The Gemara objects again: the *braitah* says they "added *dinim*," implying a new category, whereas the addition of *kenasot* is an expansion within an existing category.

### Courts Districts

Rav Acha bar Yaakov therefore proposes: *lo nitzrecha ela le-hoshiv batei dinim be-chol pelech u-felech u-ve-chol ir va-ir* — what was specifically added for Jews was the obligation to establish courts in every district and in every city, not merely to have a functional legal system but to ensure its geographic comprehensiveness throughout the land. This sounds categorical enough to justify saying "they added *dinim*." However, a *braitah* then challenges even this: *ke-shem she-nistavu Yisrael le-hoshiv batei dinim be-chol pelech u-felech u-ve-chol ir va-ir, kach nistavu bnei Noach* — just as Israel was commanded to establish courts in every district and city, so too were *bnei Noach*. This obligation was not uniquely added to Israel; it was always part of the universal commandment. Taken together, the course of this discussion makes clear that *dinim* for *bnei Noach* encompasses both the creation of court systems with geographic coverage and a body of substantive civil law — a conclusion that supports the Ramban's understanding over the Rambam's more minimalist reading.

### Menashe List

Rava resolves the impasse: *hai tana de-vei Menashe hu* — the *tana* who says *dinim* was added to Israel at Marah as a new category is from the school of Menashe, who works from a different list of seven altogether. The Tana de-vei Menashe's list: *avodah zarah, giluy arayot, shefichut damim, gezel, eiver min ha-chai, sirus*, and *kilayim* — that is, he removes *dinim* and *birkat Hashem* from the standard seven and substitutes *sirus* and *kilayim*. According to this tradition, *dinim* was never part of the universal Noahide obligation; it is genuinely a commandment added to Israel. This explains why his tradition describes *dinim* as added at Marah without contradiction. We thus emerge with not just variant opinions about what the seven commandments include, but a fundamental dispute over whether *dinim* belongs to the universal moral order or to the specifically Israelite legal covenant.

The discussion leaves us with a rich picture of the *sheva mitzvot bnei Noach* as a subject of live rabbinic debate: their content, their derivation, their procedural requirements, and their relationship to the expanded obligations of the Jewish legal system all remain active questions as the Gemara continues.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 57

## Classic Seven Mitzvot

### Overview & Context

Daf 57 continues the extended discussion of *sheva mitzvot bnei Noach*. The sugya begins approximately nine lines from the bottom of 56b, at the words *hai Tana d'bei Menashe hu*. By way of orientation, the classic seven commandments are: the three cardinal prohibitions — *avodah zarah*, *giluy arayos*, and *shfichus damim* — together with *ever min hachai*, *birchat Hashem*, *gezel*, and *dinim*. All seven are initially derived from *pesukim* concerning Adam rather than being limited to the covenant with Noach.

The preceding discussion had already touched on several major themes. First, *dinim* was explored at some length. The Rambam understands *dinim* as requiring the establishment of a court system — courts in every city and region — while the Ramban understands it more broadly as substantive law, rooted in the *pasuk* concerning Avraham: *l'maan asher yetzaveh et banav v'et beito acharav v'shamru derech Hashem la'asot tzedakah u'mishpat*, to do righteousness and justice. The *gemara* had further explored whether *knassos* — fines — are included within *dinim*. According to Rashi, *knassos* go beyond mere compensation and the righting of wrongs; they are punitive rather than restorative, which would arguably place them within the broader *tzedakah u'mishpat* framework. The conclusion of that discussion is that *dinim* encompasses substantive civil law oriented toward creating a just society.

A second theme that was established and will recur throughout the daf is the procedural distinction between how a Jewish court adjudicates and how a non-Jewish court adjudicates *sheva mitzvos*. This can be distilled into three contrasts: *edah, eidim, v'hasra'ah* — the size of the court, the requirement for witnesses, and the requirement for warning. With respect to the court: for Jews, even capital cases require a *beit din* of 23; a non-Jewish court may consist of even a single judge. With respect to witnesses: Jews require two valid witnesses; non-Jews may rely on circumstantial evidence or hearsay. With respect to warning: Jews require *hasra'ah*, prior warning to the offender, while non-Jews may be adjudicated without any such warning.

### Tana D'Bei Menashe

The *gemara* now identifies the opinion that *dinim* was added to the Israelites only at Marah as belonging to *Tana d'bei Menashe* — the school of Menashe — precisely because that school substitutes *dinim* and *birchat Hashem* for two other commandments. The *gemara* states: *d'mappik dach v'ayil sach* — it removes *dalet-ches* (*dinim* and *birchat Hashem*) and inserts *samech-kaf* (*sirus* and *kilayim*).

The formulation of *Tana d'bei Menashe* is thus: *sheva mitzvos nitztavu Bnei Noach* — the seven commandments given to the descendants of Noach are *avodah zarah*, *giluy arayos*, *shfichus damim*, *gezel*, and *ever min hachai*, together with *sirus* (sterilization and castration) and *kilayim* (crossbreeding of animals and grafting of different species). Both of these substitutions are deeply rooted in *Bereishis*: *sirus* connects to *peru u'revu*, the imperative to procreate, and *kilayim* to *l'minehu*, the principle of species distinction established at creation.

### R. Yehuda View

Rabbi Yehuda offers a more minimalist position: *Adam HaRishon lo nitztaveh ela Avodah Zarah bilvad* — the first human being was commanded in nothing other than *avodah zarah* alone. Rashi suggests this need not mean that the remaining commandments were not eventually given; rather, the point is that they should not all be rooted in *Adam HaRishon*. The derivation turns on the verse *vayetzav Hashem Elokim al HaAdam*: the prohibition against eating from the *etz hadaat* does not apply to later generations, but what does carry forward is the fundamental idea embedded in the very fact of divine command — that there is a God who commands. *Vayetzav Hashem Elokim* conveys belief in and acceptance of God, and the rejection of *avodah zarah*, the substitution of any other divinity, flows from that foundational moment. Additional commandments, on this view, came later at the time of Noach.

### R. Yehuda ben Beteira

Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira takes a similar approach but broadens it modestly. He adds *birchat Hashem* to the obligations incumbent upon *Adam HaRishon*: if the core of what was demanded at the beginning was the recognition and acceptance of God, then cursing God — attacking the very foundation of that theological relationship — is equally foundational. *Birchat Hashem* is not a separate category but flows directly from the same principle.

*V'yesh omrim af al hadinim* — some add *dinim* as well. The *gemara* then asks: *keman azla ha de'amar Rav Yehuda amar Rav* — like whom does this teaching go? The teaching expounds *vayetzav Hashem Elokim*: *Elohim ani* — know that I am your God; *lo tekaleluni* — do not curse Me; *lo temiruni* — do not replace Me with another deity. What does the third clause — *yehei morai aleichem*, let My fear be upon you — come to include? According to this, *dinim*.

The connection between fear of God and the obligation of *dinim* requires some explanation. Rashi's interpretation is that truly fearing God means judging justly, because the fear of human beings leads to the perversion of justice, while the fear of God ensures honest judgment — *lo tateh mishpat ki hamishpat l'Elohim hu*. However, that reading presupposes the obligation to judge and uses the divine fear merely as a motivator for doing so properly. A more fundamental reading would be: what kind of God are you accepting? The pagan gods are amoral — they represent no absolute moral code. The Jewish conception of God is inseparable from moral truth: *chotamo shel Hakadosh Baruch Hu emet*. If you genuinely accept a God of this character, and if the fear of that God rests upon you, then you understand that society must be structured around justice. The obligation of *dinim* flows from the theological content of the acceptance of God itself.

This connects powerfully to the *pasuk* about Avraham: *v'shamru derech Hashem la'asot tzedakah u'mishpat*. There is something profound in saying that the most basic foundation — prior to Noach, prior to *ever min hachai* or *giluy arayos* — is belief in God and the understanding that this belief entails responsibility for a just society. This resonates, incidentally, with Mendelssohn's idea of natural law.

What unites these positions — Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira, and those who add *dinim* — is the recognition that *Adam HaRishon* received only the foundational universal principles: acceptance of God, not cursing God, and perhaps the framework of justice. The more specific commandments — explicit prohibitions of murder, of *ever min hachai*, and so forth — came later, at Noach.

---

## Sourcing from Noach

### Individual Sources

The *gemara* now turns to *Tana d'bei Menashe*'s approach: since this school substitutes *sirus* and *kilayim* for *birchat Hashem* and *dinim*, how does it derive its list from *pesukim*? The *gemara* poses the dilemma sharply: *ei darish vayetzav* — if *Tana d'bei Menashe* learns the commandments from the *pasuk* about *Adam HaRishon* (*vayetzav Hashem Elokim*), then it should include *birchat Hashem* and *dinim*, which are derived from that very *pasuk*. *Ei lo darish vayetzav* — and if it does not derive anything from that *pasuk*, then where does it derive any of the commandments at all?

The *gemara* answers: *le'olam lo darish vayetzav* — *Tana d'bei Menashe* does not base its system on the *pasuk* by *Adam HaRishon* at all. Instead, *kol chada v'chada b'apei nafsha ketiva* — each commandment is derived individually, and strikingly, all of them are derived from *Noach* rather than from *Adam*. This raises a significant conceptual question: were the *sheva mitzvos* given to *Adam HaRishon*, or to Noach, or in two stages? The difference is not merely historical. Noach came after ten generations of human failure, after the corruption that led to the destruction of the world. One way to understand the trajectory of *Sefer Bereishis* is that humans keep failing, requiring progressively more detailed guidance — first the basic idea of God alone, then the broader Noachide code, and ultimately the 613 commandments given to Israel. *Tana d'bei Menashe* links all seven to the Noachide period rather than to *Adam*.

### Avodah Zarah & Giluy

This section begins at the top of 57a. *Avodah zarah* and *giluy arayos* are derived together from the verse *vatishachet ha'aretz lifnei Ha'Elokim* — the earth was corrupted before God. The school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches: *kol makom shene'emar hashchasa eino ela dvar ervah va'avodas kochavim* — wherever the word *hashchasa* (corruption) appears, it refers to sexual immorality and idolatry. The proof for the association with sexual immorality is: *ki hishchis kol basar es darko al ha'aretz* — all flesh corrupted its way upon the earth. Rashi explains that the word *derech* evokes natural conduct, and *basar* carries a corporeal connotation, together pointing to the corruption of the natural pattern of sexuality — cross-species coupling and similar violations. The association of *hashchasa* with idolatry is proved from the verse *pen tashchisun va'asisem lachem pesel* — lest you act corruptly and fashion for yourselves an idol.

This does not constitute an explicit commandment in the ordinary sense; rather, if people are being punished for these acts, it may be inferred that they were commanded not to do them. The underlying principle is that every punishment presupposes a prior prohibition. This logic, of course, raises a question about Kayin: if the prohibition of murder was only commanded explicitly at the time of Noach — and this is indeed where the *gemara* will derive it — how could Kayin have been held responsible? The *gemara* does not explicitly address this. One resolution, drawing on a broader philosophical framework about the sin of the *etz hadaat*, is that the sin of the Garden of Eden consisted not merely in disobeying God but in arrogating to humanity the authority to determine what is good and evil — displacing divine moral judgment with human moral judgment. If that was the sin, then its aftermath is precisely that humans accepted responsibility for moral determination and are held accountable accordingly, regardless of explicit commandment. *Kayin* cannot claim he was never told murder was wrong, because the acceptance of autonomous moral judgment carries with it full moral accountability. This reading fits with the Rambam-Mendelssohn tension between commanded law and natural law: the sense of the *gemara* here is not that the *sheva mitzvos* are self-evident natural law that humans could have figured out independently, but rather that they are genuine divine commandments — for without commandment, the punishment would be unjust.

### Shfichus Damim

*Shfichus damim* is derived from the explicit divine command to Noach: *shofech dam ha'adam ba'adam damo yishafach* — one who sheds the blood of a person, by a person shall his blood be shed. This is among the few obligations stated expressly in the Noachide context, and it is noteworthy that the source is here rather than the Kayin narrative. The school that roots the prohibition in *Adam HaRishon* would read the Noachide verse differently: *katlei hu d'ka megalei* — it is not establishing the prohibition anew, but revealing the punishment. The prohibition was already known from the time of Adam; the verse by Noach tells us that the punishment is death.

### Gezel Source

*Gezel* is derived from the verse addressed to Noach: *ki yerek esev nasati lachem et hakol* — as the green vegetation I have given you everything. Rav Levi explains: *ki yerek esev v'lo k'yerek gina* — like grass that grows wild, not like the produce of a cultivated garden. Wild vegetation is ownerless; produce of a garden belongs to its owner. The implication is that while God permits the taking of what is ownerless, what belongs to another may not be taken — hence the prohibition of *gezel*.

The school that derives *gezel* from *Adam HaRishon* reads this verse differently: *hu l'mishrei basar hu d'asa* — the verse comes to permit Noach to eat meat. The understanding is that *Adam HaRishon* was permitted only vegetation; the flesh of animals was not given to him. Here, by Noach, meat is for the first time permitted, as God now includes the animals in the category of what may be consumed. On this reading the verse is not about theft at all.

### Ever Min Hachai

The prohibition of *ever min hachai* is derived from the verse: *ach basar b'nafsho damo lo socheilu* — but flesh with its life, its blood, you shall not eat. The rabbinic reading of this verse is: flesh of an animal while its blood and life force remain within it — that is, while the animal is still alive — may not be eaten. Do not eat the limb of a living animal. It is worth noting that the plain reading of the *pasuk* — and one that is entirely defensible as *peshat* — is a prohibition on eating blood: eat the flesh, but not while its blood is still within it, meaning drain the blood from the meat first. The rabbis, however, read it as a prohibition on *ever min hachai*.

The school that roots *ever min hachai* in *Adam HaRishon* reads this Noachide verse differently: *hahu l'mishrei shratzim hu d'asa* — it comes to clarify that the blood of rodents is not in the category of blood but is treated like their flesh, and therefore does not render them subject to the *ever min hachai* prohibition. The conceptual distinction underlying the prohibition of *ever min hachai* is the separateness of the life force from the body — a kind of body-soul dualism where the blood represents a life force distinct from the physical flesh. Rodents are not understood in these terms; their blood is considered like their flesh, and so the prohibition does not apply to them.

This analysis also resolves a prior difficulty: if *Adam HaRishon* was forbidden to eat meat entirely, why would a prohibition on *ever min hachai* be necessary? The answer is that *Adam HaRishon* was not required to be vegetarian in the sense of being forbidden from eating any animal flesh whatsoever. Rather, he was forbidden to kill animals for food. He was, however, permitted to eat from the flesh of animals that had died naturally. Consequently, a separate prohibition was needed to forbid tearing a limb from a living animal — even if one were not killing the animal, ripping a limb from it while alive was independently prohibited.

### Sirus & Kilayim

*Sirus* is derived from the command given to Noach: *shirtzу ba'aretz ur'vu vah* — swarm upon the earth and multiply in it — a form of *peru u'revu*. The opposing school reads this verse as a blessing rather than a command, and therefore draws no prohibition from it: *l'vircha d'alma* — it is a blessing for the world, not an imperative.

*Kilayim* is derived from the verse describing the animals brought into the ark: *meh'of l'minehu* — the birds according to their species. The requirement to maintain species distinction in the ark implies a prohibition on crossbreeding. The opposing school reads this verse as reflecting companionship — animals naturally prefer the company of their own kind — rather than as a prohibition: *l'tzavsa d'alma* — for the sake of fellowship, not as a legal boundary.

What is striking about *Tana d'bei Menashe*'s list is the exclusion of *dinim* — a prohibition whose absence seems conceptually difficult. If the seven commandments are meant to constitute the foundations of a just society, the omission of any obligation to establish and maintain a system of law is puzzling. *Sirus* and *kilayim*, while certainly rooted in the deepest structures of creation — the imperatives of procreation and species integrity — seem to belong to a different register than *dinim*. One might speculate that *dinim* is excluded on the grounds that it is sufficiently self-evident as natural law that it need not be explicitly commanded — a partial accommodation between the Mendelssohn natural-law view and the Rambam's commanded-law view. However, this does not sit entirely comfortably, since *shfichus damim* — which is no less intuitive — remains among the commanded prohibitions.

---

## Death Penalty Issues

### Three Mitzvot View

Having surveyed the scope and sources of the *sheva mitzvos*, the *gemara* turns to a distinct question: for how many of these commandments is a *ben Noach* actually executed? The widespread popular understanding is that the death penalty applies to all seven, and even for theft of less than a *prutah*. But the *gemara* reveals a spectrum of opinions.

*Amar Rav Yosef amar bei Rav al shalosh mitzvos ben Noach neherag* — Rav Yosef in the name of the school of Rav: a *ben Noach* is executed for only three. The mnemonic is *gimmel-shin-resh* (*gesher*): *giluy arayos*, *shfichus damim*, and *birchat Hashem*. This is a notably unusual grouping — it omits *avodah zarah*, which for Jews forms the first of the three cardinal sins, and substitutes *birchat Hashem* in its place.

### Four Mitzvot View

Rav Sheshes challenges this position. *Bishlama shfichus damim d'chtiv* — granted, murder is explicit: *shofech dam ha'adam ba'adam damo yishafach*. But for the other two — *giluy arayos* and *birchat Hashem* — where is the capital liability derived? If the answer is that we extend the death penalty from *shfichus damim* to the other *sheva mitzvos*, then *afilu kulhu nami* — extend it to all seven. If we are not doing that, we need a specific *pasuk* for each.

The *gemara* identifies the derivation: by *birchat Hashem*, the verse says *ish ish ki yekalel elohav v'nasa cheto* — followed ultimately by *ragom yirgmu*. The phrase *ish ish* is understood as including non-Jews, thereby establishing that the capital liability of the *birchat Hashem* prohibition extends to *bnei Noach*. Similarly, by *giluy arayos*, the verse reads *ish ish el kol she'er besaro lo tikrevu legalot ervah* — again, the double *ish ish* signals inclusion of non-Jews. For *avodah zarah*, there is also a verse using *ish ish*: *ish ish mi-bnei Yisrael u'min ha-ger ha-gar b'Yisrael asher yiten mi-zar'o la-Molech mos yumos* — making it four, not three.

The conclusion: *ella amar Rav Sheshes hani amri bei Rav al arba mitzvos ben Noach neherag* — the correct version of the teaching in the name of Rav's school is that a *ben Noach* is executed for four commandments: the three cardinal sins of *avodah zarah*, *giluy arayos*, and *shfichus damim*, together with *birchat Hashem*, which is in a sense an extension of *avodah zarah* — the rejection of God's exclusive sovereignty.

This is conceptually satisfying: these four are precisely the commandments for which Jews are also executed, at least in their most serious forms. The remaining three — *gezel*, *ever min hachai*, and *dinim* — while prohibited, do not carry the death penalty on this view.

### Azharah Shelo Mita

The *gemara* now tests this conclusion against a *braisa* that discusses the scope of the *avodah zarah* prohibition for *bnei Noach*. The *braisa* states: acts of *avodah zarah* for which a Jewish court would execute Jews — a *ben Noach* is *muzhar* (warned/prohibited) regarding those. Notably, the *braisa* does not say *neherag* (executed); it says *muzhar* (cautioned, prohibited). The inference is stark: *azharah in, mitah lo* — there is a prohibition, but not a death penalty. If so, the *braisa* itself seems to undercut the position that *bnei Noach* are executed for *avodah zarah*.

The answer offered is that of Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: *azharah shelahen zu hi mitatan* — their warning is their death penalty. On its most common philosophical interpretation, this principle means that any violation of a divine prohibition is in principle deserving of death, since God who prohibits is also the source of all life; any transgression of the divine will constitutes a forfeiture of the right to life in principle, and all lesser punishments represent divine leniency. This is a harsh and austere theological stance. Rav Soloveitchik noted, in a related context, that the final passage of the *Neilah* service includes the phrase *me-chamas yadeinu* — from the *chamas* of our hands — suggesting that any sin involves a kind of theft from God, since we were given our lives to serve the divine will, and any violation represents a misappropriation of that life.

However, Rashi indicates that this is not the intended meaning here. The *gemara* at this juncture is working with the position that only four of the seven commandments carry the death penalty, not all seven. Therefore the phrase *azharah shelahen zu hi mitatan* is not a philosophical statement about the nature of divine prohibition; it is a purely textual observation. The *braisa*, by using the word *muzhar* (warned), is not carefully distinguishing between warning and execution; it is simply not being specific. When it says they are warned against *avodah zarah*, it means they are executed for it — the word *azharah* is being used loosely to encompass the full consequence.

### Seven Mitzvot Death

The students of Rav — *Rav Huna, Rav Yehudah, v'kulehu talmidei de-Rav* — take the broadest position: *al sheva mitzvos Bnei Noach neherag* — a *ben Noach* is executed for all seven. The logic is: *gali Rachmana b'chada v'hu ha-din le-kulehu* — the Torah reveals the death penalty explicitly for one of the commandments (murder), and the same rule extends to all of them. This is the position that is most commonly cited and that underlies the widespread understanding of the *sheva mitzvos*: any violation, even theft of less than a *prutah*, is in principle punishable by death. It is here that the phrase *azharah shelahen zu hi mitatan* takes on its fuller philosophical resonance — any divine prohibition directed at *bnei Noach* carries the implicit consequence of death.

---

## Gezel Scope & Liability

### Gezel Braita

The *gemara* now questions whether the death penalty truly applies to theft: *v'al gezel ben Noach neherag?* And it cites a *braisa* that discusses the scope of the *gezel* prohibition. The *braisa* lists: *ganav* (burglary), *gezel* (robbery), *v'chen yefat toar* (taking a captive woman in war — which the *braisa* treats as a species of theft: the captor forcibly removes a woman from her family and husband, appropriating her as property), and *v'chen kayotze bahen* — similar cases.

The *braisa* then states: a *goy* who steals from a *goy*, or a *goy* who steals from a Jew — *assur*. A Jew who steals from a *goy* — *mutar*.

This is a deeply troubling passage, and it is important not to elide its difficulty. The text uses the word *Kusi* (Samaritan) throughout rather than *goy* — a form of self-censorship that appears even in editions that restore other censored passages. The ruling that a Jew may steal from a non-Jew is stated baldly. Rashi on this passage reads the *braisa* as holding that it is entirely *mutar*, with no rabbinic or Torah-level prohibition. The *gemara* in *Bava Kamma*, which discusses *gezel goy* more extensively, at minimum adds that even if it is technically permissible, it is prohibited where *chillul Hashem* would result. But bracketing that consideration, the *braisa* here seems to permit it outright. This is a *gemara* that demands acknowledgment of its difficulty rather than apologetics. The danger of teaching such material without problematizing it is that it can be internalized as a normative attitude — that stealing from or causing harm to a non-Jew is of no moral consequence. This has real-world implications, including in contemporary Israel where such *gemaras* have been cited in the context of practical political attitudes.

Returning to the technical question: the *braisa* says the non-Jewish thief is *assur*, not *chayav*. If all seven commandments carry the death penalty, why does the *braisa* use the weaker language of prohibition rather than liability? *V'ee ita nitni chayav* — it should have said *chayav*, deserving of punishment.

The *gemara*'s answer is that the word *assur* was chosen to create the proper contrast: since the *braisa* wanted to conclude with *mutar* (permissible) in the case of a Jew stealing from a *goy*, the natural contrast for the non-Jewish case is *assur* rather than *chayav*. The word *mutar* calls for its antonym *assur*, not for *chayav*. This is confirmed by the *braisa*'s treatment of murder, where no such contrast is needed. The *braisa* states: a *goy* who kills a *goy*, or a *goy* who kills a Jew — *chayav*. A Jew who kills a *goy* — *patur*. There, the *braisa* explicitly says *chayav*, because it cannot say *mutar* for the Jewish case (murder of a non-Jew, while apparently not punishable by a Jewish court, is not *mutar* — *lo maalin velo moridin*), and therefore the contrast is *chayav* versus *patur* rather than *assur* versus *mutar*.

The Rambam's text in *Hilchot Rotzeach u'Shmirat Nefesh* is instructive here. He opens by stating: *kol ha-horeg nefesh harei zeh over* — anyone who kills a person transgresses the prohibition of *lo tirtzach*. This formulation applies universally, without qualification by the identity of the victim. There is, however, a scholarly debate about whether this formulation is original or represents a later editorial modification; some hold that the original text read *kol ha-horeg nefesh mi'Yisrael*. The question of whether the prohibition of murder fully encompasses the killing of a non-Jew — and if so, what the legal consequences are — is thus an ongoing and unresolved tension within the *halachic* literature.

The broader point for the *sugya*: the use of *assur* in the theft *braisa* does not indicate an absence of the death penalty. It is simply a function of the rhetorical structure of the *braisa*, which required the word *mutar* at its conclusion and therefore used *assur* as its counterpart at the outset. The death penalty remains in force; the language is not being precise.

### Less Than Prutah

Rav Pappa explains what the phrase *v'chen kayotze bahen* — similar cases — teaches in the context of *gezel*: *lo nitzrecha ela l'pachos mishaveh prutah* — the additional clause is needed only to include cases of less than a *prutah*. That is, even theft of less than the minimum denomination of currency constitutes *gezel* for a *ben Noach* and carries the attendant liability. This is the *chiddush*: one might have thought that an amount too small to be treated as money at all could not constitute theft, but the *braisa* teaches otherwise.

### Jew vs. Non-Jew Threshold

This raises an immediate question: if a non-Jew who steals from a Jew is also *assur*, why would the theft of less than a *prutah* from a Jew not be included? The *gemara* answers: *ha bar mechila hu* — a Jew will be *mochel*, will forgive the debt. This is the *gemara*'s explanation for why less than a *prutah* does not trigger liability when stolen from a Jew: the Jewish victim will simply waive the amount. Non-Jews, by contrast, will not be *mochel* even a trivial sum.

This yields a sharp and somewhat ironic contrast: the stereotyped generosity of the Jew — quick to forgive a petty debt — is precisely what limits the legal liability of a non-Jew who steals from him, while the non-Jew's insistence on full recovery even of minimal amounts means that any taking, however small, constitutes a real wrong.

### Restitution vs. Punishme…

But this answer creates a new difficulty: if the reason less than a *prutah* from a Jew is not actionable is that the Jew will be *mochel*, why should the non-Jewish thief transgress at all? After the theft, the Jew says *machel* — forgiven — so no harm was ultimately done. The *gemara* responds: *tzara b'shaita miha ita* — at the moment of the taking, there was a genuine harm. The act of appropriating something from another, however small the amount and however willing the victim is to forgive it afterward, constitutes the violation. The subsequent *mechila* does not retroactively undo the act.

At this point, the *gemara* also addresses why the theft of less than a *prutah* from a non-Jew by another non-Jew does not need the *kayotze bahen* clause: *kevan d'lav bnei mechila ninhu gezel maalya hu* — since non-Jews are not of the type to waive small amounts, less than a *prutah* is simply ordinary theft, requiring no special derivation.

This distinction points to a deeper structural difference between how *gezel* functions for Jews and for non-Jews. By a Jew, the entire framework of theft law is oriented toward restitution: *v'heshiv et ha-gezeilah*, the verse emphasizes returning what was taken. Since the focus is on restitution, the threshold is significant — below a *prutah*, there is nothing meaningful to restore, and therefore no violation is established. A wound that causes financial injury of less than a *prutah* is handled differently: since wounding is independently culpable beyond the financial damage, lashes apply even where there is nothing to restore. But theft, which is defined entirely by the property interest, has no independent act requiring punishment when the value is below the threshold. By non-Jews, there is no restitutionary framework — the liability is purely punitive. Since the line between a *prutah* and less than a *prutah* has no operative significance in a punitive system, any taking is equally an act of *gezel* regardless of amount.

### Withholding Wages

The *gemara* offers an alternative interpretation of the *kayotze bahen* clause. Rav Acha bar Brei d'Rav Ika proposes: *lo nitzrecha ela l'koves sachar sachir* — the additional clause is needed to include withholding a worker's wages. This is a qualitatively different case: it is not an active taking but a passive failure to pay what is owed. One might have thought that *gezel* requires an affirmative act of misappropriation; withholding wages is an omission. The *braisa* teaches that it is nonetheless included. The *gemara* in *Bava Metzia* similarly holds that a Jew who withholds wages transgresses *lo tigzol*, though it is regarded as a *chiddush* there too.

---

## Keyotzei Bo Cases

### Yifat Toar Case

The *braisa* included *yifat toar* — taking a captive woman in war — among the cases similar to *gezel*. This is an interesting categorization: *yifat toar* can also be understood as an aspect of *giluy arayos*, particularly if she is a married woman and the captor has relations with her. The *braisa*, however, frames it as theft: the captor is forcibly removing a woman from her family, from her husband, from her community — appropriating her as property. The *gemara* extends the *kayotze bahen* of *yifat toar* as follows: *ben Noach she-yiched shifcha l'avdo uva aleha — neherag aleha*. If a *ben Noach* designated a female slave to his servant and then himself had relations with her, he is executed. This is not a case of *arayos* in the technical sense, since there is no marriage bond for slaves. But by taking a woman designated to another — appropriating her as his own — he has committed an act analogous to theft, a species of *kayotze bahen* within the *gezel* category.

### Murder Cases

*Keyotze bo d'shfichus damim lo tanya* — there are no *kayotze bahen* cases taught in connection with murder. Murder is categorical: it either is or is not the taking of human life. There are no peripheral or analogous cases that carry liability without being fully constitutive of the prohibition. The *gemara* notes, via *Abaye*, that if one were ever to find a *baraisa* that does list *kayotze bahen* cases for murder, it would be attributable to Rav Yonatan ben Shaul.

### Self-Defense Rodef

The relevant *baraisa* of Rav Yonatan ben Shaul teaches: *rodef achar chaveiro lehorgo yachol lehatzilo b'echad me'eivarav v'lo hitzilo* — if someone was pursuing another with lethal intent, and it was possible to stop the pursuer by wounding him in a limb, yet the one being pursued killed him outright, then the defender *neherag alav* — is executed. This is not a Jew versus non-Jew distinction; it applies equally to Jews and non-Jews. The case presupposes an objective assessment that the threat could have been neutralized with less than lethal force, and that the defender nonetheless chose to kill. Under those circumstances, the killing constitutes a form of unjustified homicide, even in a self-defense context.

This is a legally and practically difficult standard. The assessment of whether a reasonable alternative existed — whether one *yachol lehatzilo b'echad me'eivarav* — is inherently uncertain in the moment of threat. The IDF rules of engagement grapple with precisely this question: at what point is a threat sufficiently neutralized that continued lethal force becomes unjustified? And when, in retrospect, is it appropriate to conclude that a defender had a feasible non-lethal alternative? The *halacha* does not resolve these evidentiary difficulties, but it establishes the principle: if the objective assessment is that the threat could have been stopped without killing, then the killing is not justified, and this constitutes the *kayotze bahen* case of *shfichus damim*.

Not everyone agrees, of course. Alternative positions hold that even if one kills when a non-lethal alternative existed, it does not constitute murder in a culpable sense — it is still self-defense. But according to Rav Yonatan ben Shaul, it is precisely these borderline cases that constitute the *kayotze bahen* of *shfichus damim*.

### Non-Jew Permissions

A final and philosophically rich question emerges from the discussion of the *rodef* case: it is not self-evident that the permission to kill a *rodef* — which the *gemara* explicitly presupposes for a *ben Noach* as well — should apply to non-Jews at all. A *ben Noach* is prohibited in murder. How do we know that the exception of self-defense carries over to the non-Jewish framework?

The present *gemara* makes it clear that it does. But the question extends further: how do the various permissions and overrides that operate within Jewish law map onto *sheva mitzvos*? For example, a Jew is obligated to accept martyrdom rather than transgress *avodah zarah*, *giluy arayos*, or *shfichus damim* under duress. Does a *ben Noach* have any obligation of martyrdom? If someone holds a gun to a non-Jew's head and demands that he commit idolatry or be killed, must he refuse and die? It is possible that a *ben Noach* has no obligation of martyrdom whatsoever — that the *yehareg v'al ya'avor* framework is entirely internal to *halacha* as it applies to Jews, and that a *ben Noach* under duress simply has no such requirement. Similarly, how do concepts like *shogeg* (inadvertent violation) interact with the Noachide framework, given the harshness of *azharah shelahen zu hi mitatan*? These questions — how the internal parameters, limits, and overrides of the commandments operate within the *sheva mitzvos* context — constitute a rich and not fully mapped area of *halachic* inquiry.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 58

## Ben Noach Execution Rules

### Source Text

The sugya opens with a passage discovered by Rav Yaakov bar Acha, who found it written in the *Sefer Aggadata d'bei Rav* — a collection that, despite its name suggesting aggadic content, appears to contain halakhic material rather than narrative legend. The citation appears at the top of 57b, the third word in from the top: *ashkah Rav Yaakov bar Acha de-iktav b'Sefer Aggadata d'bei Rav* — Rav Yaakov bar Acha found written in the *Sefer Aggadata d'bei Rav*.

### One Judge, One Witness

The text that Rav Yaakov bar Acha found reads: *ben Noach neherag b'dayan echad u-v'ed echad she-lo b'haztara mipi ish v'lo mipi ishah v'afilu karov* — a *ben Noach* can be executed by one judge, with one witness, and without a prior warning, provided the testimony comes from a man and not a woman, and — strikingly — even from a relative.

### Jewish vs. Non-Jew Rules

This stands in sharp contrast to the halakha as it applies to Jews, which requires at minimum twenty-three *dayanim* for capital cases, two *edim*, and a formal *haztara*. The requirement of *ish v'lo ishah* — that testimony come from a man and not from a woman — applies in both systems alike, making it one of the few points of symmetry between them.

### ish velo isha

The limitation of *ish v'lo mipi ishah* means that neither the judge nor the witness in such a proceeding may be a woman. This rule applies both in the Jewish system and in the Noachide system, even as the other procedural requirements diverge dramatically.

### Relatives Permitted

What is perhaps most striking is the phrase *v'afilu karov* — even a relative may testify. In a Jewish court, a relative serving as either judge or witness disqualifies the proceeding entirely. In Noachide law, however, this restriction does not apply, and the testimony of a kinsman is admissible.

## Feticide Liability

### Fetus Killing

Also recorded in the *Sefer Aggadata d'bei Rav* in the name of Rabbi Yishmael: *af al ha-ubarim* — that even one who kills a fetus is subject to capital liability under Noachide law. This is a significant extension of the prohibition against murder, applying it to the taking of fetal life.

### Textual Source

The Gemara asks *minayan* — from where do we derive this? The answer is *amar kra: ach et dimchem l'nafshoteichem edrosh* — "however your blood which belongs to your souls, I will demand" (Bereishit 9:5). This pasuk and the verses that follow serve as the textual anchor for the entire Noachide judicial system developed in this sugya, though one might fairly observe that the derivations are not always the most straightforward in their exegetical logic. Nonetheless, each rule is grounded in a specific word or phrase from these pesukim.

### Single Judge Inference

The Gemara picks up on the singular form *edrosh* — "I will demand" — and derives from it that even one judge suffices to adjudicate a capital case involving a *ben Noach*: *afilu b'dayan echad*.

### Beast Precedent

The continuation of the pasuk reads *mi-yad kol chaya edroshenu* — "and of every beast I will demand it." Since a beast cannot receive a formal warning, having no capacity for consciousness or understanding, and yet the Torah mandates that the beast be put to death for killing a human being, this becomes the precedent establishing that a *ben Noach* can likewise be executed without a prior *haztara*.

### Single Witness

The phrase *mi-yad ha-adam edroshenu* — "from the hand of man I will demand it" — is read as establishing that a single human witness suffices: *afilu b'ed echad*.

### Male Witness Only

The further phrase *mi-yad ish* — specifically "from the hand of a man" — teaches *ish v'lo miyad ishah*: a man and not a woman. This applies equally to the *dayan* and the *ed* who function in such a proceeding.

### Relative Testimony

Finally, the pasuk adds *achiv* — "his brother." From the word "brother" the Gemara derives that even a relative may testify. In ordinary Jewish law this would be categorically disqualifying; here it explicitly broadens the category of valid witnesses to include kinsmen.

The Gemara then turns to the reason underlying Rabbi Yishmael's ruling that feticide is a capital offense for a *ben Noach*. The textual basis is: *shofech dam ha-adam ba-adam damo yishapech* — "one who sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed." Rabbi Yishmael reads *shofech dam ha-adam ba-adam* and asks: *eizehu adam she-betoch adam* — when is there a human being inside another human being? The answer: this describes a fetus inside its mother's womb. And therefore, one who kills a fetus — even under the limited procedural requirements of Noachide law, with one witness and one judge — is liable for murder.

## All Deaths via Chenek

### Chenek Only Rule

The *Tanna Kamma* who does not include feticide in the Noachide capital code raises the question of why not. The answer comes from a different school: *Tanna d'bei Menashe*, who maintains that *kol mitah ha-amurah l'vnei Noach einah ela chenek* — any death prescribed for a *ben Noach* is executed exclusively by strangulation, *chenek*.

### Ba-Adam Reread

Rather than reading *ba-adam* as "inside a person" — the reading that supports Rabbi Yishmael's derivation of feticide — *Tanna d'bei Menashe* attaches *ba-adam* to the *seifa* of the pasuk, *damo yishapech*, and reads it as specifying the *method* of execution rather than the *subject* being killed.

### Blood Remains Inside

Having redeployed *ba-adam* as a description of method, *Tanna d'bei Menashe* asks: *eizehu shefichut damim shel adam she-hu b'gufo shel adam?* — what form of bloodshed involves the blood remaining within the body of the person? The answer is strangulation, *chenek*. Unlike stoning, beheading with a sword, or other forms of execution in which blood is visibly expelled from the body, strangulation kills while keeping the blood interior. This therefore becomes the exclusive mode of capital punishment for Noachide law.

## Women's Status

### Women Included

Rav Hamnuna challenges the exclusion of women from Noachide judicial proceedings. He cites the famous pasuk in which Hashem describes His relationship with Avraham: *ki yedativ l'maan asher yetzaveh et banav v'et beito acharav v'shamru derech Hashem la-asot tzedakah u-mishpat* — "for I have known him, so that he will command his sons and his household after him, and they will guard the way of Hashem to do charity and justice." Since Avraham is himself a *ben Noach*, and the pasuk explicitly includes both *banav* and *beito* in the obligation of *tzedakah u-mishpat*, it would seem to follow that women are included in *mishpat* — the judicial dimension of Noachide law.

### Avraham's Mission

Rav Hamnuna reads the phrase *banav v'et beito* as encompassing both male descendants and the women of the household. Both are commanded to maintain the ways of Hashem and to practice *tzedakah u-mishpat*. From this, one might conclude that women are not merely subject to Noachide law as defendants but are in some sense participants in its application.

### Sons vs. Household

The key interpretive question is what *banav* refers to and what *beito* refers to. Rav Hamnuna understands *beito* — the household — as including women, and therefore argues they should be included in *mishpat*, i.e., in the judicial process. The question of whether this means they are subject to the laws as defendants, or whether they can serve as judges and witnesses, is the crux of the inquiry.

### Nifkada Definition

The relevant term is *nifkada* — "appointed" or "designated." The phrase *v'ishah lo nifkada l'dinin* means she is not appointed to serve in the judicial capacity. The debate is thus whether the pasuk in question is speaking about women's subjection to the law as governed parties, which everyone appears to accept, or about their role within the apparatus of adjudication itself.

## Sons/Charity Split

### Din vs. Tzedakah

The Gemara adds that *bar Bereida* not only pressed the question but supplied the answer: *banav l'dinin, beito l'tzedakah* — the sons are commanded with respect to *mishpat*, judicial law, while the household — i.e., the women — are entrusted with *tzedakah*, charitable giving. The two applications of *tzedakah u-mishpat* in the pasuk are thus divided along these lines, resolving Rav Hamnuna's challenge by assigning women to one dimension of the verse and men to another.

### Woman as Victim

Rav Avia Sava raises a further question to Rav Pappa: perhaps a *bat Noach* — a non-Jewish woman — should not be killed at all, not because of her exclusion from the judicial role but because of the pasuk's language regarding victims. Since the pasuk concerning Noach uses *mi-yad ish* — "from the hand of a man" — one might read this as excluding women both from giving testimony and from being victims of the homicide prohibition.

### Anyone Kills Anyone

Rav Yehuda responds by citing the broader pasuk: *shofech dam ha-adam ba-adam damo yishapech*. The phrase *shofech dam ha-adam* encompasses any killer — male or female — and the victim *ha-adam* similarly encompasses any human being. The identity of the killer or the victim is not restricted by gender.

### Adultery Exemption

The Gemara then raises the question of whether a *bat Noach* who commits adultery might be exempt from liability. The basis for the question is the pasuk *al ken ya'azov ish* — "therefore a man shall leave" — which speaks specifically in terms of the male. Since the commandment to establish a marital bond is framed in masculine terms, one might argue that women are not bound by it in the same way and therefore cannot be liable for adultery.

## One Flesh Principle

### Ve-Hayu Principle

Rav Yehuda answers this by pointing to the continuation of the same pasuk: *v'hayu l'vasar echad* — "and they shall become one flesh." This phrase explicitly encompasses both the man and the woman, as it takes both to constitute "one flesh."

### Reading Back

The Gemara describes this as *hadar arebinhu kra* — the verse loops back and re-includes them together. Once the pasuk concludes with a phrase that applies to both genders, we read that inclusion retroactively back into the earlier words of the verse, even though those words used only the masculine form *ish*. Both men and women are therefore bound by the Noachide prohibition against adultery.

## Kutim & Arayot

### Ish Ish Rule

The Gemara cites a *baraita*: *tanu rabbanan, ish ish* — what does the doubling of the word *ish* in Vayikra 18 teach? The extra word comes to include the *Kutim* — the Samaritans — establishing that they are warned against *arayot* just as Yisrael is: *she-muzharin al ha-arayot k'Yisrael*.

### Separate Systems

The Gemara immediately questions this derivation. Was this not already established from a different source — from the word *leimor* in the *arayot* section, used a daf or two earlier to derive that non-Jews are commanded regarding *arayot*? The Gemara resolves the apparent redundancy: the two derivations govern two distinct systems. The *leimor* derivation establishes that non-Jews are commanded regarding their *own* system of *arayot* — *arayot dideyhu*. The doubling of *ish ish* establishes that they are also bound when interacting with the Jewish system — *arayot didan*. These are two separate bodies of law, each with its own source.

### Nafka Mina

The practical consequence of distinguishing these two systems is spelled out from the *seifa* of the earlier passage: if a non-Jew commits *arayot* with a Jew, he is adjudicated under Jewish law — *nidon b'dinei Yisrael*. If he commits *arayot* within his own system, he is judged by Noachide law. The two sets of rules carry different procedural standards and different penalties, making the distinction between the systems consequential.

## Exemption Debate

### One-One Standard

The Gemara asks: *l'mai hilchata* — what is the practical difference? Rav Nachman, citing Rabbah bar Avuha, answers: the distinction matters for the evidentiary and procedural requirements. When a non-Jew is judged under his own system — Noachide law — one witness and one judge suffice, with no *haztara* required. When judged under Jewish law, the full apparatus of two witnesses, twenty-three judges, and a formal warning applies.

### Lower Standard Issue

The Gemara raises a sharp objection: *atu migra gara?* — is this not a perverse result? If a non-Jew commits adultery with a non-Jew, the lower Noachide standard applies and he can be executed more easily. But if he commits the same act with a Jew, the Jewish standard kicks in, requiring far more stringent procedural conditions — making it *harder* to execute him. This seems to invert the logic: one would expect greater protection for Jewish victims, not a higher evidentiary bar that makes punishment more difficult.

### Betrothed Woman

Rabbi Yochanan resolves the difficulty by reframing the question entirely. The point of distinction between the two systems is not about the general evidentiary standard but about one specific case: *na'arah me-orasah* — a betrothed young woman. The institution of *eirusin*, formal betrothal, exists only in Jewish law. Non-Jews do not have a status of *eirusin* separable from full marriage. Therefore, if a non-Jew commits adultery with a *na'arah me-orasah*, Noachide law has no category for it at all — for them, she is simply unmarried. In such a case, we apply Jewish law, which does recognize her betrothed status and imposes the appropriate penalty.

## Na'arah vs. Eshes Ish

### Eirsusin Unique

The institution of *eirusin* — the formal betrothal that creates a binding marital status even before *nissu'in* — is unique to Jewish law. Non-Jews do not divide marriage into these two stages. As a result, the category of *na'arah me-orasah*, a woman who is legally a wife in the most serious sense yet has not yet entered the marital home, simply does not exist in the Noachide framework.

### Jewish Law Applies

When a non-Jew commits *arayot* with a *na'arah me-orasah*, since Noachide law has no corresponding category, Jewish law must govern the case. This is the single narrow exception that Rabbi Yochanan identifies as requiring the application of Jewish rather than Noachide law.

### Adultery Standard

By contrast, the category of *eshes ish* — a fully married woman — does exist in Noachide law. Non-Jews recognize marriage and prohibit adultery. Therefore, a non-Jew who commits adultery with a married Jewish woman can be adjudicated under Noachide law, with its single judge, single witness, and no *haztara* requirement.

## Death Penalty Mismatch

### Jewish Penalties

A *baraita* is cited that creates a new difficulty. It states: one who has relations with a *na'arah me-orasah* is punished by *sekila* — stoning; one who has relations with an *eshes ish* is punished by *chenek* — strangulation. This language describes the Jewish system of penalties, which is appropriate for the *na'arah me-orasah* case since, as established, that case is adjudicated under Jewish law. But the *eshes ish* case presents a problem.

### Non-Jewish Penalty

If the *eshes ish* case is governed by Noachide law — as Rabbi Yochanan maintains — the penalty should be *sayif*, beheading. *Tanna d'bei Menashe* holds that all Noachide executions are performed by *chenek*, but setting that aside, the language of the *baraita* describes *chenek* specifically in the context that sounds like Jewish law adjudication. If the *eshes ish* case is truly being handled under Noachide law, why does the *baraita* use the language of the Jewish penalty system?

### Eshes Ish Redefined

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves this by asking a fundamental question: *mai eshes ish?* — what exactly does "married woman" mean in this context? He proposes a refined definition: the *baraita* is speaking of a woman who has entered the *chuppah* but has not yet had marital relations — *she-nichnesah la-chuppah v'lo niv'alah*. For Jews, the *chuppah* itself completes the *nissu'in* and creates the full status of *eshes ish*. But for non-Jews, who have no *chuppah* ceremony in the Jewish sense, the finalization of marriage requires the act of consummation — *bi'ah*. Therefore, a woman in the post-*chuppah*, pre-*bi'ah* state occupies a zone that Jewish law recognizes as full marriage but Noachide law does not. In this narrow category, Jewish law must be applied — hence *chenek*, the Jewish penalty, rather than *sayif*.

## Post-Chuppah Status

### Chuppah Without Sex

The case of *nichnesah la-chuppah v'lo niv'alah* — she entered the *chuppah* but was not yet intimate — thus becomes the second exception, alongside *na'arah me-orasah*, in which Jewish law is applied to a non-Jewish defendant. For non-Jews, the marriage is not finalized until consummation; without *bi'ah*, she does not yet have the status of a full *eshes ish* in their system.

### Sex Finalizes

The underlying principle is that in Noachide marriage law, the sexual act is what finalizes the union. Without it, even a woman who has gone through whatever ceremony exists in the non-Jewish community is not yet considered a married woman for the purposes of Noachide *arayot* law.

## Post-Chuppah Status (II)

### Beulas Baal Only

A *baraita* confirms this position: non-Jews recognize *beulas baal* — a woman who has had marital relations with her husband — but they do not recognize the category of *nichnesah la-chuppah v'lo niv'alah*. The post-ceremony, pre-consummation status simply does not exist in Noachide law.

## Arayot Obligation

### Meir's Principle

The Gemara introduces a *baraita* that records a dispute between Rabbi Meir and the *Chachamim* concerning which *arayot* bind non-Jews. Rabbi Meir holds: any *ervah* for which the Jewish *beit din* imposes the death penalty — a *ben Noach* is warned against that *ervah* as well. Conversely, if the Jewish *beit din* does not impose death for a given *ervah*, the *ben Noach* is not warned against it.

### Broader Arayot

The *Chachamim* dispute this sharply: *harbeh arayot yesh she-ein beit din shel Yisrael memitin aleihen u-ven Noach muzhar aleihen* — there are many *arayot* for which Jewish law does not prescribe death, and yet a *ben Noach* is still obligated and warned against them. The Noachide system of *arayot* is not merely a subset of the Jewish system; it has its own scope and may in some cases be broader.

### System Selection

The *baraita* further articulates the principle of system selection: if a non-Jew commits *arayot* with a Jewish woman, he is judged by Jewish law — *nidon b'dinei Yisrael*. If he commits *arayot* with a non-Jewish woman, he is judged by Noachide law — *nidon b'dinei ben Noach*.

### Exceptions Listed

The *baraita* identifies the exceptions to this framework — cases where a non-Jewish defendant is pulled into the Jewish system even when the interaction is with a Jewish woman within categories Noachide law would not normally recognize: specifically *na'arah me-orasah*, and additionally the case of *nichnesah la-chuppah v'lo niv'alah*.

## Ger Lineage

### Conception/Birth

The Gemara now raises a challenge to Rabbi Meir's formulation from a *baraita* concerning the *ger* — a convert — whose conception (*horato*) occurred before his mother's conversion but whose birth (*lidato*) occurred after she converted: *ger she-hayetah horato shelo bi-kedushah v'lidato bi-kedushah*. This individual presents a unique status: he was conceived as a non-Jew but born as a Jew.

### Maternal Kin Bar

The *baraita* rules: *yesh lo she'er ha-em v'ein lo she'er ha-av* — he retains relatives through his mother but not through his father. Since his mother converted while carrying him, he is born as a Jew with a full Jewish mother, and the maternal kinship bonds carry over. He therefore cannot marry anyone to whom he is related through his mother.

### Paternal Kin OK

By contrast, his connection to his father's line existed entirely in the pre-Jewish period. Since the entire paternal relationship belongs to his non-Jewish past, the kinship bonds through his father do not carry over. He may, in principle, marry someone related to him through his father.

### Line Split

The practical implications of this distinction are spelled out in detail. If he marries his half-sister through his mother — a daughter she had previously — the marriage must be dissolved: *yotzi*. But if he marries a half-sister through his father, the marriage stands: *yekayem*. The same logic applies to his father's sisters. If his father's sister is a maternal half-sister of his father — sharing a grandmother — then *yotzi*. But if she shares only a grandfather with his father, then *yekayem*, the marriage is sustained. The principle emerging is that the maternal connection is determinative: kinship through women creates binding *arayot* prohibitions, while purely paternal kinship, rooted in the pre-conversion non-Jewish world, does not.

## Father/Mother Sisters

### Maternal Sister

Turning to the *ger*'s maternal aunts: if he seeks to marry his *achot ha-em min ha-em* — his mother's sister who shares the same mother — everyone agrees this is prohibited and the marriage must be dissolved.

### Half-Sister Debate

The dispute arises regarding *achot ha-em min ha-av* — his mother's half-sister who shares only a father with his mother. Rabbi Meir says *yotzi* — this too must be dissolved. The *Chachamim* say *yekayem* — this marriage may stand.

### Meir's Logic

Rabbi Meir's underlying principle is: *kol ervah she-hi mishum she'er em yotzi, mishum she'er av yekayem* — any *ervah* arising from a maternal kinship connection requires dissolution; any arising only from a paternal kinship connection is sustained. The maternal line is consistently the more restrictive one, generating prohibitions that the paternal line alone does not produce.

## Permitted Marriages

### Brother's Wife

The *baraita* continues: the *ger* is permitted to marry his brother's wife — *mutar b'eshet achiv*. The brother relationship, rooted in the pre-conversion non-Jewish world, does not carry over into the *ger*'s new Jewish status, and therefore the prohibition of *yibum*-related *arayot* does not apply.

### Uncle's Wife

Similarly, the *ger* is permitted to marry *eshet achi aviv* — the wife of his uncle, his father's brother. Again, the paternal-line kinship does not generate *arayot* prohibitions for the *ger*.

### Father's Wife

The *baraita* adds — and this is significant — that the *ger* is also permitted to marry his father's wife: *l'atuyei eshet aviv*. When the *baraita* says *she'er kol ha-arayot mutarot lo* — and all other *arayot* are permitted — this includes specifically his father's wife.

### Woman/Daughter Rule

If the *ger* married a woman and her daughter simultaneously — *nasa isha u-vitah* — he must maintain relations with one and dissolve the other: *kones achat u-motzi achat*. Ideally, *l'chatchila*, he should never have entered such an arrangement. This reflects that even for the *ger*, the prohibition of a woman and her daughter applies in some form.

### Mother-in-Law

If his wife dies, he is permitted to his mother-in-law — *mutar b'chamato*. However, there are those who say he remains *asur* to his mother-in-law even after his wife's death: *yesh omrim asur b'chamato*.

## Rashi's Clarification

### Father's Wife

Rashi points out something that requires attention: the *ger* is permitted to marry his father's wife even though Jewish law imposes the death penalty for that relationship. This seems to directly contradict Rabbi Meir's principle that wherever Jewish *beit din* executes, the *ben Noach* — and by extension the *ger* in this pre-conversion state — is warned.

### Mother-in-Law

Similarly, the *ger* is permitted to his mother-in-law — again, a relationship for which Jewish law imposes capital punishment. Yet the *baraita* permits it for the *ger*.

### Sisters Bar

Conversely, the *ger* is prohibited from marrying his sister and certain aunts even though Jewish law does not impose the death penalty for those relationships. Yet Rabbi Meir apparently holds that wherever Jewish law does not kill, the *ben Noach* is not warned.

### Rashi Problem

The apparent contradiction is direct: the *baraita* about the *ger* seems to falsify Rabbi Meir's stated principle in both directions — permitting what Rabbi Meir says should be forbidden, and forbidding what Rabbi Meir says should be permitted. The Gemara addresses this by noting that there are in fact two different versions of Rabbi Meir's position, aligned with two different *Tannaim*.

## Meir Variations

### Al Kein Pasuk

The resolution begins with the pasuk *al kein ya'azov ish et aviv v'et imo* — "therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother." This verse, which appears in the context of marriage and is famously invoked at weddings, carries significant halakhic content in the Noachide context. The words *aviv* and *imo* — his father and his mother — are interpreted by Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Akiva in quite different ways.

### Eleazar View

Rabbi Elazar reads *aviv* as referring to the paternal aunt — *achot aviv* — and *imo* as referring to the maternal aunt — *achot imo*. The prohibition for a non-Jew against marrying his aunt is derived from these words. A non-Jewish man "leaves" not his literal parents but the family relationships embodied by his parents' sisters.

### Akiva View

Rabbi Akiva disagrees entirely. He reads *aviv* as *eshet aviv* — his father's wife — and *imo* as his literal mother, *imo mamash*. On this reading, the pasuk is teaching that a man must leave behind — i.e., not have relations with — his father's wife and his own mother. The aunts are simply not in view here.

### Bestiality Ban

The pasuk continues: *v'davak b'ishto* — "and he shall cleave to his wife." From *v'davak*, the Gemara derives *v'lo b'zachar* — not to another male — establishing the Noachide prohibition against male homosexual relations. Further, from *b'ishto* — his wife — and not *eishes chaveiro* — his fellow's wife — the prohibition against adultery is established. And from *v'hayu l'vasar echad* — "and they shall become one flesh" — since only humans can become one flesh in the sense of producing children, this verse implicitly excludes bestiality, which cannot produce offspring: *yatzu behemah v'chayah she-ein na-asim basar echad*.

## Eleazar Challenge

### Father Objection

Having stated Rabbi Elazar's position that *aviv* refers to the paternal aunt, the Gemara challenges: why do we need a special derivation from *aviv* to prohibit the paternal aunt? Why not simply say that the paternal aunt is prohibited because of the prohibition against the father himself?

### Father Covered

The answer: the father is already excluded by the later verse, *v'lo b'zachar* — not with a male. Since a man cannot have relations with any man, that obviously encompasses his own father. Therefore, *aviv* cannot be referring to the father himself — he is already covered. The word *aviv* must therefore be pointing to a different relationship, and Rabbi Elazar identifies it as the paternal aunt.

## Akiva Challenge

### Mother Parallel

The Gemara challenges Rabbi Akiva's reading that *imo* means the mother literally. If *aviv* means *eshet aviv* — the father's wife — what is the basis for treating *imo* differently and reading it literally as the mother? Rabbi Akiva answers: the mother is analogous to the father's wife — *damya l'imo*. Just as the father's wife is prohibited not because of a marriage-based category (*eshes ish*) but because of her intimate connection to the father, so too the mother is prohibited through that same family-based logic rather than as an *eshes ish*. In other words, the prohibition of the mother is a *she'er*-based prohibition, not an *ervah*-based one.

## Eleazar Challenge (II)

### Mother Objection

The Gemara challenges Rabbi Elazar from the other direction. If *imo* refers to the maternal aunt, why do we need a specific derivation? Why not simply derive the prohibition from the prohibition of the mother herself?

## Akiva Challenge (II)

### Father Objection 2

Returning to Rabbi Akiva, the Gemara asks: if *aviv* means *eshet aviv* — the father's wife — why do we need to derive it from *aviv*? Should it not already follow from the prohibition of *eshet chaveiro* — another man's wife — which applies to all married women?

### Post-Death Question

The answer is that the prohibition of *eshet aviv* extends even after the father's death. An ordinary *eshes ish* prohibition dissolves when the husband dies — a widow is free to remarry. But the *eshet aviv* relationship carries a different quality: she remains prohibited to the son not merely as someone's wife, but because of her connection to the father, analogous to the way a mother remains prohibited regardless of the father's status.

### Household Rule

The Gemara challenges Rabbi Akiva's reading of *imo* as the literal mother: this should already be prohibited by the category of *eshet chaveiro*, since she was his father's wife and thus falls under the general prohibition against another man's wife. The answer, as worked out above, is that the mother may not have been his father's wife at all — she may have been a woman his father violated, *imo me-anusato*, never having been formally married. In that case, she would not be covered by *eshet chaveiro*, and a separate derivation from *imo mamash* is required.

## Meir Dispute Core

### Eleazar Logic

The core dispute between Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Akiva is now laid bare. Rabbi Elazar holds that *aviv* and *imo* in the pasuk are constructed as parallel, equivalent categories. If *aviv* refers to a female relative connected through the father's line, then *imo* by parallel must refer to a female relative connected through the mother's line. The logical outcome is that both words refer to the same category — sisters, specifically aunts — distinguished only by which parental line they come through. Rabbi Elazar's reading thus creates a symmetrical structure: *aviv* = paternal aunt, *imo* = maternal aunt.

### Akiva Logic

Rabbi Akiva rejects this categorical equivalence. He does not require *aviv* and *imo* to be parallel. Instead, he reads each independently: *aviv* refers to *ervat aviv* — his father's wife, who is the paradigmatic *ervah* connected to the father — while *imo* refers to his literal mother, *imo mamash*. Crucially, on Rabbi Akiva's reading, *achot aviv* — the paternal aunt — is not *ervat aviv* but *she'er aviv*, a kinship-based prohibition rather than a marital one.

### Ervah vs. She'er

The distinction between *ervah* and *she'er* is fundamental to understanding this dispute. *Ervah* refers to a prohibited relationship defined by its connection to a specific sexual or marital bond — a wife, and by extension the intimacy associated with that bond. *She'er* refers to a prohibited relationship defined by blood kinship alone, without the marital component. Rabbi Akiva argues that the paternal aunt is *she'er aviv*, not *ervat aviv*, and therefore is not captured by the word *aviv* in the pasuk.

## Aunt Marriage Case

### Amram/Yocheved

The Gemara brings a textual proof: *vayikach Amram et Yocheved dodato* — "and Amram took Yocheved his aunt" (Shemot 6:20). This apparently demonstrates that marrying an aunt was practiced before the giving of the Torah.

### Which Side?

The question is immediately raised: which kind of aunt was Yocheved? Was she Amram's *dodat min ha-em* — his aunt through his mother — or his *dodat min ha-av* — his aunt through his father?

### Genealogy

The genealogy makes clear that Yocheved is Levi's daughter, and Amram is Levi's grandson through Kehat — Levi's son. Yocheved is therefore Kehat's sister and Amram's father's sister: she is his *dodat min ha-av*, his paternal aunt. She is not his aunt through his mother.

### Permission Inferred

From the Amram-Yocheved marriage, the Gemara infers that marrying one's father's sister — the paternal aunt — was permitted in the pre-Sinaitic period, which is precisely the period that governs Noachide law.

## Abraham's Sister

### Abraham's Words

A second proof is brought from Avraham's own words regarding Sarah: *v'gam omnah achoti bat avi hi ach lo bat imi* — "and indeed she is my sister, the daughter of my father, but not the daughter of my mother."

### Maternal Bar

The implication of Avraham's formulation is significant: had Sarah been the daughter of his mother — a maternal half-sister — she would have been prohibited to him. By specifying that she is *bat avi* and not *bat imi*, Avraham signals that the paternal connection is the permissive factor and the maternal connection would have been the prohibiting one.

## Niece Interpretation

### Niece Reading

The Gemara offers an alternative interpretation: perhaps *achoto* in the relevant context means not "sister" but "niece" — *bat achiv*, the daughter of his brother.

### No Side Difference

If the word refers to a niece rather than a sister, then the distinction between paternal and maternal sides becomes irrelevant for this context, since the prohibition or permission of niece-marriage does not depend on which side the relationship runs through.

### Kinship Relation

Another possibility is raised: *kurba d'achot* — a relationship of "sister-type kinship" without being a direct sibling. This refers to a close collateral relative on the father's side — perhaps a paternal first cousin — where the connection is through the father's line without any direct maternal descent being involved.

## Adam & Daughter

### Adam's Choice

The Gemara raises a striking question: why did Adam not marry his own daughter? Adam and Chava had daughters — why was marriage with them not the arrangement that was made?

### Kayin Precedent

The answer given is: in order that Kayin could marry his sister. Had Adam married his daughter, that arrangement would have precluded Kayin from marrying the sister he ultimately married — presumably because of the precedent it would set or the structural arrangement of the family unit.

### Divine Justification

The basis for permitting Kayin to marry his sister is the verse: *ki amarti olam chesed yibaneh* — "for I said: the world shall be built with kindness" (Tehillim 89:3). The propagation of humanity required these early marriages, and the verse provides a divine sanction for what would otherwise appear to be a prohibited arrangement.

### Absence Implies Ban

The implication is notable: had this verse not existed, one would have concluded that marrying a sister is *asur* — prohibited. The very need to derive a permission from *olam chesed yibaneh* presupposes that without it, such a marriage would fall under the general Noachide prohibition.

### Permanence Rule

Once the permission was granted, however, it remains permanently in effect: *d'keivan d'ishtarei ishtarei* — once it was permitted, it stays permitted. The Gemara does not treat this as a temporary dispensation for the generation of Kayin but as an established permission that cannot be withdrawn once granted.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 59

## Arayos Dispute

### Retzicha & Fetuses

Today's *daf* is 59, and we are continuing from where the previous session left off, in the middle of 58b, picking up approximately twelve lines from the top, at the *tashma* concerning Kayin marrying his sister. The broader discussion at this point concerns the scope of *arayos* that apply to *Bnei Noach*.

The previous session raised a number of important preliminary issues. The first concerned *retzicha*: is there a unique *halacha* for *Bnei Noach* in this area, and how does it apply to *ubarim*, to fetuses? For *Yisrael*, abortion is not treated as a capital crime; for *Bnei Noach*, however, it is included in the *sheva mitzvos Bnei Noach* by virtue of the phrase *adam ba'adam*. One might suggest that this reflects a broader principle: by *Bnei Noach*, the concept of *shiurim* — formal minimum measures that define whether a prohibited act has been committed — does not apply in the same way. Anything that falls broadly under the rubric of a prohibition is included, without a minimum threshold. However, this will require qualification, because later in the *Gemara* we will encounter areas where, by contrast, the formal definitions actually seem *narrower* for *Bnei Noach* than for *Yisrael*.

This question has practical relevance. If a non-Jewish physician performs an abortion, there is a clear issue of *lifnei iver* with respect to the *sheva mitzvos Bnei Noach*. Whether that in turn reflects upon the status of abortion as an *averah* for Jews — not necessarily a capital crime, not *retzicha*, but some form of prohibition — is a question that will surface in the *Tosafot* later in this session.

### Women's Status

A further point reviewed from the previous session: women occupy an interesting position within the framework of *Bnei Noach*. On the one hand, the adjudicatory standards for *Bnei Noach* are notably non-formal — a single witness (*ed echad*) suffices and *hasra'ah* is not required — yet women were specifically excluded from serving in that judicial capacity. In the substantive obligations of the *sheva mitzvos Bnei Noach*, however, women are fully included.

### Marriage Concepts

With respect to *arayos*, one central distinction that emerged in the prior session is the definition of marriage for *Bnei Noach*. For a *ben Noach*, marriage is defined exclusively by *be'ulat ba'al* — the act of intercourse within a marital relationship. There is no concept of *erusin* for *Bnei Noach*. Accordingly, the category of *na'arah me'urasah* — a betrothed young woman — does not exist in the *Bnei Noach* framework. Nevertheless, if a non-Jew had intercourse with a Jewish *na'arah me'urasah*, since she constitutes an *ervah* under Jewish law, and since the act involved a Jewish woman, it would be punishable — governed by Jewish law, including *skilah*, rather than by the standards of *Bnei Noach*.

### Akiva vs. Eliezer

With that background established, the *Gemara* returns to determining the scope of *arayos* for *Bnei Noach*. Two principal positions have emerged. Rabbi Akiva limits the prohibited *arayos* for *Bnei Noach* to those relationships for which a Jew would be liable to the death penalty, deriving this from the *pasuk* of *al kein ya'azov ish et aviv ve'et imo* — which he reads as encompassing father, mother, father's wife, a male, an animal, and so forth, all of which carry a *chiyuv mita*. Rabbi Eliezer, by contrast, does not focus on the death penalty; rather, he centers his analysis on the principle of *achva* — the sisterhood relationship — and accordingly prohibits sisters, a father's sister, a mother's sister, and similar relationships, even where the violation carries only *karet* rather than *mita*. There is one point of agreement between all opinions: familial relationships are traced matrilineally, not patrilineally, which is practically sensible since the mother's identity is always certain.

---

## Adam & Kayin

### Kayin's Sister

With this framework in place, the *Gemara* introduces a *tashma* — a source that bears on the dispute. The question posed is: *mifnei mah lo nasa Adam et bito* — why did Adam not marry his own daughter? He had a wife in Chava, but in theory, after her sin, one might have expected Chava to die; even granting that she did not, the question remains why Adam, who could theoretically have taken any of the women available to him (limited as that pool was), did not choose a daughter. The answer given is: *kedei sheyisa Kayin et achoto* — so that Kayin could marry his sister. The *pasuk* cited is *ki amarti olam chesed yibaneh*: Adam's setting aside a woman he might otherwise have claimed was an act of *chesed* for his son. The implication that follows — *ha lav hachi asira* — is that without this special circumstance, a sister would have been forbidden to *Bnei Noach*. This appears to support Rabbi Eliezer, who prohibits sister relationships, and to work against Rabbi Akiva, since marrying one's sister carries only *karet*, not *mita*, and Rabbi Akiva should therefore permit it to *Bnei Noach*.

### General vs. Special

Rabbi Akiva's response is: *kivan de'ishtarei ishtarei* — once Kayin was permitted to marry his sister, the permission became generalized for all *Bnei Noach*. Since marrying a sister is not a *chiyuv mita* for *Yisrael*, Rabbi Akiva maintains that *Bnei Noach* are altogether *mutar* in this area. Rabbi Eliezer, for his part, reads the permission granted to Kayin as a special *chesed* — an exceptional allowance — and does not generalize it.

### Rashi Chesed

Rashi draws attention to a striking linguistic detail in the *parsha* of *arayos* itself: the *pasuk* concerning a man who marries his sister uses the word *chesed* — *ve'ish asher yikach et achoto bat aviv... chesed hu*. It is a peculiar term in the context of a prohibition. Rashi, both here and in his commentary on the *Torah*, connects this usage directly to the episode of Kayin: the permission granted for that union was a *chesed*, an act of grace, though in principle a sister is forbidden to *Yisrael*. The *Gemara* thus presents a hermeneutic tension: was the allowance for Kayin a special dispensation that defines the general *Bnei Noach* rule (Rabbi Eliezer), or was it an exception that once granted became universally normative for *Bnei Noach* (Rabbi Akiva)?

### Rav Huna Daughter

The *Gemara* then introduces a third position. *Amar Rav Huna: Kuti mutar bevito* — a non-Jew is permitted with his daughter. This is a striking ruling.
