Both Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Eliezer, despite their differences, would prohibit a daughter: marrying one's daughter carries a *chiyuv mita* for *Yisrael*, which would include it under Rabbi Akiva's criterion, and it is not a sister relationship, which is Rabbi Eliezer's criterion, yet it would still be covered by a general prohibition. Rav Huna's position takes a far narrower reading of the *pasuk* of *al ken ya'azov ish et aviv ve'et imo*: only those specific relationships explicitly derivable from that *pasuk* through *drashot* — father, mother, father's wife, a male, an animal — are prohibited. Sister and daughter are simply not textually included, and therefore *Bnei Noach* are *mutar* in those cases. This is also the position of the Rambam.

### Reconciliation

A potential objection presents itself: if a daughter is *mutar* for *Bnei Noach*, why did Adam not marry his daughter? The answer restates the *tashma*'s conclusion: *kedei sheyisa Kayin et ha'achot* — halachically, Adam *could* have done so, but he refrained as a *chesed* in order to leave a woman available for Kayin to marry as a sister. The fact that Adam did not marry his daughter proves nothing about the prohibition; it reflects only his *chesed*.

### Three Positions

An alternative formulation of Rav Huna is also reported: *Kuti assur bevito* — the daughter is forbidden. The proof offered is *teida shelo nasa Adam et bito* — the very fact that Adam did not marry his daughter demonstrates the prohibition for *Bnei Noach*. The *Gemara* rejects this: *veloha* — this is not a valid proof. As explained, Adam refrained not because of a prohibition but in order to allow Kayin to marry a sister, as expressed by the verse *olam chesed yibaneh*. Accordingly, three distinct positions emerge in summary: Rabbi Eliezer, who focuses on the principle of *achva* and prohibits sisterhood relationships while setting aside relationships defined through marriage (such as a father's wife); Rabbi Akiva, who focuses on *chayavei mita min haTorah* and accordingly prohibits the relationships that carry a death penalty while permitting sisters; and the third view — likely a refinement within Rabbi Akiva's position — which adopts the most restrictive reading of the *pasuk*, limiting the prohibitions to what is explicitly textually derived and thereby permitting even a daughter. It should be noted that under all views, familial relations for *Bnei Noach* are defined matrilineally, such that under Rabbi Eliezer a sister through the father's side would be *mutar*, while a full sister through the mother was permitted to Kayin as either a special exception (Rabbi Eliezer) or as the general rule (Rabbi Akiva).

---

## Slave Conversion

### Slave Relations

The *Gemara* now turns to a related but distinct category: the converting slave (*eved*). *Amar Rav Chisda: eved mutar be'imo* — a slave who undergoes conversion is permitted with his mother — *mutar bevito* — and with his daughter. The novelty here requires emphasis: nobody holds that a *ben Noach* is *mutar be'imo*. Mother is a universally prohibited relationship. And certainly *Yisrael* is prohibited with his mother. So how does this slave fall outside all categories?

### Quasi-Newborn

The underlying principle is *k'katan shenolad dami* — the converting slave is treated as one who has been newly born. Upon undergoing *tevilah* and conversion, he enters a quasi-Jewish status. Accordingly, the laws of *Bnei Noach* no longer apply to him. But what accounts for the *heter* with his mother and daughter? In principle, as a quasi-Jew, the negative prohibitions of Jewish law should bind him, and mother is prohibited to every Jew. The answer lies in the logic of *k'katan shenolad dami*: he is no longer halakhically related to his pre-conversion family. Technically, the mother he was born to is no longer, in Jewish legal terms, his mother.

### Paradox

This gives rise to a pointed paradox. We know from material covered in the prior session that when a non-Jew converts, the familial prohibitions from the non-Jewish period are *retained* by Rabbinic enactment — specifically to prevent someone from concluding that Jewish law is more lenient than non-Jewish law (*shelo yomru azavnu issur chumur venachnu ba'in le'kal*). That principle, rigorously applied when a full convert enters Jewish status, is evidently not applied here to the *eved*. The distinction seems to be that the *eved* is in an intermediate, quasi-Jewish state: Jewish law applies to him in virtually all respects, yet his pre-conversion family ties are not recognized for purposes of the prohibition. If he were now to father a daughter, that daughter *would* be prohibited to him — because his new familial relations, formed post-conversion, are fully operative.

The irony is complete: the Rabbinic enactment that protects against the perception of leniency kicks in once he becomes a full Jew, retroactively treating his pre-conversion mother as prohibited. But in the *eved* state, before that transition is complete, this concern is apparently set aside.

### Limbo Status

What remains somewhat puzzling is why the concern about the appearance of leniency does not apply here at all, given that the *eved* is a quasi-Jew, governed by Jewish law in most areas and living within a Jewish household. The best way to understand it may be that the *eved* occupies a genuinely liminal status — neither fully *Bnei Noach* nor fully *Yisrael*, in a kind of *nisht ahin nisht aher* category. The *Gemara* seems to tolerate the ambiguity of that transitional state rather than importing the full stringency of either legal framework into it. That said, there is something inherently strange about allowing this *limbo* to persist, and one might read into the *Gemara*'s implicit tolerance of that strangeness a certain hesitation about keeping people in this undefined condition too long.

---

## Yichud Marriage

### Designated Woman

The *Gemara* now introduces a different scenario. *Ben Noach she'yichad shifcha l'avdo* — a *ben Noach* who designated a maidservant for his slave — and then the gentile master himself had intercourse with her — *neherag aleha* — is liable to the death penalty. Why? At an earlier point in the *Gemara*, this was explained as a form of *gezel*: since the woman was designated for the slave, the master, by taking her, is effectively stealing her from his slave — treating her as an object of property. The Rambam, however, takes a different approach: he categorizes this case under *arayos* for *Bnei Noach*, specifically as a form of *eshes ish*.

The Rambam's reasoning is illuminating. For free persons, the *Bnei Noach* framework defines marriage through *be'ulat ba'al* — intercourse within an established marital relationship — and there is no parallel institution for slaves, since historically the institution of slave marriage was not socially recognized in the same way (families were routinely separated, and formal marriage was not accorded to enslaved persons in antiquity). Nevertheless, the *halacha* recognizes a de facto societal marriage for slaves through the mechanism of *yichad lo* — designation. What makes this even more striking is that, on the Rambam's reading, *yichad lo* constitutes marriage even *before* intercourse — it is earlier in the process than *be'ulat ba'al*, the standard marker for free persons. The Rambam thus understands the *chiddush* of this case as establishing that for slaves, *yichud* — social designation — replaces intercourse as the constitutive act of marriage.

### Yichud Definition

This framework means that for purposes of *arayos* and the prohibition of *eshes ish* within the *Bnei Noach* system, enslaved individuals acquire marital status through a different mechanism than free persons — one grounded in social recognition rather than in a formal legal act or in the act of intercourse itself.

### Recognition Point

*Me'eimasai* — from when does that designated status take effect? *Amar Rav Nachman: mi-d'karu lah rivisa d'planya* — from the time that people call her "the young woman of so-and-so," meaning when she is societally recognized as belonging to that slave's household. The marker is communal perception: once the surrounding community identifies her as this man's woman, the designated status has attached.

### Hair Uncovered

When does the status dissolve? *Amar Rav Huna: mi-she-par'ah rashah ba-shuk* — once her hair is uncovered in the marketplace. This reflects a broader societal reality that the *Gemara* acknowledges elsewhere as well: in ancient society, married women covered their hair. The *Gemara* derives that hair-covering is *das Yehudis* from the fact that the *sotah*'s hair is uncovered — implying that covered hair was the standard societal norm for married women. The dissolution of the slave's designated marital status follows the same logic of social reality: once her hair is publicly uncovered, the community understands that she is no longer designated.

### Rambam Divorce

For free non-Jews, the question of how marriage ends is equally important. The Rambam provides a clear formulation: *u'me'eimasai tihyeh eshes chaveiro k'grusha shelanu* — when does another man's wife become as a divorcée for us? *Mi-she-hotziah mi-beiso v'yeshalachah l'atzmah* — once he has sent her out from his home. Or alternatively, *o mi-she-teitzei hi mi-tachas reshuso v'telech lah* — if she leaves on her own, departing from his domain. *She'ein lahem gerushin b'chsav* — they have no written *get*. *V'ein ha-davar taluy bo l'vado* — the matter does not depend on the man alone. Rather, *kol zman she-yirtzeh hu o hi lifrosh zeh mi-zeh porshin* — whenever either party wishes to separate, they may do so.

This is a highly significant ruling: *Bnei Noach* divorce can be initiated by either party, husband or wife, with no formal document required. Either walking out of the marital home suffices.

### De Facto Marriage

This flows directly from the foundational principle that *Bnei Noach* marriage rests on *be'ulat ba'al* — on the lived reality of a couple cohabiting as husband and wife — rather than on any formal legal act. The Jewish system, by contrast, involves an act of *kiddushin* as a form of *kinyan*, initiated by the man, and it is dissolved only by *gerushin* initiated likewise by the man through the delivery of a *get*. The formal asymmetry of acquisition and dissolution is baked into the Jewish marital structure. The *Bnei Noach* system, lacking *erusin* entirely, is grounded in a de facto reality that both parties generate and either party can end. It is not analogous to *kiddushei biah* — intercourse as a formal act of *kiddushin* — but rather to something closer to common-law marriage: the ongoing reality of shared life, participated in by both, constitutes the marriage, and its cessation by either terminates it.

### Modern Aguna

This *Bnei Noach* model of marriage has attracted the attention of certain contemporary scholars and advocates in Israel who, confronting the *aguna* crisis, have proposed that Jews might contract marriage according to the *Bnei Noach* framework — based on *be'ulat ba'al* alone, bypassing *kiddushin* entirely — such that either party could walk away without needing a *get*. Whether *Bnei Noach* law can apply to Jews in this way, and whether such a scheme is legally achievable, remains deeply contested. But it is a fascinating instance of this *Gemara's* implications being brought to bear on a very live contemporary problem.

---

## Silo Kdarka

### Unnatural Acts

The *Gemara* now enters a distinct area. *Amar Rabbi Chanina: ben Noach she'ba al ishto she'lo k'darka chayav* — a *ben Noach* who has intercourse with his own wife in an unnatural manner is liable. This is surprising: we are no longer speaking about prohibited women, but about the nature of the act itself within marital intercourse. The source is the *pasuk* of *ve'davak* — he shall cleave to his wife — and the negative implication: *ve'lo she'lo k'darka*.

### Ve'davak

Why does *she'lo k'darka* fall outside the scope of *ve'davak*? One approach is simply physical: the bodies do not come together in the manner suggested by the word *ve'davak* — "cleaving." Rashi adds a different dimension: based on the *Gemara*'s assumption elsewhere that unnatural intercourse is generally not pleasurable for the woman, he understands *ve'davak* as requiring emotional adhesion, and that emotional adhesion — the genuine bonding implied by cleaving — is present only when both parties derive pleasure from the act. *She'mitoch she'eina nehenit ba'davar eina nidbeket imo* — since she does not experience pleasure, she does not truly cleave to him.

### Another's Wife

The *Gemara*, however, raises an immediate objection to Rabbi Chanina's formulation. *Amar Rava: mi ikka midi de'le'Yisrael lo mechayav u'le'Kuti mechayav?* — is there anything that is not a transgression for a Jew but *is* a transgression for a non-Jew? Some manuscripts have this even more starkly: *de'le'Yisrael shari u'le'Kuti assur* — that something is fully permitted for a Jew but prohibited for a non-Jew? This reflects a general *Gemara* principle. Indeed, with respect to this very act, the *rishonim* debate whether *she'lo k'darka* within marriage poses any problem for Jews — the simple reading of the *Gemara* is that for Jews it is not a transgression — and if so, how can it be a *chiyuv* for non-Jews?

Rava therefore reframes the principle entirely: *ben Noach she'ba al eshet chavero she'lo k'darka patur* — a *ben Noach* who has intercourse with *another man's wife* in an unnatural manner is *exempt*. A man and his own wife may have intercourse in any manner they choose. The prohibition of *she'lo k'darka* is not about the nature of the act within the marital relationship; rather, the *pasuk*'s prohibition of *eshes ish* is derived from *ve'davak be'ishto* — cleaving to *his* wife — implying *ve'lo be'eshet chavero*. What is prohibited with another man's wife is the act of *ve'davak*; but intercourse with another man's wife performed *she'lo k'darka* does not constitute that act of *ve'davak*, and therefore, for a *ben Noach*, is not a transgression.

### Narrow Definition

This is a remarkable ruling: unnatural intercourse with another man's wife, which for a Jew would constitute a severe violation of *arayos* and carry a *chiyuv mita* or *karet*, is simply not a transgression for a *ben Noach*. The formal definition of the prohibited act is narrower for *Bnei Noach* than for *Yisrael*.

### Shiurim Limits

This is worth pausing over, because it stands in tension with the earlier observation that *Bnei Noach* does not operate with *shiurim* — that their prohibitions cast a broader net than *Yisrael's*. We saw that anything broadly included in *gezel* or *retzicha* is forbidden to *Bnei Noach* even without the formal minimum measures that govern Jewish law. Yet here, in the realm of *arayos*, the formal definition of what constitutes a prohibited act is actually *narrower* for *Bnei Noach*. This asymmetry — broader liability in some areas, narrower in others — is striking and not immediately obvious to explain.

---

## Violence Acts

### Hit Jew Death

*Amar Rabbi Chanina: oveid kochavim she'hikkah et Yisrael chayav misa* — a non-Jew who strikes a Jew is liable to the death penalty. This goes beyond *retzicha*, which covers killing; here the *Gemara* is speaking of mere battery. The proof is drawn from Moshe's killing of the Egyptian: *vayifen koh vachoh vayach es haMitzri*. What had the Egyptian done? He was beating an Israelite — not, as far as the text indicates, with lethal intent. Yet Moshe killed him. The *Gemara* reads from this that even the act of beating a Jew is a *chiyuv misa* for a non-Jew. The historical and social context — a people living under the physical oppression of a foreign power — is palpable in this *halacha*.

### Slapping Cheek

Rabbi Chanina adds a further teaching: *ha-soter lo'o shel Yisrael* — one who slaps the cheek of a Jew — presumably a non-Jew, though the text is not entirely explicit — is *ke'ilu soter lo'o shel Shechinah* — as though he slapped the cheek of the Divine Presence. The *pasuk* cited is *mokash adam... yela kodesh* — striking a person is as striking the cheek of the Holy One. It is hard not to note the contrast with a certain famous dictum in another tradition, which counsels turning the other cheek to one who strikes it. The *Gemara* takes the diametrically opposite position: striking a Jew is not a forgivable affront between persons, but an offense against God Himself.

### Lifted Hand

*Amar Reish Lakish: ha-magbiah yado al chaveiro* — one who raises his hand against his fellow — *af al pi shelo hikah, nikra rasha* — even without having struck him, is called a *rasha*. The *pasuk* is: *vayomer la-rasha lamah takkeh re'echa* — Moshe said to the wicked one, "Why *will you* strike your fellow?" The verb is future tense — *takkeh*, not present — meaning Moshe called him a *rasha* not because he was already striking but because he *was about to*. The grammatical reading of *tashma mina* is explicit: *lamah hikisa lo ne'emar ela lamah takkeh* — the text does not say "why did you strike" but "why will you strike," demonstrating that the status of *rasha* attaches at the moment of raising the hand, before any blow is landed. It is worth noting that Reish Lakish himself was reputed to have come from a rough background, which lends a certain personal resonance to his concern with the transgression of violence. One might also note that the *pshat* of the text — both combatants were fighting, and Moshe identified who was at fault — does not require the reading the *Gemara* offers; nevertheless, the *Gemara* derives from it this principle of pre-blow culpability.

### Sinner Status

*Ze'eira amar Rabbi Chanina* offers a more lenient characterization: *nikra chotei* — such a person is called a *sinner* rather than a *rasha*. The *pasuk* brought is from the narrative of Eli's sons: *ve'im lo lakachti be'chozkah* — "if you do not give me the sacrifices, I will take them by force." The *pasuk* subsequently records: *vatehi chatas ha-ne'arim gedolah me'od* — the sin of Eli's sons was very great. So one who threatens forcible taking — which likely implies striking — is characterized as a *chotei*, which carries somewhat less weight than the designation *rasha*.

### Cut Hand

*Rav Huna amar tikatzeitz yado* — the hand of such a person deserves to be cut off. The *pasuk* is *uzroa ramah tishaveir* — a raised arm shall be broken/cut off. And this was not merely theoretical: in one actual case involving a habitual offender, Rav Huna did in fact cut off his hand. This is an extraordinarily severe measure, and it raises an immediate question about its legal basis.

### Din Debate

Rashi explains that Rav Huna acted in the framework of *beit din makin ve'onshin shelo min hadin* — the court's authority to administer punishment beyond the formal requirements of the law when circumstances demand it. This man was a habitual aggressor, and the extrajudicial punishment was necessary. Tosafot, however, reads Rav Huna differently: Tosafot holds that Rav Huna believed this to be the actual *din* — not a special *knas* or extraordinary measure, but the genuine *halacha* that a raised hand deserves amputation. This is a sharp dispute. The physical punishment of cutting off a hand has no parallel in the standard repertoire of *halachic* penalties, which reach as far as *malkos* and the various forms of *misat beit din* but not amputation. Rashi's reading is therefore far more comfortable: it was a *shelo min hadin* ruling, an exceptional judicial response to an exceptional situation. But even under Rashi's understanding, the severity is notable — *beit din* can impose unprecedented forms of punishment when the need arises, including, in appropriate cases, measures that would otherwise exceed what the formal *din* prescribes.

---

## Shabbat Ban

### Shabbat Prohibition

*Va'amar Reish Lakish: oved kochavim she'shavas chayav misa* — a non-Jew who rests on *Shabbos* is liable to the death penalty. This is one of the most famous and striking statements in this section of the *Gemara*. The ironies are sharp: the Jewish people spent centuries fighting for the right to a day of rest and were often persecuted for observing *Shabbos*; yet, according to Reish Lakish, non-Jews are *prohibited* from doing precisely that.

### Day Night Work

The *pasuk* is drawn from the covenant with Noach: *yom valaila lo yishbotu* — day and night shall not cease. Although the simple reading of this verse concerns the continuation of natural rhythms and seasons, the *Gemara* reads it as a directive: non-Jews may not cease from their labors. Day and night, there is no permitted cessation.

### Weekday Rest

*Amar Ravina: afilu sheini be'Shabbos* — even if a non-Jew takes rest on a Monday, or on any weekday at all, this is problematic. This is in addition to *Shabbos* and Sunday.

### Rashi Secular

Rashi's reading is carefully delineated: *lo teima shevisa deka'amar Reish Lakish leshum chova ka'amar* — do not think that the *shevisa* Reish Lakish speaks of refers specifically to adopting a day as a religious obligation, like *Shabbos* for *Yisrael* or Sunday for Christians. Rashi emphasizes *menucha be'alma* — even a purely secular day of rest. The *chiddush* of Ravina's statement is that even *sheini*, a Monday, with no religious character whatsoever, is included. The implication, as Rashi reads it, is that *Bnei Noach* are not entitled to any day off at all, whether religious or secular.

### Passive Violation

The *Gemara* anticipates the obvious question: if a non-Jew who rests on *Shabbos* is *chayav misa*, why is *Shabbos* not counted among the *sheva mitzvos Bnei Noach*? The answer: *shev v'al ta'aseh, kum va'aseh lo ka'chashiv* — the *sheva mitzvos* list includes only prohibitions that are violated by active transgression. *Shabbos* is violated by being passive — by doing nothing. A prohibition violated by inaction alone is not included in the formal count. This answer implicitly takes the *Shabbos* prohibition quite seriously as a real *chiyuv* for *Bnei Noach*.

### Slave Rest

A related question arises: what about Jewish slaves? An *eved Kena'ani* has quasi-Jewish obligations. Does he get *Shabbos* rest? And conversely, if a non-Jewish slave had not yet undergone *tevilah* and did not yet have the quasi-Jewish status of an *eved Kena'ani*, does the prohibition against taking a *Shabbos* rest apply to him? One might also note the parallel to animals: the *Torah* requires animals to rest on *Shabbos*, which would presumably apply to a non-Jewish slave as well. Whether that obligation on the master's part supersedes the prohibition on the slave's resting is not fully resolved here.

### Dinim Exception

The *Gemara* raises a parallel question about *dinim*: *v'dinim, kum va'aseh hu v'ka'chashiv?* — but *dinim*, the obligation to establish courts of justice, involves a positive obligation (*kum va'aseh*), yet it is counted among the *sheva mitzvos*. The answer is that *dinim* is different: it has both an active and a passive dimension. The active dimension is actively perverting justice — *lo ta'avur mishpat*, the prohibition on corrupt judgment. The passive dimension is the failure to establish courts at all. Since *dinim* can be transgressed through active wrongdoing, it is appropriately included in the formal list. *Shabbos*, by contrast, can only be transgressed passively, by resting, and therefore does not make the list. This further confirms that included in *dinim* is not merely the institutional obligation to establish a court system, but also the active prohibition of perverting justice.

### Rambam Religious

The Rambam reads this entire passage differently from Rashi — and his reading connects directly to the next topic, the prohibition on non-Jews learning *Torah*. For the Rambam, the problem of a non-Jew keeping *Shabbos* is not about a secular day off or about depriving oneself of one's right to work. Rather, it is about *creating a new religious practice*. The Rambam makes this explicit: *velo manichim osan lechadesh das vela'asos mitzvos l'atzman mida'atan* — we do not allow them to innovate a religion or to create *mitzvos* for themselves on their own initiative. His formulation: *ela yihyeh ger tzedek veyekabel kol hamitzvos o ya'amod betorato velo yosif velo yigra* — a non-Jew must either become a full *ger tzedek* and accept all the *mitzvos*, or remain within *his* religious framework — the *sheva mitzvos Bnei Noach* — without adding or subtracting. Accordingly, even taking rest on a weekday is problematic if done as a religious practice. And crucially, the Rambam holds that while a non-Jew who does these things is in principle *chayav misa*, the sanction is actually more like *chayav karet* — not literal execution: *makkin oso ve'onshin oso umodi'in oso she-hu chayav misa al zeh aval eino neherag*.

---

## Torah Learning Ban

### Inheritance Pasuk

*Va'amar Rabbi Yochanan: nochri she'osek ba-Torah chayav misa* — a non-Jew who engages in Torah study is liable to the death penalty. The source: *Torah tziva lanu Moshe morasha* — Torah that Moshe commanded us is an inheritance. *Morasha lanu — lanu morasha velo lahem* — it is our inheritance, not theirs.

### Morasha Drasha

Why then is the prohibition of Torah learning not listed among the *sheva mitzvos Bnei Noach*? The *Gemara* addresses this through two competing *drashot* on the word *morasha*. According to the first: *migo d'gazal leh* — since the non-Jew steals it from us — it is already subsumed under *gezel*, one of the *sheva mitzvos*. According to the second, the word *morasha* is read as *me'orasah* — betrothed: the Jewish people are betrothed, as it were married, to the *Torah*. On this reading, a non-Jew who engages with *Torah* is analogous to one who has intercourse with a *na'arah me'orasah* — a betrothed young woman. Notably, this is a clever inversion: *na'arah me'orasah* is not naturally part of the *Bnei Noach* framework, since *Bnei Noach* only recognize *be'ulat ba'al* and have no concept of *erusin*. A non-Jew would normally not transgress the prohibition of *na'arah me'orasah* unless the woman was Jewish, because Jewish law governs that act in relation to a Jewish woman. Here, the *Torah* is cast as the Jewish woman who is *me'orasah* to the Jewish people — and the non-Jew who violates that bond transgresses accordingly.

### Kohen Gadol

The *Gemara* now introduces a directly contrasting *braisa*. Rabbi Meir asks: *minayin she'afilu oveid kochavim she'osek ba-Torah she-hu k'kohen gadol* — how do we know that even a non-Jew who engages in Torah study is like a *kohen gadol*, the highest possible religious status? The *pasuk*: *eileh ha-mitzvos asher ya'aseh osam ha-adam va-chai ba-hem* — these are the commandments that a person shall do and live by them. *Kohanim, Levi'im v'Yisraelim lo ne'emar* — the text does not say *Kohanim*, *Levi'im*, or *Yisrael*. It says *ha-adam* — any person. *Ha lamadta she'afilu oveid kochavim v'osek ba-Torah harei hu k'kohen gadol*. This is an extraordinary, universalist statement: the study and practice of *Torah* is open to all humanity on equal terms, and a non-Jew who engages in it stands on par with the highest Jewish religious office.

### Reconciliation

The *Gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction between Rabbi Yochanan's prohibition and Rabbi Meir's expansive statement: *hatam b'sheva mitzvos did'hu* — Rabbi Meir's ruling applies when the non-Jew studies *Torah* within the context of his own *sheva mitzvos* — that is, learning the laws that pertain to him. Engaging with the broader corpus of *Torah* beyond that boundary is the transgression Rabbi Yochanan identifies.

### Universalist

That said, one should recognize what is actually at stake in these texts. The *braisa* cited — likely a *Tosefta* — contains a broader collection of universalist statements that go beyond the *Gemara's* harmonizing conclusion. One version reads not merely *osek ba-Torah* but *osek ba-Torah v'oseh es ha-Torah* — engaged in *Torah* and actually fulfilling it, meaning performing *mitzvos*. The collection includes the *pasuk* of *v'yavo goy tzaddik shomer emunim* — and a righteous nation that observes faithfulness shall come — on which the *braisa* similarly comments: *Kohanim, Levi'im v'Yisraelim lo ne'emar, ela v'yavo goy tzaddik*. Even a *goy tzaddik* enters the gates of God. And the *pasuk* of *ha-adam asher ya'aseh osam ha-adam va-chai ba-hem* — "a person" shall do them and live by them — applies to any person, with no ethnic qualification.

### Unique Framework

These statements articulate a strikingly universalist religious vision, and it is worth pausing to appreciate their significance. It is, in fact, remarkable — unusual within the broader history of religions — for a community to maintain that someone can fulfill the divine will, attain *olam haba*, and stand before God as righteous *without belonging to that community*. The very existence of the *sheva mitzvos Bnei Noach* as a coherent alternative framework for non-Jewish religious life is itself a major *chiddush* in the theology of world religions. It is not the dominant *Chazalic* voice — it tilts toward minority opinion — but it is present and powerful. Moreover, the *Torah*-as-equalizer trope connects to a familiar rabbinic theme: *afilu mamzer v'osek ba-Torah harei hu k'kohen gadol* — even a *mamzer* who studies *Torah* is like a *kohen gadol* — derived from *yekarah hi mipeninim, yekarah hi mi-kohen gadol ha-nichnas lifnai v'lifnim*. All internal Jewish hierarchy dissolves before *Torah* learning; and, on these readings, so too does the Jewish/non-Jewish boundary. The *Gemara* works to contain these statements within the structure of *sheva mitzvos*, but the original formulations carry a universalism that transcends that containment.

---

## Ever Dam

### Blood Included

*Ve'amar Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel: af dam min hachai* — even blood from a living animal is prohibited for *Bnei Noach*, not only *eiver min hachai* (a limb from a living animal).

### Double Prohibition

The *braisa* is brought: *ach basar benafsho damo lo tocheilu* — this verse is the source for *eiver min hachai*. Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel reads it as generating a double prohibition: *karei bei basar benafsho lo tocheilu, damo benafsho lo tocheilu* — "flesh while alive you shall not eat" *and* "blood while alive you shall not eat." Since the word *damo* was included alongside *basar*, he derives an independent prohibition on *dam min hachai*.

### Blood Distinct

The Rabbis respond: *hahu lemishrei sheratzim hu de'ata* — that textual element comes to teach something else. Specifically, it comes to distinguish between *eiver min hachai* in a standard animal and in a *sheretz* (rodent). In a standard animal, the blood is considered sufficiently distinct from the flesh that the prohibition of *eiver min hachai* applies separately to each. In a *sheretz*, however, the blood is legally considered merged with the flesh and therefore does not generate an independent category.

### Lifeblood

Returning to Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel, the *Gemara* continues: *rak chazak levilti achol ha-dam ki ha-dam hu ha-nefesh* — the verse's emphasis on *ki ha-dam hu ha-nefesh*, "for the blood is the soul," is understood similarly to what was seen regarding *Bnei Noach* — as indicating that *dam min hachai* is a distinct prohibition. The Rabbis demur: *hu le-dam ha-kazeh she-ha-neshamah yotzet bo* — the phrase *dam hu ha-nefesh* identifies only lifeblood, the blood from which life departs, as the category that carries *karet*. This is not blood as an independent prohibition of *dam min hachai*; it is rather a specification of *which* blood is the subject of the blood prohibition in general. Rashi explains further: the blood that constitutes *dam hu ha-nefesh* is not necessarily the first blood to flow — not the initial squirt — but the arterial blood, the sustained lifeblood. Technically all blood is biologically the same, but *Chazal* identified a particular quality of blood — the blood that the life itself depends upon — as the operative category for the prohibition carrying *karet*. The Rabbis thus resist the inference that *dam min hachai* is a separate and independent prohibition for *Bnei Noach*.

---

## Repetition Rule

### Why Repeat

The *Gemara* now raises a structural question: *lama li lemichtav le-Bnei Noach v'lama li lemishni be-Sinai* — if *eiver min hachai* was already prohibited to *Bnei Noach*, and *Yisrael* are themselves descendants of *Bnei Noach*, why did the prohibition need to be repeated at *Har Sinai*?

### Ever Application

The answer invokes the principle of Rabbi Yosi be'Rabbi Chanina, which the *Gemara* will now articulate. The repetition at Sinai was necessary to establish that *eiver min hachai* applies to *both* groups — *Bnei Noach* and *Yisrael* alike — rather than being absorbed entirely into the Jewish framework and ceasing to apply universally. Without the repetition, one might have mistakenly concluded otherwise.

### Both Groups

*D'amar Rabbi Yosi be'Rabbi Chanina: kol mitzvah she'ne'emrah le-Bnei Noach v'nishneis be-Sinai lezeh u'lezeh ne'emrah* — any commandment that was given to *Bnei Noach* and repeated at Sinai applies to both groups. This part is intuitive: if a law was given universally and then reaffirmed at Sinai, it remains universal.

### Only Yisrael

The counterintuitive half of the principle follows: *le-Bnei Noach v'lo nishneis be-Sinai, le-Yisrael ne'emrah v'lo le-Bnei Noach* — if it was given to *Bnei Noach* and not repeated at Sinai, it applies only to *Yisrael* and not to *Bnei Noach*. This is, as acknowledged, a deeply puzzling rule. The intuitive expectation would be the opposite: if a law was given to *Bnei Noach* but never repeated or incorporated into the Sinaitic corpus, one would expect it to remain binding on *Bnei Noach* and perhaps not apply to *Yisrael*, who received their own comprehensive legal system. Yet the *Gemara* inverts this: it is the *Bnei Noach* who are released from such a law, while *Yisrael* remains bound by it. The practical consequence for *eiver min hachai*: had it not been repeated at Sinai, one would have concluded it applied only to *Yisrael*. Since it was repeated, we know it applies to both.

### Gid Hanasheh

What is the one example of a *mitzvah* that was said before Sinai and not repeated at Sinai, such that it applies only to *Yisrael*? *Ve'anu ein lanu* — the only case is *gid hanasheh*, according to Rabbi Yehuda. This requires clarification. The *pasuk* says *al kein lo yochlu Bnei Yisrael et gid hanasheh* — therefore the children of Israel shall not eat the *gid ha-nasheh*. Rabbi Yehuda holds that this commandment was given at the time of Yaakov Avinu — i.e., before Sinai — and was not repeated at Sinai. The *Rabbanan* disagree: they hold the *mitzvah* was only given at Sinai and the *pasuk* was written earlier in the narrative but is not the original promulgation. Under Rabbi Yehuda's reading, *gid hanasheh* is the paradigmatic case of a pre-Sinaitic law that was never repeated — and it applies only to *Yisrael*, not to *Bnei Noach*. Of course, as the *Gemara* itself notes, there is an irony: the *pasuk* explicitly says *Bnei Yisrael* — on its face, it seems to confine the prohibition to *Yisrael* from the outset.

### Logic Objection

The *Gemara* raises the objection that logic would seem to demand: *adaraba* — shouldn't we say the opposite? Since it was *not* repeated at Sinai, we should say it applies only to *Bnei Noach* — that is, it retained its original pre-Sinaitic, universal character — and not to *Yisrael*, who received their own comprehensive code at Sinai?

### Avodah Zara Proof

The *Gemara* answers with empirical evidence rather than theoretical argument: *mide'isti ovdei kochavim be-Sinai* — we know that the prohibition of *avodah zara* was repeated at Sinai. And *ve'ashkachan de'anshu ovdei kochavim alavah* — we know that non-Jews are punished for *avodah zara* (the nations of Canaan were driven out for this very sin). And we know *Yisrael* is punished for *avodah zara*. Thus: a law that was stated to *Bnei Noach* and repeated at Sinai applies to *both* groups. *Shema mina lezeh u'lezeh ne'emrah* — this is confirmed by the case of *avodah zara*. This settles the first half of the principle.

### No Contradiction

The *Gemara* then addresses the counterintuitive second half — the rule that a law stated to *Bnei Noach* but not repeated at Sinai applies only to *Yisrael* — with a different logical argument: *leka midi de'le-Yisrael shari vel'ovdei kochavim assur* — there cannot exist a law that is permitted for *Yisrael* yet prohibited for *Bnei Noach*. It is inconceivable that the more comprehensive legal system governing *Yisrael* would permit something that the more basic *Bnei Noach* code forbids. Therefore, if a law was given to *Bnei Noach* and then incorporated into the Sinaitic corpus — even if it was not explicitly re-stated — it must apply to *Yisrael*. And conversely, the failure to repeat it would signal that it has been, in some sense, absorbed exclusively into the *Yisrael* framework rather than retained as a universal *Bnei Noach* obligation. The discussion of this principle, and its further ramifications, will continue in the next session.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 59b

## Repetition at Har Sinai

### Ever Min Hachai Setup

The discussion on this *daf* begins at the very bottom of 59a, arising from a question about why the *Torah* needed to repeat the prohibition of *ever min hachai* — the limb of a living animal — once it had already been included among the laws of *bnei Noach*. The *Gemara*'s response establishes a principle that is both important and, on closer inspection, quite striking.

### Core Principle

The *Gemara* articulates the following rule: anything that was said to *bnei Noach* and then repeated at *Har Sinai* applies to both Jews and non-Jews. That much is straightforward. But the second half of the principle is more surprising: anything said only to *bnei Noach* and *not* repeated at *Har Sinai* applies only to *Yisrael*. This is why *ever min hachai* had to be repeated — so that it would apply to both. The lone example of something said to *bnei Noach* that was *not* repeated and therefore applies only to *Yisrael* is *gid hanasheh*, though this is itself somewhat puzzling, since the verse explicitly states *al ken lo yochlu bnei Yisrael* — "therefore the children of Israel shall not eat."

### Gemara Challenge

The *Gemara* immediately presses the obvious difficulty: if something was said to *bnei Noach* and not repeated at *Har Sinai*, why should the absence of repetition mean it shifts to apply *only* to Jews? On the contrary — *aderaba* — one might argue the opposite: since it was not repeated at *Sinai*, perhaps it was given only to *bnei Noach* and not to *bnei Yisrael* at all.

### Higher Kedusha

The *Gemara* rejects this possibility by invoking a principle seen elsewhere: *leika mida d'l'Yisrael sharei u'l'Akum assur* — there is nothing that could be permitted to a Jew and forbidden to a non-Jew. Since Jews move toward a higher level of *kedusha*, the system cannot permit to Jews what it forbids to non-Jews. If something was forbidden to *bnei Noach*, it must equally — or even more stringently — be forbidden to Jews. Therefore, rather than concluding that unrepeated laws apply only to *bnei Noach* and not to us, we say the reverse: they apply to *Yisrael* as well.

---

## Exceptions & Mechila

### Yefat Toar

The *Gemara* now tests this principle against apparent counter-examples. The first is *yefat to'ar* — the beautiful captive taken in war. The *Torah* permits this for *bnei Yisrael*, yet it had previously been categorized under the prohibition of *gezel* (theft) for *bnei Noach*. Is this not a case of something forbidden to them and permitted to us?

The *Gemara* responds: *hasam mishum d'lav bnei kibush ninhu* — the mechanism of conquest, whereby captured territory legally becomes the possession of the conquering nation, applies to the wars of *bnei Yisrael* but not to the wars of gentiles. For Israel, the conquest creates a legal transformation of ownership; for non-Jews, that mechanism does not operate, and therefore what would otherwise be *gezel* remains *gezel* for them. The distinction is not in the underlying concept but in the absence of the operative mechanism. One might note — and indeed this was raised — that the *Torah* itself contains explicit verses indicating that God gave certain territories to various nations. This makes the *Gemara*'s answer difficult to fully resolve, and it must be left as a tension in the text.

### Pruta & Mechila

The second challenge concerns theft of less than a *perutah* — the minimum monetary unit. The *Gemara* had previously stated that *bnei Noach* are liable even for stealing less than a *perutah*, whereas for Jews such an act does not constitute actionable theft. Is this not something forbidden to them and permitted to us?

The *Gemara* answers: *hasam mishum d'lav bnei mechila ninhu* — the difference is not a fundamental legal distinction in the law of theft but rather a function of *mechila*, forgiveness or remission. In practice, Jews tend to forgive such trivial amounts, and once the victim has forgiven the offense, the act retroactively loses its character as *gezel*. For non-Jews, this dynamic of *mechila* does not similarly operate, and therefore the theft retains its prohibited character.

*Rashi* reads this somewhat differently, emphasizing that even Jews are commanded on *gezel*, and that the smaller amount fails to register as *gezel* only because people naturally forgive it. The underlying prohibition is the same; what changes is whether the practical reality of *mechila* transforms the nature of the act.

### Tosafot Analysis

*Tosafot* raises a probing question: given that these apparent exceptions have been explained away, why does the *Gemara* not also raise the issue of *hashchatat zera* related to *peru u'rivu* as a similar counter-example? *Tosafot* also notes a more pressing case — abortion, where a *ben Noach* is liable for killing a fetus (treating it as full *retzichah*), whereas for a Jew there is an exemption from the death penalty and the act is not classified as murder. Is this not a genuine case of something more stringently forbidden to them than to us?

*Tosafot*'s resolution is that the principle only prohibits something being *fully permitted* to Jews while being forbidden to non-Jews. As long as the act is not completely permitted — even if it is less weighty for Jews than for non-Jews — the principle is not violated. The *Gemara* therefore does not raise abortion as a challenge, because abortion is not actually *permitted* to Jews; it is merely categorized differently.

---

## Abortion & Murder

### Tosafot Questions

The question *Tosafot* raises is: why does the *Gemara* not ask about abortion as a counter-example to the rule that nothing forbidden to *bnei Noach* can be permitted to *Yisrael*? For *bnei Noach*, killing a fetus is considered murder and punishable by death. For Jews, the fetus does not have the status of a full life in terms of capital liability, and one who destroys a fetus is *patur* from execution. Is this not a case where something is forbidden to them yet effectively permitted to us?

### Not Fully Permitted

*Tosafot* answers this by distinguishing between degrees of prohibition. The rule that nothing can be forbidden to non-Jews and permitted to Jews does not require that both groups be equally liable; it only requires that the act not be *fully mutar* for Jews. *Tosafot* draws a parallel to *Shabbat*: gentiles are forbidden to rest on a *Shabbat* day, and for Jews it is a *mitzvah* — yet that is not a violation of the principle, because *mitzvah* represents an elevation of obligation, not a relaxation into permissibility.

Similarly, *Tosafot* argues that abortion is not truly *mutar* for Jews. The act remains *assur* — it is simply that the classification and the consequences differ. This resolution implies that the prohibition on abortion operates at a *d'Oraisa* level, since if it were only a *d'Rabbanan* prohibition, it would not adequately resolve the conceptual difficulty. If abortion were fundamentally permitted by *Torah* law and only restricted by rabbinic decree, one could still say that the *Torah* itself placed Jews in a more permissive position than non-Jews — which is precisely what the principle rules out.

The most stringent position in modern *halachic* literature on abortion is that of Rav Moshe Feinstein, who characterizes it as *retzichah* — murder — though without the accompanying death penalty. This formulation is consistent with *Tosafot*'s framework: the act is *assur d'Oraisa*, a serious biblical prohibition, even though it does not carry capital punishment for Jews. One should note that another *Tosafot*, discussing this issue in a different context, uses the word *mutar* rather than *patur* — and Rav Moshe Feinstein found this so untenable that he concluded it must be a *ta'us sofer*, a scribal error, and that the text must have originally read *patur*.

### Mother's Life Priority

*Tosafot* raises one further difficulty. The *Gemara* in the chapter of *Ben Sorer u'Moreh* rules that once the baby's head has emerged, one may not sacrifice the infant's life to save the mother, since one may not set aside one life in favor of another. However, before the head emerges, the *halacha* permits — indeed requires — performing an abortion to save the mother's life. In this case, the act is not merely *patur* for Jews; it is an actual *mitzvah*. Yet for *bnei Noach*, who treat the fetus as a full life, performing an abortion would constitute *retzichah* even to save the mother. Here, then, is a genuine case where something is a *mitzvah* for *Yisrael* and forbidden for *bnei Noach*.

*Tosafot* responds that when an act is a *mitzvah* for Jews, it does not fall under the rubric of the problematic principle at all. The principle addresses what is *mutar* for Jews and *assur* for non-Jews; a *mitzvah* represents an entirely different category — not leniency but obligation. We are not comparing a relaxation with a prohibition; we are comparing a divine command with a prohibition. These are incommensurable, and the principle does not speak to such cases.

### Ranking Even in Murder

*Tosafot* adds a further observation: even granting that *bnei Noach* treat abortion as *retzichah*, it is possible that even for them, saving the mother's life might be permitted. Even within the category of murder, one may recognize rankings — acknowledging that a fetus, though classified as a living person whose killing constitutes *retzichah*, is nonetheless not a fully formed life in the same sense as the mother. The *heter* of *rodef* — the permission to kill a pursuer to save a victim — seems to apply to *bnei Noach* as well, as an earlier passage in the *Gemara* suggests. *Tosafot* therefore entertains the possibility that even for non-Jews, choosing the mother's life over the fetus's life may be permitted, or even obligatory, notwithstanding the classification of the act as *retzichah* in principle.

---

## Milah & Avraham

### Milah Exception

The *Gemara* now examines *milah* as a potential counter-example to the general principle. *Milah* was given to *bnei Noach* — specifically, as it says, *v'atah et briti tishmor*, "and you shall keep My covenant," referring to *Avraham*, who is considered a representative of *bnei Noach* — and it was repeated at *Har Sinai*, where the verse states *u'vayom hashemini yimol b'sar orlato*, "on the eighth day the flesh of his foreskin shall be circumcised." According to the principle, something given to *bnei Noach* and repeated at *Sinai* should apply to both. Yet *milah* applies only to Jews, not to non-Jews generally. How does this fit?

### Repetition for Detail

The *Gemara* answers: *hahu l'mishrei Shabbat hu d'ata* — the verse in the *Torah* that mentions *milah* at *Sinai* is not there to repeat or re-command the *mitzvah* itself; its purpose is solely to teach that *milah* overrides *Shabbat* (*bayom*, "on the day," meaning even on *Shabbat*). Since the repetition serves only to convey a legal detail — a *prat* about the *mitzvah* — it does not qualify as a genuine repetition in the sense that would bring it under the principle. True repetition, for purposes of this rule, means that the *mitzvah* was re-stated at *Sinai* for its own sake, as a *tzivui*. A repetition that exists only to teach a subsidiary *halacha* does not count.

This approach effectively narrows what qualifies as "repeated at *Har Sinai*," providing a mechanism by which the *Gemara* can consistently maintain its structural principle while accounting for all the apparent exceptions.

### Peru V'Rivu

The *Gemara* then raises the case of *peru u'rivu* — the commandment to procreate. This was originally given to *bnei Noach*, as the verse says *v'atem peru u'revu*; and it appears to have been repeated at *Sinai*, since *Moshe* told the people *shuvu lachem l'ohaleichem* — "return to your tents" — which the *Gemara* reads as a re-issuance of the *mitzvah* of *peru u'rivu*. Yet *peru u'rivu* applies only to Jews, not to *bnei Noach*. This is another apparent violation of the principle.

The *Gemara*'s resolution in this case is different. The statement *shuvu lachem l'ohaleichem* was not an independent repetition of the *mitzvah* of *peru u'rivu* at all. Rather, it served a technical legal purpose: to lift a temporary prohibition. Leading up to *matan Torah*, the Jewish people were forbidden from conjugal relations — *al tigshu el isha*. Since a decree enacted by a *beit din* through formal enactment requires an explicit act to reverse it — *kol davar she'be'minyan tzarich minyan acher le'hatiro* — *Moshe*'s statement served as that explicit retraction. The verse was functioning as a cancellation of the earlier edict, not as a new statement of the *mitzvah* of *peru u'rivu*. Therefore, it does not qualify as a repetition of the *mitzvah* at *Sinai*.

*Tosafot* notes a significant difficulty in this entire discussion: why should we assume that *peru u'rivu* does not apply to *bnei Noach* at all? The verses in *Bereishit* in which God commands *pru u'revu* seem to apply to all humanity, and the fact that the obligation is not listed among the *sheva mitzvot* might simply reflect that the *sheva mitzvot* lists prohibitions rather than positive commands (*kum asei*). However, *Tosafot* points out that *peru u'rivu* carries within it a prohibition dimension as well: one who is commanded in *peru u'rivu* is thereby commanded not to destroy seed (*hashchatat zera*), which is a *shev v'al ta'aseh* — an act of omission constituting a violation. If *peru u'rivu* applied to *bnei Noach*, *hashchatat zera* would have been enumerated among the *sheva mitzvot*. Since it is not, *Tosafot* infers that *peru u'rivu* was not given to *bnei Noach*. Some *Rishonim* dispute this and hold that *bnei Noach* are indeed commanded in *peru u'rivu*, but this *Gemara* assumes they are not — a conclusion that is admittedly difficult to reconcile with a plain reading of the *pesukim*.

### Avraham's Line

The *Gemara* offers an alternative and more satisfying answer specifically for *milah*: *mila me'ikara l'Avraham hu d'ka mazhar lei Rachmana* — *milah* was never given to all of *bnei Noach* in the first place. It was given exclusively to *Avraham* and his descendants: *v'atah et briti tishmor ata v'zar'acha acharecha l'dorotam* — you and your seed after you. The word *inshi achareini lo* — nobody else was included. Since *milah* was given not to *bnei Noach* as a category but only to a subset — *Avraham*'s specific line — it was never subject to the general principle.

This raises an interesting conceptual question: when Jews today perform *bris milah*, which *tzivui* are they fulfilling — the command given to *Avraham*, or the verse that appears later in the *Torah* specifying the eighth day? This *Gemara* seems to imply that the primary source is the command to *Avraham*, which carries forward specifically through his designated line.

The *Gemara* then asks: if *milah* belongs to *Avraham* and his seed, does that include *bnei Yishmael*? The *Gemara* answers with the verse *ki v'Yitzchak yikarei lcha zara* — "for through Yitzchak shall your seed be called." *Yishmael*, though biologically *Avraham*'s son, is not the designated *zera* of *Avraham* in this covenantal sense. The *Gemara* then asks about *bnei Esav*: the answer is *b'Yitzchak v'lo kol Yitzchak* — within *Yitzchak*, but not all of *Yitzchak*'s descendants are included. The covenant narrows further to *Yaakov*, so that the family of *Avraham Yitzchak v'Yaakov* — the ancestral line of *Bnei Yisrael* — constitutes the intended recipients of the covenant of *milah*.

### Keturah Question

Rav Oshaya challenges this resolution by asking: if *milah* applies only to *Avraham*'s line through *Yitzchak* and *Yaakov*, why did *Avraham* circumcise the children of *Keturah*? *Rashi* understands this question as referring to *Avraham*'s actual children from *Keturah* — not their descendants as a nation — and the assumption is that *Avraham* did in fact circumcise them.

### Eternal vs. Temporary

Rabbi Yosi b'Rabbi Avin and Rabbi Yosi b'Rabbi Chanina answer: the verse *es briti hafar* indicates that at the moment of the original command, *Avraham* was personally required to circumcise all his children then living. This was an immediate, one-time obligation — "you shall observe My covenant" applied to *Avraham*'s household at that time. The eternal, ongoing *mitzvah* applying to future generations, however, is limited to the line of *Yitzchak*. There is thus a distinction between the temporary scope of the original command — which covered all of *Avraham*'s sons at that moment — and the permanent covenantal obligation that carries forward only through the Abrahamic family narrowly defined.

---

## Adam & Meat Eating

### Adam Vegetarian

The *Gemara* now turns to a different subject. Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: *Adam HaRishon lo hutar lo basar le'achila* — *Adam HaRishon* was not permitted to eat meat. The *Gemara* derives this from the verse in *Bereishit* which says that all vegetation shall be for food — for you and for all the animals — implying that you and the animals alike share in the vegetation, but you do not get to eat the animals: *v'lo chayat ha'aretz lachem*.

It is worth noting that *Rashi* interprets this *Gemara* more narrowly: the prohibition was not on eating meat as such, but on killing an animal for the purpose of eating it. According to *Rashi*, if an animal died on its own, *Adam* would have been permitted to eat it — and it is precisely for that reason that the prohibition of *ever min hachai* needed to be stated, since without it one might eat a limb from a living animal. But the straightforward reading of the *Gemara*'s statement — and the *pshat* of the verse — is that *Adam* was not permitted to eat meat at all. On this reading, the commandment of *ever min hachai* would belong to *Noach*'s generation, as an earlier opinion in the *Gemara* had suggested.

### Meat Permitted

When *bnei Noach* arrived — that is, with the generation of *Noach* — meat was permitted: *keyerek esev natati lachem et hakol* — "like the green herb I have given you everything." Just as you eat vegetation, so now everything, including animals, is given to you for food.

### Ever Min Hachai Details

The *Gemara* then derives the scope of *ever min hachai* from the verse *ach basar benafsho damo lo socheilu* — "but flesh with its life-force, its blood, you shall not eat." This establishes the prohibition of *ever min hachai* for *bnei Noach*. The *Gemara* then asks whether this prohibition might extend even to *sheratzim* — rodents and creeping things. From the word *ach* — "but" — which serves as a limiting term, the *Gemara* derives that *sheratzim* are excluded. The reason is offered by Rabbi Huna: *mi shedamo choluk mibesaro* — an animal to which the prohibition applies is one in which blood and flesh are distinguishable from each other; *yatzeu sheratzim she'ein damam choluk mibesaram* — rodents are excluded because their blood is not seen as distinct from their flesh.

---

## Mastery & Serpent

### Fish & Birds Work

The *Gemara* raises a challenge based on the verse *uredu bidgat hayam* — "and have dominion over the fish of the sea." The word *uredu*, "have dominion," might seem to imply that *Adam* was permitted to eat fish. The *Gemara* responds: *lo limlacha* — no, the dominion refers to using them for labor. The *Gemara* then asks with evident irony: can fish actually perform labor? The answer given is yes — and an example offered is a question posed by Rechava: if one were to harness a goat and a *shivuta* (a type of fish) together to pull a plow, would that constitute a violation of *kilayim*? The question itself presupposes that fish could in principle be used to do work.

The same challenge is raised from the verse *u've'of hashamayim* — "and over the birds of the heaven." Birds too are said to be under *Adam*'s dominion, which might imply permission to eat them. Again the *Gemara* responds: *lo limlacha* — for labor. And again the question: can birds do labor? Here the *Gemara* answers affirmatively with more confidence: Rabba bar Rav Huna describes using ducks or roosters to thresh grain. This occasions a brief discussion involving Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Yehuda, who maintains that an animal's right to eat while working depends on whether it performs labor with all four of its limbs — raising the question of what to make of an animal that works only with its lower limbs.

The verse *b'chol chayah haromeset al ha'aretz* — mastery over all the wild creatures that creep on the earth — is then cited, and the *Gemara* explains that this phrase serves specifically to include the *nachash*, the serpent. This introduces a *Baraita* from Rabbi Shimon ben Menasia.

### Serpent Servant

Rabbi Shimon ben Menasia laments: *chaval al shamash gadol she'avad min ha'olam* — what a loss, that such a great servant has been lost to the world. Before the serpent sinned, it walked upright on legs. Had it not been for the serpent's role in the sin of *Adam*, it could have served as an extraordinary attendant. Rabbi Shimon ben Menasia describes the lost potential in vivid terms: every individual Jew could have had two fine serpents to serve him — one sent to the north and one to the south — to bring precious stones and gems. And furthermore, since the serpent moved along the ground, it would overturn the soil beneath it with a strap attached to its tail, providing usable earth for one's garden. This passage is sometimes read as containing a degree of gentle humor: the greatest creature that was lost would have fetched the most precious jewels in the world — and also turned our garden soil.

### Meat from Heaven

This leads into a challenge from a *Baraita*: Rabbi Yehuda ben Teima stated that *Adam HaRishon* was reclining in *Gan Eden* like a king at a banquet, with heavenly angels roasting meat for him and filtering wine. The serpent saw all this splendor and was seized with jealousy — and this was the motivation for seducing *Chava*. But does this not contradict the ruling that *Adam* was not permitted to eat meat?

The *Gemara* resolves the contradiction: *hasam b'vasar hayored min hashamayim* — the meat at that banquet had not come from a living animal; it was a miraculous meat that descended directly from heaven. The *Gemara* then pauses to ask whether such a thing is possible — *mi ika basar hayored min hashamayim?* — and answers affirmatively with the story of Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta. While traveling, he was confronted by roaring lions that threatened to devour him. He recited the verse *hakefirim sho'agim lateref* — "the young lions roar for prey" — as a kind of prayer. In response, two large portions of meat descended from heaven. The lions ate one and left the other. Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta brought the remaining portion to the *beit medrash* and asked whether it was *tahor* or *tamei* — kosher or otherwise. The scholars ruled: *ein davar tamei yored min hashamayim* — nothing *tamei* descends from heaven.

Rabbi Zeira then posed the question to Rabbi Abahu: what if something in the shape of a donkey were to descend from heaven — would it be permitted? Rabbi Abahu responded with a tone suggesting the question was self-evidently unnecessary: since nothing *tamei* ever descends from heaven, even if it descended in the form of a donkey, it would be kosher. This brief exchange — combining the miraculous with questions of *kashrut* — gives rise to a brief but illuminating digression touching on the contemporary issue of laboratory-grown meat, which some *poskim* address by beginning with this very *sugya* about meat whose origin bypasses the life of an actual animal.

---

## Blasphemy Setup

### Witnesses Testify

The *Gemara* now returns to the major topic of the *Mishna*: the laws governing blasphemy (*birkat Hashem*). Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha had described the court procedure for trying a blasphemer. The witnesses testify using a euphemism — *yake Yose es Yosi*, "may Yose smite Yosi" — substituting the name "Yosi" in place of God's actual name, so that the explosive content of the curse is never directly repeated in court until the very end, when the final testimony must be delivered with God's name stated explicitly.

### Four-Letter Name

Rav Achai bar Yaakov teaches: *eino chayav ad sheyivarech shem bein arba osios* — one is not liable for the death penalty unless the blasphemy was uttered using God's four-letter name, the *Yud-Kei-Vav-Kei*. A *kinui* — a substitute name of God, such as *El* or *Elohim* — would not suffice to incur capital liability, even if it might constitute a lesser transgression.

The *Gemara* asks whether this principle is even necessary to state, since the *Mishna*'s use of the example *yake Yose es Yosi* — where the name *Yosi* carries four letters — already implies it. The *Gemara* responds that one might have thought *Yosi* was simply chosen arbitrarily as a convenient placeholder, with no implication about the four-letter name. Rav Achai bar Yaakov therefore makes explicit that the four-letter name is required. An alternative reading of Rav Achai bar Yaakov's statement is that from *yake Yose es Yosi* we learn that even the four-letter name — as opposed to the longer expanded name of 42 letters — is sufficient. *Rashi* explains that the *shem hamiforash* refers to the 42-letter name, and the question was whether the four-letter name alone suffices. The *Gemara* concludes that it does.

### Standing Requirement

After all the testimony has been heard and the verdict reached, everyone who was present stood when God's name was finally uttered. Where do we derive the obligation to stand?

Rav Yehuda bar Ami derives it from the story of *Ehud* and *Eglon*, King of Moav. The verse says: *vayomer Ehud dvar Elohim li eilecha* — "Ehud said, I have a word of God for you." *Vayakom me'al hakisay* — and Eglon rose from his throne. From here the *Gemara* constructs a *kal vachomer*: if *Eglon*, a non-Jew, who knew God only by a *kinui* — the name *Elohim* — nonetheless stood up when God's name was enunciated, then surely a Jew, upon hearing God's explicit name, is obligated to stand.

This is a striking *Gemara*. One might have assumed from the context of the *Mishna* that the standing was connected specifically to the horror of hearing God being cursed. But this derivation suggests that the obligation to stand is connected simply to the enunciation of God's name — which would seem to imply a much broader requirement to stand whenever God's name is articulated. Yet we do not, in practice, maintain such a rule. It is worth noting, then, that the *Gemara* derives this *din* specifically from the context of blasphemy proceedings.

---

## Keriah & Tears

### Ravshakeh Story

The *Gemara* then asks the source for *keriah* — the tearing of garments — when one hears God's name being blasphemed. The verse states that *Elyakim ben Chilkiyahu*, *Shevna the scribe*, and *Yoach ben Asaf* came to King Chizkiyahu *keruei begadim* — with torn garments — after hearing Ravshakeh, the envoy of the King of Assyria, curse and blaspheme God. They then reported the words of Ravshakeh to the king, and the verse records that *hamelech Chizkiyahu vayikra et begadav* — the king also tore his garments. This establishes the practice of *keriah* upon hearing blasphemy.

### Gezera Shava

The *Gemara* then asks how we know that the tear made for blasphemy is never sewn up — as is the rule with *keriah* over the death of a parent. The connection is made through a *gezeirah shavah* by Rabbi Abahu. The verse here uses the word *keruei vegdeihem* — "with torn garments" — and an analogous scene involving *Elisha*, who tore his garments upon the departure of *Eliyahu* in the fiery chariot. There, the verse says *vayikra'em lishnayim kera'im* — "he tore them into two tears." The *Gemara* notes: we already know from *vayikra'em lishnayim* that he made tears; why does the verse add the word *kera'im*? *Melamed shehem keruim le'olam* — to teach that they remain torn forever, never to be sewn up.

Since in the *Elisha* narrative the tear is effectively a *keriah* over a father-figure — *Eliyahu* in relation to *Elisha* — the *gezeirah shavah* links the unsewn tear of *keriah* over a parent to the *keriah* performed upon hearing blasphemy. Both are permanent and may not be repaired.

---

## Keriah Conditions

### Firsthand Secondhand

The *Gemara* now details who is obligated to perform *keriah* and under what conditions. A *Baraita* teaches: *echad hashomeia* — both one who directly hears the blasphemy, *ve'echad shomeia mipi shomeia* — and one who hears it secondhand — are obligated to tear their garments. We can infer this from the court proceeding itself, where the *dayanim* heard the blasphemy only through the testimony of the witnesses and still performed *keriah*.

However, the witnesses themselves are not required to repeat their *keriah*: *shekevar kare'u besha'ah sheshame'u* — they already tore their garments at the time they first heard the offense. The *Gemara* presses: so what if they already tore once — they are hearing it again now, so should they not tear again? The answer comes from the verse itself: it was *hamelech Chizkiyahu* who tore — implying that those who reported the incident to him, and who had already torn, did not tear again. This establishes the principle: once *keriah* has been performed for a particular incident of blasphemy, one need not tear again upon hearing it repeated in the context of testimony. But if the same individual were to blaspheme on a different occasion, *keriah* would again be required.

### Jew & Explicit

Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel: *hashomeia azkarah mipi oved kochavim eino chayav likroa* — one who hears a *kinui* — a substitute name of God — from a non-Jew is not obligated to perform *keriah*. The question is raised: why then did they tear their garments over Ravshakeh? The *Gemara* answers: *Yisrael mumar haya* — Ravshakeh was not a gentile; he was a Jewish apostate.

Rav Yehuda further states in the name of Shmuel: *ein korin ela al shem hameyuchad bilvad* — *keriah* is performed only when God's four-letter, explicit name is used; a *kinui* does not trigger the obligation.

### Rabbi Chiya View

Rabbi Chiya disputes both of Shmuel's rulings. He states: *hashomea azkara bazman hazeh eino chayav likroa* — in our time, one who hears God's name invoked in the context of cursing is not obligated to tear, *she'ilmalei atah omer kein, nitmalu kol hab'gadim kera'im* — because if you were to rule otherwise, our garments would be filled with tears.

The *Gemara* analyzes this statement. If Rabbi Chiya is speaking of Jews blaspheming constantly, that is implausible. The context must therefore be non-Jews cursing God — and if we are speaking of non-Jews, and they are doing so constantly, they could hardly be using God's explicit four-letter name, since non-Jews do not generally know or pronounce it. The only coherent context is non-Jews using a *kinui*. Yet Rabbi Chiya exempts us from *keriah* only because it is *bazman hazeh* — in our time, where it is so prevalent. The implication is that *b'ikara* — in principle — even hearing a non-Jew curse God using a *kinui* would have required *keriah*. This is the exact opposite of Shmuel's position, which required both a Jewish blasphemer and God's explicit name. Rabbi Chiya's position requires neither, though the practical exemption in our time renders the distinction moot for the common case.

---

## Second & Third Witness

### Reish Lakish

The *Mishna* describes the court procedure: the second witness says *af ani kamohu* — "I also heard the same as him" — and the third witness says the same. This raises a significant legal question about the validity of testimony.

Reish Lakish derives from this procedure a ruling about testimony in general: *af ani kamohu kasher b'dinei mamonot u'v'dinei nefashot* — technically, saying "me too" — i.e., affirming the content of a previous witness's testimony without independently restating it — is valid testimony in both monetary cases and capital cases. This is the *d'Oraisa* standard. The rabbis normally require a more explicit and independent statement of testimony from each witness. But how do we know that "me too" works *d'Oraisa*? *Ve'hacha keivan d'lo efshar okmuha ad'raita* — here, since we cannot ask the second witness to repeat the curse in full — doing so would require re-uttering the blasphemy, which is itself deeply problematic — the *Gemara* allows the testimony to stand on its minimum *Torah*-valid form. *De'i salka daitach pasul* — if you were to think that "me too" is wholly invalid as testimony, we would have a situation where the perpetrator escapes execution simply because we cannot ask the witnesses to repeat a curse. Clearly this cannot be the intent of the law. Therefore the *Gemara* concludes that "me too" is technically valid *d'Oraisa*, even if rabbinic practice generally demands more explicit testimony.

### Me Too Testimony

The validity of *af ani kamohu* as testimony thus has implications beyond the specific case of blasphemy. It establishes that the minimum *Torah* standard for testimony does not require each witness to independently narrate the full content of what they observed, provided the first witness has already done so and the subsequent witness affirms it. Rabbinic enactment raises this standard, but the underlying *d'Oraisa* rule is as stated.

### Third Witness

The requirement that the third witness also say *af ani kamohu* reflects the position of Rabbi Akiva, who holds that where there are three witnesses and one is found invalid, the entire testimony is invalidated — *stama k'Rabbi Akiva d'makish gimmel l'bet*. Rabbi Akiva applies an equation between a group of three witnesses and a group of two, such that disqualification of any member disqualifies the whole. This is why the court takes care to elicit testimony from all the witnesses present: once all three have testified formally, if any one of them is later found to be invalid, the consequences of that invalidity — namely, the invalidation of the entire testimony — follow accordingly.

---

## Avoda Zara Intro

### Classic Forms

The *Gemara* now transitions to the *Mishna* dealing with *avoda zara* — worship of foreign gods. The *Mishna* enumerates the acts that constitute *avoda zara* punishable by death. These are the four classic forms of divine worship: *shechita* (slaughter/sacrifice), *haktara* (burning incense), *nisuch* (pouring libations), and *hishtachavaya* (prostration). These four acts constitute the normative forms of service in the *Beit HaMikdash*, and performing any of them before a foreign deity is *chayav misa*.

### Verbal Acceptance

Beyond these four acts, the *Mishna* adds a fifth category: *hamekabelo alav l'eloah* — one who accepts a foreign god as his deity. This is highly significant. *Avoda zara* typically connotes a physical act of worship, yet here the *Mishna* rules that a purely verbal declaration of acceptance — "you are my god" — also constitutes *avoda zara* punishable by death.

*Rashi* notes a further distinction within this category: *mekabelo alav l'eloah* may refer to acceptance even when not in the presence of the idol, while the phrase *ve'omer lo eli ata* — "and says to it, you are my god" — refers to addressing the idol directly in its presence. These are two distinct manifestations of the same underlying offense.

This has considerable historical and halachic importance. During forced conversions in the medieval period, Jews were often compelled to make verbal declarations of acceptance of another religion without necessarily performing any physical act of worship. The *Mishna*'s ruling here establishes that such a verbal acceptance alone falls within the category of *avoda zara*.

### Adoration Acts

The *Mishna* then delineates acts that are prohibited but do not reach the threshold of capital punishment. These are acts of adoration — *gifeuf* (hugging), *nishuk* (kissing), *nichbad* (sweeping before the idol), *marbetz* (settling the dust), *rachitza* (washing the idol), *sacha* (anointing with oil), *malbish* (clothing it), and *man'il* (putting shoes on it). All of these are transgressive — *over b'lo ta'aseh* — but the negative prohibition violated is *v'lo ta'aseh k'ma'aseihem*, which *Rashi* reads as a general prohibition against engaging in acts that imitate or pay homage to idol worship, even when those acts fall short of formal *avoda*.

### Vows & Oaths

Similarly, one who vows in the name of a foreign god or swears by its name transgresses a *lo ta'aseh* — *shem elohim acherim lo tazkiru, lo yishama al picha* — "the names of foreign gods shall not be mentioned; they shall not be heard upon your lips." Taking an oath or vow in the name of another deity violates this prohibition, though it does not constitute *avoda zara* in the technical sense and is not punishable by death.

### Unique Worship

Finally, the *Mishna* addresses unique or idiosyncratic forms of worship specific to a given idol. Two examples are given. The first is *Ba'al Pe'or*: one who exposes himself and defecates before *Ba'al Pe'or* — which was apparently that idol's established form of worship — is liable to the death penalty, *zo hi avodato*, because this is the manner in which it is worshiped, however degrading the act might appear in any other context. The second is *Markolis*: a deity associated with travel and roadways, worshiped by throwing a stone onto a configuration of three stones. *Hazorek even l'markolis* — one who throws a stone to *Markolis* — is liable, again because this constitutes the established form of worship for that deity.

The principle that emerges is: any act that constitutes the genuine, established form of worship for a particular idol renders one liable for *avoda zara*, regardless of whether that act would ordinarily seem worshipful or even degrading. Similarly, the four classic forms of worship (*shechita*, *haktara*, *nisuch*, *hishtachavaya*) render one liable before any idol, even if that is not the specific form of worship associated with it — because these are the normative forms of divine service. All other acts, however intimate or deferential, constitute at most negative prohibitions, not capital *avoda zara*.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 61

## Avodah Zarah Intro

### Overview & Acceptance

The daf begins on 61b, immediately following the *mishna*, as the Gemara turns to the topic of *avodah zarah* — one of the cardinal offenses punishable by *sekilah*. Before enumerating the classic forms of worship, the Gemara makes a striking preliminary observation: the act of accepting a foreign deity as one's god is itself considered an *avodah*. One might have supposed that this falls only under the prohibition of *lo yihiyeh lecha elohim acherim* — the general negative commandment against acknowledging other gods — but not under the specific category of *avodah*, of worship. Nevertheless, the Gemara treats it as a genuine act of *avodah zarah* in its own right.

The generic term *ovedet* — the classic or paradigmatic form of worship — denotes both what the worshippers of a given deity themselves regard as the central act of veneration, and those forms of worship that are universally recognized as classic, particularly those performed in the *Beit HaMikdash*.

### Five Forms of Worship

The Gemara proceeds to clarify the *mishna*'s phrase *echad ha-oved*, asking what it encompasses. Rabbi Yirmiyah explains: whether one worships *kedarkah* — in the manner specific and natural to that deity — or whether one performs any of four additional acts, even if those acts are not the natural form of worship for that particular god, one is liable. Those four acts are *mezabeiach* (slaughtering), *maktir* (burning on the altar), *menaseiach* (libation), and *mishtachaveh* (prostration), and the liability applies *afilu shelo kedarkah* — even if this is not the deity's usual mode of worship.

The Gemara then notes that the act of throwing blood — *zerikat hadam* — was not separately listed. Abaye explains that this is subsumed under the category of *menaseiach*, since both involve the offering of a liquid substance upon the altar. The verse is adduced: *kol bal asich niskeihem midam* — "let me not pour their libations of blood" — confirming that the throwing of blood is included within the concept of libation. Conceptually, of course, the two are distinct: the libation is the offering of wine, while the throwing of blood is the climactic act of the animal sacrifice. Nevertheless, for purposes of this halachic enumeration, they are grouped together.

### Source & Derivation

The Gemara then asks: *minayin milei* — what is the scriptural source for this entire framework? A *baraita* is cited. The verse states *zoveach le'elohim yecharam bilti l'Hashem levado* — "one who slaughters to other gods shall be put under the ban, except only to God alone" (Shemot 22:19). The *baraita* proceeds through a careful derivation.

Had the verse said only *zoveach yecharam* — "one who slaughters shall be put under the ban" — one might have supposed it was referring merely to one who slaughters *kodshim* outside the *Beit HaMikdash*, the prohibition of *shechutei chutz*. The addition of *le'elohim* clarifies that the verse is speaking of one who slaughters to foreign gods — *avodah zarah*. Thus the base case is established: slaughtering to a foreign deity is prohibited and punishable.

But the verse goes on to say *bilti l'Hashem levado*. The *baraita* reads this phrase as a sweeping exclusivity clause: all acts of worship have been emptied out — reserved exclusively — for God. This phrase extends the prohibition beyond *zevichah* alone to include *maktir* (burning the fats), *menaseiach* (libation), and — through the inclusive force of the phrase — the throwing of blood as well. Rashi notes that the classic *avodot* performed in the *Beit HaMikdash* are *shechitah*, *kabbalat hadam*, *holachat hadam*, and *zerikat hadam*.
