One might ask why *kabbalah* and *holachah* are not included in the *baraita*'s enumeration. Rashi explains that no verse elsewhere in *Tanach* identifies *kabbalah* or *holachah* as acts of *avodah zarah*, whereas the other forms — slaughtering, burning, libation, and blood-throwing — do appear in other scriptural contexts as recognized modes of foreign worship. Rashi's formulation is thus an intersection: those acts that are classic to the *Beit HaMikdash* and that also appear in verses as recognized forms of *avodah zarah* are the ones that carry liability. As for *holachah* — even within the *Beit HaMikdash* context, it functions more as a preparatory step than as an act of worship in its own right, and accordingly it carries only a *lav* but not the death penalty.

The extension to *nisuach* through outside verses fits naturally with the broader halachic world of *stam yeinam* and *yayin nesech*, where libation to a foreign deity is a well-established category. Rashi characterizes this set as an intersection of what is classic *avodat pnim* and what appears in verses as classic *avodah zarah* — and once included, these acts carry the full prohibition even when performed for a deity to which this particular form of worship is not customary.

## Paradigm Debate

### Counterfactual Setup

Having established the basic framework, the Gemara now poses a sustained counterfactual: why is *zevichah* — slaughtering — the paradigm that defines the general category, with *hishtachavah* treated as a separate special case? Why not reverse the structure and make *hishtachavah* the general category?

The Gemara first explains how *hishtachavah* enters the picture at all. The verse from Devarim — *vayelech vaya'avod elohim acherim vayishtachu lahem* — "he went and worshipped other gods and prostrated to them" — establishes that *hishtachavah* is an act of *avodah zarah*. Unlike slaughtering, burning, or libation, prostration is not a formal act of worship within the *Beit HaMikdash* in the same technical halachic sense, yet it is universally recognized as a form of reverence for the divine. The subsequent verse in that passage — *ve'hotzeisa es ha'ish hahu ... el she'arecha* — specifying execution — tells us that prostrating before a foreign deity incurs the death penalty.

The *baraita* then frames the structural principle: *zevichah*, it says, was among the general class of worships, and it was singled out — *yatzas* — to become the paradigm, *liddon al haklal*, to define the set. The singling-out is purposive: just as *zevichah* is an *avodat pnim* — an act of worship within the *Beit HaMikdash* — and carries the death penalty, so too any act that shares those characteristics is included in the set defined by the paradigm. Forms of adoration such as hugging, kissing, or putting on the shoes of an idol are thereby excluded — they are not *avodat pnim* and the verse *zoveach* limits the class to acts with that character.

*Hishtachavah*, by contrast, exits to stand alone — *yatzas hishtachavah liddon b'atzmah* — as a separately enumerated exception. And then there is the third category: *avodat kedarkah*, the specific form of worship particular to that deity, derived from the verse *eicha ya'avdu hagoyim ha'eileh et eloheihem* — "how do these nations worship their gods?" — which extends liability to the unique worship of each particular idol even when it resembles none of the above.

Now Rabba bar Rav Chanan poses the question to Abaye directly: why not invert the structure? Let *hishtachavah* define the general class — since it is broad and non-specific, encompassing any act of respectful reverence — and let *zevichah* be the exceptional case, singled out to teach something specific about the act of slaughtering alone. If *hishtachavah* were the general class, the class would include every form of adoration, making the set much larger.

### Machshavim Debate

The Gemara considers what *zevichah* would then be needed to teach, if *hishtachavah* were already the general paradigm. The answer proposed is the principle of *machshavim me'avodah le'avodah* — the case where one slaughters an animal not as the act of worship itself, but with the intent to use the blood afterward as the act of worship. In other words: one slaughters an animal for the purpose of throwing its blood before a foreign deity, where the *zevichah* is preparatory and the *zerikah* is the intended act of worship.

This scenario has a direct parallel in the laws of *kodshim*: one who slaughters an animal with intent to perform an act — such as throwing the blood — at the wrong time renders the sacrifice *pigul*. Does the same logic apply to *avodah zarah*? If one slaughters an animal for the purpose of using its blood in *avodah zarah*, is the animal thereby forbidden in benefit as an animal offered to a foreign deity?

Rabbi Yochanan says the animal is *assur* — forbidden — applying the same logic as *kodshim*: since the slaughter was performed with intent directed toward *avodah zarah*, the animal acquires the status of an offering to *avodah zarah*. Reish Lakish, however, says the animal is *mutar* — permitted — because the act of slaughter was not itself an act of worship; no worship was yet performed on the animal directly.

Tosafot adds a pointed remark: even according to Reish Lakish, who permits the animal, it remains forbidden for consumption — not because of its status as an offering, but because the person performing the slaughter was, in the course of doing so, engaged in *avodah zarah*, rendering his *shechitah* halachically invalid. Tosafot then entertains a further subtlety: perhaps the person only became an *apostate* through the very act of this *shechitah*, meaning he was not yet a *mumar* at the moment he began — *bishchitah zu na'aseh mumar* — in which case perhaps even eating might be permitted, since the *shechitah* was valid at its inception.

Returning to the structural question: if *hishtachavah* is the general paradigm, then the specific word *zoveach* in the verse needs to teach something — and according to Rabbi Yochanan, it need not teach *machshavim me'avodah le'avodah*, since he derives that principle from *kodshim* by analogy. The word *zoveach* would therefore be extra and without purpose under the counterfactual arrangement. This is exactly what the Gemara needs: if *zoveach* would be superfluous when *hishtachavah* is the paradigm, that proves the arrangement cannot work — and so the original structure, with *zevichah* as the paradigm, is confirmed.

But the Gemara presses: Rav Papa challenges that Rabbi Yochanan also needs the word *zoveach* — not to establish that the animal is forbidden (which he derives from *kodshim*), but to establish that the *person* is liable for the death penalty. The animal's status and the person's liability are separate questions. The verse *zoveach* may be needed to teach that even in this preparatory-slaughter scenario, the person has performed an act of *avodah zarah* and is *chayav misa*.

Rav Acha son of Rav Ika then pushes in the opposite direction: perhaps the person's liability is obvious even without a verse — from the case of one who prostrates before a mountain. The mountain itself is not rendered forbidden; a mountain cannot become prohibited, as we learn from the verse *eloheihem al he'harim v'lo he'harim eloheihem* — "their gods are on the mountains, but the mountains do not become their gods." Yet the person who worships the mountain is executed, as the verse makes clear. So the principle that an act can constitute *avodah zarah* even when the object itself is not rendered forbidden is established without need of an additional verse. The status of the object and the liability of the person are categorically independent. In that case, Reish Lakish too might not need the word *zoveach* for this purpose, making it genuinely superfluous.

### Mountain & Peor

The Gemara then returns to the question of what would have been done with the verse *eicha ya'avdu hagoyim ha'eileh et eloheihem* had *hishtachavah* been the general paradigm. In the actual structure, this verse serves to include the *avodat kedarkah* — the unique, natural form of worship particular to each deity. But if *hishtachavah* already served as the all-encompassing general class, what would this verse need to exclude?

The Gemara considers: perhaps the verse would exclude acts of worship that are degrading rather than honorable — for example, defecating before an ordinary idol that is normally worshipped through sacrifice. This is analogous to *poreh atzmo le'Peor*, the act of defecating before Ba'al Peor, which is indeed the natural mode of worship for that deity. But what if someone performed that act before an idol that is not Ba'al Peor?

The Gemara responds that this exclusion would be unnecessary — it already flows from the nature of *hishtachavah* itself. *Hishtachavah* as a class encompasses only *derech kavod* — acts performed in a manner of honor. By extension, *af kol derech kavod* — any act performed in a dignified, reverential manner — would be included, and acts of degradation would be automatically excluded. The verse *eicha ya'avdu* would then be redundant.

### Eichah Ye'avdu Phrase

The Gemara therefore revises the question: perhaps the verse *eicha ya'avdu* is needed instead to exclude *poreh atzmo le'Markolis*. Markolis is a deity worshipped by the throwing of stones — itself an act that has an element of degradation to it. One might reason that since Markolis too is worshipped through an act that involves a kind of dishonor, perhaps any degrading act performed before any deity would be included. The verse *eicha ya'avdu* comes to exclude this: only acts that constitute *derech kavod* are included in the general category, and an act of degradation before a deity not customarily worshipped that way is not included, even if such acts are done before *other* deities.

At this point, Rabbi Eliezer's teaching is introduced: how do we know that one who slaughters an animal *le'Markolis* — to a deity worshipped through stone-throwing, not through sacrifice — is liable? The verse *ve'lo yizbechu od et zivcheihem* — "they shall no longer slaughter their sacrifices" — which serves as the prohibition, and *zoveach le'elohim yecharam* as the source for the death penalty. The phrase *eicha ya'avdu* establishes the general prohibition, and where it does not naturally apply — i.e., where this is not the natural form of worship for that particular deity — these other verses fill in the liability. The interplay between the general class of *zevichah*, the special case of *hishtachavah*, and the *avodat kedarkah* derived from *eicha ya'avdu* produces the complete and internally consistent structure. This is what would have been lost had *hishtachavah* been made the paradigm.

## Liability Threshold

### Rabba's Question

A new sugya opens with a classic *tzarich iyun*: Rabba bar Rav Chanan raises an apparent contradiction between two *mishnayot*. The first *mishna* states that one is liable for *avodah zarah* only when one actually performs the worship — *oved in*, one who worships, yes, but one who merely says he intends to worship, no. Yet a second *mishna* later in the tractate states that one who says *e'evod* — "I will worship" — or *elech ve'e'evod* — "I will go and worship" — or *nelech vene'evod* — "let us go and worship" — is already liable, even before performing any act of worship. The two *mishnayot* appear to be in direct tension.

### Acceptance Principle

Before turning to the proposed resolutions, it is worth noting the background principle invoked by Tosafot. The Gemara elsewhere states that *machshavah tovah hakadosh baruch hu metzarfah lema'aseh* — God counts a good intention as equivalent to the deed when circumstances prevent its fulfillment — but *machshavah ra'ah ein hakadosh baruch hu metzarfah lema'aseh* — He does not count an evil intention as equivalent to the deed. The single exception to this rule is *avodah zarah*. Tosafot accordingly explains the second *mishna* by appeal to the principle that accepting a foreign god as one's god is itself an act of *avodah zarah* — the same principle introduced at the very outset of the Gemara. When a person, in response to incitement, says "I will go and worship," he is not merely expressing a future plan; he is, through that verbal commitment, accepting that deity as his god — and that acceptance is an independent act of *avodah zarah*, independent of any subsequent act of worship.

The first *mishna*, then, must be read as describing a case where the person specifically makes clear that he does not accept the deity as his god until the moment he actually performs the worship — *eini mekabla alai ela ba'avodah*. In that case, no acceptance occurs at the verbal stage, and no liability arises until the worship is performed.

### Rav Yosef's Answer

Rav Yosef offers a different resolution: the two *mishnayot* reflect a disagreement among *Tannaim*, not two aspects of a single consistent system. One *mishna* holds that a verbal commitment already constitutes liability; the other holds it does not. This is a *machlokes* between the *mishnayot*.

Rav Yosef then appends a further argument: the distinction he initially proposed between an individual being incited (*yachid hanisas*) and a group being incited (*rabbim hanisatin*) is the basis for the difference. When an individual is incited and says yes, we assume he will follow through — *lo mimlach veta'ei basrei* — and therefore he is already liable from the moment of his verbal agreement. When masses are incited, the outcome is less certain — *mimlachi velo ta'u basrei* — the group dynamic may produce second thoughts, and it is possible that despite their initial assent the masses will not ultimately follow through. Therefore the masses are not liable until actual worship occurs.

Rav Yosef grounds this distinction in the verse *lo tove lo velo tishma eilav* — the prohibition in Devarim commanding the person being incited not to consent and not to listen to the inciter. The inference is: *ha-avah v'shama — chayav* — if one did consent and did listen, one is already liable. This verse, Tosafot notes, marks a conceptual shift: the liability of the person who says yes in the context of incitement derives not merely from the acceptance of a foreign deity as a god, but from the unique halachic category of responding to a *meisit*. The verse specifically addresses the context of being incited, and within that context, verbal assent triggers liability.

### Abaye's Challenge

Abaye challenges Rav Yosef's distinction between the individual and the masses. He cites a *baraita* that discusses the verse *ki yesitcha achicha ben imecha* — "when your brother, your mother's son, incites you" — and concludes that the verse applies equally whether the one being incited is an individual or a group. The *baraita* does distinguish between the two, but only with respect to the severity of punishment and the treatment of property, not with respect to the stage at which liability arises. The individual's punishment is more severe on his person — *sekilah* — but his property is spared. The group's punishment is lighter on their persons — *hereg by the sword*, as in *ir hanidachat* — but their property is destroyed. For all other matters, Abaye argues, individual and group are governed by the same rules. The difference Rav Yosef proposed — that the individual is liable upon verbal assent while the group is not — has no basis in this *baraita*.

### Rava's Answer

Rava offers yet another resolution, one that does not depend on the individual-versus-masses distinction. He maintains that both *mishnayot* could be dealing with a case where one is incited by others. The difference lies in the quality of the incitement itself. If the inciter has made an elaborate and persuasive case — *kach ocheles kach shosah kach meitivah kach meriah* — "this is how it eats, this is how it drinks, this is how it rewards its followers, this is how it punishes its enemies" — then when the person says yes, we assume that the persuasion was effective and the commitment is real. In that case, the verbal assent triggers immediate liability. But if the incitement was perfunctory — "let's go worship" — with no elaborate sell job, then the yes is shallow and we do not assume the person will follow through. In that case, liability requires actual worship.

Rava derives this from the verse *me'elohei ha'amim asher sevivoseichem ha'kerovim eilecha o ha'rechokim mimecha* — the verse warns against being drawn to the gods of surrounding nations, whether near or far. Rava reads the reference to near and far as indicating the form the incitement takes: the inciter will tell you to ignore the gods you know locally — which you can see are powerless — and will entice you with the allure of foreign gods you have never encountered. The very structure of the verse presupposes a sustained rhetorical effort. This confirms that the context of *lo tove lo velo tishma eilav* is precisely such an elaborate incitement — and therefore the liability that triggers upon saying yes applies specifically in that context.

### Rav Ashi's Answer

Rav Ashi resolves the contradiction differently. The second *mishna*, in which verbal assent suffices for liability, is referring specifically to a Jew who is already an apostate — already established as *oved avodah zarah*. For such a person, saying yes means yes; there is no reason to assume a subsequent change of heart. But for any other person, even after a full and compelling incitement, verbal assent alone does not constitute liability. Actual worship is required. The first *mishna* describes the ordinary case; the second *mishna* is the exceptional case of the *mumar*.

### Ravina's Answer

Finally, Ravina resolves the apparent contradiction by rejecting the premise that there is any contradiction at all. He reads the two *mishnayot* as articulating a *lo zu af zu* — "not only this, but also this" — structure of escalating stringency. The first *mishna* teaches that one who actually worships is liable. The second *mishna* goes further: one need not even worship — merely saying one will go and worship already incurs liability. According to Ravina, this applies even to someone acting entirely on their own initiative, without any incitement from others. The two *mishnayot* are additive, each adding a layer of liability, with no contradiction between them.

The range of positions spans a wide spectrum. The easiest resolution conceptually — and the one that Tosafot ultimately privileges — is that verbal commitment in the context of incitement constitutes an act of *kabbalat elohus*, acceptance of a foreign deity, which is itself an enumerated act of *avodah zarah*. When that acceptance has not yet occurred — either because the person explicitly withholds it, or because the incitement was insufficiently persuasive, or because the person is acting alone without an inciter — the verbal statement does not rise to the level of *avodah zarah*, and only actual worship triggers liability.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 62

## Ahavah Umiyirah

### Acts Without Belief

The daf opens with a discussion that is formally situated not in *Maseches Avodah Zarah* but here in *Sanhedrin* — and this itself is worth noting, since it is in this tractate that the Torah defines precisely which acts of *avodah zarah* carry the death penalty. The *gemara* introduces the case with the word *itmar*, signaling an *amoraic* dispute: what is the law governing one who performs an act of *avodah zarah* — slaughtering an animal (*zivuach*), burning incense (*kitur*), pouring a libation (*nisuch*), bowing down (*hishtachavah*), or any act recognized as the particular mode of worship of a given idol — but does so *me'ahavah umiyirah*, out of love and fear, rather than out of genuine theological belief?

### Rashi Clarifies

*Rashi* explains that *meahava umiyirah* means out of love and fear of a *person*, not of the idol itself — *meahavas adam umeyiras adam velo chashva beliba lelohut*. He did not believe in his heart that this object is divine. The historical resonance is clear: in the medieval period, Jews converted to Christianity not out of conviction but out of social ambition or out of fear of forced conversion and persecution — yet they went through the full motions of worship. The question is whether performing the recognized acts of *avodah zarah* with full awareness that these are the prescribed acts of that worship, but without the attendant belief, constitutes *avodah zarah* for which one is *chayav*.

This question is sharpened by the structure of the *mishnah* itself, which lists specific acts of worship and then separately mentions *vehamikabel alav beloha* — one who accepts the idol as his god. Normally, the performance of the act implicitly carries that acceptance, but what if we know that is not the case?

### Abaye vs. Rava

The *amoraic* dispute is stated directly. *Abaye amar chayav*: Abaye holds one is liable. *Rava amar patur*: Rava holds one is exempt.

### Rava's Counterargument

Rava's reasoning is straightforward: *ei kiblah alei beloha in, ei lo lo* — if one accepted it as a god, yes, one is liable; if not, no. The act without the belief does not constitute *avodah zarah*.

### Abaye's Proof

Abaye attempts to derive his position from the *mishnah*'s formulation. The *mishnah* says "one who worships" and then lists the specific acts. Abaye argues that the opening phrase — "one who worships" — extends liability even to one who does the act regardless of motivation or accompanying belief. Rava, however, deflects this reading: as Rabbi Yirmiya has explained elsewhere in the *sugya*, *oved* refers to a case of worship performed in the normative manner of that idol (*kidarka*), while the specific acts of *zivuach*, *kitur*, and *nisuch* are liable even when performed in a non-standard manner (*shelo kidarka*) because they are classic modes of divine service. The word *oved* is not adding a case of *meahava umiyirah*.

### Haman & Bowing

Abaye then brings a *braisa* as proof. The verse states *lo tishtachaveh lahem velo ta'avdeim* — do not bow down to them and do not worship them. *Lahem atah mishtachaveh aval atah mishtachaveh la'adam kemoscha*: one may not bow to an idol, but one may bow to a fellow human being, as indeed occurs throughout the Torah — Yaakov bows to Esav, and so on — as a gesture of greeting or submission, not of worship. One might then ask: perhaps one could even bow to someone who presents himself as a god and demands worship, like Haman? The assumption among the *rishonim* is that Haman did present himself in this way, which is why Mordechai's refusal was so provocative — had it been merely a show of political deference, the provocation would be inexplicable. The *braisa* therefore adds *velo ta'avdeim*: do not worship them — that extra phrase comes to include even a human being who treats himself as a god. One is forbidden from bowing even to such a person.

This appears to support Abaye, since people would have been bowing to Haman *out of fear* — and yet the *braisa* says this is forbidden as *avodah zarah*. If *miyirah* exempts, why would the *braisa* need to prohibit it?

### Rava's Distinction

Rava responds: *keHaman velo keHaman* — like Haman, but not exactly Haman. The case is like Haman in the sense that the prohibition concerns a human being who presents himself as a god. But it is not exactly the Haman case in the critical respect: *de'ilu Haman miyirah v'hacha lav miyirah* — in the actual Haman case, had people bowed to him, they would not have been *chayav* for *avodah zarah*, because they would have done so out of fear, not out of genuine acceptance of Haman as a deity. The *braisa* uses Haman as the paradigmatic example of a human being claiming divinity, but that very case — where the bowing is done *miyirah* — is precisely the case Rava considers exempt from *chiyuv misa*.

---

## Martyrdom

### Question Posed

This leads directly to what *Tosafot* identifies as the pressing question. If, according to Rava, an act of *avodah zarah* performed out of *miyirah* is not technically *avodah zarah* at all, why does the law of *yehareg v'al ya'avor* apply? If someone holds a sword to a Jew's throat and demands that he bow down to an idol, he should simply bow — since according to Rava it would not constitute a genuine act of *avodah zarah*. This is a very strong question.

### Tosafot Resolves

*Tosafot*, at the bottom of the amud, addresses this directly: *af al gav deve-perek ben sorer u-moreh amar ba-avodat kochavim yehareg v'al ya'avor, yesh omrim de-chayav limsor atzmo le-chatchilah, mi-kol makom heicha de-lo masar atzmo lo michayav misa*. Yes, one is obligated to give up one's life — but the obligation of *yehareg v'al ya'avor* is not identical to the question of whether the act constitutes a technical violation of *avodah zarah*.

### V'Ahavta Principle

The source of *yehareg v'al ya'avor* is not the laws of *avodah zarah* per se but the obligation derived from *v'ahavta et Hashem Elokecha* — the commandment to love God, to not betray one's faith. Consider: if someone holds a gun to a Jew's head and demands he deny God, accept atheism, or convert to Islam — none of those involve *avodah zarah* technically — yet *yehareg v'al ya'avor* still applies. What demands martyrdom is the act of betraying one's relationship with God, not merely whether the specific transgression meets the formal definition of *avodah zarah*. This is why, *Tosafot* explains, even according to Rava, *yehareg v'al ya'avor* would apply to the Haman case.

### Rambam View

The *Rambam* draws a related but distinct distinction in his *Iggeres Teiman*, dealing with Jews who had converted under duress and wished to return. Even though *yehareg v'al ya'avor* applied and they should have given their lives, when they ultimately submitted under compulsion, the coercion (*ones*) means that the technical act of *avodah zarah* may be treated differently. They may have been *meizid* in violating the *mitzvah* of *mesiras nefesh* — the obligation of martyrdom derived from *v'ahavta es Hashem Elokecha* — but with respect to the formal act of *avodah zarah*, they were *ones*. This reinforces *Tosafot*'s framework: the act under duress, even if required of one to resist unto death, is categorically distinct from whether the act itself constitutes the *chiyuv* of *avodah zarah*. This same logic, incidentally, could explain why *Tosafot* offers *kiddush Hashem* as the reason Mordechai would not bow to Haman even according to Rava — it was *yehareg v'al ya'avor* precisely because it would have appeared to the world as an act of betraying God, even if, technically, it was not *avodah zarah* under compulsion.

---

## Kohen Gadol Rules

### Braita Introduced

Abaye brings yet another proof, this time from a *braita* concerning a *kohen mashiach* — that is, a *kohen gadol* — who sins in the domain of *avodah zarah*. The general rule for a *kohen gadol* is that his *korban chatas* differs from that of an ordinary Israelite: he brings a *par* (ox) rather than a *seirah* (female goat or sheep), and critically, he is only liable if he both ruled incorrectly for himself and then acted on that ruling — a dual requirement learned from the case of the *par he'elem davar shel tzibur*, the bull brought when the *sanhedrin* itself rules incorrectly. When it comes to *avodah zarah*, however, the Torah specifies a male goat — a *seir* — even for an individual Israelite who transgresses *beshogeg*. Since the *kohen gadol* brings the same offering as the Israelite for this transgression, the question arises: does the *kohen gadol* still require the double condition (erroneous ruling plus act), or does he follow the Israelite's rule and become liable through mistaken action alone?

### Rabbi vs. Sages

The *braita* records a dispute. *Rebbi* says: for the *kohen mashiach* in a case of *avodah zarah*, it is sufficient that he commits *shiggas ma'aseh* — a mistaken act — and he need not have issued a mistaken *psak* for himself first. The *chachamim* say: even here, *he'elam davar* is required — he must have ruled incorrectly for himself — since his general liability still follows the framework of the *kohen gadol*, notwithstanding the identical *korban*. Both agree, however, that the *korban* itself is *k'seirah k'yachid* — like the offering of an ordinary individual. And both agree further that the *kohen gadol* does not bring an *asham taluy* even in a case of doubt about *avodah zarah*, since the *asham taluy* applies only under conditions that the *kohen gadol*'s circumstances do not meet.

### Shiggas Ma'aseh

The *gemara* now asks: what exactly is the case of *shiggas ma'aseh* by *avodah zarah*? This is the crux. For *Shabbos*, a person can transgress *beshogeg* straightforwardly — he forgot it was *Shabbos*, or he forgot that a particular act was forbidden on *Shabbos* — and he nonetheless committed the act. But for *avodah zarah*, what does it mean to err unintentionally? The *gemara* examines three scenarios.

### Three Scenarios

First: he passed by what he thought was a *beis haknesses* and bowed down, intending to worship God. *Harei libo lashamayim* — his heart was directed toward Heaven. This is not *shogeg*; it is not *avodah zarah* at all, since there was no act of worshipping anything alien. Second: he saw a statue and bowed before it. If he accepted it as a deity — *meizid hu* — he is fully liable and not in the category of *shogeg*. If he did not accept it as a deity but bowed as a gesture of respect — *lo klum hu* — it is nothing, not *avodah zarah* at all. The *gemara* arrives at an apparent impasse: either the facts are wrong (and then it is not *avodah zarah* at all), or he accepted it as a god (and then he is *meizid*, not *shogeg*).

### Ahavah Umiyirah Case

The *gemara* concludes: *ela lav me'ahavah umiyirah* — the only coherent case of *shiggas ma'aseh* by *avodah zarah* is precisely the *meahava umiyirah* scenario. He knew this was an idol, he knew these acts were defined as acts of *avodah zarah*, but he believed — incorrectly — that performing them under circumstances of love and fear rendered him exempt. That belief was his *shogeg*. This is the mistake that was not about the act itself but about the *halacha* governing his circumstances. The *gemara* notes that this is the very point Abaye needs: the only way a *kohen gadol* can transgress *avodah zarah* through *shiggas ma'aseh* alone, without a full *he'elam davar* in the manner of a typical erroneous *psak*, is precisely the *meahava umiyirah* case. His mistake was thinking that *meahava umiyirah* was permitted — not that *avodah zarah* itself was permitted, which would be gross ignorance — and so while it was a mistaken *halachic* position, it was sufficiently distinct from the normal *he'elam davar* of a *kohen gadol* to qualify as *shiggas ma'aseh* alone. This is somewhat fine-grained reasoning, and the *gemara* itself acknowledges it as such.

### Rava's Case

For Rava, who holds that *meahava umiyirah* is genuinely exempt, this scenario cannot serve as the *shiggas ma'aseh* case — because there is no *chiyuv* there at all. Rava therefore must say the case is *be'omer mutar legamrei*: the *kohen gadol* thought *avodah zarah* was entirely permitted. This is such a gross misunderstanding that it does not constitute the normal *he'elam davar* of a *kohen gadol*, who typically knows the basic contours of the prohibition but errs in a detail. Rather, *he'elam davar* is *kiyum miktzas uvitul miktzas* — knowing the general framework but getting a specific application wrong. To think the entire prohibition of *avodah zarah* is nonexistent is so far from normal *psak* error that it qualifies as *shiggas ma'aseh* without *he'elam davar*. The *gemara* acknowledges: *omer mutar haynu he'elam davar* — isn't thinking something is permitted the very definition of *he'elam davar*? And replies: *omer mutar legamrei* — when one thinks the entire prohibition is nonexistent, that is categorically different. It is not a case of the normal *he'elam davar* that a *kohen gadol*'s framework contemplates.

Before moving on, a brief word on the *Rambam*'s position regarding *meahava umiyirah* more broadly. Unlike *Rashi* and most *rishonim*, *Rambam* explains *meahava umiyirah* as doing the acts of *avodah zarah* out of love or fear of the *deity itself* — wanting to curry favor with it or avoid its displeasure — but without truly accepting it as a supreme being. According to *Rambam*, that kind of transactional relationship with an idol — hoping it will provide benefit, fearing its wrath — does not constitute the full acceptance of a god. Real acceptance of something as a god means believing it to be the supreme being and acting accordingly. Anything short of that, for *Rambam*, is not the *emunah* — or its antithesis — that the prohibition is aimed at. This yields a remarkably rigorous standard for what it means to truly commit *avodah zarah* in the Rambam's view.

---

## Multiple Acts

### Zakkai Teaching

The *gemara* now introduces a new teaching: *Tani Rabbi Zakkai kamei de-Rabbi Yochanan* — Rabbi Zakkai taught in front of Rabbi Yochanan. If someone performed *zivach, kitar, niseach, v'hishtachavah* — slaughtered, burned incense, poured a libation, and bowed down — all in one *he'elam*, one continuous state of forgetfulness, *eino chayav ela achas* — he brings only one *korban chatas*. The reasoning is that since all these are simply forms of *avodah*, performing them in one unbroken state of ignorance is analogous to eating multiple *kezaysim* of *chelev* without interruption — where one brings only a single *korban*, since it is all one act in one *he'elam*.

### Yochanan Rejects

Rabbi Yochanan's response was terse and unequivocal: *puk tani li-vara* — go teach this outside. It is not accepted. This is a strong rejection, implying the ruling is simply wrong and outside the bounds of accepted teaching.

### Fire Debate

Rabbi Abba explains the background to this rejection by invoking the dispute between Rabbi Yosi and Rabbi Natan regarding the verse *lo teva'aru esh b'chol moshvoseichem b'yom ha-Shabbas* — do not kindle fire on Shabbos. The Torah singles out fire from among all the *melachos*. Why? Rabbi Yosi says: *hav'arah lelav yatza* — it is singled out to teach that fire is merely a *lav*, a negative prohibition, without the death penalty. Rabbi Natan says: *lechalaik yatza* — it is singled out to teach that fire is treated as a distinct category, and from this we derive the principle that all *melachos* are treated separately (*chiluk melachos*), so that doing multiple *melachos* in one *he'elam* generates multiple *korbanot*. Rabbi Abba suggests that the same logic applies by *avodah zarah*: just as fire is singled out from other *melachos*, *hishtachavah* is singled out from *lo ta'avdeim*. According to Rabbi Yosi, that would mean *hishtachavah* is merely a *lav* but not a basis for *chiluk*; according to Rabbi Natan, it teaches *chiluk avodos*. Rabbi Zakkai's teaching would then align with Rabbi Yosi. So why did Rabbi Yochanan reject it outright?

### Hishtachavah Distinction

The *gemara* points to a fundamental asymmetry that makes this parallel untenable. By *Shabbos*, there is a *machloket* between Rabbi Yosi and Rabbi Natan precisely because Rabbi Yosi has another source entirely for *chiluk melachos* — the *pasuk* of *me'achas mehena*, as we will see — and therefore he can say fire's singling out teaches a *lav*, not *chiluk*. But by *avodah zarah*, if one does not learn *chiluk avodos* from *hishtachavah*, there is nowhere else to learn it. And since the principle of *chiluk avodos* by *avodah zarah* parallels the principle of *chiluk melachos* by *Shabbos* — which is universally accepted — it follows that *everyone* must agree that *hishtachavah* teaches *chiluk avodos*. There is no room for a view like Rabbi Yosi's here, because by *Shabbos* Rabbi Yosi only disagrees about *fire* because he has *me'achas mehena* as his source for *chiluk*. By *avodah zarah*, absent any alternative source, *hishtachavah* must be doing that work universally.

### Yosef Clarifies

Rav Yosef puts the argument precisely: *dilma ad kan lo ka'amar Rabbi Yossi hatam hav'arah lelav yatza denafka lei sidur melachos me'achas meihena* — perhaps Rabbi Yosi only says fire teaches a *lav* because he already derives the principle of treating each *melacha* separately from *me'achas mehena*. Since he has that source, he can deploy fire to teach something else. But for *avodah zarah*, where no such alternative source exists, *d'kulei alma hishtachava l'chalek yatza* — everyone agrees that *hishtachavah* is singled out to teach *chiluk avodos*. That is why Rabbi Yochanan rejected Rabbi Zakkai's teaching outright: it goes against a principle that is unanimously held.

---

## Me'Achas Mehena

### Pasuk Explained

The *gemara* now turns to the *pasuk* itself: *ve'asah me'achas mehena* — and he does from one of these. From this phrase, Rabbi Yonasan derives multiple distinct teachings: *achat, me'achat, heina, meheinah* — one, from one, many, from many — and then two further compound cases: *achas she'hi heina* and *heina she'hi achas* — one that is many, and many that is one.

### Shimon Case

*Achat* — one: if one intended to write the name *Shimon* on *Shabbos* and wrote it in full, one is *chayav*. *Me'achas* — from one: if one only wrote *shin mem* — the word *sheim* — having intended to write *Shimon*, since those two letters already constitute a complete word, one is *chayav* even though one did not complete the intended act. The partial act, insofar as it constitutes a completed *melacha*, is sufficient.

### Categories

*Heina* — many: this teaches that there are *avos melacha*, multiple primary categories of *chilul Shabbos*. *Meheinah* — from many: this teaches *toldos*, derivative forms of those primary categories.

### One That Is Many

*Achas she'hi heina* — one that is many: *shegagas Shabbas v'shigagas melachos* — one knew it was *Shabbos* but forgot each individual *melacha* separately — forgot that kindling fire was forbidden, forgot that kneading was forbidden, and so on. Since each forgetfulness is distinct, each *melacha* generates a separate *he'elam* and therefore a separate *chatas*. One act of identity — knowing it is *Shabbos* — combines with multiple distinct acts of forgetfulness about the individual *melachos*, yielding multiple *korbanot*.

### Many That Is One

*Heina she'hi achas* — many that is one: *shegagas Shabbas v'zadon melachos* — one knew full well that each individual *melacha* was forbidden, but forgot that it was *Shabbos* at all. Since there is only one thing forgotten — that it is *Shabbos* — everything falls within a single *he'elam* and one brings only one *korban*. The principle that emerges is clear: it is the structure of one's forgetfulness, not the number of acts, that determines the number of *korbanot*. And this principle of *chiluk melachos* is learned from *me'achas mehena*, which means that even Rabbi Yosi, who uses fire for a different *drasha*, already possesses this principle and need not derive it from fire.

### Avodah Framework

The *gemara* then applies this framework to *avodah zarah*. Could one apply the same *pasuk* of *me'achas mehena* to derive *chiluk avodos* there as well? The attempt is made:

*Achas* — one: *zvicha*, slaughtering an animal — that is a complete act. *Me'achas*: one *siman* — one of the two passages of the trachea and esophagus, analogous to *sheim miShimon*. *Heina*: the primary acts — *zivuach, kitur, nisuch, v'hishtachavah* — the four recognized forms of worship. *Meheinah*, the derivative: the *gemara* gives the example of *shiber makel l'faneha* — breaking a stick before the idol. This is considered analogous to *shechita*, though the *gemara* qualifies that this applies only where the stick is itself a meaningful object of worship for that particular idol — for instance, if worshippers normally dance with this stick before it — making its destruction a meaningful act of devotion comparable to *shechita*. This is treated as a *tolda* of *zivuach*.

Then the compound cases. *Achas she'hi heina* — one knew this was *avodah zarah* but forgot separately that *nisuch* was forbidden and forgot separately that *hishtachavah* was forbidden: each forgetfulness is distinct, generating multiple *korbanot*. *Heina she'hi achas* — *shiggas avodas kochavim b'zadon avodos*: one knew these individual *avodos* were forbidden but forgot *avodah zarah* altogether, yielding one *korban*. But this last scenario circles back to the same difficulty already encountered: what does it mean to forget *avodah zarah* while knowing that specific acts are forbidden? If one did not realize this object was an idol, one has not committed *avodah zarah* at all; if one knew it was an idol and accepted it as a god, one is *meizid*. The *gemara* returns to the same answer as before: *ela mei'ahavah umiyirah* — the overarching thing one forgot was that *meahava umiyirah* constitutes *avodah zarah*. For Abaye, this works as a genuine *shogeg*. For Rava, who holds one is exempt *meahava umiyirah*, the only available scenario is *be'omer mutar* — thinking *avodah zarah* entirely permitted — which the *gemara* equates with the single overarching forgetfulness, analogous to forgetting it is *Shabbos*. In that case, one brings a single *korban* regardless.

---

## Me'Achas Inapplicable

### Different Korbanos

Having worked through how *me'achas mehena* might apply to *avodah zarah*, the *gemara* now withdraws the entire suggestion. The *pasuk* of *me'achas mehena* appears in the section of the Torah dealing with standard *korban chatas* obligations, where the Torah explicitly distinguishes between different classes of people: a *kohen mashiach* brings a *par*, a *nasi* brings a *seir*, and an individual brings a *kisbah* or *seirah*. The diversity of *korbanot* — and the distinctions that *me'achas mehena* is meant to navigate — presupposes this very structure.

### Same Korban

By *avodah zarah*, however, the *mishna* establishes — and the *amoraim* agree — *v'shavin she'bis'eirah k'yachid*: everyone, from the *kohen gadol* to the ordinary Israelite, brings the same offering. The entire framework of differentiated *korbanot* simply does not apply.

### Hishtachavah Source

Since *me'achas mehena* is embedded in a context that presupposes distinctions of *korbanot* that do not exist in the *avodah zarah* section, it cannot be applied there. The *gemara* concludes: *v'su lo midi* — and nothing more need be said. The *chiluk avodos* of *avodah zarah* is derived, as established, from *hishtachavah* alone.

---

## Shmuel Teaching

### Shabbos Stricter

When Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda came, he clarified that what Rabbi Zakkai actually taught before Rabbi Yochanan was not the teaching about bringing one *korban* for multiple *avodos*. Rather, the *braisa* was a comparative one: *chomer b'Shabbos mish'ar mitzvos v'chomer b'sh'ar mitzvos mi'be'Shabbos* — there are ways in which *Shabbos* is stricter than other *mitzvos*, and there are ways in which other *mitzvos* are stricter than *Shabbos*. The strictness of *Shabbos*: if one performs two separate *melachos* in one *he'elam*, one is liable separately for each — *chayav al kol achas v'achas*.

### Other Mitzvos

*Ma she'ein kein b'sh'ar mitzvos*: for other *mitzvos*, where there is no principle of *chiluk* among sub-forms of the same prohibition, doing the same violation multiple times in one *he'elam* yields only one *korban*. If one ate *chelev* and *chelev* without interruption of awareness, it is all one *he'elam* and one *korban*.

### Reverse Stringency

The reverse strictness: *b'sh'ar mitzvos, shogeg belo miskavein chayav* — for other *mitzvos*, one who acts *beshogeg* without specific intent (*lo miskavein*) is nonetheless liable for a *korban*. For *Shabbos*, by contrast, *mis'asek* — performing one action while intending another — is exempt: *meleches machsheves asra Torah*, the Torah prohibited only deliberate creative work. So if one meant to pick up an object and accidentally performed a *melacha*, one is *patur* by *Shabbos*, whereas certain other prohibitions would hold one liable even in that scenario.

---

## Analogy Test

### Consistency Question

Having introduced this *braisa*, the *gemara* must now determine whether it can be made to work consistently.

### Proposed Parallel

The *gemara* proposes that the comparative structure can be made coherent. The strictness of *Shabbos* — that two distinct *melachos* in one *he'elam* generate two *korbanot* — can be illustrated by *ktzira v'techina*, harvesting and grinding, two genuinely distinct categories. The corresponding leniency of other *mitzvos* — where sub-forms of one prohibition yield only one *korban* — could be illustrated by *avodah zarah*, as per Rabbi Ami's teaching: *ziveach v'kitar v'niseach b'he'elam echad eino chayav ela achas* — if one slaughtered, burned incense, and poured a libation in a single *he'elam*, one brings only one *korban*, since these three are all derived from *lo ta'avdeim* and arguably constitute one category. This would make the *braisa* coherent as a genuine contrast: *Shabbos* distinguishes among its categories and imposes multiple *korbanot*; *avodah zarah* (in the sub-category of *zivuach, kitur, nisuch*) does not.

### Rejection Reason

The *gemara* rejects this, however, because the second half of the *braisa* — the reverse strictness — cannot be accommodated. The *braisa* says that other *mitzvos* are liable even where *Shabbos* is exempt, specifically in the case of *shogeg belo miskavein* — unintentional action without specific intent, i.e., *mis'asek*. For *Shabbos*, *mis'asek* is *patur*; for other *mitzvos*, *chayav*. But as the *gemara* has now established, there is no genuine case of *mis'asek* for *avodah zarah* that yields liability.

### Mistaken Action

The *gemara* runs through the scenarios once more. If one bowed before what one thought was a synagogue — *harei libo lashamayim*, one's heart was directed heavenward — it is not *avodah zarah* at all. If one saw a statue and bowed: if one accepted it as a deity, one is *meizid*; if not, it is nothing. There is no middle case — no case structurally parallel to *mis'asek* on *Shabbos* — where one performs an act thinking it will not be *avodah zarah* but it turns out to be, and yet one is *chayav*.

### Avodah Gap

This is the fundamental structural gap. By *Shabbos*, *mis'asek* is possible because the act of creative work can occur independently of whether one's conscious intention was directed toward it. By *avodah zarah*, the act is constituted in part by what is in one's mind — specifically, one's orientation toward the object of worship — and so the gap that *mis'asek* exploits on *Shabbos* simply does not exist here. If the mental element is absent, the act is not *avodah zarah*; if it is present, one is fully *meizid*.

### Unresolved

The *gemara* returns, at the conclusion of the *amud*, to the options already explored: *meahava umiyirah* and *omer mutar*. For Abaye, *meahava umiyirah* could serve as the analogue — one thought it was permitted and acted on that mistaken belief; for Rava, only *omer mutar* is available. But *omer mutar* is also a case where one would be *chayav* a *korban* for *Shabbos*, so it cannot serve as the case where *avodah zarah* is *chayav* and *Shabbos* is *patur*. The *braisa* cannot be made to work by *avodah zarah*, and the *gemara* leaves the question open — the *daf* will continue from here.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 63

## Abaye/Rava Debate

### Oved Me'ahava Review

Yesterday's discussion centered on the important debate between Abaye and Rava regarding *oved me'ahava umiyirah* — one who worships an idol out of love or fear, but without genuine theological belief in that idol as a god. The Rambam's position, while somewhat puzzling, seems to interpret this as a fear directed toward God — yet still not constituting actual belief in the idol. The simpler reading of the debate, however, is that the person is acting for entirely exterior motives, performing what externally appears as an act of worship but without the internal component of genuine belief.

This raises the fundamental question: to what degree does an act of *avoda zara* require the context of sincere belief to be halachically significant? That is the core of the Abaye-Rava debate. Rava holds that in the absence of belief, the person is actually exempt. The act may look like worship from the outside, but without the inner acceptance of the idol as a divine being, it does not constitute a full act of *avoda zara*.

### Martyrdom Obligation

Given Rava's position, one might ask: if worship without belief does not technically constitute *avoda zara*, why should martyrdom — *yeihareig ve'al ya'avor* — ever be required in such a scenario? After all, if the act carries no halachic weight, why give up one's life to avoid it? And even setting aside the belief question entirely, if a person is being physically compelled to perform the act, they are acting under *ones* and are halachically exempt in any case.

The *Rishonim*, Tosafot among them, resolve this by distinguishing between two separate obligations. The exemption from liability addresses one question — whether the person transgressed — but the obligation of martyrdom addresses a completely different one. Even where a person would be technically exempt for the act performed under compulsion, the failure to submit to martyrdom itself constitutes a failure to fulfill the *mitzvah* of *ve'ahavta es Hashem Elokecha* — loving God with one's entire being. The *mitzvah* of martyrdom, in other words, is not contingent on the technical status of the forced act as *avoda zara*. It flows from the prohibition against renouncing one's faith and accepting another religion — an independent obligation entirely.

This also explains why conversion to Islam, which most *poskim* and *Rishonim* do not categorize as *avoda zara* — since Islam posits the same God, merely with a different historical narrative — could nonetheless implicate the martyrdom obligation. The question of martyrdom is not whether the compelled religion technically constitutes *avoda zara*; it is whether one is renouncing one's Judaism.

### Intentional/Unintentional

Abaye's position and Rava's position diverge in a specific domain. Where everyone agrees — including Abaye — is in cases where the person does not realize they are standing before an idol, or believes they are merely showing honor without treating the object as a divine being. In those cases, even Abaye would concede there is no act of worship. The dispute is narrower: where the act is performed with full awareness that this is an idol and that one is performing a recognizable act of worship, but without the accompanying internal belief — that is the contested terrain.

---

## Chiluk Avodot Issue

### Multiple Acts Problem

Yesterday's discussion also introduced the question of *chiluk melachot* by *Shabbos* versus *chiluk avodot* by *avoda zara* — whether performing multiple distinct acts of idol worship in a single state of forgetfulness requires multiple *chata'ot* or only one. By *Shabbos*, forgetting entirely that it is *Shabbos* means that no matter how many *melachot* one performs, only a single *korban* is required. But if one remembers it is *Shabbos* while forgetting that a particular act is a *melacha*, one brings a separate *korban* for each *melacha* — that is *chiluk melachot*, the principle that each *melacha* is distinct. The question is whether a parallel principle of *chiluk avodot* applies to *avoda zara*, making each form of worship a separate *korban*.

### Rav Zakkai Rejected

A *baraita* attributed to Rav Zakkai appeared to hold that even if one performed *zivuach*, *kitor*, and *niseich* — slaughtering, burning incense, and libation — in a single state of forgetfulness, only one *korban* is required. Rabbi Yochanan rejected this outright, insisting on the principle of *chiluk avodot*. A second *baraita* appeared to raise the same difficulty, and Rabbi Yochanan likewise refused to accept it.

---

## Shabbat/Other Aveirot

### Baraita Structure

At the point where the current sugya resumes — approximately twelve lines from the bottom of the page — the Gemara asks *mai kushya*: why is this *baraita* actually a problem? The Gemara proposes a resolution: *dilma le'olam eima lach* — perhaps the two halves of the *baraita* are simply addressing different subjects. The *reisha*, the first part that contrasts multiple sin offerings versus one, is speaking about *avoda zara*: multiple *melachot* on *Shabbos* yield multiple *korbanot*, while multiple *avodot* of *avoda zara* yield only one. That position works if one accepts that there is no *chiluk avodot* by *avoda zara*.

The *seifa* — the second half of the *baraita*, which addresses whether one brings a *korban* in a case of unintentional transgression — is then not about *avoda zara* at all. It is contrasting *Shabbos* with other *aveiros* in general. This reading would allow both halves of the *baraita* to function coherently, each addressing a different set of circumstances.

### Shogeg Lo Miskavein

How would the contrast between *Shabbos* and other *aveiros* work in this context? The Gemara introduces the category of *shogeg belo miskavein* — an unintentional act where the person was not even attempting to perform the transgression in question.

### Ruku u-Valo'o Example

The Gemara's example for other *aveiros* is the case of *roku u-valo'o*: a person has something liquid in their mouth, believes it is their own saliva, and swallows it — only to discover it was forbidden fat. This would still obligate a *korban*, even though the person was not intending to eat anything at all.

### Grass Picking Example

The parallel case by *Shabbos* is one who intended to pick up a blade of grass that appeared already to be detached from the ground — *sheniskavein l'hagbi'ah es ha-talush* — and in the process of picking it up, inadvertently severed it from the soil — *ve-chatach es ha-mechubar*. In that case, one is exempt from a *korban*.

### Shogeg vs. Misasek

The comparison of these two cases illuminates a fundamental distinction: the difference between *shogeg* and *misasek*. *Shogeg* describes a person who performed exactly the act they intended but made an error — either in law, thinking the act was permitted, or in fact, thinking the substance was something it was not. In either case, the act performed is recognizably the same type of act the person intended to do, and a *korban* is required for *Shabbos* and for other *aveiros* alike.

*Misasek* is qualitatively different. Here the person was attempting to perform one act and ended up performing a completely different one. The *roku u-valo'o* case might appear to be *misasek* — after all, one was trying to swallow saliva, not eat forbidden fat. But the Gemara treats it as sufficient to obligate a *korban*. Intuitively, this can be understood as follows: swallowing saliva is not what we would ordinarily call eating, in the same way that if someone asked whether you ate or drank anything today, you would not count swallowing your own saliva as an affirmative answer. At an anthropological level, the bodily act of swallowing saliva and the social act of eating food are simply different kinds of things. The person thus tried to do something other than eat, and performed a different act — that is *misasek*.

By contrast, if one was trying to eat one food and ate a different food by mistake, that remains a classic *shogeg*: you intended to eat, and you ate. The error was in the object, not in the category of the act itself. Similarly, if a person intended to cut one blade of grass but cut a different one, that is *shogeg* for *Shabbos*. But if a person intended merely to pick something up — not to perform any act of detachment at all — and inadvertently cut it from the ground, that is *misasek*: they tried to do something other than cut, and ended up cutting.

The general rule, applicable not only to *Shabbos* but across all *aveiros*, is that *misasek* carries no liability — not even a *korban*. The act is so disconnected from what the person was trying to do that it cannot be meaningfully attributed to them. It is as though one reached out to shake a hand and accidentally switched on a light: one did not really turn on the light, the light turned on incidentally.

### Chalavim V'arayot

The single exception to this exemption for *misasek* is forbidden fats and forbidden sexual relations — *chalavim va'arayot*. In those cases, even a *misasek* is liable for a *korban*. The Gemara's explanation, as stated by Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel, is *sheken nehene*: the person derived bodily benefit from the act. When someone derives direct physical pleasure from an act — whether through eating or through sexual congress — the fact of that benefit prevents them from fully disassociating themselves from the act. You cannot say "the forbidden fat got eaten" when the reality is that your body received that experience. The benefit binds you to the act regardless of your intention.

By *Shabbos*, by contrast, even a *misasek* yields no *korban*, because the Torah requires *meleches machsheves* — intentional work. The *Torah* forbade only acts that were fully and purposively intended.

A brief observation is worth noting here, though the Gemara itself does not pursue it this direction: the Gemara frames forbidden foods and sexual relations as the exception, while *Shabbos* stands as the rule. Yet one could argue it ought to be the reverse. *Shabbos* is exceptional in that even someone who tries to perform transgression A and inadvertently performs transgression A-prime — slightly different from what was intended — may still be exempt, whereas by other *aveiros* that is ordinary *shogeg* and fully liable. The narrow precision demanded by *meleches machsheves* is itself an exceptional feature of *Shabbos*, not of *chalavim va'arayot*.

### Rabbi Yochanan's Method

The Gemara then supplies the reason Rabbi Yochanan refused to accept this entire resolution. Rabbi Yochanan operates by the principle that a problematic *mishna* or *baraita* cannot be resolved by splitting it — reading the *reisha* as addressing one set of circumstances and the *seifa* as addressing an entirely different set. He insists that a *baraita* must be interpretable as a unified whole under a single set of conditions.

The Gemara supports this by citing a famous episode in which Rabbi Yochanan struggled with a *mishna* in Bava Metzia involving a barrel. The resolution offered — that the first half addressed a case where the barrel was replaced in the original location and the second half addressed a different location — was technically workable, but Rabbi Yochanan refused to accept it. He declared that he would carry the garments of anyone who could explain that *mishna* consistently according to a single *tanna* and a single set of circumstances — *movilna manei batrei levei masusa* — as a gesture of profound gratitude. Since no such resolution was available, he continued to regard the *mishna* as a genuine difficulty. That same methodological stance prevents him from accepting the split reading of the *baraita* under discussion.

---

## Rav Ami Teaching

### Rav Ami's Position

The Gemara now turns to a direct statement of Rav Ami: if one performed *ziveiach*, *kiter*, and *niseich* — the three acts of slaughter, incense-burning, and libation — in a single state of forgetfulness, *eino chayav ela achat*: one is liable for only one *korban*.

### Lo Ta'avdeim Proof

Abaye explains Rav Ami's reasoning: the verse says *lo ta'avdeim* — do not worship them — subsuming all acts of *avoda* under a single generic term. The *hakatuv* thereby treats all those acts as a unified category, which is why a single *korban* covers all three performed in one *he'lem* — one state of unawareness. One might object that the same logic could apply to *Shabbos*, where the verse says *lo ta'aseh kol melacha*, but the Gemara does not develop that counter-argument here and moves on.

### Hishtachava Problem

This reasoning immediately raises a difficulty: the verse also says *lo tishtachaveh* — do not bow down — and *hishtachava* is conspicuously absent from Rav Ami's list of three acts. Moreover, the prohibition of *hishtachava* appears three times in the Torah. Why the repetition, and how does it relate to the unifying logic of *lo ta'avdeim*?

### Three Hishtachavot

Abaye explains that each of the three instances of *lo tishtachaveh* serves a distinct purpose. One addresses *hishtachava k'darkah* — bowing down in the standard manner of that *avoda zara*'s worship. One addresses *shelo k'darkah* — bowing down even when it is not the normal mode of worship for that idol. And the third is *l'challek* — to indicate that *hishtachava* is a separate and distinct act that generates its own *korban* independently from the other three.

This explains why *hishtachava* was absent from Rav Ami's list: the three acts that fall under *lo ta'avdeim* are treated as one, but *hishtachava*, having been singled out three times, stands apart. According to Rav Ami's view, then, performing all four acts in a single *he'lem* would yield two *korbanot* — one for the three classic *avodot* grouped under *lo ta'avdeim*, and one for *hishtachava* on its own.

The Gemara then notes that when Abaye presents this explanation of Rav Ami's position, he is explicating a view he does not himself accept. Tosafot clarifies the overall picture: Rabbi Yochanan's rejected position was the more extreme one — Rav Zakkai's view that all four, including *hishtachava*, constitute a single *korban*. What Rav Ami proposes is an intermediate position: not four separate *korbanot*, not one for everything, but two — one for the three acts unified under *lo ta'avdeim*, and one for *hishtachava*. The Yerushalmi goes even further, positing a third *korban* for an act of *avoda k'darkah* that is distinctive to a particular *avoda zara* — so that there would be three categories in total: the three standard *avodot*, *hishtachava*, and the act characteristic of that specific idol.

### K'Darkah Definition

The Gemara then revisits the definition of *k'darkah* in the context of *hishtachava*. One might object: if bowing down in the standard manner of a given *avoda zara* is already covered by the general verse — *eich ya'avdu ha-goyim ha-eleh* — which captures whatever form of worship is natural and customary for a given idol, why is a separate *pasuk* needed for *k'darkah* bowing?

The Gemara resolves this: the *k'darkah* addressed by the separate *pasuk* is not the fully normative, primary mode of worship for that idol. Rather, it refers to a case where bowing down would not be considered bizarre or offensive to that idol's cult — its worshippers might accept it as a reasonable gesture even if it is not what they typically do. This is distinguished from *shelo k'darkah* in the fully anomalous sense: bowing down before an idol like *Peor*, whose worship involved explicitly degrading acts, would be considered entirely wrong by that idol's own devotees. Between these poles lies the intermediate case — not the standard worship, but not wholly alien to it either — and it is for this intermediate case that the additional *pasuk* is required.

---

## Verbal Acceptance

### Eli Ata Statement

The Mishna includes among the acts of *avoda zara* that carry the death penalty the act of *mekablo alav b'elo'ah* — verbally accepting an idol as one's god — specifically the declaration *eli ata*: "You are my god."

### No Source Cited

What is striking about the Gemara's treatment of this case is what it does not do: it provides no *pasuk*, no derivation, no scriptural basis for the claim that this verbal declaration constitutes an act of *avoda zara* punishable by death. We were given verses for slaughter, libation, and bowing down. We were given derivations for *k'darkah* and *shelo k'darkah*. Yet for the most fundamental act — verbally declaring a deity to be one's god — the Gemara offers no source at all. This is, on reflection, a remarkable lacuna that will be worth returning to.

### Rav Nachman Teaching

Rav Nachman, citing Rabbah bar Avuha citing Rav, states: *keivan she'amar lo eli ata chayav* — as soon as one says "You are my god" to an idol, one is liable. The Gemara probes what precisely this adds. If the ruling concerns liability to execution — *le-ktala* — that is already explicit in the Mishna and requires no new teaching. What Rav must therefore be adding is liability to bring a *korban* — that is, if one made this declaration *be-shogeg*, thinking it was permitted, one must bring a sin offering.

This raises a significant difficulty. There is a principle derived from the verse *ve-asah me-achat me-henna* that a *korban* for *avoda zara* requires a physical act. Verbal declarations generally do not satisfy this requirement. Indeed, it is sometimes easier to incur the death penalty than to become liable for a *korban*: blasphemy against God — *megadef* — is punishable by death based solely on a verbal act, yet one would not automatically assume a *korban* follows from that.

### Rabbi Akiva Debate

The Gemara explains: *ve-afilu le-rabbanan* — but even granting the rule that verbal acts are insufficient for a *korban*, the Gemara questions whether this ruling about *eli ata* can stand. A *baraita* teaches explicitly: *eino chayav ela davar she-yesh bo ma'aseh* — one is only liable to bring a *korban* for *avoda zara* if there is an act associated with it — citing *zivuach*, *kitor*, *niseich*, and *hishtachava* as examples.

Reish Lakish intervenes at this point with a sharp observation: since when is *hishtachava* — bowing down — considered an "act" for this purpose? Bowing down involves merely moving one's own body; one is not interacting with, or effecting any change upon, anything external. The Gemara appears to place speech and bowing down in the same category of minimal, borderline acts.

This is the crux of the debate between Rabbi Akiva and the *rabbanan*. Rabbi Akiva holds that one who blasphemes — *megadef* — brings a *korban be-shogeg*, meaning he treats speech as a sufficient act for *korban* purposes. The *rabbanan* disagree. Abaye assumes here that bowing down occupies the same halachic space as speech: if speech is enough, bowing down is enough; if speech is insufficient, so is bowing down.

The Yerushalmi, it should be noted, suggests a distinction between the two. Speech, one might argue, is not primarily a physical act at all: its significance lies not in the movement of the lips but in the thought expressed through those lips. Speech is the outward expression of a mental reality, making it more a cognitive act than a physical one. Bowing down falls between these poles: like speech, one does not interact with or change anything external to oneself, yet unlike speech, its significance is not primarily the communication of an idea. Whether a signed gesture would be treated as speech or as a physical act along this analysis remains an intriguing open question — but the Gemara's operative position is to treat the two as equivalent.

So the Gemara's conclusion is that the ruling about *eli ata* generating a *korban* can only stand according to Rabbi Akiva, who holds that a minimal act — including a verbal one — suffices for *korban* liability.

### Heksha Linkage

The Gemara then notes: *le-Rabbi Akiva peshita* — within Rabbi Akiva's position, there is no novelty here. If verbal blasphemy brings a *korban*, surely verbal acceptance of *avoda zara* does too. What then is Rav's teaching adding?

The Gemara answers: one might have thought Rabbi Akiva limits his position about verbal acts bringing a *korban* to *megadef* specifically, because the verse concerning *megadef* explicitly mentions *karet* — *ish ish ki yekalel elohav ve-nasa cheto* — and ordinarily *korban* liability is tied to what would be punishable by *karet* if done intentionally. Since *megadef* bears an explicit *karet* marker, Rabbi Akiva is willing to impose a *korban* despite the verbal-act limitation. By *avoda zara*, however, the death penalty is explicit, but *karet* is not stated. One might therefore suppose that even Rabbi Akiva would not impose a *korban* for the verbal declaration of *eli ata*.

To this the Gemara responds: *kamashma lan de-hekkesha hikkesh* — the Torah teaches through a *heksha*, a linkage, that all acts of *avoda zara* are united in a single framework. The verse reads: *vayishtachavu lo vayizbechu lo vayomru eileh elohecha Yisrael asher he'elucha me-eretz Mitzrayim* — they bowed down to it, slaughtered to it, and declared "these are your gods, Israel, who brought you out of Egypt." By placing the verbal declaration in the same verse as slaughter — the clearest physical act — the Torah links all three: slaughter, bowing down, and verbal acceptance. Since slaughter unquestionably requires a *korban*, so too, via this *heksha*, do the other two. This is the source that justifies the ruling — at least according to Rabbi Akiva — that *eli ata* generates a *korban*.

---

## Tosafot/Ramban Views

### Tosafot Position

Returning now to the question the Gemara left open — the absence of any *pasuk* for why *eli ata* makes one liable to execution — there is a significant conceptual debate between Tosafot and the Ramban.

Tosafot, addressing the *mishna* directly, argues from the *heksha* just cited — *vayishtachavu lo vayizbechu lo vayomru* — that the verbal declaration is not merely a precursor to worship but is itself the most fundamental act of worship. Every religion's most basic expression of devotion is the verbal declaration of fealty to its deity. In this sense, saying *eli ata* is not a thought in one's head — that would merely be a possible transgression of *lo yihyeh lecha elohim acheirim al panai* without constituting *avoda zara* — but the performance of the most primary act of worship. Verbal acts of belief stated internally are one thing; the act of verbally declaring, "You are my God," is the foundational act of worship for every religion that has ever existed. Tosafot learns this from the *pasuk* linking the declaration to the other acts of worship at the *eigel*.

### Ramban Position

The Ramban reads the conceptual structure very differently. He holds that the fundamental prohibition of *avoda zara* is not the act of worship as such — the slaughter, the bowing, the libation — but rather the act of accepting another being as one's God. The primary *lav* is *lo yihyeh lecha elohim acheirim al panai*. From this perspective, *eli ata* requires no derivation at all: it is the very essence of what *avoda zara* prohibits. What needs explanation, for the Ramban, is not why verbal acceptance is forbidden but rather how the other acts — slaughter, bowing, libation — are also *avoda zara*. The answer is that those acts are understood within their context as expressions of that acceptance, and the verses address them to make that explicit.

### Golden Calf Intent

This difference has direct implications for the question raised regarding the golden calf: were the Israelites who worshipped the *eigel* rejecting God and accepting the calf as a competing deity, or were they worshipping God through an image? The Torah prohibits *lo saasun kol tmuna biyom dibber Hashem* — do not make an image — addressing worship of God through a physical representation, quite apart from worshipping another god entirely. Either the calf was accepted as a different god, or it was used as an image through which to worship the same God. Either way, the act constitutes *avoda zara* and *chayav misa*.

For the Ramban, who sees the essence of *avoda zara* as accepting another god, only the first interpretation — actual theological rejection of God — would fall squarely under *lo yihyeh lecha*. Worshipping God through an image might still be prohibited and punishable, but the *chiyuv misa* as the core of *avoda zara* is most naturally located in the act of acceptance. Rambam, by contrast, treats both as equally prohibited. These are important distinctions, though the full theological discussion lies beyond what the Gemara itself addresses.

---

## Golden Calf Agada

### Rabbi Yochanan View

The Gemara now turns to a remarkable *agadic* passage. Rabbi Yochanan states: *ilmala vav shebe'heelucha* — were it not for the plural form in the word *heelucha* ("who brought you up") — *nitchayvu resha'im she-beYisrael kelaya*: the wicked among Israel would have deserved complete destruction. The people said "these are your gods" — *eileh elohecha* — in the plural, not "this is your god" in the singular. That plural, Rabbi Yochanan argues, shows that even at the moment of the calf's worship, the people did not exclude God. God remained among the gods they acknowledged, and because they did not fully reject God, they were not deserving of annihilation.

### Rabbi Shimon Objection

A competing *tannaitic* position — cited as *acheirim omrim* — agrees with Rabbi Yochanan's formulation, only to be challenged by Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai. Rabbi Shimon objects: *vahalo kol ha-mishtatef shem shamayim ve-davar acher ne'ekar min ha'olam* — anyone who combines God's name with something else deserves to be destroyed. Saying "these are your gods" — placing God and the calf in the same category — is not a mitigating factor; it is equally, perhaps even more, damnable than outright rejection. So what, according to Rabbi Shimon, does the plural *heelucha* teach? *She'ivu elohut harbeh* — it indicates that they yearned for many gods, showing the depth of their theological rebelliousness, not the survival of their faith in God.

At the surface level, Rabbi Shimon's position implies something counterintuitive: that combining God with other gods is worse than rejecting God entirely. This is difficult to accept on its face.

### Maharsha Resolution

The Maharsha finds this simple reading unacceptable. He proposes an alternative reading of the second position: what saved the people was not the mere plurality of the word but the preservation of a theological hierarchy — God remained supreme and transcendent in their minds, while they sought to worship lower, subordinate divine beings. This is meaningfully different from either equating God with the calf or rejecting God outright. Keeping God supreme while directing practical worship at lower beings is the one configuration that, in the Maharsha's reading, allowed for national survival and eventual forgiveness.

Had they fully pushed God aside, they would have been annihilated, as Rabbi Yochanan originally feared. Had they equated God with the calf, placing them on the same plane, that too would have been intolerable — as Rabbi Shimon argues. But retaining God as the ultimate sovereign while channeling devotional acts toward lesser powers was, the Maharsha suggests, the sin that could be forgiven. The plain sense of Rabbi Shimon's answer remains more extreme, but the Maharsha smooths it considerably.

---

## Non-Classic Acts

### Hugging/Kissing Acts

The Mishna addresses a category of acts involving an idol that do not constitute classic worship: hugging it, kissing it, sweeping before it, washing it, anointing it, clothing it, honoring it in similar ways. These carry a *lav* — a negative prohibition — but not the death penalty, since they are not the normative forms of worship.

### Avdimi Teaching

When Avdimi came from Eretz Yisrael, he transmitted in the name of Rabbi Elazar: for all of these acts of honor and adoration, one receives lashes — *loke* — with the exception of one who vows in the name of another god or swears in the name of another god. For vowing and swearing, Avdimi says, there are no lashes.

### No Lashing Vows

Why no lashes for vowing and swearing in the name of another god? The Gemara's initial answer is straightforward: *mishum de-havei lav she-ein bo ma'aseh* — because it is a prohibition not involving a physical act. It is purely verbal, and the general rule is that lashes require a physical act of transgression.

### Generic Lav Problem

This answer, however, immediately generates a counter-question: if vowing and swearing receive no lashes because they are verbal, why should the acts of hugging, kissing, and so forth receive lashes at all? These acts seem to fare better on the *ma'aseh* dimension — they are physical — so what is the difficulty? The Gemara explains: *mishum de-havei lav she-bichlalut* — these acts fall under a generic *lav*. The prohibition is derived from *lo ta'avdeim*, which is a broad, abstract term encompassing many different potential acts. When a prohibition is too general and abstract to specify what particular conduct it forbids, one does not receive lashes for violating it.

This raises an obvious difficulty: the prohibition of *melacha* on *Yom Tov* — *kol melachas avodah lo ta'asu* — is also seemingly broad. One does receive lashes for *melacha* on *Yom Tov*, and the phrasing appears equally generic. Why is that not a *lav she-bichlalut*?

### Tosafot Solution

Tosafot addresses this directly. The principle of *lav she-bichlalut* disqualifies lashes only where the prohibition is so abstract that it fails to specify what conduct is meant. Tosafot gives examples: the prohibition against eating anything other than roasted meat from the *Korban Pesach* — *tzali esh* — is more specific, because even though it excludes multiple modes of preparation, you know what it is referring to. Similarly, the prohibition applying to a *nazir* — *kol asher ye'aseh mi-gefen* — specifies a category concretely enough to support lashes. By contrast, the prohibition *lo ta'avdeim* in the context of hugging, kissing, and acts of honor that are not classic worship is far too abstract: the verse says "do not worship them," and these are not even standard worship at all. Applying that phrase to them is so attenuated that it cannot be the basis for lashes.

The *meleches avodah* formulation on *Yom Tov*, by contrast, contains an adjective — it specifies *laborious* work, not any work, adding enough specificity to escape the *lav she-bichlalut* problem.

The Gemara reinforces the principle through the famous verse *lo sochlu al ha-dam* — do not eat while the blood is still flowing — which *Rishonim* derive to encompass a wildly diverse range of prohibitions: eating from an animal before it has fully expired, eating sacrificial meat while the blood has not yet been presented on the altar, the mourner's meal for relatives of those executed by the court, and the prohibition on the court eating on the day they administer a death sentence. Rabbi Yochanan adds that this verse also serves as the source for the prohibition warning the *ben sorer u-moreh*. Rashi explains the last as: do not engage in eating that will bring about your blood being spilled. The Gemara concludes that despite all these distinct applications, one receives lashes for none of them — *al kulam eino lokei* — because a prohibition that encompasses such heterogeneous cases is the quintessential *lav she-bichlalut*.

The Gemara then reverses Avdimi's ruling entirely.
