The version transmitted by Ravin in the name of Rabbi Elazar states the opposite: *al kulan eino lokei* — one receives no lashes for any of the acts in the Mishna — except precisely for vowing and swearing in the name of another god. For those, one does receive lashes, because the prohibition is specific and explicit — derived from the verse *shem elohim acherim lo tazkiru, lo yishama al picha* — not a vague generic formulation. But since the *rabbanan* hold that lashes require a physical act, the issue requires the position of Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that lashes apply even to a *lav she-ein bo ma'aseh* — a prohibition that lacks a physical component — to explain why lashes would apply to swearing as well.

The evidence for Rabbi Yehuda's position is the *baraita* concerning *lo sosiru* — do not leave the *korban* overnight. Rabbi Yehuda says one does not receive lashes there because the *asei* of burning it corrects the *lav*. This implies that absent the corrective *asei*, Rabbi Yehuda would impose lashes even for a passive transgression. Rabbi Yaakov disagrees: the reason there are no lashes is not the corrective *asei* but rather the inherent rule that a *lav she-ein bo ma'aseh* never supports lashes. The inference from Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning is that he holds lashes do apply to passive violations — and consequently to verbal acts as well.

---

## Vows/Oaths Prohibition

### Lo Tazkiru Verse

The Gemara now turns to the verse *ve-shem elohim acherim lo tazkiru* — "and the name of other gods you shall not mention" — and unpacks its scope through a *baraita*.

### Mention Examples

The *baraita* derives from *lo tazkiru* the prohibition against mentioning the names of other gods in everyday speech. The example given: one may not say to a friend, *shemor li be-tzad avodas kochavim peloni* — wait for me by that such-and-such idol — because in doing so one has casually invoked the name of a foreign deity.

### Lo Yishama Meaning

The verse continues: *lo yishama al picha* — it shall not be heard through your mouth. This phrase extends the prohibition beyond incidental mention to active religious use: *she-lo yidor bishmo ve-she-lo yekayeim bishmo* — one may not take a vow in the name of another god, and one may not fulfill a vow in the name of another god. This is a weightier form of engagement: the deity's name is being invoked in a formal religious act of commitment.

### Causing Others Oath

From the same phrase — *lo yishama al picha* — the *baraita* also derives that one may not cause others to swear by the name of another god. The scope extends even to non-Jews: if your conduct results in a non-Jew taking an oath in the name of their deity, you have violated *lo yishama al picha*. One further derivation from this phrase: *azhara le-madiach* — a warning against the one who incites an entire town toward *avoda zara*. While the incitement of an individual is prohibited by an explicit verse — *ve-chol Yisrael yishme'u ve-yira'un* — the analogous prohibition for inciting a community was not otherwise stated, and *lo yishama al picha* provides the source.

A note on the relationship between the two prohibitions: why does one need a verse prohibiting vows and oaths in the name of another god, if one is already prohibited from merely mentioning the name? One might say — and this appears to be the Rambam's position — that the *ikkar* prohibition, the core biblical prohibition, is the use of the divine name in a formal religious act: the vow or the oath. The prohibition against casual mention is secondary, perhaps rabbinic in character. Tosafot, however, understands even the casual mention as a biblical prohibition. This distinction has practical implications for how one treats the invocation of divine names associated with other religions in everyday discourse.

### Partnership Prohibition

The Gemara notes that Abba de-Shmuel's teaching is supported by this analysis: *asur le-adam she-ya'aseh shutafus im ha-oved kochavim* — it is forbidden to enter into a business partnership with an idolater. The concern is concrete: *shema yitchayeiv lo shvua* — the idolater may become obligated to take an oath in the course of the partnership, and when he does so, he will naturally swear in the name of his deity. Since the Jew would have been the proximate cause of that oath being taken, they will have violated *lo yishama al picha*. The obligation of honesty in commerce, in the absence of forensic accounting, was enforced through oaths — and this makes partnership with an idolater a structurally problematic arrangement.

---

## Tosafot Christianity

### Rabbeinu Tam Allow

The discussion of *lo yishama al picha* raises a pressing practical question: how did medieval Jews conduct financial dealings with Christians, who would inevitably be called upon to take oaths in the course of litigation or commerce? Rabbeinu Tam rules that it is permitted to take an oath from a Christian, at least to prevent financial loss. His reasoning is grounded in a principle found in the first chapter of *Avoda Zara*: one may collect a debt from a non-Jew even before his holiday because this is considered *ke-matzil mi-yadam* — saving one's assets from their possession.

### Saints Names Argument

Tosafot's first argument in support of Rabbeinu Tam's position is substantive: *bizman hazeh kulam nishba'in be-kadashim shelahem ve-ein tofsim bahem elohut* — in the present era, Christians take oaths by their *kadashim*, their saints, and they do not attribute divine status to those saints. A saint is not a god. Therefore, when a Christian swears by a saint's name, they are not swearing by *shem elohim acherim* — the name of another god — and the prohibition of *lo yishama al picha* is not triggered.

### Combining Names

The second complication is that Christian oaths typically invoke not only saints but also God — combining the divine name with the saint's name. This raises the concern of *mishtatef shem shamayim ve-davar acher* — combining God's name with something else. Tosafot addresses this: even if such combination were problematic for Jews, it is not a violation that non-Jews are prohibited from making. *Bnei Noach lo huzharu be-chach* — the laws given to the descendants of Noah do not include a prohibition against combining God's name with a saint's name in an oath. Therefore, causing a Christian to take such an oath is not *lifnei iver* — placing a stumbling block before the blind — since the Christian does not transgress in doing so.

### God Father Concept

The third and perhaps most theologically arresting point Tosafot makes — and this is the point that would prove to be historically consequential — is that when Christians say "God," they are referring to *avihem she-bashamayim* — God the Father. This is, Tosafot argues, the same God that Jews believe in. The name is not the name of another god; it refers to the Creator and sovereign of the universe, the God of Israel. The problem with the Christian oath, to the extent one exists, lies not in the invocation of God but in the additional elements — and those, as just established, are not a problem for non-Jews.

### Later Reinterpretation

These three arguments allow Tosafot to permit, in cases of financial necessity, taking an oath from a Christian: the saints' names are not divine names, the combination with God's name is not prohibited for non-Jews, and the word "God" itself refers to a shared theological referent. Tosafot is making a narrow halachic argument about the mechanics of oath-taking and the application of *lo yishama al picha* in medieval Europe.

What is historically remarkable is how this passage was subsequently read. The observation that Christians combine God — understood as God the Father, creator of heaven and earth — with other elements, and that this combination is not *avoda zara* for non-Jews, was later taken to make a far broader claim: that even if Christianity as a whole constitutes *avoda zara* from the perspective of Jewish law, it may not constitute *avoda zara* for non-Jews, provided they retain some version of the monotheistic God concept. For *bnei Noach*, adding other elements to that core God concept — including the other persons of the Trinity — may not violate the Noahide prohibition against *avoda zara*.

It bears emphasis: this is not what Tosafot was saying. Tosafot was addressing a specific, narrow question about causing a Christian to invoke a combined oath-formula in a business or legal dispute. But the passage was read to yield a broad halachic framework for how to characterize Christianity's theological status vis-à-vis the Noahide laws — a reinterpretation that became extremely influential in subsequent halachic literature on the status of Christianity. The precise scope of *lo yishama al picha* — how far the prohibition of mentioning the name of another god extends, whether it applies only to formal religious acts or to casual invocation, and whether it is biblical or rabbinic — and the theological implications of Tosafot's recognition of a shared divine referent in Jewish and Christian discourse remain live questions.

# Sanhedrin 64

## Foreign God Names

### Ulla in Kalanbo

The daf opens in the middle of a discussion concerning swearing by and mentioning the names of foreign gods, picking up from the previous session's analysis of the *Tosfos* bearing on how *halakha* treats Christianity. The Gemara now presents the case of Ulla.

*Ki ata Ulla bat be-Kalanbo* — when Ulla came, he lodged in a place called Kalanbo, which was apparently the name of some foreign god. Rava challenged him: *ve-heicha bat mar* — where did you sleep? The issue was not the lodging itself but that Ulla had spoken the name of the town. Rava cited the verse *ve-shem elohim acherim lo tazkiru* — you shall not mention the names of other gods. How, then, could Ulla have said the name Kalanbo?

Ulla responded with a ruling in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *kol avodat kochavim de-ksiva be-Torah mutar lehazkir shemah* — any form of idolatrous worship whose name is already written in the Torah may be mentioned. Torah is understood here in its broader sense as *Tanakh*. The verse *kara Bel kares Nevo* — Bel bowed down, Nevo crouched — already contains the name Nevo, and the name Kalanbo (*Kal Nevo*) incorporates that name. Since it appears in *Tanakh*, it may be stated.

### Scriptural Examples

One might ask: what of a foreign god's name that does not appear anywhere in *Tanakh*? To address this, the Gemara brings a *Mishnah* from the laws of *zav*, in which Rav Mesharshaya teaches that one large emission is equivalent to three if it spans the time required to walk from Migiddon to Shilo — that is, the time needed for two immersions and two dryings in between. The relevance here is that Migiddon, from the root *Gad* (gimmel-dalet), is the name of an idolatrous deity, and the *Mishnah* uses it freely. The Gemara then asks where this name appears in *Tanakh*, and Ravina answers: *Gad nami k'siv* — the name Gad also appears explicitly in *Tanakh*, as the verse states *ha-orkhim le-Gad shulchan* — those who set a table for Gad, this idol.

A tangential question arises regarding names like the days of the week or the months of the year, which derive from Babylonian gods. The general assumption is that gods no longer actively worshipped pose no problem, and that if the language of daily life is suffused with such references, conversation would become nearly impossible. The names of the months, notably, were brought back from Babylonia, and some of them are the names of Babylonian deities. Whether they were still being actively worshipped at the time is a genuine question left open.

### Mocking Idolatry

Rav Nachman then states a broader principle: *kol leitzanuta asura chutz mi-leitzanuta de-avodat kochavim* — all mockery is forbidden except mockery of *avodah zarah*, which is permitted. The proof text is the same verse from the prophet: *kara Bel kares Nevo, kirsu karu yachdav, lo yachlu malet massa* — Bel bowed, Nevo crouched, they crouched together, they could not escape the burden. The imagery implies that these gods were unable to manage their food and were forced to defecate — a deliberate literary mockery of idolatrous deities already found in the *nevi'im*. Eliyahu HaNavi famously employs a similar rhetorical strategy, and the Torah itself participates in this mockery, a point the Gemara reinforces shortly.

Another verse: *dibru la-aglot* — speak to the calves, referring to the *eglei zahav* of the northern kingdom, called *Beit Aven* (the house of sin) rather than *Beit El*. The verse continues: *yaguru shochen shamron* — those who dwell in Samaria shall fear, *ki avel alav amo* — for the nation will mourn for their calf when it is taken into exile. The priests, however, *yagilu* — will rejoice — *al kvodo ki gala mimenu* — over its honor having departed. The Gemara reads this as *al tikrei kvodo ela kveido* — do not read "its honor" but "its weight," meaning the priests will be relieved of the burden of managing all the waste of these calves.

---

## Motives for Idolatry

### Starving Calves

Rabbi Yitzchak opens a new inquiry: *mai de-chsiv ve-ata yosifu lachato vayaasu lahem massecha mikaspam kithvunam* — now they have added sin and made for themselves a molten image from their silver, according to their image, *atzabim*. *Mai kithvunam atzabim* — what does it mean "according to their image"? The teaching is: *melamed she-kol echad ve-echad asa dmut yirato* — every individual fashioned a likeness of his own deity and kept it in his pouch. Whenever he thought of his god, he would take it out, embrace it, and kiss it — it became a personal talisman.

The Gemara then turns to the verse: *mai zovchei adam agalim yishakun* — those who slaughter people will kiss the calves. Rabbi Yitzchak in the name of Rabbi Ammi explains: *she-hayu meshartei avodah zarah nosnim eineihem be-baalei mammon* — the attendants of the idols would set their eyes on wealthy individuals. They would then starve the calves — the very objects of worship — and fashion images of those wealthy people, placing the images before the calves' feeding troughs. When they brought out these starving calves and the wealthy worshippers were present, the calves, having seen only their images, would run toward them and rub against them. The priests would declare: *avodah zarah chafetz be-cha* — the god desires you, and would urge the person to offer himself as a sacrifice. That is the meaning of *zovchei adam* — the slaughter of people to the calves.

As for *agalim yishakun*, the kissing of the calves — Rava corrects the reading. The verse should be understood as: they kiss the calves *in order to* slaughter people, not as a subsequent reward. Rashi explains that it was the calves who rubbed and kissed the people, not the priests kissing the calves afterward. Rava himself offers a second reading: *kol hazoveach et bno l'avodat kochavim* — whoever slaughters his son to the gods — the priest would tell him, *doron gadol hikriv lo* — you have brought a great offering; *yavo ve-yishak lo* — come and kiss the god. That is the sense of *zovchei adam* paired with *agalim yishakun*.

The Gemara then continues with a list of idols worshipped by the various nations enumerated in Melachim. The people of Babylonia made *Succoth Benot* — which is a hen. The people of Cuth made *Nergal* — a rooster. The people of Hamath made *Ashima* — a bald goat, so called because it has no wool. The Avvim made *Nivchan* and *Tartak* — a dog and a donkey, the dog deriving from the root *nivach* (to bark). The Sepharvim burned their sons in fire for *Adrammelech* and *Anammelech*, the gods of Sepharvaim — a mule and a horse respectively. *Adrammelech* derives from *adar*, meaning it honors its master by bearing his burden, while *Anammelech* derives from *ani*, meaning it answers and follows its master even into battle.

The Gemara adds that even Chizkiyahu, king of Judah, nearly became a victim of this ritual — his father Achaz, of whom it is written *gam et bno he'evir ba'esh*, had passed his son through the fire. Since Chizkiyahu is the only son we know of, it must have been him they attempted to burn. He was saved, Rashi explains, because his mother had anointed him with the oil of a salamander — a creature said to emerge from an oven in which fire has burned for seven years — which rendered him impervious to flame.

### Sexual Freedom Motive

With all these forms of *avodah zarah* enumerated — and now knowing which names may be spoken freely since they appear in *Tanakh* — the Gemara returns to a deeper question: if these idols are such a mockery, why did Israel ever stray after them?

Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav states: *yodin hayu Yisrael be-avodat kochavim she'ein bah mamash* — Israel always knew that idolatry was meaningless. *Ve-lo avdu avodat kochavim ela le-hatir lahem arayot be-farhesya* — they only worshipped idols in order to permit themselves illicit sexual relations in public. The motivation was not theological conviction but the desire for freedom from the Torah's demanding constraints in the realm of sexuality. It may also be that some pagan worship rituals themselves involved sexual acts, but even setting that aside, the Torah is extraordinarily demanding in matters of sexual restraint, and people wanted greater freedom.

This evokes a perennial question: when someone abandons religious observance, is it truly for theological reasons or for other motivations? The teaching suggests that in Israel's case, the questions were, as it were, the answers — the desire for freedom came first, and the theological posture followed.

### Child & Idol

Rav Mesharshya challenges Rav Yehuda: *ki zachor benehem mizbechotam* — they would remember their altars as one remembers a cherished son. Rabbi Elazar describes the emotional intensity: *ke-adam she-yesh lo ga'aguim al bno* — like a person who aches with longing for a son far away. Surely this reflects genuine passion and not mere opportunism?

The answer given is *batar d'idabku beih* — that was after they had already begun to cleave to idolatry. The initial motivation may have been the desire for sexual license, but once they spent extended time as *ovdei avodah zarah*, they began to develop a genuine, deep attachment. The point is psychologically acute: there are things that initially motivate a person, and then — once committed to an entire way of life — it is too late, because the desire has been thoroughly internalized.

A second challenge is raised from the verse *ve-natati pigrechem al pigrei giluleichem* — I will place your corpses upon the corpses of your idols. The word *giluleichem* is itself a mockery — a near-homophone for *galal*, excrement. This leads into the story of Eliyahu HaTzaddik.

Eliyahu was going about Jerusalem during a famine, tending to those bloated from starvation. He found an infant, bloated and lying in a refuse heap. He asked where the child was from, and the child replied he was the sole survivor of a once-prominent family. Eliyahu asked: if I teach you something that will give you life, will you learn it? The child agreed. Eliyahu said: recite *Shma Yisrael Hashem Elokeinu Hashem Echad* — accept God as your God and abandon idolatry; that is what will give you life.

The child replied: *chas she-lo lehazkir be-shem Hashem* — God forbid that I should speak God's name — citing an actual verse, *chas le-hazkir be-shem Hashem*. He said: *she-lo limdu avi ve-imi* — my father and mother never taught me this. He immediately took his small idol from his cloak, embraced it, kissed it — until his stomach burst and he fell upon his idol, fulfilling the verse: *ve-natati pigrechem al pigrei giluleichem* — I will place your corpse upon the corpse of your idols — and in the most visceral sense, since his entire belly had exploded.

Could one say, then, that Israel engaged in idolatry merely to permit themselves sexual sins, when they were willing to die for their idols? Again: *batar d'idabku beih* — that is after they began to cleave to it. That is a profound observation: once something is truly internalized, a person will sacrifice everything for it, regardless of what originally drew them in.

### Second Temple Yeitzer

The Gemara now transitions to a famous *agadata* about the leaders of the *Bayit Sheni* period. In the time of Nechemya, *vayiz'aku be-kol gadol el Hashem Elokeihem* — the leaders called out in a great voice to God. What did they say? Rav Yehuda, and some say Rav Yonatan, teaches: *Baya Baya* — woe, woe. They were speaking about the *yetzer hara* for *avodah zarah*. This is the force that destroyed the Temple, burned the sanctuary, caused the righteous to be murdered, sent Israel into exile — *ve-adayin hu meraked beinan* — and it is still dancing among us, here at the threshold of the Second Temple era, with people still feeling drawn to *avodah zarah*.

*Clum yahvteya lan ela le-kabuli bei agra* — the only reason God gave us this desire was so that we could receive reward by conquering it. But, they declared, *lo ihu beinan ve-lo agra beinan* — we want neither it nor its reward. We are better off without it.

The leaders fasted for three days and prayed to God to remove the *yetzer hara* of *avodah zarah*. A little note fell from heaven bearing the word *emet* — truth — signifying divine assent. Rav Chanina notes: *chotamo shel HaKadosh Baruch Hu emet* — God's seal is truth. From the Holy of Holies emerged something resembling a fiery lion cub. The *navi* told the people: *hainu yitzra de-avoda zara* — that is the *yetzer hara* of *avodah zarah*.

This is a striking detail. The *yetzer hara* for *avodah zarah* emerges from the *Kodesh Kodashim* itself. One might understand this as a profound theological statement: the *Beit HaMikdash*, with all its physical grandeur and the *keruvim* in the inner sanctum, represents a kind of divine concession to the human need for a tangible, concrete focal point for worship. The line between that legitimate concession and the *yetzer hara* of idolatry is genuinely thin. The lion cub is also not at full strength — it is a cub — suggesting that once one begins pursuing *avodah zarah*, the *yetzer* grows stronger. Perhaps too it emphasizes how narrow the boundary is between genuine *kedushah* and its corruption.

They seized it, but as they grabbed it, a single hair fell from it, and the sound traveled four hundred *parasangs*. Concerned that heaven might reverse its decision out of compassion, they followed the *navi*'s counsel and placed the *yetzer hara* in a lead cauldron, sealing it with a leaden stone — fulfilling the verse in Zechariah: *zot ha-risha*, this is the wicked one, cast into the vessel, and the leaden stone placed over its mouth. Its voice was muffled. It was not destroyed; it was subdued.

Emboldened by their success, the leaders now prayed that they might similarly subdue the *yetzer hara* of sexual sin — since they were in a moment when heaven was receptive to their requests. God granted their request. They locked it away for three days — and immediately no fresh eggs could be found. The hens had stopped laying. All aspects of reproductive and sexual function were intertwined with this *yetzer*. They realized they could not simply eliminate it; they could not ask for half — *palga me-reki'a lo yahavi* — heaven does not give halfway. They could not ask to remove only the desire for sexual transgression while preserving healthy sexuality.

So as they released it, they managed to injure it slightly: *kachlinhu le-einei* — they blurred or blinded its eyes — *ahani bei* — and this had one measurable effect: *d'lo igrei inish bi-krovatei* — the desire for incest was diminished. The lust for a non-spouse or a *niddah* remained, but the incest drive was somewhat tamed. Not eliminated, but tamed.

Notice the intertwining of the two *yeitzarim* throughout this entire passage: Israel first worshipped *avodah zarah* to permit themselves sexual freedom; when they finally sought to remove the *yetzer hara* of *avodah zarah*, they immediately turned to the *yetzer* of sexuality. The two are deeply linked. According to this account, the deep human draw toward *avodah zarah* was something that had been internalized over centuries of pursuit — the initial motivation was sexual freedom, but what emerged was a genuine, autonomous *yetzer* for idolatry itself, one that had to be captured and sealed away. This *agadata* will be revisited in a later *perek* as well.

---

## Case Examples

### Pagan Woman

Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav relates: *ma'aseh be-nochrit achat she-hayta chola beyoter* — a non-Jewish woman was gravely ill and on the verge of death. She declared: *im ta'amod hahi isha me-cholya* — if this woman recovers from her illness — *telech ve-ta'avod le-chol avodah zarah she-ba-olam* — I will go and worship every god in the world, covering all my bases in case any one of them was responsible for my recovery. She recovered, and set off on her tour of the world's deities.

When she came to the temple of *Peor*, she asked the priests: *be-mah ovdin le-zo* — how does one worship this god? They told her: you eat beets, drink mead, and then *matrizin be-faneha* — you defecate, in a quite unrestrained fashion, before it. She said: *mutav she-tachazor hi isha le-chola* — I would rather return to my sickness and die than worship a god in this disgusting manner. Even this non-Jewish woman, who had set out to worship every deity, drew the line at the worship of *Peor*.

This sets up a pointed contrast. The verse says of Israel: *ha-nitzmadim le-Baal Peor* — you who cleaved to Baal Peor. The word *nitzmadim* evokes *tzamid patil* — a hermetically sealed jar lid, completely vacuum-packed, utterly adhered. When Israel ran after Baal Peor, nothing could separate them from it. And compare that with how they related to God: *ve-atem ha-dvekim ba-Hashem Elokeichem* — you who cling to God — the word here is merely *dvekim*, like two dates stuck together, easily pulled apart. A severe condemnation: Israel was far more passionately attached to its *avodah zarah* than it ever was to God.

A *baraita* reads this in a softer key. *Nitzmadim* need not be read as the tight seal of a jar but as *k'tzamid al yedei isha* — like a bracelet on a woman's arm, loosely hanging, with air between it and the skin. By this reading, Israel's attachment to Baal Peor was not so extreme — and *ve-atem ha-dvekim ba-Hashem Elokeichem*, your clinging to God, is the truly profound bond. The two versions thus present opposite evaluations of Israel's relative attachment to idolatry versus God.

### Savta ben Alas

The Gemara brings a further story: *ma'aseh be-Savta ben Alas* — the case of Savta ben Alas (or, according to some readings, from the city of Alas), a Jew who worked as a donkey driver. He rented his donkey to a non-Jewish woman and took her on a journey. When they arrived at a temple of *Peor*, she said: wait here while I go in to perform my worship and then come out. After she emerged, he said to her: wait here by the donkey while I also go in. She said: *ve-lo Yehudi ata* — are you not a Jew? He replied: *u-mah ichpat lach* — what concern is it of yours? He entered, *paar be-fanav* — defecated before the idol — and then wiped himself on the idol's nose. The attendants of the *avodah zarah* praised him effusively, saying that no one had ever worshipped their god in such a perfect manner. A final ironic mockery: the most degrading act imaginable was understood by the worshippers as the highest form of devotion.

These narratives together close out a sustained exploration of the *yetzer hara de-avodah zarah* and its deep entanglement with sexual drive, the process of internalization, and the Gemara's persistent undercurrent of mockery directed at idolatrous practice.

---

## Molech Act & Intent

### Defecation Intent

The Gemara now returns to strictly *halachic* discussion. *Ha-po'er atzmo le-Baal Peor harei zo avodato* — if one defecates before Baal Peor, that constitutes its act of worship and is therefore *avodah zarah*. This is so *af al gav de-michavein le-vazuya* — even if the person's intent was to degrade the idol, to perform an act of contempt or shame toward it. Intent to disgrace does not exempt one; the act itself is the act of worship.

### Throwing Stones

Similarly: *ha-zorek even le-Markulis harei zu avodato* — one who throws a stone to Markulis has performed its act of worship — *af al gav de-michavein le-mirgemei* — even if one intended the throw as an act of stoning, that is, of attacking the idol rather than venerating it. The act is determinative.

### Rav Menashya

A related episode illustrates the point. Rav Menashya was traveling to a place called Bei Tortah. People warned him: there is an idol there. He noticed the idol and, to show his contempt, *shakal patta shada bah* — took a clod of earth and threw it at the idol. Then they added: by the way, it is *Markulis*. He said: the *Mishnah* says one who throws a stone *to* Markulis — I threw it *at* it. He went to the *beit midrash* to confirm his reading, and they told him: no, even *be-Markulis* — even throwing at it — constitutes *avodah zarah*, since even a contemptuous throw is the established mode of worship.

He then asked: should he go and remove the stone, so that it should not remain there as his offering to the *avodah zarah*? They told him: *echad ha-notlah ve-echad ha-notnah chayav* — both placing a stone and removing a stone constitute acts of worship. The reason: *chada ve-chada revacha le-chavereih shevik* — each stone that is removed makes room for the next worshipper to add his own. Removal is itself a participatory act in the cult. He who inadvertently commits the act and then attempts to undo it has only compounded the transgression.

This raises a fundamental question that the *Rishonim* must address. Earlier, the Gemara discussed — particularly in the debate between Abaye and Rava — whether one who worships an idol *me-ahava u-me-yira* (from love or fear of a person, not genuine theological conviction) is liable. Rava's position seemed to require that worship be motivated by genuine belief. If so, how can throwing a stone in contempt, or defecating in degradation, constitute *avodah zarah*?

Tosafot addresses this in two ways. One approach holds that in these cases one would not be subject to the death penalty — only a *korban* would be required, since the act was performed without the proper intent, analogous to *shogeg*. Even if the intent completely changes the character of the act, the formal act of *avodah zarah* was performed, and that carries its own consequence.

Tosafot's second approach holds that even contemptuous worship implies a background belief in the deity. The person who defiles the idol is not saying it does not exist; he may believe in it but be expressing anger, or he may be performing the degrading act in a paradoxically worshipful way — the way one might take a *lulav* resentfully and still have taken the *lulav*.

A third approach, drawn from commentators on the Rambam, introduces a significant distinction: the requirements of intent — *ahava ve-yira* — apply specifically when someone is fashioning a new god from nothing, or when someone designates an object ad hoc as a deity for the first time. In such a case, the inner act of acceptance is constitutive; without it, nothing has happened. But when a god already has an established following, recognized rituals, and an interpreted cult, the act speaks for itself. If one performs the established act of worship of an established religion, it is *avodah zarah* regardless of what is occurring in one's mind, because the act carries established meaning within the community of worshippers. This reading significantly limits the scope of the earlier *ahava ve-yira* discussion: that discussion pertains only to cases involving a newly designated deity.

---

## Molech Prohibition

### Molech vs Idolatry

The *Mishnah* at the start of a new section lists, among the transgressions punishable by *sekilah*, both *avodah zarah* and the worship of *Molech* as distinct categories. That they are listed separately suggests that *Molech* worship may not simply be a subspecies of *avodah zarah* but a distinct transgression altogether. Rabbi Avin teaches that the *Mishnah* follows the opinion that *molech lav avodah zarah hi* — the Molech ritual is not *avodah zarah*. It is a pagan ritual but not the worship of a deity. This is comprehensible: one can imagine rituals believed to engage metaphysical forces without constituting the worship of a god in the conventional sense.

A *baraita* records the dispute explicitly: the majority opinion holds that the prohibition applies equally to *Molech* and to any other form of *avodah zarah* — *echad ha-Molech ve-echad she'ar avodah zarah chayav*. Rabbi Eliezer bar Rabbi Shimon disagrees: *la-Molech chayav, she-lo la-Molech patur* — one is liable only for the Molech ritual specifically, not for performing this act in the service of any other deity.

The reasoning behind this debate is exegetical. If Molech worship is a form of *avodah zarah*, the Torah would not need to single it out — it would already be prohibited by the general prohibition against *avodah zarah*. The Torah's singling it out must therefore add something: namely, that one is liable even when performing this act not in its conventional manner, which would apply to any deity. Conversely, if Molech is not *avodah zarah*, the Torah mentions it because it is a distinct pagan ritual — and then the prohibition is inherently limited to this specific ritual, performed specifically to the Molech, whatever that entity is.

### Two Components

Rabbi Yannai clarifies the requirements articulated in the *Mishnah*: *eino chayav ad she-yimsarenu le-meshartei avodah zarah* — one is not liable unless one hands the child over to the attendants. The verse says *lo titten le-ha'avir la-Molech* — do not give over to pass through to the Molech. Two distinct acts are required: handing over and passing through fire. If one handed over without the fire-passing, or passed through fire without the formal hand-over to the priests, one is not liable. Both components must be fulfilled.

The *Mishnah* itself states this explicitly: *eino chayav ad she-yimsor la-Molech ve-ya'avir ba-esh* — one is not liable until one hands over to the Molech and passes through fire. *Masar la-Molech ve-lo he'evir ba-esh* — handed over but did not pass through; *he'evir ba-esh ve-lo masar la-Molech* — passed through but did not hand over: in either case, *eino chayav*.

A *braita* elaborates: *ve-natata lo* — perhaps passing through fire without handing over the child to a priest would be sufficient for liability? No — *talmud lomar lo titten* — the verse says "do not give," so the giving over is essential. Conversely: *masar la-Molech ve-lo he'evir* — perhaps handing over without the fire-passing suffices? No — *talmud lomar le-ha'avir* — the verse specifies the passing through. Each component is derived independently.

The *braita* then asks: *masar ve-he'evir she-lo la-Molech yachol yehei chayav* — perhaps one is liable even if the act was performed for some other deity, not the Molech? No — *talmud lomar la-Molech* — the verse specifies to the Molech. Each word of the verse — *lo titten, le-ha'avir, la-Molech* — is read as limiting or expanding the law in a distinct way.

### Verse Integration

The next question is whether fire is definitionally required. The verse in the Molech prohibition (*lo titten le-ha'avir la-Molech*) does not mention fire. However, a parallel verse in Devarim states: *lo yimatze becha ma'avir beno u-vito ba-esh* — let not be found among you one who passes his son or daughter through fire. The Gemara integrates the two: *mah le-hallan ba-esh, af kan ba-esh* — just as that verse involves fire, so too the Molech prohibition involves fire. And conversely, *u-mah kan Molech, af le-hallan* — just as the first verse specifies Molech, the fire-verse too refers to Molech. The two passages describe the same ritual, and reading them together supplies both elements — fire and the specific deity — to the combined prohibition.

### Definition of Zera

The *Mishnah* speaks of giving over one's *zera* — seed. The verse *lo yimatze becha ma'avir beno u-vito ba-esh* specifies *bno u-vito* — his son or his daughter. A *braita* asks: from son or daughter alone, I might think the prohibition extends only to direct children. How do I know it applies to grandchildren — *ben bno u-vat bito*? The verse *ki mi-zaro natan la-Molech* — for he gave from his seed — uses the word *zera*, which is broad enough to include grandchildren. A second verse, *be-tito mi-zaro la-Molech*, supplies an additional *derashah*: *zaro* in the singular might suggest only *zera kasher* — legitimate offspring. How do I know that even *zera pasul* — a *mamzer* — is included? The extra phrase *mi-zaro* is read to include even such a case.

Rav Acha the son of Rava raises an additional ruling: *he'evir kol zaro patur* — if a person passed all of his children through the Molech ritual at one and the same time, he is exempt, since the verse says *mi-zaro* — from his seed — but not *kol zaro* — all of his seed. Tosafot clarifies: this cannot mean that performing the act for one child and then later for another retroactively exempts the first violation. Rather, the case is either one in which the person had only a single child (so that one child constitutes all his seed) or one in which all the children were passed through simultaneously.

Rav Ashi then raises questions left unresolved: *he'eviro suma mahu, yashen mahu* — what is the ruling if the child was blind, or if the child was asleep at the time? *Ben beno bat bito mahu* — what about grandchildren? The grandchildren question is resolved from the *braita* above. The questions of blind or sleeping children are left unresolved.

### Manner of Passing

The *Mishnah* requires that the child be passed *derekh ha-avara* — in the normal manner of passing. Abaye explains: *sharga de-livnei mi-beinitzia* — there would be a row of bricks running down the center, with fires burning on either side; the child would walk along the bricks between the two fires. Rava offers a different image: *ke-mashvarta de-puraya* — like the jumping over a bonfire that people do on *Purim*. The child would jump over a fire pit.

A *baraita* supports Rava's position: *eino chayav ad she-ya'avirenu derekh ha-avara* — one is liable only for the normal mode of passing. *He'eviro be-regel patur* — if one merely walked through without the jumping motion, one is exempt. Since walking disqualifies, the act must consist of leaping, not walking — consistent with Rava's description of jumping over a fire pit rather than walking between two fires.

### Recipients

The liability extends downward through the generations — son, daughter, grandchildren — but not upward or laterally. *Aviv ve-imo, achiv ve-achoto* — passing one's father, mother, brother, or sister through the fire: *patur* — exempt. The prohibition is directed at one's descendants, not one's ancestors or siblings.

### Self-Sacrifice

*He'evir atzmo patur* — if a person passed himself through the Molech fire, he is also exempt, according to the majority. *Rabbi Elazar be-Rabbi Shimon mechayiv* — Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon holds him liable.

Ulla explains Rabbi Eliezer bar Rabbi Shimon's reasoning: the verse *lo yimatze becha ma'avir beno u-vito ba-esh* contains the word *becha* — in you. He reads *becha be-atzmecha* — do not even do this to yourself. The self is included in the prohibition.

The Gemara challenges: the Rabbis also use *becha* in other contexts to derive similar points. The *Mishnah* teaches that one's own lost object takes precedence over one's father's — *shelo kodemet le-shel kol adam* — and this is derived from the verse *efes ki lo yihyeh becha evyon*, read as: do not let yourself become poor. If the Rabbis use *becha* to mean "you yourself," why do they not do so here?

The Gemara answers: *hatam me-Efes* — there, it is not merely the word *becha* that does the work; it is the word *efes* (eliminate, make disappear) in conjunction with *becha* that teaches one must eliminate poverty from oneself first. The word *becha* alone, in the Molech verse, does not carry the same force for the majority, and therefore they exempt one who passes himself through the fire. Rabbi Eliezer bar Rabbi Shimon, however, reads *becha* independently and derives from it that one is liable even for oneself.

The daf concludes here, with only a few lines remaining to be addressed in the following session.

---

# Sanhedrin 65

## Kareit in Avodah Zarah

### Three Kritot Intro

The daf opens on 64b with a statement by Rabbi Yossi bar Abin Chanina: *shalosh kritot b'avodah zarah* — there are three separate instances of *kareit* stated in the Torah in connection with *avodah zarah*. The immediate question is: why does the Torah find it necessary to write *kareit* three times in this context? What work does each one do?

### K'Darkah vs Lo K'Darkah

The Gemara answers that the three serve distinct purposes. One *kareit* addresses worshipping *avodah zarah* *k'darkah* — in the manner that that particular idol is normally worshipped, such as throwing stones at the idol known as *Markolis*. A second addresses worship *lo k'darkah* — in a manner that departs from the idol's usual mode of worship. The third addresses *le-Molech* — the act of passing one's child through the fire for the sake of Molech.

It should be noted that two of the three verses referenced here relate specifically to Molech. The Gemara's point is that one of those two Molech-related verses is pressed into service to derive the general rule of *lo k'darkah*, while the other addresses Molech directly.

### Molech as Avodah Zarah

The Gemara then turns to a specific dispute: what is the view of the one who holds that Molech is simply a subspecies of *avodah zarah*? For that opinion, the *kareit* assigned to Molech would seemingly be redundant — worship of *avodah zarah* already carries *kareit*, whether *k'darkah* or *lo k'darkah*. What, then, does this third *kareit* add?

The answer given is that it teaches the case of *he-avir beno le-Markolis* — one who passes his child through for Markolis rather than for Molech. This constitutes a *lo k'darkah* form of the Molech ritual applied to a different idol, and the separate *kareit* establishes this as a distinct *chiyuv*. The Mishnah elsewhere, it should be noted, does not enumerate this case among those liable to *skilah*, since the liability in question is *kareit* rather than *mitat beit din*; the four modes of execution in the Mishnah require a full *maaseh*, whereas *kareit* can obtain independently.

### Megadef & Two Kareits

The Gemara then presents a parallel question for the one who holds that *megadef* — blasphemy — is itself a form of *avodah zarah*. For that opinion, why is there a *kareit* specifically for *megadef*? The Gemara answers by citing a *braita*: *hikaret tikaret* — the doubled language implies two instances of *kareit*, one in *olam hazeh* and one in *olam haba*. That is, the verse about *megadef* teaches that one who blasphemes is cut off in both this world and the world to come.

### Rabbi Akiva Response

Rabbi Yishmael objects: we already know from another verse, *ve-nikhreta ha-nefesh ha-hi*, that *avodah zarah* carries *kareit* — including both *olam hazeh* and *olam haba*. Does the existence of a third verse imply a third world? Rabbi Akiva responds that this is simply a case of *dibra Torah kile-shon bnei adam* — the Torah speaks in the manner of human beings, using emphatic repetition for rhetorical force. The doubled language of *hikaret tikaret* does not introduce new legal content; it is ordinary stylistic emphasis, and we already derive the two-world *kareit* from the earlier verse.

---

## Ba'al Ov & Yidoni

### Ba'al Ov Defined

The Gemara moves to the beginning of the Mishnah on 65a, which introduces two additional categories of those liable to *skilah*: the *ba'al ov* and the *yidoni*. The Mishnah defines the *ba'al ov* as *zeh ha-pitom ha-medaber mi-shichyo* — this is the *pitom*, a particular type of practitioner, who speaks from his armpit. The *yidoni* is defined as *zeh ha-medaber be-piv* — one who speaks from his mouth. Both carry the death penalty of *skilah*. The Mishnah adds that one who consults either of these practitioners — who seeks them out to learn from them — violates a *lav*, an *azharah*, and may be liable to bring a *korban*.

### Omission Query

The Gemara raises a comparison between our Mishnah and the Mishnah in Masechet Kritot. Our Mishnah lists both *ba'al ov* and *yidoni*. The Mishnah in Kritot — which enumerates all the Torah transgressions that carry *kareit* and for which one who acts inadvertently must bring a *korban chatat* — mentions *ba'al ov* but omits *yidoni* altogether. The question is: why the asymmetry? Both seem structurally comparable, and yet Kritot singles out only one.

### Rabbi Yochanan

Rabbi Yochanan explains that both *ba'al ov* and *yidoni* are in fact included in the Mishnah in Kritot — they are stated together in a single *lav* in the Torah, and therefore teaching one is sufficient to encompass the other. The Mishnah in Kritot mentions *ba'al ov* alone, but *yidoni* is implicitly covered.

### Reish Lakish

Reish Lakish disagrees. In his view, *yidoni* is omitted from the Mishnah in Kritot because there is no *maaseh* involved in *yidoni* — no qualifying act. Since *kareit* (and the attendant obligation of a *korban chatat* for inadvertent transgression) requires a *maaseh*, *yidoni* simply does not qualify for inclusion in that Mishnah. The Gemara will elaborate at length on what *maaseh* means in this context.

### First Mentioned

The Gemara then asks: according to Rabbi Yochanan, who says both are subsumed under a single *lav* and are therefore jointly included in the Mishnah in Kritot — if both are included, why does that Mishnah specify *ba'al ov* rather than *yidoni*? Rabbi Yochanan answers: *mishum de-fatach bei kra* — because the Torah consistently introduces this pair by mentioning *ba'al ov* first, as in *ba'al ov o yidoni* or *ba'al ov ve-yidoni*. The Mishnah simply follows the Torah's own word order and uses the first of the pair as representative.

### Disagreement

The Gemara then asks the reverse: why does Reish Lakish not accept Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning — namely, that both are taught under a single *lav* and therefore both are included? Rav Pappa explains on Reish Lakish's behalf: *chalukin hen be-mitah* — they are separated from one another in the verse concerning the death penalty. The Torah writes *ki yihyeh vahem ov o yidoni*, using the word *o* — "or" — which constitutes a *chalukah*, a separation, between them. Once the Torah separates them in this way, one cannot assume that teaching one implicitly includes the other.

### Chalukah Types

The Gemara now asks the converse: why does Rabbi Yochanan not accept Reish Lakish's argument from the *chalukah* in the verse about the death penalty? Rabbi Yochanan's response is that there are two distinct types of *chalukah*: *chalukah de-lav* — a separation that occurs in the context of a standard negative commandment — which is halachically significant and prevents one term from covering the other; and *chalukah de-mitah* — a separation that occurs in the context of the death penalty — which is not halachically significant in this sense. The word *o* in a verse about a *lo ta'aseh* constitutes a genuine *chalukah*, but the same word appearing in a verse about liability to *mitat beit din* does not carry the same legal weight. It is therefore the *chalukah de-lav* that matters for the Mishnah in Kritot, and since in the verse about the *lav* the two are not separated, Rabbi Yochanan holds that they remain jointly covered.

### According Akiva

The Gemara now turns to explain why Rabbi Yochanan does not accept Reish Lakish's principle that a *maaseh* is required. Rabbi Yochanan's answer is that the Mishnah in Kritot was taught according to the view of Rabbi Akiva, who holds that a *maaseh* is not required in order to incur *kareit*. Since Rabbi Akiva does not require a *maaseh*, there is no reason on that basis to exclude *yidoni* from the list — and yet the Mishnah in Kritot does exclude it, which is why Rabbi Yochanan offers his alternative explanation based on the shared *lav*.

Reish Lakish responds: even conceding that the Mishnah in Kritot follows Rabbi Akiva, one must distinguish between *maaseh rabbah* — a substantial act — and *maaseh zuta* — a minimal act. Rabbi Akiva's position is that a *maaseh rabbah* is not required; but even Rabbi Akiva agrees that *maaseh zuta* is required. And *yidoni* involves no *maaseh* even of the minimal variety, which is why it is omitted.

---

## What Is Maaseh?

### Megadef Maaseh

This extended discussion of *maaseh* prompts the Gemara to ask: what *maaseh* is involved in *megadef*? Blasphemy is a transgression that carries *kareit*, and yet it appears to involve nothing more than speech. The Gemara's answer is *akimat sefatav havei maaseh* — the bending or compression of the lips constitutes a *maaseh*. This is a striking claim: bodily movement of the speech organs, without any further physical effect on the world, is categorized as a qualifying act.

This has implications beyond the immediate context. The question of whether speech constitutes a *maaseh* arises in contemporary discussions of, for example, whether verbally activating a voice-controlled device on *Shabbat* involves a *maaseh*. The sugya here speaks precisely to that question.

It is also worth noting what the Gemara focuses on: the movement of the lips, rather than the production of sound. This will become significant in a later dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish.

### Ba'al Ov Maaseh

The Gemara asks the parallel question: what *maaseh* is involved in *ba'al ov*? The answer given is *hakashat zeroatav havei maaseh* — the striking or waving of the arms is a *maaseh*. Again, a bodily movement that produces no direct physical change to the environment is classified as a qualifying act. The Gemara appears to be working against a background assumption that a *maaseh* must effect something in the external world — and it is precisely that assumption it is pushing back against.

### Braita Examples

A *braita* is then cited: one is not liable unless the act contains a *maaseh* — the *braita* gives examples: slaughtering (*zevichah*), burning incense (*kitor*), pouring a libation (*nisuch*), and bowing (*hishtachavayah*). These represent paradigmatic acts of *avodah zarah*.

Reish Lakish comments that the inclusion of *hishtachavayah* — bowing — in this list indicates that this *braita* must follow the opinion of Rabbi Akiva, who does not require a substantial *maaseh*. The *Rabbanan*, by contrast, would not count bowing as a sufficiently significant *maaseh* to trigger liability for *kareit*.

Rabbi Yochanan disagrees: even according to the *Rabbanan*, *kefifat komato* — the physical bending of one's body — constitutes a *maaseh* substantial enough to incur liability. The *braita* need not be attributed exclusively to Rabbi Akiva.

The Gemara then presses Reish Lakish: if bowing is insufficient for the *Rabbanan*, how can waving the arms (*hakashat zeroatav*) of a *ba'al ov* be sufficient? Bowing involves a more pronounced physical movement than arm-waving, and if the former is inadequate, the latter surely is as well. The Gemara resolves this by concluding that when Reish Lakish said that arm-waving is a *maaseh*, he too was speaking according to the view of Rabbi Akiva — not according to the *Rabbanan*. The *Rabbanan* would not regard arm-waving as a sufficient *maaseh* either.

The Gemara then points out a further difficulty: if the *Rabbanan* reject both bowing and arm-waving as insufficient acts, they should also exclude *ba'al ov* from the Mishnah in Kritot — and not merely exclude *megadef*. We know there is a *braita* in Kritot where the *Rabbanan* disagree with Rabbi Akiva and exclude *megadef* from *kareit* liability; but given the conclusion just reached, they should have excluded *ba'al ov* as well. Why does the *braita* omit this?

### Ulla Incense

Ulla proposes an answer: the *ba'al ov* included in the Mishnah in Kritot — the one whom even the *Rabbanan* agree is liable for *kareit* — refers not to the arm-waving practitioner, but to one who burns incense to a demon (*mekattar la-shed*). Burning incense is clearly a substantial physical act — a *maaseh gamur* — and even the *Rabbanan* would recognize it as such.

### Rava Objection

Rava objects immediately: one who burns incense to a *shed* is not a *ba'al ov* at all — he is an *oved avodah zarah*, a practitioner of full-fledged idolatry. The act of burning incense to a demon falls under the category of *avodah zarah*, not *ba'al ov*, and therefore cannot serve as the referent for *ba'al ov* in Kritot.

### Lechever

Rava therefore proposes a different identification: the *ba'al ov* in Kritot refers to one who burns incense as part of *chovev chever* — a form of necromantic witchcraft directed at a dead person rather than at an idol. This is not *avodah zarah*, and it does involve a physical act.

### Abaye Types

Abaye qualifies this further, distinguishing between different forms of *chovev chever*. There is a *chever gadol* and a *chever katan* — a major and a minor form of this practice. One who performs the more serious variety is *chayav skilah*; one who performs the lesser form is *chayav malkut* only. Rava accepts this distinction, affirming that the Torah's mention of *chover chaver* indicates *skilah*, while the lesser form carries only lashes.

### Bees & Scorpions

Abaye concludes with a practical ruling: one who conjures bees and scorpions — causing them to attack one another through incantation — falls into the category of *chovev chever* and is *chayav malkut*, even if his intent was not to cause human harm. The only exception is a life-threatening situation. Rashi notes that if it is a matter of *pikuach nefesh*, the conjuring would be permitted. A question lingers, however, since some forms of this practice border on *avodah zarah*, for which *pikuach nefesh* would not ordinarily serve as a justification — the precise categorization of the act would determine the answer.

---

## Speech vs Silence

### Bowing Dispute

The Gemara returns to the earlier dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish. Rabbi Yochanan holds that bowing (*kefifat komato*) is a *maaseh* even according to the *Rabbanan*, while Reish Lakish holds it is not.

### Heart Intent

Rava introduces a different consideration. Rabbi Yochanan holds that bowing is a *maaseh* for the *Rabbanan*, but that *akimat sefatav* — the movement of the lips in speech — is *not* a *maaseh* according to the *Rabbanan*. One might ask: are they not structurally identical? Both involve physical movement of the body with no further effect on the environment. Rava explains that *megadef* is different, because the act originates in and is driven by the heart — *ho'il ve-yeshno be-leiv*. It is not merely a mechanical physical movement but an expression of inner intent. That, Rava suggests, is what disqualifies it for the *Rabbanan* — or rather, that is what distinguishes it in some way.

### Eidim Challenge

Rav Zeira challenges this from the case of *eidim zomemin*, conspiring witnesses. *Eidim zomemin* do not receive *kareit* even when their false testimony was aimed at causing another person to receive *kareit*. The principle of *kaasher zamam* — that they receive what they sought to inflict — does not extend to *kareit* for *eidim zomemin*. The stated reason is *she-ein bahem maaseh* — there is no *maaseh* involved. But if Rava's reasoning is correct — that something is considered a *maaseh* when it comes from the heart — why would *eidim zomemin* be exempt? Surely their false testimony came from the heart as well.

### Voice Not Maaseh

Rava responds: *eidim zomemin* are different because *yeshnan be-kol* — their act was performed through their voice. And a voice, in this context, does not constitute a *maaseh*. It is not the element of *leiv*, of inner intent, that drives the analysis; it is the distinction between lip-movement and voice-production that is operative. *Megadef* involves *akimat sefatav* — the physical movement of the lips — while testimony in court operates through the voice.

### Voice Maaseh

This brings the Gemara to the explicit dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish on the general question of whether voice constitutes a *maaseh*. The case used to frame the dispute is *chasamah be-kol ve-hinhigah be-kol* — if one muzzles an animal (violating the prohibition against muzzling an ox while it threshes) by shouting at it, or if one drives a *kilayim* team of mismatched animals by voice alone. Rabbi Yochanan rules liable (*chayav*); Reish Lakish rules exempt (*patur*). This is directly relevant to the contemporary question of whether speaking to a voice-activated device on *Shabbat* constitutes a *maaseh*. Notably, the *Ein Mishpat* indicates that the *halacha* follows Rabbi Yochanan.

### Lip Movement

More precisely: Rabbi Yochanan holds that *akimat piv havei maaseh* — moving the lips is a *maaseh* — while Reish Lakish holds the opposite.

### Girsa Variants

Rava, returning to *eidim zomemin*, offers a final formulation of why they are different. The standard text of the Vilna *Shas* reads *ho'il ve-yeshnan be-reiah* — their act was one of *seeing*, meaning their testimony was grounded in what they observed, and observation alone cannot constitute a *maaseh*. However, the *Rif* cites a variant reading in the name of Rav Hai Gaon: *ho'il ve-yeshnan be-ai* — their act was performed through saying "I" (or some similar declarative statement). Even on this reading, a difficulty remains: if speaking is a *maaseh* according to Rabbi Yochanan, why are *eidim zomemin* exempt? Some suggest that there is something distinctive about speech in a formal judicial proceeding — that the context of the court somehow transforms or weights the act differently — but the matter remains a subject of considerable discussion in the commentators.

---

## Precise Definitions

### Ba'al Ov Defined

A *braita* is cited that gives precise technical definitions of the two practitioners. The *ba'al ov* is one who speaks *bein ha-prakim* — from between the joints — *u-vein atzilei yadav*, and from the armpits. The voice or communication emanates from the cavities of the body.

### Yidoni Defined

The *yidoni* is one who takes the bone of an animal called a *yadua* and places it in his mouth, whereupon *vehu medaber me-elav* — the bone speaks of its own accord. This is something resembling ventriloquism, with the notable difference that it is the bone, not the practitioner's own voice, that produces the speech.

### Tanakh Challenge

The Gemara raises a *meitivei* against the definition of *ba'al ov*. It is unusual that a *meitivei* — a challenge from a more authoritative source — comes here from a verse in *Tanakh* rather than a *tannaic* text, but the logic is the same: a verse is inherently more authoritative than any *baraita*. The verse is *ve-hayah ke-ov me-eretz kolech* — "your voice will be like an *ov* from the earth." The implication seems to be that the voice of the *ba'al ov* is heard directly from the ground, not filtered through the joints or armpits of a human practitioner.

### Spirit Between

The Gemara resolves this: the verse does not mean the voice comes out of the ground directly. Rather, the spirit ascends from the ground and then *salika ve-yatvei bein ha-prakim* — rises and positions itself between the joints, and speaks from there. The voice is ultimately heard from the joints, not from the earth itself.

### Saul's Woman

A second *meitivei* is raised from the episode of Shaul and the woman at Ein Dor: *va-tomer ha-isha el Shaul elohim ra'iti olim min ha-aretz* — "the woman said to Shaul: I have seen divine beings rising from the earth." Again, the text seems to indicate that the communication came directly from the ground.

### Dwelling Place

The Gemara resolves this second challenge in the same way as the first: the spirits rose from the earth but then went and positioned themselves *bein ha-prakim* — between the joints — and it was from there that they made themselves heard. The ground is the origin of the ascent, not the locus of the communication. The definition in the *braita* stands: the *ba'al ov* operates through the joints and armpits, and the apparent contradiction from these biblical passages is resolved by understanding that the spirits merely pass through the earth on their way to their actual dwelling place within the human body of the practitioner.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 66

## Ba'al Ov & Yidoni

### Ba'al Ov Definition

We pick up in the middle of 65b, approximately fifteen lines down, at the *tanu rabbanan*. The discussion concerns *ba'al ov*, and it follows an extended treatment of what constitutes a *ma'aseh* — specifically whether speech qualifies as an act. The *gemara* had established that speech is characterized as *yeshna b'kol* (it exists by means of voice) and *yeshna b'lev* (it exists by means of thought or inner expression), meaning the physical movement of the lips is not what gives it its legal character; it is fundamentally an expression of thought. That reasoning generated various subsidiary questions, including notable exceptions such as *eidim zomemim* and the case of yelling at an animal to stop plowing. With that prior discussion as backdrop, the *gemara* now turns to the specific acts of witchcraft that carry capital liability — chiefly *ba'al ov* and *yidoni*.

The *tanu rabbanan* defines *ba'al ov* as encompassing two distinct forms: *echad ha-ma'aleh b'zichuro* — one who causes the spirit to ascend through the male organ, where, as Rashi explains, the spirit rests upon the practitioner's penis — and *echad ha-nish'al b'gugoles* — one who consults through a skull, in the manner of the famous Hamlet scene, causing the spirit to speak from within the skull. Either method constitutes *ba'al ov*.

### Two Forms of Ba'al Ov

The *gemara* then asks: *ma bein zeh l'zeh* — what is the practical difference between the two forms? When performed through the first method, the dead spirit does not ascend in the natural manner; it rises feet-first rather than head-first. Moreover, *eino oleh b'Shabbos* — it will not ascend on *Shabbos*. By contrast, when performed through the skull, *oleh k'darko* — the spirit ascends naturally, head-first, and *oleh b'Shabbos* — it will rise even on *Shabbos*.

At this point the *gemara* raises a pointed objection: *oleh*? What does it mean that it "rises" in the case of the skull? *L'heicha salik* — where is it going? *Hakamay manach* — it is right there in front of you, sitting in the skull. The notion of a body rising does not quite apply when you are simply making a skull speak. The *gemara* therefore emends: *ela eima oneh k'darko* — say rather that it *answers* naturally, *v'oneh b'Shabbos* — and it answers even on *Shabbos*. One interpretation offered is that in the first method, the spirit resides within the sorcerer's joints or knuckles, whereas in the second it resides directly within the skull — which perhaps explains why the skull method can function on *Shabbos* without the need for any additional sorcerous preparation.

### Turnus Rufus Exchange

The *gemara* now introduces a famous exchange: *V'af she'ela zo sha'al Turnusrufus es Rabbi Akiva* — this same question was posed by Turnus Rufus to Rabbi Akiva. Turnus Rufus asked: *ma yom mi-yomayim* — why is *Shabbos* special? What distinguishes it from any other day of the week — why not Wednesday? Rabbi Akiva responded by turning the question back on his interlocutor: *u-ma gever mi-govrin* — why are you such a distinguished person? What sets you apart from any ordinary person? Turnus Rufus answered that his master, the Caesar, had appointed him. Rabbi Akiva replied: *Shabbos nami d'mari tzevi* — similarly, *Shabbos* is distinguished because God designated it so. There need not be anything intrinsically different about the day itself.

Turnus Rufus then clarified that this was not his real question. His question was: *mi yeimar d'idna Shabbasa* — who can say that what you call *Shabbos* today is actually *Shabbos*? Perhaps, over thousands of years, the count has been lost. Perhaps the day you observe is off by one, two, or more days. Rabbi Akiva replied: *d'mari tzevi* — and again, God confirmed it.

### Sambatyon Evidence

Rabbi Akiva then offered concrete evidence. *Nehar Sambatyon yochiach* — the Sambatyon River proves it. This is a river — apparently believed in antiquity to be a real river — that roars and churns throughout the entire week and rests silently on *Shabbos*. The very name *Sabbatyon* is embedded with *Shabbos*. That is one proof.

Then: *ba'al ov yochiach* — the *ba'al ov* also proves it, since we just established that a spirit raised through the first method cannot be raised on *Shabbos*, demonstrating that *Shabbos* is a day of special sanctity even in the realm of the dead. And finally: *kivro shel aviv yochiach* — your father's grave proves it. *She'ein ma'aleh ashan b'Shabbos* — smoke rises from it every day of the week but not on *Shabbos*, because those in *Gehennom* are granted a day of rest; the fires do not burn on *Shabbos*.

At this, Turnus Rufus was far from pleased. *Bizito, biyashto, v'kilalto* — you have degraded, disgraced, and cursed my father, he said, since the proof implies his father was burning in *Gehennom*. Luckily, Rabbi Akiva survived the exchange.

### Necromancer Distinction

Returning to *ba'al ov*, the *gemara* raises a conceptual difficulty: *sho'el ov haynu doreish el ha-meitim* — is not the *ba'al ov*, who raises and consults the spirit of the dead, identical to the category of *doreish el ha-meitim* mentioned in the Torah? And yet *doreish el ha-meitim* appears to be a mere *lav*, a negative prohibition, without capital punishment. How do they differ?

The *gemara* resolves this: *doreish el ha-meitim k'detanya* — *doreish el ha-meitim* is an entirely distinct category. It refers to *zeh ha-mar'iv atzmo v'holeich v'lan b'veit ha-kevarot* — one who starves himself, fasts for extended periods, and goes to sleep in a cemetery, in order to have the spirit of the dead rest upon him. Rashi explains that the purpose is *kidei she-tishreh alav ruach tum'ah* — so that a spirit of impurity will dwell upon him and assist him in his witchcraft. This is different from directly summoning and communicating with the dead; it is a more indirect form of contact, in which the spirit simply takes up residence in the practitioner.

## Doreish El HaMetim

### Cemetery Fasting Definit…

The *gemara* elaborates on this definition of *doreish el ha-meitim*: self-imposed starvation in cemeteries, undertaken so that a spirit of impurity will rest upon the practitioner. There are parallel traditions of sleeping in cemeteries and hearing the dead speak, or even hearing heavenly voices from behind the divine curtain — but in this case, it is specifically about the *ruach tum'ah* taking up residence and facilitating acts of witchcraft, rather than direct necromantic communication.

### Akiva's Lament

When Rabbi Akiva would reach this verse — *doreish el ha-meitim* — *hayah bocheh*, he would weep. His reasoning, as the *gemara* presents it, is striking: *u-ma ha-mar'iv atzmo kidei she-tishreh alav ruach tum'ah shoreh alav ruach tum'ah* — if someone who goes through this effort in order to have an impure spirit rest upon him actually succeeds, then *ha-mar'iv atzmo kidei she-tishreh alav ruach taharah* — how much more so should someone who undergoes a similar process of self-abnegation in order to have the *ruach taharah*, the divine spirit of purity, rest upon him — such as to attain prophecy or a profound connection with the divine — succeed! *Al achas kamma v'khamma* — all the more so!

And yet it does not succeed. *Aval ma e'eseh she-avonoteinu garmu lanu* — but what can we do? Our sins have prevented this. The verse is cited: *ki im avonoteikhem hayu mavdilim beineikhem l'vein eloheikhem* — for your sins have created a separation between you and your God. Were it not for sin, Rabbi Akiva teaches, ascetic spiritual practice directed toward the divine would succeed.

### Rava's Creation

Rava draws the implication further: *i ba'ei tzaddikei, baru alma* — if truly righteous individuals, those who are not separated from God by their sins, were to desire it, they could create worlds — for it is only the sin that divides. The verse is cited again: *ki avonoteikhem hayu mavdilim* — it is only the separation caused by sin that prevents this.

## Rabba's Golem

### Golem Creation

In that spirit — Rava, or as some versions have it *Rabbah* — *bara gavra*, actually created a person. This is the *golem*. Rashi notes, and the *gemara* implies, that this was accomplished through the *Sefer Yetzirah*, a work attributed to Adam Harishon that is said to contain the secrets of creation through the combination of the letters of the divine name. Having created this being, *shadrei l'kamei d'Rabbi Zeira* — he sent him to Rabbi Zeira.

### Golem's Speechlessness

Rabbi Zeira did not initially recognize what he was dealing with. He assumed Rabba had sent him a student and began engaging the figure in conversation. *V'lo hava kama'ader lei* — but the *golem* could not respond. He was entirely speechless.

This is not incidental. Speech is considered the uniquely human characteristic. Onkelos, in his Aramaic translation of the verse in Bereishit where it says *va-yihi ha-Adam l'nefesh chayah* — and the man became a living soul — renders it as the man became a being of speech, *ruach memalela*. Even granting that a righteous sage could, through the powers of *Sefer Yetzirah*, construct a humanoid being, that being cannot possess genuine speech, because speech is not merely a physical act of moving the lips — it is an expression of divine breath, the very quality God breathed into the human being. Without that, no created being can speak. Intelligence, too, may be a distinguishing quality — philosophers have debated precisely what makes human beings unique — but even if degrees of intelligence exist in the animal kingdom, speech in this deeper sense remains distinctively human. A *golem* created without divine breath cannot cross that threshold.

### Return to Dust

Rabbi Zeira, now perceiving what stood before him, said to it: *min chavraya at* — you are one of those magicians, from those *chaveirim*, a term that itself suggests an indirect critique. And then: *hadar l'afra* — return to your dust. And the *golem* was dissolved.

Whether *min chavraya at* constitutes a critique is worth noting. Technically, Rabba did not perform this act through sorcery; he employed *Sefer Yetzirah*. And yet the phrase carries weight. There is a famous *teshuvah* of the *Chacham Tzvi* addressing whether a being created through *Sefer Yetzirah* could count toward a *minyan*. The contemporary novel *He, She, and It* by Marge Piercy, a work of Jewish feminist science fiction, engages precisely these questions — the creation of an android in a post-apocalyptic society, socialized through the legends of the Maharal's *golem*, with questions about what defines humanity — though the *Maharal*'s *golem* in that retelling turns out to be a woman. The conclusion of the halachic literature, it seems, was that the *golem* does not count.

## Weekly Golem Practice

### Friday Calf Creation

The *gemara* then reports: *Rabbi Chanina v'Rabbi Oshaya hava yatvi kol ma'alei shabsa* — Rabbi Chanina and Rabbi Oshaya would sit together every *erev Shabbos* and *aski b'Sefer Yetzirah* — they would engage in the study of *Sefer Yetzirah*. And through this, *mivrei lehu igla taltsa* — they would create a third calf. The "third calf" is regarded as the choicest cut. Whether "third" means third of its age or the third born is debated: if it refers to its age, Rashi says they created the animal at that stage of development; if it refers to birth order, Rashi says they could not actually create a third-born animal but the one they created possessed the same taste and quality as one. In any case, *ve-achli lei* — and that was what they ate for *Shabbos*.

### Erev Shabbat Significance

The theological resonance here is striking, and somewhat unsettling, given the surrounding context. All the preceding material concerns forbidden practices of witchcraft, various categories of *chiyuv mita*, and yet here we read of *amoraim* apparently doing something that looks remarkably similar — and doing it as an act of *kavod Shabbos*. The juxtaposition seems intentional. Moreover, the specific timing of *erev Shabbos* is significant: humans and animals were created on *erev Shabbos*. Creating a living being on *erev Shabbos* thus mirrors the pattern of divine creation. There is evidently a distinction the *gemara* draws between the forbidden acts of witchcraft and the legitimate, if extraordinary, application of *Sefer Yetzirah* — but the text leaves that distinction more implied than articulated.

## Me'onein Forms

### Shimon's Definition

The *gemara* now turns to *me'onein*, one of the additional categories of prohibited practices that do not carry capital punishment. What is a *me'onein*? Rabbi Shimon offers a definition: *zeh ha-ma'avir shiva minei zachar al ha-ayin* — one who passes seven types of male semen over the eye. Rashi explains this as a means of giving someone an ability to perform witchcraft, connecting the word *me'onein* to *ayin* (eye).

### Illusionists Definition

The Sages, however, offer a different definition: *zeh ha-ochez et ha-einayim* — one who seizes the eyes, that is, an illusionist who uses hand motions and sleight of hand to make people believe they are witnessing genuine magic when in fact they are not. This raises an important contemporary question about the permissibility of stage magic and performance illusion. The consideration is that if everyone in the audience understands it is purely entertainment and no one genuinely believes real supernatural forces are at work, the practice may well be permissible. The concern would arise if the performance were so spectacular that, despite theoretical knowledge that it is an illusion, some part of the viewer's mind registers it as real — but arriving at that level of technical mastery is, as one might say, something we should all aspire to.

### Akiva Astrology

Rabbi Akiva offers yet another definition: *zeh ha-mechashev itim ve-sha'ot* — one who calculates times and hours. This connects *me'onein* to *onah*, meaning a period or season, and refers to astrological or sign-based prognostication: determining propitious or inauspicious moments for various activities.

### Omen Examples

The *gemara* elaborates with practical illustrations of what this looks like: *ha-yom yafe la-tzet* — today is a good day to go out, you will be successful in romance; *le-machar yafe li-kach* — tomorrow is good for doing business; *limudei arvei shevi'it chitim yafot* — those who plant on the eve of the seventh year will have good wheat. The final example — *ikurei kitniyot mi-or ra'ot* — pulling up one's legumes will prevent them from going bad — is not practical agrarian advice but rather a reading of mystical or astrological signs. None of these examples represent rational empirical observation; they are the sort of pronouncements based on what the practitioner claims to perceive in hidden cosmic indicators.

## Rambam-Ramban Debate

### Rambam Rationalism

At this juncture it is essential to note the fundamental dispute between the Rambam and Ramban regarding all of these categories. The Rambam takes an unambiguously rationalist position: all of this — witchcraft, necromancy, *ba'al ov*, the raising of spirits — is *narishkeit*, nonsense. None of it actually works. The entire reason the Torah imposes legal liability is because the practitioner presents himself as doing these things, creates the appearance of doing them, deceives people into believing they work. The *chiyuv* is essentially for the fraud and the social harm caused by that presentation. According to the Rambam, the Torah never endorsed the reality of these phenomena.

### Ramban Supernaturalism

The Ramban responds sharply. He acknowledges that the Rambam's view is intellectually appealing and that many readers will find it congenial — but he insists it is not the *peshat* of the Torah. The Torah, says the Ramban, prohibits these practices precisely because they actually work. The prohibition is not against claiming to do something that does not exist; it is against employing genuine supernatural forces that the Torah wishes to keep outside the domain of human practice. The narrative of the Witch of Ein Dor — where Shaul engages a necromancer who appears to raise the spirit of Shmuel — is cited as a clear case in point: the straightforward reading of that story is that it worked. The prohibition exists because the phenomenon is real, not because it is fake.

## Menachesh Superstitions

### Basic Omens

The *gemara* next defines *menachesh*: *zehu omer pito nafla mipiv maklo nafla miyado* — this is someone who says, "The bread fell from his mouth — that is a sign of such-and-such; the stick fell from his hand — that is a sign of something else." The move here is from astrological calculation to the kind of superstitious omen-reading associated with everyday occurrences.

### Detailed Omens

The list continues: *beno koreh lo me-achorav* — his son called to him from behind; *orev koreh lo* — a raven called out to him; *tzvi hifsiko ba-derech* — a deer crossed his path; *nachash mi-yemino* — a snake appeared to his right; *ve-shu'al mi-smolo* — a fox to his left. Each such occurrence is treated as a portent of something. This is the domain of superstition as distinct from astrology or sleight of hand — the interpretation of natural, random events as meaningful signs.

## Daily Superstitions

### Morning Avoidance

Closely related is the matter raised under the heading *al tatchil bi*: "don't start with me." Rashi illustrates with the example of a tax collector: if someone comes to collect from you, you say, "Don't start with me — ask someone else first, come to me second." The underlying concern is that being the first target of an unfortunate event early in the day will be a *siman ra* for the rest of the day. This represents the superstitious belief that one's fortune for a given period is set by what happens at its beginning.

## Me'onein Forms (II)

### Rosh Hashanah Simanim

This naturally raises a question with considerable practical relevance, particularly around this time of year: what about the *simanim* of Rosh Hashanah — the symbolic foods? Are those not precisely this kind of omen-reading? The distinction drawn in the *poskim* is fundamental. The *simanim* are not predictions and not signs in the operative sense; they are symbolic and aspirational. The formula *yehi ratzon* — may it be Your will — frames them explicitly as a prayer and an expression of hope, not as a reading of what the future will be based on what is happening now.
