The forbidden form of omen-reading is *causative*: "because this occurred, this outcome is predicted." The *simanim* of Rosh Hashanah are the opposite: they are acts of symbolic expression and aspiration toward a desired future, directed toward God.

## Daily Superstitions (II)

### Weekly Timing

The same pattern of *al tatchil bi* extends across other temporal thresholds: *Rosh Chodesh hu* — it is the new month, so bad things at this moment will be a *siman* for the entire month; *Motzaei Shabbos hu* — it is Saturday night, so something unfortunate at this moment sets a bad *siman* for the entire week. These are all prohibited as forms of the same superstitious omen-reading.

## Animal Divination

### Animal Charms

The *gemara* then cites *lo tenachashu v'lo te'onenu* and explains: *elu ha-menachashim be-chulda be-ofot u-ve-dagim* — these are people who give incantations or make prognostications using a weasel, birds, or fish. Rashi explains that this refers to when people go out on a journey or begin some undertaking and perform these acts of *nichush* in connection with these animals.

### Entrails Reading

One wonders whether this category might also encompass the practice of examining entrails — the inspection of the internal organs of slaughtered animals for omens — which was common throughout the ancient world. The *gemara* does not elaborate further on this point, and we move on.

## Chilul Shabbat

### Shabbat Violation Types

The *mishnah* now transitions from witchcraft-related offenses and the cursing of parents to *chilul Shabbat* and then the cursing of parents — the second major grouping of capital offenses addressed in this section of the *perek*. The *mishnah* states: *ha-mechalel et ha-Shabbat be-davar she-zedonno kares ve-shigagato chatat* — one who desecrates *Shabbos* through an act whose intentional violation carries *kares* and whose unintentional violation requires a *chatat* offering. This is essentially the category of the thirty-nine *melachot*.

The formulation implies, as the *gemara* notes, that there exist acts properly characterized as *chilul Shabbat* that do not fall into this capital category — acts that violate *Shabbos* without generating the full weight of *kares* and *chatat*. Not every *Shabbos* violation falls into this bin: failing to recite *Kiddush*, for instance, would not be called *chilul Shabbat* in this technical sense. The *gemara* asks what *chilul Shabbat* without these consequences looks like.

### Techumim Exception

The answer: *techumim ve-aliba de-Rabbi Akiva* — the prohibition of *techumim*, going beyond the *Shabbos* boundary, according to Rabbi Akiva. The verse *al yetze ish mi-mekomo be-yom ha-Shabbat* — let no man go out from his place on the *Shabbos* day — is, according to Rabbi Akiva, a biblical prohibition. Yet it is not a *melachah*; it does not carry *kares* or the requirement of a *chatat*. It is a biblical violation of *Shabbos* that falls outside the capital framework.

### Fire-Kindling Exception

Similarly: *ha-beirah ve-aliba de-Rabbi Yosi* — the kindling of fire according to Rabbi Yosi. The Torah singles out fire: *lo tiv'aru esh be-chol moshvoteichem be-yom ha-Shabbat* — you shall not kindle fire in any of your dwelling places on the *Shabbos* day. This could be read as the paradigmatic act of *chilul Shabbat*. But Rabbi Yosi holds that the Torah singled it out specifically to teach that it is a *lav* — a negative prohibition — and that one who transgresses it does *not* receive the death penalty. It is *chilul Shabbat* without the capital consequence.

## Cursing Parents

### Name Requirement

The *mishnah* then states: *ha-mekalel aviv ve-imo eino chayav ad she-yekalelam ba-shem* — one who curses his father or mother is not liable for capital punishment unless he curses them using God's explicit name. The mere use of an epithet or a non-explicit divine name is insufficient for the death penalty.

### Meir vs. Sages

*Kilelam be-kinui* — if he used a *kinui*, one of the non-explicit names of God such as *El* or *Elohim* (as opposed to the Tetragrammaton), *Rabbi Meir mechayev* — Rabbi Meir holds him liable for capital punishment. *Ve-chachamim potrin* — the Sages exempt him. This parallels a similar dispute in the context of blasphemy, where the same disagreement arises: must one use God's explicit name to be liable, or does a *kinui* suffice?

### Sages Identified

The *gemara* asks: *man chachamim* — who are these Sages who require the explicit name? The answer: *Rabbi Menachem be-Rabbi Yosi hi* — it is Rabbi Menachem the son of Rabbi Yosi, as taught in a *baraisa*.

### Shem Derasha

Rabbi Menachem be-Rabbi Yosi derives this from the verse regarding blasphemy: *be-nokvo shem yumat* — when he articulates the Name, he shall be put to death. The question is: why does the verse say *shem* — the name — as an extra word? The verse could have simply said *be-nokvo yumat*. Earlier in the *gemara*, that word *shem* was used to teach that one must curse God's own name *with* God's name — meaning God must function as both subject and object. But here, Rabbi Menachem reads the extra *shem* as teaching something about an entirely different case: *limed al ha-mekalel aviv ve-imo she-eino chayav ad she-yekalelam ba-shem* — it instructs us concerning one who curses his parents that he is not liable unless he curses them with God's explicit name.

## Ish Ish Inclusivity

### Gender Inclusivity

The *gemara* now proceeds to unpack the full verse governing the cursing of parents: *ish ish ki yekalel aviv ve-imo mot yumat aviv ve-imo kilel damav bo*. The double formulation *ish ish* — any man, any man — serves to expand the category: *le-rabot bat, tumtum, ve-androginos* — it includes a female, a *tumtum* (a person of indeterminate sex), and an *androginos* (a person of mixed or dual sex characteristics). The doubling of the term *ish* signals inclusivity beyond the literal male.

### Both or Either

The verse continues: *asher yekalel et aviv ve-et imo* — who curses his father and his mother. Reading the *vav* as "and," one might conclude that the offense requires cursing *both* parents simultaneously. *Ein li ela aviv ve-imo* — I would know only the case of both together. *Aviv shelo imo, imo shelo aviv minayin* — but how do I know that cursing the father alone, without the mother, or the mother alone, without the father, is also prohibited?

The answer comes from the end of the verse: *aviv ve-imo kilel damav bo* — his father and his mother he cursed, his blood is upon him. From the structure of the verse — where *aviv* is juxtaposed to *kilel* in one clause and *imo* is juxtaposed to *kilel* in the same clause — we learn: *aviv kilel, imo kilel* — cursing either one alone is sufficient for liability.

### Vav Interpretation

This is the position of Rabbi Yoshiyah. Rabbi Yonatan disagrees, arguing that no such elaborate derivation is necessary. *Mashma shem ke-echad u-mashma echad bifnei atzmo* — the *vav* carries both meanings simultaneously: "and" as well as "or." The default reading of a *vav* in the Torah is disjunctive — it means one *or* the other — and one would only read a *vav* as requiring both together when the text explicitly says *yachdav*, together, as in the prohibition of *shaatnez* (*lo tilbash shatnez tzemer u-fishtim yachdav*) or the prohibition against plowing with ox and donkey (*lo tacharosh be-shor u-va-chamor yachdav*). Absent the word *yachdav*, a *vav* means one or the other. Therefore, according to Rabbi Yonatan, no special derivation from the verse's structure is needed.

The verse concludes: *mot yumat biskilah* — he shall be put to death by stoning. The *gemara* confirms that the death prescribed is *sekilah*, deriving this from a *gezeirah shavah*: *ne'emar kan damav bo ve-ne'emar le-halan dmeihem bam* — the expression "his blood is upon him" appears here and appears there (in another context established as *sekilah*), linking the two.

## Parent Curse Derash

### Damav Bo Link

The *gemara* now addresses the question of the *azharah* — the negative prohibition — for cursing a parent. The punishment has been derived, but where does the Torah prohibit it? The verse is *Elohim lo tekalel* — do not curse *Elohim*. This refers to God or to judges. How do we get from there to ordinary parents?

The *gemara* reasons as follows: if the father were a *dayan* — a judge — he would be covered by the prohibition *Elohim lo tekalel*. If he were a *nasi* — a prince or king — he would be covered by *ve-nasi be-amcha lo ta'or* — do not curse a prince among your people. But what if he is neither a judge nor a king? Then the *gemara* attempts a *binyan av mi-shneihem* — a common-denominator argument drawing from both cases.

### Uniqueness Problem

The challenge is that the unique characteristics of a *nasi* differ from those of a *dayan*. *Lo rei nasi ke-rei dayan ve-lo rei dayan ke-rei nasi* — the distinguishing feature of a king is not like that of a judge, and vice versa. A *dayan* carries the weight of obligatory compliance: you are commanded to follow the judge's ruling, as the Torah states that one must not deviate from the decision of the court in the Temple Mount to the right or to the left. A king carries a different weight: you are forbidden to rebel against him, to engage in acts of uprising or defiance — but you are not obligated to follow the legal pronouncements of a king in the way you are obligated to follow a judge's rulings. Each, in its own way, is weightier than the other. Therefore, one cannot simply derive from one to the other, or from both to an ordinary citizen, by means of a *binyan av*.

### Nation Commonality

What is the common denominator? *She-hem be-amcha* — they are members of your people, your nation. And the verse itself provides this foothold through the word *be-amcha* in the verse *ve-nasi be-amcha lo ta'or*. From this, one could extend: *ve-af ani, avikha she-be-amcha ve-ata muzhar kilato* — and I will include also your father, who is among your people, and you are forbidden to curse him.

However, a counterargument is immediately raised: *ve-halo hatzad hashaveh she-beineihem she-ein ken gedulatam garma lahem* — the true common denominator between judge and king is that their *high status* is what generates the prohibition. Their greatness is what demands deference. That cannot straightforwardly extend to an ordinary person, including a parent.

### Cheresh Proof

The *gemara* therefore invokes the third case: *lo tekalel cheresh* — do not curse a deaf person. *Ba-umlalin she-be-amcha ha-katuv medaber* — there the Torah is speaking not of people of high status but of society's most vulnerable — those who are marginalized, who cannot even hear the curse directed at them, people against whom one might feel free to act with impunity. The prohibition is designed to protect precisely them. Now we have two poles: on one end, those of the highest social status (judge and king), whose dignity demands protection; on the other, the most vulnerable (the deaf person), who need the Torah's protection precisely because they are powerless. Together, they span the full range of society.

One might ask: does the person cursed have to hear the curse? Clearly not — the case of the *cheresh* alone establishes that the curse is prohibited even when the object cannot hear it. More broadly, if a person went into a room with two witnesses and cursed his father or mother without the parent hearing, he would still be *chayav mita*.

### Logic Resolution

Despite spanning both extremes, the *gemara* resists the simple common denominator. *Ma le-nasi be-amcha she-ken gedulatan garma lahen* — one could object that the king and judge are prohibited to curse because of their elevated status, which is the unique factor that generates the prohibition. And *ma le-cheresh she-ken umlalin garma lo* — conversely, the deaf person is protected because of his vulnerability. Each has something unique about it. Therefore, the simplest common denominator — being a member of the Jewish nation — is not sufficient without the third case.

The *gemara* resolves this with the following logic: if the Torah had provided only two of the three cases — either judge plus deaf person, or king plus deaf person — we could have derived the prohibition for an ordinary person through a *binyan av*, despite the unique features of each, because together they would cover both extremes. But one of them would have been redundant given that we could have derived it from the other two. Since the Torah included all three, and two would have sufficed for the derivation, the third extra case — whichever one it is — is available to teach something further. *Im eino inyan le-gufo, tenahu inyan le-aviv* — if the extra case is not needed for its own subject matter (because the prohibition there could already be derived), apply it to teach about the father. And so the full prohibition against cursing one's father or mother is established.

It bears noting that this prohibition against cursing applies to all people — it is a general *lav* covering every member of the Jewish nation. What distinguishes the case of one's parents is not a separate prohibition but the penalty: cursing any ordinary person is a violation of a negative commandment; cursing one's father or mother is punishable by death.

## Elohim Meanings

### Elohim Dispute

The derivation just completed presupposed that *Elohim lo tekalel* refers to a judge — allowing the word *Elohim* to serve as the prohibition against cursing judges, from which the argument proceeded. But this leads to a fundamental question. As the *gemara* notes: *hani nicha le-man de-amar Elohim chol* — this works well for the position that *Elohim* in that verse is secular, meaning a judge. But *ela le-man de-amar kodesh* — what of the position that *Elohim* refers to God, and that the verse is the source for prohibiting blasphemy? A *baraisa* presents this explicitly: *Elohim chol divrei Rabbi Yishmael* — Rabbi Yishmael holds that *Elohim* in this verse is secular, referring to a judge, and it is the prohibition against cursing a judge. *Rabbi Akiva omer Elohim kodesh* — Rabbi Akiva holds it is sacred, referring to God, and it is the basis for prohibiting blasphemy.

According to Rabbi Akiva, then, we lack a verse explicitly prohibiting cursing a judge (we have only the verse about the king), and therefore the full derivation above — which required the judge as a separate pole — may be problematic. And yet another *baraisa* notes: *Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov omer, azharah le-mevarech et ha-Shem minayin? Talmud lomar Elohim lo tekalel* — where is the prohibition against blasphemy? From *Elohim lo tekalel*. So according to that view (aligned with Rabbi Akiva), it is that verse that prohibits cursing God, not cursing a judge.

### Double Lamed

The *gemara* resolves this through the technique of the double *lamed* in the word *tekalel*. The verse could have said *lo takel* with a single *lamed*. Why the doubled form? *Shema mina tartei* — derive two things from it. The doubled *lamed* teaches that *Elohim* in this verse bears *both* meanings simultaneously — it refers both to God and to a judge. Therefore, the verse serves as the source for the prohibition against cursing God *and* as the source for the prohibition against cursing a judge, without needing to limit it to one or the other.

### Deriving Judge

But this raises a further difficulty: even if we accept both meanings, can one direction of derivation be accomplished by *kal va-chomer*? If *Elohim* means God and the prohibition applies to cursing the divine, can we derive from that, by an argument *a fortiori*, that cursing a human judge is also prohibited? Or conversely, if *Elohim* means a judge, can we then derive that cursing God is also forbidden? The problem is that *ein matzinin min ha-din* — one cannot derive a punishable prohibition by *kal va-chomer* alone. The double *lamed*, therefore, is not just a mnemonic; it is doing genuine legal work. *Dilma ha-kodesh az-har ha-chol lo az-har* — perhaps the verse only prohibits cursing the sacred (God) but not the profane (a judge). The doubling of the *lamed* forecloses that possibility and teaches both simultaneously.

## Na'arah Me'Orasah

### Four Conditions

The *gemara* now returns to the domain of sexual offenses, moving from the incest cases treated earlier to the case of adultery in its most aggravated form. Ordinary adultery — a married woman with a man who is not her husband — carries the death penalty of *chenek*, strangulation, the lightest of the four capital punishments. The case of *na'arah me'orasah*, a betrothed maiden, carries *sekilah*, the most severe. The *mishnah* establishes that one is not liable for *sekilah* in this category unless all of the following conditions are met: *ad she-tiyeh na'arah* — she must be a *na'arah*, between the age of twelve and approximately twelve and a half; *besulah* — she must be a virgin; *me'orasah* — she must be betrothed, neither single nor fully married; and *be-veit aviha* — she must still be under her father's jurisdiction, conceptually in his house.

This last condition requires elaboration. It is not about the physical four walls of the father's home. Once the father has handed her over to the husband's messengers who have come to bring her to her husband's house, even though the *chuppah* has not yet occurred and she has not yet arrived at her husband's home, she is conceptually no longer in her father's domain. *Prat le-shemasar av li-shlukhei ha-ba'al* — this excludes the case where the father has transferred her to the husband's agents; at that point she is in transition and the *sekilah* category no longer applies.

Similarly, the *mishnah* addresses the case of *ba alehah shenayim* — two men who had intercourse with her. One might immediately object that the second man would find her no longer a virgin. But the case under discussion is specifically one where the first act was anal intercourse, raising the question of how virginity is defined. Does virginity mean the hymen has not been ruptured? Or does it mean no act of intercourse has taken place, regardless of the anatomical consequence? This question recurs in other contexts — notably at the beginning of Kesuvos, where a woman's *kesubah* entitlement of 200 *shekel* (for a virgin) versus 100 (for a non-virgin) depends on this same definition, and where the same question arises for a woman whose hymen was ruptured through means other than intercourse. In the case of the *na'arah me'orasah*, the conclusion is: *ha-rishon bi-sekilah ve-ha-sheni be-chenek* — the first man receives *sekilah*, the second receives *chenek*, because even the act of anal intercourse renders her no longer a *besulah* for purposes of this category.

### Age Requirement

The *tanu rabbanan* restates the conditions: *na'arah* — not a *bogeres*, the fully mature woman over twelve and a half whose full complement of signs of puberty has appeared; *besulah* — not one who has had intercourse; *me'orasah* — not single and not *nesuah*; *be-veit aviha* — and conceptually still in her father's house, excluding the case where she has been transferred to the husband's agents.

Rav Yehudah says in the name of Rav: *zu divrei Rabbi Meir* — these are the words of Rabbi Meir, reflecting the view of our *mishnah* as requiring precisely that she be a *na'arah*, not younger. *Aval chachamim omrim na'arah me'orasah afilu ktanah be-mashma* — but the Sages say that *na'arah me'orasah* includes even a *ketanah*, a girl under twelve who has been legally betrothed by her father. According to the Sages, the word *na'arah* does not exclude the younger girl; it only excludes the *bogeres* who is too old.

This debate between Rabbi Meir and the Sages is not unique to the context of *sekilah*; it appears also in the law of the fine (*kenas*) for one who seduces a *na'arah besulah*, and in the law of the husband who falsely claims his wife was not a virgin. In all those contexts the same dispute surfaces: does *na'arah* restrict the category to girls precisely in that age range, or does it merely set the upper limit?

### Until Language

Rav Achai mi-Difti challenged Ravina: how do we know that our *mishnah* sides with Rabbi Meir and excludes a *ketanah*, rather than siding with the Sages and merely excluding a *bogeres*? The answer lies in the precise language of the *mishnah*: *einno chayav ad she-tiyeh na'arah* — he is not liable *until* she is a *na'arah*. The word *ad she-tiyeh* — "until she becomes" — carries temporal force: it means that at a younger stage (as a *ketanah*) she was *not* in this category, and only upon reaching the status of *na'arah* does the category apply. If the *mishnah* had intended to side with the Sages and include a *ketanah*, it would have phrased the condition differently: *einno chayav ela al na'arah me'orasah* — he is not liable except regarding a *na'arah me'orasah* — which would set the *na'arah* as a sufficient but not exclusive condition, leaving open the possibility that a younger girl is also included. The word "until" decisively indicates that our *mishnah* is Rabbi Meir, and that younger than *na'arah* is excluded.

## Ketanah Me'Orasah Case

### Punishment Query

Rav Yaakov bar Abba bar Adda posed the following question to Rav: if a man had intercourse with a *ketanah me'orasah* — a betrothed girl below the age of *na'arah* — according to Rabbi Meir, what is his punishment? The girl herself would not be liable, since she is a minor. But what of the man? Does he go completely free — *le-gamrei mi-pater lei* — because she falls between the categories, too young for the *sekilah* category and yet seemingly not covered by the ordinary adultery case with its *chenek* penalty? Or does he merely escape *sekilah* — *mi-sekilah mema'et lei* — and remain liable for *chenek* as in a standard case of adultery?

The answer offered is: *mistabra mi-sekilah mema'et lei* — it stands to reason that he is only exempted from *sekilah* specifically; he remains liable for *chenek*. He has committed what is effectively an act of adultery, even if the aggravated category of *na'arah me'orasah* does not apply.

The *gemara* then raises a complication from the verse *u-meitu gam sheneihem* — and they shall both die — *ad she-yihyu sheneihem shavin* — which seems to require that both parties be in the same status. Rashi reads this as suggesting that perhaps a man would not be liable at all if his partner is a minor and is not herself subject to punishment. Tosafot takes a different approach to avoid the difficulty, but following Rashi: the *gemara* is asking whether the symmetry demanded by *sheneihem* means that if she is not punishable, he is not either.

### Rav's Silence

Rav fell silent — *shasik Rav* — and had no immediate response. Shmuel then asked: *mai ta'ama shasik Rav* — why was Rav silent? The answer seems obvious. *U-meitu ha-ish asher shakhav imah levado* — the verse says "the man who lay with her shall die *alone*," explicitly indicating the case where the man is executed and the woman is not, because she was coerced and not culpable. This shows that the execution of one party does not require the punishment of the other. The *gemara* responds that this is indeed a *tannaitic* dispute.

## Equal Status Debate

### Yoshiyah Adult Rule

The verse *u-meitu gam sheneihem* — they shall both die — is interpreted by Rabbi Yoshiyah (following Rashi's reading) as requiring both parties to be adults. If one of them is a minor, the man would not be liable for capital punishment — a position strikingly at odds with the general principle that the age of one party does not determine the other's liability.

### Yonatan Counter

Rabbi Yonatan disagrees, relying precisely on the other verse: *u-meit ha-ish asher shakhav imah levado* — the man who lay with her shall die alone. This verse demonstrates that one can execute the man even when the woman is not punished. Therefore, even if she is a minor and not liable, he can still be put to death. Equal status is not required.

### Rava Necrophilia

If so, what does *u-meitu gam sheneihem* teach? Rava answers: *le-ma'utei ma'aseh chidudin* — it comes to exclude acts that, while of a sexual character, involve only one living partner. Rashi understands this as acts that are pleasurable for only one party. But the more compelling reading, as the *gemara* suggests, is *ma'aseh Hordos* — the act associated with Herod, referring to necrophilia: intercourse with a woman who is already dead. In that case there are not truly two parties to the act, and the verse's emphasis on *both* dying excludes such a case from capital liability. It requires both parties to be alive — *sheneihem* — for the offense to be capital. But it does not require them to be of equal legal status in terms of age or capacity.

## Levado First Man

### Virginity Definition

From the word *levado* — alone — the *gemara* derives a teaching about which of multiple men who had intercourse with a *na'arah me'orasah* carries the *sekilah* penalty, in the context of anal intercourse that leaves the hymen intact.

### Ten Men Case

A *baraisa* states: *ba al asara benei adam* — if ten men had intercourse (specifically anal intercourse) with this *na'arah me'orasah*, such that her hymen remained intact throughout. One position holds that *kulam bi-sekilah* — all of them receive *sekilah*, since she is technically still a *besulah* by the criterion of an unruptured hymen. Rabbi holds otherwise: *ha-rishon bi-sekilah ve-khulam be-chenek* — only the first receives *sekilah*; all subsequent ones receive *chenek*, because after the first act she is no longer considered a *besulah*, regardless of the anatomical state of the hymen. This is derived from *levado*: only one man — the first — is alone in the *sekilah* category for this woman. No subsequent man can achieve *sekilah* for her.

This resolves the question of how *levado* functions: according to one reading, the verse teaches that in the case of a *ketanah*, the man is punished alone (with *chenek* rather than *sekilah*); according to Rabbi's position, *levado* teaches that only the first man achieves *sekilah* and all others are limited to *chenek*.

## Bat Kohen Sreifah

### Parallel Categories

The final *mishnah* in the passage concerns the *bat kohen*, the daughter of a kohen, who *zonet* — who commits sexual defilement. The Torah prescribes for her the penalty of *sreifah*, burning, rather than the *sekilah* of an ordinary *na'arah me'orasah*. Rabbi holds that this is precisely the parallel category: just as the ordinary *na'arah me'orasah* receives *sekilah*, the *bat kohen* in the equivalent situation receives *sreifah*. The same conditions that apply to one apply to the other; the only difference is the nature of the penalty.

Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua states: *Rabbi ke-Rabbi Yishmael sevira lei* — Rabbi's position follows Rabbi Yishmael, *de-amar arusah yatzta li-sreifah ve-lo nesuah* — who holds that the *bat kohen* receiving *sreifah* is specifically when she is *arusah*, betrothed (as in the standard *na'arah me'orasah* case), not when she is *nesuah*, fully married.

### Techilah Defilement

What does the verse *bat ish kohen ki techel li-znot* mean? *V'hachi ka'amar* — this is what it is saying: *im techilat bi'atah be-znut bi-sreifah* — if it is the first act of intercourse that constitutes her defilement in the context of *zenut*, she receives *sreifah*. The first act of intercourse is the operative one. *Idach avatarah be-chenek* — all subsequent acts bring only *chenek*, not *sreifah*, because after the first act she is no longer a *besulah*.

The parallel verse *u-meit ha-ish asher shakhav imah levado* is cited here as well: just as we established for the ordinary *na'arah me'orasah* that *levado* means only the first man gets *sekilah*, so too here *levado* means only the first act of intercourse brings *sreifah* for the *bat kohen*. *Mah hatam bi-techilah bi'ah ka-mishtayei kra, hacha nami di-techilah bi'ah ka-mishtayei kra* — just as there the verse speaks of the beginning of intercourse, here too.

### Yosef Alternative

Ravibi bar Abaye then reports that Rav Yosef interpreted this differently. *Rabbi ke-Rabbi Meir sevira lei* — Rabbi's position actually follows Rabbi Meir, not Rabbi Yishmael. *De-amar niset le-echad min ha-pesulim mitatah be-chenek* — Rabbi Meir holds that if the *bat kohen* has been married to one of the men who would invalidate her for a *kohen* — a *mamzer*, a *chalal*, or others in that category — her penalty is *chenek*, not *sreifah*.

### Defilement Types

On this reading, the distinction is not between the first and subsequent acts of intercourse, but between two types of defilement. *Im techilah achaltatah be-znut bi-sreifah* — if the first thing that defiles her is the act of sexual *zenut* itself, she receives *sreifah*. But *idach* — if she has already been defiled not through intercourse but through marriage to an invalidating partner (*chilul* through the marriage itself), then she receives *chenek*. The word *techel* is thus read as *chilul* — defilement — and *techilah* — beginning — simultaneously: it is the *beginning* of defilement, and that beginning must be through the act of intercourse, not through a prior disqualifying marriage.

The verse *levado* is cited on this reading not as a substantive derivation but as *simana be-alma* — merely a mnemonic device, a way of remembering the principle. It echoes the same idea — that it is the first, the singular, the beginning — without serving as the primary source for the legal rule.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 67

## Mesit & Witness Rules

### Mesit Definition

The daf opens at the very top, continuing the list of sins punishable by *skila*. The *mishnah* begins with the *mesit* — the person who seduces, induces, or entices another to commit *avodah zarah*. The *mishnah* qualifies him as a *hedyot*, a commoner, and the *gemara* will explain the significance of this term. The implicit contrast in the first clause is with a *navi sheker* — a false prophet who incites to idolatry — since, as we will see in the *gemara*, Rabbi Shimon holds that a *navi sheker* who induces idolatry receives *chenek* rather than *skila*.

The second clause, which specifies that the *mesit* entices *the individual*, contrasts not with a *navi* but with the *madiach* — the one who entices an entire city. There is thus a three-tiered structure: the *mesit* seduces an individual, the *madiach* seduces an entire city, and the *ir hanidachat* is the city that has been fully seduced, whose inhabitants are all executed and whose buildings are destroyed entirely. The first clause of the *mishnah* contrasts with the *navi sheker*; the second is understood to contrast with the *madiach*, which is the subject of the next *mishnah*.

What constitutes the act of enticement? The *mishnah* describes it as follows: the *mesit* says, "There is a god in such-and-such a place — here is what it eats, here is what it drinks, here is how it benefits its worshippers, here is how it harms those who transgress." He promotes and extols the idol.

### Hidden Witnesses

The *mishnah* then states a sweeping rule: *kol chayavei misos shebatorah ein machminim aleihem chutz mizzo* — for all other capital offenses in the Torah, one may not have witnesses lie in wait. The entire framework of capital law is designed to make execution extraordinarily difficult: witnesses must be present, they must administer *hatra'ah* (prior warning), the accused must acknowledge the warning with an *af al pi chen* and then immediately proceed to commit the act. All of these safeguards ensure that the person acted with full awareness and genuine intent.

The *mesit* is the sole exception. Because what he does is considered so grievous — it is not enough for him to sin himself, he must go and corrupt others — the Torah itself declares *lo sachmol alav velo sechasseh alav*, "do not have compassion for him and do not conceal it." Therefore, witnesses may be hidden against him, no prior warning need be administered, and there is no requirement that the conditions of formal testimony in *beis din* be fulfilled in the ordinary way.

### Two-Witness Case

The *mishnah* proceeds to the case where the *mesit* speaks to two people directly: *amar lishnayim, hen edav* — the very two people he attempts to seduce become the witnesses against him. They may bring him to *beis din* and he is stoned. The question naturally arises: how do we establish that he acted with *mezid* without formal *hatra'ah*? It seems that in this case, the ordinary requirement to demonstrate intentionality may be modified — the context of deliberate seduction itself serves as the operative evidence. Some *mefarshim* hold that even here a form of dissuasion would be offered, though others argue that were the target to give any such response before two witnesses, the *mesit* would recognize the trap and retreat — not out of *teshuvah*, but out of self-preservation — and then proceed to entice the next person. The *mishnah* therefore permits, in the two-witness case, proceeding without the usual formalities.

### Wall Concealment

A more complex scenario follows: *amar le'echad* — the *mesit* approaches only a single individual, and that individual, unwilling to be enticed, wishes to see the *mesit* brought to justice. He tells the *mesit*: "I have friends who would also like to hear your ideas," thereby creating the possibility of two witnesses. But what if the *mesit* is clever — *im hayah arum* — and suspects something, or simply never speaks his enticements in the presence of more than one person at a time? The *mishnah* prescribes: *machminim lo eidim achorei hageder* — witnesses are hidden behind a wall, so that the *mesit* believes he is in private.

The procedure is carefully choreographed. The person being targeted says to the *mesit*: "Tell me again what you were saying before, now that we are alone" — *emor mah she'amarta li b'yichud* — either meaning "now that we are in private" (as Rashi explains) or "tell me clearly again." The *mesit* then says: let us go worship such-and-such *avodah zarah*. The target responds: "How could we abandon our God in heaven and go worship wood and stone?" — *heich naniach et eloheinu shebashamayim v'neilech v'na'avod eitzim va'avanim?* If the *mesit* recants, *mutav* — good. But if he doubles down and says, "No, that is indeed what we are obligated to do," then *ha'omdim me'achorei hageder*, the witnesses behind the wall bring him to *beis din* and he is stoned.

This second scenario differs from the first in an important respect: a form of *hatra'ah* has effectively been administered. By responding "how could we abandon our God?", the target has attempted to dissuade the *mesit* and made clear the gravity of what is being proposed. While this does not follow the formal structure of *hatra'ah* — the witnesses behind the wall are not identified, and the language of *chayav mitah* is not used — it is at minimum sufficient to establish *mezid*: if the *mesit* then reaffirms his position, he is clearly acting with full intentional awareness.

### Avodah Zarah Acts

The *mishnah* concludes with an enumeration of the specific acts that constitute *hasatah* — enticement. *Ha'omer e'avod* ("I will worship"), *eilech v'e'avod* ("I will go and worship"), *neilech v'na'avod* ("let us go and worship") — and the same formula applied to each of the four primary acts of idolatrous worship: *zivuch* (animal sacrifice), *kitor* (burning incense), *nisuch* (pouring libation), and *hishtachavayah* (prostration). Even the formula *eilech v'e'avod* — "I will go and worship," without explicitly inviting the other person along — constitutes *hasatah*, because when someone enthusiastically declares his intention to go worship an idol before you, the implication is that you will follow.

A subtlety remains: the opening of the *mishnah* describes the *mesit* as one who talks up the idol — recounting its powers and habits — while the closing section specifies the direct declaration of worshipping. It is not entirely clear whether the full act of *hasatah* requires both components together, or whether either alone suffices. The *gemara* does not fully resolve this point.

---

## Gemara Attributions

### Mishna Reading

The *gemara* opens by noting that the *mishnah* describes the *mesit* as the *hedyot* — the commoner. The implication, on one reading, is that a *navi sheker* who incites to idolatry does not receive *skila* but rather *chenek*. Similarly, the contrast with the individual — *hamesit et hahedyot* — implies that one who seduces the many receives *chenek* rather than *skila*.

The *gemara* concludes: *masnitin mani Rabbi Shimon hi* — the *mishnah* follows the view of Rabbi Shimon.

### Rabbi Shimon

The *baraisa* is cited: a *navi* who acted as a *madiach* — according to the *chachamim* — receives *skila*; Rabbi Shimon says *chenek*. Those who seduce the *ir hanidachat* — according to the *chachamim* — receive *skila*; Rabbi Shimon says *chenek*. So it is Rabbi Shimon who holds that both the *navi sheker* who incites to idolatry and the seducers of the *ir hanidachat* receive the lighter penalty of strangulation, while the *chachamim* maintain *skila* across all categories. Intriguingly, Rabbi Shimon's position assigns the *lesser* penalty to the *navi sheker* and *madiach* relative to the *mesit*.

But the *gemara* immediately raises an objection: *eima seifa* — look at the end of the *mishnah*. The next *mishnah* begins: *hamadiach, ze ha'omer neilech v'na'avod avodat kochavim*. And as Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav, *midichei ir hanidachat shanu kan* — the word *madiach* here refers to the seducers of the *ir hanidachat*. If the *madiach* of an *ir hanidachat* also receives *skila*, then the *mishnah* as a whole cannot follow Rabbi Shimon. We would have a *mishnah* that begins like Rabbi Shimon and ends like the *chachamim*.

### Ravina's Resolution

Ravina resolves this: *kulla Rabbanan hi* — the entire *mishnah* reflects the view of the *chachamim*. The opening clause is not to be read as a contrast implying that other categories receive a different punishment. Rather, it follows the principle of *velo zu af zu* — the *mishnah* is not narrowing the law but expanding it. It says: here is the *mesit*, an individual who entices a single person — he receives *skila*. And other categories? The *navi sheker* is a different category, but he too receives *skila*. The *madiach* of an *ir hanidachat*, as the next *mishnah* states, also receives *skila*. The *mishnah* is mapping the landscape of the categories, not excluding the others from *skila*.

### Rav Pappa View

Rav Pappa offers an alternative reading. He accepts that Ravina has correctly identified the structure — *mesit* enticing an individual receives *skila*, *madiach* of an *ir hanidachat* in the next *mishnah* also receives *skila* — but he addresses a remaining gap: where does the *mishnah* address the contrast between a *mesit* who is a commoner and one who is a *navi*? Ravina's reading does not seem to resolve this.

Rav Pappa says: when the *mishnah* describes the *mesit* as a *hedyot*, it is not contrasting him with a *navi* at all. The word *hedyot* here means: we treat him with contempt. *Lerachmana* — the Torah calls him a commoner to communicate the halachic posture we adopt toward him: *machminim alav*, we hide witnesses against him, we treat him without the ordinary dignity of the *hatra'ah* process. The *baraisa* that follows elaborates: you light a candle in the inner chamber, you seat the witnesses in the outer chamber in the dark — so they can see him and hear his voice, but he cannot see them — and the procedure of the *mishnah* plays out. So the point of calling him a *hedyot* is not categorical distinction but rather the license to use the entrapment method.

---

## Mechashef Category

### Real vs. Illusion

The *mishnah* continues: *hamachshef* — the sorcerer. The Torah in *Shemot* uses the feminine form, *mechashefah*, but the rule applies equally to men and women. The *mishnah* defines the culpable *mechashef* as one who performs a genuine act — *ha'oseh ma'aseh chayav* — as opposed to *ha'oches et ha'einayim*, the illusionist who deceives the eye. If someone uses genuine witchcraft or sorcery to effect a real change in the world, he is liable for execution. If he is merely an illusionist who makes something appear differently than it is, he is not *chayav mitah*. A striking implication of this distinction — one that runs throughout this section of the *gemara* — is that *chazal* understood real witchcraft to be an actual, effective phenomenon, not merely a superstition.

### Akiva Example

Rabbi Akiva, citing Rabbi Yehoshua, offers an illustrative case: *shnayim loktin kishuin* — two people appear to wave their hands and magically harvest cucumbers from the patch. One is liable and one is exempt. How can this be? *Ha'oseh ma'aseh chayav* — the one who actually performed a real act using sorcery is liable. *Ve'ha'oches et ha'einayim patur* — the one who merely created the illusion of picking cucumbers without actually altering anything is exempt.

### Punishment Dispute

A *baraisa* is then cited addressing the nature of the *mechashef*'s punishment. The Torah says *mechashefah lo techayeh* but does not specify the mode of execution. How do we determine which of the four death penalties applies?

Rabbi Yossi HaGlili argues by *gezerah shavah*: just as the Torah uses the phrase *lo techayeh* by *mechashefah*, it also uses *lo techayeh kol neshama* in the context of warfare against the enemy, where the mode is *sayif* — the sword. Therefore, the punishment for a *mechashef* is also death by the sword.

Rabbi Akiva disagrees and argues his own *gezerah shavah*: the phrase *lo yichyeh* appears at Har Sinai — *yaro yerare o sakel yisakel lo yichyeh* — in a context that explicitly mentions *skila*. Therefore, by connecting *mechashefah lo techayeh* to *lo yichyeh* at Har Sinai, the punishment is *skila*.

Rabbi Yossi pushes back: I derived *lo techayeh* from *lo techayeh* — the exact same phrase. You are combining *lo techayeh* with *lo yichyeh*, which is a different formulation. Rabbi Akiva responds on two fronts. First, both of his cases involve a *Yisrael* — a Jew — whereas Rabbi Yossi's comparison draws from the *lo techayeh* of warfare against non-Jews. Second, since there are multiple possible death penalties for Jews — *skila*, *sreifa*, *hereg*, *chenek* — the specification of one at Har Sinai is meaningful and informative about which penalty applies in analogous cases. When it comes to non-Jews, there is only ever one penalty, *sayif*, making the comparison less instructive for determining which of multiple Jewish penalties to select. Our *mishnah* follows Rabbi Akiva: *skila*.

### Ben Azai

Ben Azai offers an independent derivation. The Torah juxtaposes the verse about the *mechashefah* with the verse *kol shochev im behema mot yumat* — one who commits bestiality shall be put to death. *Samchu inyan lo* — the *parshiyos* are juxtaposed. Just as bestiality carries *skila* (which Ben Azai assumes is established elsewhere), so too the *mechashef* receives *skila* by virtue of the juxtaposition.

### Rabbi Yehuda

Rabbi Yehuda objects: *vechi mipnei shesamchu inyan lo notzei ze beskila?* — just because they are juxtaposed we are going to bring this person out and stone him? Rashi explains *notzei* as removing him from the other penalty categories to assign him the most severe, though there is also a powerful visual dimension to the phrase: can we really execute someone by stoning on the basis of a textual adjacency?

This objection is the source for the general rule that Rabbi Yehuda is not *doresh smuchin* — he does not derive law from the mere juxtaposition of passages, except in Sefer Devarim, which is a separate matter.

Rabbi Yehuda offers his own derivation instead: *ov v'yidoni bichlal machashifim hayu* — *ov* and *yidoni* are themselves types of sorcery, subsumed within the category of *mechashef*. The Torah nevertheless singles them out — *velama yatzu? lehakish lahen* — in order to allow a *hekesh*, a comparison, back to the general category. Since *ov* and *yidoni* are punished by *skila*, and they are linked by *hekesh* to *mechashef*, the *mechashef* too is punished by *skila*.

### Two Kesuvim

The *gemara* then presses: if Rabbi Yehuda does not *doresh smuchin*, and instead relies on the principle that when a case is singled out from a general category it teaches back to the whole — this is the rule of *davar sheyatza min haklal lelamed, lo lelamed al atzmo yatza ela lelamed al haklal kulo yatza* — then both *ov* and *yidoni* were singled out. That gives us *shnei kesuvim habayim ke'echad* — two verses making the same point. And the rule is that when two verses make the same point, one does not derive a general principle from them; each instance is treated as its own isolated exception.

This objection, however, actually confirms something about Rabbi Yehuda's position: *kasavar Rabbi Yehuda, shnei kesuvim habayim ke'echad melamdim* — Rabbi Yehuda holds that even when two verses are singled out together to make the same point, they *do* teach the general principle. This is a known position of Rabbi Yehuda documented elsewhere in the *gemara*, and its source is precisely this passage.

---

## Theology & Shed Powers

### Heavenly Powers

Rabbi Yochanan asks: *lama nikra sheman mechashefim?* — why are sorcerers called *mechashefim*? He reads it as an acronym: *shemacheshim pamalya shemala* — they weaken the heavenly household, the divine retinue above. Witchcraft is understood as an assault on the order maintained by the heavenly powers, a subversion of the natural and divine order.

This raises a sharp theological question. If the sorcerers weaken the *pamalya shemala*, does that mean that witchcraft actually constrains God? The *gemara* addresses this through a story about Rabbi Chanina. A woman was attempting to gather the dust from beneath his feet — apparently in order to perform sorcery against him. Rabbi Chanina told her: if you succeed, go and do it — *ein od milvado ksiv*, the Torah has written "there is none besides God." Rabbi Chanina's trust in God was absolute: whatever power witchcraft might have, God transcends it entirely.

The *gemara* then asks: but Rabbi Yochanan said that sorcerers *do* weaken the heavenly powers — implying that witchcraft works! The resolution: *shani Rabbi Chanina denafish zchusei* — Rabbi Chanina was different; his merit was exceptional. The general assumption, the *gemara* makes clear, is that witchcraft does operate effectively under normal circumstances. It is only for a person of Rabbi Chanina's extraordinary spiritual stature that God would override the ordinary functioning of those forces. For everyone else, the assumption must be that these powers operate — just as one cannot step off a cliff and rely on *ein od milvado*. Rabbi Chanina was making a bold theological statement rooted in his personal trust in God, not a general halachic claim that witchcraft never works.

### Egyptian Magic

Rabbi Aivo bar Nagri, citing Rabbi Chiya bar Abba, addresses the terminology used for the Egyptian magicians in the Torah. When the text says *belateihem* — without the letter *heh* — this refers to *maasei shedim*, the work of demons. The root *lat* suggests concealment or invisibility; the magicians summoned *shedim*, lesser spirits, to perform their operations. When the text says *belahateihem* — with the *heh*, the root *lahat* meaning flash or flame — this refers to *maasei keshafim*, direct magical powers not mediated through *shedim*. The verse *ve'et lahat hacherev hamitpachet* — the flashing of the turning sword — is cited in support: the flashing motion evokes this kind of direct sorcerous power.

### Vessel Particularity

Abaye offers a practical diagnostic: *dekaphid amana shed, delo kaphid amana keshafim* — if the practitioner is very particular about the specific vessels and implements used, this indicates *shedim* are at work. One may recall from the *gemara* in Berachot the elaborate specifications — a black cat, the daughter of a black cat, first-born, and so forth — all of that specificity is characteristic of *shedim*, who apparently require precise conditions to be invoked. If the practitioner is indifferent to the vessels, the operation is direct *keshafim*.

### Keshafim Categories

Abaye then articulates a tripartite framework, comparing the laws of *keshafim* to the laws of Shabbat. Some forms of sorcery carry *skila* — just as deliberate *melachah* on Shabbat. Some are *patur aval assur* — exempt from court penalty but still forbidden, analogous to rabbinically prohibited labor on Shabbat. And some are *mutar lechatchilah* — entirely permitted from the outset.

What falls into the *mutar lechatchilah* category? The example is Rav Chanina and Rav Oshaya. Every *erev Shabbat* they would study *Hilchot Yetzirah* — the laws of creation, understood by some to refer to the *Sefer Yetzirah* — and would thereby create a *igla tilta*, a fine third-born calf, which they would eat on Shabbat. This is the permitted category. The operative distinction appears to be: if one employs divine names and divine creative power, it is not in the category of forbidden *keshafim*; if one employs the power of demons or magic, it is. Rashi at one point suggests the calf came into being automatically through the learning, but the context — deliberately studying to produce Shabbat food — strongly implies intentionality, and the distinction rests on the source of power invoked.

### Creation Debate

Rav Ashi adds an observation: *chazeina lei le'avuha deKarna* — he once saw the father of Karna, evidently a practitioner of illusion or sleight of hand, who blew his nose and silk scarves came streaming out of his nostrils — a classic illusionist's trick performed, apparently, in an unusual fashion.

The *gemara* then returns to the Egyptian sorcerers and the plague of lice. When the *chartumim* said *etzba Elokim hi* — "it is the finger of God" — they acknowledged they could not replicate it. Why not? Rabbi Elazar derives from here: *ein hashed yachol livrot biryah pachos mikis'orah* — a *shed* cannot create a creature smaller than a barley kernel. The lice were too small for the *shedim* to gather or create, hence the magicians' failure.

### Shed Creation

Rav Pappa takes a more sweeping position: *ha'Elokim, afilu kegamla nami lo matzei barei* — in God's name, the *shedim* cannot create anything at all, not even something as large as a camel. The question of size is beside the point. The distinction is not about size but about *kinuf* — gathering. *Hanei michnaf lehu, vehanei lo michnaf lehu* — what the magicians using *shedim* can do is send the *shedim* to gather existing matter from elsewhere and bring it together. What they cannot do is create *ex nihilo*. The lice were too small and too numerous to be gathered from elsewhere, which is why the magicians failed. Rabbi Elazar and Rav Pappa thus disagree about whether *shedim* can create at all: Rabbi Elazar holds they can, but are limited by size; Rav Pappa holds they cannot create anything and can only gather what already exists.

---

## Witchcraft Examples

### Rav's Camel

Rav told Rabbi Chiya: *le-didi chazi hahu taya* — I once saw a certain nomadic Arab who took his sword, chopped his camel in half, banged on a bell, and the camel rose back up whole. Rabbi Chiya immediately asked: afterward, was there blood and excrement on the ground? Presumably there was not. Therefore, Rabbi Chiya concluded: *ella hi achizat einayim havei* — it was pure illusion. The camel was never actually cut; the whole scene was a deception of the eye.

### Alexandria Donkey

Zeiri came to Alexandria in Egypt and purchased a donkey. When he brought it to drink water, the magic reversed itself — for water, it appears, is the agent that dissolves these kinds of spells — and the donkey became a plank of wood. He had been sold an enchanted board. He went to reclaim his money, and the sellers told him: if you were not the distinguished Zeiri, we would not give you your money back. Anyone who buys anything in Alexandria without first testing it with water is simply not exercising due diligence. The marketplace in Egypt is one where *keshafim* are rife, and the prudent buyer knows to test.

### Inn Encounter

A figure named Yanai came to an inn and ordered water. A wheat-and-water mixture was brought. He noticed that the barmaid's lips were moving — a telltale sign of an attempt at sorcery — and he quietly poured out a small amount of the liquid. Scorpions emerged from it, revealing what had been hidden in the drink. He then announced to the proprietors: "I drank your water; now you drink mine" — and served them a drink over which he had performed his own enchantment. The woman was transformed into a donkey. He rode her into the marketplace. Her friend came, apparently aware of what had happened, and dissolved the spell with water. Yanai was then seen riding on a woman in the middle of the marketplace — the story is not without its disturbing dimensions — and the episode ends there.

### Marketplace Exposure

The donkey-woman episode described above — the transformation, the public exposure, and the dissolution of the spell by water — illustrates both the operation of *keshafim* in these stories and the recurring role of water as the agent of reversal. In both the Alexandria donkey and the inn incident, water is what breaks the enchantment, a detail the *gemara* presents matter-of-factly as practical knowledge.

---

## Frog Plague

### Frog Debate

Returning briefly to the world of Egyptian plagues, the *gemara* addresses the verse *va-ta'al ha-tzefardea va-techas et eretz Mitzrayim* — the frog (singular) arose and covered the land of Egypt. Rabbi Elazar states: *tzefardea achat haytah* — there was one frog, and it propagated, multiplying its young until they filled all of Egypt.

The *gemara* notes this is actually a *tannaitic* dispute. Rabbi Akiva holds: there was one frog, and from it all of Egypt was filled — all of the frogs came from this single progenitor. Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah said to him: *Akiva, mah lecha etzel aggadah?* — Akiva, what are you doing with *aggadah*? Stay in your lane. *Kelach midiburecha, v'lech etzel Negaim v'Oholot* — stop speaking about these matters and go to *Negaim* and *Oholot*, the most complex areas of halachic reasoning, where your expertise lies.

### Rebuke

Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah's own reading: there was one frog, yes — but not that all the frogs propagated from it biologically. Rather, this one frog let out a croak, *sharka lahem*, and that called all the other frogs to come. The frog was a leader that summoned the masses, not a single organism that spawned them all.

Why was Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah so exercised by Rabbi Akiva's reading? The text does not make fully explicit what troubled him so deeply. The two positions may not appear so dramatically different — one emphasizes miraculous biological propagation, the other a miraculous form of leadership and ingathering. Perhaps Rabbi Elazar felt that the *aggadic* exposition required a more careful interpretive hand, and that the domain of *aggadah* belonged to its own specialists, while Rabbi Akiva's true mastery lay in the rigors of *Negaim* and *Oholot*.

# Sanhedrin 68

## Opening & Arba Mitot

### Daf Overview & Kishuf

Today's *daf* is Sanhedrin 68, and it serves a dual purpose: completing *perek* Arba Mitot and beginning the *perek* of *ben sorer u-moreh*. We pick up with the final lines of the *mishnah*, where Rabbi Akiva addresses the *issur* of *kishuf* — witchcraft. Rabbi Akiva's ruling distinguishes between two scenarios: if one actually performs an act of sorcery, one is *chayav*; if the act was mere illusion, one is *patur*. The example given is making it appear as though one has gathered an entire field of vegetables — if actually done, there is a *chiyuv sekilah*; if only an illusion, one is exempt.

It is worth noting that the *gemara* earlier, in dealing with the *issur* of *kishuf* a few *dafim* back, cited one interpretation according to which even creating the illusion of performing sorcery — without actually doing anything — could constitute an *issur* of *lo te'onenu*. Different understandings exist regarding exactly what *lo te'onenu* prohibits, and interesting questions arise about how it applies in contemporary contexts where audiences are generally aware that no real magic is being performed. In any event, this would be at most an *issur d'oraita* without rising to the level of a *chiyuv misah*.

## Rabbi Akiva's Source

### Source Dispute

The *gemara* opens 68a with a challenge to the *mishnah*. Since Rabbi Akiva cites Rabbi Yehoshua as his source, the *gemara* asks: *amar Rabbi Akiva me-Rabbi Yehoshua gemar lei?* — did Rabbi Akiva really learn this from Rabbi Yehoshua? A *brayta* is cited suggesting he actually learned it from Rabbi Eliezer, his primary *rebbe*. The *gemara* thus poses a tension: the *mishnah* attributes the teaching to Rabbi Yehoshua, while the *brayta* points to Rabbi Eliezer.

## Opening & Arba Mitot (II)

### Illusion vs. Actual Deed

The clarification is that Rabbi Akiva in fact learned from both. He received the teaching from Rabbi Eliezer, and he also received it — with fuller comprehension — from Rabbi Yehoshua. This resolution will be elaborated upon after the *gemara* recounts the famous narrative surrounding Rabbi Eliezer's death.

## Rabbi Akiva's Source (II)

### Rabbi Eliezer Background

To provide context for the *brayta*, it is necessary to recall who Rabbi Eliezer was and what defined his final years. Rabbi Eliezer is the central figure of the *tanur shel Achnai* episode: all the *chachamim* ruled that a particular oven was *tamei*, while Rabbi Eliezer ruled it *tahor*. He caused the walls of the *beit midrash* to bend inward, the river to flow backward, and even brought forth a heavenly voice affirming his position — yet the rabbis replied *lo bashamayim hi*, and the majority ruling prevailed. Because Rabbi Eliezer refused to accept the principle of majority rule, he was placed in *cherem*, and the other rabbis were barred from entering his space or learning with him directly. It is against this backdrop that the deathbed narrative unfolds.

## Rabbi Eliezer's Deathbed

### Hurcanus Incident

*Kesheh-chalah Rabbi Eliezer* — when Rabbi Eliezer fell ill, Rabbi Akiva and his colleagues came to visit him. He was seated beneath his canopy bed while they remained in the outer chamber of his house. It was a Friday, *erev Shabbat*, and his son Hurcanus entered to remove his *tefillin*, since one does not wear *tefillin* on *Shabbat*. Rabbi Eliezer rebuked him sharply, and Hurcanus left in a state of distress. He turned to the assembled colleagues and said: it appears that my father's mind has become confused — perhaps a sign of the delirium of a dying man, given that he would not allow the removal of his *tefillin* before *Shabbat*.

Rabbi Eliezer, who had overheard this, responded that his *da'at* was entirely sound — *miyushevet* — and that it was his son and perhaps his son's mother who had the problem. He then posed a sharp rhetorical question: *heich manichin issur sekila ve-oseqin be-issur shevut?* — how is it that you are neglecting a concern that could rise to the level of *sekilah*, namely the obligation to light *Shabbat* candles before nightfall, while busying yourselves with my *tefillin*, which at worst would be an *issur d'rabonon*?

The reasoning is as follows: in the era of the *gemara*, the requirement to light candles before *Shabbat* was understood as ensuring that lights were burning in the home before *Shabbat* arrived, and one had to take care to do so with sufficient time. As for *tefillin*, one does not wear them on *Shabbat* because *Shabbat* is not *zman tefillin*, and there is an *issur shevut* — an *issur d'rabonon* — related to going outdoors wearing them into a *reshut ha-rabbim*. Even that would only be *d'rabonon*, since even without *zman tefillin*, wearing them in the house is akin to a *malbush*, a garment. So the worst that could follow from Rabbi Eliezer's still wearing *tefillin* was a rabbinic prohibition, whereas the proper priority at that moment should have been the *Shabbat* candles. You have your priorities entirely wrong.

When the *chachamim* perceived that his *da'at* was indeed sound — and perhaps also recognized that he was still his characteristically pointed self — they entered and sat before him, but at a distance of four *amos*, since he remained in *nidduy* and they were not permitted to enter within his four *amos*. He asked them: why have you come? They said: we came to learn Torah from you. He replied: and why did you not come until now? They answered that they had not had the opportunity — *lo hayah lanu pnai* — clearly not wishing to name the actual reason, dancing around the *nidduy* that had kept them apart.

### Harsh Prophecy

Rabbi Eliezer then said: *tamei ani im yamutu misat atzman* — I would be astonished if you were to die a natural death. This is a strikingly harsh statement, and it is one that carries terrible historical resonance given what we know of the fate of Rabbi Akiva and his contemporaries in the era of martyrdom. Rabbi Akiva then asked directly: *sheli mahu?* — and what of mine? Rabbi Eliezer replied: *shelcha kasha mishel-lahen* — yours will be worse than theirs. And of course we know the horrific nature of Rabbi Akiva's death. Rashi explains that Rabbi Akiva's fate was considered the most severe because he had the greatest opportunity to learn from Rabbi Eliezer, and therefore the loss sustained by the *nidduy* and the estrangement was greatest in his case.

### Lament on Knowledge

At that moment, Rabbi Eliezer took his two arms — *natal shtei zero'osav* — and placed them upon his heart. He said: *oy lachem shtei zero'osai* — woe to you, my two arms, for they are like two *sifrei Torah* that have been rolled up. The image is powerful: an arm, in its shape, resembles a closed scroll — sealed, containing everything within it, but inaccessible unless opened. And that was precisely his lament: he carried within himself a vast expanse of *Torah*, but no one was opening him up to receive it.

He continued: *harbeh Torah lamadeti velo chasarti merabbosai afilu kechelev hammelakkeik min hayam* — I learned so much Torah and yet I did not diminish my teachers even as much as a dog lapping water from the sea. The image here is not really about taking something away from one's teachers, but about the vastness of what remained. What he received, even with all that he learned, was but a drop in the ocean. And then for his students: *velo chissaruni talmidai ella kemikchol bishapaferess* — my students did not take from me more than an eyelash applicator drawn from its tube. Notably, the proportion is somewhat larger — the eyelash applicator does take more than a dog from the sea — and Rabbi Eliezer uses this slightly less severe image when speaking of what his students received from him rather than about himself; he reserves the harsher self-deprecation for his own relationship to his teachers. In either case, the essential point is the same: I had an ocean of *Torah* to give, and only the tiniest fraction was ever transmitted.

### Gourds Halachot

Rabbi Eliezer then made his lament explicit. He said: *ela she-ani shoneh shlosh meiot halachot b'vaheret azah* — I have three hundred *halachot* concerning the bright *tzara'at* spot known as *baheret azah*, *v'lo hayah adam she-she'alani bahen davar me'olam* — and not a single person ever asked me about them. The image of the two arms as rolled-up *sifrei Torah* finds its fullest expression here: all of that knowledge, sealed inside, with no one to open it up.

And further: *v'lo od* — and not only this — *she-ani shoneh bishlosh meiot halachot*, some say *shloshet alafim halachot*, in the planting of *kishu'in* — gourds, or cucumbers — *v'lo hayah adam she-she'alani bahen davar me'olam chutz me-Akiva ben Yosef*. Three hundred *halachot*, or according to some versions three thousand, concerning the planting of gourds — and not a single person ever asked him about them, with one exception: Rabbi Akiva.

### Magic Encounter

*Pa'am achat ani v'hu hayinu mehalchin baderech* — once, Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva were walking along the way, and Rabbi Akiva said to him: *Rabbi, lamdeni bi-netiat kishu'in* — Rabbi, teach me something of what you know about the planting of gourds. It seems, reading the context, almost as though Rabbi Akiva was asking in order to give Rabbi Eliezer the opportunity to teach these *halachot* that no one else had ever requested — not because he was necessarily in need of this knowledge himself.

*Amarti davar echad v'nitmalleh kol hasadeh kishu'in* — Rabbi Eliezer said one word and the entire field filled with cucumbers. And then Rabbi Akiva said: you have taught me the planting — *lamdeni akiratan* — now teach me the uprooting. *Amarti davar echad v'nitkabbetzu kullam l'makom echad* — Rabbi Eliezer said another word and they all gathered into one place.

This immediately raises a serious question: how could Rabbi Eliezer actually perform this act? Is there not a *chiyuv sekilah* for actually doing *kishuf*? This is distinct from the *tzara'at* material, which involves genuinely detailed *halachic* questions about what renders a spot *tamei* or *tahor*. The knowledge of *kishuf* is of a different character — it is practical magical knowledge, the performance of which the *Torah* makes a capital offense. The tragedy here is layered: not only was Rabbi Eliezer's *Torah* sealed away due to the *nidduy* and the estrangement from his students, but even the vast knowledge he possessed raises questions about its halachic relevance and what it truly empowered his students with.

This passage also reflects a broader portrait of Rabbi Eliezer that emerges from multiple sources. The *mishnah* in Pirkei Avot describes him as a *bor sud she-eino m'abed tipah* — a plastered cistern that does not lose a drop. A cistern, of course, has no spring of its own; it holds only what was poured into it, and does not generate new water. This is contrasted with the *ma'ayan hamisgaber*, the ever-strengthening wellspring. And the *gemara* in Sukka and elsewhere notes that Rabbi Eliezer would say he never taught anything that he had not received from his teachers. His entire understanding of *Torah she-be'al peh* was one of receiving and transmitting, not of human creativity. This is precisely what drove the *tanur shel Achnai* conflict: he could not accept *lo bashamayim hi*, the principle of rabbinic authority and creative interpretation. He had his tradition; it was true; no majority vote could change that. And so he died as he lived — committed utterly to what he had received, lamenting what he had been unable to pass on.

### Vessel Debate

The sages, perhaps seizing the opportunity to elicit some of the *Torah* he had lamented no one ever asked him about, now posed to him several practical *halachic* questions. They asked about *hakadur, ha'amos, v'hakamia, umishkolet ktana* — a leather ball packed tightly with stuffing, a cobbler's form used to shape shoes, a small pouch used as a charm to hold jewels (Rashi understands this as an amulet for preventing illness, where the stones are never meant to be removed), and a small weight covered in leather. The general principle governing leather vessels is that a *kli* can become *tamei* only if it has a *beit kibul*, a receptacle. The question in each of these cases is whether an object that was hollow and thus had a receptacle, but was then filled and sealed with stuffing not meant to be removed, retains its status as a vessel with a *beit kibul*.

This was a known dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the *chachamim*, and the sages wished to confirm that he still held his position. Rabbi Eliezer affirmed that they remain *tamei* — *hen tme'im* — and added that their purification is achieved with the stuffing in place: *vetaharatan b'ma shehen*. The stuffing does not constitute a *chatzitza* that would prevent *tevilah* from being effective. This may seem ironic, since the entire reason the object is considered to have a *beit kibul* is because it contains filling — yet for purposes of *tevilah*, that same filling is not treated as a separate entity creating an interposition. Nevertheless, that is Rabbi Eliezer's ruling, consistent throughout, as inflexible and certain as ever.

### Final Ruling & Death

They then asked about *min'al she'al gabei ha'amos mahu* — what is the status of a completed shoe that is still resting on the cobbler's form? It is fully finished, but has not yet been removed from the form. Is it already considered a completed *kli* capable of becoming *tamei*, or does removal from the form constitute the final step of completion? This too was a matter of dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the *chachamim*, and again he was asked whether he maintained his position.

*Amar lahen hu tahor* — he said to them: it is *tahor*. And as he spoke that word — *yatza nishmatoh b'tahara* — his soul departed in purity. The symmetry is striking: the great dispute that defined his final decades was the *tanur shel Achnai*, in which all the *chachamim* ruled *tamei* and he alone ruled *tahor*. He died with the word *tahor* on his lips. He lived exactly as he died — rigorously consistent in every position, unwavering. A pure ending, one might say, entirely of a piece with the life.

### Nidduy Ended & Eulogy

*Amad Rabbi Yehoshua al raglav v'amar hutar haneder* — Rabbi Yehoshua arose and declared: the *neder* is undone, the *nidduy* is released. Even in death, there are rules that can apply to someone who was under excommunication, and Rabbi Yehoshua formally declared that with Rabbi Eliezer's death, the *nidduy* was concluded.

*Lemotzaei Shabbat paga bo Rabbi Akiva min Keisari l'Lod* — on *motzaei Shabbat*, Rabbi Akiva encountered the funeral procession making its way from Caesarea to Lod — it appears Rabbi Eliezer had died in Caesarea, though he was from Lod, and was being brought there for burial. *Hayah makkeh bivesaro ad shedamo shotet la'aretz* — Rabbi Akiva was striking his own flesh in grief until his blood poured to the ground. Tosafot raises the question of the *d'oraita* prohibition of *veseret lanefesh lo titenu bivesarchem*, the prohibition against making cuts in one's flesh for the dead — though it appears this was not a deliberate incision but an expression of anguished grief.

*Patach alav bishura* — he opened with a eulogy in the processional formation. He quoted the words Elisha spoke when Elijah departed: *avi avi rechev Yisrael ufarashav* — my father, my father, the chariot of Israel and its horsemen. And then he added his own words: *harbeh ma'ot yesh li ve'ein li shulchani lehartzo'tam* — I have so much coinage and no money changer to exchange it. I have no one to help me clarify and make usable all of the teachings I carry.

The image chosen by Rabbi Akiva is telling. A money changer does not create new wealth; he takes existing coinage and changes it — verifies its authenticity, breaks it into smaller denominations, makes it usable. Rabbi Akiva, who represented the diametrically opposite pole from Rabbi Eliezer — all human creativity, all *chiddush* — here describes what he lost in Rabbi Eliezer in terms of the most conservative possible function: someone who could test his coins, help him verify and clarify. It is an extraordinarily fitting and moving valediction.

## Educational Witchcraft

### Learning & Understanding

After this deeply layered and powerful narrative, the *gemara* returns to its original question: *alma me-Rabbi Eliezer gamra* — apparently Rabbi Akiva learned the principle about *kishuf* and the planting of *kishu'in* from Rabbi Eliezer, not from Rabbi Yehoshua. The *gemara* resolves the tension as follows: *gamra me-Rabbi Eliezer v'lo savra* — he learned it from Rabbi Eliezer, but did not fully understand it. *Hadar gamra me-Rabbi Yehoshua ve'asbera nihalei* — he then learned it again from Rabbi Yehoshua, and Rabbi Yehoshua explained it to him so that he understood it fully. This resolution is entirely apt given everything we now know of Rabbi Eliezer: the transmitter of received knowledge who was not necessarily the one to open it up and make it comprehensible.

### Witchcraft Permission

*Heichi avdi hachi?* — but now the *gemara* presses a harder question. How could Rabbi Eliezer actually have performed this act? *Ve'anan tenan oseh ma'aseh chayav* — the *mishnah* itself rules that one who performs *kishuf* as an actual deed, not merely an illusion, is *chayav*. And it sounds very much as though what Rabbi Eliezer did on that road was for real.

The *gemara* answers: *v'shani* — this case is different. The act was performed for educational purposes, to understand and to teach, not in order to actually practice sorcery. This is derived from the *pasuk*: *lo tilmad la'asot* — you shall not learn to do as the abominations of the nations. *La'asot iy ata lamed* — you may not learn in order to do. *Aval ata lamed lehavin ule'horot* — but you may learn for the purpose of understanding and teaching. And the *gemara* concludes that on this basis one may even actually perform the act, if doing so is genuinely for educational purposes. This is, to say the least, a striking ruling — that the very act which carries a *chiyuv sekilah* may be performed when the intent is understanding and transmission rather than practice.

With that, the *gemara* recites *hadran alach Arba Misos*, and *perek* Arba Misos concludes. Though the *perek* is named for the four methods of execution, its content has in practice focused almost entirely on the cases requiring *sekilah* — and even as we move forward, that continues, as *ben sorer u-moreh* is likewise a case of *sekilah*. The extraordinary depth devoted to *ben sorer u-moreh* in the *mishnayot* and *gemara* — far exceeding the treatment of the other cases — is itself significant, and is presumably connected to the famous principle that *ben sorer u-moreh* never actually occurred. The *Torah* gave it so that one could study it and receive reward: *drush v'kabel sechar*.

## Ben Sorer u-Moreh Intro

### Future Conduct

The new *perek* begins on 68b. *Ben sorer u-moreh* is another category requiring *sekilah*, and the *mishnah* opens by asking: *eimatai na'aseh ben sorer u-moreh?* — when does a young man actually become a *ben sorer u-moreh?* What is the period of culpability?

Before examining the technical criteria, it is important to note a foundational principle that the *gemara* will make explicit: the *ben sorer u-moreh* is not executed for the gravity of his current sin. Eating and drinking to excess, disobeying his parents — these are not crimes that in themselves would ordinarily warrant death. Rather, *al shem sofo neherag* — he is executed on account of his future. The *Torah* looks ahead and perceives that he is on a trajectory toward becoming a murderous bandit, and decrees that it is better for him to die while still innocent than to be killed after he has become guilty.

This is an obviously striking and counterintuitive principle, and it is clearly connected to why the *gemara* insists that *ben sorer u-moreh* never actually happened — the halakhic system surrounds the case with so many conditions and restrictions that in practice no one could ever be executed under it. But the principle is important to state up front.

The Ramban adds a crucial dimension here. In the section of *Shoftim*, there are several *mitzvot* where the *Torah* adds the phrase *v'chol Yisrael yishme'u v'yira'u* — and all of Israel will hear and fear. Ramban reads this as indicating that part of the purpose of the death penalty in these cases is not the gravity of the individual's sin per se, but the broader societal function of protecting key institutions. One such case is *zaken mamre*, the elder who defies the ruling of the Sanhedrin: the harsh punishment exists to protect the authority of the court itself, which is a foundational social institution. Similarly here, the parental relationship is an institution whose authority the *Torah* invests with enormous significance, and the punishment of the *ben sorer u-moreh* is designed to uphold it in the broader social consciousness — *v'chol Yisrael yishme'u v'yira'u*.

## Age Requirements

### Hair Criteria

The *mishnah* specifies the window of culpability: *mi-she'yavi shtei se'arot* — from the time he produces two pubic hairs, meaning from age 13 when he becomes *halachically* obligated — *v'ad sheyakif zakan* — until his beard fills out. The *mishnah* immediately clarifies: *ha-tachton v'lo ha-elyon* — the lower beard, not the upper beard, meaning his pubic hair. *Ella she-dibru chachamim bilshon nekiyah* — but the Rabbis expressed themselves euphemistically and called it a beard.

### Ben v'lo Ish

How does the *Torah* establish these boundaries? The *mishnah* cites the *pasuk*: *ki yihyeh l'ish ben* — when a man has a son who is *sorer u-moreh*. From this the *mishnah* derives: *ben v'lo bat* — a son and not a daughter; *ben v'lo ish* — a son and not a fully grown man. So on one side, he must be old enough to be obligated in *mitzvot*, and on the other side, he must not yet have fully developed physically into a man.

This raises an immediate question: the *mishnah* ends by noting that *katan patur shelo ba l'chlal mitzvot* — a minor is exempt because he has not yet entered the realm of *mitzvot*. But why do we even need to state this? And why is the *gemara*'s opening question — *katan minailan d'patur?* — framed as though the default assumption might be that a minor should be *chayav*?

The *gemara* explains: *ki katani ta'ama* — the *mishnah* does state the reason right there. But the deeper point is this: the *ben sorer u-moreh* is not executed for his current sin. *Atu ben sorer u-moreh achatei neherag?* — do you think he is being killed for what he actually did? No — *al shem sofo neherag*, he is killed for what he will become. And if that is so, then why should he have to be technically an adult? The logic of the punishment is prospective, not tied to present liability — *afilu katan nami*, perhaps even a minor should be included. Moreover, the *pasuk* itself says *ben v'lo ish*, a son and not a man, which literally suggests someone who is not yet a man at all — namely, a minor. Both logic and the *pasuk* thus point toward including minors.

### Vigor Window

The resolution comes from *Rav Yehuda amar Rav*: the *pasuk* reads *ki yihyeh l'ish ben*, and the juxtaposition of *le'ish ben* teaches *ben hasamuch ligvurato shel ish* — a son who is close to the vigor of a man. Rashi suggests reading the phrase almost in reverse: *ki yihyeh ben le'ish* — when the son has just become a man. The window of culpability is thus the period after he has technically reached *halachic* adulthood by producing two pubic hairs, but before he has fully filled out physically into an *ish*.

*Ad sheyakif zakkan ha-tachton v'lo ha-elyon* — until the lower beard fills out, not the upper. Rabbi Chiya taught this using the term *atara* — the crown — as a further euphemism.
