And when Rav Dimi came from Eretz Yisrael, he specified further: *hakafat gid v'lo hakafat beitzim* — the hair surrounding the shaft, not the hair surrounding the testicles.

## Minor Paternity

### Rav Chisda's Rule

Rav Chisda introduces a further dimension of the requirement. *Katan sheholid ein beno na'aseh ben sorer u-moreh* — if a minor fathered a child, that child cannot become a *ben sorer u-moreh*. The derivation comes from the same *pasuk*: *ki yihyeh l'ish ben* — *le'ish ben v'lo le'ben ben* — when a man has a son, but not when a child has a son. The son of someone who himself was a minor when he fathered that child does not qualify.

### Verse Analysis

The *gemara* challenges this immediately: is this not the same *pasuk* used by *Rav Yehuda amar Rav* to teach the *vigour window*? How can the same juxtaposition of *le'ish ben* be used to teach both that the father must be an adult and that the son must be at the transitional moment of early manhood?

The *gemara* responds with a precise textual observation. Had the *Torah* wished only to teach Rav Chisda's point — that it must be a man's son, not a child's son — it could have written *ki yihyeh ben ish*, which would naturally carry the connotation of *ben le'ish* and not *ben le'ben*. The fact that the *Torah* wrote *ki yihyeh l'ish ben* — placing *l'ish* before *ben* — allows both teachings to be derived simultaneously. *Shema mina tarti*: both that we are speaking of a son who has just reached the vigor of manhood, and that the father must himself have been an adult, not a minor, at the time of fathering.

### Rava's Position

The *gemara* notes that Rav Chisda's ruling implicitly assumes that a minor *can* father a child — otherwise the rule would be superfluous. This places Rav Chisda in tension with Rava, who holds that a minor *cannot* father a child at all. Rava derives this from the laws of *gezel ha-ger*: when someone steals from a convert, denies it under oath, later admits the theft, and the convert has since died, the thief must return the money to whoever is the convert's heir. If there is no heir — *v'ein l'ish go'el* — the money goes to the *kohen*.

The *gemara* notes that ordinarily, virtually every Jew has some relative who can serve as heir. The only case in which one could have no heir is a convert — a *ger* — who has left behind no Jewish relatives and has no children. The *pasuk* says *ish* — a man — implying that if the deceased was an adult man, one must investigate whether he has heirs. But if he was a minor — *katan* — *i ata tzarich lachzor alav*, you need not investigate, because *be-yadu'a she-ein lo go'alim* — it is a certainty that he has no heirs. And why is that a certainty? Because a minor cannot father a child. That is Rava's derivation: a minor is biologically and *halachically* incapable of fathering a child, and therefore no investigation into his potential heirs is necessary.

The *gemara* thus sets up a genuine dispute between Rav Chisda and Rava regarding whether a minor can father a child, and how we will see this play out will be taken up on the next *daf*.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 69

## Minor Fathering Child

### Rav Chisda vs Rava

The *daf* opens four lines from the top of 69a, at the words *etvei Abaye*. The context is the beginning of the laws of *ben sorer u'moreh*, the wayward and rebellious son. We have already positioned a debate between two *amoraim*: Rav Chisda taught that if a minor fathers a child, that child cannot himself become a *ben sorer u'moreh*, because the *pasuk* reads *le'ish ben*—a man has a son—implying that the father must be a man, not a child. The *gemara* understands this teaching to presuppose that an underage boy, someone under thirteen, is at least capable of fathering a child. This is understood to be in conflict with the position of Rava, who teaches—based on the case of *gezel ha'ger*, stealing from a convert and swearing falsely, whereupon the convert dies—that one need not be concerned about whether the convert left heirs if he was a minor, because a minor cannot father a child. So we have a direct debate between Rav Chisda and Rava over whether a minor is biologically capable of fathering offspring.

### Shifcha Charufa Case

Abaye challenges this framework. The *pasuk* in the case of *shifcha charufa*—a slave woman who is partly betrothed to a slave—reads *ve'ish ki yishkav et isha shichvat zera*, "and a man who lies with a woman as a seminal emission." Rashi notes that this is one of the places where the Torah explicitly describes the act as *shichvat zera*, and it is accordingly one of the contexts where *halacha* requires *gemar biah*, full penetration, rather than mere *ha'ara*, simple insertion.

From the word *ish*, "a man," one might think the law applies only to an adult man. The *talmud lomar*, the additional *vav* in *ve'ish*, teaches that even a boy nine years and a day old—whom we recognize as capable of an act of intercourse—is included. But the *gemara* notes that this *pasuk* speaks of *shichvat zera* in a context requiring that the act be *ra'uy l'hazri'a*, appropriate for seminal emission. From here, Abaye argues, we see that an underage child can indeed emit seed. Does this not demonstrate that a minor's seed is potent?

### Seed Potency Issue

The *gemara* concedes the point about emission but refuses the conclusion: *yesh lo v'eino molid*—he has seed but it cannot procreate. The semen exists but is not yet fertile. The analogy given is *kitzvu'a shelo heivia shlish*: grain that has not yet reached a third of its ripening. There is grain there, but were you to plant the kernel, it would not yield new growth. So too, the minor's seed is present but lacks generative potency.

### Yazid Drasha

The *beis Chizkiyah* offers a *drasha* in support. The *pasuk* in *Parshat Mishpatim* reads *vechi yazid ish al re'ehu lehorgo be'arma*, "and when a man acts with premeditation against his fellow to kill him with cunning." The *drashah* turns on the word *yazid*. The *beis Chizkiyah* connects it to the verb found in *vayazed Yaakov nazid*, Yaakov cooked a stew—*yazid* carries the sense of cooking, of ripening. The teaching thus reads: *ish mazid u'mazria*, only a man whose seed has "cooked" and ripened within him can be fertile; *ve'ein katan mazid u'mazria*, a minor's seed has not yet undergone that ripening process.

Rav Mordechai asked Rav Ashi: what is the source that the word *mazid* carries the connotation of cooking and ripening? He answered: *dichsiv vayazed Yaakov nazid*—precisely the verse about Yaakov's stew. This is consistent with Rava's position that only once a person is an adult, after *bar mitzvah*, is his seed fertile.

### Ben v'Lo Av

The *gemara* now introduces a teaching from the school of Rabbi Yishmael: *ben v'lo av*—the *ben sorer u'moreh* must be a son, not yet a father. This excludes a case where the *ben sorer u'moreh* has himself already fathered a child. This is distinct from what we had been discussing, which was excluding the case where a *ben sorer u'moreh* was fathered by a minor. Here we are excluding the case where the *ben sorer u'moreh* is himself already a father.

But a question arises: since we have established that a *ben sorer u'moreh* is already *bar mitzvah*, is there even enough time—within the narrow window of his eligibility—for him to have fathered a child, assuming that a boy's seed only becomes potent at *bar mitzvah*? The *gemara* will now investigate this tension.

---

## Three-Month Window

### Conception Timing

The *gemara* asks: *heichei dami*, what exactly is the case that the teaching of *ben v'lo av* comes to exclude? If we say the woman became pregnant *basar d'aisei shtei searos*—after he brought two pubic hairs, meaning after he reached *bar mitzvah* and his seed was potent—and she gave birth *mikamei d'leikef zakan*, before the lower beard fills out (which marks the upper end of his eligibility as a *ben sorer u'moreh*), then *mi ka shechiach kulei hai*? Is there really time for all of that to happen within his window of eligibility?

### Rav Chisda Three Months

This is where the teaching of Rav Chisda becomes critical. Rav Chisda states—and it is worth noting, as an aside, that the name Chisda is the Aramaic cognate of *tzitzit*—*kol yamav shel ben sorer u'moreh eino ela gimel chodashim bilvad*: the entire period of eligibility for *ben sorer u'moreh* is only three months. Given that constraint, if conception could only occur after *bar mitzvah*, the woman would not give birth within the three-month window. So it would seem that the *drasha* of *ben v'lo av* has no practical application.

The *gemara* therefore suggests the only viable reading: the conception took place before he was *bar mitzvah*, *d'ibar mikamei d'laisi shtei searos*, and the woman gave birth while he was still within his three-month window. And from this, the *gemara* attempts to derive: *u'shma mina katan molid*—we see that a minor can indeed father a child, since the only way to construct the case is if the conception occurred before he was thirteen.

But the *gemara* rejects this inference. It says: *u'leolam d'ibar basar d'aisei shtei searos v'olid basar d'akef zakan*—the conception was after *bar mitzvah*, and the birth was after the three months, after the lower beard filled in. In that case, he is already no longer eligible as a *ben sorer u'moreh* on other grounds, and the exclusion of *ben v'lo av* is indeed without a practical case—and the *gemara* acknowledges this.

When Rav Dimi came from *Ma'arava*, he explained the teaching of *ben v'lo av* more precisely. What they say in the West is: *ben v'lo hara'ui likroso av*—he is excluded not when he has already become a father in fact, but once he has become someone who is *fit to be called a father*, i.e., someone who is *ra'uy lehachriso av*. This is precisely the conceptual foundation for Rav Chisda's three-month window.

The reasoning is as follows: starting from the day a boy becomes *bar mitzvah*, his seed is potent. If he were to have intercourse that very day, and if we allow the possibility of a seven-month pregnancy, the fetus might be visible—*halachically* showing—after three months. At that point, one can already point to him and say: this man is the father of the child this woman is carrying. He is therefore already *ra'uy lehachriso av*, fit to be called a father. So the window of *ben sorer u'moreh* closes three months after *bar mitzvah*, not because he has necessarily become a father, but because he has reached the stage where he is theoretically capable of being identified as one.

The *drasha* of *ben v'lo av* is thus not excluding an actual father but someone who has entered the theoretical category of fatherhood. And that is precisely the limit Rav Chisda defines.

### Three Months vs Beard

The *gemara* now raises an apparent conflict: *v'hanan tnan misheyavi shtei searos v'ad sheyakef*—our *mishnah* teaches that the window extends until the full beard fills out, *yikef zakan*. That could be longer than three months. How does Rav Chisda's three-month limit coexist with the *mishnah*'s criterion of the beard?

### Whichever Comes First

The *gemara* resolves this cleanly: whichever criterion is reached first closes the window. *Hikif zakan af al gav delo malu gimel chodashim*—if the lower beard fills out before three months have elapsed, the window closes even if three months have not yet passed. *Malu gimel chodashim af al gav delo hikif*—if three months pass before the beard fills out, the window closes even if the beard has not yet filled in. Each criterion reflects a distinct reason for closure. The beard filling in marks that the boy is no longer a *ben* teetering on the edge of manhood—he is a full adult. And three months marks the point at which he is already *ra'uy lehachriso av*. Whichever comes first applies.

---

## Rav Kuspai Teaching

### Seven-Month Pregnancy

Rav Yaakov from Har Pakod was sitting before Ravina and said in the name of Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua: we can learn from the teaching of Rav Kuspai, who said in the name of Rav Shabtai that *kol yamav shel ben sorer u'moreh eino ela gimel chodashim bilvad*, that the window is only three months. From this limit, we can infer something about seven-month pregnancies: *yoledet leshiva ein ubra nikar leshlish yameha*—for a woman who gives birth after seven months, the fetus is not visible at a third of the gestational period, but only after three full months.

The *gemara*'s background assumption is that viable births occur either after nine months or after seven months, but not in the eighth month—the eighth-month infant was understood not to survive, which is a distinct discussion. The question is: if a pregnancy is only seven months, does the fetus become visible proportionally sooner than in a nine-month pregnancy?

### Proportional Argument

The argument runs as follows. In a normal nine-month pregnancy, we say the fetus is visible after three months—a third of the gestational period. If the same proportion applied to a seven-month pregnancy, the fetus would be visible after two and a third months. If so, why is the window of *ben sorer u'moreh* set at three full months? The very day after *bar mitzvah*, a boy could theoretically have impregnated someone with a seven-month pregnancy, and that fetus would be visible after two and a third months—making him *ra'uy lehachriso av* at two and a third months, not three. Since Rav Kuspai sets the window at three full months, it must be that even for a seven-month pregnancy, the fetus only becomes visibly apparent after three months—not proportionally earlier.

### Majority in Capital

The response given is: *zil batar ruba*—go by the majority. Even if there might be a seven-month pregnancy where the fetus becomes visible earlier, when defining the parameters of *ra'uy lehachriso av*, we go by the majority of cases. In most circumstances, a woman will not show until three months. So the window is defined as three months by majority, even if the minority case might push it earlier.

### Rav Huna Objects

This answer was then brought before Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua, and he objected sharply: *uvdinei nefashot mi azlinan batar ruba?* Do we go by *rov* in cases of capital law? *Ben sorer u'moreh* is a capital crime, and the Torah says *v'shafetu ha'eda vehitzilu ha'eda*—the court has an obligation to try to save the person. Surely when defining the *shiurim* of eligibility for a capital offense, we should try to narrow the window as much as possible and not rely on majority to extend it. If there is even a minority possibility that a boy could be *ra'uy lehachriso av* at two and a third months—because of a seven-month pregnancy—we should adopt that shorter window to protect him. Going by *rov* here seems to work *against* the accused.

### Ravina Responds

Ravina responded to Rav Huna's objection: do you think we never go by *rov* in *dinei nefashot*? We most certainly do. And the proof is from the *mishnah*: if one witness says the murder occurred on the second of the month and another says it was on the third, their testimony is not considered a contradiction—*eydutan kayemet*. The reason is that it is common for people to be uncertain about which day *Rosh Chodesh* fell, depending on whether the prior month was full or deficient. We therefore assume, by *rov*, that both witnesses are referring to the same event and one of them is simply mistaken about the calendar—a normal, prevalent error. We do not treat this as a *hakhasha*, a contradiction, that would disqualify both witnesses.

Now, if we never applied *rov* in capital cases, we would be compelled to say the witnesses are actually contradicting one another—*ve'achshishei hu d'kamakhashishi ahadadi*—and we would have to disqualify the testimony. But we do not do that. Instead, we go by the majority pattern of human behavior and say: most people make calendar errors of this type, and so they are not contradicting each other. This shows that we do go by *rov* even in *dinei nefashot*.

Ravina's reasoning makes an important conceptual distinction. Going by *rov* in capital cases does not mean we execute someone on probabilistic evidence. Rather, the application of *rov* here is structural: it defines what counts as a contradiction, what parameters establish eligibility, what we regard as the normal course of events when setting up legal categories. When we ask "at what point is a boy *ra'uy lehachriso av*?"—that is a definitional question, answered by majority. It is not asking whether we will convict someone on probability alone.

### Three-Year-Old Girl

Rabbi Yirmiyah of Difti adds a further proof. We have taught in the *mishnah*—and it appears as well in *Mishnah Niddah*—that *bat shalosh shanim v'yom echad miskadeshet b'biah*: a girl of three years and one day can be betrothed through *biah*, an act of intercourse, which is considered a legally effective act. This has several *halachic* ramifications. If her *yavam* performed *yibum* with her, it is effective. If someone had intercourse with her after such a marriage, he would be liable as one who committed adultery with a married woman, *aishes ish*, and would be executed. If she was a *niddah*, the man who had intercourse with her becomes an *av hatumah* himself, and the objects beneath him are rendered *tamei* in the manner of a *mishkav* of a *niddah*, one degree removed. If she is married to a *kohen*, she may eat *terumah*, since she is fit for *biah*. Intercourse with someone invalid for *kehunah* renders her unfit to marry a *kohen*. And if one of the *arayos* had intercourse with her—a father, a case of *aishes ish*, or whatever the applicable category—that person is executed, while she is exempt as a minor.

Now, why does all of this apply already at three years old? One might ask: should we not be concerned that she will turn out to be an *aylonis*—a woman with certain infertile and masculine characteristics—in which case the original *kiddushin* would retroactively be *kiddushei ta'us*, a mistaken betrothal, and the *kiddushin* was never valid? If so, the man should not be liable for *aishes ish* at all. The answer is: *zil batar ruba*—the vast majority of women are not an *aylonis*, and we go by that majority. We do not suspend the legal effect of the *kiddushin* out of concern for a rare exception.

The *gemara* pushes back: when the *mishnah* says one is *chayav* for intercourse with her, perhaps it means only liable to bring a *korban* in a case of *shogeg*, not liable to execution—and so there is no proof that *rov* applies in capital cases specifically. But the *mishnah* explicitly says *humatu aleha*, they are executed on her account. So we are dealing with *dinei nefashot* after all.

The *gemara* then tries another evasion: perhaps the case of *aishes ish* in the *mishnah* is not about *kiddushin* where there is a concern of *kiddushei ta'us*, but rather about a case of the father himself having intercourse with her—which is incest, *arayos*, and has nothing to do with the validity of *kiddushin*. The *gemara* acknowledges that the *mishnah* refers to *kol ha'arayos*, all the forbidden relationships, which does include cases of *aishes ish* through valid *kiddushin*. Therefore, we are not concerned about the minority possibility of *aylonis*, and we see that *rov* applies even in *dinei nefashot*.

The *gemara* attempts one final escape: perhaps the entire *mishnah* is speaking about a case where the man explicitly stipulated at the time of *kiddushin* that he accepts her even if she turns out to be an *aylonis*—and therefore there is no concern of *kiddushei ta'us* at all, and no *rov* is needed. In that case, you cannot prove from here that we go by *rov* in capital cases. The *gemara* leaves this as a live possibility.

---

## Beis Shammai/Hillel

### Mother-Son Case

The *gemara* now introduces a *baraisa*: *hamisuleles bifnei bna katan*, a woman who is engaged in physically intimate contact with her minor son—Rashi describes the phrase as *lashon pritzus*, language of licentiousness—and her son performed *ha'ara'ah*, mere insertion. *Beis Shammai* says she is now *pasul min hakehunah*, disqualified from marrying a *kohen*, since she has had an act of intercourse with her son. *Beis Hillel* says she remains *kasher*. The central question is what the dispute turns on, since we know that an act of intercourse with a minor is only considered legally significant when the minor is at least nine years old.

### Nine vs Eight

Rav Chiya the son of Rava bar Nachmani said in the name of Rav Chisda—and some attribute it as Rav Chisda said in the name of Ze'iri—that everyone agrees on two extreme points: once the son is nine years and a day old, *she'biaso bia*, his act is definitely considered an act of intercourse, and whether intentional or not, she is disqualified from a *kohen*. And everyone agrees that if the son is under eight years old, *ein biaso bia*, his act is not considered intercourse at all, and she remains eligible.

### Eight-Year Dispute

The dispute is specifically about a boy who is eight years old. *Beis Shammai* says *gamina midoros harishonim*—we learn from the earlier generations, and the *gemara* will demonstrate from *pesukim* that earlier generations could father children at eight years old. Therefore, an eight-year-old's act is considered intercourse. *Beis Hillel* says *lo gamina midoros harishonim*—we do not extrapolate from the earlier generations to our present reality. Whatever was possible in biblical times, when people lived hundreds of years and human physiology may have differed, does not define the *halacha* for us today. For us, the threshold is nine years and a day.

It is worth noting that the framing of this debate specifically in the context of a mother and her minor son is somewhat striking, since the same question of when a minor's act is considered intercourse arises in many other contexts. Nonetheless, this is how the *gemara* chooses to present the dispute.

---

## Earlier Generations

### Batsheva Genealogy

The *gemara* asks: *vedoros rishonim minalan de'olid*, where do we know that the earlier generations could father children at eight years old?

The first attempt is from the genealogy of Batsheva and Achitofel. The *pasuk* identifies Batsheva as the daughter of Eliam (*halo zos Batsheva bas Eliam eshes Uriya Hachiti*), and a second *pasuk* identifies Eliam as the son of Achitofel the Gilonite (*Eliam ben Achitofel ha'Giloni*). So Batsheva is the granddaughter of Achitofel. Another *pasuk* records the birth of Shlomo to Batsheva, who was named Yedidya because God loved him (*vayishlach beyad Nasan Hanavi vayikra shemo Yedidya ba'avur Hashem*).

From there, the *gemara* strings together a series of chronological data points. Two years after Shlomo was born, *Avshalom*'s shearers were at work—so Shlomo is two years old. Then Avshalom fled to Geshur and remained there three years—Shlomo is now five. Then Avshalom returned to Yerushalayim and did not see his father's face for two years—Shlomo is seven. At that point, Achitofel saw that his counsel had not been followed, saddled his donkey, went home, gave his final instructions, and hanged himself. So Shlomo was seven years old when Achitofel died.

How old was Achitofel when he died? The *pasuk* states *anshei damim u'mirma lo yechetzu yemeihem*—men of blood and deceit will not live half their days. And a *baraisa* teaches: the lifetime of Do'eg was only thirty-four years, and the lifetime of Achitofel was only thirty-three years. The reasoning is *yemei shnoseinu bahem shiv'im shana*—seventy years is the norm, and these men did not reach half of that.

Now the arithmetic: Achitofel died at thirty-three, at which point Shlomo was seven. Subtract seven from thirty-three: Achitofel was twenty-six when Batsheva gave birth to Shlomo. Over the course of that twenty-six years, three generations of births occurred—Achitofel to Eliam, Eliam to Batsheva, Batsheva to Shlomo—accounting for approximately two years of pregnancy time in total. Subtract two from twenty-six, leaving twenty-four years divided over three generational births. That is eight years per generation: each one fathered or bore a child at age eight.

### Objection Explained

The *gemara* immediately challenges this calculation. Perhaps the two men in this chain—Achitofel and Eliam—each fathered at nine, not eight. And perhaps Batsheva was even younger than eight when she gave birth to Shlomo—perhaps as young as six. After all, we know *mishum d'itita baria*, a woman is biologically more robust and could theoretically mature earlier. Moreover, there was already a child born to Batsheva before Shlomo—the child who died shortly after birth—so the timeline becomes even more compressed. This means Batsheva would have had to be even younger than six, which only reinforces that the two men might have been nine and Batsheva extremely young—and you cannot prove from this chain that anyone gave birth at eight.

### Abraham Genealogy

The *gemara* therefore turns to a second passage. *Eileh toldot Terach, Terach holid et Avram et Nachor v'et Haran*. Assuming these sons are listed in birth order, and assuming each is one year apart from the next, Avram is two years older than Haran. Another *pasuk* tells us that Avram and Nachor took wives, and Nachor's wife was Milkah, the daughter of Haran—*avi Milkah v'avi Yiskah*. The *pasuk* also mentions a daughter of Haran named Yiskah. Rabbi Yitzchak identifies Yiskah with Sarah: *Yiskah zo Sarah*. Why is she called Yiskah? Because she could see with *ruach hakodesh*. Alternatively, *yiskah* connotes that all would look upon her beauty. Either way, Sarah is identified as a daughter of Haran, Avram's younger brother.

Now the calculation: Avram was a hundred years old and Sarah was ninety when Yitzchak was born, making Avram ten years older than Sarah. But Avram is also two years older than Haran, Sarah's father. If Haran is two years younger than Avram, and Avram is ten years older than Sarah, then when Sarah was born, Avram was ten. That means Haran at that moment was eight—making Haran eight years old when Sarah was born. Or, more precisely, given that conception precedes birth by nine months, Haran would have been about seven when he impregnated Sarah's mother—which the *gemara* acknowledges is a slight imprecision, though the logic points toward eight.

### Birth Order Objection

The *gemara* objects: *dilma Avraham zuta de'achu hava*—perhaps Haran was the oldest son and Avram was the younger, and they are not listed in birth order at all. *V'derech chochmatam kachashev lehu*—the Torah sometimes enumerates children according to their wisdom or stature rather than their birth order. And proof that such non-chronological ordering occurs is from Noach's sons. The *pasuk* says Noach was five hundred years old when he gave birth to Shem, Cham, and Yafet—listed in that order. If we assume they are one year apart in birth order, Shem is two years older than Yafet. The *mabul* occurred when Noach was six hundred, making Shem a hundred years old at that time. But a subsequent *pasuk* says: *Shem ben mea shana vayoled et Arpachshad shnatayim achar ha-mabul*—Shem was a hundred years old and fathered Arpachshad two years *after* the flood. If Shem was a hundred at the time of the flood, he would have been a hundred and two two years after—yet the *pasuk* says he was a hundred when he fathered Arpachshad. *Bar mea ve'tartein shnin havei*—he should have been a hundred and two. The resolution: *ela derech chochmatam kachashev lehu*—Shem, Cham, and Yafet are listed in order of their stature, not their birth. Shem was actually two years younger than the *pasuk*'s listing implies if read as birth order, which resolves the arithmetic. And so here too by Avram, Nachor, and Haran—the listing may reflect stature, not age—and you cannot prove that Avram was the oldest.

### Bezalel Proof

Since neither the Achitofel-Batsheva chain nor the Avraham-Haran genealogy provides an airtight proof, Rav Kahana said: I presented these arguments before Rav Zvid of Nehardea, and he said to me—you try to prove it from there, but we prove it from here, from the chain of Bezalel.

The *pasuk* states: *u'Vetzalel ben Uri ben Chur le'mateh Yehuda*—Bezalel was the son of Uri, the son of Chur. Another *pasuk* records that Caleb married Efrat and she bore him Chur. So the chain is: Caleb fathered Chur, Chur fathered Uri, Uri fathered Bezalel.

When did Bezalel build the *mishkan*? He had to have been at least thirteen years old, as derived from the *pasuk* *ish ish mi'melachto asher hem osim*—the word *ish* requiring full majority. A *baraisa* teaches: in the first year after leaving Egypt, Moshe constructed the *mishkan*; in the second year, the *mishkan* was erected and the *meraglim* were sent. So when the *meraglim* were sent, Bezalel was at minimum fourteen years old.

Now, the *pasuk* records Caleb saying: *ben arba'im shana anochi bishlo'ach Moshe eved Hashem*—I was forty years old when Moshe sent me as a spy. So when the *meraglim* were sent, Caleb was forty. At that point, Bezalel was fourteen. Subtract fourteen from forty: Caleb was twenty-six when Bezalel was born. Over those twenty-six years, three births occurred—Caleb to Chur, Chur to Uri, Uri to Bezalel—accounting for approximately two years of pregnancy time. Subtract two from twenty-six, leaving twenty-four years divided across three generations. That is eight years per generation: *ishtakach de'kol chad v'chad bitamnei aolid*—each one fathered his child at age eight.

This chain, unlike the previous attempts, is not susceptible to the objections about birth order or alternative arithmetic. It is this proof from Bezalel that the *gemara* accepts as establishing that *doros harishonim* did indeed father children at eight years old—which is the foundation for *Beis Shammai*'s position that an eight-year-old's act of intercourse is *halachically* significant.

---

## Not a Daughter

### Rabbi Shimon Logic

The *mishnah* states: *ben v'lo bas*—the *ben sorer u'moreh* must be a son, not a daughter. A *baraisa* records Rabbi Shimon's reasoning: *b'din hu she'tei bas re'uya lihyos k'ben sorer u'moreh*—by logical reasoning, a daughter should equally qualify. Why? *She'kol metzuyin etzla b'aveira*—because all manner of sin is found in her vicinity. If the concern behind *ben sorer u'moreh* is that someone who is heading down a destructive path should be put to death before he becomes a full-fledged criminal who murders for his indulgences, then the same concern applies to a girl who is on such a path, since she could turn to prostitution and cause great harm. The logical grounds are arguably even stronger.

### Ben v'Lo Bas

Yet despite Rabbi Shimon's logic, the conclusion is unambiguous: *ela gezeras ha'kasuv hu, ben v'lo bas*—it is a divine decree, the *pasuk* says *ben*, a son, and not *bas*, a daughter. No matter how compelling the logical argument in favor of including a daughter, the explicit language of the Torah determines the *halacha*. The category of *ben sorer u'moreh* applies only to a boy.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 70

## Age of Puberty Proofs

### Tanakh Fertility Age

The sugya of *ben sorer u-moreh* raises the question of when, precisely, a boy first becomes capable of siring children. The Gemara has already established that the relevant window begins at thirteen, with the appearance of two pubic hairs, and closes three months later — a limit derived from the principle that once a boy can impregnate someone, the pregnancy would become visible within that period, at which point he could no longer be called *ben* without the connotation of fatherhood. The underlying theoretical framework is that he is *nidon al shem sofo* — judged on account of what he will become — a glutton and drunkard who will turn to robbery and even murder to feed his habit. The Rambam, it should be noted, shifts the emphasis away from the individual's anticipated trajectory and toward the verse *ve-khol Yisrael yishme'u ve-yira'u*: the execution serves to protect the institutions of communal authority — divine, judicial, and parental — just as it does in the cases of the *zaken mamreh*, the false prophet, and *edim zomemim*.

At this juncture, however, the Gemara introduces a striking historical claim: in the generations of the *Tanakh*, boys were capable of fathering children at the age of eight. This is not merely an antiquarian curiosity but bears directly on the *halakhic* debate between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding what age constitutes a legally significant act of intercourse. The Gemara now undertakes to prove, through a series of genealogical calculations, that the men of earlier biblical generations were indeed capable of procreation at eight.

### Shlomo Genealogy

The first proof proceeds from the relationship between Shlomo, Bat Sheva, Eliam, and Achitophel. The Gemara cites the verse identifying Bat Sheva as the daughter of Eliam (*halo zot Bat Sheva bat Eliam eshet Uriah ha-Chiti*), and cross-references this with the identification of Eliam as the son of Achitophel the Gilonite. It then notes the verse recording Shlomo's birth (*vayishlach be-yad Natan ha-navi vayikra shemo Yedidyah*) and proceeds to reconstruct the timeline from Shlomo's birth to Achitophel's death.

Rashi observes that Shlomo is Bat Sheva's second son — the first having died — and the chain of verses that follows tracks the years of Avshalom's movements after Shlomo's birth.

### Absalom Timeline

The calculation unfolds through a sequence of *pesukim*. After Shlomo's birth, two years pass (*vayehi li-shnatayim yamim*) before the sheep-shearing incident involving Avshalom. Avshalom then flees to Geshur and remains there for three years (*vayehi sham shalosh shanim*), bringing the total to five years since Shlomo's birth. He then returns and dwells in Jerusalem for two more years (*vayeishev Avshalom bi-Yerushalayim shnatayim yamim*), for a cumulative total of seven years.

It is at this point — seven years after Shlomo's birth — that Achitophel, seeing that his counsel has not been followed, returns home and takes his own life (*vayachvosh et ha-chamor vayeilech el beito vayetzav el beito vayichanek*). The verse *anshei damim u-mirma lo yechetzu yemeihem* establishes that the wicked die before half their years, with the standard lifespan reckoned as seventy. A *baraita* confirms: Doeg's total years were thirty-four; Achitophel's were thirty-three.

### Eight-Year Calculation

Achitophel died at thirty-three, seven years after Shlomo was born. He was therefore twenty-six years old when Shlomo was born. Shlomo, however, was Achitophel's great-grandson: Achitophel fathered Eliam, Eliam fathered Bat Sheva, and Bat Sheva gave birth to Shlomo. Three generations of begetting thus had to occur within those twenty-six years.

Accounting for the time of the three pregnancies — rounding to approximately two years total for three gestations, assuming seven-month pregnancies where possible — the Gemara subtracts two years from twenty-six, leaving twenty-four years to be divided across three generations. The arithmetic yields eight years per generation: *ishtakach de-khol chad ve-chad be-tamnei olid* — each one fathered a child at age eight.

### Age Nine Alternative

The Gemara immediately raises an objection: *dilma tarvaihu be-tisha olidu* — perhaps the two men in this chain (Achitophel and Eliam) each fathered a child at nine rather than eight. This would be marginally more comfortable, since *halakha* already recognizes nine as the age at which intercourse becomes legally significant, even if we no longer hold that boys can father children at that age. The response is that if the men were nine, then Bat Sheva would have had to give birth at six, which is implausible. But the Gemara notes that *ishta barya* — a woman is constitutionally more vigorous — and moreover, Shlomo was not Bat Sheva's first child, which would push her age at first conception even lower, to seven. The chain therefore cannot be used to establish the minimum age of paternity for the men, since the variable of Bat Sheva's age cannot be fixed with sufficient precision.

### Abraham Genealogy

The Gemara therefore turns to a second proof, drawn from the family of Avraham. The verse records that Terach fathered Avram, Nachor, and Haran (*Terach holid et Avram et Nachor ve-et Haran*). A tradition holds that Avram was one year older than Nachor and Nachor one year older than Haran, making Avraham two years older than Haran.

The verse then records that Avram and Nachor took wives — Avram taking Sarai, and Nachor taking Milkah the daughter of Haran, *avi Milkah va-avi Yiskah*. Rabbi Yitzchak identifies Yiskah as Sarai: she was called Yiskah (*sokhah*) because she perceived with *ruach ha-kodesh* — as the verse confirms: *kol asher tomar elecha Sarah shema be-kolah* — or, alternatively, because all gazed upon her beauty. Thus Avraham married his niece, the daughter of his younger brother Haran.

A subsequent verse establishes that Avraham was one hundred years old when he laughed at the prophecy of a son, and that Sarah was ninety (*ha-le-ven me'ah shanah yivaled ve-im Sarah ha-bat tishim shanah teled*) — a difference of ten years. Since Avraham was two years older than Haran, and ten years older than Sarah, it follows that Sarah was born when Haran was eight years old: Avraham was ten when Sarah was born, and Avraham was two years older than Haran, so Haran was eight at Sarah's birth. *Mishtakach ki oladah Haran le-Sarah be-tamnei olidah* — Haran fathered Sarah at eight.

### Birth Order Debate

The Gemara immediately challenges this proof: *dilma Avraham zuta de-akhva hava* — perhaps Avraham was not listed first because he was the oldest, but rather because the Torah lists children in order of wisdom or importance rather than birth order. If Avraham was actually the youngest of the three brothers, the age calculation collapses.

The Gemara supports this possibility from the sons of Noach. The verse lists them as Shem, Cham, and Yefet (*vayoled Noach et Shem et Cham ve-et Yafet*), which would imply Shem is the eldest. But a subsequent verse states that Shem was one hundred years old when he fathered Arpachshad two years after the flood (*Shem ben me'ah shanah vayoled et Arpachshad shnatayim achar ha-mabul*). Since the flood began when Noach was six hundred years old and Noach's first child was born when he was five hundred, Yefet should have been ninety-eight at the flood — yet Shem is said to be one hundred two years after the flood, making him ninety-eight at its onset, not older. The conclusion is that the verse *eleh toldot Shem: Shem ben me'ah shanah* means Shem was actually the youngest, listed first only because of his importance. It is further confirmed by the verse *achi Yafet ha-gadol* — Yefet was the eldest. *Derech chochmatan kachshiv lehu* — the Torah orders by wisdom, not birth.

Rav Kahana reports that he raised this entire discussion before Rav Zvid of Neharda'a, who responded that he did not rely on the proofs from Avraham's genealogy or from Shlomo and Bat Sheva. Rather, the demonstration comes from Betzalel.

### Betzalel Mishkan

The third proof begins with the verse *u-Vetzalel ben Uri ben Chur le-mateh Yehudah*, identifying Betzalel as the craftsman of the *mishkan*. A related verse identifies Chur as the son of Kalev and Efrat (*vayikach lo Kalev et Efrat va-teled lo et Chur*), and we proceed on the assumption that this is the same Chur.

The Gemara establishes that Betzalel must have been at least thirteen when he worked on the *mishkan*, derived from the verse *ish ish mi-melakhto asher hemah osim* — *ish* implies a full-grown man, i.e., a *bar mitzvah* of thirteen. A *baraita* records that in the first year after the Exodus the *mishkan* was constructed, and in the second year it was erected and the spies were sent.

### Caleb Timeline

The calculation proceeds as follows. Kalev declares at the time of the conquest of Canaan: *ben arba'im shanah anochi bi-shloach Moshe eved Hashem oti* — I was forty years old when Moshe sent me as a spy (*ve-ata hinei anochi ha-yom ben chamesh u-shmonim shanah*). He was eighty-five at the time of the declaration; the spies were sent in the second year of the Exodus. The *mishkan* was built in the first year. Therefore, when the *mishkan* was being built, Kalev was thirty-nine years old.

Subtracting Betzalel's age of thirteen yields twenty-six: Kalev was twenty-six when Betzalel was born. Now, between Kalev and Betzalel stand two generations: Kalev fathered Chur, Chur fathered Uri, and Uri fathered Betzalel. Accounting for approximately two years of pregnancies across three gestations, and dividing the remaining twenty-four years by three, each generation must have fathered a child at eight. *Ishtakach de-olid be-tamniya olid* — it is established that they gave birth at eight.

It is noted that the calculation is, if anything, more compelling given that Kalev had already had children by a previous wife before this chain, which would only tighten the arithmetic further.

### Tosafot Age Shift

This entire discussion occasions a remarkable comment by Tosafot on the previous *daf* (69a). The *mishna* had stated that if a minor *ger* dies it is known he has no heirs, since he could not have fathered children. But if, as the Gemara has now demonstrated, boys in earlier generations could father children at eight — and if *bar mitzvah* was always thirteen — then a boy who died as a minor at, say, twelve-and-a-half could theoretically have had children in the earlier period. Why then would we assume he had no heirs?

Tosafot answers: *de-af al pi she-be-dorot ha-acharonim nasnu chachamim shiur be-vas yud beis shanah ve-yom echad u-ve-katan ben yud gimmel shanah ve-yom echad* — even though in later generations the Sages fixed the age of majority at twelve for a girl and thirteen for a boy with two pubic hairs, in the earlier generations when puberty arrived much younger (*she-hayu memaharim lehavi sa'arot*), the *zeman gadlut* — the legal threshold of adulthood — was correspondingly earlier. The *halakhic* definition of adulthood was not a fixed number but tracked the biological reality of puberty in each era.

This is a striking position. The suggestion that the *halakhic* age of majority itself changed with the historical shifting of the age of puberty — and that this is not a rabbinic innovation but a direct consequence of the Gemara's own analysis — is the kind of observation that might seem heretical if stated carelessly. Yet here is Tosafot stating it plainly, and deriving it directly from the *gemara* we have just learned. Tosafot goes on to address the apparent tension with Betzalel's requirement of thirteen, working out the resolution, though we need not enter into every detail of that answer here.

---

## Daughter Exclusion

### Shimon's Logic

The *mishna* specifies *ben* — a son — to the exclusion of a daughter. A *baraita* records that Rabbi Shimon argued that by rights a daughter should be subject to the law of *ben sorer u-moreh* just as a son is. His reasoning: *she-ha-kol metzuyin etzelah ba-aveirah* — a wayward daughter is even more likely to draw others into sin, making herself sexually available to feed whatever habit she has developed. This danger to society is at least as grave as the concern that a son, addicted to gluttony and drunkenness, will turn to robbery and murder.

### Gezeirat HaKatuv

The response to Rabbi Shimon is categorical: *ella gezeirat ha-katuv hi ben ve-lo bat* — this is a *gezeirat ha-katuv*, a scriptural decree, limiting the law to sons only. As the Gemara has ruled in several prior contexts within this sugya, the verse says *ben* and the analysis ends there, regardless of how logically compelling the argument for extension might be.

---

## Gluttony Definition

### Measure Requirements

The *mishna* on *Sanhedrin* 70a turns to the question of when the conduct of the *ben sorer u-moreh* triggers liability. The operative verse characterizes him as *zolel ve-sovei* — a glutton and a drunkard. The *mishna* defines this quantitatively: *mi-she-yokhal tartimar basar ve-yishteh chatzi log yayin* — he must have eaten a *tartimar* of meat and drunk half a *log* of wine. Rabbi Yosi disputes and doubles both amounts: a *maneh* of meat and a *log* of wine.

### Mitzvah Gatherings

Eating at a *chavurat mitzvah* — a gathering convened for a religious purpose, such as a wedding feast — does not create liability, even if the boy eats the requisite amounts there. Similarly exempt are those who eat *ma'aser sheni* in Jerusalem, since that too is a *mitzvah* context. Also listed is eating at the gathering for *ibbur ha-chodesh*, the intercalation of the month, to which we will return.

### Both Required

The *mishna* further specifies that eating every kind of food in great quantity, but without meat, or drinking every intoxicating beverage, but without wine, does not qualify. The verse *zolel ve-sovei* requires both: *ad she-yokhal basar ve-yishteh yayin*. The *mishna* acknowledges that there is no strict proof (*ein ra'ayah la-davar*) that *zolel* means specifically meat and *sovei* means specifically wine, but there is a *zeikher la-davar* — a textual resonance — in the verse *al tehi be-sov'ei yayin be-zolelei basar lamo*, which pairs the two. Rashi notes that this is perhaps simply one illustration of *zolel ve-sovei*, not a definitional limitation; nevertheless, the *halakha* requires both.

### Tartemar Amount

Rav Zeira confesses that he does not know independently what a *tartimar* is. His solution is to reason from context: since Rabbi Yosi doubles the *tanna kamma*'s amount for both meat and wine — a *log* versus half a *log* — and Rabbi Yosi specifies a *maneh* for meat, it follows by inference that the *tanna kamma*'s *tartimar* is half a *maneh*. *Nimtza tartimar chatzi maneh.*

### Cheap Purchase Rule

Rav Chana bar Molda said in the name of Rav Huna: *eino chayav ad she-yikach basar be-zol ve-yishteh yayin be-zol* — he is not liable unless he purchased the meat and wine cheaply. The concern underlying *ben sorer u-moreh* is not mere gluttony at a given moment but the fear of addictive behavior that will lead him toward a life of crime. Rashi makes this explicit: if a person only consumes very expensive wine and meat, *lo shakhia'h le-himashekh* — he is unlikely to be drawn after it compulsively, since he cannot sustain such expenditure. The word *bezol* also echoes the word *zolel*, yielding a pun that the Gemara notes (*dichsiv zolel ve-sovei*). The concern, then, is not the individual act of overindulgence but the pattern it presages.

### Dilution Standards

Ravina clarifies the nature of the wine and meat required. *Yayin chai mazug ve-lo mazug* — the wine must be diluted but not too diluted, retaining sufficient potency. *Basar chai bashil ve-lo bashil* — the meat must be cooked but not fully cooked, like the meat eaten hurriedly by thieves over coals. This intermediate state — *ke-vasar kiba de-akhli ganvei* — is itself evocative: it is the food of a man already on the path of crime, eating in haste.

### Seduction Theory

Rashi explains the underlying logic of both requirements. With respect to wine: *mamshikhah she-meshubakh hu* — the wine must be of a quality that draws a person after it. If the wine is either too raw and harsh or too diluted and weak, it will not create the compulsive pull that is the real concern. Similarly for meat: if it is fully and properly cooked, then the person who insists on such refined preparation will never adapt to the lifestyle of a thief, who eats on the run. The intermediate states — semi-cooked meat and wine diluted to a pleasant but potent degree — are precisely the conditions under which addictive behavior is most likely to take hold. *Lo mamshikhah yayin mazug* — over-diluted wine does not draw a person after it; *aval bashil shapir lo mamshikhah* — perfectly cooked meat does not either.

### Salted/Fresh Wine

Rabba and Rav Yosef both rule that if he ate salted meat (*basar maliach*) and drank wine directly from the pressing floor (*yayin mi-gitto*), he does not become a *ben sorer u-moreh*. These represent the opposite extremes: salted meat is preserved and lacks the freshness that makes meat genuinely seductive; wine straight from the press is essentially grape juice, barely fermented and not yet intoxicating in any meaningful way.

A *baraita* from the laws of *erev Tisha be-Av* is adduced in support: one may eat salted meat and drink newly pressed wine on *erev Tisha be-Av*, because these do not constitute the pleasurable indulgence that is prohibited on that day.

### Duration Limits

The Gemara then establishes the precise durations. Rabbi Chanina bar Kahana rules that meat is considered *basar maliach* — and thus no longer fresh enough to create concern — once it has sat in salt for as long as *shlamim* meat may be eaten: two days and an intervening night. Wine is considered *yayin mi-gitto* as long as it is still *toses* — still bubbling after pressing — which a *baraita* establishes as three days.

The Gemara then probes whether the same thresholds apply to *ben sorer u-moreh* as to *erev Tisha be-Av*. The answer is that the two laws rest on different principles. The prohibition on *erev Tisha be-Av* turns on *simcha* — joy — and even somewhat aged salted meat or slightly fermented wine still imparts a certain pleasure. *Ben sorer u-moreh*, by contrast, turns on *imshuchei* — the addictive pull. *U-ve-khol she-hu lo mimshakh* — even a brief period of salting suffices to eliminate the seductive quality for purposes of this law. Wine, by the same logic, may not create the relevant pull until it has fermented for forty days, by which point it is fully wine and no longer *yayin mi-gitto*.

---

## Wine Ethics

### Wine Purpose

Having treated the technical requirements for liability in *ben sorer u-moreh*, the Gemara opens an extended *aggadic* discussion on wine — its dangers, its proper uses, and its moral valence. Rabbi Chanan states: *lo nivra yayin ba-olam ella le-nachem avelim u-le-shalem sakhar la-resha'im* — wine was created in this world only to comfort mourners and to pay out reward to the wicked.

### Wicked Reward

Rashi explains the second purpose carefully. The statement is not ironic — not that the wicked will drown themselves in wine and thus seal their own destruction. Rather, Rashi reads it straightforwardly: wine brings pleasure (*she-mit'adnim bo ba-olam ha-zeh*), and for the wicked, this pleasure constitutes the *sakhar* — the reward for whatever *mitzvot* they performed — being cashed out in this world, leaving them with nothing for *Olam Ha-ba*. The verse cited is *tenu shekhar le-oved ve-yayin le-marei nafesh* — give strong drink to the one who is lost, and wine to the bitter of soul.

### Wine Color Warning

Rabbi Yitzchak interprets the verse *al tere yayin ki yitadam* — do not look at wine because it is ruddy. The *derashah* reads: do not be seduced by the ruddiness that wine brings to the faces of the wicked in this world (*she-ma'adim pneihem shel resha'im ba-olam ha-zeh*), for it will whiten their faces — shame them — in the world to come (*u-malbin pneihem le-Olam Ha-ba*). The lesson is that wine's apparent blessing to the wicked is in truth part of the mechanism by which their reward is exhausted in this life.

### Wine Blood

Rava offers a different reading of the same verse: *al tere yayin she-acharito dam* — do not run after wine, because its end is blood. The pursuit of wine leads to the shedding of blood — whether one becomes a *ben sorer u-moreh* and eventually turns to violence, or simply destroys oneself through dissipation.

### Head/Poor Pun

Rav Kahana notes a *ketiav u-keri* — a discrepancy between how a word is written and how it is read — in the word *tirosh*, the Torah's term for wine. Written without a *vav* it can be read *tirash*. *Zakha — na'aseh rosh*: if one merits, wine makes one a head, a leader. *Lo zakha — na'aseh rash*: if one does not merit, wine impoverishes. The same substance elevates or destroys depending on the character of the one who uses it.

### Joy/Desolation Pun

Rava finds a parallel *ketiav u-keri* in *yismach*, the word for joy in *yayin yismach levav enosh*. Written one way it could be read as *yishma*, evoking *shemamah* — desolation. *Zakha — mesamcho*: wine makes one joyous. *Lo zakha — meshammehu*: it makes one desolate. Again, the same reality, bifurcated by merit.

### Rava's Wisdom

Rava adds a personal testimony: *chamra ve-reichani pakhin* — wine and fragrances sharpened my intellect. Used in moderation and at appropriate moments, these sensory pleasures were not distractions but aids to the clarity of mind needed for *Torah* learning. This serves as the Gemara's clearest affirmation that the discussion is not about prohibition but about proper use.

### Noah's Thirteen Woes

The Galilean preacher known as *Over Galila* made a *derashah*: *yud gimmel vavim ne'emru be-yayin* — thirteen *vavim* are stated in connection with wine in the narrative of Noach. Each *vav* represents *vai* — woe. The thirteen verses run in sequence: *vayachel Noach ish ha-adamah* (1), *vayita karem* (2), *vayesht min ha-yayin* (3), *vayishkar* (4), *vayitgal be-tokh ohalo* (5), *vayar Cham* (6), *vayaged li-shnei echav ba-chutz* (7), *vayikach Shem va-Yefet et ha-simlah* (8), *vayasimu al shekhem shneihem* (9), *vayeilekhu achoranit* (10), *va-yekhasu et ervat avihem* (11), *u-fneihem achoranit* (12), *vayikatz Noach mi-yeino* (13). One thing led inexorably to the next: the pattern of descent from the first act of planting the vineyard to the final exposure and violation was unbroken. This chain is the clearest illustration in the *Torah* of the dynamic the Gemara has been describing — the seductive quality of wine drawing a person further and further down a path from which there is no easy return.

### Noah's Violation

The Gemara then addresses what precisely Cham did to Noach. Rav and Shmuel dispute: one says he castrated him, the other says he sodomized him. The support for castration is the fact that Noach cursed Cham's fourth son Canaan — *arur Kena'an* — because Cham prevented him from having a fourth son by castrating him: *mitokh she-kilkelo ba-revi'i killelo ba-revi'i*. The support for the other view is the *gezeirah shavah* between *vayar Cham* here and *vayar otah Shekhem ben Chamor* by the violation of Dinah — the same language of seeing implies the same act. The Gemara resolves that perhaps both occurred: *chada ke-ha ve-chada ke-ha* — one as well as the other. The castration would explain why Noach cursed the fourth son, and the violation is derived from the linguistic parallel.

### Adam Parallel

The Gemara then reports a remarkable statement: Rav Chisda said in the name of Rav Ukva, and some say Mar Ukva said in the name of Rav Zakai, that the Holy One Blessed be He said to Noach: *lo hayah lekha lilmod me-Adam ha-Rishon* — did you not have from whom to learn? Could you not have learned from Adam the First? The parallel is powerful. Just as Noach emerged to begin civilization anew upon a devastated earth, so Adam had emerged into a pristine world. And just as Adam's first sin brought ruin, Noach's first act of planting a vineyard brought ruin upon himself and his family. God's rebuke is: you had the precedent before you; you knew that wine — the fruit of the vine — was precisely what had led the first man astray.

### Fruit Identity

This brings the Gemara to a three-way *machloket* among the *Tanna'im* regarding what the forbidden fruit of the *etz ha-da'at* actually was.

Rabbi Meir holds it was the grapevine: *she-ein lekha davar she-mevi yelala le-adam ella yayin* — there is nothing that brings woe upon a person like wine. The connection to our entire discussion is obvious, and the *derashah* of God's rebuke to Noach assumes this view.

Rabbi Yehudah holds it was wheat: *she-ein ha-tinok yode'a likro aba ve-ima ad she-yit'om ta'am dagan* — a child does not know how to say father and mother until it has tasted grain. The *etz ha-da'at* is an *etz* of knowledge and intellect; wheat, which develops a child's capacity for speech and thought, is the substance that corresponds to *da'at tov ve-ra*. Furthermore, the verse describes the tree as desirable for eating and beautiful to the eyes — a description that suits a stalk of wheat.

Rabbi Nechemya holds it was a fig tree: *she-ba-davar she-kilkelu vo nitkanu* — the very thing through which they sinned became the thing that repaired them, for after eating they sewed together fig leaves to cover themselves (*vayitperu aleh te'enah*). Rashi reads this as *midah ke-neged midah* in the mode of divine providence: the same instrument God uses to wound, He uses to heal.

Tosafot, however, does not accept Rashi's formulation and offers a different explanation. When Adam and Chavah sinned, they sought shelter among all the trees of the garden, but every tree refused to receive them — *berukh zeh ha-ganav she-ganav da'atei de-Vara'ei*, blessed is this thief who tried to steal the mind of his Creator — each tree distancing itself from association with the sin. Only the fig tree, which had itself been the instrument of the sin, opened its doors to them in a kind of shared complicity: *al yedei she-akhlah mimenu patkha lo delaseiha ve-kibblah oto*. It was not divine *midah ke-neged midah* from above, but the natural consequence of the fig tree's own involvement.

---

## Bathsheba's Teaching

### Solomon's Youth

The Gemara now reads the opening of *Mishlei* 31 as a record of Bat Sheva's *mussar* to the young Shlomo. The passage begins: *divrei Lemuel melech, massa asher yisartu imo* — the words of Lemuel the king, a moral teaching with which his mother chastised him. Rashi explains *massa* here as a *parashat tochechah*, a section of remonstrance. Rav Yochanan said in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai: the verse teaches that his mother bound him to a post (*kafato imo al ha-'amud*) and subjected him to physical discipline.

The scenario implied is that Shlomo, in his youth — before assuming the full weight of kingship — had been consorting with other kings and princes and falling into their habits of drinking wine. His mother took it upon herself, in the most direct manner, to correct this.

### David's Piety

The verse *mah beri u-mah bar bitni u-mah bar nedari* — what, my son, and what, the son of my womb, and what, the son of my vow — is read as three separate complaints. The first, *mah beri*, is interpreted: everybody knows that your father Dovid was God-fearing. If you conduct yourself this way, people will say *imo garemah lo* — it is his mother's fault.

### Conception Sacrifice

The second complaint, *mah bar bitni*, is more intimate. All the other wives of your father's household, once they became pregnant, were no longer permitted to enter the king's presence. But I (*ve-ani dechakti ve-nikhnasti*) forced my way in, insisting on continuing marital relations even while pregnant, in order to produce a son who would be *mezuraz u-meluban* — vigorous and pure. The *midrashic* tradition held that marital relations during pregnancy strengthened the child. Bat Sheva made a personal sacrifice of propriety and comfort in order to produce the most capable possible son. And now, she implies, that very vigor is being squandered on wine.

### Mother's Vow

The third complaint, *mah bar nedari*, is addressed to the divergence between Bat Sheva's hopes and Shlomo's behavior. All the other wives of the king made vows that they might produce a son fit for kingship. But Bat Sheva's vow was different: *yehei li ben zariz u-mimalei ba-Torah ve-hagun li-nevuot* — let me have a son who is swift, filled with Torah, and worthy of prophecy. She did not merely want a king; she wanted a king who was a prophet and a *talmid chakham*. To see such a son pursuing wine was to see her deepest aspirations betrayed.

### Kings' Folly

The verse continues: *al la-melakhim Lemuel, al la-melakhim sheto yayin* — not to kings, Lemuel, not to kings to drink wine. The Gemara reads *Lemuel* as Shlomo himself and understands the verse as Bat Sheva's direct address: why are you spending your time with those kings who drink wine and get drunk and say *lama lanu El* — what do we need God for? The name *Lemuel* is broken down as a hint: he who has God before him (*le-El*) should not behave as those kings behave. Similarly, *ve-roznim iy shekhar* — those to whom all the secrets of the world are revealed (*mi she-kol razei olam galuyim lo*) — should they drink wine and become drunk? The one who will be given divine wisdom has no business imitating the dissipation of ordinary kings.

### Solomon's Repentance

Rabbi Yitzchak then asks: where do we see that Shlomo ultimately accepted his mother's rebuke? From the verse *ki va'ar anochi me-ish ve-lo binat adam li* — I am more brutish than any man and I have not the understanding of men. The Gemara reads *me-ish* as *mi-Noach* — I was as foolish as Noach — and *binat adam li* as referring to *Adam ha-Rishon* — I lacked the wisdom of Adam the First. Shlomo confesses that he repeated the very mistakes of Noach and Adam, following wine into self-destruction. His mother's words reached him, his youth of dissipation ended, and he became *Shlomo ha-Melech* — the wisest of all men.

---

## Exemptions

### Mitzvah Company

The *mishna* had stated that eating at a *chavurat mitzvah* does not create liability for *ben sorer u-moreh*. Rav Abbahu now specifies a condition for the non-*mitzvah* case: *eino chayav ad she-yokhal be-chavura she-kulah serikin* — he is not liable unless he ate in a gathering that is entirely composed of worthless people. This implies that if even one respectable person is present, there is no liability.

### Mitzvah Reason

The Gemara challenges this from the *mishna* itself: the *mishna* states that eating at a *chavurat mitzvah* exempts him. At such a gathering there are presumably decent people present — yet the *mishna* still exempts him. If the reason for exemption in the case of a fully-*sarikin* gathering is the presence of worthless company, then the reason in the *chavurat mitzvah* case must be something else — namely, the *mitzvah* nature of the gathering itself, not the quality of the attendees.

The Gemara resolves: *ta'ama de-mitzvah* — the reason for the *mishna*'s exemption is purely the *mitzvah* context, and this applies regardless of who is present. If a boy ate at a *chavurat mitzvah* even among entirely worthless people, he would still be exempt because *keivan de-be-mitzvah ka-asik lo mimshakh* — since the occasion is a *mitzvah*, the fear of compulsive addictive behavior developing from this particular meal is absent. The exemption for a gathering of *serikin* without a *mitzvah* context requires that the company all be worthless; in the *mitzvah* context the company is irrelevant.

### Ibur Chodesh

The *mishna* also exempts eating at the gathering for *ibbur ha-chodesh* — the gathering at which the court would announce that the preceding month was a full thirty-day month. The Gemara observes that this gathering apparently involved eating meat and drinking wine (*u-meimra de-vasar ve-yayin maski*). But a *baraita* states that the participants at such a gathering ate only bread and legumes (*ein olim lah ella be-pat dagan u-kitnit bilvad*). The resolution: even if everyone else was eating only bread and legumes and the boy brought his own meat and wine and ate those separately, since *keivan de-be-mitzvah ka-asik lo mimshakh* — the *mitzvah* context insulates even his separate indulgence from the *din* of *ben sorer u-moreh*.

### Night/Day Dispute

A final *baraita* teaches the parameters of the *ibbur ha-chodesh* gathering: it requires a minimum of ten people, it is conducted with bread and legumes only, and — *ein olim lah ella le-or iburo* — it takes place at nightfall leading into the new month. The verse supports a nighttime gathering. However, a contradictory *baraita* states that it is conducted by day and not by night. Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba's instruction to his sons — *achifu ve-ulu, achifu u-feku* (go early and arrive, go early and depart) — is cited as evidence of a daytime schedule, implying that they would gather during the day while beginning celebrations the night before. The resolution appears to be that the primary gathering occurred during the day, with the celebration commencing the night prior.

Under any interpretation, the *mitzvah* context of the *ibbur ha-chodesh* gathering suffices to exempt a boy who eats meat and wine there from becoming a *ben sorer u-moreh*.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 71

## Qualifying Conditions

### Previous Restrictions

The daf begins in the middle of the laws of *ben sorer u'moreh*, the rebellious son. The Gemara has already established a series of limiting conditions: the son must be within the narrow window of thirteen years and three months of age, with two pubic hairs; the eating must involve specific quantities of meat and wine; and the meal must occur in a neutral setting — neither in the context of a *mitzvah* nor of an *aveira* — with all participants at the meal being, as it were, dissolute characters.

### Maaser Sheni

The Gemara continues, at approximately ten lines from the bottom of 71b, with the case of *achal maaser sheni b'Yerushalayim* — one who ate *maaser sheni* in Jerusalem. This is in principle possible to constitute meat and wine, since the money of *maaser sheni* may be used to purchase meat, and wine may be brought directly. Nevertheless, the Gemara rules: *kivan d'orchai hu ka achil lei lo mamshech* — since he is eating in a natural, regulated manner, within the structure of those laws and parameters, the behavior will not lead to the habituating, addictive pattern that defines the *ben sorer u'moreh*. Notably, the Gemara does not simply say it falls under the category of *bemitzvah ka asik* — being engaged in a *mitzvah* — even though the Gemara had previously invoked that reasoning. The phrasing here seems to emphasize the structured, lawful nature of the eating rather than the *mitzvah* dimension per se.

### Chicken Meat Debate

The Gemara then addresses *achal neveilot u'treifot shkatzim u'remasim* — eating various non-kosher meats. Rava rules: *achal basar of eino naaseh ben sorer u'moreh* — eating chicken does not qualify, since chicken is not red meat, and it is the red meat that carries the gluttonous character relevant to this *din*. The Gemara raises an objection: the Mishnah explicitly includes *shkatzim u'remasim* — rodents and insects — which are not red meat. The Gemara resolves this: *hatam hu d'naaseh ben sorer u'moreh* — in that case it qualifies because these are forbidden foods, not because of the species of meat. The Mishnah is cited to teach that one may have a small proportion of chicken alongside the red meat: *ki t'nan nami matnitin l'hashlim* — the Mishnah is addressing a case where the overwhelming majority of the *maneh* or half-*maneh* consists of red meat, and a small remainder may be other things. That remainder must still be kosher; *treifa* would not qualify even in that supplemental role.

### Red Meat Proportion

The precise proportion is not given — the Gemara does not specify whether 51% suffices or a larger share is required — but the principle stands: the bulk must be red meat, and the allowable remainder is a minor portion.

### Mitzvah vs. Aveira

The Gemara then generalizes: if one ate in the context of a *mitzvah* or in the context of an *aveira*, the *din* of *ben sorer u'moreh* does not apply.

### Meal Contexts

The Gemara provides illustrations. An example of *dvar mitzvah* is *tanchumei avelim* — the meal eaten with mourners to provide comfort. An example of *dvar aveira* is a *taanit tzibur* — a communal fast day — when eating is prohibited. Both of these examples are striking, as neither is explicitly biblical: *tanchumei avelim* falls for the Rambam under the general principle of *v'ahavta l'reiacha kamocha*, while *taanit tzibur* is rabbinic in origin. The Gemara's discussion clarifies that *dvar mitzvah* and *dvar aveira* refer to the context of the meal, not necessarily to the food itself — as was clear from the earlier case of *ibur hachodesh*, which was certainly not biblical. In the case of *shkatzim u'remasim*, the food itself was the *dvar aveira*; in the case of a *chaburat mitzvah*, the context sanctifies it — but the underlying principle is the same.

### Biblical Defiance

The Gemara then provides the verse-based reason for these exclusions: *amar kra einenu shomeia b'koleinu* — the verse says, "he does not listen to our voice," *b'koleinu v'lo b'kolo shel Makom* — meaning he must be defying specifically the parents' authority, not God's. If the act also constitutes defiance of divine command, or if it fulfills a divine command, the singular character of parental defiance is altered. Until this point, the Gemara had primarily grounded these exclusions in the concern of *lo mamshech* — that the behavior would not become habitual or addictive. Here the Gemara shifts to a more formal textual ruling, invoking the language of the *pasuk* itself. Rashi notes explicitly: *af al gav d'lo avar ella al de'rabbanan* — even when the violation is only rabbinic, as in *taanit tzibur*, it still falls under *kolo shel Makom* and thus takes the case outside the parameters of *ben sorer u'moreh*. There is reason to believe the Yerushalmi applies this same logic to explain why a *bar mitzvah* who performs a *mitzvah* cannot be a *ben sorer u'moreh*: *einenu shomeia b'koleinu* means the issue at stake is the defiance of parental authority, and anything that implicates divine authority — whether as compliance or as additional defiance — alters that equation. The clearest reading remains that the setting must be neutral: neither *mitzvah* nor *aveira*.

---

## Meat & Wine Specificity

### Meat & Wine Only

The Mishnah states: *achal kol machal v'lo achal basar, shasa kol mashke v'lo shasa yayin, eino naaseh ben sorer u'moreh* — no matter how much one eats, if it is not meat, or no matter how much one drinks, if it is not wine, one does not become a *ben sorer u'moreh*. The requirement is derived from the verse *zolel v'sove*, glutton and drunkard, which is read specifically as referring to meat and wine.

### Intoxicants Excluded

The Gemara then specifies what is excluded from the category of qualifying drink. *Achal kol machal v'lo achal basar l'atuyei d'veila kilit* — even pressed figs, which according to the Gemara do produce a mild intoxicating effect, do not qualify as "meat." *Shasa kol mashke v'lo shasa yayin l'atuyei devash v'chalav* — similarly, honey and milk are excluded from the category of qualifying drink, even though they too can produce a mild intoxicating effect. Notably, *shechar* — liquor — is not mentioned, which is itself somewhat surprising. A *baraita* confirms this: *achal d'veila kilit v'shasa devash v'chalav v'nichnas l'mikdash chayav* — one who consumes those substances and enters the *Beis Hamikdash* is liable, because the prohibition of entering while intoxicated covers *kol midi d'meshaker* — anything that causes intoxication, based on *yayin v'shechar al tesht*. But that prohibition is grounded in the state of intoxication, while *ben sorer u'moreh* is grounded in the specific language of *zolel v'sove*, which is read as referring only to meat and wine.

### Temple vs. Ben Sorer

The distinction is therefore between two different legislative contexts: the law of intoxication in the *Beis Hamikdash*, which is broad enough to encompass any intoxicant, and the law of *ben sorer u'moreh*, which requires the specific substances of meat and wine by virtue of the verse's wording.

### Schnapps Tangent

This distinction surfaces naturally in connection with a *teshuvah* concerning whether a *kohen* who made *kiddush* on schnapps on *Yom Tov* may subsequently perform *birchas kohanim*. Since the prohibition on *avodah* applies to any intoxicating substance — not only wine — the question turns on how much one must consume and precisely what constitutes intoxication for this purpose. Tosafos notes an apparent exception in the practice of *birchas kohanim* on *Shemini Atzeret* following *shacharis*, suggesting a more lenient reading in that particular context, but the underlying *machlokes* is whether even a small quantity — such as one ounce for *kiddush* — is sufficient to disqualify.

---

## Theft from Parents

### Theft Component

The Mishnah introduces a further requirement that the son must have stolen money. This is striking, because the *psukim* make no explicit mention of theft. The verse reads: *ki yihyeh l'ish ben sorer u'moreh einenu shomeia b'kol aviv u'v'kol imo v'yisru oso v'lo yishma aleihem v'safsu vo aviv v'imo* — and then the parents declare *bneinu zeh sorer u'moreh einenu shomeia b'koleinu zolel v'sove*. The only explicit characterization is *zolel v'sove*, glutton and drunkard. Where, then, does the requirement of theft originate?

The answer likely lies in the word *sorer u'moreh* itself — or in *einenu shomeia b'koleinu* — suggesting that the act must constitute a direct affront to parental authority, not merely irresponsible behavior. It is worth noting in this context that *kibbud av va'em*, as understood by the *acharonim*, does not technically require obedience to parental commands, particularly once a child has reached adulthood. *Kibbud* refers to acts of service — providing food, clothing, attending to needs. *Yira* prohibits publicly defying or embarrassing parents. But simply declining to follow instructions, when done respectfully, is generally not a violation of *kibbud av va'em*. If so, then mere gluttony and drinking — even in defiance of the parents' wishes — might not constitute the kind of direct assault on parental authority that the *Torah* envisions. *Chazal* therefore understood that the offense must involve something that more directly injures the parents — specifically, stealing from them. Compellingly, simply taking the food itself from the house would not rise to this level. Taking money, purchasing meat and wine, and consuming them elsewhere involves the son behaving as an outsider — violating property in a way that explicitly treats the family home and parental authority as foreign. This distinction between taking food at hand and actively stealing to fund the behavior seems to underlie the entire construct.

### Eating Locations

The Mishnah then enumerates the possible combinations of theft source and eating location. *Ganav mishel aviv v'achal birshus aviv* — stole from the father and ate in the father's domain: not a *ben sorer u'moreh*. *Mishel acherim v'achal birshus acherim* — stole from others and ate elsewhere: not a *ben sorer u'moreh*. *Mishel acherim v'achal birshus aviv* — stole from others and ate in the father's home: not a *ben sorer u'moreh*. Only *ad sheyignov mishel aviv v'yochal birshus acherim* — until he steals from the father and eats elsewhere — does the *din* of *ben sorer u'moreh* apply.

Rabbi Yehuda adds: *ad sheyignov mishel aviv u'mishel imo* — one must steal from both father and mother, derived from *einenu shomeia b'koleinu*, since both parents are named in the verse.

### Accessibility Logic

The Gemara explains the underlying logic of the Mishnah's ruling with remarkable clarity. *Ganav mishel aviv v'achal birshus aviv*: *af al gav d'shachiach lei bias* — even though the money is readily available at home, he is afraid of being caught while eating there. *Mishel acherim v'achal birshus acherim*: *af al gav d'lo bias* — even though he is not afraid of being caught while eating, *lo shachiach lei* — the money is not readily available, since stealing from others is not repeatable in the same way. *V'chol shekein mishel acherim v'achal birshus aviv*: both deficiencies are present — the money is not available and he fears being caught. Only *mishel aviv v'yochal birshus acherim* — *d'shachiach lei v'lo bias* — combines readily available money with freedom from fear of detection, and this combination is what gives rise to the concern about habitual, escalating behavior. The analogy is instructive: someone with a drug habit will typically steal from their parents' wallet, where money is always accessible, and consume elsewhere, where they will not be caught. That precise pattern is what the Torah identifies as the dangerous behavioral trajectory.

One might ask whether stealing repeatedly from others — demonstrating rebelliousness even more boldly — should equally qualify. The Gemara's answer is that the parameters of *ben sorer u'moreh* are defined not by maximum rebelliousness but by the specific configuration that gives rise to a predictable, repeatable pattern. Stealing from others is episodic; stealing from one's own home provides ongoing, easy access. The system requires that particular combination.

### Both Parents' Money

Rabbi Yehuda requires that the theft be from both father and mother, derived from the verse's mention of *b'koleinu* — our voice — encompassing both. The Gemara immediately raises the difficulty: *imo mana lah* — from where does the mother have money? The principle *mah shekansah isha kanah ba'alah* establishes that whatever a wife acquires, her husband acquires. How can theft from the mother be a meaningful category?

### Mother's Ownership

Rabbi Yose the son of Rabbi Chanina answers: *misuda hamuchenes l'aviv u'l'imo* — from the meal being prepared for the father and mother. Even if she does not technically own the food, it is designated for her consumption, and stealing it constitutes stealing from her in a meaningful sense. However, the Gemara notes that *geneivah* implies clandestine taking, and if one is merely taking food from the kitchen, the character of the act may differ. The Gemara ultimately revises this: *ela eima midmei suda hamuchenes l'aviv u'l'imo* — the son stole money that had been set aside to purchase a meal for the parents. Even though the mother does not hold legal title to that money, it is regarded as theft from her. The Gemara further suggests: *d'akni lei echad v'amar la al menas she'ein l'baalech reshus bahen* — alternatively, someone could have transferred property to her on the explicit condition that her husband has no rights to it, in which case she would hold independent title. The question of whether *nichsei milog* — property in which the husband holds the right to *peiros* but the wife retains title — would satisfy this requirement is left somewhat open.

### Purchased Goods

Rav Huna, cited by Rabbi Chana bar Molda, states: *eino chayav ad sheyikneh basar b'zol v'yochal v'yayin b'zol v'yishteh* — he is not liable unless he purchases the meat and wine cheaply and eats and drinks them. The critical word is *ad sheyikneh* — he must steal money and *purchase* the goods. If he merely takes food directly from the home, the *din* does not apply. The reason connects to the underlying concern with habitual behavior: a person willing to steal money, sell or exchange it, and use the proceeds to purchase wine and meat has demonstrated a level of initiative and commitment to the addictive pattern that mere opportunistic eating at home does not.
