There is also a dimension of rebelliousness: taking the family's cash and engaging in commerce with it treats the son as an outsider to the household, violating the parents' authority in a more thoroughgoing way.

---

## Parental Authority

### Both Parents Required

The Mishnah states: *haya aviv rotzeh v'imo einah rotzah* — if the father wished to prosecute and the mother did not, or vice versa, *eino naaseh ben sorer u'moreh* — he is not a *ben sorer u'moreh*. Both parents must equally desire to bring him to *beis din*: *eino naaseh ben sorer u'moreh ad sheyihyu shneihem rotzim*.

### Mother's Fitness

Rabbi Yehuda adds: *im lo haysa imo re'uyah l'aviv eino naaseh ben sorer u'moreh* — if his mother was not a fitting wife for the father, he is not a *ben sorer u'moreh*. This formulation raises an immediate question, since the Torah speaks of mother and father, not of husband and wife. Why should the permissibility of the union between the parents be relevant? The Torah's language speaks only in terms of the parental relationship — *einenu shomeia b'kol aviv u'v'kol imo* — not of the marital status of the parents.

### Same Attributes

The Gemara asks: *mai einah reuyah*? What does "not fitting" mean? If it means a woman forbidden to the father — say, his sister or some other *arayos* prohibition — that should not matter: *sof sof avuh avuh ninhu v'imei imei ninhu* — ultimately he is still the father and she is still the mother, and the Torah never requires marriage. The Gemara therefore concludes: *ella b'shaveh l'aviv ka'amar* — Rabbi Yehuda means she must be equal to the father. A *baraita* confirms and elaborates: *Rabbi Yehuda omer im lo hayta imo shavah l'aviv b'kol u'v'mareh u'v'komah eino naaseh ben sorer u'moreh* — if she does not share the same voice, the same appearance, and the same height as the father, he is not a *ben sorer u'moreh*. The Gemara then derives: since the verse requires *b'koleinu* — our voice — meaning a shared voice, and the voice must be the same, so too *mareh* and *komah* must be the same. This seems reminiscent of the requirement that the two goats of *shnei se'irim* on *Yom Kippur* be identical in appearance and height.

### Unified Voice Logic

The Maharsha offers a penetrating explanation of both the requirement and its logic. If the parents had different voices, different appearances, or different heights, the *beis din* would assume that the son was effectively only defying one parent — since no child, the Maharsha reasons, would willingly defy two parents who were truly united and presenting a genuinely unified front. If both parents were visually and aurally indistinguishable in their authority — *kol echad* — we could believe the son defied both. If they were distinguishable, we would assume he really only defied one of them, and therefore the claim fails.

Read more conceptually, the requirement is not literally about physical resemblance but about the unity of parental voice. Parents who present a divided front — where one quietly concedes while the other insists, or where one says "listen to your mother" while privately sympathizing with the child — cannot truly claim the son defied *both* of them. *Einenu shomeia b'koleinu* demands that the son have genuinely defied a unified authority. When parents operate in unison — speaking in a single voice, presenting a single front — they can credibly bring this claim. When they do not, even if one parent comes to *beis din*, the defiance was at most of one parent's authority, not a rebellion against the unified household. The literal reading of the Gemara — same voice, same appearance, same height — expresses this conceptual requirement in concrete, if stringent, terms.

### Parent Discord

The Mishnah's requirement that both parents must desire prosecution follows naturally: if only one parent brings the son to *beis din*, the son has not truly defied joint parental authority. The verse *v'safsu vo aviv v'imo* — the father and mother shall seize him — demands their joint action. Notably, even the mother's refusal is sufficient to halt the proceedings entirely, notwithstanding that within much of the *halachic* framework regarding women's authority, the mother's power is often subordinate. Here, her unwillingness alone is an absolute bar.

---

## Never Occurred

### Never Was/Will Be

The Gemara now cites the famous *baraita*: *ben sorer u'moreh lo haya v'lo asid lihyot* — the *ben sorer u'moreh* never occurred and never will occur. *V'lama nechtav? Derosh v'kabel sachar* — and why was it written? Interpret it and receive reward. The Gemara asks: *k'man*? Like whose opinion does this go? *K'Rabbi Yehuda* — like Rabbi Yehuda, who requires the parents to share voice, appearance, and height. The practical impossibility of finding two parents meeting all of those criteria means the *din* will never be applied.

### Moral Objection

But the Gemara then offers an alternative: *ibayit eima Rabbi Shimon hi* — alternatively, it goes like Rabbi Shimon. A *baraita* records Rabbi Shimon's position: *vechi mipnei she'achal zeh tartimar basar v'shata chatzi log yayin italki harei aviv v'imo motzi'in oto l'saklo*? Just because a boy ate a certain portion of meat and drank half a *log* of Italian wine, are his father and mother going to bring him to be stoned? *Ella lo haya v'lo asid lihyot.* It cannot be, and it will never be.

### Parental Mercy

One might ask: Rabbi Shimon is not claiming it is technically impossible; he is expressing moral incredulity. Why does that mean it will never happen? The Maharsha reads the passage carefully: Rabbi Shimon is not arguing that the Torah's requirement is unjust. He is arguing that no parents would ever actually do such a thing. *Hen vadai lo yagia l'sof da'ato v'yachos alav* — what parents would conclude that this child is truly lost and have him executed? They will have *rachmanus* on their child. That is the Maharsha's reading of *lo haya v'lo asid lihyot* — not a metaphysical impossibility, but a certainty rooted in the nature of parental love.

### Parental Lesson

What, then, is the *derosh v'kabel sachar*? The Maharsha explains: the Torah was not unaware that parents would never carry through on this. The *parsha* was written precisely so that parents would read it and internalize its lesson. The Torah is telling you: we are declaring that this child is fit to be executed — because if you do not intervene now, he is heading toward a life of crime, addiction, and ruin. We know you will have *rachmanus* on him. But take heed. Start placing limits. Show some firmness. *Aval al yedei zeh yochichu v'yisru es bneihem v'yekablu al zeh sachar* — by rebuking and disciplining their children, parents fulfill the Torah's purpose and receive *sachar* for it.

The Maharsha adds a striking personal observation: *aval bazman hazeh einu sam leiv l'zeh* — in his own day, no parents were truly taking this lesson to heart. *D'chol echad mechapeh al bno* — every parent was covering for their child. And even when children deserved rebuke, parents stood by. *Hana'arim holchim rov yameihem b'vittul Talmud Torah* — the children were spending most of their days in idleness from Torah study. *Lo charvah Yerushalayim ella bishvil shebitlu tinokos shel beis rabban* — and the Maharsha cites the principle that Jerusalem was destroyed only because the schoolchildren ceased their learning. Nothing, it seems, is new under the sun.

### Yonatan Witness

Against the position of *lo haya v'lo asid lihyot*, Rabbi Yonatan states: *ani ra'isi v'yashavti al kivro* — I myself witnessed a *ben sorer u'moreh*, and I sat upon his grave. His testimony is simply registered, without further resolution.

---

## Parallel Cases

### City Apostasy

The Gemara continues: *k'man azla ha d'tanya — Ir Ha'nidachas lo haysah v'lo asidah lihyos* — the *ir ha'nidachas*, the city gone astray into idolatry, likewise never occurred and never will occur. *V'lama nichtavah? Derosh v'kabel sachar.* The Gemara does not explain precisely why it would never occur, though one might observe that in the period of the *Beis Rishon*, when idolatry was pervasive, the very conditions for convening a *beis din* prepared to prosecute a whole city would be absent — the verse says *ish hayashar b'einav ya'aseh, ein melech b'Yisrael*, meaning there was no central authority capable of enforcing such a ruling. The combination of a city willing to engage in idolatry and a *beis din* capable and willing to prosecute it to this degree may simply never converge.

### Mezuzah Exception

The Gemara asks whose position this goes like: *k'Rabbi Eliezer*. A *baraita* records: *kol sheyesh bah afilu mezuzah achas einah na'asis Ir Ha'nidachas* — any city that has even one *mezuzah* cannot become an *ir ha'nidachas*. The reason: the verse requires gathering all the property of the city to the *rechovah* and burning it — *v'es kol shelalah tikbotz el toch rechovah v'sarafta ba'eish*. But a *mezuzah* cannot be included in that burning, for *lo ta'asun ken l'Hashem Elokeichem* — one may not destroy holy objects. If any *mezuzah* is present, the full procedure cannot be carried out, and the city cannot be declared an *ir ha'nidachas*.

A natural question arises: does the presence of a *mezuzah* only prevent the burning of the city's property, or does it also prevent the execution of the inhabitants? For those individuals who personally worshipped idolatry, one might argue they remain individually liable. The larger controversy — touched upon here — concerns the Rambam's ruling that the *ir ha'nidachas* procedure includes the execution of the families of the perpetrators, including wives and children. The Ramah finds this position shocking. But assuming that only actual perpetrators are liable, the *mezuzah* may affect only the property-burning component.

### City Witness

Again, Rabbi Yonatan counters: *ani re'itiha v'yashavti al tilah* — I myself saw a city that had been destroyed, and I sat upon its ruins. He is a witness against the position of *lo haya v'lo asid lihyot* in this case as well.

### Tzaraat House

The Gemara then turns to the third parallel case: *bayit hamenuga lo haya v'lo asid lihyos* — a house afflicted with *tzara'at* never occurred and never will occur. *V'lama nichtav? Derosh v'kabel sachar.* This case lacks the moral dimension of the first two. The Gemara presents it as a further instance of the general pattern, going like the position of Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon.

### Lentil Bean Measure

Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon rules: *le'olam ein habayit tamei bayit hamenuga* until the affliction appears as two *gerisin* in size — the minimum *nega tzara'at* being one *geris*, equivalent to a lentil bean (or, according to some, a *pul hashelomi*, a fava bean). The affliction must appear on two different stones, on two different walls, in a corner. That is, the spot must span the corner: each stone bearing a patch of one *geris*, for a combined area of two *gerisin* long by one *geris* wide. The derivation: the verse sometimes reads *kir* (singular wall) and sometimes *kirot* (plural walls) — *eizu kir shehu kekirot? hevei omer zeh keren zavit* — the wall that is like multiple walls is the corner wall, which belongs to two faces of the structure. This technical requirement — two afflicted stones at a corner, each bearing a full *geris* of *nega* — may be why, as a practical matter, the *din* never arose.

### Tzaraat Dump Site

A *baraita* records Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Tzadok: *makom haya bitchum Azza v'hayu korin oto churbata sagirta* — there was a place in the region of Gaza called the "ruin of *tzara'at*," which was apparently a dump site for stones removed from afflicted houses. Rabbi Shimon of Kfar Akko adds that he once traveled to the Galilee and saw a place marked as containing stones with *tzara'at*, which people were warned to avoid so as not to contract impurity. These testimonies indicate that the destruction or removal of stones from afflicted houses did in fact occur, even if the full formal procedure may have been rare.

---

## Parental Qualifications

### Arm Requirement

The Mishnah enumerates a series of physical qualifications required of the parents. *Hayah echad mehem gidam* — if one of the parents was without arms, the *din* does not apply, for the verse states *v'safsu vo aviv v'imo* — the father and mother shall seize him — *v'lo gidmin*, which they cannot do without arms.

### Mobility Requirement

*O chiger* — if one was lame, *v'hotziu oso* — and they shall bring him out — *v'lo chigrin* — which they cannot do without the mobility to bring him themselves.

### Speech Requirement

*O ilem* — if one was mute, they cannot say *bneinu zeh* — this our son — *v'lo ilmin.*

### Vision Requirement

*O suma* — if one was blind, the declaration *bneinu zeh* also involves identification, pointing to the son — *v'lo sumin*, which they cannot do without sight.

### Hearing Requirement

*O cheresh* — if one was deaf, *einenu shomeia b'koleinu* — he does not listen to our voice — cannot be established, because without hearing, one cannot know whether the son was truly defying the parental voice rather than simply not hearing it. *V'lo chirshin.*

---

## Court Procedure

### Warning & Lashing

The Mishnah states: *matrin bo bifnei shlosha u'malkin oto* — one warns him and lashes him in front of three. The term *matrin* here is *veyisru oto* — "they afflicted him" — from the verse, which encompasses both the physical lashing and the formal warning. The initial process proceeds as follows: the parents bring their son before *beis din*, present witnesses testifying to the theft and the eating and drinking, the son is warned, and he receives lashes. The nature of this *hatra'ah* requires attention, as will be discussed below.

### Three-Judge Court

The court for this initial stage — administering lashes — is a court of three judges, *bifnei shlosha*, as is standard for *malkes*.

### Twenty-Three Judges

*Chazar v'kilkel nidon b'esrim u'shlosha* — if he repeated the offense, he is judged by a court of twenty-three, since it has now become a capital case.

### Same Judges Required

*V'eino niskal ad she'yihyu sham shlosha rishonim* — he cannot be stoned unless the three judges from the original proceeding are present in this court of twenty-three. The basis is the verse *bneinu zeh sorer u'moreh* — *ze* — this one, who was lashed before you. The identification of the son as the same individual who was previously lashed requires the presence of those who witnessed the lashing, rendering the three original judges an indispensable component of the capital court.

### Witness Testimony

The Rambam's account of the full procedure is illuminating. In the first stage, two witnesses testify that the son stole from the father and ate and drank the required quantities — that is his initial offense. He receives lashes and a warning. If he then repeats the behavior — *chazar v'ganav* — the parents bring him to *beis din* again with witnesses who testify to the renewed eating and drinking, *achar she'hitru vo*, following the warning that was given. Only then does the capital proceeding before twenty-three judges commence.

---

## Lashes Source

### Veyisru Etymology

The Gemara asks: *malkut b'ven sorer u'moreh heicha ktiva* — where in the *pasuk* of *ben sorer u'moreh* is the requirement of lashes actually derived? Rabbi Abbahu answers: *lamadnu veyisru min veyisru* — we derive the *veyisru* of *ben sorer u'moreh* from the *veyisru* of *motzi shem ra*, the man who falsely accuses his wife. In the passage of *motzi shem ra* the verse says the elders should afflict him — and we know there that it means lashes. How do we know it means lashes in the case of *motzi shem ra*? From the word *ben* — derived from *vehayah im bin hakot harasha*, the classic verse establishing the institution of lashes, where the word *bin* (or *ben*) grounds the lashing procedure.

### Derivation Chain

The chain is thus: the *veyisru* of *ben sorer u'moreh* is learned from the *veyisru* of *motzi shem ra*, which is itself derived from the lashing verse *vehayah im bin hakot harasha*, whose use of *bin* connects it to the *ben* of *ben sorer u'moreh*. This interlocking derivation establishes lashes as the penalty for the initial offense of the *ben sorer u'moreh*.

### Judges Continuity

The Gemara then reaffirms: *chazar v'kilkel nidon b'esrim u'shlosha* — and the reason we need the *ze* of *bneinu ze* to include the original three judges in the court of twenty-three has now been established. Were it only to teach *v'lo sumim* — that the parents cannot be blind — the verse could have said *bneinu hu*. The fact that it says *ze* — this one — carries the additional implication that the court must recognize the son as the same individual who was previously before them, requiring the presence of those original three judges.

---

## Warning Nature

### Parental Hatra'ah

Rashi's comment on the Mishnah's phrase *matrin bo* is essential for understanding the nature of the warning. Rashi clarifies that this *matrin* is not the standard *hatra'ah* — the judicial warning given by witnesses immediately before an act, enabling subsequent punishment. In the normal structure of *hatra'ah*, witnesses warn the perpetrator at the moment before the transgression: "do not do this, or you will be liable to such-and-such punishment." Here, no such warning precedes the initial theft and eating.

### Authority Assertion

Rather, this *hatra'ah* is a parental one — *einenu shomeia b'koleinu* — an assertion of parental authority. The parents are saying: we have told this son to stop, and he has defied us. The warning is an expression of their authority over him and his rebellious refusal to accept it, not a procedural trigger for the subsequent lashing.

### Warning Uncertainty

There is also a *safek* in the structure: the warning is uncertain in its sequence. *V'od zu safek hatra'ah hu im over hu im lav, shelo miyad bishneihem over* — the warning is given, and only later, not immediately, does the son go out and repeat the offense. This further distinguishes it from the classic *hatra'ah*, which must immediately precede the act. The entire punitive structure of *ben sorer u'moreh* departs from ordinary rules.

### Parental Mussar

Rashi explains: *ela mochiachin oso. D'ba'inan v'yisru oso, shelo yargil* — they rebuke him so that he does not become habituated. It is *mussar*, parental discipline and exhortation: do not do this again. *V'im lo shama, malkin oso b'veis din* — and if he does not listen, he is then brought to *beis din* and given lashes. Rashi's formulation here suggests that the warning preceded the lashing — consistent with the reading of the verse's sequence — so that the lashes are administered as a consequence of having been warned and having persisted nonetheless. Whether this warning occurs at the first offense or only at the second, and whether it must occur in the presence of witnesses, remains somewhat open, but the essential character of the *hatra'ah* here is parental rather than judicial: an expression of authority, an act of *mussar*, and a demand for obedience — not the technical mechanism for enabling punishment.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 71b

## Ben Sorer U-Moreh

### Mishnah Overview

The first *mishnah* on 71b reads: *barach ad she-lo nigmar dino ve-achar kach hikif zakan hatachton patur; ve-im mishe-nigmar dino barach ve-achar kach hikif zakan hatachton chayav*. That is, if the *ben sorer u-moreh* fled before his judgment was completed and subsequently aged past the eligible period, he is exempt; but if he fled only after the *gmar din* had already been rendered, he remains liable even after aging out of the relevant stage.

### Gmar Din Timing

The operative principle is straightforward: everything turns on when the *gmar din* occurred. The status of *ben sorer u-moreh* applies only during a narrow window of months. Once he ages out of that window, the entire *parshah* no longer applies to him. If, however, the court had already concluded its judgment — finding him guilty — while he was still within the eligible age, that determination follows him. Even if he escapes and is apprehended only years later, he is still executed, because the *gmar din* was rendered at the time he was *chayav*. But if no *gmar din* was reached during that period, and he subsequently aged out, there is nothing to execute him for — had he remained present, no sentence could have been passed.

---

## Ben Noach Conversion

### Initial Case

Against this backdrop, Rabbi Chanina introduces a parallel case involving a *ben Noach*. A non-Jew who cursed God — *beirach et Hashem*, always expressed as a euphemism — and subsequently converted to Judaism: what is his status? Rabbi Chanina rules that he is *patur*, exempt from punishment, for the following reason: *ho'il ve-nishtaneh dino ve-nishtaneh mitato* — since both the judicial process and the mode of execution have changed.

### Dinav & Mitato

Two distinct changes must be identified. The first is *dino* — the court process. For a non-Jew, capital adjudication requires only a single witness, a single judge, and no formal *hatra'ah* (warning). For a Jew, capital cases require a court of twenty-three, two witnesses, and proper warning. These are categorically different procedures. The second change is *mitato* — the manner of execution. The *gemara* later makes clear, per Rashi, that the standard execution for a *ben Noach* is *sayif* (beheading), while the punishment for a Jew who curses God is *sekilah* (stoning). So in the case of *birkat Hashem*, not only is the court process transformed upon conversion, but the very form of death changes as well.

### Rashi's Explanation

Rashi addresses both dimensions explicitly. On *nishtaneh dino*: *de-ilu me-ikara nidon be-echad ve-lo dayan echad ve-lo hatra'ah* — originally he was judged with a single witness, a single judge, and without warning. This is radically different from the Jewish capital process. On *nishtaneh mitato*: *de-kol mitat ben Noach sayif ve-atah ba ve-nidon be-sekilah* — every *ben Noach* punishment is by the sword, whereas now he would be judged by stoning. Since he was never condemned under that new framework, *ve-lo itchayav be-ha mita*, he was never rendered liable to *that* form of death, and therefore he is *patur*.

### Patur Reasoning

The logic of Rabbi Chanina's ruling, then, is not simply that something changed — it is that *both* the judicial framework *and* the execution method changed upon conversion. This dual transformation is what severs his prior liability. Had only one of these things changed, the case would look different. But where the entire structure of judgment and punishment is replaced, the act committed under the prior framework cannot straightforwardly generate liability under the new one.

---

## Proof Attempts

### First Part Proof

The *gemara* now attempts to derive support for Rabbi Chanina's ruling from the *mishnah* itself. The first part of the *mishnah* states that if the *ben sorer u-moreh* fled *before* the *gmar din* and then aged out, he is *patur*. Perhaps this supports Rabbi Chanina — in both cases, something changed before judgment was finalized, and in both cases, the person goes free.

### Rejection

The *gemara* rejects this parallel: *lo, shani hacha de-i avad hashta lav bar katala hu*. The cases are not comparable. The reason the *ben sorer u-moreh* is exempt when he ages out is categorically different: had he performed the same act *after* aging out, he would never have been liable in the first place. The offense is age-specific. By contrast, a *yehudi* who curses God is liable regardless of age, and similarly a *ben Noach* who curses God is liable as a non-Jew and would remain liable as a Jew. The *ben sorer u-moreh* case cannot be analogized to the *ben Noach* case precisely because in the former, the very act loses its criminal character once the age has passed, whereas in the latter, the criminal character persists across both identities — only the procedural and punitive framework differs.

### Second Part Proof

The *gemara* then attempts to derive support from the *second* part of the *mishnah*: *im mishe-nigmar dino barach ve-achar kach hikif zakan hatachton chayav*. If the *gmar din* occurred while the *ben sorer u-moreh* was still eligible, and he then fled and aged out, he is nonetheless *chayav*. This now seems to challenge Rabbi Chanina, because the implication is that a judgment rendered under the earlier circumstances follows a person even when those circumstances change. The *ben Noach*, by contrast, gets off even though he committed a clear transgression — suggesting an inconsistency.

### Challenge to Proof

The *gemara* responds: *gmar din kaamart? Hatam gavra katila hu* — you invoke *gmar din*? There, the man was already a condemned person. A *gmar din* had been rendered; the sentence was fixed and only awaited execution. In the *ben Noach* case, there was no *din* at all — he was never brought to court, never adjudicated. You cannot derive a conclusion about what happens when circumstances change *after judgment* and apply it to a case where there was no judgment at all. The two situations are structurally incomparable, and therefore neither the first nor the second part of the *mishnah* settles the question of Rabbi Chanina's ruling.

---

## Ben Noach & Adultery

### Case Setup

The *gemara* turns to a new set of cases, now working within the *dinim* of *ben Noach* directly. *Ben Noach she-hika et chaveiro u-va al eshet chaveiro ve-nitgayer — patur*. A non-Jew who struck another person or committed adultery with another's wife and then converted is exempt. *Asa ken be-Yisrael ve-nitgayer — chayav*. But if he committed these acts against a Jew and then converted, he is liable. The question the *gemara* raises is why: if conversion changes his *din* and his *mitah*, should he not be *patur* in both scenarios?

### Why No Patur?

The answer rests on the principle already established by Rabbi Chanina: *nishtaneh dino ve-nishtaneh mitato* — *both* the court process *and* the mode of execution must change. We can readily concede that the court process changes upon conversion — a Jew faces a fundamentally different judicial framework. The question is whether the *mitah* also changes. *Ve-ha dino ishtani, mitato lo ishtani* — the *din* changed, but the *mitah* did not. If the mode of execution remains the same whether he is judged as a non-Jew or as a Jew, then only one of the two required elements has changed, and that is insufficient to exempt him.

### Murder vs. Adultery

The *gemara* considers the two cases separately. *Bishlama rotzeach* — the murder case is relatively straightforward. As a *ben Noach*, murder is punished by *sayif*. As a Jew, murder is also punished by *sayif*. The *mitah* is unchanged. Therefore, since neither the court process change alone nor any change in punishment suffices — only both together — the converted murderer remains *chayav*.

Adultery with a married woman — *eshet ish* — presents a greater difficulty. As a *ben Noach*, the adultery would be punished by *sayif*. But as a Jew, adultery with an *eshet ish* is punished by *chenek* (strangulation). So here, unlike the murder case, the mode of execution *does* change. Given that both *dino* and *mitato* have changed, why is the convert still *chayav*?

### Eshet Ish Case

The resolution lies in a careful examination of *kal v'chomer* and the ordering of the *mitot*. The established hierarchy, according to the *Chachamim*, places *sekilah* as the most severe, followed by *sereifah*, then *hereg* (*sayif*), and then *chenek*. On this ordering, going from *sayif* to *chenek* is a *downgrade* — the punishment becomes *lighter*. The principle is *kala be-chamura mishtachacha*: a lighter punishment is subsumed within a heavier one. If one was already liable to the more severe *sayif*, one is certainly still liable when the punishment is the lesser *chenek*. Because the change in *mitah* is a downgrade rather than an upgrade, it does not constitute a sufficient *nishtaneh mitato* to exempt him. He is still liable.

The answer to the adultery case with a *na'arah me'orasah* (a betrothed young woman) is different. A *na'arah me'orasah* is subject to *sekilah* — both before conversion and after. Since both *dino* and *mitato* remain effectively the same (*sekilah* to *sekilah*), there is no transformation sufficient to exempt him. And crucially, non-Jews have no halachic category of *na'arah me'orasah* — betrothal has no analogous legal structure in Noachide law. Therefore, when the text speaks of a *ben Noach* committing adultery with another's wife, this cannot refer to a non-Jewish *na'arah me'orasah*. By elimination, it must refer to a fully married woman, an *eshet ish*, which brings us back to the *sayif*-to-*chenek* scenario — a downgrade that does not suffice for exemption.

---

## Kal V'Chomer

### Mitot Ordering

The question of whether a change in *mitah* is sufficient to exempt a converted offender depends entirely on the *direction* of that change. The *Chachamim* order the four capital punishments from most to least severe: *sekilah*, *sereifah*, *hereg* (*sayif*), *chenek*. A *ben Noach* is always subject to *sayif*, which sits above *chenek* on this scale. Moving from *sayif* to *chenek* upon conversion is therefore a downgrade — and a downgrade is considered subsumed within the original, heavier sentence. You cannot say *nishtaneh mitato* in a meaningful sense when the conversion results in a *lesser* penalty.

### Downgrade vs. Upgrade

The logic runs as follows: if one was already held liable to *sayif*, then being now liable to *chenek* — a lighter form of execution — does not constitute a change sufficient to sever that liability. Conversely, if the *mitah* were to *upgrade* — that is, if conversion would subject him to a *more* severe form of execution — then we would genuinely say *nishtaneh mitato*, and in conjunction with *nishtaneh dino*, he would be *patur*. The rule is therefore: a downgrade in *mitah* is not enough; an upgrade, where the new punishment is genuinely worse than the original, is what triggers the exemption.

### Rabbi Shimon View

This entire analysis, however, is complicated by Rabbi Shimon's position. Rabbi Shimon holds that the execution method for *bnei Noach* is always *chenek* — *kol mitah amura be-vnei Noach einah ela chenek*. This stems from a *baraita* from the school of Menashya. If Rabbi Shimon is correct, then the *ben Noach* who committed adultery starts at *chenek*, and as a Jew committing adultery with an *eshet ish* would also face *chenek* — same *mitah*, no change, and he would be *chayav*. That part works. But the murder case now becomes a problem. According to Rabbi Shimon, the *ben Noach* murderer starts at *chenek*; but a Jewish murderer is executed by *sayif*, which is *more* severe than *chenek*. That would be an upgrade — and an upgrade, as established, generates *nishtaneh mitato* and should exempt him.

### Murder Reconciliation

The resolution for Rabbi Shimon's view on the murder case returns to the *kal v'chomer* logic, but now running in the opposite direction. According to the *Chachamim*, *ben Noach* is *sayif* and Jewish murderer is *sayif* — no change, remains *chayav*. According to Rabbi Shimon, *ben Noach* is *chenek* and the Jewish murderer would be *sayif* — *chenek* to *sayif* is a downgrade (since *sayif* is more severe than *chenek* on Rabbi Shimon's ordering where *chenek* is actually the mildest). Wait — here the reasoning must be tracked carefully: Rabbi Shimon holds *chenek* is *chamur* — the *most severe* — which inverts the *Chachamim*'s scale. If that is his position, then moving from *chenek* (most severe, for the *ben Noach*) to *sayif* (less severe) for the Jewish murderer is a *downgrade* even on Rabbi Shimon's scale, and a downgrade does not constitute *nishtaneh mitato*. He therefore remains *chayav*. A *baraita* is cited as supporting the *Chachamim*'s position: *tanya kavatei de-rabanan de-amrinan kala be-chamura*.

The case of *eshet ish* under Rabbi Shimon similarly resolves: since he holds all *ben Noach* execution is *chenek*, and adultery with an *eshet ish* as a Jew is also *chenek*, the *mitah* does not change at all — and he remains *chayav*.

---

## Ben Azzai

### Preemptive Logic

Ben Azzai articulates the underlying rationale of the *ben sorer u-moreh* ruling: *yamut zakai ve-al yamut chayav* — let him die relatively innocent rather than die later when he is truly guilty. The punishment is not simply retrospective accountability for what he has already done; it is preemptive. The *Torah* foresees where this trajectory leads and authorizes his execution before he has descended further into criminality.

### Reshaim & Tzadikim

The *mishnah* continues with a series of contrasts between *reshaim* and *tzaddikim*. The death of the wicked is beneficial — *mitatan shel reshaim hana'ah lahem ve-hana'ah la-olam* — both for themselves, because their sinning stops and they do not accumulate further guilt, and for the world, because others are spared the consequences of their continued wrongdoing. The converse holds for *tzaddikim*: their death is a loss for them and for the world. Wine and sleep are beneficial for *reshaim* — at least while drinking or sleeping they are not actively causing harm — and harmful for *tzaddikim*, who are prevented from performing *mitzvot*. Dispersion of *reshaim* is good, because it prevents them from organizing for evil; dispersion of *tzaddikim* is harmful, because it deprives them of communal support. Conversely, the gathering of *reshaim* is destructive, while the gathering of *tzaddikim* is beneficial.

### Rabbi Yose HaGlili

Rabbi Yose HaGlili expands on the preemptive logic. Is it really conceivable, he asks, that a boy should be put to death merely because he ate a *tartimar* of meat and drank half a *log* of Italian wine? *Ela higiah ha-Torah le-sof da'ato shel ben sorer u-moreh* — rather, the *Torah* traces the endpoint of his trajectory. He will eventually exhaust his father's estate; when his money runs out he will take to the crossroads to rob people, and if confronted he will kill. *Amrah Torah: yamut zakai ve-al yamut chayav* — let the *Torah* intervene now, while he is still relatively innocent, rather than wait for him to commit the crimes that will make his guilt complete.

---

## Machteret Case

### Nidon Al Shem Sofo

The *mishnah* introduces another instance of *nidon al shem sofo* — being judged on the basis of one's ultimate destination rather than one's immediate act: *haba ba-machteret nidon al shem sofo*. The thief who tunnels into a home is judged based on what he is presumed to be heading toward. The *Torah* states: *im ba-machteret yimatzei ha-ganav ve-hukah va-met ein lo damim* — if the thief is found in the act of tunneling and is struck and killed, the homeowner bears no blood-guilt.

### Permission to Kill

This dispensation is remarkable: the thief has not yet killed anyone, and yet the homeowner is permitted to kill him. The justification is *nidon al shem sofo* — he is judged by where his path leads. The assumption is that if confronted, the thief will kill to protect himself and complete his theft. Because of this presumed lethal intent, the homeowner is authorized to act preemptively.

The clause *im zarchah ha-shemesh alav — damim lo, shalem yeshalem* is cited in contrast: if the "sun shines on him" — which the *gemara* will explain not literally but as a conceptual modifier — then the homeowner would be liable for killing him, and the thief must make full restitution for what he has stolen or broken.

### Damages Liability

The *mishnah* raises a further question about civil liability: *haba ba-machteret she-shibbar et ha-chavit — yesh lo damim chayav, ein lo damim patur*. If the tunneling thief broke a barrel in the course of his entry, does he owe damages? The answer depends on his *damim* status — whether there would have been liability for killing him. This invokes the principle of *kam lei bi-derabba mineih*: a person subject to the greater punishment (death) is not also assessed the lesser punishment (financial liability) for acts committed in the same episode. If the thief was in a situation where the homeowner would have been permitted — indeed authorized — to kill him, then he is subject to the death penalty in principle, and therefore cannot simultaneously be required to pay for the barrel he broke. Conversely, if the homeowner would not have been permitted to kill him — if there was no *ein lo damim* — then no death penalty applies, and he is fully liable for the property damage.

### Raba's Logic

Raba explains the underlying reasoning of the entire *machteret* dispensation: *chazakah ein adam maamid atzmo al mamono* — it is a presumption that a person will not stand passively by while his property is stolen. The thief understands this. His internal reasoning is: *ei azilna kayei appai lo shavik li* — if I go in, the owner will confront me and not simply let me take his property. *Ve-chi kayei appai katilna lei* — and if he confronts me, I will kill him. It is this presumed murderous intent — embedded in the very act of tunneling — that transforms the thief into a *rodef*, a pursuer, in the eyes of the *Torah*. The principle *ba le-horgecha hashkem le-horgo* then applies: one who comes to kill you, you may preempt and kill first. The *Torah*'s dispensation of *ein lo damim* therefore rests on the presumption that the homeowner, by encountering the thief, has effectively entered a life-threatening confrontation.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 72

## Haba b'Machteret Intro

### Perek 8 Overview

The eighth *perek* of Sanhedrin is frequently taught in schools, and for good reason: it contains some of the most practically and philosophically charged material in the entire tractate. Having just concluded the *mishna* of *ben sorer u-moreh*, we now turn to the *mishnayyot* dealing with *haba b'machteret* — the burglar who breaks in through a tunnel — and the laws of self-defense that emerge from that case. The *perek* will go on to address the *rodef*, the obligation to intervene when another person's life is threatened, and eventually reaches the case of a woman in mortal danger from childbirth, where the fetus itself is the threat. The philosophical and *halachic* stakes throughout are considerable.

### Nidon Al Shem Sofo

The link to *ben sorer u-moreh* is the concept of *nidon al shem sofo* — being judged based on one's future outcome. By *ben sorer u-moreh*, the *Torah* looks into the future trajectory of the rebellious son and condemns him based on what he will become. The *mishna* applies the same phrase to *haba b'machteret*. But as the *Gemara* immediately makes clear, the two applications are fundamentally different in kind.

By *ben sorer u-moreh*, we are projecting decades into the future and declaring this child a *rasha* on the basis of what he will eventually do. By *haba b'machteret*, we are not projecting a future crime at all. Rather, by understanding what the burglar is prepared to do *right now* — specifically, that he is willing to use lethal force if necessary to complete his theft — we recognize that the person whose home he is entering faces an immediate, present threat to his life. The *nidon al shem sofo* here is not a preventive judgment about a career criminal; it is a recognition that the circumstances confronting us at this very moment constitute a life-threatening situation.

### Torah Source

The *pesukim* in question read: *im ba-machteret yimatze ha-ganav ve-huka va-met ein lo damim* — if a burglar is found in a tunnel and is struck and killed, there is no blood-guilt. But then: *im zarcha ha-shemesh alav damim lo* — if the sun has risen over him, there is blood-guilt. The *peshat* reading is that while the burglar is inside the tunnel, the homeowner acts under the perception of an immediate threat to his life and may use lethal force; once the burglar has exited the tunnel — once "the sun has risen," meaning he is presumably fleeing and no longer threatening — the owner no longer has justification to kill him, and doing so would constitute murder.

This becomes the *Torah* foundation for the right of self-defense, including the use of lethal force. The *mishna* then adds an important further dimension: *haba b'machteret v'shibar et ha-chavit, im yesh lo damim chayav, im ein lo damim patur* — if the burglar broke something in the course of his entry, and it is a case of *yesh lo damim* (where killing him would be prohibited), he must pay for what he broke; but if it is a case of *ein lo damim* (where killing him is permitted), he is exempt from payment. This triggers the application of the principle of *kim lei b'derabba minei*.

---

## Self-Defense Principle

### Reframing Nidon

*Rava* opens by asking: *mai ta'ama de-machteret?* — what is the underlying rationale of the tunnel case? The answer: *chazakah, ein adam ma'amid atzmo al mamono* — we can reliably assume that a person will not stand passively by while another takes his property. The burglar understands this. He knows that if he enters and the owner confronts him, the owner will resist. The *Gemara* then renders the burglar's calculation explicitly: *ee azlina kaei le'apai ve-lo shavik li* — if I go in, the owner will stand before me and will not simply let me take his things. *Ve-ee kaei le'apai katlinan lei* — and if he stands before me, I will be prepared to kill him. It is precisely this calculus — the burglar's advance readiness to use lethal force — that transforms the situation into one of genuine self-defense.

*Ve-ha-Torah amrah: im ba le-horgecha hashkem le-horgo* — and the Torah says: if someone is coming to kill you, get ahead of him and kill him first. This principle is the bedrock. It is worth noting that there is a discussion as to whether killing in self-defense is a *reshut* — a permission — or a *mitzvah*. The language of the *Gemara* strongly implies the latter: *im ba le-horgecha hashkem le-horgo* reads as an obligation, not merely a dispensation. This applies both to the potential victim acting in self-defense and to bystanders who have an obligation to intervene to save the threatened person.

An important limitation bears mention: *yakhol le-hatzilo be-echad me-evarav* — if one could reasonably have stopped the attacker without killing him, one may not use lethal force. In the heat of a confrontation this remains genuinely difficult to assess, and courts must always evaluate what was reasonably available in that moment of fear. Equally, one is not obligated to surrender one's property preemptively — to say, as the *Chofetz Chaim* famously did when his home was burglarized, *ani mochel*, I forgive you, just take my things. The right to protect one's property, and by extension one's life, is what the *Torah* is affirming here.

### Qim Lei Expansion

The application of *kim lei b'derabba minei* to *haba b'machteret* raises a conceptual difficulty. Classically, *kim lei* operates as follows: when a person commits an act that simultaneously incurs both a capital punishment and a monetary obligation, the court cannot impose the monetary sanction — the greater punishment, the capital one, subsumes the lesser. The classic illustration is a murderer who, in the act of killing, also destroys the victim's garment: even if he is never executed in practice — even if the killing was *be-shogeg* and there are no witnesses — since it is the *type* of act that carries a capital penalty, no monetary liability is imposed.

The problem here is that *haba b'machteret* is not a court-imposed capital punishment. The owner who kills the burglar is not acting as an agent of *beit din*; he is acting in self-defense. The burglar cannot be brought before a court and executed after the fact. Yet the *mishna* and *Gemara* nonetheless apply *kim lei*. This can be resolved in one of two ways.

The first, more conventional reading is that *kim lei b'derabba minei* is broader than previously assumed. It is not limited to court-imposed sanctions. Rather, it reflects a more general principle: when a person is engaged in an act so severe that someone is entitled to take his life — whatever the grounds for that entitlement — no secondary monetary obligation can be simultaneously imposed. The magnitude of the life-forfeiting act overwhelms the relevance of any property damage incurred along the way.

The second reading, which is less commonly articulated but emerges, arguably, from the texture of the *Gemara* itself, is more radical: rather than seeing self-defense as merely personal protection and then expanding *kim lei* to cover it, we might instead reconceptualize self-defense itself as a form of quasi-judicial action. When someone's life is threatened and there is no *beit din* present to intervene, the threatened person — or the intervening bystander — effectively acts as a representative of the legal system. The principle of *avid inish dina l'nafshei* — that a person may take the law into his own hands to protect his own property — is understood by the *Rambam* as resting on the fact that *me-ikar ha-din* one person can serve as a *dayan*. By analogy, the defender of life is deputized, as it were, to function as an arm of the court. If the court cannot be present, someone must act in its stead, and that person acts within a framework of law rather than as a vigilante. Under this model, *kim lei* applies in the conventional sense because we conceptualize the killing as, in effect, a court-imposed judgment — just one executed at the moment of threat rather than afterward.

### Two Models

These two models — self-defense as personal right versus self-defense as court-representative action — have meaningful *halachic* consequences and will recur throughout the *Gemara's* discussion. The *Rambam's* explanation of *avid inish dina l'nafshei* anchors the second model more firmly. When the *Gemara* raises as a *hava amina* that perhaps self-defense should be prohibited on *Shabbat* because court executions are not carried out on *Shabbat*, this bizarre-sounding suggestion only makes sense if at some level the killing is being conceptualized as court-mandated. One would never think to prohibit self-defense on *Shabbat* on the grounds that it resembles a *Shabbat* execution unless one had already, at least partly, conceptualized it that way.

---

## Qim Lei & Damages

### Rav's Statement

*Amar Rav*: *haba ba-machteret ve-natal kelim ve-yatza patur* — a burglar who came through the tunnel, took vessels, and left is exempt. *Mai ta'ama? Bi-damei kanahu* — what is the reason? He acquired them with his blood. The wordplay is pointed: *damim* means both "blood" and "money." Since his life was forfeit — since he could have been killed — he incurs no monetary obligation, not even the obligation to return what he took.

At first glance this seems reasonable: he broke in, he could have been killed, he is spared any liability. But Rava immediately expresses discomfort. *Mistavra milta de-Rav be-shivrei* — it makes sense to limit Rav's ruling to a case where the stolen object was *broken*, *de-laisnahu*, because then the object no longer exists and the question is purely one of monetary compensation. There we can say no compensation is owed. *Aval natal lo* — but if he simply *took* the TV and it is sitting intact in his possession, surely that is still the owner's property. If the owner's property happened to roll into a stranger's yard, the stranger would have to give it back. Why should the burglar be any different?

Despite Rava's preference to limit the ruling, the *Gemara* acknowledges — with something approaching an oath — that Rav himself appears to have meant his statement even in the case where the stolen object remains intact. So the question becomes: what is the theoretical basis for Rav's extreme position?

### Rava's Limitation

Rava's own reasoning for limiting Rav's statement is clean and intuitive: when the object is broken, the question is whether the burglar owes money — a monetary obligation — and *kim lei* exempts him from that obligation. When the object is intact, it is not a question of imposing a new obligation but simply of returning someone else's property. *Kim lei* does not entitle you to keep another person's property; it merely exempts you from monetary penalties. Rava maintains this position as the operative ruling.

### Ownership vs Liability

To understand what lies behind Rav's position, the *Gemara* examines a foundational question in the laws of theft. The question is this: when a *ganav* steals an object, what precisely happens at that moment? Does he incur an obligation to *return* the object, with monetary compensation as a fallback if the object is gone? Or does he, from the very instant of taking, become the owner of the object and owe its monetary value to the victim — with returning the intact object merely being a way to discharge that monetary debt?

The evidence that seems to favor the second view is the rule that a *ganav* who steals an object must compensate the owner even if the object was subsequently destroyed through no fault of the *ganav* — even through an *oness*, a completely uncontrollable accident. If, in normal circumstances, negligence or fault would be required for liability, why should the *ganav* bear the loss from an accident that would have destroyed the object even in the owner's hands? The *Gemara* answers: *alma bi-reshutei kaimi* — this shows that from the moment the *ganav* takes the object, it is conceptually "in his possession," meaning he owns it and owes its value. That is why accidents befall him: because the monetary obligation — not the duty of return — was created at the moment of theft.

Rav builds on this: if the *ganav* owns the object and merely owes money, then by *kim lei* — since his life was forfeit in committing the act — the money obligation disappears. And since it is the money obligation that is the real legal relationship, not a duty of return, the *ganav* gets to keep the object.

The *Gemara*, however, rejects this reasoning on Rava's behalf. *Ve-lo hee* — this is incorrect. *Ki ukimna rachmana bi-reshutei, le-inyan onsin* — the *Torah* places the stolen object "in the *ganav's* possession" only for the purpose of strict liability in cases of accident. *Aval le-inyan miknei, bi-reshuta de-marei kai* — but in terms of actual ownership, the object remains the owner's. The analogy is to a *sho'el*, a borrower: a borrower must compensate even for accidents, not because he owns the borrowed object, but because *kol hana'ah shelo* — all the benefit is his — and the *Torah* therefore imposes strict liability. Similarly, the *Torah* imposes strict liability on the *ganav* for accidents, but that strict liability does not transform him into the owner. The object remains the owner's; the *ganav* merely bears an extraordinary liability. Accordingly, Rava's position stands: when the object is intact, the burglar must return it, and *kim lei* does not help him because there is no monetary obligation being imposed — only the return of the owner's own property.

---

## Mishnah Teaching

### Broken Vessels

The *mishna* states: *haba ba-machteret ve-shibar et ha-chavit, im yesh lo damim chayav, im ein lo damim patur* — if he broke the barrel, when it is *yesh lo damim* he pays, when it is *ein lo damim* he does not. The *Gemara* parses what this implies about the case where he *took* the barrel rather than broke it.

The implication of the *mishna* seems fairly direct: it specifies the case of *breaking* and says that in a *yesh lo damim* scenario he is liable. This implies that if he merely *took* the barrel, he would have to return it even in an *ein lo damim* case — which is precisely Rava's position against Rav. The *Gemara*, however, defends Rav by arguing that the *mishna* chose to discuss the case of breaking not because the case of taking would be different, but because the case of breaking offers a *chidush* regarding the *yesh lo damim* scenario: even though the barrel is broken, the *ganav* is still liable. One might have thought that breaking — being less direct than taking — carries a different rule; the *mishna* teaches us otherwise. The implication regarding the *ein lo damim* case is therefore *lav davka* — not precise enough to constitute a contradiction of Rav's position.

### Taking vs Breaking

The *Gemara* presses on what *chidush* the *mishna* could really be offering. If the burglar broke something, of course he has to pay — he is a *mazik*, a tortfeasor. And even if he broke it accidentally, one already knows from elsewhere that *adam muad le-olam bein be-shogeg bein be-mezid bein be-ones bein be-ratzon* — a person is always liable for damage he causes, whether intentional, unintentional, or even coerced. So what precisely is the *mishna* adding? The *Gemara* concedes: *kashya* — it is a difficulty. Rashi takes care to note that *kashya* is different from *tiyuvta*: a *kashya* means the source does not work particularly well for this position, but since the *mishna* does not explicitly say that when the burglar *takes* the barrel he must return it — only that when he *breaks* it he must pay — the *mishna's* implication is not precise enough to flatly contradict Rav's view. A difficulty, yes; a refutation, no.

---

## Wallet on Shabbat

### Simultaneous Violations

*Motiv Rav Bibi bar Abaye*: Rav Bibi bar Abaye raises a challenge — or, as becomes clear, what initially appears to be a challenge but actually serves as support for Rav. The case: *ha-gonev kis ba-Shabbat chayav* — someone who steals a wallet on *Shabbat* is liable for the theft. Why? Because normally the two obligations — the monetary one for theft and the capital one for *chillul Shabbat* — do not arise simultaneously. The act of theft (*akviyat ha-chefetz*, taking possession) occurs the moment he lifts the wallet inside the private domain, while the act of *chillul Shabbat* occurs when he carries it into *reshut ha-rabim*. Since the theft obligation precedes the *Shabbat* violation, *kim lei* does not apply: there was already a monetary obligation before any capital-level transgression occurred.

But: *haya megarer ve-yotze* — if instead he was dragging the wallet along the ground and only completed the act of theft at the precise moment he brought the wallet into *reshut ha-rabim* by lifting it there, then the *geneivah* and the *chillul Shabbat* occur simultaneously — *issur geneiva ve-issur skilah ba'im ke-echad*. In that simultaneous case, *kim lei* would apply and he would be exempt.

This case appears to support Rav's position: the wallet is presumably still in existence, and yet the *Gemara* implies the *ganav* would not have to return it. This would be exactly what Rav maintains.

### Wallet Must Return

The *Gemara* resolves this by issuing a practical ruling: *ve-hilchata, de-shadinu be-nahara* — the exemption in that simultaneous case applies only when the wallet has been thrown into the river, meaning the money is spent and the wallet is gone. If the wallet were still intact, of course it would have to be returned. The debate between Rav and Rava is thus preserved: it is precisely the case of the intact stolen object that divides them. Rav holds even then the *ganav* keeps it; Rava holds he must return it.

### Rava's Rams Story

The *Gemara* then relates a famous episode: *Rava ignavu lei dichrei be-machterta* — remarkably, Rava himself had rams stolen from him through a tunnel. The thieves apparently had a change of heart — perhaps moved by the approach of *Erev Yom Kippur* — and came to return the rams. *Ve-lo kablinhu* — Rava refused to accept them. *Amar: hova nafik mi-pumei de-Rav* — he said, a ruling of liability issued from Rav's mouth, and even though I think Rav is wrong and that these thieves are legally obligated to return my rams, I will not accept them back.

*Tosafot* raises the obvious question: even in a *kim lei* context, there is an acknowledged obligation *latzeit yedei shamayim* — to fulfill one's moral and divine obligations even when the court will not enforce them. Why then did Rava not accept the rams? *Tosafot* answers: the thieves were returning the rams *because* they believed they were legally obligated to do so. Rava therefore refused, saying: according to Rav, you are not legally obligated. I disagree with Rav, but if you are returning the property only because you think you are compelled to, I will not accept it. If you wish to return the rams beyond your legal obligation, as an act of genuine moral restitution, I will accept. The distinction Rava is drawing — between what the court demands and what conscience requires — is important: there is a meaningful difference between legal obligation and moral obligation even in *halachic* discourse.

At bottom, the entire debate between Rav and Rava is, as noted, fundamentally a *Bava Kama* question about the nature of the *ganav's* obligation at the moment of theft — whether he becomes the owner and owes money, or whether he owes the object itself with monetary compensation as a secondary fallback. That *Bava Kama* question is being resolved here, in *Sanhedrin*, in the context of *haba ba-machteret*. This is why students who study *Bava Kama* regularly find themselves reading this passage in *Sanhedrin*.

---

## Mishnah Teaching

*[See above — this macro segment is fully addressed in its own section.]*

## Conditions for Killing

### Conflicting Baraitot

A *baraita* teaches: *ein lo damim* — there is no blood-guilt. And then: *im zarcha ha-shemesh alav damim lo* — if the sun has risen upon him, there is blood-guilt. The *Gemara* asks: does the sun shine only upon him? *Mah hu im zarcha ha-shemesh alav?* What does the sun imagery mean? The first *baraita* reads it as a standard of certainty for the *owner*: *ela im barur lecha ha-davar ke-shemesh she-ein lo shalom imach, hargehu* — if it is as clear to you as the sun that he has no peace with you and is prepared to kill you, then you may kill him. *Ve-im lav, al tahargehu* — but if there is any doubt, you may not.

A second *baraita*, however, reads the sun imagery in reference to the second half of the verse — the case where it *is* blood-guilt. *Im zarcha ha-shemesh alav damim lo* — if it is as clear as the sun that there is *peace* between you, that this person would not harm you, *al tahargehu, damim lo* — only then is killing prohibited. *Ve-im lav, hargehu* — but if any doubt exists, you may kill him.

These two *baraitot* appear to be in direct tension. The first says you may kill only when it is certain the threat exists. The second says you may not kill only when it is certain the threat does not exist. The vast gray area of genuine uncertainty falls on opposite sides of the line in the two texts.

### Father-Son Distinction

The *Gemara* resolves the contradiction — *lo kashya* — with a distinction that is both legally and psychologically penetrating. *Kan be-av al ha-ben, kan be-ven al ha-av* — one *baraita* addresses the case of a father breaking in to steal from his son; the other addresses the case of a son breaking in to steal from his father.

When a father breaks into his son's home, we begin from a presumption that a father would never be prepared to kill his own child. That presumption is so strong that the son may use lethal force *only* when it is unambiguously clear — like daylight — that his father has crossed that threshold and genuinely intends to harm him. Short of that certainty, the son may not act. This is the first *baraita*.

When a son breaks into his father's home, no such presumption obtains. Children kill parents for all manner of reasons, and the evidence that one's child has descended to theft provides no reliable guarantee of restraint. There the father is permitted to use lethal force unless it is as clear as the sun that his son would not harm him. Short of that, he acts in self-defense.

The *halachic* upshot of both cases together is: in any standard case of genuine uncertainty, protect your own life. The rule requiring certainty before acting applies only where we begin with a strong presumption that the intruder would not harm you — as in a father-son relationship where paternal love is so profound that it is treated as categorically restraining. But in any ordinary case, doubt resolves in favor of self-defense.

### Love vs Threat

The *Gemara* illustrates this with a striking personal example. *Amar Rav*: *kol de-ati alai be-machteret, katlinan lei* — anyone who came through a tunnel toward me, I would kill him — *livar mi-Yoni bar Kenis ve-Rav Chanina bar Shila*, these two I would not kill even if I saw them emerging from a tunnel. The students are naturally startled.

*Eileima mishum de-tzadik hu* — perhaps because they are so righteous they would surely never use lethal force? But the *Gemara* pushes back: *hacha be-machtarta* — but he is coming out of the tunnel! Whatever I knew of him yesterday, the act of desperation that has driven him to this point makes the past character reference unreliable. This is a profound observation: moral character, however established, does not inoculate against the extremes to which desperation can drive a person.

The true reason Rav would not kill those two men: *kim li be-gaveih de-meracheim alai ke-racheim av al ha-ben* — I know from personal experience that this person's love for me is like a father's love for a son. Not piety in the abstract, but a particular and known bond of love so deep that no desperation could overcome it. *Ke-racheim av al ha-ben* — and this echoes, not incidentally, the *pasuk* of *Yom Kippur*, the divine compassion of a father for his child. The exception that proves the rule: absent such personal certainty of love, assume the worst and act accordingly.

---

## Shabbat Application

### Killing Permitted

A *baraita* teaches: *damim lo bein be-chol bein be-Shabbat* — when it is *yesh lo damim*, you may not kill him, whether on a weekday or on *Shabbat*. And *ein lo damim* — you may kill him to defend yourself — *bein be-chol bein be-Shabbat*, whether on a weekday or on *Shabbat*. There is no suspension of the right of self-defense because the day happens to be *Shabbat*.

### Court Punishment Model

The *Gemara* finds the *ein lo damim* case obvious and asks why the *baraita* needs to state it. The answer given — and this is remarkable — is that one might have thought to apply the logic of court-imposed executions: *midi de-havei a-harugei beit din, de-be-Shabbat lo katlinan lehu* — just as the court does not execute criminals on *Shabbat*, perhaps one may not kill the burglar in self-defense on *Shabbat* either.

This is a stunning *hava amina*. No one would say you cannot defend your life on *Shabbat* if the underlying logic were purely *pikuach nefesh* — saving a life, which overrides *Shabbat* unambiguously. The only way this *hava amina* makes sense is if, at some level, the killing of the burglar is being conceptualized as a court-imposed punishment that the defender is administering on the court's behalf. The *baraita* therefore teaches: *ka-mashma lan de-katlinan* — you kill him regardless. Whether the *kol mashma lan* entirely abandons the court-punishment framework or merely refines it — holding that this is still a quasi-judicial act but one that may and must be carried out on *Shabbat* — is left somewhat open.

### Obligation Save Life

The *yesh lo damim* clause presents a different and equally striking teaching. *Bishlama ein lo damim* — the *ein lo damim* case is the one that needs explanation, as discussed above. But *yesh lo damim bein be-chol bein be-Shabbat* — when the burglar's killing would be prohibited, this is prohibited whether on a weekday or *Shabbat*. The *Gemara* initially wonders why this needs to be stated: *hash-ta be-chol lo katlinan lei, be-Shabbat mibaya* — if you cannot kill him on Wednesday, obviously you cannot on *Shabbat*.

*Amar Rav Sheshet*: the clause addresses a different scenario entirely. Imagine the burglar was coming to rob — but it was a case like a father and son, or someone known to be incapable of harming the homeowner, so there is no right to kill him. He dug the tunnel on *Shabbat*, violating it throughout. Then the tunnel collapses on him. Must the homeowner save his life, even if doing so requires violating *Shabbat*? The answer is yes. *Lo nitzrecha ela le-fakei'ach alav et ha-gal* — the *baraita* is teaching that you must remove the rubble. The obligation to save life (*pikuach nefesh*) applies even to this man, even at this moment.

This is a morally demanding ruling: the very person who a moment ago was robbing you, desecrating *Shabbat* in the process, must be rescued on *Shabbat* if the tunnel collapses. *Yesh lo damim* means not only that it is prohibited to kill him — it means he retains his full human claim on life and on your efforts to preserve it.

Rashi notes the flip side explicitly: when the burglar was in an *ein lo damim* situation — when he could have been killed — and the tunnel collapses on him, there is apparently no obligation to save him. Rashi's reasoning seems to be that since he forfeited his life, *ein lo damim*, he is already as a dead man and one need not be *mechalel Shabbat* to save him. This is difficult to understand on pure self-defense grounds: once the tunnel collapses, the threat is neutralized, and he is simply a human being under rubble. The logic becomes more intelligible under the court-punishment model: he is someone the legal system has effectively already condemned, and therefore there is no obligation to rescue him at the cost of a Torah prohibition. But Rashi's position here remains arresting.

---

## Third Parties & Methods

### Third Party Intervention

The *baraita* states: *ve-huka va-met ein lo damim, be-chol adam* — when the burglar is killed in the *ein lo damim* scenario, there is no blood-guilt, and this applies to *any person* who kills him. The *Gemara* explains why this needs to be stated.

One might have thought that only the homeowner — the *ba'al ha-bayit* — has the right to kill the burglar. The logic would be: it is the homeowner whose life is in danger, because *ein adam ma'amid atzmo al mamono* — the owner will not stand by and let his property be taken — and the burglar knows the owner may confront him and has resolved to kill if necessary. But a bystander's life is not directly threatened. The burglar did not calculate that a random passerby would resist him. So what entitles a stranger to intervene with lethal force?

*Ka-mashma lan de-rodef hu* — the *baraita* teaches that the burglar has the status of a *rodef*, a pursuer. And as the next *mishna* will address in detail, anyone may — and must — intervene to stop a *rodef* from taking another's life. It is not merely a right of personal self-defense; it is a communal obligation to protect the potential victim. The intervention of a third party is thus not vigilantism but a fulfillment of *lo ta'amod al dam rei'echa*. The right of intervention is obligatory, and the question of how much personal risk the intervener must accept is itself a significant discussion among the *acharonim*.

An interesting debate among *acharonim* concerns whether the license to kill the *rodef* is *hutra* — fundamentally not an act of killing at all, as implied by *ein lo damim* — or merely *dechuya*, a prohibited act pushed aside by overriding necessity. The practical difference may bear on the requirement of *yakhol le-hatzilo be-echad me-evarav*: whether an outsider is held to a stricter standard than the victim himself in exhausting alternatives before resorting to lethal force.

### Any Means Necessary

The *baraita* continues: *ve-met be-chol mita she-ata yakhol le-hamito* — he may be killed by whatever means are available. You are not restricted to a particular method. The *Gemara* asks: why does this need to be stated?

### Murderer Execution

The *Gemara* attempts to derive this principle from the laws of executing a convicted murderer. A *baraita* states: *mot yumat ha-makeh rotzeach hu* — the killer shall surely be put to death. *Ein li ela be-mita ha-amura bo* — I know only that the prescribed method (which is the sword) is to be used. But the verse also says *mot yumat* — he shall surely die — *mi-kol makom*, from any circumstances, implying that if the prescribed execution cannot be carried out, any available means may be used.

The *Gemara* considers whether one could derive the rule for *haba ba-machteret* from this precedent. It concludes that one cannot, because the case of *rotzeach* and the case of *go'el ha-dam* (the blood-avenger) together constitute *shnei ketuvim ha-ba'im ke-echad* — two scriptural instances that teach the same principle — and the rule is that such paired instances do not serve as the basis for general derivation; they are treated as the exception rather than the rule. Therefore the *baraita* must explicitly state that in the case of *haba ba-machteret* as well, any available means may be used.

What is telling here again is the logic of the discussion. The natural argument for using any available means against someone who is about to kill you is simply: do whatever you must to save your life. The *Gemara's* framework, however, approaches the question through the lens of court-imposed punishments and their applicable methods — *harugei beit din* — and derives the rule by analogy to the execution of a murderer. This persistent framing reinforces the second model introduced at the outset: that the killing in self-defense is being conceptualized as quasi-judicial, with the defender acting as an arm of the legal system.

---

## Tunnel Warning

### Beyond Literal Tunnel

The *baraita* asks: *ein li ela machteret* — do I know only that the law applies when the entry is through a literal tunnel? What about entry through the roof, the courtyard, or other means? *Talmud lomar: im yimatze ha-ganav mi-kol makom* — "if the thief is found" — wherever he is found, however he entered. The tunnel is not the *halachically* defining feature. *Mipnei she-rov ganavim metzuyyin ba-machteret* — the *Torah* mentions the tunnel simply because it is the common case; it is descriptive, not restrictive.

### Tunnel as Warning

A second *baraita* makes the same point with identical logic, extending the law to entry through a roof, courtyard, or covered portico. But then it adds a crucial principle: *machterato zo hi hatraato* — his tunnel is his warning. This phrase deserves careful attention.

Rashi explains: by going to the extraordinary length of digging a tunnel to gain entry, the burglar has demonstrated that he is prepared to do anything, including kill, to complete his mission. The tunnel functions as the equivalent of a declaration — a warning — that lethal force is on the table. No further *hatraa* from the homeowner is needed. Since the burglar has already shown, by his actions, that he knows and accepts the risk of lethal confrontation, we may proceed to act accordingly.

### Back Door Hatraa

But what if the burglar enters through the back door without digging? In that case, Rashi holds, the presumption of readiness to kill does not automatically apply. The burglar may simply be taking advantage of an easy entry point without any intention of violence. For the homeowner to be entitled to use lethal force in that scenario, classic *hatraa* would be required: witnesses, a warning addressed to the burglar, and the burglar's acceptance of the warning — *yodea ani ve-al menat kein ani oseh* — I know the consequences and I proceed nonetheless.

This is a striking application. Classic *hatraa* is the procedural requirement for a *beit din* to impose a capital sentence: witnesses must warn the perpetrator, he must acknowledge the warning and accept it, and only then does criminal liability attach. Rashi is importing that entire framework here, into the context of personal self-defense. The homeowner, before using lethal force against a non-tunnel burglar, must essentially conduct a *hatraa* as though he were a court. This again powerfully reinforces the second model: the defender is not merely a private individual acting in extremis, but someone who, when circumstances require, operates as a representative of the legal system, with all the procedural obligations that implies.

The tunnel, then, serves a dual function. Practically, it identifies the class of burglars who are presumed to be armed with violent intent. Conceptually, it marks the threshold at which the procedural requirements of the legal system are satisfied by the very act of the burglar himself, without any further formality. *Machterato zo hi hatraato*: the tunnel is the warning, the verdict, and the sentence, all at once.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 73

## Haba BeMachteret & Rodef

### Haba BeMachteret Review

Today's daf is 73, and we begin by picking up at the bottom of 72b, which flows naturally into the new sugya. The preceding material concerned the *haba bemachteret* — the burglar who breaks through a tunnel — and established that the homeowner may act in self-defense. The *gemara* there recognized that while self-defense is what permits the killing, there are aspects of the discussion that suggest something further: the act of killing the intruder may be conceived of not merely as self-defense but as a type of *beit din din*, a quasi-judicial proceeding.

### Hatra'ah & Din Model

This impression was reinforced by the *gemara*'s formulation *machtarto zo hi hatra'ato* — his tunnel-entry is his *hatra'ah*, his warning. One reading of this phrase, which Rashi adopts, is simply that the act of breaking in through the tunnel demonstrates the intruder's readiness to use lethal force, and that demonstrated readiness is what permits the homeowner to respond. But the very use of the word *hatra'ah* evokes the formal warning required in capital cases adjudicated by *beit din*, suggesting that the framework here mimics a court procedure. Rashi goes so far as to describe a scenario where warning is given in front of witnesses and the intruder acknowledges it, which sounds very much like the classical *din* model rather than pure self-defense.

### Katan Rodef

With that tension in the background, the *gemara* now introduces a ruling of Rav Huna: *katan harodef nitan lehatzilo benafsho* — if a minor is pursuing someone with intent to kill, the potential victim may be saved even at the cost of the minor's life. This ruling functions as a precise counterpoint to the *din* model. A minor cannot be brought before a court, cannot be held legally liable for his actions, and yet Rav Huna rules that lethal intervention is permitted. The implication is clear: this is not about judging the pursuer. It is entirely about saving the person being pursued. The *gemara* makes this explicit — *lo shena gadol lo shena katan*, it makes no difference whether the *rodef* is an adult or a minor, because the operative principle is the protection of the *nirdaf*, the victim.

---

## Din vs Victim Model

### Fetus & Mother Case

Rav Chisda challenges Rav Huna with a well-known *mishnah*: if a fetus is endangering the mother's life during labor, one may dismember the fetus in the womb to save the mother, since at that stage the fetus has not yet attained the full status of a life. However, once *yatza rosho* — once the head has emerged — one may no longer touch the infant, because *she'ein dochin nefesh mipnei nefesh*, one life is not pushed aside for another. The difficulty is apparent: if the *rodef* principle operates purely to protect the *nirdaf* without any requirement of blameworthiness, why can we not treat the emerging infant as a *rodef* threatening the mother and intervene accordingly?

### Mishmaya Ka Radfu

The *gemara* responds: *shani hasam mishmaya ka radfu* — there it is different, because she is being pursued by heaven. This phrase requires unpacking. The earlier analysis suggested that the *rodef* framework does not require legal responsibility — a ten-year-old who knows what he is doing but is not yet *bar onesh* may still be stopped. But one might argue that there must at least be some degree of blameworthiness or fault, even if not formal legal culpability, in order to label someone a *rodef* and permit lethal intervention against him. If that is the standard, then perhaps below a certain age no one could ever be considered a *rodef*.

Alternatively, one might say that fault is entirely irrelevant — what matters is only the physical reality that one party is endangering another, and if we can identify pursuer and pursued, we protect the pursued. Even an infant falling from a roof and about to destroy a raft full of people would, on this reading, qualify as a *rodef*, innocent though it may be.

But the case of difficult childbirth resists both frameworks. The Rambam characterizes it as a completely natural event. Childbirth encounters complications; it always has. There is no identifiable pursuer here in the relevant sense. *Mishmaya ka radfu* means, on this reading, that there is no *rodef* — the infant is not pursuing anyone in any meaningful sense, either legally or even physically in the way that something out of the ordinary and threatening qualifies. The situation is simply the natural process of birth, and one cannot apply the *rodef* category to it.

This connects to cases discussed in other contexts: the crying baby in a hiding place whose silence might require suppression to protect others is framed as endangering lives, and that framing is what makes the concept of *rodef* applicable. What the *gemara* is doing here is carefully delimiting when the *rodef* label can and cannot be applied.

### Rodef Warning Case

The *gemara* then considers whether a support can be found for Rav Huna's position. The case presented describes a *rodef* who is running after another person to kill him, and a bystander who says to the *rodef*: "Look, this man is a *Yisrael*, a *ben brit*, and the Torah has said *shopech dam ha'adam ba'adam damo yishapech* — one who sheds blood, his blood shall be shed." This looks very much like a formal *hatra'ah* — the pursuer is being warned of the specific prohibition and its consequence. The *gemara* then asks: does this warning help or hinder the case for Rav Huna? At first glance it seems to import a *din* model into the *rodef* scenario, which would work against applying the rule to a *katan*.

### Rashi & Katan

Rashi explains the *gemara*'s reasoning differently from what one might initially suppose. The support for Rav Huna lies in the fact that nowhere in the description of this warning does the pursuer respond with *al menat ken ani oseh* — "I am doing this accepting full knowledge and responsibility." *Kabbalat hatra'ah* — the formal acceptance of the warning — is absent. Rashi reads this absence as evidence that one does not need to apply the full *din* model: there is no requirement for the *rodef* to formally accept the warning in order to permit intervention. The *gemara* responds that this proves nothing about Rav Huna's position, because the case follows the view of Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that a *chaver* — someone demonstrably knowledgeable — does not require formal warning at all. For such a person, it suffices that he has been informed; he need not explicitly confirm *yode'a ani ve'af al pi ken*.
