So the absence of *kabbalat hatra'ah* in the case reflects that leniency, not a wholesale departure from the *din* model.

Yet this response is puzzling. If the *rodef* framework is truly not a *din* model but purely about protecting the *nirdaf*, why is the warning being issued at all? The time spent delivering a formal warning could be used to intervene and save the potential victim. The very appearance of the *hatra'ah* in the scenario implies that the *din* model has not been entirely displaced. The contrast between the two models, with the case of the *katan* as the critical *nafka mina*, seems to be what the *gemara* is genuinely holding in tension — without fully resolving it.

### River Case

A further case is introduced: a *rodef* who is on the opposite bank of the river, where intervention to save the *nirdaf* is physically impossible. Here, the warning given to the pursuer serves only one possible purpose — to enable a subsequent prosecution before *beit din*. The *gemara* states explicitly: *bei dina ba'ei hatra'ah*, for *beit din* proceedings you need *hatra'ah*. This case, then, does not represent the *rodef* scenario in its pure form; it is a *beit din* scenario using *rodef* language. It does not undermine Rav Huna.

### Machteret Hatra'ah

Rav Huna's final position is stated clearly: he holds like the *tanna* of the *machteret* case, who said *machterto zo hi hatra'ato*. But crucially, Rav Huna reads that phrase not as saying "the tunnel counts as the required *hatra'ah*" — which would still presuppose that *hatra'ah* is in principle necessary — but rather as saying: *almah mishum d'machzikinan lei rodef lo ba'ei hatra'ah* — once we establish that the man is a *rodef*, threatening another person's life, there is no requirement of *hatra'ah* at all. The phrase does not introduce a surrogate for the *din* requirement; it abolishes the requirement in this context entirely. It is about protecting the victim, and that principle applies regardless of whether the *rodef* is an adult or a *katan*, regardless of blameworthiness, and regardless of formal warning. What matters is only whether one can identify a pursuer and a pursued — and if one can, the pursued is protected even at the cost of the pursuer's life.

This *sugya* thus distills two models with precision. The *din* model would require that the act in question be treated like a capital case, with formal warning and acceptance. The victim-protection model asks only whether someone's life is imminently endangered by an identifiable pursuer. The *nafka mina* — a *katan rodef* — perfectly illustrates the difference, and Rav Huna's ruling comes down squarely for the victim-protection model.

---

## Mishna: Who to Save

### Mishna Introduction

The *gemara* now transitions to the *mishnah* on 73a, which lists the cases in which one may save potential victims at the cost of the pursuer's life: *harodef achar chaveiro lehargo* — one pursuing another to kill him; *ve'achar hazachar* — one pursuing a male for sexual assault; and *ve'achar hana'arah hame'orasah* — one pursuing a betrothed maiden. The *mishnah* will be extended by the *gemara* to cover additional cases.

### Rape & Severity

An important observation emerges here: rape alone is not sufficient to authorize lethal intervention. The *gemara*'s treatment of rape is notable. While the *Torah*'s comparison of the violated *na'arah me'orasah* to a murder victim (*ki ka'asher yakum ish al re'ehu uretzacho nefesh ken hadavar hazeh*) could be read as equating rape with murder in severity, and the Chazon Ish does develop something along those lines, the *gemara* does not treat rape as independently warranting lethal force. Rather, rape is treated in a framework closer to that of physical assault — a serious crime with penalties, but not automatically one that permits taking the pursuer's life.

What is required, the *gemara* makes clear, is a combination: the victim must be genuinely being pursued against her will, *and* the act being committed must be one that carries a penalty of death or *karet*. So the case of the *na'arah me'orasah* qualifies, as does any case of *arayot* within the category of *chayvei mitot beit din* or *chayvei karet* — a married woman, a sister, a brother's wife. But rape of an unmarried woman, which does not carry that level of sanction, does not suffice to authorize lethal force. One may still intervene with non-lethal force to protect such a victim — there is a discussion in Bava Kamma that addresses the use of physical force to stop someone who initiates assault — but lethal force requires both elements.

This combination is worth pausing over. It is tempting to say that after establishing that the *rodef* framework is purely about victim protection, we have completely abandoned the *din* model. But the requirement that the act carry a capital or *karet* sanction introduces something that looks at least partially like a *din* consideration. Perhaps the severity of the offense functions not as a *din* criterion but simply as a threshold — the graver the crime, the greater the license to use extreme measures to prevent it. That reading would allow one to hold that the criterion is still about protecting the victim rather than adjudicating the perpetrator, since it is the magnitude of the harm to the victim that determines how far intervention may go. Either way, it is clear that when we are not dealing with murder, something beyond bare victim-status is required.

### Excluded Cases

The *mishnah* then states: *aval rodef achar behemah* — but one who is pursuing an animal for purposes of bestiality — and *umechallel es haShabbos*, and *ve'oveid avodah zarah*, these are cases where *ein matzilin oso b'nafsho* — one does not intervene with lethal force. The pattern is now explicit: terrible sin without a human victim does not qualify. Great sin plus human victim does. If there is a victim without a correspondingly weighty sin, equally no. The *mishnah* is beautifully clear on this structure.

### Matzilin Oso

The phrase *matzilin osan b'nafsho* — literally "they save him with his soul" — presents an interesting grammatical problem. In the case of a *mekallel Shabbos* or *oved avodah zarah*, where there is no victim, who exactly is being saved? The phrase seems to be borrowed from the victim-rescue context, but it sits oddly in a context where no victim exists. Rashi resolves this by reading *matzilin osan min ha'aveirah b'nafshan* — they save the would-be perpetrator *from sinning*, with his own life as the price. On this reading, the intervention is framed as rescuing the sinner from the gravity of his own sin — better that he should die than commit such a transgression. But this reading creates its own difficulty: if saving someone from sin justifies taking his life, why should it not apply equally to *mechallel Shabbos* or *oved avodah zarah* even in the *mishnah*'s excluded cases? Tosafot notes this tension, observing that in the cases clearly involving a victim, the grammar of *matzilin* plainly refers to saving the victim rather than the perpetrator. The very ambiguity of the phrase encapsulates the deeper tension in the *mishnah* between the offense-oriented and victim-oriented frameworks.

---

## Kal VaChomer Source

### Lo Ta'amod Source

The *gemara* now asks: from where is the *rodef achar chaveiro lehargo* derived — that one may save the potential murder victim even at the cost of the pursuer's life? The *gemara* initially proposes *lo ta'amod al dam rei'echa*. But this verse, as the *gemara* immediately notes, is needed for something else entirely: *minayin l'ro'eh et chaveiro shehu tovei'a banahar o chayah gorareto o listim ba'in alav shehu chayav lehatzilo* — how do we know that if one sees his companion drowning, or being dragged by an animal, or attacked by bandits, he is obligated to rescue him? The verse *lo ta'amod al dam rei'echa* teaches that basic obligation, including the requirement to spend money, hire people, and go to significant lengths — not merely the minimal personal effort implied by the *mitzvah* of returning lost objects (*vehasheivoto lo*, which is read by the *gemara* as *aveidat gufo*, restoring a person's own life to him). So *lo ta'amod* is the source for the obligation to save life in general; it cannot simultaneously be the source for the permission to use lethal force in the *rodef* scenario.

### Kal VaChomer

The *gemara* therefore derives the lethal-intervention rule from *kal vachomer*: by the *na'arah me'orasah* the *Torah* writes *ein moshia lah* — there was no one to save her — which implies that had someone been available, he would have saved her by whatever means necessary. Since she was being harmed but not killed, this teaches that one may intervene with lethal force even to prevent a non-lethal serious offense against a victim. If so, *rodef achar chaveiro lehargo al achat kama vekhamah* — how much more so is lethal intervention permitted when the very life of the *nirdaf* is at stake.

### Makish Analysis

The *gemara* immediately objects: *ve'chi onshin min hadin* — one cannot impose punishment on the basis of a *kal vachomer*. Again, the evocation of the *din* model is striking — the language of punishment infiltrates a discussion that, as we have argued, is about protecting the victim. The *gemara* responds by shifting to a *gezerah shavah*: the verse *ki ka'asher yakum ish al re'ehu uretzacho nefesh ken hadavar hazeh* explicitly compares the case of rape to murder. The *gemara* asks: what does murder teach us about rape? We already know the woman is blameless. And it answers: *harei zeh ba lilamed v'nimtza lamed* — it comes to teach but ends up learning. Murder is brought to illuminate rape, but it is the case of the *na'arah me'orasah* that winds up being the teacher. From *na'arah me'orasah* — where *ein moshia lah* implies lethal intervention would have been permitted — we derive that by murder (*rotzeach*) equally, *nitan lehatzilo benafsho*, one may save the potential victim with the life of the pursuer. And *na'arah me'orasah* itself is derived from *devet Rabbi Yishmael*'s reading of *ve'ein moshia lah*: if there *were* someone who could save her, he would save her by *chol davar sheyachol lehoshiya* — with any and every means available.

### Expanded Cases

The *gemara* then cites the *braita*: *echad harodef achar chaveiro lehorgo ve'achar hazachar ve'achar hana'arah me'orasah ve'achar chayvei mitot beit din ve'achar chayvei keritot* — any case of *arayot* of sufficient severity falls within the rule. Both capital offenses and those incurring *karet* are included.

---

## Sexual Offenses & Pegam

### Lesser Violations

The *braita* continues: *anesa l'kohen gadol grusha vechalutza l'kohen hedyot* — if the offense is a lesser prohibition, such as a *kohen* raping a *grushah* or a *kohen gadol* raping an *almana*, then *ein matzilin otah b'nafsho* — one does not intervene with lethal force. The distinction is not from the perspective of the victim's suffering, but from the perspective of the weight of the *aveirah* from the *Torah*'s standpoint.

### Nistafcha Status

The *braita* also states: *nistafcha ba'aveirah ein matzilin otah b'nafsho* — if the act has already been committed, one can no longer intervene. This is not a matter of coming too late to prevent the specific act, though that is an intuitive reading. The *gemara* will make clear that the principle runs deeper.

### Pegam Explained

The concept of *pegam* — defilement or spoliation — is central to understanding this entire section. The *gemara* frames the victim's status through a particular social and halakhic lens: every woman belongs, in some sense, to a man — either her current husband or her future husband. When a man rapes a woman, he is *pogeim* her — he spoils her in relation to that man. If she is married and has had intimate relations with her husband, she has not been *pogeim*; but when another man violates her, that violation constitutes the *pegam*. A single woman who has not yet been married stands in relation to her future husband; any man who violates her is *pogeim* her with respect to him.

This is why the concept of *nistafcha* operates the way it does. If a woman has already been violated by one man — even through no fault of her own — then when a second man pursues her, he is not *pogeim* her in the same sense. She has already been *nistafcha*, and therefore the lethal intervention designed to prevent that *pegam* no longer applies. The conceptual framework is uncomfortable from a contemporary perspective, but it is the *gemara*'s own framing, and the subsequent analysis only makes it more explicit.

### Na'arah Basadeh

The case of *na'arah basadeh* addresses a scenario where the woman could be saved without lethal force. If non-lethal intervention is available and sufficient, one may not take the pursuer's life. The permission to use lethal force exists only where there is no lesser means of rescue.

---

## Pesukim Analysis

### Four Terms Needed

The *gemara* now asks why all four textual terms — *na'ar*, *na'arah*, *chet*, and *mavet* — are required. Could not the derivation have been accomplished with fewer? The answer is that each term excludes a different potential error in scope.

If only *na'ar* (without the *heh*) had been written, I might have thought the rule applies only to a male victim being raped, *mishum delav orchei* — because for a man to be penetrated is not the natural order and therefore that scenario demands the most severe protective response. I would not have derived the same for a female victim.

If only *na'arah* had been written, I might have thought the rule applies only where there is *pegam* — the spoiling of a woman — and therefore not to a male victim, *dela ka pagim lei*. The *pegam* concept is gender-specific in this framework; a man being raped, however traumatic, does not carry the same dimension of *pogeim* him.

If only those two terms were given — *na'ar* and *na'arah* — I might have thought the rule is limited to those particular cases of unusual assault (*lav orchei*) or *pegam*, and would not extend to other *arayot* involving, say, a married woman where the act is not rare and the *pegam* is less acute.

So *chet* is needed to include other cases of weighty sexual sin beyond *na'arah me'orasah*. And *mavet* is needed to make clear that even the most severe category — *chayvei mitot beit din* — is included; otherwise I might have stopped at *karet*. And *chet* is also needed to prevent limiting the rule only to capital offenses — without it, I would read *mavet* exclusively and exclude *karet*. Each term does necessary work.

### Exclude Behemah

Given that *chet* and *mavet* together already cover the scope of weighty sexual offenses, what function do *na'ar* and *na'arah* serve? The *gemara* answers: one of them excludes the case of *behemah* — an animal victim. Without these terms, one might have thought that sexual assault on an animal also triggers lethal intervention, since the act of bestiality carries severe sanctions. The term *na'ar*/*na'arah* signals that the framework requires a human victim.

### Rebbi Shimon Position

Rebbi Shimon ben Yochai holds a distinct position: *oved avodah zarah nitan lehatzilo benafsho* — one who is about to worship idols may be stopped with lethal force, even though there is no human victim. For Rebbi Shimon ben Yochai, the weightiest of sins — *avodah zarah* — is sufficient on its own to authorize the use of lethal force, without requiring a victim. This represents the offense-oriented model in its fullest articulation. Given this view, what does he need *na'ar* and *na'arah* for? *Chad le-mi'utei behemah* — one still excludes the case of an animal victim from the sexual-offense track. And *chad le-mi'utei Shabbos* — one would have thought, given that he permits lethal force to stop *avodah zarah*, that the same should apply to *chillul Shabbos*, which the *Torah* equates in various ways to *avodah zarah*. The verse therefore teaches that *Shabbos* is excluded on the sexual-offense track even for Rebbi Shimon ben Yochai.

### Rebbi Elazar Position

Rebbi Elazar bar Rebbi Shimon goes a step further than his father. He holds *mechallel Shabbos nitan lehatzilo benafsho* — one desecrating the Sabbath may also be stopped with lethal force, since *Shabbos* is explicitly compared to *avodah zarah* and the two are treated as equivalent in severity. On this view, what remains for *na'ar* and *na'arah* to exclude? *Chad le-mi'utei behemah* — even the most severe-sin approach still requires either a human victim or one of the two uniquely grave offenses; bestiality therefore falls outside the authorization for lethal force. The other term simply becomes redundant since both *Shabbos* and *avodah zarah* are already included, and *na'ar*/*na'arah* need not work as hard.

The *gemara* thus clarifies that the consensus position of our *mishnah* is the hybrid: weighty sin plus human victim. Some *tanna'im* take a position that the most serious offenses — *avodah zarah* and by extension *Shabbos* — are sufficient without a victim. One might note that even those cases admit of a victim-oriented reading in a broader sense: *avodah zarah* committed within a community endangers the community's religious identity; *chillul Shabbos* poses a parallel threat. The community itself can be understood as the victim. But that framing extends beyond what the *gemara* explicitly states.

---

## Rebbi Yehuda Dispute

### Woman's Request

The *mishnah* includes a dispute involving Rebbi Yehuda: *af omeret hanichu lo shelo yehargenah* — even if the woman says "leave him alone, otherwise he will kill me," Rebbi Yehuda holds one may not kill the pursuer. This is initially puzzling: she is still clearly a victim of rape, she is not consenting, and her very statement reveals that she fears for her life. Why should her plea to stand down affect the halakha?

### Rabanan View

The *gemara* explains the dispute. Rava frames it as follows: *bemakpedet al pigmah* — she is still clearly concerned about her *pegam*; her statement that she does not want him killed is driven by fear for her life, not by any willingness to be violated. She is still very much a victim, objecting to the rape. The *Rabanan* hold: *apigma kapid Rachmana* — the *Torah*'s concern is protecting her from *pegam*, and since she is genuinely objecting to it — *makpedet al pigmah* — she remains a victim in the halakhic sense, and one may intervene. Her expression of fear for her life does not transform her into a willing participant.

### Rebbi Yehuda Theory

Rebbi Yehuda, however, offers a fundamentally different account of why the *Torah* authorized lethal intervention in the first place. He holds: *hai d'ka'amar Rachmana katlei mishum d'masra nafshah l'ktala* — the reason the *Torah* says to kill the pursuer is not primarily to protect the woman from *pegam*, but because there exist circumstances in which a woman would actually give up her life rather than be violated. There are women — Rashi describes them as *tznuot*, women of particular modesty and self-restraint — who would choose death over rape. In such cases, her life is genuinely at risk, and it is that risk to her life that authorizes lethal intervention. The *rodef* here is threatening not just her *pegam* but her actual existence.

### Application

Given this framework, the application follows directly. When the woman says *hanichu lo shelo yehargenah* — "leave him alone, he will kill me otherwise" — she is communicating clearly that she is not among those who would sacrifice her life to avoid violation. She is declaring that she will not *masar nafshah l'ktala*. For Rebbi Yehuda, that declaration removes the very rationale for lethal intervention: if her life is not at risk — because she herself confirms she will not choose death — then there is nothing that requires us to kill the pursuer. The intervention was always about the life risk, and she has eliminated that risk by her own declaration.

### Application

This is a striking position. Rebbi Yehuda is not saying the rape itself is unimportant. He is saying that the specific legal authorization for lethal intervention was always predicated on the possibility of mortal risk, and once that predicate is removed by the woman's own statement, the authorization lapses. The question of whether a woman is *obligated* in *yehareg ve'al ya'avor* — to die rather than transgress — connects naturally to this analysis and will be addressed in tomorrow's material.

### Pegam Severity

Rav Pappa raises a question to Abaye: if the *Rabanan* hold that the entire framework is about protecting a woman from *pegam*, why does the *mishnah* not authorize lethal intervention in the case of an *almana* being raped by a *kohen gadol*? She too is being *pegem*! The answer given is: *pgima raba kapid Rachmana, pgima zuta lo kapid Rachmana* — the *Torah* is concerned only with a major *pegam*, not a minor one. And the severity of the *pegam* tracks the severity of the *aveirah*: because intercourse of a *kohen gadol* with an *almana* is a less weighty prohibition than *chayvei mitah* or *chayvei karet*, the resulting *pegam* is correspondingly lesser, and it does not cross the threshold that triggers the authorization of lethal force. This is a significant observation: the size of the *pegam* is not an independent measure of harm to the woman, but rather a function of the gravity of the transgression. The more severe the *aveirah*, the more severe the *pegam*, and the more justified the lethal intervention.

This brings us full circle to the tension running through the entire daf. Is the framework about the *din* — the severity of the offense as adjudicated by the *Torah*? Is it purely about protecting the victim? Is it about *pegam* as a kind of victim-harm that tracks the offense? The *gemara* does not resolve these tensions into a single formula. What emerges instead is a sophisticated interplay: the authorization for lethal intervention requires both a genuine human victim being pursued against her will and an offense of sufficient gravity, where the gravity of the offense is itself bound up with the nature and severity of the harm done to the victim.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 74

## Rape & Ketubah Fine

### Mishnah: Fine Cases

The daf opens by continuing the discussion of cases in which one would be permitted — indeed obligated — to use lethal force to protect a woman from being sexually violated. As established in the preceding pages, this license extends only to acts of intercourse that carry the penalty of *karet* or the death penalty, not to every act of rape. With that framework in place, the Gemara picks up near the bottom of 73b and transitions into a new difficulty raised by a *mishnah* in a different context.

The *mishnah* under discussion enumerates *naarot* — maidens — who are entitled to the statutory *knas* (the fine paid by a rapist or seducer to a girl who is not yet married), even in cases where the man would ordinarily be forbidden to marry her. One such case is *haba al achoto* — a man who violates his sister. Though he has transgressed one of the *arayot* and cannot marry her, he nonetheless pays the fine. The *mishnah* further specifies that if the act was one that carries the death penalty (*chayav mita*), there would be no *knas*, invoking the principle of *kam lei bid'raba minei* — the greater penalty (death) absorbs the lesser one (the monetary fine). But if the act carried *karet*, not the death penalty, the *knas* would still apply.

### Kam Lei Principle

This invocation of *kam lei* generates a difficulty. In the context of the *machteret* (the housebreaker), the Gemara had already established that once a person is doing an act for which his life may be taken, he incurs no monetary obligations in connection with that act — a principle analogous to *kam lei*. If, then, a man is raping a girl and committing an act of *chayav karet*, and we would be permitted to kill him to stop the rape, why does he owe the *knas* at all?

### Gemara's Question

The Gemara poses this question directly: given that bystanders could have killed this man to protect the girl, the act he is performing is one for which his life is forfeit. By the logic of *kam lei*, he should not be obligated in any monetary payment. Why, then, does the *mishnah* say he pays the *knas*?

### Ha'arah & Pagum

The Gemara reports that the rabbis raised this difficulty before Rav Chisda, and he offered the following resolution: *mishaat ha'ara'ah d'fagmah, ishtarei mikatla* — from the very moment that *ha'ara'ah* begins, that is, the initial stage of penetration (or, according to one opinion, the mere external contact of the genitals), she has already been *nifgam* — she has been defiled, she has become, in the Gemara's terminology, spoiled goods. And once she has been *nifgam*, we can no longer kill him in the middle of the act. The license to use lethal force was predicated on protecting her from that very disgrace, and once the disgrace has occurred — from that very first moment — the license evaporates.

The force of this ruling is deeply disturbing to modern sensibilities. The man continues to rape her, and yet the license to intervene has already lapsed, because the harm that justified intervention has already been done. He is thus no longer performing an act for which we could kill him. And therefore — *mamona lo mishalem ad gmar bia* — the monetary obligation, the *knas*, does not crystallize until the act is complete. By that point, since he could no longer be killed during the act, there is no *kam lei* to speak of, and he pays.

Rashi explains that the *knas* does not arise until the end of the act because the fine is for rupturing the hymen, which only occurs upon completion. Tosafot disputes this, arguing that the fine is not specifically for the hymen and would technically be incurred at the very first instant of penetration. According to Tosafot, in a normal case the obligation begins at that first moment of *ha'ara'ah* — but in this case, at that precise first moment, the perpetrator could still be killed, so *kam lei* would apply. The instant after that first moment, he can no longer be killed — she is already *nifgam* — and that is when the obligation of the *knas* takes hold.

### Timing of Pagam

The Gemara then notes that this resolution works well according to the opinion that *ha'ara'ah* means *nishika* — the external touching or "kissing" of the genitals, before penetration. In that case, there are two distinct moments: the moment of *nishika* (at which she becomes *nifgam* and the license to kill him ends), and the moment of actual penetration (at which the *knas* obligation begins and she is no longer considered a *besulah*). These two moments are distinguishable, and so the analysis holds.

But according to the opinion that *ha'ara'ah* means *hachnasat ha'atara* — the insertion of the crown of the penis, the beginning of penetration itself — the analysis breaks down. At that single moment, she both becomes *nifgam* and loses her status as a *besulah*. If the *pagam* occurs at the moment of penetration, and we could still have killed him at that moment, then after that moment she is no longer a *besulah* — and the *knas* only applies to a *besulah*. So there is no remaining window in which the *knas* could apply.

### Case Resolutions

Rav Chisda himself offers a solution to this impasse. The case that generates the *knas* despite *chayav karet* is one where he first engaged in anal intercourse and then vaginal intercourse: *shelo kedarka*, and then *kedarka*. The first act does not cause her to lose her status as a *besulah*, since it is not vaginal penetration. During that first act, we could have killed him, but she has already been *nifgam*. By the time he proceeds to the vaginal act — which does carry the *knas* — she is already *nifgam* and we can no longer kill him, yet she is still a *besulah*, so the *knas* applies.

Rava offers a second resolution: the case is one where the woman herself says not to kill him, out of fear that he will kill her if intervention is attempted (*minachsa shelo yargenu*), and this follows the position of Rabbi Yehuda. Rabbi Yehuda holds that the license to use lethal force is not merely to protect her from *pagam* but because her life is at risk. Once she declares that her life is not at risk and she does not want him killed, we may not intervene. Since we are not permitted to kill him, *kam lei* does not apply, and the *knas* is owed.

Rav Pappa offers the most straightforward resolution: the case involves *mefutah* — seduction, not rape — and this is *divrei hakol*, accepted by all opinions. The Torah's *knas* applies both to rape and to seduction. In a case of seduction, there is no victim to protect and no license to kill the man, so *kam lei* never arises, and the *knas* applies normally.

### Non-Lethal Intervention

Abbaye's answer introduces a principle that will occupy the Gemara throughout the next section. Abbaye says the case is one where it was possible to stop the perpetrator by injuring one of his limbs rather than killing him — *b'yakhol lehatzilo b'echad mei-evarav* — and this follows the position of Rabbi Yonatan ben Shaul. Since it was possible to neutralize him without lethal force, we were not permitted to use lethal force, and therefore the man was never in the category of someone whose life is forfeit. Accordingly, *kam lei* never applies, and the *knas* is owed in full.

---

## Rodeph Doctrine

### R. Yonatan ben Shaul

The Gemara now opens a dedicated analysis of Rabbi Yonatan ben Shaul's principle: *rodeph shehaya rodeph achar chaveiro l'horgo, v'yakhol lehatzilo b'echad mei-evarav, v'lo hitzil, neherag alav* — if a pursuer was chasing another person to kill him, and it was possible to stop him by injuring one of his limbs, and instead the intervener killed the pursuer outright, the intervener has committed an act of murder. In practical terms, since the intervener would need to have been warned and to have accepted the warning before being subject to execution, the actual execution of the intervener in a *beis din* setting is difficult to achieve — but the Gemara's point is that the act is categorized as *murder*.

This is a striking ruling, and the Gemara does not take it as self-evident. The obvious concern is that imposing this kind of caution on would-be rescuers — requiring them to first attempt a less-than-lethal intervention — may result in the victim not being saved at all. How much caution can reasonably be demanded of an intervener when a life is in the balance, without that caution itself becoming irresponsible? This is precisely why the Gemara seeks a derivation for Rabbi Yonatan ben Shaul's position: it is not the intuitively obvious rule, and it is not universally held, though the *halacha* does follow it.

### Miscarriage Case

The proof for Rabbi Yonatan ben Shaul's principle comes from the law of the miscarrying woman. The Gemara cites the verse: *vechi yinatzu anashim* — when men fight. Rabbi Elazar explains that this describes a fight to the death, as evidenced by the continuation of the passage: *ve'im yihye ason venatata nefesh tachat nafesh* — if there is a fatality, you give a life for a life. The verse's promise of execution tells us that these men were attempting to kill one another; otherwise, accidental killing would not generate the death penalty.

Now the same passage continues: *v'lo yihye ason, anosh ye'anesh* — if there is no fatality but a pregnant bystander is struck and miscarries, the striker must pay a fine. The Gemara asks: how can he ever be obligated to pay this fine? He is engaged in an act of attempted murder, for which he could be killed. Under *kam lei*, that should eliminate any monetary obligation, including the payment for the miscarriage. The answer, says Rabbi Yonatan ben Shaul, is that the verse is discussing a case where the pursuer *could* have been neutralized *b'echad mei-evarav* — with one of his limbs. In such a case, we are not permitted to kill him. Since he cannot be killed, he is not in the category of *chayav mita*, and therefore *kam lei* does not apply. He therefore owes the fine for the miscarriage.

To make this vivid: imagine two people fighting to the death. One of them, in the course of pursuing the other, accidentally strikes a pregnant bystander who miscarries. He is liable the payment. Why? Because in this specific scenario it was possible to stop him short of lethal force — perhaps by grabbing him, striking his arm, shooting him in the leg — and since that was possible, we were not permitted to use lethal force against him. He therefore was never in the category of a person who could be killed, *kam lei* never applies, and the monetary obligation for the miscarriage stands.

### Different Victims

The Gemara, however, challenges this proof. Perhaps Rabbi Yonatan ben Shaul's principle is unnecessary to explain the payment for the miscarriage. Perhaps the explanation is simpler: *misa lizeh ve'tashlumin lizeh* — death is owed to one party and payment is owed to a different party. The principle of *kam lei* might apply only when the victim of the fatal act and the victim of the monetary claim are the same person. Here, the man he is trying to kill and the pregnant woman are two entirely separate individuals, with separate claims before entirely separate tribunals. Perhaps *kam lei* does not operate across different victims.

To draw this out: if someone fires a bullet at Reuven, and the bullet passes through Shimon's stained-glass window before killing Reuven, one might argue that Reuven's relatives' murder claim and Shimon's property claim are entirely separate cases. *Kam lei* eliminates monetary claims that arise from the same act directed at the same victim; it might not reach across to eliminate claims by third parties who were incidentally damaged.

If so, the proof for Rabbi Yonatan ben Shaul's principle from the miscarrying woman is unnecessary: even without that principle, the man could be killed — and yet he would owe the woman's husband for the miscarriage, simply because she is a different victim.

### Rava on Damage

The Gemara rejects this alternative. Rava teaches explicitly: *rodeph shehaya rodeph achar chaveiro, veshibar et ha-keilim, bein shel nirdaf bein shel kol adam — patur* — a pursuer chasing another person who breaks vessels in the course of the chase, whether those vessels belong to the victim or to a third party entirely, is exempt from payment. The reason: *mischayav b'nafsho hu* — he is doing an act for which he can be killed, and therefore all monetary obligations dissolve, regardless of to whom they would be owed.

This is precisely the case of *misa lizeh ve'tashlumin lizeh*: the pursuer owes death in his relationship with the victim, and the broken vessels belong to a third party. And yet Rava rules he is exempt from paying for those vessels. The principle of *kam lei* operates across different victims. Therefore, the alternative explanation of the miscarrying woman collapses: if the pursuer could be killed, he would be exempt from the miscarriage payment to the husband as well. The only way to explain why he *does* owe the payment is Rabbi Yonatan ben Shaul's principle: in this case, he could not be killed — because he could have been stopped *b'echad mei-evarav*.

### Good Samaritan

Rava's teaching continues with a careful taxonomy of the various parties' obligations. The *nirdaf* (the person being pursued) who, in fleeing, breaks the pursuer's vessels, is exempt — the pursuer has forfeited his life and his property to protect the victim, and so any damage done to the pursuer's property in service of that protection is covered under that forfeiture. But if the *nirdaf* breaks the vessels of a third party in fleeing, he is liable: *she-matzil atzmo b'mamon chaveiro* — he is saving his own life at the expense of another's property, and even though he was permitted to do so, the third party bears no obligation to absorb that loss.

The third case is the intervener — the Good Samaritan — who pursues the pursuer to stop him from killing the victim. If this intervener breaks vessels in the process of intervention, he is exempt, whether those vessels belong to the pursuer, to the victim, or to a third party. The exemption for the pursuer's property is obvious: the pursuer's property, like the pursuer's life, is forfeit. The exemption for the victim's property is also understandable — we assume the victim would consent to having his property used to save his life. But why should the Good Samaritan be exempt from paying a third party whose property he has damaged?

The Gemara answers candidly: *ve'lo min ha-din* — strictly speaking, as a matter of pure law, he should not be exempt. But *she'im i atah omer ken, nimtza ein adam shematzil et chaveiro miyad ha-rodeph* — if you held interveners liable for incidental damage to third parties, no one would intervene. The policy rationale is decisive: we exempt the Good Samaritan from such payment to encourage rescue. The Gemara notes that this is precisely the logic behind secular "good Samaritan" laws, which do not oblige intervention but do protect those who intervene in good faith from civil liability for inadvertent harm.

---

## Intervention & Aveirot

### Animal Case

A brief but important limiting principle is stated: if someone is "pursuing" an animal — that is, about to commit an act with an animal — one may not use lethal force to intervene. Since there is no human victim whose life or dignity is at stake, the entire logic of the *rodeph* doctrine does not apply.

### Avodah Zarah

The Gemara now cites a *beraita*: Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai teaches that one who is about to commit *avodah zarah* — idol worship — may be stopped with lethal force (*nitan lehatzilo b'nafsho*). The derivation is a *kal vachomer*: if to protect the honor of an ordinary person (*pegam hedyot*) one may use lethal force, then certainly to protect God's honor (*pegam gavoah*), which is desecrated by an act of *avodah zarah*, lethal force is permitted.

This is a striking position, because it moves away from the framework of protecting a human victim and into the framework of preventing a severe sin. One way to understand this is that the victim of *avodah zarah* is God — that an act of idol worship is a violation of God's honor, analogous to the violation of a human victim's honor in a case of rape. Whether this violation is inherent in the act itself, committed even in private, or whether it is the community's tolerance of public *avodah zarah* that creates the *chillul Hashem* — that is itself a question worth pressing. But Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai's position is that the license to use lethal force is not contingent on the victim being human.

The Gemara asks whether one may derive a *halachic* ruling permitting lethal force from a *kal vachomer*. The answer is that Shmuel holds one may (*onshin min ha-din*), and Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai's ruling follows that view.

### Shabbat Violation

Rabbi Elazar berabbi Shimon extends his father's position: one who violates *Shabbat* may also be stopped with lethal force. He holds like his father that *onshin min ha-din*, and he links *Shabbat* to *avodah zarah* through a *gezeirah shavah* — the word *chillul* appears in the verse regarding *Shabbat* and in the verse regarding *avodah zarah* — thereby extending the license for lethal intervention from *avodah zarah* to *Shabbat* desecration. The underlying logic parallels that of *avodah zarah*: a public desecration of *Shabbat* unchallenged by the community becomes a *chillul Hashem*, a violation of God's honor that demands intervention.

This is not the normative ruling. But it illuminates a coherent worldview in which communal tolerance of public sin — particularly sins that symbolize rejection of God's sovereignty — constitutes its own *chillul Hashem*, which in turn activates the logic of the *rodeph* framework.

---

## Martyrdom Principle

### Three Categories

The Gemara now transitions to the foundational discussion of *yehareg ve-al ya'avor* — the principle that one must die rather than transgress. This transition is organic: having discussed when bystanders may or must kill a *rodeph* to prevent murder or sexual violation, and having seen the view that lethal intervention is appropriate even for *avodah zarah*, the Gemara now asks the parallel question from the other direction — when must a person surrender his own life rather than commit a sin?

Rabbi Yochanan transmits in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak that the Sages voted and concluded in the attic of the house of Nitza in Lod: with respect to all other *aveirot* in the Torah, if one is told "transgress or be killed," one should transgress and not be killed. The exceptions are *avodah zarah*, *giluy arayot*, and *shfichut damim* — idol worship, forbidden sexual relations, and murder. For these three, one must die rather than transgress. It is worth noting that these three categories correspond precisely to what the Gemara has been discussing: the cases where one may use lethal force to stop a perpetrator are murder, *giluy arayot*, and — according to some — *avodah zarah*. The parallel is not coincidental. The same offenses that justify killing someone to protect others also obligate a person to sacrifice himself rather than commit them.

### Avodah Zarah Debate

The Gemara immediately raises a challenge. A *beraita* records that Rabbi Yishmael permits transgressing *avodah zarah* under threat of death, deriving this from the verse *vechai bahem* — "and he shall live by them, and not die by them." Rabbi Yishmael treats *avodah zarah* no differently from other *aveirot* in this respect. However, he qualifies this: *yachol afilu befarhesya* — one might think this applies even in public. To this he responds: the verse also says *ve-nikdashti betoch bnei Yisrael* — "I shall be sanctified among the Children of Israel" — implying that when the act occurs publicly, it must be resisted even at the cost of one's life. In public, the symbolic weight of the act is entirely different: publicly submitting to *avodah zarah* communicates that one values one's life above one's faith, and the *kiddush Hashem* achieved by public martyrdom is the counter-message that faith is paramount.

The Gemara explains that the ruling requiring martyrdom for *avodah zarah* even in private follows Rabbi Eliezer.

### Ahavat Hashem

A *beraita* records Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning: the verse *ve-ahavta et Hashem Elokecha bechol levavecha uvechol nafshecha uvechol meodecha* — "you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your possessions." Rabbi Eliezer asks: if the verse already says *bechol nafshecha* — with all your life — why add *bechol meodecha* — with all your possessions? And if it says *bechol meodecha*, why add *bechol nafshecha*? The answer: for a person whose body is more precious to him than his money, the verse says *bechol nafshecha* — you must give up your life. For a person whose money is more precious than his life, the verse says *bechol meodecha* — you must give up your possessions.

The critical point is that this reasoning operates through *ahavat Hashem* — the love of God — not through the public logic of *kiddush Hashem*. An act of *avodah zarah*, even in private, even when forced, is a momentary betrayal of one's fidelity to God. Just as an act of infidelity in a marriage undermines the relationship even if it is forced and even if it is a single act — the commitment of *ve-ahavta* demands an absoluteness of devotion that cannot be compromised even under compulsion. And therefore, even in private, one must give up one's life rather than perform an act of *avodah zarah*.

It is worth observing that the very area most contested in the martyrdom framework — *avodah zarah* — is the same area contested in the *rodeph* framework. By the *rodeph* doctrine, all authorities agree that lethal intervention is required to protect a murder victim or a rape victim, but it is debated whether lethal intervention is permitted to prevent *avodah zarah*. Similarly in the martyrdom framework, all agree that one must die rather than commit murder or *giluy arayot*, but whether one must die rather than commit *avodah zarah* in private is debated. The *psak halacha* is that one must die rather than commit *avodah zarah* even in private, but one may not use lethal force to prevent another person from committing *avodah zarah*. The two principles do not overlap perfectly, but the structural parallel is striking.

### Giluy Arayot

The Gemara derives the requirement to die rather than commit *giluy arayot* from the verse dealing with the rape of the betrothed maiden: *ki ka'asher yakum ish al re'ehu uretzacho nefesh, ken hadavar hazeh* — "as a man rises against his fellow and murders him, so is this matter." The link to murder teaches in both directions. First, just as by the betrothed maiden one uses lethal force to protect her (*ein moshia lah*), so too for murder one may use lethal force to protect the victim. Second — and this is the point relevant here — just as for murder one must die rather than commit the act, so too by *giluy arayot* one must die rather than transgress.

### Murder Case

The Gemara then asks: where do we know that for murder itself one must die rather than commit it? The answer is *sevara* — logical reasoning, without need of a verse. The case is reported directly: someone came before Rabbah and said that the non-Jewish governor of his city had commanded him to kill a particular person, threatening death if he refused. Rabbah replied: *liktlocha ve-lo tiktol* — let him kill you, and do not you commit murder. Why? *Mi yeimar de-dama didach sumak tefei? Dilma dama de-hahu gavra sumak tefei.* — Who says your blood is any redder than his? Perhaps his blood is redder than yours.

The logic is that the license to violate an *aveira* under compulsion derives from the Torah's intent to protect life. But when a life will be taken regardless — either yours or his — what gives you license to commit murder? Your right to self-preservation does not extend to taking another's life, because there is no principled reason why your life is more valuable than his. Rashi frames this somewhat differently: the Torah permits *aveirot* under duress in order to protect life, but where a life will be taken no matter what, the entire rationale for permitting the *aveira* dissolves.

---

## Public & Persecution

### Gezerot Malchut

When Rav Dimi came from Eretz Yisrael, he transmitted in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *lo shanu ela she-lo bishat gzeirat hamalchut* — the permission to transgress under duress rather than surrender one's life applies only when the government is not engaged in a systematic campaign to uproot the faith. But during a *sha'at hashmad* — a time of religious persecution, when the governing power is actively trying to eradicate Jewish practice — even a *mitzvah kala*, the most trivial commandment, one must die rather than transgress. The reasoning is historical and existential: religions survive because people are willing to martyr themselves for them. Once individuals begin calculating that their lives are more valuable than their faith, the cumulative effect is that the faith itself is extinguished. Only the willingness to die for even small things signals to an oppressive regime that it will not succeed.

### Ravin's Position

When Ravin came from Eretz Yisrael, he transmitted a stricter ruling in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *lo amru ela betzina* — the permission to transgress rather than die applies only when the act occurs in private. But *aval befarhesya* — when the act is public — even when there is no *sha'at hashmad*, even a *mitzvah kala* requires martyrdom.

### Parhesya Definition

This raises the question of how much of a public setting is required. The Gemara records that Rav Yaakov stated in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *ein farhesya pachutah mei-asara bnei adam* — *parhesya* requires no fewer than ten people. It is obviously assumed that these must be Jews, as derived from the verse *ve-nikdashti betoch bnei Yisrael* — "I shall be sanctified among the Children of Israel" — which specifies the Jewish community as the relevant audience for *kiddush Hashem*.

The Gemara records a further question from Rav Yirmiya: what if nine of the ten are Jews and one is not a Jew? The answer is drawn from a *gezeirah shavah*: the word *toch* appears both in the *kiddush Hashem* verse and in the verse *hibadlu mitoch ha-eidah hazot* regarding the spies, where there were ten — all of whom were Israelites. Just as there, all ten were Jews, so here all ten must be Jews.

It is worth noting the conceptual distinction between *parhesya* of ten people and the formal *minyan* of ten men required for certain communal prayers. In the context of *parhesya*, there is significant opinion that women count among the ten, since this is not a *minyan* for prayer but a measure of communal impact. The same verse (*betoch bnei Yisrael*) that generates the requirement of ten for *minyan* is here read to generate the requirement of ten for *parhesya*, yet in one context it is read to require men only, and in the other it may be read to include women. The same verse admits of different framings in different contexts.

### Self-Interest Exception

The Gemara introduces a critical qualification to the *parhesya* rule. When a person is coercing a Jew to transgress for the coercer's own benefit — *hana'at atzman* — this does not constitute the kind of public transgression that requires martyrdom, even if it occurs in front of many people. Rava illustrates: if a non-Jew tells a Jew to cut a particular herb on Shabbat and give it to his animal — otherwise he will kill him — the Jew should cut the herb and not be killed. The coercer wants the herb for his animal; this is an act of self-interest, not an attempt to demonstrate that he can make Jews transgress. Everyone present understands this. There is no symbolic undermining of the faith.

But if the same non-Jew says to cut the herb and throw it in the river — that is, without any benefit to himself — then the entire purpose of the coercion is to force a public act of *chillul Shabbat*. In that case, *liktlo ve-lo liktol* — let him kill the Jew, and the Jew should not transgress. Rava states the principle: *la'avorei milta ka ba'ei* — he is trying to cause the transgression itself. And when that is the purpose, it becomes an act requiring martyrdom.

### Esther Exception

The Gemara raises the case of Esther. Her situation was publicly known — she was taken into the king's palace, and everyone was aware. Why did she not give up her life rather than submit?

Abbaye answers: *Esther karka olam hayeta* — Esther was the ground; she was passive. This is a significant halakhic concept. Several *rishonim* understand this to mean that *halacha* categorizes the woman as passive in the act of intercourse — the act is done *to* her, not by her. Since *yehareg ve-al ya'avor* applies to actively committing a transgression, a woman in this position is not subject to the same demand. Tosafot draws a parallel: if someone threatens to kill you unless you allow yourself to be thrown onto an infant and crush the infant's head, you may allow it — you are not doing the act, the other person is.

Rava offers a simpler answer: *hana'at atzman shani* — Achashveirosh acted for his own pleasure and self-interest, not for the purpose of forcing Esther to transgress. This is the *hana'at atzman* exception. Even where the act is public (*befarhesya*), if the coercer is acting for his own benefit, martyrdom is not required. Rava extends this principle to explain another practice: the practice of providing fire-pans to Zoroastrian fire rituals under duress — clearly a public act, but permitted because the Zoroastrians wanted the fire-pans for their own worship, not to cause Jews to transgress.

The deeper question raised by the *karka olam* principle is whether it reflects a general *halachic* characterization of women as passive in all acts of intercourse, or only in the specific context of rape — where, as the Ramban notes, the woman frequently has no choice in the matter even if she wishes to give her life. The Esther case complicates the simpler reading, since Esther was not being raped in the conventional sense. The major *rishonim* debate this at length, including the question of whether *yehareg ve-al ya'avor* in cases of *giluy arayot* applies equally to women. The foundation of that debate is laid here on this *daf*, and it remains one of the most significant unresolved questions of this *sugya*.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 75

## Yeihareg Ve'al Ya'avor

### Three Cardinal Sins

Today's daf is 75. We pick up at the very bottom of 74b, having just concluded the extended discussion of *yeihareg ve'al ya'avor* — when one is obligated to surrender one's life rather than transgress. The basic conclusion is that in private, this obligation applies only to the three cardinal sins: *avodah zarah*, *gilluy arayot*, and *shefichut damim*. In public, however, and for a particular reason — namely, when the transgression is demanded specifically as an act of undermining the faith — or during a general period of *sha'as hashmad*, the act becomes one of *kiddush Hashem*, and even a minor prohibition triggers the obligation to give one's life. There was also a nuanced discussion regarding whether the public context requires that the coercion be specifically *l'ha'avir* — intended to make one transgress — as opposed to *hana'as atzmoh*, where the persecutor acts for personal benefit, not ideological subversion. And we examined at length the question of women, *karka olam*, and whether the formulation is *yeihareg ve'al ya'avor* or *teihareg ve'al ta'avor*.

### Bnei Noach Kiddush Hashem

We now turn to a different angle on this topic. The Gemara records: *bei'u minei mei-Rabbi Ami* — they asked Rabbi Ami: is a *ben Noach* obligated in *kiddush Hashem*, or is he not so obligated? In other words, must a non-Jew give up his life rather than violate one of the *sheva mitzvos bnei Noach*?

### Tosafot's Question

Tosafot raises a preliminary question: why do we begin by assuming that a non-Jew is *not* obligated to die for his commandments, and then seek proof that he is? For Jews, we know from the verse *v'chai bahem* — "and he shall live by them" — that the Torah's commandments are intended to sustain life, not to require one to forfeit it. But non-Jews have no such verse. Might we not assume, even without a verse, that there is no obligation to die for one's commandments? Tosafot concludes that perhaps *v'chai bahem* is not independently necessary to establish this point; perhaps even without any verse we would have assumed that one does not surrender life for *mitzvos*. That seems to be the baseline assumption for *bnei Noach* as well — and the question is whether they are nonetheless obligated in *kiddush Hashem*.

It should be noted that the Gemara does not appear to be asking specifically about the three cardinal sins, even though *bnei Noach* are also prohibited in *avodah zarah*, *gilluy arayot*, and *shefichut damim*. Those three were previously framed not through the language of *kiddush Hashem* but through specific verses — *rotzeach* through the logic of whose blood is redder, *gilluy arayot* derived from that reasoning, and *avodah zarah* grounded in *ahavas Hashem*. The concept of *kiddush Hashem* specifically pertains to contexts of *sha'as hashmad* or being coerced to transgress *b'farhesya* with the intent to make one violate. The present question, then, seems to concern all *sheva mitzvos* — one must imagine a case, for instance, of a pagan government compelling observant non-Jews to violate their seven commandments.

## Seven Mitzvot Abizrayhu

### Abaye's Seven Mitzvot

The Gemara now addresses this question. Abaye says: *tashma* — come and hear a proof — *sheva mitzvos nitztavu bnei Noach*: non-Jews were commanded in seven commandments. If there were also an obligation of *kiddush Hashem*, that would make eight. The very enumeration of seven implies that *kiddush Hashem* is not an independent eighth obligation.

### Rava's Abizrayhu

Rava responds: *inhu v'chol avizrayu* — when the tradition says seven, it means the seven commandments along with all their appurtenances, the things connected to them. The word *avizrayu* — cognate to the modern Hebrew *avizarim*, meaning accessories or peripherals — denotes the ramifications and extensions of each commandment. So if there is a commandment not to steal, the question of whether one must submit to death rather than steal under threat to one's life is a dimension of the scope of that prohibition, not an independent eighth commandment. Similarly, for each of the *sheva mitzvos*, the question of whether *kiddush Hashem* applies is part of that commandment's inner structure. The fact that *kiddush Hashem* is not listed as an eighth obligation is therefore not a counter-proof.

The Gemara then asks: *mai hava alah* — what was the conclusion? Adda bar Ahava said in the name of the school of Rav: it is written, *ladavar hazeh yislach Hashem l'avdecha* — "For this thing may the Lord forgive your servant." This is the statement of Naaman, who had been cured of his leprosy and now addresses Elisha. He says: when my master goes to the house of Rimon to prostrate himself, and he leans upon my arm, and I too bow down — for this act may God forgive me. And the verse continues: *vayomer lo lech l'shalom* — and Elisha said to him, "Go in peace."

## Naaman Case

### Naaman Source

Adda bar Ahava uses this episode as a source bearing on the question of *kiddush Hashem* for non-Jews. Elisha gives Naaman his blessing — apparently endorsing, or at least not prohibiting, Naaman's bowing in the house of idolatry.

### Bowing Analysis

This is striking in its own right. Naaman is not bowing as an act of worship; he does not believe in the idol, and he intends no act of devotion. He is merely physically supporting the king, who is prostrating himself. The Gemara elsewhere discusses a case of someone who bends down to pick up coins in front of an idol — that is not *avodah zarah b'shogeg*, it merely looks like it from the outside. Similarly, Naaman's bowing is not an act of worship at all; it merely has the outward appearance of one.

### Private vs Public

Given that Elisha simply bade him go in peace, the Gemara reasons: if there were a problem of *kiddush Hashem* for non-Jews, Elisha should have said something to him rather than giving his unqualified blessing. The Gemara, however, pushes back: perhaps the distinction is *ha b'tzina ha b'farhesya* — perhaps this took place in private, and therefore *kiddush Hashem* was not at issue; had it been public, the obligation might have applied.

### Rashi's Definition

But in what sense was this "private"? The king publicly goes to the house of idolatry — how could this be private? Rashi explains that the definition of *farhesya*, "public," in the context of *kiddush Hashem*, requires the presence of ten Jews. So if we were to say that *kiddush Hashem* applies to non-Jews, it would mean only that they may not transgress their *sheva mitzvos* in the presence of ten Jews — but transgression in front of an entirely non-Jewish public would not implicate *kiddush Hashem*. This is admittedly quite strange: a non-Jew's *kiddush Hashem* would be defined relative to a Jewish audience.

### Tosafot's Alternative

Tosafot offers a different reading. His *girsa* of the Gemara reads *v'im issa leima lei ha b'tzina ha b'farhesya* — if there were a problem of *kiddush Hashem*, why didn't Elisha say to Naaman: this is acceptable in private, but do not do it in public? The point is that since Elisha gave Naaman a blanket blessing without qualification, it seems he was declaring the matter entirely permissible in all contexts, whether private or public. According to Tosafot's reading, the Gemara's conclusion is that there is no obligation of *kiddush Hashem* for non-Jews at all.

One additional oddity bears noting. Recall that in the previous discussion, *kiddush Hashem* among Jews was defined not merely as a public transgression, but specifically as one in which the coercer acts *l'ha'avir* — to make one transgress — and not *l'hana'as atzmoh*, for personal benefit. The Naaman case is a perfect instance of *hana'as atzmoh*: there is no attempt to undermine anyone's faith; this is simply a political ritual. It is thus somewhat strange that the Gemara treats this as a potential scenario of *kiddush Hashem* at all, unless it presupposes that the question is specifically about *avodah zarah* — which, even in a diluted form, may operate by different rules.

## Lust Story

### Case Setup

The Gemara continues with a different case related to the theme of *yeihareg ve'al ya'avor*. Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: there was once a certain man who set his eyes upon a particular woman. His heart was consumed with lust — an overwhelming, uncontrollable desire. They came and consulted doctors, who concluded: *ein lo takana ad shettibael* — there is no cure for him unless he has intercourse with this woman.

### Sages' Response

The Sages ruled: let him die rather than have intercourse with her. The doctors then suggested a lesser remedy: perhaps if she were merely to stand before him naked, that would satisfy his desire. The Sages again ruled: let him die rather than have her stand before him naked. A third proposal was raised: perhaps she could speak with him from behind a fence — out of sight, but in conversation, perhaps offering him some relief. And again the Sages ruled: let him die rather than have this conversation.

### Woman's Status

Rav Yitzchak bar Idi and Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani debated the identity of this woman. One said she was a married woman, an *eishet ish*; the other said she was an unmarried *pnuyah*. If she was married, the ruling is understandable — but the Gemara then asks: if she was single, why were the Sages so insistent? His life, at least according to the doctors, was genuinely at stake. What justifies such stringency for a *pnuyah*?

### Pgam Mishpacha

Rav Pappa answers: *mishum pgam mishpacha* — out of concern for the disgrace to the family. It is worth noting the contrast with an earlier context where the concept of *pgam* was raised: in the laws of the *rodef*, the one pursuing a woman to violate her, the *pgam* was only invoked in cases of biblically serious forbidden relations — those carrying *kares* or the death penalty. Here there is no such weight, yet we still speak of *pgam*. It is somewhat striking that the concern is framed as a *pgam* to the family, with the woman's own dignity apparently subsumed within it — though the implication may simply be that such a concern extends even to lesser cases.

### Societal Protection

Rava adds *mishum pgam mishpacha* as well, but Rav Acha the son of Rav Ika offers a different rationale: *kedei shelo yiheyu bnot Yisrael prutzos ba'arayos* — so that Jewish women should not become accustomed to licentiousness. Even if in this specific case there is no formal *halachic* prohibition at the level of biblical law, the Sages cannot countenance a social license for this kind of behavior. If it were permitted for a man to claim that his illness requires such conduct, it would open the door to the degradation of women in Jewish society.

One might ask: why not simply have the man marry her? The Gemara answers: *lo miyasva da'ateih* — that would not settle his mind or resolve his pathological state.

### Stolen Pleasures

This is explained in light of a teaching of Rabbi Yitzchak: *miyom shecharav Beit HaMikdash, nital ta'am biyah venitnah le'ovrei aveirah* — from the day the Temple was destroyed, the genuine pleasure of marital intimacy was taken away and given over exclusively to those who transgress sexually. There is a heightened gratification in forbidden acts, as the verse says: *mayim gnuvim yimtaku v'lechem setarim yinam* — "Stolen waters are sweet and bread eaten in secret is pleasant" (Mishlei 9:17). Bread, in many contexts, serves as a metaphor for sexual intimacy.

### Analysis

This *sugya* raises a number of important questions. On one level, the Sages are insisting on the prohibition even at the cost of a man's life — and yet the Gemara makes clear that at least when she is a *pnuyah*, this is not because of the technical laws of *yeihareg ve'al ya'avor*. The second answer — Rav Acha's societal concern — is explicitly framed as a rabbinic and societal protective measure, not a formal *halachic* ruling about *yeihareg ve'al ya'avor*. The first answer, regarding *pgam mishpacha*, occupies an intermediate position.

When the woman is a married *eishet ish*, however, some *rishonim* derive from this case the principle that *yeihareg ve'al ya'avor* for the three cardinal sins extends not only to the act itself but to *avizraihu* — its appurtenances. Even though no actual act of adultery is being discussed — merely standing naked before him or conversing from behind a fence — because these are connected to and arouse the forbidden relationship, they too fall under the obligation of *yeihareg ve'al ya'avor*. This principle may also illuminate the earlier discussion of Naaman: perhaps even *maris ayin* of *avodah zarah*, something that merely resembles idolatrous prostration, also triggers *yeihareg ve'al ya'avor*. By extension, one might ask whether *yichud* — forbidden seclusion — falls under this rubric; *yichud* is not even *maris ayin* but rather something that may *lead to* the forbidden act, and the questions expand considerably: what if the connected prohibition is *de'oraisa* but not the grave sin itself? What if it is merely *derabbanan*? These are precisely the questions that flow from this case, and the matter generates serious *halachic* debate, even in modern contexts — the question of whether mixed swimming falls under *avizraihu* of *gilluy arayot* has been posed in earnest.

There is also an additional dimension to the case: the man's desire originates from within himself. No one is holding a weapon to his head — the illness is self-generated through his own lust. This raises the question of whether the calculus is genuinely the same as a case of external coercion. Furthermore, the Sages' firmness reflects an awareness that tolerating this behavior would encourage others to claim similar exemptions for similar desires, which would undermine the very fabric of social and moral restraint.

## Ben Sorer Conclusion

### Reflection

This *sugya* leads naturally to a reflection on where we are in the chapter. The entire *perek* began with the concept of *ben sorer u'moreh* — the rebellious son — which is itself framed around the principle of *al shem sofo*, punishing based on where a trajectory leads. There is a thematic resonance in ending the chapter with a case about protecting society from licentiousness: in both instances, the Torah and the Sages are not responding solely to the immediate act but to what that act portends for the individual and for the community. Extra precautions are warranted not because this single act is necessarily catastrophic in isolation, but because of what it opens up. Just as *ben sorer u'moreh* is about preemptive societal protection, so too is the ruling here — particularly in Rav Acha's formulation — about maintaining boundaries that prevent society from unraveling.

### Hadran

*Hadran al ben sorer u'moreh.* We conclude the chapter.

## Nisrafin

### Order Review

We now move on to the next chapter. The preceding material dealt with those executed by *sekilah* — stoning — of which *ben sorer u'moreh* was one, and that framework gave rise to the extended discussions of *yeihareg ve'al ya'avor*, *ba bamachteres*, and related cases. From *sekilah* we proceed to *sereifah* — burning — the next category in the order of the four death penalties, an order familiar from the *vidui* of Yom Kippur: *sekilah, sereifah, hereg, chenek*.

### Mishnah List

The Mishnah states: *ve'eilu hanisrafin* — and these are the ones who are executed by burning. The primary case is *haba al isha u'vittah* — one who has intercourse with a woman and her daughter. As we will see in the Gemara, the explicitly stated case in the Torah is a man who has intercourse with his mother-in-law — which is itself an instance of a woman and her daughter (the wife and her mother). The additional case is *bat kohen shezinisah* — a *kohen*'s daughter who commits fornication, and there is a well-known debate about exactly which case of the *bat kohen* is meant.

## Isha U'Bita Categories

### Case List

The Mishnah enumerates the cases included within the category of *isha u'bita*: his own daughter (*bitto*), his daughter's daughter and son's daughter (*vat bitto u'vat bino*) — that is, his granddaughter, even from a relationship that was not with his wife. Also included is his wife's daughter (*vat ishto*), even if she is not his biological daughter — his stepdaughter — and his step-granddaughter. And then: *chamoto* — his mother-in-law, the case explicit in the Torah as carrying *sereifah*, *em chamoto* — his grandmother-in-law on the maternal side, and *em chamiv* — his grandmother-in-law on the paternal side.

### Biblical Sources

We now examine the relevant verses. The first is Vayikra 18:17: *ervat ishah u'vittah lo tegaleh, et bat binah v'et bat bittah lo tikkah l'galot ervatah, she'erah henmah zimah hi* — "You shall not uncover the nakedness of a woman and her daughter; you shall not take her son's daughter or her daughter's daughter to uncover her nakedness, they are her kindred — it is *zimah*." This verse establishes the *issur* — the prohibition — regarding the wife's daughters and granddaughters, and it contains the critical word *zimah*.

The second verse is Vayikra 20:14: *v'ish asher yikkah et ishah v'et immah zimah hi, ba'esh yisrefu oto v'etahen* — "And if a man takes a woman and her mother, it is *zimah*; they shall be burned in fire, both he and they." Here we have both the word *zimah* and the explicit punishment of *sereifah*.

The structure of the *derashah* becomes clear: the prohibition is stated in one verse, the punishment in another, and they must be linked. The verse in chapter 18 gives us the *issur* for the wife's daughter and granddaughter; the verse in chapter 20 gives us the *onesh* — burning — for the case of woman and her mother. We must now determine how to extend *sereifah* to all the cases listed in the Mishnah, and how to ensure that each case has both a stated prohibition and an established punishment.

A third verse, Vayikra 18:10, addresses a man's own granddaughters: *ervat bat binkha o vat bittkha lo tegaleh ervatan ki ervatkha henmah* — "The nakedness of your son's daughter or your daughter's daughter — do not uncover their nakedness, for they are your own nakedness." Notably, this verse mentions granddaughters but skips over the daughter herself; we will later derive the prohibition regarding one's own daughter through a *kal va-homer*. The word *hena* — "they" — in this verse will also prove exegetically significant.

The general task before us: the only case that explicitly receives *sereifah* in the Torah is the mother-in-law. The other forbidden relationships are explicitly stated as prohibitions, but their punishment must be derived. We will need to connect the prohibition of 18:17 with the punishment of 20:14 through the shared word *zimah*, and then extend the *sereifah* upward one additional generation to reach the grandmother-in-law.

## Mishnah Formulation

### Mishnah Question

The Gemara now examines the Mishnah's language. The Mishnah opens with the case of *haba al isha u'vittah* — one who comes upon a woman and her daughter. But the primary case explicit in the Torah is a man who has relations with his mother-in-law — that is, *haba al isha she'nasa bittah*, the woman whose daughter he has married. The Gemara notes that the Mishnah does not say this; it says simply "a woman and her daughter," without specifying that this is his wife's mother. What, then, is the Mishnah's primary case?

### Concrete vs Abstract

One might read "a woman and her daughter" as an abstraction: any woman and her daughter, and then the Mishnah proceeds to list specific instantiations. But the Gemara resists this reading. It insists on reading the Mishnah as beginning with a concrete case found in the Torah. Since the Mishnah describes a woman and her daughter without specifying that one of them is married to the man, the most natural concrete reading that fits the Torah's explicit case of *sereifah* is: the grandmother-in-law (*em chamoto*) is the "woman," and the mother-in-law (*chamoto*) is the "daughter." The man is not married to either of them — he is married to the daughter of the mother-in-law, i.e., his wife — and both the grandmother-in-law and mother-in-law are therefore described abstractly as "a woman and her daughter." The Gemara thus reads the Mishnah's opening not as a broad abstract category but as pointing to two specific women mentioned explicitly in the verses as carrying *sereifah*: *miklal d'trivaihu ksivi b'hedya* — it implies that both are written explicitly in the Torah. Everything else in the Mishnah is derived through *drasha*.

### Abaye Position

This reading follows Abaye, who holds that the Mishnah's primary case is grandmother-in-law — *masnisin mane Rabbi Akiva* — and according to Abaye's reading of that debate, Rabbi Akiva maintains that the grandmother-in-law is implicit in the *psukim* as well. The end of the Mishnah, which lists grandmother-in-law, would then according to Abaye be adding only *em chamiv* — the grandmother-in-law on the father's side — since the grandmother-in-law on the mother's side is, in his view, already explicit.

### Rava Reading

Rava, however, offers a simpler reading: *tanya haba al isha she'nasa bittah* — simply read the Mishnah as saying "one who comes upon a woman whose daughter he has married." The opening of the Mishnah refers directly to the concrete biblical case of the mother-in-law. There is no need to interpret it as grandmother-in-law and mother-in-law simultaneously. According to Rava, the debate he identifies elsewhere concerns a different question — whether the mother-in-law remains forbidden after the wife dies — and no one maintains that grandmother-in-law appears explicitly in the *psukim*. The end of the Mishnah is therefore doing the full work of extending the category to include grandmother-in-law on both sides, and when it also mentions mother-in-law again, this is because it is enumerating all the derived cases comprehensively.

## Zimah Gezeirah Shava

### Baraita Question

The Gemara now turns to the derivation of *sereifah* for the other cases. A *baraita* is cited: *v'ish asher yikkah et ishah v'et immah* — a man who takes a woman and her mother. The *baraita* asks: I know only that this specific case — the mother-in-law, the woman and her mother — carries *sereifah*. How do I know that the wife's daughter, her daughter's daughter, and her son's daughter also receive *sereifah*?

### Zimah Connection

The *baraita* answers: *ne'emar kan zimah v'ne'emar le-halan zimah* — the word *zimah* is said here (in 20:14, the verse establishing *sereifah*) and the word *zimah* is said there (in 18:17, the verse prohibiting the wife's daughters and granddaughters). The *gezeirah shava* links the two: just as "there" — in 18:17 — the prohibition extends to the daughter and granddaughter, so too "here" — in 20:14 — the punishment of *sereifah* extends to the daughter and granddaughter. Thus the *zimah*-*zimah* link allows us to carry the punishment of burning from the mother-in-law case to all the cases governed by 18:17.

The *baraita* continues: *minayin la'asot zecharim ki-nekevot* — how do we know to make males like females? And: *minayin la'asot lemata ke'lema'ala* — how do we know to make below like above? These formulations are, for now, cryptic. The rest of the *amud* is devoted to unpacking them.

### Application Problem

But first, a difficulty. The *baraita* says the *zimah*-*zimah* connection extends *sereifah* to the daughters and granddaughters. The Gemara asks: the cases of a man's own daughters and granddaughters — which are listed in the Mishnah — do not contain the word *zimah* in their verse (18:10). So how can we apply the *gezeirah shava* of *zimah*-*zimah* to extend *sereifah* to them?

## Hena Hena Solution

### Three Generations

Abaye offers his interpretation of the *baraita*. First he addresses *zecharim ki-nekevot* — "males like females." This does not mean granddaughter through a son versus granddaughter through a daughter (which are both explicit in the same verse). Rather, it means: descendants of the wife (*she'er haba mimena*) — her daughters and granddaughters — are already covered by the *zimah* verses. How do we know that descendants of the husband (*she'er haba mimenu*) — his own daughters and granddaughters from other relationships — also receive *sereifah*? That is the question of *zecharim ki-nekevot*: making the male line like the female line.

### Hena Link

The *baraita* answers that this too is derived from *zimah*-*zimah*. But the Gemara objects: *uv'hai she'er didei lo ktiv bei zimah* — the verse governing a man's own daughters and granddaughters (18:10) does not contain the word *zimah*. So the *zimah*-*zimah* connection cannot directly apply. Rava then says in the name of Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi: *atya hena hena, atya zimah zimah* — there is a dual link. The verse 18:17 contains both *she'erah hena* — "they are her kindred" — and *zimah hi*. And the verse 18:10, governing a man's own descendants, contains *ki ervatkha hena* — "for they are your own nakedness." The shared keyword *hena* links 18:10 to 18:17, and the *zimah* in 18:17 then links to the *zimah* of 20:14 which carries *sereifah*. So the *hena*-*hena* connection bridges the prohibition of 18:10 into the *zimah* network, and from there *sereifah* applies.

### Zimah Teaches Both

The *baraita*'s second cryptic phrase is *minayin la'asot lemata ke'lema'ala* — how do we know to make below like above, or above like below? Abaye now explains this as follows: *minayin la'asot shalosh dorot lema'ala kishlosh dorot lemata* — how do we know to go three generations upward as we go three generations downward? (The count includes the wife as the first generation.) The verse governing the wife's daughters and granddaughters (18:17) goes two generations down from the wife. By parallel, the law of the mother-in-law, which is one generation up from the wife, should extend two generations upward — reaching the grandmother-in-law. The *zimah*-*zimah* link enables this: the same connection that carries *sereifah* downward to two generations of descendants carries the principle upward to two generations of forebears. And when it says *ne'emar lemata zimah v'ne'emar lema'ala zimah, mah lemata shalosh dorot af lema'ala shalosh dorot* — the *zimah* below (the descendants) goes three generations, so too the *zimah* above (the forebears) goes three generations.
