---

# Sanhedrin 80

## Murderer Mixed Up

### Nine Convicted + One

The daf opens at the bottom of 79b. The *mishna* establishes that if a murderer becomes mixed up with others, all go free — and *Rabbi Yehuda* says they are all placed in *kippa* (a form of confinement). The immediate question is what kind of "others" the murderer was mixed up with, and what exactly makes everyone's status uncertain.

The first explanation, attributed to Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel, holds that the "others" were themselves convicted murderers — people who had received a *gmar din*. The one individual who had been mixed in was someone whom the court knew to be a murderer, and the court had deliberated his case, but had not formally concluded judgment. The principle *ein gomerim dino ela bifnei ba'al din* — that a verdict cannot be finalized except in the defendant's presence and with direct identification — meant that even bringing all ten before the court could not yield a valid *gmar din* on the unconvicted man, since the court could not point to him specifically and declare "*ploni chayav*." In this reading, the *chachamim*'s position that all go free is puzzling — you have nine convicted murderers and one who is unambiguously known to be a murderer, yet everyone is released? *Rabbi Yehuda*'s position makes considerably more sense: we cannot set nine convicted murderers free simply because of this procedural impasse, so we confine them all in *kippa*.

### Reish Lakish Position

*Reish Lakish* offers a different reading of the *mishna*, holding that the case involves people — not animals — and that all parties would go free by universal agreement. His reasoning is not made entirely transparent, but his point of departure is a parallel case involving oxen. According to *Reish Lakish*, the *mishna*'s reference to a *rotzeach* mixed with others is actually about a *shor haniskal* — a condemned ox — mixed with nine other oxen that are also *shorei niskelin*. That is a difficult reading of the term *rotzeach*, as the word is never ordinarily applied to an ox, and the *mishna*'s language is strained by this interpretation. Nevertheless, *Reish Lakish* uses it to construct the parallel: just as one cannot complete a *gmar din* on a person without being able to identify him directly, the principle *kemisas haba'alim kach misas hashor* — the ox's death penalty follows the same procedural rules as a human's — means one cannot complete a *gmar din* on an ox under these conditions either.

The consequence in *Reish Lakish*'s reading is bizarre: you would let all the oxen go free — even the nine who already have a *gmar din* against them. These animals are already *assur b'hana'ah*, so they cannot be eaten, and yet you release them to pasture for the remainder of their lives. *Rabbi Yehuda*'s position — that you place them all in *kippa* and confine them until they die — avoids the grotesque outcome of releasing already-condemned animals, but raises its own concerns about *tza'ar ba'alei chayim*.

### Abba Chalafta Problem

Both *Rav Yehuda* in the name of *Shmuel* and *Reish Lakish*'s explanations, however, collapse when the *gemara* examines a *braisa* that explains the *mishna*. The *braisa* quotes *Rabbi Yosei* as saying: this principle applies "*afilu Abba Chalafta beineihem*" — even if Abba Chalafta himself was among those mixed up with the murderer. The figure of Abba Chalafta is not incidental: he was *Rabbi Yosei*'s own father, a man of towering righteousness — which is precisely why the *braisa* names him.

This *braisa* dismantles both prior readings. It obviously rules out *Reish Lakish*'s ox-based reading, since no ox is ever confused with Abba Chalafta. But it also challenges *Rav Yehuda*'s reading. If we are dealing with nine convicted murderers and one unfinished case, what is the point of invoking Abba Chalafta? Obviously, if Abba Chalafta is present, everyone goes free — that is not a novel point. And for *Rabbi Yehuda*, who says to confine them all: how could you put Abba Chalafta in *kippa*? The *braisa* makes no sense under either reading.

### Rava's Two Shooters

*Rava* therefore proposes a radical reinterpretation of the *mishna*'s opening. The *mishna*, he says, must be read as follows: *shnayim she-hayu omdim v'yatza chetz mibeineihem* — two people were standing, an arrow was shot from between them, and someone was killed. We do not know which of the two fired the arrow. Both are exempt because neither can be positively identified as the killer. This is the *mishna*'s core case — and *Rabbi Yosei* says: even if one of the two was Abba Chalafta, even if one is the world's most righteous individual and the other is a known low-life, as long as no witness saw who fired, both go free. You cannot infer guilt from character. This reading is, as *Rava* acknowledges, something close to an addition to the *mishna*'s text, but it alone renders the *braisa* coherent.

The word *rotzeach shenisarev b'acherim* in this reading no longer means a known murderer who became physically mixed into a group, but rather a situation in which the identity of the murderer is unknown from the outset because the two individuals were already intermingled. The term *rotzeach* refers to a human being, not an ox, which also resolves the linguistic strangeness of *Reish Lakish*'s position.

*Rava* then inserts an entirely new case — not found explicitly in the *mishna*'s text — about a *shor* that received a *gmar din* and became mixed up with nine innocent oxen. This is the case that generates the debate between *chachamim* and *Rabbi Yehuda* at the end of the *mishna*.

---

## Shor Haniskal Case

### Revised Ox Case

Under *Rava*'s reinterpretation, the ox-case at the end of the *mishna* involves one *shor haniskal* — an ox with a completed *gmar din* — that became mixed with nine innocent oxen. *Tosafot* notes this as a preferable reading, and it is easy to see why: now the scenario actually makes sense. One condemned ox cannot be identified among nine permissible ones. What should be done?

The initial instinct might be to say that we simply cannot act — since we cannot identify which ox is the *shor haniskal*, perhaps all go free. But the subsequent analysis overturns this.

### Bittul Animals

The pivotal question is whether the *shor haniskal* is *batel* — nullified — within the majority of innocent oxen. If it were *batel berov*, the mixture would be treated as permissible and the owners could benefit from all the animals.

The answer is that *ba'alei chayim* — living creatures — are *chashiv*, independently significant, and therefore cannot be nullified in a mixture. This principle is developed at length in *Zevachim* and constitutes one of the extended *Tosafot* passages on this daf. The logic of *bittul* is that a thing loses its distinct identity when subsumed into a larger quantity. This works most naturally with liquids (*lach belach*), where a trace amount genuinely ceases to be perceptible as a separate entity. With solid objects (*yavesh beyavesh*), the analysis is more complex, since each unit remains physically distinct. A dominant approach treats solid mixtures analogously to liquids when the individual units lack independent significance — sixty potatoes are viewed as a mass, and one problematic potato loses its identity within them.

The critical exception is when individual units are *davar shebimniyan* — things sold or counted by number — or when they are independently significant in some other way. Live animals fall squarely into this category: each animal is its own distinct entity, not merely one item in an undifferentiated herd. Because each is significant, *bittul* does not apply.

### All Assur Consequences

The practical consequence is stark. Since the *shor haniskal* is not *batel*, its prohibition does not dissolve into the majority. The owners cannot use any of the ten oxen — they cannot identify which one is the *shor haniskal*, and the prohibition of *hana'ah* from a *shor haniskal* now attaches to all of them because none can be certified as permissible. All ten become *assur b'hana'ah*.

### Stoning vs Locking Up

Once all ten are *assur b'hana'ah*, the *chachamim* say: stone them all. This is their ruling — and note how different it is from the earlier, incorrect reading of the *mishna* that had the *chachamim* releasing all the oxen. Under *Rava*'s corrected reading, it is precisely the *chachamim* who say to kill all ten. Their reasoning is direct: since all are already forbidden, we might as well stone them and ensure that at least the right one is executed. There is no injustice to the innocent nine, since their owners cannot benefit from them regardless.

*Rabbi Yehuda* disagrees. Stoning is a formal judicial procedure — we learned its elaborate procedure earlier in the tractate. To demand that *beit din* carry out a full stoning procedure on ten oxen because one of them happens to be a *shor haniskal* is excessive. *Rabbi Yehuda*'s position is *konesan l'kippa* — confine them all, let them die in confinement, and thereby ensure no one benefits from the condemned animal. Whether this fully discharges the *chiyuv* of *sekilah* on the *shor haniskal* is left open, but *Rabbi Yehuda* holds it is preferable to performing a formal *sekilah* procedure on ten animals.

### Cow Birth Braisa

A *braisa* is then cited as support for this framework. The *braisa* discusses a female cow (*parah*) that killed a person and was therefore subject to *sekilah* as a *parah haniskeles*. The *braisa* then considers the status of a calf she may have been carrying.

The rule the *braisa* establishes is: if the cow gave birth before *gmar din*, the calf is *mutar* — it was not part of the animal when judgment was finalized, so the *gmar din* did not encompass it. If, however, the cow was pregnant at the time of *gmar din* and gave birth afterward, the calf is *assur* — the *gmar din* was passed on the mother together with the fetus, which is viewed as part of her body under the principle of *ubar yerech imo*. Just as additional weight gained after goring would be included in the animal's condemnation at *gmar din*, the fetus present at *gmar din* is considered part of the mother's body at that moment and becomes forbidden along with her.

The initial purpose in citing this *braisa* is not primarily about the fetus — that analysis comes momentarily — but for the subsequent line, which addresses the *shor haniskal* that became mixed through multiple herds.

### Herds Mixed Extension

The *braisa* continues: *nit'arev b'acherim v'acherim b'acherim* — the *shor haniskal* (or the *parah haniskeles*) became mixed with a second herd, and then one animal from that second herd became mixed with a third herd. This seems extreme, but the *braisa* rules that the contamination carries through: even the third herd becomes forbidden. One might have argued that the probability of the *shor haniskal* being the specific animal that migrated into the second or third herd is low — most likely it was one of the innocent animals that moved. Yet the *halacha* does not permit that reasoning, and every herd into which any animal from the prior forbidden group migrated becomes *assur b'hana'ah*.

This raises a pointed practical question: if your animal wandered into someone else's herd inadvertently, have you ruined that entire herd? And can the injured party collect compensation? The case touches on the principle of *hezek she-eino nikar* — damage that is not physically visible — and since the mixing occurred without intent (*be-shogeg*), there is generally no liability for such damage. The owner of the innocent herd may have suffered enormous loss with no remedy.

As for the practical ruling: what is done to all these animals? The first opinion in the *braisa* is *konesan l'kippa* — they are confined, paralleling *Rabbi Yehuda*'s position in the *mishna*. *Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Shimon* says *meviyan l'veit din v'sokelan* — bring them all to court and stone them, which parallels the *chachamim*'s position. This confirms the framework that *Rava*'s reading of the *mishna* has established: it is the ox-case, and the debate is between confinement and stoning.

---

## Fetus Goring Cases

### Four Scenarios

Having introduced the *braisa*'s ruling about the fetus of a *parah haniskeles*, the *gemara* now turns to explore it in depth. The relevant variables are three distinct events: the act of goring, the pregnancy, and the *gmar din*. Depending on the order in which pregnancy and birth occur relative to goring and *gmar din*, the status of the calf varies entirely. It is helpful to organize the cases systematically.

### Case 1: Assur

The first case is where the cow was pregnant when it gored, remained pregnant through the *gmar din*, and gave birth afterward. In this scenario, the fetus was present at both the act of goring and the *gmar din*. Its status is clearly *assur*: when the court finalized judgment against the mother, the fetus was part of her body — *ubar yerech imo* — and the *gmar din* encompassed it. That it was subsequently born does not change its status. This case is relatively straightforward.

### Rava's Chidush

Now consider a different scenario: the cow was pregnant when it gored, but gave birth before *gmar din*. At the moment judgment was finalized, the calf was no longer part of the mother's body. The surface reading of the *braisa* — which declares the calf *mutar* whenever birth preceded *gmar din* — would seem to render this calf permissible.

*Rava*, however, states explicitly: *vlado nogahat assur* — if a fetus was in the mother when she gored, it is forbidden. *Rava* adds the parallel case: *vlado nirva'at assur* — if a man performed an act of bestiality on the animal while she was pregnant, the fetus is also forbidden. This is conceptually striking in the second case, since the act was done *to* the fetus rather than *by* it, and the fetus plainly contributed nothing to the act. Yet *Rava* treats presence during the act as sufficient to implicate the fetus independently. The upshot is that even if the fetus was not present at the *gmar din*, having been present during the goring requires a separate *gmar din* to be conducted on the calf itself.

The *gemara* notes that *Rava*'s statement uses the language of *assur* and *mutar* rather than *soklin oso* — this is because *Rava*'s original context was a case with fewer than two witnesses, where stoning is not possible, but where the fetus would be disqualified from use as a sacrifice. The implication, however, is that with two witnesses, stoning would similarly apply.

The *braisa*, then, appears to contradict *Rava*: it says that birth before *gmar din* renders the calf *mutar*, which would cover this very scenario. The resolution — offered by Ravina — requires rereading the *braisa* carefully.

### Case 2: Mutar

The second scenario is where the cow was not pregnant at the time of goring, became pregnant afterward, and gave birth before *gmar din*. Here the fetus was present at neither the act nor the *gmar din*. Its status is *mutar* — the judgment touched neither it nor its participation in any relevant act.

This is the case the *braisa* is actually addressing when it says *mutar*. The *braisa*'s contrast, properly read, is between a fetus that was part of neither endpoint (permitted) and one that was part of the *gmar din* (forbidden). *Rava*'s case — the fetus present at goring but not *gmar din* — is simply not addressed by the *braisa* at all. *Rava*'s ruling stands as an independent principle, and there is no contradiction.

### Zeh V'Zeh Gorem

Before Ravina's resolution is reached, the *gemara* raises a significant conceptual problem regarding case 2 — specifically the sub-scenario where the cow became pregnant after the *gmar din* and then gave birth. In this scenario, the cow is already a *shor haniskal* at the time she conceives. The calf is a product of a forbidden animal. Should it not be forbidden as a product of something that is *assur b'hana'ah*, just as the cow's milk produced after *gmar din* would be forbidden?

The counter-consideration is *zeh v'zeh gorem*: the calf was not produced by the mother alone. The father — a permissible animal — also contributed to the calf's existence. If two causes jointly produce an outcome, and one cause is forbidden while the other is permissible, is the outcome forbidden or not? This is the principle of *zeh v'zeh gorem*. If one holds that *zeh v'zeh gorem* renders the outcome forbidden, then the calf born after *gmar din* is *assur*. If one holds that *zeh v'zeh gorem* is *mutar*, then the father's permissible contribution breaks the chain of prohibition and the calf is permitted.

The *gemara* presses: if *zeh v'zeh gorem* is *mutar*, then what exactly is the *braisa* declaring *assur* in its second case, and what is it declaring *mutar* in its first? The cases need to be reidentified in a way that does not depend on this disputed principle.

### Ravina Resolution

Ravina resolves the difficulty by offering a precise reading of the *braisa*'s two cases. The *mutar* case is: the cow was not pregnant at the time of goring, became pregnant after the goring, and gave birth before *gmar din*. In this scenario, the fetus was part of neither the goring nor the *gmar din*, and no question of *zeh v'zeh gorem* need arise at all — the mother was not yet a *shor haniskal* when the fetus was conceived, so the fetus is simply the offspring of a permissible animal. It is unambiguously *mutar*.

The *assur* case is: the cow was not pregnant at the time of goring, became pregnant after goring, was pregnant at *gmar din*, and gave birth after *gmar din*. At the moment of *gmar din*, the fetus was part of the mother's body — *ubar yerech imo* — and the judgment encompassed it. After it was born, it remains forbidden.

*Rava*'s case — present at goring, absent at *gmar din* — is not addressed by the *braisa*, and stands as *Rava*'s own *chidush*: such a fetus requires its own *gmar din*. The case of a fetus conceived after *gmar din* — the *zeh v'zeh gorem* case — is similarly left aside by the *braisa*, which deals only with the two clean cases. With Ravina's reading, all apparent contradictions dissolve.

---

## Mixed Death Penalties

### Lighter Penalty

The *gemara* proceeds to the next section of the *mishna*: *kol chayvei misas* — all those liable to death penalties. When people convicted of different categories of capital punishment become mixed together, the *mishna* rules that the lighter death penalty is applied to all. This ruling presupposes the extended debates about which death penalty is heavier or lighter that appeared earlier in the tractate, and which led to the well-known disagreement between *Rabbi Shimon* and the *chachamim* on the relative severity of *sekilah* and *sereifa*.

### Hatra'ah Specificity

But the *gemara* seizes on a different problem entirely. The *mishna*'s ruling assumes that we may give everyone in the mixed group the lighter death penalty — even those who were originally warned about and convicted for a heavier one. This is a significant assumption about the nature of *hatra'ah*.

*Hatra'ah* is not simply a formal warning that a forbidden act is being committed. Part of its function is that the defendant explicitly accepts upon himself the consequences — including the specific death penalty. *Beit din*'s license to execute derives partly from this acceptance. If a person was warned that a particular transgression carries, say, *sayif* (decapitation), and he accepted that warning, can the court now impose *chenek* (strangulation) instead — even if *chenek* is lighter? The argument that it is lighter would seem to be a benefit to the defendant, so perhaps it is permissible. But this requires reasoning that a warning specifying one death penalty implicitly constitutes a warning for all lighter penalties as well.

The *gemara* asks: *shema mina* — may we infer from this *mishna* that *musra l'davar chamur havei musra l'davar kal*? That a person warned about a more severe punishment is considered warned about a lighter one as well?

### Generic Hatra'ah

*Rabbi Yirmiah* answers that the *mishna* need not be read as affirming that inference at all. The *mishna* may be dealing with a case where the *hatra'ah* was *stam* — generic. The witnesses warned him that he would be *chayav misa* without specifying which death penalty. In that case, he accepted upon himself death generically, and the court retains flexibility to impose whichever form of execution is appropriate — including the lighter one when the convicted population is mixed. The question of whether a specific *hatra'ah* for a heavy penalty covers a lighter one remains open.

### Tanna Kamma Debate

The *gemara* then brings a *braisa* that bears directly on the question of *hatra'ah* specificity. The *braisa*'s context is the special case of a *meisis* — someone who seduces others to commit *avodah zarah* — for whom the normal warning requirement is waived. For all other *chayvei misas*, the *braisa* states, one must warn the defendant. What does that warning consist of? *Ad she-yodi'u she-hu chayav misas beis din* — one must inform him that he is liable to the death penalty of *beit din*.

*Rabbi Yehuda* disagrees: *ad she-yodi'u b'eizo misa hu neherag* — one must specify which death penalty he will receive. This is the *braisa*'s central debate.

The *tanna kamma* derives his position from the *mekoshesh* — the wood-gatherer who violated *Shabbos* in the wilderness. That individual was clearly warned, yet the Almighty had to instruct Moshe which death penalty to apply, because no one had yet specified it. This demonstrates, says the *tanna kamma*, that a generic warning suffices — no specification of the execution method is required. *Rabbi Yehuda* counters that the *mekoshesh* case was a *hora'as sha'ah*, a one-time exceptional ruling arising from the unique circumstance that no death penalty had yet been explicitly delineated for that transgression. Once the system of capital punishment was fully established, specification became required.

### Lighter Penalty Tension

Within *Rabbi Yehuda*'s position, an interesting tension now emerges. If the *hatra'ah* must specify a particular death penalty, and the defendant accepted that specific penalty, then the court's license is circumscribed by that acceptance. Giving a lighter penalty — one the defendant was never warned about — may exceed the court's authority, even if it benefits the defendant. The *mishna*'s ruling that all receive the lighter penalty in a mixed case may therefore not apply when the *hatra'ah* was specific.

The *gemara* elsewhere discussed the principle *mos yumas harotzeach* — that if a convicted murderer cannot be executed by the officially prescribed method, he may be killed in whatever way is available, as in the case of a murderer who flees and can only be stopped by other means. How does this square with the notion that *beit din* may not deviate from the specific method to which the defendant consented? The two principles pull in opposite directions, and the *gemara* leaves the tension unresolved.

### Tosafot Resolution

*Tosafot* addresses this tension directly, noting that even if a specific *hatra'ah* forecloses the lighter death penalty under normal circumstances, the license of *mos yumas harotzeach* may be limited to particular cases — specifically, a murderer who is fleeing and cannot be apprehended for formal execution. When there is no such urgency and no such impossibility, and when other alternatives exist (such as confinement), there may be no license to impose an unwarned-for death penalty, even a lighter one. The general permission to execute in an alternative manner applies only under the specific conditions of impossibility, not as a blanket override of the *hatra'ah* requirement. *Tosafot* acknowledges this reading in their commentary elsewhere and points the reader there.

---

## Niskalin Nisrafin

### Hizkiya's Teaching

The *gemara* now turns to the final clause of the *mishna*: *haniskalin b'nisrafin* — those condemned to *sekilah* get mixed with those condemned to *sereifa*. *Rabbi Shimon* holds that *sereifa* is the more severe penalty, and therefore rules that all receive *sekilah*, the lighter of the two.

*Rabbi Hizkiya* taught this *mishna* to his son *Rami* in the version: *hanisrafin baniskalin* — a person condemned to *sereifa* got mixed into a group condemned to *sekilah*. In this formulation, the *nisraf* (the minority) has mixed into the *niskalin* (the majority), and *Rabbi Shimon* rules they all receive *sekilah*. *Rabbi Shimon*'s reasoning is that *sereifa* is more severe, so *sekilah* is lighter.

### Rav Yehuda Challenge

*Rav Yehuda* — who was also *Rabbi Hizkiya*'s son, and thus *Rami*'s brother — challenged his father's formulation. He said: Father, you should not teach it this way. The problem is that the version *hanisrafin baniskalin* — one *nisraf* mixed into a majority of *niskalin* — could yield the ruling that all receive *sekilah* for a completely different reason: simply because the majority of the group is already condemned to *sekilah*, and we apply majority rule. In that reading, *Rabbi Shimon*'s novel claim that *sereifa* is more severe would be entirely redundant — the outcome follows from majority rule alone, not from the severity hierarchy. The teaching therefore fails to demonstrate *Rabbi Shimon*'s *chidush*.

### Hizkiya Response

*Rabbi Hizkiya* accepted the critique and replied: how then do you think I should teach it? *Rav Yehuda* proposes the reverse: *haniskalin banisrafin* — those condemned to *sekilah* get mixed into a group condemned to *sereifa*. Now only one person deserves *sekilah*, while the majority deserves *sereifa*. Yet *Rabbi Shimon* rules that all receive *sekilah*. This is a genuine *chidush*: even though the majority receives *sereifa*, and even though by majority rule one might impose *sereifa* on everyone, *Rabbi Shimon* insists on *sekilah* for all because it is the lighter penalty.

But the *gemara* immediately identifies a new problem: in this version, when the *chachamim* respond — saying that all should receive *sereifa* because *sekilah* is the more severe penalty — their position can equally be explained by majority rule. The majority of the group gets *sereifa*, so perhaps the *chachamim* are simply following the majority, not expressing a view about severity at all.

### Gemara Resolution

The *gemara* resolves this by noting that it is *Rabbi Shimon* who lays down the case first and formulates the ruling. The *chachamim* respond only within the scenario *Rabbi Shimon* has established. The goal is for *Rabbi Shimon*'s position to constitute the *chidush* — and in the version *haniskalin banisrafin*, *Rabbi Shimon* does indeed make a striking claim: even though only one person was condemned to *sekilah* and the overwhelming majority faces *sereifa*, he rules that all receive *sekilah* because it is lighter. That is a genuine *chidush*, stated boldly as the base position.

The *chachamim* then respond within that same scenario: we disagree; *sekilah* is actually the more severe penalty, so all should receive *sereifa*. The *chachamim*'s ruling in this scenario happens to align with majority rule — but that is incidental. They are principally expressing disagreement with *Rabbi Shimon*'s severity hierarchy. The *gemara*'s conclusion is that one should teach the *mishna* in the version that places *Rabbi Shimon*'s *chidush* in its strongest, most striking form.

---

## Parental Respect

### Shmuel's Rebuke

The *gemara* closes with a brief but pointed discussion about *kavod av va'em* — the honor owed to one's father — prompted by the very exchange just described. When *Rav Yehuda* said to his father *Rabbi Hizkiya*, "*Abba*, do not teach it this way," *Shmuel* — *Rav Yehuda*'s great teacher, who often addressed him affectionately as *shinena* (sharp one) — heard of this exchange and rebuked him: one does not speak to one's father in that manner.

### Braisa Correction

A *braisa* is cited in support of this principle. The *braisa* states: even if a father was transgressing Torah and you were obligated to prevent him, you may not say to him, "*Abba*, you have transgressed Torah." To say "you have done something wrong" to one's father, even when he clearly has, is not a permissible mode of correction.

### Indirect Method

Rather, says the *braisa*, one should say: "*Abba kach kasuv ba-Torah*" — Father, here is what is written in the Torah. *Rashi* explains this as offering the relevant verse in a way that implies the point without directly accusing the father of wrongdoing. Even that, however, could be construed as criticism if delivered with an accusatory tone. The *gemara* therefore clarifies that one should say it in a rhetorically indirect manner — raising the *pasuk* as if noting something of interest, not as a rebuke: "You know, there is a *pasuk* here, *lo sevaru esh b'chol moshvoseichem*…" The point is conveyed, but the delivery is not confrontational.

Applying this to the case of *Rav Yehuda* and his father: instead of saying "Father, do not teach it that way," he should have said something like, "Would it not be a greater *chidush* to teach it this way?" — framing the correction as a question or an observation, not as a direct criticism of his father's teaching.

The *gemara* leaves open whether the rule is more lenient when intervention is needed to prevent an ongoing transgression, as opposed to commenting on what has already been done. But the principle is clear: one must find a way to communicate the correction that does not constitute a direct accusation or expression of disrespect toward a parent.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 81

## Two Sins, Stringent Puni…

### Intro: Two Violations

The *mishna* opens with a case of *mi shenischayev shtei misos beis din* — a person who has incurred two separate death penalties from among the four modes of execution discussed throughout this tractate. The rule is *nidonin b'chamura*: he is executed by the more stringent of the two methods. The underlying logic is straightforward — the fact that he is also liable for a lighter execution should not, counterintuitively, reduce his punishment.

### Single Act, Two Violatio…

A second case in the *mishna* appears at first glance to be identical, but involves a single *aveira* carrying two separate capital liabilities simultaneously. The *gemara* will elaborate on the classic example: a man who has relations with his mother who is also a married woman — generating both a prohibition of *isha uvita* and a prohibition of *eshet ish*. The *tanna kamma* rules the same as in the first case: *nidon b'chamura*, he receives the more stringent execution. Rabbi Yosi, however, disagrees. He holds *nidon b'zika rishona sheba lo* — the punishment is determined by the first *zika*, the first legal status this woman held in relation to him. The *gemara* will work out the precise implications of this position.

### Sequential Sins Obvious

The *gemara* opens with an objection: *pshita* — is this not obvious? Of course the weightier punishment applies; should a person be rewarded for having committed two *aveiros* by receiving only the lighter execution?

### Rava's Case: Judgment Pa…

Rava clarifies that the *mishna* is addressing a less obvious case. The scenario is one of sequence: a person sinned and received a judgment — *nigmar dino* — for a lighter offense, such as *chenek* (strangulation). Then, after that judgment had already been rendered, he went ahead and committed an additional, graver sin, one deserving of a weightier execution such as *sreifa* (burning) or *sayif* (the sword). The *havah amina* — the initial assumption one might have entertained — is that since his judgment has already been passed, *hai gavra ktila hu*, he is already considered as a man condemned to die. One might therefore think that the subsequent, graver transgression carries no legal consequence beyond the existing judgment. The *mishna* teaches otherwise.

### New Judgment Passed

The *gemara* therefore establishes that a new court proceeding is conducted and a new judgment is passed to execute him by the graver method. The *mishna* thus comes to exclude the mistaken assumption that the prior judgment renders the condemned man legally inert with respect to any further capital liability.

## Ezekiel Evidence

### Ezekiel 18 Citation

The *gemara* then raises a question: where is the scriptural basis for the rule that one liable for two death penalties is judged by the more stringent? The text cites Ezekiel 18, which describes a wayward son who commits multiple offenses: he sheds blood (*shofech dam*), eats upon the mountains (*el he-harim achal*), defiles his fellow's wife (*es eshes re'eihu tima*), oppresses the poor (*ani v'evyon honah*), steals and does not restore (*gezeilos gazal chavol lo yashiv*), and lifts his eyes to the idols (*el hagilulim nasa einav to'evah asah*). At the conclusion of this catalogue, the verse declares *mot yumat damav bo* — he shall surely die, his blood is upon him. The phrase *damav bo* is a recognized marker for execution by *skilah* (stoning).

The *gemara* analyzes the offenses listed. Bloodshed (*shofech dam*) deserves *sayif*. Defiling his fellow's wife — adultery, *eshet ish* — carries *chenek*. Looking toward the abominations (*avodah zarah*) carries *skilah*. Yet the verse concludes that he receives *skilah*, the most severe. This demonstrates that even when a person has already incurred a lighter capital liability, he is nonetheless judged by the graver punishment that any subsequent transgression merits.

### Rav Pappa's Challenge

Rav Pappa bar Yitzchak challenges this reading entirely. He argues that all the offenses enumerated in the passage can be read as deserving *skilah*, making the verse prove nothing about the principle of applying the more stringent penalty across different categories of execution. His reinterpretation: *shofech dam* refers to *ben sorer u-moreh*, the wayward and rebellious son, who is judged *al shem sofo* — on account of what he will eventually become — and whose execution is indeed by *skilah*. The defilement of *eshet re'eihu* refers specifically to *na'arah ha-me'orasah*, the betrothed maiden, whose seducer is also executed by *skilah*. And *avodah zarah* is of course *skilah* as well. Accordingly, the verse may simply be listing multiple offenses all of which independently carry *skilah*, and the conclusion *mot yumat damav bo* tells us nothing about graded punishments.

### Rebuttal: Purpose

The *gemara* responds: if that reading were correct, *mai kamashma lan Yechezkel?* — what exactly is Ezekiel teaching us? If all the offenses equally carry *skilah*, the prophet has said nothing new. One might rejoin that Ezekiel is simply repeating and reviewing existing Torah law. But the *gemara* rejects this as well: if that were his purpose, *ibei leh le-mehadder ke-di-mehadder Moshe Rabbeinu* — he should have done so in the manner of Moshe Rabbeinu, who reviewed the commandments in *Mishneh Torah* with clarity and expansion. Ezekiel's subtle and indirect formulation makes no sense if he is merely rehearsing what the Torah already states more plainly. It follows that Ezekiel must be coming to teach us something new — specifically, the principle of our *mishna*: that when multiple capital liabilities are incurred, the graver execution is applied.

## Ezekiel Interpretation

### Rav Acha's Derasha

Rav Acha b'Rebi Chanina turns to a related passage in Ezekiel — the positive counterpart to the one just discussed. A few verses earlier, the prophet describes the righteous individual: *el he-harim lo akhal* — he did not eat upon the mountains — *ve-einav lo nasa el gillulei beis Yisrael* — he did not look to the abominations. He did not defile his fellow's wife, and he did not approach a *niddah*. The passage concludes: *tzaddik hu chaya yichye* — he is righteous, he shall surely live. The *gemara* observes that these formulations cannot merely mean the person passively avoided grave sins; they must describe positive virtues.

### Not Eating Mountains

*El he-harim lo akhal* — he did not eat upon the mountains — is interpreted as *she-lo akhal bi-zechut avotav*: he did not rely upon the merit of his forefathers for his sustenance and reward. His righteousness is his own; the mountains, a common metaphor for those from whom one descends, are not the source of his spiritual provision.

### Virtues: Humility

The phrase *ve-einav lo nasa el gillulei beis Yisrael* — he did not lift his eyes to the abominations — is read as *she-lo halach bi-komah zekufah*, he did not walk with an upright, arrogant bearing that effectively displaces the divine presence. Humility is thus linked, by way of the verse's idiom, to the rejection of *avodah zarah*. The defilement of one's fellow's wife (*es eshes re'ehu lo timme*) is read as *she-lo yarad le-ommanuto shel chaveiro* — he did not encroach upon his fellow's livelihood. The wife, as an emblem of one's entire domestic and personal life, serves here as a metaphor for professional livelihood. Finally, *ve-el ishah niddah lo yikrav* — he did not draw near to a *niddah* — is interpreted as *she-lo ne'enah mikuppah shel tzedakah*: even if poor, he declined to benefit from the communal charity fund, seeking a particular kind of purity and wholeness. The verse then concludes: *tzaddik hu chaya yichye*.

### Rabban Gamliel Weeps

When Rabban Gamliel reached this verse, he would weep. His concern: *man de'avid le-kulhu hu de-chaya* — is it really only one who fulfills all of these qualities who will live? *Be-chada mineyhu lo?* — and one who possesses only some of them, is that insufficient? The standard implied by the verse, read this way, seemed impossibly exacting.

### Rabbi Akiva Response

Rabbi Akiva responded by invoking a parallel verse. In the laws of *arayos*, the Torah concludes: *al titame'u be-chol eleh* — do not defile yourselves with all of these. One does not read that verse to mean that violating all of them simultaneously is forbidden while any single transgression would be permitted. Rather, the intent is: *be-achat mikol eleh* — even one is forbidden. So too here: the positive formulation in Ezekiel means that even one of these virtues, even a single good deed, is sufficient to warrant the blessing of life. Rabban Gamliel's tears were therefore unfounded, and the verse does not set an impossible threshold.

## One Sin, Two Penalties

### Mother-in-Law Case

The *gemara* now turns to the substantive analysis underlying Rabbi Yosi's position in the *mishna*. A *beraita* is cited explaining what Rabbi Yosi means when he says one is judged according to the first *zika*.

### MIL Becomes Married

The first scenario: a man's *chamot* — his mother-in-law — was never a married woman during any period relevant to him. From the time he became obligated in *mitzvos*, she had already been widowed or was otherwise single. The first and only relevant prohibition she held for him was as his wife's mother, which carries the penalty of *sreifa*. She subsequently married, becoming an *eshet ish* as well. Rabbi Yosi rules *nidon be-chamoto*: he is judged as one who violated the mother-in-law prohibition, and the punishment is *sreifa*. The *issur* of *eshet ish*, which carries the lighter penalty of *chenek*, does not displace the first status.

### Married Becomes MIL

The second scenario presents the *chiddush*. This woman had always been a married woman — *eshet ish* — during the relevant period of this man's life. She was therefore primarily forbidden to him as *eshet ish*, carrying *chenek*. He subsequently married her daughter, so she became additionally forbidden as his *chamot*. Rabbi Yosi rules *nidon be-eshet ish*: he is judged only by the first status, *eshet ish*, and receives the lighter penalty of *chenek* — not *sreifa*. This is the application of *ein issur chal al issur*: once a prohibition has attached to a person or object, a subsequent prohibition of the same or even greater severity does not take legal effect. Rabbi Yosi holds that the first status defines the relationship.

### Rav Adda Challenge

Rav Adda bar Ahava raises a challenge to Rava. In the first scenario — where she was initially the *chamot* and subsequently became a married woman — why not say that the status of *eshet ish* does in fact take effect, making it a case of *issur mosif*, an expanding prohibition? This would be consistent with the principle, transmitted by Rabbi Abbahu, that even Rabbi Yosi concedes the rule of *ein issur chal al issur* does not apply where the second prohibition is an *issur mosif* — a prohibition that broadens the scope of those forbidden. When she was only the *chamot*, she was forbidden exclusively to this one man. When she became a married woman, she became forbidden to every man in the world other than her husband. The second status thus expands the universe of those to whom she is prohibited, which is precisely the definition of *issur mosif*.

### Rabbi Abbahu Teaching

Rabbi Abbahu's teaching is that Rabbi Yosi would concede in a case of *issur mosif* that the second prohibition does take effect. If so, in the first scenario the man would be liable both as one who violated his *chamot* and as one who violated an *eshet ish*. The question is whether this affects his punishment.

### Response: Irrelevant Sta…

The response is pointed: *Adda brei, Adda, masya bisrei katlei katlas lei?* — Do you want to kill him twice? Yes, the second status takes effect, and yes, she is also forbidden to him as an *eshet ish* — but this is entirely irrelevant to the question of execution. Since we are speaking of intentional transgression (*be-meizid*), the man is already subject to *sreifa* on account of the *chamot* prohibition. The lighter *chenek* of *eshet ish* adds nothing to his sentence. As both Rashi and Tosafos note, the question becomes meaningful only in the case of unintentional transgression (*be-shogeg*). There, if the second status takes effect as an *issur mosif*, the man would be required to bring two *korbanos* rather than one. But in the realm of capital punishment, the superimposition of a lesser *issur* upon a greater one does not alter the outcome.

## Repeat Offender

### Mishna: Kippah

The next *mishna* introduces a famous institution: *mi she-lakah ve-shanah beis din machnisin oso la-kippah* — one who received lashes and repeated the same offense is confined to the *kippah* by the court.

### Kippah: Barley Death

The *mishna* specifies: *u-ma'achilin oso se'orin ad she-kreiso misbaka'as* — he is fed barley until his stomach bursts. The *Bavli*'s understanding of this is that the diet administered in the *kippah* literally brings about the offender's death. The mechanism involves first reducing his stomach through meager rations, and then feeding him barley which absorbs water and expands, causing the stomach to rupture. The *Yerushalmi*, by contrast, reads this passage more moderately, as simply describing a prison regime of unpleasant but non-lethal meager rations. The difference is significant: on the *Bavli*'s reading, the *kippah* is a covert form of capital punishment; on the *Yerushalmi*'s reading, it is an institution of imprisonment.

### Justification Question

The *gemara* asks what justifies this extra-legal measure at all. Simply repeating a sin twice — even if one received lashes for it — is hardly a basis, anywhere in the Torah, for confinement and indirect execution. What authorizes the court to act in this way?

### Kares Justification

Rabbi Yirmiyah, citing Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish (Reish Lakish), clarifies: *hacha be-malkiyos shel krisos askinan* — we are not speaking of any sin that carries lashes, but specifically of a sin for which the *karet* penalty applies. *Karet* is a divinely imposed excision — a form of heavenly death — but when witnesses give warning (*hasra'ah*), the earthly penalty of lashes is applied instead. Since the offender is intrinsically one who deserves divine death, *de-gavra bar katla hu*, the court is granted the authority to bring about that death in this manner. Moreover, *u-karuvi hu de-la mikrav* — he has displayed utter indifference to his own soul and life by repeatedly committing sins that carry *karet*, and so the court, as it were, helps actualize the death he has already invited upon himself: *makrivin lei es katlei iluyei*.

### One vs. Multiple Kares

Rav Yaakov refines the principle further. The rule applies only when the person repeatedly committed the same *karet* offense — *be-malkus shel kares achas*, sins of one specific *karet* category. If, however, the person committed two or three different *karet* transgressions — eating *chametz* on Pesach, eating blood, eating *chelev* — this does not trigger the *kippah* confinement. The reason: in such a case, *issurei hu de-ka tayeim*, he is sampling various forbidden pleasures. He is driven by a variety of different appetites. This does not demonstrate the same pattern of complete recklessness or self-destructive abandon as does repeatedly violating the same prohibition. The pathology is different, and accordingly the legal response is different.

## Hazaka: Two or Three

### Mishna: Two Times

The *mishna* holds that a pattern is established after *two* instances — the offender received lashes once, repeated the offense, and on the third commission of the sin is confined to the *kippah*. The *gemara* challenges this: is the *mishna* not inconsistent with the position of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who holds that a *hazaka* — an established behavioral pattern — requires three occurrences, not two?

This debate has a well-known context elsewhere: a woman whose successive husbands die in sequence. The concern is whether there is a causal relationship between her and their deaths. The question is at what point we regard this as an established pattern: after two husbands (the position of Rabbi) or after three (the position of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel). The *gemara* frames the present debate as a parallel dispute.

The *gemara* suggests that the *mishna* may simply be following Rabbi's view that two instances suffice to establish a *hazaka*, and would therefore not accord with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.

### Baraita: Two Lashes

A *beraita* specifies: on the first and second commission of the sin the offender receives lashes, and on the third commission he is confined to the *kippah*.

### Abba Shaul: Three Times

Abba Shaul disagrees: even on the third commission he receives lashes; it is only on the fourth commission that he is confined to the *kippah*.

### Lashes vs. Sins

At first glance, this debate appears easily explicable as a replay of the dispute between Rabbi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: the *tanna kamma* requires two instances before the pattern is established (following Rabbi), while Abba Shaul requires three (following Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel). The *gemara* considers this interpretation — that what establishes the pattern is the repeated defiance of lashes (*malkus machzikos*). According to this reading, the *tanna kamma* says that defying lashes twice — by sinning on a third occasion — establishes the pattern, while Abba Shaul says one must defy lashes three times before the *kippah* is imposed.

### Sins Count

Ravina, however, resists this framing and insists that all parties in fact hold like Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, that three instances are required. The real dispute, he argues, is not about how many times lashes must be defied, but about what is being counted. The *tanna kamma* holds *aveiros machzikos* — it is the sins themselves that establish the pattern. The person sinned once, sinned again, and sinned a third time; three sins have now been committed and the *kippah* is imposed. Abba Shaul holds *malkus machzikos* — it is the defiance of lashes that establishes the pattern. One must have defied lashes three times, meaning the sin must have been committed four times (each of the first three followed by lashes, and then the fourth sin triggering the *kippah*). On Ravina's reading, no one in this *sugya* dissents from Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's requirement of three instances; they differ only on whether those three instances are three sins or three acts of defying the lash.

## Warnings Without Lashes

### No Lashes Case

The *gemara* now confronts a case where lashes were never actually administered. Witnesses were present and warnings (*hasra'ah*) were given — but the offender never verbally acknowledged the warning (*af al pi chen*) or otherwise responded in the technically required manner that would permit lashes to be administered. In one variant, he nodded his head (*hirkin rosho*) rather than explicitly accepting the warning. The result is that his willfulness was apparent but lashes could not formally be given.

### TK: Third Warning

The *tanna kamma* rules: the first and second times, the court gives him the warning; on the third occasion, he is confined to the *kippah*. This is a striking *chiddush*: even without lashes having been administered, the *kippah* is imposed. Three warnings suffice to establish the pattern.

### AS: Kippah Warning

Abba Shaul disagrees. He maintains that to impose *kippah* confinement, the court must first warn the offender explicitly that the consequence of another violation will be confinement in the *kippah* itself. He cannot issue this warning until the offender has already established himself as a habitual violator. Accordingly, three violations must first occur to establish the *hazaka*; only then may the court warn him regarding the *kippah*. A fourth violation after that warning triggers the actual confinement.

### Kippah Requires Warning

This raises an obvious question: since lashes are not in play at all in this scenario, what is Abba Shaul's reasoning for requiring a fourth instance? If the pattern is established by the sins themselves (as the *tanna kamma* holds), three sins should suffice. Why does Abba Shaul demand a fourth?

Ravina explains that the underlying dispute is whether *kippah* itself requires prior *hatra'ah* — a formal warning specifically directed at the *kippah* penalty. The *tanna kamma* holds that no such specific warning is needed; the general warnings already given suffice, and once the pattern of three violations is established, the *kippah* follows. Abba Shaul holds that *kippah* does require its own prior *hatra'ah*. Since this warning cannot be issued until the *hazaka* of three violations has already been established, the *kippah* can only be imposed after a fourth violation — the one following the warning. Tosafos notes the difficulty in explaining precisely why Abba Shaul cannot issue the *kippah* warning earlier, and the question is left without a fully satisfying resolution.

## Kippah Structure

### Height of Kippah

Having established the principle and mechanism of the *kippah*, the *gemara* briefly describes its physical structure. Rav Yehuda teaches: *malei komaso* — the *kippah* was precisely as high as the person confined within it. It was a solitary enclosure affording no room beyond the prisoner's own stature, a form of total confinement.

### Scripture Hint

The *gemara* asks where there is a scriptural allusion to the legitimacy of this institution. Reish Lakish finds a hint in the verse *timosis rasha ra'ah* — the evil of a wicked person will bring about his death. This supports the *gemara*'s earlier reasoning: since the *kippah* is understood as a mechanism of bringing about death for one who is intrinsically deserving of it by virtue of his repeated *karet* violations, there is biblical warrant for arranging the circumstances of that death.

### Know Not Your Time

A second teaching of Reish Lakish is appended, connected by the theme of death. He cites the verse: *ki gam lo yeda ha'adam es ito* — a person does not know his time — *kedagim shenechazim be-metzudah ra'ah*, like fish caught in an evil net. The *gemara* asks what *metzudah ra'ah* refers to. Reish Lakish answers: *chikah* — a fishing hook. The image is striking: a tiny instrument capable of ensnaring a massive creature. One never knows what seemingly minor thing may prove fatal. With this rather sobering reflection, the discussion of the *kippah* concludes.

## Murderer, No Witnesses

### Murderer Confined

The next *mishna* introduces a second application of *kippah* confinement: *ha-horeg nefesh she-lo be-eidin* — one who kills without the kind of testimony legally sufficient for court-ordered execution. Such a person is confined to the *kippah* and given *lechem tzar u-mayim lachatz* — meager rations of bread and water.

### Evidence Types

The *gemara* asks: if there were no proper witnesses, how do we know he committed the murder? Three scenarios are suggested. Rav says: *be-eidus meyuechedes* — there were two witnesses but they observed the act from separate vantage points and did not see one another, failing the technical requirement of joint testimony necessary for a capital conviction. Shmuel says: *she-lo be-hasra'ah* — witnesses were present but did not issue the formal warning (*hasra'ah*) required to render the act judicially actionable. Rav Chisda, citing Avimi, says: *de-iskachish be-bedikos ve-lo iskachish be-chakiros* — the witnesses contradicted themselves on peripheral examination questions (*bedikos*) but remained consistent on the essential substantive questions (*chakiros*). The contradiction on incidental matters was technically sufficient to disqualify their testimony for capital purposes, yet the underlying evidence of guilt remained compelling. A precedent for such rigorous cross-examination is cited: the case of Ben Zakkai, who pressed witnesses even on the stems of figs — trivial details — precisely to probe the reliability of testimony.

### Why Murderers

One might ask why the *kippah* is specifically applied to murderers in this context — rather than, say, to someone who desecrated Shabbos without a valid *hasra'ah*. Rav Chisda's framing makes the answer clear: this is not a formal legal proceeding but a societal response to a genuine and demonstrated danger. The entire structure of the *kippah* for the murderer operates outside the formal rules of Torah adjudication, precisely because those rules — essential as they are — have in this case produced an outcome incompatible with protecting society. The murderer is known; only a technical deficiency in the legal process has prevented formal execution.

### Combined Mishnayos

A textual question arises from the contrast between the two *mishnayos*. The *mishna* of the repeat offender specifies *se'orin* — barley — and *ad she-kreiso misbaka'as*, until the stomach bursts. The present *mishna* specifies *lechem tzar u-mayim lachatz* — sparse bread and pressed water. Are these contradictory regimens?

The *gemara* resolves the tension by reading the two *mishnayos* as describing a single combined process. The murderer is first given meager rations of bread and water, which cause his stomach to contract and shrink. Then barley is introduced, which, absorbing liquid, expands and causes the stomach to rupture — *kreiso misbaka'as*. The two *mishnayos* describe sequential stages of the same fatal regimen. Since the rupture is the mechanism of death on the *Bavli*'s reading, it applies to the murderer as well — there is no reason the murderer should be subject to a less severe outcome than the *karet* recidivist. The combination of the two *mishnayos* resolves the apparent contradiction and produces a unified account.

## Zealotry Kna'im

### Three Zealot Cases

The final *mishna* of the daf introduces the institution of *kana'im pogim bo* — zealots who may strike without formal court process. Three cases are enumerated. First: one who steals the *kasva*, a vessel of the *beis hamikdash*. Second: one who curses God through a *kosem*, a prognosticator. Third — and most famous — *ha-ba al ha-aramis*, a man who has intercourse with a non-Jewish woman. In all three cases, *kana'im pogim bo*: a zealot may act and kill the offender in the moment, without judicial authorization. The court neither prosecutes these cases through formal channels nor imposes extra-legal punishment; it is specifically the domain of private zealous action.

A further case is appended, though it operates somewhat differently: a *kohen* who performs the Temple service while *tamei* (*kohen she-shimesh be-tumah*). His fellow *kohanim* do not bring him before *beis din* — apparently because no formal capital penalty applies — but the young *kohanim* (*pirchei kehunah*) take him outside the *azarah* and break open his skull with logs. And the case of a *zar* — a non-*kohen* — who performs Temple service: Rabbi Akiva holds this is punishable by *chenek* through the court; the Sages hold it is *bidei shamayim*, a heavenly punishment.

### Kasva Temple Vessel

Rav Yehuda identifies the *kasva* as a *kli shares* — a sacred Temple vessel. The term appears in a verse describing the components of the *shulchan*, referring to the boards or supports associated with it. The *gemara* seeks a scriptural hint for the death penalty attached to stealing such a vessel: *ve-lo yavo'u lir'os ke-vala es ha-kodesh ve-meisu* — they shall not come to see as the holy things are being swallowed up, lest they die. The phrase *ke-vala es ha-kodesh* — consuming or taking possession of the sacred — is read as a basis for treating the theft of sacred vessels as a capital-adjacent offense. Rashi notes, however, that this remains only a *remez*, a hint, and does not constitute a formal derivation. Moreover, even if there is some basis for a death penalty, the further inference — that private zealots rather than the court are the appropriate agents — is not derived from this verse and remains unexplained by the *gemara*.

### Prognosticator Curse

The second case, *ha-mekallel be-kosem*, is explained by a *beraita* taught by Rav Yosef. The offense involves invoking a *kosem* — a prognosticator or diviner — as a vehicle for cursing God. The formulation described is: *yakei kosem es kosmo* — may the *kosem* strike his own [i.e., the one who gave him his power of divination], treating the *kosem* as a divine or semi-divine figure capable of acting against God. A parallel formulation cited by the Sages includes: *yakehu kosem lo u-le-kono u-le-maknehu* — may the *kosem* strike this person, and his God, and his Creator — adding both a curse against another person and an invocation against the Creator. While not technically *mekallel ha-shem* in its formal sense — which requires using God's name to curse God — this language approximates blasphemy closely enough to fall into this category.

The *gemara* does not here explain the basis for the rule of *kana'im pogim bo* in this case — any more than it resolved that question for the theft of the *kasva*. The underlying rationale, presumably some notion of protecting the sanctity of God and the Temple, is left implicit. The *gemara* similarly does not bridge the gap between recognizing an offense as serious and authorizing private zealous killing rather than formal judicial response. These are questions the *gemara* leaves open, and we will continue from here tomorrow.

# Sanhedrin 82

## Boel Aramit Status

### Intro & Question

The daf opens on the final line of 81b with the principle of *kanayim pogim bo* — the doctrine that zealots may act extrajudicially against certain transgressors — and the paradigmatic case through which that doctrine is explored: *v'haboh al ha'aramit*, one who engages in relations with a non-Jewish woman.

The discussion transitions immediately to the top of 82a, where Rav Kahana poses a question to Rav.

### Rav Kahana's Q

*Ba'ei minei Rav Kahana me'Rav*: Rav Kahana asked Rav — if the *kanayim* do not act, what is this person's legal status? What precisely is the sin, and what punishment does he incur? The underlying difficulty is that the biblical prohibition of *lo titchaten bam* addresses intermarriage in the context of *ishus*, of a quasi-matrimonial relationship. But where a man merely fornicates — casual relations outside any such context — what exactly is the transgression, and what is its formal severity? *Mahu?*

Rav, however, could not answer: *inshi Rav l'gmarei* — Rav forgot his tradition on the matter.

### Dream & Pasuk

The resolution came through an unusual channel. *Akri'u l'Rav Kahana b'chelmeih* — a *pasuk* was read to Rav Kahana in a dream:

> בָּגְדָה יְהוּדָה וְתוֹעֵבָה נֶעֶשְׂתָה בְיִשְׂרָאֵל וּבִירוּשָׁלַיִם כִּי חִלַּל יְהוּדָה קֹדֶשׁ ה' אֲשֶׁר אָהֵב וּבָעַל בַּת אֵל נֵכָר
> *(Malachi 2:11)*

Rav Kahana came to Rav and reported the dream. *Ad d'kavi Rav l'gmarei* — this prompted Rav to recover his forgotten teaching, and he proceeded to interpret the verse.

### Rav's Drasha

Rav reads the verse as encoding four distinct transgressions. *Bagdah Yehudah* — "Judah betrayed" — *zu avoda zarah*, this refers to idolatry, as confirmed by another verse: *u'v'chen bagadetem bi beit Yisrael neum Hashem* — "you have betrayed Me, O house of Israel." The language of betrayal (*bagidah*) captures the essence of our covenantal relationship with God: to worship foreign gods is to commit the ultimate act of infidelity.

*V'toevah naasta b'Yisrael u'biYerushalayim* — "an abomination was committed in Israel and Jerusalem" — *zeh mishkav zachor*, this refers to male homosexual intercourse, as the Torah states: *v'et zachar lo tishkav mishkevei isha toevah hi*. Both of these initial references describe sins that are *chayav misah*.

*Ki chillel Yehudah kodesh Hashem* — "for Judah has desecrated what is holy to God" — *zu zonah*, this refers to prostitution, as the verse states: *lo tiheyeh kadeshah mibnot Yisrael v'lo yiheyeh kadesh mibnei Yisrael*. Notably, this transgression is not *chayav misah*; it is a *lav*.

Finally, *u'vaal bat el nechar* — "and he has coupled with the daughter of a foreign god" — *zeh haboh al hakutit*, one who has relations with a non-Jewish woman. The continuation of the verse reads:

> יַכְרֵת ה' לָאִישׁ אֲשֶׁר יַעֲשֶׂנָּה עֵר וָעֹנֶה מֵאָהֳלֵי יַעֲקֹב וּמַגִּישׁ מִנְחָה לַה' צְבָאוֹת
> *(Malachi 2:12)*

Rav interprets this to mean: if he is a Torah scholar, *lo yiheyeh lo er b'chachamim v'oneh b'talmidim* — he will have no standing among the sages, no regular place among students; he will be cut off from the *beit midrash*. If he is a *kohen*, *lo yiheyeh lo ben magish mincha l'Hashem tzevaot* — he will have no son to bring offerings on the altar.

This raises a striking question: the punishment described here does not obviously constitute *chiyuv misah*. The verse's phrasing about being "cut off" is ambiguous — is this *karet* or merely the loss of social status? And between the clear capital cases at the beginning of the verse and this final case, there is the intermediate category of *zonah*, a mere *lav*. The *rishonim*, as we shall see the *gemara* return to, feel that the doctrine of *kanayim pogim bo* — which effectively licenses taking the transgressor's life — cannot be coherently grounded unless we assume this person bears at minimum some sense of *chiyuv misah bidei shamayim*. That forces a focus on the word *yicharet* in the verse — which at least implies *karet* — and that is the direction in which the *halacha* will ultimately be read.

### Intermarriage & G-d

Rabbi Chiya bar Abba adds a dimension beyond formal penalty. *Kol ha-ba al kutit ke'ilu mis'chaten ba-avoda kochavim* — whoever has relations with a non-Jewish woman, it is as though he has made the idols themselves his *machatanim*, his family by marriage. The source: *u'vaal bat el nechar* — he has coupled with the daughter of a foreign god. The *gemara* immediately asks: *ve-chi bas yesh lo l'el nechar?* Does a foreign deity actually have a daughter? The point, of course, is not literal. Rather, through this relationship one draws the entire apparatus of foreign worship into the fabric of the Jewish family. This is why intermarriage has always been perceived — rightly — as an existential threat to Jewish continuity and identity, far beyond whatever formal halachic category it may occupy. One is not merely transgressing a prohibition; one is importing *avoda zara* into the household of Israel.

### Yehoyakim Story

Rabbi Chiya bar Abba continues with a separate teaching. He reports that written on the skull of Yehoyakim — one of the late kings of Judah during the period of the First Temple, who permitted idolatrous worship to continue despite prophetic rebuke — were the words *zot ve-od acheres*: this punishment, and yet another one is still to come.

The grandfather of Rabbi Pereda — identified in the context as Rabbi Chiya bar Abba himself, though the *gemara* curiously does not name him as such — *ashkecha le-hahu gulgolta de-vashadya be-sha'arei Yerushalayim*: he found a skull that had been cast out and left to roll about at the gates of Jerusalem. He tried to bury it: *kavra*, and then *ve-hadar n'vag* — it resurfaced. He buried it again, and again it pushed its way back up. At that point he recognized it must be something extraordinary.

*Hai gulgolta shel Yehoyakim* — this must be the skull of Yehoyakim, as the prophet had declared: *kevuras chamor yikaver, sachov vehashlech mehaleh l'sha'arei Yerushalayim* — he shall be buried with the burial of a donkey, dragged and cast out from the gates of Jerusalem. A divine decree had been set: his body would not rest in the earth.

Yet even recognizing this, he felt compelled to show the former king some dignity. *Malka hu ve-lav orech ara l'vizzuyei* — he was nonetheless a king, and it is not fitting to degrade him so. So he took the skull, wrapped it in silk, and placed it in a box in his room.

His wife discovered it, and — naturally — went to her neighbors with the alarming find. They drew the worst possible conclusion: *hai de-it'sa kamaisa* — this must be the skull of his first wife, whom he apparently cannot let go. So she threw it into the oven and burned it to ash. *Ve-hainu dich'siv al gulgolto: zot ve-od acheres* — that was the *ot acheres*, the second punishment: not only was he denied burial, but his very remains were ultimately incinerated.

When Rabbi Chiya bar Abba came, he said: now I understand what was written on it.

### Hasmon. Edict

The *gemara* returns to the formal question of *boel aramit*. When Rav Dimi came from Eretz Yisrael, he reported: *beit dino shel Chashmonai gazru* — the *beit din* of the Hasmonean era issued a rabbinic enactment. It is noteworthy that the *gemara* attributes this specifically to the Hasmoneans — a period of religious reformation and heightened concern about Hellenization and cultural assimilation.

The edict: *haba al hakutit chayav alei mishum nashka* — one who has relations with a non-Jewish woman is treated rabbinically as having violated four prohibitions, encoded in the acronym *nashka*: *niddah* (even though the laws of *niddah* technically apply only to a Jewish woman, she is treated as one rabbinically); *shifcha* (a slave woman, who is categorically forbidden); *goya* (for her very status as a non-Jew, which in the Torah applies only to marriage, but is extended rabbinically to casual relations as well); and *alef* for *eshet ish* (a married woman — even though her marriage is not technically recognized as *ishus* in the full halachic sense, we treat her as a married woman for this purpose).

When Ravin came, he reported a variant: *mishum nashgaz* — replacing *eshet ish* with *zonah* (prostitute), yielding *niddah, shifcha, goya, zonah*. *Aval mishum ishut leit lah* — he does not recognize even a rabbinic status of *eshet ish* for a non-Jewish woman. His reasoning: non-Jewish men do not hold their wives to fidelity, so there is no meaningful marriage to recognize; instead, we assign her the status of a *zonah*.

Rav Dimi, by contrast, holds the opposite: *nashayehu vadai lo mafkere* — non-Jewish husbands do in fact take their wives' fidelity seriously, and therefore one should recognize *eshet ish* rather than *zonah*.

All of this elaborates the formal rabbinic prohibitions that underlie the case where *kanayim pogim bo* applies. As the *gemara* notes, it is striking that intermarriage is treated with a social severity exceeding many formal transgressions of far greater halachic weight. The answer lies in the existential dimension already articulated — this is a genuine threat to Jewish continuity — and it is that dimension which the doctrine of *kanayim pogim bo* expresses at its most dramatic level.

---

## Kanayim Framework

### No Ruling Given

*Itmar nami* — it was also taught: Rav Chisda said, *haba limalech ein morin lo* — if someone comes to ask whether he may go and kill a person caught in the act of relations with a non-Jew, we do not rule for him that it is permitted. The entire mechanism of *kanayim pogim bo* operates outside the formal legal system. We are, in a sense, retrospectively accepting what the zealot has done — even, in the right circumstances, praising it — but we cannot prospectively endorse it. There is an inherent tension here: the *halacha* exists, yet we refuse to teach it to one who asks. To license vigilantism openly would be to invite disorder and create a population of self-appointed executioners. So the principle remains operative yet judicially untransmitted.

Rabba bar bar Chana said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *haba limalech ein morin lo*.

### Zimri & Pinchas

And not only that, but the *gemara* goes further to illustrate how radically the operative window is circumscribed. *Ela she-im pirash Zimri ve-harago Pinchas neherag alav* — if Zimri had separated from Kozbi and Pinchas killed him when they were no longer in the act, Pinchas would have been guilty of murder. *Neherag alav.* He would be subject to execution.

The doctrine of *kanayim pogim bo* applies — if it applies at all — only at the precise moment of intercourse. Miss that window by even a moment, and what was a potential act of *kana'uth* becomes unlawful killing. The narrowness of this ruling is striking: not only do we refuse to give advance permission, but the conditions for post-facto endorsement are extraordinarily tight.

### Rodeph Status

There is a further, and quite remarkable, dimension. *Nehepach Zimri ve-harago le-Pinchas ein neherag alav* — if Zimri had turned around and killed Pinchas as Pinchas was coming for him, Zimri would not have been executed for it. Why? *She-harei rodeph hu* — because Pinchas in that moment is a *rodeph*, a pursuer seeking his life. From a purely legal standpoint, even at the very moment that *kanayim pogim bo* could apply — even while Pinchas is entirely within whatever latitude exists for zealot action — Zimri retains the right of self-defense, because Pinchas is pursuing him with lethal intent.

The *gemara* is here holding two ideas simultaneously: we can, after the fact, accept or even honor what Pinchas did; and yet, from within the legal system at that identical moment, Pinchas was a *rodeph* whom Zimri could lawfully kill. These two frames coexist, each fully operative. The *gemara* is not resolving the tension so much as insisting that both propositions are true at once.

---

## Pinchas Narrative

### Judges Confront

The *gemara* now turns to the biblical narrative itself. *Vayomer Moshe el shophtei Yisrael: hargu ish anashav ha-nitzmadim le-va'al pe'or* — Moshe said to the judges of Israel: each of you kill those of your men who attached themselves to Baal Peor. Trials began and executions were carried out.

### Zimri's Act

*Halach shivto shel Shimon etzel Zimri ben Salu* — the tribe of Shimon went to Zimri. They said to him: *hen danin dinei nefashot ve-atah yoshev ve-shotek?* — they are executing people, presumably from our own tribe, and you sit here silent?

*Mah asah* — what did Zimri do? *Amad ve-kibetz esrim ve-arba'ah elef mi-Yisrael* — he gathered twenty-four thousand Israelites. The *gemara* identifies these as the very twenty-four thousand who would die in the ensuing plague, presuming them to have been perpetrators themselves. *Ve-halach etzel Kozbi* — and he went to Kozbi, the daughter of Tzur, one of the princes of Midian.

He said to her: *hashmi'i li* — be with me. She responded: *bat melech ani* — I am a princess. *Ve-chen tzivani abba: lo tishme'i ela le-gadol she-ba-hem* — my father instructed me to submit to no one less than the greatest among them, meaning Moshe. Zimri replied: *af hu nasi shevet hu* — I too am a tribal chieftain. *Velo od ela she-hu gadol mimenu* — indeed I am greater than Moshe. *She-hu sheni la-beten* — I, as head of Shimon, am the second tribe; Moshe, as head of Levi, leads only the third. Therefore, by her father's own standard, she should comply with him.

*Tafshah be-vloritah* — he seized her by her hair, and *ve-hevi'ah etzel Moshe* — brought her before Moshe. Addressing him as *ben Amram* — conspicuously stripping him of the title of *Moshe Rabbeinu* — he challenged: *zu asurah o muteret?* Is this woman forbidden to me or permitted? *Ve-im tomar asurah* — and if you say forbidden — *bat Yitro mi hitirah lach?* Who permitted you the daughter of Yitro? Rashi comes quickly to Moshe's defense, noting that the daughter of Yitro had stood at Har Sinai and entered the covenant, thereby becoming Jewish. But the challenge had its effect.

### Moshe Lost

*Ba-otah sha'ah nitalmah mimenu halacha* — at that moment, the *halacha* escaped Moshe. This was not, apparently, the question of why he had been permitted to marry the daughter of Yitro, but rather the operative *halacha* of what to do about Zimri — the principle of *kanayim pogim bo* itself. Perhaps because he was being personally attacked, perhaps for some other reason, Moshe could not access the ruling.

One might pause here: God had already commanded through Moshe to judge and execute those who attached themselves to Baal Peor. Why, then, is *kanayim pogim bo* described as extra-legal? The answer the *gemara* implies is that such a command would require a full judicial process — witnesses, trial, formal verdict. What Pinchas did was something else: an immediate, extrajudicial act. That is why it required its own distinct category of *halacha*.

*Ga'u kulam bivchiyah* — they all broke out weeping. *Ve-hainu dich'siv: ve-hemah vochim petach ohel mo'ed* — as the verse states, "and they were weeping at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting."

### Pinchas Acts

*Ve-cheitiv vayar Pinchas ben Elazar* — and the verse says: Pinchas son of Elazar saw. *Mah ra'ah?* — what did he see? Here the *gemara* records three interpretations.

Rav says: *ra'ah ma'aseh ve-nizkar halacha* — he saw the act unfolding and remembered the *halacha* of *kanayim pogim bo*. He then went to Moshe: *achi avi abba* — brother of my grandfather, for Pinchas was the son of Elazar the son of Aharon, making Moshe his great-uncle. It is interesting that he does not say *Moshe Rabbeinu*, especially against the backdrop of Zimri's contemptuous *ben Amram*. He asked: *lo kach limadtani bi-ridtecha me-Har Sinai?* — is this not what you taught me when you came down from Har Sinai? *Haba al ha-kutit kanayim pogim bo.* Moshe responded: *karyana de-igarta ihu lehevei parvenka* — the reader of the message should be its executor. Notably, Moshe did not say "yes, do it" — that would violate *ein morin lo* — but rather pointed back to Pinchas as the one who had articulated the ruling.

Shmuel offers a different reading of what Pinchas saw. He was guided by the principle: *ein chochmah ve-ein tevunah ve-ein etzah neged Hashem* — there is no wisdom, no understanding, and no counsel against God. *Kol makom she-yesh chillul Hashem ein cholkin kavod la-rav* — whenever there is a desecration of God's name, one does not defer to religious authority that is failing to act. Pinchas did not look up a *halacha*; he rose because he knew he had to defend God's honor.

Rabbi Yitzchak said in the name of Rabbi Elazar: *ra'ah she-ba malach ve-hishchit ba-am* — he saw the angel coming to destroy among the people; the plague was beginning. He understood that something had to be done immediately to stop it.

Three distinct accounts: a man acting from precise legal knowledge; a man acting from moral imperative; a man acting from urgent necessity in the face of catastrophe.

*Vayakom mitoch ha-edah vayikach romach be-yado* — he rose from the congregation and took his spear. The *gemara* derives from the phrase *mitoch ha-edah* — from the midst of the congregation — that *ein nichnasim bi-khli zayin le-veit ha-midrash*: one does not bring weapons into the *beit midrash*. He had to first leave the study setting before arming himself.

*Shalaf shinana, hinichah be-unkalo* — he removed the spearhead and placed it in his cloak, concealing it. He then leaned on the wooden shaft as though it were a walking stick, entering the territory of the tribe of Shimon while saying: *heichan matzinu she-shivto shel Levi gadol mi-shel Shimon?* — where have we ever found that Levi is greater than Shimon? He was posing as someone who also wanted to participate. The tribe of Shimon said: *hanichu lo, af hu la-asot tzorcho nichnas* — let him through, he too wants to take care of his needs. The onlookers reportedly remarked: *habitu perushim et ha-davar* — even the separated ones, even the pious, are doing this now. And so he was admitted.

### Six Miracles

Rabbi Yochanan teaches: *shisha nissim na'asu lo le-Pinchas* — six miracles were performed for Pinchas in the course of his act.

First, that Zimri could have separated from Kozbi and did not, which would have immediately stripped Pinchas of any license to act.

Second, that Zimri could have spoken up — he was surrounded by twenty-four thousand tribal members — and did not call for help when he saw Pinchas draw the spear.

Third, *she-kivein be-zachruto shel ish u-vi-nekevutah shel isha* — that his spear passed precisely through their genitalia as they were engaged in the act, so that everyone could see the nature and justice of what had occurred. This is understood by the *gemara* as implicit in how the *pesukim* can be read, and is directly relevant to the parameters of *kanayim pogim bo*: the act had to be witnessed in flagrante.

Fourth, *she-lo nishmetu min ha-romach* — they did not slip off the spear. Pinchas carried them out of the tent on the spear so the people could witness it, and miraculously they remained impaled upon it.

Fifth, *she-ba malach ve-higbiya et ha-mashkof* — the angel came and raised the lintel of the tent's doorway so that Pinchas, carrying the spear with both bodies upon it, could pass through without stooping, which would have caused them to fall.

Sixth, *she-ba malach ve-hishchit ba-am* — the angel began bringing the plague to the people, distracting the crowd and preventing them from attacking Pinchas in retaliation.

### Divine Praise

*Ba ve-chavtan lifnei ha-Makom* — Pinchas then brought the two of them and cast them down before God. He cried out: *Ribono shel olam! Al elu yiplu esrim ve-arba'ah elef mi-Yisrael?* — Master of the Universe, for these two, twenty-four thousand of Israel should fall? The verse confirms: *vayihyu ha-meitim ba-mageifah esrim ve-arba'ah elef*.
