The *gemara* reads the verse *vaya'amod Pinchas vayefalel* — Pinchas stood up and *vayefalel* — not, Rabbi Elazar insists, in the sense of *vayitpallel*, he prayed, but in the sense of *pelilot*, he made an argument. *Melamed kivyachol she-asah pelilot im kono* — he argued with God, challenging the justice of so many deaths.

*Bikshu malachei ha-sharet le-dachfo* — the ministering angels sought to push Pinchas away. Who is this human to argue with God? God said to them: *hanichu lo — kanai ben kanai* — leave him alone; he is a zealot, son of a zealot. Rashi reads this as a reference to Shimon and Levi at the incident of Dinah, though it might equally evoke the Levites who rose at Har Sinai. *Meshiv cheimah ben meshiv cheimah* — one who turns away Divine wrath, descended from one who turned away Divine wrath: Aharon, who brought the *ketoret* to halt a plague, was Pinchas's great-grandfather. Now Pinchas himself has acted to stop one. He comes by his *kana'uth* honestly, and it is entirely *le-shem shamayim*.

### Tribe Contempt

The other tribes, however, were not so generous in their assessment. *Hitchilu shevatim mevazim* — the tribes began to mock him. *Ra'item ben Puti zeh* — have you seen this son of Puti? The reference is to the verse identifying Pinchas's grandfather on his mother's side: *Elazar lakach lo mi-bnot Putiel lo le-isha* — Elazar had married from the daughters of Putiel. The *gemara* identifies Putiel with Yitro, *she-pittem agalim la-avoda zara* — who fattened calves for idol worship. So they sneered: this descendant of an idol-worshipper's family — *ve-harag nasi shevet mi-Yisrael?* — has killed a prince of a tribe of Israel?

*Ba ha-katuv ve-yichasao* — the verse comes and traces his lineage to defend him: *Pinchas ben Elazar ben Aharon ha-kohen*. Not through his mother, but through his grandfather: he is the grandson of Aharon ha-kohen. God said to Moshe: *hekdem lo shalom* — go and bring him peace first.

### Covenant Peace

*She-ne'emar: lachen emor hineni nosein lo et briti shalom* — as it is said: "Therefore declare: I hereby give him My covenant of peace." The atonement that Pinchas brought through his act, the *gemara* states, was to be a source of ongoing atonement: *ve-ra'uyah kapara zo she-tehei mechaperes ve-holeches le-olam* — this atonement was fitting to endure for all time, as expressed by *bris kehunas olam*: an eternal covenant of priesthood. There is something profoundly suggestive in the fact that the man of violence is given a covenant of peace — and indeed, in the book of Yehoshua, Pinchas ultimately becomes a diplomat, a man of peace. The warrior becomes the negotiator; that trajectory is already embedded in the divine response here.

---

## Names & Acts

### Gematria 424

Rav Nachman said in the name of Rav: what is meant by the verse *zarzir masnayim o tayish u-melech al-kum imo* (Proverbs 30:31)? The plain sense speaks of a greyhound, a he-goat, and a king whom none can stand against — impressive and slightly puzzling company. The *gemara* reads the verse as a reference to the story of Zimri.

*Arba meot ve-esrim ve-arba be-ilot ba'al oso rasha oso ha-yom* — that wicked man had relations 424 times on that day. The *gematria* of the word *zarzir* is 424. The word *masnayim* refers to the hips — the act of intercourse. Zimri is the *zarzir masnayim*. *Ve-himtin lo Pinchas* — and Pinchas waited for him, reading *masnayim* now as the root *himtin*, waited — until *ad she-tashash kocho*, until Zimri was exhausted. *Ve-hu eino yodea she-melech al-kum imo* — but Pinchas did not realize he did not have to wait; the King against Whom none can rise was with him all along, and God would have protected him regardless.

A *baraita* of Rabbi Yosef offers a different count: not 424 but 60 acts of intercourse, *ad she-na'aseh ke-beitza muzeret* — until he became like a scrambled or spoiled egg, meaning either his body or his semen was spent and he was left utterly weakened. *Ve-hi hayeta ke-aruga malei mayim* — and she was like a garden bed filled with water. Rav Kahana adds: *u-moshava beit sa'ah* — her capacity was a *beit sa'ah*, an area of considerable size. Rabbi Yosef further teaches: *kavrah shelo amah amah* — the dimensions attributed to her were an *amah* wide. These are the *gemara*'s very graphic descriptions of the flagrant nature of their fornication.

### Kozbi Shvilnai

Rav Sheshes teaches: *lo Kozbi shemah* — her name was not actually Kozbi. *Ella Shvilnai* — her true name was Shvilnai, daughter of Tzur. Shvilnai, as the *gemara* will show, was a name that had entered popular speech as a byword for a notorious prostitute.

*Ve-lamah nikra shemah Kozbi?* — why then is she called Kozbi? *She-kozva aviha* — because she betrayed her father: her father had instructed her to submit only to Moshe, and she allowed herself to be taken by Zimri. Alternatively — *davar acher* — the name *Kozbi* can be read as *kos bi im zeh*: "slaughter for me through this one," meaning she told her father that through this fornication she would bring destruction upon Israel.

*Ve-hainu de-amri inshi* — and because her real name was Shvilnai, she appears in the following popular sayings: *bein kani le-urvani Shvilnai mai ba'ya?* — between the reeds and the willows, what is Shvilnai doing there? The implication is obvious: what else would she be doing in a secluded spot among the reeds and willows? Similarly: *be-hadi kilfei di-knei Shvilnai mai ba'ya?* — among these peeled reeds, what is Shvilnai doing? Same meaning, same insinuation. *Gafta le-ima* — she has brought her mother along into her evil as well; Rashi explains that calling her a *zonah* was taken to implicate her mother as a *zonah* also.

### Zimri's Names

Rabbi Yochanan states: *chamesh shemos yesh lo* — Zimri bore five names.

He was called *Zimri* — *al she-na'asah ke-beitzah muzeret*, because through the act he was reduced to the state of a spoiled egg.

He was called *ben Salu* — *al she-histil avonot shel mishpachto*, Rashi explaining that he caused people to investigate or speak about the sins of his family, bringing disgrace upon his lineage.

He was called *Shaul* — *al she-hish'il atzmo le-dvar aveirah*, he lent himself out to a matter of sin.

He was called *ben ha-Kena'anit* — *al she-asah ma'aseh Kena'an*, he acted with the licentiousness of Canaan, Canaan being classically associated with sexual transgression in the Torah.

*U-mah shemo?* — and what is his real name? *Shelumiel ben Tzurishaddai shemo* — his name is Shelumiel ben Tzurishaddai, who appears in the book of Bamidbar as the designated chieftain of the tribe of Shimon at the time of the offerings of the *nesi'im*. The *gemara* identifies Zimri with that figure. It is an interesting footnote that the Yiddish word *shlemiel* appears to derive from *Shelumiel* — and the *gemara*'s association of that name with Zimri gives the etymology a certain dark resonance.

---

## Kohen Tumah

### Kohen Head

The *gemara* turns to another case in the *Mishnah*: a *kohen* who performs the *avodah* in a state of *tumah*. The *Mishnah* teaches that his fellow *kohanim* — specifically the younger priests, *pirchei kehunah* — would not bring him to *beit din*, but would take him outside the *azarah* and crack open his head with logs.

### Divine Death Q

Rav Acha bar Hunah asked Rav Sheshes: *Kohen she-shimmesh be-tumah — chayav misah bidei Shamayim o ein chayav misah bidei Shamayim?* — is this transgression deserving of divine death, or not? Because the question is: on what basis do his fellow priests crack open his head? Rav Sheshes responds: *tanisuha* — the answer is in the *Mishnah* itself, and the question can be resolved by reasoning from it.

### Lashing Logic

If we say he is *chayav misah bidei Shamayim*, then *nishvkei de-liktil bidei Shamayim* — let God handle it. Why do the priests act? And yet if we say he is not *chayav misah bidei Shamayim* — the *gemara* presses back in the other direction as well. *Midei dumi de-amar Rachmana patur ve-anan katlinan leh?* — could it be that God exempts him and we execute him without any underlying sense of *chiyuv misah?* Surely that cannot be right either.

The *gemara* raises the case of *kippah*: *mi she-lakah ve-shanah beit din machnisim oto la-kippah* — one who is flogged and repeats his transgression is placed in the *kippah* and caused to die. But surely he is not formally *chayav misah* for the transgression that earned him lashes. The *gemara* pushes back: *Rachmana patrei ve-anan katlinan leh?*

The answer given is that of Rabbi Immi citing Reish Lakish: *be-malkut she-nitnah le-karet askinan* — we were discussing specifically lashings that are given for a sin that is *chayav karet*. The person is ultimately a *bar katla*, deserving of death at some level. That is exactly how the case of *kippah* was explained earlier. So too, the underlying assumption in all these cases is that there must be some form of *chiyuv misah* or *chiyuv karet* lurking beneath the surface.

---

## Death Framework

### Stolen Vessel

The *gemara* now conducts a rapid review of all the *Mishnah*'s cases against this framework. *Ve-ha-gonev et ha-kasvah* — what about stealing the *kli sharet*, the sacred vessel? Rav Yehudah said: *bi-kheli sharet askinan, u-remizah, velo yavo'u lirot ke-vala et ha-kodesh va-yamuto* — we connect it to the *pasuk* of "swallowing up the holy thing, and they shall die." There is a textual link to death even here.

### Cursing Kosem

*Ve-ha-mekalel et ha-kosem* — and what of cursing with the prognosticator, the *kosem*? This was not addressed when the *Mishnah* was first introduced, so the *gemara* addresses it now. *De-tani Rav Yosef: yakeh kotzam et kosmo* — Rav Yosef taught in a *baraita* that the *kotzam* should smite the *kosmo*, meaning God. *De-machzi ke-mevarekh et ha-Shem* — it resembles blasphemy. Thus, even if not formally *chayav misah*, the act is sufficiently proximate to blasphemy that some connection to the death penalty is implied.

### Karet Focus

*Ve-ha-boel aramit?* — and what of *boel aramit*, the case that opened the entire discussion? *Akriyuh le-Rav be-chelmeih ve-akriyuh li-kra* — the *pasuk* was read to Rav in his dream, and he remembered his tradition. Rashi, commenting on this passage, makes explicit what the *gemara* had only gestured toward earlier: *akriyuh le-Rav be-chelmeih — yikharet Hashem — amar: bar karet hu* — they read to Rav in his dream *yikharet Hashem*, and he said: this man is subject to *karet*. Whereas the *drasha* earlier had focused on the loss of status among scholars and the inability to bring offerings, the *rishonim* — and Rashi here — insist that the operative reading must emphasize the *karet* dimension of the verse. The principle of *kanayim pogim bo* cannot be coherently grounded without assuming some form of *chiyuv karet* or *chiyuv misah*.

### Chiyuv Mitah

The *gemara*'s overall posture, then, is this: it remains somewhat uncertain whether to read all these cases as requiring a clear *chiyuv misah* or as demonstrating that we can at times impose death even without it. But the consistent thrust of the *gemara*'s analysis has been to find, in each case, some textual or logical hook that ties the transgression to at least a heavenly death or *karet*. In the case of *boel aramit*, that hook is the word *yikharet* in the verse from Malachi. In the other cases, the connections vary — whether through *pesukim* about swallowing holy things and dying, or through proximity to blasphemy — but the pattern is consistent: the *gemara* refuses to endorse extrajudicial lethal action against someone unless there is, at some level, a basis for regarding him as deserving of death.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 83

## Tamei Kohen & Avoda

### Kanaim Pogim Bo Setup

The daf begins at the bottom of 82b, picking up in the midst of the *mishna*'s discussion of *kana'im pogim bo* — cases where zealots may strike down a transgressor without formal trial. One example that emerged, though not placed explicitly under the *kana'im pogim bo* rubric, concerns a *kohen* who performs the *avoda* while in a state of *tumah*. The *mishna* relates that his fellow *kohanim* would remove him and crack his skull open. The question the *gemara* is wrestling with is what the jurisprudential basis for this extreme extrajudicial response is: does it reflect an underlying *chiyuv misa bidei shamayim* — that heaven regards this transgressor as deserving death — and therefore the zealots are given license to act? Or does the opposite inference follow — if God is going to punish him, why must human beings intervene?

### Gemara's Position

The *gemara*'s inclination is firmly toward the former reading: the very fact that extra-legal killing is permitted, or that colleagues may strike the offender down, signals that at some level we recognize the act as one deserving of death — specifically, death at the hands of heaven. The burden now falls on the *gemara* to defend this position.

### Intermediary Avodot

A *breita* is introduced as a challenge. The *breita* enumerates a series of *avodot* that are not *gmar avoda* — not a final, completed act of service, but intermediate stages in the offering process: *hayotzek*, pouring the oil on a *mincha*; *habolel*, mixing the oil in; *hapotet*, breaking the baked *mincha* into pieces; *hamoleach*, applying salt before placing it on the altar; *hamenif*, waving it; *hamagish*, pressing the *mincha* to the corner of the altar; *vehamessader et hashulchan*, arranging the showbread on the table (whose actual offering consists of burning the incense atop it each *Shabbat*); *hameitiv et hanerot*, cleaning out the *menorah* lamps — notably not the lighting itself, which for a separate reason is not classified as *avoda* at all; *vehakomet*, taking the handful of the *mincha*; and *vehamikabel hadam*, catching the blood of the *korban* before it is thrown.

For all of these intermediary acts performed *bechutz* — outside the *Beis Hamikdash* — one is *patur*, exempt from the punishment of *shchutei chutz* and its *karet*. And now, at the top of 83a, the *breita* continues: one is similarly not liable *lo mishum zarut velo mishum tumah* — neither because a *zar*, a non-*kohen*, performed the *avoda*, nor because a *tamei kohen* performed it — and *velo mishum mechusar begadim* and *velo mishum rachatzat yadayim veraglayim*. In all these cases, when the act is merely an intermediate stage, there is no liability.

## Responses & Defenses

### Negative Prohibition

The *gemara* presses the inference: if the *breita* says that when an *avoda tama* — a final, complete act of service — is performed, one *is* liable, what exactly is that liability? *Mai lav misa?* Presumably *misa bidei shamayim*, since the whole list revolves around *misa* or *karet*. The *gemara* attempts to deflect: *lo belav* — perhaps it means only a simple negative prohibition, not death. The listing in the *breita* of liability for a completed act does not necessarily prove that the specific case of a *tamei kohen* rises to *misa bidei shamayim*.

### Secondary Challenge

But the *gemara* immediately recognizes a problem with this deflection. If the liability even for a completed *avoda* performed by a *tamei kohen* is only a *lav*, then the *breita*'s statement that there is *no* liability for an intermediary act implies that there would not even be a negative prohibition for such an intermediate act — no violation whatsoever. Yet another *braisa* directly addresses this: *azharah leyotzek ubolel minayin* — how do we know there is a negative prohibition for pouring oil and mixing, specifically when the *kohen* is *tamei*? The answer given is the verse *kedoshim yihyu velo yechalelu* — they shall be holy and they shall not desecrate. When *tamei*, they lack the status of *kedoshim*, and this verse thus supplies a negative prohibition even for the intermediate acts.

The *gemara* attempts another retreat: perhaps this *azharah* is only rabbinic in force, with the verse functioning as a mere *asmachta*. But the *gemara* is not satisfied to leave the matter there.

### Explicit Braita

A direct challenge is lodged: *meisivei* — we have an explicit *braisa* that states *ve'eilu hein shebemisa*, the following incur *misa bidei shamayim*, and that list explicitly includes *tamei sheshimesh* — a *tamei kohen* who performs the *avoda*. The *gemara* concedes: *tiyuvta*. This is a definitive refutation of the position that the *tamei kohen*'s liability is only a *lav*. The *kohen* who is *tamei* and performs the *avoda* is indeed *chayav misa bidei shamayim* — which simultaneously justifies the license given to his colleagues to intervene and coheres with the broader structure of the list, in which completed *avoda* incurs *karet* or *misa bidei shamayim* while intermediary acts incur only a negative prohibition.

## Full Braita List

### Braita Opening

The *gemara* now turns to examine the entire *braisa* in full — *gufa*, let us look at the body of the text. The *braisa* opens: *ve'eilu shebemisa* — the following carry the penalty of *misa bidei shamayim*.

### Teruma Cases

The first two entries concern eating *teruma*. *Ha'ochel et hatevel* — one who eats *tevel*, grain from which *teruma* has not yet been separated, is *chayav misa bidei shamayim*. Then, *vekohen tamei she'achal terumah tehorah* — a *kohen* who is *tamei* and eats *teruma* that is *tehorah* is likewise *chayav misa bidei shamayim*, for although a *tahor kohen* may eat *teruma*, a *tamei kohen* eating *tehorah teruma* is a serious violation. The third entry is *vezar she'achal et hateruma* — a non-*kohen* who eats *teruma*. The parallel between a *zar* and a *tamei kohen* is already emerging here as a structural motif.

### Avodah Cases

Continuing the parallel: *vezar sheshimesh* — a non-*kohen* who performs the *avoda* in the *Beis Hamikdash*, and *vetamei sheshimesh* — a *tamei kohen* who performs the *avoda*. Both are on the list.

### Extended Cases

The *braisa* then extends to more attenuated forms of *tumah*: *vetvul yom sheshimesh* — even a *tvul yom*, one who has immersed in the *mikvah* but for whom nightfall has not yet come, so the *tumah* has not been fully removed, still carries a residual *tumah*, and performing the *avoda* in this state is *chayav misa*. Then *umechusar begadim* — a *kohen* who is not wearing the *bigdei kehuna*, and *umechusar kapparah* — one whose *tumah* requires not only immersion and nightfall but also a *korban* the following morning, such as a *zav*. Until that *korban* is brought, he retains a status of *tumah*, and performing *avoda* renders him *chayav misa*. Finally, *veshelo rachatz yadayim veraglayim* — a *kohen* who has not washed his hands and feet before performing the *avoda*.

### Non-Mita Violations

The *braisa* then pivots to a category of violations that *do* desecrate the *avoda* — rendering the service invalid — yet do not incur *misa bidei shamayim*, only a simple negative prohibition. These are *shtuyei yayin* — a *kohen* who is intoxicated, *parua rosh* — a *kohen* whose hair has grown wild beyond thirty days, and — as a separate group — performing the *avoda* as an *arel* (uncircumcised *kohen*), as an *onen* (one in the immediate state of mourning after a family death), or while sitting rather than standing. All of these invalidate the *avoda* and constitute a *lav*, but the *kohen* is not *chayav misa bidei shamayim*.

### Baal Mum & Meila

Two additional cases are subjects of dispute. Regarding *ba'al mum* — a *kohen* with a physical blemish — *Rebbi* holds that performing the *avoda* is *bemisa*, for the blemish removes him from the category of a valid officiating *kohen* much as *tumah* does. The *chachamim*, however, maintain that it is only *be'azhara*, a simple negative prohibition. A second dispute concerns *hameizid bemeila* — one who intentionally commits *meila*, misappropriating consecrated objects. This is somewhat distinct from the *kohen*-service cases, but *Rebbi* again holds it is *bemisa*, while the *chachamim* say it is only *be'azhara*. As the *gemara* notes, this dispute is relevant to an earlier discussion of *hagonev et hakasva* — stealing a *kli sharet* — which also appeared under the *kana'im pogim bo* framework, and sits more comfortably with *Rebbi*'s position.

## Ochel Tevel Derivation

### Tevel Question

Having enumerated the full *braisa*, the *gemara* proceeds to examine each entry and establish its scriptural basis. The first: *ha'ochel et hatevel minalan* — how do we know that eating *tevel* incurs *misa bidei shamayim*?

### Lo Yechalelu Source

*D'amar Shmuel mishum Rabbi Eliezer* — Shmuel said in the name of Rabbi Eliezer, directly addressing this: the verse states *velo yechalelu et kodshei benei Yisrael et asher yarimu laHashem* — they shall not desecrate the sanctified things of Israel, that which they will separate as *teruma* to God. The context of the verse is *teruma*, but the *derasha* pivots on the word *yarimu* in the future tense: *ba'atidim litrom hakatuv medaber* — the verse is speaking about that which is *yet to have teruma taken from it*, i.e., *tevel*. Eating *tevel* is thus a violation of this verse. This also accounts for the *Rambam*'s ruling that the prohibition of *misa* applies to *tevel* only before *teruma* has been separated, not to grain from which *teruma* has been taken but *ma'aser* has not yet been separated.

### Chillul Connection

But this verse establishes only that there is a prohibition. How do we derive *misa bidei shamayim* specifically? *Veyalif chillul chillul miteruma* — through a *gezera shava* on the word *chillul*: the verse here uses *yechalelu*, while a verse concerning *teruma* eaten by a *tamei kohen* states *umetu vo ki yechalleluhu* — they shall die when they desecrate it. Since both verses use the language of *chillul* and both concern *teruma* (one actual, one yet to be separated), we derive: *ma halan bemisa af kan bemisa* — just as there it is *misa*, here too it is *misa*.

### Teruma vs Notar

A challenge is immediately raised: why learn *tevel* from *teruma*? There is also a *chillul* connection to *notar* — the verse states *ki et kodesh Hashem chillel* regarding leftover sacrificial meat, and *notar* carries *karet*, not *misa bidei shamayim*. One might therefore argue: *mah halan bekaret af kan bekaret* — perhaps the *ochel tevel* incurs *karet*, not *misa*.

The *gemara* responds that learning from *teruma* is more cogent — *mistabra miterumah hava lei lemilaf* — because of the multiple points of correspondence between *tevel* and *teruma*. First, *tevel* and *teruma* share the same name: one is actual *teruma*, the other is grain destined for *teruma*. Second, neither applies in *chutz la'aretz*, whereas *notar* arises in the context of *korbanot* which are not brought outside *Eretz Yisrael*. Third, both admit of *heter* — *tevel* can be fixed by separating *teruma*, and the *tamei kohen* can be fixed by immersing in a *mikvah*; *notar*, once it has become *notar*, cannot be rectified. Fourth, in both cases the verse uses *yechalelu* in the plural (*berabbim*), whereas *notar* uses the singular *chillel*. Fifth, both apply to grain (*peirot*) and not to *korbanot*, whereas *notar* is specific to sacrificial contexts. Finally, neither *tevel* nor *teruma* can acquire the status of *pigul* or *notar*, as they are not *korbanot*.

The *gemara* does press the counter-argument: one could also argue for learning from *notar* — *sheken psul ochel*, the food item itself is *pasul* in both cases (*tevel* and *notar*), unlike *teruma tehorah* eaten by a *tamei kohen* where the *teruma* is perfectly valid; and *ein lo heter bemikvah*, neither *tevel* nor *notar* can be rectified by going to a *mikvah*, whereas the *tamei kohen* can. These are two genuine points of comparison to *notar*. The *gemara* resolves that the points connecting *tevel* to *teruma* are simply more numerous: *hani nefishei*.

### Ravina's Gezerah Shava

Ravina adds an additional — and in a sense dispositive — consideration: *chillul derabbim mechillul derabbim adif*. Setting aside all the substantive comparisons, the words are identical: *lo yechalelu* appears both in the *tevel* verse and in the *teruma* context. That lexical identity constitutes a proper *gezera shava*. This is what anchors *tevel* to *misa bidei shamayim* rather than to the *karet* of *notar*.

## Tamei Kohen Teruma

### Veshomru Source

The *gemara* now addresses the second entry in the *braisa*: *vekohen tamei she'achal terumah tehorah minalan* — how do we know that a *tamei kohen* eating *tehorah teruma* is *chayav misa bidei shamayim*? Again, Shmuel provides the source: *minayin lekohen tamei she'achal terumah tehorah shehi bemisa bidei shamayim?* The verse states *veshamru et mishmarti velo yisu alav cheit umetu vo* — they shall keep My charge, they shall not bear sin on account of it, and they shall die because of it — and the continuation is *ki yechalleluhu*. The context of this passage is *tumah* and the keeping of *mishmarti*, which the *gemara* associates with *teruma* (based in part on Rashi's observation that the *pesukim* describe the progression from *tvila* and *ha'arev shemesh* to eating *teruma*, and that after sunset but before the morning *korban*, the only thing newly permitted is *teruma*, not *korbanot*). The verse thus explicitly supplies the punishment of *misa* for a *tamei kohen* who eats *teruma*.

It is worth noting the full arc of this *limud*: it was precisely this verse's *chillul* language — *ki yechalleluhu* — that served as the anchor for the *gezera shava* through which we derived *misa* for eating *tevel*. So the *tevel* derivation above was itself dependent on establishing the *teruma* case here, which is now being derived directly from its own verse.

### Tehorah Requirement

The *gemara* notes a critical limitation embedded in the verse: *tehorah ein tmeiah lo* — the *misa* penalty applies only when the *teruma* itself is *tehorah*. If both the *kohen* and the *teruma* are *tamei*, there is no *misa*. This follows from Shmuel citing Rabbi Elazar: *umetu vo ki yechalleluhu* — the death penalty is triggered by *desecration*, and *perat lazu shemechulelet ve'omedet* — the verse excludes the case where the *teruma* is already desecrated, already *tamei* in its own right. The act of a *tamei kohen* eating already-*tamei teruma* does not constitute a new act of *chillul*, and therefore the *misa* penalty does not apply. One might wonder how the *tamei kohen* can eat *tehorah teruma* without rendering it *tamei* through contact — the *gemara* implies scenarios such as someone else placing it in his mouth, or grain that never came into contact with liquid after harvest and therefore could not contract *tumah* in the first place.

## Zar Eats Teruma

### Rav's Position

The next entry in the *braisa* is *vezar she'achal et haterumah* — a non-*kohen* who eats *teruma*. Here a striking dispute emerges. Rav states: *zar she'achal et haterumah lokeh* — a *zar* who eats *teruma* receives lashes. The use of *lokeh* rather than any heavier formula implies that *misa bidei shamayim* is not incurred — the punishment is only the negative prohibition and its associated flogging.

### Challenging Rav

Rav Kahana and Rav Assi challenge Rav directly: why not say *bemisa*? They point to the very verse that just established the *tamei kohen*'s liability. The *pesukim* read: *veshamru et mishmarti velo yisu alav cheit umetu vo* — carrying the explicit penalty of *misa* — and the very next verse states *vechol zar lo yochal kodesh*, no non-*kohen* shall eat *kodesh* (i.e., *teruma*). The juxtaposition of these two *pesukim* would seem to extend the *misa* of the first verse to the prohibition stated in the second.

### Rav's Defense

Rav deflects by pointing to the verse separating these two *pesukim*: *ani Hashem mekadeisham* — I am God who sanctifies them. This phrase, Rav argues, *hifsik ha'inyan* — creates a paragraph break, closing out the discussion of the *tamei kohen* and beginning a new independent topic. The *zar*'s prohibition against eating *teruma* therefore stands alone, without any *misa* appended to it from the prior *pasuk*. This is, as the *gemara* acknowledges, a reasonable reading of the text.

## Zar Eats Teruma (II)

### Meisivei Challenge

The *gemara* raises an objection from the very *braisa* we have been analyzing: *ve'eilu hein shebemisa zar ha'ochel et hateruma* — the *braisa* explicitly lists a *zar* eating *teruma* among those who incur *misa bidei shamayim*. This appears to be a direct contradiction of Rav's position.

### Rav as Tanna

The *gemara* resolves this by invoking the principle *masnisa derav ka ramis? rav tanna hu ufaelig* — you are challenging Rav from a *braisa*? Rav occupies the transitional generation between *tanna'im* and *amora'im* and is entitled to dispute a *mishna* or *braisa*. Rav maintains that whatever the *braisa* asserts, the scriptural basis for extending *misa* to a *zar* who eats *teruma* cannot be adequately grounded in the *pesukim* as he reads them.

## Avodah Performers

### Zar Verse

The *gemara* turns to *vezar sheshimesh* — the non-*kohen* who performs the *avoda* in the *Beis Hamikdash*. Here there is no need for derivation or *gezera shava*: *dichsiv vehazar hakarev yumos* — the Torah states in three explicit words that a *zar* who draws near to perform the service shall die. This is among the most direct statements of *misa* in the entire *parasha* of *avodah*.

### Tamei Avodah

The case of *vetamei sheshimesh* — a *tamei kohen* who performs the *avoda* — now receives its derivation in the *gemara*'s own voice, as elaborated by Rav Chiya bar Avin in a question posed to Rav Yosef. *Minayin letamei sheshimesh shehu bemisa?* The relevant verse is *dabru el Aharon ve'el banav veyinazru mikodshei benei Yisrael velo yechalelu et shem kodshi* — they shall separate themselves from the holy things of Israel and not desecrate My holy name. The context is explicitly *tumah*: the verse forbids *avodah* while *tamei* but does not itself state the penalty. However, the verse uses the language of *chillul* — *yechalelu* — and *veyalif chillul chillul miteruma*: we have already established that by *teruma* the verse states *umetu vo ki yechalleluhu*, linking *chillul* to *misa*. Thus: *mah halan bemisa af kan bemisa* — just as the *tamei kohen* eating *teruma* is *chayav misa*, so too a *tamei kohen* performing the *avoda* is *chayav misa*. And the logic is compelling: if eating *teruma* while *tamei* is *misa bidei shamayim*, all the more so is performing the *avoda* while *tamei*.

### Notar Alternative

The *gemara* again raises the challenge: *veneilaf chillul chillul minotar* — why not derive from *notar*, where the verse similarly states *ki et kodesh Hashem chillel*, yielding *karet* rather than *misa*? The concern is *mah halan karet af kan karet*.

### Teruma Superior

The *gemara* again resolves that learning from *teruma* is superior — *mistabra miterumah hava lei lemilaf*. The points of comparison are the same as before but now tailored to the *avodah* context: *sheken guf tamei* — both cases involve the *person* being *tamei* (as opposed to *notar* where the issue is with the object), and *mikveh berabbim* — both can be resolved by *mikvah* immersion, and both use *yechalelu* in the plural. The counter-argument — that *notar* and *avoda* share the quality of *kodesh panim* (inner sanctity of the *Beis Hamikdash*), and that *pigul* and *notar* are both relevant in the *avoda* context but not in *teruma* — is noted. But as before, the *gemara* resolves: *chillul derabbim chillul derabbim adif* — the identical language of *yechalelu* connecting the *avoda* verse and the *teruma* verse is the decisive anchor.

## Extended Tamei Cases

### Tvul Yom Case

With the core cases established, the *gemara* extends the analysis to progressively more attenuated forms of *tumah*. *Tvul yom sheshimesh* — a *kohen* who has immersed in the *mikvah* but for whom nightfall has not yet arrived, rendering him a *tvul yom* with only residual *tumah* — is also *chayav misa bidei shamayim* for performing the *avoda*. The source is a *braisa* in which Rabbi Simai asks: *remez letvul yom she'im avad chilel minayin?* — how do we know that a *tvul yom* who performed the *avoda* has *desecrated* it, rendering the service invalid? The verse cited is *kedoshim yihyu leloheihem velo yechalelu*. The *gemara* notes that we do not need this verse to establish the basic prohibition against a fully *tamei kohen* performing *avoda*, since that is derived more explicitly from *veyinazru mikodshei benei Yisrael*. The surplus verse — *kedoshim yihyu velo yechalelu* — is therefore applied: *tenahu inyan letvul yom*, it extends the prohibition to the *tvul yom*. The verse establishes that even the *tvul yom* desecrates the *avoda* by performing it.

From there, *veyalif chillul chillul miteruma*: since the verse again employs *yechalelu*, we connect it to the *teruma* verse's *umetu vo ki yechalleluhu*, and derive *mah halan bemisa af kan bemisa* — the *tvul yom* who performs *avoda* is *chayav misa bidei shamayim*. The *gemara* does not revisit the *notar* alternative here, having already established the priority of the *teruma*-based *gezera shava*.

### Begadim Requirement

The *braisa*'s inclusion of *mechusar begadim* — a *kohen* not wearing the prescribed *bigdei kehuna* — is derived from a verse cited by Rabbi Abahu in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, with some transmitting it in the name of Rabbi Elazar berabbi Shimon. The verse is *vechagarta osam avnet* — you shall gird them with the sash — followed by *vehaysa lahem kehunah lechukat olam* — and it shall be for them an eternal priestly ordinance. From this, the *gemara* draws the foundational principle: *bizman shebigdeihem aleihem kehunasam aleihem* — when their garments are upon them, their *kehuna* is upon them; *ein bigdeihem aleihem ein kehunasam aleihem* — when their garments are not upon them, their *kehuna* is not upon them. A *kohen* performing *avoda* without his vestments is therefore treated as a *zar* — *vehavu lehu zarim* — and since a *zar* who performs *avoda* is *chayav misa*, so too is the *mechusar begadim*.

## Extended Tamei Cases (II)

### Tosafot on Begadim

Tosafot raises a pointed question here (*hiksha Rav Yaakov deOrleans*): there is an explicit verse in *Parshas Tetzaveh* that seems to state directly that a *kohen* performing *avoda* without his *begadim* is *chayav misa* — why does the *gemara* need the circuitous derivation via the *ein kehunasam aleihem* principle? Tosafot answers that the explicit verse in *Tetzaveh* mentioning death is written in the immediate context of the *michnasayim* — the linen undergarments protecting against exposure of *ervah* — and could be read as pertaining specifically to that, not to the general principle of *mechusar begadim*. Rashi on the *pesukim* there actually reads the verse as referring to *misa* for lacking *bigdim* generally, but the Ramban sides with the *gemara*'s understanding as reflected in Tosafot: the *gemara* clearly derived the *mechusar begadim* case through the *ein kehunasam aleihem* principle, implying that the explicit verse was not taken to cover this case, and was instead understood as referring narrowly to the *michnasayim* context.

### Kappurim Case

The final *tumah*-related entry is *mechusar kippurim* — one whose *tumah* requires not only *mikvah* immersion and nightfall but also a *korban* brought the following morning, such as a *zav* or *zava*. Even after immersion, until the *korban* is brought, this person retains a status of *tumah*. The derivation is from the verse *vechiper aleha hakohen vetahera* — the *kohen* shall atone for her and she shall become *tehorah*. Rav Huna explains: *vetahera miklal shehi tmeiah* — the verse's statement that she becomes *tehorah* only upon atonement implies that prior to bringing the *korban* she retains a *tamei* status. And since we have already established that a *tamei kohen* performing *avoda* is *chayav misa bidei shamayim*, it follows that a *mechusar kippurim* who performs *avoda* is likewise *chayav misa*.

### Tosafot on Kappurim

Tosafot raises a natural question: why not simply say that *mechusar kippurim* is *tamei* and therefore — by the already-established rule that *tamei* incurs *misa* — he is *chayav misa*? The answer is that the *mechusar kippurim*'s *tumah* is even more attenuated than that of the *tvul yom*, and so one might have thought it insufficient to trigger the full *misa* liability. Tosafot therefore explains that we would not have been able to make this argument for *mechusar kippurim* had we not first derived via the *kedoshim yihyu* verse that even the *tvul yom*'s diminished *tumah* is sufficient. Once we know that a *tvul yom* — despite having already immersed — is still considered *tamei* enough for *misa*, the verse of *vetahera* that reveals a residual *tumah* for the *mechusar kippurim* can similarly be treated as establishing a cognizable *tumah* status, and the general rule applies.

## Final Mita Cases

### Washing Requirement

The *braisa*'s entry of *shelo rachatz yadayim veraglayim* — a *kohen* who has not washed his hands and feet before performing the *avoda* — has an explicit source: *dichsiv bevo'am el ohel moed yirchatzu mayim velo yamutu* — when they come to the Tent of Meeting they shall wash with water so that they shall not die. The verse itself states the penalty unambiguously.

### Wine Prohibition

Equally explicit is the source for *shtuyei yayin* — a *kohen* who is intoxicated and performs the *avoda*: *yayin vesheichar al tesht atah uvanecha itcha bevo'achem el ohel moed velo yamutu* — do not drink wine or strong drink when you enter the Tent of Meeting, so that you shall not die. Here again the *misa* is written into the verse directly.

### Hair Requirement

The case of *parua rosh* — a *kohen* who has allowed his hair to grow wild beyond thirty days — is not derived from the *Torah* itself but from a verse in Yechezkel: *rosham lo yegalechu ufera lo yeshaleichu* — they shall not shave their heads nor let their hair grow wild. The *gemara* then notes that the very next verse in Yechezkel states *veyayin lo yishtu* — and they shall not drink wine, juxtaposing the *parua rosh* prohibition with the *shtuyei yayin* prohibition: *itkesh parua rosh leshtuei yayin* — *parua rosh* is thereby linked to *shtuyei yayin* via *hekesh*. Since we know that *shtuyei yayin* is *bemisa*, by the same token *parua rosh bemisa* as well. The *gemara* is aware that ordinarily one does not derive *halacha* from the *nevi'im*, but notes that *chiyuv misa bidei shamayim* is not a practical *halacha* that we enact, and moreover, Yechezkel in such contexts is typically understood as articulating principles that were already established or implicit in the earlier tradition.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 84

## Intro & Context

### Pinchas & Kaneim

Daf 84 is the final daf of the *Nisrafim* chapter, and we pick up from the bottom of 83b. The preceding *sugya* was devoted to the fascinating topic of *kana'im pogim bo* and the story of Pinchas. In this connection, it is worth noting a striking passage in the *Yerushalmi* — which has not been examined here in detail — where it states explicitly that what Pinchas did was *she-lo birtzon chachamim*, against what the rabbis would have sanctioned. The *Yerushalmi* goes further: at the moment Pinchas acted, *Bnei Yisrael* were prepared to place him in *cherem*, and only a divine voice declaring *hinneni noten lo et briti shalom* forestalled that outcome. This reinforces a tension already present in the *Bavli*: while *kana'im pogim bo* is a recognized halakhic category, it operates entirely outside the framework of law — consistent with the *Bavli*'s own position that Zimri could have turned around and killed Pinchas as a *rodef*. The *Yerushalmi* is a fitting complement to that understanding.

### Mitat Bidi Shamayim

The previous daf was largely devoted to cataloguing cases in which one incurs *chiyuv misa bidei shamayim* — death at the hands of Heaven. This may have begun as a digression, but it connects organically to the broader theme of the chapter, which is concerned with court-imposed executions. Running alongside that discussion, the *Gemara* naturally surveys those transgressions that are punishable not by a human court but by Heaven. The vast majority of these cases involve either *avoda* in the *Beit HaMikdash* or matters of *kodshim*.

### Arel, Onen, Yoshev

Before moving into the specific analyses, the *Gemara* draws a general distinction: while a *zar* who performs the *avoda*, a *kohen* who is *tamei*, or a *kohen* not wearing the *bigdei kehuna* are all subject to *misa bidei shamayim*, there is a separate category of disqualified *kohanim* whose service is invalidated but who are not subject to *misa bidei shamayim*. These are: the *arel* (an uncircumcised *kohen*), the *onen* (a *kohen* who has lost an immediate relative on the day of death), and the *yoshev* (a *kohen* who performs the service while sitting rather than standing). All three invalidate the *avoda* but incur only a *lav* — a negative prohibition — not death at the hands of Heaven.

---

## Arel

### Yechezkel Source

Where does the prohibition against an *arel* performing the *avoda* come from? Rav Chisda states that this is not derived from the Torah of Moshe Rabbeinu at all. The source is Yechezkel ben Buzi: *kol ben nechar arel lev ve-arel basar lo yavo el mikdashi* — no foreigner who is either of uncircumcised heart (i.e., an apostate) or of uncircumcised flesh may enter God's sanctuary to serve. The fact that this is only known from Yechezkel and not from the written Torah is itself noteworthy, and indeed, the concern about including Yechezkel in the canon precisely because of such passages — where he supplements or appears to stand in tension with the Pentateuch — is well known. The presumption here is that the prohibition always existed and Yechezkel's prophecy revealed it; but the *Gemara*'s language — "we did not learn this from Moshe's Torah" — does not make that entirely clear.

### Arel as Lav

Since the prohibition against an *arel* performing the *avoda* is derived solely from Yechezkel, there is plainly no basis to say that it carries *misa bidei shamayim*. The *Gemara* characterizes this prohibition as a *lav* — a negative biblical prohibition — noting that the language of Yechezkel is indeed formulated as a prohibition, even though it is not a prohibition from the Pentateuch. Precisely because there is no Pentateuchal source, there is certainly no ground to assert a death penalty.

---

## Onen

### Onen Source

The case of the *onen* is derived from the verse concerning the *kohen gadol*: *u-min ha-mikdash lo yetzei ve-lo yechalel et mikdash elohav* — he does not leave the Temple and does not desecrate the sanctuary of his God. The verse addresses the *kohen gadol* specifically: because he is required to remain in the *Beit HaMikdash* even after the death of an immediate relative, his service there is not rendered a *chilul*. The implicit inference — *ha-acher*, the ordinary *kohen* who does not leave when he becomes an *onen* — would desecrate the service. While this does not state a negative prohibition explicitly, it clearly indicates that performance of the *avoda* in such a state is forbidden and renders the *avoda* invalid.

### Chilul from Teruma

Rav Adda bar Ahava poses a question to Rava: since the verse uses the language of *chilul* — desecration — should we not learn from a *gezeira shava* of *chilul-chilul* that the *onen* who performs the service is subject to *misa bidei shamayim*, just as a *tamei kohen* who eats *teruma* is subject to *misa bidei shamayim*? The verse in the context of *teruma* states *ve-lo yisu alav cheit u-mesu bo ki yichaleluhu* — the theme of *chilul* accompanied by death was indeed the basis established on the previous daf for deriving *misa bidei shamayim* in other cases. Should the same logic not apply here?

### Chilul Limitation

The answer is that no *gezeira shava* can be drawn here. The *chilul* by the ordinary *kohen* who is an *onen* is not explicitly stated in the verse — it is only inferred implicitly from the verse concerning the *kohen gadol*. The *Gemara* states: *ha miklal ka-ati*, it comes only from implication; *havi davar haba min haklal*, it is something derived by inference; *ve-chol davar haba min haklal ein danin oso bi-gzeira shava* — one does not apply a *gezeira shava* to something that itself was derived only by implication. Tosafot note that there are cases where a *gezeira shava* is applied even to an implicit derivation, but the principle stated here is that such an implicit inference does not provide a sufficiently firm basis to extend the penalty to *misa bidei shamayim*. The implicit derivation is strong enough to establish the *lav* — the verse's statement *ve-lo yechalel et mikdash elohav* perhaps serving as the biblical prohibition for any act that constitutes *chilul* — but not strong enough to import the death penalty from *teruma*.

---

## Yoshev

### Standing Requirement

The case of the *yoshev* — a *kohen* who performs the *avoda* while seated — is derived from the verse: *ki bo bachar Hashem elohecha mikol shvatecha la'amod l'sharets* — for God has chosen him from among all your tribes to stand and to serve. Rava, citing Rav Nachman, derives from this that the *sheirus* in the Temple is mandated specifically in a posture of *amida* — standing — and not *yeshiva*. This gives rise to a *lav*, even if only implicit in the word *la'amod*.

### Yoshev as Lav

As with the *arel* and *onen*, the *Gemara* makes clear that the *yoshev* who performs the *avoda* renders the service invalid — he is *mechallel ha-avoda* — but that this does not rise to the level of *misa bidei shamayim*. The basis is not sufficiently strong. The *Gemara* notes that the *braisa* used the language of *lav*, though the *lav* here may be understood as meaning simply that it is prohibited, whether or not it rises to the level of a formal biblical *lav*. Regardless, all agree there is no basis for a death penalty.

---

## Baal Mum (III)

### Rebbi's View

With *baal mum* — a *kohen* with a physical blemish who performs the *avoda* — we return to a dispute that connects directly to the subject of our *mishna*. It is interesting to observe that while the *Gemara* introduced this whole discussion as something of a digression, the issue of the *baal mum* circles back to the precise structural context in which we find ourselves: the debate over what punishment attaches to various forms of unauthorized *avoda*. Just as our *mishna* records a dispute between Rabbi Akiva and the *chachamim* regarding a *zar* who performs the *avoda*, so too there is a parallel dispute here regarding the *baal mum*.

Rebbi holds that a *baal mum* who performs the *avoda* is subject to *misa bidei shamayim*. The *chachamim* hold it is a *lav*, a negative prohibition, but not *misa bidei shamayim*.

---

## Structure

### Final Chapters

Having concluded the chapters on *sekila*, *sreifa*, and *hereg* — with all their attendant digressions into *ben sorer u-moreh*, *rotzeach*, *rodef*, *kana'im pogim bo*, and *misa bidei shamayim* — what remains is *chenek*, the final mode of execution. The chapter *Elu Hen Ha-Nechnakin* covers all cases punishable by strangulation. Following that comes the final chapter, *Chelek*, which opens with the principle that all Israel has a *chelek l'olam haba* — with the exception of those enumerated cases who do not. The progression is theologically coherent: the tractate moves through all four modes of court-imposed death, and then turns to the question of what happens afterward — affirming that even those executed by the court ultimately retain their portion in the World to Come, with only a narrow category of individuals excluded.

### Bavli vs Yerushalmi

Notably, the *Yerushalmi* reverses the order: it places *Chelek* before *Elu Hen Ha-Nechnakin*. This is genuinely difficult to understand. Why, after treating *nisrafin* and *hereg* and all those digressions, would one move immediately into an aggadic discussion of who has a *chelek l'olam haba* and only then return to *nechnakin*? Furthermore, many tractates conclude with an aggadic passage that serves as a fitting capstone, and the end of *Chelek* — which is largely *aggadic* in character — does provide such a conclusion for the tractate as a whole, whereas *Elu Hen Ha-Nechnakin* ends with a purely technical halakhic discussion of *chenek*. (One might note in this connection that *Makot* was originally part of *Sanhedrin*, and *Makot* does end with an *aggadic* passage, which would address the structural concern about a proper ending — but the point about the logical ordering of the chapters remains.) The *Bavli*'s sequence is far more coherent.

### Chanuk Default

*Chenek* is the default category: any capital offense that carries an unspecified death penalty in the Torah receives *chenek*. One might therefore expect *chenek* to be a very large category. In practice, it is not as expansive as one might think, since the Torah frequently specifies a mode of execution, and those specifications have all been assigned to their respective chapters.

---

## Chanuk Cases

### Chanuk List

The *mishna* lists those who are executed by strangulation: the one who strikes his father or mother (*hamakeh aviv v'imo*); the kidnapper (*gonev nefesh mi-Yisrael*); the rebellious elder (*zaken mamre al pi beit din*); the false prophet (*navi hasheker*); one who prophesies in the name of *avoda zara*; a man who commits adultery (*haba al eishet ish*).

The *zaken mamre* and *navi hasheker* categories will receive extended treatment, as they do not appear elsewhere in *Shas* in this concentrated form. For the case of *navi hasheker* in particular, the *Gemara* is going to wrestle with the question of what mode of execution applies — a dispute that connects directly back to the *zar sheshimesh* debate we are about to examine.

### Bas Kohen

The *mishna* also addresses the case of *zommei bat kohen u-vo'alah* — conspiring witnesses who testify against a *bat kohen*, along with the man involved. We know that a *bat kohen* who commits adultery receives *sreifa* — the verse states *et aviha hi mechalelet ba-eish tisaref*. Yet the verse continues *hi ba-eish tisaref* — she is burned, but her partner is not. He receives whatever he would have received had she not been a *bat kohen*, which is *chenek*. The conspiring witnesses who testified against her likewise receive *chenek* — not *sreifa* — even though what they intended to do to her was to bring about her burning. This is derived both from the principle *hi ba-eish tisaref* — that the unique punishment is hers alone — and from the verse *ka-asher zamam la'asot le-achiv, le-achiv ve-lo le-achoto*: the *midah keneged midah* principle applies to "his brother," not "his sister," meaning that when the intended punishment is one uniquely assigned to a woman and to no one else, the conspiring witnesses do not receive that same punishment but rather receive *chenek*.

---

## Baal Mum (III)

### Blemish Source

Returning now to *baal mum*: what is the source for Rebbi's position that a blemished *kohen* who performs the *avoda* is subject to *misa bidei shamayim*? The verse states: *el ha-paroches lo yavo ve-el ha-mizbeach lo yigash ki mum bo — ve-lo yechalel et mikdashai* — he shall not come to the *paroches* and shall not approach the *mizbeach*, for he has a blemish, and he shall not desecrate My sanctuary. Since the verse explicitly uses the language of *chilul* — *ve-lo yechalel* — Rebbi draws a *gezeira shava* of *chilul-chilul* from *teruma*: just as *mita bidei shamayim* attaches to *chilul* in the context of *teruma*, so too it attaches here. *Mah halan b'misa af kan b'misa*.

---

## Baal Mum (III)…

### Psul HaGuf

The *Gemara* now asks which source is the more apt basis for this analogy: should we learn *baal mum* performing the *avoda* from *tamei kohen* eating *teruma*, or from *nosar*? It makes more sense to learn from *teruma*: *shekein psul ha-guf* — both cases involve a personal disqualification residing in the person himself. The *tamei kohen* has a personal impurity; the *baal mum* has a personal blemish. *Nosar*, by contrast, is a defect in the object, not in the person. *Psul ha-guf mi-psul ha-guf*.

On the other hand, one might argue the reverse: learn from *nosar* rather than *teruma*, because *nosar* involves the *kodesh* context — it is *pnim*, within the *Beit HaMikdash*, the realm in which *pigul* and *nosar* are relevant concepts — whereas *teruma* is outside the *Beit HaMikdash*. A *baal mum* performing the *avoda* is an act entirely situated within the *Beit HaMikdash*, and therefore *nosar* is perhaps the better comparand.

The *Gemara* resolves this by noting that there is actually a still better comparand than either: a *kohen tamei* who performs the *avoda*. The case of *tamei kohen* serving shares both *psul ha-guf* — a personal disqualification — and the *mikdash pnim* context, since it involves the *Beit HaMikdash* where *pigul* and *nosar* are operative concepts. Learning *baal mum* from *tamei kohen* serving thus captures all the relevant features simultaneously, making it the most natural analogy.

### Chachamim View

What do the *rabanan* say in response to Rebbi? The verse in the context of *teruma* states *ve-meitu bo ki yichaleluhu* — and they shall die *bo*, "in it." The word *bo* functions as a limiting term, and the *chachamim* read it as *bo ve-lo be-vaal mum* — "in it," i.e., in that specific case of *teruma*, but not in the case of *baal mum*. Of course, the limiting word *bo* could in principle have been used to exclude any number of cases; why specifically exclude *baal mum*? Tosafot engage this question at length and discuss why it is *baal mum* rather than *tamei* that is excluded. The *chachamim*'s reasoning appears to be that the *baal mum* is less fully excluded from the Temple's sacrificial realm than the *tamei* kohen: the Torah explicitly states that a *baal mum* shares in the sacrifices that are brought — *chelek ke-chelek yochalu* — making it intelligible that his performing the *avoda* is not quite as severe as that of the *tamei kohen*, and thus does not carry *misa bidei shamayim*.

---

## Me'ilah

### Rebbi on Me'ilah

The next case is *me'ila* — the misappropriation of or deriving benefit from sanctified property. This connects back to our *mishna*, since one of the cases cited there under *kana'im pogim bo* was *gonev et ha-kisva*, stealing a Temple vessel (*kisva* being identified by the *Gemara* as a *kli shares*). *Me'ila* need not involve outright theft; any intentional derivation of benefit from sanctified property suffices. Here too, Rebbi holds that the violation of *me'ila bi-mezid* is punishable by *misa bidei shamayim*, while the *chachamim* hold it is merely a *lav*.

---

## Me'ilah (II)

### Cheit Comparison

What is Rebbi's basis? Rav Abba states: the verse in the context of *me'ila* uses the word *cheit* — *ve-chata bi-shgaga mi-kodshei Hashem* — and the verse in the context of *teruma* also uses *cheit* — *ve-lo yisu alav cheit u-mesu bo ki yichaleluhu*. Rebbi applies a *gezeira shava* of *cheit-cheit* from *teruma*: just as *teruma* carries *misa bidei shamayim*, so too does *me'ila*. *Mah halan b'misa af kan b'misa*.

### Chachamim Exclude

The *chachamim* again invoke the limiting word *bo* from the *teruma* verse — *ve-meitu bo ki yichaleluhu* — reading it as *bo ve-lo bi-me'ila*: the death penalty is confined to *teruma* and does not extend to *me'ila*. The same difficulty applies here as with *baal mum*: why does *bo* specifically exclude *me'ila* rather than some other case? The *Gemara* does not resolve this fully, and it remains an open question which case *bo* excludes and on what principled basis.

---

## Zar Sheshimesh

### Yishmael vs Akiva

The final entry in this list brings us back to our *mishna* directly: *zar sheshimesh be-mikdash* — a non-*kohen* who performs the Temple service. The *mishna* had recorded a dispute between Rabbi Akiva and the *chachamim*: Rabbi Akiva said *chenek*, and the *chachamim* said *misa bidei shamayim*. Note the structure: all the preceding debates were between *misa bidei shamayim* and a mere *lav*; here the dispute is elevated — *misa bidei shamayim* versus *chenek*, actual court-imposed execution. It is therefore necessary to understand why this particular transgression is treated differently. A *braisa* of the school of Rabbi Yishmael addresses this directly.

### Adas Korach

Rabbi Yishmael notes that the verse states *ve-ha-zar ha-karev yumat* — the stranger who draws near shall be put to death. The question is whether this means death by Heaven or death by the court. Rabbi Yishmael draws a comparison to the verse concerning *Adas Korach*: *kol ha-karev ha-karev el mishkan Hashem yamut* — all who draw near to the Tabernacle of God shall die. In that case, God Himself struck down those who drew near improperly. *Mah l'halan bidei shamayim af kan bidei shamayim*: just as there death came from Heaven, so too by the *zar* who serves, death is at the hands of Heaven. The conceptual parallel is precise: both cases involve someone unauthorized drawing near to a sacred space and being killed as a result.

### False Prophet

Rabbi Akiva disagrees. He too reads *ve-ha-zar ha-karev yumat* as specifying a mode of death, but he connects it by *gezeira shava* to a different verse — *ve-ha-navi ha-hu o cholem ha-chalom ha-hu yumat*, the verse concerning the false prophet. Both use the identical word *yumat*. *Mah l'halan bidei beit din af kan bidei beit din*: just as the false prophet is executed by the court, so too the *zar* who serves is executed by the court.

### Skila vs Chenek

If the *zar* is executed by the court, as Rabbi Akiva maintains, the question becomes: by which mode? Rabbi Akiva's position, as stated in the *braisa*, is that we learn from *navi sheker* — and *navi sheker*, according to the *rabanan*, is executed by *skila*. Thus Rabbi Akiva would say *biskila af kan biskila*, execution by stoning. Rabbi Yonatan ben Nuri, however, holds that *navi sheker* is executed by *chenek*, and therefore the *zar* too would receive *chenek*.

### Three Opinions

This produces a three-way dispute: Rabbi Yishmael holds *misa bidei shamayim*; Rabbi Akiva (as reported in the *braisa*) holds *skila*; Rabbi Yonatan ben Nuri holds *chenek*. But our *mishna* records Rabbi Akiva as saying *chenek* — which is Rabbi Yonatan ben Nuri's position in the *braisa*. The *Gemara* resolves this with the formula *trei tanna'ei aliba d'Rabbi Akiva*: there is a dispute among Rabbi Akiva's students about what Rabbi Akiva actually held. The *mishna* represents Rabbi Shimon's transmission of Rabbi Akiva's view — Rabbi Shimon said *chenek* in the name of his teacher Rabbi Akiva. The *braisa* represents other students who understood Rabbi Akiva to have said *skila*.

The underlying dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva is also clarified. Rabbi Akiva holds *donin yumat mi-yumat* — both the *zar* and the false prophet use the identical term *yumat*, and therefore the *zar* is executed by the court just as the false prophet is. *Ve-ein donin yumat mi-yamut* — one does not draw a *gezeira shava* from *yamut*, the different form used in the verse about *Adas Korach*. Rabbi Yishmael holds the opposite: *donin hedyot mi-hedyot ve-ein donin hedyot mi-navi* — we compare a common person who performs unauthorized service to another case involving common people acting outside their authorized role, namely *Adas Korach*, and we do not compare the common person to a *navi*, even a false one. Rabbi Akiva counters: *keivan she-hidiach ein lecha hedyot gadol mi-zeh* — since the false prophet leads people astray, he is in a category of the most ordinary sort of sinner rather than being a genuine prophet, so the comparison is valid.

What is particularly striking is the radical nature of Rabbi Akiva's position: virtually every other *mikdash*-related violation catalogued in this *sugya* is punishable by *misa bidei shamayim* at most, or simply a *lav*. Even a *tamei kohen* who enters the *Beit HaMikdash* incurs *karet*, not court-imposed death. The idea that a *zar sheshimesh* — which could be seen as a comparably serious transgression — would be punishable by the court strikes many as radical. And yet, this is precisely the position our *mishna* adopts, with the *chachamim* saying *misa bidei shamayim* and Rabbi Akiva saying *chenek*.

With this, *Elu Hen Ha-Nisrafin* concludes: *Hadran alach Elu Hen Ha-Nisrafin*.

---

## Makeh Aviv

### Source

The opening *mishna* of *Elu Hen Ha-Nechnakin* establishes *chenek* as the default mode of execution: *makat aviv ve-imo* — striking one's father or mother — carries the death penalty. The source is the verse *makeh aviv ve-imo mot yumat*, and the *Gemara* notes that any death penalty stated in the Torah without further specification is *chenek*.

### Makeh Not Killing

The *Gemara* immediately asks: perhaps *hamakeh* means to kill the parent — in which case this verse would be telling us that killing one's parent is punishable by *chenek*, whereas killing a stranger is punishable by the sword (*sayif*). Should we not be concerned that this would actually make the punishment *lighter* for the more severe act? The *Gemara* notes that this objection works well according to those who hold that *chenek* is a lighter death than *sayif*. But what of the opinion that *chenek* is the *weightier* form of death? According to that view, killing one's parent and receiving *chenek* would be a harsher punishment than killing a stranger and receiving the sword — which would be entirely coherent. The *Gemara* resolves the question from the verse *makeh ish ve-meit mot yumat* — when the Torah means to speak of killing, it says so explicitly: *makeh ... ve-meit*. And further: *o be-eiva hikahu be-yado va-yamut* — he struck him with anger and he died. The inference is: *shema mina kol heikha de-chtiv hikah stam, lav mita hi* — wherever the Torah says "striking" without adding "and he died," the reference is to striking alone, not to killing. *Makeh aviv ve-imo* therefore refers to striking a parent without killing him.

### Animal Comparison

The *mishna* on 84b states: *hamakeh aviv ve-imo eino chayav ad she-ya'aseh bahen chabura* — one is not liable until one makes a wound. The *Gemara* derives this from the verse that directly compares the smiting of an animal to the smiting of a person: *makeh nefesh behema yeshalmena nefesh tachat makeh adam yumat*. The comparison is precise: just as for a *behema*, the word *nefesh* indicates that some blood must have come out — since *nefesh* in this context connotes blood (*ki ha-dam hu ba-nefesh yechaper*) — so too for striking a parent, it is only when blood comes out, i.e., a *chabura* is made, that the prohibition is violated.

One might object: we use this same verse (*makeh nefesh behema... makeh adam yumat*) to derive the principle of *kim lei bi-drabbah minei*, and does it really mean that you are only required to pay damages for wounding an animal if blood comes out? The *Gemara* presses this: what if one throws stones at an animal and breaks its bones without causing any visible wound or bleeding — is one truly exempt from payment? Clearly not. So the *nefesh behema* cannot be establishing a *chabura* requirement for monetary liability in animal damage. The *Gemara* responds: since *nefesh* is in fact not needed to teach us anything about animal damages — one is obviously liable even without drawing blood — *im eino inyan le-nefesh behema, tenahu inyan le-nefesh adam*: redirect it to the case of *nefesh adam*, i.e., striking a parent. The *nefesh* comes specifically to teach that the offense against a parent requires a *chabura*.

### Refuah Exception

If *makeh* does not mean killing, and if the *chabura* requirement is the threshold, one might think any deliberate wounding of a parent transgresses the prohibition. The *Gemara* asks about the analogy further: *mah makeh behema li-refuah patur, af makeh adam li-refuah patur* — just as wounding an animal for the purpose of healing it exempts one from monetary liability, so too wounding a person in the course of medical treatment is exempt from the prohibition of *makeh avi ve-imo*. The comparison thus teaches a critical *halacha*: the prohibition does not apply when the wounding is for therapeutic purposes.

### Bloodletting

This immediately raises the question: *ben mahu she-yakiz dam le-aviv* — may a son perform bloodletting on his father? Bloodletting (*hakzat dam*) was a standard medical procedure in the *Gemara*'s world, involving deliberately opening a vein or cutting to release blood — an act that by its very nature produces a *chabura*. Two sources are offered. Rav Matna says: *ve-ahavta le-re'acha kamocha* — the general principle of love for one's fellow. This is a striking application of so broad a verse to override what would otherwise be a capital prohibition; yet here the *Gemara* deploys the principle to show that wounding a parent for therapeutic purposes is not what the Torah meant to prohibit. Rav Dimi bar Chinena offers the derivation from the *behema* comparison itself: *mah makeh behema li-refuah patur, af makeh adam li-refuah patur*.

One might argue — and a student raises a version of this point — that perhaps *makeh* itself, understood properly, would not apply to a therapeutic procedure: the word *makeh* implies an act of aggression or violation, not a surgical intervention performed with consent and for benefit. This is a conceptually powerful observation. The *Gemara* does not explicitly adopt this framing here, choosing instead to derive the exemption from the *behema* comparison and from *ve-ahavta le-re'acha kamocha*, but the intuition behind the question is sound.

### Accidental Wounding

The *Gemara* concludes with a case that is genuinely surprising. The *mishna* in the context of *Shabbos* permits using a sewing needle to remove a splinter on *Shabbos*, presumably because it is a permitted use of an implement. The *Gemara* asks: should we not be concerned that in the process of removing the splinter one might accidentally cause some bleeding — which would render one liable for *chilul Shabbos*? The answer given is *hatam me-kalkeil* — there, causing blood to come out is a *me-kalkeil* act, a destructive act, which is exempt from *Shabbos* liability. But the *Gemara* then raises a further question about removing a splinter from someone else in a non-*Shabbos* context: if one accidentally causes a *chabura* while performing what is otherwise a beneficial act — extracting a splinter from a friend — is that a *shiggas lav* of *makeh* the person? The *Gemara*'s conclusion is that it is indeed treated as a *shiggas lav*, even though the intent was entirely beneficial and the wound was unintended.

This conclusion is genuinely puzzling. The language of *eino miskaven* — unintentional action — would normally suggest exemption, and the therapeutic purpose would seem to fall under the *li-refuah patur* rule. Why this case constitutes a *shiggas lav* — even an accidental one — when the intent was beneficent and the blood came out as an unwanted byproduct, is not resolved at this point in the *sugya*. The *Gemara*'s treatment seems to rest on the fact that the bleeding, while unintended, was not incidental to the purpose of the act in the same way that bloodletting is the *point* of the therapeutic procedure. Because the splinter removal is aimed at something other than the blood — the blood is a possible but not necessary or desired byproduct — it may not fall under the rubric of *makeh li-refuah*. Whether this is fully coherent will be reviewed when the *sugya* continues.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 85

## Wounding vs. Medical Care

### Wound Requirement

The daf opens in the middle of a discussion concerning *makei av ve'imo* — one who strikes a parent — and the requirement that the act produce a *chaburah*, a wound. The prohibition is not triggered by a mere blow; there must be actual physical injury.

### Yerushalmi: Permanent vs…

An interesting debate in the Yerushalmi concerns whether this wound requirement demands a *permanent* injury or whether any drawing of blood — even the minimal sort that would constitute a wound for purposes of *Shabbos* — suffices. From the Bavli's treatment of the subject, it is clear that the latter, more lenient threshold applies: any meaningful blood loss qualifies.

### Bavli: Medical Procedures

The Bavli raises a related and more practically charged question: what about drawing a parent's blood for medical purposes, such as therapeutic blood-letting, or accidentally causing bleeding while removing a thorn or splinter? At one point the Bavli seems to permit such procedures; yet elsewhere it records that certain *Amoraim* refused to allow their sons to perform even thorn removal on them, fearing that the son might inadvertently draw blood and thereby commit what would be a *shogeg* on an *issur sekilah*. If it is a third party rather than a parent, the concern is somewhat lesser — a *shogeg* on an *issur malkus* — but a concern nonetheless.

### Tosafos: Psik Reisha

This raises an immediate difficulty. If the son does not *intend* to draw blood, why should there be any concern at all? The general principle is that an *eino miskavein* — an unintended act — is not prohibited, provided the result is not a *definite* consequence. Tosafos addresses this directly: the cases under discussion must involve circumstances where the drawing of blood would be a *psik reisha* — a certain, inevitable outcome of the procedure being performed. Once the result is inevitable, the actor cannot claim lack of intent to shield himself from liability.

### Surgical Intent Question

Even granting the *psik reisha* analysis, one would have thought that the *context* of a medical procedure fundamentally redefines the nature of the act. The *havah amina* — the intuitive preliminary assumption — of the Gemara seems to be that performing a procedure for health purposes, or invoking the principle of *ve'ahavta l're'acha kamocha*, ought to remove the act entirely from the category of *makeh*. A physician who wounds in order to heal is not, conceptually, in the same category as one who wounds to harm.

### Third Party Surgery

What makes the Gemara's concern all the more striking is that it extends even to cases involving a *third party* — not a parent at all. Surely one cannot argue that surgery on a stranger is conceptually forbidden as an act of striking. The Gemara appears to grant that for a third party the context ought to reshape the legal category entirely; yet the concern persists, at least formally.

### Mekalkel and Tikkun

The Gemara resolves the related *Shabbos* dimension by invoking the concept of *mekalkel* — a destructive act that achieves no constructive purpose. For *Shabbos*, a prohibited labor (*melachah*) requires a *tikkun*, a constructive outcome; an act that is purely destructive (*mekalkel*) does not trigger the Shabbos prohibition. This is precisely why removing a splinter on Shabbos, even if blood is drawn, does not violate the Shabbos prohibition — the act is *mekalkel*, not constructive.

### Shabbat vs. Parent

However, this *mekalkel* reasoning cannot be imported into the domain of interpersonal injury. By a parent — or by any friend — the entire *problem* is precisely that one is injuring them, that one is *mekalkel* the other person's body. The *mekalkel* character of the act is not a defense; it is the very essence of the offense. Thus the resolution that works for *Shabbos* offers no relief in the context of striking a parent or friend.

### Rabbi Shimon: Wounding

The Gemara then raises Rabbi Shimon's position, which holds that wounding is inherently *mekalkel* — not because of contextual framing but by its very nature — and therefore would never constitute a forbidden *melachah* on *Shabbos* on those grounds. At most, it could be characterized as a *melachah she'einah tzerichah l'gufah* — a labor performed without need of the labor itself. The large *Tosafos* in *Hilchos Shabbos* works through the implications of *mekalkel* and *melachah she'einah tzerichah l'gufah* according to Rabbi Shimon's view, though those details are peripheral to our immediate topic.

### Strange Conclusion

The Gemara's ultimate conclusion is genuinely strange: by *Shabbos*, the act is permissible because it is either *mekalkel* or *eino miskavein* — unintended — and *Shabbos* has specific requirements of intent and constructive purpose. But with respect to a parent, or even with respect to a friend, the act fundamentally remains problematic. The *Rif* records the same ruling, noting that the *Amoraim* would not allow their sons to remove thorns because of the risk of drawing blood — without offering a further explanation. One would have expected that context of medical care or repair would entirely preclude the category of *makeh*; yet the Gemara declines to draw that conclusion.

---

## Son as Shaliach Beis Din

### Rav Sheshes' Question

The Gemara now turns to a question posed to Rav Sheshes: what if the *beis din* were to appoint a son as its *shaliach* — its agent — to administer lashes to a father who has been condemned, or to pronounce a *cherem* upon him? This question was raised earlier in the daf as a hypothetical; here it surfaces as a formal legal inquiry. In the case of cursing, one would need to assess whether the precise formulation used in a rabbinically administered *cherem* would even technically constitute the biblical prohibition of a son cursing a father — a question that depends on the separate debate regarding whether *shem hameforash* is required. But putting those details aside, the core question is: does court appointment provide the son legal cover to perform acts that would otherwise render him liable?

### General vs. Specific Lic…

Rav Sheshes' interlocutor first challenges the premise: since when does *anyone* have permission to hit or curse a fellow Jew? The general prohibition against striking and cursing another person applies universally. The answer is that the agent of the court operates under a specific mandate — the court's appointment provides the necessary license. For a normal person acting as *shaliach beis din*, this license is real and operative. The more interesting question — and the one the Gemara is really pressing — is whether such a license would function when the agent is the *son* of the condemned, and whether *beis din* appointment could, in principle or in fact, grant the son that standing. One might frame the distinction not merely as a question of whether the court *would* make such an appointment, but whether such an appointment would be halachically effective — whether the halacha could ever recognize the son in that role vis-à-vis his own father.

### Kvod Shamayim Override

The Gemara's answer invokes *kvod shamayim* — the honor of Heaven. Just as a normal person may perform acts in defense of Heaven's honor that would otherwise be prohibited (the Gemara alludes to the principle of *ein chochma ve'ein tevuna ve'ein eitza neged Hashem*, and to related contexts such as *kana'in pog'in bo*), so too the son, when acting in the capacity of defending Heaven's honor through his court mandate, may be permitted. This framing is noteworthy. Rather than grounding the permission in the formal legal mechanism of *shelichut* — agency — the Gemara frames it in terms of *purpose*: what is the actor trying to accomplish? This parallels the earlier discussion about medical procedures, where the Gemara likewise focused on the purposive context of the act. Equally noteworthy is that the Gemara draws no distinction between a son and a third party in this framework: just as a stranger may act for *kvod shamayim*, so may a son.

### Mechilta Derivation

The Gemara then raises a challenge from a *Mechilta*. The *Mechilta* addresses the question of how we know there is a prohibition against hitting at all — specifically, against hitting a parent. The source it identifies is the verse *lo yosif lehakoso maka raba* — the court-appointed lash-giver is commanded not to give extra lashes beyond the prescribed amount. From this, the *Mechilta* reasons: if even one who has explicit license to administer lashes is commanded not to administer *extra* lashes, how much more so is someone who had no license to strike in the first place absolutely prohibited from doing so?

### Mechilta Interpretation

The initial reading of the *Mechilta* suggests a specific application: the person who is "commanded to give lashes" refers to the general *shaliach beis din*, while "the person who is never commanded to give lashes" refers specifically to a son vis-à-vis his father — someone who would never be assigned that role. This would directly answer Rav Sheshes' question: a son is never given the court's license to strike a father, and therefore remains under an absolute prohibition.

### General Prohibition

The Gemara rejects this reading. *Aidei va'aidei lo shna b'no v'lo shna acher* — the *Mechilta* is not drawing a distinction between a son and a third party at all. Rather, it is establishing the *general* prohibition against hitting any fellow Jew. The reasoning is straightforward: when a court-sanctioned lash-giver may not give extra strikes, we derive by *kal va'chomer* that one with no such sanction at all may not strike anyone. The relevant distinction is not son versus stranger, but authorized strike versus unauthorized strike. *Kan b'makom mitzvah, kan shelo b'makom mitzvah* — the distinction is between a case where there is a *mitzvah* to administer lashes and one where there is none.

Parenthetically, this is worth noting: the same generic prohibition that forbids any Jew from hitting another Jew — derived from *lo yosif lehakoso* — also serves as the source for the specific prohibition against a child striking a parent. The two are grounded in the same textual derivation.

---

## Execution & Gavra Katila

### Father at Execution

The Gemara introduces a new case: a father is being led out to execution — *hayotzei leihareg* — and his son comes and strikes him, and also curses him. The son's motivation is understandable: he may wish to publicly dissociate from his father's crime, or the sin may have been perpetrated against the family itself. Regardless of motivation, the ruling is that the son is *chayav* — liable.

### Third Party Exempt

By contrast, if a third party — a stranger — strikes and curses this condemned man, he is *patur* — exempt. Even though striking and cursing a fellow Jew would ordinarily be prohibited and punishable (by lashes or monetary compensation, depending on the circumstances), in this case the stranger incurs no liability.

### Son vs. Third Party

This asymmetry demands explanation. If the condemned man has lost some legal status — if his impending execution changes his standing in any significant way — why should that change affect the third party but not the son? And conversely, if the condemned man retains sufficient legal standing to protect him from a stranger's blow, why should the son not benefit from the same protection?
