### Rav Chisda: Resistance

Rav Chisda offers the first answer. The case under discussion is one where the condemned man is *mesarvin bo latzeit* — actively resisting, refusing to cooperate in being led to his execution. He is grabbing onto things, fighting back, making the process impossible. The court's agents need to use force to move him, and in the course of doing so they may strike him and possibly shout at him in terms that technically constitute a *kelalah*. A stranger acting as a court agent has explicit license to use such force. The son, however, is never assigned that agency role — and therefore lacks the license. This neatly answers our earlier question: the son cannot function as the court's agent in such matters, and that is precisely what distinguishes him from a third party here.

### Rav Sheshes: No Resistan…

Rav Sheshes, however, re-reads the case. He interprets it as involving a situation where there is *no* resistance — the condemned man is cooperating fully and is being led quietly to his execution. In that scenario, there is no court mandate to use force, and the third party is not acting as a court agent. So why, on Rav Sheshes' reading, is the stranger *patur*? The answer must be something more fundamental about the condemned man's legal status itself.

Rav Sheshes invokes the concept of *gavra katila* — "a dead man walking." The condemned man is legally regarded as already dead, and this status fundamentally alters the legal consequences of acts committed against him. Just as a pot hurtling toward the ground has, in some sense, lost its value before it even reaches the floor (an analogy the Gemara in *Bava Kamma* explores), so too a man hurtling toward execution may have lost the legal protections normally afforded a living body.

### Exemption from Payment

But the Gemara pauses before fully accepting this. If the person is *gavra katila*, one might exempt the third party from *nezek* — physical damage — since there is no longer monetary value in a body about to be destroyed. But what of *boshet* — embarrassment — and *tza'ar* — pain? Those are real and present even if the body is about to be forfeited. Rav Sheshes himself elsewhere rules that if one embarrasses a person who is sleeping and the person then dies before waking up, the perpetrator is still *chayav* to pay *boshet* — because the embarrassment falls upon the family. Here, too, the condemned man is alive and does experience pain and shame; the family remains present to collect. So the *gavra katila* status does not automatically eliminate all monetary exposure.

### Minor Injuries & Lashes

The Gemara then focuses the discussion. Rabbi Ami says in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *kol hakah she'ein bah shaveh prutah lokeh* — any blow that causes less than a *perutah*'s worth of damage results in *malkus* rather than monetary payment, since there is nothing to compensate. This raises the question: if the third party is *patur*, and the act was a blow causing less than a *perutah*'s worth of damage, should the stranger not receive lashes for the underlying prohibition of striking a fellow Jew?

### Damages vs. Transgression

The Gemara clarifies: *mai patur dekamar patur mimamon* — when the text says the third party is *patur*, it means *patur* from monetary payment. This seems like a surprisingly deflated reading of "exempt," but the Gemara's apparent logic is as follows: *boshet* and *tza'ar* may well be payable; *nezek* — physical damage — is not, because the body has, in the relevant legal sense, no ongoing monetary value. This parallels the dropped-pot scenario: damage to something already in the process of destruction has no compensable value.

But this raises an acute problem: if the stranger is merely exempt from *mamon* — monetary payment — while the son is described as *chayav*, does this mean the son is *chayav b'mamon*? That seems absurd — if the body has no monetary value for the third party, why would it have monetary value for the son? The Gemara resolves this: *ella b'dino* — when the son is called *chayav*, it means *chayav misa*, liable to the death penalty for striking his father. The stranger is *patur* not merely from money but from *malkus* — and the reason requires further elaboration.

### Oseh Ma'aseh Amcha

The Gemara now introduces the governing principle. The stranger is *patur* because the verse states *ve'nasi b'amcha lo ta'or* — do not curse a *nasi* among your people — from which is derived the general prohibition against cursing any Jew. The operative word is *b'amcha* — "among your people," which the Gemara reads as *b'oseh ma'aseh amcha* — one who acts in accordance with the conduct of your people. This condemned man, having committed a sin severe enough to warrant execution, is no longer within the category of *oseh ma'aseh amcha*. The prohibitions against cursing and striking, which are grounded in the shared community of Israel, no longer protect him.

This principle raises deep questions about its scope and application. What degree of transgression removes a person from the category of *oseh ma'aseh amcha*? Is it limited to someone literally being led to execution — *mekuyam she'b'amcha*, in the narrower formulation of Rav Mari, meaning someone who has lost their legal right to remain alive — or does it extend to someone who is simply not observant? These questions will prove consequential.

With respect to *kelalah* — cursing — the exemption flows directly from the *nasi b'amcha* verse. With respect to *haka'ah* — striking — the Gemara derives the parallel exemption by way of analogy: *d'akish haka'ah l'kelalah*, hitting is linked to cursing. The two acts — verbal and physical assault — stand or fall together when the question is whether the victim falls within the protected community.

### Death & Cursing

But if the justification for exempting the stranger is that it is "as if" the condemned man is already dead — and Rav Sheshes' entire framework rests on this — then one must ask: does the same not apply to the son? The Gemara cites the upcoming *mishnah*, which teaches that cursing a parent *after death* remains prohibited and that the son is *chayav*. If the condemned father is legally "as if dead," the stranger is exempt because it is as if he is cursing a dead man — a dead man not being under the protection of *nasi b'amcha*. But the son remains *chayav* for cursing even a genuinely dead parent. The *gavra katila* equivalence to death therefore does not help the son: for the son, the prohibition against cursing and striking a parent extends even into death.

The Gemara attempts an answer: perhaps the father did *teshuvah*, in which case he reverts to the status of *oseh ma'aseh amcha* and the stranger would also be prohibited. But this creates the inverse problem — if the father did *teshuvah*, why is the stranger exempt? Any answer that works globally to explain the stranger's exemption undoes the son's liability, and any answer that explains the son's liability seems to pull the stranger back in. The Gemara cycles through these possibilities.

### Blood = Nefesh

Rashi provides the critical resolution regarding the hitting question. The *mishnah* states that striking a parent *after death* is *patur*. If the condemned father is legally treated as already dead, why is the son *chayav* for striking him? Rashi explains: the reason striking a parent after death is *patur* is specifically because the definition of a punishable strike requires *chaburah* — a wound — and a wound is defined by the drawing of blood. Blood represents *nefesh*, the life force. After genuine death, blood drawn from the body no longer carries that quality of *nefesh* — it is no longer "living blood." Therefore, there is no *chaburah* in the halachic sense, and no liability.

### Son Still Liable

Here, however, the condemned father is still biologically alive. The characterization of *gavra katila* is a legal fiction for certain purposes — but it does not change the physiological reality. The blood still pumps. Drawing blood from this man still constitutes a *chaburah* in the full halachic sense, because it is still taking living blood — *nefesh* — from a living body. The legal fictions of death that exempt the stranger from the general prohibitions of *nasi b'amcha* do not dissolve the biological reality that makes the son's act a genuine *chaburah*. The son therefore remains liable for both striking and cursing his condemned father: for cursing, because the prohibition applies even to a dead parent; for striking, because the strike is still a *chaburah* in the full sense since the blood is still biologically alive.

Rashi states this explicitly: *hayotzei leihareg it beh chaburah dechai hu ela desofo lamus* — the one being led to execution still has the quality of *chaburah* because he is alive; it is only that his end is death.

The conclusion, then, is two-fold. One reading of this entire passage — the reading based on Rav Chisda's approach, where the condemned is *resisting* — yields a clean answer to our earlier question: a son cannot serve as the court's agent to strike or curse his father, even under explicit mandate. The court's appointment simply does not create operative *shelichut* for a son in this domain. The other reading — Rav Sheshes' approach, where there is no resistance — yields a more complex picture grounded in the *gavra katila* status and the son's unique continuing obligation toward a parent that survives even after death.

Finally, the Gemara records: *amar Rabba bar Rav Huna vechen tana d'bei Rabbi Yishmael — lechol ein haben na'aseh shaliach l'aviv l'hakoto ul'kallelo*, chutz m'meisit. In general, a son cannot be made a court agent to strike or curse his father — except in the case of a *meisit*, one who seduces others to idolatry, regarding whom the Torah says *lo tachmol velo techaseh alav* — show no compassion, do not cover for him. In that case there is such an overriding mandate to eradicate the threat that even the son could legitimately fill that role. This implies that where the son genuinely serves as a recognized court agent — as in the *meisit* case — he would indeed be exempt. The general rule is simply that in virtually all other cases, the son will never be a recognized agent of the court for such purposes against his own father.

---

## Execution & Gavra Katila

*(continued)*

A parenthetical observation: the question of *oseh ma'aseh amcha* and how severely a parent's conduct must compromise their standing before it affects the obligations of *kibbud av va'em* and *shiva* is not merely theoretical. Some authorities have applied the *rasha* category to contemporary situations — for instance, ruling that a child need not sit *shiva* for a parent who was not *shomer Shabbos*. This application is highly questionable given the concept of *tinok shenishba* and the need to redefine who falls into the category of *rasha* in the modern context. A more straightforward approach to these situations is grounded in the general principle of *chayecha vechayei chaveirecha chayecha kodmin* — your own life takes precedence. Even within the framework of *kibbud av va'em*, the *poskim* note that while a child is expected to endure a remarkable degree of personal humiliation (as illustrated by the famous story of a mother publicly humiliating a rabbi who remained silent), this applies after the fact; a child is permitted — and perhaps obligated — to protect himself *in advance* from harm, even if doing so would cause embarrassment to a parent. The prior obligation to oneself is operative even within the parent-child relationship.

---

## Mishna Distinctions

### Mishna Overview

The *mishnah* now states explicitly what has been discussed throughout: *hamakeh aviv ve'imo eino chayav ad she'ya'aseh bahem chaburah* — one who strikes a parent is not liable unless he produces a wound. It then notes: *ze chomer bimekalel mibemakeh* — this is a stringency of cursing over striking. *Shehamekalel le'achar mita chayav, vehamakeh le'achar mita patur* — if one curses a parent after the parent's death, one is liable; if one strikes a parent after death, one is exempt, for the reasons Rashi explained: striking requires *chaburah*, and a wound requires living blood.

### Textual Excess

The Gemara now explains the source for the rule that cursing applies even after a parent's death. The verse in *Vayikra* (20:9) reads: *ki ish ish asher yekalel et aviv ve'et imo mot yumat aviv ve'imo kilel damav bo*. The verse concludes with a repetition — *aviv ve'imo kilel* — that appears redundant: we already know from the earlier part of the verse that one who curses a parent is put to death. What does this repetition add? The answer is: it extends the prohibition *le'achar mita* — even after the parent's death.

### Inferential Logic

The Gemara builds the inferential logic as follows. We know that striking a parent — *haka'ah* — is limited to cases where the parent is alive; the nature of the act requires a living body. One might therefore reason: cursing, too, should be limited to a living parent. Indeed, if anything, cursing should be *narrower* than striking in certain respects, since striking applies regardless of whether the parent is an *oseh ma'aseh amcha*, whereas cursing is limited by the *nasi b'amcha* requirement. Since striking — the apparently broader prohibition — does not apply after death, perhaps cursing — in certain ways the narrower prohibition — should also not apply after death.

### Textual Override

The Gemara rejects this inference. The extra repetition of *aviv ve'imo kilel* overrides the logical deduction. Precisely because one might have argued *kal va'chomer* that if striking does not apply after death, cursing — more limited in some ways — certainly should not, the Torah repeats the phrase to teach that cursing does apply after death. The logical inference is overridden by the explicit textual expansion.

### Rabbi Yoshiyah: Either P…

But wait — can the repetition of *aviv ve'imo kilel* simply be deployed for the *le'achar mita* derivation? This depends on whether the verse is "available" for that purpose. The Gemara notes that according to Rabbi Yoshiyah, the repetition is not available, because Rabbi Yoshiyah uses it for something else entirely. Rabbi Yoshiyah holds: when the verse says *asher yekalel et aviv ve'et imo*, one might have thought that the son is only liable if he curses *both* parents simultaneously. The repetition of *aviv ve'imo kilel* teaches otherwise — *aviv kilel* is enough, and *imo kilel* is enough — either parent alone suffices to incur liability.

### Rabbi Yonatan: Both Pare…

Rabbi Yonatan disagrees. He holds that a conjunctive *vav* can be read as either "and both" or "or either one," depending on context. Unless the text explicitly says *yachdav* — together (as in *sha'atnez*, where the Torah specifies *tzemer u'fishtim yachdav*) — the default reading is that either one suffices. Therefore, no special repetition is needed to teach that cursing one parent alone is sufficient. The repetition of *aviv ve'imo kilel* remains "available" according to Rabbi Yonatan, who uses it to teach the *le'achar mita* extension.

### After-Death Derivation

According to Rabbi Yoshiyah, who has used the repetition for the "either parent" derivation, where does the *le'achar mita* extension come from?

### Oseh Ma'aseh Amcha Intro

The *braita* in the course of this discussion also passes through the *oseh ma'aseh amcha* principle — the limitation that cursing applies only to one who acts as a member of the covenant community. This emerges as a kind of byproduct of the textual analysis, but it will become central in the subsequent discussion.

### Verse Allocation

The Gemara resolves the question of textual economy as follows. Rabbi Yoshiyah derives the *le'achar mita* extension from a different verse — the verse in *Shemot*, which states independently: *mekalel aviv ve'imo mot yumat*. This verse, which appears separately from the main passage in *Vayikra*, is available to teach the *le'achar mita* application. Meanwhile, the verse in *Vayikra* is, for Rabbi Yoshiyah, deployed to teach that each parent individually suffices. For Rabbi Yonatan, the *Shemot* verse is used to teach that daughters, *tumtum*, and *androgynos* are included among those who can incur liability — since no gender-specific language appears in that verse. And the repetition in *Vayikra* — *aviv ve'imo kilel* — teaches the *le'achar mita* extension. The Gemara thus works through the allocation of verses across the various derivations, ensuring that each *tanna* has a coherent source for each rule.

---

## Mishna Distinctions (II)

### Mishna Silence

A *braita* presses a question: if hitting is, in one dimension, *broader* than cursing — specifically because hitting applies regardless of whether the parent is an *oseh ma'aseh amcha*, whereas cursing does not — why does the *mishnah* fail to state this as a distinct ruling? The *mishnah* notes that cursing is more stringent than hitting in the dimension of *le'achar mita*. But it says nothing about hitting being more stringent than cursing in the dimension of *oseh ma'aseh amcha*. Why the asymmetric presentation?

### Linking Makeh & Kalal

The Gemara answers: the author of the *mishnah* holds *makkishin hakah l'kelalah* — hitting and cursing are linked by analogy. Since the general prohibition against cursing is bounded by *b'amcha* — *nasi b'amcha lo ta'or* — and since the prohibition against hitting is derived by linking it to cursing, both prohibitions share the same scope. Just as cursing applies only when the victim is an *oseh ma'aseh amcha*, so too hitting applies only when the victim is an *oseh ma'aseh amcha*. The two are not distinct in this dimension; therefore there is no asymmetry to report, and the *mishnah* is silent on this point because its author sees the two prohibitions as coextensive in scope.

---

## Oseh Ma'aseh Amcha Debate

### Kuti Braita 1

The Gemara now brings two conflicting *braitot* concerning a Samaritan — a *Kuti*. The first *braita* teaches: *Kuti atah metzuveh al haka'ato ve'ei atah metzuveh al kilelato* — you are prohibited against striking a Samaritan, but you are not prohibited against cursing him. Hitting remains forbidden; cursing does not.

### Kuti Braita 2

The second *braita* teaches the opposite allocation: *ei atah metzuveh lo al kilelato velo al haka'ato* — you are not prohibited against either cursing or striking a Samaritan. Both acts are permitted.

### Gerim Debate

The initial assumption is that this debate turns on a factual question about the status of Samaritans: are they *geirei emet* — genuine converts whose conversion was valid — or *geirei arayot* — "converts of the lions," whose forebears converted under duress out of fear of lions (as described in *Melachim II*) and whose Jewishness is therefore questionable? If they are *geirei emet*, they are Jews, and the prohibitions of striking and cursing would be operative — at least in principle. If they are *geirei arayot*, they are not Jews, and those prohibitions would not apply.

### Why Distinguish?

Even granting that the two *braitot* debate their Jewish status, it remains puzzling why the first *braita* would distinguish between hitting (prohibited) and cursing (not prohibited). If they are genuinely Jewish, both should be prohibited; if not, neither should be. What would justify the asymmetric result? The answer, one might suggest, lies in the nature of the two acts. Cursing — public denunciation — may serve a social purpose, reinforcing communal norms and boundaries, and therefore even if the Samaritan is halakhically Jewish, publicly condemning someone who does not follow rabbinic law may be permissible or even warranted as an expression of communal standards. Physical injury, however, cannot be justified on such grounds: regardless of a person's level of observance, inflicting bodily harm remains a moral and legal transgression in a way that verbal condemnation does not.

### Shor Evidence

The Gemara refutes the initial assumption. The *braita* itself indicates that both *braitot* treat Samaritans as halakhically Jewish: *hainu dekatni alah shor keyisrael* — the *braita* concludes that the Samaritan's ox is treated like a Jewish ox for purposes of tort law. Under the *mishnah* in *Bava Kamma*, a non-Jewish ox that gores a Jewish ox is liable for full damages, while a Jewish ox that gores a non-Jewish ox is entirely exempt — because the non-Jewish ox lacks the legal standing of its Jewish counterpart. If the Samaritan's ox is treated as a Jewish ox, it means both *braitot* assume that Samaritans are considered Jews. The debate between them cannot therefore be about whether they are *geirei emet* or *geirei arayot*.

### Real Dispute

The true dispute, the Gemara concludes, is not about the Samaritans' Jewish status — both *braitot* agree they are halakhically Jewish — but about the scope of the *oseh ma'aseh amcha* limitation and whether it applies equally to hitting and cursing.

### Linked View

One view holds *makkishin hakah l'kelalah* — hitting and cursing are linked. Since Samaritans, though Jewish, are not *oseh ma'aseh amcha* in the relevant sense (they follow different laws and belong to a distinct communal group), the *nasi b'amcha* limitation exempts from cursing — and since hitting is linked to cursing, it also exempts from hitting. Both acts are therefore permitted.

### Unlinked View

The opposing view holds that hitting and cursing are not linked in this respect. The exemption from cursing flows from the specific language of *b'amcha* in the cursing verse, which limits the prohibition to those who act as genuine members of the covenant community. But hitting does not share that textual limitation; its prohibition is grounded in a different source, and there is no reason to extend the *b'amcha* qualification to it. Physical injury therefore remains prohibited regardless of whether the victim is *oseh ma'aseh amcha*.

### Cursing Non-Observant

The principle now crystallizes: cursing a Jew who is not *oseh ma'aseh amcha* does not transgress the prohibition of *nasi b'amcha lo ta'or*. The person has placed themselves, through their conduct, outside the scope of that protection.

### Parent Application

The same principle extends to parents. If a parent is not *oseh ma'aseh amcha*, cursing that parent does not trigger liability under the *nasi b'amcha* verse. Whether striking such a parent is also exempt depends on the debate just outlined: those who link hitting and cursing would say yes, those who do not link them would say no.

### Logical Question

This generates a striking conclusion when read against the opening discussion of the daf. There, we found that even performing a medical procedure on a parent — even removing a thorn — was treated by the Gemara as problematic because of the potential for blood-drawing, and the rabbis in question would not allow their sons to perform such procedures. Yet here, at the close of the daf, we arrive at the position that if the parent is not *oseh ma'aseh amcha*, the prohibition against cursing that parent may not apply at all — and the prohibition against striking may also not apply, depending on one's view. The scope of these prohibitions, so severe at their core that they reach into medical procedures and past death itself, is nonetheless bounded by the community of observant practice in ways that are genuinely consequential.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 86

## Gonev Nefesh Intro

### Kidnapping Definition

The Mishnah on 85b concludes the laws of one who strikes a parent and transitions to the next capital offense under the category of *chenek*: *hagonev nefesh miYisrael*, the kidnapping of a fellow Jew. When we hear the word "kidnapping" today, our minds go immediately to ransom — holding someone captive in exchange for payment. But in the context of the *pesukim*, kidnapping was fundamentally about stealing a person to sell them as a slave.

### Yosef/Slave Trade

The paradigmatic case in the Torah is the story of Yosef. The brothers seized him and sold him off as a slave — and it is precisely this act that is commemorated with such anguish in the *Elleh Ezkerah* prayer. The historical slave trade operated in much the same way: captives were taken — sometimes as a byproduct of war, sometimes through deliberate raids — and then sold. The *gonev nefesh* prohibition addresses precisely this phenomenon.

### Tikkun Olam Limit

A related issue appears in Gittin, where one of the enactments made *mipnei tikkun olam* is that one may not pay an exorbitant sum to redeem a captive — the principle being that doing so only encourages further kidnapping, much as negotiating with terrorists emboldens further hostage-taking. The limit set is *yoter mikedei demaihen* — one may not pay more than the captive's standard market value. What is that standard? In the ancient world, it was the slave market price. If someone demands a ransom far beyond that, the community is forbidden to pay it, lest the practice be incentivized. Tosafot in Gittin raises various complications — what if it is a close family member, and so on — but the baseline principle is clear: the standard redemption price serves as the ceiling.

The *pasuk* that governs the capital offense reads: *ki yimatze ish gonev nefesh me'achiv mibnei Yisrael vehit'amer bo umacharo umet haganav hahu* — if a man is found having stolen a fellow Israelite, having made use of him, and having sold him, that kidnapper shall be put to death. Unstated execution (*stam mita*) means *chenek*, strangulation. The offense thus has three components: stealing, using, and selling — with the use serving as a condition rather than as the primary act. The core transgression is stealing and selling, with the *vehit'amer bo* functioning as contextual framing for what follows.

---

## Mishnah Requirements

### Reshut Requirement

The Mishnah states: *hagonev nefesh miYisrael eino chayav ad sheyachnisenu lirshuto* — one is not liable for kidnapping until one has brought the victim into one's own domain. This parallels the general law of *gneivah*, which requires some act of *kinyan* — an act demonstrating legal control — before liability attaches. However, there is a significant conceptual tension here, since one cannot technically perform a *kinyan* on a free person. Accordingly, some *Rishonim* suggest that the standard act of *hagbahah* — lifting the object — may be insufficient here. The *pasuk* says *gonev nefesh mibnei Yisrael*, which may imply a more substantive taking: literally bringing the person under one's control by moving them into one's domain. The Mishnah's formulation — *ad sheyachnisenu lirshuto* — supports this reading.

### Rabbi Yehuda Use

*Rabbi Yehuda omer: ad sheyachnisenu lirshuto veyishtamesh bo* — Rabbi Yehuda adds a further requirement: not only must the kidnapper bring the person into his domain, he must also make use of the victim. Rabbi Yehuda derives this from the *pasuk* itself: *vehit'amer bo umacharo* — he made use of him and then sold him. According to Rabbi Yehuda, this use must constitute at least a *shaveh prutah*'s worth. The *tanna kamma*, by contrast, requires some use but not necessarily to that minimum monetary threshold — even a use worth less than a *prutah* suffices. The *Rambam* rules in accordance with the *tanna kamma*.

### Own Son Debate

The Mishnah addresses a further case: *hagonev et beno* — one who kidnaps his own son. Rabbi Yishmael the son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka holds one liable (*mechayev*), while the *chachamim* exempt (*potrin*). The reasoning will be developed in the Gemara.

### Half-Slave Case

The Mishnah then turns to the case of *ganav mi shechetzyo eved vechetzyo ben chorin* — kidnapping a person who is half-slave and half-free, such as someone owned by two partners where one partner has freed his share. Rabbi Yehuda holds one liable; the *chachamim* exempt. This case is notable because the victim was not fully free to begin with, yet Rabbi Yehuda maintains that stealing and selling such a person is sufficient to incur capital liability.

One might ask whether the *purchaser* of the kidnapped person bears liability as well. The purchaser does not incur the death penalty, since that requires both stealing *and* selling, and the buyer has done neither. If, however, the buyer knows the person is free and takes possession knowingly, he would be transgressing the prohibition of stealing — participating in the enslavement of a free person — though he would not be liable for having sold him. There are thus two distinct prohibitions at play, which will be elaborated in the Gemara.

---

## Eimur Requirement

### Eimur Value Debate

The Gemara opens by asking: *vtanna kamma lo baey imur?* — how can the *tanna kamma* not require the use (*eimur*) of the victim, when it is explicit in the *pasuk*? The Gemara answers in the name of Rabbi Acha the son of Rava: the debate between the *tanna kamma* and Rabbi Yehuda concerns the *minimum* value of the use. The *tanna kamma* holds that even use worth less than a *shaveh prutah* suffices — any degree of use will do. Rabbi Yehuda requires use worth at least a *prutah*. Both agree the use requirement exists; they disagree on its threshold.

### Eimur Logic

This raises a deeper question: what is the conceptual purpose of the *eimur* requirement? Why should making use of the victim matter, given that the central prohibitions are stealing and selling?

The answer, it seems, is that the act of use creates the context of enslavement. Simply picking someone up and immediately transacting a sale might technically involve stealing and selling, but it does not fully transform a free person into a slave in the eyes of the perpetrator. When the kidnapper makes use of the victim — treats them as one treats a slave — he thereby defines the victim as a slave and himself as the one who has effected that transformation. The *eimur* is not about extracting monetary value from the victim; it is about creating the enslaving context. This explains why even a use worth less than a *prutah* satisfies the *tanna kamma*: what matters is not the monetary significance of the use but its qualitative character — that the kidnapper has treated this person as a slave. The *eimur*, on this reading, is what ensures that the kidnapper is not merely an incidental participant in a transaction but the one who has concretely enslaved this person.

### Pregnant Woman Case

Rabbi Yirmiyah poses a challenging question: *ganavo umacharo yashan* — what if he stole and sold someone who was asleep? And: *machar isha le'ubarrah mahu* — what if a man steals a pregnant woman and sells her specifically for the sake of her fetus, retaining ownership of the woman herself but conveying the fetus to the buyer?

These cases probe the nature of the *eimur* requirement. The fetus does not yet have an independent legal identity; the *pasuk*'s requirement that a born person be stolen and sold (*gonev nefesh me'achav mibnei Yisrael*) applies to those already born. So the woman herself is the one being stolen, but she was sold only insofar as her fetus was conveyed. Is that a valid *mechira* of the woman? And is the use of a sleeping person — who is entirely unaware of what is happening to them — a valid *eimur*?

The Gemara clarifies that the question is not whether the person can be used in some technical sense. For a sleeping person: *yashen dizaga aleih* — one lies on the sleeping person, using him as a cushion or rest. For the pregnant woman: *de'ukma be'apei zika* — one stands behind her as a windbreak, and because she is pregnant she provides greater protection from the wind, with the fetus effectively doing the work. So there *is* a technical use in both cases.

But the Gemara ends with *teiku* — the question remains unresolved. What is the deeper issue? It appears that the *eimur* is not merely a checkbox to verify. Rather, it functions to establish that the person has been enslaved — that the status of enslavement has been imposed upon them. If the victim is asleep throughout and never becomes aware that they are being treated as a slave, one might question whether the *eimur* has achieved its purpose of creating the enslaving context. Similarly, if what was sold is the fetus rather than the woman as such, even if she was technically "used," the nature of the sale does not reflect her enslavement. The question *yesh derech imur bekach o ein derech imur bekach* — is this a normal mode of *eimur* — really asks whether the use and the sale together constitute an act of enslavement, or merely a collection of technical acts that individually satisfy criteria but together fail to define the person as a slave. The *eimur*'s purpose is to ensure that the kidnapper is the one who has transformed a free person into a slave, and where the victim is wholly oblivious or the sale applies only to the fetus, that transformation may not have occurred in any meaningful sense. The question is left unresolved.

---

## Text Derivations

### Women/Gentile

The Gemara presents a *baraita*: the *pasuk* reads *ki yimatze ish gonev nefesh me'achiv* — if a *man* steals. One might think this applies only when a man is the kidnapper. How do we know a woman who kidnaps is also liable? A second *pasuk* reads *vegonev ish* — and one who steals a man — which drops the specification of the kidnapper's gender, thereby including a female kidnapper. But now it specifies the victim as *ish* — a man — which would seem to exclude a female victim.

This produces an impasse: one *pasuk* gives us any kidnapper but only a male victim; the other gives us any victim but only a male kidnapper. How do we know a woman is liable for kidnapping another woman, or for kidnapping a minor? The Gemara resolves this from a third formulation: *umet haganav hahu* — that kidnapper shall die — employing an inclusive formulation that encompasses all combinations. Whether kidnapper or victim is male or female, the prohibition applies.

It is worth noting that Tosafot raises a general question in this context: since the general rule is *kol ha-Torah kulah bilshon zachar ne'emar* — the entire Torah is written in the masculine — and we apply *huksha ishah le'ish* to extend all prohibitions equally to women unless context demands otherwise, why do we sometimes need a special derivation to include women? Tosafot engages this question in various places and offers different answers; the question is simply worth flagging here.

A second *baraita* adds: *echad hagonev et ha'ish ve'echad hagonev et ha'isha* — whether the stolen person is a man or a woman — since the *pasuk* says *nefesh*, which encompasses either. Additionally, *ve'echad ger ve'echad eved meshuchrar vekatan chayav* — a convert, a freed slave, and a minor are all included in the category of victims, since *me'achav* (his brothers) is not read so narrowly as to exclude these. All are "brethren" in the relevant sense.

### Slave Excluded

By contrast, *hagonev et ha'avadim patur* — one who steals a currently enslaved person is exempt. The question is whether this exemption derives from the word *me'achav* — brothers, from which slaves are excluded — or from the substantive nature of the crime, which requires the enslavement of a *free* person. Taking someone from one master and delivering them to another does not constitute the act of enslaving a free person; that person was already a slave.

### Sell to Family

A *baraita* teaches that one who sells the kidnapped person back to the victim's own father, brothers, or other close relatives is still *chayav*. This is challenged by a *tanna* who taught before Rav Sheshes: Rabbi Shimon's position, derived from the *pasuk* in Devarim (*gonev nefesh me'achav* — stealing from his brethren), is that one must actually remove the victim from the family's domain. If one sells him back to the family, one has not taken him *me'achav*, and one is therefore *patur*.

Rav Sheshes responds: the *baraita* you cited must be corrected to accord with Rabbi Shimon's view — the one who sells back to the family is *patur*. The Gemara then asks why this reading is necessary — perhaps the *baraita* and Rabbi Shimon reflect different opinions. The answer: *lo salka datach*. Rabbi Yochanan establishes the rule that an anonymous *Mishnah* follows Rabbi Meir, an anonymous *Tosefta* follows Rabbi Nechemyah, an anonymous *Sifra* follows Rabbi Yehuda, and an anonymous *Sifrei* follows Rabbi Shimon — all students of Rabbi Akiva, as opposed to the *midreshei halacha* of the school of Rabbi Yishmael. Since the *baraita* expounding the *pasuk* in Devarim is drawn from a *Sifrei* context, it must represent Rabbi Shimon's view, and therefore must be corrected to say *patur*.

Returning to the case of *hagonev et beno* — kidnapping one's own son — the Gemara asks what the *chachamim*'s reason for exemption is. Abaye answers: *kara ki yimatzei, prat l'matzuy* — the *pasuk* says *ki yimatzei*, implying that the stolen person is one who is "found" (i.e., discovered in a place they do not normally belong). A son who lives in his father's domain is already "found" there — he is not a person who is unexpectedly present in the kidnapper's possession. The closest parallel is the *mitzvah* of *shilu'ach haken*: the *pasuk* there says *ki yikarei* — if you chance upon a nest — and the same derivation of *prat l'matzuy* exempts one who is raising birds at home, since the nest is not "chanced upon" but is constantly available.

Rav Pappa challenges Abaye: the same logic should apply to one who commits adultery with a neighbor's wife if they live under the same roof and the woman is therefore constantly "available" to him. Abaye responds that he is not deriving from *ki yimatzei* in that *pasuk* at all, but from the phrase *venimtza beyado* in the *pasuk* in Shemot — *vegonev ish umacharo venimtza beyado mot yumat*. That phrase implies that the victim was "found" in the kidnapper's possession in a sense suggesting they did not belong there — i.e., the victim must be someone who would not normally be under the kidnapper's control.

Rava applies this to a practical ruling: *mikrei dardeki* — schoolteachers of young children — and *masnei rabbanan* — teachers of older students — are *kimtzuim biyadan dami*, treated as if the students are already in their possession, since the children are regularly entrusted to them. If such a teacher were to kidnap one of their own charges, they would be *patur* — which is admittedly striking, since these are precisely the positions of trust where such concerns are most acute.

---

## Half-Slave Debate

### Boshet/Brotherhood

The Mishnah's case of kidnapping a half-slave is illuminated by a parallel debate about *boshet* — embarrassment damages — which appears to produce a curious reversal of positions between Rabbi Yehuda and the *Rabbanan*.

The *baraita* cites the verse *ki yinatzu anashim yachdav ish ve'achiv* — when two men fight, a man and his brother — as the source for the obligation to pay *boshet*. From the word *achiv* (his brother), the *baraita* derives: *mi she'yesh lo achva* — only one who stands in a relationship of brotherhood can claim *boshet* payments. *Yatza eved she'ein lo achva* — a slave is excluded because slaves do not have legal brotherhood. What does this mean? Tosafot clarifies: it does not mean that biological ties are simply irrelevant. A convert, after all, is also severed from prior biological family, yet a convert's children are considered relatives to one another once they have converted. The point by slaves is different: the law never recognized the family structure of enslaved persons. Even a slave's children bore no legal familial connection to him. This reflected — and entrenched — the reality that slave families were routinely broken apart. Because a slave has no *achva* — no legally recognized brotherhood — Rabbi Yehuda holds there is no *boshet* payment for embarrassing one.

### Half-Slave Liability

The *Rabbanan* dispute Rabbi Yehuda on the *boshet* question: *achiv hu b'mitzvot* — a slave is still one's "brother" in the world of *mitzvot*, because a slave is obligated in *mitzvot* and thereby remains part of the Jewish community in a meaningful sense. Accordingly, the *Rabbanan* hold that slaves *can* claim *boshet* payments.

This produces the curious flip in the kidnapping context. The Gemara asks: *vehacha heichi darish Rabbi Yehuda* — how does Rabbi Yehuda read the kidnapping *pesukim* to arrive at his position that kidnapping a half-slave incurs liability?

Rabbi Yehuda reasons as follows. The *pasuk* says *gonev nefesh me'achav mibnei Yisrael* — stealing from his brothers among the children of Israel. *Me'achav* would, on his view, already exclude slaves (since slaves have no *achva*). *Bnei Yisrael* provides an additional exclusion. *Mi-Bnei Yisrael* — the prefixed *mem* — provides yet a third. Having already excluded slaves through *me'achav*, the additional exclusions of *Bnei Yisrael* and *Mi-Bnei Yisrael* now constitute *mi'ut achar mi'ut* — a double exclusion — and the principle is *ein mi'ut achar mi'ut ela l'rabos*: when the Torah is so insistent about excluding something that it excludes it twice, the effect is actually to *include* it. Thus Rabbi Yehuda winds up including the half-slave within the prohibition.

The *Rabbanan*, by contrast, do not read *me'achav* as excluding slaves at all — since *achiv hu b'mitzvot*, the slave retains brotherhood. For them, only *Bnei Yisrael* and *Mi-Bnei Yisrael* serve as exclusions — one for a full slave, and one for a half-slave. They therefore have two straightforward exclusions, and the half-slave remains exempt.

The irony is apparent: Rabbi Yehuda, who is more aggressive in excluding slaves from *boshet*, winds up via the *mi'ut achar mi'ut* principle including the half-slave in the kidnapping prohibition. The *Rabbanan*, who are more inclusive on *boshet*, wind up excluding the half-slave from the kidnapping prohibition. The positions appear reversed because the hermeneutical logic moves in opposite directions.

---

## Two Prohibitions

### Two Sources

Having established the elements of the crime, the Gemara asks: *azhara l'gonev nefesh minayin* — where is the prohibitory warning (*azharah*) against kidnapping? Rabbi Yoshiya says it derives from *lo tignov* in the Ten Commandments. Rabbi Yochanan says it derives from *lo yimachru mimcheras aved* — they shall not be sold as a slave is sold — the verse in Vayikra addressing the treatment of a Jew who sells himself into servitude. The Torah declares: *ki avadai heim asher hotzesi osam me'eretz Mitzrayim* — they are My servants whom I brought out of Egypt — and therefore *lo yimachru mimcheras aved* — they shall not be sold in the manner of slaves.

The Gemara resolves that these authorities do not actually disagree: *mar kachashiv lav d'geneivah u'mar kachashiv lav d'mechira* — one is identifying the prohibition against stealing a person, and the other is identifying the separate prohibition against selling a person. There are thus two distinct prohibitions. Capital liability requires the violation of both — stealing *and* selling — but each act is independently prohibited. This raises an interesting theoretical question: could one violate the prohibition of *lo yimachru mimcheras aved* without having first stolen anyone? For instance, if someone fraudulently represents a free person as their slave and "sells" them to an unknowing buyer who then takes possession — has the "seller" transgressed the prohibition against selling even absent the act of theft? This question is left open.

### Lo Tignov Context

The Gemara then presents a *baraita* establishing why *lo tignov* in the Ten Commandments refers to kidnapping rather than property theft. The *baraita* says: *atah omer b'gonev nefashos o eino ela b'gonev mamon* — you might think this verse speaks of property theft. The answer: *tze ulemad mishlosh esrei middos shehatorah nidreshet bahem* — go and learn from the thirteen hermeneutical principles, one of which is *davar halamed me'inyano* — a matter is understood from its context. What is the surrounding context? *Lo tirtzach, lo tin'af, lo tignov* — the preceding commandments are all capital offenses. Since the context is capital crime, *lo tignov* here must refer to a form of stealing that constitutes a capital crime — namely, kidnapping.

### Lo Tignovu Context

A second *baraita* establishes the complementary point for the verse in Vayikra: *lo tignovu* — in the plural — speaks of property theft. Again: *atah omer b'gonev mamon o eino ela b'gonev nefashos?* The same hermeneutical principle applies. The surrounding context in Vayikra is: *lo tishakru velo techachashu velo tignovu* — do not lie, do not deny, do not steal — a passage concerned with monetary matters and interpersonal deception rather than capital crimes. Therefore *lo tignovu* there refers to property theft, not kidnapping.

---

## Davar Debate

### Chizkiyah/Yochanan

Since there are two distinct elements of the crime — stealing and selling — the Gemara turns to the question of how testimony combining both elements functions. The specific framing involves *eidim zomemim* (false witnesses), but as the Gemara makes clear, the underlying question is when testimonies given by different sets of witnesses can be combined to establish liability.

*Eidei gneivah ve'eidei mechira* — two witnesses testify that the accused stole the victim, and two separate witnesses testify that he sold the victim. Both sets are subsequently proven to be *eidim zomemim* — contradicted by *hazamah*. The question: are they subject to the death penalty that they sought to impose? Chizkiyah says no; Rabbi Yochanan says yes. Chizkiyah holds *ke'Rabbi Akiva de'amar davar velo chatzi davar* — following Rabbi Akiva, who requires that testimony constitute a *davar*, a complete and legally operative matter, not merely a *chatzi davar*, a partial one. Neither set of witnesses alone testified to the complete crime; each testified only to one element. Rabbi Yochanan follows the *Rabbanan*, who accept *chatzi davar* — partial testimony can combine with other partial testimony to establish the complete crime.

The underlying issue before the *hazamah* question is: can two separate sets of witnesses, each testifying to only one element of the crime, combine to convict? For Chizkiyah, the answer is no, because each testimony standing alone has no legal effect — it proves nothing actionable. For Rabbi Yochanan, the testimonies combine and the full crime is established.

### Ben Sorer Moreh

The Gemara notes: *u'modeh Chizkiyah b'eidim ha'achronim shel ben sorer u'moreh she'huzmu she'neheragim* — Chizkiyah concedes that in the case of the *ben sorer u'moreh* (the wayward son), the *second* set of witnesses, if proven *zomemim*, are killed. Why? Because the *first* set of witnesses testified to an act — the initial theft and eating — that by itself was sufficient to administer lashes. Once the court accepted that testimony and administered lashes, the second testimony builds on something already legally operative. The second witnesses are not combining a *chatzi davar* with another *chatzi davar*; they are adding to a *davar* that was already complete in itself, advancing the matter to its capital conclusion. *Hanei kulla milta ka'avdi* — the second witnesses are doing something complete.

The Gemara then asks whether the same logic should apply to the witnesses who testified to the *gneivah* (theft) in the kidnapping case. If those witnesses already established liability for lashes — since *lo tignov* is an independent prohibition — then the second witnesses who testify to the *mechira* (sale) should be able to build on that accepted testimony, just as in the *ben sorer u'moreh* case.

### Lashes Acceptance

The question becomes: does the *gneivah* testimony, standing alone, give rise to lashes? A *baraita* records a dispute between Chizkiyah and Rabbi Yochanan on exactly this point — *chad amar lokin, chad amar ein lokin* — one says lashes are administered for the theft alone, one says they are not. The Gemara reasons that Chizkiyah is the one who says lashes *are* administered. The logic: since Chizkiyah holds that the two testimonies cannot combine to impose the death penalty, there is no basis to invoke the principle of *nitan l'azharas mitat beit din* — that a prohibition which can lead to a capital sentence does not give rise to lashes in lieu thereof. For Chizkiyah, since the theft testimony cannot lead to a capital conviction (because it cannot combine with the sale testimony), the theft transgression remains an ordinary *lav* for which lashes are appropriate. For Rabbi Yochanan, who holds that the two testimonies *do* combine and can produce a capital conviction, the theft prohibition is *nitan l'azharas mitat beit din*, and therefore no lashes are administered for it.

This creates the following internally coherent structure for each opinion. According to Chizkiyah: the theft testimony is accepted by itself and produces lashes; but the two testimonies do not combine for capital purposes; accordingly, the *eidei gneivah*, if proven *zomemim*, cannot be killed. According to Rabbi Yochanan: the theft and sale constitute a single unified capital offense; no lashes are administered for the theft alone; but the two testimonies fully combine, and if the *eidei gneivah* are proven *zomemim*, they are killed along with the *eidei mechira* as co-conspirators in the same capital case.

The question of the relationship between the theft and sale — whether they are two distinct acts or one unified crime — thus generates consequences across lashes, capital liability, and the treatment of false witnesses. Rav Pappa then clarifies the scope of the dispute. *Be'eidei mechira dechulei alma lo peligi deneheragim* — on the question of *eidei mechira* (the sale witnesses) alone becoming *eidim zomemim*, everyone agrees they are killed, because the theft witnesses testify to something that produces lashes, the court accepts that testimony, and the sale witnesses build on it entirely to bring about capital conviction. If the sale witnesses are lying, they are subject to the death penalty they sought to impose. *Ki peligi be'eidei gneivah* — the debate concerns only whether the *eidei gneivah*, if proven *zomemim*, are also killed.

Chizkiyah says they are not killed: *gneivah lechudei kai u'mechira lechudei kai* — stealing and selling are two independent legal acts, each standing alone. These first witnesses were simply part of a distinct court proceeding that resulted in lashes, not part of the capital case. Rabbi Yochanan says they are killed: *gneivah d'as'chalata d'mechira hi* — the theft is the beginning of the selling, the initiation of one unified capital crime. All the witnesses are part of the same capital proceeding, and the *eidei gneivah* who are proven false share in the liability of *eidim zomemim* for the capital offense.

---

## Separate/One Crime

### Separate Acts

Chizkiyah's position is thus that *gneivah* and *mechira* are two separate transgressions. This is consistent with his view that testimony regarding each one stands independently — each produces its own legal consequence, but neither is merely a component of the other. The first act (theft) is a violation of *lo tignov*; the second (sale) is a violation of *lo yimachru mimcheras aved*. Together they compound into a capital offense, but conceptually and procedurally they remain distinct.

### Unified Crime

Rabbi Yochanan's view is that the theft is conceptually the beginning of the sale — *as'chalata d'mechira* — and the entire sequence constitutes one unified capital crime. This is why no lashes are given for the theft alone (it is *nitan l'azharas mitat beit din*), and why the theft witnesses are treated as full participants in the capital proceeding, subject to the death penalty as *eidim zomemim* if proven false.

### Abaye Summary

Abaye summarizes the full landscape of agreements and disagreements. *Ha-kol modim b'ben sorer u'moreh b'eidim harishonim she'ein neheragim* — everyone agrees that the first witnesses in the *ben sorer u'moreh* case, if proven *zomemim*, are not subject to the death penalty. Their testimony was accepted for lashes alone; they can plausibly claim *le'halkoso banu* — we came only to have him lashed — and since they are not part of the capital proceeding, they do not receive the death penalty as *eidim zomemim*.

*Ve'ha-kol modim b'ben sorer u'moreh b'eidim ha'acharonim she'neheragim* — everyone agrees that the second witnesses in the *ben sorer u'moreh* case, if proven *zomemim*, are killed. Their testimony was built entirely upon the accepted first testimony and served exclusively to bring about capital conviction. *Hanei kulla d'var ka'avdi* — they did something complete and operative, aimed at execution.

*U'machlokes b'ben sorer u'moreh b'shnayim omrim l'fanenu ganav v'shnayim omrim l'fanenu achal* — the actual dispute between Chizkiyah and Rabbi Yochanan concerns a *ben sorer u'moreh* case where two witnesses testify to the theft and two others testify to the eating. This is a case of *chatzi davar*: neither testimony alone is sufficient to convict, and the debate about *davar velo chatzi davar* applies directly. This is where their disagreement operates.

---

## Sequential Witnesses

### Rav Assi Position

Rav Assi rules: *eidei mechira b'nefesh she'huzmu ein neheragim mishum she'yecholim lomar avdi macharti* — witnesses who testified only to the sale, and were proven *zomemim*, are not subject to the death penalty, because they can plausibly claim: "We were testifying that he sold his own slave." The testimony of sale, standing entirely alone without accompanying testimony of theft, does not establish any crime at all — for all the court knows, the person being sold was a legitimate slave. Not only does their false testimony not combine to impose capital liability, but the testimony is meaningless even to establish a lesser violation.

### After-Fact Combine

Rav Yosef notes that Rav Assi's ruling follows Rabbi Akiva's principle of *davar velo chatzi davar*. Abaye corrects him: this conclusion holds even according to the *Rabbanan*, who accept *chatzi davar* testimony. The *Rabbanan* only permit combination of two partial testimonies when *both* have been given and together they establish the complete crime. Here, the sale witnesses testified alone, without any corroborating theft witnesses. *Delo atu eidei gneivah* — the theft witnesses never came. Of course their testimony is meaningless — this is not a question of *davar* vs. *chatzi davar* at all. The Gemara responds: *tzricha d'af al gav d'atu l'vasaf* — the ruling is necessary for the case where the theft witnesses *subsequently* arrive. One might think: now that the theft has been established, can the court retrospectively combine the earlier sale testimony with the newly arrived theft testimony, and treat the sale witnesses as *zomemim* in a capital proceeding? The answer is no — and this is the operative ruling.

### Remiza/Signals

Why not? The Gemara acknowledges the argument: the sale witnesses could claim complete innocence, saying they had no idea theft was involved. The Gemara then addresses a case where *remiza* — signals — were observed. *De'ka meramze remuze* — the first witnesses and the second witnesses were seen signaling to one another, suggesting coordinated conspiracy. One might think that *remiza milta hi* — that such signaling is legally significant and establishes their complicity, making them liable as *eidim zomemim* once the testimony is combined in retrospect. The Gemara rules: *remiza lav klum hi* — signals are legally inconsequential. Unless the witnesses were part of a single coordinated testimony from the outset, their subsequent signals cannot transform what was initially innocent partial testimony into a capital conspiracy.

The practical implication is worth noting: a sophisticated conspirator who wished to avoid liability could arrange for the witnesses to testify sequentially rather than together. If the plot succeeds, the combined testimony convicts. If the witnesses are proven *zomemim*, only the sale witnesses will have testified to something that, by itself, threatened a capital outcome — and even that is mitigated by the *avdi macharti* defense. The *remiza* ruling forecloses the ability of the court to treat coordination as sufficient to unify what were legally separate acts of testimony.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 87

## Zaken Mamre Overview

### Opening Context

The daf before us, 87a, opens a sustained treatment of *zaken mamre* — the rebellious elder — which is among the most conceptually rich topics in all of Shas. It is here that the *zaken mamre* receives his primary discussion, and it is here that he is classified among those who receive *chenek*.

### Mishna & Pasuk

The *mishna* frames the rebellion of the *zaken mamre* as directed *al pi beis din* — against the authority of a properly constituted court. As support, the *mishna* cites the verse *ki yipale mimcha davar lamishpat*, "if a matter is hidden from you regarding judgment." This is somewhat puzzling. Later in the same passage, the Torah states explicitly *ha'ish asher ya'aseh b'zadon l'vilti shemo'a el hashofet* — the man who acts presumptuously, refusing to listen to the judge — making the context of rebellion against *beis din* entirely clear. It is worth noting that by *Ben Sorer u-Moreh*, the Torah specifies *al pi aviv v'imo* to indicate parental authority, because that specification is needed. Here the context seems self-evident. Yet the *mishna* still finds it necessary to anchor the law in a *pasuk*, which invites further reflection.

### Three Courts

The *mishna* then introduces a structural point of cardinal importance: *shlosha batei dinim hayu sham* — there were three *batei dinim* on *Har HaBayit* itself. This is distinct from the broader hierarchy of local and regional courts, a topic the *Yerushalmi* addresses at the outset of the *masechet*. Here we focus specifically on the courts within the Temple Mount. One *beis din* sat *al petach Har HaBayit*, at the entrance to *Har HaBayit*; one sat *al petach ha-Azara*, at the entrance to the *Azara*; and the third sat in *Lishkat HaGazit*, the Chamber of Hewn Stone — the seat of the *Sanhedrin* — which was built half within the *Azara* and half outside it.

### Rashi's Geography

*Rashi* clarifies the geography with precision. The first *beis din*, at *petach Har HaBayit*, is identified as *sha'ar hamizrachi she-p'nim min ha-chel lifnei Ezrat Nashim* — the eastern gate, situated inside the *chel* and before *Ezrat Nashim*. The second court was positioned further in, somewhere before *Ezrat Yisrael*. The third — *Lishkat HaGazit* — was, as *Rashi* states, *b'nuya b'toch Azara chetzyo b'kodesh v'chetzyo b'chol*: built within the *Azara* but spanning into the non-sacred area. The reason for this arrangement becomes clear from *Masechet Yoma*: it is forbidden to sit within the *Azara* itself, so the court was constructed straddling the boundary, permitting the judges to be seated in the permitted portion while still maintaining their connection to the sacred space of the *Beis HaMikdash*.

### Appeal Process

The *mishna* describes the dispute process with a particular stylization worth examining. When there was a legal disagreement in a local court, the dissenting voice — the individual who refuses to accept the ruling — presents the case upward. He says: *kach darashti ve-kach darshu chaverai, kach limadeti ve-kach limdu chaverai* — here is how I interpret it, and here is how my colleagues interpret it; here is what I have learned, and here is what they have learned. Notably, it is this dissenting figure who presents the case in full; the opposing majority does not appear to speak for itself.

When the *beis din* receives the appeal, the *mishna* says: *im sham'u, omrim lahem* — if they have heard, if they possess a tradition, they tell them. *Ve-im lav* — if they do not — the parties proceed to the next level. The language distinguishes pointedly between *kach darashti* and *kach limadeti*: the former reflects independent interpretive reasoning from *pesukim*, while the latter reflects received tradition.

### Tradition vs. Intellect

This distinction opens a profound structural question. Suppose the receiving court lacks an explicit tradition on the matter but is nonetheless unanimous — all its members agree, by reason and analysis, that the dissenter is wrong. May the dissenter be turned away on those grounds alone? Reading the *mishna* carefully, it appears not. The only thing that definitively ends the dissenter's ability to demand a higher ruling is an explicit tradition against his position. If the court's opposition rests purely on their own intellectual analysis — however unanimous — the dissenter may reply: "That is just your interpretation. Perhaps I am right and you are wrong." And he continues upward.

There is something both beautiful and demanding about this. Until the matter reaches the final arbiter, any individual may maintain, however outnumbered, that the majority is mistaken. This is not obstinacy that the law condemns — it is intellectual integrity that the law respects, so long as it does not cross into active defiance of the binding ruling.

### Final Authority

Once the case reaches *Beis Din HaGadol* in *Lishkat HaGazit*, the dynamic shifts entirely. *She-mimenu yetze Torah le-chol Yisrael* — from there Torah goes forth to all of Israel. The authority there is not merely majoritarian; it is constitutive. At that point, even if their ruling rests on reasoning rather than tradition, even if it is decided by vote, their decision is final and binding. *Mi-kach hora'ah yotzei.* This prompts a natural question: what if the *Beis Din HaGadol* itself votes and it is close — say, thirty-six to thirty-five? Presumably, normal principles of majority rule would apply there. The individual has exhausted his path of legitimate challenge. What is striking is the parallel: the famous case of Rabbi Eliezer ben Hyrcanus, who famously refused to be bound by majority vote and adhered to his tradition even against the *Beis Din* — which illustrates how powerful and rare it is when someone actually holds that position to its end. Once you reach *Beis Din HaGadol*, there must legally be a conclusion. Even if the dissenter is ultimately right, and even if everyone else is wrong, that court has the final say.

## Intellectual Freedom

### Teaching After Ruling

After the *Beis Din HaGadol* rules against him, the *zaken mamre* returns home. *Shana ve-limmed ba-derech shehaya lomed* — if he continues teaching in the manner he always had, he is *patur*, exempt. He may return and say openly: I know what *beis din* ruled. I believe they are wrong. Here is my reasoning, and here is why I believe the true *halacha* is otherwise — but of course, legally, you must follow their ruling. That is entirely permitted.

### Ruling vs. Opinion

The liability arises only *ve-im hora la'asos* — if he issues an active ruling directing people to follow his position rather than theirs. *She-ne'emar v'ha'ish asher ya'aseh b'zadon*: the *pasuk* uses the language of *action*, teaching that the offense is not voicing disagreement but translating that disagreement into a *hora'ah*, a binding directive to act. *Eino chayav ad sheyoreh la'asos* — he is not liable until he rules in a way that produces action.

The implications for intellectual freedom are remarkable. A scholar may dispute the highest court of Israel from now until the end of his days, articulating why he believes they are in error, provided he does not arrogate to himself the role of directing others to act contrary to their ruling. The law is not about objective correctness — it is about who holds binding decisional authority. And it protects the scholar's right to maintain and express his position even after that authority has spoken. One might add: by continuing to teach and attract students, such a scholar may, over time, influence the very composition of future courts. What looked like a lone voice might eventually reshape the *halacha* through legitimate means.

### Talmid Exemption

*Talmid she-hora la'asos patur* — a student who has not received *semicha* and thus does not yet hold the status to sit on a *beis din*, if he issues a ruling telling people to defy *Beis Din HaGadol*, is nonetheless exempt. One might think the opposite: his *chutzpah* in defying the *Sanhedrin* without even possessing the standing to do so ought to make his offense worse. But the law reasons differently — precisely because he lacks that standing, he is not perceived as a genuine threat to the court's authority. Nobody receives his pronouncement with the same weight as they would that of a fully credentialed elder. *Nimtzeu chumro kulo*: what is formally his shortcoming — that he has not yet attained the status of a *beis din* member — turns out to be his leniency, exempting him from the law's reach entirely.

## Pasuk Analysis

### Yipla & Mufla

The *gemara* now opens a systematic analysis of the verse *ki yipale mimcha davar*, unpacking each term to identify the categories of person and case to which *zaken mamre* applies. The word *yipale* is related to *mufla* — a term denoting expertise and recognized authority. The verse thus signals at the outset that we are speaking of someone who is *mufla she-be-veit din*, a figure of genuine stature fit to sit on a *beis din* — not a mere student. This is the first criterion established by the *pasuk*.

### Mimcha & Yoetz

The word *mimcha* — "from you" — is rendered *zeh yoetz*, an advisor. At first blush this sounds like a personal qualification, but as the *gemara* will develop, it refers to authority over *kiddush hachodesh* and *ibur shana*. The *gemara* supports this by citing the verse *mimcha yatza choshev al Hashem ra'ah yoetz beliya'al* — "from you emerges one who devises evil against God, an advisor of wickedness." The precise connection remains somewhat opaque at this stage, but the *gemara* will return to it when demonstrating how a dispute about calendar intercalation can constitute a debate qualifying a *zaken mamre*.

### Davar Definition

*Davar* — a matter — is interpreted as referring to *halacha*, specifically *halacha l'Moshe mi-Sinai*. This is significant: the offense of *zaken mamre* is not limited to disputes over *pesukei* d'Oraita. Even when the underlying disagreement concerns a received oral tradition — a *halacha l'Moshe mi-Sinai* — the *zaken mamre* framework applies. The *pasuk* uses the word *davar* precisely to encompass this category.

### Mishpat & Din

*Lamishpat* — "for judgment" — is glossed by *Rashi* (following the later *gemara*) as referring to *gezeirah shavah*. It is admittedly difficult to derive that *mishpat*, meaning judgment, connotes a hermeneutical principle like *gezeirah shavah*. Nevertheless, the implication is meaningful: the categories being debated range from *halacha l'Moshe mi-Sinai* (the orally transmitted tradition, *davar*) to *gezeirah shavah* (the interpretive-hermeneutical derivation, *lamishpat*). Together they span the full spectrum of how *halacha* is established beyond the explicit text.

### Blood Types

*Bein dam l'dam* — between blood and blood — refers to the three types of *dam* associated with female *tumah*: *dam niddah*, *dam leidah*, and *dam zivah*. Each of these will be shown to have its own *tannaitic* debate, and each debate carries implications for a *chiyuv kares*.

### Types of Judgments

*Bein din l'din* — between judgment and judgment — encompasses three modes of adjudication: *dinei nefashot*, capital cases; *dinei mamonot*, monetary cases; and *dinei makkot*, cases involving lashes. Each category, as the *gemara* will show, has its own internal disputes with *tannaim*, and each can be connected — however indirectly — to a scenario involving a *chiyuv kares*.

### Leprosy Types

*Bein nega l'nega* — between affliction and affliction — covers three types of *tzara'at*: *nig'ei adam*, afflictions of a person; *nig'ei batim*, afflictions of houses; and *nig'ei vegadim*, afflictions of garments. Each of these has *tannaitic* debates regarding the criteria for *tumah* and *tahara*, and each will be illustrated in turn.

### Verbal Acts

*Divrei* — matters involving speech — refers to *charamim*, *arachin*, and *hekdeshot*: consecrations, valuations, and dedications. These are cases where the legal consequence flows entirely from a verbal act — what the earlier word *yipale* suggests through its root meaning of *hafla'ah*, a pronounced verbal commitment. The *zaken mamre* can equally disagree about the scope and application of such verbal acts.

### Disputes & Rituals

*Rivot* — disputes — is interpreted as referring to *hashka'at sotah*, the ritual of having the *sotah* woman drink the bitter waters in the context of a husband's accusation, and to *arifat eglah arufa*, the breaking of the heifer's neck in the case of an unsolved murder. Both of these rituals share a defining characteristic: they address situations of factual indeterminacy — the *sotah* procedure arises from a *dispute* between husband and wife, while the *eglah arufa* responds to a killing whose perpetrator remains unknown. *Rashi* notes that the word *rivot* fits them both because they each arise from unresolved conflict or uncertainty, not merely from interpersonal friction.

### Gifts to Poor

*Be-sha'arecha* — "in your gates" — is read as referring to *leket*, *shikcha*, and *pe'ah*, the agricultural gifts designated for the poor. The verse's reference to what is adjudicated "in your gates" encompasses obligations that are distributed locally and whose scope and parameters could equally be the subject of dispute.

### Going Up

*Ve-kamta ve-alita* — "you shall arise and go up" — teaches that the *Beis HaMikdash* stands at a greater elevation than the rest of *Eretz Yisrael*, whether literally or spiritually. The *gemara* then extends this further: *Eretz Yisrael gevu'ha mi-kol ha-aratzot* — Israel is higher than all other lands. The proof-text is the verse in *Yirmiyahu* predicting that in the future, people will no longer speak of God as the One who *brought up* the Jewish people from Egypt, but as the One who *brought up* and gathered them from all the lands — *he'ela va-asher hevi et zera beis Yisrael me-eretz tzafona u-mi-kol ha-aratzot* — using the verb of ascent for the journey from all lands to Israel. *Tosafot* acknowledges that there are mountains in Israel higher than the Temple Mount, so the statement is at minimum partly spiritual in force.

### Court Location

*El ha-makom asher yivchar Hashem* — the place that God will choose — teaches that the court must literally be situated in that designated place on *Har HaBayit*. *Melamed she-ha-makom gorem*: the location is causally constitutive of the law. If the *Beis Din HaGadol* is not actually sitting in the *Beis HaMikdash* on *Har HaBayit*, the *zaken mamre* does not incur liability — regardless of everything else. This is the final clause of the *braita*.

## Three Tannaitic Views

### Rabbi Meir Position

A *braita* now presents three distinct *tannaitic* positions on the conditions that trigger *zaken mamre* liability. *Zaken mamre eino chayav ela al davar she-zedono karet u-shegagato chatat, divrei Rabbi Meir* — Rabbi Meir holds that the *zaken mamre* is liable only when the matter he is ruling on is one for which willful violation incurs *karet* and inadvertent violation incurs a *korban chatat*. The underlying logic is that the *zaken mamre* belongs to a special class of authorities whose rulings carry unique legal weight — alongside the *Beis Din HaGadol* whose erroneous collective ruling occasions the *par he'elem davar shel tzibur*, and the *kohen gadol* who brings a special *korban* when he has ruled and acted on his own ruling. These special *hora'ah*-related *korbanot* all arise from rulings concerning weighty sins — those for which one ordinarily brings a *chatat* if performed *be-shogeg* and incurs *karet* if performed *be-mezid*. The *zaken mamre*, though he himself is acting *be-mezid* and the problem is not primarily that he *machshil* others, is read through this same legal lens: the category of sin he is ruling about must meet this threshold of gravity.

### Rabbi Yehuda Position

Rabbi Yehuda disagrees with this criterion. *Al davar she-ikaro mi-divrei Torah u-ferusho mi-divrei soferim* — he requires not that the sin be of a certain weight, but that it be of a certain jurisprudential character. Specifically, Rabbi Yehuda requires that the matter being ruled on be grounded in a verse of the Torah but given its content through Rabbinic interpretation. The reasoning is structural: the defining role of *Beis Din HaGadol* is to be the authoritative interpreter of the Torah's text. *Al pi ha-Torah asher yorucha* — "according to the Torah that they teach you" — defines their authority as interpretive. When the *zaken mamre* rules in the same domain, he puts himself forward as a competing interpreter of the Torah. That is the genuine threat. If, by contrast, he simply rules against an explicit *pasuk* or against a *halacha l'Moshe mi-Sinai* without invoking the interpretive process at all, he is doing something reprehensible, and he may be *machshil* people, but he is not positioning himself as a rival interpretive authority. He is not competing for the same role they hold. Therefore, according to Rabbi Yehuda, only when the ruling is in the domain of Torah-rooted, rabbinically-developed interpretation does the *zaken mamre* become liable. This position is intellectually compelling, though it sits somewhat in tension with the *halacha l'Moshe mi-Sinai* category included in the *braita*, which is not based on a *pasuk* at all.

### Rabbi Shimon Position

Rabbi Shimon goes furthest. *Afilu dikduk echad mi-dikdukei sofrim* — even a single point of precision from among the details of Rabbinic teaching suffices. It is not entirely clear how far *dikdukei sofrim* extends for Rabbi Shimon. The term can refer to genuinely Rabbinic enactments — in which case the *zaken mamre* could incur liability even by defying a ruling about something like *muktzah* or *netilat yadayim* — or it can refer to fine points in the interpretation of earlier authoritative rulings, which would still be an act of competing interpretation even if the underlying text is Rabbinic rather than Biblical. Under the latter reading, Rabbi Shimon differs from Rabbi Yehuda only in extending the scope of interpretive authority beyond *divrei Torah* to *divrei soferim*, but the essential nature of the conflict — competing to be the authoritative interpreter of binding law — remains the same. Under the broader reading, Rabbi Shimon encompasses even pure legislative disagreements, not merely interpretive ones. The precise scope remains unresolved.

### Rabbi Meir's Reasoning

*Mai ta'amei de-Rabbi Meir?* The *gemara* asks for Rabbi Meir's source. He derives it through a *gezeirah shavah* — *gmar davar davar*. The word *davar* appears here in *ki yipale mimcha davar* and appears there in the context of the *par he'elem davar*, *ve-ne'elam davar me-einei ha-kahal* — when the *Beis Din HaGadol* rules erroneously and the community acts on it. In that context, the *hora'ah* that occasions the communal *korban* is specifically a *hora'ah* regarding something for which one incurs *karet* if done *be-mezid* and brings a *chatat* if done *be-shogeg*. Since both passages speak of a *hora'ah* situation using the same word *davar*, Rabbi Meir learns by *gezeirah shavah* that just as there the ruling must concern a *karet*/*chatat* sin, so too here the *zaken mamre*'s ruling must concern the same category. *Ma hailan davar she-chayav al zedono karet ve-al shigagato chatat — af kan davar she-chayav al zedono karet ve-al shigagato chatat.*

### Rabbi Yehuda Reading

Rabbi Yehuda's derivation comes from the phrase *al pi ha-Torah asher yorucha*. He reads *Torah* as referring specifically to the scriptural text, and *yorucha* as the act of teaching based on that text. The *pasuk* is thus saying: follow what they derive and teach based on the Torah's verses. This defines the *beis din*'s authority as hermeneutical — their role is to interpret scripture. Only when the *zaken mamre* places himself in that same interpretive role, ruling on a matter *she-ikaro mi-divrei Torah*, does he genuinely compete with their authority and incur liability. The straightforward reading of the *pasuk* — that *Torah* refers to the ruling itself and *yorucha* to the act of instructing — is set aside in favor of this more precise construction.

## Kiddush Hachodesh Debate

### Request & Setup

Having set out the three positions, the *gemara* turns to demonstrating them in practice. *Amar lei Rav Huna bar Chinana le-Rava: targema li le-ha masnisin aliba de-Rabbi Meir* — Rav Huna bar Chinana asks Rava to explain how the *braita*'s enumerated categories all work according to Rabbi Meir's position, which requires each disputed matter to carry the weight of a *karet*/*chatat* sin. Rava redirects the task to Rav Papa: *puk targema lei* — go and explain it to him. The *gemara* will now go through each category in the *braita* and show, according to Rabbi Meir, how the relevant dispute could implicate a *chiyuv kares*. Crucially, what this exercise really does is demonstrate that in every single category — *kiddush hachodesh*, *halacha l'Moshe mi-Sinai*, *gezeirah shavah*, blood types, judicial procedure, *tzara'at* — there exist genuine *tannaitic* disputes. The point is not that the *zaken mamre* is saying something offensive. He may be entirely correct. The problem is solely that he continues ruling after *beis din* has ruled. Every area he might dispute is an area where the *tannaim* themselves dispute, and the *gemara* is showing that the debate between *zaken mamre* and *beis din* could be just such a classic *tannaitic* disagreement.

### Yoetz Qualification

The first term — *zeh yoetz* — is now expanded: *she-yodea le-aber shanim ve-likboa chadashim*, he must be someone capable of ruling on *ibur shana* and *kiddush hachodesh*. This can be understood as a personal qualification for the *zaken mamre*, but it also identifies the type of matter they could be disputing: a ruling about *kiddush hachodesh* itself.

### Month Addition Debate

The *gemara* illustrates with a *mishnah*: two witnesses came and testified that one may add an intercalary month all through the month of *Adar* — *kol Adar*. The dispute is with those who had said the deadline was only *ad ha-Purim*, until *Purim*. This could be precisely the type of debate between a *zaken mamre* and *beis din* — can the year be intercalated after *Purim* has passed?

### Pesach Connection

How does this connect to a *chiyuv kares*? The answer is direct: a dispute over whether the year is intercalated is a dispute over when *Pesach* falls. *De-i le-hai gisa ka sharei chametz be-Pesach ve-i le-hai gisa ka sharei chametz be-Pesach* — whichever position you adopt, if the other position is correct, you will be eating *chametz* on *Pesach* according to that position, and eating *chametz* on *Pesach* is *chayav karet*. The calendar dispute thus directly implicates a *karet* sin, satisfying Rabbi Meir's criterion.

## Eleven Days Debate

### Niddah & Zava
