The next category is *davar* — understood as *halacha l'Moshe mi-Sinai* — and the *gemara* illustrates it with the *halacha* of the eleven days. To understand this debate, some background is essential. A woman's menstrual period, according to Torah law, renders her a *niddah* for seven days from the onset of bleeding. After the seventh day she immerses in a *mikvah*. Following this seven-day *niddah* period, there is a window of eleven days — days eight through eighteen from the onset — during which she can potentially become a *zavah*. A *zavah gedolah*, a major *zavah*, is a woman who bleeds on three consecutive days within this eleven-day window. Such a woman requires seven clean days before she may immerse. A *zavah ketanah* — one who bleeds on only one or two days in the window — requires one clean day. If she bleeds on day nineteen, she returns to the status of *niddah*. This structure of seven *niddah* days followed by eleven *zavah* days is itself a *halacha l'Moshe mi-Sinai* — it has no explicit source in a *pasuk*.

### Day Ten Dispute

The specific dispute concerns day ten of the eleven-day window. If a woman bleeds on day ten, may she immerse without first observing a clean day, or must she wait for day eleven to be clean before immersing? *De'itmar: asiri ke-teshi'i o asiri ke-achat asar?* Rabbi Yochanan holds *asiri ke-teshi'i* — day ten is like day nine. Just as a woman who bleeds on day nine must observe a clean day before immersing, so too one who bleeds on day ten must ensure that day eleven is clean. Resh Lakish holds *asiri ke-achat asar* — day ten is like day eleven. Since a woman bleeding on day eleven requires no clean day, similarly a woman who bleeds on day ten requires none.

### Mikva Implications

The reasoning of each position follows the structure of the eleven-day period. Rabbi Yochanan notes that day ten remains within the eleven-day window where *zavah* status can accumulate; therefore, the same requirement of a clean day applies as on any other day within that window. Resh Lakish reasons that on day ten, it is already impossible for the woman to become a *zavah gedolah* — even if she bleeds on days ten, eleven, and twelve, day twelve would mark the beginning of a new *niddah* period, not a third *zavah* day — and therefore the protective requirement of a clean day is inapplicable, just as on day eleven itself. The *nafka mina* for a *chiyuv karet* is transparent: if the woman does not require a clean day but her husband believes she does, they will abstain unnecessarily; if she does require a clean day but follows the lenient ruling and immerses, she remains *tamei* and subsequent relations with her husband are *chayav karet*.

## Gezeirah Shavah Debate

### Daughter Derivation

The third category — *lamishpat*, interpreted by *Rashi* as *gezeirah shavah* — is illustrated by the prohibition against a man having relations with his daughter who is not his wife's daughter. There is no explicit verse in the Torah prohibiting this directly. Rava transmits in the name of Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi that it is derived through a double *gezeirah shavah*: *atya henah henah, atya zimah zimah* — two parallel verbal identifications from separate verses establish that a man is forbidden to have relations with such a daughter.

### Kareis Connection

This prohibition falls into the gravest category of forbidden relations. The connection to *chayav karet* — or indeed to something even graver — is direct. *Tosafot* observes that this is actually the only example in this entire passage that is not itself a matter of debate among *tannaim*. Nevertheless, it is entirely conceivable that a *zaken mamre* might reject the *gezeirah shavah* on which the prohibition rests — this is, after all, the nature of disputes about *gezeirot shavot* — and rule that such relations are permitted. In that case, people who follow his ruling would violate a prohibition that is undeniably a *chiyuv karet* or worse, satisfying Rabbi Meir's criterion completely.

## Blood Impurities

### Green Blood Debate

The category *bein dam l'dam* — disputes among the three types of blood: *dam niddah*, *dam leidah*, and *dam zivah* — is now illustrated in sequence. For *dam niddah*, the *gemara* cites *biplugta de-Akavya ben Mehalalel ve-Rabanan*. *Dam ha-yarok* — greenish or yellowish blood — is the subject: Akavya ben Mehalalel rules that such blood renders a woman *tamei* as *dam niddah*, while the Sages rule it *tahor*. If a *zaken mamre* ruled as Akavya and people treated such blood as *tahor*, and then a woman had relations with her husband while still in the *niddah* status, the result would be a *chiyuv karet*. Conversely, if he ruled as the Sages and people treated it as *tahor* when in fact it is *tamei* — same result.

### Leidah Wellsprings

For *dam leidah*, the *gemara* cites *biplugta de-Rav ve-Levi*. This is the well-known debate about the source of a woman's blood during her *yemei tohar* — the period of purity following childbirth. After giving birth to a boy, a woman is *tamei* for seven days, like a *niddah*. Then, from day eight through day forty, even if she bleeds, she is *tahor* — her blood is *dam tohar*, which does not convey *tumah*. Beginning from day forty-one, her blood is once again *tamei niddah*-blood. The question is: why is the blood between days eight and forty *tahor*?

Rav holds *ma'ayan echad hu — ha-Torah tim'ato ve-ha-Torah tihara*: there is one wellspring, one source of blood in the woman. The Torah declared it *tamei* during the first seven days and declared it *tahor* during the subsequent period. The blood's physical source is unchanged; its legal status has simply been redefined by the Torah for that span. Levi holds *shtei ma'ayanot hen*: there are two distinct wellsprings. During the *yemei tohar*, the blood comes from a different source — not the uterine source that generates *niddah*-blood — and at the end of day forty, *nistam ha-tahor ve-niftach ha-tamei*: the *tahor* source closes and the *tamei* source reopens.

### Continuous Bleeding

The practical difference between these positions, the *nafka mina*, arises when a woman bleeds continuously across the transition point — for instance, from the end of day seven into day eight, or from day forty into day forty-one without a break. If there are two wellsprings, then continuous bleeding across the boundary is impossible to attribute to a single source. The physical continuity of the bleeding suggests it is coming from the same source throughout — which would undermine the premise of two separate sources. In that case, Levi's position might lead to the conclusion that the blood is *tamei* even during the *yemei tohar*, since the evidence points to a single source. But if the Torah has simply changed the legal status of blood from the same source, as Rav holds, then a continuous bleed from day seven to day eight is automatically *tahor* from the moment of transition, just as a continuous bleed from day forty to forty-one becomes *tamei* at the transition point, because the legal category changes regardless of physical continuity.

### Zivah Childbirth

For *dam zivah*, the *gemara* cites *biplugta de-Rabbi Eliezer ve-Rabbi Yehoshua*. The context is a woman who bleeds during her eleven-day *zavah* period while experiencing the pains of labor. Under Torah law, blood that flows as a result of childbirth — *zov machamat vlad* — does not render a woman a *zavah*, even if it appears during the eleven-day window. The question is: what constitutes a sufficient break between the labor pains and the delivery to sever the legal connection between them, such that the woman becomes a *zavah* after all?

*Hishtah shlosha yamim betoch achat asar yom* — if a woman experienced childbirth pains for three consecutive days during her eleven-day window, that would normally make her a *zavah gedolah*. But if those pains are connected to an imminent birth, the bleeding is attributed to childbirth rather than *zivah*. The dispute concerns the minimum break required: *im shaftah me-eis le-eis, ve-yaldah* — if she had a full twenty-four-hour relief from labor pains and then gave birth, Rabbi Eliezer rules *yoledes be-zov* — she is both a *yoledes* and a *zavah*. The twenty-four-hour break severs the connection between her earlier pains and the ultimate delivery, so the three days of bleeding are classified as *zivah*-blood rather than childbirth-blood. Rabbi Yehoshua is more lenient: *lailah va-yom ke-leil Shabbos ve-yomo* — the break that disqualifies her must consist of a full night followed by a full day, patterned after the calendrical day of *Shabbat*. Moreover, *ve-shavsa min ha-tzaar v'lo min ha-dam* — what must cease for this period is not the bleeding but the *pain*. Only if she has had this precise form of relief — a full night and full day without labor pains — does she become a *zavah*. Under Rabbi Yehoshua's view, a twenty-four-hour break that does not fall night-first-then-day is insufficient, making her *zavah* status harder to establish. Again, whether a woman is a *zavah* or not has direct implications for relations with her husband, and therefore for a *chiyuv karet*.

## Dinei Mamonos

### Two-Judge Ruling

The category *bein din l'din* is now taken up, beginning with *dinei mamonot*. The *gemara* cites *biplugta de-Shmuel ve-Rabbi Abahu*. Shmuel rules that *shnayim she-danu, dineihen din* — if two judges adjudicated a monetary case, their ruling is legally binding, albeit the court that did so is described as *beis din chatzuf*, a brazen court. Rabbi Abahu rules *le-divrei ha-kol ein dineihen din* — the ruling is universally invalid and has no binding legal force.

### Marriage Scenario

The connection to *chayav karet* may not be immediately obvious, since what is being debated is the validity of adjudication, not the substance of the monetary law. *Rashi* explains the mechanism: suppose two parties are disputing ownership of an object — a cloak, a coin, whatever — and two judges rule in favor of one of them. That person then uses the object to effect *kiddushin* with a woman: *harei at mekudeshet li*. If the two-judge ruling is valid, the object belonged to him, the *kiddushin* takes effect, and the woman is his wife. If she then cohabits with another man, that is adultery — *chayav karet*. If the ruling is invalid, he never legitimately owned the object, the *kiddushin* is void, and she has not committed adultery. Any monetary dispute, therefore, can be linked — through the mechanism of marriage effected by means of the disputed object or sum — to a potential *chiyuv karet*, satisfying Rabbi Meir's standard.

## Dinei Nefashos

### Rabbi View

Continuing through *bein din l'din*, the *gemara* addresses *dinei nefashot*. Rabbi holds *nefesh tachas nafesh mammon*: in the case of a person who intended to kill one individual but inadvertently killed another — the classic case where Reuven aimed at Shimon and killed Levi — the verse *ve-nasata nefesh tachas nafesh* is read as requiring monetary compensation rather than execution. Rabbi's derivation relies on a *gezeirah shavah*: just as *nesina* in the context of the miscarriage case means payment, so *nesina* here means payment as well.

### Chachamim View

The Sages dispute this: in their reading, either the person is executed, or — even if execution is not applicable — the principle of *kim lei bi-d'rabba minei* applies, barring any monetary obligation where a capital punishment looms. The person who killed inadvertently while aiming elsewhere either faces execution or faces nothing at all; he does not pay damages.

### Payment Marriage Link

The connection to *karet* follows the same structural logic as *dinei mamonot*: if monetary damages are owed according to Rabbi's ruling, and the killer uses that payment to effect *kiddushin* with a woman, then whether she is his wife or not — and consequently whether subsequent relations with another man constitute adultery — depends on whether the payment was legitimately his. The *gemara* does not belabor the point, having established the logical pattern.

## Dinei Makkos

### Three Judges

The third sub-category of *bein din l'din* is *dinei makkot*. The *mishna* itself records the dispute: *makkot bi-shlosha* — lashes are administered by a court of three judges, as the standard ruling requires.

### Twenty-Three Judges

*Mishum Rabbi Yishmael amru: be-esrim u-shlosha* — in the name of Rabbi Yishmael, it was taught that lashes require a court of twenty-three. The debate concerns the minimum court composition for a valid *makkot* proceeding.

### Compensation Link

The link to *chayav karet* follows the by-now-established pattern. *Rashi* explains: if a person was lashed by a court of three judges, and Rabbi Yishmael's position is correct that twenty-three were required, then the lashes were administered illegitimately. The recipient is entitled to compensation for the unlawful punishment. If he receives that compensation and uses it to effect *kiddushin*, the status of his marriage depends on whether the payment was validly owed — which depends on whether the original *beis din* proceeding was valid. From there the chain leads to potential *karet* in the same manner as all preceding cases.

## Tzaraas of People

### Spot vs. Hair

The category *bein nega l'nega* begins with *nig'ei adam*, afflictions of a person. The *gemara* cites the well-known debate from the *mishna*: *im baheres kodem le-se'ar lavan, tamei* — if the white spot appeared before the white hair, he is *tamei*. *Im se'ar lavan kodem la-baheres, tahor* — if the white hair preceded the spot, he is *tahor*.

### Safek Status

The case of *safek* — when it is unknown which came first — yields a ruling of *tamei* according to the first opinion.

### Rabbi Yehoshua

Rabbi Yehoshua's position is recorded with the single word *keiha* — "it is dim." Rava explains: *keiha tahor* — Rabbi Yehoshua means that in this situation of doubt, the ruling is *tahor*. This is his compact way of expressing disagreement with the stringent position. *Rashi* connects the *karet* implication to the following scenario: if the person is ruled *tahor* erroneously and he enters the *Beis HaMikdash*, there is a potential *karet*-level violation — entry while *tamei* can implicate severe punishment — or other scenarios in which a disputed *tzara'at* ruling creates the conditions for a severe sin.

## Tzaraas of Houses

### Corner Requirement

For *nig'ei batim*, the *gemara* cites Rabbi Eliezer the son of Rabbi Shimon, who holds that a house never becomes *tamei* from *tzara'at* unless the spot appears in a very precise configuration: *kishnei gerisim al shtei avanim bi-shtei ktalim be-kern zavis* — the equivalent of two beans' size spread across two stones on two walls, at a corner. The spot must literally wrap around an interior corner of the house, spanning both adjacent walls.

### Size Specs

The dimensions Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Shimon specifies are: *archo kishnei gerisim, rovcho ke-gris* — the length of the affliction is two beans, the width is one bean. This means the spot is rectangular in proportion, oriented along the corner.

### Kiros Derivation

His textual source: the verse uses both *kir* (singular wall) and *kiros* (plural walls). *Eizo kir she-hi ke-kiros? Hevei omer: zeh kern zavis* — what kind of wall is like walls (plural)? The answer is the corner: a corner is simultaneously one wall that is also two walls meeting. This derivation limits the scope of house *tzara'at* significantly compared to the Rabbinic majority position, creating a genuine dispute about when a house becomes *tamei*.

## Tzaraas of Clothes

### Full Spread

The final category is *nig'ei vegadim*, and the authority cited is Rabbi Nosson ben Avtulmos. The question he addresses is: if a spot of *tzara'at* began on a garment and then spread to cover the entire garment, what is the status? Rabbi Nosson ben Avtulmos rules *tahorah* — it is pure. Just as a person whose *tzara'at* spreads to cover his entire body from head to toe is declared *tahor* (the principle of *parcha be-chulo tahor* for a person), so too a garment whose *tzara'at* spreads to cover it entirely is *tahor*.

### Head to Toe

The derivation proceeds by *gezeirah shavah*: *ne'emar kerachat ve-gabachat be-adam, ve-ne'emar kerachat ve-gabachat be-vaged* — the same language of a bald spot and a smooth patch appears both in the context of a person's head and in the context of a garment. *Mah lehalan parcha be-chulo tahor, af kan parcha be-chulo tahor* — just as when the affliction covers the person entirely he is *tahor*, so too when the affliction covers the garment entirely it is *tahor*. The Sages presumably dispute this ruling, and the debate between them constitutes the *tannaitic* controversy that a *zaken mamre* and *beis din* could reproduce.

The *gemara* will continue tomorrow, completing the catalogue and reinforcing the overarching point: in each and every domain the *braita* lists, there are genuine disputes among *tannaim*, any one of which could in principle be the very disagreement that defines the confrontation between a *zaken mamre* and *beis din*. The *zaken mamre* may well be right. But once *beis din* has ruled, his continued ruling in opposition — and not the substance of what he says — is what the Torah declares intolerable.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 88

## Zaken Mamre Overview

### Opening & Zaken Mamre

The daf begins on 88a, four lines from the top, at the word *divrei*. We are in the midst of discussing *zaken mamre*, and the focus is on how the *braisa* interprets the *pasuk* underlying this law. The verses — *divrei rivos bish'arecha bein dam l'dam bein din l'din divrei rivos bish'arecha vekamta ve'alisa* — are parsed phrase by phrase, with each element mapped onto a different halachic domain in which a potentially decisive debate might arise. The governing question is how these domains relate to the earlier position of Rabbi Meir, who requires that the underlying matter be one for which one would be *chayav kares* if done intentionally (*be-meizid*) or *chayav chatat* if done inadvertently (*beshogeg*).

### Divrei Rivos Pasuk

The *braisa* identifies the phrase *divrei rivos* — "words of contention" — as referring to *archin*, *charamin*, and *hekdeshos*: the laws of valuations, dedications (*cherem*), and sanctified items. These are domains in which halachic status is created through an act of speech, a *hafla'ah*, and in which disputes can arise that carry serious downstream consequences.

### Rebbi Meir's Position

The thread connecting these cases to Rabbi Meir's requirement — that the contested matter involve *kares* or *chatat* — runs through a common mechanism: if the halachic status of money or an item is in doubt, and that money or item is then used to effect *kiddushei isha*, the validity of the marriage hangs in the balance. If the *kiddushin* did not take effect and the woman subsequently had relations with another man, the question of adultery — which carries *kares* or worse — becomes directly implicated. This chain of reasoning is what allows each of the following categories to qualify under Rabbi Meir's standard.

---

## Archin Debate

### Archin, Charamin, Hekdes…

The *braisa* proceeds to specify what debate in each domain exemplifies the point. For *archin*, it is the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the *rabbanan*, as recorded in a *braisa*: if someone says *erech ploni alai* — pledging the Torah-mandated *erech* valuation of a person — but the individual in question is an infant less than one month old, the Torah's *erech* schedule does not apply to such a child. What then?

### Erech Pachus Miben Chode…

Rabbi Meir rules *nosein damav* — the pledgor must pay the infant's market value as a slave, even though the term used was *erech* rather than *dmei*. His reasoning is the principle of *ein adam motzi dvarav l'vatala*: a person does not make a declaration without intending some practical consequence, so we interpret the pledge as if he had said *dmei ploni alai*. The *chachamim*, however, rule *lo amar klum* — he said nothing legally effective, since the formula he used (*erech*) has no applicability to an infant under one month. 

Now, if one follows Rabbi Meir's view, the money is *hekdesh* and belongs to the *Beis HaMikdash*. If one follows the *chachamim*, it is ordinary money the pledgor may keep. Should this money then be used for *kiddushei isha*, and the woman was unaware of its sanctified status, the *kiddushin* would be void according to one view but valid according to the other. If she subsequently cohabited with another man, the question of adultery — and thus *kares* — turns entirely on this underlying dispute about whether the money was *hekdesh*. This is how the *archin* debate connects to Rabbi Meir's criterion.

---

## Charamin Debate

### Stam Charamin Ruling

For *charamin*, the debate is between Rabbi Yehuda ben Beseira and the *rabbanan*. If someone declares an item *cherem* without specifying to whom it goes, Rabbi Yehuda ben Beseira rules *stam charamin l'bedek habayis* — it goes to the Temple treasury — citing the verse *kol cherem kodesh kodashim hu l'Hashem*, which indicates that any *cherem* is consecrated to God. The *chachamim* rule *stam charamin l'kohein* — it goes to the *kohein* — citing the verse *k'sdeh hacherem l'kohein tihyeh achuzaso*, which assigns a field of *cherem* to the *kohein*'s possession. According to the *chachamim*, the earlier verse teaches only that a *cherem* declaration can take effect even upon items already sanctified — *al kadshei kodashim v'al kadshei kalim* — but does not indicate that *stam charamin* goes to the Temple.

The same practical consequence follows: if the item is *hekdesh* it cannot be used for *kiddushin*, while if it belongs to the *kohein* as ordinary property, someone in possession of it who attempts to use it to marry a woman creates a question about the validity of those *kiddushin* — and again, the chain leads to potential *kares* or worse.

---

## Hekdeshos Debate

### Tzinor Shel Hekdesh

For *hekdeshos*, the relevant dispute is between Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov and the *rabbanan*. The *braisa* records that Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov rules: *afilu tzinor shel hekdesh tzarich asara bnei adam lifdoso* — even the smallest item of *hekdesh*, like a small implement, requires ten people to effect its redemption. The majority view holds that ten people — including a *kohein* — are required only for redeeming *karka* (land), while ordinary *hekdesh* requires only three, and even that requirement is essentially to ensure a proper valuation. If someone redeemed an item with only three people rather than ten, whether the item is still *hekdesh* or has been validly redeemed depends on this dispute.

Rashi notes the *kiddushin* mechanism again: if the redeemed item is still *hekdesh*, it cannot be used to betroth a woman. But Rashi also offers an independent path to *chiyuv kares*: if the item was genuinely *hekdesh* and someone who was *tamei* ate from its meat as a *korban me'ilah*, they would be *chayav kares* for eating *kodshim* in a state of *tum'ah*. Whether there was a *korban* at all, however, turns on whether the original object was truly *hekdesh* — which in turn depends on the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov and the *rabbanan*.

---

## Four Rivos Cases

### Hashka'at Sotah

The word *rivos* — contentions — is next identified with three specific *mitzvos* that presuppose some act of conflict or suspicion: the drinking of the *sotah* waters (*hashka'at sotah*), the breaking of the *egla arufa*, and the purification of the *metzora*. Each of these is then matched to a specific *tannaic* dispute. The survey serves the dual purpose of illustrating the range of *divrei rivos* and demonstrating how each generates a case that can implicate *kares* or *chatat*.

For *hashka'at sotah*, the debate is between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua, cited from the *Mishna*. When a husband performs *kinuy* — warning his wife not to enter into seclusion with a particular man — Rabbi Eliezer rules *mekana al pi shenayim u-mashka al pi ed echad*: the warning requires two witnesses, but her actual seclusion can be established by a single witness (or by the husband himself). Rabbi Yehoshua rules *mekana al pi shenayim u-mashka al pi shenayim*: both the warning and the seclusion require two witnesses.

The halachic consequence is as follows. If there were two witnesses to the *kinuy* and only one witness to the seclusion, Rabbi Eliezer would regard her as obligated to undergo the *sotah* ritual, and if she refused, she would lose her *ketubah* and be divorced without it. Rabbi Yehoshua would regard her as under no obligation and she would retain her *ketubah* rights. If she then sold her *ketubah* note and the buyer attempted to collect, the question of whether the money rightfully belongs to him depends on whether she had a valid *ketubah* claim. Money that may not legitimately belong to one party and is then used for *kiddushin* — validity uncertain — brings the matter once again into the domain of potential adultery and *kares*.

### Arifas Egla Arufa

The debate surrounding *arifas egla arufa* involves the question of from which point on the corpse the measurement to the nearest city is taken — since the city determined to be closest is the one obligated to bring the *egla*. Rabbi Eliezer holds that one measures from the navel (*tiburo*), viewing that as the bodily seat of vitality. Rabbi Akiva holds that one measures from the nose (*chotamo*), since breath is the defining sign of life. Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov holds that one measures from the neck (*tzavaro*) — the place where a person would normally be killed — regardless of where the actual wound was inflicted.

It may happen that two different cities each brought an *egla* in good faith, each believing itself to be the closest city according to one of these views. An *egla arufa* is forbidden in *hana'ah* — in deriving any benefit from it. If an item forbidden in *hana'ah* is used to betroth a woman, the *kiddushin* is invalid; if it is not forbidden because it is not the genuine *egla arufa*, the *kiddushin* is valid. The ramifications for adultery and *kares* follow in the same pattern as the cases above.

### Taharat Metzora

For the purification of the *metzora*, the dispute is between the *tanna kamma* and Rabbi Shimon (with Rabbi Eliezer also mentioned). The Torah requires that the blood of the *asham* offering be placed on the *metzora*'s right thumb, right big toe, and right earlobe. The question is: what if the *metzora* lacks a thumb, big toe, or ear? The *tanna kamma* holds *ein lo taharah olamit* — there is simply no remedy; such a person can never be purified. Rabbi Eliezer holds that one places the blood where the thumb would have been. Rabbi Shimon holds *noten al smolo v'yotzei* — one may place it on the left thumb or toe.

Rashi's approach to connecting this to *kares* is that if the person is genuinely *tahor* after going through the process according to one of the lenient views, they may enter the *Beis HaMikdash* without incurring *kares*. If they are still *tamei*, entering the *Beis HaMikdash* would be *chayav kares*. Tosafot, however, objects that entering the *Beis HaMikdash* while *tamei* may be *chayav kares* but is not subject to a *chatat* when done inadvertently — and we also require the possibility of *chatat*. Tosafot therefore constructs a different scenario: the person touched *terumah*, and whether it was *terumah tme'ah* or *terumah tehorah* depends on whether the person was truly *tahor* after the disputed purification process. That *terumah* is then used to effect *kiddushin*, and if it was *terumah tme'ah* the *kiddushin* fails, bringing us back to the chain of implications for adultery and *kares*. The Gemara itself does not spell out these connections; it is Rashi and Tosafot who work through the details.

### Leket Shikcha Pe'ah

The final term, *bisharecha* — "in your gates" — is associated with *leket*, *shikcha*, and *pe'ah*, the agricultural obligations to leave gleanings, forgotten sheaves, and the edge of the field for the poor. Each of these has its own threshold debate.

For *leket*: two stalks that fall during harvesting constitute *leket* and belong to the poor, but three do not, since three is already a substantial amount. For *shikcha*: two forgotten sheaves are considered *shikcha*, but three are not. On both of these, Beis Shammai rules that up to three constitute *leket* or *shikcha*, and four does not — thereby being more expansive in what belongs to the poor. If a poor person took what he believed was rightfully his *leket* and the question is whether it truly was his, and he uses that produce or its proceeds to betroth a woman, the familiar mechanism applies.

For *pe'ah*, the relevant dispute is in the name of Rabbi Yishmael versus the *rabbanan*. The primary *mitzvah* is to designate *pe'ah* while the grain is still standing — by simply not harvesting the edge of the field. If one failed to do so and already cut the grain, one may still designate *pe'ah* from the bundled sheaves. If one failed at that stage, one may designate it from the pile (*kari*) — but only before *mirach*, the smoothing over of the pile, which marks the point of *gmar melacha* at which the grain becomes obligated in *terumah* and *ma'aser*. Once *mirach* has occurred, the grain is *chayav* in *terumot u'ma'asrot*, and when the *pe'ah* portion is given to the poor person it must be given free of those obligations — meaning the owner must first separate *terumah u'ma'aser* and then give the remainder. In the name of Rabbi Yishmael, the authorities teach that even once one has ground the grain into flour and formed dough — *af mishiyina ha'isa* — if one has not yet given *pe'ah* one is still obligated to do so. The *chachamim* disagree. Whether the poor person has rights to a portion of that dough, whether the proceeds of its sale truly belong to him, and what happens if he uses that money to betroth a woman — all of this flows from this dispute about whether *pe'ah* can still be designated at the dough stage.

---

## Tradition vs. Logic

### Rav Kahana's Scenarios

Having established the categories of *divrei rivos* and their connection to *kares* and *chatat*, the Gemara turns to a fundamental question about the inner workings of the *zaken mamre* case itself: does it matter whether the sage's dissent is rooted in his own received tradition (*mipi hashemuah*) or in his own reasoning (*kach hu be'einai*)?

Rav Kahana presents a principled analysis structured around four possible combinations. First: *hu omer mipi hashemuah vehein omrim mipi hashemuah* — he says he has a tradition and they say they have a tradition. In that case, *eino neherag* — he is not executed. He genuinely holds a different received tradition; how can he be held morally accountable for not submitting to theirs? Second: *hu omer kach hu be'einai vehein omrim kach hu be'eineinu* — both sides argue from their own reasoning. Again, *eino neherag*. Even granting that the majority view prevails as *halacha*, he is entitled to his own logical conviction and is not simply compelled to abandon it. *Vekhol shekein* — the third case follows a fortiori: if he says he has a tradition and they respond with a logical argument, certainly he is not executed. His received tradition surely outweighs their inference.

The sole case in which execution applies, according to Rav Kahana, is the fourth and final combination: *hu omer kach hu be'einai vehein omrim mipi hashemuah* — he argues from his own logic and they present a received tradition. In this situation, he had no basis to maintain his position. His argument cannot overcome their tradition, and he should have submitted. The failure to do so, despite having no legitimate reason for holding firm, is what makes him *chayav misah*.

This reading of *zaken mamre* reflects a particular understanding of the institution's purpose: not primarily the blanket protection of rabbinic authority, but the requirement that a sage submit to superior authority when there is genuine reason to do so. If there is a legitimate basis for his disagreement — his own tradition, his own reasoning against their reasoning — he may personally maintain his view; he simply may not go out and instruct others to act on it.

### Rebbi Elazar's View

Rabbi Elazar disagrees sharply. He holds *neherag kedei shelo yirbu machlokes beYisrael* — he is executed in every case, in order that disputes not proliferate in Israel. According to Rabbi Elazar, the reasoning behind *zaken mamre* is not about the merit of the individual's position but about the institutional integrity of the *Beis Din*. The *halacha* is *acharei rabbim l'hatot*, and the *Beis Din*'s decision is the binding determination of *halacha* — even if one has an authentic competing tradition, and even if one is genuinely convinced the majority is wrong. The protection of the institution overrides the individual sage's epistemic standing.

### Akavya ben Mahalalel

As support for Rav Kahana's more limited position, the Gemara observes: *teda shelo hargu es Akavya ben Mahalalel* — note that Akavya ben Mahalalel was not executed. Akavya famously disputed four rulings with the *chachamim* and refused to retract, yet he was not put to death as a *zaken mamre*. Moreover, when he was dying, he told his son to follow the majority — explaining that he himself had held firm because he had received his tradition from a broader consensus, whereas his son was relying on a single authority (Akavya himself) and should therefore submit to the majority. This is precisely the scenario of competing traditions: Rav Kahana holds that in such a case, a sage is not executed.

One must note, however, as the Gemara itself will address, that being exempt from execution does not necessarily mean his conduct was entirely unproblematic. The Gemara will clarify: the reason Akavya was not executed was that *shelo hora halacha l'ma'aseh* — he did not actually issue a practical ruling for others to act upon. What makes one a *zaken mamre* is not the disagreement in principle, but setting oneself up as an opposing authority whose rulings are acted upon.

---

## Mishna Language Analysis

### Derashti vs. Lamadti

The Gemara now turns to the language of our *mishna*. The *mishna* describes the *zaken mamre* as saying: *kach darashti v'kach darshu chaverai* — "this is what I expounded, and this is what my colleagues expounded" — and also: *kach lamad'ti v'kach limdu chaverai* — "this is what I learned, and this is what they learned." The double formulation is striking: *darashti* implies derivation through one's own reasoning, while *lamad'ti* suggests received tradition. Since the *mishna* includes both formulations, it seems to imply that the *zaken mamre* applies regardless of which type of disagreement underlies the dispute — which would appear to contradict Rav Kahana, who limits liability to the single scenario in which logic confronts tradition.

### Gemara Reconciliation

The Gemara answers with a simple *lo* — no, you need not read the double language that way. The *mishna* can be reconciled with Rav Kahana's view by understanding the two phrases as describing the single qualifying scenario: *hu amar kach b'einai v'hein omrim mipi shmua* — he says "this is what I derived through my own reasoning" (*darashti*), and they say "this is what we received as tradition" (*lamad'ti*). Even though the *mishna* uses both terms across its two clauses, the combination maps onto Rav Kahana's lone case of liability. The Gemara admittedly does not elaborate at length on how precisely the double language of the *mishna* yields this reading, but it maintains the reading is available.

---

## Tosefta: Original Disput…

### Rebbi Yose on Original D…

The Gemara cites a *tosefta*, familiar from *Sotah*, *Chagigah*, and other places. Rabbi Yose states: *mi-techila lo hayu marbin machloket b'Yisrael* — originally, disputes did not proliferate in Israel. In the context of *Chagigah*, the *zugos* — the pairs of *Nasi* and *Av Beis Din* who preceded Hillel and Shammai — debated only one or two points, such as the question of *smicha* on *korbanos* on *Yom Tov*. The system worked because there was always a method to resolve any disagreement: when a question arose, it would travel up through successive levels of the court hierarchy until it reached an authoritative resolution, and the mechanism of that resolution was predominantly *shemuah* — received tradition.

### Three-Court System

The *tosefta* describes the structure in detail, corresponding to the picture painted in our *mishna*. The *Beis Din* of 71 sat in the *Lishkas HaGazis*. Two *batei dinim* of 23 sat respectively at the entrance to *Har HaBayis* and at the entrance to the *azarah*. And the many other *batei dinim* of 23 were spread throughout all the cities of Israel.

When a contested question arose, it was first brought to the local *Beis Din*. If they had a tradition (*im shamu*), they would answer. If not (*v'im lav*), the matter traveled to the regional court nearest the city. If that court had a tradition, they answered; if not, the question moved to the court at the entrance to *Har HaBayis*, then to the court at the entrance to the *azarah*, with the same inquiry at each level. It is striking that at no stage below the *Beis Din HaGadol* does the *tosefta* describe any court attempting to resolve the matter through its own reasoning. The sole question at each level is *im shamu* — do you have a tradition? If not, the matter moves up. The use of independent human analysis was the absolute last resort, reserved for the *Beis Din HaGadol* alone.

The *tosefta* notes that the *Beis Din HaGadol* would sit in the *Lishkas HaGazis* from the time of the morning *tamid* offering until the afternoon *tamid*, and on *Shabbos* and *Yom Tov* they would convene in the *Cheil* — the area surrounding the *Beis HaMikdash* within *Har HaBayis*. The *tosefta* specifies that on those days they sat in the *Beis HaMedrash* rather than the *Lishkas HaGazis*, since convening there might give the appearance of adjudicating capital cases, which is prohibited on *Shabbos* and *Yom Tov*, even though they wished to continue learning *Torah*.

### Sanhedrin Vote System

When the question finally reached the *Beis Din HaGadol*, the same question was first posed: *im shamu*, did they have a tradition? If so, they answered. Only if there was no tradition did they proceed to analysis and a vote. *Rabu hamitame'im timu* — if the majority ruled *tamei*, it was *tamei*; *rabu hamitaharim tiharu* — if the majority ruled *tahor*, it was *tahor*. This is the foundational mechanism of *halacha acharei rabbim*. The implication for *zaken mamre* is clear: once the *Beis Din HaGadol* has issued a ruling — whether based on tradition or, as a last resort, on analysis and majority vote — the *zaken mamre* who continues to dissent and act on his opposing view is in defiance of the binding determination.

### Shammai & Hillel Effect

The *tosefta* then identifies the historical turning point: *mishe'rabu talmidei Shammai v'Hillel shelo shimshu kol tzorkan* — once the students of Shammai and Hillel, who had not devoted themselves sufficiently to their teachers' instruction, became numerous, *rabu machlokos b'Yisrael* — disputes proliferated throughout Israel, and *v'na'asis haTorah k'shtei Toros* — the *Torah* became as if it were two *Toros*.

It is worth pausing on what this means. If the system was designed to resolve every dispute, why did the proliferation of students who lacked complete training cause unresolvable debates? One might suggest: when the number of disputed issues is small, the court hierarchy can realistically handle every case that comes before it. When everything under the sun becomes disputed, it is practically impossible to bring each question all the way through the system to resolution.

But the deeper point, which the *tosefta* makes unmistakably clear, is about the primacy of *mesora*. The entire system — the repeated inquiry of *im shamu* at every level — frames *mesora* as the *ikar*. Human analysis was a concession of last resort, not the primary engine of *halacha*. The failure of Shammai and Hillel's students is described as a failure of transmission: they did not properly internalize all that they needed to. If *halacha* were primarily a product of human reasoning, the debate about how much time a student spent with his teacher would be beside the point — good reasoning is good reasoning regardless. The *tosefta* frames it otherwise. This reflects one strand of understanding *Torah she-ba'al peh* — that the *ikar* is the *mesora*, and that human analysis, however necessary, is a departure from the ideal.

---

## Judge Qualifications

### Judge Requirements

The *tosefta* continues by describing the qualifications required to ascend through the court system. To serve as a local judge, one must be *chacham u-shfal berech v'da'at ha-beriyot nocha heimenu* — wise, of humble bearing ("low of knee"), and someone who is pleasant in the eyes of people — meaning one who commands genuine public respect. If such a judge distinguished himself in his local capacity, he could be elevated: *ma'alin oto le-Har HaBayis*, then to the *azarah*, then to the *Lishkas HaGazis*. Advancement through the system was meritocratic, rooted in demonstrated wisdom, humility, and the confidence of the community.

The Gemara appends a related tradition. The question was asked: who is deserving of *olam ha-ba*? The answer given: one who is *anvatanuto u-shfal berech* — humble and lowly of bearing — who *shayeif ayil shayeif nafik*, bowing as he enters and bows as he exits, one who constantly bends himself for *Torah*; who *garis be-Oraita tadira* — studies *Torah* constantly; and who *lo machzik tivuta le-nafsheih* — never credits himself for his learning. The *rabbanan* looked at Rav Ulla bar Abba as one who exemplified these qualities.

---

## Halacha L'Ma'aseh Requir…

### Acting or Teaching Requir…

Returning now to the *mishna* — *chazar le-iro ve-shanah*, if the *zaken mamre* returns to his city and resumes teaching his ruling, he does not become *chayav* until he crosses the threshold of *halacha l'ma'aseh*: he must either act on his ruling himself or instruct others who then act upon it. A *braisa* records this explicitly: *eino chayav ad she-ya'aseh ke-horato* — he is not *chayav* until he acts according to his teaching — *o she-yoreh le-acherim ve-ya'asu ke-horato* — or until he rules for others and they act accordingly.

### Why Zaken Mamre Needed

The Gemara immediately raises a challenge to the second element of the *braisa* — the case where he teaches and others act — is straightforward: *me-ikara lav bar katla hu ve-hashta bar katla hu*. Before others acted, he was not yet *chayav misah*; once they act upon his ruling, he is. The transition is what makes him liable. But regarding the first element — the case where he himself acts on his ruling — a difficulty arises. If the underlying matter is something like *Shabbos* desecration, and he goes ahead and acts on his view that the practice is *mutar*, why do you need the *zaken mamre* framework at all? Even without the *zaken mamre* framing, if a person performs a *melacha d'Oraita* on *Shabbos* in violation of accepted *halacha*, he is *mechalel Shabbos*. What does the *zaken mamre* status add?

### Transition Eliminates Ha…

The Gemara's first answer is that the *braisa* is speaking of a case involving *chelev* and *dam* — violations that carry *kares* rather than *misa b'Beis Din*. In such a case, *me-ikara lav bar katla hu ve-hashta bar katla hu*: before the *zaken mamre* designation, eating *chelev* in violation of accepted *halacha* would make him *chayav kares*, not *chayav misa*. Once he has gone before the *Beis Din HaGadol*, received their ruling, returned, and acted on his opposing view, he is now *chayav misa*. The *zaken mamre* framing thus elevates the consequence from *kares* to execution.

But what about a case of *chayavei mitos Beis Din* — where the underlying violation itself already carries the death penalty? The Gemara then offers the key answer: *me-ikara ba'ei hatra'ah ve-hashta la ba'ei hatra'ah*. Before the *zaken mamre* framing, any execution for the underlying violation would require *hatra'ah* — a formal warning at the moment of commission. Now, however, because he has already stood before the *Beis Din HaGadol* and been told explicitly that he is wrong, and despite that he has returned to his city and acted on his view, the process of the *Beis Din*'s adjudication itself functions as the effective warning. He does not require a fresh *hatra'ah* at the moment of the act; what the *zaken mamre* framework accomplishes is to make him *chayav misah* for the sin of *zaken mamre* itself — without the need for *hatra'ah* — even though the underlying violation, taken in isolation, would have required it.

### Meisis & Avodah Zarah

The Gemara presses further. What if the case involves *avodah zarah* and he was acting as a *meisis* — one who entices others to idolatry — a category that already does not require *hatra'ah*? In that case, it seems, the *zaken mamre* framing adds nothing with respect to eliminating the *hatra'ah* requirement, since *meisis* dispenses with *hatra'ah* independently. Why then would we invoke *zaken mamre* at all?

The Gemara answers: *manah me'ikara i amar ta'ama mekablina minei, hashta i amar ta'ama lo mekablina minei*. In an ordinary *meisis* case, if the accused stood before the court and offered a reasoned explanation for why he believed his conduct was *mutar* under the circumstances, the court would be in a position to consider his argument and potentially exonerate him. Here, however, once he has gone through the *zaken mamre* process — brought his question to the *Beis Din HaGadol*, received their authoritative ruling, and defied it — no argument he now offers can be entertained. The sin is no longer simply *meisis*; it is the sin of *zaken mamre*. It is for that sin, and not the underlying violation, that he is executed. And for that sin, the entire prior proceedings serve in place of both *hatra'ah* and any opportunity to offer exculpatory reasoning.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 89

## Zaken Mamre Definition

### Chomer Sofrim

The *daf* opens with the *mishna* found at the bottom of 88b, approximately ten lines from the end, which introduces the principle of *chomer bedivrei sofrim midivrei torah* — that rabbinic interpretation can carry greater weight than what is stated explicitly in the verses themselves. The context is the *zaken mamre*, the rebellious elder.

### Tefillin Examples

The *mishna* illustrates this principle through the laws of *tefillin*. If a *zaken mamre* were to declare that there is no such thing as *tefillin* at all — thereby denying something stated explicitly in the *psukim* of the *Torah* — he would be *patur*, exempt from the *chiyuv* of a *zaken mamre*. The reason is that such a statement does not constitute a *hora'ah*: the *zaken mamre* is defined by his positioning himself as a *posek* in defiance of the *Beis Din*, and a flat denial of explicit *Torah* law does not rise to the level of a competing legal ruling.

However, if he were to claim that the *shel rosh* requires not four *batim* but five, then he is *chayav*. This position engages with the halachic question of what constitutes *tefillin* — accepting the institution while disputing its parameters — and that constitutes a true *hora'ah*. It is thus counterintuitive but correct: one is more liable for deviating on a matter whose details derive from rabbinic interpretation than for denying something stated outright in the text.

This *mishna* reflects the opinion of *Rebbi Yehuda*, who derives from the phrase *al pi hatorah asher yorucha* that the *zaken mamre* can be liable for any matter that has both a *Torah* basis (*al pi hatorah*) and a dimension requiring interpretation (*asher yorucha*). This is the broader view, as distinct from *Rebbi Meir*, who requires that the matter be one for which an ordinary person would incur *kares* and *chatas*.

### Mosif Gore'a Principle

*Rebbi Elazar* then cites *Rebbi Oshaya* with a considerably narrower definition. He states: *eino chayav ela al davar she'ikaro midivrei torah uperusho midivrei sofrim veyesh bo lehosif ve'im hosif gore'a* — one is only liable as a *zaken mamre* for something whose root is in the *Torah*, whose elaboration derives from rabbinic interpretation, and where there is the possibility of addition such that adding actually subtracts. The *gemara* concludes: *va'anu ein lanu ela tefillin* — the only example that fits all these criteria is *tefillin*.

This formulation is narrower than the *mishna* and is said to align with *Rebbi Yehuda*. It introduces the *mosif gore'a* principle: not merely that one added to a *mitzvah* object, but that by adding, one rendered the original invalid. As will be seen, this is a demanding criterion that eliminates most potential cases.

### Lulav/Tzitzit Analysis

The *gemara* challenges *Rebbi Elazar's* restriction by proposing additional candidates. Regarding *lulav*: its root is in the *Torah*, its details are rabbinic elaboration, and adding an extra *min* might seem to invalidate the *arba minim*. But the *gemara* responds that the answer depends on whether one holds that the *lulav* requires binding (*egged*). If no binding is required, then each species stands independently (*hai lechudei kai vehai lechudei kai*), and adding an extra species does not redefine the bundle and does not invalidate it. If binding is required, then a bundle that included an extra species would be *garu ve'omed* — invalid from the very moment of its construction. There would never be a moment when a valid bundle existed only to be subsequently invalidated by the addition.

The same logic applies to *tzitzit*. Adding an extra string might seem to invalidate the *tzitzit*, but it depends on whether the *kesher elyon* — the top knot — is *de'oraisa*. If it is not (a minority view), the extra string stands independently and does not invalidate. If it is *de'oraisa*, which is indeed the accepted *pesak*, then the extra string creates an invalid object from the outset — *garu ve'omed* — rather than invalidating something previously valid.

The *gemara* then presses the same challenge against *tefillin*: if one begins with four valid *batim* and attaches a fifth as a separate unit, the fifth stands independently and does not invalidate the four. If one constructs five *batim* as a single unit from the start, then again the object is *garu ve'omed* — never valid to begin with. The difficulty, then, is: how is *tefillin* any different from *lulav* or *tzitzit*?

### Bayis Chitzon Exposure

*Rav Zeira* resolves the problem: *bayis chitzon she'eino ro'eh es ha'avir pasul* — the outer compartment of the *shel rosh* must be exposed to the open air, and if it is not, it is invalid. When a fifth *bayis* is added to what was a valid set of four, even if the fifth stands as a separate unit and does not redefine the whole as a set of five, it nonetheless invalidates the outer compartment of the original four by covering it and preventing its exposure to the air. This is the unique mechanism by which *tefillin* satisfies the *mosif gore'a* criterion: there is a valid object to begin with, and the act of adding genuinely invalidates it — not by redefining the unit, but through this distinct *pesul* of the *bayis chitzon*.

It should be noted that no *psukim* are brought in the *gemara* to explain why *Rebbi Elazar* requires this *mosif gore'a* criterion as the essential definition of *zaken mamre*. The derivation remains analytically interesting but without explicit scriptural grounding in the text as presented.

## Execution Procedures

### Jurisdiction Rules

The next *mishna* continues the laws of the *zaken mamre* and turns to the question of where and when he is executed. The *mishna* states: *ein memisin oso lo beveis din shebe'iro velo beveis din shebeyavneh* — he is not executed either in his local *Beis Din* or in the *Beis Din* of *Yavneh*. *Rashi* and *Tosafos* both raise the obvious difficulty: why is *Yavneh* mentioned at all? The *Beis Din* of *Yavneh* rose to prominence precisely after the *Beis HaMikdash* was destroyed, yet the *zaken mamre* requires the *Beis Din* in the *Beis HaMikdash* to have jurisdiction. The *mishna*'s mention of *Yavneh* thus indicates that even a major court sitting outside the *Beis HaMikdash* cannot execute the *zaken mamre*.

### Beis Din HaGadol

Execution can only occur under the authority of the *Beis Din HaGadol she'birushalayim*. This is not only the venue of the *gmar din* but also the place of execution itself. It is worth noting, however, that the *Rambam* makes explicit that the actual adjudication — the determination of liability — can be conducted in the *zaken mamre's* local *Beis Din*. He is then brought to *Yerushalayim* for execution. Notably, the opening *mishna* of *Sanhedrin* does not list the judgment of the *zaken mamre* among the matters requiring a *Beis Din* of seventy-one; the elevated venue is required specifically for the execution, not the trial itself.

### Regel vs. Immediate

The *mishna* records a dispute regarding timing. According to the *Tanna Kamma* in the name of *Rebbi Akiva*: *umeshamrin oso ad haregel umemisin oso baregel* — one waits until the *regel* and executes him then, as the *pasuk* states: *vechol ha'am yishme'u veyira'u velo yezidun od* — all the people will hear and fear and no longer act presumptuously. The rationale for waiting is that the *regel*, when all of Israel gathers in *Yerushalayim*, maximizes the deterrent effect and reinforces the authority of the *Beis Din HaGadol*.

*Rebbi Yehuda* disagrees: *ein me'anin es dino shel ze* — one does not delay and cause *inui hadin*, the suffering of prolonged judgment, once the *gmar din* has been rendered. According to *Rebbi Yehuda*, execution is immediate, and the requirement of public awareness — *veyishme'u veyira'u* — is satisfied by sending written notifications throughout all locations: *ish ploni nischayev misa beveis din*. *Rebbi Yehuda* presses the textual point: the *pasuk* does not say *yir'u* — they will see — but *yishme'u* — they will hear. Hearing about the execution through dispatched messages is sufficient; there is no need for the physical gathering of the *regel*.

The consequence of *Rebbi Yehuda's* position regarding venue is also noteworthy: since the trial occurs in the local *Beis Din* and execution follows immediately upon the *gmar din*, execution would take place locally rather than in the *Beis Din HaGadol*. The elevation to *Yerushalayim* was driven by the logic of waiting for the *regel*; once that is removed, execution proceeds where the judgment was rendered.

### Four Akhraza Cases

The *gemara* introduces a *baraisa*: *arba'ah tzerichin akhraza* — four categories of individuals require a public proclamation throughout all of Israel upon their execution, as derived from the formulation *vechol Yisrael yishme'u veyira'u*. These four are: *ha-meisis* (one who seduces others to *avodah zarah*), *ben sorer u-moreh*, *zaken mamre*, and *edim zomemin*. In each case, some form of the phrase *veyishme'u veyira'u* appears in the relevant *psukim*. The one variation is by *edim zomemin*, where the *pasuk* reads *vehanish'arim yishme'u veyira'u* — only the remaining will hear and fear — because the *gemara* explains: *de-lav kol amma chazu le-sahaduso*, not everyone is qualified to serve as a witness, and so the deterrent effect is directed specifically at those who can.

### Institution Protection

*Ramban*, in his commentary on the *Torah*, offers a striking insight that illuminates the entire list. In each of these four cases, he observes, the individual is being executed not simply because his act alone deserves the death penalty, but in order to protect critical institutions. The *ben sorer u-moreh* is executed to protect the institution of parental authority. The *edim zomemin* are executed to protect the integrity of the courts — even when the person they falsely accused was not actually put to death. The *zaken mamre* is executed to protect the decisory authority of the *Beis Din* — its power not merely to adjudicate but to interpret and rule. And the *meisis* is executed to protect divine authority, even if nobody actually worshipped *avodah zarah* as a result.

This is why in each case the *Torah* insists on *veyishme'u veyira'u*: the deterrent must be public and pervasive, because what is at stake is not merely one individual's sin but the integrity of the foundational structures that sustain Jewish life. It also explains why the punishment can appear disproportionate to the concrete harm caused — the harm being protected against is institutional, not individual.

## Navi HaSheker

### Four Categories

The *mishna* now moves to the next category of *chenek*: the *navi ha-sheker*, the false prophet. Four types are identified. First: one who prophesies something he never heard — he fabricates a prophecy entirely. Second: one who prophesies something that was communicated to another *navi* but not to him — technically also *mah shelo shama*, since he himself received no such prophecy, but the *mishna* specifies this case because one might have thought that since it was a genuine divine communication to someone, it carries some legitimacy. The *pasuk* on which these are based is: *ach ha-navi asher yazid ledaber davar bishmi es asher lo tzivisiv ledaber* — the prophet who presumptuously speaks in my name what I did not command him to speak. Both categories fall under *mitat beis din*, execution by human agency.

### Heaven's Punishment

Three other categories are left to divine judgment — *misatan bidei shamayim*. These are: one who suppresses his own prophecy (*ha-koveish nevuato*), one who violates the word of a *navi* (*ha-mavater al divrei navi*), and a *navi* who violates his own prophecy (*navi she'avar al divrei atzmo*). The derivation is from the *pasuk*: *ve-ha'ish asher lo yishma el devarai* — the man who does not hearken to my words — with the *gemara* reading it both ways: *lo yishma*, he does not obey, and *lo yashmia*, he does not cause them to be heard. Both acts — disobeying the *navi* and failing to transmit the prophecy — are addressed by the same verse, and the consequence is *anochi edrosh me'imo* — I, God, will seek it from him, indicating *mitat shamayim*.

The *mishna* then lists two additional categories of *chenek* that do not belong to the *navi ha-sheker* laws. One who prophesies in the name of *avodah zarah* — even if the content he delivers happens to align with correct *halacha* — is also subject to human execution. And one who commits adultery with a married woman (*haba al eishet ish*) is executed by *chenek* once the woman has formally entered the *reshut* of the husband for *nisuin*, even if the marriage has not yet been consummated. The special case of a *bat kohen* who commits adultery requires *sreifah* for her, while the adulterer still receives *chenek*, and *edim zomemin* who attempted to convict her receive *chenek* as well, since it is written *hi ba'esh tisaref* — only *she* is burned, excluding all the men involved, who revert to the baseline punishment of adultery.

### Scriptural Sources

The *baraisa* then maps each category to its scriptural source, tracking closely with the *gemara's* exposition of the same verse. The phrase *et asher lo tzivisiv ledaber* — what I did not command him — is read to mean: I did not command *him*, though I may have commanded a colleague. *Lachaveiro tzivitiv* — I commanded his friend — establishes the second category of one who transmits another's prophecy as his own. The phrase *va'asher yedaber beshem elohim acherim* covers the case of prophesying in the name of *avodah zarah*. And the conclusion *umeis hanavi hahu* — that *navi* shall die — is a *stam misah* in the *Torah*, which by convention means *chenek*.

### Tzidkiyah Case

The *gemara* identifies *Tzidkiyah ben Kena'anah* as the paradigmatic case of one who prophesies what he never heard. As described in *Tanach*, he fashioned iron horns and declared *ko tenagach et Aram* — so shall you gore Aram — presenting this as divine prophecy to *Achav*. The difficulty is immediate: *mai hava leh le-me'evad*? How can *Tzidkiyah* be held liable if he apparently received some vision or spirit that led him to believe he had a genuine prophecy?

The *gemara* provides the context. God asked which spirit would seduce *Achav* to go up and fall in battle at *Ramot Gil'ad*. A spirit came forward and said *ani afatenu* — I will seduce him. God said *tzei va'aseh chen* — go and do so. *Rav Yehuda* explains the word *tzei*: *tzei me-mechitzati* — depart from my domain — indicating that while God permitted this false spirit to act, it was not acting on God's behalf. *Rebbi Yochanan* identifies this spirit as *ruach Navot ha-Yizre'eli*, the spirit of *Navot* whom *Achav* had murdered, now returning to bring about *Achav's* downfall in battle.

The problem, then, is one of culpability: *Tzidkiyah* believed himself to be a genuine recipient of divine prophecy. How can he be punished?

### Signon Principle

The *gemara* answers that *Tzidkiyah* should have attended to the teaching of *Rebbi Yitzchak*: *signon echad oleh le-chama nevi'im ve-ein shenei nevi'im mitnab'im be-signon echad* — a single theme or content may be given to many prophets, but two prophets never prophesy in precisely the same language. Each *navi* receives a prophecy refracted through his own personality and intellect, and the expression is always uniquely his own. This is demonstrated from the comparison of *Ovadia* and *Yirmiyah*, who each prophesied the theme of *zdon libcha hishi'acha* — the brazenness of your heart has misled you — but with different precise formulations.

In the episode of *Achav*, all the prophets were delivering their prophecy in exactly the same words. This linguistic uniformity should itself have been a signal that what they were saying was not genuine prophecy. The *gemara* questions the anachronism — how would *Tzidkiyah* have known *Rebbi Yitzchak's* teaching? — and answers that *Yehoshaphat* was present and was already articulating this very principle. As the *pasuk* records, *Yehoshaphat* asked *ha'ein po navi la-Hashem od* — is there not another true prophet of God here? — and when challenged, he explained: *kach mekubbani mibeis avi abba, signon echad oleh le-chama nevi'im ve-ein shenei nevi'im mitnab'im be-signon echad*. This was his received tradition from his ancestral house.

One might still ask whether this logical awareness is sufficient to establish *mezid* — intentional wrongdoing — for one who had a genuine experiential sense of prophetic reception. The *gemara* does not resolve this tension cleanly, but the implication appears to be that since *Tzidkiyah* should have recognized, on the basis of the known principle, that the identical language of all the prophets was a disqualifying sign, he is held to have spoken knowingly and is thus liable.

### Chananya Case

The case of *mah shelo ne'emar lo* — prophesying something told to another — is illustrated by *Chananya ben Azur*. *Yirmiyah* had stood in the upper marketplace and declared in the name of God: *hineni shover es keshes Elam* — I will break the bow of Elam — one of the nations that had joined *Bavel* in its campaign against Israel. *Chananya* then proceeded to the lower marketplace and declared, on his own account: *koh amar Hashem shavarti es ol melech Bavel* — so says God, I have broken the yoke of the king of *Bavel*.

*Rav Pappa* challenges *Abaye*: this does not quite fit the category, because what *Yirmiyah* heard was about *Elam*, not about *Bavel*. So *Chananya* was not simply transmitting *Yirmiyah's* prophecy — he made a separate claim that was not said to *Yirmiyah* either. *Abaye* responds: since the *kal vachomer* was fully available — if God will break the bow of *Elam*, which came only to assist *Bavel*, then how much more so will God break *Bavel* itself — *keivan d'isyahiv lei kal vachomer le-midrash, ke-man de'is'mar lei dami*. It is as though it were explicitly said to *Yirmiyah*. Accordingly, *Chananya's* error lies not in constructing an unreasonable inference, but in presenting his own logical derivation as though it were a received divine prophecy — and that is precisely what makes him a *navi sheker*.

### Suppression Proof

The *gemara* addresses the case of *ha-koveish nevuato* — suppressing prophecy — and cites *Yonah ben Amittai* as the example, who fled rather than deliver his prophecy. A *Tanna* who studied before *Rav Chisda* stated that one who suppresses his prophecy incurs *malkus*. *Rav Chisda* pressed back with a practical objection: *man de'achal tamre be-arba lo lakei* — who could possibly issue a warning? How can one be forewarned and thus liable for *malkus* for an act that is both passive and entirely private in its occurrence?

*Abaye* resolves this: *chavrei nevi'ei* — his fellow prophets would know, because *ki lo ya'aseh Hashem Elokim davar ki im gila sodo el avadav ha-nevi'im* — God does not act without first revealing His secret to His servants the prophets. Thus, a colleague who received the same awareness of the prophecy could, in principle, issue a forewarning. The *gemara* raises a further question: perhaps God had retracted the prophecy, which would explain why it was not delivered. The response is that if a retraction had occurred, all the fellow prophets who knew of the original prophecy would also have been informed of its retraction. The case of *Yonah* is then raised as a seeming counterexample — *Yonah* remained outside *Ninveh* to see what would happen even after the people repented, suggesting he was not informed of the shift. The *gemara* answers that the original prophecy *ninveh nehepaches* — *Ninveh* will be overturned — was inherently ambiguous. *Yonah* did not know whether it meant the city would be destroyed or the city's conduct would be overturned in repentance. There was no retraction; rather, there was a clarification of the original prophecy's meaning.

### Michah Case

The paradigmatic case of *ha-mavater al divrei navi* — one who violates the word of a prophet — is drawn from the episode in *Tanach* where *ish echad mibnei ha-nevi'im* asked his fellow to strike him. The *gemara* understands this figure to be *Micha*: he sought to appear beaten so that he could deliver a message to *Achav* with appropriate dramatic weight. His colleague refused, even though a *navi* had directed him. The *pasuk* records that this man was subsequently killed by a lion — an expression of divine punishment for failing to obey the word of a prophet.

### Ido HaNavi Case

The case of *navi she'avar al divrei atzmo* — a prophet who violated his own words — is *Ido HaNavi*. He had declared by divine command that he would neither eat bread nor drink water, and an individual claiming also to be a prophet told him: *gam ani navi kamocha* — I too am a prophet like you — and instructed him that it was permissible to eat and drink. Despite knowing what God had commanded him, *Ido* listened to this other man and ate. The *pasuk* records that he too was found and killed by a lion on his journey home. The lion is the instrument of divine punishment — *bidei shamayim* — in both this case and the case of *Micha's* colleague, while *Yonah*, who suppressed his prophecy, was swallowed by a fish before ultimately being spared.

### Proving Navi Status

The *gemara* transitions to a broader and striking question: how does one establish that a person is genuinely a *navi*, such that violating his words carries the halachic consequence of *mitat shamayim*? The *gemara* suggests initially that the answer lies in signs (*os*) — the *Torah* indicates that a prophet who gives a sign that is fulfilled can be treated as genuine. But the case of *Micha's* colleague poses a problem: *Micha* told the man to strike him without providing any sign to prove his prophetic status. How was the man then obligated to listen?

The *gemara* answers: *heicha de-muchzak shani* — where one is already established as a *navi*, the rules are different. If a person is *muchzak* as a prophet, he need not produce a sign for each individual instruction; his prior status carries the obligation.

*Rashi* explains that *muchzak* here means that the person is known to be a *tzaddik* and a *navi emes* — righteous and a true prophet. How does one acquire that status? *Rashi* implies that it comes from a track record of predictions that proved accurate, even if these do not meet the technical definition of a wondrous sign. *Rambam* engages similarly with the question of how character and prior prophetic performance combine to establish *muchzak* status, though the precise threshold remains open to interpretation.

The *gemara* then reinforces the principle with two famous cases. *Ve-ei lo teima hachi, Avraham be-Har HaMoriah heicha shama lei Yitzchak* — if not for the *muchzak* principle, how did *Yitzchak* consent to being slaughtered? *Avraham* had not produced a sign in any conventional sense. Yet *Avraham's* standing as someone in whom divine communication was manifest was sufficient for *Yitzchak* to accept his father's instruction. Similarly, *Eliyahu be-Har HaKarmel* directed the people to bring a *korban* outside the *Beis HaMikdash*, an act that would otherwise constitute a severe *issur de'oraisa* of *shechutei chutz*. They listened because *Eliyahu* was *muchzak* as a prophet, and a *navi muchzak* may instruct a temporary deviation from a prohibition. The *gemara* concludes: *ela heicha de-muchzak shani* — it is the established status of the prophet that creates the obligation to listen, even absent a contemporaneous sign.

## Akeidah Narrative

### Satan's Challenge

Having mentioned *Avraham* at *Har HaMoriah*, the *gemara* digresses to explore the *Akeidah* narrative through *midrashic* elaboration. *Rebbi Yochanan* in the name of *Rebbi Yosi ben Zimra* asks: what were the *devarim* — "things" — that preceded the divine test of *Avraham*? The verse states *vayehi achar ha-devarim ha-eileh ve-ha-Elokim nissah es Avraham* — and it was after these things that God tested *Avraham*. The answer: *achar devarav shel Satan* — after the words of the *Satan*.

The background is the feast *Avraham* made upon the weaning of *Yitzchak*. The *Satan* approached God and objected: this elderly man, granted the fruit of his womb after a hundred years, made a great celebration — but from the entire feast did not bring even a single turtledove or young bird as a *korban* before God. Is this how he shows gratitude? God replied: *kelum asah ela bishvil beno* — everything he does is for the sake of his son. If I were to ask him to sacrifice his son, *mi-yad zovcho* — he would agree immediately. And immediately: *ve-ha-Elokim nissah es Avraham*.

### Mashal Analogy

*Rebbi Shimon ben Abba* explains the word *na* in the phrase *kach na et bincha* — please take your son. The word *na* is a language of entreaty, of request. He offers a *mashal*: a human king who had one great warrior who helped him prevail in many wars. When a particularly difficult battle arose, the king said to him: "Please, stand with me in this battle" — not because the general had ever failed, but so that no one could say the previous victories were easy and meant little. God similarly said to *Avraham*: "I have tested you with many tests and you have withstood them all. Now please, stand with me in this one, so that no one will say the earlier tests had no real substance."

### God's Command

The command unfolds incrementally. *Kach et bincha* — take your son. *Avraham* replied: I have two sons — *Yishmael* and *Yitzchak*. *Et yechidecha* — your only son. But each is unique to his mother, *ze yachid le'immo veze yachid le'immo*. *Asher ahavta* — the one you love. *Teravyehu rachmina aleihon* — I love both of them. The beauty of this exchange, as the *midrash* presents it, reveals something profound about *Avraham's* character: even after being commanded to sacrifice *Yitzchak*, *Avraham* does not distance himself emotionally from *Yishmael*. He acknowledges his full love for both sons. Finally, God says *et Yitzchak* — *Yitzchak*.

### Incremental Disclosure

Why the drawn-out exchange? *Kedai shelo titaref da'ato alav* — so that *Avraham* not be overwhelmed and disoriented by the shock of the command all at once. The gradual disclosure allows *Avraham* time to internally acclimate to what is being asked of him, so that he can proceed with full composure rather than in a state of psychological collapse.

### Satan's Logic

As *Avraham* set out toward *Har Moriah* with *Yitzchak*, the *Satan* moved to intercept him. He cited verses from *Iyov*: *hanissa davar eleicha tileh* — will a matter be tested against you and you will grow weary? *Hinneh yissarta rabbim ve-yadayim rafot techazzek* — behold you have instructed many and strengthened weak hands. *Koshel yekimun milecha* — your words have lifted up those who would stumble. *Ki atta tavo eleicha ve-tileh* — now it has come upon you and you are weary.

In context, these are words spoken to *Iyov* by a companion, urging him not to lose faith after having strengthened so many others. The *midrash* reads the *Satan* as deploying these verses as a challenge to *Avraham*: you have been the pillar of faith for so many, strengthening others — and now God tests you with this terrible demand? After all you have sacrificed and built? The *Satan* may also be suggesting that the *Akeidah* will undermine the very ethical and spiritual edifice that *Avraham* has spent his life constructing.

### Abraham's Trust

*Avraham* replied: *ani be-tummi elech* — I walk in my integrity. His response is the inverse of *Iyov's*: where *Iyov* demanded justification, *Avraham* accepted without question. God has asked; he will do it. Doubt may exist, the logic may be elusive, but his commitment is absolute.

### Satan's Deception

When the *Satan* saw that this approach had not deterred *Avraham*, he changed tactics. He said: *ve'elai davar yugnav* — a thing was stolen to me, I received a kind of secret. *Kach shamati me'achorei ha-pargod* — this is what I heard from behind the heavenly curtain: *hasseh le'olah ve'ein Yitzchak le'olah* — it is a sheep that will be brought as the *olah*, and *Yitzchak* will not actually be sacrificed. The *Satan's* intent here was apparently to deflate the value of the test — if *Avraham* proceeded believing that at the end there would be no actual sacrifice of *Yitzchak*, his compliance would not constitute the same level of *emunah* and sacrifice.

### Liar's Fate

*Avraham* responded: *kach onsho shel badai, afilu omer emet ein shom'in lo* — this is the punishment of a liar: even when he speaks the truth, no one believes him. I know what God asked of me; I will not be swayed by what you claim to have overheard. *Nechama Leibowitz* observes, in a related vein, that the *Satan* in this and similar *midrashim* — including one in which the *Satan* warns *Avraham* that the world will call him a murderer — may be understood as an externalization of *Avraham's* own inner turmoil and conflict. The *midrash* does not simply portray an untroubled march to *Har Moriah*, but rather gives form to the genuine anguish and struggle that any such test would involve. Indeed, without some measure of internal resistance, the concept of a test would be empty.

### Ishmael's Challenge

*Rebbi Levi* offers an alternative reading of *vayehi achar ha-devarim ha-eileh*. In his view, it refers not to the words of the *Satan* but to *achar devarav shel Yishmael* — after the words of *Yishmael* to *Yitzchak*. On the occasion of the celebration, *Yishmael* said to *Yitzchak*: *ani gadol mimcha ba-mitzvot* — I am greater than you in *mitzvot*, for *ata malta ben shmonat yamim* — you underwent your *bris milah* as an eight-day-old infant, while *va'ani ben shalosh esre shana* — I underwent it at thirteen, when I was fully aware and could have refused. *Yitzchak* replied: you think one limb is such an accomplishment? *Im omer li Ha-Kadosh Baruch Hu zaveach atzmecha lefanai* — if God were to say to me, offer yourself before Me, *ani zoveach* — I would do it. And immediately: *ve-ha-Elokim nissah es Avraham*.

What is particularly compelling about this version is that it draws *Yitzchak* into the center of the narrative. The *Akeidah* is not merely a test of *Avraham*; it is also a fulfillment of *Yitzchak's* own declaration of readiness and faith. *Yitzchak* is not a passive subject but a willing participant, and the *midrash* establishes that his willingness was not merely coerced compliance but an expression of genuine commitment to divine service.
