# Sanhedrin 90

## Navi Shehidiach

### Intro: Navi & Avodah Zar…

The daf opens in the middle of a discussion about a *navi* who prophesies something he did not actually receive, or who prophesies in the name of another god — both of which carry the penalty of *chenek*. There is also the related case of one who fails to heed the words of a prophet, which carries *misa b'yedei shamayim*. These categories prompt the broader question of how one identifies a true prophet and why one is obligated to obey him — a question that ultimately opens into the *agadata* of *akeidas Yitzchak*, exploring why Yitzchak listened to Avraham.

The present discussion, however, turns to a distinct case that has appeared earlier in the sugya: not a *navi* who prophesies in the name of *avoda zara*, but one who claims to have received a prophecy and uses it to incite others to worship *avoda zara*. This case appears in the Torah directly before the *parsha* of the *mases* — the individual who privately entices others to idolatry, whose punishment is *skila*. The question is: what is the punishment for a *navi* who does the same thing publicly?

### Tanu Rabbanan Debate

A *tanu rabbanan* addresses this directly. The *navi shehidiach* — the prophet who incites to *avoda zara* — receives *skila*, just like the individual *mases*. Rabbi Shimon disagrees and holds that such a *navi* receives *chenek*. The same dispute applies to the *midichei ir nidachas*, those who cause an entire city to worship *avoda zara*: the Rabbis say *skila*, Rabbi Shimon says *chenek*.

This is striking. An individual *mases* receives *skila*, the most severe of the four capital punishments. One would expect that a *navi* who incites masses to *avoda zara* — surely a graver offense — would carry at least the same penalty. Yet Rabbi Shimon rules that both the *navi* and the *midichei ir nidachas* receive the lesser punishment of *chenek*.

### Gezeira Shava

The Gemara explains the Rabbinic position first. The verse in the *navi shehidiach* passage uses the language *ki vikaish lehadichacha*, and the very next section on the individual *mases* uses the identical phrase *ki vikaish lehadichacha*. This *gezeira shava* — a verbal analogy between the two passages — establishes that just as the *mases* receives *skila*, so too does the *navi shehidiach*: *mah le'halan biskila af kan biskila*.

Rabbi Shimon, however, rejects this *gezeira shava*. The verse in the *navi shehidiach* passage simply says *u'mas* — an unqualified death. The rule is that any *misa* stated in the Torah without specification is *chenek*. Rabbi Shimon therefore holds that the *navi shehidiach* receives *chenek*, rendering the ironic result that a *navi* inciting to *avoda zara* receives a lesser punishment than an ordinary individual doing the same.

### Midichei Ir Nidachas

The same debate plays out regarding the *midichei ir nidachas*. The Rabbis are consistent: since the *mases* gets *skila* and since the same *gezeira shava* of *hadacha* language applies here as well — either drawn from the *mases* directly, or from the *navi shehidiach* who already received *skila* — the *midichei ir nidachas* also receive *skila*.

Rabbi Shimon, by contrast, draws the *gezeira shava* of *hadacha hadacha* from the *navi* rather than from the *mases*. Having established that the *navi shehidiach* receives *chenek*, Rabbi Shimon applies the same ruling to the *midichei ir nidachas*.

The Gemara presses Rabbi Shimon: why not learn the *midichei ir nidachas* from the *mases* instead? The answer is *danin mases rabbim mimases rabbim*: the *midichei ir nidachas* are a case involving the masses, and the *navi shehidiach* similarly involves the masses. It is therefore more appropriate to draw the analogy from that case rather than from the individual *mases*, which involves a *yachid*. The Gemara then suggests the opposite — perhaps the ordinary people who are *midichei ir nidachas* should be compared to the ordinary *mases*, not to the *navi*. To this, Rabbi Shimon replies: *keivan shehidiach ein lecha hediyot gadol mizeh* — a *navi* who incites to *avoda zara* has forfeited his prophetic status and is no more than a common person. Once the *navi* is placed in the *chenek* category, the *midichei ir nidachas* follow.

### Rav Chisda Framework

Rav Chisda steps back to clarify what kind of case the *navi shehidiach* involves. He explains that the dispute between the Rabbis and Rabbi Shimon concerns a *navi* who is either *oker haguf de'avoda kochavim* — completely uprooting the prohibition against *avoda zara*, effectively saying all idolatry is now permitted — or who is engaged in *kiyum miktzas u'bitul miktzas de'avoda kochavim*, partially permitting some forms of idolatry while prohibiting others. Either of these falls within the scope of Devarim 13 and is the subject of the dispute.

## Oker Haguf vs. Miktzas

### Two Types False Prophecy

To understand Rav Chisda's framework fully, it is necessary to distinguish between two categories of false prophecy. The first is the *navi shehidiach*, the prophet who incites to *avoda zara*, governed by Devarim 13. The second is the *navi sheker* more broadly — a prophet who testifies to a prophecy he did not receive — which is governed by Devarim 18 and is the subject of the *mishna* we encountered earlier. The punishment for the *navi sheker* is *chenek*, and that is undisputed.

The question Rav Chisda is addressing is how to situate various types of prophetic transgression within one or the other of these two categories.

### Devarim 13 vs. 18

The relevant verse in Devarim 13 reads: *ki yakum bekirbecha navi o cholem chalom* — if a prophet or dreamer arises and gives you a sign or wonder, and says *nelcha acharei elohim acherim*, let us follow other gods and worship them. The *navi* is inducing *avoda zara*. The verse then mandates his execution: *umes hanavi hahu*, and it concludes with *lehadi-chacha min haderech asher tzivecha Hashem elokecha laleches bah* — to lead you astray from the path that God commanded you to walk.

The relevant verse in Devarim 18 is different in character. It reads: *ach hanavi asher yazid ledaber davar bishmi es asher lo tzivisiv ledaber* — the prophet who presumptuously speaks in My name what I did not command him — *va'asher yedaber beshem elohim acherim umes hanavi hahu*. That *umes* is unqualified, yielding *chenek*. This is the generic *navi sheker* — not someone inciting to *avoda zara*, but someone falsely claiming prophetic authority.

One marker that distinguishes the *navi sheker* from the *navi shehidiach* is *oker kol haguf*: a *navi* who claims there is no longer a *mitzvah* to perform some commandment — say, that *tefillin* are no longer required — is *oker kol haguf* with respect to that *mitzvah*, which identifies him as a *navi sheker* and places him squarely in the Devarim 18 category, carrying *chenek* by consensus. By contrast, a *navi* who temporarily overrides a *mitzvah* in a specific circumstance — as Eliyahu did on Har HaCarmel — is not a *navi sheker* at all. That kind of partial, time-bound override is permitted and carries no liability.

### Rav Chisda: Laleches

Rav Chisda's framework is challenged by a *braisa* that expounds on the word *laleches* in the verse from Devarim 13. The *braisa* derives: *laleches* — this refers to a *mitzvas asei*; *bah* — this refers to a *mitzvas lo sa'asei*. The implication is that the case of the *navi shehidiach* in Devarim 13 can encompass even a prophet who leads people astray from a positive commandment, not only one who incites to outright *avoda zara*.

This creates a difficulty for Rav Chisda, who limits Devarim 13 to cases involving *avoda zara*. If the passage is solely about *avoda zara*, what would a *mitzvas asei* in that context even look like, since all the prohibitions of *avoda zara* are negative commandments? Rav Chisda resolves this by interpreting *ve'nitz'atzem* — the positive commandment to destroy places of *avoda zara* worship. A *navi* who tells people not to fulfill this positive obligation of demolishing idolatrous shrines would be included in the *navi shehidiach* category under Devarim 13. This preserves Rav Chisda's position that Devarim 13 remains entirely within the domain of *avoda zara*.

### Rav Hamnuna View

Rav Hamnuna challenges Rav Chisda's framework directly. In his view, the category of *oker haguf* — completely uprooting a principle — is itself what defines the *navi shehidiach* classification, regardless of whether the subject matter is *avoda zara* or other *mitzvos*. A *navi* who claims there is no longer any obligation to observe *tzitzis*, for example, is not simply a *navi sheker* in the narrow Devarim 18 sense; he is fundamentally challenging the authority of the Torah, which is conceptually equivalent to inciting *avoda zara*. Both represent a root-level attack on the foundations of faith, not merely a false or unauthorized prophecy.

Under Rav Hamnuna's view, then, the line between Devarim 13 and Devarim 18 is drawn differently. Devarim 13 applies to any case of *oker haguf* — whether the *navi* is uprooting *avoda zara* restrictions or any other *mitzvah*. The *kiyum miktzas u'bitul miktzas* of *avoda zara* also falls under Devarim 13 since the Torah explicitly says *min haderech afilu miktzas haderech* — even a partial deviation regarding *avoda zara* places one in the graver category. The word *laleches* accordingly refers to *oker kol haguf* by any *mitzvas asei*, placing that squarely within the *navi shehidiach* category. And *kiyum miktzas u'bitul miktzas* by *shear mitzvos* — other commandments — remains exempt entirely, as that is the domain of legitimate prophetic override.

### Abaye vs. Rava

The dispute between Rav Chisda and Rav Hamnuna generates a corresponding dispute between Abaye and Rava in their reading of a subsequent *braisa*. The *braisa* states: one who prophesies to uproot a principle of the Torah is *chayav*; one who prophesies to establish some and cancel some — Rabbi Shimon exempts; and regarding *avoda zara*, even if he says worship it today and abolish it tomorrow, all agree he is *chayav*.

Abaye follows Rav Chisda. On his reading, the first clause — *hamisnabe l'akor davar min hatorah chayav* — refers to *shear mitzvos* that are completely uprooted. This places the *navi* in the *navi sheker* category of Devarim 18, and the liability is *chenek*, with no dispute. The second clause — *l'kayem miktzas u'levatel miktzas* — addresses *shear mitzvos* with partial override; here Rabbi Shimon (and in truth all opinions) concur that there is no liability, since such override is the legitimate domain of prophetic authority. The final clause about *avoda zara* governs the dispute between the Rabbis and Rabbi Shimon, with the Rabbis imposing *skila* and Rabbi Shimon *chenek* — *mar ki isa u'mar ki isa*.

Rava follows Rav Hamnuna. On his reading, the opening clause — *hamisnabe l'akor davar min hatorah* — is not limited to *shear mitzvos* but applies broadly: whether the *navi* is uprooting *avoda zara* restrictions or any other *mitzvah*, if he is *oker kol haguf*, he falls into the *navi shehidiach* category of Devarim 13. The clause *l'kayem miktzas u'levatel miktzas* then addresses *shear mitzvos* with partial override, and all agree there is no liability. The final clause about *avoda zara* — even temporary worship — again belongs to the *navi shehidiach* category, with the liability following each authority's position: *mar ki isa u'mar ki isa*.

## True Prophet Override

### Prophet Override Rule

Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav Yochanan states a general principle: in all cases, if a *navi* instructs you to transgress a Torah commandment, you must listen to him — except when it comes to *avoda zara*. This is consistent with the framework developed above. A legitimate *navi* exercising *kiyum miktzas u'bitul miktzas* over *shear mitzvos* is operating within the proper scope of prophetic authority, and one is obligated to comply. The sole exception is *avoda zara*, which is always in the *navi shehidiach* category — never a case of legitimate override. This is true no matter how compelling the sign he produces: even if he were to halt the sun in the middle of the sky, one must not heed him.

### God's Test Rationale

Rabbi Yossi HaGlili offers an explanation for why the Torah permits such extreme temptation. The Torah assessed the full danger and power of *avoda zara* and therefore granted a kind of authority even to those prophesying in its name. The intention was to test the people: could they withstand even the most dramatic signs and wonders produced in favor of idolatry? The instruction not to heed such a prophet — no matter how spectacular his demonstration — is precisely because the Torah knows the temptation is real and formidable. The precise formulation of this idea is admittedly difficult to parse, but the thrust is that the Torah deliberately allows for the possibility of extreme temptation in this domain, in order to train Israel to resist it absolutely.

### Rabbi Akiva Response

Rabbi Akiva objects. It is, he says, inconceivable — *chas v'shalom* — that God would empower a violator of His will to produce miraculous signs in the service of *avoda zara*. The more plausible explanation for how such a person could display apparent wonders is the case of someone like Chananya ben Azur: a person who was initially a true prophet and received genuine prophetic capacity from God, but who subsequently became a *rasha*. The signs he is able to produce are residual from his prior authentic prophetic status. That is how a person can seem to perform wonders while inciting to *avoda zara* — not because God grants such power to transgressors, but because the power was granted earlier, when he was still a true prophet.

## Chenek: Edim & Others

### Edim Zomemin & Bat Kohen

The *mishna* concludes its enumeration of those who receive *chenek* by addressing *edim zomemim* — perjured witnesses — in the case of a *bas Kohen* who commits adultery while married, and the men involved in that adultery. The distinctive feature of this case is that the *bas Kohen* herself receives *sreifa* — burning — while the adulterer receives *chenek*, the standard punishment for adultery by an ordinary married woman. The *edim zomemim* who conspired to have her executed also receive *chenek*.

### Rabbi Yossi Gezeira

The Gemara asks for the source of these rulings. Rav Acha the son of Rav Ika cites a *braisa* in which Rabbi Yossi expounds the verse *v'asisem lo ka'asher zamam la'asos l'achiv* — you shall do to him as he plotted to do to his brother. This establishes a general principle: wherever *edim zomemim* appear in the Torah, they receive the same punishment that would have been inflicted on the accused, and similarly, those who commit *arayos* with a woman receive the punishment applicable to her relationship. The difficulty arises when, as in the case of *bas Kohen*, the man and the woman receive different punishments.

### Zomemin Follow Man

In the case of the *bas Kohen*, the Torah specifies *hi ba'esh tisaref* — she shall be burned — but the men involved are not subject to *sreifa*. The question then is: when the *edim zomemim* are refuted, do they follow the punishment designated for her or for him? The Gemara resolves this from the verse *la'asos leachiv* — what he plotted to do to his brother, not to his sister. In a case where the man's and woman's judgments diverge, the *edim zomemim* follow the man's ruling, and therefore receive *chenek* rather than *sreifa*.

With that, the *perek* of *eilu hein hanichnakin* is complete, and the masechta turns to its final chapter.

## Olam HaBa Introduction

### Kol Yisrael Opening

The last *perek* of Sanhedrin opens with the famous declaration: *kol Yisrael yeish lahem cheilek l'Olam HaBa* — all Israel has a portion in the world to come — deriving this from the verse *ve'ameich kulam tzadikim le'olam yirshu aretz netzer matai ma'aseh yadai lehispa'er*: your people are all righteous; they shall inherit the land forever, the branch of My planting, the work of My hands, that I may be glorified.

It is worth noting that this opening declaration was not originally part of the *mishna* itself. Rashi remarks on this — and though his comment appears to have been excised, the Maharsha preserves it. The *mishna* actually began with *eilu she'ein lahem cheilek l'Olam HaBa*, a list of exclusions. The affirmative declaration *kol Yisrael yeish lahem cheilek l'Olam HaBa* was prepended precisely because it would be jarring to begin with the exclusions without first establishing that the default is inclusion. The opening therefore functions as a frame: everyone has a portion — *except* the following.

This framing, however, sits in tension with other teachings in *Shas* that suggest only *tzadikim* have a portion in *Olam HaBa*. On Rosh Hashanah, for instance, *tzadikim* are immediately granted *Olam HaBa*, *reshaim* face *Gehennom*, and *beinonim* are suspended in judgment. Similarly, when one converts, one is told not to assume that conversion automatically confers *Olam HaBa* — *Olam HaBa eino ela letzadikim*. The *mishna* here bridges this tension through the verse *ve'ameich kulam tzadikim*: by default, all Jews are classified as *tzadikim*. There is a genuine unresolved strand of tradition, however, as to whether *Olam HaBa* is a default that can only be forfeited, or an achievement that must be earned.

### Excluded Categories

The *mishna* then enumerates those who forfeit their portion. The first category is one who says *ein techiyas hameisim min haTorah* — there is no resurrection of the dead rooted in the Torah. Note that the disqualification is not merely denying resurrection as such; one must specifically deny that it is derived from the Torah. Second is one who denies *Torah min hashamayim*. Third is the *apikorus*, whose precise meaning the Gemara will elaborate upon.

Rabbi Akiva adds two further categories: one who reads in *seforim chitzoniyim* — external books excluded from the canon — and one who whispers an incantation over a wound while reciting the verse *kol hamachalah asher samti bemitzrayim lo asim alecha ki ani Hashem rofecha*. Even citing a *pasuk* as part of a healing incantation places one in this category.

At first glance, these final two exclusions seem categorically different from denying *techiyas hameisim* or *Torah min hashamayim*. Reading sectarian literature or whispering a verse over a wound appears far less severe than denying foundational doctrines of faith. One way to understand the grouping is that *Chazal* are drawing lines of communal identity and sectarianism: there were sects in their time — likely including certain strands of Jewish Christianity — that denied *techiyas hameisim* and *Torah min hashamayim*, and some of these practices were associated with those movements. The exclusions may therefore share a common thread: each marks one as aligned with a sectarian movement that has severed its connection with mainstream Israel, whether through doctrinal denial or through characteristic sectarian behavior.

Abba Shaul adds a final exclusion: *hahogeh es Hashem be'osyosov* — one who articulates the divine name as it is spelled, letter by letter.

### Kings & Commoners

The *mishna* then lists specific historical figures who, despite being Israelites, do not receive a portion in *Olam HaBa*. Three kings are named: Yerovam, Achav, and Menashe. Rabbi Yehuda holds that Menashe does have a portion, citing the verse *vayitpalel eilav* — Menashe prayed to God — and God heard his plea and restored him to Jerusalem and his kingship. The Sages respond: God restored him to his *malchus*, his earthly kingship, but not to *chayei Olam HaBa*.

Four commoners complete the list: Bilam, Doeg, Achitofel, and Geichazi. The Gemara will develop each of these cases in turn.

## Resurrection Proofs

### Denial Consequence

The Gemara asks: why does one who denies *techiyas hameisim min haTorah* forfeit a portion in *Olam HaBa*? The answer is measure for measure: *hu kafar b'techiyat hameisim l'fichach lo yihiyeh lo chelek b'techiyat hameisim*. By denying resurrection, one disqualifies oneself from experiencing it. In identifying the consequence this way, the Gemara implicitly equates *Olam HaBa* in this context with *techiyas hameisim* — not the individual soul's existence after death, but the future resurrection of the body in historical time. This is worth pausing over. The Rambam's conception of *Olam HaBa* centers on the immortal soul's existence in a purely spiritual realm, a world that runs parallel to ours and receives souls after death. The Gemara's *pshat* here is quite different: *Olam HaBa* is the world that will arrive in the future, the era of resurrection, the culmination of history. The one who denies it will not share in it.

### Mida K'Neged Mida

The Gemara then pauses to establish the principle of *mida k'neged mida* as a divine operating principle. Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan derives it from the episode of Elisha and the officer. Elisha had prophesied during a famine that by the next day grain would be available at remarkably cheap prices at the gates of Shomron. The officer upon whom the king leaned scoffed: could God make windows in the heavens? Elisha responded: *hincha ro'eh b'einecha u'misham lo tochal* — you will see it with your own eyes, but you will not eat from it.

Indeed, as the verse records, the Aramean army panicked and fled, leaving abundant provisions, and the people rushed out through the gate — trampling the officer there, exactly as foretold.

The Gemara challenges: perhaps the officer's fate was simply due to Elisha's personal curse, since the curse of a sage takes effect even when unwarranted (*kilelat chacham afilu al chinam hi ba'ah*). If so, this episode merely demonstrates the power of a sage's curse, not a general divine principle of *mida k'neged mida*. The Gemara responds: if that were the entire point, the verse need only have said that they trampled him and he died. Why specify *b'sha'ar* — at the gate? The word *sha'ar* echoes the context of the grain prices at the gate — *b'sha'ar Shomron* — and thus the specific detail signals that the punishment was calibrated to the sin: he mocked the prophecy about the *sha'ar*, and he was destroyed at the *sha'ar*. This demonstrates that an overarching principle of *mida k'neged mida* is at work.

### Terumah Proof

The Gemara proceeds to demonstrate *techiyas hameisim* from the Torah itself. The verse states: *venatatem mimenu et terumat Hashem l'Aharon HaKohen* — you shall give from it the *terumah* of God to Aharon the *Kohen*. The Gemara notes: would Aharon actually be alive to receive *terumah* when the Israelites enter the land? He did not enter *Eretz Yisrael* at all. The verse must therefore be teaching that Aharon is destined to be resurrected, and Israel will give him *terumah*. This is the derivation of *techiyas hameisim min haTorah*.

The school of Rabbi Yishmael, however, reads *l'Aharon* not as a literal reference to Aharon himself but as meaning "like Aharon" — a *Kohen* of Aharon's character. The requirement to give *terumah* applies specifically to a *Kohen* who, like Aharon, is a *chaver* — one who can be trusted regarding the laws of *tumah* and *taharah*.

### Terumah Conditions

This leads into a brief but significant digression on the laws governing to whom *terumah* may be given. Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yochanan asks: from where do we know that one may not give *terumah* to a *Kohen am ha'aretz* — an unlearned *Kohen* who cannot be relied upon to maintain the proper standards of purity? The source is a verse in Chronicles: *vayomer la'am yoshvei Yerushalayim latet menat haKohanim v'haLevi'im lema'an yechezku b'Torat Hashem* — he said to the people of Jerusalem to give the portions to the *Kohanim* and *Levi'im* so that they may be strengthened in God's Torah. The implication is that only one who strengthens himself in God's Torah has a claim to a *manat* — a portion. One who does not strengthen himself in God's Torah has no such claim.

Rav Acha bar Adda in the name of Rav Yehuda adds that giving *terumah* to a *Kohen am ha'aretz* is like placing it before a lion: just as with a lion one cannot know whether he will claw into his prey and devour it or not, so too one cannot know whether this *Kohen* will eat the *terumah* in a state of *taharah* or *tumah*. Rabbi Yochanan adds that one who gives *terumah* to a *Kohen am ha'aretz* may bring about his death, as the verse states *umetu vo ki yechalelu'u* — they shall die in it if they desecrate it by eating it in *tumah*. The school of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov further teaches that one thereby causes the *Kohen* to incur *avon ashmah* — the iniquity of guilt — as the verse states *v'hisi'u otam avon ashmah b'ochlam et kodsheihem*.

### Simai's Proof

After the digression, the Gemara returns to the proofs for *techiyas hameisim*. A *braisa* records Rabbi Simai as asking: from where do we derive *techiyas hameisim min haTorah*? From the verse: *v'gam hakimoti et briti itam latet lahem et Eretz Kena'an* — I established My covenant with them to give *them* the land of Kena'an. The verse does not say *lachem*, to you — the descendants — but *lahem*, to them — the *avot* themselves. Since the *avot* did not receive the land in their lifetimes, the verse implies that they will receive it at the time of the resurrection. This, Rabbi Simai concludes, is a proof for *techiyas hameisim* from the Torah.

### Minim Challenges

The Gemara then relates that *minim* — heretics, often understood as referring to Jewish Christians — challenged Rabban Gamliel: from where do you derive that God resurrects the dead? Rabban Gamliel replied that he could demonstrate it from the Torah, from the *Nevi'im*, and from the *Ketuvim*. He proceeded to offer proofs from each, but the *minim* rejected each one.

From the Torah, he cited the verse *hinecha shochev im avotecha v'kam* — behold, you will lie down with your fathers, and arise. The *minim* responded that the continuation of the verse — *v'kam ha'am hazeh v'zanah acharei elohei nechar ha'aretz* — shows that it is the nation that rises and strays, not that the dead individual will literally be resurrected.

From the *Nevi'im*, he cited *yichyu meisecha neveilasi yakumu* — your dead shall live, my corpses shall arise — and *ki tal orot talecha ve'aretz refaim tapil* — for the dew of light is Your dew. The *minim* responded that perhaps this refers only to the particular resurrection of dry bones performed by Yechezkel, not a general doctrine of universal resurrection.

From the *Ketuvim*, he cited *vechichecha keyayin hatov...dovev siftei yeshenim* — your palate is like good wine...causing the lips of the sleeping to murmur. The *minim* pushed back, suggesting that *dovev siftei yeshenim* does not imply physical resurrection but merely that the lips of the dead murmur — a reference to the teaching of Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak: anyone who cites a *halacha* in the name of a deceased sage causes his lips to murmur in the grave, as it is said *dovev siftei yeshenim*. In other words, the *minim* deflected each proof by offering an alternative reading.

### Final Proof

After each attempted proof was met with a rebuttal, Rabban Gamliel produced a verse they could not contest: *asher nishba Hashem la'avoteichem latet lahem* — which God swore to your forefathers to give *them*. The verse does not say *lachem*, to you, but *lahem*, to them — the *avot* themselves. Since the forefathers never received the land in their lifetimes, the oath implies a future fulfillment through resurrection. This is the same proof Rabbi Simai had offered, and it was decisive. *Mikan l'techiyas hameisim min haTorah.*

### Alternative Proof

The Gemara records an alternative tradition, according to which Rabban Gamliel's clinching proof was a different verse: *ve'atem hadeveikim baHashem elokeichem chayim kulchem hayom* — and you who cleave to God are all alive today. The inference is: just as you are alive today, so too will you remain alive in *Olam HaBa*. *Mah hayom kulchem chayim af l'Olam HaBa kulchem chayim.* The verse thus links continued life to cleaving to God, implying that this bond endures even beyond death — and that those who do cleave will be alive in the world to come as well.

# Sanhedrin 91

## Chapter Order & Olam HaBa

### Perek Order Correction

We begin the last *perek* of Sanhedrin, *Perek Chelek*. Before proceeding, a correction is in order regarding something mentioned before *Yom Tov*, when we started *Elu Hen Hanhenakim*: at that time it was suggested that some authorities list *Chelek* as the tenth *perek* and *Elu Hen Hanhenakim* as the eleventh, but that logically *Chelek* should be seen as the final *perek*, because after working through all the *misos beis din* there is a natural transition to discussing who lacks a *chelek l'olam haba*, and the *masechet* then concludes with a broader *aggadic* sweep. That is the position of Rashi, and it explains our received order. It was also noted that the *Yerushalmi* has the order reversed.

On further reflection — and confirmed by examining the *Tosefta*, where the sequence is more firmly embedded — it is clear that the correct order is actually the reverse of what we have in our editions. The reason is structural: there is one of the *arba misos* that had not yet been treated, namely *Ir Nidachas*, which falls under the category of *hereg*. And *Ir Nidachas* is in fact treated at the very end of *Chelek*. This means *Chelek* must be the second-to-last *perek*, not the last. The sequence runs: *srefa* is covered, then *chenek*, then *hereg* — and under *hereg* we have *retzicha* and *Ir Nidachas*. *Chelek* ends with *Ir Nidachas*, completing *hereg*, and then *Elu Hen Hanhenakim* follows as the final *perek* on *chenek*. This is clearly the order of both the *Yerushalmi* and the *Tosefta*.

This still raises an obvious question: why insert such an extensive *perek* about who has a *chelek l'olam haba* before one has even finished discussing all the *arba misos beis din*? A partial answer is that *Ir Nidachas* itself generates the question of whether the inhabitants of the *ir nidachas* have a *chelek l'olam haba* — so there is a sense of building toward that discussion. Beyond that, the section on *rotzeach* had already broadened the discussion beyond formal *misos beis din* to include the *ba b'machteret*, the *rodef*, people executed under special circumstances despite lack of formal proof, those who received repeated *malkus*, and *kana'im pogin bo*. There was even a mention of *misah bidei shamayim*. So it appears that once the *gemara* was already ranging into punishments that are not technically *misos beis din*, a decision was made to include the discussion of *olam haba* as a natural extension. It remains a somewhat puzzling editorial choice, but structurally *Chelek* is evidently the penultimate *perek*, not the final one.

### Rambam vs Gemara

The major theme of this *perek* is *olam haba* — who receives a portion in *olam haba* — and it is important to clarify at the outset precisely what the *gemara* means when it uses that term.

Commonly, we assume *olam haba* refers to the world of souls, the realm to which the soul proceeds after death — not a future world that does not yet exist, but a parallel world of souls that already exists, subjectively "the next world" for each individual. That is the Rambam's conception of *olam haba*, and it is emphatically not the *peshat* of this *gemara* or of this *perek* as a whole.

The evidence is immediate: the *perek* opens by identifying among those who have no *chelek* in *olam haba* the *kofer be-techiyat hameitim*, one who denies resurrection of the dead. The *gemara* then asks: why should denying *techiyat hameitim* cost one a portion in *olam haba*? And it answers: one who denies *techiyat hameitim* will not receive it. As the Ritva observes, we were speaking of *olam haba* — so what has the denial of resurrection to do with *olam haba*? The answer embedded in the *gemara* is that *techiyat hameitim* is understood as the necessary precursor to *olam haba*. Deny it, and you forfeit *olam haba* as well.

The *peshat* of the *gemara*, then — and this is explicit throughout the *mishna'yot* and the *gemara* — is that *olam haba* refers to the world that will follow this world, not subjectively but objectively, for all of humanity, in time. After this-worldly history reaches its conclusion, *mashiach* will come, the dead will rise, and a qualitatively different world will be created. The *gemara* even records a tradition that for a period of one thousand years God will wipe the slate entirely clean before creating a new world.

### Eschatological Terms

It is worth mapping the principal terms that appear in the *gemara* and how they relate to one another. The major categories are: *gan eden* and *gehennom*, *mashiach*, *techiyat hameitim*, and *olam haba*.

According to most *rishonim*, reading the *gemara* in its plain sense — beginning with the Ra'avad, the Ramban, the Ritva, and others — the sequence is: *mashiach* arrives, *techiyat hameitim* follows, and then *olam haba* begins. A central question among those *rishonim* is what the nature of *olam haba* will be. The *gemara* states that in *olam haba* there is no eating or drinking, but the *tzaddikim* sit with their crowns and derive benefit from the radiance of the *shekhinah*. Does this mean purely disembodied souls? Or, since *techiyat hameitim* precedes *olam haba*, will existence be embodied? Many *rishonim* hold that bodies will exist but will be elevated to such a spiritual level that they will require no physical sustenance — analogous to *Moshe* on *Har Sinai*, sustained entirely by proximity to the divine, yet still embodied.

### Torah Rewards Problem

One further dimension of this *sugya* requires mention: the relationship between the this-worldly rewards described in the *Torah* and the otherworldly framework the *gemara* develops. The *Torah* itself is strikingly this-worldly in its promise of reward and punishment — *venasati gishmeichem be-ito* and the entire system of *blessings* and *klalos* in the *parshiyot* are all couched in terms of rain, prosperity, and national flourishing. The problem of *tzadik v'ra lo* and *rasha v'tov lo* became increasingly acute, particularly in periods of persecution and martyrdom, when this-worldly reward seemed manifestly absent.

The Ramban's approach is that the *pesukim* of reward and punishment are addressed at the national level — when all of *Klal Yisrael* collectively observes the *mitzvos*, the national framework functions. The Rambam takes a different approach: the *blessings* described in the *Torah* are not the ultimate reward for *mitzvos* but rather instrumental — if one performs *mitzvos*, God provides the material conditions that make continued performance easier; if one sins, God allows adversity to multiply, making further observance more difficult. The *brachot* and *klalos* are thus a divine pedagogical mechanism, not an ultimate ledger of reward.

Either way, neither Rambam nor Ramban treats the this-worldly *pesukim* as the final accounting for *mitzvos* and *aveiros*. The shift to an otherworldly reckoning is where the *gemara*'s emphasis lies.

### Rambam & False Messiahs

The Rambam's conception of *mashiach* is also quite distinctive and deserves attention. The Rambam rules in accordance with the opinion of Shmuel that *ein bein olam hazeh limot hamashiach* — the only difference between the present era and the messianic period is whether Israel is subject to foreign domination. The Rambam in *Mishneh Torah* cites this position as if it were the consensus voice of the Sages — *amru chachamim ein bein olam hazeh limot hamashiach* — whereas in the *gemara* itself Shmuel's position reads more like a minority opinion. One of the Rambam's *nosei kelim* pointedly notes: *Shmuel amrah* — it is Shmuel who said this, not the *chachamim* collectively.

The broader point is that the Rambam systematically de-miraculizes the messianic era, seeking to redirect attention away from speculation about future wonders and toward present Torah observance and *mitzvos*. The Rambam was particularly impatient with the kinds of questions the *gemara* itself raises — will the resurrected wear clothes or not? Will they be the same age they were at death? If a man was married twice, which wife will he be reunited with? — dismissing such speculation as idle.

David Berger observed decades ago, however, that the Rambam's de-miraculization of messianic times produced a paradoxical effect: by establishing that the messianic era need not involve obvious miracles, the Rambam inadvertently furnished intellectual cover for claimants to messianic status. Three movements or figures illustrate this. First, Shabbetai Zvi — or more precisely, his prophet Natan — explicitly cited the Rambam to argue that the absence of miracles posed no obstacle to the messianic claim. Second, religious Zionism and the concept of *atchalta de'geulah* — that sovereignty without miracles can be read as the beginning of redemption — similarly draws on this framework. Third, those associated with the Lubavitcher Rebbe likewise cite the Rambam extensively in contexts that de-emphasize the miraculous as a criterion.

The irony Berger identifies is precise: an argument designed to suppress messianic speculation and focus Jewish attention on this world wound up lowering the bar for messianic claims.

---

## Proofs for Resurrection

### Romans & Deut 31:16

The *gemara* records that Romans posed a question to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya: from where do we know that the Holy One resurrects the dead and that He knows the future? Rabbi Yehoshua replied that both can be derived from a single *pasuk*: *vayomer Hashem el Moshe hinecha shochev im avotecha ve-kam* — "And God said to Moshe, you will lie down with your fathers and you will rise up" (Devarim 31:16). The verse thus contains both a prediction of the future and an indication that *Moshe* will arise — hence *techiyat hameitim* and divine foreknowledge together.

The Romans countered: perhaps *ve-kam* does not refer to *Moshe* rising, but to *ha-am hazeh ve-zanah* — "this people will rise and go astray." Rabbi Yehoshua conceded the point on *techiyat hameitim* but replied: *nekutu miha palga bi-yadeichu* — at least you have half of the proof in your hands. Even read your way, God predicts what the people will do in the future, establishing divine foreknowledge, *yodea mah she-atid lihyot*. It is noted that this seems almost superfluous given the breadth of prophetic prediction throughout *Nevi'im*, but the *gemara* cites it nevertheless. Rabbi Yochanan similarly transmitted this tradition in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai.

### R. Yochanan's Version

The *gemara* adds that this teaching was also transmitted independently: Rabbi Yochanan said in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai that the same *pasuk* — *hinecha shochev im avotecha ve-kam* — serves as the source for both the resurrection of the dead and divine foreknowledge of the future.

### Minim & Forgery

A *baraita* records that Rabbi Eliezer the son of Rabbi Yosi declared: with this very matter I exposed the books of the *minim* as fraudulent. The *minim* in this context were asserting that *techiyat hameitim* has no basis in the *Torah* — a claim that makes them an unusual fit for the typical identification of *minim* with Jewish Christians, who generally accepted resurrection. It appears more likely that these are Jewish sectarians of another variety — possibly *tzadokim*, or, as one authority suggests, *kutim* (Samaritans). The Samaritan identification is intriguing because the *gemara*'s language of forged or corrupted scripture fits naturally in a context where two groups each claim the authentic text of the *Torah*: Rabbi Eliezer says *ziyaftem toratchem* — you have corrupted your *Torah* — and since the Samaritans maintained their own version of the *Torah*, the charge of textual corruption lands with particular force. Whether the original text read *minim* or *kutim* would require a manuscript investigation, but the substantive point is that some form of Jewish sectarians rejected *techiyat hameitim min haTorah*, and it is against them that the following arguments are marshaled.

Rabbi Eliezer's proof comes from the *pasuk*: *hikaret tikaret hanefesh hahi avonah bah* (Bamidbar 15:31). The verse uses a doubled verb — *hikaret tikaret* — and concludes with *avonah bah*, "its sin remains upon it." He reads *hikaret* as referring to this world and *tikaret* as referring to *olam haba*, while *avonah bah* — "its sin remains with it" — implies there must be a future period in which the soul still carries its sin, i.e., a future reckoning. Since *karet* in *olam haba* implies the existence of *olam haba*, and since *olam haba* in the *gemara*'s understanding presupposes *techiyat hameitim*, the *pasuk* implicitly affirms resurrection.

### Karet Exegesis

Rav Papa raised a challenge to Abaye: why not derive both *techiyat hameitim* and *olam haba* directly from the doubled verb *hikaret tikaret* alone, without requiring *avonah bah*? Abaye responds that the *minim* would not have been persuaded by double language — they would have invoked the principle of *dibrah Torah kilshon bnei adam*, that the *Torah* sometimes uses emphatic doubling without intending two separate referents. Hence *avonah bah* is needed as an additional pointer.

A *baraita* then records a dispute between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yishmael on this matter. Rabbi Akiva reads *hikaret tikaret* as referring to two worlds — *hikaret* for this world and *tikaret* for *olam haba* — in addition to the import of *avonah bah*. Rabbi Yishmael objects: there is another *pasuk* regarding *megadef* that also uses the expression *ve-nichretah* alongside a form of *karet* — yielding potentially three "worlds," which is impossible. He therefore reads *ve-nichretah ba-olam hazeh* and *hikaret l'olam haba* as covering the two worlds, while attributing the doubling simply to the stylistic principle of *dibrah Torah kilshon bnei adam*. Both authorities, however, agree that one *pasuk* addresses this world and the other addresses *olam haba*. The question of what each derives from *avonah bah* is then resolved by appeal to a separate *baraita*.

---

## Disputes w/ Rulers

### Cleopatra Question

The *gemara* records that Cleopatra the queen asked Rabbi Meir a question — though chronologically the dates present a difficulty, since Cleopatra died in 30 BCE while Rabbi Meir flourished around 150 CE. She stated that she already knew the dead would come to life — citing the verse *ve-yatzitzu me-ir ke-esev ha-aretz*, "they will sprout from the city like the grass of the earth" — but her question was practical: when they rise, will they be naked or clothed?

### Grain Analogy

Rabbi Meir responded with a *kal va-chomer* from a grain of wheat: if a grain of wheat, which is buried naked, emerges covered in multiple layers — kernel, chaff, and all its various coverings — then the *tzaddikim*, who are buried in their garments, how much more so will they arise clothed. The *kal va-chomer* moves from the simple case of a grain buried without covering yet emerging with covering, to the more richly endowed case of the righteous who are already interred with garments.

### Caesar & Dust

A separate exchange involves Caesar and Rabban Gamliel. Caesar challenged: you say the dead will come to life — but by then they will be dust, and how can dust live? Rabban Gamliel's daughter intervened, telling her father to leave the response to her. She posed a rhetorical question to Caesar: in our city there are two potters — one fashions vessels from water alone, and one from clay. Which is greater? Caesar answered: the one who fashions from water. She replied: if God can fashion a human being from water — from semen — then from clay, which is far better building material, how much more so. The first human being was fashioned from earth, so if God could create life from the liquid medium of conception, the reconstitution of a body from existing clay poses no difficulty whatsoever.

### Glass Kal Va-Chomer

The school of Rabbi Yishmael taught a parallel *kal va-chomer* from glass vessels: glass vessels, which are made merely by human breath, can be broken and then refashioned by melting and reblowing. Human beings, who were created by the breath of the Holy One — as the *parasha* we had read describes the divine *neshima* — how much more so can God reconstitute them after they decompose.

### Palace Analogy

A *min* posed a similar challenge to Rabbi Ami: you claim the dead will live, but they become dust — how can dust come back to life? Rabbi Ami responded with a parable: a mortal king commanded his servants to go and build him a great palace in a place where there was no water and no dirt. They did so. It fell. He said to them: go and rebuild it in a place where there is water and dirt. They declared: impossible. The king grew angry and said: if you could build it in a place with no materials at all, how much more so can you rebuild it where you have water and dirt. The parable maps directly onto resurrection: God created human life originally from essentially nothing — *ex nihilo* — so when God now has actual material to work with, reconstituting a body from existing dust is, if anything, easier.

### Mouse & Squirrel

To further reinforce the point, Rabbi Ami adds: if you do not believe me, go to the valley and observe the *achbar* — what appears to be a squirrel or field mouse — which today is half flesh and half earth, and by tomorrow will be entirely flesh, having emerged from the soil. Here in this present world we already observe life generated from earth, without a miracle. The objection that such a process takes a long time rather than happening instantaneously is then addressed by the next example.

### Snail Evidence

To demonstrate that transformation can occur rapidly, the *gemara* points to the *chalazon*: if you ascend a mountain where there is but one snail, and rain falls overnight, by morning the mountain will be filled with snails. Rashi explains this by noting that the eggs of the snails all hatch simultaneously — so the operative phenomenon is that eggs hatch overnight. The argument being made is that God can bring life into being swiftly, within a single night, demonstrating that *techiyat hameitim* need not require an extended gradual process. There is a note that the Rashi on this passage has been questioned as perhaps not being the authentic Rashi text — this requires further investigation.

### Ex Nihilo Argument

The section concludes with an exchange involving Gviha ben Psisa — apparently a hunchback — and a *min*. The *min* says: woe to you sinners who claim the dead will come to life — if the living die, how will the dead reverse entropy and return to life? Gviha ben Psisa replied in kind: woe to you sinners who say the dead will not come to life — if one who never existed can come to life (as every new birth demonstrates, life being drawn from essentially nothing), then one who once already lived — *kal va-chomer* — how much more so can that person return to life. The *min* responded angrily — you call me a sinner? — and threatened to kick Gviha so hard as to straighten his hunchback. Gviha replied calmly that if he could do that, he would be a master physician and would deserve a generous fee.

---

## Alexander Disputes

### African Claim Refute

The *gemara* now transitions to a series of disputes adjudicated before Alexander the Great, connected to the narrative by the figure of Gviha ben Psisa. A *baraita* from *Megillat Taanit* records that on the 24th of Nissan certain legal attacks against Judah and Jerusalem were dismissed. The *gemara* proceeds to describe the cases.

The people of Africa (*bnei Afrikaya*) came before Alexander to dispute with Israel. They claimed: the land of Canaan is ours — it is written *Eretz Knaan*, the land of Canaan, and Canaan was our ancestor. Gviha ben Psisa asked the Rabbis to grant him permission to go and dispute on their behalf before Alexander. His framing was tactically shrewd: if they defeat him, simply say he was a commoner and that the sages have not yet spoken; if he wins, attribute the victory not to himself but to the *Torat Moshe*, which prevailed.

Permission granted, Gviha asked the Africans for their proof. They cited the *Torah*'s designation of the land as *Eretz Knaan*. He responded: I will also bring proof from the *Torah*. It is written, *vayomer arur Canaan eved avadim yihyeh l'echav* — "Cursed is Canaan, he shall be a slave of slaves to his brothers." The principle is straightforward: a slave who acquires property — to whom does the slave belong, and to whom do the slave's acquisitions belong? To the master. Since Canaan was declared a slave, whatever land he possessed belongs to his masters. Furthermore, there are many years of unpaid service owed.

Alexander turned to the Africans: give him an answer. They requested three days. He granted the time. They found no response. They immediately fled, leaving behind fields that were planted and vineyards that were tended — which the Jews then came into possession of. The *gemara* adds that it was a *shemitah* year. The *Maharsha* clarifies that this does not mean the Africans abandoned their landholdings in Africa — they abandoned the lands they had been claiming in *Eretz Yisrael*, and since it was *shemitah*, the windfall came at a propitious moment.

### Egyptian Reparations

The Egyptians came next before Alexander, invoking the *pasuk*: *va-Hashem natan et chen ha-am hazeh b'einei Mitzrayim va-yashi'ilum* — God gave the people favor in Egyptian eyes and they lent them silver and gold. The Egyptians demanded: you borrowed from us, now return the silver and gold.

Gviha ben Psisa again sought and received permission from the Rabbis to dispute on their behalf, with the same framing as before. He asked the Egyptians for their source; they cited the *Torah*. He replied: I too will bring proof only from the *Torah*. The verse states, *umoshav bnei Yisrael asher yashvu b'Mitzrayim shloshim shana v'arba me'ot shana* — the Jewish people dwelt in Egypt for 430 years. He therefore demanded: give us back wages for 600,000 men enslaved over 430 years. He did not even compute the interest.

Alexander turned to the Egyptians: give him an answer. They requested three days. He gave them the time. They found no answer, abandoned their planted fields and vineyards, and fled. Again it was a *shemitah* year, and the Jews benefited from the windfall.

### Ishmaelite Claim

The descendants of Yishmael and the children of Ketura came before Alexander with a more moderate claim: the land of Canaan is ours *and* yours — let us partition it. Their proof: it is written *ele toldot Yishmael ben Avraham* and *ele toldot Yitzchak ben Avraham* — both Yishmael and Yitzchak descend from Avraham, so both have a claim.

Gviha ben Psisa again came forward with the same procedural framing and received permission. He asked for their proof; they cited the *Torah*. He replied: I will also bring proof from the *Torah*. It is written, *vayiten Avraham et kol asher lo l'Yitzchak* — Avraham gave everything he had to Yitzchak. And it is further written, *v'livnei hapilagshim asher l'Avraham natan Avraham matanot* — to the sons of the concubines Avraham gave gifts, and while he was still alive he sent them away from his son. The legal principle: a father who gives a bequest (*agtin* — likely a Latin term for bequest) to his children during his lifetime and sends them away, thereby making clear that this portion is their entirety — does the other creditor (*ba'al chov*) retain any further claim? He does not. Avraham made it explicit that Yitzchak receives everything, and the sons of the concubines received their severance gifts and were dismissed.

The Ishmaelites and children of Ketura found no answer, abandoned their planted fields and vineyards, and fled. Again it was a *shemitah* year.

### Witchcraft Gifts

The *gemara* pauses to ask: what exactly were the *matanot* — the gifts — that Avraham gave the sons of the concubines? Rabbi Yirmiya bar Abba taught: this teaches that he transmitted to them a *shem tum'ah* — names of impurity, i.e., the names and knowledge used for *kishuf*, for witchcraft. The *Maharsha* notes that this would accord with the view that *bnei Noach* were not forewarned against *kishuf*. It remains unclear why Avraham would specifically bequeath this knowledge to them, and the *gemara* does not elaborate further.

---

## Body-Soul Judgment

### Dualism Problem

Antoninus posed to Rabbi a fundamental problem about divine justice in light of body-soul dualism: can the body and the soul each argue their way out of judgment separately? The body says: it was the soul that sinned — proof being that from the moment the soul departed, the body lies motionless as a stone in the grave, incapable of any act. The soul says: it was the body that sinned — proof being that from the moment it separated from the body, the soul hovers like a bird through the air, incapable of action on its own. Each party, taken alone, has a colorable defense.

### Dualism Philosophy

This *sugya* raises a broader philosophical point worth noting. The body-soul dualism so familiar to us — the idea that the soul is capable of autonomous existence apart from the body, and that the body is merely a vessel — is deeply Greek in origin. Biblical Judaism is considerably less committed to this framework. In fact, the requirement for body-soul dualism in the Jewish metaphysical picture arises precisely and almost exclusively from the need to account for the intermediate stage: the period between a person's death and the future *yom ha-din*. If one conceives of the soul as naturally continuous with the body, and resurrection as the moment of re-ensoulment, the intermediate stage still requires some framework for the soul's existence between death and resurrection — and that is where body-soul dualism becomes functionally necessary. Strip away the intermediate stage and the dualism is far less compelled. The *gemara* here engages with this intermediate state directly, as each party's argument presupposes a period of separate existence.

It is also worth noting that the question of what happens to the soul during this intermediate period — whether it hovers, enters *gan eden*, or undergoes some form of judgment — is addressed in various *gemarot*, though perhaps less extensively than one might expect given how central that question is to popular Jewish understanding of what happens after death.

### Lame & Blind Tale

Rabbi's response to Antoninus takes the form of a *mashal*: a mortal king had a beautiful garden with magnificent ripe figs, and he appointed two guardians — one lame and one blind. The lame guardian said to the blind: I can see the fine figs in the garden; come carry me, and let us take them to eat. The blind man carried the lame man, and together they ate the figs. When the owner of the garden came and asked for his figs, each party pleaded innocence: the lame man said he had no legs to walk there, the blind man said he had no eyes to see. What did the owner do? He placed the lame man back upon the blind man and judged them together as a single unit — since neither could have acted alone, and the act required their conjunction, they are judged as one.

So too God: each party alone neither sinned nor can be judged, but God will restore the soul to the body and judge them as a unified entity. The parable makes the crucial point that the very partnership that enabled the sin is what must be reconstituted for judgment.

### Heaven & Earth Verse

Rabbi concludes with a *pasuk* as proof: *yikra el hashamayim me-al ve-el ha-aretz la-din immo* — He calls to the heavens above and to the earth below, to judge His people (Tehillim 50:4). *Yikra el hashamayim me-al* refers to the soul, called down from the heavens; *ve-el ha-aretz la-din immo* refers to the body, summoned from the earth. Together — heaven and earth, soul and body — they are brought for judgment.

This *pasuk* carries an important implication that reinforces the broader framework of the *perek*: God does not judge the soul alone, nor the body alone. What is judged is the reconstituted person, the body and soul once reunited. This is the *yom ha-din* of the future time — a judgment that presupposes *techiyat hameitim* as its prerequisite. The *mashal* is thus not merely a response to Antoninus's logical puzzle about divine justice; it is simultaneously an affirmation of why *techiyat hameitim* is theologically necessary.

---

## Sun & Bowing

### Sun Question

After this extended discussion of body-soul unity and judgment, the *gemara* records another exchange between Antoninus and Rabbi, this one ranging into natural philosophy. Antoninus asked: why does the sun rise in the east and set in the west? Rabbi replied: if it were the reverse — rising in the west and setting in the east — you would ask the same question. This answer establishes that the direction itself is not the real question.

### Midday Arc

Antoninus pressed: that is not my question. What I am asking is: why does the sun set in the west specifically? Rashi's reading seems to suggest that the underlying question is why the sun does not simply reverse its course and return the way it came, rather than completing a full arc to the west. Antoninus sharpened this further: why does the sun not travel to the midpoint of the sky, bow toward its Creator there, and then retreat back in the direction it came? That would still accomplish the apparent purpose of showing deference — the way one properly takes leave of a king by backing out rather than turning away.

### Workers & Travel

Rabbi responded: *mishum po'alim u'mishum ovrei drachim* — on account of workers and travelers. If the sun reversed its course at midday and darkness fell in the middle of the day, workers in the field and travelers on the road would be caught without light and unable to complete their journeys or tasks. The value of the continuous arc from east to west — full daylight until a proper nightfall — is that it ensures uninterrupted productive hours. One listener raised the fair point that even if the sun reversed direction, it would not set instantly — it would gradually darken just as it gradually darkens in the ordinary course of a sunset — which suggests the question may have a slightly different nuance. The discussion on this point remains open, and the *sugya* closes there.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 92

## Textual Notes

### Daf 92 Overview

Daf 92 continues within *Perek Chelek*, one of the most expansive loci of *aggadata* in the entire *Gemara*, devoted to *olam haba* and the many theological and eschatological questions surrounding it.

### Rashi Attribution

Before resuming the *sugya*, two points that arose in the previous session warrant brief mention. The first concerns whether the Rashi commentary on this section is genuine. It was Y. N. Epstein who first raised the question and proposed that the commentary was composed by a student of Rashi — the *Rivas* — rather than Rashi himself. Based on scholarship from roughly four decades ago, however, the overwhelming weight of evidence appears to favor authentic Rashi attribution, and nothing in the commentary itself reads in a way that feels distinctively different from Rashi's characteristic approach. The debate exists, but the strong position is that this is indeed Rashi's work.

### Minim/Kuthim Variant

The second point concerns a *Gemara* from the previous daf that discussed a verse in the context of *minim* — sectarians — where the phrase *vi-af-tem toraschem* ("you have forged your Torah") appeared awkward in context. A student noted that the Koren Steinsaltz edition reads *kuthim* — Samaritans — which fits the passage far more naturally. What is surprising upon consulting the manuscripts, which are available online in their entirety, is that every extant manuscript reads *kuthim* as well. It appears that the Samaritan reading was the original text. How the word *minim* found its way into printed editions — when normally the censorship process runs in the opposite direction, replacing *minim* with *kuthim* so as to avoid a politically charged term — remains unclear.

---

## Rabbi-Antoninus Dialogue

### Intro to Dialogue

The *Gemara* returns to the dialogue between Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi and Antoninus, whom the tradition identifies with Marcus Aurelius — though how historically accurate this identification is remains an open question. The preceding discussion had addressed the body-soul relationship and how divine judgment can hold each accountable: since the soul and body each could claim that the other was responsible for sin, God reunites them and judges them together. This sits well with the understanding that *yom hadin* follows *techiyas hameisim*, when body and soul are rejoined. The broader framework of body-soul dualism, which pervades this section, is itself worth noting: it is more originally a Greek idea than a distinctively Jewish one, though by the Talmudic period it had become thoroughly integrated into rabbinic discourse.

### Soul Entry Timeline

Antoninus poses a question to Rabbi: *neshama mishe'as nitna ba-adam* — from when is the soul placed within a person? Is it *mish'at pekida*, from the moment of conception, or *mish'at yetzira*, from the moment of formation — that is, the point forty days after conception when the fetus begins to take on human form?

Rabbi initially answers: *mish'at yetzira*, from the time of formation. Before this stage, the Gemara elsewhere describes the embryo as merely water, and Rabbi's intuition is that the soul enters only once the body begins to acquire some human shape.

This exchange touches on a broader question embedded in the *Bereishit* narrative. The Torah describes *nishmat chayim* breathed into Adam, yet the same expression *nefesh chaya* appears in relation to animals and even sea creatures. The precise distinction between *neshama* and *nefesh* is not fully resolved, though the breathing of life by God into the human being does suggest something qualitatively distinct. The question of whether the *neshama* under discussion is the distinctively human divine spark — the *tzelem Elokim* — or simply the animating life-force present in all creatures, bears on how one reads the entire exchange.

### Flesh Spoilage Argument

Antoninus challenges Rabbi's position with a compelling logical argument: *efshar chatichat basar omedet shlosha yamim belo melach ve'eina masracha?* Can a piece of raw flesh sit for three days without salt and not spoil? By implication, if the soul only enters at forty days, what prevents the developing embryo from decomposing in the womb during those first forty days? Presumably it is the presence of the soul that preserves the flesh from decay. But then the soul must be present from the very beginning — from the moment of conception.

### Soul at Conception

Rabbi's response is immediate: *davar zeh limadani Antoninus* — this point Antoninus taught me. And once he recognized the argument's force, he found a verse that supports it: *upkudat'cha shamra ruchi* — "your visitation has guarded my spirit." The word *pekida* — visitation or conception — appears in the same root as *v'Hashem pakad et Sarah*, God's quickening of Sarah, and denotes the initial moment of divine engagement. From the moment of *pekida*, the spirit is already present, preserving the flesh.

The *Maharsha* reads the verse to mean that the spirit actively guards the flesh from the moment of conception — it is the soul's presence that prevents decay, which is precisely the logic Antoninus had employed.

### Philosophical Context

One might ask whether this discussion carries any practical *halachic* implications — particularly with respect to the question of abortion and the legal standing of an embryo before forty days. Some have sought to draw a line from here, arguing that if the soul enters at conception, then perhaps the embryo's legal standing should reflect that even from the earliest stage.

This argument is, however, largely dismissed by the *poskim*. The reason is that there exists a substantial body of *halachic* literature — actual *Gemarot* bearing directly on abortion law — and the *poskim* treat this passage as a philosophical discussion, not as a *halachic* ruling about the legal status of the embryo. It is worth noting that in contemporary *halachic* questions where no direct *Gemarot* exist — such as questions of maternity and paternity in cases of artificial insemination or surrogate motherhood — authorities do sometimes turn to *aggadic* sources. But because explicit *halachic* *Gemarot* exist on abortion, those take precedence and this passage remains in the domain of philosophy.

One might press: if the soul is already in the flesh, surely that should have some legal significance. One possible response is that the *neshama* discussed here may not refer to the distinctively human divine soul — the *tzelem Elokim* — but rather to the animating life-force shared with animals. One could equally ask when the soul of an animal enters the womb during gestation, and why that flesh does not decay either. The verse *nishmat chayim* may be operating at a different level than the *neshama* at stake in Antoninus's biological argument.

### Yetzer Hara Timeline

Antoninus then turns to a second question: *me'eimatai yeitzer hara sholeit ba-adam* — from when does the *yetzer hara* exercise dominion over a person? Is it from *mishat yetzira*, the time of formation, or from *mishat yetzia*, the time the infant exits the womb?

It is worth noticing that the three key terms in this passage — *yeitzer*, *yetzira*, and *yetzia* — share a common root, a linguistic resonance that may or may not be deliberate. Notably, the question here does not include *mishat pekida* as a possibility, unlike the previous exchange about the soul. The *yetzer hara* in this context should probably not be understood in its most extreme sense of an evil drive toward immorality, but more broadly as the animating desires and drives of a person — the raw impulse-life that motivates behavior.

Rabbi's initial answer is again: *mishat yetzira*, from the time of formation.

### Fetal Motion Objection

Antoninus challenges this: *im kein boeit be-mei imo ve-yotzei* — if that were so, the fetus would already be trying to kick its way out of the womb. If the *yetzer hara* — understood as drives and desires and the will to assert oneself — were already present in the fetus, why would the fetus remain placid inside the womb rather than pushing insistently to be free? Of course, some women would argue that this is precisely what their babies seemed to be doing for nine months. But the force of Antoninus's objection is that a being governed by drives should not be content in such a constrained state.

The *Gemara* on *ki yeitzer leiv ha-adam ra mi-ne'urav* — which appears in the passage of Noach — is relevant here. Rashi there, citing *Bereishit Rabbah*, interprets *mi-ne'urav* as *mi-shenina'ar latzeit mi-mei imo* — from the time it stirs to exit the womb. That formulation places the onset of the *yetzer hara* not at actual birth but at the moment the infant is pushing its way out. This is somewhat in tension with the *Yaakov* and *Esav midrashim*, in which Esav's *yetzer hara* manifests already in the womb, though the *Maharsha* addresses some of that tension.

### Yetzer at Birth

The resolution follows the now-familiar pattern: *ela mishat yetzia* — it must be from the moment of exit. And again Rabbi acknowledges: *davar zeh limadani Antoninus u-mikra mesaye'o* — Antoninus taught me this, and the verse supports it: *l'fetach chatat roveitz* — sin crouches at the doorway. The doorway is understood as the opening of the womb. The *yetzer hara* enters the moment a person enters the world.

---

## Resurrection Concepts

### Reish Lakish Paradox

The *Gemara* now shifts to a series of apparent contradictions about the nature of the future world, beginning with Reish Lakish. Two verses seem to present opposing pictures. One verse states: *bam iver u-fise'ach harah ve-yoledet yachdav* — among them are the blind and the lame, the pregnant and the birthing together. Another verse declares: *az yidaleig ka-ayal pise'ach*, then the lame will leap like a hart, and *ve-taron leshon ileim*, the tongue of the mute will sing forth. The first verse implies that disability will persist into the messianic age; the second implies complete healing. How are these reconciled?

This type of question — will the dead be resurrected in their prior physical condition or already healed — is precisely the sort of inquiry Rambam criticized as beneath the dignity of serious theological discussion. Yet the *Gemara* engages it directly, which itself demonstrates that Rambam's position was not the consensus.

### Resurrection with Healing

The resolution: *omdim be-mumam u-mitrapin* — they are resurrected with their blemishes and then they are healed. One can reflect on why this sequence should be theologically significant. Perhaps the continuity between the person who died and the person who is resurrected requires that they arise in recognizable form — as themselves, with their physical history intact — before restoration takes place.

### Ula's Death Paradox

Ula similarly points to a contradiction between two verses. One verse reads: *bila hamavet lanetzach umacha Hashem dima me'al kol panim* — death will be swallowed up forever, and God will wipe away the tears from every face. This appears to promise a future world entirely without death. Yet another verse reads: *ki hana'ar ben me'ah shanah yamut* — one who dies at a hundred years will be considered to have died young, and: *lo yihyeh misham od ul yamim* — there will no longer be a burden of days. This verse envisions vastly extended lifespans, but still envisions death.

### Jewish vs. Non-Jewish Et…

The resolution: *lo kashya — kan be'Yisrael kan be'ovdei kochavim*. The verse promising the complete elimination of death applies to Jews; the verse describing century-long lifespans as youthful death applies to non-Jews. In the future world, Jews will live forever, while non-Jews will live for extraordinary lengths of time but will not be immortal.

This resolution immediately raises a broader question: what is the status of non-Jews in the future world at all? Several possibilities present themselves. One view holds that the distinction between Jews and non-Jews will be maintained, with non-Jews recognizing God but retaining their own distinctive identity. A second possibility is that all non-Jews will become Jewish. A third possibility flows from the opinion that *mitzvot betelot le'atid lavo* — commandments will no longer be operative in the future era — in which case the very category of religious particularism may dissolve, and the distinction between Jew and non-Jew may cease to exist. All three frameworks remain live options within the tradition.

### Non-Jews' Role Future

The *Gemara* presses the question: *ve'ovdei kochavim mai ba'u hatam?* — who invited the non-Jews? What are they doing in the future world at all? The answer draws on a verse: *ve'amdu zarim ve-ra'u tzonchem u-venei nechar ikareichem ve-chormeichem* — foreigners will stand and tend your flocks, and the children of strangers will be your farmers and your vintners. The non-Jews will be present not as recipients of divine reward in their own right, but as the labor force that enables the Jewish people to be fully engaged in their transcendent existence. This framing, striking as it is, sets up a broader discussion about the role of non-Jews in the future world that will continue further in the *Gemara*.

---

## Yemos HaMashiach vs. Ola…

### Light Paradox

Rav Chisda points to another contradiction, this one concerning the luminaries. One verse states: *ve-chafra halevana u-vosha hachama ki malach Hashem tzeva'ot* — the moon will be shamed and the sun will be embarrassed, for God will reign as king. In the radiance of divine presence, the light of the sun and moon will be overwhelmed and humbled. Another verse, however, states: *va-yhi or halevana ke-or hachama ve-or hachama yihye shiv'atayim ke-or shivat ha-yamim* — the light of the moon will be like the light of the sun, and the light of the sun will be sevenfold, like the light of the seven original days of creation. This verse envisions a vast amplification of natural light.

### Two Periods Resolved

The resolution: *lo kashya — kan li-yemot ha-mashiach kan le-olam haba*. These verses describe two distinct periods. In *yemot hamashiach*, the messianic era, the sun and moon will shine with dramatically increased brilliance. In *olam haba*, by contrast, the physical existence associated with natural light may no longer obtain at all, and the divine radiance will overwhelm whatever luminaries remain.

### Samuel's Naturalism

Now the *Gemara* introduces Shmuel's famous position: *ein bein olam hazeh li-yemot hamashiach ela shib'ud galuyot bilvad* — there is no difference between this world and the messianic era except the subjugation of exile. Rambam's version of this formulation reads *shib'ud malchuyot*, the subjugation of foreign kingdoms, but the substance is the same. Messianic times, according to Shmuel, will not involve any miraculous transformation of nature. It is critical to note that this opinion is presented in the *Gemara* as the view of Shmuel alone. Rambam famously cites it as if it represents the consensus of the sages — *ameru chachamim* — but in its original context it is a single, dissenting position.

How does Shmuel's view reconcile the verses Rav Chisda raised? *Lo kashya — kan bi-machaneh tzadikkim kan bi-machaneh shechina*. The difference lies in proximity to the divine presence, borrowing from the concentric structure of the wilderness camp: those in the innermost circle, close to the *Mishkan*, experience God's radiance overwhelming all natural light, while those at greater distance still perceive the amplified light of sun and moon.

Crucially, Shmuel's naturalism about *yemot hamashiach* does not mean he denies a miraculous *olam haba*. Shmuel is arguing only that the messianic period itself will be continuous with this world, minus exile. The otherworldly transformation — the *machaneh shechina* overwhelming natural light — belongs to *olam haba*, which even Shmuel affirms.

### Wounding & Healing

Rava points to yet another apparent contradiction. One verse states: *ani amis ve-achayeh* — I will kill and bring to life. Another verse states: *machatzti va-ani erpa* — I will wound and I will heal. The tension between them: if God kills and revives, what is the role of wounding and healing? The resolution: *mah she-ani meimis ani mechayeh, va-hadar mah she-machatzti va-ani erpa* — first God will resurrect the dead, and then, as we established earlier, they will be healed. The sequence is: death, resurrection with blemishes, and then healing — consistent with what was established in the resolution of Reish Lakish's contradiction.

---

## Techiyas Hametim Proofs

### Kill & Revive Proof

The *Gemara* now turns to a sustained *tannaitic* effort to establish *techiyas hameisim min ha-Torah*. The verse *ani amis ve-achayeh* is brought as a primary source. A *baraita* raises the obvious objection: perhaps the verse simply means that one person dies and another comes to life — the ordinary course of the world, in which each generation replaces the one before. The response comes from the parallel phrase in the same verse: *machatzti va-ani erpa*. Just as wounding and healing apply to the same individual — a person is wounded and that same person is healed — so too death and revival must apply to the same individual. The one who died is the one who is brought back to life. This is *mikan teshuvah la-omrim ein techiyas hameisim min ha-Torah* — a response to those who deny that resurrection has any basis in the Torah.

### Future Tense Argument

Rabbi Meir asks: where is the basis for *techiyas hameisim* in the Torah? He cites the Song of the Sea: *az yashir Moshe u-vnei Yisrael et ha-shira ha-zot l'Hashem*. The word is *yashir* — will sing — not *shar*, sang. The future tense indicates that Moshe will sing again in the future. *Mikan l'techiyas hameisim min ha-Torah*. A parallel proof: *az yivneh Yehoshua mizbe'ach l'Hashem* — *yivneh*, will build, rather than *bana*, built. Yehoshua will build an altar in the future.

### Solomon Idol Problem

The *Gemara* raises an immediate objection: if the future tense in these verses proves resurrection, consider: *az yivneh Shlomo bama l'Chemosh shikutz Moav* — Solomon will build a high place for Chemosh, the abomination of Moab. Does this mean Solomon will be resurrected to engage in idolatry? The resolution: regarding idolatry, the principle applies that Scripture ascribes to a person the intention to sin as if the sin were committed. The future tense there means Solomon desired to build it, and the verse therefore treats it as though he did. By contrast, regarding Moshe and Yehoshua, we know from context that these are real future events — Moshe will actually sing praise again. The future tense carries a different valence depending on context.

### Dwelling in God's House

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi derives the proof from: *ashrei yoshvei veitecha od yehalelucha sela* — praised are those who dwell in Your house; they will yet praise You. The verse says *yehalelucha* — will praise — not *hilelucha*, have praised. *Mikan l'techiyas hameisim min ha-Torah*.

### Singing Continuity

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi draws a corollary: *kol ha-omer shira ba-olam hazeh, zocheh ve-omra le-olam haba* — whoever sings God's praises in this world will merit to sing them in the world to come. The proof text is the same verse: *ashrei yoshvei veitecha od yehalelucha sela*. Those who dwell in God's house — whether this means the *beit knesset* or some broader sense of sacred space — and who praise God now, will praise God again in the future. The pattern across these proofs is consistent: the future tense of praise implies that those who sang will sing again, which implies their continued or renewed existence.

### Prophets' Unified Voice

Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan adds: *kol tzofayich nas'u kol yachdav yeranenu* — the sound of your visionaries lifted their voice together and sang forth. The proof again lies in the future tense: *yeranenu*, they will sing — not *rinnenu*, they sang. *Mikan l'techiyas hameisim min ha-Torah*.

Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba further states in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *atidin kol ha-nevi'im kulam omrim shira be-kol echad* — in the future, all the prophets will sing praise in a single voice. This remarkable statement connects to the *Gemara* encountered earlier regarding *signon echad* — that different prophets could perceive the same divine vision yet articulate it in their individual styles.
