In the future, the clarity of divine perception will be so complete that all individual variation dissolves, and all the prophets will speak, and sing, in perfect unison.

---

## Teaching Torah Obligation

### Withholding Theft

Rabbi Yehuda in the name of Rav states: *kol ha-mone'a halacha mi-pi talmid ke-ilu gozlo mi-nachalat avotav* — whoever withholds a *halacha* from a student is as though he stole from that student's ancestral inheritance. The proof: *Torah tziva lanu Moshe morasha kehilat Yaakov* — the Torah that Moshe commanded us is the inheritance of the congregation of Jacob. Since Torah is the national inheritance of all Israel from the six days of creation, it cannot be withheld from any member of that nation.

### Withholding Curses

Rav Chana bar Bizna in the name of Rabbi Shimon Chasida intensifies this: *kol ha-mone'a halacha mi-pi talmid, afilu ubarin she-be-mei imma mekalelin oto* — even the fetuses in their mothers' wombs curse out anyone who withholds Torah from a student. The prooftexts work through a chain of associations: *mone'a bar yikvuhu le'om* — one who withholds grain (*bar*) will be cursed (*yikvuhu*) by nations (*le'om*). *Ve-ein le'om ela ubarin*, as the verse *u-le'om mi-le'om ye'ematz* — one nation shall prevail over the other — uses *le'om* to mean unborn children. *Ve-ein kavo ela klala* — to *kovo* means to curse, as in *mah ekov lo kavo El*. And *ve-ein bar ela Torah* — grain (*bar*) means Torah, as in *nashku bar pen ye'enaf*.

### Pierced Like Sieve

Ulla bar Shmuel adds a vivid image: *menakvin oto ke-khivara* — such a person will be pierced through like a sieve. The wordplay: *yikvuhu* in the verse can be read not only as cursing but as piercing, as in *vayikov chor be-dalto*, to bore a hole in a door. Abaye adds that this is like the perforated implement used by launderers to sprinkle water. The resonance is striking: the one who tries to hoard Torah and hold it inside himself will find himself punctured through — everything he tried to keep for himself will drain away.

### Teaching Reward

If one does teach, what is the reward? Rava in the name of Rav Sheshet states: *zocheh le-vrachot ke-Yosef* — one merits blessings like Joseph. The verse: *u-vracha le-rosh mashbir* — blessing is upon the head of the one who provides sustenance. And *ein mashbir ela Yosef*, as in *Yosef hu ha-shalit al ha-aretz hu ha-mashbir le-chol am ha-aretz* — Joseph provided sustenance to all the people of the land. Just as Joseph provided for all who came to him, so the teacher of Torah is rewarded with blessing.

### Extended Teaching Effort

The *Maharsha*'s interpretation of this entire passage is particularly powerful. He reads *kol ha-mone'a halacha mi-pi talmid* not merely as a prohibition against outright refusal to teach, but as an obligation to extend oneself in teaching — specifically, to persist until the student has genuinely mastered the material. The *Maharsha* writes: *she-eino lomed im ha-talmid ke-Rav Preida, she-haya lamed im talmido arba me'ot pe'amim ad she-hayta shegurah lo ba-peh* — one is obligated to learn with a student like Rav Preida, who would teach a student 400 times until the material was fluent in that student's mouth. The prohibition is not only against refusing to teach the easy students; it is against refusing to invest the effort required for the difficult ones.

The *Maharsha* continues: *u-fi she-omer ha-rav she-ein ha-talmid hagun*, when a teacher dismisses a student as unworthy or unteachable — *harei gozlo mi-nachalat avotav*, he steals that student from the inheritance of the fathers. The basis: *she-ha-Torah hi morasha le-chol Yisrael mi-sheshet yemei bereishit* — Torah is the inheritance of all Israel from the six days of creation, and *le-fi beri'utam ve-tiv'am mi-sheshet yemei bereishit mukhanim kol Yisrael lilmod Torah* — by their very created nature, all of Israel are prepared and capable of learning Torah. This *Gemara* speaks with particular force to the communal obligation to ensure that every child has genuine access to Torah education — including those children for whom learning requires extraordinary effort and accommodation.

### Teaching in Olam HaBa

Rav Sheshet extends the theme: *kol ha-melamed Torah ba-olam ha-zeh, zocheh u-melamdah le-olam haba* — whoever teaches Torah in this world merits to teach it in the world to come. The verse: *u-marveh gam hu yoreh* — the one who saturates will also teach. This continues the pattern observed throughout this section: the activities one excels in in this world are precisely the activities one will continue in *olam haba*. Teaching Torah is not merely rewarded with something external; it becomes the very substance of one's existence in the world to come.

---

## Righteous Attributes

### Da'at Meaning

Rabbi Elazar states: *gedolah de'ah she-nitnah bein shtei otiyot* — great is *de'ah*, knowledge or intellect, for it was placed between two of God's names. The verse: *ki El de'ot Hashem* — for God is a God of knowledge. The divine name *El* precedes, and the name *Hashem* follows, and between them stands *de'ot*. The *Maharsha* emphasizes that this positioning is not merely formal but substantive: *El* represents *midat ha-din*, the divine attribute of strict judgment, while *Hashem* represents *midat ha-rachamim*, the attribute of mercy. True *de'ah* — authentic intellectual and moral understanding — therefore encompasses the capacity to know when *din* is called for and when *rachamim* is appropriate. The wisdom to navigate between these two divine qualities is itself what *de'ah* means at its deepest level.

### Da'at & Beis HaMikdash

Rabbi Elazar makes a parallel claim: *gadol Mikdash she-nitan bein shtei otiyot* — great is the *Beit HaMikdash*, for it too was placed between two of God's names. The verse: *pa'alta Hashem mikdash Hashem konenu yadecha* — You fashioned, O God, the sanctuary of God, your hands established it. Examining the names of God in the verse reveals that the first *Hashem* is *Alef-Dalet-Nun-Yud*, God's *midat hadin*, and the second is the *yud-keh-vav-keh*, the *shem hameforash* associated with *midat harachamim*. The *Beit HaMikdash* stands between these two qualities, just as *de'ah* does.

The *Maharsha* connects this to the teaching that Betzalel knew how to *letzaref et ha-otiyot* — to combine the letters of God's name — and through that capacity he fashioned the *Beit HaMikdash*. The *de'at* to understand and harness the interplay of divine names is what made the *Mishkan* possible. This creates a theologically rich equivalence: *de'ah* in the human being corresponds to what the *Beit HaMikdash* achieves in the world. The implication is significant — in the absence of the *Beit HaMikdash*, the person who has developed genuine *de'ah* represents a living point of divine connection.

### Vengeance Question

Rav Adda Karchinaos challenges: *ela me'ata gedola nekama she-nitnah bein shtei otiyot* — if the criterion for greatness is appearing between two of God's names, then vengeance too should be considered great, since the verse reads *Kel nekamot Hashem, Kel nekamot hofi'a* — God of vengeance, O God, appear — with *nekamot* appearing between two divine names.

The response: *le-milta hachi nami* — yes, in its proper context, vengeance too is a divine quality. When the exercise of *nekama* is genuinely appropriate, it partakes of the same divine character as *de'ah* and *mikdash*. The *Maharsha* invokes Pinchas here as the paradigm case — an act of zealous intervention that the rabbis regarded with significant ambivalence (the *Yerushalmi* states that the sages actually wished to place Pinchas in *cherem*, and only a divine voice declaring *hineni noten lo et briti shalom* stayed their hand). The point is that *nekama* as a *midah* is not simply rejected — but *midat harachamim* will almost always counsel against it, leaving only an extraordinarily narrow space in which it is appropriate.

Ulla elaborates: *shtei hofa'ayot halalu lama?* — why does the verse mention *hofi'a* twice in connection with *nekamot*? *Achat le-midah tovah ve-achat le-midat pur'anut* — one for reward and one for punishment. Rashi understands the rewarding manifestation as referencing *hofi'a meHar Paran*, the revelation of Torah at Sinai, in which the nations who refused the Torah were implicitly judged while Israel received it — though the connection to *nekama* in that context is admittedly indirect.

### Intellect Wealth

Rabbi Elazar continues: *kol adam she-yesh lo de'ah le-sof mitasher* — anyone who has *de'ah* will ultimately become wealthy. The verse: *u-ve-da'at chadarim yimale'u, kol hon yakar ve-na'im* — through knowledge, rooms are filled with all precious and pleasant treasure. This can be read literally — a sharp intellect provides the tools for material success — or figuratively, as a description of a richly lived inner life in which one possesses the things truly worth having.

### No Compassion Lack Da'at

Rabbi Elazar further states: *kol adam she-ein bo de'ah assur le-rachem alav* — it is forbidden to show compassion to someone who lacks *de'ah*. The verse: *ki lo am binot hu — al ken lo yerachamenu osehu ve-yotzro lo yechunenu* — for they are not a people of understanding; therefore their Creator will not have compassion on them, and their fashioner will not show them grace.

This requires careful interpretation. Taken at face value, it raises challenging questions: does Rabbi Elazar mean that anyone who is not intellectually gifted forfeits the right to compassion? Almost certainly not. What is being described is a person who has the capacity to develop their intellect and moral reasoning but chooses not to — who squanders opportunities for growth. The verse is about willful non-engagement, not congenital limitation. Even so, the statement raises important practical questions about where communal resources and compassion should be directed. Notably, even in cases where someone has acted with profound self-destructiveness — endangering their own life — one is still obligated to violate Shabbat to save them. The statement about withholding compassion is likely about orientation and priorities rather than a literal prohibition on assistance.

### Bread to Foolish

Rabbi Elazar also states: *kol ha-noten pito le-mi she-ein bo de'ah, yissurin ba'in alav* — one who gives their bread to someone lacking understanding will be visited with suffering. The verse: *lachmecha yasim mazor tachtecha ein tevunah* — your bread will become a *mazor* beneath you, there being no understanding. And *ein mazor ela yissurin*, as the verse *vayar Efraim et cholyo vi-Yehuda et mazoro* uses *mazor* to mean affliction.

The verse's logic implies that indiscriminate provision to someone who refuses to develop their capacities is not an act of generosity but of enabling — it entrenches the very pattern that leads them toward ruin. The practical analogy is to the question of enabling destructive behavior: sometimes genuine compassion requires withholding easy support. This connects back to the interplay between *midat hadin* and *midat harachamim* — sometimes what looks like mercy is in fact the greater cruelty.

### Exile from Ignorance

Finally: *kol adam she-ein bo de'ah, le-sof goleh* — anyone who lacks *de'ah* will ultimately go into exile. The verse: *lachen gala ami mi-bli da'at* — therefore my people went into exile for lack of knowledge. The loss of rootedness, of home, of stability — all these are the natural consequence of failing to cultivate understanding.

---

## Torah Support & Conduct

### Night Torah Study

Rabbi Elazar states: *kol bayit she-ein divrei Torah nishma'in bo va-lailah, esh ochalto* — any house in which words of Torah are not heard at night, a fire shall consume it. The verse: *kol choshech tamun li-tzfunav, tochalehu esh lo nupach, yera sarid be-ohalo* — all darkness is stored up for what is hidden away; an unblown fire consumes it; evil is upon the remnant in one's tent. *Ve-ein sarid ela talmidei chachamim*, as the verse *u-vaseridim asher Hashem koreh* uses *sarid* to mean those whom God calls out — and therefore the absence of Torah scholars from the home signals this darkness.

The *Maharsha* observes that night is the crucial time precisely because it is free from the legitimate demands of livelihood. During the day, one must work; that is understood. But at night, when there are no external obligations and one's true priorities are revealed in how one uses discretionary time, the absence of Torah study is a statement about character. The question of whether one opens a book that develops the mind or settles into purely passive entertainment is, in the *Maharsha*'s reading, what this *gemara* is addressing.

### Support Scholars

Rabbi Elazar adds: *kol she-eino mehaneh talmidei chachamim mi-nechesav, eino ro'eh siman bracha le'olam* — anyone who does not benefit Torah scholars from their property will see no sign of blessing. The *Maharsha* frames this as the complementary obligation for those who genuinely cannot devote their own time to Torah study: even if one's livelihood fully occupies one's days, the obligation to support those who do learn remains. To spend one's working life accumulating property and share none of it with those who dedicate themselves to Torah study is to court the withdrawal of divine blessing.

### Leftover Bread

Rabbi Elazar further states: *kol she-eino meshayer pat al shulchano, eino ro'eh siman bracha le'olam* — anyone who does not leave some bread on the table sees no sign of blessing. The verse: *ein sarid le-ochlo al ken lo yachil tuvo* — there is no remnant left to eat; therefore his goodness will not endure. Leaving bread on the table is a sign that God has given one more than enough — *achalnu ve-hoteir*, we ate and there was still something left over. The *Maharsha* adds that leaving crumbs also creates the opportunity for the poor to benefit afterward.

A seeming contradiction: does not Rabbi Elazar elsewhere state that one who leaves crumbs (*pesitim*) on the table is considered as if engaging in idolatry? The verse: *ha-orchim la-gad shulchan ve-ha-memalim li-mni mimsach* — those who set a table for the idol *gad* and fill vessels with libations. The resolution: *ha de-ika sheleima ba-hadeih* — the prohibition applies when a whole loaf of bread is left alongside the crumbs, which mimics an idolatrous ritual. *Ha de-leika sheleima ba-hadeih* — when only some remaining bread is left over from the meal, without the ceremonial character of a full loaf, this is the proper sign of blessing, not idolatry.

### Proper Conduct

Rabbi Elazar states: *kol ha-machlif be-diburo ke-ilu oved avoda zara* — anyone who changes his words, meaning misrepresents himself, is as if engaging in idolatry. The verse from the *Yaakov* and *Esav* narrative: *ve-hayisi be-einav ke-mtatei'a* — I will be in my father's eyes like a deceiver. And the parallel: *hevel heima ma'aseh tatu'im* — they are nothingness, they are pure deception — used of idolatry itself. The essential falseness of idolatry and the essential falseness of misrepresentation of oneself partake of the same spiritual category.

Rabbi Elazar adds: *kol ha-mistakel be-erva kashto ninarat* — one who gazes at forbidden nudity will have his bow shaken out. Rashi offers two interpretations: the literal — a man gazing at a woman's nakedness — or, in Rashi's preferred reading, a man who fixates mentally on sexual sin. The punishment is the loss of virility. The verse: *arya te'or kashtecha* — nakedness (*arya*, read as *erva*) will rouse your bow — the bow being understood as the instrument of masculine power.

### Humility & Privacy

Rabbi Elazar concludes this series: *le-olam hevei kavel ve-kayam* — always be accepting and enduring. The *Maharsha* offers two readings of *kavel*: either "submissive" or, from the Aramaic, "dark" — that is, not drawing attention to oneself, remaining in the background. Do not publicize your success. Do not be a complainer. Stay quiet and you will survive.

Rabbi Zeira supports this from a *mishnah*: *bayit afel ein potchin lo chalonot lir'ot nigo* — a dark house, one does not open windows in it to examine the blemishes. If one remains humble and unassuming, one is not inviting scrutiny of one's own imperfections. *Shma minna* — the principle is confirmed.

---

## Resurrection Proofs Natu…

### Never Satisfied Three

Rabbi Tavi in the name of Rabbi Yoshiya asks about the verse: *she'ol ve-otzer rachem eretz lo save'ah mayim* — the grave, the womb, and the thirsty earth are never satisfied. What connection is there between the depths of the underworld and the womb?

### Womb & Underworld

The *Gemara* draws the parallel: *mah rachem machnis u-motzi*, just as a womb receives and releases — it receives the semen and releases the child — so too the underworld receives the dead and releases them. *Af she'ol machnis u-motzi* — the underworld too receives souls in and releases them again. This is another proof of *techiyas hameisim*, arrived at through the structural parallel between two things that both receive and both release.

### Kal Vachomer Womb

The *Gemara* adds a *kal va-chomer*: *mah rachem she-machnisin lo be-chashai, motzi'in mimeno be-kolei kolos* — what goes into the womb goes in privately, in intimacy, yet what comes out does so with loud cries, publicly, as every birth is announced to the world. The underworld is the opposite: *she-ol she-machnisin bo be-kolei kolos* — what goes into the underworld does so loudly, with the entire procession of a funeral, publicly observed. *Eino din she-motzi'in mimeno be-kolei kolos?* — how much more so should what comes out of the underworld be announced with great fanfare and miracle. *Mikan techiyas hameisim min ha-Torah*.

---

## Righteous Future State

### No Return to Dust

A *tanna de-vei Eliyahu* teaches: *tzadikkim she-atid ha-Kadosh Baruch Hu le-hachayotan einan chozrin la-afaram* — the righteous whom God will revive in the future will not return to dust. This settles a question about what follows *techiyas hameisim*: it is not a temporary resurrection that eventually ends in a second death, but a permanent one for the righteous. The verse: *ve-haya ha-nishar be-Tzion ve-ha-notar bi-Yerushalayim kadosh ye'amer lo, kol ha-kasuv la-chayim bi-Yerushalayim* — all who are inscribed for life in Jerusalem will be called holy. *Mah kodesh le-olam kayam, af heim le-olam kayamin* — just as what is holy endures forever, so do they.

### Thousand Year Renewal

But a practical question arises: if there is a transitional period in which God is remaking the world — a process that will take a thousand years, corresponding to the verse *va-nisgav Hashem levado ba-yom hahu* — what will happen to the resurrected righteous during that interval? The world will be in a state of *tohu va-vohu*, dissolution and primordial chaos. The righteous, having been promised that they will not return to dust, must somehow persist through this cosmic transition.

### Eagle Wings Period

The answer: *ha-Kadosh Baruch Hu oseh lahem knafayim ke-nesharim, la-shut al pnei ha-mayim* — God will give them wings like eagles, and they will soar over the primordial waters. The image is a deliberate echo of *ve-ruach Elokim merachefet al pnei ha-mayim* — the spirit of God hovering over the waters at creation. The bodies of the righteous, sustained by divine power, will hover over the waters of the re-forming world. The verse: *al ken lo nira be-hamir aretz, be-mot harim be-lev yamim* — therefore we will not fear when the earth is transformed, when the mountains fall into the heart of the sea.

### Believer Strength

The *Gemara* addresses a possible objection: will this hovering existence be painful or exhausting? *Talmud lomar: ve-kovei Hashem yachalifu koach, ya'alu ever ke-nesharim, yarutzu ve-lo yig'u, yelchu ve-lo yi'afu* — those who trust in God will renew their strength; they will rise with wings like eagles; they will run and not grow weary; they will walk and not grow tired.

---

## Ezekiel Dry Bones

### Ezekiel as Proof

The *Gemara* now raises the question: *ve-nilaf mi-meitim she-hechiya Yechezkel* — why not derive the proof for *techiyas hameisim* from the dead that Yechezkel revived? If God actually revived dry bones through Yechezkel, this would serve as perhaps the most dramatic and direct evidence that resurrection is possible — and, at least for the bones that were revived, as an actual instance of it. The *Maharsha* frames this as the question: even if Yechezkel's revival does not prove that there will be universal *techiyas hameisim* in the messianic future, it at least proves that God has the power to raise the dead from dust and bones. Why is that not invoked as evidence?

### Miracle vs. Metaphor

The answer: the *Gemara* here follows the opinion that *be-emet mashal haya* — in truth, it was only a *mashal*. The vision of the dry bones in the valley was not an actual miracle but a parable for Israel's national restoration: the people felt that their hope was lost and they were as good as dead, and the vision reassured them that God would restore them to national life. Since it was not a real event, it cannot serve as evidence for anything.

The phrase is striking: *be-emet mashal haya* — in truth it was a *mashal*. The word *be-emet* sitting next to *mashal* is almost paradoxical. Rabbi Nechemiah indeed presses on exactly this: *im emet lama mashal, ve-im mashal lama emet?* — if it was true, why call it a *mashal*, and if it was a *mashal*, why say in truth? The resolution: *ela be-emet mashal haya* — it simply means: truly, in reality, it was only a parable. Nothing more than that.

### Eliezer: Actual Event

Rabbi Eliezer, however, holds that it actually happened: *meisim she-hechiya Yechezkel amdu al ragleihem va-amru shira u-meisu* — they stood on their feet, sang praises, and then died. They were revived for the purpose of the lesson, and then died again. What *shira* did they sing? *Hashem meimis be-tzedek u-mechayeh be-rachamim* — God caused us to die with justice and revives us with compassion, for we did not deserve the resurrection.

Rabbi Yehoshua adds an alternative version of the *shira*: *Hashem meimis u-mechayeh, morid she'ol va-ya'al* — God causes death and gives life, brings down to the depths and raises up again.

### Yehuda: Pure Metaphor

Rabbi Yehuda holds: *emet mashal haya* — it was truly just a *mashal*. The vision referred to the state of the Jewish people in exile, as the verse itself confirms: *ha-atzamot ha-eleh kol beit Yisrael heimah* — these bones represent the entire house of Israel. The people said *yavshu atzmoteinu ve-avda tikvatenu nigzarnu lanu* — our bones are dried out and our hope is lost. The vision is an extended metaphor for national desolation and the promise of restoration.

### Actual Aliyah & Children

Rabbi Eliezer son of Rabbi Yose HaGlili goes furthest: *meisim she-hechiya Yechezkel alu le-Eretz Yisrael ve-nasu nashim va-olidu banim u-vanot* — the dead whom Yechezkel revived went up to the Land of Israel, married, and had children. Remarkably, Rabbi Yehuda ben Beseira rose to his feet and testified: *ani mi-bnei veneihem, ve-halu tefillin she-hiniach li avi avi me-hem* — I am among their descendants, and here are the *tefillin* that my grandfather's grandfather bequeathed to me from them.

### Ephraim Identity

Who were these dead? Rav identifies them as *benei Ephraim she-manu la-keitz ve-ta'u* — the children of Ephraim who calculated the timing of the redemption and erred, leaving Egypt prematurely and being killed in battle. The verse supports this: the genealogy in *Divrei HaYamim* traces the descendants of Ephraim through Shuthelach and records that *Ezer and Elad were killed by the men of Gat who were born in the land* — meaning that these children of Ephraim had somehow made it to the Land of Israel before the Exodus. And: *va-yitabbel Ephraim avihem yamim rabbim va-yavo'u echav le-nachamo* — Ephraim mourned for them for many days. There may also be a subtle warning embedded in this identification: so much of the surrounding discussion concerns anticipating when the *keitz* will be. The *benei Ephraim* are the paradigm case of what happens when one tries to force the end prematurely.

### Alternative Identities

Shmuel identifies them differently: *elu benei adam she-kafru bi-techiyas ha-meitim* — these were people who denied the resurrection of the dead. The entire two dappim of the Gemara have been building proofs for *techiyas hameisim*; here are the paradigmatic deniers. Why were they resurrected if denial of resurrection forfeits one's portion? Precisely to demonstrate the truth to them — they were revived as a proof, not as a reward.

Rabbi Yirmiyah bar Abba identifies them as *benei adam she-ein bahem lachluchit shel mitzvah* — people who have not even a trace of moisture, not even a trace of *mitzvot* within them. Completely dried out morally. And yet God revived them — perhaps demonstrating that *kol Yisrael yesh lahem chelek le-olam haba*, or perhaps they were resurrected only for the moment of judgment.

Rabbi Yitzchak Nafcha identifies them as the people who covered the entire *Heichal* with images of *shekatizm u-remasim* — vermin and creeping things. The verse from Yechezkel's own vision: *va-avo va-ereh, ve-hineh kol tavnis remes u-veheimah sheketz ve-chol gillulei beit Yisrael mechukkah al ha-kir saviv saviv* — he entered and saw carved on the wall all manner of creeping things and abominations surrounding the sanctuary. The verbal parallel *saviv saviv* connects Yechezkel's vision of the defiled *Beit HaMikdash* to his vision of the valley of bones.

---

## Divine Vindication Narra…

### Dura Valley Resurrection

Rabbi Yochanan identifies the dead of the valley as *meitim she-be-bikat Dura* — those who died in the valley of Dura. The valley of Dura stretched from *Nahar Eshel* to *Ravat*. At the time when Nevuchadnezzar exiled Israel, there were among the exiles young men *she-hayu meganin et ha-chamah be-yofyan* — so extraordinarily beautiful that they made the sun itself look dim by comparison.

### Dead Strike King

The *Gemara* then provides the narrative framework: when Nevuchadnezzar was about to cast Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah into the furnace, God commanded Yechezkel to go and resurrect the dead in *bikat Dura*. Once he revived them, *ba'u atzamot ve-tapchu lo le-oto rasha al panav* — the resurrected dead came and slapped Nevuchadnezzar in the face, right at the moment he was presiding over the furnace. Nevuchadnezzar was bewildered: *ma tivan shel elu?* — who are these people who have walked into my presence and struck me? He was told: *chavreihen shel elu, mechayei meitim be-bikat Dura* — the friends of these three — meaning Yechezkel — has revived the dead you killed in the valley of Dura. The implicit warning was clear: you are about to throw their companions into the fire, and it will not end in your favor.

### Nebuchadnezzar Conversion

Nevuchadnezzar opened his mouth and said: *atvohi kama ravrevin, ve-timhohi kama takiffin, malchuteh malchut alam ve-shaltaneh im dar ve-dar* — how great are God's miracles, how wondrous are God's wonders, His kingdom is an eternal kingdom and His dominion endures for all generations. A wicked king, confronted with the undeniable demonstration of divine power through the resurrection of those he had slaughtered, burst forth in praise.

### Angel Intervention

Yet this moment of praise was not to be completed. Rabbi Yitzchak states: *yutzak zahav roteach le-toch piv shel oto rasha* — molten gold should have been poured down the throat of that wicked man. For *she-ilmale ba malach u-staro al panav* — had an angel not come and slapped him on the face, he would have gone on to sing God's praises so extensively and so powerfully that he would have *bikeish le-ganot kol shirot ve-tishbachot she-amar David be-sefer Tehillim* — his praises would have surpassed and thereby embarrassed all the psalms and praises that David composed in the book of Tehillim. Nevuchadnezzar was such a *rasha* that he did not deserve that opportunity. The angel intervened to stop him. His recognition of God's greatness was real — but it was cut short precisely because a man of his deeds should not be the one to attain that ultimate level of praise.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 93

## Five Groups/Dry Bones

### Five Categories

The *gemara* on 92b asks: *uman nin hu meisim shehechaya Yechezkel* — who are the dead that *Yechezkel* revived in the valley? The *gemara* identifies five distinct groups, and there is reason to suggest that for approximately two thousand years those five categories may not have resonated with the same force as they do in the last hundred years or so — and that is perhaps what has prompted a second look.

### Bnei Ephraim

The first group is *bnei Ephraim shemanu laketz veta'u* — those who miscalculated when the slavery was to end. We know the Egyptian servitude was decreed for four hundred years, though the precise starting point was disputed. This group hastened the *geulah*, pushed ahead prematurely, and paid dearly for it: *haragu anshei Gat hanoladim ba'aretz* — the Philistines of Gat who were already settled in the land attacked and killed them, because the time was not yet ripe. These are the people who press for faster redemption before redemption is ready.

### Rejected Resurrection

Shmuel's opinion is that the dead revived by *Yechezkel* were *bnei adam shekafru bitchiyas hameisim* — people who denied the concept of *techiyas hameisim*, who lost all faith in a future. The *pasuk* cited in connection with this group — *yaveshu atzmoiseinu ve'avda sikvaseinu*, "our bones have dried and our hope is lost" — is, of course, the very verse that the modern State of Israel inverted into *lo avda sikvaseinu*, "we have not lost our hope." The second group, then, consists of those who did lose that hope — people who perhaps assimilated, who were not necessarily lost physically but who lost faith in the Jewish people's collective future. When they died, *Yechezkel*'s prophecy of the dry bones encompasses them as well.

### Dry Practitioners

Rabbi *Yirmeya*'s opinion is particularly striking: *elu bnei adam she'ein bahen lachluchis shel mitzvah* — these are people who have no moisture of *mitzvah* in them. Notably, he does not say *she'ein bahen mitzvos* — that they have no *mitzvos* — and that distinction is significant. The *gemara* could have said simply that these are people without *mitzvos*. Instead, by borrowing the imagery of *ha'atzamos hayeveshos* — the dry bones — the text layers an extra degree of intensity onto the dryness. Rabbi *Yirmeya* is pointing to the *dati'im yeveshim*, as one might characterize them: people who observe the letter but not the spirit, who do *mitzvos* on the outside without allowing them to penetrate. One is reminded of Rabbi *Akiva*'s image of water gradually wearing through rock — to what degree do we allow *mitzvos* to truly affect us, or do we perform them while remaining wholly untouched within?

### Temple Desecrators

Rabbi *Yitzchak Nafcha* identifies a fourth group: *bnei adam shechipu et haheichal kulo shkatzim uremasim* — people who plastered or covered the sanctuary entirely with the most abhorrent creatures. The image is provocative and can be understood metaphorically as people who not only abandoned the religious path but actively defiled and smeared it — the *mumar lehachis*, the one who rebels specifically to spite.

### Beautiful Youth/Dura

The fifth category, stated by Rabbi *Yochanan*, is entirely different in character. It is worth recalling what we know about Rabbi *Yochanan* himself — that in his youth he was renowned for his exceptional beauty, to the degree that stories are told of *Reish Lakish* encountering him at the river and of Rabbi *Yochanan* sitting at the entrance to the *mikveh* to inspire women through the sight of his beauty. With that context in mind, it is notable that the fifth group he identifies is *bachurim shehayu meganim et hachama beyofyam* — young men so beautiful they outshone the sun itself. These are *metim shebe-Bik'at Dura* — the dead of the *Bik'at Dura*, the valley of Dura in Syria, along what may have been the route of the exile. When *Nevuchadnezzar* drove Israel into exile, there were among them young men of such physical beauty that the Chaldean women who saw them were overcome with desire. They told their husbands, the husbands told the king, the king commanded that these men be killed, and still the women were drawn to them even afterward. The king had them trampled. Those are the fifth group included in *Yechezkel*'s resurrection.

### Modern Context

This fifth category invites reflection across historical distance. For roughly two thousand years — and especially in the era of caricature and persecution leading up to and through the Nazi period — the Jewish people did not walk through the world with an image of themselves as beautiful. And yet in the last seventy to a hundred years, a new image has emerged: the *tzabar*, sun-tanned, strong, and vital, and with it a new kind of Jewish presence in the world. When one considers all five of these groups together — the overly militant who hasten the end, the assimilated who have lost hope, those who perform *mitzvos* without any inner moisture, those who actively desecrate the sacred, and those beautiful young men cut down in the exile — one sees the full scope of *kol Yisrael*. Every one of these categories is included in *Yechezkel*'s vision and in the promise of revival.

---

## Furnace & Revival

### Six Miracles

*Tanu Rabbanan*: *besha'ah shehipil Nevuchadnezzar harasha et Chananyah Mishael va'Azaryah lekivshan ha'esh amar lo HaKadosh Baruch Hu leYechezkel lech vehachayeih metim beVik'at Dura* — at the very same moment that *Nevuchadnezzar* cast *Chananyah*, *Mishael*, and *Azaryah* into the furnace, the Holy One Blessed Be He said to *Yechezkel*: go and revive the dead in *Bik'at Dura*. The simultaneity is arresting. *Chananyah*, *Mishael*, and *Azaryah* were evidently the last three people in the entire exile who refused to bow down to *Nevuchadnezzar*'s statue — a golden colossus sixty *amot* in height. The text does not tell us of two hundred thousand others taken to the furnace who happened to survive; it tells us of three. Everyone else had bowed. *Nevuchadnezzar* was about to annihilate the final remnant of Jewish resistance, and at that precise moment — *besha'ah* — God commands *Yechezkel* to revive the dead. It is one of those moments in the *gemara* that reads differently in this century than it may have in 1500.

The *baraita* then enumerates: *shisha nissim na'asu be'oto hayom* — six miracles occurred on that day — *ve'elu hen*: the furnace rose, the furnace was breached, its foundation dissolved (*humak sodo*), the graven image fell on its face, four kingdoms were burned, and *Yechezkel* revived the dead in *Bik'at Dura*.

### Furnace Rising

What precisely is the *kivshan* — the furnace into which *Chananyah*, *Mishael*, and *Azaryah* were thrown? The *kivshan* is a kind of kiln or hot furnace sunk into the ground, with the fire buried beneath. This architectural feature is critical to understanding the sequence of miracles. If the furnace is below ground level, anything cast into it becomes invisible from the outside, and the full scope of a miracle occurring within it would be obscured. Therefore, for the miracle to be witnessed in its entirety, the furnace first had to rise from its sunken position. Then — *nifratz hakivshan* — it was breached or cracked open, making visible what was inside.

### Furnace Lime/Base

The third miracle, *humak sodo*, presents some interpretive difficulty. The conventional reading is that the *kivshan* was constructed from limestone — *sid* — and that this limestone base dissolved or melted. *Rashi* addresses this in the *dibur hamatchil* of *humak sodo* and offers two possibilities. In one formulation he reads the word as *yesodo* — its foundation — indicating that the structural base of the furnace came apart. In another he reads it as *humak sido* — *hasid hakivshan namas merov chamimut* — the limestone of the furnace melted from the intensity of the heat. He then adds: *kach shamati* — this is what I heard — *v'haya nimshechet lirachok mehahavel shel oto hasid nisrefu otan sheyashvu* — and that the heat and vapor emanating from that melting limestone spread outward and consumed those who were standing nearby.

### Officials Burned

This leads directly to the next element of the narrative: four of *Nevuchadnezzar*'s officials were themselves burned. *Nevuchadnezzar* had dispatched eight ranks of officials and governors — the *gemara* works through the list appearing in *Daniel* — yet when *Chananyah*, *Mishael*, and *Azaryah* emerged from the furnace, only four ranks of officials are described as witnessing it. There is a tradition that the other four were burned in the fire. According to *Rashi*, the *dibur hamatchil* of *humak sodo* makes this explicit: *nisrefo otan she'hishlichu Chananyah Mishael va'Azaryah l'toch kivshan ha'esh* — those who had thrown *Chananyah*, *Mishael*, and *Azaryah* into the furnace were themselves consumed by it.

---

## Dignity/Garments

### Royal Garments

*Tnai devei Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov*: *afilu b'sha'at hasakanah lo yeshaneh adam et atzmo min harabbanut* — even in a moment of mortal danger, a person should not alter his dignified bearing or his station. The *pasuk* that generates this teaching is from *Daniel*: *be'edin gavraya ilech kaftu besarbalehon patishehon vecharbelatehon* — these men were bound in their tunics, cloaks, and hats, fully clothed in their royal garments when they were cast into the fire. They did not strip away their dignity even at the moment of their execution. From this the school of Rabbi *Eliezer ben Yaakov* derives a general principle: even under threat, one does not shed one's *rabbanut*.

### Pirkei Avot

This teaching stands in apparent tension with a principle in *Pirkei Avot* — *snai et harabbanut*, distance yourself from *rabbanut*, from positions of prominence and closeness to the ruling authorities. The two statements seem to pull in opposite directions. The resolution lies in distinguishing between the two situations: *Pirkei Avot* counsels against seeking out or cultivating proximity to power in the first place, while Rabbi *Eliezer ben Yaakov* addresses what one does when already enmeshed in that situation through no choice of one's own. Once you are there, maintain your dignity.

### Historical Dignity

An image that captures this distinction: there is a film about two girls who are close friends in Vienna in 1938 — one from a family that joins the Nazi party, the other Jewish. When the Nazis come and compel the Jews to scrub the streets with toothbrushes, the Jewish grandfather turns to his granddaughter and says: help me choose my finest tie — I want to look especially well today. That is the teaching. One does not seek out the confrontation. But when the confrontation arrives, one does not strip away who one is.

---

## Tzadikim>Angels

### Greater Status

*Amar Rabbi Yochanan*: *gdolim tzadikim yoter mimalachei hasharet* — the *tzadikim* are greater than the ministering angels. One dimension of this is straightforward: an angel has a single function and performs it perfectly, while a *tzaddik* operates across the full complexity of human life and still chooses righteousness. A further question is how to order the different categories of the spiritually elevated relative to one another — we know separately that *bemakom sheba'alei teshuvah omdim tzadikim lo omdim*, that *ba'alei teshuvah* stand in a place where *tzadikim* cannot — but the claim here is that the *tzadikim* of the caliber of *Chananyah*, *Mishael*, and *Azaryah* stand above even the ministering angels.

### Fourth Figure

The source for this emerges from the verse in *Daniel* itself: *anah ve'amar ha ana chazei gavrin arba sharin mehalechin bego nura, vechaval lo itai behon, verevi'aya domeh l'var elohin* — I see four men walking unharmed in the midst of the fire, and the fourth one resembles a son of God, that is, an angel. Yet when *Chananyah*, *Mishael*, and *Azaryah* emerge from the furnace, only three come out. The fourth figure — the one who appeared angelic — is gone. One possibility is that this figure entered the fire in order to save them and was consumed in doing so; another reading is that he was an angel who stepped in and did not emerge. The *tzadikim* came out; the angel did not. This is part of what the *gemara* means in asserting that the *tzadikim* are greater.

---

## Nations Slap Haters

### Nations React

*Amar Rav Tanchum bar Chanilai*: *besha'ah she'yatzu Chananyah Mishael va'Azaryah mi'kivshan ha'esh, ba'u kol umot ha'olam ve'taphchu l'soneihen shel Yisrael al pneihem* — at the moment that *Chananyah*, *Mishael*, and *Azaryah* emerged from the furnace, all the nations of the world went and slapped the enemies of Israel across the face. This is of course *sagi nahor* — a euphemism — and the ones being struck are the Jews themselves who had capitulated. The nations turned to them and said: *yesh lachem eloh kaze ve'atem mishtachavim la'tzelem* — you have a God of this magnitude, capable of saving men from a furnace, and you bow down to a graven image?

### Admission of Sin

*Mi'yad patchu ve'amru*: immediately those same people opened their mouths and declared, from *Daniel*: *Lecha Hashem ha'tzedakah u'lanu boshet ha'panim k'hayom ha'zeh* — to You, *Hashem*, belongs righteousness, and to us belongs *boshet ha'panim*, shame of face, as on this day.

### Shir HaMa'alot

This *pasuk* connects to something encountered regularly without necessarily being fully registered. In *Shir HaMa'alot* recited before *bentching* on *Shabbat*, we read: *az yomru va'goyim higdil Hashem la'asot im eleh* — then the nations said, *Hashem* has done great things for these people — followed immediately by *higdil Hashem la'asot imanu* — *Hashem* has done great things for us. The sequence seems counterintuitive: one might expect the Jewish people to proclaim God's greatness first, and then the nations to affirm it. But *beshuv Hashem et shivat Tzion* — in the context of exile — we gradually absorb the way we are perceived by those around us. When the *goyim* themselves declare *higdil Hashem la'asot im eleh*, something shifts, and we find ourselves able to say: *higdil Hashem la'asot imanu*. We sometimes need the external affirmation to recover the internal one.

### Shame Concept

On *boshet ha'panim*: there is something valuable in a sense of shame that keeps one properly oriented — a *yirei boshet*, as various commentaries explore, is someone in whom humility functions as a moral anchor. The risk is when that sense of shame is not internally generated but rather absorbed from an external, hostile gaze — when we begin to see ourselves through the eyes of those who diminish us, and become hunched. The glory of *Chananyah*, *Mishael*, and *Azaryah* emerging from the fire, and the slap it delivers to those who had abandoned faith, is precisely the restoration of a proper interiority.

---

## Palm Tree/Tamar

### Palm/Israel

*Amar Rav Shmuel bar Nachmani amar Rabbi Yonatan*: the verse in *Shir HaShirim* reads, *amarti e'eleh ve'tamar ochazah ve'sansinav* — I said I will climb the palm tree and take hold of its branches. Who is the speaker? *HaKadosh Baruch Hu*. And what is the *tamar*? *Amarti e'eleh ve'tamar elu Yisrael* — the palm tree is Israel. The *tamar* is a rich symbol: *tzaddik katamar yifrach*, the *tzaddik* flourishes like a palm; and the *lulav*, the palm branch, contains within it the *lev*, the heart — the *tamar* has one heart, and the Jewish people are meant to be a people of one heart, unified in focus toward *Hashem*.

### One Branch

*Ve'achshav lo alah b'yadi* — and now it has not quite come up in my hand. There is something deeply moving in this formulation. God, who can sustain three men in a furnace, who can command *Yechezkel* to revive the dead, says: it is genuinely difficult to bring the Jewish people fully to where they ought to be. The attempt was made and was not entirely successful — *ela sansan echad shel Chananyah Mishael va'Azaryah*, only a single branch of *Chananyah*, *Mishael*, and *Azaryah* was achieved.

### Tamar/Judah

An alternative reading that deserves to be noted: *tamar* can also be understood as *Tamar*, the wife of *Yehudah*, about whom there is a tradition that she was willing to be thrown into a furnace of fire in order to preserve the lineage of the Jewish people. The implication of the *kal vachomer* is plain: if she was prepared to make such a sacrifice for the sake of a human being, how much more so should such willingness apply in service of *Hashem*. The connection to *Yehudah* and *Yehudim* gives the metaphor an additional layer of resonance.

---

## Vision/Red Horse

### Darkness/Night

*Amar Rabbi Yochanan*: the verse in *Zechariah* reads — *raiti halaila vehineh ish rocheiv al sus adom vehu omed bein hahadasim asher bametzula* — I saw in the night, and behold a man riding a red horse, standing among the myrtles in a deep place. What is the *laila* — the night? *Bikesh HaKadosh Baruch Hu lehafoch et kol ha'olam kulo le'laila* — the Holy One Blessed Be He sought to turn the entire world to night, because the whole of it had abandoned the path. Only three people remained who had not.

### God/Red Horse

*Vehineh ish rocheiv* — and behold a man riding. The word *ish* is a loaded term throughout *Tanach*. When *Moshe* looks around and sees *ve'ein ish*, when the *mishnah* in *Avot* says *bemakom she'ein anashim heye ata ish* — sometimes *ish* refers to *Eliyahu*, sometimes to an extraordinary human figure. Here, the *gemara* identifies the *ish* as *HaKadosh Baruch Hu* Himself, because it is written in *Shirat Hayam*: *Hashem ish milchama Hashem shemo* — that is His name, He is the *ish*. And the horse is red: *bikesh HaKadosh Baruch Hu lehafoch et ha'olam kulo ledam* — He sought to turn the entire world to blood. The color red, the night, the blood — these are all metaphors for the catastrophic destruction that was imminent when the faith of the Jewish people was on the verge of being annihilated entirely.

### God Cools

*Keivan shenistakel beChananyah Mishael va'Azaryah nitkarera da'ato* — but when He looked upon *Chananyah*, *Mishael*, and *Azaryah*, His mind cooled. We have, in the language of the *gemara*, a passionate God — one moved to fury and moved to relent.

### Myrtles/Righteous

*Vehu omed bein hahadasim asher bametzula* — He stands among the myrtles in a deep place. Is God literally standing in a forest of myrtle trees and feeling calmed by the scenery? The *gemara* resolves: *ve'ein hadasim ela tzaddikim* — the *hadasim* are none other than the *tzaddikim*. He stands among the righteous — specifically, *Chananyah*, *Mishael*, and *Azaryah* — and His anger is assuaged.

### Esther/Hadassah

And here *Esther* returns to the discussion, because *hadasim* bring *Hadassah* in their wake. The verse states: *vayehi omen et Hadassah* — and he raised *Hadassah*. *Esther* had two names. The significance of the name *Hadassah* — connecting her to the *hadas*, the myrtle — is that the righteous are called *hadasim*, and she belongs in their company.

### Three Leaves

One commentary notes that a *hadas* leaf grows in clusters of three. What do the three leaves represent? Various groupings of three suggest themselves: *Torah*, *avodah*, *gemilut chasadim*; *Avraham*, *Yitzchak*, *ve'Yaakov*; or simply *Chananyah*, *Mishael*, *va'Azaryah* themselves. The *hadasim* carry this threefold symbolism, and somehow within it the *tzaddikim* are always represented. Whether this also builds on the *lulav* and its component species — having just spoken of the *tamar* — is a further layer worth sitting with, even if not fully resolved.

### White Horse

*Amar Rav Papa*: *shema mina sus yachivra malei lealma* — from here we learn that a white horse is a good sign. If one dreams of a white horse, it is a favorable omen.

---

## Where They Went

### Three Opinions

After *Chananyah*, *Mishael*, and *Azaryah* walked out of the furnace — where did they go? *Verabanan leichan azlu?* The *gemara* records three opinions among the *Amoraim*, and then notes that these positions already appear among the *Tannaim*, making it a *kitnai* — the dispute is not new.

### Evil Eye Death

*Amar Rav*: *be'ayin hara metu* — they died from the *ayin hara*. After all this, *davka* because of all this — the intensity of attention, the envy, the *kin'ah* — they were struck down. There is a position in *Bava Metzia* that ninety-nine percent of deaths in the world are attributable to the *ayin hara*. What does that say about the nature of human beings and how we look at one another?

### Spat Upon

*Shmuel amar*: *berok tav'u* — they were spat upon in contempt and disdain. The world's reaction to their emergence from the furnace was, for some, not reverence but derision.

### Went to Israel

*Rabbi Yochanan* says: *alu le'Eretz Yisrael venasu nashim ve'holidu banim uvanot* — they went up to *Eretz Yisrael*, married, and had sons and daughters. This is itself a form of *techiyas hameisim* — the *atzamot yeveshot* revived and took root in the land.

### Tannaitic Sources

The *gemara* notes that this is *kitnai* — these three positions already appear in the earlier generation: Rabbi *Eliezer* holds *be'ayin hara metu*, Rabbi *Yehoshua* holds *berok tav'u*, and the *chachamim* align with Rabbi *Yochanan* — *alu le'Eretz Yisrael venasu nashim ve'holidu banim uvanot*.

### Anshei Mofet

The *chachamim*'s view is supported by a *pasuk* from *Zechariah*: *shema na Yehoshua Kohen Gadol ata vere'echa hayoshevim lefanecha ki anshei mofet hema* — hear, *Yehoshua* the high priest, you and your fellows who sit before you, for they are *anshei mofet* — men of a miracle, men around whom miracles occur. The *gemara* asks: who are these *anshei mofet* who sit before *Yehoshua*? *Eizehem anashim shenasa lahem mofet? Hevei omer zeh Chananya Mishael va'Azarya* — these are *Chananyah*, *Mishael*, and *Azaryah*, around whom the great miracle was performed.

---

## Where Was Daniel?

### Three Reasons

This leads immediately to the obvious question: *veDaniel leichan azal* — where was *Daniel*? Is it conceivable that *Daniel* bowed to the idol while only those three refused? The *gemara* offers three explanations for his absence, each from a different *Amora*, and each carrying its own theological and historical texture.

---

## Daniel in Tverya

### Tverya Aqueduct

*Amar Rav*: *lemichra nahara raba biTverya* — Daniel went to dig the great river aqueduct in *Tverya*, the national water infrastructure, the *movila artzi*, in Israel. He is described as going to establish the hydraulic foundation for the eventual center of Jewish life in the land.

### Tverya Center

What is *Tverya*? One etymology traces the name to *Tiberius*, the Roman ruler. But in Hebrew, *tabur* is the navel, the belly button — and so *Tverya* functions as the *tabur* of *Eretz Yisrael*, the center of the land. Daniel goes to dig water — to bring *Torah*, as it were, to revive the center — and we know from history that *Tverya* did indeed later become a center of Jewish scholarship and life.

---

## Daniel/Seeds

### Alfalfa Seeds

*Ushmuel amar leatoyei bizra deaspasta* — Shmuel says Daniel went to bring seeds, specifically a superior variety of alfalfa that was not yet available in the land. Shmuel's role in *halacha* is that of the preeminent *dayan* in monetary law, the economic authority — and fittingly, his Daniel is an economic advisor to the king who takes advantage of his position to bring vital agricultural resources to *Eretz Yisrael*.

---

## Daniel/Pigs

### Egyptian Pigs

*Amar leatoyei chazirei deAlexandria shel Mitzrayim* — Rabbi *Yochanan* says Daniel went to bring pigs from Alexandria in Egypt. The surprise this generates — *ini?* — is acknowledged. What is the nature of these Egyptian pigs? *V'ha tanya*: there is a *baraita* that states that no cow or pig leaves Alexandria of Egypt unless its womb has been surgically cut, ensuring that the uniquely valuable Egyptian breed cannot be reproduced outside Egypt. The Egyptians maintained a monopoly on their special breeds through this practice.

### Thodos Practice

This practice is associated with *Thodos HaRofe* — *Thodos the doctor* — who is credited with its development or implementation. The animals whose wombs were not cut were the very young ones — those not yet slated for breeding — who would simply be eaten.

### Unauthorized Pigs

Rabbi *Yochanan*'s explanation continues: *zutari aytei belo da'ata d'atu* — Daniel, when he went there, took young ones without the authorization of those who controlled the Egyptian supply. He took them before they could be operated on, because taking adults would have presented a different set of concerns. The rabbis' explanation, then, is that Daniel's mission on behalf of *Nevuchadnezzar* — as royal advisor — took him to Alexandria, and he used the opportunity to secure these animals for the benefit of the community.

---

## Where Was Daniel? (II)

### God's Reason

*Tanu Rabbanan*: there were three parties to the decision that Daniel should not be present in *Bavel* when *Chananyah*, *Mishael*, and *Azaryah* were thrown into the furnace. *HaKadosh Baruch Hu amar*: *yeizal Daniel mehacha d'lo limru bizchuto inatzel* — let Daniel leave from here, so that people will not say that the three of them were saved from the furnace through Daniel's merit. It should reflect their own righteousness alone — the miracle should belong to them and not be attributed to the presence of a greater figure.

### Daniel's Reason

*V'Daniel amar*: *eizal mehacha d'lo lekayem bi pesilei eloheihem tisrefun ba'esh* — Daniel said: I should leave from here lest the verse *pesilei eloheihem tisrefun ba'esh* — you shall burn their idols in fire — be fulfilled through me. This requires the next point to be understood.

### King's Concern

*V'Nevuchadnezzar amar*: *yeizil Daniel mehacha d'lo limru kali leh l'elohei beneura* — *Nevuchadnezzar* said: Daniel should leave from here so that people will not say that *Nevuchadnezzar* burned his own god in the fire. For *Nevuchadnezzar* effectively worshiped *Daniel*, and to throw someone whom the king treats as a god into a furnace would be to do precisely what the Torah commands regarding idols — burn them in fire. From Daniel's perspective, he did not want to become an idol; from *Nevuchadnezzar*'s perspective, he did not want to be seen as burning his own god.

### King Worshipped

Where do we derive that *Nevuchadnezzar* worshiped *Daniel*? *Mna lan d'sagid leh?* The source is a verse in *Daniel* itself: *be'edayin malka Nevuchadnezzar nefal al anpohi u'l'Daniel sagid* — then King *Nevuchadnezzar* fell on his face and worshiped *Daniel*. That verse establishes the premise for all three parties' reasoning.

---

## False Prophets

### False Prophets Intro

The *gemara* now turns to two other figures who appear in the context of *galut Bavel* and involve fire — but in a very different register. A verse in *Yirmiyahu* is cited: *koh amar Hashem Tzevaot Elokei Yisrael el Achav ben Kolaya v'el Tzidkiya ben Maaseiya haniva'im lachem bishmi lasheker* — thus says *Hashem Tzvaot*, the God of Israel, concerning *Achav ben Kolaya* and *Tzidkiyah ben Maaseiyah*, who are prophesying to you falsely in My name. These are not the famous *Achav* king of Israel or *Tzidkiyahu* king of Judah — they are false prophets active among the Jewish exiles in *Bavel*.

### Curse Comparison

*V'lukach mehem klala l'chol galut Yehuda asher b'Vavel lemor yesimcha Hashem k'Tzidkiya u'ch'Achav asher kalam melech Bavel ba'esh* — and from them shall be taken a curse for all the exile of Judah in *Bavel*, saying: may *Hashem* make you like *Tzidkiyah* and *Achav* whom the king of *Bavel* roasted in the fire. Compare this to the blessing *yesimcha Hashem keEphraim ucheMenashe* — Ephraim and Menashe lived through the exile in Egypt and strengthened the Jewish people. Here we have figures who lived through *galut Bavel* and instead weakened and corrupted the Jewish people, and whose names become a curse rather than a blessing.

### Roasted Seeds

*Asher srafam lo ne'emar ela asher kalam* — the verse does not say they were *burned*, it says they were *klam* — roasted. *Amar Rabbi Yochanan mishum Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai melamed sheasaan kekliyot* — we are taught that they were made like toasted seeds, like grain roasted on a fire. The connection between *klala* — curse — and *kalam* — roasted — is striking even if not formally derived.

### Sexual Sin

Why this particular punishment? *Yaan asher asu nevalah beYisrael vayinafu et neshei rei'ehem* — because they committed an abomination in Israel and committed adultery with the wives of their neighbors. *Mai avud* — what exactly did they do? The *gemara* now tells the story.

### Seduction Plan

*Achav amar lah koh amar Hashem hashmeyi el Tzidkiyah* — *Achav* said to the daughter of *Nevuchadnezzar*: this is the word of *Hashem* — you should be intimate with *Tzidkiyah*. And *Tzidkiyah amar koh amar Hashem hashmeyi el Achav* — *Tzidkiyah* said to her: this is the word of *Hashem* — you should be intimate with *Achav*. Each one was using false prophecy to push the king's daughter toward the other.

### Daughter Reports

*Azlah ve'amrah leih leavuh* — she went and told her father. *Amar lah*: he said to her — and here the *gemara* notes something remarkable: *eloheihem shel elu soneh zimah hu* — the God of these people abhors this kind of behavior. The Babylonian king, without Torah study, knows that the God of Israel is *soneh zimah*. *Ki atu legabach shadreinhu legabi* — when they come to you, send them to me. She did so: *ki atu legabah shadratehu legabei avuh* — when they came to her, she sent them to her father.

### Prohibition Confirmed

*Amar lehu man amar lachon* — he said to them: who told you this? They answered: *HaKadosh Baruch Hu*. He replied: *veha Chananyah Mishael va'Azaryah she'altinhu ve'amru li assur* — but I asked *Chananyah*, *Mishael*, and *Azaryah*, and they told me it is forbidden. This is a remarkable detail: it means that *Nevuchadnezzar* had already, at some earlier point, considered the possibility of his daughter having relations with a Jewish prophet — and had consulted *Chananyah*, *Mishael*, and *Azaryah*, who rendered it *assur*.

### King's Test

*Amru leih anan nami nevi'ei kevathaihu ledidhu lo amar lehu ledidan amar lan* — the false prophets said: we are also prophets just like them. To them He did not say it; to us He did. *Amar lehu*: fine. *Ana beina deivadkinechu* — I will test you just as I tested *Chananyah*, *Mishael*, and *Azaryah*. I will put you to the same proof.

### Joshua Chosen

*Amru leih inun tlata havu ve'anan terein* — they said: there were three of them; we are only two. Three survived, two cannot be expected to. *Amar lehu bacharu lachon man deito bahadayichu* — the king said: choose yourselves a third to accompany you. *Amru Yehoshua Kohen Gadol* — they chose *Yehoshua* the *Kohen Gadol*. Their reasoning: *savri tfei Yehoshua denafish zechuteih umagen alan* — they calculated that *Yehoshua*'s merit was so great that it would shield them. As the *gemara* will go on to show, this calculation did not succeed.
