---

# Sanhedrin 93b

## False Prophets & Fire

### Nebuchadnezzar's Test

The sugya opens near the bottom of 93a, picking up the narrative of two false prophets who had been exploiting their prophetic claims to take advantage of women. Nebuchadnezzar decided to test them as he had tested Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah — by throwing them into the fire. The false prophets, knowing they could not survive on their own merits, proposed bringing a third person whose merit might protect them: Yehoshua Kohen Gadol. They reasoned, *savri leisye Yehoshua de-nevitz zechusei u-magen alan* — let Yehoshua come, for his great merit will shield us. So they brought him, and all three were thrown into the furnace. The false prophets were consumed entirely; Yehoshua Kohen Gadol, however, had only his garments singed. The Gemara cites the verse, *vayar'eini es Yehoshua ha-kohen ha-gadol omeid lifnei malach Hashem*, and the subsequent verse, *halo zeh ud mutzal me-eish* — is this not a brand plucked from the fire? — as the scriptural basis for this account.

Nebuchadnezzar then addressed Yehoshua directly: *yadana de-tzaddika at* — I know you are a righteous man. But then he asked: *ela mai ta'ama ahanya becha purta nura* — why did the fire affect you even slightly, when it had no effect whatsoever on Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah? Yehoshua replied: *innu tlatah havu va-ana chad* — they were three and I was only one. Nebuchadnezzar countered: but Avraham was alone when he was saved from the fire, according to the *midrash*. Yehoshua answered: *hasam lo havu resha'im ba-adei ve-lo is-yehav reshusa l'nura* — there, no wicked men were present with him, and the fire was given no permission to operate. Here, by contrast, the wicked ones were present, and the fire had been granted permission — it burned them, and since it was genuinely burning, it touched me slightly as well. The Gemara adds the folk saying: *trei udi yaveshi ve-chad rativa* — two dry logs and one wet one: the dry ones, once alight, cause even the wet one to catch.

### Yehoshua's Punishment

Yet the Gemara presses further: even granting that the presence of the *resha'im* explains the fire's general power, why did Yehoshua specifically suffer any effect at all? There must have been something in his own record that warranted it. Rav Papa answers: *she-hayu banav nosim nashim she-einam hagunot li-khunah ve-lo michah ba-hen* — his sons had married women who were not fitting for *kehunah*, and he did not protest. The verse that describes him as wearing *begadim tzo'im* — soiled garments — is read not literally but symbolically. As the Gemara asks rhetorically: would Yehoshua actually go about in soiled clothes? Rather, it teaches that his sons' unsuitable marriages splattered back upon him, not as a personal transgression but as a failure to rebuke. A measure of that defilement clung to his garment — something external yet attached — and that accounts for the slight singeing he suffered.

## Ruth & Six Blessings

### Barley Midrash

Rabbi Tanchum cites a *derashah* of Bar Kappara in Tzippori: what is the meaning of the verse *sheish se'orim ha-eileh nasan li* — "these six barleys he gave me," spoken by Ruth? The Gemara considers and rejects both the plain reading — that Boaz gave her six literal kernels, which would be no gift at all — and the alternative that it was six *se'ah*, which would be too heavy for a woman to carry. The answer: *ela remez ramaz lah* — it was six kernels, but he was giving her a symbolic hint, *she-atidim shishah banim latzei mimmenah she-mitbarchin be-sheish sheish berachot* — that six distinguished descendants would emerge from her, each blessed with six blessings. Those six descendants are: David, Mashiach, Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah — all, the Gemara will explain, from the Davidic household or at minimum from the tribe of Yehudah.

### David's 6 Blessings

The six blessings of David derive from the verse in which one of the lads — identified later as Doeg — spoke to Shaul about the son of Yishai: *yode'a nagen, ve-gibor chayil, ve-ish milchama, u-nevon davar, ve-ish to'ar, va-Hashem imo* — he knows how to play music, he is valorous, a man of war, understanding in speech, handsome, and God is with him. Six attributes, six blessings.

Yet Rav Yehudah in the name of Rav makes a striking observation: *kol ha-pasuk hazeh lo amaro Doeg ela bi-leshon hara* — this entire verse was said by Doeg with an evil tongue. The praise is genuine in content, but the intent was to make Shaul jealous of David. This is *lashon hara* not because the words are false, but because of the malicious purpose animating them. Rashi explains that each praise was framed to provoke royal envy.

The Gemara then unpacks how each praise, read through this lens, actually refers to David's Torah brilliance: *yode'a nagen* — he knows how to ask penetrating questions in learning; *gibor* — he knows how to answer them; *ish milchama* — he knows how to engage in the *give and take* of Torah debate, *lisah u-litein be-milchamtah shel Torah*; *nevon davar* — he can infer one matter from another, *mevin davar mitoch davar*; *ish to'ar* — he can demonstrate the correct *halacha*, *mareh panim ba-halacha*; *va-Hashem imo* — *she-halacha ke-moto be-chol makom*, the *halacha* follows his opinion everywhere.

As each praise was reported to Shaul, the king brushed it aside: *efes, Yonatan beni kamohu* — my son Yonatan is just as good. But when Doeg said *va-Hashem imo*, Shaul could not dismiss it, for that was something even he himself lacked — *bi-milta de-bidida nami lo hava bei*. At that point, *chalash da'atei ve-itkana bei* — Shaul despaired and became jealous of David — which was, the Gemara says, precisely Doeg's goal. The contrast is sharpened by the verses: by Shaul it says *u-ve-chol asher yifneh yarshia* — wherever he turned he acted wickedly — while by David it says *u-ve-chol asher yifneh yatzliach* — wherever he turned he succeeded.

The Gemara then asks: how do we know the anonymous speaker was Doeg? The verse here says *echad mi-ha-ne'arim*, and the same superlative language, *meyuchas she-ba-ne'arim*, appears in connection with Doeg ha-Edomi, called *avir ha-ro'im* — the chief among Shaul's attendants — in a parallel passage.

## Mashiach 6 Blessings

### Mashiach Smells Truth

The six blessings of Mashiach are drawn from the passage in Yeshayahu: *ve-nachu alav ruach Hashem* — and the spirit of God will rest upon him — followed by *ruach chochmah u-vinah, ruach eitzah u-gevurah, ruach da'at ve-yirat Hashem*. The counting yields six when *da'at* and *yirat Hashem* are treated as a pair or when *ruach Hashem* functions as the overarching heading rather than a numbered item. Rashi, sensitive to the same difficulty, brackets the concluding clause *ve-chtiv va-haricho be-yirat Hashem* as a separate point about Mashiach's special faculty — not an additional blessing in the count, but an explication of how *yirat Hashem* manifests in him.

Rav Alexandri interprets this faculty homiletically: *melamed she-hit'ino mitzvot ve-yissurin ke-reichayim* — Mashiach will be laden with *mitzvot* and afflictions like a millstone, suggesting that his path will not be untroubled. This resonates with the motif of the afflicted servant and the wars of *Gog u-Magog* that precede the final redemption.

Rava, however, stays close to the plain sense: *de-morach ve-dayin* — Mashiach will be able to smell out the truth. The verse makes this explicit: *ve-lo le-mar'eh einav yishpot ve-lo le-mishma oznav yochiach* — he will not judge by what his eyes see or his ears hear — yet *ve-shafat be-tzedek dalim* — he will judge the poor with righteousness. How, if not through sight or sound? Through a supernatural sense of smell, a divine intuition that bypasses the normal channels of evidence.

### Bar Koziba Test

Bar Koziba — whose very name is the Gemara's play on *kazav*, falsehood, in contrast to the honorific *Bar Kochba* — ruled, or led his rebellion, for two and a half years. He declared himself the *mashiach*. The rabbis responded by citing precisely this Gemara: by the *mashiach* it is written *de-morach ve-dayin* — he can smell out the truth. *Nechezi anan i morach ve-dayin* — let us see whether he can do this. When they observed that he could not, *katluhu* — they killed him.

This passage raises several difficulties. First, why would the rabbis kill him? Even the Rambam, who writes at the end of *Hilchot Melachim* that Mashiach is not required to perform miracles, addresses this question differently: he says they knew Bar Kochba was not the *mashiach* because he died without fulfilling the messianic promises. The Ra'avad challenges the Rambam directly, pointing to this very Gemara: they knew because he failed the test of *de-morach ve-dayin*. Commentators suggest that even according to this Gemara, *katluhu* need not mean the rabbis themselves executed him; it may mean they did not protect him when the Romans moved against him — a re-reading that softens the tension with historical record and with the question of what legal category a false messianic claim would occupy. Some suggest it resembles *navi sheker*, a false prophet, though Mashiach is not the same as *navi*.

It is worth noting that even this test is not a demand for wholesale transformation of reality. It is a supernatural capacity, but a specific and limited one — which brings it somewhat closer to the Rambam's general orientation than might first appear.

## Daniel's Group

### Exiles' Perfection

The Gemara now turns to Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah — four of Ruth's six descendants — each of whom received six blessings. The verse at the opening of Sefer Daniel describes those taken into exile: *asher ein bahem kol mum* — without any blemish — one; *ve-tovei mareh* — of good appearance — two; *u-maskilim be-chol chochmah* — wise in all wisdom — three; *yodei da'at* — knowledgeable — four; *u-mevinei mada* — understanding — five; *va-asher koach bahem la'amod be-heichal ha-melech* — possessing the stamina to stand in the king's palace — six.

Rabbi Chama bar Chanina explains the phrase *ein bahem kol mum* with striking specificity: *afilu ke-rivda de-chusilta lo hava behu* — they did not even have the puncture mark left by a blood-letting instrument. They had never needed medical bloodletting; their physical perfection was absolute.

He explains *va-asher koach bahem la'amod be-heichal ha-melech* as well: *melamed she-hayu onsin et atzmam min ha-schok u-min ha-sicha u-min ha-sheina, u-ma'amidin al atzmam be-sha'ah she-nitzrechin le-nekaveihem mipnei eimas malchut* — they disciplined themselves to suppress laughter, idle talk, and sleep, and even to hold their bodily needs, out of awe of the royal court. Like sentinels who cannot break formation, they stood in absolute self-mastery.

The concluding verse, *va-yihyu va-hem mi-bnei Yehudah Daniel Chananyah Mishael va-Azaryah*, prompts a dispute. Rabbi Elazar says *kulam mi-bnei Yehudah hen* — all four were descendants of Yehudah, consistent with the midrash of Ruth's six descendants from the Davidic line. Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani disagrees: Daniel was from Yehudah, but Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah were from the other tribes.

### Saris Dispute

The Gemara brings the prophecy, *u-mi-vanecha asher yetzu mimecha asher tolid yikachu ve-hayu sarisim be-heichal melech Bavel* — your children will be taken and become *sarisim* in the palace of the king of Babylonia — and debates what *sarisim* means here.

Rav says *sarisim mamash* — they were literally castrated, as was standard for those serving in close proximity to the royal harem. Rabbi Chanina disagrees: *she-nistarsa avodah zarah bi-ymeihem* — idolatry was "eunuchized" in their days, rendered impotent through the events described in Sefer Daniel, where the false gods were exposed and defeated.

One might ask: does not the phrase *saris ha-melech* in contexts like Esther unambiguously denote literal castration? The Gemara acknowledges this — yes, castration was the practice — but entertains the metaphorical reading as an alternative for these particular individuals.

The Gemara then tests each position. *Bishlama* for Rabbi Chanina's view: the verse in Yeshayahu, *koh amar Hashem la-sarisim asher yishmeru et shabatotai*, makes sense only if the *sarisim* is being used metaphorically — why would the Torah highlight a shameful physical condition as the defining characteristic of these great men? For Rav's view — that they were literally castrated — the verse from Yeshayahu poses a challenge: why single them out as *sarisim* if that is simply a degrading physical state? The Gemara answers: *ha ve-ha havu behu* — according to Rav, both things were true of them: they were literally castrated, *and* idolatry was rendered impotent in their days. The verse highlights the latter.

The earlier verse's praise that they had no *mum* refers to when they were taken into captivity, before castration occurred. The later verse, *ve-chaval lo isai behon*, refers to the fire: it does not mean they had no wound in general, but that *lo chavala ve-lo reicha* — the fire left neither burn nor smoke on them. The double language indicates two different types of freedom from fire-damage, not a general absence of bodily blemish.

### Book Names

The Gemara pivots to a discussion of why the book containing the words of Nechemya ben Chachalyah is called Ezra rather than Nechemya. Rabbi Yirmeyah bar Abba answers: *mipnei she-hechzik tovah le-atzmo* — because Nechemya claimed credit for himself, as evidenced by the verse *zochrah li Elokai le-tovah* — remember this for me, O God, for good. One who demands to be remembered does not end up remembered, at least not by having the book named after him.

The Gemara challenges: did not David say something similar — *zochreini Hashem bi-rtzon amecha, pakdeini bi-shu'asecha*? The answer distinguishes the two: David was *rachamei de-ka-baei* — petitioning for mercy, not demanding credit. The end of the verse, *pakdeini bi-shu'asecha* — visit me with Your salvation — reveals the supplicatory register, not a demand. There is also a grammatical distinction: *zochreini* — remember me — differs from *zochrah li* — remember this [accomplishment] for me — the latter implying a specific claim to credit.

A second reason is advanced: *she-sipar bi-gnusan shel rishonim* — Nechemya spoke disparagingly of his predecessors, complaining that the earlier governors had burdened the people, as stated in the verse *ve-ha-pachot ha-rishonim asher hayu le-fanai hichbidu al ha-am*. One who disparages earlier generations forfeits the right to have the book named after him.

The Gemara then asks: it says *ve-af al Daniel she-kadmu mimenu siper* — even Daniel, who preceded him, Nechemya disparaged. But how do we know Daniel was greater than those who were Nechemya's contemporaries? The verse in Daniel states: *va-er'ei ani Daniel levadi et ha-mar'eh ve-ha-anashim asher hayu imi lo ra'u et ha-mar'eh aval charadah gedolah naflah aleihem va-yivrachu be-hechavei* — I, Daniel, alone saw the vision, while the men with me did not see it, yet great terror fell upon them and they fled to hide. Rabbi Yirmeyah (or Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba) identifies those men as Chaggai, Zechariah, and Malachi — the prophets of the Second Temple era who were Nechemya's contemporaries. Since Daniel surpassed them in vision, he was surely greater than Nechemya as well. Rashi notes that this passage may have been imported from Tractate Megillah and was not originally part of this sugya, and indeed acknowledges that it is absent from many manuscripts.

### Daniel's Vision

The Gemara refines the comparison: *inhu adifi minei ve-ihu adif minhaihu* — in one respect those prophets were greater than Daniel, and in another Daniel was greater than them. They were greater because *de-inhu nevi'ei ve-ihu lo navi* — they were full prophets with direct divine communication, whereas Daniel was not. Daniel was greater because *de-ihu chaza ve-inhu lo chazu* — he saw the vision while they could not.

This raises an obvious question: if they did not see the vision, why were they overcome with terror? The answer: *af al gav de-inhu lo chazu mazlaihu chazu* — even though they themselves did not see, their *mazal* — some non-conscious, intuitive dimension of their perception — registered the supernatural event, producing overwhelming fear even without conscious awareness of what was occurring.

### Fear & Demons

Ravina draws a practical inference: *ha-i man de-miv'as* — one who is suddenly, inexplicably gripped by fear — *af al gav de-ihu lo chazi, mazlei chazi* — even though he sees nothing consciously, his *mazal* perceives something real. The fear is not irrational; something is actually present.

What should one do? *Linshof mi-duchtei arba garmidei* — jump four *amot* from where one stands, for a *shed* or evil spirit may be about to attack, and moving disrupts its proximity. Alternatively, one may recite *Keri'at Shema*, which affords protection. If one is in a place of *tino'fet* — a lavatory or similarly impure location — where *Shema* cannot be recited, one should say: *iza de-vei tavcha shamina minai* — the goats of the slaughterhouse are fatter than I am — meaning: if you are a *sheid* looking for a victim, I am not worth your trouble; go to the slaughterhouse.

## Chizkiyahu Mashiach

### No Shirah = No Mashiach

The Gemara now turns to the verse *le-marbeh ha-misrah u-le-shalom ein ketz* — "of the increase of dominion and peace there will be no end" — a passage that evokes messianic abundance. The curiosity the Gemara addresses is orthographic: the word *le-marbeh* is written in Yeshayahu with a *mem sofit* — a closed *mem* — in the middle of the word, where an open *mem* would normally appear. Why the anomaly?

Rav Tanchum, citing a *derashah* of Bar Kappara in Tzippori, explains: *bikesh ha-Kadosh Baruch Hu la'asot Chizkiyahu Mashiach* — God wished to make Chizkiyahu into the Mashiach, and to transform the war of Sancherev into the war of *Gog u-Magog*. The historical moment, in other words, was poised to become the messianic denouement of history.

What prevented it? *Midat ha-din* spoke before God: You created David, who composed all of Sefer Tehillim — *kama shirot ve-tishbachot* — and yet You did not make him Mashiach. Now Chizkiyahu, for whom You performed all these miracles against Sancherev, and who did not respond with *shirah* — you would make *him* Mashiach? *L'kach nistatem* — therefore the *mem* was sealed, closed. Either Chizkiyahu's own voice was sealed — he did not sing — or God's intention to crown him as Mashiach was sealed.

This raises a profound question the lecturer flags explicitly: what exactly is the criterion for Mashiach? Is it not about the righteousness of the generation, the spread of Torah, the merit of the people? How is the presence or absence of *shirah* the pivotal factor? And what does it mean that this was almost a "bottom-up" process — that a particular historical confrontation with Sancherev could have *become* Gog u-Magog, as if the eschatological script were being improvised from unfolding events rather than determined in advance from above?

### Earth's Song

The land itself then opened and sang *shirah* on Chizkiyahu's behalf: *patchah ve-amrah shirah lefanav, she-ne'emar mi-kanaf ha-aretz zemirot shamanu, tzevi la-tzaddik* — from the edge of the earth we have heard songs, glory to the righteous one. The earth offered to discharge the *shirah* that Chizkiyahu had omitted, petitioning God: *asehu Mashiach* — still make him the Mashiach.

Then *sar ha-olam* — the angel charged with the ongoing governance of the world, according to Rashi — added his own petition: *tzevyono aseh la-tzaddik zeh* — do the will of this righteous man. A *bat kol* responded: *razi li razi li* — the secret is Mine, the secret is Mine. The message: it is not merely about the *shirah*. There are reasons, inscrutable to all these pleading advocates, why the moment of redemption has not yet come.

The *navi* — presumably Yeshayahu — cried out: *oy li oy li ad matai ad matai* — woe to me, woe to me, how long, how long? The *bat kol* replied with the verse from Yeshayahu: *bogdim bagadu u-voged bagadu* — the treacherous have dealt treacherously. Rava (or Rav Yitzchak) reads this with a *zayin* rather than a *dalet*: *ad de-asu bezuzai u-vezuzai de-vezuzai* — until the despoilers and despoilers of despoilers come. The point: the wars of *Gog u-Magog* must involve real anguish and suffering for Israel. The episode of Sancherev, for all its drama, left the population of Judea completely unscathed — and that cannot serve as the tribulation that precedes final redemption. The Mashiach cannot come until Israel has passed through a genuine period of collective anguish.

The passage from *Massa Dumah* — the prophecy addressed to *Dumah*, identified by Rabbi Yochanan as the angel charged with the souls — follows: *shomer mah mi-laylah, shomer mah mi-leil* — watchman, what of the night? All the souls gathered before *Dumah* asking when the long night of exile would end. The response: *ata voker ve-gam lailah* — morning is coming, but there must first be night. *Im tiv'ayun be'ayu* — if you want it, pray for it. *Shuvu asayu* — return and come, which Rashi reads as: do *teshuvah* and the redemption will follow. The passage closes with a gesture toward longing and active preparation for the Mashiach's arrival.

A *baraita* adds in the name of Rabbi Pappias: it was a *gnai* — a disgrace — for Chizkiyahu and his entire circle that they did not sing *shirah*, to the point that the earth itself had to sing on their behalf. The same *baraita* draws a parallel: it was a *gnai* for Moshe and the six hundred thousand who crossed the sea that they did not say *baruch* — until Yitro came and said *baruch Hashem asher hitzil eschem*. The Gemara explores the two opinions of Rav and Shmuel about the word *vayichad Yitro* — Rav reads it as Yitro cutting his own flesh in circumcision; Shmuel reads it as his flesh becoming covered with goosebumps. Rav then adds the folk proverb: *giura ad asara darei lo tivzei Armaya kamei* — do not disparage a non-Jew in the presence of a convert for ten generations. Yitro, despite his praise of God, still felt some vestigial bond with the Egyptians who had been drowned — illustrating how deeply prior identity runs.

## Sancherib Account

### Sancherib's 8 Names

The Gemara cites the verse *lachen yeshalach Adon Hashem Tzeva'os be-mishmanav razon* — therefore the Lord God of Hosts will send among his fat ones leanness — and interprets it as a play on the word *shemoneh*, eight: let Chizkiyahu, who has eight names, come and take account of Sancherev, who likewise has eight names. The word *be-mishmanav* is read as alluding to both.

Chizkiyahu's eight names come from the verse in Yeshayahu: *ki yeled yulad lanu ben nitan lanu* — a child is born to us, a son is given to us — followed by *pele, yo'etz, el, gibbor, avi, ad, sar, shalom*. Each word is treated as a distinct name, yielding eight. The Gemara anticipates the objection: does that not give nine, including the name Chizkiyahu itself? It answers that *Chizkiyahu* — meaning *chizko Yah*, God strengthened him — is merely a descriptive epithet, or alternatively, *Chizkiyahu she-chizak et Yisrael la-avihem she-ba-shamayim* — he strengthened Israel's bond with their Father in Heaven — which is again a description, not a proper name.

Sancherev's eight names are drawn from the various royal names and epithets he bore in the biblical record: Tiglath Pileser (read as one name), Pulneser, Shalmaneser, Pul, Sargon, Asnappar, Rabba, and Yakira — eight in total. Similarly, the name Sancherev itself is treated as a descriptive: either *she-sicho riv*, meaning he was always contentious, or *she-sach ve-nichar devarim klapei ma'alah* — he spoke and snorted blasphemies against Heaven.

### Paroh vs. Sancherib

Rabbi Yochanan asks: why was Sancherev merited to be called *Asnappar Rabba ve-Yakira* — the great and glorious one? Because *shelo sipar bi-gnushah shel Eretz Yisrael* — he did not speak disparagingly of the Land of Israel. His declaration — *ad bo'i ve-lakachti eschem el eretz ke-artzechem* — I will take you to a land *like* your land — was notably restrained. He acknowledged that their land was good but promised an equivalent, without claiming the destination was superior.

Rav and Shmuel debate whether this restraint was cunning or stupidity. According to the view that he was shrewd: had he claimed to offer a better land, the Israelites would have called him a liar, since nothing surpasses the Land of Israel. According to the view that he was foolish: if the new land is only equivalent, what incentive do the people have to leave? The Gemara then notes ruefully that the ten tribes themselves behaved worse than Sancherev in this respect. When they arrived at their place of exile and found it pleasant, they said it was *just as good as*, or even *twice as good as*, the Land of Israel — expressing contentment with exile. This attitude is offered as a partial explanation for why the ten tribes remained lost.

The Gemara addresses the verse *tachas kevodo yekad yekod ki-ykod esh* — beneath his glory shall burn a burning like the burning of fire. Rabbi Yochanan interprets: *tachas kevodo ve-lo kevodo mamash* — the *kavod* is not literal. Just as Rabbi Yochanan would call his garments *machbadutai* — that which honors me — so *kavodo* here refers to Sancherev's garments, and the verse means his body will burn beneath his clothes. Rabbi Eliezer disagrees: *tachas kevodo mamash* — *kavod* refers to the body itself, and beneath the body will burn — meaning the souls will be burned, as in the case of Nadav and Avihu, where *srefat neshama ve-guf kayam* — the soul was consumed and the body remained intact.

### Isaiah's Prophecy

The Gemara raises the verse: *atah ha-mibaledei Hashem alisi al ha-makom ha-zeh le-hashchiso* — was it without God that I came up against this place to destroy it? *Hashem amar elai: aleh el ha-aretz ha-zot ve-hashchisei* — God told me: go up and destroy it. Sancherev claims divine mandate. What is the basis for this claim? He had heard Yeshayahu's prophecy: *ya'an ki ma'as ha-am ha-zeh et mei ha-Shiloach ha-holchim le-at u-mesos et Retzin u-ven Remalyahu* — because this people has despised the gentle waters of Shiloach and rejoiced in Retzin and the son of Remalyahu.

Rav Yosef observes that without the Aramaic *targum* of this verse one would not understand what it means. The *targum* explains: since this people has despised the kingdom of the House of David — which governs them with gentleness, like the soft-flowing waters of Shiloach — and has instead embraced the rulership of Retzin and the son of Remalyahu, that is, the kings of the northern kingdom, God will bring the King of Assyria against them.

Rabbi Yochanan cites the verse *me'eras Hashem be-veit rasha u-nevei tzaddikim yevorach* — the curse of God is in the house of the wicked and the dwelling of the righteous will be blessed. He identifies the wicked man as Pekah ben Remalyahu, who despite eating forty *se'ah* of doves for dessert was never satisfied, and the righteous man as Chizkiyahu, who was content with a *litra* of vegetables. The spiritual condition of a person is mirrored in how much suffices him.

Yeshayahu prophesied: *ve-Hashem ma'aleh aleihem et mei ha-nahar ha-atzumim ve-ha-rabim et Melech Ashur* — God will bring upon them the mighty waters of the river, the King of Assyria. The subsequent verse adds: *ve-chalaf bi-Yehudah shataf ve-avar ad tzavar yagi'a* — he will pass through Yehudah, flood and pass, reaching up to the neck. Sancherev read this prophecy as his license to conquer Yehudah as well.

The Gemara then asks: if Sancherev was fulfilling a divine mandate, why was he punished? The answer: *navi a'aseret shevatim itnabi* — the prophet was speaking about the ten tribes. *Ihu yahav da'atei a-kula Yerushalayim* — Sancherev extended his ambitions to all of Yerushalayim. The prophecy said the flood would reach the neck — not drown the head. He overreached.

The prophet then came and told Sancherev: *ki lo mu'af la'asher mutzak lah* — there is no weariness for those who are distressed by her. Rabbi Elazar bar Berachyah interprets: *ein am zu ayef mu'af* — this people, weary as it is, weary in Torah — *lo yimasru b'yad mi ha-metzik lah* — will not be delivered into the hands of the one besieging them. You conquered the ten tribes, who *heikilu me'aleihem ol Torah* — treated the yoke of Torah lightly. But now you face the later ones, *Yehudah* and *Binyamin*, who *hichbidu aleihem ol Torah* — who bore the yoke of Torah with full weight. They are *re'uyim la'asot lahem nes* — fit to have a miracle performed for them — like those who crossed the *Yam Suf* and the *Yarden*. If Sancherev retreats, good. If not, *ani e'eseh lo galil ba-goyim* — I will make him as dung among the nations.

## Chizkiyahu Mashiach (II)

### God's Oath

The verse *acharei ha-devarim ve-ha-emet ha-eileh ba Sancherev Melech Ashur* — after these words and this truth, Sancherev King of Assyria came and besieged Yehudah — seems troubling. After the *emet*, the truth that Chizkiyahu was in the right, Sancherev is rewarded with the ability to lay siege? Ravina resolves this: *l'achar she-kafatz ha-Kadosh Baruch Hu ve-nishba* — after God jumped up and swore. Why did God swear? Because God recognized that if He offered Chizkiyahu the gift of Sancherev's defeat in advance, Chizkiyahu would decline: *lo hu be'ina ve-lo bi'utei be'ina* — I want neither him nor the dread of him. No one wants to endure a siege, even for a glorious outcome. So God did not consult Chizkiyahu. He simply swore: *d'mayiteina lei le-Sancherev* — I will bring Sancherev — so that Sancherev would be destroyed on Chizkiyahu's mountain, *ve-al harai avusenu*, and the yoke of Assyria would be lifted from Chizkiyahu's shoulders. The verse's *emet* refers to God's unilateral oath, and only afterward did Sancherev come. Then the miracle occurred and wiped out Sancherev's army.

Rabbi Yochanan adds: *yavo Sancherev ve-si'ato ve-ya'aseh avus le-Chizkiyahu ve-si'ato* — let Sancherev and his company come and serve as a feeding trough for Chizkiyahu and his company. The bodies of the fallen army would lie in the field and become fodder for animals. This is the reading of *avusenu* — we will make of them a feeding trough.

The verse *va-Hashem yeshalach bo davar va-yipol be-Yisrael* — God will send a word against him and it will fall upon Israel — leads to the concluding image: *ve-chuval ol mipnei shamen* — and the yoke will be destroyed because of oil. Rabbi Yitzchak Nafcha interprets: *chuval ol shel Sancherev mipnei shamno shel Chizkiyahu* — the yoke of Sancherev was broken by the merit of Chizkiyahu's oil, *she-hayah dolek be-vatei knesiyot u-ve-vatei midrashot* — which burned perpetually in synagogues and study halls. This brings us back to the theme of Torah learning as the decisive merit.

## Chizkiyahu's Torah

### Sword at Door

The Gemara now elaborates on what Chizkiyahu actually did to earn this merit. *Na'atz cherev al petach Beit ha-Midrash* — he planted a sword at the entrance of the *Beit ha-Midrash* — and declared: *kol mi she-eino osek ba-Torah yidaker ba-cherev ha-zot* — whoever is not engaged in Torah will be run through by this sword. Once everyone was inside, the sword at the door ensured they stayed.

### Universal Learning

The results were sweeping. *Badku mi-Dan ve-ad Be'er Sheva ve-lo matzu am ha-aretz* — they searched from the northern border of Israel to the south and found no ignoramus. *Mi-Gevat ve-ad Antipatris ve-lo matzu tinok ve-tinoket, ish ve-isha, she-lo hayu beki'in be-hilchot tuma ve-tahara* — from city to city they found not a single child, man, or woman who was not fully conversant in the laws of *tuma ve-tahara*, the most intricate and recondite domain of halachic knowledge.

This is the picture that now comes into focus: it was not merely that Chizkiyahu was personally righteous. Torah had genuinely permeated the entire nation. The Rambam's own criterion for messianic times — a king who returns the people to Torah and spreads the knowledge of God — was being met. The lecturer emphasizes that this makes the loss of the messianic moment all the more poignant. In the end, the Gemara acknowledges that the failure to sing *shirah* may not have been the only factor preventing the redemption; but now, at least, we understand why the generation of Chizkiyahu was considered genuinely worthy of it.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 95

## Chizkiyahu & Torah

### Chizkiyahu Mashiach

Today's *daf* is 95, and we are picking up at the bottom of 94b, in the middle of the *aggadetot* concerning *Chizkiyahu HaMelech* and the well-known teaching that he might have been the *Mashiach* had he only sung *shira*. The *Gemara* then raises the possibility that there may have been other reasons, known only to God, why he was not the *Mashiach*. What follows is the *Gemara's* own elaboration of why *Chizkiyahu* came so close to that distinction — and the answer it emphasizes is not merely that he was a righteous king, but that he returned the entire people to *Torah*. This aligns with the *Rambam's* conception of Messianic times, wherein the king *Mashiach* returns the people to righteousness, to the *mitzvot*, and to the worship of God. Seen through this lens, the *Gemara* is laying out what *Chizkiyahu HaMelech* actually accomplished: a universal return to *Torah* study. Everybody — man and woman, boy and girl — knew even the most obscure areas of *Torah*, including all of the laws of *tuma v'tahara*.

### Universal Torah Knowledge

The *Gemara* paints a remarkable picture of *Chizkiyahu's* generation. The universal mastery of *Torah* was not confined to scholars; it was a society-wide phenomenon. Even the most recondite areas of law were known by all.

### Abundance & Neglect

The *Gemara* then cites the verse (Isaiah 7:21): *v'haya bayom hahu yichye ish eglat bakar u'shtei tzon* — on that day a person will live from a single calf and two sheep. And further (Isaiah 7:23): *v'haya bayom hahu yihye kol makom asher yihye sham elef gefen b'elef kessef l'shamir v'lashayit yihye* — any place where there had been a thousand vines worth a thousand pieces of silver will be given over to the worm. At first glance this hardly sounds like a blessing. The *Gemara* explains: even though the streets were lined with gold and the vines were worth fortunes, the people simply left it all to be consumed by bugs and worms, because they were entirely absorbed in sitting in the *Beis Medrash*. They had no interest in material or monetary pursuits. The single calf and two sheep is similarly read: people were not raising whole flocks because they were wholly uninterested in material accumulation. All they were doing — and one must be careful here not to project this forward to Messianic times, since the *Gemara* is reading these verses about *Chizkiyahu's* own era — was sitting and learning *Torah*.

---

## Spoils & Acquisition

### Spoils Distribution

The *Gemara* transitions now to the aftermath of *Sancheriv's* defeat, citing the verse: *v'atshav shalchem osef hachasil* — you will gather in the booty as the gathering of the locust. The *navi* said to Israel: *isfu shalchem* — go take in the booty, strip the fallen soldiers, take in the wealth of the troops. The people asked: *livoz o lachlok* — is this to spoil freely or to distribute? *Rashi* explains: the question was whether each person could keep what he took for himself, or whether the booty had to be divided equally — or perhaps distributed to the poor. Could they simply keep it?

### Locust Metaphor

The *navi* answered: *k'osef hachasil* — like the gathering of the locust. *Mah osef hachasil kol echad v'echad l'atzmo* — every locust for itself. *Af shalchem kol echad v'echad l'atzmo* — so too with your booty, every man for himself, keep what you take.

### Ten Tribes Spoils

The people then raised a further objection: *halo mammonot shel shvatim ur'vavu* — but *Sancheriv* had exiled the ten tribes, and some of the wealth he was carrying had originally belonged to those Israelites. Could they really take what rightfully belonged to their fellow Jews, wherever they might be?

### Conquest Nullifies

The *navi* responded with the image of *geivim*: *k'meshek geivim shokek bo* — like the roar of water rushing into pools. Just as a pool of water transforms a person from *tamei* to *tahor*, so too the money of Israel that had fallen into the hands of the nations has been purified — *mityaher* — and is free to be taken.

What does this mean practically? The parenthetical note in the *Gemara* — which appears to be a later gloss, as indicated by its placement in parentheses — invokes *Rav Papa's* principle: *Ammon u'Moav ki'aharu b'Sichon*. The lands of *Ammon* and *Moav* could not ordinarily be taken by Israel. Yet once *Sichon* had conquered them, those lands were no longer considered lands of *Ammon* and *Moav* — they became *Sichon's* lands, and Israel could take them. This is how nations always acquire territory: by conquest. Once a conquering army takes over, the land stops belonging to the original nation.

### Yeush & Property

The principle here is not simply that a non-Jew taking from a Jew automatically severs the Jew's ownership. The *Gemara* in *Bava Kamma* makes clear that normal laws of property ownership apply regardless of who is doing the taking. If a non-Jew steals something from a Jew, the original owner remains the owner unless certain conditions are met — a combination of *yeush* (the owner's relinquishment of hope of recovering the item) and *shinui reshus* (a change of legal domain). The same analysis applies whether the thief is Jewish or not.

The specific context that does sever ownership is when property is taken by a conquering army or by a *sikarikon* — a strongman operating entirely outside the law — from whom there is genuinely no legal recourse. In that situation the reality is so total, the loss so complete, that one truly stops owning the property. A prayer said on behalf of recovering it would be a *brachah levatalah*. The point the *Gemara* is making, then, is not narrowly about non-Jews taking from Jews; it applies equally to nations taking from nations. Here, once *Sancheriv* conquered and carried off the wealth of the ten tribes, those tribes lost their monetary claims, and Israel could legitimately take it.

---

## Sancheriv's Campaign

### Ten Stages Listed

*Amar Rav Huna eser masa'ot nasa Sancheriv b'oso hayom* — Rav Huna teaches that on the very day *Sancheriv* was approaching *Yerushalayim* to lay siege to it, he made ten journeys. The *Gemara* then enumerates these stages based on the verses in Isaiah 10: he came to *Ayas* (one); he passed through *Migron* (two); at *Michmash* he left his weapons (three); they passed through the pass (four); they lodged at *Geva* (five); *Ramah* trembled (six); *Givas Shaul* fled (seven). Then, accounting for the *navi's* address to the Jewish people — *tzahali koleich Bas Gallim* — this is not counted as a stage; it is the prophet speaking to *Knesset Yisrael*, calling her *Bas Gallim*, daughter of those who performed *mitzvot* like the waves of the sea.

### Lion's Six Names

The *Gemara* asks: *mi dami?* — how is this consistent? When speaking of *Nevuchadnetzar*, the verse uses the word *aryeh* for lion, but here the verse uses *layish*. *Amar Rabbi Yochanan shisha shemot yesh la'ari* — Rabbi Yochanan teaches that a lion has six names: *ari*, *kfir*, *lavi*, *layish*, *shachal*, and *shachatz*. These are simply synonyms, and there is therefore no contradiction.

### Nov's Sin

*Amar Rav Huna*: the verse *od hayom b'Nov la'amod* — still this day he will stand at *Nov* — refers to the very same day on which *Sancheriv* made his ten journeys toward *Yerushalayim*. That day was the one on which punishment for the sin of *Nov* was still outstanding. *Nov ir hakohanim* had been destroyed in the days of *Shaul*, and that sin had not yet been fully accounted for. The anniversary of that destruction was the day *Sancheriv* drew close. *Oto hayom nishtayer me-avona shel Nov* — that day still carried the weight of the sin of *Nov*.

### Astrologers' Prophecy

*Amru leh Kalda'ei* — the Chaldean astrologers told *Sancheriv*: *ei azlat ha'idna yachlat lah* — if you go today, you will be victorious. *V'ei la, lo yachlat lah* — if not, not. The journey normally required ten days. *Saga b'chad yoma* — he traveled it in a single day, so intent was he on seizing the propitious moment. This is what accounts for the ten journeys of a single day: it was a ten-day march compressed into one.

### Sancheriv at Jerusalem

When *Sancheriv* arrived at *Yerushalayim*, his attendants piled up mattresses upon mattresses and raised him aloft so that he could survey the entire city. *Ki chazya, zutra b'eineih* — when he saw it, it was trivial in his eyes. He declared: *halo da hi karta d'Yerushalayim?* — is this the city of Jerusalem? *D'alah argishit kol mashiryai* — for this I have mobilized all my forces? *V'al da kavshit kol medinata* — for this I have conquered every province? *Halo hi ze'ira* — it is such a small city, *v'chalsha mikal karkei ammaya* — weaker than all the cities of the other nations that I have conquered with the strength of my hand. He stood up and shook his head in derision, waving his hand back and forth contemptuously — over the *Har HaBayit* and over the *Azarot* of *Yerushalayim*. The *Gemara's* description here is vivid and almost literary in quality; one senses it may draw on some older source.

### Postponement Decision

The astrologers urged him: *mishkei yadei ha'idna* — let us conquer it now. But precisely because *Sancheriv* had now trivialized *Yerushalayim*, he no longer felt the urgency. *Amar lehu: tamhu lemachar* — wait until tomorrow. Give yourselves a rest; we have rushed here, everyone is exhausted. This is nothing; we will deal with it tomorrow. He commanded each of his soldiers to take a stone from the city wall — *Rashi* suggests this was as a token of the imminent conquest, to throw the stones at the city on the morrow. They made camp and slept.

### Annihilation Night

Before *Sancheriv* could act on his plan, that very night: *vayehi balaylah hahu vayetzei malach Hashem vayach bemachaneh Ashur me'ah ushemonim vachamishah elef* — the angel of God went out and struck 185,000 in the Assyrian camp. *Vayashkimu vaboker vehinei kulam pegarim meitim* — when they arose in the morning, they were all dead carcasses.

### Justice & Sleep

*Amar Rav Papa*: *hainu d'amri inshi, pash dina bat dina* — that is what people say: if the judgment sleeps over, it is nullified. This aphorism is evocative of the *Sanhedrin's* own principle of *linat hadin* — the requirement that a capital case be deliberated overnight — where part of the rationale is precisely to avoid hasty execution. But here the point is the converse: by letting the opportunity sleep, *Sancheriv* discarded it. *Pash dina* — the ruling passes, the moment dissolves. If you postpone something, you lose it. Do not procrastinate.

There is a deeper dimension here as well. The description of *Sancheriv* trivializing *Yerushalayim* — seeing nothing there worth conquering — reflects the perspective of someone entirely without love for the city. For one who has no emotional connection, *Yerushalayim* is simply an unremarkable provincial town. And yet, looking at the broader narrative, the day carried within it a genuine metaphysical vulnerability for Israel — the unresolved weight of *Nov's* sin. The passage invites us to read all of these elements together as the unfolding of a divine plan: the propitious day, the rush, the trivialization, the delay, and ultimately the miraculous annihilation — all working toward a divinely orchestrated conclusion. The parallel is apt: *Haman* cast the *pur* on the day that seemed most dangerous for Israel, and that very day was turned around. Just as a parent who watches a child stumble toward punishment does not wish it, and yet the outcome is ultimately guided by a larger design.

---

## David & Nov Sin

### Yishbi & Causality

The word *Nov* having appeared, the *Gemara* now pivots to the earlier and more fundamental episode from which *Nov's* sin originated — the time of *David HaMelech*. The verse (Samuel II 21:16) reads: *v'Yishbi b'Nov asher b'yelidei haRafah* — and *Yishbi b'Nov*, who was among the descendants of *Rafah*, a Philistine giant whose spear weighed three hundred talents of copper and who was newly girded and intent on killing *David* while *David* was in the land of the *Plishtim*.

*Amar Rabbi Yehuda amar Rav*: the name *Yishbi b'Nov* means *ish sheba al iskei Nov* — a man who came on account of the affair of *Nov*. This is a striking *Gemara*. Even long before the time of *Sancheriv*, the sin of *Nov* was already being repaid — in the time of *David* himself.

*Amar lei HaKadosh Baruch Hu l'David*: God said to *David*: *ad masai yehei avon zeh tamun b'yadecha* — how long will this sin remain buried in your hands? *Al yadecha neherag Nov ir kohanim* — through you, *Nov ir kohanim* was destroyed. *David* had not personally destroyed *Nov*; he had fled there, knowing that *Shaul* was pursuing him, no doubt believing that *Shaul* would never dare destroy an entire city of *kohanim*. Nevertheless, the choice *David* made jeopardized them, and through that choice they were wiped out. The *Gemara* continues: *v'al yadecha nitrad Doeg HaEdomi* — and through you, *Doeg HaEdomi* was drawn in; *Doeg* was the one who incited *Shaul's* jealousy and carried out the slaughter. And *v'al yadecha nehergu Shaul v'shloshet banav* — through you, *Shaul* and his three sons were killed, for *Shaul's* sin of destroying *Nov* brought punishment upon him and his children.

This is genuinely troubling, and it deserves to be said plainly: *David* was the victim. *Doeg* was the instigator, *Shaul* the perpetrator. Yet the *Gemara* still says *al yadecha* — through you. Note that it does not say *mipanecha* — because of you, or that it was *David's* fault. The language is causal, not one of blame. And that itself raises a profound distinction: the difference between fault and causality. Even when one is a victim, one must anticipate the consequences of one's choices. That logic is at least intelligible when it comes to *David's* decision to shelter at *Nov* — he could have anticipated the risk he was placing that city under. It becomes far harder to understand with respect to *Doeg* and *Shaul*, who were the actual perpetrators. Perhaps the point is that there is enough in history to go around — not that *Shaul* and *Doeg* are exonerated, but that *David's* indirect role in setting in motion a chain of events is not invisible.

### David's Choice

*Birtzoncha yichlu zar'acha* — God offered *David* a choice: either your descendants will be wiped out, or you will be handed over to an enemy. *Amar lefanav: Ribbono Shel Olam, mutav emaser beyad oyev v'lo yichleh zar'i* — Master of the Universe, I would rather be handed over to the enemy than have my descendants destroyed.

### Demon Deer Trap

One day *David* went out hunting to a place called *Biza*. *Ata shatan v'idmei lei k'tavya* — the *Satan* appeared to him in the form of a deer. *David* shot an arrow but could not reach it. The deer kept drawing him further, until *Patak beih geira, v'lo mata, mashchei, ad d'amtayei l'eretz Plishtim* — he kept pursuing it until he found himself in the land of the *Plishtim*. The image is reminiscent of the arrow that fell short in the story of *David* and *Yehonatan*, though here the purpose is entrapment.

### Olive Press Miracle

When *Yishbi b'Nov* spied *David*, he recognized him: *hainu hai d'katlei le'Golyat achi* — this is the one who killed *Golyat* my brother. *Kafteih* — he bound *David* up; *kamteih* — he folded him; *otveih v'ramei tutei bei badya* — and placed him underneath an olive press to crush him to death. The image is almost comic in retrospect — rather than simply killing him, he subjects him to an elaborate contraption, reminiscent of those theatrical villains of fiction who construct elaborate death-traps rather than acting directly. A miracle intervened: *macha lei ar'a* — the ground beneath *David* sank slightly, and he was not crushed. The verse captures this: *tarchiv tza'adi tachtai* — You have broadened my steps below me; *v'lo ma'adu karsulai* — and my ankles did not slip. *Hahu yoma apanya de'ma'alei Shabta hava* — that day was *erev Shabbat*.

### Avishai's Rescue

*Avishai ben Tzeruiah* — one of *David's* generals and the brother of *Yoav ben Tzeruiah* — was that same *erev Shabbat* washing his hair, in four buckets of water, when he noticed drops of blood in the water. Some say a dove came and began flapping and moaning in distress in his presence.

*Amar*: the Jewish people are compared to a dove, as it says *kanfei yona nechpasa bakesef*. If a dove is in distress, it must represent the king of Israel. *Shma mina David malka d'Yisrael betzara* — from this I conclude that *David* is in danger. He went to *David's* home and found him gone. He then asked a *halachic* question that is itself revealing: the *Mishnah* rules that one may not ride a king's horse, sit on his throne, or use his scepter. *Besha'as hassakana mai?* — what is the law when the king is in danger? He went and posed the question to the *Beis Medrash*, and they ruled: *besha'as hassakana shapir dami* — in a time of danger, of course it is permitted. He rode *David's* mule and set out — the land foreshortening for him, as we will discuss shortly. Why specifically *David's* mule rather than a faster horse? The *Gemara* does not explain; perhaps riding the royal animal carried some practical benefit of free passage, or perhaps the episode simply reports what occurred.

On the way, *Bahadi deka masgei, chazayei l'Orpah imei d'hahu* — as he rode, he came upon *Orpah*, the mother of *Yishbi b'Nov*. *Imei d'hahu dahavas navla* — she was knitting. When she saw *Avishai* coming, understanding that he was pursuing her son, she broke off her spindle and hurled it at him, intending to kill him. She missed. She then called out to him: *Alem, ayisei li pilchi* — young man, could you bring me back my spindle? He picked it up and *patkyei beresh mocha v'katlah* — drove it into her forehead and killed her. A notable detail here is the identification of this *Orpah* with the *Orpah* of the Book of Ruth, sister-in-law to *Ruth* and thus sister-in-law to *Naomi*. The *Gemara* in *Sotah* makes this identification explicit: the mother of *Yishbi b'Nov*, and of *Golyat*, was none other than that same *Orpah* — an inglorious end for a figure who also appears in a context of loyalty and kindness.

### Bound Prisoner

*Kad chazei Yishbi b'Nov Avishai*: when *Yishbi b'Nov* saw *Avishai* approaching, he calculated that now there were two against one. Despite the fact that *David* was still bound, he did not trust the odds. So *patkeih l'David l'eila* — he hurled *David* upward into the air, and *v'datz leh romchei* — thrust his spear below so that *David* would fall directly onto it. The *Gemara* notes that this could raise the question from earlier in *Sanhedrin* as to whether one who merely throws another upward is liable as a *rotzeach* if the victim falls onto a weapon. *Neipul v'niktal* — let him fall and be killed.

### Hovering Between

*Amar Avishai shem* — *Avishai* invoked one of the divine names, *u'kmei l'David bein shamaya l'ara* — and this stopped *David's* fall, leaving him hovering between heaven and earth. One might ask: why could *David* not invoke the divine name himself? The *Gemara* answers with one of its most resonant principles: *ein chavush matir atzmo mi-beis ha-asurim* — a bound prisoner cannot free himself from prison. *Rashi* explains: *ein da'ato mechuvvenet lomar ha-shem* — his mind is not properly focused to invoke the name. There is an unmistakably psychological dimension to this line. When one is the one in crisis, in anguish, the very mental state that the crisis creates prevents one from finding one's own way out. Under other circumstances, that same person might have helped another in identical danger. But for oneself, in one's own distress, the capacity is not there.

### Reverse Prayer

*Amar Avishai* to *David* as he hovered: *mai ba'at hacha?* — what are you doing here? How did this happen? *David* told him: this is what God had said to me, and this is how I had responded — I chose to be handed over to the enemy rather than have my descendants destroyed.

*Amar lei Avishai: hafich tzlutach* — reverse your prayer. Ask that your descendants be destroyed instead. *Dar brich kira lizbun v'at lo titzta'er* — let your grandson sell wax for a living, but let yourself not be in pain. The *Gemara* cites this as an apparently common folk expression: let your grandchildren be beggars as long as you yourself live comfortably. *Avishai* was giving *David* practical advice to revise his prayer. Whether the *Gemara* is endorsing this view or merely reporting what *Avishai* counseled is unclear, and the advice sits uncomfortably given *David's* characteristic acceptance of responsibility. *David* responded: *ee hachi, sayyatan* — if that is what you counsel, then help me — either to descend safely or to pray the reverse prayer. *Hainu d'ichtiv: vayazor lo Avishai ben Tzeruiah* — and that is the verse: *Avishai ben Tzeruiah* came to *David's* aid. *Rav Yehuda amar Rav: she'azro bi-tfilah* — he assisted him through prayer, reversing the original petition.

*Amar Avishai shem* — *Avishai* then invoked another divine name — *v'achsei* — and brought *David* all the way down safely to the ground, away from the spear.

### Taunting Strategy

Even after *David* was rescued, *Yishbi b'Nov* continued pursuing both of them. They came first to a place called *Kubi*, where they considered making a stand. They came then to *Bei Trei*, where they said: *bitrei guryan katlohu l'arye* — can the two of us kill the lion? The reading *b'timyah* — in astonishment rather than resolve — may actually be the correct one: they were not certain they could overcome him by force alone. So instead they taunted him.

### Mother's Memory

*Amrei lei: zil ishtakach l'Orpah imach bekivra* — go find your mother in the grave. *Ki idkaru lei shma d'imeih, kechesh cheileih* — when they mentioned his mother's name, his strength left him, *v'katlohu* — and they were able to kill him. The mention of his mother — whose inglorious death *Avishai* had brought about on the road — was the instrument that broke him.

### Oath of Protection

*Az nishbe'u anshei David lo leimor lo teitzei od itanu lamilchama v'lo techabeh et ner Yisrael* — then *David's* men made him swear that he would no longer go out to war with them. He was too precious, the light of Israel, and they had come too close to losing him.

---

## Land Jumping

### Eliezer's Journey

*Tanu rabanan: lishlosha kaftza lahem ha'aretz* — the *Rabbanan* taught that the land foreshortened its journey for three righteous figures. The first is *Eliezer eved Avraham*: *d'ichtiv va'avo hayom el ha'ayin* — I came today to the wellspring — demonstrating that the very day he departed he had already arrived at his destination in *Charan* to find a wife for *Yitzchak*.

### Avishai's Speed

*Avishai ben Tzeruiah ha d'amran* — *Avishai ben Tzeruiah* we have just discussed. Despite the vast distance between *Yerushalayim* and *Eretz Plishtim*, he traversed it with miraculous speed on *David's* mule. It is notable that *Sancheriv*, who also had a foreshortened journey — traveling ten days' worth of road in a single day — is not included in this list of three, though the *Gemara* had mentioned him just before.

### Jacob's Return

The third is *Yaakov Avinu*: *d'ichtiv vayeitzei Yaakov miBe'er Sheva vayelech Charanah* — and *Yaakov* left *Be'er Sheva* and went to *Charan* — and immediately: *vayifga bamakom* — he encountered the place. The juxtaposition implies that the moment he left *Be'er Sheva* he had already arrived at *Charan*. But then *Beis El* enters the picture. *Ki mata l'Charan, amar: efshar avarti al makom shehitpalelu bo avotai va'ani lo hitpalalti bo?* — when he came to *Charan*, he thought: is it possible that I passed by the place where my forefathers prayed and I did not pray there? The framing is striking: it is not primarily about the place's inherent sanctity, but about the practice of the *avot* — he wants to follow in their custom.

*Ba'ei l'mehadar* — he decided to return. *Keivan d'hirher bedaiteih l'mehadar, kaftza lei ar'a, miyad vayifga bamakom* — the moment he formed the intention to return, the land jumped, and he was immediately at *Beis El*. So the first *kfitzat haderech* was from *Be'er Sheva* to *Charan*, and the second was the return to *Beis El*.

*Davar acher: ein pegia ela tefila* — and additionally, the word *pegia* connotes prayer, as in *v'al tifga bi* — do not intercede with me. This dovetails naturally with the *Gemara's* point, since the entire purpose of *Yaakov's* return was to pray — so *vayifga bamakom* signifies both his encounter with the place and his prayer there. The *Gemara* also identifies this as the basis for *Yaakov* being the *mataken* of *tefillat arvit*.

*Vayalon sham ki va hashemesh* — and he slept there because the sun had set. *Rashi* reads the verse to indicate that the sun set suddenly and unexpectedly — it is not *vayavo hashemesh vayalon sham* (the sun came and he slept) but *vayalon sham ki va hashemesh* (he slept because the sun had come) — the sequence implies that the sunset was unexpected, as though the sun had set prematurely.

*Amar HaKadosh Baruch Hu: tzaddik zeh ba l'veis maloni v'yiftar belo linah?* — this righteous one has come to My inn and shall he leave without sleeping over? The image of God calling *Beis El* His inn is charged with meaning. There is also a parallel to the law that one who brings a *korban* and whose *tefilla* or *paschal* offering is involved must sleep over and not rush away. The narrative itself shifts: it begins with *Yaakov's* motivation — following the practice of his forefathers — and then pivots to God's perspective — *My house, you've arrived, stay.* From *Yaakov's* angle, the place is where the *avot* prayed; from God's angle, it is His home and *Yaakov* is His guest.

*Miyad ba hashemesh* — so too the sun set before its time. The *Gemara* then notes the parallel: *vayizrach lo hashemesh v'hu tzoleia al yereicho* — the sun shone for him after his struggle with the angel. *V'chi lo bilvad zaracha? V'halo l'chol ha'olam kulam zaracha?* — did the sun shine for him alone? Does it not shine for everyone? *Ella amar Rabbi Yitzchak: shemesh sheba'ah ba'avuro zaracha ba'avuro* — the same sun that had set for him when he returned to pray at *Beis El*, that same sun shone for him again after his nightlong struggle with the angel.

The *Gemara* then addresses whether *David's* descendants were in fact destroyed, given that his original prayer was reversed. The verse (Kings II 11:1) says: *v'Asalya em Achazyahu ra'asah ki mes benah vatakam vatabad et kol zera hamamlacha* — *Atalya* saw that her son had died and she rose and destroyed the entire royal family. Yet *va'ishtayeir Yoash* — *Yoash* was left over and became the next king, from whom further descendants came. *Hacha nami ishtayeir Avyasar* — similarly, from *Nov ir hakohanim*, one person escaped: *v'yimaleit ben echad l'Achimelech ben Achituv u'shmo Avyasar*. *Amar Rav Yehuda Amar Rav: v'ilmalei lo nishayar Avyasar l'Achimelech ben Achituv, lo nishayar mizar'o shel David afilu pali* — had *Avyasar* not survived from *Nov*, not a single remnant of *David's* line would have remained, and there would have been no *Malchei Yehuda* and no *Mashiach*. The precariousness of history, viewed through the *Gemara's* lens, is deeply unsettling: entire chains of consequence, the continuation of the messianic line, hanging by the survival of a single individual.

---

## Army Composition

### Officer Breakdown

*Amar Rav Yehuda Amar Rav*: *ba'aleihem Sancheriv harasha b'arba'im vachamishah elef ish* — *Sancheriv* came against them with 45,000 men who were *bnei melachim*, princes, *yoshvim bikronot shel zahav* — seated in golden covered wagons — accompanied by *shiglonot v'zonot*, queens and concubines. A good point arises here: the word *shiglonot* is one of those words in *Tanach* that is customarily read as *tishkavena* rather than as written, since the written form implies something unseemly; it is noteworthy that it appears here juxtaposed with *zonot*. Presumably *Rashi* renders it as *princesses*, though the parallel to *zonot* may suggest something closer to concubines.

### Total Army Size

Then *ushmonim elef giborim levushei shiryon klipa* — 80,000 valorous soldiers clad in plate armor. *Uvshishim elef achuzei cherev ratzim lefanav* — and 60,000 sword-fighters running before him. The arithmetic: 45,000 plus 80,000 plus 60,000 equals 185,000 — precisely the number the verse records as having been slain by the angel. But this was not *Sancheriv's* entire army; these were the elite, the *rashei gavsot*. *V'hashar parashim v'agronim v'raglim* — the rest were cavalry, supply troops, and infantry.

The *Gemara* then notes that a comparable force came against *Avraham* when he fought the four kings, and that the same number will come in the war of *Gog uMagog* — a connection that reinforces the *Gemara's* earlier thread: *Chizkiyahu*, who was nearly the *Mashiach*, anticipates Messianic times, and the parallels with *Avraham* as well as with the future war of *Gog uMagog* reflect the principle of *ma'aseh avot siman l'banim*.

### Officers Distinction

*U'v'matnita tana*: a *Baraita* teaches that the length of *Sancheriv's* camp was 400 parasangs, and the total number of his troops was 260 myriads (*ribuv*) of thousands (*alafim*) minus one. The *Gemara* asks whether the "minus one" refers to one myriad, one thousand, one hundred, or one individual — and leaves the question as *teyku*. The figure, depending on how it is read, ranges from roughly two and a half million to two billion six hundred million — numbers that exceed even the world population of that era, and which the *Gemara* itself does not attempt to rationalize. What it does convey is the sheer magnitude of the force bearing down on *Yerushalayim*.

The *Baraita* also describes the army's passage through a river: the first wave had to swim through (*besichi*), so deep was the water. So many men then passed through that the middle group could walk with the water only up to their necks — *ad tzavar yagia*. By the time the last group crossed, the river had been so depleted that they walked on dry land and there was no water left in the river to drink, requiring water to be brought from elsewhere — *ani karti v'shatiti mayim*.

### Annihilation Methods

The *Gemara* then asks: *bameh hikam?* — with what did the angel strike them? Various *Amoraim* offer different readings.

*Rabbi Eliezer omer*: *beyad hikam* — with a hand. *Shene'emar vayar Yisrael et hayad hagedolah* — the same great hand that struck *Paroh* and Egypt was the hand that would pay back *Sancheriv*.

*Rabbi Yehoshua omer*: *be'etzba hikam* — only with a finger. *Shene'emar vayomru hachartumim el Paroh etzba Elokim hi* — it is the finger of God, says the verse by *Paroh*; that same finger would pay back *Sancheriv*.

*Rabbi Eliezer beno shel Rabbi Yossi HaGlili omer*: God said to *Gavriel*: *magalecha metushah?* — is your scythe sharpened? *Gavriel* responded: *Ribbono Shel Olam, metushah v'omedet misheshet yemei vereishit* — it has been sharpened and standing ready since the six days of creation. The point here is not merely that the same power that punished *Paroh* punished *Sancheriv*, but that the very instrument was prepared at the dawn of creation — it was always part of the plan.

*Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai omer*: that was the season when fruits were ripening, and *Gavriel's* assigned role was to oversee that ripening. God said to him: *keshetehei yotzei levashel peirot, hizakek lahem* — when you go out to ripen the fruits, take care of *Sancheriv's* troops along the way. *Shene'emar midei avro yikach etchem* — as he passes through, he will take you. *Ki vaboker vaboker ya'avor bayom uvalailah* — he passes by day and by night. *Amar Rav Papa: hainu d'amri inshi: agav urchach leba'al devavach ishtama* — that is what people say: along your way, make yourself known to your enemy. On your way past, settle an account.

One might raise the question from elsewhere that a *malach* is not supposed to perform two tasks simultaneously. The *Gemara* does not address this directly here.

*V'yesh omrim*: *bechotmam nashaf bahem u'metu* — God blew into their nostrils and they died. *Shene'emar v'gam nashaf bahem vayivashu* — and they dried up.

*Rabbi Yirmeyah bar Abba amar*: *kapayim sipek lahem* — God clapped His palms, producing something like a great sonic concussion. *Shene'emar vegam ani akeh chapi el kapi vahanichoti chamati* — I will strike palm against palm and My fury will abate.

### Angels' Song

*Rabbi Yitzchak amar*: *oznayim gilah lahem* — God made their ears hear. *V'sham'u shirah mipi chayot u'metu* — they heard the *shira* sung by the heavenly *chayot*, and they died. This is the most striking opinion among those offered. Rather than a violent image — a divine hand, a finger, a blade — the troops were annihilated by hearing something beautiful. Their souls, confronted with the transcendent, departed. It is a very different conception of divine power. And it is worth noting that this ties back to the *shira* theme that runs throughout the *daf*: *Chizkiyahu* did not sing *shira*; the land sang *shira* in his place; *Nevuchadnetzar* sought to humiliate the *shirot* of *David HaMelech*; and now here, the angels' *shira* becomes itself the instrument of divine retribution against *Sancheriv's* host.

### Survivor Counts

How many survived? *Rava amar asara* — Rava says ten, based on the verse *ushear etz yaaro mispar yihyu v'naar yichtivem* — the remnant will be so few that a young lad could write down their number. How many can a lad write? Ten — the number of his fingers, or alternatively the number *yud* formed by a single drop of ink.

*Shmuel amar tisha* — nine, from the verse about the remnant of the olive-picking: *shnayim u'shlosha gargarim berosh amir v'arba'a v'chamisha biseifia* — two and three at the top, four and five at the branches: 2 plus 3 is 5, plus 4 plus 5 is 9.

*Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi amar arba'a asar* — fourteen, because adding all terms: 2 plus 3 plus 4 plus 5 equals 14.

### Five Survivors

*Rabbi Yochanan amar chamisha* — five. These five were: *Sancheriv u'shnei banav* — *Sancheriv* and his two sons (who, as already cited, ultimately killed him in the house of his god *Nisroch*) — and *Nevuchadnetzar v'Nevuzaradan*. The implication is sobering: fine, *Sancheriv's* army was annihilated; but *Nevuchadnetzar* and his general *Nevuzaradan* walk away, and they will return for *Yerushalayim*.

### Angel Recognition

*Nevuchadnetzar d'chtiv* — the textual proof for *Nevuchadnetzar* being among the survivors comes from the Book of *Daniel*, where *Nevuchadnetzar*, upon seeing the four figures in the furnace, declares that the fourth *damei l'var elohin* — resembles a divine being, an angel. How did *Nevuchadnetzar* know what an angel looked like? *V'ee lav d'chaza* — if he had not seen one before, *mena hava yada* — how would he have known? The answer is that he had seen the destroying angel at *Sancheriv's* camp, and that encounter remained with him. The five survivors carried with them the memory — and the consequences — of what they had witnessed.

We will stop here and continue tomorrow.
