# Sanhedrin 96

## Sennacherib's Defeat

### Divine Razor

The *gemara* opens with a statement of Rabbi Abahu: *ilmalei mikra katuv iy efshar le'omro* — were it not that the verse was written, it would be nearly heretical to say the following. The verse in question is from Yeshayahu: *bayom hahu yigalach Hashem betaar hasechira be'evrei nahar bimelech Ashur et harosh use'ar haraglayim vegam et hazakan tispeh* — on that day God will shave with the hired razor, by way of the river, with the king of Assyria, the head and the hair of the legs, and even the beard He will destroy. The verse, taken plainly, depicts God Himself administering a shave to Sennacherib. Because such an anthropomorphic image might seem irreverent, Rabbi Abahu prefaces it with his caveat. The *gemara* then proceeds to narrate how this verse was actually fulfilled.

### God as Old Man

*Ata Kudsha Brich Hu ve'idmi lei k'gavra saba* — God came and appeared to Sennacherib in the form of an old man. The disguised figure said to him: you have been traveling throughout all the lands of the east and the west, you have brought with you the sons of all the other kings — all those princes who accompanied your great army — *vekataltinhu*, and you got them all killed. *Mai amrat lehu* — what are you going to say to these kings when they ask where their children are? Sennacherib replied that this was precisely his own fear — *hahu gavra bahu pachta nami yasiv*, that very thing is what he himself was afraid of. He then asked the disguised figure: *heichi naavid* — what should I do? The answer came: *zil veshani nafshech* — go and disguise yourself.

### Scissors Quest

The question then arose: *b'mai eshani* — how exactly should he disguise himself? The old man replied: go fetch me a *mispara*, a scissors, and I will give you a haircut. Sennacherib asked where he might obtain scissors. He was directed to a certain house. When he arrived, he found the heavenly angels there, appearing to him as ordinary men, grinding *kashisa* — palm kernels. Sennacherib asked if he could borrow a scissors. The men replied: *tchon chad giyura dekashisa u'niten lach* — grind a measure of these seeds for us and we will give it to you. So Sennacherib — once the conqueror of nations — ground a measure of palm kernels, and they gave him the scissors. The episode is unmistakably humiliating, evoking something of the degradation visited upon Samson at the millstone, though the precise moral lesson of the narrative remains somewhat elusive.

### Beard on Fire

As Sennacherib was making his way back to the old man with the scissors, it had grown dark. The old man said he could not cut hair in the dark — *zil aytei nura*, go bring fire. Sennacherib went and obtained a light. *Bahadei dekanafach leih itli beih nura bedikneih* — as he was blowing on the flame to keep it going, the fire caught his beard. *Azal gazyah lereisheih vedikneih* — he then shaved off his own hair and beard so that his whole face would not catch fire. Rather than God performing the shave, Sennacherib ended up doing it himself.

*Amru hainu dechsiv vegam et hazakan tispeh* — this, says the *gemara*, is the fulfillment of the verse: the beard will be *destroyed*, not merely shaved, for it was burned away by fire. The distinction in language — *tispeh*, destruction, rather than *yigalach*, shaving — is now explained by the manner in which it came to pass.

### Rav Papa's Saying

Rav Papa appends a popular saying: *hainu de'amri inshi gerirta l'arma'ah shapir leih* — this is why people say, singe an Aramean and it will be good for him. *Itli leih nura bedikneih velo shachach chucha mineih* — if his beard catches fire, his smile of relief will not leave his face, so grateful is he for the result. The precise significance of this folk saying in context is admittedly opaque.

### Recognition & Vow

*Azal ashchach dapa miteivuta deNoach* — Sennacherib, now making his way back to Assyria, found a plank from Noah's ark. *Amar hainu elaha raba deshizbeih leNoach mitufana* — he recognized it as belonging to the great God who had saved Noah from the flood. This recognition — perhaps drawing on the flood narratives preserved among ancient nations — prompted him to realize he had been fighting against the God of Israel. He then said: *ei azilna vehu gavra umatzlach* — if I return to my country and succeed, *mekarvna lehu letrin benohi kaimach* — I will offer my two sons as sacrifices before You.

### Sons Kill Father

*Shamu benohi vekatluhu* — his sons heard this vow and killed him. This provides the backstory to what the *pesukim* record explicitly: *vayehi hu mishtachaveh beit nisroch elohav veAdrammech veSharezer benohi hikuhu bacharev* — and it was as he was bowing down in the house of his god Nisroch that Adrammelech and Sharezer his sons struck him with the sword.

---

## Historical Cycles

### Angel Layla

With the story of Sennacherib's destruction now complete, the *gemara* draws a broader observation about the cyclical nature of Jewish history. The same heavenly forces that intervened against Sennacherib's armies echo the intervention on behalf of Abraham against the four kings, and point forward to the future wars of *Gog uMagog*. The *gemara* turns to the verse: *Vayechalek Aleihem Layla* — and the night divided against them, referring to Abraham's pursuit of the kings who had captured Lot.

Rabbi Yochanan teaches: *oto malach shenizdamen lo le-Avraham Layla shemo* — the angel who came to Abraham's assistance was named *Layla*, Night. The verse's word *layla* is therefore to be read not merely as the time of night but as the name of the angel who assisted. The proof is from a verse in Iyyov: *ve-ha-layla amar hora gaver* — and the Night said, a man has been conceived — where Night is personified and speaks, indicating it represents an angelic being.

### Night Fights

Rabbi Yitzchak Nafcha offers a different reading. *She-asah imo ma'aseh layla* — rather than an angel named Night, the *layla* in Abraham's verse means that the night itself fought for him, just as we find by another episode: *Min ha-shamayim nilchamu ha-kochavim mi-mesilotam nilchamu im Sisra* — from the heavens the stars fought from their paths against Sisera. There too celestial forces — elements of the night sky — intervened against an enemy of Israel.

Reish Lakish notes a parallel with the splitting of the sea, where *velo karav zeh el zeh kol ha-layla* — the Egyptians and Israel did not approach one another throughout the night, and the destruction came at the close of the night.

*Tava de-Nafcha mi-bar Nafcha* — Reish Lakish then remarks that the explanation of Rabbi Yitzchak Nafcha is better than that of Rabbi Yochanan, who is himself known as *bar Nafcha*. The second interpretation is preferable: it is not that some angel bears the name Night, but that the stars and forces of the night sky came to fight.

### Abraham at Dan

*Vayirdof ad Dan* — and he chased them until Dan, in the north of the Land of Israel. Rabbi Yochanan teaches: *keivan sheba oto tzaddik ad Dan tashish kocho* — when that righteous man, Abraham, reached Dan, his strength ebbed and he was unable to continue the pursuit. Why? *Ra'ah benei banav she-atidin la'avod avodah zarah be-Dan* — he saw prophetically that his descendants would one day worship *avodah zarah* in Dan, where Jeroboam would place one of the golden calves: *vayaseim et ha-echad be-Veit El ve-et ha-echad natan be-Dan*. The future sin of his descendants sapped Abraham's strength at that very location.

### Nebuchadnezzar at Dan

*Ve-af oto rasha lo nitgaber ad she-higia le-Dan* — and similarly, that wicked one, Nebuchadnezzar, did not gain his full strength until he reached Dan, because he was coming to punish Israel for that very sin. *Shene'emar mi-Dan nishma nachrat susav* — as it is written, from Dan can be heard the snorting of his horses. All of Jewish history is interconnected: the strength Abraham lost at Dan is the very strength that Nebuchadnezzar gained there.

The *gemara* then introduces a statement attributed to Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira of Nitzivin, or alternatively Rabbi Yehoshua ben Lakish, transmitted by Rabbi Zeira: *hizaheru be-zaken she-shachach talmudo machamat onso* — be careful to continue showing respect to an elder scholar who has forgotten his learning due to old age and through no fault of his own. And equally: *ve-hizaheru bi-venei amei ha-aretz she-mehen tetzei Torah* — be careful regarding the children of the unlearned, for from them Torah may emerge.

The placement of this teaching at this juncture will become clear from the passage that follows, which the *gemara* now turns to.

---

## Jeremiah's Complaint

### Racer Parable

*Tzadik atah Hashem ki ariv eilecha ach mishpatim adaber otach madua derech reshaim tzalcha shalu kol bogdei vaged* — Righteous are You, O God, even when I contend with You; but I must speak justice with You: why does the path of the wicked succeed, why do all those who rebel against You have peace? *Netatam gam shorashu yelechu gam asu peri* — You have planted them and they have taken root, they have gone on and been fruitful. This is Jeremiah's complaint, read through the lens of the story of Nebuchadnezzar, who has just been shown gaining his strength at Dan. Why was Nebuchadnezzar permitted to succeed?

*Ma ahadru lei* — what did they respond to him? The answer comes from the very next verse: *ki et raglim ratzta vayelauch veeich titchareh et hasusim uve-eretz shalom atah voteiach veeich taaseh bigon ha-Yarden* — because you have run against foot-racers and they have wearied you, how do you think you can compete against horses? And in a land of peace you are confident — how much more will you struggle at the swelling of the Jordan?

The *gemara* offers a parable. A man boasted that he could run three *parsa'ot* against horses, even through a swamp. A foot-racer challenged him. They ran merely three *milin* on dry land — a quarter of the claimed distance — and the boaster grew weary. *Umah lifnei ragli kach lifnei susim al achat kama vechama* — if this is how you fare against a foot-racer, how much more would you lose against horses? *Umah gimmel milin kach gimmel parsaot al achat kama vechama* — if three *milin* weary you, how much more three *parsa'ot*? *Umah bayabasha kach bein bitzei hamayim al achat kama vechama* — and if dry land undoes you, how much worse through a swamp?

### Four Steps Reward

*Af atah umah bishchar daled pesiot sheshilamti lo leoto rasha sheratz achar kevodi* — and so too with you, Jeremiah: if merely for the reward of four steps that this wicked man ran in My honor, I am granting him this power — that he becomes the instrument of Jerusalem's destruction — imagine what the reward will be for those who truly served Me. Note that it should be said that a marginal note in the *gemara* indicates that the *Midrash* and the *Yalkut* read three steps rather than four, which would align with the three *parsa'ot* of the parable.

The destruction of Jerusalem is not the *reason* Jerusalem is destroyed — that is the sins of Israel. But someone had to serve as the instrument, and Nebuchadnezzar was selected for that role as a reward for this act of honor toward God. Even for so small a thing, this is what he receives.

### Patriarchs' Reward

*Kesheni meshalem sachar le-Avraham Yitzchak ve-Yaakov sheratzu lefanai k'susim al achat kama vekama* — when I eventually get around to rewarding Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, who ran before Me like horses, their reward will be incomparably greater. The argument, then, is one of proportionality. If the tiny and almost incidental act of Nebuchadnezzar earns him such power, consider what the accumulated merit of the patriarchs will ultimately yield.

### Jeremiah Consoled

*V'linviim nishbar libi b'kirbi* — and for the prophets — which Rashi understands here as a reference to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob — my heart was broken within me, I could not perceive where their ultimate reward would come from. *V'rachafu kol atzmotai hayiti k'ish shikkor v'kagever avru yayin* — all my bones trembled, I was like a drunken man, like a man overcome by wine. *Mipnei Hashem umipnei divrei kodsho* — because of God and because of His holy words. After God's explanation, Jeremiah is consoled: the very scale of Nebuchadnezzar's reward for so little is itself a guarantee of the infinitely greater reward that awaits those who truly served God.

---

## Four Steps Story

### Baladan's Letter

*Hani arba pisiot mai* — but what exactly are these four steps? The *gemara* now explains. *Ba'eis hi shalach Merodach Baladan ben Baladan Melech Bavel sefarim* — at that time Merodach Baladan the son of Baladan, king of Babylonia, sent letters and a gift to Hezekiah when he heard that Hezekiah had recovered from his illness. Why was this worthy of such a diplomatic gesture? *Mishum d'chala Chizkiyahu vayechazak* — merely because a king was sick and recovered? The *gemara* explains that another verse in Divrei Hayamim adds: *lidrosh hamofes asher haya ba'aretz* — because a wonder had been performed in the land.

### Sun Clock Wonder

What was the wonder? Rabbi Yochanan explains: *oso hayom shemeis bo Achaz shti sha'os haya* — on the day that Achaz, the wicked father of Hezekiah, died, the sun set ten hours early; the day had only two hours of light. God did this so that people would not come out to eulogize the wicked king and make a spectacle of his funeral. Then, *v'ki chala Chizkiyahu v'ispach hadrinu Kudsha Brich Hu l'hanach eser sha'ei* — when Hezekiah fell ill and recovered, God extended the day by ten hours. Ten hours taken away for the father, ten hours restored for the son.

The source is explicit: *Hineni meshiv tzel hama'alos asher yarda b'ma'alos Achaz bashemesh achornit eser ma'alos* — behold I will return the shadow of the sun clock of Achaz backward ten units. *Vatishev hashemesh eser ma'alos b'ma'alos asher yorada* — and the sun returned ten gradations on the steps where it had descended.

When Baladan heard of this, he said: *ika gavra ki hai velo be'ina leshadurei lei shalma* — there is such a great man, that the sun itself reversed for him, and I have not sent him greetings? He instructed his scribes: write to Shalma Lemalka Chizkiyah — peace to King Hezekiah; *Shalma Lekarta De'yerushalayim* — peace to the city of Jerusalem; *Shalma Le'elaha Raba* — peace to the great God.

### Nebuchadnezzar Corrects

*Nevuchadnetzar Safra De'baladan Hava* — Nebuchadnezzar was Baladan's scribe at the time. *Hahi sha'ata lo hava hatam* — at that moment he was not present, having been sent on some errand. When he returned and heard what had been written, he said: *karitu lei Elaha Raba vekatvitu lei levasof* — you called their God the great God, and you put God at the end of the letter? If you truly acknowledge Him as great, He comes first — before Jerusalem, and certainly before Hezekiah. He directed them to rewrite the letter: *Shalma Le'elaha Raba, Shalma Lekarta De'yerushalayim, Shalma Lemalka Chizkiyah* — God first, then His city, then the king.

The scribes responded with a famous phrase: *karyana de'igarta ihu leihavei parvanka* — let the one who reads the proclamation be the one to execute it. You want the letter rewritten your way? You go deliver it yourself.

### Four Steps Run

*Rahat batrei karahat arba pesiyot* — Nebuchadnezzar ran after the messengers who had already been dispatched. He ran four steps — or, according to the *Midrash* and *Yalkut*, three steps — to catch up with them and redirect the letter. These are the four steps he ran in God's honor.

### Gabriel Stops Him

*Ata Gavriel ve'ukmei* — the angel Gabriel came and stopped him after those four steps. Rabbi Yochanan teaches: *ilmale ba Gavriel ve'he'emido lo hava takana lesonayehem shel Yisrael* — had Gabriel not come and halted him precisely there, there would have been no remedy for Israel. If Nebuchadnezzar had been permitted to run further — a greater distance, a more sustained effort in God's honor — his reward would have been correspondingly greater and the destruction he could have wrought correspondingly worse. Gabriel therefore stopped him at exactly four steps, limiting both his merit and the scope of what he would be empowered to do.

Here a brief but memorable digression: on the day of the shiur the teacher had been overcharged fifty cents at a sidewalk fruit stand. A block and a half away, the vendor came running after him to return the change — a gesture reminiscent of stories told about the *Chafetz Chaim*. The relevance, as Rashi will soon make explicit, is the theme of *benei am ha-aretz* and the importance of not underestimating anyone's potential for honesty and greatness.

### Baladan's Name

*Mai Baladan ben Baladan* — why does Merodach Baladan share his father's name? The *gemara* explains: *Baladan malka hava v'ishtanei apay ve'hava ke'kalba* — Baladan was king, but his face changed and came to resemble a dog. His son took over the kingship. *Ki hava kasiv hava kasiv shemei u'shemei de'avuha* — whenever the son would write his own name, he would include his father's name alongside it, styling himself Baladan son of Baladan, as if his father were still reigning, in order to honor him. This fulfills the verse: *ben yechabeid av v'eved adonav* — a son honors his father and a servant his master.

### Son Honors Father

The second part of that verse — *v'eved adonav* — is illustrated by Nebuzaradan. The relevant verse reads: *u'vachodesh hachamishi b'asor lachodesh bishnas tsha esrei shana l'melech Nevuchadnezzar melech Bavel ba Nevuzaradan rav tabachim lifnei melech Bavel b'Yerushalayim* — in the fifth month, on the tenth of the month, in the nineteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylonia, Nebuzaradan the chief slaughterer came before the king of Babylonia in Jerusalem.

But this raises an obvious question: *u'mi salik Nevuchadnezzar l'Yerushalayim* — since when was Nebuchadnezzar in Jerusalem? The verse elsewhere records that Tzidkiyahu was brought to Nebuchadnezzar in *Rivlah* — which Rabbi Abahu identifies as Antioch — clearly outside the Land of Israel. Rav Chisda and Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avdimi offer two resolutions. One holds that Nebuzaradan had the image of Nebuchadnezzar engraved on his chariot — *dmus dyukno hayesa chakuka* — so that wherever he went, it was as though Nebuchadnezzar were present. The other holds that *eimateih yetirah hayetah lo mimenu* — Nebuzaradan had such intense awe of Nebuchadnezzar that he always felt his master's presence before him, *v'domeh k'mi she'omed lefanav* — as though he were perpetually standing in front of him. Either by an external symbol or through internalized reverence, the servant honored the master.

This, Rashi explains, is also the connection to the earlier teaching about the children of *amei ha-aretz*. The *gemara* will shortly note that descendants of Sennacherib and Haman sat and taught Torah. The point, as the *Maharsha* articulates it more fully, is not that one should honor those students because of their illustrious wicked ancestry, but rather that one should never give up on educating the children of bad homes. Hezekiah was the child of the wicked Achaz. The descendants of Sennacherib became *Shemayah and Avtalyon*. The message is: do not assume that a child's environment determines his fate. Teachers can influence students, and that responsibility must not be abandoned.

---

## Jerusalem's Destruction

### Iron Hammers Fail

Rava teaches: *t'ein t'las me'ah kudnayasa narga d'parzla d'shalt b'parzla shad'reih Nebuchadnezzar l'Nebuzaradan* — Nebuchadnezzar sent Nebuzaradan a burden of 300 mules laden with iron hammers so sharp they could break through iron itself. *Kulyahu balyu b'chada dasha d'Yerushalayim* — and all 300 were destroyed trying to break through a single gate of Jerusalem. As the verse says, *p'sachah yachad b'khishil v'kheyalfos yahalomun* — they came at its opening with hammers and axes and could not prevail.

### Heavenly Voice

Nebuzaradan then sought to withdraw. Whether it was Nebuzaradan or Nebuchadnezzar who hesitated, the concern voiced was: *mistafina d'la l'avdu bi k'heicha d'avdu b'Sancheiriv* — I am afraid they will do to me what they did to Sennacherib. Then *n'phek kahlah* — a heavenly voice emerged and said: *sh'var bar sh'var* — leaper son of a leaper, *m'to zimna d'mikdash d'yechariv v'heichala d'yikli* — the time has come, the Temple is to be destroyed and the *heichal* to be burned. Left with a single hammer, Nebuzaradan struck the gate *b'kupah* — with the back of the hammer, not even the sharp edge — *v'iftach* — and it opened. What 300 iron hammers could not accomplish, one blow accomplished once God permitted it.

He then slaughtered his way through the city until he reached the *heichal* and set it alight. The flames rose toward heaven. *Darchu bei min shamaya* — from heaven they trampled down the fire, so that it would be unmistakably clear that this was a this-worldly destruction and not a heavenly one. As the verse says: *Gat darach Hashem livtulat bat Yehuda* — God has trampled upon the daughter of Judah as in a winepress. The trampling here refers to pressing down the flames.

### Nebuzaradan Humbled

When Nebuzaradan began to feel haughty at his conquest, *nafak bat kol ve'amra* — a heavenly voice came forth and said: *ama ketila katalt* — you have killed a nation that was already killed. *Heichala kalya kalit* — you have burned a Temple that was already burned. *Kimcha techina techinat* — you have ground flour that was already flour. Do not take any credit. The verse cited is: *Kechi rechain utchaini kemach* — take a millstone and grind flour. Prophesying the exile, the verse says *kemach* — flour — not wheat, because what you are grinding was already flour. Nebuzaradan was merely actualizing a divine decree that had already been issued.

### Zechariah's Blood

*Chaza dmyei deZecharya dehava ka ratach* — Nebuzaradan then saw the blood of Zechariah the prophet, which was still boiling. This Zechariah — a *kohen* and *navi* who had prophesied the destruction of Jerusalem and was killed by the people in the Temple courtyard for it — had blood that had never ceased to boil. This story is well known from the *Kinot* of Tisha b'Av.

Nebuzaradan asked the people what the boiling substance was. They told him it was blood of sacrifices that had been spilled. He slaughtered an animal and compared the blood — it was not the same. He threatened to flay their skin with an iron comb if they did not tell him the truth. They confessed: this was the blood of a *kohen* and prophet who prophesied against Israel about the destruction of Jerusalem, *vekatluhu* — and they killed him.

*Ana mefayisne leh* — I will appease him, said Nebuzaradan. He brought the *Rabbanan* and slaughtered them over the blood — perhaps because as leaders they bore responsibility. The blood did not stop. He brought schoolchildren — innocent, surely offering their blood should suffice. Still it did not stop. He brought the young *Kohanim*. Still it did not stop. *Ad dikatlinhu tishim ve-arba'in ribo* — until he had slaughtered 940,000 people, and still the blood boiled. Finally Nebuzaradan approached and said: *Zecharia Zecharia tovim shebahen ibadeti nicha lach de-aktilinnhu lechulhu* — Zechariah, Zechariah, I have destroyed the best of them; do you want me to kill them all? *Miyad nach* — immediately the blood stopped boiling.

### Nebuzaradan Repents

*Hirher teshuva bedatei* — Nebuzaradan began to contemplate *teshuva*. He said to himself: *mah hem she-lo ibdu ela nefesh achas kach* — these people killed only one innocent person, and look how God demanded such justice for that one life. *Hahu gavra mah tehei alei* — I, who have now killed hundreds of thousands in my misguided attempt to appease the blood — what will become of me? *Azal shadar priteita leveiteih ve-isgayar* — he sent a final testament to his house and converted.

The *gemara* then records: *Tanu Rabbanan* — the Rabbanan taught: Na'aman was a *ger toshav*, a Noahide who worshipped God but did not become part of the Jewish people. But *Nevuzaradan ger tzedek hayah* — Nebuzaradan became a full righteous convert.

### Wicked Descendants

*Mibnei banav shel Sisra limdu torah biyerushalayim* — the descendants of Sisera taught Torah in Jerusalem. *Mibnei banav shel Sancheriv limdu torah berabbim* — the descendants of Sennacherib taught Torah to the masses. *U-man ninhu Shemaya ve-Avtalyon* — who were they? Shemayah and Avtalyon. *Mibnei banav shel Haman limdu torah bivnei brak* — and the descendants of Haman taught Torah in Bnei Brak. No matter what family one comes from, the descendants can become the greatest of Torah teachers.

### Descendants Rejected

*Ve-af mibnei banav shel oso rasha bikesh hakadosh baruch hu lehachnisan tachas kanfei hashchina* — even the descendants of that wicked man, Nebuchadnezzar himself, God wished to bring under His wings. *Amru malachei hashareis lifnei hakadosh baruch hu* — but the ministering angels said before God: *Ribono shel olam mi she-hechriv es beischa ve-saraf es heichalecha tachnis attah tachas kanfei hashchina* — the one who destroyed Your house and burned Your Temple — You will bring him under Your wings?

*Hainu dechsiv ripeinu es bavel velo nispasa* — that is what is meant by the verse: I sought to heal Babylonia, but it was not healed, because ultimately the descendants of Nebuchadnezzar were not accepted. Yet the man who actually carried out the destruction — Nebuzaradan — was accepted as a convert. There is something striking in this contrast: the one who followed orders, who personally slaughtered hundreds of thousands, was accepted in *teshuva*; while the family of the one who gave the orders was not. The *gemara* leaves us to grapple with the question of who may be accepted after terrible deeds, and under what circumstances.

Ulla and Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani dispute what the verse *ripeinu es bavel velo nispasa* refers to: Ulla says it refers to Nebuchadnezzar and his descendants; Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani says it refers to the bitter rivers of Babylonia, which were never healed and whose water remained bitter.

---

## Ammon & Moab

### Bad Neighbors

*Ulla amar Ammon u'Moav shcheinei ra'im l'Yerushalayim havu* — Ulla said: Ammon and Moab were bad neighbors to Jerusalem. *Keivan d'sham'inhu l'nevi'ei d'ka mitnabu l'churbana d'Yerushalayim* — when they heard the prophets prophesying the destruction of Jerusalem, they seized the opportunity and sent word to Nebuchadnezzar: *puk v'ta* — come, this is your moment.

### Fear of Fate

Nebuchadnezzar was reluctant: *mistafina d'la l'yavdu bi ki heichi d'avdu b'kama'ei* — I am afraid they will do to me what they did to the earlier ones, meaning Sennacherib and Sisera and those who had previously tried and failed to destroy Israel.

### Messages to Attack

Ammon and Moab then sent him a series of reassurances, each quoting and interpreting verses from Mishlei. First: *ki ein ha'ish b'veito halach b'derech merachok* — God is not at home, He has gone on a long journey. The *gemara* notes that *ish* here means God, as in *Hashem ish milchama*. Nebuchadnezzar replied that God was probably nearby and would return when His people were in danger. They countered: *halach b'derech merachok* — no, He has gone on a long way journey and is not coming back soon. He replied that there were still righteous people who would cry out and bring God back. They countered with another verse: *tzror hakesef lakach b'yado* — He has taken His money with Him and is not coming back; and *kesef* means the righteous, as derived from a verse in Hoshea connecting *kesef* with the redemption from Egypt. Even the righteous have departed. Nebuchadnezzar replied that the people might repent and pray God back. They countered with a final verse: *l'yom hakisei yavo l'veito* — God has set a time for His return, and *kisei* means a designated time, as in *bakese l'yom chagenu*. He has set a time of seventy years before He returns. So for now He has entirely left and will not return for the foreseeable future. The time is set; this is the window.

### Winter & Mountains

Nebuchadnezzar raised another objection: *sitva hu v'ramia tina d'ati etaltal m'mitra* — it is winter, the rains and snow will prevent a campaign. This hesitation is itself noteworthy — there is a certain reluctance throughout this passage that may account for the *gemara*'s willingness to consider some small measure of merit even in Nebuchadnezzar. Indeed, the siege did begin in *Tevet*, in winter, as we mark on *Asara b'Tevet*. They responded: *ta shina d'tura* — come by way of the mountains, and the mountains will shelter you from the elements, as the verse says: *shalchu char moshel eretz misela midbara el har bat tziyon* — send a messenger through the rock of the wilderness to the mountain of Zion.

### Graves as Quarters

Nebuchadnezzar objected further: *ee asina leit li dukhta di asvina beh* — if I come, I will have nowhere to quarter my troops. They replied: *kivros shelahem me'ulim mi-paltrin shelcha* — their graveyards are better than your palace. As Rashi explains, the Israelites buried in caves, and those cave-graves offered more than enough space to quarter an army.

The proof-text is: *ba-et ha-hi ne'um Hashem yotziu et atzmot malchei yehuda ve'et atzmot sarav ve'et atzmot hakohanim ve'et atzmot hanevi'im ve'et atzmot yoshvei yerushalayim mikivreihem ushetachum lashemesh velayarei'ach ulechol tzeva hashamayim asher ahevum va'asher avadum va'asher halchu achareihem* — at that time God declared that they would take out the bones of the kings of Judah, and of their officers, and of the *Kohanim*, and of the prophets, and of the inhabitants of Jerusalem from their graves, and spread them before the sun and the moon and all the host of heaven — those heavenly bodies which the people had loved and served and followed. The bones are taken from the caves because Nebuchadnezzar's troops are quartered in those very caves, emptied out to make room.

# Sanhedrin 97

## Mashiach Introduction

### Opening Context

The *daf* opens two lines from the bottom of 96b, picking up from the preceding discussion of *Sancheriv* and *Nevuchadnezzar* and the fall of those empires. The connection to what follows is not entirely clear on the surface. One possible reading is that the prior sugya focused on those who came to war against Israel and inaugurated the *galus*, and the Gemara now naturally raises the next question: when will *Mashiach* come? This transition carries the discussion into a sustained and remarkable section of Sanhedrin 97 dedicated to the nature of redemption, the signs of *Mashiach*'s coming, and the dangers of trying to calculate the appointed time.

### Bar Nafli

*Amar leh Rav Nachman le-Rav Yitzchak*: Rav Nachman said to Rav Yitzchak, *mi shemi'a lakh eimat ati Bar Nafli* — have you heard when the son of Nafli will come? Rav Yitzchak responded: who is this Bar Nafli? Rav Nachman replied: *Mashiach*. Rav Yitzchak pressed further: you are calling *Mashiach* "Bar Nafli" — the son of those who have fallen? Rav Nachman confirmed this, citing the verse *ba-yom ha-hu akim et sukkat David ha-nofelet* — on that day I will raise up the fallen booth, the fallen dominion, of King David.

What is striking here is that the emphasis falls not on the glory and triumph that *Mashiach* will bring, but on the suffering and collapse from which he will emerge. The very name given to *Mashiach* — Bar Nafli, son of the fallen — frames the redemption as something that rises out of hardship and tragedy.

### R. Yochanan: Generation…

*Hachi amar Rabbi Yochanan*: Rabbi Yochanan taught that in the generation when the son of David comes, *talmidei chakhamim* will be diminished — their numbers will shrink. The rest of the people will have their eyes dimmed with anguish and mourning. Tremendous afflictions and harsh decrees will come in rapid succession — before the effects of the first tragedy have passed, the next is already on its way. This portrait of the generation preceding *Mashiach* is entirely consistent with the epithet Bar Nafli: it will be a time of great difficulty and suffering, with the redemption emerging from the depths of the fall.

## Shmita Cycle

### 7-Year Progression

*Tanu rabbanan*: our rabbis taught regarding the *shavua* — the seven-year *shmita* cycle — in which *Mashiach* will come. The progression unfolds year by year. In the first year, rain will fall on one city but not another, producing sporadic famine alongside relative plenty. In the second year, pangs of hunger will spread to everyone. By the third year, a great famine will set in — men, women, and children will die, along with the righteous and people of good deeds; the *Torah* will be forgotten by those who had learned it, overwhelmed by hunger. In the fourth year, *sova ve-eino sova* — there will be satiation but not full satiation, the pendulum beginning to swing upward. By the fifth year, great satiation returns: people will eat, drink, and rejoice, and the *Torah* will return to those who had learned it. This is the shape of a U-curve. In the sixth year, *kolot* — sounds — will come; Rashi understands these as sounds heralding the arrival of *Mashiach*. In the seventh year, great wars will take place, presumably including the war of *Gog u-Magog*. And finally, *bemotzei shvi'is*, at the conclusion of the seventh year, *ben David ba* — *Mashiach* will come.

The Gemara's description is striking enough that one who is so inclined might read it as a lens through which to view more recent history — the devastation of the third year echoing the Holocaust, in which men, women, and children perished and entire *Torah* communities were destroyed, followed by an upward arc of rebuilding. That reading remains, of course, speculative, but the structure of the passage invites it.

### Rav Yosef Challenge

Rav Yosef raised an objection: *ha kama shevi'isa dahava ken velo asa* — we have had several *shmita* cycles that seemed to follow this pattern, and yet *Mashiach* did not come.

### Abaye Response

Abaye responded by sharpening the challenge: *bishishis kolos bishvi'is milchamos mi hava* — did we actually have the sixth year with those sounds heralding *Mashiach*, and the seventh year with those specific wars? That did not happen. And moreover, *kesidran mi hava* — nor did the events occur in the precise sequence described. Some years of famine and some years of plenty, yes, but not in the exact U-shaped order laid out in the *braita*. Furthermore, even granting that such events occurred, it does not follow that when this pattern appears *Mashiach* will necessarily come — only that these are the conditions preceding his arrival.

## Generation Collapse

### Social Breakdown

*Tanya* — it was taught. Rabbi Yehuda says: in the generation when *Mashiach* comes, *batei va'ad* — houses of assembly, places where sages would gather, even the *beis midrash* — will become houses of fornication. The Galilee will be destroyed. The *Gavlan* — understood by some as the Golan or the northern region near *Har Chermon* — will be laid desolate. The people of the border cities will wander from city to city and will not be given rest or welcome, *velo yechanenu*. For those who would read this in a contemporary lens, the image of border communities evacuated and wandering from city to city, unsettled, could hardly be more vivid.

### Wisdom Spoiled

*Ve-chochmat ha-sofrim tisrach* — the wisdom of the sages will be spoiled. *Ve-yirei cheit yim'asu* — those who fear sin will be despised. Values will be turned upside down. *U-fnei ha-dor kipnei kelev* — the face of the generation will be like the face of a dog. The Maharsha explains that dogs appear friendly and loyal while concealing betrayal beneath the surface. *Ve-ha-emet ne'ederet* — and truth will be absent and lost.

### Truth Lost

The Gemara asks: what does *vatehi ha-emet ne'ederet* — truth will be lost — actually mean? *Amri d'vei Rav*: this teaches that truth will gather itself into flocks and wander away. The Maharsha explains that with respect to *Torah* and *talmidei chakhamim*, this does not mean truth will vanish utterly, but rather that those who carry truth will have to abandon the corrupt centers of civilization and seek out places of their own in which to dwell.

The verse continues: *ve-sar me-ra mishtolel* — one who turns from evil will be mocked. *Amri d'vei Rabbi Shila*: anyone who turns away from evil will be seen as a fool in the eyes of the general population. Good will be viewed as stupidity.

*Amar Rava*: from the outset, Rava says, *me-reish hava amina leit kushta b'alma* — I used to say there is no real truth in this world. This world is one of *sheker*; no one can stand fully by the principle of truth. Then one of the rabbinic students — *Rav Tavut* by name, some say *Rav Tavyomi* — told Rava the following. This student was renowned for his absolute commitment to truth: even if given all the wealth in the world, *lo hava meshanei be-dibburei* — he would not misrepresent himself or say an untruth. And he told Rava that he had once come to a certain place called *Kushta* — Truth — where no one ever fudged anything, and no one died before his ripe old age. He settled there, married a woman from the city, and had two sons.

### Rava's Story

One day his wife was washing her hair when a neighbor knocked on the door. He thought: *lav orach ar'a* — it is not appropriate to say my wife is in the bath. So he told the neighbor: she is not here. His two sons then died. The people of the city came to him and asked what had happened. He explained that he had slightly misrepresented the situation to protect his wife's privacy. They said to him: please, *puk me-asra* — leave our city, lest you incite death among our people.

This is a genuinely arresting story, and it leaves one somewhat unsettled. On the one hand, it illustrates in dramatic terms the absolute standard of truth maintained in that city, and the lethal consequence of even the smallest departure from it. On the other hand, the Gemara elsewhere permits fudging in certain contexts — such as *kevod ha-beriyot*, human dignity and privacy — which is precisely what he was trying to protect. One is left wondering what the ultimate message is: is this a story demanding the harshest possible commitment to literal truth even at the cost of another's privacy? The Gemara does not resolve the tension explicitly.

## Alt. Accounts

### R. Nehorai

*Tanya* — it was taught. Rabbi Nehorai says: in the generation when *Mashiach* comes, *nearim yalbinu pnei zekenim* — youth will cause the faces of elders to go white with embarrassment. The elders will be expected to stand before the young rather than the reverse. A daughter will rise against her mother, a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law. The face of the generation will be like the face of a dog. And a son will not be ashamed before his father. The passage distributes the specific failures interestingly: sons toward fathers, daughters toward mothers, daughters-in-law toward mothers-in-law.

### R. Nechemiah

*Tanya* — it was taught. Rabbi Nechemiah says: in the generation when *Mashiach* comes, *ha-azut tirbeh* — brazenness will increase. *Ve-ha-yoker ya'avot* — that which deserves honor will be perverted. Rashi reads this as the proper showing of honor being turned on its head. The vine will give its fruit and there will be plentiful wine — that is the one seemingly positive note — yet *ve-ha-yayin be-yoker*, the wine will be very expensive. Rashi understands this to mean that demand will be so high, driven by widespread drunkenness, that price will be extreme despite abundance.

*Ve-nehepcha kol ha-malkhut le-minus* — and the entire kingdom will turn to *minut*, heresy. Since the Romans of Rabbi Nechemiah's time — the second century — practiced *avodah zarah*, and *minut* in the Gemara often refers to a form of Jewish heresy, specifically to what would become Christianity, this is most naturally read as a prediction that the Roman Empire would convert to Christianity. Constantine's conversion of Rome to Christianity occurred at the beginning of the fourth century, roughly two centuries after Rabbi Nechemiah. He may have sensed the direction in which things were moving. And though that conversion has long since occurred, *Mashiach* has not yet come, suggesting this is one necessary sign among many, not a sufficient condition alone.

### R. Yitzchak Sign

*Mesayei lei le-Rabbi Yitzchak* — Rabbi Nechemiah's teaching supports Rabbi Yitzchak's position, for Rabbi Yitzchak said: *ein Ben David ba ad she-tit'hapekh kol ha-malkhut le-minut* — *Mashiach* will not come until the entire kingdom turns to heresy. For Rabbi Yitzchak this is the defining prerequisite. That turning occurred approximately 1,700 years ago, yet we still await *Mashiach*.

*Amar Rava mai kra* — Rava asks, what is the scriptural basis? *Kulo hafakh lavan tahor hu* — if the entire diseased area turns white, it is pure. The image of *tzara'at* spreading until it covers everything completely, which counterintuitively signals purity, is invoked as a parallel: when the darkness spreads completely, that becomes the sign of the turn toward redemption.

## Arrival Conditions

### Divine Judgment

*Tanu rabbanan* — our rabbis taught. The verse reads: *ki yadin Hashem amo* — God will judge His people — *ki yireh ki azlat yad ve-efes atzur ve-azuv* — when He sees that their power is gone and there is none guarded or supported. From this verse the Gemara derives multiple conditions for *Mashiach*'s arrival.

### Hand Extended

Four distinct readings are offered. First: *ein Ben David ba ad she-yirbu ha-mesorot* — *Mashiach* will not come until informers against Jews to the government greatly multiply, reading *azlat yad* as a hand extended against them. Second: *ad she-yim'atu ha-talmidim* — until the *talmidei chakhamim* are diminished, for as Rashi notes, *Torah* is what would strengthen Israel and its absence leaves them unsupported. Third: *ad she-tichleh perutah min ha-kis* — until no money remains in the pocket, reading *azlat yad* as the hand reaching into one's pocket and finding nothing. Fourth — and perhaps closest to the plain sense of the verse: *ad she-yit'yashu min ha-ge'ulah* — until they despair of redemption entirely. It is at the moment of the greatest loss of hope, when it feels as though there is nothing left to hold and support Israel, *kibi-yakhol ein somekh ve-ozer le-Yisrael* — as though there is none supporting or helping Israel — that *Mashiach* will come.

## Computing End Danger

### R. Zeira Warning

Rabbi Zeira's practice was the following: when he found rabbis deeply engaged in trying to compute when *Mashiach* would come, he would say to them — *bi-metuta*, please, *lo terachakuha* — do not push it further away. The very act of preoccupying oneself with calculating the moment of arrival, Rabbi Zeira teaches, delays rather than hastens the coming.

This is not merely the principle of a watched pot never boiling. There is a deeper concern. The tradition of *Mashiach* gives the Jewish people hope when oppressed and in exile; it orients the believer toward an ultimate redemption. But *Torah* and *mitzvot* have always been profoundly this-worldly. Preoccupying oneself with computing a future arrival date distracts from the work that needs to be done in the present — which is, in fact, the very work that would bring *Mashiach* closer.

### 3 Unbidden Things

*De-tanya* — as was taught in a *braita*: three things come *be-hesech ha-da'at* — when one is not paying attention to them. These are *Mashiach*, a found object (*metziah*), and a scorpion (*akrav*). If one goes about deliberately looking for a *metziah*, one will not find it; it is only when going about one's business that one stumbles upon a lost object. Likewise a scorpion strikes when one is not alert. The Maharsha attempts to link all three by connecting them to the question of what the messianic era will look like — whether it will be reward or punishment, a *metziah* or an *akrav*. But the broader point seems to be that such computations are not only futile; they actively distract from the present-world labor that gives the belief in *Mashiach* its meaning.

## Cosmic Timeline

### 6000 Years

*Amar Rav Katina*: the world has a lifespan of 6,000 years — *sheis alfei shanei havei alma* — and one thousand years of destruction thereafter, after which a new world will be created. The source is the verse *ve-nisgav Hashem levado ba-yom ha-hu* — God will stand alone on that day — combined with the principle that one day in God's eyes is a thousand years. That millennium will be a period in which God alone stands; all of creation will be destroyed, and a new world will come into being at the end of that thousand years.

Abaye offers a variant: *terei charuv* — two thousand years of destruction — citing the verse *yechayeinu mi-yomayim, ba-yom ha-shlishi yekimenu ve-nichyeh le-fanav* — He will revive us after two days; on the third day He will raise us up and we will live before Him. On this reading, *techiyat ha-meitim* — the resurrection — occurs at the transition from the second to the third thousand-year period, which would coincide with the beginning of the era of *yemot ha-Mashiach*.

### Shmita Analogy

*Tani kevatei de-Rav Katina* — a *braita* supports Rav Katina's position. Just as the *shmita* year is one year in seven during which the land lies fallow, so too the world will lie fallow for one thousand years out of every seven thousand. The scriptural support comes from the same verse — *ve-nisgav Hashem levado ba-yom ha-hu* — as well as the psalm: *Mizmor Shir le-Yom ha-Shabbat, yom she-kulo Shabbat* — a day of complete rest. The tension here is worth noting: we pray for *Olam ha-Ba* in terms of *Shabbat* as *me'ein Olam ha-Ba*, a foretaste of perfection — yet here the "day of complete rest" sounds far more cataclysmic and destructive than any idyllic, Edenic image. The two conceptions sit in some tension. Finally: *ki elef shanim be-einekha ki-yom etmol ki ya'avor* — a thousand years in Your eyes are like a yesterday that has passed.

### 3 Epochs

*Tana d'vei Eliyahu* divides the 6,000 years into three epochs of two thousand years each. The first two thousand years are *tohu* — void and emptiness — covering the period from creation until *Avraham Avinu*. By conventional chronology *Avraham* was born in the year 1948 from creation. Rashi connects the beginning of the *Torah* epoch to the moment when *Avraham* and *Sarah* began bringing people under *kanfei ha-Shekhinah* — Rashi dates this to when *Avraham* was 52 years old, corresponding approximately to the year 2000 from creation. Until that moment the world is a desolate world. The *Ramban* on *Bereishit* attempts a parallel structure dividing the world into epochs of one thousand years, each corresponding to a day of creation, but that is a separate framework.

The second two thousand years are the epoch of *Torah* — beginning with *Avraham* and *Sarah* bringing people closer to God and culminating with *Ma'amad Har Sinai* and the full flourishing of *Torah* and *mitzvot* within the Jewish people. Calculating forward, two thousand years from approximately year 2000 brings us to year 4000 from creation — corresponding roughly to the year 250 of the common era, the end of the period of the *Tanna'im* and the beginning of the Talmudic period. This is the epoch of *Torah* in the fullest sense.

The third two thousand years are *yemot ha-Mashiach* — the era in which *Mashiach* can come. This is the period that was, from the Gemara's perspective, already in progress. The Gemara adds: *uvavonoteinu she-rabu, yatze'u mehem mah she-yatze'u* — but due to our great iniquities, years have passed in this final epoch without *Mashiach* arriving. Those are lost opportunities. Yet *Mashiach* can still come at any point within this remaining two-thousand-year window.

The Gemara then records that *Eliyahu* told Rav Yehuda the brother of Rav Sila the *chasid*: the world will last no fewer than 85 *yovlot* — jubilee cycles. At 50 years per *yovel*, 80 *yovlot* equals 4,000 years; adding the remaining five brings us to 4,250, meaning *Mashiach* cannot come before approximately the year 500 of the common era. When Rav Yehuda asked whether *Mashiach* would come at the beginning or the end of that final *yovel*, and whether the entire period must be completed first, *Eliyahu* answered each time: *eini yodea* — I do not know. Rav Ashi summarizes: before that point, do not anticipate *Mashiach*; from that point onward, look for him.

## Specific Computations

### Roman Scroll

Rav Chana bar Tachlifa sent the following to Rav Yosef: I found a certain man — possibly a non-Jew — carrying a scroll written in *Ashuris*, the square Hebrew script, and in the Hebrew language. He told me he had hired himself out as a mercenary to the Roman army and found this scroll in the storehouses of Rome — evidently among items plundered when Rome conquered Israel. Written in it was: *le-achar arba'at alafim u-masayim ve-tish'im ve-achat shana le-olam* — after 4,291 years from creation, the world will come to its end. The *hagahah* records a variant reading but the figure is essentially consistent with the 4,250 computed earlier.

### End Wars

The scroll continues: some of that ending will come through *milchamos taninim* — wars of sea creatures, possibly the *Livyasan*, which some read as a metaphor for wars between great national superpowers. Some will come through *milchamos Gog u-Magog*. And *she'ar yemot ha-Mashiach* — the remainder of the time — will be the period of *Mashiach*.

### 7000 Years

*Ve-ein ha-Kadosh Barukh Hu mechadesh et olamo ela le-achar shivat alafim shana* — God will not renew His world until after seven thousand years. This clarifies the sequence: *Mashiach* comes sometime after the 4,290-year mark, the wars of *Gog u-Magog* follow, but the full renewal and re-creation of the world does not occur until the end of the seventh millennium.

### R. Acha Variant

Rav Acha the son of Rava offers a variant: *le-achar chameishot alafim shana* — after five thousand years. This makes the sequence slightly more coherent: *Mashiach* and the wars of *Gog u-Magog* arrive sometime in the fifth millennium, and the world renews at the end of that millennium, all within the seven-thousand-year framework.

## Computation Impossible

### R. Nasan Verse

*Tanya* — Rabbi Nasan says: *mikra zeh nokeiv ve-yored ad ha-tehom* — this verse pierces and descends to the very depths. The verse in question is from *Chavakuk*: *ki od chazon la-mo'ed ve-yafei'ach la-ketz ve-lo yekhazeiv; im yitmahmeah chakkeh lo, ki vo yavo lo ye'acher* — for the vision is yet for its appointed time, it declares toward the end and will not lie; if it tarries, wait for it, for it will surely come and will not delay. The plain sense of *ve-yafei'ach la-ketz* is that it declares the end; but as we will see, the Gemara also reads *yafei'ach* as "blow away" — meaning blow away and destroy all the calculations that have been made. Rabbi Nasan's point is that this verse is fathomless — you cannot reach the bottom of it, and no computation will succeed.

### Three Rejected

The Gemara proceeds to dismiss three specific rabbinic computations. The first is the calculation based on the verse in Daniel: *ad idan ve-idanin u-felag idan* — until a time, times, and half a time. Rashi explains that *idan* means 400 years, the duration of the Egyptian exile; two *idanin* plus a half gives 1,400 years. Counting 1,400 years from the time of Daniel — just before the *Beit ha-Mikdash* of 420 years — brings one to approximately the year 1000 of the common era. That did not come to pass.

The second computation belongs to Rabbi Simlai, who expounded: *he'ekhaltem lechem dim'ah va-tashkemo bi-dema'ot shalish* — I fed them bread of tears and gave them tears to drink in full measure. Rashi reads *shalish* as "a third," understanding the Egyptian and Babylonian exiles — 400 and 70 years respectively, totaling 470 — as one third of the ultimate exile. Multiplying by three yields 1,410 years, essentially identical to the first calculation. Counting 1,410 years of exile from the *Churban ha-Bayit* brings one to approximately the year 1500. That too did not come to pass.

The third is Rabbi Akiva's, who expounded: *od achat me'at va-ani mar'ish et ha-shamayim ve-et ha-aretz* — just a little more and I will cause heaven and earth to tremble. The Gemara understands that Rabbi Akiva read this as indicating *Mashiach* would come very soon after the *Churban* — which is why he believed Bar Kokhba was *Mashiach*.

The Maharsha reads the verse from Chavakuk as elegantly dismissing all three. *Ki od chazon la-mo'ed* — there is yet another vision of what *mo'ed* means (addressing the *idan ve-idanin* computation). *Ve-yafei'ach la-ketz* — and blow away the interpretation of the third (Rabbi Simlai's). *Ve-lo yekhazeiv* — and it is not Bar Koziva — for Barkochba was referred to by the sages as *ben Koziva*, meaning the liar. Thus the verse simultaneously undermines all three attempted computations.

### 3 Kingdoms

The Gemara adds: *malkhut rishon shivim shanah, malkhut shniya chamishim u-shtayim, u-malkhut Ben Koziva shtei shanim u-mechtza* — there was a kingship of 70 years (the successful phase of the *Beit Chashmonai*), a kingship of 52 years (Herod), and the rule of Bar Kokhba for two and a half years. The precise connection to what immediately precedes is not fully spelled out, but the Maharsha reads it as a response to Rabbi Akiva's expectation: Rabbi Akiva thought that "just a little more" meant *Mashiach* was imminent in his day and that Barkochba was the *Mashiach*. But the Gemara is pointing out that even after all of those brief sparks of Jewish self-sovereignty passed — Hasmonean, Herodian, and Bar Kokhba — *Mashiach* still did not come. All of those were not the true *Mashiach*; they passed, and *Mashiach* will come only afterward.

## Curse Computers

### Tiphach Curse

*Amar Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani amar Rabbi Yonatan*: *tipach atzmotam shel mechashvei kitzin* — may the bones of those who compute the ends of days be blasted. The word *ve-yafei'ach la-ketz* in the verse is now read as an imprecation: blow away, destroy, those who blow toward the end — those who try to calculate when it will arrive.

### Computation Failure

The reason for this severity is explained: those who compute set a date, *Mashiach* does not come by that date, and then they say *Mashiach* will never come — *shuv eino ba*. The false expectation generated by calculation leads directly to despair of redemption altogether, which is far worse than never having made the calculation.

### Just Wait

The alternative, drawn from the rest of the verse, is: *chakkeh lo* — simply wait for him. *Im yitmahmeah, chakkeh lo* — if he tarries, wait for him. And lest one wonder whether God Himself is waiting and hoping for this time — *lachen yechakveh Hashem la-chananchem ve-lachen yarum le-rachamchem* — therefore God waits to show you grace; therefore He rises to show you compassion. God too is, so to speak, waiting and longing for the redemption.

### Justice Prevents

This raises a penetrating question: if we are waiting and God is waiting, *mi me'akev* — who is preventing *Mashiach* from coming? *Midat ha-din me-akevet* — the attribute of justice is what delays it. Everyone wants the redemption; but we must earn it, and the divine attribute of justice stands in the way until we do.

This leads naturally to a further question: if *midat ha-din* is what prevents it, and waiting for *Mashiach* does not overcome *midat ha-din*, then why is it important to wait for him at all? Why should we cultivate a sense of longing for something that will not arrive merely because we long for it? The Gemara implicitly asks whether such waiting distracts from the work — the *teshuvah* and *ma'asim tovim* — that would actually be effective.

### Reward Waiting

*Lekabel sakhar* — to receive reward, *shene'emar ashrei kol chokhei lo* — as it says, praiseworthy are all who wait for Him. The act of waiting itself, expressing a genuine belief in ultimate redemption, carries its own value and its own reward. The proper balance is clear: have faith, believe in redemption, work toward a better world because one believes it is achievable — but do not allow the anticipation of that future moment to consume the work that needs to be done right now. The two must be held in tension.

## 36 Righteous

### Abaye 36

*Amar Abaye*: the famous statement — *lo pachot almaya mi-tlasin ve-shita tzadikim*, the world has no fewer than thirty-six *tzadikim* — *d'mekablei appei Shekhinah be-chol dara* — who receive the countenance of the Divine Presence in every generation.

### Gematria 36

The proof: *ashroi kol chokhei lo* — praiseworthy are all who wait for *him*. The word *lo* — for him — has the numerical value of 36: *lamed* equals 30, *vav* equals 6.

### Rava Objection

But does this not contradict Rava's statement? Rava taught that the row of people standing before the *Kadosh Barukh Hu* stretches *tamnei srei alfei parsa* — eighteen thousand *parasangs*, citing the verse *saviv shemonah asar alef* — around him eighteen thousand. How can only thirty-six receive the Divine Presence if eighteen thousand stand before God?

### Clear/Cloudy Lens

*Lo kashya* — there is no difficulty. The thirty-six are those who *mistaklei be-ispaklaria ha-meirah* — who see God through a clear, luminous lens. The eighteen thousand are those who see through a clouded lens — they are present before God, but their perception is indirect and dimmed. The thirty-six occupy the innermost circle, the most direct apprehension of the Divine.

One textual nuance: Abaye uses the word *dara*, which in this context can mean either "in every generation" or "row" (as Rava uses it in his statement). Reading Abaye as meaning "in every generation" fits better with the broader context of the *lamed vav tzadikim* as a phenomenon of every era.

### S.b.Y. Few

But is even thirty-six too large a number? *Ve-ha'amar Chizkiyah amar Rabbi Yirmeyah mishum Shimon bar Yochai*: Chizkiyah said in the name of Rabbi Yirmeyah in the name of Shimon bar Yochai — *ra'iti bnei aliyah ve-hen mu'atin* — I have seen those of true spiritual stature, and they are very few. Presumably this is from his period of seclusion in the cave. If there are a thousand, he said, I and my son are among them. If there are a hundred, I and my son are among them. If there are two — it is me and my son. How could there be thirty-six who receive the Divine Presence at the highest level?

*Lo kashya* — not difficult. *Ha d'ayli b'var, ha d'ayli be-lo var*: there are those who enter the divine presence only with permission — these are the thirty-six — and there are those so elevated that they enter even without permission. It is the latter category, those who need no permission, that may be as few as two. Whatever precisely this means, the distinction is between levels of intimacy with the divine: the thirty-six enjoy the highest access; the even smaller number — perhaps only two — enjoy an intimacy that transcends even the framework of permission.

## Repentance Debate

### R. Eliezer: If

*Amar Rav*: *kalu kol ha-kitzin* — all of the computed ends of days have expired and run out. The matter now depends entirely on *teshuvah u-ma'asim tovim* — on our repentance and good deeds. *Ve-Shmuel amar*: Shmuel says, *daiyo la-avel she-ya'amod be-evlo* — it is enough for the mourner to stand in his mourning. We have suffered long enough; God will bring *Mashiach* regardless. This appears to be the position that *Mashiach* will come even without *teshuvah*, and it leads directly into the debate of the *Tanna'im*.

*K'tana'ei* — this dispute echoes a debate among *Tanna'im*. Rabbi Eliezer says: *im Yisrael osim teshuvah nigalin ve-im lav ein nigalin* — if Israel does *teshuvah* they will be redeemed; if not, they will not be redeemed. The position is clear and absolute.

### R. Yehoshua: Evil King

Rabbi Yehoshua responded: you mean to say that if Israel does not do *teshuvah* they will never be redeemed — that there will be no *Mashiach*? *Ela* — rather, *Ha-Kadosh Barukh Hu ma'amid lahem melekh she-gezeirotav kashot ke-Haman* — God will raise up against them a king whose decrees are as harsh as Haman's. *Ve-Yisrael osim teshuvah u-machziram le-mutav* — and as a result, the external pressure will cause Israel to repent and improve their ways. Rabbi Yehoshua does not say *Mashiach* will come without *teshuvah*; the point is that God is committed to bringing the redemption regardless, and if Israel will not generate *teshuvah* from within, God will compel it from without.

### Scripture Quotes

*Tanya idach* — a second *braita* records the debate. Rabbi Eliezer cites: *shuvu banim shovavim erpa meshuvoteikhem* — return, wayward children, I will heal your waywardness — proving that *teshuvah* is the prerequisite. Rabbi Yehoshua counters: *chinam nimkartem ve-lo be-khesef tiga'elu* — you were sold for nothing and you will not be redeemed with money. *Chinam nimkartem* — you gave yourselves over to *avodah zarah* for nothing. *Ve-lo be-khesef tiga'elu* — and your redemption will not come through *teshuvah u-ma'asim tovim*. On this reading Rabbi Yehoshua appears to be saying that the redemption will not be contingent on our *teshuvah* and good deeds at all.

To harmonize this with his earlier position, the best reading is that Rabbi Yehoshua means: the redemption need not come through self-initiated *teshuvah*; God will compel Israel's return if necessary, and it is that divinely-induced *teshuvah* — not Israel's own *teshuvah* — that brings the redemption.

### Ownership Forced

Rabbi Eliezer then cites: *shuvu elai ve-ashuva aleikhem* — return to Me and I will return to you — which requires Israel to move first. Rabbi Yehoshua responds with: *ki anochi ba'alti vakhem ve-lakachti etkhem echad me-ir u-shnayim mi-mishpachah va-heveti etkhem Tzion* — because I have taken ownership over you, and I will take you, one from a city and two from a family, and bring you to Zion. The image is of God seizing Israel and forcing the ingathering even against their will — an act of divine compulsion, not of Israel's own initiative.

### Despised Redeemed

Rabbi Eliezer cites: *be-shuvah va-nachat tivvashe'un* — through returning and rest you will be saved — reading *shuvah* as *teshuvah*. Rabbi Yehoshua counters with: *ko amar Hashem go'el Yisrael kedosho, li-vzoh nefesh le-mita'ev goy le-eved moshlim, melakhim yir'u ve-kamu sarim ve-yishtachavu* — so says God the Redeemer of Israel, to the one despised, abhorred by nations, a slave to rulers — kings will rise and officers will prostrate themselves. The message: even in a state of utter degradation and unworthiness, God will redeem Israel.

Rabbi Eliezer's position is consistent throughout: *teshuvah* is the necessary and indispensable prerequisite for redemption. This also aligns with Rav's ruling. Shmuel's position — and Rabbi Yehoshua's — is somewhat less clear in its full extent: does it mean God will force *teshuvah* upon Israel and then redeem them, or that redemption will ultimately come irrespective of the moral condition of Israel because God's ownership and commitment to His people is unconditional? The *sugya* will continue to develop this question.

# Sanhedrin 98

## Eliezer vs. Yehoshua

### Intro: Teshuvah Debate

The opening of Daf 98 returns us to the debate between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua regarding the conditions under which Mashiach will come. Rabbi Eliezer holds that Israel must perform *teshuvah*, while Rabbi Yehoshua maintains that God will compel it if necessary. One might ask whether both Tannaim ultimately agree that *teshuvah* is required in principle, differing only on the mechanism. The answer may well be yes — but the deeper disagreement concerns the nature of the *teshuvah* itself.

### Nature of Teshuvah

Is the *teshuvah* in question a sincere, self-motivated return to God, or a coerced repentance — a *teshuvah* performed, as it were, with a gun to one's head? This distinction operates not only at the individual level but at the level of civilization itself. If one follows Rabbi Eliezer's approach, then the requirement for *teshuvah* implies something far more demanding than personal moral improvement: it implies that we must transform the world into a more righteous place, that the Messianic era can only be ushered in through genuine collective moral achievement. Rabbi Yehoshua's position, by contrast, envisions a *teshuvah* imposed by God — and even if such compelled repentance technically occurs, it would not reflect an intrinsic transformation of the world's character.

This touches on the fundamental question of whether the Messianic era is something humanity brings about or something God imposes upon history. If one takes the Rabbi Eliezer approach seriously, then bringing about the Messianic period is very much under human control — it requires genuinely turning the world into a better place, not merely producing a generation that performs *teshuvah* under duress.

### Generational Worthiness

This connects to the concept of *dor shekulo zakai* — an entirely meritorious generation — versus *dor shekulo chayav* — an entirely sinful generation. Rabbi Yehoshua's position, that God will bring it regardless, is consistent with the notion that Israel need not be collectively righteous; the generation could be entirely sinful. But even if one holds that *teshuvah* is necessary, there is a significant difference between a generation that genuinely transforms itself and one that does so only under the pressure of calamity — just as one might argue that repentance performed on *Yom Kippur* out of habit does not necessarily reflect a changed world. One might note, with a degree of dark irony, that it is far more within our current power to produce a *dor shekulo chayav* than a *dor shekulo zakai*.

### Shmuel & Rav Alignment

How does this debate map onto the positions of Rav and Shmuel? Shmuel's position — *dai lo la'avel sheya'amod be'evlo*, it is enough for the mourner to stand in his mourning — implies that the suffering of exile is itself sufficient and that God will bring Mashiach in His own time without requiring *teshuvah* at all. This seems to diverge even from Rabbi Yehoshua's framing, since Rabbi Yehoshua at least gestures toward God compelling *teshuvah*, whereas Shmuel's focus is simply on the inexorable arrival of the appointed time. The point is that the various formulations — Rabbi Yehoshua's *teshuvah* forced by God, Shmuel's simple faith in the appointed time — are all variations on a single theme: it is not our moral achievement that brings Mashiach, but God's unilateral action. In none of these versions is human-initiated transformation of the world the operative factor.

---

## Textual Debate

### Eliezer's Verse

The Gemara records the actual textual exchange. Rabbi Eliezer cites a verse from Isaiah: *Im tashuvu Yisrael ne'um Hashem elai tashuvu* — "If you return to Me, Israel, says God, return to Me." This verse makes the coming of redemption conditional upon Israel's repentance — the classic prooftext for his position.

### Yehoshua's Verse

Rabbi Yehoshua responds by citing a passage from Daniel. He says: *V'shamati et ha'ish levush habadim asher mima'al l'meimei haye'or* — "I heard the man dressed in linen who was above the waters of the river," who lifted up his right and left hands to the heavens and swore by the One who lives forever: *Ki l'mo'ed mo'adim vachatzi* — "in a time, the time of the times and a half." And: *U'kechalot napetz yad am kodesh tichlena kol eleh* — "when the spreading forth of the hand of the holy nation comes to an end, then all of this will be completed." The import of this prophecy is clear: there is a fixed time, and at that time, when the people are at their lowest and most powerless state, the Messianic era will arrive. The people need not be performing *teshuvah*; it comes at an appointed moment regardless.

### Eliezer's Silence

The Gemara records: *V'shatak Rabbi Eliezer* — Rabbi Eliezer fell silent. He had no response. This is striking. It seems that what silenced him was not just any counterargument but specifically the prophecies in Daniel, which are the most explicitly eschatological texts in all of Scripture — the most precise and detailed descriptions of the end of days, of the time of resurrection or of Mashiach's coming (even if the word *mashiach* does not appear there explicitly). The vividness and specificity of Daniel's prophetic vision apparently struck Rabbi Eliezer as unanswerable, and he conceded the point, at least on the textual level.

---

## Signs of Mashiach

### Prosperity Sign

The Gemara now shifts away from the debate about *teshuvah* and turns to the question of how one recognizes the Messianic period. Rabbi Abba declares: *Ein l'cha ketz meguleh mizeh* — there is no more revealed sign of the end than this verse: *Va'atem harei Yisrael anafchem titnu ufriychem tis'u le'ami Yisrael* — "And you, mountains of Israel, your boughs will give forth and your fruit you will bear for My people Israel." The sign of the Messianic era, Rabbi Abba says, is prosperity — the land flourishing and yielding its fruit abundantly. This is the clearest, most openly revealed *ketz* one could point to.

### Scarcity Sign

Rabbi Elazar — note, this is Rabbi Elazar, not Rabbi Eliezer — disagrees, or rather offers what he considers an even better sign. He cites the verse: *Ki lifnei hayamim hahem sechar adam lo nihya usechar behema einena* — "For before those days there was no hire for man and no hire for beast." The sign he points to is the opposite of prosperity: a time of profound scarcity and economic collapse, when one cannot hire out people or animals for wages. This is consistent with earlier Gemara discussions that portrayed the period immediately preceding Mashiach as one of tremendous hardship.

### Affliction Period

The verse continues: *Ulayotzei velavo ein shalom min hatzar* — "And for those who go out and come in there is no peace from the oppressor." The Gemara asks: what does this phrase mean? Rav Abba explains: *Af talmidei chachamim* — even Torah scholars, who are normally associated with the verse *Shalom rav le'ohavei Toratecha* — "great peace for those who love Your Torah" — even they will have no peace. They will be unable to sit and study, forced instead to constantly exert themselves to earn a living during this period of extreme want. Rashi understands the *tzar* referenced in the verse as referring either to the general *tzarot* — the sufferings of that period — or to the *yetzer hara*, which would bring us back to the theme of a sinful generation.

### Equal Prices

Shmuel adds another sign: *Ad sheyishvu kol hashearim kulam shekulim* — until all prices become equal. Rashi offers two readings of this: either everything becomes equally cheap — wine costs no more than flour — or everything becomes equally expensive, with flour priced as dearly as wine. Both readings describe a period of economic distortion, though the two readings point in opposite directions regarding whether the Messianic era is preceded by abundance or collapse.

---

## Conditions for Mashiach

### Fish Scarcity

The Gemara now presents a series of statements about the conditions under which Ben David will come. Rabbi Chanina states: *Ein Ben David ba ad sheyitvakesh dag lechola velo yimatze* — the Son of David will not come until it reaches a point where one cannot even obtain a fish for a sick person who needs it. The destitution will be so extreme that even the smallest comfort cannot be procured. He cites the verse from Ezekiel: *Az ashkiya meimeihem venaharotam kashemen olichem* — "Then I will sink their waters and make their rivers run like oil" — meaning the rivers will be so thick, so stilled, that one cannot pull a fish from them. The following verse then continues: *Bayom hahu atzmiach keren leveit Yisrael* — "On that day I will cause the pride of the house of Israel to flourish."

### Loss Sovereignty

Rabbi Chama bar Chanina teaches: *Ein Ben David ba ad shetichleh malchut hazala miYisrael* — the Son of David will not come until even the most lowly, the most negligible form of sovereignty is removed from Israel. Rashi explains: *Shelo tehe lahem shum shiltonut leYisrael afilu shiltonut kala vedala* — Israel will not possess even the slightest, most trivial form of authority; they will be utterly subjugated to the non-Jewish powers. This is a challenging statement in its contemporary implications. One might ask: is the restoration of Jewish sovereignty in the Land of Israel a sign that we are moving *closer* to the Messianic era, or does this teaching suggest the opposite — that as long as Israel retains some form of rule, Mashiach will not come, and that total subjugation is the necessary precondition? The verse cited is *Vecharat hazalzalim bemazmerot* — cutting off even the smallest branches — with *zalzalim* read as representing even the slightest remnant of sovereignty. The following verse: *Ba'et hahi yuval shai l'Hashem tzevaot* — "At that time a gift will be brought to God."

### Remove Haughty

Rabbi Zeira citing Rabbi Chanina: *Ein Ben David ba ad sheyichlu gasei haruach miYisrael* — the Son of David will not come until the haughty ones are eliminated from Israel. The verse: *Ki az asir mikirbecha alizei ga'avasecha* — "Then I will remove from your midst those who exult in pride." The following verse adds: *Vehisharti bekirbecha am ani vadal vechasu beshem Hashem* — "I will leave among you a humble and poor nation, and they shall take refuge in God's name." Here, interestingly, the poverty may not be financial destitution but rather a quality of spiritual humility — a nation poor in arrogance rather than in wealth. This potentially points toward a more righteous period rather than simply a time of affliction.

### End Judges

Rav Simlai, citing Rabbi Elazar the son of Rabbi Shimon, teaches: *Ein Ben David ba ad sheyichlu kol shoftim veshotrim miYisrael* — the Son of David will not come until all judges and officials are eliminated from Israel. The verse: *Va'ashiva yadai alayich ve'etzrof kavar sigayich* — "I will turn my hand against you and smelt out your dross" — and then: *Va'ashiva shoftayich kevarishona* — "I will restore your judges as in former times." The implication is that God will first purge all of the current judges — who are themselves dross — before restoring true judges of the caliber of antiquity.

### Righteousness Redemption

Ulla teaches — some textual versions read *Ein Yisrael nifdis* — *Ein Yerushalayim nifdis ela bitzedaka* — Jerusalem will be redeemed only through righteousness. The verse: *Tzion bemishpat tipadeh veshaveha bitzedaka* — "Zion will be redeemed through justice, and those who return to her through righteousness." Not *berachamim*, not through divine mercy alone — it must be earned. This is the basis on which the Vilna Gaon, in *Birkat HaMazon*, omits the word *berachamav* from the blessing *Boneh Yerushalayim*, since Zion is redeemed *bitzedaka* and not merely through mercy.

### Haughty & Magi

Rav Papa adds a series of parallel statements. *Ee batlu yeheiri batlu amgushi* — if the haughty ones cease, the Magi will also cease. The *amgushi* appears to refer to a priestly class in ancient Persia — the Zoroastrian Magi — who are associated with the oppressive non-Jewish powers. *Ee batlu dayani batlu gezirpati* — if the [corrupt] judges cease, so too will the *gezirpati*, some form of Persian official or oppressor. The prooftexts: for the haughty and the Magi, the verse *Ve'etzrof kavar sigayich ve'asira kol bedilayich* — "I will smelt your dross and remove all your dross," with Rashi explaining *bedilayich* as those who separate Israel from God, i.e., the Magi. For the judges and oppressors, the verse *Hesir Hashem mishpatayich pina oyvayich* — "God has removed your judges, turned away your enemies." The thrust of all these teachings is the same: poor and arrogant leadership is what keeps Israel from God and is ultimately responsible for Israel's suffering at the hands of foreign powers.

---

## Hope in Affliction

### Shrinking Generation

Rabbi Yochanan offers a teaching of profound pastoral importance: *Im ra'ita dor shemisma'et veholech* — if you see a generation where things are going from bad to worse, declining and shrinking — whether in terms of moral quality or material circumstances — *chakei lo*, nevertheless wait for him, continue to long for Mashiach.

### Divine Response

The prooftext: *Ve'et am ani toshia* — "And a poor nation He will redeem." When things are at their worst, that is not necessarily a sign that the Messianic era is most distant; it may be precisely the opposite — that God's redemption is most imminent. A second teaching from Rabbi Yochanan reinforces this: *Im ra'ita dor shetzarot rabot ba'ot alav k'nahar* — if you see a generation upon which many afflictions are coming like a rushing river — *achakeh lo*, still wait for him. The verse: *Ki yavo k'nahar tzar ruach Hashem nosesah vo* — "When affliction comes like a river, the spirit of God surges within it" — *usamich lei uva l'Tziyon goel* — and immediately following: "And a redeemer will come to Zion."

### Hope in Exile

This teaching carries enormous significance for understanding how Jews historically endured persecution. The belief in Mashiach was not merely theological doctrine but a psychological lifeline. The principle of *af al pi sheyitmahmeha im kol ze achakeh lo* — even if he delays, I will wait for him — is not passive resignation but active hope. The possibility that precisely when things are at their worst, redemption may be nearest, gave people the capacity to endure what would otherwise be unbearable. This also maps onto the broader debate: Rabbi Yehoshua's position, that God will bring it regardless of our merit, is what sustains hope in dark times. If Mashiach could only come when we had transformed the world into a righteous place, then suffering would suggest distance from redemption. But if God brings it when He sees there is no other way, then suffering itself becomes a potential harbinger of redemption. Notably, the Gemara at this point makes no mention of *teshuvah* at all — consistent with Rabbi Yehoshua's framework, God's intervention operates independently of human moral achievement.

### Hasidic Story

This dynamic is captured in a famous Hasidic exchange. A rabbi delivers a *drasha* urging his congregation to be *metzapeh l'viat haMashiach* — to constantly long and wait for Mashiach, to know that at any moment he could come and take the Jewish people to *Eretz Yisrael*. A man goes home inspired and tells his wife. She is unmoved — life is good here, the community is comfortable, the business is running, she has no desire to pick up and move to Jerusalem. He returns to the rabbi and reports her response. The rabbi asks: but what about the *pogromtchiks* — the violent enemies who bring persecution? He goes back and tells his wife the rabbi's question. She replies: tell the rabbi that Mashiach should come and take the *pogromtchiks* to *Eretz Yisrael*. The story, with its wry irony, makes a serious point: genuine longing for Mashiach is most naturally felt by those who need to be saved from their current reality, who feel the weight of exile and suffering.
