The desire for redemption is inseparable from the experience of exile.

---

## Merit or Force

### Zakai or Chayav

Rabbi Yochanan sharpens the dichotomy he introduced earlier: *Ein ben David ba ela b'dor shekulo zakai o kulo chayav* — the Son of David will not come except in a generation that is entirely meritorious or entirely sinful. The prooftext for *dor shekulo zakai*: *Ve'amech kulam tzadikim l'olam yirshu aretz* — "Your people will all be righteous, they will inherit the land forever." The prooftext for *dor shekulo chayav*: *Vayar ki ein ish vayishtomem ki ein mafgia* — "He saw that there was no man and was astounded that there was no one to intercede" — and then: *L'ma'ani e'eseh* — "For My own sake I will act," says God.

### Merit vs. Intervention

This is a sharper and more theologically precise formulation than Rabbi Yehoshua's earlier statement. Rabbi Yehoshua spoke of God bringing some external pressure to compel *teshuvah*, meaning there is still *teshuvah* in the equation, even if forced. Rabbi Yochanan's formulation removes *teshuvah* from the picture entirely in the case of *dor shekulo chayav*. It is not that God makes them repent — it is that when all is lost, when not a single righteous man remains and there is no one even to intercede, God acts for His own sake. The logic is essentially eschatological emergency: if Mashiach does not come now, everything will be lost entirely. As one student observed, this parallels the Egypt narrative — the forty-ninth level of defilement, the point at which another moment of delay would mean total assimilation and loss. The Gemara does not explicitly draw this connection here, but the structure is identical. And importantly, the correspondence between *dor shekulo zakai* and prosperity on the one hand, and *dor shekulo chayav* and affliction on the other, is suggested but not made explicit by the Gemara.

---

## Be'itah Achishena

### Two Verses

Rabbi Alexandri presents a teaching in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: *Rami* — he posed a contradiction between two verses. It is written *be'itah* — "in its time I will bring it" — and immediately adjacent, it is written *achishena* — "I will hasten it." If there is a fixed time, how can it be hastened? If it can be hastened, how is there a fixed time? The resolution: *Zachu, achishena* — if they merit, I will hasten it. *Lo zachu, be'itah* — if they do not merit, it will come in its fixed time.

### Reassurance vs. Empowerm…

This resolution introduces a theological framework meaningfully different from the *dor shekulo zakai o dor shekulo chayav* model. The *be'itah achishena* framework insists on a fixed time: there is an absolute outer limit beyond which God will bring redemption regardless. In this sense it is reassuring — even if we keep failing, there is a moment at which God has committed to act. One need not be driven to anxiety by the thought that human moral failure could indefinitely delay the end of history. But this reassurance comes at a cost. The vision is a fundamentally disempowering one. Human action can only hasten the timetable; it cannot be the fundamental cause of redemption. The deepest initiative lies with God, and we can at most adjust the schedule somewhat by our merit. This stands in real tension with a different, more demanding orientation — the view that it is our responsibility to bring the world to a Messianic state, that *tikkun olam* is not just a way to hasten God's plan but is itself the operative mechanism of redemption. The *be'itah achishena* model is not that vision; it is, rather, a reassurance that God has a plan and we can only modestly accelerate it. The *dor shekulo chayav* model is different still — there the issue is not a fixed timetable but a moral cliff edge: either all are righteous and Mashiach comes through merit, or all are lost and God intervenes. Neither model gives us unlimited agency.

---

## Glory or Humility

### Clouds vs. Donkey

Rabbi Alexandri presents a second contradiction, again in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: *Rami* — there is a verse that says *Ve'aru im ananei shamaya kevar enosh ata* — "And behold, with the clouds of heaven, one like a man was coming" (Daniel), suggesting Mashiach arrives with extraordinary glory and majesty. Yet another verse says *Ani verochev al hachamor* — "Humble and riding on a donkey" (Zechariah). The resolution follows the same structure: *Zachu, im ananei shamaya* — if they merit, he comes with the clouds of heaven, with glory and grandeur. *Lo zachu, ani verochev al hachamor* — if they do not merit, he comes humble on a donkey. The manner of Mashiach's arrival thus reflects the moral state of the generation receiving him. A generation that has achieved spiritual greatness receives a glorious redemption; a generation that is spiritually diminished receives a redemption that matches its lowly state.

### Shapur's Offer

The Gemara records an exchange between the Persian king Shapur and Shmuel. Shapur said to Shmuel: *Amritu Mashiach al chamara ati* — I hear that you Jews say Mashiach comes on a donkey. *Ishdar lei susaya* — I'll send him a horse, one of my finest. Why does he need to ride a donkey? Shmuel replied: *Mi is lach bar chivor gavnei?* — Do you have a horse of a hundred different colors? Rashi's reading is that Shmuel was essentially deflecting with a nonsensical answer — Mashiach does not come on just any donkey, he comes on a supernal donkey, and Shapur's horse is irrelevant to the matter. The exchange is mildly absurdist but the underlying point is that the imagery of the donkey is not to be taken as a practical transportation problem awaiting a royal equestrian solution.

---

## Rabbi Yehoshua's Vision

### Elijah's Location

The Gemara now presents one of its most celebrated *agadot*. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi once encountered Elijah, who was standing at the entrance to the cave of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai. The significance of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's cave in this context is not elaborated by Rashi, who treats it as a historical detail. One might note that Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai famously fled to a cave to escape the Romans — which may carry thematic resonance with the Rome imagery that follows — though Rashi does not draw this connection explicitly.

### Ask Mashiach

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi asked Elijah: *Atina l'alma de'asei?* — Will I enter the World to Come? Elijah replied: *Im yirtzeh adon zeh* — if God wills it. Rashi explains *adon zeh* as referring to God, not to Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai — the question of why Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai would determine anyone's entry into the World to Come would be difficult to answer. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi adds: *Shnayim ra'iti ve'kol gimel shamati* — I saw two there, meaning himself and Elijah, but I heard a third voice. Rashi identifies this as the *Shechinah*. Rabbi Yehoshua then asked Elijah: *Eimatai asi Mashiach?* — When will Mashiach come? Elijah replied: *Zil shaylei l'didei* — go ask him yourself.

### Gates of Rome

*Ve'heikha yasiv?* — And where is he sitting, that I might find him? Elijah replied: *A'pitcha de'karta* — at the entrance to the city. Our version reads "the city," but the actual *girsa* of the Gemara specifies *Roma* — the gates of Rome. He is sitting there among the poor who are ill, those whose bodies are afflicted with wounds and sores.

### Ready Any Moment

The Gemara elaborates on how Mashiach can be identified among the sick poor. All the others, when they dress their wounds, take off all their bandages at once, treat all their wounds together, and then rebandage everything at once. *Ihu shari chad ve'asir chad* — he alone takes off one bandage at a time, treats it, and rebandages it before moving to the next. Why? *Dilma mive'ina de'lo i'akev* — perhaps I will be needed, and I do not want to be delayed. At any moment the call could come, and he must be ready to respond immediately. He cannot afford to have all his dressings off at once.

### Mashiach Answers

Rabbi Yehoshua went to Rome, found Mashiach, and greeted him: *Shalom alecha rabbi u'mori* — peace to you, my teacher and master. Mashiach replied: *Shalom alecha bar livai* — peace to you, son of Levi. Rabbi Yehoshua asked: *L'eimatai asi mar?* — When will the master come? Mashiach replied: *Hayom* — today.

Rabbi Yehoshua returned to Elijah. Elijah asked what Mashiach had told him. Rabbi Yehoshua reported: he greeted me as *bar livai*, calling me by my father's name — which Elijah explains is itself the answer to Rabbi Yehoshua's earlier question, since addressing him thus and saying *shalom alecha* signifies that both Rabbi Yehoshua and his father will enter the World to Come. But then Rabbi Yehoshua objected: *Shakorei kashkar bi* — he lied to me! *De'amar li hayom atina ve'lo asa* — he said he was coming today and he did not come.

### If You Listen

Elijah replied: *Hachi amar lach* — this is what he was saying to you: *Hayom im bekolo tishmau* — today — if you listen to God's voice. This *midrash* is of extraordinary beauty. Mashiach is always coming today. Every day is *hayom* — today — if only the people would listen to God's voice. Redemption is not postponed to some distant future moment; it is perpetually available, perpetually conditional on the same thing: *im bekolo tishmau*.

### Mashiach Symbol

The imagery of Mashiach sitting at the gates of Rome among the sick poor carries deep symbolic weight. Rome represents the sovereignty that oppresses the Jewish people — whether the literal Roman Empire or, in later generations, Christendom, the Holy Roman Empire, and the forces that keep Israel in subjugation. Mashiach afflicted and bandaging his wounds at the gates of Rome represents the Jewish people themselves: present at the threshold of the oppressive power, not fully absorbed into it but under its dominion, suffering its effects. The teaching about dressing wounds one at a time — never fully exposed, always ready to leap up at a moment's notice — is a model for how to live in exile: attend to your wounds as you must, but always with eyes lifted toward the possibility of instantaneous redemption. Do not become so absorbed in your suffering that you lose the orientation of readiness. *Hayom im bekolo tishmau* — the redemption could come at any moment, not after some extended preparation but today, if the conditions of the heart are met.

The appearance of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's cave in this narrative may carry additional resonance: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai fled into a cave specifically to escape Roman persecution and to be able to continue performing *mitzvot* in freedom. The interplay of Roman oppression, the cave, and the encounter with Elijah and Mashiach may all be part of a unified symbolic landscape, even if Rashi does not develop it explicitly.

The Ramban, in his *Sha'ar HaGemul* (collected in *Kitvei HaRamban*), assembles many of the *midrashim* from *Chelek* and elsewhere about *Olam HaBa*, *techiyat hameitim*, and *sechar va'onesh*. This very *agadata* featured prominently in the famous Barcelona disputation between Ramban and the apostate Frai Paul. The adversary argued: the Talmud itself says Mashiach was sitting at the gates of Rome — that is Jesus, since Rome had long since become Christian. Ramban responded on multiple levels. First, the text shows plainly that Mashiach had *not* yet come — the whole point of the narrative is that Rabbi Yehoshua was asking *when* he would come, and Mashiach himself said "today if you listen" — meaning he had not come yet. Second, Ramban distinguished three categories of Jewish literature: the Bible, which all Jews accept as fully binding; the Talmud, which is the authoritative commentary on the *mitzvot* of the Torah; and *Midrash*, which is homiletical literature — like sermons that someone wrote down — which one may choose to believe or not. He said: I do not believe in this *agadata* literally, so it is not a proof for your claims. But even if you do believe in it literally, it does not support the Christian claim, because Jesus was not born after the destruction of the Temple, and the chronology does not match. The disputation offers a fascinating window into how our Gemara was read, debated, and deployed in the medieval world.

---

## Rome's Gate

### When Will Come

The students of Rabbi Yosi ben Kisma asked him: *Eimatai ben David ba?* — When will the Son of David come? He replied: *Mityarei ani shema tevakeshu mimeni ot* — I am afraid that if I tell you, you will ask me for a sign to confirm it. They assured him they would not ask for a sign.

### Gate's Cycles

He told them: *Lechesyipol hasha'ar hazeh veyibaneh veyipol veyibaneh veyipol ve'ein maspikin livnoto ad sheben David ba* — when this gate — the gate of Rome — falls, is rebuilt, falls again and is rebuilt again, and falls a third time before they can complete rebuilding it, then Ben David will come. The imagery extends beyond a single physical gate: Rome will collapse, something will rise in its place and collapse, and when the third collapse occurs faster than it can be rebuilt, the Messianic era arrives.

### Water to Blood

The students then — despite their promise — pressed him for a sign. He responded: *Im kach yehafechu mei me'arat Pamyas ledam* — if so, let the waters of *Pamyas* — which feeds, it seems, into the Jordan River — turn to blood. The evocation of the Egyptian plagues is unmistakable. *Venehefechu ledam* — and they turned to blood.

### Burial Request

As he was dying, Rabbi Yosi ben Kisma made a request of those around him: *Hamiku li aroni* — bury my coffin deep in the earth. He explained why: every palm tree in *Bavel* will have a horse of the Persian armies tied to it, so vast will be the armies of *Gog uMagog* that march through. Such will be the scale of the military forces assembled for the final war before the Messianic era.

### Gog & Magog War

And when those armies advance into *Eretz Yisrael*: *Ve'ein kol aron ve'aron shebe'eretz Yisrael she'ein sus Madai ochel bo teven* — every single coffin in the Land of Israel will be dug up and used as a feeding trough for the Median horses. This is why Rabbi Yosi ben Kisma wanted to be buried deeply: so that even his body would not be exposed to the anguish of that terrible period preceding Mashiach. The narrative marks a transition — from the question of when Mashiach comes to the nature of the *chevlei Mashiach*, the birth pangs of Mashiach, and the war of *Gog uMagog* that will precede it.

---

## Nine Months

### Evil Rule Period

Rav teaches: *Ein ben David ba ad shetifshot hamalchut haresha'ah al Yisrael tishah chodashim* — the Son of David will not come until the evil kingdom has spread its dominion over Israel for nine months. Some textual versions read *al kol ha'olam kulo* — over the entire world — rather than specifically over Israel. Rashi reconciles the two readings: *hainu kol ha'olam sheYisrael mefuzarim bo* — it means the entire world in which Israel is dispersed. Whether one reads the verse as applying to Israel specifically or the entire world, the point is that there will be a period of comprehensive domination by a single foreign power before Ben David arrives.

### Birth Pangs

The nine-month period is, of course, evocative: it is the duration of a human pregnancy. The Messianic era is being *born*, and the birth is preceded by birth pangs. The prooftext from Micah: *Lachein yitnem ad eit yoledah yaladah* — "Therefore He will give them up until the time when she who travails has given birth" — *veyeter echav yeshuvun al benei Yisrael* — "and the remnant of his brothers shall return to the children of Israel." This verse, on Rashi's reading, is consistent with understanding *al Yisrael* as referring to scattered Israel throughout the world: only after these nine months of gestation and travail will the scattered remnant return.

---

## Chevlei Mashiach

### Ulla's Wish

Ulla declares: *Yeitei velo eichminei* — let Mashiach come, but let me not see him. That is, let it happen, but not in my days. Ulla does not want to live through the *chevlei Mashiach* — the terrible suffering that precedes and accompanies the Messianic arrival. This is a remarkable statement: one should certainly long for Mashiach, but the desire not to personally witness the birth pangs is understandable.

### Rava & Yosef

Rava says the same: *Yeisei velo echaminei* — let it come but let me not see it. Rabbi Yosef, however, takes the opposite position: *Yeisei ve'ezkeh* — let it come and may I merit — *da'eisiv betulla dechufisa dechamra* — to sit in the shade of the dung of Mashiach's donkey. He is willing to endure any suffering whatsoever, however degrading the circumstances, in order to be alive at the time of Mashiach's coming.

### Yissurin Parallel

Abaye asks Rava: *Mai ta'ama* — why do you not wish to live through the Messianic era? This discussion has a direct parallel in the beginning of *Berachot*, in the discussion of *yissurin shel ahavah* — sufferings of love. In that Gemara, certain rabbis were afflicted and asked whether they cherished their sufferings as a sign of divine love and a vehicle for additional reward. Many responded: *Lo hein velo secharan* — neither them nor their reward. The attitude of Ulla and Rava toward the *chevlei Mashiach* is structurally identical.

### Torah & Kindness

A *Baraita* is cited: the students of Rabbi Eliezer asked him — what can a person do to be protected from the *chevlei Mashiach*? Rabbi Eliezer replied: *Ya'asok baTorah uvigmilus chasadim* — one should engage in Torah study and acts of kindness. If one is immersed in Torah and *gemilus chasadim*, one may be shielded even if the birth pangs occur in one's own lifetime.

### Fear of Sin

Abaye points out to Rava: but you have both Torah and *gemilus chasadim* — so why are you afraid? Rava responds: *Shema yigrom hacheit* — perhaps sin will cause it. Despite one's Torah and acts of kindness, one cannot be certain that some sin will not expose one to the sufferings. One cannot presume that one's merits are intact.

### Jacob's Fear

This is the principle of Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi, who noted a contradiction in the narratives about Jacob. God explicitly promised Jacob: *Hinei anochi imcha ushmarticha bechol asher telech* — "I am with you and will protect you wherever you go." Yet when Jacob returned and confronted the possibility of facing Esau, the Torah says *Vayira Yaakov me'od vayetzer lo* — "And Jacob was very afraid and distressed." Why was Jacob afraid if he had God's explicit promise of protection? *Mistafei shema yigrom hacheit* — he feared that perhaps sin had caused him to forfeit the protection. God's promise of protection is conditional on continuing to merit it. Even a direct divine promise does not constitute an unconditional guarantee independent of ongoing human conduct.

### Lost Miracle

This principle is further demonstrated by a *Baraita* that notes: the verse *Ad ya'avor amcha Hashem* refers to the first entry into *Eretz Yisrael*, while *ad ya'avor am zu kanita* refers to the second. *Emu'ata*, from this point one may derive: *Re'uyim hayu Yisrael la'asot lahem neis biviah shniyah* — the Jewish people should have had miracles performed for them at the time of the second entry into the Land, in the era of the Second Temple, comparable to the miracles of the first entry under Joshua. It should have been a time of full sovereignty, miraculous war, and divine intervention — not a return accomplished under the permission of the Persian king. But *ella shegaram hacheit* — sin caused the miracle not to materialize. Even where miracles were implicitly promised, they were forfeited through sin. Therefore, even Rava, with his Torah and *gemilus chasadim*, cannot be certain that he has not sinned in some way that would expose him to the *chevlei Mashiach*.

---

## Universal Suffering

### Lion Bear Snake

Rabbi Yochanan says he would prefer not to see Mashiach come in his days. Reish Lakish responds to him: *Mai ta'ama* — why? Is it perhaps because of the verse from Amos: *Ka'asher yanus ish mipnei ha'ari ufegasho hadov* — "As when a man flees from a lion and a bear meets him" — *uva habayit vesamach yado al hakir unishacho nachash* — "and he enters the house, leans his hand on the wall, and a snake bites him." The Messianic period will be one of running from one disaster to the next, with no escape and no safe harbor.

### Modern Examples

Reish Lakish says: do not take this imagery too literally. *Bo ure'ei dugmaso ba'olam hazeh* — come and see its analogue in this very world, in the present era. *Bizman she'adam yotzei lasadeh ufaga bo santeir* — when a person goes out to his field and encounters a *santeir* — a government official who does property assessments and determines field boundaries, levying taxes or altering the lines of one's land — *domeh kemi shepega'o ari* — it is as if a lion has met him. *Nichnas la'ir ufaga bo gabbai* — he enters the city and the tax collector confronts him — *domeh kemi shepega'o dov* — it is as if a bear has met him. *Nichnas leveiso umatza banav uvnotav mutalim bera'av* — he returns home and finds his children and daughters lying hungry and starving — *domeh kemi shenishacho nachash* — it is as if a snake has bitten him. The verse need not be fulfilled through supernatural calamity; it is the ordinary grind of economic oppression, governmental harassment, and domestic destitution. One should not, therefore, be so terrified of the period of Mashiach as if it will bring unprecedented cosmic catastrophe; even now we see its fulfillment in everyday life.

### Birth Pangs Verse

The verse from Isaiah: *Sha'alu na ure'u im yalad zachar* — "Ask now and see: has a male ever given birth?" — *Madua raiti kol gever yadav al chalatzav k'yoleda* — "Why do I see every man with his hands on his loins like a woman in labor?" — *Venehefechu kol panim l'yerakon* — "and all faces have turned to pallor and jaundice?" This describes a time of profound collective affliction. The verse *kol gever* — every man — is read as a reference to the One for whom all power belongs, i.e., God, as explained by Rav Yitzchak citing Rav: even God is in the anguish of these birth pangs. The birth pangs of Mashiach are not only experienced by human beings.

### God's Suffering

The Gemara elaborates: *U'mai venehefechu kol panim l'yerakon?* — what does the turning of all faces to jaundice represent? Rabbi Yochanan explains: *Pamalia shel ma'ala u'pamalia shel mata* — both the heavenly court above and the earthly assembly below. At the time of *Gog uMagog*, everyone suffers — the heavenly hosts and human beings alike. The reason God suffers is given: *Besha'ah she'amar HaKadosh Baruch Hu, halalu ma'aseh yadai v'halalu ma'aseh yadai* — at the time when God says, "These are My handiwork and those are My handiwork." Even if Israel emerges victorious and the nations that oppressed her are defeated, those nations are also God's creatures. The destruction of any human beings — Jewish or non-Jewish — causes God suffering. The Messianic war, even when won, is a time of grief for the Creator.

### Ox & Horse

Rav Papa adds a folk saying to illustrate: *Ratzya v'nafal tora v'azlu v'shadyu l'susa b'urya* — your ox went and fell, and so they put a horse at the feeding trough in its place. Rashi explains the image: you had an ox, you lost it, a horse was installed in its place, and now you have grown attached to the horse. To then replace the horse back with the original ox disrupts a new equilibrium and causes its own pain. In the Divine economy: God had the Jewish people in a position of favor and blessing. The Jewish people sinned and were displaced; the nations of the world were placed in their position of relative divine favor, so to speak, filling the stall. Now, when the time comes to restore the Jewish people and displace the nations, even that reversal — however just — carries cost. God must, as it were, remove creatures who have occupied that role, and that is painful. The Messianic restoration is not a simple, painless rectification; it involves transitions that cause suffering at a cosmic level.

---

## Hillel's Position

### Mashiach Benefits

Rav Gidel citing Rav: *Atidin Yisrael d'achli shne Mashiach* — Israel will benefit from the Messianic era; they are the ones who will enjoy its prosperity. Rav Yosef responds: *Pshita* — this is obvious. Who else would benefit — *Chivi u'Vili*? Rashi explains that *Chivi u'Vili* are just placeholder names for nobody in particular. Of course it is Israel that will benefit from the Messianic era. Why would this need to be stated?

### Hillel Claim

The answer is: *L'apukei m'de'Rabbi Hillel* — to exclude the position of Rabbi Hillel. For Rabbi Hillel said: *Ein Mashiach l'Yisrael shekvar achluhu b'imei Chizkiyahu* — there is no Mashiach for Israel, because they already consumed him — already received the fulfillment of the Messianic promises — in the days of Hezekiah. This statement, buried deep within a daf saturated with Messianic speculation, is arresting. One Amora holds that all of the prophetic promises of Mashiach were already fulfilled by Chizkiyahu HaMelech, that there is no future Mashiach to come. Rashi confirms: *She'Chizkiya haya Mashiach* — Hezekiah was the Mashiach, and the consolations promised by the prophets were realized in his era. Rav Gidel's statement — that Israel will benefit in the Messianic times — is therefore specifically formulated to reject this position.

### Dogma Questions

This raises profound questions. If one holds that belief in Mashiach is a binding article of faith — that one who denies it is an *apikorus* — what is the status of Rabbi Hillel, who apparently denied it? One might suggest that in his time the question was still open, and it was only subsequently settled that there will indeed be a Mashiach. But this raises a further and deeper question: can one *pasken* — can one render a binding halachic-like ruling — on matters of *emunah*? Is the existence of Mashiach a dogmatic fact that simply is or is not, independent of rabbinic decision? Or can it be the subject of deliberation and determination in the way that ritual questions are? The fact that our Gemara presents it as a disputed matter — where one Amora openly denies a future Mashiach and the response is not a ruling against him but a counter-argument from another sage — is itself significant. As the Rambam formulates this among his thirteen principles, the question of whether issues of *emunah* can be *paskened* the way *halacha* is *paskened* is a genuinely fascinating one, and our daf provides an extraordinary case study for that inquiry.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 99

## Purpose of Creation

### World Created For

The *daf* begins by picking up at the bottom of 98b, where the *Gemara* transitions from the *aggadeta* surrounding *Techiyat Hameitim*, *Olam Haba*, and *Yemot Hamashiach* — the themes provoked by the *mishna*'s list of those who have no portion in the world to come — toward the remainder of that list. Before doing so, the *Gemara* offers a remarkable three-way debate about the very purpose of creation.

*Amar Rav*: the world was created for the sake of David. *U'Shmuel amar l'Moshe*: for the sake of Moshe Rabbeinu. *V'Yochanan amar l'Mashiach*: for the sake of *Mashiach*.

Of the three positions, *l'Moshe* is perhaps the most classically rabbinic: the world exists for *Torah*, for learning and performing *mitzvot*. *L'Mashiach* is also readily understood — the world is oriented toward a future redeemed and perfected reality. But what is the meaning of *l'David*? Rashi's answer is elegant: it is *bizchut tishbachot she'haya omer lifnei Hakadosh Baruch Hu* — on account of the praises that David would offer before God. So the three visions are *tefillah*, *Torah*, and *tikkun olam* in its deepest sense.

There is also something worth noting in the contrast between *l'David* and *l'Mashiach*. David, after all, is himself a *Mashiach* — yet he is a figure who inhabits the imperfect world, a righteous king who nonetheless sins with Bat Sheva and does *teshuvah*. This may represent a tension between two orientations: whether the purpose of existence is to strive for the highest future ideal, or to live the most perfected life possible within the flawed world we actually inhabit. This resonates with Shmuel's position elsewhere — *ein bein olam hazeh l'yemot Hamashiach ela shibud malchuyot* — the messianic era differs from this world only in that foreign domination will cease.

### Names of Mashiach

The *Gemara* then asks: *u'mah shemo* — what is the name of *Mashiach*? What follows is a charmingly self-referential series of opinions. *Debei Rabbi Shila amri Shilo shemo* — the school of Rabbi Shila says his name is *Shilo*, deriving it from the verse *ad ki yavo Shilo*. *Debei Rabbi Yannai amri Yanun shemo* — the school of Rabbi Yannai says his name is *Yanun*, from the verse *yehi shemo l'olam lifnei shemesh Yanun shemo*. *Debei Rabbi Chanina amri Chanina shemo* — the school of Rabbi Chanina says his name is *Chanina*, from *asher lo eten lachem chanina*. And *yesh omrim*: his name is *Menachem ben Chizkiyah*, from *ki rachak mimeni menachem*.

Note that in each case, the school names *Mashiach* after its own *rebbe*. This is not mere self-promotion; rather, it reflects a genuine theological sensibility — that *Mashiach* could in theory arrive in any generation, and a figure of the stature of one's own *rebbe* might be that person. Each school is saying: the potential is real and present. This is precisely the teaching from the *daf* before — *im bekolo tishma'u*, if you listen to his voice today. So the naming exercises are less about pinpointing a historical individual and more about cultivating a living sense of messianic imminence.

*V'rabanan amri*: the rabbis say his name is *Chivara d'vei Rabbi* — the sick one, the leper of the house of *Rebbe*. This returns to the image of the suffering servant: *achen cholyenu hu nasa, umachovenu sevelam, va'anachnu chashavnuhu nagua umukeh elohim ume'uneh* — our illnesses he bears, our wounds he suffered, we considered him smitten by God and afflicted.

### Mashiach Leadership

On this passage, *Amar Rav Nachman*: *im min chayya hu* — if he is among the living, *kegon ana* — I would be a fitting example. Rashi offers two readings of this phrase, but the Maharsha notes that Rav Nachman was a figure of political leadership among the Jews, and *Mashiach* is, among other things, a political head. The verse he cites supports this: *vehaya adiro mimenu umoshlo mikirbo yetzei* — the glorious one will be from within them and the ruler will emerge from their midst. The tension between this image of powerful kingship and the earlier image of the leprous suffering servant is openly acknowledged — these are different visions of *Mashiach* that do not fully reconcile.

*Amar Rav*: if he is comparable to someone living, *kegon Rabbeinu Hakadosh* — like Rabbi Yehuda Hanasi, who embodied the combination of religious and political authority. If comparable to someone who has passed, *kegon Daniel ish chamudot* — Daniel, who exercised a kind of mixed authority within a non-Jewish political system while maintaining his religious identity.

### David vs. Mashiach

*Amar Rav Yehuda Amar Rav*: God will raise up for Israel another David — not merely a descendant of David, but another David. The verse reads *ve'avadu et Hashem eloheihem ve'et David malkam asher akim lahem* — and they will serve Hashem their God and David their king, whom I will raise for them. Crucially, the verse says *akim* — I will raise — not *heikim* — I have raised — pointing toward a future event.

Rav Papa then asks of Abaye: does not another verse call him *nasi* — a prince — rather than *melech*, a king? The *Gemara* resolves this through the analogy of *Keisar upalgi Keisar* — the Caesar and the half-Caesar. Rashi explains: the newly born David — whatever it means to call him a new David rather than simply *Ben David* — will be the king, while the resurrected King David himself will be second in command.

---

## Messianic Duration

### Length Calculations

The *Gemara* now turns to a different question that grows out of an adjacent discussion. The verse *hoi hamit'avim et yom Hashem* — woe to those who yearn for the day of God — is expounded by *Darash Rav Simlai*: why are you longing for that day? *Hu choshech velo or* — it will be a day of darkness, not light. He offers a *mashal*: a rooster and a bat were both waiting for daybreak. The rooster says to the bat — I understand why I wait for dawn, it is my time. But why do *you* wait for light? The daylight will not benefit you.

The point is not that the messianic day brings suffering to the righteous — it does not. Rather, the wicked are being warned: you are like the bat who yearns for a dawn that will only harm you. The day of *Mashiach* will be a day of judgment for those who have wronged Israel.

This is followed by the opening of 99a: *Ve-hainu d'amar lei ha-hu mina le-Rabbi Abbahu* — a certain sectarian asked Rabbi Abbahu: when will *Mashiach* come? Rabbi Abbahu replied: when darkness covers those people — meaning you. The sectarian objected: are you cursing me? Rabbi Abbahu responded: it is a verse — *ki hinei ha-choshech yechaseh eretz va-arafel le-umim, ve-alayich yizrach Hashem, u-chevodo alayich yeira-eh* — darkness will cover the earth and thick cloud the nations, but upon you God will shine forth.

The *Gemara* then turns to the question of how long the messianic period will last. *Tanya*: Rabbi Eliezer says *yemot ha-Mashiach* will last forty years, deriving this from the verse *arbaim shana akut be-dor* — forty years I seized the generation — read together with *samcheinu kiyemos inisanu* — make us rejoice like the days of our affliction. The days of affliction in the wilderness were forty, and those forty transfer to forty years of the messianic era. Rashi notes a variant reading of four thousand years, based on the principle that one day of God equals a thousand years.

Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya says seventy years, from *ve-haya ba-yom ha-hu ve-nishkachat tzor shivim shana ki-ymei melech echad* — Tyre will be forgotten for seventy years, like the days of one king. The *Gemara* asks: which is the distinctive, singular king? *Hevei omer zeh Mashiach* — that must refer to *Mashiach*.

*Rabbi* says three generations, from the verse *yira-ucha im shemesh ve-lifnei yarei-ach dor dorim* — they will fear You with the sun and before the moon, generation of generations. Rashi explains that the moon represents the Kingdom of the House of David. *Dor dorim* — one generation plus two equals three.

This raises a question: does the messianic period lasting multiple generations imply that individuals will live for extraordinary lengths of time, or simply that the *Melech Mashiach* will die, his son will rule, and so on, with the messianic epoch continuing across natural lifespans? The *Gemara* leaves this open.

Now Rabbi Hillel — a minor figure in the *Gemara*, not to be confused with the great Hillel — makes a striking statement: *ein lahem mashiach l'Yisrael, she-kvar achaluhu bi-ymei Chizkiyahu* — there will be no *Mashiach* for Israel, for they already consumed that with Chizkiyahu; he was the fulfillment of all the prophetic visions. *Amar Rav Yosef*: *shrei lei mareih le-Rabbi Hillel* — may God forgive Rabbi Hillel for such an error. Chizkiyahu lived during the first *Beit Ha-Mikdash*, yet the prophet Zechariah — the one who prophesied during the second *Beit Hamikdash* — was still proclaiming *gili me'od bat Tzion, hineh malkeich yavo lach, tzadik ve-nosha hu ani ve-rochev al chamor* — rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion, your king will come to you, righteous and redeemed, poor and riding on a donkey. How could those visions have already been fulfilled in Chizkiyahu's time?

Rashi's reading of Rabbi Hillel's position is illuminating: Rabbi Hillel is not denying a future redeemed world. Rather, he holds that God Himself will reign directly — *hakadosh baruch hu yimloch b'atzmo v'yigaleim l'vado* — and there will be no human Davidic king as intermediary. It almost sounds like leaping straight to the *Olam Haba* period, a world governed directly by the divine presence without the medium of a human king.

What is theologically remarkable is how the *Gemara* responds. Rav Yosef says *shrei lei mareih* — God should forgive him — not out of horror at heresy, but essentially because the position is refuted by a *pasuk*. The *Gemara* does not react with shock that a rabbi denied the existence of *Mashiach*. This bears on the broader question of *emunah* as *psak*: can dogma be adjudicated? David Bleich, in his introduction to *In Perfect Faith*, argues that yes, *emunah* can be *paskened*, that we have *paskened* against Rabbi Hillel, and that denying *Mashiach* is now *kefirah* in a way it was not before we did so. Marc Shapiro, by contrast, argues that questions of dogma concern eternal truths — either *Mashiach* is coming or not — so the framing of *psak* is somewhat misplaced. What we can say is that Rabbi Hillel was always wrong as a matter of what will actually happen. The question of *psak* may apply more precisely to the *consequences* of holding incorrect beliefs. In any event, the *Gemara*'s relatively calm handling of Rabbi Hillel's position is striking.

### History Duration

*Tanya idach* — another *braita* returns to calculating the duration of *yemot ha-Mashiach*. Rabbi Eliezer again says forty years, now from the verse *vaya'anchecha vayarivecha vaya'achilecha et ha-man* — God afflicted you and made you hungry and fed you the *man*, referring to the forty years of wandering — combined again with *samcheinu kiyemos inisanu*. Rabbi Dosa says four hundred years, from *ve-avadum ve-inu osam arba meos shanah* — they will enslave and afflict them four hundred years — again with the same rejoicing verse equating future joy with past affliction. *Rabbi* says three hundred and sixty-five years, like the days of the solar year — *ki yom nakam b'libbi u'shnas geulai ba'ah* — a day of vengeance is in my heart, and the year of my redemption is come, reading the "day" as each day of the year and the "year" as the total. Again Rashi here carries a variant reading of three hundred and sixty-five thousand years.

On the phrase *ki yom nakam b'libbi*, Rabbi Yochanan comments: *l'libbi galis', l'eivarai lo galis'* — I have revealed it to my heart but not to my limbs. God has not even articulated to Himself, as it were, what that day will be, so deeply hidden is it. Resh Lakish adds: *l'libbi galis', l'malachei hashareit lo galis'* — I admitted it to myself but did not tell even the angels.

*Tanya Avimi brei d'Rabbi Abbahu*: *yemos hamashiach l'yisrael shivas alafim shanah* — seven thousand years. This is derived from the rejoicing of the *chatan* over the *kallah* — just as there are seven days of *sheva brachos*, so one day per thousand years yields seven thousand years.

*Amar Rav Yehuda Amar Shmuel*: *yemos hamashiach k'yom she'nivra ha'olam v'ad achshav* — the messianic period will equal the entire span of world history from creation until now. The *pasuk* is *ki-ymei hashamayim al ha'aretz* — like the days of the heavens upon the earth. Whether this implies that individuals will live for that extraordinary span, or simply that the messianic epoch as a whole will endure that long, is left open.

*Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak amar*: *ki-ymei Noach v'ad achshav* — from the days of Noah until now — citing the verse *ki mei Noach zos li asher nishbati me'avor mei Noach od al ha'aretz*. Rashi explains: God's oath after the flood was not to destroy the world; so when *Mashiach* comes, the oath covers the length from Noah until now, after which the world will be destroyed and *Olam Haba* will be recreated.

### Prophetic Visions

*Amar Rabbi Chiya bar Abba Amar Rabbi Yochanan*: *kol hanevi'im kulam lo nisnab'u ela l'yimos hamashiach* — all the prophets prophesied only about the messianic period. The visions of lions lying down with lambs, swords beaten into plowshares — these describe the messianic era. But when it comes to *Olam Haba* itself, *ayin lo ra'asah Elokim zulasecha* — no eye has seen it, God, other than You; *ya'aseh l'mechakeh lo* — You will do it for the one who longs for it.

### Shmuel's View

This position argues with Shmuel. *D'amar Shmuel*: *ein bein ha'olam hazeh l'yimos hamashiach ela shibud malchuyos* — there is no difference between this world and the messianic era except subjugation to foreign powers. For Shmuel, the messianic period is thoroughly this-worldly, and therefore the prophetic visions must be oriented toward the truly transcendent *Olam Haba*. For Rabbi Yochanan, the messianic period itself is miraculous — and *Olam Haba* surpasses even prophetic vision entirely.

---

## Hidden Reward

### Reward Levels

The same teaching of Rabbi Chiya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan is then cited in a second formulation: *kol hanevi'im lo nisnabu ela l'ba'alei teshuvah* — all the prophetic visions were only for those who sinned and repented. But for *tzaddikim gemurim* — those who never sinned at all — *ayin lo ra'asah Elokim zulasecha*: their reward is utterly beyond prophetic sight.

### Baalei Teshuvah

This claim that the *tzaddikim gemurim* occupy a higher plane than the *ba'alei teshuvah* argues with Rabbi Abbahu: *d'amar Rabbi Abbahu, makom she'ba'alei teshuvah omdim sham tzaddikim einam omdim* — the place where *ba'alei teshuvah* stand, the fully righteous cannot stand. His proof is the verse *shalom shalom l'rachok v'lakarov* — peace, peace to the distant and to the near — where peace is extended first to *rachok*, those who were once far and have drawn near, and only then to *karov*, those who have always been near. *B'reisha rachok* — first to those who started distant. So the *ba'alei teshuvah* receive precedence.

Rabbi Yochanan reads the same verse differently to support his position: *rachok* refers to one who is distant from sin — i.e., never sinned — while *karov* refers to one who had been close to sin and only now has distanced from it. The reading is admittedly strained.

### Eden Reward

Then the *Gemara* asks directly: *mai ayin lo ra'asah* — what is this unseen reward? After all the majestic build-up — "no eye has ever seen, not even through the prophetic lens" — the *Gemara* proceeds to answer, and the answers are, perhaps deliberately, somewhat deflating. *Amar Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi*: *zeh yayin hameshummar be'anavav misheshes yemei bereishis* — it is wine that has been stored in its grapes since the six days of creation. The unseen reward is the finest wine imaginable. This reads almost like a gentle puncturing of the preceding rhetoric.

Resh Lakish says: *zeh Eden* — it is Eden itself. The *Gemara* responds: but did not the first human being live in Eden? He lived only in the *gan*, the garden — but not Eden itself. And if you say the *gan* and *Eden* are the same, the verse teaches otherwise: *v'nahar yotzei me'Eden l'hashkot es hagan* — a river flows out of Eden to water the garden. Eden is distinct from and greater than the garden. It is in that unexplored Eden that the reward awaits.

There is, however, a deeper reading — not the material pleasures of wine or botanical paradise, but the sense of direct divine presence. As other *Gemara* passages describe *Olam Haba*: the righteous sit with crowns on their heads and bask in the radiance of the *Shechinah*. In that light, *Eden* is less a place than an encounter — an unmediated experience of the divine that no prophetic eye has glimpsed.

---

## Torah from Heaven

### Prooftext

Having completed the extended discussion of *Techiyat Hameitim*, *Olam Haba*, and *Yemot Hamashiach*, the *Gemara* turns to the next item on the *mishna*'s list: *Ha-Omer Ein Torah Min Ha-Shamayim* — one who says that *Torah* is not from heaven. The operative verse is *ki devar Hashem bazah* — for the word of God he has despised — followed by *hikaret tikaret ha-nefesh ha-hi avonah bah* — that person shall be surely cut off, his sin is with him. While *karet* alone attaches to many sins, the double language *hikaret tikaret* is here read as *karet* in this world and *karet* in the next — loss of a portion in *Olam Haba*.

*Tanu Rabbanan*: *ki devar Hashem bazah* — *zeh ha-omer ein Torah min hashamayim* — this is the one who says *Torah* is not from heaven. Furthermore, even if a person says the entire *Torah* is from heaven *chutz mipasuk echad* — except for one verse — claiming Moshe said it on his own without divine instruction — *zehu ki devar Hashem bazah*. Even one word of God, denied, constitutes despising God's word. The same applies to one who denies a single rabbinic inference: *chutz midekduk zeh, chutz migezeirah shavah zo* — everything except this one *kal vachomer*, everything except this one *gezeirah shavah* — even that partial denial is *ki devar Hashem bazah*. The Maharsha notes that the emphasis here is on *davar* — speech — suggesting that even the oral dimension, not only the written text, falls within the scope of this prohibition.

### Apikoros Definition

*Davar acher*: *ki devar Hashem bazah* — *zeh apikoros*. This demands careful attention. There is a widespread assumption that *apikoros* means heretic — specifically, one who rejects articles of Jewish dogma — and this assumption derives from the Rambam, who systematized the *ikarei emunah* and used *apikoros* as his hook for the category of those who deny fundamental beliefs. But that is not what the *Gemara* means by the term.

From the *Gemara*'s perspective, an *apikoros* is someone who acts in a disrespectful and demeaning manner toward *Torah* or toward *Torah* scholars. The classic *Gemara* definition is *mevazeh talmidei chachamim* — one who demeans scholars of *Torah*. This is precisely the language of *ki devar Hashem bazah* — *mevazeh*, to demean — demonstrating that treating those who embody and represent *Devar Hashem* in a contemptuous manner is itself a form of despising God's word.

So the two entries from the *mishna* — *ein Torah min hashamayim* and *apikoros* — are both expressions of the same root: treating *Devar Hashem* with contempt, whether by denying it is divine or by demeaning its human representatives.

*Davar acher*: *ki devar Hashem bazah* — *zeh megaleh panim ba-Torah*. This phrase is often encountered with the addition *shelo ke-halacha* — one who explicates *Torah* contrary to *halacha* — and read as referring to heretical or deviant interpretation. But the *Gemara* does not use the phrase *shelo ke-halacha* here; that is a later gloss. *Megaleh panim ba-Torah* means what it literally says: *gillui panim* — to bare one's face, to act brazenly and insolently toward the *Torah*. It describes an attitude of brazen disrespect, not an act of textual misinterpretation. The gloss *shelo ke-halacha* appears in only one place, and even there it is clearly secondary.

Continuing: *zeh meifer brit basar* — one who has reversed the covenant of the flesh, undoing circumcision surgically. *Hikaret tikaret* — cut off in this world and cut off in the next.

What emerges from this entire passage is significant: what is being catalogued here is not primarily a list of incorrect dogmas. It is a collection of attitudes and actions — disrespect toward *Torah*, toward *talmidei chachamim*, toward one's covenantal relationship with God. It is the Rambam who transforms this material into a system of dogma with formal consequences for unbelief. The *Gemara* itself is far more interested in relationship and orientation than in propositional correctness. Even the *Chatam Sofer*, it should be noted, was troubled by the Rambam's systematization of thirteen *ikarei emunah*, arguing that fundamentally there are only two — God exists, and God gave the *Torah* — from which everything else follows.

### Interpretations

*Mikan amar Rabbi Eliezer HaModai* in *Pirkei Avot*: one who desecrates the sacrifices, one who demeans the *mo'adot* — Rashi says this refers to *Chol HaMoed*, the more vulnerable liminal period — one who undoes *brit milah*, one who acts brazenly toward *Torah*, and one who shames his friend in public — *af al pi sheyesh beyado Torah uma'asim tovim ein lo chelek l'Olam Haba* — even with much *Torah* and good deeds, has no portion in the world to come. Whether all of these are derived from the single verse *ki devar Hashem bazah* involves some creative reading: the sacrifices are things sanctified by God; the *mo'adim* are time sanctified by God; *malbish pnei chaveiro* may relate to human beings being created *betzelem Elokim*. Rashi seems to read it roughly this way.

*Tanya idach*: another *braita* adds that even one who says the entire *Torah* is from heaven except for this one *pasuk*, or this one inferential derivation, or this one *gezeirah shavah* — each of these is *ki devar Hashem bazah*.

---

## Attitudes Toward Torah

### Learn and Teach

*Tanya*: *Rebbi Meir omer* — whoever learns *Torah* and does not teach it, *zehu ki devar Hashem bazah*. The Maharsha explains the link to the verse: teaching requires verbalization — *dibbur* — while learning alone does not necessarily. To refuse to transmit is to be *mevaze* the *davar* of God, demeaning the verbal, living quality of *Devar Hashem*. Once again, the *Gemara* slides naturally between matters of faith, matters of attitude, and matters of action — without privileging the dogmatic over the relational.

*Rebbi Nasan omer*: whoever is not careful to repeat the *mishna* — to go over it again and again — is in a sense despising God's word, because the *mishna* is what makes the *pesukim* meaningful.

*Rebbi Nehorai omer*: whoever can engage in *Torah* and chooses not to — whoever sets other priorities above *Devar Hashem* — that too is *ki devar Hashem bazah*.

*Rebbi Yishmael omer*: this designation properly belongs to *oved avodah zarah*. His point seems to be that if we are going to be reading into this verse the severe consequence of having no *chelek l'Olam Haba*, we should reserve that for genuinely weighty acts. The *Gemara* asks how *avodah zarah* is derived from *ki devar Hashem bazah*. *Detani Debei Rebbi Yishmael*: *ki devar Hashem bazah* — *zeh hamevaze dibbur shene'emar lo l'Moshe mi-Sinai* — one who rejects the prime *dibbur* given at Sinai: *Anochi Hashem Elokecha* and *Lo yihiyeh lecha elohim acheirim* — the very words all of Israel heard directly. Rejecting *avodah zarah* is rejecting the foundational speech-act of revelation.

### Chazarah

*Rebbi Yehoshua ben Korcha omer*: whoever learns *Torah* and does not review it — *eino chozer aleha* — is likened to one who plants without harvesting. There is no point in the planting if you are not going to follow through with the harvest. The seed will simply rot in the ground. Doing *chazarah* is the act of cultivation that allows what was planted to take root, grow, and become something lasting. Failing to do so may itself be a form of *ki devar Hashem bazah* — it signals that you do not value it enough to follow through.

### Forgetting

*Rebbi Yehoshua omer*: whoever learns *Torah* and actually forgets it — *kol halomed Torah u'meshach'cha* — is likened to *ishah she'yoledes ve'koveres* — a woman who gives birth and then buries her child. The image is devastating. The previous metaphor allowed for some hope — perhaps something will grow despite the lack of harvesting — but this metaphor allows for none. To have invested all that effort in bringing something to life, only to watch it die — *why did you go through all this?* There is something almost like the concept of *chevlei leidah shel Mashiach* echoing here: you endure the labor pains of birth only to have the child taken from you. The follow-through — the *chazarah* — requires less effort than the initial learning, and yet it is the thing that sustains everything.

### Torah Labor

*Rebbi Akiva omer*: *zemer bechol yom zemer bechol yom* — your *Torah* should be a song every day. The Maharsha suggests that *zemer* here might mean *zomer* — to prune, to tend to what you have planted — but the more natural reading is musical. The way to keep *Torah* alive is to make it into a song: something you repeat again and again, something you return to naturally. Memory attaches powerfully to music; the children in the old *chadarim* had a *niggun* to the learning, and we remember melodies with a tenacity we rarely achieve for ordinary words. Rashi confirms: *haya mesader limudcha af al pi shesedurah beficha ke-zemer* — arrange your learning even when it is already arranged in your mouth, like a song. And the reward? *Vehu yigrom lecha shetehe l'Olam Haba be-simcha u-ve-shirim* — it will bring you to *Olam Haba* with joy and with song.

*Amar Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi*: what is the verse? *Nefesh amal amla lo ki akaf alav pihu* — if you labor, it will labor for you, because his mouth has devoted itself to it. Rashi: *mipnei she-amal ba-Torah, Torah omelet lo* — because you labored in *Torah*, *Torah* labors for you. The Maharsha reads this as the hidden secrets of *Torah* being revealed to you in *Olam Haba*. But there is also a more immediate reading: there is a percolating effect in deep learning. You work at something, you cannot quite reach it, you step away — and then the understanding arrives, because something in your mind was still processing it. If you have made it into a song and keep returning to it, then even when you are not consciously engaged, the *Torah* continues to work within you. *Hu amal be-makom zeh ve-Torato amla lo be-makom acher* — you labor here, and your *Torah* labors for you somewhere else.

*Amar Rabbi Eliezer kol adam le-amal nivra* — every person is created for labor. The verse in *Iyov*: *ki adam le-amal yulad*. The *Gemara* asks: does this mean labor of the mouth or physical labor? Refining further: if it means the mouth, does it mean *Torah* or ordinary speech? The answer builds through a chain: *lo yamush sefer ha-Torah ha-zeh mipicha* — let this *sefer Torah* not depart from your mouth — resolving that the labor of the mouth means *Torah*. And *Rava* adds: *kulhu gufei deruftaki ninhu* — all people are laborers in some sense. *Tovei le-dizakei de-havei deruftaki d'Oraisa* — fortunate are those who merit that they become laborers in *Torah*.

### Lishmah

It is striking that a *sugya* ostensibly about *Torah min ha-shamayim* has given so much space to *chazarah*, forgetting, the labor of *Torah*, and singing. The *Gemara* is less interested in dogma as a propositional category and more in the lived relationship one cultivates with *Torah* — whether one values it enough to review it, invest in it, and let it permeate one's life.

*Ve-no'ef isha chaser lev, amar Reish Lakish*: *zeh ha-lomed Torah l'prakim* — this refers to one who learns *Torah* intermittently, when convenient, every now and then. The verse is about the adulterer who lacks heart, and Resh Lakish maps it onto the person whose relationship to *Torah* is not like a marriage — ongoing, committed, primary — but like an affair: occasional, disconnected, without depth. A deep and sustaining relationship with *Torah* requires constancy. *Ki na'im ki tishmerem be-vitnecha yikonu yachdav al sfatecha* — they are pleasant when you keep them in your belly; they will be established well on your lips.

---

## Menashe Example

### Menashe

*Ve-ha-nefesh asher ta'aseh be-yad rama* — and the soul that acts with a high hand. *Zeh Menashe ben Chizkiyah* — this refers to Menashe ben Chizkiyah. *She-haya yoshev ve-doresh b'agadot shel dofi* — he would sit and expound on teachings that he considered foolish or degraded. He would say: did Moshe have nothing better to write than *va-achot Lotan Timna ve-Timna hayta pilegesh l'Elifaz* — that Lotan's sister was Timna and Timna was the concubine of Elifaz? What is the need for all these genealogies?

There is a question as to exactly which verses bother him. Perhaps it is the entire genealogical section of Esav's descendants. The common thread between the Timna passage and the mandrakes — *vayeilech Reuven bimei ketzir chitim vayimtza dudaim basadeh* — may be a concern about passages that seem to deal with sexual or carnal themes (*pilegesh*, the aphrodisiac properties attributed to mandrakes). But whether his complaint is about irrelevance, impropriety, or simply the apparent mundaneness of certain passages, his essential posture is dismissive: why does this belong in the *Torah*?

### Divine Rebuke

*Yatzta bat kol ve'amra lo* — a heavenly voice came out and said to him: *teshev be'achicha tedaber, beven imecha titen dofi* — will you sit and speak against your brother, will you ascribe foolishness to your mother's son? *Eileh asita ve-hecherashti, dimita hayot eheyeh chamocha* — you have done this and I was silent, and you thought that my silence meant I was with you. *Ochichecha* — I will now rebuke you, and *ve-erecha l'einecha* — I will lay my argument before your eyes.

The *bat kol*'s rebuke carries a powerful point about silence as perceived complicity. Because God did not immediately punish Menashe for his dismissiveness, Menashe assumed endorsement. The verse captures the danger of interpreting divine patience as divine agreement.

*Ve-alav meforash ba-kabalah*: the prophets make explicit what happens to such a person — *hoi moshchei he'avon be-chavlei hashav uche'avot ha'agalah chata'ah* — woe to those who drag iniquity with ropes of nothingness and like the cords of a wagon drag sin. *Amar Rabbi Assi*: *yeitzer hara betichilah domeh la-chut shel kuvya* — the evil inclination initially is like a spider's thread. *Ul'vasof domeh ke'avot ha'agalah* — but if allowed to continue, it thickens into ropes as heavy as a wagon's cord.

The principle illustrated is: Menashe began with what might seem like a relatively modest position — asking why certain *pesukim* are necessary. But that attitude, if unchecked, grows. It is one thing to ask, in genuine curiosity, what the purpose is of a particular passage. It is something else entirely to declare it foolish or beneath inclusion in the *Torah*. That posture of dismissal can metastasize into something far darker. Small disrespect, left unchallenged, becomes deep rejection.

### Timna Story

*De'ata le-mai achot Lotan Timna, mai hi?* The *Gemara* now explains the *purpose* of those verses that Menashe mocked. *Timna bat melachim havaia* — Timna was a daughter of kings: *aluf Lotan, aluf Timna* — and every *aluf* is a form of royalty, a king without a crown. *Ba'aya l'igurei* — she wished to convert. *Atai eitzel Avraham, Yitzchak ve-Yaakov, ve-lo kibluha* — she came to Avraham, Yitzchak, and Yaakov, and they refused to accept her.

*Halacha ve-hayta pilegesh l'Elifaz ben Esau* — she then became a concubine to Elifaz ben Esav. *Amra mutav shetehei shifchah l'umah zo ve-lo tehei gvirah l'umah acheret* — better to be a maidservant to this nation than a great woman in any other nation. *Nafak minah Amalek* — and from her came Amalek, the nation that attacked Israel and represents the archetype of evil in Jewish history.

*Mai ta'ama? De-lo ibei lehu le-rachakah* — why did Amalek emerge from her? Because the Avot should not have pushed her away. Rashi is explicit: *she-haya lahem le-gayera* — they should have converted her. This is a striking and oft-cited *Gemara* on the consequences of turning away sincere converts. Timna had no malice; she sought to attach herself to the Jewish people with great devotion. The responsibility for what emerged from her rejection lies, the *Gemara* says, with those who sent her away.

### Mandrakes

*Vayelech Reuven bimei ketzir chitim* — and Reuven went during the wheat harvest. *Amar Rav bar Rav Yitzchak Amar Rav*: the point of this verse is to show us the virtue of the righteous — *mitovatan shel tzadikim she-ein poshtim yedeihem be-gazal* — they do not extend their hands in theft. Rashi explains: after the field had been harvested, it was customary and acceptable for others to enter. Reuven went precisely at that time, making clear that he was not trespassing or taking what was not his.

*Vayimtza dudaim ba-sadeh* — and he found *dudaim* in the field. *Mai dudaim?* Rav says *yavrochei*. Levi says *sigli* — Rashi identifies this as a violet. Rabbi Yonatan says *savisky*, some type of spice or flower. The exact botanical identification remains uncertain.

---

## Torah Power

### Peace and Protection

*Amar Rabbi Alexandri*: *kol ha-osek ba-Torah lishmah* — whoever occupies himself with *Torah* for its own sake, *mashim shalom be-pamalia shel ma'ala u-ve-pamalia shel mata* — makes peace in the family above and the family below, in heaven and on earth. The verse: *o yachazek be-maozi ya'aseh shalom li shalom ya'aseh li* — two instances of peace, one above and one below.

*Rava amar*: *ke-ilu bana paltarin shel ma'ala ve-shel mata* — it is as if he built a palace above and below. The verse: *va-asim devarai be-ficha, ub-tzel yadi kisiticha linto'a shamayim ve-lisod aretz* — I have placed My words in your mouth and covered you in the shadow of My hand, to plant the heavens and to found the earth. True love and connection to *Torah* simultaneously serves God and sustains this world.

*Rabbi Yochanan amar*: *af megin al kol ha-olam kulo* — moreover, it protects the entire world. *Ub-tzel yadi kisiticha* — in the shadow of My hand I have covered you. The learning of *Torah* is the opposite of *mevaze Devar Hashem*; it is what keeps the world protected and sustained.

*Levi amar*: *af me-karev et ha-geulah* — it brings the redemption closer. *Ve-lomar le-Tzion ami atah* — and to say to Zion: you are My people.

### Teaching Creation

*Resh Lakish amar*: *kol ha-melamed et ben chavero Torah* — whoever teaches his friend's son *Torah* — *ma'ala alav ha-katuv ke-ilu asa'o* — the verse treats him as though he created that person, giving him a spiritual life. The verse: *ve-et ha-nefesh asher asu ve-Charan* — the souls that they made in Charan. By spreading God's word and drawing a person into *Torah*, one participates in a kind of spiritual birth.

*Rabbi Eleazar amar*: *ke-ilu asan l'divrei Torah* — it is as if you made the words of *Torah* themselves. By loving *Torah* enough to spread it, you help bring *Torah* into actual existence in the world.

*Ve-Rava amar*: *ke-ilu asa'o l'atzmo* — it is as if you made yourself. In teaching and spreading *Torah*, you transform yourself in the process. *Va-asitem otam — al tikrei otam ela atem* — do not read "them" but "yourselves."

### Encouraging Mitzvot

*Amar Rabbi Abbahu*: *kol ha-ma'aseh et chavero le-dvar mitzvah* — whoever encourages or compels his friend to perform a *mitzvah* — *ma'ala alav ha-katuv ke-ilu asa'o* — it is as though he himself performed it. The proof: *u-matcha asher hikita bo et ha-Ye'or* — your staff with which you struck the Nile. But did *Moshe* strike the Nile? It was *Aharon* who struck! Rather, this teaches that because *Moshe* directed and enabled *Aharon*, the act is attributed to him. The one who inspires another to do a *mitzvah* receives the credit as though he had done it himself.

The *daf* closes here. Tomorrow the *Gemara* will take up the definition of *apikoros* — and as the lecturer flags in advance: from the *Gemara*'s own perspective, it is emphatically not the apostate, and it is not defined by one's stance on the *ikarei emunah*. That transformation of the term belongs to the Rambam, and it is a transformation the *Gemara* itself does not recognize.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 100

## Epikoros Definition

### Perek Chelek Intro

Perek Chelek — the tenth chapter of Sanhedrin — is among the most consequential chapters in all of *shas*, cataloguing those who forfeit their share in the world to come. We begin our treatment of Daf 100 from the bottom of 99b, where the *gemara* introduces the category of *epikoros* as one of the individuals enumerated in the *mishnah* who has no share in *olam haba*. Before arriving at the *epikoros* proper, however, the *gemara* opens with several teachings about those who engage in Torah study and their cosmic significance.

Rava teaches that whoever occupies himself with Torah is as if he built a heavenly and earthly palace, as it is written: *va'asim devarai beficha uvtzel yadai kisiticha lintoa shamayim uliyased aretz* — "I have placed My words in your mouth and with the shadow of My hand I have covered you, to plant the heavens and establish the earth." Resh Lakish adds that such a person protects the entire world, as it is written *uvtzel yadecha kisiticha* — I cover you with the shadow of My hand. And Levi adds that one who studies Torah even hastens the redemption, as it is written *uletzion ami ata*.

Resh Lakish further teaches that one who teaches another's child Torah is credited by Scripture as if he created him, drawing from the verse regarding Avram and Sarai: *ve'et hanefesh asher asu veCharan* — "and the souls that they made in Charan." Rava goes further: one who teaches Torah to another is as if he created himself, reading *va'asitem otam* — "and you shall do them" — not as *otam*, them, but as *atem*, you. Rabbi Abahu adds yet another dimension: one who causes another to perform a *mitzvah* is credited as if he performed it himself, deriving this from the verse *umatcha asher hikita bo et hayeor* — "your staff with which you struck the Nile" — though it was Aharon who actually struck it, not Moshe. The *midrash* tells us that Moshe felt a warm relationship with the Nile, which had protected him, and so had Aharon perform the act in his place. Yet Scripture credits the staff — and thus Moshe — with the deed, to teach that one who causes another to perform a *mitzvah* is as if he himself performed it.

### Epikoros Etymology

With this prologue established, the *gemara* turns to the *epikoros*. We tend to understand the term as a Greek word, and indeed it does derive from the Greek philosophical tradition associated with Epicurus. But the *Maharal* connects it to a Hebrew root: *hefker*, ownerlessness. What does it mean to conduct oneself with *hefker*? It does not necessarily mean the person openly denies God. Rather, he treats the world as though it has no owner, as though it is unguided — as though *he* himself is the master of the place. He does not say there is no God; it simply does not cross his mind. This is the essence of *apikorsut*: not theological atheism so much as a posture of radical disregard for divine sovereignty and rabbinic authority.

### Three-Tier Definition

Alongside the *epikoros*, the *gemara* introduces the related concept of *mevazeh* — one who disgraces or demeans. There is a three-tier structure that emerges: one who is against God (the *epikoros* in the strictest sense), one who is *megaleh panim baTorah* (who distorts or misreads the Torah in a brazen way), and one who *mefer brito shel Avraham* (who nullifies the covenant of Abraham). These three tiers can be understood as offenses against God, against Torah, and against Israel respectively — mirroring the framework of the *sugya* concluded just above.

### Mevazeh Dispute

Now the *gemara* must define more precisely who falls into which category. The question is: who is the *epikoros* and who is the *megaleh panim baTorah*, and which is the more severe offense?

Rav and Rav Chanina both say: the *epikoros* is one who disgraces a *talmid chacham* directly — *hamevazeh talmid chacham atzmo*. Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, by contrast, say: the *epikoros* is one who shames his fellow in front of a *talmid chacham* — *hamevazeh chaveiro bifnei talmid chacham*.

The *gemara* examines both positions. According to the view that shaming one's fellow in front of a *talmid chacham* constitutes *apikorsut*, then directly disgracing a *talmid chacham* would be the more serious category of *megaleh panim baTorah*. But according to the view that directly shaming a *talmid chacham* is the *apikoros*, then what would *megaleh panim baTorah* look like? The *gemara* offers as an example Menashe ben Chizkiyah, the notorious king of Judea, who embodies a brazen distortion of Torah. There is also a reversed teaching — *ve'ika dematni la aseifa* — where the formulations are attributed in the opposite order, yielding the same internal tension.

Why must the shaming occur specifically in front of a *talmid chacham* for one view to qualify as *apikorsut*? The entire thrust of this *sugya* concerns the respect owed to *talmidei chachamim* as a barometer of one's relationship with the entire way of life — with *halacha*, with *Hashem*, with everything. It is not unlike the experience of a parent who hears someone say, "I respect you, but I cannot stand your children." That friendship is over. The *talmid chacham*, the Torah, and God form a single package, and dismissiveness toward any element of the chain reflects a broader orientation of *hefker*.

---

## Epikoros Examples

### Rabbis' Benefit

Having laid out the definitional framework, the *gemara* now proceeds to offer concrete examples of *apikorsut*, each more refined than the last. Rav Yosef opens: the paradigmatic *epikoros* is the person who says, *mai ahano lan rabanan ledidehu karu ledidehu tanu* — "What benefit do the Rabbis bring us? They study for themselves and teach for themselves." This is a strikingly contemporary-sounding complaint, and the *gemara* takes it with great seriousness.

### Abaye Response

Abaye responds sharply: this is not merely *apikorsut*, it actually rises to the level of *megaleh panim baTorah* — the more severe category. The person who claims the Rabbis do nothing for us has fundamentally misunderstood the structure of the world. The proof text is from Yirmiyahu: *im lo briti yomam valailah chukot shamayim va'aretz lo samti* — "Were it not for My covenant day and night, I would not have established the laws of heaven and earth." The Torah and those who maintain its covenant are the very engine that keeps the universe running. Before the world was created, Torah existed; the covenant is the foundation of creation itself. To say the Rabbis do nothing is to deny this entire structure.

### Divine Merit

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak adds a supporting verse: *venasati lechol hamakom ba'avuram* — "I will forgive the entire place for their sake." This is drawn from the context of Sodom and Amorah: the whole place would have been preserved not because each individual merited preservation, but because the merit of the righteous upheld it. The principle generalizes: the righteous, those who maintain the covenant through Torah study, hold up the entire world on their behalf.

### Talmidei Chachamim

This raises the question of what exactly is meant by *talmidei chachamim* in this context. It need not refer only to those who have mastered the entirety of *shas* and *poskim*. It can refer more broadly to those who study Torah and thereby serve as a kind of glue holding the world together — even if the precise mechanism remains beyond our full understanding. It is worth noting that *talmid chacham* and *tzaddik* are not equivalent categories: one can be a *talmid chacham* without being a *tzaddik*, though in this context the emphasis is on those whose Torah study upholds the covenant and thereby benefits the world.

### Attribution Error

The next example is more refined and perhaps more surprising. The *gemara* says: another form of *apikorsut* is the student who sits before his teacher, hears a teaching that he then applies or transmits in another context, and says *hachi amrinan hatam* — "this is what we have taught there" — rather than *hachi amar mar* — "this is what my teacher taught." By saying "we have taught" rather than attributing the ruling to a named rabbi, the student subtly erases the chain of tradition. The oral tradition depends on precise attribution; to blur that chain, even inadvertently, is a form of *apikorsut*. One might be surprised that such a slip carries so grave a designation, but the *gemara* is clearly drawing the *siyag* — the protective fence — very deliberately. The concern is that each generation without proper attribution makes the next generation more vulnerable to complete severance from the tradition.

### Binyamin's House

Rava offers the example of the members of the house of Binyamin the doctor, who said: *mai ahano lan rabanan* — "what good have the Rabbis done for us?" Their specific formulation of the complaint: *me'olam lo sharu lan urva velo asru lan yona* — "they have never permitted us a raven nor forbidden us a dove." This is an audacious claim. The raven, *orev*, is never *kosher* and never will be permitted. The dove, *yona*, is always permitted and never will be forbidden. What have the Rabbis decided, then? They just tell us the obvious.

### Rava's Test

Rava's response to this challenge is pointed. When a *tereifah* question arose from the house of Binyamin — an animal potentially forbidden due to a defect — Rava would make a point of probing the case. When he found grounds to permit it, he would say to them: *techazu d'kashrina lechu urva* — "See, I am permitting you a raven." When he found grounds to forbid it, he would say: *techazu d'kaserna lechu yona* — "See, I am forbidding you a dove." His point: the Rabbis' expertise is not in deciding what color is white or black, but in adjudicating precisely those difficult, ambiguous cases — the cases that look like a raven but might be a dove, or look like a dove but might be a raven. Rabbinic authority manifests exactly where certainty is absent.

### Rav Pappa Case

Rav Pappa offers the final and most refined example: one who refers to the Rabbis as *hanni rabbanan* — "those Rabbis." The offense lies in the dismissive, casual, third-person plurality — speaking about rabbinic figures without specific attribution, in a tone of *zilzul*, of contempt. No individual rabbi is identified; they are simply lumped together in an off-handed reference.

### Rav Pappa Repents

What makes this example all the more striking is the *gemara*'s immediate sequel: *ishtali* Rav Pappa — Rav Pappa himself forgot, and he used this very expression. His response was to sit in a fast. This incident illuminates the *siyag* at work: the category of *apikorsut* proper is one thing, but the Rabbis have drawn the fence so close that even Rav Pappa — sitting and teaching this very *sugya* — stumbled into it momentarily and felt the weight of that stumble acutely. The concern is ultimately about protecting the integrity of the oral tradition as a living, attributed chain passing from teacher to student.

---

## Megillat Esther Case

### Scroll Wrapping

The *gemara* now presents an incident that illustrates *apikorsut* through disrespect toward a canonical text. Levi bar Shmuel and Rav Huna bar Chiya were sitting in the *beit midrash* of Rav Yehuda, wrapping Torah scrolls in their scarves — the kerchief-wrappers used to dress the scrolls, a practice preserved in some Sephardic and German communities to this day.

### Esther No Scarf

When they came to Megillat Esther, they said: *ha Megillat Esther lo ba'aya mitpachat* — "the Megillah does not need a scarf." Their reasoning was presumably that the Megillah occupies a somewhat lesser formal status than the other scrolls of *Tanakh*.

### Rav Yehuda Rebuke

Rav Yehuda rebuked them immediately: *ki hai gavna nami mechazei k'apikoruta* — "Even speaking in this way already looks like *apikoruta*." The casual dismissal of Megillat Esther's dignity — the slight *zilzul* embedded in saying it needs no wrapping, as if it were of lesser sanctity — crosses into the territory the *gemara* has been carefully mapping. Disrespect toward a canonical rabbinic text, even through a seemingly minor act, carries the appearance of *apikorsut*.

---

## Rabbi Respect

### Rabbi by Name

Rav Nachman provides yet another dimension: the person who has no share in *olam haba* is *hakore rabbo bishmo* — one who calls his rabbi by his first name alone, without title or honorific.

### Geichazi Case

Rabbi Yochanan grounds this in a biblical episode: why was Geichazi punished? *Mipnei shekara l'rabbo bishmo* — because he called his teacher by name. Geichazi was the attendant of Elisha, and when he came before the king, he said: *vayomer Geichazi adoni haMelech* — "my master the king" — presenting the case of the woman whose son Elisha had revived, but referring to Elisha simply by name without any title or introduction. This bare use of the name, without the honorific due to his teacher, was sufficient to incur severe punishment.

### Eldad Meidad

A contrasting case is mentioned: Eldad and Meidad, when they came to Moshe to report that people were prophesying in the camp, said *adoni Moshe kla'em* — "my master Moshe, restrain them." Even this formulation — combining the honorific *adoni* with the name Moshe — was subject to debate: was it appropriate for them to address Moshe by name to his face, or would even *adoni* alone have been more fitting? The discussion underscores how carefully calibrated the *gemara*'s expectation of respectful address truly is.

---

## Future Redemption

### Future Stream

Rabbi Yirmiyah and Rabbi Zeira are sitting together and teaching. They say: in the future, *HaKadosh Baruch Hu* is going to bring forth a stream from the Holy of Holies — *nachal mibeit kodshei hakodashim* — and upon it will be all kinds of delicacies.

### Yechezkel Pasuk

The source is a verse from Yechezkel: *ve'al hanachal ya'aleh al sfato mizeh umizeh kol etz ma'achal lo yibol alehu velo yitam piryo lechodashav yevaker ki memav min hamikdash hem yotzim vehayah piryo lema'achal ve'alehu litrufah* — "And on the banks of the stream there shall grow all trees of food whose leaves shall not wither and whose fruit shall not cease, for their water issues from the sanctuary; their fruit shall be for food and their leaf for healing." The fruit trees lining this stream from the *Mikdash* will yield fruit that does not fall and leaves that serve as medicine. The *gemara* will return to the word *litrufah* — "for healing" — shortly.

### Old Man's Mark

An old man was sitting nearby and listening. He interjected: *yashar* — well done — and noted that Rabbi Yochanan had said the same thing. Rabbi Yirmiyah turned to Rabbi Zeira with some unease: *ki hai gavna mechezi afkiriuta*? Does this not smell a little of *afkiriuta*? Who is this old man to be giving them marks on their *drasha*, and then to mention that Rabbi Yochanan had said the same thing afterward, rather than first? Is there something presumptuous — something tinged with *hefker* — in the way he spoke up?

### Zeira Defense

Rabbi Zeira reassures him: *siyu'a ka mesaye'ach lach* — he was supporting you, not challenging you. The old man meant well; he was offering corroboration, not acting as a judge. But Rabbi Zeira adds: if you want a case that truly has the flavor of *apikoruta* — one that crossed a genuine line — let me tell you what happened with Rabbi Yochanan.

---

## Precious Stones

### Yochanan Stones

Rabbi Yochanan was sitting and teaching: *atid HaKadosh Baruch Hu lehavi avanim tovot umargaliot shehen shloshim al shloshim amot* — in the future, the Holy One Blessed Be He is going to bring precious gems and stones thirty *amot* by thirty *amot*. Given that an *amah* is approximately 18 to 24 inches, this means stones somewhere between 45 and 60 feet in dimension.
