These stones will be carved ten by twenty and will stand as the gates of Yerushalayim, as it is written: *vesamti kadchod shimshotayich usha'arayich le'avnei ekdach* — "I will set your windows of precious stone and your gates of sparkling gems."

### Student Mockery

A student mocked him. He said: *hashta kibeita detziltzal lo mashkechinan kulei hai mashkechinan* — "Right now we cannot even find a gem the size of an egg; you expect us to find stones thirty by thirty to be placed in the gates of Yerushalayim?" His skepticism was directed squarely at the literal content of Rabbi Yochanan's teaching.

### Angelic Vision

Some time later, this student sailed at sea — or perhaps, in one reading, experienced a vision; the *gemara* leaves this somewhat open. He saw ministering angels who were busy sawing precious gems: *dekah mensari avanim tovot umargaliyot*. He asked them: *hani leman* — what are these stones for? They answered: *atid HaKadosh Baruch Hu l'ha'amidan b'sha'arei Yerushalayim* — these are the stones that will be placed in the gates of Yerushalayim.

### Yochanan Rebuke

When the student returned, he chanced upon Rabbi Yochanan sitting and teaching. He said to him: *Rabbi drosh ulecha na'eh lidrosh — keshem she'amarta kach ra'iti* — Rabbi, go ahead and teach, it is fitting that you teach; what you said, I saw. One might expect this to be a moment of reconciliation, of confirmation. Instead, Rabbi Yochanan's response was withering. He said: *reika* — empty one. *Ilmalei ra'ita lo emanta* — had you not seen it for yourself, you would not have believed. *Melagleg al divrei chachamim ata* — you are mocking the words of the sages. The problem was not that the student doubted; the problem was that his belief required empirical confirmation. He could not extend faith to the tradition without personal proof — and that itself constituted a form of *ligleg*, of mockery toward rabbinic teaching.

### Bones Punishment

Rabbi Yochanan then *yahav beih eineh va'asao gal shel atzamot* — he fixed his eyes upon him and turned him into a pile of bones. This is not the only place where Rabbi Yochanan does something of this kind, and there is debate about how literally to understand it. One possibility is that it is metaphorical — connecting to the valley of dry bones in Yechezkel — seeing the student as someone who was all body and no soul, all matter and no spirit. Another reading is that Rabbi Yochanan's gaze carried a genuine transformative power, reducing a person who had scorned the tradition to its barest physical residue. The *gemara* notes that in other places Rabbi Yochanan sometimes revives those he has reduced in this way, and sometimes does not.

---

## Yechezkel Analysis

### Window Measurements

The *gemara* now raises a textual challenge to Rabbi Yochanan's own teaching. He spoke of stones thirty by thirty *amot*; but a *meitivei* notes that the verse may be referring only to the measurements of the windows — not to stones of that dimension filling entire gates. The thirty-by-thirty figure, on this reading, would apply only to the window apertures, allowing the teaching to remain internally consistent.

### Komemiyut Height

The *gemara* continues its analysis of the future dimensions of the redeemed world with a separate passage. The verse in Vayikra, in the section of blessings: *va'olech etchem komemiyut* — "I will lead you upright" — is subjected to close scrutiny. The word *komemiyut* could have been written *komiyut*, but the doubling of the root implies two heights stacked together. What does this mean?

### Height Dispute

Rabbi Meir says: *matayim amah* — two hundred *amot*. The reasoning: *Adam Harishon* was one hundred *amot* tall, and in the messianic future the righteous will stand two hundred *amot* tall, corresponding to two of *Adam Harishon*'s heights — the doubled root of *komemiyut* yielding two full statures. Rabbi Yehuda disagrees: only one hundred *amot* — corresponding to the height of the *Heichal* and its walls, as it is written: *asher baneinu kintiyim megudalim binureihem bnoteinu k'zaviyot mechutavot tavnit heichal* — a verse from Tehillim describing the majestic proportions of a future flourishing. The objection that a two-hundred-*amah* person would tower over a hundred-*amah* sanctuary is addressed by Rabbi Yochanan: do not worry about it, the measurements will work out.

### Medicinal Leaves

Returning to the verse in Yechezkel, the *gemara* asks: *mai ve'aleihu litrufa* — what does "and their leaves for healing" mean? The leaf of the tree is described as *litrufah* — for healing — rather than simply *trufa*, healing. What does the additional *lamed* add?

### Trufa Wordplay

Rabbi Yitzchak bar Abudimi and Rav Chisda offer a wordplay. The word *trufa* — tav, reish, peh, heh — can be read as *lehatir peh*, "to open the mouth." One says it refers to *peh shel ma'ala* — the mouth above, that is, those who cannot speak; the other says it refers to *peh shel mata* — the mouth below. This second interpretation is expanded: Chizkiyah says it means *lehatir peh* of those who are mute; Bar Kappara says it means *lehatir peh* of barren women — *akarut* — since the womb is sometimes called a mouth in the language of *Niddah*. In the future redemption, neither barrier — neither muteness nor barrenness — will remain closed.

### Litrufa Meaning

Rabbi Yochanan himself disagrees with these interpretive elaborations. He says: *litrufah mamash* — the leaf is literally a medicine, in the plain sense of the word. There is no need to allegorize. Rav Shmuel bar Nachmani offers yet a third reading: *letoar panim shel ba'alei hapeh darash* — to beautify the appearance of those who speak, that is, the *talmidei chachamim* who teach Torah. In the future, the teachers of Torah will radiate a special luminosity.

---

## Reward Doctrine

### Blackening Face

The *gemara* continues with a series of teachings about the relationship between toil in this world and reward in the next. Rav Yehuda bar Rav Simeon teaches: *kol hamashchir panav al divrei Torah ba'olam hazeh* — one who blackens his face over Torah study in this world — *HaKadosh Baruch Hu mavhik zivo la'olam haba* — the Holy One Blessed Be He will cause his radiance to shine in the world to come. The source is *Shir Hashirim*, which describes a beloved who is weathered and dark from toil, but whose ultimate countenance is luminous and cedar-like. The principle is that the toil, the self-expenditure, the darkening of one's face in this world through diligent study, is precisely what is transformed into radiance in the world to come.

### Starvation Satiation

Rav Tanchum bar Rav Chanilai adds a parallel teaching: *kol hamariv atzmo al divrei Torah ba'olam hazeh* — one who starves himself, who withholds food from himself for the sake of Torah study in this world — *HaKadosh Baruch Hu masbi'o la'olam haba* — God will satiate him in the world to come. The verse is from Tehillim: *yirveyun mideshen beitecha venachal adanecha tashkem* — He will sate them from the richness of His house and give them to drink from the river of His delights. The movement is consistent: what one surrenders in this world for Torah is repaid and exceeded in the world to come.

### Full Measure

Rav Dimi adds a teaching from the West — from the tradition of Eretz Yisrael, transmitted in the name of Rava bar Mari: *atid HaKadosh Baruch Hu latet lechol tzaddik vetzaddik melo omso* — in the future, God is going to give to each and every righteous person His full load, His full measure. The proof text from Mishlei: *lehanchil ohavai yesh ve'otzroteihem amale* — "to cause those who love me to inherit *yesh*, and I will fill their treasuries." The word *yesh* — *yud* and *shin* — has a *gematria* of 310 (10 plus 300), and so the tradition crystallizes: each righteous person will receive 310 worlds, with their treasuries filled to capacity.

### Abaye Challenge

Abaye challenges this: *vechi efshar lomar ken* — is it really possible to say so? That God unloads His entire measure of good upon us? Does not another verse say *mi madad beshalo mayim veshamayim bezeret tichen* — "who measured the waters in the hollow of His hand and meted the heavens with a finger"? The heavens themselves are measured by a mere finger — *zeret*, perhaps a pinky — suggesting that God's measure is vastly disproportionate to anything a human being could receive. How, then, can we say He gives His full load to each righteous person?

Abaye's interlocutor responds with a gentle reproach: are you not versed in the *agadata* of the West, transmitted from Rava bar Mari? The statement is not a claim about precise arithmetic equivalence but rather about fullness and intention — that God's gift to the righteous is complete and overflowing, each receiving a world unto themselves.

### Yehoshua Counter

Rav Yehoshua raises a further challenge: if the principle is *mida keneged mida* — measure for measure — how does that work when a person gives everything he has to the poor in this world, and we say God gives him everything back in the world to come? The heavens are measured by a finger. The scales seem incommensurable. The *gemara* accepts the challenge and moves to address the underlying tension between the doctrine of *mida keneged mida* and the vast asymmetry between human capacity and divine generosity.

---

## Measure Doctrine

### Two Measures

The *gemara* clarifies: there is a distinction between *midat tovah* — the measure of goodness — and *midat pur'anut* — the measure of punishment. They are not symmetrical. The measure of goodness is greater than the measure of punishment. Rabbi Meir states this as a general principle: *bemida she'adam moded modedin lo* — in the measure that a person measures, it is measured back to him. But the *gemara* nuances this carefully. It is not a simple tit-for-tat; the *midot* in question are not quantities but qualities — if one exercises *rachamim*, one merits *rachamim*; if one exercises *din*, one encounters *din*. The mistake would be to reduce this to a ledger of three *mitzvot* earning three credits. The principle is larger and more organic than that.

### Doors Chimneys

The textual evidence for the asymmetry between the two measures: in the context of *midat tovah*, the verse says *vayetzav shechakim mima'al vedaltei shamayim patach vayamter aleihem man leechol* — "He commanded the clouds above and opened the doors of heaven and rained down upon them manna to eat." The full doors of heaven swing open. But in the context of *midat pur'anut* — the flood — the verse says only *va'arubbot hashamayim niftachu* — "and the floodgates of heaven were opened." Not the broad doors, but the *arubbot*, the chimneys, the narrow openings. Even in the worst catastrophe in human history, the opening was smaller than the generosity of the good. The measure of punishment is thus inherently less expansive than the measure of goodness.

### Fire Comparison

But this raises its own problem. Another verse, from Yeshayahu, describes the fate of the wicked in eschatological terms: *veyatzu vera'u bepigrei ha'anashim haposh'im bi ki tula'atam lo tamut ve'isham lo tichbeh* — "And they shall go out and see the carcasses of the men who rebelled against Me, for their worm shall not die and their fire shall not be quenched." If the fire of punishment keeps burning forever without being extinguished, how can we say the measure of punishment is the smaller of the two? In this world, if a person stretches a finger toward fire, he is immediately burned — and the burning stops. But the punishment described here burns without end. That seems like more punishment, not less.

### Strength Resolution

The *gemara*'s answer is, as noted, striking in its psychological depth. *Ela keshem shenoten HaKadosh Baruch Hu koach baresha'im lekabbel pur'anutam kach noten HaKadosh Baruch Hu koach batzaddikim lekabbel tovatam* — just as God gives the wicked the strength to endure and absorb their punishment, so too God gives the righteous the strength to receive and contain the goodness that comes to them. The comparison runs in both directions: punishment that burns forever is tolerable because God grants the capacity to bear it; goodness that overflows every boundary is receivable because God grants the capacity to receive it. The latter point is the more profound one — it takes a certain kind of strength, a certain spiritual capacity, to receive good. Without that capacity, even abundant blessing cannot be internalized. God provides both.

---

## External Books

### Rabbi Akiva Ruling

We return to the *mishnah*. Rabbi Akiva teaches: *af hakoreh basefarim hachitzoniyim* — also one who reads *in* the external books — has no share in the world to come.

### Book Categories

What are the *sefarim chitzoniyim*? There are essentially three concentric circles: the *Tanakh*, the *sefarim chitzoniyim*, and what we might call the emerging Christian writings — *Berit Hechadashah*. The historical context is critical: the Rabbis are operating in a period when nascent Christianity is pressing its claim to continuity with the Jewish biblical tradition. The *sefarim chitzoniyim* include texts like Ben Sira — whose author is sometimes associated in tradition with descendants of Yirmiyahu — as well as *sifrei tzadokim*, the Sadducean writings. These are books external to the Jewish canonical tradition, not external to those who wrote them; they saw themselves as within the tradition. Rav Yosef adds that reading in the book of Ben Sira is also forbidden.

### Immersion Meaning

The key to understanding Rabbi Akiva's prohibition lies in the preposition *bet* — *hakoreh basefarim hachitzoniyim*, not *hakoreh et hasefarim hachitzoniyim*. In Hebrew, *koreh et*, reading the newspaper, is ordinary reading. *Koreh be*, reading *in* a text, implies immersion, depth-study, a soul-level engagement. The prohibition is not on knowing what these books contain; it is on immersing oneself in them the way one immerses in Torah. The *gemara* itself is about to demonstrate that the Rabbis knew perfectly well what Ben Sira said — they will quote it repeatedly. The issue is not knowledge; it is the orientation of deep study.

### Boundary Protection

The second dimension of the prohibition is protective and sociological. Once someone begins immersing himself in these external books, the path to accepting their claims — ultimately the path to the *Berit Hechadashah* — becomes more direct. The Rabbis are treating this as an impassable road: not because the content is necessarily false in every line, but because the trajectory leads somewhere they are determined to foreclose. The fence is drawn not at the destination but at the first steps of the journey.

---

## Ben Sira Examples

### Fish Skinning

Having established the prohibition, the *gemara* proceeds in an almost paradoxical way: it quotes Ben Sira extensively, demonstrating that the Rabbis knew the text and inviting analysis of what exactly could justify the prohibition. The implicit argument is precisely that the content alone is not the problem.

The first example: Ben Sira writes, do not skin the fish from its ear, because it will cause damage; rather, fry it whole in fire and eat it with two loaves of bread. Is that the reason the book is forbidden? The *gemara* responds: *i pshatei*, if the meaning is simply the prohibition of waste, the Torah itself says *lo tashchit et etzecha* — *bal tashchit*, do not destroy. And *i midrasha*, if the passage is allegorical and refers to sexual conduct — skinning the fish from the ear as a metaphor for *shelo kedarka*, non-normative intercourse — the Rabbis teach that principle too. Either way, the content of this passage is already present in the Jewish tradition.

### Daughters Treasure

A second example: Ben Sira says a daughter is to her father a *matmonet shav* — a false treasure. *Mipachada lo yishan balaila* — he does not sleep at night from worry about her. When she is young, he fears she will be seduced; when she is a teenager, he fears she will go astray; when she is older, he fears she will not marry; when she is married, he fears she will not have sons; when she is old, he fears she will practice witchcraft. Is that grounds to prohibit the book? The *gemara* responds: the Rabbis said the same thing. *I efshar la'olam belo zcharim uvelo nekevot* — the world cannot exist without males and females. But *ashrei mi shebanav zcharim, oi lo lemi shebanav nekevot* — fortunate is the one whose children are sons, and woe to the one whose children are daughters. The sentiment, with all its ancient and discomfiting assumptions, appears in the Rabbinic tradition as well.

### Pain Heart

A third example: Ben Sira writes, *lo ta'ayil davya belibecha* — do not carry pain in your heart — *degavrei govrin katil davya* — because pain can kill mighty men. Surely that cannot be the reason for the prohibition? *Ha Shlomo amra* — Shlomo said the same thing. In Mishlei, the verse reads: *de'agah belev ish yashchena* — worry in a man's heart, *yashchena*, let him crush it. Or perhaps: let him discuss it. This is the *gemara*'s beautiful wordplay on the unusual verb *yashchena*, which ordinarily means to hunch or be weighed down. Both readings are legitimate derivations.

### Worry Handling

Rav Ammi and Rav Assi each offer one interpretation. One says *yassichenah mida'ato* — push it away from your mind. Suppress it, set it aside, do not let it consume you. The other says *yassichenah le'achirim* — speak of it to others. Articulating one's worry to another person alleviates the burden and prevents the sorrow from becoming destructive. Both approaches are responses to the same verse, and both find expression in the Rabbinic tradition independently of Ben Sira. And so once again, the content of the *sefer chitzon* is not the problem — the prohibition must rest on grounds other than the specific teachings contained within it, grounds that the *gemara* has not yet fully articulated and will presumably continue to develop.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 101

## Ben Sira & Apocrypha

### External Books Ban

Today's daf is 101. We pick up in the middle of 100b, where — if one looks at the left-hand column between Rashi and the Gemara — one finds a reference to Mishlei 12. The discussion concerns *ben Sira*, because one of the individuals listed as lacking a *chelek olam haba*, according to one opinion, is someone who is *kore besfarim chitzonim* — who reads from the apocrypha, from external books, presumably works that did not make it into the canon but were attributed with some degree of holy significance. To that category, a *tanna* adds even one who reads from *ben Sira*.

Now, this addition does not appear in the Mishnah itself. The Mishnah records only Rabbi Akiva's formulation of *kore besfarim hachitzonim*; it is in a *baraita* of Rav Yosef that *sefer Ben Sira* is included. The Gemara then asks: what exactly is so problematic about *ben Sira*?

### Gemara Quotes Ben Sira

Before proceeding to the Gemara's answer, one must appreciate a striking irony at the outset: the Gemara demonstrates complete fluency in *ben Sira* in the very course of discussing whether one is permitted to read it. It goes on to quote verse after verse from *ben Sira*, and at certain points even uses the word *dechtiv* — a term the Gemara ordinarily reserves for scriptural citation. The subtext is clear: either the Gemara does not rule like Rav Yosef, or — to the extent that it does — one has to understand Rav Yosef's concern in a much more limited sense.

### Interpretation Debate

The most natural reading of that limitation is that the prohibition applies only when one treats these non-canonical texts *as* scripture — as holy writ — or when one studies them in a manner that elevates them to the status of *Torah*, effectively blurring the line between the canon and what lies outside it. Reading *ben Sira* the way one might read Poor Richard's Almanac, or Confucius, for whatever wisdom one finds there — that is presumably not the concern. The problem is assuming the text is divinely inspired and therefore treating everything in it as authoritative and binding.

One student raised a subtle grammatical observation worth noting: the Mishnah uses the formulation *kore basfarim hachitzonim*, with a *bet*, rather than *kore et hasefer* or *kore sefer*. The *bet* may itself be suggestive — it implies a mode of engagement, a manner of reading, rather than the mere act of picking up the book. One might also suggest that the concern is not only about elevating the apocrypha to scriptural status in isolation, but about blurring lines more broadly: once one begins treating pseudo-biblical works as equivalent to the canon, the category of "what counts as scripture" becomes destabilized — and from there one cannot know where the erosion stops.

It was also noted, correctly, that immediately before Rav Yosef's statement about *ben Sira*, there is a *baraita* that concludes with a reference to *sifrei minim* — heretical books, which in this context likely refers to early Jewish-Christian writings. That juxtaposition is telling.

### Ben Sira Problems

Having framed the discussion, the Gemara turns to identifying which specific passages in *ben Sira* are problematic. The first verse offered is: *lo ta'il davya belibakh, dgavya gavrin ketila* — do not let anguish enter your heart, for anguish has slain the mightiest of men. The Gemara asks: what is wrong with that? It is essentially the same as what Shlomo says in Mishlei: *de'aga belev ish yis-chena* — anguish in the heart of a man lays him low. And indeed, Rav Ami and Rav Assi then offer two readings of that very Mishlei verse: one says *yesichenah mi-da'ato*, that one should try to suppress or set aside the worry; the other says *yesichenah le-acherim*, that one should speak about it to others — in effect, go find someone to talk to.

The Gemara proceeds to identify more genuinely problematic material. One verse reads: *mena rabbim mi-toch beitecha, velo ha-kol tavi el beitecha* — keep the masses out of your house, and do not bring everyone home. The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi himself said the same thing — that a person should not crowd his house with too many guests — citing the verse *ish re'im lehitro'ea*, which is interpreted to mean that having too many acquaintances in one's home can lead to destruction of one's property or peace. So this verse from *ben Sira* is not problematic — it aligns perfectly with rabbinic teaching.

Then comes what the Gemara presents as genuinely foolish material. The verse reads: *zal dikan korteman* — a man with a thin beard is wise; *avdikan sachsachan* — a man with a thick beard is a fool. Then: someone who blows on his cup to cool it clearly cannot be very thirsty; someone who asks what would go nicely on his bread evidently cannot be very hungry — so take the bread away from him. And someone with a split down the middle of his beard — no one can stand up against him, presumably because he is always stroking it conspiratorially. Rashi offers the reading that such a man is sly and calculating.

So the problem with *ben Sira* comes into focus: the book contains material that is genuinely wise and parallel to received tradition, but it also contains material that is simply foolish — physiognomic speculation dressed up with the same literary gravity as serious moral teaching.

### Rav Yosef's Defense

Rav Yosef himself addresses this directly: *milei ma'alyata de-it bei darshinan le-hu* — the good material in it, we can still expound. Fine; some of it is foolish. But the worthy passages can still be treated with the weight of *derash*. And one student astutely noted that it is Rav Yosef himself — the very authority who declared *sefer Ben Sira* included in the ban — who now qualifies his own ruling. Perhaps his original statement was never meant to prohibit reading altogether, but rather to warn against treating the text as holy writ indiscriminately. By standing up and expounding its better passages, he is clarifying that the proper relationship with *ben Sira* is selective and critical, not reverential.

### Ben Sira on Women

The Gemara then proceeds to cite a series of passages from *ben Sira* that Rav Yosef commends as worthy of *derash*. A good woman is a good gift — *ishah tovah matanah tovah* — and should be given to a man who fears God. A wicked woman, by contrast, is like a plague of *tzara'at* to her husband. The Gemara interjects — *mai takan-teih?* what is his remedy? — and the answer comes: let him drive her from his house and he will be healed of his plague.

A beautiful woman makes her husband fortunate — *ishah yafah ashrei ba'alah* — and his days will be as though doubled. But — *ha'alem einecha me-eshet chen* — hide your eyes from a charming woman who belongs to your friend, lest you be caught in her net. Do not incline yourself toward your friend's home, and do not go there to drink with him wine and beer, *ki b'toar isha yafa rabim hushchatu* — because through the appearance of a beautiful woman many have been destroyed, and numerous are those she has brought down.

*Rabim hayu pitzei rochel* — many are the wounds of the perfume merchant, because he spends his time among women, and is either suspected of improper relations or actually falls into them — with the result that husbands come and beat him. *Hamargilim l'dvar erva* — those who habituate themselves to exposure to forbidden sexual scenarios are asking for catastrophe. *Ki nitzotz mav'ir gachelet* — it is like a spark landing on a smoldering ember. The image is apt: the ember of desire is always there, banked and controlled; a small provocation is all it takes to ignite a conflagration.

The Gemara then returns to show scriptural parallels to other *ben Sira* passages. The verse in Yirmiyah — *kichlov malei of, ken bateihem m'lei'im mirmah* — a cage full of birds, so their houses are full of deceit — parallels the *ben Sira* warning to keep the masses out of one's home. Then: *rabim yihiyu dorshei shlomecha* — let many seek your welfare; that is, have many friends. But *galei sodecha l'echad me'alef* — share your secret with only one in a thousand. And *mishochevet cheikecha shmor pitchi picha* — even from the one who sleeps in your bosom, your wife, guard the words of your mouth.

Finally: *al tatzar tzarot machar* — do not borrow tomorrow's anguish today, *ki lo teda ma yeled yom* — for you do not know what the day will bring. And perhaps even more starkly — *shema l'machar einenu* — perhaps by tomorrow you will no longer be alive, in which case you will have spent today worrying about a world that will not even be yours. The point is not fatalism, but the futility of unproductive anxiety. As one student observed, the line *v'nimtza mitzta'er al olam she'eino shelo* — you will have anguished over a world that is not yours — can be read not only to mean a day you will not live to see, but a reality that will never materialize. Rashi appears to support something of that reading, though the simpler meaning is the former.

---

## Poor Person Verse

### Rav's Comparison

The last citation from *ben Sira* bridges into the next topic. The verse *kol yemei ani ra'im* — all the days of a poor person are evil — appears in Mishlei. *Ben Sira* adds: *af leilot* — even the nights are bad, because a poor person cannot rest easily. His roof is lower than all his neighbors' roofs, so their rainwater runs down onto his. His vineyard is on the mountaintop where the soil is thin, so what little topsoil there is rolls down to everyone else's fields. Even sleep does not redeem him.

The Gemara then takes up the verse from Mishlei directly. Rabbi Zeira said in the name of Rav: what does it mean that all the days of a poor person are evil? *Elu ba'alei Talmud* — these are the people who learn Gemara, because the work of Talmud learning is genuinely hard. One strains the mind, the answers are not always clear, the process is exhausting. By contrast, *vetov lev mishteh tamid* — and a good heart is always a feast — *elu ba'alei Mishnah*, these are the students of Mishnah, because Mishnah is clear, apodictic, accessible. One has a good time learning it. Of course, the framing raises the obvious question: is being always at a feast the right goal? Is ease the correct measure of value? The contrast is not an endorsement of the easier path — it simply describes the experiential reality of the two modes of study.

### Rava Disputes

Rava says the opposite — *ipcha*. One must think not only about the difficulty of the process but about what it yields. Rav Mesharshiya said in the name of Rava: what does the verse mean — *masi'a avanim ye'atzev bahem* — one who carries stones is anguished by them? *Elu ba'alei Mishnah* — these are the Mishnah scholars. They labor under an enormous burden of material, but it is like hauling boulders: in the end, what do they have? A mass of memorized facts without deep understanding. By contrast, *ubokei'a etzim yisachen bahem* — one who chops wood provides warmth thereby. *Elu ba'alei Talmud* — the Gemara scholars, who break the material down into its component parts, who analyze, who get to the depth. The chopping is vigorous, productive work; the warmth it generates is real and lasting.

A student noted further that this image carries an additional dimension: a stone is inert and fixed, while wood is organic and alive. Mishnah is a fixed, closed text; Gemara is continuously growing and expanding. That resonance enriches the metaphor considerably.

### Multiple Readings

The Gemara then presents a series of additional readings of the verse, each interpreting "the poor person" differently.

Rabbi Chanina says: *ze mi sheyesh lo ishah ra'ah* — the one whose days are all evil is the man with a bad wife. Conversely, *vetov lev mishteh tamid* — the one whose heart is always at a feast — is the man with a good wife.

Rabbi Yannai says: *ze istanis* — the poor person is the fastidious individual, one who is forever troubled by germs, by the environment, by conditions that others do not even notice. Conversely, the one at the feast is *ze she-da'ato yafah* — the one who is, so to speak, easy with everything, for whom the world presents no particular irritants. The phrase *da'ato yafah* here does not mean refined — there is a Mishnah that uses *nefesh hayafah tochalena* to describe someone who has no problem eating something others might find repulsive, meaning someone who is simply unbothered. That is the sense here.

Rabbi Yochanan says: *ze rachmani* — the one whose days are all evil is the deeply empathetic person, one who feels everything around them, absorbs others' pain, has no emotional boundaries. *Vetov lev mishteh tamid ze achzari* — and the one at the feast is the hard-hearted person. This is not a normative endorsement; it is a description of a reality. The person without conscience, who is never troubled by others' suffering, moves through the world lightly. That may be the easiest way to live — it is not the right way.

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says: *ze she-da'ato ktzarah* — the poor person is one who is always importing trouble: borrowing others' anxieties, worrying about every possible future misfortune that might befall him. Rashi offers the additional reading that *da'ato ktzarah* means *ragzan* — someone who is short-tempered, who is easily angered and upset. Either way, *vetov lev mishteh tamid ze she-da'ato rechavah* — the one at the feast is the expansive-minded person, who neither carries borrowed anxieties nor reacts disproportionately to provocation.

### Shabbat Objection

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi then raises an apparent difficulty with the verse itself: *kol yemei ani ra'im* — how can one say *all* the days are evil? What about Shabbat and Yom Tov? Even a poor person ensures proper food for Shabbat — that is rather the entire point of Shabbat. The answer given is *ki deShmuel* — like the teaching of Shmuel: a change in one's normal diet can itself become a source of discomfort. If someone eats much better food on Shabbat than during the rest of the week, the change in routine may produce its own adverse effects by the following day. It was noted that Shmuel was a physician, which lends a particular weight to this medical observation.

---

## Scripture Misuse

### Shir HaShirim Song

The Gemara now transitions from books that lack canonical status — and the risk of treating them as scripture — to the opposite problem: taking canonical scripture and treating it in ways that are unworthy of it. The consequence here is not *ein lo chelek l'olam haba*, but the Gemara's language makes plain that the behavior is seriously objectionable.

*Tanu Rabbanan*: one who reads a verse of *Shir HaShirim* and makes it into a kind of song, or one who recites a verse in a drinking house *b'lo zmano* — not in its proper time, not in the right context — brings evil into the world. The phrase *b'lo zmano* resists precise definition, and the Gemara seems to leave it that way deliberately; some things cannot be fully quantified, but one knows the difference between singing *Shir HaShirim* in its proper context and turning it into a bar song. The issue is not melody per se — after all, much of *Tanakh* was composed to be sung — but the context in which it is done and the spirit in which it is treated.

### Torah's Complaint

The Gemara offers a powerful image for what is at stake. *Mipnei she-haTorah chogeret sak* — because the Torah puts on sackcloth. The personification is striking: by turning the Torah into something trivial, one strips it of its dignity, and the Torah itself dresses in mourning. It stands before God and cries: *Ribono shel Olam*, your children have made me like a flute played by wastrels — like a harmonica, like background noise in a tavern. That is what I have become.

And then God defends the people. *Besha'ah she-ochlim v'shotim bameh ya'asoku* — when they are eating and drinking, what would you have them do? At least they are engaging with Torah. The parallel is irresistible: it recalls the Chassidic story of the porter who changes a tire while davening Mincha — the Misnaged is scandalized, but the Chassid says to God: even with grease on their hands, Your children are thinking of You. God here is defending the Jewish people to the Torah itself: they could be singing something far worse; at least this is Torah.

But the Torah responds: *Ribono shel Olam*, if they are students of *mikra*, let them discuss Torah, Nevi'im, and Ketuvim; if they are students of Mishnah, let them discuss Mishnah, *halakhot*, and *aggadot*; if they are students of Talmud, let them discuss the laws of Pesach on Pesach, the laws of Shavuot on Shavuot, the laws of Sukkot on Sukkot. The key distinction is between discussing and singing. Talking about *psukim* at the table is not the same as converting them into entertainment. A *d'var Torah* at a meal is not the same as the *beit midrash* — no one requires that — but there is a difference between lighter Torah conversation and turning the Torah into a pop song. Notably, the Gemara links *ba'alei Talmud* with *halakhot* rather than with free-form analysis — though the assumption is presumably that one is *schmoozing* in learning, not issuing formal rulings, since one should not teach *halacha* in a state of inebriation.

### Context Matters

Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Chananya offers the positive formulation: *kol hakoreh pasuk bizmano* — one who reads a verse in its proper time and context — *tovah le'olam*, it is good for the world. *Shene'emar vidavar be'ito mah tov* — how good is it to speak in its proper time. The problem is never intrinsic to the singing or the meal setting; the problem is the context and the spirit. The same act in the right setting is good; in the wrong setting it dishonors the Torah.

---

## Incantations Forbidden

### Lochesh Definition

The Mishnah lists among those who forfeit their share in the world to come the one who whispers an incantation — *halochesh al hamakah* — over a wound, using a verse from Torah. The example given is *kol hamachala asher samti beMitzrayim lo asim alecha* — all the illness that I placed upon Egypt I will not place upon you. Already it is somewhat striking that this should appear on the same list as one who denies the divine origin of the Torah or the resurrection of the dead. One wonders whether the Mishnah means something different by placing items on this list — perhaps indicating behavior that is condemned rather than technically prohibited, or that forfeits the *chelek olam haba* not through heresy but through disrespect of a different kind. The weight of being on this list alongside fundamental denials of faith is not easy to explain.

### Spitting Requirement

Rabbi Yochanan qualifies the ruling: the problem is specifically *uve-rokek bah* — if one spits while reciting the verse. Spitting and then uttering God's name — or a verse that invokes God's healing — is a form of disrespect to the divine name. That is what triggers the severe consequence. Even granting that reading, the question of whether *ein lo chelek l'olam haba* is truly the appropriate weight for this is an uncomfortable one.

### Without Name Still Bad

Rava extends the ruling further: even if one recites a verse that does not contain God's name — such as *nega tzara'at ki tihyeh ba'adam vehuva el hakohen* — it is still problematic. One might have thought that the absence of God's name makes it categorically different and less objectionable. Rava rules that it does not.

Rabbi Chanina goes further still: even *Vayikra el Moshe* — a verse that does contain God's name but has no direct healing content, no incantatory relevance to the wound — is nonetheless forbidden to recite over it in this manner. The act of deploying scripture as a magical incantation over a wound, regardless of which verse is chosen, remains in the category of that which the Gemara condemns here.

---

## Healing Practices

### Permitted Acts

The Gemara now turns to a series of permitted and forbidden practices, many relating to Shabbat, which provides the occasion for discussing the *lechishah* issue in its broader context.

*Tanu Rabbanan*: one may apply oil and rub it into the abdomen on Shabbat. The reason is that applying oil to the skin was a normal, everyday practice; doing so even for therapeutic purposes does not present the appearance of *refuah* in a way that would be prohibited. It does not look like medical treatment because it looks like ordinary grooming.

A subsequent *baraita* refines this: one may do so, provided one does not do it in precisely the same manner as one would during the week — a *shinui* is required. Rav Chama bar Chanina says the modification is to apply the oil first and rub afterward — rather than beginning to rub and then adding oil, which would more obviously suggest medicinal intent. Rabbi Yochanan says one may apply and rub simultaneously — but again, not begin with the rubbing before the oil is present.

### Snake Incantations OK

*Velochashim lechishat nechashim ve'akrabim beShabbat* — one may recite incantations to prevent snakes and scorpions from biting on Shabbat. This is permitted because it is not a physical act of trapping; one is simply reciting words. And since the concern is mortal danger, it is permitted even on Shabbat. One may also place a vessel over an inflamed eye on Shabbat to cool it. Eye disease was apparently extremely prevalent in the ancient world — infected hands touching the eyes caused serious problems — and applying a cold metal object to reduce inflammation was a recognized treatment. This is permitted on Shabbat, interestingly, and is not classified as *refuah*. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel qualifies: this applies only if the vessel is not *muktzeh*; if it is *muktzeh*, it is forbidden to move it for this purpose.

### Demon Inquiry Ban

*Ve'ein sho'alin bidvar shedim beShabbat* — one may not inquire of the *sheidim* on Shabbat. Rashi explains the nature of such inquiries: one might ask the *sheidim*, for instance, where one has lost something. The *sheidim*, apparently, may respond. The reason this is forbidden on Shabbat is that it is *dover davar* — weekday activity, the conduct of mundane commerce, which is inappropriate on Shabbat.

Rabbi Yossi goes further: *af bechol assur* — it is forbidden even on weekdays. The question is the basis: is there a formal prohibition, or is it purely *sakana* — danger? Rav Yosef says — and there is a variant in the text as to whether the ruling is like Rabbi Yossi or not — that even Rabbi Yossi's concern is not a formal *issur* but a concern for safety. Once one engages with *sheidim*, one may expose oneself to forces one cannot control and cannot safely navigate.

This raises the question of where this falls relative to *lo tenachashu* and the other prohibitions on magic and divination. The line between what is technically *assur* and what is merely dangerous — *darchei ha'Emori*, signs, inquiries — is genuinely complicated, and the Gemara's treatment here reflects that complexity without resolving it with precision.

### Dangerous Oil Story

A story illustrates the danger of incantations over oil. Rabbi Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta arrived at a certain inn. They brought him oil in a vessel — already a bad sign, as will become clear. He rubbed it on himself, and blisters or boils broke out on his face. He went out to the marketplace, and a certain woman saw him and said: I see here the spirit of *Cheimat* — apparently a known *sheid*. She performed some neutralizing ritual, and he was healed.

The lesson: incantations are performed over oil when it is in a vessel, not over oil held in the hand. Therefore, oil poured directly from someone's hand is safe, whereas oil poured from a vessel — if there is reason to suspect the one who handled it — may carry injurious incantations within it. One should not anoint oneself from such a vessel if the circumstances are suspicious.

The story of Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef — who was swallowed by a cedar tree while being pursued by a *sheid*, and was miraculously saved when the tree burst open — is cited earlier in the same sugya as further illustration of why one should not casually involve oneself with *sheidim*.

---

## Healing Meaning

### Egypt Verse Paradox

Rav Abba raised a question to Rabba bar Mari about the verse that serves as the Mishnah's example of the forbidden incantation: *kol hamachala asher samti beMitzrayim lo asim alecha ki ani Hashem rofecha* — all the illness that I placed upon Egypt I will not place upon you, for I am the Lord your healer. The paradox is straightforward: if God is promising not to make one sick — *lo asim alecha* — then why does one need God as a healer? If the illness is never placed upon the person, what is there to heal?

### Two Conditions

Rabbi Yochanan resolves this: *mikra zeh me-atzmo nidrash* — the verse explains itself if one reads it carefully. The full verse reads: *vayomer im shamoa tishma le-kol Hashem Elokecha... kol hamachala asher samti beMitzrayim lo asim alecha ki ani Hashem rofecha*. There are two distinct parts. If you hearken carefully to the voice of God — *im shamoa tishma* — then *lo asim*: you will not be made sick at all. But even if you do not fully listen — *v'im lo tishma* — and the illness therefore does come upon you, even then: *ki ani Hashem rofecha* — know that I am still your healer. You may yet turn to Me and I will heal you. The promise of *refuah* is not rendered redundant by the promise of protection; rather, the verse is addressing two different situations depending on whether the condition of obedience is met.

---

## Rabbi Eliezer Death

### Fever & Tears

Rabba bar bar Chana said: when Rabbi Eliezer fell ill, his students entered to visit him. He said to them: *chama azah yesh ba'olam* — there is a powerful sun in the world. Rashi understands this as a reference to his own burning fever, expressing the intensity of his suffering. His students began to weep — *hitchilu hen bochin* — and Rabbi Akiva was laughing.

### Akiva Laughs

The other students asked Rabbi Akiva: why are you laughing? And he turned it back on them: why are you crying? They answered: how can we not weep? Here is a *sefer Torah* — Rabbi Eliezer had long been understood in those terms, as a repository who preserved and transmitted everything he had received without creative addition, not a *ma'ayan ha-mitgaber* but a *sefer Torah* — and this *sefer Torah* is in anguish. How could we not cry?

Rabbi Akiva said: that is precisely why I am laughing. As long as I watched my rabbi and saw that his wine did not spoil, his flax was undamaged, his oil did not go rancid, his honey did not congeal — I was worried. I feared that perhaps, *chas ve-shalom*, he had already received his full reward in this world, and there would be nothing left for him in the world to come. Now that I see him suffering, I am happy — he will receive his reward in the world to come.

This moment operates on multiple levels, not all of them comfortable. Rabbi Eliezer had been in *cherem*, cut off from his colleagues; one might ask whether material well-being fully measures whether someone has been *sharui be-tza'ar*. And there is an additional layer of irony: it is Rabbi Akiva who makes this argument, given the terrible end Rabbi Akiva himself would face. But the pastoral logic is distinct from the biographical one. Rather than weeping alongside the suffering man — which, however genuine, may only compound his misery — Rabbi Akiva offers a reframe: your suffering is not a punishment, it is a sign that your reward is being preserved for the world to come. Whether or not that always works as pastoral care, it is at least offering something that might help.

Rabbi Eliezer's response is telling: *amar lahem samchuni* — prop me up, support me, let me sit up. *D'eshma divrei Akiva talmidi* — I want to hear what Akiva my student is saying. He says something that is not what the others are saying — the others' words, however sincere and moving, are essentially the kind of tribute one finds in a eulogy. What is Akiva saying that is different?

Rabbi Akiva replied to his teacher's question — *minayin lach?* where do you derive that *yisurin* are beloved? — *mikra ani doreish*: from a verse, from Scripture.

### Four Elders Visit

A *baraita* records a second account: when Rabbi Eliezer fell ill, four elders came to visit him — Rabbi Tarfon, Rabbi Yehoshua, Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, and Rabbi Akiva. Their mode of address is notable; they are called *zkenim*, elders, though Rabbi Yehoshua was a colleague and Rabbi Akiva was still a student.

Rabbi Tarfon spoke first: you are better to Israel than a drop of rain. Rain gives life — but only in this world. My teacher gives life to Israel in this world and in the world to come.

Rabbi Yehoshua spoke: you are better to Israel than the sun. The sun illuminates only in this world. My teacher illuminates both in this world and in the world to come.

Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya spoke: you are better to Israel than a father and mother. Parents — and it is notable that the text says *av v'em*, naming both — care for their children only in this world. My teacher cares for Israel in this world and in the world to come.

### Beloved Sufferings

Then Rabbi Akiva spoke: *chavivin yisurin* — sufferings are beloved. The effect on Rabbi Eliezer is immediate: *amar lahem samchuni* — prop me up, hold me up, I want to hear what my student Akiva is saying. *She-amar chavivin yisurin* — he has said that sufferings are beloved. The other tributes, however sincere, have the quality of things one says. Akiva has said something genuinely surprising, something with intellectual substance that catches attention.

Rabbi Eliezer asks: *minayin lach?* And Rabbi Akiva says: *mikra ani doreish* — I will derive it from a verse.

### Menashe Example

The verse is from Chronicles: *ben shtem esreh shanah Menashe b'molcho v'chamish v'chamishim shanah malach b'Yerushalayim vaya'as hara b'einei Hashem* — Menashe was twelve years old when he became king, he reigned fifty-five years in Jerusalem, and he did what was evil in the eyes of God. And elsewhere it is written that Chizkiyahu's men transcribed the proverbs of Shlomo.

The argument: Chizkiyahu taught *Mishlei* — with all its moral guidance on how to live a good life — to the entire world. Did he teach it to his own son Menashe? Obviously yes. And did all that moral education do Menashe any good? Clearly not. *Mikol torach shetarach bo, mikol amal she'amal bo* — no matter how much Chizkiyahu invested in giving Menashe a proper upbringing, *lo he'elu l'mutav* — it did not put him on a straight path. *Ela yisurin* — it was only *yisurin*, only suffering, that set Menashe straight.

As it says: God spoke to Menashe and his people, but they did not listen. And God brought against them the commanders of the Assyrian king's army; they captured Menashe with hooks and bound him in copper chains and led him away. He then humbled himself greatly before the God of his fathers, prayed to Him, and God listened to his supplication and restored him to Jerusalem and to his kingdom. And Menashe knew that the Lord is God.

*Halamadnu shekhavivin yisurin* — from this we learn how beloved sufferings are. How powerful their capacity to transform a person that all the moral instruction in the world could not achieve.

One must sit with the strangeness of this as a message to Rabbi Eliezer. Menashe's *yisurin* were the consequence of extraordinary wickedness — the suffering that woke him up to repentance. Rabbi Eliezer is not Menashe. How is this meant to be uplifting? One is left without a fully satisfying resolution. The parallel the Gemara draws elsewhere is instructive: *Vayasar hamelech et taba'ato* — Achashverosh handing his signet ring to Haman — accomplished more than all the words of all the prophets in spurring Israel to *teshuvah*. The *fear* of impending harm, the lived experience of suffering and consequence, reaches places that *mussar* cannot. That is the principle Rabbi Akiva is articulating. Whether it fully lands as consolation in this context is another question.

---

## Three Protesters

### Cain's Complaint

The Gemara records that three individuals came before God not merely in prayer but with something resembling a righteous complaint — *ba'alila*, with a claim. They were Kayin, Esav, and Menashe.

Kayin: *gadol avoni minaso* — is my sin too great to bear, or is my punishment too great to bear? He said before God: *Ribono shel Olam*, is my sin greater than the sin of the sixty myriads who will sin with the golden calf? You will forgive them — *ve'ata soleiach lahem* — and you cannot forgive me? This is not supplication; it is a challenge. A demand that justice be applied consistently.

### Esau's Challenge

Esav: *habracha achat hi lecha avi* — do you have only one blessing, Father? The complaint is directed to Yitzchak rather than to God, but it carries the same quality of pressing a claim. Is there only one blessing available? Give me the one that belongs to me.

### Menashe's Ultimatum

Menashe: *batkhila kara l'elohoot harbei u'levasof kara l'elohei avotav* — at first he called upon many other gods, and only at the end called upon the God of his fathers. Rashi explains the implicit challenge: having tried every other deity and found them unresponsive, Menashe's prayer to God carries an implicit ultimatum — if You are real, answer me as You answer others; prove yourself distinct from the gods who did not answer. The structure of the prayer, coming after all alternatives have been exhausted, constitutes its own form of pressure on the divine.

---

## God's Name Rules

### Name Pronunciation

The final ruling on this daf: Abba Shaul says — *af hahogeh et Hashem be'otiyotav* — one who pronounces the divine name as it is spelled is among those who forfeit their *chelek l'olam haba*. A *tanna* specifies: this applies in the *gevulin* — outside the Temple — and *b'lashon agah*, which is not entirely clear but appears to mean in the vernacular or in a casual register. The implication may be that pronouncing it in Hebrew — the sacred tongue — in a deliberate, reverent manner outside the Temple is at least somewhat less objectionable than doing so casually in the vernacular, though the precise line here is difficult to draw with confidence. We will continue from here tomorrow.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 102

## Intro & Overview

### Previous Topics

The daf under discussion is 102b, and with it we transition into a new section of *Perek Chelek*. By way of orientation, the opening portion of the perek addressed *olam ha-ba* and *techiyas ha-meisim* — the denial of resurrection as a disqualification from the World to Come — along with *yemos ha-mashiach* and ancillary topics such as one who pronounces the Divine Name in its letters, the category of *apikoros* (which, for the Gemara, refers not to a dogmatic heretic in the Rambam's sense but to one who disrespects rabbinic authority), and the prohibition against *sefarim chitzonim*, which led into an extended discussion touching on Ben Sira.

### Second Mishnah Intro

We now arrive at the second *mishnah* of *Perek Chelek* — printed in most editions as a distinct *mishnah* — which begins to identify specific individuals who have no portion in the World to Come. The *mishnah* states that three kings and four commoners (*hedyotos*) are excluded. The three kings are *Yerovam ben Nevat*, *Achav*, and *Menashe*.

### Three Kings Focus

A significant portion of the Gemara's analysis focuses on each of these three kings in turn, examining both the textual basis for their exclusion and the deeper moral and historical dimensions of their failures. Strikingly, the discussion is not a simple catalogue of wickedness; it also probes the greatness these figures once possessed, why they merited positions of leadership in the first place, and what ultimately led to their downfall.

---

## Yerovam Etymology

### Yerovam Name Play

The Gemara opens its treatment of *Yerovam* with a series of etymological plays on his name. *Tanu Rabbanan*: *Yerovam* — *she-riva am*, he trampled the people. Rashi understands the root *rova* in this context as connoting trampling or, alternatively, as suggesting sexual domination, though the more natural reading here is simply that he abused and downtrodden the people. A second interpretation: *she-asah merivah ba-am* — he created strife and contention among the people, splitting the nation in two. A third: *she-asah merivah bein Yisrael le-avihem she-bashamayim* — he drove a wedge between the people of Israel and their Father in Heaven, leading the ten tribes into *avoda zara* through the golden calves. As the Gemara will elaborate, while the division of the kingdom itself was prophetically ordained and carried out through the word of a *navi*, it was the manner in which Yerovam led the people astray that constituted his singular transgression.

### Ben Nevat Names

The Gemara then turns to the patronymic: *ben Nevat* — *ben she-nibat ve-lo ra'ah*, a son of one who saw but did not truly see. Nevat perceived a vision whose import he failed to grasp. A *tana* teaches that Nevat, Micha, and Sheva ben Bichri are all the same person — that is, the father of Yerovam goes by multiple names. The name *Micha* derives from *she-nismachmach ba-binyan*: according to the *midrash* cited by Rashi, when Moshe observed Jewish infants being embedded in the walls of Egyptian construction projects and protested to God, God responded that these children would grow up to be *resha'im* in any case. One child was saved — Micha — who later became the source of idolatrous influence in Israel for generations. The name *Sheva ben Bichri* was simply his given name.

### Three Who Saw

*Tanu Rabbanan*: three people *nibtu ve-lo ra'u* — they saw but failed to perceive correctly. They are Nevat, Achitophel, and the astrologers of Pharaoh.

### Nevat Fire Vision

What did Nevat see? *Ra'ah esh yotze me-amato* — he saw fire issuing from his body. He interpreted this as a sign of his own kingship. *Ve-lo hi* — he was mistaken. The fire referred to Yerovam, who would emerge from him and become king.

### Achitophel Leprosy

Achitophel saw leprosy blazing across his bed — *tzara'at she-zarcha lo al ha-mitah* — and concluded that this portended his own kingship. *Ve-lo hi*: it referred instead to Bat-Sheva his daughter, from whom Shlomo would descend.

### Astrologers Vision

The astrologers of Pharaoh saw a vision involving water — the very waters alluded to in the phrase *mei Merivah*, as Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina explains. They perceived that the savior of Israel would be struck through water. This led them to counsel Pharaoh to drown all newborn Jewish boys, reasoning that the one destined to redeem Israel would be caught in that decree. *Ve-hein lo yad'u she-al iskei mei Merivah lokeh* — what they failed to understand was that Moshe's undoing would come not through drowning as an infant but through the waters of Merivah, decades later.

---

## Yerovam Merit & Fall

### Biblical Proof

Returning to the main subject: how do we know that Yerovam has no portion in *olam ha-ba*? *De-ketiv*: *vayehi ba-davar hazeh le-chatat beit Yerovam u-lehachid u-lehishmid me-al pnei ha-adamah* — "And this matter became a sin for the house of Yerovam, to cut off and to destroy from the face of the earth." The Gemara reads the double language: *lehachid ba-olam hazeh*, to be cut off from this world, *ve-lehishmid le-olam ha-ba*, and to be destroyed from the World to Come.

### Yerovam Merit

Rabbi Yochanan asks: *mipnei mah zachah Yerovam le-malchus?* Given all his evil, why did he merit becoming king in the first place? *Mipnei she-hochiah et Shlomo* — because he rebuked Shlomo. Reading the narrative in *Tanach*, it is evident that Shlomo had acted improperly, and Yerovam was the one who first gave him *musar*, which ultimately led to the prophetic designation of Yerovam as the ruler over ten tribes, serving simultaneously as a reward for Yerovam's integrity and a punishment for Shlomo's failings.

Then the Gemara asks: *u-mipnei mah ne'enash?* Where were the seeds of his downfall already visible in that original act? *Mipnei she-hochiacho be-rabbim* — because he publicly humiliated Shlomo. The willingness to give *musar* was admirable, but the manner — before others, without proper respect for the king — already revealed something troubling. The verse says: *ve-zeh ha-davar asher herim yad ba-melech Shlomo* — "and this is the thing that he lifted his hand against King Shlomo." The specific act, notes Rav Nachman, was *she-chalatz tfilav befanav* — that he removed his *tefilin* in Shlomo's presence, an act of studied disrespect and perhaps a kind of brazen undressing before the king.

The verse that prompted this confrontation relates that Shlomo built up the *Millo* and closed the breach in the city of David. Yerovam challenged him: your father David intentionally left openings in the walls of Jerusalem to facilitate the *oleh la-regel* — the pilgrimage — so that all could enter freely. You have sealed them, imposing *angarya* — a king's levy — for the benefit of Bat Pharaoh, your Egyptian queen, by collecting tolls at the gates.

### Seeds Downfall

Rav Nachman observes: *gasut ruach she-hayah bo be-Yerovam tardato min ha-olam* — the arrogance inherent in Yerovam destroyed him from the world, and *olam* here encompasses *olam ha-ba*. The public rebuke was an expression of that arrogance; the removal of *tefilin* before the king was another. These were not merely incidental lapses — they were symptoms of the quality that would ultimately express itself in the most consequential way.

### Jerusalem Fear

The Gemara now cites the verse: *vayomer Yerovam be-libo: atah tashuv ha-mamlachah le-veit David im ya'aleh ha-am ha-zeh la'asot zevachim be-veit Hashem bi-Yerushalayim* — Yerovam reasoned to himself that if the people continued to make pilgrimage to Jerusalem three times a year, they would inevitably return their loyalty to the house of David and to Rechavam. *Ve-shav lev ha-am ha-zeh el adoneihem el Rechavam melech Yehudah* — their hearts would follow the king whose religious center they attended. *Ve-haraguni ve-shavu el Rechavam melech Yehudah* — they would kill me and go back to Rechavam. It is worth noting the sharp irony: Yerovam's original rebuke to Shlomo was precisely that he had obstructed *aliyah la-regel*, and yet Yerovam's own political survival now depended on preventing that same pilgrimage.

### Azarah Status

The Gemara adds a further dimension to Yerovam's calculations. *Gemiri*: there is a received tradition that only the kings of the house of Yehudah were permitted to sit in the *Azarah* — the Temple courtyard — while all others, including kings of other tribes, were required to stand. *Keivan de-chazu leh le-Rechavam de-yativ ve-ana ka'imna* — when the people saw Rechavam seated and Yerovam standing, they would conclude that Rechavam was the king and Yerovam the servant. One might ask: what if Yerovam simply sat as well, claiming equal status? The Gemara answers that doing so on Rechavam's territory would constitute *mored be-malchus* — rebellion against the king — an act for which he could be put to death. The phrase *mored be-malchus* is admittedly a surprising one given that Yerovam had already established a separate kingdom; as the Gemara seems to intend it here, it means specifically transgressing the special prerogatives of the Davidic crown, or perhaps more precisely, a brazen challenge to God's *malchus* itself. Either way, the conclusion is the same: Yerovam could not accompany the pilgrims to Jerusalem without exposing either his subordinate status or his sedition.

### Golden Calves

*Miyad vayiva'atz ha-melech vaya'as shenei eglei zahav* — immediately Yerovam took counsel and fashioned two golden calves. *Vayomer aleihem: rav lachem me'alot Yerushalayim* — he told the people, it is too great a burden to go up to Jerusalem. *Hineh elohecha Yisrael asher he'elucha me-eretz Mitzrayim* — consciously echoing the language of the original *eigel ha-zahav* in the wilderness. He placed one in Beit El and one in Dan, establishing two convenient cult sites so that the people would have no need to make the arduous journey southward. The *gasut ha-ruach* that had been visible from the beginning expressed itself here fully: he would do anything, even transform Israel into an idolatrous nation, to preserve his power and status.

### Manipulation Deception

The Gemara asks: *mai vayiva'atz* — what did it mean that he "took counsel"? Rabbi Yehuda explains: *she-hoshiv rasha etzel tzadik* — he seated a wicked person alongside a righteous person. He circulated a document requiring all citizens of the ten tribes to affirm their loyalty and obedience to him. The exchange would proceed as follows: Yerovam's agent would ask, "Will you sign to do whatever I command?" — *kol de-amina lachon aviditu*? The people would answer yes. Then: "Even to worship *avodat kochavim*?" At this point the *tzadik* would recoil — *chas ve-shalom!* — and the *rasha* seated beside him would say: "Do you think someone as righteous as Yerovam would actually intend such a thing? He is merely testing our commitment; of course he does not mean it literally." And so the *tzadik* was persuaded to sign.

### Achiya Signed

By the end of this process, Yerovam had secured the assent of every stratum of the population — including, shockingly, *Achiya ha-Shiloni*, the very prophet who had initially designated Yerovam as king. *Ve-af Achiya ha-Shiloni ta'ah ve-chatam* — even Achiya ha-Shiloni was deceived and signed.

### Yehu Yerovam

The Gemara uses the story of Yehu to demonstrate both Achiya's greatness and the significance of his having signed. Yehu was a great *tzadik*, as the verse attests: *ya'an asher hetivota la'asot ha-yashar be-einai* — God praised him for having done all that was right, having wiped out the entire house of Achav as commanded. Yet the verse continues: *ve-Yehu lo shamar lalechet be-Torat Hashem Elohei Yisrael be-chol levavo lo sar me-chatat Yerovam* — Yehu himself did not depart from the sins of Yerovam. The Gemara asks: *mai garmeh* — what caused this righteous person to go astray?

Abaye answers: *berit kerutah la-sefatayim* — a covenant is formed by one's lips. When Yehu, in the course of his campaign against the prophets of the *Ba'al*, declared *Achav avad ha-Ba'al me'at, Yehu ya'avdenu harbe* — "Achav served the Ba'al a little, but Yehu will serve him greatly" — he did so as a ruse to lure them in. Nevertheless, those words having passed his lips, they held power over him and ultimately drew him toward the worship he had only feigned.

Rava disagrees: *chotamto shel Achiya ha-Shiloni ra'ah ve-ta'ah* — he saw the signature of Achiya ha-Shiloni on Yerovam's loyalty document and was thereby led astray. If a man of Achiya's stature had signed, Yehu reasoned, there must be legitimacy to it. This connects the account of Yehu back directly to the earlier discussion of how Yerovam's deception had implicated even the most righteous figures, whose endorsement then perpetuated his influence across generations.

The Gemara then cites the difficult verse from Hoshea: *ve-shachata shetim he'emiku, va-ani musar le-chulam* — "those that went astray went deep, and I am a reproof to all of them." Rabbi Yochanan reads this as God saying: they went deeper than I did. *Ani amarti: kol she-eino oleh la-regel over be-aseh* — I said only that one who fails to make the pilgrimage transgresses a positive commandment. *Ve-hen amru: kol ha-oleh la-regel yidaker ba-cherev* — but they decreed that anyone who goes up to the Temple will be killed by the sword. That was Yerovam's prohibition against pilgrimage: not mere disobedience but a policy of lethal enforcement.

---

## Cloth & Covenant

### Times Places Trouble

The Gemara observes that the encounter between Yerovam and Achiya ha-Shiloni was not coincidental in its timing. *Tana mishmei de-Rabbi Yosi*: the verse says *vayehi ba-et ha-hi* — and it was at that time. *Et hi mezumenet le-puranut* — that time was designated for calamity. The Gemara expands this principle: just as there are times designated for punishment — *uve-et pekudatam yovedu* — there are also times designated for blessing — *uve-et ratzon aniticha, et mezumenet le-tovah*. This is not merely coincidence; certain periods are intrinsically charged with either benevolent or destructive potential. Rashi makes explicit that *vayom pokdi* refers to Tisha B'Av, a day designated for disaster from the time of the *meraglim*, through the destruction of the First and Second Temples alike — a recurring moment of concentrated catastrophe.

The same *tana*, Rabbi Yosi, makes a parallel observation about a different verse: *uve-yom pokdi u-fakadeti aleihem chatatam* — this too is a designated time, connected directly to the sin of the *eigel*, and Rashi again identifies it with Tisha B'Av. Times of disaster recur; and certain sins continue to accumulate their punishment across multiple such moments.

### Shechem Disasters

From designated times the Gemara turns to designated places: *vayeilech Rechavam Shchem ki Shechem ba kol Yisrael lehamlikh oto* — Rechavam went to Shechem because all Israel gathered there to crown him. *Tana mishmei de-Rabbi Yosi: makom mezuman le-puranut*. Shechem is a place historically associated with catastrophe. It was in Shechem that Dinah was violated; it was in Shechem — or its environs, since Rashi identifies Dotan as essentially a suburb of Shechem — that the brothers sold Yosef; and it was in Shechem that the kingdom of the house of David was rent in two.

The Gemara also preserves, in passing, that *Yerovam yatza mi-Yerushalayim* — Yerovam departed from Jerusalem. Rabbi Chanina bar Papa comments: *she-yatza mi-pitka shel Yerushalayim* — he left the faith, the lot, the essential spiritual covenant of Jerusalem. The word *pitka*, a kind of note or slip, is used here in an unusual but evocative sense: Yerovam severed himself from the destiny of the holy city.

### New Cloak

The meeting between Achiya ha-Shiloni and Yerovam is described as taking place while Achiya wore a new cloak: *ve-hu mitkaseh be-salma chadashah*. *Mai salma chadashah?* Rav Nachman explains: *ke-salma chadashah — ein bah shum dofi* — just as a new garment has no blemish or stain, so too the Torah of Yerovam had no blemish at that time. Before his descent into sin, his Torah learning was flawless and unblemished. A second interpretation: *she-chidshu devarim she-lo shama ozen me-olam* — the garment was "new" because the Torah insights they discussed were so brilliant and unprecedented that no ear had ever heard anything like them. They did not immediately turn to political matters; first they learned Torah together, and the learning itself was the "new cloak."

### Field Alone

The verse continues: *u-shneihem levadim ba-sadeh* — and the two of them were alone in the field. Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav explains: *she-kol talmidei chachamim domim lifneihem ke-isvei ha-sadeh* — that all other Torah scholars of the generation appeared before them like blades of grass in a field; their stature was so far above their contemporaries. An alternative reading: *she-kol ta'amei Torah megulim lahem ka-sadeh* — all the hidden reasons of Torah were open and revealed to them, as exposed to view as a field.

This leads to a passage from Micha: *lachen titni shilluchim al Moreshet Gat, batei Achziv le-achzav le-malchei Yisrael* — therefore send farewell messengers to Moreshet Gat; the houses of Achziv will prove a deception to the kings of Israel. Rabbi Chanina bar Papa reads this as a divine rebuke: the one who killed the Philistines — King David, who slew Golyat of Gat — gave you the inheritance of Gat. And now you are sending farewell notices to his children, stealing the kingdom away from the house of David? Rashi explains: *le-malchei beit David atem mechazvim, ve-halachtem acharei malchei Yisrael* — you are deceiving the kings of the house of David and going after the kings of Israel instead.

This brings the Gemara to a statement by Rabbi Chanina bar Papa: *kol ha-neheneh min ha-olam ha-zeh be-lo bracha ke-ilu gozel le-Hakadosh Baruch Hu u-Knesset Yisrael* — anyone who derives benefit from this world without making a *bracha* is as though he stole from God and from the Jewish people. The proof text: *gozel aviv ve-imo ve-amar ein pesha, chaver hu le-ish mashchit* — one who steals from his father and mother and says it is no sin is a companion to a destructive person. *Ve-ein aviv ela ha-Kadosh Baruch Hu* — "father" is God, as the verse says *halo hu avicha kanecha*; *ve-ein imo ela Knesset Yisrael* — "mother" is the Jewish people, as the verse says *shema beni musar avicha ve-al titosh Torat imecha*.

The relevance here lies in the final clause: *chaver hu le-ish mashchit — chaver hu le-Yerovam ben Nevat she-hishchit Yisrael le-avihem she-ba-shamayim* — he is a companion to Yerovam, who destroyed the people by separating them from their Father in Heaven. The parallel is pointed: *avoda zara* draws people's worship away from God; similarly, when a person encounters the world without a *bracha*, without recognizing the divine source of what he enjoys, he is effectively separating his experience of the world from God — much as Yerovam directed the people's worship toward the golden calves. The connection to *Knesset Yisrael* as the aggrieved "mother" is somewhat less explicit in the proof text, though one might suggest that just as Yerovam's sin corrupted the whole people, one who models indifference to *brachos* may lead others astray as well.

The section on Yerovam concludes: *vayidach Yerovam et Yisrael me'acharei Hashem ve-hecheti'am chata'ah gedolah* — he drew Israel away from God and caused them to sin greatly. Rabbi Chanin offers an image: *ki-shtei maklot ha-matizah zo et zo* — like two sticks, one of which is struck so hard by the other that it goes flying far away. The separation Yerovam effected was not a modest drift but a violent and radical rupture.

---

## Cheit HaEigel Legacy

### Gold Complaint

The mention of the golden calves prompts the Gemara to step back and address the sin of the *eigel ha-zahav* in the wilderness. *Amru de-vei Rabbi Yannai*: the verse in Devarim contains the place name *Ve-Di Zahav*. The *derasha* reads this as *dai zahav* — too much gold. Moshe said before God: *Ribono shel Olam, bishvil ha-kesef ve-ha-zahav she-hishpata lahem le-Yisrael, ad she-yomru dai, garam lahem la'asot lahem elohei zahav* — it was the superabundance of silver and gold that You poured upon Israel that caused them to make the golden calves. The *mashal*: a lion does not trample and roar when it is fed from a trough of grain; only when it devours flesh does it become fierce and boisterous. Excess prosperity breeds arrogance and ultimately leads to transgression.

### One Calf Two

Rabbi Yoshiyah notes: *ad Yerovam hayu Yisrael yonkim me-eigel echad* — until Yerovam, Israel suffered the consequences of only the one golden calf made in the wilderness. *Mi-kan ve-eilach mishnayim u-shloshah agalim* — from that point forward, they were burdened by the sins of two more: the two calves Yerovam erected at Beit El and Dan, added to the original of Moshe's time, making three altogether.

### Twenty-Fourth

Rabbi Yitzchak teaches: there is no calamity that comes upon the world that does not contain *echad me-esrim ve-arba be-hachra litra shel eigel ha-rishon* — one twenty-fourth of a scale-tipping measure of the original sin of the golden calf. The language evokes the practice of adding a tiny counterweight to a scale to ensure accurate measure: every catastrophe carries within it a fraction of that primordial sin. One might further suggest that the image implies something about causation — that tiny residual weight is sometimes the very thing that tips the scales toward punishment, even if the sin itself has long seemed settled.

### 24 Generations

Rabbi Chanina adds the longitudinal dimension: *le-achar esrim ve-arba dorot nigbah pasuk zeh* — this verse, in which God declares He will visit the sin of the *eigel* upon Israel, was finally collected after twenty-four generations. The verse: *vayikra be-oznai kol gadol leimor: kirvu pekudot ha-ir ve-ish kli mashchito be-yado* — the cry of Yechezkel announcing the coming destruction of the city, each destroying angel armed with his weapon of ruin. Rashi demonstrates that this moment — the destruction of Jerusalem — fell precisely twenty-four generations after the *cheit ha-eigel*. The *pekudot* of Yechezkel thus fulfills the *u-fakadeti* of Shemot. One might also hear in this a note of closure: the debt was ultimately discharged completely, rather than stretching indefinitely.

---

## Teshuva Complexity

### Teshuva Gan Eden

*Achar ha-davar ha-zeh lo shav Yerovam mi-darko ha-ra'ah* — after all this, Yerovam did not return from his evil path. The Gemara asks: *mai achar* — after what? What event should have prompted him to return? Rabbi Abba explains: *achar she-tefaso ha-Kadosh Baruch Hu le-Yerovam be-vigdo* — after God, as it were, took Yerovam by the collar and said to him: return. *Va-ani u-ven Yishai netayel be-Gan Eden* — I, you, and the son of Yishai — King David — will stroll together in Gan Eden. God offered Yerovam not merely forgiveness but the most exalted spiritual companionship imaginable.

### Pride Rejection

Yerovam's response: *mi be-rosh?* — who walks first? *Ben Yishai be-rosh* — David goes first. *Ei hachi lo be'ina* — then I don't want it. This exchange crystallizes everything the Gemara has been building toward. The man who started off giving *musar* to a king, the man whose downfall the Gemara traces entirely to *gasut ha-ruach*, refused divine pardon because it came with a subordinate position. He would rather forfeit *olam ha-ba* than walk behind David.

### Abbahu Sickness

Rabbi Abbahu was accustomed to lecture extensively about the three evil kings of *Perek Chelek*, dwelling on their misdeeds and punishments. At a certain point he fell ill — *chalash* — and understanding the possible significance of this, he accepted upon himself to cease. *Ve-kidel aleih de-lo darash*. Once he recovered, he resumed his lectures. His students challenged him: did you not commit to stop? He replied: *inhu mi-hadru behu de-ana ahadar bi?* — did they stop sinning, that I should stop preaching? The exchange is left somewhat unresolved, but the story serves as a prelude to what follows, suggesting that excessive focus on these kings' wickedness is itself potentially problematic.

### Rav Ashi Plan

Rav Ashi was engaged in a sequential study of *Perek Chelek*. At the point where he was about to reach the section on the three kings, he stopped for the day and announced: *le-machar niftach be-chaverin* — tomorrow we will begin with our colleagues. His decision to call the three evil kings "colleagues" was an expression of genuine recognition: even these figures, with all their profound wrongdoing, were men of vast Torah learning, and as such they merited a degree of collegial respect from those who studied Torah in later generations.

That night, Menashe appeared to him in a dream.

### Menashe Challenge

*Amar: chavrecha ve-chavrei de-avuch karita lan?* — you called us your colleagues and your father's colleagues? The impertinence of that designation! Then Menashe posed a question: *me-heicha de-ba'it le-mishra ha-motzi?* — where does one break the bread when reciting *ha-motzi*? Rav Ashi admitted he did not know. Menashe was incredulous: you perform *ha-motzi* every single day and you do not know the proper place from which to break it — and you consider yourself our colleague? Rav Ashi, rather than defending himself, asked Menashe to teach him. *Agmar li, ul-machar darishna mi-shmach be-pirka* — teach me, and tomorrow I will transmit this teaching in your name in the public assembly. Menashe replied: *me-heicha de-karim bishula* — from where the baking forms a crust. Rashi suggests this means one takes from the outer, firmer crust rather than the soft interior, or from the part that is more thoroughly baked.

### Seduction Defense

Then Rav Ashi turned the conversation around: *me-achar de-chakimtu kulei hai, mai ta'ama ke-pachitu la-avodat kochavim?* — given your tremendous wisdom, why did you worship idols? Menashe's answer has become one of the most cited passages in this perek: *i havit hatam, havat nakitat be-shipulei glimach ve-rahitat basrai* — if you had been there, you would have picked up the skirts of your cloak and run after it. The seductive power of *avodat kochavim* in that era was so overwhelming that one cannot judge from a later vantage point. The moral and cultural force of that pull is simply not accessible to those who did not live through it.

### Colleagues Rabbis

The next morning, Rav Ashi addressed the assembled scholars differently than he had planned. *Le-machar amar lehu le-rabbanan: niftach be-ravvata* — let us begin with the great ones. Not "colleagues" — *chaverin* — but "our rabbis" — *rabbanan* or *ravvata*. They were *resha'im*, yes, but they were also great figures whose depth of Torah and whose complexity of character demand a certain reverence, or at the very least, humility.
