This is a striking recalibration. The lesson of Menashe's dream appearance is not merely a charming anecdote about where to break *challah*; it is a demand for intellectual and moral modesty. The ease with which later generations pronounce judgment on those who served *avoda zara* reflects a failure to appreciate the pressures and temptations of those times.

This principle suffuses the entire discussion of the three kings: the Gemara's portrait of Yerovam is not one-dimensional villainy but a complex interweaving of genuine Torah greatness, corrupted by arrogance and fear, ultimately expressing itself in catastrophic national sin. And Menashe's rebuke to Rav Ashi asks that we carry that complexity with us.

---

## Achav

### Achav Names

The Gemara turns to Achav. Again, a series of name-plays: *ach la-shamayim* — using *ach* not as "brother" but as an exclamation of woe, a cry of anguish: woe to heaven, i.e., his very existence is a source of grief to heaven. The proof text: *ach le-tzarah yulad* — a woe, one born for trouble. *Av la-avodat kochavim* — a father to *avoda zara*, meaning he cherished and cultivated idolatry. The proof text: *ke-rachem av al banim* — as a father has compassion on his children.

### Achav Worse

The verse says: *vayehi ha-nekel le-lechto be-chatat Yerovam ben Nevat* — it was trivial for him to walk in the sins of Yerovam. Rabbi Yochanan explains: *kalot she-asa Achav ke-chamurot she-asa Yerovam* — the lightest of Achav's sins were as weighty as the gravest of Yerovam's. He did Yerovam's program, and then multiplied it tenfold. Yet the verse still attributes his evil with reference to Yerovam — *mipnei mah tala ha-katuv be-Yerovam?* — because Yerovam was the *techila le-kalkalah*, the originator of the corruption. All subsequent evil among the kings of Israel flowed from the precedent and culture that Yerovam had established.

### Every Furrow

Rabbi Yochanan adds: *ein lecha kol telem ve-telem be-Eretz Yisrael she-lo he'emid alav Achav avoda zara ve-hishtachavah lo* — there was not a single furrow in all of the land of Israel upon which Achav did not erect an idol and bow before it. The verse from Hoshea — *gam mizbechotam ke-galim al talmei sadai* — their altars like mounds along the furrows of the fields — is read with literal comprehensiveness: every field, every furrow, every inch of cultivated land in Eretz Yisrael was desecrated with idolatrous worship.

### Mashtin Proof

How do we know Achav has no portion in *olam ha-ba*? *De-ketiv: ve-hichrati le-Achav mashtin be-kir* — I will cut off for Achav every *mashtin be-kir*, which the Gemara reads as a reference to *talmidei chachamim*, and *atzur va-azuv be-Yisrael* — whether constrained in this world or abandoned in the next. The double language again: *atzur ba-olam ha-zeh, ve-azuv le-olam ha-ba*. Both categories of persons associated with Achav's regime will be destroyed — and by extension, Achav himself is without portion.

### Omri City

Rabbi Yochanan asks: *mipnei mah zachah Omri le-malchus?* — why did Omri, Achav's father, merit kingship despite his own wickedness? *Mipnei she-hosif kerach echad be-Eretz Yisrael* — because he added one city to the land of Israel. The verse: *vayiken et ha-har Shomron me-et Shemer be-kicharayim kesef, vayiven et ha-har, vayikra et shem ha-ir asher banah shem Shemer: Shomron* — he purchased the hill of Samaria from Shemer for two talents of silver, built it up, and named it Shomron after its former owner. That single act of building and expanding Israel's territory secured Omri a dynasty.

### Achav Torah

Rabbi Yochanan then asks the same question about Achav: *mipnei mah zachah Achav le-malchus* — and for how long? *Kaf-chet shanim* — twenty-two years, a substantial reign. *Mipnei she-kibed et ha-Torah she-nitnah be-chaf-bet osiyot* — because he honored the Torah given in twenty-two letters of the Hebrew alphabet.

### Sefer Torah

How did Achav honor the Torah? The Gemara cites the episode in which Ben-Hadad, the hostile king, sent messengers to Achav demanding: your silver and gold are mine, your wives and children are mine; and further, my servants will come and search your house and take whatever is most desirable to you. Achav responded by agreeing to the first demands but refusing the last: *ve-hadavar hazeh lo uchal la'asot* — this thing I cannot do.

*Mai machmad eynecha?* — what was the most desirable possession he refused to surrender? *Lav sefer Torah?* — must it not be the *Sefer Torah*? The Gemara considers an objection: perhaps it was his idols — given his devotion to *avoda zara*, perhaps that was what he refused to relinquish? *Lo salka da'atcha*: the text records that *vayomru elav kol ha-zkenim ve-chol ha-am* — all the elders and all the people told him not to comply. Unanimous popular support for the refusal is inconceivable if the issue were idols — surely somewhere among all the people there would have been someone unwilling to take a stand in defense of *avoda zara*. But the one thing that would command truly unanimous assent — from every stratum of the population, including the *zkenim* who were actual *talmidei chachamim* — was the defense of the *Sefer Torah*. And that is indeed the reading Rav Yosef offers: those *zkenim* were genuine sages, not, as he says of the elders who supported Avshalom's rebellion, *savei de-vahata* — foolish old men. The proof: by Avshalom the verse does not say *ve-chol ha-am*, whereas here it does. Universal popular assent seals the identification.

Because Achav protected the *Sefer Torah*, even from the overwhelming military threat of Ben-Hadad, he merited twenty-two years of kingship — one year for each letter of the *aleph-beit* in which the Torah was given.

---

## Achav Beinoni

### Beinoni Status

Rav Nachman makes a striking claim: *Achav shakul hayah* — Achav was precisely balanced, a *beinoni*. His merits and transgressions were exactly equal.

### Seduction Proof

The proof: God asked *mi yefateh et Achav* — who will seduce Achav? If Achav had been wholly wicked — a complete *rasha* — seduction would have been unnecessary. One seduces someone who is not already committed to the sin. The very need for divine orchestration of temptation demonstrates that Achav retained some measure of resistance, that the scales were not already decided.

### Sold Evil

Rav Yosef objects: the verse says *asher hitmaker la'asot ha-ra be-einei Hashem* — he sold himself to do evil. A *beinoni* does not sell himself; only a fully committed *rasha* does.

### Izevel Gold

Furthermore, *asher hesatah oto Izavel ishto* — Izavel seduced him. And the *baraita* records: *be-chol yom hayta shokelet shiklei zahav la-avodat kochavim* — every single day Izavel would weigh out gold shekels to finance *avodat kochavim*. Taken together — that he sold himself to evil and that Izavel actively drove the idolatrous enterprise — Rav Yosef concludes that Achav was a complete *rasha*, not a *beinoni*.

### Tzedakah Half

The Gemara resolves this: *vatran be-mamoneh hayah* — Achav was extremely generous with his money. *U-mitoch she-henah talmidei chachamim mi-nechasav, kiperu lo mechtzah* — and because Torah scholars benefited from his wealth, God waived half his sins. So while Rav Nachman was right that the scales appeared balanced — balanced enough that seduction was required to tip them — the reason for the balance was not that Achav was intrinsically a *beinoni* in his moral constitution. Rather, the extraordinary *tzedakah* of supporting Torah scholarship neutralized precisely half the weight of his transgressions. The *cheshbon* came out even, but only because of this one overriding merit. Once again the Gemara insists: one never knows the full weight of a single *mitzvah*, and the support of Torah study in particular carries consequences that may offset sins of the gravest order.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 103

## Achav & Idolatry

### Three Evil Kings

The present sugya continues in Perek Chelek, on 103a, amid the discussion of the three evil kings: *Yerovam*, *Achav*, and *Menashe*. *Yerovam* was dealt with previously — he split the kingdom, made the two golden calves, and led all the people into *avodah zarah*. Indeed, every subsequent king of Israel who did evil is described in terms of *Yerovam*: they continued to do evil as he had done. We now turn to *Achav*, one of the most terrible kings, notorious for his partnership with *Izevel*, the murder of *Nabot*, and his introduction of widespread idolatry. The *Gemara* notes, however, that he enjoyed a long reign — understood through the *midrash* as a reward for having treasured and protected the *Sefer Torah*.

### Achav's Merits

Beyond his protection of the *Sefer Torah*, the *Gemara* records that while his wife *Izevel* was channeling funds toward *avodah zarah*, *Achav* was directing his own wealth toward the support of *talmidei chachamim*. These merits, however qualified, earned him some measure of divine favor during his lifetime.

### Nabot's Spirit

The *Gemara* now picks up approximately ten lines from the bottom of the page, quoting the verse in which God addresses the spirits assembled before Him, asking who will go and seduce *Achav* into entering the battle in which he will fall. *Vayetze haruach vayaamod lifnei Hashem* — one spirit came and stood before God. *Vayomer ani apatenu* — I will seduce him. God asked: *bameh*, how? The spirit replied: *etze vehayiti ruach sheker befi kol nevi'av* — I will become a false spirit in the mouths of all of his false prophets, and they will all prophesy that he should go to war, and he will fall. God responds: *tepateh gam tuchal tze vaaseh ken* — go, seduce him, and you will succeed.

*Mai ruach?* What was this spirit? Rabbi Yochanan says: *rucho shel Nabot haYizre'eli* — the spirit of *Nabot haYizre'eli*, the man whose vineyard *Achav* had stolen and whose murder *Achav* had engineered. This spirit now finds his justice. It is worth pausing here: much of this discussion concerns *olam haba*, which in this context refers to the world following the Messianic era, though the more familiar notion of the afterlife — where the soul goes after death — also operates in fewer sources and becomes dominant in later tradition. Here, the disembodied soul of *Nabot* is obtaining his reckoning.

*Mai tze?* Why did God need to say *tze*, "go out," if He had simply given the spirit his commission? *Amar Ravina: tze mimichitzati* — get out of my presence. As the verse says, *dover shekarim lo yikon leneged einai* — one who speaks falsehood will not stand before me. God essentially says: this is a necessary task, but once you are going out to speak falsehood, I no longer want you near me. It is worth noting the distinction: the original commission was *pitu'i*, seduction, which is not the same as outright lying — yet the spirit's execution of the task would involve falsehood, and for that God sends him away.

*Amar Papa: hainu de'amrei inshi, dipara kinei machriv beiteh* — that is what people say: the one who finally exacts vengeance for his jealousy ultimately destroys his own home. You may find satisfaction in acting on those feelings of revenge, but the outcome will be deeply destructive for yourself.

### Desecrating Torah

The *Gemara* then quotes the verse *vayaas Achav et ha'asheirah*, that *Achav* made the *asheira*, and *vayosef Achav laasot lehachis et Hashem elokei Yisrael mikol malchei Yisrael asher hayu lefanav* — he did more to anger God than all the kings who came before him. What did he do that so pointedly expressed his wickedness? Rabbi Yochanan says: *shekatav al daltot Shomron* — he wrote on the doors of *Shomron*: *Achav kafar be'elokei Yisrael* — *Achav* has rejected the God of Israel. He made it into a philosophical declaration: I reject you; I want nothing to do with you. And therefore, *ein lo chelek l'olam haba* — he has no portion in the world to come.

The *Gemara* then cites a verse about *Achazyahu* hiding in *Shomron* — though on its face the verse concerns *Achazyahu*, the *Gemara* appears ultimately to be reading it as referring to *Achav*. *Amar Rabbi Levi: shehayah koder azkarot* — what he would do is take a *Sefer Torah*, cut out or scrape away God's names, *vekotev avodat kokhavim tachtehen* — and write in their place the names of *avodah zarah*. He preserved the form of the *Sefer Torah* but replaced every divine Name with the name of an idol.

---

## Menashe's Repentanc (III)

### Menashe's Status

We now turn to the third king, *Menashe*. The *Gemara* begins with a play on his name: *shenashyah* — he forgot God. *Davar acher*: *shehishia et Yisrael l'avihen shebashamayim* — he caused Israel to be forgotten by their Father in heaven, or he caused Israel to forget God.

*Umanlan d'lo ati l'alma d'ati* — how do we know he has no portion in the world to come? The verse states: *ben shtem esreh shanah Menashe bemolcho vachamishim vechamesh shanah malach b'Yerushalayim* — he was twelve years old when he began to reign and he reigned for fifty-five years. *Vaya'as Asherah ka'asher asah Achav melech Yisrael* — and he made an *asheira* just as *Achav* king of Israel had done. The *Gemara* applies a *gezeirah shavah*: just as *Achav* has no portion in the world to come, so too *Menashe* has no portion in the world to come.

However, *Rabbi Yehuda omer Menashe yesh lo chelek l'olam haba* — Rabbi Yehuda holds that *Menashe* does have a portion in the world to come, as the verse says: *vayitpallel Menashe el Hashem vay'ater lo HaElohim* — *Menashe* prayed to God and God was importuned by him and responded. Rabbi Yehuda reads this as indicating genuine *teshuvah*, in contrast to *Achav*.

*Amar Rabbi Yochanan ushneihem mikra echad darshu* — both opinions are interpreting a single verse: *unatatim l'za'avah l'chol mamlechot ha'aretz biglal Menashe ben Yechizkiyahu* — I will make them a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth, because of *Menashe* son of *Yechizkiyahu*. *Mar savar*: one reads this as *biglal Menashe she'asah teshuvah v'inhu lo avid* — because *Menashe* demonstrated that even the most wicked person could do *teshuvah*, and this in turn, by contrast, indirectly brings judgment upon those who did not. *Umar savar* — and the other, which is closer to the simple meaning of the text, reads it as *biglal Menashe d'lo avid* — because of the evil that *Menashe* actually perpetrated, for which the people will ultimately pay.

---

## Achav & Idolatry (II)

### No Share in Olam HaBa

The question arises regarding the *pasuk haraita ki nikhna Achav lifnai — yaan ki nikhna mipanai lo avia hara'ah beyamav*, the moment of *Achav*'s apparent humility before God. The assumption appears to be that this represented a moment of submission but not genuine *teshuvah*, and therefore it extended *Achav*'s days but did not reverse his ultimate judgment.

---

## Menashe's Repentanc (III)

### Rabbi Yehuda's View

*Amar Rabbi Yochanan*, at the top of 103a: *kol ha'omer Menashe ein lo chelek l'olam haba merappe yedeihen shel ba'alei teshuvah*. This is a striking statement. Rabbi Yochanan is not saying the view is factually wrong — he is making a point about which version of the story one chooses to tell. If one opts to emphasize the sheer wickedness of *Menashe* and declares that even after doing *teshuvah* it made no difference, that is not a religiously constructive message. The choice of interpretive framing carries moral consequences.

### Two Interpretations

The two views trace back to the same verse, and the debate reflects a genuine ambiguity: does *biglal Menashe* refer to the evil he committed, or does it refer to his *teshuvah* and what his repentance demonstrated? The *peshat* reading favors the former; the more theologically productive reading favors the latter.

One might raise the parallel of *Acher*, about whom the *Gemara* is extraordinarily harsh, with formulations like *chutz m'Acher* — even *teshuvah* would not help him. The answer is that Rabbi Yochanan is not asking anyone to claim that a person did *teshuvah* when he demonstrably did not. *Acher* showed no basis for *teshuvah*. The point here is specifically that when the verses genuinely permit a reading in which *teshuvah* occurred — when that is a legitimate interpretive option — one should adopt that version rather than the more damning one.

### Repentance Narrative

The account of *Menashe*'s *teshuvah* appears in *Divrei HaYamim* and is absent from *Sefer Melachim*, and scholars have noted the possibility of a difference in theological perspective between those two books. The *Gemara*, for its part, does not adjudicate the factual question but emphasizes the religious imperative: where *teshuvah* can reasonably be affirmed, affirm it.

### 33 Years of Good

A *tanna* taught before Rabbi Yochanan: *Menashe asa teshuvah shloshim v'shalosh shanim* — *Menashe* was on the righteous path for thirty-three years. The calculation proceeds from the verse: *ben shtaim esre shana Menashe b'molcho v'chamishim v'chamesh shana malach b'Yerushalayim* — he was twelve years old at his accession and reigned for fifty-five years. *Vaya'as hara kechol asher asu Achav melech Yisrael* — and he did evil like *Achav*. But *Achav* only reigned for twenty-two years. The *tanna* is asked: how long did *Achav* reign? Twenty-two years. How long did *Menashe* reign? Fifty-five. The years of evil — equated with the length of *Achav*'s reign by the *gezeirah shavah* — amount to twenty-two. *Pashu lei tlatin v'tlat* — that leaves thirty-three years of goodness. *Menashe* spent more than three-fifths of his life on the right path.

### Tunnel to Heaven

*Amar Rabbi Yochanan mishum Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai: mai dichtiv, vayishma elav vayichater lo* — what is the meaning of the phrase? The *pasuk* as it actually reads is *vaya'ater lo*, with an *ayin*, meaning God was importuned by or responded to him. But the version before Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai apparently had a *chet* instead of an *ayin*, reading *vayichater*, from the root meaning to dig. The *drasha* proceeds from this variant: *melamed she'asa lo HaKadosh Baruch Hu k'min machteret barakia* — God fashioned for *Menashe* something like a tunnel through the heavens, *kedei lekabelo b'teshuvah mipnei middat hadin* — in order to receive his *teshuvah*, circumventing, as it were, the *middat hadin*, the divine quality of strict justice, which would not otherwise have permitted it.

This is a striking image. One might ask: why should justice ever prevent *teshuvah*? The *Gemara*'s answer seems to be that while *teshuvah* in principle has the power to reverse even the gravest sin, there are cases where the *middat hadin* strains against accepting it — where it seems, from a rigorous standpoint of justice, almost inconceivable that all the evil a person has done could simply be wiped away. *Menashe* represents precisely such a case. And yet God does not simply reject the *teshuvah*; instead He tunnels through His own *middat hadin* to accept it. The imagery is extraordinarily powerful: God Himself is, as it were, sneaking around His own justice in order to embrace this repentance.

### Textual Variants

The question of the textual variant is addressed in the *Masoret HaShas*, which notes in brackets: *b'pasuk ketiv vaya'ater lo* — the actual verse reads *vaya'ater* with an *ayin*, and indeed the *Gemara* itself had quoted this form just moments earlier. *V'efshar d'beDivrei HaYamim shehaya lifnei Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai haya katuv vayichater* — it is possible that the text of *Divrei HaYamim* that lay before Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai actually read *vayichater* with a *chet*, representing a variant textual tradition. *Tosafot* in *Shabbat* likewise notes that the *Tannaim* and *Amoraim* sometimes had slightly different versions of the biblical text than the one we possess.

*Rashi* is also sensitive to this difficulty. He writes *vayichater lo u'mibachutz ketiv vaya'ater lo* — on the outside it says *vaya'ater*. It is not entirely clear what *Rashi* intends — whether he means the *drasha* is drawing on a hidden or secondary meaning beneath the surface reading — but he is evidently troubled by the discrepancy between the *darshan*'s text and the received version.

---

## Yehoyakim & Tzidkiyahu

### Resetting Creation

*V'amar Rabbi Yochanan mishum Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai: mai dichtiv, bereshit mamlechut Yehoyakim ben Yoshiyahu* — what is meant by the phrase "the beginning of the reign of *Yehoyakim*"? And similarly: *u'chtiv bereshit mamlechut Tzidkiyahu* — and it also writes "the beginning of the reign of *Tzidkiyahu*." What is striking is the choice of the word *bereshit*, which obviously evokes the opening word of the Torah — *bereshit bara Elokim*. The text could simply have said *barishona* or *bashana rishona*. Why *bereshit*? *V'ad idna lo havu malchei?* Were there no kings before these? Was this truly a beginning?

*Ela bikesh HaKadosh Baruch Hu lehachazir et ha'olam kulo l'tohu vavohu* — rather, God wanted to return the entire world to void and nothingness, *bishvil Yehoyakim*, on account of the evil of *Yehoyakim*. *Mistakel bedoro venitkara daato* — but He looked at the generation and was appeased, for the people themselves were still relatively righteous, and so He stayed His hand.

*Bikesh HaKadosh Baruch Hu laasot olam kulo tohu vavohu bishvil doro shel Tzidkiyahu* — then, in the time of *Tzidkiyahu*, God again wanted to reverse the world to *tohu vavohu*, this time because of the wickedness of the entire generation. *Nistakel beTzidkiyahu venitkara daato* — but He looked at *Tzidkiyahu* and was appeased, for at least *Tzidkiyahu* himself was righteous.

### Silent Enablement

How did the situation reverse itself so quickly between *Yehoyakim* and *Tzidkiyahu*? *Rashi* explains: at the end of *Yehoyakim*'s reign — the period of the exile of *hachoresh vehamasger*, all the *talmidei chachamim* and righteous people — were taken to *Bavel* first. They were removed during *Yehoyakim*'s reign, so that by the time of *Tzidkiyahu*, none of them remained. That is how the two reigns present such mirror-image portraits: a righteous populace under a wicked king, followed by a wicked populace under a righteous king.

### Tzidkiyahu's Silence

The *Gemara* then notes: *uveTzidkiyahu nami ktiv vayaas hara be'einei Hashem* — but the verse also says that *Tzidkiyahu* did evil in the eyes of God. How can *Tzidkiyahu* be called righteous if the verse characterizes him as evil? *Shehaya beyado limchot velo micha* — because it was within his power to protest and he did not protest. His "evil" was passive enablement: he silently permitted the sins of those around him when he had the standing to intervene.

This principle — that the silent bystander who could have acted bears genuine moral responsibility — is treated with full seriousness by the *Gemara*. The failure to protest constitutes a form of complicity, and *Tzidkiyahu* is characterized accordingly.

### Gate Degraded

*Vayavo'u kol sarei melech bavel vayeshvu beshaar hatavech* — all the officers of the king of *Bavel* came and sat in the gate of *hatavech*, the middle gate. *Amar Rabbi Yochanan mishum Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai: makom shemechatchen bo halachos* — this is the place where legal rulings would be rendered, the seat of the *Sanhedrin* on the Temple Mount and in the *azarah*. *Rashi* notes: *hatavech*, from the root *choteich*, cutting — the *hei* and *chet* exchanged — because this was the place where matters of *halacha* were "cut," decided. *Rashi* further explains: *nehepach lemoshav leitzim* — it became a place of entertainment and mockery, a complete reversal of what had been.

*Amar Rav Papa: hainu de'amrei inshi, b'asra d'marei tali lei zainiei, taman kulba ra'aya kuzya tali* — that is what people say: in the same place where the master would hang his weapons, there a lowly shepherd now hangs up a water jug. This captures the outrage — not only of the mighty fallen, but of the sacred desecrated, the most solemn seat of judgment reduced to a resting place of foreign officers.

---

## Escalating Desecrati (II)

### Lazy Man's Field

*Amar Rav Chisda amar Rabbi Yirmiyah bar Abba*: what is meant by the verse *al sadeh ish atzel avarti* — I passed by the field of a lazy man — *v'al kerem adam chasar lev* — and by the vineyard of a man lacking understanding — *ve'hineh ala kulo kimshonim* — and behold it was all filled with thorns and thistles — *kasu fanav charullim* — its face covered with weeds — *v'geder avanav nehersa* — and the stone walls were broken through? The image of the broken wall is what anchors the *drasha*, evoking the destruction of the *Beit HaMikdash*.

### Stages of Ruin

The *Gemara* now works backwards through the verse, identifying each element with one of the evil kings. *Al sadeh ish atzel avarti zeh Achaz* — the lazy man is *Achaz*, who was passive in restoring the people to righteousness. *V'al kerem adam chasar lev zeh Menashe* — the vineyard and the man lacking understanding is *Menashe*. *Ve'hineh ala kulo kimshonim zeh Amon* — the thorns and thistles are *Amon*, because, as we will see, the *mizbe'ach* had been neglected until it was filled with what the *Gemara* will describe as cobwebs from disuse, as if weeds had grown up over everything. *Kasu fanav charullim zeh Yehoyakim* — the weeds covering the face correspond to *Yehoyakim*. *V'geder avanav nehersa zeh Tzidkiyahu* — and the broken walls are *Tzidkiyahu*, *shenechrav Beit HaMikdash beyamav* — for it was in his days that the *Beit HaMikdash* was destroyed. Even though *Tzidkiyahu* himself was not guilty of active wrongdoing, by his time the walls had already fallen.

### Four Excluded Groups

*V'amar Rav Chisda amar Rabbi Yirmiyah bar Abba: arba kitos ein mekablot pnei Shechinah* — four groups do not merit receiving the divine presence: *kat leitzim*, the mockers; *kat shakranim*, the liars; *kat chanifim*, the flatterers; and *kat mesaprei lashon hara*, those who speak evil of others. It is worth noting that all four of these categories concern speech — either the corruption of honest communication or its weaponization against others. There is something significant in that connection: encountering *Shechinah*, whether in prayer or in the ultimate redemption, requires a kind of integrity in language that these four groups have fundamentally violated.

*Kat leitzim* — the mockers — are excluded as the verse says, *dover shekarim lo yikon leneged einai*, one who speaks falsehood will not stand before me; this same verse was cited earlier in the context of the *ruach* of *Nabot*. *Kat chanifim* — flatterers — are excluded as the verse says *ki lo lefanav chanef yavo*, flattery will not come before Him. *Kat mesaprei lashon hara* — evil speakers — are excluded as the verse says *ki lo el chafetz resha atah*, you are not a God who desires evil; *rashi* reads the context as *lo yegurcha ra*, evil does not dwell with you.

*V'amar Rav Chisda amar Rabbi Yirmiyah bar Abba: mai dichtiv, lo te'uneh elecha ra'ah v'nega lo yikrav b'oholecha* — what is the meaning of the verse "evil will not befall you and no plague will come near your tent"? *Lo te'uneh elecha ra'ah shelo yishlot becha yetzer hara* — the evil inclination, understood here primarily in its sexual dimension, will not have dominion over you; having it is human, but being controlled by it is the danger. *V'nega lo yikrav b'oholecha* — and no plague in your tent: *shelo timtza ishtecha safek niddah b'sha'ah shetavo min haderech* — that you will not find your wife in a status of doubtful *niddah* at the moment you return from a long journey. As *Rashi* observes, *safek niddah* is in some ways harder than *vadai niddah*, because with certainty one can simply accept the situation, whereas with doubt one is left grappling with rationalization.

*Davar acher*: *lo te'uneh elecha ra'ah shelo yeva'atucha chalomot ra'im v'hirhurim ra'im* — you will not be disturbed by bad dreams and troubling thoughts. *V'nega lo yikrav b'oholecha shelo yihiyeh lecha ben o talmid shemakdiach tavshilo barabbim* — you will not have a child or a student who publicly "burns his stew," that is, who goes off the path in a way that reflects badly upon you. The concern here is for one's tent understood not as the domestic space of marital life but as the tent of Torah — one's family and one's disciples. *Ad kan bercho aviv* — to this point are the blessings of the father. As *Rashi* notes, *David* is blessing *Shlomo*, and these are characteristically paternal concerns: the sexual dimension, the disciples, the continuity of righteous progeny.

*U'mikan v'ilech birchato imo* — and from this point begin the blessings of the mother. *Ki malachav yetzaveh lach lishmorcha bechol derachecha, al kapayim yisau'necha, al shachal vafeten tidroch* — God will command His angels to guard you in all your paths, to carry you upon their palms, to allow you to tread upon snakes and serpents. A mother's blessing is for safety and protection. *Ad kan birchas imo* — to this point the blessings of the mother. *Mikan va'ilach birchas hashamayim* — and from here God Himself blesses: *ki bi chashak va'afalteihu, asagveihu, ki yada shemi, yikra'eini ve'eneihu, imo anochi betzarah, achaltzeihu va'achabdeihu, orech yamim asbi'eihu ve'ar'eihu bishu'asi* — because he trusted in Me I will deliver him; I will protect him because he knows My name; he will call to Me and I will answer; I am with him in his trouble; I will rescue him and honor him; I will satisfy him with long life and show him My salvation.

*Amar Reish Lakish: mai dichtiv, veyimana mersha'im oram vezroa ramah tishaver* — God withheld from the wicked their light, and the outstretched arm will be broken. *Mipnei mah ayin shel rasha'im teluyah?* — why is the *ayin* of *resha'im* suspended above the word in the text? Without the *ayin*, the word would read *rashim*, the poor. *Keivan shena'asah adam rash milmata* — when a person is impoverished below, meaning, as *Rashi* reads it, not materially poor but lacking in friends, with everyone arrayed against him — *na'asah rash milma'alah* — he becomes poor above as well; God's favor does not rest upon him either. The principle resonates with *matza chein veseichel tov be'einei Elokim ve'adam* — finding favor in the eyes of both God and man as interconnected realities.

*Velo nischivei klal* — but if so, why write the word with an *ayin* at all? Why not just write *rashim*? *Rabbi Yochanan veRabbi Elazar, chad amar mipnei kevodo shel David* — because the rule is not universal: righteous people can also be without friends. *David* himself faced constant opposition — from *Shaul*, from rebellions, from all sides — and the principle would be false as applied to him. *Vechad amar mipnei kevodo shel Nechemya ben Chachalyah* — and the other says because of *Nechemya*, who also faced tremendous opposition despite his righteousness. So the word is written with an *ayin* to signal that the pattern holds for the wicked, not as an iron rule about everyone lacking friends.

---

## Menashe's Repentanc (III)

### Torah Scholar

*Tana mna lan: Menashe hayah shoneh chamishim vachamishah panim beToras Kohanim* — a *tanna* taught: *Menashe* would expound fifty-five different interpretations of *Vayikra*, *keneged shenei malchuso* — corresponding to the years of his reign. *Achav shemonim vechamishah* — *Achav* had eighty-five different interpretations. *Yerovam me'ah ushloshah* — and *Yerovam* one hundred and three.

This is a remarkable acknowledgment: all three of these notoriously wicked kings were, simultaneously, towering *talmidei chachamim*. One message is that human beings are genuinely complex — they are never simply all evil or all good. But there is a harder religious message as well. One might be tempted to say: if people can be such great Torah scholars and still behave with such depravity, what is the point of Torah learning? The *Gemara* does not shy away from this tension. It does not pretend that Torah scholarship inevitably produces moral rectitude. One can have a person who is a *talmid chacham* of the highest order and simultaneously the wickedest of kings. We do Torah because God commanded it; we hope it transforms us — and often it does — but it is not a guarantee, and the *Gemara* is honest about that.

---

## Escalating Desecrati (II)

### Four-Faced Idol

The *Gemara* addresses a textual question: one verse uses the singular *pessel* — a single idol — while another verse uses the plural *psilim* — multiple idols. Which is it? *Amar Rabbi Yochanan: b'techila asa lo partzuf echad* — at the beginning, *Menashe* made an idol with a single face, which he placed in the *Beit HaMikdash*. *U'vasof asa lo arba'ah partzufim* — but ultimately he gave it four faces, *kedei she'taknit Shechinah* — in order to provoke the *Shechinah*. God sees in all directions; *Menashe* wanted that no matter which direction God looked, he would see the face of the idol staring back at Him. This is *lehachis* — spite — taken to its architectural extreme.

### Narrow Bed Image

*Achaz he'emido ba'aliyah* — *Achaz* had placed an idol in the upper chamber, on the rooftops, as the verse says: *v'es hamizbechos asher al hagag aliyas Achaz* — the altars on the rooftop of the upper chamber of *Achaz*. It was somewhat concealed, elevated rather than displayed in the main space. *Menashe he'emido b'heichal* — *Menashe* placed the idol in the *Heichal* itself, as the verse says: *vayasem es pessel ha'asheirah asher asa babayis asher amar Hashem el David v'el Shlomo bno* — he set the carved image of the *asheira* in the very house about which God had said to *David* and to *Shlomo* his son: *babayis zeh uviYerushalayim asher bacharti mikol shivtei Yisrael asim es shmi l'olam* — in this house and in Jerusalem which I have chosen from all the tribes of Israel I will place My name forever. That is the house into which *Menashe* placed his idol.

*Amon hechniso l'veis kadshei hakodashim* — *Amon* brought it into the Holy of Holies. The verse that serves as the hook here is *ki katzar hamatza mehishtarei'a* — for the bed is too short to stretch out on — *v'hamaseichah tzarah k'hiskanes* — and the blanket too narrow to gather around oneself. The literal meaning refers to a couch and a cover, but the *drasha* builds on both. *Amar Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani amar Rabbi Yonatan: ki katzar hamatza zeh m'lehishtareir alav shnei rei'im k'echad* — this bed, which is the *Beit HaMikdash* and the *Kodesh HaKodashim*, is too narrow for two masters to rule within it simultaneously, too narrow for two gods.

*Mai v'hamaseichah tzarah?* The word *maseichah* is the same term used for a cast idol. *Amar Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani Rabbi Yonatan ki havai mati l'hai kra havah bachi* — when he would reach this verse he would weep. *Mi shekasuv bo kones k'ned mei hayam* — the One of whom it is written that He gathers the waters of the sea like in a flask — *ta'aseh lo maseichah tzarah?* — that for Him there should be a *tzarah*, a competing wife, a rival, an idol? The word *tzarah* carries its full double meaning: the idol is simultaneously a rival deity and a *tzarah* in the sense of a co-wife, a competing claimant to God's own dwelling. *V'hamaseichah tzarah k'hiskanes* — the idol, the *tzarah*, when it was entered into the *Kodesh HaKodashim*. The imagery is devastating: the God who contains all the waters of the ocean has been given a rival who is crowded alongside Him in His innermost chamber.

### Achaz Seals Torah

Returning now to fill in the pattern of these kings' escalating violations: *Achaz bital es ha'avodah* — *Achaz* brought the Temple service to a halt. *V'chasam es haTorah* — and he sealed the Torah, preventing its study, as the verse says: *tzur te'udah chasum Torah belimudai* — seal the Torah among my learners.

### Menashe Cuts Names

*Menashe kadar es ha'azkaros* — *Menashe* cut out or scraped away God's names from the *Sefer Torah*, as was noted earlier in a different connection, replacing them with names of *avodah zarah*. *V'haras es hamizbeiach* — and he destroyed the *mizbe'ach*, going beyond merely stopping the service to physically demolishing the altar.

### Amon's Violations

*Amon saraf es haTorah* — *Amon* was not content with merely preventing Torah study; he burned the Torah scrolls. *V'he'ela shamamit al gabei hamizbeiach* — and he brought up a *shamamit* — apparently a type of lizard, perhaps a gecko or salamander — upon the altar. Even if the *mizbe'ach* had only been partially damaged rather than totally destroyed, the image is of total desolation: the altar of God overgrown, defiled, hosting vermin rather than offerings. This circles back to the earlier *drasha* of the lazy man's field, with its thorns and weeds: the *Beit HaMikdash* has become like an abandoned field.

---

## Spiting God

### Amon's Incest

*Achaz hitir es ha'erva* — *Achaz* permitted forbidden sexual relations for the population. *Menashe ba'al achoso* — *Menashe* went further and actually had relations with his own sister. *V'Amon ba al imo* — and *Amon* had relations with his own mother. The verse says *ki hu Amon hirbah ashmah* — he multiplied his transgression. What makes *Amon*'s sin so particularly severe in the *Gemara*'s reading is not merely that it represents the outermost boundary of *arayos* but that it seems to have been entirely devoid of the ordinary pull of desire.

His mother said to him: *klum yesh lecha hana'ah mimakom sheyatzata mimenu?* — Do you have any pleasure from the place from which you emerged? The implication is that there is no erotic dynamic here, no *yetzer hara* in the ordinary sense. *Amar lah: klum ani oseh ela lehachis et bori* — I am only doing this to spite my Creator. The sin was not the product of temptation overcome but of pure, calculated contempt for God.

### Yehoyakim Blasphemes

*Ki ata Yehoyakim* — when *Yehoyakim* came, he said: *kama'ei lo yadu le'argezei klum* — the kings who came before didn't even know how to anger God properly. *Anu klum anu tzrichim le'oro?* — Do we even need God's light? *Hai it lanu zehav parvayim de'anan mishtamshin bei* — we have this beautiful gold of *Parvayim* that gives us light. Who needs God? *Lekatzetz et oro* — let God take away His light; it makes no difference to us.

Those around him pushed back: *velo kesef vezahav shelo hu?* — does not the gold itself belong to God? *She'ne'emar: li hakesef veli hazahav ne'um Hashem Tzeva'ot* — as the verse says, Mine is the silver and Mine is the gold, says the Lord of Hosts. *Amar lahem: kvar natnu lanu* — it has already been given to us, *she'ne'emar: hashamayim shamayim l'Hashem veha'aretz natan livnei adam* — the heavens are God's heavens, but the earth He gave to humanity.

### Relationship vs. Sin

The contrast between *Amon* and *Yehoyakim* on the one hand, and the earlier wicked kings on the other, raises a question worth examining carefully. *Amon* and those before him were doing genuinely terrible things — burning Torah, committing the most severe sexual violations, placing idols in the *Kodesh HaKodashim* — and they were doing it *lehachis*, to spite God. *Yehoyakim*, on the other hand, is in some sense just saying words: why do we need God, we have gold. This seems far less dramatic. Yet the *Gemara* treats *Yehoyakim*'s position as distinctively troubling.

The distinction appears to be this: *lehachis* — doing something to spite God — still presupposes a relationship. Even the most defiant act of spite is an act within a relationship; it acknowledges that the other party exists and can be hurt. *Amon* saying "I am doing this only to anger my Creator" is, paradoxically, still a form of engagement with God. *Yehoyakim* is doing something different: he is attempting to sever the relationship entirely, to declare that God is irrelevant, that we have no need of Him. It is better to be in a fighting relationship than in no relationship at all. The old observation applies: *lehachis mi* — to spite whom? — is the reply of one who has already stepped outside any relationship entirely.

### Yehoyakim Unlisted

*Amar lei Rava l'Rabba bar Mari: mipnei ma lo manu et Yehoyakim?* — Why, given everything discussed, is *Yehoyakim* not on the list of kings without a portion in the world to come? The verse says about him: *v'yeter divrei Yehoyakim v'to'avotav asher asa v'hanimtzah alav* — and the rest of the acts of *Yehoyakim* and his abominations which he committed and what was found upon him. *Mai v'hanimtzah alav?* What does "found upon him" mean?

*Rabbi Yochanan veRabbi Elazar, chada amar shechakak shem avodah zarah al amato* — one says he had the name of an idol tattooed on his membrum, expressing how thoroughly his desire for *avodah zarah* had consumed him. *V'chada amar shechakak shem shamayim al amato* — and the other says he had God's name tattooed there, as an act of contempt and desecration. Either way, *Yehoyakim* was extraordinarily wicked.

So why is he not on the list? *Amar lei: bimlachim lo shamati* — I have not heard an explanation for the kings. There are kings who seem as though they ought to be on the list and are not, and the *Gemara* acknowledges this openly. The Mishnah's list of kings who have no portion in the world to come is not exhaustive, and for the omissions among the kings, no satisfying explanation is available. *Behedyotot shamati* — for the list of non-royal figures, there are explanations for why some who might be expected to appear are absent.

---

## Michah's Kindness

### Michah's Bread

*Michdei maan lo manu et Michah?* — While we are on the question of unexpected omissions from the list, what about *Michah*, who erected an idol and practiced *avodah zarah* in the early period of Israelite history? Why is he not condemned? *Mipnei shepito metzuya l'ovrei drachim* — because his bread was always available to passersby. Even as he was engaged in his idolatrous worship, his home was open and his table was set for travelers. *Shene'emar kol over v'shav el ha'Leviyim* — anyone who came and went among the Levites was welcome. In the context of *Michah*'s *pesel v'avodah zarah*, this hospitality is what saves him from total condemnation.

### Gerev & Shiloh

The *Gemara* offers a *drasha* on the verse *v'avar bayam tzarah v'hikah bayam galim* — he passed through the ocean and smote its waves. *Amar Rabbi Yochanan: zeh peslo shel Michah* — this refers to the idol of *Michah*, which was carried through the splitting sea when *Michah* left Egypt. According to this tradition, *Michah* was among those saved from the Egyptian slave labor — some say he had been built into the buildings the slaves were constructing — and he brought his idol with him through the *Yam Suf*.

*Tanya Rabbi Natan omer: miGerev l'Shiloh, gimel milin* — from *Gerev*, the location of *Michah*'s idolatrous sanctuary, to *Shiloh*, where the *Mishkan* stood, was only three *mil* — approximately three miles. *V'hayah ashan hama'aracha v'ashan pesel Michah mitarvim zeh b'zeh* — the smoke of the offerings on the *mizbe'ach* of the *Mishkan* and the smoke of *Michah*'s idol would mingle together. The proximity was not incidental; it was a direct affront, a competing worship placed within sight and smell of God's own dwelling.

### God's Mercy

*Bikshu malachei hasharet l'dochfo* — the ministering angels wanted to push *Michah* away, to destroy him entirely. *Amar lahem HaKadosh Baruch Hu: hanichu lo, shepito metzuya l'ovrei drachim* — God said: leave him, because his bread is available to passersby. This is a remarkable statement. The same *talmidei chachamim* who were great scholars did not find their scholarship counterbalancing their sins. Yet *Michah*'s *hachnasat orchim* — his hospitality to travelers — tips the scales in his favor sufficiently that even the angels' desire to destroy him is overridden by divine mercy.

### Pilegesh B'Giva

*V'al davar zeh ne'enash anshei Pilegesh b'Giva* — and it was because of *Michah*'s sin that the men of *Pilegesh b'Giva* were punished. *Amar lahem HaKadosh Baruch Hu: bichvodi lo mechitem v'al kvodo shel basar vadam mechitem?* — God said to them: You did not protest on behalf of My honor when the idol of *Michah* was erected right in your locale, and yet you came forward to defend the honor of a human being in the matter of the *pilegesh b'Giva*? That failure to protest against *Michah*'s idol — which stood so close to the *Mishkan* that their smokes mingled — is what ultimately brought punishment upon the men of that generation. The lesson parallels what was said of *Tzidkiyahu*: silence in the face of desecration is its own form of culpability.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 104

## Extending Food Merit

### Michah Food Merit

The *daf* opens by returning to a question carried over from the previous discussion: why was Michah not included among those enumerated as having no portion in the world to come? The Gemara's answer was that Michah made his food available to passersby, and that merit shielded him from the list. This serves as the springboard for a broader teaching about the remarkable power of extending food to others.

### Distance/Bring Close

Rabbi Yochanan teaches in the name of Rabbi Yosei ben Kisma: *gedolah legima* — great is the tasting and extending of food. He then expands this teaching in his own name, enumerating four dimensions of food's power. First, *meracheket et hakrovim* — it can distance those who are close. Second, *umikarrevet et harichokim* — it can bring near those who are far. Third, *uma'alemet einayim min harisha'im* — it causes God, as it were, to turn a blind eye from the wickedness being committed. Fourth, *umashra Shechinah al nevi'ei habaal* — it even has the power to cause the *shechina* to rest upon a prophet of the *baal*, of *avodah zarah*, for the merit of one who extended food to him. And fifth, *sheshigagato olah zadon* — even negligence in failing to provide food is treated as though it were intentional wrongdoing.

### Ammon Moab

The first principle — that food distances those who were close — is demonstrated from Ammon and Moav. The explicit *pasuk* states: *al devar asher lo kidmu etchem balechem uvamayim* — because they did not greet you with bread and water. That simple failure to extend bread and water caused these two nations, who bordered Israel and were related to us through Lot, to be permanently distanced from the community of Israel.

### Yitro Merit

The second principle — that food brings near those who are far — is demonstrated from Yitro. Rabbi Yochanan teaches: *bischar kir'an lo veyochal lechem* — in the reward of Yitro's daughters calling Moshe and giving him food, *zachu benei banav veyashvu belishkat hagazit* — his descendants ultimately merited to sit in the *Lishkat HaGazit*, the chamber of the *Sanhedrin* within the *Beis HaMikdash* itself. The *pasuk* from Divrei Hayamim identifies these descendants as the *sofrim* who dwelt in Yavetz — the Tiratim, Shimatim, and Suchatim — who are identified as *hakeinim*, and the *pasuk* in Shoftim confirms that *bnei Keini chotein Moshe* — the sons of the Keini, Moshe's father-in-law — went up with the children of Yehuda toward the desert of the south near Arad.

One might ask what precisely is meant by calling Ammon and Moav "close" and Yitro "far." One reading is geographical: Ammon and Moav bordered Israel while Yitro was geographically distant. Another reading would cast it in terms of family relation: Ammon and Moav were blood relatives descended from Lot, while Yitro was an outsider. Rashi, however, is uncomfortable with the second reading, since he holds that Yitro descended from the *benei Keturah* through Midyan — ultimately tracing back to Avraham. Rashi therefore reads the distinction as purely geographical.

### Divine Blindness

The third principle — that extending food causes God to overlook wickedness — is demonstrated from Michah himself. As we said, Michah's habit of extending food to those who passed his home is precisely the reason he was not included in the list of those without a portion in the world to come.

The fourth principle — that the *shechina* can rest upon a prophet of the *baal* in the merit of extending food — is drawn from the story of Iddo HaNavi. A false prophet, one who was in truth a prophet of the *baal*, deceived Iddo and brought him to his house and fed him. The *pasuk* then records: *vayehi devar Hashem el hanavi asher heshivo* — and the word of God came to that prophet, the very one who had brought Iddo back and hosted him. The power of extending food was sufficient to draw a direct communication from God even to one who was a prophet of idolatry.

### Yehonatan David

The fifth principle — that negligence in failing to provide food is counted as intentional sin — is taught by Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav. *Ilmale hilvehu Yehonatan l'David shtei kikrot lechem* — had Yehonatan only given David two loaves of bread when David was fleeing from Shaul, *lo neherga Nov ir hakohanim* — the city of Nov, the city of the *kohanim*, would not have been massacred by Shaul. *V'lo nitrad Doeg Adomi* — and Doeg HaEdomite, who slandered David at that time, would not have been *nitrad*, excluded from *olam haba*, as a consequence of his sin. *V'lo neherag Shaul v'shloshet banav* — and Shaul and his three sons would not have been killed as a result of that cascade of events. All of this tragedy traces back to the negligence — not malice, mere negligence — of failing to provide food when it was needed.

---

## Kings Not Listed

### Achaz Yotam

Having concluded the discussion of Michah and the importance of extending food, the Gemara now turns to a series of evil kings in Israel's history who were not included in the list of those without a portion in the world to come, and asks why. *U'mipnei ma lo manu et Achaz* — why was Achaz not listed?

Rabbi Yirmiyah bar Abba answers: *mipnei shemutal bein shenei tzaddikim bein Yotam l'Chizkiyahu* — because he was sandwiched between two righteous men. His father was Yotam and his son was Chizkiyahu. The lineage runs: Uziyahu, Yotam, Achaz, Chizkiyahu. Because of both his father and his son, he was not listed.

A prior question is worth noting: does being omitted from the list mean that he actually merits *olam haba*, or is it merely that *chazal* chose not to call him out explicitly? This distinction will recur throughout. When the Mishnah listed the three kings and four *hedyotot*, was that list exhaustive and definitive, or was it a deliberate enumeration that left others unmentioned for their own reasons? The question remains open, but it should be kept in mind as the discussion unfolds.

A separate reason is offered by Rav Yosef: *mipnei shehayah lo boshet panim mi'Yeshayahu* — because Achaz felt shame before Yeshayahu. When God told Yeshayahu to go meet Achaz by the upper pool, at the field of the *kovess* — the launderer — Achaz, upon seeing Yeshayahu, could not face him. Some say *d'chavshinehu l'apei* — he buried his face and passed by. Others say he placed a launderer's sprinkling implement over his face as a kind of mask and slipped away. Either way, he was overcome with embarrassment before the prophet. This reason sounds less like a technicality about whether to include him in a list and more like a genuine moral attainment — the capacity for shame — that may qualify him for a portion in the world to come.

### Son Father Merit

The Gemara asks about Amon — another notoriously wicked king who is also absent from the list. *Mipnei kevodo she-Yoshiyahu* — because of the honor of Yoshiyahu, who was Amon's son, and who was one of the most righteous kings in Israel's history.

This immediately raises a counterpoint: *Menashe nami lo nimnei* — by the same logic, Menashe should not have been listed either. Menashe is definitively on the list. And Menashe's father was Chizkiyahu. So if we protect a son because he had a righteous son, why not protect Menashe because he had a righteous father?

The Gemara responds with a fundamental principle: *bra mazakei aba aba lo mazakei bra* — a son brings merit to the father, but a father does not bring merit to the son. The logic is intuitive. A wicked person who failed to learn from his own righteous father cannot claim protection from that father's merit — if anything, the father's righteousness makes the son's wickedness more culpable. But a wicked person who nevertheless raised or fathered a righteous son — something of that goodness reflects back on the father and works in his favor.

This is reinforced by the *pasuk*: *ve'ein mi-yadi matzil* — no one can save from My hand — and the Gemara reads this to mean that *ein Avraham matzil et Yishmael ve'ein Yitzchak matzil et Esav*. Avraham's righteousness could not save Yishmael; Yitzchak's righteousness could not save Esav. A good father cannot protect a bad son.

With this principle established, the Gemara notes: *hashta de-atit le-hachi* — now that we have this principle, we can actually revisit Achaz as well. Rather than needing the reason of shame before Yeshayahu, we can say simply: *mishum kevodo shel Chizkiyahu* — because of the honor of Chizkiyahu, his son. The merit of the righteous son protected the father from being named on the list.

### Amon Yoshiyahu

Returning now to Amon: the answer that his righteous son Yoshiyahu shielded him from the list follows directly from the principle just established. The son's merit works retroactively in the father's favor. Amon was wicked, but Yoshiyahu was exceptional, and that is sufficient reason — at least — for his exclusion from explicit enumeration.

### Yehoyakim Skull

*Mipnei ma lo manu et Yehoyakim* — and why was Yehoyakim not included? The Gemara gives a striking answer, tied to a dramatic story. The answer is *mishum de-Rabbi Chiya bar Avin* — because of the case involving Rabbi Chiya bar Avin.

Rabbi Chiya bar Avin taught — and this Gemara appeared earlier in the tractate — that it was written on the skull of Yehoyakim: *zot ve-od acheret* — this, and one more. The *pasuk* had foretold that Yehoyakim would receive the burial of a donkey, meaning he would be cast out and left unburied. The inscription on his skull indicated that that curse had befallen him, and yet one more punishment was to come.

The grandfather of Rabbi Preida — identified as the same Rabbi Chiya — found this skull, cast aside at the gates of Jerusalem, which is precisely what the *pasuk* had said would happen. Written on it were the words *zot ve-od acheret*. He buried the skull, and it would not stay buried — it kept rising back to the surface. He buried it again, and again it would not remain. Understanding then that this was the skull of Yehoyakim — of whom it is written *kvurat chamor yikaver* and *sachov ve-hashlech*, that he would be cast away — he recognized that a proper burial was simply impossible for this man. Yet it was still the skull of a king, and *lo ikshar lezalzulei beih* — it was not proper to treat it with such degradation. So he wrapped it in silk and placed it in a box so that at least it would not be kicked around.

His wife saw the skull in the box. She assumed it must be a first wife whose memory he could not release — *dehalo ka menashe lah*, he simply could not forget her. Consumed by jealousy, she fired up the oven and burned the skull entirely. And that, says the Gemara, is what *zot ve-od acheret* meant: the first curse of unburied, dishonored remains, and the second curse of being completely incinerated. Because of this extreme and distinctive punishment that had already befallen him, Yehoyakim was not listed among those explicitly excluded from *olam haba*. Whether that omission means he genuinely has a portion there, or only that *chazal* chose not to list him, remains, as before, ambiguous.

---

## Chizkiyahu Sins

### Arrogance Sign

A *braisa* is introduced: *bishvil hatov be'einecha asiti* — because of the phrase "I did what was good in Your eyes," attributed to Chizkiyahu's prayer when he was deathly ill. By taking credit for his own righteousness in this way, Chizkiyahu displayed a form of arrogance. And that arrogance led, by the principle of *aveira goreres aveira*, to further sin.

Specifically, when Yeshayahu came to him with the divine promise that his prayer had been heard and he would live another fifteen years, Chizkiyahu demanded a sign. *Ma os* — what will be the sign? This is presented as *chutzpah*: he had just received an extraordinary reprieve, a prophetic promise of renewed life, and yet he demanded confirmation. Moreover, when given the choice of a sign — whether the sun should stand still for ten hours or move backward — he chose the backward movement because mere stillness was insufficiently dramatic. Arrogance upon arrogance.

### Babylon Exile

*Uvishvil ma os* — and because he demanded a sign, *nochrim achlu al shulchano* — foreigners ate at his table. The king of Babylonia sent emissaries when he heard that Chizkiyahu had been ill, and somehow — whether through the connection to the miraculous sign or through the arrogance that now flowed freely — Chizkiyahu welcomed them and hosted them. *Achlu al shulchano uvishvil she'nochrim achlu al shulchano garam galus le'vanav* — and because they ate at his table, it caused the exile of his children.

The specific sin that brought about this consequence was that Chizkiyahu showed these emissaries everything: his silver and gold, his fragrances, his fine oil, his treasuries. Rava asks: what is *Beis Nechoso* — the "treasure house" mentioned in the *pasuk*? One view is that he had his wife attend to the guests, which was not *tzanua* for the queen. Shmuel says it simply means his treasury, which fits the plain context. Rabbi Yochanan understands it as a reference to some kind of weapon. After this display, the prophecy came: his children would be taken into exile and become eunuchs in the palace of the king of Bavel. *Uvaneha asher yetzu mimecha asher toulid yikachu vehayu sarisim beheichal melech Bavel.*

### Non-Jews Home

The Gemara uses this episode as support for a broader teaching of Chizkiya the Amora: *kol hamizamen akum letoch beiso umeshamesh elav garam galus le'vanav* — anyone who invites a non-Jew into his home and attends to him — serving him in a way that demonstrates deference or subservience — brings about exile for his children. The *pasuk* about Chizkiyahu's children being taken captive is cited as proof.

The chain is therefore: arrogance in prayer led to demanding a sign, which led to receiving the Babylonian emissaries, which led to displaying the royal treasuries to them, which led to the prophecy of exile for his children. One sin generates the next — *aveira goreres aveira* — until the consequences extend across generations.

---

## Eicha Verses

### Vadad Alone

Now that the discussion has touched on the destruction of the *Beis HaMikdash* — the culmination of the evil kings' legacy — the Gemara pivots to a *derasha* on the opening verses of *Eicha*, the Book of Lamentations, proceeding through them in order.

First, a general observation: Rava in the name of Rabbi Yochanan asks *mipnei ma laku b'Eicha* — why were they punished with *Eicha*? The answer is that the *gematria* of *Eicha* is thirty-six, corresponding to the thirty-six *kritot* in the Torah — the gravest violations for which one incurs *karet* — which they had transgressed. A second question: *mipnei ma laku b'alef-bet* — why is *Eicha* structured as an *alef-bet* acrostic? Because they transgressed the Torah that was given in *alef-bet* — that is, in the full breadth and entirety of the Hebrew language. The *alef-bet* represents the complete scope of Torah from beginning to end, and their sin was correspondingly total.

Turning now to the opening phrase itself — *Eicha yashva vadad*, how does she sit alone — Rava in the name of Rabbi Yochanan notes that God had originally promised: *vayishkon Yisrael betach badad ein Yaakov el eretz dagan v'tirosh af shamav yaarfu tal* — Israel will dwell in security, alone, like the eye of Yaakov, in a land of grain and wine, its heavens dripping with dew. That *badad* was the *badad* of strength: self-sufficient, secure, not dependent on the nations. Now, *yashva badad* means something entirely different — alone and desolate, abandoned. *Achshav yehiye badad moshavam* — now their dwelling place is a different kind of aloneness, the aloneness of abandonment.

### City Widow

*Ha'ir rabati am haita k'almana* — the city that was so populous has become like a widow. Rava in the name of Rabbi Yochanan asks: what made Jerusalem so densely populated? The answer is that they would marry a younger woman to an older man and an older woman to a younger man. Rashi explains that this is not about legal minors but about younger and older in a relative sense: by matching someone of lesser fertility with someone of greater fertility, both couples were able to begin having children immediately, maximizing the population. Matching two very young people together, by Rashi's account, would have delayed reproduction.

Then Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav adds a crucial qualifier: *k'almana v'lo almana mamash* — like a widow but not literally a widow. A literal widow's husband is dead and will never return. Jerusalem is compared instead to *k'isha shehalach baala l'medinat hayam v'daato lachazor aleha* — a woman whose husband has gone overseas but intends to return. The relationship is not severed. God has not abandoned us forever; the return is anticipated.

### Ruler Vassal

*Rabati bagoyim sarati bamdinot hayta lamas* — she who was great among the nations, a prince among the provinces, has become a vassal. Rava in the name of Rabbi Yochanan notes: wherever the Jewish people would go, *nasim sarim l'adoneihem* — they would become princes to their very masters.

### Two Captives

A *baraisa* illustrates this: there was an episode involving two Jewish captives taken on Mount Carmel. Their captor was walking behind them. As they walked, one captive said to the other: that camel walking ahead of us is blind in one eye, it is carrying two skins — one of wine and one of oil — and the two people leading it are one Jew and one non-Jew.

The captor overheard this and demanded — perhaps with something between admiration and hostility toward this stiff-necked people — *me'ayin atem yode'im*, how could they possibly know all this? They explained each inference in turn. The camel ate only from one side of the road — the side it could see — revealing that it was blind in the other eye. They knew the skins contained wine and oil because wine drips and is absorbed into the ground, while oil drips and floats on the surface; they had observed both phenomena as they walked behind the camel. As for the men leading it: the non-Jew relieved himself directly on the road, while the Jew stepped to the side — *mipnei tzniyut*.

The captor ran after the caravan, confirmed every detail, and was so astonished that he kissed these two captives on their heads, brought them home, made a great feast for them, and danced before them. The masters had become servants; the captives had become the *sarim*. And he declared: *Baruch shebachar b'zaro shel Avraham v'natan lahem michochmato* — blessed is He who chose the seed of Avraham and gave to them from His wisdom — *u'v'chol makom she'hein holchin nasim sarim l'adoneihem* — wherever they go, they become princes to those who would be their masters. He released them, and they returned home in peace.

---

## Eicha Crying

### Spies Night

The Gemara moves to the next phrase in *Eicha*: *bachoh tivkeh balaylah* — she shall surely weep in the night. The double language of weeping — *bachoh tivkeh* — prompts the question: *shtei bchiyot hallalu lama*, why the double weeping? Rava in the name of Rabbi Yochanan answers: *echad al Mikdash Rishon v'echad al Mikdash Sheni* — one for the First *Beis HaMikdash* and one for the Second *Beis HaMikdash*. The lamentation in *Eicha* already anticipates both destructions.

Why specifically at night? *Al iskei laylah* — because of the original nighttime sin. The *pasuk* in Bamidbar records: *vatissa kol ha'edah vayitnu et kolam vayivku ha'am balaylah hahu* — the entire congregation lifted its voice and wept that night, the night of *chet hamiraglim*, the sin of the spies, when they despaired and wanted to return to Egypt. According to tradition, that night was the night of Tisha B'Av. God responded: *atem bchitem bchiya shel chinam v'ani ekba lachem bchiya l'dorot* — you have wept for nothing, and I will establish this night as a night of weeping for all future generations.

Three additional explanations are offered for the significance of *balaylah*. First, *shekol habocheh balaila kolo nishma* — when one cries at night, the voice carries further, since the world is quiet and there is no ambient noise. Second, *kochavim umazalot bochim imo* — the very stars and constellations seem to weep along, for at night one perceives the full cosmos, and the entire universe shares in the grief. Third, *hashomea kolo bocheh kenegdo* — the sound of nighttime crying is so clear and unobstructed that those who hear it are overwhelmed with sympathy and cry along.

This last point is illustrated by an episode involving Raban Gamliel. A woman in his neighborhood had lost her son and cried for him at night. Raban Gamliel heard her crying and could not help but cry along — *ad shenishru risei einav* — to the point that his very eyelashes fell out. The next morning his students noticed his reddened eyes and understood what had happened. Unwilling to see their master suffer so, they removed her from the neighborhood.

### Husband Youth

*V'dimasah al lochayah* — her tears upon her cheek. Rav in the name of Rabbi Yochanan interprets *lochayah* as suggesting moisture, the freshness of youth: the crying is *k'isha shebochah al baal ne'urim* — like a woman who weeps for the husband of her youth. The *pasuk* cited is *eli k'visulah chogeret sak al baal ne'urah* — a wail like that of a young woman girding herself in sackcloth for the husband of her youth.

### Enemies Head

*Hayu tzareha l'rosh* — her enemies became the head over her. Rav in the name of Rabbi Yochanan states: *kol hameitzik l'Yisrael naasah rosh* — whoever oppresses Israel becomes a head, a leader among nations. This is a striking statement, and the Gemara itself seems aware that it requires careful handling: one would not want it read as an endorsement of oppressing the Jewish people. The general understanding is that God, out of a kind of respect for Israel, would not allow a weak or minor nation to subjugate them — only a truly mighty nation could be permitted to do so.

The proof-text offered is *ki lo muaf laasher mutzak lah* — there is no weariness to the one who afflicts her. This is read as a separate but related teaching: those who oppress Israel never seem to grow weary of it. The Gra notes that this *drash* on the *pasuk* does not actually prove the prior point about oppressors becoming great nations; rather it is a distinct observation — anti-Semites and those who persecute Israel throughout history never seem to exhaust themselves in doing so.

### Complaint Blessing

*Lo aleichem kol ovrei derech* — let it not befall you, all you who pass by. Rav in the name of Rabbi Yochanan derives from here: *mikan l'kuvlanah min haTorah* — from here we see the concept of making a complaint or lament in a way that also extends a blessing to those nearby. Rashi explains that when one bemoans one's own tragedies, one should add: but may this not befall you — *lo aleichem* — as a way of protecting the listener. The lament itself becomes an expression of care for others.

Rav Amram in the name of Rav adds another layer: *asuni ke'ovrei al dat* — my punishments have made me appear as though I transgress my own religion. The sufferings visited upon Jerusalem make it look, to outside observers, as though God has abandoned His people — as though they must have been the worst of transgressors.

### Jerusalem Sodom

This is then connected to the statement: *ve'ilu biSdom ketiv vaHashem himtir al Sdom* — when it comes to Sodom, God rained down fire and brimstone. *Ve'ilu biYerushalayim ketiv mimarom shalach esh be'atzmotai vayirdena* — and by Jerusalem it says God sent fire from on high into my very bones and crushed them. The same image of heavenly fire applied to Jerusalem as to Sodom implies that Jerusalem's sin was as great as Sodom's — or greater.

Indeed, the *pasuk* states explicitly: *vayigdal avon bat ami mechatat Sdom* — the sin of my people was greater than the sin of Sodom. This raises an obvious question: *vachi maso fanim yesh badavar* — is there favoritism here? If Jerusalem's sin was greater than Sodom's, why was Jerusalem not destroyed as utterly as Sodom?

Rabbah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan answers: *midah yeteirah hayetah biYerushalayim shelo hayetah biSdom* — there was a distinctive quality in Jerusalem that was absent in Sodom. The *pasuk* about Sodom reads: *hineh zeh hayah avon Sdom achotech gaon sivat lechem veyad ani ve'evyon lo hechezikah* — Sodom had bread in abundance but did not support the poor and destitute. It was stingy and hardhearted.

By contrast, the *pasuk* about Jerusalem reads: *yedei nashim rachmaniyot bishlu yaldeihen* — the hands of compassionate women cooked their own children. Rashi offers two readings of this juxtaposition. The first — striking in its moral audacity — is that even in the act of cooking their own children in the extremity of the famine during the siege, the women of Jerusalem shared what they had with their neighbors, as the end of the *pasuk* indicates that they ate it together. Even amid unimaginable horror, the people of Jerusalem retained a measure of compassion for one another — and that quality distinguished them from Sodom. The second reading is darker: the comparison is not exculpatory but rather shows that Jerusalem's destruction was in some ways worse than Sodom's — Sodom was annihilated but had known wealth, while Jerusalem's destruction came through terrible privation and suffering. In that sense there was no favoritism; they suffered more, not less.

### Spies Mouth

The Gemara then notes: *sillah kol abbirai Hashem bekirbi* — God has crushed all my mighty ones within me — and interprets this *ke'adam she'omer lechavero nifsala matbeia zu* — like a person who says to his friend: this coin has been invalidated. A coin is invalidated when it is flattened and the image stamped upon it is destroyed. So too, God flattened and obliterated the mighty of Jerusalem.

Moving to *patzu alaich pihem* — they opened their mouths against you — the acrostic in *Eicha* reaches the letter *peh*. The Gemara notes a well-known anomaly: in *Eicha*, the *peh* precedes the *ayin* in the acrostic, whereas in standard Hebrew order *ayin* precedes *peh*. Rabbah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan explains: *bishvil meraglim she'amru befihem mah shelo ra'u be'eineihem* — because of the spies, who said with their *peh*, their mouth, what they had not seen with their *ayin*, their eye. Their mouth preceded their eye — they fabricated their report, giving voice to things they had never actually witnessed. The inversion of *peh* before *ayin* in *Eicha* is the literary memorial to that original inversion.

### Bread Judges

A final *pasuk* — not from *Eicha* but on the same theme — is cited: *ochlei ami achlu lechem Hashem lo kara'u* — those who devour my people eat bread, they do not call out to God. Rabbah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan derives: *kol haohel milachman shel Yisrael toeim ta'am lechem* — whoever eats from the bread of Israel truly tastes what good bread is. Rashi understands this as referring to the enemies who stole and took from Israel's food — when they took what was ours, they experienced the real taste of bread. And conversely, *she'eino ochel milachman shel Yisrael eino toeim ta'am lechem* — one who does not eat Jewish bread has never truly tasted bread. Why did it come to this — that our enemies were able to steal and consume our food? *Hashem lo kara'u* — because we did not call out to God.

Two opinions are offered for who precisely *Hashem lo kara'u* refers to. Rava says *elu hadayanim* — these were the judges, who failed to bring God's presence into their courts and did not administer true justice. Shmuel says *elu melamdei tinokot* — these were the schoolteachers, who were lax in their responsibility to have children read *pesukim*, diligent in their teaching. Both sins — the corruption of the courts and the neglect of Torah education — are identified as the underlying causes of the national catastrophe.

---

## List Authority

### Great Assembly

Having completed the *derasha* on *Eicha*, the Gemara returns to the foundational question of the entire discussion: who composed the list of those without a portion in *olam haba*? Rav Ashi answers: *Anshei Knesset HaGedolah mana'um* — it was the Men of the Great Assembly, at the beginning of the period of the Second *Beis HaMikdash*, who deliberated and determined who would be explicitly enumerated.

### Shlomo David

Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav then relates that the *Anshei Knesset HaGedolah* sought to add one more name to the list. They did not even say the name directly — such was the respect they maintained — but it was Shlomo HaMelech, whose wives, according to the plain meaning of the *pesukim*, had led him into idolatry.

At that moment, *ba'ah dmut dyukno* — the image, the *dyukan*, the icon of his father David, appeared before them and prostrated itself at their feet. The *Anshei Knesset HaGedolah* were unmoved. *Ba'ah esh min hashamayim velichecha esh besafseleihem* — fire came from heaven and singed their benches. They remained unmoved. Remarkably, the Gemara presents this almost as a parallel to the *lo bashamayim hi* principle — except that here the domain is not *halacha* but the determination of who merits *olam haba*.

### God Final Say

Then a *bat kol* emerged and spoke: *chazita ish mahir bimlachto lifnei melachim yityatzev bal yityatzev lifnei chashuchim* — have you seen a man diligent in his work? He will stand before kings; he will not stand before the darkened ones. The *bat kol* identified this verse as referring to Shlomo. He had built the *Beis HaMikdash* in seven years while his own palace took thirteen. His diligence in God's house was exceptional. Such a person *lifnei melachim yityatzev* — will stand before kings, meaning in *Gan Eden* — *bal yityatzev lifnei chashuchim* — not before the darkened ones, not in *Gehinnom*.

Still the *Anshei Knesset HaGedolah* did not relent. A second *bat kol* emerged with a final declaration: *hime'imach yeshalmenah* — is it from you that payment will come? *Ki ma'asta ki atah tivchar velo ani* — because you have made your determination: do you think you choose and not I? God declared: it is I who decide who receives *olam haba*.

This is a powerful and fitting conclusion. The *Anshei Knesset HaGedolah* had the authority and wisdom to compose their list, and their deliberations were taken with the utmost seriousness — fire from heaven and two heavenly voices notwithstanding, they did not simply yield. But God's final word reasserts divine sovereignty: the human list is a human list. The eschatological fate of every individual — whether explicitly named or conspicuously omitted, whether included for reasons of honor, punishment, shame, or the merit of a righteous child — ultimately rests not with any assembly but with God alone. And this returns us, in the most clarifying way, to the question that has threaded through the entire discussion: what does it actually mean to be on the list, or left off it? The answer, in the end, is that the list reflects the wisdom and considered judgment of the *Anshei Knesset HaGedolah* — but *atah tivchar velo ani* is turned on its head. It is not they who choose. It is God.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 105

## Shlomo & Divine Voice

### Bat Kol & Shlomo

Today's *daf* is 105, picking up at the bottom of 104b. The discussion has centered on the list of kings who lack a portion in the *olam haba*, with the previous *daf* concluding on a remarkable note: the *Anshei Knesset HaGedolah* sought to include Shlomo among those kings, and God responded by sending fire from heaven accompanied by a *bat kol*. The dynamic here invites comparison with the famous story of the *tanur shel Achnai*, but with a crucial difference. That episode concluded with *lo bashamayim hi* — the authority to determine *halacha* rests with the rabbis, not with heavenly voices. Here, however, the resolution runs in the opposite direction.

### God Decides Olam HaBa

The *bat kol* declares: *hame'imcha yishalmena* — will compensation come from you? *Ki ma'asta* — you have chosen who to despise. *Ki ata tivchar, v'lo ani* — do you think you get to choose, and not I? The message is unmistakable: while the *rabbanim* derive their authority over *halacha* from *psukim* and *derasha*, the question of who enters *olam haba* is ultimately God's domain. The list the Sages compile is, in a meaningful sense, beside the point — God reserves that judgment for Himself. This answers a question that naturally arises: who authorized the *rabbanim* to determine who has a portion in *olam haba* or not?

### Tashlumin Interpretation

Rashi explains that the key word in the *bat kol* is *yishalmena*, which he connects not to *shalom* but to *tashlumin* — compensation. The question God poses is whether the rabbis are the ones who will compensate, that is, make good on these judgments. The answer is no. That authority belongs to God alone.

---

## Dorshei Reshumot

### Reject Exclusions

The *Dorshei Reshumot* — those who interpret *psukim* in the manner of *aggadata* — go even further than God's protest over Shlomo. Rather than merely objecting to a particular inclusion on the list, they reject the entire framework of exclusion. *Kulam ba'im l'olam haba* — everyone, even those wicked kings, receives a portion in *olam haba*. Their proof derives from a creative and remarkably ingenious *derasha* on a *pasuk* in Psalms.

### Psalm Interpretation

The *pasuk* reads: *li Gilead v'li Menashe, v'Ephraim ma'oz roshi, Yehuda mechokki, Moav sir rachtzi, al Edom ashlich na'ali, alai Pleshet hitro'ai* — to me is Gilead and to me is Menashe; Ephraim is the strength of my head; Yehuda is my scepter; Moav is the pot in which I will bathe; on Edom I will cast my shoes; upon the Philistines I will shout in triumph. Read simply, the *pasuk* contrasts God's chosen tribes of Israel with nations like Edom and Moav that are treated contemptuously. The *Dorshei Reshumot*, however, read it as a divine declaration of ownership and inclusion for a roster of sinners.

### Figure Identifications

The *derasha* proceeds as follows: *li Gilead* — to me is Gilead: *zeh Achav*, that is Achav, *she'nafal b'Ramot Gilead*, who fell at Ramot Gilead. Rashi explains that God is saying, in effect, I will carry his sin — he too will receive *olam haba*. *V'li Menashe k'mashma'o* — and to me is Menashe, taken literally as King Menashe rather than the tribe, meaning God has him covered as well. *Ephraim ma'oz roshi zeh Yerovam* — Yerovam, who comes from the tribe of Ephraim, is also included. *Yehuda mechokki zeh Achitofel* — Yehuda is my scepter, referring to Achitofel, who comes from Yehuda. Achitofel is one of the four commoners (*hedyotot*) who will be introduced shortly; this *derasha* already incorporates him.

### Commoners Included
