*Moav sir rachtzi zeh Geichazi* — Moav is the pot in which I bathe, referring to Geichazi, *she'laka iskei rechitza*, whose entire episode with Na'aman centered on bathing. *Al Edom ashlich na'ali zeh Doeg HaEdomi* — on Edom I cast my shoes: the connection between *Edom* and *Edomi* is direct.

### Making Friends

The *pasuk* concludes: *alai Pleshet hitro'ai* — upon the Philistines I will triumph. What does this refer to? The angels before God ask: if David, who slew Goliath the Philistine and bequeathed the city of Gat to Israel's children, comes before You, what will You do for him, given that You are protecting Doeg — who informed against David to Shaul and brought about such tragedy? God replies: *alai la'asotan rei'im zeh la-zeh* — it is upon Me to make them friends with one another. Similarly, Achitofel and Doeg were enemies of David; God assures the angels He will reconcile them all. This is a beautiful and inventive *derasha*, managing to include every figure on the list of sinners within a single *pasuk* while resolving the apparent injustice to David at the same time.

---

## People & Prophets

### Teshuvah Nitzachat

The *Gemara* now shifts from the kings to the people themselves, introducing a verse: *Madua shovevah ha'am hazeh Yerushalayim meshuvah nitzachat* — why does this people persistently rebel, a rebellion that is *nitzachat*, enduring. Rav reads *shovevah* as referring to a *teshuvah* — not repentance, but a response — and *nitzachat* as meaning devastating, unanswerable. His claim is that the people of Israel responded to the prophet with a *teshuvah nitzachat*, a reply so powerful that it could not be answered.

### Fathers & Prophets

What was that response? Rav explains: the prophet said to Israel, *chizru b'teshuvah* — repent. He then argued: *avoseichem shechatu heichan heim* — your fathers who sinned, where are they now? They are dead. You don't want to share their fate, so repent. The people replied: *u'nevi'eichem shelo chatu heichan heim* — and your friends the prophets who did not sin, where are they? Also dead. If everyone dies regardless, that argument gives us no particular reason to repent.

The *Gemara* cites the verse: *avoseichem ayeih heim vehanevi'im haleolam yichyu* — your fathers, where are they? And the prophets, do they live forever? The prophet's rejoinder is either that even the prophets are mortal, yet God's word endures and the people should acknowledge that — or, alternatively, that at least your forefathers, when rebuked, admitted their wrongdoing and returned. As it says: *ach devarai vechukai asher tzivisi es avadai hanevi'im* — even My words which I commanded through My servants the prophets were eventually heeded, the people admitted their sin. One reading of this ends with Israel doing *teshuvah* — which, of course, would make it a less than fully devastating response. The tension in these readings is left unresolved.

### Slave Analogy

Shmuel offers a different version of the *teshuvah nitzachat*. Ten people came and sat before the prophet. He told them to repent. They replied: *eved shemachro rabo v'ishah shegerashah ba'alah, klum yesh lazeh al zeh klum* — if a master sells his slave, or a husband divorces his wife, they have nothing further to do with one another. God has sent us into exile; God has, in effect, abandoned us. Do not tell us to repent — it is over. This indeed sounds like an unanswerable response.

### No Divorce

Yet the *Gemara* shows that it was not unanswerable — because God responded through the prophet Yeshayahu: *eizeh sefer kerisus imchem asher shillachtiyah* — show me the bill of divorce I sent your mother. *Umi minoshai asher macharti eschem lo* — who is the creditor to whom I sold you off? The answer: *hein ba'avonoseichem nimkartem uvifsha'eichem shullechah imchem* — it was through your own sins that you sold yourselves; it was through your own transgressions that your mother was sent away. God did not divorce Israel. Israel brought the exile upon itself — and therefore Israel, not God, holds the power to end it. The slave argument is thus refuted: you were never sold to anyone but your own sin; you can return.

---

## Nebuchadnezzar Drasha

### David & Nebuchadnezzar

Rav, citing Reish Lakish, raises a striking observation: the verse refers to both David and Nebuchadnezzar as God's *avdi* — My servant. What possible comparison is there between God's faithful servant David and the destroyer Nebuchadnezzar? The explanation is as follows: God foreknew that Israel would make the very argument about the slave being sold — that once God sent them into exile via Nebuchadnezzar, they would claim to be cut off from any further relationship with God. To preempt this, God designated Nebuchadnezzar as His own *eved*, His own slave.

### Acquired Property

The operative legal principle is: *eved shekanah nechasim, eved l'mi, nechasim l'mi* — if a slave acquires property, who owns the slave and who owns the property? The master owns both. By establishing Nebuchadnezzar as His slave, God ensured that whatever Nebuchadnezzar acquired — including the Israelites he took into captivity — belongs to God.

### Never Left Servitude

The implication is profound: you never left God's servitude. Even in Babylonian captivity, you remained God's people, because Nebuchadnezzar himself was God's slave and his possessions were God's possessions. The claim that exile constitutes a severance of the divine relationship is therefore untenable.

---

## Redemption & Kingship

### God's Anger Verse

Another verse addresses the people's resistance directly. They say: *nihyeh kagoyim kemishpachot ha'aratzot lisharet etz va'even* — let us be like the nations, like the families of the lands, worshipping wood and stone. God responds through Yechezkel: *chai ani neum Hashem Elokim, im lo b'yad chazakah uvizro'a netuyah uvicheimah shefuchah emloch aleichem* — as I live, says the Lord God, even if it requires a powerful hand, an outstretched arm, and outpoured fiery wrath, I will reign over you. There is no escaping the divine relationship, no matter how much Israel resists.

### Accept Anger

Rav Nachman responds to this verse with a striking declaration: *ko ki hai ritcha lirtach Rachmana alan, dilfarkinan, velimloch aleichan* — let God pour out all that anger upon us, let us endure all of it, as long as in the end He redeems us and reigns over us. This is a remarkable contrast to the view mentioned earlier in the *masechta* — that some *rabbanim* preferred not to live in the days of *yemot haMashiach* because they feared the suffering of *chevlei Mashiach*. Rav Nachman takes the opposite position: whatever divine anger may come, redemption makes it worthwhile.

---

## Yetzer Hara Claim

### Evil Inclination

The *Gemara* presents yet another version of the people's response to prophetic rebuke. Rabbah bar bar Chana teaches: the prophet said to Israel, *chizru b'teshuvah*. They replied: *ein anu yocholim, yetzer hara sholet banu* — we cannot; the *yetzer hara* rules over us. We are simply unable to resist it.

### Deflect to God

The prophet responded: *yisru yitzrechem* — subjugate your evil inclination, bring it under control. The people replied: *elohav yorenu* — let the God who created the *yetzer hara* teach us how to control it, and then we will do so. This final deflection — placing the responsibility for overcoming the *yetzer hara* back on God — serves as another instance of the people's resistance to *teshuvah*.

The discussion of the people's sinfulness here connects, thematically, to the broader discussion of the kings: the people, in a sense, get the leaders they deserve, and vice versa. The question also arises whether the *dorshei reshumot*'s inclusive approach — covering the kings and the *hedyotot* alike — reflects the general principle of *kol Yisrael yesh lahem chelek l'olam haba*. That line, it should be noted, was a later addition to the *Mishnah*, not original to it, and its normative status is itself debated. Urbach, among others, has argued about whether this principle represents the standard theology of *Chazal*. The standard view seems to be that *tzaddikim* receive *olam haba*, *resha'im* go to *Gehinnom*, and *beinonim* fall somewhere in between. Yet the very fact that the *Mishnah* lists only a small number of individuals who are excluded implies that the default assumption is inclusion. The *dorshei reshumot* push that inclusivity to its furthest limit — even the most wicked among Israel retain their portion.

---

## Four Commoners

### List of Four

The *Mishnah* now turns to the four *hedyotot* — commoners — who have no portion in *olam haba*: Bilam, Doeg, Achitofel, and Geichazi. Note that the *derasha* of the *dorshei reshumot*, which we just encountered, included Doeg, Achitofel, and Geichazi but conspicuously omitted Bilam. This is deliberate: the principle of *kol Yisrael yesh lahem chelek l'olam haba* applies to Jews. For non-Jews, the standard is different — one must be among the *chasidei umot ha'olam* to merit *olam haba*, and that is precisely the discussion the *Gemara* is about to enter.

### Bilam Etymology

The *Gemara* now derives multiple meanings from the name *Bilam*. First: *b'lo am* — without a nation. Second, *davar acher*: *she'bala am* — who swallowed, wiped out, a nation. Third, he is identified as *Ben Be'or*, and the *Gemara* derives from *be'or* — *she'ba al be'ir* — that he, or his father, had intercourse with an animal. The *Gemara* will develop this point more explicitly later in connection with Bilam and his donkey.

### Genealogy

The *Gemara* then presents the tradition that Be'or, Bilam's father, is the same person as Cushan-Rishathaim, who is in turn the same person as Lavan Ha-Arami. One individual with multiple names, living across an extraordinarily long span of history — from the era of Yaakov through the period of the *Shofetim*. Why the multiple names? *She'ba al be'ir* — the name Be'or reflects his act with an animal. *Cushan-Rishathaim d'avad shtei risha'os b'Yisrael* — Cushan-Rishathaim, whose name encodes "two evils against Israel": one in the days of Yaakov, when as Lavan he sought to destroy Yaakov and thereby wipe out the Jewish people in its infancy, and once in the period of the *Shofetim*, when he oppressed Israel. Bilam himself would constitute a third attempt. *U'ma shemo? Lavan Ha-Arami shemo* — his true name is Lavan Ha-Arami. The *Gemara* seems to be connecting Bilam's lineage to a pattern of implacable enmity toward the Jewish people across generations.

The *pasuk* itself uses both *Ben Be'or* and *b'no Be'or* — one reading meaning "son of Be'or," the other potentially meaning "Be'or is his son." Rabbi Yochanan explains: when it says *b'no*, it means that in the realm of prophecy, Be'or was *Bilam's* subordinate — Bilam's junior. His father was, as it were, a lesser prophet than he was.

---

## Gentiles & Olam HaBa

### Bilam Excluded

The *Gemara* makes an observation from the *Mishnah*'s singling out of Bilam: *Bilam hu d'lo asi l'alma d'asi* — it is Bilam specifically who does not come to *olam haba*. The implication is that *other* non-Jews do have a portion in *olam haba*. Which non-Jews? The question prompts a discussion of the *masnisin*: whose view does our *Mishnah* represent?

### Eliezer Position

The *Gemara* answers: it reflects the position of Rabbi Yehoshua, as opposed to Rabbi Eliezer. As the *braita* teaches: Rabbi Eliezer interprets the verse *yashuvu resha'im lish'olah kol goyim shochechei Elohim* — the wicked shall return to the underworld, all nations who forget God. *Yashuvu resha'im lish'olah* — these are the sinners of Israel. *Kol goyim shochechei Elohim* — these are the sinners among the nations. But his deeper *derasha* reads the verse as establishing an identity rather than a subset: by definition, *all* the nations are categorized as those who forget God. All gentiles, on this reading, are treated as *resha'im* — not merely the wicked among them, but the entire category.

### Yehoshua Position

Rabbi Yehoshua disputes this. His position is that *resha'im* refers only to the wicked — among both Israel and the nations — and that the qualifier *shochechei Elohim* narrows the verse to those specifically who forget God, not to all gentiles universally. From this, Rabbi Yehoshua concludes: *ha yesh tzaddikim b'ovdei kochavim sheyesh lahem chelek l'olam haba* — there are righteous people among the nations who do have a portion in *olam haba*. The debate, then, is whether *kol goyim shochechei Elohim* is read as an identity (*all* nations *are* forgetters of God) or as a restrictive clause (those *among* the nations who forget God are the ones excluded).

### Tosefta Clarity

The debate is considerably clearer in the *Tosefta* (*Perek* 13), and it is worth presenting that version. The *Tosefta* opens with a related but distinct question: *bnei rish'ei Yisrael ein lahem chelek l'olam haba* — the children of the wicked of Israel have no portion in *olam haba* — based on the verse *hinei yom ba bo'er katanur*, in the words of Rabban Gamliel. Rabbi Yehoshua disagrees and says they do come to *olam haba*. His reasoning: first, *shomer peta'im Hashem* — God protects the simple, and these children were raised in wickedness through no fault of their own, a case akin to *tinok shenishba*. Second, he cites the verse from Daniel about cutting down the tree while leaving the roots — punish the parent, but allow the possibility of redemption to remain for the children.

Turning to the main debate: the *Tosefta* has Rabbi Eliezer saying: *kol rish'ei ovdei kochavim ein lahem chelek l'olam haba, shene'emar: yashuvu resha'im lish'olah — elu rish'ei Yisrael; kol goyim shochechei Elohim — elu rish'ei ovdei kochavim*. Rabbi Yehoshua responds with precision: had the verse said *yashuvu resha'im lish'olah, kol goyim* and then stopped, you would be right — all the nations are treated as wicked. But since the verse adds *shochechei Elohim* — those who forget God — it demonstrates that there are those among the nations who are not forgetters, and therefore: *ha yesh tzaddikim b'ovdei kochavim sheyesh lahem chelek l'olam haba*. The *Tosefta* thus lays out the structure of the argument with considerably more clarity than the *Gemara*'s version.

### Rambam Ruling

One might ask whether one can even *pasken* in matters of theology. As we saw, the *bat kol* itself declared that God decides who enters *olam haba*. Nevertheless, the Rambam rules that *chasidei umot ha'olam yesh lahem chelek l'olam haba* — the righteous among the nations have a portion in *olam haba* — aligning with Rabbi Yehoshua's position. This ruling carries profound theological significance. It is a remarkable feature of Jewish thought that one need not be Jewish to merit *olam haba*. As far as one can tell, Judaism is the only major religion that explicitly provides a path to salvation — or its equivalent — for those outside the faith. Other traditions may be more inclusive in certain respects, but the notion of a divinely mandated code for non-Jews (*sheva mitzvos b'nei Noach*) that carries with it genuine eschatological standing is, to the best of our knowledge, unique.

### Sheva Mitzvot

This leads directly to the question of the *sheva mitzvos b'nei Noach*. If God gave the nations a binding set of laws, and if the fundamental system of divine reward and punishment is ultimately rooted in *olam haba*, then it would be strange indeed to say those laws carry no ultimate reward. The linkage between the *sheva mitzvos* and the *chasidei umot ha'olam*'s portion in *olam haba* would seem to follow naturally. How Rabbi Eliezer's position coheres with the existence of the *sheva mitzvos b'nei Noach* is genuinely difficult to understand.

The Rambam adds an important qualification: a non-Jew merits the status of *chasidei umot ha'olam* only if he observes the *sheva mitzvos b'nei Noach* because he believes God commanded them — specifically, because God commanded Moshe at Sinai that the earlier Noahide covenant remained binding. If he observes them purely out of his own rational judgment, without grounding them in divine command, the Rambam says *eino m'chasidei umot ha'olam*. Here, a famous textual dispute arises among the *acharonim*. Some versions of the Rambam read *v'lo m'chachameihem* — he is neither among the pious of the nations nor among their wise men. Other versions read *ela m'chachameihem* — he is not among the pious, but he is among their wise men. The difference is significant: the first version implies he has no standing at all; the second grants him the status of *chacham* even without the theological grounding. The Rambam does not explicitly state in either version that such a person lacks *olam haba*; that conclusion is implied but not stated directly.

### Radbaz View

Some *nosei keilim* of the Rambam were uncomfortable with the implication that non-Jews who observe only seven *mitzvos* might receive the same portion in *olam haba* as Jews who observe the full *taryag mitzvos* — a disparity in obligation with an apparently equal reward. The Radbaz addresses this directly, arguing that while the *chasidei umot ha'olam* do have a portion in *olam haba*, that portion is not equivalent in quality to the portion of Israel. It is a portion, but a lesser one. This formulation allows for both the inclusion of righteous gentiles and the preservation of a meaningful distinction corresponding to the difference in covenantal obligation.

---

## Bilam's Sign

### Righteous Death

Returning to Bilam: *v'af oso rasha nasan siman b'atzmo* — even that *rasha* gave a sign by which to know whether he would receive *olam haba*. Bilam himself declared: *tamus nafshi mos yesharim vetehi achrisi kamohu* — let my soul die the death of the righteous, and let my end be like theirs. This statement contains his own criterion: if he were to die like the righteous, he would share their ultimate destiny and receive *olam haba*.

### Death in Battle

But Bilam did not die like the righteous. He died in battle, killed when Israel smote the Midianites. That violent death is itself the sign that he does not receive *olam haba*. His own words serve as the standard against which his fate is measured — and he falls short of it.

---

## Moav & Midyan

### Common Enemy

The *Gemara* now examines the background of the encounter between Balak and Bilam. The verse records: *vayelchu ziknei Moav v'ziknei Midyan* — the elders of Moav and the elders of Midyan went together. This is historically striking: *Midyan uMoav lo hayah lahem shalom me'olam* — Midyan and Moav had never had peaceful relations with one another. They were perpetual enemies. Yet here they cooperated. The reason, of course, is that they faced a common threat in Israel.

### Dog Parable

The *Gemara* illustrates this with a *mashal*: there were two dogs in a flock who were enraged at one another, *tzehuvim zeh lazeh* — their hackles raised against each other. A wolf came and attacked one of them. The first dog reasoned: if I do not help my fellow dog, the wolf will kill him today and come for me tomorrow. So they united and killed the wolf together. Here too, Balak was protecting his people of Moav, and they joined with the leaders of Midyan to address what they perceived as the threat of Israel. Rav Pappa adds the folk saying: *karkushta v'shunra* — the weasel and the cat, sworn enemies, *avdu hilula mitarva d'vish gada* — made a feast together from the fat of one who suffered misfortune. Common interest bridges even the deepest enmity.

The *Gemara* then explains why the officers of Midyan departed after Bilam asked them to stay the night. Bilam said: *linu poh halailah vahashivosi eschem davar* — stay here tonight, and I will bring you God's word. The Midianite officers replied: *klum yesh av shesonei es bno* — is there a father who hates his own son? They recognized that the God of Israel is Israel's father, and concluded that God would never agree to curse His own people. Seeing that any appeal to Bilam was therefore pointless, they left.

This prompts Rav Nachman to observe: *chutzpah afilu klapei shamaya mahani* — brazenness works even toward Heaven. For at first, God told Bilam *lo teleich imahem* — do not go with them. Yet Bilam kept pressing, and ultimately God said *kum leich itam* — arise and go with them. The *chutzpah* of his persistence, whether directed at the officers of Moav by asking them to remain another night in hopes of a different divine response, or directed at God Himself by daring to ask again after being refused, produced results. Rashi connects the *chutzpah* to Bilam's invitation to the officers to stay, suggesting it was bold of him to imply he might obtain a different answer; on a straightforward reading, the *chutzpah* was simply in approaching God again after a clear refusal.

Rav Sheshes adds a related observation: *chutzpah malchusa bela taga* — *chutzpah* is like kingship without a crown. Boldness confers informal power exceeding one's formal standing. David himself acknowledged this: *va'anochi hayom rach umishuach melech v'ha'anashim ha'eileh bnei Tzeruyah kashim mimeni* — I am today a young anointed king, and the sons of Tzeruyah are more powerful than I. Even David, the anointed king, found himself constrained by their audacity.

---

## Bilam's Flaws

### Lameness

Rabbi Yochanan enumerates several physical and moral deficiencies of Bilam. He was lame in one leg — *chiga b'raglo achas haya* — as derived from *vayelech shefi*, where Rashi reads *shefi* as indicating a displaced, dislocated limb. By contrast, Shimshon was lame in both legs, derived from the double language of *shefifon alei orach*, referring to a descendant of Dan who bit horses' heels: the doubled root indicates lameness in both legs.

### Blindness

Bilam was also blind in one eye — *suma b'achas me'einav haya* — as derived from his self-description *sh'sum ha'ayin*. Rashi reads the word *sh'sum* as meaning "open" in one eye, which by implication means the other is closed. The derivation is unusual, but the conclusion is that Bilam's vision was impaired in one eye.

### Necromancy

He also engaged in a form of *kosem b'amato* — necromancy involving his genitalia — derived from the phrase *nofel v'galui einayim*, which is compared to the verse about Haman's fall: *hineh Haman nofel al hamita asher Ester aleha*, where falling clearly carries sexual connotations. There is a dispute between Mar Zutra and Mar bar Ravina: Mar Zutra says the first interpretation stands — Bilam practiced necromancy in a sexually deviant manner. Mar bar Ravina says: rather, *sheba al atono* — he actually had intercourse with his donkey. Each interpretation uses a different comparative verse. Those who hold *ba al atono* derive it from the language of *kara shachav k'ari* in Bilam's prophecy, compared to *bein ragleha kara nafal shachav* in the episode of Yael and Sisera, where the language is clearly sexually charged.

---

## Donkey Argument

### God Knowledge

This leads into one of the more striking passages of the *daf*. Bilam describes himself as *v'yodea da'as elyon* — one who knows the thoughts of the Most High. The *Gemara* responds with biting irony: *hashta da'as behemto lo hava yada, da'as elyon hava yada?* — he did not even know the mind of his own animal, yet he claims to know the mind of God? Bilam could not see the angel standing before him, which his donkey could clearly perceive. But the *Gemara* takes this a step further: Bilam was not merely outclassed perceptually. He was actually bested in argumentation by his donkey.

### Constant Companion

The occasion for the argument was this: the officers of Moav asked Bilam why he was riding a donkey rather than a horse. Riding a horse would have been more dignified, more fitting for a person of his stature. Bilam replied that the donkey was practical — *d'shadei lehu birtiva*, it grazes on the wet grass of the swamp, so the cost of maintaining it is low. The donkey then spoke: *halo anochi asonecha* — am I not your donkey? You are using me today as if this is an ad hoc arrangement, but I am your regular mount. Bilam countered: I use you only for carrying burdens, not for riding. The donkey replied: *asher rachavta alai* — no, I am the one you always ride. Bilam dismissed this: *akrai b'alma* — occasionally, not regularly. The donkey rejected this too: *me'odecha ad hayom hazeh* — from your very beginning until today, I have always been your mount.

### Spousal Acts

The donkey then raises the stakes entirely: *v'lo od ela she'ani osa lach ma'aseh ishus balailah* — not only that, but I perform spousal acts for you at night. The word *hasken haskanti* — have I ever treated you this way before — is compared to *v'tehi lo sochenes*, the description of Avishag who kept David warm at night, reading *sochenot* as denoting intimate service.

### Outsmarts

The point of the entire exchange is pointed: if Bilam cannot hold his own in an argument with his donkey — a donkey that knows his history, his habits, and his most intimate arrangements better than he does — how plausible is his claim to know the thoughts of the Most High?

---

## Cursing Moment

### When Angry

What, then, was the genuine power Bilam possessed? The *Gemara* explains: *shehaya yodea l'chaven osa sha'a she'haKadosh Baruch Hu ko'es bah* — he knew how to time his action precisely to the moment in each day when God becomes angry. Had he managed to deliver his curse at that precise moment, it would have been effective.

### Shittim-Gilgal

This is the background for the prophet's reminder to Israel: *ami zachor na mah ya'atz Balak melech Moav, umah ana oso Bilam ben Be'or min haShittim ad haGilgal* — My people, remember what Balak king of Moav schemed, and what Bilam son of Be'or answered him, from Shittim to Gilgal, *l'maan da'as tzidkos Hashem* — so that you may know the righteous acts of God. What righteous acts? The *Gemara* explains:

### Avoided Anger

God says to Israel: know how great was My kindness to you — *shelo ka'asti kol otan hayamim* — throughout all those days, from Shittim to Gilgal, I deliberately refrained from becoming angry, so that Bilam should have no opening through which to curse you. This is implied by Bilam's own words to Balak: *mah ekov lo kaboh E-l, umah za'am lo za'am Hashem* — how can I curse whom God has not cursed, and how can I be wrathful when God has not been wrathful? This is read as testimony that throughout that entire period, *lo za'am Hashem* — God did not become angry — removing any possibility for Bilam's curse to take effect. Bilam knew the mechanism, but God chose not to activate it.

The general principle is that God does experience *za'am* — wrath — each day, but only for a moment: *ki rega b'apo chayim birtzono*. Bilam's unique skill was knowing precisely which moment that was. The verse *lech ami bo b'chadrecha, sgor d'latecha ba'adecha, chavi k'mat rega, ad ya'avor za'am* — go, My people, enter your chambers, close your doors, hide for a brief moment until the wrath passes — also alludes to this fleeting moment of divine anger.

### Three Hours

When exactly does God become angry? The *Gemara* specifies: during the first three hours of the day — from dawn until approximately mid-morning — when *k'chivra d'charbalta d'tarnagolta*, the comb of the rooster turns white. The *Gemara* clarifies that the rooster's comb is ordinarily white but has red streaks throughout most of the day. During that brief window, *leit bei sarki sumki* — the red streaks disappear entirely, and the comb is pure white. That is the moment.

### Rooster Story

This leads to a story about a *mina* — a heretic or sectarian — who lived in the neighborhood of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and caused him great anguish. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi decided he would use that propitious moment to curse the man. He took a rooster, tied it to his bedpost by its legs, and sat watching for that precise moment of pure white. The *Gemara* notes, with something close to rueful humor: a watched rooster, it seems, never turns white. When that moment arrived, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi had dozed off. When he awoke, he concluded: *shma mina lav orach ara* — it is clearly not appropriate behavior. *Ktiv gam anosh l'tzaddik lo tov* — punishing another, even a *min*, is not fitting for a righteous person. *Afilu b'minei lo iba'i leh l'meimar hachi* — even against heretics one should not resort to cursing. The entire exercise led him to a moral conclusion rather than a curse.

There is a broader question lurking here: is the whole framework — that God becomes angry at a specific moment, and that Bilam knew how to exploit it — mechanistic? Does the one who knows the moment effectively compel a divine response? The answer, as the *Gemara* makes clear, is no. God chose not to become angry precisely because He foresaw the danger. *Olam keminhago noheg* — the world operates according to its nature — but God retains the capacity to override that nature. Bilam knew the mechanism; God simply chose not to engage it.

---

## Love & Hatred

### Love Breaks Hierarchy

The *Gemara* teaches in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar: *ahavah mevateles shurah shel gedolah* — exceeding love destroys the normal boundaries of conduct expected of people of stature. A great person will normally delegate tasks beneath his dignity to servants or attendants. But when love overrides judgment, those boundaries dissolve. The proof is from Avraham: *vayashkem Avraham baboker* — Avraham rose early in the morning himself, and personally saddled his donkey for the *Akeidah*, an act he would normally have delegated. Whether motivated by love of God or by love of Yitzchak, the force of the emotion caused him to bypass the normal conventions of his station.

### Hatred Breaks Bounds

Symmetrically: *sin'ah mevateles shurah shel gedolah* — hatred equally causes people of stature to cross normal behavioral boundaries. The proof is from Bilam: *vayakam Bilam baboker vayachavosh es atono* — Bilam rose in the morning and saddled his own donkey. Bilam would not ordinarily saddle his own animal; his hatred of Israel was so consuming that he eagerly did so himself, without waiting for his servants.

---

## Balak's Merit

### Wrong Motivation

The *Gemara* now introduces the principle of *shelo lishmah ba lishmah* — doing something for the wrong reason can ultimately lead to doing it for the right reason, or at least to producing good. Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav states: a person should always engage in Torah and *mitzvos*, even *shelo lishmah*, even for impure or extrinsic motives, *shemitoch shelo lishmah ba lishmah* — because from doing it for the wrong reason, he will ultimately come to do it for the right reason.

### Forty-Two Sacrifices

The proof is Balak. Balak brought forty-two sacrifices — seven bulls and seven rams per occasion, across three occasions, totaling forty-two — for the explicit purpose of enabling Bilam to curse Israel. This is almost the inverse of *shelo lishmah*: not merely a less-than-ideal motive, but an actively malevolent one. Yet he was offering these sacrifices to God, and there is an assumption that even the most corrupt motivation behind a genuine religious act leaves some residue of merit. The question of what exactly made these sacrifices a *mitzvah* — given that they were offered outside the *Mishkan*, constituting *chutz* — is complicated, but the *Gemara* assumes some form of divine service was involved.

### Ruth's Origin

By the merit of those forty-two sacrifices, *vayatsa mimenu Rut* — Ruth emerged from Balak's lineage. Rabbi Yosi bar Chunya specifies the genealogy: Ruth was the daughter of Eglon, who was the grandson of Balak, king of Moav. The *ba lishmah* here operates in an unusual register: ordinarily the principle means that impure motivations, if channeled into genuine action, will eventually reform themselves into pure ones in the actor. Here, Balak himself never improved — but the merit he accumulated through the act generated a reward that materialized generations later in the form of Ruth, ancestress of David.

---

## King's Blessing

### Throne Question

Rava poses a question to Rabba bar Mari: the verse says *yeteiv Elokim es shem Shlomo mishemcha, viyagdel kiso mikisecha* — may God make the name of Shlomo good from your name, and make his throne greater than yours. This was said to David when he designated Shlomo as his successor. But is it proper etiquette to say to a king that his son's throne should exceed his own? That would seem to be a slight — implying that the father's kingship was somehow deficient.

### Derive From

The answer: *mishimcha* does not mean "greater than your name." It means *me'ein kamre leh* — deriving from your name, taking something of the greatness of your name as its source. May Shlomo's greatness be an extension of David's, not a surpassing of it.

### Yael Analogy

The *Gemara* proves this reading from a parallel case: *tivorach minashim Yael* — Yael should be blessed among women, *eshet Chever HaKeini, minashim ba'ohel tivorach* — from among the women of the tent she should be blessed. The *nashim ba'ohel* — the women of the tent — are identified as Sarah, Rivka, Rachel, and Leah, the matriarchs. Could one possibly mean that Yael is greater than the matriarchs? Clearly not. *Ela me'ein kamre* — the blessing means that her greatness derives in some way from theirs, that she is blessed in the manner of those great women. *Hacha nami me'ein kamre* — so too by Shlomo, the blessing means deriving from David's greatness, not exceeding it.

### No Jealousy

The *Gemara* adds an observation from Rabbi Yose bar Chanina: *bechol adam mitkanei chutz mibno v'talmido* — a person is jealous of everyone except his son and his student. The absence of jealousy toward one's son is illustrated precisely from this episode: David's court could say "let Shlomo's throne be greater" without causing David offense, because a father naturally wants his son to surpass him. The same applies to a student: one genuinely wishes one's student to excel and surpass even oneself — as illustrated by Elisha asking for *pi shnayim b'ruchacha*, a double portion of Eliyahu's spirit, and by Moshe placing both hands on Yehoshua when God had only specified one — an act born of wholehearted generosity rather than reluctant compliance.

---

## Mouth Control

### Three Views

The *Gemara* returns to Bilam. *Vayasem davar b'fi Bilam* — and He placed a word in the mouth of Bilam. Three interpretations are offered. Rabbi Elazar says: *malach* — God sent an angel who accompanied Bilam to ensure that the words coming from his mouth were blessings rather than curses. Rabbi Yochanan, or Rabbi Yonatan, says: *chitah* — God placed a hook or bit in Bilam's mouth, physically dragging and controlling his speech the way a rider controls a horse with a bit.

### Prevent Curse

The purpose in either interpretation is the same: ensuring that Bilam could not curse Israel despite every intention to do so. Tomorrow's *daf* will develop this theme further, examining each of Bilam's blessings and showing how the very structure of the language reveals that Bilam was reaching for curses — and how God's control of his mouth transformed each intended curse into its opposite. This is, after all, what the *psukim* themselves say: *vayahafoch Hashem Elokecha lecha es hakelalah libracha* — God transformed the curse into a blessing, precisely because God loved Israel.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 106

## Bilam's Reversed Curses

### Intro & Vayasem Davar

The daf begins roughly eleven lines from the bottom of the page, with the verse *vayasem davar b'fi Bilam* — "God placed a word in the mouth of Bilam." This serves as the launching point for a broader discussion of how exactly God controlled Bilam's speech, and what Bilam had actually intended to say.

### Angel vs. Hook Debate

*Rabbi Eliezer* understands *vayasem davar* to mean that an angel was given to Bilam to instruct and constrain what he said. *Rabbi Yochanan*, by contrast, reads it as *chaka* — a fishhook — meaning God dragged the words out of him. The *Gra* suggests these two positions are not truly in conflict: one describes the mechanism of preventing Bilam from saying what he wanted to say, while the other describes the mechanism of compelling him to say the right thing. One blocks the tongue; the other forces it.

### Reversing the Blessings

*Amar Rabbi Yochanan*: from the blessings of that wicked person you can deduce — simply by reversing them — what he had wanted to curse Israel with, because God reversed his curses into blessings. The *pasuk* itself states *vayafoch Hashem Elokecha lach es hakelalah libracha* — "God reversed the curse into a blessing."

Working through the blessings in sequence: Bilam had wanted to say that Israel should have no *batei knesiyos u'batei midrashot* — synagogues and study halls — and instead was forced to say *Ma Tovu Ohalecha Yaakov*, "How beautiful are your tents, O Jacob." He wanted to say that the *shechinah* should not rest upon them, and instead uttered *mishkenotecha Yisrael* — your dwelling places, drawing on the same root as *shechinah*. He wanted to say that their kingship should not be extended, and instead produced the image of *kenachalim nitayu* — rivers stretched out — a symbol of enduring dominion. He wanted to say they should have no olive trees or vineyards, and instead said *keganos alei nahar* — like gardens by the river. He wanted their aroma not to be fragrant, and instead gave them *k'ahalim nata Hashem* — like *ahalim* planted by God. The word *ohel* can denote both a tent and the aromatic substance *ahalot* mentioned in *mor ve'ahalot*, and so the blessing carries a double meaning. He wanted to say they should have no kings of stature, and instead said *kearazim alei mayim* — like cedar trees by the water. He wanted to say there should be no king son of a king — no dynastic continuity — and instead gave the image of *yizal mayim midalyav*, water flowing from one bucket to the next. He wanted to say their kingship should not dominate other nations, and instead said *vezaro bemayim rabim* — his descendants over many waters. He wanted to say their kingship should not be powerful, and instead gave *vayarom meAgag malko*. He wanted to say their kingship should not inspire fear, and instead declared *vetinesa malchuso*.

Every one of these metaphors, when reversed, reveals what Bilam had been reaching for — a comprehensive curse across the dimensions of divine presence, kingship, land, fragrance, and fear.

### Curses Reverted Except O…

*Amar Rabbi Abba bar Kahana*: in the end, *kulam chazru leklalah* — all of the blessings reverted to their originally intended curse. Whether this happened because of Bilam's original intent, or simply because of Israel's subsequent sins, is an open question, but the observation stands: the kingship is gone, the land with its olive trees and vineyards is gone, so much of what the blessings described has in fact been lost. *Chutz mi'batei knesiyos u'mibatei midrashot* — the sole exception is the very first blessing, *Ma Tovu Ohalecha Yaakov*. No matter the depth of exile, synagogues and study halls have persisted. The *pasuk* is then read carefully: *kelalah velo kelalot* — "the curse" in the singular, implying that only one of the curses remained permanently reversed into a blessing, while the others ultimately reasserted themselves.

### Beloved's Wounds vs Enem…

*Amar Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani amar Rabbi Yonatan*: what is meant by the verse *ne'emanim pitzei ohev vena'atarot neshikot soneh* — "trustworthy are the wounds of a beloved, but the kisses of an enemy are unreliable"? Better is the curse that *Achiyah HaShiloni* the prophet cursed Israel with than the blessings that *Bilam HaRasha* bestowed upon us. The wounds of a friend — even when painful — are rooted in genuine care, while an enemy's kindness conceals a hidden agenda. As one student aptly noted, this fits the verse precisely: Achiyah's curse came from genuine prophetic concern for Israel's welfare, while Bilam's blessing was rooted in an attempt to destroy.

### Reed vs Cedar Metaphor

When *Achiyah HaShiloni* wanted to curse Israel, he used the image of a reed: *vehika Hashem et Yisrael kaasher yanud hakaneh bamayim* — "God will smite Israel as the reed sways in the water." On the surface this appears harsh — Israel will not be firm, they will sway. But consider what a reed in water actually is. No matter how many waters rush past it, the reed remains rooted where it was planted. Even if cut down, *vegizo machalif* — it grows back. Its roots are numerous and deep. Even if all the winds of the world blow against it, they do not uproot it from its place; rather, *hu holech uva imahem* — it sways along with them. And when the winds finally cease, *amad hakaneh bimkomo* — the reed stands exactly where it always stood. The curse is therefore a genuine blessing: we will suffer, we will sway, but we will endure.

*Bilam HaRasha*, by contrast, when he blessed Israel, compared us to a cedar tree — *kearazim alei mayim*. And what is a cedar? *Eino omed bimkom mayim* — it does not grow from water. Its roots are shallow. If cut down, it does not regenerate. True, because of its rigidity, ordinary winds do not even move it — it will not bend at all. But *keivan shenashva ruach dromit* — once a powerful southern wind strikes it, *miyad okarto vehofachto al panav* — it is immediately uprooted and overturned. Within the blessing lurks a hidden curse, and within the curse a hidden blessing.

There is a further dimension to the reed's virtue: *ela shezacha kaneh litol himenu kulmus lichtov mimenu Sefer Torah* — the reed merits being fashioned into a quill with which a *Sefer Torah* is written. The resilience is not merely physical but ultimately spiritual in its orientation.

---

## Keini & Yitro Story

### Bilam Addresses Keini

The *daf* continues: *vayar et haKeini vayisa meshalo vayomar* — he saw the Keini and lifted his parable and said, *eitan moshavcha vesim basela kinecha* — strong is your dwelling place, and you set your nest in the rock, with *kinecha* playing on the name *Keini*. The *Gemara* identifies the *Keini* here as *Yitro*. Bilam says to him rhetorically: *lo hayita imanu b'otah eitzah* — weren't you with us in that council? How did you merit such greatness? The question *ma hoshivcha eitan olam* — who caused you to dwell with the mighty ones of the world, i.e., Israel — is rhetorical, given that Yitro had been part of the original plot.

### Three Counselors Plot

This brings the *Gemara* to the *derasha* of *Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba* [citing] *Rabbi Simai*: *shlosha hayu b'ota eitza* — there were three participants in the counsel against Israel at Pharaoh's court: Bilam, Iyov, and Yitro. *Bilam she'ya'atz neherag* — Bilam gave the advice and was killed. *Iyov she'shatak nidon b'yisurin* — Iyov was silent; he had not the courage to speak against Pharaoh, and so he suffered. This is presented as the *Gemara*'s explanation for all of Iyov's sufferings — silence in the face of evil is itself a moral failing. It is not merely about active participation; failing to stand against evil, remaining a silent bystander, carries its own consequence. There is a resonance here with Iyov's narrative as well, where the first rounds of suffering are met with silence, and eventually he does speak.

### Yitro's Escape & Reward

*Yitro she'barach* — Yitro fled. He could not speak up — perhaps he would have been killed — but he refused to remain in place as a passive participant. He separated himself from the evil. And because of that separation, *zachu b'nei vanav layshev b'Lishkat HaGazit* — his descendants merited to sit in the Chamber of Hewn Stone, where the *Sanhedrin* convened in the *Beit HaMikdash*. And that is the meaning of *eitan moshavcha*: you dwell among the mighty, because you were present at the counsel but then rejected it and fled.

The *pasuk* cited is *umishpachot sofrim yoshvei Yabetz* — the family of scribes who dwelt in *Yabetz*, which is read as an allusion to the *Lishkat HaGazit*. *Hema haKinim haba'im me'Chamat avi beit Rechav* — these are the Kenites who came from Chamat, father of Beit Rechav. The identification is then clinched by the verse *u'vnei Keini choten Moshe* — the sons of Keini, the father-in-law of Moshe — establishing that *Keini* is the *mishpachat sofrim*, the family of scribes, and that *yoshvei Yabetz* means dwelling in the *Lishkat HaGazit*.

The image of Yitro simply running away might seem like avoidance, but the *Gemara* treats it as genuine moral courage. When facing a tyrant, options are limited: one can speak up and be killed, or one can flee — but remaining silent and in place is complicity. Moshe himself fled when Pharaoh was about to apprehend him. Running away, in this context, is a form of moral self-preservation and an act of dissociation from evil.

---

## Bilam's Final Prophecies

### Keini Parable

The *daf* continues with Bilam's final utterances: *eitan moshavcha vesim basela kinecha* — strong is your dwelling place, and you set your nest in the rock. The full force of this parable, as the *Gemara* has developed it above in relation to Yitro, affirms the reward that comes to one who dissociates from evil even without the ability to actively resist it.

### Woe & Lion Metaphor

*Vayisa meshalo vayomar oy mi yichye mi'shumo El* — he lifted his parable and said: woe, who will live from God's placing of these things? *Amar Rabbi Shimon ben Levi*: from the word *mi'shumo* — from His name — woe is the person who gives himself life through the name of God, i.e., *mi she'mechayeh atzmo b'shem El*, the one who makes himself into a god. *Rashi* offers two readings: one is the person who literally goes around claiming to be a divine figure; the other is the person who decides to live a godless life devoted entirely to sensory and physical pleasure, treating himself as the ultimate authority. The former reading likely carries the *pshat*, though *Rashi*'s second explanation has also been noted by scholars as a not-so-shielded critique of certain religious movements.

*Amar Rabbi Yochanan*: the verse means something closer to the plain sense — *oy lah l'uma she'timatze b'sha'ah she'HaKadosh Baruch Hu oseh pidyon l'vanav* — woe to the nation that finds itself in the way when God comes to redeem His children. The metaphor Rabbi Yochanan deploys is striking: *mi matil ksuto bein lavi l'lviyah b'sha'ah she'niska'akin zeh im zeh* — who would throw his garment between a lion and a lioness when they are copulating? Lions appear indolent most of the time, but when they act, their full power is unleashed. The nation that interposes itself at that moment of divine redemption faces total annihilation.

### Assyria Ever Kittim

The *pasuk* continues: *v'tzim miyad Kittim* — legions from the hand of *Kittim*. *Amar Rav Libun Aspir* — this is an identification whose precise historical referent is debated. The Soncino commentary offers several possibilities: some read *Aspir* as deriving from the Persian *aswar*, meaning knight, yielding the sense of a cavalry legion. *Kittim* is generally taken to denote Rome. One reading, attributed to Jastrow, interprets the entire passage as a reference to Leo the Isaurian, the Byzantine emperor who led the iconoclastic movement and provoked a prolonged conflict between the eastern and western halves of the empire — which would explain the term *Libun* as a reference to the "white" faction. Whatever the precise historical identification, the thrust is of a powerful military formation arising from the coastal regions associated with Rome.

*V'inu Ashur v'inu Ever* — they will afflict Assyria and they will afflict Ever. The *Gemara* then makes a subtle distinction: up to Assyria they will kill (*ad asher katli miktal*), but beyond that point — *mikan v'eilach m'shabdi shibudei* — they will no longer kill but only subjugate.

### Bilam's Real Advice

*Hineni holech l'ami* — I am going back to my people. Bilam says to Balak: *l'cha i'atzcha asher ya'aseh ha'am hazeh l'amcha b'acharit hayamim* — let me advise you what this nation will do to your nation in the end of days. On the surface, this refers to the fate of Moab at the hands of Israel. But the *Gemara* understands it as the verse in which Bilam gave Balak his advice to use the Moabite and Midianite women to seduce Israel — because a later verse states *hein heinah hayu l'vnei Yisrael al dvar Bilam*, they were against Israel through the word of Bilam.

This creates a textual difficulty: the verse should read *amcha l'am hazeh* — what your nation should do to this nation — not the other way around. *Amar Rabbi Abba bar Kahana*: this is the speech pattern of *adam she'mekalel atzmo v'toleh klilato b'acherim* — a person who curses himself but frames it as speaking about others. *Rashi* offers an alternative explanation: Bilam phrased it normally, intending to advise how to bring about Israel's downfall, but the *pasuk* as written inverted the formulation — a kind of euphemism, declining to write the destructive counsel directly. Either way, the *Gemara* reads this as the locus of Bilam's advice to Balak to seduce Israel into sin.

*Amar lahem eloheihem shel eilu sonei zimah hu* — the God of this people hates sexual immorality. *V'heim mitavin l'chlei pishtan* — and they happen to desire fine linen garments. Come, let me give you counsel. The convergence of these two observations forms the basis of the strategy that follows.

---

## Seduction Strategy

### Marketplace Setup

*Asei lahen kla'im* — make curtains for them, set up a kind of open-air market or street fair. *Vehoshiv bahen zonot* — station prostitutes in the booths. *Zkeinah mibachutz veyaldah mibifnim* — the older woman on the outside, so it will not be immediately apparent that seduction is the purpose, and the younger, more attractive woman on the inside. *Veyimkru lahen klei pishtan* — and have these booths sell fine linen garments, which will draw Israelite men to browse.

The plan was executed on a large scale: *mehar sheleg ad beit hayeshimot* — from Mount Sheleg to Beit Hayeshimot, an enormous expanse was set up in this fashion, with prostitutes stationed throughout, the older women at the entrance and the younger women inside. It is worth noting that this setup appears to draw on a real social phenomenon familiar to the *Gemara*'s audience — there are parallel references in the opening of *Avodah Zarah* to Roman markets that included prostitutes among the commercial offerings.

### Gradual Seduction

*Uvesha'ah sheYisrael ochlin veshotin vesmeichim veyotzim letayel bashuk* — when Israel were eating and drinking and rejoicing and going out to stroll in the market, the older woman would call out: would you be interested in fine linen garments? He would ask the price; the older woman would give the fair market rate. Then he would be drawn toward the younger woman inside, *veyaldah omeret lo befachot* — and she would offer him a discount. This exchange happens two or three times, drawing him back repeatedly, each visit extending his time in the company of the younger woman, ostensibly in the course of a commercial negotiation.

### Idol Worship Test

After multiple visits, the younger woman would say: *harei atah k'ven bayit* — you are practically family here. *Shev go rolei le'atzmecha* — sit, look through the wares yourself. And she would produce a flask of Ammonite wine — *utzlochit shel yayin Amoni munach etzlah*. The *Gemara* inserts a historical note: *ve'adayin lo ne'esar yayin shel nochrim* — the wine of non-Jews had not yet been forbidden at that time. This is not merely informational; it also hints at why the prohibition was eventually enacted, since social wine-drinking between Jewish men and non-Jewish women clearly created the conditions for exactly this kind of boundary erosion.

Once he had drunk the wine, *ba'ar bo* — his passion was inflamed — and he asked her to be intimate with him. At that point she reached into her bosom and produced her idol: *avod lazeh* — worship this first, and then I will agree. He recoiled: *halo Yehudi ani* — I am a Jew. And she responded: *u'ma ichpat lach* — what does it matter? *Kum u'vakesh mimcha iypur* — I am only asking you to defecate before it. And *hu eino yodea she'avodato be'kach* — he does not know that that is in fact the mode of worship of the *Baal Peor*.

The dynamic being described is one of incremental compromise. Each step is minimized, each line crossed is framed as trivial — until, as *Rashi* inserts, she then says: and now, if you truly want to be with me, you must deny the Torah of Moshe your teacher. The sequence illuminates how moral collapse occurs: not through a single dramatic fall, but through the accumulation of small steps, each of which seemed manageable in isolation, until one has traveled so far from one's original position that what was once unthinkable becomes the price of one more step. This is the pedagogical warning embedded in the narrative — the same logic by which the rabbis cautioned against the dangers of any context that begins eroding boundaries.

### Baal Peor Plague

*Shene'emar heima ba'u ba'al pe'or* — they came to *Baal Pe'or*, *vayinazru laboshet* — and they strayed to their shame, *vayihyu shikutzim be'ahavam* — and they became abominations through their desire. The seduction strategy succeeded, and Israel was drawn into the sin of *Baal Pe'or*. The consequences were the plague of 24,000 dead, as the *Gemara* will note shortly.

---

## Shittim Debates

### Shittim Name Debate

*Vayeshev Yisrael bashitim* — Israel dwelt in the *Shitim*. *Rabbi Eliezer omer shitim shemo* — that was simply the name of the place. *Rabbi Yehoshua omer she'nitasku b'divrei shtut* — no, the name reflects what happened there: they engaged in matters of foolishness, the word *shitim* being read as related to *shtut*. This debate between *Rabbi Eliezer* and *Rabbi Yehoshua* follows a consistent pattern: *Rabbi Eliezer* takes names at face value while *Rabbi Yehoshua* reads meaning into them.

The *Gemara* then records their dispute about the nature of the seduction itself. *Rabbi Eliezer omer arumot pagu bahen* — they encountered the women naked, a blatant and direct form of enticement — though it is not entirely clear which *pasuk* this is derived from. *Rabbi Yehoshua omer shenatan b'kulam ba'al keri* — the entire nation experienced seminal emission, which is associated with the *Shitim* and the *ba'al keri* condition.

### Refidim Weakness

Because one dispute of *Rabbi Eliezer* and *Rabbi Yehoshua* about a place name has been cited, a second is brought alongside it, concerning *Refidim* and the attack of Amalek. *Rabbi Eliezer omer Refidim shemo* — that was simply the name of the place where Amalek encountered Israel. *Rabbi Yehoshua omer sherifu atzman midivrei Torah* — no, their hands had grown weak from Torah, the word *rifyon* being embedded in *Refidim*, and it was that spiritual weakness that gave Amalek its opening. *Shene'emar lo hifnu avot el banim merifyon yadayim* — "the fathers did not turn to the sons from the weakness of the hands."

### Fornication Begins

*Amar Rabbi Yochanan*: *vayachel ha'am liznot b'vnot Moav* — the people began to fornicate with the daughters of Moav. The word *vayachel*, "they began," invites a broader reflection on the pattern in which the word *vayeshev* — dwelling, settling — appears in *Tanach* and is followed by trouble. Several examples are cited: *vayeshev Yaakov b'eretz megurei aviv* and then the episode of Yosef and his brothers; *vayeshev Yisrael b'eretz Goshen* and then *vayikrevu yemei Yisrael lamut*; *vayeshev Yehuda v'Yisrael lavetach ish tachat gafno v'tachat te'enato* and then — several chapters later — the rise of *Hadad ha'Adomi* against Shlomo. These examples are admittedly of varying force; the last requires going some seven chapters forward to find the adverse development. The point being made is that *vayeshev* functions as a kind of *lashon tza'ar*, a term of distress — settledness and comfort precede a fall — though the examples are not all equally compelling.

---

## Bilam's Death

### Bilam Seeks Payment

*V'et malchei Midyan hargu al chalaleihem* — they killed the kings of Midian along with their slain. And then: *v'et Bilam ben Be'or hargu bacharev* — they killed Bilam son of Be'or by the sword. What was Bilam doing in Midian? He had left Balak and returned to his own people. The *Gemara* asks *mah ba'ei hatam* — what was he doing there? *Amar Rabbi Yochanan*: *shehalach litol schar esrim v'arba'ah elef she'naflu mi'Yisrael* — he had gone to collect payment for his advice, which had caused a plague that killed 24,000 of Israel. He went back to receive his reward — and it was there that he met his death.

### Camel's Horn Parable

*Amar Mar Zutra bar Tuvia amar Rav: hainu d'amri inshi* — that is what people say: *gamla azla lemib'ei karnei* — a camel went to ask for horns, and *udnei d'havu lei gezizi minei* — had the ears it had cut off. Not content with what it had, it reached for more, and in doing so lost what it already possessed. The application is transparent: Bilam was not satisfied with whatever he had received from Balak, went back to collect more, and was killed in the process.

The *Gemara*'s point is reinforced by a striking analogy. A man was paid to bring rain to San Diego. He performed his cloud-seeding procedure, it subsequently rained for many days, and the flooding caused some ten million dollars in damage. A year later he returned to collect his ten thousand dollar fee. The city presented him with a ten million dollar bill for the damages. If you want to take credit for the rain, you take responsibility for the flood as well. Bilam wanted payment for his deadly counsel — and the payment he received was death.

### Prophet to Magician

The *pasuk* in *Yehoshua* refers to Bilam as *hakosem* — the magician or diviner — rather than *navi*, prophet. This is noted as a deliberate demotion. *Amar Rabbi Yochanan: bitechilah navi ulevasof kosem* — he began as a prophet but ended as a mere practitioner of magic. *Rashi* explains: *shenatan einav bemalchut venittela heimenu nevuah* — because he set his eyes on the kingship, God removed the gift of prophecy from him. *Amar Rabbi Yochanan: hainu d'amrei inshi* — that is what people say: *misagnei v'shalti havai, izin legabi nagrei* — this woman descended from kings and ministers and wound up serving carpenters. The mighty have fallen.

### Four Deaths of Bilam

*Hargu benei Yisrael becherev el chalaleihem* — the *Bnei Yisrael* killed him by sword upon their corpses. The phrase *el chalaleihem* is read as superfluous and carrying additional import. *Amar Rav*: *shekiyemu bo arba mitot sekilah sreifah hereg vechenek* — they inflicted upon Bilam all four forms of capital punishment: stoning, burning, slaying, and strangling. *Rashi* explains the derivation from the word *chalaleihem*, which implies multiple deaths. The practical sequence, as *Rashi* reconstructs it, involved hanging, burning on the stake to which he was suspended, decapitation, and strangulation.

### Bilam's Age at Death

A *min* — a sectarian, quite possibly a Jewish Christian — approached *Rabbi Chanina* and asked: *mi shemia lach Bilam bar kamah havai* — have you heard how old Bilam was when he died? *Rabbi Chanina* replied that it is not explicitly written, but from the verse *anshei damim umirmah lo yechetzu yemeihem* — men of blood and deceit will not live to half their days — one can infer he was either thirty-three or thirty-four years old. The sectarian responded: *shappir ka'amrat* — you have spoken well. And then he added: *ledidi chazi li pinkasei deBilam* — I actually happened to see Bilam's ledger or diary, and it was written therein: *bar tlatin utlat shanin Bilam chagira* — thirty-three years old was Bilam the lame one. *Katilei Pinchas lista'ah* — Pinchas the bandit killed him. From the perspective of whoever wrote in Bilam's ledger, *Pinchas* is cast as the wicked one. The note about *Pinchas* leading the military campaign serves, from *Rashi*'s perspective, to explain how *Pinchas* is credited with the killing even without personally wielding the sword.

The likely subtext of this exchange is a veiled reference to Jesus, who died at approximately thirty-three years of age. The *min*'s knowing response — "you have spoken well" — and the elaboration from Bilam's supposed diary suggest that this was precisely the point being probed and implicitly addressed.

*Amar Mar brei deRavina levrei*: in all of *Perek Chelek*, when studying the wicked figures who have no portion in the World to Come, one should not invest too much in elaborating their evil — *levar miBilam harasha*, with the sole exception of Bilam. Because Bilam is the one non-Jew on the list, *dechamah demishkachat bei derosh bei* — as much as you can expound about his wickedness, by all means do so.

---

## Doeg the Edomite

### Doeg's Name Meaning

The *daf* now turns to *Doeg ha'Adomi*. The name *Doeg* appears in two distinct spellings: one with the letters *dalet-vav-alef-gimmel* and another rendering. *Amar Rabbi Yochanan*: at the outset, when *Doeg* was righteous and on the correct path — but already showing his potential for evil — the Holy One Blessed be He was anxious, *do'eg* — worried — about him. That is the first spelling. After he ultimately actualized his destructive potential, God said *oy* — woe — that this one went forth in the direction he did, either lamenting his birth or lamenting his apostasy. That is the second spelling, with the *vav-yod-yod* rendering *dovay*, woe.

### Scholar Contradictions

*Amar Rabbi Yitzchak*: what is meant by the verse *mah tithallel be-ra'ah ha-gibor chesed El kol hayom* — why does the mighty one glorify himself in evil, with God's kindness extended to him all day? The Holy One Blessed be He said to *Doeg*: were you not a great and valorous person in Torah? How did you come to glorify yourself in evil? Was not God's kindness poured out upon you throughout your years of learning and success?

And then: *vela-rasha amar Elohim mah le-cha lesapper chukkai* — to the wicked one God says: what business do you have reciting My laws? The Holy One said to *Doeg the wicked*: when you reach the sections dealing with murderers — say you are teaching *Makkot* or *Sanhedrin* and you are discussing the laws of those who kill — how do you have the audacity to give a *shiur* on that after what you have done? *U-parshat mesapprei lashon hara* — and when you come to the sections dealing with *lashon hara* — how can you teach My Torah? You are a living contradiction to everything the Torah represents.

This is a point the *Gemara* has made before: Torah scholarship does not automatically produce a righteous person. One can be enormously knowledgeable, capable of delivering brilliant *shiurim*, and be a thoroughly corrupt individual. The verse *ki siftei kohen yishmeru da'at ve-Torah yevakshu mi-pihu ki malakh Hashem Tzeva'ot hu* — "for the lips of the priest shall preserve knowledge, and Torah shall be sought from his mouth, for he is an angel of God" — expresses the demand that a Torah teacher be a living embodiment of what Torah is about, not merely its intellectual conduit.

### Learning Without Heart

*Amar Rabbi Ami*: *ein Torato shel Doeg ela mi-sefatav u-lachutz* — Doeg's Torah never penetrated him. It remained only from the lips outward. It never transformed who he was. Whether this was true from the outset or whether he initially had genuine piety that was subsequently lost, the point stands: the possibility exists of someone who gives magnificent *shiurim* and is a moral anathema to everything those *shiurim* are about.

*Amar Rabbi Yitzchak*: what is meant by the verse *veyiru tzaddikim ve-yira'u ve-alav yischaku* — the righteous saw and were afraid, and then they laughed at him? Initially, *yira'u* — they feared — that people would follow *Doeg*'s bad example, because here was a *talmid chacham* who might lead others astray. But ultimately, *yischaku* — they laughed — because when *Doeg* met his downfall, it was clear that no one would be drawing lessons from his path.

### David's Petition

*Amar Rabbi Yitzchak*: what is meant by the verse *chayil bala vayaki'ennu, mibitno yorishenu El* — he swallowed great wealth and disgorged it, God drove it from his innards? *Amar David lifnei Hakadosh Baruch Hu*: Master of the Universe, let *Doeg* die. *Amar leih*: *chayil bala vayaki'ennu* — he has swallowed great Torah. I will not bring death upon him until he has disgorged it, until he has forgotten his Torah. David then said: *mibitno yorishenu El* — then You, God, drive it from him. If that is what it takes, cause him to forget his Torah, so that justice can be done.

*Amar Rabbi Yitzchak*: what is meant by *gam El yitatzcha lanetzach* — even God will crush you forever? The Holy One Blessed be He wanted to give *Doeg* a portion in the World to Come — consistent with the position mentioned earlier that even these figures retain some access to *olam haba*. But David objected. There is tension here between two parties with legitimate claims: God, who would extend mercy even to *Doeg*, and David, who is the wronged party and refuses to concede. Neither is simply right or wrong; the passage is designed to embody that complexity.

God then said: fine, if not *olam haba*, then at least let Torah be said over in his name in the *Beit Midrash* — *limru shma'ta bei midrasha mishmeih*. David said: *yechat-cha ve-yisach-cha me-ohel* — let him be cut off even from the tent of Torah. Should he at least have descendants who are *talmidei chachamim*? *Ve-shoresh-cha me-eretz chayim sela* — let his root be cut off from the land of the living. No descendants, no Torah credit, nothing. This is a striking exchange, given that elsewhere the *Gemara* notes that even the descendants of those who sought to destroy Israel eventually converted and produced Torah scholars. The question of what to do with the Torah legacy of a morally corrupt genius remains genuinely unresolved.

### Lost Greatness

*Amar Rabbi Yitzchak*: what is meant by *ayeh sofer ayeh shokel ayeh sofer et ha-migdalim* — where is the counter, where is the weigher, where is the one who counts the towers? *Ayeh sofer* — where is the one *she-sofer kol otiyot she-ba-Torah* — who could count every letter in the Torah? *Doeg* possessed that capacity. How did someone with such mastery go so wrong? Or: how did such mastery come to be forgotten? *Ayeh shokel* — where is the one who could weigh all the *kal va-chomerim* in the Torah? *Ayeh sofer et ha-migdalim* — where is the one *she-hayah sofer shalosh me'ot halachot psukot be-migdal ha-poreiach ba-avir* — who could enumerate 300 decided laws regarding a tower floating in the air? *Rashi* explains this as a reference to a chest (*migdal*) positioned half inside and half outside a house and exposed to the air (*avir*), raising complex questions about whether *tumah* passes inward or outward — some of the most intricate territory in the tractate of *Ohalos*. That *Doeg* could navigate 300 decided *halachot* in that domain marks him as a scholar of the first order.

### Questions vs Answers

*Amar Rabbi Ami*: *arba me'ah ba'ei ba'u Doeg ve-Achitofel be-migdal ha-poreiach ba-avir* — *Doeg* and *Achitophel* together could ask 400 questions about a tower floating in the air. *Ve-lo ifshat lehu chad* — yet they could not resolve even one of them. This introduces a subtle qualification: before, *Doeg* was credited with 300 *halachot psukot* — decided law, actual conclusions. Here, the number rises to 400 but the result is only unresolved questions. Someone can be brilliant at generating questions without being able to reach conclusions.

### Heart Over Knowledge

*Amar Rabbah*: *rabuta le-mib'ei ba'ei* — is it such a great feat to ask questions? Anyone can ask questions. This cuts deeper: the obsession with *Doeg* and *Achitophel*'s scholarly accomplishments misses the point. Torah scholarship is not equivalent to being a good person or a true servant of God.

*Bishnei de-Rav Yehudah kuli tanuyei bi-Nezikin* — in the years of *Rav Yehudah*, all they studied was *Nezikin*. They did not study *Nashim*, they did not study *Moed*, and certainly not *Taharos*. *Va'anan ka matninya tuva b'Uktzin* — and we know even *Uktzin*, the most obscure tractate in *Taharos*, with thirteen major *yeshivot* of discussion. By sheer breadth and depth of knowledge, our generation is far ahead of *Rav Yehudah*. And yet: *Rav Yehudah shalyif msanei v'ata mitra* — all *Rav Yehudah* had to do was remove his shoe as a gesture of preparatory prayer, and rain would come. *Va'anan tzavchinan ve-leika d'mashgiach ban* — we pray and cry out the whole day and no one pays attention to us.

*Ela Hakadosh Baruch Hu liba ba'ei* — God wants the heart. *D'chtiv v'Hashem yireh lalevav* — as it is written, "God sees to the heart." The phrase carries a play on words: *liba ba'ei*, wanting the heart, echoes the word *libay ba'ei*. God does not want brilliant Talmudic questions. He wants religious sincerity. The message connects directly back to everything said about *Doeg*: Torah that remains only from the lips outward, Torah that is never internalized, Torah that does not transform — that is Torah that produces a *Doeg*, not a servant of God. And as the verse states: *sod Hashem lireiaiv* — God discloses Himself to those who fear Him. The one whose Torah is purely intellectual, disconnected from genuine *avodas Hashem*, will not arrive at the correct *halachic* conclusion. The fear of God is not a supplement to Torah learning; it is a prerequisite for the Torah yielding its deepest truths.

*Amar Rav Mesharshiya*: *Doeg ve-Achitofel lo havu savri shma'ata* — they did not truly understand what they were learning. *Masiv Mar Zutra*: but it is written about such a person *ayeh sofer ayeh shokel ayeh sofer et ha-migdalim* — how can you say they didn't know how to learn? *Ela d'lo havu salki shma'ata aliba d'hilchasa* — rather, they could engage with the material but they could not arrive at the *halacha*. And why? *D'chtiv sod Hashem lireiaiv* — because God speaks to those who fear Him. Their learning, being a purely intellectual game and not genuine *avodas Hashem*, could not penetrate to the correct *halachic* conclusion.

### Three Destructive Angels

*Amar Rabbi Ami*: *lo mes Doeg ad she'shachach talmudo* — *Doeg* did not die until he had forgotten his Torah. *Shene'emar hu yamut b'ein musar u've-rov ivalto yishgeh* — he will die without instruction, and in his great foolishness he will err.

*Rav Ashi amar*: he became a *metzora*, a leper. The textual derivation is complex: the word *hatzamta* — you have cut off — is connected via the word *l'tzmisus* in the Torah, which the Targum renders *l'chalutin*, meaning permanent or full-status. And the *Mishnah* teaches: *ein bein musgar u'muchlat ela priah u'frima* — the only difference between a quarantined leper and a full *metzora* is the rending of garments and the growing of hair. The chain of verbal connections is intricate, working toward establishing that *Doeg* attained the status of a full *metzora*.

*Amar Rabbi Yochanan*: *shlosha malachei chavala nizdamnu lo l'Doeg* — three angels of destruction met *Doeg*. *Echad she'shikach talmudo* — one caused him to forget his Torah, consistent with *David*'s petition that *Doeg*'s learning be removed before his death. *V'echad she'saraf nishmato* — one burned his soul. *V'echad she'pizer afro b'vattei khnesiyos u'vattei midrashos* — and one scattered his ashes in synagogues and study halls. In this way, *Doeg* achieves a kind of presence in the *Beit Midrash* — through his ashes — even as he has been denied any living portion in its life and legacy.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 107

## Doeg's Three Judgments

### Doeg's Three Punishments

Rabbi Yochanan teaches: *shlosha malachei chavala nizdamnu lo le'Doeg* — three destructive angels chanced upon Doeg the Edomite. One caused him to forget his Torah learning, one burned his soul, and one scattered his ashes in *batei knesiyot uvavatei midrashot*. The imagery is striking — Doeg, who so thoroughly undermined David's life, ends with his very dust scattered throughout the houses of study and prayer. There is something almost paradoxical in this: the element that was Doeg was not erased from the world but dispersed into its holiest spaces.

### Doeg & Achitofel Apart

Rabbi Yochanan further notes: *Doeg ve'Achitofel lo rau ze et ze* — Doeg and Achitofel never encountered one another. This is fortunate for David, because had these two forces converged simultaneously, he would not have survived. Doeg operated during the lifetime of Saul, while Achitofel appeared later, during David's own reign.

### Half-Lives of Evil Men

Rabbi Yochanan adds that neither Doeg nor Achitofel lived beyond half their years. A *baraita* corroborates this: *anshei damim umirma lo yechetzu yemeihem* — men of bloodshed and deceit will not live out half their days. Doeg lived only thirty-four years; Achitofel only thirty-three.

This teaching is, of course, complicated. We are fully aware that righteous people sometimes die young, and that wicked people sometimes live long lives. The Gemara's intent is worth noting without pressing too hard for a tidy resolution: there is some understanding that righteousness carries with it a blessing of longevity, and its absence is reflected in a shortened life. Let us note it and proceed.

---

## David & Achitofel

### Three Titles Descent

Rabbi Yochanan observes a striking descent in how David refers to Achitofel across three Biblical verses. Initially David called him *rabo* — his teacher and master. Later he called him *chaveiro* — his friend. And still later he called him *talmido* — his student.

The *pasuk* supporting the first: *ata enosh ke'erki alufi umyudai* — you are like my teacher, the one who gives me knowledge. The second title, "friend," emerges from the continuation of that same *pasuk*: *asher yachdav namtik sod beveis elokim nehalech beragesh* — together we share secrets and walk in the house of God. And for the third, "student," the Gemara cites: *gam ish shlomi asher batachti vo ochel lachmi higdil alay akev* — the man of my peace whom I trusted, who ate my bread.

### Betrayal of Trust

The end of that final *pasuk* is telling: *higdil alay akev* — he raised his heel against me. This is the sensitive spot David identifies — Achitofel had such intimate access, such a deep place in David's confidence, that when he betrayed that trust, the wound was uniquely devastating. Of course David had trusted him so completely; otherwise Achitofel's counsel would never have carried such weight in his life.

---

## David's Trial Request

### Temptation Principle

Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: *le'olam al yavi adam atzmo lidei nisayon* — a person should never bring himself to be tested. The proof: David, King of Israel, brought himself to be tested and he failed. This is the lens through which the Gemara examines the entire episode that follows.

It is very common, when approaching the story of David and Bathsheba, to read it with knowing eyes — as though we already understand what happened and why. The effort here will be to resist that reflex and to follow the commentaries in searching for a more nuanced understanding of what the *nisayon* was and where exactly David's *chet* lay. Perfect answers may not be available, but the questions are worth holding.

### Nisayon Etymology

What is this word *nisayon*? One explanation connects it to the Hebrew word *nes* — a flag or banner. A *nisayon* is meant to be something that elevates and displays a person's greatness, not something that causes failure. A teacher does not quiz students on material they do not know; questions are posed so that students can demonstrate what they have mastered, raising their esteem and strengthening the teacher's reputation. The *nisayon* of the Patriarchs — *v'HaElokim nisa es Avraham* — was of this character. It was meant to show their success, not to expose them.

### David's Prayer Question

How did David bring the *nisayon* upon himself? The Gemara relates: David said before God, *mipnei mah omrim Elokei Avraham Elokei Yitzchak v'Elokei Yaakov v'ein omrim Elokei David?* Why does the prayer invoke the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob — but not the God of David?

The *chutzpah* of this request is already a kind of self-endangerment. Some suggest David could foresee that his name would appear somewhere in the *tefillah* — he is associated with *Magen David*, and appears in the *Haftarah* blessings — but the request here is more specific. David wants to be the fourth wheel of that *merkavah*, so to speak: if Abraham is *chesed*, Isaac is *gevurah*, and Jacob is *tiferet*, then *malchus* — the fourth *sefirah* — should be his.

### God's Warning

God responds: the Patriarchs were tested by Me, and you have not yet been tested. David then says: *bachaneni Hashem venaseni* — O God, test me and try me. And the Gemara reports that God agreed — but did something for David that He had not done for the Patriarchs: He told David in advance both that a test was coming and that it would be in the domain of *ervah*, of sexual matters. Every possible forewarning was given.

The human side of us acknowledges that even knowing a test is coming, one can still fail. But when we speak of David HaMelech — the author of *Tehillim*, the founder of our Messianic dynasty — we must recognize that we are not dealing with an ordinary person, and that our reading of what follows must accordingly be more careful.

---

## David & Bathsheba

### Evening Rising

Immediately following, the Gemara cites the *pasuk* from Shmuel: *vayehi le'et ha'erev vayakom David me'al mishkavo vayit'halech al gag beit hamelech vayar isha rochetzet me'al hagag veha'isha tovat mareh me'od* — it was at the time of evening and David rose from his bed and walked upon the roof of the king's house, and he saw a woman bathing from the roof, and the woman was very beautiful.

Several features of this *pasuk* deserve attention if we wish to read it charitably. Why is David rising in the evening? One favorable explanation is that the moment David learned he would be tested in matters of *ervah*, he resolved to invert his schedule entirely — to be awake and moving through the world at the hour when others sleep, deliberately placing himself in a situation of constant disorientation so as to avoid the ordinary circumstances that might lead to temptation.

What is he doing on the roof? He is the king — he could walk in the streets to great acclaim. Yet he chooses the roof, perhaps seeking solitude, perhaps preparing to compose *Tehillim*.

### Forgotten Halakha

Rav Yehuda says that David *hafach mishkavo lailah lemishkavo shel yom* — he switched his sleep schedule, converting the nighttime to his daytime and vice versa. But in doing so, he forgot one *halakha*: *eivar katan yesh ba'adam masbi'o ra'ev umar'ivo savei'a* — there is a small limb in a person: when it is satiated it is hungry, and when it is starved it is satisfied. The Gemara's reference, of course, is to the sexual drive. Rashi, in his second comment on the page, understands that David had relations with his wife as part of this switched schedule — and yet, as the Gemara implies, he had still not fully reckoned with this dimension of human nature.

### Roof Vision
