# Sanhedrin 108

## Yehoshua & Yeishu

### Four Lepers Setup

The daf begins by picking up where the previous discussion left off: the Gemara on 107b, wrapping up the individuals who have no *chelek l'olam haba*, had arrived at the figure of Geichazi. Notably, the Gemara handles Geichazi somewhat differently than the others — rather than engaging in the usual technique of *darshhaning* his name or deriving his exclusion from a *pasuk*, it moves almost immediately into the narrative of how Elisha attempted to bring him to *teshuvah* and he refused. The textual support is comparatively thin, yet the Gemara introduces the principle that animated Geichazi's resistance: *kach mekublani mibeit ava, kol ha-choteh u-machti et ha-rabbim ein maspikin beyado la'asot teshuvah* — one who sins and causes the masses to sin is not given the opportunity to repent. Even if that formulation does not in itself entail the loss of *olam haba*, the Gemara had to explain in what sense Geichazi was *machti et ha-rabbim* — since his episode with Naaman hardly seems to have caused widespread sin — and concluded it was his involvement with Yerovam's golden calves and his keeping students away from Elisha.

Now the Gemara transitions: *v'arba'ah anashim hayu metzoraim petach ha-sha'ar* — the four lepers at the gate of the city. Rabbi Yochanan identifies them as Geichazi and his three sons. This closes the Geichazi episode. And now the Gemara reaches the passage that has been excised from standard printed editions. The expunged text runs in parallel to the Elisha-Geichazi narrative, because the Gemara had already stated: *tanu rabbanan, leolam tehei smol docheh veyamin mekarevet* — one should always push away with the left and draw near with the right — *lo k'Elisha she-dachfo l'Geichazi bishtei yadav*, not like Elisha who pushed Geichazi away with both hands, *velo k'Yehoshua ben Perachia she-dachfo l'Yeishu HaNotzri bishtei yadav*, and not like Yehoshua ben Perachia who pushed away Yeishu HaNotzri with both hands.

### Alexandria Flight

The *Braisa* then asks: *v'Yehoshua ben Perachia mai hi* — what is the story with Yehoshua ben Perachia that parallels the Elisha and Geichazi narrative? *Ki dekatlinu Yannai Malka l'rabbanan* — when King Yannai was killing the rabbis, Yehoshua ben Perachia and Yeishu fled together to Alexandria of Egypt, since according to this tradition Yeishu was his student. When peace was restored, Shimon ben Shatach sent him a message in the poetic form: *mi-Yerushalayim ir ha-kodesh lichi Alexandria shel Mitzrayim, achoti ba'ali sharuy betochech va'ani yoshevet shomem* — from me, Jerusalem the holy city, to you, Alexandria of Egypt, my sister, my husband dwells among you and I sit desolate. The allegorical "husband" is Yehoshua ben Perachia himself, and the message signals that it is safe to return.

### Inn & Appearance

Yehoshua ben Perachia arose and began to travel back. He came to a certain inn, *itrami lei hahu ushpiza*, and they gave him great honor. He remarked, *kamah yafah aksanya zo* — how fine this *aksanya* is — meaning, how wonderful this innkeeper has been, or perhaps how fine the inn itself is. Yeishu, however, took his remark differently: *Rebbi, eineiha terutot* — Rabbi, but her eyes are somewhat slanted. Yehoshua ben Perachia was enraged: *rasha, be-chach ata osek* — wicked one, is this what you are occupied with? I was speaking of the warmth and hospitality we were shown, and you are evaluating her looks? The reaction was severe: he took out 400 *shofarot* and placed Yeishu in *cherem*.

### Excommunication

What follows is the parallel to the Elisha-Geichazi story, and in some respects the reaction here seems even more extreme. Yeishu came before him repeatedly — *ata lekameih kama zimnin* — and each time said, *kablan*, take me back, accept me, I wish to do *teshuvah*. Each time, Yehoshua ben Perachia paid him no attention. Where at least the initial response of Elisha to Geichazi carried some justification, here the *cherem* itself appears to have been a significant overreaction, and now the continued refusal to accept Yeishu back compounds it. This is the very dynamic the Gemara is criticizing: not merely that he pushed away with his left hand, but that he was *docheh bi-shtei yadayim* — pushing away with both hands.

### Final Rejection

One day, Yehoshua ben Perachia was in the middle of reciting *keriat shema* when Yeishu appeared before him again. This time, Yehoshua ben Perachia's heart softened — *savar lekabuleih* — he was prepared finally to accept him back. He signaled with his hand, *achvei lei bideih* — gesturing, apparently, for Yeishu to wait a moment while he finished the *shema*. But Yeishu misread the gesture entirely: *hu savar midadcha dachi lei* — he understood it as yet another rejection, as if to say, get away from me. That was the final straw.

### Brick Worship

Yeishu departed, *azal zakaf levinta ve-hishtachavah lah* — he went and stood up a brick and bowed down to it. When Yehoshua ben Perachia then came after him and urged him to repent, Yeishu replied with the same formulation Geichazi had used: *kach mekublani mimcha, kol ha-choteh u-machti et ha-rabbim ein maspikin beyado la'asot teshuvah*. The Gemara then adds: *keshaf ve-heisit ve-hidiah et Yisrael* — he practiced *kishuf*, he seduced and he led Israel astray. This is the sense in which he was *machti et ha-rabbim*, which the brick incident apparently initiated.

### Kishuf & Context

The term *kishuf* is significant. One approach to all the narratives in the Gospels about miraculous acts — the fish and loaves, the water — is simply to dismiss them as fabrication. But the Gemara here offers a different framework: Yeishu was a practitioner of *kishuf*, of magic, and what appeared to be miraculous was in fact sorcery. This framing does not require calling him an *oved avodah zarah* in the strict sense; it positions him as someone who seduced the people away from the traditional rabbinic path through means that could be categorized as *kishuf*. The *heisit* fits within an *avodah zarah* framework, but need not be limited to it.

There is an obvious historical difficulty: Yannai and Yehoshua ben Perachia predate the figure of Yeishu by roughly a century, so the story as told is historically incoherent. But this need not mean the rabbis were not thinking of Jesus when they told it. The Gemara is not writing history; it is constructing a narrative. The historical framing may serve a literary-theological purpose. Having Yeishu as a student of a great rabbi who traveled to Alexandria grounds the story in recognizable rabbinic experience: the student who was close and went astray, and the Alexandria setting explains where the *kishuf* was learned — Egypt, the ancient home of sorcery. That framework answers the implicit question: where did he acquire the power to mislead people? He was in Alexandria, in the world of Egyptian magic. The detail is not incidental.

It is also worth noting the structural point the Gemara is making. There were in theory four possible modes of relating to a student or disciple who errs: one could draw near with both hands; one could push with the left and draw near with the right — *smol docheh veyamin mekarevet* — which is the ideal; one could push with the right and draw near with the left, a harsher approach but still ultimately welcoming; or one could push away with both hands. Neither Elisha nor Yehoshua ben Perachia managed even the third option. They were *docheh bi-shtei yadayim* in the most complete sense.

---

## Mussar & Balance

### Both Hands Rejection

The Gemara's criticism of both Elisha in the Geichazi episode and Yehoshua ben Perachia in the Yeishu episode is unified under the same rubric: *docheh bi-shtei yadayim*. The ideal is *smol docheh veyamin mekarevet* — pushing away with the left, drawing near with the right — meaning that even when *mussar* must be administered, even when a student's behavior demands a hard response, the ultimate orientation must be toward *kiruv*, toward bringing the person back. Both of these figures failed this standard categorically.

### Left & Right

The *Braisa* now articulates the principle in its positive form: *leolam tehei smol docheh veyamin mekarevet* — always let the left push away and the right draw close. The imaging of left and right is not arbitrary, as noted below, but the primary point is structural: *mussar* and correction belong to the left hand, the minor hand; embrace and closeness belong to the right, the dominant hand. The proportion matters. Even when the left hand must act, the right hand must simultaneously draw near.

### Yetzer & Balance

Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar applies this principle to three domains: the *yetzer*, children, and wives. With respect to the *yetzer* — which in this context refers primarily to sexual desire — the principle of *smol docheh veyamin mekarevet* implies that total suppression is as dangerous as total indulgence. Rashi explains: *ta'avato, im yarchikennah mimenu legamrei, yimna yishuvo shel olam* — if one distances oneself from it entirely, the continuity of the world is foreclosed; *ve-im yekarvenah legamrei, yavo lidei issur she-eino yachol lichbosh yitzro midvar aveira* — and if one indulges it entirely, one will inevitably cross into transgression, since the desire, once fully given its head, becomes uncontrollable. But beyond Rashi's formulation, there is a broader human dimension: if fundamental parts of who we are are denied entirely, they find other outlets, often destructive ones.

Critically, the Gemara frames the ideal as *smol docheh*, not *yamin docheh*. The corrective impulse — the suppressive impulse — belongs to the minor hand. The welcoming, acknowledging, properly channeling impulse belongs to the dominant right. The orientation is ultimately one of integration, not asceticism.

### Children & Wives

The same structure applies to children and wives. Rashi reads the *ishah* here not in a sexual context but in the context of correction: when a husband must rebuke his wife's conduct, or when a parent must discipline a child, the left hand may and sometimes must push away — but the right hand must simultaneously draw near. Push too hard and the child rebels; fail to push at all and the child has no guidance. The Raavad in *Ba'alei HaNefesh* reads the wife passage in the sexual register as well, understanding it as addressing two distinct dimensions: a man's relationship to his own *yetzer* and his responsiveness to his wife's needs — two sides of the same concern about proper channeling rather than suppression.

### Chesed & Din

The symbolism of the right and left hands maps onto a deeper conceptual structure: *yamin* is *chesed*, kindness; *smol* is *din*, judgment. Correction, boundary-setting, and reproof belong to the register of *din*. But *din* must always be held within the larger embrace of *chesed*. There is also a structural insight about what happens when both hands act simultaneously in opposite directions: if one pushes with the left and draws near with the right at the same time, the effect is a reorientation — the person is turned around, given a new perspective, fundamentally redirected. This is the deepest form of *mussar*.

---

## Aging & Illness

### Abraham's Aging

The Gemara now takes a striking turn, reframing three categories of human experience — old age, illness, and recovery from illness — as gifts rather than afflictions, each one instituted at the prayer of a righteous figure.

*Ad Avraham lo hayah ziknah* — until Abraham, no one experienced old age. People died, but they retained the appearance of youth until their final day. The consequence was that Abraham and Isaac looked identical — *kol de-chazi l'Avraham amar Yitzchak, kol de-chazi l'Yitzchak amar Avraham* — anyone who saw one thought he was the other. This created a kind of social confusion: the wisdom and experience of the elder could not be read from his face; society had no visual marker by which to orient its deference. Abraham prayed that *ziknah* should become visible — *d'leihavei lei ziknah* — and the result is recorded in the verse *va-Avraham zaken ba ba-yamim*, which the Gemara identifies as the first instance in the Torah of anyone being described as having grown old. The gift of *ziknah*, the Gemara suggests, allows a society to honor its elders, to recognize their accumulated wisdom, to relate to them differently than to youth. This presupposes, of course, a culture that respects the elderly — and the contrast with contemporary youth-obsessed culture, where the marks of age are to be erased rather than honored, is not lost.

### Jacob's Illness

*Ad Yaakov lo hayah chulsha* — until Jacob, no one became ill. Death arrived without warning and without preparation; people simply expired when their time came. Jacob prayed that illness should precede death — *ba'ei rachamei ve-havah chulsha* — and the result is recorded in the verse *va-yomar l'Yosef, hinei avicha choleh*. Rashi explains the gift: illness gives time to prepare. The person who is dying can gather his family, offer *berakhot*, complete unfinished emotional and spiritual business. The family has time to transition. There is no sudden void. Jacob, who himself gave *berakhot* to his sons on his deathbed, exemplifies exactly what this gift makes possible: the deliberate, conscious passage out of the world, with the people one loves gathered close.

The Gemara notes that in prior generations there were *berakhot* given — Abraham blessed Isaac, Isaac blessed Jacob — but not from a deathbed, not in the context of final parting. They just happened to give *berakhot* at some point. The gift of *chulsha* creates the context in which the final blessing becomes a true *vidui*, a true leave-taking.

### Elisha's Recovery

*Adei Elisha lo hava inish chalish d'mitpach* — before Elisha, no one had ever fallen ill and recovered. Sickness was invariably terminal; it was simply the process of dying, manifesting physically. Elisha prayed, and the possibility of illness followed by recovery was introduced into the world. The proof-text is the verse describing Elisha's own death: *v'Elisha chala et chalyo asher yamut bo* — implying that this final illness was the one by which he would die, meaning he had previously been ill and had *not* died. The gift here is twofold: it gives individuals the opportunity to survive and do *teshuvah*, and it gives God, so to speak, the instrument of *yissurin* — suffering as a wake-up call, as a minor punishment that redirects before the final reckoning arrives. The stories in Tanakh of people who fall ill, pray, and recover now make sense within this framework: illness as divine intervention that opens a door rather than closes one.

---

## Dor HaMabul

### No Judgment

The Gemara arrives at the next *Mishnah*, which continues the enumeration of those who have no *chelek l'olam haba*, now moving from individuals to entire groups. The *Mishnah* also introduces a distinction that runs throughout the subsequent discussion: the difference between having no *chelek l'olam haba* and not even being *omed b'din* — not even being resurrected to stand in judgment.

The general eschatological framework the Gemara operates with is roughly as follows: *Mashiach* will come, *techiyat ha-meitim* will occur, everyone will be resurrected, and on the day of judgment the righteous will receive *olam haba* while the *resha'im* will return to *Gehinnom*. *Ein lo chelek l'olam haba* presumably means one is resurrected but at the judgment is not retained — one does not remain for *olam haba*. But there are categories of sinners who do not even reach resurrection — they are not *omed b'din* at all — and this is treated as a worse punishment still, as though one's case is too contemptible even to receive a hearing.

*Dor HaMabul ein lahem chelek l'olam haba* — the generation of the Flood has no portion in the world to come. The proof-text is *lo yadon ruchi ba-adam l'olam* — My spirit will not contend with man forever. *Lo din* — no judgment; *velo ruach* — no spirit. They are not even resurrected. Why is not being judged worse than being judged and condemned? One reflection: at least a judgment means that one's life was worth adjudicating, that something was at stake, that the case warranted hearing. To be dismissed without a hearing is to be told that one's existence does not rise even to the level of a meaningful *din*.

### Dor HaPlagah

*Dor HaPlagah ein lahem chelek l'olam haba* — the generation of the dispersion, the builders of the Tower of Babel, also have no *chelek l'olam haba*. The proof-text is *va-yafetz Hashem otam mi-sham al pnei kol ha-aretz* — God scattered them — read as: *va-yafetz* in this world; *u-mi-sham hefitzam* for the world to come. Crucially, however, the *Mishnah* does not say that *Dor HaPlagah* is not *omed b'din*. They are scattered — they lose *olam haba* — but they apparently do stand in judgment. What precisely their sin was, and why God viewed it so severely, is not fully transparent from the narrative.

### Disputes on Groups

*Anshei Sedom ein lahem chelek l'olam haba*, and they stand for *din*. The proof-text is *v'anshei Sedom ra'im v'chatta'im la-Hashem me'od* — *ra'im ba-olam hazeh, v'chatta'im l'olam haba*. They do, however, stand in judgment.

Rabbi Nechemiah disagrees: both *Dor HaPlagah* and *Anshei Sedom* are not *omed b'din*. His proof-text is *al ken lo yakumu resha'im ba-mishpat, v'chatta'im ba-adat tzaddikim* — the *resha'im* will not stand in judgment; the *chatta'im* will not stand in the congregation of the righteous. He reads *resha'im* as *Dor HaMabul* and *chatta'im* as *Anshei Sedom*, and he argues that the second clause does not simply restrict where they stand but removes them from *din* entirely.

The *Tannaim* respond to Rabbi Nechemiah: *einam omdim ba-adat tzaddikim* — they do not stand *with the righteous*, but that does not mean they receive no judgment at all. The *chatta'im* stand in judgment; they simply stand *ba-adat resha'im*, among the wicked. They will be judged, and they will be found guilty. The distinction between *resha'im* and *chatta'im* maps neatly onto the language of the Sedom verse itself: *ra'im v'chatta'im*, where the more severe term *ra'im* might correspond to those who get no hearing, and *chatta'im* to those who do.

### Meraglim & Midbar

The *Mishnah* includes a line about the *Meraglim* — the spies: *ein lahem chelek l'olam haba*, derived from *vayamutu ha-anashim motzei dibat ha-aretz ra'ah ba-magefah lifnei Hashem* — *vayamutu ba-olam hazeh, ba-magefah l'olam haba*. This line is, however, textually redundant and rendered moot by the following statement: *Dor HaMidbar ein lahem chelek l'olam haba, v'einam omdim b'din* — the entire generation that lived through the forty years in the wilderness has no *chelek l'olam haba* and does not even stand in judgment. Since the *Meraglim* were part of *Dor HaMidbar*, the broader category absorbs the narrower one, which is why the *Meraglim* line was excised.

This ruling about *Dor HaMidbar* is genuinely difficult. In *Chazal*'s eyes, *Dor HaMidbar* is often described as a generation of exceptional righteousness — they received the Torah, they witnessed the *Shekhinah*. And even setting aside their virtues, the nature of their sins does not obviously warrant the most severe eschatological punishment. Perhaps the reasoning relates to the collective, consequential nature of their sin: the rejection of the Land of Israel, the foreclosure of the national destiny for an entire generation. Whatever the explanation, the proof-text — *ba-midbar hazeh yitamu v'sham yamutu* — does not transparently convey *einam omdim b'din*; it seems to speak to *ein lahem chelek l'olam haba* at most.

### R. Eliezer View

Rabbi Akiva holds the severe position on *Dor HaMidbar*. Rabbi Eliezer fundamentally disagrees: *alehem hu omer, isfu li chasidai, kortei vriti alei zavach* — it is about them that the verse says, gather for Me My pious ones, who made My covenant over sacrifice. Far from having no *chelek l'olam haba*, *Dor HaMidbar* in Rabbi Eliezer's view are the *chasidim* who will be gathered to God. Rabbi Eliezer likely held that it was specifically the *Meraglim* who forfeited their *chelek l'olam haba*, while the broader *Dor HaMidbar* does not.

The *Adat Korach* presents a unique case: they are still alive, buried in the netherworld, and the question is not resurrection but return. *Einah atidah la'alot* — they are not destined to ascend. Rabbi Akiva: *va-tichas aleihem ha-aretz ba-olam hazeh, va-yovdu mitoch ha-kahal l'olam haba*. Rabbi Eliezer, consistent with his broader view, says: *Hashem memit u-mechayeh, morid she'ol vaya'al* — God brings them down and God will bring them up. Rabbi Eliezer likely maintained that the *Meraglim* lose their *chelek l'olam haba*, *Adat Korach* will eventually ascend, and *Dor HaMidbar* overall will be among the *chasidei* gathered to God. Rabbi Akiva denies all of them.

---

## Flood Disputes

### Akiva & Beteira

A *Braisa* now records the views of additional *Tannaim* on *Dor HaMabul*. Rabbi Akiva's position is: *vayimach et kol ha-yekum asher al pnei ha-adamah* — God wiped out everything that stood, *ba-olam hazeh*; *vayimachu min ha-aretz*, wiped out, *l'olam haba*. They are erased from both worlds.

Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira sharpens the formulation: *lo chayim v'lo nidonim* — they neither live (in the resurrection) nor are they judged. His proof-text is the same verse already cited in the *Mishnah*: *lo yadon ruchi ba-adam l'olam, lo din v'lo ruach*. He adds a second reading: *she-lo tehei nishmasam chozeret le-nadana* — their *neshamah* does not return to its sheath. The *ruach* will not return to its vessel; they are not resurrected, and there is no day of judgment for them.

### Menachem's View

Rabbi Menachem bar Rabbi Yose goes further still, raising a difficulty: at the time of *techiyat ha-meitim*, when God restores souls to dead bodies, what happens to *Dor HaMabul*? He resolves it as follows: *nishmasam kashah lahem be-Gehinnom* — even at the moment of resurrection, their soul continues to suffer in *Gehinnom*. The precise mechanism is difficult to parse. One reading is that they are not resurrected in this world at all; rather, the restoration of their soul does not bring them back to the surface but intensifies their suffering wherever they remain below, in *Gehinnom*. Another reading is that they are somehow simultaneously present in the resurrection and still suffering — a kind of dual state, reminiscent of a Horcrux in its structural strangeness.

The proof-text Rabbi Menachem cites is *taharoo chashash, teildoo kash, ruchachem esh tochalechem* — you shall conceive of chaff and give birth to straw; your spirit, a fire will consume you. The image of chaff and straw, materials that ignite easily and burn to nothing, evokes a soul that is present only to be destroyed by fire — there is nothing substantial to resurrect, or whatever is resurrected is immediately consumed.

---

## Causes of Sin

### Wealth & Pride

The Gemara now examines the root causes of *Dor HaMabul*'s sin, offering two competing explanations. The first is attributed to Rabbi Yochanan: *Dor HaMabul lo nitga'u ela bi-shvil tovah she-hishpia lahem HaKadosh Baruch Hu* — their arrogance arose solely from the overflowing goodness God had showered upon them. The Gemara then brings a series of verses from *Iyov* to illustrate the extraordinary comfort of their lives. *Bateihem shalom mi-pachad, v'lo shevet Eloha aleihem* — their homes were free of fear, they never felt the rod of divine suffering. *Shoro avar v'lo yag'il, taplet parato v'lo tishakeil* — their oxen went and did not miscarry its seed; their cow gave birth without miscarriage. *Yishalchu khi-tzon avileihem, v'yaldeihem yerakedun* — they sent their children out like a flock, and their children danced. *Yis'u b'tof v'khinor* — they carried drums and harps. *Yivlu yemeihem b'tov, u-shnoteihem bi-ne'imim* — their days were spent in goodness, their years in pleasantness. And then, suddenly: *u-ve-rega she'ol yeichatu* — in a moment they descended to the depths.

### Mocking God

The abundance led to a complete rejection of divine need. *Va-yomru la-El, sur mimenu, v'da'at derachecha lo chafatznu* — they said to God: leave us, we have no desire to know Your ways. *Mah Shaddai ki na'avdenu, u-mah no'il ki nifga bo* — who is God that we should serve Him, what benefit do we gain from entreating Him? And when pushed further, they specified: *klum tzrichin anu lo ela le-tipah shel geshamim* — what do we even need from God? Only a drop of rain. And even for that, *yesh lanu neharot u-ma'ayanot she-anu mistafkim bahem* — we have rivers and wellsprings enough for ourselves. Who needs rain?

### Divine Judgment

God's response: *ba-tovah she-hishpati lahem ba hikh'isuni* — the very goodness I poured out to them is what they used to anger Me, to throw in My face. And you want to talk about water? *Bah ani dan otam* — by that same water I will judge them. *V'ani hineni meivi et ha-mabul mayim.*

### Eye & Lust

Rabbi Yosi offers a different etiology: *Dor HaMabul lo nitga'u ela bi-shvil galgal ha-ayin* — their downfall came not from their wealth but from the lust of the eye. This picks up a theme that traces back to the very first sin: one sees, one desires, one takes. The verse cited is *va-yikchu lahem nashim mi-kol asher bacharu* — they took for themselves women from whoever they chose. The *galgal ha-ayin* — the wheel of the eye, the aperture — is what drove the desire and ultimately the taking.

### Creation & Taking

*U-lefichach danam ba-mayim* — therefore God judged them with water, *she-domeh le-galgal ha-ayin* — which resembles the eye. The connection is linguistic and visual: *ma'ayan* shares its root with *ayin*; both describe an aperture, an opening from which something flows. The punishment mirrors the sin in its physical form. *Nivke'u kol ma'ayanot tehom rabbah* — all the wellsprings of the great deep burst forth. *V'aruvot ha-shamayim niftachu* — and the windows of heaven were opened. Eye — aperture — water: the imagery is woven through the judgment.

The contemporary resonance is unmistakable. Powerful men who believe they may take whatever they desire, who see women as objects available to them, enact the very pattern the Gemara is describing: *ra'u, va-yit'avvu, va-yikahu* — they saw, they desired, they took.

### Rabba Echo

Rabbi Yochanan draws attention to a verbal echo running through the narrative: *Dor HaMabul be-rabbah kilkelu u-ve-rabbah nidonu* — they corrupted with *rabbah* and were judged with *rabbah*. The word appears first in the account of their sin — *va-yar Hashem ki rabbah ra'at ha-adam* — and then in the account of their judgment — *kol ma'ayanot tehom rabbah*. The verbal correspondence between sin and punishment is deliberate and structural.

### Hot Springs

Rabbi Yochanan adds a topographical note: *shloshah nish'tayru mehem* — three of those primordial hot springs of the *mabul* still exist in the world. *Belu'a de-Gader, Chamei Teverya, ve-Einah Rabbati de-Biram* — the springs at Gader, the famous hot springs of Tiberias, and the great spring of Biram. These remnants of the flood's waters endure as a physical trace of that judgment.

---

## Flesh Corruption

### Mixed Species

*Ki hish-hit kol basar et darko al ha-aretz* — all flesh had corrupted its way upon the land. Rabbi Yochanan reads this as: *she-hirbi'u behemah al hayah ve-hayah al behemah* — they caused animals to crossbreed with other animals, crossing not merely different species but categories — domesticated with wild, *behemah* with *hayah* — *ve-ha-kol al adam ve-adam al ha-kol* — and humans with all of these. The word *basar* — flesh — signals the sin of the flesh; *hish-hit*, corruption, describes what the crossing of these natural boundaries represented.

### Animal Exception

Rabbi Abba bar Kahana observes that after the *mabul*, the animals returned to mating only within their own *min* — *ve-khullam hazaru* — all of them went back to their kind, except for one bird called *tushlami*, known for its promiscuity, which continued its prior behavior. All others returned to the natural order that had been violated.

### Power of Theft

*Va-yomer Elohim le-Noach, ketz kol basar ba le-fanai*. Rabbi Yochanan comments: *bo u-re'eh kammah gadol koha shel hamas* — come and see how great is the power of *hamas*, of theft and violence. They had committed every variety of sin — the sexual perversions we have described, the arrogance, the mocking of God — *ve-lo nichtam aleihem gezar dinam ad she-pash'tu yedeihem be-gezel* — yet the decree of their judgment was not sealed until they extended their hands into outright theft. Theft is, in a sense, the culmination of the pattern: you see, you desire, you simply take what belongs to another. *She-ne'emar ki male'ah ha-aretz hamas mi-peneihem ve-hinneni mash-hitam et ha-aretz* — the earth was filled with *hamas* from before them, and I will destroy them with the earth.

### Hamas Testifies

*Ve-khtiv ha-hamas kam le-matteh rasha* — and *hamas* rises as a rod for the wicked. Rabbi Elazar reads this striking verse as follows: the *hamas* literally stood up like a rod, *ve-ha-hamas amad lifnei HaKadosh Baruch Hu, ve-amar lefanav, Ribbono shel Olam, lo me-hem* — *hamas* itself stood before God and said: Master of the Universe, I can no longer be among them. Even the *hamas* got fed up. Even theft reached a point where it testified against the generation. And God responded in kind: *lo me-hem, ve-lo me-hamonam, ve-lo me-hemahem, ve-lo noah ba-hem*.

### Noah's Favor

That final phrase, *ve-lo noah ba-hem*, introduces the figure of Noah — a pun on his name. *Ve-af al Noach nichtam gezar din* — even Noah had the decree of judgment sealed against him. The proof-text is read by *tana de-vei Rabbi Yishmael*: even Noah was included in that verdict. The reason he was saved was not that he was objectively innocent of the decree — *ella she-matza hen be-einei Hashem* — but that he found unearned favor in God's eyes. The *chen* was not a function of his strict desert; it was something else, something of grace.

The verse *va-yinnahem Hashem ki asah et ha-adam ba-aretz* is then read in two ways by *ika de-amrei*: one, God was consoled by the fact that He had arranged for burial in the earth — *yafeh asiti she-hitkaneti lahem kevarot ba-aretz*, I did well in establishing for them graves in the ground; or two, *lo yafeh asiti* — I did not do well, I regret having made graves for them in the earth. Rashi reads both interpretations not as being literally about burial but as metaphors for whether God was comforted or regretful about the destruction of humanity — either finding consolation in the ending of the wicked generation, or regretting that He had brought that destruction at all, wishing He had given them yet another chance.

---

## Noah Debate

### Yochanan View

The Torah describes Noah as *ish tzaddik tamim hayah be-dorotav* — in his generations. Rabbi Yochanan focuses on that qualifier: *be-dorotav* — for his generation, but not compared to other generations. The implication is that Noah's righteousness was relative; measured against the extraordinary evil of his surroundings he looked righteous, but against a generation of actual *tzaddikim* he would not have stood out.

### Lakish View

Resh Lakish reads the same word in the opposite direction: *be-dorotav, kol she-ken be-dorot acherim* — if he could be a *tzaddik* in that generation, how much more so in others. His ability to resist the overwhelming evil of his environment is evidence of a powerful inner core; had he lived in a more righteous world, that core would have been nurtured to still greater heights.

### Wine Mashal

Rav Chanina illustrates Rabbi Yochanan's view with a *mashal*: a barrel of wine placed in a cellar full of vinegar — *be-mikomo reicho nodef*, in its place the wine's fragrance is noticeable and striking, because it rises above the pervasive smell of vinegar. *Shelo be-mikomo ein reicho nodef* — not in its place, in a cellar of other fine wines, it would be unremarkable. The imagery is carefully chosen: everyone agrees that Noah resisted the vinegar of his generation. But Rabbi Yochanan's point is that the resistance itself does not establish absolute greatness. The wine is still only wine; surrounded by vinegar it seems remarkable, but placed among other fine wines it is merely ordinary. There is also a darker implication: prolonged exposure to vinegar accelerates the wine's own turning; Noah's sustained immersion in his generation's evil was not without cost.

### Perfume Mashal

Rabbi Oshaya offers the counter-*mashal* for Resh Lakish's view: a small flask of *palyaton* perfume placed in a filthy, malodorous place. *Be-mikomo reicho nodef* — in that smelly setting, the perfume's fragrance is noticeable; it cuts through the stench. *Kol she-ken be-mekom ha-besamim* — how much more would its true fragrance emerge in a setting of spices and other fine aromas. Here the emphasis falls differently: because of the overpowering bad smell surrounding the perfume, the full power of the scent cannot be appreciated. You smell it, but you do not smell it at its potential best. In a setting of other beautiful fragrances, the full range of its quality would emerge. A personal note has been offered on Resh Lakish's framing — that someone who himself came from a difficult background, as Resh Lakish did, might be particularly attuned to what it means to be good in a bad environment, and to the question of what he might have become had his upbringing been different.

---

## Flood Narrative

### Animals Mashal

*Va-yimach et kol ha-yekum asher al pnei ha-adamah* — the question is raised: *im adam chata, behemah mah chat'ah* — if the humans sinned, what did the animals sin? The answer is given in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Karcha through a *mashal*: a man who prepared a wedding feast for his son, arranging every variety of delicacy, and then his son died before the wedding. He arose and scattered all the food, tore down the wedding canopy. *Amar: klum asiti ela bi-shvil beni, akhshav she-meit, chuppah lamah li?* — I made all of this for my son's sake; now that he is dead, what do I need the wedding feast for? So too, *Hakadosh Baruch Hu* said: I created domesticated animals and wild animals only for the sake of human beings. If I am going to destroy human beings, I have no need for any of it. *Akhshav she-adam choteh, behemah ve-hayah lamah li?*

### Fish Spared

*Mi-kol asher be-charavah meitu* — everything on the dry land died, *velo dagim she-ba-yam* — but not the fish of the sea. The fish were spared because they did not participate in the unnatural reproduction that characterized the generation's sin. Fish reproduce through external spawning rather than direct copulation, and so the charge of *hish-hit kol basar et darko* did not apply to them.

### Noah Warns

*Darash Rabbi Yosi de-min Keisari*: the verse *kal hu al pnei mayim, tukulal chelkatam ba-aretz* is read to teach that Noah the righteous was warning the generation and telling them: *asu teshuvah, asu teshuvah* — repent, repent — *ve-im lav, HaKadosh Baruch Hu mevi aleikhem et ha-mabul, u-makfeh nivlatchem al ha-mayim ki-zikin* — and if not, God will bring the flood and your corpses will float on the water like flasks, as it says *kalu al pnei ha-mayim*. Moreover, *kol ba'ei olam* will use you as a curse for all future generations: *tekulal chelkatam ba-aretz* — your portion will be a curse upon the earth.

Rava then *darshens*: *lapid buz le-ash-tut sha'anan, nachon le-mo'adei ragel* — a torch of contempt for those at ease, ready for the appointed time of the heel. The *Gemara* teaches that Noah would rebuke them with words as sharp as torches, *devarim she-hem kashim ke-lapidim*, and they would respond with contempt, *buz*. *Amru lo: pachach!* — they mocked him as a fool. *Zaken, teivah zu lama?* — hey, old man, what are you building this box for? He told them: God will bring the flood. *Mabul shel mah?* — what kind of flood?

### Mocking Response

The population had an answer ready for every scenario. If it is a flood of fire — *yesh lanu davar, ve-alita shemo* — we have something called *alita* that protects against fire. If it is a flood of water rising from the earth — *yesh lanu ashashiyot shel barzel she-anu mechafim bahem et ha-aretz* — we have iron plates with which we will cover the ground and stop the water from rising. And if it is rain from the heavens — *yesh lanu davar, ve-akash shemo* — we have something called *akash* that will serve as a dome of protection. They had engineered a response to every possible mode of flood.

### Between Heels

God's response to all their preparations: *hu mevi mi-bein ikvei ragleikhem* — He can bring it from between your very heels. *Nachon le-mo'adei ragel* — ready at the appointed time of the heel. The *akev*, the heel, is also used as a metaphor for the genital area, which leads directly into the next passage about the nature of the flood waters.

---

## Flood Waters

### Hot Waters

A *Braisa* states: *mei ha-mabul kashim ke-shichvat zera* — the waters of the flood were as hot and dense as semen. The proof-text is *nachon le-mo'adei ragel*. This is a striking statement that connects the mode of judgment directly to the mode of sin: a generation that sinned sexually is judged by waters that carry the character of sexual fluids.

### Rotchin Measure

Rav Chisda articulates the principle of measure for measure: *be-rotchin kilkelu, be-rotchin nidunu* — they sinned with hot liquid and were judged with hot liquid. Semen as a hot liquid used for procreation — the very gift of creation — was perverted through the sexual sins of the generation, and the waters of judgment came in the same mode. It is important to note that the Gemara here is describing the sin of perverted procreation — crossbreeding with animals, the corruption of *kol basar* — rather than the sin of *shichvas zera levatala*. The later poskim who invoke this passage in the context of masturbation are drawing on it in a secondary application; the Gemara's own context concerns something different.

### Verbal Echo

A final verbal correspondence: *khtiv hacha, va-yashoku ha-mayim* — and the waters abated; *khtiv hatam, ve-chamat ha-melekh shakhakhah* — and the king's anger abated. The word *shakhakh* connects the subsiding of the flood to the subsiding of divine wrath, a verbal echo that runs through the narrative of judgment and its conclusion.

---

## Seven Days

### Metushelach Mourning

*Va-yehi li-shvat ha-yamim u-mei ha-mabul hayu al ha-aretz* — and after seven days, the waters of the flood were upon the earth. Why did God wait seven days from the decree to the execution? Rav offers the first explanation: *eilu yemei evlo shel Metushelach* — these were the days of mourning for Metushelach. The chronology of the Torah confirms that Metushelach died precisely in the year of the flood. The Gemara understands that God delayed the *mabul* to allow the mourning period for Metushelach to be observed — *le-lamedcha she-hespadan shel tzaddikim me'akvin et ha-pur'anut lavo* — to teach you that eulogizing the righteous holds back the arrival of punishment. Even when the decree has been sealed, the honor due to a *tzaddik* creates a pause in the execution of divine judgment.

### Creation Reversal

*Davar acher*: the seven days reverse and echo the seven days of creation. The *Noach* narrative is structured as an anti-creation story: where creation separates the waters from the dry land, the flood re-merges them; where creation establishes categories and boundaries, the flood dissolves them. The seven days of waiting are a mirror image of the seven days of creation — *she-shinah lahem HaKadosh Baruch Hu sidrei Bereishit* — God reversed the order of creation. When Noah and his family emerge from the *teivah*, God says *peru u-revu*, echoing the blessing of creation; the flood is the undoing and the renewed creation alike.

### 120 to 7

*Davar acher*: *she-kava lahem HaKadosh Baruch Hu zman gadol ve-achar kach zman katan* — God had given them a long deadline and then a short one. The 120 years of Noah's building the *teivah* constituted the long grace period. When that expired, God gave them seven more days — a shorter, final window. There is a certain psychological truth here: the long deadline recedes into abstraction, while the short, urgent one focuses the mind. A week to do *teshuvah* — that is pressing. That is something one might actually act upon.

### Taste of Olam HaBa

*Davar acher*: *she-hit'imam me'ein olam haba* — God gave them a taste of *olam haba*. The seven days, associated with *Shabbat*, offer a foretaste of the world to come. They were given this experience *kedei she-yedu mah tovah manu mei-hem* — so that they should know what goodness they had withheld from themselves through their sins. The extraordinary abundance they had experienced in their earthly lives, and used to reject God, was now given a final, spiritual dimension — a glimpse of what could have been theirs — before the flood came.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 109

## Dor HaMabul & Ark

### Husband & Wife

The Gemara opens on 108b with a striking question about the *pasuk* describing the animals that entered the ark: *mi-kol ha-behemah ha-tehorah tikach lekha shiv'ah shiv'ah ish ve-ishto* — "of every clean animal you shall take seven and seven, a man and his wife." The question is obvious and almost comic: *ish ve-ishto le-behemah mi itei?* — since when do animals have marriages? The answer given by Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan is that the phrase does not mean they were actually married in any formal sense, but rather that the animals taken were those that had maintained a kind of fidelity — *me-otam she-lo ne-evdah bahem averah*, those upon whom no *averah* of interspecies copulation had been committed.

### Gate Test

This immediately raises the question: *mi-na yada* — how was Noach supposed to know which animals qualified? Rav Chisda answers that Noach passed the animals before the *tevah*: *she-he-eviru lifnei ha-tevah*. Any animal that the *tevah* admitted — *kol she-hatevah koletato* — was thereby known to have been faithful, while any animal the *tevah* rejected was known to have sinned. It is not entirely clear from the Gemara's language whether this involved some kind of magnetic or divine pull, but the principle is that the ark itself served as the mechanism of selection.

### Animals Volition

Rabbi Abahu offers an alternative: *me-otam ha-ba-im me-eleihen* — the animals simply came of their own accord. This reading draws on the *pasuk* that says the animals *came to* Noach, using the active voice, implying that God arranged for them to present themselves rather than Noach having to select them.

### Ark Wood Type

The *pasuk* instructs Noach to make the ark from *atzei gofer*. The Gemara asks: *mai gofer* — what is this wood? Rav Adda citing the school of Rabbi Shila says it refers to a type called *mavliga*; others say it is called *gulmish*. Both are understood to belong to the cedar family.

### Tzohar Light

The *pasuk* instructs: *tzohar ta'aseh la-tevah* — make a *tzohar* for the ark. Rabbi Yochanan explains that God told Noach to set in it precious stones and gems — *avanim tovot u-margaliyot* — so that they would illuminate the interior like the midday sun: *kedei she-yihyu me'irot lakhem ke-tzohorayim*. As Rashi notes, there are two interpretations of *tzohar*: some understand it as a window, others as a luminous jewel. The Gemara here follows the jewel interpretation, with the sunlight presumably refracting off the stones to spread light throughout the ark's interior.

### Ark Design

The *pasuk* continues: *ve-el amah tekhalenah milma'lah* — bring it to a cubit at the top. The Gemara explains: *de-be-hachi hu de-kaima* — that is simply good engineering. A tapered, angled roof that comes to a peak at the top distributes structural pressure in a way that makes the vessel more durable. The principle is not unlike the architectural logic of an arch or a dam built at an angle, where the incoming force actually strengthens the structure rather than breaking it.

### Three Levels

The verse also mandates three levels: *tachtiyim sheniyim u-shelishiyim ta'aseha*. A *tanna* teaches: *tachtiyim le-zevel* — the lowest level was designated for dung and excrement; *emtza'iyim le-behemah* — the middle level for the animals; *ve-elyonim le-adam* — and the upper level for the people. While this allots a great deal of space to the human inhabitants, the tapered design of the roof may account for the narrowing of that level.

### Raven Argument

The Gemara takes up the episode of the raven. Resh Lakish observes: *teshuvah nitzachit heshiv orev le-Noach* — the raven delivered to Noach a *teshuvah nitzachit*, an argument so compelling it could not be refuted. This is the same concept encountered earlier in the Gemara, where an argument is called *nitzachit* not necessarily because it is correct, but because no response can be mounted against it.

The raven's argument was as follows: *rabkha soneini ve-atah snatani* — your Master hates me, and you hate me. God took seven pairs of the clean animals and only two of the unclean, and now you are sending me — one of only two ravens in the world — on this mission. *Im pogea bi sar chama o sar tzina* — if the angel of heat or cold encounters me, *lo nimtza olam chasar briyah achat* — the world will be left lacking an entire species. Why not send from a species with seven, where the loss of one would still leave six? The raven then adds, somewhat absurdly: *o shema le-ishti atah tzarikh* — or perhaps you have designs on my wife?

### No Intercourse

Noach responds to the last point, calling the raven *rasha* — wicked. *B'mutar lach ne'esar* — even what is permitted to me, namely my own wife, is forbidden to me on the ark. *U'v'ne'esar li lo kol shekein* — certainly an animal, of the very type of transgression that brought about the destruction of the world through interspecies mixing, is unthinkable. Noach answers the silly point while leaving the stronger argument technically unanswered — a feature the Gemara implicitly acknowledges.

The Gemara then asks: *u'mei'heichan ne'asru* — from where do we derive that intercourse was forbidden on the ark? The answer comes from a careful reading of two *pesukim*. When they entered the ark, the verse lists them in the order: *atah u'vanecha v'ishtecha u'nshei vanecha itacha* — you, your sons, your wife, and your sons' wives — men and women listed separately. But when they left, the verse reverses the pairings: *atah v'ishtecha u'vanecha u'nshei vanecha* — you and your wife, your sons and their wives — couples reunited. Rabbi Yochanan derives from this conspicuous structural difference that *neasru b'tashmish hamitah* — they were forbidden conjugal relations during the entire time on the ark.

### Three Violators

A *baraita* teaches: *shlosha shimshu b'teivah* — three violated this prohibition on the ark, *ve-chulam laku* — and all three were punished. These three were: the dog, the raven, and Ham.

*Kelev nikshar* — the dog is now leashed, tied up, as its punishment. *Oreiv rak* — the raven spits; Rashi explains that this refers to the raven's mode of reproduction, though this explanation is difficult to understand as a punishment. *Ve-Cham laka b'oro* — Ham was smitten in his skin. Rashi identifies this as the origin of the dark-skinned descendants of Ham, specifically *sheyatza mimenu Kush*, the Ethiopians. While never made explicit in the *pasuk* itself, this has been a long-held reading within rabbinic tradition, though it carries the obvious difficulty that the Gemara uses the word *laka* — implying something negative — while any sensitivity to the topic requires care. One might also note that this provides a possible retrospective explanation for why Noach sent the raven first: having violated the prohibition, perhaps it was sent out of the ark as a form of consequence.

### Dove's Preference

The Gemara turns to the dove. Rabbi Yirmiyahu notes that the verse says *vayishlach et ha-yonah me'ito* — he sent the dove *from with him* — and derives from the word *me'ito* that *diratan shel ofot tehorim im ha-tzadikim* — the kosher birds prefer to dwell together with the righteous.

The verse then reports that the dove returned with *aleih zayit taraf b'fiha* — an olive leaf torn in its mouth. Rabbi Elazar expounds: the dove said before God: *Ribono Shel Olam, yihyu mezonosai merurin k'zayit umasurin b'yadcha* — let my food be as bitter as an olive but dependent upon You, *v'al yihyu metukin k'dvash umasurin b'yad basar v'dam* — rather than sweet as honey but dependent on human beings. The dove preferred the hardship of foraging freely under divine providence over the comfort of domestication and reliance on people. The words *taraf* meaning food and *b'fiha* meaning "in its mouth" are thus read as the dove's spoken declaration. The proof that *taraf* means food comes from the verse *hatrifeni lechem chuki* — provide me with the bread of my portion.

### Dove Metaphor

This *drasha* is best understood not merely as a general lesson about self-reliance, but as a metaphor for the Jewish people. The dove represents Israel: even when our sustenance in this world is bitter as an olive, we prefer a direct dependence on God to the easier path of dependence on foreign powers. That interpretation gives the entire passage its depth and purpose — the dove's declaration is Israel's declaration about its own condition in exile.

### Animals' Families

The Gemara notes that the verse states *le-mishpechoseihem yatze'u min ha-teivah* — they came out by their families. Rabbi Yochanan comments: *bi-mishpechosam ve-lo hem* — by their families but not themselves. The *Maharsha* acknowledges that no one is entirely certain how to parse this teaching. One possibility is that the verse emphasizes they emerged in family groupings rather than individually, but the precise import of the contrast remains unclear.

## Life on Ark

### Eliezer Questions

Rav Chana bar Bizna reports that Eliezer, the servant of Avraham, posed a question to Shem the elder — *Shem rabba* — invoking the verse *le-mishpechoseihem yatze'u min ha-teivah* as a springboard: *atun heichi avisun* — what was it like for you on the ark?

### Feeding Schedule

Shem replied: *tzar gadol haya lanu ba-teivah* — the hardship we endured on the ark was immense. Every creature had to be fed according to its natural cycle: *birya she-darkah le-ha'achilah ba-yom he'echelanu ba-yom, she-darkah le-ha'achilah ba-laylah he'echelanu ba-laylah* — daytime animals were fed by day, nighttime animals by night. The care was round the clock and without respite.

### Chameleon Diet

There was a particular difficulty: *hai ziksa lo hava yada abba mai achal* — father did not know what the chameleon ate. One day Noach was sitting and splitting open pomegranates — *hava yaseiv ve-pali rimona* — and a worm fell out of the pomegranate, which the chameleon promptly ate. From that point on, *hava gaval lei chizra* — he would knead or prepare for it some kind of porridge or mixture, and when it became wormy the chameleon would eat it.

### Lion's Fever

The lion presented a different challenge: how does one feed a lion on an ark full of the very animals one is trying to preserve? The answer was providential: *ishata zinsei* — God afflicted the lion with a fever for the duration of the voyage, so that it had no appetite for food. As Rav teaches: no less than six and no more than twelve months will a fever sustain and nourish — presumably meaning that the fever sustained the lion for the full twelve months of their time on the ark.

### Phoenix

There was also a creature called *orchina* — understood to be a phoenix or a bird of extraordinary longevity. Shem recounts that Noach found it resting quietly in one of the ark's compartments and asked: *lo ba'at me-zoney* — don't you need food? The bird replied: *chazisach de-hava trida* — I saw how busy you were with all the other animals, *amina lo atzrachach* — so I thought, I will not burden you. Noach blessed it: *yehei ra'ava de-lo samus* — may it be God's will that you never die. The verse cited in support is from *Iyov*: *ve-cha-chol arbeh yamim* — like the sand I will multiply days — understood as a reference to this immortal bird.

### Kings' Battle

Shem then turned the conversation around, addressing Eliezer directly: *ki asun aleichon melachim mizrach u-maarav* — when the kings of the east and west came against you, *atun heichi avisun* — how did you manage?

### Abraham Miracle

Eliezer answered: God brought Avraham, and me at his right hand, and the two of them would throw *afra* — dirt — at the enemy armies, and it would turn into swords; they threw chaff, and it turned into arrows. The *pasuk* from Tehillim is invoked: *Ne'um Hashem l'Adoni shev li-mini* — sit at my right hand. And the *pasuk* from Yeshayahu, familiar from the *haftarah* of *Lech Lecha*: *mi he'ir mi-mizrach* — who stirred from the east? — *yiten ke-afar charbo ke-kash nidaf kashto* — his sword is like dust, his bow like driven chaff. Thus the *pshat* of the *pasuk* itself encodes the miracle: the dust became swords, the chaff became arrows.

## Nachum & Crown

### Gam Zu Letovah

The Gemara now introduces Nachum Ish Gamzu, about whom it was said that *kol d'havei sareik lei amar gam zu letovah* — whatever happened to him, he would say: this too is for the good. One might observe that the truest test of the *gam zu letovah* attitude is not when bad things are miraculously transformed into good ones, but precisely when the difficulty remains difficulty — and yet one maintains that disposition. Nevertheless, what follows is a story in which the bad indeed turns good, through a miracle tied directly to the very tradition Eliezer just described.

### Crown Mission

One day the Jewish people wished to send a precious gift to the *Keysar* — the Roman emperor. *Nishdar behadei Nachum Ish Gamzu* — they decided to send it through Nachum Ish Gamzu, *de-melumad be-nissim hu* — because he was known to have miracles happen to him. This itself is a revealing detail: the confidence placed in Nachum was not because he was wise or diplomatic, but because his way of living — his *gam zu letovah* posture — made him someone through whom things worked out.

### Theft & Dirt

When Nachum arrived at an inn and disclosed that he was carrying a crown of precious jewels as tribute to the emperor, the innkeepers rose in the night, *sharinu le-sifteih* — opened his luggage — *ve-shaklu kol d'havei gabeih* — took everything inside — *u-malinu afra* — and refilled the box with dirt so that Nachum would be none the wiser. He continued on his journey, entirely unaware of the substitution.

### Caesar Suspects

When he arrived and presented the box to the *Keysar*, and the emperor opened it to find only dirt, he concluded: *achuchei kamachaichu bi Yehuda'ei* — the Jews are mocking me. Nachum was taken out to be executed. He said: *gam zu letovah* — this too is for the good.

### Eliyahu Appears

At that moment Eliyahu appeared — *admi l'hu*, disguised as one of the Roman officers — and suggested to them: *dilma hai afra me-afra d'Avraham Avinu hu* — perhaps this dirt is the very dirt of Avraham our patriarch, the miraculous dirt of which it was said *d'hava shadi afra havei charvei* — he threw dirt and it became swords — *gila havei girei* — he threw chaff and it became arrows.

### Dirt Tests

They tested it: *badku ve-ishtakach hachi*. There was a certain fortified city that had resisted all Roman conquest until that point. They threw some of this dirt at it, and the city fell. The miracle was confirmed.

### Gold Reward

Nachum was brought into the royal treasury and told to take whatever he wished. He filled his box with gold. On his return journey, the innkeepers who had stolen the original contents asked him what he had brought to the emperor that merited such reward. He told them simply: *mai d'shakli me-hacha ampeiti l'hasam* — whatever I took from here is what I brought there. Taking him at his word, the innkeepers gathered dirt and brought it to the emperor as a gift — and were executed for their trouble. The story has the structure of a folk tale, reminiscent of the Chelm story in which a man brings back gold for his onions, and his neighbor, trying to replicate the success, brings garlic and receives only onions in return.

## Dor HaPlaga

### No Share

The Gemara moves from *Dor HaMabul* to *Dor HaPlaga* — the generation of the dispersion. The *Mishnah* has established that they too have no share in *Olam HaBa*. The question is: *mai avdu* — what exactly did they do wrong?

### Tower Motive

The school of Rabbi Shila offers the classic answer: *nivneh migdal ve-na'aleh la-rakia* — they sought to build a tower and ascend to heaven — *ve-nakeh oto be-kardumot* — and strike God with axes. The motivation, seemingly, was control over rain: since rain descends from the heavens and is the one resource entirely dependent on divine will, they wished to seize control of that mechanism.

### Valley Problem

The objection raised in Eretz Yisrael is sharp: *im ken yivnu echad be-tura* — if they wanted to reach heaven, why does the verse say *va-yisu bik'ah* — they traveled to a valley? One does not build a tower to heaven in a valley. This is acknowledged as a formidable question — a *kushiya nitzchit* of sorts — and the Gemara never provides a satisfying answer to it, even as it continues to work within the framework that reaching heaven was indeed the goal.

### Three Groups

Rabbi Yirmiyah bar Elazar resolves part of the difficulty by noting that the builders were not a monolithic group: *necheliku l'shalosh kitot* — they divided into three factions, each with distinct motivations. A unified construction project can harbor diverse intentions, and indeed the Gemara suggests that what united them on the surface concealed fundamental disagreements about purpose.

### Dwelling Group

The first group said: *na'aleh ve-neshev sham* — let us ascend and take up residence there. Whether to protect themselves from a future flood or to consider themselves somehow elevated beings, they did not seek to make war against God. Their punishment was accordingly proportional: *hepitzam Hashem* — they were scattered. Their offense was about where they wished to live, so the response addressed precisely that.

### War Group

The second group said: *na'aleh ve-na'aseh milchamah* — let us ascend and wage war against God. They wished to surpass the divine. Their punishment, as *midah keneged midah*, was to be made subhuman: *na'asu kofim ve-ruchot ve-shedim ve-lilin* — they were turned into monkeys, spirits, demons, and *lilin*. They aspired to divinity; they were stripped of their humanity — or more precisely, as one might add, they were made *be-tzelem Elohim* and chose to read that image as actual divinity, so God removed even that *tzelem* from them.

### Idolatry Group

The third group said: *na'aleh ve-na'avod avodah zarah* — let us ascend and worship idols. Their punishment was *balal Hashem sephat kol ha'aretz* — God confounded the language of all the earth. The *midah keneged midah* here is not immediately obvious. Rashi explains that the confusion of language prevented them from coordinating their *avodah zarah*. A deeper reading would suggest that this group's sin was the worship of intermediaries — not outright denial of God but the insertion of celestial middlemen between Israel and the divine, which distorts and corrupts the very concept of monotheism. In response, God took the means of communication — itself a conduit — and made it an obstacle. Just as they turned access into obstruction by interposing intermediaries, God turned language from a vehicle of unity into a barrier of confusion.

### Natan View

A *baraita* adds the view of Rabbi Natan: *kulam le-shem avodat kochavim nitkavnu* — all three groups intended idolatry. He derives this through a *gezerah shavah*: the verse here says *ve-na'aseh lanu shem*, and elsewhere the Torah says *ve-shem Elohim acherim lo tazkiru* — the word *shem* links both passages to idolatry.

### Tower Fate

Rabbi Yochanan teaches regarding the fate of the tower itself: *migdal shlish nisraf* — one third was burned; *ve-shlish nivla* — one third was swallowed into the ground; *ve-shlish kayam* — one third still stands and can theoretically be visited.

### Tower Hidden

If a third of it remains, why has no one found it? Rav answers: *avir migdal meshake'ach* — the air around the tower causes forgetfulness. Anyone who comes near it and then departs cannot remember where they were or what they saw. It is a kind of divinely imposed amnesia that renders the surviving structure effectively invisible to human experience.

### Bad Omens

Rav Yosef then notes that *Bavel u-Borsif* — Babylon and its neighboring locale of Borsif — are *siman ra le-Torah*. Since the tower stood there and caused forgetting, the very air of that region is associated with the loss of Torah memory. This is deeply ironic, of course, given that Babylon ultimately became the center of the greatest Torah tradition in the diaspora. Rav Assi interprets *Borsif* as *bor shapi* — a pit that draws out, that pulls away — presumably a reference to the sapping of Torah retention.

## Anshei Sedom

### Sedom No Share

Having treated *Dor HaMabul* and *Dor HaPlaga*, the Gemara turns to *Anshei Sedom*. Notably, throughout this entire discussion the Gemara has not paused to explain the underlying logic of the hierarchy articulated in the *Mishnah* — why some groups are *omdin ba-din* but lack *Olam HaBa*, why others receive neither, and what distinguishes one category from another. The Gemara simply moves forward with what each group did and what their fate is.

### Wicked & Sinners

The verse in Bereishit describes the people of Sodom as *ra'im ve-chata'im la-Hashem me'od* — wicked and sinners before God greatly. The Gemara expounds the double language. Rav Yehuda interprets: *ra'im be-gufam* — wicked with their bodies; *ve-chata'im be-mamonam* — and sinners with their money. An alternative *baraita* inverts the mapping of the words but preserves the same two categories: bodily transgression and monetary transgression.

### Two Sins

The bodily sin is identified through the *pasuk* spoken by Yosef when he refused the wife of Potifar: *ve-eich e'eseh ha-ra'ah ha-gedolah ha-zot ve-chatati l'Elohim* — and how shall I commit this great evil and sin against God? That *pasuk* uses the root *ra'ah* for sexual transgression. The monetary sin is derived from *ve-hayah becha chet* — there will be a sin upon you — which the Torah uses in the context of failing to give to the poor. These two sins — sexual immorality and neglect of the poor — are in fact the same two identified as the core failures of *Dor HaMabul*, where both *chamas* and *hishchit kol basar* were central to their *gezar din*.

The verse continues: *la-Hashem* — against God — which the Gemara reads as *birchat Hashem*, blasphemy. And *me'od* — greatly — is interpreted either as doing these sins with full deliberate intent rather than through *yetzer ha-ra*, or in the *baraita* as *shefichus damim* — the shedding of blood — supported by the verse about Menashe: *gam naki shafach Menashe harbeh me'od*.

### Sedom Abundance

The Gemara then explains the origin of Sodom's wickedness in a way that exactly parallels the Gemara's earlier treatment of *Dor HaMabul*: *lo nisga'u ela bishvil tovah she-hishpia lahem ha-Kadosh Baruch Hu* — they became arrogant only because of all the goodness God lavished upon them. The verses from *Iyov* are marshaled to describe this abundance: *eretz mimena yatza lechem* — bread came forth from the land; *ve-tachteha nehepach ke-mo esh* — beneath it turned like fire; *makom sapir avaneha ve-afros zahav lo* — its stones were like sapphires and it had gold dust. It was a land of extraordinary natural wealth.

The verse continues: *nasiv lo yedau ayit ve-lo shezafaso ein ayah* — the path was unknown to the vulture and unseen by the eye of the hawk — understood metaphorically to mean that no bandits or enemies ever attacked this blessed land. *Lo hidrichuhu benei shachatz* — the sons of pride did not trample it; *lo adah alav shachal* — the lion did not gather against it. The land was uniquely protected and bountiful.

### Prevent Strangers

Their response to this abundance was: *lama lanu ovrei drachim* — why do we need passersby? *She'ein ba'im etzlenu ela lachasrenu mi-mamonenu* — they only come to take from our wealth. *Bo'u ve-nishkach torat regel me'artzenu* — let us eliminate the right of passage from our land.

The *pasuk* from *Iyov* is cited: *peretz nachal me'am gar ha-nishkachim mini regel* — they burst forth a river from the people who dwell there, causing passersby to be forgotten from their land. The interpretation offered is that God responded by diverting a stream of fire and brimstone from the heavenly course — *peretz nachal* as the divine punishment directed against those who made the foot-traveler forgotten in their midst.

### Leaning Wall

Rabba expounds a verse in Tehillim: *ad ana tehotetu al ish teratzechu chulchem ke-kir natui gader ha-dechuyah* — how long will you oppress a person, will you all murder like a leaning wall, like a pushed-over fence? The *Midrash* is: the people of Sodom would identify wealthy individuals, invite them to walk beside a leaning wall, and then push the wall onto them — *ve-dochin oto alav* — and after killing them they would raid their property. The desire for wealth, which one might think would be satisfied given their extraordinary abundance, instead became self-consuming — generating covetousness and ultimately murder.

### Tunnels & Perfume

Rabba expounds a second verse: *chatar ba-choshech batim* — they dig through houses in the darkness — *yomam chatmu lamo* — in the daytime they seal themselves in. The Gemara explains: the people of Sodom would identify wealthy homeowners and approach them with a seemingly generous request — *ha-yu notnin eineihem be-ba'alei mamon u-mafkidim etzlo afarsamon* — would you mind storing some of our precious *afarsamon* perfume in your treasure house? The wealthy person obliged. Then at night — *ba'in u-merichim oto ke-kelev* — they would come and sniff it out like a dog, following the scent of the perfume precisely to the storehouse, *ve-bain ve-chotrin sham* — and dig tunnels right to it — *ve-notlin et mamono* — and steal the contents. The verse from Tehillim is cited: *yashuvu la'erev yehemu che-kelev vi-sovavu ir* — they return at evening, they howl like dogs and circle the city.

### Tzipori 300

Rabbi Yose expounded this *drasha* publicly in Tzipori, recounting how Sodom's thieves would deposit perfume in wealthy homes to mark them for nighttime tunnel-breaking. That very night, three hundred people in Tzipori attempted to replicate the technique and tunneled into homes across the city. The townspeople confronted Rabbi Yose angrily: *yahavitu orcha le-ganve* — you have given a method to thieves. He replied: *mi hava yadana de-atun ganve* — I did not know I was delivering my *shiur* to a room full of thieves. The episode raises a genuine question: what was novel about the technique? Tunneling was not new; presumably the *chiddush* was the use of perfume as a locator. The number three hundred is likely an exaggeration, but the anecdote points to the real dangers of public exposition of criminal methodology, even in the context of Torah study.

### Yose's Death

The Gemara then notes: *ki nach nafshi de-Rabbi Yose* — when Rabbi Yose died — *shafu marzeiva de-Tzipori dama* — the gutters of Tzipori ran with blood. The image is arresting. On one level it speaks to the magnitude of communal mourning for a great sage. On another level, following immediately upon a story about theft, murder, and the abuse of wealth, it functions as a subtle commentary on the city of Tzipori itself — a wealthy, cosmopolitan city not unlike the Rome whose corruptions the Gemara has been cataloguing. The blood flowing in the streets of Tzipori upon the death of its great teacher may be the Gemara's quiet critique of what that city stood to lose.

## Sedom Laws

### Ox Tax

The Gemara now catalogs the perverse legal and social structures of Sodom. Their communal regulation for watching the town's oxen ran as follows: *de-is lei tora marei chad yoma, de-leis lei marei trei yoma* — whoever owns an ox watches for one day; whoever owns no ox watches for two days. The logic is inverted from anything fair: the burden falls heaviest on those who have least stake in the outcome. This is a paradigm of regressive social policy, designed to oppress the poor under the guise of civic duty.

### Orphan Logic

Into this system stepped an orphan, the son of a widow — someone at the very bottom of Sodom's social hierarchy — who was given the oxen to watch. He proceeded to slaughter them all, and then announced his own counter-regulation: *de-is lei tora nishkal chad mashka, de-leis lei nishkal trei mashkei* — whoever owns an ox takes one hide; whoever owns no ox takes two hides. The Sodomites protested: *mai hai* — what is this absurdity? He replied: *sof dina ke-techilat dina* — the end of the law mirrors the beginning of the law. Your own principle, applied consistently, yields exactly this. They had no answer.

### Bridge Toll

The taxation of passage was similarly structured to extract maximum payment from those least able to resist. Anyone who crossed by the bridge paid one *zuz*. Anyone who crossed through the river — to avoid the toll — paid two *zuz*. There was no way to pass through or around Sodom without paying, and the attempt to avoid one fee simply generated a higher one. Similarly, if a person had a pile of bricks or a spread of garlic and onions to sell, every passerby would help themselves to one item — *ana chada de-shakeil, I'm only taking one* — until by day's end the entire stock was gone, with each individual thief technically having taken almost nothing.

### Four Judges

The four judges of Sodom bore names that announced their function: *Shakrai* — Liar; *Shakrurai* — Great Liar; *Zaifi* — Forger; *Matzli Dina* — Perverter of Justice. Their court operated in deliberate inversion of every principle of justice.

### Wife & Donkey

If someone struck his neighbor's pregnant wife and caused her to miscarry, the judges would rule: *hav niyalah* — give your wife to him, so he can impregnate her and thereby restore what was lost. If someone cut off the ear of his neighbor's donkey, the ruling was: give your donkey to the person whose donkey you maimed, *ad di-ka'atya* — until the ear grows back, during which time the maimer gets use of the whole animal.

### Launderer

If someone wounded his neighbor and caused bleeding, the judges ruled that the wounded party owed the assailant a medical fee — *agra de-shakeil lach dama* — because he had performed a service by letting blood, as a professional bloodletter would. The launderer who refused to pay the bridge toll, was beaten for his refusal, came before the judges, and was told he owed eight *zuzei* for having crossed through the water — plus the bloodletting fee to the man who beat him. Eliezer, the servant of Avraham, happened to pass through Sodom on one of his journeys and was similarly beaten. He came before the judge and proceeded to smash a stone on the judge's head, then coolly informed him: the bloodletting fee you now owe me — pay it to this man who beat me. And my own money I shall keep. With that, he bested the entire system at its own game.

## Eliezer Sodom

### Procrustes Bed

Sodom maintained a guest bed for travelers — *mi-ttat Sodom* — which operated on a grotesque principle of uniformity. If a visitor was too long for the bed, *gayzei lei* — they would cut off his legs to make him fit. If he was too short, *matchilei* — they would stretch him until he fit. The phrase *mittat Sodom* has entered the language as the paradigm for forcing others to conform to one's own structure, regardless of the violence it does them.

### Bed Refusal

When Eliezer came to Sodom and was offered the use of this bed, he declined with an ingenious excuse: *nidra nadini mi-yoma de-miset imi* — I took an oath on the day my mother died that I would never sleep on a bed. He thus escaped by invoking an oath rather than by revealing that he knew what the bed was for.

### Starving Poor

When a poor person somehow found his way into Sodom, the city's response was a masterpiece of performative generosity masking lethal cruelty. Every resident would give the poor man a *dinar* — and write his own name on it. But no one would sell him food. The poor man thus accumulated money he could not spend, surrounded by people whose names were inscribed on the coins they had given him and who would not permit him to use them.

### Coin Recovery

When he died of starvation — *kad hava mayit* — each resident came and took back his coin, identified by the name written on it. The cruelty was layered: the appearance of charity, the agony of wealth without recourse, and the final retrieval of every coin from the corpse.

### Wedding Law

Sodom also enacted a law that anyone who invited a guest to a wedding feast would be stripped of his garments as punishment, since outsiders at communal celebrations were considered intolerable.

### Eliezer Crashes

Eliezer arrived in Sodom during a wedding feast and was denied food. He planted himself at the end of the table and when the person next to him asked who had invited him, Eliezer told him: you did. The man, terrified that others would hear him accused of inviting an outsider and strip him of his clothes, fled. Eliezer moved to the next seat and told that person the same thing. He worked his way around the entire table in this manner — *ve-chen avid le-chulehu* — until everyone had fled and he sat and ate the entire feast alone.

### Woman Righteous

There was one young woman in Sodom who secretly brought bread to a poor person, hiding it in her water jug as she went to draw water. When this was discovered, the people of Sodom covered her with honey — *shafyuha devash* — placed her atop a wall — *ve-okmuha al igra de-shura* — and left her there until the bees came and consumed her.

### Outcry Sealing

Rav Yehuda teaches that it was this act — *al iskei riva* — the affair of this young woman — that sealed Sodom's fate. The verse *va-yomer Hashem za'akat Sedom va-Amorah ki rabbah* — the outcry of Sodom is great — refers to the cry of this single righteous woman, the last act of goodness in the city, extinguished with honey and bees.

## Korach & Tribes

### Korach Fate

The Gemara concludes the chapter with two brief entries. *Adat Korach ein lahem chelek la-Olam HaBa* — the congregation of Korach has no share in the World to Come. The verse is invoked: *va-techas aleihem ha-aretz* — the earth covered them — in this world; *va-yovdu mi-toch ha-kahal* — they were lost from the assembly — in the World to Come. In this world they were swallowed by the earth; in the next world they are excluded from the *kahal*.

### Tribes Exile

Similarly: *aseret ha-shevatim ein lahem chelek la-Olam HaBa* — the Ten Tribes have no share in the World to Come. The verse: *va-yashlichem el eretz acheret* — He cast them to another land — in this world; *va-yovdu mi-toch ha-kahal* — lost from the assembly — in the next world. These are the words of Rabbi Akiva.

### Akiva Redemption

Rabbi Akiva's position is the stricter view. He holds that just as they were cast to another land and lost from the community in this world, so too they are lost from *Olam HaBa*. The verse's double language — exile in this world and loss from the *kahal* for the next — seals their fate on both planes.

### Eliezer View

Rabbi Eliezer offers a more expansive reading. He cites: *va-yomer Hashem Hashem memit u-mechayeh morid she'ol va-ya'al* — God brings death and life, brings down to the grave and raises up. Since God has the power to resurrect even those brought to death and to the grave, the Ten Tribes can still be revived and redeemed. This presumably applies to *dor ha-midbar* as well, among whom we would otherwise have assumed *chelek la-Olam HaBa* was more secure.

### Beteira Compassion

Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira takes an even more compassionate stance regarding *adat Korach* specifically: *harei hen ka'aveida ha-mitbakeshet* — they are like a lost object that is being sought. God has not abandoned them; God is actively looking for them. The verse cited is from Tehillim: *ta'iti ke-seh oved bakesh avdecha ki mitzvotecha lo shachachti* — I have strayed like a lost sheep; seek your servant, for I have not forgotten Your commandments. Even the congregation of Korach, in all their rebellion, did not forget God's *mitzvot* — and God, for His part, has not stopped seeking them. The session concludes here, with the exposition of the *pesukim* about Korach's congregation to continue in the next *shiur*.

# Sanhedrin 110

## Adat Korach

### Mishnah: No Olam Haba

The *Gemara* on this *daf* opens by citing a *Baraita*: *adat Korach ein lahem chelek le'olam haba* — the congregation of Korach has no share in the World to Come. The proof text is the verse describing their end: *vatechas aleihem ha'aretz*, the earth covered over them, *vayovdu mitoch hakahal*, and they were lost from the congregation.

### Vatechas vs. Vayovdu

The *Gemara* reads the verse in two parts. The first clause, *vatechas aleihem ha'aretz*, refers to *olam hazeh* — their physical destruction in this world. The second clause, *vayovdu mitoch hakahal*, refers to *olam haba* — they were severed from the congregation of Israel in the World to Come as well. This is *divrei Rabbi Akiva*.

### Aveidah Mitbakeshet

Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira offers a strikingly different characterization: *harei hen ke'aveidah hamitbakeshet* — they are like lost property that is being sought. The souls of Korach's congregation are not annihilated; they are lost, but the implication is that God, as it were, desires to find them again. Their fate is not final — they remain, in some sense, retrievable.

### Bakesh Avdecha

The *pasuk* adduced in support comes from Tehillim: *ta'iti kaseh oved bakesh avdecha ki mitzotecha lo shachachti* — "I have gone astray like a lost sheep; seek your servant, for I have not forgotten your commandments." The operative word is *bakesh*, seek — paralleling *ke'aveidah hamitbakeshet*. One might find it significant that the verse adds *ki mitzotecha lo shachachti*: unlike the other figures studied earlier in this *perek* who committed grave *aveirot* such as *avodah zarah*, there is no indication that *adat Korach* abandoned the rest of the *mitzvot*. Their sin was the rebellion itself — a quarrel over leadership, not apostasy. Perhaps that is precisely why Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira sees them as still reachable: God's point has been made in this world, but they need not be permanently cut off from *olam haba*.

---

## Korach's Story

### Vayikach Korach

The *Gemara* now turns to a sustained analysis of the rebellion narrative. The *parsha* opens with the grammatically peculiar phrase *vayikach Korach* — "and Korach took" — without specifying what he took.
