The debtor agrees he owes the thousand *zuz* but says the repayment deadline is ten years from now, not thirty days. The *mishna* says we assess *kama adam rotze liten v'yihyu elef zuz b'yado bein notnam mikan v'ad shloshim yom u'vein notnam mikan v'ad eser shanim* — how much would someone be willing to pay to have a thousand *zuz* in hand, given the difference between a loan repayable in thirty days versus ten years?

### Value Calculation

The logic is straightforward: having access to a thousand *zuz* for ten years rather than one month is enormously more valuable. A borrower can put that capital to productive use over a decade. The proportional difference is substantial — perhaps roughly a hundredfold. This makes the *edim zomemim*'s potential liability in this case quite significant, since the difference in value between the two terms is large.

### Shemita Cancellation

At this point Rav Yehuda quotes Shmuel: *hamalveh et chavero l'eser shanim, shevi'it mashmatato* — if one lends money to a friend for ten years, the *shemita* year will cancel the debt through *shmitat kesafim*. This creates an immediate tension with the *mishna*. If a ten-year loan is simply cancelled by *shemita*, what meaningful difference in value is the *mishna* actually assessing? A loan that gets wiped out is worth nothing to the lender.

### Lo Yigosh After Shemita

The Gemara answers on behalf of the first version of the *sugya*: *af al gav d'hashta lo karinan beih lo yigosh, sof ati lidei lo yigosh* — even though at the time of *shemita* it is not yet called *lo yigosh* (since the loan is not yet collectible during the *shemita* year), in the end, when the loan becomes collectible after the loan term expires, collecting it will constitute a violation of *lo yigosh*. This is a significant extension of the prohibition: one might have thought *lo yigosh* applies only when the lender actually presses the borrower *during* the *shemita* year. Here the Gemara holds that even a loan whose collection period will simply *overlap* with *shemita* — or more precisely, whose eventual collection will lead to a *lo yigosh* situation — already poses a halakhic problem.

### Alternative Shemita View

The Gemara then presents an alternative version of the *sugya* — *ika de'amri* — in which Rav Yehuda quotes Shmuel in the opposite direction: *hamalveh et chavero l'eser shanim, ein shevi'is mashmatato* — a ten-year loan is *not* cancelled by *shemita*. In this version, the proof is derived from the *mishna* itself: the *mishna* presupposes that a ten-year loan has meaningful assessable value, which would be impossible if *shemita* cancelled it entirely. Rav Kahana then explicitly invokes the *mishna* as his proof.

In this version, the ruling on *lo yigosh* is inverted: *ve'af al gav de'asi lidei lo yigosh, hashta miha lo karina bei lo yigosh* — even though eventually collecting the loan will implicate *lo yigosh*, at the time of *shemita* itself the loan is not yet collectable, so *shemita* has no present cancelling effect. The violation of *lo yigosh* occurs at the future moment of collection, not during the *shemita* year, and that is not sufficient to cancel the loan preemptively.

### Rava's Exclusion

Rava resolves the tension in both versions by pointing to a specific category of loans that fall outside *shmitat kesafim* entirely. *Hacha b'mai askinan* — what cases is the *mishna* discussing? Either *malveh al hamashkon* — a loan secured by collateral — or *hamoser shtarosav l'veit din* — a case where the lender has deposited his loan deed with the court for collection. Whether this latter mechanism is identical to *pruzbul* or something distinct is itself a matter of *machloket rishonim*. The *mishna* in Masechet Shevi'it teaches: *hamalveh al hamashkon vehamoser shtarosav l'veit din ein mashmitin* — these loans are not cancelled by *shemita*. The *mishna* in Makkot, Rava argues, is discussing precisely such cases.

### Conditions on Torah Law

The Gemara then raises a related question: what if someone lends money and stipulates *al mnat shelo tishmeteni shevi'it* — on the condition that the *shemita* year will not cancel this loan? Rav Yehuda quotes Shmuel: *shevi'is mashmatato* — *shemita* cancels it nonetheless. The principle at stake is whether one can make a *tenai* that overrides a *mitzvah* written in the Torah — *matneh al mah she-katuv ba-Torah tena'o vatel*.

The Gemara tests whether this is actually Shmuel's position by noting that elsewhere Shmuel appears to hold that such a condition *can* work, in the context of *ona'ah* — overcharging. A seller who says *al mnat she-ein lecha alai ona'ah* — on condition that you have no *ona'ah* claim against me — according to Shmuel, there is no *ona'ah*. Rava disagrees and says *ona'ah* still applies regardless.

Rav Anan clarifies the apparent contradiction in Shmuel's positions. The distinction is: if one says *al mnat she-ein lecha alai ona'ah* — on condition that *you* will not hold *me* liable for *ona'ah*, meaning a personal waiver of the right to sue — that is valid, because one may waive one's own right. But if one says *al mnat she-ein bo ona'ah* — on condition that the *law* of *ona'ah* simply does not apply — that is an attempt to nullify a Torah law, which is invalid.

The same distinction applies to *shemita*. If someone stipulates *al mnat shelo tishmeteni shevi'it* — asking the borrower to agree not to invoke *shemita* cancellation against him — *ein shevi'is mashmatato*: that condition works, because the borrower is waiving his own personal invocation of the law. But if someone stipulates *al mnat shelo tishmeteni shevi'it* in the sense of trying to nullify *shemita*'s legal force as such — *shevi'is mashmatato*: *shemita* cancels it anyway.

---

## Default Loan Terms

### Thirty-Day Minimum

A *baraita* is cited: *hamalveh et chavero stam, eino rashai letov'o pachot mishloshim yom* — if one lends to a friend without specifying a repayment date, one may not demand repayment before thirty days. The assumption built into an unspecified loan is that the minimum term is thirty days.

This is interesting to set alongside a parallel from Nazir, where the Gemara derives *stam nezirut shloshim yom* — that an unspecified term of *nezirut* is thirty days — from a *gezera* based on the word *yihiyeh* in the verse. There, it is presented as a matter intrinsic to the ritual law of *nezirut* and derived from *psukim*. Here, in a purely financial context, the same timescale emerges. It is striking that *Chazal* anchor both a ritual institution and a commercial norm to the same thirty-day baseline, and in the commercial context they feel the need to derive it from a verse rather than simply asserting it as a market convention.

### Written vs. Oral

Rabba bar bar Chana suggests before Rav that this thirty-day minimum applies only to a loan documented in a *shtar*. His reasoning: *de-la avid inish de-tarach de-katav shtar batzir mi-tlatin yomi* — no one goes to the trouble of drafting and executing a written contract for a loan intended to be repaid in less than thirty days. The very fact that a *shtar* was written implies a minimum term of thirty days. But for a verbal loan — *malveh al peh* — perhaps no such assumption attaches, and the lender could demand repayment much sooner.

### Shmuel's Challenge

A *baraita* is then cited that explicitly contradicts Rabba bar bar Chana's distinction: *echad ha-malveh bi-shtar ve-echad ha-malveh al peh* — whether the loan was written or oral, the thirty-day minimum applies equally. Shmuel reportedly told Rav Matna: *lo titeiv akareicha ad de-parshaht lah l'ha shmaita* — I will not let you leave your seat until you explain this teaching. How can the thirty-day minimum apply identically to both written and oral loans, given that the reasoning based on the effort of drafting a *shtar* would seem to distinguish them?

### Gezera from Shemita

The resolution comes from the verse in Devarim: *karvah shnat hasheva shnat hashmitah* — the seventh year, the year of release, is approaching. The apparent redundancy — having said "the seventh year," why add "the year of *shemita*"? — generates a *drasha*: *yesh shmitah acheret she-hi kazot* — there is another *shemita* that resembles this one. *Ve'eizu zu? Hamalveh et chavero stam she'eino rashai letov'o pachot mishloshim yom* — which *shemita*? The rule that an unspecified loan may not be collected before thirty days. Just as the *shemita* year creates a protected window during which debts cannot be pressed, the unspecified loan creates a protected window of thirty days during which the lender cannot demand repayment. This derivation applies equally to written and oral loans, since it is grounded in the verse's analogy rather than in any inference from the act of drafting a contract.

### Fiscal Year Analogy

The Gemara then connects this to a broader principle: *shloshim yom beshanah chashuv shanah* — thirty days within a year counts as a full year for certain purposes. This principle surfaces across a range of legal contexts. In the laws of *chazaka*, as discussed in the third *perek* of Bava Batra, questions arise about how to count the years of undisturbed possession that establish legal tenure. In the laws of *metzarin* — neighbors' rights — and in questions of fiscal-year calculations for leases and agreements, the same thirty-day threshold functions as a minimum unit that can stand in for a full year. The discussion of this principle at the end of the amud connects the loan minimum back to a fundamental and recurring *halakhic* construct about how time is measured and how partial periods are treated in Jewish law.

---

---

# Makkot 4

## Shemita Kesafim

### Shemita Tangent

The discussion of *shemita* in the preceding pages arose as a tangent from our *mishnah*, which contemplated the possibility of a loan extended for a ten-year term. The immediate difficulty was that *shemita* would inevitably intervene during such a period, forgiving the loan and apparently rendering the entire scenario impossible. That question prompted an extended treatment of how *shemitat kesafim* operates, anchored in a statement of *Amar Rav Yehuda Amar Shmuel*. We now turn to three further statements of Rav Yehuda — two quoting Rav and one returning to Rav — each of which introduces its own independent legal discussion.

### Hapote'ach Beit Hatzavar

The first statement: *Amar Rav Yehuda Amar Rav* — one who opens the neck of a new shirt on *Shabbat* is *chayav chatat*, liable for a biblical violation of *Shabbat*. The underlying principle is that this act constitutes a constructive form of tearing. In the manufacturing practice of the Talmudic period, the neck seam of a new garment would be basted shut, and the purchaser would rip it open when first wearing the garment. The tearing of those stitches is, on one level, destructive — it breaks the thread — but on another level it is constructive, because it creates a functional opening in the garment that allows it to be worn. This is why it cannot be dismissed under the general principle of *kol hamekalkelin peturin*, that destructive acts on *Shabbat* carry no liability. Here the destruction is in service of a constructive result, and so the act is classified as genuinely constructive.

### Lid of Barrel Challenge

*Matkif lah Rav Kahana* — Rav Kahana challenges Rav Yehuda's ruling: *vekhi mah bein zeh lemegufat havit?* What is the difference between opening the neck of a shirt and opening the lid of a barrel? The same logic would seem to apply — one is removing a covering to make the vessel usable. This question has evident practical resonance. The *poskim* have addressed at length whether opening a bottle cap on *Shabbat* falls into this category, a discussion that originated with the earlier and more pressing question of opening tin cans. The key variables are whether the cap constituted a functional *kli* in its own right before being opened, whether it was designed to be opened and reclosed, and whether opening it creates something genuinely new. Related questions arise with resealable bags and sealed boxes: if the item will be used across multiple occasions after opening, one has arguably fashioned a new functional vessel. The *Chazon Ish* and others devoted considerable attention to these distinctions.

### Chibur vs. Non-Chibur

Rav Yehuda's response to Rav Kahana: *zeh chibur vezeh eino chibur* — the neck of the shirt is actually sewn shut, making it a connected part of the garment itself, whereas the lid of the barrel is a separate piece and not genuinely attached. Since the shirt's neck constitutes a *chibur*, a joined unit with the garment, ripping it open is a meaningful constructive act upon the garment as a whole. The barrel lid, being a non-attached separate piece, involves no such consideration. Rav Kahana's challenge is thereby answered, and the ruling stands: opening the shirt neck on *Shabbat* does carry liability, while opening the barrel does not present the same problem.

### Three Logs & Wine

A second statement: *Ve-amar Rav Yehuda Amar Rav* — if one has three *log* of water into which a *kortov* of red wine has fallen, and the color of the water has been visibly affected such that *mareihen kemarei yayin*, they appear like wine, and then this liquid falls into a *mikveh*, *lo pesaluhu* — it does not disqualify the *mikveh*. The question is what happens when a small amount of wine colors a larger body of water and that colored water is then introduced into a *mikveh*.

### Dye Water Challenge

*Matkif lah Rav Kahana* once more — Rav Kahana presses again: *vekhi mah bein zeh lemei tzeva?* How is this different from dye water? The process of dyeing fabric involves dissolving pigment in water and immersing the material in the solution. The remaining dye water retains color. The *mishnah* in *mikvaot* records Rabbi Yossi's position that *mei tzeva poslin et hamikveh bishelosha lugin* — dye water can disqualify a *mikveh* in a quantity of three *log*. If colored water disqualifies the *mikveh*, why should wine-colored water be any different?

### Wine vs. Dye Water

*Amar lei Rava* — Rava intervenes to defend Rav Yehuda's ruling. *Hatam maya de-tziva mikru* — that liquid is called dye water. *Hacha chamra maziga mikrei* — but here, when a small amount of wine falls into water, the resulting liquid is not dye water but *chamra maziga*, diluted wine. In Talmudic practice, wine was routinely consumed heavily diluted — sometimes one part wine to three parts water, or even one part to five — yet it retained enough color to appear like wine and was still called wine. The character of the liquid has been transformed: it is no longer water with something foreign added, but rather a different kind of liquid altogether, namely *yayin mazug*. And since *yayin mazug* is simply wine, it is actually less problematic for the *mikveh* than colored water, because it is not water at all. This creates what is, at first glance, a counterintuitive result: a small amount of wine that colors the water and shifts its character into *yayin mazug* actually makes the liquid *less* stringent from the *mikveh*'s perspective. The same analysis applies to *mei peirot* such as fruit juice — these are categorized as a different liquid rather than water, and so the concern is of a different and lesser order.

### Appearance vs. Volume

A *braita* from *Tractate Mikvaot* is raised involving Rabbi Chiyya, which indicates that such a liquid *horeidu et hamikveh* — it diminishes the valid water count of the *mikveh*. *Amar Rava lo kashya ha Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri ha Rabbanan* — Rava resolves the apparent contradiction by identifying it as a *machloket* between Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri and the other *Rabbanan*. The relevant *mishnah* presents two parallel cases: three *log* of water, minus one *kortov*, into which a *kortov* of wine fell, such that the water appears like wine — it does not disqualify the *mikveh*; and three *log* of water, minus one *kortov*, into which a *kortov* of milk fell, such that the water appears like water — it similarly does not disqualify the *mikveh*. *Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri omer hakol holekh achar hamarei* — Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri holds that everything follows appearance, not volume. The question of whether there are a full three *log* of disqualifying liquid is determined entirely by how the mixture looks, not by measuring out the precise amounts of each component.

### Rav Pappa's Question

This leads to the question raised by Rav Pappa: *Rav tani chaser kartov be-reisha* — did Rav, when teaching this *mishnah*, include the qualification of *chaser kortov* in the first clause, the case involving wine, holding that the *tana kama* would consider a full three *log* of wine-colored water to be disqualifying, while Rav himself ruled like Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri? Or did Rav not read *chaser kortov* into the first clause at all — meaning his statement about the wine case applied to a full three *log* of water, and Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri's dispute was only with the second clause of the *mishnah*, the milk case, while Rav's ruling is in fact consistent with *divrei hakol*, with both the *tana kama* and Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri? For Rav Pappa, this remained an unresolved question. For Rava, the answer was evident — Rav's position accords only with Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri, not with the *Rabbanan*, as Rava had already explained.

### Rav Yosef's Claim

*Amar Rav Yosef* — Rav Yosef declares: *lo shemia li ha shmaita* — he had never heard this entire teaching, meaning he had no recollection of Rav's manner of reading the *mishnah* and the interpretive question that surrounded it.

### Abaye's Counter

*Amar lei Abaye* — Abaye responds to his own teacher: *at amarat lan nilan vehachi amarat lan nilan* — you yourself taught it to us, and this is precisely how you taught it. The discrepancy is striking. Whether Rav Yosef's amnesia reflects a gap in memory — he suffered a severe illness that affected his recollection — or whether Abaye simply retained what his teacher had once said with greater precision, the episode illustrates the fragility of oral transmission and the indispensability of diligent students. Abaye proceeds to reconstruct the teaching: Rav did not read *chaser kortov* into the first clause concerning wine; Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri's disagreement is with the second clause concerning milk; and Rav's ruling accords with *divrei hakol*, both the *Rabbanan* and Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri.

---

## Barrel into Ocean

### Chavit into Yam

A fourth statement from Rav Yehuda quoting Rav: *chavit mele'a mayim she-nafla le-yam hagadol* — a barrel filled with water that fell into the ocean. *Ha-tovel sham lo alta lo tvila* — if a person immerses *there*, the *tevila* does not count. The word "there" is itself the subject of debate among the *Rishonim*: does it refer to the area of the ocean where the water from the barrel dispersed, or does it mean within the barrel itself if the water remained inside?

### Mayim She'uvim

The concern that drives this ruling is *chaishinan lishlosha lugin she-lo yiheyu bemakom echad* — we worry that within the forty *se'ah* zone one would draw around the *mikveh* area, there are three *log* of *mayim she'uvim*, drawn water, which would disqualify the *mikveh*. Normally one might think that a barrel of water poured into an entire ocean is entirely inconsequential — surely it is *batel*, nullified, in so vast a body. Yet the *halacha* treats the water as localized. One mentally circumscribes a forty-*se'ah* zone within the ocean, and within that zone the drawn water from the barrel may represent three *log* of *mayim she'uvim*, enough to disqualify the *mikveh*. This spatial subdivision of the ocean is itself a remarkable conceptual move.

### Density Differences

One of the more striking interpretations of this *sugya* is attributed to Rabbi Moshe HaDarshan, cited by the *Ra'avad* and quoted in the *Ritva*. Rabbi Moshe HaDarshan — better known from Rashi's citations of him in his *Torah* commentary, and understood more as a *darshan* than as a *Talmud* scholar — offers an explanation grounded in physical science. He invokes the difference in density between fresh water and salt water. Salt water is denser and therefore does not readily mix with fresh water poured into it. The barrel of fresh water that spills into the ocean may sit as a distinct, unmixed mass for some period before dispersing. This is why, in the ocean specifically, the concern for *mayim she'uvim* applies — the freshwater and saltwater do not instantly homogenize, creating a localized zone of drawn water.

### Ocean vs. River

*Ve-davka le-yam hagadol* — this concern is specific to the ocean, *d'ka'i ve-kaima*, because the water largely remains in place, even accounting for waves and currents. *Aval nahara be-alma* — in an ordinary river, the ruling does not apply. The current constantly moves the water downstream, so that if one immerses at the spot where the barrel fell in, the drawn water will no longer be present. This raises separately the question of whether a river may serve as a *mikveh* at all. If it is fed by a spring, it has the status of a *mayan* and immersion in flowing water is entirely valid. If it is composed of rainwater, it must be stationary to qualify as a *mikveh* — *be'ashboran* — which is derived from the *Sifra*. The extensive discussion of this issue in *Tosafot* and the *Ran* in *Nedarim* touches on *Masechet Niddah*, *Shabbat*, and *Bechorot*. For present purposes, the river is invoked simply to show that flowing water disperses the drawn water and so the concern does not arise there.

### Wine Barrel

A *braita* supports and extends the ruling: *chavit mele'a yayin she-nafal le-yam hagadol* — a barrel of wine that fell into the ocean. *Ha-tovel sham lo alta lo tvila* — immersion there does not count. The same *chaishinan* formula appears, though the concern here is not technically *mayim she'uvim* — wine is not water, so it is not disqualifying on those grounds — and the precise textual formulation of the *braita* is somewhat difficult in this respect.

### Terumah Impurity

The *braita* continues: *ve-khen kikar shel terumah she-nafela sham tamei* — if a loaf of *terumah* bread fell into that same area, it becomes *tamei*. One might have argued from a *status quo* reasoning that since the *terumah* was *tahor* to begin with, it should remain *tahor*. The *braita* uses the conjunction *ve-khen*, "and similarly," to signal that this follows as a further inference. *Ka mashma lan* — the teaching comes to tell us that not only does the *mikveh* lack the power to remove the *tumah* of one who immerses, but the *mashkin* present in that zone — the wine, the drawn water — render the *terumah* *tamei*. The logic does not permit us simply to leave the *terumah* in its prior status; rather, we actively assess it as impure.

---

## Eidim Zomemim

### Monetary Conspiracy

We return now to the *mishnah* and the topic of *eidim zomemim*, conspiring witnesses. *Me'idim anu be'ish ploni she-chayav le-chavero matayim zuz* — if witnesses testify that a certain individual owes his friend two hundred *zuz*, and they are subsequently shown to be *zomemim*, *lokin u-meshalmim* — they receive lashes and they pay. This ruling is contested between Rabbi Meir and the *Chachamim*, and it represents the first of several *machlokot* that run through this section of the *mishnah*.

### Rabbi Meir: Two Violatio…

The verse *ve-asitem lo ka-asher zamam la-asot le-achiv* mandates reciprocal punishment — they tried to impose a monetary loss, so they pay money. But they also violated the prohibition against false testimony. According to Rabbi Meir: *shelo hashem hamevi'an lidei makot mevi'an lidei tashlumin* — the legal category that renders them liable for lashes is not the same legal category that renders them liable for payment. Two distinct violations are at play, and therefore both punishments apply simultaneously.

### Sages: No Double

*Ve-chachamim omrim kol ha-meshalem eino lokeh* — the *Chachamim* disagree and establish a principle of mutually exclusive penalties: in any circumstance where a person pays money, he does not also receive lashes. The same wrongful act cannot generate two forms of corporal and financial punishment. The underlying verse *kedei rish'ato* — "according to his wickedness" — implies that one is held liable for a single wickedness at a time, not two simultaneously.

---

## Lashes Dispute

### Lashes Testimony

A second scenario: *me'idim anu be'ish ploni she-hu chayav malkot arba'im* — the witnesses testify that a certain individual has committed a transgression punishable by forty lashes, and they are shown to be *zomemim*.

### Rabbi Meir: Eighty

According to Rabbi Meir, *lokim shmonim* — they receive eighty lashes. *Mishum lo ta'aneh ve-rei'acha ed shaker* — because they violated the prohibition against false testimony, and *u-mishum ve-asitem lo ka-asher zamam* — because they violated the reciprocal punishment principle. Since these are two distinct prohibitions, they generate two distinct sets of lashes. The practical figure in either case, of course, is thirty-nine per set — yielding seventy-eight — since the Torah's prescription is understood as a maximum of thirty-nine for any single violation.

### Sages: Forty Only

*Ve-chachamim omrim ein lokin ela arba'im* — the *Chachamim* hold that only forty lashes are administered, one set for one violation. The *gemara* explains the *Chachamim*'s reasoning from the verse *kedei rish'ato*: *mishum rishah achat atah mechayvo ve-i atah mechayvo mishum shtei rishayot* — you hold him liable for one act of wickedness, not two. For being *eidim zomemim*, you receive one set of *makot*, not two.

### Motzi Shem Ra

*Amar Ulla* — Ulla identifies the source for Rabbi Meir's position: *gamar mi-motzi shem ra* — Rabbi Meir derives the principle by analogy to *motzi shem ra*, the case of a husband who falsely accuses his wife of infidelity during the period of *erusin*. In that case, the husband receives both *makot* and pays a *knas*. Rabbi Meir generalizes: *mah motzi shem ra lokeh u-meshalem af kol lokeh u-meshalem* — just as *motzi shem ra* involves both lashes and payment, so too in all analogous cases of *eidim zomemim* one both receives lashes and pays. The choice of *motzi shem ra* as the paradigmatic case follows the logic of *binyan av*: one finds a generative example and derives a general principle from it. Ulla is not citing Rabbi Meir explicitly on this point; he is reconstructing the reasoning on Rabbi Meir's behalf.

### Knas vs. Restitution

An objection is raised: *mah motzi shem ra she-ken knas* — the payment in *motzi shem ra* is a *knas*, a punitive fine, not ordinary monetary restitution. One cannot straightforwardly apply it to the case of *eidim zomemim*, where the witnesses were trying to impose a restitution-style payment, not a *knas*. If the source case involves a *knas* and the target case involves ordinary *mamon*, they may not be comparable.

### Rabbi Akiva Position

*Savar lah ke-Rabbi Akiva de-amar eidim zomemim knasa hu* — the defense of Rabbi Meir is that he holds like Rabbi Akiva's position, already seen in an earlier *daf*, that the entire institution of *eidim zomemim* and its attendant punishment is itself a *knas*. If the payment imposed on *zomemim* is itself a *knas* rather than simple restitution, then the analogy to *motzi shem ra* is entirely consistent: both cases are *knas*, and therefore the same principle applies — one both receives lashes and pays.

---

## Passive Violations

### Notar Principle

The *gemara* now introduces a *braita* that uses the case of *notar* as its organizing example. *Notar* is the prohibition against leaving over sacrificial meat past the permitted time — *lo totiru mimenu ad boker*. Certain *korbanot*, notably the *korban chatat*, *korban pesach*, and others, must be consumed within a defined period; any meat remaining by morning must be burned: *ve-hanotar mimenu ad boker ba-esh tisrof*.

### Rabbi Yehuda Position

*Samach lei assei achar lo ta'aseh lomar she-ein lokin alav* — when the Torah places a positive commandment immediately following a prohibition, this signals that one does not receive lashes for violating that prohibition, since a corrective action remains available. This is the principle of *lav hanitak la-aseh*, a prohibition given over to a positive commandment as its remedy. This is the position of *divrei Rabbi Yehuda*.

### Lav She'ein Bo Ma'aseh

*Lo min hashem hazeh hu zeh* — Rabbi Akiva disagrees and says the reason is not *lav hanitak la-aseh* but rather *lav she-ein bo ma'aseh*: a prohibition that is violated without any active step. The prohibition of *notar* is violated passively — one simply fails to eat the meat, and by not eating it, the meat becomes *notar*. Since no physical action was performed, there is no punishment, for the principle is that a *lav she-ein bo ma'aseh* carries no *malkot*.

### Inference Question

From Rabbi Yehuda's formulation, one may infer — *michlal* — that Rabbi Yehuda holds the opposite position: that a *lav she-ein bo ma'aseh* does in fact carry *malkot*. If his reason for exempting *notar* from lashes is the *lav hanitak la-aseh* structure, then in the absence of that structure, a passive prohibition would still generate punishment. The question then becomes: from where does Rabbi Yehuda derive this position?

### Ulla Source

*Amar Ulla gamar mi-motzi shem ra* — Ulla says Rabbi Yehuda learns it from *motzi shem ra*. Just as *motzi shem ra* is a *lav she-ein bo ma'aseh* — the husband simply makes an accusation, no physical action is performed — and yet he receives *makot*, so too every *lav she-ein bo ma'aseh* carries lashes.

### Lo Tachmod

One of the more instructive discussions of what constitutes *ein bo ma'aseh* arises in connection with *lo tachmod*, the prohibition against coercing someone until they sell you something they did not wish to sell. The *Rambam* holds that there are no *makot* for *lo tachmod* because it is a *lav she-ein bo ma'aseh* — the violation consists of sustained pressure, a speech act, not a physical deed. Yet in a preceding *halacha*, the *Rambam* states that the prohibition is triggered only when the coercion succeeds — when the other party finally agrees to sell. One might ask: is not the relentless verbal pressure itself an action? The *Ra'avad* disagrees with the *Rambam*'s categorization entirely, holding that the exemption from *makot* derives not from *lav she-ein bo ma'aseh* but from *lav hanitan letashlumin* — it is a prohibition whose violation is remedied through payment, like *genevah* and *gezelah*, and therefore does not generate *malkot*. The contours of what counts as *ein bo ma'aseh* remain genuinely contested.

### Reish Lakish Source

*Ela amar Reish Lakish gamar me-eidim zomemim* — Reish Lakish proposes an alternative: Rabbi Yehuda derives his principle not from *motzi shem ra* but from *eidim zomemim*. Just as *eidim zomemim* constitutes a *lav she-ein bo ma'aseh* — the witnesses appear in court and testify, performing no physical act against the defendant — and yet they receive *malkot*, so too every *lav she-ein bo ma'aseh* generates punishment.

### No Warning Needed

An objection to using *eidim zomemim* as the paradigmatic case: *mah le-eidim zomemim she-ken ein tzrichin hatra'ah* — *eidim zomemim* is one of the few *aveirot* that does not require prior warning. We learned in *Masechet Sanhedrin* that certain categories of violations are exempt from the requirement of *hatra'ah*, and *eidim zomemim* is among them. The reason is partly logical impossibility: the proof of the conspiracy — *o imanu heyitem*, "were you not with us?" — only becomes relevant when the witnesses to the witnesses appear in court, potentially weeks after the original testimony. There would be no moment at which a warning could practically be administered. The *derisha ve-chakirah* process in court arguably functions as a quasi-warning, but the *Sages* nonetheless classified *eidim zomemim* as *ein tzrichin hatra'ah* because no formal warning in the classic sense is possible at the time of the violation.

### Common Denominator

Since we now have two potential sources — *motzi shem ra* and *eidim zomemim* — the argument proceeds through the standard Talmudic methodology of *tzad hashaveh*. *V-lo rei zeh ke-rei zeh ve-lo rei zeh ke-rei zeh* — each case has features that the other lacks, so neither alone can serve as a proof. *Hatzad hashaveh shebehen* — the common denominator between the two is *lav she-ein bo ma'aseh ve-lokin alav*: both are passive prohibitions and both carry *malkot*. *Af kol lav she-ein bo ma'aseh lokin alav* — from their shared characteristic we derive the general rule that every *lav she-ein bo ma'aseh* carries *malkot*.

### Not Exceptional

One might press: *mah le-tzad hashaveh shebehen she-ken knas* — both cases have the characteristic of being a *knas*, and therefore they may be exceptional rather than generative. The response is that this is not a problem for Rabbi Yehuda, since *Rabbi Yehuda lo savar lah ke-Rabbi Akiva* — Rabbi Yehuda does not hold like Rabbi Akiva that *eidim zomemim* is a *knas*. The further challenge — *ela mah le-tzad hashaveh shebehen she-yesh lahen tzad chamur*, that both cases are unusually severe and therefore exceptional — does not trouble Rabbi Yehuda either. *Rabbi Yehuda tzad chamur lo parich*. Rashi explains: *ho'il ve-chumro shel zeh eino chumro shel zeh* — since the source of stringency in each case is different from the other, it cannot be identified as the defining characteristic that makes each case exceptional. The two cases are therefore not treated as rare exceptions but as generative examples from which a general principle is derived. Consequently, Rabbi Yehuda holds that *lav she-ein bo ma'aseh* carries *malkot*, and Rabbi Meir's position — that *eidim zomemim* involves two violations — can be understood consistently within a framework where *lokeh u-meshalem* is possible.

---

## Sages' Interpretation

### Lo Ta'aneh Warning

The *gemara* now turns to how the *Rabbanan* interpret the verse *lo ta'aneh ve-rei'acha ed shaker*. In the *mishnah*, Rabbi Meir had cited this verse as the source for the second violation — false testimony — generating a separate set of lashes alongside the *ka-asher zamam* principle. But if the *Rabbanan* use only one of these as the basis for punishment, what do they do with the verse? *Hahu mibayelei le-azharah le-eidim zomemim* — they use it not as an independent prohibition generating lashes, but as the *azharah*, the formal warning, for the violation of *eidim zomemim* itself. The requirement of a separate *azharah* alongside the *onesh* typically applies in capital cases, and since *eidim zomemim* can in some scenarios carry a capital penalty, the separate mention of *lo ta'aneh* is needed to provide that formal warning. The *Rabbanan* thus understand *lo ta'aneh* and *ka-asher zamam* as two elements of a single legal structure rather than as two independent prohibitions.

### Hachrazah Source

*Amar Rabbi Yirmeyah* — Rabbi Yirmeyah explains how Rabbi Meir derives his *azharah* for *eidim zomemim* if he does not use *lo ta'aneh* for that purpose. *Nafka lei min vahanish'arim yishme'u ve-yira'u ve-lo yosifu od* — he derives the *azharah* from the verse describing the proclamation that follows punishment, the requirement that the broader public be informed of what was done to the conspiring witnesses. According to Rabbi Meir, the first part of that verse — the injunction that others should not continue such conduct — serves as the *azharah* against *eidim zomemim*, while the second part — *yishme'u ve-yira'u*, they shall hear and be afraid — provides the basis for the *hachrazah*, the formal public announcement. The *Rabbanan*, by contrast, use *vahanish'arim yishme'u ve-yira'u* exclusively for the *hachrazah* requirement. *Ve-Rabbi Meir hachrazah mi-yishme'u ve-yira'u nafka* — Rabbi Meir divides the verse, extracting both the *azharah* and the *hachrazah* from its two clauses, leaving him free to use *lo ta'aneh* as the source for an independent second violation.

---

## Division of Penalties

### Money Divided

The *mishnah* continues: *mishalshilin be-mamon ve-ein mishalshilin be-malkot*. When *eidim zomemim* are subject to a monetary penalty, the payment is divided among all the conspiring witnesses. If four witnesses conspired to impose a debt of a thousand *zuz*, and they are exposed as *zomemim*, they each pay two hundred and fifty — the total is divided equally among them.

### Lashes Not Divided

Physical punishment, however, is not divided. *Ve-ein mishalshilin be-malkot* — if the same four witnesses conspired to testify that someone had worn *shatnez* and is therefore liable for forty lashes, and they are exposed, each of the four witnesses receives the full thirty-nine lashes. There is no halving or quartering of the corporal punishment across the group.

### Half-Death Analogy

*Amar Abaye* — Abaye derives this rule through a textual parallel. The Torah uses the word *rasha* in the context of those liable for *malkot*, and it uses the same word *rasha* for those liable for capital punishment. *Mah lehalan ein mita lachatzi* — just as there is no such thing as a half-death in capital cases, *af kan ein malkot lachatzi* — there is likewise no such thing as half-*malkot*. The analogy is presented as a gezeirah shavah in structure: the shared term links the two domains and imports the indivisibility of capital punishment into the realm of *malkot*. One might ask whether the parallel is truly compelling — death is obviously impossible to divide, whereas lashes are physically divisible — and indeed the question is pressed in the *gemara*. The response involves understanding *malkot* as a subcategory, or near-equivalent, of the range of punishments that includes capital penalties. The tradition enumerates multiple modalities of punishment: *sekilah*, *srefah*, *hereg*, *chenek*, *kipah*, exclusion from *olam haba*, and *malkot* — and *malkot* is understood as occupying a position within that continuum, functioning as a punishment that carries the character of *kapparah* just as capital punishment does. The sense is that any punishment administered by *beit din* is intended as both deterrent and atonement, and *malkot* achieves this only when administered in its prescribed complete form.

### Ka'asher Zamam

*Rava amar* — Rava offers an independent derivation. *Ba'inan ka-asher zamam la-asot le-achiv ve-lo ika* — the principle of reciprocal punishment requires that what is done to the *zomemim* must correspond precisely to what they sought to do to their intended victim. If the victim would have received thirty-nine lashes, the witnesses must each receive thirty-nine lashes. Giving each witness only ten lashes — apportioning one-quarter of the punishment across four conspirators — does not satisfy the requirement of *ka-asher zamam*, because no individual witness was attempting to give the defendant one-quarter of a flogging.

### Money Joins, Pain Doesn't

One immediately asks: if Rava's logic is that the punishment must mirror exactly what was intended, why does money get divided? Should each witness not pay the full sum as well? *Mamon mitztaref* — monetary amounts join together. Two hundred and fifty plus two hundred and fifty plus two hundred and fifty plus two hundred and fifty equals a thousand, and that thousand matches the monetary harm the witnesses sought to impose. *Malkot lo mitztaref* — but physical suffering does not aggregate across persons. Ten lashes experienced by four individuals is qualitatively different from thirty-nine lashes experienced by one. The subjective human experience of corporal punishment is not additive across bodies; the pain of one person cannot be summed with the pain of another to yield an equivalent. And so while monetary penalties are divisible because the total amount can be reconstructed by summing the parts, *malkot* are not divisible because the individual experience of thirty-nine lashes is an irreducible unit. Each witness must bear the full weight of what they sought to impose — not a fraction of it.

---

---

# Makkot 5

## Edim Zomemim Basics

### Witnesses & Conspiracy

The second *mishnah* on daf 5a opens with a foundational statement about *edim zomemim*: *ein ha-edim na'asim zomemim ad she-yazumu et atzman* — witnesses cannot be declared conspiratorial and subjected to the reciprocal punishment until their testimony is proven conspiratorial through their own persons. The *mishnah* then asks *keitzad* — how does this work in practice?

The *mishnah* gives the following case: witnesses testify that so-and-so killed someone. Another set of witnesses then comes forward and says, "How can you testify to this murder? The murder victim — or the murderer — was with us in a different place at that very time." The *mishnah* rules: *ein elu zomemim*. These are not *edim zomemim*, and the conspiratorial punishment does not apply.

What the second set of witnesses has done is undermine the *content* of the testimony — they have shown that the alleged murder could not have happened as described, because the victim or perpetrator was elsewhere. But this is a fundamentally different kind of challenge than *hazamah*. It is *hakhashah* — contradiction of the facts — and while it may invalidate the testimony, it does not make the witnesses *zomemim*.

By contrast, if the second group of witnesses says, "How can you testify to this? *You* were with *us* in a different place on that day" — then the rule is *harei elu zomemim*. The decisive element is not whether the murder could have occurred, but whether *these witnesses* could have been present to observe it. The falsehood must attach to the witnesses themselves, to their very capacity to have witnessed what they claim. This is the essential mechanism of *hazamah*.

### Hakhashah vs Hazamah

The distinction between *hakhashah* and *hazamah* is the structural heart of this *mishnah*. *Hakhashah* attacks the truth of the alleged events; *hazamah* attacks the ability of the witnesses to have been present at those events. Only *hazamah* triggers the reciprocal punishment of *edim zomemim*.

The *mishnah* continues: if yet another set of witnesses comes and *hizimum* — proves the second group of witnesses to have been elsewhere as well — those too become *zomemim*. And if yet another group comes and does the same to the third group, and so on — *afilu me'ah*, even a hundred times — *kulam yeiharegu*, all of them are executed. Each successive group has been proven unable to have witnessed what they claimed, and so each is swept into the category of *zomemim*.

*Rabbi Yehuda* disagrees. His objection is grounded in the observation that with multiple groups contradicting each other in a chain, the process can reverse itself: the first group says the defendant committed murder, the second group invalidates them, the third group invalidates the second, which in principle restores credibility to the first — and so on indefinitely, back and forth. *Rabbi Yehuda* characterizes such a situation as an *istatit* — a cabal, an organized conspiracy — and holds that *ve-eino neherag ela kat harishona bilvad*, only the first group of witnesses, the ones who actually came to cause the defendant's death, should be executed. The subsequent groups, in his view, are too entangled in what appears to be a broader conspiratorial scheme to be held individually liable in the same way.

The *Gemara* will elaborate on this further, but already at this stage the *tanna kamma* and *Rabbi Yehuda* are in clear tension over how to handle cascading layers of *hazamah*.

### Sheker in Testimony Core

The *Gemara* asks *mena hanei milei* — what is the source for the principle of *hazamah*? *Rav Adda* cites the verse *ve-hineh ed sheker ha-ed sheker ana* — the witness is a false witness, he has spoken falsely. The operative requirement is *ad she-tishaker gufa shel edut* — the falsehood must occupy the core of the testimony itself. This is why *hazamah* targets specifically the question of where the witnesses were at the time of the alleged crime and whether they could have witnessed it. Undermining the facts of what happened — who was where, whether the crime took place — does not constitute the kind of falsehood that the *pasuk* demands.

*Debei Rabbi Yishmael* derives the same principle from a different verse, using the phrase *la-anot bo sara* — to testify falsely about him — with the requirement being *ad she-tisreh gufo shel edut*, until there is a *sara*, a turning aside or flaw, at the very core of the testimony.

*Rava* notes that *lesareh* carries the connotation of *lasur* — to turn aside. The difference in emphasis between *Rav Adda* and *Rabbi Yishmael*'s school is subtle but worth noting: according to *Rav Adda*, the focus is on *sheker*, outright falsehood; according to *Rabbi Yishmael*'s school, the operative concept is *sara*, a flaw or deviation, which might represent a somewhat lower threshold — not necessarily total fabrication, but a defect at the core of the testimony that is sufficient to undermine it. Whether this represents a substantively different standard or simply a different *drasha* arriving at the same conclusion remains an open question.

---

## Geography & Time

### Visibility Test

*Rava* proceeds to apply these principles to concrete spatial and temporal cases. The first case: two witnesses testify that on the eastern side of a certain building, so-and-so killed someone. A second pair of witnesses then says, "How can you testify to this? You were with us on the western side of that same building at that time." What is the law?

*Rava* rules: *chazinan* — we go and investigate. If it is physically possible to see the eastern side of the building from the western side — that is, if the geometry of the structure permits a sightline from one side to the other — then *ein elu zomemim*, they are not *zomemim*, because we cannot rule out that they had visual access to what they claimed to have witnessed. But if it is impossible to see from one side to the other, *harei elu zomemim* — they are *zomemim*.

The *Gemara* asks *peshita* — isn't it obvious that one should simply investigate this question? The answer is that one might have thought we should be concerned about *nahora barya*, exceptionally good eyesight. Perhaps the witnesses possessed extraordinary vision that would have allowed them to see what normal people could not. *Ka mashma lan* — the ruling teaches us that we do not take such a possibility into account. We assess the case based on normal human capacity. The consequence is that witnesses who genuinely did observe the murder through some unusual circumstance — a perfect alignment of windows, a sliver of sightline — could in theory be declared *zomemim* and executed, while the actual murderer goes free. The system operates based on normal assumptions, not exceptional ones.

### Travel Distances

*Rava* presents a second case of the same structure, now involving geography rather than architecture. Two witnesses testify that on Sunday morning in Sura, so-and-so killed someone. A second pair of witnesses comes and says, "On Sunday you were with us in Nehardea." Again, *chazinan* — we investigate. Is it possible to travel from Sura to Nehardea in a single day, from morning to evening? If yes, *lo havu zomemim* — they are not *zomemim*, since they might have witnessed the murder in the morning and then traveled to Nehardea. If no, *havu zomemim* — they are *zomemim*.

Again the *Gemara* asks *peshita* — why is this not obvious?

### Flying Camel Principle

The answer is that one might have thought we should be concerned about *gamla parcha* — a flying camel, some extraordinary mode of transportation that would allow travel beyond normal human capacity. *Ka mashma lan* — the ruling teaches us that we do not factor in such possibilities. We assess travel based on normal means.

This "flying camel principle" appears elsewhere in the *Bavli* — toward the end of *Gittin* and *Sotah*, for instance — and reflects an awareness, at least theoretical, of faster-than-ordinary transport. The *Bavli* entertains such possibilities in ways the *Yerushalmi* does not. The halakhic point, however, is clear: miraculous or superhuman possibilities are not factored into *hazamah* determinations. We go by what is normally possible.

This principle has interesting modern implications. Since *Hazal* measured time by distance — the standard of seventy-two minutes corresponding to the time to walk four *mil* — and since modern transportation renders distances that once took a full day traversable in a short time, questions arise in various halachic contexts about whether such measurements are governed by distance or by the underlying time unit. The flying camel principle suggests that *Hazal* measured based on normal conditions of their era, which invites reflection on how those standards apply today.

---

## Multiple Hazamot

### Defendant Guilty, Differ…

*Rava* now presents a case that adds a further layer of complexity. Two witnesses testify that on Sunday, so-and-so killed someone. A second pair comes and says, "You were with us on Sunday" — they *hazim* the first pair. But the second pair adds: "In fact, the same person killed the same victim — but on Monday." Or even, they say, "He killed him on Friday" — multiple days removed from what the first pair claimed.

The ruling is *neheragin* — the first pair is executed as *edim zomemim* — because *be-idna de-ka-shahadi gavra lav bar katla hu*, at the time that they testified, the defendant was not yet subject to the death penalty. Their testimony was what would have caused his execution. Even though the defendant is still a murderer, and even though the second pair's testimony about the actual murder will now proceed independently, the first pair testified falsely about the specific act of murder, and that false testimony was what endangered the defendant's life. The two determinations — *edim zomemim* for the first pair, and liability for the defendant based on the second pair's testimony — are treated as separate tracks.

The *Gemara* asks *mai ka mashma lan tanina* — what is this teaching us that we don't already know from a *mishnah*? A *mishnah* from tomorrow's daf is quoted: *lephichach nimtset achat mehem zomemet, hu va-hen neheragin, va-hashniya petura* — if one of the two groups of witnesses is found to be *zomemet*, both the murderer and that set of witnesses are executed, while the second group is exempt. But the *seifa* of that *mishnah* adds: *ma she-ein ken be-gmar din* — this does not apply when there has already been a *gmar din* about the murder case. It is this *seifa* that *Rava*'s teaching here comes to elaborate upon.

### Gmar Din Already Issued

The case of *gmar din* already having been issued is the crucial distinction. Two witnesses testify that on Sunday, the final verdict in so-and-so's murder case was issued by the court. A second pair of witnesses comes and says that on Sunday the first pair was with them elsewhere. The second pair adds: actually, the verdict was finalized on Friday. Or even, they say, it was finalized on Monday. The ruling: *ein elu neheragin* — the first pair, even though proven to be *zomemim*, is not executed.

Why not? Because *be-idna de-ka-mashadi gavra bar katla hu* — at the time being testified about, the defendant was already a convicted man. The *gmar din* had already been issued. The first pair of witnesses was not testifying about a crime; they were testifying about a court ruling. Their false testimony about *when* the verdict was issued does not alter the defendant's legal status — he was already subject to execution. The witnesses' testimony is therefore not what causes his death. It is the prior ruling of the court that does so. Since the mechanism of *edim zomemim* operates through reciprocity — the punishment they sought to bring upon the defendant is visited upon them — and since their testimony was not the operative cause of the death sentence, they cannot receive the death penalty as *edim zomemim*.

This principle reflects a profound legal insight: at *gmar din*, the locus of responsibility for the defendant's fate shifts from the witnesses to the court. Before *gmar din*, the testimony of the witnesses is what holds his fate in the balance. After *gmar din*, the court's ruling has taken over. Any subsequent testimony is merely about the facts of the court's decision, not about the crime itself. Thus even if such testimony is proven false through *hazamah*, the witnesses cannot receive the reciprocal punishment.

This principle connects to a broader theme regarding *gmar din* as a legal status point — the moment at which a person becomes, in a meaningful legal sense, a *bar katla*, a dead man walking. *Mishnayot* in *Arachin* and elsewhere discuss the implications of this status for various halachic questions, such as whether someone who takes a personal *erech* vow after *gmar din* has done so as a living person or as someone whose life is already forfeit in a legally operative sense. The *gmar din* is not merely procedural; it is a genuine legal transformation.

One might wonder: in practice, could such a scenario arise in *Babylonia*, where *dinei nefashot* were not conducted? *Rava* frames his cases using Sura and Nehardea — cities in *Bavel*. Presumably such examples would have applied before the *churban*, when capital jurisdiction existed, though the question is worth noting.

### Monetary Penalties & Gma…

The same principle extends to monetary *knas* cases. *Ve-chen le-inyan tashlumei knas* — the same logic applies to fines imposed by a court. Two witnesses testify that on Sunday so-and-so stole a cow and slaughtered it or sold it — an act that incurs the fourfold or fivefold payment of *daled* or *hei*. A second pair of witnesses says, "On Sunday you were with us." The second pair also testifies that in fact the theft and slaughter occurred on Monday, or even on Friday. The ruling: *meshalmin* — the first pair pays. Because *be-idna de-ka-mashadi gavra, gavra lav bar tashlumin hu* — at the time they testified, the defendant had not yet been declared liable to pay the fine. Their testimony was the operative cause of his financial liability, so the reciprocal punishment applies to them.

But if the witnesses testify that on Sunday the court finalized its ruling that the defendant owed the *knas*, and a second pair says, "On Sunday you were with us, and in fact the court finalized the ruling on Friday" — or even on Monday — then *ein meshalmin*, the first pair does not pay. Because *be-idna de-ka-mashadi, gavra bar tashlumin hu* — at the time of the *gmar din* being testified about, the defendant's financial liability had already been fixed by the court. Their testimony is about the court's ruling, not the underlying act, and the ruling is what created the obligation. Once the *gmar din* has occurred, the witnesses' role is no longer operative, and *hazamah* of their testimony about the timing of the verdict does not trigger the reciprocal penalty.

---

## Rabbi Yehuda's Position

### Rabbi Yehuda: Only First

Returning to the *mishnah*'s dispute, *Rabbi Yehuda* says: *istatit hi zo* — this whole scenario of multiple cascading sets of *hazamah* witnesses constitutes a cabal, an organized conspiracy. Therefore, *ve-eino neherag ela kat harishona bilvad* — only the first group is executed.

### Rava's Clarification

*Rava* clarifies *Rabbi Yehuda*'s position: *im eino ella kat achat, neherget* — if there is only a single pair of *hazamah* witnesses against the first set, those first witnesses are executed. *Ei ika tefei, ein nehergin* — but if there are multiple groups in the chain, none of them are executed, according to *Rabbi Yehuda*. The suspicion of *istatit* — of coordinated conspiracy — falls over the entire structure, and once that suspicion takes hold, no single group can be singled out for execution.

### Bilvad & Kasya

Yet *Rabbi Yehuda*'s formulation uses the word *bilvad* — "only" — as in "only the first group." This word implies that there is indeed a case with *more* than one group, from which we exclude all but the first. But *Rava*'s explanation posits that in the scenario *Rabbi Yehuda* addresses, when there are multiple groups, *none* of them are executed. So why does *Rabbi Yehuda* say "only the first"? This creates a *kashya* — a difficulty — that the *Gemara* leaves unresolved.

One could suggest that *bilvad* simply means: in a case where there are two sets of witnesses total — one original set and one set of *hazamah* witnesses — we kill the first set *bilvad*, since there is no further group to cast suspicion on the entire chain. But the *bilvad* still sits awkwardly given *Rava*'s formulation. A note suggests that *Rabbi Yehuda*'s statement in the *mishnah* may need to be read as referring specifically to a scenario where the *hazamah* applies only to the first group alone — but this reading, too, requires further research. The *Gemara* leaves it as a *kashya*.

---

## Woman & Chazakah

### Woman Case Intro

The *Gemara* now introduces a different case involving multiple sets of contradicting witnesses. A woman came before the court; witnesses were brought on her behalf, and they *ishtakur* — they were shown to contradict each other during the court's cross-examination, *drishat beit din*. Then she brought additional witnesses, and they too contradicted each other. Then she brought yet another group who did not contradict each other.

### Reish Lakish & Chazakah

*Reish Lakish* rules: *huchzekah zo* — this woman has now established a *chazakah*, a presumption, that she corrupts or tampers with witnesses. Two consecutive instances of her witnesses contradicting each other under examination is sufficient to establish this presumption. According to *Reish Lakish*, the *chazakah* is established by two instances.

### Rabbi Elazar's Objection

*Rabbi Elazar* objects: *im hi huchzekah, kol Yisrael mi michuzku?* — if she has established a *chazakah*, does that mean all of Israel is presumed to be lying? The suspicion attaches to one person, yet we would be casting doubt on the testimony of entirely different witnesses who testified on her behalf. We should not, argues *Rabbi Elazar*, allow suspicion of a single individual to undermine the presumed reliability of unrelated witnesses.

### Rabbi Yochanan Intervenes

The *Gemara* relates that on another occasion, when *Reish Lakish* made this ruling in the presence of *Rabbi Yochanan*, *Rabbi Yochanan* responded with the same objection: *im huchzekah zo, kol Yisrael huchzaku* — if she has established a *chazakah*, does that mean all of Israel is presumed to be suspect? It becomes clear that *Rabbi Elazar* had in fact heard this position from *Rabbi Yochanan* but had not attributed it to him.

When *Reish Lakish* realized this — that *Rabbi Elazar* had stated *Rabbi Yochanan*'s view without attribution — he turned to *Rabbi Elazar* with displeasure, *be-fanim ze'ufot*. *Reish Lakish* had learned so much of his *Torah* from *Rabbi Yochanan* that had he known this ruling was from *Rabbi Yochanan*, he would have retracted his own position rather than dispute it. He was upset that *Rabbi Elazar* had cited the position without naming its source. *Rabbi Elazar*, in turn, was embarrassed by *Reish Lakish*'s reaction: *shamat mili mi-bar Nafha ve-lo amarta li mi-shmeh* — you heard this from *Rabbi Yochanan* and you didn't tell me it was in his name?

### Known vs Future

The *Gemara* then asks whether this dispute between *Reish Lakish* and *Rabbi Yochanan* simply maps onto the dispute between *Rabbi Yehuda* and the *rabanan* in the *mishnah*. The *Gemara* rejects this: each *amora* can defend their position even within the opposing *tanna*'s framework.

*Reish Lakish* can say: *ana de-amri lakh afilu rabanan* — my position is consistent even with the *rabanan*. The *rabanan*'s rule in the *mishnah* — that all multiple groups of *zomemim* are executed — applies *hacha*, in the *mishnah*'s case, because once the chain of events has concluded, *de-ika hadra*, there is no way to revisit the case. But in our case of the woman, *ika de-ka mahadar* — the process is still open, the *drishat beit din* is still available, we can still investigate these witnesses. In such an open-ended situation, *Reish Lakish* would say the *chazakah* should not cast suspicion.

*Rabbi Yochanan* can similarly say: *ana de-amri afilu Rabbi Yehuda* — my position is consistent even with *Rabbi Yehuda*. *Rabbi Yehuda*'s rule in the *mishnah* — that only the first group is executed — applies when all the witnesses are already before us. But in our case of the woman, *hanei yad'ei be-sahaduta ve-hanei lo yad'ei be-sahaduta* — the earlier groups knew about each other's testimony and contradicted each other during examination, whereas future witnesses would not have the same prior knowledge. That distinction changes the analysis; the *chazakah* is operating on future unknown witnesses, not on witnesses who are already known to be in conflict with each other.

---

## Timing & Tzedukim

### Timing of Execution

The next *mishnah* states: *ein edim zomemim neheragim ad she-yigamer ha-din* — *edim zomemim* are not executed until the *gmar din* has been issued. This establishes a clear temporal boundary: between the acceptance of testimony (*kabbalat edut*) and the *gmar din*, *hazamah* can be applied and the witnesses executed. But before *gmar din*, and after execution of the defendant, the reciprocal punishment does not apply.

### Tzedukim's View

*Sheharei ha-Tzedukim omrim ad she-yehareg* — the *Tzedukim* hold that the reciprocal capital punishment for *edim zomemim* applies only after the defendant has actually been killed. They derive this from *nefesh tachat nefesh* — a life for a life — arguing that the reciprocity requires an actual death to have occurred. Only once the false witnesses have caused a real execution should they themselves be executed.

### Nefesh Tachat Nefesh

The *chachamim* respond by citing a different verse: *ve-asitem lo ka-asher zamam la-asot le-ahiv* — you shall do to him as he plotted to do to his brother. The critical point is *ve-harei ahiv kayyam* — his brother, the defendant, is still alive. The *Torah*'s formulation *ka-asher zamam*, "as he plotted," indicates that the *zomemim*'s punishment is triggered by what they *intended* to do, not by the completed act. Therefore, as long as the defendant has not yet been executed, the *hazamah* can still be applied.

If so, one might think that the *zomemim* should be executed as soon as the testimony is accepted — *mi-she-kiblu edutan yeihareigu*. This is where *nefesh tachat nefesh* comes in: the verse teaches that there must be a *nefesh* at stake — that is, the defendant's life must already be forfeit in a legally operative sense — before the reciprocal punishment takes effect. And a *nefesh* becomes forfeit at the *gmar din*, not at the moment of the *kabbalat edut*. Thus *nefesh tachat nefesh* functions not to push the threshold later, as the *Tzedukim* argue, but to confirm that the threshold is *gmar din*: only after the verdict is final has the defendant's life been legally placed at risk by the witnesses' testimony.

The three time points are thus: *kabbalat edut* — too early; *gmar din* — the threshold; actual *hariga* — too late. This interacts deeply with the broader halachic significance of *gmar din* as a legal transformation in the defendant's status, touching questions discussed in *Arachin* and elsewhere about what it means to be a *bar katla* from the moment the verdict is rendered.

### Kal Vachomer Limits

The *Gemara* records a remarkable exchange. *Tana be-ribbi* — a certain scholar — formulates the principle: *lo haragu, neheragin; haragu, ein neheragin* — if the *zomemim* did not cause the defendant to be killed, they are themselves executed; if he was already killed, they are not. His father — apparently *Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi* himself — responds: *lav kal va-chomer hu?* Is this not derivable by *kal va-chomer*? If we execute them when they failed to kill him, how much more so should we execute them when they actually succeeded in causing his death?

The son replies: *limadetanu rabbeinu* — my teacher, did you not teach me that *ein onshin min ha-din* — we cannot impose punishments derived through *kal va-chomer*?

The proof is brought from the laws of incestuous relationships. The *Torah* mentions separately a paternal half-sister and a maternal half-sister, specifying punishment for relations with each. One might think to derive by *kal va-chomer* that a full sister — who is both a paternal and maternal sibling — should certainly be prohibited, since even each half-relationship alone is punishable. But the *Torah* writes explicitly *ervas achoso gila* — he uncovered his sister's nakedness — rather than allowing us to derive it. The very need for the explicit verse proves that we cannot derive the punishment from a *kal va-chomer*. Moreover, even the *azhara* — the prohibition, not merely the punishment — cannot be derived for capital offenses through *kal va-chomer*; the *Torah* provides explicit verses for both the *onesh* and the *azhara* of the full sister.

For offenses incurring *malkot*, the connection is learned through a *gezeirah shavah* from the word *rasha*. For cases of manslaughter requiring *galut*, the connection is learned through a *gezeirah shavah* from the word *rotze'ah*. In neither case is *kal va-chomer* the operative mode of deriving a punishment.

---

## Tavai & Shetach

### Tavai Executes

The *Gemara* cites a *baraita*: *Rabbi Yehuda ben Tavai* declared — *ereh be-nechama im lo haragti ed zomem* — "I should merit to see the times of *mashiach* if I did not execute an *ed zomem* in order to contradict the position of the *Tzedukim*." The *Tzedukim*, as we have seen, held that *edim zomemim* should not be executed unless the defendant had already been killed. *Rabbi Yehuda ben Tavai* took it upon himself to execute an *ed zomem* specifically before the defendant was killed — that is, in accordance with rabbinic law and against the *Tzeduki* position — as a public demonstration of the correct ruling.

### Shetach Rebukes

*Shimon ben Shetach* responded immediately: *ereh be-nechama im lo shafachta dam naki* — "You should merit to see the times of *mashiach* if you have not spilled innocent blood." His rebuke was based on a specific halachic point: *ein edim zomemim neheragin ad she-yizomu sheneihem* — *edim zomemim* cannot be executed until *both* of them have been proven to be *zomemim*. And similarly, *ein lokin ad she-yizomu sheneihem* — you cannot administer *malkot* until both have been proven. *Rabbi Yehuda ben Tavai* had executed only one of the two witnesses, without establishing *hazamah* against both. By the halachic standard, he had therefore killed someone unjustly.

### Tavai's Repentance

*Rabbi Yehuda ben Tavai* immediately accepted *Shimon ben Shetach*'s authority and undertook not to issue any halachic ruling except in *Shimon ben Shetach*'s presence. Furthermore, for the rest of his life he would go prostrate himself on the grave of that *ed zomem* whom he had wrongfully executed. He would cry there, and his voice could be heard. The people developed an urban legend: they believed the sound they heard was the voice of the unjustly executed man crying out from the grave. *Rabbi Yehuda ben Tavai* clarified: *koli sheli hu* — it is my own voice. And as proof, he added: *ted'u, le-machar hu met, ein kolo nishma* — you will know this is so when I die, because then the voice will no longer be heard.

### Rav Acha's Comment

Many generations later, *Rav Acha berei de-Rava* said to *Rav Ashi*: *dilma be-dina kam bahadei; inami piyusei piyusei* — perhaps that *ed zomem* had a legal claim against *Rabbi Yehuda ben Tavai*; he could still appease him. Even if the executed witness had a legitimate grievance, the act of ongoing repentance and appeasement — the prostrations, the weeping, the lifelong penance — still had value and purpose. The *Gemara* closes the sugya on this note.

---

---

# Makkot 6

## Eidim Zomemim Unit

### Two vs. Three Witnesses

The daf opens at 5b, at the *mishna* that continues the discussion of *eidim zomemim* while also establishing the general parameters defining a *kat eidim* — a unit of witnesses. The *mishna* begins by citing the verse *al pi shnayim eidim o shlosha eidim yumet hamet*: by the mouth of two witnesses or three witnesses shall the condemned be put to death. The *mishna* asks: if two witnesses are already sufficient to establish a matter, why did the Torah need to specify three? Surely that is obvious.

### Equal Weight Principle

The answer is that the Torah places two and three on equal halakhic footing: *lehakkish shnayim lishlosha v'shlosha lishnayim*. Just as three witnesses can render two witnesses *zomemim* — by declaring *immanu hayitem b'oto hamakom*, you were with us in that place, you could not have witnessed what you claimed — so too can two witnesses render three witnesses *zomemim*. Two carries the same weight as three. Once the minimum threshold of two is met and a *kat eidim* is formed, the number beyond that is irrelevant.

### Extension to Many

The *mishna* then extends this principle further: *u'minayin afilu me'ah?* — how do we know this applies even to a hundred witnesses? The answer is *talmud lomar eidim*: the Torah uses the general term *eidim*, witnesses, rather than specifying the number. Any group of *eidim*, regardless of size, has equal halakhic weight.

### Rabbi Shimon View

*Rabbi Shimon* adds a related principle: just as when there are two witnesses, both must be proven *zomemim* before the law of *ka'asher zamam* can be applied — neither one alone is the full unit — so too when there are three, all three must be proven *zomemim* together. One might have thought that if two out of three are proven *zomemim*, those two could be punished on their own, since after all two witnesses are sufficient to convict and these two are the ones whose testimony carried the verdict. Rabbi Shimon rejects this: the entire group is treated as a single unit, and you must invalidate the whole unit before the *halakha* of *eidim zomemim* applies. And once the principle is established for three, it extends to a hundred as well.

### Rabbi Akiva View

*Rabbi Akiva* makes a further point: *lo ba hashlishi lehakel ela lehakhmir alav vela'asot dino k'yotzei b'eilu* — the Torah's mention of the third witness comes not to be lenient but to be stringent, teaching that the third witness receives the same punishment as the first two. The reasoning is this: the first two carried the full weight of the testimony and would have been sufficient to convict the defendant on their own. When all three are found *zomemim*, one might argue that the third, who contributed nothing beyond what was already in place, should not receive the full punishment. Rabbi Akiva says otherwise — because he joined himself to the group, his *din* is identical to theirs.

*Rashi* clarifies that Rabbi Akiva does not dispute the principle that all three must be proven *zomemim* together. His *chidush* is specifically about the third's punishment, not about when the *halakha* applies. The *mishna* then draws a moral inference: *al achat kamah vechamah yeshaleim sachar lenitpal le'osei mitzvah ke'osei mitzvah* — if one who attaches himself to wrongdoers is punished like them, all the more so will one who attaches himself to those performing a *mitzvah* be rewarded as though he were the primary actor, since *middat hatov* is greater than *middat hadin*.

---

## Pasul Invalidates

### One Disqualifies All

The *mishna* now establishes another principle that flows from the equation of two and three. Just as when two witnesses testify and one is found to be a *karov* — a relative of a litigant — or *pasul* — disqualified by virtue of a transgression — the entire testimony collapses, because without him only one valid witness remains and one witness is nothing, so too if one of three witnesses is *karov* or *pasul*, *eidusan beteilah*: the entire testimony of the group is void. One bad apple spoils the entire unit. This is a significant *chidush*: one might have thought that the disqualified witness simply does not combine, leaving two valid witnesses intact. The *halakha* rejects this — he is part of the unit and his *pesul* disqualifies everyone. And again, this extends to a hundred.

### Capital vs. Civil

*Rabbi Yosi* then limits this rule: *bameh devarim amurim bedinei nefashos* — this principle, that one invalid witness voids the entire group, applies only to capital cases. But in *dinei mamonos*, civil and monetary cases, *tiskayeim ha'eidus bash'ar*: the invalid witnesses are simply set aside and the valid ones retain their standing.

### Tosafot Reasoning

*Tosafot* offers a sharp explanation for this distinction. The reason two witnesses are a unit at all is that one witness alone counts for nothing in *dinei nefashos* — *lo yakum eid echad be'ish*. Therefore, if one of two is disqualified, you are left with nothing. But in *dinei mamonos*, a single witness does carry halakhic weight: he can obligate an oath, a *shvuah*. Accordingly, there is no foundational reason in *dinei mamonos* to treat one remaining valid witness as equivalent to nothing. The *chidush* of one invalidating all simply does not apply there, and the remaining valid witnesses stand.

### Rabbi's Position

*Rabbi* disagrees. He maintains that the principle applies equally to both *dinei mamonos* and *dinei nefashos*: *echad dinei mamonos ve'echad dinei nefashos*. However, *Rabbi* introduces a different qualification.

### Hatra'ah Requirement

*Ve'eimasai* — when does the disqualified individual actually become part of the group and thereby invalidate it? Only *bizman she'hisru bahen*: when the *pasul* witness actively gave *hatra'ah*, warning the perpetrator of the consequence of his act. By giving *hatra'ah*, he makes himself a participant in the *eidut* and thereby becomes part of the unit in a way that can disqualify it. But if he merely happened to be present — if, as *Rabbi* puts it, two brothers happened to witness the same murder — we cannot simply declare that their presence voids the testimony of the entire assembled group of witnesses. *Mah ya'asu shnei achim shera'u b'echad sheharag et hanefesh?* What would two brothers do if they happened to witness someone commit murder? The system cannot function if the accidental presence of any *pasul* observer brings down every *eidut*.

---

## Toch Kedei Dibbur

### Rava Definition

*Rava* adds a condition governing when multiple witnesses form a single *kat*: *vehu she'he'idu kulam betoch kedei dibbur* — it is only when all the witnesses testify within *toch kedei dibbur* of one another that they are considered a unified group.

### Time Measure

*Rav Acha miDifti* raises a question to *Ravina*: what is the measure of *toch kedei dibbur*? The standard measure is the time it takes a student to greet his teacher — *shalom alecha Rebbe u'mori* — which is roughly a second. If that is the standard, how can a hundred witnesses ever form a single unit? Each one's testimony would take far longer than that, and by the time the hundredth witness testified, they would be far outside the window of the first. The answer is: *kol chad ve'chad betoch kedei dibbur shel chaveiro* — each successive witness must begin testifying within *toch kedei dibbur* of the conclusion of the previous witness's testimony. The chain links continuously, each to the one before, and in this way even a large group can form a unified unit.

### Tosafot Limitation

*Rashi* understands *Rava*'s requirement to apply generally — that for witnesses to constitute a single *kat eidim* for any purpose, they must testify within *toch kedei dibbur* of one another. *Tosafot* disagrees sharply. *Tosafot* notes that it is clear from the *hatra'ah* discussion, and from later *sugyot*, that *nimtza echad meihem karov o pasul* does not require *toch kedei dibbur*. For that *halakha*, witnesses form a unit at the moment they witness the event, not the moment they testify. Indeed, the *mishna*'s discussion of what happens when two brothers witness a murder presupposes that one becomes part of a group of witnesses by being present at the scene — not by testifying in *toch kedei dibbur*. *Tosafot* therefore limits *Rava*'s rule: the requirement of *toch kedei dibbur* applies specifically to *eidim zomemim*, to the question of whether all witnesses must be proven *zomemim* together before *ka'asher zamam* can be applied.

### Why Different Standards

Why should *eidim zomemim* require *toch kedei dibbur* to form a unit while other *eidut* does not? *Tosafot* explains: ordinary witnesses become a unit at the moment they witness an actual event. The event is what binds them. But *eidim zomemim*, by definition, did not witness an event — they fabricated testimony. There is no external event that created their bond as a group. Therefore, for *eidim zomemim*, the constitutive act that makes them a unit is the act of testifying in *beit din* itself, and that testimony must be linked by *toch kedei dibbur* for them to be treated as a single *kat*.

---

## Perpetrators/Victims

### Murderer Disqualifies?

The *Gemara* now returns to the principle of *nimtza echad meihem karov o pasul* and the question *Rabbi* raised: what about two brothers who happen to be present? *Rav Pappa* poses the problem to *Abaye* in its sharpest form. According to *Rabbi Yosi*, who does not require *hatra'ah* for a *pasul* witness to combine with the group and disqualify it, is it not the case that in virtually every capital case the testimony should be thrown out? *Ela me'ata harog yatzil* — let the murder victim save the murderer. The victim was present, is a *karov* to himself, and perhaps a *soneh* — an enemy — of the murderer. According to *Rabbi Yosi*, should not his presence disqualify the entire *eidut*?

The *Gemara* answers: the victim was killed *keshehorgo meiachorav* — from behind, and therefore did not see the act. What about the perpetrator of forbidden *bi'ah*? Let the passive partner save the active one. Again: *kesheravo meiachorav* — it occurred from behind, and he did not see. But *Rav Pappa* presses further: let the perpetrator himself — the murderer, the one committing the act — save himself. He saw the event. He is a *karov* to himself. *Ishtik* — *Abaye* had no answer.

### Rava Solution

When *Rav Pappa* came before *Rava*, *Rava* resolved the difficulty: *yakum davar bemekayemei davar hakatuv medaber* — when the Torah says the matter shall be established, it speaks of those who *establish* the matter, those who stand outside the action and give it its legal standing.

### Who Counts as Witness

*Rashi* explains most clearly: perpetrators and victims occupy categorically different roles from witnesses. An *eid* is someone external to the act itself — someone who observes and establishes what occurred. The perpetrator and the victim are not *bemekayemei davar*; they are the actors. They never enter the category of *eid* at all, and therefore their presence as *karov* or *pasul* is simply irrelevant to the *eidut*.
