This resolves the problem entirely: *Rabbi Yosi*'s principle about *nimtza echad meihem karov o pasul* operates only within the class of witnesses, not across the boundary into the class of actors.

---

## Witness vs. Spectator

### Rava's Inquiry

The *Gemara* now returns to *Rabbi Yosi*'s unanswered problem: what happens when two brothers simply happen to be present among a crowd of witnesses to a murder? *Rabbi Yosi* never required *hatra'ah*, so he has no mechanism to distinguish an active participant in the *eidut* from a passive bystander. *Rava* provides the answer: *heichi amrinan lehu* — this is what we say to the witnesses: *lemechzei asitu o la'asudei asitu?* Did you come to watch, or did you come to testify?

### If Testifying Intent

If they respond that they came to testify — that they positioned themselves with awareness that they might be called upon to bear witness — then they are treated as *eidim*. They are *mitztaref*, they join the group, and if one is *karov* or *pasul*, *eidusan beteilah*.

### If Spectating Intent

If they say they merely came to observe — they were bystanders, not intending to testify — then they are not classified as *eidim* and do not combine with the group. Consequently, their *pesul* does not disqualify the others.

### Two Brothers Problem

This distinction resolves the problem of two brothers who happened to witness a murder. *Mah ya'asu shnei achim shera'u b'echad sheharag et hanefesh?* They were spectators, not witnesses. Their mere presence cannot bring down a valid *eidut*, and the system is not paralyzed every time relatives happen to be in the vicinity of a crime.

### Tosafot Civil Cases

*Tosafot* notes that this discussion of intent — did you come to testify or to spectate — is addressing *Rabbi*'s position specifically in the context of *dinei mamonos*, where there is no *hatra'ah* to serve as the external marker of a witness's active participation. In *dinei nefashos*, according to *Rabbi*, the act of giving *hatra'ah* itself establishes whether someone has assumed the role of witness. But in *dinei mamonos*, there is no *hatra'ah*, and so the court must inquire directly into the person's intent.

---

## Practical Rulings

### Rav Yehuda Ruling

*Rav Yehuda* rules in the name of *Shmuel*: the *halakha* follows *Rabbi Yosi* — the principle that one *pasul* witness voids the entire *eidut* applies only in *dinei nefashos*, not in *dinei mamonos*, and no *hatra'ah* is required as a precondition for the *pasul* witness to be counted as part of the group.

### Rav Nachman Ruling

*Rav Nachman* rules: the *halakha* follows *Rabbi* — the principle applies in both *dinei nefashos* and *dinei mamonos*, and in *dinei nefashos* at least, *hatra'ah* by the *pasul* witness is required for him to be considered part of the group.

### Wedding Problem

This immediately raises a practical difficulty that all the *rishonim* grapple with: why is every wedding not invalidated? At every wedding there are relatives present among those who witness the *kiddushin*, and if the *halakha* follows *Rabbi* that this principle applies even in *dinei mamonos* — and *kiddushin* is certainly not less serious than a monetary matter — then *nimtza echad meihem karov o pasul* should void every marriage contracted in the presence of relatives.

### Wedding Solutions

Several answers are offered. One is that the relatives are simply spectators, not witnesses, and the *Gemara*'s principle that intent determines whether one is classified as an *eid* applies here: people attending a wedding are presumed to come to celebrate, not to testify. The formal designation of specific witnesses — *eidim meyuchadim* — to the exclusion of all others present serves to confirm this status explicitly, marking everyone else as spectators. *Tosafot* raises an additional consideration: a relative may not even know the *halakha* of *nimtza echad meihem karov o pasul*, and therefore cannot be said to have consciously presented himself as a witness in a way that activates the rule. *Tosafot* also suggests that perhaps the *halakha* of *nimtza echad meihem karov o pasul* requires actually appearing and testifying before *beit din*, rather than merely being present at the scene — though this sits in some tension with the earlier discussion that suggests the group is formed at the moment of witnessing.

---

## Two Windows Mishna

### Setup of Mishna

The next *mishna* on 6b presents a case: two witnesses observe a murder from one window, and two other witnesses observe the same murder from a second window across the street, while one additional person standing in the middle of the street below gives *hatra'ah* to the perpetrator.

### Visibility Requirement

The governing condition is whether the witnesses on opposite sides can see one another. The *mishna* requires that some members of each group see some members of the other group — the seeing must be mutual, going in both directions. It is not necessary that all four witnesses see all four others, but at minimum one witness from each group must see at least one from the other group.

### Unified Testimony

If that condition is met — if one witness from each side sees one witness from the other — then all four are considered a single *kat* of four. To make any of them *eidim zomemim*, all four must be proven *zomemim* together, and if one is found *pasul*, all four are disqualified.

### Separate Testimony

If the condition is not met — if the witnesses on one side cannot see any witness on the other side — then they constitute two separate *katot*, two independent groups. In that case, one group can be made *zomemim* without the other group being affected.

### Paradoxical Outcome

This produces a striking result. If one *kat* of two is proven *zomemim* — *immanu hayitem b'oto hayom* — those two are executed under *ka'asher zamam*. But the other *kat* remains valid. They testified truthfully about a murder that actually occurred. Accordingly, the murderer is also executed. The irony is stark: both the murderer and the *eidim zomemim* are put to death. One might ask — if he actually committed the murder, why are the *eidim zomemim* executed? As the *Gemara* addressed earlier, the answer is that when they testified, the defendant had not yet been found guilty in court and was not yet *chayav mita*. Their testimony sought to impose a death sentence on someone not yet legally subject to it. They are therefore *eidim zomemim* regardless of what the other group's testimony subsequently establishes.

---

## Rabbi Yosi Witnesses

### Person in Middle

The *mishna* then turns to the role of the person in the middle giving *hatra'ah*, and *Rabbi Yosi* offers a ruling about a broader requirement.

### Both Must Warn

*Rabbi Yosi omer: le'olam ein neheragim ad she'yihyu shnei edav matrin bo* — a defendant can never be executed unless the witnesses themselves — the two who will testify against him — are the ones who gave him the *hatra'ah*. The idea behind *hatra'ah* is not merely that someone warned the perpetrator; it is that the very people who observed the act and will testify about it must be the ones who warned him. The perpetrator must know that those observing him are witnesses, he must hear their warning, understand the consequence, reject it, and commit the act under their gaze. If the warning came from an external person — the man in the middle of the street — while the actual witnesses were looking on from their windows, that does not constitute sufficient *hatra'ah* according to *Rabbi Yosi*.

### Pasuk Source

*Rabbi Yosi* derives this from the verse *al pi shnayim eidim*: it is by the *mouth* of the two witnesses — they must be the ones speaking the warning.

### Tosafot Analysis

*Tosafot* clarifies an important point about the *mishna*'s structure. In the *reisha* of the *mishna* — the case where the witnesses from the two windows do see one another and form a single *kat* — the man in the middle giving *hatra'ah* does not play any combining role. The combination of the two groups is achieved entirely through their visual contact with one another. The only function of the man in the middle becomes apparent in *Rabbi Yosi*'s ruling at the *seifa*: he represents the problematic scenario in which the *hatra'ah* was not given by the witnesses themselves but by an outside party. Whether the witnesses can see the *matreh* or hear his voice, and whether that suffices for the *tanna kamma* who does not share *Rabbi Yosi*'s requirement, is a question *Tosafot* explores — but for *Rabbi Yosi*, that external *hatra'ah* is simply insufficient regardless.

---

## Rava on Warning

### Visibility Combines

*Rava* states: *im hayu ro'in et hamatra o hamatra ro'eh osan mitztarfin* — if the witnesses see the *matreh* or the *matreh* sees them, they combine. At first this seems difficult to reconcile with the *mishna*, where combination of the two groups of witnesses required mutual visibility between members of the groups themselves.

### Tosafot Application

*Tosafot* explains that *Rava* is addressing a different scenario from the *mishna*: not two groups of two, but two individual witnesses — one from each side — who are not yet a valid *kat* on their own. In that case, if each of the two individual witnesses sees the *matreh*, or the *matreh* sees them, the *matreh* functions as a connecting link that draws them into a single unit of two. *Tosafot* further reasons that if this combining role applies to one-and-one, it would logically apply to two-and-two as well — making all four into a single *kat* of four through the *matreh*'s mediation, even though the *mishna* did not explicitly address this mechanism. One might distinguish the cases — two-and-two is each already a valid *kat*, and arguably no further combination is needed — but *Tosafot* treats *Rava*'s principle as applicable in both settings.

### Warning Sources

*Rava* adds a further statement: *matra she'amru afilu mipi atzmo va'afilu mipi hashed* — the *matreh* whose warning suffices under the *tanna kamma*'s view (as opposed to *Rabbi Yosi*'s stricter requirement) need not be a qualified witness or even a recognized authority. The warning is valid even if it comes *mipi atzmo* — from the victim himself — or *mipi hashed* — from a voice with no identified source.

### Rashi Explanation

*Rashi* explains: *mipi atzmo* refers to the victim of the act — if *Shimon* is about to be killed and cries out to *Reuven*, "Do not kill me! If you do, you will be *chayav mita*!" — that constitutes valid *hatra'ah*. *Mipi hashed* means some unidentified voice — whether a minor, a woman, a non-Jew, or simply an unrecognized source — that delivers the warning. This is a significant *chidush*, because ordinarily one might think that *hatra'ah* must come from a source of authority to have legal standing. *Rava* teaches that the function of *hatra'ah* — at least according to the *tanna kamma* — is to establish that the perpetrator acted in willful defiance of a known consequence, and any warning sufficient to convey that consequence can serve that purpose.

---

## Separate Testimony

### Civil Combination

*Rav Nachman* rules: *eidus miyuchedes kesheira b'dinei mamonos* — testimony from separate, individual witnesses who did not see one another is valid for monetary cases. The verse *lo yumas al pi ed echad* — he shall not die by one witness — uses the language of *death*, applying the disqualification of *eidus miyuchedes* specifically to *dinei nefashos*. For *dinei mamonos*, one-and-one who each witnessed the same event from separate vantage points without seeing each other do combine into a valid pair of witnesses.

### Challenge to System

*Rav Zutra* challenges this: if *eidus miyuchedes* can combine for *dinei mamonos*, why not use the same combination to benefit the defendant in *dinei nefashos*? For instance, in the *mishna*'s case of two groups of two witnesses who do not see one another — where one group is proven *zomemim* and executed while the other's testimony stands — why not combine all four into a single *kat* and then declare *nimtza echad meihem karov o pasul*, voiding the entire *eidut* and sparing the murderer? We have a principle of *v'hitzilu ha'edah* — the court should seek to acquit in capital cases. *Alma tnan hu v'hen neheragim* — but the *mishna* explicitly says both the murderer and the *zomemim* are executed, which means we do not use such combination. *Kashya.*

### System Integrity

The response is that while the principle of seeking to acquit in *dinei nefashos* is real, it does not license distorting the halakhic structure itself. If the foundational rule is that in *dinei nefashos* separate witnesses who did not see one another do not combine, then they simply do not combine — one cannot invoke that non-combination selectively to generate a *nimtza echad meihem karov o pasul* that would not otherwise exist.

### Distinctions Explained

*Tosafot* addresses why *eidus miyuchedes* combines in *dinei mamonos* but not in *dinei nefashos*. The answer follows the same reasoning established earlier: in *dinei mamonos*, a single witness has halakhic standing — he can obligate a *shvuah*. He is not a legal nullity. Therefore, one witness plus one witness produces two witnesses. In *dinei nefashos*, a single witness is legally nothing — *lo yakum eid echad be'ish*. One plus one remains one, and no valid *kat* is formed.

---

## Two Rabbi Yosis

### Questioning Requirement

*Rav Pappa* raises a difficulty against *Rabbi Yosi*'s requirement that the witnesses themselves give the *hatra'ah*. The *mishna* elsewhere records that *Rabbi Yosi* holds: *hasoneh neherag mipnei she'hu k'muad u'mushra* — a known enemy who kills the person he hates is executed even without *hatra'ah*, because his hatred demonstrates his willfulness. If *Rabbi Yosi* is willing to dispense with *hatra'ah* entirely in that case, how can he insist that the *hatra'ah* must specifically be given by the witnesses?

### Clarification

The *Gemara* resolves this: *hahu Rabbi Yosi b'Rabbi Yehuda hi* — the *Rabbi Yosi* who can waive *hatra'ah* for a *soneh* is not the same *Rabbi Yosi* as in our *mishna*. That position belongs to *Rabbi Yosi ben Rabbi Yehuda*.

### Scholar Exception

*Detanya*: *Rabbi Yosi ben Rabbi Yehuda omer: chaver ein tzarich hatra'ah* — a *talmid chacham* does not require *hatra'ah*, *lefi she'lo nitna hatra'ah ela lehavchin bein shogeg le'meizid* — because the entire purpose of *hatra'ah* is to distinguish between unintentional and intentional violation. A scholar who knows the law cannot claim ignorance of the prohibition, and therefore *hatra'ah* for that purpose is unnecessary. The same logic underlies the case of the *soneh*: his demonstrated hatred establishes that his act was willful. This view treats *hatra'ah* purely as a tool for determining the defendant's state of mind.

### Authority Requirement

The *Rabbi Yosi* of our *mishna* holds a fundamentally different conception of *hatra'ah*. For him, *hatra'ah* is not merely about establishing *meizid* versus *shogeg*. It is an act of formal authority — the witnesses, who represent the legal system, must confront the perpetrator directly, warn him, and he must defy them under their observation. This is why it must be the witnesses themselves who deliver the warning: the act of rejection must be a rejection of the witnesses' authority specifically, not merely a demonstration of willfulness in general. Accordingly, there is no contradiction: *Rabbi Yosi ben Rabbi Yehuda*'s leniency operates within a framework where *hatra'ah* is purely about frame of mind, while *Rabbi Yosi*'s stringency reflects a broader conception of what *hatra'ah* must accomplish.

A subtle distinction also applies regarding the two types of *shogeg* at stake. A *talmid chacham* cannot claim ignorance of the law — he knows that *chilul Shabbos* is prohibited. But he could still claim ignorance of the facts — perhaps he did not realize the walls had fallen and it was *reshut harabim*, or that the substance was *chametz* rather than *matzah*. Similarly, the *soneh* who kills is presumed willful in his act, but one might ask whether he necessarily knew the legal consequence of *mita*. These distinctions point to the complexity underlying both positions.

---

## Interpreter Requirement

### Pasuk Requirement

The *mishna* adds a second *drasha* on the phrase *al pi shnayim eidim*: *shelo tehei Sanhedrin shoma'as mipi hameturgeiman* — the *Sanhedrin* may not hear witness testimony through an interpreter. The witnesses must testify directly, *al pi* — by their own mouths — to the court.

### Rava Case

The *Gemara* relates that foreign litigants once came before *Rava*, and he appointed a *turgeiman* — an interpreter — to mediate. The *Gemara* asks: how could he do this? Has not the *mishna* prohibited exactly this? The answer: *Rava meida hava yada mah dehavu amri* — *Rava* understood their language and heard them directly.

### Hearing vs. Speaking

*V'ahadurei hu d'lo hava yada* — what *Rava* could not do was respond to them in their language, and so the interpreter was used to convey *Rava*'s responses back to the witnesses, not to relay the witnesses' words to *Rava*. The *mishna*'s prohibition is one-directional: the *beit din* must hear the witnesses' testimony directly. There is no formal requirement that the court communicate back to witnesses in a language they understand without intermediary assistance, though questions of accuracy in the interpreter's transmission of the court's words remain a matter of trust rather than formal *halakha*.

---

## Guarantor Relatives

### Facts of Case

The *Gemara* closes by presenting a case: *Ilai* and *Tuvya* are relatives of an *areiv* — a guarantor on a loan between a borrower and a lender — and they are called to testify about the terms of the loan transaction.

### Initial Analysis

*Rav Pappa* was inclined to accept their testimony. His reasoning: *gabei loveh u'malveh rechikei ninhu* — they are not related to the borrower or to the lender. The case before the court is ostensibly between those two parties, and *Ilai* and *Tuvya* have no familial tie to either. The *halakha* of disqualification by kinship should not apply to them.

### Rav Huna Objection

*Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua* challenged *Rav Pappa*: *ei leit lei l'loveh, lav batar arva azil malveh?* — if the borrower cannot repay, does the creditor not turn to the guarantor to collect? The guarantor is not a peripheral figure; he is potentially the primary target of collection. This litigation is therefore also a litigation that directly affects the guarantor's financial interests. A case involving the guarantor's money is a case the guarantor is a party to, and those related to him are as compromised as if they were related to the borrower or lender directly.

### Ruling Applied

The *halakha* therefore follows: relatives of the *areiv* are disqualified from testifying in the case, just as relatives of the primary litigants are disqualified. The *areiv*'s stake in the outcome is sufficient to render the case *his* case as well, and the rules of kinship-based disqualification apply accordingly.

---

---

# Makkot 7

## Escaped Convicts & Sanhe…

### Escaped Convict

The second chapter of *Makkot* opens with a *mishna* concerning a convicted person who escapes and is subsequently apprehended: *mi shenigmar dino uvarach* — one whose *din* has been concluded and who has fled. If he returns and appears before the same *beit din*, *ein sotrin et dino* — the court does not retry his case. The *mishna* continues: wherever two witnesses come forward and declare that such-and-such a person was sentenced in the *beit din* of so-and-so, with these and these as his witnesses, *harei ze ye'hareg* — that person is put to death on the basis of their testimony alone, without any new proceeding.

### Sanhedrin Authority

The *mishna* then introduces a new topic: *sanhedrin noheget ba'aretz uvachutz la'aretz* — a *sanhedrin* can be established whether in *Eretz Yisrael* or outside of it. Based on the context of the *gemara*, this refers to a *sanhedrin* of twenty-three. The *mishna* also introduces the famous teaching that a *sanhedrin* which executes one person in seven years is called a *chavlanit* — destructive.

### Same vs. Different Court

The *gemara* opens by inferring from the *reisha* of the *mishna*: it is specifically before the *same* *beit din* that the case is not retried, which implies that before a *different* *beit din* the case would be reopened and the court would seek grounds for acquittal. Yet the *seifa* seems to contradict this, since it states that even when two witnesses appear anywhere and testify to the sentence, the condemned is executed immediately without any retry. How are these two clauses reconciled?

*Abaye* resolves the apparent contradiction: *kan b'Eretz Yisrael, kan b'chutz la'aretz* — the *seifa* is speaking of *Eretz Yisrael*, where a different *beit din* would indeed reopen the case, while the *reisha* speaks of outside *Eretz Yisrael*, where even a different *beit din* does not retry the matter. The asymmetry is striking, and it raises a genuine conceptual question: why should the mere fact of escape trigger a renewed search for acquittal? The logic of the institution is not immediately apparent.

### Escape Across Borders

A *braita* is cited in support: *Rabbi Yehuda ben Dostai* says in the name of *Rabbi Shimon ben Shetach* that if one escapes from *Eretz Yisrael* to *chutz la'aretz*, the case is not retried; but if one escapes from *chutz la'aretz* to *Eretz Yisrael*, the case is retried — *mipnei zechutah shel Eretz Yisrael*, because of the merit of *Eretz Yisrael*.

### Merit of Eretz Yisrael

*Rashi* explains the concept of *zechutah shel Eretz Yisrael* as follows: *ulai toil limtzo lo petach shel zechut* — perhaps the merit of *Eretz Yisrael* will somehow influence the proceedings and the court will find a basis for acquittal. There is something counterintuitive here: the stronger and more skilled a *dayan* is, the more capable he is of finding grounds for acquittal. This is precisely what *Rabbi Tarfon* and *Rabbi Akiva* claimed — *ilu hayinu b'Sanhedrin, lo neherag adam me'olam* — had they sat on the *sanhedrin*, they would always have found a way to exonerate the accused. And *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* responded: *af hem marbin shofchei damim beYisrael* — by publicly announcing such a policy, they would only be increasing bloodshed in Israel, since the deterrent effect of capital punishment would be eliminated. The parallel concern applies here: allowing a convicted person to escape from *chutz la'aretz* to *Eretz Yisrael* and obtain a new hearing creates an obvious incentive for flight.

### Biblical Source

The *gemara* then turns to the derivation that a *sanhedrin* of twenty-three operates both in *Eretz Yisrael* and outside it. The *tanna'im* cite the verse *v'hayu eleh lachem l'chukat mishpat l'doroteichem* — these shall be for you a statute of judgment for your generations. The verse continues with *b'chol moshvoteichem* — in all of your dwellings — which extends the obligation to establish courts beyond *Eretz Yisrael* alone.

### Court Jurisdiction

If so, the *gemara* asks, why does the *pasuk* also use the word *b'sharecha* — in your gates — which ordinarily refers specifically to the gates of cities in *Eretz Yisrael*? The answer is that the two formulations do different work: *b'sharecha atah moshiv batei dinim b'chol pelech u'pelech u'v'chol ir va'ir* — in *Eretz Yisrael* you establish courts in every district and in every city, whereas *u'v'chutz la'aretz atah moshiv b'chol pelech u'pelech ve'i atah moshiv b'chol ir va'ir* — outside of *Eretz Yisrael* you establish a *beit din* in every province but not in every individual city. The *sanhedrin* presumably defines what constitutes a *pelech*, and on that basis determines where courts are to be set up.

## Destructive Sanhedri (II)

### One Per Seven Years

The *mishna* teaches: *sanhedrin hahoreget echad be'shavua nikret chavlanit* — a *sanhedrin* that executes one person in seven years is called destructive.

### Seventy-Year Standard

*Rabbi Eliezer ben Azariah* then offers an alternative: one execution every seventy years rises to the level of being called *chavlanit*.

### Unresolved Dispute

The *gemara* records the question: when *Rabbi Eliezer ben Azariah* says one in seventy years, does he mean that even that rate is called *chavlanit*, or does he mean that one per seventy years is *orach ar'a* — the proper and reasonable standard? The *gemara* leaves this unresolved: *teku*.

### Tarfon & Akiva View

*Rabbi Tarfon* and *Rabbi Akiva* declare: *ilu hayinu b'Sanhedrin, lo neherag adam me'olam* — had we sat on the *sanhedrin*, we would never have allowed anyone to be executed.

## Capital Conviction I (II)

### Witness Interrogation

The *gemara* immediately asks: *heichi havu avdei* — how would they have actually achieved this? This is not merely a moral position; it is a question about procedure. *Rabbi Yochanan* and *Rabbi Elazar* both answer that they would interrogate the witnesses about the victim's physical status.

### Tereifah Status

In a case of murder, the judges would ask the witnesses: *re'item terefah* — did you see that the victim was a *terefah*, someone with a mortal internal condition who is in any case destined to die imminently? *Horeg shalem horeg* — or did you see that the person was whole and healthy? *Rav Ashi* adds a further complication: even if the witnesses claim the victim was *shalem* — complete and uninjured prior to the killing — one might still ask whether the precise location where the sword struck happened to coincide with an existing *terefah* wound, leaving the matter unresolved.

## Destructive Sanhedri (II)

### Shimon ben Gamliel

*Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* responds to the position of *Rabbi Tarfon* and *Rabbi Akiva*: *af hem marbin shofchei damim beYisrael* — by pursuing a policy of never convicting anyone, they would effectively increase bloodshed in Israel, since the absence of any credible threat of capital punishment removes the deterrent entirely.

## Capital Conviction I (II)

### Shechita Comparison

*Tosafot* raise a pointed question: if we are truly concerned that a victim might have been a *terefah* before the killing, why do we not raise the same concern in the context of *shechita*? When one slaughters an animal, we do not require the *shochet* to demonstrate that the animal was not already a *terefah* prior to slaughter. Both situations involve a *chazaka* that a living creature is presumed not to be a *terefah*. If that *chazaka* is sufficient for *shechita*, why is it not sufficient in capital cases to establish that the victim was *shalem*? Clearly the concern cannot be absolute, because if it were, the *Torah* could never sanction an execution — which would effectively nullify the entire institution of capital punishment, much as the Talmud elsewhere discusses with *ben sorer u'moreh* and *ir ha-nidachat*.

### Unknown Answer Disqualif…

*Rabbeinu Tam* addresses the issue differently. He explains that the strategy of *Rabbi Tarfon* and *Rabbi Akiva* did not rest on the *terefah* question per se. Rather, the method was *she-marbe be-vedikot* — to multiply questions put to the witnesses until eventually one witness contradicts the other, producing a *hakchashah* that disqualifies their testimony entirely. The key principle *Rabbeinu Tam* articulates is this: if the witnesses are asked a question and respond *ein anu yodim* — we don't know — this response itself disqualifies them. Witnesses who cannot provide complete answers to the court's examination may become *pesulim*, and the *edut* collapses. This is why the phrase *lo neherag adam me'olam* is *lav davka* — not strictly literal. Most of the time, *Rabbi Tarfon* and *Rabbi Akiva* would succeed in tripping up the witnesses through extensive questioning; occasionally they would not. It follows, as *Tosafot* make clear, that this is not a claim to literally abolish the death penalty, but rather a description of a vigorous commitment to evidentiary scrutiny.

### Sexual Relations Evidence

The *gemara* turns to a different category of capital crime: *boel et ha-erva* — one who has illicit sexual relations. *Heichi avdei* — how would *Rabbi Tarfon* and *Rabbi Akiva* have handled this case? *Abaye* and *Rava* both state that the witnesses would be asked: *re'item k'michul ba-shfoferet* — did you see the actual act of penetration, like a brush entering a tube? This is the standard metaphor used throughout the Talmud for the act of intercourse. If the witnesses could not give such direct testimony, there would be no conviction.

### Sufficient Appearance

The *rabbanan*, however, hold a different standard. The *gemara* cites *Shmuel* who says: *bimna'afim, mi-she-yiru k'mna'afim* — in cases of illicit relations, once witnesses see the parties behaving in the manner of those engaged in the act, that is sufficient. The question this raises is significant: if the *rabbanan* do not require actual testimony of penetration, how can they convict? The answer is that *Shmuel*'s principle allows conviction on the basis of contextual observation, without requiring the witnesses to testify to the act itself. The *Rambam* rules in accordance with the *rabbanan*, and the *Shulchan Aruch* follows the *Rambam* on this point.

## Accidental Homicide

### Exile Category

With the conclusion of the first chapter, the *gemara* begins the second: *elu hen ha-golin* — these are those who go into exile. The Torah provides for *arei miklat*, sanctuary cities, to which a person who accidentally kills another must flee. There he is protected from the *go'el ha-dam*, the blood avenger from the victim's family, who is otherwise permitted to kill the manslayer. The chapter enumerates who is and who is not included in this obligation.

### Downward Motion Cases

The *mishna* presents several paradigmatic cases of accidental homicide that do incur exile. If one was rolling a log along a roof — *Rashi* explains this was a common method of sealing rooftops with pitch — and the log fell and killed someone below, that person is exiled. Similarly, if one was lowering a barrel — *meshalshel be-chavit* — and it fell and killed someone. And if one was descending a ladder and fell onto someone and killed them, *harei zeh goleh* — that person is exiled.

### Upward Motion Cases

By contrast, the *mishna* lists cases that are excluded from exile: if one was pulling the log upward and it fell and killed someone, or one was raising the barrel and the rope broke, or one was ascending a ladder and fell and killed someone — in all these cases, *harei zeh eino goleh* — that person is not exiled.

### General Rule

The *mishna* then articulates the governing principle: *kol she-be-derech yeridato goleh, ve-shelo be-derech yeridato eino goleh* — any case in which the harmful event occurs through a downward motion incurs exile; any case in which it does not occur through a downward motion does not incur exile.

### Negligence vs. Exile

This raises an important conceptual distinction. In several of the excluded cases — for instance, pulling a barrel upward when the rope snaps — the person may well be negligent and could be liable to pay damages. The exclusion from *galut* does not necessarily mean full exemption from legal responsibility; it means specifically that the obligation to go to an *ir miklat* does not apply. The *gemara* will make clear that in some excluded cases liability for negligence remains, while in others the *gemara* excludes the individual altogether. There appear to be two dimensions to *ir miklat*: protection from the blood avenger, and a kind of existential atonement for having caused a death, however unintentionally. Both dimensions are operative in the institution, which makes the precise contours of the *derech yeridato* rule all the more significant.

### Biblical Source

*Shmuel* derives the entire principle from the verse *va-yipol alav va-yamot* — and it fell upon him and killed him — implying that exile is incurred only when the killing occurs through the natural manner of falling, which is a downward motion.

## Excluded Categories

### Intentional Exclusion

The *braita* proceeds to expound the relevant *pesukim* term by term. The word *bishgaga* — unintentionally — comes to exclude the *mezid*, someone who kills deliberately. This person is not exiled because he is *bar katla* — subject to execution, not exile.

### Omer Mutar Dispute

The *gemara* notes that excluding the *mezid* on the basis of *bishgaga* seems obvious — of course an intentional killer is not sent to an *ir miklat*. *Rava* therefore proposes a more refined reading: *bishgaga* comes to exclude the *omer mutar* — one who believes that killing is permitted and kills on that basis. Such a person is not simply a *mezid* in the usual sense, yet *Rava* argues he is *karov le-mezid* — close to being intentional — and therefore the *braita*'s exclusion applies to him.

*Abaye* pushes back: if someone genuinely believes killing is permitted, he is an *oness* — acting under a form of compulsion arising from mistaken belief — and ought not be labeled a *mezid* at all. *Rava* responds that while the *omer mutar* is not a full *mezid*, his proximity to intentionality is sufficient for the *braita* to treat him as falling outside the category of *shogeg* entitled to exile. Importantly, *karov le-mezid* is not identical to *mezid*: such a person would not be executed, but neither would he receive the protection of *galut*. How one could genuinely believe that murder is permitted is indeed difficult to conceive; the case is perhaps most analogous to one who mistakenly believes his victim is a *rodef*, though that remains a distinct *halachic* category.

A parallel analysis applies to the phrase *bivli da'at* — without knowledge — which excludes one who *intended* to kill. That exclusion, too, seems obvious since an intentional killer is *chayav mita*. *Rabba* therefore reinterprets it as excluding one who intended to kill an animal and accidentally killed a person, or intended to kill a *kuti* and killed a *Yisrael*, or intended to kill a child who was not halachically viable and killed a viable one. We know from elsewhere that *ha-mitkaven la-harog zeh ve-harag zeh patur* — one who intends to kill one person and kills another is exempt from execution. One might nonetheless have thought such a person incurs *galut* — the *braita* tells us he does not. Notably, the *braita* does not address the case where one intends to kill one *Yisrael* and kills a different *Yisrael* — leaving open the possibility that in that case, *galut* does apply.

### Corner Exception

The *pasuk* uses the word *be-feta* — suddenly — and the *braita* derives from this that the two parties must be in close proximity to one another. *Befeta* implies immediacy and closeness. This comes to exclude the case of *keren zavit* — a corner. *Rashi* explains that *leshon feta hu be-samuch* — the language of *feta* implies the two are near one another, *betakif*, immediately accessible. The case: one person is walking out of one alleyway and entering another, turning left or right, with a knife in hand — and another person comes around the corner and is accidentally stabbed. In this case there is no *galut*, because the parties were not in a position to see and be seen by one another; the word *feta* implies proximity of awareness, not merely physical proximity at the moment of impact.

This is admittedly counterintuitive. Walking through a public space with a knife outstretched represents a high degree of negligence; the case of two people rounding a corner and colliding might seem more like a genuine accident. Yet the *halacha* holds that the corner case is excluded from *galut* — though liability for damages may still apply — while the straight-line encounter could incur exile. The *derech yeridato* principle, combined with the *befeta* requirement, generates results that are not always intuitively obvious.

### Enmity Exclusion

The phrase *be-lo eivah* — without prior hatred — excludes the *soneh*, someone who harbored enmity toward the victim. If a person who hates someone else "accidentally" kills that person, the preexisting hatred disqualifies the act from being classified as pure *shgaga*, and the killer does not receive the protection of *galut*.

### Intent Mismatch

The *braita* then addresses a case involving a mismatch between intent and result by way of *hadafo* — pushing — establishing that the act must be *bishgaga*, without deliberate intent, and the harmful motion must be a downward one. The *braita* includes in the category of *chayav galut* a downward motion that is *tzorech aliyah* — functionally necessary to an upward motion. One might have thought that because the downward swing is merely a means to an upward motion, it should be classified as *aliyah* and thus exempt from *galut*. The *braita* teaches otherwise: *lehavi yeridah she-hi tzorech aliyah* — this case is included.

### Wrong Target/Distance

The phrase *be-lo tzediyah* — without premeditation — comes to exclude two specific situations: one who intends to hit one side of a person and actually strikes another side, and one who intends to throw something two *amot* and actually throws it four. In both cases, the person is not *chayav galut*. Whether this is because the degree of negligence is too low or too high relative to the *galut* threshold is a matter of judgment; in either case, the person likely retains liability for damages.

### Mutual Access

Finally, the verse *ve-asher yavo et re'eihu ba-ya'ar* — and he goes with his fellow into the forest — generates a general principle: *mah ya'ar reshut le-nizak ule-mazik lehikaneis lesham* — just as in a forest both the damaged and the damager have permission to enter, so too *galut* liability requires that both parties had equal right of access to the location where the accident occurred.

## Ladder Case

### Rung Falling Question

*Rabbi Abbahu* poses a question to *Rabbi Yochanan*: *haya oleh be-sulam ve-nishmeta ha-shleiva mitachtav ve-naflah ve-hargah mahu* — if one is climbing up a ladder and, as he pushes down on a rung, the rung is dislodged and falls and kills someone, what is the law? Is this considered a downward motion — *yeridah* — triggering *galut*, or an upward motion — *aliyah* — exempting him?

### Downward for Upward

*Rabbi Yochanan* replies: *kevar nagata bi-yeridah she-hi tzorech aliyah* — you have already touched upon this in the *braita*. The *braita* explicitly stated that a downward motion which is necessary for the purpose of going up — *yeridah she-hi tzorech aliyah* — is included in the category of *chayav galut*. The act of pushing down on the rung in order to propel oneself upward is precisely this: a downward motion performed in service of ascent. It is therefore *chayav galut*.

### Mishna Challenge

An objection is raised from the *mishna* itself: the *mishna* formulates the general rule as *kol she-be-derech yeridato goleh, ve-shelo be-derech yeridato eino goleh*. What is the phrase *she-lo be-derech yeridato* coming to include? The challenger suggests it comes to include precisely the ladder case — i.e., climbing up and having a rung fall — as an instance of something that is *not* in the way of descent and is therefore *eino goleh*. If so, the *mishna* itself contradicts *Rabbi Yochanan*'s answer.

### Butcher Example

*Rabbi Yochanan* turns the argument around: *ule-ta'amach*, according to your reasoning, what does the positive clause — *kol she-be-derech yeridato* — come to include? You need both clauses to be adding something. *Rabbi Yochanan* resolves this by reading both clauses of the *mishna*'s general rule as referring to the case of a *katzav* — a butcher chopping meat.

### Four Butcher Cases

A series of four *braitot* addresses the butcher case. The first teaches: *lefanav chayav, le-achorav patur* — liable if the blade falls in front of him, exempt if it falls behind him. The second teaches the reverse. The third holds liable in both directions; the fourth exempts in both. The apparent contradictions among these four *braitot* are resolved by attention to the direction of the butcher's arm motion at the precise moment the blade is released.

### Motion Direction

The resolution: whenever the *braita* says *chayav lefanav*, it refers to a downward motion in front — *yeridah she-lefanav*; whenever it says *patur le-achorav*, it refers to an upward motion behind — *aliyah she-le-achorav*. Systematically, upward motions result in *patur*, downward motions in *chayav*. There are four possible combinations — down-front, down-back, up-front, up-back — and the four *braitot* address them in differing combinations, all consistent with the overarching principle of *derech yeridato*.

### Tannaitic Dispute

The *gemara* then raises the possibility: *leima katanai hi* — perhaps the dispute between *Rabbi Abbahu* and *Rabbi Yochanan* reflects an underlying *tannaitic* dispute. The very case they debated — one who is climbing up a ladder and a rung falls — appears in two conflicting *braitot*, one ruling *chayav* and one ruling *patur*. Perhaps one *tanna* holds it is *yeridah* and the other holds it is *aliyah*.

### Two Liability Types

The *gemara* rejects this interpretation: *lo, de-chulei alma aliyah hi, ve-lo kashya — kan le-nizkin, kan le-galut*. Both *tanna'im* may agree that the motion is fundamentally *aliyah* — ascent — and there is no contradiction, because the two *braitot* are addressing different legal frameworks: one speaks of liability in *nezikin*, where one may be *chayav* to pay damages even for an upward motion involving negligence; the other addresses *galut*, where the *aliyah* classification exempts one from exile.

### Rung Sagging

Alternatively, both *braitot* may indeed be discussing *galut*, and the distinction is factual: *ha de-itlia, ha de-lo itlia* — one case involves a rung that had been eaten by worms and therefore sagged slightly under the person's weight before breaking off. That sagging constitutes a downward motion, making the rung's fall *derech yeridah*, and the person is *chayav galut*. The other *braita* involves a rung that had not been so compromised, with no sagging — and that person is *patur*.

### Poor Fastening

A third resolution: *ha de-mihadek ve-ha de-lo mihadek* — one case involves a rung that was not well fastened in the first place. When stepped upon, it too would sag under the pressure before coming loose, again constituting a downward motion at the critical moment. A well-fastened rung that simply snapped without any preliminary downward motion would leave the climber *patur* from *galut*. The practical implication is that liability may turn on fine distinctions in the physical condition of the ladder — distinctions that are difficult to assess in advance, which is precisely why the question of whether one must clear the area before climbing even a new ladder remains genuinely open.

---

---

# Makkot 8

## Makkot Intro

### Structure & Size

Makkot is a small *maseches*, comprising only three *perakim*. This brevity is somewhat anomalous, since *masechtos* are generally organized according to the number of their chapters, and three places it at the low end. Nevertheless, its position in the order of *shas* is not arbitrary.

### Sanhedrin Link

Makkot is clearly a continuation of Sanhedrin. The general assumption — difficult as it is to formally prove — is that it originally existed as part of Sanhedrin itself, which would have then comprised some fourteen *perakim* in total. In some manuscript traditions, it does not appear immediately following Sanhedrin, which complicates the picture somewhat. What is clear is that Makkot opens with *eidim zomemim* precisely because it is picking up from the *mishna* in Sanhedrin that discussed *zomemei bas kohen uvo'alah* — a *mishna* that, as Rashi notes on the first *daf* of Makkot, was the final *mishna* of the second-to-last *perek* of Sanhedrin. This provides further evidence that *Chelek* is not, as we might assume from our printed editions, the last chapter of Sanhedrin. The final *perek* of Sanhedrin dealt with *chenek*, the last of the *arba misos*, and concluded with the material about *zomemei bas kohen* — which then flows directly into Makkot's treatment of *eidim zomemim*. The order of *perakim* in our editions of Sanhedrin is, on this evidence, incorrect.

### Conceptual Move

Conceptually, what Makkot represents is a transition away from the *arba misos beis din* toward the other functions of *beis din* as a judicial institution. The first *perek* began with *eidim zomemim* but quickly broadened into procedural questions about *eidus* — what renders witnesses *pasul*, how separate groups of witnesses may be combined, whether witnesses must be able to see one another, and so on. It also dealt with questions such as whether a defendant who flees to a different *beis din* can have his case reopened, and the obligation to establish courts and adjudicate capital crimes whether in *Eretz Yisrael* or *Chutz La'aretz*. In this way, the end of the first *perek* served as a conclusion to the entire discussion of capital punishments, together with the procedural rules of testimony that apply specifically in capital cases.

### Galus & Lashes

The remainder of Makkot concerns itself with non-monetary, non-capital bodily punishments — specifically the two forms that *beis din* administers beyond execution. The second *perek*, which we are now studying, deals with *galus*, exile to the *arei miklat*. This institution is fascinating in its own right: the *Torah* seems to be deliberately channeling what might otherwise have become vigilante justice — the *go'el hadam* pursuing the killer — into a controlled judicial framework. The *galus* serves simultaneously as protection for the unintentional killer and as a form of *kappara* for one who did cause a death, however inadvertently. The third and final *perek* then deals with lashes, the other major non-monetary punishment administered by *beis din*.

---

## Exile Logic

### Lack of System

The *perek* of *Elu Hein Hagolin* presents a significant interpretive challenge: there does not seem to be a consistent underlying principle governing which cases of unintentional homicide result in exile and which do not. Already from the first *daf* of Makkot, the cases seem to resist systematization. One principle exempts a person who threw in one direction and the object went in the other — presumably because such a person is entirely blameless. Another principle exempts a person who tried to throw only partway toward the victim but the object covered the full distance. Yet this creates an obvious difficulty: if you're exempt when it goes the wrong direction and also exempt when it goes further than intended toward the person, when exactly are you liable? Rashi suggests the classic case is when you intended to throw it in that direction and the victim happened to walk into the path — but there is a *mishna* that exempts that scenario as well. What is the underlying logic?

Even setting aside questions of negligence, there are cases that seem purely formalistic — as we are about to see with the chopping of wood, where the question of whether it is the axe head that flies off or a wood chip that flies off determines *galus* liability, and it is genuinely difficult to understand why one should be categorically different from the other. And more troubling still, cases that appear virtually identical are sometimes treated differently. The honest answer is that this *perek* operates with a very high degree of specificity that does not always resolve into a neat internal logic, and that does not always seem to be internally consistent.

### Yerida Letzorech

One concept introduced in the preceding *sugya*, which deserves mention here, is the doctrine of *yerida letzorech aliyah* — downward motion for the sake of upward motion. The examples the *Gemara* gives include pressing down on the rung of a ladder or a butcher bending down before pulling upward. The phrase itself has become a significant concept in *Chassidus* literature, applied to the spiritual experience of someone who, having achieved a level of religious seriousness, suddenly finds themselves falling into a *chet* they believed they had long surpassed, and is tempted to despair. The *Gemara*'s framework offers a reframe: the descent may itself be in service of a greater ascent.

### Rung Falls

What is interesting — and the *Gemara*'s treatment is not entirely consistent on this point — is how exactly to define which direction constitutes the relevant motion. Rashi says that if you are simply pressing your foot down onto a rung and the rung remains steady, that is not a *yerida* in the relevant sense, because the rung itself is not descending. But if the rung is loose and it pushes downward, then that qualifies as *yerida*. Tosafot notes, importantly, that the mechanism of the case is not that the person fell and struck someone below, but that the rung itself fell. So the question becomes whether the rung going down counts as *yerida* when the purpose of pressing on it was to climb upward. One could plausibly categorize this case many different ways, and the *Gemara* itself seems to shift in how it frames it by the end of the *sugya*.

---

## Axe Head Debate

### Mishna Setup

The *mishna* at the bottom of 7b presents the following case from the *Torah*'s paradigm of unintentional homicide: the verse in Devarim describes two people who go into the forest together to chop wood, and states *v'nashal habarzel min ha'etz* — the iron was let loose from the wood — and kills someone. The question turns on what "the wood" refers to. It can be read as the wooden handle of the axe, yielding the interpretation that the iron head of the axe flew off the handle and killed someone. Alternatively, it can be read as the wood being chopped, yielding the interpretation that a splinter flew off the wood that was being struck and killed someone.

This is precisely the debate between Rabbi and the *Chachamim*. *Nishmata habarzel mikito v'harag* — the iron head came loose from its handle and killed. Rabbi says *eino goleh*, he does not go into exile. The *Chachamim* say *goleh*, he does go into exile. Then: *Min ha'etz hamitpakeia* — from the wood that was being split — a splinter flew off and killed. Rabbi says *goleh*. The *Chachamim* say *eino goleh*.

The *Gemara* does not explicitly explain why each reading should produce a different *din*. One could reason that the flying axe head is more analogous to *metassek* — a completely incidental, unanticipated consequence entirely disconnected from the intended act of chopping. You reach back, the head flies off — there is no way in which your chopping motion caused this in any ordinary sense of causation. A splinter, by contrast, is the direct and predictable result of the blow. So perhaps Rabbi's position makes sense on a negligence framework: only when you were producing the thing that caused the death — the splinter — does the death count as traceable to your action in a way that warrants *galus*. The *Chachamim*'s position is harder to parse on this framework, unless they say the reverse — that the splinter represents too much negligence, or perhaps that the axe head represents a sufficiently predictable hazard. Alternatively, as the *Gemara* will go on to suggest, there may be a formal rather than negligence-based distinction at play, involving the concepts of *kocho* and *koach kocho*.

### Rabbi's Argument

A *brayta* records Rabbi's own argument to the *Chachamim*. He asks: does the verse say *v'nashal habarzel me'etzO* — from its handle? No. It says *min ha'etz* — from the wood. Moreover, he points out a *gezera shava* within the passage itself: the word *etz* appears both in the description of the scenario — they came into the forest *lachtov etzim*, to chop wood — and in the description of the accident — *min ha'etz*. *Ma etz ha'amur lemala min ha'etz hamitpakei'a* — just as the word *etz* in the opening of the scenario refers to the wood being chopped, so too the word *etz* in the description of the accident must refer to the wood being chopped. This is a strong contextual argument.

### Rav's Answer

The *Gemara* then asks a pointed question. Rav states that both Rabbi and the *Chachamim* are actually deriving their respective positions from the very same verse — *v'nashal habarzel min ha'etz*. This seems obvious, and the *Gemara* acknowledges it. The real question is the grammatical reading. Rabbi holds *yesh eim l'masoret*, that the written form of the word — *venishal*, in the transitive — governs. The transitive form means the iron *caused* the wood to fly off, i.e., a splinter was produced. The *Chachamim* hold *yesh eim lamikra*, that the traditional oral reading — *venashal*, the intransitive — governs, meaning the iron itself flew off.

But the *Gemara* immediately objects: Rabbi is generally understood to hold *yesh eim lamikra* — indeed, there is a *brayta* in the name of Rabbi Yochanan listing Rabbi, Rabbi Yehudah ben Ro'ei, Beit Shammai, Rabbi Shimon, and Rabbi Akiva as all holding *yesh eim lamikra*. So how can Rabbi suddenly invoke *yesh eim l'masoret* here?

The *Gemara* resolves this: *hainu dekamar lehu ve'od* — that is precisely why Rabbi added the *ve'od* argument to his contextual proof. Since the context makes clear that *etz* in this passage means the wood being chopped, not the handle, and since the verse does not say *me'etzo* but *min ha'etz*, even according to the principle of *yesh eim lamikra* we are entitled to read the verb in the transitive form. Tosafot's explanation of how these two considerations combine is particularly instructive: given the weight of contextual evidence pointing toward "the wood being chopped," we are justified in invoking the written form's transitive reading — *venishal* — rather than the intransitive *venashal* that would normally dominate under *yesh eim lamikra*. The context licenses the departure from the default reading.

### Dirt & Dates

Rav Pappa extends the debate of Rabbi and the *Chachamim* to an analogous case: *man deshada pissa l'dikla* — someone who threw a clump of dirt at a palm tree, *v'azei tamrei v'katlo* — and as a result dates flew off and killed someone. This case falls under the same dispute. Why? Because structurally, it mirrors Rabbi's category: the person used one object — the clump of dirt — to make another object — the dates — fly off and cause death, without directly handling the lethal projectile. The *Gemara* notes that this might initially seem obvious, but it is not. The point is that the *Gemara* is not analyzing degree of negligence here — for on a negligence analysis, throwing things at trees really is not so different from chopping wood in terms of the hazard one should anticipate. Rather, the *Gemara* is examining formal similarity: in both cases, one object is used to propel another. This is underscored by the *Gemara*'s framing of the question, which we turn to next.

### Kocho Debate

The *Gemara* raises the possibility that the dirt-and-dates case might actually be *more* removed from the actor than Rabbi's case of the axe, and might therefore be exempt even according to Rabbi. In the axe case, you are holding the axe when the splinter flies off — the splinter is your *kocho*, one degree removed from you. In the dirt-and-dates case, you are not holding the clump of dirt when it strikes the tree; your energy transferred to the clump, and that is your *kocho*, and then from the clump to the dates is *koach kocho* — two degrees removed. Perhaps even Rabbi would agree that *koach kocho* is too attenuated to create liability. The *Gemara* therefore teaches that this is not the case — the clump of dirt you throw is treated analogously to the axe you are swinging, and the dates are in the same position as the splinter.

The *Gemara* then asks what would constitute *koach kocho* according to Rabbi, since the dirt-and-dates case does not reach that threshold. The answer is a Rube Goldberg-style case: you throw a clump and it hits a branch, the branch hits a cluster of dates, the dates fall and kill someone — that third degree of removal would be *koach kocho* in the relevant sense, and everyone would agree you are exempt. The implication for understanding the dispute is important: one way to frame why the *Chachamim* exempt in Rabbi's axe-splinter case is that they consider the splinter to be one degree removed from you — not *kocho* in the relevant sense, but already *koach kocho*, since you were not holding the wood, only the axe, and the splinter came from the wood. This would explain the formal distinction the *Chachamim* draw. It does not, however, explain why Rabbi would exempt when the axe head flies off, so the formal framework only takes us partway.

---

## Public Domain

### Mishna Stones

The following *mishna* presents the case of *hazorek even l'reshus harabbim v'harag* — one who throws stones into the public domain and thereby causes a death. The *mishna* rules *harei ze goleh*, he goes into exile — even though this might seem to represent a high degree of negligence, placing it closer to the *meizid* end of the spectrum. Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov adds a qualification: *im misheyatza ha'even miyado hotzi halah es rosho v'kiblah, harei ze patur* — if after the stone left his hand the person who was struck walked into the stone's path, the thrower is exempt.

### Own Courtyard

The *mishna* then turns to a related case: throwing stones in one's own courtyard. Here the rule is that *im yesh reshus l'nizak likannes l'sham* — if the person who was killed had permission to be there, such as a guest, a postman, anyone invited or allowed onto the property — then *goleh*, exile applies. *V'im lav, eino goleh* — but if the person had no right to be there, the thrower is exempt. This rule is derived from the *brayta* which expounds the verse *v'asher yavo es re'eihu baya'ar* — one who goes with his friend into the forest: just as the forest is a place where both the injurer and the injured have equal permission to be, so the rule of *galus* applies only when both parties had a right to be in that location.

### Abba Shaul

Abba Shaul makes a different *drasha* from the same model case. *Ma chatavas etzim reshus, af kol reshus* — just as the chopping of wood in the *Torah*'s paradigm is a discretionary act, so the law of *galus* applies only to discretionary acts. *Yatza av hamakeh es bno v'rav harodeh es talmido* — this excludes cases where what a person is doing constitutes a *mitzvah* context: a father striking his son for educational purposes, a teacher striking a student. Also excluded is *shliach beis din*, the court officer who administers lashes, whose act is explicitly mandated. In these *mitzvah* contexts, if an accident results in death, there is no *galus* liability.

There is, however, another dimension to these exemptions worth noting. In the case of the father hitting his son or the teacher hitting his student, what is happening is a willful infliction of physical force on another person. One might have expected a different analysis altogether: even setting aside the *mitzvah* context, there is something conceptually distinct about an act that involves directly, physically striking someone, as opposed to all the other scenarios — the axe, the stone — where the harm is the unintended byproduct of some other activity. In a bar fight where someone accidentally strikes a fatal blow, for instance, the degree of intentional physical involvement is very different from a wood-chopping accident. Yet the *mishna*'s framing suggests that outside the *mitzvah* exemption, even such cases could fall under *galus* liability if the degree of negligence were in the right middle range — which raises its own interesting questions about the boundaries of the institution.

### Negligence Levels

The *Gemara* opens its analysis of the public domain case by asking how one can be *chayav* for throwing stones into *reshus harabbim* — isn't that simply *meizid*, fully intentional-grade negligence? The *Gemara* answers, citing Shmuel bar Yitzchak: the case involves someone knocking down his wall — a purposeful act of deconstruction, not random stone-throwing. Still, the *Gemara* asks, doesn't even that constitute excessive negligence?

A further refinement emerges: *besoteir koslo l'ashpah* — we are dealing with someone knocking debris into an adjacent space that is technically a *reshus harabbim* but functions as a dump — an abandoned yard where people do not ordinarily go. This is not quite the same as throwing into a busy thoroughfare.

The *Gemara* then poses the question precisely: *hai ashpah heichi dami* — what exactly is the case of this dump? If *ishkichi bei rabbim* — people regularly frequent it — then *poshea hu*, you are negligent and too blameworthy for *galus*. If *lo shkichi bei rabbim* — nobody goes there — then *onus*, you are entirely free of blame and too blameless for *galus*. This is the essential search for the middle ground: not *poshea* and not *onus*.

Rav Pappa resolves it: the case that falls precisely in the middle is *l'ashpah she'asuya lifanos bah balailah v'ein asuya lifanos bah bayom* — a dump that people use to relieve themselves at night, when it is too public during the day for such activity, but which is not ordinarily used during the day. The person was clearing debris during the daytime. Since the place is genuinely not frequented in the daytime, you are not *poshea*. But since you know people use it at night, that knowledge ought to be on your radar — and since occasionally, *v'ika d'mikrei v'yasiv*, someone does wander there during the day when they have no choice, this is precisely the combination that places you in neither the *poshea* nor the *onus* category. It is exactly the right middle position.

Tosafot notes an additional structural observation: in the *Torah*'s model case, both the *mazik* and the *nizak* are in the same domain together. Here, the person causing the harm is in his private domain while the harm occurs in the public domain. This formal distinction means the dump case is an extension of the *Torah*'s paradigm, not a direct application of it — though from the standpoint of the calibrated negligence analysis, it maps cleanly onto the same framework.

### Self-Placement

Returning to Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's ruling that one is exempt when the person walked into the stone's path after it was released, the *Gemara* derives this from the word *u'matza* in the verse — *u'matza es re'eihu* — the axe head found his friend. The *Gemara* argues that *matza* implies the friend was already there; it connotes discovery of something pre-existing, not something that arrived subsequently. *Prat l'mamtzi es atzmo* — this excludes a case where the person made himself found, i.e., placed himself in the path of the danger.

The *Gemara* then questions whether *matza* consistently carries this meaning, citing a verse about redeeming a sold house: *u'matza kedei geulato* — he finds the means to redeem it. In that context, the *Gemara* understands *matza* to mean *now* he comes to have the funds, not that the funds were pre-existing. Rava resolves the apparent contradiction: *hacha me-inyana de-kra v'hasam me-inyana de-kra* — each instance of *u'matza* is understood from its own context. In the redemption case, the surrounding verb *v'hisiga yado* — "his hand reaches" — connotes a newly achieved capacity, and so *u'matza* there means he newly acquires the funds. In the homicide case, the whole scenario is structured around a setting that was already in place — the forest, the friends going together — and so *u'matza* means the friend was already present in that setting when the act occurred.

The practical implication remains formalistic rather than fault-based: the thrower's negligence level is identical whether the victim was standing there when he threw or walked in a moment later. Yet the law distinguishes between the two based on the physical sequence of events. When the victim was present at the moment of the act, it is described as the actor doing it to the victim. When the victim walked in afterward, it is described as the victim placing himself in the situation — *mamtzi es atzmo*. This is not a question of comparative fault, but of how the legal system categorizes the event.

---

## Discretion vs Mitzvah

### Mitzvah Chopping

The *Gemara* raises a challenge against the assumption underlying Abba Shaul's *drasha* that the *Torah*'s model case of wood-chopping is discretionary. One of the *Rabbanans* asks Rava: *mimai de-vi-chritat etzim de-reshut* — how do we know that the verse is speaking about discretionary chopping? *Dilma bi-chritat etzim de-sukkah* — perhaps it is talking about chopping wood to build a *sukkah*, which would be a *mitzvah*. Or *bi-chritat etzim de-ma'aracha* — perhaps it refers to chopping wood for the temple altar. If so, maybe even in a *mitzvah* context the *Torah* mandates *galus*, and there is no exemption at all.

### Means Not Mitzvot

Rava responds: *keivan de-i matza katuv eino choteh* — since if the wood were already chopped, there would be no *mitzvah* to chop new wood for a *sukkah* or for the altar. The act of chopping is merely a *machshir mitzvah*, a means of obtaining necessary material, not an intrinsic *mitzvah* act. Therefore *lav mitzvah* — it falls into the discretionary category regardless of its ultimate purpose. Building a *sukkah* is a *mitzvah*; procuring the lumber is not. The *Torah*'s model case therefore remains one of discretionary activity.

### Ravina Challenge

Ravina then challenges Rava with a pointed *kushya*: if the dividing line between discretionary and *mitzvah* is whether the act is a means or an intrinsic *mitzvah*, then consider the cases of the father hitting his son and the teacher hitting his student — those too are merely means to an end. If the child is already behaving correctly, there is no *mitzvah* to strike him; the physical force is only a means of achieving education, *chinuch*. On Rava's logic, the means-to-a-*mitzvah* should fall in the discretionary category, not the *mitzvah* category. So why does the *mishna* exempt these cases as *mitzvah* acts?

### Intrinsic Mitzvah?

The *Gemara* at this point offers a troubling answer: *af al gav d'gamir, nami mitzvah* — even if the child is learning properly and doing everything right, it is still a *mitzvah* to give him some physical discipline. *Mitzvah ka-avid, d'ksiv yaseir bincha veyinichaka* — the verse in Mishlei states, "Chastise your son and he will give you rest" — implying an intrinsic positive value to parental discipline beyond mere instrumentality. By this reading, a father striking his son is not just a means but an inherently obligatory act with its own *mitzvah* status. This is, frankly, a deeply disquieting conclusion, and the *Gemara* itself registers the discomfort — or at least one should register it on the *Gemara*'s behalf.

### Retraction

Rava retracts. *Hadar amrah Rava, lav milsa hi* — that was not correct; abandon what I just said. It is not the case that striking a child is an intrinsic *mitzvah*. The problem then resurfaces: on what basis are the cases of the father, the teacher, and the *shliach beis din* excluded from the *Torah*'s paradigm?

Rava's revised position shifts the distinction from intrinsic *mitzvah* status to *necessity*. *Va'asher yavo es re'eihu baya'ar* — the verse says *va'asher yavo*, someone who *happens to come* into the forest, *d'ba'i ayil vd'ba'i lo ayil* — meaning one who had a choice whether to go or not. This is the defining feature: the act was not necessary. And a *mitzvah* context, even one where the act is merely a means, counts as a *mitzvah* category precisely because it involves acts that were necessary — that had to be done.

### Shabbat Parallel

The *Gemara* parallels this analysis with a *sugya* elsewhere concerning *Shabbat*. The verse in Shemot says "in plowing and in harvesting you shall rest." Rabbi Yishmael interprets this as referring to *Shabbat*, and reads it to mean: *ma charish reshus, af katzir reshus* — just as plowing is always discretionary (there is never a *mitzvah* to plow), so too it is only discretionary harvesting that is prohibited on *Shabbat*. But if the harvesting is a *mitzvah*, it is permitted. The paradigmatic case: *yatza katzir ha-omer shehu mitzvah* — the harvesting of grain for the *omer* offering is a *mitzvah* and therefore permitted on *Shabbat*, even though harvesting in general is prohibited.

Rabbi Akiva, by contrast, reads the same verse as referring to *shvi'is* rather than *Shabbat*, and draws the principle of *tosefes shvi'is* from it — that one must add time before and after the *shmitta* year. Under Rabbi Akiva's reading, the verse is not limiting the prohibition of plowing to discretionary contexts; it is instead extending it.

### Omer Pushback

A member of the *Rabbanans* challenges Rava using this parallel: *vemi decharisha direshut* — who told you plowing is discretionary? Perhaps the verse is referring to plowing for a *mitzvah* purpose — specifically, plowing to grow wheat for the *omer*, which would make it a *mitzvah* context. And yet the verse still prohibits it on *Shabbat* — meaning there is no exemption for *mitzvah* contexts, contrary to Rabbi Yishmael's position.

Rava's response is the same as before: *keivan de-im matza charush eino choreish* — if the field were already plowed, there would be no *mitzvah* to plow it again. Therefore plowing is never necessary; it is always discretionary in the relevant sense. The same logic applies as in the *galus* context.

Ravina then challenges once more, this time specifically within the *Shabbat* framework: you are saying the distinction between discretionary and *mitzvah* is whether the act is necessary. Consider the *omer* harvest: *matza katzur eino kotzeir* — if the grain were already cut, would there be a *mitzvah* to cut it again? Presumably not. So on Rava's logic, the *omer* harvest should also be classified as discretionary, not *mitzvah*. Yet we know it is a *mitzvah* — that is the whole basis for permitting it on *Shabbat*.

### Final Necessity

The final resolution is that the line between discretionary and *mitzvah* — in both the *galus* context and the *Shabbat* context — is not intrinsic *mitzvah* value versus means-to-a-*mitzvah*, but rather necessity versus non-necessity in context. The *omer* harvest is a necessary act in a way that plowing is not: it must be performed as an act of harvesting at the right time, and if not done cannot simply be substituted by pre-existing cut grain. Plowing, even for a *mitzvah* purpose, is not like that — if the field is already plowed, nothing is lost.

What emerges from the entire discussion is that the relevant distinction drawn from *va'asher yavo* — "one who happens to come," suggesting discretion — is not a mechanical inquiry into whether the act is intrinsically obligatory or merely a means. It is a question of contextual necessity. Acts that had to be done, that could not simply have been replaced by a pre-existing state of affairs, count as *mitzvah*-adjacent for purposes of these exemptions. Acts that were not necessary in this sense — even if done in service of a *mitzvah* — remain in the discretionary category. And crucially, striking a child, which the *Gemara* initially tried to classify as an intrinsic *mitzvah*, is better understood as a necessary act of *chinuch* in context — which is what places it in the exempt category, without requiring us to say that hitting a child for no reason constitutes a *mitzvah* in itself.

---

---

# Makkot 9

## Father & Son Exile

### Mishnah Overview

The second chapter of Makkot, *Elu Hen HaGolin*, concerns those who are exiled for unintentionally killing another person. The Mishnah on this daf reads:

> *Ha'av goleh al yedei haben vehaben goleh al yedei ha'av hakol golin al yedei Yisrael veyisrael golin al yedeihen chutz miger toshav veger toshav eino goleh ela al yedei ger toshav.*

The father is exiled on account of his unintentional murder of his son, and the son is exiled on account of his unintentional murder of his father. Everyone — a category we will unpack shortly — is exiled for killing a *Yisrael*, and a Jew is exiled for killing any member of this group, except when the victim is a *ger toshav*. The *ger toshav* himself is exiled only when he has killed another *ger toshav*.

Three distinct categories appear in the background of this Mishnah. The *ger toshav* is someone who is not Jewish but who fulfills the seven Noahide laws and resides among the Jewish people. The *oved kochavim* is a non-Jew who has accepted none of these obligations. The *eved Kena'ani* is a Canaanite servant living within a Jewish household. These three, together with *Yisrael*, form the spectrum of persons whose status the Mishnah addresses.

### Why Father & Son?

The Mishnah's decision to single out the father and son is immediately striking. After all, any person who kills another unintentionally is subject to exile — why must the Mishnah specify this particular relationship? The Gemara will probe precisely this question, alongside the broader issue of who exactly is included in *hakol* and on what basis any member of that group might be excluded.

### Father Striking Son

The Gemara opens with a challenge to the first clause: *ha'av goleh al yedei haben*. The father is exiled for the unintentional killing of his son — yet earlier we were told that a father who strikes his son and thereby unintentionally kills him is *yatza*, excluded from exile. How do we reconcile the two statements? The cases must differ in some meaningful way.

### Teaching Torah & Craft

The Gemara's answer turns on the context of *degamir* — the son has already learned. The question, then, is what exactly the father was teaching when the fatal blow occurred. The Mishnah's specification applies to a father teaching his son a profession, *shulya deNagrai* — an apprenticeship in carpentry, for instance — rather than Torah. One might object that teaching a son a trade is itself obligatory, since the verse *ur'eh chayim im ha-ishah asher ahavta* implies that providing one's child with a livelihood is a religious duty. The Gemara's resolution is that the case concerns a son who has already acquired both Torah learning and a professional skill, and the father is now teaching him an entirely different craft, *umanuta achrita*. This specificity is what the Mishnah is highlighting.

The discussion then turns to the second clause, *vehaben goleh al yedei ha'av*. The Gemara raises a *remini*: we already know from a general principle that anyone who kills another unintentionally is exiled, but there is an explicit exclusion — *prat lemakeh aviv* — for one who kills his father, who receives a more severe punishment rather than exile. So in what sense does the Mishnah say the son is exiled *on account of* the father?

Rav Kahana proposes a resolution: *lo kashya* — this is not a contradiction. The two statements reflect the positions of Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis respectively, and their disagreement hinges on the hierarchy of capital punishments. Rabbi Shimon maintains that *chenek* (strangulation) is more severe than *sayaf* (beheading by sword), while the Rabbis hold the reverse — *sayaf* is more severe than *chenek*. The principle at stake is that unintentional commission of an act punishable by a given mode of execution can be atoned through exile, but only if that mode of execution falls below a certain threshold of severity. According to Rabbi Shimon, for whom strangulation is more severe, the son who unintentionally kills his father — whose intentional act would be punishable by strangulation — cannot be atoned through exile. According to the Rabbis, who rank beheading as more severe, the unintentional commission of an act punishable by the sword *can* be atoned through exile. Hence the Mishnah's statement that the son is exiled reflects the Rabbinic position, while the exclusion reflects Rabbi Shimon's.

Why exactly the severity of the mode of execution determines eligibility for exile remains difficult to fully unpack. It appears to rest on *gezeirat hakatuv* — a scriptural decree that simply establishes the categories without compelling logical derivation. The *ir miklat* itself is in many respects a *gezeirat hakatuv*, and the same applies to the categories of who may enter it.

### Son Killing Father

Rava offers an alternative explanation that focuses on the nature of the son's act itself. He argues that when a son kills his father, even unintentionally, two transgressions are necessarily involved: he must have struck him (*chavurah*) and the blow must have been fatal. This double dimension lends the act a quality that borders on intentionality. Since had the act been intentional (*bemezid*) the son would be liable to execution (*bar katla*), unintentionally (*beshogeg*) he is exiled. The Mishnah therefore specifically mentions the son's exile in relation to the father to teach us that despite the compounded nature of the transgression, exile remains the appropriate atonement in the unintentional case. As the *Aruch LaNer* notes, a scriptural verse is still needed, since the logical argument alone is not fully compelling.

---

## Categories of Killers

### Hakol Golin

The Mishnah's phrase *hakol golin al yedei Yisrael* — everyone is exiled for the killing of a Jew — prompts the Gemara to ask: *le'ituyei mai*? What is the Mishnah adding with the word *hakol*? The answer: *le'ituyei eved ve'Kuti* — it comes to include the Canaanite servant and the Samaritan (*Kuti*).

### Servants & Samaritans

A *baraita* elaborates: *eved ve'Kuti goleh velokeh al yedei Yisrael, ve'Yisrael goleh velokeh al yedei Kuti ve'eved*. A Canaanite servant and a Samaritan are exiled for the unintentional killing of a Jew, and are also flogged on account of a Jew. Conversely, a Jew is exiled for the unintentional killing of a *Kuti* or servant, and is likewise flogged on their account. The Gemara immediately distinguishes the two penalties: exile applies for killing (*de'katlei*), and lashes apply for cursing (*de'lateih*).

### Cursing Non-Jews

This is where the analysis becomes complicated, particularly regarding lashes for cursing. The verse states *venasi be'amcha lo ta'or* — you shall not curse a leader among your people — and the Gemara understands *be'amcha* to refer specifically to one who acts as part of your people, *oseh ma'aseh amcha*. How then does a Jew incur lashes for cursing a *Kuti* or non-Jew? The lines are murky, and the Gemara acknowledges the difficulty.

### False Testimony Case

Rav Acha bar Yaakov attempts to resolve this by suggesting the case involves false testimony followed by *hazama* — refutation. If someone testified falsely and was subsequently subjected to *hazama*, the *edim zomemim* receive the punishment that would have befallen the defendant. Perhaps the lashes derive from this mechanism. The Gemara immediately challenges this: is a *eved* (Canaanite servant) even eligible to testify? The answer is that he is not, so this framing cannot stand either.

### Insignificant Blow
