A more refined resolution is then offered by Rav Acha son of Rav Ika. The specific case under discussion involves *haka'ah she'ein bah shaveh prutah* — a blow that does not cause damage worth even one *prutah*. Rav Ami citing Rabbi Yochanan teaches: one who strikes another with a blow worth less than a *prutah* — since there is no monetary payment due — incurs lashes for violating the Torah prohibition. The case of lashes in the *baraita* is thus this precise scenario: a blow too minor to generate financial liability, but serious enough to constitute a violation warranting corporal punishment.

---

## Ger Toshav Status

### Ger Toshav Intro

The Mishnah states that a Jew is exiled for unintentional killings across the board *chutz miger toshav* — except with respect to the *ger toshav*. Some commentaries note that the text as it stands is ambiguous — is the exception about a *ger toshav* being the victim, or the *ger toshav* as the perpetrator? The Gemara itself flags the difficulty, with some suggesting the correct reading should be *chutz miger toshav* rather than *chutz me'al yedei ger toshav*.

What is at stake is a fundamental question: is the *ger toshav* categorically equivalent to the *oved kochavim*, or does his acceptance of the Noahide laws and his residence among the Jewish people grant him a distinct intermediate status? *Alma ger toshav oved kochavim hu* — is the *ger toshav* simply a non-Jew? The Gemara poses this as an open question.

### Two Pesukim

Two verses in Bamidbar seem to point in opposite directions. Bamidbar 35:15 reads *livnei Yisrael vela-ger vela-toshav betocham tihyena sheish ha-arim* — the six cities of refuge shall be for the children of Israel, and for the *ger*, and for the *toshav* among them. This verse, using the formulation *la-ger vela-toshav* (reminiscent of Avraham's *ger ve-toshav anochi*), implies that the *arei miklat* are available to all residents of the land. Yet Bamidbar 35:12 states *vehayu lachem ha-arim lemiklat* — the cities shall be for *you* — from which we derive *lachem velo lagerim*: for you and not for the strangers. The contradiction is direct.

### Rav Kahana's Answer

Rav Kahana resolves the tension: *lo kashya*. One verse applies to a *ger toshav* who killed another *ger toshav*, and the other applies to a *ger toshav* who killed a *Yisrael*. As a resident of the land, the *ger toshav* is eligible for the *ir miklat* when he has killed one of his own kind. But if he kills a Jew, exile cannot serve as atonement and he faces execution. The two verses thus address distinct scenarios rather than conflicting rules.

### Baraita Contradiction

The Gemara raises a fresh contradiction from a *baraita*: *lefichach ger ve-oved kochavim she-haregu neheragin* — therefore, a *ger* and an *oved kochavim* who kill are executed. The *baraita* groups the *ger* together with the *oved kochavim*, and argues by analogy: just as with the *oved kochavim* it makes no difference whether he killed someone of his own kind or someone of a different status — he is executed regardless — so too the *ger* should be executed regardless of whom he killed. This undercuts Rav Kahana's distinction, which depended on *whom* the *ger toshav* killed determining the outcome.

### Downward vs Upward

Rav Chisda proposes a different resolution: *lo kashya — kan she-harago derech yerida, kan she-harago derech aliya*. The distinction is not about whom was killed, but *how* the killing occurred — whether it was in a downward motion (*derech yerida*) or an upward motion (*derech aliya*). A downward killing, such as dropping an object that falls onto someone below, is understood as carrying a lesser degree of culpability — more plausibly accidental. An upward killing, such as throwing something that strikes someone, implies a more active and directed motion. The rule, as Rav Chisda formulates it, is: *derech yerida de-Yisrael gali ihu nami sagi lei be-galut* — in a downward-motion case, if a Jew would be exiled, the *ger toshav* similarly suffices with exile. *Derech aliya de-Yisrael patur ihu neherag* — in an upward-motion case, where a Jew would be exempt from exile (*patur* here meaning exempt from *galut* but liable to some other consequence), the *ger toshav* is executed.

### Rava's Challenge

Rava challenges Rav Chisda's framework by means of a *kal vachomer*. If in the downward-motion case — where the Jew would be exiled — the *ger toshav* is also only exiled, fine. But in the upward-motion case — where a Jew would be exempt from exile — shouldn't the *ger toshav* also at most be exempt from exile, rather than being executed? The *kal vachomer* seems to run in exactly the opposite direction from Rav Chisda's conclusion. The argument resists easy resolution, and the Gemara shifts course.

### Permitted Killing Case

Rava proposes an alternative framing: *be'omer mutar* — the case concerns a *ger toshav* who killed another *ger toshav* believing that the killing was permitted. This introduces a new axis of analysis, one that goes beyond the physical mechanics of the killing and focuses on the killer's state of mind.

### Mutar Anuss Category

Abaye challenges Rava on precisely this point. He distinguishes between *mutar anuss* — one who believed the act was permitted due to circumstances genuinely beyond his control — and *mutar mezid* — one whose belief that the act was permitted itself reflects a kind of recklessness or quasi-intentionality. Rava's response is that one who says *mutar* — that the killing is permitted — is *karov lemezid*, close to intentional. Even within the domain of *shegaga*, there is gradation: unintentional killing can range from the truly coerced and unavoidable to the nearly deliberate.

This distinction maps roughly onto the difference between negligence and recklessness in legal reasoning: a driver exercising every caution who is struck by another vehicle occupies an entirely different moral and legal category from one driving recklessly in poor conditions after drinking. It is the same external outcome — an unintentional death — but the internal quality of the act differs fundamentally.

### Mistaken Identity

The Gemara observes that Abaye and Rava are consistent with their respective positions elsewhere: *ve'azdu letameihu de'itmar kesavor behemah venimtza adam, Kena'ani venimtza ger toshav*. Another mode of *shegaga* — one that operates independently of the physical mechanics — is mistaken identity. The killer thought he was killing an animal (*behemah*) but it turned out to be a human being (*adam*); or he thought he was killing a *Kena'ani* servant and it turned out to be a *ger toshav*. Like the famous image in *The Little Prince* — what adults see as a hat is in fact a snake that has swallowed an elephant — the same act can be entirely different in nature depending on what the actor perceived.

Rava rules that in the case of *omer mutar* — believing the killing to be permitted — the person is *chayav*, liable, because his actions border on intentional. Rav Chisda rules that such a person is *patur* in the capital sense, treating him as a victim of circumstances beyond his control, an *omer mutar anuss*. The tension between the two positions — one emphasizing the culpable proximity to intentionality, the other emphasizing the involuntary nature of the error — remains unresolved.

---

## Avimelech Story

### Avimelech & Sarah

Rava now brings a proof from the story of Avimelech and Sarah to support his position that *omer mutar* borders on intentional. The Gemara cites the verse spoken by God to Avimelech in a dream: *hincha met al ha-ishah asher lakachta* — you are going to die on account of the woman you have taken. Avimelech had taken Sarah from Avraham, believing she was Avraham's sister — a paradigmatic case of acting in error, under circumstances he believed to be legitimate.

The Gemara asks: what does *hincha met* mean here? Is this a death penalty to be administered *bidei adam* — by a human court? The Gemara considers this and concludes: *bidei shamayim* — the judgment is from heaven. The proof comes from the verse in which God says *mehato li*, you have transgressed against Me. The Gemara then draws a parallel with Yosef, who when resisting Potiphar's wife declared *vehatati lelohim* — I would sin against God. The Gemara asks: was Yosef not equally sinning against a man? It answers: *ella dino masur le'adam* — yes, but the judgment for such an act is ultimately rendered by people, by a human court. And the same applies here: *hacha nami dino masur le'adam* — in Avimelech's case too, his judgment is given over to human reckoning. This is Rava's point: even though Avimelech acted in genuine ignorance of the full situation — he was told she was a sister — God declares him deserving of death. The *omer mutar* does not escape liability simply by virtue of his error.

### Return of Sarah

Abaye raises an objection to this reading. Avimelech himself protested: *hagoy gam tzadik taharog* — will You slay a nation even though it is righteous? And God did not simply reject his plea outright. Does this not imply divine acceptance that Avimelech was, to some degree, innocent?

The Gemara responds that the return of Sarah was mandated regardless — *mikol makom* — on multiple grounds. God's instruction *ve'atah hashev eshet ha'ish ki navi hu* — now return the wife of this man, for he is a prophet — does not mean, as a superficial reading might suggest, that Sarah must be returned *only because* Avraham is a prophet and that she could have been retained had he been an ordinary man. That reading is immediately rejected as absurd. Rather, as Rav Shmuel bar Nachmani says in the name of Rabbi Yonatan, God's message to Avimelech was this: return the wife unconditionally. And as for your claim of righteousness — *halo hu amar li achoti hi*, he told me she was his sister — consider that claim more carefully.

### Ben Noach Lesson

The Gemara then shifts to an examination of how Avraham knew that Avimelech's intentions were not pure. The teaching is: *achsanai hu sheba la'ir al iskei achila ushtiya shoalin oto* — when a guest comes to town, the host's proper concern is food and drink, asking after the traveler's wellbeing and the journey. *Klum shoalin oto ishtecha zo achotecha zo* — would any proper host immediately ask a guest, "Is that your wife or your sister?" The fact that Avimelech asked precisely this question revealed the nature of his interest.

From this the Gemara derives: *mikan sheben Noach neherag shehaya lo lilmod velo lamad* — from here we learn that a *ben Noach* who should have learned and did not learn is liable to execution. Avimelech, as a *ben Noach* — analogous to the *ger toshav* who lives among the Jewish people — had the obligation to learn proper norms from those around him. His failure to internalize basic ethical conduct, revealed by the very nature of his inquiry, strips him of the defense of pure ignorance. Avraham intuited from Avimelech's question alone that his surroundings were dangerous — which is precisely why he had instructed Sarah beforehand. The *ger toshav* who fails to learn from the Jewish community around him bears moral responsibility for what follows.

---

## Blind & Hater

### Blind Person

A new Mishnah introduces two further special cases. *Hasuma eino goleh divrei Rabbi Yehuda; Rabbi Meir omer goleh* — the blind person does not go into exile; this is the view of Rabbi Yehuda. Rabbi Meir says that the blind person does go into exile.

### The Hater

The Mishnah then addresses the *soneh* — the hater. It is important to note that the Hebrew *soneh* is not the same as *oyev*, an enemy. An enemy is someone openly opposed to you; a *soneh* is someone who harbors hatred toward you, potentially while maintaining outward relations. The verse we recite when opening the *aron* — *vayehi binsoa ha'aron vayomer Moshe: kumah Hashem veyafutzu oyvecha vayanusu mesanecha* — distinguishes between *oyvecha* (your enemies) and *mesanecha* (those who hate you), two distinct categories. The Mishnah's ruling concerns the latter. *Hasoneh eino goleh* — the hater does not go into exile.

### Hater Executed

Rabbi Yosi goes further: *hasoneh neherag mipnei shehu kemuad* — the hater is executed because he is considered like one who has already been warned. The logic is that a person harboring hatred toward the victim possesses an internal disposition that makes the killing quasi-intentional. The *soneh* does not require formal *hatrah* (prior warning) because the animus itself functions as the operative warning.

### Shimon's Distinction

Rabbi Shimon draws a more nuanced line: *yesh soneh goleh ve'yesh soneh she'eino goleh* — there is a hater who is exiled, and there is a hater who is not exiled. The operative principle: *kol shehu yachol lomar lada'at harag eino goleh, veshelo lada'at harag harei zeh goleh* — anyone of whom it can be said that he killed knowingly does not receive exile; one who killed without that knowledge of intent goes into exile. Rabbi Shimon thus distinguishes within the category of *soneh* based on whether the particular killing evidenced deliberate direction of the hateful impulse.

### Belo Re'ot Exclusion

The Gemara seeks the textual basis for these positions in the phrase *belo re'ot* — "without seeing" — which appears in the context of the *ir miklat*. *Tanu Rabanan: belo re'ot perat lesuma divrei Rabbi Yehuda* — the phrase "without seeing" excludes the blind person from the *ir miklat*, according to Rabbi Yehuda. Rabbi Meir, however, reads *belo re'ot* in the opposite direction — as specifically including the blind person. The verse in question describes someone who enters a forest to chop wood (*va'asher yavo et re'ehu baya'ar lachtov etzim*), swings the axe, and the iron head flies off and kills someone nearby — a paradigmatic case of unintentional killing. It is in this context that *belo re'ot* appears.

### Mi'ut Principles

The dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Meir turns on a technical principle of *mi'ut* (exclusion). Rabbi Yehuda reads *belo re'ot* as a *mi'ut* — an exclusion — that removes the blind person from eligibility for the *ir miklat*. Rabbi Meir counters that we also have the phrase *bivli da'at* (without knowledge) in the same context, which would be a second exclusion. The hermeneutical rule is that *ein mi'ut achar mi'ut ela lerabbot* — two consecutive exclusions in the same passage do not compound each other but rather expand the scope; the second exclusion comes to include rather than exclude. Therefore, Rabbi Meir concludes that the blind person is included in the *ir miklat*.

Rabbi Yehuda responds that *bivli da'at* is not functioning as a second *mi'ut* parallel to *belo re'ot* — it addresses a distinct category, namely the one who acts without any awareness at all, as opposed to one who acts with directed intent (*perat lemitkaven veda'at*). The two phrases operate on different axes entirely and do not trigger the double-exclusion rule.

---

---

# Makkot 10

## Blind Person Debate

### Intro: Blind Person

The daf opens in the middle of a tannaitic dispute regarding the culpability of a blind person who unintentionally caused a death. Rabbi Yehuda holds that a blind person does not go into exile, while Rabbi Meir holds that he does. One might initially frame this debate as a question about degree of responsibility — how much awareness and caution can we attribute to a blind person navigating the world? — but the Gemara anchors the disagreement firmly in hermeneutical analysis of the relevant verses rather than in any general theory of responsibility.

### Hermeneutics: Exclude/In…

The Gemara introduces a *baraita*: the phrase *belo re'ot*, "without seeing," implies that the killer could have seen his victim but failed to do so — which, according to Rabbi Yehuda, excludes (*prat l'suma*) a blind person for whom there was never any possibility of seeing at all. Rabbi Meir reads the same phrase in the opposite direction: *belo re'ot* comes specifically to include (*l'rabbot et hasuma*) even someone who cannot see.

### R. Yehuda: 'Without Seei…

The Gemara then asks: what is Rabbi Yehuda's textual basis? The verse states, "and one who comes with his friend into the forest" — which encompasses even a blind person. Then follows the phrase *belo re'ot*, "without seeing," which implies that the killer could have seen, thereby excluding the blind person for whom sight was never possible. On this reading, Rabbi Yehuda's interpretation is internally coherent and flows naturally from the text.

### R. Meir: Two Exclusions

Rabbi Meir's position requires more explanation. He concedes that *belo re'ot* carries an exclusionary force. However, there is a second verse, *bivli da'at*, "without awareness," which similarly comes to exclude — implying someone who could have been aware, as opposed to someone who could not have been. Now there are two exclusionary phrases, each pointing toward limiting the class of those who go into exile. The Gemara applies the classic rabbinic principle: *mi'ut achar mi'ut* — a double exclusion functions not as exclusion but as inclusion. Since both phrases converge in excluding the blind person, their combined effect is to include him. This is admittedly a striking piece of hermeneutics; the obvious rejoinder is simply that if the intention were to include, the Torah could have remained silent on both counts. The interpretive move is recognized as somewhat counterintuitive, even if the underlying legal position need not be.

### R. Yehuda: Intent Issue

Rabbi Yehuda, having already used *belo re'ot* for his exclusion of the blind person, must account for the second phrase, *bivli da'at*. He uses it to exclude intentional killing — not outright premeditated murder, but rather a case in which someone intended to kill one thing and inadvertently killed a person, such as aiming at an animal and striking a human being. That class of actor, who was in some sense aiming and choosing, falls outside the category of accidental homicide warranting exile.

---

## R. Yossi: Hater

### R. Yossi: Execution

The Mishna had established that a *soneh* — someone who bore a known enmity toward the victim — does not go into exile, grounding this in the verse *ve-hu lo soneh lo mitmol shilshom*, "and he was not his enemy from yesterday or the day before." The underlying logic is that when an enemy kills someone even under apparently accidental circumstances, we suspect the act was intentional. Rabbi Yossi now goes a step further: the *soneh* is actually executed.

### Responsibility Levels

The reasoning reflects a broader structural principle in these laws. *Galut* — exile — occupies a precise middle position on the spectrum of culpability. Someone too far removed from responsibility, such as the blind person in Rabbi Yehuda's view, does not deserve exile because he bears no meaningful fault. Someone too far toward culpability — such as the *soneh* — also does not receive *galut*, not because he is innocent but because he is too suspect to merit the protective *kapara* of exile. We cannot execute him for lack of absolute proof, but we will not grant him the benefit of the city of refuge either. Rabbi Yossi, however, holds that the presumption of intent is strong enough to execute him outright.

### Warning Problem

A significant difficulty immediately presents itself: where is the *hasro'ah*, the formal warning required before capital punishment can be administered? The witnesses may have observed what looked like an accident — a rope breaking, a barrel slipping — and even if they find the circumstances suspicious given the defendant's known enmity toward the deceased, the formal technical requirement of warning someone immediately before his act seems to be entirely missing. The Gemara addresses this.

---

## R. Yossi b. R. Yehuda

### Chaver: No Warning

The Gemara resolves the problem by attributing the position of Rabbi Yossi to the broader ruling of Rabbi Yossi bar Rabbi Yehuda: a *chaver* — a learned person who is expert in the law — does not require *hasro'ah*. The *baraita* states this explicitly: *chaver eino tzarich hasro'ah*.

### Purpose of Warning

The reason is that *hasro'ah* serves a single essential function: to distinguish between *shogeg* and *meizid*, between one who acts without knowledge and one who acts in deliberate defiance. The formal warning achieves this by ensuring, first, that the person is fully aware of what he is about to do and, second, that he knows it is forbidden. The Gemara in Sanhedrin elaborates that *hasro'ah* does even more — it creates the reality that the person is acting in direct rejection of legal authority, and by accepting the consequences (*hitir atzmo l'misa*), he licenses the court to execute him. But Rabbi Yossi bar Rabbi Yehuda maintains that the sole indispensable function of warning is to establish willful intent, and nothing more.

### Hater: No Warning

Combining the two elements: a *soneh* who is also a *chaver* satisfies both requirements without formal warning. As a *chaver*, he knows the law and therefore knows his act is forbidden. As a *soneh*, we presume he is not acting by accident. Together, these facts substitute for the *hasro'ah*. The court may proceed to execution.

It must be said that this remains a striking conclusion. Even sworn enemies sometimes have genuine accidents, and the move from presumption to execution is a significant one. The question of how a *soneh* is established in the first place — what proof suffices to label someone a formal enemy of the deceased — is itself an open question, though it may be that this status was already presumed and on record prior to the incident. Whether witnesses observing an apparently accidental event can honestly attest to the intentionality of the act, or whether we are relying on a prior presumption to supply that element, is a tension that runs more naturally into a discussion of Sanhedrin than of Makkot.

---

## R. Shimon: Context

### Shimon: May/May Not

Rabbi Shimon takes what might be called a contextual or circumstantial approach. He holds that a *soneh* sometimes goes into exile and sometimes does not, depending on whether the particular circumstances of the killing make it possible to say (*yachol lomar*) that the act was intentional. This is an important nuance: Rabbi Shimon does not simply rule categorically based on the status of the parties, but requires an evaluation of the act itself.

### Rope Break vs. Slip

A *baraita* provides the concrete illustration. *Nifsak goleh* — if the rope broke, he goes into exile. *Nishmat eino goleh* — if it slipped out of his hands, he does not go into exile. The intuition is that if the rope broke (*nifsak*), the most natural explanation is that it was an accident, and even a *soneh* should receive *galut*. If it slipped out of his hands (*nishmat*), the circumstances lend themselves to the possibility that the release was intentional — he let go deliberately — and this opens up enough of a reasonable suspicion, even if not more likely than the innocent interpretation, to deny him exile.

### Contradiction: Two Barai…

A second *baraita*, however, appears to say the exact opposite: Rabbi Shimon holds that a person never goes into exile unless the tool slips (*nishmat*) from his hand. This would make the slipping case the one that leads to exile and the breaking case the one that does not — a direct reversal of the first *baraita*. The Gemara acknowledges the contradiction sharply: *kashya nifsak anifsak, kashya nishmat anishmat*.

### Resolution: Friend/Enemy

The Gemara resolves the first contradiction — *nishmat* versus *nishmat* — by distinguishing between the nature of the relationship. Where the actor is a *soneh*, the slipping (*nishmat*) case results in no exile because we suspect intentionality. Where the actor is an *ohev*, a friend, the slipping case does result in exile because there is no such suspicion and the act looks purely accidental. This resolution is clean and consistent.

### Rabbi/Rabbanan Debate

The second contradiction — *nifsak* versus *nifsak* — is resolved differently. The Gemara invokes the dispute between Rabbi and Rabbanan regarding the axe-head case. Rabbanan hold that even when the actor is left holding part of the instrument while another part flies off and kills someone, exile is warranted. Rabbi holds that in such a case — where the actor retains a portion — there is no exile; the *goleh* case is specifically where, like a splinter, no part of the instrument remains in the actor's hand. Accordingly, one *baraita* presents the *nifsak* case from the perspective of Rabbanan (exile), and the other presents it from the perspective of Rabbi (no exile). Rabbi Shimon in the two *baraitot* is thus being read as operating according to two different tannaitic frameworks, which is itself somewhat unsettling — one might ask why a single *amora* would present Rabbi Shimon's ruling according to two competing tannaitic opinions rather than resolving the matter. The Gemara leaves this as its answer without further elaboration.

A note on the underlying dispute: Rabbi himself reads the Torah's paradigm case not as the axe-head flying off (*hashel habarzel min ha'etz* meaning the iron flies from the wood), but as the axe causing a chip of wood to fly off from the wood being chopped. The *Torah* case and the *Rabbanan* case are thus in dispute over the very reading of the scriptural paradigm.

---

## Cities of Refuge

### Six Cities Total

The Gemara now turns to the *arei miklat* — the cities of refuge. The Mishna establishes that there were three on each side of the Jordan: three designated by Moshe in the Transjordan and three designated by Yehoshua in the land of Canaan, as the verse states: "You shall give three cities across the Jordan and three cities you shall give in the land of Canaan."

### Simultaneous Operation

A key operational principle follows: the three cities in the Transjordan did not function as operative *arei miklat* until the three in the land of Israel had been designated as well, a process that occurred only after fourteen years of conquest and apportionment. The verse states *sheish arei miklat tihyena* — there should be six — and the Gemara derives: *ad sheyiyu sheshtan koltot ke'achas*, until all six are operating simultaneously.

### Roads Between Cities

Highways were constructed connecting the cities to one another. This is somewhat surprising — one might expect the roads to lead from the general population toward the cities, since a fugitive fleeing from anywhere in the land needs to reach a city quickly. The focus on roads between the cities themselves, rather than roads leading to them, is not entirely clear, though it may be that establishing a network of clear roads connecting the six created a kind of major route structure that made access from adjacent regions more direct. The verse *tachin lecha haderech v'shilashta* — "you shall prepare the road and divide into thirds" — is cited as the source.

### Talmidei Chachamim

Two *talmidei chachamim* were dispatched to accompany the person fleeing to the city of refuge. The concern was that the *goel hadam* — the blood avenger — might pursue the fugitive en route and kill him before he reached safety. The *talmidei chachamim* were to speak to the *goel hadam* and dissuade him from violence. One might note that two scholars seem a curious choice for what amounts to a security detail; presumably their authority and ability to invoke the law carried more weight than physical deterrence. The system reflects a broader effort to bring what had been a practice of vigilante justice under institutional and rabbinic control — a dynamic that has an analogue in the *sotah* procedure as treated in Gemara Sotah, where the court similarly inserts itself by having *talmidei chachamim* accompany the husband.

### R. Meir: Self-Defense

Rabbi Meir holds that the fugitive himself may speak to the *goel hadam* and argue his own case, citing the verse *vezeh d'var harotzeach* — "and this is the matter of the killer" — as indicating that the killer himself has a voice in the proceeding. The practical implication is somewhat unclear. The *tanna kamma* does not appear to prohibit self-advocacy; the difference may be that Rabbi Meir dispenses with the need for accompanying *talmidei chachamim* entirely, believing that the fugitive's own words suffice, while others may hold that self-advocacy would be counterproductive or that the *talmidei chachamim* serve an independent institutional function regardless.

### Initial Custody Rule

Rabbi Yose bar Rabbi Yehuda introduces a general procedural rule: at the outset (*batchila*), whether the homicide appears to be *shogeg* or *meizid*, all such individuals are first sent to the city of refuge. Rashi clarifies that *batchila* here does not denote an earlier historical practice that was later changed; rather, it describes the first step in the process — regardless of the suspect's claims of innocence, the initial response is to direct everyone to the *ir miklat* in order to control the situation. Afterward, the *beit din* summons the person and tries the case.

### Three Outcomes

From the city of refuge, three outcomes are possible. One found guilty of intentional murder (*mechuyav mita*) is executed. One who is fully exonerated (*lo nischayev mita*) is released entirely. And one who committed a genuine *shogeg* killing (*nischayev galut*) is returned — in the sense of formally confirmed — to the city of refuge. The verse *v'heshivu oso ha'eidah el ir miklato* is cited as the source for this last category.

---

## Geographic Distribution

### Named Cities

The *baraita* lists the six cities by name. On the west bank of the Jordan, in the land of Israel: Hebron in Judah, Shechem in Mount Ephraim, and Kedesh in Naftali. On the east bank: Betzer in the wilderness, Ramous in Gilead, and Golan in Bashan.

### Parallel Arrangement

The cities were arranged in parallel, like rows in a vineyard (*k'min shtei shurot shebakarem*), such that the cities on one side of the Jordan corresponded directly to those on the other. This implies not only that they were matched pairs but that each set was arrayed in a straight line north to south, so that Chevron corresponded to Betzer, Shechem to Ramous, and Kedesh to Golan.

### Equal Spacing

The verse's instruction *ushilashta* — "you shall divide into thirds" — is understood to require equal spacing: the distance from the southern border to Chevron equals the distance from Chevron to Shechem, which equals the distance from Shechem to Kedesh, which equals the distance from Kedesh to the northern border. This technically divides the land into four equal segments with three evenly spaced cities — hence the word "thirds" refers to the three intervals created by three points, even though the land is effectively quartered.

### Gilead Murderers

A geographic asymmetry presents itself: three cities serve the two and a half tribes of Transjordan, while three also serve the much more populous west bank. Why the equal distribution? Abaye explains: *be-Gilad shechichi rotzchim* — murderers were prevalent in Gilead. The verse supports this: *Gilead kiryat poalei aven, akuva mi-dam* — Gilead is a city of evildoers, steeped in blood. Rabbi Elazar adds that *akuva mi-dam* means they would *plot* to kill (*oklavim laharog nefashot*), not merely act in passion. The higher frequency of homicides in the Transjordan justified having three cities serve that smaller population.

### Shechem Murderers

Another problem: even within the land of Israel itself, the arrangement is not fully equitable. The cities in the north and south are farther apart, meaning that an inhabitant of the peripheral regions faces a longer maximum journey than someone in the center, where Shechem sits. The average distance to an *ir miklat* for someone in the middle of the land is correspondingly shorter than for someone at the edges. Abaye answers again: *be-Shechem nami shechichi rotzchim* — Shechem too had a disproportionately high rate of murderers, justifying placing a city of refuge there at the center of the land. The verse from Hoshea is cited: "As troops of robbers wait for a man, so does the band of priests — they murder in the way toward Shechem." The reference to priests (*kohanim*) is explained by Rabbi Elazar: just as *kohanim* band together to go to the threshing floors to collect *terumah*, so the people of that region would band together to commit murder. The explanation is admittedly somewhat elliptical, but the association of Shechem with violence is established through the verse.

### Six vs. Forty-Two

The Gemara notes that the Torah also commands the addition of 42 cities of refuge beyond the primary six (the cities of the Levites designated to function as secondary *arei miklat*). Abaye distinguishes between them: the six primary cities provide sanctuary whether the fugitive arrived there intentionally seeking refuge or merely happened to be present (*bein le-daat bein she-lo le-daat*). The 42 secondary cities provide legal sanctuary only if the fugitive went there specifically for the purpose of seeking refuge (*le-daat*); incidental presence does not protect.

---

## Hebron & Kadesh

### Hebron: Suburbs

The Gemara raises a textual difficulty: is Hebron really an *ir miklat*? The verse states that Caleb was given Hebron, as Moshe had promised him — which seems inconsistent with it being a public city. Abaye resolves this: what was given to Caleb was the *suburb* (*parvara*) of the city, its surrounding fields and outlying areas. The verse itself says, "the fields of the city and its courtyards they gave to Caleb ben Yefuneh" — meaning only the surrounding land, not the city itself, which retained its status as a public *ir miklat*.

### Kadesh: Village

A parallel question is raised about Kadesh: can it be an *ir miklat* if the Torah elsewhere lists it among the fortified cities (*arei mivtzar*)? A *baraita* rules that *arei miklat* must be medium-sized towns — not small villages and not large cities. A major fortified city would fall into the prohibited category of *kerachim gedolim*. Two answers are offered. Rav Yosef says there were simply two separate places named Kadesh — one the fortified city, the other the *ir miklat*. Rav Ashi offers a different resolution, analogous to the Hebron answer: just as there is a city called Selikum and a separate place called "the *akra* of Selikum" (i.e., the fortified citadel of Selikum), so too there is Kadesh the large fortified city and Kadesh the town nearby, which is the *ir miklat*. On this reading, the two Kadeshes are not entirely separate localities but a city and its smaller adjacent community.

---

## Requirements & Rules

### Town Size

Returning to the *baraita* itself: *arei miklat* must be medium-sized towns — not too small and not too large. Extremes in either direction would be inappropriate.

### Water & Markets

The cities must be settled only where there is water; if natural water is unavailable, water must be brought in artificially. They must also have markets (*shevakim*), since the inhabitants require access to food and provisions.

### Population Needs

The cities must be placed where there is an *ochlusin* — a surrounding population — so that they are not isolated. Rashi explains that this requirement serves a security function: an isolated *ir miklat* would be vulnerable to attack by a *goel hadam* and others; the presence of surrounding towns reduces that vulnerability. If the internal population of the city itself (*diyureihem*) declines, it must be replenished — by whatever means necessary — and the repopulated city must include *kohanim*, *Leviyim*, and *Yisraelim* in a proper social diversity.

### Weapon Prohibition

Weapons (*klei zayin*) may not be sold in the *ir miklat*, nor may trapping implements (*klei metzudah*). The reason is self-evident: the city of refuge must not become a place where a *goel hadam* can conveniently acquire the means to kill the fugitive he is pursuing.

### Nets & Ropes

Rabbi Nechemia's position extends the prohibition to trapping implements generally. The *chachamim* permit selling trapping implements but agree that nets (*metzudot*) may not be spread out within the city, and ropes (*chavalim*) may not be laid or strung there either — *kedei shelo tehei regel Goel HaDam metzuyah* — so as not to encourage the *goel hadam* to frequent the city on the pretense of conducting his craft, as he might find occasion to use such things against the fugitive. The precise distinction between what the *chachamim* permit and what they prohibit remains somewhat unclear even after the Gemara's explanation.

### Verse: 'And Live'

Rabbi Yitzchak derives from the verse *venas el achat he'arim ha'eleh vachai* — "he shall flee to one of these cities and live" — that the city of refuge must genuinely sustain life: *avid lei midei d'tehavi lei chiyuta*, one must provide the fugitive with everything necessary for his subsistence once he arrives.

### Student-Teacher Exile

A *baraita* rules: if a student goes into exile, his *rebbe* goes with him — derived from the same word *vachai*, "and live," understood as encompassing spiritual life. Without Torah study, the student cannot truly live; without his teacher, he cannot learn. The obligation that the teacher accompany his exiled student into the city of refuge is an application of this principle. This is admittedly a striking imposition on the teacher, who is uprooted from his home and community and, presumably, from his other students — for the sake of one student who accidentally killed someone. The Gemara does not pause to address this tension but moves forward with the ruling.

Rabbi Zeira draws an additional lesson: one should not teach a student who is unworthy (*talmid she'eino hagun*). The implicit assumption is that when someone accidentally causes a death, some degree of moral or spiritual deficiency is involved — whether because divine providence arranges such accidents specifically as punishment for negligence in the sanctity of human life, or because a person of truly refined character would be so vigilant that such accidents would not occur. The *rebbe*'s fate of exile is thus the consequence of having accepted such a student.

---

## Torah as Sanctuary

### Torah Refuge

Rabbi Yochanan teaches: how do we know that words of Torah provide sanctuary (*koltin*)? From the juxtaposition of the verse citing *Betzer bamidbar* (one of the *arei miklat*) with the immediately following verse *vezot haTorah* — "and this is the Torah." The Torah itself thus serves as an *ir miklat*.

### Active Study

The Gemara qualifies this: there is no contradiction between a ruling that Torah provides sanctuary and the requirement to actually go to a city of refuge. The resolution is that Torah provides its protection only *b'idna d'asik bah* — during the time when one is actively engaged in study. The moment one stops, the protection lapses. This naturally raises a question: if Torah provides sanctuary for a *talmid chacham*, does he still need to go to an *ir miklat*? The Gemara's focus here is on the protection aspect alone. But *galut* serves not only as protection but as *kapara* and punishment — which Torah study, however potent, does not substitute for. The Gemara does not resolve this tension explicitly in this passage.

### David Story

The protection afforded by active Torah study is illustrated by the story of David — or, more precisely, by an analogous account involving Rav Chisda. The *malach hamavet*, the angel of death, could not approach him because the words of Torah never left his lips (*d'la hava pasik pumieh migirsa*). The angel of death then went and sat in the cedar tree of Rav's study house. When the tree split — startling Rav Chisda into a moment of silence — the angel was able to claim him. The story dramatizes the principle that Torah protection is contingent on continuous, uninterrupted study; the moment it ceases, one is exposed. Notably, Rabbi Yochanan's teaching about *koltin* is clarified to refer not to protection from the *goel hadam* but from the *malach hamavet* himself: *koltin* means the Torah protects from death.

---

## Merits & Rewards

### Reuben: First

Rabbi Tanchum bar Chanilai asks: why did Reuben merit being the first mentioned in connection with the *hatzalah* — the rescue provided by the *arei miklat*, whose first-cited cities were those in the territory of Reuben? Because Reuben was the first to attempt rescue: *Vayishma Reuven Vayatzileihu Miyadam* — Reuben heard and saved Yosef from his brothers' hands. He did not succeed in the end, but he was the one who spoke up and tried to prevent the killing. That merit was rewarded by making the Transjordanian cities — situated in his territory — the first mentioned in the Torah's discussion of refuge.

### Sun Shines

Rabbi Simlai expounds the verse: *Az yavdil Moshe shalosh arim b'ever haYarden mizrach shamesh* — "Then Moshe set apart three cities across the Jordan toward the sunrise." God said to Moshe: *mizrach shamesh lerotzchin* — let the sun shine for the murderers, meaning, ensure that even those fleeing to the cities of refuge have what they need. The term *rotzchin* — murderers — is striking given that these are people who committed unintentional homicide, but the word is used in the verse (*vezeh d'var harotzeach*) without distinction. An alternative reading treats *mizrach shamesh* as a statement of approbation: you, Moshe, have caused the sun to shine for those who needed it.

### Love of Mitzvos

Rabbi Simlai then expounds the verse from Kohelet: *ohev kesef lo yisba kesef* — one who loves money will never have enough. *Kesef* is read not as money but as *mitzvos*. Moshe knew that the three Transjordanian cities would not go into effect until the three in the land of Israel were designated — a milestone he would never live to see. He could have reasoned that there was no point in designating cities that would not yet function. Instead, he acted on the principle *mitzvah sheba'ah leyadi akaymena* — a *mitzvah* that comes to hand, I will perform, even if I will not live to see it take effect. This is the *ohev kesef* — one who loves *mitzvos* so much that he can never have enough, and seizes every opportunity regardless of whether he will see the fruit.

### Teaching Masses

The verse continues: *u'mi ohev be'hamon lo tevuah* — and one who loves with the masses will not have grain. The word *tevuah* (grain) functions as a metaphor for Torah knowledge. Rabbi Simlai reads the phrase to mean: who is worthy to teach Torah to the masses? Only the one who has all the grain — i.e., comprehensive Torah knowledge. Rabbi Elazar draws on the verse *mi yemallel gevurot Hashem yashmia kol tehillato* — who can speak of the mighty deeds of God and proclaim all His praise? Only one who can truly *yashmia kol tehillato*, who can give voice to the fullness of God's glory through comprehensive mastery of Torah.

The *rabbanan* — and Rabbah bar Mari — reverse the equation: *mi ohev be'hamon lo tevuah* is read with *lo* spelled with a *vav*, meaning "he has grain." Anyone who loves those who study Torah — i.e., who loves *talmidei chachamim* — will himself merit Torah. Rashi specifies: *haTorah mechazeret alav v'al zaro* — the Torah will pursue him and his children. The Aramaic formulation makes this concrete: *hai man derachim rabbanan havu lei banin rabbanan* — one who loves Torah scholars will have children who are Torah scholars. The Rabbis then cast their eyes toward Rabbah the son of Rav, who exemplified this love and whose children were indeed Torah scholars.

A further reading of the same verse: anyone who loves to learn Torah with the masses — in a large *beit medrash*, amidst the *kol Torah* of a community — will be granted Torah. This shifts the emphasis from loving *talmidei chachamim* to the act of communal learning itself. And *Ravina* reads it from the perspective of the teacher: anyone who loves to teach the masses (*lelamed be'hamon*) will not err (*lo to'eh*). This is then connected to the famous teaching: much Torah did I learn from my teachers, more from my colleagues, and the most from my students.

---

## Community Learning

### Love Community

The theme of communal Torah study is now developed directly. The one who loves to be among the masses engaged in Torah — who seeks out large gatherings of learners — is described as deserving of Torah knowledge.

### Sin: Solitary

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chanina expounds the verse: *cherev el habadim veno'alu* — a sword upon the *badim* and they shall grow foolish. He reads *badim* as a reference to *talmidei chachamim* who sit and learn Torah *bad be-vad* — each one alone, isolated from one another. Three consequences follow from solitary study. First, such scholars will grow weary and their learning will be ineffective. The word *veno'alu* is linked to the root of *noalnu* — "we have been foolish" — appearing in two other verses. Second, the learning itself is undermined: the scholar becomes dull from isolation. Third — and most sharply — it is an outright *cheit*, a sin: *shechot'in*, they actually transgress, as implied by the juxtaposition *asher noalnu va'asher chatanu*.

### Gates of Study

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi expounds: *omdot hayu ragleinu bish'arayich Yerushalayim* — our feet were standing in your gates, Jerusalem. What enabled our legs to stand firm in the battles of Torah? The gates of Jerusalem — meaning the places where masses gathered, the markets and public spaces — because it was there that Torah was studied communally, in the thick of human life. It was that communal, public engagement with Torah that gave the people their spiritual strength.

### David's Joy

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi expounds a final verse: *shir hama'alos le-David samachti be'omrim li beit Hashem neilech* — I rejoiced when they said to me, let us go to the house of God. David said before the Holy One: I heard people saying, when will this old man die so that his son Shlomo can come and build the Temple and we can be *oleh le-regel*? And I rejoiced. Rather than being wounded that they wished for his death, David heard only the desire to draw close to God — that they wanted to make the pilgrimage, that they wanted the Temple built.

God responded to David: *ki tov yom bachatzeirecha me'alef* — one day in Your courtyards is better than a thousand. The verse is read: *tov li yom echad she'ata osek ba-Torah lefanai me'alef olot she'asid Shelomo bincha lehakriv al gabei hamizbe'ach* — more precious to Me is one day that you sit and learn Torah before Me than the thousand sacrifices that your son Shlomo will one day offer on the altar. Whether this was meant to reassure David that his contribution was not diminished — or simply as a statement of the supreme value of Torah — the message is unmistakable: a single day of Torah study outweighs a thousand sacrifices. And here the daf concludes.

---

---

# Makkot 10b

## Roads to Arei Miklat

### Crossroads & Signs

The daf opens at the very last line of 10a with a *baraita* concerning the infrastructure of the *arei miklat*. The *Mishna* had described paths interconnecting the various cities of refuge with one another — a system that, on reflection, is not the most practical arrangement. What a fleeing manslaughterer truly needs are paths leading from every point in the land *toward* the *arei miklat*, not merely between them. Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov addresses precisely this concern: *miklat haya katuv al parashat derakhim* — at every crossroads throughout the country, a sign would be posted reading "*miklat*," indicating the direction to turn. In this way, wherever the *rotzeach* found himself, he could immediately orient himself and make his way to safety. It is worth pausing on the Gemara's consistent use of the term *rotzeach* for the person who killed *beshogeg* — a striking choice, and one the Gemara does not explain away.

### Prepare the Way

Rav Kahana identifies the scriptural basis for this entire infrastructure: *takhin lekha ha'derekh* — "prepare the way" (Devarim 19:3). The verse is read actively and expansively: one must make the way directed and prepared so that it is genuinely accessible. Implicit in this, as the Gemara notes, is not only the erection of signs but the ongoing maintenance of the roads themselves.

### Opening Homily

Rav Chama bar Chanina, when delivering a *derasha* on the *parasha* of *arei miklat*, would open with a classic rabbinic *ptichta* — that form of homiletical introduction found throughout *Midrash Rabbah*, in which one begins with an apparently distant verse and gradually winds one's way to the topic at hand. His *ptichta* verse was: *tov ve'yashar Hashem al ken yoreh chata'im baderekh* — "God is good and just, and therefore He will show sinners the path" (Tehillim 25:8). The point of departure is that even someone who bears some moral culpability — for negligence that led to a death is not pure accident — is nonetheless shown the path by God. And if this is what God does for *chata'im*, sinners, then *kal vachomer* how much more so does He do for the righteous.

### Evil Produces Evil

Resh Lakish's *ptichta* takes a different approach. Rather than beginning from a distant verse in *Nach*, he opens directly within the *parasha* itself: *ve'asher lo tzadah ve'ha'elohim ina leyado* — "and one who did not lie in wait, but God delivered him into his hand" (Shemot 21:13). This raises an immediate difficulty: if God orchestrated the death, if the killer was merely God's instrument, why must he go into exile at all? Resh Lakish weaves in the verse *ka'asher yomar meshal ha'kadmoni me'resha'im yetze resha* — "as the ancient proverb says, from the wicked comes wickedness" (Shmuel I 24:14). The point, as Rashi explains, is that the killer was already a person of moral failing, and therefore even though divine providence shaped the circumstances, the exile is still deserved.

---

## Providence & Justice

### Rashi Resolution

The apparent contradiction — that God caused it and yet the killer is liable — is precisely what the Gemara elaborates upon through the famous parable. The scenario described is one of two people who each committed killing, one *bemezid* and one *beshogeg*, neither of whom had witnesses. Both escaped human judgment. Divine justice, the Gemara explains, then arranges the resolution.

### Inn Parable

The parable unfolds as follows: *HaKadosh Baruch Hu mazminam le'pundak echad* — God arranges that both individuals arrive at the same inn. The intentional murderer sits beneath a ladder, while the one who killed unintentionally is descending that same ladder — and note that the direction matters, he is coming *down* — and falls upon the murderer and kills him. Justice is thus served on both accounts: *zeh she'harag bemezid neherag* — the intentional killer is killed as he deserved to have been by a court, *ve'zeh she'harag beshogeg goleh* — the one who killed accidentally goes into exile as he deserved for his original act. Divine providence has arranged the circumstances, but each party receives precisely what justice required of him. One student noted that the verse *me'resha'im yetze resha* appears in the context of David's address to Shaul — David's refusal to kill Shaul despite the opportunity — which enriches the resonance of Resh Lakish's citation.

---

## Divine Guidance

### Three Sources

The Gemara transitions to a broader principle articulated by Rabbah bar Rav Huna in the name of Rav Huna — or according to some versions, Rav Huna in the name of Rav Elazar: *b'derech she'adam rotzeh lalechet bah molichin oto* — in the path that a person wishes to travel, heaven facilitates his going. This principle is derived from three distinct parts of *TaNaCh*.

### Bilam Example

From the Torah: when Bilam wished to go with the Moabite princes, God initially said *lo telech imahem* — do not go with them. But Bilam persisted, and God relented: *kum lech itam* — arise and go with them. This is the principle made concrete: since Bilam insisted on going, God did not continue to obstruct him. One student pressed the point that God here does not merely *permit* but actively *instructs* Bilam to go, which is somewhat more than simply not standing in one's way. Rashi's formulation in this context is *ein me'akvin b'yado* — one does not hold him back.

### Isaiah's Teaching

From the Prophets: *ani Hashem elohecha m'lamdecha l'ho'il madrichacha b'derech telech* — "I am the Lord your God who teaches you for your benefit, who guides you in the path you will walk" (Yeshayahu 48:17). The key word is *telech* — the path *you will walk*, not the path *you ought to walk*. God guides a person along the road that person has already chosen.

### Proverbs Example

From *Ketuvim*: *im laleitzim hu yalitz ve'la'anavim yitein chein* — "if one deals with mockers, He will mock, but to the humble He gives grace" (Mishlei 3:34). Rashi reads *hu yalitz* to mean that if a person wishes to go ahead and mock or pursue evil, God will enable that as well — *ein me'akvin b'yado*, one does not obstruct him. The Gemara uses this as a metaphor for the *rotzeach* running toward the *ir miklat*: the Torah facilitates his reaching it, because God directs people along the paths they have chosen.

---

## Go'el HaDam Liability

### Rav Huna View

Rav Huna rules: *rotzeach she'galah l'ir miklat u'metza'o go'el hadam v'harago — patur* — a manslaughterer who has fled toward the city of refuge and is killed along the way by the *go'el hadam*, the *go'el hadam* is exempt from liability. The basis is a reading of the verse in Devarim (19:6): *pen yirdof go'el hadam acharei harotzeach ki yeicham levavo v'harago baderech v'lo ein mishpat mavet* — lest the *go'el hadam* pursue the killer while his heart is hot and kill him on the way, and *v'lo ein mishpat mavet* — and he will not deserve the death penalty. The plain reading of the verse seems to be that the manslaughterer does not deserve to die, since *ki lo sonei hu lo mitmol shilshom* — he did not hate the deceased from the past, i.e., it was accidental. But Rav Huna reads the verse differently: *v'lo ein mishpat mavet* refers not to the *rotzeach* but to the *go'el hadam* — it is the *go'el hadam* who will not be liable for having killed the *rotzeach* before he reached the city. And it is precisely because the *go'el hadam* can act with impunity during this window that the Torah commands *tachin lekha ha'derekh* — you must ensure the road is prepared so the *rotzeach* can arrive as quickly as possible.

### Braita Challenge

A *braita* is cited in objection: *v'lo ein mishpat mavet berotzeiach hakatuv medaber* — the verse is speaking about the killer himself, not about the *go'el hadam*. The proof is that the following phrase, *ki lo sonei hu lo mitmol shilshom* — he did not hate him from the past — is manifestly speaking about the *rotzeach* and his lack of prior malice toward the victim. Since that phrase clearly refers to the *rotzeach*, the immediately preceding phrase, *v'lo ein mishpat mavet*, must refer to him as well. The *go'el hadam* reading of Rav Huna is therefore challenged.

### Braita Resolution

The Gemara resolves this by showing that Rav Huna's position is in fact supported by another *tanna*. A second *baraita* argues the inverse: since the phrase *ki lo sonei hu lo mitmol shilshom* unambiguously refers to the *rotzeach* — and would be redundant if the entire verse were about him — *v'lo ein mishpat mavet* must refer to a *different* subject, namely the *go'el hadam*. The *baraita* works through the logic explicitly: *ata omer b'go'el hadam hakatuv medaber o eino ela berotzeiach* — one might say it refers to the *go'el hadam* or perhaps to the *rotzeach*; but since the closing phrase *ki lo sonei* is already clearly about the *rotzeach*, the opening phrase *v'lo ein mishpat mavet* must be about the *go'el hadam*. This is accordingly a genuine *tannaitic* dispute, and Rav Huna holds in accordance with the *tanna* who reads the verse as referring to the *go'el hadam*'s exemption. The *pshat* of the broader passage — that the Torah establishes the *arei miklat* lest the killer be caught on the road — remains consistent with this reading: the killer is exposed until he arrives, which is precisely why the road must be prepared.

---

## Talmidei Chachamim

### Mishna Requirement

The *Mishna* states: *mosrin lo shnei talmidei chachamim shema yehorgenu baderech v'yedabru elav* — two *talmidei chachamim* are appointed to accompany the manslaughterer as he flees, lest the *go'el hadam* kill him on the road, and they are to speak to the *go'el hadam*.

### Persuasion vs Halacha

What precisely are these scholars to say? One might assume — given that they are *talmidei chachamim* — that their role is to convey *halacha*: to inform the *go'el hadam* that if he kills the *rotzeach* he will himself be liable to the death penalty, since the *rotzeach* is now under legal protection. This would also confirm that the manslaughterer is indeed protected while still in transit. But the Gemara raises an alternative: perhaps they are simply functioning as persuaders, not as *halachic* instructors. The *baraita* spells out what they would say: *al tinhag bo minhag shofchei damim bisshgagah ba miyado* — do not treat this person as a murderer; what happened was an accident. One might question how persuasive this is likely to be when addressed to a *go'el hadam* running in the heat of passion, but the Gemara takes the position seriously.

### Emissary Value

Rabbi Meir holds that the manslaughterer can and even should speak on his own behalf: *hu medaber al yedei atzmo* — he speaks for himself, as implied by the verse *ve'zeh devar ha'rotzeach* — "and this is the matter of the killer" (Devarim 19:4). The Rabbis respond: *harbeh shelichuto oseh* — an emissary often accomplishes what direct speech cannot. A person defending his own life before the family member of the one he killed is unlikely to be the most effective advocate for himself; an intermediary carries a different kind of authority and neutrality.

### Intent Distinction

One might ask: if their role is merely persuasion — telling the *go'el hadam* the death was accidental — why is this not obvious? If the man is fleeing to the *ir miklat*, is it not self-evident that he killed *beshogeg*? The Gemara responds: *peshita d'bemezid bar galut hu?* — obviously an intentional killer would not be heading to the *ir miklat* for refuge! So what is the information the scholars are conveying? The Gemara answers that this is not as obvious as it seems, because according to the following *tanna*, it is not only the *shogeg* who flees to the *ir miklat*.

### Rabbi Yose View

Rabbi Yose bar Yehuda teaches: *batchila echad shogeg v'echad mezid makdimin l'ir miklat* — initially, both the inadvertent killer and the intentional murderer proceed to the *ir miklat*. The *ir miklat* functions at first as a holding place for all who killed, pending the convening of *beit din*. The court then summons them: *u'veit din sholchin u'mevi'in otam misham* — *beit din* sends and retrieves them from there. The one found liable for intentional murder is executed; the one found entirely innocent is freed (*v'hitzilu ha'edah et harotzeach miyad go'el hadam*); and the one found liable for manslaughter is returned to the *ir miklat*. Since, according to Rabbi Yose bar Yehuda, an intentional killer might also be found in the city, the *talmidei chachamim* serve a real informational function: they are conveying to the *go'el hadam* that this particular person killed *beshogeg*.

*Rebbi* disagrees with Rabbi Yose bar Yehuda. He reads the *pesukim* describing *beit din* retrieving a *mezid* from the *ir miklat* not as reflecting a *beit din*-administered system but as describing cases where the *mezid* went there *voluntarily*: *me'aleihen hen golin* — they go on their own initiative. Why would an intentional murderer run to the *ir miklat*? Because *kasvorin hen echad shogeg v'echad mezid koletet* — they mistakenly believed the *ir miklat* protects everyone, whether *shogeg* or *mezid*. *V'einan yodim she'bishgagah koletet u'vemezid einah koletet* — they did not know that in fact only the *shogeg* is protected there, not the intentional killer. This also raises the pointed question of how the *go'el hadam* — or anyone — can determine before trial whether the *rotzeach* is a *shogeg* or *mezid*, since the trial has not yet occurred. One must presumably act on the available presumption, with the *talmidei chachamim* conveying what is known about the circumstances at the time.

---

## City Requirements

### Majority Murderers

Rav Elazar rules: *ir she'rubbah rotzchim einah koletet* — a city whose population is predominantly composed of those who killed does not function as a city of refuge. The source is a verse in Yehoshua (*va'yedaber b'oznei ziknei ha'ir hahi et devarav*), read as implying that the population of the *ir miklat* must be distinct from the *rotzeach* who takes refuge there — *v'lo shehushevu devarav l'devarav* — their words and his words are not equivalent; they are a separate civic population, not a community uniformly composed of killers. The *ir miklat* requires a functioning, normal civic body to confer its status of sanctuary upon the minority who are the refugees.

### No Elders

Rav Elazar further rules: *ir she'ein bah zekenim einah koletet* — a city without elders cannot function as an *ir miklat*. The Yehoshua verses specify that the *rotzeach* speaks before the elders of that city, and that requirement is understood as substantive, not merely descriptive.

### Ammi vs Assi

A direct *machlokes* between Rav Ammi and Rav Assi follows. One holds *koletet* — the city still provides protection even without elders — and the other holds *einah koletet* — it does not. The one who rules it does not protect reads the elders requirement as *me'akev*, indispensable. The one who permits it reads the mention of elders as *mitzvah b'alma* — describing the ideal situation, but not a condition that invalidates the city's function if absent.

### Related Extensions

The same dispute between Rav Ammi and Rav Assi is applied analogously to *ben sorer u'moreh* and *eglah arufah*. Regarding *ben sorer u'moreh*: one holds that such a case can be adjudicated in a city without elders, reading the requirement of *ziknei iro* as merely the ideal procedure; the other holds it cannot, since the Torah explicitly requires the parents to bring him before *the elders*. Regarding *eglah arufah*: one holds that the ritual can be performed even in a city without elders, and one holds it cannot. Tosafot raises a question here: there is a *Gemara* elsewhere that when the closest town lacks elders and a more distant town has them, the more distant town performs the *eglah arufah* — which would seem to confirm that elders are genuinely required. Tosafot resolves this by distinguishing the case: when there is a choice between a town with elders and one without, one assigns the responsibility to the town that has them. But if no surrounding town has elders, the ritual proceeds regardless. The *eglah arufah* case is particularly compelling for requiring elders, since the entire *inyan* is the city taking collective responsibility — a function that cannot easily be delegated to an external institution the way *ben sorer u'moreh* might be transferred to the *beit din* of another town.

---

## Harsh Language

### Question Posed

Rabbi Chama bar Chanina asks: *mipnei mah ne'emrah parashat rotzchim b'lashon azah* — why is the section concerning the *rotzeach* and the *arei miklat* in Yehoshua expressed in harsh language? Elsewhere in *Sefer Yehoshua*, when God speaks to Yehoshua, the text consistently uses *vayomer* — "and He said." But when it comes to this passage, the verb shifts repeatedly to *vayedaber*, *daber*, *dibarti* — forms of *dibur*, which *Chazal* understood as connoting a harder, more severe register of speech.

### Torah Seriousness

The first answer offered is *mipnei shehi Torah* — because this is the fulfillment of a *mitzvah* of the Torah. The repeated use of *vayedaber* and its cognates evokes the formulaic *Vayedaber Hashem el Moshe lemor* of the Chumash, signaling that what Yehoshua is now doing carries the weight and gravity of divine command. The harsher language conveys the seriousness and import of what is being enacted.

### Vayedaber Meaning

The Gemara then asks: *leimar dechol dibur lashon kasheh* — does *dibur* always indicate harshness? It cites a counter-example: *diber ha'ish adonei ha'aretz itanu kashot* — the man, the lord of the land, spoke harshly with us (Bereishit 42:30), where the harshness is explicit. But then it cites *az nidberu yirei Hashem* — then those who feared God spoke with one another (Malachi 3:16), where the *baraita* says *ein nidberu ela lashon nachat* — *nidberu* means pleasant speech. And *yadber amim tachteinu* is similarly cited as a form of *dibur* that connotes leading or guiding rather than harshness. The Gemara's resolution is *dibur lachud yadber lachud* — *dibur* as a noun-form connotes harshness, while *yadber* in the sense of "to lead" or "to guide" is a distinct usage with a softer valence.

### Rav Yehuda Debate

Rav Yehuda and the Rabbis dispute the underlying reason for the harsh language. One holds *mipnei sheshicham* — because Yehoshua delayed in fulfilling the *mitzvah* of establishing the cities of refuge, so the harsh divine speech represents a rebuke. The other holds the reason is simply *mipnei shehein shel Torah* — as stated above, because it is biblical in character and must be expressed with commensurate gravitas.

---

## Joshua's Writing

### Dispute on Content

The Gemara now addresses a related question prompted by a verse in Yehoshua: *vayichtov Yehoshua et hadevarim ha'eleh besefer Torat Elohim* — "and Yehoshua wrote these words in the book of the Torah of God" (Yehoshua 24:26). What exactly did Yehoshua write? Rav Yehuda and Rav Nechemiah dispute this. One holds he wrote the *shemoneh pesukim* — the last eight verses of the Torah in *Devarim*, which according to one opinion in *Bava Batra* were written by Yehoshua rather than Moshe, since they describe Moshe's death. The word *hadevarim* in the verse is particularly apt, evoking *Sefer Devarim* itself (*eleh hadevarim*). The other opinion holds that what Yehoshua wrote was the *parshat arei miklat* — the section concerning the cities of refuge as it appears in *Sefer Yehoshua* itself.

### Rashi Interpretation

The Gemara asks: if the second opinion is correct, in what sense was it written *besefer Torat Elohim* — in the Torah scroll of God? Rashi's reading resolves this elegantly: *sefer Torat Elohim* in this verse refers not to the *Sefer Torah* of Moshe but to *Sefer Yehoshua* itself. The book of Yehoshua is here called *sefer Torat Elohim* — the book of God's Torah — and what Yehoshua wrote within it was the *parshat arei miklat*. The Gemara then offers a further harmonization: one could also read the verse as saying that Yehoshua wrote *in his own book* the words that are already written *in the Sefer Torah of God* — meaning he recorded the fulfillment of the Mosaic command, with the phrase *besefer Torat Elohim* modifying *hadevarim ha'eleh* (those words which are in the Torah), not describing where he wrote them.

---

## Torah Stitching

### Flax Dispute

Since the Gemara has been presenting a series of disputes structured as *chad amar* / *chad amar*, it now appends another such dispute. If a *Sefer Torah* is sewn together with flax rather than with *gidin* — sinews derived from animal intestine — is it *kasher* or *pasul*? Rav Yehuda and Rav Meir disagree.

### Tefillin Connection

The one who rules *pasul* invokes the verse *lema'an tihyeh Torat Hashem beficha* — "so that the Torah of God shall be in your mouth" (Shemot 13:9), by which the *Gemara* connects *tefillin* to *Sefer Torah*. There is a *Halacha l'Moshe miSinai* that *tefillin* must be sewn together with *gidin*. Since the verse creates a *hekesh* between *tefillin* and *Sefer Torah*, the same requirement applies: *mah tefillin Halacha l'Moshe miSinai litforan b'gidin, af kol litforan b'gidin* — just as *tefillin* requires sinews by received tradition, so too *Sefer Torah*. The one who rules *kasher* argues that the *hekesh* between *tefillin* and *Sefer Torah* extends only to the specific *derasha* of *b'ficha* — that the parchment must come from a *mutar b'ficha*, an animal whose flesh is permitted for consumption — but does not extend to all the subsidiary *halachos* of *tefillin*. Since the *gidin* requirement is a detail of *tefillin*, it does not transfer via this *hekesh* to *Sefer Torah*.

### Rav Chazina Testimony

Rav Chazina adds a striking piece of testimony: *l'didi chazi li tefillin d'bei chavivi* — I myself saw the *tefillin* of the household of my beloved (Rabbi Chiyya), *d'tzafiri b'kitna* — that they were sewn with flax. This is a remarkable report, since even those who rule *kasher* for a *Sefer Torah* stitched with flax do not say the same for *tefillin*, for which the *gidin* requirement is unambiguous. The Gemara concludes: *v'leit hilchata k'vateih* — and the *halacha* is not in accordance with this practice.

---

## High Priest Death

### High Priest Types

The Gemara now transitions to the *Mishna* dealing with which *Kohen Gadol*'s death releases the manslaughterer from the *ir miklat*. The *Mishna* enumerates: the *Kohen Gadol* anointed with the *shemen hamishcha* (as was the case in the first *Beit HaMikdash*); the one who became *Kohen Gadol* through the wearing of the eight special garments alone, without the oil of anointing (as occurred toward the end of the first *Beit HaMikdash* when the *shemen hamishcha* was lost); and even a *Kohen Gadol* who had been removed from his office — one who, for example, had a *pesul* that temporarily disqualified him from serving on *Yom Kippur*, requiring a substitute to serve, so that one now has both a sitting and an ex-*Kohen Gadol*. Even the death of such a former *Kohen Gadol* would free the manslaughterer.

### Rabbi Meir's View

Rabbi Meir adds a fourth category: even the *mashuach milchama* — the Kohen anointed to address the troops before battle (Devarim 20:2-4), who is accorded a status of distinction above ordinary *Kohanim* — counts as well, and his death would also free the *rotzeach*.

### Care Packages

The *Mishna* records a remarkable social practice consequent upon this law: *imoteihem shel Kohanim mesafkot lahen michya u'chsut* — the mothers of the *Kohanim Gedolim* would provide food and clothing to the residents of the *arei miklat*. The reason given is *k'dei shelo yitpallelu al b'neihem sheyamutu* — so that those confined in the *ir miklat* should not pray for their sons to die. The logic runs in two directions: gratitude for the care packages might prevent the residents from wishing death upon the benefactor's son, and, more practically, if the *Kohen Gadol* dies and the manslaughterer is freed, the care packages stop as well. The entire arrangement reflects a deep assumption about the efficacy of prayer.

### Prayer Efficacy

The Gemara sharpens this into a question. If the concern is that the manslaughterers not pray for the *Kohen Gadol*'s death, there is a verse that seems to make such prayers futile: *ke'tzippor lanud ke'dror la'uf ken kilelat chinam lo tavo* — like a bird that wanders, like a swallow that flies, so too a causeless curse shall not come to rest (Mishlei 26:2). Why should a prayer for an innocent person's death accomplish anything at all? A certain elder (*hahu saba*) cites the teaching of Rav's academy: *she'hayah lahem levakesh rachamim al doram v'lo bikshu* — the *Kohanim Gedolim* were culpable because they *should have* prayed for their generation, for the safety of the people under their watch, and they failed to do so. This failure means that when tragedy strikes — even accidental deaths — the leadership bears a share of the responsibility. Thus, when those confined in the *ir miklat* pray for the *Kohen Gadol* to die, it is not entirely a causeless curse; the *Kohen Gadol* himself carries some culpability for not having done more to prevent the conditions that led to the tragedy.

### Leadership Responsibility

An alternate version of the *Mishna* reads the mothers' motivation differently: not *shelo yitpallelu al b'neihem sheyamutu* — that they should not pray for their sons to die — but *k'dei she'yitpallelu aleihem shelo yamutu* — so that the residents would actively pray for their sons to *live*. The Gemara finds this version even more demanding. If the reason the *Kohanim Gedolim* don't die is only because the *rotze'achim* are praying actively for them to live, the implication is that absent such prayers, the *Kohanim Gedolim* would in fact die. But what would they have done to deserve death? Again the elder's answer applies: *she'hayah lahem levakesh rachamim al doram v'lo bikshu* — they should have prayed for their generation and did not. A leader who fails to carry the welfare of the community in prayer, who does not function as an advocate before God for those under his authority, bears a degree of culpability when harm befalls them. The Gemara reinforces this with the account of the lion that attacked a man within three *parsangs* of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi — a great *amora* who regularly had conversations with Eliyahu HaNavi — and Eliyahu did not speak with him for three days afterward, implicitly holding Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi accountable for what occurred in his vicinity.

---

## Power of Curses

### Wise Person Curse

Rav Yehuda teaches in the name of Rav: *kilat chacham afilu bechinam hi ba'ah* — the curse of a *chacham*, even if it was issued without cause — *bechinam* — will still come to pass. The word *chinam* here is critical: it is the same word that appears in *kilelat chinam lo tavo* — a causeless curse shall not come to rest — yet even this protection does not apply when the one who issued the curse is a *chacham*.

### Achitofel Case

The proof comes from Achitofel. When David was excavating the foundations for the *Beit HaMikdash*, he dug so deep that he tapped into the subterranean waters — the *tehom* — and the waters began rising, threatening to inundate the world. David called out: *man yadei'a lichtov shem achaspa u'mishda bitehoma* — who knows how to write God's name on a shard and throw it into the depths? And he added: *kol hayodeia davar zeh ve'eino omro yechanek bigrono* — whoever knows this and does not come forward, let him be choked in his throat.

### Waters Deep Story

Achitofel reasoned through the problem by *kal vachomer*: he arrived at the solution and presented it. David wrote God's *shem* on a shard of pottery, *shadi atehoma* — threw it into the depths — and the waters receded and stood in their place. The parallel account in the *Yerushalmi* adds the detail about David removing a piece of pottery from the hole in the first place, and the tradition of the fifteen *Shir HaMa'alot* being recited to restore the water to an appropriate level.

### Achitofel Logic

The *kal vachomer* that Achitofel constructed was this: *umah la'asot shalom bein ish le'ishto amrah Torah shemi shehichtav bikedusha yimacheh al hamayim* — in order to make peace between a husband and wife, the Torah permits God's name, written in holiness, to be erased into the water of the *sotah* ritual. *Lechol ha'olam kulo lo kol sheken* — certainly for the sake of the entire world, the same should be permitted. One might ask what the *hava amina* even was — why would there be a prohibition? Perhaps it was understood in terms of *Lo ta'asun ken l'Hashem Elokechem*, or perhaps even as approaching the category of *yehareg ve'al ya'avor*. Regardless, Achitofel ruled: *shari* — it is permitted. Now, crucially, it appears that Achitofel himself had not known the answer in advance; he derived it under the pressure of David's curse — which means the curse functioned *bechinam*, without genuine cause, for Achitofel had not been willfully withholding anything.

### Achitofel Death

Despite having provided this crucial service, Achitofel met his end shortly thereafter. The verse records: *va'yar Achitofel ki lo na'astah atzato vayachavosh et hachamor vayakam vayelech el beito el iro vayetzav el beito vayechanek* — Achitofel saw that his counsel had not been followed — in the context of the succession dispute — and he went to his city, set his affairs in order, and hanged himself. The self-imposed end is striking. Nevertheless the Gemara's point stands: the curse of David, *even though it was bechinam*, came into effect because a *chacham* issued it, and Achitofel — the foremost *chacham* of the generation — was caught within its scope.

---

## Conditional Curses

### Nidui Conditional

Rabbi Abahu teaches: *kilat chacham afilu al tnai hi ba'ah* — the curse of a *chacham* takes effect even when issued conditionally, i.e., even if the condition upon which it was suspended was ultimately not met, or was met in such a way that the curse ought not to apply. This leads Rav Yehuda to articulate a consequent *halacha*: *nidui al tnai tzarich hafara* — excommunication issued conditionally still requires formal release (*hafara*), even if the condition was never triggered.

### Eli Curse

The proof-text for Rabbi Abahu's principle is from Eli and Shmuel. Eli said to the young Shmuel: *koh ya'aseh lecha Elokim v'choh yosif im techached mimeni davar* — so shall God do to you and more, if you conceal from me anything (Shmuel I 3:17). The condition was: if you withhold. *Aval kol hadevarim nagad lo Shmuel* — yet Shmuel told him everything and concealed nothing — so the condition was not met. And yet the verse subsequently records that Shmuel's sons did not walk in his ways, taking bribes, in precisely the manner that Eli's sons had been condemned. The curse thus took effect in a transferred form: not upon Shmuel personally, but upon his children, mirroring the fate of Eli's own household — even though the condition upon which the curse was nominally suspended had been fulfilled.

### Yehuda Curse

The proof for Rav Yehuda's ruling about *nidui al tnai* requiring *hafara* comes from Yehuda. When Yehuda pledged to Yaakov regarding Binyamin — *im lo hevi'otiv eleicha v'hitzagtiv lefaneicha v'chatati l'avcha kol hayamim* — if I do not bring him back and present him before you, I shall be considered a sinner to you all my days — this is read as a self-imposed *cherem*, albeit conditional. The question is: did Yehuda fulfill the condition? In a sense, yes: Binyamin returned safely. Yet the *Gemara* understands that the *nidui* nonetheless took effect and required *hafara*, as evidenced by the fate of Yehuda's bones in the *aron*.

### Moses Blessing

Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan derives this from the juxtaposition in Moshe's *berachot* at the end of *Devarim*: *yechi Reuven v'al yamot* — let Reuven live and not die — immediately followed by *vezot li'Yehuda*, without the formulaic introduction *li'Yehuda amar* that introduces every other *berachah*. The close juxtaposition is deliberate. *Kol otan mem shanah she'hayu Yisrael bamidbar atzmotav shel Yehuda hayu megulgallim ba'aron* — throughout all forty years in the wilderness, Yehuda's bones were rolling within the *aron*, his soul unable to find rest.
