This continued *ad she'amar Moshe bikeish alav rachamim* — until Moshe prayed on his behalf. Moshe's prayer is read as a sequence tracking through the verse: *Shema Hashem kol Yehuda* — the bones reconnected into a skeleton; *v'el amo tevi'enu* — Yehuda's soul was admitted into the heavenly *yeshiva*; *yadav rav lo* — he was able to participate in *halakhic* debate; *v'ezer mizarav tihyeh* — he was able to resolve difficulties put to him. Each phrase corresponded to a further stage of restoration. The *hafara* required was nothing less than the prayers of Moshe himself.

### Tosafot's Distinction

Tosafot raises a sharply practical question: in the medieval period, the primary mechanism by which rabbinic authorities secured communal compliance was the *cherem al tnai* — the conditional excommunication. If one does not do such-and-such, one is in *cherem*. But if even a *nidui al tnai* requires formal *hafara*, this would seem to undermine the entire apparatus, since presumably no *hafara* is issued every time a member of the community complies with a rabbinic enactment. Tosafot resolves this by drawing a distinction based on the nature of the condition. In Yehuda's case, the condition — bringing Binyamin safely back and presenting him before Yaakov — was not fully within his control: Yosef might have prevented it, Binyamin might have died along the way. Because the condition was partially outside Yehuda's ability to guarantee, the *cherem* took effect from the outset regardless of outcome. But when the condition of a *cherem* is entirely within the person's own control — for instance, the rabbinic enactment that says "if you do such-and-such, you are in *cherem*" — then from the moment the *cherem* is issued, we presume the person has no intention of violating it, and therefore it does not take effect at all at the outset. It takes effect, if ever, only at the moment the person actually chooses to violate the condition. This distinction preserves the rabbinic authority that depended on the *cherem al tnai* as an enforcement tool.

---

## Practical Application

### Gmar Din

The *Mishna* establishes that the operative moment determining which *Kohen Gadol*'s death will free the manslaughterer is *gmar din* — the conclusion of his trial and the formal pronouncement of sentence. It is not sufficient that the manslaughterer has simply arrived at the *ir miklat*; there must be a completed judicial proceeding in which *beit din* formally adjudicated his guilt and sentenced him to exile. The *beit din* taking control of the process — sentencing, returning people from the *ir miklat* for trial, and assigning them back — is foundational to how this institution functions. Once *gmar din* has occurred, the manslaughterer's fate is tied to the *Kohen Gadol* who is in office at that moment.

### Succession Rule

If a *Kohen Gadol* dies during the *proceedings* but before *gmar din*, and a new *Kohen Gadol* is appointed in the interim, and *gmar din* then occurs during the new *Kohen Gadol*'s tenure — *chozer bemitato shel sheni* — it is the death of the second *Kohen Gadol* that will free the manslaughterer. The logic is that the operative *Kohen Gadol* is the one in office at the moment of *gmar din*.

### No High Priest

If there is simply no *Kohen Gadol* in office at the time of *gmar din* — *nigmar dino belo Kohen Gadol* — then *eino yotze misham le'olam*, the manslaughterer is never freed. There is no mechanism by which his release can be triggered. Similarly, if a *Kohen Gadol* himself committed an act of manslaughter and there is a new *Kohen Gadol* in office by the time of his *gmar din*, he too is never freed, since the current *Kohen Gadol* is himself. The source for extending the release to multiple categories of *Kohen Gadol* — anointed, invested by garments, retired — is the three-fold repetition of *Kohen Gadol* in the relevant verses of Bemidbar (35:25, 28, 32), each repetition coming to include one further category. Rabbi Yehuda's fourth category, the *mashuach milchama*, is derived from a fourth verse that mentions only *haKohen* without the qualifier *haGadol* — and the other opinion holds that this verse is simply one of the three already counted.

### Absolute Restrictions

Once confined to the *ir miklat*, the manslaughterer may not leave for any reason whatsoever: not to give testimony even in the context of a *mitzvah*, not for monetary testimony, not even for capital testimony. Even if all of Israel has need of him — *v'afilu sar tzva Yisrael k'Yoav ben Tzeruyah* — even if he is a military commander as distinguished as Yoav ben Tzeruyah, he may not go forth. The verse *asher nas shamah* — "to which he fled" — is read expansively: *sham tehei diraso, sham tehei misaso, sham tehei kevuraso* — there shall be his dwelling, there his death (if the *Kohen Gadol* does not die in time), and there his burial. The force of *pikuach nefesh* and other overriding considerations might seem to challenge this, and the *Gemara* acknowledges the strangeness of forbidding someone of Yoav's stature from leading an army, yet the prohibition is absolute.

### Environs Protection

Not only the city itself but its *techum* — its surrounding boundary, defined as 2,000 *amos*, the same measure used for the *techum Shabbat* — provides equivalent protection. If the manslaughterer steps outside this boundary, however, the protection lapses immediately.

---

## Outside City Killing

### Yose HaGalili

The *Mishna* concludes with a debate about the status of the manslaughterer who has left the *ir miklat* or its *techum* and is found by the *go'el hadam*. Rabbi Yose HaGalili rules: *mitzvah b'yad go'el hadam* — there is a *mitzvah* for the *go'el hadam* to kill the manslaughterer who has left the protected area. Furthermore, *urshut b'yad kol adam* — any other person has *permission* to kill him. This is a striking position: the person killed *beshogeg*, yet once he has violated the boundaries of his city of refuge, he is open not merely to the *go'el hadam* but to all. One might read Rabbi Yose HaGalili less as expressing a judgment that the manslaughterer *deserves* death and more as a mechanism to ensure that the conditions of confinement are taken with absolute seriousness — the existential risk of leaving is what keeps the person within the *ir miklat*. Nevertheless, the ruling remains troubling.

### Akiva Position

Rabbi Akiva disagrees: *reshut b'yad go'el hadam* — the *go'el hadam* has permission but no *mitzvah* to kill the manslaughterer outside the city. The *pshat* of the *pesukim* indeed seems to favor Rabbi Akiva's position: the Torah establishes the *arei miklat* precisely to protect the *rotzeach* from the *go'el hadam*, and there is no indication that it *wants* the *go'el hadam* to act when the opportunity presents itself. The Torah cannot entirely eradicate all elements of vigilante justice — it must tolerate them to a degree — but it confers no positive mandate upon them.

### Third Party Liability

The final question concerns a third party — someone other than the *go'el hadam* — who kills the manslaughterer outside the *ir miklat*. Two versions of the *Mishna*'s text exist here. According to the standard reading: *kol adam chayavin alav* — any person who kills him would be liable for murder. According to the alternative *girsa*: *ein chayavin alav* — one would not be liable for having killed him. This remains a deeply unsettled question about how far the Torah intended to reach in tolerating, permitting, or indeed sanctioning the logic of the blood avenger — and how much it meant to constrain it absolutely, tolerating only the narrowest exception in favor of the *go'el hadam*'s permission, while treating any broader extension as murder.

---

---

# Makkot 11

## Roads to Arei Miklat

### Tanya: Pathways

The daf opens at the very last line of 11a with a *tanya* touching on the infrastructure surrounding the *arei miklat*. The *mishnah* had spoken of paths interconnecting the various cities of refuge — but what is truly needed is not merely roads running between one *ir miklat* and another, but roads leading from every point in the land toward these cities. All roads, in other words, should lead to the *arei miklat*.

The *tanu rabbanan* that follows makes this concrete.

### R. Elazar b. Yaakov

Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov teaches: *miklat haya katuv al haparashat drachim* — the word *miklat* was written at every crossroads throughout the country. Whenever a traveler arrived at a fork in the road, a sign indicated which way to turn in order to reach the nearest city of refuge. The stated rationale is *kedai sheyakir rotzeach viyifneh lishama* — so that the killer would be able to see and turn in the right direction. It is worth pausing on the language: the person who killed unintentionally is nonetheless consistently referred to as *rotzeach*, a striking usage that runs throughout this entire section of the *gemara*.

### Tachin Lecha Haderech

Rav Kahana then asks: *mai kra?* — what is the scriptural basis for this obligation to signpost the roads? The answer is *tachin lecha haderech* — "prepare the way for yourself" (Deuteronomy 19:3). The *derasha* reads this as: *aseh lecha hachanah laderech*, make the way prepared and direct so that the fleeing killer can reach the city with ease. This verse speaks not only to the physical maintenance of roads but to every form of advance preparation that facilitates the journey.

### Rav Chama Petichta

Rav Chama bar Chanina would open his *petichta* — his homiletical introduction — to the *parasha* of *arei miklat* from the verse *tov veyashar Hashem al ken yoreh chataim baderech*: "God is good and just, and therefore He will show sinners the path" (Psalms 25:8). The classical form of Rabbinic *midrash*, particularly as one encounters it throughout *Bereishit Rabbah* and *Shemot Rabbah*, works by beginning from a verse that appears distant from the topic and then weaving one's way toward the core passage — much as one might open a *derashah* on *Parshat Toldot* with a verse from *Mishlei* and then gradually connect it to the narrative of Avraham and Yitzchak.

Here the connection is pointed: the person heading to the *ir miklat* has sinned — for the death was not a pure accident, since some negligence was involved, and this is why the *gemara* calls him *rotzeach*. And yet God desires to create the paths that will protect him and help him arrive safely. The *drasha* concludes: *im lachataim yoreh, kal vachomer latzadikim* — if God guides sinners on the path, how much more so the righteous.

### Reish Lakish Petichta

Reish Lakish would open his *petichta* differently. Rather than beginning from a distant verse, he jumps directly into the *parasha* itself: *va'asher lo tzadah veha'elokim inah leyado* — "and he did not intend it, yet God delivered him into his hand" (Exodus 21:13). He then weaves in the verse *ka'asher yomar hamashal hakadmoni meirsha'im yeitzei resha* — "as the ancient proverb says, from wicked people comes evil."

### Divine Causation Debate

The difficulty that Reish Lakish identifies is one of profound theological weight. The verse *va'asher lo tzadah veha'elokim inah leyado* seems to say that God caused this death to happen — that the killer was merely God's *kli*, His instrument. If so, why should he be exiled at all?

The answer lies in the other verse: *meirshaim yeitzei resha* — evil comes from wicked people. Even if God is orchestrating the events, this person was already culpable in some respect, and the exile is the appropriate consequence for that culpability.

The *gemara* explains the scenario: *bishnei bnei adam shehargu et hanefesh* — two people who killed: one intentionally (*bemeizid*) and one unintentionally (*bishogeg*), and neither had witnesses. Both escaped legal consequence. So what does God do? *Hakadosh Baruch Hu mazminam lefundak echad* — He arranges that they both end up at the same inn. The intentional killer sits beneath a ladder; the unintentional killer descends the ladder and falls on him, killing him. Justice is served on both accounts: *zeh sheharag bemeizid neherag* — the one who murdered deliberately is now killed as he deserved, and *zeh sheharag bishogeg goleh* — the one who killed accidentally is now sent into exile as he deserved. God orchestrated the outcome, but the result maps precisely onto what justice required for each person from the start.

A student pointed out that the verse *meirshaim yeitzei resha* appears in the context of the story of David and Saul — specifically, David's declaration that he would not kill Saul even when he had the opportunity. That context, centered on restraint from murder, makes the verse especially apt here.

### God's Guidance Principle

Rabbah bar Rav Huna said in the name of Rav Huna — and some say Rav Huna said it in the name of Rav Elazar — that from the Torah, the Prophets, and the Writings we learn: *bederech she'adam rotzeh lalechet bah molichin oto* — in the path that a person wishes to walk, Heaven leads him.

## Sources for Choice

### Bilaam Example

From the Torah: by Bilaam, God first says *lo telech imahem* — do not go with them. But Bilaam keeps pressing, and eventually God says *kum lech itam* — arise and go with them. Because he persisted, God accommodated his desire. This is the principle of *bederech she'adam rotzeh lalechet*: if you insist on going, God will not stand in your way.

### Isaiah Example

From the Prophets: *ani Hashem Elohecha melamedcha leho'il madrichcha bederech telech* — "I am the Lord your God who teaches you for your benefit, who guides you in the path that you will walk" (Isaiah 48:17). The verse is read not as "the path you *should* walk" but as "the path you *will* walk" — the path you have already chosen. Even if that path leads toward wrongdoing, God will guide you along it. A student raised the question of *lifnei iver* — does facilitating another's sin not itself constitute a prohibition? The response is that the principle here is primarily one of *non-interference*: God does not compel a person against his chosen course.

### Proverbs Example

From the Writings: *im laleitzim hu yalitz vela'anavim yitein chein* — "if with mockers, He will mock, but to the humble He grants grace" (Proverbs 3:34). Rashi understands *im laleitzim hu yalitz* to mean: if someone chooses to be a mocker, to pursue wrongdoing, God will make it possible — *ein me'akvin beyado*, He will not obstruct him.

The broader thematic point is clear and ties back to the opening of the daf: *tachin lecha haderech* — preparing the road to the *arei miklat* is part of this same divine principle of enabling a person to pursue the path he has chosen, here the path toward refuge and life. But the same divine dynamic operates in the inverse direction as well: God will not block the path of one who chooses wickedness.

## Protection En Route

### Rav Huna's Rule

Rav Huna states: *rotzeach shegalah le'ir miklat umatz'o goel hadam vehargo, patur* — if a manslayer is fleeing to the *ir miklat* and the *goel hadam* intercepts and kills him along the way, the *goel hadam* is exempt. The manslayer is not legally protected until he actually arrives within the city.

The reasoning is based on the verse *pen yirdof goel hadam acharei harotzeach ki yeicham levavo vehisigo vehargo baderech velo ein mishpat mavet* — lest the *goel hadam* pursue the killer, and when his heart is hot overtake him and kill him on the road, and there would be no judgment of death (Deuteronomy 19:6). Rav Huna reads *velo ein mishpat mavet* as referring to the *goel hadam*: if he kills the fleeing man before he reaches the city, the *goel hadam* bears no capital liability. This is precisely why the Torah commands *tachin lecha haderech* — you must prepare the road and ensure the manslayer can reach the *ir miklat* as quickly as possible, because until he arrives he is exposed.

### Textual Ambiguity

A *meitivei* is raised from a *braita*: *velo ein mishpat mavet, berotzeach hakatuv medaber* — this verse is talking about the killer himself, not the *goel hadam*. The *braita* argues: you might think it refers to the *goel hadam*, but when the verse adds *ki lo sonei hu lo mitmol shilshom* — "for he did not hate him previously" — that phrase clearly describes the killer, establishing that his act was unintentional. Therefore *velo ein mishpat mavet* in the prior clause is also about the killer, meaning he himself does not deserve the death penalty.

The *gemara* responds that Rav Huna's position aligns with a different *tanna*, *ki hai tanna*, who holds that *velo ein mishpat mavet* does refer to the *goel hadam*. According to that *tanna*, the verse is read as follows: since *ki lo sonei hu lo mitmol shilshom* is established as referring to the killer (his lack of prior hatred demonstrating the unintentional nature of the act), the *velo ein mishpat mavet* clause becomes redundant if it too refers to the killer — and is therefore read instead as establishing the exemption of the *goel hadam*.

A student offered an additional textual observation: in Deuteronomy 19:4, *velo sonei lo mitmol shilshom* appears in a verse that is already explicitly framed around the *rotzeach*, making it natural to attribute that phrase to the killer throughout. The counterargument is that precisely because that first mention is already established, the second appearance of *lo sonei lo* can carry a distinct reference — and that permits reading *velo ein mishpat mavet* as directed at the *goel hadam* rather than at the killer.

This is a critically important debate: does the manslayer enjoy legal protection while en route, or is he entirely exposed until the moment he passes through the city gate? The *peshat* of the *pesukim* — as the lecturer notes — most plausibly supports the latter reading: the Torah establishes the *ir miklat* specifically because the manslayer has no protection until he gets there, which is why preparing the roads matters so much.

### Two Sages Rule

The *gemara* now turns to the *mishnah*: *mosrin lo shnei talmidei chachamim shema yehargenu baderech veyedabru elav* — two Torah scholars are assigned to accompany the manslayer, lest the *goel hadam* kill him on the way, and they speak to the *goel hadam*. The question arises: what do they say? If they are *talmidei chachamim*, presumably they speak *halacha* — they inform the *goel hadam* that the man is protected and that killing him would render the *goel hadam* liable to the death penalty. That reading would imply that the manslayer is indeed legally protected during transit. Alternatively, the two sages are there not to deliver a *halakhic* warning but simply to persuade.

A *braita* supports the persuasion reading: *veyedabru elav devarim re'uyim lo* — they speak to him things that are fitting for him to hear. *Omrim lo: al tinhag bo minhag shofchei damim, bishgaga ba leyado* — they say: do not treat this man as a murderer; what happened was an accident. Of course, as one might observe, such words are a difficult sell when the *goel hadam* is running in the heat of passion. The role of *talmidei chachamim* may be that their authority and their manner of speaking lend a certain weight that could not otherwise be achieved.

### Intermediary Debate

Rabbi Meir holds: *hu medaber al yedei atzmo* — the manslayer himself may speak in his own defense, citing the verse *veze devar harotzeach* (Deuteronomy 19:4). The Rabbis respond: *harbeh shelichut oseh* — a messenger or intermediary can accomplish far more than one can accomplish on one's own. When a person is trying to argue for his own life against the man whose relative he killed, the chances of success are considerably lower than if trained scholars speak on his behalf.

### Sage Function

The *gemara* then asks: *peshita* — is it not obvious that the statement *bishgaga ba miyado* (it was an accident) needs to be said? After all, *deveizid bar galuta hu* — if it were intentional, surely this man would not be running to the *ir miklat*. The *gemara* answers: not necessarily obvious, because in fact everyone runs to the *ir miklat* initially — including those who killed intentionally. The two sages are therefore not merely persuading but also informing. The *goel hadam* genuinely may not know whether the fleeing person is *shogeg* or *meizid*.

## Court Procedures

### Initial Refuge

Rabbi Yose bar Yehuda teaches: *bit'chilla, echad shogeg ve'echad meizid makdimin le'ir miklat* — initially, both the unintentional killer and the intentional murderer are sent to the *ir miklat*. The city functions as a kind of holding place pending trial.

### Court Classification

Once there, *beit din sholchim umevi'im otam misham* — the court then asserts control, summoning the accused from the city of refuge. *Mi she'nitchayav mita haragu* — one found guilty of intentional murder is executed, as the verse states: *ve'shalchu ziknei iro velakchu oto misham venatnu oto beyad goel hadam vamet*. *Mi she'lo nitchayav patruhu* — one found entirely innocent is freed, as in *vehitzilu ha'eda et harotzeach miyad goel hadam*. And *mi she'nitchayav galut machzirin oto limkomo* — one convicted of *shogeg* manslaughter is returned to the *ir miklat*, as in *veheshivu oto ha'eda el ir miklato asher nas shamma*.

This framework also clarifies the role of the *talmidei chachamim* accompanying the fleeing man. Even before the trial, they may speak to the *goel hadam* based on the presumption of what is known at that moment — that the circumstances appear consistent with *shogeg*. A student raised the question of whether the *talmidei chachamim* would similarly protect even the *meizid* runner on the grounds that the court has not yet rendered its verdict and vigilante action should be avoided in all events. The answer is that while the *braita* frames their speech as conveying *shogeg*, there is reason to suppose the protective function extends more broadly — the court, not the *goel hadam*, should be the arbiter.

### Rabbi's View

Rabbi (Rebbe) disagrees with Rabbi Yose bar Yehuda. He holds: *me'atzman hen golim* — when the *meizid* killer is found in the *ir miklat*, he went there on his own initiative, not under *beit din* supervision. *Soverin hen echad shogeg ve'echad meizid koletet* — those who killed intentionally mistakenly believed the *ir miklat* protects everyone. *Ve'einan yodim she'bashogeg koletet uvemeizid einah koletet* — but in fact the city protects only the *shogeg*, not the *meizid*. According to Rabbi, *beit din* would not dispatch a *meizid* to the *ir miklat*; they would retain him locally. The *peshat* of the *pesukim* that describe *beit din* recalling someone from the *ir miklat* for execution describes a person who went there of his own accord, believing himself protected.

This generates a further question: if the *ir miklat* does not protect a *meizid* killer, can the *goel hadam* enter the city and kill him with impunity? And if the trial has not yet been held, how can anyone — including the *goel hadam* — know with certainty whether the person is *shogeg* or *meizid* before the verdict is rendered? The *gemara* does not resolve this entirely, and the lecturer acknowledges the strangeness of a situation in which the *rotzeach* might be killed before having the opportunity to defend himself.

## City Requirements

### Murderers Rule

Rabbi Elazar rules: *ir she'rubah rotzechim einah koletet* — a city in which the majority of inhabitants are themselves people who killed *bishogeg* cannot function as an *ir miklat*. The city of refuge is not merely a geographical location but a community. The presence of an ordinary, non-fugitive population is what confers upon the city its status and gives meaning to its function as a sanctuary. The *ir miklat* works because the manslayer is a protected minority within a normal civic community.

The source: *vediber be'oznei ziknei ha'ir ha'hi et devarav* — in Yehoshua, the text describes the manslayer speaking in the ears of the elders of that city. The elders and the townspeople must be categorically distinct from the manslayer; *lo she'hushu devav l'dvarav* — their situation cannot be equated with his.

### Elders Requirement

Rabbi Elazar further rules: *ir she'ein bah zekeinim einah koletet* — a city without elders cannot function as an *ir miklat*. The source is the same passage in Sefer Yehoshua, which makes the presence of *ziknei ha'ir* an explicit element of the *ir miklat* framework.

### Elders Debate

This ruling is itself subject to dispute. Rav Ami and Rav Assi debate: *chad amar koletet* — one holds the city still provides refuge even without elders, *ve'chad amar einah koletet* — the other holds it does not. According to the view that it does not: *beinan ziknei ha'ir ve'leika* — the verse demands elders and they are absent. According to the view that it does: *mitzva be'alma* — the mention of elders in the verse is describing the ideal arrangement, not an indispensable condition.

### Ben Sorer Debate

The same dispute between Rav Ami and Rav Assi is applied to the case of a city without elders in the context of the *ben sorer umoreh*. One holds: *na'aseh bah ben sorer umoreh* — a rebellious son can be prosecuted in such a city. The other holds he cannot: *beinan ziknei iro ve'leika* — the verse requires that the parents bring the child to the elders of his city, and if they are absent, the proceeding cannot be held. The view that it can proceed holds: *mitzva be'alma* — this is the preferred procedure, but if no local *beit din* exists, one may take the child to the *beit din* of the next town.

### Egla Arufah Debate

The same framework applies to *eglah arufah* — the rite performed when a corpse is found outside a city and responsibility must be assumed. One of Rav Ami and Rav Assi holds: *mevi'ah eglah arufah* — the ritual may be performed even in a city without elders. The other holds: *einah mevi'ah* — it cannot. The view that it cannot: *beinan ziknei ha'ir ha'hi ve'leika* — the verse explicitly requires the elders of that city, and this requirement is particularly compelling here, since the entire logic of the ritual is that the *city itself* takes communal responsibility for the death. Unlike the *ben sorer umoreh* case, one cannot simply transfer the responsibility to the elders of a neighboring town, because the ritual is about this city's particular accountability.

### Tosafot Resolution

Tosafot raises a difficulty. There is a *gemara* elsewhere that rules, when there are multiple surrounding towns and one is closer but lacks elders while a farther one has elders, the *eglah arufah* is performed by the town with elders. This implies that elders are indeed a *sine qua non* for the rite. How then can anyone hold *mitzva be'alma* — that it is merely preferred?

Tosafot resolves the contradiction as follows: when there is a choice between a town with elders and one without, the rite is assigned to the one with elders — even if it is not the geographically nearest town. But if *none* of the surrounding towns has elders, then the rite proceeds without them. The *mitzva be'alma* position, properly understood, holds that elders are ideal but not absolutely essential when no alternative exists.

## Scripture's Tone

### Harsh Language

Rabbi Chama bar Chanina poses a question: *mipnei mah ne'emar parashat rotzchim bileshon azah* — why does the passage in Sefer Yehoshua concerning the *rotzeach* and the *arei miklat* employ particularly harsh language? Specifically, while elsewhere in Sefer Yehoshua God speaks to Yehoshua with the word *vayomer*, here the text repeatedly uses *vayidaber* — a term that *chazal* consistently understood as conveying a sterner, more severe register of speech. The word *daber* even sounds harder, with its emphatic consonants.

### Torah Explanation

Rav Huna's initial answer: *mipnei she'hen shel Torah* — because these laws originate in the Torah itself. The repeated use of *vayidaber* and *dibarti* in this passage evokes the classic Sinaitic formula *vayidaber Hashem el Moshe lemor*, signaling that what Yehoshua is now implementing is the fulfillment of a weighty divine command from Sinai. The *vayidaber* language marks this as a moment of supreme gravity.

### Language Challenge

The *gemara* challenges: is it really true that every instance of *dibur* carries a harsh connotation? Several counter-examples are adduced. *Diber ha'ish adonei ha'aretz itanu kashot* — there, Yosef "spoke harshly" to his brothers and *dibur* is indeed harsh. But *az nidberu yirei Hashem* — "then those who feared God spoke to one another" — this is a pleasant, warm exchange, not a harsh one. And *yadber amim tachtenu* — this *yadber* connotes leading or guiding nations, again not harsh.

The *gemara* resolves: *dibur lachud, yadber lachud* — the *dikduk* distinguishes between *dibur* (speech, which leans harsh) and *yadber* (to lead or guide, which can be pleasant). These are distinct usages of the same root.

The debate then pivots: *peliga Rabbi Yehuda veRabbanan*. One opinion holds that the harshness of the language reflects the fact that these *mitzvot* are of Torah origin and carry special weight; the other holds that God was actually displeased with Yehoshua for tarrying in implementing the commandment to designate the cities.

### Joshua Writing

Since the discussion now centers on Sefer Yehoshua, the *gemara* connects to another question. The verse *vayichtov Yehoshua et hadevarim ha'eleh bisefer Torat Elohim* — "and Yehoshua wrote these words in the Book of the Torah of God" — raises the question of what exactly Yehoshua wrote in the *sefer Torah*.

### Anger View

One opinion holds that the harsh *vayidaber* language reflects God's displeasure — Yehoshua was slow in fulfilling the commandment of establishing the cities of refuge, and God's speech to him was therefore stern. This anger view does not sit easily alongside the plain reading of the Yehoshua narrative, but it fits a pattern in Rabbinic literature of holding leaders to an elevated standard of alacrity in fulfilling *mitzvot*.

### Eight Verses Debate

Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Nechemya debate the question of Yehoshua's writing. One holds: *shemona pesukim* — Yehoshua wrote the final eight verses of the Torah, the *pesukim* at the end of Devarim that describe the death of Moshe. This connects to the famous debate in Bava Batra about who wrote those verses, with one opinion there attributing them to Yehoshua. The verse in Yehoshua referring to *sefer Torat Elohim* would then be a reference to the *sefer Torah* of Moshe — meaning Yehoshua wrote the closing verses of Moshe's Torah. The word *hadevarim* in that verse additionally evokes *Sefer Devarim*, giving the identification added resonance.

The other opinion holds: *parshat arei miklat* — what Yehoshua wrote was the section dealing with the *arei miklat*, which appears in Sefer Yehoshua itself. According to Rashi, *sefer Torat Elohim* in this verse refers not to Moshe's Torah but to Sefer Yehoshua, which is itself a book of divine teaching. On this reading, Yehoshua recorded in his own book the fulfillment of what had been commanded in the Torah — he wrote the *arei miklat* passage as the implementation of what God had commanded through Moshe.

The *gemara* notes: *bishlama le'man de'amar shemona pesukim*, the identification of *sefer Torat Elohim* as Moshe's Torah is straightforward. But *le'man de'amar arei miklat*, one must explain: *hachi ka'amar vayichtov Yehoshua besifro et hadevarim ha'eleh hakevuvim bisefer Torat Elohim* — Yehoshua wrote in his own book those matters that are recorded in the Torah of God. The *sefer Torat Elohim* is Moshe's Torah, and Yehoshua's book records the fulfillment of its commands.

## Binding Materials

### Flax vs. Sinews

A further debate is introduced: *sefer she'tefaro be'pishtan* — what is the status of a *sefer Torah* in which the parchment sections have been sewn together with flax rather than with *gidin* — sinews? Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Meir disagree: one holds it is *kasher*, the other *pasul*.

### R. Yehuda Pasul

The view that it is *pasul* derives from the verse *le'maan tihye Torat Hashem be'ficha* (Exodus 13:9). The *gemara* uses this verse to connect *tefillin* and *sefer Torah*: it is a *halacha le'Moshe mi'Sinai* that *tefillin* must be sewn with *gidin*, and the same verse equates *tefillin* with *sefer Torah*. *Vehikish kol haTorah kullah letefillin* — just as *tefillin* require *gidin*, so too does a *sefer Torah*.

### Limited Derivation

The opposing view holds: *ki hikish le'le'maan tihye Torat Hashem be'ficha, lehilchotav lo hikish* — the *hekesh* between *tefillin* and *sefer Torah* is limited. The verse connects them only for the *derasha* of *beficha* — namely, that the *klaf* must come from the hide of a permitted animal, one that is *mutar beficha*, fit for consumption. For other *halachot* of *tefillin*, including the requirement of *gidin*, no *hekesh* is made to *sefer Torah*. A *sefer Torah* therefore does not require sinew binding.

Rav Chazina adds a brief practical note: *chazeina lehu letefillin d'bei chavivi* — he saw the *tefillin* in the home of his beloved, referring to Rabbi Chiya, *detfiri bechitna* — that they were sewn with flax. He then notes: *ve'leis hilcheta kevasei* — the *halacha* does not follow this practice for *tefillin*. The ruling is stated simply and the *gemara* moves on.

## High Priest Death

### Mishnah Categories

The *mishnah* now enumerates the categories of *kohen gadol* whose death releases the manslayer from the *ir miklat*: *echad mashuach beshemen hamishcha* — one anointed with the oil of anointment, as was practiced in the first *Beit HaMikdash*; *ve'echad hamerubeh bigvadim* — one who attained the status of *kohen gadol* through investiture in the eight garments alone, a practice that became necessary toward the end of the first Temple period when the *shemen hamishcha* was no longer available; and *ve'echad she'avar mimishichuto* — even a former *kohen gadol*, one who had served in that capacity but was temporarily displaced — for example, because a *pul* rendered him unfit to serve on *Yom Kippur* and a replacement served in his place. Even such a retired *kohen gadol*, his death would free the manslayer.

## High Priest Death (II)

### Mothers' Care

Because the death of any sitting *kohen gadol* releases the manslayer, *imoseihem shel kohanim mesapkos lahen michya uchsus* — the mothers of the *kohanim gedolim* would send generous care packages to the manslayers confined in the *arei miklat*. The motivation: *kedei shelo yispallelu al beneihem sheyamusu* — so that the manslayers would not pray for their sons to die. If you have been receiving food and clothing from this man's mother, you might feel some gratitude toward her son and refrain from wishing him dead. Or equally, once the *kohen gadol* dies and the manslayer is free to leave, the care packages stop — and perhaps the manslayer would rather remain in comfortable exile than lose his benefactress.

### Curse Efficacy

But this raises a question: why should the prayer of these manslayers have any effect? The verse states: *ke'tzipor lanud kederor la'of, ken kilat chinam lo tavo* — like a bird that flutters and a swallow that flies free, so a causeless curse will not land (Proverbs 26:2). If there is no deserving basis for it, why should God answer a prayer calling for the death of an innocent *kohen gadol*?

### Culpability

An elder answered: *amar hahu saba mipirkei d'Rava shmia li* — I heard this from the teaching of Rava. *She'haya lahem levakesh rachamim al doram velo bikshu* — the *kohanim gedolim* bear a share of culpability: they were obligated to pray for their generation, to intercede before God so that such tragedies of accidental death would not occur — and they did not do so. More broadly, the *kohen gadol* as spiritual leader bears responsibility for the moral and physical welfare of his people. If he failed in that responsibility, the deaths that occurred under his watch are not entirely beyond his accountability, and a prayer calling for his death is therefore not entirely without basis.

This principle runs deep. Leadership confers not only honor but responsibility for what happens within one's domain.

### Prayer Variant

Some manuscripts record the text of the *mishnah* differently: not that the mothers sought to prevent prayer for the *kohen gadol's* death, but *kedei she'yitzalu aleihem shelo yamutu* — they sent care packages so that the manslayers would actively pray for the *kohen gadol* to live. But the *gemara* objects: on this reading, the implication would be that if the manslayers did *not* pray for the *kohen gadol's* life, *amai meiti* — why should the *kohen gadol* die? *Mah hava lei lemi'evad* — what wrong had he done to deserve death? The *gemara* responds with the Babylonian formulation of the irony: *Tuvia chata veZigud minged?* — Tuvia sinned and Zigud gets punished? Here the parallel is: the *rotzeach* killed and the *kohen gadol* deserves death? The Eretz Yisrael formulation of the same irony: *Shechem nasiv uMavgai gazir?* — Shechem took Dinah and the men of his city had to undergo circumcision?

The *gemara* resolves even this version with the same teaching of Rava: *she'haya lahem levakesh rachamim al doram velo bikshu* — the *kohanim gedolim* themselves bear responsibility for not having prayed sufficiently for their generation. It is not unjust that they require the prayers of the manslayers to preserve their lives; they forfeited a degree of their own protection by failing in their pastoral duty. This is presented as even weightier than before: not merely that the curse might be answered, but that the *kohanim gedolim* begin with a measure of deserving — and need prayer to counteract it.

## Justice Excursus

### Sage's Curse

Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: *klalat chacham afilu bechinam hi ba'ah* — a curse issued by a Torah scholar takes effect even if it is undeserved, even a *klalat chinam*. The authority of a *chacham* is such that his words carry independent force regardless of whether the underlying deserving exists.

### Ahitophel Story

The source is Ahitophel. When David was digging the foundations of the *Beit HaMikdash*, he dug so deep that he tapped into the primordial depths — the *tehom* — and the waters began to rise, threatening to flood the world. David asked whether anyone knew how to stop this, and declared: *kol hayodeia davar zeh ve'eino omro yechanek bigrono* — whoever knows the answer and does not say it, let him choke in his throat.

Ahitophel reasoned through a *kal vachomer*: if to make peace between husband and wife, the Torah permits God's name — written in sanctity — to be dissolved in water (*sotah*), then certainly to save the entire world, God's name can be written on pottery and cast into the depths to seal the waters. *Amar leih shari* — it is permitted. He wrote the divine name, cast the shard into the depths, and the waters receded.

Now, the condition in David's declaration was *if* someone knows and *does not say*. Ahitophel did say — in fact, he may not even have known the answer until the pressure of David's words caused him to work it out. The curse was therefore a *klalat chinam* — it should not have applied to Ahitophel at all. And yet: *ve'Ahitophel ra'ah ki lo ne'estah atzato... vayechanek* — Ahitophel saw that his counsel was not followed in the matter of the succession, went home, gave final instructions, and died by choking — precisely the death David's words had threatened. The *klalat chacham* took effect despite being causeless.

### Eli Samuel

Rabbi Abbahu adds: *klalat chacham afilu al tnai hi ba'ah* — a sage's curse takes effect even when stated conditionally. The source is Eli and Shmuel. Eli said to Shmuel: *koh ya'aseh lecha Elokim vecho yosif im techahed mimeni davar* — so should God do to you and add to it, if you conceal anything from me. Shmuel did not conceal; he told Eli everything. The condition was fulfilled — or rather, the condition for the curse's activation was *not* met, since Shmuel told the truth. The curse should have been null.

And yet the verse records: *velo halchu vanav bidrachav* — Shmuel's own children did not walk in his ways. They took bribes, precisely as Eli's sons had abused their priestly authority. The implication is that Eli's words — *koh ya'aseh lecha Elokim* — carried the force of a curse: *do to you what was done to me*. Even though Shmuel satisfied the stated condition, the inner logic of the conditional curse was fulfilled: Shmuel too would suffer the heartbreak of wayward sons.

### Tosafot Curse

Tosafot raises the challenge: in the Middle Ages, rabbinic leaders regularly used conditional *cherem* — *nidui al tnai* — as an enforcement mechanism. If you do not comply, you are in *cherem*. But if even a conditional curse of a *chacham* takes effect regardless of whether conditions are met, has not everyone upon whom such a *cherem* was declared been placed in a state requiring *hafarah*?

Tosafot distinguishes: the cases of David and Eli both involved conditions over which the subject had no full control. Ahitophel genuinely may not have known the answer until the pressure brought it forth; Shmuel told the truth, yet the outcome was beyond his control. Because the condition lay outside the person's power to determine, the curse took effect from the outset.

### Medieval Herem

But where the condition involves something fully within the person's control — *kegon shemandit adam shelo ya'aseh hadavar*, where a person is told: if you do such-and-such you will be in *cherem* — the *nidui* does not take hold from the outset. *Dekivan devyado hu, mis'at hanidui anu yodim bevadai shelo bedato la'asot hadavar* — since we can presume that a person does not intend to violate and thereby enter *cherem*, the *cherem* does not take effect unless and until he actually violates the condition. This distinction was critical for medieval rabbinic authorities, for whom *cherem al tnai* was a primary instrument of communal governance.

### Lion Story

A narrative illustrates the principle of leadership responsibility introduced earlier. A certain man was attacked by a lion within three *parsei* of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi — within what might be called his zone of communal authority. As a result, Eliyahu, who had been in the habit of speaking to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi regularly, did not speak to him for three days. The implication is that the attack occurred within a community for which Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi bore some degree of responsibility. Had he taken sufficient measures — teaching his community greater vigilance, implementing protections — perhaps this would not have happened.

### Smoke Detectors

This principle finds a contemporary resonance: a rabbi who on *Yom Kippur* delivered his central *derashah* on the obligation to ensure working batteries in smoke detectors was articulating precisely this point. The spiritual leader of a community bears responsibility for the physical safety of those in his care. If something preventable occurs within his community, questions may rightfully be asked of him.

### Judah's Bones

The *gemara* returns to the question of conditional curses by examining the case of Yehuda. When Yehuda pledged *im lo hevi'otiv eilecha vehatzagtiv lefanecha vechatati le'avi kol hayamim* — if I do not bring Binyamin back and present him before you I will be a sinner to my father all my days — this is read as a form of self-imposed *cherem*: acceptance of outcast status should the condition not be fulfilled.

Did Yehuda fulfill it? In a sense he did — Binyamin came safely to Yaakov in Mitzrayim, even if not directly "presented" before him as Yehuda had promised. Yet the *gemara* shows that the self-curse took effect nonetheless: *atzmotav shel Yehuda hayu megulgalim ba'aron* — Yehuda's bones rolled within the *aron* throughout the forty years in the desert, a sign that his soul found no rest.

At Moshe's prayer, the resolution came in stages. *Yihi Reuven ve'al yamot* — Moshe prayed for Reuven's eternal life, for Reuven had admitted his sin with Bilhah, and it was Yehuda's own public confession that had prompted Reuven's. *Vezot liYehuda* — Moshe then turned to Yehuda: is this what Yehuda deserves? *Shema Hashem kol Yehuda* — God heard and the bones reconnected, *alu eivrav laShafe*, forming a proper skeleton. But Yehuda's soul still could not enter the heavenly *yeshiva* — *ve'lo havu ka'ma'ylei lei bimetivta derakia* — until *ve'el amo tevi'enu* brought him in. Even then, *lo hava yada limishkal umitarach bishemata* — he could not argue well in Talmudic discourse with the other souls. *Yadav rav lo* — his hands were strengthened, and he could debate. Yet *lo hava yada lifrokei kushya* — he could not resolve difficulties. *Ve'eizer mitzarav tihye* — finally he received help even in that.

The case of Yehuda explains why *nidui al tnai* in uncontrollable circumstances takes hold from the outset: Yosef might have detained Binyamin; Binyamin might have been lost or stolen along the way. Because Yehuda's ability to fulfill the condition was not entirely in his hands, the self-imposed *cherem* attached immediately.

## Release Conditions

### Judgment Timing

The *mishnah* now addresses the determinative moment: which *kohen gadol's* death frees the manslayer? The answer is the *kohen gadol* who was in office at the time of the manslayer's *gmar din* — the conclusion of his trial, when *beit din* issued its sentence of exile to the *ir miklat*.

### No HP at Judgment

*Nigmar dino belo kohen gadol* — if there happened to be no *kohen gadol* at the time of *gmar din* — for instance, a vacancy had not yet been filled — *eino yotze misham le'olam*: he never goes free. There is no *kohen gadol* whose death can be tied to his release.

### HP Succession

If the *kohen gadol* died during the proceedings, before *gmar din*, and a new *kohen gadol* was appointed in his place, and only thereafter was the *gmar din* rendered — *chozer bemitat hasheni* — the manslayer's release is contingent on the death of the second *kohen gadol*, the one in office at the moment of *gmar din*.

### Kills HP

*Kohen gadol sheharag* — if the manslayer himself killed a *kohen gadol*, he is never released, because the *kohen gadol* whose death would theoretically free him is the very person he killed, and there can be no mechanism for release built around that.

### No Departure

While confined to the *ir miklat*, the manslayer may not leave under any circumstances. *Lo le'edut mitzvah* — not even to testify in fulfillment of a *mitzvah*; *ve'lo le'edut mamon* — not for monetary testimony; *ve'lo le'edut nefashot* — not even for capital testimony. *Ve'afilu Sar Tzva Yisrael keYoav ben Zeruiah* — even if he is the commander of Israel's armies and they are at war and need him. This last point raises obvious questions about *pikuach nefesh* — how can a negative prohibition override the security of the nation? The *gemara* grounds the rule in the verse *asher nas shamma*: *sham tehei dirato, sham tehei mitato, sham tehei kevurato* — there shall be his dwelling, there his death (if the *kohen gadol* does not die first), there his burial.

### Territorial Scope

The protection of the *ir miklat* extends not merely to its physical walls but to its surrounding *tchum* — the two-thousand-*amah* boundary that defines the Sabbath domain, *tchum Shabbat*. *Keshem she'ir koletet kach tchum kolet* — just as the city itself provides refuge, so too does its full perimeter.

## Outside Boundaries

### R. Yose: Mitzvah

*Ve'rotzeach sheyatza chutz latchum umatz'o goel hadam* — if the manslayer has left the *tchum* of the *ir miklat* and the *goel hadam* encounters him: Rabbi Yose HaGelili holds *mitzvah beyad goel hadam* — it is a *mitzvah* for the *goel hadam* to kill him. Furthermore, *reshut beyad kol adam* — any ordinary person is permitted to kill him.

### R. Akiva: Reshut

Rabbi Akiva holds: *reshut beyad goel hadam* — the *goel hadam* is permitted but not obligated; there is no *mitzvah* here. *Ve'chol adam chayavin alav* — on one reading of the final clause, any other person who kills him is liable for murder; on an alternate *girsa*, *ein chayavin alav* — they are not liable, but neither do they have any affirmative permission.

### Ethical Problem

The ethical difficulty of Rabbi Yose HaGelili's position is striking. This man killed *bishogeg* — unintentionally. He has served his exile. Why should leaving the *ir miklat's tchum* make him deserving of death, and why should that killing constitute a *mitzvah*? One way to read Rabbi Yose is less as a statement about the man's culpability and more as a mechanism of enforcement: the severity of the consequence is what keeps the manslayer within the city. If leaving carried no penalty, the institution of *ir miklat* would have no teeth.

Rabbi Akiva's position is more consistent with the spirit of the *pesukim*, which seem at every turn to be trying to *protect* the manslayer rather than to deliver him into further danger. The Torah tolerates the residual element of vigilante justice embodied by the *goel hadam* — it cannot entirely legislate away the grief and rage of a bereaved family — but it does not endorse it as a *mitzvah*. On Rabbi Akiva's reading, the Torah channels and limits this impulse without sanctifying it. Whether anyone who kills the manslayer outside the *tchum* would bear murder liability remains, on some versions of the text, an open question — itself a reflection of how profoundly difficult it is to assign full moral responsibility in these cases.

---

---

# Makkot 12

## Kohen Gadol Death

### Intro & Gmar Din

The *gemara* on daf 12a picks up immediately following the *mishna* on 11b, which addresses the question of who counts as the *kohen gadol* for purposes of releasing the *rotzeach* from the *ir miklat*. The basic rule established by the *mishna* is that the determining moment is *gmar din* — the moment of final sentencing. Whoever holds the office of *kohen gadol* at the time the judgment is passed is the *kohen gadol* whose death eventually frees the exile. This holds even if the *kohen gadol* dies before the convicted person has actually traveled to the *ir miklat*: the connection is forged at *gmar din*, not at the moment of arrival. Conversely, if there is no *kohen gadol* at the moment of *gmar din*, the exile is permanent — the person never goes free. And if there are multiple changes in the office, what matters is who held it at *gmar din*.

### Kal Vachomer & Kapara

The *gemara* opens by asking *mai ta'ama* — what is the underlying rationale for the ruling that if the *kohen gadol* dies even before the convicted person has entered the *ir miklat*, he nonetheless goes free? Abaye proposes a *kal vachomer*: if someone who has already been in exile goes free upon the *kohen gadol*'s death, surely someone who has not yet entered exile at all — who is in a sense already partway out — should likewise go free.

The *gemara* immediately challenges this *kal vachomer*. One might argue precisely the reverse: the person who went into exile received some measure of *kapara* through the experience of exile itself, whereas the person who never entered *galus* has not yet undergone that atonement. On this reading, the exile who has already experienced *galus* has earned his release, but the person who has not yet entered cannot benefit from the same logic.

The *gemara* then delivers what appears to be a decisive clarification, almost as a throwaway remark: *midi galus kamchapra? Misas kohen hi de'mechaphra* — do you think it is the *galus* that atones? No. It is the death of the *kohen* that atones. This statement raises a significant difficulty, because earlier in the *masechet* the *gemara* itself speaks explicitly about exile as a form of *kapara*, stating that the unworthy go into exile so that it serves as atonement for them.

### Tosafot Kapara

*Tosafot* addresses this tension directly, citing the passage at the beginning of the *masechet* that treats *galus* as *kapara*: *alma galus mechaper*. *Tosafot* asks: surely the exile itself does atone — how then can the *gemara* dismiss this? *Tosafot* answers by distinguishing between two different forms of *kapara*. There is the *kapara* that atones for the underlying sin of negligent homicide — and that is indeed the experience of exile. But there is a separate question of what serves as the release mechanism, what "atones" in the sense of enabling the person to be freed from the obligation of exile altogether. That function is performed by the death of the *kohen gadol*. *Tosafot* phrases this as *kapara liftur migalus* — the atonement that frees one from exile — and says it is the *misas kohen gadol* that accomplishes this, even for someone who never entered exile at all.

The result is a striking and somewhat ironic situation: the person who goes free before ever entering the *ir miklat* is released from the *chiyuv* of exile through the *kohen gadol*'s death, yet never undergoes the experiential *kapara* of *galus* that would atone for the original act of negligence. The *gemara* says: *de'misas kohen gadol to'il liptoro migalus m'kal vachomer* — the death of the *kohen gadol* suffices to free him from exile by means of *kal vachomer*. These are two distinct processes operating in parallel.

### Kohen Appointed Mid-Trial

The *mishna* addresses a further case: what if a new *kohen gadol* was appointed during the course of the trial proceedings themselves? The rule is that it is the *kohen gadol* who holds office at the moment of *gmar din* who determines the exile — even if he was appointed only partway through the proceedings.

### Anointed in His Day

Rav Kahana derives this from a verse: *v'yashav bah ad mos hakohen hagadol asher mashach oso b'shemen hakodesh* — he shall dwell in the *ir miklat* until the death of the *kohen gadol* who anointed him with the holy oil. The *gemara* asks: *v'chi hu meshacho?* Did the convicted person actually anoint the *kohen gadol*? Obviously not. Rather, says the *gemara*, *asher mashach* means *shenimshach b'yamav* — who was anointed during his time, that is, during the period of the exile's lifetime or, more precisely, during the relevant period of proceedings. This reading encompasses even a *kohen gadol* who was anointed partway through the trial, since the verse attaches the release to whoever held anointed office at the moment of *gmar din*.

### Kohen Responsibility

The *gemara* then raises a conceptual difficulty regarding this newly appointed *kohen gadol*. Part of the underlying logic of the institution — that the *kohen gadol*'s death frees the exile — has to do with the *kohen gadol* bearing some degree of responsibility for preventable deaths in the society under his watch. Leaders of the religious establishment are responsible for cultivating a society in which such tragedies do not occur. But if this *kohen gadol* was only appointed during the trial proceedings, what responsibility does he bear for the original death?

The *gemara* answers: *mah hava lei l'meivad? Haya lo l'vakesh rachamim sheyigmor dino l'zechut v'lo vikesh* — what should he have done? He should have prayed that the judgment be concluded in the person's favor, and he failed to do so. This is admittedly difficult to parse. Even if the convicted person genuinely deserved to be exiled, the *kohen gadol*'s responsibility is framed as his failure to pray on his behalf. The *gemara* never fully resolves the philosophical tension here. It is perhaps best understood in light of the broader principle, noted by a participant in the discussion, of *mitat tzadikim mechaperet* — the death of the righteous atones — and the *kohen gadol*'s unique status as the head of the religious establishment, such that his death carries atoning power regardless of the specific circumstances of his appointment.

---

## Burial & Bones

### Death Pre-Kohen

Abaye states: *naktinan*, we take it as an established principle, that if a person received *gmar din* and then died before going to the *ir miklat*, the question arises of what is to be done with his body.

### Burial in Ir Miklat

Abaye rules: *molichin et atzmotav l'sham* — his bones are brought to an *ir miklat* and he is buried there. The source is the verse *lashuv lashevet ba'aretz ad mot hakohen* — to return to dwell in the land until the *kohen* dies. The *gemara* reads *lashevet ba'aretz* — literally "to dwell in the land," meaning under the land — as a reference to burial. The *mishna* itself (readable in the narrow line within the *gemara* text) states explicitly: *sham tei dirato, sham tei misato, sham tei kevurato* — there is his dwelling, there is his death, there is his burial. Burial in the *ir miklat* is thus not incidental but part of the *din* of exile itself. Even a person who never lived in the *ir miklat* is subject to this aspect of the *din* that was passed upon him.

### Disinterment & Return

The *gemara* cites a *baraita*: if the exile died while residing in the *ir miklat* — before the *kohen gadol* died — and was buried there, and subsequently the *kohen gadol* died, the verse states *yashuv harotzeach el eretz achuzato* — the murderer shall return to the land of his inheritance. The *gemara* interprets *eizehu yeshuv she'hi eretz achuzato* through the same lens: *hevei omer zu kevurah* — this "return" refers to burial in his ancestral plot.

The Rambam's reading of this passage is notably different from a more surface-level reading. Rather than reading the phrase about carrying the bones *al kivrei avotav* as a brief symbolic visit followed by reburial in the *ir miklat*, the Rambam understands the sequence as follows: the person was buried in the *ir miklat* during the period of exile; when the *kohen gadol* died, the exile ended retroactively, and at that point the bones are disinterred and reinterred with his fathers in his ancestral land. Just as a living exile would physically return upon the *kohen gadol*'s death, his bones are accorded the same return. The verse *yashuv harotzeach* applies equally to bones as to a living person, enabling his remains ultimately to rest in his ancestral burial place.

---

## Pasul Kohen

### Ben Grusha Discovered

A new case is introduced: *nigmar dino*, a person received his *gmar din*, with a particular individual serving as *kohen gadol* — call him Reuven. Reuven's death is thus the event that will eventually free this exile. Subsequently, it is discovered that Reuven's mother was in fact a *grusha*, rendering him a *chalal* — a *pasul kohen* who was never halachically fit for the *kehunah* in the first place. The question is whether, in retrospect, there was any valid *kohen gadol* at the moment of *gmar din*, and what the consequences are for the exile.

### Misas/Batla Kehunah

Rabbi Ammi and Rabbi Yitzchak Nafcha debate the matter. One holds *meita kehunah*: the discovery of his *pesul* is treated as the death of his *kehunah*, equivalent to the death of a *kohen gadol*, and the exile goes free. The other holds *batla kehunah*: retroactively his *kehunah* is nullified, meaning there was no valid *kohen gadol* at *gmar din*, and the exile remains permanently confined to the *ir miklat*.

### Korban Validity

The *gemara* wonders whether this debate maps onto an earlier tannaitic dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua. The *mishna* (in a different context) describes a case where a *kohen* is found to be a *ben grusha* or *ben chalutzah* in the midst of bringing *korbanot* on the *mizbe'ach*. Rabbi Eliezer rules: *kol korbanot she'hikriv pesulin* — all the *korbanot* he ever brought are retroactively invalid, because he was never a *kohen* at all. Rabbi Yehoshua rules *machshir* — he validates them, holding that his invalidity takes effect only from the moment of discovery, not retroactively.

The connection to the *ir miklat* debate seems straightforward: the opinion that holds *meita kehunah* — treating discovery as equivalent to the *kohen gadol*'s death, freeing the exile — parallels Rabbi Yehoshua's position that the *kohen*'s status was valid until the moment of discovery. The opinion that holds *batla kehunah* — that retroactively there was never a valid *kohen gadol* — parallels Rabbi Eliezer's position that everything is retroactively annulled.

### Gemara Resolution

The *gemara* rejects this mapping, however, and offers a more refined resolution at the top of 12a. *Aliba de'Rabbi Eliezer kulei alma lo pligi* — according to Rabbi Eliezer, there is no debate in the *ir miklat* case at all. If Rabbi Eliezer holds that the *pesul* is fully retroactive, then clearly there was no *kohen gadol* at *gmar din*, and the exile never goes free. The debate between the two opinions is only *aliba de'Rabbi Yehoshua* — according to Rabbi Yehoshua, who holds that the *kohen*'s status was valid until discovery. Even granting that, one could argue that the discovery acts like a *misas kehunah* and frees the exile — that is the first opinion. The second opinion, however, holds *batla kehunah* even within Rabbi Yehoshua's framework, and would say that even Rabbi Yehoshua's leniency does not extend to this case.

### Korban Exception

The reason the second opinion can hold *batla kehunah* even according to Rabbi Yehoshua is that Rabbi Yehoshua's ruling in the *korbanot* case rests on a specific verse: *bareich Hashem cheilo ufo'al yadav tirtzeh* — God should bless his *cheil* (related to *chullin* or *chalal*) and the acts of his hands shall be accepted. The *drasha* is that even if he turns out to be a *chalal*, as long as this was not known at the time, God accepts the *korbanot*. This is a specific *halacha* applying to *korbanot* — a practically necessary rule to prevent the cascade of invalidation that would otherwise require enormous numbers of people to bring replacement offerings. But *ad kan* — this is the limit of Rabbi Yehoshua's ruling. It is a *halacha* confined to *korbanot*. In the context of *ir miklat*, where no such verse applies, even Rabbi Yehoshua would agree that if the *kohen gadol* was a *chalal*, there was never a valid *kohen gadol* at *gmar din*, and the exile remains permanently confined. Thus the debate within Rabbi Yehoshua's position comes down to whether the discovery itself acts as a species of *misas kehunah* capable of freeing the exile, or whether — absent the special *halacha* of *korbanot* — the retroactive nullification leaves the exile with no path to freedom.

A further digression in the *gemara* concerns the case of Yoav ben Tzeruiah, who is cited in the context of a *kohen gadol* or a figure whose presence in the *ir miklat* is required by the nation at large. The question of *pikuach nefesh* is raised — what happens if the person confined to the *ir miklat* is someone the nation needs urgently, such as a military commander? The *gemara* does not develop this point directly.

Regarding Yoav ben Tzeruiah himself: David on his deathbed instructed Shlomo to ensure that Yoav would not die in peace, because Yoav had shed blood in a time of peace by killing two major Israelite generals. Yoav, understanding the principle of sanctuary, fled to the *mizbe'ach* and grasped its horns. Shlomo sent Benaiahu ben Yehoyada, who killed him there. The *gemara* (cited by Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav) teaches that Yoav made two fundamental errors — and Abaye adds a third. First, he erred in thinking the altar provided sanctuary while grasping its horns: the verse says *me'im mizbechi*, which the *gemara* reads as referring to the roof or top surface of the altar, not the horns. Second, he erred because the sanctuary applies only to the *mizbe'ach beit olamim* — the altar of the permanent *Beis Hamikdash* — whereas Yoav grasped the temporary altar erected by David before the *Beis Hamikdash* was built. Third, according to Abaye, he erred because the sanctuary of the altar protects only a *kohen* who is actively engaged in the *avodah*, and Yoav was a *zar*.

It is striking that the *gemara* does not list a fourth error: that Yoav killed *b'meizid*, intentionally, and the verse *v'chi yazid ish al re'ehu l'horgo b'ormah me'im mizbechi tikachenu lamus* explicitly states that an intentional killer is dragged from the altar to be executed. The Rambam addresses this omission in a remarkable passage. He rules that the altar sanctuary applies to someone who killed *b'shogeg*, and also — under different conditions — to someone fleeing the king's power or a *beit din* acting in *hora'at sha'ah* emergency capacity, even without a standard *din*. For such a person, the Rambam rules, the sanctuary is absolute and they may never be removed, even if they are a *zar*, even if they held on to the horns rather than the rooftop. This would encompass Yoav's case, since Shlomo's mandate to execute him did not come from a formal *beit din* process. The Rambam's source may be the *Yerushalmi*, as the reading diverges significantly from our *gemara*'s analysis.

The *gemara* concludes this section with a *midrashic* application by Reish Lakish. Since the discussion has touched on the three errors of Yoav, Reish Lakish observes that the *sar shel Romi* — the divine power overseeing Rome — will make three parallel errors in the eschatological era. The verse in Yeshayahu, *mi zeh ba me-Edom chamutz begadim mi-Botzrah*, depicts God arriving blood-soaked from Edom after slaying that power. Three errors: the angel fled to *Botzrah* rather than *Betzer*, one of the actual *arei miklat* — confusing the names; the *ir miklat* sanctuary only protects a *shogeg*, and this angel was a *meizid*; and the sanctuary protects only human beings, and this is an angel.

---

## Burial & Bones (II)

### Levites' Cemetery

Rabbi Abbahu rules: *ir miklat lo nitnu l'kevura* — the cities of refuge were not designated for burial. He derives this from the verse *u-migrasheihem yiheyu lahem livhemtam u-l'rekhusham v'sham l'khol chayatam* — the open lands around the cities were designated for living creatures. *L'chayim nitnu v'lo l'kevura* — they were given for the living, not for burial.

This seems to contradict the *halacha* established earlier that exiles are buried in the *ir miklat*. The *gemara* resolves this cleanly: *rotzeach shani*, the *rotzeach* is different, because the *Torah* explicitly specifies that the exile dwells there, dies there, and is buried there. That explicit ruling overrides the general principle. The general principle — that these cities are not for burial — applies to the *Leviyim* themselves, the permanent residents. The *Leviyim*' cemetery is located outside the boundaries of the *ir miklat*, not within it.

### Tchum Refuge

The *mishna* states that just as the city itself provides sanctuary, so too does the *tchum* — the surrounding area of two thousand *amah* — serve as a refuge zone. The basis is the general structure of the *arei ha-Leviyim*: the *Torah* speaks of a *migrash* of one thousand *amah* and a *sadeh* extending to two thousand *amah* around the city, and both zones together constitute the effective *tchum*.

A question is raised from the verse *v'yashav bah* — he shall dwell *in it*, implying only within the city itself, not in its environs. Abaye resolves this: *kan liklot kan ladur* — these are two separate provisions. The verse *v'yashav bah* concerns where the exile must live — his permanent dwelling must be inside the city. But the *tchumim* surrounding the city retain their protective function as sanctuary even without being his residence. He must reside in the city; he is protected throughout the *tchum*.

A further complication: there is a general *halacha* of *arei ha-Leviyim* prohibiting building in the *migrash* area, meaning the exile cannot construct a dwelling outside the city boundaries even if he wished to. Rav Sheshet resolves this by noting that the prohibition on dwelling outside applies specifically to building structures. One could potentially inhabit caves or subterranean spaces in the *tchum* without violating the prohibition. The practical upshot is that the exile must live in the city proper but is protected throughout the *tchum*.

---

## Goel HaDam

### Yose vs. Akiva

The *gemara* now turns to what happens if the *rotzeach* exits the *ir miklat*. Rabbi Yose HaGlili and Rabbi Akiva debate the status of the *goel hadam* in such a case. Rabbi Yose HaGlili holds that it is a *mitzvah* for the *goel hadam* to kill the *rotzeach* who has left the bounds of the *ir miklat*, and if there is no *goel hadam* available, then *reshus b'yad kol adam* — any person has permission to do so. Rabbi Akiva holds that the *goel hadam* has *reshus* — permission, not an obligation — and any other person who kills the *rotzeach* would be liable for murder. The crux of the debate turns on the reading of the verse *v'ratzach goel hadam et ha-rotzeach*: Rabbi Yose HaGlili reads *v'ratzach* as prescriptive — he shall kill; Rabbi Akiva notes that it does not say *yirtzach* and reads it as descriptive — if he kills. The verb is genuinely ambiguous and neither position has a decisive grammatical advantage.

Most people would instinctively identify with Rabbi Akiva's position; the idea of *mitzvah* for the *goel hadam* strikes most as difficult to embrace, even if the verse permits it. The Torah's framework here is plausibly understood as accommodating the pre-existing reality of blood vengeance while channeling and limiting it — the *ir miklat* system is an attempt to insert legal structure into what would otherwise be pure vigilante justice.

### Tannaim Sources

A *baraita* supports the analysis. The *Torah* states *v'ratzach goel hadam et ha-rotzeach — ein lo damim* — the *goel hadam* kills the *rotzeach* and bears no blood guilt. The *baraita* in accordance with Rabbi Yose HaGlili reads this as: it is a *mitzvah* for the *goel hadam* to do so; if no *goel hadam* is available, the permission passes to any person. In accordance with Rabbi Akiva: the *goel hadam* alone has *reshus*, and any other person would be guilty.

### Mar Zutra Opinion

Mar Zutra bar Tuvia in the name of Rav takes a position that departs from both *tanna'im*: a *rotzeach* who exits the *tchum* and is killed by the *goel hadam* — the *goel hadam* himself is liable for murder. This is the most restrictive possible reading and, as the *gemara* notes, contradicts both Rabbi Yose HaGlili and Rabbi Akiva, since both agree the *goel hadam* is at minimum permitted. The *gemara* asks: *k'man* — like whom? And answers that Mar Zutra follows a third *tanna* whose opinion we have not yet seen.

### Standing Before Eidah

That third *tanna* is derived from a *braita* in the name of Rabbi Eliezer: *ad omdo lifnei ha-eidah l'mishpat* — the verse says he shall not be killed until he stands before the court for judgment. Rabbi Eliezer applies this principle not only to the initial trial but also to the case of someone who has left the *ir miklat*. When the *Torah* states *v'ratzach goel hadam et ha-rotzeach* — he kills the *rotzeach* who left — one might think this grants the *goel hadam* immediate, independent authority to act. *Talmud lomar*: *ad omdo lifnei ha-eidah l'mishpat* — no. Even now, the killing may only occur after the person has stood before a court.

This is a remarkable step in the direction of fully judicializing the *goel hadam* function. The *goel hadam* is not acting as a private avenger but as an instrument of the court. The *rotzeach* who leaves the *ir miklat* has, by that act, made himself liable to death — but the execution of that judgment requires judicial process. One possible reading: the *goel hadam* must bring the person before a *beit din*, the *beit din* finds him liable, and only then may the *goel hadam* carry out the killing. As the discussion notes, this transforms the entire *goel hadam* institution into something closely analogous to a *shaliach beis din*.

Rabbi Yose HaGlili and Rabbi Akiva, the *gemara* notes, do not use *ad omdo lifnei ha-eidah l'mishpat* for this purpose. They have a different *drasha* from that verse — specifically, Rabbi Akiva uses it to derive that if an entire *sanhedrin* witnessed a murder, they may not themselves adjudicate the case; the witnesses must bring their testimony to a separate *beit din*, because *ad omdo lifnei ha-eidah l'mishpat* requires the defendant to be able to "stand before" the court in a genuine sense, which is impossible if the court itself observed the crime.

### Intentional Exit

A *baraita* asks: *im yatzo yetzei ha-rotzeach* — the verse says "if he leaves, he leaves." Does this expose the *rotzeach* to being killed regardless of how he came to be outside the *ir miklat*? What if he left *b'shogeg* — accidentally, without intent? *Talmud lomar*: the double language *yatzo yetzei* could imply *mi-kol makom*, by any means. Yet another *braita* distinguishes: *b'meizid neherag, b'shogeg goleh* — if he left intentionally he is liable to be killed; if unintentionally, he simply returns to the *ir miklat*. The two *baraitot* thus conflict, and the *gemara* resolves that the question turns on the principle of *dibrah Torah ki-leshon b'nei adam* — whether one gives interpretive weight to the doubled expression or reads it as ordinary language.

### End Not Harsher

Abaye weighs in decisively with a logical argument: *mistabra* — it stands to reason — to adopt the position that reads *yatzo yetzei* as ordinary language and restricts the *goel hadam*'s license to the case of intentional exit. His reason: *shelo yehei sofo chamur mi-tchilato* — the end should not be harsher than the beginning. At the beginning, when the original killing occurred: *b'meizid neherag, b'shogeg goleh* — intentional killing incurs death, unintentional killing incurs exile. The same logic should apply at the end: if he left the *ir miklat* intentionally, *neherag*; if unintentionally, *goleh* — he simply returns. It would be incoherent for the regime surrounding the *ir miklat* to be harsher than the original sentencing framework that put him there.

This argument also reinforces the broader pattern visible throughout this sugya: the entire institution is being progressively reframed in terms of *din* — legal judgment with the categories of *shogeg* and *meizid*, intentionality, court authorization — rather than raw blood vengeance. The language of *neherag*, "he is killed," rather than "the *goel hadam* kills him," reflects this judicial framing.

---

## Father & Son

### Son's Status

A *baraita* rules: *av she-harag bno na'aseh lo goel hadam* — a father who accidentally killed his son: the surviving brother may serve as *goel hadam* against the father to avenge his brother's blood. Another *baraita* contradicts this: *ein bno na'aseh lo goel hadam* — a son may not serve as *goel hadam* against his father.

The *gemara* considers whether this maps onto the debate between Rabbi Yose HaGlili and Rabbi Akiva — the former expanding the scope of the *goel hadam* institution, the latter restricting it.

### No Shaliach

The *gemara* rejects this mapping: *v'tisbra* — does it even make sense, regardless of whether the *goel hadam*'s function is a *mitzvah* or a *reshus*, to permit a son to act against his father in this way? The principle is established by Rabbah bar Rav Huna and confirmed by the school of Rabbi Yishmael: *ein haben na'aseh shaliach l'aviv lehakoto ulekallelo* — a son cannot serve as the *beit din*'s agent to administer corporal punishment or impose *cherem* on his own father. The son must recuse himself from any judicial function directed against his father. The one exception is *mesit* — one who seduces others to idolatry — where the *Torah* explicitly commands *lo tachmol alav v'lo techaseh alav*, leaving no room for compassion.

The very framing of this ruling — that the *goel hadam* cannot act against a father because a son cannot be a *shaliach beit din* against his father — once again encodes the *goel hadam* as a judicial agent rather than a private avenger.

### Grandson Allowed

The *gemara* resolves the contradiction between the two *baraitot*: *lo kashya, ha bno v'ha ben bno* — there is no contradiction. The *baraita* that prohibits it refers to the son acting against his father. The *baraita* that permits it refers to the grandson — the son of the man who was killed — acting against his grandfather, the killer. That is permitted. The father-son relationship creates the disqualification; the grandfather-grandson relationship does not.

---

## Tree Boundary

### Crown Rule

The final *mishna* of the *daf* addresses a classic question in halachic boundary law: a tree that stands astride the boundary of the *ir miklat*. If the trunk (*ikar*) stands within the *tchum* and the crown (*nof*) extends outside, or the trunk is outside and the crown extends inside — where is the person in the tree considered to be? The *mishna* rules: *hakol holech achar hanof* — everything follows the crown. This reverses the usual presumption, often formulated as *shadinan nofo batar ikaro* — we treat the crown as following the trunk — and says instead that the crown determines the person's location.

### Maaser Sheni

The *gemara* immediately raises a *reminehu* — a contradiction from a *baraita* dealing with *Maaser Sheni* in Yerushalayim. The relevant law is that *Maaser Sheni* must be eaten within the walls of Yerushalayim. The *baraita* states: a tree whose trunk is inside Yerushalayim and whose crown extends outside, or whose trunk is outside and crown extends inside — *miknegd ha-chomah velifnim ke-lifnim, miknegd ha-chomah velachutz ke-lachutz* — the dividing line is the wall projected straight upward. You are wherever the vertical line of the wall places you. This makes no reference to crown or trunk; it simply asks whether you are in the airspace inside or outside the wall.

This seems to contradict the *mishna* in our *masechet*, which says to follow the crown.

The *gemara* offers an initial resolution: these two cases are not comparable because the governing principle differs. By *Maaser Sheni*, the *Torah* attached the law to the *chomah* — the physical walls of Yerushalayim — so the relevant question is always one of airspace relative to the projected wall. By *ir miklat*, the *Torah* attached the law to *dirah* — dwelling — as in the verse *ki be-ir miklato yeishev*. The question is not airspace but where one is considered to be dwelling. *Benofo midayer, be-ikaro lo midayer* — one can conceivably build a dwelling in the crown of a tree; nobody dwells in a trunk. Therefore by *ir miklat* the crown determines the locus of "dwelling."

### Yehuda Debate

The *gemara* then complicates matters further: *rami Maaser a-Maaser* — there is a contradiction even within the *Maaser Sheni* sources themselves. A *mishna* in *Maasrot* states that by Yerushalayim one follows the *nof* (crown) for determining whether one may eat *Maaser Sheni*. This contradicts the *baraita* that said to follow the projected wall.

Rav Kahana resolves: *lo kashya, ha Rabbi Yehuda ve-ha Rabbanan* — the two sources reflect a tannaitic debate. The *braita* recorded in a *baraita*: Rabbi Yehuda says that by a cave, one follows the opening (*achar pitchah*), and by a tree, one follows the crown (*achar nofo*). This is Rabbi Yehuda's position — both for *Maaser Sheni* in Yerushalayim and for *ir miklat*, follow the crown.
