The opposing position (the *Rabbanan*) would say you follow where you actually are in the airspace, consistent with the *baraita* about the projected wall.

### Lechumra Reading

The *gemara*, however, does not accept that Rabbi Yehuda's ruling applies fully and symmetrically in all directions. There is a general principle — cited by *Rashi* — of *shadinan nofo batar ikaro*: normally the crown follows the trunk, not the reverse. Given this background assumption, the *gemara* reasons: one cannot say that Rabbi Yehuda intends to fully override this principle in both directions. Rather, *d'shamat lei l'Rabbi Yehuda gabei Maaser l'chumra* — Rabbi Yehuda's ruling that one follows the crown should be understood as applying only *l'chumra*, only in the stringent direction.

What does *l'chumra* mean by *Maaser Sheni*? There are two relevant restrictions: eating *Maaser Sheni* requires being inside Yerushalayim; *pidyon* (redemption) of *Maaser Sheni* may only be done outside. To be *machmir* both ways means: if the trunk is inside and the crown is outside, we follow the crown (*l'chumra*) and say this person may not eat *Maaser Sheni* there, because the crown is outside. But we also do not allow *pidyon*, because the trunk is inside and the general principle is to follow the trunk — so *l'chumra* for that as well, we say he may not redeem. If the trunk is outside and the crown is inside, we follow the crown (*l'chumra*) and say he may not redeem without *pidyon* because he is considered inside; but we also say he may not eat without *pidyon* because the trunk is outside. The result is that Rabbi Yehuda's rule about following the crown is always applied to impose the maximum stringency — never to grant leniency.

### Rava Cases

Rava observes that this *l'chumra* reading works cleanly by *Maaser Sheni*, but creates a problem by *ir miklat*. By *ir miklat*, *l'chumra* in one direction is clear: if the trunk is outside and the crown inside, we treat the person as inside and say the *goel hadam* cannot kill him — that is a stringency in the sense of protecting the *rotzeach*. But what about the reverse case: trunk inside, crown outside? To follow the crown *l'chumra* here would mean treating him as outside the *ir miklat* and allowing the *goel hadam* to kill him — even though he is physically standing inside the *ir miklat* at the trunk of the tree. *Ha gavra kai* — the man is standing inside! Treating him as exposed to death on the grounds that his crown is outside is not a *chumra* in any meaningful sense; it is an absurdity. You would be using a legal fiction to allow someone to be killed who is physically inside the protected zone.

### Rav Ashi Crown

Rav Ashi offers the *gemara*'s final resolution. *Mai acharei nof, af acharei nof* — when the *mishna* says one follows the *nof*, this means: we follow the *nof* to protect the person, to extend the mantle of the *ir miklat* in his favor. The rule is asymmetric by design. If the person is at the trunk inside the *ir miklat* and the crown extends outside, he is inside — obviously, since he is standing inside. If the person is at the trunk outside but the crown extends inside, we follow the *nof* and consider him inside the *ir miklat*, thereby protecting him. The crown is used to expand the zone of protection, never to contract it.

This reading also clarifies Rava's earlier point about the cases: *be-ikaro dechulei alma lo peligi delo matzi katil* — if the person is at the trunk inside the *ir miklat*, everyone agrees he cannot be killed. *Kai benofo* — if he is physically up in the crown in the outside zone, everyone agrees he can be killed. The debate that remains — per Rava — is the narrow case of whether the *goel hadam* may enter the *ir miklat*, use the trunk as a ladder (*darga lenof*), climb up to the crown, and kill the person there. That is a distinct question about the *goel hadam*'s ability to pass through protected territory to reach an exposed location, and the *tanna'im* debate it. Rav Ashi's formulation resolves the broader structural question: the *mishna*'s rule that one follows the crown is a rule for the benefit of the *rotzeach* — the crown of the tree, wherever it reaches, casts its protective shadow.

---

---

# Makkot 13

## Manslayer's 2nd Crime

### Manslayer 2nd Kill

The daf opens on 12b, roughly a third of the way from the bottom, with the first of two *mishnayos* that close out the topic of *arei miklat* and the accidental killer. The *mishnah* poses the following case: *harag b'oso ha'ir* — what is the *halacha* if someone already exiled to a *ir miklat* for an accidental killing now kills again within that same city?

The answer is *goleh mishchuna lishchuna* — he must exile himself from the neighborhood he has been living in and relocate to a different neighborhood within the same *ir miklat*. He cannot move to a different *ir miklat* entirely, since he is not permitted to leave the city he is already confined to. Yet the *mishna* imposes some form of exile upon him, and so his exile takes the form of a neighborhood displacement within the existing city.

This raises an interesting question. If he were to leave the neighborhood to which he has been internally exiled, would he expose himself to being killed by the *goel hadam* of the second killing? Presumably not — he remains within the *ir miklat* itself, which continues to protect him. So there is an intriguing asymmetry here: he could technically violate the terms of his internal exile without thereby exposing himself to the blood avenger. Nevertheless, there is no alternative available to the *halacha*, and this is what it prescribes.

### Ben Levi Goleh

The *mishnah* then addresses a different scenario: *u'ven Levi goleh me'ir le'ir* — if a Levite accidentally kills someone, he is exiled from one of the *arei Levi'im* to another. Since all the *arei Levi'im* serve as *arei miklat*, this is the natural form his exile takes. Unlike the person who committed an earlier accidental killing and was already confined to a *ir miklat*, the Levite who kills has not yet been placed in exile at all. He was simply living in a Levite city, which happened to also be a *ir miklat*. He must therefore be properly exiled, and that means departing for a different *ir miklat*.

### Midbar Precedent

The *gemara* opens with a *braisa* built on the *pasuk* in Shemos: *vesamti lecha makom* — I will give you a place to which the accidental killer may flee. The *drashah* reads *lecha* as *bechayecha*: this will happen in your own lifetime, Moshe, before the people cross into *Ever HaYarden*. This was already operative immediately after *yetzias Mitzrayim*. The *braisa* continues: *mimkomecha* — "from among your places," meaning the *arei miklat* would be drawn from the *arei Levi'im*, and all of them may function as *arei miklat*.

The *pasuk* adds *asher yanus shama* — that he shall flee there — and from this the *braisa* derives: *melamed shehayu sham galim bamidbar*, that this institution of exile was already operative even in the wilderness, before the formal *arei miklat* had been designated. The precise derivation is not fully elaborated, but that is the *braisa*'s conclusion. And so the question arises: where would an accidental killer go in the *midbar*, when there were no designated cities? *Lemachaneh Leviyah* — to the Levite camp. Since the *arei miklat* were to come from the *arei Levi'im*, the *machaneh Leviyah* itself functioned as the *ir miklat* in the wilderness.

From here the *braisa* derives: *mikan amru ben Levi sheharag goleh mipelech lepelech* — a Levite who kills is exiled from his city to another. This is, at one level, simply logical: what else could be done with a Levite who kills? He goes into exile and travels to a different *ir miklat*. But the *mikan amru* is really pointing to the second half of the *braisa*: *ve'im gola lepelcho pelcho kolto* — if he exiles himself within his own city, that same city can absorb and protect him.

What exactly does this mean? *Tosafos* explains that it refers to the case analogous to the *rotze'ach* in the first part of the *mishnah*: the person who commits his second killing while already confined to a *ir miklat* has no choice but to exile himself to another neighborhood. But a Levite — or any person who happens to be living in a *ir miklat* and has only now killed for the first time — has a choice. He can either relocate to a different *ir miklat* entirely, or he can remain in his current city but confine himself to a particular neighborhood, in effect exiling himself internally.

Why would anyone choose the former option over the latter? The answer is straightforward. If one stays within the same city but exiles to a single neighborhood, one is permanently restricted to that narrow area. If one relocates to an entirely different *ir miklat*, one can circulate freely throughout that city. So there is a real practical trade-off.

The *braisa*'s *mikan amru* also provides the conceptual source for this option. In the *midbar* there was only one *machaneh Leviyah*. If a *ben Levi* had killed someone there, the only possibility would have been to exile himself within that same encampment — there was nowhere else to go. This establishes the principle that internal exile within the same city is a valid form of *galus*.

### City Absorbs Him

*Rav Aha b'rei d'Rav Ika* then asks: what is the *pasuk* that supports this? He cites: *ki be'ir miklato yeshev* — in his city of refuge he shall dwell — and reads it to mean: *ir shekaltaso kevar*, even a city that has already absorbed and protected him can continue to serve as his *ir miklat*. This appears to reach beyond the *ben Levi* case and applies as well to someone who was already functioning within a *ir miklat* — that city can absorb him anew. This is a distinct *chiddush* from the *ben Levi* discussion: Rav Aha is addressing the earlier case, where the man who kills a second time remains protected by the same *ir miklat* that had already received him.

---

## Manslayer Rehab

### Shemitta Parallel

The next *mishnah* opens with the phrase *kayotzei bo* — similarly — though what follows is not similar to the preceding *mishnah* in any obvious way. It is, in fact, a transcription of a *mishnah* from the tenth *perek* of *Shevi'is* (perek 10, *mishnah* 8). The context in *Shevi'is* is that *shemitah* annuls outstanding debts, and the question arises: if a debtor nonetheless wishes to repay, what should the creditor do?

The *mishnah* in *Shevi'is* teaches: *hamachazir chov bashevi'is, yomar lo meshamet ani* — if someone comes to repay a debt during the *shemitah* year, the creditor should declare, "I annul it." If the debtor then responds *af al pi chen* — nevertheless, I still wish to pay — then *yekabel mehen*, the creditor may accept it. The basis is *shene'emar vezeh devar hashemitah* — "and this is the matter of the *shemitah*." The word *davar* teaches that what matters is the verbal declaration: the creditor says the words "I annul," checks that obligation, and thereafter, if the debtor chooses to give the money back voluntarily, it is received as a gift rather than as a loan repayment.

### Honors Despite Crime

The *mishnah* then brings the parallel: *kayotzei bo rotze'ach* — similarly, a *rotze'ach* who has been sent to his *ir miklat*, and the people of the city wish to honor him, *yomar lahem rotze'ach ani* — he must declare, "I am a killer, I cannot accept this honor." If they respond *af al pi chen* — nevertheless — then *yekabel mehen*, he may accept the honor. The source is *shene'emar vezeh devar harotze'ach* — "and these are the words of the killer." Just as *devar* in *shemitah* means you say the words of annulment, here *devar* means the *rotze'ach* must say the words identifying his status. Having done so, and with the community wishing to honor him despite that declaration, he may accept.

### Taxes & Rent

The *mishnah* continues at the top of 13a. The question arises: do the inhabitants of the *ir miklat* provide free lodging and support to the exiled killer, or must he pay for his own expenses? *Ma'alim hayu sachar laleviyim* — they would charge the Levites rent — *divrei Rabbi Yehudah*. According to *Rabbi Yehudah*, the exiled person must pay rent and, as *Tosafos* clarifies, this extends also to property taxes and any other civic financial obligations. Being exiled there does not exempt one from the ordinary financial responsibilities of residence.

*Rabbi Meir* disagrees: *lo hayu ma'alim lahem sachar* — no, they would not charge him rent or other expenses. He is, in a sense, like a prisoner who does not pay for his confinement.

The *gemara* explores the basis for this dispute through *Rav Kahana*, who holds: *machlokes beshesh* — the debate applies only to the six primary *arei miklat*. As for the other 42 Levite cities, both opinions would agree that the exiled person must pay his own way. The reasoning: the *pasuk* says *v'hayu lachem ha'arim* — these cities shall be *lachem*, for you. One opinion (*Rabbi Yehudah*) reads *lachem* as meaning only that they serve the protective function of refuge — *lachem liklita* — but not that all expenses are covered. The other (*Rabbi Meir*) reads *lachem lechol tzarcheichem* — for all your needs, meaning the community bears those costs.

*Rava*, however, pushes back. He argues that the phrase *lachem lechol tzarcheichem* is clearly expansive — it certainly means that at least for the primary six *arei miklat*, there would be no charge, by everyone's agreement. Therefore, *Rava* reframes the entire dispute: *machlokes b'arbayim veshtayim* — the debate is only about the remaining 42. One opinion holds that *ve'aleihem titnu* — the command to add those 42 Levite cities means they too serve purely as refuge (*kehanei liklita*), just like the primary six, and therefore there are no charges for the exiled killer there either. The other opinion holds that only the primary six carry that full benefit, while the remaining 42 do not. But for the original six, says Rava, *divrei hakol lo hayu ma'alim lahem sachar* — by everyone's agreement, no rent was charged.

### Status Recovery

After addressing the financial question, the *mishnah* turns to a broader rehabilitative question: *vachozer lisrarah shehayah bah* — does the exiled person return to the social standing and position he held before? *Divrei Rabbi Meir* — Rabbi Meir says yes. Rabbi Meir is the more lenient voice in both debates: he says the person need not pay rent, and he says the person fully recovers his prior status upon returning home after the *kohen gadol*'s death.

*Rabbi Yehudah*, consistent with his position in both disputes, is more stringent: *lo haya chozer lisrarah shehayah bah* — no, he does not return to the position he previously held.

### Eved Ivri Rehab

The *gemara* introduces a *braisa* that illuminates the debate through the case of the *eved Ivri*. The *braisa* cites the *pasuk*: *veshav el mishpachto ve'el achuzat avotav yashuv* — he shall return to his family and to the inheritance of his fathers. This verse speaks of the Hebrew slave who goes free at *yovel*. The *braisa* derives: *lemishpachto shav* — he returns to his family. But does he return to the inherited status and position his forefathers held? *Rabbi Yehudah* says no: *eino shav lema shehecheziku avotav*. He went and sold himself into servitude; that cannot simply be erased. Whatever ancestral post or inherited position he held before does not automatically revert to him. *Rabbi Meir* disagrees: *af hu shav lema shehecheziku avotav* — he does return to the very standing his ancestors held. The *pasuk* says *el achuzat avotav ke'avotav* — to his fathers' inheritance, just like his fathers — and that includes whatever posts and status they occupied.

### Eved/Manslayer Link

The *braisa* then draws the connection to the *rotze'ach*: *ke'yotzeh bo, vechen begola* — and similarly when it comes to exile. The *pasuk* regarding the exiled killer says *yashuv harotze'ach el eretz achuzato* — he shall return to the land of his inheritance. Rabbi Yehudah reads this literally: *l'eretz achuzato yashuv eino shav lema shehecheziku avotav* — he returns to the land, but not to the ancestral status. *Rabbi Meir* says *af hu shav lema shehecheziku avotav* — he too returns to what his forefathers held.

How does Rabbi Meir derive this from a *pasuk* that only says *eretz achuzato*, making no mention of ancestral status? The answer is *gamar shiva shiva mehatam* — a verbal linkage (*gezeirah shavah*) between the word *yashuv* here and the word *yashuv* in the *eved Ivri* context, where the *pasuk* explicitly says *ve'al achuzat avotav yashuv*. Just as the *eved Ivri* returns *el achuzat avotav* — to the standing of his forefathers — so too does the *rotze'ach* return to that standing, according to Rabbi Meir. There is a striking and genuine belief in full rehabilitation here: both the *eved Ivri* and the *rotze'ach* are returned, in Rabbi Meir's view, not merely to physical home and family, but to the full ancestral position that had been theirs before.

---

## Galus to Malkos

### Perek Transition

*Hadran alach elu hein hagolin* — so concludes the *perek* on *galus*. The daf now pivots to *ve'elu hein halokin* — these are those who receive *malkus*. The transition deserves a moment's reflection. *Sanhedrin* concluded with the laws of *chayvei misos*, and *Makkos* picks up from there as an extension of *Sanhedrin*. Once *chayvei misos* have been addressed, the tractate turns to the other major punishments that *beis din* imposes: exile (*galus*) for the accidental killer, and now *malkus* for those who transgress a range of prohibitions.

There is also a structural symmetry worth noting. The first *perek* of *Makkos* opened with the case of *edim zomemim* who testified that someone is a *ben gerusha* or *ben chaluza* — the accused does not receive that status, but the false witnesses receive *malkus*. Similarly, a witness who falsely testified that someone is *chayav galus* does not cause the person to be exiled but receives *malkus* himself. So the first *perek* introduced both *malkus* and *galus*, and the second and third *perakim* then expand upon each in turn.

### Sexual Prohibitions

The third *perek* opens with those who incur *malkus*. In principle, any active violation of a *lo ta'aseh* — provided it involves a deed, is not *nitak l'asei* (capable of being corrected by the performance of a positive commandment), and is not subject to capital punishment — incurs *malkus*. There are 365 negative commandments, so the category is vast. The *mishnah* does not enumerate all of them but focuses on cases that carry some *chiddush*.

The first category listed is *chayvei krisos*: those who are liable for *kares* through forbidden sexual unions. The *mishnah* lists: *haba al achoto* — one who has intercourse with his sister; *ve'al achot aviv* — his father's sister; *ve'al achot imo* — his mother's sister; *ve'al achot ishto* — his wife's sister; *ve'al eshet achiv* — his brother's wife; *ve'al eshet achi aviv* — his father's brother's wife; *ve'al haniddah* — a woman who is in the state of *niddah*. All of these are *arayos* that carry the penalty of *kares*, and the *chiddush* of the *mishnah* is that even so, if witnesses warned the person that he would receive *malkus*, he receives *malkus*.

### Priestly Marriages

The *mishnah* continues with the forbidden marriages of *kohanim*: *almana l'kohen gadol* — a widow whom a *kohen gadol* marries — and *gerusha vechaluza l'kohen hedyot* — a divorced woman or a *chaluza* married by an ordinary *kohen*. These are forbidden to the respective *kohanim* and incur *malkus*.

The *chaluza* case carries its own complexity. *Rashi* treats *chaluza* as a *d'oraisa* prohibition that carries full *malkus*. *Tosafos* takes the more standard *gemara* position that *chaluza* is *d'rabbanan*, with the consequence being only *makas mardus* rather than biblical *malkus* — though if the woman is both a *gerusha* and a *chaluza*, the plain reading of the *mishnah* would seem to treat *chaluza* as *d'oraisa*. The *mishnah* also includes: *mamzeres ve'nesina le-mamzer* — a *mamzeret* or a *nesina* (a descendant of the Gibeonites, one of the *shiv'as amim*) to a regular *Yisrael* — and conversely, *bas Yisrael le'nesin u'le'mamzer*. These are straightforward *lavin*, not involving *kares*, and the reason they are grouped here will become clearer in what follows.

### Double Status

The *mishnah* then raises the case of a woman who is simultaneously an *almana* and a *gerusha*. If a *kohen gadol* has intercourse with her, he has violated two separate *lavin* in a single act — the prohibition against a *kohen gadol* marrying an *almana*, and the prohibition against marrying a *gerusha*. He is therefore liable for two separate sets of *malkus*: *chayav aleha mishum shtei shemos*.

However, if the woman is both a *gerusha* and a *chaluza*, the *mishnah* rules *eino chayav ela mishum shem echad bilvad* — he is liable for only one set of *malkus*. A *chaluza* is a subcategory of *gerusha*: both represent a severing of the marital bond, and the *chaluza* is effectively a type of *gerusha*. Whether one holds *chaluza* is *d'oraisa* or *d'rabbanan*, it remains a subset of the same prohibition, and only one punishment applies.

### Temple Impurity

The *mishnah* continues with matters involving the *beis hamikdash* and sacred food. *Ha'tamei she'achal es ha'kodesh* — one who is *tamei* and eats *korbanos*; *ve'ha'ba el ha'mikdash tamei* — and one who enters the *beis hamikdash* while *tamei*. These too carry *kares*, and the *mishnah* teaches they are nonetheless subject to *malkus* under the right conditions.

The *mishnah* adds: *ve'ochel chelev ve'dam ve'nosar u'figul* — eating forbidden fats, blood, *nosar* (a *korban* left beyond its permitted time), and *pigul* (a *korban* whose *shechita* was performed with an intent to consume it outside the permitted time or place). All of these carry *kares*, yet *malkus* can apply. The *mishnah* also includes *ve'tamei* — eating *korbanos* that themselves are *tamei*, which does not carry *kares* but is included here in the same breath.

### Forbidden Foods

The *mishnah* lists: *ve'ha'shocheit u'ma'aleh ba'chutz* — one who *shochets* a *korban* outside the *beis hamikdash*, or who offers up the *eimurim* outside; *ve'ochel chametz ba'Pesach* — eating *chametz* on *Pesach*; *ve'ha'ochel ve'ha'oseh melacha b'Yom Kippur* — eating or performing *melacha* on *Yom Kippur*. These are all *chayvei kares*, and the same principle applies.

The *mishnah* then moves to prohibitions involving the *shemen ha'mishchah* and *ketores*: *ha'mifatem es ha'shemen* — one who compounds the anointing oil in the manner prescribed by the *Torah* for unauthorized use; *ve'ha'mifatem es ha'ketores* — one who similarly compounds the incense; *ve'ha'sach be'shemen ha'mishchah* — one who applies the actual anointing oil to their own flesh. These too incur *kares* and are subject to *malkus*.

The *mishnah* then lists: *ve'ochel neveilos u'treifos shekatzim u'remasim* — eating an animal that died without *shechita*, a *treifa*, and various forbidden insects and rodents. These carry a *lav* and *malkus*, which is not particularly surprising — but as the end of the *mishnah* will demonstrate, the mention of *shekatzim u'remasim* here is deliberate and sets up the closing debate.

It continues: *achal tevel u'ma'aser rishon she'lo nitlah trumaso* — eating *tevel* (untithed produce) or *ma'aser rishon* from which the *terumah* had not yet been separated; *u'ma'aser sheni ve'hekdesh she'lo nifdu* — or *ma'aser sheni* and *hekdesh* that had not been redeemed. All of these are forbidden consumptions that incur *malkus*.

### Minimal Amount

The *mishnah* closes with a debate: *kama yochal min ha'tevel ve'yehei chayav?* — how much must one eat of *tevel* in order to be liable? *Rabbi Shimon omer kol she'hu* — Rabbi Shimon says even the tiniest amount suffices. The *Sages* disagree: *k'zayis* — an olive-sized portion is required, as is the standard measure for eating-related prohibitions.

Rabbi Shimon challenges the Sages: *i ata modeh li b'ochel nemalah shehu chayav kol she'hu?* — do you not agree that one who eats an ant is liable even for the tiniest amount, even less than a *k'zayis*? The Sages respond: *mipnei she'hu k'beriasah* — yes, but that is because the ant is a whole, self-contained creature; it constitutes a *beryah*, an entire entity, and that intrinsic wholeness gives even the smallest specimen halakhic significance. By contrast, *tevel* is grain — fungible, undifferentiated — and therefore requires the standard minimum measure.

Rabbi Shimon retorts: *af chitah achas k'beriasah* — why isn't a single grain of wheat also a *beryah*, a self-contained natural unit? And therefore, he argues, even eating one kernel of *tevel* should render a person liable. The debate continues into the *gemara*.

---

## Lashes + Karet

### Akiva's View

The *gemara* opens this discussion by noting what the *mishnah* does and does not include. The *mishnah* lists *chayvei krisos* — those liable for *kares* — and teaches that *malkus* applies to them as well. But the *mishnah* conspicuously omits *chayvei misos beis din* — those liable for capital punishment. The inference is that if someone who is liable for the death penalty is warned by witnesses that he will receive *malkus*, he does not in fact receive *malkus*.

On whose view does this *mishnah* operate? *Masnisin mani Rebbe Akiva hi* — the *mishnah* follows the position of Rabbi Akiva.

### Yishmael Both

A *braisa* is then cited presenting the full spectrum of opinions. *Rabbi Yishmael* says: *echad chayvei krisos ve'echad chayvei misos beis din yeshno bichlal malkus arbaim* — whether a transgression carries *kares* or carries the death penalty of *beis din*, the person is included in the category of receiving forty lashes.

This statement can be understood in two ways. One reading is that the transgressor can receive both punishments: both *malkus* and execution, or both *malkus* and *kares*, for the same act. The other reading is that even when the witnesses warned only of *malkus* — without specifying the full punishment — Rabbi Yishmael would allow *malkus* to be imposed even for capital offenses. The *gemara* initially proceeds on the more expansive reading: that both punishments may apply simultaneously.

### Akiva Karet OK

*Rabbi Akiva* draws a distinction. *Chayvei krisos yeshno bichlal malkus arbaim* — yes, those liable for *kares* are included in the category of receiving forty lashes. The reasoning: the ordinary concern against double punishment rests on the principle of *k'dei rishaso* — according to his wickedness, as the *pasuk* says — and the rabbinic principle derived from this, *mishum rishah achas ata mechayvo ve'i ata mechayvo mishum shtei rishayus*: you make a person liable for one act of wrongdoing, not for two punishments from the same act. But *malkus* and *kares* together do not constitute double punishment in a prohibited sense, because *she'im asu teshuvah beis din shel maalah mochalin lahem* — if the person repents, the heavenly court forgives him and *kares* is not actually executed. Since *kares* is conditional on the absence of repentance, it does not collide with the imposition of *malkus* in the way that a certain punishment would.

For capital cases, however, *Rabbi Akiva* says *chayvei misos beis din eino bichlal malkus arbaim* — those liable for the death penalty do not receive forty lashes. Here the prohibition against double punishment applies fully: *she'im asu teshuvah ein beis din shel mata mochalin lahem* — even if a person repents, the earthly *beis din* does not forgo the execution. Repentance is between the person and God and does not affect the court's obligation to carry out the sentence. Therefore, you cannot impose both *malkus* and execution. One punishment precludes the other, and the graver punishment — death — takes precedence.

### Yitzchak No Lashes

*Rabbi Yitzchak* takes the opposite position from Rabbi Akiva's ruling on *kares* cases. He argues: *chayvei krisos bichlal hayu* — those liable for *kares* were originally subsumed within the general category of *malkus*, since any *lav* in principle carries *malkus*. But then the Torah made a specific mention of *kares* in connection with the case of one who sleeps with his sister. The entire concluding section of the *arayos* laws states *kol asher yaaseh mikol ha'to'eivos ha'eleh ve'nichresu* — all who do these abominations shall be cut off — applying *kares* broadly across the forbidden unions. Why then did the Torah single out *kares* specifically in the *achoto* case?

*Laduno b'chareis ve'lo b'malkos* — to teach that the only punishment assigned to that transgression is *kares*, not *malkus*. And this becomes the paradigm: wherever the Torah assigns *kares*, that is the punishment to the exclusion of *malkus*. So Rabbi Yitzchak holds that *chayvei krisos* receive *kares* alone, with no *malkus* at all.

All three positions are thus fully laid out: Rabbi Yishmael holds that both *malkus* and the more severe punishment — whether *kares* or death — can apply together. Rabbi Akiva holds that *malkus* applies alongside *kares*, but not alongside capital punishment. Rabbi Yitzchak holds that *kares* offenses carry only *kares* and exclude *malkus* entirely.

### Yishmael Source

The *gemara* now analyzes Rabbi Yishmael's source. *Mai taama d'Rebbi Yishmael?* The verse states: *im lo sishmor laasos es kol divrei ha'Torah hazos* — if you do not observe and fulfill all the words of this Torah — and then: *v'hifla Hashem es makosecha* — God will make your smitings wondrous. The word *hafla'ah* — wondrous or extraordinary — is unfamiliar as a punishment term. But the *gemara* reads it as a homonym: elsewhere the Torah says *v'hipilo ha'shofet* — the judge shall cast him down — *v'hikahu l'fanav arba'im yakenu* — and he shall be struck forty times. *Hevei omer hafla'ah zu malkos hi* — this *hafla'ah* is *malkus*.

So the verse *im lo sishmor laasos es kol divrei ha'Torah hazos* establishes that anyone who violates anything in the Torah — *kol divrei ha'Torah*, including prohibitions that carry *kares* or capital punishment — receives *malkus*. This is the broad basis for Rabbi Yishmael's position.

### Lav Definition

The *gemara* immediately challenges: *ai hachi, chayvei asei nami?* If the source verse speaks of "all the words of this Torah," why not extend *malkus* to the failure to observe a positive commandment (*asei*) as well? The *gemara* answers: *im lo sishmor kesiv* — the verse says "if you do not *observe* to do," which implies an active violation of something one was supposed to guard against. As *Rabbi Avin* in the name of *Rabbi Ila'a* teaches: wherever the Torah says *hishamer, pen*, or *al* — guard yourself, lest, do not — that formulation always denotes a *lav ta'aseh*, a negative prohibition against active transgression. So *lo sishmor* here means the failure to guard against doing something forbidden, not the mere failure to do something required.

The *gemara* presses further: *lav she'ein bo ma'aseh nami?* If the source verse generates *malkus* for all *lavin*, why not include a *lav* that involves no action — a purely passive violation? The *gemara* answers: *laasos kesiv* — the word *laasos*, "to do," demands that the violation be an active one.

Then: *lav hanitak l'asei nami?* Why not impose *malkus* for a *lav* that is *nitak l'asei* — connected to a positive commandment capable of correcting the violation? Here the *gemara* invokes the paradigm case.

### Chasima Model

The answer is *dumya d'lav d'chasimah* — the laws of *malkus* are modeled on the prohibition of *chasimah*, muzzling an ox while it threshes: *lo sachsom shor b'disho*. The *parasha* about the administration of *malkus* — *v'hipilo ha'shofet v'hikahu l'fanav* — is juxtaposed in the Torah directly to this prohibition of muzzling. This juxtaposition establishes the paradigm: the prohibition against muzzling the ox defines what type of *lav* incurs *malkus*. It must be a *lav ta'aseh* involving an active deed, and it must not be *nitak l'asei*, not correctable by a subsequent positive act. The muzzling prohibition fits both criteria, and all other *lavin* that incur *malkus* must be similar.

The *gemara* then resolves the broader discussion: *hashta d'asis l'hachi, kulhu nami dumya d'lav d'chasimah* — now that we have arrived at the muzzling paradigm, that itself determines the full scope of *malkus*. One need not derive it from the broad verse of *v'hifla Hashem es makosecha* at all; the verse *v'hipilo ha'shofet v'hikahu l'fanav*, juxtaposed to the muzzling prohibition, is the operative source. Anything comparable to the *lav* of *chasimah* — including transgressions that carry *misas beis din* — falls within the category of *malkus* punishments. The broad verse from which Rabbi Yishmael derived his position that even capital offenses carry *malkus* may simply be emphasizing that the full scope of "all the words of the Torah" are potentially included, without independently adding *chayvei misos* if they would otherwise be excluded by the muzzling paradigm.

The *gemara*'s analysis of Rabbi Akiva's response to this — and how Rabbi Yishmael would address the principle that one cannot be doubly punished — is to be continued in the following daf.

---

---

# Makkot 14

## Lashes & Karet

### Three Positions

The opening *mishnah* of *Eilu Hein HaLokin* lists a substantial number of sins for which one incurs *karet*, and the *mishnah* presents this list as reflecting the position of Rabbi Akiva. The *gemara* on 13b frames this within a three-way debate recorded in a *braisa*.

### Rabbi Ishmael

Rabbi Ishmael holds that one receives *malkos* for any negative transgression, even if the ultimate punishment is court execution — and certainly if the punishment is *karet*. This is a striking and unfamiliar position. The *gemara* explains it is based on the principle that lashes leading up to a more severe bodily punishment — whether imposed by the court or by the heavenly court — are all considered, in effect, one extended death. One does not receive both a monetary fine and lashes, since those represent two fundamentally different categories of punishment. But lashes administered prior to a harsher bodily consequence are considered part of a single drawn-out continuum.

### Rabbi Akiva

Rabbi Akiva takes a more nuanced position. He agrees that one does receive *malkos* when the accompanying punishment is *karet*, but he disagrees when the accompanying punishment is *misat beit din* — court execution. His reasoning flows from the verse *kedei rishato* (Deuteronomy 25:2): "according to his wickedness" — meaning, the court holds a person liable for one wickedness, not two. Double punishment by the court is impermissible.

Rabbi Ishmael would counter that this prohibition on double punishment applies only when the two punishments are of different types — monetary fine combined with execution, or monetary fine combined with lashes. But execution combined with lashes is all one extended death, and that is not a prohibited doubling. Rabbi Akiva's response to this is what distinguishes his position: he holds that *karet* does not fall within the category of double *beit din* punishment, because the person liable to *karet* might yet do *teshuvah* — and thus *karet* is not an inevitable second punishment.

### Gemara's Question

The *gemara* presses Rabbi Akiva on this reasoning. Even if *teshuvah* theoretically averts *karet*, the individual standing before the court has not yet done *teshuvah*. At this moment, he is deserving of *karet*. How, then, can the fact that he *could* escape it be sufficient reason to treat it as non-existent for purposes of the double-punishment concern? This question drives the *gemara* forward.

---

## Gezeirah Shavah

### L'Einei L'Einecha

Rabbi Abbahu answers that Rabbi Akiva's position is not purely a matter of logical reasoning about the nature of *karet* — it is derived explicitly from a *pasuk*. The Torah itself includes those liable to *karet* within the category of those who receive *malkos*, through a *gezeirah shavah* on the word *einei*. By *karet*, the Torah writes *v'nichresu l'einei bnei amam* — "they shall be cut off before the eyes of their people" (Leviticus 20:17). By *malkos*, the Torah writes *v'niklah achicha l'einecha* — "your brother shall be degraded before your eyes" (Deuteronomy 25:3). The shared formulation *l'einei* / *l'einecha* creates a verbal analogy that explicitly links *karet* offenses to the punishment of *malkos*.

### Abba bar Mammal

Rabbi Abba bar Mammal challenged this derivation. If one can construct a *gezeirah shavah* between the *karet* verse and the *malkos* verse, why not construct an equally valid *gezeirah shavah* and reach the conclusion of Rabbi Ishmael — that even those liable to court execution receive *malkos*? By *misat beit din*, the verse in the context of *avodah zarah* writes *im me'einei ha'eidah ne'estah lishgagah* — "if it was hidden from the eyes of the congregation" (Numbers 15:24). Both that verse and the *malkos* verse contain the word *einei* / *einecha* — why not link those as well?

### Linguistic Distinction

The *gemara* responds that the two links are not equally precise. The *karet* verse uses *l'einei* and the *malkos* verse uses *l'einecha* — both share the prefix *lamed*, making this a close parallel. The *misat beit din* verse, by contrast, uses *me'einei* — with a *mem* prefix rather than a *lamed*. The *gemara* thus rules: *danin l'einei m'l'einei v'ein danin me'einei m'l'einei* — one may construct a *gezeirah shavah* from *l'einei* to *l'einei*, but not from *me'einei* to *l'einei*.

The *gemara* itself questions whether this distinction carries real weight. After all, the school of Rabbi Ishmael taught that *v'shav hakohen* and *u'va hakohen* — "the priest shall return" and "the priest shall come" — are treated as a *gezeirah shavah* in the laws of *tzara'at* of the house, even though these are entirely different words that simply share the same sense. If imprecise wording can be sufficient, why is the *mem*-*lamed* difference decisive? The *gemara* raises this as a standing question.

### No Double Punishment

Rabbi Shmuel bar Yitzchak resolved the underlying question by returning to Rabbi Akiva's own language. The verse *kedei rishato* — understood as "the court imposes one punishment" — establishes that *beit din* may not administer two punishments. This prohibits *misat beit din* together with *malkos*, since both are *beit din* punishments. But *karet* is a divine punishment, not a *beit din* punishment. There is no prohibition on *beit din* imposing *malkos* when God separately imposes *karet*, because these operate on entirely different planes. The question of whether the person will ultimately suffer *karet* — something he can avert through *teshuvah* — is between him and God, not a matter for the court below. The court's concern is exclusively with its own sanctions, and *malkos* stands on its own as the *beit din* response to a violated *lav*.

---

## Rava's Reframe

### Rava's Premise

Rava now significantly reframes the entire debate. He argues that Rabbi Ishmael could not have meant that a person receives both *malkos* and *misat beit din* simultaneously from the court. Everyone would agree that *beit din* does not impose two punishments — *ein lokeh u'mes*. Rava thus eliminates the most radical reading of Rabbi Ishmael's position.

### Warning Mismatch

If everyone agrees that *beit din* does not administer both *malkos* and *misat beit din*, then what exactly is the debate between Rabbi Ishmael and Rabbi Akiva? According to Rava, the debate concerns a case where witnesses gave an incorrect *hasra'ah* — where they warned the transgressor that his act carries *malkos*, without mentioning *misat beit din*. Perhaps the witnesses had compassion and downplayed the severity, warning him only of lashes. He acknowledged the warning and proceeded anyway. Now, the court cannot impose *misat beit din* because the warning did not match that punishment. The question is: can the court impose *malkos*?

Rabbi Ishmael says yes. Even though the *lav* that this person violated normally carries *misat beit din*, every *lav* has within it an inherent capacity to generate *malkos*. Since *misat beit din* will not be imposed, *malkos* steps in. Rabbi Akiva disagrees: a *lav* that was assigned as the vehicle for *misat beit din* cannot be repurposed to produce *malkos*. The *lav* is dedicated, so to speak, to the heavier punishment, and when that punishment cannot be imposed due to a mismatched warning, the person goes free rather than receiving the lesser sanction.

### Rabbi Akiva Refined

Under Rava's reframing, Rabbi Akiva's concern about *karet* cases takes on a different dimension. If Rabbi Akiva holds that a *lav* assigned to one punishment cannot function to generate a different punishment, then why can a *lav* that accompanies *karet* generate *malkos*? The *lav* is, after all, associated with a *karet* offense. The answer, as Rav Mordechai reported in the name of Avimi of Hagronya in the name of Rava, is: *chayvei kerisos lo tsrichi hasra'ah* — for God to impose *karet*, no *lav* is required. This is demonstrated by the two cases of *karet* that carry no accompanying *lav* at all: failure to bring the *korban pesach* and failure to perform *bris milah*. In both cases, the Torah imposes *karet* for a passive omission — no prohibition was transgressed. This proves that *karet* operates entirely independently of any *lav*.

### Karet & Lav

Since *karet* does not require a *lav*, the *lav* in a *karet* case is not "used up" by the *karet*. It is genuinely free to serve as the basis for *malkos*. This is the economy of the *lo ta'aseh*: for Rabbi Akiva, a *lav* can only serve one purpose, and a *lav* assigned to *misat beit din* cannot generate *malkos*. But a *lav* in a *karet* case is not assigned to *karet* — *karet* exists without it. Therefore, the *lav* is available to produce *malkos* independently.

The *gemara* momentarily considers a challenge to this: perhaps the *lav* in *karet* cases is needed not for *karet* itself, but for the *korban* that accompanies *karet* offenses. After all, we observe that *pesach* and *milah* — the two *karet* offenses that lack a *lav* — also have no *korban* for their omission. Does this not show that the *lav* is part of the *korban* package?

The *gemara* rejects this. The reason *pesach* and *milah* carry no *korban* is not because of any *lav*. The paradigm for *korbanos* is *avodah zarah*, and the rule is *mah avodah zarah shev v'al ta'aseh* — just as *avodah zarah* involves an active transgression, every *korban* arises only from an active violation. *Pesach* and *milah* are sins of omission — of *kum va'aseh*, of failing to act — and therefore they fall outside the category of offenses requiring a *korban*, regardless of the presence or absence of a *lav*. A *korban* is owed whenever there is *karet* combined with an active transgression. The *lav* has no role in generating the *korban* obligation.

The conclusion is clean: *karet* does not need the *lav*. The *korban* does not need the *lav*. The *lav* is therefore entirely free to serve as the basis for *malkos*. Rabbi Akiva's position is consistent: he applies *malkos* to *karet* cases because the *lav* is unencumbered, and he withholds *malkos* from *misat beit din* cases because there the *lav* is dedicated to the court execution.

---

## Ravina's View

### Teshuvah Option

Ravina offers a final account of Rabbi Akiva's reasoning, returning to what he characterizes as the original formulation. Rabbi Akiva's position, at its core, is that *karet* does not constitute a definite second punishment. The person who has violated a *karet* offense and is now before the court has not yet done *teshuvah* — that is true. But *karet* is not a punishment that *beit din* imposes; it is something God may or may not carry out, and crucially, the transgressor retains the ability to escape it entirely through repentance. Since there is no certainty that *karet* will materialize, imposing *malkos* does not constitute giving the person two definite punishments. Double punishment — in the relevant sense — means administering two certain, irrevocable sanctions. *Karet* does not qualify.

It is worth noting that throughout all these opinions, not one of them claims that receiving *malkos* exempts the person from *karet*. Rabbi Ishmael says both are received. Rabbi Akiva says *malkos* is administered alongside *karet*, but the two operate on separate planes and neither cancels the other. Ravina clarifies Rabbi Akiva's reasoning but does not alter the substance: the *malkos* is simply not the mechanism by which *karet* is averted.

---

## Rabbi Yitzchak

### Karet Exclusion

Rabbi Yitzchak takes the most restrictive position of all: one does not receive *malkos* for any *karet* offense whatsoever. His reasoning, as presented through the *Tosafos* reading, begins from an inclusive premise. Those liable to *karet* were originally included within the general category of *lav* violators who receive *malkos* — so by default, one might have assumed *malkos* applies. The question is therefore: why did the Torah explicitly single out *karet* for the case of one's sister (*achoto*)?

### Achoto Proof

The verse in *Kedoshim* (20:17) contains a notably elaborate formulation: *v'ish asher yikach es achoso bas aviv o vas imo v'ra'ah es ervasah v'hi sir'eh es ervaso chesed hu v'nichresu l'einei v'nei amam ervas achoso gilah avono yisa*. Unlike the other *arayos* offenses, which receive their *karet* from the general concluding verse at the end of *Acharei Mos*, the sister case receives an explicit, dedicated mention of *v'nichresu* in *Kedoshim*. Rabbi Yitzchak reads this singling-out as a deliberate exclusion: it tells us that the *karet* here operates *instead of malkos* — *ladunu b'kares v'lo b'malkos*. The Torah is specifying that one who sleeps with his sister is punished through *karet* and not through *malkos*.

---

## Achoto Interpretation

### Thirty-Six Sins

The *mishnah* in *Kerisus* enumerates thirty-six transgressions for which one incurs *karet*. Rabbi Yochanan explains why the *mishnah* specifies this number: it is to teach that even if a person commits all thirty-six in a single lapse of awareness (*he'elam echad*), he is *chayav* for each one individually — up to a maximum of thirty-six *korbanos*.

### No Malkos

Rabbi Yitzchak uses the singling-out of *karet* in the *achoto* verse for the purpose just described: to establish that *karet* offenses do not carry *malkos*. The explicit *v'nichresu* in the *achoto* passage signals an exclusion from the general rule that *lav* violations incur *malkos*.

### Multiple Statuses

Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Ishmael — the *rabbanan* — who hold that *karet* offenses do carry *malkos*, need a different explanation for why the Torah singled out *karet* by the sister. They use it to teach the principle of *l'chaleik* — division. Even when a person commits multiple *karet* offenses in a single lapse of awareness, each offense counts separately and generates a separate *korban*. The explicit mention of *v'nichresu* by *achoto* establishes that every distinct *karet* transgression is treated independently, rather than collapsed into a single *korban*.

But the *gemara* presses further. The principle that different women and different sins generate different *korbanos* seems obvious: they are separate bodies, separate acts, separate offenses. The deeper question is whether the same principle applies when the *multiple* status categories all converge upon a single individual.

### Rasha Bar Rasha

The *gemara* resolves this by specifying the precise case the verse is addressing: *lachayiv al achoto she'hi achot aviv she'hi achot imo* — to establish liability for a woman who is simultaneously his sister, his father's sister, and his mother's sister. Three overlapping prohibitions, one woman, one act. The *gemara* asks how such a situation is even possible, and answers: *rasha bar rasha* — a wicked person, son of a wicked person. Rashi describes the scenario: a man has relations with his mother and produces two daughters; he then has relations with one of those daughters and produces a son; that son then has relations with his aunt — who is simultaneously his sister (sharing the same father) and his mother's sister (by direct lineage). The result is a single woman who carries three distinct forbidden statuses. It is for precisely this case — one body, multiple statuses — that the *v'nichresu* of *achoto* teaches that each status generates a separate *korban*.

---

## Separate Karbanos

### Five Women

The *gemara* cites a tradition to clarify the broader principle. The foundational case for separate *korbanos* from separate sins in one *he'elam* is a man who has relations with five different *niddah* women in a single lapse of awareness: he is *chayav* a separate *korban* for each one. This is the paradigm case of the same *aveirah* but different women — different bodies, and therefore obviously different *korbanos*.

Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua were once asked by Rabbi Akiva — while they were all on their way to the meat market at Imaum to purchase an animal for Rabban Gamliel's son's wedding feast — what the law would be if a man slept with a woman who was simultaneously his sister, his father's sister, and his mother's sister. Would he bring one *korban* or three? They answered: *zo lo shamanu* — we have no explicit tradition on this. But they did have a tradition regarding five different *niddah* women in a single act of forgetfulness: each one requires a separate *korban*. From that they wished to reason: if *different women* and the *same aveirah* generate separate *korbanos*, then surely *different aveirot* in a *single woman* should generate separate *korbanos* as well — *kal vachomer*.

The other position challenged this *kal vachomer* as *pricha* — refutable. Different bodies are inherently more distinct than different status categories. Since the *kal vachomer* is reversible, it cannot serve as a definitive proof.

### Achoto Seifa

The *gemara* therefore returns to derivation from scripture. Where does Rabbi Yitzchak — who uses *v'nichresu* to exclude *malkos* from *karet* offenses — learn the principle of separate *korbanos* for multiple overlapping status categories? He derives it from *achoto d'seifa* — the word *achoto* that appears at the end of the *achoto* verse: *ervas achoto gilah*. It could have said simply *ervatah gilah*. The repetition of *achoto* signals that the accumulation of *achot*-related statuses in one person generates separate liabilities.

### Full Sister

Rabbi Akiva uses *achoto d'seifa* for something different. The prohibition against sleeping with one's sister, stated in *Acharei Mos* (Leviticus 18:9), explicitly mentions only a half-sister — *bas avicha o vat imecha* — one's sister on the father's side or the mother's side. It never explicitly prohibits a full sister, one who shares both parents. Yet the punishment passage in *Kedoshim* covers *achoto* broadly, and the extra *achoto* at the end — *ervas achoto gilah* — serves to establish that the prohibition extends to a full sister as well. Without the explicit *pasuk*, one might have thought the prohibition could be derived by *kal vachomer* from the half-sister case, but the rule is *ein onshin min hadin* — one does not derive punishments from logical inference. The verse is therefore necessary to ground the prohibition explicitly.

### Pitum & Sach

Rabbi Akiva still must account for the *v'nichresu* at the beginning of the *achoto* passage — which he uses for the three-in-one case of overlapping status categories — and *achoto d'seifa*, which he uses to establish the prohibition for a full sister. There is a third use of an extra *achoto* at the beginning of the passage, which Rabbi Akiva employs to address a distinct question: what is the law when two separate *lav* prohibitions share a single *karet*?

The case is the *pitum ha-ketores* — the incense compounded for the *Beis Hamikdash* — and *sach ha-shemen* — anointing with the *shemen ha-mishcha*. The Torah separately prohibits compounding the incense for private use and anointing oneself with the sacred oil, yet states a single *karet* referring to both violations. If a person committed both in a single *he'elam*, does he bring one *korban* or two? Since the principle of separate *korbanos* follows the *lavin* and not the *karet*, Rabbi Akiva derives from this *achoto* that even when two *lavin* share one *karet*, they each generate a separate *korban*. This is comparable to the principle already established for the *arayos* — one global *karet* does not merge multiple distinct violations.

Rabbi Yitzchak, who does not use *achoto d'seifa* for the multiple-statuses case and does not use *v'nichresu* for the three-in-one, derives the *pitum* and *sach* rule from the position of Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Oshaya: wherever there are two *lavin* and a single *karet*, they are automatically treated as separate for purposes of *korban* — no special verse is required, as it follows logically from the structure of the *lavin*.

---

## Isha Dava Case

### Flow Location

Rabbi Yitzchak requires yet another derivation to account for the extra *karet* mentioned by the case of *isha dava* — a woman who is flowing. The verse in *Kedoshim* (20:18) states: *v'ish asher yishkav es isha dava v'gila es ervatah es mekora he-erati v'hi gilta es mekor dameha v'nichretu sheneihem*. The *v'nichretu* here is an extra mention of *karet* for a case already subsumed under the general *karet* rules. Rabbi Yochanan, in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, derives from this verse a fundamental rule: *minayin l'niddah ad she-yeitzei midveih derech ervatah* — how do we know that a woman does not acquire the status of *niddah* unless the blood flows specifically through the genital area? The verse links the flow of *dava* with *ervatah* — connecting the issue of flow to the place of nakedness. This teaches that a nosebleed or blood from another area of the body does not create the status of *niddah*.

The *gemara* presents this as one of several competing uses of the extra *karet* in the *isha dava* passage. Those who do not need it for this *halacha* can use it for the principle of separate *korbanos* in cases analogous to *pitum* and *sach*; those who derive that principle from Rabbi Elazar's logical rule need the *isha dava karet* for Rabbi Yochanan's teaching. Each opinion thus has its verses accounted for, and none is left without a source.

---

## Tamei Kodesh

### Mishnah's List

After the extended discussion of *arayos* and *karet*, the *gemara* now turns to individual entries in the *mishnah*'s list of those who receive *malkos*. Among them is the case of a *tamei* person who eats *kodesh* — sacrificial meat. The *mishnah* includes this among the violations that carry *malkos*, which requires both a punishment (*onesh*) and a prohibition (*azhara*) in the form of a *lav*.

### Prohibition Source

For the case of a *tamei* person entering the *Beis Hamikdash*, both elements are clearly present. The punishment — *v'nichreta* — appears in the verse *es mishkan Hashem timei v'nichreta* (Numbers 19:20). The prohibition appears in *v'lo yetam'u es machaneihem* (Numbers 5:3). But for a *tamei* person who eats *kodesh*, while the punishment is explicit — *hanefesh asher tochal mi-besar zevach hashlamim asher l'Hashem v'tumato alav v'nichreta* (Leviticus 7:20) — where is the *azhara*, the prohibitory *lav* that grounds the *malkos*?

There is a verse that initially appears to supply this prohibition: *u-vakodashim lo yocheil ad asher yithar* (Leviticus 22:4) — do not eat *kodashim* until you have become *tahor*. This sounds explicit. But the *gemara* will establish that this verse refers to *terumah*, not to *kodshim* proper, and so a different source must be found.

### Resh Lakish

Resh Lakish derives the *azhara* from the verse *bechol kodesh lo tiga v'el hamikdash lo tavo* (Leviticus 12:4), which appears in the context of a woman after childbirth. The word *tiga* — "touch" — Resh Lakish understands to encompass eating as well.

### Rabbi Yochanan

Rabbi Yochanan takes a different approach. He does not learn from *bechol kodesh lo tiga* at all; he derives the prohibition from a *gezeirah shavah* on the word *tumato*. The verse of *karet* for eating *kodesh* while *tamei* says *v'tumato alav v'nichreta*. The verse dealing with *misat beit din* for entering the *Beis Hamikdash* says *tamei yihye od tumato bo* (Numbers 19:13). By linking the two via the shared word *tumato*, Rabbi Yochanan extends the prohibition from the *Beis Hamikdash* context — where both punishment and prohibition exist — to the eating of *kodesh* context.

---

## Terumah vs. Kodesh

### Aharon's Seed

The reason Rabbi Yochanan cannot use *ish ish mi-zera Aharon v'hu tzarua o zav bakodashim lo yocheil* (Leviticus 22:4) as a prohibition against eating *kodesh* while *tamei* — even though that verse seems maximally explicit — is that the verse specifies *mi-zera Aharon*, the seed of Aaron. This phrase includes not only the male *kohanim* but all of Aaron's descendants, male and female alike. The question is: what is the one category of sacred food that all descendants of Aaron, men and women, share equal access to? The answer is *terumah*. *Kodashim* proper can only be eaten by male *kohanim* under specific conditions; *terumah* is the food shared by all of Aaron's household. Therefore, the prohibition in *ish ish mi-zera Aharon* is understood to be addressed to the eating of *terumah* in a state of *tumah*, not to *kodashim*.

### Touching vs. Eating

This forces the question of how Resh Lakish handles the *terumah* prohibition. If Resh Lakish uses *bechol kodesh lo tiga* for eating *kodesh* while *tamei*, where does he derive the prohibition against eating *terumah* while *tamei*? He takes it from *ish ish mi-zera Aharon*. And if Rabbi Yochanan uses *bechol kodesh lo tiga* for the prohibition against touching *terumah* while *tamei* (reading *lo tiga* in its plain sense), then both authorities use the same set of verses but assign them differently. Rabbi Yochanan: *bechol kodesh lo tiga* = prohibition against touching *terumah*; *ish ish mi-zera Aharon* = prohibition against eating *terumah*. Resh Lakish: *bechol kodesh lo tiga* = prohibition against eating *kodesh*; *ish ish mi-zera Aharon* = prohibition against eating *terumah*.

---

## Resh Lakish's Derivations

### Eating Kodesh

Resh Lakish derives the prohibition against a *tamei* person eating *kodesh* from *bechol kodesh lo tiga*. Even though the verse literally says *lo tiga* — "do not touch" — Resh Lakish understands it to be addressing eating. This creates an immediate internal tension: Resh Lakish himself also maintains that a *tamei* person who *touches kodesh* receives *malkos*. How can a single verse serve both purposes?

### Touching Kodesh

The *gemara* states directly: *deitmar tamei shenaga bekodesh — Resh Lakish amar lokeh* — a *tamei* person who touches *kodesh* receives *malkos*, and the source is *bechol kodesh lo tiga*. Rabbi Yochanan disagrees: *eino lokeh* — one does not receive *malkos* for touching *kodesh*. For Rabbi Yochanan, *bechol kodesh lo tiga* is addressed only to touching *terumah*, and there is no *malkos* for touching *kodesh* at all. *Tosafos* notes the irony in Rabbi Yochanan's position: he derives a prohibition from *lo tiga* for touching *terumah*, which is a lesser sanctity, while holding that there is no such prohibition for touching *kodesh* proper, which is holier. *Tosafos* suggests that for Rabbi Yochanan, *lo tiga* regarding *terumah* may not be a genuine prohibition at all but rather a statement that touching *terumah* while *tamei* renders it impure — a consequence rather than a prohibition.

### Beis HaMikdash Link

The *gemara* works out how Resh Lakish derives *both* the prohibition against eating *kodesh* and the prohibition against touching *kodesh* from a single verse. The answer lies in the structure of *bechol kodesh lo tiga v'el hamikdash lo tavo*. The word *tiga* in its plain sense addresses touching — that is the prohibition against touching *kodesh* while *tamei*. The second half of the verse — *v'el hamikdash lo tavo* — creates a *hekesh*, a textual analogy, linking *kodesh* to the *mikdash*. Just as entry into the *mikdash* while *tamei* is a grave violation that carries *karet*, this analogy imports the same gravity for an act involving *kodesh*. And since touching *kodesh* does not carry *karet* — only eating *kodesh* while *tamei* does — the *hekesh* to the *mikdash* must be pointing to eating. Thus *lo tiga* teaches the prohibition against touching, and the *hekesh* to the *mikdash* teaches the prohibition against eating.

### Before Blood

Resh Lakish uses the verse for yet a third purpose. The *gemara* states: *tamei she'achal basar kodesh lifnei zrikat damim — Resh Lakish amar lokeh* — a *tamei* person who eats sacrificial meat *before* the blood of the offering has been sprinkled (*zrikat damim*) receives *malkos*. Rabbi Yochanan again disagrees: *eino lokeh*. Rabbi Yochanan's position is consistent with his overall approach: he derives the prohibition against eating *kodesh* while *tamei* from the *gezeirah shavah* of *tumato tumato*. That *gezeirah shavah* is anchored to the *karet* verse for eating *kodesh*, and that *karet* applies only once the meat is fit to be eaten — that is, after *zrikat damim*. Before the blood is sprinkled, the meat is not yet at the stage where eating it in *tumah* constitutes a fully culpable act.

Resh Lakish, by contrast, derives the prohibition from *bechol kodesh lo tiga*, and the word *bechol* — "every" or "any" — broadens the scope. *Lo shena lifnei zrika v'lo shena achar zrika* — it makes no difference whether it is before or after *zrikat damim*: the prohibition covers *any* act of eating *kodesh* while *tamei*. The word *bechol* is the textual basis for this extension.

### Braisa Support

The *gemara* concludes with a *braisa* that supports Resh Lakish: *tanya k'vaseih d'Resh Lakish* — it was taught in accordance with Resh Lakish. The *braisa* reads: *bechol kodesh lo tiga — azhara le'ochel*. The question is posed: when it says *lo tiga*, does it mean a prohibition against touching, or a prohibition against eating? The *braisa* answers by invoking the *hekesh*: *bechol kodesh lo tiga v'el hamikdash lo tavo — makish kodesh l'mikdash*. Just as entry into the *mikdash* while *tamei* involves a *netilas nefesh* — a taking of life, that is, a *karet* offense — so too the act involving *kodesh* that rises to that level of severity must be one that carries *karet*. Touching *kodesh* does not carry *karet*; eating *kodesh* while *tamei* does. Therefore, the prohibition of *lo tiga* is ultimately about eating — *ela ba'achila*. For Resh Lakish, *lo tiga* thus operates on two levels simultaneously: its plain meaning addresses touching *kodesh* while *tamei*, and its contextual meaning — via the *hekesh* to the *mikdash* — addresses eating *kodesh* while *tamei*, with the word *bechol* further extending that prohibition to the period before *zrikat damim*.

---

---

# Makkot 15

## Lav Nitak L'Asei Intro

### Definition & Examples

The daf opens with a principle that is conceptually richer and less technically complicated than much of what precedes it in the third *perek*: the *lav she'nitak l'asei*, a negative prohibition that is connected to a positive commandment in such a way that the *asei* functions as a corrective or remedy, thereby exempting the transgressor from lashes. The governing assumption is that when an *asei* is positioned in the Torah as the means of fixing a violation of a *lav*, the person who performs that remedial act is not subject to *malkus*. One frequently cited example is the prohibition against stealing coupled with the verse *v'heshiv es ha'gezeilah* — return the stolen object. Though in that case the exemption from lashes rests also on a broader principle that monetary transgressions do not incur lashes, the conceptual framework is similar.

### Mother Bird Case

The cleaner, more paradigmatic case is the prohibition of taking the mother bird: *lo tikach ha'eim al habanim* — do not take the mother with her young. The Torah then instructs *shalei'ach t'shaleich es ha'eim* — send the mother bird away. This is the classic instance of *lav she'nitak l'asei*, and the structure is significant: the *asei* appears after the *lav* and can be read as the corrective response to a transgression already committed. Note that the act of sending away the mother bird is not exclusively remedial — one could perform it even without having transgressed, simply by sending the mother away before taking the young. Read on its own terms, the verse might simply mean: rather than taking the mother with her chicks, send her away. But because the *asei* follows the *lav* in the text, the Talmud reads it also as: if you did transgress, here is what you must do to fix it. The same physical act serves both purposes. And precisely because it is read as a corrective mechanism, the *lav* is understood as subject to repair, and the transgressor is therefore not given lashes.

### Asei Precedes Lav

The statement transmitted by Rabbah bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan introduces a critical qualification: *kol lo ta'aseh she'kidmo asei, lokin alav* — any negative commandment that was preceded by a positive commandment, one receives lashes for its violation. This is a departure from what one might assume, and its logic runs as follows. When the *asei* comes after the *lav*, it is naturally read as a repair mechanism — "don't do this, but if you did, here is how to fix it." When, however, the *asei* precedes the *lav*, the *asei* cannot serve as a remedy for the transgression, because it appeared in the Torah before the transgression was even defined. In such cases, the *asei* is simply an independent positive obligation, not a corrective one. Rabbi Yochanan's example by analogy would be *Shabbos*: the verse *bayom hashvi'i tishbos* commands rest on the seventh day and appears before the negative prohibition against *melacha*. No one reads that *asei* as a remedy for violating *Shabbos* — it is plainly a reinforcing obligation, not a fix. And therefore, if the *asei* came first, the *lav* is not undermined by it, and one who transgresses receives lashes.

---

## Tamei Entry Case

### Tamei Precedent

When Rabbah bar bar Chana was asked whether he had actually transmitted this ruling in Rabbi Yochanan's name, he initially disavowed it. Rava responded forcefully — *Ha-elohim amarta!* — insisting that he had indeed said it, and moreover that the position is well-grounded in both a *pasuk* and a *mishnah* working in concert.

### Gemara Support

The scriptural support: the Torah writes *veshilchu min hamachaneh kol tzaru'a vechol zav vechol tamei lanafesh* — send out from the camp all who are impure. That is the positive commandment, and it appears first. Only afterward does the Torah state *velo yetame'u es machanehem* — they shall not defile the camp. That is the negative prohibition. The *asei* of leaving the camp precedes the *lav* of defiling it.

Now one might have thought: if a *tamei* person entered the *Beis Hamikdash*, perhaps he could remedy the transgression by simply leaving. After all, there is an *asei* connected here — the obligation to depart from the camp when impure. But the *mishnah* rules explicitly that one who enters the *Beis Hamikdash* in a state of *tumah* receives lashes. This demonstrates that the positive commandment to leave does not serve as a corrective that exempts from lashes — and the reason, consistent with Rabbi Yochanan's principle, is that the *asei* appeared before the *lav*. It is an additional independent obligation, not a mechanism of repair. The *pasuk* and the *mishnah* together, then, confirm Rabbi Yochanan's position rather than undermining it.

### Retraction Reason

If the position is so well-grounded, why did Rabbah bar bar Chana retract it in the first place? The Gemara explains: *mishum dekashya lei ones* — because of a difficulty posed by the case of rape. The Torah instructs that the man who has violated a woman must take her as his wife — *lo tihyeh le'ishah* — and may never divorce her: *lo yuchal leshalcha kol yamav*. Here the *asei* of taking her as a wife comes before the *lav* of divorcing her. And yet, as we will see, the *halacha* treats remarriage as a remedy that exempts him from lashes if he did divorce her. That apparent counterexample is what led Rabbah bar bar Chana to withdraw. The Gemara will work to resolve this tension.

---

## Rape & Divorce Case

### Rape Exception

A *beraisa* teaches the details of this case. If a man who raped a woman subsequently divorces her, what is his status with respect to lashes? The *asei* of *lo tihyeh le'ishah* — she shall be his wife — comes first in the verse, before the *lav* of *lo yuchal leshalcha*. According to Rabbi Yochanan's principle, one would expect this to be a case where the preceding *asei* does not remedy the transgression, and lashes should follow.

### Remarriage Exemption

Yet the *beraisa* rules: *im Yisrael hu, machazir ve'eino lokeh* — if he is a non-*kohen*, he remarries her and is thereby exempt from lashes, because the remarriage constitutes a fix. If, however, he is a *kohen*, he cannot remarry her — she is now a *gerushah* and forbidden to him — and so he receives lashes without any possibility of remedy. The case of the *yisrael* thus appears to contradict Rabbi Yochanan directly: here the *asei* precedes the *lav* and yet functions as a corrective. This is the *kushya* that drove Rabbah bar bar Chana to retract.

The Gemara acknowledges the difficulty and seeks to explain how, within Rabbi Yochanan's framework, the case of the rapist can be read as an exception — or more precisely, why the *asei* of marrying her can here be understood as a fix even though it preceded the *lav*.

### Ulla Superfluous Logic

Ulla proposes a resolution rooted in the principle of *im eino inyan* — redirecting a superfluous verse to teach something else. His argument begins: the Torah did not need to state the obligation of marriage in the case of the *oneis*, the rapist. Why not? Because we could have derived it through a *kal vachomer* from the case of the *motzi shem ra*, the man who falsely reports that his wife was not a virgin at marriage. In that case too, the Torah states *lo tihyeh le'ishah lo yuchal l'shalchah kol yamav* — she shall remain his wife and he may never divorce her. The *motzi shem ra* did not commit any physical act against the woman; his offense was entirely verbal. And yet the Torah imposed upon him the obligation to remain married to her. If even the slanderer — who committed no physical act — has this *mitzvah*, then certainly the rapist, who committed a far more serious physical offense, should have it as well. Thus the verse's statement of the marriage obligation in the rape case is superfluous. Since it is superfluous, the principle of *im eino inyan l'fanav, taneihu inyan l'acharyav* applies: redirect it to teach something for after the fact — namely, that if he divorced her, he must remarry her, and that act of remarriage functions as a repair of the transgression.

---

## Rape vs. False Report

### Challenge to Kal Vachomer

The Gemara objects to Ulla's *kal vachomer*. One cannot derive the marriage obligation of the rapist from that of the *motzi shem ra* so easily, because the *motzi shem ra* case carries exceptional punishments: the Torah imposes both lashes *and* a monetary fine — *v'yisru oso v'anshu oso mei'ah kesef* — a combination normally not applied in a single case. The severity of the *motzi shem ra's* punishment may reflect the unique heinousness of his act, making it an atypical case from which one cannot extrapolate to others. So the *kal vachomer* fails: perhaps the obligation to remain married is specific to the *motzi shem ra* on account of the exceptional punishment, and cannot be extended to the *oneis*.

### Redundancy Resolved

The Gemara then reverses the direction: rather than deriving the *oneis* from the *motzi shem ra*, why not learn the *motzi shem ra* from the *oneis*? One would reason: the *oneis* does not incur the doubled punishment of lashes and a fine — he is not an exceptional case in that sense. And yet the Torah requires him to remain married to the woman he violated. A fortiori, the *motzi shem ra*, whose punishment is far heavier, should certainly be required to remain married. If so, the statement of the marriage obligation in the *motzi shem ra* passage is the superfluous one. And being superfluous, we apply *im eino inyan l'fanav, taneihu inyan l'acharyav*: it is not needed to establish the obligation at the outset in the *motzi shem ra* case — that follows from the *oneis* — but rather to teach that if he transgresses and divorces her, he must remarry her as a corrective.

But here too the Gemara objects: you still cannot learn one case from the other without challenge, because each case possesses a characteristic that the other lacks. The *oneis* is weightier in that he committed an actual physical act — *asah ma'aseh* — against the woman. The *motzi shem ra* is weightier in that his punishment is uniquely severe. Each case has a dimension of gravity absent from the other, so neither can be simply derived from the other by *kal vachomer* or analogy, and therefore each requires an independent textual source. Neither verse is in fact superfluous, and Ulla's argument collapses.

### Already Married

At this point the Gemara observes what seems in retrospect almost obvious, and notes wryly that it took some time to arrive at: in the case of the *motzi shem ra*, the verse need not have stated *lo tihyeh le'ishah* — she shall be his wife — because they are already married. The entire premise of that case is an existing marriage in which the husband falsely accuses his wife of pre-marital infidelity. There is therefore no need to instruct him to take her as a wife; she already is. All the Torah needed to say was that he may not divorce her. The statement that she shall be his wife is therefore unambiguously superfluous in the *motzi shem ra* case — not because of any *kal vachomer*, but simply because there is no marriage to establish.

This being so, the redundant phrase in the *motzi shem ra* passage teaches: *im eino inyan l'fanav, taneihu inyan l'acharav* — since it is not needed to establish a marriage obligation at the outset, it is redirected to teach that even after he transgresses and divorces her, remarrying her constitutes a remedy and exempts him from lashes.

But this still leaves the original problem unresolved. We have now established that in the *motzi shem ra* case the *asei* of remarrying serves as a corrective after the fact. But by the *oneis*, the *asei* of taking her as a wife appears before the *lav* of not divorcing. According to Rabbi Yochanan, a preceding *asei* is not a fix. How then do we know that in the *oneis* case, remarriage exempts him from lashes?

The Gemara attempts to say: learn the *oneis* from the *motzi shem ra* — since we see that in the *motzi shem ra* case the *asei* of marrying functions as a corrective, apply the same logic to the *oneis*. But the Gemara immediately concedes that this learning cannot stand, since we have already established that neither case can be derived from the other: *mah l'motzi shem ra sheken lo asah ma'aseh* — the *motzi shem ra* committed no physical act, and perhaps the Torah grants him a corrective precisely because his offense was less severe, whereas the *oneis*, having committed an act of physical violation, may not be granted that lenience.

The Gemara acknowledges: *ein hachi nami* — indeed, the *motzi shem ra* verse teaches its own case, that if he divorces her he can remarry to fix it, but this tells us nothing about the *oneis*. The *oneis* case, where the *asei* precedes the *lav*, remains problematic.

---

## Kol Yamav Solution

### Kol Yamav Teaching

Rava resolves the difficulty differently, setting aside entirely the comparison to the *motzi shem ra*. He focuses instead on the phrase *kol yamav* — all his days — in the verse *lo yuchal leshalcha kol yamav*. Why does the Torah need to say *kol yamav*? The prohibition of divorcing her is already stated; the phrase *kol yamav* is additional. Rava says: *kol yamav be'amod vehachazir* — the phrase *kol yamav* is teaching that the obligation of maintaining the marriage extends across his entire life, and if he divorces her, he must remarry her. This phrase, being superfluous on a plain reading of the prohibition, is what teaches that remarriage functions as a corrective in the *oneis* case — and does so without relying on any comparison to the *motzi shem ra*.

### Two Readings

There are, however, two distinct ways to understand how *kol yamav* achieves this result, and they lead to meaningfully different conceptual frameworks.

The first reading, associated with Rashi, keeps *kol yamav* attached to the negative prohibition itself. On this reading, the transgression of divorcing her is not defined as the mere act of delivering a *get*. Rather, the prohibition is violated only when he has divorced her *permanently* — for all his days. If he divorces her and subsequently remarries her, he has not in fact transgressed the *lav*, because the divorce did not endure for *kol yamav*. On this reading, the *asei* of marrying is entirely beside the point as a remedial mechanism; the man who remarries her never transgressed in the first place. The exemption from lashes is not because the *asei* fixed the *lav*, but because the *lav* was never fully violated.

The second reading, which Tosafot and Rashi in another context prefer, attaches *kol yamav* to the *asei* of *lo tihyeh le'ishah* — she shall be his wife for all his days. On this reading, the *asei* of marriage is not merely an obligation that precedes the *lav* in the text; it extends forward across his entire life and functions as an ongoing corrective. Even if he divorced her, the *asei* is telling him: make sure she remains your wife for all your days, which means that remarrying her after a divorce is itself the fulfillment of the *asei* — and that fulfillment exempts him from lashes.

The practical difference between these two readings is considerable. On the first reading — Rashi's primary interpretation — the man who divorces and does not remarry has not technically transgressed *so long as* she remains available for remarriage. He can always say he intends to remarry her. A court could not give him lashes while remarriage remains possible, because he has not yet divorced her *kol yamav*. It is only when remarriage becomes permanently impossible — for instance, if she marries someone else or dies — that he has transgressed. On the second reading, the question is whether the *asei* has been fulfilled or not, and a different framework for assessing when lashes are due applies.
