This connects directly to the broader debate between the *bitlo* and *kiymo* models, to which the Gemara now turns.

---

## Rav Papa Challenge

### Ox Paradigm

Rav Papa challenges Rabbi Yochanan's principle from a different angle. The foundational paradigm for *malkus* is derived from the juxtaposition of the passage mandating lashes — *vehaya im bin hakot harasha, vehipilo hashofet vehikahu lefanav* — with the prohibition of *lo tachsom shor bedisho*, do not muzzle an ox while it threshes. That case establishes the model: a negative prohibition, transgressed through an active physical deed, with no *asei* connected to it whatsoever. Rav Papa's question: even granting Rabbi Yochanan's point that when the *asei* precedes the *lav* it is not a corrective but merely an independent additional obligation — still, is such a *lav* truly comparable to the paradigmatic case of muzzling the ox? The ox case has no *asei* at all. The case where an *asei* precedes the *lav* does have an *asei*, even if that *asei* does not function as a fix. Should the mere presence of an *asei* not be sufficient to distinguish this case from the paradigm and exempt the transgressor from lashes, even without the *asei* serving as a remedy?

### Obligation Not Fix

Rabba responds: *mishum dechtav bei Rachmana asei yetira migra gara?* — does the fact that the Torah wrote an additional *asei* thereby weaken the *lav*? Once we have conceptually established that the *asei* which precedes the *lav* is not a corrective but an independent additional obligation, its presence does not diminish the *lav*. If anything, having both a positive obligation and a negative prohibition makes the entire matter weightier, not lighter. The comparison to the paradigm of muzzling the ox is not made arbitrarily on the basis of formal similarity alone; what matters is whether the *lav* is in some way weakened. A preceding *asei* that carries no remedial function does not weaken the *lav* — it reinforces the overall stringency of the obligation.

### Nitak Disrupts Lav

Rav Papa then presses further: if a non-remedial *asei* does not weaken the *lav*, why should a remedial *asei* — the classic case of *lav she'nitak la'asei*, where the *asei* comes after and is meant to fix — exempt from lashes? Should we not say the same thing: just because there is an *asei*, it does not weaken the *lav*?

Rabba's response is decisive. Here the word *nitak* — detach, undermine — is operative, and crucially, it refers not to what happens to the *asei* but to what happens to the *lav*. When the *asei* follows the *lav* in order to serve as a corrective, the *asei* is there to *natek* the *lav* — to dislodge, neutralize, or undermine the *lav* itself. The *lav* is not simply accompanied by an additional obligation; rather, the *asei* is positioned in the text precisely to attenuate the force of the *lav*. That is a qualitative difference: the *lav* is intrinsically weakened by the corrective *asei* that trails it. By contrast, when the *asei* precedes the *lav*, it adds an obligation; it does not undermine the *lav*. These are categorically distinct cases. The absence of lashes in the case of *lav she'nitak la'asei* is therefore not arbitrary — it flows from the structural fact that the *asei* is designed to neutralize the transgression. And when the *asei* precedes, no such neutralization is at work, and lashes apply.

This is also the basis for the exemption from lashes in the case of a *lav she'ein bo ma'aseh* — a passive transgression. Just as a passive act is categorically weaker than an active one and therefore falls outside the paradigm of muzzling the ox, so too a *lav* accompanied by a subsequent corrective *asei* is categorically weaker — the *asei* has disrupted the *lav* — and lashes similarly do not apply.

---

## Bitla vs. Kiyma

### Tana Teaching

A *tana* taught before Rabbi Yochanan the following formulation: *kol mitzvat lo ta'aseh she'yesh ba kum aseh* — any negative commandment that is accompanied by a positive commandment positioned to remedy it — *kiyyem aseh she'bah, patur; bitel aseh she'bah, chayav*. If one fulfilled the *asei* — sent away the mother bird — one is exempt. If one negated the *asei* — killed the mother bird, rendering its fulfillment impossible — one is liable.

### Excluded Middle

The difficulty with this formulation is immediate and striking. The *tana* has articulated two poles — fulfillment and negation — but has said nothing about the vast middle ground between them. In the case of the mother bird: what is the *halacha* for the person who took the mother bird, did not send her away, but also did not kill her? He simply walked away. He has neither fulfilled the *asei* nor actively negated it. The *tana's* formulation leaves this case entirely unaddressed.

Rabbi Yochanan identifies the problem precisely. He poses it as a choice: are you saying *kiyymo patur, lo kiyymo chayav* — if you fulfilled it you are exempt, if you did not fulfill it you are liable? In that case, the framework is *kiyma versus lo kiyma*, and the excluded middle is covered by the "not fulfilled" side: a person who merely walked away without sending the mother bird free has not fulfilled the *asei* and would be liable. This is the more intuitive reading: you transgressed the *lav*, you can remedy it by doing the *asei*, but if you have not done so, you remain liable. Alternatively, are you saying *bitlo chayav, lo bitlo patur* — if you actively negated the *asei* you are liable, if you did not actively negate it you are exempt? In that case, someone who merely walked away — who neither sent the bird away nor killed it — would not be liable at all, because he did not take the affirmative step of negating the *asei*.

These are not equivalent positions, and the *tana's* formulation, as stated, does not cleanly commit to either. Rabbi Yochanan insists: choose one or the other. Present it as a question of fulfillment (*kiyma*) versus non-fulfillment, or as a question of active negation (*bitla*) versus non-negation. As formulated, the *beraisa* creates an irresolvable excluded middle.

The two positions have very different practical implications. Under the *kiymo* model, the person who walks away from the bird without sending it free is liable to lashes — he transgressed the *lav* and failed to fulfill the remedial *asei*. Under the *bitlo* model, the same person is exempt — he has not actively negated the *asei*, and as long as the *asei* remains theoretically performable, he incurs no lashes. On the *bitlo* model, lashes are extraordinarily difficult to impose in almost any real case, because short of actively rendering the *asei* impossible to perform, the transgressor remains technically exempt.

### RY vs. RL Debate

Rabbi Yochanan resolves the ambiguity by instructing the *tana* to reformulate: *tani bitlo v'lo bitlo* — teach it in terms of active negation and its absence. You are only *chayav* if you actively negated the *asei*; anything short of that renders you exempt. Resh Lakish, by contrast, insists on the *kiymo* formulation: *kiymo v'lo kiymo* — if you fulfilled the *asei* you are exempt; if you have not yet fulfilled it, you are liable.

---

## Hasra'at Safek Root

### Warning Timing

The Gemara probes the root of this dispute. What underlying principle generates the disagreement between Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish? The answer: *be'hasra'at safek kamiflagi* — they disagree about the validity of doubtful warning, *hasra'at safek*. To understand why this matters, consider the moment at which the warning is administered in the mother bird case. There are witnesses who see a man approaching a nest and they warn him: do not take the mother bird; if you do, you will receive lashes. Is that a *hasra'at vadai* — a definite warning, meaning a warning that his act will definitely constitute a transgression? Or is it a *hasra'at safek* — a doubtful warning, meaning a warning about an act that may or may not ultimately constitute a transgression?

### Active Completion

Under the *bitlo* model, the act of taking the mother bird is inherently incomplete as a transgression. The transgression is not fully constituted until the person has also actively negated the *asei* — say, by killing the mother bird. At the moment of taking the bird, the person has done the first half of the transgression but not the second. The warning at that moment is therefore not definitive — the witnesses cannot say with certainty that this act will result in full liability. The act is a *hasra'at safek* because it remains possible that the person will send the bird away and thereby avoid liability entirely.

### RY Safek Valid

This is the precise axis of the dispute. Rabbi Yochanan holds that *hasra'at safek shema hasra'ah* — a warning even in a case where it is not yet certain that a full transgression will occur is nonetheless a valid warning. Because Rabbi Yochanan accepts *hasra'at safek*, he can hold the *bitlo* position: the transgression is conceptually understood in two stages, and the warning at the first stage is still valid. Resh Lakish, on the other hand, holds *hasra'at safek lo shema hasra'ah* — a doubtful warning does not qualify as a valid warning. Therefore, for Resh Lakish, the only way to give a person valid lashes with a proper warning is to take the *kiymo* approach: hold that the act of taking the bird is itself the complete transgression, the warning is unambiguously definitive, and the subsequent fulfillment of the *asei* functions as a post-hoc remedy. Under this model, the moment of taking is the moment of full transgression, the warning is *vadai*, and lashes are properly grounded.

---

## Loaf of Bread Case

### Bread Oath

The Gemara confirms that Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish carry their respective positions consistently into a related case: one who takes an oath that he will eat a loaf of bread today, and the day passes without his having done so. Both agree that he does not receive lashes — but they disagree about the reason.

### Passive Exempt

Rabbi Yochanan says he is exempt *mishum d'havei lav she'ein bo ma'aseh* — because this is a passive transgression. He did nothing; the day simply elapsed. The principle that a *lav she'ein bo ma'aseh*, a prohibition violated through inaction rather than action, does not incur lashes, is the operative rule here. For Rabbi Yochanan, this is a straightforward application of that exemption. Rabbi Yochanan is not troubled by *hasra'at safek* as a category — he accepts it — so the problem with the bread case is not the nature of the warning but the nature of the act.

### RL Safek Invalid

Resh Lakish locates the exemption elsewhere: *mishum d'havei hasra'at safek* — because the warning in such a case is a doubtful warning. When one warns a person at midday that he must eat the bread or face lashes, the person has not yet transgressed, and it is uncertain whether he will. The warning is not definitive. Since Resh Lakish holds that *hasra'at safek lo shema hasra'ah*, the warning is invalid, and lashes cannot be administered without a proper warning. For Resh Lakish, the passive character of the transgression is not the operative concern — the problem is that *hasra'at vadai* could never be properly administered in such a case.

These two explanations are rooted in the same underlying disagreement. Rabbi Yochanan, who accepts *hasra'at safek* and therefore can embrace the *bitlo* model, locates the exemption in the passive nature of the act. Resh Lakish, who requires *hasra'at vadai* and therefore must hold the *kiymo* model in the *lav she'nitak la'asei* context, locates the exemption in the invalidity of the warning. Both agree on the outcome in the bread case, but their reasoning reflects two coherent and divergent ways of understanding when a negative prohibition is truly violated and when the machinery of *malkus* may legitimately be set in motion.

---

---

# Makkot 16

## Lav Hanitak Le'aseh

### Definition & Examples

We open on daf 16 in the midst of the *machloket* between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish — and this is, as one might say, the welcome-to-Gemara roller coaster. The subject is *lav hanitak le'aseh*: cases in the Torah where a negative commandment is paired with a positive one, such that if the transgressor does the forbidden act, the Torah then instructs him to perform a remedial positive act. The classic illustration is *shiluach haken*: the Torah prohibits taking the mother bird together with her young, and immediately pairs that prohibition with the positive command *shaleach teshalach et ha'em* — you shall send the mother away. Another paradigmatic example, which opens our sugya at the top of daf 16, is the verse in Shemot 12 concerning the Pesach sacrifice: *velo totiru mimenu ad boker*, do not leave over from it until the morning — and yet *vehanotar mimenu ad boker ba'esh tisrofu*, whatever remains until the morning shall be burned in fire. The Torah thus attaches a positive obligation to the negative prohibition.

### Core Dispute

The central dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish concerns precisely when *malkot* — lashes — are incurred for a *lav hanitak le'aseh*. The basic framework: ordinarily, negative commandments carry lashes. But a *lav* that is linked to a positive commandment does not generate lashes, because the person retains the potential to perform the corrective *aseh*. The question is: at what point does that potential expire, and the lashes kick in?

Reish Lakish holds that as soon as the person has violated the *lav* and has not yet performed the *aseh*, he is already liable. Rabbi Yochanan holds the opposite: only when the possibility of fulfilling the *aseh* has been entirely cancelled — actively and irrevocably — does he become liable for lashes. Until that moment, the *lav* and the *aseh* remain connected, and no lashes apply.

### Lav Categories

To appreciate the structure of the dispute, one must recall two foundational principles. *Lav she'ein bo ma'aseh* — a negative commandment whose transgression involves no physical act — does not carry lashes. *Lav she'yesh bo ma'aseh* — a prohibition transgressed through an active deed — does carry lashes. The case of *lav hanitak le'aseh* introduces a third, more complicated category, which is why the sugya demands such careful unpacking.

### Lav + Aseh

The Gemara presents the verse regarding the Pesach sacrifice: *velo totiru mimenu ad boker, vehanotar mimenu ad boker ba'esh tisrofu*. This is adduced as a case of *lav hanitak le'aseh*. The text says *bah hakatuv liten aseh achar lo ta'aseh lomar she'ein lokin alav divrei Rabbi Yehuda* — the Torah came to place a positive act after the negative, to teach that one does not receive lashes for it: these are the words of Rabbi Yehuda. As we shall see, Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish each draw their respective positions from different teachings of Rabbi Yehuda — and a tension between two of his rulings will have to be resolved.

## Rabbi Yochanan

### Pesach Example

Rabbi Yochanan reads the *peshat* of this passage with precision. The Gemara states: *Rabbi Yochanan dayek hachi — ta'ama de'va katuv, ha lo va katuv lokei*. The reason lashes do not apply is specifically because the Torah wrote the positive commandment — *ba'esh tisrofu* — providing a remedial act. Had the Torah not provided this *aseh*, the violator would indeed receive lashes. This implies that it is the existence of the *aseh* — and the ongoing potential to fulfil it — that exempts from *malkot*. The violator retains that exemption as long as the *aseh* can still be performed.

### Hatra'at Safek

This leads directly to the question of *hatra'at safek* — a doubtful or uncertain forewarning. For lashes to apply, *hatra'ah* — a valid warning — is required. In a *lav hanitak le'aseh*, if I warn someone that he is about to transgress the prohibition, my warning is necessarily uncertain: I cannot tell him definitively that he has transgressed, because he still has time to fulfil the *aseh*. According to Rabbi Yochanan, this *hatra'at safek* is nonetheless considered a valid *hatra'ah* — and lashes apply once the *aseh* becomes impossible to fulfil.

## Reish Lakish

### Lav She'ein Bo

Reish Lakish reads the same Gemara differently. The Gemara states: *ve'Reish Lakish dayek hachi — ta'ama de'va katuv, ha lo va katuv lokei*. For Reish Lakish, the reason that lashes apply when the text does not provide a remedial *aseh* is that without it, this is a *lav she'ein bo ma'aseh* — a prohibition violated without a physical act. Ordinarily, *lav she'ein bo ma'aseh ein lokin alav*; yet the Gemara qualifies this, and the discussion proceeds to the further implication: *hatra'at safek*, for Reish Lakish, does *not* constitute a valid *hatra'ah*. These seemingly opposed conclusions — lashes applying earlier in Reish Lakish's view but *hatra'at safek* not being valid — generate the structure of the coming analysis.

### Makeh Aviv

To examine the status of *hatra'at safek*, the Gemara pivots to a case concerning *makeh aviv ve'imo* — one who strikes his father and mother. A *baraita* teaches: *hika zeh ve'chazar ve'hika zeh, kilel zeh ve'chazar ve'kilel zeh, hika shneihem be'vat achat o kilel shneihem be'vat achat — chayav*. The case involves a child whose paternity is uncertain: the mother divorced one man and remarried shortly thereafter, such that when a child was born, it is unclear whether the child belongs to the first or second husband. If this child struck or cursed one putative father and then the other — or struck or cursed both simultaneously — one of them is certainly his father and he is liable. The reason: *hatra'at safek shema hatra'ah* — a doubtful warning counts as a warning.

## Makeh Aviv Case

### Paternity Doubt

The scenario is as follows. A woman was married to, say, Reuven. They divorced, and without waiting the requisite three months for establishing paternity, she remarried — let us say Levi. A child was born. The child may belong to Reuven, in a pregnancy of nine months, or to Levi, in a pregnancy of seven months. This child now strikes Reuven, having been forewarned; returns and strikes Levi; or strikes both simultaneously; or curses one and then the other or both at once. In all these scenarios he is declared *chayav*, because at least one of the two men struck is certainly his father, and the warning given — even if directed at someone who may not be the father — counts as a valid forewarning.

### Rabbi Yehuda's Rule

Rabbi Yehuda, however, introduces a critical distinction: *be'vat achat chayav, zeh achar zeh patur*. If both were struck simultaneously, he is liable; if sequentially, he is exempt. The reason: when the acts are sequential, *hatra'at safek* does not constitute a valid *hatra'ah* — the warning preceding each individual act was directed at a person who may not be the father at all, and that is not a sufficient forewarning. When both are struck simultaneously, the single warning covers a single moment in which one father is certainly being struck.

This ruling stands in tension with the position Reish Lakish derives from Rabbi Yehuda in the context of *lav hanitak le'aseh*. The Gemara thus presents *trei tanna'ei aliba de'Rabbi Yehuda* — two different traditions in the name of Rabbi Yehuda — and resolves: *ei le'Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish, trei tanna'ei aliba de'Rabbi Yehuda; ei le'Rabbi Yochanan, lo kashya — ha deideh, ha de'rabeih*. For Reish Lakish, the conflict reflects a genuine dispute among transmitters of Rabbi Yehuda's view. For Rabbi Yochanan, there is no conflict: one ruling reflects Rabbi Yehuda's own position, the other reflects his teacher's.

## Negative Commandment

### Negative Commands

The Gemara now cites a broader principle transmitted through a chain of Amoraim: *Rav Idi bar Avin amar Rav Amram amar Rav Yitzchak amar Rav Yochanan* — and Rav Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Yossi ha-Glili: *kol lo ta'aseh she'ba'Torah* — every negative commandment in the Torah — *lav she'yesh bo ma'aseh lokin alav, lav she'ein bo ma'aseh ein lokin alav*. If transgressed through a physical act, lashes apply; if not through an act, they do not.

### Exceptions

Three explicit exceptions to the general rule that *lav she'ein bo ma'aseh* carries no lashes are listed: *chutz min ha'nishba u'meimar ve'ha'mekalel et chaveiro ba'Shem* — one who swears falsely, one who performs *temurah* by substituting one sanctified animal for another, and one who curses his fellow using God's name. These three carry lashes despite involving no physical act.

### Rabbi Yehuda Issue

This generates a *kashya de'Rabbi Yehuda a'de'Rabbi Yehuda* — a contradiction between two positions attributed to Rabbi Yehuda. In the case of *lo totiru*, Rabbi Yehuda rules that no *malkot* apply — it is a *lav hanitak le'aseh*. But in the case of the son striking both putative fathers, *malkot* do seem to apply. Striking another person is *lav she'yesh bo ma'aseh*, and the *hatra'ah* issue works differently in each context. The Gemara registers this tension as requiring resolution.

## Resolution

### Reish Lakish Position

For Reish Lakish, the resolution is that *hatra'at safek* counts as a valid *hatra'ah*. He learns the principle of *lav hanitak le'aseh* from one strand of Rabbi Yehuda's teaching and the principle of *hatra'at safek* from another, treating the apparent contradiction as reflecting different *tanna'im* transmitting Rabbi Yehuda's view.

### Rabbi Yochanan Position

For Rabbi Yochanan, there is no contradiction at all: *lo kashya — ha deideh, ha de'rabeih*. One ruling reflects Rabbi Yehuda's own position, the other reflects his teacher's position, and Rabbi Yochanan consistently attributes each to its proper source. Rabbi Yochanan's specific contribution is understanding the *lav she'ein bo ma'aseh* dimension in this context: the striking of the putative father is indeed *lav she'yesh bo ma'aseh*, and the *hatra'at safek* functions as a valid *hatra'ah* in his view.

## Overview Examples

### Two Views

To summarize before proceeding to the cases: as long as the *lav hanitak le'aseh* remains connected to the possibility that the person will yet fulfil the positive commandment — and that possibility has not been cancelled — no lashes apply. This is articulated through the formulas *kiyamo ve'lo kiyamo* (whether he fulfilled or did not fulfil the *aseh*) on Reish Lakish's side, and *bitlo ve'lo bitlo* (whether he actively cancelled or did not cancel the *aseh*) on Rabbi Yochanan's side. For Reish Lakish, the moment the *aseh* is not fulfilled, liability begins. For Rabbi Yochanan, liability begins only when the person has done something to actively and irrevocably foreclose the possibility of fulfilling the *aseh*.

### Four Examples

The Gemara will examine four primary examples of *lav hanitak le'aseh* and test whether each satisfies both frameworks — the *kiyamo ve'lo kiyamo* approach and the *bitlo ve'lo bitlo* approach. The four cases are: *shiluach haken* (sending away the mother bird), *lo tigzol* (robbery and its return), the case of *ones she'gerash* (the rapist who divorces the woman he was obligated to keep), and *pe'ah* (the corner of the field). The critical question in each case is: at what point can the *aseh* no longer be performed — and was that point brought about by the person's own action?

## Shiluach Haken

### Torah Passage

The Gemara cites *tanan hatam — hanotel em al habanim*, and the relevant Torah passage is read: *ki yikarei kan tzippor lefanecha baderech, bechol etz o al ha'aretz, efrochim o beitzim, veha'em rovetzet al ha'efrochim o al habeitzim, lo tikach ha'em al habanim. Shaleach teshalach et ha'em, ve'et habanim tikach lach, lema'an yitav lach veha'arachta yamim*. The structure is clear: a negative commandment — do not take the mother together with the young — paired with a positive commandment — send the mother away. This is the textbook case of *lav hanitak le'aseh*.

### Rabbi Yehuda

*Rabbi Yehuda omer lokeh ve'eino meshaleach*. Rabbi Yehuda holds that the violator receives *makot* and does *not* send the mother away. His reasoning is that the order of the verse is to be read in reverse: one is first supposed to send the mother, and only then may one take the young. Under this reading, the *aseh* was supposed to precede the *lav*, and therefore the *aseh* cannot serve as a corrective to the *lav* after the fact — it does not cancel it. Consequently, lashes apply.

### Chachamim

The Chachamim read the verse in its straightforward order: first the prohibition against taking the mother, then the positive command to send her. *Vechachamim omrim meshaleach ve'eino lokeh* — one sends the mother and does not receive lashes. They articulate the general rule: *zeh haklal — kol mitzvat lo ta'aseh sheyesh bah kum aseh ein chayavim aleha* — any negative commandment that carries with it a positive remedial act does not generate liability for lashes, so long as the *aseh* remains available.

### Two Cases

*Amar Rabbi Yochanan — ein lanu ela zot ve'od acheret*. Rabbi Yochanan offers what should be the most reassuring statement in the entire sugya: there are only two cases of *lav hanitak le'aseh* in which *malkot* actually apply, this one and one other. When Rabbi Elazar asked where the other case is, Rabbi Yochanan said: go look for it. *Nafak dak ve'ashkach* — he went, searched, and found it. The rest of the sugya is devoted to identifying why only two cases ultimately result in *malkot*, as all the other candidates fail the *bitlo ve'lo bitlo* test for one reason or another.

## Ones She-Gerash

### Context

The case of *ones she'gerash* — the rapist who divorces the woman he was compelled to marry — is introduced as a candidate for the second case of *lav hanitak le'aseh* where lashes apply. The Torah states *lo tuchal le'shalcha kol yamecha* — you may never send her away for all the days of your life. This negative commandment is paired with an implicit positive: he must maintain her as his wife. While the moral dimension of this case is deeply troubling by modern sensibilities, the Talmudic logic reflects a protective mechanism for the woman in the social context of the ancient world, where a woman who had been violated had severely diminished marriage prospects, and the Torah therefore imposed on the perpetrator a lifelong obligation.

### Israelite vs. Kohen

The Gemara distinguishes: *im yisrael hu — machzir ve'eino lokeh*. If he is an ordinary Israelite, he can bring her back — he can still fulfil the positive *aseh* — and he therefore does not receive lashes. *Ve'im kohen hu — lokeh ve'eino machzir*. If he is a *kohen*, once he has divorced her she becomes a divorcee, and a *kohen* is forbidden to marry a divorcee. He can no longer fulfil the remedial *aseh*, so he receives lashes. This makes it a case where the *aseh* has been cancelled.

### Kiyam Problem

The Gemara asks: this works well for the opinion that follows *kiyamo ve'lo kiyamo* — since the *aseh* is no longer fulfilled, lashes apply. But for the opinion that requires *bitlo ve'lo bitlo* — that the person must have *actively* cancelled the *aseh* — this case poses a difficulty. In *shiluach haken*, the cancellation is clear: if one kills the mother bird, one has actively destroyed the object of the *aseh*. But in *ones she'gerash*, how does one actively cancel the *aseh* in a comparable way? You cannot kill the woman — *de'i de'katla, kam leih biderabbah mineih*, he would be liable for a far graver offense. What act, analogous to killing the bird, forecloses the possibility of ever returning her?

### Solutions

*Amar Rav Shimi me'Chozna — kegon she'kibla kiddushin me'acher*. Rav Shimi suggests: the cancellation occurs when she has accepted *kiddushin* from another man — she is now betrothed to someone else and he can no longer take her back. But this is challenged: *Rav Ashi amar — shavitah shali'ach? Ei hi ka'mavatla leih, ei lo shavitah shali'ach, kol kimeineih ve'lo klum hi*. Did he appoint her as his agent to accept betrothal on her behalf? If she herself is the one nullifying his obligation, that is not *his* act of cancellation. And he cannot have appointed himself an agent to facilitate her betrothal to another, since he has a prior binding obligation to her.

An alternative solution is then offered: *ela amar Rav Shimi mi'Naharde'a — kegon she'hadira b'rabim*. What if he made a public vow — a *neder b'rabim* — that he will never take her back? This vow, if irrevocable, would foreclose the *aseh*.

## Vow Annulment

### Neder Types

The Gemara distinguishes between two types of vow: *neder she'hudar b'rabim* — a vow made publicly — and *neder al da'at rabim* — a vow made with the agreement or understanding of the community, incorporating the community's will into its very fabric. The question is which of these cannot be annulled.

### Ameimar

*De'amar Ameimar: hilcheta — neder she'hudar b'rabim yesh lo hafarah; al da'at rabim ein lo hafarah*. Ameimar's ruling: a vow made publicly *can* be annulled — one can return to the public setting and undo it. But a vow made *al da'at rabim* — with the community's assent incorporated into its very terms — cannot be annulled, since it is no longer the individual's vow alone to retract. It is only this latter type that would permanently foreclose the man's ability to fulfil the *aseh* of taking back the woman he violated.

## Gezel, Mashkon

### Gezel

The Gemara asks: are there not more examples? *Ve'ha'ika siman — gezel, mashkon, u'fe'ah*. Taking these in order: *gezel* — the Torah says *lo tigzol*, do not rob, and then *ve'heshiv et ha'gezeilah*, return what you have taken. This is a *lav hanitak le'aseh*, and it works straightforwardly for both the *kiyamo ve'lo kiyamo* and *bitlo ve'lo bitlo* frameworks.

### Mashkon

*Mashkon*: the Torah says *lo tavo el beito la'avot avoto, hashev tashiv lo ha'avot k'vo ha'shemesh* — do not enter the poor person's home to seize his collateral, but return it to him at sunset. Again, a negative paired with a positive. *U'mashkachat lah be'kiymo ve'lo kiymo u'vitlo ve'lo bitlo* — this case can be found to work under both formulas. However, a complication arises: *hatam keivan de'chayav be'tashlumin ein lokeh u'meshalem* — since the violator is liable for monetary restitution, he cannot receive both lashes and payment. The rule is that one does not receive both *malkot* and *tashlumim* (with the sole exception of *motzi shem ra*). Therefore *gezel* and *mashkon* may not be the best examples — the person can always pay the monetary equivalent, and the *aseh* is never truly foreclosed.

### Ger Dies

*Matkif lah Rabbi Zeira: ha'ika mashkono shel ger u'met ha'ger* — what about the collateral of a *ger* who dies? A convert who dies leaves no halachic heirs; his estate is ownerless. If someone holds a *ger*'s collateral and the *ger* dies, the collateral cannot be returned — to whom would one return it? The possibility of fulfilling the *aseh* has been foreclosed.

### Not Bitul

The Gemara responds: *hatam gavra bar tashlumi hu, ve'shibuda de'gera hu de'ka paka* — the person was always liable for monetary payment, and it is the *ger*'s death that dissolves the lien. The point is that the *ger*'s death was not caused by the violator's own action. Unlike the case of killing the mother bird — where the person actively destroys the object of the *aseh* — the *ger* dying on him is not something he did. Furthermore, even if one destroyed the *mashkon* itself, one can still pay its monetary value, meaning the *aseh* is never truly, actively cancelled by the person. *Gezel* and *mashkon* therefore fail the *bitlo ve'lo bitlo* test, and do not generate *malkot* under Rabbi Yochanan's framework.

## Pe'ah

### Torah Requirement

The Gemara then turns to *pe'ah*: *ve'ha'ika pe'ah de'rachmana amar lo techaleh pe'at sadecha... le'ani ve'la'ger ta'azov otam* — do not destroy the corner of your field; leave it to the poor person and to the stranger. Again, a negative and a positive. *De'mashkachat lah be'kiymo ve'lo kiymo, bitlo ve'lo bitlo* — this case, the Gemara suggests, can work under both formulations.

### Time Framework

The question is: how much time does the person have to fulfil the *aseh*, and when is it actively foreclosed? The Gemara cites a *mishnah*: *mitzvat pe'ah le'hafrish min ha'kamah* — ideally, the *pe'ah* is given from the standing grain. *Lo hifrish min ha'kamah — mafrish min ha'omerim* — if he cut the whole field without leaving a corner, he may give from the sheaves. *Lo hifrish min ha'omerim — mafrish min ha'keri ad she'lo mireach* — he may give from the pile of grain before it is smoothed and rendered liable for tithes.

### Making Dough

*Mircho — ma'aser ve'noten lo*: once it has been processed to the point of *miru'ach*, it must be tithed, and the tithe goes to the Levi. But can one still give *pe'ah* at this stage? The discussion presses further: when does the window definitively close?

### Rabbi Yishmael

*Ki de'Rabbi Yishmael de'amar: af mafrish min ha'isah* — Rabbi Yishmael extends the obligation even further, holding that one may still give *pe'ah* from the dough. By this point, the grain has been transformed into a fundamentally different substance — no longer standing sheaves, no longer loose grain, but *isah*, dough.

### Challah Exclusion

*Ve'de'Rabbi Yishmael nami mashkachat lah de'achal isah* — but even within Rabbi Yishmael's extended framework, one can find a case of active cancellation: if the dough has been rendered *challah* — set aside as *challah* and thus subject to the prohibition of consumption without separation — then one can no longer distribute it to the poor as *pe'ah*. The form has been changed so fundamentally, and a new *issur* has been created, that the *aseh* of *pe'ah* is now actively foreclosed. This is the *bitul* we have been looking for.

## Conclusion

### Only Two Cases

*Ela zot ve'od acheret* — and so Rabbi Yochanan is vindicated. After examining all the candidates — *ones she'gerash*, *gezel*, *mashkon*, and *pe'ah* — we are left with exactly two cases of *lav hanitak le'aseh* in which a person can genuinely, actively foreclose the *aseh* and thereby incur *malkot*. The first is *shiluach haken*: if one kills the mother bird, one has destroyed the very object of the positive commandment and can never fulfil it. The second is *pe'ah*: if one processes the grain all the way to dough and then renders it *challah*, one has actively transformed the *pe'ah* into something that can no longer be distributed as required. In all other cases, either the *aseh* remains perpetually available (and no *bitul* is possible), or any apparent *bitul* is not attributable to the person's own act.

## Vow Annulment (II)

### Teacher Case

There remains one loose end from the case of *ones she'gerash*: we concluded that a *neder al da'at rabim* could theoretically foreclose the *aseh*, making it a third case of *malkot* — yet Rabbi Yochanan said there are only two. The resolution: even a *neder al da'at rabim* can be annulled when the matter involves a *dvar mitzvah*. The Gemara illustrates this with a famous story: *ki ha de'hahu makrei dardekei de'hava pasha beinokei* — there was a teacher of young children who was harsh and neglectful with his students. Rav Acha imposed a *heider* on him, barring him from teaching. Later, Ravina reinstated him, because no teacher of equivalent skill could be found — *de'lo ishtakach de'dayek kavatei*. Since the children's education constitutes a *dvar mitzvah*, the *neder* could be annulled, and the man was reinstated. The same logic applies to *ones she'gerash*: even if the man took a *neder al da'at rabim* never to take her back, since taking her back is itself a *dvar mitzvah* — the positive commandment *lo tuchal le'shalcha* — the *neder* can be annulled, and the *aseh* remains theoretically available. Therefore, this case does not generate *malkot*, and we are left with only two.

## Eating Prohibited

### General Rule

The Mishnah returns to the broader category of those who receive lashes: *ha'ochel nevelot u'treifot shekatzim u'remasim* — one who eats animals that died without proper *shechita*, *treif* animals, *shekatzim* and *remasim*, the various categories of prohibited creeping things. The Gemara now examines specific cases within this category, moving from the general to the particular.

### Binta

*Amar Rav Yehuda: hai man de'achal binta devei karva — malkin leih mishum sheretz hashortetz al ha'aretz*. Rav Yehuda rules that one who eats the *binta* — a small creature found inside cabbage — receives lashes on account of the verse *kol sheretz hashortetz al ha'aretz sheketz hu lo ye'achel*, in Vayikra 11. A subsequent report notes: *hahu de'achal binta devei karava — venagdei Rav Yehuda*, indicating that Rav Yehuda actually administered lashes in such a case.

Tosafot raises the obvious question: if this is simply a *sheretz gamur*, why does the Gemara need to tell us? The answer Tosafot provides is that the *binta* may be a small fish — *kemo dag katan hanimtza bamachreshah* — a creature that, had it been found in water, would have been permitted because it possesses *kaskasim*, scales. Found outside the water, however — inside the ground or inside a head of cabbage — it is no longer a kosher fish. The novelty is that one might have thought its former status as a potentially kosher species exempts it; the Gemara teaches that it does not, and *malkot* apply.

### Sheratzim Lashes

*Amar Abaye: achal putita — lokei arba'ah*. One who swallows a *putita* whole — which Rashi identifies as a water creature — receives four sets of lashes. *Achal nemalah — lokei chamesh mishum sheretz hashortetz al ha'aretz*. Eating an ant incurs five sets of lashes. *Tzirah — lokei shesh mishum sheretz ha'of*: eating a wasp incurs six sets of lashes, with the additional count coming from the category of *sheretz ha'of*, flying creeping things. The reason for swallowing whole is that the laws of *kezayit* — the minimum volume for liability — apply when eating pieces; a whole living creature, however, constitutes a *biryah* and generates its own liability regardless of size.

### Lo Teshaktzu

*Amar Rav Achai: hamash'he et nekavav over mishum lo teshaktzu* — one who unduly delays attending to bodily needs transgresses the prohibition *lo teshaktzu*, do not make yourselves abominable. Whether this transgression generates *malkot* is implied by the context.

### Bloodletter Vessel

*Amar Rav Bibi bar Abaye: hai man de'shati be'karna de'umna — ka'avar mishum de'lo teshaktzu*. One who drinks from the vessel of a bloodletter — a vessel used in the course of medical bloodletting — also transgresses *lo teshaktzu* by virtue of the disgusting nature of the act.

### Smashed Ants

*Amar Rava bar Rav Huna: rissek tesha nemalim ve'hevi echad chai ve'hishliman le'kezayit — lokei vav*. If one crushed nine ants and added one living ant, bringing the total to a *kezayit*, he receives six sets of lashes. The breakdown: *chamesh mishum biryah* — five for the whole creature (*biryah*), and one for the *kezayit* of the crushed ants.

### Quantity Dispute

*Neveilah — Rabba amar Rabbi Yochanan: afilu shenayim vehu. Rabbi Yosef amar: afilu echad vehu. Ve'lo paligi — ha be'rabbata, ha be'zutarta* — Rabba citing Rabbi Yochanan says the case involves two crushed creatures; Rabbi Yosef says even one. The Gemara resolves: they do not actually disagree. One ruling refers to large ants, the other to small ones. The practical upshot: one must not eat revolting things. The halachic scaffolding in which one receives six *malkot* and requires prior warning for each — while vivid — reflects the Gemara's systematic precision in applying the principles of liability to every conceivable case.

## Tevel & Tithe

### Tevel Maaser

*Achal tevel u'maaser rishon* — among those who receive lashes are those who eat *tevel*, untithed produce, and *maaser rishon*, first tithe. *Amar Rav: achal tevel shel maaser ani — lokeh* — one who eats produce that should have been given as *maaser ani*, the poor tithe, receives lashes.

### Rabbi Yosi

*Amar Rabbi Yosi: yachol lo yehei chayav ela al ha'tevel she'lo huram mimenu kol ikkar* — one might have thought that liability arises only for produce from which no separation whatsoever has been made. But Rabbi Yosi extends the liability: even if *terumah gedolah* was separated but not *maaser rishon*, or *maaser rishon* but not *maaser sheni*, or even if *maaser ani* specifically was not separated — in all these cases, the produce retains its status as *tevel* and may not be eaten.

### Tithe Obligation

The textual derivation proceeds through a *gezerah shavah*: the verse states *lo tuchal le'echol bish'arecha* — you may not eat within your gates — and elsewhere the Torah states *ve'achlu bish'arecha ve'save'u* in reference to *maaser ani*. The verbal parallel between *bish'arecha* in the prohibition and *bish'arecha* in the description of *maaser ani* links the two: the prohibition of eating *tevel* extends to produce from which *maaser ani* has not been separated. *Ve'amar Rachmana lo tuchal* — and the Torah says you may not. The presence of this negative commandment is what generates *malkot* for eating such produce.

# Makkot 17

## Intro & Review

### Opening Overview

Today's *daf yomi* covers Makkot 17, picking up at the bottom of 16b, approximately ten lines from the bottom. The preceding material involved a sustained discussion of *lav hanitak la'aseh* — a negative prohibition that is linked to a positive commandment — and the related principles of *bitlo v'lo bitlo* and *kiyum v'lo kiyum*: whether one has actively nullified or fulfilled the positive commandment that accompanies the prohibition. Classic cases included the get given to a divorcée one is forbidden to remarry, and whether actively remarrying her constitutes a nullification of the positive commandment.

### Multiple Aveiros & Bal T…

The preceding sugya also addressed the consumption of non-kosher food, including a characteristic *gemara* discussion about the multiple *aveiros* incurred when eating particular insects, and an important treatment of the prohibition of *bal teshaktzu* — the commandment not to render oneself abominable. The *gemara* focused this prohibition on eating repulsive substances, including, in a somewhat unexpected case, drinking from a vessel used in the process of bloodletting, where one ends up ingesting blood in the course of drinking. That digression, though brief, carries significant practical weight for the general concept of *bal teshaktzu*.

---

## Tevel & Ma'asrot

### Tevel Definition

The *gemara* now turns to the case in the *mishnah* dealing with the consumption of *tevel* — grain from which *terumos u'ma'asros* have not been properly separated — as well as the eating of *ma'aser sheni* outside of Jerusalem without redemption.

### Rav's Position

The *gemara* states: *achal tevel she-hu ma'aser ani, lokeh* — Rav rules that one who eats *tevel* from which only *ma'aser ani* has not yet been separated still incurs *malkos*.

### Hierarchy of Separations

This requires some context. Classic *tevel* is produce from which *terumah* has not been taken. Eating *terumah* is a prohibition that carries *chiyuv misah bidei shamayim*, and *tevel* that has not had *terumah* separated partakes of that severity. Similarly, if *ma'aser rishon* has not been taken, the *ma'aser rishon* within it contains *terumas ma'aser*, which is forbidden to non-*kohanim* — it too has an *issur* dimension. And *ma'aser sheni* that has not been separated is forbidden to eat outside Jerusalem.

### Ma'aser Ani Case

But what of *tevel* where the only thing not yet separated is *ma'aser ani*? In the years governed by *ma'aser ani* rather than *ma'aser sheni*, once *ma'aser ani* is separated it has no *issur* status — it simply belongs to the poor. So the question is whether consuming grain from which only *ma'aser ani* has not yet been separated rises to the level of *tevel* punishable by *malkos*, or whether it amounts to no more than a form of *gezel* — wrongfully withholding property owed to the poor — without the full gravity of *tevel*.

### Braitah: Rabbi Yosei

Rav's ruling is established as following a *tanna*, as it is taught in a *braitah*: Rabbi Yosei asks, might one think that *chiyuv* applies only to *tevel* from which nothing at all has been separated? Perhaps if *terumah gedolah* was taken but not *ma'aser rishon*, or *ma'aser rishon* but not *ma'aser sheni*, each of these partial states still involves something with genuine *issur* or *kedushah* status — but how do we know that one is liable even when only *ma'aser ani* has not been taken?

### Scriptural Basis

The derivation proceeds from Deuteronomy: *lo suchal le'echol bish'arecha ma'aser deganecha tiroshecha v'yitzharecha* and so on — a list of things forbidden to be consumed outside one's gates, i.e., outside Jerusalem. Later the verse says *ve'achlu bish'arecha ve'save'u*, referring to the poor eating *ma'aser ani* within one's gates. Through a *gezerah shavah* on the word *bish'arecha*, the prohibition of *lo suchal le'echol* is linked to *ma'aser ani*: just as there it refers to *ma'aser ani*, so here the *ma'aser* mentioned in the prohibition refers to *ma'aser ani*. There is no prohibition against eating *ma'aser ani* itself outside Jerusalem, so the only possible meaning is that grain from which *ma'aser ani* has not been separated retains the status of *tevel* and the prohibition applies. Even the weakest form of *tevel* — produce awaiting only the *ma'aser ani* separation — is included in the *mishnah*'s case.

---

## Demai Debate

### Demai Definition

The *gemara* continues: *amar Rav Yosef, kitnai* — this matter is itself a dispute among *tannaim*. The *gemara* quotes: Rabbi Eliezer says one need not designate a portion of *demai* grain as *ma'aser ani*, while the Sages say one must designate it — though one need not physically separate it.

*Demai* refers to grain purchased from an *am ha'aretz* — the ordinary working farmer — concerning whom, as the tradition records in connection with Yochanan the High Priest, there was established uncertainty about whether *terumos u'ma'asros* had been properly taken. The one separation the *am ha'aretz* was presumed to take was *terumah gedolah*, because its minimum amount is virtually negligible — a single grain suffices for an entire storehouse — and because eating *terumah* as a non-*kohen* carries extreme severity. Everything beyond that was uncertain.

### Separating from Demai

Accordingly, the Sages required one who purchased grain from an *am ha'aretz* to take *ma'aser rishon* and *ma'aser sheni*, even without certainty that these had not already been taken. The reason is that this is an *issur* concern, not purely a monetary one, and the principle of *hamotzi mechavero alav hara'aya* — the burden of proof falls on the claimant — governs only monetary disputes. Once the issue becomes one of *issur*, one must act conservatively.

### Separation Process

To illustrate: suppose one purchases a hundred units of grain. One separates ten units as *ma'aser rishon*. Of those ten, one unit is designated as *terumas ma'aser* — which must genuinely be given to a *kohen*, as it has clear *issur* status. The remaining nine are *ma'aser rishon* proper. Now, a *levi* may claim those nine, but since one cannot be certain the grain was not already tithed, this becomes a monetary dispute, and one may retain and eat the nine units. For *ma'aser sheni*, one separates it out and redeems it. For *ma'aser ani*, one separates it in principle, but since the claim of the poor is also a monetary matter — Gloria, as it were, representing the poor, cannot prove that those units weren't already taken — one may consume the designated *ma'aser ani* oneself without physically removing it.

This is the position of the *chachamim*: one must at least verbally designate a portion as *ma'aser ani* — the process of naming it removes the grain from its *tevel* status — even though one need not physically set it aside.

### Rabbi Eliezer vs. Chacha…

Rabbi Eliezer's position is that one need not even designate *ma'aser ani* in the case of *demai*. The *gemara* initially considers whether this means Rabbi Eliezer disagrees with the ruling of Rav entirely — that is, perhaps Rabbi Eliezer holds that even in a case of definite *tevel* from which only *ma'aser ani* remains unseparated, there is no *tevel* status, and one who eats it commits only *gezel*, not *tevel*. After all, how else can one explain his position that no designation is required? Before designation, the grain is *tevel*; if he says no designation is needed, he must believe it is not *tevel*.

### Gemara Analysis

Abaye challenges this reading: *ei hachi, adamiflagi b'sfeiku liflgu b'vadai* — if they genuinely dispute the *tevel* status of grain awaiting *ma'aser ani*, they should argue directly about a case of definite *tevel*. The fact that the debate is specifically framed around *demai* suggests something narrower is at stake.

### Debate Conclusion

The *gemara* concludes that the debate is not about *tevel* status at all — both Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages agree that definite *tevel* awaiting *ma'aser ani* is fully *tevel*. Rather, the debate concerns the behavior of the *am ha'aretz*: does he or does he not, in practice, separate *ma'aser ani*?

Rabbi Eliezer holds that *am ha'aretz* do separate *ma'aser ani*, even though they neglect other separations. The reasoning, as Rashi explains, is somewhat counterintuitive. It is not primarily out of sympathy for the poor. Rather: since *ma'aser ani* carries no *issur* obligation after separation — it is purely a monetary obligation to the poor — an *am ha'aretz* can separate it without incurring any new *issur* headaches. By contrast, separating *ma'aser rishon* obligates one to deal with *terumas ma'aser* and its attendant obligations, and separating *ma'aser sheni* requires eating in Jerusalem or redemption. The *am ha'aretz* finds these burdensome. But *ma'aser ani* merely creates a monetary obligation — one he can technically discharge while still consuming the rest. So he does it. *Keivan d'mamona hu, afrushei mafrish* — since it is a monetary matter, he separates it.

The *chachamim*, however, hold that *am ha'aretz* does not bother with *ma'aser ani* either — *keivan d'tarcha leih milsa, lo mafrish* — any burden, however minor, is enough for him to forgo. Accordingly, one who purchases grain from an *am ha'aretz* must at minimum verbally designate a portion as *ma'aser ani* before consuming it. Both sides agree, however, that in a case of definite *tevel* — where one knows with certainty that *ma'aser ani* has not been taken — the grain is *tevel*, and eating it is punishable by *malkos*.

---

## Quantity for Lashes

### Mishnah's Question

The *mishnah* next asks: *kama yochal min ha-tevel* — how much *tevel* must one eat to incur *malkos*? This launches a significant dispute. Rabbi Eliezer holds that even the smallest amount — even a single kernel of grain — is sufficient.

### Ke'Briato Concept

The *mishnah* uses the phrase *kebriato* — in its natural, created state. One grain of wheat is a discrete, whole unit. The question is whether qualitative wholeness of a natural unit can substitute for the quantitative *shi'ur* of a *kezayit* that is normally required to incur *malkos* for eating forbidden food.

This raises a deeper conceptual question. The standard *shi'ur* of *kezayit* might reflect either a threshold of meaningfulness — one must eat enough for it to matter — or it might reflect a question of whether the act constitutes "eating" in the legal sense. Rabbi Eliezer seems to say that a whole unit, by virtue of being qualitatively complete, is legally significant even below a *kezayit*.

### Ant vs. Grain

Rav Bibi cites Resh Lakish: the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages concerns specifically one grain of wheat. If one is eating flour, *divrei hakol kezayit* — everyone agrees that a *kezayit* is required, since flour is simply a quantity of an undifferentiated substance. Rabbi Yirmiyah citing Resh Lakish, however, reads the dispute more broadly: Rabbi Eliezer holds there is no minimum quantity required for *malkos* under any circumstances.

To press his argument, Rabbi Shimon (not Rabbi Eliezer — a clarification the *gemara* makes) challenges the Sages: *ee atem modim li be'ochel nemala she-kol she-hu she-chayav* — surely you agree that one who eats even a single ant incurs *malkos*? The Sages respond: *mipnei she-hu kebriato* — yes, because the ant is in its natural created state, a whole living creature. Rabbi Shimon replies: *af chitah achat kebriato* — one grain of wheat is equally in its natural state. The Sages' distinction: *biryas neshamah chashuvah, chitah lo chashuvah* — a creature that once possessed life is qualitatively significant in a way that an inanimate kernel is not.

### Rabbi Shimon Position

The *gemara* then cites a *braisa* that confirms Rabbi Yirmiyah's reading: *Rabbi Shimon omer kol she-hu le-malkos* — the smallest amount suffices for *malkos*. And then a striking ruling: *lo amar kezayis ela le-inyan korban* — the *kezayit* requirement was stated only with respect to bringing a *korban*.

This is genuinely surprising. One might have assumed the opposite: that for a *korban* — an internal, metaphysical act of atonement before God — perhaps even the smallest amount triggers guilt, while for society to actually impose physical punishment, a more substantial threshold is needed. Rabbi Shimon inverts this. For *malkos* — the public, judicial punishment — there is no minimum. For the *korban* — the individual's obligation to bring an atonement offering — the *kezayit* is required. The reasoning is not developed further here, but the inversion is itself remarkable.

### Tosafot's Logic

*Tosafot* offers an explanation for the underlying distinction that is more logically compelling than simply appealing to whether something once had life. The real difference between the ant and the grain of wheat is not biological but structural: it concerns how the Torah defines the prohibited object.

When the Torah says not to eat a *sheretz* — an insect — it names a discrete, defined entity. If one eats an ant, one has consumed precisely the object the Torah prohibited. The ant eaten is the prohibited thing itself, whole and complete. Similarly, if the Torah prohibits eating a *gid ha-nasheh*, eating the sinew in its entirety means one has consumed the defined prohibited object.

By contrast, *tevel* — like *chazir* — is not a defined discrete object. It is a category of substance, of which there can be more or less. Eating a small piece of *tevel* means one has eaten *some* of a prohibited substance, not the prohibited thing as a whole. In such cases, where the Torah's prohibition attaches to a substance rather than to a discrete object, a quantitative *shi'ur* is necessary. *Tosafot* puts it this way: a useful test for whether something qualifies as a *biryah* — a whole unit — is whether cutting it in half causes it to lose its name. Cut an ant in half: you no longer have an ant. Cut a kernel of wheat in half: you still have *tevel*, only less of it.

---

## Mishnah Cases

### Mishnah List

The *mishnah* enumerates additional cases that incur *malkos*. Among them: *ha'ochel bikurim ad shelo kara aleihem* — one who eats *bikurim* before the declaration has been made. Since *bikurim* may only be consumed by *kohanim*, this refers to a *kohen* who ate from the *bikurim* after they were brought to the Temple and handed over, but before the recitation of *Arami oved avi*. Also listed: *kodshei kodashim chutz le-kla'im* — eating the holiest sacrifices outside the Temple precincts. Even a *kohen* who is ordinarily permitted to eat a *chatat* may not do so outside the *azarah*, and doing so incurs *malkos*.

### Kodshim Kalim

The *mishnah* continues with *kodshim kalim* — the lighter sacrifices, such as *shelamim* — eaten outside Jerusalem, and *ma'aser sheni* eaten outside Jerusalem's walls. Both are permitted for consumption, but only in their proper location. Also mentioned: breaking a bone of a *pesach* offering that was *tahor* and fit to be eaten. The verse *v'chol etzem lo tishberu bo* prohibits this, and the *gemara* reads *bo* — specifically in the *tahor* case, not in the case of a *pesach* that became *tamei*. If the *pesach* was *tamei* and could not be eaten, breaking its bone does not incur *malkos*. Similarly, leaving over from a *korban* — *lo tosiru mimenu ad boker* — does not incur *malkos*, because it is a *lav she-ein bo ma'aseh*: it is a passive violation. Alternatively, it may be because *notar* is subject to the positive commandment to burn it the next morning — making it a *nitak la'aseh* — or because of *hatra'as safeik*. Multiple reasons converge.

### Mother Bird Case

The *mishnah* then presents the case of *shiluach ha-ken* — taking the mother bird together with her young. Rabbi Yehuda rules: *lokei v'eino meshaleach* — one incurs *malkos* and sending the mother bird away afterward does not exempt one. The obligation to send the mother bird away is not a *nitak la'aseh* that retroactively repairs the violation; it is a prior, independent obligation that one should have fulfilled before taking the mother. Once one has transgressed, subsequent sending does not undo the violation.

### Kiyum Asei Bitul Lav

The *chachamim* disagree: *meshaleach v'eino lokeh* — one sends the bird away and does not receive *malkos*. They articulate the general principle: *kol mitzvas lo ta'aseh she-yesh bah kum asei, ein chayavin aleha* — any negative commandment accompanied by a positive commandment to "stand and do" — to affirmatively correct — does not incur *malkos*. This is, of course, the principle of *lav hanitak la'aseh* that dominated the preceding two days of learning.

---

## Rabbi Shimon Derashah

### Akiva vs. Shimon

Rabba bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan states that the *stam mishna* — the anonymous formulation — follows Rabbi Akiva. The *chachamim* elsewhere hold that for *bikurim*, the act of *hanacha* — placing the basket before the altar — is the critical act that permits the *bikurim* to be eaten, while the *kria* — the declaration — does not prevent consumption if omitted. Rabbi Akiva, whose position this *mishnah* reflects, holds that it is specifically the *kria* that matters, not merely the placing down.

The *gemara* then asks: why attribute the *stam mishnah* to Rabbi Akiva — why not say it follows Rabbi Shimon? The answer: this is coming to inform us that Rabbi Akiva himself holds like Rabbi Shimon. Interestingly, Rabbi Shimon was a student of Rabbi Akiva — yet here, the formulation is that Rabbi Akiva's view aligns with Rabbi Shimon's. The *gemara*'s reason for focusing on Rabbi Shimon specifically is that the ensuing *braisa* attributed to Rabbi Shimon not only makes this point about *bikurim* — that the *kria* is what permits the *bikurim* to be eaten — but presents a comprehensive *derashah* establishing that a wide range of *korbanot* and sanctified items, if consumed in circumstances that render them forbidden, incur *malkos*. Since this *derashah* directly illuminates several cases in the *mishnah*, the *gemara* pivots to Rabbi Shimon's formulation.

### Devarim 12 Derashah

The *gemara* presents the *braisa*: Rabbi Shimon offers a sustained *derashah* on a verse in Deuteronomy 12. The verse in question is: *lo suchal le'echol bish'arecha* — you shall not be able to eat within your gates — followed by a list of items: *ma'aser degancha, tiroshcha, v'yitzharecha, u-vechorot bekarcha v'tzonecha, v'chol nedarecha asher tidor, v'nidvosecha, u-serumas yadecha*.

The *peshat* of the verse is that all of these items must be eaten in Jerusalem — they may not be consumed in one's home cities. But Rabbi Shimon's *derashah* proceeds differently: he takes each term in the list and uses it to derive a specific *lav* — a distinct negative prohibition — that generates liability for *malkos* in a particular scenario, not necessarily about location but about the timing or status of consumption.

### Lo Tuchal Phrase

What grounds this reading is the observation that the same list appears earlier in the same chapter in a positive formulation: *ve-achalta lifnei Hashem Elokecha ba-makom asher yivchar, ma'aser degancha, tiroshcha, v'yitzharecha, u-vechorot bekarcha v'tzonecha, v'chol nedarecha asher tidor, v'nidvosecha, u-serumas yadecha* — you shall eat all of these before the Lord your God in the chosen place. The negative formulation in *lo suchal le'echol bish'arecha* therefore could have simply said *lo suchal le'ochlem* — you shall not eat them — with a single pronoun encompassing everything. Instead, it repeats each item individually. The repetition is the key.

### Terumas Yadecha

*U-serumas yadecha* — this refers to *bikurim*, which is often called *terumah*. Rabbi Shimon asks: what is this coming to teach? If it means one may not eat *bikurim* outside Jerusalem, that is derivable from a *kal vachomer* from *ma'aser sheni*: if *ma'aser sheni* — the lighter case — incurs *malkos* when eaten outside Jerusalem, *bikurim* — which unlike *ma'aser sheni* is forbidden to non-*kohanim*, indicating greater sanctity — certainly incurs *malkos* for that. Since one could derive this through *kal vachomer*, the explicit mention of *bikurim* must be teaching something else. What, then, does it teach? *Le-echol bikurim ad shelo kara aleihem she-lokeh* — that eating *bikurim* before the declaration incurs *malkos*.

### Nedavot & Todah

*V'nidvosecha* — voluntary offerings — refers to *todah* and *shelamim*. Again, Rabbi Shimon asks: if this merely prohibits eating them outside Jerusalem, it is derivable from *ma'aser* by *kal vachomer*. So the explicit mention teaches something else: *le-echol be-todah u-shelamim lifnei zerikah she-lokeh* — one who eats from a *todah* or *shelamim* before *zerikat ha-dam* — before the blood has been sprinkled on the altar — incurs *malkos*. This prohibition is not about location but about time: eating before the act that renders the *korban* fit for consumption.

As Rashi notes, these prohibitions were already known as requirements from other sources; what was not previously established was that violating them constitutes a *lav* generating *malkos*. That is precisely what Rabbi Shimon derives here.

### Bechoros Case

*U-vechorot* — *bechoros*, firstborn animals. Once the prohibition of eating *todah* and *shelamim* before *zerikah* is established, Rabbi Shimon argues through *kal vachomer* that the same applies to *bechor*. But the explicit mention of *bechor* is therefore teaching something beyond the *zerikah* issue: *le-echol min ha-bechor afilu le-achar zerikah she-lokeh* — one incurs *malkos* for eating from a *bechor* even after *zerikah*, referring to a non-*kohen*. The fact that a non-*kohen* may not eat a *bechor* was known; but that it constitutes a *lav* producing *malkos* is derived here.

### Bechoros Outside Temple

*U-vchorot bekarcha v'tzonecha* — continuing through the list — along with the more general reference to animals — now encompasses *kodshei kodashim*, the holiest sacrifices such as *chatat* and *asham*. By layering the argument: what was established for *bechor* — a non-*kohen* may not eat it even after *zerikah* — extends by *kal vachomer* to *kodshei kodashim*. But the explicit mention of *chatat* and *asham* teaches something additional still: eating them *chutz la-kla'im* — outside the Temple precincts — incurs *malkos*.

### Olah Prohibition

Finally, the term for animals in the verse encompasses the *olah* — the burnt offering. Once all prior categories have been addressed, the *olah* is mentioned to teach that no one — not even a *kohen*, not even after *zerikah*, not even inside the Temple — may eat an *olah* at all. *Le-echol min ha-olah le-achar zerikah afilu bi-fnim she-hu lokeh* — eating from an *olah* in any circumstance incurs *malkos*.

---

## Critique of Arguments

### Rava's Praise

Rava responds to Rabbi Shimon's *derashah* with striking admiration: *de-yaldei imei ke-Rabbi Shimon teyalad* — whoever's mother gives birth to him should give birth to him like Rabbi Shimon. That is: one should be blessed to produce a mind like Rabbi Shimon's. The ingenuity lay in the layering — establishing each prohibition on the foundation of the prior one, working backwards through the list so that each successive item could be shown to be heavier than its predecessor, and therefore the explicit mention must be teaching something new.

### Kal Vachomer Challenge

But Rava immediately adds: *v'af al gav d'is lei pircha* — even though every single *kal vachomer* argument can be challenged. The praise is for the intellectual architecture, not for the logical inviolability of each step.

### Weight Examples

The challenges proceed systematically. Can one say *bikurim* is categorically weightier than *ma'aser sheni*, thereby making the *kal vachomer* from *ma'aser* to *bikurim* valid? *Shekein assurim le-zarim* — *bikurim* is forbidden to non-*kohanim*, while *ma'aser sheni* is not: this supports the *kal vachomer*. But *adaraba* — in the other direction — *ma'aser chamur shekein assur le-onein*: one who is in the immediate mourning state of *aninut* may not eat *ma'aser sheni* — *lo achalti be-oni mimenu* — whereas *bikurim* may actually be consumed by an *onein*. So *ma'aser* is weightier in that respect, and the *kal vachomer* is not absolute.

Similarly, the *kal vachomer* from *todah u'shelamim* to *bechor* can be challenged: *todah u'shelamim* require *semichah*, *nesachim*, *tenufah*, and the giving of *chazeh va-shok* to the *kohen* — a far more elaborate ritual structure — making them weightier in those respects than *bechor*, which is sanctified automatically from birth but involves a simpler procedure. And so on down the list: in each case, the supposedly "lighter" item can be shown to be weightier in some dimension, undermining the *kal vachomer*.

### Kal Vachomer Fails

The conclusion is that none of Rabbi Shimon's *kal vachomer* arguments is logically airtight. Yet Rava's admiration stands: the ingenuity of the structure — working backwards through the list, layering each prohibition to allow the next to be derived — remains impressive even if the individual *kal vachomer* steps cannot withstand scrutiny.

---

## Ain Mazirin Principle

### Ain Mazirin Problem

But there is a more fundamental difficulty, beyond the question of whether each *kal vachomer* holds: *ve-chi mazhirin min ha-din?* — can one derive a prohibition itself from a *kal vachomer*? Even setting aside the debate about *ein onshin min ha-din* — whether a punishment can be imposed based on a *kal vachomer* — the principle that *ein mazhirin min ha-din* is universally accepted: one cannot establish the very *isur* of something through a *kal vachomer* alone. There must be an explicit verse. Rabbi Shimon's entire structure depends on deriving that these things are prohibited through *kal vachomer* from *ma'aser*. That cannot be the source of the prohibition.

### Yatira Solution

The *gemara*'s answer — and this is the punchline — is *kra yesera hu*: the verse is extra. This is Rabbi Shimon's actual mechanism, and it resolves everything. The prohibition of *lo suchal le'echol bish'arecha* could have simply said *lo tuchal le'ochlem* — you may not eat *them* — with a single pronoun encompassing all items previously listed. Instead, it repeats every single item individually.

### Scriptural Support

The redundancy is demonstrable: the immediately preceding verse in Deuteronomy lists these exact items in the positive: *ve-achalta lifnei Hashem Elokecha ba-makom asher yivchar* — you shall eat before the Lord in the chosen place — and then enumerates: *ma'aser degancha, tiroshcha, v'yitzharecha, u-vechorot bekarcha v'tzonecha, v'chol nedarecha asher tidor, v'nidvosecha, u-serumas yadecha*. The negative verse then repeats the identical list. One word — *them* — would have sufficed. The Torah chose instead to enumerate each item.

### Word Repetition

Why does the Torah repeat each word individually? Rabbi Shimon's answer: to establish a distinct *lav* for each category. Each term in the negative formulation creates its own independent prohibition — not merely restating the location restriction that could have been inferred, but generating a new *lav* that applies to that category and to everything weightier than it.

### Separate Lavim

This is the resolution to *ein mazhirin min ha-din*. Rabbi Shimon is not deriving prohibitions through *kal vachomer* alone. He is deriving them from the *yatira* — the extra words in the verse. Each word, being superfluous as a mere repetition of the location prohibition, must therefore be teaching an independent *lav* applicable to that item and to the heavier categories above it. The *kal vachomer* serves only as the explanatory framework — demonstrating why the earlier prohibition does not need to be explicitly stated for the heavier items, and therefore why the explicit mention of each heavier item must be teaching something new. But the *lav* itself comes from the verse.

Rava accordingly rules: *zar she-achal min ha-olah lifnei zerikah chutz la-choma le-Rabbi Shimon lokei chamesh* — a non-*kohen* who eats from an *olah* before *zerikah* outside the walls incurs five sets of *malkos*, because he has violated the prohibition of eating an *olah* at all, the prohibition against eating outside the Temple precincts, the prohibition as a non-*kohen*, the prohibition of eating before *zerikah*, and the prohibition of eating outside Jerusalem. Each of the prohibitions layered through Rabbi Shimon's *derashah* applies, and each generates its own set of *malkos*. This is the whole point of the *derashah*: not merely to establish that these things are *assur* — that was already known — but to establish that each of them constitutes an independent *lav* for which one incurs *malkos*.

---

---

# Makkot 18

## Shimon's Five Lashes

### Shimon's Derivation

The daf opens at the top of 18a with a recap of Rabbi Shimon's derivation of multiple distinct prohibitions from the verse *lo tuchal leechol bish'arecha* — "you shall not be able to eat within your gates." Rabbi Shimon holds that the Torah could have stated a single general prohibition covering all these cases, yet it spells out each category individually: *maaser*, *shelamim*, *bechor*, *kodshei kodashim*, *olah*, and *bikkurim*. Each repetition signals an independent *lav* — a negative prohibition carrying *malkos* — for eating a sacred item either in the wrong place or before the proper preparatory act has been performed.

The specific cases are as follows. *Bikkurim* eaten before the declaration (*kriya*) was made. *Shelamim* eaten before *zrikas hadam*, the sprinkling of the blood. *Bechor* eaten by a non-*kohen* (*zar*) even after the blood was properly sprinkled. *Kodshei kodashim* consumed outside the *beis hamikdash*, even by a *kohen* and even after *zrikas hadam*. And *olah*, which of course cannot be eaten by anyone under any circumstances. Each of these is a distinct prohibition derived from the elaboration of this verse.

### Why Repeat?

The Gemara presses: if a single phrase like *lo sochlun* — "you shall not eat them" — would have conveyed the prohibition for all, why does the Torah enumerate each category explicitly? The answer the Gemara arrives at is that each individual word is there *leyachadei lehu lavei lechol chad v'chad* — to designate a separate *lav* with its own prohibition and its own potential for *malkos* in each distinct case.

### Kal V'Chomer Problem

Yet this resolution does not fully resolve the underlying difficulty. Even if we accept that each category carries an independent *lav*, there remains the principle of *ein mazhirin min hadin* — one cannot establish a prohibition through logical inference alone. The logical inference at work here is the *kal v'chomer*: if something is prohibited in a lighter case, it is certainly prohibited in the more stringent case. For example, if *shelamim* cannot be eaten before *zrikas hadam*, then certainly *bechor* cannot. If a *zar* cannot eat *bechor*, then certainly a *zar* cannot eat *kodshei kodashim*. If *kodshei kodashim* cannot be eaten outside the *beis hamikdash*, then certainly *olah* cannot be eaten outside the *beis hamikdash*. The *kal v'chomer* runs from the weaker case to the stronger — and the rule of *ein mazhirin min hadin* says this inferential extension cannot, under normal circumstances, generate lashes.

The Gemara and Rishonim struggle with this. Rashi and Tosafos each in their own way attempt to retreat from the straightforward reading, suggesting perhaps that the weaker cases do not actually generate *malkos* in the extended applications. But the plain sense of the Gemara appears to embrace precisely that conclusion — that here, somehow, the extension via *kal v'chomer* does carry full legal weight, generating lashes even in the stronger cases inferred from the weaker. Tosafos in a lengthy discussion ultimately acknowledges the difficulty without arriving at a fully satisfying resolution: the Gemara seems committed to the position that if lashes apply in the lighter case, they apply in the heavier case by force of the *kal v'chomer*, even though this appears to violate *ein mazhirin min hadin*.

### Rava's Five Lashes

The Gemara then cites Rava with a striking concrete illustration: *zar she'achal min ha'olah lifnei zrika chutz lachoma* — a non-*kohen* who ate from an *olah* before *zrikas hadam*, outside the walls of Yerushalayim (and outside the *beis hamikdash*) — according to Rabbi Shimon receives five sets of *malkos* from a single act of eating. The count: one, for eating an *olah* which can never be eaten by anyone; two, for eating *kodshei kodashim* outside the *beis hamikdash* — the *kal v'chomer* from *kodshei kodashim* reaches *olah*; three, for eating as a *zar*, a non-*kohen* — the *kal v'chomer* from *bechor* reaches *olah*; four, for eating before *zrikas hadam* — the *kal v'chomer* from *shelamim* reaches *olah*; and five, for eating outside Yerushalayim altogether, in addition to being outside the *beis hamikdash*. Five distinct violations, five distinct sets of *malkos*, from a single act. This is what makes clear that each prohibition is real, that each applies through the *kal v'chomer* to more severe cases, and that we are genuinely speaking of *malkos* and not merely of a theoretical prohibition.

---

## Additional Lashes?

### Kodshei Kodashim

Having established the five, the Gemara asks: why not a sixth? There is an additional verse — *ve-zar lo yochel ki kodesh heim* — "a non-*kohen* shall not eat, for they are holy," which prohibits a *zar* from eating *kodshei kodashim*. Should that not add another set of *malkos*?

The Gemara answers: *hani mili heicha delekohanei chazi* — that verse applies only where the item is fit for *kohanim* to eat. The verse begins *ve'achlu otam asher kuppar bahem* — "they shall eat from those with which atonement was made" — making explicit that this prohibition against *zar* consumption is predicated on the food being something that *kohanim* are in principle permitted to eat. Here, an *olah* cannot be eaten even by *kohanim*, so this particular prohibition does not apply. Interestingly, one could raise the same question about the *bechor*-derived *zar* prohibition earlier in the chain — for that prohibition too, one might have thought it only applies when the item is fit for *kohanim*. But the verse is more explicit in its formulation here, and the Gemara treats this exclusion as operative.

### Boundary Violation

The Gemara raises another candidate: the verse *u-vasar basadeh tereifah lo socheilu, lakelev tashlichun oto* — "flesh in the field that is torn you shall not eat, you shall cast it to the dogs." The *derasha* is: *basadeh* — "in the field" — suggests that meat which has left its proper boundary becomes prohibited. This prohibition, *chutz limechitzoso*, has wide application: to *korban* meat taken outside Yerushalayim, to *kodshei kodashim* taken outside the *beis hamikdash*, and even to a fetal limb that protruded from its mother's womb and was retracted before *shechita*. Surely this should add another prohibition to our case?

Here Tosafos offers a classic distinction — the *gavra-cheftza* analysis, the difference between the person and the object. The prohibition derived from *chutz limechitzoso* focuses on the *status of the meat itself*: once the meat left its boundary, the meat is forbidden, regardless of who is eating it or where the person is standing. By contrast, the prohibitions already counted focus on the *person's act*: is this person eating in the wrong place? These are conceptually distinct prohibitions, and in principle a scenario could exist where one applies without the other — for instance, if one leans over the boundary and consumes meat that itself remains inside. So why does this verse not add a sixth *lav*?

The Gemara answers: *hani mili heicha de-vifnim chazi* — this prohibition only applies to meat that could have been eaten had it remained within its boundaries. Here, the *olah* cannot be eaten even within the *beis hamikdash*, so the prohibition of leaving its boundary does not attach. However, this means that in a case involving a *shelamim* improperly removed, this verse could theoretically generate a second set of *malkos* — subject to the question, raised by Rashi and Tosafos, of whether the verse is too broad to function as a *lav she-biklalos*, an overly generic prohibition.

### Pasul Meat

The Gemara tries again: another verse — *lo ye'achel ki kodesh hu* — "it shall not be eaten, for it is holy" — is expounded by Rabbi Eliezer as follows: the phrase *ki kodesh hu* teaches that any sanctified meat which has been invalidated (*pasul*) carries a prohibition against eating. The derivation is from *nosar* — meat left over past its allotted time, which is holy meat that became *pasul* — but the principle is generalized: *kol she-be-kodesh passul, ba hakasuv ve-itein lo sa'aseh al achilaso*, any sanctified item that became invalid has a Torah prohibition against its consumption. Should not *olah* meat eaten outside its boundary fall under this category as well?

The Gemara's answer follows the same logic as before: *hani mili heicha di-kodem pesulo chazi* — this prohibition applies only to meat that was initially valid and became invalidated. It applies when something was once fit for consumption and then became *pasul*. Since an *olah* was never fit for consumption in the first place, this prohibition of eating *pasul* sanctified meat does not apply. The same logic would apply to *piggul* — an offering rendered invalid through improper sacrificial intent — which carries its own explicit Torah prohibition though the verse states the *onesh* without an explicit *lav*, raising a question about where the *lav* itself is learned; in principle, the same framework would apply.

### Eliezer's Olah

The Gemara raises yet another possible source for an additional prohibition: a *braita* in which Rabbi Eliezer states that the verse *kalil tihye be-lo ye'achel* — "it shall be wholly burnt, it shall not be eaten" — establishes a *lo sa'aseh* against eating an *olah*.
