This is a far more explicit and direct prohibition against eating an *olah* than the generic verse of *lo tuchal leechol bish'arecha*, from which Rabbi Shimon learned it. Should not this provide an additional *lav*, yielding a sixth count of *malkos*?

The Gemara concedes the point: *ai hachi nami* — indeed, Rava's count does include this verse. When Rava said one of the five lashes comes from eating an *olah*, that prohibition is in fact grounded in this explicit verse of Rabbi Eliezer — *kalil tihye be-lo ye'achel* — rather than in the general verse of *lo tuchal leechol bish'arecha*. The Gemara, notably, does not address the inverse question of why Rabbi Shimon would then need to learn the prohibition of eating an *olah* from his verse at all, given this more explicit formulation. The Gemara simply establishes that the most explicit source governs which *lav* produces *malkos* in that particular case, and the number remains five rather than growing larger.

### Kohen & Chattat

The Gemara now introduces a new statement: *Rav Giddal said in the name of Rav* — a *kohen* who ate from a *chattat* or *asham* before *zrikas hadam* receives *malkos*. This parallels the earlier discussion about *shelamim* eaten before *zrikas hadam*, but now applied to *kodshei kodashim* like *chattat* and *asham*. The question is: what is the source?

### Lav from Asei

Rav's statement is grounded in the verse *ve'achlu otam asher kuppar bahem* — "they shall eat from those through which atonement has been effected." The derivation is: *le'achar kappara in, lifnei kappara lo* — after the blood has been thrown, yes; before, no. The verse, framed positively, implicitly prohibits eating before atonement is completed. And Rav apparently held that *lav haba miklal asei lav* — a prohibition derived implicitly from a positive commandment carries the full legal weight of a *lav*, yielding *malkos*.

### Rava Objects

Rava challenges this immediately. The principle that an implicit negative derived from a positive commandment has the force of a *lav* is not accepted. The Gemara cites the verse about kosher animals — *ve-zos ha-beheima asher tochelu* — which implicitly prohibits eating non-kosher animals. If *lav haba miklal asei* had the weight of a *lav*, the explicit verse *et zeh lo tochelu* — "this you shall not eat" — would be superfluous. The Gemara presses the point: we never apply *lav haba miklal asei* to generate *malkos*. The Torah must state the prohibition explicitly as a negative for it to function as a *lav* with *malkos*. Violating an implied prohibition transgresses a positive commandment, not a negative one. Rava therefore rejects the original formulation of Rav's ruling.

### Zar Exempt

Accordingly, the Gemara revises the position and introduces the corrected version: *ela i itmar hachi itmar* — here is how it was actually stated. Rav Giddal said in the name of Rav: *zar she'achal michattat ve'asham lifnei zerika patur* — a *zar* who ate from a *chattat* or *asham* before *zrikas hadam* is exempt from the particular violation of *zarus*.

### Zarus Relevance

The reasoning is derived from the same verse: *ve'achlu otam asher kuppar bahem* — the *kohanim* shall eat from those through which atonement has been effected. The verse establishes when *kohanim* are permitted to eat. And the principle is: *kol heicha dekaryanan beih ve'achlu otam asher kuppar bahem, karinan bei v'zar lo yocheil* — only when the item is in the state where *kohanim* may eat from it does the prohibition of *zarus* — the violation of a non-*kohen* eating what belongs to *kohanim* — become operative. Before *zrikas hadam*, when no one may eat from the *korban*, the item is not yet in a state that is "relevant for *kohanim*," and therefore the distinct category of *zarus* does not apply. A *zar* eating before *zarikas hadam* may transgress the prohibition of eating before the blood was thrown — which applies to everyone — but does not add the distinct violation of *zarus* on top of it.

This principle stands in apparent tension with Rava's earlier case of five *malkos*, where eating as a *zar* was counted as one of the five even though the item was an *olah* eaten before *zrikas hadam*. That tension runs through the *sugya*: Rava evidently holds that all these prohibitions layer together regardless of whether the *korban* is fit for *kohanim*, while this ruling insists that *zarus* only applies when the item is in a state fit for *kohen* consumption. The two positions represent a genuine disagreement about when the concept of *zarus* is activated.

---

## Bikkurim Dispute

### Hanacha Makev

The Gemara now pivots to a fresh topic introduced at the outset: what makes *bikkurim* permissible for the *kohen* to eat — the *kriya* (the declaration recited by the owner) or the *hanacha* (the placing down of the basket before the altar)?

Rabbi Elazar said in the name of Rabbi Oshaya: *bikkurim hanacha me'akves bahem kriya ein me'akves bahem* — it is the placing down that is the critical act, not the declaration. This position stands in contrast to our *mishna*, which implies that the *kriya* is what matters, as it lists eating *bikkurim* before the declaration among acts that carry *malkos*. The verse in *parashas bikkurim* says *ve-hinachto lifnei Hashem Elokecha* — you shall place it before the Lord your God — and it is this act of placing, according to this view, that transitions the *bikkurim* into a state permissible for *kohen* consumption.

### Rot Proof

But the same Rabbi Elazar citing Rabbi Oshaya taught elsewhere: *hifrish bikkurim kodem le-chag ve-avar alav hachag, yirkavu* — if one separated *bikkurim* before *Sukkos* and the festival passed without bringing them, they must be left to rot. The rationale the Gemara proposes: since these *bikkurim* were separated at a time when the *kriya* was obligatory and now the *kriya* can no longer be performed (the declaration is only said during the period of joy associated with the harvest, from *Shavuos* through *Sukkos*; after *Sukkos* one may still bring *bikkurim* until *Chanukah*, but may no longer make the declaration), they can never achieve their proper status and must be left to rot.

But this creates a contradiction. If the *kriya* is not *me'akev* — if the placing down alone suffices — why must they rot? Why not simply bring them and perform the *hanacha*? *Mai lav mishum d'lo matzi le-mikrei alaihu* — is it not because they can no longer perform the *kriya* over them, proving that *kriya* is indeed essential?

### Zeira's Principle

The resolution invokes the famous principle of Rabbi Zeira: *kol haraui lebila ein bila me'akeves bo* — anything fit for mixing is not prevented by the absence of actual mixing; *ve-kol she'ein raui lebila bila me'akeves bo* — but where mixing is not even possible, the absence of mixing does disqualify it. The context of this rule is the *minchah* offering: the flour and oil ideally should be mixed (*belila*), yet if they were not mixed, the *minchah* is still valid — provided the mixture was physically possible. A *minchah* of more than sixty units of flour (*esronos*) cannot be effectively mixed by human hands, and in that case, the lack of mixing renders it invalid.

The logical structure is subtle: it is not that the act of mixing is required for validity; rather, the *capacity* for mixing is required. If the *minchah* is the kind of thing that could theoretically be mixed, then even without actual mixing it is valid. But if it is constitutionally incapable of being mixed, the absence of mixing disqualifies it — because the disqualification flows from an inherent deficiency in the object itself.

Applied to *bikkurim*: one who holds that *kriya* is not *me'akev* does not mean that *kriya* is irrelevant. The position is more nuanced: *kriya* need not actually be performed, but the *bikkurim* must have the *capacity* for *kriya* to be performed over them. *Bikkurim* separated before *Sukkos* were obligated in *kriya*; after *Sukkos* passes, they are no longer capable of *kriya*; and therefore — even though actual *kriya* is not required — the absence of the capacity for *kriya* disqualifies them. That is why they must rot. The view that *hanacha* is *me'akev* and *kriya* is not a halfway concession: *kriya* must be possible, even if it need not be performed.

### Yochanan Contradiction

Rav Acha bar Yaakov reported that Rav Ashi teaches this principle — that *hanacha* is *me'akev* and *kriya* is not — in the name of Rabbi Assi citing Rabbi Yochanan. But this generates a contradiction within Rabbi Yochanan's own teachings: *remi d'Rabbi Yochanan a'Rabbi Yochanan*.

For Rabbi Assi himself had once asked Rabbi Yochanan: from what point do *bikkurim* take on the sanctity that makes a *zar* who eats them liable? Rabbi Yochanan replied: for *bikkurim* that are *re'uyim le-keria* — fit for the *kriya*, meaning separated before *Sukkos* — the operative moment is when someone performs the *kriya* over them. For *bikkurim* that are not fit for *kriya*, meaning separated or brought after *Sukkos*, the operative moment is *mi-she-yiru pnei ha-bayit* — once they have been brought before the *beis hamikdash*, seen the face of the Temple.

The contradiction is double: *kashya keria a-keria, kashya hanacha a-hanacha*. On the one hand, one tradition has Rabbi Yochanan saying *kriya* is not *me'akev*, while the other has him saying *kriya* is indeed the operative moment. On the other hand, one tradition says *hanacha* is *me'akev*, while the other says that when *kriya* is not applicable the key is *re'iyat pnei ha-bayit*, not *hanacha*.

### Shimon vs. Rabbanan

The Gemara resolves the first contradiction — *keria a-keria lo kashya, ha Rabbi Shimon ha Rabbanan* — by noting that Rabbi Yochanan was articulating different positions. In one statement he reports Rabbi Shimon's view, according to which *kriya* is indeed what matters — *terumat yadecha* is the phrase from which Rabbi Shimon derived that *bikkurim* before *kriya* carry *malkos*, consistent with our *mishna*. In the other statement Rabbi Yochanan speaks for the Rabbanan, who hold that it is the *hanacha* that is *me'akev*. The apparent contradiction is resolved: in one case Rabbi Yochanan presents Rabbi Shimon's position, in the other his own (or the Rabbanan's) position.

The second contradiction — *hanacha a-hanacha* — remains. In one tradition Rabbi Yochanan says *hanacha* is *me'akev*; in the other, he says that when *kriya* is not applicable the key is *re'iyat pnei ha-bayit*, not *hanacha*. The Gemara resolves this as well: *ha Rabbi Yehuda ve-ha Rabbanan* — one tradition reflects the opinion of Rabbi Yehuda, the other reflects the Rabbanan.

### Hinachto Debate

The *braita* explains Rabbi Yehuda's position. The verse says *ve-hinachto lifnei Hashem Elokecha* — "you shall place it down before the Lord your God." Rabbi Yehuda reads this as referring to the act of *tenufa*, waving, rather than literal placing down. His argument: there is a separate verse, *ve-hinicho lifnei mizbei'ach*, which already teaches literal placing down. Since the word *ve-hinachto* cannot mean the same thing as *ve-hinicho*, Rabbi Yehuda derives that *ve-hinachto* refers to *tenufa*. The implication, as Rashi explains, is that since the *Torah* only mentions the act of placing down once explicitly, it is *not* designating that act as the critical *me'akev* moment — and therefore according to Rabbi Yehuda, *hanacha* is not the determinative act. What is the determinative act? *Re'iyat pnei ha-bayis* — entry into the *beis hamikdash*.

The Rabbanan, by contrast, read both *ve-hinicho* and *ve-hinachto* as referring to placing down — two mentions of the same act, emphasizing its significance as the *me'akev* moment. Where then does the Rabbanan learn *tenufa*? This brings in Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, who represents the opposing view on the source of *tenufa*: the verse says *ve-lakach ha-kohen ha-tene mi-yadecha* — "the *kohen* shall take the basket from your hand." This teaches that the *kohen* is the active party in waving. The Gemara then develops this through a *gezeira shava* of *yad-yad* connecting *bikkurim* and *shelamim*: by *bikkurim* the verse says the *kohen* takes it from your hand, emphasizing the *kohen's* active role; by *shelamim* the verse says *yadav tavi'ena* — his hands shall bring it — emphasizing the owner's active role. The two are combined: *meni'ach kohen yadav tachat yad be'alim u-menif* — the *kohen* places his hands beneath the owner's hands and they wave together, since ultimately it is the owner's *korban* and he remains the primary actor.

### Zar Chiyuv

A further dimension is introduced by Rav Adda citing Rabbi Yitzchak: *bikkurim eimasai mechayvin aleihem?* — from what point do *bikkurim* render a *zar* liable? This question parallels the earlier discussion regarding *korbanot*: the prohibition of *zarus* — a non-*kohen* eating from something designated for *kohanim* — only becomes operative when the item is in a state fit for *kohen* consumption. Until then, a non-*kohen* who eats may transgress a general prohibition of eating *bikkurim* before their time, but does not incur the distinct *zarus* liability, which is characterized by *chiyuv misa bidei shamayim*. Once the operative moment is passed — whether that moment is *kriya*, *hanacha*, or *re'iyat pnei ha-bayis* depending on one's position — the *bikkurim* are now in a state fit for *kohanim*, and a *zar* who eats from them compounds the transgression with *zarus*. The answer given here for those who follow the position of *re'iyat pnei ha-bayis*: liability commences from the moment the *bikkurim* enter the *beis hamikdash*.

### Re'iya Pnei Bayis

Rabbi Eliezer's position is cited in support of this framework: *bikkurim miktzasam bachutz u'miktzasam bifnim* — if part of the basket is outside the *beis hamikdash* and part is inside, those portions that are outside retain the status of *chulin* for all purposes, while those inside have the status of *hekdesh* in all respects. The critical dividing line is the threshold of the *beis hamikdash*: what has entered is sanctified and now generates the full *zarus* prohibition; what remains outside has not yet reached that status. This illustrates with precision that according to this view, *re'iyat pnei ha-bayis* — the act of being brought before the *beis hamikdash* — is indeed what transforms the status of the *bikkurim* and activates the *kohen*'s right to eat them.

### Sheshes's View

The *sugya* closes with Rav Sheshes restating the position clearly: *bikkurim hanacha me'akeves bahem kriya einah me'akeves bahem* — it is the placing down that is the critical act, and the declaration is not *me'akev*. This is presented as a view that runs against our *mishna*, and which the Gemara notes is supported by a *tanna* whose identity and source will be the subject of the following day's learning.

---

---

# Makkot 19

## Bikurim Permissibil (III)ity

### Bikurim Timing Question

The daf opens in the middle of an ongoing discussion regarding when *bikurim* become permissible for a *kohen* to eat. This question has a natural flip side: before the decisive moment — whether that moment is the *hanachah* (placement before the altar) or the *kriyah* (the declaration) — the *bikurim* are forbidden to everyone, much like a *korban* before the blood is sprinkled. After that moment, a *kohen* may eat them, while a non-*kohen* who eats them violates *zarus*, the prohibition against a non-*kohen* eating priestly portions.

### Rav Yehudah Opinion

Rav Yehudah opens with the following formulation: *Bikurim — eimasai mechayevin aleihem?* When is a non-*kohen* liable for eating them as a *zar*, in a manner that would render him *chayav misah bidei shamayim*? *Misheyiru pnei habayis* — from the moment they have been brought within the *Beis Hamikdash*. This is neither the *hanachah* nor the *kriyah*, but rather the physical entry into the Temple. This position reads the word *hanachah* in the relevant verse as referring to waving rather than to placement, and therefore emphasizes the act of bringing the *bikurim* inside the *Beis Hamikdash* as the determinative moment.

### Rabbi Eliezer Position

The Gemara asks: *keman* — whose view does Rav Yehudah follow? It answers that this corresponds to the position of Rabbi Eliezer in a *baraisa*: if one has a basket of *bikurim* and half of it is inside the boundary of the *azarah* while half is outside, the portion outside remains like *chulin* in all respects — meaning it has not yet acquired the status of *hekdesh* and does not implicate *zarus* — while the portion inside the *azarah* is fully sanctified in all respects. Once the *bikurim* cross the line into the *azarah*, they acquire full *kedushah* and can only be eaten by a *kohen*, with a non-*kohen* incurring the violation of *zarus*.

### Rav Sheshes Opinion

Rav Sheshes takes a different position: *bikurim — hanachah me'akeves bahen; keriyah ein me'akeves bahen.* It is the placing down before the altar that is essential, not the declaration. This stands against the plain reading of the *mishnah*, which seems to indicate that it is the *kriyah* that matters. The Gemara asks whose view this follows, and answers that it corresponds to the position recorded in a *baraisa* cited by Rabbi Yose, who transmitted three rulings in the name of three elders. The first of these — cited in the name of Rabbi Ishmael — forms the transition into a new and closely related topic.

---

## Ma'aser Sheni Statu (III)

### Rabbi Ishmael Query

Rabbi Yose transmits the following question in the name of Rabbi Ishmael: *Yachol ya'aleh adam ma'aser sheni bazman hazeh biYerushalayim v'yochlenu* — might a person bring *ma'aser sheni* in the present day to Jerusalem and eat it there? This is a genuine and interesting question. *Ma'aser sheni* must be eaten in Jerusalem. So too must *kodshim kalim*, *bechor*, and *bikurim*. But there is an important distinction between *ma'aser sheni* and the others with respect to the *Beis Hamikdash*.

### Korbanot vs Non-Korbanot

*Bechor* and *kodshim kalim* require concrete rituals performed at the *Beis Hamikdash*: the blood of *korbanos* must be dashed on the altar, and *bikurim* must be waved and placed *lifnei mizbach Hashem Elokecha* — before the altar of God. By contrast, *ma'aser sheni* requires only that one eat it *lifnei Hashem Elokecha* — in the presence of God, meaning in Jerusalem. There is no ritual act tied to the altar itself. This gives rise to a reasonable suggestion: even without a *Beis Hamikdash*, perhaps one should be able — or even be obligated — to bring *ma'aser sheni* to Jerusalem and eat it there. In practice today, *ma'aser sheni* is redeemed and its monetary value is set aside, but the question is whether the eating in Jerusalem should still apply.

### Logical Distinction

The *baraisa* sets up a logical argument for why *ma'aser sheni* should indeed require the *Beis Hamikdash*: just as *bechor* requires being brought to Jerusalem and cannot be eaten nowadays, the same should apply to *ma'aser sheni* which also requires being brought to Jerusalem. But this argument is immediately challenged: *mah l'bechor shekein te'un dam ve'eimurim legabei mizbe'ach* — the reason *bechor* cannot be eaten nowadays is that it requires the blood to be dashed on the altar and the fats to be burned. *Ma'aser sheni* has no such requirement. One might therefore argue that *ma'aser sheni* can indeed be eaten in Jerusalem today.

---

## Bikurim Permissibil (III)ity…

### Bikurim as Proof

The *baraisa* responds by invoking *bikurim* as a counter-proof. *Bikurim* are not a sacrifice and do not require blood dashed on the altar, yet it is taken as given that *bikurim* cannot be brought to Jerusalem and eaten there nowadays. This demonstrates that the inability to eat in Jerusalem is not solely a function of the altar-based sacrifice requirement. Something about *bikurim* also prevents it. What is that something? *Mah l'bikurim shekein te'unim hanachah* — *bikurim* must be placed before the altar. So while *bikurim* are not a *korban*, they still have a concrete link to the altar through the act of *hanachah*. This is precisely the reason the *baraisa* mentions *hanachah* as the distinguishing feature of *bikurim* rather than *kriyah* — and that is the side-point relevant to our earlier discussion. The *baraisa* uses *hanachah* as the key feature of *bikurim*, which suggests that *hanachah* is what makes *bikurim* permissible, not the *kriyah*.

---

## Ma'aser Sheni Statu (III)

### Textual Link Analysis

Since both *bechor* and *bikurim* have altar-based requirements that *ma'aser sheni* lacks, one might ask: why not derive the requirement for *ma'aser sheni* from the common denominator of *bechor* and *bikurim* — that both require Jerusalem and the *Beis Hamikdash* — and apply that to *ma'aser sheni*? The Gemara responds: *mishum de'ika l'mifrach* — there is a valid rebuttal, namely that the common feature of *bechor* and *bikurim* is *shekein yeish bahen tzad mizbe'ach* — both are concretely connected to the altar in some way. From that shared feature one cannot derive a ruling for *ma'aser sheni*, which has no altar connection whatsoever.

The *baraisa* therefore turns to a textual source. The verse states: *ve'achalta sham lifnei Hashem Elokecha ma'aser degancha tiroshcha ve'yitzharecha uvechoros bekarcha ve'tzonecha* — "And you shall eat there before the Lord your God your tithe of grain, wine, and oil, and the firstlings of your herd and flock." This verse juxtaposes *ma'aser* and *bechor* in a single context of eating before God in Jerusalem. The *baraisa* derives: *makish ma'aser l'bechor* — just as *bechor* can only be eaten when there is a *Beis Hamikdash*, so too *ma'aser*. The linkage in this verse is in fact close to the *peshat* of the *pesukim*: both items are treated as belonging to the same category, eaten together before God in Jerusalem. The same Jerusalem that is required for *bechor* — one with a standing *Beis Hamikdash* — is the same Jerusalem required for *ma'aser*: *af ma'aser eino ela lifnei habayis*.

---

## Bikurim Permissibil (III)ity…

### Rav Ashi Challenge

Having established, as a side-point, that the *baraisa* emphasizes *hanachah* rather than *kriyah* as the distinctive feature of *bikurim* connecting them to the altar, the Gemara returns to the original debate and subjects this inference to scrutiny. Rav Ashi challenges the proof: *nehi de'ikuva leika* — granted that according to Rav Sheshes, *kriyah* is not absolutely required to render the *bikurim* permissible, nevertheless, *mitzva mi leika?* Is there no *mitzva* to recite the declaration? Surely everyone agrees there is a *mitzva* of *kriyah* by *bikurim*. If that is the case, when the *baraisa* lists what is distinctive about *bikurim* and what connects them to the altar, it should have mentioned *kriyah* as well — even if it is not strictly *me'akev*, it is still a feature that connects *bikurim* to the altar. The failure to mention *kriyah* therefore cannot be taken as proof that *kriyah* is not essential.

Rav Ashi then supplies his own explanation for why the *baraisa* omitted *kriyah*: *kivan de'ika bikurei hager* — since a *ger* who brings *bikurim* cannot recite the declaration, because he cannot say *asher nishba Hashem la'avoteinu latet lanu* — "which God swore to our forefathers to give us." This prompts a brief but important digression. There is in fact a *tannaitic* dispute about this very point: one *tanna* holds that upon converting, the *ger* adopts not only the religion but the history of the Jewish people, and therefore can recite *la'avoteinu latet lanu*. The *Rambam*, in his celebrated letter to Ovadya HaGer, rules decisively that a *ger* does say *Elokeinu ve'Elokei avoteinu* and that Avraham Avinu is the *ger*'s father as well, making the *ger* fully part of the people and its history.

In any event, the operative point is that since there exist cases where *kriyah* is not performed by a *ger* — or similarly, when *bikurim* are brought after *Sukkot* — the *baraisa* could not cite *kriyah* as a universal feature of *bikurim*. It therefore cited only *hanachah*, which always applies. The logical conclusion is: *lo psika lei* — it was not a categorical rule applicable in all cases. The absence of *kriyah* from the *baraisa*'s list therefore says nothing about whether *kriyah* is or is not *me'akev*. The only thing that can be inferred is that *hanachah* is the universally applicable feature. The debate between *hanachah* and *kriyah* as the decisive moment remains formally unresolved.

---

## Ma'aser Sheni Statu (III)s…

### Gezeirah Shavah

Returning to the central question of *ma'aser sheni*, the Gemara now asks why the common denominator argument — deriving the *Beis Hamikdash* requirement for *ma'aser sheni* from both *bechor* and *bikurim* together — fails. The answer, as noted, is that the shared characteristic of *bechor* and *bikurim* is their connection to the altar. The *baraisa* therefore relies instead on the textual juxtaposition in the verse linking *ma'aser* and *bechor* — a *hekesh* — to establish that just as *bechor* requires the *Beis Hamikdash*, so does *ma'aser sheni*: *af ma'aser eino ela lifnei habayis*.

---

## Kedushah Status

### Kedushah Rishonah

Having established through the *hekesh* that *ma'aser sheni* requires the *Beis Hamikdash*, the Gemara probes a deeper dimension of the question. The inquiry becomes: what does one hold about the *kedushah* of Eretz Yisrael and Jerusalem? *Ei kasavar kedushah rishonah kidshah l'sha'atah vekidshah l'asid lavo* — if one holds that the original *kedushah* of the *Beis Hamikdash*, as established in the time of Yehoshua or Shlomo, persisted even after the destruction of the first *Beis Hamikdash* and continues to apply even now after the destruction of the second, then everything retains its full *kedushah* today. If so, the question arises: why is it obvious that one cannot bring *bechor* nowadays? The answer is that according to the principle *makrivin af al pi she'ein bayis* — one may bring sacrifices even without a standing *Beis Hamikdash* — in theory one could bring *bechor* today, provided one constructs a *mizbe'ach* on the site of the *azarah*. This is the very principle cited in the context of those who wish to bring a *korban Pesach* on Har Habayis.

Conversely, *va'ei kasavar kedushah rishonah kidshah l'sha'atah velo kidshah l'asid lavo* — if one holds that the original *kedushah* did not survive the destruction — then the *kedushah* of Jerusalem no longer exists at all. In that case, why would anyone think one could bring *ma'aser sheni* to Jerusalem and eat it there? There is no *kedushah* of Jerusalem remaining to render the eating permissible, and the question of Rabbi Ishmael would be moot. The Gemara's point is that without a distinction between types of *kedushah*, the analysis leads to an all-or-nothing conclusion: either both *bechor* and *ma'aser sheni* can be brought to Jerusalem (if *kedushah* remains), or neither can (if it does not).

### Kedushah Categories

This is where *Tosafot*'s reading of the Gemara opens a particularly illuminating conceptual dimension. *Tosafot* maintains a different *girsa* than the standard text, and following *Tosafot*'s reading, the answer offered by Ravina draws on a crucial distinction between different categories of *kedushah*. There is the *kedushah* of Eretz Yisrael as a whole, and there is the distinct *kedushah* of Jerusalem and the site of the *Beis Hamikdash*. These are not the same.

The *kedushah* of Eretz Yisrael — grounded in the divine promise to Avraham, Yitzchak, and Yaakov, and described by the verse *einei Hashem Elokecha bah mereshit hashanah ve'ad acharis shanah* — is not contingent on the physical structure of the *Beis Hamikdash*. It can therefore persist even after the Temple's destruction. Grain growing in Eretz Yisrael today is genuinely obligated in *ma'aser sheni* on a Torah level, because the *kedushah* of the land endures.

By contrast, the unique *kedushah* of Jerusalem — particularly the *kedushat hamikdash* on the Temple Mount itself — may well be linked to the physical structure. When that structure no longer stands, the question of whether Jerusalem retains its special status is genuinely open. This yields a precise and elegant formulation of Rabbi Ishmael's question: *ma'aser sheni* originates in the *kedushah* of Eretz Yisrael, which endures. It requires no altar ritual. One might therefore argue that the eating of *ma'aser sheni* in Jerusalem is tied to a different dimension of Jerusalem's holiness than the eating of *bechor* or *bikurim* — one tied to the capital of the land rather than to the altar of the Temple. If so, perhaps *ma'aser sheni* can be eaten in Jerusalem even today, when the *kedushat hamikdash* may no longer apply.

### Ravina Position

Ravina's answer, according to *Tosafot*'s reading, is: *le'olam kasvar kidshah l'sha'atah vekidshah l'asid lavo* — one holds that the *kedushah* does in fact persist. The *kedushah* of the Temple site and of Jerusalem endures. Yet the reason one cannot eat *bechor* in Jerusalem today is not that the *kedushah* is absent, but that there is no physical *mizbe'ach*. The question then becomes: does *ma'aser sheni*, which never required the altar for its eating in the first place, also require a physical *mizbe'ach*?

### Blood/Flesh Link

To sharpen this question, the Gemara introduces a hypothetical case: *bechor she'nizrak damo kodem churban habayis* — a *bechor* whose blood was properly dashed on the altar just before the Temple was destroyed, and whose flesh remains uneaten after the destruction. The blood-sprinkling was completed; the altar was present for the bringing. But now there is no *mizbe'ach*. Can the flesh be eaten without one? This scenario is introduced not because it commonly occurs, but because it conceptually isolates the act of eating from the act of bringing, allowing one to ask: is the presence of a physical altar required for the eating of *bechor* as well, even once it has been properly brought? And if it is, that has implications for *ma'aser sheni*, which also requires no altar-based bringing — only the eating in Jerusalem.

### Flesh-Blood Linkage

The Gemara answers by linking the flesh to the blood: *umakshinan besaro ledamo — mah damo bemizbe'ach af besaro bemizbe'ach*. Rashi cites the verse: *es damam tizrok al hamizbe'ach uvasaram yihyeh lach* — "their blood you shall dash on the altar, and their flesh shall be yours." The juxtaposition of blood and flesh in this verse creates an *hekesh*: just as the blood requires the altar, so the flesh requires the presence of an altar for its permissible consumption. A *bechor* whose blood was dashed before the destruction still cannot be eaten once the *mizbe'ach* is gone, because flesh and blood are treated as a single integrated *halachah* — *dam u'vasar chada milta hi* — and not as two independent applications that could be separately derived.

This in turn resolves the case of *ma'aser sheni*. Through the *hekesh* linking *ma'aser* to *bechor*, we know: just as *bechor* requires a physical *mizbe'ach* for its permissible eating — even when it has already been properly brought — so too *ma'aser sheni* requires the presence of a physical *mizbe'ach*. The *kedushah* of Jerusalem and the Temple site may well persist, but without a standing physical altar, neither *bechor* nor *ma'aser sheni* may be eaten. The Gemara also addresses a potential challenge regarding double-derived *limudim* (*davar halamad behekesh chozer umelamed behekesh*), but notes that since *ma'aser dagan chullin hu* — *ma'aser* of grain is, relative to *korbanos*, considered non-sacred — the restriction against chained *hekeshim* does not apply. And since blood and flesh are ultimately one *halachah*, the derivation is properly a single link: *ma'aser* is connected to *bechor*, and what applies to *bechor* applies to *ma'aser*.

---

## Ma'aser Tumah Violation

### Redundancy Issue

Having concluded the discussion of *ma'aser sheni*'s dependence on the *Beis Hamikdash*, the Gemara turns to a new topic within the same subject matter. The *mishnah* in the present chapter states that one of the violations for which lashes are incurred is eating *kodshim kalim* or *ma'aser sheni chutz lachomah* — outside the walls of Jerusalem. But the first *mishnah* of the chapter already taught that one of the cases warranting lashes is eating *ma'aser sheni ve'hekdesh she'lo nifdah* — *ma'aser sheni* or consecrated property that has not been redeemed. The Gemara raises the question: is this not the same violation? Eating *ma'aser sheni* outside of Jerusalem is a problem precisely because it has not been redeemed. Why does one *mishnah* frame the violation as "unredeemed *ma'aser sheni*" while the other frames it as "eating outside Jerusalem"?

### Resolution Offered

Rav Yosef bar Chanina resolves the apparent redundancy: the second *mishnah* — *seifa* — which describes the violation as eating *chutz lachomah* is speaking of a case where both the *ma'aser sheni* and the person are *tahor*. The only problem is that it is outside Jerusalem and unredeemed. Had it been redeemed or had the person been inside Jerusalem, there would have been no violation.

### Two Violations

The first *mishnah* — *reisha* — by contrast, is speaking of a case where either the person or the *ma'aser sheni* itself is *tamei*. In such a case, the violation is not simply that one ate outside Jerusalem; rather, even inside Jerusalem one would be forbidden to eat it. If one is *tamei* or the *ma'aser sheni* is *tamei*, the problem is that it has not been redeemed, because the proper response to *tumah* — even within Jerusalem — is redemption. The two *mishnayos* therefore describe two distinct violations: eating unredeemed *ma'aser sheni chutz lachomah* when both are *tahor*, and eating unredeemed *ma'aser sheni be'tumah* even within Jerusalem.

### Rabbi Shimon Source

This raises a further question: how do we know that eating *ma'aser sheni* while *tamei* incurs lashes at all? The *baraisa* quotes the declaration recited upon the separation of *ma'aser*: *lo vi'arti mimenu b'tamei* — "I did not consume from it in a state of *tumah*" — *bein she'ani tamei v'hu tahor, bein she'ani tahor v'hu tamei* — whether I was *tamei* and it was *tahor*, or I was *tahor* and it was *tamei*. This establishes that there is indeed a prohibition, but for lashes one needs an explicit negative commandment, not merely an implicit inference from a positive declaration. The *baraisa* therefore asks: *v'heichan muzhar al ha'achilah?* — where is the explicit prohibition against eating?

### Pasuk Analysis

The Gemara interjects before the *baraisa* reaches its answer: *tumat haguf behadya ketiv* — the prohibition against eating holy items while one's body is impure is stated explicitly in the verse: *nefesh asher tigah bo v'tamah ad ha'erev velo yochal min hakodashim* — "a person who touches it shall be impure until evening and shall not eat from the holy things." This includes *ma'aser sheni*. What remains to be established is the prohibition on eating *ma'aser sheni* when it itself is *tamei* even if the person is *tahor*. For that the Gemara cites: *lo tuchal le'echol bish'arecha* — "you cannot eat within your gates" — referring to *ma'aser*. The word *bish'arecha* — "in your gates," i.e., outside Jerusalem — is compared to another verse (*bish'arecha tochelenu*) in which *tamei* and *tahor* persons may eat together from an animal redeemed from *korban* status due to a blemish. From that context, eating "in your gates" carries the connotation of eating in any manner, including in a state of *tumah*. The Torah therefore says: *lo tuchal* — you cannot eat *ma'aser sheni* in that manner. Do not eat *ma'aser sheni be'tumah*, whether you are *tamei* or whether it is *tamei*.

---

## Ma'aser Redemption

### Redemption When Tamei

The *mishnah*'s implication that when *ma'aser sheni* becomes *tamei* it should be redeemed raises a further question: from where do we know that *ma'aser sheni* that has become *tamei* can be redeemed even while one is inside Jerusalem? Ordinarily, redemption of *ma'aser sheni* is performed before arriving in Jerusalem. Rabbi Elazar derives the permissibility of redemption within Jerusalem in cases of *tumah*: *minayin l'ma'aser sheni she'nitma she'podin oto afilu biYerushalayim?* — from the verse: *ki lo tuchal se'eto* — "for you are unable to carry it [to Jerusalem]."

### Se'eto Interpretation

The word *se'eto* is interpreted not as "carry" but as "eat." The derivation is supported by the verse regarding Yosef's gifting of food portions to his brothers: *vayisa masa'ot me'et panav* — where *masa'ot* refers to food portions, showing that the root *s-a-t* can denote a food allotment. The verse therefore means: because you cannot eat it in a state of permissibility, you are permitted to redeem it even within Jerusalem. One can thus redeem *ma'aser sheni* that has become *tamei* even inside Jerusalem rather than having to bury it.

### One Footstep Rule

Having established that *tumah* permits redemption within Jerusalem, Rabbi Bibi in the name of Rabbi Assi extends this to the case of *ma'aser sheni* that is *tahor*: *minayin l'ma'aser sheni tahor she'podin oto afilu bipsi'ah achat chutz lachomah?* — from where do we know that even *tahor ma'aser sheni* can be redeemed when one is even a single footstep outside the walls of Jerusalem? The source verse *ki yirchak mimcha hamakom* — "when the place is far from you" — might suggest a minimum distance. But since the Torah also says *lo tuchal se'eto* — you cannot even lift it — the emphasis is on any displacement at all: if there is any movement required to bring the *ma'aser sheni* into Jerusalem, that is sufficient to permit redemption. The principle of *natata devarecha lish'iurin* — that the Torah does not leave its measures undefined — supports this: since no minimum distance is specified, any distance outside the wall suffices.

### Partial Entry Scenario

The Gemara now turns to the Gemara's further inquiry, raised by Rabbi Chanina and Rav Oshaia sitting together: what is the rule regarding the *afpiskei* — the thresholds or gates — of Jerusalem? A preliminary case is ruled obvious: if the person is outside and his load is inside, *kaltuhu mechitzot* — the walls have absorbed it, and it is considered inside Jerusalem. It cannot be redeemed (unless it is *tamei*). The more genuinely uncertain scenario is the reverse: the person is inside Jerusalem but his load — his *ma'aser sheni* — is still outside the gates, in his pack on his back with the pack extending past the threshold.

### Fullness Principle

An elder from the school of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai teaches from a *baraisa*: *ki yirchak mimcha hamakom — mimlu'acha* — "when it is far from your fullness," meaning the entirety of you. Rashi explains that when one carries something on one's back, that person and the pack are a single unit. Since part of that unit — the person — is already inside Jerusalem, the whole unit is considered inside. Once any part of you has entered, you have entered fully, and redemption is no longer possible for *tahor ma'aser sheni*.

### Rav Pappa Query

Rav Pappa presses the boundary of this principle with a final question: *nakti leh b'kanya mai?* — what if the food is not in a backpack but is being held at a distance on a stick, in the manner of a traveler carrying his pack on a pole? The person is inside Jerusalem; the stick extends outward and the *ma'aser sheni* bag hangs at the far end, outside the walls. Is the *ma'aser sheni* considered to be "with" the person who is inside, or does the separation afforded by the length of the stick make a legal difference? The Gemara concludes: *teyku*. The question stands unresolved, and the discussion of what constitutes "entry" into Jerusalem — and at what point redemption of *ma'aser sheni* becomes impossible — continues to the next daf.

A final note of significance: at this point in the commentary of Rashi on Maseches *Makkot*, the following parenthetical remark appears, five lines from the top of the narrow column: *Rabbeinu — gufo tahor v'yatza nishmato b'tahara* — a reference to the tradition that Rashi departed this world while pronouncing the word *tahor*, his soul departing in purity. From this point forward, the commentary is no longer Rashi's own but that of his student Rabbeinu Yehuda bar Nosson, known as the *Rivan*. *Mikan va'eilach l'shon talmido Rabbeinu Yehuda Bar Nosson.*

---

---

# Makkot 20

## Maaser Sheni Entry

### Rav Assi's Rule

The daf picks up on 19b, where the Gemara is engaged with a list of prohibitions that carry *malkos*, including the eating of *maaser sheni* outside of Yerushalayim, *kodashim kalim* consumed outside of Yerushalayim, and similar cases. Following that broader discussion, the Gemara now focuses specifically on *maaser sheni*.

Rav Assi said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *maaser sheni me'imatai chayavin alav?* — from when is one liable for *maaser sheni*? The intuitive answer seems obvious: when you eat it outside of Yerushalayim. But that is precisely the *chiddush* — that answer is not correct. The rule is *misheyira pnei hachomah*: the *maaser sheni* must first have been brought inside the walls of Yerushalayim, and only then, if it is taken back out and eaten outside, does one incur *malkos*. If the *maaser sheni* was separated but never brought into Yerushalayim, there is a violation of a positive commandment but not the *lav* that carries *malkos*.

### Walls Requirement

The reasoning behind this requirement follows from a careful reading of the relevant *pesukim*. The positive commandment is *lifnei Hashem Elokecha tochalennu* — you shall eat it before Hashem your God. The *lav* is *lo tuchal le'echol bish'arecha* — you may not eat it in your gates — referring to *maaser deganecha tiroshecha veyitzharecha*. The Gemara reads these two verses in conjunction: wherever it is appropriate to say *lifnei Hashem Elokecha tochalennu* — wherever the produce has reached the stage where it is fit to be eaten as *maaser sheni* before Hashem — that is precisely the context in which the Torah then says *lo tuchal le'echol bish'arecha*.

### Pesukim Analysis

The logic is that *maaser sheni* is unlike other things that must be consumed in Yerushalayim, which typically acquire their sanctified status *within* Yerushalayim. *Maaser sheni* begins outside. The Torah's positive command — eat it before Hashem — becomes operative only once it has been present inside Yerushalayim, having been fit to be eaten in that sacred context. Only then does the accompanying *lav* — do not eat it in your gates — become applicable. Before it has ever entered Yerushalayim and been in that state of readiness, *lo karina bei lo tuchal le'echol bish'arecha*: the prohibitory verse simply does not apply, and therefore there is no *lav* to carry *malkos*.

---

## Tosefta Fig Case

### Fig Setup

A challenge is now raised from a *Tosefta*. Rabbi Yosi describes the following scenario: a *kohen* holds a fig that is *tevel* — produce from which the required separations have not yet been made. The *kohen* declares: the tip of this fig (by the stem) is designated as *terumah*; the northern portion is *maaser rishon*; and the southern portion is *maaser sheni*. He has been making his designations verbally, giving the whole fig a structure of separated gifts, though without having actually physically removed anything. The case is set in a *maaser sheni* year and he is standing in Yerushalayim — or, in the alternate version, it is a *maaser ani* year and he is outside.

If he eats the fig in such a state, *achlah lokeh achas* — he receives one set of *malkos*. The reason: although it appears as if he has done everything correctly and is eating *maaser sheni* in Yerushalayim, he has not yet separated *terumat maaser* from the *maaser rishon*, which means the entire fig retains the status of *tevel*, and it is for eating *tevel* that he is lashed.

### Tosefta Implications

A further dimension emerges. *Vezar she'achlah lokeh shtayim* — if a non-*kohen* were to eat this fig, he receives two sets of *malkos*: one for eating *tevel* and one for eating *terumah*. And here the *Tosefta* introduces a striking irony: *she'ilu betchilah achlah eino lokeh ela al achat* — had the non-*kohen* eaten the fig at the very outset, before any designations were made at all, he would have received only one set of *malkos*, since the whole thing was undifferentiated *tevel*. But now that the *kohen* has made his declarations, there is both *terumah* and *tevel* of *maaser rishon* present, yielding an additional prohibition.

The Gemara turns to the implications of the *Tosefta* for our original rule. The fact that the *Tosefta* sets its case in Yerushalayim — and on that basis the *maaser sheni* does not generate *malkos* — implies, *ha bigvulin lokeh shalosh*: had the same situation occurred outside of Yerushalayim in a *maaser sheni* year, the *kohen* would have received *malkos* for the *maaser sheni* as well. But this directly contradicts Rav Assi's teaching, for the *maaser sheni* in this case had never been brought inside the walls. It appears that eating *maaser sheni* outside of Yerushalayim generates *malkos* even without prior entry into the city.

### Gemara Challenge

The Gemara responds with what it acknowledges is a somewhat forced *ukiimta*: *d'oil v'afkei* — the *Tosefta* is speaking of a case where the produce had been brought into Yerushalayim and then taken back out. In the *Tosefta*'s scenario, the *kohen* is in Yerushalayim and therefore receives no *malkos* for the *maaser sheni*. The implicit contrast is not with a case where the produce was never in Yerushalayim, but with a case where it was in Yerushalayim and then brought back out — in which case he *would* receive an additional set of *malkos*.

But the Gemara immediately presses: *ee hachi mai l'meimra?* — if that is all the *Tosefta* is telling us, what is the *chiddush*? That eating *maaser sheni* outside after having brought it in and taken it out is forbidden is entirely obvious. There must be something more novel here.

---

## Matnot Status

### Solution Framework

The Gemara answers: *hocha b'mai askinan kegon d'oiliuhu bitveilaihu* — the case under discussion is one where the fig was brought into Yerushalayim while still in its *tevel* state, before any separations had been made at all. And the position being expressed is *d'kasavar matnos shelo hurmu k'mi shehurmu damyan* — that gifts which have not yet been separated are treated as if they have already been separated.

The *chiddush* now becomes clear. The *kohen* had the fig in hand, brought it into Yerushalayim before performing any *hafrasha*, and then either performed the separations in Yerushalayim — in which case the *maaser sheni* is in Yerushalayim and he eats it there without *malkos* — or brought it back out first and then made his declarations. In the latter scenario, the *Tosefta* teaches that he would incur an additional set of *malkos* for the *maaser sheni*, because the fact that the *tevel* fig was brought into Yerushalayim is already considered as if the *maaser sheni* component was brought into Yerushalayim. Since that portion was conceptually present when the fig entered the city, it counts as having been brought in and brought back out.

### Matnot Principle

The novel principle at work here is that *matnos shelo hurmu k'mi shehurmu damyan* — the priestly and levitical gifts that have not yet been physically separated are nevertheless regarded, for certain legal purposes, as if they are already separately present within the produce. When the undivided fig enters Yerushalayim, the *maaser sheni* "within" it is already treated as having entered, even though no designation has yet occurred. This is what transforms an otherwise straightforward case into a meaningful *chiddush* in the *Tosefta*.

### Reb Yosi Debate

A difficulty now arises. This *Tosefta* is attributed to Rabbi Yosi. Does Rabbi Yosi in fact hold that unseparated gifts are treated as if already separated? A *Baraita* quoted in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda citing Rabbi Yosi suggests the opposite: *lo necheleku Beis Shammai u'Beis Hillel al peiros shelo nigmera melachtan v'avru b'Yerushalayim sheyifteru maaser sheini shelahem v'yochlu b'chol makom* — Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel did not dispute that if produce which had not yet reached the stage of *gmar melacha* — the completion of processing that renders it liable in *maaser* — was brought into Yerushalayim and taken back out, the *maaser sheni* separated from it afterward may still be redeemed and eaten anywhere. In that case, everyone agrees there is no *klitas mechitzos*, no status-affixing by the walls. The debate between Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel concerned only produce that *had* reached *gmar melacha* and was therefore *tevel* proper, which was then brought in and out of Yerushalayim.

---

## Mechitzot Distinction

### Beis Shammai Hillel

The dispute between Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel, as presented in this *Baraita* from Rabbi Yosi, concerns the case of *peiros* that completed their *gmar melacha* — they are fully *tevel* and liable in *maaser* — and were then brought into Yerushalayim and subsequently taken back out while still unseparated. The question: once you later separate the *maaser sheni*, can it be redeemed and eaten anywhere? Or has the *maaser sheni* already had its status fixed — *klitas mechitzos* — by virtue of having been present within the walls of Yerushalayim, even while still embedded in the *tevel*?

### Shammai-Hillel Views

Beis Shammai holds: *yachzir maaser sheni l'sham v'yeiachel b'Yerushalayim* — you must bring the *maaser sheni* back to Yerushalayim and eat it there. In their view, the *maaser sheni*'s status was fixed when the *tevel* fig passed through the walls — *matnos shelo hurmu k'mi shehurmu damyan* — and the *maaser sheni* is now as if it genuinely entered Yerushalayim. It cannot subsequently be redeemed. Beis Hillel, however, maintains *yifdeh v'yeiachel b'chol makom* — it may be redeemed and eaten anywhere. Beis Hillel does not treat the unseparated gift as legally present for the purpose of *klitas mechitzos*.

This seems to create an internal contradiction within Rabbi Yosi's own position. The *Tosefta* (attributed to Rabbi Yosi) appears to invoke the principle that unseparated gifts are treated as already present — yielding *malkos* when the fig is brought in and taken out — yet the *Baraita* (also from Rabbi Yosi) attributes that very principle to Beis Shammai, while Beis Hillel (the accepted *halakha*) rejects it. How can the *Tosefta* rest on a principle that we rule against?

### Rabbah's Solution

Rabbah resolves the tension with a foundational distinction: *mechitzah l'echol d'Oraisa, mechitzah liklot d'Rabanan*. The requirement that *maaser sheni* be eaten within the walls of Yerushalayim is a Biblical obligation. The rule that once *maaser sheni* enters Yerushalayim its status is fixed and it can no longer be redeemed — *klitas mechitzos* — is a Rabbinic enactment. These are two legally distinct applications of the walls of Yerushalayim.

### Lashes vs. Redemption

Given this distinction, the Gemara can now differentiate the two cases. With respect to *malkos* — which is grounded in the Biblical prohibition *lo tuchal le'echol bish'arecha* — we apply the *d'Oraisa* standard. Even when the *maaser sheni* is not yet separated, we treat the unseparated gift as present: *metivlo shelo huram k'mi shehuram dami*. Since the *tevel* fig entered Yerushalayim, the *maaser sheni* within it is regarded as having entered, rendering it fit for its required context of consumption. Taking it back out and eating it therefore violates the Biblical *lav* and carries *malkos*.

With respect to the Rabbinic question of whether the *maaser sheni* can still be redeemed after being brought in and taken out as *tevel* — which is the dispute between Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel — the Rabbinic enactment of *klitas mechitzos* is limited to cases where the *maaser sheni* was actually separated before entering Yerushalayim. *V'ki gazur Rabanan ki isa b'einei b'tivlo lo gazur Rabanan* — when the Rabbis enacted this restriction, they restricted it to cases where the *maaser sheni* was genuinely present, not merely present in potential. Beis Hillel accordingly rules that the *maaser sheni* may still be redeemed, and this ruling does not contradict the *d'Oraisa* position that carries *malkos* in the Biblical domain.

---

## Ravina Clarifies

### Stick Connection

Ravina offers an alternative reading of the *Tosefta* case, returning to close the discussion of the original question. He proposes: *kegon d'nakit lei bekanya* — the scenario is one in which the produce was connected to the outside by a stick. The person was standing inside Yerushalayim, but the produce itself was in a bag located just outside the walls, physically connected to him by a stick.

### Partial Presence

This connects to a question raised earlier by Rav Pappa. In that scenario, the produce was never fully inside Yerushalayim in any conventional sense, yet the person's own presence inside the city, combined with this physical connection, creates an ambiguous status — something halfway between being inside and outside. According to Ravina, the *Tosefta*'s *chiddush* is precisely this: that even such a case of partial or indirect presence would be treated as the *maaser sheni* having been "brought in" to Yerushalayim and then "taken out," such that eating it outside would generate *malkos*. This is not at all obvious, and therefore the *Tosefta* is saying something genuinely novel — that even this attenuated form of presence within the walls suffices to trigger the Biblical consequence. What does *not* happen, and what the Gemara consistently rejects across both readings, is that *malkos* applies to *maaser sheni* which was always, entirely outside of Yerushalayim from start to finish.

---

## Mourning Prohibitions

### Korach Prohibition

The Gemara now moves to the next *Mishnah*, which introduces several prohibitions relating to mourning practices. The *Mishnah* opens with *hakoreiach karcha berosho* — one who makes a bald spot on his head as an act of mourning over the dead — and immediately invokes the *pasuk* from *Emor* addressed to the *Kohanim*: *lo yikchu korcha berosham u'feas zkhanam lo yegaleichu*. Two separate types of appearance-altering practices are grouped together: making a bald patch as an expression of grief, and shaving the corners of the beard.

### Peyot Beard Terms

The *Mishnah* uses different verbs for the two prohibitions involving hair on the head and the beard, and those distinctions are legally meaningful. For the head, the term is *makif* — one who "rounds off" or "encircles" the corner of the head. For the beard, the term is *mashchis* — one who "destroys" the corner of the beard. These terms are not interchangeable. The *pasuk* for the beard reads *lo sashchis es peas zkhanecha*, using the language of *hashchasa*, destruction. The Gemara understands *hashchasa* by the beard to require the use of a *ta'ar* — a straight-edge razor that cuts the hair completely flush against the skin. A shaver or clipper that operates with a scissor-like mechanism — where the hairs pass through a guard and are cut by a blade against a shield — is what the Gemara calls *misparayim k'ein ta'ar*: scissors operating like a razor. Such an instrument does not constitute *hashchasa* by the beard and would not incur Biblical *malkos*.

For the *peyos* of the head, by contrast, the operative term in the *pasuk* is *lo takifu*, framed around the act of "rounding" rather than "destroying." There, the scissor-motion standard is more disputed, and the accepted position is that even a *misparayim k'ein ta'ar* raises concern, making its use on the *peyos* problematic in a way that it is not for the beard.

### Sritat Incisions

The *Mishnah* then addresses *sritat* — incisions made on the skin as a sign of grief over the dead. The *pasuk* is *v'saret lanefesh lo sitnu bivsarchem*. Even a single incision made for a deceased person renders one liable to *malkos*. The *Mishnah* then presents a striking case: *soreit srita achas al chamisha meisim* — one who makes a single incision as an expression of mourning for five different deceased relatives simultaneously. Even though it is a single physical act, the *Mishnah* teaches that one receives separate *malkos* for each *meis*. Each dead person for whom the act is performed imparts a distinct identity to the incision, making it as if one incised separately for each. The same logic applies in reverse: *chamisha sritos al meis echad* — five separate incisions all performed for a single deceased person — yields separate *malkos* for each incision, provided there was a separate *hasra'ah* before each one.

### Peyot Locations

The *Mishnah* enumerates the locations of the *peyos*: on the head, there are two — one on each side, at the area where the sideburn meets the hairline. On the beard, there are five: two on each side — corresponding roughly to the upper cheek and the lower cheek — and one at the bottom at the chin. Rabbi Eliezer, however, holds: *im nitlu kulan ke'achas eino chayav ela achas* — if all five locations on the beard were shaved in a single act, one is liable for only one set of *malkos*. In Rabbi Eliezer's view, the act of shaving the beard is a single unified prohibition, regardless of how many of the five designated spots are affected. According to the *Chachamim*, each of the five locations is a distinct prohibition, and if all five are removed — even in a single sweeping act — one incurs five separate sets of *malkos*, assuming the requisite warnings were given.

Rabbi Eliezer adds a further stringency: *v'eino chayav ad sheyitlenu beta'ar* — for the standard view, one is only liable for the beard if a straight-edge razor is used. But *Rabbi Eliezer omer afilu likto bemelaket o berahitni chayav* — Rabbi Eliezer holds one is liable even for using tweezers or a similar depilatory instrument. In Rabbi Eliezer's view, the prohibition is not limited to an act of cutting with a razor; any act of removal from the designated locations of the beard suffices.

---

## Korach Analysis

### Korcha Derivation

The Gemara begins its analysis with the prohibition of *korcha* — making a bald spot on the head for the dead. A *Baraita* raises the question: perhaps even if one makes four or five bald spots, he is only liable once, on the grounds that it is all part of a single act? The *Baraita* rejects this, deriving from the repeated use of the word *korcha* — *lo yikrechu korcha* by the *Kohanim* and *lo sasimu korcha* by *Yisrael* — that one is *chayav al kol korcha v'korcha*, liable separately for each and every bald spot made.

### Biblical Limits

The *Baraita* then asks about the phrase *berosham* in the *pasuk* for *Kohanim* — why does it say "on their heads" when the broader principle presumably applies? Because by *Yisrael* the *pasuk* specifies *bein eineichem* — between your eyes — one might think only a bald spot made precisely between the eyes generates liability. The *Baraita* therefore uses *berosham* to teach that the prohibition extends to the entire head, not only to the space between the eyes. This raises an asymmetry: perhaps the fuller prohibition — applying to the whole head — belongs to *Kohanim* alone, given that they carry additional obligations? One might then confine the *Yisrael* prohibition to *bein einayim* only.

### Unifying Verses

To resolve this, the Gemara employs a *gezeira shava*: the word *korcha* appears both in the *pasuk* addressing *Kohanim* (*lo yikrechu korcha*) and in the *pasuk* addressing *Yisrael* (*lo sasimu korcha*). Through this *korcha-korcha* linkage, everything derived from one verse applies to the other: just as by *Kohanim* one is liable for each individual bald spot and the prohibition covers the entire head, so too by *Yisrael* — *chayav al kol korcha v'korcha v'chayav al harosh k'vein einayim*. And critically, the *gezeira shava* also imports the limitation found by *Yisrael*: just as by *Yisrael* the prohibition is *al hameis* — for the dead — so too by *Kohanim* the prohibition is *al hameis*. The *pasuk* for *Kohanim* does not explicitly mention mourning for a deceased person, but via the *gezeira shava* it is unified with the *Yisrael* prohibition under the single framework of mourning. The phrase *bein eineichem* in the *Yisrael* verse, meanwhile, is not taken as a strict limitation; the *berosham* of the *Kohanim* verse — the whole head — overrides it, and *bein eineichem* is understood as a non-exclusive reference rather than a definitional constraint.

---

## Multiple Lashes Rule

### Hasra'ah Problem

Having established that one is liable separately for each bald spot, the Gemara now asks: what exactly is the scenario in which making four or five bald spots results in four or five sets of *malkos*? The question is not trivial, because the requirements for *malkos* demand not only a prohibited act but a valid *hasra'ah* — a warning given immediately before the act — and each separate set of *malkos* requires its own prior warning.

### Nazirite Comparison

The Gemara illustrates the principle by reference to the *Mishnah* concerning a *Nazir*: *Nazir shehayah shoseh yayin kol hayom eino chayav ela achas* — a *Nazir* who drinks wine the entire day receives only one set of *malkos*. Even if the drinking is not continuous — even if he pauses, takes a walk, resumes later — as long as there is only a single *hasra'ah*, only one set of *malkos* applies. But if the witnesses said to him "do not drink" and he drank, and then they said again "do not drink" and he drank again, *chayav al kol achas v'achas* — he is liable for each separately. The *hasra'ah* must immediately precede the specific act; it does not carry forward to subsequent acts.

This principle creates a problem for the case of multiple bald spots. If the person was warned once and then proceeded to make five bald spots — whether in rapid succession or in a single sweeping gesture — the single *hasra'ah* would seem to apply only to the first act. Why should a special *pasuk* of *korcha v'korcha* be needed to establish multiple liability if the *hasra'ah* requirement would in any case limit liability to one?

### Five Fingers Solution

Rav Huna resolves this: *d'shach chamish etzba'otav nasha* — the case is where one dipped all five fingers into a depilatory substance and then, in a single simultaneous act, placed all five fingers on five different spots on the head. In this scenario, *d'havei leh hasra'ah l'chol chada v'chada* — the single *hasra'ah* functions as the warning for all five acts, because all five acts were performed simultaneously in one motion. The *hasra'ah* is not "used up" by the first act and then unavailable for the subsequent ones; since all five happened at once, the single warning stands immediately before each one of them simultaneously. The *chiddush* of the verse *korcha v'korcha* is precisely that this single simultaneous act is conceptualized as five distinct violations — one for each bald spot created — and therefore yields five sets of *malkos*.

This is a significant illustration of how *hasra'ah* interacts with complex acts. A single continuous act of drinking, even if it spans a full day, is one act and yields one set of *malkos*. Multiple separate acts, even clearly distinct ones, require separate *hasra'os* to generate separate *malkos*. But a single simultaneous act that by its nature touches five prohibited locations in one moment is treated as five acts for purposes of *malkos*, with the single *hasra'ah* covering all five simultaneously.

---

## Korcha Shiur

### Size Opinions

The Gemara turns to the question of minimum size: *v'kamah shiur korcha?* — what is the smallest bald spot for which one is liable? Rav Huna says *kedei sheyeira merosho* — enough to be visible from the head, that is, an observable patch of baldness. Rabbi Yochanan says in the name of Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon: *k'gris* — the size of a *gris*, a type of bean. A *Baraita* records these as a *Tannaitic* dispute. Rabbi Yehuda bar Chaviva then reports that in fact three *Tannaim* debate the matter: one says *k'gris*, one says *kedei sheyeira merosho*, and one says *k'shtei searot* — just two hairs. Some versions substitute *k'adasha* — the size of a lentil — for the two-hairs opinion, yielding a three-way dispute between a bean, a lentil, and visible-from-the-head.

### Tzara'at Parallel

A mnemonic device is offered to help remember the relevant *shiurim*: *v'simancha b'bahares k'gris u'michyah k'adasha* — recall the laws of *tzara'at*. The white patch of *tzara'at* must be at least the size of a *gris* to be a *nega*, and the area of *michyah* — the patch of healed skin within a *nega* that is halakhically significant — must be the size of an *adasha*, a lentil. Since these are familiar units in the context of bodily marks, they serve as natural reference points for the comparable *shiurim* of *korcha*.

### Hair Shiur

The Gemara then turns to the *shiur* for hair removal as it applies to *shabbat*, which has bearing on *korcha* as well. A *Baraita* teaches: *hanoteil kimlo pi hazug b'shabbat chayav* — one who removes as much hair as fills the mouth of scissors on *shabbat* is liable. Rav Yehuda explains that the measure is two hairs. A variant *Baraita* appears to contrast the *shabbat* standard from the *korcha* standard by stating them separately — *lekorcha shtayim* — but this is resolved by reading both as expressing the same measurement: the fill of the mouth of scissors equals two hairs, and two hairs is likewise the standard for *korcha*. Rabbi Eliezer disagrees: *achas* — even one hair is sufficient to make one liable.

### White Hair Exception

An important exception is noted: *umodim chachamim l'Rabbi Eliezer b'melaket levanot mitoch shachorot afilu achas shehu chayav* — the *Chachamim* concede to Rabbi Eliezer that if someone plucks a white hair from among black hairs, even a single hair renders one liable. The reason is that the act is qualitatively significant: by removing that single white hair, the person has made his entire head of hair appear uniformly black. The significance is not quantitative but functional — the appearance of the person is meaningfully altered by even one hair. In the ordinary case of *korcha*, one hair makes no perceptible difference; two hairs at least constitute something that can be identified as a minimal act. But here, the single white hair does the entire work of changing the appearance, and therefore even one hair crosses the threshold.

### Grooming Lo Yilbash

The Gemara adds that this prohibition against plucking white hairs from among black ones is not limited to *shabbat* but applies even on weekdays: *vedavar zeh afilu b'chol assur mishum shene'emar lo yilbash gever simlat isha* — because a man may not wear the garment of a woman. The verse *lo yilbash gever simlat isha* is understood to extend beyond literal cross-dressing to encompass any grooming practice that is characteristically feminine — that is, practices by which a woman attends to her appearance. A man who plucks white hairs to make his hair appear uniformly black is engaging in the kind of appearance-management that is associated with women's grooming, and this falls within the prohibition of *simlat isha*. The definition here is notably broad: the end result is not a feminine appearance as such — the man simply has black hair — but the *practice* is one associated with feminine self-presentation, and that is sufficient. The Gemara elsewhere discusses the case of a man arranging his appearance in a mirror, which *Rishonim* note is highly contextually dependent; what constitutes a characteristically feminine practice is culturally variable, and many *Rishonim* limit the application of this prohibition accordingly to practices that remain genuinely gender-specific in the relevant society.

---

---

# Makkot 21

## Overview: Lashes

### Daf Overview

The daf before us continues the tractate's sustained engagement with a cluster of bodily prohibitions that incur *malkot*: making a bald spot on the head in mourning, cutting the *peot* (sideburns), destroying the corners of the beard, incisions in the flesh, and tattooing. The Mishnah enumerates all of these, and the Gemara on this daf works through them with considerable technical precision, examining the anatomical definitions, the identity of the liable parties, the required implements, and the relationship between a single physical act and multiple distinct transgressions.

### Makif & Peot

The Torah's prohibition against cutting the sideburns uses the term *makif* — literally "one who circles" or "cuts around." This is in contrast to the prohibition concerning the beard, which uses the word *mashchit* ("destroy"), a distinction that turns out to carry significant halachic weight. Because the beard prohibition employs the language of *hashchata*, the manner of cutting becomes central: only a method that constitutes destruction — reaching the root — triggers liability. The sideburn prohibition, by contrast, uses only *makif*, raising the question of what specific act is targeted.

According to Rashi and the *Rivan* (the commentary that serves as our primary *rishon* for this portion of the tractate), *makif* refers specifically to making a straight line — essentially leveling off the entire section of hair from one anatomical boundary to another, cutting it completely away. It is not merely any trimming of the area; it is the wholesale removal of that defined region. Several *rishonim*, including Rambam, understand the prohibition differently — Rambam speaks of forty hairs — but the basic contour of Rashi's reading is that the violation requires the complete excision of the *pe'ah*.

### Sof Rosho Definition

The Gemara opens with a *Baraita*: *at rosho sof rosho* — "the end of the head." The Gemara asks: what is *sof rosho*? The answer: *ze hamoshve tzadav le-achorei ozno* — this is the one who makes the temples (*tzadaav*) level with the back of the ear. The Gemara then adds: *ule-padachto le-achorei ozno* — and also to his forehead and the back of the ear. The picture that emerges is a straight line drawn from the forehead, along the temple, to the back of the ear — an entire section swept away in one motion.

This definition aligns well with Rashi's reading. The practical implication is that the prohibition on *peot ha-rosh* is triggered by that complete removal, not by trimming incrementally. It is worth noting that the prevailing practice in many communities is considerably stricter than even this reading of the Gemara would require, a reflection of layers of custom and stringency that have accumulated over the centuries.

---

## Actor vs Recipient

### Echad Hamakif

A *Tanna* taught before Rav Chisda: *echad ha-makif ve-echad ha-nikaf lokeh* — both the one who performs the haircut and the one who receives it are liable for *malkot*. This is a striking statement. The Torah says *lo takifu* — "do not make circuits" — which appears to be directed at the one performing the act. The one sitting passively while another cuts around his sideburns seems, on a plain reading, to be entirely outside the scope of that prohibition.

Rav Chisda's reaction captures this intuition vividly. He responds with an Aramaic idiom: *man de-achil tamrei be-arvilei loki?* — "Is someone who eats dates through a sieve going to get lashes?" The image is of someone who accomplishes nothing at all. The idiom cuts to two related but distinct issues: first, whether the *nikaf* transgresses any prohibition at all; and second, even if he does transgress, whether his passivity disqualifies him from *malkot*, given the principle that a *lav she-ein bo ma'aseh* — a prohibition violated without a physical act — does not ordinarily incur lashes.

### Lav She'ein Bo

The Gemara identifies the position that the *nikaf* receives lashes as that of Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that *lav she-ein bo ma'aseh lokin alav* — even a passive violation incurs *malkot*. What is notable here is that nobody in the Gemara appears to contest the underlying transgression of the *nikaf*; the debate is only over whether he is liable for lashes. The existence of the prohibition as applied to the recipient seems to be taken as established, the question being solely whether the passive nature of his participation shields him from corporal punishment.

### Lo Takifu & Mesayeia

Three resolutions are offered. First, the *Rivan* suggests that the plural form *lo takifu* — "you [plural] shall not circuit" — encompasses both parties: the one doing the cutting and the one submitting to it. Second, Rava proposes: *b'makif l'atzmo* — when a person cuts his own sideburns, he is simultaneously both the *makif* and the *nikaf*, and in that case, by universal agreement (*divrei ha-kol*), he is liable under both aspects of the prohibition and would receive two sets of lashes.

Third — and this is Rav Ashi's solution, which also aligns with what emerges naturally from the situation — the *nikaf* is liable because he is a *mesayei'a*: he actively assists in the act. When the barber says to tilt the head, hold steady, or position in a certain way, and the recipient complies, that participation constitutes sufficient action to make him an active transgressor and render him liable for *malkot*.

This generates an important conceptual distinction. In our case, everyone already agrees that the *nikaf* is a transgressor; the *mesayei'a* principle is invoked to establish that his participation is sufficiently active to warrant lashes. That is categorically different from a case where a person was not a transgressor to begin with and one wishes to argue that their *mesayei'a* makes them one. The *poskim* debate the latter scenario separately. One contemporary application involves a woman who arrives at the *mikvah* on Friday night having forgotten to cut her nails — in a community where the practice required complete cutting — and the question of whether she may assist a non-Jew in doing so on *Shabbos*. Her *mesayei'a* in holding her hand in position raises the question of how much participation is needed to transform her from a bystander into a transgressor. The *sugya* here is directly relevant, though the categories must be handled with care.

---

## Beard Cutting

### Five Corners

The Mishnah refers to *pe'at ha-zakan* — the corners of the beard — and the Gemara specifies that there are five such corners: two on each side of the face and one below. The *Rivan* explains the anatomical picture as follows: the *pe'ah* of the head runs from the bone near the ear to the temple, while the *pe'at ha-zakan* runs from that same bone downward along the jaw to the chin, and then again symmetrically on the other side, together with the strip below. The boundary point is thus the bone in the middle of the ear — from that bone upward defines the *peot ha-rosh*, and from that bone downward defines the *pe'at ha-zakan*.

A point worth noting is that the beard prohibition does not encompass the mustache. It appears, at least tentatively, that a straight razor may be used on the mustache without transgressing the prohibition — though this is not a common practice. The Amish custom of growing the beard while trimming the mustache is presumably rooted in exactly this distinction.

---

## Flesh Incisions

### Sherit for Dead

The Gemara cites a *Baraita* on *ve-saret la-nefesh* — the prohibition against cutting the flesh. One might have thought that any act of self-cutting made in grief — even over a collapsed house or a sunken ship — would be prohibited. The *Baraita* teaches: *talmud lomar la-nefesh* — the verse says "for a soul," indicating that liability applies only when the incision is made as a mourning rite for one who has died. An incision expressing anguish over financial loss or property is not included.

### One Act, Multiple Dead

The *Baraita* continues: if one makes five separate incisions for a single dead person, he is liable for each one — *talmud lomar ve-saret*, the use of the noun form teaching that each individual incision is counted separately. The added implication, as with the parallel case of the five bald spots mentioned earlier in the tractate, is that if the five incisions are made simultaneously — one can imagine a multi-pronged implement doing all five at once — that too counts as five separate violations in a single act.

Rabbi Yose adds a further dimension: if one makes a single incision on behalf of five different dead persons, he is liable five times — *l'chayev al kol nefesh va-nefesh*, one violation for each soul. This is the ruling in the Mishnah, though the Gemara notes that it represents Rabbi Yose's position rather than the anonymous, uncontested view.

### Sherita vs Gedida

The Gemara now addresses the relationship between *sherita* (incision by hand) and *gedida* (incision with a tool, such as a knife). The general assumption is that they are separate acts described by separate verses: *ve-saret la-nefesh* covers hand-incision, and *lo tisgodedu* (from Deuteronomy) covers tool-incision. Rabbi Yose, however, holds that *sherita* and *gedida* are one and the same act — the two words simply describe the same prohibition without distinguishing by method. The practical consequence of his view is that the verse *la-nefesh* and the word *la-met* (found in the context of *lo tisgodedu*) are then redundant with each other, and that redundancy is what Rabbi Yose uses to derive that a single incision over multiple dead persons is itself multiple violations.

### Samuel's Ruling

Shmuel states: *ha-masaret bi-khli chayav* — one who makes an incision *using a tool* is liable, and he uses the word *masaret* (*sherita*) rather than *gedida*. This implies that Shmuel holds like Rabbi Yose, that *sherita* encompasses both hand and implement, and the two terms are not distinguishing by method. The Gemara raises an objection from a *Baraita* that explicitly states *srita beyad u-gedida bi-khli* — that *sherita* is by hand and *gedida* is by instrument — but resolves it: Shmuel follows the position of Rabbi Yose.

---

## Avoda Zara Context

### Pagan Ritual

A *Tanna* taught before Rabbi Yochanan: for a dead person, whether the incision is by hand or by tool, one is liable; for *avodah zarah*, liability differs by method. Making incisions in the flesh was a recognized pagan ritual — the paradigmatic Talmudic example being the prophets of Baal on Har Carmel who *va-yisgodedu ke-mishpatam, ba-charavot u-va-ramachim* — they made incisions as was their practice, with swords and spears. That is an instrument, a *kli*.

The Gemara therefore asks: but the verse shows pagan incisions being done with tools — so how can the rule say that for *avodah zarah* the tool is exempt? The Gemara reverses the formulation: by hand is exempt; by tool, one is liable.

### Rambam on Paganism
