The Rambam in *Moreh Nevukhim* argues that many of the prohibitions discussed throughout this passage — bald spots, flesh incisions, cutting the beard, and, as we will see, tattooing — are rooted in their association with pagan ritual practice. The Torah is not necessarily prohibiting excessive mourning per se; rather, these were the actual forms that pagan mourning and pagan worship took, and the Torah targets them for that reason. This framing has implications for how one analyzes the boundaries of each prohibition.

### Hand vs Tool

The resulting legal map is as follows: for incisions made over the dead, liability applies whether the incision is made by hand or with a tool. For incisions made in the context of *avodah zarah*, liability applies when made with a tool, not by hand. This is the inverse of what one might initially expect. The Tosafot explain the *avodah zarah* case in terms of the category of *avodah she-lo ke-darkhah* — worship performed in a manner atypical for a given idol, which incurs *malkot* without the death penalty. Since making incisions was so widespread a feature of pagan worship generally, it constitutes a recognizable act of adulation toward any idol, even one not normally worshipped this way. By contrast, an act that no one would recognize as reverence — even if the worshiper intends it as such — would not qualify. The line is whether an outside observer would identify it as an act of *kavod* to a deity.

---

## Beard Cutting (II)

### Rabbi Eliezer Debate

Returning to the beard: Rabbi Eliezer holds that if one removes all five corners of the beard simultaneously, he is liable only once — *kasavar chad lav hu*, it is one prohibition. The Sages apparently count each corner as a separate prohibition. The precise nature of this debate is somewhat puzzling, since one would think that separate warnings between acts would result in separate liability in any case, and a single warning would not generate multiple sets of *malkot* regardless. The debate may be most meaningful in the case of truly simultaneous removal of all five corners at once — analogous to the earlier case of the bald spots, where one act could generate multiple violations if the five spots were made in a single motion.

### Razor vs Scissors

The Mishnah rules: *ve-eino chayav ad she-yitlenu be-ta'ar* — he is not liable unless he removes it with a razor. Rabbi Eliezer adds that even tweezers (*malket* and *rehitani*) incur liability.

The Gemara derives the razor requirement from two separate verses: *pe'at zekanam lo yegaleichu* (applied to *kohanim*, but read together with the parallel prohibition applying to all of Israel) and *lo tashchit et pe'at zekanecha*. These two verses are not read as establishing two separate *lavin*, but rather as jointly defining the act that is prohibited: it must be both *giluach* (shaving) and *tashchit* (destruction — i.e., reaching to the root). The Gemara then maps the three implements:

A razor satisfies both conditions — it reaches the root (*tashchit*) and is a normal act of shaving (*giluach*). Scissors do not reach the root — they cut above the surface of the skin — and therefore lack *tashchit*, even though they constitute *giluach*. Tweezers, by contrast, do reach the root by pulling the hair from it, satisfying *tashchit*, but the *Rivan* explains they are not *giluach* because they do not involve a normal manner of shaving — they are not *derekh giluach*. An alternative reading is that *giluach* implies a cutting or slicing action, and tweezers perform neither; they pluck. Either way, only a razor satisfies both conditions and therefore only a razor incurs liability. Hence Rabbi Eliezer, who holds that tweezers are liable, must explain tweezers as constituting *giluach* — the *Rivan* explains that for Rabbi Eliezer, *giluach* is defined more broadly, perhaps as anything that produces the end result of removal, which he prioritizes over the question of method.

### Electric Shavers

The question of electric shavers is not addressed explicitly in the Gemara, but the analysis of the razor-versus-scissors distinction generates the analytical framework within which *poskim* have debated it. The issue is whether an electric shaver satisfies *tashchit* (getting to the root) and *giluach* (the appropriate method of shaving).

On the question of *tashchit*: a standard electric shaver works through a foil mechanism — the foil rests against the skin, hair enters the foil, and the blade cuts within. Because the foil intervenes between blade and skin, the blade never achieves the proximity to the skin that a straight razor does. Some *poskim* therefore argue that electric shavers do not constitute *tashchit*, since they do not cut at the root in the way a razor does. This explains why the conversation about electric shavers often focuses on how close a particular model shaves — the claim that it "shaves as close as a blade" is precisely what would be halachically concerning under this analysis.

On the question of *giluach*: if one follows the view that the distinction between razors and scissors lies in the razor's slicing action versus the scissors' two-blade cutting action, then an electric shaver presents a further question. The foil-and-blade mechanism of a shaver resembles the scissors model — the foil holds the hair while the blade cuts it. This would suggest it is more like scissors than a razor, and therefore even if it were to reach the root, it might still be permitted because it is not *derekh giluach* in the razor sense. Others argue the opposite, contending that the blade inside is doing a slicing motion regardless of the foil.

The Tosafot in another tractate develop the concept of *misparayim ke-ein ta'ar* — scissors operating very close to the skin, functioning almost like a razor — and rule it permissible even so. This *chiddush* does not appear explicitly here but underlies much of the discussion. If scissors are permitted even when approaching razor-level closeness, the question becomes: what exactly is it that makes a razor different? The three answers — closer to the root; slicing versus cutting; more *derekh giluach* — each point in a different direction when applied to an electric shaver.

It should also be noted that the *misparayim ke-ein ta'ar* leniency does not apply to *peot ha-rosh*. The verb *mashchit* is absent from the *pe'ah* prohibition, and the methodology of the beard prohibition therefore does not carry over. So while scissors may be permitted for the beard even when cutting very close, they are not permitted for the sideburns under the same logic — though, as the Gemara indicated earlier, the *pe'ah* prohibition may require a more sweeping act of removal than any question of implement would address.

---

## Tattooing

### Ketiva & Ke'aka

The Mishnah on *ketovot ka'aka* — tattooing — states that liability requires both *ketiva* (writing or marking) and *ke'aka* (incision into the skin). Neither element alone is sufficient. The mechanism described by Rashi is that ink is applied to the skin and then an incision is made into it, causing the ink to be absorbed beneath the surface where it remains permanently.

### Ink Without Cut

If one wrote the ink marking without making the incision, or made the incision without applying ink — such as the temporary tattoo-like markings sometimes made today — there is no liability. One is not liable until both the writing and the incision have occurred together: *eino chayav ad she-yikhtov ve-yaka'keia*. The Mishnah also specifies the substances — ink (*dyo*), *kochal* (another pigment), and any substance that leaves a lasting mark — thus indicating that the critical feature is permanent pigmentation beneath the skin, not any particular material.

### Rabbi Shimon's Name

Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Shimon holds that liability applies only if one writes *ha-shem* — the Name — into the skin. His derivation: *ke-sovet ka-aka lo titenu bachem Ani Hashem* — "you shall not place a tattooing inscription upon you; I am the Lord." The plain reading would suggest one must literally write the words *Ani Hashem* to be liable.

The Gemara, however, pushes back immediately. Rav Acha son of Rava asks Rav Ashi: does one really have to write the words *Ani Hashem* literally? That cannot be the intent. Rav Ashi explains with reference to a teaching of Bar Kappara: the liability arises not from writing the name of God, but from writing the name of *avodah zarah*. The verse is read as follows: "Do not inscribe a tattoo upon yourselves — [because I am] *Ani Hashem*," meaning: *do not bear the brand of another*. The prohibition is against tattooing the name of a foreign deity onto one's body, marking oneself as belonging to that god. The Gemara notes that this reading aligns naturally with the Rambam's framework, which roots these prohibitions in their pagan context.

### Ashes in Wounds

Rav Malkiya said in the name of Rav Adda bar Ahava: it is forbidden to rub *efer mikleh* — ashes — into a wound, because when the wound heals, the ash remains beneath the skin and creates the appearance of a tattoo. This is prohibited *mipnei she-nireh ki-ketovot ka'aka* — because it looks like a tattooed inscription.

This raises an immediate question: if ash rubbed into a wound for a medical purpose leaves a permanent mark, is that prohibited? The answer from the Gemara appears to be yes, at least in the general case. Rav Ashi, however, qualifies this: *kol makom she-yesh sham makah, makato mochiach alav* — wherever there is a wound, the wound itself demonstrates the purpose. That is, if it is evident from the wound that the incision or the marking was made for healing and not for ornamentation or religious branding, there is no violation.

The *Rivan* adds a further qualification to the prohibition on ashes: the term *mikleh* — referring to ashes charred from a fuel stove, which leave a particularly lasting and dark impression — distinguishes this case from ordinary dust or dirt, which would not create the same appearance. The Ritva understands the distinction as separating this type of ash from regular ash; the *Rivan* seems to be distinguishing *efer* (ash) from *afar* (ordinary dirt), clarifying that it is specifically the type of ash that leaves a permanent subdermal pigment. Whatever the precise scope, the principle is that the prohibition applies when the substance leaves a lasting mark beneath the skin.

Rav Imi bar Abba was stringent even about the residue left by a lancet — a cutting instrument used for piercing boils — lest it incidentally leave a mark beneath the skin.

---

## Tattooing (II)

### Breast Reconstruction

A directly contemporary question flows from Rav Ashi's ruling. Women who undergo mastectomy and subsequent reconstructive surgery often receive tattooing to recreate the areola around the reconstructed nipple, restoring natural appearance. Does this constitute a biblical violation of *ketovot ka'aka*?

Several considerations bear on the analysis. According to the Rambam's *Moreh Nevukhim* framework, these prohibitions are rooted in their pagan context — but of course the Rambam's explanation of *ta'amei ha-mitzvot* does not translate into a halachic exemption simply because the original social context is absent; that is not how *ta'amei ha-mitzvot* operate in practice.

A more textually grounded argument advanced by one *acharon* is that *ketovot ka'aka* as a *de-Oraita* prohibition requires actual *ketiva* — writing, i.e., letters or at least a recognizable depiction — and that a purely cosmetic mark not constituting writing might be only *de-rabbanan* at most. However, as the lecture notes, the Gemara itself prohibited the mere rubbing of ashes into a wound because it *appears* as a tattoo, without any suggestion that the absence of letter-formation reduces the prohibition. The *Gemara* did not draw that distinction, and its absence is significant.

The *makah mochiach* principle of Rav Ashi — that a wound demonstrates the medical purpose — is the more solid ground. If the tattooing is clearly done as part of documented medical reconstruction, and the medical purpose is self-evident, one can argue that the *makah mochiach alav* principle applies: the context makes clear it is not *avodah zarah* branding, not cosmetic marking for its own sake, and not a violation of the prohibition's intent. Many *poskim* lean on the combination of these considerations, treating such cases as at most *de-rabbanan* and permissible given significant medical and psychological need.

---

## Multiple Acts Principle

### Nazir Wine Case

The Mishnah teaches: if a *nazir* was drinking wine the entire day, he is liable only once — *eino chayav ela achat* — because there was a single warning and the drinking constitutes one continuous process. If, however, he received warnings between drinks — *amru lo al tish-teh, al tish-teh* — and continued drinking each time, he is liable for each separate act of drinking.

### Warnings Divide Acts

The underlying principle is that a single continuous action, performed without intervening warnings, constitutes one transgression regardless of how many times the prohibited behavior is repeated during that stretch. An intervening warning (*hatara*) serves to separate what would otherwise be a continuous act into distinct, independently countable violations. The warning functions as a break — it signals that the person has been notified and is now making a fresh, conscious choice to transgress again.

### Ongoing Actions

The Mishnah applies this principle to a series of cases. A *nazir* who spent the entire day in a cemetery — even moving from one to the next — incurs only one set of lashes, either because each subsequent entry lacked its own warning, or because the entire sequence of contaminations is treated as one continuous state. If he received a warning before each entry and continued, he is liable for each one.

Similarly, a person who was shaving continuously all day — cutting very slowly — incurs only one set of lashes. If warned repeatedly between strokes, each warned stroke is a separate transgression. This case also returns to the question of the five corners: since the five corners of the beard are distinct prohibitions, the question of how warnings and continuous action interact with multiple anatomical sites is directly relevant, though the Gemara does not resolve it in detail here.

### State vs Action

The case of *kilayim* — wearing *sha'atnez* — introduces a critical distinction. If a person wore *sha'atnez* all day without interruption, he is liable only once regardless of any number of warnings, because wearing *sha'atnez* is a *state*, not a repeated act. Remaining in a state of violation, even a prolonged one, does not multiply into separate transgressions by virtue of warnings alone.

However, if he took off the forbidden garment and put it back on — *poshet ve-lovesh* — and received a warning between each such act, he is liable for each. The taking off and putting back on transforms what would be a continuous state into a series of discrete physical acts, each of which can be independently warned and independently punished. The distinction is thus between an ongoing state (in which the person is continuously transgressing but performing no new act) versus a repeated action (in which the person is actively performing the prohibited act anew each time).

---

## Eight Violations

### Choresh Telem Echad

The Mishnah concludes with the celebrated *choresh telem echad* — a single furrow that can generate liability for eight separate prohibitions simultaneously. The Mishnah enumerates: *ha-choresh be-shor va-chamor* — plowing with an ox and a donkey, which is the *kilayim be-vehema* prohibition; *ve-hem mukdashim* — and they are sanctified, so that the ox is a *bechor* (a firstborn animal that may not be worked: *lo ta'avod bi-vchor shorecha*) and the donkey is *hekdesh bedek habayit* (consecrated to Temple maintenance, so that working it involves *me'ila*); *ve-kilayim b'kerem* — the plowing simultaneously covers over seeds of mixed kinds in a vineyard, constituting *kilayim* in the category of *kilay ha-kerem* (as the Gemara explains, the plow covering seeds over the earth constitutes a form of planting); *u-vi-shevi'it* — it is the *shmitta* year, during which plowing is forbidden; *ve-Yom Tov* — it is also a festival day, during which agricultural labor is prohibited; *ve-Kohen ve-Nazir be-veis ha-tumah* — and the person plowing is both a *kohen* and a *nazir*, both of whom are forbidden from entering or remaining in a space containing the dead.

That is the list as constructed, yielding eight.

### Chananya's Objection

Chananya ben Chakinai raises an objection in the Mishnah itself: *af ha-lovesh kilayim* — one might add yet another violation if the person is wearing *sha'atnez* while plowing. The Sages respond: *eino min ha-shem* — wearing *sha'atnez* is not connected to the act of plowing; it is an independent state unrelated to the furrow. Chananya responds pointedly: *af nazir lo min ha-shem* — then neither is the *nazir* being in a cemetery connected to the act of plowing! Being a *nazir* or a *kohen* in a cemetery is equally extraneous to the furrow itself. This is a strong argument. The Sages appear to have no fully compelling rejoinder within the framework of the list as they have constructed it.

### Methodological Note

The Sages' response, and indeed the entire exercise, functions not as a definitive halachic ruling but as a demonstration of the principle of multiple simultaneous violations in a single act. There is no authoritative conclusion about exactly which eight — or how many — violations are generated; the list is designed to illustrate how densely a single physical act can be laden with distinct prohibitions when the right combination of circumstances obtains.

### Tosafot's Count

Tosafot note a difficulty with the count and resolve it by redefining one of the entries. Rather than treating the donkey as *hekdesh bedek habayit* — which generates one violation — Tosafot hold that only the ox is *hekdesh*, as a *bechor*, and the donkey is not separately consecrated. To restore the count to eight, Tosafot identify two distinct violations of *kilayim* in the plowing: *kilay ha-kerem* (mixed planting in the context of a vineyard) and *kilay zera'im* (mixing two different species of grain). If the person is covering over a grape seed along with two different types of grain, both the *kilay ha-kerem* and the *kilay zera'im* prohibitions are triggered simultaneously, yielding two separate violations from the single act of covering the seeds — and thereby restoring the count to eight without requiring the donkey to be *hekdesh*.

---

---

# Makkot 22

## Single Act, Multiple Acts

### Continuity & Warnings

The daf opens in the middle of a discussion concerning the relationship between multiple transgressions and a single continuous act. The governing principle, familiar from earlier in the tractate, is that a single unbroken act produces only one set of lashes, regardless of how many times the forbidden conduct is repeated, so long as only one warning was issued at the outset. If, however, a separate warning was administered before each successive iteration of the act, each such iteration constitutes a distinct transgression warranting its own set of lashes. The *mishnah* applies this principle to the case of *shaatnez*: if a person removes and re-dons a garment containing a forbidden wool-linen mixture, each donning following a separate warning generates a new liability for lashes.

### Rav Assi's Position

The *gemara* opens with a statement of Rav Bibi in the name of Rav Assi: *lo poshet velo lovesh mammash ela afilu machnis umotzi beit hatzavar ukli shelo* — one need not actually strip the garment completely and redress. Even if a person merely withdraws one arm from a sleeve and then reinserts it, that partial removal followed by partial reinsertion constitutes a new act of "putting on," sufficient to generate a new transgression if accompanied by a fresh warning.

### Wearing vs. Putting On

Rav Acha the son of Rav Ika demurred, gesturing to indicate that only a full withdrawal and reinsertion — *yulei ve'afukei* — would qualify. According to the *Rivan*'s explanation, he requires complete removal and redressing. Rav Ashi goes furthest. He holds that one need not even perform any physical movement at all, provided only that sufficient time has elapsed — *kedei lifshot velilvosh*, enough time to remove and replace the garment. In other words, the mere continued wearing of *shaatnez*, given the theoretical opportunity to have removed it, constitutes a new punishable act.

### Act Definition

Rav Ashi's position is genuinely puzzling. If the *issur* is simply *lo tilbash shaatnez* — the ongoing state of wearing — then one would expect that the choice not to remove the garment when one had the opportunity would suffice: I had the chance to remove it and did not, therefore I have chosen to continue wearing it. That would be a coherent theory of passive liability. But Rav Ashi introduces the additional requirement that enough time passed to both remove *and* replace the garment, not merely to remove it. This suggests he is conceptualizing the violation not as an ongoing state of *levisha* but as a virtual, theoretical act of *levishas* — a renewed putting-on — that he imagines occurring during that window of time. This is a striking middle position: the violation is modeled as an act of donning, yet it is entirely notional, not physical.

One might extend this framework to analogous cases, such as a *nazir* who continues drinking. There, the relevant act is drinking, not the picking up of a cup, and so the theory of virtual repetition would presumably apply there as well. But why specifically the time to both remove and replace, rather than merely the time to remove? The answer seems to lie precisely in Rav Ashi's conceptual framing: since he is treating the ongoing wearing as a constructive, theoretical act of re-donning, the minimum window he requires is the time it would take to accomplish that complete act.

---

## Plowing & Kilayim

### Mishna's 8 Sins

The *gemara* shifts to the second part of the *mishnah*, which enumerates how a person can transgress eight separate *lavin* in the course of plowing a single furrow: *yesh choresh telem echad vechayav alav mishum shemoneh lavin*. One furrow, eight prohibitions. The *mishnah* specifies, among other things, the prohibition of *kilayim b'kerem* — planting mixed species in a vineyard.

### Covering = Planting

Rav Yannai reports a ruling issued in a gathering of scholars: *bechabura nimnu vegamru, hachofer bekilayim lokeh* — they took a vote and concluded that one who covers *kilayim* seeds with dirt receives lashes, because that covering constitutes a form of planting. The prohibition, *lo tizra karmicha kilayim*, speaks of *zeriya* — planting — and covering seeds with earth is deemed a form of *zeriya*, since it is the act of bringing the seed into productive contact with the soil.

### Yochanan's Reply

Rabbi Yochanan responded: *lav mishnateinu hi zo?* — is this not already implicit in our own *mishnah*? He asks: how is it that the *mishnah* lists the prohibition of *kilayim* as one of the lashes incurred by plowing a furrow? Plowing a furrow is not planting a seed — one might presume it generates no *kilayim* violation at all. The only coherent answer is *lav demichasseh behadi de'azil* — that as the plow advances, it turns over dirt that covers the pre-existing seeds, and that covering constitutes a form of planting. The *chiddush* of Rav Yannai, Rabbi Yochanan is saying, is already embedded in the *mishnah* itself.

### Pearl Analogy

Rav Yannai responded with a memorable rejoinder: *ei lav de'dalina lach chaspa mi mishkachat marganita tutei* — had I not lifted the pottery shard for you, you never would have found the pearl hidden beneath it. This is a sharp and accurate observation about the nature of insight. Once the idea is stated — that covering with dirt is a form of planting — the *pshat* of the *mishnah* appears obvious, even inevitable. But before the idea was articulated, it was not obvious at all. Rabbi Yochanan can only say "of course, it is already in the *mishnah*" because Rav Yannai first revealed it. The best test of a genuine *pshat* is precisely that once stated it becomes self-evidently correct — yet the fact that it required articulation proves it was a discovery.

### Reish Lakish Agrees

Reish Lakish added: *ei lav de'kalsach gavra raba* — had this great man not praised you, meaning, had Rabbi Yochanan not confirmed by his response that the idea is already embedded as *pshat* in the *mishnah*, Reish Lakish would have said the *mishnah* follows Rav Yannai's *chiddush* as a minority position. But since Rabbi Yochanan agreed and treated it as plain *pshat*, it is clearly the straightforward reading of the *mishnah*. The implication is that Reish Lakish is himself persuaded by Rabbi Yochanan's confirmation.

### Rabbi Akiva View

This agreement having been established, the *gemara* notes that had Rabbi Yochanan not endorsed that *pshat*, one could have read the *mishnah* entirely differently. The *mishnah* could have reflected the position of Rabbi Akiva, who holds that *af hamekayem* — even one who merely allows *kilayim* to remain in his field, without doing anything active — transgresses. This is a remarkable *chiddush*: passive toleration of *kilayim* is itself a punishable act, just as, in the earlier discussion, merely continuing to wear *shaatnez* may itself constitute an active violation. Indeed it is worth noting that both cases involve *kilayim* — one in the domain of *beged kilayim shaatnez*, one in *kilayim b'kerem* — and both raise the identical structural question: why is a passive state treated as an actionable *maaseh* sufficient to generate lashes?

The *gemara* here does not resolve why Rabbi Akiva's *kilayim* constitutes a *lav she'yesh bo maaseh* rather than a *lav she'ein bo maaseh*, which ordinarily does not generate lashes. The same question, left unanswered, applies to Rav Assi's position on *shaatnez*. The two problems are parallel.

### Verse Exegesis

The source for Rabbi Akiva's position is a *braisa* that derives it from a close reading of the verse: *sadchecha lo tizra kilayim*. On the surface, the verse prohibits the act of *zeriya* — planting. Rabbi Akiva, however, reads the verse as *kilayim sadchecha lo* — the *kilayim* shall not be in your field — separating the verb *tizra* from the object *kilayim sadchecha*, and reading the latter phrase independently to forbid the mere presence of *kilayim* in one's domain.

### Active vs. Passive

The *gemara* offers a possible way of reconciling the active-versus-passive tension within Rabbi Akiva's ruling. When the *mishnah* says one gets lashes for plowing a furrow while *kilayim* is present, perhaps the act of plowing is not itself a form of planting the *kilayim* — the plow does not plant them — but rather it constitutes an active demonstration that one intends to maintain the *kilayim* in the field. A person who sits inside the house while *kilayim* grows in his field is entirely passive. A person who goes out to the field and plows, cultivates, weeds, and fertilizes that field, without destroying the *kilayim*, is actively showing his desire to preserve them. This active demonstration transforms what would otherwise be passive toleration into the kind of affirmative conduct that warrants lashes. On this reading, the two questions resolve each other: the act is not planting *kilayim* per se, but rather the cultivation-as-endorsement that Rabbi Akiva's reading of *kilayim sadchecha lo* targets.

It is worth noting, almost parenthetically, that Rav Yannai's *chiddush* about covering as planting appears to be anticipated by the *braisa* itself, which states *hamechapeh bekilayim lokeh* — one who covers seeds of *kilayim* with dirt receives lashes. This seems already to encode the idea. The *gemara* leaves this without comment.

---

## Yom Tov Violations

### Ula's Challenge

Having established the *mishnah*'s scenario — plowing a furrow on *Yom Tov* with *kilayim* present — the *gemara* proceeds to ask why the *mishnah* stops at eight transgressions. Ula challenges Rav Nachman: *dilki nami mishum zorea b'Yom Tov* — the person should also receive lashes for the prohibition of planting on *Yom Tov*. Since the act of plowing is itself a form of planting the *kilayim*, and this is occurring on *Yom Tov*, the same furrow should generate two separate *Yom Tov* violations: one for plowing (*choresh*) and one for planting (*zorea*). Why does the *mishnah* not count both?

The initial response — *tana v'shiyer*, the *tanna* listed an incomplete list — is immediately rejected. The entire rhetorical point of the *mishnah* is to tell you the maximum: it explicitly says *shemoneh lavin*, eight. If nine could be derived from the identical scenario, the *mishnah* should have said nine.

### Shabbat vs Yom Tov

Rava resolves the difficulty with a fundamental distinction: *yesh chiluk melachos b'Shabbos v'ein chiluk melachos b'Yom Tov*. On *Shabbos*, each distinct *melacha* carries its own identity as a separate *aveira*. This is demonstrated by the rule that one who forgot it was *Shabbos* and performed all the *melachos* brings thirty-nine separate *korbanos* — each *melacha* is conceptually distinct. On *Yom Tov*, however, there is no such differentiation among *melachos*. Breaking *Yom Tov* by plowing and breaking *Yom Tov* by planting are not two separate *aveiros*; they are simply two different modes of committing the single *aveira* of violating *Yom Tov*. It is as though one received a single warning not to break *Yom Tov* and then broke it twice — whether by making two furrows or by making one furrow and planting — the result is one set of lashes, because the identity of the transgression is unified.

### Gid HaNasheh

This thesis faces an immediate challenge from Abaye, who cites a *mishnah* that appears to treat different *melachos* on *Yom Tov* as distinct *aveiros*. The case: one who cooks a *gid hanasheh* — the sciatic sinew, which is treated in this *mishnah* as flesh — in milk on *Yom Tov* and then eats it. The *mishnah* counts five separate sets of lashes: (1) eating a *gid hanasheh*, (2) eating *basar b'chalav*, (3) cooking *basar b'chalav*, (4) cooking without a permitted purpose (*she-lo letzorech*) — since one cooked something one cannot eat, the cooking serves no legitimate *Yom Tov* function — and (5) *havarah*, kindling the fire.

Crucially, both (4) and (5) are *Yom Tov* violations, and they are counted as two separate *aveiros*. This directly contradicts Rava's position that different *melachos* on *Yom Tov* are not distinct.

### Havarah Issue

The *gemara* initially attempts to address this by reinterpreting the fifth transgression: perhaps it is not *havarah* at all.

### Hekdesh Wood

The *gemara* proposes two revisions to the case. First, perhaps the fire was kindled with *atzei asheirah* — wood belonging to *avodah zarah* — making the fifth violation a transgression of deriving benefit from idolatrous property: *v'lo yidbak b'yadcha me'umah min hacherem*. This is immediately rejected, because if *asheirah* wood were involved, there should be yet a sixth transgression — *lo tavi to'evah el beitecha*, the prohibition against bringing such wood into one's possession.

The *gemara* therefore settles on a second revision: the wood was *atzei hekdesh* — consecrated property — and the prohibition is derived from the verse *v'ashreichem tisrefun ba'eish, lo taasun kein la-Hashem Elokeichem*, which is read to forbid the destruction of *hekdesh*. This is clearly not the *pshat* of the *mishnah*, as the *mishnah* makes no mention of *asheirah* wood or *hekdesh* wood. But it is the answer the *gemara* works with.

### Yom Tov Unified

The conclusion, then, is as follows: the *mishnah* about the *gid hanasheh* does not, in fact, count two separate *Yom Tov melachos* as two *aveiros*. The fifth transgression is not *havarah* as a *Yom Tov* violation but rather the forbidden use of *hekdesh* wood, which is an entirely independent prohibition. With that revision accepted, Rava's principle stands: two different *melachos* on *Yom Tov* are treated as a single *aveira* of breaking *Yom Tov*, not as two distinct *aveiros*. Plowing and planting in the *mishnah*'s scenario are simply two ways of breaking *Yom Tov*, and since a single warning was issued, only one set of lashes results. This is an important and counterintuitive principle, and it stands in sharp contrast to the *Shabbos* framework, where each *melacha* retains its distinct identity.

---

## Added Transgressions

### Nachal Eitan

Having resolved the internal tension within the *mishnah*'s scenario, the *gemara* opens a more playful register, entertaining ways that additional transgressions could theoretically be appended to the furrow-plowing case by modifying the scenario's circumstances. Rav Hoshaya asks: why not also include the prohibition of planting or plowing in the *nachal eitan* — the valley designated for the *eglah arufah* ritual? The verse *asher lo ye'aveid bo v'lo yizara* prohibits working or planting in that valley. Since the *mishnah*'s scenario already involves planting and plowing, one could simply specify that the field is located in the *nachal eitan* and gain another transgression.

### Erasing Name

Rav Chanina asks: why not include one who erases God's name in the course of plowing? The prohibition of erasing a divine name is derived from *v'ibadtem et shemam... lo ta'asun kein la-Hashem Elokeichem*. One could imagine the plow passing over a piece of parchment on which God's name is written, causing its erasure. By this point, the *gemara* is beginning to construct scenarios that are only incidentally related to the act of plowing itself.

### Leprous Spot

Rabbi Abbahu presses further: why not include one who cuts off a leprous spot (*baheret*), which is forbidden under *hishamer b'nega hatzaraas*? One could imagine — and the *gemara* is clearly now approaching the absurd — a person positioning a diseased limb in the path of the plow in order to excise the spot. The *gemara* is simply enumerating any conceivable violation that could, under some contrived circumstance, accompany the act of plowing.

### Choshen & Ephod

Abaye continues: one who displaces the *choshen* — the High Priest's breastplate — from the *ephod* transgresses a prohibition derived from *lo yizach hachoshen*. One could imagine the High Priest standing in the field, being jostled by the plow. Abaye adds further: one who removes the staves of the *aron* from their rings likewise violates *lo yasuru*. The scenario now involves, somehow, the Ark of the Covenant being in the path of the furrow.

### Asheira Wood

Rav Ashi returns to more realistic territory: one who plows with a plow constructed from *asheirah* wood derives benefit from *avodah zarah* property, in violation of *v'lo yidbak b'yadcha me'umah min hacherem*. This is at least not incidental to the act of plowing itself — the wood is integral to the implement.

### Fruit Trees

Ravina asks: why not include one who cuts down good fruit trees? If the furrow passes through an orchard and the plow fells productive fruit trees without purpose, that would constitute *bal tashchis*, derived from *ki mimenu tochal v'oso lo tichrot*. This too is a reasonably natural adjunct to the act of plowing.

### Oath Not to Plow

The most substantive addition is raised by Rav Zeira to Rabbi Mani: why not include a case where the person swore an oath not to plow? An oath of that kind would add a violation of *shevua* to the other transgressions. However, if one specifies that the oath was not to plow on *Yom Tov* — which fits the *mishnah*'s existing scenario — the *shevua* would not take effect at all, for the principle of *mushba ve'omed me'Har Sinai*: one cannot take an oath to repeat a Torah obligation or prohibition, since one is already "sworn from Sinai" to observe it. The oath is therefore redundant and does not generate additional liability.

---

## Issur Kolel

### Oath Problem

The problem with adding the *shevua* violation is thus the doctrine of *mushba ve'omed me'Har Sinai*. An oath not to plow on *Yom Tov* cannot take effect because the Torah has already imposed that prohibition.

### Generic Oath

The resolution: specify that the oath was not simply *not to plow on Yom Tov* but rather *shevua shelo achrosh bein b'chol bein b'Yom Tov* — a generic oath never to plow at all, on weekdays as well. Since the oath clearly does take effect on ordinary weekdays — where there is no prior prohibition — it has a legitimate scope of application and is not entirely redundant.

### Kolel Principle

This triggers the principle of *issur kolel*: when a prohibition encompasses a broader range of situations, it takes effect even in the specific area where it is technically redundant. Because the oath not to plow is valid on weekdays, it is a genuine *issur* with real force across a wide domain. By virtue of that broader applicability, it takes effect *even* on *Yom Tov*, adding a *shevua* violation on top of the pre-existing *Yom Tov* prohibition. This is the one addition in this entire sequence that the *gemara* treats with full analytical seriousness. All the previous cases — the *choshen*, the *aron*, the leprous spot, the erased name — were almost entirely incidental to the act of plowing, constructed violations of extreme artificiality. This case, by contrast, genuinely concerns an oath about plowing, and the question of why it was not included in the *mishnah* is a real halachic question deserving a real answer.

---

## Oaths Not Listed

### Reversible Excluded

The *gemara* offers an answer to why the *mishnah* nonetheless omits the *shevua* case: *midei d'islei b'she'ila lo katani* — the *mishnah* does not list prohibitions that are subject to reversal through *she'ila*, i.e., petitioning a sage for release. An oath, even one governed by *issur kolel*, can in principle be annulled through *hataras nedarim*, and the *mishnah*'s catalog of transgressions is limited to absolute, irrevocable prohibitions.

### Bechor Challenge

The *gemara* immediately challenges this: one of the cases in the *mishnah* involved an animal that was *hekdesh* — consecrated property — and sanctification is created through a verbal act, similar to an oath, and is in principle reversible through *she'ila*. The *gemara* responds: *b'bechor* — the *mishnah* refers not to an animal consecrated by a human verbal act, but to a *bechor*, a firstborn animal, whose sanctity is Torah-imposed without any speech act by its owner and therefore admits of no annulment.

### Nezir Challenge

A stronger challenge: the *mishnah* also includes a *nazir* in a cemetery. *Nezirut* is created through a vow — a verbal declaration — and is equally subject to *hataras nedarim*. Why is *nezir* included if reversible prohibitions are excluded?

### Nezir Shimshon

The *gemara* responds: *b'nazir Shimshon* — the *mishnah* refers specifically to a *nazir Shimshon*, which cannot be revoked. The *Rivan* explains: the defining feature of *nezirus Shimshon* is that it was not self-imposed through a voluntary declaration but was decreed by divine mandate — the angel announced to Shimshon's parents that *nazir yiheyeh ha-yeled*, the child shall be a *nazir*. Because the *nezirut* originated not from the person's own speech act but from a divine command, it cannot be undone through *she'ila* — there is no human petitioner to release it, and the originating authority is not a human vow.

This leaves the *mishnah* in an awkward posture: does the *halachic* category of *nazir Shimshon* require an actual angelic visitation? The *Rivan* entertains but rejects the alternative explanations. One might have said, for instance, that the category applies when a parent accepted the *nezirut* on a child's behalf — in which case the child, when grown, cannot individually revoke it, even if the parent theoretically could. Or one might argue that among the distinctive features of *nezirus Shimshon* as a formal category is simply that it is irrevocable regardless of who accepted it. The *Rivan* inclines toward the angel-visitation explanation, acknowledging that this limits the category to extraordinary circumstances.

### Hataras Nedarim

A further difficulty: one of the unique features of *nazir Shimshon* is that, unlike ordinary *nezirus*, it does not prohibit contact with the dead — as the story of Shimshon himself makes clear, since he was perpetually engaged with mortality. If *nazir Shimshon* does not restrict contact with the dead, how can the *mishnah* use it as the paradigm case for lashes in a cemetery? The *gemara* notes as well that *nazirus Shimshon* is explicitly mentioned in the formula of *hataras nedarim* recited on *Erev Rosh Hashanah*, where different textual versions either include *nazirus Shimshon* among the vows being released or specifically except it. This very ambiguity in the *nusach* reflects the underlying debate about whether *nezirus Shimshon* is subject to *she'ila* at all.

### No Issur Kolel

The *gemara* ultimately abandons the entire approach. *Ela hai tanna issur kolel leis lei* — the *tanna* of our *mishnah* simply does not hold of the principle of *issur kolel*. On this view, even a generic oath not to plow ever does not take effect on *Yom Tov*, because on *Yom Tov* the person was already prohibited by the Torah and remains, as it were, *mushba ve'omed me'Har Sinai*. The *tanna* rejects the mechanism by which a broader *shevua* could piggyback on its weekday validity to generate liability for *Yom Tov* as well. Consequently, no version of the *shevua* scenario produces a genuine additional *aveira* for the *mishnah* to count, and its absence from the list requires no further explanation. The *mishnah* may freely include reversible prohibitions — the argument from *she'ila* is abandoned — but the *shevua* case simply fails as a matter of this *tanna*'s *halachic* framework.

---

## Lashes Count

### 39 Not 40

The *mishnah* now turns to the administration of lashes itself. The Torah prescribes forty lashes — *arba'im yakenu lo yosif* — yet the *mishnah* records that the number administered is thirty-nine: *arba'im chaser achat*.

### Verse Reread

The derivation rests on a reading of the phrase *bemispar arba'im*: the number that is within, or adjacent to, forty — meaning the highest number that falls short of forty. The *gemara* formulates this as *minyan shehu samuch le-arba'im* — a count that approximates forty — yielding thirty-nine. Rabbi Yehuda dissents from this reinterpretation.

### Rabbi Yehuda

Rabbi Yehuda holds that the full forty lashes are administered, and he derives from the verse *mah makkot ha-eleh bein yadecha* that the fortieth lash is given between the shoulder blades. The *gemara* notes, however, that this verse's plain meaning concerns false prophets who, in the messianic era, will attempt to disavow their prophetic past and attribute their bruises to an ordinary altercation: *asher hukkeiti beit me'ahavai*. The rabbis read it instead as governing corporal punishment administered in school settings, not court-ordered lashes — a reading invoked once before in the tractate.

### Assessment

Having already departed from the Torah's explicit number of forty, the *mishnah* goes further: not every offender receives even the thirty-nine. The court first assesses (*omeid*) how many lashes the person can withstand, and whatever number is determined must be divisible by three, since the lashes are divided across three locations on the body. The logic seems to be: once the rabbis have established that forty does not mean forty, the number itself is no longer sacrosanct, and the court's authority to calibrate the punishment appropriately becomes operative.

### Lock-In Rule

A critical rule governs the assessment: once the process of lashing has begun, the court is locked into its original number. If the assessment was thirty-nine and the person proves unable to withstand the full amount after lashing has commenced, he goes free entirely — the court cannot simply reduce the number mid-process, because its authority is limited to the assessment made prior to commencement. Symmetrically, if the assessment was eighteen and the person proves more resilient than expected once lashing begins, the court cannot increase the number; he receives only the assessed eighteen and goes free of any additional liability. The principle is: *laka in, lo laka lo* — only once lashing has begun are these constraints in force; prior to commencement, the assessment may in principle be revised.

### Rabbinic Authority

Rava famously marks the passage with an observation about rabbinic authority: *kama tipsha'i she'ar inshi de-kaimi mikmei Sefer Torah v'lo kaimi mikmei gavra raba*. How foolish are ordinary people, who rise before a *Sefer Torah* when it enters a room but do not rise before a great Torah sage. The proof: the Torah writes forty, and the rabbis said thirty-nine, and their word prevails. The *Sefer Torah* says forty; the *gavra raba* says thirty-nine; and at the end of the day, it is the sage's interpretation that determines what "forty" means in practice. Just as, in constitutional terms, the text of a constitution is ultimately given meaning by the court interpreting it, so too the Torah's numbers are given operative meaning by the rabbinic sages. Their interpretive authority supersedes the raw text.

This observation also illuminates why the departure from forty was felt necessary in the first place. Once the number forty is opened up to reinterpretation — once it has been established that forty can mean thirty-nine — the entire principle of a fixed, irrevocable count is undermined, and the authority to calibrate the punishment further, based on the individual's capacity, flows naturally from that same source of rabbinic interpretive power.

### Reassessment

The *mishnah*'s implication — that reassessment is permissible before lashing begins but not after — is challenged by a *braisa* that appears to prohibit reassessment even before commencement. If the court assessed forty and then reconsidered before a single lash was struck, concluding the person could not withstand forty, the *braisa* says he goes free entirely. Similarly, if assessed at eighteen and then found capable of more before lashing began, the court is still bound to eighteen. This seems to prohibit pre-commencement reassessment as well, contradicting the *mishnah*.

### Same Day

Rav Sheshet resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between assessments made for the same day and assessments made in advance for a future day. If the assessment and the lashing are scheduled for the same day, a reassessment conducted before lashing begins is treated as a correction of an obvious error — analogous to a retraction made within the immediate frame of the original decision — and is permissible. If, however, the assessment was made on one day for a lashing to take place on a different day, no reassessment is permitted even before the process begins, because the original assessment was made as a considered, forward-looking determination, not an in-the-moment judgment subject to instant revision. The *gemara* acknowledges that this distinction is not fully transparent — one might argue that a lashing on a different day is precisely the situation where new information about health or capacity should most readily allow reassessment — but Rav Sheshet's formulation is the *gemara*'s resolution of record.

---

## Two Sins One Act

### Bundle or Separate

The final *mishnah* addresses a person who performs one act that transgresses two separate *lavin* simultaneously — such as, in the *mishnah*'s scenario, plowing with *kilayim* on *Yom Tov* or on *Shemita*, where a single furrow generates two distinct punishments. The question is how the administration of two separate sets of lashes is structured.

### Single Counts

If the court makes a single bundled assessment (*omed echad*) for both transgressions together, the offender receives whatever number of lashes that unified assessment yields — perhaps thirty-nine, perhaps thirty-six, perhaps forty-two — and that total counts toward both sets of liability simultaneously. The lashes are not divided into a first set for transgression one and a second set for transgression two; rather, one continuous administration of lashes discharges both obligations within whatever the court's assessment permits.

### Dual Sessions

The alternative is that the court makes two separate assessments, treating each transgression independently. In that case, the offender receives the first set of lashes today, heals, and returns for the second set on a subsequent occasion. The practical consequence of choosing between the bundled and separate models is significant: the separate model will almost always result in the offender receiving more total lashes.

### Braisa

A *braisa* challenges the bundled model, asserting *ein omdin omed echad bishnei lavin* — one may not make a single assessment for two transgressions. This appears to mandate the separate model categorically.

### Threshold of 42

Rav Sheshet resolves the contradiction by introducing a threshold. The key question is whether the offender can withstand forty-two or more lashes. This number is not arbitrary: thirty-nine lashes satisfy the first transgression in full; the minimum number of lashes that can be attributed to the second transgression while still constituting a coherent unit (divisible by three) is three. Therefore, thirty-nine plus three equals forty-two. Only if the court's assessment reaches at least forty-two can the lashes meaningfully encompass both transgressions. At forty-two or above, a single assessment that bundles both transgressions is possible: the first thirty-nine satisfy transgression one, and the remainder — three, six, nine, or whatever the assessment yields beyond thirty-nine — begins to address transgression two.

### Below 42

If the person can only withstand forty-one or fewer lashes, the bundled model is unavailable. In that range, even the full administered count cannot reach thirty-nine for transgression one and still leave any remainder for transgression two, since there is no number below forty-two that both fully satisfies transgression one and contributes something to transgression two. Consequently, below the threshold of forty-two, the court must proceed with two separate sessions: it administers lashes for transgression one today, waits for the offender to recover, and holds a second session for transgression two. Whether at or above the threshold the court *must* use the bundled model, or merely *may*, appears to be at the court's discretion — it can opt for either approach. But below forty-two, the separate model is mandatory. The *gemara* concludes here, and the discussion continues in the following session.

---

---

# Makkot 23

## Malkot Procedure

### Overview

Makkot 23 concludes with what is, in many respects, a deeply unsettling passage to study. The final two *mishnayot* of the tractate deal with the precise mechanics of *malkot*—how lashes are actually administered—and then pivot to some of the most profound theological statements in the entire *masechta*. We begin at the bottom of 22b, with the *mishnah* that opens: *keitsad malkin oto*—how do we administer the lashes?

### Binding & Position

The procedure begins with binding the offender's hands to a post. The post stands roughly one and a half to two *amot* high, and the person receiving the lashes leans against it—not standing upright and not sitting, but tilted sideways—so that lashes can be delivered both to the front and to the back. The *mishnah* states: *kofet shtei yadav al ha-amud heylach ve-heylach*—his two hands are tied to the post on either side, so that he cannot resist or interfere with the procedure.

### Degradation Principle

The *chazzan ha-knesset*—the attendant—grabs hold of the offender's garments. *Im nikreu nikreu ve-im nifremu nifremu ad she-hu megaleh et libo*: if they are torn, they are torn; if they unravel, they unravel—until the person's heart is exposed. The exposure is required so that one can see exactly where the lashes land, but the *mishnah* is careful to specify that this exposure goes only as far as is necessary. The principle at work throughout this entire procedure is *nikleh*—degradation. There is a deliberate point to the *bizayon*, the humiliation, but it is bounded: degradation is the vehicle, not the destination.

This dynamic is reminiscent of what we find with the *sotah*, where a comparable form of controlled exposure takes place. Here too, the underlying principle is that the offender must undergo a defined experience of *nikleh* and emerge from it redeemed—as we will see later, the *pasuk* concludes *veniklah achicha le'einecha*, "and your brother will be degraded before your eyes," which the *gemara* reads as: once he has been degraded, he becomes *achicha*—your brother once again.

### Strap Construction

Behind the attendant, a stone is placed on which he stands—*ve-even netunah me-achorav, ve-hazan ha-knesset omed aleha*. In his hand is a strap of calf skin, doubled over: *retzuah be-yado shel egel kefulah*. It is doubled once and then again—*echad li-shnayim ve-shnayim le-arba'ah*—so that it has multiple layers. On the sides of this strap hang two additional straps of donkey leather—*shtei retzuot shel chamor olot ve-yordot*—that rise and fall with each strike. Based on Rashi, these elements appear to have been woven together, though the Steinsaltz illustrations present their own reconstruction.

### Measurements

The handle of the strap has a specific measurement: *yad tefach ve-rochvah tefach*—a *tefach* in length and a *tefach* in width. The tip of the strap should reach as far as the belly of the person being lashed: *ve-roshah maga'at al pi kreiso*. The distribution of lashes is likewise precisely defined: *u-makeh oto shlish mil-fanav ve-shtei yadot me-achorav*—one third of the lashes on the front (over the heart) and two thirds on the back.

### Striking Position

The flogger strikes with one hand and with full force: *ve-hamakeh beyado achat bechol kocho*. This is derived from the *pasuk* of *vehippilo ha-shofeyt*—"the judge shall fell him"—which, as we will discuss at greater length, yields two separate teachings from a single word. Counterintuitively, the tradition understands a one-handed strike as producing greater force than a two-handed strike, and that is the standard applied here.

### Verses & Word Count

Three individuals are present during the procedure: the *makeh* (the one who strikes), a *koreh* (one who reads *psukim* aloud), and a third who counts the lashes and coordinates the strikes. The *koreh* recites the following verses throughout the procedure.

The first passage is from Devarim (28:58–59): *im lo tishmor la'asot et kol divrei ha-torah ha-zot... vehifla Hashem et makotecha*—"if you do not observe all the words of this Torah... Hashem will make your plagues extraordinary." After completing this section, *vechozer le-tichilat ha-mikra*—he returns to the beginning of the reading. The second passage is from Devarim (29:8): *ushmartem et divrei ha-brit ha-zot va'asitem otam*—"and you shall observe the words of this covenant and fulfill them." The procedure closes with the verse from Tehillim (78:38): *ve-hu rachum yechaper avon velo yashchit*—"and He, being merciful, atones for iniquity and does not destroy," again followed by a return to the beginning of the reading.

One of the commentators notes that the *teivot*—the word count of these *psukim*—can be arranged to reach the number 39. One reckoning: the first passage from Devarim runs to 21 words, then *vehifla Hashem et makotecha* adds 13 more, for 34. Add the first five words of *ushmartem et divrei ha-brit ha-zot*, and one arrives at 39. Another reckoning, advanced by the Maharsha, is that the three closing verses are each precisely 13 words, totaling 39. Both calculations are plausible and appear in the sources.

There is a notable element of *teshuvah* embedded in this structure. The procedure does not conclude on a note of pure punishment; rather, *ushmartem et divrei ha-brit ha-zot*—"guard the words of this covenant"—is placed deliberately to give the offender an orientation toward repentance, not merely chastisement. The closing verse of *ve-hu rachum* similarly frames the moment as one of divine mercy rather than naked retribution. The juxtaposition is striking: *ve-hu rachum, yechaper avon*—He is merciful—is declared even as the strike lands. One might read this as an expression of the principle that punishment in this system functions as education and purification, in the spirit of *chosech shivto soneh beno*—one who withholds the rod hates his child.

A question naturally arises about how the verses were coordinated with the strikes—whether each word corresponded to one strike, or whether the *psukim* were recited continuously as a backdrop to the grouped lashes of 13, 13, and 13. This remains unclear. The *mishnah* itself notes that the *koreh* adjusts his pace: *bezman she-makah merubah ma'arich, bezman she-makah mu'etet mekatzeir*—when there are more lashes he prolongs the reading, when fewer he shortens it. This suggests that the verse-reading was not a rigid one-word-per-strike system, but rather something timed broadly to the duration of the procedure, though the precise mechanics are not spelled out.

### Death Liability

The *mishnah* continues: *umet tachat yado patur*—if the person being lashed dies in the course of the procedure, the flogger is exempt from liability. This is because the process was preceded by a medical assessment that determined the person was fit to receive the prescribed lashes. If death occurred within the parameters of that authorized procedure, the flogger bears no criminal responsibility.

However, if the flogger added even one extra lash beyond what was prescribed—*hosif lo od retzuah achat va-met*—and the person died as a result, the flogger is subject to *galut*, exile to an *ir miklat*, the same consequence as one who kills *be-shegegah*, unintentionally.

### Nikleh Dismissal

The *mishnah* introduces a final basis for dismissal from the lashing: *nitkalkel bein be-rei bein be-mayim, patur*—if the offender becomes soiled, whether by what one would delicately call number two or number one, the lashing stops immediately. The reasoning is tied to the principle of *nikleh*: the degradation has already occurred, and continuing the lashes would exceed what the Torah intended. Rabbi Yehudah draws a distinction between men and women in this regard—for a man, the dismissal is triggered by the former; for a woman, by the latter. The implications of this distinction are discussed in greater detail below.

---

## Smichuyot & Sources

### Why Nikleh

The *gemara* opens its analysis of the *mishnah* with a foundational question: *mai ta'ama? mishum nikleh*—what is the reason for this entire procedure? It is because of *veniklah achicha le'einecha*, the *pasuk* in Devarim that frames the lashing in terms of degradation. The idea that the offender becomes *achicha*—your brother—after undergoing this humiliation is what gives the entire procedure its internal coherence. Everything that looks gratuitously harsh—the tearing of the garments, the exposure, the leaning posture—is in the service of *derech bizayon*, a defined path of degradation that, when completed, restores the offender to the community.

### Calf-Skin Source

A more difficult question follows. Rav Sheshet in the name of Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah asks: *minayin la-retzuah she-hi shel egel*—from where do we derive that the strap must be made of calf skin? The answer: *de-chtiv arba'im yakenu ve-samich lei lo tachsom shor be-disho*—the *pasuk* of "forty lashes shall be given to him" (*arba'im yakenu*) is written in proximity to the *pasuk* of "you shall not muzzle an ox while it threshes" (*lo tachsom shor be-disho*). From the proximity of these two verses, we learn something about the material of the strap—a *shor* (ox) is connected, and *shor* is connected to *egel* (calf). Admittedly, this requires some inferential steps that are not fully transparent to us, and the *gemara* itself is working from a received tradition here. There is an additional resonance: the tradition that the *parah adumah* (red cow) atones for the sin of the *egel ha-zahav* (the golden calf). One commentator suggests that *egel* etymologically connects to *ma'agal*—going in circles, self-absorption—while *parah* relates to *lifroth*, to be fruitful, to give outward. Whether that etymology illuminates the connection to the lashing strap or not, it remains a suggestive piece of the larger picture.

### Smichuyot Concept

The technique being employed here is *smichuyot*—the principle that *psukim* placed in proximity to one another in the text illuminate each other. When two commandments or narratives stand side by side, the Sages understood that the juxtaposition itself carries legal or homiletical significance. This is a well-established mode of deriving *halacha* and *aggadah* in rabbinic literature, though the specific connections are not always fully recoverable. We possess the conclusions; some of the intermediate reasoning belongs to the *Torah she-be'al peh* that was not written down and has been lost to us.

### Smichuyot Examples

Rav Sheshet in the name of Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah brings several further examples of *smichuyot*.

The first: *minayin le-yevamah she-nafelah lifnei muke shchin she-ein chosmin otah*—from where do we learn that a *yevamah* who falls before a *yavam* whom she finds repulsive (described here as *muke shchin*, afflicted with a severe skin condition) cannot be compelled to marry him? The answer: *lo tachsom shor be-disho* is in textual proximity to *ki yeshvu achim yachdav*—the opening of the laws of *yibbum*. Just as we do not muzzle the ox in its moment of labor, so too we do not "muzzle" the *yevamah* by forcing her into a marriage that is intolerable to her. The *smichut*, the proximity, teaches the one from the other.

The second: *kol ha-mevazeh et ha-mo'adim ke-ilu oved avodah zarah*—anyone who treats the *mo'adim* with contempt is as though he has worshipped idols. The *mo'adim* referred to here are understood to be *Chol Ha-Mo'ed*, the intermediate days of Pesach and Sukkot—for the full *yom tov* days carry their own explicit obligations. The textual basis: *Elohei masechah lo ta'aseh lach* ("do not make molten gods") is in proximity to *et chag ha-matzot tishmor* ("you shall observe the festival of matzot"). The verse prohibiting idolatry stands directly beside the command to observe the festival, and from this proximity we derive the severity of degrading *Chol Ha-Mo'ed*.

The third: *kol ha-mesaper lashon ha-ra, ve-chol ha-mekabel lashon ha-ra, ve-chol ha-me'id edut sheker—ra'uy le-hashlicho la-klavim*—one who speaks *lashon ha-ra*, one who receives it, and one who gives false testimony, all deserve to be thrown to the dogs. The textual basis: *basar ba-sadeh tereifah lo tochelu la-kelev tashlichun oto* ("flesh torn in the field, you shall not eat; throw it to the dogs") stands in proximity to *lo tisa shema shav* ("do not carry a false report"), which is read homiletically as *lo tashi*—do not cause others to carry it. The letter in *tisa* can be read as either an *ayin* or an *aleph*, and the *gemara* here is willing to play on that ambiguity. The connection between discarding treife meat and discarding false speech is made through the proximity of these two *psukim*.

One cannot help but notice a certain tension: in other contexts in the *gemara*, great precision is brought to bear on individual letters—distinguishing an *ayin* from an *aleph*, a *yud* from a *vav*—and entire legal edifices are built on those distinctions. Here, the *gemara* itself seems to wave away the philological precision in the service of the *smichut*. This is, in a sense, the honest face of *Torah she-be'al peh*: we have the tradition, we have the conclusion, and we work with what we have, even when the derivation raises more questions than it answers.

### Donkey Strap

The *mishnah* mentioned that alongside the doubled calf-skin strap, there are *shtei retzuot shel chamor*—two straps of donkey leather. The *gemara* explains this through a teaching cited by a certain Galilean in the presence of Rav Chisda: *yada shor konehu ve-chamor evus ba'alav*—"an ox knows its owner, and a donkey its master's feeding trough" (Yeshayahu 1:3). The *chamor* is the animal that recognizes its provider and appreciates its sustenance. *Yisrael lo yada*, says the prophet—Israel did not recognize theirs. The *gemara* therefore says: *amar Hakadosh Baruch Hu, yavo mi she-makir evus ba'alav ve-yipara mi-mi she-eino makir evus ba'alav*—let the one who recognizes its master's trough come and call to account the one who does not. The donkey strap becomes a kind of testimony: an animal that knows its provider administers the reminder to the human being who forgot his.

---

## Size & Attendants

### Tefach Sizing

The *mishnah* specified that the handle of the strap should be a *tefach* in length and width. Abaye observes: *shema mina, kol chad ve-chad le-fum gabeih avdinan lei*—from this we infer that the strap is sized individually to the person being lashed. Since *tefach* varies by person, a bespoke strap must be fashioned for each individual, ensuring that neither too many nor too few lashes are effectively delivered.

### Loop Solution

Rava immediately raises the practical problem: *im ken, nafishu lehu retzuot tuva*—if so, the *beit din* would need an enormous stock of straps, one for every possible size. He resolves the difficulty: *avakta it leih, ki ba'ei miktar beih, ki ba'ei marpei leih*—the strap has a loop; when the attendant needs it tighter, he tightens it; when he needs it looser to fit the individual, he loosens it. One adjustable strap suffices for all.

### Distribution Source

The Gemara then asks: from where do we derive the specific distribution of one third to the front and two thirds to the back? Rav Kahana answers from the *pasuk*: *ve-hippilo ha-shofeyt ve-hikkahu le-fanav kedei rish'ato be-mispar*. The word *le-fanav*—"before him"—is read to indicate one portion to the front. The construction of the verse implies the remainder goes to the back: *rish'ah achat mil-fanav, shtei rishot me-achorav*—one punishment to the front, two to the back.

The *gemara* then asks further: from where do we derive that the strap must be doubled? Rav Chisda in the name of Rabbi Yochanan says: from the same word *ve-hippilo*. The word can be read as *ve-hikpilo*—and he shall double it. But this raises a question: if we use *ve-hippilo* to teach doubling, how can we simultaneously use it to derive the posture (that the judge "fells" him)? The *gemara* resolves: *shema mina tartei*—we derive both teachings from the same word. The single term yields two conclusions: the doubled strap and the tilted posture.

### Attendant Qualifications

The *mishnah* states that the one who strikes must do so with one hand and with full force. The *baraita* adds: *ein ma'amidin chazanin ela chasrei koach vi-yeterei mada*—we appoint only those who are lacking in physical strength but rich in knowledge. The reasoning is that such a person will be careful, attentive to the condition of the offender, and restrained enough not to exceed the prescribed measure.

### Attendant Dispute

Rabbi Yehudah disagrees: *afilu chasirei mada vi-yeterei koach*—one may appoint even someone deficient in knowledge, provided he is physically strong. Rava supports Rabbi Yehudah's position from the *pasuk*: *lo yosif pen yosif*—"he shall not add, lest he add." This redundant warning—"do not add, lest you add"—would be unnecessary if the attendant were already a thoughtful, learned person. The very fact that the Torah warns against excess implies the attendant is someone who needs to be told. The Sages who favor the learned attendant respond: *ein mezarzin ela la-mezoraz*—we caution even the cautious. The reminder is appropriate regardless of the attendant's disposition.

The *baraita* specifies the mechanics further: *keshe-hu magbia, magbia bi-shtei yadav; u-keshe-hu makeh, makeh be-yado achat*—when raising the strap, he raises with two hands; when striking, he strikes with one. This ensures the blow is measured and controlled rather than carried by the momentum of a two-handed swing.

### Three Judges

Three *dayanim* are present at the procedure. *Ha-gadol she-ba-dayanim korei*—the most senior judge reads the *psukim*. *Ha-sheni moneh*—the second counts the lashes. *Ve-ha-shlishi omer hakehu*—the third gives the signal to strike.

The *baraita* adds: *be-zman she-makah merubah ma'arich, be-zman she-makah mu'etet mekatzeir*—when the number of lashes is large, the *koreh* prolongs his reading; when the number is small, he shortens it. The reading is calibrated to the duration of the procedure as a whole.

---

## Dismissal Rules

### Maka Raba

The *gemara* now turns to the *baraita* on the prohibition against adding lashes. The *pasuk* itself says *maka raba*—a great blow. One might think this prohibition applies only to exceeding by a significant amount. The *baraita* clarifies: *maka raba ein li ela maka raba, maka mu'etet minayin—talmud lomar lo yosif*—even adding a single small lash is prohibited, as the verse states "he shall not add." If so, what does *maka raba* add? The *baraita* answers: it teaches us that even the prescribed lashes themselves already constitute *maka raba*—a great blow. One should not minimize or dismiss what the offender has already endured.

### Nitkalkel Dismissal

The *gemara* returns to the question of dismissal through *nitkalkel*—soiling. *Tanu rabanan: echad ha-ish ve-echad ha-isha be-rei, ve-lo be-mayim—divrei Rabbi Meir*—the *baraita* records that according to Rabbi Meir, both men and women are dismissed from lashing only in the case of the more severe soiling (number two), not the lesser. Rabbi Yehudah distinguishes: for a man it is number two, for a woman it is number one. The Sages say: for both men and women, either form of soiling is sufficient grounds for dismissal.

### Meir vs. Yehudah

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves an apparent contradiction in Rabbi Yehudah's position by explaining that while there may appear to be leniency extended to the woman, the operative conclusion is that for both men and women, the more severe soiling dismisses them from the procedure. *Shneihem shavim be-rei*—both are equal with respect to that standard.

### Escape & Breakage

The *gemara* raises a delightful case. Shmuel states: *kefatuhu ve-ratz mi-beit ha-din, patur*—if the offender was bound and somehow escaped from the court, he is exempt. The logic is that the act of escaping—in full view of everyone—already constitutes sufficient *bizayon*. The humiliation has occurred; there is nothing more to administer.

A parallel case distinguishes strap breakage from escape. If the strap broke during the second lash, the offender is dismissed. But if it broke during the very first lash, he is not—*barishona ein potrim oto*. Why? Because unlike the person who escaped—who actively underwent the humiliation of fleeing bound from the court—the person whose strap broke at the first strike has experienced only one lash, and the degradation associated with the process has not yet been sufficiently established. *Hatam ratz, hacha lo ratz*—in the one case, he ran; in the other, he did not.

### Sequence Rules

A final *baraita* addresses the timing of dismissal relative to the order of events. *Amduhu le-shilkeh, kala potrim oto*—if the court assessed him, and in the course of the assessment he became degraded, he is exempt. However: *le-cheshe-yatza mi-beit ha-din, kala malkin oto*—if he was degraded after leaving the court but before the lashing began, he is flogged anyway. *Ve-lo od ela afilu kala ba-techila malkin oto*—even if the degradation came at the very outset, he is still subject to lashing in that case.

The *pasuk* establishes the necessary sequence: *ve-hikkahu... ve-niklah*—first the lashing, then the degradation. If the degradation preceded the lashing entirely, it does not fulfill the Torah's intended order. The offender must first receive the lashes and then emerge from the procedure degraded—not the reverse. *Ve-lo she-lakah kvar be-veit din*—the lashing in the *beit din* must precede the *nikleh*.

---

## Malkot & Karatah

### Kareit Absolution

We arrive at the final *mishnah* of *Makkot*, and it is a remarkable one. *Kol chayavei keritot she-laku nifteru al yedei kritatan*—all those who are liable for *kareit*, if they received lashes, are absolved of their *kareit*. The textual basis: the proximity of the *kareit* passages to the verse *veniklah achicha le'einecha*—"and your brother will be degraded before your eyes." Once he has been degraded, *harei hu ke-achicha*—he is restored as your brother. These are the words of Rabbi Chananya ben Gamliel.

### Kal Vachomer

Rabbi Chananya ben Gamliel continues: *mah im over aveirah achat noten nafsho aleha, ha-oseh mitzvah achat al achat kamah va-chamah she-tinaten lo nafsho*—if one who commits a single transgression may forfeit his life on account of it, then one who performs a single *mitzvah* surely receives his life back, and more, *kal va-chomer*.

### Reward Ratio

Rashi's comment on this *kal va-chomer* is illuminating. The phrase *she-tinaten lo nafsho* reflects the principle that *midah tovah merubah mi-midat pur'anut*—the measure of divine goodness exceeds the measure of divine punishment. The ratio is *echad me-chamesh me'ot*—one to five hundred. How so? In the measure of punishment, the verse states *poked avon avot al banim al shileshim ve-al rive'im*—sin is visited upon the sons to the third and fourth generation, which gives us the factor of four. In the measure of goodness, the verse states *oseh chesed la-alafim*—kindness is done to thousands. The minimum plural of "thousands" is two thousand. Two thousand divided by four equals five hundred. The measure of goodness therefore exceeds the measure of punishment by a factor of at least five hundred to one.

### Shimon Derivation

Rabbi Shimon offers an alternative derivation that dispenses with the *kal va-chomer* entirely. He says: *mimkomo hu lomed*—we learn it from the verses themselves. The *pasuk* of *ve-nichretu ha-nefashot ha-osot* (those who commit transgressions shall be cut off) stands in proximity to *asher ya'aseh otam ha-adam va-chai ba-hem*—"which a person shall do and live by them." We are now at the top of 23b. The juxtaposition of *kareit* and *chai bahem* teaches directly that life is the reward for observance, without any inferential structure required.

### Reward for Inaction

This leads to a striking corollary: *ha kol ha-yoshev ve-lo avar aveirah notnim lo sachar ke-oseh mitzvah*—anyone who sits and refrains from a transgression is given the reward as though he had performed a positive *mitzvah*. The mere absence of sin, the deliberate non-act, is credited as a positive achievement.

### Blood Abstention

Rabbi Shimon the son of Rabbi extends this principle with a *kal va-chomer* of his own. The *pasuk* states *rak chazak le-vilti achol ha-dam ki ha-dam hu ha-nafesh*—"only be strong not to eat the blood, for the blood is the life." Blood is something that most people find instinctively repulsive; one would not eat it without being commanded otherwise. Yet by refraining from blood, one receives a reward. *Kal va-chomer*: *gezel va-arayot she-nafsho shel adam mitavah lahem*—theft and sexual immorality, which the soul genuinely desires—one who removes himself from those receives reward extending to his children, his children's children, and to the end of all generations: *al achat kamah va-chamah she-yizkeh lo u-le-dorotav ve-dorot dorotav*.

### Chananya ben Akashya

The *mishnah* closes with one of the most frequently cited statements in all of rabbinic literature: *Rabbi Chananya ben Akashya omer: ratza Hakadosh Baruch Hu le-zakot et Yisrael, le-fichach hirbah lahem Torah u-mitzvot*—the Holy One, Blessed be He, wished to confer merit upon Israel, and therefore multiplied for them Torah and *mitzvot*, as it is written: *Hashem chafetz le-ma'an tzidko, yagdil Torah ve-yadir*—"Hashem desired, for His righteousness, to make the Torah great and glorious."

The implication of Rabbi Chananya ben Akashya's teaching is that the abundance of *mitzvot* is itself an act of divine beneficence. A Torah with fewer commandments would have given us fewer opportunities for merit. Even those *mitzvot* that require little effort—or whose transgression is instinctively avoided—provide an occasion for reward. The comprehensive scope of *halacha* is thus not a burden but a gift, a divine strategy for maximizing the *zechuyot* of Israel.

---

## Kareit Dispute

### Yochanan Dispute

The *gemara* opens with a sharp rejoinder: *amar Rabbi Yochanan, chalukim alav chaveirav shel Rabbi Chananya ben Gamliel*—Rabbi Yochanan states that Rabbi Chananya ben Gamliel's colleagues dispute his ruling. The position that *malkot* can absolve *kareit* is not universally accepted. One can immediately see why the ruling is controversial: it opens the door to a kind of calculus whereby a person who is liable for *kareit* might seek to receive lashes—perhaps even engineering an early exit from the procedure through *nitkalkel*—as a means of shedding the more severe heavenly penalty.

### Yitzchak Position

The *gemara* then invokes Rabbi Yitzchak: *de-amar malkut be-chayavei keritot leika*—Rabbi Yitzchak holds that *malkot* simply cannot be applied to those liable for *kareit*. They are not interchangeable punishments.

### Shabbat vs. Yom Kippur

The *gemara* frames the underlying conceptual issue through the well-known distinction between Shabbat and Yom Kippur: *ein bein Shabbat le-Yom Ha-Kippurim ela she-zeh zedono bi-dei adam ve-zeh zedono be-kareit*—the difference between them is that willful transgression of Shabbat is punished *bi-dei adam* (by a human court, through *skilah*), while willful transgression of Yom Kippur carries *kareit*, a heavenly punishment. If Rabbi Chananya ben Gamliel's position were accepted fully—that *malkot* can substitute for *kareit*—then both Shabbat and Yom Kippur would ultimately be reducible to human-court punishments, collapsing the distinction between them. Rabbi Yitzchak's position is adduced from a *baraita*: *chayavei keritot be-chlal hayu*—those liable for *kareit* were originally included in the general category of lashing. The fact that the *kareit* of *achoto* (sleeping with one's sister) was singled out teaches that it is to be judged by *kareit* specifically, and not converted into *malkot*.

### Ashi Resolution

Rav Ashi offers a resolution that cuts through the apparent contradiction. *Zeh ikar zedono bi-dei adam, ve-zeh ikar zedono bi-dei shamayim*—in the case of Shabbat, the primary punishment is by human authority; in the case of Yom Kippur, the primary punishment is by the heavenly court.
