Rabbi Meir takes the opposite approach: he says *kol ha-se'irim kaparatan shavah al tumat mikdash ve-kodashav* — all the goats perform equivalent atonement for *tumat mikdash ve-kodashav*. There is no meaningful distinction between the *musaf* goat of Yom Kippur, the goats of *rosh chodesh*, and the goats of the *regalim*; all of them address the full range of *tumat mikdash* cases without differentiation. The case of *tahor she-achal et ha-tamei* is also covered by this general equivalence.

### Interchangeable Offerings

Given that these categories differ in what they atone for, the *mishnah* raises a practical question: what if the Yom Kippur goat became lost and was subsequently found on *rosh chodesh* of *Marcheshvan* — could it be used as the *musaf* goat for *rosh chodesh*?

One would expect the answer to be no: if each goat serves a distinct atonement function, a goat consecrated for one category should not be substituted for another. But Rabbi Shimon's response is *yikrevu* — yes, they may be used interchangeably. When pressed by his colleagues — *harei ein kaparatan shavah*, their atonement is not equivalent, so *heichi kreivim zeh ba-zeh*, how can you use one for the other? — Rabbi Shimon replies: *kulam ba'im le-chapper al tumat mikdash ve-kodashav* — they all come to atone for *tumat mikdash ve-kodashav*. Though each functions differently at the level of species, so to speak, they share the same genus. They are all variants of the same fundamental category of sin. Consequently, if you bring the Yom Kippur goat on *rosh chodesh*, it will function with the atonement capacity appropriate to *rosh chodesh*; if you bring a *rosh chodesh* goat on the *regalim*, it will function for the *regalim* category. When and where you bring it determines which specific function it performs, but since they are generically interchangeable, substitution is permitted.

### R. Shimon b. Yehuda

Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda transmits a different version of Rabbi Shimon's position, one that generates a more elegant internal structure. According to this version, the categories are not parallel but cumulative. The *se'irei rashei chodashim* atone for *tahor she-achal et ha-tamei* — one category. The *regalim* goats atone for *tahor she-achal et ha-tamei* plus the case of no *yediah* at all — two categories. The *musaf* of Yom Kippur atones for all three: *tahor she-achal et ha-tamei*, the case of no awareness, and the case of *yediah* only at the end. Each level of the calendar's sacred time adds an additional layer of atonement capacity.

This version also generates an interesting question about interchangeability: if the *rosh chodesh* goat can only atone for category C, and Yom Kippur's goat can atone for categories A, B, and C, then it is easy to understand using the Yom Kippur goat for a lesser day — it contains the capacity for C within it. But how can you take a *rosh chodesh* goat, which was only designated for C, and use it on Yom Kippur, where the requirement is atonement for A, B, and C? You would seemingly be using a goat of limited capacity to perform atonement it was never designed to provide. Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda's reply is the same: *kulam ba'im le-chapper al tumat mikdash ve-kodashav* — since they all belong to the same fundamental category, you may bring the *rosh chodesh* goat on Yom Kippur, and by virtue of being brought on Yom Kippur, it will perform the full Yom Kippur atonement. The time and context of the offering determines its scope; the generic interchangeability of all these goats — rooted in their shared purpose of addressing *tumat mikdash* — permits this flexibility.

## Scapegoat & Other Sins

### Se'ir Mishtale'ach

Having discussed the full array of goats and their functions in addressing *tumat mikdash ve-kodashav*, the *mishnah* turns to an entirely different dimension of Yom Kippur atonement. *Al she'ar aveirot she-ba-Torah* — for all other violations of the *Torah* — the full range of sins across all 612 other commandments, whether light or weighty, intentional or unintentional, whether the sinner was aware or unaware, whether it involved a positive commandment or a negative prohibition, and even if the transgression carried the penalty of *karet* or *mitot beit din* — for all of these, *se'ir ha-mishtale'ach mechaper* — the scapegoat atones.

This is the goat sent to *Azazel*, driven off the cliff into the barren land. Its function, as the *Torah* states, is to carry all the sins of the Jewish people — *ve-nasa avonotam el eretz gezeirah*. Notably, the *mishnah* here says only the *se'ir* atones, not Yom Kippur itself. Elsewhere in the *mishnah*, the *day* of Yom Kippur is mentioned alongside the *korban* as performing *toleh* or *kaparah*. Here only the *se'ir* is named — which of course creates a practical difficulty in the post-*Mikdash* era, when there is no *se'ir ha-mishtale'ach*. The resolution adopted by later *halachic* tradition is that the day of Yom Kippur itself is *mechaper* in the absence of the *korban*.

### Kohanim vs. Yisrael

The *mishnah* then states that the *se'ir ha-mishtale'ach* atones equally for *Yisrael*, for *kohanim*, and for the *kohen mashiach* — the *kohen gadol* himself. So where does the distinction between *kohanim* and *Yisrael* manifest? The *mishnah* answers: *she-ha-par mechaper al ha-kohanim al tumat mikdash ve-kodashav* — the *par*, the special bull sacrificed by the *kohen gadol*, atones for the *kohanim* specifically with respect to *tumat mikdash ve-kodashav*. In other words, the elaborate inner service of Yom Kippur involves two parallel tracks: a goat whose blood is brought into the *Kodesh Kodashim* for the atonement of *Yisrael*, and a bull whose blood is brought in for the atonement of the *kohanim*, in both cases specifically for *tumat mikdash ve-kodashav*. For all other sins, the *se'ir ha-mishtale'ach* covers everyone equally.

### R. Shimon on Kohanim

Rabbi Shimon, however, sees the distinction as running deeper. He observes that the inner service involves two instruments — blood and verbal *viduy*. *Keshem she-dam ha-se'ir ha-na'aseh bifnim mechaper Yisrael, kach dam ha-par mechaper al ha-kohanim* — just as the blood of the goat atones for *Yisrael* with respect to *tumat mikdash*, the blood of the bull atones for the *kohanim* with respect to *tumat mikdash*. So far, this parallels the anonymous position of the *mishnah*.

But Rabbi Shimon extends the parallel to the *se'ir ha-mishtale'ach*. The scapegoat carries the people's sins in part because of the *viduy* that the *kohen gadol* pronounces over it — the *ana Hashem chatati aviti pashati ani u-veiti* — by which the sins of the people are symbolically transferred to the goat before it is sent off. Now, the *kohen gadol* also recites *viduy* over the *par*, the bull — and Rabbi Shimon argues that just as the *viduy* over the scapegoat carries the sins of *Yisrael* away, so the *viduy* over the *par* carries the sins of the *kohanim* — all their sins, not only *tumat mikdash*. The blood of the *par* atones for the *kohanim*'s *tumat mikdash*, and the *viduy* over the *par* atones for all the remaining sins of the *kohanim*, paralleling precisely what the *se'ir ha-mishtale'ach* does for *Yisrael*.

The implication is striking: even for ordinary violations — *chillul Shabbat*, eating *chazir*, any run-of-the-mill transgression — *kohanim* and *Yisrael* have separate tracks of atonement on Yom Kippur. One might find this theologically challenging, as it suggests that *kohanim* occupy a categorically distinct position even in the realm of personal sin and divine forgiveness. Perhaps the intention is that *kohanim*, as the religious exemplars charged with maintaining the sanctity of the *avodah*, bear a higher standard and therefore require a distinct mechanism of atonement even for sins that in other respects parallel those of *Yisrael*. The symmetry Rabbi Shimon draws — blood and *viduy* for *Yisrael*, blood and *viduy* for *kohanim* — is aesthetically elegant, even if its theological implications require careful thought. We will return to these themes as we continue into the *masechet*.

---

---

# Shevuot 3

## Opening & Mishnah Struct…

### Intro & Mishnah Summary

We begin Shevuot 3 by picking up immediately after the very long *mishnah* that constitutes the entire first *perek*. The *mishnah* draws on the structural principle of "two which is four" — *shtayim she-hein arba* — which applies to *shevuot*: two categories of oaths in the past and two in the future. From there, however, the *mishnah* extends this same structural framework to an extensive series of cases involving *tumah*, covering the different ways in which a person who is *tamei* either enters the *Beit HaMikdash* or eats *korbanot*, with the consequence of bringing a *korban oleh veyored* — the sacrifice of variable value. The *mishnah* goes on to enumerate the various sacrificial rites — on *Yom Kippur*, *Rosh Chodesh*, and the *regalim* — that atone for the sin of *tumat mikdash*.

### Impurity & Atonement

The *mishnah*'s sustained focus on *tumat mikdash* is striking. It catalogs the personal *korban oleh veyored* brought when the violation was known at the outset, then forgotten, then recalled — as well as the range of communal *Yom Kippur* sacrifices that address various configurations of this sin.

### Yom Kippur & Scapegoat

In the *Torah*, *Yom Kippur* is centrally concerned with a kind of metaphysical cleansing of the *mikdash* itself, because all sin is understood to defile the sanctuary in a cosmic sense. The *mishnah*, however, shifts the focus away from this metaphysical dimension. Rather than the grand purification of the *mikdash*, the *mishnah* emphasizes atonement for the individual who accidentally entered the sanctuary while *tamei*. Toward the end of the *mishnah*, there is a return to broader scope: the *mishnah* notes that for all other sins — whether *meizid* or *shogeg*, whether punishable by death or relatively minor — the goat sent off the cliff on *Yom Kippur* atones.

### Why Temple Impurity?

This raises a genuine structural question: why do the first two chapters of a tractate named for oaths devote themselves almost entirely to the laws of *tumat mikdash*? At least part of the answer may lie in the final line of this *mishnah*. Having concluded *Sanhedrin* and *Makkot*, which deal exhaustively with the penalties for transgression — death sentences, lashes, exile — one might feel the overwhelming weight of all that sin and its consequences. Our *mishnah* offers an answering perspective: no matter how grave the transgression, even one for which the court would impose a death sentence, this single ritual on *Yom Kippur* — the dispatching of the goat — achieves atonement.

### Context: Sanhedrin & Mak…

The end of *Makkot* offered one reframing of the weight of all those transgressions: it is all *le-zazkot et Yisrael*, to ease the burden on the Jewish people — simply refrain from transgression and receive an enormous reward, so the entire weight of the forbidden is reimagined as an invitation to merit. Our *mishnah* provides a complementary answer: however heavily one has sinned, the mechanisms of *Yom Kippur* atonement remain available. So there is a conceptual bridge between the close of *Makkot* and the opening of Shevuot.

### Oath-Impurity Analogy

Beyond this thematic continuity, there is an analogy being drawn that may explain the deeper reason why *tumat mikdash* receives such extended treatment within a tractate devoted to oaths. The *korban* for a false oath and the *korban* for *tumat mikdash* are structurally identical — both are the *korban oleh veyored* — and in the *Torah* these two cases appear side by side. This juxtaposition is not merely textual coincidence; the *gemara* will make explicit that they appear together because they are genuinely analogous.

### Oaths & God's Presence

There is a further conceptual connection worth exploring. The entire *masechet* concerns the invocation of an oath — typically in God's name, either explicitly or implicitly — as a mechanism for establishing truth. When a person swears an oath, they are in effect summoning the divine presence to testify to the veracity of their claim; God is, as it were, brought into the world to bear witness. When that oath is false, the person has defiled the very space they created by that invocation. In the absence of the *mikdash*, the sworn oath in God's name is among the primary loci of divine presence in the world — and to violate it through falsehood carries something of the quality of *metamei ha-mikdash*, defiling the sanctuary. This, it may be argued, is why a *masechet* devoted to oaths opens with two full chapters on *tumat mikdash*: the two are understood as manifestations of a single underlying concern.

### Q&A: Yom Kippur & Sins

One might ask how *Yom Kippur* atonement relates to sins between one person and another — particularly in cases where the *Sanhedrin* would impose capital punishment. The answer is that *Yom Kippur* rectifies the relationship between the person and God, but human justice runs on a parallel track. A person could achieve the most complete *teshuvah* imaginable and be fully atoned for before Heaven, while the *beit din* would still be obligated to carry out its sentence. The system of earthly justice cannot simply dissolve its procedures on account of repentance, even repentance that is genuine and total — and this remains true in secular legal systems as well, which permit only very limited acknowledgment of transformation or remorse. Furthermore, when the sin involves another person, the *mishnah* in *Yoma* makes clear that *Yom Kippur* cannot atone until the offender has made things right with the person he has wronged. One cannot make things right with God while the interpersonal injury remains unaddressed.

---

## Gemara: Why This Order?

### Michti Question

The *gemara* opens with the word *michti* — "having just come from" — and poses its first question: *tanna me-heicha salik?* — from where did our *tanna* just depart? The tractate of Shevuot follows *Makkot*. *Mai shena de-tani Shavuot?* — why does Shevuot come after *Makkot*? This is a question not about the internal structure of our *masechet* but about the ordering of tractates within *Seder Nezikin*.

### Tractate Ordering

The scholarly consensus is that tractate ordering follows a principle of size — number of chapters, number of *mishnayot*. Even though Shevuot has more chapters than *Makkot*, if one treats *Sanhedrin* and *Makkot* as a single extended tractate — which the structure of those two *masachtot* effectively invites — then Shevuot follows naturally as the next tractate by size.

### Full List in Shevuot

But the *gemara* goes on to ask a more pointed question. We have here not one but several instances of the two-which-is-four pattern: oaths, *tumah*, *tzara'at*, and *Shabbat*. Each of the relevant tractates — *Shabbat* in *Seder Moed* and *Negaim* in *Seder Taharot* — contains the corresponding two-which-is-four in its own opening *mishnah*, but only the portion directly relevant to that tractate. Here in Shevuot, the full list appears. *Mai shena hacha de-tani lehu le-kulhu?* — why here do we collect all of them together? And conversely, why do *Yetziat ha-Shabbat* and *Mara'ot Negaim* present only their respective portion?

### Torah's Juxtaposition

The *gemara* answers: *amri shevuot vi-yedi'ot ha-tumah de-gabi hadadi kesivan* — oaths and the laws of *tumah* in the *mikdash* are written side by side in the *Torah*. As we saw in the opening verses reviewed earlier, the *Torah* treats the *korban oleh veyored* for a false oath and the *korban oleh veyored* for *tumat mikdash* within the same passage.

### Same Parsha Teaching

These two cases are not merely physically adjacent; they appear together because they are genuinely similar — they share the same *korban*, the *oleh veyored*, and belong to the same *parsha* addressing the same legal mechanism.

### Reasoning for Collection

Once it is established that oaths and *tumat mikdash* belong together, and given that there is no independent tractate devoted to *tumat mikdash*, these two must be addressed within a single tractate. Since two elements of the list are already being brought together, the editorial logic follows: *ve-aydi de-tani tarti, tani kulhu* — since we are going to present two items from the list, we may as well present the entire list here.

### Rabbi's Compilation

This reflects a broader pattern in the editorial work of *Rebbi* in compiling the *Mishnah*. Earlier collections of *mishnayot* often gathered materials with a shared formal structure — parallel constructions, repeated patterns — even when the underlying topics differed entirely. A particularly prominent example is the series beginning *ein bein* in *Megillah*, where some twenty disparate topics are organized around the single formal framework of "there is no difference between X and Y except Z." Such collections were likely compiled as independent units, and when *Rebbi* edited the tractates, he typically distributed the relevant lines to their proper thematic locations. Here, however, the full list is preserved intact, and the *gemara* explains why: the underlying connection between oaths and *tumat mikdash* made Shevuot the natural home for the complete collection.

---

## Opening Structure Explai…

### Short Material First

Having explained why oaths and *tumat mikdash* appear together and why the full list is presented here, the *gemara* addresses a remaining structural question. The *mishnah* opens with the phrase *shevuot shtayim she-hein arba* — oaths are two which is four — clearly announcing oaths as its theme. Yet the tractate then immediately devotes two full chapters to *tumat mikdash* before returning to oaths at all. Why not proceed directly into the laws of oaths?

The *gemara* answers: *aydi de-zutri mileyhu* — since the material on *tumat mikdash* is relatively short. Two chapters is not nothing, but measured against the full seven chapters of the tractate, it is the shorter element. Rather than interrupting the sustained treatment of oaths midway through with a digression, the better editorial approach is to dispose of the shorter material first.

### Cut & Untie Metaphor

The *gemara* uses a vivid phrase: *pasik sharei lehu* — cut it off and untie it. The image is of completing a discrete task cleanly and fully, so that it does not remain as an open thread. The two chapters on *tumat mikdash* represent a self-contained body of law; better to address it in its entirety before moving on.

### Then Focus on Oaths

Once the *tumat mikdash* material has been fully resolved — *batar hachi tani shavuot de-nafishi mileyhu* — then the tractate turns to oaths, which is its true and primary subject and on which there is a great deal to say across the remaining chapters. The structure of the tractate, in other words, reflects a deliberate editorial choice: address the shorter digression first, then give undivided attention to the main topic.

---

## Tosafot on Shaving Laws

### Sidelocks & Razors

Before turning to the substance of the *gemara* on oaths, there is an important body of *halachic* material in *Tosafot* that addresses an issue which came up at the end of *Makkot* — the prohibition of shaving the beard and sidelocks — but which was not treated fully in the *Tosafot* there. The relevant *Tosafot* appears here on daf 2b. *Tosafot* states: *nire de-af al gav de-al ha-zakan eino chayav ela be-ta'ar* — even though for the beard one is only liable if one uses a *ta'ar*, a straight razor, as was discussed at the end of *Makkot* (which is why contemporary shavers are permitted for the beard, on the basis that a shaver does not constitute a *ta'ar*, since the prohibition requires *giluach she-yesh bo hashchatah* — a shaving that involves complete destruction of the hair at the root) — *u-ve-hakafat ha-rosh chayav af be-misparayim ke-ein ta'ar*: for *hakafat ha-rosh*, the sidelocks, one transgresses even by using scissors functioning like a razor.

### Beard vs. Sidelocks

This marks a fundamental distinction. For the beard, only a genuine *ta'ar* — a straight razor applied directly to the skin — triggers the prohibition. For the sidelocks, the standard is broader: any implement that functions like a razor, even scissors operating in a razor-like fashion, is prohibited.

### Rambam's View

The *Rambam* disagrees with this position of *Tosafot*. The *Rambam* holds that *misparayim ke-ein ta'ar* — scissors functioning like a razor — are in fact permitted for the sidelocks. The practical difference between the two authorities is significant.

### Modern Shavers Prohibited

The accepted *halacha* follows *Tosafot*, and this is why one who uses a shaver for the beard — which is permitted because the shaver's mechanism does not constitute a *ta'ar* in the halachic sense — may nevertheless not use that same shaver on the sidelocks. Since a shaver operates by bringing a blade flush against the skin in a manner functionally equivalent to a razor, it falls under the category of *misparayim ke-ein ta'ar* and is prohibited for *hakafat ha-rosh*. This explains the common practice of shaving the beard with an electric shaver while leaving the sidelocks untouched — not merely unshaved, but specifically not shaved with any razor-like instrument. Attachments or trimming devices that do not make direct skin contact may be treated differently, depending on how closely they approximate a *ta'ar*, but any device pressed flush against the skin in the area of the sidelocks is problematic.

### Giver & Receiver

The following *Tosafot*, on daf 3a, addresses a second important question in connection with the passage from *Makkot*: *nire de-mashchit ve-nishchat sheneihem chayavim* — it appears that both the one who performs the shaving and the one who receives it are liable. This is not self-evident. The prohibition is expressed as an act performed by one person upon another, and one might have supposed that only the barber transgresses. *Tosafot* makes clear that both parties bear liability.

### Non-Jewish Barber

This leads to a consequential practical ruling. *Tosafot* takes up the case where the barber is a *goy* — a non-Jew who is not obligated in *mitzvot*. One might reason that since the barber himself has no obligation, the Jew receiving the shave cannot be said to have caused a transgression on his behalf, and therefore bears no personal liability. *Tosafot* rejects this reasoning: it does not matter from the perspective of the one receiving the shave whether the one administering it is obligated in *mitzvot* or not. The prohibition on the one receiving the shave is independent. Accordingly, one may not present oneself to a non-Jewish barber for a straight-razor shave of the beard or sidelocks. The liability attaches to the recipient regardless of the status of the one performing the act.

---

## The Four Categories

### Carrying on Shabbat

The *mishnah* now presents the full list of two-which-is-four cases. *Yetziot ha-Shabbat shtayim she-hein arba* — the acts of carrying on *Shabbat* are two which is four. The canonical description of this is drawn from the opening *mishnah* of *Masechet Shabbat*, which presents the scenario of a homeowner inside a private domain and a poor person standing in the public domain. The paradigmatic form of the *melachah* of carrying (*hotza'ah*) is bringing an object from the *reshut ha-yachid*, the private domain, to the *reshut ha-rabbim*, the public domain — or vice versa. The scriptural basis for this being the primary form is *Moshe*'s instruction to the people not to bring any more donations for the *mishkan* from their private homes into the public collection area, establishing that the transfer between private and public domains is the prototypical prohibited act.

### Four Carrying Ways

The two primary cases are: the homeowner extends his hand out and places an object in the hand of the poor person (transfer from private to public, initiated from within), or the poor person extends his hand inward and takes the object from the homeowner (transfer from private to public, initiated from without). These are the *shtayim* — the two. The *arba* — the four — are the mirror image: the poor person extends his hand inward and places something into the private domain of the homeowner (*hachnasas he-ani*), or the homeowner extends his hand out and takes something from the poor person (*hachnasas ba'al ha-bayit*). All four constitute violations of *Shabbat*, and in this case the two-which-is-four structure maps cleanly onto a uniform *halacha*: all four are prohibited with equal force.

### Leprosy Types

*Mara'ot nega'im shtayim she-hein arba* — the visible signs of *tzara'at* are two which is four. The *Torah* specifies two primary types of skin discoloration that constitute *tzara'at*: *se'eit* and *baheret*. Each of these primary categories has its own subcategory — *se'eit* and its *toldah*, *baheret* and its *toldah*, the latter being called *sapachat*, a secondary type of marking that is equally *metamei* but is conceptually treated as derivative of the primary category. All four types carry the same *halachic* consequence: the person is a *metzora*. Again, the two-which-is-four is not merely a formal categorization; it reflects a uniform legal reality.

### Authorship Question

With the list laid out, the *gemara* now asks: *mani masnisin?* — who is the author of our *mishnah*? The answer, which will require some working through, is: *lo Rabbi Yishmael ve-lo Rabbi Akiva* — neither *Rabbi Yishmael* nor *Rabbi Akiva*.

---

## Ishmael vs. Akiva

### Ishmael on Future Oaths

The reasoning unfolds as follows. *Ee Rabbi Yishmael — ha-omer eino chayav ela al ha-atid lavo* — *Rabbi Yishmael* holds that one is only liable to bring a *korban* for a false oath about the future. The verse in the *Torah* reads *ki tishava levate bisefatayim le-hara o le-heitiv* — when one swears to do harm or to do good — and the context of the *korban oleh veyored* is explicitly tied by *Rabbi Yishmael* to this formulation, which is future-oriented: one swears about what one will or will not do. The two-which-is-four in that case would be: I will do something and I do it (oath fulfilled, no transgression), I will do something and I don't (oath violated, *korban*), I won't do something and I don't (oath fulfilled), I won't do something and I do (oath violated, *korban*). For *Rabbi Yishmael*, past-oriented oaths — I swear that I did something I didn't do, or that I didn't do something I did — do not generate a *korban*. They may carry other consequences, but the *korban oleh veyored* applies only to the future-oriented cases. So *Rabbi Yishmael* does not hold of the full two-which-is-four for *shevuot*; he holds of only two.

### Akiva's Position

*Rabbi Akiva*, by contrast, does hold of the full two-which-is-four for oaths: one brings a *korban* for violating an oath whether it was past-oriented or future-oriented. But *Rabbi Akiva* holds a different position regarding *tumat mikdash*. The *Torah* states *ki tiga be-chol davar tamei asher yitma bah ve-ne'elam mimenu* — if one touches any *tamei* thing and it becomes hidden from him. The simple reading is that what is hidden is the *tumah* itself — *he'elem tumah* — and this generates two cases (eating *korban* while *tamei*, or entering the *Beit HaMikdash* while *tamei*), which is the primary two. The additional two that make it four come from *he'elem mikdash* — one forgot not just that one was *tamei* but that the place one was entering was the *Beit HaMikdash*, or forgot the sanctity of the *korban* one was eating. *Rabbi Akiva* holds that one is only liable for the case of *he'elem tumah* — forgetting that one was *tamei* — and not for *he'elem mikdash* — forgetting that one was in the sanctuary. So for *Rabbi Akiva*, the *tumat mikdash* category yields only two cases, not four.

### Neither Holds Both

The problem is thus clearly defined. *Rabbi Yishmael* holds of the full two-which-is-four for *tumat mikdash* but only two for oaths. *Rabbi Akiva* holds of the full two-which-is-four for oaths but only two for *tumat mikdash*. Neither sage holds of the complete two-which-is-four for *both* categories simultaneously. Yet our *mishnah* presents the full list across both categories as if they are parallel and complete. So who authored our *mishnah*?

### Partial Application Answ…

The *gemara* first attempts to resolve this by suggesting that the two-which-is-four in our *mishnah* need not mean uniform liability in all four cases. Perhaps the *mishnah* is merely cataloguing four conceptually distinct types, some of which generate liability and some of which do not — *mehem le-chiyuv u-mehem le-patur*. On this reading, *Rabbi Yishmael* could be the author: he acknowledges four types of oaths even though only two generate a *korban*, and he holds of all four *tumat mikdash* cases with full liability. Similarly, *Rabbi Akiva* could be the author: he holds of all four oath cases with full liability, and he acknowledges four types of *tumat mikdash* even though only two generate a *korban*. The *gemara*, however, rejects this approach. The rest of the *mishnah* makes it evident that two-which-is-four means uniform *halacha* applies to all four. The *tzara'at* cases and the *Shabbat* cases are all equally *metamei* or equally prohibited — the structure of the *mishnah* signals legal equivalence, not merely formal categorization. So the partial-application reading is forced and is set aside.

---

## Lashes Not Korban

### Lashes Interpretation

The *gemara* pivots to an entirely different interpretive approach. Perhaps our *mishnah*'s two-which-is-four is not about *korban* at all. Perhaps it is about *malkot* — lashes. On this reading, the *mishnah* is asserting that all four types of false oaths (past positive, past negative, future affirmative, future negative) generate lashes when violated willfully. This sidesteps the dispute between *Rabbi Yishmael* and *Rabbi Akiva* about which cases generate a *korban*, since now the *mishnah* is speaking of an entirely different legal consequence.

### Past Oaths & Lashes

For past-oriented oaths, it is relatively clear that lashes apply, and the *gemara* will elaborate this through *Rava*'s comparison.

---

## Lashes Not Korban (II)

### Rava's Comparison

*Rava* states: *be-ferush ribetah Torah shvuat sheker dumya de-shvuat shav* — the *Torah* explicitly compared a false oath (*shvuat sheker*) to a vain oath (*shvuat shav*). The *shvuat shav* — the oath taken in vain — generates lashes by virtue of the verse *ki lo yenakeh Hashem et asher yisa shemo la-shav*: God will not cleanse the one who takes His name in vain. The *gemara* understands this to mean that while God will not cleanse him, the earthly court will — by administering lashes, which constitute an atonement that releases the person from the Heavenly consequence. This is the same principle articulated at the end of *Makkot*: the punishment administered by the court below serves as an instrument of divine cleansing.

### Utterance & Violation

The reason the comparison works — *mah shav le-she'avar af sheker nami le-she'avar* — is that both a vain oath and a past-oriented false oath share the same essential characteristic: the violation occurs at the moment of utterance. A *shvuat shav* is an oath about something obviously true or obviously impossible; the moment it leaves one's lips, whether trivially true or trivially false, the transgression is complete. A past-oriented *shvuat sheker* works the same way: whether I swear that I ate eggs this morning when I did not, or that I did not eat them when I did, the lie is already done the instant I speak it. There is no future act required to complete the transgression.

---

## Four Oath Cases

### False Past Positive

The first of the four cases: I swear that I ate something when in fact I did not. This is a past-oriented false oath, a *shvuat sheker le-she'avar*. The violation is complete the moment I utter the oath. By *Rava*'s comparison to a *shvuat shav*, lashes apply.

### False Past Negative

The second case: I swear that I did not eat something when in fact I did. This is equally past-oriented and equally a *shvuat sheker le-she'avar*. The same reasoning applies, and lashes follow.

### Future: Will Eat

The third case: I swear that I will eat a loaf of bread tomorrow, and then I eat it — but I swear falsely in the moment, or I take the oath earnestly and then violate it. The complication here is that unlike the past-oriented cases, the violation does not occur at the moment of utterance. Nevertheless, when the future moment arrives and I actively eat the bread in violation of the oath, I have performed a concrete act. *Nami lav she-yesh bo ma'aseh hu* — this is a negative prohibition accompanied by an act. The act of eating is the transgression, and since lashes apply to violations involving an active deed, lashes are given here.

### Future: Won't Eat

The fourth case: I swear that I will eat a loaf of bread, and then I do nothing — I simply fail to eat it. This is the case that generates the difficulty. The day passes, the bread sits uneaten, and I have violated my oath — but purely through inaction.

### Passive Transgression Pr…

The problem is severe: how does one receive lashes for a purely passive transgression? The moment of utterance was not false — at that moment I fully intended to eat the bread — so one cannot assimilate it to the past-oriented cases via *Rava*'s comparison. And since the violation consists entirely of *not* performing an act, there is no positive deed that could anchor the lashes. This is the classic *lav she-ein bo ma'aseh* — a negative prohibition without a concrete act — and it raises the question of whether such a transgression can ever generate *malkot*.

---

## Yochanan & Passive A (II)

### Yochanan Follows Stam

*Rabbi Yochanan* follows the principle that *halacha* is determined by the *stam mishnah* — an unattributed *mishnah* in the *Mishnah* of *Rebbi*. Our opening *mishnah*, which is unattributed, thus presents itself as the authoritative ruling. If our *mishnah* is speaking of lashes, and it asserts the full two-which-is-four including the case of the passive non-performance, then *Rabbi Yochanan*'s principle would seem to commit him to the position that one does receive lashes for a passive transgression.

### Opening Mishnah Suggests

This is indeed what our *mishnah*, on the interpretation the *gemara* has been developing, appears to teach: that all four types of false oath — including the case of "I will eat" followed by not eating — generate *malkot*.

### Eggs Case: No Lashes

Yet *Rabbi Yochanan* himself rules otherwise. Together with *Reish Lakish*, he holds that if a person swears he will eat a loaf of bread today and the day passes without his eating it, *ein lokeh* — he does not receive lashes. Both *Rabbi Yochanan* and *Reish Lakish* agree on the *halacha*; they disagree only on the reason.

---

## Yochanan & Passive A (II)

### Two Reasons for No

*Rabbi Yochanan* says: *ein lokeh mishum de-havei lav she-ein bo ma'aseh* — he does not receive lashes because this is a passive transgression, and any negative prohibition that lacks a concrete act does not generate lashes: *ve-chol lav she-ein bo ma'aseh ein lokin alav*. *Reish Lakish* offers a different reason: *ein lokeh hatrat safek hi* — he does not receive lashes because the warning (*hatra'ah*) required before administering lashes is doubtful in efficacy. For lashes to apply, a valid warning must immediately precede the transgression. Here, the warning would have to be issued in the morning — "you must eat bread today or you will receive lashes" — but at that moment it is entirely unknown whether the person will transgress; perhaps he will eat. The warning does not immediately precede a clear imminent act, and so it is a *hatrat safek*, a doubtful warning, which is insufficient to establish liability for *malkot*.

---

## Support in Notar Mishnah

### No Lashes for Notar

The *gemara* seeks to support *Rabbi Yochanan*'s position by identifying another *stam mishnah* that would allow him to rule against our opening *mishnah*. The candidate it first considers is a *mishnah* which states: *aval ha-motir be-tahor* — one who leaves over the meat of a valid *korban* past the deadline, *eino lokeh et ha-arba'im* — does not receive lashes. This was reviewed in *Makkot*.

### Passive = No Lashes

Why does one not receive lashes for leaving over *notar*? The straightforward answer would be that this is a passive transgression — one simply failed to eat the meat in time — and any passive transgression is exempt from *malkot*. If this is the reason embedded in the *stam mishnah* about *notar*, then *Rabbi Yochanan* has his supporting *stam mishnah*: another unattributed *mishnah* that implies the same principle he is invoking.

### Yehuda's Reason

But the *gemara* challenges this inference. The *mishnah* about *notar* may exempt from lashes for an entirely different reason — the reason of *Rabbi Yehuda*: *mishum de-ba kasuv litein asei achar lo ta'aseh* — because the *Torah* comes to attach a positive commandment (*asei*) after the negative prohibition. When a negative prohibition is linked to a corrective positive *mitzvah* — a *lav ha-nitak le-asei* — lashes do not apply, because there is a remedial act available. The *Torah* says: do not leave over any meat until morning — and whatever is left over shall be burned in fire. The positive commandment to burn the *notar* follows the prohibition against leaving it over, and that linkage may be the reason lashes do not apply, not the principle of *lav she-ein bo ma'aseh*.

### Yaakov's Principle

*Rabbi Yaakov* explicitly rejects the *Rabbi Yehuda* explanation: *lo min ha-sheim zeh* — the exemption from lashes for *notar* does not rest on the connection to a positive commandment. Rather, *ela mishum de-havei lav she-ein bo ma'aseh* — it is simply because leaving over the meat is a passive transgression, and *lav she-ein bo ma'aseh ein lokin alav* — any passive transgression is exempt from lashes as a general principle. So the *mishnah* about *notar* follows *Rabbi Yaakov*'s principle. However, the *gemara* points out that this is uncertain: the *mishnah* about *notar* can be read as following either *Rabbi Yehuda* or *Rabbi Yaakov*, and without knowing which, we cannot confidently derive the general principle from it.

---

## Which Mishnah Prevails?

### Unclear Reasoning

The problem, then, is that the *mishnah* about *notar* does not provide a reliable basis for *Rabbi Yochanan* to override our opening *mishnah*, because it is unclear whether the *notar* exemption rests on the *lav she-ein bo ma'aseh* principle or on the *lav ha-nitak le-asei* principle.

### Two Oaths Mishnah

The *gemara* therefore turns to a different *stam mishnah* — one that addresses the exact scenario at issue. The *mishnah* states: *shvuah she-lo ochal kikar zu* — one takes an oath that he will not eat this loaf of bread. *Shvuah she-lo ochlena* — and then takes a second oath not to eat it. *Ve-achalah* — and then he eats it. *Eino chayav ela achat* — he is only liable once, for one set of lashes. Why? Because the second oath could not take effect: since he was already obligated by the first oath not to eat the bread, he is *mushba ve-omed* — already bound by a prior oath — and a second oath on the same subject has no legal force. So the first oath did take effect, and when he ate the bread, he actively violated it and received lashes.

### Active Violation Only

The *mishnah* then concludes: *zo hi shvuat bituy she-chayavin al zidonah malkot ve-al shigagata korban oleh veyored* — this is the *shvuat bituy* for which one is liable to lashes for willful violation and a *korban oleh veyored* for unwitting violation. The *gemara* reads the phrase *zo hi* — "this is the one" — as a pointed exclusion. *Zo hi de-chayavin al zidonah malkot* — this particular type of violation — where you said you would not eat and you actively ate — is what generates lashes. *Aval ochal ve-lo achal* — but if you said you would eat and then you failed to eat, *lo laki* — you do not receive lashes. The *stam mishnah* about two oaths thus provides *Rabbi Yochanan* with his supporting source: an unattributed *mishnah* that directly addresses our case and implies that passive non-performance does not generate *malkot*.

---

## Rabbi's Compilation Expl…

### Rabbi's Contradiction

This resolution raises a new difficulty. Both *mishnayot* — our opening *mishnah*, which apparently says lashes apply even in the passive case, and the later *mishnah* about two oaths, which implies they do not — are *stam mishnayot*, unattributed rulings that *Rebbi* incorporated into the *Mishnah*. How can *Rebbi* himself have compiled two *mishnayot* that contradict each other on so fundamental a question?

### Initial Teaching

The *gemara* explains that this reflects a process of intellectual development. *Me-ikara savar lav she-ein bo ma'aseh lokin alav ve-satma* — initially, *Rebbi* held that a passive transgression does incur lashes, and he taught this ruling as an unattributed *mishnah*, which became our opening *mishnah* of Shevuot, presenting the full two-which-is-four including the passive case.

### Later Change

*Ve-hadar savar ein lokin alav* — subsequently, *Rebbi* reconsidered and concluded that passive transgressions do not generate lashes. He changed his ruling. The later *mishnah* about two oaths — *zo hi* — reflects this revised position: lashes attach only to active violation.

### Cannot Revoke

But *Rebbi* faced a practical impossibility: *ve-mishnah lo zaza mi-mekomah* — the original *mishnah* could not be uprooted from its place. By the time *Rebbi* changed his mind, the earlier *mishnah* had been disseminated, learned, and memorized by students across the academies. One cannot simply instruct a community to stop learning an established *mishnah* and declare it void; the tradition had already taken root.

### Later Clarification

So *Rebbi* took a different approach. Unable to revoke the earlier ruling, he composed and disseminated a later *mishnah* — the *mishnah* about two oaths — which, through the interpretive phrase *zo hi*, makes clear that lashes apply only to the active case. This later *mishnah* effectively signals the correct *halacha* to those who know how to read it, even as the earlier *mishnah* remains in place.

### Summary & Resolution

The resolution of the *gemara*'s long inquiry is thus as follows. Our opening *mishnah* — *shevuot shtayim she-hein arba* — is speaking of *malkot*, not *korbanot*, and this is what allows it to present a complete two-which-is-four that neither *Rabbi Yishmael* nor *Rabbi Akiva* would endorse if the subject were *korbanot*. The two past-oriented cases clearly generate lashes via *Rava*'s comparison to *shvuat shav*. The two future-oriented cases are the *chiddush*: the *mishnah* asserts that even the passive case — "I will eat" followed by not eating — generates lashes. However, this assertion reflects *Rebbi*'s initial position, which he subsequently revised. The later *mishnah* about two oaths, which *Rabbi Yochanan* relies upon, establishes the authoritative ruling: a passive transgression of a *shevuah* does not generate *malkot*. Only active violation does.

---

---

# Shevuot 4

## Mishnah Problem

### Mishnah Overview

The *daf* opens eleven lines into Shevuot 4a, at the words *b'mai okimta* — "how did you explain it?" — and the central question concerns the proper understanding of the *mishnah*. The *mishnah* had enumerated four topics that each exhibit the pattern of *shtayim she'hen arba*, "two that is four." The first concerns *tumas mikdash v'kodashav*: one who is *tamei* and enters the *Beit HaMikdash*, or who is *tamei* and eats a *korban*. The basic "two" that everyone agrees triggers liability is unawareness of one's *tumah* status. The "four" arises because those same two forbidden actions — entering the *Mikdash* or eating *kodshim* — can each be committed in a second type of unawareness: not being aware that the place was the *Beit HaMikdash*, or not being aware that the food was *kodshim*. That is the two that is four for *tumah*.

The second case is *shavuah*. The basic "two" are future-oriented oaths: swearing one will eat something and then not eating it, or swearing one will not eat and then eating. The "four" comes from adding past-oriented oaths: declaring "I ate" when one had not, or "I did not eat" when one had. The *mishnah* continues with *tzaraat* and *Shabbat* as additional instances of the same pattern.

### Gemara Problem

The *gemara* identifies a fundamental difficulty: no single *tanna* holds both of these "two that is four" positions simultaneously. Regarding *tumah*, it is only Rabbi Yishmael who maintains that liability extends even to cases where one forgot that the location was the *Mikdash* or that the food was *kodshim*. Rabbi Akiva holds that liability applies only when one forgot that one was *tamei* — not when the forgotten element was the *Mikdash* or the *kodshim* themselves. Thus the first clause of the *mishnah*, the two that is four by *tumah*, can only accord with Rabbi Yishmael. Conversely, regarding *shavuah*, it is only Rabbi Akiva who holds that one brings a *korban* not merely for a future-oriented oath but also for a past-oriented one. Rabbi Yishmael does not extend *korban* liability to past oaths. So the second clause — the two that is four by *shavuah* — can only accord with Rabbi Akiva. The *mishnah* thus appears to be internally inconsistent, combining the positions of two incompatible *tannaim*.

### Malkut Solution

The solution proposed the previous day was as follows: the entire *mishnah* is attributed to Rabbi Yishmael, and the cases it discusses are not about bringing a *korban* at all but about *malkut* — lashes administered for willful transgression. If every case in the *mishnah* involves someone acting intentionally and receiving lashes rather than bringing an atonement offering, then the debate between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yishmael about what triggers *korban* liability becomes entirely irrelevant. Both *tannaim* would agree on the contours of liability when the question is *malkut*. One might ask how this applies to the *shavuah* case, which can involve passivity — swearing one will eat and then simply not eating. The answer given was that Rabbi Yishmael holds one receives *malkut* even for a passive violation. The proposed reading was thus that the entire *mishnah* speaks of willful acts subject to *malkut*.

## Testing Malkut

### Tzaraat Solution

The *gemara* now tests whether the *malkut* framework can accommodate every clause of the *mishnah*. It raises the *tzaraat* case first: *mar'os nega'im mai malkus ika?* — what is the scenario of *malkut* when it comes to the appearances of *tzaraat*? If the *mishnah* were discussing *korban*, Tosafot notes one could understand it as referring to the *korban* brought at the conclusion of the *tzaraat* purification process. But if the *mishnah* is about *malkut*, what negative prohibition does one transgress merely by being afflicted with *tzaraat*?

The *gemara* answers: *bikotzes baharto* — we are speaking of a case where one cuts off one's leprous spot in order to prevent becoming *tamei*. This is explained by reference to the principle of Rabbi Avin in the name of Rabbi Illai: wherever the *Torah* uses the language of *hishamer*, *pen*, or *al* — "guard yourself," "lest," or "do not" — it constitutes a *lo sa'asei*, a negative prohibition. The *Torah* states *hishamer b'nega hatzaraat*, "guard yourself regarding the affliction of *tzaraat*," and *Chazal* understand this to prohibit cutting off one's *tzaraat* spot to avoid *tumah* liability. Violating this prohibition would incur *malkut*, and the two that is four in this case would require knowing which features of one's condition render one *tamei*. Tosafot raises a complication from another *gemara* that suggests *malkut* applies even when one merely risks having *tzaraat* and attempts to prevent the *kohen* from seeing it — which would seem to indicate the prohibition is broader than the *gemara* here implies. Nevertheless, the *tzaraat* case can at least be accommodated under the *malkut* framework.

### Shabbat Issue

The *gemara* then turns to the *Shabbat* case and encounters a more serious obstacle: *yetzios Shabbos mah malkus ika? lav shenitan le'azharas misas beis din hu?* The negative prohibition against performing labor on *Shabbat* is one whose assigned punishment is *misas beis din* — execution by the court. The well-established rule is that any *lav shenitan le'azharas misas beis din* — a negative prohibition whose designated sanction is capital punishment — cannot serve as the basis for *malkut*. If the warning given to the violator mentioned lashes rather than execution, the court cannot impose the death penalty, but neither can it impose lashes, because *malkut* is not the punishment assigned to that prohibition. Accordingly, the willful desecration of *Shabbat* cannot generate *malkut*, and the *malkut* framework appears to break down at this point.

### Rabbi Yishmael

This is precisely why, the *gemara* explains, the solution attributed the *mishnah* to Rabbi Yishmael specifically: *v'mishum hacha kamukmina k'Rabbi Yishmael*. Rabbi Yishmael holds the exceptional position that *lav shenitan le'azharas misas beis din lokin alav* — even a negative prohibition that carries capital punishment can result in *malkut* if the individual was warned about lashes rather than execution. Under Rabbi Yishmael's view, then, one could indeed receive *malkut* for *Shabbat* violation if warned accordingly.

The *gemara* then raises a meta-question: it had originally attributed the *mishnah* to Rabbi Yishmael because of the *tumah* problem — Rabbi Akiva's position on *tumah* does not yield two that is four. So why is the *Shabbat* issue now being presented as the reason for the attribution to Rabbi Yishmael? The *gemara* clarifies: the *mishnah* could not be Rabbi Akiva to begin with because of the *tumah* problem, not because of *Shabbat*. The *Shabbat* issue is simply an additional reason that reinforces the attribution to Rabbi Yishmael. Moreover, now that the framework has shifted from *korban* to *malkut*, the distinction between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yishmael on *tumah* and *shavuah* — which was entirely a dispute about *korban* liability — disappears. Under *malkut*, both *tannaim* would agree, and the entire *mishnah* could be read consistently. The sole reason the *mishnah* must specifically go like Rabbi Yishmael is his unique position on *lav shenitan le'azharas misas beis din*.

The *gemara*, however, is not yet satisfied. It objects: *i hachi, yedios hatra'os mibei lei* — if we are talking about willful violations subject to *malkut*, then the *mishnah* should have spoken of "warnings" (*hatra'os*), not "awarenesses" (*yedios*). The *gemara* offers a strained response — *tani yedios d'hatra'os*, read "awareness" as referring to awareness of the warning — but this is an obviously forced reading, since the term *yedios* is never employed outside the context of inadvertent unawareness. The argument is losing force.

## Back to Korban

### Two That Is Four

The *gemara* now delivers what proves to be a decisive blow against the *malkut* interpretation. *I hachi, shtayim she'hen arba, tartai hu de-avyan* — if we are discussing willful violations subject to *malkut*, then by *tumah* there are only two cases, not four. The only reason one arrives at four is by asking: what did the person forget? Did one forget one's *tumah* status, or did one forget that the location was the *Mikdash*, or that the food was *kodshim*? That fourfold structure emerges only when the cases are organized around categories of forgotten information. But if one is acting willfully, there is nothing forgotten, and the count collapses back to two: entering the *Mikdash* while *tamei*, and eating *kodshim* while *tamei*.

### Oleh Vayyored

Beyond the structural problem, the *gemara* delivers its knockout argument: *ve-su, harei zeh be-oleh ve-yored* — the *mishnah* itself states, at its conclusion, that the transgressor brings a *korban oleh ve-yored*, a sliding-scale offering. The *mishnah* explicitly names a *korban*. The *malkut* interpretation is therefore impossible. This point, the *gemara* implies, could have been stated from the outset.

### Original Problem

With the *malkut* solution entirely dismantled, the *gemara* returns to its original difficulty. The *mishnah* is clearly discussing *korban*, and the problem is now restored in full: the two that is four for *tumah* goes like Rabbi Yishmael, while the two that is four for *shavuah* — encompassing past-oriented oaths — goes like Rabbi Akiva. The two clauses reflect incompatible *tannaic* positions, and the question of how they coexist in a single *mishnah* demands a new answer.

## Rav Yosef

### Rebbi Synthesis

*Ela amar Rav Yosef: Rebbi hi ve-nasiv lah aliba de-tannai.* Rather, says Rav Yosef, the *mishnah* was composed by Rebbi — Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, the editor of the *Mishnah* — and he deliberately incorporated the positions of different *tannaim* in different clauses. *Bi-yedi'os nasiv lah ke-Rabbi Yishmael* — for the *tumah* cases, Rebbi adopted the position of Rabbi Yishmael that liability extends to forgetting the *Mikdash* and *kodshim*. *Bi-shvu'os nasiv lah ke-Rabbi Akiva* — for the *shavuah* cases, Rebbi adopted the position of Rabbi Akiva that the *korban* extends even to past-oriented oaths. One can understand why Rebbi would have composed the *mishnah* this way: he wished to collect instances of the pattern "two that is four" — from *Shabbat*, from *nega'im*, from *shavuah*, and from *tumas mikdash v'kodashav* — and chose the most expansive reading available in each domain, even if those readings derived from different *tannaim*. They are not inherently contradictory; there is no logical reason that one must hold the same way across both domains.

### Rav Kahana

Rav Ashi reports that when he presented this analysis of Rav Yosef before Rav Kahana, Rav Kahana objected to it. *Lo teima nasiv lah aliba de-tannai ve-lei lo sevira lei* — do not say that Rebbi is merely compiling the positions of various *tannaim* without personally subscribing to them. That would be a problematic portrait of the *mishnah*'s editor: we cannot simply say Rebbi assembled a *mishnah* from positions he may not personally hold. Rather, *ela Rebbi ta'ameh de-nafshei mefaresh* — Rebbi is expressing his own considered opinions in the *mishnah*. He personally holds the two-that-is-four by *tumah* along the lines of Rabbi Yishmael, and he personally holds the two-that-is-four by *shavuah* along the lines of Rabbi Akiva. The *gemara* will now demonstrate this from textual evidence.

## Proving Tumah

### Two Nelam

The *gemara* cites a *baraita* establishing the foundational principle of *tumas mikdash v'kodashav*: *minayin she'eino chayav ela she-yesh bo yediya ba-techila ve-yediya ba-sof ve-helam bein-tayim* — how do we know that one is not liable unless there was awareness at the outset, awareness at the conclusion, and a period of forgetting in between? Unlike most *shogeg* violations, where one simply was unaware at the time of the act, *tumas mikdash v'kodashav* requires that the person had initially known of their *tumah* status, then forgot, then sinned, and only subsequently became aware again. The source for this requirement is the doubling of the word *ve-nelam* — "and it was hidden" — in the relevant *pesukim*: *ve-nelam mimenu ve-hu tamei* and again *ve-nelam mimenu*. The *talmud lomar* is *venelam venelam shtei pe'amim*, said in the name of Rabbi Akiva.

### Rabbi Akiva

Rabbi Akiva's reading of the double *ve-nelam* is that the duplication implies a double awareness — that one must have known and then forgotten, and known again. The two occurrences of *ve-nelam* together require an initial knowledge followed by concealment, and a subsequent knowledge at the end.

### Rebbi Reading

Rebbi disagrees with Rabbi Akiva's derivation, not with its conclusion. *Eino tzarich* — one does not need both instances of *ve-nelam* to establish that requirement. From a single *ve-nelam*, Rebbi infers the necessity of initial awareness: the word *ve-nelam*, "it became hidden from him," implies by its very structure that there was something to become hidden — that is, prior knowledge. Furthermore, the *pasuk* adds *ve-hu yada*, "and he knew," establishing a second moment of awareness at the end. So Rebbi derives both the initial *yediya* and the concluding *yediya* from a single *ve-nelam* together with *ve-hu yada*.

If the first *ve-nelam* already teaches initial awareness and the second *ve-hu yada* teaches final awareness, what purpose does the second *ve-nelam* serve? *Lechayev al helam tumah ve'al helam mikdash* — the Torah is making one liable not only for forgetting one's *tumah* status but also for forgetting that the location was the *Mikdash* or that the food was *kodshim*. The second *ve-nelam* thus extends liability to a second category of hidden information.

### Tumah Conclusion

This is a crucial finding. Rebbi explicitly disagrees with Rabbi Akiva on how to read the double *ve-nelam*, and he uses that second *ve-nelam* to establish a different proposition entirely — that there are two categories of *helam*, two types of concealment that can trigger liability. This is precisely the Rabbi Yishmael position: that one is *chayav* even when it is the *Mikdash* or the *kodshim* that was forgotten, not merely when the *tumah* itself was forgotten. Rebbi, in other words, personally holds the first clause of the *mishnah* — the two that is four by *tumah* — on his own reasoning, not merely as a citation of Rabbi Yishmael.

## Shavuah Logic

### Gap Identified

The *gemara* now acknowledges a gap in the proof: *ashkechan bi-yedi'os d'islei ta'amei de-nafshei* — good, we have demonstrated that Rebbi holds his own view regarding the *tumah* cases. But *shavuos d'leis lei ta'amei de-nafshei minalan?* — when it comes to *shavuah*, we have no text where Rebbi ever explicitly expressed his own view that the *korban* applies to past-oriented oaths as well. The Rabbi Akiva position on *shavuah* depends on a specific hermeneutic approach, and we do not have a direct statement from Rebbi embracing it. How, then, can we say that Rebbi personally holds this second clause of the *mishnah* rather than merely citing Rabbi Akiva?

### Ribui u'Mi'ut

The *gemara* answers: *sevara hu* — it can be derived logically. Why does Rabbi Akiva hold one is *chayav* for a past-oriented *shavuah*? Because *didarash ribui u'mi'ut* — Rabbi Akiva employs the hermeneutic method of *ribui u'mi'ut*, a broadening-and-narrowing interpretive framework. And *Rebbi nami darish ribui u'mi'ut* — Rebbi likewise employs the *ribui u'mi'ut* approach. If Rebbi uses the same interpretive methodology as Rabbi Akiva, he will inevitably arrive at the same conclusion regarding the scope of *shavuah*. To understand why this is compelling, the *gemara* must explain the *ribui u'mi'ut* principle in detail.

## Ribui u'Mi'ut

### Klal u'Prat

The *gemara* explains *ribui u'mi'ut* in contrast to the more familiar method of *klal u'prat*. The principle of *klal u'prat* holds that when the *Torah* states a general proposition and then specifies a particular example, the law is restricted to that specific example. A classic illustration involves the *menorah*: *ve'asita menoras zahav tahor mikshah te'aseh ha-menorah*. The phrase *ve'asita menorah* is general; *zahav tahor* is a specification; *te'aseh ha-menorah* is again general. Under *klal u'prat*, once the *Torah* specifies "pure gold," that particular example becomes the operative category.

### Klal u'Prat u'Klal

When the pattern is *klal u'prat u'klal* — general, specific, general — the final generalization reopens the category but does not return it to full breadth. The rule is *eino dan ela ke'ein ha-prat*: one may include only things similar to the specific example. Applied to the *menorah*, the second general term *te'aseh ha-menorah* broadens beyond gold specifically but only to other metals — things sufficiently like gold. Wood, for instance, would be excluded as too different from the *prat*.

### Broader Approach

*Ribui u'mi'ut* proceeds differently. Under this approach, the initial broad statement and the subsequent narrowing example do not function as *klal* and *prat* in the technical sense; the specific example is understood as a *mi'ut*, a narrowing, not a specification. Because the general term was stated first, one does not conclude from the specific example that only that example applies. Already at the stage of *ribui u'mi'ut*, one has concluded that a wide category is intended, and the specific example merely indicates the boundary in one direction. When the *Torah* then broadens again — *ribui u'mi'ut u'ribui* — the result is a substantially wider category than *klal u'prat u'klal* ever produces. Under *klal u'prat u'klal*, the final broadening returns one only to things similar to the specific example. Under *ribui u'mi'ut u'ribui*, the final broadening reaches everything except what is most unlike the specific. Returning to the *menorah* example: the *ribui u'mi'ut u'ribui* reading would conclude that the *menorah* may be made of virtually any material except pottery, which would be considered wholly different from gold. The *klal u'prat u'klal* reading, by contrast, limits the category to metals.

### Shavuah Applied

This hermeneutic difference has direct bearing on the *shavuah* case. The *Torah* states *ki tishava levate bisefatayim lehara o lehetiv, lechol asher yivate adam bishvuah* — "when one enunciates with one's lips to do harm or to do good, anything that a person enunciates by oath." Under *klal u'prat u'klal*: *ki tishava levate bisefatayim* is the general statement; *lehara o lehetiv* — harm or benefit — is the specific; *lechol asher yivate adam* is the broadening. The *klal u'prat u'klal* result is: any oath similar to harm-or-benefit, which means future-oriented oaths. The category broadens slightly from the specific examples of harm and benefit to include neutral future commitments, but it remains tethered to the future, since *lehara o lehetiv* refers to prospective actions.

Under *ribui u'mi'ut u'ribui*, by contrast, the initial *levate bisefatayim* is the *ribui* — a broad term for any oral utterance. *Lehara o lehetiv* is the *mi'ut*, the narrowing. Already at the stage of *ribui u'mi'ut*, one has abstracted to any future-oriented oath, not merely beneficial or harmful ones. Then *lechol asher yivate adam* functions as the second *ribui*, the final broadening, and now reaches past-oriented oaths as well. The only category excluded — the most dissimilar thing — would be *nishba levatel et ha-mitzvah*, an oath to nullify a commandment, which is a categorically different type of commitment. Thus Rabbi Akiva's *ribui u'mi'ut* approach yields liability for past-oriented *shavuah*, whereas the *klal u'prat u'klal* approach of Rabbi Yishmael yields only future-oriented liability.

## Pidyon HaBen

### Rabbi Yishmael

The *gemara* now demonstrates Rebbi's use of *ribui u'mi'ut* from a concrete case: the redemption of the firstborn son, *pidyon ha-ben*. Rebbi rules *bechol podin bechor adam chutz min ha-shtarot* — one may redeem a firstborn son with anything except promissory notes. A *shtar* has no intrinsic value of its own; it merely represents a debt, and therefore cannot serve as payment for *pidyon ha-ben*. Everything else — including land, slaves, and movable property — is valid according to Rebbi.

### Rabbis

The Rabbis disagree: *bechol podin bechor adam chutz me'avadim u'shtarot ve-karka'ot* — one may not use slaves, land, or promissory notes. Their reasoning follows *klal u'prat u'klal*: *u'fduyav miben chodesh* is the general statement; *be'erkcha kesef chameshet shekalim* — "silver, five *shekalim*" — is the specification, which refers to something that is chattel and possesses intrinsic monetary value; *tifdeh* is the second general term. By *klal u'prat u'klal — eino dan ela ke'ein ha-prat* — one may only include things similar to the specific: *mah ha-prat meforash davar ha-mitaltel ve-gufo mamon* — just as silver is both movable and intrinsically valuable, so too anything redeemed must be movable and intrinsically valuable. This excludes land (*karka*), which is not movable; slaves (*avadim*), which are legally equated with land; and promissory notes (*shtarot*), which, though movable, have no intrinsic value.

Rebbi's *ribui u'mi'ut* reading, by contrast, produces a much broader category. The two general statements — *u'fduyav* and *tifdeh* — work together with the narrowing term *kesef chameshet shekalim*, and the final broadening includes everything except that which is most unlike silver: namely, *shtarot*, which have no intrinsic value whatsoever. Everything else, including land and slaves, remains valid.

## Consistency Challenge

### Ravina Challenge

This proof for Rebbi's *ribui u'mi'ut* approach now faces a challenge. Ravina objects: *ha ve-Rebbi klal u'prat darash* — but look, there is a case where Rebbi explicitly employs *klal u'prat*, not *ribui u'mi'ut*. If Rebbi were a consistent practitioner of *ribui u'mi'ut*, he should apply it everywhere. The case Ravina cites undermines the claim that Rebbi's *pidyon ha-ben* ruling reflects his general hermeneutic approach.

### Awl Case

The case concerns the boring of a slave's ear with an awl at the doorpost, the ritual performed when an *eved ivri* elects to remain in servitude. The *Torah* mentions specifically a *martzea* — an awl. A *baraita* asks: *ein li ela martzea, minayin le-rabos ha-sov ve-ha-sira ve-ha-machat ve-ha-makdeach ve-ha-michtav?* — from where do we know that one may also use a thorn, a sharpened piece of wood, a metal needle, an inscribing tool, or similar instruments? The *talmud lomar* offered is *ve-lakachta* — "and you shall take" — anything that can be taken in the hand. This is the position of Rabbi Yoshiya b'Rebbi Yehuda, who employs *ribui u'mi'ut* and arrives at the broad conclusion that any hand-held instrument suffices.

Rebbi disagrees. He rules that only something made of metal qualifies — *mah martzea meyuchad shel mateches af kol shel mateches* — just as the awl is specifically of metal, so must any substitute be metal. This is a *klal u'prat* derivation: Rebbi takes the specification (*martzea*, specifically metal) as genuinely restrictive and broadens only to other metals. The *gemara* identifies the methodological difference explicitly: *Rebbi darish klal u'prat, ve-Rabbi Yoshiya b'Rebbi Yehuda darish ribui u'mi'ut*. Rebbi's narrow ruling in the awl case reveals that he is in fact a *klal u'prat* man — which directly contradicts the claim that his broader ruling in *pidyon ha-ben* reflects a general commitment to *ribui u'mi'ut*.

## Pidyon HaBen (II)

### Two Generalizations

The *gemara* resolves the internal tension in Rebbi's rulings. *De'alma klallei u'prattei darish* — generally, Rebbi follows *klal u'prat*. The *pidyon ha-ben* case is an exception, and the reason lies not in a general preference for *ribui u'mi'ut* but in a specific structural feature of those *pesukim*. The relevant *baraita* from the school of Rabbi Yishmael establishes that when two general statements appear immediately adjacent to one another before the specific term appears, the sequence is no longer treated as *klal u'prat u'klal* but as *ribui u'mi'ut u'ribui*. The *baraita* derives this from the double use of *b'mayim* — "in the water" — in the context of aquatic creatures, where the word appears twice in succession and only then is followed by the more specific *b'yamim u'vanachalim*, "in the seas and rivers." *B'mayim b'mayim shtei pe'amim ein zeh klal u'prat ela ribui u'mi'ut* — two consecutive general terms transform the analysis from *klal u'prat* to *ribui u'mi'ut*. In *pidyon ha-ben*, the two generalizations *u'fduyav miben chodesh* and *tifdeh* appear adjacent to each other, and only then does the specific term *be'erkcha kesef chameshet shekalim* follow. Because of this structural feature, Rebbi applies *ribui u'mi'ut* in that case specifically — not because he is generally a *ribui u'mi'ut* exponent.

## Two Klalim

### Mayim Baraita

The *baraita* from the school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches: *b'mayim b'mayim shtei pe'amim ein zeh klal u'prat ela ribui u'mi'ut* — when two general expressions appear before the specific, it is *ribui u'mi'ut*, not *klal u'prat*. The principle is clear: the presence of two adjacent *klalim* before the *prat* signals a fundamentally different hermeneutic mode.

### Amora Dispute

An *amora* dispute is recorded regarding how to handle such a *klal klal u'prat* sequence. Ravina cites a tradition from the scholars of *Eretz Yisrael* — *kol makom she-ata motzei shtei klalos ha-smuchos zeh la-zeh, hatel prat beineihem ve-donam b'klal u'prat* — wherever you find two adjacent general terms, insert the specific between them and analyze the sequence as a standard *klal u'prat u'klal*. This is a competing approach to reading double generalizations. The resulting debate, then, is whether two adjacent *klalim* before the *prat* shift one to *ribui u'mi'ut* (as the school of Rabbi Yishmael holds) or whether the *prat* is simply inserted mentally between them and the whole sequence is treated as *klal u'prat u'klal* (as the *Eretz Yisrael* tradition proposes).

### Pidyon Exception

For Rebbi, the resolution is now clear. His general methodology is *klal u'prat*, as demonstrated by the awl case. *Pidyon ha-ben* is an exception precisely because the structural condition identified by the school of Rabbi Yishmael obtains there: two generalizations appear side by side before the specification. That structural anomaly, and only that, leads Rebbi to apply the broader *ribui u'mi'ut* framework in that specific instance.

## Final Position

### Concession

This resolution, however, creates a new problem for the *gemara*'s argument about *shavuah*. The *gemara* had argued that since Rebbi uses *ribui u'mi'ut*, he necessarily shares Rabbi Akiva's conclusion that *shavuah* liability extends to the past. But now it has been established that Rebbi is fundamentally a *klal u'prat* man who applies *ribui u'mi'ut* only as an exception in *pidyon ha-ben* due to the unusual structure of those *pesukim*. There is no such structural anomaly in the *shavuah pesukim*. Therefore Rebbi, applying *klal u'prat u'klal* to the *shavuah* verses, would arrive at Rabbi Yishmael's conclusion: the *korban* applies only to future-oriented oaths. *Hashta de'amrat Rebbi klallei u'prattei darish, ba'al korchecha kashya shavuos* — now that one has conceded that Rebbi employs *klal u'prat*, one is forced to conclude that Rebbi himself would not hold that a past-oriented *shavuah* triggers *korban* liability.

### Complete Answer

The *gemara* thus arrives at its final resolution: *ela bi-shvu'os nasiv aliba de-Rabbi Akiva, ve-lei lo sevira lei* — regarding *shavuah*, Rebbi includes the two that is four by quoting Rabbi Akiva's broader position, even though he himself does not personally hold that view. Rebbi's own methodology — *klal u'prat* — would yield only future-oriented *shavuah* liability, consistent with Rabbi Yishmael's reading. But in composing the *mishnah*, Rebbi wished to record another instance of the pattern "two that is four," and for that he incorporated Rabbi Akiva's expansive ruling on *shavuah* without personally subscribing to it. The two clauses of the *mishnah* thus reflect, as Rav Yosef originally proposed, different *tannaic* positions — but with an important qualification: in the *tumah* case, Rebbi personally holds the position he records (that of Rabbi Yishmael, as shown from the *baraita*), while in the *shavuah* case, he cites Rabbi Akiva's view for the sake of completeness, without it representing his own *halachic* conclusion.

# Shevuot 5

## Yedi'ot HaTumah

### Mishnah Setup

The Gemara opens with the phrase *gufa*, indicating a return to the core matter. The Mishnah has established that one is liable for a *korban* only where there exists *yedi'ah batchilah* — knowledge at the outset — and *yedi'ah basof* — knowledge at the conclusion — with an *he'elam*, a lapse of awareness, in between. This framework applies to the laws of *tumah*: one must have had some awareness regarding *tumah*, then entered a state of forgetfulness or ignorance, and subsequently regained awareness. The two axes of this structure concern either forgetting that one is *tamei* or forgetting that the place entered is the *Mikdash* — or in the related context of *kodesh*, forgetting the sanctity of the food one is consuming. These are the two or four permutations that the Mishnah generates.

### R. Akiva's View

The Gemara asks: from where is this principle derived? The answer is *talmud lomar vene'elam vene'elam shtei pe'amim* — the Torah uses the word *vene'elam* twice, and Rabbi Akiva derives from this doubling that two distinct *yedi'ot* are required. The repetition of the term is not incidental; it is the exegetical anchor for the two-knowledge requirement.

### R. Yishmael Challenge

Rabbi Yishmael takes a different approach. He maintains that one need not derive the two *yedi'ot* from the doubled expression, since even the single use of *vene'elam* implies prior knowledge — *miklal sheyada*. The logic is linguistic: *vene'elam* denotes something that became hidden or concealed, which presupposes that it was previously known. The verse in context further states *vehu yada ve'asham* — "and he knew and became guilty" — indicating an awareness that follows the forgetting. Rabbi Yishmael thus holds that a single occurrence of *vene'elam* already implies two states of knowledge, rendering the second appearance of *vene'elam* available for a different derivation: to create liability separately for *he'elam tumah* and for *he'elam mikdash*, two distinct categories of lapse.

### Rava's Sotah Proof

The Gemara challenges the premise that *vene'elam* inherently means "knew and then forgot." Rava raises a difficulty from the laws of *sotah*. The verse concerning the *sotah* uses the same root: *vehi ne'elmah mei'einei ishah* — "and she was hidden from her husband's eyes." If *vene'elam* always implies prior knowledge followed by forgetting, then in the *sotah* case, one would be forced to say the husband once knew of the infidelity, then forgot, and only then proceeded to bring his wife for the *sotah* procedure. This is obviously untenable: the entire premise of the *sotah* process is that the husband *does not know* whether his wife was unfaithful. The *sotah* procedure is not a post-hoc ritual for confirmed knowledge; it is a mechanism for resolving genuine doubt.

### Sotah Analysis

Abaye raises a further difficulty from within the *sotah* laws themselves, citing the principle *venikah ha'ish me'avon veha'ishah hi tisa et avonah* — the husband is absolved of sin and the woman bears her own guilt. A Baraita teaches: *bizman sheha'ish menukeh me'avon hamayim bodkin et ishto* — the bitter waters work only when the husband himself is free of sin. If the husband had known of the adultery, covered it up, and then submitted his wife to the ordeal, this very act of concealment would constitute an *avon* on his part — and the waters would not work. The entire efficacy of the *sotah* procedure is contingent on the husband's innocence, which would be forfeit if he had knowledge and then "forgot." Thus, *vene'elam* in that context cannot possibly mean prior knowledge followed by forgetting.

### Torah Examples

Additional instances from Torah further undermine the reading of *vene'elam* as implying prior knowledge. The verse describes divine wisdom as *ne'elamet mei'einei kol chai u-me'of hashamayim nisterah* — hidden from all living creatures and concealed from the birds of the sky. If *vene'elam* required prior knowledge, this would imply that someone once possessed full understanding of divine wisdom and then forgot it. But the very next verse states *lo yada enosh erchah* — no human has ever known its true measure. The *chukim* of the Torah cannot be fully grasped; the notion that some person once knew them and then forgot is impossible. These examples demonstrate conclusively that *vene'elam* need not imply prior knowledge; it can simply mean that something was, and remains, concealed.

### Abaye's Solution

Abaye therefore proposes a reinterpretation of what "knowledge" means in this context. He invokes the principle *yediat beit rabo shemah yediah* — the knowledge one absorbs in one's teacher's house, meaning the knowledge acquired in childhood education, counts as the relevant *yediah*. This is not the knowledge of a specific incident — not a conscious, moment-to-moment awareness that one has become *tamei* — but rather a general conceptual familiarity with the laws of *tumah v'taharah*.

### Rashi Explanation

Rashi elaborates on this distinction in illuminating detail. The phrase *yediat beit rabo she-lamad b'veit rabo she-hanogea b'tumah tamei* means that a person learned as a child — particularly in an era like that of Chizkiyahu, when Torah knowledge was widespread — that contact with a source of *tumah* renders one *tamei*. Additionally, *vehu yada she-hirgish k'she-naga*: he was aware, at least on some level, that he had touched something. So it is not that he was entirely oblivious. What he did not do is *hitbonenah tumah b'libo she-nitma* — he did not mentally put the pieces together and consciously register: I touched that *sheretz*, that *sheretz* is *tamei*, therefore I am now *tamei*. He possessed, in effect, a kind of subconscious or background knowledge — the conceptual framework was there, the triggering incident was there, but the conscious synthesis never occurred. It is something like knowing the speed limit and being aware that traffic is moving quickly, but not actively registering in the moment that one is speeding.

### Rav Pappa Q

Rav Pappa presses Abaye with a question arising from the Mishnah itself. The Mishnah had enumerated different permutations, one of which involves a case where there is *ein bah yediah batchilah* — no knowledge at the outset — and *yesh bah yediah basof* — knowledge at the conclusion. If Abaye's principle is that *yediah* means general conceptual knowledge acquired in one's education, how can there be a case of no initial knowledge? Surely everyone knows the basic laws of *tumah* — that contact with impure objects renders one *tamei*. Rav Pappa formulates his challenge precisely: *mi leika d'lo yada yediat beit rabo d'leit lei yediat beit rabo?* Is there truly someone who lacks even this background level of knowledge?

### Tinok Shenishba

The answer is *mashkachat lah b'tinok shenishba l'vein hanachrim* — yes, one can find such a case in the *tinok shenishba*, the Jewish child taken captive and raised among non-Jews. Literally this refers to a Jewish infant kidnapped and raised without any Jewish education or exposure to Torah law. In the world of the Talmud, such kidnappings were not uncommon.
