The concept has been significantly expanded in later halachic discourse to encompass any Jew who grew up entirely without Jewish education — raised in an assimilated household, with no exposure to *halachah* — who would simply not know why, for instance, one cannot turn on a light on *Shabbat*. For such a person, the very conceptual framework that Abaye identifies as the necessary *yediah* is absent. In that case, the Mishnah's permutation of *ein bah yediah batchilah* is perfectly applicable: there was genuinely no prior knowledge of any kind, and only later, through some form of education or exposure, does the person acquire *yediah basof*.

### Historical Waves

This discussion prompted a broader reflection on the variation in Jewish knowledge and observance across history. The Gemara elsewhere notes that at the time of Chizkiyahu, Torah knowledge was so pervasive that even the youngest child knew the *halachot* of *tumah v'taharah*, and a survey from one end of *Eretz Yisrael* to the other found universal familiarity — the image of *meHodu v'ad Kush* applied internally to Jewish learning. Yet there were other periods of sharp decline, when large segments of the population had little knowledge of basic observance, drawn instead toward idolatry. The *Beit Sheni*, for all its outward grandeur, was ultimately destroyed precisely because of such failures. At the same time, other Gemaras note moments of extraordinary scholarly flourishing — the famous comparison where Rav Yehuda had only to remove his shoe during a drought before rain came, while in later generations great learning seemed to coexist with diminished spiritual potency. Knowledge and righteousness, it emerges, do not always track together, and they both move in waves throughout Jewish history. There is, the discussion implies, nothing new under the sun: there have always been more observant and less observant Jews, the content and locus of observance simply shifting from one era to the next.

---

## Yetziot HaShabbat

### Mishnah Setup

The Gemara now turns to the Mishnah's second item: *yetziot HaShabbat*. The familiar formulation from Tractate Shabbat reads: *yitziot HaShabbat shtayim she'hen arba bifnim u'shtayim she'hen arba bachutz* — the exits of Shabbat are two that are four inside, and two that are four outside. The immediate arithmetical consequence of this formulation is striking: the Shabbat Mishnah enumerates not four but eight cases in total. This stands in contrast to our Mishnah in Shevuot, which states only *shtayim she'hen arba* — two that are four — with no mention of a second set. The Gemara will work to explain this discrepancy.

### Three Components

Before proceeding to the individual cases, it is essential to establish what constitutes a prohibited act of transfer on *Shabbat*. Three components are required for full liability *mi'd'Oraita*: *akirah* (lifting — removing an object from its resting place), *ha'avarah* (transference across the boundary between domains), and *hanachah* (placing down — depositing the object in the new domain). All three must be performed by a single person, acting in the usual manner. If the labor is divided between two people, neither is *chayav*; each has performed only part of the prohibited act.

The relevant domains are *reshut hayachid* — the private domain — and *reshut harabim* — the public domain. A third category, *makom patur*, also exists and plays a role in more complex traversals, but the core prohibition involves transfer between the private and public domains.

Regarding the two that are four in our Mishnah: Rashi explains that *shtayim she'hen arba mi'divreihem hosifu shtayim le'asur lechatchila im asah patur* — the two that derive from rabbinic enactment are *patur aval assur*: one is exempt from a *korban* but the act is still prohibited. So two cases carry full Torah-level liability and two additional cases are rabbinically prohibited, accounting for the "four" of the formulation.

### Case 1: Ani Outside

The Mishnah in Shabbat begins: *he'ani omed bachutz u'ba'al habayit bifnim* — the poor man stands outside and the homeowner is inside, this being the standard configuration. The first case: *pashat he'ani et yado lifnim venatan letoch yado shel ba'al habayit* — the poor man extends his hand into the interior domain and places an object into the hand of the homeowner. In this case, the *ani* has performed both the *akirah* (lifting the object from its place in the public domain) and the *hanachah* (depositing it in the homeowner's hand in the private domain). The *ani* is therefore *chayav*. The homeowner has done nothing that carries liability.

### Case 2: Ani Takes

The second case, presented as an alternative: *o she'natal mitocha vehotzi* — or the *ani* reaches his hand into the interior, takes an object from it, and withdraws. Here too the *ani* has performed both the *akirah* — lifting the object from the homeowner's domain — and the *hanachah* — coming to rest with it in his own domain outside. Again, the *ani* has done everything; the *ani* is *chayav*.

### Case 3: Baal Habayit Out

The third case: *pashat ba'al habayit et yado lachutz venatan letoch yado shel ani* — the homeowner extends his hand outside and places an object into the outstretched hand of the poor man. Here the homeowner has performed the *akirah* from within and the *hanachah* into the public domain. The *ba'al habayit* is *chayav*; the *ani* is *patur*.

### Case 4: Ani Takes Out

Fourth: *o she'natal mitocha vehichnis* — or the homeowner, with his hand extended outside, takes an object from the *ani*'s hand and brings it back inside. Again, the homeowner has performed the complete prohibited act — *akirah* from the public domain and *hanachah* within his own private domain. The *ba'al habayit* is *chayav*; the *ani* is *patur*.

### Cases 5-8: Divided Labor

The Mishnah then turns to the cases of divided labor. *Pashat he'ani et yado lifnim venatal ba'al habayit mitocha* — the *ani* extends his hand inside, but the homeowner takes the object from his hand. Or: *she'natan lo letochah vehotzi* — the homeowner places something into the *ani*'s extended hand, and the *ani* withdraws. In both of these sub-cases, *shnehem peturim* — both are exempt — because the *akirah* was performed by one party and the *hanachah* by the other. Similarly mirrored are the cases where the homeowner extends his hand outside: *pashat ba'al habayit yado lachutz venatal ani mitochah* — the *ani* takes from the homeowner's extended hand; or *she'natan letochah vehichnis* — the *ani* deposits an object into the homeowner's extended hand and the homeowner draws it back inside. Again, *shnehem peturim*. These four cases of divided labor — *patur aval assur* — complete the set of eight.

### Gemara Q

Having reviewed the Mishnah in Shabbat, the Gemara poses its question about our Mishnah in Shevuot: *mai shna hacha detani shtayim she'hen arba vetu lo* — why does Shevuot state only "two that are four" without the additional "inside" and "outside"? Why does Shabbat say *shtayim she'hen arba bifnim u'shtayim she'hen arba bachutz*, while Shevuot contents itself with the shortened formulation?

### Preliminary Answer

A preliminary answer is offered: *hatam de-ikar Shabbat hu tani avot ve-toldot, hacha delav ikar Shabbat hu avot tani ve-toldot lo tani* — there, in Tractate Shabbat, the subject matter is Shabbat itself, and so both *avot* and *toldot*, both the primary cases and their derivatives, are fully elaborated. Here, in Shevuot, Shabbat is not the central topic; only the *avot* are taught and the *toldot* are not. So the truncated formulation is appropriate to the secondary context.

### Rav Pappa Object

The Gemara is unsatisfied with this. Rav Pappa presses: if *yetziot* refers to the cases of actual *hotza'ah* — the acts of removal — then there are really only two such cases, not four. If the formula "two that are four" is supposed to enumerate only the cases where one is *chayav*, then the inside and outside distinction would need to be mentioned in order to reach four *chiyuvim*. And if the "four" includes cases of *patur*, then one cannot say this Mishnah discusses only *chiyuvim*. The formulation is internally inconsistent. The question, in short, is: *chiyyubi mai ninhu yitziot? Yitziot tartin havyen* — if *yetziot* means acts of taking out, there are really only two of them.

### Yetziah Broad Use

The resolution requires expanding the semantic range of the word *yetziah*. Even in the Mishnah in Shabbat, where the text says *yitziot HaShabbat* and then describes both *yetziah* (removal from private to public) and *hachnasah* (bringing in from public to private), the term *yetziah* is used to encompass both. The Mishnah counts *hachnasot* as *yetziot* because it is using *yetziah* in a broad sense — denoting any transfer between domains, regardless of direction. This is what allows the formulation "two that are four" to hold: two general categories of transfer, each with two concrete cases, yielding four total *chiyuvim*.

### Baraita Source

Support for this usage is drawn from a Baraita listing the thirty-nine *avot melachot*, where one of the categories is stated as *hamotzi mereshut lereshut chayav* — one who transfers from domain to domain is liable. The formulation *mereshut lereshut* is conspicuously general: it does not say *mi-reshut hayachid li-reshut harabim* but simply "from one domain to another." This breadth is intentional. If the prohibition applied only to removing something from the private to the public domain, the Baraita would have specified that direction. The open formulation indicates that bringing something *in* — from public to private — is equally prohibited and equally subsumed under the term *hotza'ah*.

### Rav Ashi

Rav Ashi states this principle explicitly: *tanna hachnasa nami yetziah kari leh* — the Tanna calls *hachnasah* also a *yetziah*. The proof is the Baraita just cited: *mi lo askinan dekama'yel leh vekakari leh hotza'ah* — are we not dealing there also with cases where one is bringing an object *in*, and yet the Baraita calls it *hotza'ah*? Clearly the term *hotza'ah* or *yetziah* is being used to denote any act of transfer between domains, not merely removal in one direction. The better conceptual term would perhaps be *ha'avarah* — conveyance or transfer — but the Mishnah and Baraita use *yetziah* to encompass both directions. What unifies them is the structure of the prohibited act: an *akirah* from one domain and a *hanachah* in the other, performed by the same person. Whether one calls the result a *yetziah* or *hachnasah* depends only on which direction the object travels; the underlying legal structure is identical.

### Raba: Reshuyot

Rava offers a still different resolution to the linguistic difficulty. Rather than expanding the meaning of *yetziah* to include *hachnasah*, Rava proposes that *yetziot* in the Mishnah does not mean "acts of removal" at all, but *reshuyot* — domains. *Reshuyot Shabbat shtayim* — the relevant domains of Shabbat are two. The two general categories are the two domains, *reshut hayachid* and *reshut harabim*, and the various permutations of transfer between them generate the four (or eight) specific cases. On this reading, the Mishnah is not claiming that there are two types of *yetziah*; it is rather orienting the entire discussion around the two domains that define the prohibition.

---

## Mar'ot Nega'im

### Four Marks Intro

The Mishnah's third item is *mar'ot nega'im* — the appearances of *tzara'at* lesions — which are described as two that are four. This topic is less familiar to most contemporary learners than *Shabbat*, and a brief orientation to the relevant laws is essential. The Torah in Parashat Tazria introduces the condition with the words: *adam ki yihyeh be'or besaro se'eit o sapachat o baheret* — a person who has on the skin of his flesh a *se'eit*, or a *sapachat*, or a *baheret*. Three terms are listed, but the halachic tradition identifies four distinct shades that trigger the laws of *tzara'at*: *baheret*, *se'eit*, *sid heichal*, and *krum habeitza*. The term *sapachat* in the verse does not name a fourth primary shade but rather denotes a secondary or derivative shade attached to one of the primaries — but which primary or primaries it attaches to is, as we shall see, precisely what is disputed.

### Visual Order

The four shades are arranged in order of decreasing whiteness. *Baheret* is the most intensely white — the Mishnah compares it to snow, and the word itself relates to the Hebrew *bahir*, meaning bright or brilliant. *Se'eit* is the white of clean wool — slightly less dazzling than snow but clearly white. *Sid heichal* is the white of the plaster used to coat the walls of the *Heichal*, the Temple sanctuary — a lime-white, somewhat more muted. *Krum habeitza* is the color of the membrane found just beneath the eggshell — not the shell itself but the thin translucent film inside it, which presents a faint, delicate white. This is the palest of the four and sits at the bottom of the scale.

### Sapachat Ambiguity

The Mishnah states *mar'ot nega'im shnayim she'hem arba* and proceeds to explain: *baheret azah kasheleg*, and *u'shniyah lah kesid haheichal* — *baheret* is intense as snow, and secondary to it is *sid heichal*. Then *se'eit ketzemer lavan*, and *u'shniyah lah kekrum habeitza* — *se'eit* is like white wool, and secondary to it is *krum habeitza*. This formulation pairs each of the two primary shades with one secondary shade: *baheret* with *sid heichal*, and *se'eit* with *krum habeitza*.

The ambiguity arises from the word *sapachat* in the original verse. Read one way, *sapachat* refers to a secondary shade attaching specifically to *baheret*, making it a modifier for *baheret* alone. Read another way, it could indicate that each of the two named primaries — *se'eit* and *baheret* — has its own *sapachat*, its own secondary shade. The practical stakes of this ambiguity concern the law of *mitztaref* — combination. Two differently shaded patches of *tzara'at* can combine to meet the minimum required size for a diagnosis of *nega tzara'at* only if they belong to the same halachic category, or to a parent-derivative relationship within a category. The question of which shades can combine with which therefore turns entirely on how the categories and their *sapachot* are structured.

### R. Akiva Setup

Rabbi Akiva holds that *baheret* and *se'eit* are the two *avot* — the two primary categories — and that *sid heichal* and *krum habeitza* are the two *toldot*, the derivative or secondary shades. Crucially, Rabbi Akiva assigns both *toldot* to *se'eit* alone. That is: *se'eit* is the *av* from which *sid heichal* and *krum habeitza* both derive, while *baheret* stands alone as the other *av* with no *toldah* of its own. On Rabbi Akiva's scheme, the structure is: *baheret* (primary, no derivative); *se'eit* (primary, with *sid heichal* and *krum habeitza* as its two secondary shades). This is a 1 and 2 with two sub-variants under 2: call it 1, 2, 2A, and 2B.

### Hanina Challenge

Hanina raises a sharp challenge to Rabbi Akiva's position, specifically as it bears on the law of *mitztaref*. If we accept Rabbi Akiva's ordering and then try to ask how the shades combine: can *sid heichal* combine with *baheret*? No, because there are two levels between them — *se'eit* intervenes, and one cannot jump two levels in the chain of parent-derivative relationships. Can *sid heichal* combine with *se'eit*? No, because though *sid heichal* is indeed closer to *se'eit* in the ordering, *se'eit* is *se'eit*'s *av* — but *sid* is a *toldah* and *se'eit* is an *av*, and a *toldah* cannot combine with anything except members of its own sub-group. On Rabbi Akiva's reading, then, *sid heichal* is left isolated: it cannot combine with *baheret* (too far up), and it cannot combine with *se'eit* in a way that would trigger the combined minimum.

### Combination Rules

The rules governing combination are: a secondary shade can combine only with its parent category or with shades that share the same parent. This means that patches of different *toldot* stemming from the same *av* can combine with one another, and a *toldah* can combine with its own *av*, but a *toldah* cannot jump over its parent to combine with a more distant shade. The structure of the combination rules thus follows precisely the structure of the category assignments, which is why the assignment of *sid heichal* as a *toldah* of *se'eit* has such significant practical consequences.

### Sapachat Resolution

The difficulty regarding *krum habeitza* is somewhat more tractable. Although *krum habeitza* sits below *se'eit* in the ordering, the verse *u'le-se'eit u'le-sapachat* — "and to *se'eit* and to *sapachat*" — indicates that *sapachat* is subsidiary to *se'eit*, *sapahat tfelah le-se'eit*. And, crucially, the Torah explicitly designates this relationship even though *krum habeitza* is lower in shade intensity. The verse's pairing of *se'eit* and *sapachat* provides the authorization for *krum habeitza* to function as *se'eit*'s derivative and to combine accordingly. *Sid heichal*, by contrast, lacks an analogous explicit authorization under Rabbi Akiva's system, and the problem remains unresolved for it.

### Non-Akiva View

The Gemara's conclusion is therefore: *mechuvarata lo ke-Rabbi Akiva* — the plainest understanding of the Mishnah's formulation does not accord with Rabbi Akiva's view. The Mishnah as we have it, which pairs *baheret* with *sid heichal* as its secondary shade and *se'eit* with *krum habeitza* as its secondary shade, reflects a different classification entirely — one in which each of the two *avot* has exactly one *toldah*. In that scheme: *baheret* is primary (1) with *sid heichal* as its derivative (1B), and *se'eit* is primary (2) with *krum habeitza* as its derivative (2B). This clean two-by-two structure is what yields the formulation "two that are four" — two *avot* each with one *toldah* — and it avoids the combinatorial problems that beset Rabbi Akiva's arrangement. The Mishnah's language, then, represents a Tannaitic view other than Rabbi Akiva's, and the discussion will continue from this point.

---

---

# Shevuot 6

## Four Shades & Combination

### Mishna vs. Rabbi Akiva

The opening discussion on 6a takes up a problem that has been building across the preceding folio: the *mishna* in *Masechet Negaim*, which lists the four shades of white that constitute *tzaraat*, appears to be at odds with the position of Rabbi Akiva. The heart of the tension lies in a statement attributed to Rav Chanina (5b): *man tanna mar'ot nega'im dela k'Rabbi Akiva* — "who is the *tanna* who taught the shades of the *negaim*? It is not Rabbi Akiva." The reason, as Rav Chanina continues, is that Rabbi Akiva holds *zu l'mala mizu v'zu l'mala mizu* — each shade is ranked above the next in a continuous ascending scale — and if that were the operating principle, one would end up rendering the lime-plaster color of the *heichal* walls permanently pure, a result that cannot be accepted.

To understand what is at stake, the four shades must be kept clearly in view. *Baheret* is the color of snow — the brightest white. *Se'et* is the color of wool. *Sid*, the lime-plaster color, is a *toldah*, a derivative of *baheret*. *Krum beitzah*, the color of an egg membrane, is the dimmest of the four. According to the *Tanna Kamma*, *sid* cannot combine with *se'et* because they belong to different species — *sid* is a derivative of *baheret*, not of *se'et*. Nor can *sid* combine directly with *baheret*, its parent category, because they are not adjacent in the ranked list. The Gemara therefore concludes: *ela mechavarta d'matnitin dela k'Rabbi Akiva* — it appears quite clear, as the Gemara puts it with a term (*mechavarta*, from the root for "white") that carries a certain resonance in the context of a discussion about shades of white, that the *mishna* does not accord with Rabbi Akiva.

### R. Yehoshua's Question

The Gemara then asks: where exactly do we derive Rabbi Akiva's distinctive position? The answer comes from a *baraita* introduced by *meha d'tanya* — "from what was taught." Rabbi Yosi relates that Yehoshua the son of Rabbi Akiva — who is generally known as Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha — posed a question to his father: *mipnei mah amru mar'ot nega'im shnayim shehen arba'ah* — why did the Sages say that the shades of *negaim* are "two which are really four"? Why enumerate all four categories explicitly? The *mishna* could simply have said *mikrum beitzah ulmala tamei* — anything whiter than an egg membrane is *tamei* — and the entire range of qualifying shades would be captured in a single formulation. The style of Tannaitic composition tends toward brevity; the principle *derech hatanna lkatzer* means that *tanna'im* typically compress their rulings and leave the reader to infer. So why the full enumeration?

### R. Akiva's Answer

Rabbi Akiva's response is twofold. First, *lomar shemitztarfin ze im ze* — to teach that the different shades can combine with one another, such that a *nega* spanning adjacent color categories can still reach the requisite minimum size of a *gris*. *Krum beitzah* can combine with *sid*; *sid* can combine with *krum beitzah* or *se'et*; *se'et* can combine with *sid* or *baheret*. Each shade combines with its neighbors in the ordered sequence — the principle of *zu l'mala mizu* expressed in practice.

But Rabbi Akiva adds a second point when pressed further: even if one were to state both the threshold (*mikrum beitzah ulmala tamei*) and the combination rule (*umitztarfin ze im ze*) in a single formulation, there would still be a reason to enumerate the four shades individually.

### Names & Recognition

That reason is the following *halacha*: *kol kohen she-eino baki bahen uvishmoteihen eino ro'eh et hanegaim* — a *kohen* who is not expert both in the shades themselves and in their names is not qualified to inspect *negaim*. This is a striking ruling. One might have assumed that visual competence alone suffices — if the *kohen* can correctly identify whether a given spot is *tamei* or *tahor*, why should it matter whether he can name the category? Yet Rabbi Akiva insists that the taxonomical and linguistic dimension is essential. The *kohen* must not only perceive the color but be able to classify it and name it correctly.

This emphasis on naming recurs across many areas of *halacha*. In the laws of *Shabbat*, knowing the name of a *melachah* is part of how the violation is constituted. At the end of *Makkot*, a *hatraah* requires specifying to the violator the name of the *aveirah* they are about to commit. Language plays a constitutive, not merely descriptive, role in halakhic categories.

---

## Kohen's Expertise

### Who Becomes Tamei

A related *halacha* from Rambam's *Hilchot Tumat Tzaraat* (chapter 9) illuminates the structure of the *tzaraat* inspection process. The first *halacha* states: *hakol mitam'in benegaim* — everyone can become *tamei* from *nega tzaraat*, including even an infant from the day of birth and slaves. However, non-Jews and even a *ger toshav* who has accepted the *sheva mitzvot* are excluded. The Rambam then adds: *vechol hanegaim adam ro'eh otan chutz minigei atzmo* — one can inspect all *negaim* except one's own. This is partly a practical constraint — one cannot see one's entire body — but also a formal structural requirement: the inspection involves a *metamei*, the inspector, standing in opposition to the *mitamei*, the one being inspected. The two roles cannot be played by the same person. There is a dialogical, relational dimension to the process of becoming *tamei* from *tzaraat* that is built into the halakhic framework itself.

### Kohen as Mouthpiece

The second relevant *halacha* from the Rambam addresses a case where the *kohen* lacks the required expertise. If a non-*kohen* — a *Yisrael* or a *Levi* — possesses the halakhic knowledge but lacks the priestly status, while the available *kohen* lacks the knowledge, the two can operate in combination: the expert advises and the *kohen* serves as the formal mouthpiece, making the declaration of *tamei*, *tahor*, *musgar*, or *muchlat*. The formal validity of the declaration derives entirely from the *kohen*'s statement, even though the substantive expertise comes from elsewhere. This produces an interesting parallel to the Talmudic passage at the end of *Sanhedrin* involving the lame man and the blind man — each contributes what the other lacks — and there the image is deployed to explain why God judges body and soul together.

### Minor/Shoteh Kohen

The Rambam extends this principle further in a direction that may seem surprising: *afilu haya hakohen katan* — even if the *kohen* is a minor — *o shoteh* — or even someone who is mentally incapacitated, a *shoteh* in the full halakhic sense whose capacity to interact functionally with the world is severely compromised — *hachacham omer lo v'hu machlit o poter o soger* — a Torah scholar can instruct this person and the *kohen* can make the legally effective declaration. Despite the general rule that a minor and a *shoteh* lack the standing to create halakhic consequences, the declaration is valid.

One might ask whether this contradicts Rabbi Akiva's requirement that the *kohen* be expert in the shades and their names. The resolution appears to be that there are two distinct tracks. When the *kohen* relies on his own abilities, he must himself be an expert. When he relies on someone else who is the expert, his role becomes purely formal — the required mouthpiece through whom the declaration must pass — and the expertise requirement is satisfied vicariously. The formal and substantive dimensions of the *kohen*'s function are separable.

---

## R. Yehoshua Korcha

### Korcha = R. Akiva

The *baraita* cited above identifies the questioner as *Yehoshua beno shel Rabbi Akiva* — Yehoshua the son of Rabbi Akiva. This same figure appears throughout *Shas* under the name Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha. The *Ge'onim* and Rashi in numerous places across the Talmud identify these as the same person, explaining that Rabbi Akiva was known by the nickname *Korcha* — the bald one — as attested by the Gemara in *Bechorot*. Rabbi Akiva began studying Torah at the relatively advanced age of forty, lived to an unusually old age, and may well have been bald by the time his reputation was fully established; once the nickname became entrenched, his son would naturally be known as *Yehoshua ben Korcha*.

### Tosafot Objection

Tosafot, however, object to this identification on grounds of propriety. To call one of the greatest *tanna'im* of his generation by an embarrassing nickname — effectively calling him "baldy" — seems deeply problematic. The Gemara itself treats conferring a degrading *kinuy* on another person as an extremely serious matter. Tosafot therefore conclude that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha must be a different person whose father was literally named *Korcha*, citing a *Gemara* in *Megillah* in support.

Against Tosafot, one might observe that the tradition identifying them as one and the same is too pervasive to dismiss easily. It is possible that Rabbi Akiva's extraordinary humility — rooted in his origins as an illiterate shepherd who began learning Torah at forty — made him genuinely indifferent to such a nickname. Rabbi Akiva is always paired in rabbinic imagination with Moshe Rabbeinu as the great Torah teacher who overcame impossible odds. Perhaps that humility extended to accepting, or at least not objecting to, a playful epithet. And once the nickname became common currency, it would naturally attach to his son's name as well.

As for who this otherwise-unknown person named *Korcha* might be if not Rabbi Akiva — *Korcha* is itself a strange name, and the identification with Rabbi Akiva remains the most economical explanation.

### Age Problems

A further difficulty involves chronology. Tosafot note that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha appears in conversation with Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who blessed him that he should live to at least half of Rabbi Akiva's years — that is, to sixty. If Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha was younger than sixty at the time of that blessing, then working backwards, the timeline grows strained: Rabbi Akiva would have had to father a child when he was well past one hundred years old, which is difficult to accept straightforwardly. The math does not work cleanly, and Tosafot leverage this as an argument against the identification. Nonetheless, the genealogical evidence embedded in the sources pointing toward this identification remains strong, and it may be that some of the *gemarot* involved carry a degree of imprecision that makes exact chronological reconstruction unreliable.

---

## Tanna Kamma Return

### Dilmah Question

Returning to the substantive halakhic question: could the *mishna* perhaps be read according to the *Tanna Kamma*'s model — that is, *se'et* and its *toldah* combine, and *baheret* and its *toldah* combine, but there is no cross-combination? The Gemara raises this reading (*vedilma se'et vetoldatah baheret vetoldatah*) and asks whether it can be sustained.

### Milk & Blood Mashal

The problem is that this reading runs into Rabbi Chanina's *mashal* explaining Rabbi Akiva's position. Rabbi Chanina describes Rabbi Akiva's view through a *mashal* of four cups of milk: into one go two drops of blood, into a second go four drops, into a third go eight, and into a fourth go twelve. (A variant reading has sixteen in place of twelve, which would make each step a clean doubling — two, four, eight, sixteen — and the Gemara notes this *ve'amrei lah* reading, suggesting the variant may have been motivated by a preference for geometric doubling.) All four cups remain white — *shekulan mar'ot lavan hen* — but each is a slightly more reddish white than the previous, a continuous gradation: *ela shezeh lemalah mizeh vezeh lemalah mizeh*. This is the visual picture underlying Rabbi Akiva's conception: the four shades form a single unbroken spectrum, not two separate paired families.

### Patuach & Chaluk

The question then becomes whether Rabbi Akiva's principle of combination (*mitztarfin ze im ze*) applies when the two shades in question are *patuach* — adjacent in the spectrum — or also when they are *chaluk* — separated, non-adjacent. Rashi explains *patuach* as *me'urav*, mixed or together. The Gemara works through the question of whether hearing that non-adjacent shades combine also tells us that adjacent shades combine, and vice versa. The difficulty is that if the shades are of different families — if *se'et* and *baheret* are genuinely distinct species — it is not obvious that adjacency in the spectrum is sufficient to permit combination. The Gemara ultimately uses this analysis as part of establishing the full scope of Rabbi Akiva's position.

---

## R. Akiva's Colors

### Beheret = Snow

The next *baraita* offers Rabbi Akiva's own description of the color scale. *Shel baheret az kesheleg* — the *baheret* color is as vivid and bright as snow. *Veshel sid deheh heimena* — and the *sid* (lime-plaster) color is darker than, or dimmer than, *baheret*.

### Se'et Omission

A question immediately arises: Rabbi Akiva mentions *baheret* (snow) and *sid* (lime-plaster), but makes no mention of *se'et* (wool color). The *baraita* should have said that the wool color is darker than snow, if that is Rabbi Akiva's view. The Gemara acknowledges this: *in hachi nami* — yes, that is correct, the *baraita* should have mentioned it. The omission is notable partly because it bears on the earlier debate about whether Rabbi Akiva would place *sid* in direct combination with *baheret* or would interpose *se'et* between them.

### Rabbi Nathan Version

Rabbi Nathan preserves an alternative version of the *baraita*: rather than saying that *sid* is darker than snow, he says it is *se'et* — the wool color — that is darker than snow. This is a textual variant that directly affects how Rabbi Akiva's ordering is understood.

### Abaye's Drasha

The Gemara then asks how we know that *baheret* is the brightest of all the colors. Abaye cites a *pasuk*: *ve'im baheret levanah hi* — "and if the *baheret* is white." From this Abaye derives: *hi levanah ve'ein acheret levanah* — it, the *baheret*, is white, and none of the others are white in the same sense. They belong to the white family, but only *baheret* is truly white. It should be noted that Abaye is not deploying a formal *middah* of *midrash*; he is reading the *pasuk* straightforwardly as an *asmachta* — a Scriptural support for a conclusion that was already known from other grounds.

---

## Four Negaim

### Beheret Amukah

The Gemara continues with a *baraita* of the Rabbanan describing each of the four *negaim* in turn. *Baheret amukah* — the *baheret* appears deep, or recessed. The *pasuk* says *amok me'or besaro* — it is beneath the level of the skin — and the Gemara connects this to a visual phenomenon: *ke'mareh chamah amukah min hatzel* — just as a brightly illuminated area outdoors appears deeper, farther away, than a shaded area. The *baheret*'s extreme whiteness creates this optical impression of recession. This reflects a genuine feature of visual perception: bright, high-contrast areas are interpreted by the brain and eye as more distant. The observation is reminiscent of the viral internet debate over the blue-and-black (or white-and-gold) dress, where different viewers perceived the same object entirely differently depending on how they processed background lighting. The *baheret*'s brightness makes the skin around it appear to recede, producing the halakhic term *amukah*.

### Se'et Elevated

*Se'et*, by contrast, conveys elevation: *ein se'et ela gevohah* — *se'et* means nothing other than height. The root *nasa* — to carry, to lift — gives *se'et* its meaning of something raised or elevated. The *masuk* in Yeshayahu, *al kol he'harim ha'ramim ve'al kol hage'va'ot hanissa'ot* — upon all the high mountains and all the elevated hills — uses the same root. Where *baheret*'s extreme brightness makes it look deep, *se'et*'s dimmer tone makes it appear elevated or raised above the skin level.

### Sapachat Derivative

*Sapachat* means something secondary or derivative: *ein sapachat ela tifeilah*. The same root appears in modern Hebrew in the word *nispach* — an appendix to a book. The *sapachat* colors are those that are subordinate or derivative — the secondary shades attached to the primary ones.

### Secondary Derivation

How do we know that there is a *sapachat* — a secondary shade — for *baheret* specifically, given that the derivation of a *sapachat* for *se'et* is more explicit in the text? Rabbi Zeira applies a *gezeirah shavah*-style comparison: the Torah uses the word *levanah* (white) in connection with both *se'et* and *baheret*. Just as the *se'et* has a secondary color (the egg membrane color), so too the *baheret* must have a secondary color (the lime-plaster color). The *matnitin* formulates this more directly: the Torah mentions the word *sapachat* in proximity to both *se'et* and *baheret*, teaching that there is a secondary color for each of the two primary *negaim*.

### White Wool Standard

What precisely is the white wool that serves as the standard for *se'et*? Rav Bibi citing Rav Assi says: *tzemer naki ben yomo* — clean wool from a sheep on the day of its birth. A newborn lamb is licked clean by its mother and has not yet been exposed to the environment, so its wool is at its purest white. The Rambam notes that one who wishes to preserve that pristine quality for use in *milat* (the soft downy inner wool) would wrap the newborn lamb in a leather covering to protect the fleece from soiling. The comparison is thus not to aged or dirty wool, but to the untouched wool of a one-day-old lamb — the whitest natural wool that exists.

---

## Combination Mashalim

### Kings & Officers

A series of *mashalim* is now offered by different Amoraim to make vivid the contrasting combination patterns of the four shades. Rabbi Chanina provides the first, explaining the *Rabbanan*'s position. The four shades are compared to two kings and two viziers (*litre malkhei ulitre ifrchei*). One king is more powerful than the other, and each king has his own officer. The key point is that each king ranks above his own vizier, not above the other king's vizier. This maps onto the *Tanna Kamma*'s model: *baheret* (king one) combines only with *sid* (its vizier), and *se'et* (king two) combines only with *krum beitzah* (its vizier). Cross-combination — *baheret* with *krum beitzah* or *se'et* with *sid* — is not permitted, just as one king does not outrank the other's officer. The *mashal* is acknowledged to be imperfect in some of its details, but it provides a useful mnemonic structure.

### Four Ranks Mashal

Rav Adda bar Abba offers a different *mashal* with four distinct hierarchical ranks: *malka* (king), *alkafta* (a high official similar to a king but subordinate), *rufila* (the grand vizier of the king), and *resh galuta* (the exilarch, still an important figure but below the grand vizier). The ranking, according to Rashi, is that the king is above the *alkafta*, and the *rufila* is the king's vizier, while the *resh galuta* is subordinate to the *alkafta*. The Gemara works through which ranks are paired: the king goes with the *rufila*, and the *alkafta* goes with the *resh galuta* — again a pattern of one going with three and two going with four. This captures the same underlying structure as the *Rabbanan*'s position.

### Persia & Rome

Rava proposes a more dramatic comparison: the four shades are like *Shvor Malka* (the Persian emperor) and *Keysar* (the Roman emperor). This brings the political realities of the Babylonian Amoraic world into the classroom. Rava lived in Babylonia under Persian rule; he names the Persian emperor first.

### Power Comparison

Rav Pappa presses Rava: *hai mineihu adif* — which of the two is actually more powerful? By putting Persia first, Rava implied Persian supremacy. His response is pointed: *puk chazi tivuta de'man sagi be'alma* — go out and see whose influence has spread throughout the world. The implicit answer is Persia, at least in Rava's estimation and at that historical moment.

Rava then cites a *pasuk* from Daniel — *ve'teichal kol ar'a ve'tedushenah ve'tedikenah* — and the Gemara notes that Rabbi Yochanan, who lived in the Land of Israel under Roman rule, interpreted this verse as referring to Rome. The contrast is illuminating: Rava in Persia points to Persian ascendancy; Rabbi Yochanan in Roman Palestine reads the apocalyptic verse of Daniel as applying to Rome. The four kingdoms described in Daniel — Babylonia, Persia, Greece, and Rome — map onto this four-part structure, and the tension between Persia and Rome that runs through the Talmudic period eventually shifts, in the medieval period, into the tension between the Muslim and Christian worlds.

Rabbi Yochanan adds: *Romi chayavet she'tiv'ah yatza be'chol ha'olam kulo* — Rome is liable because its *tiva'ah*, its stamp, its characteristic mark, has spread throughout the entire world.

### Garment Mashal

Ravina, several Amoraic generations later, offers a final *mashal* grounded in everyday material observation: *glima de'amar ve'shafsei de'sina de'kitna ve'shachakei* — a wool garment and a linen garment, new and worn. When wool and linen are brand new, both are very white. As each ages and is worn, it darkens and discolors. The wool garment in its new state corresponds to one shade; as it wears, it transitions to its paired category. The linen garment does the same in its own pair. The point, as with all the preceding *mashalim*, is that one goes with three and two goes with four — the *Rabbanan*'s model of two independent paired families, not Rabbi Akiva's continuous spectrum.

A parenthetical note: the minimum size for a *nega* to be halakhically significant is a *gris* — the size of a bean, roughly equivalent to nine lentils or a coin of approximately the size of a nickel or dime, depending on the *posek*. The question of combination between adjacent shades is therefore a question about whether two spots of different colors can be combined to reach that minimum size threshold. In *Hilchot Niddah* the *gris* functions as a *de'rabbanan* standard, and the *Shulchan Aruch* advises finding the largest available bean to be more lenient; here it operates as a *de'oraita* requirement, which makes the overlap between the two contexts a subject deserving further exploration.

---

## Korban Scope

### Baraita Scope

The final *sugya* on this *daf* turns to the scope of the *korban oleh veyored* — the variable offering that scales with the offender's means — in the context of *yedi'ot hatumah*, awareness of one's impure state. A *baraita* is cited: *minayin she'ein hakatuv medaber ela betumat mikdash vekodashav* — from where do we know that when the Torah speaks of bringing a *korban oleh veyored* for *yedi'at hatumah*, it refers specifically to *tumat mikdash vekodashav* — the impurity of the Temple and its sancta — rather than to *tumah* in general or to other categories of prohibited contact?

### Warning & Punishment

The *baraita* advances a logical argument: *ho'il vehizhir ve'anash al hatumah vehayav korban al hatumah* — since the Torah warned about *tumah* (*hizhir*) and imposed punishment (*anash*) for deliberate violation (*b'zadon*), and also requires a *korban* for inadvertent violation (*b'shogeg*), the warning, punishment, and *korban* must all refer to the same category of violation. The warning and punishment, as Rashi notes, apply only to *zadon tumah* in the context of *mikdash vekodashav* — entering the *Beit HaMikdash* or eating *korbanot* while *tamei*. There is no general prohibition against becoming *tamei*; the prohibition attaches to the subsequent action that desecrates something sacred. Therefore the *korban* obligation must be coextensive with that same category of *tumat mikdash vekodashav*.

### Terumah Exception

One might object that *terumah* should also be included: eating *terumah* while *tamei* is a prohibited act for which there is both a warning and a punishment — *mita bidei shamayim*, a divinely imposed death — and for which one might expect a *korban oleh veyored* to apply as well. The Gemara acknowledges that eating *terumah* while *tamei b'shogeg* does incur a *korban*, but that *korban* is a *korban kavua* — a fixed offering, specifically a *korban chatat* requiring an animal sacrifice. The *korban oleh veyored*, by contrast, is a variable offering that applies specifically to the categories listed together in the Torah.

### Terumah Exclusion

The exclusion of *terumah* from the scope of the *korban oleh veyored* is derived textually through the juxtaposition in the Torah of *tumat mikdash vekodashav* with *shmi'at kol* (hearing a voice — the oath of testimony, *shevuat ha'edut*, treated in the fourth *perek* of this *masechta*) and *bitui sfatayim* (utterance of the lips — *shevuat bitui*, treated in the third *perek*). These three categories — *tumat mikdash vekodashav*, *shevuat ha'edut*, and *shevuat bitui* — are linked together in the Torah's formulation, and all three share the *korban oleh veyored* as the consequence for inadvertent violation. *Terumah* is excluded from this grouping: the text is read as *bah bah* — a limiting particle — to signal that *terumah*, despite carrying its own severe consequences, does not fall under the *korban oleh veyored* framework. The distinction in sanctity is relevant: *korbanot* must be eaten either within the *Beit HaMikdash* or within Jerusalem, and the level of purity required is correspondingly higher. The more severe *karet* punishment applies to *tumat mikdash vekodashav* when done deliberately; *mita bidei shamayim* applies to *terumah*. Different levels of sanctity, different punishment structures, and different *korban* obligations reflect a coherent underlying framework, even if the precise derivation may seem formally compressed at first glance.

---

---

# Shevuot 7

## Four Knowledge States

### Four Awareness Scenarios

The Gemara's discussion on this amud requires us to take a few lines back to the bottom of 6b in order to properly unpack the Mishnah's framework. The Mishnah enumerates four distinct configurations of awareness — *yedi'ah* — and concealment — *he'elam* — as they relate to a transgression. The four possibilities are: awareness at the beginning and awareness at the end, with *he'elam* in the middle; awareness at the beginning but no awareness at the end; no awareness at the beginning but awareness at the end; and no awareness at either the beginning or the end.

### Knowledge-Concealment-Kn…

The Mishnah now addresses the case of *et she-yesh bah yedi'ah ba-techilah* — a situation in which there is *yedi'ah* at the outset, a period of *he'elam* in the middle, and *yedi'ah* again at the end.

### Mezid vs. Shogeg Distinc…

One might ask: why is there no fifth category — full awareness at both beginning and end with no *he'elam* at all? The answer is that a person who is fully aware of what he is doing wrong at every moment would be classified as a *mezid*, acting intentionally, and would therefore fall into an entirely different legal category. The present discussion concerns only those cases that involve some gap in awareness, situating the transgressor in the realm of *shogeg* rather than *mezid*.

---

## Vayikra 5 Source Texts

### Vayikra 5 Reading

The Gemara throughout this amud and into 7b grounds its discussion in the opening verses of Vayikra 5. Because the Gemara itself does not reproduce the full text, it is worth pausing to read them. The passage opens with *ve-nefesh ki techeta ve-sham'ah kol alah ve-hu ed o ra'ah o yada im lo yagid ve-nasa avono* — a case of a witness who fails to testify to what he has seen or heard. It continues: *o nefesh asher tiga be-chol davar tame* — a person who touches any unclean thing — *o bi-nevelat chayah teme'ah o bi-nevelat behemah teme'ah o bi-nevelat sheretz tame ve-ne'elam mimeno ve-hu tame ve-ashem* — whether the carcass of an unclean *chayah*, an unclean *behemah*, or an unclean creeping thing, and the fact escaped him, yet he is unclean and thus guilty. A further verse states: *o ki tiga be-tum'at adam le-chol tum'ato asher yitma bah ve-ne'elam mimeno ve-hu yada ve-ashem* — one who touches human *tumah* in any of its forms, and though he had known it, that fact escaped him and he later realizes his guilt. The passage then shifts to the topic of this tractate: *o nefesh ki tishava levate bi-sfatayim le-hara o le-heitiv le-chol asher yevate ha-adam bi-shvuah ve-ne'elam mimeno ve-hu yada ve-ashem le-achat me-eleh* — one who utters an oath for any purpose and the matter later escapes his awareness. The section closes: *ve-hayah ki yesham le-achat me-eleh ve-hitvadah asher chata aleha* — when he realizes his guilt in any of these matters, he shall confess his sin.

### Satum (Unclear) Verses

These verses present an immediate difficulty: we are in a tractate devoted to *shvuot*, to oaths, and yet the middle verses pivot abruptly to matters of *tumah* and ritual defilement before returning to the topic of *shevuah*. These middle verses are what the tradition calls *satum* — obscure, sealed off, unclear in their purpose. The project of this amud and the next is to work through them methodically and determine precisely what legal situation they are describing.

### Intel Museum Metaphor

The process is not unlike viewing technicians in a semiconductor fabrication facility — workers clothed in full protective gowns, handling particles invisible to the naked eye, engaged in operations whose logic is entirely opaque to the outside observer, yet which ultimately produce something of enormous consequence. So too here: we are working with *psukim* that are *stumim*, deeply obscure, and we are unpacking them layer by layer through comparison with other verses, eventually arriving at a definitive conclusion about what these middle passages of Vayikra 5 actually govern.

---

## Tumah = Mikdash & Kodshim

### Tannaitic Proof

The Gemara now asks, through a *tanu rabanan*: how do we know that the verses under discussion speak exclusively of *tumat mikdash ve-kodashav* — defilement of the Temple and its sacred foods? The question is a fundamental one, since the text itself does not say so explicitly.

### Vedin Hu Logic

The Gemara proposes a logical argument — *ve-din hu*. The Torah has already both prohibited and prescribed punishment for the intentional defiling of something sacred: that is, there is an *azhara*, a warning, and a prescribed *onesh*, a punishment. The same Torah also creates liability for a *korban* when this is done *beshogeg*, unintentionally. The Gemara then draws the following analogy: just as the warning and punishment for *tumah* apply only to the *tumah* of the *mikdash* and its *kodshim* — *tumat mikdash ve-kodashav* — so too the liability to bring a *korban* for *tumah* applies only to *tumat mikdash ve-kodashav*. The structure is clean: the Torah's framework of prohibition, punishment, and sacrificial remedy is internally consistent, and the same domain that triggers punishment triggers *korban* liability.

### Terumah Objection

The Gemara immediately raises an objection: *ve-eima tumah* — perhaps the scope of this obligation is broader, and it should also include the *tumah* of *terumah*, the priestly tithe. After all, *terumah* also carries both an *azhara* and a punishment. The Gemara answers: *lo ash'kahan avon mitah de-chayav aleha korban* — we do not find a sin whose prescribed punishment for intentional violation is *mita bi-yedei shamayim* — death at the hands of Heaven — for which one is also liable to bring a *korban*.

Here a crucial distinction must be kept in mind. The punishment for intentionally defiling something connected to the Temple is *karet* — a cutting off that affects the transgressor's future generations. The punishment for intentionally eating *terumah* in a state of *tumah*, by contrast, is *mita bi-yedei shamayim* — a premature death that affects only the transgressor himself, not his descendants. These are two distinct categories of divine punishment, and they are not interchangeable.

### Offering Types (Oleh/Yor…

The *korban* at issue here is not a *korban kavua*, a fixed offering, but the *korban oleh ve-yored* — the sliding-scale offering described in Vayikra 5, whose form varies according to the transgressor's means, ranging from an animal to birds to flour. The rule is that one brings a *korban oleh ve-yored* for unintentional violation of a transgression whose intentional commission carries *karet*. This is the link established by the Mishnah: the *korban oleh ve-yored* is brought for *shemiat kol* and *vitui sefatayim* — the hearing of an oath-taking and the utterance of an oath — as well as for *tumat mikdash ve-kodashav*.

The Gemara now presses further: perhaps the word *bah* — "through which," appearing in Vayikra 5:3 — serves as a *mi'ut*, a restrictive particle, to exclude *terumah* from the scope of this *korban oleh ve-yored*. But then a counter-possibility is raised: perhaps the *bah* comes instead to exclude *mikdash* from the same obligation, teaching that for defiling the Temple one cannot achieve atonement through the *korban oleh ve-yored* alone and must bring a *korban kavua*. The Gemara is genuinely uncertain which exclusion the particle is effecting.

It is at this point that Rava, with characteristic depth, invokes a verse from Proverbs to describe Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's coming derivation: *doleh mayim mi-borot amukim* — one who draws water from deep wells. What follows is presented in a *braita*.

---

## Rabbi Yehuda's Chayah-Be…

### Chayah & Behemah Question

The *braita* cites Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who asks: since *chayah* — a non-domesticated animal — is in some contexts a broader category that includes *behemah* — a domesticated animal — why does the verse in Vayikra 5 need to mention both *bi-nevelat chayah teme'ah* and *bi-nevelat behemah teme'ah* separately? If *chayah* already encompasses *behemah*, *behemah* is redundant.

### Gezeirah Shavah

Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's answer is that the repetition of *behemah teme'ah* is deliberate: it enables a *gezeirah shavah*. The expression *behemah teme'ah* appears here in Vayikra 5 and also in Vayikra 7:21, which speaks of someone who eats from a *shelamim* offering while ritually impure. Just as the *behemah teme'ah* in Vayikra 7:21 refers to the *tumah* of *kodesh* — sacred food — so too the *behemah teme'ah* in Vayikra 5 refers to the *tumah* of *kodesh*. This establishes that the central verses of Vayikra 5 pertain to *tumat kodashim* specifically.

### Itkesh Mikdash-Kodshim

But this only accounts for the *kodshim* — the sacred foods. How do we connect the *tumah* of the *mikdash* itself? For this, the Gemara turns to a different verse: *be-chol kodesh lo tiga ve-el ha-mikdash lo tavo* — from Vayikra 12:4, the opening of *Parashat Tazria*, regarding the *yoledet*, the woman after childbirth. The verse prohibits her from touching any sacred item and from entering the Temple. From this juxtaposition — *itkesh mikdash le-kodesh* — the Temple is placed alongside the sacred foods in a single legal framework. The *tumah* of the *mikdash* and the *tumah* of the *kodshim* are thereby linked.

### Terumah First Argument

With both *mikdash* and *kodshim* now connected, the question of *terumah* resurfaces. Since the verse in Vayikra 12:4 says *be-chol kodesh lo tiga* — "she shall not touch any sacred thing" — and the Sages elsewhere derive from *be-chol kodesh* that this phrase includes *terumah* in its prohibition, perhaps *terumah* should also fall within the scope of the *korban oleh ve-yored*?

### Exclusion with Bah

The Gemara answers: *ha mi'et rachmana bah* — the Torah restricted the scope of this *korban* through the word *bah*, "through which," in Vayikra 5:3. This word functions as a *mi'ut*, an exclusionary particle, and its effect is to exclude *terumah* from the obligation to bring the sliding-scale *korban*.

---

## Three Karot Mystery

### Rava's Three Categories

The discussion now takes a new turn. Rava states that the word *karet* appears three times in the context of *shelamim* — the peace offering. Why three times? *Achat li-khlal ve-achat li-frat ve-achat le-tumah ha-ktuva ba-Torah stam ve-eini yodeia ma hi* — one mention is for the general case of a ritually impure person eating the *shelamim*, one is for a specific instance, and one is for an instance of *tumah* that is written in the Torah without specification, "and I do not know what it is." This frank acknowledgment — that Rava himself cannot identify the referent of the third *karet* — is striking. The implication, however, is that this unaccounted-for mention is available to be applied somewhere. Perhaps it addresses the *tumah* of *kodesh*, and if it is not needed there — since Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's derivation already covers that — then perhaps it can be applied to *tumat mikdash* instead.

The logic runs as follows: one who intentionally defiles the Temple by entering it in a state of *tumah* is liable to *karet*. It is therefore reasonable that for doing so unintentionally, *bishgaga*, he should be liable to bring the *korban oleh ve-yored*. The third, otherwise unassigned mention of *karet* with *shelamim* is thus brought to bear on this case.

### Rabbi Abahu Alternative

The Gemara then presents Rabbi Abahu's alternative reading. Rabbi Abahu agrees that there are three mentions, but he assigns the third not to an unknown *tumah* but rather to *devarim she-einam ne'echalim* — things that are not eaten. This is a different legal application for the same surplus textual mention.

### Rabbi Shimon: Uneaten It…

Rabbi Shimon goes further and offers a limiting principle: for items that are not generally eaten — such as certain forms of *ketoret* — one is not liable to *karet* on account of *tumah* if one consumes them. The rationale is that *karet* applies specifically to the consumption of sacred food in a state of impurity, and items not designated for eating fall outside that category.

The Gemara then applies this principle to a specific case: the third mention of *karet* in connection with *shelamim* is needed to include the case of an impure person who eats from the internal *chatat* — the *sa'ir ha-pnimi* offered inside on *Yom Kippur*. One might have thought that since this offering is not brought on the outer altar — its blood is applied inside the sanctuary — and since Rabbi Shimon holds that such offerings are not subject to *pigul*, one might conclude they are also not subject to *karet* for *tumah*. The third mention teaches otherwise: even for the internal *chatat*, an impure person who eats from it is liable to *karet*. The relationship between *pigul* and the inner *chatat* spans much of Masechet Zevachim and cannot be fully resolved here, but the principle stands.

### Nahardei Tumot Formula

The *amora'im* of Nehardea, citing Rava, offer yet another formulation. Rather than speaking of three occurrences of *karet* with *shelamim*, they speak of three occurrences of *tumah* with *shelamim* — *shalosh tumot bi-shlamim lama*. The structure of the derivation is the same: *achat li-khlal ve-achat li-frat*, and a third whose referent is unspecified. Since Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's derivation from *chayah u-behemah* already accounts for the *tumah* of *kodashim*, the third mention can be redirected to *tumat mikdash*. And since the Torah in any case needed to write the *karet* formulation three times for the purposes of Rabbi Abahu's derivation, the additional mention of *tumah* alongside each is not superfluous — the punishment cannot be stated without stating the act for which it is prescribed.

---

## Tumato Gezeirah Shavah

### Tumato Comparison

To provide an independent basis for the conclusion that *tumat mikdash* is subject to the *korban oleh ve-yored*, Rava proposes a *gezeirah shavah* from the word *tumato*. The word *tumato* — "his impurity" — appears in Vayikra 5:3, and it appears again in Bamidbar 19:13, in the context of the *parah adumah*, the red heifer: *tamei yihye od tumato bo*.

### Mikdash Conclusion

Just as the verse in Bamidbar 19:13 explicitly addresses *tumat mikdash* — the *parah adumah* passage concerns one who defiles the Tabernacle — so too the use of *tumato* in Vayikra 5 is to be read as referring to *tumat mikdash*. The conclusion follows: one who unintentionally defiles the Temple is liable to bring the *korban oleh ve-yored*.

### Ba Particle Inclusion

Having resolved the status of *mikdash* and *kodashim*, the Gemara returns to the word *ba* — the restrictive particle in Vayikra 5:3. If *ba* is a *mi'ut*, a limitation, what does it include through its exclusion? The Gemara answers: *le-rabbot nevelat of tahor* — to include the case of someone who becomes ritually impure through eating an improperly slaughtered carcass of a kosher bird. But this raises an immediate difficulty: we just said *ba* is a *mi'ut* that excludes *terumah*. How can the same particle both exclude and include?

### Double Limitation = Incl…

The Gemara resolves this through the principle of *mi'ut achar mi'ut* — a double limitation. The verse actually contains two restrictive elements in close proximity: the phrase *o ki yiga ba-davar* — "or if he touches" — already implies a limitation through its particularity, and *ba* constitutes a second limitation on top of the first. The rule of hermeneutics is that a *mi'ut achar mi'ut* — a restriction following upon a restriction — does not intensify the exclusion but rather reverses it, creating inclusion. The double *mi'ut* thus functions as a positive statement: the obligation of the *korban oleh ve-yored* applies to one who contracts *tumah* through any form of impurity that can be transmitted via contact — *negia* — but not to one whose impurity cannot be transmitted through touching.

This concludes the extended discussion of *et she-yesh bah yedi'ah ba-techilah* — the scenario of awareness at the outset, *he'elam* in the middle, and awareness again at the end. The conclusion, following the Rambam's reading of this as a tradition supported by derivation rather than explicit scriptural statement, is that the *korban oleh ve-yored* applies solely to unintentional defilement of the Temple and its *kodshim*.

---

## Knowledge Then Obscurity

### Awareness Cycle

The Gemara now moves to the second configuration: *yesh bah yedi'ah ba-techilah ve-ein bah yedi'ah ba-sof* — awareness at the beginning but no awareness at the end. In this scenario, the person became aware that he had transgressed — that he had defiled the Temple or its *kodshim* — but that awareness was never recaptured. The uncertainty is indefinite; it may persist for the rest of the transgressor's life. No *korban oleh ve-yored* can be brought, because the *korban* requires the transgressor to know what he is bringing it for, and he cannot bring a *korban* while the *yedi'ah* remains absent.

### Sa'ir Bifnim Atonement

For this case, the Mishnah assigns atonement through the *sa'ir ha-na'aseh bifnim* — the goat offered inside the sanctuary on *Yom Kippur* — and through *Yom Kippur* itself. So long as the *yedi'ah* does not return, the *sa'ir bifnim* and the day of *Yom Kippur* provide atonement collectively for what remains unknown.

---

## Three Classic Tumot

### Yom Kippur Pasuk

The source for this is Vayikra 16:16, the central verse of the *Yom Kippur* service: *ve-chipper al ha-kodesh mi-tum'ot b'nei Yisrael u-mi-pish'eihem le-chol chatatam ve-chen ya'aseh le-ohel mo'ed ha-shochen itam be-toch tum'otam* — and he shall atone for the holy place from the *tumot* of the children of Israel and from their transgressions, for all their sins; and so shall he do for the Tent of Meeting which dwells with them in the midst of their impurities. The Gemara will now unpack this verse carefully, attending both to its scope and to the grammatical nuances it contains.

### Three Cardinal Sins

The Gemara identifies three forms of *tumah* that the verse might be understood to address: *tum'at avodah zarah*, *tum'at giluy arayot*, and *tum'at shefichut damim* — the defilement associated with idolatry, forbidden sexual relations, and murder. Each of these three is linked to the language of *tumah* in the Torah: idolatry through *lema'an tame mikdashi* in Vayikra 20; forbidden relations through *ve-lo titame'u vahem* in Vayikra 18; and murder through *ve-lo tetame et ha-aretz* in Bamidbar. The question is then whether the *sa'ir* of *Yom Kippur* can atone for all three when violated unintentionally.

### Mitumot vs. Kol Tumot

The Gemara answers through the letter *mem* that prefixes *tum'ot* in Vayikra 16:16: the verse says *mi-tum'ot b'nei Yisrael* — "from the impurities of Israel" — not *kol tum'ot b'nei Yisrael* — "all the impurities of Israel." The prefixed *mem* functions as a limiting particle, indicating that the *sa'ir* atones not for all *tumot* but only for some. The question becomes: which *tumah* is included and which is excluded?

### Rabbi Yehuda vs. Rabbi Shimon

Rabbi Yehuda holds that the limiting *mem* is understood through comparison with another context where a *tumah* was explicitly differentiated from the general category. The case we have just analyzed — *tumat mikdash ve-kodashav* — is precisely such a case. Therefore, the *sa'ir ha-pnimi* atones specifically for *tumat mikdash ve-kodashav* in the configuration of *yesh bah yedi'ah ba-techilah ve-ein bah yedi'ah ba-sof*: the person knew at the outset but never regained awareness.

Rabbi Shimon disagrees with Rabbi Yehuda's methodology. Rabbi Shimon holds that one need not derive this through external comparison; it follows from the verse itself. The verse says *ve-chipper al ha-kodesh* — "he shall atone for the *kodesh*" — and then *mi-tum'ot* — "from *tumot*." The specification *al ha-kodesh* already restricts the scope to the *tumah* of things that are *kodesh*, and the limiting *mem* of *mi-tum'ot* simply confirms that only certain *tumot* of the *kodesh* are included. The *sa'ir pnimi* thus atones for *tumat mikdash ve-kodashav* without needing to derive that conclusion from any external verse.

The Gemara then asks whether the *sa'ir* might atone for every act of *tumah* connected to the *kodesh*. The answer is no: the verse concludes *u-mi-pish'eihem le-chol chatatam* — and the *chata'im* are compared to the *pish'aim*. Just as *pish'aim* — intentional transgressions — are not subject to *korban*, so too the *chata'im* atoned by the *sa'ir* are those that are not subject to *korban* either — namely, cases where *yedi'ah* never returned and no *korban oleh ve-yored* could therefore be brought.

---

## Specific Transgression C…

### Avodah Zarah Cases

The Gemara now turns to the practical application of this framework to each of the three cardinal categories. With regard to *avodah zarah*: if someone commits idolatry intentionally — *be-mezid* — he is liable to the death penalty; if unintentionally — *be-shogeg* — he is required to bring a *korban*. Where, then, is the space for the *sa'ir* to operate? The Gemara identifies two specific situations. First: *be-mezid ve-lo hitru beh* — intentional transgression but without the required prior warning. Without formal *hatrah*, the death penalty cannot be administered, and since the act was intentional, the *korban* does not apply either. The *sa'ir* fills this gap. Second: *be-shogeg ve-lo ityada leh* — unintentional transgression that was never brought to the transgressor's awareness. Since *yedi'ah* never arrived, no *korban* could be brought; the *sa'ir* of *Yom Kippur* provides atonement in its place.

### Giluy Arayot Cases

The identical structure applies to *giluy arayot*. Intentional violation carries the death penalty; unintentional violation requires a *korban*. The *sa'ir* operates in the two parallel gaps: *be-mezid ve-lo hitru beh* — intentional but without warning — and *be-shogeg ve-lo ityada leh* — unintentional but without the transgressor ever becoming aware.

### Shefichut Damim Cases

The same analysis extends to *shefichut damim*. Intentional killing is punishable by death. Unintentional killing requires exile to one of the cities of refuge — the subject of much of Masechet Makkot. The *sa'ir* again addresses the two exceptional situations: intentional killing without prior warning, and unintentional killing of which the perpetrator never became aware.

The discussion pauses here, at 8a, six lines from the top, to be continued.

---

---

# Shevuot 8

## Tumat Mikdash vs. Sin

### Intro: Tumat vs Sin

The daf opens by continuing a sustained inquiry into the precise function of the *korbanot* brought on *Yom Kippur*, and by extension on the *regalim* and *Rosh Chodesh*. The governing assumption, established in the preceding sugyot, is that all of these *korbanot* relate to *tumat mikdash* — the defilement of the sanctuary by someone who entered while ritually impure or who consumed *kodashim* in a state of impurity. The standard *korban* in the *Torah* for such a violation is the *oleh veyored*, the variable-cost offering whose price scales with the offender's means. That *korban* applies specifically when there was *yedi'ah bitchilah veyedi'ah besof* — awareness at the outset that one had become *tamei*, a period of forgetting, and renewed awareness at the end — with the transgression occurring during the interval of *helem*. The various *korbanot* associated with *Yom Kippur*, the *musaf* of *Yom Kippur*, and the *regalim* address distinct configurations of awareness, covering cases where one or both endpoints of knowledge are absent.

Before the *Gemara* can turn to those distinctions, however, it must first establish which category of *tumah* is even under discussion. The verse in *Vayikra* (16:16) reads: *vechipper al hakodesh mitumot benei Yisrael umipisheihem lechol chatotam* — "and he shall atone for the sanctuary from the impurities of the Children of Israel and from their transgressions, for all their sins." The plain sense of this verse, and one that many biblical commentators embrace as the *pshat*, is that *tumot* here does not refer to the technical ritual impurity of contact with corpses or bodily discharges, but rather to the metaphysical pollution generated by sin itself. According to this reading, grave transgressions — especially the three cardinal sins — contaminate the land and the *Mikdash*, driving God's presence inward. Once a year, the *Kohen Gadol* enters the innermost sanctum to cleanse what has accumulated and restore the conditions under which God can continue to dwell among Israel: *hashochen itam betoch tumotam*, "He who dwells among them amid their impurities." The impurity in that phrase does not refer to someone who touched a carcass; it refers to the reality that a sinful people nonetheless merits divine indwelling, enabled in part by this annual act of cosmic housekeeping.

The *Gemara* acknowledges this reading — at least as a *hava amina* — before ultimately setting it aside on technical grounds.

### Three Great Sins

The *Gemara* raises the possibility explicitly: *yachol al shalosh tumot halalu yehei zeh mechaper* — perhaps this *korban* atones for the three *tumot* associated with *avoda zara*, *gilui arayot*, and *shefichut damim*, the three cardinal sins for which the *Torah* itself uses the language of *tumah*. The rejection comes from the phrase *mitumot velo kol tumot* — "from the impurities," with the prefix implying a subset, not the totality of all *tumot*. The *Gemara* thus concedes that in principle some *tumot* could be intended, but not all of them; the question becomes which ones.

The logic of selection follows a principle of analogy: *mah matzinu shechilak hakatuv michlal kol tumot betumat mikdash vekodashav af kan betumat mikdash vekodashav* — just as we find that the *Torah* gave distinct, separate treatment to the *tumah* that involves the sanctuary and its sanctified objects (*tumat mikdash vekodashav*), so too here, it is that same category of *tumah* that is being addressed. This is the position of *Rabbi Yehuda*.

### Oleh Veyored

What does it mean that the *Torah* gave *tumat mikdash* "separate treatment" — *chilek hakatuv*? *Rabbi Yehuda* explains: *demayti oleh veyored* — it is the one offense for which the *Torah* prescribes a sliding-scale *korban*, an *oleh veyored*, making it easier for the sinner to obtain atonement by adjusting the cost to his means. This leniency signals that the *Torah* is actively facilitating atonement for this particular sin. By analogy, when *Yom Kippur* provides atonement for *tumat mikdash*, it is extending the same spirit of accessibility — addressing a sin for which the *Torah* has already demonstrated a desire to lower the barriers to *kapara*.

### Lenient vs Stringent

The question arises: why not say the *Torah* gave special treatment to *avoda zara* — after all, by *avoda zara* the *Torah* requires a female goat (*se'irah*) specifically, excluding the sheep that is normally available? *Rav Kahana* draws the crucial distinction: *anan chilek lehakel ka'amina vehai chilek lehachmir* — the principle we are applying is "separate treatment in a lenient direction." The *oleh veyored* is lenient because it makes atonement more accessible. The restriction to a goat by *avoda zara*, by contrast, is a *stringency* — it limits the offender's options. We are not looking for any instance of separate treatment; we are looking for separate treatment that eases the path to atonement. That criterion is met only by *tumat mikdash vekodashav* and the *oleh veyored*.

### Yoledet Case

The *Gemara* then considers the *yoledet* — the woman who gives birth and brings an *oleh veyored* as part of her post-partum purification. This offering is also variable in cost, just like the *korban* for *tumat mikdash*. Perhaps, the *Gemara* suggests, the *Yom Kippur* service atones for the *tumah* of the *yoledet*. *Rashi* understands the scenario as a woman who gave birth before *Yom Kippur* and had not yet brought her *korban*; perhaps *Yom Kippur* exempts her. *Tosafot*, noting a difficulty with this reading — since an established *korban* obligation is not ordinarily discharged by the *Yom Kippur* service — suggests instead a case of doubt, such as uncertainty about whether a miscarriage occurred before or after 40 days of gestation, where the obligation itself is ambiguous.

### Tumah and Sin

The response comes from *Rav Oshaya*: *lechol chatotam velo lechol tumotam* — "for all their sins," not "for all their impurities." The *Yom Kippur* service must address something that contains both a *tumah* dimension and a *sin* dimension. *Avoda zara*, *gilui arayot*, and *shefichut damim* have both. *Tumat mikdash* has both — the *tumah* of entering the *Mikdash* while impure, and the sin of having done so. But the *yoledet*'s offering involves no sin at all; she has done nothing wrong. Therefore, *lechol chatotam* excludes her case: the *Yom Kippur* *korban* cannot be addressing the *tumah* of the *yoledet*.

The *Gemara* then raises the view of *Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai*, who holds that the *yoledet* is, in fact, considered a sinner. His reasoning: during the agony of labor, a woman is presumed to take an oath that she will never again be intimate with her husband. The *korban* she brings is therefore a *chatat* in part to address this rash oath. According to *Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai*, the *yoledet* case does have a sin component — so why doesn't the *Yom Kippur* service apply to her? The answer is that *Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai* uses a different methodology altogether — he derives which *tumah* is at stake directly from context (*mimkomo hu muchra*), as will be explained shortly.

### Chatat Cleansing

This discussion opens a broader reflection on the nature of *chatat* itself. The word is commonly translated as "sin offering," and we naturally assume it is about personal guilt and divine forgiveness. But this framing may be post-*Mikdash* thinking. The verb *lechatei* can mean to cleanse or purify, not only to sin. A *chatat* can function as the culminating act of a process of purification — not as an acknowledgment of wrongdoing, but as the mechanism that restores a person to full ritual standing. The *metzora* provides the clearest example, as does the *yoledet*. Neither has sinned in the conventional sense, yet both bring a *chatat*. What the *chatat* does in those cases is address the *tumah* — to clean up, as it were, the disruption that occurred in the world, whether through birth or through affliction.

This suggests a fundamentally different way of understanding *korbanot* in general. Rather than centering on the individual's guilt, punishment, and need for forgiveness, the *korban* framework centers on rupture and repair — what was damaged in the world, the sanctuary, the relationship between *Bnei Yisrael* and *Hashem*, and how to restore it. The *chatat* is not primarily about me and my stain; it is about fixing what my action broke, or completing a process of transition from one status to another.

### Tinok Shenishba

A striking illustration of this principle is the case of the *tinok shenishba* — a child taken captive and raised among non-Jews, who grew up with no knowledge of his Jewish identity. If such a person spent decades performing *melacha* on *Shabbat* in complete and blameless ignorance, and then discovered his origins, is he required to bring a *korban*? The *Gemara* says yes — one *korban*, not one for every *Shabbat* or every *melacha*, but one nonetheless. This is remarkable: the person is entirely without fault. Yet the *korban* is still required. Why? Because the framework is not about guilt; it is about the objective fact that a disruption occurred in the world, and something is needed to address that, irrespective of personal culpability. You broke it, you fix it — even if it was not your fault. This case powerfully demonstrates that the *chatat* is not reducible to a mechanism of divine forgiveness for personal wrongdoing.

### Metzora Case

The *Gemara* next considers the *metzora* — the person afflicted with *tzaraat* — who also brings an *oleh veyored* as part of the purification process. The suggestion is that perhaps the *Yom Kippur* service addresses the *tumah* of the *metzora*. Again, *Rav Oshaya*'s principle applies: *lechol chatotam velo lechol tumotam* — there must be both *tumah* and sin. The *Gemara* acknowledges the tradition cited by *Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani* in the name of *Rabbi Yonatan* that *tzaraat* comes as punishment for seven categories of sin, including *lashon hara*. So there is indeed a sin component. Why, then, can't *Yom Kippur* serve the *metzora*?

The answer is subtle: *hasam negaei d'achpar leih* — there, the affliction of *tzaraat* itself served as the atonement for the sin. The suffering of *tzaraat* was his *kapara*. By the time he brings the *korban*, the sin has already been atoned for through the ordeal of the affliction itself. The *korban* at that point functions only to address the *tumah* and restore him to full participation — *l'ishtruye b'kodashim*, to permit him to eat *kodashim* again. With the sin already atoned for through suffering, the *korban* is a purely *tumah*-related act, and the *lechol chatotam* requirement remains unmet.

### Nazir Tamei

The *Gemara* then raises the case of the *nazir tamei* — the *nazir* who became impure and brings a *chatat* as part of his re-purification. This *chatat* is of birds rather than animals, making it an inexpensive and accessible offering — another instance of *chilek hakatuv* in a lenient direction. One might therefore suggest that this is the type of sin the *Yom Kippur* service addresses.

Once again, *Rav Oshaya*'s principle is invoked: the *chatat* of the *nazir tamei* relates only to *tumah*, not to sin. But here, too, the *Gemara* raises a counter-position: *Elazar Hakappar* teaches that a *nazir* is considered a sinner, because *shetziar atzmo min hayayin* — he denied himself the pleasure of wine. The verse says *asher chata al hanefesh*, "who sinned against the soul," referring to self-deprivation as a form of transgression. If the *nazir tamei*, by extending his *nezirut* beyond its justified purpose through the incident of impurity, compounds this sin — then there is both a *tumah* and a sin dimension. Why, then, couldn't the *Yom Kippur* service apply?

*Tosafot* addresses the difficulty by suggesting that an original *nezirut* of limited duration serves a legitimate purpose that counterbalances the self-denial; once the *nazir* becomes *tamei* and the *nezirut* is extended beyond its original scope and purpose, the sin element becomes more pronounced. Even so, the *Gemara* ultimately resolves the question by invoking *Rabbi Shimon*'s position: anyone who finds this line of reasoning unsatisfying can fall back on *Rabbi Shimon*'s methodology, which derives the answer directly from context.

### Rabbi Shimon Context

*Rabbi Shimon* does not need to work through the process of identifying *chilek hakatuv* and then filtering by the requirements of *tumah* plus sin. He reads the *pasuk* directly: *vechipper al hakodesh mitumot benei Yisrael* — it is a *tumah* that directly affects the *mikdash* itself.
