Because the *ketores* is prepared in bulk at the start of the year and is understood from the outset to be designated for use throughout the entire year, it is not yet considered to be "at the cusp of being offered." The clock for *lina* begins only when the *ketores* has been transferred into the vessel from which it will actually be offered — not merely the *machteshet* which confers *kedushat haguf*, but the subsequent *kli* that represents readiness for immediate offering. The *machteshet* confers *kedushat haguf*, but *lina* — which tracks the transition from readiness to offering — is measured from the later stage of preparation, when a specific portion is taken for use on that day. This explanation elegantly accounts for why the *braita* and the *mishna* can both be accurate, each speaking of a different halakhic threshold.

### Ketores Full Kedusha

With this resolution in place, the *Gemara* returns to its original point: the *ketores* does indeed have *kedushat haguf* from the moment of grinding, and yet it can be redeemed at the end of the year. This constitutes solid support for Rabbi Yochanan's position regarding the surplus *tamidim*. Just as the *ketores* — an item bought with communal funds, possessing *kedushat haguf* — can be redeemed at year's end, so too the leftover *tamidim* can be redeemed without a blemish. But the *Gemara* immediately presses further: *v'chi kdusha shebahem l'heichan halcha?* — the fact of the *ketores* precedent does not yet explain the *mechanism* by which the *kedusha* can be dissolved. That explanation is what must now be supplied.

---

## Lev Beis Din

### Rabba's Answer

Rabba provides the central resolution of the *sugya*: *lev beis din matneh aleihem* — the *beis din* implicitly stipulates conditional sanctity. The *beis din* that represents the Jewish public and that purchases these items with the funds of the *terumat halishka* understands from the outset that there will be surplus. Their implicit stipulation is: *im hutzrechu hutzrechu* — if the items purchased turn out to be needed and used on the *mizbeach*, then they are fully sanctified with *kedushat haguf*. *V'im lav yehiyu dmeihem* — but if they turn out not to be used, then they were never intended to carry *kedushat haguf*; they were intended only as *kedushat damim* for the monetary value they represent. At year's end, the leftover *ketores* or unused animals are therefore in the same category as someone who sanctified a non-sacred object for its monetary value — they carry only *kedushat damim* and can be redeemed straightforwardly, without any need for a blemish.

### Abaye's Challenge

Abaye objects: did not Rabba himself rule that if one sanctifies a male unblemished animal for *kedushat damim* — intending only that the proceeds be used by the *Beis HaMikdash* — the sanctity nonetheless automatically upgrades to *kedushat haguf*? The logic is that if the animal itself could serve as an *olah*, it is pointless to speak of merely selling it and using the money; the animal simply becomes the *olah* directly, eliminating the middleman. If so, the same reasoning should apply here: even if the *beis din* stipulates *kedushat damim*, the moment the stipulation lapses and the animal is deemed unused, it stands there as a perfectly fit animal — and should automatically be elevated to *kedushat haguf*.

### Earmarking Answer

The *Gemara* resolves this by distinguishing between different varieties of *kedushat damim*: *ha de-amar lidmei olah v'ha de-amar lidmei nesachim* — the automatic upgrade to *kedushat haguf* operates only when the *kedushat damim* is specifically earmarked for the purpose of an *olah*. If someone sanctifies a sheep and declares that its proceeds should be used for an *olah*, then since the *kedushat damim* is targeted toward acquiring something to be offered on the *mizbeach*, and this animal itself could serve in that role, the upgrade happens automatically. But if the *kedushat damim* is earmarked for wine offerings, or for repairs to the *Beis HaMikdash*, or for any other purpose besides an *olah* to be offered on the *mizbeach* itself, the upgrade does not occur. The sanctity remains *kedushat damim* directed toward its declared purpose, and the animal is sold accordingly.

### Application

The application to the present case follows naturally. The *beis din*'s implicit stipulation earmarks any surplus not for use on the *mizbeach* but for other *Beis HaMikdash* needs — specifically, the funds remaining from the *terumat halishka* at year's end were known to be redirected toward communal *nedava* offerings or *Beis HaMikdash* maintenance. Since the *kedushat damim* of the surplus is thus earmarked for non-*mizbeach* purposes, it does not trigger the automatic upgrade to *kedushat haguf*, and the animals or *ketores* can be redeemed without a blemish.

---

## Uncommon Cases

### Lost YK Animals

Abaye is still not satisfied and raises a further challenge from a *mishna*: *paro v'se'iro shel Yom HaKippurim she-avedu* — if the bull and goat of Yom Kippur that were designated for the *Kodesh HaKodashim* service were lost, and replacements were set aside in their stead, and then the originals were found, what is to be done with them? Similarly, the goats brought when the entire community sinned through *avodah zarah* on the basis of a *beis din* ruling — if those designated animals were lost and replacements brought, and the originals were then found, what then? The *mishna* states: *kullan yamutu* — they must all be left to die. This is the view of Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that a *chatas* whose owners have achieved atonement through a replacement animal — a *chatas shekapru be'alav b'acher* — must be left to die. This applies even to a communal *chatas*.

Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon disagree: *yiru ad sheyista'avu v'yimkeru v'yiplu dmeihem l'nedava* — they should be left to graze until they develop a blemish, at which point they can be redeemed, and the proceeds used as an *olah* donation. This is because the principle that a *chatas* must be left to die applies only to an individual's *chatas*, not to a communal one. The question then becomes: according to Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon, why must one wait for a blemish? Why not simply invoke *lev beis din matneh aleihem* — these are communal animals, implicitly stipulated to carry only *kedushat damim* if they cannot be used for their designated purpose? And according to Rabbi Yehuda, who says they must be left to die, why does *lev beis din* not rescue the situation at all?

### Rare vs Common

The answer is straightforward: *sha'ani avudim d'lo shechichi* — the case of an animal that gets lost is uncommon. Rashi adds that these particular *korbanot* themselves are not common occurrences. The principle of *lev beis din matneh aleihem* operates only where surplus or non-use is anticipated and standard. When the *beis din* purchases *ketores* in bulk at the start of the year, it is known with certainty that there will be leftover. When four extra *tamidim* are kept in reserve, it is known that some will remain. The *beis din* makes its implicit stipulation precisely because it is thinking about what will typically occur. An animal that gets lost is a freak occurrence that no one anticipates, and the *beis din* does not formulate its stipulation with such outlier scenarios in mind.

### Parah Adumah

No sooner is this distinction established than the *Gemara* introduces a counter-case: *v'harei parah d'lo shechicha* — but consider the *parah adumah*, which is also uncommon. Yet a *braita* teaches that a *parah adumah* can be redeemed in a wide range of circumstances: if any defect is found (*parah nifdes al kol psul shebah*), if it died before *shechita*, if it was slaughtered in the wrong location, or even if a more beautiful specimen was found (*matza acheres na'ah himenu tipadeh*). In all of these situations, the *parah* can be redeemed — and the case of finding a more beautiful animal explicitly involves no blemish whatsoever. The only exception is after it has been slaughtered in the proper location on the proper pyre, at which point it can no longer be redeemed — not because redemption is legally impossible, but, as Rashi explains, because it would be demeaning to the sanctified item at that stage. The question stands: if the lost Yom Kippur animals cannot be rescued by *lev beis din* because their loss is uncommon, how can the *parah adumah* be redeemed in these scenarios if the *parah adumah* is itself an uncommon occurrence?

### Parah as Bedek

The *Gemara* answers: *sha'ani parah d'kodshei vedek habayis hi* — the *parah adumah* is categorically different because it belongs to *kodshei bedek habayis*, not *kodshei mizbeach*. This is a distinction worth pausing over. There are two orthogonal axes in the laws of sanctity: *kedushat haguf* versus *kedushat damim* (intrinsic sanctity versus monetary sanctity), and *kodshei mizbeach* versus *kodshei bedek habayis* (altar sanctity versus Temple-maintenance sanctity). These are not synonymous. One could have something that is *kedushat haguf l'bedek habayis* — a beam designated for construction of the *Beis HaMikdash*, for instance, is intrinsically sanctified but not for the *mizbeach*. The *parah adumah* occupies this category: it is used — not sold — so it is not simply *kedushat damim*, but the purpose of its use is not as a *korban* on the *mizbeach*. It is slaughtered outside the *Beis HaMikdash*, its blood is sprinkled facing the *Beis HaMikdash* but not within it, and its body is burned. It is therefore *kedushat haguf l'bedek habayis*, not *kodshei mizbeach*.

Because it is *kodshei bedek habayis* rather than *kodshei mizbeach*, it can be redeemed without a blemish — this is the standard rule for *kodshei bedek habayis* and requires no special invocation of *lev beis din*. This explains why finding a more beautiful *parah* allows redemption of the original: from the outset, its sanctity was of the *bedek habayis* variety, which carries no prohibition against redemption for a wholesome animal.

The *Gemara* confirms this by identifying the ruling with Rabbi Shimon specifically, who holds that *kodshei mizbeach* requires *ha'amada v'ha'aracha* — the animal must be presented alive before a *kohen* for evaluation in order to be redeemed — whereas *kodshei bedek habayis* does not require this. That is why the *parah adumah* can be redeemed even if it died: *kodshei bedek habayis* has no requirement of *ha'amada v'ha'aracha*.

A difficulty then arises: the *braita* states that Rabbi Shimon holds the *parah* has a *sha'as hakosher* — a moment when it could theoretically have been eaten — and this is the basis on which *parah* is considered susceptible to the *tumah* of food. Reish Lakish explains that this *sha'as hakosher* refers to the moment immediately after *shechita*, because Rabbi Shimon holds that the *parah* could have been redeemed even at that point. If Rabbi Shimon would allow redemption even after proper *shechita*, then the *braita* that prohibits redemption once the *parah* is slaughtered on its pyre cannot be Rabbi Shimon's view. This leaves open the question of who authored that *braita*, and whether the ruling permitting redemption of a dead *parah* can still be attributed to Rabbi Shimon's reasoning about *kodshei bedek habayis*.

### Parah Cost Clause

The *Gemara* therefore retreats to an alternative explanation: *ela sha'ani parah ho'il v'dameha yekarin* — the *parah adumah* is different because its price is very high. Since the *parah adumah* is extraordinarily costly, there is always an implicit understanding on the part of *beis din* that it must be possible to redeem it if circumstances require — and this implicit stipulation constitutes a form of *lev beis din matneh aleihem* that operates even in uncommon cases.

This explanation is admittedly difficult to fully comprehend in terms of its practical logic. If the animal has died or been replaced, what precisely is being salvaged by redemption? The answer offered by the *Gemara* via Rav Kahana is that even if all one can salvage is the leather — like the ear of a camel that died in one's care — people will want to feel that something was recouped from a very costly investment. The *beis din* therefore built its stipulation around that psychological and financial reality, allowing at minimum the salvage value to be realized. This may be the practical content of *dameha yekarin* as a basis for *lev beis din*.

The upshot of the entire discussion is therefore as follows. The *ketores* and the surplus *tamidim* — anticipated surpluses from communal purchases — can be redeemed without a blemish because *lev beis din matneh aleihem* applies in standard, foreseeable cases. The lost bull and goat of Yom Kippur — a freak occurrence — receive no such benefit; one must either let them die (Rabbi Yehuda) or wait for a blemish (Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon). The *parah adumah* presents its own sui generis analysis: it is *kodshei bedek habayis*, not *kodshei mizbeach*, and can be redeemed without a blemish on that basis; and additionally, because of its great cost, *lev beis din* furnishes a supplementary basis for flexibility in its redemption.

---

## Regalim Substitution

### Mishna Position

The *Gemara* now turns back to our *mishna*, where the Rabbis challenge Rabbi Shimon: *mahu sheyakrivu zeh b'zeh* — can the communal *korbanot* of one *regel* substitute for the *musaf korbanot* of another? Rabbi Shimon answers: *yikrevu* — yes, they may. When pressed as to how, given that each set of *korbanot* atones for slightly different dimensions of *tumat mikdash v'kodashav*, Rabbi Shimon replies: *kulam ba'in l'chaper al tumat mikdash v'kodashav* — all of them come to atone for *tumat mikdash v'kodashav*, and that is sufficient commonality to allow substitution among them.

### Why Not Lev Beis Din

The *Gemara* then asks: *v'amai? leima lev beis din matneh aleihem* — why did Rabbi Shimon need to invoke the reasoning that all these *korbanot* share the same atonement category? Why could he not have simply said that since these animals were purchased with communal funds, the *beis din* implicitly stipulated from the outset that if one set cannot be used for its original designation, it may be applied toward a related need? This would be a simpler and perhaps more powerful argument. Tosafot acknowledges the difficulty of why this argument is not deployed here, given that we have been somewhat restricting the scope of *lev beis din* to anticipated surpluses — and the scenario of *korbanot* being lost and then recovered is arguably more like the uncommon lost-animal cases. Nevertheless, the question stands as to why Rabbi Shimon does not reach for *lev beis din* as a basis.

### School Dispute

The *Gemara*'s answer is decisive: *Rabbi Shimon ka'amart? Rabbi Shimon leit lei lev beis din matneh aleihem* — Rabbi Shimon simply does not accept the principle of *lev beis din matneh aleihem*. He rejects it entirely. Therefore he cannot invoke it; it is not part of his halakhic framework.

### Rabbanan vs Shimon

The proof is brought by a chain of tradition: *amar Rav Idi bar Abin amar Rav Amram amar Rabbi Yochanan* — the very statement with which this *daf* opened, in Rabbi Yochanan's name via Ulla, is now quoted again with its full attribution. Regarding the surplus *tamidim*, *l'divrei Rabbi Shimon ein nifdin temimim* — according to Rabbi Shimon, the surplus *tamidim* cannot be redeemed while still unblemished; one must wait for a blemish. *U-l'divrei Chachamim nifdin temimim* — but according to the Sages who disagree with Rabbi Shimon, the surplus *tamidim* can be redeemed even while unblemished.

The entire principle of *lev beis din matneh aleihem* that the *Gemara* has been developing across this *daf* — the implicit stipulation of the *beis din* that governs how communal sanctity operates with respect to surplus — is thus the position of the Rabbanan, not of Rabbi Shimon. Rabbi Shimon holds that once *kedushat haguf* has adhered in an animal, no stipulation can pre-empt it, and a blemish is required for redemption. The Rabbanan hold that the *beis din*'s implicit prior stipulation can qualify the nature of the *kedusha* itself, such that anticipated surplus never fully acquires *kedushat haguf* and can therefore be redeemed without a blemish. This is the fundamental *machloket* that will be elaborated further in the *daf* that follows.

---

---

# Shevuot 12

## Lev Beis Din & Tmidin

### Lev Beis Din Masneh

The daf begins at the very bottom of 11b, picking up where the previous session left off with a remarkable teaching of Rabbi Yochanan concerning *tmidin* — the communal daily sacrifices. The problem arises at the turn of the new year: funds collected in the previous year must give way to funds of the new year, leaving any communal sacrifices purchased with last year's money in an uncertain position. The general rule is that one may not redeem a sanctified animal unless it has developed a *mum* — a blemish that renders it unfit for sacrifice. Yet Rabbi Yochanan had asserted that in this case, the communal animals may be redeemed even without a blemish. The reason he offered was *lev beis din masneh aleihem* — an implicit stipulation by the court. Because the *beis din* is fully aware that this situation will arise, their original act of sanctification was never meant to be absolute. It was, in effect, conditional: if the animal turns out to be unnecessary as a *korban*, it was purchased merely as an asset, with only a generic *kedushas stam* rather than as a fully committed sacrificial offering.

The *Gemara*, having accepted this principle, then turned it back upon our *mishna*, where Rabbi Shimon is challenged. Rabbi Shimon had ruled that a goat designated for one *musaf* — whether for a *regel*, *Yom Kippur*, or *Rosh Chodesh* — may be used for a different *musaf* if the original is lost and subsequently recovered. The challengers pressed him: if all these *musafin* perform slightly different variations of *tumas mikdash v'kodashav*, how can one substitute for another? Rabbi Shimon's answer was that they are all variations on a single theme, and since they all address *tumas mikdash v'kodashav*, they are interchangeable. But the *Gemara* now asks: why didn't Rabbi Shimon simply invoke the principle of *lev beis din masneh aleihem*? If an implicit stipulation exists that the *beis din* can redirect the animal, then the problem dissolves without needing to argue they are all functionally equivalent.

### Challenging R. Shimon

The implication of the question is telling: since Rabbi Shimon did not appeal to this mechanism, he apparently does not accept it. The *Gemara* thus surfaces a tension between Rabbi Shimon's position and Rabbi Yochanan's general principle.

### R. Yochanan Concedes

Rabbi Yochanan concedes the point directly. His formulation, transmitted through Rabbi Idi bar Avin in the name of Rav Avin, is as follows: *tmidin shelo hutzrechu l'tzibbur* — if *tmidin* were left over from the previous year — *l'didi Rabbi Shimon ein nifdim tmimim*: according to Rabbi Shimon, they cannot be redeemed without a blemish. Rabbi Shimon does not hold of the *chidush* of *lev beis din masneh aleihem*. *L'didi chachamim nifdim tmimim*: Rabbi Yochanan clarifies that his statement about redeeming without a blemish was made according to the *chachamim*, not according to Rabbi Shimon.

### Shimon vs. Yochanan

With that concession in hand, the *Gemara* proceeds to ask a sharper question: who exactly are these rabbis who disagree with Rabbi Shimon and whose position supports Rabbi Yochanan's teaching? Since Rabbi Yochanan has now acknowledged that Rabbi Shimon parts ways with him, the *Gemara* wants to identify the *tanna* whose authority undergirds Rabbi Yochanan's claim that communal animals may be redeemed without a blemish. This sets the stage for an extended examination of the Tannaitic sources.

---

## Tannaitic Sources

### Rabbanan de'Pligi

The *Gemara* now recapitulates the Tannaitic support previously marshaled for Rabbi Yochanan's position, but with a crucial refinement: it will demonstrate that none of the cited sources unambiguously extends the principle of *lev beis din masneh aleihem* to the specific case of the *tmidin*, where the alternative of simply waiting for a blemish is available.

### Ketores Distinction

The first candidate is the case of the *ketores* — leftover incense from the previous year, which may be redeemed and repurchased with new funds. One might think this parallels the case of the *tmidin*, since it likewise involves redeeming an item in its unblemished state. However, the *Gemara* dismisses this: *shani ketores de'lav bar re'iyah hi* — the *ketores* is categorically different, because there is simply nothing else one can do with it. Unlike an animal, the *ketores* cannot be set out to graze until it develops a blemish. When you have no alternative, the principle of *lev beis din masneh aleihem* must supply the escape route. But an animal, in theory, can wait. So the *ketores* case establishes that the mechanism exists in some form, but does not prove that it extends to a situation where another option is available.

### Parah Adumah Case

The second candidate is the *parah adumah* — the red heifer — where similarly, the ruling permitted redemption and repurchase under certain circumstances. Here too, the *Gemara* notes that most scenarios involving the *parah adumah* are ones where no alternative exists: the animal died, or was otherwise rendered unusable, and the community had no choice. However, one scenario remains troubling — if a superior animal was found, could one redeem the first and purchase the better one? In that case, one could, in principle, simply wait for the first animal to develop a blemish. Yet the *Gemara* answers: *dilma shani Parah de'damei yakrin* — perhaps the *parah adumah* is special because its cost is so significant, and there may be particular reasons to allow greater flexibility there that would not carry over to the *tmidin*. The bottom line is that the *parah adumah* case cannot serve as proof for the broader principle either.

### Challenging R. Shimon

The *Gemara* then turns to the third possible source: the rabbis who challenged Rabbi Shimon in the *mishna* itself. When they pressed him — "What would happen if a goat designated for one *musaf* was lost, and later recovered; could you use it for another?" — the implicit assumption in their challenge might be that they themselves had no problem with using one for another, because they held *lev beis din masneh aleihem*. They were asking Rabbi Shimon: fine for us, but how does it work for you?

This reading, the *Gemara* acknowledges, requires that the challengers be Rabbi Yehuda and not someone else — for it assumes that they, like Rabbi Shimon, hold that each *korban* performs a distinct function, but they resolve the practical difficulty through the mechanism of *lev beis din*. The reconstructed dialogue would run: "It is understandable according to us — *bishlama ledidi de'amina lev beis din matneh aleihem*, I understand why you can use one for another even though they each atone for something slightly different, because *beis din* implicitly stipulates. But according to you, who denies that stipulation and thus cannot change the animal's status without a *mum* — *amai yikrevu*? Why can they be used interchangeably?"

### Rabbi Meir Reading

However, the *Gemara* immediately offers an alternative reading: *dilma Rabbi Meir hi* — perhaps the challenger is Rabbi Meir. Rabbi Meir holds that all the goats of *Yom Kippur*, the *regalim*, and *Rosh Chodesh* perform the exact same *kapparah*, covering the full range of *tumas mikdash v'kodashav* identically. On this reading, the challenge runs differently: "It is understandable according to me — *bishlama ledidi de'amina kol hanei kapparah achat hi*, all these goats do precisely the same thing, which is why if you lose one you can use another in its place. But according to you, Rabbi Shimon, who holds that they do not perform an identical function — *amai yikrevu*? Why can you use one for the other?" This second reading of the challenge, as the *Gemara* presents it, is actually the more straightforward one: the challenger's own position is that the goats are fully identical in function, not that *beis din* stipulates.

### No Explicit Tanna

The conclusion is sobering. Since the reading of the challenge as reflecting *lev beis din masneh aleihem* is uncertain — the challenger may simply be Rabbi Meir, whose position requires no such mechanism — there is no explicit *tanna* who applies *lev beis din* to the case of an unblemished animal when the option to wait for a *mum* exists. Rabbi Yochanan is thus left without a clean Tannaitic source. The *Gemara* resolves this with the phrase *Rabbi Yochanan gemara gemiri lah* — it is simply a tradition he holds, without deriving it from any explicit *tanna*: *ledivrei Rabbi Shimon ein nifdin, ledivrei chachamim nifdin*.

Tosafot raises an interesting question in this context: what compelled Rabbi Yochanan to concede that Rabbi Shimon disagrees with him at all? Rabbi Shimon's position — that you may use a goat from one *musaf* for another — does not require *lev beis din masneh aleihem*. Rabbi Shimon simply says they are all addressing *tumas mikdash v'kodashav* and are therefore interchangeable by nature. Why should Rabbi Yochanan infer from Rabbi Shimon's silence about *lev beis din* that he rejects the principle entirely? The *Gemara* does not address this directly, but once Rabbi Yochanan made his concession, the broader consequence followed: no *tanna* explicitly endorses the redemption of an unblemished animal in a case where one could simply wait for a *mum*. And yet Rabbi Yochanan maintains this as his understanding of the *chachamim*'s position. Whether this statement is accepted as authoritative *halacha* or represents a position the *Gemara* is straining against is, as always, a question worth pursuing — the *Rambam*'s treatment of the passage would bear directly on that question.

---

## Leftover Qorbanos

### Mai Avdinan Lehu

The *Gemara* now pivots to a directly practical question, posing it from the vantage point of Rabbi Shimon who denies *lev beis din masneh aleihem*: *mai avdinan lehu* — what do we do with them? The scenario is the leftover *tmidin* from the previous year. Unlike the earlier discussion about a goat that got lost and was recovered in the same year, here the difficulty is structural: there is a clear demarcation that communal funds from one year cannot be used for *korbanos* of the following year. So one cannot simply offer last year's *tamid* as this year's *tamid*, even though it is the identical type of sacrifice. What then is to be done with these animals?

The *Gemara* clarifies that Tosafot regards this entire discussion as a question of *lechatchila* only — *b'dieved*, if the sacrifice was in fact offered, it would be valid. But the question remains: short of waiting for a *mum* to develop, what legitimate use can be made of these leftover communal animals?

### Kayitz Hamizbeach

Rabbi Yitzchak, in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, provides the answer: *makitzin bahen es hamizbeach* — one uses them for *kayitz hamizbeach*, keeping the altar active. The term *kayitz* — related to the word for summer — evokes the image of a lull in Temple activity, a period when traffic has slowed and the altar risks falling idle. In such moments, a communal *olah* is brought not to fulfill any specific obligation but simply to maintain the rhythm of the Temple's *avodah*, to signal that business continues as usual. This is *kayitz hamizbeach*: a freewill communal offering whose purpose is to keep the altar in constant use.

### Leftover Funds Usage

To understand why this works, one must appreciate a special *halacha* governing the disposition of leftover communal funds. If, at year's end, money remains in the communal treasury that was collected for purchasing *korbanos*, it cannot simply be redirected to the new year's obligatory sacrifices. Nor is it returned. Instead, there is a specific mechanism: leftover funds from the previous year may be used to purchase *korbanos* for *kayitz hamizbeach*, even for the following year. This is not circular — it reflects a halakhic determination that *kayitz hamizbeach* offerings occupy a distinct status, more flexible than the obligatory communal sacrifices and thus eligible to be funded from residual prior-year assets.

The practical upshot is as follows. If one has leftover *money* from last year, it may go toward *kayitz hamizbeach* this year. If one has leftover *sheep* from last year — animals originally designated as *tmidin* — the same applies: since they are *olah olah* (the animal was set aside as an *olah*, and it will be brought as an *olah*), the identity has not fundamentally changed, and the flexibility afforded to *kayitz hamizbeach* accommodates this carry-over.

Rashi explains explicitly: when the altar is idle, one brings these animals as *olos lenidvas tzibur* — freewill communal burnt offerings — as established in the earlier *sugya* regarding the *se'ir* that was not brought for one occasion but could be brought for another. The *Gemara* notes that one of the specific uses of leftover funds — alongside others such as Temple repair — is this *kayitz hamizbeach* fund. A *beraisa* confirms: *mosros* — leftover communal funds — go toward *kayitz hamizbeach*, in the form of offerings comparable to what Rashi describes as a kind of delicacy brought to the altar, keeping it continually engaged.

One important limitation: the *halacha* of *ein olas ha'of b'tzibbur* — there is no communal bird *olah* — means that the *kayitz hamizbeach* sacrifice must be a full animal offering, not a bird. Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda, in the name of Rav Shimi of Neharde'a (citing a tradition passed through Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak), explains that *mosros l'nidvas tzibbur azli* — leftover funds must go toward communal freewill offerings — *ve'ein olas ha'of b'tzibbur*: a bird *olah* can only be brought by an individual, not as a communal sacrifice. The derivation from the *pasuk* emphasizing *korbano* — his personal offering — establishes that *olas ha'of* is restricted to private individuals. Rashi cites this scriptural basis. Tosafot, however, questions how absolute this rule is: if it were entirely black-and-white, Rava's apparent mockery of the ruling would be difficult to understand. Tosafot entertains the possibility that *b'dieved*, a communal bird *olah* might be valid, and that the restriction is primarily *lechatchila*.

---

## Chatas Status Change

### Identity Change Issue

The discussion thus far has addressed leftover *tmidin* and generic communal funds. A fundamentally harder case now arises: what of a leftover *chatas* from the previous year? Here the problem is compounded, because a *chatas* is not a *se'ir* of a *musaf* that can flow into another *musaf*; nor is it an *olah* that can be redirected as *kayitz hamizbeach*. It is a sin-offering with a fixed identity. Once the new year has begun, a *chatas* purchased with last year's funds cannot be offered as this year's *chatas musaf*. And unlike the *tmidin*, one cannot simply use it for *kayitz hamizbeach*, because *kayitz hamizbeach* calls for an *olah*, and this animal is a *chatas*.

The *Gemara* makes this explicit: *modeh Rabbi Shimon b'siyumei chatas she'ein miketzin b'gufan ela bidmeihen* — even Rabbi Shimon concedes that with leftover *chatos*, you cannot use the animal itself for *kayitz hamizbeach*; you can only use its money value. The process is: let it graze until it develops a *mum*, redeem it, and then apply the redemption money toward an *olah* for *kayitz hamizbeach*. It cannot leapfrog directly to *kayitz hamizbeach* in its current form.

But this raises a natural question: why not? If the animal's inevitable trajectory is toward an *olah* — once it develops a *mum*, is redeemed, and the money is used to purchase an *olah* — why not short-circuit the process and simply offer it directly as an *olah* now? The *Gemara* explains with the principle noted at the top of 11b, in the ruling of Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Shimon: *yiru ad sheyistavu, v'yimakru, v'yipelu dmeihem l'nedavah, she'ein chatas tzibur meisah* — a communal *chatas* that cannot be brought does not simply die as a personal *chatas* would; instead, it is left to graze until it acquires a *mum*, is redeemed, and the money is donated for a communal freewill *olah*. The funds are absorbed into the communal *nedavah* fund, the *kayitz hamizbeach* reserve. This is a settled *halacha*: by the *chatas tzibur*, you wait for the *mum*, redeem it, and the money goes to *nedavah*.

### Gezeirah Risk

The *Gemara* then articulates the reason one cannot bypass this process and simply bring the animal as an *olah* in its current form. The answer given is: *gezeirah le'achar kapparah atu lifnei kapparah*. It is a rabbinic safeguard: once the *chatas* has been superseded — once another sacrifice has been brought in its stead or the time for its use has passed — its practical identity has shifted toward that of an *olah*, and in principle one might think the animal itself could simply be offered as such. But if we were to permit that, we might come to do the same thing even when the animal could still serve as a *chatas* — when the conditions rendering it obsolete have not yet materialized. To prevent this confusion, the rabbis require that the identity change be effected through a concrete act: the development of a *mum*, followed by redemption.

This is a striking *Gemara*. One would have expected the ruling to rest on a more principled foundation: namely, that a *chatas* does not change its identity automatically, and that some concrete act is required to transform it. Instead, the *Gemara* frames the restriction as a *gezeirah* — a preventive measure against confusion. The implication seems to be that in truth, once the *chatas* can no longer serve its original function, it has already, in some sense, taken on the character of an *olah*, and one might legitimately offer it as such. The *gezeirah* is what stands in the way.

### Tosafot View

Tosafot, however, is uncomfortable with this framing. Other *gemaros* strongly imply that the identity of a *chatas* does not shift automatically — that something concrete must occur to effect the change. One important formulation from elsewhere in the *Gemara* is the concept of *nitak lire'iyah*: once the animal has been actively designated for pasture — placed in a pen to await a *mum* — that concrete act changes its identity. It is no longer a *chatas* in any operative sense; it is now on its way to being an *olah*. But this happens because of the concrete act of designation, not automatically by virtue of the passage of time or the bringing of a substitute. Tosafot thus reads the *gezeirah* explanation of our *Gemara* as somewhat anomalous, and understands the underlying rule to be that without such a concrete act, the animal retains its *chatas* identity regardless.

### Tannaitic Parallels

The *Gemara* brings three Tannaitic parallels, each introduced with the phrase *af anan nami tanina* — "we too have taught this" — all converging on the same point that the animal itself cannot be brought as an *olah* directly; only its redemption money may be so used.

The first, brought by Abaye, involves the *par* and *se'ir* of *Yom Kippur* that were lost and replaced, as well as the *se'ir* of *avoda zarah* in a similar situation. Rabbi Yehuda rules that these die — treating them as a *chatas shenitkapru ba'aleiha*, a *chatas* whose owners have achieved atonement through another means, which, like a personal *chatas*, must be left to die. Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon disagree: *yire'u ad sheyista'avu v'yimakru v'yipelu dmeihem linedavah, she'ein chatas tzibur meisah* — a communal *chatas* does not die; it grazes until it develops a *mum*, is redeemed, and the money goes to a communal *olah*. Why not simply bring the animal itself as an *olah*, given that its money is destined for that purpose anyway? *Gezeirah le'achar kapparah atu lifnei kapparah* — we worry the practice will be confused with cases where the *chatas* could still function as such.

The second parallel, adduced by Rav Ashi, involves the *hasheni* — the extra goat that remains when one of the *Yom Kippur* pair is lost or rendered unfit and a replacement pair is procured. The extra surviving goat must graze until it develops a *mum*; it is then redeemed and its money goes to a *nedavah*. Again, why not bring it as an *olah* directly, since its *Yom Kippur* function has been fulfilled by another? The same answer: *gezeirah le'achar kapparah atu lifnei kapparah*.

The third, adduced by Ravina, addresses the case of an *asham* — a guilt-offering — whose owners either died or achieved atonement through another *korban*. Unlike a personal *chatas*, which in Rabbi Eliezer's view must die, the *asham* follows a parallel track to the communal *chatas*: *yireh ad sheyista'ev v'yimakru v'yipelu damav linedavah* — graze until blemished, redeem, and the money goes to a *nedavah*. Rabbi Eliezer says it dies, like a *chatas*; Rabbi Yehoshua says its money may be used to bring a personal *olah* — *yavi bedamav olah*. The distinction between the view that the money goes to a communal *nedavah* fund versus that it funds a personal *olah* parallels the distinction between the communal and individual contexts. In all these cases, however, the animal itself may not be brought as an *olah*: *amru lo gezeirah le'achar kapparah atu lifnei kapparah*.

The *Gemara* thus establishes a consistent framework. Leftover money from last year: may be used for *kayitz hamizbeach*. Leftover *tmidin* from last year: may be used for *kayitz hamizbeach*. Leftover *chatas* or *asham* from last year: must wait for a *mum*, be redeemed, and the money then goes to *kayitz hamizbeach*. The body of the animal itself cannot serve directly as an *olah*. And the *Gemara*'s stated reason — that it is a *gezeirah* against confusion — leaves open the more principled question of whether an automatic identity change ever truly occurs, a question Tosafot pursues at length by reference to the language of *nitak lire'iyah* in parallel *gemaros*.

---

## Sakin Moshechtan

### Communal Bird Restriction

The *Gemara* at this stage has established that *kayitz hamizbeach* offerings must take the form of communal animal *olos*, not bird offerings. The restriction *ein olas ha'of b'tzibbur* — derived from the *pasuk*'s emphasis on individual ownership — is clear in the *lechatchila* sense, though Tosafot raises the question of whether it extends to *b'dieved*. The *Gemara*'s citation of Rav Shimi of Neharde'a establishes the Amoraic chain of transmission for this ruling and explains why Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak felt entitled to defend it against Rava's apparent skepticism.

### Sakin Moshechtan

Having established this, the *Gemara* now introduces a statement of Shmuel that supports Rabbi Yochanan's broader framework. Rav Yehuda quotes Shmuel: *korbanot tzibur — sakin moshechtan lama she-hen* — communal sacrifices, the knife drags them to what they are. This is a compact and somewhat cryptic principle that requires unpacking, and Rashi and Tosafot offer strikingly different explanations.

### Rashi on Sakin

According to Rashi, the principle means the following. Even though a communal animal was originally designated for a specific *korban*, if circumstances have changed — most relevantly for our *sugya*, if it is now the new year and the animal can no longer serve as last year's *tamid* — when the *shechita* is performed with a generic, unstated intent, the knife "drags" the animal to whichever legitimate identity it can assume. Rashi reads this as supporting the *halacha* that last year's sheep designated as a *tamid* can be used this year for *kayitz hamizbeach*: even though it was originally sanctified for a *tamid*, when the *kohen* takes the knife to it now for *kayitz hamizbeach*, that act of *shechita* defines what it is. The *beraisa* that immediately follows supports this reading: *modeh Rabbi Shimon b'sa'ir shelo karav b'regel yikarev b'Rosh Chodesh* — Rabbi Shimon himself concedes that if a goat was not brought on the *regel*, it may be brought on *Rosh Chodesh*; and if not on *Rosh Chodesh*, on *Yom Kippur*; and if not on *Yom Kippur*, on another *regel*. The reason given is *she'mitechilah lo ba ela l'chaper al mizbeach hachitzon* — all these *musafin* were always coming to atone via the outer altar, and all addressed *tumas mikdash*, so one may be substituted for another. Rashi reads the principle of *sakin moshechtan* as extending this flexibility: the knife, at the moment of *shechita*, seals the identity of the offering among the range of legitimate possibilities.

Significantly, the *beraisa* also implies that Rabbi Shimon's flexibility has a temporal limit. When the list of occasions runs out — after the final *regel* before the new year arrives — he stops. He does not say that the goat may be carried over into the following year. This supports the general understanding that once the new year's *korbanos* are funded by new money, last year's animals cannot simply be inserted into this year's *musaf* cycle, even according to Rabbi Shimon.

### Tosafot on Sakin

Tosafot, citing the *Aruch*, reads the principle of *sakin moshechtan* quite differently, and in a way that connects more directly to *lev beis din masneh aleihem*. Before *shechita* is performed, the animal's specific sacrificial identity has not been fully determined. It has been sanctified generically — set aside as a communal *korban* — but which *korban* precisely it is remains somewhat fluid, held open by the implicit condition of the *beis din*. Then, when the *kohen* takes the knife to it and performs *shechita* with a particular intent, the act of *shechita* draws the animal toward and solidifies that specific identity. The knife does not change the identity from something fixed to something new; rather, it resolves a genuine ambiguity that was always present.

On this reading, Tosafot says explicitly: *terem moshcham la'sakin, ein lomar eizeh tamid eizeh musaf, ela tluyim v'omdim b'tnai lev beis din* — before the knife draws them, one cannot say definitively whether this sheep is the *tamid* or the *musaf*; they are suspended in a state of conditionality, depending on the stipulation of the *beis din*. Then the knife comes and settles the matter.

This understanding illuminates the relationship between *sakin moshechtan* and *lev beis din masneh aleihem*. In the more radical formulation of *lev beis din*, a *korban* sanctified for one purpose is redirected entirely — for instance, from a *korban* to *bedek habayit*. Here, the *lev beis din* is operating within a narrower range: the animal was sanctified generically for some communal *korban* to be determined, and the *shechita* specifies which one. This is a less radical application of the same underlying idea: the *beis din*'s implicit intention is that the animal will serve whatever function the *shechita* designates within the legitimate range. Tosafot sees this as consistent with, and indeed illuminating of, Rabbi Shimon's own position — even Rabbi Shimon, who rejects the more radical *lev beis din*, may accept this more modest form of pre-*shechita* fluidity, which is why he permits using a goat from one *musaf* for another.

---

## Yom Kippur Atonement

### Shear Aveiros

With the Temple-law discussions concluded, the *Gemara* now turns to a new section of the *mishna* that addresses the atonement scope of the *sa'ir hamishtaleiach* — the goat sent off the cliff on *Yom Kippur*. Having labored through the complex mechanics of communal sacrifice identity and redemption over the course of the preceding pages, we arrive at what most people consider the primary concern: *al shear aveiros shebatorah* — upon all the remaining transgressions of the Torah, the scapegoat atones. The *mishna* enumerates: light transgressions and heavy ones, intentional and unintentional, those one has become aware of and those one has not, positive commandments, prohibitions, those carrying *kares*, and those carrying *mita beis din*.

### Redundancy Analysis

The *Gemara* immediately notes apparent redundancies in this list. *Hainu kalos hainu aseh* — "light" (*kalos*) seems to be the same as *aseh* and simple *lo ta'aseh*, and "heavy" (*chamuros*) seems to be the same as *krisot* and *misos beis din*. If you have already listed *aseh* and *lo ta'aseh* and *kares* and *misa beis din*, what additional information do "light" and "heavy" contribute? The *Gemara* resolves this: the pairing is meant to explain each other. "Light" means *aseh* and *lo ta'aseh*; "heavy" means *kares* and *misa beis din*. They are simply more precise elaborations, not independent categories.

### Hoda vs. Lo Hoda

A second apparent redundancy concerns *hoda* and *lo hoda* — "became aware" and "did not become aware." *Hoda hainu meizid* — if one became aware, that would seem to mean one was willful; *lo hoda hainu shogeg* — if one did not become aware, that would seem to mean one sinned unintentionally. But the *mishna* has already mentioned *shogeg* and *meizid*. What do *hoda* and *lo hoda* add?

Rav Yehuda explains: *hoda* and *lo hoda* do not refer to one's state of knowledge at the time of sinning but to one's subsequent awareness. One who sinned *bishogeg* — unintentionally — may or may not later discover that he has sinned. If he does discover it definitively, he incurs a personal obligation to bring a *chatas*, and *Yom Kippur* does not exempt him from that obligation; the *chatas* must still be brought. But *hoda* and *lo hoda* in the *mishna* refer to a different situation: one who becomes aware that he *might* have sinned, triggering the obligation of an *asham talui*. The terms are thus not synonymous with *shogeg* and *meizid* but refer specifically to the degree of awareness regarding a potential sin. The *Gemara* thus explains that *bein noda lo sfekan bein lo noda lo sfekan*: whether or not one has become aware that one might have transgressed — i.e., whether or not the *asham talui* obligation has been triggered — the scapegoat of *Yom Kippur* covers this.

### Asham Talui Exception

This distinction sharpens the exceptional status of the *asham talui* in relation to *Yom Kippur*. If, on the eve of *Yom Kippur*, one is aware that one may have eaten *chelev* — perhaps two pieces of meat were in front of him, one of which was *chelev*, and he is now uncertain which he ate — he would normally be obligated in an *asham talui*, the guilt-offering for a doubtful transgression. Once *Yom Kippur* passes, however, that *asham talui* obligation lapses. If it later emerges that he definitely sinned, he then incurs the obligation of a *chatas*; but the *asham talui* is not required after *Yom Kippur* has passed. The scapegoat thus covers both the case where one is unaware of a potential sin and the case where one is aware of the uncertainty — in either case, the *asham talui* is discharged.

What *Yom Kippur* does not cover is a definite *chatas* obligation already established by certain knowledge of having sinned. That must be addressed directly, through the appropriate *korban*.

### Kalos & Chamuros

The *mishna*'s full list, as parsed by the *Gemara*, thus divides into the following framework. *Kalos* — light transgressions — encompass positive commandments (*aseh*) and prohibitions (*lo ta'aseh*). *Chamuros* — heavy transgressions — encompass those punishable by *kares* or *misa beis din*. Across all of these categories, whether committed *bishogeg* or *b'meizid*, and whether or not the person has become aware of a possible violation (in the sense relevant to *asham talui*), the *sa'ir hamishtaleiach* of *Yom Kippur* provides atonement. The remaining discussion of exactly which forms of *tumas mikdash v'kodashav* are addressed by the inner *sa'ir* — including the case where one was not aware at the outset but was aware at the end, based on the *pasuk*'s reference to *pish'eihem* alongside *chata'osam* — will continue on the following *daf*.

---

---

# Shevuot 13

## Yom Kippur Atonement

### Opening & Transition

Today's daf is 13, and we are finally turning from the last part of the *mishnah*, which devoted its opening portion to working out the distinct functions of the various *musafim* — the *chatat* offerings and their relationship to *tumat mikdash* — and then a lengthy derivation establishing that *shevuot shtayim she'hein arba* follows the same structural pattern as other cases of "two that are four." The final portion of the *mishnah*, however, shifts to a topic more directly connected to our own lives: not the question of *tumat mikdash* and the *korbanot* that address it, but the broader question of what the goat of *Yom Kippur* atones for.

### Goat of Yom Kippur

The *mishnah* states that the goat sent over the cliff on *Yom Kippur* atones for sins whether they are weighty or light, *mezid* or *shogeg*, or whether the sinner knew or did not know — with the *gemara* clarifying that "knew or did not know" refers to a case of initial *shogeg* where there is now uncertainty as to whether an *asham* is required. One thing the goat does not accomplish is releasing someone from the obligation of a *chatat*: if you sinned *beshogeg* and are certain of it, the *chatat* obligation remains. But with that established, we pick up at the bottom of 12b.

### Lack of Teshuvah

The *gemara* asks: what is the case where the goat atones for a positive *mitzvah* one failed to perform? If one did not do *teshuvah* — *idelo avid teshuvah* — why should a sacrifice atone at all? *Zevach reshaim to'evah* — the sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination. The *gemara* is framing the question in a striking way: it is not merely asking whether atonement is deserved, but suggesting that if one remains entirely unrepentant toward a particular sin, the very act of bringing a sacrifice in that context borders on the contemptible — a kind of invalid or unwanted offering. On the other hand, if one *has* done *teshuvah* — *id'avid teshuvah* — then *kol yoma nami*: any day on which *teshuvah* is done for a *mitzvat aseh* suffices, and *Yom Kippur* with the goat seems superfluous.

### Teshuvah for Mitzvat Aseh

A *baraita* is cited: *avar al mitzvat aseh ve'asah teshuvah*, if one transgressed a positive *mitzvah* and did *teshuvah*, *lo zaz mi-sham ad she-mochalin lo* — one does not move from there before God forgives. The imagery evokes something like *Choni HaMa'agal* standing his ground: immediate forgiveness is available upon *teshuvah* for a *mitzvat aseh*. So who then needs the goat, and who needs *Yom Kippur*?

### Omed BeMiddo

Rabbi Zeira answers: this case concerns someone who is *omed be-meredo* — standing in a state of rebellion. The point is subtle and important. The failure to do *teshuvah* is not a passive oversight; it is an active ongoing choice to remain unrepentant, an implicit declaration of indifference. Nevertheless, *Yom Kippur* forgives even this.

### Ramban on Teshuvah

This connects to a remarkable observation of the Ramban in his *drasha le-Rosh Hashanah* — a work that is essentially a fifty-page commentary on *Masechet Rosh Hashanah*, with only its final paragraph devoted to *mussar*. There the Ramban writes that the opportunity for *teshuvah* God has granted us is simultaneously a great gift and a great liability. It is a gift because *teshuvah* earns forgiveness. But it is a liability because: had God never given us *teshuvah*, a person who sinned would have sinned only once. Now that *teshuvah* exists, choosing not to do *teshuvah* is itself an ongoing sin — every passing moment becomes a renewed act of *omed be-meredo*, a continued embrace of one's transgression. This is precisely what Rabbi Zeira captures: not doing *teshuvah* is not simply the absence of an action; it is an active posture of rebellion. And yet, *Yom Kippur* still atones.

---

## Rabbi's Position

### All Sins Atoned

The *mishnah*, the *gemara* tells us, follows the position of *Rabbi* — that is, Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi. A *baraita* states his teaching explicitly: *al kol averos she-ba-Torah bein asah teshuvah bein lo asah teshuvah Yom HaKippurim mechaper* — for all the transgressions in the Torah, whether one has done *teshuvah* or has not done *teshuvah*, *Yom Kippur* atones. The vision is of a kind of divine amnesty: God desires that each year, every person begin with a clean slate. Even a willful *mechalel Shabbat* with no remorse whatsoever — come *Yom Kippur*, the slate is wiped clean.

It is worth noting a subtle but critical shift that occurs here and continues throughout the day's discussion: the *gemara* has quietly transitioned from speaking about the goat going over the cliff as the instrument of atonement to speaking of *Yom Kippur* itself as *mechaper*. This shift is obviously momentous for us, who no longer have the goat. The *gemara* allows this transition to happen organically without drawing explicit attention to it.

### Three Exceptions

There is, however, an exception — in fact, three. *Chutz* — excepted from the blanket atonement of *Yom Kippur* are: *porek ol*, *megaleh panim ba-Torah*, and *mefeir brit basar*.

### Porek Ol Defined

*Porek ol* means casting off the yoke — an outright rejection of God and His *mitzvot*. This is not mere willful sinning driven by desire or appetite; it is an ideological rejection of the entire covenantal relationship.

### Megaleh Panim

*Megaleh panim ba-Torah* is frequently misread, particularly when a gloss of *she-lo ka-halacha* is inserted, suggesting it refers to someone who interprets a *halacha* incorrectly. That misreading obscures what is actually a far more serious category. The phrase *gilui panim* means acting brazenly, with insolence. Applied to *Torah*, it describes someone whose relationship to the words of the *Torah* is one of dismissive scoffing — not sincere philosophical questioning, but a contemptuous "ugh, why would God have said such a thing?" — a posture of mockery and denigration toward the *Torah* itself.

### Rashi on Megaleh Panim

Rashi makes this vivid. Three lines from the top of the relevant passage he writes: *ba al divrei Torah be-chutzpah u-vegillui azut panim, ke-gon Menashe she-haya yoshev ve-doresh be-agadot shel dofi* — like Menashe who would sit and expound stories of *Torah* in a manner of derision: Why did Moshe need to write the story of Timna who was a concubine? What is the episode of Reuven going out in the days of the wheat harvest doing in the *Torah*? Not as a genuine question, but as contemptuous dismissal. Rashi thus reads *megaleh panim* as describing a specific relationship to the *Torah* — one of brazen scoffing — rather than to God or *mitzvot* directly. The Rambam in his *Peirush HaMishnayot*, by contrast, reads it as referring to someone who sins *le-hachis*, in active defiance and provocation.

### Mefir Brit

*Mefeir brit basar* — annulling the covenant of the flesh — refers to reversing *brit milah*. The word *basar* makes clear this is not merely metaphorical. It is the cancellation of the physical covenant. Whether this extends to someone who grows up in a household that never performed the *brit* and makes a conscious ideological choice to remain uncircumcised is an interesting question; the language suggests active rejection rather than mere passivity.

For these three, *teshuvah* does work — *she-im asah teshuvah Yom HaKippurim mechaper* — if *teshuvah* is done, *Yom Kippur* then atones. But without *teshuvah*, *Yom Kippur* does not atone for these three. By contrast, one might wonder whether the classic three cardinal sins — *gilui arayot*, *shefichut damim*, and *avodah zarah* — fall within or outside this framework. According to Rabbi, as long as the person has not crossed into ideological rejection of God, Torah, or the covenant — as long as they remain within the *berit* even while sinning grievously — *Yom Kippur* atones even for those sins without *teshuvah*.

One should also be clear about what atonement without *teshuvah* means and does not mean. As Rav Soloveitchik once articulated, there is a distinction between *kapparah* — the erasure of culpability, the cleaning of the slate — and the personal transformation that genuine *teshuvah me-ahavah* accomplishes. A person whose slate is wiped clean by *Yom Kippur* without *teshuvah* is still, *be-gavra*, a *rasha* — they have simply escaped punishment for their past sins. *Teshuvah* in its deepest sense transforms who a person is, converting the *rasha* into a *tzaddik*. The mechanisms are not equivalent.

### Hikareit Tikareit

How does Rabbi derive that these three are not covered by the general atonement of *Yom Kippur*? A *baraita* cites: *ki devar Hashem baza* — because he has denigrated the word of God. Rashi explains that *devar Hashem* in its primary sense refers to *Anochi Hashem Elokecha* — the first word of the *aseret ha-dibrot* — so that *ki devar Hashem baza* describes the person who denigrates God's word entirely: *ze ha-porek ol u-megaleh panim ba-Torah*. And *ve-et mitzvato hefar* — he has annulled His commandment: *ze ha-mefeir brit basar*. What *mitzvah* symbolizes the covenant more than any other? The *brit* of the flesh.

Then the verse continues: *hikaret tikaret* — he shall surely be cut off. The doubling is exegetically significant. *Hikaret* — before *Yom Kippur*. *Tikaret* — after *Yom Kippur*. The verse is teaching that even after *Yom Kippur* passes, these three are not atoned for. This is Rabbi's proof that *Yom Kippur* does not atone for these three — not that he needs a proof that *Yom Kippur* atones for everything else, which seems to be his starting assumption.

### Avona Bah

But the verse then adds: *avona vah* — the sin is in her, or more precisely, the sin persists with the person. *Lo amarti ela bi-zman she-avona vah* — this is only said when the sin continues to persist, when the person is still grasping it. Once *teshuvah* is done — once the person is no longer holding fast to the sin — even these three receive atonement. Implicitly, this also establishes Rabbi's view for everything else: since the verse specifies that these three are not atoned for specifically due to *avona vah* — because the sin persists — we can derive that for everything else, *Yom Kippur* atones even without *teshuvah*.

---

## Rabbanan's Position

### Olam HaBa Reading

The *rabanan* who disagree with Rabbi — who hold that *Yom Kippur* does *not* atone without *teshuvah* — read the verse differently. *Hikaret* — cut off in *olam hazeh*. *Tikaret* — cut off *le-olam haba*. On this reading, the doubling of *hikaret tikaret* says nothing about *Yom Kippur* at all; it is describing the punishment of *karet* in its two dimensions across this world and the next. The reference to *olam haba* then implies that we are discussing what happens after death.

### Death Atones

For the *rabanan*, therefore, the verse is about *misa* — death. Death, *misa memarkeset*, cleanses. The *rabanan* hold that death atones even for those who have not done *teshuvah*, at least for all sins other than the three cardinal ones. Rashi adds that this works in conjunction with *Yom Kippur*. The term *memarkeset* is telling: it suggests something more like scouring than the gentle *mechaperes* — the erasure is complete but the process is more severe, perhaps less total in its redemptive quality.

For the big three, the *rabanan* hold that even death atones only if *teshuvah* was done. And as for *Yom Kippur*: in the view of the *rabanan*, *Yom Kippur* always requires *teshuvah*.

### Atonement Chart

To map the positions clearly: Rabbi holds that *Yom Kippur* atones for everything without *teshuvah*, with the exception that for the three — *porek ol*, *megaleh panim*, and *mefeir brit* — one needs *Yom Kippur* plus *teshuvah*. The *rabanan* hold that *Yom Kippur* always requires *teshuvah*, and that death (*misa*) atones without *teshuvah* for everything other than the three, while the three require *teshuvah* even for death to atone.

### Mitzvat Aseh Agreement

One important point of agreement: for a *mitzvat aseh*, both Rabbi and the *rabanan* agree that *teshuvah* alone suffices — no *Yom Kippur* and no other mechanism is required. Forgiveness is immediate upon genuine *teshuvah*.

---

## Mishnah Attribution

### Challenge to Mishnah

The *gemara* now asks: if our *mishnah* follows Rabbi — who holds that *Yom Kippur* atones even without *teshuvah* — how does that square with the apparent evidence from the end of the *mishnah*?

### End of Mishnah

The *seifa* of the *mishnah* states: *echad Yisrael ve-echad Kohanim ve-echad Kohen Mashuach* — all three categories, the ordinary Israelite, the *Kohen*, and the *Kohen Gadol*, receive equal atonement. This reflects the position that when it comes to *she'ar aveiros* — the sins other than *tumat mikdash* — the goat that goes over the cliff provides atonement equally for all. Whereas for *tumat mikdash*, Kohanim have a distinct atonement through the ox and Israelites through the goat, for all other sins they share one vehicle. Now, this position — that they share equally in the goat for *she'ar aveiros* — is identified as belonging to Rabbi Yehudah. If the *seifa* is Rabbi Yehudah, the *gemara* argues, so must be the *reisha*, and the *mishnah* should therefore not be attributed to Rabbi.

### Rav Yosef's Solution

Rav Yosef responds: the *mishnah* is indeed Rabbi — *Rabbi hi* — and Rabbi simply adopts Rabbi Yehudah's position regarding the equality of Kohen and Yisrael for the goat. *Ve-savar lah ke-Rabbi Yehudah*. In other words, Rabbi, as author of the *mishnah*, held like Rabbi Yehudah on this particular *halacha* while maintaining his own distinctive position that *Yom Kippur* atones without *teshuvah*.

### Abaye's Challenge

Abaye presses further: was Rav Yosef being precise in saying that *Rabbi* holds like Rabbi Yehudah — as opposed to saying the *mishnah* is Rabbi Yehudah who holds like Rabbi? After all, either formulation could account for the evidence.

### Mutual Agreement

Rav Yosef responds: *davka ka-amina* — yes, I was being precise. Rabbi holds like Rabbi Yehudah, but Rabbi Yehudah does not hold like Rabbi regarding *Yom Kippur* atoning without *teshuvah*. Why phrase it with Rabbi as the one borrowing? *Orcha de-milsa* — it is simply more natural to say that the later authority, Rabbi (who postdates Rabbi Yehudah), embraced an earlier position, rather than the reverse. But the precision is real: Rabbi Yehudah actively disagreed with Rabbi's core position on *teshuvah* and *Yom Kippur*.

---

## Baraita Evidence

### Sifra Source

The evidence comes from a *baraita* drawn from the *Sifra* — the collection of tannaitic legal exegesis on *Vayikra*, whose anonymous voice is by tradition attributed to Rabbi Yehudah. The *baraita* opens: *yachol yehei Yom HaKippurim mechaper al shavim ve-al she-einam shavim* — perhaps *Yom Kippur* should atone both for those who have done *teshuvah* and for those who have not?

### Logical Derivation

A logical analogy is offered: *chatas* and *asham* atone, and *Yom Kippur* atones; just as *chatas* and *asham* only atone for those who have done *teshuvah* — since bringing a sin-offering includes the act of *viduy*, verbal confession — so too *Yom Kippur* should atone only for those who have done *teshuvah*. *Af Yom HaKippurim ein mechaper ella al shavim*.

### Counter-argument

But this analogy is challenged: *mah le-chatas ve-asham she-ein mechaperim al ha-mezid ke-shogeg* — one could distinguish *chatas* and *asham* by saying their atoning power is inherently limited, applying only to unintentional sins. Their restricted scope explains why *teshuvah* is also required: the most forgivable sins (unintentional at the outset, repented at the end) earn the atonement of a *chatat*. *Tomar le-Yom HaKippurim she-mechaper al ha-mezid ke-shogeg* — but *Yom Kippur* is explicitly described in the *pasuk* as atoning even for willful sins, *u-mipisheihem le-chol chatosam*. Since *Yom Kippur* possesses this expanded atoning power, perhaps it functions as a complete and unconditional mechanism, working even without *teshuvah*.

### Ach Limitation

The *baraita* responds with a verse from Vayikra 23: *ach be-yom hazeh yechapper*. The word *ach* introduces a limitation. *Ach* — only, but. *Yom Kippur* does not have total scope. And therefore: it atones only for those who have done *teshuvah*. Even if the sin was *mezid*, *Yom Kippur* still requires *teshuvah* to function. The combination is: yes, it can cover even willful sins, but only when accompanied by *teshuvah*.

### Sifra Attribution

This entire *derasha* comes from the *Sifra*. *Stam Sifra mani? Rabbi Yehudah* — the anonymous voice of the *Sifra* is Rabbi Yehudah. The *baraita*'s conclusion that *Yom Kippur* works only *al shavim* — only for those who have returned — is therefore explicitly Rabbi Yehudah's position. This confirms Rav Yosef's claim: the part of our *mishnah* that implies *Yom Kippur* atones even without *teshuvah* cannot be Rabbi Yehudah; it must be Rabbi.

---

## Sifra Contradiction

### Violating Yom Kippur

The *gemara* now raises a striking contradiction between two anonymous passages of the *Sifra* — *rami stam Sifra a-stam Sifra*. The first *Sifra* we just cited says *Yom Kippur* works only for those who have done *teshuvah*. But a second *baraita* says the opposite, and in a dramatically expanded direction: *yachol lo yehei Yom HaKippurim mechaper ela im kein hisana bo ve-kara mikra kodesh ve-lo asah bo melachah* — one might think *Yom Kippur* atones only for one who fasted on it, acknowledged its sacred character, and refrained from *melachah*.

### Non-Observant Scenario

The *gemara* then entertains a scenario that borders on the radical: what about someone who did none of those things? Who did not fast, did not acknowledge the day, and actively performed *melachah*?

### Day of Atonement

*Talmud lomar: Yom Kippurim hu* — the verse simply states, it is *Yom Kippur*. *Mikol makom* — regardless. The day carries its atoning power independent of the person's acknowledgment or observance. This is a far more expansive claim than anything in the first *Sifra* passage, and it seems to posit that *Yom Kippur* atones even for someone actively violating it.

### Abaye's Resolution

Abaye resolves the contradiction by attribution: *ha Rabbi ve-ha Rabbi Yehudah*. The first *Sifra* — requiring *teshuvah* — is Rabbi Yehudah's position. The second *Sifra* — atoning even for the violator — is Rabbi's position.

### Rava's Position

Rava disagrees: *ha ve-ha Rabbi* — both passages represent Rabbi's position. The tension between them will be resolved not by attributing them to different authorities but by reading them in a more nuanced way.

---

## Rava's Interpretation

### Teshuvah for Violation

Rava's resolution is elegant. Both *Sifra* passages represent Rabbi. The earlier statement — that *Yom Kippur* requires *teshuvah* — is not a general statement about all sins. It refers specifically to the violation of *Yom Kippur* itself. *Ve-modeh Rabbi be-kareit di-yoma* — Rabbi concedes that *Yom Kippur* does not atone for its own violation without *teshuvah*.

### Other Sins Atoned

And yet — and this is the crucial move — even someone who violates *Yom Kippur* still benefits from *Yom Kippur*'s atonement for all his other sins. Violating *Yom Kippur* does not strip the day of its atoning power vis-à-vis everything else. The person eating on *Yom Kippur* will emerge, if he does not repent for the eating itself, with that particular sin unatoned — but his *mechalel Shabbat* and whatever else he has done throughout the year will be atoned for by the day.

### Karet Problem

This creates an internal pressure: if Rabbi holds that *Yom Kippur* atones for everything including its own violation, then why does the *Torah* prescribe *karet* for eating on *Yom Kippur*? If I am eating and *Yom Kippur* is atoning for me with every bite, what is left to punish? *De-i lo tima hachi kareit di-yoma le-Rabbi leit leh* — if you do not make this concession, Rabbi would have no scenario in which someone who eats on *Yom Kippur* receives *karet*, which the *Torah* explicitly prescribes.

### Karet Scenarios

The *gemara* briefly entertains the possibility of constructing a scenario where *Yom Kippur* atones for its own violation and *karet* still applies in some edge case: perhaps someone ate at night and died before the day of *Yom Kippur* arrived (*ke-gon de-avid be-layla u-mis ve-lo havi yemama le-khapporei leh*), since the *pasuk* says *ki ba-yom hazeh yechapper* — it is the *day* that atones. Or perhaps someone ate and choked as they were swallowing (*de-achal umtza ve-chankei u-mis*), dying before the *aveira* was complete enough for atonement to apply. Or someone ate right up until *shekiat ha-chama* with no remaining time for atonement to take effect.

### Rabbi's Agreement

Ultimately, Rava establishes: Rabbi agrees that *Yom Kippur* does not atone for its own violation without *teshuvah*. The two *Sifra* passages are both Rabbi's, and they are not contradictory: the first addresses the one thing *Yom Kippur* cannot atone for without *teshuvah* (its own violation), and the second addresses everything else (which *Yom Kippur* atones for regardless, even if one is violating the day). To the earlier framework of Rabbi's three exceptions — *porek ol*, *megaleh panim*, *mefeir brit* — we now add a fourth category requiring *teshuvah* according to Rabbi: the violation of *Yom Kippur* itself.

---

## Rambam's Ruling

### Concern for Incentive

One might reasonably worry about the practical implications of Rabbi's position. If people learn that *Yom Kippur* wipes the slate clean without *teshuvah*, the incentive to actually engage in *teshuvah* would be severely weakened.

### Teshuvah Essential

The Rambam rules definitively in *Hilchos Teshuvah*: *kol mitzvot she-ba-Torah bein asei bein lo ta'asei, im avar adam al achat mehem bein be-zadon bein bi-shigaga, she-ya'aseh teshuvah ve-yashuv me-cheto chayav le-hitvadot* — for every commandment in the *Torah*, positive or negative, intentional or unintentional, the obligation is to do *teshuvah* and *viduy*. And further: all the various mechanisms of atonement — *mitat beit din*, *korban*, and the rest — are insufficient without *teshuvah*.

### Se'ir HaMishtaleach

Concerning the *se'ir ha-mishtaleach*, the Rambam states: *she-hu kapparah kol Yisrael* — it is an atonement for all of Israel, atoning for all transgressions in the *Torah*, light and grave, *mezid* and *shogeg*, our *mishnah* — *ve-hu she-asah teshuvah*. Even the *se'ir ha-mishtaleach* requires *teshuvah*. The Rambam is applying the *rabanan*'s framework — or Rabbi Yehudah's — rather than Rabbi's more expansive position, plainly because he does not want *Yom Kippur* to become a reason to defer *teshuvah*.

### Without Temple

Finally: *bi-zman ha-zeh she-ein Beit ha-Mikdash kayam, ein lanu mizbe'ach kapparah, ein sham ela teshuvah. Ha-teshuvah mechaperet al kol ha-aveiros* — in our time, without the *Beit ha-Mikdash*, we have no altar of atonement, and there is nothing but *teshuvah*. *Teshuvah* alone atones for everything.

---

## Kohen Equality

### Mishnah Statement

The *mishnah* states: *echad Yisrael ve-echad Kohanim ve-echad Kohen Mashuach* — the Israelite, the *Kohen*, and the *Kohen Gadol* are all equal. The question is what precisely they are equal in, because the *mishnah*'s formulation seems to say they are all the same and then immediately asks what distinguishes them.

### Clarification

Rav Yehudah clarifies: *echad Yisrael ve-echad Kohanim ve-echad Kohen Mashuach miskapprin bi-se'ir ha-mishtale'ach bi-she'ar aveiros* — all three categories receive atonement from the *se'ir ha-mishtaleach* for all sins other than *tumat mikdash*. In the domain of *she'ar aveiros*, there is no distinction among them.

### Tumat Mikdash Distinction

The distinction exists only for *tumat mikdash*: *ella she-ha-par mechapper al Kohanim al tumat mikdash*. For the sins of *tumat mikdash*, the ox atones for the *Kohanim* and the goat atones for *Yisrael*. The *Kohanim* require separate atonement for *tumat mikdash* for two reasons: they are present in the *Mikdash* constantly and therefore more likely to render it impure, and they bear the special responsibility of maintaining and protecting its purity.

### Rabbi Yehudah Confirmed

This idea — that for *she'ar aveiros*, Kohanim and Yisrael share equally in the *se'ir ha-mishtaleach* — is Rabbi Yehudah's position, as the *gemara* confirms will be demonstrated from a *baraita*.

---

## Atonement Sources

### Mikdash Cleansing

The *baraita* from the *Sifra* begins with the *Kohen Gadol*'s service on *Yom Kippur* and traces through the various spaces it atones for: *ve-kipper et Mikdash ha-Kodesh* — he should atone for the sanctuary.

### Inner Sanctuary

*Zeh lifnai ve-lifnim* — that is the innermost chamber, the *Kodesh Kodashim*. *Et Ohel Mo'ed zeh Heichal* — the *Heichal*, where the *shulchan* and *menorah* stood. *Ve-al ha-mizbe'ach ke-mashma'o* — the altar, which Rashi explains refers to the *mizbe'ach ha-zahav*, the inner golden altar where the incense was offered.

### Outer Areas

*Yekhapper — elu azarot* — the *azarot*, the outer courtyards including the *ezrat Kohanim* and *ezrat Yisrael* where the outer altar stood. All of these spaces are atoned for through the blood of the ox and the blood of the goat.

### Both Groups

Then the *pasuk* concludes: *ve-al ha-Kohanim ve-al kol am ha-kahal yekhapper* — for the Kohanim and for all the congregation of the people he will atone. *Kohanim ke-mashma'o am ha-kahal elu Yisrael* — the Kohanim and the people of Israel. At this point, the blood of the ox is working for the Kohanim and the blood of the goat is working for Yisrael, for their respective *tumat mikdash* obligations.

### Extra Yechapper

But the verse ends with a final word: *yekhapper* — he will atone. What does this extra *yekhapper* come to include? *Elu ha-Levi'im. Hushvu kullam le-kapparah achat* — the Levites. They are all made equal to a single atonement. But wait: one has an ox and one has a goat. In what sense are they all equivalent? The *baraita* answers: *she-miskapprin bi-se'ir ha-mishtaleach bi-she'ar aveiros — divrei Rabbi Yehudah*. The equivalence indicated by that final *yekhapper* is that for all sins other than *tumat mikdash*, they all receive atonement through the *se'ir ha-mishtaleach*. That is Rabbi Yehudah's reading.

---

## Yehudah vs. Shimon

### Yehudah: Equality

Rabbi Yehudah holds that for *she'ar aveiros* — all sins other than *tumat mikdash* — both Kohanim and Yisrael receive atonement from the same source: the *se'ir ha-mishtaleach* that goes over the cliff. The extra *yekhapper* in the verse establishes their equality in this domain.

### Shimon: Separation

Rabbi Shimon disagrees. He too reads the *pasuk* carefully: the blood of the inner goat atones for *tumat mikdash* for Yisrael; the blood of the ox atones for *tumat mikdash* for Kohanim — *keshem she-dam sa'ir ha-na'aseh bi-fnim mechapper Yisrael al tumat mikdash ve-kodashav kakh dam par mechapper al Kohanim al tumat mikdash ve-kodashav*. So far there is agreement. But Rabbi Shimon argues that even for *she'ar aveiros*, there is a parallel split. The *se'ir ha-mishtaleach* does not atone for Kohanim for *she'ar aveiros*; something else does.

### Shimon's Link

What is his proof? *Ve-lakach et shenei ha-se'irim* — take the two goats: the inner goat and the *se'ir ha-mishtaleach*. These two are linked by the verse. Just as the inner goat is specified as *asher la-am* — belonging to the people — and therefore atones only for Yisrael (not for Kohanim) with respect to *tumat mikdash*, so too the *se'ir ha-mishtaleach*, being linked to the inner goat, atones only for Yisrael for *she'ar aveiros* as well. *Af se'ir ha-mishtaleach eino mechapper al Kohanim bi-she'ar aveiros*.

### Bull Viduy

What then atones for the Kohanim for *she'ar aveiros*? The *viduy* recited over the ox. The *Kohen Gadol* places his hands on the ox and confesses: *chatasi, avisi, pashati, ani u-veiti* — and it is this *viduy* on the ox that carries the atonement for the Kohanim's other sins, just as the *viduy* on the *se'ir ha-mishtaleach* carries that atonement for Yisrael. The ox, therefore, has two distinct atoning functions: its blood atones for *tumat mikdash* for Kohanim, and its *viduy* atones for *she'ar aveiros* for Kohanim.

### Same Result

On this reading, the extra *yekhapper* in the verse is not establishing that they all share the same vehicle of atonement. Rather, *hushvu kullam le-kapparah achat* means only that they all end up atoned — *de-bnai kapparah ninhu* — the outcome is the same. But the process differs: *kol chad ve-chad mechapper mi-denafshei* — each group receives atonement from its own distinct source.

### Yehudah Counter

Rabbi Yehudah responds to Rabbi Shimon's linkage argument: yes, the two goats are linked by the verse — but they are linked only in the sense that *shehayu shavin be-mareh u-ve-komah u-ve-damim*: they must be identical in appearance, equal in height, and purchased at the same price. *Hu de-asa* — that is all the linkage establishes. It does not follow that because one is exclusively for Yisrael, so too must the other be exclusively for Yisrael.

### Own Source

For Rabbi Yehudah, therefore, the *se'ir ha-mishtaleach* atones for *she'ar aveiros* for everyone — Kohen and Yisrael alike. For Rabbi Shimon, even in the domain of *she'ar aveiros*, each group draws atonement from its own separate source: Yisrael from the *se'ir ha-mishtaleach*, and Kohanim from the *viduy* of the ox.

---

---

# Shevuot 14

## Kohanim Atonement

### Intro: Two Views

The discussion at the close of the first chapter of Shevuot centers on a fundamental question: what atones for the *kohanim*? We know that *Yisrael* atones through the *seir*, the goat, but whether the *kohanim* are included in that atonement is the subject of a dispute between two *tanna'im*. Rabbi Yehuda holds that when the *seir* atones for *Yisrael* and the verse says *ba'ad asher la'am* — for the people — this phrase includes everyone, *kohanim* included. Rabbi Shimon, by contrast, holds that the *kohanim* achieve their *kapparah* through a different mechanism entirely.

### Sewage Metaphor

The underlying structure of the entire *kapparah* system on *Yom Kippur* can be visualized as a great purifying operation — all transgression flows toward one central point of cleansing, and if that final stage is not resolved, what flows back into the system remains impure and unusable. The entire enterprise depends on clarity about where each stream of *chata'im* is directed.

### Three Funnels

Concretely, the *par* — the bull — belongs to *Aharon*, and the people have the *seir*. But the precise boundary remains to be determined. Is the *par* exclusively for *Aharon* himself, given that the verse says *vichapper ba'ado* — he shall atone for him? Or does it extend to *Aharon*'s immediate family? And, as the *gemara* will demonstrate, will all the *kohanim* ultimately be folded into *Aharon*'s household?
