Both agree that the *korban* is owed only when *helam tumah* — one forgets one is *tamei*; both agree there is no *korban* for *helam mikdash* alone. *Rabbi Akiva* learns this from the word *v'hu tamei* and its attendant *v'ne'elam*, focusing on the word *tamei*. *Rabbi Eliezer* focuses on the word *sheretz*. But as a matter of *halacha*, they say the same thing.

### Rav Sheshet's Version

The *Gemara* adds: *v'iseima Rav Sheshet mishmosh dorshin ika beinaihu* — this reading is alternatively attributed to *Rav Sheshet*, with the note that *d'Rav Sheshet machlif* — *Rav Sheshet* would sometimes invert the attribution, assigning *Rabbi Eliezer*'s formulation to *Rabbi Akiva* and vice versa. Whether this was deliberate — to signal that they are not really disagreeing — or simply because the distinction was so minor that the attributions were interchangeable, the effect is the same: both *Tannaim* are making the identical halakhic point, differing only in which word of the *pasuk* they derive it from.

---

## Helam Zeh V'Zeh

### Rava's Inquiry

*Rava* poses a question to *Rav Nachman*: according to *Rabbi Akiva* and *Rabbi Eliezer*, the *korban* is owed only for *helam tumah*, not for *helam mikdash*. What happens when both were forgotten — when a person forgot both that he was *tamei* and that the place he entered was *Mikdash*? Is he *chayav* or *patur*?

The question is subtle. On one reading, *Rabbi Akiva* and *Rabbi Eliezer* require only that the person not have known he was *tamei* — they do not require that he be aware of the *Mikdash*. If so, the mere forgetting of *tumah* should suffice to create the *chiyuv*, regardless of whether the *Mikdash* was also forgotten. On another reading, perhaps their ruling is that the specific configuration of not-knowing-*tumah* while knowing-*Mikdash* is what triggers the *korban*, and in the absence of awareness of either element, neither side of the equation is met.

### First Response

The first answer given is the intuitive one — *harei helam tumah b'yado v'chayav*: since the element of forgetting *tumah* is present, and that is all that is required, he is *chayav*.

### Alternative Response

The alternative answer reverses this: *aderaba harei helam Mikdash b'yado v'patur* — since the element of forgetting the *Mikdash* is also present, and forgetting the *Mikdash* is what exempts, he is *patur*.

### Rav Ashi's Analysis

*Rav Ashi* proposes a more sophisticated approach: *chazinan* — let us assess the facts. *Ei mi'tumah ka parish* — if awareness of the *tumah* alone would have caused the person to separate, because it would have triggered his memory that this was a *korban* or a *Mikdash*, then *harei he'elam tumah b'yado v'chayav*: the fundamental forgotten element was the *tumah*, and he is *chayav*. *Im mi'mikdash ka parish* — if becoming aware that this was the *Beit HaMikdash* would have been sufficient to cause him to separate, because that would have triggered his memory that he was *tamei*, then *harei he'elam mikdash b'yado v'patur*: the fundamental forgotten element was the *Mikdash*, and he is *patur*.

The logic is that whichever forgotten element, if restored, would have triggered recall of the other, is the more primary forgotten element and determines the outcome.

### Ravina's Question

*Ravina* objects to *Rav Ashi*'s framework. He points out that this assessment is ultimately circular: *kelum parish mi'tumah ella mishum mikdash* — the only reason a person would separate upon being reminded of his *tumah* is because he would then realize he is about to enter the *Mikdash*. Conversely, *kelum parish mi'mikdash ella mishum tumah* — the only reason being reminded of the *Mikdash* matters is because he would then recall he is *tamei*. The two are so interdependent that asking which would trigger the other does not resolve the question; it simply rephrases it. Both were forgotten, and the analysis goes in circles.

### Rashi's Conclusion

After the exchange of *Rav Ashi* and *Ravina*, *Rashi* draws a conclusion from the *Gemara*'s direction. Looking at the words *ela lo shna* — "it makes no difference" — *Rashi* resolves the question as *patur*. This is a somewhat surprising result; one might have expected that since forgetting *tumah* was present, the *chiyuv* should attach. Nevertheless, *Rashi* concludes that when both were forgotten simultaneously and neither can be identified as the primary, the person is exempt.

---

## Shnei Shvilin

### Both Paths Case

The *Gemara* now introduces a *baraita*: *shnei shvilin echad tamei v'echad tahor* — there are two paths, and it is known that a corpse is buried beneath one of them, though not which. Anyone who walks on the *tamei* path will certainly become *tamei*. A person walks on both paths and then, having forgotten, enters the *Beit HaMikdash*. He is certainly *tamei* — one of the two paths made him so — and he forgot about it before entering. The ruling of the *Tanna Kamma* is: *chayav*. He is *chayav* a *korban*. There was definite *tumah*, and when he enters the *Mikdash* he is unaware of it — this is the classic *helam tumah* scenario.

### Separate Days Case

A more complex case follows: a person walks on the first path and then, while still in a state of doubtful *tumah*, enters the *Beit HaMikdash*. He then undergoes the sprinkling of *parah adumah* ashes and immersion in a *mikvah* — the process for clearing a *safeik tumah* acquired from a *meis* — and is now *tahor* in relation to path A. He then walks on path B, forgets, and enters the *Beit HaMikdash* again. Now, on either the first entry or the second entry, he sinned: on one of those days, he entered the *Mikdash* while *tamei*, albeit while in a state of *safeik tumah* at the time he was aware. In hindsight, the combination of the two episodes establishes that he definitely sinned on one of the two occasions. The *Tanna Kamma* rules: *chayav*.

### Rabbi Shimon Patur

*Rabbi Shimon* exempts in this case. Moreover, *Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda* in the name of *Rabbi Shimon* goes further — exempting even in the first case, where the person walked both paths before entering the *Mikdash*.

### Gemara Questions

The *Gemara* is puzzled by *Rabbi Shimon*'s position in the first case. *V'amai*? *Mimma nafshach, tamei hu* — make up your mind; the person is definitively *tamei*. He walked path A and path B. One of those was certainly the *tamei* path. He then entered the *Mikdash*. Why is he *patur*?

### Rava's Explanation

*Rava* explains the case: *kegon shehalach berishona uveshaah shehalach bashniya shachach shehalach berishona* — the scenario is that the person walked path A and then, at the moment he walked path B, he had already forgotten that he walked path A. So at no point was he ever aware that he was *vaday tamei*. When he was on path A, he knew he was *safeik tamei*. When he moved to path B, he forgot path A and again knew only that he was *safeik tamei* — aware of one doubtful source but not the other. He was therefore, in reality, *vaday tamei*, but he never possessed awareness of being *vaday tamei*. The question is whether this partial and overlapping awareness of *safeik* constitutes sufficient *yedi'ah* to form the basis of a *korban*.

### Miktzas Yedia Debate

This is precisely the disagreement between the *Tanna Kamma* and *Rabbi Shimon*. *Tanna Kamma savar amrinan miktzas yediyah kechol yediyah* — the *Tanna Kamma* holds that partial awareness of one's definite *tumah* is treated as full awareness: since the person was in reality certainly *tamei*, even a partial awareness of that *tumah* suffices to create the *yedi'ah batchilah* required for *chiyuv*. *V'Rabbi Shimon savar lo amrinan miktzas yediyah kechol yediyah* — *Rabbi Shimon* disagrees. Partial awareness of definite *tumah* does not count as full awareness, and without full awareness of his *vaday tumah*, there can be no *chiyuv*.

---

## Safek Yedia Analysis

### Yochanan: Exception Rule

The *Gemara* now addresses the earlier case — *shnei shvilin* with entries on separate days — in which the *Tanna Kamma* says *chayav* even though at no point was the person aware of *vaday tumah*, only of *safeik tumah* on each separate occasion. *Rabbi Yochanan* says: *kan asu safeik yediyah kiyediyah* — here, the law treats doubtful awareness as equivalent to full awareness. He acknowledges that this is an exception, indicated by the phrase *kan asu* — "here they made it so." The underlying rationale he will explain.

### Reish Lakish Reading

*Reish Lakish* reads the same case differently. He says: *ha mani Rabbi Yishmael hi d'amar lo beinan yedia batchila* — this case follows *Rabbi Yishmael*, who holds that one need not have been aware at the outset at all. Since *Rabbi Yishmael* does not require *yedi'ah batchilah*, even a person who was oblivious throughout can be *chayav* once he ultimately becomes aware. For *Rabbi Yishmael*, the absence of initial certain awareness is not a disqualifier, and therefore this case presents no difficulty.

---

## Cheilev and Safek Awaren…

### Safek Cheilev Cases

The *Gemara* now introduces a parallel case involving *cheilev* in order to challenge both *Rabbi Yochanan* and *Reish Lakish* from their readings of another *mishnah*. The case: *achat safek cheilev v'noda* — a person ate a piece of meat that was possibly *cheilev* and became aware of the doubt. *Safek cheilev v'noda* — then he ate another piece of possibly *cheilev* and became aware again. The combination of these two doubtful events raises the question of how many *korbanot* are owed.

### Rabbi's Ruling

*Rabbi* — *Rebbi Yehudah HaNasi* — rules: just as, if both pieces had been definite *cheilev*, he would have brought a separate *chatat* for each piece, so too here, since there are two separate moments of becoming aware of a *safeik issur*, he brings a separate *asham talui* for each episode. Two doubtful sins, two separate *ashmot taluyim*.

### Rabbi Shimon's View

*Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda* and *Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon* in the name of *Rabbi Shimon* rule otherwise: *eino mevi ela asham talui echad* — he brings only a single *asham talui*. They cite the verse *al shigagato asher shagag*: *HaTorah ribeta shegagot harbei v'asham talui echad* — the Torah speaks of many errors, yet only one *asham talui*. The implication is that for all doubtful sins of the same category, however many separate episodes of doubtful eating occurred, only one *asham talui* is brought.

### Reish Lakish Analogy

*Reish Lakish* reads *Rebbi*'s ruling as establishing a principle: *yedi'ot sfekot mitchalakot l'chata'ot* — doubtful awarenesses divide for separate *chata'ot*. His reasoning by analogy is as follows: in the case of definite *cheilev*, if a person ate two pieces in a single state of unawareness and then became aware, he brings one *korban*; if awareness intervened between the two pieces, he brings two. So the awareness — even a doubtful one, *yedi'at safeik* — divides the acts into separate obligations. If this is true for definite *cheilev* where the intermediate awareness is of a *safeik*, then by analogy, where the pieces themselves are *safek cheilev*, a *safeik* awareness divides for separate *ashmot taluyim*. Moreover, *Reish Lakish* suggests a more radical reading of *Rebbi*: even in a case where the *cheilev* is definite but the intervening awareness was only a doubtful one, that doubtful awareness is sufficient to divide it into two separate *chata'ot*. Certainly then, for *safek cheilev* with *safeik* awareness, there are two *ashmot taluyim*.

### Yochanan Disagreement

*Rabbi Yochanan* reads *Rebbi* differently. He says: *keshem she'yidi'at vaday b'alma mitchaleket l'chata'ot* — just as definite awareness divides for separate sin-offerings, *kach yedi'at safeik mitchaleket l'ashamos* — so doubtful awareness divides for separate *ashamos*. This is an analogy, not an equation: definite awareness divides for *chata'ot*, while doubtful awareness divides — not for *chata'ot* — but for separate *ashmot taluyim*. For *Rabbi Yochanan*, a *safeik* awareness is never sufficient to divide for a *chatat*; it can only divide for an *asham talui*.

---

## Safek Yedia Analysis (II)

### Why Exception Applies

This creates a direct contradiction: *Rabbi Yochanan* just stated, in the context of the two-paths case, that *safeik yedi'ah* counts as full *yedi'ah* in *tumat mikdash* — and now he appears to hold that *safeik yedi'ah* does not suffice as a general matter to create the full obligations of a *chatat*. The *Gemara* resolves this by pointing to the exceptional nature of *tumat mikdash*: *hacha hu d'lo kesiv yediyah b'hedya* — here, in *tumat mikdash*, the Torah never explicitly stated that awareness is required. We know of the awareness requirement only from the word *v'ne'elam* — "it was hidden from him" — which implies, by inference, that at some point it was known. Since the requirement of awareness is itself only an inference from *v'ne'elam*, and not an explicit statement like *v'hu yada* or *o hoda eilav*, the standard for what counts as awareness is lower. A doubtful awareness — being aware that one might be *tamei* — suffices.

---

## Reconciling Contradiction

### Exception in Tumat

*Rav Ashi* makes explicit what the *Gemara* has been building toward: *tumat mikdash* is an exception. Elsewhere, a *safeik yedi'ah* does not function as full *yedi'ah*. Here it does.

### Lo Kesiv Yedia B'Hedya

The reason is anchored in the text: *lo kesiv yediyah b'hedya* — awareness is not explicitly written. *Mi'v'ne'elam hu d'ka'asi* — we derive the awareness requirement only from the word *v'ne'elam*, "it was hidden," which implies prior knowledge only by implication. Since the *yedi'ah* requirement is inferred rather than stated, and the inference is correspondingly weaker, the type of awareness required is accordingly more lenient. Doubtful awareness — being aware that one might be *tamei* — suffices to satisfy this inferred requirement.

### Other Korbanot Different

By contrast, in the standard *korban chatat* framework, the Torah writes *o hoda eilav* — "or it became known to him." This is an explicit statement of awareness, not a mere inference. Accordingly: *yediyah ma'alyasa be'inan* — a full, genuine awareness is required. A *safeik* awareness does not qualify.

### Inference Logic

The weaker textual basis for the awareness requirement in *tumat mikdash* yields a weaker standard for what that awareness must be. Since we are only inferring the requirement from *v'ne'elam*, we do not read into it the full rigor of explicit awareness language.

### Reish Lakish Alternative

*Reish Lakish* maintains his alternative reading: rather than explaining the case of the two paths as an exception where *safeik yedi'ah* functions as full *yedi'ah*, he attributes that ruling to *Rabbi Yishmael*, who requires no initial awareness at all.

### Emphasizing Yishmael

The *Gemara* asks: why not simply read the case according to *Rebbi*'s opinion, since *Rebbi* also holds that *safeik yedi'ah* can be significant? *Reish Lakish* answers: *ka mashma lan d'Rabbi Yishmael lo ba'ei yediyah batchilah* — he wanted to make the affirmative point that *Rabbi Yishmael* requires no initial awareness whatsoever. This is never stated explicitly by *Rabbi Yishmael*; it is inferred from the fact that *Rabbi Yishmael* uses both instances of the word *v'ne'elam* in the *pasuk* to establish *helam tumah* and *helam mikdash* as the two operative categories, and therefore has no extra *v'ne'elam* from which to derive a requirement of *yedi'ah batchilah*. The *Gemara* notes that one might have said: even without a *pasuk*, *Rabbi Yishmael* could hold the requirement as a matter of tradition — *mi'gemara it lei*. *Reish Lakish*'s attribution makes the point that *Rabbi Yishmael* truly has no such requirement, neither from a *pasuk* nor from tradition.

With that, the *Gemara* concludes the first *perek* — *hadran alach yediyot ha'tumah* — and we leave the world of *tumat mikdash* after an extensive twenty *dapim* that occupied nearly half the *masechta* before the main subject properly begins.

---

## Shebuot Introduction

### Main Topic Begins

We now turn at last to the third *perek*, which brings us to the central topic of the *masechta*: *shevu'ot* — oaths. It is worth pausing to note how striking it is that approximately forty percent of *Shevuot* concerned *tumat mikdash v'kodshav* rather than oaths themselves. One possible connection is that a *shevuah*, unlike a *neder*, involves directly invoking God's name — the classic *shevuah* is *beshem Hashem*. Even when the name is not explicitly stated, it may be inferred. In that sense, a *shevuah* brings a divine presence down as witness and guarantor of one's claim, much as the *Mikdash* was the one place where the divine presence was, so to speak, geographically present on earth. But that connection remains loose. Why *Rebbi*, who authored the *Mishnah*, chose to place the laws of *tumat mikdash* here rather than in *Seder Taharot* or *Kodshim* remains genuinely unclear.

### Shebuot Structure

The *mishnah* opens with the familiar structure: *shavuot shtayim shehen arba* — there are two categories of oaths that expand to four.

### Torah's Emphasis

The Torah addresses the case of *ki tishava levatei bisfasayim lehara o lehaitiv* — swearing an utterance with one's lips to do bad or to do good. This indicates a future-oriented oath, a commitment about what one will or will not do. The *lehara o lehaitiv* formulation, as will be elaborated, corresponds broadly to active versus passive commitments.

### Four Oath Types

The two cases mentioned in the Torah become four: *shevuah she-ochal v'she-lo ochal* — swearing that one will eat or that one will not eat (future-oriented oaths), and *she-achalti v'she-lo achalti* — claiming that one did eat or did not eat (past-oriented claims). When a person swears falsely or forgetfully about past claims, that too generates a *korban* obligation under the extended framework. These four are the foundational structure of the *perek*.

---

## Rabbi Akiva: Kol Shehu

### Oath Violation Standard

The *mishnah* presents the following case: *shevuah shelo ochal v'achal kol shehu chayav* — if one swears not to eat something and then eats even the smallest amount, one is *chayav* a *korban*. This is not the standard *kezayit* minimum that governs most food-related prohibitions. The position cited is that of *Rabbi Akiva*.

### Rabbi Akiva's Logic

*Rabbi Akiva*'s colleagues challenge him: *heichan matzinu b'ochel kol shehu shechayav* — we have never found that eating a minimal amount generates a *chiyuv*. What is the basis for this? *Rabbi Akiva* answers: *v'chi heichan matzinu b'medaber u'meivi korban* — when have we ever found that a speech act obligates a *korban*? An oath is unique in that one brings a *korban* for violating something one said. Since this is a fundamentally different category of obligation — one generated by speech rather than by a physical act — the measure of violation is determined differently.

### Rashi's Analysis

*Rashi* explains the underlying logic: *bishvil bitul diburo* — the *korban* is brought because of *bitul diburo*, the negation of one's word. The obligation is rooted not in the physical act of eating but in the invalidation of the commitment one made. Since the whole framework is about fidelity to speech, the relevant question is what one's speech meant.

### Intent vs. Fixed Amount

This distinction is fundamental. For a prohibition like *neveilah*, the Torah defines the relevant act in terms of a *kezayit* — a fixed physical quantity, because the prohibition is about the physical act of consumption. An oath, however, is created by the person through his own words, and what constitutes a violation of that oath depends on what he intended when he spoke. If a person swore not to eat something, and then ate even a tiny amount, he has violated the spirit and the letter of his commitment — no one would say his oath permitted eating a small quantity. The amount is therefore determined not by a fixed *Torah* standard but by the scope of the oath as he formulated it. *V'keivan d'mishum bitul diburo hu, af ze bitul diburo she-amar lo ochal v'daato le'esor atzmo b'chol shehu* — since it is about negating one's word, and the intent of "I will not eat" encompasses even the smallest amount, a *kol shehu* suffices to constitute the violation.

This principle — that the measure of an oath violation is tied to the intent and scope of the oath rather than to fixed physical quantities — will be explored further as the *Gemara* on this *mishnah* unfolds.

---

---

# Shevuot 20

## Two Oaths That Are Four

### Opening

We begin Daf 20 by moving from the extended discussion of *tum'ah* and entry into the *Beit HaMikdash* into the subject that stands at the heart of our *masechta*: *shevuot*, oaths. The immediate focus is the question of when one incurs liability to bring a *korban* — specifically the *korban oleh v'yored* — upon violating an oath. In time the tractate will address oaths in a judicial context, the reason this material appears in *Seder Nezikin*, but we begin here with the foundational structure.

### Mishna Structure

The *Mishna* opens with the familiar formula: *shevuot shtayim she-hein arba* — two oaths that are four. The basis is the verse, *nefesh ki tishava levate bisfatayim lehara o le-heitiv* — a person who swears an utterance with his lips to do harm or to do good (Vayikra 5:4). "Doing harm" is understood to refer to swearing one will *not* eat something; "doing good" refers to swearing that one *will* eat. These are the first two. The "four" includes two further cases involving the past: swearing that one did eat something, or that one did not. Violating any of these — whether the underlying act was performed wittingly or unwittingly — generates liability for a *korban*.

### Rabbi Akiva

The *Mishna* then records the view of Rabbi Akiva: *shevuah shelo ochal ve-achal kol shehu chayav* — if one swears not to eat and eats even the smallest amount, he is liable. The Sages challenge him: *heichan matzinu be-ochel be-kol shehu she-hu chayav*? Where do we ever find that eating the smallest amount incurs liability? Ordinarily, whether for a *korban* or for *malkot*, the minimum threshold is a *kezayit*. Rabbi Akiva replies: *u-khe-heichan matzinu be-medaber mevi korban*? Where do we ever find that someone brings a *korban* merely for a speech act? And yet here, in the case of oaths, that is precisely the rule. If one swore to eat something and then did not eat — a purely passive failure — the liability stems entirely from the words spoken. Or in the case of a false oath about the past, again there is no action at all; the *korban* is incurred solely on account of the speech. The lesson, says Rabbi Akiva, is that when it comes to *shevuot*, the operative category is *medaber* — the utterance itself.

### Rashi's Explanation

Rashi explains the connection between Rabbi Akiva's two points as follows. Since the liability of an oath is rooted entirely in one's words, we interpret the scope of those words by what a person actually meant when speaking. Unlike a Torah prohibition, where the minimum quantity is fixed externally — a *kezayit*, for example, is defined by the Torah — an oath has no externally determined threshold. The person himself sets the terms through his language. Therefore, when someone says "I will not eat," without specifying an amount, we assume he meant even the smallest quantity. The prohibition is not a category of forbidden food with a fixed *shiur*; it is a violation of one's own verbal commitment, and that commitment is interpreted according to its natural scope.

---

## Context in Oaths

### Linguistic Ambiguity

The *Gemara* opens with an inference from the *Mishna*. If the *Mishna* speaks of a *shevuah she-ochel* — an oath that one will eat — this implies that the word *ochel* straightforwardly means "I will eat." But the *Gemara* immediately challenges this from a *Baraita*: the phrase *shevuah she-ochal lach* — an oath that I will eat of yours — is treated in that source as if it means the opposite, namely that one is binding oneself not to eat. How can the same words bear such different meanings?

### Abaye: Context Matters

Abaye resolves the tension: *le'olam de-achilna lach* — yes, *ochal* ordinarily means "I will eat." But the apparent contradiction is not a contradiction at all, because *lo kashya* — there is a distinction. *Kan de-misarvin bo le-echol* — in the case where others are pressuring the person to eat; *kan de-ein misarvin bo le-echol* — and in the case where no such pressure exists. When someone is being urged to eat and keeps refusing — "come on, just a little" — and finally says *shevuah she-ochal lach*, the context makes clear that what he means is: I am bound by oath against eating anything of yours. He is pushing back against the pressure, not affirming his intention to eat. In that setting, *she-ochal* functions as *she-lo ochal*.

### Pressure Scenarios

The *Mishna*, Abaye continues, is dealing with *she-ein misarvin bo le-echol* — the case where no one is pressuring him, so the straightforward meaning applies: it is an oath that he will eat. The *Baraita*, by contrast, is addressing *misarvin bo le-echol*, where the pressure context inverts the sense of the words. Abaye captures this dynamic succinctly: the one who keeps saying "no, no" and is pressed repeatedly — *de-ka'amar lo achilna ve-lo achilna* — when he finally says *shevuah she-ochal*, everyone understands he means *shelo ochal*. Language does not operate in a vacuum.

### Rav Ashi

Rav Ashi offers an alternative reading of the same *Baraita*. *Tani shevuah she-ee ochal lach* — the text of the *Baraita* should actually be read as *she-ee ochal*, meaning "that I will not eat," not *she-ochal*. In his view, *she-ochal* is a phonetic contraction of *she-ee ochal*, the word *she-ee* being an abbreviated form of negation — a linguistic phenomenon found, for example, in Palestinian Hebrew, where a prefixed *lamed* sometimes contracts the word *lo*. The *Gemara* pushes back: if the *Baraita* explicitly says he won't eat, where is the novelty? Rav Ashi answers: one might have thought the person slipped and said *she-ee ochal* when he meant *she-ochal*. The *Baraita* therefore establishes that if one says *she-ee ochal*, we take him at his word.

The question of whether Rav Ashi is substantively disagreeing with Abaye on whether context determines meaning is worth noting. It seems most likely that Rav Ashi is simply offering an alternative textual reading of the *Baraita* — since the *Baraita* does not supply the context of pressure, it is not fair to assume it — rather than disputing the *halakhic* relevance of context as a matter of principle. And indeed, throughout *Nedarim* and *Shevuot*, the principle of *piv v'libo shavin* — that what matters is not merely the formal words but the underlying intent — makes clear that context is genuinely operative.

---

## Technical Terms

### Mivta Definition

The *Gemara* now moves to a *Baraita* that examines what linguistic formulations constitute a binding *shevuah*. The starting point is the term *mivta*. The verse states: *ki nefesh ki tishava l'vatei bisfatayim* — when a person swears, *l'vatei*, to enunciate with his lips. The root *bet-tet-alef* gives rise to the technical term *mivta* — "enunciation." When someone says *mivta* I will eat such-and-such, or *mivta* I will not eat such-and-such, the word *mivta* functions as a technical term with the force of the word *shevuah* itself. This is confirmed by an additional verse: *u-ndareha aleha o mifta sfateha asher asra al nafshah* — where the word *mifta* appears entirely on its own, without the word *shevuah*, yet clearly refers to an oath. So *mivta* is a standalone technical term for a *shevuah*.

### Issur as Technical Term

The *Baraita* then introduces a second term: *issar*. This too is derived from a verse: *le'esor issar al nafsho* — to make something forbidden upon himself (Bamidbar 30:3), and *kol neder v'chol shevuat issar* (ibid. 30:14). However, the *Baraita*'s treatment of *issar* is more ambiguous than its treatment of *mivta*, and this ambiguity drives the major dispute of the *sugya*.

### Mifas Concept

Central to understanding this section is the concept of *mifas*, or *hatfasa* — "grabbing" or "association." In the context of *nedarim*, *hatfasa* works as follows: if object A is already forbidden to me by a *neder*, and I say "this object B is like that object A," I have transferred the forbidden status of A onto B. This is called *matfis b'neder* and is uncontroversial; it is the classic mechanism of a *neder* throughout *Masechet Nedarim*. The term *davar hanadur* — a vowed object — is operative here: my power to change the status of an object through speech derives from associating it with something already rendered forbidden through speech.

The conceptual distinction between *nedarim* and *shevuot* is critical. A *neder* operates on an *object* — it changes the status of a thing, analogous to the way one can consecrate something to the *Beit HaMikdash*. A *shevuah*, by contrast, operates on a *person* and an *action* — it is a call upon God to witness one's commitment or the truth of one's statement. The two categories are therefore structurally distinct: the association-logic of *hatfasa* fits naturally into the world of *nedarim*, where status is the currency, but it is not self-evident that the same mechanism applies to *shevuot*.

### Baraita Framework

Having laid this groundwork, the *Baraita* presents the case of *issar* and the question of whether *matfis b'shevuah* — doing a *hatfasa* onto a *shevuah* — has the force of actually uttering a *shevuah*. The *Baraita*'s language at this point generates a dispute between Abaye and Rava, both as to how the *Baraita* should be read and as to the underlying *halakhic* question it addresses. Tosafot's reading of this passage differs from Rashi's, and the analysis below follows Tosafot.

---

## Abaye vs. Rava

### Abaye Position

Abaye reads the *Baraita* as follows. The word *mivta* is a *shevuah* — a standalone technical term. The word *issar* in the Torah, by contrast, does not function as a standalone technical term at all. Rather, it describes a scenario of *matfis b'shevuah* — of associating something with a pre-existing *shevuah*. And the pivotal question the *Baraita* then raises is: when someone does a *hatfasa* onto a *shevuah*, is that *kemotzi shevuah mipiv dami* — equivalent to having actually uttered a *shevuah* — or not? If it is equivalent, one is liable; if not, one is exempt.

### Tosafot Explanation

Tosafot's reading is that the technical word *issar* itself is not at issue in this section of the *Baraita*. Rather, the *Baraita* is describing a scenario — when the Torah uses the language *le'esor issar al nafsho*, it is characterizing a case of *hatfasa*, of piggybacking onto a pre-existing *shevuah*. The question the *Baraita* then raises concerns what language is required to make that *hatfasa* operative. Does it suffice to say "this is like that," or must one include the action-language of "I will not eat" in order for the statement to carry the weight of a *shevuah*?

### Apple Illustration

To make this concrete, consider the following scenario. A person takes a *shevuah* — using the word *shevuah* or *mivta* — that he will not eat a particular apple (apple number one). He then wants to extend that commitment to a second apple. If he says "I will not eat apple number two, just as I will not eat apple number one," he has used the action-language of a *shevuah* — "I will not eat" — and linked apple two to apple one. This, according to Abaye, is *matfis b'shevuah* in a manner *kemotzi shevuah mipiv dami*, and he would be liable if he eats apple two.

If, however, he says only "apple two is like apple one" — focusing on the objects without the action-language of "I will not eat" — that statement is in the idiom of *neder*, not *shevuah*, and would not bind him as a *shevuah*.

A still more elegant reading of Tosafot produces the following refinement. *Issar* in the Torah describes the case where someone links apple two to apple one — that much is the classic case, and one is certainly liable. But then the *Baraita* moves to a further case: *issar issar* — what if the person says "I will not eat apple three just as I will not eat apple two"? This is a *hatfasa* of a *hatfasa*, two degrees removed from the original *shevuah*. Are you liable?

The answer depends on how one understands the liability in the first case. If you are liable in the first case because the *hatfasa* is *kemotzi shevuah mipiv dami* — as if you yourself uttered a *shevuah* about apple two — then apple three would equally be as if you uttered a *shevuah* about it, and you would be liable. But if you are liable in the first case not because it is equivalent to uttering a *shevuah*, but merely because the statement is *connected* to a *shevuah*, then apple three is connected only to something connected to a *shevuah* — two degrees removed — and you would be exempt.

This raises a beautiful conceptual question. What exactly is the nature of a *hatfasa*? Does saying "I won't eat apple two like apple one" function as a technical utterance — so that the act of linking is itself *kemotzi shevuah mipiv dami*, the equivalent of having said the word *shevuah*? Or does it merely create a derivative association — linked but not equivalent? The same question arises in a different key with the *Rambam*'s ruling that one who answers *Amen* to another's *brachah* is *kemotzi brachah mipiv dami*: is "Amen" itself the equivalent of having said the *brachah*, or is it merely a form of association through *shome'ah k'oneh*?

For Abaye, the word *issar* in the Torah points to *hatfasa* as the operative mechanism, and *hatfasa b'shevuah* — done with the action-language of "I will not eat" — is *kemotzi shevuah mipiv dami*. Liability follows.

### Rava Position

Rava disagrees fundamentally. *Matfis b'shevuah lav kemotzi shevuah mipiv dami* — performing a *hatfasa* onto a *shevuah* does not have the force of uttering a *shevuah*. For Rava, *hatfasa* is a mechanism that belongs to the world of *nedarim*, not *shevuot*. A *shevuah* requires the technical language of a *shevuah* — either the word *shevuah* itself, the word *mivta*, or, Rava adds, the word *issar* — which he regards not as a description of a *hatfasa* but as a genuine third technical term.

On Rava's reading, the *Baraita* is not saying that the word *issar* describes a *hatfasa*. Rather, *issar* is a technical term in its own right — like *mivta* — but with an inherent ambiguity: *hetilo hakatuv bein neder l'shevuah* — the Torah has placed it between a *neder* and a *shevuah*, with the word *neder* appearing two words before it and *shevuah* appearing two words after it in the verse. The result is that *issar* can function as either a *neder* or a *shevuah* depending on how it is used. If one says "*issar* this apple is forbidden to me" — focusing on the status of the object — it is a *neder*. If one says "*issar* I will not eat this apple" — focusing on one's action — it is a *shevuah*. The word is context-sensitive, but in both cases it is a proper technical term, not a description of *hatfasa*.

This position is encapsulated in the formula: *hotzio b'lashon neder neder, b'lashon shevuah shevuah* — if expressed in the language of a *neder*, it is a *neder*; if expressed in the language of a *shevuah*, it is a *shevuah*.

---

## Issur in Nedarim

### Baraita on Issur

The *Gemara* now turns to a *Baraita* that directly addresses the question of *issar*: *eizehu issar ha'amur b'Torah* — what is the *issar* spoken of in the Torah? The *Baraita*'s answer describes a case of *hatfasa*, which, on the surface, would seem to constitute a direct proof for Abaye's position.

### Wine and Meat Case

The *Baraita* presents the following scenario. Someone has already committed, by *neder*, not to eat meat or drink wine on the anniversary of his father's death, or on the anniversary of some other significant event, or on *Tzom Gedaliah* — the fast of Gedaliah ben Achikam. Now, on a different day, he says: meat and wine are forbidden to me today *just as* they are forbidden on that day. This is a paradigmatic *hatfasa b'neder*: the object (meat, wine) is forbidden on the reference day by virtue of a *neder*, and the speaker is associating the current day's prohibition with that pre-existing vowed status. Shmuel adds the qualification: *vehu she-nadar bo me'oto hayom* — this works only if he had indeed taken a *neder* on the reference day from that day onward. The association must connect to a genuine *davar hanadur*, a pre-existing vowed object.

### Rava's Reinterpretation

This *Baraita* poses a difficulty for Rava. If the *Baraita* introduces itself with *eizehu issar ha'amur b'Torah* — asking what the *issar* of the Torah is — and then describes a case of *hatfasa*, it seems to confirm Abaye's reading that *issar* refers to *hatfasa*, not to a standalone technical term.

Rava's response is to reread the *Baraita*. The *Baraita* should be understood as asking not *eizehu issar ha'amur b'Torah* but rather *eizehu issar neder ha'amur b'Torah* — what is the classic case of a forbidden *neder* spoken of in the Torah? On this reading, the word *issar* is not being defined as *hatfasa*; the *Baraita* is simply illustrating what a classic *neder* looks like. And the answer is: a *neder* classically takes the form of *hatfasa* — associating a new object or occasion with something already forbidden as a *davar hanadur*.

For Rava, then, the *Baraita* is not a proof about the technical term *issar* at all. It is a description of classic *neder* formation, and it is entirely consistent with his view that the technical term *issar* is distinct from *hatfasa* and functions as a proper term for either a *neder* or a *shevuah* depending on context.

---

## Abaye vs. Rava (II)

### Neder vs. Shevu'a

The deeper conceptual ground of Rava's position comes into focus here. The reason *hatfasa* is the natural and indeed essential mechanism of a *neder* is that a *neder* derives its force from the speaker's power to change the status of objects through speech — a power that is itself derived from the world of *korbanot* and *hekdesh*. When I say *konam this apple upon me*, I am associating this apple with the category of things sanctified to the *Beit HaMikdash*. My speech operates on the object. The verse *ad she-yidor b'davar hanadur* — which requires that a *neder* connect to something already vowed — reflects precisely this structure: the speech-power to change the status of objects flows from the established category of objects that are already vowed.

A *shevuah*, by contrast, operates not on objects but on persons and actions. It is a calling upon God to witness — either the truth of a factual claim or one's commitment to a future course of action. In this domain, saying "A is like B" — associating one object with another — does not engage the logic of a *shevuah* at all. A *shevuah* requires that I place myself and my actions before God. Therefore Rava holds that *hatfasa b'shevuah* is simply not *kemotzi shevuah mipiv dami* — it does not have the force of actually taking an oath.

Abaye and Rava thus represent two fundamentally different views of whether the mechanism of association, which is intrinsic to *nedarim*, can be transposed into the domain of *shevuot*.

---

## Issur in Nedarim (II)

### Davar Hanadur

The principle that a *neder* must connect to a *davar hanadur* — something already forbidden through a *neder* — is not merely a rule for *hatfasa* situations; it reflects the constitutive logic of *nedarim* as a whole. Even when one says simply *konam this apple upon me*, one is implicitly associating the apple with the general category of *korban* — of things rendered forbidden through a speech-act of sanctification. The *davar hanadur* requirement means that the power of one's speech to prohibit derives always from association with an already-established vowed category. This is why *hatfasa b'neder* — saying B is like A, where A is already a *davar hanadur* — is a paradigmatic *neder*: it makes explicit what is implicit in every *neder*.

### Tzom Gedaliah

The *Baraita*'s inclusion of *Tzom Gedaliah* as a reference-day introduces a non-obvious dimension. On first consideration, one might think that *Tzom Gedaliah* cannot serve as a *davar hanadur*: the prohibition against eating on *Tzom Gedaliah* is rabbinic in origin, not the product of a personal *neder*. If I say "this meat is forbidden to me today like it is on *Tzom Gedaliah*," am I connecting to something forbidden by a *neder*, or merely to a rabbinic fast — which is not a *davar hanadur* at all?

The *Gemara* addresses this directly. *Salka datach amina*: one might have thought that since the food would be forbidden on *Tzom Gedaliah* even without any personal *neder*, any personal *neder* one adds on top of the rabbinic prohibition never truly takes effect as a distinct layer of *neder*-prohibition. If the *neder* layer never took hold, then when one says "today is like *Tzom Gedaliah*," one is connecting not to a *davar hanadur* but merely to a *taanis* — and *hatfasa* onto a *taanis* would not be a *neder*.

The *Gemara* therefore teaches: *kamashma lan* — the *Baraita* comes to tell us that one *can* add a *neder*-layer on top of a rabbinic fast, and that layer is effective as a *davar hanadur*. The reason this is possible is that the principle of *ein issur chal al issur* — one prohibition cannot take effect on top of another — does not apply here, because the existing rabbinic prohibition and the new Torah-level *neder* are prohibitions of different types. The rabbinic *taanis* does not block the personal *neder* from taking effect as a distinct and additional layer. Once that *neder*-layer is in place, *Tzom Gedaliah* does become a genuine *davar hanadur*, and subsequent *hatfasa* onto it is valid.

---

## Rabbi Yochanan

### Yochanan's View

The *Gemara* closes this section by noting that Rabbi Yochanan takes the position of Rava. When Ravin came from Eretz Yisrael, he transmitted: Rabbi Yochanan taught that whether one says *mivta lo ochal lach* or *issar lo ochal lach*, either formulation constitutes a *shevuah*. Both *mivta* and *issar* are technical terms that independently create a binding oath. Rabbi Yochanan thus aligns with Rava's view that *issar* is a standalone technical term — not a description of *hatfasa* — and that both terms function equivalently as formal expressions of a *shevuah*.

---

---

# Shevuot 21

## Oath Classifications

### Nedarim vs Shvuot

The sugya of Daf 21 opens against the backdrop of a fundamental conceptual distinction that pervades the entire masechta: the difference between a *neder* and a *shvuah*. A *neder* changes the status of an object — the prohibition created by vow inheres in the thing itself, not in the person. The *shvuah*, by contrast, relates to the person; it is a declaration about what one will or will not do. Given this distinction, the governing prohibition for a *neder* is *lo yachel devaro* — one may not allow the words to be negated by acting in a manner that disregards the status one has created in the object. But when it comes to a *shvuah*, the relevant prohibition depends on which type of oath is at issue, and that question is precisely what the Gemara is working through.

### Past vs Future Oaths

The question the Gemara has been navigating is what prohibition one transgresses when taking a false *shvuah*. There are two classic categories. First, one may take a false oath about events in the past — the paradigmatic case being *achalti velo achalti*, swearing that one ate when one did not, or that one did not eat when one did. Second, one may take an oath to do something in the future and then fail to fulfill it.

### First Opinion

The first opinion in the Gemara holds that a past-oriented false oath constitutes a *shvuat shav* — an oath in vain — on the grounds that such words have no operative impact; one has lied, but the *shvuah* did not bind one to any future course of action, rendering it essentially purposeless. A future-oriented oath that one fails to keep, according to this view, transgresses *lo tishavu bishmi lashaker* — the prohibition against taking a false oath in God's name — because one initially made a binding commitment and subsequently falsified it.

### Second Opinion

The second opinion, which the Gemara now takes up, is arguably more intuitive. According to this view, using an oath to lie about the past is a *shvuat sheker* — a false oath — because one is straightforwardly lying under oath. A future-oriented oath that one violates, however, is governed by *lo yachel devaro*, precisely as a *neder* is. The logic is that a future oath creates an obligation, and when one disregards that obligation, one has negated the binding force of one's words — the same conceptual structure that underlies *lo yachel devaro* for vows.

### Rambam's View

It is worth noting that both of these positions are contested by the Rambam, who takes the simpler and perhaps most straightforward approach: whether the false oath concerns the past or the future, it is classified as a *shvuat sheker*. If one lies about the past under oath, that is *sheker*; if one swears to do something in the future and fails to keep it, one has retroactively made one's oath false, which is equally *sheker*. This, however, is not the view being developed in the sugya at this point.

---

## Source Derivation

### Rav Pappa's Analysis

*Amar Rav Pappa*: the attribution of the second opinion — that past oaths are *shvuat sheker* and future oaths fall under *lo yachel devaro* — to Rabbi Abahu in the name of Rabbi Yochanan was not an explicit statement, but an inference (*mikhlala itmar*). The tradition was transmitted through a chain: Rabbi Idi bar Avin said in the name of Rav Amram, who said in the name of Rav Yitzchak, who said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan — and Rabbi Yochanan cited Rabbi Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Yose HaGlili.

### Lavin Without Action

That tradition reads: any prohibition (*lo ta'aseh*) in the Torah that involves an action (*lav sheyesh bo ma'aseh*) incurs lashes; one that involves no action (*lav she'ein bo ma'aseh*) does not incur lashes. The exceptions are taking an oath (*nishba*), performing *temurah* — attempting to transfer the sanctified status of one *korban* onto another animal — and cursing another person in God's name. All three of these exceptions are speech acts, which ordinarily would not be classified as "actions" for the purpose of the rule. Yet the Torah prescribes lashes for them. The rule thus stands: speech acts generally do not generate lashes, but these three are uniquely treated as actionable.

### Lashav Derivation

The Gemara now asks: where is the source for lashes in the case of a *shvuat shav*? Rabbi Yochanan, in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, derives it from the verse *lo tisa shem Hashem Elokecha lashav, ki lo yenakeh Hashem* — do not take God's name in vain, for God will not cleanse the one who does so. The *derashah* runs as follows: the heavenly court (*beit din shel ma'alah*) will not cleanse such a person, but the earthly court (*beit din shel matah*) will administer lashes — and through those lashes, cleansing is achieved. This is a striking inversion of what one might initially understand: lashes here function not merely as punishment but as a vehicle for atonement. The verse's declaration that God will not forgive is read not as an absolute negation of all forgiveness, but as a limitation on *divine* clemency — leaving open the path of human-administered punishment as the mechanism of cleansing.

### Pappa-Abaye Debate

Rav Pappa challenges this reading: perhaps the verse means precisely what it says — *lo yenakeh klal*, that there is absolutely no forgiveness for one who takes God's name in vain? Abaye responds: if the verse had simply said *ki lo yenakeh*, that would support Rav Pappa's reading. But the verse specifically reads *ki lo yenakeh Hashem* — *God* will not cleanse. The emphasis on God as the one who withholds cleansing implies that *He* specifically will not do so, but the earthly court may administer lashes and thereby achieve cleansing. This is the textual basis for the rule that a *shvuat shav* incurs lashes (*malkot*).

### Double Lashav Extension

Having established the source for lashes regarding *shvuat shav*, the Gemara asks: what is the source for lashes regarding *shvuat sheker* — a *false* oath? Rabbi Yochanan, speaking in his own name this time, answers: the word *lashav* appears twice in the passage. The verse says *lo tisa shem Hashem Elokecha lashav*, and then the verse concludes *ki lo yenakeh Hashem et asher yisa et shemo lashav*. Why the repetition? One mention of *lashav* suffices to address *shvuat shav*; the second is therefore redirected (*taneihu inyan*) to teach that lashes are also incurred for *shvuat sheker*. The doubled *lashav* functions as an extension from the known case — an oath in vain — to the adjacent case of a false oath.

---

## Which Oath Gets Lashes

### Abahu's Question

Following this derivation, Rabbi Abahu poses a sharp analytic question: the verse teaches that *shvuat sheker* incurs lashes — but which case of *shvuat sheker* are we actually talking about? The point of the derivation was to demonstrate that even a *lav she'ein bo ma'aseh*, a prohibition transgressed without an action, can incur lashes. So what case fits that description?

### Future Active Eliminated

The first candidate — swearing that one will not eat and then actively eating — is immediately eliminated. If one swore not to eat and proceeded to eat, this is a *lav sheyesh bo ma'aseh*, a prohibition transgressed through a physical act. This case needs no special derivation; it follows the standard rule. The verse's teaching would be superfluous if directed at this case.

### Future Passive Eliminated

The second candidate — swearing that one *will* eat and then passively failing to do so — would qualify as a *lav she'ein bo ma'aseh*, since the violation consists of simply not eating. But does one actually incur lashes in this case? The Gemara notes that this very question was addressed explicitly.

### Eating Case Analysis

The case is stated: if one swears to eat a particular loaf of bread that day (*shvua ochel kikar zu hayom*), and the day passes without one having eaten it (*ve'avar hayom velo achlah*), Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish both rule that one does not incur lashes — though they disagree about the reason.

### Yochanan's Rationale

Rabbi Yochanan holds that one is exempt because this is a *lav she'ein bo ma'aseh* — a prohibition violated without action — and the general rule is that such a prohibition does not incur lashes (*kol lav she'ein bo ma'aseh ein lokin alav*).

### Resh Lakish's Rationale

Resh Lakish offers a different reason: *hatra'at safek*, a doubtful warning. For lashes to be administered, there must be a valid *hatra'ah* — a warning delivered immediately before the transgression. In this case, if one warns the person at the end of the day not to violate the oath, one cannot know at that moment whether the person will ultimately eat or not. Since the transgression will only be realized when the day ends without eating, any warning delivered beforehand is inherently uncertain as to whether it will prove to have been necessary. Rashi emphasizes that a *hatra'ah* must be delivered immediately before the transgression, and in this case the moment of warning is never one of certainty. A *hatra'at safek* — a doubtful warning — is not a valid *hatra'ah*.

### Past Oath Conclusion

With future-oriented violations thus excluded — whether the violation is active (covered by the standard rule) or passive (exempt from lashes in any case) — Rabbi Abahu concludes that the only case of *shvuat sheker* for which the verse needs to teach that lashes are incurred is the past-oriented case: *achalti velo achalti*. One swears about what one has or has not done, and swears falsely. That is the case. The violation is immediate, it is accomplished through speech, and it is precisely for this case that the derivation from the doubled *lashav* is necessary.

---

## Rava's Explanation

### Torah's Doubling

Having concluded that lashes for *shvuat sheker* apply specifically to the past-oriented case, the Gemara asks what distinguishes this case conceptually from a future-oriented false oath. *Amar Rava*: the Torah deliberately doubled the word *lashav* to signal that the *shvuat sheker* which incurs lashes is the one that resembles a *shvuat shav* — an oath in vain. *Mah shav l'she'avar, af sheker nami l'she'avar* — just as *shvuat shav* pertains to the present or past (something obviously true, obviously false, or entirely purposeless), so too the *shvuat sheker* that incurs lashes pertains to the past.

### Conceptual Parallel

The deeper conceptual point is this: both *shvuat shav* and a past-oriented *shvuat sheker* share the same structural feature — the transgression is constituted by the speech act itself. When one swears by something patently true or patently false, or swears that one ate when one did not, the very act of uttering the oath is the violation. One is using God's name either purposelessly or to deceive in that very moment. The oath itself — the words spoken — *is* the sin.

### Immediate Violation

This stands in sharp contrast to a future-oriented oath. When one swears to do something and then fails to do it, the moment of oath-taking is not itself the transgression. Part of the structure of the violation depends on what happens afterward: whether one keeps or does not keep what one said. Even according to the Rambam, who classifies this as *shvuat sheker*, the falsification occurs when one fails to fulfill the oath — which means the violation is not fully realized at the moment of speech. It is, in a sense, a two-stage transgression: the oath creates an obligation, and the future failure to uphold it turns the oath into a lie. The conceptual question — whether the violation is in the original speech act or in the subsequent non-compliance — is precisely what determines whether lashes apply and in what circumstances. For a past-oriented oath, the lie is instantaneous and complete at the moment of speaking. That is why it earns *malkot* even without any subsequent physical act.

---

## Mishna Shvuat Bituy

### Multiple Oaths Rule

The Gemara now raises a challenge to Rabbi Abahu's conclusion from a *mishnah*. The *mishnah*'s case involves someone who takes a series of oaths not to eat a particular loaf: *shvuah shelo ochal kikar zu*, then again *shvuah shelo ochlena*, then again. He then eats it. The ruling is *eino chayav ela achas* — he is liable for only one, because *ein shvuah chala al shvuah* — one oath cannot take effect upon a pre-existing oath. Since he was already bound by the first oath, the second and third add nothing.

### Shvuat Bituy Definition

The *mishnah* then identifies this as the case of *shvuat bituy* — an oath of enunciation, future-oriented — and declares: *zo hi shvuat bituy shechayavin al zedonah malkot ve'al shegagasah korban* — this is the oath of enunciation for which one incurs lashes if one willfully violates it and brings a *korban olah veyored* if one violates it unintentionally. The *korban olah veyored* is a sliding-scale offering — the specific type prescribed for inadvertent violation of *shvuat bituy*. The phrasing *zo hi* — "this is" — appears to be exclusive: this is the case, implying that other cases are not included.

One might ask: why does the *mishnah* need to specify *zo hi* if the case is obvious? The exclusionary force of the phrase is the point. What is it excluding? The most natural candidate is the past-oriented case, *achalti velo achalti*. If the *mishnah* says "this" future-oriented oath is where one incurs lashes and brings a *korban*, one might infer that a past-oriented false oath does not.

### Shvuat Shav Contrast

The *mishnah* then turns to *shvuat shav* and similarly uses the phrase *zo hi* — "this is the *shvuat shav* for which one incurs lashes for willful violation but is exempt from bringing a *korban* for inadvertent violation." The contrast with *shvuat bituy* is instructive: both incur *malkot* for intentional transgression, but *shvuat shav* carries no *korban* at all, even if violated unintentionally.

### Exclusion Question

This raises a structural question. The *mishnah* covers two cases — future oaths and oaths in vain — and uses the phrasing *zo hi* for each. The only case the *mishnah* does not explicitly address is *achalti velo achalti*, the past-oriented false oath. Both clauses of the *mishnah* seem to exclude this case, but do they exclude it for the same reason, or for different reasons? And what exactly is each clause excluding it *from*?

---

## Past Oaths Resolution

### First Clause: No Offering

Rabbi Abahu proposes a reading. The first clause — which identifies the future-oriented *shvuat bituy* as the one for which an unintentional violation brings a *korban* — is excluding the past-oriented case from the *korban* requirement. That is, *zo hi* in the first clause is saying: it is the future oath that generates both lashes and a *korban*; the past-oriented case does not generate a *korban*. This exclusion reflects the position of Rabbi Yishmael, who holds that only future-oriented oaths carry the *korban* obligation — the two explicit cases in the Torah that require a *korban olah veyored* are both future-oriented, and Rabbi Yishmael limits the *korban* liability to *asid lavo*, the future.

### Second Clause Tension

If the second clause — the one discussing *shvuat shav* — is similarly using *zo hi* to exclude the past-oriented case, one might infer that it is excluding *achalti velo achalti* from *malkot* as well. This would create a significant problem, because Rabbi Abahu has argued that the past-oriented false oath is precisely the case that *does* incur lashes. For that to be what the *mishnah* implies — that this most egregious case, swearing falsely about the past, carries no lashes — would be deeply counterintuitive. As one might observe: of all the categories of false oath, the deliberate use of God's name to deceive about a matter of fact is the most brazen, and yet we would be contemplating the possibility that it carries no penalty at all?

### Both Akiva View

The Gemara considers whether both clauses might reflect the same position and, if so, whose. If the first clause follows Rabbi Yishmael — past oaths exclude *korban* — and the second clause follows Rabbi Akiva — who holds that past oaths *do* incur a *korban*, the same as future oaths — then the two clauses are internally inconsistent: one says no *korban* for past oaths, the other implies there is. The Gemara therefore proposes: *kula Rabbi Akiva* — the entire *mishnah* follows Rabbi Akiva, who holds that past false oaths carry the same liability as future ones.

### Correct Exclusions

Under this reading, the first clause's exclusion is not of past oaths from lashes, but of a different case of future oath from *korban* and *malkot*. Specifically, the first clause contrasts the future oath violated through *action* — one swears not to eat and eats — with a future oath violated *passively* — one swears to eat and fails to. The former incurs both lashes and a *korban*; the latter incurs a *korban* but not lashes, since it is a passive violation. The phrase *zo hi* in the first clause is pointing to the active violation as the paradigm.

### Future Oaths Focus

The second clause, similarly, is not excluding past-oriented oaths from lashes — on the contrary, under Rabbi Akiva's view, they *do* incur lashes. Rather, both clauses are oriented around future oaths and are distinguishing between active and passive modes of violation. The *mishnah* is thus internally consistent: throughout, it is Rabbi Akiva who holds that past false oaths incur both lashes and a *korban*, and the *mishnah*'s exclusions are all drawn from within the category of future oaths, distinguishing the active violator (who gets lashes and is liable for a *korban*) from the passive one (who brings a *korban* but does not receive lashes). This is the settled conclusion the Gemara reaches.

---

## Kezayit Requirement

### Tiny Amount Dispute

The Gemara now shifts to a related question: if one takes an oath not to eat and then eats only a tiny amount (*kol shehu*) — less than a *kezayit* — has one transgressed?

### Akiva: Words Violation

Rabbi Akiva holds that even a tiny amount constitutes a transgression. His reasoning, stated in reply to the *Chachamim*, is striking: "Since when do we find that a person incurs lashes merely for speaking?" — meaning, it is already unusual that a *shvuah* generates lashes through speech alone, without any physical act. Since the entire structure of this prohibition is grounded in the violation of one's words, the act of eating is relevant not as an act of eating per se but as the act that falsifies one's statement. And falsifying one's statement requires no minimum measure: even the smallest amount of eating means one has violated what one said.

### Rabbis: Kezayit Standard

The *Chachamim* disagree. Their position is that a *kezayit* — the standard olive-sized minimum for eating-related prohibitions — is required here as well. The violation is still defined by eating, and eating is halachically defined by the *kezayit* threshold.

### Oath Concepts

The conceptual stakes of this dispute are significant and are best articulated through the analysis of Rav Soloveitchik, who draws on Rashi's framework. The question is: what is the nature of the transgression when one violates a *shvuah* about eating? One approach — reflected in *Tosafot* — treats the *shvuah* as particularly weighty precisely because it generates liability through speech alone, and argues that the severity of the prohibition implies one must have intended even the smallest amount. A different approach, articulated more precisely by Rashi and developed by Rav Soloveitchik, locates the issue structurally: the *shvuah* creates an obligation through words, and therefore the violation is of the *words* rather than of the physical act of eating. When the violation is constituted by falsifying a speech act, there is no minimum measure for the falsification. A small lie is still a lie.

---

## Akiva's General Position

### General Tiny Bit Query

The Gemara raises a broader question about Rabbi Akiva's position: does he hold, throughout the Torah, that even a tiny amount (*kol shehu*) suffices to transgress eating prohibitions? This would align him with the view of Rabbi Shimon.

### Shimon's Position

Rabbi Shimon explicitly holds that for *malkot*, any amount of forbidden food suffices — a *kol shehu* transgresses and incurs lashes. However, for bringing a *korban*, one still needs a *kezayit*. The *kezayit* threshold remains operative for the *korban*, but not for the *malkot*.

### Logical Extension

The Gemara reasons: if Rabbi Akiva holds like Rabbi Shimon generally — that a *kol shehu* suffices to incur lashes throughout the Torah — then his argument to the *Chachamim* in the case of *shvuot* would be trivially easy. He could simply say: I hold that even a tiny bit always violates eating prohibitions everywhere in the Torah. The *Chachamim* would have no particular difficulty answering him on the grounds of the uniqueness of *shvuot*. The fact that the debate is framed specifically in terms of *shvuot* suggests that something unique about oaths is driving his position.

### Oath Uniqueness

The resolution is that the debate is indeed uniquely about *shvuot*. Rabbi Akiva does not necessarily hold Rabbi Shimon's general position; his argument is specific to the structure of *shvuah* obligations. The *Chachamim*'s position is similarly extreme on their side: even though there is a theoretical basis for saying that *shvuot* require no minimum measure — given that the violation concerns one's words — they maintain the standard *kezayit* threshold even here. The debate thus illuminates a point of genuine principle about the nature of oath-obligations rather than a simple application of a general rule.

---

## Kezayit Evidence

### Nazirite Case

The Gemara brings a textual proof. The rabbis cite Rabbi Akiva's own ruling in a *nazir* case: if a *nazir* dips his bread in wine and eats a *kezayit* — even if the *kezayit* is a combination of wine and bread rather than wine alone — he is liable, since *heter mitztaref le'issur*, permitted food combines with the forbidden food to reach the requisite measure. This principle, unique to *nazir*, allows combining the bread (permitted) with the wine (forbidden) to constitute the full *kezayit*.

### Kezayit Inference

The critical inference: Rabbi Akiva himself requires combining to reach a *kezayit* in the *nazir* case. If he held generally that any amount transgresses — like Rabbi Shimon — there would be no need to combine at all. Even a tiny drop of wine would suffice. The fact that he demands a *kezayit* even through combination demonstrates that he does not hold Rabbi Shimon's general position.

### Unique Oath Position

The conclusion is thus established: Rabbi Akiva holds the standard *kezayit* requirement for eating prohibitions generally. His position that a *kol shehu* suffices for *shvuot* is specific to the unique nature of oath-violations, grounded in the principle that the transgression is one of words rather than of eating per se.

---

## Oath on Forbidden Foods

### Issur on Issur Rule

The *mishnah* now addresses a further question: can a *shvuah* take effect on foods that are already biblically prohibited? The general principle of *ein issur chal al issur* — no new prohibition can attach to something already forbidden — would seem to prevent any *shvuah* from having operative effect on, say, forbidden meats. One is already prohibited from eating them; the oath would appear to add nothing.

### Case Description

The *mishnah*'s case: one takes an oath not to eat, and then eats *neveilot* (animals not slaughtered according to *halacha*), *tereifot* (animals with certain defects), *shkatzim* (creeping creatures), and *remasim* (crawling creatures) — all biblically forbidden foods.

### Mishna Ruling

The *mishnah* rules that one is liable. Despite the principle of *ein issur chal al issur*, the *shvuah* takes effect, and violating it generates liability.

### Shimon Exemption

Rabbi Shimon, however, exempts. For Rabbi Shimon, *ein issur chal al issur* applies absolutely: since these foods are already forbidden, a new *shvuah* cannot superimpose an additional prohibition upon them. Therefore, eating them does not constitute a violation of the oath — the oath never took effect on them to begin with.

---

## Oath Inclusive Language

### Inclusive Scope

The Talmud addresses how the majority position — that one is liable — is coherent in light of *ein issur chal al issur*. The first approach, attributed to Rav, Shmuel, and Rabbi Yochanan, is the principle of *becholel devarim hamutarim im devarim ha'asurim* — including permitted things together with forbidden things within the scope of the oath. If one swore not to eat anything, the oath takes effect on all the permitted foods in that category; since it takes effect on the permitted foods, it simultaneously takes effect on the forbidden foods as well. The oath is not directed solely at forbidden foods — it encompasses permitted and forbidden alike — and therefore it is operative across the entire scope. Rabbi Shimon rejects this principle and maintains that even under such inclusive language, the *shvuah* never generates a new prohibition for what was already forbidden.

### Resh Lakish's Approach

Resh Lakish offers a different approach. The oath takes effect on forbidden foods if one specifies a minimal measure — for example, stating that one will not eat even half a *kezayit*. The biblical prohibition on *neveilah* and similar foods attaches to a *kezayit*; below that threshold, there is no biblical transgression (though there may be a rabbinic one). When the *shvuah* explicitly prohibits an amount smaller than the minimum for the biblical prohibition, it creates a genuinely new restriction — the oath forbids what the Torah does not, and therefore the oath has operative effect at that level. Alternatively, even without explicit specification, the oath takes effect according to Rabbi Akiva's position that a *shvuah* forbids even a *kol shehu* — which goes beyond the biblical prohibition that only attaches at the *kezayit* level.

### Akiva's Effect

Rabbi Akiva's position that a *shvuah* generates liability for any amount is thus directly relevant here. Since the biblical prohibition on forbidden foods is only violated by a *kezayit*, an oath that forbids even a *kol shehu* creates a new prohibition for amounts below the *kezayit* threshold. In this sense, the oath is not superimposing itself on an existing prohibition — it is creating a distinct, oath-based restriction at a level where the Torah's prohibition does not operate.

### Proof of Akiva

This analysis also provides a proof for the conclusion reached earlier — that Rabbi Akiva holds his *kol shehu* position specifically with respect to *shvuot* and does not hold like Rabbi Shimon generally. For if Rabbi Akiva held like Rabbi Shimon that a *kol shehu* of forbidden food *always* transgresses the biblical prohibition, then even the *kol shehu* level would be *mushba ve'omed me'Har Sinai* — already foresworn at Sinai, already covered by the biblical prohibition. The oath would add nothing. The fact that Resh Lakish can invoke Rabbi Akiva's position as the basis for the oath's effectiveness at the *kol shehu* level proves that Rabbi Akiva does not extend his *kol shehu* rule to forbidden foods generally. His position is unique to *shvuot*.

---

## Oath vs Vow Measure (III)

### Word vs Act

The conceptual framework underlying the *kezayit* debate now comes into fuller relief. For normal eating prohibitions, the transgression is defined by the act of eating — and the act of eating is halachically significant only at the *kezayit* level. For vows (*nedarim*), a similar logic applies: when one says this food is forbidden to me, violating the vow consists of eating it, and eating is quantified by the *kezayit*. For a *shvuah*, however, the violation is of one's word: one swore not to eat, and eating any amount at all falsifies that statement. The violation is not primarily the act of eating; it is the act of rendering false what one swore.

### Qualitative Significance

The Gemara's earlier discussion of *biryah* — a qualitatively whole unit, such as an ant — is relevant here. Normally, a quantitative threshold is required to give halachic significance to a small amount of food. But certain things carry qualitative significance independent of quantity: a *biryah* is a whole, complete organism, and its integrity as a unit gives it significance regardless of its size. Similarly, explicitly specifying a tiny amount in one's oath gives that tiny amount qualitative significance: one has singled it out and defined it as the threshold of one's commitment.

### Word Falsification

The underlying principle, then, is that the *kezayit* requirement is a function of the act of eating being the operative locus of the violation. Where the violation is instead of a spoken commitment — where the sin is that one's words have been rendered false — the minimum measure for eating is irrelevant. Any amount that falsifies the statement is sufficient. This is the coherent basis for Rabbi Akiva's position, and it rests on a fundamental distinction between prohibitions constituted by physical acts and prohibitions constituted by the breach of a verbal commitment.

---

## Oath vs Vow Measure (III)

### Konamos Parallel

This same logic extends to *konamos* — vows using the technical term *konam* (a paraphrase of *korban*, used to give an object a quasi-sanctified status). The Gemara takes for granted that a *konam*-vow is violated even by a *kol shehu*, with essentially universal agreement among the *rishonim*. The reason is precisely parallel to the analysis of *shvuot*: when one declares a food *konam* to oneself, the violation consists not of the act of eating per se but of transgressing the status one has conferred upon the object. Since the transgression is about the object's status rather than the act of consumption, the *kezayit* measure — which defines the act of eating — does not apply.

---

## Offering on False Oath

### Speech Act Offering

The Gemara next raises a fundamental question about the structure of oath-violations: is it truly the case that one brings a *korban* for a transgression accomplished entirely through speech? This is unusual. Generally, a *korban* is brought when one has committed a substantive physical act — eating forbidden food, performing a forbidden labor — not merely for the act of speaking.

### Counterexamples

Two counterexamples are considered. First, *megadef* — one who blasphemes God. Blasphemy is a speech act, yet one does not bring a *korban* for it; the prohibition is violated the moment one speaks, but it generates no offering. Second, a *nazir* who brings a *korban* upon completing his *nezirut*: this is a *korban* associated with a process initiated by speech (the vow of *nezirut*), but the *korban* at the end is not for *violating* the *nazir*'s vow — it is the prescribed offering that concludes the term of *nezirut* properly.

### Narrowed Definition

The Gemara progressively narrows the definition. The relevant category is not simply "speech acts" in general, but specifically: a speech act that creates a personal prohibition (*oser le'atzmo*) which is subsequently violated. Blasphemy creates no ongoing prohibition; the *nazir*'s concluding *korban* is not for violation. What is unique to *shvuot* is that the speech act establishes a binding personal obligation, and the *korban* is brought when that obligation is inadvertently breached.

### Hekdesh Analogy

The analogy to *hekdesh* — consecrated objects — is raised as particularly apt. When one consecrates an object, speech creates a new status that is subsequently binding; if one misuses that object, one violates *me'ila* and brings a *korban*. The structure is: words create a status; violation of that status generates a *korban*. This is structurally identical to *shvuot*: words create an obligation; inadvertent violation of that obligation generates a *korban olah veyored*.

### Vow Liability

Does the same apply to *konamos* — vows? If a *konam*-vow functions like *hekdesh*, then violating it would constitute *me'ila*, and one would bring a *korban* for its violation just as for misuse of consecrated property.

### Vow No Me'ila

The Gemara resolves this by ruling that *konamos* do not have the status of *hekdesh* for purposes of *me'ila* (*ein me'ila be'konamot*). A *konam*-vow creates a personal prohibition and generates *malkot* for willful violation, but it is not considered a form of consecration that triggers the *me'ila* framework. Therefore, there is no *korban* for violating a *konam*-vow — only *malkot*. The *korban olah veyored* for inadvertent oath-violation is thus a unique feature of *shvuot*, distinguishing them from all other speech-act prohibitions.

---

## Rava's Refinements

### Explicit Statement

*Amar Rava*: the debate between Rabbi Akiva and the *Chachamim* about whether a *kol shehu* suffices to violate a *shvuah* is limited to the case where one took the oath in general terms — *shvuah shelo ochal*, "I will not eat," without specifying a measure. In such a case, Rabbi Akiva holds that even a tiny amount constitutes a violation, while the *Chachamim* require a *kezayit*. But if one explicitly stated a tiny amount — "I will not eat even a *kol shehu*" — all agree that even a tiny amount suffices to violate the oath. This is simply because one has defined one's own threshold explicitly.

### Biryah Comparison

Rava compares an explicit specification to a *biryah*. Just as a *biryah* — a qualitatively whole unit — has inherent significance that exempts it from the *kezayit* requirement, an explicit declaration that a tiny amount is the threshold gives that amount a defined significance. When significance is established — whether through qualitative integrity or through explicit verbal designation — the ordinary quantitative threshold is set aside.

### Tasting Case

Similarly, if one swore not to *taste* (*shelo et'om*) rather than not to *eat*, all agree that any amount constitutes a violation. Tasting inherently refers to a small amount — that is the ordinary meaning of the word. One who swears not to taste something has defined the threshold by the nature of the word itself. The Gemara anticipates the objection that colloquially, people say "I'll just have a taste" when they mean to eat normally — but that vernacular usage does not override the precise halachic definition of *tasting* as a minimal amount.

---

## Oath vs Vow Measure (III)

### Debate Scope

*Amar Rav Pappa*: a further clarification. The dispute between Rabbi Akiva and the *Chachamim* regarding the *kol shehu* threshold applies specifically to *shvuot* — oaths, where one uses the language of a personal action ("I will not eat"). It does not apply to *konamos* — vows using the language of object-status.

### Vow Consensus

When one declares a food *konam* to oneself, all opinions agree — including the *Chachamim* — that even a tiny amount violates the vow. This is not limited to cases where one has explicitly specified a tiny amount; even a standard *konam* declaration is universally held to be violated by any measure.

### Vow Reason

The reason follows directly from the structural analysis developed throughout this sugya. A *shvuah* uses the language of eating: "I will not eat." The violation is therefore framed by the act of eating, and eating is normally defined by a *kezayit*. A *konam*-vow, by contrast, does not use the language of eating at all. One says this object is *konam* to me — one confers a status on the object without referencing the act of consumption. When the violation is of the object's status rather than of the act of eating, the *kezayit* threshold that defines a halachically significant act of eating is simply not relevant. Any engagement with the object — any amount at all — constitutes a transgression of its status. This is the conclusion that unifies the sugya's extended analysis of measures, speech acts, and the nature of oath-obligations.

---

---

# Shevuot 22

## Akiva vs. Tanna Kama

### Eating Defined

The daf opens in the middle of a *tashma* passage, picking up a discussion that concerns one of the foundational disputes of the tractate: when a person takes an oath not to eat, does the word "eat" carry its halachically defined meaning — a *kezayit*, an olive's bulk — or does it mean something else? The debate between Rabbi Akiva and the *tanna kama* turns on precisely this question.
