The *tanna kama* holds that since an oath is grounded in language, and the halachic definition of eating throughout the Torah is a *kezayit*, that definition applies here as well. Rabbi Akiva disagrees. Since a *shevua* is fundamentally about a person's words and intentions, and since one could theoretically take an explicit oath not to eat even the tiniest amount — a *kol shehu* — the very model of a *shevua* applying to a *kol shehu* exists. Therefore, even when unstated, that is how we interpret the oath.

### Rabbi Shimon

The Gemara raises a complication. There is a position, familiar from Makkot, associated with Rabbi Shimon, who holds that in general, the Torah's prohibitions on eating apply even to a *kol shehu* — a small amount — at least for the purposes of *malkus*, lashes. The amount of a *kezayit* is reserved, in his view, only for the obligation to bring a *korban*. The Gemara therefore asks: perhaps Rabbi Akiva's position that even a *kol shehu* triggers an oath violation is not rooted in anything unique about *shevuot* at all — perhaps he simply follows Rabbi Shimon's general approach that a *kol shehu* suffices for transgression.

This raises an immediate difficulty, noted by both Rashi and Tosafot. The context of our Mishnah is entirely about when one brings a *korban* for violating an oath — not about *malkus*. And even Rabbi Shimon himself agrees that a *korban* requires a *kezayit*. So what does Rabbi Shimon's position regarding *malkus* have to do with the question of a *korban* for a *shevua*?

### Rashi's Word-Breaking

Rashi offers what may be called an incisive structural reading. He reasons as follows: when a person eats a prohibited substance, eating more of it represents a greater violation. A small amount earns lashes; a larger amount — a *kezayit* — triggers *karet* if done willfully, or a *korban* if done inadvertently. There is a sliding scale, and the *kezayit* marks a qualitative threshold. But the violation of a *shevua* is categorically different. The wrong being committed is not the eating of the forbidden substance itself — it is the breaking of one's word. And breaking one's word is binary: either one has broken it or one has not. Eating more of the forbidden substance does not constitute a greater breaking of the word. The moment one eats, the word is broken. That is why, according to Rashi, the *kezayit* threshold does not map onto the *shevua* context in the same way.

### Tosafot on Karet

Tosafot takes a different approach. Rabbi Shimon normally links the *kezayit* requirement for a *korban* to the associated punishment of *karet*: since *karet* is a severe divine sanction, one must have committed a substantial transgression — a *kezayit* — to warrant it, and the *korban* mirrors that standard as the substitute for unintentional *karet*-level violations. However, the *korban* brought for violating a *shevua* has no *karet* attached to it at all — even a willful false oath does not incur *karet*. This is itself a peculiarity: one brings a *korban* for something that carries no *karet*. But Tosafot draws from this an important inference: precisely because there is no *karet* associated with a *shevua*, the *kezayit* threshold — which is calibrated to *karet* — need not apply. If a *kol shehu* suffices for *malkus* in ordinary prohibitions (per Rabbi Shimon), then in the domain of *shevuot*, where the *korban* is untethered from *karet*, a *kol shehu* should similarly suffice for the *korban*.

### Challenge to Akiva

The Gemara then challenges the assumption that Rabbi Akiva follows Rabbi Shimon in general. When the *tanna kama* asked Rabbi Akiva, "Where do we ever find that one is liable for eating a *kol shehu*?" — why didn't Rabbi Akiva simply respond, "I follow Rabbi Shimon throughout the entire Torah"? The fact that he did not say this implies that Rabbi Akiva does not in general hold like Rabbi Shimon. Rather, the Gemara explains, Rabbi Akiva was arguing within the framework of the *Rabbanan*'s own position — *ledivreihem*. He was saying: even according to you, who normally require a *kezayit*, you should concede that *shevuot* are different and that a *kol shehu* should apply. The *Rabbanan*, tersely and unabashedly, respond: no.

### Nazir Proof

The Gemara adduces further proof that Rabbi Akiva does not generally follow Rabbi Shimon. The Mishnah elsewhere teaches: a *nazir* who dipped his bread in wine and there was enough wine — when combined with the bread — to constitute a *kezayit*, is liable. Rabbi Akiva requires that the combination reach a *kezayit*. If Rabbi Akiva normally followed Rabbi Shimon that even a *kol shehu* suffices, why would the *nazir* need the wine to combine with the bread up to a *kezayit* at all? Even a small amount of wine should have been sufficient. It is therefore clear that Rabbi Akiva's standard position is that a *kezayit* is required, and *shevuot* represent a deliberate exception in his view.

### Non-Kosher Foods

A Mishnah is cited: if someone takes an oath "I will not eat" and then eats *neveilot*, *treifot*, *shekatzim*, or *remasim*, he is liable. Rabbi Shimon exempts. The Gemara asks the obvious question: why should the oath take effect on non-kosher food at all? The principle of *mushba ve'omeid me-Har Sinai* holds that one is already foresworn from eating these things by virtue of the covenant at Sinai — a *shevua* cannot take effect upon a pre-existing *shevua*.

### Three Answers

Three *Amoraim* — Rav, Shmuel, and Rabbi Yochanan — answer in agreement: the oath takes effect because the person said "I will not eat anything," encompassing all food in the world. Since the oath validly applies to the permitted foods, it simultaneously attaches to the forbidden foods as well — *bekolel devarim hamutarim im ha-asurim*. The forbidden foods are caught within the broader net of the oath.

Reish Lakish disagrees sharply. Even the all-inclusive formulation would not help; the oath still would not take effect on prohibited foods. The only ways the oath can take effect on non-kosher food, he says, are two: either one explicitly takes a *shevua* not to eat even a *chatzi shiur* — a half-*kezayit* — in which case the oath targets an act that the Torah itself does not explicitly forbid at that measure; or, according to Rabbi Akiva, one uses the generic formulation "I will not eat," which Rabbi Akiva interprets as applying to even a *kol shehu*, and since the Torah's prohibition of non-kosher food attaches only at the *kezayit* level, the *shevua* creates an additional prohibition at the sub-*kezayit* level where none previously existed.

### Akiva Implicit

This last point illuminates Rabbi Akiva's position sharply: according to him, any oath phrased using the word "eating" — even without explicit specification — is interpreted to mean a *kol shehu*. This is because the model of a *shevua* applying to a *kol shehu* inherently exists (since one could always have said it explicitly), and Rabbi Akiva understands the implicit oath to carry that meaning. The Gemara then confirms this reading: if Rabbi Akiva followed Rabbi Shimon in general, then by eating non-kosher food even in a small amount, one would already be foresworn from Sinai — there would be nothing for the *shevua* to add. The fact that Rabbi Akiva says the *shevua* does take effect demonstrates that normally even Rabbi Akiva requires a *kezayit*, and only in the domain of *shevuot* does he hold that the *kol shehu* applies.

### Explicit vs. Implicit

Rava summarizes the scope of the debate: the dispute between Rabbi Akiva and the *tanna kama* applies only when one used the generic formulation "I will not eat" without specifying an amount. But if one explicitly said "I will not eat even a tiny amount," all opinions would agree that even a *kol shehu* creates a violation. And further: if one used the word *"taam"* — "I will not taste" — all would agree that even a *kol shehu* is intended, since "taste" carries no fixed halachic definition. One might have thought otherwise — perhaps "taste" is used colloquially to mean a substantial sample — but Rava maintains that since there is no established halachic measure for "taste," we interpret the word in its most minimal sense. "Eat," however, carries a well-established halachic definition, and the *tanna kama* applies it.

---

## Eating Exceptions

### Briah Exception

Having established the general rule that a *kezayit* is the default measure for an oath of eating, the Gemara proceeds to identify apparent exceptions that the *Rabbanan* must address when they claim there is no precedent for liability with less than a *kezayit*. The first is the *briah* — a whole creature. One who eats a whole ant is liable even though an ant is far smaller than a *kezayit*. The Gemara responds: *birya shani* — a complete organism is different.

There are two explanations for this. First, just as a *kezayit* confers quantitative significance on an act of eating, a whole creature confers qualitative significance — it represents a complete act. Second, the verse explicitly prohibits eating a *sheretz*, a *sheketz*, and so on; when one eats an entire specimen of that creature, one has violated precisely what the verse says, even if it is smaller than a *kezayit*. By contrast, when the Torah prohibits eating meat generically, the question of "how much?" requires external definition.

### Hekdesh Measure

The Gemara raises a second apparent exception: *hekdesh*, consecrated property. One who derives benefit from consecrated property is liable for *meilah* even for an amount less than a *kezayit*. The Gemara responds: there is no absence of a minimum amount here — the measure is simply different. *Meilah* is calibrated not to acts of eating but to acts of deriving benefit, and the threshold for benefit is a *shaveh prutah*, a penny's worth. A different scale applies, but the principle of requiring a minimum amount remains intact.

### Explicit Tiny Amount

The third exception raised is the case of explicit specification. If someone says "I will not eat even a tiny amount," he is liable for a *kol shehu* — and the *Rabbanan* themselves would concede this. So there exists a case where liability attaches below a *kezayit*. Why, then, do the *Rabbanan* claim there is no such precedent?

The Gemara responds that an explicit oath of this kind is comparable to a *briah*: just as a whole creature is qualitatively significant despite its small size, an explicit statement lends weight and significance to an otherwise trivial act. By default, eating a tiny amount is a meaningless act, beneath the threshold of halachic significance. But if a person explicitly designates that tiny amount as the subject of his oath, he has given it weight — he has made it significant. On the alternative explanation of *briah*, the parallel is more direct: the verse says "do not eat a rat," and if one eats a rat, one has done exactly what the verse prohibits; similarly, if one says "I will not eat a tiny amount" and then eats a tiny amount, one has violated precisely what one said. But the *Rabbanan*'s point is that this is an exception created by explicit designation, not the default interpretation of the word "eat."

### Dirt Question

Rava raises a question: if someone takes a *shevua* that he will not eat dirt and then eats dirt — what is the measure? On one hand, he used the word *achila* — eating — which might import the standard *kezayit* measure. On the other hand, eating dirt is not a normal act of eating in any conventional sense; people do not eat dirt as food. Perhaps in this context, *achila* is simply shorthand for "putting in one's mouth and swallowing," and no standard halachic definition of eating applies, making even a *kol shehu* sufficient. The Gemara leaves this unresolved: *teiku*.

The Gemara notes that this question is relevant to a broader principle. When the *Rabbanan* say there is never liability for a *kol shehu*, they are speaking of normal foodstuffs subject to normal acts of eating. Dirt, which is not *bar achila* — not something that is biologically eaten — may occupy a different category entirely, and the *Rabbanan*'s categorical statement need not address it.

### Konamot

The Gemara then raises *konamot* as a possible exception. A *konam* is a form of *neder* in which a person borrows the language of *korbanot* to prohibit something to himself — "this bread is *konam* to me" means roughly "this bread is to me as a *korban*." Because the word *konam* itself is not a word of eating — it does not say "I forbid myself to eat this" but simply "this is forbidden to me" — the status it creates is not defined by an act of *achila*. Rashi notes that the person is not saying "*konam* this bread from eating" but simply declaring the bread *konam*, which means utterly prohibited in all ways.

As Rav Pappa argues, *konamot* do not require a *kezayit* even according to the *tanna kama*: since no word of *achila* was used, the standard halachic definition of eating does not apply, and even a tiny benefit constitutes a violation. The Gemara characterizes this as *k'mefaresh dami* — equivalent to an explicit specification — because by using the language of *konam* rather than *achila*, the person has, in effect, specified that his prohibition is not of eating in the halachic sense but of something broader.

### Konam Meilah

This raises the question of what measure *does* govern a *konam*. Since the language of *konam* parallels the language of *hekdesh*, it might follow that the relevant measure is a *shaveh prutah*, as in *meilah* from consecrated property. Tosafot presses this point: even if *konam* does not require a *kezayit*, it should not have *less* structure than *hekdesh*, which still requires a minimum of a *shaveh prutah*. The Gemara seems to imply that there is no minimum measure for a *konam* in some respects, which Tosafot finds difficult to resolve.

The deeper issue is whether there is *meilah* by *konamot* at all. *Meilah* normally applies to items that are objectively *hekdesh* — sanctified for all persons. A *konam* creates only a subjective status, forbidding the item to the one who declared it but not to others. Can such a subjective prohibition generate *meilah*? This question drives the subsequent discussion.

---

## Combination Rule

### Baraita Rule

The Gemara introduces a *baraita* that presents a striking asymmetry: two *konamot* combine to reach the minimum threshold, while two *shevuot* do not combine. If a person says "*konam* this apple is forbidden to me in eating, and *konam* this apple is forbidden to me in eating," and eats a half-*kezayit* from each, the two amounts combine and he has violated his *konam*. But if a person says "*shevua* I will not eat this, and *shevua* I will not eat this," and eats a half-*kezayit* from each, the two amounts do not combine and he has not violated either oath. The question is why this difference exists.

### Rabbi Meir

Rabbi Meir dissents from the *baraita*: he holds that *konamot* are like *shevuot* — presumably meaning they too do not combine. This requires explanation, since the logic behind each position is not immediately apparent. The Gemara explores whether Rabbi Meir means that *konamot* are like *shevuot* in that they do not combine, or whether the text should be reversed — that *shevuot* are like *konamot* and do combine.

### When Konamot Combine

The Gemara first establishes why *konamot* combine. Rav Pappa explained earlier that when one says *"konam"* without using the word *achila*, there is no minimum amount at all. But the *baraita* speaks of a case where one did use the word *achila* — "the eating of this is *konam* to me, and the eating of this is *konam* to me" — and therefore a *kezayit* is indeed required. The question then is: if each *konam* specifies a separate object, why should amounts from each combine? Eating a half-*kezayit* of the first apple did not violate the *konam* on the first apple, and eating a half-*kezayit* of the second apple did not violate the *konam* on the second apple. Where is the violation?

The Gemara resolves this: the person said "the eating of these two is *konam* to me" — formulating them as a single unit. Since both apples are grouped under one prohibition, any eating from either one, or from both together, counts toward that single prohibition, and the amounts combine.

### Oath Separation

Why, then, do *shevuot* not combine even when formulated similarly — "I swear I will not eat from this one and from this one"? Rav Pinchas explains that *shevuot* are subject to the rule of *chaluka lekorbanos* — they are divided into separate sin offerings. When one says "*shevua* I will not eat from this and from this," halacha treats this as two separate oaths, each governing its own object. The source is the verse *"vehaya ki yesham le'achas me'eleh"* — "and he shall be guilty regarding one of these" — from which the *Sifrei* derives that even a single formulation covering two items is reckoned as two distinct oaths. This means that eating a *kezayit* from each incurs two separate *korbanos*, as though one had violated two different prohibitions, like eating *chelev* and *dam*, which never combine.

### Rav Pinchas

The implication of Rav Pinchas's rule is that two *shevuot* covering different objects are always treated as entirely separate, regardless of how they were phrased. If one eats a half-*kezayit* from each, one has not completed the act required to violate either oath individually, and since they are separate they cannot combine. This is the fundamental structural difference between *konamot* and *shevuot*: a *konam* covering two items remains one *konam*; a *shevua* covering two items is treated as two *shevuot*.

Rabbi Meir's position, on the Gemara's revised reading, is that *shevuot* are like *konamot* — that is, *shevuot* do combine. Rabbi Meir does not deny that there may be two *korbanos* in principle, but he holds that the rule of *chaluka lekorbanos* does not preclude combination when assessing whether the minimum amount for liability has been reached.

### Ravina's Answer

Ravina offers an alternative approach to the entire question. He proposes that Rav Pappa's principle — that *konamot* require only a *kol shehu* — was stated specifically with regard to *malkus*, not with regard to a *korban*. The *baraita* that discusses combination, however, concerns a *korban*, not *malkus*. And what *korban* would be relevant to a *konam*? Since a *konam* borrows the language of *hekdesh*, the applicable *korban* is the *korban me'ila* — brought for improperly benefiting from consecrated property. A *korban me'ila* requires a *shaveh prutah*, not a *kezayit*. Therefore, the *baraita* teaches that two *konamot* combine to reach a *shaveh prutah*'s worth for the *korban me'ila*, while two *shevuot* do not combine to reach the *kezayit* needed for a *korban shevua*.

### Ravina Challenged

This interpretation requires that the *Rabbanan* who disagree with Rabbi Meir hold that there is *meilah* by *konamot* — otherwise there would be no *korban* to discuss. The Gemara therefore examines a *baraita* on this point.

### Konam vs. Hekdesh

The *baraita* distinguishes between two cases. If one says "this loaf is *hekdesh*," the item is objectively consecrated — both the person and others would transgress *meilah* by deriving benefit from it, and it can be redeemed, since it has genuine *hekdesh* status. If one says "this loaf is *hekdesh* for me" — a formulation that parallels *konam* — the status is subjective: the person himself transgresses *meilah* by eating it, but others do not, and it cannot be redeemed, since the *hekdesh* is not an objective metaphysical reality. This is Rabbi Meir's position. The *Chachamim*, however, hold that in the case of "this loaf is *hekdesh* for me," neither the person nor others transgress *meilah*, because the status is not sufficiently objective to constitute real *hekdesh*.

The problem is that the *Chachamim*'s position — no *meilah* for *konamot* — is the opposite of what Ravina's explanation of the *baraita* requires. Ravina needs the *Rabbanan* (who hold that *konamot* do combine) to affirm *meilah* by *konamot*, but the *Chachamim* here deny any *meilah* by *konamot*.

### Resolution

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by inverting the attribution in the *baraita* on *meilah*. It is Rabbi Meir who holds there is no *meilah* by *konamot* at all — and when Rabbi Meir says in the earlier *baraita* that *konamot* are like *shevuot* and do not combine, he is consistent: there is no *meilah*, hence no *korban*, hence no reason to speak of combination for a *korban* threshold. The *Chachamim*, on the other hand, hold that there is *meilah* for the person himself — "he transgresses, his fellow does not" — and it is therefore the *Rabbanan* who affirm combination for *konamot*, since combining to a *shaveh prutah* enables the *korban me'ila*.

When Rabbi Meir argues *ledivreihem* — within the *Rabbanan*'s framework — he says: even granted that you hold there is *meilah* by *konamot*, you should still agree that *konamot* are like *shevuot* and do not combine. The *Rabbanan* reject this, maintaining that the rule of *chaluka lekorbanos*, which prevents *shevuot* from combining, does not apply to *konamot*, which remain a single unified prohibition over all covered objects.

---

## Rava's Questions

### Dirt Measure

Returning now to the unresolved questions left earlier, the Gemara formally records Rava's question: *shevua shelo ochel afar — bechama?* If someone takes an oath not to eat dirt and then eats dirt, what is the operative measure? Is it a *kezayit*, because he used the word *ochel* — eating — which normally carries a halachic definition? Or is it a *kol shehu*, because dirt is not a normal foodstuff and therefore "eating" in this context cannot carry its standard halachic weight? The Gemara leaves this as *teiku* — unresolved.

### Grape Seeds

Rava then raises a second question: if someone takes a *shevua* not to eat *chartzan* — grape seeds — what is the measure? Two considerations pull in opposite directions. On one hand, grape seeds are eaten — they are consumed as part of a grape — and in that sense they belong to the category of normal food. This would suggest that "eating grape seeds" should be interpreted as a *kezayit*. On the other hand, people do not eat grape seeds on their own; they are not independently consumed as a food. This might place them in the same category as dirt — something not genuinely *bar achila* in the standalone sense — and the measure would be a *kol shehu*. This question, too, is left unresolved: *teiku*.

### Rav Ashi

Rav Ashi poses a further question related to these themes: what is the law for a *nazir* who takes a *shevua* not to eat grape seeds? A *nazir* is already biblically prohibited from eating grape seeds. The *shevua* would therefore be redundant at the level of a *kezayit* — the Torah already forbids that. For the *shevua* to add anything meaningful, it would have to apply at the sub-*kezayit* level, a *kol shehu*. Should we therefore interpret the *nazir*'s oath as implicitly targeting the *kol shehu*, in order to give his words meaning?

### Non-Redundancy

The question is whether halacha adopts a principle of charitable or purposive interpretation — reading an oath to mean whatever it would take for the oath to be non-redundant and effective — or whether we simply take the word "eat" at face value, apply its standard measure, and accept that the oath turns out to be redundant and ineffective. This is a genuinely significant structural question about how *shevuot* are interpreted.

### Neveilah Biology

The Gemara brings a *tashma* to resolve the issue. The Mishnah teaches that one who takes a *shevua* "I will not eat" and then eats *neveilot* and *treifot* is liable. We have already seen this passage and the debate about *mushba ve'omeid*. But the Gemara now highlights Reish Lakish's position: the *shevua* takes effect on non-kosher food only if one explicitly specified "I will not eat a *chatzi shiur*," or, according to Rabbi Akiva, by default because *shevua* always means *kol shehu*. And crucially, Reish Lakish does not say: "since you're already prohibited from *neveilah* at the *kezayit* level, we will naturally interpret your *shevua* to mean *chatzi shiur* so that it should be meaningful." He does not do so. We require an explicit statement.

### Dirt Not Edible

This resolves Rav Ashi's question about the *nazir*. We do not adopt a principle of non-redundancy that would re-interpret an oath to give it effect. If a *nazir* says "I will not eat grape seeds" without specifying a smaller amount, his words mean a *kezayit*, and since he is already foresworn at that level, the *shevua* is redundant and does not take effect. The parallel to *neveilah* is direct: one who says "I will not eat *neveilah*" means a *kezayit*, and we do not creatively re-interpret the oath to save it from redundancy.

However, the Gemara distinguishes between *neveilah* and dirt precisely on the question of biological edibility. *Neveilah* is *bar achila* — it is genuinely edible in the physical sense. The vast majority of humanity eats it. There is, as the Gemara puts it, a lion crouching upon it — meaning the Torah is the sole external force prohibiting it — but the food itself is edible. Therefore, when one says "eat *neveilah*," one is speaking of eating something that is biologically food, and the standard *kezayit* measure applies. Dirt, by contrast, is *lav bar achila hu klal* — it is not edible at all as a biological matter. When one says "eat dirt," one is not invoking the halachic act of eating in any normal sense, and it remains unresolved what measure, if any, applies. The Gemara's *teiku* on dirt thus stands, while Rav Ashi's question about the *nazir* and grape seeds is answered: we read "eat" at its face value, do not rescue the oath from redundancy by creative interpretation, and the *shevua* of the *nazir* regarding grape seeds does not take effect. The Gemara closes here, leaving the continuation for the following Mishnah.

---

---

# Shevuot 23

## Previous Material Review

### Opening & Overview

The present daf opens by picking up with the *mishna* at the bottom of 22b. The preceding material covered a wide range of foundational topics in *hilchot shevuot*, and the discussion now turns to questions of how the framing of a *shvua* affects the number of *korbanot* incurred upon its violation.

### Topics Summary

Among the principles already examined: the distinction between *shvuat shav* and *shvuat sheker*, the mechanism of *hatfasat shvua*, the status of *konam*, the meaning of *achilah* in various formulations, and the question of whether the minimum measure triggering liability is a *kolshehu* or a *kezayit*. The principle of *mushba v'omed* — that an oath cannot take effect on something one is already forbidden to do — has also figured prominently. These concepts now provide the backdrop for the *mishna*'s treatment of single versus multiple oaths and their corresponding *korbanot*.

---

## One Oath vs. Multiple

### Eating Includes Drinking

The *mishna* opens with the case of *shvua shelo ochal* — a person who takes an oath not to eat — and then proceeds to eat and drink. Although eating and drinking are two distinct acts, the *mishna* teaches that both fall under the single rubric of *achilah*: consuming, broadly understood. Implicit in this ruling, and soon to be the focus of the *gemara*, is the principle that *shtiyah* — drinking — is included within the word *ochal*. Since both transgressions flow from one *shvua*, the person is *eino chayav ela achas*: liable for only one *korban*, even if he was not made aware between the two acts. This parallels the rule for other repeated violations of the same *aveira* — eating two *kezaysim* of *chametz* on *Pesach* or of forbidden fat without intervening awareness yields one *korban*, not two.

### Two Oaths, Two Korbanot

The *mishna* then introduces the case of *shvua shelo ochal v'shelo eshteh* — a person who takes an oath that he will not eat and will not drink. One might have supposed that since he uses only a single utterance of the word *shvua*, the whole statement constitutes one oath. The *chiddush* of the *mishna* is that we regard this as two distinct *shvuot*, because he identified two separate acts. Accordingly, if he then eats and drinks — even without intervening awareness — he is *chayav shtayim*: obligated in two *korbanot*. The two acts are treated as two separate sins, as though he had taken the oath not to eat one day and the oath not to drink the next.

### Shabbat Melachot Analogy

There is a further *chiddush* embedded here. One might object: even granting that these are two separate *shvuot*, is he not still transgressing the same underlying *aveira*? After all, the prohibition is the same — violating the sanctity of one's word through a false oath — and so perhaps a single *korban* should suffice regardless of how many *shvuot* were involved.

The best analogy is *Shabbos*. If a person forgot both that it was forbidden to cook on *Shabbos* and that it was forbidden to kindle a fire, and he then kindled a fire and cooked without becoming aware between the two acts, he brings two *chata'ot* — two separate sin offerings — because those are two distinct *melachos*. Yes, he transgressed one underlying sin of violating *Shabbos*, but the Torah's principle of *chiluk melachos* treats each *melacha* as a discrete transgression warranting its own *korban*. The same logic applies here: *shvuah* likewise recognizes that two separately articulated *shvuot*, even if they address overlapping subject matter, are treated as two distinct transgressions requiring two *korbanot*.

---

## Bread & Liquid Types

### Bread Types Cases

The *mishna* continues with cases involving different categories of food and drink. If a person takes an oath *shelo ochal* — not to eat — and then eats three types of bread: wheat bread, barley bread, and spelt bread, he is *eino chayav ela achas*. All three are merely three ways of transgressing the same *shvua*; one *korban* suffices.

By contrast, if he explicitly formulates his oath as *shvua shelo ochal pas chitin u'pas seorin u'pas kusmin* — that he will not eat bread of wheat, bread of barley, and bread of spelt — this is treated as three distinct *shvuot*. Eating all three makes him *chayav al kol achas v'achas*: liable for each separately, for three *korbanot*.

### Liquid Types Cases

The same structure governs liquids. A person who takes a *shvua shelo eshteh* and then drinks many different liquids is *eino chayav ela achas* — one *korban* for multiple violations of the same oath. But one who explicitly swears *shelo eshteh yayin v'shemen u'dvash* — that he will not drink wine, oil, and honey — and then drinks all three, is *chayav al kol achas v'achas*.

It is worth noting that oil and honey raise an intuitive question: these are not beverages in the ordinary sense. Drinking oil is hardly a normal act; honey one might more naturally describe as eating. The *chiddush* may be that since these are liquids, they fall under the prohibition of *shtiyah* even when they are not commonly consumed in that form.

### Inedible Foods & Drinks

The *mishna* further rules that if a person takes an oath not to eat and then consumes foods or liquids that are *einam reuyim l'achilah* — unfit for consumption — he is *patur*. The same standards that govern other dietary prohibitions apply: you must consume something that is halachically considered food. Just as a person eating dirt on *Yom Kippur* or *Pesach* would not be *over* the prohibition, dirt and similarly unfit substances are outside the scope of the oath.

### Konam Conditional Oath

The *mishna* then addresses the case of a person who makes a conditional *konam*: *konam ishti nehenis li im achalti hayom* — if I have eaten today, my wife is forbidden in benefit to me. This mechanism functions as an alternative to a standard *shvua*: rather than swearing directly, a person backs his denial with a conditional *neder*, making something forbidden to him contingent on the truth of his assertion.

If such a person then ate *neveilot u'treifot shekatzim u'remasim* — non-kosher food — the *mishna* rules *harei ishto asurah*: his wife is indeed forbidden, because eating non-kosher food counts as eating for this purpose. The question of whether a *shvua* can take effect on forbidden food is the subject of debate between the *tanna kamma* and *Rabbi Shimon*, who exempts. As will be developed in the *gemara*, Rabbi Shimon's exemption may rest on the principle of *mushba v'omed*: one is already forbidden from *Sinai* to eat that food, so a *shvua* cannot add a new layer of prohibition.

---

## Achilah Includes Shtiyah

### Svara Explanation

Rabbi Chiya bar Avin said in the name of Shmuel: if a person takes a *shvua shelo ochal* — not to eat — and then drinks, he is *chayav*. This makes explicit what the *mishna* implies: *shtiyah bichlal achilah*, drinking is subsumed within eating.

The *gemara* offers two routes to this conclusion: *iba'it eima svara* — logical reasoning — or *iba'it eima kra* — a scriptural proof. The *svara* is based on ordinary usage: when one person says to another *neito midi* — let's go have something — and they then go and eat and drink, it is natural to say that the invitation to "taste something" or "have something" encompasses drinking as well. The *svara* is admittedly not airtight: that one might drink while being invited to eat could simply mean the drinking is incidental to the eating, not that the word *ochel* refers to the drink. Some textual variants have the example as going to get something to drink upon such an invitation, which would be a stronger illustration — but then the operative word is "taste," not "eat," and the proof still does not establish that the word *achilah* itself encompasses drinking. So the *svara* is suggestive but not conclusive.

### Resh Lakish Proof

Resh Lakish offers a more authoritative grounding in a *pasuk*. The *gemara* cites *ve'achalta lifnei Hashem Elokecha bamakom asher yivchar*, referring to the laws of *ma'aser sheni*, where the Torah says *ma'asar deganecha tiroshecha v'yitzharecha* — the tithe of your grain, your wine, and your oil — and uses the word *ve'achalta*, "and you shall eat it." Since *tirosh* is wine — a liquid — and the Torah describes consuming it with the word *achilah*, this demonstrates that *achilah* can include drinking.

### Rav Acha Proof

The *gemara* pushes back: perhaps *ve'achalta* in the context of *ma'aser sheni* refers not to drinking wine straight but to consuming it in a dish — the *anigron*, described by Rabbah bar Shmuel as a dish made from beet water, or the *achsigron*, made from cooked vegetables. If wine was consumed as part of a cooked preparation, one might be said to "eat" wine without any implication that *achilah* encompasses drinking.

Rav Acha bar Yaakov therefore adduces a different verse, also from the laws of *ma'aser sheni*: *ve'natata hakesef be'chol asher t'aveh nafshecha, ba'vakar u'va'tzon u'va'yayin u'va'shechar* — you shall give the money for whatever your heart desires, for cattle, for sheep, for wine, for *shechar* — and the verse concludes *ve'achalta lifnei Hashem Elokecha*, "and you shall eat it before the Lord your God." The word *shechar* denotes something intoxicating, *midi de'meshaker*, and if it can intoxicate, one must be drinking it straight rather than consuming it in a small admixture through food.

The *gemara* tests this as well: perhaps *dveilah k'ilit* — pressed figs from K'ilit — are also capable of intoxication, as the *baraisa* indeed teaches that eating those figs, or drinking honey or milk, constitutes a state of intoxication sufficient to disqualify one from performing the Temple service. So perhaps *shechar* here refers to such solid intoxicants.

The *gemara* resolves this by means of a *gezeirah shavah*: *shechar shechar mi'nazir*. The same word *shechar* appears in the laws of the *nazir* — *mi'yayin v'shechar yazir* — and there we know it refers to wine-derived liquids and not to solid intoxicants like pressed figs. Therefore here too, *shechar* refers to something one drinks, and yet the *pasuk* describes it with *ve'achalta* — establishing that *achilah* encompasses *shtiyah*.

### Svara vs. Pasuk Debate

This passage — *iba'it eima svara, iba'it eima kra* — has long been cited as a window into a foundational principle of *Torah she'ba'al peh*. The *gemara*'s willingness to say "if you want, I can prove it with logic, if you want, I can prove it with a verse" implies that human reason and scriptural derivation are of equivalent weight as sources of halachic knowledge. This is, in fact, the precise opposite of fundamentalism, which would insist on deriving everything from the simple meaning of a verse to the exclusion of independent reasoning. Here the *gemara* treats them as interchangeable.

Tosafot, on 22b, notes that this phrasing appears in a number of places throughout the *gemara* and raises the question sharply: *v'teima, keivan d'ika svara, lama li kra?* — If we already have the logical proof, why do we need the verse? Why did the Torah bother to indicate this if we could have derived it ourselves? Tosafot's answer is that this depends on the cogency of the *svara*: when the logic is not entirely compelling on its own, the *pasuk* serves to confirm and validate the reasoning. The present case is actually a good illustration of that principle — the *svara* was not persuasive, and so the *kra* does the heavier lifting. One may also note that elsewhere the *gemara* goes further still, suggesting that a sufficiently strong *svara* can override a *pasuk*, as when the *gemara* says *shavik likra d'ihu dachik u'mokei anafsheh* — set aside the verse, it is strained, and the logic stands on its own.

---

## Shtiyah vs. Achilah

### Rava's Proof

Rava observes that the *mishna* itself confirms the principle *shtiyah bichlal achilah*. The *mishna* states: *shvua shelo ochal v'achal v'shata, eino chayav ela achas* — if he took an oath not to eat and then both ate and drank, he is liable for only one *korban*. If drinking were simply not included in *achilah*, then the *mishna*'s ruling would be trivially obvious: of course you bring only one *korban* when you eat after having sworn not to eat, regardless of whether you also happen to scratch your back or drive somewhere. The fact that the *mishna* found it necessary to tell us that eating and drinking together yields only one *korban* proves that drinking is indeed a violation of the oath — but since both violations stem from the same *shvua*, it is one *korban*. Were drinking simply irrelevant to the oath, no ruling would have been needed.

### Abaye's Challenge

Abaye poses a sharp challenge. Grant, he says, that *shtiyah bichlal achilah* — drinking is included in eating. Then consider the case of *shvua shelo ochal v'shelo eshteh*. The moment the person finishes saying the words *shvua shelo ochal* — before he has even uttered the rest of the sentence — he is already *issur lei bi-shtiyah*: forbidden in drinking as well, since drinking is subsumed in his oath not to eat. When he then adds *v'shelo eshteh* — and not to drink — why should those words create any new prohibition? The principle of *ein shvua chalah al shvua* should apply: one oath cannot take effect on something already forbidden by an earlier oath. The result should be that the second clause never takes effect, and if he then eats and drinks, he is liable for only one *korban* — for violating the first oath. Yet the *mishna* says he is *chayav shtayim*.

### Rava's Response

Rava replies that the *mishna* should be understood as stating the clauses in reverse order: the person first said *shelo eshteh* — not to drink — and then said *shelo ochal* — not to eat. In this sequence, drinking was separately prohibited by the first clause, and eating — together with its implicit inclusion of drinking — was prohibited by the second. Since *shtiyah bichlal achilah* but *achilah* is not included in *shtiyah*, the oath not to drink prohibited only drinking, while the subsequent oath not to eat now prohibited eating and thereby also redeclared the prohibition on drinking under a new *shvua*. Thus both oaths are in force, and the *mishna*'s ruling of *chayav shtayim* follows.

### Context Defines Scope

Abaye presses further: if Rava reverses the order of the *mishna* to make it work, then Rava is conceding that if the clauses were stated in the natural order — *shelo ochal v'shelo eshteh* — drinking would indeed not take effect as a second prohibition, yielding only one *korban*. But then the *mishna* ought to have taught the more novel case: that even when formulated as *shelo ochal v'shelo eshteh*, you are *eino chayav ela achas*. Teaching that case would have been a greater *chiddush*.

The *gemara* resolves this with an important conceptual point: *keivan d'amar shelo ochal v'hadar amar shelo eshteh, gali adatei de'hach achilah d'amar, achilah geridasa hi* — when a person says "I will not eat and I will not drink," the very fact that he adds the clause about drinking reveals that in his formulation, *achilah* means eating alone, in the narrow sense, without the extension to drinking. Context governs the scope of the word. When *ochel* appears by itself, it encompasses all forms of consumption including liquids; but when a person pairs it explicitly with *eshteh*, he signals that in this sentence *ochel* refers only to solid food. Accordingly, the two clauses create two genuinely independent prohibitions — one on eating and one on drinking — and the *mishna* correctly rules *chayav shtayim*.

---

## Alternative Phrasing Rule

### Bread Repetition Analysis

The *gemara* turns to the *mishna*'s ruling that naming bread of wheat, bread of barley, and bread of spelt separately creates three distinct *shvuot*. The underlying principle, which the *gemara* now develops, is that separate naming produces separate *shvuot* only if there was an alternative, grouped phrasing available that would have expressed the same content as a unified oath. Because the person chose to name them separately rather than bundling them, we treat each as its own *shvua*.

The *gemara* immediately raises a problem: perhaps the person was not creating three separate *shvuot* at all, but was simply specifying three particular types of bread to exclude others. Maybe he just wanted to say he would not eat *these* three types of bread and not, say, rye.

### Separation Principle

The *gemara* works through this methodically. If the person simply wanted to prohibit these three and no others, he should have said *chitin u'seorin v'chusmin* — wheat, barley, and spelt — without the word *pas*. But that phrasing would have meant he could not chew on the raw grains themselves; the word *pas* — bread — was necessary to make clear that bread is the subject. Very well, then he should have said *pas chitin u'seorin v'chusmin* — bread of wheat, barley, and spelt — in a single phrase. The *gemara* notes that this formulation might have been ambiguous: it could be read as bread of wheat on the one hand and raw barley and spelt on the other.

So the required phrasing would have been *pas chitin v'shel seorin v'shel kusmin* — bread of wheat and of barley and of spelt — using the connective *shel* to make clear that all three follow under *pas*. It is worth noting that this alternative phrasing is no shorter — in fact, it is slightly longer — than what was actually said. The *gemara*'s point is not that the alternative is easier to say, but that it would have more clearly expressed a unified prohibition. Since such a phrasing was available and the person did not use it, we conclude that the repetition of *pas* before each grain was deliberate and signals three separate *shvuot*.

The *gemara* presses further: even *pas chitin v'shel seorin v'shel kusmin* might have been misunderstood as referring to a bread made of all three grains mixed together — a *taaroves*. To dispel that reading entirely, one would have had to say *pas chitin v'chein shel seorin v'chein shel kusmin* — bread of wheat and similarly of barley and similarly of spelt. This formulation, though considerably more cumbersome, would have been entirely unambiguous. The key principle that emerges is that we do not require the alternative phrasing to have been the natural or easy way to speak; we only require that some alternative phrasing *could* have conveyed the unified sense. Since such alternatives exist, the fact that the person said *pas pas pas* — bread of wheat, bread of barley, bread of spelt — is treated as signaling separation, and each is a distinct *shvua*.

### Rav Papa's Context

When the *gemara* turns to the case of wine, oil, and honey, it faces a different challenge. There, the person simply names three distinct liquids; there is no obvious single word that would have encompassed precisely those three and no others. So why does naming them separately create three *shvuot*?

Rav Papa explains: we are dealing with a case where these three items were physically present before the person — *munachim lefanav*. In that context, the person could easily have said *shvua shelo eshteh eilu* — I swear I will not drink any of these — and that would have expressed a single unified prohibition on all three. Or he could have said *shvua delo shatina kegon elu* — I will not drink anything like these — to encompass these types generally. The *gemara* tests and refines these alternatives: *kegon elu* might have been taken to refer to that specific quantity rather than the type; so a still more precise formulation would be *shvua shelo eshteh mi'min elu* — I will not drink from these types of liquids. And if even that left some ambiguity — whether "these types" excludes the very items before him — one could have said *shelo eshteh elu u'mi'mineihem* — these and anything of their type. Since such a phrasing was possible and would have clearly unified the oath, we read the person's choice to name wine, oil, and honey individually as creating three separate *shvuot*.

### Rav Acha Bar Acha

Rav Acha brei de'Rav Ika provides yet another context in which the separation principle applies to the liquids case. He describes a *pessirah* setting: a friend is pressing the person to come drink with him, urging him to join for wine and oil and honey. In that context, the person could simply have said *shvua shelo eshteh imcha* — I swear I will not drink with you — and that single phrase would have covered all the liquids that were being offered. The fact that the person instead named wine, oil, and honey individually shows that he was identifying each one separately, and that identification — which in this context required more deliberate effort — creates three distinct *shvuot*. The *gemara* does not explicitly require that naming individually always be more effortful than a unified alternative; but Rav Acha's formulation suggests that when the individual naming required greater specification than a simpler bundled phrasing would have, that distinguishes the items as separate *shvuot*.

---

## Litigation Oaths

### Return Goods Cases

The *gemara* now cites a *mishna* from later in the *masechta* dealing with oaths in the context of litigation. One who claims: "Give me wheat, barley, and spelt that I deposited with you," and the respondent takes a single oath — *shvua she'ein lecha beyadi klum*, I swear I owe you nothing — and is lying, he is *eino chayav ela achas*: one *korban* for one *shvua*. However, if he takes an oath specifically denying each item — *shvua she'ein lecha beyadi chitin u'seorin v'chusmin* — and he is lying about all of them, he is *chayav al kol achas v'achas*: liable separately for each, for three *korbanot*.

An important distinction applies here between this *shvuat shav* or *shvuat sheker* in a litigation context and the future-oriented *shvuat bituy* discussed earlier. By a future oath — *shelo ochal* — if a person repeats the same oath twice, the principle of *ein shvua chalah al shvua* means the second oath never takes effect and only one *korban* is incurred. By an oath in litigation about the past, by contrast, each separate false oath generates its own independent liability, even if the content is redundant.

### Half-Pruta Combination

Rabbi Yochanan observes: *afilu pruta mikam mitztarefes* — even a half-*pruta*'s worth of each type can combine to create liability. The practical difficulty is this: a person is only liable for a litigation oath if he is denying something worth at least a *pruta*. If he swore a single global oath — I owe you nothing — and in fact owed half a *pruta* of wheat and half a *pruta* of barley, the two amounts combine to meet the *pruta* threshold and he is liable on the global oath. But if he made three separate specific oaths — no wheat, no barley, no spelt — and owed only half a *pruta* of each, no individual oath covered a full *pruta*'s worth. The combination across separate oath-categories is what Rabbi Yochanan addresses.

### Rav Acha vs. Ravina

Rav Acha and Ravina debate how to read the formulation *shvua she'ein lecha beyadi chitin u'seorin v'chusmin*. One opinion holds that this contains four *shvuot*: a global oath — I owe you nothing — plus three specific oaths, one for each type of grain. Under this reading, one is *chayav* both on the specifics and on the general. The other opinion holds that no global oath is embedded in the statement; the statement consists only of three specific oaths, and the general framing is merely introductory, not itself a separate *shvua*. The practical difference concerns both the number of *korbanot* and the application of Rabbi Yochanan's half-*pruta* rule. Under the view that a global oath exists, half-*pruta* amounts of different types can combine to create liability on the global oath, explaining Rabbi Yochanan's statement. Under the view that only the specifics exist, it is harder to account for cross-category combination, and Rabbi Yochanan's statement must refer back to the earlier single-oath case.

---

## Litigation Oaths (II)

### Rava's Application

Rava applies these principles back to the case of the oath not to drink wine, oil, and honey. One might ask whether the formulation *shvua shelo eshteh yayin v'shemen u'dvash* should similarly be read as containing a global oath — a general prohibition on drinking — embedded within the specific names. Rava rejects this: *hachi hashta?* How can you compare? In the litigation context, it is possible to be liable separately on a general oath and on specific oaths because each repetition of a false oath creates independent liability regardless of overlap. But in the future-oriented context of *shvuat bituy*, if you read the opening words as a general prohibition on all drinking, the specific prohibitions on wine, oil, and honey could never take effect — they would be cases of *mushba v'omed*, already subsumed under the general. Since the *mishna* clearly holds the person liable separately for each of the three, we must conclude that no general oath is embedded in the statement; the person's liability rests only on the three specific *shvuot*. Reading a global prohibition into the sentence would, paradoxically, eliminate the specific *shvuot* that are the very basis of the multiple-*korban* ruling.

---

## Treif Food Paradox

### Treif vs. Inedible

The *mishna* appears to present a contradiction. It first rules that one who takes an oath not to eat and then consumes foods that are *einam reuyim l'achilah* — not fit for eating — is *patur*. It then rules that one who takes an oath not to eat and consumes *neveilot u'treifot shekatzim u'remasim* — non-kosher meat and forbidden creatures — is *chayav*. The question is immediate: isn't non-kosher food also "not fit for eating"?

The obvious resolution, which the *gemara* has in fact noted elsewhere, is that there is a difference between something that is physically unfit for consumption — such as dirt or rotten matter — and something that is physically edible but halachically forbidden. Non-kosher food falls in the second category: it is fit to be eaten in the physical sense and is therefore within the scope of an oath not to eat. Inedible substances are outside that scope entirely, just as eating dirt on *Yom Kippur* would not constitute a violation of the *Yom Kippur* fast.

### Stam vs. Meforash

The *gemara* initially offers a different resolution: *reisha bi-stam v'seifa bi-meforesh* — the first clause deals with a general oath while the second deals with an explicit oath. Under this reading, a simple, unspecified *shvua shelo ochal* might not be understood to include non-kosher food, perhaps treating it as effectively inedible for halachic purposes. But if a person explicitly specifies in his oath that he will not eat, say, *chazir*, then it does take effect, in the same way one could explicitly swear not to eat dirt — such a *shvua* would be binding even on something ordinarily outside the scope of eating.

### Mushba V'Omed Problem

The *gemara* immediately recognizes that this answer raises a deeper problem: *amai mushba v'omed me'Har Sinai hu?* Even if the person is explicit, why should the *shvua* take effect at all? He is already forbidden from eating non-kosher food by the oath of Sinai. The principle of *mushba v'omed* holds that a personal oath cannot create a new prohibition on something already prohibited; the new *shvua* simply has nothing to grip.

### Bundling Solution

Rav, Shmuel, and Rabbi Yochanan all offer the same answer: *be'kollel dvar hamutar im dvar ha-asur* — the *shvua* takes effect when the person bundles a permitted item together with a forbidden one. If the person says, "I swear I will not eat apples and *chazir*," the oath takes hold on the apples — which were previously permitted — and by virtue of that grip, it extends to encompass the *chazir* as well. The *shvua* is not floating unsupported; it is anchored in the permitted item and radiates outward to cover the forbidden one as part of a unified prohibition.

### Reish Lakish Alt.

Reish Lakish disagrees. Merely bundling a permitted item with a forbidden one, in his view, is insufficient to make the *shvua* take effect on the forbidden item. The forbidden item — say, *chazir* — is already the subject of a standing prohibition, and a *shvua* cannot add to that regardless of what else is included in the same statement.

For Reish Lakish, the only way a *shvua* takes effect with respect to forbidden food is if the oath forbids something that was, until that moment, permitted to do. That condition is satisfied in one of two ways. First, if the person explicitly specifies less than a *kezayit* — *meforesh chatzi shiur* — because eating less than a *kezayit* of non-kosher food is not biblically prohibited, a *shvua* can forbid that sub-threshold amount and thereby genuinely create a new prohibition. Second, even without explicit specification, according to the view of Rabbi Akiva — who holds that a person's *shvua* can make even the smallest amount forbidden to him, *d'amar oser et atzmo be'chol she'hu* — the general statement of the oath automatically extends to quantities that are otherwise permitted, and the *shvua* takes effect on that basis. For Reish Lakish, then: *ee ata motzei ella im mefaresh chatzi shiur va'aliba de'rabbanan* — you cannot find a case where the *shvua* takes effect on non-kosher food unless the person explicitly specified less than a *kezayit*, according to the rabbis — *ee b'stam aliba de'Rabbi Akiva* — or unless one follows Rabbi Akiva, for whom even a general oath automatically applies to sub-*kezayit* amounts. This debate between Rav, Shmuel, and Rabbi Yochanan on the one hand and Reish Lakish on the other will be developed further in the discussion to follow.

---

---

# Shevuot 24

## Inedible vs. Non-Kosher

### Setting Up Contradiction

The *gemara* on 23b opens with a discussion of the oath "*shevua shelo ochal*" — an oath not to eat. The *mishnah* rules that if a person takes such an oath and then consumes food that is not fit for eating (*ochalin she'ein reuyin la'achilah*) or drink that is not potable (*mashkin she'ein reuyin lishtiyah*), he is *patur* — exempt from liability. Yet later in the same *mishnah*, the ruling shifts: if someone takes an oath not to eat and then eats *nevelos u'treifos*, carcasses and non-kosher animals, *shekatzim u'remasim*, creeping things and the like — he is *chayav*, liable.

The *gemara* flags this as an internal contradiction: *hagufa kashya*. The opening clause appears to treat halachically unfit food as equivalent to physically unfit food, exempting a person who eats it; yet the closing clause imposes liability for eating non-kosher food, which is also halachically unfit for consumption. *Mai sh'na reisha u'mai sh'na seifa* — what distinguishes the first case from the last?

The *gemara* offers an initial resolution: *reisha bistam, seifa bimfaresh* — the opening clause speaks of an unspecified oath ("I will not eat"), while the closing clause speaks of one who was explicit ("I will not eat non-kosher food"). When a person issues a generic oath not to eat, non-kosher food falls outside its scope because it is not considered fit for eating; but when he explicitly names non-kosher food, the oath takes effect directly on it. Of course, this reading is not explicit in the *mishnah* itself, and it is complicated by the position of *Reish Lakish*, who holds that even an explicit oath cannot take effect on something already forbidden — the principle of *ein issur chal al issur*.

### Rava's Answer: Dirt

Rava's resolution, which will emerge more fully later, is that the *mishnah*'s exemption in the opening clause refers to something that is physically inedible, like dirt (*afar*). When the *mishnah* says a person is *patur* for eating something "not fit for eating," it is not referring to *treif* food — which, though halachically forbidden, is still entirely edible in a physical sense — but to substances that no person would eat under ordinary circumstances, such as dirt or the like. This distinction will become central to the *gemara*'s ultimate resolution.

### Oath on Top of Torah

Even granting that the closing clause of the *mishnah* involves an explicit oath concerning non-kosher food, the *gemara* presses further: *amai? mushba ve'omed me'Har Sinai hu* — why should such an oath take effect at all? The person is already bound from Sinai not to eat *treif* food. This is the problem of *mushba ve'omed*: a pre-existing oath or prohibition blocks a subsequent one from taking hold. Since every Jew is already, in effect, sworn at Sinai to observe the dietary laws, a personal oath to abstain from non-kosher food should be redundant and legally inoperative — it cannot take effect on top of an existing prohibition.

---

## Issur Kolel Solution

### Broader Prohibition Works

*Rav*, *Shmuel*, and *Rabbi Yochanan* all offer the same solution to the *mushba ve'omed* problem: *bekolel devarim hamutorim im ha'asurim* — the oath encompasses both permitted and forbidden foods simultaneously. When a person swears that he will eat neither kosher food nor non-kosher food, the oath takes effect on the kosher food, which is otherwise permitted. Since the oath has a broader scope — *issur kolel* — it "grasps" the permitted food and, by extension, pulls the already-forbidden food into its orbit as well.

This is worth pausing over. The underlying concern is that a new prohibition cannot ordinarily take effect on something already prohibited. But *issur kolel* supplies an exception: when the new prohibition is wider in scope — encompassing objects not previously forbidden — it takes effect on those objects, and simultaneously reinforces its hold on the object that was already forbidden. The mechanism is that the oath's broader reach gives it independent footing.

It is worth noting a tension here with what has been discussed in preceding *dapim*: when a person says "I will not eat X and Y," we generally treat that as two separate *shevuos*, requiring two separate *korbanos* for violation. If that is so, one might have expected an oath about kosher food and an oath about non-kosher food to be evaluated independently — in which case the kosher-food oath takes effect, but the non-kosher-food oath does not, without any *kolel* mechanism. Presumably the *gemara* here envisions a case where all the food stands before the person and the oath sweeps over everything at once as a single undivided declaration — though this tension deserves attention.

### Reish Lakish Disagrees

*Reish Lakish* disagrees. He holds that *issur kolel* does not solve the problem when the second prohibition is a *shevua* — a self-imposed oath. According to *Reish Lakish*, the only way an oath can take effect on non-kosher food is by targeting something that is presently permitted by Torah law. He therefore offers a different mechanism: *ee bimfareish chatzi shiur v'aliba d'Rabbanan* — the oath explicitly forbids even less than a *kezayis*. Since the Torah only prohibits consuming a *kezayis* of forbidden food, a lesser amount is technically permitted on a biblical level. An oath forbidding even a *chatzi shiur* — less than the full prescribed amount — takes effect precisely because it addresses something the Torah has not prohibited. Alternatively, according to *Rabbi Akiva*, who holds that an oath forbids even the smallest quantity, the problem is solved in a different way — but *Reish Lakish*'s primary solution works by targeting the gap below the biblical threshold.

Here a sharp and elegant inner logic emerges: *Reish Lakish* himself is the one who holds that a *chatzi shiur* is not biblically forbidden. His own solution thus perfectly coheres with his own position. *Tosafos* notes this and raises the converse: the reason *Rabbi Yochanan* does not avail himself of *Reish Lakish*'s *chatzi shiur* solution may be that *Rabbi Yochanan* holds a *chatzi shiur* is itself biblically prohibited — in which case an oath targeting it still runs into the *mushba ve'omed* problem. The *gemara* does not state this explicitly, but *Tosafos* treats it as the elegant underlying logic. *Tosafos* further raises the question of how firmly something must be biblically prohibited before a *shevua* cannot take effect on top of it — whether a prohibition derived from a positive commandment, or the attenuated kind inferred from a subtle textual hint, suffices to block a *shevua*.

### Self vs. Automatic

The *gemara* pursues the question of why *Reish Lakish* refuses to accept *Rabbi Yochanan*'s *issur kolel* solution. The *gemara* puts the question directly: *ki amrinan issur kolel* — when do we apply the principle of *issur kolel*? The answer *Reish Lakish* would give is: *b'issur haba me'elav* — only when the broader prohibition arrives on its own, without being self-generated. If the second prohibition is externally and automatically imposed by the Torah, then when it encompasses both permitted and forbidden things, it takes hold of the forbidden things too. But if the second prohibition is generated by the person himself through a *shevua*, it cannot achieve this effect.

### Already Sworn Status

The distinction *Reish Lakish* draws between automatic and self-imposed prohibitions deserves careful examination. One way to understand it is that he views *ein shevua chala al shevua* — the rule that one oath cannot take effect on top of another — as a distinct principle, separate from the general rule of *ein issur chal al issur*. Even if *issur kolel* can override the general *ein issur chal al issur* when the second prohibition is broad enough, the specific rule governing oaths operates differently: a *shevua* is categorically incapable of taking hold of something already bound by a prior oath, including the foundational oath of Sinai.

*Tosafos* adds a different dimension: it is not merely that the person created the second prohibition, but that the *shevua* is inherently subjective — it applies only to the individual who utters it. Compare this to *Yom Kippur*, which imposes an objective, world-facing prohibition on all food. Because *Yom Kippur* objectively changes the forbidden status of the apple, it simultaneously changes the forbidden status of the *treif* hamburger. But a *shevua* is a private, personal declaration. Its effect on the apple does not carry the same objective weight, and therefore it lacks the power to add another layer of prohibition to something already objectively forbidden. The example clarifies this: when *Yom Kippur* arrives, all food — kosher and non-kosher alike — becomes forbidden. The *treif* hamburger is now doubly forbidden, once as *treif* and again as *Yom Kippur* food. Everyone agrees that *Yom Kippur*, as an automatic and objective prohibition, achieves this. But according to *Reish Lakish*, a personal self-generated oath cannot replicate that result, because its subjective nature renders it too weak to impose an additional layer of prohibition on something already objectively off-limits.

The question is also raised whether the same reasoning applies to a *neder* followed by a *shevua* on the same item — and presumably, yes, once something is already forbidden to the person, even by a prior self-generated prohibition, the subsequent *shevua* cannot take hold.

The *gemara* now notes a further elegance: this explains why *Rabbi Shimon* exempts a person who violates such an oath. According to *Reish Lakish*, the *tanna kamma*'s ruling that one is liable can only be explained by the *chatzi shiur* mechanism — the oath took effect specifically on a quantity below the biblical threshold. *Rabbi Shimon* rules that even a *chatzi shiur* carries lashes (*kol shehu lemakot*), meaning that even less than a *kezayis* was already prohibited. In that case, there was no gap for the oath to fill, and so the oath cannot take effect at all — explaining *Rabbi Shimon*'s exemption perfectly.

According to *Rabbi Yochanan*, by contrast, the reason the *tanna kamma* rules one is liable is *issur kolel* — the broader oath sweeps in the non-kosher food alongside the kosher. *Rabbi Shimon* then rejects this reasoning because he rejects *issur kolel* entirely. The *gemara* cites the *baraisa*: *Rabbi Shimon omer ha-ochel neveila be-Yom HaKippurim patur* — one who eats a carcass on *Yom Kippur* is exempt from the *Yom Kippur* sin offering. The *Yom Kippur* prohibition, though broader in scope, cannot take effect on something already forbidden. *Rabbi Shimon* denies *issur kolel* root and branch, with the result — as one student correctly observed — that many of the *gemara*'s famous exercises in stacking multiple violations onto a single act would simply not apply according to his view.

---

## Lav v'Hein Requirement

### Reversible Oaths

The *gemara* now introduces a requirement for an oath that has not yet been explicitly presented in this tractate, though the *gemara* here takes it largely for granted: the principle of *lav v'hein* — an oath must be capable of being taken in both directions. This is derived from the *pasuk* (*Vayikra* 5:4) that speaks of an oath *l'hareia o l'heitiv* — to do harm or to do good — which the *gemara* understands to mean that a binding oath must be reversible: one must be able to swear to do the thing or to refrain from doing it. If the reverse formulation would itself be invalid — for instance, an oath to commit a transgression (*shevua l'vatel et hamitzva*) — then the original oath also cannot take effect.

This requirement creates a new problem in our discussion. If a person swears not to eat non-kosher food, one might ask: can he validly swear to eat non-kosher food? Surely not — that would be a *shevua* to perform a *mitzvah*-violation. Without the valid reverse, the original oath cannot take effect either.

### Half-Measure Solution

According to *Reish Lakish*, this is not a problem. Since his mechanism involves the *chatzi shiur* — forbidding less than the minimum biblical amount — the reverse is entirely coherent. One can validly swear to eat less than a *kezayis* of non-kosher food, since that quantity is not biblically prohibited. Thus the oath forbidding even that amount satisfies the *lav v'hein* requirement: both directions of the oath are theoretically valid.

### Generic Oath Solution

According to *Rabbi Yochanan*, whose mechanism is *issur kolel*, the *lav* direction — swearing not to eat — is entirely valid: the broader oath not to eat anything takes effect on both kosher and non-kosher food. But what of the *hein* — the positive direction? Swearing that one *will* eat non-kosher food is a *shevua* to transgress, which is invalid. The *gemara* asks: *ela hein heichi mishkachat lah* — where do you find the *hein*?

The answer, which the *gemara* now articulates, resolves the difficulty cleanly. The *gemara* invokes *Rava*'s core ruling: *shevua shelo ochel v'achal afar patur* — if one swears not to eat and then eats dirt, he is exempt. What this teaches is that *treif* food is not, in fact, classified as inedible. The original assumption — that a generic oath not to eat exempts one from eating non-kosher food because it is "unfit" — was incorrect. *Treif* food is entirely edible in the physical sense; only something like dirt is genuinely inedible. Therefore, a generic oath not to eat — without any specification — encompasses *treif* food automatically. It is not necessary to name non-kosher food explicitly.

### Back to Rava's Answer

This resolves the *lav v'hein* difficulty as well. When a person says simply "I will not eat today," the oath encompasses all food — kosher and non-kosher alike. *Treif* food is considered edible; dirt is not. The *issur kolel* operates naturally: since the oath takes effect on the apple, it takes effect on the hamburger as well. And the *lav v'hein* requirement is satisfied: the reverse oath — "I will eat today" — is perfectly valid, because it covers all food, and if the person swears to eat today and eats *treif* food, he has fulfilled his oath. There is no problem of swearing to commit a transgression, because the oath is not directed specifically at the non-kosher food; it is a generic oath about eating in general.

By contrast, if a person were to say explicitly, "I swear not to eat non-kosher food," the reverse would be "I swear to eat non-kosher food" — which is invalid, and so the oath would fail the *lav v'hein* test entirely.

This also dissolves the earlier need to suppose that the *mishnah*'s closing clause involves an explicit naming of non-kosher food. The person simply says a generic oath not to eat, and since *treif* food is physically edible, it is included. The *issur kolel* mechanism then accounts for how this oath takes effect on top of the pre-existing Torah prohibition — the oath covers the apple, and because it is broader, it also covers the hamburger.

*Rav Mari* adds that this conclusion is also implied by the *mishnah* itself in a different case: if a man declares that his wife will be forbidden to him *konam*-style if he has eaten anything today (*im achalti hayom*), and it emerges that he had earlier eaten non-kosher food — his wife is forbidden. This shows that eating non-kosher food counts as eating. The *gemara*, however, qualifies this: *hatam keivan d'mei-ikara achal* — in that case, the man had already eaten the non-kosher food before the declaration. Having already eaten it, he has demonstrated through his actions (*achshavei*) that the food is edible to him. This is the principle of *achshavei*: a person's act of consumption can elevate an item's classification into the category of food, at least for purposes of a vow or oath. The *gemara* therefore cautions that this case cannot serve as proof for ours — where the oath precedes any act of eating. Before a person has eaten *treif* food, it may still be considered outside the category of edible things as far as a generic oath is concerned. Nevertheless, the *gemara* maintains its ruling: *treif* food is considered edible even prospectively, the only true exclusion being something like dirt.

---

## Kolel vs. Mosif

### Rava's Mechanism

*Rava* now asks a foundational question: *mai ta'ama d'man d'is lei issur kolel* — what is the underlying rationale for *issur kolel*? Why should an oath or prohibition that takes effect on a permitted object simultaneously reinforce its hold on an already-forbidden object? His answer: *midi de'hava a'issur mosif* — it works just like *issur mosif*. The mechanism of *issur kolel* is analogous to — and can be understood through — the already-established mechanism of *issur mosif*.

*Rava* continues: the one who exempts (*man d'patar*) — i.e., *Rabbi Shimon*, who rejects *issur kolel* — would say that *issur mosif* works when dealing with a single object (*b'chada chaticha*), but not when dealing with two different objects (*b'shtei chatichos*). The distinction is critical.

### Sister-to-Wife Example

The clearest illustration is the case of a man's sister who subsequently marries another man. Call the man *Reuven* and the sister *Leah*. Before the marriage, *Leah* is forbidden to *Reuven* as a sister. When *Leah* then marries *Mordechai*, a new prohibition takes effect — the prohibition of *eshet ish*, a married woman. Does *Reuven* now violate two prohibitions if he has relations with her: both the prohibition of a sister and the prohibition of a married woman?

This is *issur mosif* — and everyone agrees it works. The marriage prohibition is not an *issur kolel* in the technical sense; it does not expand the number of *objects* that are forbidden. Rather, it changes the status of *Leah herself*. Before the marriage, she was forbidden to one person (*Reuven*) as a sister. After the marriage, she is forbidden to the entire world as a married woman. Her own status has been transformed, and that transformation affects even *Reuven*, to whom she was already forbidden. The new prohibition took hold of *Leah* as an object — changing what she is — and because her status changed globally, it changed vis-à-vis *Reuven* as well.

### What is Kolel

*Issur kolel*, by contrast, works differently. Here the new prohibition does not change the status of the forbidden object itself. Instead, it expands the range of objects or actions that are forbidden. The paradigm case: *Yom Kippur* arrives. Before *Yom Kippur*, the apple was permitted and the *treif* hamburger was forbidden. *Yom Kippur* makes the apple forbidden. *Yom Kippur* is now broader (*kolel*) — it encompasses the apple, which was previously permitted. And because it encompasses a new set of things, it takes hold simultaneously on the hamburger, adding a second layer of prohibition there.

The key point is that the hamburger's own status has not changed. *Issur kolel* does not transform what the hamburger *is*; it simply means that the new prohibition, by sweeping in more objects, also re-prohibits the hamburger. This is a weaker mechanism than *issur mosif*, which changes the object's own status — and this is why *Rabbi Shimon* accepts *issur mosif* but rejects *issur kolel*: he holds that merely adding more forbidden objects does not supply sufficient grounds to stack a second prohibition on what was already forbidden.

### What is Mosif

*Issur mosif* thus has a precise and distinct definition: it changes the status of a single object or person, expanding the scope of who is forbidden access to that object, or the ways in which the object is itself prohibited. The *notar* example — leftover sacrificial matter — illustrates this well with an object rather than a person. The *chelev* (forbidden fat) of a sacrifice that has become *notar* (leftover past its permitted time) now cannot even be placed on the *mizbe'ach* — something that was previously possible with that fat. The object's own prohibited status has expanded. That is *mosif*.

When a person becomes *tamei* (ritually impure), by contrast, the *chelev* itself has not changed. What has changed is the person's relationship to an entire world of *korbanos*: all sacrificial food is now forbidden to him. Because more objects are now forbidden to him, the prohibition adds another layer onto the *chelev* as well. That is *kolel* — expanding the universe of forbidden things, not transforming the status of the object itself.

Similarly, when *Yom Kippur* arrives, the *chelev* has not become more forbidden on its own terms. But the *tamei* person's world of forbidden food has expanded enormously — all food is now prohibited — and that expansion generates yet another layer of prohibition on the *chelev*. Another *kolel*.

The test question: when an animal is *makdish*-ed — consecrated as a *korban* — does that represent *kolel* or *mosif* with respect to the *chelev* already inside the animal? The consecration does not expand the *chelev*'s own prohibition; rather, it makes new objects — the meat of the animal — forbidden, thus expanding the number of forbidden objects. That is *kolel* with respect to the *chelev*.

### Rabbi Shimon Rejects

*Rabbi Shimon* rejects *issur kolel* entirely. The *gemara* cites the *baraisa*: *Rabbi Shimon omer ha-ochel neveila be-Yom HaKippurim patur* — one who eats a carcass (*neveila*) on *Yom Kippur* is not liable for the *Yom Kippur* prohibition. Precisely because the *neveila* was already forbidden before *Yom Kippur*, the *Yom Kippur* prohibition — even though it is broader in scope — cannot take effect on it a second time. *Rabbi Shimon* holds that the *kolel* mechanism, no matter how broad the encompassing prohibition, cannot stack a new *issur* onto what was already prohibited.

The consequence of *Rabbi Shimon*'s position is wide-ranging. The famous *gemara* constructions in which a single act generates multiple *chatat* obligations depend on both *issur mosif* and *issur kolel*. According to *Rabbi Shimon*, cases built on *issur kolel* collapse: you cannot get a second liability for *Yom Kippur* eating if the food was already *treif*. *Issur mosif*, by contrast, *Rabbi Shimon* does accept — because there the object itself genuinely changes status, which is a qualitatively different kind of stacking.

---

## Five-Prohibition Meat

### The Setup

The *gemara* now turns to a dramatic illustration of these principles. *Yesh ochel achila achas ve'chayav aleha arba chatat ve'asham echad* — there is a case where one act of eating a single piece of food generates liability for four *chatat* sin-offerings and one *asham* guilt-offering. The case involves a person who is *tamei* (ritually impure), who eats *chelev* (forbidden fat) that had the additional status of *notar* (leftover sacrifice), that came from a *mukdashim* (sanctified animal), on *Yom Kippur*.

### Forbidden Fat

The first prohibition is *chelev* itself. From the moment an animal is born, the forbidden fat within it carries an inherent prohibition. This is the baseline *issur*, independent of anything the person does or any subsequent status the animal acquires.

### Made into Sacrifice

The second prohibition arises when the animal is consecrated — made a *korban*. The consecration creates an *issur hekdesh* on the entire animal.
