With respect to the *chelev* specifically, this is *issur kolel*: the consecration does not change the *chelev*'s own forbidden status, but it makes additional objects (the meat of the animal) forbidden. Because the scope of the new prohibition encompasses more objects — and the *chelev* is among them — a second layer of prohibition attaches to the *chelev* as well.

### Leftover Status

The third prohibition arises from the *notar* status: the sacrifice was not consumed or burned in its permitted time, and the remaining fat is now *notar*. This changes the status of the *chelev* itself — it was previously capable of being burned on the *mizbe'ach*, and now even that is foreclosed. Because the *notar* status expands the ways in which the *chelev* is prohibited — no longer merely forbidden to human consumption, but now forbidden even to the altar — this is *issur mosif*. The object's own status has been altered, and a new prohibition layers onto it as a result.

### Impurity Adds

The fourth prohibition comes from the person's *tumah*. When the person becomes *tamei*, the *chelev* itself does not change. But the *tamei* person's forbidden world expands enormously: all *korbanot* and sanctified foods are now forbidden to him. Because the *tumah* prohibition encompasses the *chelev* alongside a whole range of other sanctified items, this is *issur kolel* — expanding the universe of prohibited objects for that person, thereby adding another layer onto the already-forbidden *chelev*.

### Yom Kippur Layer

The fifth prohibition is *Yom Kippur*. When *Yom Kippur* arrives, the prohibition expands even further: now all food — not just sanctified foods — is forbidden. The *chelev* was already forbidden on multiple grounds, but *Yom Kippur* adds yet another layer via *issur kolel*, because the *Yom Kippur* prohibition encompasses even the apple and the bread that were previously permitted.

The offerings thus generated are: four *chatat* offerings (for the *chelev*, the *notar*, the *tamei* person eating sanctified food, and *Yom Kippur*) and one *asham* for the *me'ilah* — the violation of sanctified property.

### Shabbat Carrying

*Rabbi Meir* proposes a sixth prohibition: if the person carried the *chelev* in a public domain on *Shabbat* while eating it — *hotzio chayav* — he adds a *Shabbat* violation to the count. The *chachamim* respond: *eino min hashem* — carrying is not part of the act of eating; it is entirely incidental to the consumption and therefore cannot be bundled into this framework. *Rashi* further notes that *Rabbi Meir* does not raise the same point for *Yom Kippur* because he understands there to be no prohibition of carrying on *Yom Kippur* as such.

---

## Why Not Oaths?

### Oath Objection

If *issur kolel* works — and the *gemara* has been building toward affirming that it does, at least according to *Rabbi Yochanan* and *Rava* — one might ask why an oath (*shevua*) was not added to the five-prohibition example. Before *Yom Kippur*, the person could have declared a *shevua* not to eat figs and *chelev*. Since the oath takes effect on the figs (which are kosher and not otherwise forbidden), and since it is a broader oath — *issur kolel* — it would also take effect on the *chelev*. One act of eating the *chelev* should then generate an additional *chatat* for the *shevua*, bringing the total to five *chatat* offerings and one *asham*. So why does the *mishnah* stop at four?

The *gemara* answers — and does so several times, each with a slightly different rationale — that the *shevua* is simply not within the scope of the discussion. In each case, the *gemara* affirms: *ein hachi nami* — the *halacha* would indeed hold true, and an oath taken in this configuration would add another layer of prohibition via *issur kolel*. The exclusion is purely a matter of which types of prohibitions the *tanna* chose to enumerate.

### Variable Offering

The first answer: *ki tanya korban kavua* — the *mishnah* was discussing only prohibitions that carry a fixed-value *korban*. All four *chatat* offerings enumerated are fixed in value. A *shevua*, by contrast, generates a *korban oleh ve'yored* — a variable-value offering whose cost depends on the financial means of the violator. The *tanna* simply chose not to include prohibitions of that type in the discussion.

The *gemara* challenges this: *ve'harei tamei she'achal es ha'hekdesh de'korban oleh ve'yored hu* — the *korban* for a *tamei* person who ate sanctified food is itself a variable-value offering. The *gemara* responds: *bi'nasi rebbi eliezer hi* — the case in the *mishnah* involves a *nasi* (king), for whom *Rabbi Eliezer* holds that the *korban* in this case is a fixed *sa'ir* (goat), making it a fixed-value offering after all.

### No Minimum Amount

*Rabbi Ashi* offers a different answer: *ki tanya midi de'chayil ki'shiur* — the *mishnah* discusses only prohibitions that take effect relative to a minimum prescribed amount (*shiur*). A *shevua*, by contrast, can take effect even on less than the minimum, since one can formulate an oath in terms of *mashu* — any amount whatsoever. The *tanna* did not wish to include prohibitions with this characteristic in the enumeration.

The *gemara* again challenges: *ve'harei hekdesh* — the violation of *hekdesh* (*me'ilah*) also does not require a *kezayis*; all one needs is a *perutah*'s worth of benefit. The *gemara* responds: even so, *me'ilah* does have a minimum — a *perutah* — and thus it still falls within the category of prohibitions with a *shiur*. A *shevua* can be formulated with literally no minimum, which places it in a categorically different class.

### No Kares Requirement

*Rav Zeira* (cited by *Rav Ashi*) offers yet another answer: *ki tanya zedono kares* — the *mishnah* discusses only prohibitions whose willful violation carries the penalty of *kares*, divine excision. All four *chatat* violations listed carry *kares* for deliberate transgression. A *shevua* does not: its willful violation incurs a standard penalty and a *korban*, but not *kares*. Therefore the *tanna* excluded it.

The *gemara* challenges: *ve'harei asham de'zedono lav* — the *asham* for *me'ilah* does not carry *kares* for willful violation; it is merely a standard negative prohibition. How can *kares* be the criterion if *me'ilah* is already in the list without it? The *gemara* responds: *be'chataos ka'amina* — the *kares* criterion applies specifically to the *chatat* offerings in the list. Within the category of *chataot*, only standard ones backed by *kares* were considered. The *asham* is a separate category and is not bound by that criterion.

### Non-Physical Acts

*Ravina* offers the final answer: *ki tanya midi de'chaila a'midi de'var achila hu* — the *mishnah* discusses prohibitions that take effect on physical food objects. A *shevua*, by contrast, can take effect on non-physical actions — one can swear to sleep or not to sleep, to stand or not to stand. Its scope extends beyond the domain of physical objects. The *tanna* did not wish to include a category of prohibition so untethered from the object-based framework of the discussion.

The *gemara* challenges: *hekdesh de'chayil nami a'etzim va'avanim* — *hekdesh* can also take effect on wood and stones, things that are not food. The *gemara* responds: that is true, but when we say *hekdesh* appears in our list, we are referring to its characteristic mode of operation in relation to physical consumables. The *shevua*, however, characteristically operates even on purely non-physical acts — *kegon she'ishan ve'shelo yishan* — such as swearing to take a nap or not to take a nap. That distinguishing characteristic of the *shevua* is what placed it outside the scope of the *mishnah*'s enumeration.

### Oath Affirmed

In every case, the *gemara*'s refrain is *ein hachi nami*: yes, the *halacha* is true. Had a *shevua* been included, it would indeed have added an additional layer of prohibition via *issur kolel*. Even though a *shevua* is self-generated — a fact that led *Reish Lakish* to reject *issur kolel* for *shevuos* — the accepted position (that of *Rabbi Yochanan*, *Rava*, and the *tanna kamma*) is that a self-imposed oath of broader scope does follow the *issur kolel* mechanism and can take effect on top of a pre-existing prohibition. The *mishnah*'s silence about *shevuos* in the five-prohibition example reflects only the *tanna*'s choice of scope, not a rejection of the principle.

---

---

# Shevuot 25

## Shevuat Bituy Overview

### Opening & Parameters

The daf opens with the *mishnah* on *shevuat bituy* — the oath addressed by the verse *lehara o leheitiv u'lechol asher yevatei ha'adam bishvuah*, the oath to do good, to do bad, or anything a person enunciates with an oath. The Torah specifies that when such an oath is violated *b'shogeg*, with the matter having become hidden from him (*vene'elam mimenu*), the person brings a *korban oleh v'yored*. The *daf* examines the basic parameters of this *shevuah* and the various debates that define its scope.

### Mishnah Four Categories

The *mishnah* opens by establishing two axes along which *shevuat bituy* operates. The first axis is *echad devarim shel atzmo v'echad devarim shel acherim* — the *shevuah* applies whether it concerns something you yourself will do or something that involves another person. This requires some nuance: an oath that Reuven will give Shimon a hundred dollars is not in your control, and such an oath would not be included. The cases involving others that *are* included are those still within the swearer's own power, as we shall see. The second axis is *v'echad devarim she'yesh bahen mamash v'echad devarim she'ein bahen mamash* — whether the oath pertains to something of concrete substance or something without substance, whether it relates to a physical object or not.

### Mishnah Examples

The *mishnah* then illustrates these categories with concrete examples. The first example — *amar shevuah she'etein l'ploni v'shelo etein*, an oath to give or not give to someone, *she'natati v'shelo natati*, that I have given or have not given — illustrates a *shevuah* involving another person that remains within one's own control. The second example — *she'ishan v'shelo ishan*, that I will sleep or will not sleep, *she'yashanti v'shelo yashanti*, that I slept or did not sleep — illustrates a *davar she'ein bo mamash*, something without physical substance: sleep is an abstract condition, not a concrete object. The third example — *she'ezrok tzror l'yam v'shelo ezrok, she'zarakti v'shelo zarakti*, that I will throw or will not throw a rock into the sea, that I did throw or did not throw — is explained by Rashi as also capturing the notion of *ein bo mamash*, not in the sense that the rock is intangible, but that the act is entirely neutral, neither beneficial nor harmful. It is neither *lehara* nor *leheitiv* in any real sense, and so it represents a completely gratuitous act.

Each example pairs a positive and a negative formulation, and both a future and a past formulation, and this double pairing will become central to the debates that follow.

### Yishmael vs. Akiva

The *mishnah* records a significant *machloket* regarding the temporal scope of *shevuat bituy*. Rabbi Yishmael holds *eino chayav ela al ha'atid lavo* — liability attaches only to an oath about what one will or will not do in the future. His source is the verse itself: *lehara o leheitiv*, to do bad or to do good — both formulations are future-oriented.

Rabbi Akiva presses back: if you are going to read the verse so literally, then the *shevuah* should only apply to things that are genuinely harmful or beneficial — *devarim she'yesh bahen hara v'hatavah* — to the exclusion of a completely neutral act like throwing a rock into the sea. How do we know that neutral acts are included? Because the verse continues *l'chol asher yevatei ha'adam bishvuah* — for anything a person enunciates as an oath — which is broadly inclusive. Rabbi Yishmael grants this point. Rabbi Akiva then turns it back on him: once you have already expanded beyond the literal meaning of *lehara o leheitiv* through the inclusive phrase *l'chol asher yevatei*, why stop there? Once neutral acts are included, past acts should equally be included through the same expansion. The *gemara* will shortly examine how far this reasoning extends.

---

## Nedarim vs. Shevuot

### Nedarim Stringencies

Before drilling down into the specifics of the *mishnah*'s examples, the *gemara* presents a *baraita* that contrasts *nedarim* and *shevuot* along their respective axes of stringency. *Chomer bin'darim mibishvuot*: a *neder* has a broader scope than a *shevuah* in one critical respect. *Nedarim chalim al devar mitzvah k'dvar reshut* — a *neder* takes effect even on objects associated with a *mitzvah*, ultimately leading to the *mitzvah*'s non-performance. A *shevuah*, by contrast, cannot do this. If someone takes an oath that he will not sit in a *sukkah* or will not take a *lulav*, that *shevuah* does not take effect, because *mushba v'omed m'har sinai* — he is already bound from Sinai to perform the *mitzvah*, and a *shevuah* cannot obligate him to do what the Torah forbids or contradict an existing obligation. A *neder*, however, operates differently: it does not confront the obligation head-on but rather attaches forbidden status to the object. By declaring the *sukkah* or *lulav* prohibited to him, the person is not directly violating his obligation — but when the time comes, he is unable to fulfill it because the object itself has been rendered forbidden. That indirect mechanism is something a *shevuah* cannot replicate.

### Shevuot Stringencies

The reverse stringency is *chomer bishvuot*: *hashvuah chalah al davar she'ein bo mamash kedavar sheyesh bo mamash* — a *shevuah* takes effect even on matters without substance, as when a person swears he will not sleep. *Ma she'ein kein binedarim* — a *neder* cannot operate this way, because a *neder* attaches to an object, and sleep is not an object. One might try to formulate it creatively — "my eyes are forbidden to me for the purpose of sleep" — but the sleep itself, as an abstract act, cannot be made *assur* through a *neder*. This contrast sets up the *mishnah*'s discussion nicely, since the examples it provides — giving, sleeping, throwing a rock — each illustrate dimensions that distinguish *shevuot* from *nedarim*.

---

## Gemara on Examples

### Giving Example

The *gemara* returns to the *mishnah*'s first example: *she'etein l'ploni v'shelo etein*, an oath to give to someone. The *gemara* asks: *mai etein*? If this refers to giving *tzedakah* to a poor person, then this *shevuah* cannot take effect — *mushba v'omed m'har sinai hu*, the person is already obligated, as the verse says *venason titein lo*, you must give. A *shevuah* cannot create a double obligation where you are already bound. The *mishnah* must therefore be speaking of *matanah l'ashir*, a gift to a wealthy person, where there is no pre-existing obligation and the *shevuah* therefore operates normally.

### Sleeping Example

The *gemara* then examines the *mishnah*'s second example — an oath about sleeping — and raises a question. Is it really true that an oath not to sleep takes effect as a *shevuat bituy*? But Rabbi Yochanan taught: if someone swears *shelo ishan gimel yamim*, that he will not sleep for three days, we administer *malkus* immediately, and he may then go and sleep. The reason: it is not possible for a person to go three days without sleeping, so this oath is patently impossible — it falls into the category of *shevuat shav*, an oath on something manifestly false, like swearing one can fly. A *shevuat shav* yields *malkus* immediately but does not create the *shevuat bituy* liability of the *korban oleh v'yored*. So how can the *mishnah*'s example about sleep be a *shevuat bituy* at all?

The *gemara* resolves this: *hasam d'amar gimel, hacha d'lo amar gimel* — the case of *shevuat shav* is where one specified three days, an explicitly impossible commitment. In our *mishnah*, no such time frame was specified. If one simply says "I won't sleep," context suggests it means tonight or some limited period, and we do not assume it means forever. Therefore it is not a *shevuat shav*, and the person's compliance or non-compliance with the oath is what determines liability.

### Rock Example & Rav/Shmuel

The third example of the *mishnah* — throwing a rock into the sea — leads the *gemara* to a new *sugyah*. The *mishnah* presents the case both in the future and past tense: *she'ezrok* and *she'zarakti*. Now a new case is introduced: *shvuah shezarak ploni tzror l'yam v'shelo zarak* — an oath that Ploni threw a rock into the sea or did not. An oath in the future that Reuven *will* throw the rock would not be valid as a *shevuat bituy*, since that is not within one's own control. But what about framing it in the past, according to Rabbi Akiva who holds that past oaths incur liability? Here one might have knowledge about what another person did, and that is not entirely outside one's purview. On this, *Rav* and *Shmuel* disagree. *Rav amar chayav*: one is liable. *Shmuel amar patur*: one is exempt.

---

## Rav vs. Shmuel Debate

### Rav's Position

*Rav* holds that one is liable for such an oath — *ita belav hachi* — because the real test for *shevuat bituy* is whether the oath can be cast in both the positive and the negative, *lav v'hein*. Since one can say either "Ploni threw the rock" or "Ploni did not throw the rock," the oath satisfies the criterion of *lehara o leheitiv*. That is the only genuine criterion: can the oath be formulated in the positive, and can the same oath be formulated in the negative? If both are coherent, the oath is valid, and if it turns out to be false, one is liable.

### Shmuel's Position

*Shmuel* holds one is exempt — *leisa b'lehaba* — because there is an additional criterion beyond *lav v'hein*: even according to Rabbi Akiva who extends liability to past oaths, that extension is only to oaths that *could* be formulated as a future-oriented oath. The paradigm for *shevuat bituy* is *lehara o leheitiv*, which is inherently future-directed. A past oath is included only by virtue of the expansion *l'chol asher yevatei*, but that expansion brings in only past formulations that are modeled on a possible future formulation. Since saying "Reuven will throw a rock into the sea" would not be a valid *shevuat bituy* — it is not within one's control — there is no future version of this oath that qualifies, and therefore the past version equally fails to qualify.

### Within Akiva Framework

One might initially suppose that *Rav* and *Shmuel* are simply replaying the dispute of Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva — whether past oaths carry liability at all. The *gemara* rejects this. *Aliba d'Rabbi Yishmael kulei alma lo peligi*: there is nothing interesting to debate within Rabbi Yishmael's framework, because Rabbi Yishmael categorically excludes all past oaths. Even a past formulation that *could* be made into a future oath — such as "I ate" or "I did not eat," which maps onto "I will eat" or "I will not eat" — is excluded by Rabbi Yishmael, who insists the verse *lehara o leheitiv* refers only to the future. If so, something that cannot even be framed in the future would be excluded a fortiori, with no need for debate. *Ki peligi aliba d'Rabbi Akiva*: the debate is entirely within Rabbi Akiva's framework. *Rav* reads Rabbi Akiva simply as including past oaths, full stop. *Shmuel* reads Rabbi Akiva more narrowly: Rabbi Akiva extends liability to the past only where the oath is modeled on a possible future formulation. Something that cannot be cast in the future — because it concerns another person's actions outside one's control — Rabbi Akiva would also not include.

### Shmuel's Reasoning

The *gemara* now develops *Shmuel*'s reasoning in greater depth. The *gemara* asks whether the debate between *Rav* and *Shmuel* might itself be a reflection of the earlier dispute between Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira and the Rabbanan. In the upcoming *mishnah*, there is a dispute about someone who takes a *shevuah lekayem et hamitzvah* — a sworn commitment to perform a *mitzvah* he is already obligated to perform — and then fails to do so. The *Tanna Kamma* says he is exempt, because such a *shevuah* is not valid as a *shevuat bituy*: since a *shevuah* to *negate* the *mitzvah* would not take effect (one cannot swear to violate an obligation), the positive and negative forms are not both valid, and the criterion of *lav v'hein* is not met. Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira argues one *should* be liable — if the oath works in one direction and you violated it, you should be accountable. The Rabbanan counter: *sheken lo asah bo lav vahen* — a *shevuah* to perform a *mitzvah* fails the *lav v'hein* test, because the reverse oath — "I will not take the *lulav*" — is not a valid *shevuat bituy* but rather a nullified oath that contravenes an obligation.

The *gemara* tentatively suggests that *Rav* follows Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira (no *lav v'hein* requirement) while *Shmuel* follows the Rabbanan (*lav v'hein* is required). But the *gemara* rejects this, establishing a more refined hierarchy. *Aliba d'Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira kulei alma lo peligi*: if Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira does not even require *lav v'hein* — the criterion most explicitly rooted in the verse *lehara o leheitiv* — he certainly would not require *lehaba*, that the oath be formable in the future, which is a less explicit requirement. So all opinions would agree that within Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira's framework, *Rav*'s position trivially follows, and no debate is needed. *Ki peligi aliba d'Rabbanan*: the live question is within the Rabbanan's framework, who do require *lav v'hein*. *Shmuel* holds that just as the Rabbanan derive from *lehara o leheitiv* that the oath must be formable in the positive and negative, they similarly require that a past oath be frameable in the future. *Rav* responds: the *lav v'hein* requirement is explicitly in the verse — *lehara o leheitiv*, positive and negative — and so it is a hard requirement. The *lehaba* requirement, by contrast, rests on the generic expansion *l'chol asher yevatei*, with no textual basis to import into it a future-formulation criterion. Accordingly, even the Rabbanan who require *lav v'hein* would not extend that logic to require *lehaba*, and therefore *Rav* and the Rabbanan alike would hold that a past oath about another person's actions is valid.

---

## Hamnuna Challenge

### Mishnah Proof

Rav Hamnuna raises a challenge to *Shmuel*'s position from a *mishnah* at the end of the chapter. The *mishnah* presents a case where someone says *lo achalti hayom* — I did not eat today — and *lo hinachti tefillin hayom* — I did not put on *tefillin* today — and another person then imposes a *shevuah* upon him (*mashbia ani aleicha*), and he responds *amen*, which is treated as equivalent to having uttered the *shevuah* himself. The *mishnah* rules him liable.

### Problem for Shmuel

Both examples are past-tense oaths, consistent with Rabbi Akiva. The first, *lo achalti* — I did not eat — poses no difficulty for *Shmuel*: one can easily formulate the future version, *lo ochel*, I will not eat. That future oath is a standard *shevuat bituy*, so the past formulation maps cleanly onto it and liability is established even by *Shmuel*'s criterion. But the second example, *lo hinachti tefillin*, is a powerful challenge. One cannot formulate the future version — "I will not put on *tefillin*" — as a valid *shevuat bituy*, because that is a *shevuah levatel et hamitzvah*, an oath to violate an obligation, which does not take effect. Here, then, is a past oath that has no valid future counterpart, yet the *mishnah* rules the person liable — precisely the outcome *Rav* predicts and *Shmuel* should deny.

### Shmuel's Answer

Rav Hamnuna himself poses the challenge and himself supplies the answer. *Hu masiv lah v'hu mefarek lah*. The *mishnah*, he explains, speaks *l'stama* — it is not internally differentiating between the two cases in terms of the *type* of liability. *Lo achalti l'korban*: the first case, not eating, generates full *shevuat bituy* liability, including the *korban oleh v'yored* if violated *b'shogeg* — because it has a valid future version. *Lo hinachti tefillin l'malkus*: the second case, not having put on *tefillin*, generates only *malkus* liability in the event of willful violation — because the *malkus* prohibition of *lo tishavu vishmi lashaker* / *lo sisa shem* operates without the constraints imposed by the *psukim* governing the *korban oleh v'yored*. The requirements of *lehara o leheitiv*, whether something must be *lehaba*, and related criteria — all of these are features of the *sugyah* of *korban oleh v'yored*. For *malkus* alone, none of these limitations apply.

This is, admittedly, a strained reading of the *mishnah*, given that the entire chapter is focused on the *korban*. The simpler reading — and the reading that flows more naturally — is *Rav*'s: *lo hinachti tefillin* generates *korban* liability even though it lacks a future formulation. *Shmuel*'s reading requires understanding that the *mishnah* silently introduces a case of mere *malkus* amid a chapter devoted to the *korban*. Nevertheless, that is how *Shmuel* must answer.

---

## Shav vs. Bituy

### Shevuat Shav Defined

*Rava* raises a further inquiry concerning the boundary between *shevuat shav* and *shevuat bituy*. To sharpen the question, the *gemara* cites a *mishnah* defining *shevuat shav*: if one swears *levatel et hayadu'a la'adam* — to deny or affirm something that is patently known — that is a *shevuat shav*. The example given is swearing *al amud shel even shehu shel zahav* — that a stone pillar is gold. *Ulla* adds a qualification: *v'hu shenikar l'gimel bnei adam* — for it to be *shevuat shav*, the falseness of the claim must be apparent to at least three people. The reasoning is clear: when something is known to everyone to be obviously false, swearing that it is otherwise is an empty, silly oath — it fools no one and is therefore *shav*, vain. But if only one or two people happen to know the truth, and the broader public does not, then a false oath on the matter is a *shevuat sheker* — a genuine lie, a deception — not a *shevuat shav*.

### Stone Example Problem

The *gemara* deduces from this: *taima d'nikar* — the reason it is *shevuat shav* is because the stone-nature of the pillar is plainly evident to everyone. *Ha lo nikar* — but if it were not obvious, say because the stone had been painted to look like gold, then it would *not* be *shevuat shav*, and the implication seems to be that it would be *shevuat bituy*, seemingly making the person liable for a *korban* if he violated it. But this creates a problem, at least for *Shmuel*: such an oath is *leisa l'haba* — one cannot formulate a future version of it. You cannot swear "I will make this stone into gold," because that is not *b'yadecha* — not within human capability.

### Rava's Answer

*Hu masiv lah v'hu mefarek lah* — Rava himself poses and resolves the question. If the falseness *is* obvious — that is, three people can see it is stone — then swearing it is gold is *shevuat shav*, and one receives *malkus* for that. If the falseness is *not* obvious — the stone is painted and appears to be gold — then the false oath is *shevuat sheker*, not *shevuat bituy*. The implicit contrast in the *mishnah* between *nikar* and *lo nikar* is not drawing a distinction between *shevuat shav* and *shevuat bituy* at all; it is drawing a distinction between *shevuat shav* and *shevuat sheker*. The *mishnah* is not speaking about the *korban* context in that contrast — it is simply delineating when an oath is empty-and-vain versus when it is an outright lie. Whether the *sheker* case would generate *korban* liability is a separate question entirely not addressed by the *mishnah*, and no inference about the *lehaba* requirement can be drawn from it. This is, in any case, a notably weaker proof than the *tefillin* case, precisely because it can be dispatched so cleanly.

---

## Abaye on Lav v'Hein

### Testimony Case Setup

The *gemara* now records a statement by Abaye: *u'modeh Rav b'omer l'chaveiro shvuah she'ani yode'a lecha edut v'ishtakhakh d'lo yada leih d'patur* — even *Rav* concedes that if someone swore "I know testimony for you" and it turned out he was mistaken, or did not in fact know, he is exempt. This is surprising at first glance. The oath "I know testimony for you" is past-tense, and it has a *lav v'hein* — one could say "I do not know testimony for you." *Rav* does not require *lehaba*, so there should be no obstacle. Why, then, does even *Rav* say the person is exempt?

### Abaye's Innovation

Abaye's innovation is the following: although the positive and negative formulations both exist — "I know" and "I do not know" — they do not occupy the *same* legal category. The positive, "I know testimony for you" (*she'ani yode'a lecha edut*), is a standard statement that would fall under *shevuat bituy* if anything. But the negative, "I do not know testimony for you," is not a *shevuat bituy* — it is a *shevuat ha'edut*, the subject of an entirely separate *parshah* in the Torah. Since the *lav* and the *hein* belong to different categories, they are not considered to constitute a proper *lav v'hein* for the purposes of *shevuat bituy*. For the *lav v'hein* criterion to be satisfied, the positive and negative formulations must both fall within the *same* category of oath. When the negative falls under *shevuat ha'edut* rather than *shevuat bituy*, the criterion is not met, and the positive oath — "I know testimony" — does not generate *korban* liability.

### Past Oaths Examples

This analysis allows the *gemara* to clarify which past oath cases are subject to the *Rav-Shmuel* debate. *Yadati v'lo yadati* — "I knew testimony" or "I did not know testimony" — this is the *machloket* between *Rav* and *Shmuel*. Both formulations are in *lav v'hein* and both are past-tense, but neither can be made future-oriented (swearing "I will know testimony" or "I will not know testimony" relates to *mitzvah* obligations and does not operate as a standard *shevuat bituy*). Similarly, *he'adati v'lo he'adati* — "I testified" or "I did not testify" — is equally the *machloket*: both are past-tense and in *lav v'hein*, but a future oath about whether to testify would be either a *shevuah lekayem et hamitzvah* or *levatel et hamitzvah*, and therefore not applicable in the *korban oleh v'yored* framework. These cases, then, sit squarely in the dispute between *Rav* and *Shmuel*.

---

## Shevuat Ha'edut Category

### Shmuel's Explanation

The *gemara* now raises a foundational question about *shevuat ha'edut* as a separate Torah category. *Bishlama leShmuel*: the question works out elegantly for *Shmuel*. *Shmuel* holds that a past oath generates *korban* liability only if it can be formulated in the future. *Lo yada'ti* — "I do not know testimony for you" — cannot be made future-oriented: "I will not know testimony" is not a proper future *shevuat bituy* (it relates to a *mitzvah* obligation). Therefore, this oath would not be a *shevuat bituy* for *Shmuel*, and it would escape the *korban* framework entirely — unless the Torah created a separate category. *Lehachi afkei Rachmana lishvuat ha'edut michlal shvuat bituy*: that is precisely why the Torah extracted *shevuat ha'edut* from the general framework of *shevuat bituy* and established it as an independent category with its own *korban*. For *Shmuel*, the need for a separate category of *shevuat ha'edut* is entirely motivated: without it, the classic case of false denial of testimony would carry no *korban* liability at all.

### Rav's Problem

For *Rav*, however, a serious question arises. *Ela l'Rav lemai hilkheta afkei Rachmana* — why did the Torah bother creating a separate category of *shevuat ha'edut*? According to *Rav*, "I do not know testimony for you" is a past-tense oath that is in *lav v'hein* — one can say "I do" or "I do not" — and the *lehaba* criterion is not required. It should therefore be a perfectly ordinary *shevuat bituy* and generate the standard *korban*. What was accomplished by creating the separate category? If *shevuat ha'edut* is just a subset of *shevuat bituy* in disguise, the Torah's separate treatment of it needs explanation.

### Abaye's Answer

The rabbinic students present before Abaye suggest: *lechiyuvei aleih tartei* — the reason the Torah created a separate category is so that one becomes liable for *two korbanot*, one as a *shevuat ha'edut* and one as a *shevuat bituy*. Abaye rejects this: *tarti lo matzis amras* — you cannot obligate someone to bring two *korbanot* for a single act. The Torah says *l'achat me'eileh* — "one of these" — and a *beraita* derives from this: *l'achat atah mechayevo v'ee atah mechayevo shtayim*, you can only hold him liable for one, not for two. Double jeopardy does not apply in this framework.

Abaye himself then provides the correct answer: *l'chiddetanya* — as we are taught in a *beraita*, by all the other cases of *korban oleh v'yored* — *tumah*, *shevuat bituy* — the Torah specifies *vene'elam mimenu*, that the matter was hidden from him, that the person sinned in a state of unawareness. But by *shevuat ha'edut*, the Torah omits this condition. The *halacha* derived from this omission is *lechayev al hameizid keshogeg* — to hold even a willful violator liable, treating *meizid* like *shogeg* for purposes of the *korban* obligation. This is admittedly a striking ruling — bringing a *korban* for a *meizid* act is highly unusual. But that is the *halacha* of *shevuat ha'edut*. The reason the Torah needed its own category, then, was to capture this unique ruling: when a person lies about testimony in precisely the *shevuat ha'edut* circumstances (a qualified witness, testimony of monetary consequence), he is liable for a *korban* even if he acted willfully.

### Ne'elam Criterion

The *gemara* then addresses the *ne'elam* criterion more specifically. By *shevuat bituy*, *shevuat tumah*, and similar cases, the Torah writes *vene'elam mimenu* — it was hidden from him — which is the basis for the requirement of *shogeg* to generate *korban* liability. By *shevuat ha'edut*, no such *ne'elam* condition is stated, and it is from this absence that the Rabbanan derived the rule that even *meizid* generates the *korban*. This structural difference — the presence or absence of the *ne'elam* language — is what formally separates *shevuat ha'edut* as its own category with its own internal logic, distinct from the standard requirements of *shevuat bituy*.

---

## Abaye Contradiction

### Earlier Abaye Statement

The *gemara* surfaces an apparent internal contradiction in Abaye's positions. Earlier, Abaye stated that even *Rav* concedes that swearing "I know testimony for you" (*she'ani yode'a lecha edut*) does not generate *korban* liability — because the corresponding negative form, "I do not know testimony for you," is not a *shevuat bituy* but a *shevuat ha'edut*, meaning the two forms belong to different categories and thus do not constitute proper *lav v'hein* for *shevuat bituy*. The implication of this statement is that *shevuat ha'edut* is its *own* separate category — entirely distinct from *shevuat bituy* — such that when the negative falls under *shevuat ha'edut*, it does not "count" as the negative version of a *shevuat bituy*.

### Later Implication

But later — in answering the question of why the Torah needed to create a separate category of *shevuat ha'edut* — Abaye's answer was that this category exists *lechayev al hameizid*, to obligate even the willful violator. Embedded in Abaye's dismissal of the students' suggestion (that *shevuat ha'edut* generates two *korbanot*) is the concession that *shevuat ha'edut* is *also* a *shevuat bituy* — just one that carries only a single *korban* because of *l'achat me'eileh*. But if *shevuat ha'edut* is also a *shevuat bituy*, then the negative form, "I do not know testimony," *is* within the *lav v'hein* of *shevuat bituy* — and Abaye's earlier statement that swearing "I do know testimony" is exempt would be incorrect. After all, the reverse oath, "I do not know," *does* exist as a *shevuat bituy* (even though it is also a *shevuat ha'edut*), and so the *lav v'hein* criterion for *shevuat bituy* should be satisfied.

### Contradiction Resolved

The *gemara* resolves this directly: *hadar beih Abaye mehahi* — Abaye retracted one of his positions. While it is not entirely clear which statement he retracted, the drift of the *gemara* is that he retracted the earlier ruling — that "I know testimony" is exempt even for *Rav*. His later position would be that *shevuat ha'edut* is simultaneously a *shevuat bituy*, and therefore the *lav v'hein* is met: "I do not know testimony" serves as the *lav* within the *shevuat bituy* framework (and it is also a *shevuat ha'edut*). Accordingly, swearing "I know testimony" would be a valid *shevuat bituy* with a proper negative counterpart, and a person who did so falsely *would* be liable — according to *Rav* — for a *korban*.

### Alternative Resolutions

The *gemara* offers an additional resolution at the opening of 26b: *chada mineihu Rav Pappa amrah* — one of these two statements was in fact made by Rav Pappa, not by Abaye, and it was attributed to Abaye. In that case, the contradiction dissolves entirely, because the two statements are from different authorities and need not be reconciled. The practical upshot in *halacha* appears to be: according to Abaye, *shevuat ha'edut* retains membership in the *shevuat bituy* category, but constitutes only one *korban* obligation (not two); whereas according to Rava's formulation, once the Torah extracted *shevuat ha'edut* as its own category — motivated by the need to create *chiyuv* for *meizid* — the act falls *only* under *shevuat ha'edut* and not under *shevuat bituy* at all, applying the principle of *davar shehayah bichlal veyatza lidon b'davar chadash*, that once something is given a new independent status it is treated exclusively by that new status.

---

---

# Shevuot 26

## Future vs. Past Oaths

### Intro to Daf 26

Daf 26 opens by examining the parameters governing when one is obligated to bring a *korban* for violating a *shvua*. The Torah's language is explicit: *lehara o leheitiv* — to do bad or to do good — which is inherently future-oriented. There is universal agreement that this phrase extends beyond oaths concerning explicitly harmful or beneficial acts to encompass even neutral activities. A further principle derived from *lehara o leheitiv* is that the oath must be reversible — it must constitute a meaningful *shvua* whether framed positively or negatively.

### Lehara/Leheitiv

The requirement of reversibility means that whatever one swears must be capable of being expressed in both its positive and negative formulations and remain a valid oath in either case. This is part of what the phrase *lehara o leheitiv* communicates structurally: the subject matter must be the kind of thing about which one could meaningfully swear either to do or to refrain from doing.

### Shvuas Sheker

A foundational distinction must be drawn at the outset. When someone swears about something in the past — for example, declaring "I ate" when in fact he did not — the most natural description of that act is a *shvuat sheker*, a false oath. Indeed, that is precisely what it is. If done intentionally, one incurs lashes; the act is classified as *shvuat sheker*. The question that animates the discussion on this daf is narrower: does such an oath also constitute a *shvuat bituy* — that is, does it fall within the Torah's category of an expressed oath whose violation triggers a *korban* when done inadvertently? The term *shvuat bituy* refers to the oath the Torah describes through the phrase *levatei bisfatayim*, to express with one's lips, for which a *korban* is brought when violated *beshogeg*. The specific question is whether a past-oriented *shvuat sheker* belongs to this category — since the structure of *shvuat bituy* normally envisions first making the oath and then potentially violating it through subsequent action, whereas in the past-oriented case the person is lying at the very moment of utterance.

### Rav/Shmuel Debate

This question was explored in the preceding daf through the debate between Rav and Shmuel concerning an oath about something in the past that could not meaningfully be reversed or restated in the future. One category of such cases involves *shvuat ha-edus* — testifying under oath about knowledge of testimony. To negate that oath, one would say "I don't know testimony," which is a valid *shvua*, but it belongs to an entirely different legal category. Similarly, declaring "I will know testimony" or "I will not know testimony" in the future is not within a person's control. Because such oaths cannot be reversed and remain within the same category, Rav and Shmuel debated whether a *korban* would be incurred at all. All of this belongs to the broader inquiry into the boundaries of *korban* liability.

## Rabbi Yishmael vs. Akiva

### Braisa on Oaths

The Gemara now returns to the central *tannaitic* dispute. *Rabbi Yishmael omer eino chayav ela al ha-asid lavo* — Rabbi Yishmael holds that liability for a *korban* applies only to future-oriented oaths. Rabbi Akiva maintains that even a past-oriented oath can generate *korban* liability.

A *braisa* records the hermeneutical reasoning. The verse begins: *o nefesh ki tishava levatei bisfatayim* — if a soul swears, to express with his lips. This is a general, inclusive statement. It then narrows: *lehara o leheitiv* — to do bad or to do good. The *braisa* derives from the opening *klal* that even oaths about neutral matters — those that involve neither harm nor benefit in any obvious sense — are included. Yet one might have thought the phrase is limited to the future. The verse then closes with a broad statement: *lechol asher yivatei ha-adam bishvua* — anything that a person expresses by oath. Rabbi Akiva reads this final phrase as including past-oriented oaths, citing the pattern of *klal u-prat u-klal*.

Rabbi Yishmael responds: *lehara o leheitiv lehaba* — the oath must be future-oriented. Rabbi Akiva then presses him: if you insist on limiting the verse so strictly, how do you include even neutral acts? Rabbi Yishmael answers that the final inclusive phrase — *me-ribui ha-kasuv* — expands the scope. Rabbi Akiva rejoins: *im riba ha-kasuv lekach riba ha-kasuv lekach* — if you concede that the verse broadens the scope once, that same broadening must also include past-oriented oaths. The Gemara notes: *shapir ka-amar lei Rabbi Akiva* — Rabbi Akiva made a compelling point. Once Rabbi Yishmael concedes that the verse expands beyond the literal *prat*, there is no principled reason to expand toward neutral acts while refusing to expand toward past-oriented ones.

### Akiva's Critique

Rabbi Akiva's critique is pointed precisely because it catches Rabbi Yishmael in an internal inconsistency. Rabbi Yishmael wants to use the *ribui* of the final phrase to include neutral acts, but not to include past-oriented acts. Rabbi Akiva demonstrates that this is hermeneutically incoherent: once expansion is granted, it must proceed along consistent lines.

### Hermeneutics Methods

Rabbi Yochanan resolves the apparent tension by locating each authority's position within the broader hermeneutical school he inherited. Rabbi Yishmael, who had closely attended upon Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKanah — *she-shimmesh es Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKanah* — and who was his foremost disciple, adopted his master's method of interpreting the entire Torah through *klal u-ferat*: general and specific principles. Rabbi Yishmael therefore reads the verse through *klal u-ferat* hermeneutics.

Rabbi Akiva, who had similarly devoted himself to Nachum Ish Gamzu — the sage known for his declaration *gam zu le-tovah* — inherited his master's method of *ribui u-miyut*: inclusion and exclusion. Rabbi Yochanan notes: *ihu nami doresh be-ribui u-miyut* — Rabbi Akiva likewise interprets through inclusion and exclusion, and therefore extracts more from the verses than Rabbi Yishmael does.

This is not the familiar debate about whether *dibrah Torah ki-leshon benei adam* — whether the Torah speaks in ordinary human language, with Rabbi Yishmael being less inclined to derive meaning from every formulation. Here, both authorities agree that the verses present a general statement, a specific one, and another general statement. The disagreement is purely hermeneutical: which system of derivation applies? One approach broadens the specific somewhat; the other yields a far more expansive result.

It is worth noting, as an aside, that the thirteen hermeneutical principles recited each morning — *yud-gimel middos she-ha-Torah nidreshes ba-hen*, attributed to Rabbi Yishmael — appear at the opening of the *Sifra*, the midrashic work on Vayikra associated precisely with the school of Rabbi Akiva. The irony is not lost, though we will not pursue it further here.

## Ribui u-Miyut

### Three Stages

The Gemara now demonstrates concretely that Rabbi Akiva employs *ribui u-miyut*, citing the relevant *braisa*: *o nefesh ki tishava* — if a soul swears — this is the first term, an inclusive statement, *riba*, which encompasses everything. *Lehara o leheitiv* — to do bad or good — this is the second term, an excluding or narrowing statement, *miyat*. *Lechol asher yivatei ha-adam* — for anything a person enunciates — this third phrase returns and broadens again, *chazar ve-riba*. The pattern is thus *ribui u-miyut ve-ribui* — inclusion, exclusion, inclusion.

What does this final *ribui* include? *Riba kol milli* — it includes everything. The Gemara asks: what does the *miyut* — the narrowing — exclude? The answer is: *mi-et dvar mitzvah* — it excludes an oath involving a matter of religious obligation. This point will be developed, but the basic structure is clear: the pattern of inclusion-exclusion-inclusion under Rabbi Akiva's methodology leads to a near-total inclusion of all oaths, both future and past, with the single exclusion being *dvar mitzvah*.

### Ribui vs. Klal

The crucial difference between *ribui u-miyut* and *klal u-prat u-klal* becomes clear when one examines what each system yields at the intermediate stage. Under *ribui u-miyut*, after the first two terms — the inclusive statement and the narrowing statement — one already arrives at the conclusion that the result is something in between: not everything, and not only the specific case. This is because the *ribui* methodology reasons as follows: if the Torah intended only the specific case, why begin with a general statement at all? Therefore, the general and specific terms, operating together, indicate a result somewhere between total inclusion and the specific example.

Under *klal u-prat*, by contrast, the specific term collapses the general entirely at stage two. The *prat* defines the scope completely — it is only at stage three, when a second *klal* appears, that the expansion beyond the specific is restored. The structure is therefore different: *klal u-prat u-klal* says you remain anchored to something *like* the specific, whereas *ribui u-miyut u-ribui* says the two inclusive terms overwhelmingly dominate, and one need only identify the single element the *miyut* removes.

A helpful analogy: if someone says "buy anything for dinner, get some chicken, buy anything," the *klal u-prat u-klal* reading says buy things similar to chicken — perhaps meat, perhaps fish, but remaining in the domain of the specific example. The *ribui u-miyut u-ribui* reading says the instruction is essentially open-ended; the one thing to exclude is whatever the narrowing term singles out.

### Dvar Mitzvah

Under the *ribui u-miyut u-ribui* framework, one begins from a position of near-total inclusion. Both the first and third terms say "everything." The narrowing term *lehara o leheitiv* identifies a single category to exclude. Given that the framework is so expansive — encompassing future oaths, past oaths, neutral acts, everything — the question becomes: what is the one thing to exclude? The Gemara's answer is *dvar mitzvah*. This is because *lehara o leheitiv* suggests the domain of voluntary, discretionary human activity, things one freely chooses to do or not to do. An oath involving a matter of *mitzvah* falls outside this domain of discretion, and therefore is excluded.

Crucially, under this system one need not confine the scope to future-oriented oaths. Because the overall thrust of the two inclusive terms is to include everything, there is no requirement that the result resemble *lehara o leheitiv* in its temporal orientation. The single exclusion is *dvar mitzvah*; everything else — past or future — is included.

## Klal u-Prat u-Klal

### Structure of Klal

Rabbi Yishmael reads the same three phrases through *klal u-prat u-klal*. The first phrase — *o nefesh ki tishava levatei bisfatayim* — is a *klal*, a general statement encompassing all oaths. The middle phrase — *lehara o leheitiv* — is a *prat*, a specific and concrete instance. The final phrase — *lechol asher yivatei ha-adam* — is a second *klal*, which broadens beyond the *prat*.

The rule of *klal u-prat u-klal* is: *ei ata dan ela ke-ein ha-perat* — you derive only what is *like* the specific instance. The *prat* here, *lehara o leheitiv*, is clearly future-oriented. Therefore: *ma ha-prat meforash le-haba af kol le-haba* — just as the specific case is explicitly future, so too everything included must be future-oriented.

What do the two *klalim* contribute? The first *klal* and the second *klal* expand beyond the precise content of the *prat*. The first broadens the category beyond acts that are literally harmful or beneficial, to include even neutral acts — *hanei klala la-asuyei afilu dvarim she-ein bahem hara-ah ve-hatavah* — as long as they are future-oriented. The *prat* then specifies that future orientation is the essential characteristic; the final *klal* broadens the scope to include any future oath, even on neutral matters. But the *prat* simultaneously limits: *le-miu-tei afilu dvarim she-yesh ban hara-ah ve-hatavah* — even those things that involve actual harm or benefit are excluded if they are past-oriented, because past orientation is unlike *lehara o leheitiv*.

The difference from *ribui u-miyut u-ribui* is now fully apparent. Under *klal u-prat u-klal*, the third term brings one back to "like the *prat*" — which requires future orientation. Under *ribui u-miyut u-ribui*, the third term is an overwhelming inclusion that makes the *miyut* do minimal exclusionary work, so one need only find the single excluded category.

### Yitzchak's Reason

The Gemara raises a challenge: why should "similar to the *prat*" be understood as requiring future orientation rather than requiring that the act involve harm or benefit? One could equally say that the relevant characteristic of *lehara o leheitiv* is its content — harm and benefit — rather than its temporal orientation, in which case past-oriented oaths about harm or benefit would be included.

Rabbi Yitzchak answers: *dumya d'lehara o leheitiv — mi she-isuro mishum bal yachel devaro* — the oath must resemble *lehara o leheitiv* in being the kind of oath whose violation consists in transgressing *bal yachel devarav*, the prohibition against breaking one's word. A future-oriented oath obligates one to act or refrain from acting in a specific way, and if one subsequently violates it, that act of violation is the transgression of *bal yachel devarav*. A past-oriented oath is categorically different: the violation occurs at the moment of utterance, because the person is lying when he speaks. The transgression is *lo tishave-u vishmi lasheker* — a prohibition against swearing falsely — not *bal yachel devarav*. These are entirely different genres of *shvua*, and therefore a past-oriented oath is not *like* the *prat*, no matter how harmful or beneficial its content might be.

### Dimi bar Avin

Rav Dimi bar Avin offers an additional reason why Rabbi Yishmael's reading limits the scope to future-oriented oaths. The verse says *o nefesh ki tishava levatei bisfatayim* — if a person swears to express with his lips. The word *vituy* normally denotes the physical act of verbal expression, but Rav Dimi bar Avin reads it to convey a broader principle: *michdi ha-shvuah kodemet le-vituy* — the oath must precede the action. In a future-oriented oath, the *shvua* is taken first and the action follows; the oath preexists the violation. This is the paradigm case: *she-ma-aseh kodem la-shvua yatza* — it therefore excludes the case of "I ate" or "I did not eat," *achalti velo achalti*, in which the action precedes the oath.

## Oness & Shogeg

### Ha'adam Bishvua

The Gemara now turns to a separate dimension of *korban* liability: the conditions of consciousness and intent required at the time of the oath. A *braisa* derives from the phrase *ha-adam bishvuah* — the person in his oath — that certain states of mind or circumstance exempt one entirely. *Prat le-oness* — this excludes one who is compelled. If a person was forced into an oath, it is not binding.

A second derivation comes from the continuation of the verse: *ve-ne-elam mimenu* — and it was hidden from him. This teaches that the *korban* is incurred only when one acted *beshogeg* — inadvertently — and not *be-meizid*, intentionally. The Gemara also notes that it says *bishvuah ve-ne-elam* — it is the *shvua* that must be forgotten, not merely the object to which the oath pertains. This distinction between *he-elam shvua* and *he-elam chefetz* will receive extended treatment in the following section.

### Kahana & Assi Case

What constitutes *oness* in the context of a *shvua*? The obvious case is physical compulsion — someone holding one at gunpoint. But the Gemara presents a more nuanced and striking example. Rav Kahana and Rav Assi were both students of Rav. They fell into a dispute about what Rav had actually ruled on some matter. One swore that Rav had said *muttar*, the other swore that Rav had said *assur*. They then came before Rav, who confirmed one of them. The one who was wrong exclaimed: *ve-ana b'shikra ishtavai* — did I swear falsely? He was genuinely convinced that he was telling the truth.

Rav replied: *libcha ansach* — your heart compelled you. Meaning: since you were fully persuaded that you were telling the truth, you are considered *anuss*. This is not a case of physical compulsion, but rather a case where one's entire subjective certainty was misdirected. The Gemara frames this under the category of *oness*, and the broader principle seems to be captured by the requirement of *ha-adam bishvua* — one must be fully present in one's oath, fully aware of all the relevant realities. If one is genuinely mistaken about a material fact underlying the oath, that kind of mistaken subjective certainty is treated as a form of *ones*, not as *shogeg*.

### Full Awareness

This raises a conceptual question: why is being sincerely mistaken about a fact classified as *oness* rather than *shogeg*? The distinction appears to be that *shogeg* by an oath involves being mistaken about the *halacha* — knowing one is lying but not knowing that doing so is prohibited or that a *korban* is required — whereas being mistaken about the underlying facts means one does not experience the act as a transgression at all. Such a person is not "present" in the *shvua* in the way *ha-adam bishvua* demands. The Torah's requirement is that the person fully stand behind the meaning of his words; if his understanding of the relevant facts is fundamentally wrong, something essential to the oath's constitution is absent. This is the framework within which the *oness* exemption operates here.

## He'elam Shvua

### Forgetting Oath

The *braisa* teaches a sharp distinction: one is *chayav* a *korban* for *he-elam shvua* — forgetting the oath — but not for *he-elam chefetz* — forgetting the object of the oath. Forgetting the oath means either forgetting that one had taken the oath entirely, or confusing its terms — for example, thinking one had sworn to eat the bread when in fact one had sworn not to eat it. Forgetting the object means remembering the oath perfectly but being confused about whether the specific item in front of one is covered by it.

### Eretz Yisrael View

In Eretz Yisrael they laughed at this distinction — *mechaichei alei be-Ma-arva*. The challenge: granted, one can readily construct a case of *he-elam shvua* without *he-elam chefetz* — a person swore not to eat wheat bread, confused the terms, and thought he had sworn to eat it; he remembers the bread but forgot which way the oath ran. But what would *he-elam chefetz* without *he-elam shvua* look like? If someone swore not to eat wheat bread and forgot that the oath was about barley — meaning he forgot which grain he had specified — then *keivan de-cheftza inshi lehu*, since the person forgot the object, that is itself a form of forgetting the *shvua*. Whether what one forgot is which action one swore to do, or which object one swore about, either way one has forgotten the particulars of one's oath. The distinction therefore collapses.

Rabbi Elazar in Eretz Yisrael concluded: *da ve-da achas* — this and that are the same; the *braisa*'s distinction is untenable, and one is *chayav* in both cases.

### Yosef's Example

Rav Yosef challenged this dismissal. There is a case, he argued, where one clearly forgets the object without forgetting the oath. Suppose one swore not to eat wheat bread. He then reaches into a basket intending to take out barley bread — *ve-alsah be-yado shel chitin* — and what he actually pulls out is wheat bread. He eats it, thinking it is barley. Here, *shvuata dachir lei* — he remembers the oath completely. *Cheftza hu de-lo yada lei* — it is the object he did not correctly identify. This is a precise analog to the classic case of *shogeg* in other areas: eating *treifa* meat that one believed to be *kosher*. One knew exactly what was forbidden; one was simply mistaken about the identity of the item before oneself.

### Ashi's Resolution

Abaye, however, challenged Rav Yosef. At the end of the day, *korban de-kamyasi alah de-hai pas* — the *korban* one would bring is for eating this particular piece of bread. From the perspective of the violated oath, what happened was that the person did not realize that his *shvua* applied to what he was eating. That, Abaye argued, is itself *he-elam shvua*. The critical question is not whether one remembered the *shvua* in the abstract, but whether one realized at the relevant moment that the *shvua* prevented the action one was about to take.

Rav Yosef responded: *keivan de-ei yada lei de-chitin hu parish minei* — had someone told him "that is wheat bread," he would have immediately stopped. He fully remembers the *shvua*; it is purely the identity of the object that he misapprehended. Rav Yosef therefore maintains that this is properly classified as *he-elam chefetz*, and on that basis one would not bring a *korban*.

Rav Ashi proposed a practical resolution: *chazinan* — we examine the case. If, upon being told "you made a *shvua*," the person would have recognized the prohibition and refrained — that is fundamentally *he-elam shvua*, and he is *chayav*. If, upon being told "that is wheat bread," the person would have recognized the problem and refrained — that is fundamentally *he-elam chefetz*, and he is *patur*. The determination depends on which awareness would have been the primary trigger for his restraint.

### Ravina's Challenge

Ravina challenged Rav Ashi's resolution: *u-klum parish mi-shvua ela mishum chefetz u-klum parish mi-chefetz ela mishum shvua* — in truth, neither the forgotten oath alone nor the forgotten object alone would have caused the person to stop. He would not have stopped eating unless both memories were restored. The reality is that both were forgotten, and the conceptual question of which would have "triggered" the other is unanswerable. Therefore, *lo shna* — it makes no difference; one cannot distinguish. Rashi, consistent with his reading of the parallel case of *he-elam tumat Mikdash*, appears to hold that in such a case one is *chayav*, since the presence of *he-elam shvua* is sufficient to obligate.

## Shogeg Definition

### Rava's Q

The Gemara now turns to the question of defining *shogeg* in the context of past-oriented oaths. According to Rabbi Akiva, a past-oriented false oath can generate *korban* liability — but only if committed *be-shogeg*. Rava asks Rav Nachman: *eizu hi shegagat shvuat bituy le-sha-avar?* — what is the example of *shogeg* for a past-oriented *shvuat bituy*? The difficulty is stark. If you know you are lying, you are *meizid*. If you do not know you are lying — if you believe you are telling the truth — we have said that is classified as *oness*. What space remains for *shogeg*?

### Not Knowing

The answer: *de-amar yodeia ani she-shvua zo asurah aval eini yodeia im chayavin aleha korban o lo* — the person knows the oath is forbidden, but did not know whether it carries an obligation of *korban*. This is a peculiar form of *shogeg*: one is fully aware that one is transgressing, yet unaware that the specific *korban* obligation applies. One might object that such a person should receive lashes rather than bring a *korban*, since he knowingly violated a prohibition. Indeed, it may be that such a person incurs both lashes and brings a *korban*; the point is that his ignorance of the *korban* obligation constitutes sufficient *shogeg* to create the *korban* liability.

Tosafot suggests an easier example of *shogeg*: one who did not realize at all that the act was a sin — perhaps thinking one was violating a positive commandment rather than a negative prohibition, or not recognizing the act as forbidden at all. This would more cleanly remove the person from the *meizid* category. But the Gemara proceeds with the narrower case.

### Munbaz

The Gemara notes that this ruling resembles the position of Munbaz, who holds in Masechet Shabbat that *shegagat korban shmah shegaga* — not knowing that one's act carries *korban* liability is itself sufficient to classify one as *shogeg*. Does the Gemara's answer here follow only Munbaz, against the majority Rabbinical position?

The Gemara answers: *afilu teima rabbanan* — even the Rabbis would agree here. The Rabbis only dispute Munbaz with respect to the rest of the Torah, where the standard rules apply: a *chatat* is brought for sins that carry *karet*, and normal *shogeg* categories are well-defined. But here, the *korban* liability for *shvuat bituy* is itself an expansion of the ordinary rules — *de-lav chiddush hu* elsewhere, but *de-chiddush hu* here, since ordinarily a simple negative prohibition does not generate *korban* liability. We learn that it does here from *avodah zarah* by way of analogy. Since the entire *korban* obligation in this context is already a broadened category, the Rabbis concede that not knowing about the *korban* obligation is sufficient to constitute *shogeg* and trigger the obligation to bring one.

## Shav Mi-Yedi'ah

### Life at Risk

Ravina poses a case to Rava: someone took an oath not to eat a particular loaf of bread, and then his life was endangered — *mistakana leh* — and he ate it. Is a *korban* brought? One might have thought that even though *pikuach nefesh* renders the eating permitted and obligatory, there remains some metaphysical dimension to having violated an oath sworn in God's name, perhaps sufficient to generate a *korban*. The Gemara immediately dismisses this: if his life was at risk, he was permitted — indeed required — to eat the bread *le-chat-chila*. There can obviously be no *korban* in such a case.

### Desire Case

The real *seifa* of the question concerns a different scenario. Someone is in anguish — *mitztayer* — intensely desiring this particular loaf of bread, and at the moment of eating he has forgotten his oath. Did he forget because his desire overwhelmed his memory? And regardless of the cause of forgetting, the critical question is: given how desperately he wanted to eat the bread, even had he remembered the oath, would he have violated it anyway? If so, does he bring a *korban* for having eaten it in a state of apparent *shogeg*?

### Rashi View

Rashi reads the case as follows: the forgetting is incidental. The person genuinely forgot his oath — perhaps it had been taken long ago. The fact that he very much wanted to eat the bread is a separate datum: we know that even had he remembered the oath, he would have violated it regardless, because his desire was so strong. The question is therefore whether one who forgets and acts, but who would have acted even had he remembered, is classified as *shogeg* and brings a *korban*.

### Would Violate

The Gemara answers by citing a principle: *shav mi-yedi-ah maiti korban al shigegato* — one who would have refrained had he been informed of the oath brings a *korban* for his inadvertence. *Lo shav mi-yedi-ah ein maiti korban* — one who would not have refrained even had he been informed does not bring a *korban*. In the case described, since the person would have violated the oath even had he remembered it, he does not bring a *korban*. He is not genuinely a *shogeg* in the operative sense, because his *shogeg* state did not functionally alter his conduct. The *korban* is *kaparah*; it is appropriate only for someone who, had he known, would have acted differently. For someone who would have willfully violated regardless, the *korban* is not the appropriate response — the violation was effectively *meizid* at the level of intent, even if technically *shogeg* at the level of awareness.

### Tosafot View

Tosafot reads the case differently. The word *mitztayer aleha* indicates something more active: the person was in such anguish over the desired food that he effectively *wished* to forget his oath so that he could eat. Tosafot reads this as a case where the forgetting itself was quasi-volitional — brought about by the person's desire to be in a state of not-knowing. The person did not neutrally forget; he was oriented toward forgetting as a means of enabling himself to eat. In this reading, the case is not one where the person happened to forget and would have violated anyway. Rather, the person willed himself into a state of forgetfulness precisely because he wished to eat. Tosafot therefore identifies this as an instance where the person is not *shav mi-yedi-ah* — not someone who would have pulled back had he known — because his entire orientation was toward eating regardless.

The two readings thus differ on the mechanism: according to Rashi, the forgetting was innocent and the disqualifying factor is the hypothetical counterfactual that he would have violated anyway. According to Tosafot, the forgetting was itself the product of desire, and the disqualifying factor is that the person essentially engineered his own unawareness in order to transgress.

## Verbal Expression

### Shmuel

Shmuel rules: *gamar be-libo tzorich she-yotzi be-sfatav* — if someone resolves in his heart to take an oath, the oath is not binding unless he actually gives it verbal expression. The source is *levatei bisfatayim* — to express with the lips. The *shvua* requires articulation.

### Bituy Contradiction

A *braisa* appears to be internally self-contradictory. It first states: *be-sfatayim ve-lo be-lev* — with the lips, not if merely resolved in the heart. It then asks: *gamar be-libo minayin* — how do I know that a heart-commitment is also binding? — and derives it from *lechol asher yivatei ha-adam*, which broadens the scope to include even mental commitment. The Gemara notes: *ha-gufa kashya* — the *braisa* contradicts itself. It begins by excluding heart-commitment and then includes it.

### Sheshet Resolution

Rav Sheshet resolves the internal contradiction by reading the two clauses of the *braisa* as addressing two different cases. The first clause — *be-sfatayim ve-lo she-gamar le-hotzi be-sfatav ve-lo hotzi* — excludes the case where someone intended to verbalize the oath but did not actually do so. He resolved to speak but never spoke. Since the speech never materialized, even though he had intended to speak, no oath is created. The second clause then asks: what if someone intended the commitment purely internally, never planning to verbalize it at all? The answer, derived from *lechol asher yivatei ha-adam*, is that this is also binding.

Rav Sheshet thus identifies two distinct exclusions within the word *bisfatayim*. The first reading excludes the case where one intended to speak but did not. The second reading, from the broader verse, includes the case where one intended to commit only mentally. This means: without Shmuel's ruling, we would have said that an entirely internal commitment, if that is all that was intended, is binding. Shmuel overrides this and requires actual verbalization in all cases.

What, then, does Shmuel do with the *braisa*? The Gemara notes: *ela le-Shmuel kashya* — for Shmuel, the *braisa* remains difficult. The *braisa*'s second clause seems to validate heart-commitment as binding, in tension with Shmuel's ruling that verbalization is always required.

## Exceptions

### Motza Challenge

The Gemara challenges Shmuel's position from the verse *motza sefatecha tishmor ve-asita* — what proceeds from your lips, you shall guard and perform — from which one might derive that only verbal commitments bind. The *braisa* then asks how heart-commitment can also obligate, and derives it from *be-chol nediv lev*, concerning donations to the *Beit Hamikdash*. If the heart-commitment of a generous donor is sufficient to create a binding obligation in that context, why should Shmuel's general rule exclude heart-commitment elsewhere?

### Two Verses Rule

The Gemara answers: *shani hatam de-ktiv kol nediv lev* — that case is different, because there the Torah explicitly says *kol nediv lev*. Moreover, this is a case of *shnei ketuvim ha-ba-im ke-echad* — two verses that teach the same exceptional rule simultaneously — and the principle is *shnei ketuvim ha-ba-im ke-echad ein melamdin* — two such verses cannot be used to derive a general rule. One verse is *terumah* — whether referring to the setting aside of grain *terumah*, for which mental designation is sufficient to effect the separation (*ve-nechshav lachem*), or to the *parshat Terumah* context of donations to the *Mikdash*, *kol nediv lev* — and the other is *kodashim*, for which the verse in *Divrei Hayamim* establishes that mental commitment to bring an offering is sufficient to generate the *neder* obligation even without verbalization. Since these are two exceptional cases taught by two separate verses, they cannot be extended to establish a general rule.

### Donation Q

The exception of *terumah* and *kodashim* has significant practical implications. The Gemara raises the alternative resolution that *chullin mi-kodshim lo gamrinan* — the laws of non-sacred matters are not derived from sacred ones. Whether the *terumah* category here refers narrowly to the separation of grain *terumah* or broadly to donations of *kol nediv lev* — donations made with a generous heart to religious causes — is a question with direct practical consequence. If someone mentally resolves to donate a sum to the synagogue, does that thought alone create a binding *neder* obligation, even without verbal declaration?

If the *terumah* exception extends to charitable pledges and donations more broadly, then heart-commitment in that domain binds without verbalization. The Gemara leaves open the precise scope of the exception, but the question is a live *halachic* one: whether silent mental commitment to donate to religious causes creates an obligation, based on whether such donations fall under the *terumah* category that the Gemara identifies as an exception to the general requirement of verbal expression.

---

---

# Shevuot 27

## Intro & Review

### Daf 27 Overview

Daf 27 continues the systematic effort to define the parameters of a binding *shevuah* — specifically, in which cases one is liable to bring a *korban* and in which cases the *shevuah* does not take effect at all.

### Rabbi Akiva & Yishmael

The previous daf established the debate between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yishmael concerning a *shevuah* made about the past: whether one brings a *korban* for such an oath. All authorities agree that a willful violation of a *shevuat shav* incurs *makkot* (lashes), but the *korban* obligation is the contested issue between these two Tannaim.

### Positive & Negative

It was established that a *shevuah* capable of generating *korban* liability must be articulable in both the positive and the negative — the requirement known as *lehara o leheitiv*, that the oath must be expressible as either doing good or doing bad. An oath that cannot be reversed and restated in its opposite form lacks this essential quality.

### Shevuot vs Nedarim

The *mishnah* also addressed distinctions between *shevuot* and *nedarim*, and introduced the category of a *shevuah bishogeg* — an unintentional oath made about the past. One might have assumed this simply means taking an oath while not knowing the facts; in fact, the *gemara* frames the paradigm case as one of *ones* (compulsion) — where the person believed he was telling the truth. Tosafot extends this analysis beyond the *korban* context to *makkot* as well.

### Expression Requirement

Finally, it was established that a *shevuah* is not binding unless it is articulated aloud — *levatay bisifatayim*, expressed through the lips. The *gemara* then raises related cases where silent acceptance does take effect, such as *terumah* and *kodshim*. The practically significant question this raises for contemporary halacha is whether accepting upon oneself a donation — say, to give a sum of money to a synagogue — requires verbal articulation to become binding. The general rule, as the *poskim* understand it, is that one must indeed speak the words aloud. Similarly, accepting a voluntary fast requires verbal expression to be effective.

---

## Negate/Fulfill Mitzvah

### Oath to Negate

The *mishnah* now on 27a states: *nishba levatel et hamitzvah v'lo biteil* — one who swore to negate a *mitzvah* and did not negate it is *patur*, exempt from bringing a *korban*. This case represents the clearest exclusion from the *korban* regime: a *shevuah* to violate a *mitzvah* cannot take effect at all. No authority holds that one can obligate oneself through oath to transgress a *mitzvah*. One might still incur *makkot* for *shevuat shav*, but the *shevuah* as such has no binding force.

### Oath to Fulfill

The *mishnah* continues: *lekayem v'lo kiyem* — one who swore to fulfill a *mitzvah* and did not fulfill it is likewise *patur*. Here the *mishnah* itself notes that logic would seem to demand liability — *shehaya din sheyehei chayav* — and indeed this is the position of Rabbi Yehuda Ben Batera.

### Rabbi Yehuda Ben Batera

Rabbi Yehuda Ben Batera reasons as follows: if taking an oath in the realm of *reshut* — a discretionary act about which one is not already foresworn from Sinai — renders one liable if he violates it, then how much more so should an oath regarding a *mitzvah*, regarding which one is *already* obligated from Sinai, be binding? One is *mushba v'omed mehar sinai* to perform the *mitzvah*, and the additional personal oath should only reinforce that obligation. Rabbi Yehuda Ben Batera therefore holds that such a *shevuah* is binding and its violation generates *korban* liability.

### Lav v'Hein Argument

The Rabbis respond: the analogy does not hold. In the realm of *reshut*, an oath satisfies the requirement of *lehara o leheitiv* — it can be framed in the positive and in the negative, *lav v'hein*. The same action can be sworn to and sworn against. But in the realm of *mitzvah*, this symmetry collapses. We already agreed that one cannot take a binding *shevuah* to negate a *mitzvah* — for example, to refrain from sitting in a *sukkah*. Therefore, the oath to sit in the *sukkah* likewise cannot serve as a binding *shevuah*, because it lacks the *lav v'hein* quality: one cannot articulate its inverse as a valid oath. Without that reversibility, it does not generate *korban* liability.

It should be noted that earlier in the *gemara*, the reason given for why a *shevuah* does not take effect on an already-obligatory *mitzvah* was framed differently: *mushba v'omed mehar sinai* — *ein shevuah chala al shevuah*, the principle that one oath does not take effect upon another. Here, the framing is the *lav v'hein* argument. These are not necessarily contradictory; one could read the Rabbis as responding to Rabbi Yehuda Ben Batera on his own terms — granting, for the sake of argument, that *mushba v'omed* strengthens rather than blocks the oath, yet still insisting that the absence of *lav v'hein* independently defeats the claim.

### Tosafot's Distinction

Tosafot offers a penetrating alternative reading of the *mishnah*, one that hinges on a textual variant. The key conceptual distinction Tosafot draws is between negative and positive *mitzvot*. The principle *ein issur chal al issur* — that a state of forbiddenness does not take effect upon an existing state of forbiddenness — is structurally parallel to *ein shevuah chala al shevuah*. Both principles address the impossibility of double *issur*, double forbiddenness.

### Tosafot's Girsa

Tosafot removes the *kaf* of comparison from the phrase *kidivrei Rabbi Yehuda Ben Batera*, reading the passage not as the anonymous voice of the *mishnah* invoking Rabbi Yehuda Ben Batera's position, but as Rabbi Yehuda Ben Batera himself conceding a point. In Tosafot's reading, Rabbi Yehuda Ben Batera is saying: I agree that taking a *shevuah* to fulfill a *negative mitzvah* — for instance, swearing not to eat *neveilah* — does not take effect. Why? Because *ein issur chal al issur* and *ein shevuah chala al shevuah*: the meat is already in a state of forbiddenness, and a *shevuah* cannot add a second layer of that same forbiddenness. But Rabbi Yehuda Ben Batera holds that taking a *shevuah* to perform a positive *mitzvah* — to sit in a *sukkah* — is entirely different and is indeed binding.

### Double Obligation

The conceptual core of Tosafot's distinction is this: one cannot be doubly *forbidden* — *ein issur chal al issur* — but one can be doubly *obligated*. The Torah obligates sitting in the *sukkah*, and a personal *shevuah* can add a further layer of obligation without any conceptual difficulty. There is no principle of *ein chiyuv chal al chiyuv*. According to Tosafot's reading, it is only in the case of negative *mitzvot* where the *shevuah* fails, because the *shevuah* would be attempting to add a second layer of forbiddenness to something already forbidden. This also illuminates why the Rabbis invoke the *lav v'hein* argument specifically for the case of an oath to sit in the *sukkah*: when dealing with a positive *mitzvah*, *ein issur chal al issur* and *ein shevuah chala al shevuah* do not apply, and the sole remaining reason the *shevuah* fails is the absence of *lav v'hein* — the inability to reverse it.

---
