## Deriving Reshut Fram (II)

### Inclusion & Exclusion

The *gemara* now presents a *baraita*: *Tanu Rabbanan*. One might have thought that a *shevuah levatel et hamitzvah* — an oath to negate a *mitzvah* — should be binding, such that if one took such an oath and then did not follow through with the violation, one would be *chayav* a *korban*. The *baraita* rejects this: *talmud lomar lehara o leheitiv* — the verse specifies doing bad or doing good. From this we derive that both the bad and the good must refer to the same category of act.

### Good=Neutral

The *baraita* reasons: *mah hatavah reshut* — the same way doing good refers to a discretionary, neutral act, so too doing bad (*af haraah reshut*) refers to a neutral act, not to an act in the *mitzvah* realm. Negating a *mitzvah* would be "doing bad" in the *mitzvah* realm, not in the neutral realm. Therefore, an oath to negate a *mitzvah* is excluded: *hotzi nishba levatel et hamitzvah v'lo biteil sheyehei patur*.

### Bad=Neutral

The derivation then runs in the opposite direction. One might have thought that an oath to fulfill a *mitzvah* — doing good in the *mitzvah* realm — should also be binding. The *baraita* again invokes *lehara o leheitiv*: the same way doing bad refers to the neutral realm, so doing good (*af hatov reshut*) must also refer to a neutral, discretionary act, not to the fulfillment of a *mitzvah*. Hence, *otzi nishba lekayem et hamitzvah v'lo kiyem shepatur* — one who swears to fulfill a *mitzvah* and fails to do so is likewise exempt.

---

## Injury & Good Acts

### Self-Injury

The *baraita* continues: *yachol nishba lehara le'atzmo v'lo hara yachol yehei patur* — one might have thought that an oath to do injury to oneself would not be binding, since *lehara* should be read as applicable only to permitted forms of "bad." The *baraita* rejects this: *mah hatov reshut af hara reshut* — doing bad to oneself falls within the realm of discretionary action, *shehareshut beyado*, one is permitted to do so. Therefore such an oath is binding, and if violated, liability follows.

This is a striking passage. Tosafot's brief comment notes that the primary function of including this case is to teach that self-injury is permitted (*adam rashai lachavel be'atzmo*). The *gemara* in Bava Kamma draws upon this *baraita* as evidence in the debate over whether self-injury is halachically permissible. It is important to flag that this *baraita* represents a position contrary to the normative ruling. The *Rambam* and the mainstream *poskim* rule that self-injury is forbidden, and the discussions around procedures such as elective surgery — what constitutes genuine injury versus an act ultimately aimed at benefit — are downstream of that ruling. But the *baraita* here assumes self-injury is permitted, and that assumption is what makes the *shevuah* binding.

### Harm Others

The *baraita* then addresses: *yachol nishba lehara le'acherim v'lo hara sheyehei chayav* — one might have thought that taking an oath to harm others and then refraining from doing so would generate *korban* liability. The answer is again *lehara o leheitiv*, *mah hatov reshut af hara reshut*: the "bad" referred to in the verse must be in a neutral, discretionary domain, not in the domain of prohibited action. An oath to harm others is not binding because injuring another person is itself a violation of a *mitzvah* — it is *levatel et hamitzvah* — and therefore falls outside the operative range of the verse.

The *baraita* itself makes explicit what form of harm it has in mind: *akeh ploni va'eftza mocho* — I will strike so-and-so and crush his head. This explicit language confirms that the "bad" in question is physical injury, not merely an absence of generosity. This clarification is significant because there are forms of conduct toward others that are unfriendly or ungracious without constituting an *aveirah*. For instance, declining to lend one's lawnmower to a neighbor, or ignoring someone — these could be "bad" in a colloquial sense without violating any prohibition (though some such conduct might run afoul of *lo tikom*, the prohibition of revenge). Those forms of "bad," if one took a *shevuah* regarding them, could potentially be binding. It is specifically the category of physical harm — which constitutes *bitul mitzvah* — that is excluded from the *shevuah* framework.

### Do Good to Others

The *baraita* concludes: *minayin lerabot hatavat acherim talmud lomar o leheitiv* — how do we know that a *shevuah* to do good to another person is binding? From the word *o* ("or") in the phrase *lehara o leheitiv*. The inclusion of doing good to others requires a textual source.

One might ask: given that we have already established *lehara o leheitiv* as the operative framework, why should doing good to another person require a separate derivation? The answer lies in the *lav v'hein* principle. Since one cannot take a binding *shevuah* to harm another — the negative of "I will do good to Michael" might be thought to be "I will harm Michael" — one might have concluded that the oath to do good is also not binding, because its reverse falls into forbidden territory.

The *gemara* here implicitly introduces a crucial three-zone model.

### Three Zones

Between the zone of "good" and the zone of "bad" lies a neutral middle ground. The oath "I will do good to Michael" — for example, I will give him *tzedakah*, or I will help him — is reversible without entering the zone of prohibition. The negation of "I will help him" is simply "I will not help him," which is entirely permissible. Not doing a favor is not a *mitzvah* violation. Therefore this oath has a valid *lav v'hein* structure: its positive and negative formulations are both within the permitted range.

By contrast, the oath "I will not harm Michael" is paradoxically *not* binding in this framework — not because the oath itself is problematic, but because its logical opposite, "I will harm him," is forbidden. Since that reverse oath could not itself be binding, the forward oath cannot satisfy the *lav v'hein* requirement. It has the positive formulation, but lacks a valid negative.

The three-zone structure therefore operates as follows: an oath to act in the zone of "good" works, because its reverse is the neutral zone — the mere absence of doing good, which is permitted. An oath to act in the zone of "bad" (toward others, in the sense of physical injury) does not work, because it is itself *bitul mitzvah*. And an oath to stay out of the bad zone — "I will not harm" — also does not work, because its reverse falls into the bad zone, which is impermissible.

---

## Deriving Reshut Fram (II)

### Circularity Problem

The *gemara* now raises what it frankly identifies as a problem of circularity in the *baraita*'s derivation. The *baraita* argued: since *hatavah* (good) is in the *reshut* realm, *haraah* (bad) must also be in the *reshut* realm — and therefore an oath to negate a *mitzvah* is excluded. Then it reversed and said: since *haraah* is in the *reshut* realm, *hatavah* must also be in the *reshut* realm — and therefore an oath to fulfill a *mitzvah* is excluded.

The *gemara* challenges: *umimai dekra d'b'milei d'reshut ketivi* — how do we know the verse is speaking of the *reshut* realm at all? *Dilma bidvar mitzvah ketivi* — perhaps the entire verse is framed in terms of *mitzvah* cases. Perhaps *lehara* means to negate a *mitzvah* and *leheitiv* means to fulfill one. If so, the whole derivation has read its conclusion into its premises.

The *gemara* acknowledges the circularity: *lo salka datach*. It cannot be dismissed, but the reason is not immediately obvious. The *gemara* invokes the principle that *hatavah* must be analogous to *haraah* and *haraah* to *hatavah* — *d'akish haraah l'hatavah*. If we were to situate both in the *mitzvah* realm, then good (*hatavah*) in that realm would be, say, eating *matzah* on *seder* night, and bad (*haraah*) in the *mitzvah* realm — while still being analogous to the good — would have to mean something that is bodily bad but a fulfillment of a *mitzvah*, like refraining from eating *chametz* on Pesach. But in that case, *hara gufa tova hi* — what presents as "bad" is fundamentally good in terms of *mitzvah*. The two categories collapse into one another, and the verse becomes redundant.

Running the argument in the opposite direction produces the same problem: *hatavah gufa ra'a hi*. If one insists on strict analogy between the two terms, whether in the *mitzvah* realm or in the *reshut* realm, one ends up with a redundancy. The *gemara* presses further: *ee hachi bidvar hareshut nami lo meshakchas lah* — if that is the objection, it applies equally in the *reshut* realm. If doing bad must be strictly analogous to doing good, then in the *reshut* realm, "bad" (say, fasting) would simply become another version of "good" (eating, just negated). The circularity cannot be resolved by pointing to the analogy between *hatavah* and *haraah* alone, whether in the *mitzvah* domain or in the *reshut* domain.

### Or Teaches Inclusion

The *gemara* resolves the circularity with a different argument entirely: *mide'itztarich o l'rabos hatavat acheirim shma mina bidvar hareshut ketivi* — the fact that the word *o* ("or") was needed to include the case of doing good to others proves that the verse is operating in the *reshut* domain, not the *mitzvah* domain.

### Implicit Exclusion

Why does the word *o* prove this? The *gemara* reasons: *de'ee salka dach'tach bidvar mitzvah ketivi* — if the verse were speaking in terms of *mitzvah* cases, then *lehara* would already include taking an oath to harm another person, even though doing so is *levatel et hamitzvah*. That would be the meaning of "bad" in the *mitzvah* realm. Once I knew the verse permitted an oath regarding something as severe as injuring another person, it would be obvious — *mibaya?* — that doing good to another person would also be covered. No separate word would be needed to include it.

But in fact the word *o* is needed to include doing good to others. Why would that inclusion be necessary? Only because we already know — from some other principle — that one cannot take a *shevuah levatel et hamitzvah*, i.e., one cannot take a binding oath to harm another person. Given that the "bad" case is already restricted in this way, one might have thought that the *lav v'hein* requirement blocks the "good" case as well (since the reverse of "doing good" might be thought to be "doing harm," which is forbidden). The word *o* therefore comes to teach that no, an oath to do good to another person is valid, because its reverse — not doing the favor — falls into the neutral zone, not the forbidden zone.

This means the verse presupposes that harming another is already excluded from the *shevuah* framework. That presupposition only makes sense if the verse is operating in the *reshut* domain, where the natural content of oaths is discretionary activity. The *mitzvah* exclusion (*levatel et hamitzvah*) is read as the one case the *Torah* by definition leaves outside the *shevuah* framework.

### Vav vs Or

The *gemara* then raises a complication: *vehai o mibaya leh lechalek* — perhaps the word *o* is not extra at all. It is needed simply to separate the two cases: the oath to do bad and the oath to do good are each independently binding, and the *o* teaches that one need not take an oath encompassing both simultaneously. Without *o*, one might have read the conjunctive *vav* in *lehara v'leheitiv* as requiring both elements present in the same oath.

The *gemara* responds: *lechalek lo tzarich kra* — a verse is not required to teach this. A *vav* can normally be read to encompass either one or both cases. This is the position of Rabbi Yochanan.

But the *gemara* then raises the view of Rabbi Yoshiya: *haniicha le'Rabbi Yochanan... ela le'Rabbi Yoshiya mai ika lemeimar?* Rabbi Yoshiya maintains that a *vav* would normally be read as "and" — requiring both elements together — and one needs an explicit *o* to read it as "or." The *baraita* brought in support reads: *ish asher yekallel et aviv ve'et imo* — a man who curses his father and his mother. Rabbi Yoshiya says: from this verse alone, I know only if he cursed them both together. The word *killel* appearing adjacent to *aviv* alone (at the beginning of the verse) and *killel* appearing adjacent to *imo* alone (at the end) teaches that cursing either one separately is also punishable — but Rabbi Yoshiya required that separate derivation, because for him a *vav* means "and" not "or." Rabbi Yonatan disagrees: a *vav* inherently encompasses both possibilities — together and apart — and the verse is simply confirming both readings. Only an explicit word like *yachdav* ("together"), as in the prohibition against plowing with an ox and a donkey, would restrict the case to the two elements being simultaneous.

The *gemara* concludes: even according to Rabbi Yoshiya — for whom the word *o* is not superfluous but structurally necessary — the exclusion of *levatel et hamitzvah* can still be derived. The source would instead be Rabbi Akiva's interpretive principle of *ribui umi'ut*. Rabbi Akiva taught that the phrase *lehara o leheitiv lechol asher yevata* functions as a *ribui* (expansion) followed by a *mi'ut* (exclusion). The expansion includes virtually everything; the exclusion removes one case. What would be the most natural single exclusion? An oath to contravene what the *Torah* itself commands. Under this reading, the *reshut* domain of the verse is established not from the word *o* but from Rabbi Akiva's interpretive framework, which identifies *levatel et hamitzvah* as the one case excluded. Once that exclusion is established, the conclusion that the verse operates in the *reshut* realm follows: *amar bishlama dvar hareshut ketiv, mimela dvar mitzvah* is excluded. If the verse covered the full *mitzvah* range — taking oaths about both fulfillment and negation of *mitzvot* — then everything in between would also be covered, and the *mi'ut* would exclude nothing meaningful.

---

## Multiple Oaths

### Three Formulations

The *mishnah* presents the following scenario: a person takes a *shevuah* that he will not eat a certain loaf of bread, then takes another *shevuah* that he will not eat it, and a third that he will not eat it. He then eats it. He is liable for only one *korban*. This is the principle of *ein shevuah chala al shevuah*: a *shevuah* does not take effect upon an already-existing *shevuah* regarding the same object. The *mishnah* then identifies this as the paradigmatic case of *shevuat bitui* — the category of future-directed oath for which willful violation incurs *makkot* and unintentional violation incurs a *korban oleh v'yored* (of variable cost depending on one's means). By contrast, a *shevuat shav* — an oath for naught, such as swearing to something patently obvious or patently false — incurs *makkot* for willful transgression but no *korban* whatsoever.

### Ein Shevua Chala

The *gemara* asks: why does the *mishnah* bother stating the oath in multiple formulations? Stating it once with different phrasing would suffice to establish the *korban* obligation. The *gemara* answers that the different formulations — *shelo ochel* and *shelo ochalnah* — are not identical in scope, and the *mishnah* teaches something from their juxtaposition and ordering.

### Rava's Wording Rule

Rava offers a crucial distinction: *shelo ochel kikar zo* — "I will not eat this loaf" — means I will not eat *from* it, and therefore even eating a *k'zayis* (an olive's volume) constitutes a transgression. *Shelo ochalnah* — "I will not eat it" — implies I will not eat *the entirety* of it, and therefore one is not liable until he has eaten the whole loaf.

### Order Matters

Given this distinction, order becomes determinative. If one first swore *shelo ochalnah* (not to eat the whole loaf) and then swore *shelo ochel* (not to eat any portion of it), the second oath takes effect because it is more stringent than the first: it creates a liability even for a *k'zayis*, something the first oath did not forbid. If, however, one first swore the stricter oath (*shelo ochel*, forbidding even a *k'zayis*) and then the broader formulation (*shelo ochalnah*, the entire loaf), the second oath is entirely subsumed by the first and does not take effect at all. The *mishnah* is constructed precisely to convey this: the order in which the formulations appear reflects which one was stated first.

### Hovering Principle

Rava adds a further principle: even when the second oath does not take effect — because the first oath already covers the same ground — the second oath does not simply cease to exist. It remains present, hovering, unable to actualize only because of the blocking effect of the first. This has a practical consequence: if one seeks and obtains a *hetter* (annulment) from a *chacham* on the first oath, the *hetter* operates retroactively — the first oath is treated as though it never took effect. Looking back from that point, the second oath was never blocked, and it therefore takes retroactive effect in the first oath's place.

### Tosafot's Girsa

Tosafot's version of the *mishnah* contains only two oath formulations, not three. Accordingly, Tosafot must derive the "hovering" principle from somewhere other than the extra third scenario. Tosafot finds it in the precise wording of the *mishnah* itself: *eino chayav ela achas* — "he is not liable except for one." Tosafot notes that the *mishnah* could have said simply *chayav achas* — "he is liable for one." The formulation *eino chayav ela achas* — "he is not liable except for one" — acknowledges that there were two oaths, both present, yet only one generates a *korban*. The phrasing *eino chayav ela achas* implies that both are acknowledged to exist; the second merely does not generate liability. *Chayav achas* would suggest the second is altogether ignored. The more elaborate phrasing therefore carries the implication that the second oath continues to hover — present and recognized, but inactive — which is precisely what enables it to take retroactive effect if the first is annulled.

### Nazir Proof

The *gemara* attempts to bring a proof for Rava's hovering principle from the laws of *nezirut*. If someone accepted two separate terms of *nezirut* upon himself, completed the thirty days of the first, and separated a *korban* to conclude it — and then, before bringing the *korban*, obtained a *she'eilah* (halachic annulment) on the first *nezirut* — the ruling is: *alsa lo shniya barishona* — the second *nezirut* is treated as having filled the first slot. The thirty days he served count toward the second *nezirut*, and the *korban* he designated for the first is counted toward the second. He has now completed the second term as well.

This seems to support Rava: the second *nezirut* was always present and hovering, such that once the first was retroactively removed, the second stepped into its place.

### Challenge to Proof

The *gemara* rejects the analogy: *hachi hashta? Hosam neziros mi isa* — in the *nazir* case, everybody agrees the second *nezirut* was always present and active, not merely hovering. How do we know this? Because even without a *she'eilah*, the practical consequence of the second *nezirut* was always clear: after completing the first term, the individual would simply proceed to observe the second. *Belo sheilah*, if no annulment had been sought, the second *nezirut* would have taken effect automatically upon completion of the first. Its continuous presence was never in doubt.

*Hacha shevuah shniya mi isa klal?* — here, by contrast, had the first *shevuah* not been annulled, the second would have had no practical effect whatsoever. There would be no moment at which the second oath visibly came into force. Because the second *shevuah* had no independent expression or consequence absent the annulment of the first, one cannot straightforwardly say it was always "present." The *nazir* proof therefore fails to establish Rava's principle, and the *gemara* leaves it as Rava's own assertion without an external proof. The discussion of this topic will continue on the next daf.

---

---

# Shevuot 28

## Heter Nedarim Timing

### Case Setup

The *daf* opens by continuing the discussion of *ein shvua chal al shvua* — the principle that a redundant oath does not take legal effect on top of an already binding one. The *Gemara* had already established that a second oath, if it adds some additional restriction beyond the first, does take effect, and that if the first oath is retroactively voided through *sheila l'chacham*, the second oath "descends" to fill its place. This sets the stage for a fundamental question about timing: how late in the game may one appeal to a *chacham* to void a *shvua*?

### Rava's Position

Rava addresses this at the bottom of 27b. The case involves someone who took an oath regarding a loaf of bread and then ate from it. Rava rules: *im shiyer heimenu kezayit, nishal aleha* — if a *kezayit* of the loaf still remains, the person may still go to a *chacham* and request *heter nedarim*, since the *shvua* retains current relevance with respect to that remaining portion. But *achala kula, ein nishal aleha* — if the entire loaf has been eaten, the moment has passed, and the *chacham* cannot void what has no present application. The principle is clear: *hataras shvua* is a forward-looking institution. It functions only when there is something remaining upon which the *shvua* can still operate.

### Rav Acha Challenge

Rav Acha the son of Rava challenges Rava's formulation before Rav Ashi. He notes that Rava's ruling is ambiguous depending on exactly how the oath was worded. If the person said *shelo ochel* — "I will not eat [from this loaf]" — then every *kezayit* constitutes an independent transgression, and someone who ate all but the final *kezayit* has already violated his *shvua* multiple times. Can we truly perform *heter nedarim* for someone who has already transgressed so severely? Alternatively, if the oath was *shelo ochlena* — "I will not eat it," meaning the entire loaf as a unit — then one does not transgress until consuming the whole thing, including the last *kezayit*. In that case, as long as even a tiny crumb remains, the person has not yet violated at all. Why then should the threshold specifically require a *kezayit*? Even less than a *kezayit* remaining should suffice to allow the *sheila*, since the *shvua* is still formally unviolated.

### Two Readings

The *Gemara* opens 28a with a dual response — *iba'it eima shelo ochel, iba'it eima shelo ochlena* — conceding that Rava's ruling is viable under either reading of the oath, and offering a separate justification for each.

Under the reading of *shelo ochel*, where each *kezayit* is a discrete transgression: yes, the person has already violated the oath multiple times over. But there remains one *kezayit* against which the *shvua* is still operative and enforceable. The *heter nedarim* is sought and granted for the sake of that remaining *kezayit* — not as a retroactive remedy for past sins. The institution of *hataras shvua* does not function to undo what has already been done; its purpose is to free the person from ongoing and future restriction. However, once the *heter* is legitimately granted for the remaining *kezayit*, it operates comprehensively: *migu d'mahani l'kezayit*, the voiding of the oath extends to cover the entire *shvua* retroactively as well. The critical point is that there must be *something* to which the *shvua* is currently relevant — a hook for the present — without which the process cannot begin.

### De Minimis Principle

The second reading, *shelo ochlena*, is somewhat harder but equally instructive. If the oath covered the loaf as a whole unit, then as long as any portion remains — even less than a *kezayit* — the person has technically not yet transgressed. So why should the requirement of a *kezayit* matter at all? The *Gemara*'s answer invokes what amounts to a *de minimis* principle: *hishir kezayit, chashiv lei tzaluyei alei; ve'i lo, lo chashiv lei tzaluyei alei* — if a *kezayit* remains, it is a matter of sufficient weight to bring before a *chacham*; if less than a *kezayit* remains, it is simply not important enough to justify the proceeding. The analogy is to bringing a claim before *beis din* for less than a *perutah* — the matter is beneath the threshold of legal concern. So even though the person has not yet violated, if what is at stake is the ability to eat only a fraction of a *kezayit*, the rabbis simply decline to entertain the appeal. The *shvua* remains technically in force, but the residual restriction is too trivial to warrant a *sheila l'chacham*.

### Tosafot Dispute

Tosafot dissents from the assumption embedded in the *Gemara*'s framing. Can one really eat an entire loaf of bread, the argument goes, without leaving behind any crumbs? Tosafot maintains that the practical threshold for transgressing a *shelo ochlena* oath is leaving less than a *kezayit* — anything below that amount is treated as negligible, and at that point the violation is considered to have occurred. Under Tosafot's reading, therefore, the dividing line is stark: if a *kezayit* remains, you have not yet violated, and *hataras shvua* is obviously available; if less than a *kezayit* remains, you have already violated, and it is too late.

This reading, however, sits uncomfortably with the *Gemara* itself, which does not seem to treat the distinction between "a *kezayit* remaining" and "less than a *kezayit* remaining" as representing a bright qualitative line between non-violation and violation. The *Gemara* reasons about both scenarios without suggesting that the former category is entirely permissible and the latter entirely violated — which is precisely what Tosafot's position would imply. Rashi, by contrast, holds that even with less than a *kezayit* remaining, the *shelo ochlena* oath has technically not yet been violated, but the remainder is too negligible to justify a *sheila*. The *Gemara*'s discussion is smoothly consistent with Rashi's approach, even if the exact practical threshold of "crumbs" requires further definition.

---

## Two Neziruyot Case

### Nazir Challenge

The *Gemara* now tests Rava's principle against a case involving a *nazir* who undertook two *neziruyot* in sequence. He completed the first *nezirut*, separated his *korban*, and then sought a *sheila* to void the first *nezirut* retroactively. The *Gemara* had already taught that if the first *nezirut* is voided, the second one "descends" to fulfill what was the first's slot. The question is whether this case poses a challenge to Rava — since the first *nezirut* appears to be entirely in the past at the time of the *sheila*.

### First Response

The *Gemara*'s initial response is that *hacha mai askinan bishelo kipper* — the case is referring to one where the *nazir* has not yet brought his *korban*. Since the *korban* is still pending, the *shvua* retains present relevance, and there is no challenge to Rava at all.

### Baraita Challenge

A more explicit difficulty then arrives: a *Baraita* teaches that the *sheila* may be performed even *after* the *korban* has been brought — *ha tanya kipper*. If the *korban* has already been offered, what future relevance remains? This appears to be a direct contradiction of Rava's principle.

### Shaving Component

The *Gemara* deflects by saying *bishelo gilach* — the *nazir* has not yet shaved his head, which is the concluding act of *nezirut*. According to Rabbi Eliezer, *tiglachas me'akeva* — the shaving is indispensable to the fulfillment of *nezirut*. Since something essential still remains undone, the *nezirut* has not been fully concluded, and the *sheila* therefore still operates upon something currently relevant. This preserves Rava's framework: the voiding is performed not on a purely concluded matter, but on something whose implications are still unresolved.

### Amemar Disagrees

A further *Baraita* pushes back even harder, indicating that the *sheila* works even after the shaving — *ha tanya gilach*. At this point, Amemar breaks with Rava's position altogether: *afilu achlo kula nishal alav* — even if everything has been done and the *shvua* or *nezirut* is entirely in the past, one may still appeal to a *chacham*. His reasoning is that it is never truly "all in the past." If the violation was *beshogeig*, the person remains obligated to bring a *korban*, and having the *sheila* granted would exempt him from that obligation — that is present relevance. If the violation was *bemeizid*, he faces potential *malkos* from *beis din*, and the *sheila* has present relevance in staving off that punishment. Thus, Amemar expands the definition of present relevance rather than abandoning the requirement entirely.

### Rav Ashi Answer

Rav Ashi offers a more elegant answer that preserves Rava's position without Amemar's expansions. He argues that the case of two *neziruyot* is simply not analogous to the case of a single *shvua* that is entirely spent. The question to pose is: *mi garam lishniyah shelo tachol, rishonah ve'einah?* — what is it that prevented the second *nezirut* from taking effect in its own right? It was the first one. As long as the second *nezirut* is still ongoing, the first one retains living relevance — it is the direct cause of the present obligation. If the first *nezirut* is voided, the second one would have been the first all along, and the person is now free from the burden of a second term. There is thus a tangible and present reason to seek the *sheila*: the first *nezirut* is currently making its weight felt through the ongoing second one. This is entirely different from a person who took a single *shvua*, violated it fully, and can point to no present consequence whatsoever.

### Beating Post Limit

The discussion of Amemar's position raises a further boundary case. Suppose someone violated his *shvua bemeizid*, and has now been bound to the post in *beis din* to receive *malkos* — the witnesses have testified, the warning was given, and the lashing is about to begin. May he appeal to a *chacham* at that very moment? The *Gemara* cites Shmuel's ruling: *kaftuhu al ha'amud, veratz mibeis din, patur* — if one was bound to the post and managed to flee *beis din*, he is exempt from further lashing, since the humiliation of the flight (*venikla achicha l'einecha*) substitutes for the punishment. One might think that being bound to the post therefore has the status of having already received the *malkos*, and that it is accordingly too late to seek a *sheila*. The *Gemara* rejects this: *hacha lo ratz* — here, the person has not fled. The exemption Shmuel speaks of arises from the running, not from the binding itself. Until the lashes are actually administered, the punishment remains pending, the *shvua* retains present relevance through its threatened consequence, and the appeal to the *chacham* remains theoretically available — a striking parallel to the idea that *teshuva* remains possible until the very last moment.

---

## Conditional Vows

### Setup & Consciousness

Rava introduces a new case: *shevuah shelo ochal kikar zo im ochal zo* — an oath structured as "I will not eat loaf B if I eat loaf A." Loaf A functions as the *tnai* (the trigger condition) and loaf B is the object of the *shvua* itself. The oath does not restrict B automatically; it only becomes binding upon B when A is eaten. This conditional structure introduces a layer of complexity that the *Gemara* now unpacks, and the key analytical tool — articulated most clearly by Tosafot — concerns the requirement of conscious awareness at critical junctures.

### Tosafot Framework

The foundational premise, as Tosafot frames it, is this: since the *shvua* on B does not take effect automatically upon being uttered but only upon the eating of A, the act of eating A is not merely a behavioral trigger — it is constitutively part of the act of *taking* the *shvua*. The *shvua* is not fully formed without the trigger being consciously pulled. From this follows a remarkable requirement: to bring a *korban* for violating B, one must have been *beshogeg* — having forgotten the oath — when eating B. But to have the *shvua* take effect on B in the first place, one must have been *bemeizid*, i.e., fully conscious and aware, when eating A. If A was eaten inadvertently, with no awareness that doing so would activate the prohibition on B, the *shvua* simply never crystallized, and there is no violation of B regardless of the circumstances in which B is subsequently eaten.

### Four Combinations

Four combinations of *shogeg* and *meizid* across A (the trigger) and B (the forbidden act) exhaust the possibilities.

### Shogeg Trigger

If A was eaten *beshogeg* — without awareness that it was activating a *shvua* — the conditional *shvua* never takes effect. Regardless of what state of mind accompanied the eating of B, there is no liability: *patur*. The conversation ends there.

### Both Mezid

If A was eaten *bemeizid* (the trigger was consciously pulled) and B was eaten *beshogeg* (the person had forgotten his oath by the time he ate B), this is the paradigmatic case of liability: the *shvua* was properly activated, the violation was inadvertent, and a *korban* is required.

If both A and B were eaten *bemeizid*, the analysis becomes sensitive to order — specifically, which was eaten first.

### Order & Warning

If A (the trigger) was eaten first *bemeizid*, and then B was eaten *bemeizid* with full awareness that the *shvua* was already in effect, this is a straightforward willful violation, and *malkos* applies.

The more complex case arises when B is eaten first — while it is still entirely permissible — and only afterward is A eaten, thereby retroactively triggering the *shvua* and making the earlier eating of B into a transgression. If both acts were *bemeizid*, one might think a warning (*hasra'ah*) could have been issued when B was being eaten, saying: if you subsequently eat A, this eating of B will have constituted a violation. Whether such a *hasra'ah* is valid is the subject of the famous debate between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish regarding *hasra'as safek* — a conditional warning given when it is uncertain at the time whether a violation will actually occur. According to the opinion that *hasra'as safek shmah hasra'ah*, such a warning suffices for *malkos*; according to the opposing view, it does not, and the person is *patur* from lashes.

There is, however, something genuinely uncomfortable about applying Reish Lakish's position here. In the standard *hasra'as safek* case, the person is typically already in the process of an act that may or may not mature into a transgression — one can see how a warning at that moment captures the spirit of *hasra'ah*. Here, by contrast, when B was being eaten, the act was entirely permissible. The person had made no decision to violate anything. Giving a warning at that point — "if you later eat A, this eating of B will have been a sin" — does not seem to correspond to the usual function of *hasra'ah*, which is to confront the person at the moment of apparent transgression and elicit a conscious act of defiance. The person eating B is doing nothing wrong; it strains the concept of *hasra'ah* to treat that as the moment of violation. This remains a genuine analytical tension.

### Rashi Alternative

Rashi offers a different reading of the *Gemara* that does not require the trigger specifically to be *bemeizid*. Rather, Rashi holds that whichever of the two loaves is eaten *first* must be done with conscious awareness. This is a somewhat harder position to explain conceptually — Tosafot finds it difficult to justify why chronological priority should determine the consciousness requirement rather than the functional role of trigger versus forbidden act. The elegance of Tosafot's reading, however imprecise its handling of the term *rishona*, is that it maps neatly onto a coherent principle: the act that brings the *shvua* into being requires consciousness; the act that violates it requires *shegagah* for the *korban* to apply.

### Rabbeinu Tam

Rabbeinu Tam contributes an additional *chiddush*: one need not eat the trigger *bemeizid* for the *shvua* to take effect on B. His scenario involves eating A consciously and permissibly — since at the moment of eating A no transgression is occurring — and then eating B while having completely forgotten the entire conditional stipulation. Rabbeinu Tam rules that in such a case the person brings a *korban*, treating the entire sequence as *beshogeg*. The reasoning is that what rendered the eating of B a transgression was the prior eating of A, and since the person had no memory of the stipulation when B was eaten, the whole act is colored by that inadvertence and classified as *shogeg* — even though the eating of A itself was entirely intentional.

---

## Reciprocal Conditions

### Dual Setup

The *Gemara* now introduces a doubly interlocked case: *lo ochel zo im ochel zo, lo ochel zo im ochel zo* — "I will not eat A if I eat B, and I will not eat B if I eat A." This creates two superimposed conditional structures, each of which designates the other loaf as its trigger and as its object respectively. The analysis now runs through the same four-quadrant grid, but applied simultaneously to both conditions.

### Dual Scenarios

The variables are: the state of mind when eating each loaf in its capacity as trigger for the *other* loaf's prohibition, and the state of mind when eating each loaf in its capacity as the forbidden object.

### Both Shogeg

If in both instances the trigger was eaten *beshogeg* — without awareness that eating it would activate the prohibition on the other — neither conditional *shvua* takes effect, and there is no liability whatsoever.

### Both Mezid Triggers

If both triggers were eaten *bemeizid* but both prohibited acts were committed *beshogeg*, the person brings two separate *korbanos*, one for each violation.

### Mixed Intent

If the triggers were *meizid* in one direction and *shogeg* in the other, only the *shvua* activated by the *meizid* trigger takes effect. The *shvua* on the other side never crystallized, and only one *korban* or one set of consequences applies.

### Complete Mezid

If everything was *bemeizid* throughout, the analysis returns to the question of order. The eating that occurred *after* its respective trigger was activated constitutes a clear and contemporaneous willful violation — *malkos* applies there. The eating that occurred *before* its trigger was subsequently activated presents the same *hasra'as safek* problem: it is subject to the debate of Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish as to whether that retroactive violation can carry *malkos* in its wake.

---

## Conditional Consciousness

### Four Vow Types

The *Gemara* brings support from the *Mishna* concerning *nidrei shegagos* — one of the four categories of vows that the Sages permit to be dissolved — alongside *nidrei ziruzin*, *nidrei havai*, and *nidrei onasin*.

### Forgotten Condition

The *Mishna* illustrates *nidrei shegagos* with the following case: a person declares, "*konam* if I have eaten or drunk today," believing he had not eaten, and the bread he designated becomes forbidden contingent on that past condition. He then remembers that he did in fact eat or drink. The *neder* is treated as never having taken effect, because at the moment of the declaration, the speaker's understanding of reality was mistaken in a way that negates the binding intent. The *Mishna* then pivots to a forward-conditional version: *she'ani ochel she'ani shoteh* — "if I will eat or drink" — where the condition is yet to occur.

### Trigger Consciousness

Here is the *chiddush*: if the person subsequently forgot about his stipulation entirely and proceeded to eat and drink, the *neder* is nonetheless *muttar* — permissible. The conditional *neder* did not take effect, because the trigger was pulled without conscious awareness that it was a trigger. This supports the broader principle: when a *shvua* or *neder* is structured around a future condition, the person must be conscious of the stipulation at the moment the condition is fulfilled. If that awareness is absent, the vow never fully crystallizes into a binding prohibition.

### Baraita Proof

A *Baraita* confirms the application: *keshem shenidrei shegagos muttarim kach shvuos shegagos muttaros* — just as inadvertent *nedarim* are permissible, so too inadvertent *shvuos*. The *Baraita* then asks *heichi dami* — how exactly does a *shvuat shegagos* work? — and answers with precisely this scenario: a *shvua* conditioned on a future event, where the condition was triggered without the person's awareness of the stipulation. *Shema mina* — this is solid support for the principle that conscious triggering is required.

---

## Eifa's Story

### Identical Past Vows

The *Gemara* now presents a charming but halachically substantive anecdote. Eifa, a scholar who studied *Shevuot* in Rabba's academy, was tested by his brother Avimi on the material. Avimi asked: if someone takes a *shvua* twice that he did not eat in the past — "*shvua shelo achalti, shvua shelo achalti*" — is he liable for both? Eifa answered that he is liable for only one, applying the principle of *ein shvua chal al shvua*.

### Past Vows False

Avimi corrected him: *ishtabishata* — you have been sloppy. The principle of *ein shvua chal al shvua* applies only to future-oriented oaths, where the question is whether a second restriction can layer atop an already existing one. A past-oriented *shvua* is a different creature entirely. The moment the first false *shvua* is uttered, the person is liable for *shvuat shav*; the oath has no ongoing force, and when the second one is uttered, it is likewise an independent false *shvua*. There is no mechanism of "one riding on top of the other" since past *shvuos* impose no lasting prohibition — each is a discrete act of false swearing, and liability attaches to each one separately.

### Nine and Ten

Having corrected his brother, Avimi pressed further. He asked: if someone first takes a *shvua* not to eat nine olives, and then takes a *shvua* not to eat ten — what is the law? Primed by the previous correction to expect double liability, Eifa answered: *chayav al kol achas ve'achas* — liable for each one.

### Not Broader

Again Avimi corrected him: *ishtabishata*. Ten is not actually a broader restriction than nine. Since one cannot eat ten without having already eaten nine, the prohibition of nine entirely subsumes the prohibition of ten: *tesha lo ochal asara lo ochil* — if you cannot eat nine, you certainly cannot eat ten. The second oath adds nothing; it cannot take effect as a *chol al shvua* because it does not enlarge the scope of the prohibition at all.

### Ten Then Nine

Now Avimi turned the tables. He asked about the reverse: first a *shvua* not to eat ten, then a *shvua* not to eat nine. Having been twice corrected toward single liability, Eifa answered: *eino chayav ella achas* — only one. Avimi corrected him a third time: *ishtabishata*.

### Nine More Restrictive

In the case of ten-then-nine, the second oath is actually *more* restrictive, not less. When the person swore not to eat ten, he could still eat nine freely — there is no violation until the tenth olive is consumed. The second oath, forbidding nine olives, now prohibits something the first oath left entirely permissible: eating nine olives without proceeding to the tenth. *Eser hu d'lo ochil, hatesha mi ochil?* — "It was ten I could not eat; who said anything about nine?" The second oath therefore genuinely adds a restriction and takes effect on its own terms. The brother had been tricked into overcorrecting in exactly the opposite direction — a lesson in thinking each case through on its own merits rather than applying a pattern from the previous case.

---

## Korban Separation

### Abaye Exception

Abaye now intervenes to defend Eifa's final, apparently erroneous answer, at least in a narrow scenario. He says: *zimnin d'mishkachas lah, leha d'Eifa kedemar* — there are circumstances in which Eifa's statement, that the ten-then-nine structure yields only a single liability, would actually be correct. Abaye grounds this in a ruling of Rava.

### Figs & Grapes

Rava's ruling addresses the following case: someone takes a *shvua* not to eat figs and grapes together — meaning a *kezayit* of figs *combined with* a *kezayit* of grapes. He then takes a second *shvua* not to eat figs alone. He eats the figs *beshogeg*, transgressing the second oath, and separates out a *korban* for that violation. He then eats the grapes separately. One might expect that the grapes, combined with the earlier eating of figs, would now constitute a violation of the first oath as well. But the *Gemara* rules otherwise: *havei lehu anavim chatzi shiur, v'chatzi shiur lo mechayeiv korban* — the grapes now constitute only a half-measure. The moment a *korban* was separated for the figs, the figs became exclusively identified with that specific violation. They are now "in their own box," categorically associated with the second *shvua* and its *korban*, and can no longer combine with other foods to create a new compound violation. The grapes alone are less than a *kezayit* toward any relevant threshold, and *chatzi shiur* does not generate *korban* liability.

### Half-Measure

The operative principle is that separating a *korban* segregates the violation. Once a *korban* is set aside for a specific transgression, the substance consumed in that transgression loses its capacity to function as part of a different combined violation. The remainder — whatever was not part of the act for which the *korban* was separated — now stands alone, and if alone it falls below the *shiur*, no additional liability follows.

### Nine & Ten Korban

Abaye applies the same logic to Eifa's case. Even though swearing not to eat ten and then not to eat nine should in principle create two distinct prohibitions — the second oath being the more restrictive one — there is a scenario in which only one *korban* results. If the person ate nine olives *beshogeg*, transgressing the second oath, and then separated a *korban* for that violation, and then ate the tenth olive, the tenth olive standing alone is *chatzi shiur* with respect to the first oath. It cannot combine with the now-segregated nine to form a compound violation of the first oath. In such a case, Eifa's answer of a single liability would be correct, even if he arrived at it by faulty reasoning.

### Tosafot Specificity

Tosafot adds a further nuance concerning the conditions under which a second oath takes effect at all. If the first oath forbids eating any nine out of a larger group, and the second oath forbids all ten, one can argue that the second oath adds nothing because one cannot eat ten without eating nine. But if the first oath was phrased to identify *specific* olives — "these nine" — and the second oath then includes a tenth olive that was previously excluded, the second oath explicitly encompasses something the first did not. Even though eating ten still requires eating nine, Tosafot argues that the specificity of the new inclusion is itself halachically significant: the second oath can be said to forbid a distinct object not referenced in the first, and on those grounds it takes effect even though the only path to transgressing it runs through the already-forbidden nine. This same principle would apply in the figs-and-grapes scenario where Tosafot reads the case differently than Rashi — if the first oath referred specifically to *zeitim* (olives) and the second added *anavim* (grapes), the addition of a specific new object may be sufficient for the second oath to bind, even though one cannot transgress the combined prohibition without eating the already-forbidden *zeitim*.

---

---

# Shevuot 29

## Daf 29 Overview

### Daf 29 Context

Daf 29 is the final daf of the third *perek* of Shevuot. With it, we wrap up the first two *perakim*, which focused on being *tamei* and entering the *Beis HaMikdash* — a theme we have discussed at length in terms of its place within this *masechet*. The third *perek* is concerned, at its core, with the *korban* that one brings when taking an oath and then violating it *beshogeg*, whether with respect to the future or to the past. But as we have seen, it also lays down the foundational parameters of oath law more broadly.

### Foundation Concepts

The *perek* has established the basic mechanics of *shevuot*: the difference between a *shevua* and a *neder*, the rule of *ein shevua chala al shevua* — that one oath cannot take hold upon another — and the concept of *mushba ve'omed*, that one who is already "standing under" an existing oath cannot create a new obligation by taking an additional one on the same matter. Similarly, we encountered the principle that a *shevua levatel es hamitzvah* — a *shevua* taken to negate a *mitzvah* obligation — does not take effect.

### Transition to Courts

Beginning with the next *perek*, our focus will shift toward the role of *shevuot* within *Seder Nezikin*: the use of oaths in the context of court deliberations, litigation, and the relationship between two parties. Questions will arise such as when one litigant is entitled to impose an oath upon the other, and what the consequences are if that oath is not taken. That discussion begins tomorrow. Today, however, we complete the third *perek*'s analysis of what makes an oath valid, binding, and consequential.

---

## Shevuat Shav

### Three Oath Types

The *Mishnah* on 29a opens with the question: *eizehi shevuat shav?* — what constitutes a *shevuat shav*, an oath taken in vain? To appreciate this, it helps to situate it against the categories we have already encountered. A *shevuat bituy* is future-oriented: if violated *beshogeg*, one brings a *korban*; if violated *bemezid*, one receives lashes. A past-oriented oath, when violated *bemezid*, constitutes a *shevuat sheker* — a false oath. If violated *beshogeg*, there is a debate between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yishmael as to whether a *korban* is brought at all. What we have not yet examined is the third category: *shevuat shav*, against which the verse reads *lo tisa et shem Hashem Elokecha lashav* — do not take God's name in vain, as distinct from *lasheker*, which is false.

### Known Falsehoods

The *Mishnah* defines *shevuat shav* beginning with a case of *nishba lishanot es hayaduah l'adam* — swearing to claim something is different from what is well known to people. The example given is: *amar al amud shel even shehu shel zahav* — one has a pillar of stone and takes an oath that it is gold. One might have assumed this was a *shevuat sheker*, a false oath, but the distinction being drawn is that something *transparently* false is not a meaningful lie — it does not deceive — and therefore the oath serves no purpose. It is, in that sense, vain. A lie that cannot function as a lie is not *sheker*; it is *shav*. The *Mishnah* similarly includes swearing that a man is a woman or that a woman is a man.

### Impossible Claims

The *Mishnah* continues with *nishba al davar she'ee efshar lo* — swearing about something that is impossible. The example given is: *im lo ra'iti gamal porei'ach ba'avir* — if I did not see a camel flying through the air; or claiming to have seen a snake as thick as the beam of an olive press. These are cases of patently impossible claims, though the precise structure of what oath is being taken here will require the *Gemara*'s attention, as we will see shortly.

Worth noting is something conspicuously absent from this *Mishnah*: the case of swearing to something patently *true*. If one swears that two plus two is four, that is also a *shevuat shav* — the oath serves no purpose because the matter is self-evident. This case appears elsewhere and is assumed to be included in *shevuat shav*, but it is not enumerated here, a point to flag.

### Negating Mitzvot

A distinct and important category in the *Mishnah* is *nishba levatel es hamitzvah* — taking an oath to negate a *mitzvah* obligation. The examples given are: *shelo la'asot sukka*, *shelo litol lulav*, *shelo l'haniach tefillin*. Each of these cases falls under *shevuat shav*.

One notices immediately that the *Mishnah* says *shelo la'asot sukka* — not to *build* a *sukka* — rather than *shelo leishev basukka*, not to *dwell* in it. One does not have a technical obligation to build a *sukka* oneself. This phrasing prompted the *Netziv* to develop the concept of *hachshar mitzvah hakatuv baTorah*: the Torah's verse *chag hasukkot ta'aseh lecha* implies a value in the making of the *sukka* even absent a strict obligation, such that this too carries some weight as a *kiyum mitzvah*. Most *Rishonim*, however, treat the phrase as *lav davka* — not to be read precisely — and assume the *Mishnah* means *shelo leishev basukka*. Still, the observation is worth making.

### Penalties

With regard to penalties: *zo hi shevuat shav shechayavin al zedonah malkot* — if one willfully takes a *shevuat shav*, one receives lashes. *Ve'al shigagatah patur* — if done in error or unawareness, one is exempt. Crucially, one does not bring a *korban* for *shevuat shav* under any circumstances. The *korban* is reserved for *shevuat bituy* in the future, and possibly the past — but not for *shevuat shav*.

The *Mishnah* also addresses a paired case: *shevua she'ochal kikar zo, shevua shelo ochelenah* — first swearing to eat a loaf of bread, then swearing not to eat it. The *Mishnah* identifies the first as a *shevuat bituy* and the second as a *shevuat shav*, since the second oath negates the binding obligation created by the first. The *Mishnah* then states: *achalah* — if he ate it — he has violated the *shevuat shav* (though he fulfilled his *shevuat bituy*); *lo achalah* — if he did not eat it — he has violated the *shevuat bituy*. The implication of the *Mishnah* seems to be that the two oaths stand in tension and one will inevitably be violated. The *Gemara* will challenge this framing, and *Tosafot* raises a preliminary question about whether these two oaths are truly contradictory in the first place — after all, one might fulfill the first by eating a *kazayit* and fulfill the second by not eating the entire loaf. *Tosafot* does not resolve this cleanly but suggests that "I will eat it" may connote eating the whole thing, while "I will not eat it" may mean not eating any of it. In any case, it is the *Gemara* that will probe the deeper difficulty.

---

## Obviousness Standard

### Ulla's Rule

The *Gemara* now takes up the question of what "well known" means for the purpose of *shevuat shav*. *Amar Ulla: vehu shenikar ligimel bnei adam* — Ulla teaches that it does not need to be transparently false to everyone; it suffices that three people know the truth of the matter. So if three people know that a pillar is made of stone — even though most observers believe it is gold because it has been painted to look so — and one swears it is gold, that is a *shevuat shav* rather than a *shevuat sheker*.

### Challenge to Rule

This is a striking ruling. One would naturally assume that if a person succeeds in deceiving most observers, the oath functions as a genuine lie and ought to constitute *shevuat sheker*. The apparent logic of the three-person standard is that facts known to three people are, in principle, publicly accessible — they can eventually come to light. But this seems deeply insufficient as a criterion. A lie can deceive a thousand people even though the facts are theoretically discoverable. The distinction between *shav* and *sheker* here seems to rest on an idealized notion of epistemic accessibility that may not correspond to social reality, particularly in an age where demonstrable falsehoods are repeated and believed with great conviction. The argument that "in theory, people could find out" is a thin basis for removing the offense from the category of *sheker*.

### What Counts as Known

One might further ask: how contextual is this three-person standard? If three members of one's family witnessed something and one swears publicly to the contrary, does that qualify as *shav* rather than *sheker* because three people know? The more defensible reading is that the three-person rule applies in a context where the knowledge is sufficiently available in the relevant setting — where one would ordinarily expect the truth to be discoverable in the community in which the oath is being taken. A purely private or confined awareness likely does not satisfy the threshold. That is how one would prefer to read the principle, though the *Gemara* does not spell this out explicitly.

---

## Impossible Oaths

### Oath Content Issue

The *Gemara* now returns to the case of the camel flying. The difficulty is pointed: *shevua she'ra'iti lo ka'amar* — the person did not say "I swear I saw a flying camel." The language in the *Mishnah* is *im lo ra'iti* — "if I did not see." This is conditional language, not a direct oath. So what exactly is the *shevua* here, and why does it constitute *shevuat shav*?

### Abuye vs. Rava

*Abaye* resolves this by proposing an alternative *girsa* — a different textual reading: *tani shevua she'ra'iti* — simply emend the *Mishnah* to read that the person swore that he *did* see a flying camel. That is patently false, and the case straightforwardly fits the category of *shevuat shav*. *Rava*, by contrast, offers a different reading of the conditional formulation: *ye'asru kol peirot sheba'olam alai bishevua im lo ra'iti gamal porei'ach ba'avir* — what the person is saying is: "All the fruit of the world shall be forbidden to me by oath if I did not see a camel fly." Since in fact he did not see one, the condition is triggered, and he has taken a *shevua* never to eat any of the world's produce.

### Tossafot's View

*Tosafot* finds the *Gemara*'s treatment here difficult and clarifies the point: the truly significant element is not the flying camel — that is essentially incidental — but rather the oath to refrain from all fruit forever, which is practically impossible. The analogy offered in the *Gemara* elsewhere is an oath never to sleep: the person receives lashes for *shevuat shav* immediately, and is permitted to sleep immediately, because such an oath cannot be fulfilled. The *ee efshar* — the impossibility — refers not to the camel's flight but to the oath's subject matter, namely the commitment to never consume any food. As *Tosafot* acknowledges, this is a very strained reading of the *Mishnah*, which emphasizes the flying camel prominently and treats it as if it were the salient feature of the case. The real point, according to *Tosafot*, is the category of a *shevua* to do something humanly impossible.

### Neder Shav

This analysis in *Tosafot* prompts an interesting further question: what if the same impossibility were framed as a *neder* rather than a *shevua*? If one said "all fruit of the world is forbidden to me" in a *neder* formulation, the effect is indirect — it forbids the objects rather than directly speaking to one's capacities. This is analogous to a *neder levatel es hamitzvah* — a *neder* that makes a *sukka* forbidden, which takes effect because it operates on the object rather than directly contradicting the obligation. *Tosafot* presents two opinions: one holds that such a *neder* on all food would take effect for the same reason; the other argues that a *neder* whose fulfillment is humanly impossible is not a valid *neder* at all.

This raises a further question: if such a *neder* does not take effect, has the person done anything wrong? Is there a concept of *neder shav*? The *Gemara* itself states simply *nidrei shav lo matzinu* — we have not found the category of a *vow in vain*. The explanation lies in the structural difference between a *shevua* and a *neder*. The prohibition of *shevuat shav* derives from *lo tisa et shem Hashem Elokecha lashav* — it is the invocation of God's name, explicitly or implicitly, that defines the wrong. A *shevua* always involves calling upon God as a witness to one's word; even without pronouncing the divine name aloud, the invocation is present by implication. A *neder*, by contrast, operates by sanctifying or prohibiting objects, without any inherent invocation of God's name. Hence, if a *neder* fails to take effect, there is nothing further that has been violated.

---

## God's Name Role

### Shevua as God's Witness

This returns us to a theme that has recurred throughout the *perek*: the fundamental character of a *shevua* is not merely a commitment about one's future actions but an act of calling upon God to witness the truth of one's statement. Whether or not one explicitly pronounces the divine name, God's presence as guarantor is always implicit in the structure of a *shevua*. This is what makes *shevuat shav* a violation of *lo tisa et shem Hashem lashav* — one has invoked God's name, directly or by implication, in a vain or false context.

### Shevua vs. Neder

This distinction between *shevua* and *neder* is precisely why *neder shav* is not a recognized category. The *Rambam* reinforces this point when he rules that while an oath without explicit mention of God's name does create a binding obligation, the full range of consequences — *malkus* and *korban* — apply only when God's name or one of His appellations is explicitly invoked. Whether the *Rambam* means that without God's name the violation is only rabbinic, or that it is biblical but lacks sufficient weight to trigger the specific penalties — analogous to a *chatzi shi'ur* — is itself a question worth examining. But the centrality of God's name to the *shevua* is unmistakable throughout.

---

## Intent & Private Meaning

### Private Meaning

The *Gemara* poses a sharp question via *Ravina*: how do we know in any given case that an oath about a camel flying is patently false? Perhaps the person had a large pet bird he nicknamed "Camel," and when he said he saw a camel fly, he was referring to his bird — *ufarkah* — and assigned that meaning perfectly consistently with his own private linguistic framework. *Ve'chi kamishtava ada'ata didei kamishtava* — when he takes an oath, perhaps he takes it on the basis of his own private meaning? This is a natural extension of the well-established principle that *shevuot* and *nedarim* require *piv ve'libo shavin* — that one's words and one's intention must be aligned — which implies that what one *means* by the words matters, not merely what the words standardly denote.

### Lips vs. Mind

The response is: *batar pumi azlinan velo azlinan batar da'atei* — we follow the lips, not the mind. The principle that intention matters functions to contextualize and clarify; it does not permit a speaker to assign a meaning to words that stands in clear contradiction to what those words normally and standardly mean. There is a difference between private *context* that clarifies an ambiguity, and private *language* that simply overrides the shared meaning of words. The former may be permitted; the latter is not.

### Court Warning

This principle is reinforced by a *baraita*: *kshe'mashbi'in oto omrim lo hevei yodea shelo al da'atcha anu mashbi'im otcha ela al da'teinu v'al da'at Beit Din* — when *Beit Din* administers an oath, they explicitly warn the person: this oath is not being taken on the basis of your understanding of the words but on the basis of ours, and of the court's. The question is why this warning is necessary. Does the fact that we must preempt the possibility of private meanings not demonstrate that, absent such preemption, one would in fact be entitled to assign private meanings?

### Rava's Stick

The *Gemara* answers: *lo, hasam mishum kanya d'Rava* — no; the warning is directed at a different concern, illustrated by the famous story of *Rava*. A person owed money and denied the debt. Before taking an oath, he secretly placed the money inside a hollowed-out walking stick, handed the stick to the creditor, and then swore that he had "given" the other party the money — which was literally true, in a manner of speaking, since the money was inside the stick now held by the creditor. Here the deception is not through private linguistic meaning but through *context* — the circumstances are constructed so that words true in one sense are understood entirely differently by everyone else. The court's warning addresses this kind of manipulation: not that you may assign idiosyncratic private meanings to words, but that you may not manufacture a context designed to make your words technically accurate while conveying a false impression.

### Context Not Meaning

The conclusion is thus that the concern is not private meaning but constructed context. The standard remains: we go by what the words normally and publicly mean, and no private redefinition overrides that standard.

---

## Moshe's Oath

### Torah Source

The *Gemara* cites a further proof from the account of *Moshe* at *Arvot Moav*, where *Moshe* imposes an oath upon *Bnei Yisrael* — not only upon those present but upon all future generations. *Amar lahen: de'u shelo al da'atchem ani mashbia etchem ela al da'at Hamakom ve'al da'ati* — know that I am not imposing this oath based on what you think the words mean; it is on God's understanding and on mine. The *Gemara* asks why *Moshe* needed to say this. If the concern were private linguistic meanings, he could simply have said: fulfill everything God commanded. But even the most explicit formulations — *kimu kol hamitzvot kulan* — might be given non-private but alternative recognized meanings. For instance, *kol haTorah kula* could be interpreted as the essence of the Torah, namely rejection of *avoda zara*, based on the rabbinic teaching that one who repudiates idolatry is as one who affirms the entire Torah. Similarly, *kimu kol hamitzvot* could be satisfied by adopting *tzitzit*, which the rabbis say is equivalent in weight to all the *mitzvot*. These are not private meanings but legitimate alternative interpretations of the language used.

### Tossafot Question

*Tosafot* raises a beautiful question here. If *Bnei Yisrael* were not going to keep the *mitzvot* commanded by God, why would a *shevua* to keep them make any difference? *Tosafot* phrases it: *ktzat kashe mai mahanya lehu hashevuah* — it is somewhat difficult: what does the oath accomplish? If they feared they would commit *avoda zara*, how much more so should they fear violating an oath? If they would transgress divine command, would they honor their own sworn word?

### Pachad Yitzchak

The answer, and it is a compelling one, is psychological and philosophical. The *Pachad Yitzchak* — Rav Yitzchak Hutner — extends this reasoning in a striking direction. He addresses the same question with respect to *Ma'amad Har Sinai* itself: why did *Bnei Yisrael* need to say "we will do" and "we will listen"? The *mitzvot* were being commanded by God regardless — what additional weight did their own acceptance carry? He argues that this points toward an irreducible category of self-imposed obligation that is independent of divine command. If all ethical obligation derived solely from God's command, then a person's own self-commitment would add nothing. But there is evidently something qualitatively distinct about the experience of standing by one's own word — of one's integrity being on the line — that is not reducible to obedience to an external command. The *shevua* does not merely replicate the divine command; it introduces a different register of obligation, one rooted in the person's own self-definition. This is why it can function as additional motivation even for someone already bound by *mitzvot*.

### Prevents Nullification

The *Gemara* ultimately provides its own explanation for why *Moshe* said *al da'at Hamakom ve'al da'ati*: *ki heichi d'lo tehei hafara lishevu'asaihu* — so that there could be no *hatara*, no annulment, of the oath. The mechanism of *hatarat nedarim* works by demonstrating that, given the actual circumstances, one would not have taken the oath. But when the oath is declared to be binding on *God's da'at* and on *Moshe's da'at*, not merely on the swearer's own intent, the swearer cannot approach a *chacham* and claim "had I known, I would not have committed to this" — because the bindingness was never predicated solely on the swearer's intent. It was anchored in a will external to the swearer's own, and that external will cannot be undone by the swearer's claim of regret. This is the primary function of *al da'at Hamakom ve'al da'ati* — not to determine the *meaning* of the words but to constrain the *unwinding* of the commitment.

---

## Cherem & Waivers

### Cherem Question

*Tosafot* raises the practical application of this principle in the context of medieval communal *cherem*. The classic formula used when communities enacted binding enactments — including *Cherem Rabbeinu Gershom* — employed the phrase *al da'as hakadosh baruch hu ve'al da'as hakahal*, on God's understanding and on the community's. Since this formula invokes *da'as rabim* — collective intent — the rule *neder she'hu al da'as rabim ein lo hafara* would seem to apply: a *neder* made on collective intent cannot be annulled. Yet *Cherem Rabbeinu Gershom* was in practice sometimes waived under extenuating circumstances. How is that possible?

### Waiver Discretion

*Tosafot* answers: *da'as hakahal kach hu* — this is precisely *what* the collective intent is. The invocation of *da'as rabim* achieves two things: first, it prevents the individual subject to the *cherem* from unilaterally seeking a *hatara* on his own; second, it vests complete discretion in the *kahal* — or the rabbis as their representatives — to waive the obligation whenever and however they see fit, without requiring any formal process of *charata*. It is not that the *Beit Din* must go through the usual process of demonstrating that had they known the circumstances they would not have imposed the *cherem*. The *da'as rabim* is precisely the authority of the collective to determine, at their discretion, when a waiver is appropriate. The individual cannot undo it; the collective can.

### God's Da'at Purpose

As for the invocation of God's name in the communal *cherem* — *tiknu hageonim lechumra be'alma* — the *Geonim* instituted the inclusion of *da'as Hamakom* to add weight and solemnity to the enactment. But unlike *Moshe's* invocation, which was made at God's explicit instruction, the communal *cherem* is ultimately grounded in *da'as hakahal* alone. The reference to God is a stringency, not essential to the legal mechanism. *Aval charamos shenigzaru hakol taluy beda'as hakahal lachud* — as far as the law is concerned, it is the community's intent that is dispositive.

---

## Contradictory Oaths

### Bread Case

The *Mishnah* presents the case of *shevua she'ochal kikar zo, shevua shelo ochelenah* — swearing to eat a particular loaf of bread and then swearing not to eat it. The *Mishnah* identifies the first as a *shevuat bituy* and the second as a *shevuat shav* — since the second oath attempts to negate an obligation already created by the first. The *Mishnah* then states: *achalah* — if he ate it — he violated the *shevuat shav*; *lo achalah* — if he did not eat it — he violated the *shevuat bituy*.

### When Does It Become Shav

The *Gemara* presses the difficulty that Michael flagged: if the second oath was already a *shevuat shav* the moment it left his lips — *harei yatza shevua leshav* — then if he does not eat the bread, why has he violated anything? The *shevuat shav* was never binding, and all he has done is fail to eat what his first oath required. There should be no violation of the second oath because the second oath was always void. The *Gemara* thus asks: *mishum shevuat shav lo mechayev?* Did he not transgress anything with respect to the *shevuat shav*?

### Both Oaths Stand

*Rabbi Yirmiyah* resolves this: *tani af al shvuat bituy* — both oaths effectively stand and operate in parallel. One always has the transgression of the *shevuat shav* — it was uttered in vain the moment it was spoken — and the question is only whether one will *additionally* violate the *shevuat bituy*. If he eats the bread, he violates the *shevuat shav* and fulfills the *shevuat bituy*. If he does not eat it, he has the *shevuat shav* transgression regardless, and additionally violates the *shevuat bituy*. There is no situation in which he escapes both violations: the *shevuat shav* is violated simply by having been uttered, and the *shevuat bituy* is violated one way or the other depending on his action.

---

## God's Name Role (II)

### Rambam's Categories

At this point it is worth citing the *Rambam*'s systematic account of *shevuat shav*, which he divides into four categories: *ha'achas shenishba al davar yadua she'ein kein* — swearing about something known to be untrue; *hashniya shenishba al davar yadua she'ein bo safek l'adam shehu kein* — swearing to affirm something that is entirely beyond doubt and requires no oath; *hashlishit shenishba levatel es hamitzvah* — swearing to negate a *mitzvah*; and *harevi'it shenishba al davar she'ein lo koach bah la'asoto* — swearing to do something beyond one's physical capacity, such as never to sleep or never to eat. The second category — the patently true oath — is notably absent from our *Mishnah* but is confirmed here by the *Rambam* as a genuine category of *shevuat shav*. Equally notable is that the *Rambam* does not enumerate *ain shevua chala al shevua* — the redundant oath — as a category of *shevuat shav*, which is itself an interesting omission.

On the question of God's name, the *Rambam* rules: if one says *alah*, *arur*, or *shevua* without mentioning God's name, the thing sworn is nevertheless prohibited. However, one does not receive *malkus* and does not bring a *korban* for violating such an oath unless it included an explicit divine name or one of God's appellations. This underscores how central God's name is to the full category of *shevua*: without explicit invocation, the oath may still be halakhically binding, but the severe penalties are reserved for the case where God's name is directly engaged. Whether this reflects a merely rabbinic level of obligation absent God's name, or a biblical obligation of lesser weight — insufficient to trigger *korban* or *malkus* but real nonetheless, in a manner analogous to *chatzi shi'ur* — remains a meaningful question.

---

## Shevuat Bituy

### Scope

The *Mishnah* turns to a summary of the scope and penalties of *shevuat bituy*. *Noheget beanshim uvenashim* — it applies to both men and women; *bikrovim uverechokim* — to relatives and non-relatives alike. The mention of relatives here anticipates the contrast with *shevuat ha'edut* in the next *perek*, where a relative cannot be a valid witness and an oath regarding testimony from a relative is therefore not binding as a *shevuat ha'edut*. *Rashi* explains that the example of relatives here means something like: whether you swear to give money to your brother or to a stranger, the oath is equally binding. *Bichsherim uvisulim* — whether the oath-taker is halakhically fit to give testimony or disqualified, as in the case of a *ganav*.

### Jurisdiction

*Bifnei Beit Din ushelo bifnei Beit Din* — the oath operates whether taken in the presence of the court or outside of it. *Mipi atzmo* — it applies only if the oath was self-initiated. The *Mishnah* adds this qualification, which will generate apparent tension with the end of the *Mishnah*, as the *Gemara* will note.

---

## Shevuat Bituy (II)

### Penalties

*Vechayavin al zedonah malkus ve'al shigagatah korban oleh veyored* — one who willfully violates a *shevuat bituy* receives lashes; one who unintentionally violates it brings the variable-cost *korban*.

---

## Shevuat Shav Scope

### Full Scope

A *shevuat shav* likewise applies to men and women, relatives and non-relatives, those who are *kasher* to testify and those who are *pasul*. In these respects it parallels *shevuat bituy* exactly.

### Jurisdiction

Similarly, *shevuat shav* applies both *bifnei Beit Din* and outside of *Beit Din*. And here too, it applies only when self-initiated — *mipi atzmo*.

### Penalties

*Vechayavin al zedonah malkus ve'al shigagatah patur* — willful violation of *shevuat shav* brings lashes; unintentional violation incurs no penalty at all — no *korban*, no lashes. This stands in direct contrast to *shevuat bituy*, where unintentional violation triggers the *korban*.

---

## Imposed vs. Self

### Contradiction

Having stated in both contexts that oaths apply only *mipi atzmo* — when self-initiated — the *Mishnah* then appears to reverse course. It states: *achat zu ve'achat zu hamushba mipi acherim chayav* — whether the oath of *shevuat bituy* or of *shevuat shav*, one is *chayav* even if the oath was imposed by others. This seems to directly contradict the requirement of *mipi atzmo* that was just stipulated. Which is it?

### Shmuel's Rule

*Shmuel* resolves the tension: *kol ha'oneh amen achar shevua kemotzi shevua mipiv dami* — one who responds *amen* after an oath administered by another is considered as if the oath came from his own lips. Packed into the word *amen* is the full content of what the other person said. When you say *amen*, you have, in effect, pronounced the oath yourself. The proof-text is the *pasuk* regarding a woman who responds *amen amen* to an oath imposed upon her — this is treated as if she herself articulated the oath. The case in the *Mishnah* that describes someone being told "I impose an oath upon you" and responding *amen* thus does not contradict the requirement of *mipi atzmo*; rather, the word *amen* itself constitutes the speech act of self-imposition.

### Confirmation

*Rav Pappa* in the name of *Rava* adds that this same principle can be derived from the rules of *shevuat ha'edut*, the oath of testimony discussed at the outset of the next *perek*. That *mishnah-baraita* specifies: *noheget beanshim velo benashim* — it applies to men but not women; *berachokim velo bekrovim* — to non-relatives but not relatives; *bichsherim velo bifsulim* — to those fit to testify but not those disqualified. These are the inverse of the categories for *shevuat bituy*. The *baraita* further distinguishes between oath initiated by the witnesses themselves and oath imposed upon them: if the witnesses themselves swore, the oath is binding whether inside or outside the court; if the oath was imposed by others, it is binding only if done *bifnei Beit Din*. This distinction depends on the presence or absence of *amen*. When they say *amen*, the oath functions as self-imposed and operates anywhere; when no *amen* is said, a court-imposed oath requires the formal setting of *Beit Din*.

### Reconciliation

This provides the clean reconciliation: *ha deana amen, ha delo ana amen* — when the person said *amen*, it is as if it came from their own lips; when they did not say *amen*, only the court context supplies sufficient authority for the imposed oath to be binding. And a striking point emerges: even without *amen*, a court-administered oath appears to be effective — meaning the person does not need to affirmatively acquiesce in some cases.
