That is itself a *chiddush*, but it is the separate mechanism of *Beit Din*'s authority, not the principle of *amen* as self-imposition.

---

## Close Reading

### Diuk Method

After establishing this halakhic conclusion, the *Gemara* asks: given that the point follows so clearly from a close reading of the *Mishnah* itself — the example given is of someone who says *amen*, and it says *chayav* — what precisely is *Shmuel* teaching us? The answer: *diuka dematnitin ka mashma lan* — he is teaching us the method of *diuk*, close textual reading, and demonstrating that by attending carefully to the precise language of the *Mishnah*, one can extract substantive halakhic conclusions that might otherwise be missed.

### Rambam's Bracha

The *Rambam* applies this same principle — *kol ha'oneh amen kemotzi shevua mipiv dami* — to the laws of *Brachot* in *Hilchot Brachot*. He creates two distinct levels. *Kol ha'oneh amen kemotzi bracha mipiv dami*: if you hear a *bracha* and respond *amen*, that *amen* is considered as if you yourself pronounced the full *bracha* — all the words of the blessing are packed into the word *amen*. A distinct lower level is the *shomea*: *vehashomea harei zeh k'oneh* — one who merely listens, without saying *amen*, is considered as if he responded *amen*. Listening is equivalent to *amen*; *amen* is equivalent to having said the full *bracha*. There are thus two degrees of removal from actually pronouncing the words — and the *Rambam* distinguishes them, because the halakhic consequences may differ, even if both permit one to fulfill the obligation. The *Rambam* clearly derives this graduated structure from the *Gemara*'s discussion here, extending the principle of *amen* as equivalent speech from the domain of *shevuot* into the domain of *brachot*.

---

---

# Shevuot 30

## God's Name & Oath Types

### Opening & Transition

We begin the fourth *perek* of Masechet Shevuot, moving on from the mechanics of how *shevuos* take effect — how one oath operates on top of another, what constitutes *sheker* versus *shav*, and related questions — to the use of a *shevua* in a legal context. The most immediate application is between litigants, but this *perek* also addresses the use of a *shevua* to compel testimony, functioning as something like a subpoena.

Before turning to the new *perek*, however, it is worth revisiting a point from the previous discussion concerning the *Ra'avad's* position on *shevuos* — a position that was not fully presented earlier due to the limitations of working without the *Ra'avad's* glosses in the app being used.

### Shevua vs. Neder

The fundamental distinction between a *shevua* and a *neder* is that a *shevua* involves an implicit or explicit invocation of God's name. This is rooted in two prohibitions: *lo tisa shem Hashem Elokecha lashav* and *lo tishavu bishmi lashaker*. This is precisely why there is a prohibition — and indeed *malkus* — for a *shvuas shav*, but not for a *neder shav*. A *neder shav* means an attempt to make something forbidden that simply did not take effect — no great harm done. But a *shvuas shav* means invoking God's name in vain, and that is inherently serious. The reason *shevuos* concern past events and specific actions is precisely because they all revolve around invoking God's name.

This raises the question: what if one did not invoke God's name at all, but simply said "I swear I will not do such and such"?

### Rambam & Ra'avad

The *Rambam* rules (*Hilchos Shevuos*, *perek* 2, *halacha* 4) that if someone takes an oath *velo hizkir shem velo kinuy* — without mentioning God's name or any divine epithet — *harei zeh assur bedavar shenishba alav*, the *shevua* is binding, but *ein lo malkus velo meivi korban*: there is neither *malkus* nor a *korban*. The practical consequence is thus entirely absent, and it may even be the case that such an oath is merely rabbinic in force.

The *Ra'avad* disagrees, at least partially. His disagreement is significant and worth reading carefully.

### Ra'avad's Two Components

The *Ra'avad* begins by noting that the *Rambam's* formulation may apply in certain contexts — specifically *ella be'edus uvifikadon*, in cases involving an oath of testimony or an oath of a *shomer* regarding the fate of an entrusted object. He notes that it is specifically in these contexts that we find the Torah's emphasis on God's name, and he marshals the relevant *Gemaras* in support.

But *aval bishvuas bituy* — when it comes to an oath about future actions — and even *shvuas shav*, everything studied until now — *afilu mifta o issur shvua*, even if one said *mifta* or *shevua* without invoking God's name, and *af al pi shelo amar lo shem velo kinuy*, even without stating God's name or any of its substitutes, the *Gemara* treats it as a full-fledged *shevua*. The *Ra'avad* enumerates additional formulations: *lav lav vehen hen* — saying "yes, yes" or "no, no" — which the *Gemara* recognizes as oath-language; *vechen yamin usmol*, invoking the right and left hand of the Creator by implication. In all these cases, the *Gemara* appears to treat the oath as fully binding.

The *Rambam* would agree that these are binding *shevuos*, but would maintain there is no *malkus* and no *korban*. The *Ra'avad*, however, argues that the *Gemara* treats them as real *shevuos* in every sense.

Yet the *Ra'avad* does not completely part ways with the *Rambam*. His final line is critical: *v'hani milei lekorban* — all of the above is in terms of the *korban* obligation and the prohibition of *bal yachal devaro*. One does not need the concept of *shem Hashem* to create an obligation, violate it, and thereby transgress *lo yachal devaro*. This is precisely how a *neder* works: a *neder* has nothing to do with *shem Hashem*, it creates a metaphysical reality about the object's status, and violating it constitutes *lo yachal devaro*. A *shevua* similarly creates a self-imposed obligation upon the person — independent of the invocation of God's name. Violating that self-imposed obligation is *lo yachal devaro*, and brings with it the obligation of a *korban*.

Where the *Ra'avad* does agree with the *Rambam* is regarding *malkus*. To incur lashes, one must transgress *lo tisa es shem Hashem Elokecha lashav* — the prohibition of *shvuas shav* — or *lo tishavu bishmi lashaker* — the prohibition of *shvuas sheker*. Both of these are explicitly tied to God's name. *Aval le-malkus be'inan shem, de-ksiv lo sisa es shem Hashem Elokecha lashav, ve-shvuas sheker nami lo tishavu bishmi lashaker*. Without God's name, there is no *malkus*. This is why *shvuas shav* incurs *malkus* while *neder shav* does not: the former involves God's name taken in vain, the latter does not.

The *Ra'avad* thus presents a two-component analysis of *shevua*. The first component is the invocation of God's name — this is what generates the prohibitions of *shvuas shav* and *shvuas sheker* and their attendant *malkus*. The second component is the creation of a self-imposed metaphysical obligation, analogous to a *neder*, which does not require God's name and which generates the obligation of a *korban* and the transgression of *lo yachal devaro* upon violation. Importantly, the *Ra'avad* adds that when it comes to *shvuas ha-eidus* specifically, he agrees with the *Rambam* — God's name is required there even for the *korban*.

With this understanding of *shevua* and the role of God's name firmly established, we turn to the new *perek* and its central subject: *shvuas ha-eidus*.

---

## Shevuas Ha-Eidus

### Parameters & Scope

The *Mishnah* opens: *shvuas ha-eidus noheges ba-anashim velo ve-nashim* — the oath of testimony applies to men and not women. This is because the *shvuas ha-eidus* in the *Torah* comes into play when a person is asked to come testify on someone's behalf and denies knowing any relevant testimony. It operates only in contexts where testimony would be legally relevant. Since women are not eligible witnesses in a *beis din*, the *shvuas ha-eidus* does not apply to them.

Likewise: *bi-rechokim velo bi-kerovim* — it applies only when one is adjuring someone who is not a relative; *bi-kesherim velo bi-pesulim* — only someone who is halachically qualified to testify, not, for example, one who has been disqualified as a *gazlan*; *ve-eino noheges ela be-re'uyin le-ha'id* — it applies only to those fit to testify. This final catch-all phrase adds something beyond what was already stated — presumably it would include a minor or someone not of sound mind, who may not have been captured by the earlier categories.

### Beit Din Requirement

The *Mishnah* then states: *bifnei beis din ve-shelo bifnei beis din*. The *Mishnah* is presenting *Rabbi Meir's* position: the *shvuas ha-eidus* applies even if the oath was administered outside of court. And *mi-pi atzmo* — even if the person imposed it upon himself outside of court — *Rabbi Meir* holds it would be binding.

As with the previous *perek*, the primary frame of reference throughout is the *korban* that the *Torah* prescribes for a false oath of testimony. The question of whether a person who acted *be-mazid* in such a case would also incur *malkus* — since this involves a *shvuas sheker* done willfully — is a point worth considering, but the basic framework of the *Mishnah* is the *korban* framework.

### No Subpoena Function

*Rabbi Meir* holds that a *shevua* outside of court is binding if the person imposed it upon himself. But if it was imposed by others: *u-vein mi-pi acherim, eino chayav ad she-yichpor be-veis din* — then it must be in court. One recalls from the previous discussion that if someone said *amen* outside of court, even in response to an oath imposed by another, *Rabbi Meir* would treat it as though one took the oath oneself. So *Rabbi Meir's* position is that a self-imposed oath outside of court creates a valid *shvuas ha-eidus*.

*Chachamim* disagree: *bein mipi atzmo uvein mipi acherim, einam chayavim ad sheyichperu b'veis din*. Regardless of who imposed the oath and where, liability only attaches when the denial takes place in court. The reasoning is that *shvuas ha-eidus* requires a context in which the testimony would be immediately relevant — where the witness is, as it were, on the stand and the testimony is needed right there. Outside of court, even if someone knows testimony, denying it represents a lesser degree of suppression. Yes, the person is still needed in court, but the denial is a step removed from the context in which it would be consequential.

This has an important practical implication: according to *Chachamim*, and to a significant degree even according to *Rabbi Meir*, the *shevua* cannot function as a subpoena. Imagine a litigant who says he borrowed money and has two witnesses, but one of them is reluctant to appear. The *beis din* must use whatever tools it has to bring that witness to court. The litigant cannot go to the witness outside of court, say *mashbi'acha ani*, and thereby legally compel him — as long as the witness is smart enough not to say *amen*, the oath has no binding force under *Rabbi Meir*, and the whole mechanism would fail to get the witness through the door in the first place.

### Liability Framework

The *Mishnah* continues: *ve-chayavin al zadon hashvua ve-al shiggasah im zadon ha-eidus*. This is a striking feature of *shvuas ha-eidus*: unlike most *korbanos* which require *v'ne'elam mimenu* — that the transgression occurred through some degree of inadvertence or unawareness — the *Torah* makes no such requirement here. A person who swears falsely that he does not know testimony, knowing full well what he is doing, still brings a *korban*. That is *zadon hashvua*.

Alternatively, there is the case of *shiggat hashvua im zadon ha-eidus*: the person knows he is lying about the testimony — *zadon ha-eidus* — but is *shogeg* with respect to the *shevua* itself, meaning he does not realize that this constitutes a prohibited oath or does not realize that a *korban* is associated with such an oath. That too triggers the obligation. One might ask: what would a simple *shogeg* in this context look like? The most obvious example would be that the person actually forgot the testimony and genuinely believed he was telling the truth. But that is not a false oath at all — we established earlier that if one believes one is telling the truth, no prohibition is violated regardless of the objective facts. So the *Mishnah* cannot offer that as its paradigmatic case of *shiggah*. The case it focuses on instead is: you know you are lying, but you do not know it is prohibited — or you know it is prohibited but do not know there is a *korban*. That constitutes *shegagah* with respect to the *shevua*, and still obligates a *korban*.

What one does not bring a *korban* for: *ein chayavin ela al shigegatah*, a full *shogeg* — meaning one who genuinely believed one was telling the truth.

For the *zadon* case: *mah hein chayavin al hazadon?* What does one bring when willfully lying? *Korban oleh veyored* — the sliding-scale *korban* calibrated to the person's means. Notably, there appears to be no *malkus* even in the fully willful case.

### Perjury vs. Denial

A useful comparison is to perjury in civil law: perjury requires intent to deceive — if one is simply mistaken, there is no crime. That maps remarkably well onto the *halachic* framework here, where liability for *shvuas ha-eidus* requires that one actually know the testimony and is consciously denying it.

One might also ask: what about giving false testimony? There is a distinction between *shvuas ha-eidus* — falsely claiming in the presence of a court, through an oath, that one does not know testimony — and actually taking the stand and testifying falsely. These are different acts. Notably, witnesses in a *halachic* court do not take an oath before testifying. If someone does get on the stand and testifies falsely, the applicable category is *eidim zomemin* — not *shvuas ha-eidus*. The question of whether false testimony per se carries *malkus* independently is a complex one discussed in Maseches Makkos, since establishing the falsity of testimony without the specific mechanism of *hazamah* is difficult.

As for the person who hires witnesses to testify falsely: the witnesses themselves may be subject to the laws of *eidim zomemin*, while the instigator — though *patur bidinei adam* — is *chayav bidei shamayim*. The *Rambam* goes so far as to call such a person a *rotzeach*. One who passively withholds testimony bears a lesser but still real degree of moral responsibility when his silence leads to an unjust outcome.

---

## Women & Witnesses

### Pasuk Interpretation

The *Gemara* asks: *mena hanei milei?* Of all the elements of the *Mishnah*, the *Gemara* chooses to focus first on *anashim velo nashim* — the exclusion of women. The *Gemara* cites a *drashah*: *ve-amdu shnei ha-anashim asher lahem hariv lifnei Hashem* — "and the two men who have the dispute shall stand before God." The plain reading would be that these are the two litigants, but the *Gemara* argues *be-eidim hakatuv medaber* — the verse is speaking of witnesses. And once we identify them as witnesses, the word *ha-anashim* — men — teaches that only men may serve as witnesses.

### Three Braitot

Three *Braitot* are presented, each working through a different derivation, reflecting an awareness that the initial argument can be challenged.

The first *Braita* reads the phrase as two parts: the second half, *asher lahem hariv*, describes the litigants, and the first half, *ve-amdu shnei ha-anashim*, must therefore describe the witnesses. Since witnesses are described as *ha-anashim*, testimony is restricted to men. The challenge: perhaps the entire verse — *ve-amdu shnei ha-anashim asher lahem hariv* — is one continuous description of the litigants, since there is no *vav* separating the clauses. If so, the phrase about "the men" cannot be separated out to refer to witnesses. In response: *ne'emar kan shnei vene'emar lehalan shnei* — there is a *gezeirah shavah* from the word *shnayim* here to *al pi shnei eidim yumat hamet*, where *shnei* explicitly accompanies witnesses. *Mah lehalan be-eidim af kan be-eidim* — just as *shnei* there means witnesses, so too *shnei* here refers to witnesses, and they must be men.

The second *Braita* offers a different approach. If the verse were about litigants, why would it say *two*? The number of litigants in a case is not fixed at two — there could be many parties. *Vechi shnayim ba'im ladin shlosha ein ba'im ladin?* Do only two come to court — can three not come? By contrast, witnesses have two as their fundamental number. True, one might argue that *conceptually* there are always two parties — the plaintiff and the defendant — even if each side is composed of many individuals. And one could say: *betove'a venitba hakatuv medaber* — the verse means the two fundamental roles. To resolve this, the *Braita* again falls back on the *gezeirah shavah* of *shnei*.

The third *Braita* takes yet another approach. *Amarta vechi anashim ba'im ladin nashim einam ba'im ladin?* If the word *anashim* is what teaches us to restrict to men, and if this verse is talking about litigants — does that mean women can never be litigants or defendants? Surely women have occasion to bring cases and to be sued. And there is a broader question: do we wish as a matter of law to exclude women from the ability to participate in court as parties? Obviously not. Therefore, the word *anashim* cannot be functioning as a legal restriction on the role of litigant — it must be describing witnesses, and from the witnesses the legal restriction flows.

### Tosafot's Question

*Tosafot* raises a penetrating question: even if we accept that the verse is describing witnesses rather than litigants, how do we know that the word *anashim* is functioning as a *legal exclusion* of women rather than a *descriptive* statement? Perhaps the *Torah* uses the word *anashim* because it is simply the normal case that witnesses are men — not because women are legally barred, but because *kol kvuda bat melech pnima*, the honor of the king's daughter is inward, women are more in the domestic sphere and less commonly found in public roles such as testifying in court. Just as the third *Braita* suggested that *anashim* may be descriptive when applied to litigants because women would typically avoid appearing in court, perhaps the same logic applies even to witnesses.

### Tosafot's Resolution

*Tosafot* resolves the question by drawing a critical distinction between the roles of witness and litigant. *Gabi eidim al korchach tzrichin lavo de-ein ed mipi ed kasher* — witnesses, if they have relevant testimony, are obligated to come to court and testify. There is no halachically valid substitute; hearsay testimony is not acceptable. A woman who witnessed something relevant cannot simply stay home and relay what she saw through her husband or any other intermediary. If she were an eligible witness, she would have no choice but to come.

A litigant, by contrast — at least on the side of the plaintiff — *yechola limsor ta'anoteha b'yad acher*, can empower a representative to argue her case. She can give power of attorney and have someone else present her claims in court. She need not appear herself.

Therefore: if the verse used the word *anashim* and the verse were describing litigants, one could explain *anashim* as merely descriptive — it is talking about the normal case where men appear in court, since women can and typically would choose to send a representative. But if the verse is describing witnesses, where women would be just as compelled to appear as men if they were eligible, then using the word *anashim* cannot be explained away as descriptive. It must be a legal term. *Tosafot's* conclusion is thus that the use of *anashim* in the context of witnesses establishes a genuine legal exclusion.

---

## Court Procedure

### Standing Requirement

Having established from the verse *ve-amdu shnei ha-anashim* that it refers to witnesses, the *Gemara* now turns to the *peshat* of the verse as applied to court procedure more broadly. *Mitzvah le-ba'alei dinin she-ya'amodu* — it is proper for litigants to stand. The judges sit and the litigants stand.

*Rabbi Yehuda* qualifies: *shamati she-im ratzu le-hoshiv et shneihem moshivin* — if the court wishes to have both litigants sit, that is permissible. There is no absolute technical requirement for standing. What is forbidden: *shelo yehei echad omed ve-echad yoshev* — one standing and one sitting. Similarly: *echad medaber kol tzorcho ve-echad omer lo katzer devarecha* — one litigant is allowed to speak at length while the other is told to cut his remarks short.

### Fair Treatment

The prohibition against differential treatment is derived not from *ve-amdu* itself but from a separate verse: *b'tzedek tishpot amitecha* — with righteousness shall you judge your fellow. The prohibition of one standing and one sitting, and one speaking freely while the other is rushed, is derived from this verse.

The word *b'tzedek* is worth pausing over, because it points to something subtler than mere formal equality. There is a difference between fairness and equality. If one litigant needs two hours to say what he needs to say and the other needs ten minutes, the court cannot cut the first one off after ten minutes in the name of equal treatment. The requirement is *tzedek* — justice — which means giving each person what they actually need, even if that results in different treatment. Equality of outcome is not always justice; sometimes justice requires accounting for different circumstances and different needs. This is the distinction between treating people equally and treating people fairly.

### L'Chaf Zechut

A second interpretation of the same verse: *davar acher, b'tzedek tishpot amitecha, havei dan et chavercha l'chaf zechut* — judge your fellow favorably. Here *amitecha* is read not in the judicial context but in the context of ordinary social interactions. Everyone judges others in daily life — the question is in which direction one tips that judgment. The instruction is *l'chaf zechut*: when you see something that could be interpreted critically or sympathetically, tip the scale toward the sympathetic interpretation, toward the side of merit. This is not a legal presumption of innocence in a court case; it is a social and moral directive about how to perceive other people's actions in everyday life.

### Emitecha & Preference

*Rav Yosef* offers a third reading: *b'tzedek tishpot amitecha* — *amitecha* means *im she'itcha b'Torah u'v'mitzvot*, one who is your fellow in Torah and *mitzvos*. The instruction *hishtadel l'dono yafe* — judge him well — is then explained by *Rashi*: if two cases come before you simultaneously, you may hear the case of a *talmid chacham* first.

This seems troubling at first — is this not favoritism? But *Rashi* and *Tosafot* limit the scope carefully: only if the two cases arrived at precisely the same time. If another case arrived first, a *talmid chacham* may not jump the line simply by virtue of his status. The principle applies only to a genuine tie, where there is no prior claim on the court's attention.

As an illustration: *Rav Ulla brei de-Rav Ilai* had a tort case before *Rav Nachman*. *Rav Yosef* sent word: *Ulla chaveirenu, amit batorah u'mitzvos* — Ulla is our colleague in Torah and *mitzvos*. *Rav Nachman* responded with some suspicion: *lama shalach li — lachanfeyei lei?* Why is he telling me this — just to flatter the litigant? He then reconsidered: the message must have been sent *lemishra d'kitrei* — to move Ulla along, to help expedite his case, presumably in a situation where Ulla's case and another had arrived simultaneously.

The *Gemara* adds a further dimension: *ai naami leshuda de-dayni* — or in a case that is entirely at the judge's discretion, with no factual basis for resolution, preferring a *talmid chacham* is legitimate. If, say, a gift was left in a will to "Reuven ben Shimon" and there are two such people in the city with no way of determining which was intended, one approach is to award it to the *talmid chacham*. This is a genuine form of preference — but it is confined to the narrow category of cases where judgment is truly indeterminate and discretion is entirely vested in the court.

---

## Witnesses Standing

### Standing Rules

*Rav Ulla* clarifies: *machloket be-ba'alei dinin* — the debate about whether litigants must stand applies to litigants. *Aval be-eidim, divrei hakol be-amida* — when it comes to witnesses, everyone agrees they must stand. This is derived from *ve-amdu shnei ha-anashim*, which, as established, refers to witnesses.

*Rav Huna* adds a further distinction: the debate about litigants applies *besha'at masa umatan* — during the deliberations. *Aval besha'at gmar din, divrei hakol dayanim biyishivah u'va'alei din be'amida* — when the verdict is actually delivered, everyone agrees that the judges sit and the litigants stand. This is derived from the verse describing Moshe: *vayeishev Moshe lishpot et ha-am vaya'amdu ha-am al Moshe* — Moshe sat and the people stood. A parallel formulation derives the same rule from the idea that witnesses are like *gmar din*: accepting testimony has a formal, almost ritual quality — *kabbolas eidus* — with a compelling and concrete effect on the proceedings. For that reason, witnesses must stand when testifying.

### Rav Huna's Widow

These principles create a practical dilemma illustrated by the following case. The widow of *Rav Huna* had a court case before *Rav Nachman*. *Rav Nachman* faced a genuine conflict: *heichi na'avid?* How should he handle her entrance? On one hand, *akum mikama* — he has a *halachic* obligation to rise in her presence. The *kavod ha-Torah* accorded to a *talmid chacham* extends even to his widow after his passing. On the other hand, *ei avidna hachi mistatmin ta'antei de-ba'al dina* — if he rises for her, the claims of her opposing litigant will be "stopped up." The other party will see that the judge honors one litigant and not the other, and however one explains the *halachic* basis for it, the psychological damage to that litigant's ability to present his case freely is real. And conversely, *lo akum mikama — eshet chaver harei hi ke-chaver* — he is not entitled to simply ignore the obligation to rise: the wife of a *chaver* — even the widow — is treated as a *chaver*.

### The Goose Ruse

*Rav Nachman's* solution was to instruct his attendant: *tzei ve-afrach alai bar avza* — go release a goose into the court. As the widow enters, the goose would fly at him, and in the commotion of dealing with the goose, he would naturally stand up — and thus fulfill his obligation to rise in her presence without the opposing litigant understanding that he had done so out of honor for her.

*Tosafot* raises a sharp question: the *halacha* of rising in honor requires a rising that communicates respect. A rising accompanied by a wild goose attack does not obviously communicate respect. *Tosafot* offers two resolutions. First: the widow herself understood the ruse perfectly — she knew he was honoring her — and the obligation of *kiyum kavod* was satisfied by her recognition of the intent, while the deception protected the opposing litigant from feeling disadvantaged. Second: the requirement to stand does not apply if one is already standing. The goose ruse caused *Rav Nachman* to rise *before* she entered, so that by the time she walked in he was already on his feet — technically not rising *for* her at all.

---

## Witnesses Standing (II)

### Half-Sitting Solution

A further complication: *Rav Huna* himself had ruled that at the time of *gmar din* the judges must sit and the litigants must stand. But *Rav Nachman* is obligated to rise for the widow, who is also a litigant in this very proceeding. How does he sit in judgment while also fulfilling his obligation to stand for her? The *Gemara* resolves this: *deyotiv keman de-shrei masanei* — he sits in a manner as if he were tying his shoes, half-risen from his chair, not fully seated. In that posture he both issues the ruling — making clear the judicial authority — and is not in a position of full dignified sitting. It is a compromise that attempts to honor both imperatives simultaneously.

---

## Kavod vs. Equality

### Voluntary Standing

*Rabbah bar Rav Huna* addresses the scenario of a *talmid chacham* and an *am ha'aretz* appearing together as opposing litigants. *Motvina lei le-tzurba me-rabbanan* — the court seats the *talmid chacham*. *Ve-la'am ha'aretz nami amrinan lei tiv* — the *am ha'aretz* is also told he may sit. The two are treated formally equally in this respect, though the manner differs slightly: the *talmid chacham* is actively seated by the court, while the *am ha'aretz* is merely invited to sit.

*Ve-i kai leit lan bah* — if the *am ha'aretz* chooses to stand nonetheless, presumably out of deference to his learned opponent, the court does not insist that he sit to enforce formal equality. One might have thought that the court should proactively enforce parity — if they are both supposed to sit, make them both sit. But the *halacha* is that the *am ha'aretz* may make this choice voluntarily, even though it places him in a psychologically weaker position.

### Forced Standing

A more troubling incident: *Rav bar Sharvaya* had a case before *Rav Pappa*. Both litigants had been seated. A court attendant arrived and struck the non-*talmid chacham* litigant, telling him he had no business sitting in the presence of a *talmid chacham*. *Ve-lo amar lei Rav Pappa tiv* — and *Rav Pappa* said nothing to counteract this. This is far worse than the voluntary case: the person is not choosing to stand out of deference; he is being physically compelled to stand by a court officer. *Heichi avid hachi?* How could *Rav Pappa* allow this?

*Rav Pappa* explained: the litigant could reason for himself that the judge had already given him permission to sit. When the court officer struck him, the litigant should understand that this reflected some personal grudge on the officer's part, not the court's position. The court officer, in other words, was acting on his own, not as an agent of the court's judgment. This seems to walk a fine line — a person standing while his opponent sits is in a disadvantaged position regardless of the explanation — but this is *Rav Pappa's* justification.

### Appearance of Bias

*Rabbah bar Avuha* raises an additional concern about the appearance of bias. *Hai tzurba me-rabbanan ve-am ha'aretz de-it lehu dina bahadi hadadei* — when a *talmid chacham* and an *am ha'aretz* have a case before a court, *lo lijkam tzurba me-rabbanan ve-leysev* — the *talmid chacham* should not go into the courtroom early and sit down. If he does, the opposing litigant will walk in and see him already settled there, perhaps exchanging pleasantries with the rabbinic judges, and the impression will be one of prior collusion and established social familiarity. *Mishum de-meichzei ke-man de-sader lei le-dinei* — it will look as if he had already been arranging matters in advance. This is an issue of *mar'it ayin* — the appearance of improper behavior — and it is significant enough to require the *talmid chacham* to stay out of the room before the proceeding begins.

This concern is not merely theoretical. There are documented situations in which a woman accompanying a party to a *beis din* for a *get* witnessed precisely this dynamic: the husband walks in, recognizes rabbinic acquaintances among the judges, and a wave of warm greetings and yeshiva reminiscences follows. Whatever the actual fairness of the proceeding, the other party's confidence in receiving equal treatment has been effectively undermined.

### Fixed Learning Time

There is an important exception: *ve-lo amaran ela de-lo kavia lei idnei* — the concern about entering the courtroom early applies only if the judge and the *talmid chacham* litigant do not have a fixed regular learning session together. *Aval kavia lei idnei, leis lan bah* — if they have an established *chavrusa* or regular class, the litigant's presence before the proceeding begins raises no concern, since his opponent can attribute their interaction to the ongoing learning relationship.

One might argue — and it is worth noting — that an ongoing *rebbe-talmid* relationship between a judge and a litigant raises its own serious questions about the ability of the judge to be impartial. But the *Gemara* does not pursue that concern here.

---

## Kavod & Sin Prevention

### Honor & Testimony

*Rabbah bar Avuha* raises yet another dimension: *hai tzurba me-rabbanan de-yada be-sahaduta* — a *talmid chacham* who knows relevant testimony, but *zila bei milta le-meizal le-vei dina de-zuta minei* — it would be beneath his dignity to appear before a court of judges who are his students or his students' students. *Lo leizil* — he need not go. His honor takes precedence, and he is not required to demean himself by presenting as a witness before judges of far lower status.

### Found Objects

*Rav Sheshet brei de-Rav Idi* cites a parallel: *matza sak u-kupa ve-ein darko litol harei zeh lo yitol* — if one finds an abandoned object in the street but it is beneath his dignity to bend down and pick it up — the test being whether he would bother to pick it up if it were his own — he is not obligated to take it in order to return it to its owner. Even though his inaction means the owner will not recover his property, one's personal dignity permits passive non-action even when it comes at a monetary cost to another. This is the principle of *kavod ha-briyot* — human dignity — taking precedence over certain monetary obligations where the individual's role is passive.

### Money vs. Sin

*V'hani mili b'mamona* — but all of the foregoing applies only in the monetary domain. *Aval b'issura* — when it comes to actual transgressions, *ein chochma v'ein tvuna v'ein etza l'neged Hashem* — there is no wisdom, no understanding, no calculation that can stand against God's honor. *Kol makom she-yesh chilul Hashem ein cholkin kavod le-rav* — wherever there is a *chilul Hashem*, honor is not accorded even to a great Torah scholar. The principle of dignity and honor yields entirely when God's honor is at stake.

### Rashi's Reading

What exactly is the case? One possibility is that the *talmid chacham* knows testimony about a capital matter, and his silence would mean that someone is wrongly convicted or wrongly acquitted. But *Rashi* reads the case differently: a *talmid chacham* is present in a judicial proceeding — perhaps as a court clerk — and his *rebbe*, who is the judge, is about to issue a ruling that would permit a woman to remarry when in fact her husband may still be alive. The *talmid chacham* knows this ruling is wrong. Despite the prohibition of contradicting or overriding one's *rebbe*, he must speak up. *Kavod ha-Torah* and deference to one's teacher do not apply when silence would lead to an *aveira* being committed.

### Ex Post vs. Ex Ante

There are thus three distinct scenarios nested within this discussion. *Rashi's* scenario — the most straightforward — involves preventing an *aveira* from being committed in real time: speak up now or an *aveira* occurs. A second scenario involves testimony that would exonerate someone from an undeserved punishment: here the motivation is protecting human life and bodily integrity, which is plainly compelling regardless of *kavod* considerations. The most complex scenario is the one most directly on point: must a *talmid chacham* lower himself to appear before inferior judges in order to ensure that a sinner receives his due punishment?

There is something qualitatively different about ex post punishment versus ex ante prevention. Preventing an *aveira* from occurring is an immediate and direct protection of God's honor. Ensuring that punishment is administered after the fact feels like a different order of claim — it is still about *kavod Hashem*, but at one remove. Whether the obligation to override one's personal dignity is equally strong in that case is the question with which this discussion concludes.

---

---

# Shevuot 31

## Witnesses Standing

### Ameimar Seats Witnesses

Today's daf is 31. We pick up on the bottom of 30b, the second wide line, continuing to deal with *shvuat ha'edut*, but as a slight digression from that subject we are also examining how one comes to give testimony, how litigants stand, and how to balance *kavod* shown to rabbinic Torah authorities while still maintaining equal treatment during a court case.

The Gemara opens with a brief narrative. Rav Yemar knew testimony relevant to Mar Zutra and came before Ameimar, who was serving as judge. Ameimar seated all the witnesses — a departure from the standard procedure, in which witnesses stand and judges sit. Ameimar's concern was that having Rav Yemar stand before him would create a stark and disrespectful difference in power and status.

### Witnesses Must Stand

Rav Ashi raised an immediate objection. Had Ulla not ruled that the debate over whether litigants must stand pertains specifically to *ba'alei dinim* — the litigants themselves? But regarding witnesses, everyone agrees they must stand: *b'edim divrei hakol b'amida*. This is not merely a procedural preference; the verse *v'amdu shnei ha'anashim* establishes a positive obligation.

### Kavod Overrides Standing

Ameimar's response was that both obligations are in the category of *asseh*: the requirement for witnesses to stand is an *asseh* derived from *v'amdu shnei ha'anashim*, and the requirement to show *kavod* for a Torah authority is likewise an *asseh*. When two *asseh*s conflict, one must choose, and *asseh d'chevod hatorah adif* — the *asseh* of honoring the Torah takes precedence. Importantly, failing to have the witness stand would not invalidate the testimony, since the obligation operates at the level of an *asseh* and does not condition the validity of what is said. Furthermore, since Ameimar applied this ruling equally to all the witnesses, there was no concern of showing differential deference to one side.

---

## Judge Non-Defensive

### Midvar Sheker Tirchak

The Gemara now cites a *baraita*: *Minayin l'dayan shelo ya'aseh sanegor lidvarav* — how do we know that a judge should not become a defense attorney for his own words? The derivation is from *midvar sheker tirchak*, "distance yourself from words of falsehood."

### Sanegor Defense

The concern here is not about outright lying. Rashi explains that the problem arises when a judge takes a position, then begins to feel uncertain about it, and rather than honestly reassessing, moves into a defensive mode to protect what he said earlier. The English phrase "don't be so defensive" captures the idea precisely. A judge who has become defensive will not honestly evaluate the merits of the case; instead, he will marshal arguments to protect his prior position. Even though this does not involve saying a direct falsehood, channeling all one's energy into defending a stated position rather than remaining detached and open to revision leads inexorably to a false conclusion. Hence, *midvar sheker tirchak*.

### Perverting Truth

This opens a broader discussion of *midvar sheker tirchak*. Two features of this verse deserve emphasis. First, the word *tirchak* — "distance yourself" — indicates that the prohibition reaches beyond outright lying to encompass any influence or perversion of the truth, any process that makes an honest assessment less likely. Second, the verse appears in the context of the court and judges. The Gemara elsewhere permits altering facts for the sake of peace, *mutar lishanos mipnei hashalom*, citing the case of Yosef's brothers, who represented to Yosef that their father had asked him to forgive them — a claim the Gemara implies may not have been literally accurate. Similarly, the *Chasam Sofer* notes that there is a distinction between an outright lie and a technically accurate statement used to mislead, though the *Ramban* argues that the technical accuracy of one's words is irrelevant if the intent and effect are deceitful.

These discussions raise the broader question of whether there is an *issur* to lie in general — independent of the court context. The verse *midvar sheker tirchak* is primarily understood as operating in the setting of the *beit din*. So on the one hand it broadens the prohibition by using *tirchak* rather than a simple negative commandment against lying; on the other hand it is very much grounded in the judicial context specifically.

---

## Midvar Sheker Applicatio…

### Talmid Bur Exclusion

The *baraita* continues with a series of applications of *midvar sheker tirchak* to the courtroom. The first: *minayin l'dayan shelo yeishev talmid bur l'fanav* — how do we know that a judge should not have an ignorant student sitting before him? Rashi explains that *leshev l'fanav* includes bouncing ideas off of someone. If the judge's interlocutor lacks discernment, the conversation will lead him astray rather than toward the truth of the matter. Even without any intent to deceive, surrounding oneself with the wrong people creates conditions that undermine honest judgment. The derivation is again from *midvar sheker tirchak*.

### Gazlan Disqualification

The next case: *minayin l'dayan she-yodeia l'chaveiro she-hu gazlan, v'chein eid she-yodeia l'chaveiro she-hu gazlan* — how do we know that a judge who knows his fellow judge is a *gazlan*, or a witness who knows his fellow witness is a *gazlan*, should not join with him? The derivation is *midvar sheker tirchak*.

This requires some analysis. The *gazlan* is not necessarily lying; he may be testifying accurately about events he genuinely witnessed. He is simply *pasul* on technical grounds. One might therefore reason: as long as they are telling the truth, what is the problem with participating alongside a technically invalid witness? The answer, as Rashi points out, is that by going forward — by allowing the court to accept testimony that the technical laws of evidence would disqualify — one is participating in a procedural deception, even if the underlying facts happen to be accurate. That too is an element of *sheker* in the process.

This principle is illustrated by a question posed to the *Rashba*. A man claimed his adversary genuinely owed him money, but he lacked sufficient evidence to prove it in court. He asked whether, based on the principle of *adam dan dina l'nafsheih* — the right to take the law into one's own hands — he might be permitted to forge evidence and bring it to court, since he was confident the debt was real. The *Rashba* rejected this, explaining that the right to act in self-help does not extend to perverting the procedures of the court. Here too, the problem is not only in the final result but in the process itself.

### Suspect Corruption

A further application: *minayin l'dayan she-yodeia be-din she-hu merumeh* — how does a judge who has come to believe that a case before him is corrupt know that he may not simply go along with it? The scenario is one where the judge cannot identify the precise lie — perhaps he saw the witnesses conferring with a party outside, or some other circumstantial sign — but it is clear to him that the entire proceeding is being manipulated.

One might think the judge can reason: *ho'il v'eidim me'idim*, witnesses have testified, the technical requirements have been met, and *yei kolar talui b'tzavar eidim* — let whatever blame there is fall upon the witnesses; I will simply rule on the evidence before me. This is not permitted. *Midvar sheker tirchak*: a judge may not be party to a falsehood even without having committed a lie himself, even without knowing precisely where the lie is located.

What exactly the judge is supposed to do in such circumstances — whether he can recuse himself mid-case, what procedural options are available — the Gemara does not specify. But it is unambiguous that simply going along and issuing a ruling while knowing the proceeding is corrupt is not an option. Notably, the judge also cannot resolve the problem by ruling in favor of the party he suspects is being wronged without a legal basis to do so: he lacks the evidence to support a contrary ruling.

### Student Correction

Next: *minayin l'talmid she-yoshev lifnei rabbo v'ra'ah zechut l'ani v'chov l'ashir minayin shelo yishtok* — how do we know that a student sitting before his *rebbe* who perceives that a poor litigant has merit, and that a rich litigant actually has a debit in the case, may not remain silent? The student faces powerful social pressures: the *kavod* owed to his *rebbe*, the social weight of a wealthy and prominent opponent, and the fact that he is not even lying — he is merely withholding information. *Midvar sheker tirchak*: silence in the face of a miscarriage of justice is itself a form of distance one must keep from falsehood.

### No Strategic Silence

The final application in this series sharpens the point. *Minayin l'talmid she-ra'ah rabbo she-to'eh be-din* — how do we know that a student who perceives his *rebbe* is making an error in judgment may not say to himself: I will let my *rebbe* go down this wrong path, allow him to reach his erroneous conclusion, and then, in order to build myself up — *avastrenu v'avneno misheli k'dei she'yikra hadin al shemi* — demolish his position and reconstruct it properly, so that the ruling is named after me?

Here the student's motive is far from pure; he seeks to inflate himself at his *rebbe*'s expense. But the Gemara's concern goes beyond his bad intent. By waiting — allowing a misquoted source or a flawed argument to stand uncorrected for even an hour while the entire discussion proceeds on that false premise — the student is countenancing a perversion of the truth for the duration of his strategic silence. *Midvar sheker tirchak* requires him to speak up the moment he perceives the error, not when it becomes advantageous for him to do so.

---

## Witness Pressure Cas (II)

### Coerced Testimony

A further series of applications follows. *Linnoshe bachavero maneh shelo yomar lo* — regarding someone owed a hundred dollars by another, the *baraita* addresses a gambit: he goes to court claiming two hundred dollars, reasoning that the debtor — being an honest man — will admit to a hundred, thereby becoming a *modeh b'miktzat*, one who partially admits a debt. This obligates the debtor in an oath (*yitchayiv li shvua*), and once he must take one oath the creditor can leverage that to force additional oaths about other disputed debts — *v'agalgela alav shvua mimakom acher*. The creditor is not falsifying the facts of what is owed; he is making a deliberately inflated claim solely to manipulate the court process and compel oaths. The derivation forbidding this: *midvar sheker tirchak*.

It might seem surprising. Every pleading in modern civil litigation opens with an inflated demand for damages. The distinction, however, is between asking a court to award a particular amount in compensation — a claim about what one wants — and misrepresenting the underlying facts of the debt itself. The gambit the Gemara is prohibiting is the latter: asserting that someone owes two hundred when you know the sum is one hundred, purely to manufacture a procedural advantage.

The Gemara then poses the same question from the debtor's side. If the creditor has in fact claimed two hundred, the debtor faces the following temptation: deny the entire claim in *beit din* so as to avoid being a *modeh b'miktzat*, and then privately admit the hundred-dollar debt and pay it outside of court. This avoids the oath obligation entirely. The Gemara forbids this strategy as well, despite the fact that the creditor's original claim was itself a lie. The debtor may not respond to a lie in the proceeding by telling his own lie. *Midvar sheker tirchak*.

The Gemara then asks: the case that Jacob must not join the two of you as a false witness — is that really just *midvar sheker tirchak*? Is this not an outright lie, subject to the prohibition of *lo ta'aneh v'reacha ed sheker*? The Gemara clarifies: the truly outright case, where Jacob testifies to knowledge he does not have, is indeed a transgression of *lo ta'aneh v'reacha ed sheker*, bearing false witness. The *midvar sheker tirchak* case is the subtler one: suppose the creditor says to Jacob — I definitely have one witness, Chanan, who saw that Michael borrowed the money. Go stand with Chanan in court. Don't say anything. Just stand there. Michael will assume you are about to testify as well, and the pressure of believing two witnesses are present will induce him to admit the debt. *V'lo tima v'lo midi* — I'm not asking you to say a single false word. Your presence does the work.

Even this — standing silently in a way that communicates to Michael that you possess knowledge you do not possess — is forbidden by *midvar sheker tirchak*. The prohibition extends to any conduct that conveys a false impression, even without a spoken word, even when the underlying fact (that Michael owes the money) is perfectly true. The Ramban makes a parallel observation in the narrative of Avraham and Avimelech: it is irrelevant whether the words spoken were technically accurate if the intended and achieved effect was deception.

### Multiple Creditors

*Minayin lishelosha sheno'shin maneh b'echad* — how do we know that if three parties have each lent money to a fourth, they may not arrange themselves so that one plays the role of plaintiff while the other two pose as disinterested witnesses? They are all parties to the case — *ba'alei davar* — and therefore not qualified to testify for one another. Yet the facts they would be testifying to are true: the money was indeed borrowed. The problem is procedural deception: presenting themselves as witnesses when the technical laws of evidence disqualify them from that role. *Midvar sheker tirchak*.

---

## Dress Equality

### Litigant Dress

*Minayin lishnayim sheba'u ladin, echad lavush smartutin v'echad lavush itzalit bat meah maneh* — how do we know that when two litigants come to court, one dressed in rags and the other wearing a garment worth a hundred *maneh* (a lavish designer outfit, as it were), the court instructs the wealthy one to either dress down to a comparable level or to bring the other to his tailor and clothe him equivalently? *Midvar sheker tirchak*.

The reasoning is transparent: people are human and respond to status cues. A litigant who appears wealthy and well-dressed will have his words treated with greater weight and deference by the court, whether consciously or not. By appearing in dramatically superior dress, the wealthier party is, in effect, tilting the proceeding in his favor — creating a procedural falsehood that skews the weight given to each side's arguments. Even if the wealthy litigant genuinely believes he has truth on his side, that confidence does not entitle him to exploit the psychological dynamics of status. Responsibility here is not his alone; the court itself is presumably entitled and obligated to insist on comparability of dress — much as defendants in criminal proceedings are dressed in ordinary clothing rather than prison garb when they appear before a jury.

### Removing Fancy Shoes

The Gemara reports that when witnesses would come before Rava bar Rav Huna, he would say to them: *shulufu puzmukaichu v'nachatu ledina* — remove your fine shoes and come down to the judgment. The *puzmukeichu* were apparently an elaborate form of footwear. Even the difference between expensive and ordinary shoes was sufficient to create a disparity of status that Rava bar Rav Huna would not tolerate.

The word *v'nachatu* — "come down" — is also noteworthy. Shoes are *maamidim et ha'adam*; they lend a person stature and elevation. There is an element of humbling before the proceeding that Rava bar Rav Huna may have been cultivating — having all parties appear barefoot before the court. Whether the same concern about comparable dress would apply to witnesses as well as litigants, so that one side's witnesses cannot appear significantly more prestigious than the other side's witnesses, is an interesting question the Gemara leaves open.

---

## Witness Pressure Cas (II)

### Power of Attorney

The passage cites the verse from *Yechezkel*, *va'asher lo tov asa besoch amo*, describing one who does not do right in his nation. Rav interprets this as referring to a person who comes into a case with a *horsha'ah* — a power of attorney. *Tosafot* explains the concern precisely: the problem is not with all representatives, but specifically with one who comes because *hu alim u'va'al ta'anot* — he is imposing, forceful, and skilled in argumentation. What may have been a balanced dispute between two ordinary parties is suddenly transformed when one side introduces a powerful legal advocate. The other side cannot compete. This, says *Tosafot*, is the case of *lo tov asa*. By contrast, if Michael is traveling to Israel and simply asks a friend to collect money owed to him — a pure act of assistance — there is nothing improper about granting that power of attorney. The question of where the legitimate business arrangement ends and the unfair manipulation of the proceeding begins is one of degree and intent.

Shmuel offers a different referent for *lo tov asa*: one who purchases a field that has legal claims (*asikin*) against it. The buyer knows that the encumbrances have driven the price far below market value, and he has the legal muscle — financial resources, lawyers, connections — to defeat those claims. He acquires the property at a fraction of its worth, at the expense of the original holder who lacked the means to navigate the legal process effectively. Whether this constitutes simply seizing a good business opportunity or genuinely wronging the original claimant is a line that is not always clear.

---

## Both Parties Present

### Anchoring Bias

*Minalan d'dayan shelo yishma divrei ba'al din kodem sheyavo ba'al din chaveiro* — how do we know that a judge may not hear one litigant's presentation of his case before the other party has arrived? The derivation is *midvar sheker tirchak*.

Two concerns underlie this rule. First, the absent party is not present to correct misstatements or provide counter-evidence, which invites falsehood. Second — and more subtle — there is a well-recognized phenomenon (sometimes called "anchoring") by which the first framing of a situation shapes all subsequent evaluation. Once a judge has heard a case presented in a particular structure, it becomes very difficult to evaluate the opposing party's arguments on their own terms; the judge will almost inevitably process them through the lens of the initial presentation. Even if the first party is not intentionally deceiving anyone and is simply telling his story as he understands it, the effect is to pervert the judge's impartiality. The judge is not allowed to permit this, even when there is no deliberate manipulation.

### Persuasive Presentation

*Minalan l'ba'al din shelo yat'im devarav l'dayan kodem sheyavo ba'al din chaveiro* — and how do we know that the litigant himself may not present his case — giving it *ta'am*, making it attractive and palatable — before the other party arrives? *Midvar sheker tirchak*.

This is distinct from the general right of a litigant to advocate. The litigants are permitted — indeed expected — to present their narratives persuasively when both parties are before the court. The role of opening and closing statements, the right to tell one's story and not merely recite bare facts: all of this is legitimate *hataamah*. The court does not require litigants to speak in neutral, objective terms. The prohibition is specifically about doing so *before* the other party has arrived, where the persuasive presentation cannot be countered in real time. Under those conditions, even legitimate advocacy becomes an instrument of distortion.

Rav Kahana frames this point through an alternative derivation: *lo tisa shema shav* — do not carry a false report. By presenting one's case in the absence of the opposing party, one is, in effect, transmitting a false report into the mind of the judge — even if every word spoken was literally true.

---

## Shvuat Ha'Edut Scope

### Mina Debate

The Gemara now turns to a significant legal debate between Rabbi Meir and the *Rabbanan* regarding the scope of *shvuat ha'edut*. The issue: is a person liable for *shvuat ha'edut* when the denial and oath occur outside of *beit din*, or only when they occur in the presence of *beit din*?

The analytical framework involves two mechanisms of legal analogy. The verse governing *shvuat ha'edut* (*v'hu ed o ra'ah o yada im lo yagid*) establishes liability when the oath is imposed *mipi acheirim* — by others — and contextually locates this in a *beit din* setting. The verse governing *shvuat ha'pikadon* establishes liability for a self-imposed oath — *mipi atzmo* — and does not specify a *beit din* context; it refers to any oath taken falsely regarding a deposit. Each case has something the other lacks: *shvuat ha'edut* has the *beit din* context; *shvuat ha'pikadon* has the *mipi atzmo* mechanism.

Both Rabbi Meir and the *Rabbanan* agree that *shvuat ha'edut* generates liability when the oath is self-imposed (*mipi atzmo*), which they learn from *shvuat ha'pikadon*. Their dispute is about what happens once that *halacha* is imported. Rabbi Meir holds *don mina u'mina*: you learn the *halacha* from its source and you retain its original context. Since *shvuat ha'pikadon* is not limited to *beit din*, the *mipi atzmo* liability in *shvuat ha'edut* likewise extends outside *beit din*. The *Rabbanan* hold *don mina v'oki b'atrah*: you learn the *halacha* from its source but then transplant it into the context of the target law. Since *shvuat ha'edut* is fundamentally a *beit din*-based obligation, once *mipi atzmo* is imported, it takes on that context and is limited to *beit din*.

Expressed visually: Rabbi Meir imports *mipi atzmo* from the *pikadon* context (outside *beit din*) and carries that context with it into *shvuat ha'edut*. The *Rabbanan* import *mipi atzmo* but immediately situate it in the *edut* context (inside *beit din*), discarding the original *pikadon* context.

### Rav Papa Explanation

The *Rabbanan* of the *beit midrash* asked Rav Papa whether he could really say the debate is not about *don mina u'mina* versus *don mina v'oki b'atrah*. Rav Papa responded that if the *Rabbanan*'s learning of *mipi atzmo* were derived from *pikadon*, then everyone — even the *Rabbanan* — would hold *don mina u'mina* and concede that *mipi atzmo* applies even outside *beit din*. Rather, *ela hainu ta'ama d'Rabbanan*: the *Rabbanan* do not learn *mipi atzmo* from *pikadon* at all. They stay entirely within the world of *shvuat ha'edut* and derive *mipi atzmo* via *kal v'chomer*: if one is liable when someone else imposes the oath, certainly one is liable when one imposes it upon oneself. This derivation is self-contained within the *beit din* context of *shvuat ha'edut*, and by the rule of *dayo* — the sufficiency principle of *kal v'chomer* — the conclusion cannot exceed its premise. Since the premise (*mipi acherim*) is limited to *beit din*, the conclusion (*mipi atzmo*) is likewise limited to *beit din*.

The *Rabbanan* of the *beit midrash* then pressed Rav Papa further: surely you can prove the debate really is about *don mina u'mina*, because the positions reverse in the parallel case of *shvuat ha'pikadon*, and that reversal is explicable only on the basis of this exact methodological disagreement.

### Pikadon Mirror

The next *mishnah* establishes that *shvuat ha'pikadon* applies to men and women, relatives and non-relatives, qualified witnesses and disqualified ones, in the presence of *beit din* and outside *beit din* — but only *mipi atzmo*. Liability for *shvuat ha'pikadon* when the oath is imposed *mipi acherim* is not stated in the verse; it must be derived from *shvuat ha'edut*. This generates the mirror-image debate.

Rabbi Meir rules that by *pikadon*, one is liable *mipi acherim* only if the denial occurs in *beit din*. The *Rabbanan* rule that one is liable *mipi acherim* whether the denial occurs in *beit din* or outside *beit din*. This is the exact reversal of their positions in the *edut* case: Rabbi Meir was more expansive about *edut* (outside *beit din* included) but more limited about *pikadon* (*beit din* only); the *Rabbanan* were more limited about *edut* (*beit din* only) but more expansive about *pikadon* (anywhere).

The logic is perfectly symmetrical and confirms the methodological underpinning of the debate. Rabbi Meir holds *don mina u'mina*: you retain the original context of the source. When learning *mipi atzmo* for *shvuat ha'edut* from *pikadon*, the original context is *outside beit din*, so that becomes the operative context. When learning *mipi acherim* for *shvuat ha'pikadon* from *edut*, the original context is *inside beit din* — so that becomes the operative context. The *Rabbanan* hold *don mina v'oki b'atrah*: you always apply the context of the target law. When the target law is *shvuat ha'edut*, the context is *beit din*, so *mipi atzmo* is limited there. When the target law is *shvuat ha'pikadon*, the context is *outside beit din* (since *pikadon* has no *beit din* requirement), so *mipi acherim* extends there too. Whichever direction one goes, Rabbi Meir preserves the source context and the *Rabbanan* apply the target context — consistently, regardless of whether the result is more or less expansive.

The Gemara then asks: from where do the *Rabbanan* know that *mipi acherim* generates liability in *shvuat ha'pikadon*? It cannot be derived by *kal v'chomer*, since *mipi acherim* is, if anything, a weaker basis for liability than *mipi atzmo* — there is no logical inference from "you are liable when someone else imposes it" that could be *more* compelling than "you are liable when you impose it yourself." The only possible derivation is from *shvuat ha'edut*, which confirms that the *Rabbanan* do learn across these two domains when necessary — and that the methodological debate of *don mina u'mina* versus *don mina v'oki b'atrah* is precisely what drives the reversal of positions.

The Gemara concludes: *miha in* — yes, from the *pikadon mishnah* I concede that that is indeed the debate. The objection Rav Papa raised — that one could not prove the debate from the *edut* case alone, since there a *kal v'chomer* was available — is well-taken; but looking at the *pikadon* case, where no *kal v'chomer* exists, confirms unambiguously that the dispute concerns the methodology of *don mina u'mina* versus *don mina v'oki b'atrah*.

---

## Oath-Taker Status

### Mipi Atzmo Outside

Rabbi Meir's position — *don mina u'mina* — means that when *mipi atzmo* is imported from *shvuat ha'pikadon* into *shvuat ha'edut*, it carries with it the original context of *pikadon*, which is not limited to *beit din*. Consequently, Rabbi Meir holds that one who spontaneously takes a false oath denying knowledge of testimony is liable for *shvuat ha'edut* even if this occurs outside of *beit din*, provided that the oath is self-imposed.

### Mipi Atzmo Inside Only

The *Rabbanan*, applying *don mina v'oki b'atrah*, situate the imported *mipi atzmo* within the context of *shvuat ha'edut* — a law whose operative sphere is *beit din*. Consequently, they hold that *mipi atzmo* liability for *shvuat ha'edut* applies only within *beit din*, not outside it. Since the *Rabbanan* derive *mipi atzmo* from a self-contained *kal v'chomer* within the domain of *shvuat ha'edut*, they have no occasion to look to *pikadon* and no reason to absorb its context.

---

## Disqualified Witnesses

### King Afuki

The *mishnah* states that *shvuat ha'edut* applies only to someone who is qualified to testify. Rav Papa identifies one category the *mishnah* is excluding: the *melech*, the king. A king is not technically *pasul* — there is no formal disqualification — but he cannot be brought to court to testify; doing so would be incompatible with the honor of his position. Since the king is not *ra'uy l'ha'id* in practice, he falls outside the scope of *shvuat ha'edut*.

### Dice Player

Rav Acha the son of Rav Yaakov identifies a second category: the *mesachek b'kubiya*, the dice player. Unlike the king, the dice player is explicitly *pasul* — but only *d'Rabbanan*, on rabbinic grounds. The disqualification stems either from the *asmachta* problem (winnings from gambling may not constitute a valid acquisition) or from the fact that one who does not engage in a productive occupation lacks the social accountability that renders testimony reliable. But from the Torah's perspective, he is a fully valid witness.

### Rabbinic Effect

This generates a genuinely interesting question. From the biblical standpoint, the dice player can testify; his oath is therefore a valid *shvuat ha'edut*, and lying under it should obligate him in a *korban*. From the practical standpoint, any time he appeared in court to testify, the court would send him home — his testimony is not accepted. If the court would never accept his testimony regardless, does it make sense to hold him liable in a *korban* for *shvuat ha'edut*?

The argument for exempting him is intuitively compelling: since as a practical matter the court will reject him, the *shvuat ha'edut* framework — premised on the denial of testimony that could actually affect a case — never becomes operative for him. Whether the rabbinic disqualification is sufficient to override the biblical liability is the question, and it illustrates the broader problem of how a *d'Rabbanan* ruling intersects with and potentially displaces *d'Oraita* consequences.

---

## Liability Cases

### Meizid Liability

The *mishnah* states that one is liable for *shvuat ha'edut* even if one acts willfully — *meizid*. The Gemara derives this from a comparison with other *oleh v'yored* obligations (where the Torah explicitly uses the phrase *v'ne'elam*, "and it was hidden from him," indicating a requirement of inadvertence). In the laws of *shvuat ha'edut*, the verse does not include *v'ne'elam*. This omission is deliberate: it signals that one is liable *l'chayev al hameizid k'shogeg*, even for a willful violation, just as one would be for an inadvertent one.

### Shogeg Liability

The *mishnah* further states that one is liable for a *shogeg* of a particular type — *shigagato im zedonah ha'edut*. This formulation means that one is *shogeg* with respect to one element (the *korban* obligation) while being *meizid* with respect to another (the oath itself). One is not liable for a pure *shogeg* — *shigagatah greidah* — without any element of willfulness.

### Shogeg Definition

Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav defines the actionable *shogeg* case precisely: *be'omer yodea ani sheshvua zo asura, aval eini yodea im chayavin aleha korban im lav* — I know this oath is forbidden, but I do not know whether one incurs a *korban* obligation for it. That is the case of *shogeg* in which one is liable. One knows one is lying; one knows taking a false oath is *assur*; but one is mistaken about whether the consequence is a *korban*. Liability follows because the *meizid* element — deliberate lying — is present, even if the *korban* obligation was unknown.

### Kahana and Assi

The Gemara then asks: is the *mishnah*'s exemption of a pure *shogeg* simply confirming what was already established by the famous case of Rav Kahana and Rav Assi? In that case, each took an oath as to what Rav had ruled on a certain matter, and one of them was mistaken. When they came before Rav and discovered the error, the one who had sworn falsely asked whether he had transgressed. Rav replied: *libcha anascha* — your heart compelled you; you genuinely believed what you said was true. Thinking one is telling the truth, even while factually mistaken, does not constitute a false oath.

Was that case not already implicit in the *mishnah*'s exemption of *shigagatah greidah*? The Gemara answers: *af al gav detanan, itzterich* — even though the *mishnah* states the exemption, the case of Rav Kahana and Rav Assi was still a *chiddush* that needed to be taught. The reasoning: one might have thought that since *shvuat ha'edut* does not use the phrase *v'ne'elam*, it requires an element analogous to *meizid* — and perhaps even believing one is telling the truth is not sufficient to remove liability entirely, because one ought to have verified the facts. In contexts where the Torah does write *v'ne'elam*, perhaps even pure inadvertence generates a *korban* for other oath types (*shvuat bitui*, for example), and perhaps the absence of *v'ne'elam* from *shvuat ha'edut* means something different altogether. The case of Rav Kahana and Rav Assi teaches unambiguously that genuinely believing one is telling the truth exempts completely — not only from the *korban* but from any transgression of false oath.

*Tosafot* adds a further point: the *mishnah*'s exemption of a pure *shogeg* may also encompass the case where one knows one is making a false statement but genuinely believes it is *muttar* to do so — that there is no prohibition against taking a false oath. Whether such a person has sufficient *meizid* consciousness to incur liability under *shvuat ha'edut* is a question *Tosafot* leaves open. The only *shogeg* explicitly identified by the Gemara as generating liability is the one defined by Rav: knowing one is lying and knowing it is forbidden, but being ignorant of the *korban* obligation.

---

---

# Shevuot 32

## Shvuos Ha'eidus Basics

### Opening & Transition

The present daf, Shevuot 32a, continues from the bottom third of 31b, where the Gemara begins transitioning from a theoretical discussion of the parameters and criteria of *shvuos ha'eidus* to the practical scenario of how the *chiyuv* actually arises and what circumstances generate an obligation to bring a *korban*.

### Mishnah Setup

The *mishnah* opens with the question *shvuos ha'eidus keitzad* — what is the scenario that generates a *shvuos ha'eidus* obligating a *korban*? The classic case is that a litigant approaches two individuals who are *kasher l'eidus* and says: "Come and testify on my behalf." The requirement that he address two witnesses — and not merely one — reflects the principle that *shvuos ha'eidus* applies only when the testimony in question could actually have been used to extract *mamon*; a single *eid* cannot independently accomplish that. The witnesses then respond with a false *shvuah*: "We swear we have no testimony on your behalf." That is the paradigmatic case that obligates a *korban*.

### Oath vs. Amen

The *mishnah* presents a second scenario as well. The witnesses first declare — without an oath — that they have no testimony. The litigant then responds: *mashpia ani aleichem*, "I impose a *shvuah* upon you," and the witnesses answer *amen*. The *mishnah* rules that they are likewise *chayavim*. The halachic basis for this is the principle that *kol ha'omer amen k'motzi shvuah mipiv dami* — answering *amen* is considered as though one personally uttered the oath. Accordingly, both scenarios in the *mishnah* are, in fact, cases of *mushpa mipi atzmo*.

### Self vs. Other Oath

This stands in contrast to a true case of *mushpa mipi acherim*, which would occur if the litigant declared *mashpia ani aleichem* that you have no testimony, and the witnesses responded only by reaffirming their position — "We're telling you we don't know" — without themselves articulating or accepting a *shvuah*. They were merely standing by their denial after having the *shvuah* placed upon them. Both scenarios in our *mishnah*, by contrast, involve the witnesses actively taking the oath themselves, through explicit utterance or through *amen*.

---

## Denial in Beis Din

### Outside BD Oaths

The *mishnah* then addresses a case where the litigant administered the oath to the witnesses five times outside of *beis din*, and when they subsequently appeared before *beis din* they admitted to knowing testimony — they are *patur*. Two distinct principles underlie this ruling, both of which the *Gemara* will develop.

### Kfira Triggers Chiyuv

The first principle is that the *kfira* — the denial of testimony — must occur in *beis din* in order to trigger the *chiyuv*. Outside of *beis din*, the witnesses have not yet testified to anything in a binding sense. They retain the ability to come before *beis din* and testify truthfully at any moment. Their repeated false oaths outside of *beis din* therefore remain open-ended and do not yet crystallize into a *chiyuv*.

### No Retraction Rule

The second principle is *kivan she'higid shuv eino chozer u'maggid*: once testimony — or a denial of testimony — has been given before *beis din*, one cannot retract it. Outside of *beis din*, by contrast, the situation remains fluid. Since the witnesses can always choose to testify truthfully when they arrive before *beis din*, the issue is still live, and the prior oaths carry no irreversible force.

### Multiple Oaths BD

The *mishnah* then considers a different case: the litigant administered the oath to them five times *before beis din*, and they denied. Here one might expect that each of the five oaths generates a separate *chiyuv*, since everything occurred in the very place where testimony could have been given. Yet the *mishnah* rules that they are *chayav* only once — *ein chayav ela achas*.

### Posul After First

Rabbi Shimon explains: *ho'il ve'einam yecholim lachzor lehodos* — once the witnesses make their first denial in *beis din*, they are no longer in a position to testify at all. *Kivan she'higid shuv eino chozer u'maggid* applies from the moment of the first *kfira* in *beis din*. After that point, every subsequent oath is meaningless as a *shvuos ha'eidus*, because the witnesses are no longer eligible to give testimony — they are, in effect, like *psulei eidus* the moment they deny in *beis din*. The first denial activates the *chiyuv* for the first *shvuah* and simultaneously forecloses any *chiyuv* for those that follow.

---

## Two Witnesses

### Simultaneous Denial

The *mishnah* then turns to the structure of *chiyuv* when two *eidim* are involved. If *kafru shneihem k'echad* — both witnesses denied at the same moment — both are *chayav*. Each one withheld testimony that, in combination with the other's, could have established the case and extracted *mamon* for the litigant.

### Sequential Denial

If, however, they denied sequentially — *zeh achar zeh* — the first is *chayav* and the second is *patur*. When the first witness denies before *beis din*, his *kfira* takes immediate effect: *kivan she'higid shuv eino chozer u'maggid* renders him no longer eligible to testify. By the time the second witness denies, he is standing alone. He is only an *ed echad*, and a single witness cannot independently support the litigant's case to extract *mamon*. Therefore the second witness is *patur* for *shvuos ha'eidus*.

### First Denies

Similarly, if the first witness denied and the second witness admitted — *kafar echad ve'hodeh echad, hakofar chayav* — the first witness is *chayav*. At the time of his denial, his testimony could have joined with that of the second witness to fully establish the case. He withheld evidence that was potentially decisive.

### Two Groups

The *mishnah* then addresses a case involving two separate groups of witnesses — *shtei kitei eidim* — both of which the litigant approached for testimony. Even if the first group denied before *beis din* and was subsequently rendered ineligible, the second group can still independently establish the testimony. Since each group of two witnesses constitutes a complete set of *eidus* on its own — *ha'eidus yecholah lehiskayem bishteihen* — the *chiyuv* applies to both groups even if their denials were sequential.

---

## Direct Demand Req.

### Shmuel's Ruling

Shmuel introduces a teaching not stated explicitly in the *mishnah*: *ra'uhu sheratz achareihem* — if the witnesses saw the litigant running after them, clearly intending to ask them to testify, and they preemptively swore that they had no testimony on his behalf, they are *patur*. Why? *Ad sheyishme'u mipi* — they must actually hear the demand verbalized directly from him. Merely observing his behavior does not suffice.

### Running After

The concern that Shmuel is addressing is whether implicit communication — specifically, running after witnesses in a context that makes the purpose unmistakable — could constitute a sufficient demand. One might have thought: *kivan de'ratz achareihem ke'man de'amar lehu dami* — since he is visibly running after them and the intent is obvious, it is as though he has made an explicit verbal demand. Shmuel's ruling forecloses that reasoning: *ka mashma lan*, verbal articulation of the demand is required.

### Necessity Debate

The *Gemara* challenges whether Shmuel's teaching is even necessary. A later *mishnah* already states that if the litigant sent his servant, or if the opposing party imposed the *shvuah*, the witnesses are *patur* — *ad sheyishme'u mipi hatoveia* — because they must hear the demand from the litigant himself. Doesn't that *mishnah* already establish that a direct verbal demand is required? The *Gemara* responds: the case of running after them is qualitatively different. There it is the litigant himself who is approaching — only the verbalization is absent. One might have thought that his physical pursuit, which clearly communicates his intent, suffices. It is therefore necessary for Shmuel to inform us that it does not.

### Pikadon Compare

The *Gemara* pushes further. Our *mishnah* opens with *amar lishnayim* — "he said to two witnesses" — and the *Gemara* asks whether this *amar* reflects a formal *halachic* requirement or merely describes the typical scenario. It raises the parallel of *shvuas ha'pikadon*, where the *mishnah* likewise uses the formulation *amar lo ten li pikadon* — "he said to him, give me back my deposit." Yet we know from the *pasuk* — *ve'hikhash be'amito* — that *shvuas ha'pikadon* applies in any form of denial, without requiring a direct verbal demand from the claimant. If *amar* in the *pikadon mishnah* is merely descriptive and not a strict requirement, perhaps *amar* in our *mishnah* is likewise merely illustrative.

### Verbal Essential

The *Gemara* attempts a counter-argument: perhaps *amar* in the context of *shvuos ha'eidus* is *davka*, a genuine requirement, and the *pikadon mishnah* adopted the same language only by association — *tana hatam atu hakha* — patterning itself on our *mishnah* even though in that case the requirement does not apply. The *Gemara* ultimately rejects this, concluding: *dilma orcha de'milsa ka mashma lan* — the *mishnayos* in both cases are simply describing the typical scenario, not specifying a formal *halachic* requirement. It is therefore entirely possible that I would have read *amar* in our *mishnah* as non-*davka*, and would have assumed that a non-verbal demand also suffices for *shvuos ha'eidus*. Shmuel comes to clarify that this is not the case — a verbalized demand is essential.

### Braisa Support
