A *braisa* corroborates Shmuel's position almost word for word: witnesses who see the litigant pursuing them, preemptively declare a *shvuah* that they have no testimony on his behalf, and are ruled *paturim* — exempt — because they never heard him verbally demand their testimony. The *braisa* adds: *ve'im be'pikadon chayavin* — but if this were a case of *shvuas ha'pikadon*, they would be *chayavin*, since the direct verbal demand is not a requirement in that context.

---

## Scriptural Basis

### Im Lo Yagid

The *Gemara* now derives the requirement that *kfira* occur specifically in *beis din* from a *pasuk*. The verse states: *im lo yagid ve'nasa avono* — "if he does not testify, he bears his sin."

### Abaye's Logic

Abaye derives from this that the denial must occur in a place where, had the witnesses chosen to testify, their testimony would at that moment create a monetary obligation for the opposing party. *Lo amarti lach ela be'makom she'ilu maggid ze mis'chayev ze mamon* — I am speaking only of a context in which actual testimony could be given and would be binding. That context is *beis din*. The phrase *im lo yagid* implies a setting in which *hagada* — giving testimony — is possible and operative.

### Papa's Question

Rav Papa immediately raises an obvious objection to Abaye: if the *pasuk* establishes a *beis din* context for the entire *parasha* of *shvuos ha'eidus*, does this mean that the *shvuah* itself must also be taken in *beis din*? Should we rule that a *shvuah* administered outside of *beis din* falls entirely outside the *parasha* and generates no *chiyuv* whatsoever?

### Multiple Chiyuvim

The *Gemara* responds by invoking the *pasuk*: *ve'haya ki yesham le'achas me'eila* — "and it shall be when he incurs guilt for one of these." While the *peshat* of this phrase refers to liability for one of the three categories of *oleh ve'yored*, the *Gemara* reads it to teach *lechayyev al kol achas ve'achas* — that one can be *chayav* separately for each individual *shvuah* in a single case. This is precisely the scenario in our *mishnah*: five oaths taken outside of *beis din*, followed by a single *kfira* in *beis din*, generate five separate *korbanot*.

### Reconciliation

This produces a revealing proof. If we were to require that the *shvuah* itself also be taken in *beis din*, it would be impossible to ever be *chayav* for multiple *korbanot* in one case. Why? Because as soon as the witnesses make their first denial in *beis din*, *kivan she'higid shuv eino chozer u'maggid* applies — they are no longer eligible to testify, and any subsequent *shvuah* in *beis din* is irrelevant. The only way to accumulate multiple *chiyuvim* is to take multiple oaths *outside* of *beis din* — where each oath is still meaningful, since at every prior moment the witnesses retained the ability to come and testify — and then trigger those *chiyuvim* through a single *kfira* inside *beis din*. The *Gemara* concludes: *shma mina shvuah chutz la'beis din, kfira be'beis din* — the oaths must occur outside *beis din*, and the *kfira* that activates them must occur inside. This conclusion is arrived at not by a simple reading of the *pasuk* but by working backwards from two established principles: that multiple *chiyuvim* are possible, and that the context of *im lo yagid* demands *beis din*.

One important caveat: in all the cases where the witnesses fall short of the criteria for *shvuos ha'eidus* — whether because the *kfira* occurred outside *beis din*, or because five oaths were taken within *beis din* rendering subsequent ones irrelevant — the witnesses may still have violated *shvuas sheker*. The *Gemara* had discussed earlier whether such cases generate a *chiyuv* for *shvuas bitui*; that discussion, however, lies beyond the scope of the present analysis. The focus here is solely on whether the parameters of *shvuos ha'eidus* have been met.

---

## Two Witnesses (II)

### K'dei Dibur

The *Gemara* returns to the *mishnah*'s ruling that when both witnesses deny *k'echad* — simultaneously — they are both *chayav*. A conceptual difficulty immediately presents itself: is it ever truly possible to say that two people did something at precisely the same moment? If one always precedes the other by even a fraction of a second, then the second witness will always be rendering himself a lone *ed echad* after the first's denial, and will always be *patur*.

Rav Chisda identifies this *mishnah* as following the position of Rabbi Yosi ha-Glili, who holds *efshar le'tzamtzem* — that genuine simultaneity is a coherent and legally recognized possibility. The underlying dispute surfaces in Bechorot, in the case of twin firstborn lambs that emerged simultaneously: the *chachamim* treat each as a doubtful *bechor*, while Rabbi Yosi ha-Glili holds that both are *bechoros* — both literally emerged first.

Rabbi Yochanan, however, offers a simpler resolution: the ruling in our *mishnah* can be explained even according to the *rabanan* who reject *efshar le'tzamtzem*. The *mishnah* does not require literal simultaneity; it is sufficient that both witnesses denied *betoch k'dei dibur* — within the span of time it takes to utter a brief utterance. The principle *betoch k'dei dibur ke'dibur dami* — that what occurs within this interval is treated as contemporaneous — is a well-established *halachic* concept, operative across many domains. In the context of speech acts in particular, actions taken within this brief window are considered to have occurred at the same time.

Rashi here specifies that *k'dei dibur* corresponds to the time it takes a student to greet his teacher: *shalom alecha Rabi* — three words. Rav Acha mi'Difti raises a pointed question to Ravina: the full declaration *shvuah she'eini yode'a lach eidus* is itself considerably longer than *k'dei dibur*. If the second witness must begin his oath within *k'dei dibur* of the first witness's beginning, it would always take too long. Ravina responds: the measure of *k'dei dibur* is not calculated from the start of the first witness's speech, but from the moment he finishes. Each subsequent speaker need only begin within *k'dei dibur* of when his fellow completed his utterance — *kol echad ve'echad toch k'dei dibur shel chaveiro*. One might add that even without this framework, one could envision the two witnesses beginning their declarations in an overlapping fashion; but at minimum, the *Gemara's* formulation is as stated.

---

## Ed Echad Debate

### Concept Debate

The *Gemara* notes that our *mishnah* — in ruling that the second witness who denies after the first is *patur* — does not follow the position of a certain *tanna*. A *braisa* teaches: *mashpia eid echad patur* — imposing a *shvuah* on a single witness generates no *chiyuv* for *shvuos ha'eidus*. This is the implied assumption of our *mishnah*. However, Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Shimon disagrees and holds him *chayav*. The *Gemara* seeks to identify the conceptual root of this dispute.

The initial proposal is that the debate turns on the fundamental nature of *eid echad*: does the testimony of a single witness *come for shvuah* — its only halachic function is to impose a *shvuah* on the opposing party — or does it *come for mamon* — its fundamental legal import is monetary, with the *shvuah* serving merely as a mechanism that can neutralize that monetary force? If an *eid echad* is understood as coming for *mamon*, one might argue that withholding such testimony is as consequential as withholding the testimony of two witnesses, and the *chiyuv* of *shvuos ha'eidus* should apply. The classic *nafka mina* of this conceptual question is the rule *mitoch she'eino yachol lishava meshalem* — when the party who would normally take the *shvuah* is unable to do so, he must pay — which would make sense if we understand the *eid echad* as fundamentally generating a monetary obligation that the *shvuah* was merely suspending.

### Eliezer Position

Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Shimon's position, ultimately, is not that an *eid echad* comes for *mamon* directly. Rather, it is founded on the principle of *davar ha'gorem l'mamon k'mamon dami* — something that causes money to be paid is treated as equivalent to money itself. Since the testimony of a single *eid* will, in the typical case, lead the opposing party to take a *shvuah* — and most people will not take a false *shvuah*, or at minimum there is a real possibility they will not — the testimony of an *eid echad* effectively has the power to bring about the payment of the debt. Because it can generate this monetary consequence, Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Shimon treats it as *eidus* that relates to *mamon*, and therefore imposes the *chiyuv* of *shvuos ha'eidus*.

### Chachamim Position

The *chachamim*, by contrast, hold *lav k'mamon dami* — what only indirectly leads to monetary consequence is not treated as monetary in itself. Unless the testimony of the *eid* would directly and immediately obligate the opposing party to pay, it does not qualify as the type of *eidus* that triggers *shvuos ha'eidus*. An *eid echad* whose testimony requires the intermediate step of a *shvuah* — which may or may not be taken — before any monetary consequence materializes, does not meet this threshold.

### Abaye's Framework

Abaye offers a nuanced statement identifying the precise contours of the dispute: *hakol modim be'eit sotah, ve'hakol modim be'eid sotah, u'machlokes be'eid sotah, hakol modim be'eid echad, ve'hakol modim be'eid she'kenegdo chashud al ha'shvuah*. This cryptic formulation contains five cases — two on which everyone agrees the witness is *chayav*, two on which everyone agrees he is *patur*, and one that falls within the active *machlokes*. We will unpack each in turn.

### Sotah Cases

The first case of universal agreement: *hakol modim be'eit sotah she'chayav be'eid tumah* — everyone agrees that a witness is *chayav* in the case of the *eid tumah* of a *sotah*. Recall that the *sotah* process involves multiple stages: the husband's warning (*kinuy*), the witness to the wife's seclusion with the warned man (*stirah*), and potentially a witness who actually observed the act of adultery itself (*eid tumah*). Regarding *eid tumah*, the *Torah* explicitly believed even a single witness — *ve'eid ein bah*, from which we derive *yesh bah* — meaning that one witness who testifies to the act of adultery is credited with the status of two witnesses for purposes of the monetary consequence: the wife is divorced and loses her *kesubah*. Since the *eid tumah* directly generates a monetary consequence in the manner of two witnesses, everyone agrees that withholding such testimony while swearing falsely constitutes a full violation of *shvuos ha'eidus*.

The second case of universal agreement runs in the opposite direction: *hakol modim be'eidei kinuy she'patur* — everyone agrees that the witnesses to the husband's warning are *patur* from *shvuos ha'eidus*. Their testimony is twice removed from any monetary consequence. First, the warning witnesses must testify; then, a witness to the seclusion must testify; then, the outcome of the *sotah* ritual must unfold before there is any monetary consequence. This is not merely *davar ha'gorem l'mamon* but *gorem de'gorem* — a cause of a cause — and everyone agrees that this is too attenuated to qualify.

### Sotah Stirah

The debated case is *eidei stirah* — the witness or witnesses who testify that the wife entered seclusion with the warned man. Even granting for the moment that two witnesses could testify to the *stirah*, their testimony does not directly obligate the wife to lose her *kesubah*. What follows from their testimony is the *sotah* process: she is brought before *beis din*, given the opportunity to drink the *sotah* waters, and only if she refuses — or if she is found guilty — does she lose her *kesubah*. For Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Shimon, since this sequence *could* lead to monetary consequence, *davar ha'gorem l'mamon k'mamon dami* applies and the *chiyuv* exists. For the *chachamim*, since there is no direct monetary consequence — too many intervening steps remain — *lav k'mamon dami* and the witnesses are *patur*. The *Gemara* notes that even in the case of two witnesses to the *stirah*, the *chachamim* maintain their position, since the indirectness of the monetary consequence is not resolved by having two witnesses rather than one.

### Shvua Impossible

Abaye also states that everyone agrees a *chiyuv* exists in cases where the party who would have been obligated to take the *shvuah* cannot do so. The mechanism here is *mitoch she'eino yachol lishava meshalem*: when the *shvuah* cannot be taken, the obligation reverts directly to payment. In such a case, the testimony of even an *eid echad* would have an immediate, direct monetary consequence, since no *shvuah* stands between the testimony and the payment. Everyone — including the *chachamim* — agrees that this qualifies as *eidus* relating to *mamon*, and that withholding it constitutes *shvuos ha'eidus*.

The scenario Abaye identifies is where *she'kenegdo chashud al ha'shvuah* — the opposing party is disqualified from taking a *shvuah* due to prior misconduct. The *Gemara* clarifies: if only the *loveh* (borrower) is suspect and cannot take a *shvuah*, the *shvuah* would transfer to the *malveh* (lender), who could then swear and collect. There remains the intermediate step of the *malveh* actually taking the *shvuah*, which the *malveh* might decline to do — so the testimony still does not *directly* obligate payment, and the *chachamim* would not necessarily agree. The relevant case is where *both* parties are suspect and neither can take a *shvuah*. In that event, the *shvuah* reverts to the *loveh*, who cannot take it, and he must pay directly. The *eid echad's* testimony would thus have immediate monetary consequence, and everyone agrees he is *chayav*.

### Abba Case

The final case where everyone agrees — *hakol modim be'eid echad de'Rabbi Abba* — involves a striking incident adjudicated by Rabbi Ami in which Rabbi Abba was present. A man had seized a chunk of metal (*naska*) from his fellow. The aggrieved party brought a single witness who testified to the seizure. The accused did not deny the act: he admitted that he took it — *chatafi vedidi chatafi*, "I grabbed it, and what I grabbed was mine." He claimed he was merely reclaiming his own property.

Rabbi Ami was uncertain how to rule. The case could not simply result in payment, since there were not two witnesses. Nor could the accused simply be released, since there was one witness whose testimony had to be addressed. Normally, one witness obligates the opposing party to take a *shvuah*. But here lies the difficulty: the *shvuah* the *Torah* would have him take — denying that he took the object — is a *shvuah* he cannot take, since he has already admitted to taking it. Rabbi Ami asked whether he might take a different *shvuah* — one affirming that he took only what was rightfully his — in lieu of the *shvuah* he cannot take.

Rabbi Abba ruled: *hava leh mechuyav shvuah ve'eino yachol lishava, ve'chol hamechuyav shvuah ve'eino yachol lishava meshalem* — he has an obligation to take a *shvuah* and is unable to do so, and in such a case he must pay. The fact that he has an explanation for his conduct does not alter the analysis. The *shvuah* the *Torah* obligates him to take is the *shvuah* that would contradict the *eid*, and that *shvuah* he cannot make. He therefore must pay.

This case parallels the preceding one: just as when both parties are suspect and the *shvuah* cannot be taken by anyone, the *eid echad's* testimony translates directly into a monetary obligation — so too here. The witness who denied knowledge of this seizure was withholding testimony that would have immediately led to payment, and therefore everyone agrees he is *chayav* for *shvuos ha'eidus*.

---

## Death Testimony

### Death Framework

Rav Papa constructs a parallel framework using the testimony of witnesses regarding a husband's death. The halachic backdrop is the leniency of *chazal* to permit a woman to remarry — and to collect her *kesubah* — based on the testimony of even a single witness, or even hearsay (*eid mipi eid*), in circumstances where testimony about death is otherwise unavailable. Since there are also monetary consequences to this testimony — the woman collects her *kesubah* — Rav Papa identifies scenarios that map precisely onto the structure of Abaye's statement: cases where everyone agrees the witness is *chayav*, cases where everyone agrees he is *patur*, and implicitly, cases falling within the active *machlokes*.

### Private Tell

The first case where everyone agrees the witness is *patur*: *d'amar la l'didah ve'lo amar lehu l'vei dina* — he told the woman privately that her husband had died, but when called before *beis din* he denied it and took a false *shvuah*. In this scenario, his testimony before *beis din* was no longer needed. The *mishnah* teaches: *ha'isha she'amra meis ba'ali tinasei* — a woman who declares her husband has died may remarry based on her own statement if she heard it from a reliable source, including a single witness. Once he told her directly, his testimony accomplished its full effect. His subsequent denial in *beis din* is therefore inconsequential, and he is *patur*.

### Refuses Both

The second case where everyone agrees the witness is *chayav*: *d'lo amar la l'didah ve'lo amar lehu l'vei dina* — he refused to tell the woman privately and refused to testify before *beis din*. In this scenario, his testimony — had he given it either to her or to *beis din* — would have had immediate monetary consequences. The woman would have been permitted to remarry and to collect her *kesubah*. This is analogous to the *eid tumah* in the *sotah* case: the testimony of a single witness, credited with the weight necessary to generate an immediate monetary consequence, and withheld through a false oath, constitutes a full *chiyuv* of *shvuos ha'eidus*.

### Monetary Effect

The *Gemara* closes with a brief observation. If the woman's *kesubah* is secured by liens on land (*karka*), one might ask whether the *chiyuv* of *shvuos ha'eidus* still applies — since the normal rule is that there is no *shvuah* with respect to *karka*. The *Gemara* rejects any inference from this case: *dilma d'tfisa metaltalei* — perhaps in the case under discussion the woman was holding chattel in escrow as security for her *kesubah*, not land. No proof can therefore be adduced here regarding the question of *shvuah* where liens on land are involved.

The underlying principle that emerges from the entire discussion is that *shvuos ha'eidus* requires that the withheld testimony have a genuine and direct monetary effect. Where that monetary connection is immediate, whether for two witnesses or for an *eid echad* in those particular circumstances recognized by all, the *chiyuv* is clear. Where the monetary consequence is indirect, attenuated, or contingent on further steps, it is precisely this point that divides Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Shimon and the *chachamim*.

---

---

# Shevuot 33

## Two Witnesses & Denial

### Intro & Framework

The daf picks up at the bottom of 32b, continuing the treatment of *shevuat edut*. Several principles have already been established. The *kefira* — the denial of knowledge of testimony — must take place in *beit din*, the place where the *edut* is actually relevant; the *shevua* itself, however, may have been taken outside of *beit din*, and the denial inside *beit din* still renders one *chayav*. A further requirement is that the *edut* being denied must be the kind capable of extracting or protecting money. This means it must be the testimony of *shnei edim*, since only two witnesses carry the legal weight to compel payment.

The complication, of course, is how one arrives at *shnei edim* when each person takes a *shevua* individually. Either they take their *shevuot* simultaneously or within *toch kedei dibbur* of one another, or the first witness to take the *shevua* undermines the sufficiency of the remaining testimony — he has, as it were, destroyed the *edut*, and thus bears the *chiyuv*. By the time the second witness takes his *shevua*, the remaining testimony is only that of *ed echad*, which is insufficient to compel payment.

There was, to be sure, a significant position advanced in an earlier *Gemara* — that of Rabbi Elazar BeRabbi Shimon — who held that even an *ed echad* is *chayav*. Two approaches were entertained: first, that *ed echad* might itself obligate payment; second, and the one the *Gemara* settled on, that even if *ed echad* only obligates a *shevua*, since the defendant might choose not to take that *shevua* and thereby trigger a monetary loss, the testimony carries sufficient potential weight to fall under *shevuat edut*. But we proceed according to the *Chachamim*, who hold that *ed echad* is not *chayav*. The upshot is that *chiyuv* falls either on both witnesses when they take their *shevuot* together, or on the first of the two when they act sequentially.

### Simultaneous vs Sequenti…

The *Mishna* states: *kafar echad ve-hoda echad* — one witness denied and one admitted. The *Gemara* raises the obvious question. If we have already established that when both deny sequentially the first is *chayav* and the second is *patur* — even though the second also denied — because the first had already nullified the *edut*, then surely it is self-evident that if one denies and one admits, the one who denied is *chayav* and the one who admitted is *patur*. What does the *Mishna* need to add?

The *Gemara* answers: *lo tzericha*. The *Mishna* is not describing the simple case. Rather, it addresses a scenario in which they *both* denied — *she-kaferu shneihem* — and then one of them retracted his denial *be-toch kedei dibbur*.

### Toch Kedei Dibbur

This picks up directly on the earlier discussion of *toch kedei dibbur* — the principle that acts performed within the brief span of completing a phrase (*shalom alecha rabbi*) are considered part of a single continuous speech act, and that a retraction made within this window remains legally effective. So: suppose Charlie denies first, making him the one who bears the *chiyuv* for the *korban*; David then denies, but at that point his denial carries no legal weight since Charlie's denial has already nullified the *edut*. If Charlie then retracts his denial within *toch kedei dibbur*, Charlie's denial is undone, and David is now left as the operative denier — even though he took the *shevua* second. The *Gemara* formulates this: *toch kedei dibbur ke-dibbur dami* — what falls within the time of speech is treated as a single continuous act.

### Rav Chisda & R.Y.G.

The *Gemara* now explains why this is significant given the structure of the *Mishna*. According to Rav Chisda, the *reisha* of the *Mishna* — both witnesses denying simultaneously — was interpreted as following Rabbi Yose HaGlili, who holds that it is possible for two acts to occur literally at the same time, or at least to be treated *halakhically* as simultaneous. On that reading, the *reisha* had not yet introduced the concept of *toch kedei dibbur* at all. The *seifa* of the *Mishna* is therefore needed to introduce *toch kedei dibbur* as its own operative principle — teaching that a retraction within that window is legally effective and can shift the *chiyuv* from one witness to the other.

### Rabbi Yochanan

Rabbi Yochanan, however, disagrees. He holds that strict simultaneity is legally impossible, and therefore the *reisha* of the *Mishna* — which describes both witnesses as *chayav* when they deny together — must already be speaking of *toch kedei dibbur*. If the *reisha* already invokes *toch kedei dibbur*, then the *seifa* seems to repeat the same principle. As the *Gemara* frames it: *reisha toch kedei dibbur, seifa toch kedei dibbur — tarti lamah li?* Why do you need both halves of the *Mishna* if each one is teaching the same thing?

The *seifa*, after all, says that one denied and one admitted — of course the one who denied is *chayav*. The only novelty would be if the one who ultimately admitted had initially denied and then retracted *be-toch kedei dibbur*. But that principle has already been introduced in the *reisha*. So what does the *seifa* add?

### Daisy-Chaining

The *Gemara* explains the mechanism that makes this question necessary. The principle of *toch kedei dibbur* had been understood as operating in a "daisy-chaining" fashion: witness one speaks and finishes; witness two begins within one or two seconds of witness one's conclusion. That brief overlap causes witness two's entire speech to be treated as a continuation of witness one's speech-act. And as long as that continuity holds, witness one retains the ability to retract — even after witness two has begun speaking, because it is all treated as one extended act.

## Deny & Admit Mix

### Contradiction Case

But this raises the question: perhaps that daisy-chaining logic applies only when both witnesses are saying essentially the same thing — *kefira u-kefira*, both denying. One might argue that *toch kedei dibbur* creates a unified speech-act only when the two speakers are delivering a coherent, consistent message. If witness one says, effectively, "I don't know of any testimony," and witness two says, "I do know testimony," they are contradicting each other. Perhaps in that case the second statement breaks the chain and the framework of *toch kedei dibbur* does not link them into a single act.

This is precisely the teaching of the *seifa*: *mah de-teima hani mili kefira u-kefira* — one might think this rule holds only when both are denying — *aval kefira ve-hoda'ah* — but when one denies and one admits, the linkage does not apply. *Ka-mashma lan* — the *Mishna* therefore teaches that it does apply even in that case. Even when the two witnesses end up delivering contradictory messages, the *toch kedei dibbur* principle still operates: the retraction is valid, and whoever is left standing as the denier bears the *chiyuv*.

### Redundancy Question

One might note that the case described in the *Mishna* is somewhat more nuanced than a pure case of one denying and one admitting from the outset. In the actual scenario, both witnesses initially denied, and it is only within the *toch kedei dibbur* window that one of them retracted and switched from denial to admission. Since they began by saying the same thing, the initial combination of their speech acts was already established; the retraction then shifts things. The *Gemara*'s point, however, is that the *Mishna* is teaching that even when the witnesses ultimately land in contradictory positions — one left denying, one having admitted — the framework of *toch kedei dibbur* remains intact, and the witness who retracted is not treated as having caused a break in the chain.

## Two Groups Case

### First Group Liable

The *Gemara* continues to the next clause: *hayu shtei kitei eidin* — there were two groups of witnesses. The *Mishna* states that if both groups denied the testimony sequentially, both are *chayav*. The *Gemara* will interpret this *Mishna* quite differently from what its plain meaning seems to convey.

On the surface, the *Mishna* appears to be teaching that if you deny someone a testimony that was *sufficient* for their case — even if that testimony was not *necessary*, because another group of witnesses could also have supplied it — you are still *chayav*. Denying sufficient testimony is enough to create a *chiyuv* even when the claimant had alternative avenues. That seems to be the straightforward message.

But the *Gemara* resists this reading. It asks: granted, the second group is *chayav*, since after the first group denied, the entire case rested on the second group's testimony. *Bishlama shniya titchayiv* — the second group's *chiyuv* is clear. But why is the first group *chayav*? The second group was still present and available — *haka kayma shniya*, the second group is standing right there at the top of 33a. If the testimony of the first group is redundant, their denial did not deprive the claimant of anything; he could simply turn to the second group. The *Gemara* thus rejects the *pshat* of the *Mishna* and insists that mere sufficiency without necessity does not create a *chiyuv*.

### Pasul Solution

Ravina resolves the difficulty: the case in the *Mishna* must be one in which the second group of witnesses was actually *pasul* at the time the first group denied. Therefore the first group's testimony was not merely sufficient but was, at that moment, the *only* valid testimony available — the second group could not have served as an alternative.

### Wives' Deaths

The specific example Ravina gives is that the two witnesses in the second group were married to sisters. Two witnesses who are brothers-in-law — related through their wives who are sisters — are disqualified from testifying together in the same case. Their wives were also, at the time of the first group's denial, *gossot* — on their deathbeds. This introduces the principle of *rov gosesin le-mita*: most dying people will die soon. One might have thought that since the wives were expected to die imminently, the second group should be considered effectively *kasher*, on the anticipation that they would shortly become eligible. The *Gemara* rejects this: *hashta miha la shchiv* — right now the wives have not died. Whatever the statistical likelihood, the second group remains *pasul* at this moment, and therefore the first group's testimony was the only valid testimony available. Their denial was a meaningful deprivation, and they are *chayav*.

The *Gemara*'s reinterpretation of the *Mishna* is striking. The *Mishna* itself appears to be saying that redundancy is irrelevant — you are *chayav* for denying testimony that was sufficient even if not necessary. The *Gemara* insists the *Mishna* must be read as a case where the second group was *pasul* — because otherwise there would be no *chiyuv* for the first group. This is a significant departure from the plain sense of the text.

### Tosafot Solution

*Tosafot* finds a middle ground. On the phrase *haka kayma shniya* — Ravina's answer — *Tosafot* notes that the *Mishna* may in fact be read according to its plain meaning, but with a nuance. *Tosafot* distinguishes between alternative witnesses who are immediately present and accessible, and alternative witnesses who exist but are not accessible at the moment — perhaps in a different town. If the second group of witnesses is right there, physically present and available, then the first group's denial is truly redundant and they are *patur*. But if the second set of witnesses exists somewhere else and is not immediately accessible to the claimant, then the first group's denial is a meaningful deprivation, and they are *chayav*.

This reading preserves something of the *Mishna*'s plain meaning while accommodating the *Gemara*'s concern about pure redundancy. The *chiyuv* depends not on a binary of necessary versus sufficient, but on the practical accessibility of the alternative testimony. When the second group is right there before the court, you are exempt; when they are unavailable even if they technically exist, your denial has deprived the claimant of something real.

## Money Requirement

### Pikadon Types

The *Gemara* now proceeds to the next *Mishna*, at the top of 33a, which begins to lay out explicitly the requirement that *shevuat edut* must concern monetary subject matter. Before examining the *Mishna* directly, it helps to recall the structure of the relevant *pesukim* in *Vayikra*.

The *parasha* of *shevuat edut* — the *korban oleh ve-yored* — opens at *Perek 5, Pasuk 1*: *ve-nefesh ki techeta ve-shama kol alah ve-hu ed o ra'ah o yada im lo yagid ve-nasa avono*. A person who heard the voice of an oath — an externally imposed demand — and who is a witness, or who saw, or who knew, and who failed to report: he bears his sin. From the phrase *im lo yagid* — if he does not tell — we derive that the demand must be directed personally at the individual by the *tove'a*, the claimant himself. The absence of the word *ve-ne'elam* teaches that even a *meizid*, one who acts intentionally, is *chayav*. But nothing in this *pasuk* describes the content of the testimony — what the *edut* must be about.

That content is derived by analogy from *shevuat pikadon*. The *parasha* of *shevuat pikadon* — a *korban asham* — appears at *Pasuk 26*: *ve-nefesh ki techeta u-ma'ala ma'al ba-Hashem ve-kichash ba-amito be-fikadon o be-tsumet yad o be-gezel o ashak et amito o matza aveidah ve-kichash bah ve-nishba la-shaker*. You denied your fellow a *pikadon* — an object given for safekeeping; or *tsumet yad* — some form of misappropriation; or *gezel* — outright theft; or *oshek* — withholding wages or money owed; or *aveidah* — a found object that you deny. *Ve-nishba la-shaker* — and you swore falsely. All of these cases concern the denial of money or monetary obligations. The link between the two *parashiyot* establishes that *shevuat edut*, too, applies only when the testimony being withheld is testimony relevant to that same kind of monetary issue.

The *Mishna* itself now directly borrows the language of the *shevuat pikadon* passage and restates it in the context of *shevuat edut*: "I impose an oath on you — if you do not come and testify for me that so-and-so has of mine a *pikadon*, or *tsumet yad*, or *gezel*, or *aveidah*." These are the four categories drawn from the *pasuk*. The witnesses then say: "*shevuah she-ein anu yodim lecha edut*" — we swear we have no testimony for you. If they made this generic denial in one *shevua*, they are *chayav* only one *korban*, *ein chayavin ela achas*, even if the denial technically covered all four categories.

But if they enumerated the objects specifically — *shevuah she-ein anu yodim she-yesh lecha be-yad ploni pikadon u-tsumet yad u-gezel va-aveidah* — naming each category, then they are *chayav al kol achat ve-achat*, a separate *korban* for each. This parallels the earlier discussion of *shevuat bitui*, where objects separately named are treated as separate *shevuot* even if only one word of *shevua* was uttered.

The *Mishna* then extends this to the sub-case of a single category with multiple objects. If I say: come and testify that so-and-so holds a *pikadon* for me consisting of wheat, barley, and spelt — *chitin use'orin ve-kusmin* — and they say generically we know no testimony, they are *chayav* only one *korban*. But if they named each item — wheat and barley and spelt — then they are *chayav* separately for each.

### Generic vs Specific

The crucial distinction is between a generic denial and a specific one. A generic *shevua* covering multiple categories or multiple objects produces a single *chiyuv*. Once the denier specifies each object or category explicitly, the law treats each denial as a separate *shevua* carrying its own *chiyuv*. This mirrors the principle seen in *shevuat bitui*, where separate enumeration creates separate *chiyuvim* regardless of whether the oath was formally repeated.

One might ask about the case of multiple *korbanot* in the same breath — that comes from separately naming categories, analogous to *shevuat bitui* where multiple named items generate separate obligations even under one formal oath.

### Knas Cases

The *Mishna* then introduces a set of cases where the monetary obligation in question is not straightforward compensation but takes the form of a *knas* — a penalty or fine. The cases listed are:

*Nezek* — full damages — which is ordinary *mamon*. *Chatzi nezek* — half damages — which in the context of a *tam* ox may be considered a *knas*. *Tashlumei kefel* — double payment imposed on a thief — which is certainly a *knas*. *Tashlumei arba'ah va-chamisha* — four or five times payment when the thief also slaughtered or sold the stolen animal — again a *knas*. *She-anas ish ploni et biti u-fita et biti* — that a certain man raped or seduced my daughter — with a *knas* of fifty *shekel*. *She-hikani bni* — my son struck me — without *chavalah* (wounding), because if it were wounding that would be *chayav misa* and *kim leih*. And finally: *she-chaval bi chaveri ve-hidlik gdishi be-Yom HaKippurim* — my friend wounded me or burned my haystack on *Yom HaKippurim*. The author of this *Mishna* holds that for a *chayav karet* — unlike a *chayav misa* — there is still a monetary obligation and *kim leih* does not apply. The *Mishna* states that in all these cases the witnesses are *chayavin* — the *knas* element does not exempt them, *knas* being treated as *mamon* for these purposes.

## Knas Testimony

### Knas Question

The *Gemara* raises the question: *mashpia edei knas mahu* — when a person adjures witnesses to testify that another owes him a *knas*, and they deny, are they *chayav* a *korban*? On the surface this seems to be exactly what the *Mishna* just taught. But the *Gemara* will scrutinize whether the *Mishna* actually establishes this.

### R.E.B.R.S. View

First the *Gemara* clarifies: *aliba de-Rabbi Elazar beRabbi Shimon lo tiba'ei lach* — according to Rabbi Elazar BeRabbi Shimon, this is not a question at all. The relevant rule here is that one who admits to a *knas* is exempt from paying it — the principle that there is no self-incrimination for a punitive fine. The question, then, is whether such an admission permanently neutralizes the obligation, or merely fails to activate it. Rabbi Elazar BeRabbi Shimon holds that admission merely fails to activate: it does not get one off the hook if witnesses subsequently appear. In his view, witnesses to a *knas* can always render the person liable even after he has admitted. Therefore their testimony is at all times capable of compelling payment, and when they deny it they are straightforwardly *chayav shevuat ha-edut*.

### Rabbanan Position

The question is acute only *aliba de-Rabbanan* — according to the Rabbis. The Rabbis hold *modeh be-knas ve-achar kach ba'u edim patur* — if the defendant admitted to the *knas* and witnesses subsequently came, the witnesses cannot override the admission; the defendant remains exempt. The difficulty is then the following: when I adjure the witnesses to testify that Michael owes me a *knas*, they might argue that their testimony would not necessarily have secured the money for me — because Michael could have stepped forward and admitted the *knas* himself, preempting the witnesses and rendering himself exempt from payment. Since the outcome depended on whether Michael would confess before they testified, their testimony was not a certain cause of my recovery.

### Definitive Testimony

This argument has a familiar ring. It echoes the earlier debate regarding *gorem le-mamon*: is testimony that might lead to money but does not definitively compel it sufficient to generate a *chiyuv* for *shevuat edut*? The Rabbis had ruled there that *gorem le-mamon lav ke-mamon dami* — causing a potential monetary outcome is not equivalent to a direct monetary outcome — and that therefore witnesses are not *chayav* unless their testimony would definitively have resulted in payment.

The *Gemara* notes, however, that there is a crucial distinction between the *knas* scenario and the earlier *gorem le-mamon* cases. In those earlier cases — the single witness whose testimony needed to be combined with the defendant's refusal to take a *shevua*, or the *sotah* case where the testimony needed to be combined with the wife's refusal to drink the water — the testimony was genuinely just one piece of a multi-part causal chain. Something positive had to happen in addition to the testimony for the money to flow.

In the *knas* case, the testimony alone will secure the money provided the status quo holds — provided Michael does nothing. The witnesses do not need anything additional to happen. The only thing that could preempt their testimony is an active intervention by Michael: he would have to run to *beit din* and confess before they testify. So perhaps the correct framing is the present status: *hashta miha lo odei* — right now Michael has not admitted. At this moment, the testimony is fully operative. Should we not define the legal significance of the testimony by the status quo at the time it was withheld?

This is the unresolved question: does the mere theoretical possibility that Michael could preempt the testimony by confessing first render the testimony non-definitive — like *gorem le-mamon* — and therefore insufficient to generate a *chiyuv*? Or do we assess the testimony by the status quo, in which it would have been decisive, and hold the witnesses *chayav*?

### False Report Case

A *braita* is cited: one adjures witnesses to come and testify that a certain person spread a false report — *shem ra* — about his daughter. This is a pure *knas* case. If they denied the testimony, *chayavin* — they are *chayav*. But if the defendant admitted on his own — *hoda mipi atzmo* — then *patur* — they would be exempt. This *braita* appears to address precisely the open question. Before the defendant's admission, the witnesses are *chayav*; after, they are exempt. The implication is that even though it was theoretically possible at any point for the defendant to admit and preempt the witnesses, so long as he has not actually done so the witnesses' denial is treated as a meaningful deprivation and they are *chayav*.

### Braita Meaning

The *Gemara* objects: *ha mani Rabbi Elazar beRabbi Shimon hi* — this *braita* follows Rabbi Elazar BeRabbi Shimon, who holds that witnesses to a *knas* can render the person liable even after admission. Under his view, the witnesses are always *chayav* when they deny, since their testimony would be effective even after the defendant admitted. The *seifa* of the *braita* — *hoda mipi atzmo patur* — is then interpreted not as the admission neutralizing later witnesses, but as the specific case where the defendant admitted when there were no witnesses at all. In the absence of any witnesses, the admission alone settles the matter; but as long as witnesses exist, they can come and testify even after an admission.

The *Gemara* acknowledges this is a forced reading of the *braita*, which in its plain sense does seem to describe exactly the scenario the question was probing: that prior to admission the witnesses are *chayav*, and after admission they are *patur*, suggesting that the *chiyuv* is assessed at the time of the denial, by the status quo, and that the theoretical possibility of a later preemptive admission does not retroactively negate it. But the *Gemara* will not allow this to resolve the question definitively, attributing the *braita* instead to Rabbi Elazar BeRabbi Shimon. The question according to the Rabbis thus remains open.

## Non-Money Cases

### Mishna Examples

The next *Mishna* addresses non-monetary testimony — cases where the witnesses are *patur* because the *edut* being withheld does not concern a monetary claim. "I impose an oath on you — come and testify for me that I am a *kohein*, that I am a *levi*, that I am not the son of a *grusha* or a *chalutzah*." These are status questions. Or: "Come and testify that so-and-so is a *kohein*, that so-and-so is not the son of a *grusha* or *chalutzah*." Or: "Come and testify that a certain man raped so-and-so's daughter or seduced so-and-so's daughter." Or: "That my son wounded me." And: "That my friend wounded me, or burned my haystack on *Shabbat*." In all these cases the witnesses are *paturim*.

The *chiddush* of this *Mishna* is layered. The case of someone demanding testimony about their own *kohein* status is genuinely novel: it directly affects that person, there is arguably monetary consequence to it (access to *teruma*, *ma'aser*), and yet it is *patur* because the deprivation is indirect, not a direct monetary claim. The cases involving third parties — testify that Reuven is a *kohein*, that Reuven raped Shimon's daughter — are more straightforward, because the basic rule of *shevuat edut* requires that the demand be made by the *tove'a* personally, the person to whom the testimony is relevant.

### Third Party Issue

The *Gemara* focuses on the third-party cases. If the *Mishna* states that witnesses who are asked to testify about *ish ploni kohein* — that a certain *other* person is a *kohein* — are *patur*, this might seem obvious since the demand was not made by the party to whom it pertains. The *Gemara* notes, however, that there is a specific *chiddush* here: the case is one where the demand was made through a *harsha'ah* — a power of attorney. One might have thought that if the person to whom the testimony is relevant granted another a formal *harsha'ah*, that agent could make the demand in the principal's name and the witnesses would be *chayav*.

The *Gemara* cites *Shmuel*: *be-vava de-harsha'ah* — our *Mishna* is speaking of the *harsha'ah* case. The *Mishna* teaches that even with a *harsha'ah*, witnesses to a *kohein* status matter are *patur*.

### Qi'yum Leih

The cases at the end of the *Mishna* — *she-chaval bi bni* (my son wounded me) and *she-chaval bi chaveri ve-hidlik gdishi be-Shabbat* (my friend wounded me or burned my haystack on *Shabbat*) — are *patur* for a different reason: *kim leih*. Where the perpetrator is subject to a capital or lashes penalty, the monetary obligation is subsumed under the greater penalty. In these cases the witnesses' testimony about the monetary dimension is therefore not testimony about operative *mamon* and generates no *chiyuv*. The *Yom HaKippurim* case in the previous *Mishna* excluded precisely this reasoning: the author there held that a *chayav karet* offense does not trigger *kim leih*, and hence the monetary obligation remains operative.

### Power of Attorney

The mechanism of *harsha'ah* as understood in *halakha* deserves attention. When Dov wishes to empower Michael to sue on his behalf and to compel testimony on his behalf, the legal structure involves something between *shlichus* and *hakna'ah* — a combination of agency and transfer. Dov effectively says: that hundred dollars Reuven owes me — I am treating it as though I have transferred it to you. Michael can then sue Reuven in his own name and demand testimony from witnesses as though it were his own claim. When Michael makes the demand of the witnesses, it is as if Dov is demanding it, and the witnesses are *chayav*.

But when the subject matter is a status question — whether Dov is a *kohein* — there is no money to transfer. Dov cannot render Michael the one to whom his *kohein* status is relevant. There is no legal fiction by which Michael acquires Dov's status for purposes of the lawsuit. Therefore the *harsha'ah* does not function, Michael is not treated as Dov, and when he demands the testimony of the witnesses it is not a demand by the *tove'a*, and they are *patur*.

### Harsha'ah Limits

A further constraint on *harsha'ah* applies even in monetary cases. The *Amora'im* of *Nehardea* held that one does not write a *harsha'ah* on *metaltelin* — movable property — once the defendant has denied owing it. The reasoning flows from the legal structure of *harsha'ah*: for the fiction to work, Dov must be able to say plausibly, "I am giving Michael the hundred dollars Reuven owes me." If Reuven has publicly denied the debt, the money is as if inaccessible — one cannot transfer what one has no current grasp of. But if Reuven has not yet denied the debt in court, the money still exists in a legally accessible sense, and Dov may write a *harsha'ah* empowering Michael.

By contrast, if the subject matter is land, the fiction is more easily sustained: the land is visible and present, Dov's ownership claim is tangible, and even after Reuven's denial the court can speak of Dov's land in a concrete sense. Hence *harsha'ah* on land remains valid even after denial.

*Rabbeinu Tam* rules as a matter of practical *halakha* that we do write a *harsha'ah* even on *metaltelin* even after denial. He explains that the reason for the Nehardean restriction was only because such a transfer *mechezi ke-shikra* — looks like a farce, since one appears to be giving something one arguably does not have access to. But *Rabbeinu Tam* holds that we do not in practice concern ourselves with things merely looking like a legal fiction, since the entire device of *harsha'ah* is a legal fiction to begin with. This represents a meaningful *halakhic* adaptation to the commercial realities of the medieval period.

## Money Derivation

### R. Eliezer Proof

The *Gemara* now turns to the *tannaitic* derivations of the requirement that *shevuat edut* must concern monetary subject matter. Four separate approaches are presented.

Rabbi Eliezer derives it through a *gezerah shavah* of the word *o* — the repeated "or" connectives found in both *parashiyot*. In *shevuat edut* the *pasuk* reads *ve-hu ed o ra'ah o yada* — multiple *o*'s. In *shevuat pikadon* the *pasuk* reads *o be-tsumet yad o be-gezel o ashak et amito* — again multiple *o*'s. Since the same grammatical pattern appears in both contexts and *shevuat pikadon* concerns exclusively monetary matters, *ne'emar kan o ve-ne'emar le-halan o mah le-halan eino medaber ela bi-tvi'at mamon af kan eino medaber ela bi-tvi'at mamon* — just as the *pikadon* case speaks only of monetary claims, so too *shevuat edut*.

### Exclusions

The *Gemara* challenges this derivation. The same connective *o* appears in the case of murder — *o be-eivah hikahu o hishlich alav bi-tzdiya* — and murder is obviously not about monetary claims. Should we then learn from murder that *shevuat edut* can apply to non-monetary testimony?

The answer distinguishes the cases: *danim o she-yesh imahem shevuah me-o she-yesh imahem shevuah* — we derive one *shevua* context from another *shevua* context. Both *shevuat edut* and *shevuat pikadon* involve oaths, and they appear adjacent in the Torah. We do not derive from the murder passage, which has nothing to do with oaths.

A second challenge: the connective *o* also appears in the *sotah* passage — *o avar alav ruach kinah* — and *sotah* involves an oath (the waters of *sotah*) yet concerns something entirely non-monetary. Should we then learn that *shevuat edut* applies even non-monetarily? The answer here: *danim o she-yesh imahem shevuah ve-ein imahem kohein* — we compare oath cases that do not involve a *kohein*. The *sotah* case uniquely involves a *kohein* who administers the oath. Therefore *shevuat edut* and *shevuat pikadon* — both oaths not administered by a *kohein* — are compared to each other, not to *sotah*.

### R. Akiva Method

Rabbi Akiva's approach is different. He derives from the phrase at the end of the *shevuat edut* passage — *ve-hayah ki yisham le-achat me-eleh* — that one is *chayav* from "some of these" situations, implying not all. *Yesh me-eleh she-hu chayav ve-yesh me-eleh she-hu patur* — in some cases of this type you are *chayav*, in others *patur*. Rabbi Akiva does not derive the specific content requirement — monetary vs. non-monetary — directly from the *pasuk*; he derives only that not all testimony cases generate a *chiyuv*, and he then rules that the dividing line is monetary versus non-monetary. The *Gemara* will note that this leaves open the question of how we know precisely where to draw the line, since the *pasuk* only tells him that there is a line somewhere.

### R.Y.H. Examples

Rabbi Yose HaGlili takes a fundamentally different approach, deriving the monetary requirement from the phrase *ve-hu ed o ra'ah o yada* — he is a witness, or he saw, or he knew. This phrasing, he argues, encompasses testimony of a certain distinctive character: *edut ha-mitkayemet be-re'iah belo yedi'ah* — testimony that consists of seeing something without knowing its legal significance — and *o be-yedi'ah belo re'iah* — or knowing something without having directly witnessed it. These two categories of testimony, he argues, exist only in monetary cases.

*Re'iah belo yedi'ah* — seeing without knowing — the *Gemara* illustrates as follows: you watched as someone counted out a hundred dollars and handed it to Michael. You witnessed the transaction but do not know whether it was a gift, a repayment, or a loan. I tell you: come to court and testify to what you saw. In the monetary context, your testimony is relevant: Michael may then be pressured to admit that the transaction was a loan. The court can work with testimony about a transaction even without knowing the parties' intent at the time, because subsequent admissions can supply the missing context. In a capital case, by contrast, partial observation without knowledge of legal significance is generally not usable testimony, because courts require objective legal determinations, not testimony that relies on subsequent admission.

*Yedi'ah belo re'iah* — knowing without seeing — is illustrated by: Michael, you admitted to me in front of Charlie and David that you owed me a hundred dollars. I now adjure Charlie and David to come and testify. They did not observe the original transaction; they merely heard Michael's admission. In a monetary case, this constitutes valid testimony — they know about the obligation through Michael's admission even if they never saw the loan. In a capital context, knowledge without direct observation of the act is not valid testimony for the charge itself.

Since both forms of testimony — seeing without knowing, and knowing without seeing — occur only in monetary contexts, *shevuat edut* is thereby limited to those contexts.

### R. Shimon Kal V.C.

The final approach belongs to Rabbi Shimon, who constructs a *kal va-chomer*. He begins with a comparison — somewhat analogous to Rabbi Eliezer's *o-o* link — establishing that *shevuat edut* and *shevuat pikadon* are compared, and that *shevuat pikadon* is monetary. He then builds a *kal va-chomer*: *shevuat pikadon* is broader in scope — it applies to women as it applies to men, *nashim ke-anashim*; to relatives as to non-relatives, *kerovim ke-rechokim*; to those who are otherwise unfit witnesses as to those who are fit, *pesulim ke-kasherim*; and one is *chayav* multiple times for *shevuat pikadon* even outside of *beit din*. And yet, despite all this breadth, *shevuat pikadon* speaks only of monetary matters.

*Shevuat edut*, by contrast, is far more restricted in its application: it does not apply to women as it does to men; it does not apply to relatives as to non-relatives; it does not apply to those who are unfit for testimony; and one is *chayav* only once and only in the context of *beit din*. *Eino din she-lo yehei medaber ela bi-tvi'at mamon* — it stands to reason that this more restricted category of testimony likewise — and indeed all the more so — speaks only of monetary matters. The *kal va-chomer* thus reinforces and derives the same conclusion: the subject matter of *shevuat edut* is limited to monetary claims.

---

---

# Shevuot 34

## Braisah Overview

### Intro & Structure

The daf opens in the middle of a long *braisah* that demonstrates how we know *shvuas ha'eidus* applies exclusively to monetary matters. The relevant verses state simply that he is a witness — *vehu eid o ra'ah o yada* — yet later in Vayikra, a separate *parsha* treats *shvuas hapikadon*, which concerns denying a monetary deposit or obligation owed to another: *o vitshumes yad o vegazel o ashak es amiso*. There the *korban* is an *asham*. The *braisah* draws a link between the two *parshot* and argues: just as *shvuas hapikadon* is entirely about monetary matters, so too *shvuas ha'eidus* is limited to monetary matters.

### O's Approach

The first method of linkage relies on the repeated use of *o* (*o, o, o*) — what the *Gemara* calls *o'in* — appearing in both passages, providing a textual parallel that ties them together.

### Rabbi Akiva

Rabbi Akiva's approach derives from the phrase *achat me'eileh*, which introduces a distinction without specifying its content. He reads this as implying that while the *parsha* governs monetary cases, not all monetary cases are included.

### Rabbi Yose HaGlili

Rabbi Yose HaGlili focuses on the nature of the testimony described in *shvuas ha'eidus* — *vehu eid o ra'ah o yada* — testimony that can be established through knowledge without seeing or through seeing without knowledge. He argues that only monetary cases permit these hybrid forms of testimony, which is why the verse's formulation signals that the entire *parsha* is limited to money.

### Rabbi Shimon

Rabbi Shimon employs a *kal vachomer*: *shvuas hapikadon* has a broader scope of application — it encompasses men and women, those eligible to testify and those who are not — and yet it is limited to monetary matters. *Shvuas ha'eidus*, which has a narrower scope, should certainly be limited to monetary matters as well. It is in the middle of this *drasha* that the daf begins.

---

## Kal Vachomer Fails

### Kal Vachomer Setup

Rabbi Shimon's *kal vachomer* is stated explicitly: if *shvuas hapikadon*, which does not treat women as men, does not treat relatives as non-relatives, does not treat the ineligible as the eligible, and limits liability to a single oath when the demand is made before *beis din* — if despite its narrower scope *shvuas hapikadon* is restricted to monetary matters, then *shvuas ha'eidus*, with its even narrower scope, certainly must be restricted the same way.

### Pikadon Narrower

The *braisah* immediately objects: *mah lapikadon sheken lo asa bo mushba k'nishba*. There are respects in which *shvuas hapikadon* is actually narrower than *shvuas ha'eidus*. First, *shvuas hapikadon* does not apply when the oath is imposed by another party — *mushba* — whereas *shvuas ha'eidus* applies even in such a case, as the Torah describes *v'shomea kol alah*, an oath imposed upon the witness. Second, *u'mezid k'shogeg*: *shvuas hapikadon*, like most *korbanos*, applies only when the violation is unintentional — *b'shogeg* — while *shvuas ha'eidus*, as derived from the absence of the word *v'ne'elam*, applies even when the transgression is willful — *b'mezid*. Since *shvuas hapikadon* is narrower in these respects, one cannot simply assume it is always the broader category from which to derive a *kal vachomer*.

### Edus Narrower

The *braisah* anticipates a counter-objection: *tomar b'edus sheken asa bo mushba k'nishba* — here, by contrast, is where *edus* is broader: it applies even when the oath is imposed, and it applies even in cases of *mezid*. The two categories thus each have domains of greater and lesser scope relative to the other.

### Need Gezeirah Shavah

Since the *kal vachomer* cannot stand — *shvuas hapikadon* is not uniformly broader, rendering the inferential chain invalid — the *braisah* concludes: *talmud lomar techeta techeta l'gezeirah shavah*. A *gezeirah shavah* is required.

---

## Gezeirah Shavah

### Techeta Link

The word *techeta* appears in both relevant passages, providing the verbal link for the *gezeirah shavah*. This connects *shvuas ha'eidus* to *shvuas hapikadon* through shared textual language.

### Two Verses

The two verses in question are Leviticus 5:1 and 5:21. The first, governing *shvuas ha'eidus*, reads: *v'nefesh ki techeta v'shomea kol alah vehu eid o ra'ah o yada im lo yagid v'nasa avono*. The second, governing *shvuas hapikadon*, reads: *v'nefesh ki techeta u'ma'ala ma'al b'Hashem v'kichash b'amiso*. The linkage is not merely the single word *techeta* but the entire opening phrase *v'nefesh ki techeta*, which opens both passages identically. This stands in contrast to the earlier *o'in* approach, which linked the passages through structural parallelism; here the link is substantive and phraseological, and it is this verbal identity that Rabbi Shimon ultimately employs.

---

## Why Not Bitui?

### Challenge to O's

Rabba bar Ulla raises a challenge against the first approach — the linkage via *o'in*. The *Gemara* had established that the *o'in* in *shvuas ha'eidus* parallel those in *shvuas hapikadon*, and that both passages share additional features: both involve a *shevuah*, and neither involves a *kohen* (excluding the case of *sotah*). But Rabba bar Ulla asks: why not link *shvuas ha'eidus* to *shvuas bitui* instead? After all, *shvuas bitui* also uses the disjunctive language and is also a *shevuah* without a *kohen*. And *shvuas bitui* — an oath about future conduct, introduced by *o nefesh ki tishava levatei visfa'taim lehara o lehitiv* — is not limited to monetary matters. If the linkage went to *shvuas bitui*, the conclusion about *shvuas ha'eidus* being restricted to money would not follow.

### More Comparisons

The *Gemara* responds: it is more reasonable to derive from *shvuas hapikadon* — *mistavra mipikadon hava lei lemeilaf* — because these two passages share an additional bond beyond the *o'in* and the *shevuah*: the phrase *nefesh ki techeta*, which appears in both, provides an extra point of comparison not present between *shvuas ha'eidus* and *shvuas bitui*.

### Bitui vs Pikadon

The *Gemara* then entertains a counter-argument in favor of linking to *shvuas bitui*: *adraba mibitui hava lei lemeilaf sheken chatat michatat*. The argument here is not about a shared word but about shared *halakha*: *shvuas ha'eidus* and *shvuas bitui* are literally in the same *parsha*, they share the same category of *korban* — a *chatat oleh veyored*, a sliding-scale sin-offering — and neither involves a *chatat* with a *chomesh*. Thus the thematic and legal affinity between *shvuas ha'eidus* and *shvuas bitui* is substantial. The two sides of the argument can now be laid out: linking to *shvuas hapikadon* offers the *v'nefesh ki techeta* verbal parallel; linking to *shvuas bitui* offers the shared *korban* type and shared *parsha*.

### Pikadon Wins

The *Gemara* resolves the competition by counting points of comparison. In favor of *shvuas hapikadon*: first, the shared phrase *v'nefesh ki techeta*; second, both apply even in cases of *mezid* — neither passage uses *v'ne'elam*, so both are not limited to inadvertent violation; third, both involve a *teviah u'kfirah*, a demand and a denial; and fourth, both are oriented toward past conduct. That gives four substantive points of comparison. Against this, the case for *shvuas bitui* offers three: the shared *chatat* type, the *oleh veyored* form, and the absence of *chomesh*. Since *haneich nefishin* — the *pikadon* side has more points — the linkage goes to *shvuas hapikadon*, and therefore *shvuas ha'eidus* is restricted to monetary matters.

---

## Rabbi Akiva's Limits

### Akiva's Position

Having established the general principle through multiple approaches, the *Gemara* now turns to Rabbi Akiva's specific contribution. Rabbi Akiva's *drasha* reads: *vehaya ki ye'asham le'achat me'eileh* — the verse states that one becomes liable for *one* of these. From this Rabbi Akiva derives that *yeish me'eileh shehu chayav v'yeish me'eileh shehu patur* — there are some cases within this category that incur liability and some that do not. The *braisah's* plain reading is that Rabbi Akiva is offering another proof that the *parsha* concerns money. But the *Gemara* reorients his position: Rabbi Akiva was actually making a narrower point — not merely confirming that the *parsha* is about money, but pointing out to the other *tanna'im* who were busy establishing that principle that *achat me'eileh* signals that not every monetary case is included.

### Land or Knas?

The *Gemara* asks: what is the distinction Rabbi Akiva draws, and where does it emerge from a debate with Rabbi Eliezer? The *Gemara* initially proposes that the debate concerns *edei karka* — testimony relating to land. There is a general principle that one does not take an oath regarding land. The question here is subtler: when witnesses are asked to testify about a claim that has implications for liens on land, does that implicate the land-oath principle? If the witnesses are not swearing about the land itself but about whether they possess certain testimony, it is unclear whether this falls under the *shvuas ha'eidus* framework at all.

### Edei Karka

The *Gemara* proposes that Rabbi Eliezer holds the witnesses are liable — *chayavin* — while Rabbi Akiva holds they are exempt — *patur* — in the case of *mashbia edei karka*. However, the *Gemara* notes that Rabbi Yochanan elsewhere rules that even Rabbi Eliezer would agree that testimony relating to land is exempt — *afilu Rabbi Eliezer patur*. If that is so, then the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva must concern something else: *edei knas*. Witnesses summoned to testify about a penalty — a *knas* — may be exempt according to Rabbi Akiva's reading of *achat me'eileh*, since the *knas* context has features that distance it from the ordinary monetary framework, including the possibility that the liable party could preempt the witnesses by confessing directly and thereby avoiding the *knas* altogether.

---

## Rabbi Yose HaGlili

### Yedia/Reiah Types

Rabbi Yose HaGlili's approach returns to the content of the verse itself: *vehu eid o ra'ah o yada*. He reads the disjunctive formulation — either he saw or he knew — as pointing to a category of testimony that operates even when seeing and knowing come apart. Two distinct sub-cases follow: *yedia belo re'iyah* — knowing without seeing — and *re'iyah belo yedia* — seeing without knowing.

### Monetary Examples

What does *yedia belo re'iyah* look like in a monetary case? The witnesses heard Michael admit that he owes Dov a hundred dollars. They did not see the original loan; their knowledge derives entirely from the admission. In monetary matters, self-admission is legally operative, so such *yedia* suffices to establish the claim. *Re'iyah belo yedia* is actually the more striking case: witnesses saw money counted out from one party to another but do not know what it represented — a loan, a gift, repayment of a prior debt. Rashi explains that this testimony has value in monetary contexts because it may pressure the other party to admit the truth, or, as Tosafot elaborates later in the *Gemara*, because the defendant may have made statements that effectively committed him to a particular interpretation of the event, such that witnesses who corroborate the act itself resolve the dispute in the plaintiff's favor.

### Not Capital

Rabbi Yose HaGlili's point is that this kind of testimony — where seeing and knowing come apart — simply does not arise in capital cases or cases of *malkus*. In those domains, witnesses must have both direct visual observation and knowledge of the legally relevant facts. Since the verse's formulation presupposes testimony of these distinctive hybrid types, it signals that the entire *parsha* concerns monetary matters.

---

## Rav Acha's Camel

### Rav Acha

Rav Pappa asks Abaye whether Rabbi Yose HaGlili's position — that *yedia belo re'iyah* works only in monetary contexts — conflicts with a *braisah* of Rav Acha. That *braisah* states: if a camel was acting wild among other camels — either goring them or, according to one of Rashi's readings, in some other aggressive manner — and a dead camel was found beside it, *b'yaduah she-zeh harago*: it is established knowledge that this camel killed the other, and one may collect damages accordingly. This is a case of *yedia belo re'iyah* in a monetary context. The question is whether the same reasoning could extend to capital cases. The *Gemara* observes: *b'dinei nefashot nami mishkachas lah* — you can construct an analogous case in capital law. And it invokes the story of Rabbi Shimon ben Shatach.

### Rabbi Shimon ben Shatach

The *braisah* records Rabbi Shimon ben Shatach's account, prefaced with the oath-formula *ereh b'nechamah* — may I see the consolation of Jerusalem. He saw a man running after another into a desolate ruin. He ran after them. He found the pursuer holding a sword, blood dripping from it, and the victim thrashing on the ground in his death throes. Rabbi Shimon ben Shatach said: "Wicked one — who killed this man? It is either you or I, and I know it was not I." Yet he could do nothing, because the Torah requires *al pi shenayim eidim o sheloshah eidim yumos ha-meis* — conviction requires two witnesses. He declared that God would exact retribution, and, the *braisah* records, before they left that spot a snake bit the killer and he died. The clear implication of Rabbi Shimon ben Shatach's lament is that had there been a second witness, the circumstantial chain of *yedia belo re'iyah* might have sufficed. This appears to concede that *yedia belo re'iyah* can function in capital cases.

### Concession/Restriction

This is a striking *Gemara*. The *Gemara* seems to concede, at least provisionally, that *yedia belo re'iyah* might work even in capital cases. Tosafot raises the obvious difficulty: where was the *hatra'ah* — the required forewarning? Tosafot answers that perhaps the murderer was a *chaver*, a Torah scholar presumed to know the law and therefore not requiring formal warning. But the deeper problem is that the entire thrust of *shas* is that capital convictions require direct eyewitness observation of the act itself — no inferences, no circumstantial chains, no drawing of conclusions from what was not seen. The case Rav Acha presents involves a monetary dispute about a camel; it does not touch capital law, and it is therefore surprising that the *Gemara* treats it as potentially applicable to *dinei nefashot*. It must be emphasized that this theoretical concession does not reflect the *halakha*. The *Gemara* appears to be making a conditional argument: even granting for the sake of argument that *yedia belo re'iyah* might work in capital cases, there remains a distinction between *dinei mamonot* and *dinei nefashot* — and that distinction is *re'iyah belo yedia*. The *Gemara* pivots: *ela re'iyah belo yedia heichi mishkachas lah?* — you simply cannot construct a case of seeing without knowing in capital law.

---

## Mamonot vs Nefashot

### Critical Facts

Why can't *re'iyah belo yedia* function in capital cases? The *Gemara* explains: *mi lo ba'ei meida im oved kochavim harag o Yisrael harag* — the witnesses must know whether the victim was Jewish or not, since killing a non-Jew does not carry the death penalty. They must also know *im adam treifa harag o shalem harag* — whether the victim was a *treifa*, a person with a life-threatening internal condition, because killing such a person would render the killer technically exempt from execution. Tosafot notes that in practice one might assume the victim was healthy and Jewish — particularly in an insular community where those assumptions are virtually certain — and that explicit testimony about these facts is only required when there is actual reason for doubt. But the principle stands: in capital cases, partial visual testimony that leaves legally critical facts unestablished cannot sustain a conviction.

### Knas Inference

The *Gemara* then asks whether this reasoning applies equally to *knas* cases, and infers that Rabbi Yose HaGlili would hold witnesses about a *knas* exempt — *mashbia ed knas patur*. The logic runs as follows: even if we grant (provisionally) that *yedia belo re'iyah* might work even in capital cases, it is *re'iyah belo yedia* that definitively cannot function there. And *re'iyah belo yedia* fails in *knas* cases for the same reason it fails in capital cases: critical facts remain unknown. The *Gemara* asks: what would the witnesses need to know? *Nochris ba'al o bas Yisrael ba'al* — was the woman involved Jewish or not? *Besula ba'al o be'ula ba'al* — was she a virgin or not? These facts determine whether a *knas* applies at all. Since *re'iyah belo yedia* leaves such facts unresolved, it cannot carry the testimony in *knas* cases either.

### Examples

The *Gemara* accordingly concludes — reading the inference as a statement rather than a question — that Rabbi Yose HaGlili holds *knas* is also excluded from *shvuas ha'eidus*. The distinction that Rabbi Yose HaGlili draws between monetary cases and other domains thus excludes not only capital and *malkus* cases but *knas* cases as well, since *re'iyah belo yedia* cannot do the necessary legal work there.

---

## Monetary Scenarios

### Pillar Scenario

Rav Hamnuna was sitting before Rav Yehuda, who posed the following hypothetical as a kind of examination: "Reuven says to Michael — *maneh maniti lach bifnei ploni u'ploni*, I counted out a hundred dollars to you in front of these two witnesses. The witnesses were standing outside watching through the window — *veha'eidim ro'in oso mibachutz* — and Michael, unaware he was being observed, denied the transaction." What happens when the witnesses are produced in court?

### Hamnuna's Analysis

Rav Hamnuna's response: *ei amar lo hayu devarim me'olam* — if Michael says the entire event never took place, then *huchzak kafran* — Michael is now established as a liar. The witnesses saw the money being counted; Michael denied it happened at all. Rashi reads the consequence as follows: Michael can no longer be believed for purposes of taking a *shvuah*, which may ultimately affect the resolution of the monetary claim.

### Michael Admits

But if Michael says *in shakli v'didi shakli* — yes, you counted out money, and it was simply mine that you were returning to me — then *ki atu edei mai mahani?* — what do the witnesses accomplish? They saw money change hands but they have no idea what it represented. Rav Hamnuna responds: *haimnu ul* — you understand it correctly, come take your seat in the *beit midrash*. The witnesses, in this scenario, do nothing. The *Gemara* thus has not yet satisfactorily explained how *re'iyah belo yedia* genuinely functions in monetary cases.

---

## Credibility Tests

### Location Case

The *Gemara* presents a further case. Someone says to his friend: *maneh maniti lach betzad amud zeh* — I counted out a hundred dollars to you by that pillar. The friend replies: *lo avarti betzad amud zeh* — I was never by that pillar. Witnesses then come forward and testify that they observed him urinating by that very pillar. Rav Yitzchak rules: *huchzak kafran* — he is established as a liar.

### Absolute Denial

Rav Nachman objects: *hai dina parsa'ah hu* — that would be Persian justice, not *halakha*. When Michael said "I wasn't by that pillar," he meant: in the context of the transaction you're describing, I was not there. He did not mean he had never in his life stood near that pillar. The witnesses' testimony about his urinating there is therefore irrelevant to this dispute. The *Gemara* then presents a modified version of the case — *ikha de'amri* — in which Michael explicitly says *lo avarti betzad amud zeh me'olam*: I was never, ever by that pillar. In that version, Rav Nachman agrees: *huchzak kafran*. If Michael made an absolute, global denial of ever having been near that location, witnesses who place him there establish him as a liar.

### Irrelevant Details

Rava challenges even the stricter version: *kol milta dela ramya aleih de'inish avid leih velav adaiteih* — anything that is not of significance to a person, he will do without registering it in his memory. Which pillar one happens to urinate by is entirely irrelevant to most people's lives. Michael could say with full sincerity that he was never at that pillar, not because he is lying, but because passing by that pillar simply did not register. One cannot therefore establish him as a *kafran* based on testimony about a detail he had no reason to track. Rava's objection illustrates the principle: only if the person made a denial about something he would necessarily have noticed and remembered can contradicting witnesses establish his dishonesty.

Tosafot, however, proposes a scenario in which *re'iyah belo yedia* does genuinely function as useful testimony. If Michael had said not merely "I wasn't there" but effectively: "if you can prove it happened, I concede I owe you" — then witnesses who corroborate the act of counting itself resolve the case entirely in the plaintiff's favor without needing to interpret what the money transfer meant. This reading, Tosafot notes, is not explicit in the *Gemara* but provides the most coherent account of why *re'iyah belo yedia* has any legal relevance at all in monetary matters.

---

## Rav Shiman's Kal

### Rav Shiman Setup

Rav Shiman states a direct *kal vachomer*: *chiyuv kan v'chiyuv bepikadon* — there is liability here (*shvuas ha'eidus*) and there is liability in *shvuas hapikadon*. *Shvuas hapikadon* has broader scope, yet it is limited to monetary matters; therefore *shvuas ha'eidus*, which is narrower, is also limited to monetary matters.

### Mocking

*Machu alav bamaarava* — they laughed at this in Eretz Yisrael. The *Gemara* asks: why is this position mockable? The answer: *dekasani mah lipikadon sheken lo asa bo mushba k'nishba mezid k'shogeg* — the *braisah* itself already established that *shvuas hapikadon* is not uniformly broader. There are ways in which *shvuas hapikadon* is narrower: it does not apply when the oath is externally imposed (*mushba*), and it is limited to *shogeg*. Since Rav Shiman's *kal vachomer* assumes *shvuas hapikadon* is the broader category, it was mocked on the grounds that this assumption is demonstrably false.

### Self-Imposed Oath

The *Gemara* then raises a further question: *mushba mipi atzmo b'eidus Rav Shiman minaleh?* — how does Rav Shiman even know that *shvuas ha'eidus* applies when the oath is self-imposed (*nishba*), not merely imposed by another? The verse describes *v'shomea kol alah*, an oath imposed upon the witness. The answer: Rav Shiman derives *nishba* via a straightforward *kal vachomer* — if you are liable when someone else imposes the oath upon you, you are certainly liable when you take it upon yourself. This *kal vachomer* operates internally within *shvuas ha'eidus* itself, and therefore does not require any cross-reference to *shvuas hapikadon*. The asymmetry thus stands: *shvuas ha'eidus* applies to both *mushba* and *nishba* (the latter by *kal vachomer*), while *shvuas hapikadon* applies only to *nishba*; and *shvuas ha'eidus* applies to *mezid* (from the absence of *v'ne'elam*), while *shvuas hapikadon* is limited to *shogeg*. In both respects *shvuas hapikadon* is the narrower category, and Rav Shiman's *kal vachomer* collapses.

---

## Meilah Comparison

### Mezid/Shogeg

Rav Huna intervenes to defend Rav Shiman and explain the mocking more precisely. He notes that the *kal vachomer* objection regarding *mushba k'nishba* is not the real problem — that can be handled by Rav Shiman's internal *kal vachomer*. The point on which the mocking is justified is the *mezid/shogeg* distinction. The question is: why does Rav Shiman assume *shvuas hapikadon* is limited to *shogeg*? After all, *shvuas hapikadon* also does not say *v'ne'elam*. By the same logic used for *shvuas ha'eidus* — absence of *v'ne'elam* implies *mezid* applies — one should conclude *shvuas hapikadon* also applies to *mezid*. Rav Huna answers: *dilma mezid d'lav shogeg b'pikadon mi'me'ilah Rabbi Shimon gamar lah* — Rabbi Shimon derives the restriction of *shvuas hapikadon* to *shogeg* from its comparison to *me'ilah*, the laws of trespass against consecrated property. *Me'ilah* incurs liability only in *shogeg*; since *shvuas hapikadon* is linked to *me'ilah* by the word *u'ma'ala ma'al b'Hashem*, it inherits *me'ilah*'s restriction.
