The word *me'ilah* thus actively limits *pikadon* to *shogeg*, just as the absence of *v'ne'elam* actively extends *shvuas ha'eidus* to *mezid*.

### Meilah Links

Rav Huna then elaborates the points of comparison between *shvuas hapikadon* and *me'ilah* that make this linkage compelling: first, both passages use the word *me'ilah*; second, in both cases the one who sins is deriving personal benefit — the one who denies the *pikadon* is withholding money that belongs to another, and the one who benefits from *hekdesh* is appropriating consecrated property for personal use; third, both incur a *korban* of fixed cost as opposed to a variable one; and fourth, the *korban* in both cases is an *asham* accompanied by a *chomesh*, a penalty of an added fifth. The Torah itself, it is worth noting, employs the word *me'ilah* — trespass — in both contexts: an act of trespass against God by appropriating *hekdesh*, and an act of trespass against God through false swearing about a deposit. The overlap in terminology and consequence is striking and provides a strong basis for the linkage.

### More Points

Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua then arrive from their studies and offer the following assessment: the linkage from *shvuas hapikadon* to *me'ilah* is actually stronger than any alternative linkage one might propose. This counting of points — more points to *me'ilah* than to *eidus* — is what justifies Rabbi Shimon's decision to derive the *shogeg*-only restriction from *me'ilah* rather than concluding that *pikadon* also extends to *mezid* by parallel to *eidus*.

---

## Gezeirah Override

### Gezeirah Impact

The *Gemara* now raises the question that was, according to Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua, the actual reason for the mocking: once Rabbi Shimon ultimately falls back on a *gezeirah shavah* — *techeta techeta* — to establish the link between *shvuas ha'eidus* and *shvuas hapikadon*, why do the prior distinctions matter at all? Normally when a *gezeirah shavah* is accepted, it equalizes the two compared domains and would eliminate any asymmetries between them. Should the *gezeirah shavah* not import *mezid* into *pikadon* and *mushba* into *pikadon* as well? And conversely, should the restrictions of *pikadon* not be reimposed on *eidus*? The mocking was directed precisely at Rabbi Shimon's insistence on maintaining distinctions even after invoking a *gezeirah shavah*.

### Shimon's Stand

The *Gemara* confirms through Rava's testimony that Rabbi Shimon does indeed hold *shvuas hapikadon* is restricted to *shogeg* even after the *gezeirah shavah* is in place. *Man tana shvuat hapikadon lo nitna l'hitkaper b'mezid — Rabbi Shimon hi*. And this generates the question: if the *gezeirah shavah* links the two passages, why does it not extend *mezid* to *pikadon* as well?

### Rava Explains

Rava explains that Rabbi Shimon acknowledges the *gezeirah shavah* resolves certain distinctions. Specifically, the *mushba/nishba* distinction: after the *gezeirah shavah* equalizes the two passages, the *mushba* that applies to *eidus* is imported into *pikadon* as well. Rabbi Shimon concedes this point. But the *mezid/shogeg* distinction is different. The *kal vachomer* and *gezeirah shavah* cannot override an active textual signal. The word *u'ma'ala ma'al* in the *pikadon* passage ties it to *me'ilah*, and *me'ilah* is explicitly *shogeg*-only. This is not a default assumption or an inference from silence — it is a positive linkage that restricts *pikadon* to *shogeg* independent of any comparison to *eidus*.

### Final Resolution

The *Gemara* articulates the final resolution: the absence of *v'ne'elam* in *shvuas ha'eidus* is itself a meaningful textual signal. The word *v'ne'elam* appears in every other parallel context — *shvuas bitui*, *tumas mikdash v'kodashav* — and its systematic absence from *shvuas ha'eidus* is not silence but active communication. It communicates *l'chayav al ha'mezid k'shogeg*: the *mezid* case is explicitly made equivalent to *shogeg* for purposes of liability. This positive signal that *eidus* applies to *mezid* cannot be reversed by the *gezeirah shavah*. Conversely, the word *me'ilah* in the *pikadon* passage provides the positive signal that *pikadon* is limited to *shogeg*; this positive restriction likewise cannot be overridden by the *gezeirah shavah*. The two signals operate in opposite directions and remain in force simultaneously. The result, as Rabbi Shimon holds: *shvuas ha'eidus* applies even in *mezid*, and *shvuas hapikadon* is limited to *shogeg* — even after the *gezeirah shavah* linking the two passages is accepted. The *rabanan* dispute this, holding that the *gezeirah shavah* overrides the *me'ilah* link and extends *pikadon* to *mezid* as well, but Rabbi Shimon insists the word *me'ilah* holds firm.

---

---

# Shevuot 35

## Mashbia Ani Aleichem

### Shevuat HaEdut Intro

We continue the *mishna* from where we left off yesterday, adding new dimensions to the laws of *shevuat ha'edut* — the oath of testimony — which operates primarily in the domain of monetary disputes. The *mishna* presents five distinct cases, each introduced by the formula *mashbia ani aleichem*, "I administer an oath upon you," illustrating the various circumstances under which this oath can or cannot generate liability.

### Promise vs Exchange

The first case: *mashbia ani aleichem im lo tavo'u v'te'iduni she'amar ish ploni liten li matayim zuz v'lo natan* — I place an oath upon you that if you do not come and testify that so-and-so promised to give me two hundred *zuz* and did not give them. The *mishna* rules: *harei elu p'turim*, they are exempt, *she'ein chayavim ela al tvi'at mamon k'pikadon* — liability attaches only to a monetary claim comparable to a deposit, where actual money was exchanged.

As *Rashi* explains in just a few lines: had the witnesses testified, they would not have rendered the other party liable for anything, because he could simply say, "I changed my mind." A mere promise, even one heard by multiple people, creates no binding monetary obligation. This is our first case of *mashbia ani aleichem*.

### Oath Precedence

The second case: *mashbia ani aleichem k'shetid'u li edut shetavo'u v'te'iduni* — I place an oath upon you that when you know testimony for me, you will come and testify. Here the *mishna* rules them exempt *mipnei shekadmah shvuah la'edut* — because the oath preceded the testimony. The proper order requires that one first witness an event and only then be bound by oath regarding it. An oath administered prospectively, before the witnesses have seen anything, is fundamentally out of sequence and generates no liability.

### Synagogue & Specificity

The third case: *amad b'vet haknesset v'amar mashbia ani aleichem she'im atem yod'im li edut shetavo'u v'te'iduni* — he stood in the synagogue and declared: I place an oath upon you that if you know testimony for me, you will come and testify. The *mishna* rules them exempt — and then adds, in what some read as a parenthetical: *ad sheyehe meyuchad lahem*, unless the witnesses are specifically designated.

One might ask why the *mishna* situates this case in the *bet haknesset* specifically. The *bet haknesset* is a place of public assembly, a gathering of the community — and the scenario is precisely that the speaker addresses an undifferentiated crowd. The *gemara* will develop this point further, but the essential problem is already visible: even if witnesses are present in that crowd, addressing a general audience without specifying who the witnesses are is insufficient to bind them.

### Disqualified Witnesses

The fourth case addresses a situation where the plaintiff explicitly designates two individuals — *mashbia ani aleichem, Ploni u'Ploni, im atem yod'im li edut shetavo'u v'te'iduni* — and the two witnesses do in fact know the relevant testimony, yet their testimony is halachically invalid. The *mishna* and the *Tosafot* at the opening of this *daf* recall what was already stated at the beginning of the *perek*: *ed mipi ed*, hearsay testimony, or a situation where one of the witnesses is a relative or otherwise *pasul*, disqualifies the testimony. Furthermore, the principle *edut she'batla miktzatah batla kulah* — testimony that is partially invalid is entirely invalid — applies here as well.

### Messenger & Defendant

The fifth and final case: *shalach b'yad avdo* — he sent the summons via his servant — or where the defendant himself, *ha'nitba*, administered the oath to the witnesses. In both situations the witnesses are exempt, *ad she'yishm'u mipi hatove'a* — unless they hear the oath directly from the plaintiff. The oath must come from the claimant himself; neither an unauthorized agent nor the opposing party can administer it in his stead.

---

## Gezeirah Shavah

### Promise Obligation

The *gemara* now interrogates the first case. Could witnesses ever be liable for failing to testify about a mere promise? The question is: *yachol yehu chayavin?* — might one think they are?

### Shevua Comparison

The *gemara* answers by invoking a *gezeirah shavah*: *talmud lomar techeta techeta*. The word *techeta* appears in two places in *Vayikra* chapter 5 — once in the opening *pasuk* concerning *shevuat ha'edut* (Pasuk 1), and once in the context of *shevuat ha'pikadon*. We compare the two: just as *shevuat ha'pikadon* requires an actual monetary claim — money that was in fact exchanged — so too *shevuat ha'edut* requires an actual monetary claim, *tvi'at mamon*, backed by real exchange. A promise alone, without actual transfer, cannot generate liability.

---

## Order Requirement

### Witness Hearing

The *gemara* addresses the second case with a *baraita*: *mashbiani aleichem k'shetid'u li edut she-tavo'u v'te'iduni — yachol yehu chayavin? Talmud lomar: v'shama kol alah v'hu ed o ra'ah o yada*. The *pasuk* says "and he heard the sound of the oath, and he is a witness, or he saw, or he knew." The *gemara* derives from this that the person must already be a witness at the time the oath reaches him — *mi she-kadma edut li-shvuah v'lo she-kadma shvuah la'edut*. The testimony must precede the oath, not the other way around. One cannot be sworn regarding testimony one has not yet acquired.

---

## Witness Specification

### Samuel's Rule

The *gemara* turns to the third case. *Shmuel* teaches: *afilu ed beineihem* — even if the actual witnesses happen to be standing among the crowd in the *bet haknesset*, the witnesses are still exempt. This might seem obvious, yet the *gemara* explains why it needs to be stated: *de-ka'i pilavei abrai* — one might have thought that since the witnesses are standing right beside the speaker, it is as if he addressed them directly. *Shmuel* therefore teaches that this is not so.

### General vs Specific

The critical distinction is between a general address to the assembled crowd and a specific designation of individuals. Simply declaring "whoever among you knows testimony" — even if the two witnesses are present and know full well that they are the relevant witnesses — does not constitute sufficient designation. Until the plaintiff actually approaches and specifies the witnesses, they are not bound.

### Baraita Distinction

A *baraita* sharpens the distinction further. *Ra'ah si'ah shel bnei adam omdim v'adav beineihem* — if he saw a group of people standing, with his witnesses among them, and said *mashbiani aleichem im atem yode'im li edut she-tavo'u v'te'iduni* — might one think they are liable? The *talmud lomar*: *v'hu ed* — "and he is a witness" — implies that the individual witness must have been specifically designated. Since *lo yiched adav*, he did not specify his witnesses, they are exempt.

However, the *baraita* continues: *yachol afilu amar kol ha-omdim kan* — what if he said "all who are standing here"? In that case, *harei yiched adav* — he has in effect specified his witnesses, because he designated everyone present. Even though this is not highly specific — it is "all of you here" rather than calling out names — it is nonetheless sufficient to constitute designation. The line between general and specific address, then, is not merely about naming individuals but about whether the language clearly embraces the witnesses as a defined, identified group.

---

## Valid Testimony

### Hearsay & Disqualificati…

Moving to the fourth case, the *gemara* presents the *baraita*: *amar l'shnayim mashbia ani aleichem Ploni u'Ploni im atem yode'im li edut she-tavo'u v'te'iduni* — and they do know testimony, but their testimony is either *ed mipi ed*, hearsay, or one of them is a relative or otherwise *pasul*. Might one think they are liable? The *talmud lomar*: *im lo yagid venasa avono*.

### Capable Witnesses

The verse says: "if he does not speak, he shall bear his iniquity." The *gemara* derives: *b're'uyim lehagada hakasuv medabeir* — the text speaks only of those who are capable of giving valid testimony. A witness whose testimony is inherently disqualified — whether because it is hearsay, or because he is a relative, or because he is *pasul* for another reason — is not within the category of persons the verse addresses. Such witnesses are therefore exempt.

---

## Messenger Authorization

### Servant & Defendant

The *gemara* now addresses the fifth case. *Tanu rabbanan*: if one sent the oath *b'yad avdo* — through his servant without authorization — or if *ha'nitba*, the defendant, administered the oath to the witnesses saying *mashbiani aleichem she'im atem yode'im lo edut she-tavo'u v'te'idu*, might one think they are liable? The *talmud lomar*: *im lo yagid venasa avono*.

### Double Lo Interpretation

The *gemara* asks: *mai talmuda?* How exactly does this *pasuk* teach us about the requirement of direct address by the proper party? *Amar Rabbi Elazar*: the word in the *Torah* appears spelled with both a *vav* and an *alef* — that is, both *lo* (to him) and *lo* (not) are simultaneously present in the written text. Reading it as *im lo lo yagid* — "if to *him* he does not say it" — teaches that liability arises specifically when the oath was not delivered to the witness by the one to whom the witness is obligated to speak. If someone else, an unauthorized party, administered the oath, the binding relationship between the witness and the person owed testimony is not established.

### Plaintiff Authority

The requirement, then, is that the plaintiff himself — *ha'tove'a* — administer the oath. This is not merely a technical formality. The *pasuk* is structured around the relationship between the witness and the party who has standing to demand testimony. A servant without *harsha'a*, without formal power of attorney, has no such standing. Neither does the defendant: the *nitba* cannot place the witnesses under oath on behalf of the *tove'a*. It is worth noting that the exclusion of a servant is not absolute — had the servant come with proper *harsha'a*, the situation would be different. But absent authorization, neither an agent nor the opposing party can fulfill what the *Torah* requires of the plaintiff himself.

---

## Oath Language

### Binding Words

The *mishna* now shifts to a closely related topic: the precise language of an oath — what words are binding, and what words are not. The *mishna* states: *mashbia, metzaveh, osrechem — harei elu chayavin*. If one uses any of these three formulas — I administer an oath upon you, I command you, I forbid you — the witnesses are liable should they deny their testimony.

### Non-Binding Phrases

By contrast, *bashamayim uva'aretz — harei elu peturin*. Invoking heaven and earth does not constitute a binding oath.

### God's Names

The *mishna* then lists the divine names and titles that do render an oath binding: *alef-dalet* (the name *Adon*), *yud-heh* (the divine name), *Shaddai*, *Tzva'ot*, *Chanun veRachum*, *Erech Apayim*, *Rav Chesed* — and all *kinuyim*, all appellations. Invoking any of these, *harei elu chayavin*. This immediately raises a question the *gemara* will take up: *alef-dalet*, the word *adon*, is an ordinary word in Hebrew — one can say *adon* in a grocery store and simply mean "sir." The question of when this word constitutes invocation of God's name and when it is mundane will require further analysis.

---

## Curses & Names

### Cursing Dispute

Since we are dealing with the power of God's names in oaths, the *mishna* addresses an adjacent question: cursing using God's name. *Ha'mikalel bekulam chayav, divrei Rabbi Meir; ve'Chachamim potrin* — one who curses using all of these names is liable according to *Rabbi Meir*, while the *Chachamim* exempt him. The case at issue is whether the *kinuyim* and divine attributes, not just the explicit names, render a curse actionable.

### Self & Family Cursing

The *mishna* continues: *ha'mikalel aviv ve'imo bekulam chayav divrei Rabbi Meir, ve'Chachamim potrin* — if one curses his father or mother using all of these names, *Rabbi Meir* holds him liable and *Chachamim* exempt. And: *ha'mikalel atzmo ve'chavero be'chulan over be'lo ta'aseh* — one who curses himself or his fellow transgresses a prohibition in all cases. The *gemara* will supply the relevant scriptural source, drawn from the *klalot* of *Ki Tavo* (Devarim 28:22): *yakecha Hashem Elohim* — and by extension: *al yakecha, ve'yivarechecha, ve'yeitiv lach* — whether the formulation is a direct curse or its inverse, *Rabbi Meir* holds one liable, while *Chachamim* exempt.

---

## Mashbia Formula

### Rav Yehuda Formula

The *gemara* now probes the *mishna*'s opening words — *mashbia ani aleichem, metzaveh ani aleichem, osrechem* — asking what exactly is being said. *Amar Rav Yehuda*: this is what the formula means: I administer an oath upon you in the manner of the oath spoken in the *Torah*; I command you in the manner of the command spoken in the *Torah*; I forbid you in the manner of the prohibition spoken in the *Torah*. According to *Rav Yehuda*, each formulation is understood as a reference to a specific category in the *Torah*.

### Abaye's Correction

*Abaye* challenges this. He points to a *baraita* in which *Rabbi Chiya* adds a fourth term — *kovelachem*, I bind you, from the root *kevel*, a chain or rope. The question is: *ve'hai kovel be'Oraita michtiv?* — where does *kovel* appear in the *Torah* as a binding formula? Since no such term appears in the *Torah*, *Rav Yehuda*'s framework — that each word points to its counterpart in the *Torah* — cannot accommodate *Rabbi Chiya*'s addition.

*Abaye* therefore reframes the entire formula: *mashbia ani aleichem bishvu'ah, metzaveh ani aleichem bishvu'ah, oserchem ani bishvu'ah, kovel ani bishvu'ah* — in each case, the operative word is *shvu'ah*, and the other terms — commandment, prohibition, binding — all qualify as invocations of oath-power. The witnesses are liable in all these formulations because in each case a *shvu'ah* is being administered. Whether this fully resolves the analytical difficulty is another question, but the practical conclusion is clear: if the word *shvu'ah* underlies any of these formulas, the witnesses are bound.

---

## Erasable Names

### Names vs Descriptions

The *mishna* listed both explicit divine names and *kinuyim* — appellations such as *Chanun veRachum* — as names that bind an oath. The *gemara* now challenges this by citing a contradiction: *yesh shemot she'nimchakim ve'yesh shemot she'ein nimchakim* — some names may be erased, and others may not. The *gemara* is thus not merely asking whether *Chanun veRachum* is a name or a description, but more precisely: what may be erased from a sacred text, and what must be preserved?

### Unerasable List

The *baraita* provides the definitive list of names that may not be erased: *El, Elohecha, Elohim, Eloheichem, Ehyeh asher Ehyeh, alef-dalet, yud-heh, Shaddai, Tzva'ot — harei elu ein nimchakim*. This list reflects the *halacha* as we observe it to this day.

### Erasable List

By contrast, the descriptive attributes — *ha'gadol, ha'gibor, ha'nora, ha'adir, ve'ha'chazak, ve'ha'amitz, ve'ha'izuz, Chanun, veRachum, Erech Apayim, veRav Chesed* — these may all be erased, *harei elu nimchakim*, because they describe qualities rather than name the divine essence.

*Abaye* explains: when the *mishna* includes *Chanun veRachum* among the binding names, it means *be'mi shehu chanun, be'mi shehu rachum* — invoking "He who is gracious, He who is compassionate," understood as pointing to God. *Rava* immediately presses: if that is the logic, then *bashamayim uva'aretz* — "by heaven and earth" — should also be understood as invoking "He whose heaven and earth it is," and should likewise be binding. The *gemara* distinguishes: *Chanun veRachum* can refer to nothing other than God — nothing else is called gracious and compassionate in this sense — and so the reference is unambiguous. Heaven and earth, however, exist as independent entities in their own right; one might construe an oath "by heaven and earth" as referring to those entities rather than to their Creator. Therefore *bashamayim uva'aretz* remains exempt.

### Heaven & Earth

This distinction might strike one as somewhat forced — everything in existence belongs to God, and it borders on a kind of conceptual heresy to treat heaven and earth as standing independently of their Creator. Yet the *halacha* draws this line: the concern is with how a speaker might be understood, and since heaven and earth can be conceived as independent referents, an oath invoking them is not sufficiently anchored to the divine name to be binding.

---

## Letter Combinations

### Alef-Lamed, Yud-Hey

A *baraita* addresses written letters: *katav alef-lamed me'Elohim, yud-heh me'Hashem — harei ze eino nimchak*. If one writes the letters *alef-lamed* with the intention of writing God's name, or *yud-heh* with the intention of writing the divine name, that text may not be erased. The key qualifier is intent. One might note that *alef-lamed* appears constantly in ordinary Hebrew — *ani holech el ha'cheder* — and *yud-heh* begins many names entirely unrelated to God. The ruling therefore is specifically conditioned on the writer's intention to inscribe a divine name.

### Shin-Dalet, Alef-Dalet

The *baraita* continues: *shin-dalet me'Shaddai, alef-dalet me'Adonai, tzadi-beit me'Tzva'ot*. Here the situation is somewhat different. *Alef-lamed* and *yud-heh* are themselves recognized divine names, which is why intent alone is decisive. But *shin-dalet* standing alone spells *sheid* — a demon — which is decidedly not a divine name. Similarly, *alef-dalet* alone means *eid* — as in *ve'eid ya'aleh min ha'aretz* — a vapor or mist, an entirely mundane word. The partial letters thus carry their own independent non-divine meanings, which makes the question of intent even more pointed in these cases.

### Tzvaot Dependency

*Rabbi Yosei* goes further: even the complete word *Tzva'ot* in its entirety may be erased, *kulo nimchak*, because the word *Tzva'ot* acquired its divine association only through its connection to Israel: *shene'emar ve'hotzeiti et tzivotai et ammi Benei Yisrael me'eretz Mitzrayim* (Shemot). The *armies* in question are the armies of Israel; the divine name is therefore contingent on that context and does not stand as an independent divine appellation. *Shmuel*, however, rules that *ein halacha ke'Rabbi Yosei* — the law does not follow *Rabbi Yosei* — without elaboration, and so we do not accept this position.

---

## Name Affixes

### Prefixes Erasable

The *gemara* addresses prepositions and other letters attached to God's name: *kol ha'tefel la'Shem bein milfanav uvein mil'acharav harei zeh nimchak* — anything appended to God's name, whether before it or after it, may be erased. The examples of prefixes: *la'Shem* — the *lamed* may be erased; *ba'Shem* — the *beit* may be erased; *ve'Hashem* — the *vav* may be erased; *me'Hashem* — the *mem* may be erased; *she'Hashem* — the *shin* may be erased; *ha'Shem* — the *heh* may be erased; *ke'Hashem* — the *kaf* may be erased. The prefix is grammatically attached but remains external to the name itself.

### Suffixes Erasable

Similarly for suffixes: *Eloheinu* — the *nu* may be erased; *Eloheihem* — the *hem* may be erased; *Eloheichem* — the *chem* may be erased. The possessive suffix is likewise external to the divine name proper.

### Suffix Sanctity

However, *acherim omrim le'acharav eino nimchak shekevar kidsho ha'Shem* — others say that what follows God's name may not be erased, because God's name has already sanctified it. And *Rav Huna* rules: *halacha ka'acherim* — the law follows this anonymous opinion. It is worth noting that the *gemara* does not identify *acherim* by name here, and a comment is made that this is one of the places where *Rabbi Meir*'s opinions were attributed to *acherim* following a dispute with *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel*, as discussed in *Horayot*.

---

## Abraham & God's Names

### Abraham Overview

The *gemara* now embarks on a sustained analysis of instances in *Tanakh* where God's name appears in a context that could be read as referring either to God or to a human figure. The *siman* for this series of passages is: *Avraham, deLotia, leNavot, beGivat Binyamin, Shlomo, Daniel*. The first principle: *kol shemot ha'amurim ba'Torah be'Avraham kodesh, chutz mizeh she'hu chol* — all the divine names that appear in the *Torah* in the context of Avraham are *kodesh*, sacred, except for one instance which is *chol*, mundane.

### Adonim Ambiguity

That one case is found in the opening of *Vayera*: the word that in many texts appears spelled *yud-yud* — indicating *Hashem* — but which in the *Torah* itself reads *alef-dalet-nun-yud*, in the plural: *Adonim*, my masters. The context is *im na matzati chein be'einecha* — "if I have found favor in your eyes." This is the moment when Avraham encounters the three angels. Grammatically, the word is plural — *my masters*, a perfectly ordinary Hebrew honorific, the kind one might use addressing a group of gentlemen. And yet the suffix *einecha* — "your eyes" — is singular. The sentence begins in the plural and resolves into the singular. This grammatical oscillation between plural address and singular reference is striking.

One might note that this kind of shift is in fact common throughout the *Torah* — a plural entity is addressed in the singular or vice versa, sometimes because of the unity of the group, sometimes because the speaker turns to address the chief of a delegation. The classic *Talmudic* example here — that Avraham turns to address the most significant of the three visitors — is one reading, but the grammatical phenomenon itself appears widely in biblical literature.

### Abraham Interpretation

*Chanina ben achi Rabbi Yehoshua* and *Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah* in the name of *Rabbi Elazar HaModa'i* hold that even this instance is *kodesh* — Avraham was not addressing the angels but speaking to God Himself. This reading aligns with the famous teaching: *amar Rav Yehudah amar Rav, gedolah hachnasat orchim yoter mehakbalat pnei ha'Shechinah* — hospitality toward guests is greater than receiving the *Shechinah*. That teaching depends on understanding that Avraham was in the midst of a divine encounter when the three men arrived, and that he said to God: wait for me while I attend to these guests. The *gemara* therefore notes: *keman azlah* — this teaching goes according to *Chanina* and *Rabbi Elazar*, who read the word as addressed to God. *Keman ke'oto hazug* — just like that pair of Sages.

---

## Lot's Address

### Lot Overview

*Kol shemot ha'amurim beLot chol, chutz mizeh she'hu kodesh* — all the divine names that appear in Lot's narrative are *chol*, mundane, except for one instance which is *kodesh*. In Lot's story, the names generally refer to the angels or to Lot's human interlocutors.

### Lot Escape

The one *kodesh* instance: *vayomer Lot aleihem, al na Adonai, hineh na matza avdecha chein be'einecha* (Bereshit 19:18). The angels have told Lot to flee to the mountain, but Lot demurs and requests to escape to a nearby city instead. The opening of the verse seems to indicate he is addressing the angels — *vayomer Lot aleihem*, he said to them — and yet the *gemara* rules this instance *kodesh*. The explanation: *mi sheyesh beyado lehamit ulehachayot zeh haKadosh Baruch Hu* — the one who has the power to give life and to take it is God alone. Since Lot is appealing to the power to save him, he must be addressing God, not an angel. The word *aleihem* is itself a difficulty the *gemara* does not fully dissolve — but based on the content of Lot's appeal, the *gemara* reads the name as directed to God.

---

## Navot & Micah

### Navot Sacred

*Kol shemot ha'amurim beNavot kodesh, beMicha chol* — all the names in the Navot story (*Melachim Aleph*) are *kodesh*, while the names in the story of *Micha* (the figure from *Shoftim*) are *chol*. *Micha* built a private temple and priestly garments in competition with the legitimate service — a figure whose acts were sinful — and in that narrative the names refer to human or contextual usage. By contrast, the names in the story of *Navot HaYizre'eli*, whose vineyard Achav sought to seize, are all sacred.

*Rabbi Eliezer* adds a refinement for the case of *Micha*: *beNavot kodesh; beMicha yesh mehem chol veyesh mehem kodesh — alef-lamed chol, yud-heh kodesh*. In *Micha*'s narrative, *alef-lamed* is mundane while *yud-heh* is sacred. The one exception where *alef-lamed* in *Micha*'s story would be *kodesh* is the phrase *kol yemei heyot beit ha'elohim be'shilo* — "all the days that the house of God was in Shilo" — because here the reference is to the *Mishkan* at Shilo, an unambiguously sacred context.

### Gibeah Dispute

The *gemara* introduces the dispute between *Rabbi Eliezer* and *Rabbi Yehoshua* regarding the narrative of *Givat Binyamin* (*Shoftim* 20 — the tragic story of *pilegesh be'giv'ah*, where a concubine was brutalized, the dismembered portions sent to the twelve tribes, and a devastating civil war erupted between Israel and the tribe of Binyamin). *Rabbi Eliezer* says the names in this passage are *chol*; *Rabbi Yehoshua* says they are *kodesh*. *Rabbi Eliezer* presses *Rabbi Yehoshua*: *vechi mavtiach ve'eino oseh?* — would God promise and not fulfill? If the names are *kodesh*, they represent divine guarantees — and those guarantees were apparently not honored in the early battles. *Rabbi Yehoshua* responds: *mah she'hivtiach asah* — what He promised, He did. The people, however, did not ask the right questions.

---

## Gibeah Promise

### Eliezer: Mundane

*Rabbi Eliezer*'s position is that the names in the *Givat Binyamin* narrative are *chol* — mundane — because the failures of the early campaigns suggest that no genuine divine promise was in effect. To call these names *kodesh* would imply that God promised victory and then withheld it, which *Rabbi Eliezer* finds untenable.

### Yehoshua: Sacred

*Rabbi Yehoshua* counters that the names are indeed *kodesh*, and that the problem lay not with God but with the people. *Ve'hem lo bachan im lintoach o lenatzeach* — they did not properly inquire whether they would emerge victorious. They went out to battle without asking the right question.

### Three Battles

The proof: *be'acharonah she'bachanu hiskimu al yadam* — in the final campaign, when they inquired properly, the answer came. The verse (*Shoftim* 20): *u'Pinchas ben Elazar ben Aharon ha'kohen omed lefanav ba'yamim ha'hem lemor: ha'osif od latzet la'milchamah im Binyamin achi im echdal* — Pinchas son of Elazar son of Aharon the priest stood before God in those days and asked: shall we continue to go out to battle against Binyamin our brother, or shall we desist? This was a complete and proper inquiry through the *Urim veTumim*, and a complete answer came. Only in this third campaign, when the question was properly formulated and directed through the high priest, did God's response align with the outcome. Therefore the names in the passage are *kodesh* — they reflect genuine divine engagement, contingent on proper human inquiry.

---

## Shlomo & Names

### Shlomo Overview

*Kol Shlomo ha'amurim be'Shir ha'Shirim kodesh, shir le'mi she'ha'shalom shelo* — every instance of *Shlomo* in *Shir ha'Shirim* is *kodesh*, a song to the One to whom peace belongs, since *Shalom* is one of the names of God and *Shlomo* contains that name. One exception: *karmi sheli lefanai, ha'elef lecha Shlomo* — my vineyard is before me, the thousand is yours, *Shlomo*. That refers specifically to King Shlomo, and is *chol*.

The *gemara* also considers *ve'yesh omrim af zeh chol*: the verse *hineh mitato she'lishomo shishim* — behold the bed of *Shlomo*, sixty — might also be *chol* according to some.

### One-Sixth Rule

This discussion opens onto *Shmuel*'s ruling: *malchuta d'katla chad mi'shita b'alma lo mi'ansha* — a kingdom that takes one-sixth does not incur divine punishment. The proportion of a thousand to *Shlomo* and two hundred to the *notrim*, the guards who watch the fruit, is understood through this arithmetic: the two hundred plus the thousand total twelve hundred, and two hundred is one-sixth of twelve hundred. A kingdom may legitimately claim one-sixth of its subjects' productivity without transgressing.

The *gemara* also offers an alternative reading: the thousand goes to the heavenly kingdom, *malchuta d'rakia*, and the two hundred to the earthly kingdom, *malchuta d'ara*, with the *notrim* — the guardians — representing earthly governance. *Shmuel* aligns with *yesh omrim* on this question. The precise interplay between *Tanna Kamma* and *yesh omrim* — whether one *pasuk* or two are *chol*, and how to account for the numbers — remains in some tension, but *Shmuel*'s ruling orients us toward the *yesh omrim* position.

---

## Daniel & Malchim

### Daniel Mundane

*Kol malchaya ha'amurim beDaniel chol* — most instances of *malka* (king) in *Daniel* are *chol*, referring to Nevuchadnezzar or other earthly rulers.

### Daniel Sacred

One exception is *kodesh*: *ant malka, melech malchaya, di elah shmaya, malchuta chasna ve'takpa ve'ykara yehav lach* — you, O king, king of kings, to whom the God of heaven has given kingdom, power, might, and glory. In this passage Daniel praises — but the object of the deepest praise is God, not the human king, and *yesh omrim* would extend this status to an additional verse.

### Ambiguous Address

That additional verse: *mari chalma l'sanach u'fishreh l'arach* — my master, let the dream be for your enemies and its interpretation for your adversaries. *Yesh omrim* say this too is *kodesh* — Daniel was addressing God. The difficulty with reading it as addressed to Nevuchadnezzar is: *sinata mai ninhu?* — who would be Nevuchadnezzar's enemies? If Daniel were speaking to Nevuchadnezzar, he would be saying that the terrible dream should befall Nevuchadnezzar's enemies — which would be Israel. *Tanna Kamma* responds: Nevuchadnezzar had many enemies among the other nations; being an enemy of Nevuchadnezzar does not necessarily identify one as Israel. Therefore, the verse can plausibly be read as addressed to Nevuchadnezzar, and the word *malka* there remains *chol* according to the *Tanna Kamma*. *Yesh omrim* disagree and hold it is *kodesh*. The passage thus closes in the familiar mode of the *gemara* — an ambiguity preserved, two legitimate readings held in tension, the ruling to be determined elsewhere.

---

---

# Shevuot 36

## Shvuat Ha'edut Basics

### Oath Language & God's Na…

We begin at the bottom of 35b, just before the lines widen and the double dots mark the new sugya. The topic at hand is *shvuat ha'edut*: what language is required, and what constitutes a valid *shvua*? The *Mishnah* had mentioned formulas such as *mashbia ani aleichem* and *metzaveh ani aleichem*, which might have suggested that no explicit *shvua* language is needed at all. The *Gemara*, however, clarifies that these phrases are shorthand for *metzaveh ani aleichem bishvua* — some keyword of *shvua* is indeed required. This was established earlier in the tractate when treating *shvuat bitui* as well: there are synonyms that function as *shvua* language, but some form of oath terminology is necessary.

The *Mishnah* further teaches that one must invoke God's name — though not necessarily the *shem Havayah* (the four-letter name *Yud-Kei-Vav-Kei*). Any of the divine names will suffice: *Aleph-Daled-Nun-Yod*, *Tzevaot*, and so forth. This requirement opens an extended *Gemara* discussion about which names of God are sufficiently sacred to trigger the prohibition against erasure, and related questions. But its relevance to our *sugya* is fundamental: it is here, finally, that the *Gemara* directly addresses the question raised as far back as the beginning of the *masechet* — must God's name form part of a *shvua*, whether implicitly or explicitly?

### Sotah Parallels

The *Gemara* begins with a challenge. The *Mishnah* states that one is *chayav* with any *kinnui* — any euphemistic or substitute name of God. But a *Baraita* raises the following: by the *Sotah*, the verse reads *veyiten Hashem otach le'alah velishvua* ("may God make you a curse and an oath"). Yet another verse had already stated *vehishbia hakohen et ha'ishah bishvuat ha'alah* ("the *kohen* adjured the woman with the oath of the curse"). Why then does the text repeat the words *alah* and *shvua*, and even invoke God's name explicitly?

The answer given is that the repetition in the *Sotah* passage comes to teach us something about *shvuat ha'edut*. In the passage governing *shvuat ha'edut*, the Torah says only *veshama kol alah* — "and he will hear the sound of a curse." Notice that the word *shvua* never appears there at all. The *Gemara* therefore constructs a link: *ne'emar kan alah vene'emar lehalan alah* — the word *alah* appears here (in *shvuat ha'edut*) and there (in *Sotah*). Just as by *Sotah* the *alah* operates within a *shvuat ha'alah* — a combined oath-curse — so too here the *alah* is a form of *shvua*. And furthermore: just as by *Sotah* the formulation invokes *shem Hashem*, so too by *shvuat ha'edut* one must invoke God's name. These are the two foundational components of *shvuat ha'edut*, and neither one appears explicitly in the verse; both are derived from the connection to *Sotah*.

## Sotah Derivation

### Rabbi Chanina bar Idi

The resolution to the tension between the *Baraita* (which seems to require the explicit *shem Havayah*) and the *Mishnah* (which permits any *kinnui*) is provided by Abaye: *ha Rabbi Chanina bar Idi, ha Rabbanan* — this is a dispute between *Tannaim*. Rabbi Chanina bar Idi is the author of the position requiring *shem Havayah*, while the anonymous *Rabbanan* are the authors of the *Mishnah*'s ruling permitting a *kinnui*.

A *Baraita* is then cited that elaborates Rabbi Chanina bar Idi's position. His argument is structured around a series of parallels: since the Torah sometimes commands the taking of an oath (as in *shvuat Hashem tihiyeh bein shneihem*) and sometimes prohibits it (*lo tishavu bishmi lashaker*), and similarly sometimes commands the pronouncement of a curse (as by *Sotah*, *veyiten Hashem otach le'alah velishvua*) and sometimes prohibits cursing (*lo tekalel cheresh*, *Elohim lo tekalel*), the internal logic follows: just as the mandated oath is with God's name, so too the prohibited oath is with God's name; and just as cursing with God's name is sometimes required (by *Sotah*: *yitein Hashem otach le'alah*), so too the prohibition against cursing invokes God's name. The invocation of God in the oath context, and in the curse context, is treated as symmetric. 

It is worth noting — and this is somewhat ironic — that the explicit prohibition against a false *shvua* is stated with God's name more directly than the affirmative requirement to take one: *lo tishavu bishmi lashaker* and *lo tisa et shem Hashem Elokecha lashav* are quite explicit. But the structure of Rabbi Chanina bar Idi's argument works in both directions. The key point is that his derivation from *Sotah* is what commits him to requiring *shem Havayah* specifically — and that is why the *Mishnah*'s permission of a *kinnui* reflects a different view.

### Rabbis' Position

The *Gemara* now turns to the *Rabbanan* and presses the question: if the *Rabbanan* accept the *gzerah shava* connecting *shvuat ha'edut* to *Sotah*, then they should arrive at the same conclusion as Rabbi Chanina bar Idi — that the *shem ha-meyuchad* is required. But if they do not accept the *gzerah shava*, then they have no source at all to tell them that the *alah* in *veshama kol alah* is even a *shvua*. The verse says only "curse," not oath. So make up your mind: either accept the *Sotah* link with its full consequences (including *shem Havayah*), or abandon the *Sotah* link entirely — in which case where does the requirement of *shvua* come from at all?

The *Gemara* answers: *nafka lehu mide-tanya* — the *Rabbanan* derive their position from a *Baraita*, and their method is distinct from a *gzerah shava*. They do not make a formal hermeneutical link to *Sotah*; rather, they look at the word *alah* as biblical scholars examining usage. They ask: what does the word *alah* mean? Looking at the *Sotah* passage, where it says *shvuat ha'alah*, they observe that *alah* appears in the context of an oath. From this they conclude — not via *gzerah shava* but simply as a matter of semantic understanding — that *alah* is *lashon shvua*, oath-language.

### Word Meaning vs. Gzerah

The *Baraita* makes this explicit: *ein alah ela lashon shevuah* — the word *alah* simply means *shvua*. And the proof: *vehen hu omer vehishbia hakohen et ha'ishah bishvuat ha'alah* — the *kohen* adjures the woman with the *shvuat ha'alah*. This is not a *gzerah shava* importing all the laws of one passage into another; it is merely reading the word *alah* in its context and discerning its meaning. Because this is semantic derivation rather than formal analogy, the *Rabbanan* do not also import the requirement of *shem ha-meyuchad*. The connection to *Sotah* tells them only what the word means — not that all conditions of the *Sotah* passage apply.

This raises an immediate and striking question: if the *Rabbanan* do not learn from *Sotah* through *gzerah shava* and do not import *shem Havayah*, then how do they know that any reference to God is required at all? The *Mishnah* after all permits a *kinnui* — *bimi she-shmo rachum*, *bimi she-shmo chanun* — but it still requires some invocation of the divine. Where does even that minimal requirement come from?

No *Rishon* directly addresses this question, and the *Gemara* itself notably does not ask it. That silence is itself significant. The implication seems to be that a *shvua*, by its very definition, is an act of calling upon God as witness. God's name is always implicit or explicit in a *shvua* — that is what the word *shvua* means. Once we have established via semantic analysis that *alah* is *lashon shvua*, we have also imported the inherent structure of a *shvua*, which necessarily involves some invocation of God. There is no need for an explicit verse to establish this, because it follows from the nature of the act itself. This is a theme that runs back to the very beginning of the *masechet*: the *Gemara* has consistently treated reference to God as intrinsic to *shvua*-language, never pausing to derive it as if it were some additional external requirement.

This is precisely where the Rambam and the Ra'avad diverge — a dispute mentioned earlier in the tractate and relevant here. The Rambam holds explicitly that no consequences of a *shvua* — no *korban*, no *lav* — apply without some reference to God's name; it need not be *shem Havayah*, but God must be invoked. The Ra'avad disagrees and holds that even without invoking God, a *shvua* can function analogously to a *neder*: it creates a binding status, and violating it would transgress *lo yachel dvaro* — not *lo tishavu bishmi lashaker* or *lo tisa et shem Hashem Elokecha lashav*, since those are specifically about *shem HaShem* — but a general obligation of not profaning one's word. The Ra'avad does concede, however, that in cases like *shvuat ha'edut* and *shvuat pikadon*, the relevant prohibitions are specifically tied to God's name and do require its invocation.

For the *Rabbanan* of our *Mishnah*, then: they require *shvua* and implicitly some reference to God — not through any explicit verse, but because that is what a *shvua* is — but they do not require *shem Havayah* specifically, since they reject the full *gzerah shava* to *Sotah*.

## Alah vs. Shvua

### Veshama Kol Alah

Having established where each view derives its requirements, the *Gemara* turns to a deeper question embedded in the text. The *Baraita* had said that *alah* means *shvua*, and it cited the *Sotah* verse *shvuat ha'alah* as evidence. But the *Gemara* now objects: *hatam shevuat ha'alah ketiv* — by *Sotah* it says the *shvua* of the *alah*. That means they are combined: it is a curse that occurs within the context of an oath. That does not demonstrate that the word *alah* by itself means *shvua*; it demonstrates that the two are joined. So how does one know that an *alah* without a *shvua* constitutes a *shvuat ha'edut*, or that a *shvua* without an *alah* constitutes one?

The *Gemara* answers with a more careful reading of the verse *veshama kol alah*. The word *kol* — "sound" or "voice" — is the key. Had the Torah wished to say only "he heard a curse," it could have said *veshama alah*. The additional word *kol* allows for a double reading: *veshama alah* — he heard a curse; *veshama kol* — he heard a voice, i.e., a *shvua* (since a *shvua* is something spoken and heard). The verse is thereby read as addressing two separate possibilities: either an *alah* alone, or a *kol* — a spoken oath — alone. Either one is sufficient to create liability for *shvuat ha'edut*.

This is a significant halakhic point. All along the discussion has used the word *shvua*, but now the *Gemara* is making explicit what was implicit in the *Mishnah*: a *shvua* is not strictly necessary for *shvuat ha'edut*. An *alah* — a pure curse, without any oath — can also suffice. If someone says to a witness, "May God curse you and bring plague on your house if you know testimony and do not come to testify," and the witness falsely denies knowing any testimony, that person brings a *korban*. This is the *Mishnah*'s case of *yakecha Hashem Elokeinu v'chen yakecha Elokeim* — "may God smite you" — which the *Mishnah* itself identifies as the *alah haketuvah baTorah*. One need not combine *shvua* and *alah*; either suffices on its own.

### Rabbi Abahu's Approach

Rabbi Abahu then provides an independent source for the equivalence of *alah* and *shvua*: *vayavei oto be'alah* — he brought him into the curse — and a parallel verse that describes the same act using the language of adjuration. The two verses, describing a single event, use the words *alah* and *shvua* interchangeably. This is a clean derivation: one verse uses *alah*, the other uses *shvua* for the same act, demonstrating that sometimes the word *alah* functions as *shvua*.

### Arur as Shvua

A *Baraita* is then cited establishing that the word *arur* — "cursed be" — likewise has multiple valences depending on context. *Bo niduy* — in some contexts it means excommunication, as in *oru Meroz*, where Ulla teaches that Barak placed Meroz under *cherem* with four hundred *shofarot*. *Bo klala* — in other contexts it plainly means a curse, as in *ve'eileh ya'amdu al ha'klala* and *arur ha'ish asher ya'aseh pesel u'maseicha* at Har Gerizim and Har Eival. *Bo shevuah* — and in other contexts it means an oath.

## Curse-Oath Equivalence

### Joshua's Arur Oath

The proof that *arur* can mean *shvua* is drawn from the verse *vayashba Yehoshua ba'eit hahi leimor arur ha'ish lifnei Hashem* — Yehoshua imposed an oath on the people saying "cursed be the man before God." The verb *vayashba* tells us this was an oath, yet the content of what was said was the curse-formula *arur ha'ish*. So the word *arur* in that context constituted the swearing.

### Saul & Yonatan

A parallel case is then adduced from the story of Shaul and Yehonatan. One verse states *vayo'el Shaul et ha'am leimor arur ha'ish asher yochal* — Shaul made the people take an *alah* (note: the very verb for *alah* is used), saying "cursed be the man who eats anything today." A subsequent verse refers back to this act with the language of adjuration: *behishbia aviv et ha'am* — when his father adjured the people. Yehonatan, who had not heard Shaul's pronouncement and had eaten from the honey, bears the verse's testimony that what Shaul said was an oath.

### Curse-Oath Unity

The *Gemara* raises the obvious objection to both cases: *ve'dilma tarti avad lehu* — perhaps in each instance both were done? Perhaps Yehoshua (or Shaul) both made them take an oath and cursed them, but the word *arur* itself does not mean *shvua*? The *Gemara* answers: *miksiv ve'arur* — the verse does not say "and cursed." There is no conjunction indicating two separate acts. The single act described was the saying of *arur*, and this was identified as an oath. Then the *Gemara* applies the same logic to both cases simultaneously: *hashta de'atit lehachi, hatam nami lo ketiv ve'arur* — now that you have established this from Shaul, the same is true of Yehoshua: there too it says simply *arur*, not "and cursed," meaning the oath and the curse are one and the same act.

This is a rich conceptual point that the *Gemara* is working out, and it is worth pausing over the underlying structure. What is the *shvua* part and what is the *alah* part? In a typical *shvuat ha'alah*, they are distinct layers: the *shvua* is the declarative swearing in God's name — "I swear by God that I know no testimony" — and the *alah* is the conditional imprecation — "and if I am lying, may such-and-such befall me." These two elements are normally bundled together. What the *Gemara* is showing is that when the *alah* element is pronounced with sufficient weight and in the right context — particularly when it is delivered as a conditional curse directed at another person's behavior — it is as if both elements are present. Saying *arur ha'ish asher yochal* in the context of a public declaration by a leader implicitly carries the force of a sworn oath. That is why the later verse can describe the same act as adjuration. And this is also the significance of the phrase *veshama kol alah*: either a *shvua* or an *alah* independently carries this combined force in the context of *shvuat ha'edut*.

## God's Name Requirement

### Shvuat Ha'alah

The *Gemara* now engages a puzzling verse in the *Sotah* passage: *yitein Hashem otach le'alah velishvua betoch amech* — "may God make you a curse and an oath among your people." The question this raises is: how can a person become an oath? The simple reading would be that people will use her as an exemplar in oaths — "may what befell that woman befall me if I am lying." But there is another, surprising way to read the verse: the word *shvua* itself is sometimes used to mean a curse, not just an oath. This is the reverse of what we have been proving — rather than showing that *alah* means *shvua*, this verse suggests *shvua* can mean *klala*.

The *Gemara* does not pursue this direction, however, because it would undermine the careful distinction being maintained. The point of the entire *sugya* is that these two concepts, though deeply intertwined and often expressed through the same vocabulary, represent distinct phenomena: the sworn statement and the conditional imprecation. That they are often inseparable in practice — and that the verse sometimes uses one word to gesture at both — is precisely what makes the analysis subtle.

### Implicit God's Name

Rabbi Yose bar Chanina then turns to the word *amen*. He teaches that *amen* has three distinct functions: *bo shvuah* — it can constitute acceptance of a *shvua* imposed on oneself, as in *ve'amra ha'ishah amen amen* by the *Sotah*, who accepts the oath by responding *amen*. *Bo kabbalat devarim* — it can constitute acceptance of an obligation upon oneself, as in *arur asher lo yakim et divrei hatorah hazot la'asot otam, ve'amar kol ha'am amen* — the people accept the curse upon themselves. *Bo emanut devarim* — it can express affirmation of a belief, as in *vayomer Yirmiyahu amen, ken ya'aseh Hashem* — affirming confidence in the truth of what was said. The function of *amen* is entirely context-dependent.

Rabbi Eliezer then adds a striking teaching: *lav shvuah* — saying "no" is an oath; *hen shvuah* — saying "yes" is an oath. The proof for *lav*: God said *velo yihyeh od hamayim lemabul* — "the waters will no longer be a flood" — and a subsequent verse refers back to this as a sworn oath (*asher nishbati*). So God's simple statement "I will not do this again" was treated as an oath. By the same logic, an affirmative statement is also an oath.

Rava qualifies this significantly: this applies only when the word is doubled — *lav lav* or *hen hen*. This emerges from the *Noach* passage itself, where two separate negative statements appear (*velo yikaret kol basar od mimei hamabul; velo yihyeh od mayim lemabul*), suggesting that a single statement is not sufficient and doubling is required.

*Tosafot* substantially downplays this ruling, explaining that *lav lav* or *hen hen* are not literally a *shvua* in the full halakhic sense, but carry a weight of quasi-promise — one should be careful, and there is some measure of consequence, but it is not a *shvua mamash*. The Rambam and Ra'avad take the *Gemara* more seriously. The Rambam explains the cases carefully: if someone explicitly had a *shvua* imposed upon them and responds *hen* — yes — that is like saying *amen* and is fully binding. Even without a *shvua* explicitly imposed, if one says *hen hen* invoking God's name, that constitutes a *shvua*, because the two components of a *shvua* — oath-language and God's name — are present. *Hen hen* serves as the technical term for the *shvua*, and the invocation of God's name satisfies the second requirement. For the Rambam, one cannot create a *shvua* by merely saying "yes, yes" without any reference to God; but if God's name is invoked together with the doubled affirmation, it is a genuine *shvua*.

The *Gemara* then introduces a dispute about cursing with a *kinnui*. A *Baraita* cites the verse *ish ish ki yekalel Elohav* — "any man who curses his God" — and asks what this adds, since the death penalty for cursing God was already stated in the verse *venoikev shem Hashem mot yumat*, which specifies the explicit utterance of the divine name. The answer given is that this additional verse extends the prohibition to the *kinuyim*, the substitute names of God. This is Rabbi Meir's position: one is *chayav misa* even for cursing God using a *kinnui*. The *Chachamim* disagree: the death penalty applies only to *shem ha-meyuchad*, and the additional verse establishes a *lav* — a negative prohibition — for cursing with a *kinnui*, without the death penalty.

Rabbi Menachem bar Yosi extends this logic to the case of cursing a parent. The verse that describes the death penalty for cursing God is read as doubly purposeful: not only does it remind us about God-cursing, but the emphasis on "the name" (*shem*) comes to teach us that cursing a parent also requires explicit use of God's name to incur the death penalty.

Rabbi Yannai adds that cursing another person or even oneself is prohibited according to everyone — not the death penalty, but a *lav* — even without using God's name. The prohibition against cursing another derives from *lo tekalel cheresh*; the prohibition against cursing oneself derives from *rak hishamer lecha ushemor nafshecha me'od*. This is a striking reading: the verse "guard yourself greatly," whose plain sense concerns remembering Sinai, is read as a prohibition against self-endangerment, and cursing oneself is treated as a form of self-endangerment — reflecting the *Gemara*'s view that a curse carries real efficacy.

## Euphemizing Curses

### Rav Kahana's Critique

A practical vignette now illustrates the above with a case of improper enunciation. Rav Kahana was sitting before Rav Yehuda, who was teaching the *Mishnah*. When Rav Yehuda came to the case of *yakecha Hashem Elokeinu* — "may God smite you" — as an example of an *alah*, he read it in the second person, directly addressing those present. Rav Kahana rebuked him: *kanei* — you should say it differently. One should not explicitly invoke a curse in the second person when teaching, as though directing the imprecation at the people in front of you. One should euphemize: say "may God curse him," in the third person, not "you."

### Third Person Usage

The *Gemara* then symmetrically records that a rabbinic student was sitting before Rav Kahana and committed the same error — reciting the verse *gam El yitatzcha lanetzach, yichtecha veyisacha me'ohel, veshershacha me'eretz chayim selah* ("God should destroy you forever, cut you down, and uproot you from the land of the living") in the second person. Rav Kahana corrected the student with the same instruction: *amar lei kanei*. One must euphemize.

The *Gemara* then asks: why do we need both stories? The answer is that one might have thought that only the *Mishnah*'s rabbinic teaching requires euphemism — perhaps a biblical verse, being God's direct word, must be quoted precisely as written. The second incident teaches that even when quoting scripture, one must phrase it in a way that does not imply the curse is being directed at those present.

## Blessing vs. Curse

### Blessing Formula

The *Gemara* now introduces a case where a person administers neither an explicit curse nor an oath, but instead a conditional blessing: "May God bless you if you testify about what you know." No explicit *klala* was pronounced, and no *shvua* formula was used — only a positive formulation. If the witness thereafter falsely denies knowing any testimony, has a valid *shvuat ha'edut* occurred?

### Rabbi Meir Position

Rabbi Meir holds that such a formulation creates *chiyuv* and the person would be obligated to bring a *korban*. His reasoning rests on the principle of *miklal lav atah shome'a hen umiklal hen atah shome'a lav* — from the negative you can infer the positive, and from the positive you can infer the negative. Saying "God will bless you if you testify" implies "God will curse you if you do not testify." In the ordinary language of human communication, this is indeed how such statements are understood, even if formal propositional logic would not strictly license the inference.

### Rabbis Position

The *Chachamim* exempt such a person. They do not accept the inference from one direction to the other as halakhically operative here. Since the curse was never stated — even implicitly, in a legally cognizable way — no *shvuat ha'edut* was created.

## Rabbi Meir Bilateral

### Monetary Stipulations

The *Gemara* now asks: does Rabbi Meir's position here not contradict his well-known general rule? In the laws of stipulations (*tenai*), Rabbi Meir consistently requires that any condition be stated in both directions — *im ken yihyeh* and *im lo yihyeh*, both the positive and the negative. If P then Q, and if not P then not Q — both must be stated for the condition to be halakhically binding. This is the rule of *tenai kaful*, the doubled condition. If Rabbi Meir normally insists on explicit bilateral formulation, why does he accept here the inference from the positive blessing to the negative curse?

The *Gemara* attempts to resolve this by reversing the positions: the text of the *Mishnah* has Rabbi Meir's name and the *Chachamim*'s name switched, so that it is actually the *Chachamim* who say one direction suffices and Rabbi Meir who says both directions are required. When Rav Yitzchak came from *Eretz Yisrael*, he taught a *Baraita* that assigned the positions as our *Mishnah* does — with Rabbi Meir saying one direction suffices. Rav Yosef argues from this that since both our local *Mishnah* and the *Baraita* brought by Rav Yitzchak assign Rabbi Meir the position that one direction suffices, we cannot simply reverse the *Mishnah*'s text.

The *Gemara* therefore distinguishes: *ki leit lei be'mamona, aval be'issura it lei* — Rabbi Meir's requirement of bilateral formulation applies in monetary matters; in cases of prohibition (*issur*), one direction is sufficient even for Rabbi Meir. This would explain why, by *shvuat ha'edut*, which involves a prohibition, Rabbi Meir is satisfied with the blessing alone implying the curse.

### Prohibition Exception

This distinction, however, creates a different problem. Ravina challenges it with the case of *shetuyei yayin upruei rosh* — priests who enter the *Beit Hamikdash* while drunk or with overgrown hair are subject to *misah bidei shamayim* (death at God's hand). The verse stating this liability reads: if you do not drink, you will not die — that is, the death penalty is only expressed in one direction, implying the converse. Since the *Mishnah* itself establishes *shetuyei yayin* and *pruei rosh* as cases of *misah*, even Rabbi Meir must agree with this. But this is an *issur* case, so Rabbi Meir should have no problem with it to begin with. Ravina's challenge thus demonstrates that Rabbi Meir cannot consistently require bilateral formulation even in all *issur* cases, since everyone — Rabbi Meir included — agrees on the single-direction verse for *shetuyei yayin*.

### Sotah Mixed Case

The *Gemara* then revisits *Sotah*, which had previously served as a test case for Rabbi Meir's *tenai kaful* rule. In the *Gemara* that deals specifically with Rabbi Meir's bilateral requirement, the *Sotah* passage posed a challenge: the verse says "if you have not sinned, you will be cleansed" — only one direction. The defense offered was *hinaki ksiv* — reading *hinaki* as *khinaki*, "you will be strangled," so that the verse implicitly contains both directions. The *Gemara* here notes that this defense implies: *ha lav hachi* — had it not been for this reading, Rabbi Meir would have had to concede that *Sotah* requires only one direction. But if *Sotah* is a case of *issur* and Rabbi Meir permits one direction for *issur*, why did *Sotah* ever pose a problem for him?

The *Gemara* resolves this: *ushani issura de'Sotah de'issura de'is lei mamona nami* — *Sotah* is not a pure *issur* case; it contains a *mamon* component as well. The *mamon* element of *Sotah* is the exemption from paying the *ketubbah* — the *Sotah*'s guilt or innocence bears on monetary consequences to the husband. Because there is a monetary dimension, Rabbi Meir applies his bilateral requirement even in the *Sotah* context.

### Ha'edut Monetary

By the same token, *shvuat ha'edut* is also not a pure *issur* case. The entire context of *shvuat ha'edut* is monetary: someone is summoning a witness to testify in a financial dispute, and the witness's testimony — or false denial — affects monetary outcomes. Because *shvuat ha'edut* has this *mamon* component, Rabbi Meir requires that both directions be stated: the blessing and the curse must each be pronounced explicitly. The *Chachamim*, who hold that one direction always implies the other, exempt a person who heard only the blessing and then falsely denied knowledge of testimony.

The final alignment is therefore as follows: Rabbi Meir requires both the blessing and the curse to be stated, because *shvuat ha'edut* is a *mamon*-connected matter, and in *mamon* matters he always demands the bilateral formulation. The *Chachamim* hold that one direction suffices, and the unstated direction is legally implied. *Shetuyei yayin* and similar pure *issur* cases are not problematic for Rabbi Meir because everyone agrees that single-direction formulation is operative there, regardless of Rabbi Meir's general rule.
