# Shevuot 39

## Oath Model & Requirements

### Oath Model

The *gemara* opens not in direct response to any particular point in the *mishna*, but to the broader phenomenon of *shevuat hadayanim* — the oath administered by the judges. The question posed is: *heichi mashbinan lei?* How do we actually impose the *shevua*? Rav Yehuda citing Rav answers that we use as our model the oath that Avraham administered to his servant, as it is written: *v'ashbiacha bashem elokei hashamayim v'elokei ha'aretz asher lo sikach isha livni mibnos hakna'ani asher anochi yoshev bekirbo* — "And I will make you swear by the Lord, God of heaven and God of earth, that you will not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites among whom I dwell."

The question immediately arises: what precisely are we deriving from this Abrahamic model? The *gemara* might have assumed that the emphasis lies on the words *bashem* — that the oath must invoke God's name specifically. Ravina raised this point with Rav Ashi, asking whether this represents the position of Rabbi Chanina bar Idi, who requires the use of *shem hameyuchad*, the distinctive and explicit Divine Name. Rav Ashi replied that the ruling holds even according to the *rabbanan*, who permit the use of a secondary divine appellation such as *El* rather than the Tetragrammaton. The derivation from the Abrahamic model therefore concerns something else entirely.

### Holy Object Req.

The practical derivation from Avraham's oath is the requirement that the oath-taker hold a holy object in hand during the *shevua*. This follows from the instruction Avraham gave his servant: *sim na yadecha tachas yerechi* — "place your hand under my thigh." The understanding is that the servant grasped the *bris milah* of Avraham, which served as a tangible symbol of a *mitzva* and of covenantal obligation to God. From this we learn that the administration of a *shevua* requires the oath-taker to hold onto something sacred — in practice, a *sefer torah*.

### Rava: No Object

The *gemara* then invokes the ruling of Rava: a judge who administers an oath invoking *Hashem elokei hashamayim* but does not require the oath-taker to hold a holy object is regarded as one who has erred in a matter of *mishna* — *to'eh bidvar mishna* — and the ruling must be reversed. The implication is that the requirement to hold a holy object is so well-established that failing to enforce it constitutes an inexcusable halakhic error, with the consequences that flow from such errors in the context of judicial rulings discussed in tractate *Sanhedrin*.

### Rav Pappa: Sefer Torah

Rav Pappa goes further still: a judge who administers an oath using *tefillin* as the held object — rather than a *sefer torah* — is also considered to have erred in a matter of *mishna*, and the ruling is likewise reversed. The holding of *tefillin* alone does not suffice; a *sefer torah* is required. One might ask whether this standard was ever met in the case of Avraham's servant, who obviously had no *sefer torah* available. The *gemara* implicitly acknowledges that Avraham simply had no alternative.

### Halakha Decision

The *gemara* then rules on both positions. The *halakha* follows Rava: if no holy object whatsoever was used, it is a clear and unacceptable error, and the oath is invalidated. However, the *halakha* does not follow Rav Pappa. The ruling is: *velo hilchesa kevashei deRav Pappa deha nakat cheftza beyadei dehalo sefer torah* — since the oath-taker was holding some holy object, even if it was only *tefillin* rather than a *sefer torah*, the *shevua* is valid after the fact.

### Standing Requirement

The *gemara* continues with further formal requirements. A *shevua* must be taken while standing — *shevua be'umad*. A *talmid chacham*, however, may be seated — *talmid chacham beyoshev*. This reflects a broader principle of deference to Torah scholars within the court system. The logic behind these various requirements — standing, use of a *sefer torah*, and so forth — appears to be that they are designed to impress upon the oath-taker the gravity of what a *shevua* is and the enormity of the consequences of a false one. A *talmid chacham* does not require the same theatrical weight to internalize that gravity, which is why the rules are relaxed for him: he may sit, and *tefillin* suffices for him *lechatchila* rather than a *sefer torah*.

### Any Language Allowed

The *Tosefta* cited from the context of tractate *Sota* establishes that *shevuat hadayanim* may be administered in any language — *shevuat hadayanim af hi bilshonam ne'emra*. The significance of this ruling will be unpacked further below in connection with the relevant *mishna* in *Sota*.

## Fear & Consequences

### World's Trembling

When the oath is about to be administered, those present address the oath-taker with the following: *hevei yodea shekol ha'olam kulo nizdazeia besha'a she'amar hakadosh baruch hu beSinai* — be aware that the entire world trembled at the moment God proclaimed at Sinai: *lo sisa et shem Hashem elokecha lashav*, "You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain." The purpose is to impress upon the person about to take the oath the full weight of what he is doing.

### No Forgiveness

The *braisa* goes on to explain what makes this prohibition singular. For all other sins in the Torah, the verse employs the language of *venakeh* — God will cleanse. But here the Torah states *ki lo yenakeh Hashem et asher yisa shemo lashav* — God will not cleanse one who takes His name in vain. The *gemara* reads the phrase *nakeh lo yenakeh* elsewhere in the Torah as meaning: God cleanses those who repent — *nakeh lashavim* — but does not cleanse those who do not repent — *velo yenakeh le'eina shavim*. There is at least some measure of *nakeh* in all other cases. But by *shevuat shav*, the Torah employs *ki lo yenakeh* without any qualifying *nakeh*, signaling that even the possibility of full cleansing is categorically denied.

### Family Punishment

Beyond the absence of forgiveness, the *braisa* identifies a second distinctive feature of false oaths: whereas for all other sins in the Torah punishment is exacted from the sinner alone, for a false oath punishment extends to his family as well — *mimenu umimishpachto*. The proof text is: *al titein et picha lachati et besarecha* — do not allow your mouth to bring sin upon your flesh. The word *basar* — flesh — is interpreted as referring to one's relatives, as the verse states: *umibesarcha lo titalem*, do not hide yourself from your own flesh.

### Hosea's Proof

Further still, the *braisa* identifies a third and even more expansive consequence: whereas for all other sins only the sinner bears punishment, a false oath brings suffering upon the entire world. This is the meaning of the world's trembling at the utterance of *lo tisa* — because swearing falsely in God's name represents a fundamental violation of the trust placed in God as witness.

The proof text is drawn from *Hoshea* 4:2: *alah vechachesh veratzoach veganov vena'of paratzu udamim bedamim naga'u* — false swearing, dishonesty, murder, theft, and adultery have burst forth and blood touches upon blood. The verse continues: *al ken te'evel ha'aretz ve'umlal kol yoshev bah bechayat hasadeh uve'of hashamayim vegam degei hayam ye'aseifu* — therefore the land mourns and all who dwell therein are bereaved, including the beasts of the field, the birds of the sky, and even the fish of the sea.

One might object that this verse lists a whole litany of sins, not only false oaths. The *gemara* addresses this by pointing to a parallel verse in *Yirmiyahu*: *mipnei alah avelah ha'aretz* — because of the oath the land mourns. This verse employs the exact same language of mourning as the verse in *Hoshea*, thereby drawing a direct line connecting the cosmic mourning of the land specifically to the sin of false swearing.

### Immediate Punishment

For all other sins, the *braisa* states, if the sinner possesses merit, punishment may be deferred for two or three generations. But for a false oath, punishment comes immediately — *nifra'im mimenu le'altar*. The proof text is from *Zechariah*: *hotzeitia neum Hashem tzevaot uvah el beit haganav ve'el beit hanishba bishmi lashaker* — I will eject it, says the Lord of Hosts, and it will come to the house of the thief and to the house of one who swears falsely in My name. *Hotzeitia* — I will eject — connotes immediacy, *le'altar*.

The *gemara* interprets *beit haganav* — the house of the thief — as referring to the one who practices *geneivat da'at*, that is, deception of others. The classic illustration here is of someone who makes a financial claim against another, who, uncertain of the facts, finds himself compelled to swear in order to extricate himself from the demanded payment. The one making the false claim has engaged in *geneivat da'at* in the most consequential sense — misrepresenting facts for financial gain and weaponizing the *shevua* to that end.

### Metaphor of Fire

The verse concludes: *velanah betoch beito vechilat'o ve'et etzav ve'et avanav* — and the sin will dwell within his house and consume it along with its timber and its stones. The *gemara* draws a remarkable lesson from this: *devarim she'ein esh ochaltan shvuat sheker mechala otan* — things that even fire cannot consume, a false oath will consume them. Even stone and timber, which resist ordinary destruction, are not immune to the devastation wrought by a false oath. The *avon* — the sin — dwells within the house and destroys everything within it.

## Oath Administration

### Right to Refuse

After instilling all of this fear and awe in the oath-taker, if the person says *eini nishba* — I will not take the oath — the court immediately releases him: *potrin oso mi-yad*. There is no penalty for refusing. Indeed, the procedure is to wrap up the matter quickly at that point. *Rashi* and *Tosafos* discuss whether he could retract his refusal, but the practice is to conclude proceedings swiftly so that no such reversal occurs.

### Distancing from Evil

If, having heard all of this, the person nevertheless declares *ha-reini nishba* — I will proceed with the oath — those present respond by distancing themselves, reciting: *suru na me-al ohalei ha-anashim ha-reshaim ha-eleh* — turn away from the tents of these evil men. This is striking: even the one who demands the oath is characterized alongside the oath-taker as belonging to the category of *resha'im*. The very act of taking a *shevua* — even if it may well be truthful — carries so enormous a moral and spiritual weight that all those in proximity must recoil. The longstanding Jewish practice of avoiding *shevuos* and *nedarim* flows from precisely this sensibility.

### Judicial Warning

When the oath is actually administered, the court declares: *hevei yodea she-lo al datcha anu mashbi-in oscha ela al da'as ha-Makom ve-al da'as Beit Din* — be aware that we are not imposing this oath according to your own private understanding, but according to the intent of God and the intent of the court. The concern is that the oath-taker might frame his words so that they sound like one thing while technically meaning something else in his own mind.

### No Reservations

This warning forecloses all attempts at mental reservation or self-serving reinterpretation. Whatever semantic sleight of hand the oath-taker might attempt to perform internally — whatever qualifying gloss he places on the words in his own mind — is irrelevant. The oath is constituted by what God means and what the court means by those words, not by whatever the oath-taker privately intends.

### Moses Precedent

The *braisa* cites a precedent for this practice in the behavior of Moshe Rabbeinu. When Moshe administered the oath to Yisrael at *Arvot Moav*, he similarly declared: *de'u she-lo al datchaschem ani mashbi-a eschem ela al da'as ha-Makom ve-al da'ati* — know that it is not according to your own understanding that I am administering this oath, but according to the intent of God and my own intent. The proof text is: *ve-lo itchem levadchem anochi koreis es ha-bris ha-zos ki es asher yeshno poh* — and it is not with you alone that I am making this covenant, but with all those who stand here. The phrase *ve-lo itchem* — not with you — is read as signaling that what you privately have in mind does not determine the content of the covenant.

### Future Generations

The *gemara* then continues to expound the verse. *Ki es asher yeshno poh* — this might be taken to mean only those physically present at the covenant ceremony. But from where do we know that it includes future generations? The verse continues: *ve-es asher eineno* — and even those who are not here — establishing that all future generations were included in the *kabbalat* *mitzvos* at Sinai and *Arvot Moav*.

The *gemara* further asks: from where do we know that the concept of *kabbalat mitzvos* — the covenantal acceptance — extended even to commandments that would only come into existence later, such as *mikra megilla*? The answer is derived from the phrase *kimu vekiblu* — they confirmed and accepted. At the time of the *megilla*, Yisrael reaffirmed and confirmed what had previously been accepted, extending the scope of covenantal obligation even to God's presence as experienced in a more hidden mode, and to all future *mitzvos* that would subsequently emerge.

## Language & Severity

### Language Clarification

The *gemara* now returns to examine the opening phrase of the *braisa*: *shevuat hadayanim af hi bilshonam ne'emra* — the oath of the judges may also be said in any language. The word *af* — also — implies a comparison to something else. The *gemara* explains that this is a reference to the *mishna* in *Sota*, which lists those things that may be said in any language, as opposed to those which must specifically be said in Hebrew. Among the items on that list the *mishna* in *Sota* includes *parshat sotah*, *viduy ma'aser*, *krias shema*, *tefilla*, *birchat hamazon*, *shvuat ha-eidus*, and *shvuat hapikadon*. The *mishna* there did not include *shevuat hadayanim*, and the *braisa* therefore comes to add it — *af* — she too may be said in any language.

### Relative Severity

The *gemara* then addresses the underlying reason why the world trembled at the utterance of *lo tisa*. It might seem that the trembling was simply because this commandment was given at Sinai — but the *gemara* notes that the entire *Aseret HaDibrot* were given at Sinai, and yet we do not say that the world trembled at each of them. Alternatively, perhaps the trembling reflects the particular severity of *lo tisa*. But here the *gemara* points to a *mishna* that categorizes the transgressions: the lighter ones are positive and negative commandments excluding *lo tisa*, while the weightier category includes *krisos*, *misos beit din*, and *lo tisa* alongside them. So *lo tisa* is certainly weightier than ordinary negative commandments, yet it is not weightier than *karet* and *misas beit din*. There are many sins carrying those penalties, and yet the world did not tremble specifically at their utterance. What, then, accounts for the trembling?

## Language & Severity (II)

### Why Trembling

The *gemara* resolves the question by returning to what the *braisa* itself says: the reason the world trembled is not that *lo tisa* is the weightiest transgression in the Torah — it is not, since *karet* and *misas beit din* are weightier in their prescribed punishment — but rather because there is categorically no *kapara* for it. The verse says *lo yenakeh*, and that absence of any qualifying *nakeh* sets *shevuat shav* apart from every other transgression. Rabbi Elazar addresses the tension in the text: it is impossible to read *venakeh* as meaning God fully cleanses, since the same verse also says *lo yenakeh*; and it is impossible to read *lo yenakeh* as meaning God never forgives at all, since the same verse also says *venakeh*. The resolution is: *menakeh hu lashavim ve'eino menakeh leshainam shavim* — God forgives those who repent but does not forgive those who do not. For all other transgressions there is some measure of *nakeh* even without complete *teshuva*. Here, there is none without it. That is why the world trembled.

### Family vs. Accessory

The *gemara* then examines the claim that family punishment is distinctive to false oaths. The *braisa* states that for all other sins punishment falls on the sinner alone, whereas for a false oath it extends to the family as well. The *gemara* challenges this: is it really true that families are never punished for other sins? The verse in connection with *avodah zarah* and the sin of giving one's child to *Molech* states: *ve-samti ani es panai ba-ish hahu u-v'mishpachto* — I will set My face against that man and his family.

### Family Liability

A *braisa* is cited in which Rabbi Shimon asks: if he sinned, what did the family sin? The answer: there is no family that has a *mocheis* — a tax collector engaged in extortion — in which the entire household is not implicated. Family members cover for him, make excuses on his behalf, assist him actively or by their silence. The *gemara* applies the parallel principle here: there is no family that harbors a bandit in which all members are not in some way implicated, *mipnei shemechaphin alav* — because they cover for him.

The *gemara* then draws the critical distinction. In those other cases — *avodah zarah* and similar transgressions — the family is punished in a different and lesser capacity: as accessories, bearing a derivative punishment commensurate with their complicity. But in the case of a false oath, the family receives the same punishment as the sinner himself, not merely an accessory penalty. This is the distinctive feature: not that the family is punished at all, but that it is punished equally.

A *braisa* is cited in which Rebbe expounds the verse *ve-hikrasti oso* — and I will destroy him. Why does the Torah need to add this given the prior mention of the family? Because the prior verse, *u-v'mishpachto*, might suggest that the entire family receives *karet*. Therefore the Torah adds *oso* — him specifically receives *karet*, but not the entire family. The upshot is that in other *aveiros* the family receives only an accessory and lesser punishment, while in the case of a false oath the punishment that falls on the family is equal to that of the sinner himself, even as *karet* remains the exclusive penalty of the individual sinner alone.

## Fear & Consequences (II)

### Cleanse Doctrine

The textual tension embedded in the phrase *nakeh lo yenakeh* — which appears to simultaneously assert both that God cleanses and that God does not cleanse — is resolved, as noted above, through the doctrine of *teshuva*. Rabbi Elazar's teaching establishes that neither reading can stand alone: *venakeh* cannot mean unconditional forgiveness, nor can *lo yenakeh* mean absolute non-forgiveness in all circumstances. The reconciliation is that God cleanses those who repent — *menakeh hu lashavim* — and does not cleanse those who do not — *ve'eino menakeh leshainam shavim*. What sets *shevuat shav* apart from all other transgressions is not that repentance is powerless — for no sin is beyond the reach of genuine *teshuva* — but rather that without *teshuva*, there is no cleansing whatsoever, no partial mitigation, no accumulated merit that can defer or soften the consequence. That is the meaning of the unreserved *lo yenakeh*, and that is why the world trembled.

---

# Shevuot 40

## False Oath Impact

### Shevua vs. Other Sins

Today's daf is formally *daf mem*, though we are picking up from the bottom of 39a, still unpacking the *baraita* that addresses the administration of an oath and the weight of a false one. That *baraita* echoes the warnings given to witnesses before testimony — how people's lives hang in the balance — except here the focus is how a false *shevua* can be destructive not only to the person who swears it, but to his family and the entire world.

The *gemara* picks up five lines from the bottom of the page: *v'chol aveirot shebatorah nifra'im mimenu* — for other sins, only the person himself is punished. But here, *v'kan mimenu umikol ha'olam kulo* — in the case of a false *shevua*, the entire world suffers.

### Collective Responsibility

This immediately raises an objection. The *gemara* asks: *v'chol aveirot shebatorah mikol ha'olam lo?* Are we saying that the rest of the world is entirely unaffected by other sins? But the verse states *vechi kashlu ish be'achiv* — a man will stumble through his brother's sin — and *melamed shekol Yisrael arevim zeh lazeh*, teaching that all of Israel are guarantors for one another. This suggests the world does suffer for others' sins!

The *gemara* resolves this: *hasam she'yesh b'yadam limchot v'lo michu* — that principle applies only where bystanders could have protested and failed to do so. They are passive enablers, and that degree of complicity accounts for their culpability. In the case of a false *shevua*, however, the metaphysical consequence extends even to those who bear no responsibility whatsoever.

### Punishment Gradations

The *gemara* further refines the distinctions. It asks: *mai ika bein rish'ei d'mishpacha l'rish'ei d'alma, bein tzadikei d'mishpacha l'tzadikei d'alma* — what is the difference between a *rasha* of the family and a *rasha* of the wider world, or between the *tzadikim* of the family and those of the world at large?

For ordinary sins, the perpetrator is punished with the full weight of his transgression — *b'sha'ar aveirot b'dinei*. Family members who enabled him, whether actively or passively, receive a weightier punishment — *v'rasha d'mishpacha b'din chamur*. Bystanders in the broader world who were passive enablers receive a lighter punishment — *v'rasha d'alma b'din hakal*. Crucially, those who are completely blameless, the *tzadikim*, are entirely exempt — *tzadikei d'hacha v'hacha peturei*.

This framework reveals two layers of distinction. First, culpability is required: one must be a *rasha* in some sense — either the perpetrator, an active enabler, or a passive one — before the punishment applies. The label *rasha* here is pointed: the person who simply did not protest is designated a *rasha* for that failure to act. Second, even among the culpable, punishment is graduated according to proximity to the wrong.

In the case of a *shevua*, the structure shifts. The perpetrator and his family enablers are punished with equal severity: *hu vchol mishpachto kidinei*. The broader world's passive enablers receive a weighty though lesser punishment: *rish'ei d'alma b'din chamur*.

### Universal Impact

Here is the major *chiddush*: *vetzadikei d'hacha d'hacha b'din kal* — even the entirely blameless, both of the family and of the world at large, receive some form of light punishment. This is the fundamental difference between a *shevua* and all other sins. For other transgressions, the *tzadikim* are exempt. For a false *shevua*, no one escapes entirely. The suffering of the world is not a function of guilt — it is a metaphysical reality set in motion by the oath itself. The *tzadikim* of the family may seem harder to envision, but there are always exceptions — infants, for instance, who could not possibly have been complicit.

---

## Oath Administration

### Refusal & Joint Liability

The *baraita* continues: *im amar eini nishba potrin oto miyad* — if he says he will not swear, he is released immediately. But if he says *harei ani nishba* — he intends to go ahead with the oath — those present invoke the verse *suru na me'al ohalei ha'anashim harishaim ha'eileh*, calling on all to distance themselves from these wicked men. This designates both the one taking the oath and the one imposing it as a *rasha*.

The *gemara* asks: *bishlama hu deka mishtava kai be'issura* — understandably the one taking a false oath transgresses. But why is the one imposing the oath also called a *rasha*? The answer comes from a *braita* of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: *shevuat Hashem tihyeh bein sheneihem* — the oath of God rests upon both of them. Both parties are, in some sense, participants in the act of swearing.

Rashi explains that both are punished because the one who imposed the oath failed to ensure proper documentary evidence or adequate witnesses, thereby allowing the situation to arrive at a *chillul Hashem*. This reasoning, though, sits uneasily in certain cases. In a situation involving *eid echad*, for instance, the claimant cannot always arrange for additional witnesses — a car accident has whatever witnesses it has. So the *gemara* may be gesturing at something more metaphysical: you set this in motion, and a false *shevua* resulted. Perhaps you could have waived your claim. The discussion here is subtly different from the earlier analysis of family and world — it is not simply about fault and guilt but about the raw reality of the *shevua* and who brought it about.

### Oath Language Standardiz…

The *baraita* continues: *uche'shemashbi'in oto omrim lo hevei yodeia shelo al da'atecha* — when administering the oath, the court informs the oath-taker that the oath is not interpreted according to his own understanding, but according to theirs.

### Hollowed Staff Case

The *gemara* asks: *lama li lemeimar lei hachi?* Why must the court say this? *Mishum kanya deRava* — because of the incident involving Rava's staff. A man who owed money hollowed out his staff, filled it with the coins he owed, and handed it to his creditor, asking him to hold it. He then swore that he had returned the money — technically true, since the creditor was at that moment holding the coins inside the staff. The debtor was thus playing semantic games, assigning private meaning to his oath. To prevent such manipulation, the court declares that the oath means only what they intend it to mean, not what the oath-taker privately has in mind.

This concludes the *baraita's* treatment of the weight and administration of a false *shevua* — the gravity of swearing falsely, the framing designed to deter the oath-taker, and the safeguard ensuring the oath means what the court says it means.

---

## Rav vs. Shmuel

### Mishnah Ambiguity

The *gemara* now shifts to a more technical *halachic* discussion. The Mishnah states that *modeh bemiktzat* requires a *ta'anah* of *shtei kesef* — two *ma'ah*, which we will call twenty dollars for convenience — and an admission of at least a *perutah*, a penny. The question is an ambiguity in the Mishnah itself: does the requirement of *shtei kesef* apply to the *claim*, or to the *denial*?

### Rav's Position

*Amar Rav kefirat ta'ana shtei kesef* — Rav says the denial must be *shtei kesef*. It is not enough that twenty dollars was claimed; the amount actually denied must be at least twenty dollars.

### Shmuel's Position

*uShmuel amar ta'ana atzma shtei kesef* — Shmuel says the claim itself must be twenty dollars, but even if you admitted to nineteen dollars and ninety-nine cents and only denied a single penny, you are still *chayav*. Conversely, even if you admitted only to a penny and denied nineteen dollars and ninety-nine cents, you are still *chayav*. Once the original claim was large enough, the *shevua* attaches.

Rav himself acknowledges an internal tension: *dika matnitan kevasi d'Rav, vekrah kevasi de'Shmuel* — the Mishnah reads more naturally like Rav's position, but the *pesukim* read more naturally like Shmuel's.

The Mishnah's formulation supports Rav because it specifies a *ta'ana* of *shtei kesef* and an admission of a *perutah*, but never explicitly mentions the case where only a *perutah* is denied — which would be Shmuel's sharpest *chiddush*. Had Shmuel been right, the Mishnah should have highlighted the remarkable ruling that one takes an oath even when denying only a penny, yet that formulation is absent. The same observation applies to a parallel Mishnah in Bava Metzia.

### Kesef O Keilim

The *pesukim*, however, read more naturally like Shmuel. The verse in the section dealing with *shomrim* states *ki yiten ish l're'eihu kesef o keilim lishmor* — if a man gives his fellow silver or vessels to watch. The *gemara* learns from the plural *keilim* that *kesef* must also be plural — at minimum two — and the question becomes: two what? The tradition establishes it means two *ma'ah*, which we are calling twenty dollars.

The verse continues with an additional derivation: *ma kesef davar chashuv, af keilim davar chashuv* — just as silver must be significant, so too *keilim* must be significant. Here Tosafot's reading is preferable to Rashi's: *keilim* must be a *davar chashuv*, meaning each vessel must be worth at least a *perutah*, even if the pair together does not reach the monetary threshold of *shtei kesef*. A *kli* carries intrinsic significance beyond its market value — one needle can sew an entire garment — and so two needles worth a *perutah* each would be sufficient to trigger *modeh bemiktzat*, even though their combined value is far below twenty dollars. When dealing with *keilim*, you do not need the *shtei kesef* threshold at all.

The verse then says *ki hu zeh* — which the *gemara* uses to establish the basic requirement of *hoda'ah bemiktzat ha-ta'anah*, partial admission within the claim, and also the requirement that the admission be *mimin ha-ta'anah*, of the same genre as what was claimed.

Shmuel reads the verse as a whole to indicate that the twenty dollars is what was claimed, not what was denied. The structure of the verse — *kesef o keilim* being what the person gave — points naturally to the claim. When the *gemara* presses that this seems to show the claim was *shtei kesef*, implicitly confirming Shmuel, Rav responds: *kesef ki asa me-ikara le-kfira hu de-asa* — the word *kesef* comes primarily to address the denial, not the claim.

Rav's argument is as follows: if the Torah had only mentioned *keilim*, I would have derived *shtei kesef* on my own by analogy, knowing that monetary thresholds require a substantial amount. The additional word *kesef* must therefore be teaching something else, something not already derivable — namely, that the *denial* itself must reach the threshold of *shtei kesef*. *Im eino inyan le-ta'anah tnehu inyan le-kfira* — if it is not needed to teach the claim, apply it to the denial.

Shmuel, for his part, maintains that without the word *kesef*, he might have known the quantity requirement but not the *davar chashuv* requirement for *keilim*. The word *kesef* is therefore necessary to teach that *keilim* must be significant objects. Both words together establish the claim threshold and the significance requirement for vessels.

The upshot is clear: the plain reading of the verses favors Shmuel, because the natural sense of *ki yiten ish el re'eihu kesef o keilim* is that this is what was entrusted — what was claimed — not what was denied. Rav's reading requires treating the word *kesef* as displaced from its plain meaning and redirected toward a different legal element. Rav himself concedes the Mishnah may read more like his position, but the verses read more like Shmuel's.

The subsequent discussion turns on how to read a series of Mishnaic cases — the case of claiming *shtei kesef* and the defendant admitting to a *perutah*, and the case of claiming *shtei kesef* plus a *perutah* with the defendant admitting only to a *perutah*. The *gemara* asks whether these cases involve disputes about monetary value or disputes about the physical coins themselves.

Shmuel argues that the Mishnah is speaking of disputes about the coins as objects, not their value. Under this reading, when one says "you have two silver coins of mine," he means the actual coins, not their monetary equivalent. Thus when the defendant admits to only a *perutah* in the first case, it is not a *modeh bemiktzat* — what was claimed (silver coins) was not what was admitted (a copper penny). Rav, by contrast, holds that whenever monetary language is used without specification of the object itself, we are speaking of value, not physical coins.

A further case is raised: one claims a *litra zahav* — a pound of gold — and the defendant says he only received a *litra kesef* — a pound of silver. Here, because the word *litra* specifies a physical quantity of a substance, we are clearly talking about the object itself, not its monetary value. This is compatible with both positions. The subsequent case — where a gold *dinar* is claimed and a silver *dinar* admitted, with the ruling being *chayav* — is explained by Rabbi Elazar as a case where the claimant gave the coin for change (*b'shata'ano b'dinar matbeiot*). In that context, what matters is not the coin itself but the obligation to provide change, so the admission that one received a silver *dinar* worth of change is indeed a partial admission of the same claim.

According to Tosafot's reading, the case of *dinar zahov zahov* — where the claimant specifies that the coin is made of pure gold — establishes that only when one explicitly emphasizes the physical nature of the object are we dealing with the object as such. The standard formulation *dinar zahov*, absent such emphasis, refers to value, not the coin. This, says Rav Ashi, is how Shmuel would read it — *kol ha-omer dinar zahov ke-omer dinar zahov zahov dami*, treating every mention of a gold *dinar* as implicitly referring to the object. But this is acknowledged to be a forced reading. If every mention of a monetary sum were taken as a reference to the physical currency rather than the value, disputes about money would routinely become disputes about objects, releasing defendants from *shevua* far too easily. The simpler reading remains Rav's: monetary language denotes value, and the reason the defendant is *patur* in the Mishnah's first case is simply that the denial did not reach *shtei kesef*.

---

## Rabbi Chiyya Braita

### Sela Case

Since the Mishnah already reads more naturally like Rav, a *baraita* of Rabbi Chiyya explicitly supports him. *Sela li beyadecha* — you have a *sela* of mine, which is worth six *kesef*. The defendant says: *ein lecha beyadi ella sela chasar bet kesef* — you only gave me four *kesef*, a *sela* less two. In this case he is *chayav*, because the denial is two *kesef*, which satisfies Rav's threshold. But if the defendant says he only owes one *kesef* — *chasar ma'ah* — he is *patur*, because the denial is only one *kesef*, below the required two. This is a clear and direct statement: it is the denial, not the claim, that must be at least *shtei kesef*, just as Rav maintains. All the evidence points toward Rav's position, though the *gemara* does not formally resolve the dispute in favor of either side.

---

## Modeh vs. Eid Echad

### Shmuel's Teaching

The *gemara* moves to a new point. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak says in the name of Shmuel: *lo shanu ella be-ta'anat milveh ve-hoda'at loveh* — the requirement of *shtei kesef* applies only to the case of *modeh bemiktzat*, where there is a lender's claim and the borrower's partial admission. But *aval ta'anat milveh ve-ha'adat ed echad* — if instead of a partial admission there is a single witness corroborating the claim, then *afilu lo ta'ano ella be-frutah chayav* — even if the entire claim is only a *perutah*, the defendant takes a *shevua*.

Tosafot observes that this ruling tracks neatly with Shmuel's general position. Shmuel had already said that in *modeh bemiktzat*, as long as the initial claim was large enough, one takes an oath even if the amount actually denied is only a penny. That principle — that a *shevua* can attach to a very small disputed amount — naturally extends to *eid echad*: once a single witness corroborates the claim, an oath is triggered regardless of how small the sum. Rav, by contrast, required the denial itself to be *shtei kesef* in *modeh bemiktzat*, and Tosafot suggests he might similarly require a *shtei kesef* denial threshold in the *eid echad* case as well.

### Rav's Eid Echad View

This practical consequence matters for *halacha*. Tosafot rules directly: *leit hilchata ke'vateih de'Shmuel be'ha de'hacha* — we do not rule like Shmuel that *eid echad* triggers a *shevua* even on a *perutah*. Since this ruling about *eid echad* is a corollary of Shmuel's position in the earlier *modeh bemiktzat* dispute, and we rule like Rav in that dispute, it follows that we rule like Rav here as well. Tosafot cites Rabbi Chiyya's *baraita* and Rav Pappa's subsequent discussion as further grounds for ruling like Rav. Accordingly, just as *modeh bemiktzat* requires a denial of *shtei kesef*, so too *eid echad* may require that the amount in dispute reaches that same threshold before a *shevua* is imposed.

### Eid Echad Basis

What is the textual basis for the rule that a single witness can obligate a *shevua* at all? The verse states *lo yakum ed echad be'ish le'chol avon u'le'chol chatat* — one witness shall not stand against a man for any transgression or sin. *Le'chol avon u'le'chol chatat hu de'eino kam* — it is for the purpose of compelling monetary payment that one witness is insufficient. *Aval kam hu li'shvuah* — but one witness can obligate a *shevua*. A *braita* formalizes this: *kol makom she'shnayim mechayvin oto mamon, ed echad mechayvo shvuah* — wherever two witnesses would obligate payment, one witness obligates an oath. This is the principle underlying Shmuel's ruling, and it is why Shmuel extends it even to a claim of a single *perutah*.

---

## Unified Claim Problem

### Shmuel on Multiple Items

The *gemara* introduces a new teaching: *Amar Rav Nachman amar Shmuel: ta'ano chitin u'se'orin v'hoda lo be'echad me'hen chayav* — if one claims that another owes him both wheat and barley, and the defendant admits to one of them while denying the other, he is *chayav*. Even though wheat and barley are two different *minim*, the claim is viewed as a unified *ta'anah*, and admitting to one of the two items constitutes *modeh bemiktzat* of the whole claim.

### Support for Shmuel

Rabbi Yitzchak responded with *yasher koach* — well said — and Rabbi Yochanan likewise stated the same principle. The *gemara* notes that since Rabbi Yitzchak acknowledged Rabbi Yochanan's agreement but did not mention Reish Lakish, one might infer that Reish Lakish disagreed. The *gemara* deflects this: according to some, Reish Lakish was still waiting to hear the statement concluded before chiming in; according to others, he happened to be in the middle of drinking and simply did not interject. Either way, no clear *masoret* emerged from Reish Lakish, which is why his position remained unknown to Rabbi Yitzchak.

### Wheat vs. Barley Alone

The *gemara* attempts to bring support from a Mishnah: *ta'ano chitin v'hoda lo bi'se'orin patur, v'Rabban Gamliel mechayev* — if one claims wheat and the defendant admits only to barley, he is *patur*; Rabban Gamliel says he is *chayav*. The *gemara* reasons: the only reason the *chachamim* rule *patur* is because the parties were talking entirely past one another, the claimant demanding wheat while the admission was barley. But if the original claim had been both wheat and barley — *chitin u'se'orin* — and the defendant admitted to one, surely he would be *chayav*, supporting Shmuel's teaching.

The *gemara* rejects this inference. The *patur* ruling in the case of wheat versus barley could equally apply even if the original claim was *chitin u'se'orin* and only one was admitted. The Mishnah may have given the starker case — full cross-talk between wheat and barley — *le'hodiecha kocho de'Rabban Gamliel*, to reveal the remarkable extent of Rabban Gamliel's position: even where the parties seem to be speaking of entirely different things, Rabban Gamliel considers it *chayav*.

### Vessels & Land Problem

A further challenge arrives: *ta'ano keilim v'karka'ot, hoda bi'keilim v'chafar bi'karka'ot, bi'karka'ot v'chafar bi'keilim patur* — if one claims both vessels and land, and the defendant admits to the vessels while denying the land, or admits to the land while denying the vessels, he is *patur*. The *gemara* proceeds to the case on 40b: *hoda be'miktzat karka patur* — if the admission consists entirely of some of the land, he is *patur*, since *karka* does not obligate a *shevua*. But *hoda be'miktzat keilim chayav* — if he admitted to some of the vessels while denying others, he is *chayav*, and the *shevua* on the vessels draws in the land as well.

The *gemara* notes that the *diyuk* here seems strong: the reason for *patur* in the earlier cases involving land must be precisely that *karka lav bar shvua hi* — land is not subject to oath. If the only reason for *patur* is the involvement of land, then in a case of two types of vessels — analogous to *chitin u'se'orin* — admitting to one while denying the other should be *chayav*. This would directly support Shmuel.

The *gemara* resists the inference. The *patur* in the vessel-and-land cases could equally apply even in a case of two types of vessels, because the parties are addressing two distinct *minim*. The reason *karka* is specifically mentioned is not to identify the unique exemption for land, but to teach the *chiddush* at the end: when one is obligated by a *shevua* on the vessels, that *shevua* extends to cover the land as well. The *gemara* then asks whether this principle is not already derived from the Mishnah *zokkim et ha-nechasim she'ein lahen achrayut lishava aleihem* — that *metaltelin* on which an oath is taken drag in real estate. The *gemara* answers: *hai ikar hi agav grara nasveih* — here is the primary source for that ruling; what is stated in Kiddushin in the context of *kinyanim* is incidental. The *gemara* concedes that the *pshat* reading of the vessel-and-land case does seem to say one would be *chayav*, but presses the point that the *patur* there can be explained on grounds independent of the two-*minim* theory.

---

## Chitin Debate Resolution

### Unified Claims Problem

The *gemara* now directly confronts the competing versions of Rabbi Yochanan's position. One transmission, quoted by Rav Nachman in Shmuel's name, had Rabbi Yochanan agreeing that *chitin u'se'orin* with admission to one is *chayav*. But Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba reports in Rabbi Yochanan's name: *ta'ano chitin u'se'orin v'hoda lo be'echad me'hen patur* — you are *patur*.

The *gemara* acknowledges the contradiction and states: *amora'ei ninhu aliba de'Rebbe Yochanan* — it is a dispute among *Amoraim* about what Rabbi Yochanan actually held. The transmission was unclear, perhaps because Reish Lakish was quietly listening and others were not present to hear the definitive statement.

The *gemara* returns to challenge the *patur* version of Rabbi Yochanan's position with the same sources raised before, now as contradictions rather than as support. The Mishnah states *ta'ano chitin v'hoda lo bi'se'orin patur, v'Rabban Gamliel mechayev*. The *diyuk*: the only reason for *patur* here is that the parties were talking past one another. If the claim was *chitin u'se'orin* and one was admitted, the implication is *chayav* — directly against this version of Rabbi Yochanan. The *gemara* gives the same answer as before: even in the *chitin u'se'orin* case you would be *patur*, and the Mishnah presents the cross-talk case only *le'hodiecha kocho de'Rabban Gamliel*. Similarly, the vessel-and-land case is re-examined and resolved identically to before.

### Rava's Challenge

Rava presses harder with a cleaner source: *tanu shor v'hoda lo b'seh, seh v'hoda lo b'shor patur* — if you are claimed to have an ox and you admit only to the sheep, or vice versa, you are *patur*, because you are speaking of entirely different objects. But *tanu b'shor v'seh v'hoda lo b'echad mehem chayav* — if the original claim was for both an ox and a sheep, and you admit to one, you are *chayav*. This is the *chitin u'se'orin* scenario stated with perfect clarity, and it says *chayav*.

### Admon's Position

Rava anticipates the response: *ha mani Rabban Gamliel hi* — that is Rabban Gamliel's position. But the *gemara* immediately pushes back: if it were Rabban Gamliel, then even the first case of ox versus sheep should be *chayav*, since Rabban Gamliel rules *chayav* even when the parties are talking past one another. So it cannot be Rabban Gamliel. *Ela ha mani Admon hi* — this must be the position of Admon.

Here the *gemara* invokes the case of Admon from elsewhere: if one claims jars of olive oil and the defendant admits to having the jars but denies the oil, Admon rules *chayav*. Implicitly, that is exactly the *chitin u'se'orin* scenario — the claimant demands oil *and* the jars, the defendant admits only to the jars. Admon holds that admitting to one item within a unified claim is *modeh bemiktzat* of the whole. So whatever the *chachamim* hold in that dispute, Admon clearly rules *chayav* in the *chitin u'se'orin* type of case.

### Rava's Resolution

Rava concludes: *v'lo dichuyi m'dachinan lach, ela Talmud aruchu b'piv shel Rabbi Yochanan* — I am not merely deflecting you. This is a well-established teaching in the mouth of Rabbi Yochanan himself. When Rabbi Yochanan rules *patur* in the *chitin u'se'orin* case, he is ruling in accordance with the *chachamim* who disagree with Admon, and when the *braita* about the ox and the sheep says *chayav*, *ha mani Admon hi* — that is Admon's position, not the standard *halacha*.

This resolves the apparent contradiction within Rabbi Yochanan's reported rulings. The version that says *chayav* in the *chitin u'se'orin* case reflects Admon's position, which Rabbi Yochanan was perhaps citing or explaining rather than endorsing as normative. The version that says *patur* reflects Rabbi Yochanan's own ruling, following the *chachamim*. Rava establishes this as the definitive and settled teaching, and the daf concludes here.

---

---

# Shevuot 41

## Modeh B'miktzas

### Shmuel's Cases

The daf begins approximately twenty lines before the bottom of 40b, at the passage commencing with the words *Rav Anan*. The Gemara there picks up a series of statements transmitted in the name of Shmuel concerning the precise requirements for *modeh b'miktzas* — the partial admission that triggers a biblical oath obligation — and, in particular, what counts as an admission that is *mimin hata'ana*, of the same type as the original claim.

### Wheat & Barley

The first case: *tano chitim vekodam vehodo lo bese'orim* — the claimant said "you owe me wheat," and was about to add "and barley," but before he could finish, the defendant pre-empted him and said, "No, I owe you barley." Shmuel's earlier statement had established that had the claimant actually said "wheat and barley" and the defendant admitted to the barley, that would constitute a valid *modeh b'miktzas* — it would be *mimin hata'ana*, of the same category as the claim — and the defendant would be obligated in a *shvua*. But in this case, only "wheat" came out of the claimant's mouth, and the defendant responded "barley." He has not admitted to any part of the stated claim, and on the face of it he appears to be a *kofer hakol*, a total denier, and would be exempt from the *shvua*.

### Intent & Scheming

The Gemara resolves the ambiguity as follows: *im kimarim chayav ve'im b'miskaven patur* — if the defendant was acting as a schemer, meaning he knew the claimant was about to include barley and deliberately cut him off in order to prevent that word from being spoken, then he is obligated in a *shvua*. But if he was acting innocently — he heard "wheat," he said "no, barley," with no strategic intent — then he is exempt.

The precise nature of the obligation in the first case is itself unclear. One possibility is that it is only a rabbinic obligation: technically, on a biblical level, the defendant has escaped the *modeh b'miktzas* structure, but the rabbis impose a *shvua* where manipulation is detected. Alternatively, the very definition of what constitutes the *ta'ana*, the claim, may be contextually determined: if the defendant demonstrably knew that "barley" was about to be part of the claim and was effectively responding to it, then the claim did include barley, and the admission falls squarely within *mimin hata'ana* even at the biblical level.

### Two Vessels

The Gemara continues: *tano shenei machtim vehodo lo b'achas mehen chayav* — if the claimant demanded two needles and the defendant admitted to one of them, he is obligated. This spells out a principle discussed earlier: *keilim*, vessels or discrete objects, operate under a distinct standard for *modeh b'miktzas*. The normal threshold requires a claim of at least two *ma'ah* — a substantial monetary amount — but in the case of *keilim*, the two-item structure is itself sufficient, regardless of market value. The Gemara phrases this as *lefikach yatzo keilim lemah shehen* — that is why *keilim* are treated as their own category, whatever their monetary worth. Tosafot qualifies this by insisting that each needle must still be worth at least a *pruta* in order to have the requisite significance, but the two-*shekel* threshold does not apply.

### Rav Pappa's Case

Rav Pappa introduces a further refinement: *tano keilim uperuta vehodo b'keilim vekhafar b'peruta patur* — if the claimant demanded two needles and a *pruta* and the defendant admitted to the needles but denied the *pruta*, he is exempt. Conversely, *hodo b'peruta vekhafar b'keilim chayav* — if he admitted to the *pruta* and denied the needles, he is obligated.

### Rav vs. Shmuel

The Gemara explains this outcome elegantly: *chada k'Rav vechada k'Shmuel* — one of these rulings follows Rav and one follows Shmuel. Rav had maintained that *kefiras ta'anas shte kessef* — not only must the claim reach the two-*ma'ah* threshold, but the denial itself must be of sufficient magnitude, either two *ma'ah* in value or two *keilim* in kind. In Rav Pappa's case, the claim is certainly sufficient — it includes two needles and a *pruta*. The question is whether the denial reaches the required standard. If the defendant denied the *pruta* and admitted the needles, the denial is too small, and he is exempt — this is *k'Rav*, following Rav's standard for the denial. If, however, he admitted the *pruta* and denied the two needles, the denial is substantial — two discrete *keilim* — and he is obligated. That ruling, in turn, follows Shmuel's principle that if two distinct types of items are claimed (*chitim use'orim*) and the defendant admits one category while denying the other, the partial admission constitutes *modeh b'miktzas* even though what was denied is entirely separate from what was conceded. Notably, Rav did not dispute Shmuel on this point. The conclusion thus synthesizes both positions: the denial must be of sufficient magnitude (Rav), and admission to one of two distinct categories of items suffices as a partial admission (Shmuel).

## Kofer HaKol

### Rav Nachman's Oath

The Gemara now returns, with the two-dot marker, to the Mishnah. The Mishnah states that if someone demands a hundred *zuz* and the other party responds "I owe you nothing," the denier is exempt — *kofer hakol patur*. The natural reaction to this is astonishment: is a total denial truly without any consequence whatsoever? The Gemara immediately addresses this. *Amar Rav Nachman mashbi'in oto shvuat hesset* — Rav Nachman rules that we do make the denier take a *shvuat hesset*.

### Presumption

What is a *shvuat hesset*? The word *hesset* likely means something like "persuasion" — Rashi understands it as a *shvua* that rabbinic authority effectively compelled; the individual technically has no biblical obligation, yet the rabbis pressed the point with considerable force. More substantively, the *shvuat hesset* is a generic rabbinic *shvua* distinct from the small, carefully defined set of cases of *nishba'in venotlin* — those specific situations where a claimant with strong circumstantial support is allowed to swear and collect. The *shvuat hesset* is far broader: it applies essentially any time a denial is made without corroboration on either side.

The rationale for imposing it on the *kofer hakol* is stated plainly: *chazakah ein adam tove'a ela im ken yesh lo alav* — there is a presumption that a person does not press a monetary claim unless there is some legitimate basis for it. If the claimant says you owe me a hundred *zuz*, the mere fact of that demand raises enough suspicion that we require the defendant to back his denial with a *shvua* before we let him walk away.

### Stalling vs. Lying

The Gemara immediately raises a counterpoint: *chazakah ein adam me'iz panav bifnei ba'al hovo* — there is also a presumption that a person would not have the audacity to deny a debt to the face of a creditor. If he denies it, perhaps he is telling the truth and the presumption favors him. The Gemara rejects this: *ishtamutei hu deka mishtamit lei* — he is merely stalling. The debtor may know perfectly well that he owes the money but is buying time: *savar ad hava lei parana lei*, he thinks, "let me get the funds together and I'll pay him later." The social pressure of total denial is therefore insufficient evidence of innocence, and the *shvuat hesset* remains appropriate.

### Loan vs. Deposit

The Gemara then cites a ruling of Rav Idi bar Avin in the name of Rav Chisda that illuminates the nature of this stalling behavior: *hakofer b'milveh kasher l'eidus, b'pikadon pasul l'eidus* — one who falsely denies a loan remains valid as a witness, whereas one who falsely denies holding a deposit is disqualified as a witness.

What distinguishes the two? When someone denies a loan, even if witnesses subsequently demonstrate that the denial was false, the denial is understood as a form of stalling — the debtor was not intending to permanently deprive the lender of his money, only to delay. Such a lie, motivated by temporary embarrassment or financial difficulty rather than an intent to steal, does not constitute the kind of moral corruption that disqualifies a witness. A deposit is different. If someone has an object in his possession and denies holding it at all, that denial can only be understood as an intent to steal — there is no temporal reprieve logic available. That constitutes a fundamental dishonesty that does invalidate witness testimony.

The implication for *shvuat hesset* is that the denial of a loan, even if false, reflects a kind of defensible human weakness rather than genuine wickedness — which is precisely why the mere fact of denial is not itself determinative. We therefore require a *shvua* to supplement the denial, rather than simply believing or disbelieving the defendant outright.

### Both Cases

The Gemara notes that *Rav Chavivi matni a'seifa* — Rav Chavivi taught Rav Nachman's ruling in connection with the second part of the Mishnah rather than the first. The second part of the Mishnah deals with a case where the defendant had initially admitted the debt — "yes, you are owed a hundred *zuz*" — and then the following day claimed to have already paid it. There, the existence of the debt is established; the question is only whether it was discharged. Rav Nachman imposes the *shvuat hesset* on this denier as well.

The Gemara then observes: *man d'matni a'reisha kol sheken a'seifa* — whoever holds that the *shvuat hesset* applies even in the first case, where there is no prior evidence of any debt at all, would certainly apply it in the second case, where the debt's prior existence is known. The *shvuat hesset* in the first version is therefore the more expansive ruling, and the second case is virtually self-evident by comparison.

## Drora D'Mamona

### Connection Req'd

According to the second version of Rav Nachman's statement — the one attributed to Rav Chavivi — the *shvuat hesset* requires *drora d'mamona*: an established monetary connection between the parties. The case of the second part of the Mishnah satisfies this because the debt was already admitted. *Aval hatam d'leika drora d'mamona* — but in a case where no such basis exists, where the claimant's demand emerges entirely without prior foundation, the *shvuat hesset* would not apply. The term *drora d'mamona* combines *mamona*, money, with *drora*, understood by the *rishonim* as something like *shaychus* — a connection or linkage — indicating that the claimant has some established, demonstrable nexus to the money being claimed, not merely a bare assertion.

### Tosafot Ruling

The question then arises: what is the *halacha*? Tosafot, citing Rabbeinu Tam, rules as follows: *hashta d'lo itmar hilcheta k'chad meihanei lishni* — since neither version of Rav Nachman's statement has been definitively adopted, we are left with two competing positions. In a case where there is no *drora d'mamona*, should we nonetheless impose the *shvuat hesset*? Tosafot applies the principle of *hamotzi meichavero alav hare'aya* — the burden of proof rests on the claimant — to the *shvua* context as well: just as we cannot extract money from a defendant without proof, we cannot extract a *shvua* from him without sufficient basis. Therefore, where there is doubt whether the *shvuat hesset* applies, we do not impose it.

At the same time, Rabbeinu Tam acknowledges that he did not object to judges who regularly applied the *shvuat hesset* even without *drora d'mamona* — judges found it useful for promoting candor and giving their verdicts greater weight. Tosafot further notes that there is something to be said for the first version of Rav Nachman's ruling — that the *shvuat hesset* applies even without any prior basis — since among the two versions of a Talmudic statement, the first formulation is typically considered the primary one and carries greater weight. However, Rabbeinu Tam adds that when there is an *ika d'amri* — an alternate formulation — we follow the more lenient view, and since imposing a *shvua* without *drora d'mamona* is the more demanding position, we refrain from it.

### Shepherd Case

Tosafot then discusses what constitutes *drora d'mamona* by reference to a case in the first chapter of Bava Metzia involving a shepherd. In that case, there was an established pattern: each day, a flock would be entrusted to a shepherd's care. On one particular day, the owners claimed to have handed over sheep without witnesses, and the shepherd denied receiving them. The court imposed a *shvuat hesset*. The question is whether this constitutes a case with *drora d'mamona* or not. On that specific day, there is no evidence of a transaction. But the pattern of daily dealings over an extended period creates a strong contextual probability that the handover occurred. Rabbeinu Tam holds that this suffices as *drora d'mamona* — the established course of dealings provides the necessary nexus to the claimed money, even in the absence of witnesses to that day's transaction.

## Shevua D'Oraita

### Mehapaich Shvua

With the nature of the *shvuat hesset* established, the Gemara turns to the structural differences between a *shvua d'Oraita* and a *shvua d'Rabbanan*. The question posed is: *mai ika bein shvua d'Oraita lishvua d'Rabbanan?* — what precisely distinguishes them? The first answer offered is *mehapaich shvua* — the reversibility of the oath obligation. This refers to the option of a party who is required to take an oath instead turning to the other side and saying: "I do not wish to swear; you swear, and I will pay."

### Mar bar Rav Ashi

The Gemara initially states that by a *shvua d'Oraita*, the oath cannot be reversed — *lo mehaphinan*. If the *nitva* (defendant) refuses to swear, he simply pays; he cannot transfer the obligation to the *tove'a* (claimant). By a *shvua d'Rabbanan*, however, the oath can be reversed — *mehaphinan*. The *nitva* may decline and place the *shvua* on the other party, who must then swear or forgo collection. Mar bar Rav Ashi disputes this, holding that even a *shvua d'Oraita* may be reversed. According to his position, if a defendant in a *modeh b'miktzas* situation refuses to swear and instead demands that the claimant swear, the claimant is indeed presented with that option. If the claimant also declines, both parties would presumably walk away.

### Seizure Question

If Mar bar Rav Ashi holds that reversal is available even for a *d'Oraita* oath, what then distinguishes a *shvua d'Oraita* from a *shvua d'Rabbanan*? The Gemara answers: *mechas l'nechsei* — whether the court proceeds to seize the defendant's property. By a *d'Oraita* obligation, if the defendant refuses to swear and refuses to reverse the oath, the court will send the equivalent of the sheriff to seize his assets. By a *d'Rabbanan* obligation — specifically a *shvuat hesset* — under one view, the court acknowledges the obligation to pay but will not back it up through seizure of property.

### Rav Yosef View

Rav Yosef, however, disputes this asymmetry. He holds that even rabbinic monetary obligations are backed by court enforcement. His position is derived from a broader principle: the Gemara cites the case of a *cheresh, shoteh, veikatan* — a deaf-mute, imbecile, or minor — who finds a lost object. There is a view that the object is "theirs" only *mipnei darchei shalom*, for the sake of civil order, without conferring true legal ownership; accordingly, if someone takes it from them, the court would not intervene. Rav Yosef, however, holds that the rabbis declared such a finder a *gezel gamur* in the rabbinic sense — a genuine owner by rabbinic decree — and therefore the court would compel restitution if someone takes the object away. The Gemara reads this disagreement as touching a global principle: whenever a rabbinic ruling creates an obligation or a right, does the court actively enforce it through seizure? The *chachamim* say no; Rav Yosef says yes. Applied to *shvuat hesset*, if the defendant refuses to swear, Rav Yosef would hold that the court treats him as owing the money and would seize assets accordingly.

### Chashud

A further distinction between *d'Oraita* and *d'Rabbanan* concerns the *chashud al hashvua* — a person suspected of swearing falsely, such as a known gambler or one previously found to have taken a false oath, who consequently cannot be asked to swear at all. By a *shvua d'Oraita*, when the defendant is disqualified from taking the oath, the court reverses the obligation: *afchinan lei shvua veshadina aidach* — the oath is transferred to the claimant, who swears and collects. By a *shvuat hesset*, however, this further step is not taken — *takanta letakanta lo avdinan* — we do not stack one rabbinic remedy atop another. The result is that a defendant known to swear falsely is, paradoxically, released from liability entirely when the underlying obligation is only rabbinic. He cannot be made to swear, and the *tove'a* cannot swear in his place.

## Refusing Oath

### Cherem Imposed

Returning to the view that by a *shvuat hesset* the court does not proceed to seizure of property, the Gemara asks: *mai avdinan lei?* — what do we do with someone who refuses to take the *shvuat hesset*? The answer is: *meshamtinan lei* — we place him in *cherem*, rabbinic excommunication. The social and communal pressure of *cherem* functions as a substitute for the coercive power of physical enforcement.

### Crude Force

Ravina challenges Rav Ashi: is *cherem* really so different from outright coercion? If *cherem* effectively forces the person to comply — Rashi notes the passage here employs a crude expression, describing the process as grabbing the man by a part of his anatomy in order to compel him to surrender his cloak — then the pressure exerted is functionally indistinguishable from sending in the sheriff.

## Refusing Oath (II)

### 30-Day Cherem

Rav Ashi responds: *meshamtinan lei ad d'mati zman negdei* — the *cherem* is maintained for thirty days, after which, under the *halacha*, one who remains under *cherem* without rectifying the matter receives rabbinic lashes, and is then released. The structure is therefore: thirty days of *cherem*, followed by lashes, followed by release. It functions like a contempt-of-court sentence of fixed duration. After that period, if the person is willing to undergo *cherem* and lashes rather than pay, he is in principle released. The practical reality is that this does represent a meaningful difference from a *d'Oraita* obligation, where property seizure would occur regardless of the defendant's willingness to endure communal sanction.

## Shtar Rules

### Debt Document

The Gemara now introduces a structurally inverse case. Rather than a claimant appearing with nothing more than a bare assertion, here the claimant produces a *shtar* — a written debt instrument with witnesses — establishing that David owes him a hundred *zuz*. David responds that the debt has been fully paid. *Lav kol kminach, zil shalim* — the court tells David he is not believed; go pay. A defendant's bare claim of repayment is insufficient to overcome a *shtar* in the other party's possession.

### Debtor Reversal

But suppose David then says: I will pay, but I want the creditor to take a *shvua* first that the debt is not yet satisfied. *Aminan lei ishtava lei* — the Gemara says we tell the creditor: go ahead and swear to him. So even when the claimant has the full weight of a *shtar* behind him, the defendant may nonetheless demand a *shvuat hesset* before paying.

### Pogem Shtaro

Rav Acha the son of Rav Yosef raises an objection to Rav Ashi: *u'mah bein zeh lepogem et shtaro?* — how is this different from the established rabbinic case of *pogem shtaro*, the creditor who himself concedes that part of the debt recorded in the *shtar* has been repaid? In that case, the rabbis specifically ordained that the creditor must take a *shvua* before collecting the remainder, precisely because his admission that part was paid introduces doubt about the whole. But if a *shvua* can be demanded even when the *shtar* is entirely intact and uncontested, why was it necessary to institute a special rule for *pogem shtaro*?

The Gemara responds: *hasam af al gav delo ta'in ihu taninan lei* — in the case of *pogem shtaro*, even if the defendant does not raise the demand himself, the court proactively imposes the *shvua* on the creditor. *Taninan lei anan* — we make the argument on the defendant's behalf. Here, by contrast — *hacha amrinan lei zil shalim lei* — the court tells the defendant to go pay; we do not suggest the *shvua* unprompted. It is only *v'i ta'in v'amar ishtava li* — if David expressly demands it — that the court then responds, *zil ishtava lei*, go and swear. The distinction is between a court-initiated oath and a defendant-initiated demand.

### Tzurva Exception

The Gemara introduces a further qualification: *v'i tzurva meRabanan hu lo mashbi'inan lei* — if the claimant is a *tzurva meRabanan*, a Torah scholar, we do not require him to take the *shvua* even upon the defendant's demand. The rationale is that demanding a *shvua* from a scholar implies a suspicion of dishonesty that is incompatible with his standing. Notably, this exemption is not mentioned in ordinary cases of *shvuat hesset* — a *tzurva meRabanan* presumably takes a *shvuat hesset* like everyone else — but here, where the scholar has the additional backing of a *shtar*, the combination is held sufficient to waive the *shvua* demand entirely.

### Objection

Rav Yeimar objects to Rav Ashi: *tzurva meRabanan mashlach glima d'inshi?* — does a Torah scholar have the right to strip people of their cloaks? If we exempt him from the *shvua* that any other creditor would have to take, we are effectively granting him an immunity that allows him to collect without any check on his claim — that is, to potentially rob people with impunity. This is reminiscent of the earlier discussion about whether a *tzurva meRabanan* should sit or stand in court relative to the other litigant. Favoritism that compromises the integrity of the judicial process cannot be tolerated.

### Case Delayed

The Gemara's resolution is striking: *lo mizdakkinan lei l'dinei* — the court simply never hears his case. Unable to ask the scholar to take a *shvua* (which would impugn his integrity) and equally unable to exempt him from it without creating an unjust favoritism, the court resolves the tension by indefinitely deferring his claim. A *tzurva meRabanan* with a *shtar* in hand — even a substantial debt document — will find his case perpetually delayed. This is, as the lecturer observes, a paradoxical outcome: the defendant's bad faith in demanding a *shvua* is accommodated at the scholar's expense, and the scholar is in effect penalized for his status. Yet that appears to be the Gemara's conclusion.

## Witnesses Required

### Rav Yehuda

The Gemara introduces a ruling in the name of Rav Yehuda citing Rav Assi: *hamalveh et chaveiro b'eidim tzarich l'poro b'eidim* — one who lends money to another in the presence of witnesses must be repaid in the presence of witnesses. Implicit in this ruling is that if the borrower cannot produce witnesses to the repayment, his claim of having paid will not be credited.

### Shmuel Position

When Rav Yehuda presented this ruling before Shmuel, Shmuel responded that the borrower may say: *paraticha bifnei ploni u'ploni vehalchu lahem limdinat hayam* — I paid you in the presence of so-and-so and so-and-so, and they have since gone overseas. In other words, Shmuel holds that even if repayment required witnesses, the borrower is not actually obligated to produce those witnesses. He may claim they were present and have since become unavailable. The practical upshot is that, for Shmuel, even a loan made with witnesses does not in the end subject the borrower to a strict production requirement; the bare claim of witnessed repayment is accepted.

### Mishnah Conflict

The Gemara notes a tension with the Mishnah. The Mishnah's earlier case — where the defendant initially admitted the debt and the following day claimed to have paid — appears to address a situation where the acknowledgment was made in the presence of witnesses. That, says the Gemara, is analogous to a loan made with witnesses (*k'man d'ozfay b'eidim dami*), and yet the Mishnah states that a claim of repayment is believed — *patur*. This seems to support Shmuel's lenient view. The Gemara identifies this as a potential *tyuvta* against Rav Assi's stricter position.

### Rav Assi

Rav Assi deflects: *ana ki amri heicha d'me'ikara ozfay b'eidim d'lo leideihimnei* — I only said that witnesses must be produced if the loan was originally made with witnesses specifically *because* the lender signaled from the outset that he did not trust the borrower and expected all transactions to be fully documented. In the Mishnah's case, the original loan was not made with witnesses; it was only the subsequent admission of debt that occurred in their presence. That circumstance does not carry the same implication of distrust and does not trigger the witness-production requirement. Therefore, the Mishnah's ruling that the borrower is believed is consistent with Rav Assi's position.

### Rav Assi

Rav Yosef teaches a variant version of the exchange. In this version, the initial ruling of Rav Assi is actually the lenient one: *hamalveh et chaveiro b'eidim eino tzarich l'poro b'eidim* — even if the loan was made with witnesses, no witnesses are required for repayment, absent an explicit stipulation. Only if the lender expressly stipulated — *al tifreini ela b'eidim*, do not pay me without witnesses — is the borrower then obligated to repay with witnesses, and presumably to produce them as proof.

### Baraita Debate

When Rav Yehuda then presented Shmuel's claim to Shmuel himself in this formulation, Shmuel responded identically: even if the lender stipulated that repayment must occur before witnesses, the borrower may still claim *paraticha bifnei ploni u'ploni vehalchu lahem limdinat hayam* — that he paid in the presence of witnesses who are no longer available. For Shmuel, the condition is interpreted narrowly: it governs the modality of repayment, not the evidentiary standard for proving it later. Unless the lender spelled out explicitly both that witnesses must be present *and* that no claim of repayment will be credited without their production, Shmuel holds that the condition does not compel the borrower to produce them.

The Gemara then examines a *baraita* that appears to contradict Shmuel. The *baraita* states: if the lender says "I lent you with witnesses, repay me with witnesses" — *o yiten o yavi ra'aya she-nasati* — then the borrower must either pay now or bring proof that he already paid, implying that the witnesses must be produced. This supports the stricter reading. However, Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira in the same *baraita* endorses Shmuel's position, holding that the borrower may satisfy the condition by claiming the witnesses went overseas.

### Rabbi Yehuda

The *baraita* therefore represents a genuine dispute among *tanna'im*: one view holds that a stipulation requiring witnesses means the witnesses must be produced for the claim of repayment to be accepted; the other, endorsed by Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira and paralleling Shmuel's position, holds that the stipulation governs the act of repayment but not the evidentiary burden.

### Rav Pappa Ruling

Rav Pappa rules in the name of Rava: *hamalveh chaveiro b'eidim tzarich l'poro b'eidim* — if the loan was made with witnesses, repayment must be made with witnesses. This is the most demanding of the positions and represents the formal ruling. However, Rav Pappa also clarifies: if there were no witnesses at the time of the loan and no explicit stipulation was made, then no witnesses are required for repayment — *ein tzarich l'poro b'eidim*. This is the generally accepted *psak* throughout the *Shas*. But if the lender stipulated *al tifreini ela b'eidim* — do not pay me without witnesses — then witnesses are required.

### Unresolved

The final and most contested question — whether the borrower who claims *paraticha bifnei ploni u'ploni vehalchu lahem limdinat hayam* is believed — remains unresolved. The text as standardly understood reads *ne'eman* — believed, following Shmuel — but the *girsa* of the Rambam reads *eino ne'eman*, not believed. The straightforward implication of the Mishnah, and the logical force of demanding witnesses at all, points strongly to the stricter position: if a stipulation requiring witnesses was made, the borrower should have to produce them, and cannot escape the requirement by claiming unavailability. Yet Shmuel — supported by Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira — holds otherwise. The Gemara does not definitively resolve which version governs, leaving the ruling dependent on one's textual tradition.

---

---

# Shevuot 42

## Shmuel's Position

### Shmuel's Rule

The daf opens by continuing from 41b, where the *gemara* concluded that according to Shmuel, one who lends money in the presence of witnesses is not required to be repaid in the presence of witnesses. The practical implication for a creditor is clear: either obtain a *shtar* at the time of the loan, or stipulate explicitly that repayment must occur in the presence of witnesses.

### Stipulation Options

When such a stipulation is made, a further question arises. Does the condition require merely that witnesses be present at the time of repayment, or does it require the debtor to actually produce those witnesses in court to prove that payment occurred? The question, in other words, is whether the debtor may claim that witnesses were present but have since traveled abroad — *medinat hayam* — and are therefore unavailable. Is such a claim sufficient, following Shmuel's permissive position, or must the witnesses be physically produced?

### Conclusion Ambiguity

The *gemara*'s conclusion on this point is not fully clear, as it depends on one's *girsa* — the textual variant — in the closing lines of the discussion. Whether we rule with Shmuel, and whether the debtor is believed to claim that witnesses existed but are now in *medinat hayam*, thus remains unresolved as the *gemara* moves forward into a series of concrete cases.

---

## Designated Witnesses

### Creditor's Stipulation

The *gemara* presents its first case. A creditor said to his debtor: when you repay me, repay me specifically in front of Reuven and Shimon. The creditor thus not only stipulated that witnesses must be present, but named the particular individuals he required.

### Different Witnesses

The debtor, ignoring this condition, repaid the creditor in front of two other witnesses — Levi and Yehuda. According to the reading of Tosafot, those witnesses subsequently traveled to *medinat hayam* and are no longer available. The debtor now claims before the court that he repaid the debt in front of Levi and Yehuda, who are abroad, and that this should suffice.

### Abaye's Position

Abaye rules in favor of the debtor. When the creditor said "repay me in front of Reuven and Shimon," he effectively meant "repay me in front of two witnesses." There is no meaningful legal distinction between one pair of valid witnesses and another; the naming of Reuven and Shimon was merely a way of expressing the requirement of witnesses generally. Since the debtor paid in front of two witnesses — and following Shmuel's position that one may claim witnesses went to *medinat hayam* — the debtor is believed and has discharged his obligation.

### Rava's Position

Rava disagrees sharply. If the creditor had simply meant "two witnesses," he would have said "two witnesses." The deliberate naming of Reuven and Shimon was purposeful: *lehachi amar lei be'appei Reuven veShimon* — precisely to foreclose the *medinat hayam* argument. The creditor knew Reuven and Shimon to be reliably available, and specified them so that the debtor could not later invoke the Shmuel defense by naming two witnesses who happen to be away on a lengthy journey. By specifying Reuven and Shimon, the creditor closed off that avenue entirely.

### Tosafot's Interpretation

Tosafot's reading of Rava's position has important consequences for a further scenario. What if the debtor did not merely claim that Levi and Yehuda went to *medinat hayam*, but instead produced Levi and Yehuda in court, and they testified that the debt was repaid? According to Tosafot, this would be entirely effective. The creditor's stipulation naming Reuven and Shimon was designed solely to prevent the *medinat hayam* evasion — to ensure that the debtor could not name absent witnesses. But if actual witnesses appear and testify to repayment, the creditor cannot invoke the stipulation to invalidate their testimony. The debt was objectively repaid and can be proven in court; the creditor has no power to stipulate away valid testimony that stands before the court. The creditor's condition related to *evidence*, not to the legal reality of repayment itself.

### Rashi's View

Rashi reads the case differently and reaches a more far-reaching conclusion. According to Rashi, by stipulating that repayment must occur in front of Reuven and Shimon, the creditor effectively established — and the debtor implicitly accepted — that any other testimony would be treated as invalid. When the debtor received the money on those terms, he agreed that the only witnesses whose testimony would be accepted in this matter are Reuven and Shimon. Thus, even if Levi and Yehuda actually witnessed the repayment and stand ready to testify, their testimony is legally null by force of the prior agreement.
