For *halacha* purposes, it is as though the debt was never repaid.

### Rashi vs. Tosafot

The debate between Rashi and Tosafot thus turns on how far the creditor's stipulatory power reaches. For Tosafot, a creditor may stipulate regarding the *mode of proof* — requiring that witnesses be producible rather than merely claimed as absent — but may not stipulate to *invalidate* testimony that is actually present. For Rashi, the parties may contractually agree to treat specific named witnesses as the exclusive valid testimony in this matter, such that even actual testimony from others is disregarded. One might ask whether, under Rashi's reading, the appearance of Levi and Yehuda might at least trigger a *shvuat hesset* — a floating oath — rather than leaving the creditor with no remedy at all. Perhaps so, but the core point is that for formal collection purposes, Rashi holds that their testimony has been rendered legally inoperative by the prior agreement.

---

## Quality Witnesses

### Halacha Knowledge

The second case involves a creditor who stipulated not named individuals but a qualitative standard: when you repay me, pay me in front of two witnesses who know *halacha*. The concern, perhaps, was that witnesses unfamiliar with the legal context might not appreciate the significance of what they were observing.

### Private Payment

The debtor disregarded this condition entirely and repaid the creditor in private, without any witnesses at all. More specifically, the creditor admits that he received the money — no dispute about that fact. But then a misfortune occurred: immediately after the debtor handed over the money, someone ran up and seized it from the creditor's hands. The parties came before Rav Nachman to adjudicate.

### Deposit Argument

The creditor argued as follows: yes, he concedes that he accepted the money from the debtor — *in, kiburei kabaltinhu* — but since the stipulation required repayment in front of witnesses who know *halacha*, when he actually accepted the money in private, he was not accepting it *as repayment of the debt*. Since the precondition for repayment was not met, the money was taken *derech pikadon* — in the capacity of a deposit. The creditor was holding the debtor's hundred *zuzi* temporarily, intending to return it until such time as the repayment could be properly conducted in front of qualified witnesses. Since he held it merely as a *shomer chinam*, and someone then stole it, he bears no liability to the debtor — and the debt itself remains outstanding.

### Rav Nachman

Rav Nachman rejected this argument outright. Since the creditor conceded that he definitely received the money from the debtor — *keivan de-ka modit de-vadai shakaltih mineih* — it constitutes full repayment, *piraon malya hvei*. If the creditor truly wished to enforce his stipulation about witnesses who know *halacha*, the remedy was simple: *zil aitinhu* — go bring such witnesses. Rav Nachman added, with apparent wit, that he and Rav Sheshet themselves — who had mastered *halacha*, *sifra*, *sifrei*, *tosefta*, and the entire *gemara* — could serve as those witnesses. The debtor could hand back the money and receive it in their presence, thereby satisfying the condition.

### Tosafot Analysis

Tosafot notes that Rav Nachman's offer was *bdichuta be'alma* — essentially a joke — not a serious ruling that the stipulation could still be fulfilled. The deeper point Tosafot draws out is this: once the creditor admits the money was received, no stipulation can reframe that accepted payment as something other than repayment of the debt. A creditor may stipulate regarding what constitutes *evidence* — he may limit what proofs will be accepted in court. But he cannot stipulate that when the debtor actually hands him money and he takes it, it will be treated legally as something other than repayment. At the point of admitted receipt, the law of repayment applies regardless of any prior condition.

### Rashi's Distinction

Rashi introduces a more nuanced point. His reasoning suggests that the creditor's argument fails not because such a stipulation is categorically impossible, but because in this case the creditor said nothing at the moment of receiving the money. Had the creditor explicitly declared at that moment — "I am accepting this not as payment of the debt, but only as a *pikadon*" — that declaration might have been effective. What defeats him here is *devarim shebelev einam devarim*: the unspoken intent to treat the payment as a deposit carries no legal weight. It was a thought in his heart, never expressed.

### R. Akiva Eiger

Rabbi Akiva Eiger in his *Gilyon HaShas* takes a more radical position. Even if the creditor had declared explicitly at the moment of receipt that he was accepting the money only as a *pikadon* and not as payment — and even if the debtor said nothing to the contrary — Rabbi Akiva Eiger holds that this would still not work. If the debtor handed over the money and declared that he was paying it as repayment of the debt, then that is what it is. The creditor, no matter how loudly he protests that he is accepting it only as a deposit, cannot override the debtor's act of repayment through his own unilateral declaration. The debtor owed a hundred *zuzi*, he gave a hundred *zuzi*, he said he was repaying the debt — the debt is paid, and no verbal formula by the creditor changes that legal reality.

---

## Denial Then Proof

### Debtor's Denial

The third case: a creditor demands repayment of a hundred *zuzi*. The debtor responds: *lo hayu devarim me'olam* — nothing of the sort ever occurred; I have no idea what you are talking about.

### Witness Testimony

The debtor then produces witnesses. Those witnesses testify both that the debtor borrowed the money *and* that he repaid it.

### Abaye's Solution

Abaye says: *mai ne'avid* — what can we do to compel the debtor to pay? If we accept the witnesses' testimony in its entirety, they say he borrowed and they say he repaid — the result is that the debt is considered discharged. If we ignore the witnesses, the debtor has denied the loan outright, which is *kofer hakol*, and without a *shtar* he cannot be compelled to pay. Either way, the debtor walks free. The witnesses effectively establish repayment regardless of the denial.

### Rava's Solution

Rava reaches a strikingly different conclusion. When the debtor declared *lo hayu devarim me'olam*, he was not merely denying the loan — he was implicitly testifying that he never repaid anything. The phrase is unambiguous: nothing of this matter ever happened. That cannot be read as "I borrowed and repaid"; it can only mean he is asserting that the entire transaction, including any repayment, never occurred. That implicit testimony — that he never paid — now stands as his own admission against himself. The principle of *hoda'at ba'al din k'mei'ah edim dami* means that one's own admission against oneself carries even greater weight than witness testimony. Therefore, we take the witnesses' testimony that he borrowed, combine it with the debtor's own implicit testimony that he never repaid, and the result is that the debt is outstanding and he must pay.

### Testimony Analysis

This is a striking position. In effect, Rava splits the witness testimony — accepting the half that establishes the loan while the other half, which establishes repayment, is overridden by the debtor's own words. Tosafot observes that had the debtor said something more ambiguous — "I did not borrow" rather than the absolutist *lo hayu devarim me'olam* — we might have interpreted the denial charitably as meaning "I no longer owe you, because I repaid." But the phrase *lo hayu devarim me'olam* cannot be read that way. It is a categorical denial of any transaction whatsoever, and by that very categorical denial the debtor has implicitly testified against his own eventual claim to have repaid.

---

## Witnesses Deny Repayment

### Debtor's Claim

The fourth case: the creditor demands payment of a hundred *zuzi*. The debtor responds that he already paid — specifically, that he paid in front of Ploni and Ploni, naming two individuals as his witnesses.

### Contradiction

The named witnesses are brought to court. Ploni and Ploni testify: *lo hayu devarim me'olam* — no such payment ever took place. They contradict the debtor directly.

### Rav Sheshet

Rav Sheshet considered ruling that the debtor's credibility has been undermined — *huchzak kafan* — in this specific case. Ordinarily, a debtor who denies owing money would be believed, perhaps subject to a *shvuat hesset*. But here, the debtor identified specific witnesses to the alleged payment, and those very witnesses denied it. His credibility in this particular dispute has been destroyed, and even if he were now willing to take an oath, the court would not believe him. He must pay. (This designation of *huchzak kafan* applies only to this specific claim; his general standing in future matters is unaffected.)

### Rava

Rava disagrees and invokes the principle: *kol milta dalo ramya aleh de'inshi lav adaiteh* — for matters that people do not generally pay careful attention to, an error does not constitute a lie, and credibility is not thereby undermined. The debtor knew he had to pay back the money, but he may not have been careful to note the precise identities of the bystanders who happened to witness the transaction.

### Knowledge Standard

Rava's *chiddush* is grounded in the general *halacha* that a debtor without a *shtar* outstanding against him is believed to claim repayment — potentially with a *shvua*, but believed nonetheless. Because the debtor knew he did not strictly need to produce witnesses to be believed, he may not have paid careful attention to exactly who Ploni and Ploni were. He believed them to be those individuals, but since he was never truly relying on them as formal witnesses — his own word being sufficient — the identification error does not rise to the level of a deliberate falsehood. *Lo ramya aleh* — it was not his legal responsibility to track the witnesses' identities — and therefore his credibility is not undermined.

---

## Gallnuts Price

### Gallnuts Claim

The fifth case: the creditor demands 600 *zuzi*. The debtor replies: did I not repay you with 100 measures of gallnuts, valued at six *zuzi* per measure? Six times one hundred equals six hundred — the debt is fully paid.

### Price Dispute

The creditor disputes the valuation. He says the gallnuts were not going at six per *zuz* that day; they were going at four per *zuz*. The debtor therefore paid the equivalent of only 400 *zuzi* and still owes 200.

### Credibility Loss

Two witnesses then testify that on the relevant day the market price — the *sha'ar* — for gallnuts was indeed four *zuzi* per measure, confirming the creditor's account. Rava rules that the debtor's credibility has been undermined: *huchzak kafan*. If the debtor now claims to have paid the remaining 200 in cash, or makes any further argument, he is no longer believed.

### Challenge

Rami bar Chama challenges this: did Rava himself not say just moments ago that matters a person does not closely track — *kol milta dalo ramya aleh de'inshi lav adaiteh* — do not undermine credibility? Perhaps the debtor simply misremembered the price.

### Rava's Answer

Rava responds with a distinction. The price of goods — the *kitzutza detara*, the market rate — is something people consciously know. When a debtor chooses to repay a large loan in gallnuts, he is making a deliberate commercial decision and necessarily knows the current rate. Unlike the identity of bystanders who happen to be present, which is not something a person ordinarily tracks, the exchange rate for the commodity he is using as payment is precisely the kind of information he is responsible for knowing. Claiming that gallnuts were worth six when witnesses establish they were worth four is therefore a conscious misrepresentation, not an innocent error, and it does undermine his credibility.

---

## Different Debt Claim

### Creditor's Admission

The sixth case: the creditor presents a *shtar* and demands a hundred *zuzi*. The debtor claims he paid. The creditor then does something unexpected — he concedes that he received a hundred *zuzi* from the debtor.

### Other Debt Claim

But the creditor asserts: *hani sitrai ninhu* — those funds were for a *different* debt. He claims there was a separate oral loan between them, and the hundred *zuzi* he received discharged that other obligation. The *shtar* debt, he insists, remains outstanding.

### Rav Nachman

Rav Nachman rules: *itra shtara* — the *shtar* has been undermined. Once the creditor admits to having received a hundred *zuzi* and cannot prove the existence of any other loan, we presume that payment was for the *shtar* debt, and the *shtar* can no longer be used to collect. According to Rashi, this means the *shtar* is entirely unusable.

### Rav Pappa

Rav Pappa disagrees: *lo itra shtara* — the *shtar* is not undermined. The creditor still holds the *shtar*, which is prima facie evidence of an outstanding debt. The debtor has not independently proven that the money he paid was for this particular debt. The creditor's claim that it was for a different obligation is plausible, and he is believed. Tosafot, citing Rabbeinu Tam, offers a middle position: the *shtar* is not nullified outright, but if the creditor wishes to collect on it, he must now support it with a *shvua* attesting that it has not been paid.

### Contextual Case

The *gemara* then introduces a variant that illuminates the limits of Rav Pappa's position. Suppose the creditor lent the debtor money specifically for cattle trading — and the debtor repaid a hundred *zuzi* at the cattle market. The creditor again claims *hani sitrai ninhu* — that was for a different debt. Here, Rav Pappa himself concedes: *itra shtara*. The *shtar* is undermined. Why? Because the circumstances create an overwhelming contextual fit between the debt and the payment. The loan was for cattle; the repayment happened at the cattle market. The creditor's claim that this was for some other unrelated debt is implausible in that setting, and he is not believed.

In the original case, by contrast, there is no such contextual connection. The payment and the loan are linked only by the amount. In that circumstance, the creditor retains sufficient credibility to claim the payment was for a separate oral debt, and the *shtar* stands.

### No Witnesses

A clarification: the entire debate over *itra* or *lo itra shtara* concerns a case where there were actually witnesses to the payment — two people who saw the debtor hand over the hundred *zuzi* — but those witnesses said nothing about the *shtar*. The debtor did not ask for the *shtar* to be returned or cancelled in their presence. That is where the dispute applies, and it is the larger *chiddush* of the position that says *lo itra shtara*: even with witnesses to a payment, the creditor's holding of the *shtar* combined with a claim of alternative debt may be sufficient to maintain the *shtar*'s validity.

### Final Rule

A third scenario resolves more simply. If there are no witnesses to the payment at all — the creditor simply admits on his own that he received the money — then everyone agrees the *shtar* is valid and the creditor is believed to say it was for another debt. The principle of *migo* applies: since the creditor could have simply denied receiving any payment at all, the fact that he admitted it and attributed it to a different loan makes his claim credible. The *gemara* notes that this parallels the case cited in the name of Abimi son of Rabbi Abbahu in Ketubot. The *halacha* is ruled as *itra shtara* in the contested case — the *shtar* is undermined when witnesses saw the payment even if the *shtar* was not mentioned — while in the case of the creditor's own unaided admission, he retains the benefit of *migo*.

---

## Stipulated Belief

### Stipulation

The seventh case involves a debtor who explicitly stipulates, as a condition of receiving the loan, that the creditor will always be believed to claim that the debt has not been repaid. This arrangement is made to reassure the creditor — perhaps the creditor feared the debtor might later claim *medinat hayam* or produce witnesses in dubious circumstances — and the debtor formally grants the creditor enhanced credibility: *mehemnat li kol eimat d'amart li lo parana* — you are believed to me whenever you say I have not repaid.

### Oath Demanded

The debtor later pays in front of witnesses. The creditor denies the repayment and, invoking the stipulation, demands that his word prevail. The debtor points to the witnesses.

### Abaye and Rava

Abaye and Rava both rule that the stipulation stands: since the debtor agreed that the creditor would be believed, that agreement carries more weight than the testimony of witnesses. The creditor is believed.

### Rav Pappa

Rav Pappa challenges this. When the debtor said the creditor would be believed, he meant *nee d'hemnai tfei m'nafshei* — that the creditor would be believed over the debtor's own claims. The debtor was granting the creditor enhanced standing compared to himself — foreclosing a simple *kofer hakol* defense — but he was not saying the creditor would be believed over witnesses. The phrase "you are believed" means more than me, not more than external testimony.

---

## Multiple Witness Equival…

### Two or Three

This leads the *gemara* to a more precise version of the stipulation: the debtor now says explicitly that the creditor is believed *k'bei trei* — like two witnesses — whenever he claims non-payment. The debtor subsequently pays in front of three witnesses. The question is whether the creditor's stipulated weight of two neutralizes or is overridden by three.

### Number Question

The further extension: what if the debtor said the creditor is believed like three witnesses, and the debtor then pays in front of four?

### Rav Pappa's Rule

Rav Pappa holds that the stipulation is limited to the number stated. If the creditor was granted the weight of two witnesses and the debtor paid in front of three, the three override the two. The creditor's stipulated credibility did not include being treated as more than two.

### Rav Huna

Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua challenges Rav Pappa. He invokes the well-known principle: *trei k'mei'a u'mei'a k'trei* — in matters of testimony, two witnesses are the equivalent of a hundred. When does the count of witnesses actually matter? Only in the context of *umdena* — assessments, such as when appraisers are brought to value property for seizure in payment of debt. There, more assessors means greater expertise, and the majority view prevails. But in formal legal testimony, two is identical in weight to a hundred. Therefore, if the creditor was granted the status of two witnesses, he equivalently has the status of any number of witnesses, and he neutralizes even three.

### Quantity Counting

The *gemara* then addresses the case where the debtor stipulated "three witnesses" rather than "two." Here, Rav Huna concedes that four witnesses would indeed override the stipulation. Why? Because once the debtor specified three rather than two, the only purpose of mentioning a larger number is to invoke the logic of counting — *keivan de'neichis le'de'ot neichis le'de'ot*. Since there is no qualitative difference between two and three witnesses in terms of testimonial weight, specifying three can only be meaningful if the debtor intended the *quantity* of witnesses to matter. Having imported numerical counting into the stipulation, four witnesses are then sufficient to override a stipulated weight of three.

### Agunah Application

This legal device — stipulating that one party will be believed against a certain weight of testimony — has practical relevance beyond the monetary cases under discussion. It is invoked in attempts to address the *agunah* problem. One proposed solution involves *kiddushin al tnai* — conditional betrothal — but such arrangements are vulnerable to the husband's ability to nullify the condition during the marriage by declaring before witnesses that he is *mevatel* the *tnai*. To foreclose this, the arrangement can include a stipulation in which the husband grants the wife the status of being believed — even against witnesses the husband might later produce — to establish that no such nullification took place. The mechanism analyzed in this *gemara*, by which one party's credibility can be contractually calibrated against a specified number of witnesses, is thus the formal underpinning of such solutions.

---

## No Oath Rules

### Mishnah Rule

The *gemara* turns to a new *mishnah*: one does not take a *shvua* — specifically a *shvuat modeh bemiktzat* — when the claim is made against one by a *cheireish*, *shoteh*, or *katan*. Equally, one does not administer an oath to a *katan*. Rashi notes parenthetically that he had forgotten to explain this *mishnah* when it was first cited and is explaining it here — *shachachti milifaresh hamishnah vehineni mefaresh kan* — a remarkably candid admission given that Rashi is known to have produced multiple editions of his commentary.

### Ki Yitein Ish

The *gemara* derives the rule from the verse *ki yitein ish el re'ehu* — "when a man gives to his fellow." The giving must be the act of an *ish*, a legally competent adult. The giving of a *katan* does not satisfy that standard. This does not mean that a minor cannot create a debt — legally, a minor can have property and a debt can arise from a transaction with him. But the Talmudic mechanism that generates the oath requirement is tied to the quality of the original giving, and that quality is absent when the lender was a *katan*.

### Exception Case

The *mishnah* continues: nevertheless, one does take an oath *to* a *katan* or to *hekdesh*. The *gemara* questions the apparent contradiction: if the rule is that oaths are not required when the claimant is a *katan*, how can one be required to swear *to* a *katan*?

### Rav Bibi

Rav Bibi resolves the contradiction: the case in which an oath is administered to a *katan* is where the money originated from the father. The *katan* comes to court and says: my father lent you a hundred *zuzi*, and the defendant admits to fifty. The oath is triggered not because the *katan* made the loan, but because the original transaction was between adults — *ki yitein ish* is satisfied by the father. The *katan* now appears as the heir pressing the father's claim. The relevant question, the *gemara* establishes, is not who is currently pressing the claim in court, but whether the original giving was by a competent adult.

---

## Self-Claim Oath

### Own Claim Rule

The *gemara* identifies the position of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov: *pe'amim she'adam nishba al ta'anat atzmo* — there are instances in which a person takes an oath based on a claim that, in a sense, originates from himself rather than from a fully standing opposing party.

### Orphan Example

The example: a person approaches an orphan and volunteers that he borrowed a hundred *zuzi* from the orphan's father and has repaid fifty — *amar lo maneh la'avicha beyadi veHe'echaltiv pras*. He thus creates a partial admission — *modeh bemiktzat* — before a party who made no formal demand. Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov rules that this person must take an oath. The *gemara* asks: if no claim was made against him, is he not simply like one who returns a lost object — *meshiv aveida* — a person who volunteers information he was under no obligation to disclose and whom we simply believe? Why impose a *shvua*?

The answer: this is not a case of pure voluntary disclosure. The *katan* — or more precisely, as the *gemara* will resolve, the orphan — did make some form of demand. It is that demand, combined with the partial admission, that triggers the oath. Rav states: *beta'ano katan* — the minor pressed a claim against him. Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov holds that even the demand of a minor suffices to establish the claim side of the equation, so that the defendant's partial admission becomes a *modeh bemiktzat* requiring an oath.

### Adult Orphan

The *gemara* pushes back: if the oath is triggered by the *katan*'s demand, why does the *mishna* call this *ta'anat atzmo* — a claim from himself — if there is actually a *katan* demanding? Moreover, why do the *Rabbanan* say he is merely *meshiv aveida* if there is a claimant? The *gemara* resolves: *le'olam gadol* — the orphan in question is actually an adult. When the *mishna* calls him a *katan*, it means he is a "minor" only in relation to the father's dealings — he is the heir, not the original party to the loan. For purposes of the Talmudic analysis, the case is one of an adult orphan pressing his late father's claim. This is why the *Rabbanan* can argue that the admission is merely *meshiv aveida*, and why Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's position must be grounded in something other than the ordinary mechanics of *ta'anat* — a claim — from a fully standing party.

---

## Chutzpah Principle

### Chutzpah Lack

The *gemara* sets out Rabbah's foundational principle explaining why *modeh bemiktzat* requires a *shvua* at all: *chazakah ein adam me'iz panav bifnei ba'al chovo* — it is an established presumption that a person will not have the *chutzpah* to deny everything in the face of his creditor.

### Partial Admission

If a debtor is lying and trying to avoid paying, he would *want* to deny everything — *be-kulei bei de-lichpariah*. But he cannot bring himself to do so in front of the very person who lent him the money, because *eino me'iz panav bifnei ba'al chovo* — he lacks the brazenness to deny it entirely to his creditor's face. This is why the partial admission cannot simply be taken at face value. The debtor cannot invoke *migo* — the argument that since he could have denied everything and been believed, he should be believed when he partially admits. He could *not* have denied everything, because he would not have had the *chutzpah* to do so.

### Oath Purpose

Yet if the debtor truly could not deny it all, why does he not admit the full amount? Because — *ishtamutei hu de-ka mishtamit mineih* — he is merely stalling. He intends to pay eventually but needs time to gather the funds. He is not a true thief; he is a person under financial pressure trying to buy time. The *shvua* is therefore imposed to induce full admission — *rami shvua ileih ki heichi de-lodei leh* — since he is not truly dishonest, the weight of an oath will prompt him to acknowledge what he actually owes.

---

## Chutzpah Principle (II)

### Father vs. Son

Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov holds that the *chutzpah* principle operates equally whether the creditor is the father himself or the father's son — *lo shena bo ve-lo shena bno eino me'iz*. One lacks the brazenness to deny a debt even to the heir of the person who lent the money. Therefore, there is no *migo* — the debtor could not simply have denied it all — and a *shvua* is required.

### Sages' View

The *Rabbanan* disagree. They hold that while a person will not have the *chutzpah* to deny the debt to the creditor himself — *be-vo hu de-eino me'iz* — he would have no such inhibition before the creditor's son — *aval bifnei bno me'iz*. If the debtor were lying and wanted to deny the debt, he would have had no difficulty doing so when facing the son rather than the father. Therefore, the *migo* argument does apply: since the debtor could have denied the entire debt to the son and been believed, the fact that he instead admitted to half establishes his credibility, making him *meshiv aveida* — a person returning a lost object — who needs no oath.

---

## Self-Claim Oath (II)

### Claim Status

The foregoing analysis crystallizes the structural dispute between Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov and the *Rabbanan*. For Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, the adult orphan pressing his father's claim generates a sufficiently weighty *ta'anah* — combined with the *chutzpah* principle that operates even vis-à-vis the son — to produce a full-fledged *modeh bemiktzat* requiring an oath. For the *Rabbanan*, because one *would* have had the *chutzpah* to deny it all to the son, the partial admission before him is credible on its own terms and the person is simply *meshiv aveida*, exempt from any oath.

---

---

# Shevuot 43

## Oath to Minor/Heir

### Mishna Overview

The daf begins in the middle of 42b, with the *mishna* that will carry us into 43. The *mishna* states that one does not take a *shvua* on the basis of a claim made by a *cheresh shoteh ve'katan* — a deaf-mute, a mentally incompetent person, or a minor — against another party. Yet the very same *mishna* then states that one is *nishba'in lekatan*, that one does take an oath *to* a *katan*. The apparent contradiction demands resolution: which is it?

### R. Elazar ben Yaakov

The first answer offered is that the *mishna*'s phrase *nishba'in lekatan* should not be read literally as referring to a minor at all. Rather, it refers to taking an oath to an heir — specifically, when the son of a deceased creditor comes to collect a debt owed to his father. The question then becomes: if that heir comes with a *bari* — a definite claim that you certainly owe his father money — and you are *modeh bemiktzas*, admitting to part of the debt, do you take an oath? One might argue that you should not, on the grounds of *migo*: since you feel no particular moral relationship to the son (as opposed to the father who lent you the money), you could just as easily have denied the debt entirely. Since you could have been a *kofer hakol*, the partial admission should function like *meshiv aveida* — a voluntary gift — and you should be exempt.

This is precisely the position of *Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov*, and the *Gemara* considers interpreting our *mishna* in accordance with his view.

The *Gemara* challenges this reading: the earlier part of the *mishna* already addresses the heir case explicitly, teaching *maneh l'aba beyadcha, ein lecha beyadi ella chamishin dinar — patur mipney meshiv aveida*. If someone says "you owe my father a hundred dollars" and you reply "I only owe fifty," you are exempt, because the partial admission is treated as returning a lost object. Why, then, does the later clause need to introduce a different rule?

The answer lies in a distinction. In the earlier clause, the heir comes with a *safeik* — a tentative claim, perhaps "I think you owe my father money." In that case, since the claim is both from an heir and uncertain, everyone agrees that any admission functions as *meshiv aveida* and there is no *shvua*. But in the later clause, the heir comes with a *bari* — "I know for certain you owe my father" — and it is specifically in that case that *Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov* holds you are not exempt by *migo*, and therefore must take a *shvuat modeh bemiktzas*. This reconciles the two parts of the *mishna*.

### Shmuel's Approach

*Shmuel* offers an entirely different and remarkably elegant reading of the *mishna*. He argues that *nishba'in lekatan* does not mean responding to a claim made *by* a *katan*, but rather taking an oath when you are coming to *collect from* a *katan* — *lifra minichsei katan*. Similarly, *lehekdesh* means *lifra minichsei hekdesh* — collecting from sanctified property.

Under Shmuel's reading, the case is not one of *modeh bemiktzas* at all. Rather: you hold a *shtar* proving that the deceased father owed you money, and you now seek to collect from the minor orphan heir. The minor cannot mount a proper defense — he lacks the capacity to examine witnesses, present counterclaims, or argue effectively. Therefore, even though all the evidence is in your favor, you must first take a *shvua* that the debt is genuinely still owed before collecting.

The case of *hekdesh* is analogous. The scenario the *Gemara* envisions is not that *hekdesh* itself borrowed money, but rather that David owed you money, you held a prior lien on his property, and David then consecrated that property to *hekdesh*. Since your lien predates the consecration, you may seize the property — and at the moment of seizure, retroactively, it is as though it never became *hekdesh*. Nevertheless, before collecting in this way, you must take a *shvua* that David has not already repaid the debt.

### Heirs & Orphans

The *Gemara* notes that the obligation to take a *shvua* when collecting from *yetomim* is already taught explicitly in a forthcoming *mishna* — *lo yifra ela bishvua*. Why does the present *mishna* need to say it again? The *Gemara* answers that the repetition conveys the *chiddush* of *Abaye Kashisha*, the elder Abaye, who taught: *yetomim she'amru gedolim* — when the *mishna* says you must swear before collecting from heirs, this applies even if the heirs are adults, and needless to say when they are minors.

One might have thought that if the heirs are adults, they can mount a full defense and no special protection is needed. The *chiddush* is that since the adult heirs were not themselves party to the original loan — it was their father who borrowed — they may lack crucial information about what transpired. Therefore the obligation to take a *shvua* before collecting applies regardless of the heirs' age. This applies both to the *shvua* itself and to the rule that one collects only from *zivoris*, third-grade land, even from adult heirs.

### Hekdesh Collection

Returning to the case of collecting from *hekdesh*: the *Gemara* observes that this too is already taught in the forthcoming *mishna* regarding *nechasim meshubadim* — encumbered property — so why does the present *mishna* need to state it separately? The answer is that the two cases are distinct and each needed to be said independently. One might have thought that the requirement to take a *shvua* applies only when a lay person (*hedyot*) holds the lien and might be defrauded, but that no one would scheme (*knunya*) to cheat out *hekdesh*. Therefore the *mishna* teaches that we do require a *shvua* even when *hekdesh* is the party with the lien, since a person who is alive and healthy may indeed conspire to defraud *hekdesh* and receive a kickback.

However, the *Gemara* cites *Rav Huna*, who rules that a *shechiv mera* — a person on his deathbed — who consecrates all his property and then adds "by the way, I owe Reuven a hundred dollars which is already liened and not included," is believed. The reasoning is *chazaka ein adam oseh knunya al hekdesh* — we may rely on the presumption that a person will not scheme to defraud *hekdesh*. Does this not contradict the requirement of a *shvua*?

The resolution distinguishes between the two cases. By a *shechiv mera*, two factors combine: first, one is reluctant to engage in such schemes on one's deathbed; second, and perhaps more importantly, the dying person himself will not live to receive any kickback — it is his children who benefit, a step sufficiently removed that we do not attribute such scheming to him. By contrast, a healthy person (*bari*) who has many years ahead of him and stands to personally benefit from the scheme — there we are certainly concerned, and the *shvua* is required.

### Encumbered Property

The case of *nechasim meshubadim* — encumbered property — involves a scenario where David owes money to two creditors: you and Charlie. You hold a prior lien, and you seek to collect from David's property. But since Charlie also has a claim on that same property, your collecting from it affects Charlie as well. The concern is that David and you might conspire: David will not contest your claim, you will seize the property as though under a prior lien — even if that lien is fictitious — and later return part of the proceeds to David under the table, leaving Charlie unable to collect. This conspiracy is called a *knunya*.

Because a third party (Charlie) stands to lose when the lienholding creditor seizes the property, David's failure to contest your claim is insufficient protection for Charlie. You must therefore take a *shvua* to forestall any such collusion. The same applies when it is *hekdesh* rather than a private individual that holds the parallel lien, as the *Gemara* establishes.

---

## Excluded Objects

### Five Exclusions

The *mishna* now introduces the following categories: *v'eilu devarim she'ein nishba'in aleihen* — these are the objects regarding which no oath is taken. The list comprises slaves (*avadim*), writs of debt (*shtaros*), land (*karka*), and sanctified objects (*hekdesh*). These four categories are excluded from the oath of *modeh bemiktzas*, from the oath of a single witness (*ed echad*), and — as the *mishna* goes on to specify — from several other *halachic* obligations as well.

The first additional exclusion concerns *tashlumei kefel* — double payment for theft. Normally, a burglar pays *kefel*, double the value of the stolen object. If he then slaughters or sells the stolen animal, he pays four or five times its value. All four categories are exempt from *kefel*, and consequently from the four-and-five payment as well, since once *kefel* is eliminated, the incremental payment above *kefel* falls away automatically.

The *mishna* then addresses the laws of *shomrim* — guardians. *Shomer chinam eino nishba, nosei sachar eino meshalem* — an unpaid guardian (*shomer chinam*) need not take an oath regarding these objects, and a paid guardian (*shomer sachar*) need not pay if something happens to them.

It is worth pausing on the classic *shvuat shomrim*. This oath is not a response to an adversarial claim of lying; rather, it functions as corroboration when the guardian reports what befell the object. The owner asks what happened, the guardian explains there was a theft or loss, and the *Torah* requires an oath to substantiate that truthful account. One might therefore have thought that this category of oath — which is not about disputed amounts but about disputed facts — might apply even to the excluded objects. The *mishna* teaches otherwise: these objects are exempt from the *shomrim* oath as well. An unpaid guardian simply asserts what happened and is exempt; a paid guardian who would normally be liable for theft or loss (and who admits as much) is nonetheless exempt from payment when the object falls into one of these categories.

An important question raised by the *Rishonim* but left unresolved explicitly in the *mishna* is whether a *shomer* of these objects bears any *chiyuv shemira* — any legal obligation of care — at all. The exemptions from oath and payment do not necessarily speak to whether the guardian incurred any duty in the first place. Furthermore, several *Rishonim* hold that *poshea hi k'mazik* — negligence is legally equivalent to direct damage. If so, a negligent guardian might be liable even for these excluded objects, not under the laws of *shomrim* but as a tortfeasor. Whether the exclusion of the *shomrim* framework also eliminates the underlying duty of care remains an open question not explicitly addressed in the *mishna*.

### R. Shimon's Kodashim

*Rabbi Shimon* draws a distinction within the category of *kodashim*: *kodashim she-chayav be-achrayutan nishba'in aleihem, ve-she-eino chayav be-achrayutan ein nishba'in aleihem* — sanctified objects for which one bears a replacement obligation are subject to the oath, while those for which one bears no such obligation are not.

The case is this: Charlie takes a *neder* — a personal vow — to bring two *olot*, two burnt offerings. He then designates two sheep for this purpose and gives them to Dov to watch. Dov claims he only received one. According to *Rabbi Shimon*, Dov must take a *shvuat modeh bemiktzas*. Why? Because Charlie's *neder* obligated him personally to bring two *olot*; if those sheep are lost, Charlie must replace them out of his own pocket. The sheep are therefore not merely *hekdesh* from Charlie's perspective — they represent a real financial exposure. Their loss *goremes le-mamon*, it causes a monetary loss. Such sanctified objects are called *davar ha-gorem le-mamon*, and *Rabbi Shimon* treats them as property rather than as *hekdesh* for purposes of the oath requirement.

This stands in contrast to a case where someone merely sanctified an animal without a personal vow: if that animal is lost, there is no obligation to replace it, and it is treated as pure *hekdesh*, exempt from the oath.

### R. Meir Laden Vines

*Rabbi Meir* introduces a further nuance regarding *karka*. The *mishna* states: *yesh devarim she-hen ke-karka ve-einam ke-karka* — there are things that are like land yet are not treated as land *halachically*, and the *chachamim* do not agree with him. His example: if Charlie says "I gave you ten vines laden with grapes to watch" (*esser gefanim te'unot*), and Dov responds "you only gave me five," *Rabbi Meir* holds that Dov must take an oath. The *chachamim* respond: anything attached to the ground (*kol ha-mechubar le-karka*) has the status of *karka* and is excluded.

A surface reading of *Rabbi Meir*'s position suggests that he holds attachment to the ground confers no *karka* status on growing things at all. But the *Gemara* limits his view considerably. *Rav Yosef* citing *Rabbi Chanina* explains: normally *Rabbi Meir* agrees that things attached to the ground are treated as *karka*. The dispute here is specifically because the grapes are *omdot libatzir* — ready for harvest. *Rabbi Meir* holds that grapes at the point of harvest are *k'vatzur dami* — regarded as if already detached and no longer part of the land. The *chachamim* hold they remain *ke-karka* until actually harvested.

---

## Quantifiability

### Mishna Rule

The *mishna* states: *ein nishba'in ela al davar she-be-mida u-ve-mishkal u-ve-minyan* — one takes a *shvuat modeh bemiktzas* only when the disputed object is quantifiable in measure, weight, or number.

### House Full Case

The *mishna*'s example of a non-quantifiable claim: *bayit malei masarti lach* — "I gave you a house full of potatoes." The respondent replies: *ela mah she-inhata atah notel* — "I don't know how much you gave me; take back whatever is here." Since neither the claim nor the response is expressed in any unit of measure, there is no *shvuat modeh bemiktzas*.

By contrast: *zeh omer ad ha-ziz ve-zeh omer ad ha-chalon* — one says the house was filled up to the protruding beam, the other says only up to the windowsill — this is *chayav*, because while no explicit unit is used, the positions of the beam and the window can be measured, and the disagreement is quantifiable.

*Abaye* proposes that the *mishna*'s distinction turns on whether the claim references *this* house specifically. If Charlie says *bayit zeh malei* — "this house, full" — its dimensions can be measured and the claim becomes quantifiable. The generic *bayit malei* is not.

*Rava* objects: if *bayit zeh malei* were considered quantifiable and therefore *chayav*, the *mishna* should have made that its *chiddush* — teaching that even *bayit malei* can suffice when a specific house is named. The fact that the *mishna* instead contrasts *bayit malei* with the *ad ha-ziz / ad ha-chalon* case indicates that even *bayit zeh malei* is insufficient. The reason is that *Rava* requires not merely that the *difference* between claim and response be quantifiable, but that each be articulated in affirmatively quantifiable terms. Saying "this house full" remains too imprecise, lacking any explicit reference to a unit or boundary point. Saying "up to the beam" or "up to the window" crosses that threshold, even without invoking units, because it specifies an objective boundary from which a measurement can be taken.

---

## Excluded Objects (II)

### Kelal-Prat-Kelal

The *Gemara* now derives the exclusion of these categories from the Biblical text using the hermeneutic of *kelal-prat-kelal* — general-particular-general. The verse *al kol devar pesha* ("on any matter of negligence") is a *kelal*; *al shor al chamor al seh al salmah* ("on ox, donkey, sheep, and garment") is a *prat*; *al kol aveidah* ("on any lost object") is a return to the *kelal*. When a *kelal-prat-kelal* structure appears, one derives only cases similar to the particulars. The particular cases — ox, donkey, sheep, garment — are all movable objects (*meitaltel*) with intrinsic value (*gufo mamon*). Therefore the rule applies only to *davar ha-metaltel ve-gufo mamon*: movable objects of intrinsic value. This same *parsha* of the *Torah* governs the oath of *modeh bemiktzas*, the obligations of *shomrim*, and the double payment of *kefel*.

### Kefel Exclusion

From this *kelal-prat-kelal*, the *Gemara* derives the exclusions from *kefel*. Land (*karka*) is excluded because it is not movable. Slaves (*avadim*) are excluded because they are legally equated to land (*hukshu le-karka'os*). *Shtarot* — writs — are excluded because, although they are physically movable, they have no intrinsic monetary value (*ein gufan mamon*); they merely represent value. *Hekdesh* is excluded because the verse says *ki yitein ish el re'ehu* — one person gives to his *neighbor*, specifically a lay person, not consecrated property.

Regarding the four-and-five payment: *tashlumei arba va-chamisha amar Rachmana, ve-lo tashlumei shlosha ve-arba'a* — the *Torah* specified four and five in the context where *kefel* already applies. Once *kefel* is eliminated for these categories, the incremental payments of four and five are automatically eliminated as well, since those amounts presuppose the *kefel* baseline.

### Shomer Obligations

The same *kelal-prat-kelal* structure appears in the *parsha* of *shomer chinam*: *ki yitein ish el re'ehu* is the *kelal*; *kesef o keilim* ("silver or vessels") is the *prat*; *lishmor* ("to watch") functions as the return to the *kelal*. The derivation excludes the identical categories: land (not movable), slaves (equated to land), *shtarot* (movable but no intrinsic value), and *hekdesh* (*re'ehu ketiv* — it says "neighbor," not consecrated property).

The *shomer sachar* exclusion is derived from a parallel *kelal-prat-kelal* in the *parsha* of the paid guardian: *chamor o shor o seh* is the *prat*; *ve-chol behemah lishmor* is the closing *kelal*. The *Gemara* does not belabor the derivation, noting that the structure and conclusions are identical. *Hekdesh* is again excluded by *re'ehu ketiv*.

As noted, the question of whether a *shomer* retains any *chiyuv shemira* — an underlying duty of care — for these objects even after the formal exemptions apply is not explicitly resolved. If *poshea hi k'mazik* — if negligence functions as direct damage — then a *shomer* who is genuinely negligent with such objects might still face liability as a *mazik* rather than as a *shomer*, though this depends on whether the acceptance of the *shomer* role generates any duty of care in the first place.

---

## Quantifiability (II)

### Rava's Standard

*Rava*'s position, introduced above in response to *Abaye*, is now stated as the governing principle: *l'olam eino chayav ad she-yit-anennu be-davar she-be-mida u-ve-mishkal u-ve-minyan, ve-yodeh lo be-davar she-be-mida u-ve-mishkal u-ve-minyan* — one is never liable for a *shvuat modeh bemiktzas* unless both the claim is articulated in quantifiable terms and the admission is likewise articulated in quantifiable terms. It is not enough that the *difference* between claim and response is quantifiable; the claim itself and the response itself must each be expressible in units of measure, weight, or number.

The implication for the *bayit malei* case is that even if one could in principle calculate the volume of a house, the claimant who says merely "a house full" has not articulated a quantifiable claim. One who says "up to the beam" or "up to the window" has done so — not in conventional units, but by specifying a measurable boundary. *Rava* holds that this distinction is meaningful: the former is insufficiently precise to anchor a *shvua*, the latter is not.

### Baraita Examples

A *baraita* supports *Rava*'s position with a series of cases. First: "I gave you a gallon (*kor*) of grain to watch" — the other responds "you never gave me any grain" — *patur*, since the denier is a *kofer hakol*. Second: "I gave you a large *menorah* to watch" — the other responds "you only gave me a small *menorah*" — *patur*. Third: "I gave you a large belt (*azur*) to watch" — the other responds "you only gave me a small belt" — *patur*.

Why is the *menorah* case exempt from a *shvua*? Not only is "large" and "small" insufficiently quantified, but more fundamentally, a large *menorah* and a small *menorah* are different objects. *Ma she-ta'ano lo hoda lo u-ma she-hoda lo lo ta'ano* — what was claimed was not conceded, and what was conceded was not claimed. *Modeh bemiktzas* requires that the admission be to a partial quantity of the very thing claimed. If someone says "I gave you this large table" and you respond "I have only a small table," you are not conceding to part of the claim — you are describing an entirely different object. The *kefel* payment by a *ganav* turns on the same structure: the stolen object must be a subset of what was claimed.

Contrast the exempt cases with those that generate a *shvua*: "I gave you a gallon (*kor*) of grain" — "I only have a half-gallon (*letach*)" — *chayav*. "I gave you a ten-pound *menorah*" — "I only have a five-pound *menorah*" — *chayav*.

### Dual Quantifiability

The *baraita* closes with an explicit formulation of the principle: *kelalo shel davar: l'olam eino chayav ad she-yit-anennu be-davar she-be-mida u-ve-mishkal u-ve-minyan, ve-yodeh lo be-davar she-be-mida u-ve-mishkal u-ve-minyan* — the general rule is that one is not liable unless both the claim and the response are quantifiable. The *Gemara* notes that this explicit statement is included specifically to rule out *bayit zeh malei* — to emphasize that even when a specific house is named, making the dimensions in principle measurable, the claim must be articulated in explicitly quantifiable terms. *Bayit zeh malei* lacks the necessary specificity.

### Menorah Subset

The *menorah* case — where a ten-pound *menorah* is claimed and a five-pound *menorah* is admitted — naturally raises the question: is this not also a case of two different objects? *Ma she-ta'ano lo hoda lo* — just as a large *menorah* and a small *menorah* are different, so too a ten-pound and a five-pound *menorah* would seem to be different objects.

*Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak* initially proposes that the case involves a *menorah shel chuliyot* — a modular *menorah* assembled from components that can be added or removed. A five-pound *menorah* assembled from fewer components is therefore literally a subset of a ten-pound *menorah* assembled from more components, and the admission is to part of the very thing claimed.

The *Gemara* challenges this: if the principle is that modular, addable objects create a subset relationship, why does the *baraita* not teach a similar case for belts, which can be expanded by adding links? The *Gemara* replies that the *baraita* simply did not enumerate every applicable case (*d'laifi lo kasani*), and similarly, one could say the *menorah shel chuliyot* is not the only possible explanation.

*Rav Papa bar Manmiyo* therefore offers a different account. The key is that a ten-pound *menorah* can physically be converted into a five-pound *menorah* by scraping down and thinning out the metal. A shorter *menorah* cannot be produced from a taller one without destroying its integrity — cutting off the base or the top renders it non-functional. But scraping the exterior to reduce weight preserves the object's form and function. Therefore, a five-pound *menorah* is indeed a potential subset of a ten-pound one, since the latter can be transformed into the former. This conversion relationship is what justifies treating the admission as *modeh bemiktzas* rather than as a claim about a different object.

---

## Mashkon Cases

### Mashkon Setup

The *mishna* now presents a series of cases involving *mashkon* — collateral. The scenario is: I lend Charlie a hundred dollars (*sela*), and Charlie gives me his watch as collateral. Subsequently the watch is lost — meaning I, as the *shomer* of the collateral, must bear its loss and reimburse Charlie. A dispute arises between us about the watch's value and what, if anything, Charlie still owes me. The *mishna* works through four permutations.

### Full Denial

First case: I say to Charlie, "I lent you a hundred dollars and the watch was worth only fifty (*shekel* = half a *sela*); you still owe me fifty." Charlie responds: "You lent me a hundred dollars and the watch was worth a hundred — I owe you nothing." Charlie is denying my entire claim against him, making him a *kofer hakol*. The *halacha*: *patur* — no oath is required.

### Partial Admission

Second case: I say to Charlie, "I lent you a hundred dollars and the watch was worth fifty; you still owe me fifty." Charlie responds: "You lent me a hundred dollars, but the watch was worth seventy-five (*shlosha dinarim* = three quarters of a *sela*); I owe you only twenty-five, not fifty." Charlie is conceding that he owes something but disputes the amount — this is *modeh bemiktzas*, and he is *chayav* to take an oath.

### Reversed Denial

Third case: Charlie reverses the roles. He says: "That watch was worth two hundred dollars (*shtayim*). You owe me a hundred dollars more than the loan." I respond: "No — the watch was worth exactly a hundred dollars, equal to the loan; we're even, you owe me nothing." I am the *kofer hakol* in this configuration. *Patur* — no oath required.

### Reversed Partial

Fourth case: Charlie says the watch was worth two hundred dollars, so I owe him a hundred. I respond: "The watch was worth only a hundred and twenty-five (*chamishah dinarim* = five quarters of a *sela*); I owe you twenty-five, not a hundred." I am now the *modeh bemiktzas* — admitting I owe something but disputing the amount. *Chayav* — I take an oath.

### Unusual Oath Rule

These first four cases, while instructive, follow the standard rules of *modeh bemiktzas* in a straightforward way. The *chiddush* of the *mishna* lies in the second case, the one where Charlie should logically be taking the oath. I claim he owes me fifty; he says he owes only twenty-five — he is the *modeh bemiktzas*. Yet the *mishna* rules: *u-mi nishba? mi she-ha-pikadon etzlo* — who takes the oath? The one who is holding the collateral — meaning, *I* take the oath, not Charlie. The *Gemara* will explain why.

---

## Mashkon Oath Reasoning

### False Oath Risk

Why does the *mishna* transfer the oath from Charlie to me? *Shema yishava zeh ve-yotzi hallah et ha-pikadon* — lest Charlie take the oath that the watch was worth seventy-five dollars and only twenty-five is owed, and then I produce the watch and demonstrate it was actually worth only fifty.

The concern is subtle and important. We are not primarily worried that Charlie is lying. Valuation of an object is inherently subjective, and each party has a natural (and perhaps unconscious) bias: the owner of lost collateral tends to recall it as more valuable; the party who owes money has reason to believe it was worth less. Charlie might take his oath in complete good faith, and yet when the watch reappears it could turn out to be worth only fifty dollars, rendering him technically a false swearer despite his sincerity. The *halacha* is concerned about protecting a person from being shown to have taken a false oath, even innocently.

### Lender Takes Oath

To protect Charlie from this predicament, the rabbis transfer the oath to me. I swear — to what? The implication is that I swear the watch was indeed worth only fifty, and on the basis of that oath I collect the full fifty dollars that I claimed. This outcome seems harsh to Charlie: not only is he denied the benefit of his own oath, but he must now pay the full amount I claimed rather than the twenty-five he was prepared to acknowledge. The protection of Charlie's integrity comes at the cost of his money.

### Rav Ashi Principle

Before accepting this outcome as final, the *Gemara* introduces a principle stated by *Rav Ashi* in a different context in *Bava Metzia*. The case is: I asked David to watch my watch. David comes to me and says, "Something happened to it — it was stolen — but I accept liability and will reimburse you." One might think David need say nothing further. He is admitting liability; what more could be required?

*Rav Ashi* holds that David must nonetheless swear *she'eina birshuto* — that the object is no longer in his possession. Why? Because David may have coveted the watch all along, and is now fabricating a theft story so he can pay its value and keep it. To foreclose that possibility, even a *shomer* who voluntarily admits liability must swear that the object is genuinely no longer with him.

### Rav Ashi Solution

With *Rav Ashi*'s principle established, the *Gemara* revisits the *mashkon* case. In that scenario, I am the *shomer* of Charlie's watch. I am saying the watch was lost and that I must deduct its value from the loan — meaning I am in the position of a *shomer* who accepts liability for the object. Applying *Rav Ashi*: before any further oath or collection occurs, I must first swear that I no longer have the watch. This addresses the fear that I might be holding onto it.

Once I have sworn I no longer possess the watch, the concern evaporates: I cannot later "produce" the watch to demonstrate that Charlie's oath was false, because I have already sworn under oath that it is not in my possession. Charlie's oath is therefore protected.

### Sequential Oaths

This is how *Rav Ashi* would read the *mishna*: *mi nishba techila? mi she-ha-pikadon etzlo* — who takes the oath *first*? I do — I swear the collateral is no longer in my possession. Only after that does Charlie take his oath about the watch's value. The ordering is crucial: if Charlie were to go first and swear the watch was worth seventy-five, the concern would remain that I could produce it and expose him. But once I have first sworn it is gone, that concern is eliminated, and Charlie may safely take his own oath.

The result under *Rav Ashi* is importantly different from the simple reading of the *mishna*. In the simple reading, I take the oath and collect the full fifty dollars, leaving Charlie worse off. Under *Rav Ashi*, both parties take oaths in sequence — I first, then Charlie — and Charlie is then able to stand by his claim that the watch was worth seventy-five and pay only twenty-five. The justice of the outcome is restored: Charlie is protected not by stripping him of his money, but by ensuring that the sequence of oaths renders his own *shvua* immune to later contradiction.

---

---

# Shevuot 44

## Shmuel's Collateral

### Shmuel's Framework

The daf opens, roughly fifteen lines into 43b, at the words *amar Shmuel*. The background is the *mishnah* already studied, which discussed a creditor who held a borrower's collateral (*mashkon*) and then lost it. The *mishnah*'s implicit assumption was straightforward: the creditor must deduct the value of the lost *mashkon* from the outstanding debt, and he owes the borrower compensation equal to that value. Against this backdrop, Shmuel introduces a strikingly different conceptual framework for thinking about *mashkon* altogether.

### Broom Handle Case

Shmuel states: *hai man de'ofei alfa zuza lechavrei umashken lei kata de'magla* — a person who lends a thousand *zuz* to his friend and receives in return a scythe handle as collateral — *avad kata de'magla, avad alfa zuzei*: if he loses that scythe handle, he has lost his thousand dollars. The *mashkon*, in Shmuel's view, is not held because of its intrinsic monetary value; it is not there so the creditor can recoup the debt by selling it. Rather, the implicit understanding of the arrangement is an exchange: you return the handle, I return your money; I return your money, you return the handle. The flip side of that exchange logic is that if the creditor cannot return the handle, the borrower need not repay the debt.

### Rashi's Exchange

Rashi explains that the *mashkon* functions as a one-to-one exchange object. The creditor holds onto it with the understanding that returning the object and receiving repayment are two sides of the same act. This is, admittedly, a puzzling arrangement from the creditor's perspective — why would any *malveh* agree to terms under which a worthless broom handle represents his entire debt? The answer is that one does not have to agree to this arrangement. The question, to be examined shortly, is whether this is the default or whether it requires explicit stipulation.

Rashi continues: *aval tartei katati* — if there were two scythe handles — *lo*: Shmuel's principle would not apply in the same way. Rashi's explanation is that the exchange logic operates as a one-to-one correspondence. If one handle is lost, perhaps the exchange relationship still inheres in the remaining handle; the creditor pays for the lost one, and the surviving handle continues to serve as the symbolic exchange object.

### One vs. Two Objects

The question naturally arises whether losing one of two handles means the debtor is discharged from half the debt. Rashi's reasoning, at least as applied to two identical objects, is that the exchange relationship might be preserved partially by the surviving object. One might have thought that the logic of Shmuel simply does not apply when the *mashkon* consists of multiple objects — that the whole premise of the exchange breaks down, and we revert to strict valuation. But that is not where the Gemara takes us.

### Multiple Collaterals

Rav Nachman goes further: *afilu tartei katati* — even with two handles — *avad chada avad chamesh me'ot, avad idach avad kulei*: lose one handle and you lose 500; lose the other and you lose the remaining thousand. With two identical objects, the debt is divided equally between them. *Aval kata venaska lo* — but if the collateral consists of a handle and a silver ingot, then this equal division would not apply. Rashi explains that the silver ingot clearly exists not as a symbolic exchange object but as something of genuine value that the creditor intends to collect from if the debt goes unpaid. The silver ingot is therefore outside the Shmuel framework entirely; if it is lost, the creditor simply reimburses the borrower for its actual value. The broom handle, however, may still function as the exchange object.

The *Nehardaei* go even further still, ruling that even a handle and a silver ingot — *afilu katva venaskla* — follow equal division: lose the ingot and you lose 500, lose the handle and you lose 500, regardless of the disparity in their actual values.

Tosafot, however, reads the case differently. Because of what follows in the Gemara, Tosafot maintains that Shmuel's framework applies even to objects of real value, and that *kata venaska lo* means not that the silver ingot is excluded from the framework, but that when the two objects are of unequal value, the debt is divided between them *proportionally* rather than equally. If the silver ingot represents ninety percent of the combined value of the collateral and the handle represents ten percent, then losing the ingot forfeits $900 of the debt and losing the handle forfeits $100.

### Shmuel vs. Mishnah

The Gemara now confronts the obvious difficulty: the *mishnah* assumes that when a creditor loses a *mashkon*, he deducts its value from the debt — not that the entire debt is extinguished. The *mishnah*'s case explicitly contemplates a dispute over the value of the *mashkon* and the resulting *shevuat modeh bemiktzat*. Under Shmuel's framework, the moment the *mashkon* is lost, the entire debt disappears, rendering the *mishnah*'s detailed analysis of partial admissions and oaths incomprehensible. If the *mashkon* — regardless of its value — represents the full debt, then Gloria, upon learning her watch was lost, owes nothing, takes no oath, and the entire litigation framework of the *mishnah* collapses.

The Gemara resolves this with a distinction: *masnisin b'defarish, Shmuel b'delo parish* — the *mishnah* speaks of a case where the terms were made explicit, while Shmuel speaks of a case where they were not. The question is which direction this distinction runs.

### Rashi vs. Tosafot

According to Rashi, the default — when nothing is said — is Shmuel's arrangement: the *mashkon* embodies the full debt, and if lost, the entire debt is forfeited. The *mishnah* represents the case where the parties explicitly stipulated otherwise, excluding the Shmuel model. According to Tosafot, the default is the *mishnah*'s model — the *mashkon* is worth only its actual value — and Shmuel's framework applies only when explicitly stipulated. Tosafot's reading is the more intuitive one: it is far more natural to treat collateral as being worth what it is worth, with the Shmuel arrangement as an exceptional explicit deal.

### Asmachta Analysis

Tosafot takes the analysis further. Even when the Shmuel arrangement is explicitly stipulated, Tosafot does not view it as a legal *concept* of what a *mashkon* is — that is, not as an inherent legal definition according to which the *mashkon* fully embodies the debt. Rather, it is simply a side deal: the parties agree that if the creditor loses the collateral, the debt is forfeited. This is the structure of an *asmachta* — a conditional penalty clause — similar to a case where one stipulates that failure to plow a field results in a ten-thousand-dollar penalty. Such deals are enforceable when properly made, but they represent agreed-upon conditions, not conceptual redefinitions of what collateral is. Rashi, by contrast, for whom the Shmuel model is the default when nothing is said, appears to view the *mashkon*-as-full-debt-embodiment as a genuine conceptual category, not merely a side deal.

---

## R. Eliezer vs. R. Akiva

### Tannaitic Setup

The Gemara now asks whether Shmuel's position reflects a broader *tannaitic* dispute. The relevant *baraita* concerns a case where a creditor lent money against a *mashkon* and the *mashkon* was subsequently lost: *hamalveh et chavero al hamashkon ve'avad hamashkon*.

### R. Eliezer Chinam

Rabbi Eliezer rules: *yishava v'yitol me'otav* — the creditor takes an oath that he was not negligent and collects his entire debt. This is a position not even contemplated in the *mishnah*. Rabbi Eliezer treats the creditor as a *shomer chinam* — an unpaid guardian — who bears no liability for loss that occurs without negligence. The creditor loses the *mashkon*, takes an exculpatory oath, and is entitled to collect the full debt as if nothing had happened to the collateral.

### R. Akiva Full Debt

Rabbi Akiva rules the polar opposite: *yachol she'yomar lo klum hilvitani ela al hamashkon* — the borrower may say, "You only lent me money in order to hold my collateral. *Avad hamashkon avdu me'otecha* — you lost the *mashkon*, you lost your money." This is recognizably aligned with Shmuel's position. The *mashkon* is the full embodiment of the debt; its loss extinguishes the debt.

### With Document

An additional clause appears: if the loan was accompanied by a written *shtar* (*b'shtar*) and the creditor held collateral, then *divrei hakol avad hamashkon avdu ma'osav* — all agree that losing the *mashkon* means losing the money. This is surprising: one might have thought that having a *shtar* — which concretizes and formalizes the debt — would make it *harder*, not easier, to extinguish the obligation. Rashi's implicit explanation (to be developed below) is that precisely because the creditor already had a *shtar*, taking additional collateral signals that the collateral was intended as the exchange object for repayment, not merely as security.

### Equal Value Condition

The Gemara analyzes the structure of the *tannaitic* dispute. The first question is: *heichi dami* — what exactly is the case? If the *mashkon* was worth the full value of the debt, *mai ta'ama d'Rabbi Eliezer* — why would Rabbi Eliezer say the creditor can simply take an oath and collect? The Gemara responds: *ela lav d'lo shavei shiur zuzei* — it must be that the *mashkon* is not worth the full value of the debt. Only then can Rabbi Eliezer's position be understood on its own terms.

### Shomer Status

The Gemara proposes that the debate between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva actually concerns *shomer* status. The underlying logic turns on whether a creditor holding a *mashkon* receives any benefit from doing so. Generally, a *shomer chinam* — who receives nothing from the arrangement — is liable only for negligence, while a *shomer sachar* — who receives compensation of some kind — bears the additional liability of theft and loss. If the *mashkon* is worth the full value of the debt, the creditor clearly benefits: he has collateral against which he can collect if the borrower defaults. That would make him a *shomer sachar*, and losing the *mashkon* would require reimbursement. If, however, the *mashkon* is of negligible value, the creditor derives little practical benefit, and the argument for *shomer chinam* status becomes plausible.

The Gemara ultimately shifts the frame: *u'vi-Rabbi Yitzchak kamifligi* — the debate of Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva concerns the principle enunciated by Rabbi Yitzchak, to which we now turn.

---

## Kinyan Mashkon

### Kinyan Principle

Rabbi Yitzchak asks: *minayin l'baal chov she-koneh mashkon* — from where do we derive that a creditor acquires (*koneh*) the *mashkon*? That is, does the creditor actually take formal possession of the collateral, such that it is legally considered his?

### Tzedakah Verse

The source is the verse *u'lecha tihyeh tzedakah* — "and it will be *tzedakah* to you." The context is the Torah's law requiring the creditor, in certain circumstances, to return the collateral every evening (the debtor's nighttime garment, for example) or every morning. The Gemara reads *tzedakah* here not merely as "righteousness" but in its rabbinic sense of charity or giving from one's own resources. The question is: if the creditor is merely returning the borrower's own property, wherein lies the *tzedakah*? There is no charitable act in returning what was never yours. The inference is therefore that when the borrower hands over the *mashkon*, it becomes the creditor's property — *kinyan* is effected — and when the creditor returns it each morning, he is giving away something that is legally his. That constitutes *tzedakah*.

Tosafot adds a nuance in the tiny note *tzedakah minayin*: *d'lo mikrei tzedakah ela im ken mechaser mamona* — it is only called *tzedakah* if the act actually causes the giver a monetary loss. Returning property that is genuinely one's own, with an obligation to provide it, does involve such a loss, which is what makes the act qualify as *tzedakah* in the full sense.

A brief digression is warranted here. The concept of *tzedakah* in the Torah is often misconceived as equivalent to outright gifting. The Torah's primary modality for supporting those in need is the interest-free loan — *im kesef talveh et ami* and related *mitzvot* — rather than the outright gift. The question of whether lending money to a poor person constitutes *tzedakah* in the formal legal sense is a genuine conceptual issue: on the one hand, the lender is giving his own money; on the other hand, he expects it back, so the loss is only contingent. The Rambam famously rules that enabling employment — a form of transaction that involves no loss at all — constitutes the highest form of *tzedakah*, which suggests that the Rambam understands *tzedakah* in broad enough terms to include arrangements that do not necessarily entail an outright financial loss.

### Enhanced Obligation

If the creditor truly takes *kinyan* of the *mashkon*, his level of responsibility is significantly elevated. The *mashkon* is no longer "her watch" — it is his watch, subject to his full obligation to return it. If something happens to it in the interim, he cannot disclaim responsibility by saying it was not his property. The obligation runs against him personally.

### Post-Loan Taking

The Gemara now introduces an important limitation: *eima d'amar Rabbi Yitzchak b'mashkono shelo b'sha'at halva'ah* — Rabbi Yitzchak's principle of *kinyan* applies only when the creditor took the collateral *after* the loan was made, not at the time of the loan itself. The logic is conceptually transparent: when a debtor, who has not repaid, is subsequently subject to a *beit din*-authorized entry into his home to seize collateral, that act of seizure closely resembles actual collection of the debt. The creditor is not merely receiving a token — he is actively recovering what is owed. In that context, the language of *kinyan* makes intuitive sense. But when collateral is tendered simultaneously with the loan, the borrower is simply providing security for a debt that has not yet matured; the notion that the creditor thereby "takes possession" in any meaningful proprietary sense is far less natural.

The consequence for the *tannaitic* debate is that Rabbi Yitzchak's *kinyan* principle does not govern the case of collateral given at the time of the loan. We therefore need a different framework to understand why Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva disagree in the at-the-time-of-loan scenario.

### Shomer Avedah

The Gemara resolves: *b'mashkono shelo b'sha'at halva'ah kulei alma lo peligi d'it lei d'Rabbi Yitzchak* — when collateral is taken after the loan, everyone agrees with Rabbi Yitzchak; the creditor has *kinyan* and bears full responsibility for loss. *V'hacha b'mashkono b'sha'at halva'ato* — the dispute concerns collateral tendered at the time of the loan. And the operative question in that case is framed as the *shomer avedah* debate, to which we now turn.

---

## Shomer Avedah Debate

### Rabbah vs. Rav Yosef

The Gemara cites a directly relevant dispute: *shomer avedah* — a person who finds a lost object and tends it while seeking its rightful owner — *Rabbah amar k'shomer chinam, Rav Yosef amar k'shomer sachar dami*. Is such a guardian a *shomer chinam* or a *shomer sachar*? The relevance to our case is that the creditor holding collateral at the time of the loan is similarly situated: he is performing some kind of custodial function, but whether he receives meaningful compensation for it is contested.

### Collateral as Mitzvah

The parallel is now made explicit. The question of whether a creditor holding a *mashkon* is a *shomer chinam* or *shomer sachar* tracks the *shomer avedah* debate precisely because, in both cases, the guardian may be said to be performing a *mitzvah*.

### Mitzvah Exemption

Rashi identifies the relevant *mitzvah* benefit: *schar mitzvah, u'malveh al hamashkon nami mitzvah avid* — the creditor earns *mitzvah* credit for having extended the loan, and this *mitzvah* provides a tangible practical benefit. The practical benefit is *osek b'mitzvah patur min hamitzvah*: one who is engaged in performing a *mitzvah* is exempt from other *mitzvah* obligations at that moment. So if the creditor is holding the *mashkon* as part of the larger enterprise of having extended an interest-free loan — itself a *mitzvah* of the Torah — and a poor person approaches him requesting charity, he may decline on the grounds that he is already occupied with a *mitzvah*. This exemption from the *tzedakah* obligation constitutes the "salary" that elevates him to *shomer sachar* status, according to Rav Yosef.

One might wonder whether this theoretical benefit — the possibility of being exempted from a *tzedakah* request that may never materialize — constitutes meaningful compensation. That is precisely what makes the question debatable.

### Loan vs. Holding

The Gemara goes on to distinguish between the *mitzvah* of lending and the act of holding the *mashkon*. The debate between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva may hinge not on whether lending money is a *mitzvah* — that is explicit in the Torah — but on whether the holding of the *mashkon* itself partakes of the *mitzvah* character of the loan. One view is that taking a *mashkon* transforms the transaction: rather than a purely altruistic loan in which only the borrower benefits, the creditor now has a stake in the object, a practical self-interest. This makes the arrangement more business-like and less *mitzvah*-like, and the creditor is no longer receiving "compensation" in the *mitzvah* sense. According to this view, the creditor is a *shomer chinam*: Rabbi Eliezer's position.

The alternative view separates the two components cleanly: the loan was a *mitzvah*, and the custodial function of holding the *mashkon* partakes of that *mitzvah* character. The creditor is therefore a *shomer sachar*: Rabbi Akiva's position.

### Using Collateral

The Gemara addresses one additional scenario briefly passed over above. The case of *malveh tzarich lemashkon* — where the creditor actively uses the *mashkon* to facilitate repayment of the debt, for example by using the borrower's hoe and crediting rental fees against the outstanding balance. (This arrangement requires the creditor to pay rental fees to avoid *ribbit*.) The question in this scenario is whether holding and using the *mashkon* in this way constitutes a *mitzvah*. The Gemara notes: *keivan d'tzarich lemashkon ein kan mitzvah* — since the creditor is deriving direct benefit from the *mashkon*, the *mitzvah* framing may not apply, and the arrangement is more purely transactional. According to this view, the creditor would be a *shomer chinam*, bearing less liability precisely because the personal benefit he derives strips the arrangement of its *mitzvah* quality — a somewhat counterintuitive result that the Gemara acknowledges.

---

## Shmuel & Shemitah

### Shemitah Scenario

The Gemara now revisits Shmuel's framework in a different legal context, asking whether the *tannaitic* dispute in the *mishnah* concerning *shemitah* reflects a debate about Shmuel's principle. The *mishnah* states: *hamalveh et chavero al hamashkon venichnesah shemitah* — a person lent money against a *mashkon* and the *shemitah* year arrived. Normally, *shemitah* annuls outstanding loans — the creditor may no longer collect. But a loan secured by a *mashkon* may be different, because holding the *mashkon* is in some sense already a form of collection.

### Whole Debt Protected

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel rules: *af al pi she'eino shaveh ella palga eino meshammet* — even if the *mashkon* is worth only half the debt, *shemitah* does not annul the loan at all. The implication is that the entire hundred dollars is protected, even though the *mashkon* is worth only fifty.

### Partial Annulment

Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi rules: *im hayah mashkon k'neged chovo eino m'shameit* — if the *mashkon* is worth the full value of the debt, *shemitah* does not annul it. *V'im lav m'shameit* — but if not, then *shemitah* does annul the loan. The implication is that the unrepresented portion of the debt — the fifty dollars not covered by the watch's value — is annulled.

### Full Embodiment

The Gemara now asks: *u'vid'Shmuel kamifligi* — is this *tannaitic* debate actually a debate about Shmuel's principle? Under Shmuel's view, the *mashkon* fully embodies the entire debt regardless of its face value. A fifty-dollar watch, in Shmuel's framework, represents the full hundred-dollar debt.
