Shmuel holds that the category of *shevuat bitui* — the oath of expression — applies only to future undertakings, things one commits to do or refrain from doing. The verse in *Vayikra* speaks of *lehara o leheitiv* — doing harm or doing good — which implies future action. An oath about what happened to an ox in the past — whether it died, was stolen, or was lost — is not the kind of oath *shevuat bitui* is designed to govern. Rav, however, holds that *shevuat bitui* applies equally to both negative and positive statements, including declarations about the past — *belav vehen*, yes or no, I ate or I didn't eat, the animal died or it didn't die. Under Rav's view, a false declaration about past events is still a *shevuat bitui* and still incurs liability.

### Stone/Sea Case

The *gemara* notes that this exact dispute between Rav and Shmuel has already been recorded once before, on 25a, in the case of *shvua she'zarak ploni tsror la-yam* — one who swears "so-and-so threw a stone into the sea," or swears that he did not. Rav holds that if this statement is false, the swearer is liable — since this is a statement that can be made in either the positive or negative form, *belav vehen*. Shmuel holds he is exempt — since this is a statement that involves no future undertaking, it falls outside the category of *shevuat bitui*. The *gemara* explains why it is nevertheless necessary to record the dispute in both contexts — the case of the stone thrown into the sea and the case of the guardians — despite their apparent identity. Each case adds something the other does not. In the case of the stone, one might have thought Rav holds the swearer liable specifically because the person swore entirely on his own initiative, *menafshei*, of his own accord. One might then have said: but in a court-administered oath, Rav would concede to Shmuel. Conversely, one might have supposed that Shmuel's exemption applies specifically to court-administered oaths, while in the case of a self-initiated oath he concedes to Rav. Since each case might be distinguished, both must be recorded.

### Court vs. Self Oaths

This brings the *gemara* to a principle of Rav Ami: *kol shevuah she'hadayanim mashbi'in otah, ein chayavin aleha mishum shevuat bitui* — any oath that is administered by the court judges does not carry liability under the category of *shevuat bitui*. This is a striking ruling deserving extended examination. The basis for it is derived from the verse in *Vayikra* chapter 5, *o nefesh ki tishava levate bisefatayim* — "or if a soul swears, expressing with its lips." The word *ki* in this verse, as Reish Lakish explains, functions in one of four possible senses: *ei, dilma, ela, deha* — if, perhaps, rather, or as. Here, the *ki* indicates that the liability for *shevuat bitui* is predicated on the person swearing *me'atzmo*, of his own volition. An oath that the court imposes does not carry the full weight of *shevuat bitui* because it is not the spontaneous expression of the individual's own speech — it is a judicially administered mechanism, and the verse's requirement of personal initiative is not satisfied.

---

## Rabbi Elazar & Conclusion

### Rabbi Elazar Rule

Rabbi Elazar states a position that synthesizes much of what has been discussed: *kulam peturim mishevuat shomrim ve'chayavim mishum shevuat bitui* — all four categories of guardians are exempt from the *shevuat shomrim* but are liable under *shevuat bitui*. This is consistent with Rav's position, and it applies across all the cases surveyed in the *mishnah*.

### Theft/Loss Exception

There is, however, an exception: *chutz misachir she-lo yodea mah atah sach shel hashoel* — except for the *sho'el* who says "I don't know what you are talking about." That case, as established earlier, renders the *sho'el chayav* in a different way. Additionally, Rabbi Elazar addresses the specific situations of *gneivah ve'aveidah* — theft and loss — for the *nose sachar* and the *socher*. In those cases, *shehu chayav, sheharei kaparah mamon* — the guardian is liable, because his *kaparah*, his atonement, comes through monetary payment. Since the *nose sachar* and *socher* bear financial responsibility for theft and loss, that monetary obligation cannot simply be sidestepped by the mechanics of oath exemption; the obligation to settle accounts monetarily stands, and the swearer cannot walk away.

### Completion

*Hadran alach arba shomrim, ve'silka lah Masechet Shevuot.* We have reached the end of *Masechet Shevuot* — a *masechet* that began with the hidden awareness of *tum'ah* in the sanctuary, moved through the mysteries of the oaths of expression, the oaths of vain utterance, and the oath of testimony, and concludes here with the intricate legal choreography of the four guardians and the conditions under which a false declaration before God carries halachic consequence. If we leave with more questions than we had when we began, that is precisely as it should be. *Hadran alach*.

---

---

# Avodah Zarah 2

## Intro to Avodah Zarah

### Calendar & Nezikin

*Masekhet Avodah Zarah* is the last large tractate in *Nezikin*, and with its commencement we find ourselves drawing close to the conclusion of that entire order.

### Subject Matter

Contrary to what one might expect from its name, *Avodah Zarah* is not primarily about the act of worshipping idols. The first half of the tractate is devoted to a different question altogether: how do we negotiate the larger world around us, especially given that this world is not only non-Jewish but also, in the rabbinic period, a pagan world? That is certainly the focus of the first two chapters.

### Terminology & Censorship

The opening *mishna* begins with the phrase *lifnei edeihem*, "before their holidays," and the original text used the word *goyim* — simply, non-Jews — or *nochri*, meaning foreigner. If one were to ask a typical *yeshiva* student what the standard term in the *gemara* is for non-Jews, he would likely answer *akum*, an abbreviation of *ovdei kochavim u'mazalot*, worshippers of stars and constellations. But the original language of the *mishna*, *gemara*, and *baraita* uses *goyim* or *nochri*, neither of which implies idolatry.

What happened was that in the Middle Ages, Jewish apostates who had converted to Christianity informed the Church about passages in the *Talmud* that expressed negative attitudes toward non-Jews. This led the Church in various places to confiscate, censor, and even burn the *Talmud*. In response, Jews engaged in a process of self-censorship, replacing *goy* and *nochri* with *akum* — so they could claim to the Church that these passages referred only to ancient pagans, not to contemporary Christians. Some passages were removed entirely, such as the discussions of Jesus in *Sanhedrin*. And when a source is particularly sensitive, the substituted term is not even *akum* but *Knani* — a Canaanite — allowing the claim that the reference concerns only those ancient peoples from thousands of years ago. One therefore knows that a passage is especially pointed when the term used is *Knani*, as in the famous question of *gezel Knani*, theft from a Canaanite, which in the original would have been *gezel goy*.

### Goyim vs. Idolaters

It is important to recognize that not all non-Jews are idolaters. Even if the vast majority were in the rabbinic period, the concern is not always rooted in their status as idolaters; sometimes it simply arises from the fact that they are non-Jews. So while there is not a perfect one-to-one correspondence between *goy* and *oved avodah zarah*, there was in the rabbinic world a high degree of practical overlap. The very first *mishna*, *lifnei edeihem shel goyim*, illustrates this: the prohibition on certain interactions before their holidays derives precisely from the connection to idolatry, even though the word used was simply *goyim*. Nevertheless, the *gemara* itself at times acknowledges non-Jews who are not idolaters and not pagans, and that distinction matters throughout the tractate.

### Tractate Structure

The tractate can be divided thematically into three broad sections. The first two chapters deal with how one navigates the larger Gentile pagan world — whether one is indirectly supporting or participating in pagan practices, or being endangered physically or religiously through certain types of interactions. The middle chapter deals with idolatry more directly: what to do when one encounters objects that may have been used in pagan worship — an idol discarded in a marketplace, or a bowl with an image of a deity on it. Was it an object of worship, or merely a decorative item? The final two chapters focus intensively on one particular domain of concern: wine. The question of *yayin nesech*, wine touched by a non-Jew under various circumstances, occupies the last two chapters in considerable detail.

The tractate is genuinely fascinating on multiple levels. Historically, it provides a remarkable window into the world of the rabbis — the references to Roman pagan practices, the texture of Greco-Roman life, bathhouses and marketplaces and legal institutions. Halakhically, it is enormously practical, given that so many of its topics — wine, cooked foods, cheese, milk, and other products — remain relevant. And philosophically, it raises enduring questions about how Jews are to perceive the outside world, how much separation is required, how much integration is possible, and what assumptions we bring to our understanding of non-Jewish society.

### Significance & Sources

Because of its profound practical dimensions, *Avodah Zarah* attracted the attention of a great many *rishonim* whose commentaries are not found on more purely theoretical tractates like *Sanhedrin* or *Shavuot*. The abundance of *rishonim* on this *masekhet* reflects the ongoing relevance of its questions to Jewish communities across the medieval world.

### Yerushalmi & Dina

One might ask whether the *Yerushalmi* presents a different orientation to these questions than the *Bavli*. This is a genuinely important question. There are issues in the tractate that bear directly on the Jewish relationship to the land of Israel — questions about protecting Jewish economic self-sufficiency and Jewish presence in the land — which have a particular character in the Palestinian context. More broadly, the experience of Jews in *Bavel* was very different from that of Jews in Roman Palestine. In *Bavel*, Jews generally enjoyed a welcoming and supportive government; in the land of Israel, the Roman occupation carried with it a long history of oppression, and the Romans were experienced not as hosts but as occupiers of the Jews' own land.

The *Mishnah* and *baraita*, as Palestinian documents, reflect that Israeli perspective. How the *Bavli* then recasts this material is worth examining closely. One clear example of the difference emerges elsewhere: the principle of *dina de'malchuta dina* — the law of the kingdom is the law — is articulated in the *Bavli* but never appears in the *Yerushalmi*. The *Mishnah* treats tax collectors as presumptive thieves; the *Bavli* pushes back, arguing that they operate under government license and their collections are therefore legally sanctioned. These are not small differences; they reflect fundamentally different postures toward the non-Jewish political order. Whether a similarly clear divergence emerges specifically within *Avodah Zarah* is a question worth keeping in view as we proceed.

---

## Mishna: Business Ban

### Mishna Text

The *mishna* opens: *lifnei edeihem shel goyim* — before the holidays of the non-Jews — *shlosha yamim* — three days before — it is *asur lasset velatet imahem*, forbidden to engage in commerce with them, buying or selling; *ul'hashilan*, to lend them objects; *ulish'ol mehem*, to borrow objects from them; *ul'halvotam*, to lend them money; *ulilovot mehem*, to borrow money from them; *ul'faran*, to repay a debt one owes them; *ulifroa mehem*, or to collect a debt they owe you.

### R. Yehuda Dispute

Rabbi Yehuda disputes one item: *nifrain mehem*, one may collect debts from them during this period, *mipnei shemeitzer hu lo* — because having to pay is an anguish to the non-Jew. The act of paying causes him distress, not joy, and therefore it cannot serve as a source of the problem that the *mishna* is concerned with.

### Response to R. Yehuda

The Sages respond: *af al pi shemeitzer hu achshav same'ach hu le'achar zman* — even though he feels anguish in the moment of payment, afterward he feels relief and even satisfaction. The debt is discharged; he is free of an obligation. Whatever momentary pain the payment causes, it ultimately generates a sense of happiness.

### Rashi's Reason

From this exchange one can infer that something causing joy is the source of the problem. But why should causing a non-Jew joy be prohibited in connection with their holiday? Rashi provides a direct explanation: *vechulan mishum de'azil u'modeh la'avoda kochavim beyom eydo* — all of these transactions are forbidden because they cause the non-Jew happiness, and when that non-Jew arrives at his holiday one, two, or three days later, he will celebrate with greater joy and will give thanks to his god. The Jew's business deal, or loan, or act of repayment becomes the occasion for an expression of gratitude to Zeus or whichever deity — "Thank you for this good fortune." The Jew has thus indirectly contributed to an act of *avodah zarah*.

### Aiding Idolatry

Why is that a problem? The *gemara*'s fundamental answer is that non-Jews are bound by the *sheva mitzvot bnei Noach*, the Seven Noahide Laws, which include a prohibition against *avodah zarah*. By providing the occasion for their idolatry, one is in some sense abetting a transgression. Even if this does not rise to the level of *lifnei iver* — placing a stumbling block before the blind, which technically requires that the other party could not have sinned without your assistance — there remains a serious concern about aiding and abetting another person's sin.

### Three Frameworks

There are in fact three distinct ways of understanding the prohibition, and they are worth distinguishing carefully. The first and narrowest framework, the one that the *gemara* itself emphasizes, is *lifnei iver* or something adjacent to it: the non-Jew will sin, and I have helped make that sin possible. From this perspective, if non-Jews were not prohibited against idolatry, there would be no problem with our business dealings whatsoever. The second framework shifts the focus: it is not that I am concerned about their sin per se, but that through this transaction I become in some way connected to their act of *avodah zarah* myself. I am not transgressing, but I am participating — the way someone who stands in a kitchen chatting and tasting food while another person cooks on *Shabbos* is not violating *Shabbos* but is in some sense implicated in what is happening around him. The third framework is in many ways the most straightforward and the most directly intuitive: when a major pagan holiday approaches, all the surrounding commerce and excitement and social activity is bound up with that holiday. By participating in that commerce — even in transactions that have no direct connection to the worship itself — one is becoming part of the cultural fabric of an idolatrous event.

### Culture vs. Sin

This third framework is the *pshat*, the plain explanation. Consider what it means to go shopping in the days before a major holiday: even if one is buying perfectly ordinary goods, one is participating in the season, contributing to the excitement, and embedding oneself in a culture organized around that holiday. The question of borrowing money is particularly illuminating: if the non-Jew lends money to the Jew, he is not being aided in his idolatry in any direct sense. Yet that transaction too is prohibited. Why? Because the issue is not whether one is enabling their worship but whether one is becoming part of the broader social and commercial energy surrounding it.

Interestingly, the *gemara* does not explicitly articulate this third explanation. But it is, in many respects, the most compelling account of why borrowing — not just lending — should be caught by the prohibition.

### Non-Idolater Recognition

One important caveat must be kept in view throughout. The *gemara* itself acknowledges the existence of non-Jews who are not idolaters. The full logic of *lifnei iver* and of concern about connecting to *avodah zarah* applies only where actual idolatrous worship is at stake. Where non-Jews are not practitioners of idolatry, the concern about their thanksgiving to pagan gods simply does not arise, and the limits of these principles must be respected accordingly.

---

## Tosafot: Sunday

### Tosafot Q

A major practical question occupied the *rishonim* of medieval Christian Europe: the principal market day was Sunday, and Christianity was widely regarded as *avodah zarah*. How could Jews do business on Sunday, which was the Christian Sabbath and day of worship, when the *mishna* explicitly prohibits commerce before and on the holidays of non-Jews? This was not an ancient theoretical problem — it was an ongoing reality that Jews faced every week. *Tosafot* frames the question directly: *al ma samkhu ha'olam lasset ulasset beyom eid ovdei kokhavim imahem* — on what basis did the entire community rely when conducting business with them on their holiday?

### Saint Days

*Tosafot* notes one preliminary distinction: *nihi de-rov eideihem min ha-kedoshim hem* — most Christian holidays are saint days. A saint day commemorates a holy person, not a god, and does not involve worship of a deity in the same sense. Nevertheless, *Tosafot* acknowledges that every week there is one day — Sunday — that is a genuine religious observance, and the question therefore remains fully in force.

### Eivah Answer

The first answer *Tosafot* offers is *de-shari mishum eivah*: it is permitted in order to avoid engendering *eivah*, hatred on the part of non-Jews. If Jews refused to participate in the Sunday market, they might provoke hostility from their neighbors. This explanation reflects a particular way of perceiving the surrounding society — as one in which antisemitism is always potentially just beneath the surface, and in which Jewish behavior must be calibrated to avoid triggering it.

### Eivah Objection

*Tosafot* himself, however, is not satisfied with this answer. The *eivah* concern is intelligible when a non-Jew approaches a Jew directly and the Jew refuses to transact with him — that refusal is visible and can provoke resentment. But if Jews simply do not appear in the market on Sunday, why would the non-Jews even notice, let alone be offended? There is no obvious mechanism by which their absence generates *eivah*. Other *rishonim* do argue that if the entire Jewish community stops frequenting the market, the non-Jewish merchants notice the loss of business and become genuinely hostile. But *Tosafot* finds this response unpersuasive.

### Darchei Shalom

An alternative framing, the flip side of *eivah*, is *darchei shalom* — the ways of peace. Rather than being motivated by fear of non-Jewish hostility, one participates in Sunday commerce as a positive expression of cultivating good relations with one's neighbors. This is not about avoiding a danger; it is about affirming a value. Living among non-Jews requires fostering interactions that are genuinely constructive and neighborly.

### Machanif Explanation

*Tosafot* then cites a source from the *Yerushalmi* that refines this further. The *Yerushalmi* distinguishes between two cases: where the non-Jew is a stranger, one is not permitted to do business with him; but where one knows the non-Jew, it is permitted *mipnei she-hu k'machanif* — because it constitutes a form of flattery, or more precisely, a form of polite social engagement. The *Yerushalmi* adds a striking illustration: if one enters a city and finds the inhabitants in the midst of a celebration, one may join in the rejoicing — *she-eino ela k'machanif* — because to refuse would be socially inappropriate.

### Politeness Frame

What does *machanif* mean here? One way to read it is simply as a form of *darchei shalom* — maintaining congenial relations. But there is a more precise understanding: when one gives a neighbor a gift on their holiday or participates in a social gathering, the act is understood by all parties as neighborliness and basic decency, not as religious endorsement or participation in worship. The social context makes clear that one is simply being a good neighbor. Just as one might give candy to children who come to one's door on Halloween — which is quite different from taking one's own children to participate in the practice — there are acts that are read as politeness rather than as religious participation. When you join a celebration already in progress, to refuse pointedly is rude; to accept a drink or a greeting is simply human. *Machanif* in this sense means being appropriately polite and socially engaged, not betraying one's values. Of course, there is a line — one would not sing the songs of their worship — but the *Yerushalmi* is pointing to a range of ordinary social behavior that falls on the permissible side.

### Rabbeinu Tam

*Rabbeinu Tam* offers a different and more technical approach. He argues that the core prohibition of the *mishna* applies specifically to selling objects that the non-Jew could use directly in his acts of pagan worship. Selling goods that cannot serve as materials for worship is simply not covered by the prohibition. This provides a clean explanation for why ordinary commerce on Sunday — selling cloth, grain, household goods — does not violate the *mishna*.

### Money Fungibility

But *Rabbeinu Tam* faces an immediate challenge. If money is the one thing non-Jews actually do offer in their worship — the collection plate passed around in church — then any financial transaction with them might seem to be providing them with their offering material. He resolves this by invoking the fungibility of money: just because a Jew sold something to a non-Jew and the non-Jew now has money does not mean that those specific coins are the ones that will end up in the collection plate. The non-Jew had money before and will have money regardless. There is no traceable causal link between the Jew's transaction and the specific funds used in worship.

### Religious Loans

There is, however, a case where caution is warranted: *umihu nakhon hu lehachmir keshebah oved kokhavim ve'omer halveini ma'ot leshikri* — when a non-Jew explicitly comes and says, lend me money for my religious observance. In this case, the purpose of the loan is stated, and the Jew is directly funding a religious purpose. *Tosafot* notes that in the actual historical context of medieval Jewry, this could arise when a prominent ecclesiastical figure — identified by the pejorative term *operier* — sought to borrow funds for some religious undertaking, perhaps even a crusade. In such a case, lending should be avoided.

### Supporting Clergy

*Rabbeinu Chananel*, however, disagrees even here. He argues that even when money is given to priests and monks — *galachim* and *khumarim* — this does not constitute a direct act of worship. The money goes to support the practitioners, to pay for their food and lodging, not to be used in the actual ritual acts themselves. Supporting the personnel of a religious institution is sufficiently indirect that it does not cross into *avodah zarah*. *Tosafot* is thus navigating a genuinely complicated medieval reality: Jews were heavily involved in money-lending, and the question of whether one could lend to churches and monasteries was live and practical.

### Christians Not Idolaters

The most striking and theologically significant answer *Tosafot* offers is preserved toward the end of this discussion. Rather than arguing that the prohibition does not technically apply, or that various practical considerations override it, *Tosafot* entertains the possibility that we need to reconsider how we categorize Christians themselves. The key passage reads: *kimla beghavaihu delo palchu le'avodat kochavim* — we know that the Christians among us do not actually worship *avodah zarah* in any meaningful sense, even if their religion, considered as a system, can be characterized as *avodah zarah*. As a precedent, *Tosafot* cites the famous case of Rav Yehuda sending a gift to a non-Jewish acquaintance on his holiday, justified because *kimli beghavei delo palach le'avodat kochavim* — he knew this individual did not actually worship *avodah zarah*.

### Religion vs. Persons

This is one of the most consequential passages in all of the *rishonim* on how to think about Jews' relationship to the Christian world. *Tosafot* here drives a wedge between Christianity as a religious system and individual Christians as persons. The religion may be classifiable as *avodah zarah*; the people practicing it may not be. The concept *Tosafot* deploys — articulated more explicitly elsewhere — is *minhag avoteihem bi'yedeihem*: they are doing what they were raised to do, following ancestral custom, not engaging in a sincere and deliberate act of pagan worship. The religion is inherited rather than chosen, practiced by rote rather than out of genuine theological conviction.

There is admittedly something patronizing about this framing. It says, in effect: I can lower the barriers between us by deciding that even though you take your religion very seriously, you are not really a sincere worshipper of a foreign god — you are just going through motions you absorbed from childhood. In the context of medieval Christendom, there is an additional irony: the people who were least enthusiastic about the Church's religion were often those in whom the older paganism was still alive. Yet for *Tosafot*, this framing served a crucial function. It allowed for substantially increased interaction with the Christian population by separating the halakhic status of Christianity as a religion from the halakhic status of Christians as individuals — without requiring *Tosafot* to make the arguably more radical claim that Christianity itself is not *avodah zarah*.

### Interest Distinction

*Tosafot* in the following passage addresses the lending question from yet another angle. *Rabbeinu Tam* notes that the *mishna*'s prohibition on lending applies specifically to lending without interest — *davka bechinam*. But lending *beribis* — with interest — is permitted even in the days leading up to their holidays, *mishum demitzta'er tuva* — because being charged interest causes the borrower considerable anguish and irritation, not joy. Since the entire concern is that commerce generates the non-Jew's happiness and thereby contributes to his joyous thanksgiving on the holiday, a transaction that causes him financial pain rather than pleasure does not trigger the prohibition.

### Debt Collection

Similarly, the question of collecting outstanding debts during their holiday period is treated leniently by *Tosafot*. The *gemara* rules in accordance with Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha that where there is no document — and one risks losing the money if collection is delayed — one may collect *mipnei she-hu k'matzil miyadam*, because one is in effect rescuing one's own funds from potential loss. *Tosafot* suggests that perhaps even where a document does exist, collection may still be permitted, since there is always the concern that the debtor will not have funds available at a later date. The combined effect of these discussions is that virtually all the commercial activities that medieval Jewish communities actually engaged in — buying, selling, lending, collecting — could be accommodated through one or another of *Tosafot*'s frameworks.

---

## Edeihem Dispute

### Aleph-Ayin

The *gemara* now returns to the very word *edeihem* — "their holidays" — with which the *mishna* opens, and reports a debate between Rav and Shmuel. *Chad tani aideihen* — one of them reads the word with an *alef* — *vechad tani eideihen* — and the other reads it with an *ayin*. *Man detani aideihen lo mishtabesh u'man detani eideihen lo mishtabesh* — neither is making a mistake. Both readings are correct and carry distinct meaning.

### Destruction Reading

The *alef* reading derives *edeihem* from the word for disaster or destruction. The supporting verse is *ki karov yom eidam* — for the day of their downfall is near — drawn from Deuteronomy 32:35, where *eid* signifies calamity. On this reading, the *mishna* is covertly referring to the non-Jews' holidays as the days of their ruin. This is an example of a practice — using a derogatory term to describe something while appearing to use a neutral one — born of the psychological needs of an oppressed minority community. Jews living in a pagan Roman world that appeared to be flourishing and dominant needed ways to maintain hope and perspective; using the word *eid* to mean both "holiday" and "destruction" was one such rhetorical strategy. The same impulse can be seen in other examples: *beit tiflotam* rather than *beit tefillotam* — the house of their nonsense rather than the house of their prayers — or *Nittel Nacht*, which is not a Hebrew coinage meaning the night from which sanctity has been removed, but simply the German *Nativity Night*, the night of the birth.

### Testimony Reading

The *ayin* reading derives *edeihem* from *eidut*, testimony. The verse is *yitnu edeihem ve-yitzdaku* — let them give their testimony and be vindicated. On this reading, the idols of the pagans will one day be called upon to testify on behalf of their worshippers — but their testimony will in fact condemn those worshippers, exposing the reality that they engaged in *avodah zarah*. Their very holidays are thus moments that generate the evidence against them.

### Mitzvot Testimony

The *gemara* then notes that the verse *yitnu edeihem ve-yitzdaku* does not straightforwardly refer to idolaters; it would seem to be addressed to *Yisrael*. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi resolves this: *kol mitzvot she-Yisrael osim ba-olam ha-zeh ba'ot u-ma'idot lahem le-olam ha-ba* — every *mitzvah* that the Jewish people perform in this world will come and testify on their behalf in the world to come. On this reading, *edeihem* — their testimony — refers to the *mitzvot* themselves, which function as witnesses for the righteous. The end of the verse, *ve-yishme'u ve-yomru emet* — they will hear and say, this is true — refers to the nations, who will be compelled to acknowledge the righteousness of the Jewish way of life even against their own interest.

### Rav Huna Source

Finally, Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua offers an alternative verse as the source for the *alef* reading: *yotzrei fesel kullam tohu, va-hamudeihem bal yo'ilu, ve-edeihem heima* — the fashioners of idols are all vanity, their cherished things will not help them, and it is they — the idols — that are their testimony. The idols they worship will not benefit them; indeed, those very idols will stand as testimony against them, confirming their idolatry. This is the same essential idea as the previous *ayin* reading, grounded in a different verse from Isaiah.

---

## Judgment Midrash

### Future Scenario

Rabbi Hanina bar Papa — and some say Rabbi Simlai — expounded: *la-atid la-vo*, in the time to come, the Holy One Blessed Be He will bring a *sefer Torah* and place it in His bosom, and will declare: whoever occupied themselves with this, let them come and receive their reward. The scene being constructed is an eschatological judgment in which the *Torah* itself serves as the criterion for reward — and the surprising development is that the nations of the world rush forward to claim that they too deserve a share in that reward.

### Nations Gather

*Misgabshin bahem dukhturin ve-irvuvya* — all the nations come crowding together in a great commotion, everyone rushing to claim their portion, as the verse says, *kol hagoyim nikbetzu yakhdav* — all the nations are gathered together. God says to them: *al tikanesu lefanai be-irvuvya* — do not come before Me all mixed together. *Ela tikanes kol uma va-uma ve-sofreha* — let each nation come separately with its own sages and learned leaders. The verse supports this: *ve-ye'asfu le-ummim*, and nations gather — *ve-ein le-um ela malkhut*, and *le-um* denotes a national identity, as in the verse *u-le'um mi-le'um ye-ematz*, one nation strives against another. What is remarkable here is the implicit insistence that nations not be painted with a single brush. There is diversity among the nations; they are not all the same, and they deserve to be evaluated distinctly.

### Clarity Issue

The *gemara* interrupts with a question: *u-mi ika irvuvya kamei hakadosh barukh hu* — is there any confusion before the Holy One Blessed Be He? Surely God can sort out all the nations simultaneously. The answer: *ela ki heikhi dela le-irvevu inhu bahadi hadadi* — the separation is not for God's sake but for the nations' sake, so that each nation can hear clearly and attend to what is being said to them. The arrangement serves clarity of communication, not any epistemic need on God's part.

### Rome First

*Miyad nikhnesah lefanav malkhut romi tekhila* — immediately the Roman kingdom enters first. The *gemara* asks: why Rome? *Mishum de-khashiva* — because it is the most important. The source is the vision of Daniel, in which the fourth beast *ve-tokhal kol ar-a ve-tedushena ve-tedukena* — ate the whole earth, trampled it and crushed it. Rabbi Yochanan identifies this beast with wicked Rome, *she-tiv'ah yatza be-khol ha-olam* — whose imprint and whose power went out throughout the entire world.

### King First

The *gemara* then asks: on what basis does the most important nation enter first? This is derived from a principle articulated by Rav Chisda: *melekh ve-tzibur, melekh nikhnas tekhila la-din* — when a king and his people come to be judged, the king enters first, as the verse states, *la'asot mishpat avdo u-mishpat amo Yisrael* — to execute judgment for His servant and for His people Israel, listing the king's judgment before the people's. Two reasons are offered for why the king goes first. The first: *lav orakhe ar-a le-meitev malka me-avrai* — it is not respectful for a king to be kept waiting outside. The second, somewhat more striking: *mikamei de-lifosh kharon af* — before God's anger builds. Since God is reviewing an endless parade of sins, to enter first, before the full weight of divine frustration accumulates, might be advantageous. The application of this reasoning to wicked Rome is admittedly somewhat strained — it is borrowed from a different context concerning the judgment of a Jewish king alongside his people — but it serves the homiletical purpose.

---

## Judgment Midrash (II)

### Rome's Claim

God asks Rome: *bemai asaktam* — what have you accomplished? Rome responds: *ribbono shel olam* — Master of the Universe — we have done great things. *Harbe shvakim tiknannu* — we established many marketplaces. *Harbe merkhata'ot asinu* — we built many bathhouses. *Harbe kesef ve-zahav hirbbenu* — we multiplied gold and silver, creating wealth and prosperity. *Ve-khulam lo asinu ela bishvil Yisrael* — and all of it we did for the sake of Israel, *kedei she-ya'asku ba-Torah* — so that they should be able to engage in Torah study. The implication: Rome created the conditions — the economic infrastructure, the social amenities, the accumulated wealth — that enabled Torah civilization to flourish. And for this they claim reward.

### God Rejects

God's response is devastating: *shotim she-ba-olam* — idiots! *Kol mah she-asitem le-tzorech atzmekhem asitem* — everything you did, you did for your own sake. *Tikantem shvakim le-hoshiv bahen zonot* — you built your marketplaces to house your prostitutes. *Merkhata'ot le-aden bahem atzmekhem* — your bathhouses were for your own indulgence. *Kesef ve-zahav sheli hu* — and as for all that gold and silver, it is Mine: *she-ne'emar li ha-kesef ve-li ha-zahav ne'um Hashem tzeva'ot* — as it is written, the silver is Mine and the gold is Mine, declares the Lord of Hosts.

### Torah Only

*Klum yesh bakhem magid zot* — is there anyone among you who can say *zot*? *Ve-ein zot ela Torah* — and *zot* refers to nothing other than *Torah*, as in the verse *ve-zot ha-Torah asher sam Moshe* — and this is the *Torah* that Moses placed. None of them actually engaged with *Torah*, and none of them truly did what they did for Israel's sake. *Miyad yatze'u be-fakhi nefesh* — they immediately departed despondent.

### Verse Interpretation

The *gemara* pauses to address the verse *yitnu edeihem ve-yitzdaku* more carefully. Is it referring to non-Jews — whose testimony condemns them — or to Jews? The answer, already sketched above in the discussion of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, is that the verse operates on two levels simultaneously. The first part of the verse — *yitnu edeihem ve-yitzdaku*, they shall present their testimony and be vindicated — refers to the Jewish people, whose *mitzvot* testify on their behalf. The second part — *ve-yishme'u ve-yomru emet*, they will hear and say, this is true — refers to the nations, who acknowledge the truth even as they are being judged against.

---

## Persia & Nations

### Persia Enter

*Ve-nikhnesah malkhut paras akhareha* — the Persian kingdom enters after Rome. The *gemara* asks: why Persia next? Because it is next in importance. The source again is Daniel's vision: *va-aru khivah akherei tinyana* — and behold, a second beast appeared, *damya le-dov* — resembling a bear. Rav Yosef expounds: this refers to the Persians, *she-okhlin ve-shosin ke-dov* — who eat and drink like a bear, *u-mesubbalin be-vasar ke-dov* — who are fleshy like a bear, *u-megadlin se'ar ke-dov* — who are hairy like a bear, *ve-ein lahem menuha ke-dov* — and who are never at rest, like a bear. This is not a flattering portrait.

### Persia Claims

God asks Persia: *bemai asaktam* — what have you done? *Harbe gisharim gisharnnu* — we built many bridges. *Harbe krakhim kavashnu* — we conquered many cities. *Harbe milkhamot asinu* — we waged many wars. *Ve-khulam lo asinu ela bishvil Yisrael, kedei she-yit'aseku ba-Torah* — and all of it was for the sake of Israel, so that they might engage in *Torah*.

### Persia Rejected

God rejects this: *kol mah she-asitem le-tzorech atzmekhem asitem* — you did it all for yourselves. *Gishartem gisharim litol mehem mekhes* — you built bridges to collect tolls. *Krakhim la'asot bahem angariya* — you conquered cities in order to conscript their populations into royal service. *Milkhamot ani asiti* — as for your wars, those are Mine: *she-ne'emar Hashem ish milkhama* — as it is written, the Lord is a Man of War. And again: *klum yesh bakhem magid zot? Ve-ein zot ela Torah* — none of you can claim any genuine relationship to *Torah*. *Miyad yatze'u milfanav be-fakhi nefesh* — they too left despondent.

### Persia Advantage

The *gemara* asks: Persia watched Rome enter and fail to establish any valid claim. Why then did Persia think it would fare better? The answer: *amri inhu satrei beit ha-mikdash* — Rome destroyed the *Beit Hamikdash*; that is a decisive strike against them. *Va-anan banina* — but we, the Persians, allowed the Jews to return to their land and rebuild the *Beit Hamikdash*. Persia therefore believed it had a meaningful moral advantage over Rome, one that might carry weight in the divine judgment.

### Other Nations

The same pattern then repeats for every nation: *ve-khen be-khol uma va-uma* — and so it is with each and every nation. Yet the *gemara* raises a further question: once all the other nations saw that even Rome and Persia, with all their historical significance and all their purported contributions, gained nothing — why did they persist and enter as well? The answer: *savri hanei ishtabdu be-Yisrael va-anan lo ishtabdanu be-Yisrael* — at least Rome and Persia actually subjugated Israel and had a direct historical relationship with the Jewish people. The other nations — those that never subjugated Israel, never had contact with her — thought that their very distance might work in their favor. Perhaps they could claim that unlike the great empires, they had never oppressed the Jews. So they entered with a different kind of argument.

### Significance

The *gemara* then asks a structural question: why does the *midrash* focus specifically on Rome and Persia and not enumerate all the other nations? *Mishum de-hanei mashkhei be-malkhusaihu ad de-ati meshikha* — because Rome and Persia maintain their dominion until the coming of the *Mashiakh*. They are the nations of enduring eschatological significance; the others, however historically real, do not bear on the ultimate end of history in the same way.

### Conclusion

What this entire *midrash* accomplishes — and it is worth stepping back to see this clearly — is a sustained meditation on a question that faced every Jew living in the Roman and later Christian world: how do we evaluate the accomplishments of the civilization around us? There is a genuine claim to be made. Rome built roads, bathhouses, legal institutions, and an economy; Persian policy permitted the return to Zion and the rebuilding of the Temple. Jews benefited from these things. Should they feel grateful? The *midrash* is constructed precisely to foreclose that gratitude without dismissing the underlying question. It places the claim in the mouths of Rome and Persia themselves, then rejects it on two grounds: first, they did everything for their own self-interest, not for Israel's benefit; and second, all the wealth and power they accumulated ultimately belongs to God anyway — *li ha-kesef ve-li ha-zahav*. Whatever good came from their civilization was not their achievement to credit; it was divine provision flowing through them. The *midrash* thus produces a particular way of seeing the world — one in which no gratitude is owed to the great powers, no sense of indebtedness to the civilization that surrounds and often oppresses the Jewish people. Whether the *gemara* elsewhere presents a more generous view is a question we will keep open as we continue.

---

---

# Avodah Zarah 3

## Nations' Defense

### Aggadata Framework

We take up the *daf* at the bottom of 3b, in the middle of the opening *aggadata*. This opening *aggadata* is significant because it functions as a framing device for the tractate as a whole: it addresses the broad question of the Rabbis' attitude toward non-Jews and the non-Jewish world. The scenario it depicts is one of a future day of cosmic judgment, in which all the nations of the world come before God to justify their actions, claiming that everything they did was somehow connected to the *Torah* or done for the sake of enabling the Jewish people to study it. God rejects all of these claims entirely.

### Idolatry vs. Torah

One point worth noting at the outset — and it is easy to overlook — is that the nations in this *aggadata* are not being held accountable for their idolatry. In the *Torah* itself, the central concern is the proclamation of a single transcendent God who is not worshipped through images, and the great struggle against the idolatry of the surrounding nations. The people of Israel entering the land were warned above all else against being led astray by the idolatrous practices of the inhabitants. The verse in *Yeshayahu* that serves as the textual basis for this *midrash* speaks of how, in the future, all idols will be exposed as falsehoods. Yet by the time of the Rabbis, the framing has shifted entirely. The dispute here is not about idolatry versus belief in God. It is about *mitzvot* and *Torah* — have you kept them, are you connected to them? The *Maharsha* observes that the image of God holding a *Sefer Torah* in his bosom captures precisely this: every nation claims that its faith is the true one, and the revelation is that it is the *Torah* that stands closest to God, not any other faith. But the central point remains that this is not a polemic about paganism — it is about what it means to live a life of *Torah* and *mitzvot*.

### Non-Jewish Works

A second theme concerns whether credit is extended to the accomplishments of the non-Jewish world — the roads, the bridges, the bathhouses, the marketplaces. In this *midrash*, those accomplishments are acknowledged, but only in order to be dismissed. They are dismissed on two grounds: first, that the nations did it all for their own sake, not for any higher purpose; and second, that God declares it all to be his anyway. The acknowledgment, in other words, is purely instrumental — it is introduced so that it can be set aside.

### Never Given Torah

The nations now bring their first claim before God. The *gemara* locates this approximately fifteen lines from the bottom of the page, beginning at *omrim lefanav*, near the citation of *Devarim* 33. They say: *Ribono Shel Olam*, how can you hold us responsible for not observing the *Torah* when you never gave it to us? Had you given it to us, we would have accepted it.

### Torah Offered

The *gemara* immediately interjects: how could they possibly make such a claim? The verse says *Vayomar Hashem miSinai ba*, God came from Sinai, and also *v'zarach miSeir lamo*, he shone from *Seir*, and *Eloah miTeiman yavo*, he came from *Teiman*. What was God doing in *Seir*, the territory of *Esav*, and in *Paran*, the territory of *Yishmael*? Rabbi Yochanan explains: this teaches that before giving the *Torah* to the Jewish people, God brought it around and offered it to every nation and tongue — *kol umah v'lashon* — and none of them accepted it, until he came to Israel and they received it. So the nations cannot honestly claim they were never given the opportunity.

### Would Have Kept

The nations revise their argument: *klum kiblanuha v'lo kiyamanuha* — if only you had given it to us, we would have fulfilled it. The *gemara* is dismissive: *al da'at tavar tuhu* — this claim shatters them. You cannot say "I would have done it had I accepted it" when you chose not to accept it in the first place.

The nations then try yet again. *Ribono Shel Olam*, did you not force it upon Israel? The verse says they stood at the foot of the mountain — *vayisyatzvu b'tachtit hahar* — and Rav Dimi bar Chama teaches that God held the mountain over them like a barrel and said: if you accept the *Torah*, good; if not, this is where you will be buried. So if you had only forced it upon us the way you forced it upon them, we would have committed ourselves to a life of *Torah u'mitzvot*.

## Noachide Mitzvot

### Track Record Test

God responds with a challenge: *harishonot yashmiunu* — let us look at the early record and see whether your claim that you would have upheld the *Torah* had any merit. You were given the *sheva mitzvot bnei Noach*. *Sheva mitzvot she'kibaltem heichan kiyamtem* — the seven *mitzvot* you did accept, where is your track record in fulfilling them? The *midrash* thus moves from dismissing the nations' claim about the *Torah* to an even more pointed indictment: they did not even fulfill the basic ethical-religious minimum that was given to them.

### Habakkuk Verse

To demonstrate that the nations did not fulfill the seven Noachide laws, the *gemara* cites a teaching of Rav Yosef from the verse in *Chabakuk*: *amad vayimodad eretz ra'ah vayater goyim* — God stood up and measured out the land, he saw and he *yatar* the nations. The word *vayater* is read as related to *mutar*, permitted. What did God see? He saw the *sheva mitzvot* that the *bnei Noach* had accepted upon themselves — and the verse notes that they accepted them, *she'kiblu aleihem*, a phrase that is itself slightly ironic given that they were never fully willing participants. God saw they did not fulfill them, and therefore declared it all *mutar* — permissible to them, as it were, releasing them from obligation.

The *gemara* pauses over this: does that mean the sinner is rewarded — *chotei niskar* — that by failing to observe, one is now relieved of the obligation entirely?

### Obligation & Reward

Mar b'rei d'Ravina clarifies. Since the nations failed to uphold the seven *mitzvot* and began living as though they were not obligated, when they subsequently do perform those same actions, they do so not from a sense of *chiuv*, of obligation, but rather out of their own inclination or personal ethic. Therefore, *af al pi she'mekaymim otam ein mekabelin aleihem sachar k'metzuveh v'oseh* — even if they observe these *mitzvot*, they are not rewarded as one who is commanded and fulfills, *metzuveh v'oseh*. Rather, they receive only the lesser reward of *eino metzuveh v'oseh*, one who performs a deed without being obligated to do so. This is grounded in the principle stated by Rabbi Chanina: *gadol hametzuveh v'oseh yoter mi-mi she'eino metzuveh v'oseh* — greater is the one who acts from obligation than the one who acts without it.

### Rabbi Meir Teaching

The *gemara* challenges this framework: but surely non-Jews do receive some reward? The *braita* is then introduced: *hayah Rabbi Meir omer minayin she'afilu oved kochavim ve'osek baTorah shehu k'kohen gadol* — Rabbi Meir taught that we learn from the verse *asher ya'aseh otam ha'adam v'chai bahem* — which specifies not *kohanim*, *leviyim*, or *Yisraelim*, but simply *ha'adam*, a human being — that even a non-Jew who involves himself in *Torah* is like a *kohen gadol*.

This is a striking teaching, and its full force requires some unpacking. The phrase *harei hu k'kohen gadol* is borrowed from a famous passage in the *Mishna* in *Horayot*, which contains what is essentially an anti-hierarchical statement about the nature of *Torah* society. The traditional structure is ordered by class: *kohen*, *levi*, *Yisrael*, and so on, with a further hierarchy of man over woman, Jew over non-Jew. But the *Mishna* there says that when all other things are equal, *Torah* learning overrides everything. A *mamzer* who is a *talmid chacham* takes precedence over a *kohen gadol am ha'aretz*. The *kohen gadol* represents the apex of the class hierarchy, and *Torah* supersedes it entirely. This is grounded in the verse *yekarah hi mipeninim* — *Torah* is dearer than pearls — read as *yekarah hi mikohen gadol shenichnas lifnai velifnim*, dearer even than the *kohen gadol* who enters the innermost sanctum. The larger *midrash* from which this teaching derives, found in the *Sifrei* (or *Sifra*), elaborates further: it reads verses that say *adam*, it reads verses that say *goy*, and in each case draws the conclusion that whoever is *osek baTorah* rises to the highest level. One particularly powerful line reads *veyavo goy tzaddik* — and notes that it does not say *kohanim leviyim veyisraelim* will enter but rather *goy tzaddik*, a righteous nation; even a non-Jew *osek baTorah* will enter. So Rabbi Meir has taken the existing principle — that *Torah* breaks class hierarchy — and extended it to its ultimate conclusion: it does not even matter whether you are a Jew.

This is a profound counter-voice to everything the *midrash* has been building until this point. It does not speak about non-Jews who build roads or bathhouses, but it does disrupt the sharp division of the world into Jew and non-Jew. It raises the possibility that among the nations there may be individuals who are greater even than Jews — certainly greater than a *kohen gadol am ha'aretz*.

One might also ask whether *osek baTorah* here means learning *Torah* or performing *mitzvot*. The verse on which the teaching is grounded — *asher ya'aseh otam ha'adam v'chai bahem* — emphasizes doing, *ya'aseh*, not learning. And indeed, a parallel formulation elsewhere reads *afilu goy v'oseh et haTorah*, a non-Jew who *does* the *Torah*. This version fits both the verse and the broader context of the *gemara*, which has been discussing the performance of *mitzvot*. The *Rambam* in fact rules that if a non-Jew performs any of the 613 *mitzvot* of the *Torah* — even *brit milah*, which one might assume to pertain exclusively to the Jewish covenant — he receives reward as an *eino metzuveh v'oseh*. So the question of whether Rabbi Meir's teaching pertains to Torah study or to the performance of *mitzvot* is itself a substantive one.

### Diffusing Radicalism

The *gemara* immediately works to contain the force of Rabbi Meir's position. Rather than allowing the teaching to stand in its radical form — a non-Jew *osek baTorah* being compared to a *kohen gadol* — the *gemara* re-reads it through the lens of *metzuveh v'oseh* versus *eino metzuveh v'oseh*. They don't receive reward equal to a *kohen gadol*; they receive the lesser reward of one who performs without obligation. This is in tension with the entire point of the *harei hu k'kohen gadol* formulation, which was meant to assert equivalence, not hierarchy. Other *gemarot* push back further still: a *goy she-shavas* — a non-Jew who observes *Shabbat* — is *chayav mita*, and accordingly some *gemarot* limit Rabbi Meir's statement to mean that a non-Jew may only study the *mitzvot* that pertain to him — the *sheva mitzvot bnei Noach* — not the *Torah* that belongs to Israel. The *gemara* here has introduced the radical voice of Rabbi Meir and then systematically bracketed and diminished it.

It is worth noting parenthetically that certain *poskim* read the *midrash*'s phrase *amad vehitiran lahem* — God declared it permitted to them — in a more *pshat* direction, invoking an argument analogous to *tinok shenishba*. A Jew who grew up with no Jewish knowledge and violates *Shabbat* cannot be held to the same standard of responsibility as one who knew and chose otherwise. Some *poskim* apply a similar framework to non-Jews regarding the *sheva mitzvot bnei Noach*: one cannot hold them accountable for obligations they have no awareness of. This reading looks more sympathetically at the very passage the *gemara* here cites in order to be dismissive.

### Learning vs. Doing

The dominant orientation of this *sugya*, however, remains one of dismissal. The question of what a non-Jew's positive actions are worth — whether *osek baTorah* means learning or doing, whether the reward is that of a *kohen gadol* or merely of *eino metzuveh v'oseh* — all of it is resolved in the direction of minimizing credit to the nations. The lens through which the opening of this tractate invites us to view the non-Jewish world is one of fundamental skepticism: they did not fulfill their minimal obligations, and even when they appear to do so, it is not from a place of genuine *chiuv* and therefore yields only attenuated reward. That is how this *sugya* is shaping the reader's perception of the larger world — not as a simple polemic about idolatry versus monotheism, but as a carefully constructed argument about religious obligation, meritocracy, and who is genuinely connected to a life of *Torah u'mitzvot*.

## Counter-Claim

### Why Israel Different

The nations, having been told that their track record with the *sheva mitzvot bnei Noach* disqualifies their claim, now press a further argument. Fine, they say — but *Yisrael shekibluah, heichan kiyamuah*? The Jewish people who received the *Torah*, where is their record of fulfilling it? Why should they be rewarded if they too failed to keep it?

### Israel's Fulfillment

God responds: *ani me'id bahem shekiyamu et haTorah kulah* — I will testify that they fulfilled the entire *Torah*.

### Bias Challenge

The nations immediately challenge this: *Ribono Shel Olam, klum yesh av sheme'id al bno?* Is there a father who testifies on behalf of his son? You are *pasul edut* — disqualified as a witness. You are *noge'a b'davar*, a party with vested interest. You have already shown favoritism, as it is written *beni bechori Yisrael* — Israel is my firstborn son.

### Heaven & Earth

God replies: very well, let us bring impartial witnesses — *shamayim va'aretz ya'idu bahem*. Heaven and earth are frequently invoked in *Tanach* as cosmic witnesses to solemn commitments: *ha'azinu hashamayim ve'adabera*, *shimu shamayim*, and so on. Based on rain and the produce of the land, they hold people accountable and can testify to whether Israel has kept the *Torah*.

### Vested Interests

The nations object again: *shamayim va'aretz nog'im be'edutam* — heaven and earth also have a vested interest. The verse states *im lo briti yomam valayla, chukot shamayim va'aretz lo samti* — were it not for my covenant, meaning the *Torah*, I would not have set the laws of heaven and earth in place. Their very existence is conditional on Israel keeping the *Torah*.

### Creation Purpose

This is the teaching of Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish: why does the *Torah* say *yom hashishi*, the *the* sixth day, with the definite article, rather than simply *yom shishi*? This teaches that the entire six days of creation were predicated on the sixth day of *Sivan*, the day of *matan Torah*. God stipulated with the act of creation: *im Yisrael mekablim et haTorah mutav, ve'im lav ani achazir etchem l'tohu vavohu* — if Israel accepts and keeps my *Torah*, good; if not, I will return the world to the primordial void. Since the continued existence of heaven and earth depends on Israel having fulfilled the *Torah*, they cannot serve as impartial witnesses — their testimony in Israel's favor is self-serving. Chizkiyah adds a supporting verse: *mishamayim hishmata din, eretz yerah v'shakata* — from heaven the judgment was heard, the earth feared and then became tranquil. If it feared, why did it become tranquil? Because it feared that Israel would not accept the *Torah* and creation would be undone — and when Israel accepted it at *Har Sinai*, the earth was tranquil.

The recurrence of this theme is worth pausing over. The entire *sugya* continues to frame what is at stake not as a struggle between monotheism and idolatry, but as the question of whether the Jewish people live a life of *Torah* and *mitzvot*. That is why the world exists. That is the lens through which this tractate — which governs the Jewish community's relationship with the surrounding non-Jewish world — asks us to approach everything that follows.

## Historical Witnesses

### Rulers Testify

Since heaven and earth are disqualified, God turns to a different category of witnesses: *mikem yavo'u ve'ya'idu bahem b'Yisrael* — from among you, the nations, witnesses will come and testify on Israel's behalf that they fulfilled the entire *Torah*.

### Nimrod & Abraham

*Yavo Nimrod ve'ya'id b'Avraham shelo avad avodah kochavim* — let Nimrod come and testify regarding Abraham that he did not worship idols. According to the *midrash*, Abraham was cast into the furnace at *Ur Kasdim* precisely because he refused to bow to idols, and Nimrod himself witnessed this.

### Laban & Jacob

*Yavo Lavan ve'ya'id b'Yaakov shelo nechshad al hagezel* — let Laban come and testify regarding Jacob that he was never suspected of theft. Laban pursued Jacob and accused him of stealing his *terafim*, and yet, as Rashi notes, Jacob could say: show me someone who worked for his employer for twenty years and did not take so much as a pin or a scissors. Laban searched and found nothing. The irony that Rachel had in fact taken the *terafim* is duly noted — but Jacob himself did not, and it is Jacob who is the subject of this testimony.

### Potiphar & Joseph

*Yavo eshet Potifar ve'ta'id b'Yosef shelo nechshad al aveirah* — let the wife of Potiphar come and testify that Joseph did not commit sexual sin. Here too we are choosing whom to look at; many of the *bnei Yisrael* worshiped the *egel* at the foot of *Har Sinai*, but those are not the subjects of this *midrash*.

### Pre-Sinai Laws

Rashi makes a point worth highlighting: Abraham, Jacob, and Joseph all lived before *matan Torah*. The *mitzvot* for which they are praised — *avodah zarah*, *gezel*, and *giluy arayot* — correspond to three of the *sheva mitzvot bnei Noach*. The *midrash* is thus making a two-stage argument: in the pre-Sinaitic period, when Israel's ancestors were still in the legal status of *bnei Noach*, they kept the *mitzvot bnei Noach*. The witnesses testifying to this are themselves non-Jews, which is precisely the point — they are the ones who observed it firsthand.

### Post-Sinai Witnesses

After *matan Torah*, a second set of non-Jewish witnesses is called. *Yavo Nevuchadnetzar ve'ya'id b'Chananyah Mishael v'Azaryah shelo hishtachavu latzelem* — let Nebuchadnezzar come and testify that Chananyah, Mishael, and Azaryah did not bow down to the statue. *Yavo Daryavesh ve'ya'id b'Daniel shelo bitel et hatfillah* — let Darius come and testify that Daniel did not cease from his daily prayers. Then the friends of *Iyov* — Bildad, Tzofar, and Eliphaz — are called; as non-Jewish prophets, they can testify through prophetic knowledge that the Jewish people kept the entire *Torah*. The verse *yitnu edeihem veyitzdaku* is cited in support: let them give their testimony and be found righteous. Notably, the original verse in *Yeshayahu* was part of a challenge to idolaters; here it has been entirely reframed as a declaration about who kept the *Torah*.

### Statue Question

Tosafot raises an important distinction regarding Chananyah, Mishael, and Azaryah. The *gemara* says they did not bow to *latzelem* — the statue — which is not the same formulation used for Abraham, who is said not to have been *oved avodah zarah*. Tosafot suggests that the statue Nebuchadnezzar demanded they bow to may not have been an actual idol but rather a symbol of fealty to the king — and that bowing to it would not technically have constituted *avodah zarah* under *halacha*. Yet they gave up their lives rather than do even that. This leads Tosafot into an important discussion relevant to its own historical context: the Jews of the Crusade period who died as martyrs in circumstances that were not technically required by *halacha* — can the idea of *kiddush Hashem* extend to such cases? Tosafot is also troubled by the *midrash* that suggests Chananyah, Mishael, and Azaryah would have bowed had they been subjected to torture. If the statue was not real *avodah zarah*, that claim becomes more understandable — one cannot be obligated to die for something that is not technically *yehareg v'al ya'avor*.

## Sukkah Test

### Final Chance

The nations, having been outmaneuvered at every turn, make one last appeal: *Ribono Shel Olam, tenah lanu merosh vena'asena* — give us one final chance and we will do it.

### Friday-Shabbat

God's reply is blunt: *shotim shebaolam* — fools! *Mi shetarach beerev Shabbos yochal beShabbos* — whoever worked on *erev Shabbat* gets to eat on *Shabbat*; whoever did not work on *erev Shabbat* — where will his food come from? The world to come is like *Shabbat*: a time to receive reward, not to perform *mitzvot*. The work must precede it. The *gemara* cites Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's reading of *asher anochi metzavcha hayom* — *hayom la'asotam velo lemachar la'asotam*, today is the time to do them, not tomorrow; *hayom la'asotam velo hayom litol secharchem*, today you do, but today is not when you collect your reward.

Strictly speaking, of course, the *gemara* acknowledges that God should not be offering them any chance at all — *ein HaKadosh Baruch Hu ba bitrunya im briyotav* — God does not wish to leave his creatures with any legitimate basis for complaint. Even an opportunity they do not deserve will be granted, to ensure they have no grounds to protest.

### Sukkah Offered

So God says: *mitzvah kalah yesh li, vesukkah shemah* — I have an easy *mitzvah* for you, called *sukkah*. *Lechu va'asu osah* — go and do it.

### Zechariah Vision

The choice of *sukkah* is not arbitrary. The *haftarah* read on *Sukkot* is from *Zechariah*, and it envisions precisely this scenario: *vehayah kol hanotar mikol hagoyim habaim al Yerushalayim ve'alu midei shanah beshanah lehishtachavot leMelech Hashem Tzeva'ot velachog et chag hasukkot* — all the remaining nations will come up to Jerusalem year after year to bow before God and to celebrate the festival of *Sukkot*. And those who do not come will receive no rain; and if the family of Egypt does not come, they will be struck with plague. *Sukkot* thus carries a universalist dimension — it is connected to rain, to sustenance, to the basic conditions of life for all humanity — which makes it a fitting test case.

### Sukkah Failure

The nations hear the offer and are enthusiastic. *Miyad kol echad ve'echad notel veholech ve'oseh sukkah berosh gago* — immediately, each one goes and builds a *sukkah* on the roof. But then God causes the sun to beat down upon them with the heat of summer — some textual variants read *kitkufat Tammuz*, like the summer period, but the standard text has *mitkufat Tammuz*, during the summer period. In any case, the point is clear: the sun is blazing.

### Sun Exemption

The *gemara* pauses: but is this fair? God said he does not come with complaints against his creatures — and here he is making things unreasonably difficult. The answer given is that for Israel too, sometimes the summer heat extends into *Sukkot*, depending on the alignment of the lunar and solar calendars. The Jews manage to sit in their *sukkot* even then. So God was not imposing an impossible standard — he was testing whether the nations could do what Jews have managed to do.

Furthermore, Rava points out: *mitzta'er patur min hasukkah* — one who is genuinely uncomfortable is *halachically* exempt from the *sukkah*. So there was actually a legitimate basis for leaving.

### Rejecting Bonds

But the nations do not simply leave. *Vekol echad ve'echad meva'et besukkato veyotzei* — each one kicks his *sukkah* in frustration and walks out. That is the crucial point. Leaving the *sukkah* when genuinely uncomfortable is permitted; kicking it as you leave is not. The verse cited is *nenatkah et mosroteimo venashlichah mimenu avoteimo* — let us cast off his bonds and throw his ropes away from us. The *Maharsha* notes that *avot* echoes *anaf etz avot*, the braided branch used for *lulav*, lending the image a *Sukkot*-flavored resonance. The nations' reaction is not simply one of incapacity — it is one of hostility. They are constitutionally unsuited to a life of regulated obligation, and the moment conditions become difficult, their response is not to seek an exemption but to reject the entire enterprise. This is how the *midrash* concludes its characterization of the nations: not merely that they fail to observe, but that they are fundamentally not the kind of people who can live this type of life.

## Divine Laughter

### God Laughs

*Miyad HaKadosh Baruch Hu yoshev umesachek aleihem* — immediately God sits up in heaven and laughs at them. The verse is *Yoshev Bashamayim Yischak* — he who dwells in the heavens will laugh — drawn from the same chapter of *Tehillim* that spoke of casting off bonds.

### One Day Laughter

Rabbi Yitzchak teaches: *ein schok lifnei HaKadosh Baruch Hu ela oto hayom bilvad* — God has laughter only on that one day, the future moment when all of the nations' claims and pretensions are exposed as folly.

### Future Converts

The *gemara* notes that some teach Rabbi Yitzchak's statement in connection with a different teaching. A *braita* states: Rabbi Yosi teaches that in the future, non-Jews will come and convert — *ba'in ovdei kochavim umitgayrin*.

### No Converts

The *gemara* immediately challenges this: would we accept them? The rule is *ein mekabelin gerim limot haMashiach* — we do not accept converts in the Messianic era, because such converts would be motivated by self-interest rather than sincere commitment. The precedent cited is that we similarly did not accept converts in the days of David and Solomon, when it was too advantageous to be part of the Jewish people.

### Dragged Converts

Nevertheless, Rabbi Yosi's point still holds, because these individuals will present themselves as converts even without formal acceptance: *shena'asu gerim grurim* — they become, in an alliterative phrase, *gerim grurim*, dragged-along converts. To demonstrate their Jewish identity, they take on the visible markers of male Jewish practice: *tefillin* on their heads and arms, *tzitzit* on their garments, and a *mezuzah* on their doorposts.

### Gog-Magog Wars

Then the wars of *Gog uMagog* approach. The timing is somewhat curious: one would generally expect the Messianic period to follow the wars of *Gog uMagog*, yet here the Messianic era has arrived and the wars have not yet occurred. In any case, these *gerim grurim* see the armies massing against the Jewish people and ask: why are you coming? *Ve'omrim lo al Hashem ve'al Meshicho* — they answer: we are coming to fight against God and his Messiah. Immediately, each of these fair-weather converts strips off his *mitzvot* and departs. *Vekol echad ve'echad menatek mitzvotav veholech*. The verse again: *nenatkah et mosroteimo venashlichah mimenu avoteimo*. Tosafot notes that *mosroteimo* — the bonds — alludes to the *tefillin* straps wound around the arm and head, and *avoteimo* — the braided cords — to the *tzitzit*. They cast it all off, and God laughs: *VehaKadosh Baruch Hu yoshev umesachek, Yoshev Bashamayim Yischak*. Rabbi Yitzchak's teaching applies here as well: *ein lo leHaKadosh Baruch Hu schok ela oto hayom bilvad* — only on that one day.

## Divine Schedule

### Twelve Hours

The *gemara* presses: is it really true that God only laughs on that single day? But Rav Yehuda, citing Rav, teaches that the day is divided into twelve hours, and God's schedule throughout the day involves something that might be characterized as a form of pleasure or laughter.

### Study Torah

In the first three hours, *HaKadosh Baruch Hu yoshev ve'osek baTorah* — God sits and engages in *Torah* study.

### Divine Judgment

In the second set of three hours, from roughly nine to noon, *yoshev vedan et kol ha'olam kulo* — God sits in judgment of the entire world. When he sees that the world's conduct would merit destruction, he does not carry it out: *miyad omed mikise hadin veyoshev al kise rachamim* — he rises from the throne of judgment and takes his seat on the throne of compassion. The world must continue.

### Sustains World

In the third set of three hours, from noon to three in the afternoon, *yoshev vezan et kol ha'olam kulo* — God provides sustenance to the entire world. The *gemara* describes the scope of this: *mikarnei re'eimim ad beitzei kinim* — from the horns of the great beast (suggested by some to be the reindeer, with its magnificent antlers) to the eggs of lice. Rashi suggests that *beitzei kinim* refers to a species of small creature rather than lice eggs literally, though the plain sense of the phrase seems to convey the extremity of God's providential reach: from the most lofty creature to the most minute, God sustains all.

### Leviathan Play

In the fourth and final set of three hours, from three to six in the afternoon, *yoshev umesachek im livyatan* — God sports with the Leviathan. The verse cited is *livyatan zeh yatzarta lisachak bo* — the Leviathan you created to play with. This is, admittedly, a strikingly anthropomorphic image, with something of a mythological flavor. But the structural point it makes is clear: God has laughter every day, *im briyotav*, with his creatures, taking pleasure in his creation. What God does *not* do every day is laugh *at* his creatures, *al briyotav*. That happens only on the one day at the end of time when the nations' folly is finally exposed.

### Post-Destruction

Rav Acha objects to Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: *mi-yom she-charav Beit ha-Mikdash ein schok lifnei HaKadosh Baruch Hu* — from the day the *Beit ha-Mikdash* was destroyed, God no longer laughs at all.

### Jerusalem Mourning

Is this provable from a verse? The verse *vayikra Hashem Elokim Tzeva'ot bayom hahu livchi u-lemisped u-lekorchah* — God called that day one of weeping and lamentation and mourning — might be limited to the day of the destruction itself. But the verse *im eshkachech Yerushalayim tishkach yemini, tidbak leshoni le-chiki im lo ezkerechi* — if I forget you, Jerusalem, may my right hand wither; may my tongue cleave to my palate if I do not remember you — shows that the mourning is perpetual, not confined to a single day. Could this not mean simply that God will never *forget* Jerusalem while still being capable of joy? The verse *hechesheiti me-olam acharish et'apak* — I have long been silent, held myself back — implies that God continually restrains himself, maintaining a posture of perpetual restraint rather than open laughter.

### Teaching Infants

If God no longer sports with the Leviathan in the fourth quarter of the day, what does he do instead? *Yoshev u-melamed tinokot shel beit raban Torah* — God sits and teaches *Torah* to the schoolchildren. These are not living children in their classrooms who need God as their teacher. They are infants and young children who died before their time. They are up in heaven, and God himself teaches them *Torah*. It is a striking and moving image: the child who is taken too young sits in a heavenly *cheder* with God as the teacher. The verse cited is *et mi yoreh dei'ah, ve'et mi yavin shmu'ah — g'mulei me-chalav, atikei mi-shadayim* — to whom will he teach knowledge, who will understand the teaching? — those weaned from milk, those torn away from the breast.

One might ask: who taught these infants before the destruction of the *Beit ha-Mikdash*, when God was occupied with the Leviathan? The *gemara* offers two answers: either it was the angel *Metatron*, who serves in some traditions as a heavenly surrogate for divine activity, or alternatively God was doing both simultaneously — teaching *Torah* and playing with the Leviathan. After the destruction, the play ceased and only the teaching remains.

### Night Tour

Finally, the *gemara* addresses what God does at night, having described his daytime schedule in such detail. Two answers are given. The first is that nighttime activity parallels daytime activity in some analogous way — *me'ein yamama*. The second is more specific and no less vivid: *rochev al kruv kal shelo veshat* — God mounts his swift cherub and tours the world, surveying creation. More expansively: *bishmonah asar elef olamot* — through 18,000 worlds, based on the verse *rechev elohim ribotayim*, which yields a figure of 20,000, from which 2,000 are subtracted to give 18,000. A third possibility is offered: *yoshev veshome'a shira mipi chayot* — God sits and listens to the celestial beings singing songs of praise, as the verse says: *yomam yetzaveh Hashem chasdo, uvelayla shiro imi* — by day God commands his kindness, and at night his song is with me.

---

---

# Avodah Zarah 4

## God's Judgment Nations

### Torah vs. Frivolous Talk

We are picking up at the bottom of 3b, deep in the middle of the *agadata*. The preceding sugya addressed how the nations will attempt to justify their actions before God, who will ultimately dismiss their claims as self-serving. God then gives them a final opportunity — the *mitzvah* of *sukkah* — which they fail entirely, and God laughs at them. The digression on divine laughter having concluded, the *gemara* now resumes with *Amar Rabbi Levi*.

### R. Levi: Punishment

Rabbi Levi teaches: *kol haposek midivrei Torah ve'osek bedivrei sicha, machilin lo gachalei resamim* — whoever interrupts words of *Torah* and involves himself in frivolous talk will be fed burning coals. The prooftext is *hakotfim maluach alei siach* — those who pluck *maluach*, which Rashi understands not in its literal sense of something salted, but as a reference to the *mei luchot*, the words inscribed on the tablets. The phrase *alei siach* is read homiletically as "for frivolous talk." The verse concludes: *veshoresh resamim lachmam* — the root of those burning coals will be their bread.

### Torah at Night

The *gemara* continues: *Amar Reish Lakish, kol ha'osek baTorah balayla, HaKadosh Baruch Hu moshech alav chut shel chesed bayom* — anyone who engages in *Torah* study at night, God draws over him a thread of *chesed* by day. The prooftext is *yomam yetzaveh Hashem chasdo uvalayla shiro imi* — by day God will command His kindness, and at night His song is with me. The verse was already cited earlier in reference to what God does at night — listening to the song of the heavenly angels. The *gemara* reads it now as asking: why does God grant a person favor in the eyes of others during the day? *Mishum devalayla shiro imo* — because at night His song is with him, meaning the person's *Torah* study.

There is something quite beautiful in the characterization of *Torah* as a *shira*, a song — a mode of expressing one's connection to God, a source of joy and praise. This idea is one that Rav Soloveitchik developed at great length. There is also a striking practical dimension: ordinarily, someone who stays up studying through the night looks haggard and exhausted the next morning. Here the *gemara* inverts that: the one who stays up learning *Torah* will glow, will find that others look upon him with admiration. The deeper point is that nighttime is unstructured, unobserved time. What a person does in those quiet hours reveals what he is truly about — whether he reaches for *Torah* or for distraction.

### Fish Metaphor

*Amar Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel*: what is meant by the verse *vata'aseh adam kedigei hayam*, and he made humans like the fish of the sea, like crawling things that have no ruler over them? Why are human beings compared to fish of the sea? *Lomar lach* — to teach you that just as fish, the moment they are lifted out of the water onto dry land, immediately die, so too human beings: *kecheivan sheporshin midivrei Torah umin hamitzvos miyad meisun* — as soon as they separate themselves from *Torah* and *mitzvos*, they immediately die. This is the classic lesson associated with Rabbi Akiva, who continued learning even after the Roman decrees prohibited it, understanding that to cease learning *Torah* would itself be a form of death — spiritual death.

The theme here is worth pausing over. The tractate of *Avodah Zarah*, in the Tannaitic and biblical periods, was primarily concerned with the literal danger of pagan worship as a seductive force. But by the time of the *gemara*, the concern has shifted. It is now about the commitment to a life of *Torah* and *mitzvos* and the way in which the larger world, by not representing that commitment, can draw a person away from it.

## Sun Righteous Wicked

### Sun Health Advice

The *gemara* offers a second interpretation of the fish metaphor: *mah dagim shebayam keivan shekadrah aleihem chamah miyad meisim* — just as fish, when the sun beats down upon them, die immediately, so too human beings. This is presumably a reference to fish that have already been taken out of the water — the sun and exposure combining to destroy them. The *gemara* then offers two readings of this second metaphor. The first: *ei ba'is eima b'olam hazeh*, this applies in the present world, in line with the teaching of Rabbi Chanina.

Rabbi Chanina states: *hakol biydei shamayim chutz mitzinim u'pachim* — everything is in the hands of heaven except cold and heat, as it is written *tzinim u'pachim bederech ikeish, shomer nafsho yirchak meihem* — cold and heat lie along the crooked path; one who guards himself will distance himself from them.
