Tosafot explains that certain forces — hurricanes, tsunamis, certain illnesses — are decreed from above and offer the individual no recourse. But heat and cold are different: they are dangers a person can identify and take measures to avoid. If it will be hot, one seeks shade or cooling; if cold, one dresses warmly. The mention of exposure to the sun therefore serves as straightforward health advice. Know that you are vulnerable to the elements. Take care of yourself.

### Future Sun Judgment

The second reading: *v'ei ba'is eima l'olam haba*, this may refer instead to the world to come, in line with the teaching of Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish. *Amar Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish: ein Gehennom le'asid lavo* — there will be no *Gehennom* in the future time. Instead, God will remove the sun from its sheath — from its protective covering. Presently we do not receive the sun at full intensity. In the time to come, God will unleash it entirely. For the wicked — *reshaim nidonin bah* — they will be scorched and destroyed by it. For the righteous — *tzaddikim misrapin bah* — that very same sun will bring healing.

### Destruction Healing

The *gemara* brings the prooftexts for both. For the wicked: *ki hinei hayom ba bo'er katanur, v'hayu kol zeidim v'chol osei rish'ah kash* — behold a day is coming burning like a furnace, and all the arrogant and all those who do wickedness will be stubble. *V'lo ya'azov lahem shoresh v'anaf* — no root in this world and no branch in the world to come. For the righteous: *v'zorcha lachem yirei shemi shemesh tzedakah u'marpei bichnafeha* — and the sun of righteousness will shine for those who fear My name, with healing in its wings. The identical phenomenon — the full, unsheathed power of the sun — produces entirely opposite experiences depending on who you are.

There is a famous parable illustrating precisely this point: the *gan eden* and *gehinnom* of the next world are the same hall, the same feast, the same abundance. The difference is that in *gehinnom* everyone tries to feed himself with arms that cannot bend; in *gan eden* everyone feeds his neighbor. It is one reality, experienced according to what one has become.

The *gemara* adds: *v'lo od ela shemisyadnin bah* — and not only will the righteous be healed, they will be pampered by the sun of the future time, as it says *v'yatzasem ufishtem k'eglei marbeik* — you will go out and spread out like the calves of the stall, Rashi understanding this to mean that they will be fattened, flourishing in full bodily pleasure.

## Government Law Fear

### Fish Swallow Gov't

*Davar acher* — a third explanation of the fish metaphor: *kol hagadol mechaveiro bolei'a es chaveiro* — every larger fish swallows the smaller one. So too with human beings: *ilmalei mora'ah shel malchus, kol hagadol mechaveiro bolei'a es chaveiro* — were it not for the fear of the government, the stronger would simply devour the weaker. It would be a completely predatory, lawless world.

### Prayer Gov't

This teaching connects directly to the *mishna* in *Avos*: *Rabbi Chanina segan hakohanim omer, hevei mispallel bishlomah shel malchus* — pray for the welfare of the government. *She'ilmalei mora'ah shel malchus, ish es rei'ehu chayim bela'u* — for were it not for the fear of the government, one man would swallow his neighbor alive. This *tefillah lishlom hamalchus* has been a persistent feature of Jewish liturgical history throughout the generations, and the *gemara* here roots it in a foundational recognition: structured authority, however imperfect, is what prevents total social collapse.

## God Strength Anger

### R. Chanina Strength

Rabbi Chanina bar Papa raises a contradiction. One verse states *Shaddai lo m'tzanuhu sagi koach* — the Almighty, we have not found Him great in strength. Yet other verses say *gadol adoneinu v'rav koach* — great is our Lord and abundant in strength — and *yeminecha Hashem nedari bakoach* — Your right hand, O Lord, is glorified in strength. Which is it?

### Judgment War

*Lo kashya* — there is no difficulty. The first verse speaks of the time of judgment — *b'shas din* — while the others speak of the time of war — *b'shas milchamah*. When God sits in judgment, He does not bring His full strength to bear. This connects to the earlier discussion: God sits in judgment and then, recognizing that the world cannot survive strict justice, rises and moves to the seat of compassion, restraining Himself. But at the time of war and punishment of the wicked — as at *Shiras Hayam* — God acts with the full force of His power.

### R. Chama Anger

Rabbi Chama bar Chanina raises a parallel contradiction. One verse states *cheimah ein li* — I have no anger. Another says *nokem Hashem uva'al cheimah* — God takes vengeance and is full of anger. *Lo kashya.*

### Israel Nations

The contradiction is resolved by context: *kan b'Yisrael, kan b'ovdei kochavim* — the former verse concerns God's disposition toward Israel, the latter toward the nations. This echoes the central theme of the entire *agadata*: the differential way in which God relates to Israel versus the nations, in judgment and in punishment.

### R. Papa Oath

Rabbi Chanina bar Papa offers an alternative resolution. *Cheimah ein li* — I have no anger — means: yes, God is by nature *ba'al cheimah*, filled with the disposition toward anger, as the verse elsewhere states. But *cheimah ein li* — I have set my anger aside. *Shekvar nishbati* — because I have taken an oath. Rashi explains: God acknowledges the anger as real and perhaps even justified, but has voluntarily foresworn acting upon it. *Mi eini shelo nishbati, ashmeyah beshait* — had I not taken that oath, I would have already brought destruction upon the world. It is the oath — not the absence of anger — that preserves creation.

## Nations Future Exam

### R. Alexandri Destroy

Rabbi Alexandri asks: what is meant by the verse *v'haya bayom hahu avakesh l'hashmid et kol hagoyim* — and it will be on that day that I will seek to destroy all the nations? The question the *gemara* raises is almost amusing in its precision: *avakesh mimi* — God will *seek*? From whom does God need to seek permission? The answer: *avakesh b'pinkas shelahem* — God will search through their records, their historical accounts. *Im yesh lahem zechut, efdem* — if they have merit, He will redeem them. *V'im lav, ashmidem* — and if not, He will destroy them. Of course, as the preceding discussion made clear, when those records are examined, they will not pass muster.

### Rava Judgment

This connects to Rava's teaching on a difficult verse in *Iyov*: *al b'ei yishlach yad, im b'pido lahen shoa* — He does not send His hand against them; if in His *pido* it is their salvation. God says to Israel: *keshe'ani dan et Yisrael, ein ani dan otam k'ovdei kochavim* — when I judge the Jewish people, I do not judge them the way I judge the nations.

### Gradual Destruction

For the nations: *avah avah avah asimenah* — destruction, destruction, destruction — I bring all their punishment at once. But for Israel: *ani nifra mehem k'pid shel tarnegolet* — I exact from them like the pecking of a hen. The punishment comes in tiny installments, distributed over time. Therefore: *lav b'ei yishlach yad* — I do not send my full hand against the Jewish people; *b'pido* — like a light pecking — *shoa* — it becomes their salvation, precisely because it is spread out rather than delivered all at once.

### Small Mitzvot

*Davar acher*: even if the Jewish people perform only a little before God — *k'pid shel tarnegolim* — like the pecking of chickens that peck in the garbage heap — *ani metzarfan l'cheshbon gadol* — I aggregate it all into something significant. *Im b'pido lahen shoa* — even those few scattered good deeds accumulate and become their salvation.

### Payment Sins

*Davar acher*: in the merit of their crying out before God, He saves them. And as Rabbi Abba teaches: *v'anochi efdem vehama dibru alai k'zavim* — I will redeem them, yet they have spoken falsehood about Me. God says: *ani amarti efdem bemamonam b'olam hazeh* — I declared I would redeem them by taking payment from them in this world — that is, their sufferings in this world are God's way of settling accounts, so that they will be fully rewarded in the world to come.

This is the classic rabbinic understanding of the asymmetry between Jewish suffering and non-Jewish prosperity: God pays the nations their reward for whatever good they have done in this world, so that they will have no claim in the next; while for Israel, God collects their debts in this world so their portion in the world to come will be complete and unencumbered. The principle is coherent, but it raises a question that the *gemara* does not entirely resolve: the earlier discussion at least argued on the merits — the nations had their chance and failed, Israel made the right choices. Here, the asymmetry feels less like justice than like a prior determination, a favoritism that precedes the reckoning rather than following from it. The answer may lie in the covenant relationship itself.

*V'heim dibru alai k'zavim* — and yet the Jewish people responded by complaining, by attributing evil to God, not realizing that their suffering was intentional and remedial.

### Afflictions Strength

This is what Rav Papi teaches in the name of Rava: *va'ani yasarti, chizakti z'ro'otam* — I afflicted them and strengthened their arms — *v'elai yachsh'vu ra* — and they considered it evil and thought ill of Me. God says: *ani amarti ayasrim b'yisurin ba'olam hazeh kedai sheyechazku z'ro'otam l'olam haba* — I meant to afflict them in this world in order to strengthen their power in the world to come. It is like being put through a rigorous training regimen: in the moment one curses the trainer, but the result is strength and health. *V'elai yachsh'vu ra* — and instead of understanding this, they attributed evil to Me.

It is worth noting, as pointed out in the scholarly notes of the Soncino edition, that these *drashot* at the opening of *Avodah Zarah* serve not only as a theological framework for understanding the relationship between Israel and the nations. They are also — and perhaps primarily — acts of *nechamah*, consolation, addressed to an oppressed minority living inside a dominant pagan culture, watching the powerful prosper and struggling to understand why. The *Kaddish DeRabbanan*, recited after a *derasha*, includes the phrase *l'eila mikol shirata v'tushbechata v'nechemata* — above all songs and praises and *consolations*. The word *nechemata* appears there because this kind of rabbinic teaching — explaining suffering, promising ultimate reward, reversing the apparent verdict of history — *was* the consolation. Seen through that lens, the opening *agadata* of *Avodah Zarah* is an extended act of comfort to a people who needed it.

## R. Abbahu Heretic

### Abbahu Reputation

*Mistabeach havah Rabbi Abahu l'minei b'Rav Safra* — Rabbi Abbahu had been praising Rav Safra to a certain *min*, a heretic — likely in this context a Jewish Christian — describing him as a great *talmid chacham*. This government official, on the basis of that praise, waived Rav Safra's taxes for thirteen years. Then one day this *min* encountered Rav Safra directly.

### Heretic Challenge

The *min* presented a verse: *rak etchem yadati mikol mishpechot haadamah, al ken efkod aleichem et kol avonoteichem* — only you have I known from all the families of the earth, therefore I will visit upon you all your sins. And he challenged: *man deit lei sanya berachamei masik lei?* — does someone who loves another direct his anger specifically at that beloved? How does God's love for Israel explain the visitation of punishment?

*Ishtik* — Rav Safra was silenced. *Lo hava beyadei lemeimar lei velo midi* — he had nothing to answer. So they threw a cloth around his neck and began to drag him off — he who was supposed to be this great Torah scholar could not explain a simple verse. When Rabbi Abbahu arrived and found what was happening, he said: *amai mitzaaritu lei?* Why are you afflicting him? They told him: you praised him to us as a great *talmid chacham*, and he cannot even explain this verse. Rabbi Abbahu responded: *eima de'amri lachon betana'ei* — when did I say that? I told you he was great in rabbinic literature. *Bekra'ei mi amri lachon?* — I never claimed he could explain biblical verses.

There is something wry and very recognizable in this exchange. Even in the Talmudic period, the *gemara* understood the phenomenon of the *talmid chacham* who knows all of *Shas* but is unfamiliar with a verse of *Tanakh*. The *Rashash*, in his commentary to the opening of *Bava Batra*, notes precisely this point from an incident involving Rebbi: when Rebbi tested someone's credentials, he asked first whether the person had learned *Tanakh* and then whether he had learned *Mishna* — which implies that it was considered possible to have mastered rabbinic literature without having learned *Tanakh*, and that these were treated as distinct bodies of knowledge.

### Scripture Debate

The *min* then asked Rabbi Abbahu: *mai shena atun deyad'itun?* — if that is the case, how is it that *you* know *Tanakh* so well, if the rabbinic world is focused on its own literature? Rabbi Abbahu responded: *anan deshachichan gabayichun* — we are among you, meaning: we regularly have these discourses with you. This strongly suggests that the *minim* here are indeed Jewish Christians, and that the disputations Rabbi Abbahu engaged in were precisely the kind of debate — common throughout the medieval period and apparently already present in the Talmudic era — in which both sides argued from shared scriptures, with Christians attempting to demonstrate that their faith was foretold in the Jewish texts. *Raminan anafshin ume'aynan* — we make the effort to study *Tanakh* thoroughly in order to know how to respond. *Inhu lo me'aynei* — those who remain cloistered in the *yeshiva* have no such need.

### Parable Love

Having established his credentials, Rabbi Abbahu returned to the question. *Emshol lachem mashal* — let me offer a parable. A man has two creditors: one who loves him and one who hates him. The one who loves him allows repayment *me'at me'at* — a little at a time, on an installment plan. The one who hates him demands the full sum at once. Therefore: when God says *because I loved you, I will visit your sins upon you* — it means precisely this: I will take my repayment from you gradually, in small installments, across time. That is the expression of love, not of anger.

## Righteous Suffering

### R. Abba Avraham

Rabbi Abba bar Kahana raises the question from a different angle, returning to Avraham's argument with God regarding Sodom. The verse is: *chalila lecha me'asot kadavar hazeh, lehamis tzaddik im rasha* — far be it from You to do such a thing, to kill the righteous together with the wicked. Avraham argued before God: *chulin hu me'asot kadavar hazeh* — it is a profane act to kill the righteous with the wicked. Now, within the context of the larger discussion — all of this concerns the justice of future punishment and why the righteous suffer in this world — the question becomes pressing: is it actually true that God does not bring death to the righteous together with the wicked? Because another verse says: *vehichrasti mimcha tzaddik verasha* — I will cut off from you both the righteous and the wicked.

### Complete Righteous

The resolution: *betzaddik she'eino gamur* — that verse applies to one who is not completely righteous. But for someone who is *tzaddik gamur*, truly and fully righteous — God does not destroy them together with the wicked. Yet this too requires qualification, for the verse also says *umimikdashi tichalu* — from My sanctuary shall you begin. And Rav Yosef taught: *al tikri mimikdashi, ela mimikudashai* — do not read "from My sanctuary," read "from those sanctified to Me" — those who have fulfilled the entire *Torah* from *alef* to *taf*. It is precisely these most devoted people who are struck first when destruction comes.

### Silent Enablers

The resolution to this apparent injustice: *keivan she'haya beyadam limchos velo michu* — since it was within their power to protest the evil being done in the world and they did not, *havu lehu ketzaddikim she'einam gmurim* — they are reckoned as those who are not fully righteous. One cannot claim the status of *tzaddik gamur* solely on the basis of personal piety, if one remains a silent enabler of evil in the community. The righteous person who sees wickedness and says nothing — who does nothing to protest or resist — bears a portion of the moral responsibility. This principle is perennial; it is precisely what allows evil to succeed.

Within the larger narrative arc, this teaching also serves a pastoral function: it addresses the uncomfortable question of why even seemingly good people suffer. One answer is that God is paying debts in installments. But another answer, offered here, is that no one is as fully righteous as they may appear if they have stood by silently while wrong was being done.

## God Wrath Daily

### R. Papa Daily Anger

Rav Papa raises a contradiction. One verse states *El zo'em bechol yom* — God becomes wrathful every day. Another verse asks *lifnei za'amo mi ya'amod* — who can stand before God's wrath? If God's wrath is daily and nothing can withstand it, why does the world continue to exist?

*Lo kashya* — no difficulty. *Kan beyachid, kan betzibur* — the individual cannot stand before God's wrath, but when God judges the entire world, the collective merit of creation prevents God's anger from consuming it. The world is perpetually deserving of destruction and perpetually preserved — by the aggregate merit of the whole.

### Instant Wrath

*Tanu Rabbanan*: God's wrath is daily — but how long does that wrath last? *Rega* — an instant. And how long is an instant? *Achas michamesh ribo ushloshes alafim ushmonah me'os v'arba'im ushmonah besha'ah* — one 53,848th of an hour. Working this out: rounding the denominator to 60,000ths of an hour, and dropping one factor of 60, one arrives at something less than a 150th of a second. *V'ein kol biryah yecholah lechaven osah rega* — no creature can identify that precise instant of God's wrath.

### Bileam Knowledge

With one exception: *chutz miBilam harasha* — except for Bilam the wicked. It is written of him: *yode'a da'as Elyon* — he who knows the thought of the Most High. This is where the *gemara* becomes genuinely pointed. *Efshar da'as behemto lo hava yada* — is it possible that someone who could not even know what his own animal was thinking — *da'as Elyon mi hava yada* — could know the mind of the Most High? The claim to divine knowledge is punctured immediately by the absurdity of the comparison. What is the proof that Bilam did not know his own animal's thoughts?

### Donkey Bileam

When people saw Bilam riding on a donkey, they said to him: why are you riding on a donkey? You should be riding on a horse — that would be more fitting for a man of your stature. He answered: *be'irtiva shadya* — it is out grazing in the swamp, it was not available. Immediately the donkey answered back: *halo anochi asonecha* — am I not your donkey, the very one you always ride? He tried to claim he only used her as a beast of burden. She replied *asher rachavta alai* — no, I am the one you always ride. He said *akrai b'alma* — only occasionally. She replied: *me'odecha ve'ad hayom hazeh* — from your entire life I have been your regular mount. And moreover: *she'ani osa lecha rechiva bayom, v'ishus balaila* — I provide you riding by day and companionship at night. The *gemara* reads *hahasken hiskanti la'asos lecha koh* through the word *sochenes*, as it appears by David and Avishag Hashunamis, meaning intimate closeness. The point: Bilam could not win an argument with his own donkey. He could not know what she was thinking. And this is the man who claimed to know *da'as Elyon*?

*Ela mai yodeia da'as Elyon? Ela shehaya yodeia kivein osah sha'ah shehakadosh baruch hu ko'es bah* — what it actually means is that Bilam knew how to identify that precise instant when God became wrathful, and therefore he could time his curses to coincide with it and channel that divine anger toward destruction.

## Israel Protection Wrath

### R. Elazar Withhold

The *navi* says to Israel: *ami zechor na mah ya'atz Balak melech Moav, umah ana oso Bilam ben Be'or, min hashittim ad haGilgal, lema'an da'as tzidkos Hashem* — My people, remember what Balak king of Moav plotted and how Bilam son of Be'or responded, from Shittim to Gilgal — so that you may know the *tzidkos* of God. What *tzidkos* are we meant to learn from that episode?

Rabbi Elazar explains: *ami reu kama tzedakos asisi imachem* — My people, see how many acts of righteousness I performed for you. *Shelo kaas'ti aleichem kol osan hayamim* — I withheld that daily instant of wrath throughout all those days. *Lo nishtayer mishoneihem shel Yisrael sarid ufalit* — had I allowed even one such instant of wrath to occur while Bilam was poised to exploit it, not a single person among Israel's enemies — which is the *gemara*'s way of saying Israel itself would have been annihilated — would have survived. The entire *parasha* of Bilam, seen through this lens, is not merely a story of curses turning to blessings. It is an account of God actively restraining His own natural wrathful response, day after day, throughout the entire episode, specifically to prevent Bilam from tapping into it.

### Bileam Admission

This is precisely what Bilam himself admits to Balak: *mah ekov lo kaboh El* — how can I curse what God has not cursed? The verse continues with the word *ezom*, which connects directly to the *zaam* — the wrath — that is the subject of this entire discussion.

### Zaim Wrath

*Umah ezom lo zaam Hashem* — how can I bring wrath when God has not shown wrath? There is a brilliance here in the *agadata*'s construction. The word *za'am* appears both in *El zo'em bechol yom* — God has that moment of wrathful anger every day — and in *lifnei za'amo mi ya'amod* — nothing can survive God's wrath — and now in Bilam's own confession: *lo zaam Hashem*. God had not become wrathful. Because God had withheld it. Therefore Bilam could do nothing.

The *gemara* then returns to the question of duration: *vekamah za'amo? rega* — an instant. And *Amar Ameimar v'isema Ravina: rega kemimrei* — a *rega* is as long as it takes to pronounce the word *rega* itself.

The *gemara* asks: *umanalan derega havei resicha* — where do we derive that a *rega* corresponds to God's wrath? From the verse *ki rega b'apo chayim birtzono* — only a moment in His anger, a lifetime in His favor. Or, as the *gemara* adds, from an even more precise verse: *chavi chimat rega ad ya'avor za'am* — hide for just a moment until the wrath passes. Here the word *za'am* itself appears in conjunction with *rega*, which is the strongest textual support.

Tosafot raises a pointed question: what could Bilam possibly have accomplished in so small a window — an instant, a fraction of a second — even if he had identified it? Tosafot gives two answers. First: he could have said a single word, *kaleim* — destroy them — and one word is sayable in the time it takes to say *rega*. Indeed, God reversed the word: rather than *kaleim*, it became *melech*, as it says *v'sruas melech bo*. Second: Rabbi Eliyahu explains that Bilam would not have needed to complete his curse in that instant — he would only have needed to *begin* during that window. Once the curse had been initiated at the moment of divine wrath, it would have continued to draw on that opening. The *Rogatchover* applies a similar principle to *davvening*: if someone begins *tefillah* a moment before the *zman* expires, that beginning within the *zman* may be sufficient to count the prayer as having been recited in time.

## Wrath Moment

### Rooster Crown

So when, practically speaking, does that instant of divine wrath occur during the first three hours of the day? *Amar Abaye: b'slas sha'ei kmaisa, ki chivra karbalta d'tarnagola* — during the first three hours of the morning, at the moment when the comb of the rooster is white. The *gemara* objects: the rooster's comb is always white. *Kol sha'ata is beih serikei sumkei* — no, normally there are red streaks running through it. *Hahi sha'ata, leis beih serikei sumkei* — at that one precise instant, the comb is pure white, with no red streaks at all.

### R. Yehoshua Heretic

With this knowledge in hand, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi decided to act. A certain *min* had been giving him a hard time *bikrai* — in disputes over biblical verses, the kind of scriptural disputations we have already described — and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi was struggling to hold his own. One day he took a rooster, placed it between the legs of his bed, and kept his eyes fixed on it, intending to identify that pure-white instant and at that moment curse the *min*. When that instant finally arrived — he had fallen asleep.

### Harm Not Just

Upon waking, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi drew a lesson: *lav orach ara lemeevad hachi* — it is not the right way to act. Even when someone is afflicting you, you do not seek to bring punishment upon them. *Verachamav al kol maasav kesiv* — God's compassion extends to all His creatures. *V'achsiv gam anosh latzaddik lo tov* — and it is written, even punishment is not appropriate for the righteous to bring.

This is not a call to passivity in the face of evil — the *gemara* already made clear that silent enabling is itself a form of complicity. The distinction is between *mecha*, protesting against evil in the world, which is obligatory, and personally seeking to bring punishment on those who have wronged you, which is categorically different. The latter draws on something more personal and less elevated: the desire for vengeance, which — even when the cause is just — belongs to the lower registers of human motivation. A righteous person does not cultivate or indulge it.

## Kings Sun Musaf

### Kings Crowns Sun

*Tana mishmeih de-Rabbi Meir*: when kings remove their crowns and prostrate themselves before the sun — setting aside their human dignity and sovereignty to worship the solar disk — God immediately becomes angry. This provides the practical context for when the moment of divine wrath occurs during the morning: it corresponds to the time when pagan kings bow to the sun.

### Musaf Alone

Rav Yosef rules: *lo litzli inish tzluta demmusafi betlas sha'ei kamaisa deyoma kama deRosh Hashanah beyachid* — a person should not pray *musaf* alone, without a *tzibbur*, during the first three hours of the day on the first day of *Rosh Hashanah*. The reason: that period is the time of judgment. *Musaf* on *Rosh Hashanah* — with *Malchiyos*, *Zichronos*, and *Shofros* — is the concentrated moment of divine reckoning. *Dilma me'ayni be'uvdai* — they may scrutinize your deeds, *vedachfu lei midchayei* — and you may be found guilty and condemned. Standing alone before that level of scrutiny is dangerous.

### Congregation Merit

But the *gemara* objects: if the first three hours are so dangerous, then even the *tzibbur* should not pray *musaf* that early. The answer: *detzibbur nefishei zechusei* — the congregation possesses far greater merit; the collective protects even those whose individual record might not withstand close examination.

The *gemara* then asks the inverse: if even an individual *davvening* alone is at risk during the first three hours, then *shacharis* on *Rosh Hashanah* should also be dangerous for someone *davvening* at home during that same period. The answer: *keivan dechi tzibura ka matzlu lo ka midchu* — since the entire community is *davvening shacharis* during those first three hours, even someone praying at home is understood to be connected to the communal prayer. He is, in effect, *davvening* together with the *tzibbur*, even if physically apart. *Musaf* is different: most congregations have not reached *musaf* in the first three hours, given the length of the *Rosh Hashanah* *davvening*. An individual who reaches *musaf* that early is therefore genuinely alone — not merely physically separate, but disconnected from the rhythm of congregational prayer — and that isolation during the height of divine judgment is what Rav Yosef cautions against.

## Lenient Torah

### Hours Judgment

The *gemara* circles back to address an apparent contradiction. Earlier it was stated that God spends the first three hours of the day in *Torah* learning and the next three hours sitting in judgment. But Rav Yosef's ruling assumed that the first three hours are the *dangerous* period of judgment. *Eifoch* — reverse the order. The first three hours are judgment; the next three are *Torah* learning.

### Torah Truth Law

*Ve'iba'is eima le'olam lo seifoch* — alternatively, one need not reverse the order at all. *Torah dechsiv bah emes* — *Torah* is truth, as it says *emes kneh ve'al timkor* — buy truth and do not sell it. When God is engaged in learning *Torah*, He operates strictly within the logic of pure truth. *Ein hakadosh baruch hu oseh lifnim mishuras hadin* — God does not go beyond the strict requirement of the law when learning *Torah*. Think of the dynamic inside a *beis medrash*: one does not argue from compassion or flexibility; one argues from rigor, from the force of the *sugya*, from what the text actually says.

### Flexibility Judge

*Din* — judgment — is different. Judgment applies law to human reality, which is not a purely abstract philosophical enterprise. Therefore: *hakadosh baruch hu oseh lifnim mishuras hadin* — when sitting in judgment, God can find latitude, can extend compassion, can look beyond the strict letter of the law. This produces the counterintuitive conclusion: it is actually *better* to approach God during the hours when He is sitting in judgment than during the hours when He is learning *Torah*. The *beis medrash* mode admits no flexibility; the *beis din* mode allows for mercy. The *gemara* acknowledges this is striking — and it is — but the underlying dynamic it describes is entirely recognizable to anyone who has observed the difference between *psak halacha* as an abstract exercise and *psak halacha* as a response to a human being standing before you with a real question.

# Avodah Zarah 5

## Torah & Future Reward

### Intro & Themes

Daf 5b opens approximately ten lines down, at the *siman* beginning *yom me'itaref ba'agal*, which serves as a heading for the various discussions to follow, after which the *gemara* proceeds *gufa*. The bulk of what we encounter here is *aggadata* — and this *aggadata* is, in a meaningful sense, the theological and moral framing of *masechet Avodah Zarah* as a whole.

The *masechet* is ultimately about navigating a world that is largely non-Jewish, often pagan, and sometimes hostile. The *aggadata* addresses the logical and emotional challenges this raises: the nations seem to prosper; we seem to suffer; their accomplishments appear impressive. The opening sections of the *masechet* have already introduced several major themes in response. First, in the future time the nations will be punished, and even their great achievements — building roads, conquering kingdoms — will be granted no credit, not even their claim that such works were done to facilitate Torah study. Second, and relatedly, what truly matters is Torah: learning it, performing its *mitzvos*. Third, the punishment of the nations will ultimately be harsher than our suffering, and our present suffering is directed toward our ultimate reward. These themes continue now as the *gemara* resumes.

### Today vs. Tomorrow

*Amar Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi*: what is meant by the *pasuk*, *asher anochi metzavcha hayom la'asotam* — that I command you today to do them? *Hayom la'asotam velo lemachar la'asotam*: today is the time to perform the *mitzvos*, not tomorrow. The *lemachar* here carries a double meaning — not only "don't delay" in the ordinary sense, but that the *atid lavo*, the *olam haba*, is not the time for doing *mitzvos*. And correspondingly: *hayom la'asotam velo hayom litol secharam* — in this world you perform the *mitzvos*, but you do not receive their reward here. The reward belongs to *olam haba*. This directly addresses the question of why those who devote themselves to Torah and *mitzvos* do not always appear as materially successful as the surrounding nations.

### Mitzvot as Witness

*Va'amar Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi*: all the *mitzvos* we perform in this world will come and testify to our righteousness in the world to come — *kol mitzvos she'osin ba'olam hazeh bo'os umididots osam la'olam haba*. Even if in this world we are mocked or degraded by surrounding nations, in the end the *mitzvos* will bear witness to our rightness. As the *pasuk* says: *yitnu adeihem veyitzdaku yishme'u veyomru emet* — they will give their testimony and be found righteous, they will hear and say it is true. *Eilu Yisrael* — these are Israel, who will demonstrate through a life of Torah and *mitzvos* that they are righteous. *Eilu ovdei kochavim* — it is the idolaters who will ultimately acknowledge this. The formulation *adeihem* also echoes back to the word *yom edam* cited at the very opening of the *masechet*, a deliberate textual resonance.

### Mitzvot Rebuke Nations

A third statement from *Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi*: all the *mitzvos* we perform in this world will not only vindicate us but will come and *slap the nations in the face* — *bo'os vetorfas al pneichem*. As the *pasuk* says: *ushmartem va'asitem ki hi chochmatchem uvinatchem le'einei ha'amim* — you shall observe and perform them, for this is your wisdom and understanding in the eyes of the nations. Note that the *pasuk* says *le'einei ha'amim*, in their eyes, not *neged ha'amim*, opposite the nations. *Melamed she-ba'at v-tarpas bifneihem* — it is as if the *mitzvos* smack the nations right in their face, demonstrating that their own lives have been worthless and that we were the truly wise ones.

One might note that the plain sense of that *pasuk* — *ki chachmatchem uvinatchem le'einei ha'amim asher yishme'un es kol hachukim v'omru rak am chacham v'navon hagoy hagadol hazeh* — seems to describe the nations recognizing Jewish wisdom *in this world*. Yet the *gemara* consistently places all of this vindication *le'asid lavo*, in the future time.

## Cheit HaEgel

### Gate for Repentance

*Va'amar Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi*: the Israelites made the *eigel* — the Golden Calf — only in order to open a *pischon peh*, an opening, for *ba'alei teshuvah*. It is worth noting that *pischon peh* ordinarily carries a negative connotation — one does not want to give a *pischon peh* to the *resha'im* or to the *apikorsim*. Here, however, the *pischon peh* is precisely what is needed: an opening for those who seek to return.

The argument is rooted in the *pasuk*: *mi yitein vehayah levavam zeh lahem l'yira osi kol hayamim* — who would only give that their heart would be like this, to fear Me all the days. This was said immediately after *Matan Torah*, when they stood at an extraordinary level of *yirat Hashem*. How could it be that within forty days they descended to worshipping the *eigel*? The very incomprehensibility of the sin suggests that it was allowed to happen only to demonstrate that even from the greatest heights, even after the most catastrophic fall, the gates of *teshuvah* remain open. Whether *Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi* means this was literally the Israelites' motivation, or rather that this was the ultimate purpose served by the event being permitted, is itself a question — but the theological function is clear.

### David & Israel

This connects to what *Rabbi Yochanan* says in the name of *Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai*: *lo David ra'uy l'oso ma'aseh* — David was not at a level where he should have been capable of that act with *Bas Sheva*, and *lo Yisrael re'uyim l'oso ma'aseh* — the Israelites at *Har Sinai* were not at a level where they should have been capable of the sin of the *eigel*. How do we know this about David? *V'libi chalal b'kirbi* — my heart is as if emptied within me, meaning he was entirely free of lust and *yetzer hara*. How do we know this about Israel? From the very same *pasuk*: *mi yitein vehayah levavam zeh* — they were at such a level of *yirat Hashem* that it is simply incomprehensible that they could have sinned. The conclusion: both events happened as they did in order to establish a model of return.

### Individual & Community

Moving to the top of *amud alef*: *l'omar lach she-im chata yachid omerim lo k'la eitzel yachid* — if an individual sins, even grievously, one can point him to the individual who sinned, meaning David HaMelech, who sinned and did *teshuvah*, and thereby show that the path of *teshuvah* is open. *V'im chatu tzibur omerim lahem l'chu eitzel tzibur* — and if an entire community has sinned, one can point them to the community that sinned and returned, namely *Am Yisrael* at the time of the *eigel*, to show that the gates are open for them as well.

The *gemara* then notes *v'tzricha* — it was necessary for both examples to exist. Had we only had the case of the individual — David — one might have argued that *teshuvah* was available because an individual's sin is not widely publicized and does not constitute so large a *chilul Hashem*, and therefore God permits recovery. But for an entire community whose sin is *mefarsam*, broadcast openly, perhaps *teshuvah* would be unavailable. And conversely, had we only had the communal case, one might argue that a whole nation merits *teshuvah* because *nafishei rachamei* — God has great compassion on the many, or their collective merit is substantial. But for a single individual whose merit is comparatively limited, *aval yachid d'lo aleem zechutei*, perhaps the path would be closed. *Tzricha* — you need both.

It is worth pausing here to notice how this *aggadata* is in conversation with the deeper themes of *masechet Avodah Zarah*. The *masechet* grapples with the temptations of the surrounding pagan world. One might wonder: if all of *Am Yisrael* could descend to *avodah zarah* at *Har Sinai* itself, does that say something about the pull of idolatry? Does it lend some legitimacy to it? The *gemara*'s answer is precisely the opposite: this happened at such a miraculous, inexplicable level that the only meaning to be drawn from it is the openness of the path of *teshuvah* — not any validation of idolatrous impulses.

## Mitzvot & Sins

### Mitzvot Proclaim

*V'hainu d'Rabbi Yishmael bar Nachmani* — and this is akin to what *Rabbi Yishmael bar Nachmani* says, that *Rabbi Yonatan* expounded: the *pasuk ne'um David ben Yishai v'ne'um hagever hukan al* — David the son of Yishai, and the man *hukan al*, raised above — means that David *hekim olah shel teshuvah*, he lifted up the yoke of *teshuvah*, he established that *teshuvah* is possible.

Continuing in the name of *Rabbi Yishmael bar Nachmani* citing *Rabbi Yonatan*: *kol ha'oseh mitzvah achat ba'olam hazeh, makdimas v'holechet l'fanav l'olam haba* — whoever performs even a single *mitzvah* in this world, that *mitzvah* will go before him and herald him in the world to come, proclaiming his righteousness. It is a striking and beautiful image: your *mitzvos* will be announced before you like a herald before a king. The *pasuk* cited: *v'halach l'fanecha tzidkecha u'kvod Hashem ya'asfecha* — your righteousness will walk before you and the glory of God will gather you in.

### Sins Chase You

However, the flip side is equally stark. *V'kol ha'over aveirah achat, melafefto u'molichto l'yom hadin* — whoever transgresses even a single sin, it clings to him and drags him to the day of judgment. You cannot shake it; it wraps around you. *Rabbi Eliezer* sharpens the image: *keshurah bo k'chelev* — it is tied to him like a dog, chasing after him relentlessly. The *pasuk* brought is *v'lo shama eileiha lishkav etzlah lihyot imah* — referring to Yosef's refusal of Potiphar's wife — and the *gemara* reads it as *lishkav etzlah ba'olam hazeh lihyot imah l'olam haba*: refusing to lie with her in this world means not having her cling to him in the world to come. The image is powerful: the good deeds you think are unnoticed will herald you magnificently; the sins you hope to escape will pursue you like a dog — unless, of course, one does *teshuvah*, as the preceding discussion has established.

## Gratitude Theme

### Existence & Sin

*Amar Reish Lakish*: *bo u'nachzik tov l'avoteinu* — let us come and hold gratitude toward our forefathers — and here he means not *Avraham Yitzchak v'Yaakov* but the generation of *Am Yisrael* who stood at *Har Sinai*. *She'malei heim lo chatu anu lo banu l'olam* — for had they not sinned, we never would have been born.

The *pasuk*: *ani amarti elohim atem u'vnei elyon kulchem* — I said that you would be like gods, like the most high. The understanding is that being like angels means, among other things, not engaging in sexual reproduction — and therefore no future generations would have been born. *Chibbaltem ma'aseichem* — but you corrupted your deeds — and so *achen k'adam t'mutun* — you will die like human beings, with all that entails. *Reish Lakish*'s move here is striking: he takes the catastrophic sin of the *eigel* and finds in it a reason for gratitude — we exist because of it. There is an obvious tension in this approach, since one might misread it as suggesting that great sins can be endorsed because of their downstream benefits. The difficulty of what precise *educational* message this carries is real and worth sitting with.

### Challenge: Later Gen

The *gemara* now challenges the implication of *Reish Lakish*'s statement. *Lemeimar de'ilu chatu lo havei moldu* — are you saying that had they not sinned, they would not have sired children? But the Torah commands *atem peru u'revu* — be fruitful and multiply — and clearly people were having children before the *eigel*. The *gemara* initially answers: *ad Sinai* — yes, up until *Har Sinai* people obviously had children, but once they reached the extraordinary *madreigah* of standing at *Har Sinai* and the experience of *mi yitein vehayah levavam zeh*, at that point they would have been like angels and would no longer have reproduced.

The *gemara* then presses further: but doesn't the Torah say at *Sinai* itself, even before *cheit ha'eigel* — *lechu imru lahem shuvu lachem le'ohaleichem* — go back to your tents? This is understood by *Chazal* as a permission to return to their wives, to *lesimchat onah*, the joy of marital intimacy. The *gemara* responds that this does not imply procreation — they could have continued marital relations for the sake of the *mitzvah* of *onah* without bearing children. This is a conceptually interesting distinction: even granting a kind of angelic elevation, the *mitzvah* of husband and wife as a married couple retains its value independent of procreation.

But a further challenge comes from the *pasuk*: *lema'an yitav lahem u'livneihem achareihem* — in order that it be good for them and their children after them. This appears to be spoken in the context of *Ma'amad Har Sinai*, before *cheit ha'eigel*, and speaks of children born later. The *gemara* answers that *le'otan ha'omedim al Har Sinai* — it refers to the children already alive who stood at *Har Sinai*, not to children yet to be born.

### Never Born Reading

*Va'amar Reish Lakish*: what is meant by *zeh sefer toldot Adam*? Did *Adam HaRishon* actually have a book? Rather, *melamed she'her'ah lo ha'Kadosh Baruch Hu le'Adam HaRishon dor dor ve'dorshav dor dor ve'chakhamav dor dor u'farnassav* — God showed *Adam HaRishon* all the future generations, their leaders, their sages, their communal figures. When God reached the generation of *Rabbi Akiva*, *Adam HaRishon* rejoiced in his Torah but was anguished by his terrible martyrdom, saying *veli mah yakru rei'ekha El* — how heavy and incomprehensible are Your thoughts, O Lord.

*Va'amar Rabbi Yosei*: *ein Ben David ba ad sheyichlu kol haneshamot shebaguf* — *Mashiach* will not come until all the souls stored in the heavenly repository called *guf* have been distributed, with each new birth drawing from that storehouse. The *pasuk*: *ki lo l'olam ariv v'lo netzach ektzof ki ruach milfanai yaatof uneshamot ani asiti* — I will not contend forever, nor will I be angry forever; a spirit from before Me will be held back because of the souls that I have created. *Rashi* explains *yaatof* as indicating that the souls are holding things back — once they are all used up, the time of *Mashiach* will arrive.

This *aggadic* passage establishes that it was always part of the divine plan for there to be future generations — God showed *Adam HaRishon* all future generations, and *Mashiach*'s arrival is contingent on the completion of those generations. The *gemara* therefore reinterprets *Reish Lakish*: *lo teima anu lo banu l'olam* — do not read him as saying we never would have been born. *Ela eima k'mi shelo banu l'olam* — rather, what he means is that it would have been *as if* we had never been born. Had that generation not sinned, they would have lived forever, and our existence would have had no significance in relation to theirs.

### Death Decreed

The *gemara* now challenges this revised understanding from a *braisa*. Going back to *mi yitein vehayah levavam zeh* — even at that extraordinary level, it was not within the cards that they could have nullified the *malach hamaves*, the angel of death. Why? *Shekvar nigzira gzeira* — the decree of death was already decreed from the time of *Adam HaRishon*. *Halo kibelu Yisrael es haTorah ela kedei shelo tehei uma velashon sholetes bahen* — the level they reached through accepting the Torah would have achieved that no nation would ever subjugate them, as the *pasuk* promises *lema'an yitav lahem ulevineihem le'olam*. But conquering death itself was never possible. The *gemara* responds that *Reish Lakish*'s position accords with a different *tanna*.

## Angel of Death

### Like Gods

*Detanya Rabbi Yosei omer*: *lo kibelu Yisrael es haTorah ela kedei shelo yehei malach hamaves sholet bahen* — at the moment of accepting the Torah, the Israelites reached a level at which the angel of death had no dominion over them. The *pasuk*: *ani amarti elohim atem u'vnei elyon kulchem* — I said you would be like gods, like the most high, *i.e.*, like angels who do not die.

### Corrupted Deeds

*Chavaltem ma'aseichem* — you corrupted your deeds — *achen k'adam temutun* — and therefore you will die like a human being. This *chavaltem ma'aseichem* is *Reish Lakish*'s interpolation into the *pasuk*, marking the hinge between the exalted possibility and the fallen reality. It is worth noting that once the *gemara* moved away from the literal reading of *Reish Lakish* — that they literally would not have been born — toward the reading that they would have lived forever, this *pasuk* fits precisely: you would have been like the most high, beyond death, but now *achen k'adam temutun*.

### Death as Suffering

*V'tanna kamma ha kesiv achen k'adam temutun* — what does the *tanna kamma* do with this *pasuk*, which seems to say explicitly that had they not sinned they would not have died? The *tanna kamma* holds that death was always decreed from *Adam HaRishon* and that the level of *Matan Torah* could only have protected them from subjugation, not from death itself. So how does the *tanna kamma* read *achen k'adam temutun*? *Mai misa aniyus* — the *misa* here does not mean literal death; it means suffering that is *like* death. Had they not sinned, no nation would have subjugated them, and they would have lived well. Now they will be subject to experiences that feel like death — poverty, blindness, illness, childlessness.

The underlying disagreement between *Rabbi Yosei* and the *tanna kamma* is thus: *Rabbi Yosei* holds that at *Ma'amad Har Sinai* they literally conquered death; the *tanna kamma* holds that death was always decreed, and the only gain from accepting the Torah at that level was immunity from national subjugation.

### Four Like Dead

*De'amar mar arba'a chashuvim k'mes* — the master taught that four types are considered like dead. *Elu hen*: *ani*, a poor person; *suma*, a blind person; *metzora*, one afflicted with *tzara'as*; and *mi she'ein lo vanim*, one who has no children.

How do we know poverty is like death? *Ki mesu kol ha'anashim* — for all the men who sought your life have died, said to *Moshe*. Who were those men? *Datan va'Aviram*. But did they actually die? We know they were alive later when they rebelled against *Moshe*. Rather, *sheyardu minechaseihem* — they had become impoverished, and therefore it is as if they had died, stripped of influence and standing. How do we know blindness is like death? *Bemakhshakhim hoshivani kemetei olam* — You have placed me in darkness like the eternally dead. For *metzora*: *al na tehi kemet* — let our sister not be like dead, said of *Miriam* when she was afflicted with *tzara'as*, banished from the community. For one without children: *havah li banim ve'im ayin metah anokhi* — give me children, and if not I am dead.

These are striking statements that deserve careful reading. The *gemara* is likely pointing to societal realities — that those who lack wealth, sight, physical wholeness, or children are sometimes rendered invisible, devalued, as if they do not exist. This does not mean that such people *ought* to be treated that way, but it reflects a reality that we are obligated to work against. The four together, then, give content to the *tanna kamma*'s reading of *mai misa aniyus* — death here means the range of profound suffering and marginalization that human beings can experience.

## Moses' Rebuke

### God's Offer

*Tanu rabbanan*: *im be-hukkotai telechu* — the *ein im ela lashon takhnunim*, the word *im* here carries a tone of pleading, as if *Moshe* is beseeching Israel to keep the *mitzvos*. As the *pasuk* says: *lu ammi shome'a li* — oh, if only my people would listen to me — *kim'at oyeveihem akhni'a* — I would subdue their enemies swiftly. *V'lu hikshavta le-mitzvotai vayehi khannahar shelomekha* — had you listened to My commandments, your peace would flow like a river.

The discussion turns to *mi yitten vehayah levavam zeh lahem*. *Amar lahem Moshe le-Yisrael, kefuyyei tovah benei kefuyyei tovah* — *Moshe* said to Israel: ingrates, children of ingrates. When God said *mi yitten vehayah levavam zeh* — if only their hearts would be like this — *hayah lahem lomar ten attah* — they should have said: give it to us, God. God was opening a door: if only you could be at this level forever. The correct response was to seize that moment and say, yes, grant us this. Instead, they turned away from the goodness being offered before their eyes.

### Ungrateful

*Kefuyyei tovah dikhtiv* — and how do we know they are ingrates? Because *Moshe*, speaking forty years later in *Sefer Devarim*, frames it this way — retroactively demonstrating that ingratitude is a pattern. The *pasuk* cited: *venafshenu katzah balekhem hakkalokel* — our soul is disgusted by this insubstantial bread. They complained about the *manna*. The *manna*, as *Rashi* explains, left no waste product — an extraordinary blessing, in that there was nothing unclean or burdensome about it. Yet Israel framed it as something unnatural and punishing, failing to recognize the tremendous gift God had given them.

### Adam's Blame

*Benei kefuyyei tovah* — and they are also the children of ingrates — *dikhtiv ha'ishah asher natata imadi hi natna li min ha'etz v'ochel* — Adam said, the woman *You* gave me, she gave me from the tree, and I ate. Adam took the goodness God had given him — a companion — and turned her into the excuse for his transgression. The pattern is the same: receiving great goodness and converting it into a complaint or a deflection rather than gratitude.

### Forty Years Later

*Af Moshe Rabbeinu lo rimzam l'Yisrael ela l'achar arba'im shanah* — even *Moshe* himself did not hint this idea to Israel until forty years had passed. Only in *Sefer Devarim*, when retelling the events of *Ma'amad Har Sinai*, did *Moshe* frame it in this way — that they had missed an extraordinary opening that God had offered them. The *pasuk*: *va'olech es'chem bamidbar arba'im shanah* — and I led you in the wilderness forty years — *v'lo natan Hashem lachem lev lada'at v'einayim lirot v'oznayim lishmo'a ad hayom hazeh* — and God did not give you a heart to understand, eyes to see, and ears to hear until this day.

### Master's Teaching

*Amar Rabbah shma mina*: from this we may infer that *lo ka'i inish ada'teih d'rabbeih ad arba'im shanin* — a person does not truly understand his master until forty years have passed. The question is who the *inish* refers to. *Rashi* understands that even *Moshe* did not grasp what God had meant at that moment — that God was opening a door with the words *mi yitten* — until forty years later. Others understand it to mean that *Bnei Yisrael* could not have appreciated what that moment signified until forty years of growth had passed, and *Moshe* knew this and therefore waited.

## Torah Controls Yetzer

### Torah & Charity

*Amar Rabbi Yochanan mishum Rabbi Banna'ah*: what is meant by the *pasuk ashreichem zorei al kol mayim m'shalchei regel hashor v'hachamor* — praised are you who sow upon all waters, who send forth the leg of the ox and the donkey? *Ashreihem Yisrael bizman she'oskim baTorah u'vigmilut chasadim* — praised is Israel when they engage in Torah and *gemilut chasadim*. *Yitzram masur beyadam* — their *yetzer hara* is delivered into their hands; they control it. *V'ein hem mesurim beyad yitzram* — the *yetzer* does not control them.

This connects directly to the larger themes of the *masechet*. The *masechet*'s halachic *takanot* — don't drink their wine, limit commercial interaction — are one layer of protection against the temptations of the surrounding world. But the deeper protection is Torah and *gemilut chasadim*. If you are truly engaged in these, your *yetzer hara* is *masur beyadecha*.

*V'ein zri'ah ela tzedakah* — "sowing" refers to *tzedakah*, which is *gemilut chasadim*, as the *pasuk* says: *zir'u lachem l'tzedakah v'kitzru l'fi chesed* — sow for yourselves for righteousness and harvest for *chesed*. *V'ein mayim ela Torah* — and "waters" refers to Torah, as the *pasuk* says: *hoy kol tzamei l'chu lamayim* — all who are thirsty, come to the waters.

### Ox & Donkey

What then is meant by *m'shalchei regel hashor v'hachamor*? *Tana d'vei Eliyahu*: a person should always make himself toward the words of Torah *k'shor l'ol* — like an ox to the yoke — *u'chachamor l'masoy* — and like a donkey to the burden. You must subjugate yourself to Torah with the acceptance of a working animal, willing to bear the full weight of the commitment. *Rashi* notes that this final teaching of *Tana d'vei Eliyahu* is somewhat distinct from the preceding point: the image of *meshalchin u-mashlichin raglei yetzer hara me'al adam me'alehem* — casting away the feet of the *yetzer hara* from upon a person — is the first interpretation, while the dedication of the ox and donkey is a parallel but independent point about the posture one must take toward Torah.

This concludes the extended opening *aggadata* of *masechet Avodah Zarah*.

## Three Days Rule

### Mishna Stated

We now return to the *mishna* and the halachic discussion: one may not conduct business with non-Jews for three days before their holidays — *gimel yamim*. The presumed concern is that they will rejoice at the good fortune of the transaction and bring that joy to their *avodah zarah* worship. However, the *gemara* here will focus more specifically on the concern that transactions may enable them to purchase items for their idolatrous rituals.

### Three Days Logic

The *gemara* asks: *u'mi be'inan kulei hai* — do they really need three full days to acquire what they need for their holiday? Is such advance preparation genuinely required? The *gemara* raises a *mishna* as a comparison: *be'arba'ah perakim ba-shanah ha-mocher behemah le-chavero tzarich le-hodi'o* — at four times in the year, one who sells an animal to another must inform him whether the animal's mother or offspring was sold that same day, because of the prohibition of *oto ve-et beno lo tishchatu beyom echad* — the mother and child may not be slaughtered on the same day. Note that the transgression belongs to whoever causes both to be slaughtered on the same day, so the seller must inform the buyer.

### Four Festivals

The four times in the year when people are assumed to slaughter immediately upon purchase — so that this notification is practically necessary — are: *erev yom tov ha-acharon shel chag*, the eve of the last day of *Sukkot*, meaning *Shemini Atzeret*. *Tosafot* notes that the first day of *Sukkot* is not listed because people are occupied with their *sukkah* and *lulav* and are not necessarily focused on preparing a major festive meal; furthermore, *Shemini Atzeret* has its own independent identity and deserves particular emphasis as a day of *simcha*. Then: *erev yom tov ha-rishon shel Pesach*, the eve of the first day of *Pesach*; *ve'erev Atzeret*, before *Shavuot*; and *ve'erev Rosh Hashanah*, before *Rosh Hashanah*. *U'ke-divrei Rabbi Yose ha-Gelili af erev Yom ha-Kippurim ba-Galil* — and according to *Rabbi Yosei ha-Gelili*, also the eve of *Yom Kippur* in the *Galil*, because of the *mitzvah* to eat on *erev Yom Kippur*.

What the *gemara* draws from this *mishna* is that even for a major feast, people buy only one day in advance — not three. There is an inherent awkwardness in the *gemara*'s reasoning here: it is applying the patterns of Jewish festival practice to the question of what non-Jewish pagans do in preparation for their idolatrous holidays. The *gemara* is working within a framework of rabbinic discourse and treating this as a question that must be resolved through the available halachic models, even if those models reflect specifically Jewish realities. One possible way to understand this is that the *gemara* is seeking a standardized model — since pagan practices vary across Rome, Syria, North Africa, and elsewhere, some fixed benchmark is needed, and the Jewish model provides the available reference point.

### Sacrifice vs. Feast

The *gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction: *hasam de'achilah, sagi be'chad yoma* — there, for a feast, one day's advance purchase is sufficient. *Hacha de'hakravah, binan tlata yomei* — here, the concern is not festive eating but sacrificial offering, and for that, three days are needed to verify the animal.

### Blemish Standards

But does inspection for sacrifice really require three days? *V'hatanya: sho'alin vedorshin behilchos hapesach kodem hapesach sheloshim yom* — the *braisa* teaches that one begins asking and studying the laws of *Pesach* thirty days before, which the *gemara* understands to include beginning the process of acquiring *korbanot*. *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* says two weeks. Why do Jews need thirty days or two weeks? *Anan de'shchichi mumei de'paslei afilu bidukim she'ba'ayin* — for us, even minute blemishes — such as a slight film over the eye — are sufficient to disqualify an animal, so *binan tlashin yomei*, we need thirty days of preparation and inspection.

### Blemish Standards

*Inhu de'mechusar eivar it lehu* — for them, the *gemara* holds, an animal is disqualified only if it is missing a limb entirely. This is a *halacha* pertaining to *Bnei Noach* who wish to bring a *korban* in the *Beis Hamikdash* — for them, a simple blemish is not disqualifying; only a missing limb renders it unfit. The *gemara* is again transparently applying the *halachos* of *Bnei Noach* and the *Beis Hamikdash* to the question of pagan sacrificial standards, which is a legal fiction of sorts: the reality of pagan sacrificial practices bears no direct relationship to these *halachos*. But the only lens the *gemara* has to work with is what it knows. Given this standard, *itlehu be'tlata yomei sagi* — three days is sufficient for them to determine whether the animal is missing a limb. Though it must be said: checking for a missing limb takes a matter of moments, not three days, and this gap in the reasoning is not fully resolved.

### Rabbi Elazar

*De'amar Rabbi Elazar minayin lemechusar eivar de'asur livnei Noach* — how do we derive that a *Bnei Noach* may not bring an animal missing a limb? *Dichsiv umikol hachai mikol basar shenayim mikol* — from the *pasuk* commanding *Noach* to bring two of every living creature into the ark, which implies a standard of completeness.

*Rashi* at this point attempts to bridge the gap between the *halachos* of *Bnei Noach* bringing *korbanot* to the *Beis Hamikdash* and the reality of pagan sacrificial practice. He writes: *lehakriv legavoah, vedumya de'korbanos shenahagu avoseihem leshamayim hem nohagim b'avodah zarah shelahem* — we assume that the same standards their ancestors maintained when bringing *korbanot* to God, they have carried over into their *avodah zarah* practice. It is an attempt to create a bridge, though the underlying strangeness remains — the *gemara* is consistently reading non-Jewish pagan practice through the prism of the only sacrificial law it knows: that of *Bnei Noach* and the *Beis Hamikdash*.

# Avodah Zarah 6

## Abaye vs. Rava

### Abaye: Marvach

The daf picks up at the bottom of 6b, where the Gemara has been surveying the various categories of forbidden business interactions with non-Jews. Abaye holds that the primary concern animating these prohibitions is *marvach*—transactions that give the non-Jew greater resources and increase. Lending money or objects to a non-Jew falls squarely within this concern. What about the reverse direction, such as borrowing from them or compelling them to pay up a debt? Those too are forbidden, but as a *gezeira*: one direction is prohibited in order to prevent the other. The core problem, for Abaye, is anything that enlarges the non-Jew's holdings.

### Rava: Azol uModeh

Rava takes a different view. For him, both directions of transaction are forbidden for the same reason: the concern of *azol umodeh*, that as a result of the interaction the non-Jew will go and give thanks to his deity. Rashi sharpened this concern by pointing to the verse *lo yishamah al picha*—that expressions of thanksgiving to a pagan god should not occur through your agency. A third and more concrete concern running through the entire *mishnah* is *lifnei iver*, the prohibition of providing a non-Jew the objects of his worship.

## Debt Collection Debate

### Yehuda: Debt Collection

With this framework in place, the Gemara turns to a specific case. Rabbi Yehuda permits collecting a debt from a non-Jew even on the eve of his holiday, reasoning that compelling repayment causes the non-Jew distress rather than joy, and therefore does not implicate the concern of *simcha*. The *Chachamim* disagree: even though the non-Jew suffers an immediate loss, in the long run he will be relieved that the debt is no longer hanging over him, and that eventual satisfaction constitutes the prohibited joy.

### Gemara's Challenge

The Gemara then presses Rabbi Yehuda: does he not accept the principle that even if something causes immediate pain, one looks at the larger picture and recognizes it will produce joy in the end? The Gemara locates evidence that Rabbi Yehuda does accept precisely this macro perspective—but in an entirely different context.

### Chol HaMoed Precedent

The parallel case comes from the laws of *Chol HaMoed*. A *baraita* teaches that Rabbi Yehuda holds a woman may not apply a lime plaster to her face on *Chol HaMoed*, because it is a *nival*—a de-beautifying—for her during the festival, and looking unkempt is not appropriate for the spirit of *Chol HaMoed*. Yet the Gemara then notes that Rabbi Yehuda concedes in the case of a plaster that can be peeled off (*kaflo*) during *Chol HaMoed* itself: although right now while it is on her face she looks unpleasant and that immediate condition is not fitting for the festival, once she peels it off she will look attractive, and *af al pi shemetzar achshav sameach hi le'achar zman*—even though it causes distress now, she will be happy afterward. The macro perspective thus governs, and the use of such a plaster is permitted.

The logic maps onto the debt collection question: just as Rabbi Yehuda looks past the present discomfort to the later joy in the *Chol HaMoed* case, why does he not do the same for the non-Jew who has just had his debt collected and will, in the long run, feel relieved?

### Rashi's Distinction

Rashi addresses this question by observing that everything permitted on *Chol HaMoed* involves activities that cause some momentary effort or inconvenience—*shechita*, meal preparation, and similar tasks—but ultimately serve the purpose of *simcha* during the festival itself. The macro logic is built into the structure of *Chol HaMoed*: you look past the present exertion because the entire enterprise is oriented toward joy within the festival period. Rashi's language is *kol mah sheheitiru la'asot bemoed metzar be'oto sha'ah...veyihyeh mishmetzar simcha le'achar zman shebetoch hamoed*—whatever they permitted to do on *Chol HaMoed* causes some distress at that moment, but leads to joy later within the festival itself. The analogy breaks down in the case of debt collection because the non-Jew's ultimate relief will not necessarily materialize within the days of his actual holiday; the timing does not align.

### Rav Nachman's View

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak offers a more structural explanation. On *Chol HaMoed* the macro perspective is the default framework universally applied—*hanei dechol hamoed dekulei alma meitzari achshav sameichi le'achar zman*—everything permitted during the festival follows that logic. But the laws governing transactions with non-Jews around their holidays may operate from a fundamentally different starting point, one that looks at the immediate and the micro rather than the larger picture.

### Ravina's Pessimism

Ravina takes yet another approach, one that is frankly pessimistic about the non-Jewish disposition. He argues that non-Jews harbor a persistent and abiding resentment—*eimat yeteirah leolam meitzar*—such that even long-term they will never genuinely feel satisfaction at having had the debt paid off. They will always have wished they had found some way to escape the obligation. On this reading, Rabbi Yehuda's position is not that he rejects the macro principle; it is that he simply does not believe the long-term *simcha* will ever materialize in this case.

## Yehoshua ben Korcha

### Documented vs. Oral

The Gemara now notes that the *mishnah*'s position—which prohibits collecting even debts before the holiday—does not accord with the view of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha. A *baraita* records his distinction: *milveh b'shtar ein nifrain meihen, milveh al peh nifrain meihen mipnei shehu k'matzil mi'yadam*—a documented loan (*milveh b'shtar*) may not be collected before their holiday, but an undocumented oral loan (*milveh al peh*) may be collected, because in that case it is as though one is rescuing one's assets from their hands. Without documentation the creditor is always at risk: the debtor could simply deny the debt. Collecting while one has the chance is therefore an act of financial self-preservation.

### Halacha k'Yehoshua

Rav Yehuda was sitting behind Rav Yabba, who was sitting before Rav Huna. Rav Huna declared: *halacha k'Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha*—we rule like Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha that collection of an undocumented debt is permitted. *Ve'halacha k'Rav Yehuda*—we also rule like Rav Yehuda in the dyer case, to be discussed below.

An additional factor supporting the ruling regarding undocumented debts is *meiti u'masur*—the ease with which the debtor could simply deny or escape the obligation. Where that risk is present, not only is there less *simcha* for the non-Jew in being compelled to pay, but the creditor's need to protect himself takes on added weight. The concern of *eivah*—hatred generated by Jewish non-engagement with economic obligations—is also implicitly in the background as a permitting factor.

## Dyer Liability Case

### Dyer Scenario

The Gemara now turns to the case of the dyer, which is not directly related to the laws of *avodah zarah* but is brought here because Rav Huna declared it in the same sitting. The *mishnah* in Bava Kamma presents the case of *tzavar l'tzava*—one who gives wool to a dyer with instructions to dye it a particular color, and the dyer dyes it the wrong color.

### Meir: Gazlan

Rabbi Meir holds that because the dyer changed the object contrary to the owner's instructions, he has effectively taken wrongful possession: he is a *gazlan*. As a *gazlan* he acquires the wool and must reimburse the owner the full value of the wool as it was before dyeing.

### Yehuda: Upper Hand

Rabbi Yehuda disagrees. The dyer acted without intent to steal; he was simply working under instructions he failed to follow. He therefore does not become a *gazlan*, and the wool remains the property of the owner—now dyed the wrong color. Because the dyer failed to follow the owner's instructions, the owner holds the upper hand. He does not owe the contracted fee. Instead: *im ha'shevach yeteir al ha'yetzia notein lo et ha'yetzia*—if the improvement in the wool's value exceeds the dyer's expenses, the owner pays only the expenses. *Ve'im ha'yetzia yeteirah al ha'shevach notein lo et ha'shevach*—if the expenses exceed the improvement, the owner pays only the improvement. The owner pays the lesser of the two, and the dyer bears the loss.

To give a concrete example: if the contracted fee was one hundred, but the dyer's actual expenses (including labor, stripped of profit) came to fifty, and the wool's value increased by eighty, the owner pays fifty. If the wool's value increased by only thirty despite the dyer's expenses of fifty, the owner pays thirty. The *shinui*—the unauthorized change—forfeits the dyer's right to his contractual fee and leaves him with only the lesser of cost or benefit.

### Gemara's Question

When Rav Yosef heard Rav Huna declare *ve'halacha k'Rav Yehuda*, he turned his face around in surprise. He understood why Rav Huna needed to rule explicitly like Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha: that was a minority opinion against the *mishnah*, a *daat yachid*, and one might otherwise assume *yachid verabbim halacha kerabbim*—when an individual opinion stands against the majority, the halacha follows the majority. So there it was necessary to announce the ruling explicitly. But why was it necessary to state that we rule like Rabbi Yehuda in the dyer case? That should be self-evident.

### Stam Mishna

The reason it should be obvious, Rav Yosef continues, is the principle of *machlokes ve'achar kach stam halacha kestam*: when a dispute appears in the *mishnah* and is followed by an anonymous, unattributed *mishnah* that sides with one position, the *halacha* follows the anonymous ruling. Here, the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda appears in Bava Kamma, but Bava Metzia contains an anonymous *mishnah* stating *kol hameshane yado al hatachtona*—whoever deviates from the terms of an agreement is in the disadvantaged position—and *kol hachozer bo yado al hatachtona*—whoever backs out of an agreement is similarly disadvantaged. That *stam mishnah* clearly encodes Rabbi Yehuda's principle: the party who deviated does not collect the contracted price but only the lesser of expenses or improvement. Since Bava Metzia follows Bava Kamma, this is a case of debate followed by a later anonymous ruling, and the *halacha* should follow the *stam* without any need for explicit declaration.

### Mishna Order

Rav Yosef raises this question, but the answer given is that Rav Huna would invoke the principle of *ein seder laMishnah*—the *mishnayot* do not necessarily appear in the order in which they were composed or taught. The fact that the dispute appears in Bava Kamma and the *stam* in Bava Metzia does not necessarily mean the *stam* postdates the dispute. Perhaps the *stam* was composed first and the explicit debate was formulated later; perhaps Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi placed them in this sequence for organizational reasons that do not reflect the intended hierarchical relationship. If the order of composition is uncertain, one cannot derive from the position of the *stam* that it was meant to resolve the earlier debate.

### Within vs. Between

The Gemara presses: if one can never infer anything from the order of *mishnayot*, the entire principle of *machlokes ve'achar kach stam* would collapse. Rav Huna clarifies: *ein seder laMishnah* applies only across separate *masechtos*, not within one *masechta*. Within a single tractate, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi organized the material with enough intention that the sequence is meaningful, and a *stam mishnah* appearing after a dispute within the same tractate does signal that we rule like the *stam*. But between two separate tractates, the organizational logic does not carry the same implication.

Rav Yosef responds: Bava Kamma, Bava Metzia, and Bava Basra are not truly three separate *masechtos*—*kulan Nezikin chada masechta hu*. They constitute one large thirty-chapter tractate that was divided into three for practical reasons. If the debate appears in Bava Kamma and the *stam* appears in Bava Metzia, they are within one masechta for these purposes, and the sequence should be meaningful. On this view, there was indeed no need to state the ruling explicitly. But on the other view—that Bava Kamma and Bava Metzia are considered distinct tractates for the purposes of sequence—the order carries no implication, and Rav Huna's explicit declaration was necessary.

### Halacha Pesuka

The Gemara offers a second resolution, independent of the question of masechta order. Even if one concedes that Bava Kamma and Bava Metzia are separate tractates and the sequence carries no implication, it should still have been obvious that we rule like Rabbi Yehuda—because of the way the *stam mishnah* in Bava Metzia is framed. *Mishum de'katani legabbei hilchata pesikta*: the ruling is presented as *halacha pesuka*, an apodictic legal principle stated in tight, absolute terms. *Kol hameshane yado al hatachtona, kol hachozer bo yado al hatachtona*: this is not a case study where the *mishnah* works through a particular scenario and attributes an answer to a named authority. It is framed as a broad *klal*, a general principle stated in the terse declarative language of binding law. When the *mishnah* speaks that way, it signals consensus and finality.

Rashi and Tosafot understand this point somewhat differently. Rashi notes that the principle *kol hameshane yado al hatachtona* was not the primary topic of the *mishnah* in Bava Metzia in which it appears—it was, so to speak, brought in from outside the immediate subject matter, which itself signals that it is being stated as a standalone *halacha psuka* rather than as a ruling tied to a specific context. Tosafot, by contrast, focuses on the language itself: *midekatni kol hameshane hu lashon halacha psuka*—the formulation *kol hameshane*, stating the rule as an all-encompassing principle, is itself the hallmark of *halacha psuka*. The framing as a *klal* rather than as a case-bound ruling is what makes explicit the binding character of the position.

## Yehoshua ben Korcha (II)

### Tosafot's Expansion

Returning to the ruling of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha on debt collection: the *halacha* as stated in the Gemara permits collection of an oral, undocumented debt (*milveh al peh*) before a non-Jewish holiday but forbids collection of a documented debt (*milveh b'shtar*). Tosafot, however, extends this leniency significantly. Tosafot reasons that the Gemara's distinction between documented and undocumented debts was predicated on a situation where Jews had sufficient leverage—perhaps some degree of governmental control—such that a documented debt was secure and the creditor could afford to wait. In the reality Tosafot faced, where non-Jews controlled the government and enforcement mechanisms, a documented debt was no more secure than an oral one: the creditor was always at risk of losing the money. Tosafot therefore rules that even a *milveh b'shtar* may be collected before the non-Jewish holiday in such circumstances, because the imperative to protect one's assets applies regardless of documentation. Tosafot also invokes the *Yerushalmi* in support of this position. It is difficult to argue that Tosafot's reality was so fundamentally different from the Gemara's, but the ruling reflects a broader pattern in Tosafot of defending established practice and protecting Jewish economic interests.

## Conflicting Rulings

### No Forum Shopping

The Gemara pivots to a *baraita* on a different topic, brought here because it involves another ruling of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha. The *baraita* states: *hanishal lachacham vetimei lo yishal lachacham veyitaher*—if someone asked a sage for a ruling and was told the object is *tamei* (or forbidden), he may not go ask another sage and seek a ruling of *tahor* (or permitted).

This prohibition raises a fundamental question about the nature of halakhic rulings. One way to understand it is through the prism of metaphysical reality: when an authorized sage issues a ruling, it creates a halakhic fact. To say something is *assur* is to make it *assur*, within the range of legitimate interpretation. A second ruling from another sage would be negating something that has already been concretized. On this reading, the problem is not merely procedural.

Alternatively, the concern may be primarily one of *kvod chacham*: you asked me for a ruling; going to someone else signals that you do not respect my judgment. One *nafka mina* between these two framings is the case where the first sage ruled leniently—*mutar*. If the first ruling creates a metaphysical reality, no such *issur* was created by a lenient ruling, and consulting someone else seems unproblematic. But if the concern is *kvod chacham*, the disrespect occurs regardless of whether the first ruling was stringent or lenient. Another question is whether, even if someone goes ahead and asks a second sage, they remain bound by the first ruling—or whether the second ruling can override it.

### Tosafot's Objection

Tosafot raises a pointed objection to the prohibition on seeking additional opinions. The entire enterprise of Tosafot as a school of learning is premised on hearing multiple voices, probing arguments, and allowing truth to emerge from the collision of perspectives. Why should a questioner be forbidden to consult multiple sages? *Ve-yidonu zeh im zeh*—let them argue with one another. *Ulai yeshivuhu midvaro*—perhaps if you received a ruling from one sage and believed it to be mistaken, going to others and raising the question would prompt a discussion that would lead the first sage to reconsider if his position was indeed wrong. The value of multiple voices is precisely that no single authority is beyond correction.

### Disclosure Exception

Tosafot resolves the tension by distinguishing between two types of follow-up consultation.
