The purpose of the decree was to sever the chain of rabbinic ordination entirely, thereby preventing the perpetuation of the authority required to adjudicate *dinei kenasos* and other matters dependent on ordained judges.

Into this breach stepped Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava, who is recalled with the formula *zachur oto ha'ish le-tov* — that man is remembered for good. Without his intervention, *dinei kenasos* would have been lost from Israel entirely. Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava is among the Ten Martyrs of the period of the Bar Kochba rebellion and its aftermath, and the full account of his heroism in preserving the chain of *smicha* — transmitting ordination to five students between two mountains while Roman soldiers closed in — will be taken up in the continuation of the daf.

---

---

# Avodah Zarah 9

## Sanhedrin's Exile

### Sanhedrin Moves

The *gemara* on daf 8b picks up the thread of a *baraita* concerning the period leading up to the destruction of the *beit hamikdash*. The *baraita* states: *arba'im shana ad lo charav habayit galta Sanhedrin veyashva la bakhanut* — forty years before the *beit hamikdash* was destroyed, the *sanhedrin* exiled itself and took up residence in the *khanut*. Although the word *khanut* suggests a shop or market stall, both *Rashi* and *Tosafot* understand it as referring to a different location on *Har HaBayit* — no longer situated within the *beit hamikdash* itself, but still within the broader Temple precinct.

The question immediately arises: *lema'i hilcheta?* — for what legal consequence does this matter? Rav Yitzchak bar Adimi answers: once the *sanhedrin* relocated, they were no longer able to adjudicate *dinei knasot*, monetary fines. The reason is that imposing fines is not merely a matter of civil restitution; it represents the *beit din* exercising coercive punitive authority, which requires both *smicha* — rabbinic ordination traceable in an unbroken chain back to *Moshe Rabbeinu* — and the physical presence of the *sanhedrin* within the *beit hamikdash*. The moment they moved, even a short distance, the legal prerequisite was no longer met.

### Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava

The *gemara* immediately challenges this framing. If the *sanhedrin* stopped adjudicating *dinei knasot* forty years before the *churban* — approximately the year 30 of the common era — how do we account for the famous account cited by Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav? The *gemara* quotes: *bram zachur oto ha'ish letov veRabbi Yehuda ben Bava shemo* — let that man be remembered for good; Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava is his name — *she'ilmalehu nishtachachu dinei knasot miYisrael* — for were it not for him, *dinei knasot* would have been forgotten from Israel.

The *gemara* presses: *ligresinu!* — could one not simply have learned the laws academically and preserved them? The answer is that the concern was not theoretical knowledge but practical application: *butlu dinei knasot miYisrael* — the actual practice of adjudicating fines would have ceased entirely. The reason was that the Roman government had issued a savage decree: whoever grants *smicha* shall be executed; whoever receives it shall be executed; the city in which it takes place shall be destroyed; and even the surrounding *tchum* shall be uprooted.

In the face of this, Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava acted with extraordinary courage. He went and situated himself between two large mountains and two large cities — specifically between Usha and Shefaram — placing himself outside the *tchum Shabbat* of either city. The intent was clear: he was not in any city, so no city could be destroyed; he was not in any *tchum*, so no *tchum* could be uprooted; and the sheer scale of the surrounding mountains and cities meant that any Roman reprisal would require leveling enormous, inhabited terrain. There, in that carefully chosen interstitial space, Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava conferred *smicha* on five *zkenim*: Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yosi, Rabbi Shimon, and Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua — the great students of Rabbi Akiva, the leading *tannaim* of their generation, active around the year 130–150 of the common era. Rav Avimi adds that Rabbi Nechemia was also among those ordained.

When the Romans became aware of what was happening, Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava told his students: *banai, rutzu* — my sons, flee. When they asked what would become of him, he answered that he would remain, immovable as a stone that cannot be overturned. He stood between his students and their pursuers, shielding them from the Roman assault. The *gemara* recounts that the Romans did not leave the spot *ad shena'atzu legufo gimel me'ot lulaniyot shel barzel* — until they had pierced his body with three hundred iron spears, making it *kichvarah* — like a sieve.

This episode, which took place roughly 150 years after the *sanhedrin* supposedly ceased adjudicating *dinei knasot*, demonstrates that the transmission of *smicha* — which enables *dinei knasot* — continued well after the forty-year mark before the *churban*. The original claim is therefore difficult to maintain as stated.

### Murderers & Capacity

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves the difficulty: *lo teima dinei knasot* — the *baraita* does not mean that the *sanhedrin* stopped adjudicating fines. Rather, *ela shelo danu dinei nefashot* — it means they ceased adjudicating capital crimes. This is not merely a question of *smicha*. While *smicha* is indeed required for any exercise of the *beit din*'s punitive power — whether *knas*, *malkut*, or *mita* — capital cases carry an additional requirement: the *sanhedrin hagadol* must be physically present within the *beit hamikdash* itself.

Why did the *sanhedrin* remove itself? The *gemara* explains: *keivan d'chazu denafishu lehu rotzchin velo yachlu lemidan* — when they saw that murderers had multiplied beyond their capacity to judge, they reasoned: *mutav nigli mimakom lemakom ki heichi d'lo litchayvu* — better to go into exile than to remain in a legal position of responsibility they could no longer fulfill.

The precise meaning of *d'lo litchayvu* invites scrutiny. *Rashi* reads it as: so that the murderers should not be held liable for the death penalty — since without a properly situated *sanhedrin* there can be no formal capital judgment. One might, however, prefer to read it as the *beit din* itself not being held accountable: better to place oneself in a position of legal incapacity than to remain formally obligated to judge while visibly powerless to do so. The distinction matters. In the latter reading, the *sanhedrin*'s relocation was an act of institutional self-protection — removing themselves from a situation where their impotence would be conspicuous and their failure to act publicly evident. The *gemara* supports the ruling with a *pasuk*: *ve'asita al pi hadavar asher yagidu lecha min hamakom hahu* — you shall act according to what they instruct you from that place — teaching that *hamakom goreim*, the place itself is a constitutive requirement for the authority to judge capital cases.

---

## Chronology Overview

### Kingdom Timeline

The *gemara* now turns to rabbinic chronology, working through the succession of foreign powers that ruled over Israel during the period of the Second *beit hamikdash*. The *baraita* records: *malchus Paras bifnei habayit shloshim ve'arba shanah* — the Persian kingdom held sway during the era of the *beit hamikdash* for 34 years. This reflects the rabbinic tradition that the Second *beit hamikdash*, rebuilt under Cyrus (*Koresh*), was constructed under Persian governance for only 34 years before the rise of Greek dominion. *Malchus Yavan bifnei habayit me'ah ushmonim shanah* — the Greek kingdom ruled during that era for 180 years. After that came 103 years of *Chashmonai* rule, followed by the Herodian period of 103 years under Roman suzerainty — together yielding the classical rabbinic figure that the Second *beit hamikdash* stood for 420 years in total.

It should be noted that secular historical reckoning places the duration of the Second Temple period at approximately 586 years, a discrepancy of over 160 years from the rabbinic count. The sources of this gap have been debated extensively; for the purposes of the *gemara*'s internal calculations, the 420-year figure is the working assumption.

The *gemara* notes that from the beginning of Greek rule through the Herodian period amounts to 206 years before the *churban*. Yet an earlier statement held that the Romans took control only 180 years before the *churban*. The discrepancy — 206 versus 180 — is 26 years, and this becomes the subject of the next discussion.

### Roman Delay Period

The *gemara* resolves the 26-year discrepancy with reference to a tradition that the Romans had entered into a pact with the Jewish people to act jointly against the Greeks. During the first 26 years of what would otherwise be counted as Roman dominion, the Romans honored this agreement and did not subjugate Israel: *kamu be'heimanuteihu bahadi Yisrael velo ishtabdu vehu* — they stood by their word with Israel and did not impose dominion over them. Therefore, when the earlier statement says the wicked government subjugated Israel 180 years before the *churban*, it counts only from the point at which Rome actually imposed its rule, not from the formal inception of Roman regional power. Those first 26 years — whether understood as a period of Roman good faith or, more simply, as a period of genuine *Chashmonai* self-rule and autonomy — are accordingly excluded from the reckoning of Roman subjugation.

---

## Three Dating Systems

### Dating Systems Intro

Rav Pappa introduces the practical concern that motivates this entire discussion: *i ta'ei tanna velo yada paratei kama havei lish'alei lesafra kama kesiv* — if a *tanna* becomes confused and does not know the *pratim*, the last two digits of the year count, he should go and ask a *sofer*, a scribe, what year he writes in his documents.

This presupposes an understanding of three distinct dating systems in use among the Jewish people. The most familiar to a modern reader is *beriyas olam* — counting years from the creation of the world — which is the system used in contemporary *ketubot* and *gittin*, typically accompanied by the phrase *livriyas olam leminyan she'anu monin* to specify which count is meant. A second system counted years from the *churban habayit*. A third system — arguably the most widespread in practice — was called *minyan shtarot*, the standard dating system used by *sofrim* for legal documents.

### Minyan Shtarot

*Minyan shtarot* began 380 years before the *churban habayit*, placing its year zero in the middle of the period of Greek dominion — specifically, as will be clarified, corresponding to the rise of the Seleucid Empire. This means that the year of the *churban habayit* was year 380 in *minyan shtarot* reckoning, and any year after the *churban* adds to that baseline.

This system was the standard employed by *sofrim* throughout the ancient Jewish world. The scribe writing a legal document would not count from the *churban* or from creation; he would write the year according to *minyan shtarot*, which had been the universal civic standard across the ancient Near East for centuries.

### Conversion Methods

The *gemara* provides the conversion formula between *minyan shtarot* and the *churban habayit* count. If a *tanna* — meaning someone using the *churban*-based reckoning — is uncertain of his last two digits, he should ask a *sofer* what the current *minyan shtarot* year is, and then add 20. Conversely, if a *sofer* using *minyan shtarot* is uncertain of his last two digits, he should ask the *tanna* his count and subtract 20.

To see why the adjustment is 20: the *churban habayit* corresponds to year 380 in *minyan shtarot*. Any subsequent year, expressed in *minyan shtarot*, will therefore exceed the *churban*-based count by 380. Since the hundreds are assumed known and only the last two digits are in question, the practical arithmetic reduces to adding or subtracting 20 — because 380 ends in 80, and adding 80 to any two-digit number and rounding for the century is equivalent to subtracting 20 (or, looking at it the other way, the *churban*-based count will lag the *minyan shtarot* by 80 in the tens and units, which when working modulo 100 is the same as being 20 ahead). The *gemara* provides a mnemonic for why one adds 20 when converting from *minyan shtarot* to *churban*-based dating: *ze li esrim shana beveitecha* — this is twenty years I have been in your house — a phrase with resonances of Israel reckoning its years within the house of the nations.

The corresponding mnemonic for the reverse — a *sofer* subtracting 20 — is *safra betzira*, the scribe reduces, with *Rashi* suggesting this evokes the *sofer*'s practice of writing words in their *chaser* form, without full spelling. The *tanna*, on the other hand, adds — *tanna tosfa* — as a *tanna* teaches a *tosefta*, implying augmentation.

### Seleucid Origin

One might reasonably ask: why should Jews date their documents from the rise of a Greek or Hellenistic empire? The answer is simply that this was the standard practice of the ancient world, and Jewish communities lived within that world. The Seleucid Empire rose to prominence around 312 BCE. The *beit hamikdash* was destroyed in 70 CE, which is indeed approximately 382 years after 312 BCE — consistent with the *gemara*'s figure of 380, given the rough approximations of rabbinic chronology. The rabbinic text frames the origin as the beginning of Greek world dominion, understanding the first six years of Greek rule as a period before that dominion became truly universal — a point the *gemara* will elaborate further.

The parallel to the modern situation is striking and the *gemara* itself seems aware of it. Just as contemporary Jews speak of dates in terms of the common era — itself derived from a non-Jewish religious reckoning — the Jews of the Talmudic period calibrated their documents to the dominant civic calendar of their world. The tractate of *avodah zara*, which is devoted to demarcating the boundaries between Israel and the surrounding culture, thus contains within it a remarkable acknowledgment: the very numbering of years in Jewish legal documents reflected immersion in the non-Jewish world. The *sofrim* of Babylonia continued using *minyan shtarot* through approximately the 9th century; the Jewish community of Egypt used it until the 14th century; and the Jews of Yemen dated their documents by *minyan shtarot* into the 20th century.

---

## Six-Thousand-Year Cycle

### Tanna D'vei Eliyahu

The *gemara* now cites a famous cosmological teaching: *Tanna D'vei Eliyahu* — from the school of Eliyahu — *sheshet alfei shana havei alma* — the world endures for six thousand years. This framework maps the six days of creation onto six millennia of human history, with the seventh thousand year corresponding to *Shabbat* — the era of *olam haba*. The Ramban's commentary on the first chapter of *Bereishit* develops this correspondence in detail, matching the symbolism of each day of creation to the character of its corresponding millennium.

The six thousand years are divided as follows: *shnei alafim tohu* — the first two thousand years are *tohu*, void and waste, evoking the *tohu vavohu* of the primordial creation, a period before *Torah* and before Avraham's transformative influence. *Shnei alafim Torah* — the next two thousand years are the era of *Torah*. *Ushnei alafim yemot HaMashiach* — the final two thousand years constitute the era of the *mashiach*, the period in which redemption is possible and expected. *Uva'avonoteinu sherabu, yatzo mehen ma she-yatzo* — but because of our many sins, the *mashiach*-era has already extended far beyond its opening threshold without the redemption's arrival.

### Torah Era Dating

This raises an immediate question: *shnei alafim Torah me'eimat* — when does the two-thousand-year era of *Torah* begin? The obvious answer would be from *matan Torah* at *Har Sinai*, but this creates a problem. *Matan Torah* occurred in the year 2448 from the creation of the world — not at year 2000. If the *Torah* era began only at year 2448, then the middle two thousand years are badly misaligned with the framework.

The *gemara* therefore says: *ela min hanefesh asher asu veCharan* — rather, the *Torah* era begins from "the souls they made in Charan" (Bereishit 12:5), which the tradition understands as referring to Avraham's activity of bringing people close to God and teaching them monotheism. And there is a received tradition that *Avraham be'hee sha'ata bar chamsin vetartei havei* — Avraham was 52 years old at that time. Since Avraham was born in the year 1948 from creation, the year 2000 corresponds precisely to the moment when Avraham, at age 52, was still in Charan, preaching the existence of God and drawing people toward belief — even before God spoke to him at the age of 75 with the command of *lech lecha*. The two-thousand-year era of *Torah* therefore begins not from *matan Torah* but from this first moment of Avraham's public monotheistic mission.

This reading reframes the standard chronology: *matan Torah* was not the inauguration of the *Torah* era but its continuation, arriving 448 years into a process that began with Avraham in Charan. The *gemara* notes that if one were to count from *matan Torah*, one would be short by 448 years — *arba me'ah ve'arba'in vetamnya shanin* — confirming that the *tanna*'s calculation only works if we start the clock at Avraham's age 52.

### Year 4000 Calculation

Working through the rabbinic chronology: from the year 2000 (Avraham in Charan) to the birth of Yitzchak at Avraham's age 100 is 48 years, bringing us to year 2048. The tradition holds that the 400 years of exile foretold to Avraham (*ki ger yihyeh zaracha*) is counted from the birth of Yitzchak, since Yitzchak was already a stranger in a land not his own from birth. From Yitzchak's birth the count runs to the Exodus: 400 years, reaching year 2448 — the year of *yetziat Mitzrayim* and, shortly after, *matan Torah* at *Har Sinai*. (The intermediate figure of 210 years marks the descent of Yaakov and his family to Egypt, with the full 400-year reckoning encompassing a longer sweep.) The First *beit hamikdash* was built 480 years after the Exodus, at approximately year 2928. It stood for 410 years, was destroyed, and after 70 years of exile the Second *beit hamikdash* was built — its destruction in the year 3828 from creation. Adding 172 years brings us to year 4000 — which corresponds to approximately 172 CE, the period marking the close of the *tannaitic* era and the transition to the *amoraim*. The *gemara* presents this as the natural terminus of the *Torah* era and the beginning of the two-thousand-year *mashiach* period.

---

## Olam/Shtarot Conversion

### Add Forty-Eight

Rav Pappa states: *i ta'ei tanna velo yada pratei kama hava, lish'alei lesafra* — if someone counting from *beriyas olam* (or, more precisely, from the year 4000, which is effectively the same system with the leading four thousand dropped) does not know his last two digits, let him ask the *sofer* who is counting *leminyan shtarot*. He should then take the *sofer*'s last two digits and *venitfei alaiyhu arba vetamne* — add 48 — and he will have his result.

The arithmetic behind this is as follows. The *churban habayit* was year 380 in *minyan shtarot* and year 3828 in *beriyas olam* — or, equivalently, year 172 after the year 4000 baseline. Since the year 4000 baseline corresponds to year 552 in *minyan shtarot* (380 plus 172 — wait: 380 is the *minyan shtarot* year of the *churban*, and the year 4000 is 172 years after the *churban*, so the year 4000 is *minyan shtarot* year 552), to convert from *minyan shtarot* to the 4000-based count, one must subtract 552 — or, working only with the last two digits and modulo 100, add 48. The formula thus emerges: take the last two digits of the *minyan shtarot* year and add 48 to obtain the corresponding last two digits in the *beriyas olam* / year-4000 count.

### Mnemonic: 48 Cities

The *gemara* supplies a mnemonic for the number 48: *arba'im ushmonah ir* — forty-eight cities. This refers to the forty-eight cities of the *Levi'im*, the priestly cities distributed to the tribe of Levi throughout the land of Israel as enumerated in *Bamidbar*. The association is simply numerical — the same figure of 48 appears in the *Torah* in a memorable context, anchoring it in memory.

### Subtract Forty-Eight

The reverse conversion works correspondingly: *ve'i ta'ei safra*, if the *sofer* using *minyan shtarot* forgets his last two digits, he should obtain the *beriyas olam* / year-4000 count and *venivtzar mineih arba'im ushmoneh* — subtract 48 — and he will recover his *minyan shtarot* position. The mnemonic again: *safra betzira*, the *sofer* reduces — just as a *sofer* writes in the abbreviated *chaser* spelling — while *tanna tosfa*, the *tanna* adds, as the *tanna* teaches an expansive *tosefta*.

To summarize the full set of conversion relationships: to move from *minyan shtarot* to *churban*-based dating, add 20. To move from *minyan shtarot* to *beriyas olam* / year-4000 dating, add 48. The inverse operations subtract those same values. All three dating systems are thus interconvertible, provided one knows which system is in use and can perform the appropriate adjustment to the last two digits.

---

## Shmita Cycle Calculation

### Add One, Divide by 7

Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua turns to an adjacent problem: given a year expressed as years since the *churban habayit*, how does one determine which year of the *shmita* cycle one is in? The key datum is that the *churban habayit* itself fell in year 1 of a *shmita* cycle. This establishes the anchor from which all subsequent *shmita* calculations flow.

The basic algorithm is: take the number of years elapsed since the *churban*, add 1 (because the *churban* year itself was year 1, so the following year was year 2), and divide by 7. The remainder gives the position within the current *shmita* cycle.

### Hundred Extraction

The *gemara* offers a computational shorthand suited to an era without Arabic numerals and long division. Rather than dividing the full number by 7, one can: extract all the hundreds; account for two additional years for every hundred extracted; add those extra years to the remaining sub-hundred number; and then divide that manageable remainder by 7.

To illustrate: suppose it is 518 years after the *churban*. Add 1: now 519. Extract the hundreds: 500, with a remainder of 19. For every hundred, add two — five hundreds yield an additional 10 — giving 29. Divide 29 by 7: four full cycles of 7, with a remainder of 1. The current year is therefore year 1 of the *shmita* cycle.

The reason this works is rooted in the structure of the *yovel* cycle. The *gemara* proceeds on the assumption that we rule like Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that the 50th year of the *yovel* itself counts as year 1 of the subsequent *shmita* cycle, rather than like the *chachamim*, who hold that the 50th year stands alone and year 1 begins anew afterward. Under Rabbi Yehuda's position, every century spans exactly two *yovel* periods of 50 years each, but because the *yovel* year doubles as the first year of the next cycle, each century of 100 years actually corresponds to 100 years minus 2 — meaning that for each century removed from the count, two years have already been "used up" within the *yovel* structure and must be added back into the sub-hundred remainder before dividing by 7.

A student might rightly observe: if we are ruling like Rabbi Yehuda and the *yovel* year serves as year 1 of the next cycle, the entire structure is simply divisible by 7, and one could simply take the year-after-*churban* number, add 1, and divide by 7 directly. This is correct, and the *gemara*'s algorithm is simply an easier method for mental arithmetic when only Roman-style numerals were available and extracting small remainders by hand was simpler than performing full long division.

### Famine Mnemonic

The *gemara* provides a mnemonic for the critical step of adding two for every hundred removed: *ki zeh shenatayim haraav bekerev haaretz* — "for these two years has the famine been in the land" (Bereishit 45:6). The number two in that verse serves as the memory hook for the two-year adjustment per hundred years in the *shmita* calculation.

---

## Messiah Timeline

### Rabbi Chanina's 400 Years

Rabbi Chanina teaches: *achar arba me'ot leChurban HaBayit, im yomar lecha adam kach sadeh shaveh elef dinarin bedinar, lo tikach* — after 400 years from the destruction of the *beit hamikdash*, if someone offers you a field worth a thousand *dinarim* for a single *dinar*, do not take it. The reasoning is that by 400 years after the *churban*, the *mashiach* should certainly have arrived, and investing in property outside the land of Israel at that point would be pointless — one would shortly be returning to Israel with the redemption.

This teaching flows naturally from the cosmological framework established earlier. If the year 4000 from creation — the onset of the *mashiach* era — fell approximately 172 years after the *churban*, then 400 years after the *churban* places us roughly 228 years into the two-thousand-year *mashiach* period. The implication is not that *mashiach* will come precisely at the 400-year mark, but that 400 years into a period designated for messianic redemption, investment predicated on continued exile outside Israel is unreasonable.

### Baraita's 4231

A *baraita* formulates the same teaching differently: *achar arba'at alafim uma'tayim ushloshim ve'achat shanah l'olam* — after 4231 years from creation, if someone offers you a field worth a thousand *dinarim* for a single *dinar*, do not take it. The *gemara* immediately asks: *mai beinayhu* — what is the difference between these two formulations?

The answer: *ika beinayhu tlas shanin* — there are three years between them. Four hundred years after the *churban*, given that the year 4000 corresponds to 172 years after the *churban*, is the year 4228 from creation. The *baraita* says 4231. The two traditions thus differ by exactly three years. Both agree, in substance, that *mashiach* should arrive at approximately the year 4228–4231 from creation — corresponding to the late 4th or early 5th century of the common era, a period that saw the collapse of Roman imperial order, the rise of Byzantine Christianity, and the subsequent emergence of Islam: a moment of profound civilizational transformation within which the Talmudic sages might well have expected divine intervention in history. *Umasnisa tefei tlas shani* — the *baraita*, counting from *beriyas olam*, came out three years later than Rabbi Chanina's *churban*-based count.

---

---

# Avodah Zarah 10

## Shtar Dating Systems

### Post-dated Shtar

The Gemara opens with a case involving a *shtar* that appeared to be dated six years into the future from the time it was being examined by the court. The rabbis sitting before Rava assumed it was a post-dated document — a *shtar meuchar* — and proposed holding it back until its stated date arrived before permitting collection. Rav Nachman, however, rejected this assumption. He explained that it was a skilled, senior scribe who wrote the document — *hai safra dukina katveih* — and that this scribe had a particular reason for the unusual date. The document was not post-dated at all; it was written for the present moment. The apparent discrepancy arose because the scribe counted from six years earlier than the conventional starting point of *minyan shtarot*. As Rav Nachman put it: *vahanach shit shanin demalku beEilam, deanan lo chashvinan lehu* — those six years during which the Greek empire ruled over Eilam, a region in Mesopotamia, are not normally included in our count; we conventionally begin from a later point in the consolidation of Greek power, specifically after Alexander's heirs established the Seleucid dynasty. This particular scribe chose to include those six years, giving the document what appeared to be a future date but was in fact entirely consistent with the present.

The broader halachic background here is the well-established discussion in the opening chapter of *Gittin* — around daf 17 — concerning the invalidity of a *shtar mukdam*, a pre-dated document. A pre-dated *shtar* is disqualified because it retroactively asserts that liens were in place earlier than they actually were, thereby undermining the legitimate claims of prior creditors. A *shtar meuchar*, by contrast, raises different concerns. The case here ultimately resolves into a question not of fraud but of which dating convention the scribe employed.

### Greek Rule in Eilam

A *Baraita* is cited to support Rav Nachman's explanation: *de-tanya Rabbi Yosei omer shesh shanim malchu be-Eilam, ve-achar kach pashitah malchutan be-chol ha-olam kulo* — Rabbi Yosei teaches that the Greeks ruled for six years specifically in Eilam before their dominion spread across the entire world. The significance of this teaching for our purposes is that there was a genuine historical ambiguity about when to mark the beginning of Greek imperial rule. The Macedonian Greeks fought lengthy wars against the Persians and other Eastern powers before consolidating control. Depending on which milestone one chose — the first assertion of power in Eilam or the later expansion across the whole empire — one might arrive at dates differing by six years. Some scribes, like the one in our case, counted from the earlier moment; the conventional system did not.

### Yetziat Mitzrayim Dating

Rav Acha bar Yaakov then issues a broader challenge to the entire assumption underlying the discussion: *matkif lah Rav Acha bar Yaakov mi-mai de-malchut Yevanim mininan dilma li-Yetziat Mitzrayim mininan* — from where do we know that we count according to the Greek kingdoms at all? Perhaps we count from *Yetziat Mitzrayim* instead! If so, the apparent six-year discrepancy in the *shtar* would be irrelevant, because the entire dating system would rest on a different foundation.

### Thousands Place Debate

This challenge prompts a deeper question about the structure of dating conventions. The Gemara raises the possibility: *ve-shavkei lah alfa kama ve-naktei* — perhaps we dropped the first thousand years and are working with the second. That is, the year written in the document might represent not a count from the Seleucid dynasty but a count from *Yetziat Mitzrayim* with the leading "1,000" omitted. This is structurally analogous to our own practice of writing the year as *taf shin ayin chet* rather than spelling out the full five-thousand-something — we routinely drop the thousands place because it changes only once a millennium.

The underlying assumption of this proposal is that a count from *Yetziat Mitzrayim* to the beginning of the Seleucid dynasty would come to approximately one thousand years, which is historically plausible. *Yetziat Mitzrayim* is generally dated to the fourteenth or thirteenth century BCE, and the Seleucid era begins around 312 BCE, placing the gap in the vicinity of one thousand years.

The question then becomes: if the date in the *shtar* represents the second millennium since *Yetziat Mitzrayim* with the thousands digit omitted, could the document be read as a *shtar meuchar* — ambiguously dated either to the present or to a thousand years hence? The concern is that the ambiguity itself might compromise the *shtar*'s validity.

This discussion naturally raises a broader point about the religious significance, or lack thereof, of year-numbering conventions. The passage of years in halachic contexts is typically important for relative counts — how long a king has reigned, when *shmitta* or *yovel* falls — rather than for any absolute cosmic significance attached to the calendar number itself. The widespread Jewish practice today of dating documents and tombstones *le-vriat ha-olam* was not the universal convention even among medieval authorities, many of whom continued with *minyan shtarot*. A document dated *le-minyan she-anu monin kan* — according to whichever conventional reckoning is currently in use — would presumably be unproblematic, since no absolute significance attaches to the number of years apart from its function as a shared reference point.

### Rav Nachman's Ruling

Rav Nachman provides a definitive ruling: *ba-golah ein monin ela l'malchei Yevanim bilvad* — in the diaspora, we count exclusively according to the years of the Greek kings. At first, Rav Acha bar Yaakov thought this was merely a dismissive deflection and was dissatisfied with the answer. But Rav Nachman then pointed to a supporting *Baraita* that says the same thing explicitly — and the Gemara notes that *Ravina* adds that this can be inferred from the *Mishnah* as well.

The Gemara's emphasis that this rule applies specifically *ba-golah* — in the diaspora — is itself worth noting. In the land of Israel, one might maintain a stronger fidelity to distinctly Jewish frameworks of counting. Outside the land, the reality of living within a foreign political and cultural structure means that we adopt the dominant chronological conventions of that structure. Why the Greek count rather than the Roman? Even by the time of the Amoraim, the Greek Hellenistic culture — particularly in the eastern Mediterranean — remained the dominant cultural framework. The Roman Empire absorbed much of Greek civilization, and Greek functioned as the *lingua franca* of the eastern empire while Latin was largely confined to administration. The Seleucid dating system thus retained its practical utility and cultural familiarity long after the Seleucid dynasty itself had ceased to exist.

---

## Royal Year Counting

### Nisan vs Tishrei

The Gemara now turns to a related but distinct question: when counting the regnal years of a king for purposes of dating documents, from which month does a new year begin? The *Mishnah* in *Rosh Hashanah* states: *be-echad be-Nisan Rosh Hashanah le-melachim ve-laregalim* — the first of Nisan is the new year for kings and for the festivals.

### Jewish Kings Nisan

Rav Chisda interprets the clause *le-melachim* as referring to the halacha of *shtarot*: when we write the year of a king's reign in a legal document, the year advances at Nisan. However, the same *Mishnah* also states that the first of Tishrei is *Rosh Hashanah le-shanim u-li-shmitin* — the new year for years generally and for *shmitta* cycles — and Rav Chisda also interprets that clause as pertaining to *shtarot*. This creates an internal contradiction: Rav Chisda has apparently assigned two contradictory rulings to the same subject.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction: *kan le-malkhei Yisrael kan le-malkhei ovdei kokhavim* — one ruling refers to Jewish kings, the other to non-Jewish kings. Jewish kings count their regnal years from Nisan, while non-Jewish kings count from Tishrei. This distinction reflects a broader pattern well known from the *Rosh Hashanah* discussions: Nisan is the beginning of the year for the Jewish people as a nation — it marks *Yetziat Mitzrayim* and the formation of Israel as *am* — while Tishrei represents the universal human new year, associated with the creation of the world.

### Seleucid Convention

The Gemara draws the practical conclusion: *ve-anan hashta mi-Tishrei mininan* — we currently count our years from Tishrei, using the Seleucid reckoning. This confirms the earlier ruling of Rav Nachman. And the Gemara uses this to further refute the suggestion of Rav Acha bar Yaakov: *ve-i salka da-atakh mi-Yetziat Mitzrayim mininan* — if we were truly counting from *Yetziat Mitzrayim*, we would need to count from Nisan, because *Yetziat Mitzrayim* is a specifically Jewish historical anchor and Jewish counting runs from Nisan. The fact that we count from Tishrei demonstrates conclusively that we are following the Seleucid, non-Jewish convention.

### Dating Convention Shift

One might ask why contemporary Jewish documents — *ketubot*, *gittin*, and the like — no longer use *minyan shtarot* at all, having shifted to dating *le-vriat ha-olam*. The answer appears to lie in a convergence of historical and intellectual factors. After fifteen hundred or two thousand years, dating documents by reference to the Seleucid dynasty, which had long since vanished from history, became increasingly artificial. Around the turn of the sixth millennium *le-vriat ha-olam* — roughly 1240 CE — there was a notable surge of Kabbalistic interest in cosmic chronology, and the significance attached to the world's entering its sixth thousand years appears to have catalyzed the shift toward the *briat ha-olam* dating convention. The transition was gradual and not uniform across communities, and some *ketubot* continued to include *minyan shtarot* even after the change became widespread.

---

## Yom Ginussia

### Coronation Day Def.

The *Mishnah* earlier in the tractate had listed *yom ginussia shel malcheihem* — the *yom ginussia* of their kings — among the occasions on which commercial dealings with non-Jews are restricted. The Gemara now asks: *mai yom ginussia*? What is this term? Rav Yehuda offers the first definition: *yom she-ma'amidin bo ovdei kokhavim et malkam* — it is the day on which the non-Jews appoint their king, the coronation day. This definition reflects an important feature of Roman governance: the emperor was not a hereditary dynastic monarch but was officially appointed by the Senate, giving the Roman succession an electoral or quasi-electoral character rather than an automatic dynastic one.

The Gemara immediately objects from a *Baraita* that lists both *yom ginussia* and *yom she-ma'amidin bo et malkam* as two distinct occasions, implying they cannot be the same thing. The response: *lo kashya ha didei ha dibrei* — one refers to the king himself and the other to his son, the prince regent, who might be formally installed during his father's lifetime as heir apparent.

### Obadiah Prophecy

This resolution raises a further difficulty: *u-mi mukmi malka bar malka* — do the Romans actually ever appoint a king's son as king? Given that imperial succession was not hereditary, was there ever really a coronation ceremony for a prince? The Gemara cites a *Baraita* in the name of Rav Yosef quoting the prophecy of *Ovadia*: *hineh katanticha ba-goyim* — behold I have made you the smallest among the nations. *She-ein moshivin melech ben melech* — one expression of this diminished status is that they cannot establish a dynasty, that each king is appointed independently rather than succeeded by his son. The *pasuk* continues *bezuy ata me'od* — you are very denigrated — *she-ein lachem lo ktav ve-lo lashon* — for they have neither their own alphabet nor truly their own language, having borrowed their script from the Greeks and relied heavily on Greek as the lingua franca of the eastern empire.

### Birthday Interpretation

Given the difficulty with the coronation interpretation, the Gemara proposes an alternative: *yom ginussia* simply means *yom ha-leda*, the birthday. But now a different *Baraita* creates a parallel problem, listing both *yom ginussia* and *yom ha-leda* separately. The same resolution applies: *lo kashya ha didei ha dibrei* — one is the king's birthday and one is the prince's birthday. The Romans made great public celebration of a young man's first shaving, a coming-of-age ceremony with some analogy to significant Jewish lifecycle moments.

### Asverus Example

The Gemara eventually returns to the coronation interpretation and resolves the objection about hereditary succession with a qualification: *al yedei she'eila mukminan* — through a special petition, the emperor can request that his son be appointed to succeed him. The example given is *kegon Asverus bar Antoninus* — such as Asverus, the son of Antoninus, who did in fact become emperor through such a request. This is a reference to the arrangement following the death of Antoninus Pius, when his two adopted sons — Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Severus — were designated as co-emperors, requiring a special imperial intervention beyond the normal mechanisms of senatorial appointment.

---

## Antoninus & Rabbi

### Antoninus Dilemma

With the mention of Asverus bar Antoninus, the Gemara transitions to the extended aggadic material concerning the friendship between Antoninus and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi. The first episode establishes the political context of their relationship. Antoninus presents Rabbi with a dilemma: *ba'ina de-yimloch Asverus bri tichotai* — I want my son Asverus to reign after me — *ve-tit'avid Tiveriya koloniya* — and I want Tiberias to be granted a remission of its taxes. The problem: *ve-i eima lehu chada avdi, tartei lo avdi* — if I ask the Senate for one of these two things they will do it, but they will not grant both requests.

### Dove Parable

Rabbi's response is characteristically oblique. Rather than speaking directly, he arranged a visual parable: *aitei gavra arkibei achavreia* — he brought a man riding piggyback on another man's shoulders — *ve-yahav lei yona le'eila bidei* — and placed a dove in the hands of the one on top — *ve-amar lei le-tata eimar le'eila limifrach midei yona* — and instructed the lower man to tell the upper man to release the dove from his hands. Antoninus correctly decoded this message: ask the Senate to appoint Asverus as emperor — that is the request that requires the cooperation of the body beneath him — and then instruct Asverus, once seated in power, to grant the tax remission to Tiberias. The two requests could be achieved sequentially if one used the successor as the vehicle for the second.

### Secret Speech

One might ask why Rabbi could not simply have told Antoninus this directly, or at minimum whispered it to him. The Gemara explains that even a whisper was considered too dangerous: *mishum de-chtiv ki of ha-shamayim yolich et ha-kol* — as the *pasuk* in *Kohelet* warns, the birds of the sky will carry the word. The danger of political intelligence leaking, even from a private conversation, is too great. The Gemara adds a parallel teaching: a secret shared between two people is a secret of the heart; shared among three, it is a secret of the street. When political intrigue is involved and powerful parties have an interest in the information, the risk of exposure demands the most indirect possible communication.

### Vegetable Codes

The same logic of coded communication governs another episode. Antoninus had a daughter named Gira who was conducting herself improperly — the implication being some form of sexual misconduct. He sent Rabbi a *gargira*, a plant whose name echoed her name. Rabbi sent back *kusbarta* — coriander — punning on *kus barta*, effectively "destroy your daughter." Antoninus then sent *karti*, leeks, playing on *karat*, "cut off," suggesting he would execute her. Rabbi responded with *chasa*, lettuce, playing on *lachus*, to have compassion, counseling mercy instead. This elaborate exchange of vegetables encodes an entire conversation about how to handle a scandalous family situation — a negotiation conducted entirely through culinary puns, both because of the political risks of speaking plainly and because the medium itself allowed plausible deniability.

### Secret Gold Gift

In another episode, Antoninus would regularly send Rabbi bags of finely granulated gold concealed under a layer of wheat — *dahava paricha be-matrata ve-chiti apumaihu* — instructing his servants to deliver what appeared to be grain to Rabbi's household. When Rabbi protested that he had no need of the money — *la tzrichna, it li tuva* — Antoninus urged him to accept it anyway: *ve-habu le-man de-batrach de-yehavu le-batrai de-atu batrach* — so that the people who come after you will be able to pay off the people who come after me. The gold was meant to provide a long-term financial cushion for the Jewish community of Tiberias, ensuring that future generations could meet their fiscal obligations to the imperial successors of Antoninus.

### Secret Tunnel

There was a tunnel connecting Antoninus's residence to Rabbi's house, through which Antoninus would travel daily to meet with Rabbi in private. Each day he would bring two slaves as escorts through the tunnel and then kill one at Rabbi's doorway and the other at his own doorway upon returning, ensuring that no one survived to reveal the secret of their meetings. He had given Rabbi explicit instructions: *be-idana de-atina la nishkach gevar kamach* — when I come to visit, there should be no one present.

The practice of eliminating those who knew about the tunnel was consistent with Antoninus's broader character as portrayed throughout these stories — pragmatic, sometimes brutal, unencumbered by sentimentality about the lives of his slaves. At the same time, the Gemara presents him as genuinely committed to his relationship with Rabbi, which required extraordinary measures of secrecy given the political risks of a Roman emperor being known to consult with the leader of a subject people. One gets the portrait of a man simultaneously Machiavellian and sincere — ruthless in his methods, but authentic in his friendship.

### Rabbi Chanina Incident

One day when Antoninus arrived through the tunnel, he found Rabbi Chanina bar Chama sitting with Rabbi, violating the standing arrangement. Antoninus reminded Rabbi of his instruction: *amina lach be-idana de-atana la nishkach gevar kamach*. Rabbi replied that Rabbi Chanina bar Chama was not to be considered an ordinary human being — *leit dein bar inish* — meaning that someone of such extraordinary spiritual stature stood in a different category entirely.

Antoninus then tested this claim. He instructed Rabbi to send Rabbi Chanina bar Chama to wake up the slave he had killed at the doorway. Rabbi Chanina bar Chama went and found the slave dead. He faced a genuine dilemma: to return and report the death would be to deliver distressing news — *ein meshivin al ha-kala'ah* — yet to simply leave would be to show disrespect to the king. His resolution was to pray over the dead slave: *ba rachamei alei ve-achayei u-shderei* — he prayed for him, revived him, and sent him in. Antoninus's reaction combined admiration with pragmatism: *yadana zuta de-itchu mechayeh metim* — I see that even the least among your students can perform *techiyat ha-meitim* — but he maintained nonetheless that he did not want visitors present during his meetings with Rabbi.

### Antoninus Service

Every day Antoninus would personally serve Rabbi — bringing him food and drink, acting in the role of attendant. When Rabbi wished to climb into bed, Antoninus would bow before the bed to serve as a step for Rabbi to mount it, in the manner that the Gemara in *Kiddushin* describes children doing for their parents as an expression of *kibbud av va-em*. When Rabbi protested that it was not appropriate to show such disrespect to the Roman emperor — *lav orch arch le-zalzulei be-malchuta kulei hai* — Antoninus responded: *mi yesimeni matza tachteicha le-olam ha-ba* — I only hope that in the *olam ha-ba* I will be worthy to be your mattress. The image is one of total self-abnegation, Antoninus measuring his own spiritual worth against Rabbi's by expressing the desire to serve him even in the world to come.

This led directly to the question that animates the next section: Antoninus asked whether he would actually have any share in *olam ha-ba* at all.

---

## Edom Olam Ha-Ba

### Esau Actions Doctrine

Antoninus asked Rabbi directly: *atena le-alma de-atei* — will I enter *olam ha-ba*? Rabbi affirmed that he would. Antoninus then challenged this: doesn't the *pasuk* in *Ovadia* say *lo yihye sarid le-veit Esav* — there will be no remnant for the house of Esau? Rabbi replied: *be-oseh ma'aseh Esav* — the verse applies only to one who actually performs the deeds of Esau. You, Antoninus, do not. Similarly, Antoninus pressed: does not *Yechezkel* say *shama Edom melacheiha ve-chol nesi'eiha* — there will be destruction for Edom's kings and all its princes? Rabbi replied: *melacheiha ve-lo kol melacheiha, kol nesi'eiha ve-lo kol sareiha* — "its kings" means not all of its kings; "all its princes" means not every single one of its officers.

### Baraita Exception

A *Baraita* is then cited that confirms and specifies this interpretation. On the clause *ve-lo kol melacheiha* — not all of Edom's kings — the *Baraita* specifies: *perat le-Antoninus bar Asverus* — this excludes Antoninus who served Rabbi. And on *ve-lo kol sareiha* — not every single officer — *perat le-Kti'a bar Shalom* — this refers specifically to Kti'a bar Shalom. The Gemara now turns to tell us who Kti'a bar Shalom was.

### Kti'a Bar Shalom

*Kti'a bar Shalom mai havah* — what was his story? There was a Roman emperor who harbored intense hatred of the Jews. He assembled the leading dignitaries of his empire and put the following question to them: if a man has a wound on his foot, should he amputate it and live, or leave it and suffer? The answer was obvious: amputate and live. The implication was plain — the Jewish people were the festering wound, and the emperor was proposing to eliminate them so that the empire could thrive. The analogy is chilling precisely because of how many times in subsequent history the same rhetoric recurred: the notion of a minority group as a parasitic drain on the body politic, requiring excision for the host to flourish.

### Four Winds Argument

Kti'a bar Shalom, however, rose to challenge the emperor's conclusion. He offered two arguments. First, *chada de-lo yachalt lehu le-kuleihu* — you simply cannot kill all of them — *dich-tiv ki ke-arba ruchot ha-shamayim perashti etchem* — for the *pasuk* in *Zecharia* says that God has spread Israel out like the four winds. The Gemara notes that the verse says *ke-arba ruchot*, "like the four winds," not *le-arba ruchot*, "to the four winds." The former does not merely mean that the Jews are dispersed in four directions — it means that just as the world cannot exist without winds, so too the world cannot exist without Israel: *keshem she-iy efshar la-olam belo ruchot, kach iy efshar la-olam belo Yisrael*.

Second, Kti'a bar Shalom warned that attempting to destroy the Jews would result in the empire being called *malchuta keti'a* — a severed, cut-off kingdom. The name *Kti'a bar Shalom* itself encodes this teaching, playing on the root *keta*, to cut off. It is worth noting the recurring observation in the Gemara that certain sages' famous teachings seem to echo their names — whether they were named in anticipation of these ideas or developed the ideas by association with their names is itself a point of scholarly interest.

### Kti'a Execution

The emperor acknowledged the force of Kti'a bar Shalom's argument — *meimar shapir ka'amarta*, you spoke well — but declared that anyone who defeats the king in argument must be thrown into a pit of ashes as punishment. Rashi understands this as a furnace; Rabbeinu Chananel describes it as a burning punishment. As Kti'a bar Shalom was being led away to his death, a Roman noblewoman called out to him: *vai lah le-ilfa de-azla be-lo michsa* — woe to the ship that tries to cross without paying the customs duty. The image was that of a soul departing the world without the proper "payment" to gain entry to the world to come.

Understanding her meaning, Kti'a bar Shalom bent over and circumcised himself on the spot, declaring: *yahavit michsi chalifet va-avarit* — I have paid my customs, now let me cross over. In the shadow of his imminent execution, he performed the sign of the covenant as a final act of commitment to the Jewish people and their God, despite having been born a Roman.

### Kti'a Bequest

As he was being taken to his death, Kti'a bar Shalom declared: *kol nichsai le-Rabbi Akiva ve-chaverav* — all of my property should go to Rabbi Akiva and his colleagues. Rabbi Akiva then went out and delivered a *drasha* on the *pasuk* that describes the priestly portions of the *lechem ha-panim* and *terumah*: *ve-hayah le-Aharon u-le-vanav*, which is interpreted as splitting the gift half to Aharon and half to all his sons collectively. Accordingly, Rabbi Akiva claimed half of the inheritance for himself alone and the remaining half to be divided among all the other rabbis — a creative and perhaps playful halachic reading that allowed Rabbi Akiva to take a disproportionate share while remaining technically grounded in precedent.

### Bat Kol Approval

Immediately following this, a heavenly voice descended and announced: *Kti'a bar Shalom mezuman le-chayei ha-olam ha-ba* — Kti'a bar Shalom has been designated for life in *olam ha-ba*. Rabbi wept upon hearing this and said: *yesh koneh olamo be-sha'ah achat, ve-yesh koneh olamo be-chamah shanim* — there are those who acquire their world in a single moment, and there are those who must acquire it over many years. The teaching is one of the most moving in the tractate. A lifetime of Torah study, *mitzvot*, and ethical striving is of immeasurable value — and yet, in certain extraordinary moments, a single act of self-sacrifice or total commitment can accomplish in an instant what others labor toward over decades. The story of Kti'a bar Shalom, a Roman officer who defended the Jews, circumcised himself as he was being led to execution, and used his final breath to leave his estate to the rabbis, stands as the Gemara's paradigmatic example of that singular transformative moment.

---

## Adrachan & Rav

### Adrachan Service

The Gemara draws a structural parallel between two great rabbinic leaders and their respective royal admirers. Just as Antoninus would personally serve Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi as his attendant — bringing him food and drink, serving as his step to mount the bed — so too Adrachan, the Persian king, would serve as attendant to Rav.

### Deaths & Eulogies

When Antoninus died, Rabbi delivered what amounted to a eulogy in the form of a terse and profound phrase: *nitpardah chavilah* — the bundle has come undone. The image is of a close bond that had kept two very different things tightly bound together; with Antoninus's death, that bond was released and the bundle fell apart. When Adrachan died, Rav likewise announced *nitpardah chavilah* — the same expression, the same sense of a uniquely close friendship across the boundaries of religion and power having been severed. The parallel structure of these eulogies signals the Gemara's interest in a broader phenomenon: the possibility of genuine, deep friendship between the greatest Torah authorities of their generations and the most powerful rulers of the surrounding world, friendships rooted not in political convenience alone but in mutual respect, personal devotion, and, as the foregoing aggadah has shown, a shared aspiration for something beyond the political.

---

## Onkelos Story

### Onkelos Conversion

The final section of the daf presents the celebrated story of *Onkelos bar Kolonimus*, who converted to Judaism. *Onkelos ha-Ger* is of course best known as the author of the authoritative Aramaic translation of the Torah that bears his name. His very name is interesting: *Kolonimus* in Greek means "good name" — *shem tov* — and the name appears widely among Italian and Greek Jewish families through the early medieval period, including the Kalonymus dynasty of *paytanim*. Thus *Onkelos bar Kolonimus* might be read as Onkelos who had a good reputation, a *ba'al shem tov*.

The Roman emperor, upon learning of the conversion of so prominent a figure, dispatched a legion of troops — *gunda de-romaye* — to apprehend him. The troops succeeded in taking hold of Onkelos, whereupon he enticed them with *pesukim* from the Torah and they all converted: *igayur*. The emperor sent a second detachment with explicit instructions: *lo temru leh velo midi* — do not say a word to him, do not let him speak.

### Four Winds Defense

When the second group arrived and took hold of Onkelos, he asked permission to say just one brief, non-Torah remark. He pointed to the hierarchical chain of imperial service: a lower official carries the torch for a higher one, who carries it for the duke, the duke for the governor, the governor for the supreme ruler. And at the top? The supreme ruler carries the torch for no one — he is served, not serving. *Amar lehu ha-kadosh baruch hu nakat nura kamei Yisrael* — but the Holy One, blessed be He, carries the torch for Israel, as the *pasuk* states: *ve-Hashem holech lifneihem yomam* — and God went before them by day, providing the pillar of cloud and fire in the desert. All of them converted.

### Torch Bearer Parable

This argument is striking and worth dwelling on. The image Onkelos presents is not of God as distant sovereign but of God as intimate servant of Israel's needs — one who humbles Godself, as it were, to provide for the Jewish people. The relational logic is powerful: if the greatest sign of status in human hierarchies is that one is served rather than serving, then God's having "carried the torch" for Israel — providing them light and guidance in the wilderness — signals a uniquely elevated status for the Jewish people in the divine economy. The Roman soldiers, embedded in a hierarchical culture where this logic was perfectly intelligible, found the argument compelling enough to abandon their mission and join the Jewish people.

### Mezuza Argument

The emperor, undeterred, sent a third detachment with even stricter orders: *lo tishta-u midi bahadeih* — do not engage with him about anything at all. As this group was escorting Onkelos away, he paused at the doorpost, placed his hand on the *mezuza*, and asked: *mai hai* — what is this? When they said he should explain it to them, he offered his argument: *minhago shel olam, melech basar va-dam yoshev bifnim ve-avadav mishamrim oto mibachutz* — normal human practice has the king sitting within, protected, while his servants stand guard outside. *Va-ilu ha-kadosh baruch hu avadav mibifnim ve-hu mishamram mibachutz* — but the Holy One, blessed be He, has His servants dwelling within while He stands guard outside, as it says *Hashem yishmor tzeitcha u-vo'echa me-atah ve-ad olam* — God will guard your going out and your coming in forever. The *mezuza* placed at the doorpost is the sign of God's watchful presence — not within the protected interior, but at the threshold, guarding those who dwell inside. All of them converted.

### Emperor Surrenders

After this fourth wave of soldiers all converted, the emperor gave up sending any more: *tu lo shadar batre* — he simply stopped dispatching troops. The story has a comic inevitability to it, each successive wave of soldiers falling to the same irresistible intellectual and spiritual force.

The Gemara's account of Onkelos here provides a kind of valediction to the themes of the entire daf. Throughout the daf we have seen the complex relationship between the Jewish people and the empires surrounding them — the halachic question of dating documents according to the regnal calendar of foreign rulers, the political friendship between Antoninus and Rabbi, the courage of Kti'a bar Shalom defending the Jews before the emperor, and now Onkelos demonstrating to successive waves of Roman soldiers that God's relationship with Israel is unlike any other relationship in the world. The practice of touching the *mezuza* upon entering and leaving a room — a *minhag* the Gemara may be connecting to this very episode — embodies that consciousness: the awareness that at the threshold of every doorway stands the divine protection that has accompanied Israel through every exile and every empire.

The *Targum Onkelos* itself, the Aramaic translation of the Torah that Onkelos produced, reflects these same sensibilities. Throughout the translation, Onkelos consistently renders anthropomorphic and anthropopathic descriptions of God in more abstract terms, substituting the *yekara de-Hashem*, the divine glory, or the *shechinta de-Hashem*, the divine presence, wherever the *pasuk* might be read as attributing physical qualities or postures to God. The very verse from Onkelos's *mezuza* argument — the torch carried before Israel in the desert — is itself one that Onkelos's translation handles with characteristic theological care. There is a profound coherence between the convert, the translator, and the teacher: the one who crossed every boundary to join the Jewish people is also the one who spent his life articulating, in the most accessible language, what makes the Jewish people's relationship with God irreducibly singular.

---

---

# Avodah Zarah 11

## Jewish Minority Cont (II)

### Integration vs. Distinct…

The tractate of *Avodah Zarah* opens up a fundamental question about how we think about the larger world. Is this tractate primarily about idolatry in the technical sense, or is it about a different type of life altogether — a life that is not oriented around *Torah* and *mitzvos*? Whatever the answer, the Rabbis are manifestly aware of the world in which they live. They know all of these pagan holidays intimately, and more than that, the entire calendar is structured around events of the larger world — the *minyan shtarot*, not the destruction of the *Beis HaMikdash* and not the creation of the world. Even the socio-structural organization of time reflects this embeddedness: the discussion of counting from *Tishrei* rather than from *Nissan* evokes a year beginning in January rather than on *Rosh Hashanah*. We are in many ways one fabric with that larger world, even as we work to retain our distinctiveness.

### Antoninus & Rabbi

The figure of Antoninus — and the question of exactly which Caesar this refers to is itself a significant one, as Keafter has a very long note attempting to identify precisely which ruler is meant, since the dates do not work for Marc Antony — appears in this context as a counterpart to *Rebbi*, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi. It is possible that this friendship has some kernel of historical fact, since part of the role of the *nesi'im* in *Eretz Yisrael* was to maintain a positive relationship with Rome. But the story as told — with Antoninus sneaking away from Rome nightly and traveling through some secret cave, crossing improbable distances in order to have private meetings with *Rebbi*, and at one point even serving as *Rebbi*'s footstool — is of course quite humorous to read. It is also a very powerful story, and one must think carefully about its intended audience.

The audience is fellow Jews who are feeling the weight of minority existence — oppressed, defenseless, wondering what it means to be part of a tradition that seems so insignificant before the overwhelming success of Rome. These stories are powerful precisely because the message comes through even as one senses how non-factual they are. The whole event that recurs once every seventy years — *Eisav* riding atop a lame *Yaakov* — seems to be the opposite message, Rome triumphant over Israel. But the punchline, as we will see at the end of the *daf*, is that even in the midst of that great display of dominance, the final proclamation is a lament: woe to us when the other one arises. Even they, deep down, recognize the ultimate truth.

## Roman History & Caesar

### Sefer Josippon Account

Before proceeding further into the *daf*, there is a small but remarkable *Tosafos* on 10b, *kol nesi'eha*, that distills in roughly six lines an entire account of Roman history. The source it draws on is *Sefer Josippon* — not the actual Josephus, but a Hebrew pseudo-Josephus written in the Middle Ages that was believed to be a translation of Josephus and became very popular in that period. The *Tosafos* introduces this with the words *da'amar Ri*, and then proceeds to tell the following story.

### Roman Oath & Caesar

*Shenishbu Romiyim shelo lehamlich aleihem od melech* — the Romans took an oath never again to install a king over themselves. This oath arose *bishvil echad shelakach isha achas bechazaka* — because of the rape of a woman, a reference to the rape of the Sabines. From that point forward, Rome decided it could never have a king. Instead, *ela shehayu memanim yashish echad* — they would appoint one elder, essentially a consul, along with *shelosh me'os yo'atzim*, three hundred advisors representing the Senate. Yet *vesof kama shanim malach aleihem echad bechazaka* — after many years, one man imposed his power over them and became a real ruling force.

### Caesar Etymology

This man's origins carry a further detail: *shemesa imo belidta venivka bitna* — his mother died in childbirth and her womb was cut open, meaning he was born through cesarean section. *Umetzauhu chai umalach aleihem* — he was found alive and ultimately ruled over them. *Venikra Keisar belashon Romi belashon karus beIvris* — he was called *Keisar* in the language of Rome, which corresponds to the word for "cut" in Hebrew. *Ve'al shemo nikre'u kol hamelachim she'achirav Keisar* — and after him, all subsequent rulers were called *Keisar*. This is, notably, reasonably close to what actually happened historically. A beautiful distillation of Roman history in roughly six lines.

## Onkelos Proselyte

### Onkelos Recognition

At the top of 11a, the *Gemara* relates the story of *Onkelos HaGer*, which functions as a similar narrative to the Antoninus and *Rebbi* story: even a non-Jew of the highest standing recognizes greatness and converts. Moreover, when Roman officers were sent to apprehend *Onkelos*, all he had to do was give them a small glimpse of the true path, and they too converted. The story functions to reinforce a sense of dignity and confidence — even in a condition of minority and oppression, the power of the faith we represent speaks for itself.

It is worth noting in this context that Jews in the Roman world likely constituted a much higher percentage of the population than Jews represent in the world today. What accounts for the dramatic decline is a combination of persecutions, forced conversions, and assimilation over the subsequent centuries. But within the Roman world, Jewish presence was far from insignificant.

## Rivka Womb Reading

### Goyim as Ge'im

The *Gemara* now takes up the verse *Shnei goyim bevitnech* — "two nations are in your womb" — said by God to *Rivka*. *Amar Rav Yehuda amar Rav al tikrei goyim ela ge'im* — do not read it as "nations" but as "haughty ones," or ones of great stature, *de'Antoninus ve'Rebbi* — referring to Antoninus and *Rebbi*. This is a classic example of the *al tikrei* reading, rerouting the plain meaning of a biblical verse through a subtle orthographic shift to generate a new layer of significance.

## Jewish Minority Cont (II)

### Yaakov-Eisav Paradigm

This brings us to a broader reflection on how Jews read history and interpret world events. Yosef Yerushalmi, in his small but essential book *Zachor*, argues that Jews did not do history in the modern sense — they did memory. The concern was not with establishing facts for their own sake, but with constructing a sense of Jewish memory, interpreting history through a biblical lens, and fitting past events into a set of archetypes that make sense of the present and provide confidence about the future. Every anti-semite becomes a *Haman*; every crisis maps onto a prior paradigm.

Within this framework, the central warring model in the *Torah* — leaving aside the Pharaoh who enslaved the Israelites — is *Yaakov* and *Eisav*: two entities in constant striving against one another. But *Eisav* becomes *Edom*, and *Edom* eventually dies out as an ancient nation. The question then becomes who, in the post-biblical period, inherits the role of *Edom* in the cosmic drama. The answer the tradition settled on is Rome. The translation was taken for granted: *Eisav* is *Edom* is Rome. And when Rome as a political entity ceased to exist, the model shifted to the relationship between Judaism and Christianity — a transition helped considerably by the fact that the Holy Roman Empire adopted Christianity as its religion. All of this history — Jews versus Rome, Judaism versus Christianity — gets read through the *Yaakov*-*Eisav* lens.

The *Gemara*'s reading of *shnei goyim bevitnech* as referring to Antoninus and *Rebbi* represents a rare moment in this paradigm: the one time when these two figures got along.

## Seasonal Produce Luxury

### Off-Season Vegetables

The *Gemara* records that both Antoninus and *Rebbi* enjoyed vegetables year-round, regardless of season: *shelo pasak me'al shulchanam lo chazeret velo kishut velo tzenon, lo biyemei hachama velo biyemei hageshamim* — neither lettuce, nor cucumbers, nor radishes ever ceased from their table, whether in summer or in winter. This is presented as a mark of extraordinary wealth, since in the ancient world access to vegetables out of season was by no means taken for granted.

The *Gemara* offers medical explanations for why these particular vegetables were valued: *tzenon mechatech ochel* — radishes help chop up and digest food; *chazeret mehappech ma'achal* — lettuce helps churn the food around in the stomach; *kishut marchiv mei'ayim* — cucumbers help expand the digestive capacity. *Tosafos* adds that the point was not merely that they had out-of-season vegetables, but that they had specifically those vegetables which were necessary for good digestion, because their tables were so overflowing with delicacies that digestive aids were a necessity.

### Cucumber Debate

The *Gemara* then raises a complication. *Ve'atanyah devei Rabbi Yishmael lama nikre sheman kishu'in mipnei shekashin legufo shel adam kecharavot* — a *Baraisa* in the school of Rabbi Yishmael states that cucumbers are called *kishu'in* precisely because they are as hard and damaging to the body as swords. This seems to contradict the positive assessment just offered. The *Gemara* resolves: *lo kashya, ha berabbeyei ve'ha bezozei* — there is no difficulty; one statement refers to large cucumbers and the other to small ones, with the large ones presumably being harmful.

## Birth & Death Days

### Birth Death Holiday

The *Gemara* returns now to the topic of pagan holidays, listing *yom leida ve'yom mita* — the day of birth and the day of death among the occasions that constitute pagan holidays for the purposes of the *Mishnah*'s prohibitions.

### Funeral Pyre Dispute

This leads to an important *halachic* discussion. Rabbi Meir holds that a death day is a pagan holiday only when it involves a funeral pyre — *mita sheyesh bah sereifa* — while a death day without a funeral pyre is not considered a pagan holiday. The Rabbis do not make this distinction. The *Gemara* reads the positions as follows: *miklal de'Rabbi Meir savar, lo shena mita sheyesh bah sereifa velo shena mita she'ein bah sereifa, palchi lah la'avodat kochavim* — Rabbi Meir's position implies that pagan worship takes place at all funerals regardless of whether there is a funeral pyre. The funeral pyre is therefore not itself the problem; it is not a *chuka* in the relevant sense. *Alma sereifa lav chuka hi* — the funeral pyre is not a *chuka*, meaning it is not per se a pagan ritual. Pagan worship occurs at all funerals whether the pyre is present or not, so the presence or absence of the pyre changes nothing.

Conversely, *ve'rabbanan savri sereifa chuka hi* — the Rabbis appear to hold that the funeral pyre is itself a *chuka*, a pagan rite, and only when it is present do we have a genuine pagan holiday. Without it, the death day does not constitute a prohibited occasion.

The *Gemara* immediately raises a challenge from a *Baraisa*: *sorfin al hamelachim ve'lo midarchei ha'emori* — one may burn for the death of Jewish kings and this is not considered the ways of the Amorite, which is another formulation for the prohibition of *bechukoteihem lo telechu*. This seems to flatly contradict the Rabbinic view that a funeral pyre is itself a pagan ritual — for if it were, how could it be permitted for Jewish kings? *Ve'ei chuka hi, anan heichi sarfinan, vehaktiv uvchukoteihem lo telechu* — if this really is a *chok*, how can we practice it?

### Chashivuta Framework

The resolution: *ela dechulei alma sereifa lav chuka hi* — in fact, everyone agrees that the funeral pyre is not intrinsically a pagan ritual. *Ela chashivuta hi* — rather, it is a signal of *chashivuta*, of great significance and importance. It marks the death of an especially important person and marks the occasion as a funeral of great weight. It is not itself a form of pagan worship, but it is a marker that a funeral of this magnitude will be accompanied by pagan worship.

This then is the actual dispute: *Rabbi Meir savar lo shena mita sheyesh bah sereifa velo shena mita she'ein bah sereifa palchei leh le'avodat kochavim* — Rabbi Meir holds that pagan worship takes place at all funerals, important or not, because pagans will always incorporate some form of worship into a death. Therefore, whether there is a funeral pyre matters not at all. *Ve'rabbanan savri mita sheyesh bah sereifa chashiva lehu ufalchei bah* — the Rabbis, however, hold that the pyre marks this as an important occasion, and it is at important occasions that pagan worship is conducted. *She'ein bah sereifa lo chashiva ve'lo palchei* — without the pyre, the funeral is not significant enough to occasion pagan worship.

The practical upshot is that we ourselves may perform this burning ritual for our kings and *nesi'im* — not because we are following pagan practice, but because the ritual itself is not pagan in content. It signals importance and honor, which is a Jewish value as much as a Roman one. An analogy: whenever a certain society dresses formally for an event, one knows they will conduct their pagan worship there. That does not make formal dress itself forbidden; the two simply co-occur. We are permitted to signal honor for our great ones in this way.

This *Gemara* opens onto a larger discussion about the scope of *bechukoteihem*. *Tosafos* is bothered because in *Sanhedrin* the prohibition of *bechukoteihem* seems to have a broader scope — for instance, the discussion of whether execution by sword constitutes *bechukoteihem*. The *Gemara* there also indicates that if a practice has a basis in *Torah* or *Nach*, it is not a problem of *bechukoteihem*. And the burning of kings, as we will see shortly, is indeed sourced in *Nach*.

*Tosafos* resolves this by distinguishing two categories within *bechukoteihem*. The first category consists of things genuinely associated with foreign religions or with *avodah zarah* — those remain off-limits regardless of whether there is a parallel in *Torah*, once they are truly associated with those other religions. The second category consists of arbitrary or irrational practices that they happen to have — like executing by sword. In that second category, if we have our own independent basis in *Torah* for the practice, it is permissible. The present *Gemara* thus narrows *bechukoteihem* to things specifically associated with *avodah zarah*, while other *Gemaros* suggest it can reach further into neutral practices of the surrounding society — though with less stringency, and more room to say we are not really deriving it from them if we have our own basis.

This question about the scope of *bechukoteihem* is in fact central to the broader conversation about Jewish integration into the surrounding world. If *bechukoteihem* prohibits only practices that are genuinely *avodah zarah*-related, then one can dress, live, and appear in many ways similar to the surrounding society while retaining one's distinctiveness through observance of *mitzvos*. If *bechukoteihem* extends to neutral everyday practices, then the demand is not merely for distinctiveness but for a more thoroughgoing separateness. *Rav Moshe Feinstein* in a *teshuvah*, asked whether it is *assur* to give secular names, points out that many great rabbis throughout history had secular names and that *lo shinu shemam umalbusham uleshonam* applied specifically before the giving of *mitzvos*, when external markers were needed to maintain distinctiveness. Now that we have *mitzvos*, he argues, one need not be as stringent about these external signs — a position that speaks directly to the difference between Modern Orthodox and *Haredi* approaches. But this is a much larger discussion; the *Gemara* here raises it only in passing.

## Burning for Kings

### Torah Source Burning

The *Gemara* now returns to the *Baraisa*: *sorfin al hamelachim ve'ein bah mishum darchei ha'emori*. The *pasuk* adduced in support comes from Jeremiah's prophecy to *Tzidkiyahu*: *beshalom tamut* — you will die in peace — *uvemisrafos avotecha hamelachim asher sarfu lefanecha* — and you will have a burning like those of the kings who preceded you. This demonstrates that these burnings were practiced throughout the period of the Judean monarchy and were accepted practice.

### What Burned

*U'keshem shesorfin al melachim kach sorfin al nesi'im* — just as this applies to kings, so it applies to *nesi'im*, the leaders of the Jewish community. *U'mahi hem sorfin? Mitatan u'chlei tashmishan* — what is burned? Their beds — which may refer either to their literal beds or to the funeral bier on which the body was carried out — and their personal effects.

### Onkelos Burning

The *Gemara* records: *u'ma'aseh shemet Rabban Gamliel hazaken, ve'saraf alav Onkelos hager shiv'im mana tzuri* — when Rabban Gamliel died, *Onkelos HaGer* burned seventy *mana* of Tyre in his honor, an enormous sum. The *Gemara* immediately questions this: *mai hem sorfin alav mitatan u'chlei tashmishan* — we said only personal effects are burned? *Eima b'shiv'im mana tzuri* — the text means that the value of the personal effects burned came to seventy *mana* of Tyre.

It is notable that it is *Onkelos HaGer* who makes such an extravagant gesture here. In the context of the whole discussion establishing that this practice is not pagan — that it is in fact rooted in *pesukim* and represents Jewish tradition — the person making the most emphatic statement of honor is one who comes from the outside culture and has now converted in. One wonders whether, had it been someone else, they might have felt less urgency to demonstrate that *Rebbi* should be treated no differently from a Roman emperor.

On the historical question of whether *Onkelos* could have been present at the death of Rabban Gamliel: the *Gemara* states that *Onkelos* was a student of *Rebbe Eliezer* and *Rebbe Yehoshua*, placing him roughly in the period of *Rabbi Akiva*, around 130 CE. Rabban Gamliel HaZaken, the elder, died well before the destruction of the Temple, creating a significant chronological difficulty. However, many *Rishonim* — including the *Rif*, the *Rosh*, and the *Ran* — do not have the word *hazaken* in the text, which would place this as a reference to the later Rabban Gamliel, who lived in approximately the right period. The *Tosefta* likewise does not include *hazaken*, which lends weight to the reading without it.

### Hobbling Animals

*U'midai achrinei lo?* — is it truly only personal effects that are subject to this practice? A *Baraisa* states: *okin al hamelachim ve'ein bo mishum darchei emori* — one hobbles animals as part of the funeral of a king and this is not considered the way of the Amorite. *Okin* refers to cutting the tendons of the animal's legs.
