This immediately prompts an obvious difficulty. Once we sell the animal, it is no longer ours — *v'neivid keivan de'zabna kinya*, why should we care what the new owner does with it on *Shabbat*?

### Gezeirah: Lending & Test…

The Gemara answers: *gezeirah mishum she'ilah u'mishum sechirut* — it is a rabbinic decree extending to cover lending and leasing. The concern is that if we permit outright sale, we will slide toward permitting the lending or renting of animals to non-Jews, where the Shabbat work prohibition remains directly implicated because the animal technically still belongs to a Jew.

The Gemara immediately challenges this: *she'ilah kanya ve'agrah kanya* — does borrowing or renting actually constitute a form of acquisition? The question of where the line falls between "this is now yours" and "this still belongs to me" is real and nuanced, and it maps readily onto familiar situations. A renter of an apartment cannot dig holes in the living room or light bonfires regardless of their sense of possession. Ownership boundaries in rental situations are not self-evident.

### Testing Near Shabbat

The Gemara offers a different and more specific rationale. *Ella amar Rav breh Rami breh de-Rav Yeivi: gezeirah mishum nisyoni* — the decree is on account of *nisyoni*, testing. When purchasing a large animal, a prospective buyer naturally wants a demonstration of the animal's capabilities: how well it carries a load, how responsive it is. The Gemara specifies the troublesome scenario precisely: *de-zamnin de-zavna la nihaleih samuch lishkiat hachamah de-ma'alei Shabta* — sometimes the sale happens close to sunset on *erev Shabbat*. The seller, eager to demonstrate the animal's quality, calls out to it, and the animal — hearing its owner's familiar voice — responds and moves under load. *Ve-amar lo ta nisyei nihali de-shama lei kalia ve-azla meichamanteih.*

The Gemara characterizes this as a violation of *mechamer*, the prohibition against driving an animal to perform labor on *Shabbat*: *hamichamer achar behema be-Shabbat chayav chatat*. The seller has not physically done anything — he has simply spoken — and yet through his voice he has activated the animal to perform *melacha*, and this constitutes a real transgression. The *Tosafot* and other *rishonim* note that this is admittedly a narrow and specific scenario — it requires the sale to be happening on *erev Shabbat*, the use of voice, the animal's recognition of its owner, and all the circumstances aligning — but it grounds the prohibition in an identifiable concern.

### Renting vs. Owning

Rav Shisha the son of Rav Idi presses the question of *sechirut* further. *Usechirut mi kanya?* — does leasing actually constitute acquisition? He cites a Mishnah that will appear on 21a: even in places where it is permitted to rent items to a non-Jew, one may not rent an apartment, *lo leveit dirah amru mipnei she-machnis letochoh avodat kochavim* — because of the concern that he will bring *avodat kochavim*, idolatrous practice, into the space.

If *sechirut* were a full acquisition, then once rented the space would be entirely the renter's and no concern would attach to the owner. The fact that we restrict what can be rented implies the owner retains some relationship to the property. *Shani avodah kochavim d'chamira* — the domain of idolatry is treated with special stringency, grounded in the verse from *Devarim*: *v'lo tavi toevah el beitecha*, do not bring an abomination into your home. Even when one has rented a space, the prohibition of allowing *toevah* into what remains legally connected to the Jewish owner applies.

Rav Yitzchak the son of Rav Mesharsheya raises yet another challenge on the *sechirut* question, this one from the laws of *terumah*. An *Yisrael* who rents a cow from a *kohen* may feed it *karshinei terumah* — a leguminous plant used as fodder that has the status of *terumah*. But a *kohen* who rents a cow from an *Yisrael*, even though he bears the obligation to feed it, may not feed it *karshinei terumah*. *V'i salka da'atach sechirut kanya, amai lo yachilena? Parah dideih hi* — if the leasing were equivalent to acquisition, the *kohen* renting the cow should be able to feed it whatever is his, since it would be his cow. The fact that he cannot do so demonstrates: *ela shma mina sechirut lo kanya*, leasing is not equivalent to purchase.

And now that we have established that *sechirut* is not full acquisition, the Gemara draws the full picture: *v'hashta d'amart sechirut lo kanya, gzera mishum sechirut, u-gzera mishum she'elah, u-gzera mishum nisyoni* — the prohibition on selling large animals to non-Jews is undergirded by all three concerns: the leasing concern, the lending concern, and the *nisyoni* concern of demonstrating the animal near *Shabbat*.

---

## Housing & Idolatry

### No Apartment Rentals

The Gemara's discussion of *sechirut* and ownership naturally raises the question of renting housing. The relevant Mishnah, which will be studied on 21a, teaches that even in locales where renting to non-Jews is permitted in general, one may not rent them a residential dwelling — *lo leveit dirah amru mipnei she-machnis letochoh avodat kochavim* — out of concern that the tenant will introduce idolatrous practice into the space.

### Ownership Boundaries

This ruling raises a fundamental conceptual question: if *sechirut* is not acquisition, then when a non-Jew rents an apartment, whose home is it really? And if it remains in some meaningful sense the Jewish owner's home, what responsibility does the owner bear for what transpires inside? The concern is not merely practical but spiritual: the character of the space and the practices conducted within it implicate the owner even after the keys have changed hands.

This maps onto intuitive analogies. A renter may possess the interior of a space without possessing it in every relevant sense — a landlord can and does restrict certain uses, whether making structural changes or activities that affect the building or neighbors. The Gemara is asking the same question from a spiritual dimension: in what sense does the Jewish owner's relationship to the property continue after he has rented it to a non-Jew?

### Toevah Prohibition

The Gemara resolves this with a principle specific to *avodat kochavim*: *shani avodah kochavim d'chamira*, idolatry carries a special stringency beyond other prohibitions. The basis is the verse in *Devarim*: *v'lo tavi toevah el beitecha* — do not bring an abomination into your home. The word *toevah* here is not merely technical but connotes something morally and spiritually repugnant. Crucially, the prohibition is not limited to practicing idolatry oneself; it extends to allowing it to enter into one's home. Even after rental, where the tenant has taken possession for purposes of ordinary use, the owner's Jewish home retains enough of its character that enabling *avodat kochavim* within it violates this prohibition.

This creates a unique category: *sechirut* may not constitute acquisition for most legal purposes, but the heightened prohibition around idolatry means that the owner cannot divest responsibility for what occurs in his property simply by signing a lease.

---

## Middleman Device

### Rav Adda's Ruling

A practical solution to these restrictions is presented in the case of *chamra l'yada d'sapsira*: Rav Adda permitted someone to sell their donkey to a non-Jew by routing the transaction through a *sapsir*, a middleman or broker, rather than conducting the sale directly.

### Middleman Advantages

Rav Adda articulates three reasons why the middleman device resolves the concerns raised above. First, *i mishum nisyoni, halo yada l'kala d'azal mechmatei* — if the concern is the *nisyoni* problem, the test-drive near *Shabbat*, that concern evaporates because the animal does not know the middleman's voice. The seller's voice is what activates the animal; the middleman's voice carries no such power. Second, *i mishum she'elah u'sechirut, keivan d'lav didei, lo moshil v'lo mogar* — if the concern is that the animal might be lent or leased back in a problematic way, this too is resolved: because the animal does not belong to the middleman, he has no authority to lend or lease it to anyone. Third, *mishum d'la naga l'vei muma* — the middleman will not handle the animal in any way that might cause a *mum*, a blemish, because he has no interest in damaging goods he is merely brokering.

One might reasonably ask whether the non-Jewish buyer could simply approach the middleman and request that he relay a request to the original owner for a test-drive or a rental arrangement. Rav Adda's ruling is a case study, and not every permissive ruling resolves every possible objection. The *nisyoni* concern in particular is tied to a very specific scenario — the seller using his own voice on *erev Shabbat* — and the middleman structure severs that specific link.

---

## Rav Huna's Case

### Sale & Challenge

The Gemara records that Rav Huna sold a cow to a non-Jew. Rav Chisda challenged him: *mai ta'ama avad mar hachi?* — master, what is your reasoning? The challenge is straightforward. The Mishnah establishes *ein mocherin behemah gasah*, and a cow is paradigmatically a *behemah gasah*. How did Rav Huna permit himself to do this?

Before Rav Huna's defense is presented, it is worth noting the shift in the underlying concern. With *behemah dakah* the primary worry was *reva'iyah*. With *behemah gasah*, the Gemara has been explaining, the concern is *melacha* on *Shabbat*. Bestiality with a large animal — a horse or cow — is simply not a realistic concern in the same way.

### Shechita Assumption

Rav Huna's defense is: *eimor l'shechitah zabna* — we may assume the animal is being purchased for slaughter, not for labor. The non-Jew wants to eat, and a cow is a plausible candidate for *shechita*. If the buyer's purpose is to slaughter the animal for food, then the Shabbat work concern never arises, because the animal will not be put to labor at all.

### Shemitah Dispute

Rav Huna then supports his position with a precedent from another domain. He cites the dispute between *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel* regarding the *shemitah* year: *Beit Shammai lo yimkor adam para choreshet bashvi'it* — Beit Shammai rules that one may not sell a plowing cow during the Sabbatical year, since the buyer will presumably use it to plow, which is forbidden during *shemitah*. *U-Beit Hillel matirin mipnei sheyachol leshochta* — but Beit Hillel permits such a sale because we can assume the buyer intends to slaughter it. The *halacha* follows *Beit Hillel*. We do not project forbidden intent onto a buyer; we assign the innocent motive — slaughter — and permit the transaction.

### Rava's Challenge

Rava challenges the comparison: *mi dami?* — are these really analogous? The core difference is that *shemitah* and *Shabbat* impose different obligations regarding animals. *Hatam ein adam mitzuveh al shvitat behemto bashvi'it* — in the Sabbatical year, a person has no commandment to ensure that his animal rests; the commandment of *shemitah* applies to the land, not to the animal. *Vehacha adam mitzuveh al shvitat behemto beShabbat* — on *Shabbat*, however, there is an explicit positive commandment to ensure one's animal rests. This commandment is one of the *aseret hadibrot* themselves. The two cases are therefore not parallel: the Beit Hillel leniency in *shemitah* operates in an area where no animal-rest obligation exists, while selling an animal that will work on *Shabbat* implicates a direct commandment.

### Abaye Extends Logic

Abaye presses back on Rava's distinction. If the rule is that wherever one is commanded regarding one's possessions one cannot sell an item that might be used in violation of that commandment, then we should find the same prohibition even in *shemitah* cases involving the land itself. *Veharei sadeh de'adam mitzuveh al shvitat sadehu bashvi'it* — a person is commanded to let his field rest during the Sabbatical year. Yet the Mishnah records: *Beit Shammai lo yimkor adam sadeh nir bashvi'it u-Beit Hillel matirin mipnei sheyachol lehovirah* — Beit Shammai forbids selling a plowed and prepared field during *shemitah*, but Beit Hillel permits because one can assume the buyer will leave it unworked this year and use it the following year. Here we have a case where the seller *is* commanded regarding the rest of his possession — the field — and yet Beit Hillel still permits the sale on the strength of an innocent assumption about use. This would seem to undercut Rava's distinction.

### Innocent Motive Test

Rav Ashi rejects the attempts to derive a clean rule from the commanded/non-commanded distinction, and proposes instead a more nuanced principle: *kol heicha d'ika lemitli talinan v'af al gav d'mitzuveh, v'chol heicha d'leika lemitli lo talinan af al gav d'eino mitzuveh*.

The determining factor is not whether one is commanded regarding the rest of the item in question, but whether it is *possible to assign an innocent motive*. Wherever we can credibly "hang" the transaction on a permitted purpose — as we can say a cow might be purchased for *shechita*, or a field might be held fallow this year and worked next — we do so, and the sale is permitted, even where a rest commandment exists. Conversely, where no such innocent motive can plausibly be assigned — as in the case of specific implements like the plow, yoke, or winnowing fork during *shemitah*, which have no plausible use other than the forbidden one — we cannot assign such a motive, and the sale is forbidden, even where no commandment specifically applies to those tools.

This is a striking principle. The operative question is not the formal structure of the commandment but the practical availability of a credible innocent reading of the transaction.

---

## Rabbah vs. Abaye

### Suspect Buyer

The Gemara now presents a case study that tests these principles in a different direction. *Rabbah zavin hahu chamra l'Yisrael hachashid limkor l'oved kochavim* — Rabbah sold a donkey to a Jew who was suspected of selling animals onward to idolaters.

### Abaye Objects

Abaye immediately challenged Rabbah: *mai ta'ama avad mar hachi?* — master, why did you do this? Rabbah defended himself: *ana l'Yisrael zavini* — I sold it to a Jew. The transaction on its face is entirely within the community; there is no prohibition on selling a donkey to a fellow Jew. Abaye pressed: *v'ha azil u'mzavin lei l'oved kochavim* — but he is going to go and sell it to a non-Jew. Rabbah pushed back: is that certain? *L'oved kochavim ka mzavin l'Yisrael lo ka mzavin?* — you're concerned he'll sell it to a non-Jew, but couldn't he just as readily sell it to a Jew? We don't know what he'll do. Must I refuse to transact with anyone who might conceivably pass something along to the wrong party?

The dynamic of this exchange is important to follow. Rabbah is taking a lenient position and Abaye is challenging him sufficiently that — as the Gemara will reveal — Rabbah ultimately changes his mind. Abaye then cites Rav Nachman's ruling to clinch the argument.

### Lifnei Iver

Running beneath this entire dispute is the principle of *lifnei iver lo titein michshol* — do not place a stumbling block before the blind. If I sell something to a person who will then use it to violate a prohibition, I have enabled that violation, and the Torah holds me responsible. The question the Gemara is pressing is: how many links in the chain does *lifnei iver* extend?

The clearest case is a direct transaction: I sell prohibited merchandise to someone who will use it for a forbidden purpose. But what of a transaction one step removed — I sell to a Jew who will sell to a non-Jew, thereby enabling the non-Jew's prohibited use? And does it matter whether the intermediate party is a Jew or a *kuti*? These gradations are not merely theoretical; they determine the practical contours of permissible commerce.

---

## Kutim vs. Goyim

### Small Animals to Kutim

Abaye advances his case against Rabbah by citing a *baraita*: *makom shenahagu limkor behemah dakah lekutim mocherim, shelo limkor ein mocherim* — in a place where it is the custom to sell small livestock to *kutim*, Samaritans, one may sell them; in a place where it is not the custom, one may not. The question is what drives this restriction on *behemah dakah* in the places where it applies, and the *baraita* will illuminate the differential treatment of *kutim* versus outright idolaters.

### Trust in Kutim

The Gemara explores the basis for distinguishing between *kutim* and *ovdei kochavim* more broadly. Is the restriction on *behemah dakah* in some places a concern about *reva'iyah*? The *baraita* presents extensive evidence that *kutim* are substantially trusted: *ma'amidin behemah b'fundekaot shel kutim, zakharim etzel nekevot u-nekevot etzel zakharim* — we may stable our animals at Samaritan inns even with males next to females and vice versa, the very arrangements we would not permit with idolaters. Furthermore, *mosrim behemah le-ro'eh shelahem* — we entrust our animals to their shepherds. And we have *yichud* with them, and we entrust our children to them to be taught *sefer* and a craft.

The basis for this trust is explicit: *kutim* accept the *Torah she-bikhtav*. They observe the written Torah, even though they do not accept the *Torah she-be'al peh*. Because of this, they are presumed to abide by the prohibitions the written Torah itself would restrain them from, including *reva'iyah*. *Alma lo chashidi* — they are simply not suspected of such misconduct.

### Fear of Resale

And yet, *behemah gasah* presents a distinct problem even with *kutim*. Given the Mishnah's blanket statement — *ein mochrin lahem behemah gasah*, with no qualification for custom, unlike the *behemah dakah* rule — there is an additional concern beyond *reva'iyah*: if we sell a large animal to a *kuti*, he might in turn sell it to a non-Jew. Even if the *kuti* himself is trusted not to misuse the animal, the chain does not end with him. And this is precisely the parallel to the case of Rabbah selling to the suspect Jew: in both cases, the concern is not the immediate buyer's conduct but what happens at the next link.

The implication Abaye is drawing is unmistakable: just as we do not sell *behemah gasah* to a *kuti* because he might sell it to an idolater, we similarly cannot sell it to a Jew who is suspected of doing the same.

### Weapons Forbidden

The *baraita* continues with a further restriction that applies to both *ovdei kochavim* and *kutim* alike, with no distinction between the two: *ein mochrin lahem lo zayin v'lo klei zayin v'ein mashchizin lahem et ha-zayin* — we may not sell them weapons or weapon accessories, and we may not sharpen weapons for them. Additionally, *ein mochrin lahem lo sadan v'lo kularin v'lo kevalim v'lo shalshelaot shel barzel* — we may not sell them a *sadan* (leg shackles for slaves), *kularin* (neck collars), *kevalim* (chains), or iron chains. And this applies equally to idolaters and *kutim*: *echad ovdei kokhavim ve-echad kutim*.

### Weapons Resale Fear

This creates an apparent tension. If we trust *kutim* so substantially — entrusting them with our animals, our children, permitting *yichud* — why are we treating them exactly like idolaters when it comes to weapons and restraints? *I nima dechashidi ashfichut damim, umi chashidi?* — if the reason is that we suspect them of bloodshed, are they really so suspected? We just said we have *yichud* with them. That level of trust is incompatible with suspecting them of violence.

The resolution: *ela mishum de'ati lezavona le'ovdei kochavim* — the concern is not that the *kutim* themselves will use these items to shed blood, but that they will sell them onward to idolaters who will. The restriction is not a character judgment about *kutim* but a practical concern about what happens downstream. This is identical in structure to the *behemah gasah* concern: we don't doubt the *kuti*'s own conduct; we worry about where the item ends up.

And this conclusion feeds directly back into Abaye's challenge to Rabbah: Rav Nachman has ruled explicitly — *kederech she'amru asur limkor le'ovved kochavim, kach asur limkor le'Yisrael hachashud limkor le'ovved kochavim* — just as it is forbidden to sell certain items directly to an idolater, it is equally forbidden to sell to a Jew who is suspected of reselling to an idolater. The chain of liability runs through the intermediary.

---

## Rabbah vs. Abaye (II)

### Rav Nachman Rules

Abaye finalizes his argument by invoking Rav Nachman's ruling explicitly: *kederech she'amru asur limkor le'ovved kochavim, kach asur limkor le'Yisrael hachashud limkor le'ovved kochavim*. This is not merely Abaye's personal opinion; it is the accepted position as stated by Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha. Just as we forbid selling to an idolater directly, we equally forbid selling to a Jew who is known to be suspected of funneling such sales to idolaters. The *lifnei iver* concern does not evaporate simply because the prohibited transaction is one step removed from the original seller.

Rabbah had attempted to deflect this: *v'chi teima, kuti lo avid teshuvah, Yisrael avid teshuvah* — perhaps one could argue that a *kuti* will not do *teshuvah* and change his ways, whereas the suspect Jew might repent and decide not to sell the donkey to an idolater after all. But Rav Nachman's ruling forecloses this: the established rule treats the suspected-Jew case identically to the idolater case, and the possibility of *teshuvah* does not lift the prohibition at the moment of sale.

### Rabbah's Retraction

Upon hearing this reasoning, Rabbah understood he had made a mistake. *Rahit batrei tlata parsei* — he ran three *parsa'ot* after the Jew to whom he had sold the donkey in order to retract the sale. Some versions of the tradition say he ran only one *parsa* — but through sand, an extraordinarily difficult effort. A *parsa* is approximately four kilometers, making three *parsa'ot* somewhere between twelve kilometers and, by some reckonings, between 7.2 and 8.7 miles. *V'lo adrachei* — but he was unable to catch him.

Nevertheless, the legal outcome is clear: Rabbah, upon reflection, agreed that the sale had been improper. The ruling stands that one may not sell to a Jew suspected of selling onward to those who would misuse the item.

---

## Necessity & Coexistence

### Bandits & Weapons

Rav Bibi bar Abba extends the principle further: just as we may not sell to a non-Jew, we may not sell to a *listim* — a Jewish bandit or outlaw. The Gemara immediately probes the contours of this rule. *Heichi dami* — under what circumstances does it apply? If the *listim* in question is suspected of murder, then the case is trivial — *peshita, hainu oved kochavim*, he is simply equivalent to an idolater for purposes of this prohibition, and of course we may not arm him. But what if this is a bandit who specializes in theft and not in killing? Why not sell to him?

The Gemara answers: *be'mashmuta de'zimnin de'avid le'atzolei nafsha* — we are dealing with a bandit who carries a weapon not because he plans to use it offensively but because he wants it for self-protection in case a situation escalates. The reason we nonetheless cannot sell to him is that the weapon is what enables his continued life of crime. The bandit's confidence in his ability to use the weapon if necessary is precisely what makes the weapon instrumentally dangerous, even if he does not plan to use it. The same *lifnei iver* logic applies: we may not supply what enables the forbidden enterprise.

### Shield Debate

The Gemara now introduces a dispute regarding a specific category of item: *trisim*, shields. *Ein mochrin lahem trisim, v'yesh omrim mochrin lahem trisim* — one opinion holds we may not sell shields to non-Jews; another permits it. Shields are protective by nature — they are defensive items, not weapons of attack. This makes the case more ambiguous than swords or spears.

The Gemara probes the reasoning of the prohibitive opinion. *Eileima mishum de'meginu aleihu* — if the reason is that shields protect them in battle, then by the same logic we should refuse to sell them *chiti u'se'ari*, wheat and barley, which sustain their armies equally. That conclusion is clearly untenable.

### Rav's Pragmatism

Rav addresses this directly: *i efshar, hachi nami* — if it were possible to refuse everything without consequence, one might indeed forbid even food staples. The underlying logic of restricting all commerce that might benefit an enemy is coherent in principle. But the practical reality is that total commercial isolation from the surrounding population would inflict massive harm — economic, social, and political — on the Jewish community. Rav's position reflects a frank pragmatism: comprehensive restriction of trade would cause greater harm than selective trade. The animosity generated by total isolation would be more dangerous than the marginal benefit gained from any particular restriction.

The principle, therefore, is not "restrict everything that could theoretically benefit an enemy," but rather a targeted prohibition on items whose primary use is violence or idolatry. Items that serve broad civilian purposes — food, protective gear used for escape rather than attack — fall outside the prohibition.

### Shields Permitted

The Gemara presents one rationale for permitting shields: *v'chi shalim zayin u'marka raki* — at the conclusion of battle, soldiers throw down their weapons and use their shields to flee. The shield is thus primarily associated with retreat and self-preservation rather than with offensive violence.

The final ruling: *amar Rav Nachman bar Abba bar Avuha halacha k'yesh omrim* — the *halacha* follows the permissive opinion. Shields may be sold to non-Jews. The assumption is that they will be used for protection and escape, not for aggression, and this suffices to assign the innocent motive that Rav Ashi's principle requires. Where we can credibly hang the transaction on a permitted purpose, we do so — and the *halacha* reflects that we should seek coexistence where it can be responsibly achieved, rather than defaulting to isolation.

The Gemara continues at the top of 16, and we will take it up there.

---

---

# Avodah Zarah 16

## Economic Reality

### Tosafot's Question

The opening of today's shiur revisits two critical issues that emerged from the previous daf's discussion of the prohibition on selling large animals — *behemah gassah* — to non-Jews. The primary concern underlying that prohibition is *Shabbat*: one must not place one's animal in a situation where it may perform *melacha* on *Shabbat*. Yet Tosafot confronts an uncomfortable reality: the practice of Jewish communities in his time did not conform to this prohibition. And unlike other areas where Tosafot resolves the discrepancy by arguing that medieval Christians are not to be classified as *ovdei Avodah Zarah*, that move is unavailable here. The prohibition on selling animals has nothing to do with *Avodah Zarah*; it concerns the *Shabbat* problem of one's animal performing labor. Tosafot must therefore find a different answer.

### Shabbat Concern

The Gemara itself had noted that selling through a middleman is permitted, because the animal would no longer recognize its owner's voice and would therefore not come when called on *Shabbat* — thus eliminating the concern that the owner would inadvertently cause his animal to labor. Tosafot, on 15a, extends this reasoning: animals today no longer recognize their owners' voices at all — a kind of *yeridat hadorot* even in the animal kingdom — and therefore the triggering concern simply does not arise. Additionally, Tosafot notes, we do not commonly lend or rent out our animals, which addresses yet another avenue of potential violation.

But Tosafot then presses himself: what of animals that *are* regularly rented to non-Jews? For those, how can we permit even the initial sale, given that the sale may lead to ongoing rental arrangements in which the animal labors on *Shabbat*?

### Takkanah Limits

Here Tosafot offers a remarkable socioeconomic argument. The prohibition, he writes — *davka bi-ymeihem* — was specifically applicable in their time and context. In the era of the *Tannaim*, particularly in the Land of Israel, there were large, dense Jewish communities. If a person had an animal he no longer needed, *she-hayu harbeh Yehudim beyachad*, he could readily sell it to a fellow Jew. He would not suffer a loss, *velo haya mafsid*. But now, Tosafot writes, *mah ya'aseh she-lo yimtzah limkor yafsid* — what is a person to do if there are only a handful of Jews in his town and no Jewish buyer exists? The rabbis never intended their *takkanah* to force people to absorb a total financial loss.

This is a striking piece of Tosafot. He is not pretending that people have technically complied. He is openly acknowledging that the practice departed from the law, and he is retroactively explaining why the rabbis' *takkanah* was never meant to apply in circumstances of genuine economic hardship. He traces this leniency back to the *Geonim* — or at minimum to the earlier authorities — as an established practice, *hilkheta badavar*. One can also sense the unstated subtext: many of these prohibitions were rooted in the realities of the Land of Israel, where Jews were engaged in agriculture and commerce within a large community, and where strengthening Jewish economic presence was a live concern. That entire societal infrastructure was simply absent in the medieval Diaspora, where Jews were often legally barred from owning land and forced into far narrower economic roles.

### Business Restriction

Tosafot then records the position of Rabbeinu Baruch, who draws a critical distinction. Even granting the economic argument, the leniency applies only when a person already owns an animal and finds himself unable to sell it to a fellow Jew — *koneh sus le-tzorech atzmo ve-nimlach alav le-mochro*. In such a case, where he would otherwise absorb a loss, *im lo yimchrenu yafsid*, Rabbeinu Baruch acknowledges the necessity. But one who purchases animals specifically to resell them for profit — *lokeach susim le-mochram kedei le-harvi'ach* — that is forbidden. The prohibition was never meant to be relied upon as the foundation of a business model.

### Davar Ha'avad

This distinction mirrors a well-known principle in *halakha*: *davar ha'avad* — preventing an existing loss — often permits actions that would otherwise be prohibited, but it does not license entering into a new commercial enterprise that depends on the leniency. There is a significant difference between telling someone they need not destroy their own investment and telling someone they may build a business on the premise that the prohibition does not apply to them. As a practical matter, of course, Tosafot is aware that people were in fact conducting regular commerce in animals with non-Jews. But his *Tosafot* is powerful precisely because it honestly acknowledges the economic realities that drove these practices rather than constructing a purely formal legal justification.

---

## Lifnei Iver

### Lifnei De-Lifnei

There is a second issue from the previous daf worth examining. The Gemara had discussed whether one may sell an animal to a *Kuti* — a Samaritan — given that the *Kuti* will in turn sell it to a non-Jew. Tosafot raises a sharp question: we established earlier, on daf 14a, that *lifnei de-lifnei* — two degrees of removal from the transgression — is permitted. Here, even if the Jew sells to the *Kuti* and the *Kuti* then violates the rabbinic prohibition by selling to the non-Jew, the Jew is only one step removed from that rabbinic violation. Why should this be worse than the *lifnei de-lifnei* case discussed earlier? Tosafot formulates the question on the bottom of 15b: *u'mai shna mi-lifnei de-lifnei de-le'eil* — what distinguishes this from the earlier case where two degrees of removal was explicitly permitted?

### Non-Jews Exempt

Tosafot's answer turns on a fundamental asymmetry between the obligations of Jews and non-Jews. In the earlier case, the item — incense intended for use in *Avodah Zarah* — was sold first to a non-Jew. That non-Jew is not commanded in *lifnei iver*. Therefore, when non-Jew number one eventually passes the item to non-Jew number two, the first non-Jew has not violated any prohibition at all. And since my direct transaction was only with non-Jew number one — *she-eino muzhar al lifnei iver* — I have not caused anyone to sin. My connection to the ultimate transgression is simply too attenuated: the person in the middle committed no violation, and I therefore bear no responsibility for what comes next.

### Differential Duty

But when I sell to a Jew who I know will then sell the animal to a non-Jew, a fundamentally different principle applies. Tosafot states it plainly: *anu metzuvim she-lo yavo shum Yisrael lidei takala al yadeinu* — we are obligated to ensure that no Jew comes to sin through our actions. Our responsibility toward a fellow Jew is not merely the negative duty of refraining from directly tripping him; it is an active concern for his *shmirat mitzvot*. This heightened responsibility operates independently of whether the technical definition of *lifnei iver* applies.

### Cheeseburger Case

The principle can be illustrated with a concrete case. The Gemara says that *lifnei iver* only applies in a situation of *trei avri de-nahara* — where the person cannot obtain the forbidden item without your help. If the cheeseburger is sitting right next to Michael and he could pick it up himself, there is no technical *lifnei iver* when you hand it to him. And yet the *Rishonim* are nearly unanimous that you may not do so. They frame the prohibition differently — *lifnei iver de-Rabbanan*, *machshil*, and other formulations — but the operative principle is clear: even absent the technical biblical prohibition, I may not facilitate a fellow Jew's *aveira*. Now consider the parallel case: Christopher asks you to hand him an *ever min ha-chai* that is right next to him. In that case, since it is not *trei avri de-nahara*, and since a non-Jew is not commanded in *lifnei iver*, it may actually be *muttar* to hand it to him.

### Responsibility Scope

The contrast is deliberate and philosophically significant. Toward non-Jews, our responsibility is limited to not actively enabling their transgression. As long as I am not the direct cause — as long as it is not *trei avri de-nahara* — I bear no obligation. Toward Jews, the scope of responsibility is broader: I am actively concerned with their *shmirat mitzvot*, not merely prohibited from directly tripping them. This is why *lifnei de-lifnei* works by non-Jews but not by Jews. By Jews, even if I am technically two degrees removed, the fact that a Jew in the middle will violate a rabbinic prohibition is something that concerns me directly — I am *machshil* that Jew in his transgression of the rabbinic prohibition, and my general responsibility to Jewish observance demands I avoid this. The formal answer Tosafot adds is that since I am selling directly to a Jew who will then violate a rabbinic prohibition, I am in effect *chad lifnei* — one degree of removal, not two — from that Jew's sin, since his transgression is the proximate consequence of my sale.

---

## Iron Ingots

### Ashisheiot

Turning to daf 16 proper, the Gemara opens with a ruling of Rav Adda bar Ahava: *ein mochrin lahen ashisheiot shel barzel* — one may not sell iron ingots to non-Jews. The reason, *mishum de-chalshina minnaihu klei zayin*, is the concern that they will melt the iron down and forge it into weapons. Raw ingots of iron have no particular function other than being processed into something else, and the presumption is that weapons are the intended product.

### Spades Question

The Gemara immediately challenges this: if the concern is that they will smelt it into weapons, then surely one should also be prohibited from selling spades and pickaxes, which are also made of iron and could theoretically be melted down and reforged into weaponry. The implicit principle underlying the challenge is that we do not assume someone will destroy a finished, useful implement — a *kli* — simply in order to fashion a weapon. One does not ruin a perfectly good spade. Iron ingots, by contrast, are purpose-built raw material.

### Persian Exception

The Gemara then introduces a further refinement. Rav Zvid clarifies that the prohibition applies specifically to Indian iron — *parzela Hindua* — which is of particularly high quality and especially well-suited for weapon-forging. And then Rav Ashi adds a crucial contextual observation: *le-Parsai de-magenu alan* — in the current situation, we sell this iron only to Persians, because the Persians protect us. The Babylonian Amoraim, operating under Persian rule rather than Roman, found themselves in a different geopolitical reality. The Persians were, by the standards of the time, a relatively welcoming host nation that took an active interest in the welfare of their Jewish population. If the Persians used this iron to forge weapons and fight wars, that was in a sense advantageous — they were fighting on the side that protected Jewish communities. The same material that in Roman hands would represent a threat here served a protective function.

---

## Young Animals

### Agnlim Vesichim

The Gemara now addresses a series of cases that extend the prohibition on selling animals to non-Jews. Young calves — *agalim* — and foals — *siachim* — may not be sold to non-Jews. The Mishnah states this categorically, regardless of whether the young animal is healthy or has a broken limb.

### Shvura

However, a *Braita* records that Rabbi Yehuda goes further and draws a distinction: he permits the sale of an animal with a broken limb — *shvura*. His reasoning is that an animal so injured cannot heal, *eina yechola le-hitrapos le-achiyos*, and will inevitably die. There is therefore no concern that it will be used as a beast of burden; the non-Jew will presumably slaughter it or it will perish. Since the entire prohibition rests on the concern that the animal will perform *melacha* on *Shabbat*, and that concern is eliminated when the animal will never be fit for work, Rabbi Yehuda permits the sale.

### Reproduction Risk

The Rabbis counter with a different concern: *v'lo marbeena lah l'yoledess*? Even a female animal with a broken limb can still conceive and give birth. The non-Jew will not slaughter it immediately; he will keep it alive, mate it with a male, and thereby expand his livestock through her offspring. Rabbi Yehuda's response is *amar lahem lich'she-tailyad* — he will deal with that concern when and if she actually gives birth. His position, as the Gemara explains, is that an animal with a broken limb is in fact not receptive to mating — *lo mikabel ha-zachar* — and therefore the reproduction concern is not a live one in practice.

### Marit Ayin

Rashi frames the Rabbis' concern differently, invoking *marit ayin*: since the female animal will not be slaughtered immediately but will remain in the non-Jew's possession for some period while it might potentially become pregnant, observers will see the animal and assume that the Jew sold it without any broken limb, leading others to conclude that selling animals to non-Jews is generally permitted. This explanation is, on its face, somewhat far-fetched. The prohibition against selling large animals to non-Jews is itself only a rabbinic enactment, and it is itself a safeguard against other concerns — we do not typically worry about *marit ayin* to protect rabbinic safeguards at this degree of remove. The layering — a *marit ayin* concern to protect a rabbinic prohibition that itself exists to prevent another violation — seems extreme, and the Gemara does not appear to treat it as the primary explanation.

---

## Horses

### Ben Beteira

The Mishnah records a special ruling of Ben Beteira: he permits the sale of a horse to a non-Jew. A *Braita* explains his reasoning explicitly — *mipnei she-hu oseh bo melacha she-ein chayavin aleha chatas*. A horse is used for riding. Even if the non-Jew rides the horse on *Shabbat*, this does not constitute a biblically prohibited act of *melacha* on the owner's part, because a horse carries its rider and the principle of *chai nosei et atzmo* — a living being supports its own weight — means that the animal is not technically carrying a load in the halakhically prohibited sense. Therefore a horse cannot cause its owner to violate a biblical prohibition on *Shabbat*, and Ben Beteira reasons that the rabbinic concern about large animals does not extend to this case. This *Braita* is notable because it makes the *Shabbat* rationale for the prohibition explicit in the name of Ben Beteira.

### Rabbi's Reasons

Rabbi, however, disagrees and prohibits the sale of a horse for two independent reasons. The first is *mishum toras klei zayin* — because horses are used in warfare and thus fall within the category of weapons. The second is *mishum toras behemah gassa* — because a horse is a large animal and the rabbis prohibited selling large animals to non-Jews as a categorical matter.

### Horse Weapon

The Gemara accepts the first reason without much difficulty: certain horses are trained to trample enemies in battle and thus can literally function as instruments of violence — *dekativi be-sichufeih*. What is worth noting here is that the concern seems to be limited to the item itself being a weapon, not merely to its use in a military context. A horse that itself tramples people is a weapon; something that merely supports the war effort more indirectly might not be included in the prohibition.

The second reason — *mishum toras behemah gassa* — is more difficult. If Ben Beteira is correct that horses present no *Shabbat* problem, what does it mean to say that a horse is prohibited because it is a large animal? The category of large animals was itself created because of *Shabbat* concerns.

### Millstone Work

Rabbi Yochanan resolves the difficulty: *lich'she-yazkin matachino be-reichayim be-Shabbat* — when the horse grows old and is no longer suitable for riding, its owner will yoke it to turn a millstone, at which point it will be performing genuine *melacha* on *Shabbat*. So while the young horse presents no problem, an aged horse does, and therefore the category of horses is not entirely free of *Shabbat* concerns. One might object that at the time of sale the horse is young and fit for riding — the millstone scenario is a distant possibility. But the answer seems to be that we do not subdivide within a category based on the age or current condition of the animal.

### Lo Plug

This points to the principle of *lo plug*: the rabbis, when they issue a categorical prohibition, do not typically invite analysis of each individual case within the category. The Mishnah itself reflects this approach — it prohibits large animals categorically, without asking whether this particular animal is old or young, whole or broken-limbed. *Lo plug* means that once a category is defined as prohibited, we do not make internal distinctions within it. The tension with Rabbi Yehuda's broken-limb exception and with Ben Beteira's horse ruling is precisely that both *Tannaim* are willing to make distinctions within the broader category — Ben Beteira because horses are fundamentally a different subcategory vis-à-vis *melacha*, and Rabbi Yehuda because a broken-limbed animal is, practically speaking, entirely outside the category of work-capable animals.

### Ruling

The Gemara ultimately rules: *halacha ke-Ven Beteira* — we follow Ben Beteira. This ruling is significant in its practical implications. Rather than taking a blanket *lo plug* approach that prohibits the entire category of large animals without qualification, the ruling of Ben Beteira directs us to actually examine the particular case and ask whether this specific animal presents a genuine concern. This affords considerably more latitude and is consistent with the earlier Gemara's permission to sell a cow when circumstances indicate it will be slaughtered.

---

## Shor Patam

### Patam Dispute

The Gemara now raises a question about a *shor shel patam* — a fattened ox. Such an animal is raised specifically for slaughter; its entire purpose is to produce meat. Given that the prohibition on selling large animals is rooted in the concern that they will be used for *melacha* on *Shabbat*, and a fattened ox seems categorically destined for the slaughterhouse rather than the field, one might think the prohibition does not apply. The Gemara poses the question as a double-sided inquiry: does Rabbi Yehuda's logic permit the sale of a fattened ox, or does he still prohibit it? And does the reasoning of the Rabbis who rejected Rabbi Yehuda's broken-limb allowance perhaps lead them to permit the fattened ox?

### Baraita Proof

The question might be framed as follows. Rabbi Yehuda permitted the sale of a broken-limbed animal on the grounds that it is permanently unfit for work — *delo chazya limlacha*. A fattened ox, one might argue, is different: leave it long enough, let it lose its excess weight, and it will eventually be fit for agricultural labor. Thus perhaps even Rabbi Yehuda would concede that a fattened ox remains within the prohibition. On the other hand, the Rabbis who rejected Rabbi Yehuda's broken-limb ruling did so on the grounds that the animal with a broken limb will be kept alive for reproduction — *stama lav lishchita kai*. A fattened ox, by contrast, is paradigmatically destined for slaughter — *stama lishchita kai* — and the Rabbis might therefore agree that it is permitted.

### Rabbi's Tribute

At this point the Gemara introduces a remarkable historical datum. Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel: the household of Rabbi — the *Nasi*, Rabban Yehuda Ha-Nasi — used to send a fattened calf to the Roman authorities on the occasion of their holiday. The Gemara uses the language *hayu makrivin*, which carries connotations of tribute and offering. Rashi is careful to interpret this as a political tribute — *mas ve-doron le-melech* — and explicitly resists the implication that the animal was used as a sacrifice; it would have been extraordinary and shocking if Rabbi had sent an animal that would be offered on the altar of a pagan deity, perhaps even in a temple dedicated to Zeus. The term *makrivin*, then, reflects the status of the act as a tribute from a subject people to their imperial overlords, framed in the language of offering, not literal sacrifice.

### Negotiation 1

What follows is equally significant. Rabbi spent forty thousand coins — an exaggerated figure conveying enormous expense — to arrange that the tribute should be delivered the day *after* the Roman holiday rather than on the holiday itself, so that he would not violate the rabbinic prohibition on conducting commerce with non-Jews on their festival day. The scale of the expenditure reflects both the seriousness with which Rabbi took the rabbinic prohibition and the degree of political pressure under which the Jewish leadership operated.

### Negotiation 2

A second payment of forty thousand coins secured an additional concession: that the animal could be delivered already slaughtered rather than alive. This addressed the concern about handing over a live large animal to non-Jews — whether framed as a prohibition on selling or giving such animals, and perhaps also with an eye toward ensuring the animal would not be used as a live sacrifice.

### Inference

The Gemara now draws an inference from this narrative. If a *shor shel patam* were straightforwardly permitted — because it is presumptively destined for slaughter and thus presents no *Shabbat* concern — why would Rabbi go to such lengths and expense to maneuver around the prohibition? The fact that he paid so much to have the animal delivered slaughtered suggests that he regarded the live delivery of a fattened ox as problematic, which in turn implies that the prohibition applies to fattened oxen. This would mean the *shor shel patam* is indeed forbidden to give or sell to non-Jews.

### Elimination Goal

Rav Ashi resolves the difficulty with a different reading of Rabbi's conduct. Rabbi's goal, Rav Ashi explains, was ultimately to eliminate the tribute obligation altogether — *Rabbi me'akar milta ba'ei*. He pursued this in stages — *ye'akar ve-ati pursa pursa* — first getting the delivery moved off the holiday, then having it delivered slaughtered, and finally paying to be rid of the obligation entirely. The expenditure at each stage was not necessarily driven by a specific halakhic concern at that precise juncture; it was a long-term political negotiation aimed at complete extrication. Therefore one cannot draw a precise inference from any single step in that process about the technical status of the *shor shel patam*. The Gemara also notes in passing that this narrative implies gifts, not merely sales or rentals, may also be included within the prohibition — an important extension of the principle. Rav Ashi's further observation, vouched for by Zvida bar Tora — a man whose trade was in fattened animals — is that a *shor shel patam*, if left to lose its excess weight, actually ends up doing the work of two animals. This confirms that the concern about eventual *melacha* is not merely theoretical.

---

## Bears Lions

### Dangerous Animals

The Mishnah moves to a distinct category of prohibition: *ein mochrin lahem dubim va-arayot* — one may not sell to non-Jews bears, lions, or anything that poses a hazard to the public — *kol davar she-yesh bo nezek larabbim*. This category differs from the preceding discussion. The concern here is not *Shabbat* labor but public safety: these are dangerous creatures that, if not managed with appropriate care, will cause harm.

### Responsibility

The Gemara's underlying assumption is worth pausing over. The implication of the *Mishnah*'s formulation — *ta'ama de-ika nezek*, the reason is because of the hazard — is that the issue is specifically the non-Jew's handling of the animal. The assumption seems to be that Jews are more conscientious about preventing public harm, while non-Jews cannot be trusted to maintain adequate control over dangerous animals. Whether this reflects a general presumption about relative responsibility, or whether it simply reflects the specific context of the Roman arena — where lions and bears were routinely deployed in gladiatorial spectacles and therefore their acquisition by Roman parties was inherently dangerous — the practical result is the same. One might also note that the *Mishnah* in Bava Kamma treats lions and bears as fundamentally incompatible with private ownership; these are animals one is required to destroy, not keep. That background makes the question of who is selling them in the first place somewhat curious.

### Stadiums

The Mishnah then lists another set of prohibitions concerning construction. One may not build with non-Jews a *basilikei*, a *gardom*, an *istadya*, or a *bima*. The stadium — *istadya* — is forbidden because it is the venue for gladiatorial combat, where captives, including Jewish captives, were forced to fight and die. Building such a structure makes one complicit in the bloodshed that occurs within it. The *gardom* and *bima* are associated with the Roman judicial and penal system. Rashi understands one as the platform or steps leading up to where the judges sit, and the other as the scaffold or structure used for public executions. The Gemara's explanation draws on the grim reality that Jewish communities frequently suffered at the hands of Roman courts and Roman executioners; any contribution to the infrastructure of Roman justice and Roman punishment is therefore prohibited.

As for the *basilikei* — the large basilica-style building — Rashi suggests this too functioned as a type of courthouse, which would bring it within the same rationale.

### Hatzalat

Despite the prohibition on *building* a stadium, the *Braita* records that one is permitted to attend the stadium for the purpose of *hatzalat nefashos* — saving lives. The mechanism is well known: at a certain point in the gladiatorial contest, the crowd votes whether to spare the defeated combatant's life. A sufficient show of support for mercy could save him. Jewish spectators attending for this purpose — to add their voices to those calling for the combatant's life to be spared — are permitted to do so, notwithstanding all the other concerns that such attendance would ordinarily raise.

### Execution Structures

The *gardom* and *bima*, as noted, relate to Roman structures of capital justice. The lectured makes clear that the context is the Roman persecution of Jews: enough Jews were tried, sentenced, and executed under Roman authority that participation in constructing the spaces where those proceedings and executions took place was intolerable. Whether the specific structure is the judicial bench, the platform, or the scaffold, the prohibition covers the full apparatus of Roman judicial violence against Jewish communities.

### Bathhouses

However, the Mishnah draws a clear line: one *may* build with non-Jews a *bimosiot* and a *beit merchatzaot* — a bathhouse. A bathhouse is, fundamentally, a neutral structure. The difficulty arises at the point where one reaches the specific niche or alcove — *kipa* — in the wall where the idol is installed. From that point onward, construction is forbidden. Until that point, one is simply building a bathhouse.

### Tashmish

Rashi's understanding of *bimosiot* — which he takes to refer to a single-stone altar upon which sacrifices are offered — creates a serious difficulty. He argues that this is *tashmish de-Avodah Zarah* — an implement used in idolatrous service — and that since it is two degrees removed from the actual act of idol worship, it is permitted. Tosafot finds this position untenable. An altar upon which idolatrous sacrifices are actively offered is directly and immediately involved in *Avodah Zarah*; this is not a remote or attenuated connection by any reasonable measure. Even if one were to grant Rashi's technical framing of *tashmish*, the notion that a Jew should be permitted to build an altar for pagan sacrifice because of some formal degree-of-removal calculation is, as Tosafot puts it, simply unacceptable — we would not allow it on any technical ground. Tosafot therefore rejects Rashi's *girsa* and reads *dimosiot* instead of *bimosiot*, understanding it as a type of bathhouse or similar structure, bringing it comfortably within the permitted category of neutral construction.

---

## Chaya Gassa

### Pirchus

The Gemara now introduces a statement of Rav Chana bar Rav Chisda — and some attribute it to Rav Chanan bar Rava — in the name of Rav, concerning *chaya gassa*, large non-domesticated animals such as deer. The *halakha* of *pirchus* — the tremors required after *shechita* to confirm the animal had viable life-force at the time of slaughter — operates differently for large and small domesticated animals. For a large *behemah*, such as a cow, it is sufficient for the animal to extend a limb; for a small *behemah*, such as a sheep, the animal must extend and then retract the limb. The question is: into which category does a *chaya gassa* fall? Rav Chana bar Rav Chisda rules that a *chaya gassa* is like a small *behemah* with respect to *pirchus* — it must extend and retract, not merely extend.

### Not Forbidden

Having established that ruling regarding *pirchus*, Rav Chana bar Rav Chisda then makes a second, independent claim: when it comes to the laws of selling to non-Jews, a *chaya gassa* is in the category of a small animal — *behemah daka* — not a large one. This matters because the prohibition on selling to non-Jews applies categorically to large domesticated animals but varies by local custom for small ones. Rav Chana's reasoning is implicit but not difficult to supply: what *melacha* does one do with a deer or similar large wild animal? Unlike an ox or donkey, a *chaya gassa* is not yoked to a plow or a millstone. Without a realistic concern about *Shabbat* labor, the prohibition should not apply.

### Baraita

The Gemara challenges this immediately. A *Braita* — the Tosefta — states explicitly: *keshem she-ein mochrim behemah gassa kach ein mochrim chaya gassa* — just as one does not sell a large domesticated animal, so too one does not sell a large non-domesticated animal. And moreover: *afilu be-makom she-mochrim behemah daka, chaya gassa ein mochrim* — even in a locale where the custom permits selling small animals, a *chaya gassa* may not be sold. The *Braita* is unambiguous. This constitutes a *tiyuvta* — a decisive refutation — of Rav Chana bar Rav Chisda's position.

### Broken Leg

Ravina attempts to resolve the apparent contradiction between the *Mishnah*'s implication and the *Braita*. The *Mishnah*'s prohibition on selling bears and lions includes the qualifier that the prohibition applies because of *nezek larabbim* — public danger. The implication is that absent the public danger concern, a lion or bear could be sold, which suggests *chaya gassa* is not categorically prohibited. But the *Braita* says it is prohibited. Ravina resolves this: the *Mishnah*'s implication that a non-dangerous *chaya gassa* would be permitted refers specifically to a lion with a broken leg — *ari shavur* — following Rabbi Yehuda's logic that an animal permanently unfit for work is excluded from the prohibition. It is only that narrow case that the *Mishnah*'s language implies is permitted; a healthy *chaya gassa* remains forbidden according to the *Braita*.

### Rav Ashi

Rav Ashi offers a different resolution with broader implications. A lion, he says, is *stam ari shavur hu etzel melacha* — as a matter of course, a lion is like an animal with a broken leg when it comes to work. Nobody uses a lion for agricultural labor. The reason the *Mishnah* implies that a non-dangerous lion or bear could be sold is not specifically because of a broken limb, but because lions are intrinsically unsuited for *melacha*. The implication for the broader category is significant: the prohibition on *chaya gassa* is not a blanket rule that excludes the entire category regardless of function. Rather, if a specific *chaya gassa* is genuinely incapable of being employed in *melacha*, it would fall outside the prohibition. But if a particular large wild animal *can* be used for work, it remains forbidden. The category is not uniformly excluded; it must be assessed functionally.

### Nachman

Rav Nachman interjects with a different sort of challenge: *man de-amar lan de-ari chaya gassa hu* — who says a lion is even classified as a *chaya gassa*? Perhaps a lion is in fact a *chaya daka* — a small wild animal — in which case the entire preceding analysis has been applied to the wrong category. This question is cryptic, and the Gemara does not develop it extensively; it may refer to certain smaller members of the cat family that might be considered *ari*.

### What Work

Having established through multiple analyses that the prohibition on *chaya gassa* remains in force wherever the animal *could* perform *melacha*, the Gemara finally asks the practical question that makes all of this concrete: *mai melacha avdi* — what kind of work would a large wild animal actually do? The answer is what gives the entire preceding discussion its practical bite. If no such animal is ever used for work, the entire functional analysis is academic.

---

## Arode

### Millstone Use

Abaye provides the answer, citing a teaching he received from Mar Yehuda in the house of Mar Yochnai: *tochni rei-chaim be-arodei* — the *arode* is used to turn a millstone. The *arode* is a wild donkey — a large, powerful animal that, though non-domesticated, is captured and harnessed to grind grain. This proves the point: there exist *chayot gassot* that are in fact employed for *melacha*, and those animals would be prohibited from sale to non-Jews.

### Source

With the substantive question resolved, the Gemara turns to an extended *sugya* tracing the transmission history of the *pirchus* ruling — the teaching that a *chaya gassa* requires the same post-*shechita* tremors as a small *behemah*. Rav Zeira narrates a chain of events. When he was studying in the academy of Rav Yehuda, Rav Yehuda stood before his students and addressed them with unusual emphasis: *smiru minai ha milta de-migavra raba shmia li* — commit this teaching to memory, for I heard it from a great authority. The teaching was *chaya gassa harei hi ke-behemah daka le-pirchus*. But Rav Yehuda could not recall whether he had received it from Rav or from Shmuel.

### Rav or Shmuel

The uncertainty itself was notable: Rav Yehuda was a direct disciple of both Rav and Shmuel, and the fact that he could not attribute the teaching to one or the other caused him enough discomfort that he flagged it explicitly while transmitting it to his own students. This kind of epistemic honesty — acknowledging uncertainty about the chain of tradition even while insisting on the importance of the ruling itself — is characteristic of the care taken in the transmission of oral Torah.

### Authorities

Rav Zeira then recounts his travels. When he arrived at a certain location — Kurkonya — he found Rav Chiya bar Ashi sitting and teaching the same ruling in the name of Shmuel. Rav Zeira concluded from this that the teaching originated with Shmuel, and he could now report back to Rav Yehuda's academy that the authority was Shmuel. But when Rav Zeira subsequently arrived in Sura, he found Rabba bar Yirmeya transmitting the same teaching in the name of Rav — not Shmuel.

### Both Authorities

Now Rav Zeira was presented with what appeared to be a discrepancy: one authority traced the teaching to Shmuel, another traced it to Rav. When he reported this to Rav Assi, he asked: should not the proper attribution credit Rabba bar Yirmeya as the transmitter, since he had heard it from him in the name of Rav? Rav Assi responded with what became a well-known phrase: *minai u-minach tistayem shmata* — from me and from you together we will resolve this teaching. The resolution was that the teaching was transmitted through *both* channels: Rabba bar Yirmeya reported it in the name of Rav Chama bar Guria in the name of Rav, and this formed one chain. The other chain went through different transmitters to Shmuel. Both are valid attributions because the teaching genuinely came from both Rav and Shmuel.

### Conclusion

The final formulation records the full chain of transmission: Rav Zeira, in the name of Rav Assi, in the name of Rabba bar Yirmeya, in the name of Rav Chama bar Guria, in the name of Rav — *chaya gassa harei hi ke-behemah daka le-pirchus*. A large wild animal requires the same post-*shechita* tremors as a small domesticated animal. This is the established ruling, and the careful reconstruction of its transmission history — tracing it through multiple independent chains back to Rav, and through a parallel chain to Shmuel — serves to confirm its authority and reliability. The practical upshot: if one slaughters a deer or similar *chaya gassa*, it must extend and retract its limb after *shechita* for the slaughter to be deemed *kosher*, just as a sheep must.

---

---

# Avodah Zarah 17

## Prohibited Buildings

### Three Basilica Types

The *mishnah* that preceded our discussion addressed a range of prohibited transactions with the Roman government, including the sale of wild animals, which the *gemara* treated as analogous in spirit to the sale of weapons — not because non-Jews would consciously deploy the animals as instruments of violence, but because we are not permitted to keep dangerous wild animals ourselves and therefore should not be facilitating their ownership by others. The *mishnah* then turns to a related prohibition: one may not assist in building a *basilica*, understood as a platform or courthouse in which Roman judges sit; a *gardom*, a scaffold on which executions — including crucifixions of Jews — were carried out; or an *istadya*, a stadium for gladiatorial games. Helping construct these structures is seen as aiding and abetting the apparatus of Roman violence against the Jewish people.

On this point, Rabbah bar Bar Chana cites Rabbi Yochanan: there are three types of *basilica*. The first is a *basilica shel malchei ovdei kochavim* — a palace or castle of idolatrous kings. The second is one situated in the context of a *merchatza*, a bathhouse. The third is associated with a storage complex. Rava then rules: two of these are permitted to build and one is forbidden. The one that is forbidden is the *basilica* in which judgment takes place — the courthouse — which he connects to the phrase about binding kings in chains, using the double meaning of *leesore* (to bind / to forbid) as a *siman*. The other two involve no judicial function and are therefore permitted.

### Basilica Classification

The *gemara* raises a challenge: the *mishnah* itself lists *basilki* alongside *gardom*, *istadya*, and *bima* as structures one may not help build. Is a *basilica* really a standalone prohibited category, or is it always understood as the *basilica* of a *gardom*, of an *istadya*, of a *bima*? The *gemara* resolves this by reading the *mishnah* as referring to a *basilica shel gardom* and a *basilica shel istadya* — a basilica of a scaffold, a basilica of a stadium — rather than treating *basilki* as an independent category prohibited in its own right. The prohibition attaches to the judicial or entertainment function embedded within the structure.

### Tosafot Altar Critique

Before turning to the narrative *aggadta* that follows, it is worth pausing on a *Tosafot* — the discussion of *bimosot* — that touches directly on the building prohibitions and reflects a striking exercise in religious common sense overriding technical classification.

*Rashi* explains *bimosot* as altars on which offerings were brought to *avodah zarah*, and holds that building such an altar is permissible because it is two degrees removed from idolatry itself: you do not place the idol on the altar, but the sacrifice, and the sacrifice in turn serves the idol. *Tosafot* is openly astounded by this. He notes first — at almost exactly the midpoint of *Tosafot bimosot* — the phrase *alma mamash tashmish avodat kochavim atzmo hu*: this is straightforwardly a direct accessory to *avodah zarah*. What greater *tashmish* of idolatrous worship could there be than an altar?

*Tosafot* then adds a second argument, one that appeals to basic religious sensibility rather than formal classification: *dinehi nami demishamesh demishamesh avodah zarah* — granted that technically, in some formalistic sense, one could call this two degrees removed (it serves the sacrifice, and the sacrifice serves the idol). But even conceding that technical point, *atu livnot imahem*? How could any *frum* Jew conceivably think it permissible to build an altar upon which incense would be offered to *avodah zarah*? Religious sensibility sometimes demands that we set aside a technical *halachic* argument. *Tosafot* therefore concludes that *Rashi*'s reading of the word should be corrected: the word is not *bimosot* (altars) but *dimosiyot* — a type of bathhouse. This aligns with the adjacent mention of *beit merchatza* (bathhouse), since the *mishnah* permits building a bathhouse even though bathhouses sometimes contained niches or apses housing idols. The operative point is that one avoids building the niche itself but may assist with the fundamentally utilitarian bathhouse structure. We are dealing with bathhouses, not with altars to *avodah zarah*.

---

## Rabbi Eliezer Trial

### Christian Context

*Keshenitpas Rabbi Eliezer leminut* — when Rabbi Eliezer was seized by the Roman government on suspicion of heresy. This requires some historical context. *Minut*, as familiar from earlier discussions in this *masechet*, very often refers specifically to Jewish Christianity. The Romans persecuted not only Jews but early Christians as well, and with considerable ferocity. Christianity posed a particular political threat: it proclaimed a king, which was interpreted as a challenge to Roman sovereignty. The famous formulation "give unto Caesar what is Caesar's" arose precisely because Christians had to navigate whether rendering tribute to Caesar — who fashioned himself a god — constituted a form of *avodah zarah*. As a result, early Christians were frequently martyred by the Roman state, and identifying a fellow Christian in dangerous times required secret signals — the fish symbol, *ICTHYS*, being the known example.

The Roman government therefore suspected Rabbi Eliezer, who had previously been known as an observant Jew (a population with which Rome had its complicated but ultimately stable relationship), of having become a Jewish Christian — the dangerous heretical sect that was at that moment being actively suppressed. The reason this episode is introduced here is transparent: we have just been discussing why one may not help build *batei mishpat*, the courthouses of Rome, given how they serve as instruments by which Jews are falsely judged and executed on trumped-up charges. The story of Rabbi Eliezer's arrest exemplifies exactly that.

### Trial & Trust

*He'aluhu l'gardom lidon* — they brought him up to the *gardom* to be judged. And here we encounter that word again: *gardom* is the very platform mentioned in the *mishnah*, the place of judgment and execution. The presiding *hegmon* — the Roman officer and chief judge — said to him: *zaken shekmotecha ya'asok bidvarim betelim halalu*? You are a great sage, a respected elder — why have you involved yourself with this heretical sect?

Rabbi Eliezer replied: *ne'eman alai hadayan* — the judge is trusted by me. He meant, of course, that he trusted the Divine Judge to vindicate him. But the *hegmon* understood it as a compliment to himself: *kasavar oto hegmon alav hu omer* — the officer thought Rabbi Eliezer was saying "I trust you, this judge, to see my innocence." *V'hu lo amar ela keneged aviv shebashamayim* — but he was referring only to his Father in Heaven. The *hegmon*, satisfied that the accused was placing his trust in the Roman court's judgment and not attempting to mount a defense, declared: *ho'il v'hemanti alecha* — since you have trusted me — *dimus patur ata* — you are exempt, free.

### Dimus Meaning

What is the meaning of *dimus*? *Rashi* explains that *dimus* was the name of the officer's god, suggesting the dismissal was framed as a religious declaration. The Soncino commentary, and more accessibly Steinsaltz, suggests it simply means freedom or exemption. *Tosafot* provides the clearest explanation: *perash berachamei* — it is the word of mercy; *ki dimus lashon rachamim hi* — *dimus* is an expression of compassion or clemency. You are pardoned. Interestingly, *dimus* and *gardom* have both survived into modern Hebrew: *gardom* persists in the name of the Acre prison where the British hanged members of the Irgun, and *bedimus* describes a retired judge — a *shofet bedimus*, a judge emeritus, one who has been relieved of his post.

When Rabbi Eliezer returned home, his students gathered to comfort him — not that he had survived, for that was clearly cause for relief, but because the very fact that he had been seized under false suspicion deeply troubled him. *V'lo kibel alav tanchumim* — he refused to accept their consolation. Something he had done, he believed, had brought this upon him, whether as Divine punishment or as behavior that had given the Romans legitimate grounds for suspicion.

---

## Rabbi Akiva Teaching

### Permission Request

Rabbi Akiva approached him and said: *rebbi, harshini lomar davar echad mimah shelimadtani* — Rebbe, permit me to say something from what you yourself taught me. This is a moment worth pausing on from a pastoral perspective. The act of asking permission before sharing difficult insight sets an entirely different tone than lecturing someone in distress. It signals sensitivity and signals that what follows is offered in service of the other person rather than imposed upon them. Rabbi Eliezer granted permission.

### Marketplace Encounter

Rabbi Akiva asked: perhaps some heretical teaching came into your hand and you derived pleasure from it — *shema minut ba leyadcha vehana'ah* — and on account of that you were seized? The phrase carries a double meaning: perhaps this intellectual engagement with a heretic both gave the Romans reason to suspect you of following the sect, and perhaps it is why God brought this upon you — since engaging such teachings, even with pleasure at their cleverness, is precisely what one is meant to avoid.

Rabbi Eliezer said: *Akiva hizkartani* — Akiva, you have reminded me. He recalled: once he was walking in the upper marketplace of *Tzippori* and he encountered a man — here the text as transmitted gives the sanitized form, naming only *Yaakov ish Kfar Sekanya*, but the original manuscripts and *rishonim* restore the full reading: *umatzati echad mitalmidav shel Yeshu HaNotzri* — he encountered one of the disciples of Jesus of Nazareth, and his name was *Yaakov ish Kfar Sekanya*. We are speaking, then, explicitly of early Jewish Christians.

### Non-Response Strategy

*Yaakov ish Kfar Sekanya* posed a *halachic* question to Rabbi Eliezer: it is written in your Torah, *lo tavi etnan zonah* — you may not bring the fee paid to a prostitute into the house of God. So what about using such money to build a *beit hakisse* — an outhouse — for the *kohen gadol*, who must reside on the Temple Mount for the seven days preceding *Yom Kippur*? Would that be a fitting use, converting money from a place of filth to a place of filth?

*Velo amarti lo klum* — Rabbi Eliezer said nothing in response. This was deliberate. The best approach to a missionary or a sectarian who seeks to draw you into debate is often silence — to engage is to invite further entanglement, which is precisely what leads a person deeper in. The man did not walk away, however, and continued: *kach limadani* — and here the original reads *kach limadani Yeshu HaNotzri*, this is what Jesus taught me — *ki meetnan zonah kibtza ve'ad etnan zonah yashuvu*: because it was gathered from the payment of a prostitute, so shall it return to the payment of a prostitute. *Mimmekom hatinofet ba'u lemakom hatinofet yelechu* — it came from a place of filth and to a place of filth it shall go. The argument is a kind of midrashic wordplay applied to a novel *halachic* conclusion.

### Prostitute Gift

*Vehenani hadavar* — and Rabbi Eliezer admitted: I was pleased by it. He found it a clever *chap* — a good reading. Now, as a pure matter of *halacha* the ruling itself is *pashut* and *muttar* in any case, since the prohibition of *etnan zonah* applies only to bringing the object directly into the *Beit HaMikdash* itself, not to these peripheral applications. But the pleasure he took in the cleverness of the argument, in the intellectual engagement — that, Rabbi Akiva was suggesting, was the problem. *Al zeh nitfasti* — it is for this that I was seized. *Ve'avarti al mah shekasuv batorah* — I transgressed what the Torah commanded: *harcheik me'aleha darkecha* — keep far from her, your path.

---

## Proverbs Interpretation

### Three Threats

Rabbi Eliezer identifies the verse from *Mishlei* — *harcheik me'aleha darkecha ve'al tikrav el pesach beisah* — as the operative *pasuk*. He reads it as referring to two distinct dangers: *harcheik me'aleha darkecha* — keep your path far from her — this is *minut*, heresy. *Ve'al tikrav el pesach beisah* — do not draw near to the opening of her house — this is *rashut*, the government. A second opinion (*ve'ika de'amrei*) holds that the first half of the verse refers to both *minut* and *rashut* together, while the second half — do not draw near to her house — refers to *zonah*, prostitution.

### Four Cubits Rule

How far must one keep one's distance from a house of heresy or prostitution? Rav Chisda rules: *arba amos* — four *amos*.

### Modern Threats

Here a striking observation demands attention. We are learning *Masechet Avodah Zarah* — a tractate devoted in its entirety to the prohibition of idolatry and maintaining distance from idolatrous practice. If someone were told, without context, that the *gemara* here cites *harcheik me'aleha darkecha* — keep far from her path — as protection against the dangers that confront Israel, what would one expect the *gemara* to identify as the primary threat? One would naturally say: a house of *avodah zarah*. Yet the *gemara* identifies three things to keep away from — heresy, government, and sexual immorality — and not one of them is *avodah zarah* in the classical sense of literal idol worship.

This speaks volumes about the world in which the *chachamim* lived. By the time of *Bayit Sheini* the *yetzer hara* for *avodah zarah* had already been extinguished — the *gemara* says this explicitly elsewhere. Even for many non-Jews in the Roman world, paganism had become largely *pro forma*, a matter of cultural convention rather than genuine religious devotion. And so the tractate that bears the name *Avodah Zarah* is really, in its lived texture, about something else entirely: about the seductions of intellectual heresy, which could draw a brilliant mind into foreign religious frameworks; about the allure of governmental power, which could compromise a person's integrity and independence; and about sexual freedom, which the larger Roman world offered in abundance.

These were the real threats. Not idols of stone and wood, but the pull of sectarian ideas, the glamour of Roman authority, and the freedom of a life unbound by the constraints of *taharah* and *kedushah*. In that sense the tractate's themes are perennial: the question of what constitutes *avodah zarah b'yameinu* — idolatry in our time — is never answered by pointing to pagan temples that no longer exist, but by identifying what actually competes with our loyalty to God and *Torah*.

On the related *halachic* matter: the *gemara* notes that the Rabbis' interpretation of *meetnan zonah* — the verse about the prostitute's fee — follows Rav Chisda's teaching that any prostitute who hires herself out for pay will eventually fall on hard times and lose her appeal, and will in the end find herself paying others for what she once sold: *uvisiteich esnan ve-esnan lo nisan lach va-tehi le-hefech* — in your giving of payment, and payment was not given to you, the dynamic has reversed.

---

## Physical Contact Rules

### Sexual vs. Neutral

This ruling of Rav Chisda's regarding four *amos* disagrees with a position of Rav Padat. Rav Padat holds: *lo asrah Torah ela kereivah shel gilluy arayos bilvad* — the Torah prohibited only *kereivah* that constitutes an actual act of forbidden intercourse. When the Torah says *lo sikrevu legallos ervah* — do not draw near to uncover nakedness — it is not speaking about physical proximity to a building or a person; it is speaking about the act of intercourse itself. The proof-text is *ish ish el kol she'er besaro lo sikrevu legallos ervah* — a man shall not draw near to any close flesh to uncover nakedness.
