If one makes one's Torah like bundles — piling on more and more, always moving to the next *daf*, the next tractate, accumulating material at speed without pausing to consolidate — *mitma'et*, it will diminish; one cannot hold on to it. But *vekovetz al yad yarbe* — if one gathers handful by handful, learning a little, reviewing it, ensuring comprehension, then moving to the next portion, reviewing again — each piece builds on the last, and in the end one truly possesses a great deal of Torah.

Rava himself acknowledges the irony: *yadei rabanan leha milta ve'avri ala* — Torah scholars know this principle and regularly violate it. It is always more exciting to move forward than to review what has already been learned. A practical habit that exemplifies the principle: upon completing a *daf* or *amud*, pausing to identify the two or three main points one wishes to retain makes an enormous difference in internalization.

### Nachman's Testimony

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak offers personal testimony: *ana avidta* — I followed Rava's method, learning gradually and reviewing, *ve'kayem biyadi* — and in the end it remained established in my hand. These teachings about the process of learning Torah — how to absorb it, how it becomes yours, and how to retain it — form a remarkable sequence of practical wisdom embedded in this *agadta*.

---

## Hunter Analogy

### Skillful vs. Deceitful

Rav Shizvi in the name of Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah cites the verse *lo yachroch rmiyah tzeido* — the deceitful one will not roast his game. The word *yachroch*, to char or roast, is read here as a play on *yichyeh velo ya'arich yamim* — the *tziyad haramai*, the deceitful hunter, will not live long or have length of days. Rashi identifies the deceitful hunter as one who goes around superficially quoting things, performing the appearance of Torah without genuine dedication. *Vachachamim omrim tziyad haramai yachroch* — but the sages say: shall the skillful hunter roast his game? Yes — the one who hunts his Torah with craft and care, takes hold of what he has caught, and then processes it — reviews it, owns it — will indeed succeed. This reading continues the imagery developed throughout this section: the game that one catches but does not secure is lost.

### Dimi's Bird Parable

When Rav Dimi came from the Land of Israel, he offered a parable: it is like a person hunting birds — *im meshaber knafeha harishonah kulam mitkayemet biyado* — if you break the wing of the first one, all the birds you subsequently catch will remain in your hand as well. The logic may be that once the first bird is secured and cannot escape, one has established the habit of retention, and everything that follows is likewise retained. *Ve'im lav ein mitkayemet biyado* — but if not, if one allows the first catch to fly away — if the learning goes in one ear and out the other — nothing will stay. The image reinforces the central message of this entire section: initial mastery and consolidation are the precondition for accumulating Torah.

---

## Tree by Waters

### Replanted Tree

The *Gemara* returns to the opening verse of Tehillim 1: *vehayah ke'etz shatul al palgei mayim* — he will be like a tree planted beside streams of water. The school of Rabbi Yannai notes the precise word: *ke'etz shatul* — like a tree that has been *replanted*, transplanted from one location to another — *velo ke'etz natua*, not like a tree that was planted once and remains forever in a single place.

### Multiple Teachers

The implication: *kol halomed Torah merav echad eino ro'eh siman bracha le'olam* — whoever learns all his Torah from a single rabbi will never see a *siman bracha*. By remaining rooted in one place, one is not stimulated by different waters, different perspectives, different ways of thinking. One may accumulate a great deal of content, but without the *bracha* of growth and expansion that comes from exposure to multiple streams of Torah.

### Chisda's Dilemma

Rav Chisda illustrates the personal cost of this truth. He gathered his students and said: *ba'ina de'eima lachon milta mistafina dishvakiton li ve'azliton* — I want to tell you something, but I am afraid that as soon as I do, you will abandon me and leave. He told them nonetheless — and they did exactly what he feared, departing immediately to study before Rava.

### Svara vs. Gmara

Rava — and the *Gemara* suggests it may be Rava who addresses the departed students — clarifies the principle: *hanei milei svara, aval gmara merav echad adif* — this applies to *svara*, to analytical reasoning and conceptual thinking, which benefits from exposure to multiple teachers and multiple frameworks. But when it comes to *gmara* — the transmission of the received text — it is better to have one rabbi. The implication may be that Rava was directing the students back to Rav Chisda for the foundational textual learning, with the freedom to seek multiple teachers for analysis.

### Terminology Consistency

At the top of 19b, the reason for maintaining a single teacher for textual learning is explained: *ki heichi d'lo liflog lishnei* — in order not to create confusion among different terminologies. Different teachers use different technical vocabularies for the same concepts — what one calls *metaltelin* and *karka*, another may call *nechasim bnei chorin* and *nechasim meshubadim*. If one absorbs the same material through multiple terminological frameworks simultaneously, the conceptual categories will blur, and one will mistake terminology for substance. The textual foundation — the *girsa* discussed earlier — must be laid with consistent framing, and only then can analysis be pursued from multiple vantage points.

---

## Three-Part Study

### Tanchum's Division

The phrase *palgei mayim* — streams of water in the plural — is taken to suggest that one's Torah should be divided into multiple channels. Rav Tanchum bar Chanina teaches: *le'olam yeshalesh adam shnotav* — a person should always divide his years into three portions: *shlish beMikra, shlish beMishna, shlish beTalmud* — a third in Scripture, a third in Mishnah, and a third in Talmud, meaning analysis. The foundational texts and the analytical tradition receive equal weight.

### Lifespan Uncertainty

The *Gemara* immediately raises an objection: *mi yada inish kama chayei* — how can one divide one's years when one does not know one's lifespan? If the division is chronological — Scripture from birth to age twenty, Mishnah from twenty to forty — one cannot know in advance how many years remain for each phase.

### Weekly Division

*Dechi ka'amrinan beyomei* — the teaching must refer to one's days, not one's years. Rashi interprets this as a weekly division: two days for Scripture, two days for Mishnah, two days for Talmud, with Shabbat devoted to review of all three.

### Bavli's Inclusion

Tosafot asks: how does one even know one will survive the week? The pointed humor aside, Tosafot's more substantive answer is that the structure of the daily liturgy already implements this division. The *psukei hatamid*, the verses recited in the morning service, fulfill the portion of Scripture; the Mishnah of *Eizehu Mekoman* fulfills the Mishnah portion; and the *Braita deRabbi Yishmael* — the thirteen hermeneutical principles — represents the beginning of *Talmud*, of analysis. Even those who do not formally divide their learning already encounter all three each day. For those who devote themselves to learning *gemara* exclusively, Rabbeinu Tam argues further: *anu she'oskim beTalmud Bavli* — we who occupy ourselves with the Babylonian Talmud need not make a strict third-by-third division, *ki hu balul beMikra uv'Mishna uv'Talmud* — because the Bavli itself is interwoven with Scripture and Mishnah. Studying the Bavli keeps one in conversation with all three dimensions, even if not in equal proportions.

### Rambam's Stages

Rambam spells out a practical scenario. He describes a person with a profession who works three hours a day, leaving nine hours for Torah: three hours of Scripture, three hours of Mishnah, three hours of Talmud. Rambam's scenario presupposes, notably, that the professional devotes three hours to work and nine to Torah — a ratio worth appreciating in itself. But Rambam also emphasizes that this three-part division applies only to the *beginning* of one's learning, when the goal is to acquire the core texts and establish foundations. Once one reaches a more mature stage, the entire effort should shift toward the higher level of intellectual analysis. Tosafot's answer and Rambam's answer are thus complementary rather than contradictory: Rambam addresses the initial stage of formation, while Tosafot addresses the ongoing reality of mature learning. Both the continued engagement with foundational texts and the movement toward higher analysis have their place within a complete Torah life.

---

## Fruit in Season

### Fruit & Leaves

The *Gemara* continues through the verse: *asher piryo yitein be'ito* — who gives his fruit in its season — and the next phrase, *ve'alehu lo yibol* — and his leaves will not wither. Rava notes that the verse conditions the promise: *im piryo yitein be'ito, ve'alehu lo yibol* — if the fruit is given in its season, then the leaves will not wither. But if not — *ve'im lav* — the subsequent verse applies: *lo chen ha'reshaim ki im ka'motz asher tidfenu ruach* — not so the wicked, for they are like chaff that the wind blows away.

### Unripe vs. Refusing

Rava interprets this through the lens of *hora'ah* — the giving of *psak halacha*. The reference to *elu melamed u'melamed* — both the one who is being taught and the one who teaches — suggests that the "fruit" is the practical ruling, the application of Torah to life. Two categories of failure are identified, and they receive opposite condemnations drawn from the same cluster of verses.

Rav Abba in the name of Rav Huna in the name of Rav cites the verse: *ki rabbim chalalim hipila ve'atzumim kol harugeha* — for many slain has she cast down, and great are all those she has killed. The first clause — *rabbim chalalim hipila* — refers to a student who has not yet reached the level of *hora'ah* yet rules anyway. The word *hipila* is connected to *nefel*, an unformed fetus; such a student is spiritually unripe, not yet fit to issue rulings, and by doing so causes many to sin — ruling too leniently, or too stringently, or simply incorrectly. *Rabbim chalalim hipila* — many casualties from the premature *posek*.

The second clause — *ve'atzumim kol harugeha* — is read differently. *Atzumim*, enormous, is connected to *le'otzeim*, to hold back or shut. This refers to the student who has reached the level of *hora'ah* and yet refuses to rule. By withholding his *psak* from those who need it, he too causes great damage — enormous are all those "slain" by his reticence.

### Age Forty

The *Gemara* asks: *ve'ad kama* — until what age should one refrain from issuing rulings? The answer: until forty years of age.

### Rava's Exception

But a challenge immediately follows: did not Rava himself give *psak halacha*, and did Rava not die at the age of forty? *Hatam bishavin* — that was a case of equivalence, or indeed of superiority: when there is no one at a greater level than you, one need not wait for the age of forty. But where there are those who surpass you in learning and authority, one should defer until that threshold is reached.

---

## Leaves Not Wither

### Mundane Wisdom

Rav Acha bar Adda — with variant attributions running through Rav Acha bar Abba and Rav Hamnuna — cites Rav on the phrase *ve'alehu lo yibol*, "and his leaves will not wither": *she'afilu sichat chullin shel talmidei chachamim tzricha talmud* — even the mundane conversation of Torah scholars requires study and attention. There is wisdom embedded in how a *talmid chacham* speaks, carries himself, and interacts with others that goes beyond the explicit content of his teaching. The *Gemara* elsewhere formulates this as *gadol shimusha yoter milimmuda* — attending upon a Torah scholar teaches more than formal study alone. One observes the tone, the word choice, the manner — and these are themselves a form of Torah. Even the leaves — not the fruit — are not to be dismissed; they too carry content and significance.

---

## All Success

### Tripled Promise

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi states: *davar zeh katuv baTorah veshunuy baNevi'im umeshulash baKetuvim* — this matter is written in the Torah, repeated in the Prophets, and said a third time in the Writings. What matter? *Kol ha'osek baTorah* — whoever occupies himself with Torah — *drachav matzlichin* (following the *Gra*'s emendation, which fits the verses better than the manuscript reading of *nechasav matzlichin*) — his paths succeed.

### Written: Covenant

The verse in the Torah: *ushmartem et divrei habrit hazot va'asitem otam lema'an taskilu et kol asher ta'asun* — you shall observe the words of this covenant and do them, in order that you may act wisely in all that you do. Success in all endeavors flows from faithfulness to the covenant and its teachings.

### Nevi'im: Meditation

The verse in the Prophets — in Yehoshua — *lo yamush sefer haTorah hazeh mipicha vehagita bo yomam valailah lema'an tishmor la'asot kechol hakatuv bo ki az tatzliach et drachecha ve'az taskil* — the book of Torah shall not depart from your lips, and you shall meditate in it day and night, in order to observe all that is written in it, for then your paths will be successful and you will act wisely. The word *tatzliach*, succeed, appears explicitly, and the *Gra*'s emendation of the *girsa* to *drachav matzlichin* aligns precisely with *tatzliach et drachecha*.

### Ketuvim: Tree

The verse in the Writings is the very passage of Tehillim 1 that the *Gemara* has been expounding throughout: *ki im b'torat Hashem cheftzo uvtorato yehgeh yomam valailah, vehayah ke'etz shatul al palgei mayim asher piryo yiten be'ito ve'alehu lo yibol vechol asher ya'aseh yatzliach* — for in God's Torah is his desire, and in his Torah he meditates day and night; he shall be like a tree replanted beside streams of water, giving its fruit in its season, whose leaves do not wither, and all that he does will succeed. The entire *agadta* on *Talmud Torah* closes with this verse, the promise of success threaded through Torah, Prophets, and Writings alike.

---

## Alexandri's Proclamation

### Who Wants Life?

Rabbi Alexandri would go to a town and make a public proclamation: *man ba'ei chayei? man ba'ei chayei?* — who wants life? Who wants life? The crowd gathered: *kanaf ve'atu kulei alma laggabeih* — everyone came to him. *Amru leih hav lan chayei* — give us life! He replied by citing the verse: *mi ha'ish hachafetz chayim ohev yamim lir'ot tov* — who is the person who desires life, who loves days, to see good? This is why the Chafetz Chayim took his name from this verse.

### Guard Your Speech

*Netzor leshoncha mera usfatecha middaber mirma* — guard your tongue from evil and your lips from speaking deceit. Do not speak *lashon hara*. This is the secret of life.

### Evil to Good

But Rabbi Alexandri continues with the next verse. One might hear *netzor leshoncha mera* and conclude: I have watched my tongue, I speak no evil — *eilech ve'etgareh beshinah*, let me now go and sleep. The abstention from evil, the avoidance of harm, might seem sufficient. It is not. *Talmud lomar sur mera va'asei tov bakesh shalom verodfehu* — the very next verse adds: turn from evil *and do good*, seek peace and pursue it. Negative commandments, the refraining from transgression, are not enough in isolation. Positive action is required.

### Torah as Good

And what is that good? *Ve'ein tov ela Torah* — there is no good but Torah. The proof-text: *ki lekach tov natati lachem Torati al ta'azovu* — for I have given you a good teaching, My Torah; do not forsake it. This brings the entire extended *agadta* on *Talmud Torah* to its culmination. All the teachings about desire and heart, about *girsa* and analysis, about multiple teachers and the right season for *hora'ah*, about the speech of Torah scholars and the universal promise of success — all of it flows from and returns to the identification of Torah as the supreme good, the elixir of life itself.

---

## Idol Niche Mishna

### Stop at Niche

The *Gemara* returns to the Mishnah. The Mishnah had stated that one may assist in the construction of a bathhouse or other building for idolaters, but *higia lekippa* — when one reaches the niche, the *kippa*, the place where they set up the idol — one must stop. One cannot participate in constructing the actual site of idolatrous worship.

### Payment Permissible

Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Yochanan rules: *im bana, scharo mutar* — if a person did build it in violation of this prohibition and thereby transgressed — creating at minimum a problem of *mesaye'a lifnei iver* at the rabbinic level — the payment one received is nonetheless *mutar*, permitted. One may keep the fee.

---

## Niche as Tashmish

### Idol vs. Tashmish

The *Gemara* asks: this ruling is obvious — why would it even occur to us that the payment should be forbidden? The niche is a *tashmish*, an appurtenance of the idol, not the idol itself.

### Both Amoraim Agree

*Meshamshei avodat kochavim hem* — such appurtenances are indeed subject to specific rules. *Umeshamshei avodat kochavim bein le-Rabbi Yishmael bein le-Rabbi Akiva einam asurin ad she-ye'avedu* — the appurtenances of an idol are forbidden, according to both Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva, only once they have actually been used in the context of idol worship. Mere designation or construction of an appurtenance does not render it *asur behana'ah*. Since the niche has not yet had an idol placed upon it, it has not yet been used in worship and is therefore not yet forbidden in benefit. Consequently, there is no reason for the payment to be forbidden, and the ruling that it is *mutar* seems self-evident.

It is worth pausing here on a conceptual distinction embedded in the *Gemara*'s reasoning. The direct, classical sense of *issur hana'ah* — prohibition of benefit — covers physical enjoyment (eating, smelling, incorporating into one's body) and monetary benefit (selling and taking the proceeds). The benefit derived from having performed labor associated with a forbidden object is somewhat distinct in category. Yet the *Gemara* treats the laborer's fee as governed by the same principle: if the object is not *asur behana'ah*, the payment for work involving it is likewise permitted. Similarly, one might have expected a *rabbinic* prohibition on the payment even where the classical *issur hana'ah* does not apply — analogous to the rabbinic rule that proceeds from business conducted on an idolater's market day (*yom hashuk*) must be discarded. The *Gemara*'s assumption appears to be that absent an explicit rabbinic extension of the prohibition, the default rule follows the standard categories of *issur hana'ah*.

### Jew vs. Non-Jew

Rabbi Yirmiyah proposes that the novelty of Rabbi Elazar's ruling lies elsewhere entirely: not in the case of a *tashmish*, but in the case of the idol itself — *avodat kochavim atzmah*. Even if one actually made the idol, Rabbi Elazar rules the payment is permitted. This is striking. The *Gemara* engages with the debate between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva regarding when an idol becomes forbidden. The key distinction is between an idol made for or by a Jew and one made for or by a non-Jew. An idol *shel Yisrael* — made on behalf of a Jew, or in Rashi's reading, owned temporarily by a Jew (perhaps a merchant intending to sell it) — is *asura mi-yad*, forbidden immediately upon its creation. An idol *shel oved kochavim* — made for and by a non-Jew — according to the opposing view is *ad she-te'aved*, forbidden only once actually worshipped.

According to the view that a non-Jew's idol is forbidden only upon worship, the ruling that the payment is permitted is indeed obvious: even the idol itself is not yet *asur behana'ah* at the moment of its construction, and therefore the laborer's payment is unproblematically permitted. But according to the view that even a non-Jew's idol is forbidden immediately upon completion — *asura mi-yad* — the ruling requires explanation. At the moment the idol is complete, it becomes *asur behana'ah*, and at that very moment the laborer's work is finished and his fee is earned. Why should the payment be permitted?

---

## Last Hammer Blow

### Makkesh Acharon

Rava bar Ula resolves the difficulty: *lo nitzrecha ela bemakkesh acharon* — the ruling is necessary specifically with regard to the last hammer blow. The idol does not become an idol — does not become *asur behana'ah* — until *gemar melachah*, until the work is complete. And *gemar melachah* is the very last hammer blow or tap that completes the object.

### Gemar Melachah

An idol in the process of being fashioned is not yet an idol. Whatever prohibitions may attach to the completed object do not apply until that final act of completion.

### Less Than Pruta

*Makkesh acharon leit beih shaveh prutah* — the last hammer blow is not worth a *prutah*. A craftsman working on an idol throughout the week is accumulating wages continuously. By the time he delivers the final tap, he has already earned essentially the entire fee. That final moment — the only moment at which the idol is actually *asur behana'ah* — corresponds to a fraction of a *prutah* of his total compensation. Since that amount is legally negligible, it is as though nothing of the forbidden object's value contaminated his payment. The bulk of his wages were earned before the prohibition came into effect.

### Wages Throughout

The *Gemara* adds: *ve'alma kasavar yeshnah lisechirut mitechilah ve'ad sof* — this analysis reveals an underlying principle about the nature of wages. Conceptually, a hired worker earns his fee continuously throughout the performance of his work, not only at the moment of its completion. Even if payment is made only upon delivery, the entitlement to that payment accrues progressively from the beginning of the labor to its end. It is therefore not the case that the laborer earned nothing for ninety-nine percent of his work and then earned everything at the moment of completion. He earned throughout — and throughout, the object was not yet *asur behana'ah*. The only moment it was forbidden was the final tap, and that moment was worth less than a *prutah*. Hence the fee is permitted in its entirety.

It is worth noting, in closing, how striking the *Gemara*'s silence is regarding any rabbinic prohibition on building idols for non-Jews. The contrast with the *Gemara*'s earlier discussion of business on idolaters' market days — where rabbinic enactments rendered proceeds forbidden — is marked. Perhaps the explanation lies in prevalence: market-day commerce with idolaters was a common enough phenomenon to demand serious rabbinic deterrence, whereas Jews constructing idols for non-Jews was a sufficiently rare scenario that the Sages left it to be governed by the underlying law of *issur hana'ah* alone.

---

---

# Avodah Zarah 20

## Jewelry Prohibition

### Mishnah & R. Eliezer

The daf begins at the bottom of 19b, continuing a series of *mishnayot* governing the permitted scope of interaction with the pagan non-Jewish world. The previous *mishnah* had addressed participation in construction projects associated with pagan courts and public spectacles, and had opened a rich digression on *moshav letzim* and the primacy of *talmud Torah*. The underlying theme was that the true line of division drawn by the Rabbis was not merely the formal boundary between Jewish and pagan, but the contrast between the seductions of the broader world and a life anchored in *Torah u-mitzvot*.

The *mishnah* now under discussion opens with what appears to be a prohibition: *ve-ein osin tachshitin le-avodat kochavim* — one may not fashion jewelry to adorn an idol. The specific items listed are a *katla* (likely a necklace), a *nezem* (likely a nose ring), and a *taba'at* (a ring). Rabbi Eliezer then adds: *be-sachar mutar* — if one is being compensated, it is permitted. This position is striking. If manufacturing the niche of a bathhouse designated for idolatrous use is forbidden, how could fashioning actual ornaments for an idol be permitted under any circumstances? And even if one were to say that *bedi'avad* the craftsman may retain his fee — a position the *gemara* had already countenanced in a previous discussion about crafting idols — to say it is *mutar le-chatchilah* seems deeply at odds with the general tenor of the tractate.

### Manuscript Evidence

Tosafot raises a fundamental question about whether this line belongs in the *mishnah* at all. The text does not appear in *Ktav Yad Kaufmann*, which is widely regarded as the most reliable extant manuscript of the *mishnah*. There is no parallel in the *Tosefta*, and no *gemara* engages with it as such.

Tosafot frames the textual difficulty as follows: *ve-ikka de-garsinan* — there are those who have this reading — but he regards it as an unlikely *girsa*, for *de-lo mistavar she-yattir shum tanna la-asot le-chatchilah tachshitei Avodah Zarah* — it is implausible that any *tanna* would permit the crafting of idolatrous ornaments in the first instance. Furthermore, one cannot invoke the argument of *mishum eivah* — that refusal would generate hostility — as one might in the case discussed later of a Jewish midwife declining to assist in childbirth. There, one might plausibly say the non-Jew will attribute the refusal to malice. But here, *de-ha vadai ika eivah* — even if there is some hostility, the non-Jew would understand why a Jew would decline to make jewelry for their idol. The *mishum eivah* defense simply does not apply.

### Rashi & Textual Issues

Tosafot adds a final and notably elegant argument from silence: *ve-nireh she-lo haya katuv be-sefer Rabbeinu Shlomo al perusho* — it appears that Rashi did not have this line in his text of the *mishnah*, and the proof is that Rashi offers no commentary on the word *katla'ot*. The word is unusual enough that had Rashi possessed this *girsa*, he would surely have explained it. This is a compelling instance of evidence derived from the absence of commentary — and, one might note, it is the same type of reasoning Tosafot deploys when Rashi's silence signals a textual problem rather than mere indifference.

The question of how such a line entered certain manuscripts, complete with an attributed position for Rabbi Eliezer, remains genuinely puzzling. One might speculate that it originated as a marginal gloss, perhaps written by someone seeking to justify commercial activity that had become commonplace. In any case, since there is no *gemara* engaging with this line, and the manuscript evidence is so weak, the *mishnah* as our *gemara* understands it begins elsewhere.

---

## Land Sales Ban

### Mishnah Rules

The *mishnah* now turns to a different subject, one that connects back to the earlier discussion about selling large and small animals. There, the *gemara* had suggested various rationales — concerns about *Shabbat* violations or bestiality — but a more straightforward reading is that many of these prohibitions reflect an underlying concern about maintaining Jewish presence and control in the Land of Israel, a concern made explicit by the *gemara*'s earlier discussion about purchasing animals, land, and slaves at market in order to reinforce that presence.

The *mishnah* states: *ein mochrin lahem bi-mechubar la-karka* — one may not sell to them anything that is attached to the ground. This effectively encompasses land itself, though land is so obvious a case it goes without saying. Trees, standing grain, and other attached property are included. However, *aval mocher mi-she-yikatzetz* — once the item has been cut, it may be sold, which is self-evident. Rabbi Yehuda adds a nuance: *mocher lahem al menat liktoz* — one may sell them standing grain on condition that it will be cut. The Rabbis reject even this, because while the grain remains standing the buyer effectively holds a temporary claim over the land itself.

### Lo Techonem Derivation

The *gemara* asks *minah hanei milei* — what is the biblical source for this rule? Rav Yosef bar Chanina answers that the verse states *lo tichrot lahem berit ve-lo techonem* — do not make a covenant with them and do not *techonem* them. The word *lo techonem* receives multiple interpretations in the *gemara*, the first being *lo titein lahem chanayah ba-karka* — do not grant them a dwelling or foothold in the land.

The *peshat* of the surrounding verses clearly addresses the seven Canaanite nations. The passage also contains the prohibition *lo titchaten bam* — do not intermarry with them — which, notably, the dominant *gemara* position limits to those same seven nations. Even the technical biblical intermarriage prohibition may not extend beyond the seven Canaanite peoples, though this is a startling conclusion that *poskim* have had occasion to address.

### Scope & Extensions

Tosafot addresses the obvious scope question: since the verse is speaking about the seven Canaanite nations, why does the *gemara* treat *lo techonem* as a general prohibition applicable to all non-Jews? Tosafot's position is that the *gemara* assumes — without extended argument — that the concerns expressed in *lo techonem* are of a nature that applies more broadly. Whether this broader application is *de-oraita* or merely an *asmachta* for a rabbinic prohibition is itself debated. It is also possible, the *gemara* allows, that we limit the scope to those actually engaged in *avodah zarah*, rather than to all non-Jews as such.

### Policy vs. Mitzvah

A closer look reveals a significant framing question. The most natural reading of these restrictions is that they are communal policy measures — responses to the precarious position of the Jewish minority under Roman rule, designed to prevent the erosion of the Jewish land base. In a context where Jews were politically vulnerable, selling land to the dominant power would have been deeply destabilizing for the community. The analogy is not difficult to find: in other communities under occupation or demographic pressure, there have been comparable norms against selling land to outsiders, understood as acts of communal solidarity and survival rather than religious injunction.

The *gemara*, however, consistently reframes these practical concerns as *mitzvah* categories — the same move it made earlier when it read the prohibition on selling large animals through the lens of *Shabbat*. The concern is no longer a communal policy responsive to historical circumstances; it becomes a timeless religious obligation derived from a biblical verse. This shift has significant implications. A policy-based norm can be revisited as circumstances change; a *mitzvah* framing tends toward absolute application regardless of context. It is precisely this tension that has given rise to contemporary halakhic debates about whether these rules apply when Jews are not a vulnerable minority but the dominant power — a question that falls well beyond the scope of this *shiur*, but whose roots lie in exactly this point.

---

## Lo Techonem: Favor

### Three Meanings

The *gemara* continues to derive multiple meanings from the single word *lo techonem*. The first derivation, *lo titein lahem chanayah ba-karka*, has already been discussed. But the *gemara* now objects: the word *lo techonem* is needed to teach something else — *lo titein lahem chein* — do not give them favor, do not express admiration for them. If the word was meant only to convey the land-dwelling prohibition, it would have been written differently. And if it was meant only to convey the favor prohibition, a different vocalization would have sufficed. The *gemara* therefore concludes *shema mina tartei* — we derive both meanings — and adds a third: *lo titein lahem matnat chinam* — do not give them a free gift.

The *lo titein lahem chein* prohibition does not mean simply "don't be kind to them." It means: do not go about publicly praising and extolling the non-Jewish world — its beauty, its achievements, its religious institutions. The concern is not merely social warmth, but the cultural and spiritual pull exerted by enthusiastic admiration. If one is constantly declaring how magnificent pagan temples are, or how brilliant non-Jewish cultural productions are, one feeds the seductive appeal of that world and implicitly denigrates one's own. This is especially acute when the objects of praise are directly associated with *avodah zarah*: extolling the grandeur of the Temple of Zeus is not a neutral aesthetic observation; it actively rehabilitates what Jewish law demands one treat as repugnant.

That said, this is a genuinely challenging *gemara* from the perspective of a more pluralistic religious sensibility. We are apparently prohibited not only from giving non-Jews land, but from complimenting them, and from giving them gifts. The most generous limiting principle available is to confine all three derivations to the context of genuine idolaters — which, in many contemporary contexts, would dramatically narrow the practical scope of the prohibition.

---

## Matnat Chinam

### R. Meir vs. R. Yehuda

The *gemara* notes that the prohibition of *matnat chinam* — giving a free gift to a non-Jew — is itself the subject of a *tannaitic* dispute. The *gemara* cites a *beraita* based on the verse in Deuteronomy: *lo tochlu kol neveila la-ger asher bi-sh'arecha titnenah va-achala o machor la-nochri* — do not eat any *neveila*; give it to the *ger* in your gates, or sell it to the foreigner. The *ger* in rabbinic reading is the *ger toshav*, the resident alien, while the *nochri* is the visiting foreigner — a stranger from another land.

The *beraita* then asks: I know only that giving applies to the *ger* and selling applies to the *nochri*; how do I derive that selling to the *ger* and giving to the non-Jew are also permitted? Through creative rearrangement of the verse's clauses, the *beraita* constructs an argument that both *netinah* and *mechirah* apply to both categories. Rabbi Meir takes this position: both giving and selling are permitted to both *ger* and non-Jew alike, the verse's framing being a matter of priority rather than exclusion. Rabbi Yehuda, by contrast, takes the verse literally — *devarim kichtavam* — *ger* receives, *nochri* is sold to. Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning: since you have an affirmative obligation to sustain the *ger toshav* (*ve-chai achicha imach* includes the *ger toshav*), you would have known to prioritize him without the verse's guidance. The fact that the verse uses the disjunctive *o* rather than a simple *vav* therefore conveys an actual prohibition: you may not give the non-Jew a free gift; you may only sell.

The *gemara* validates Rabbi Yehuda's reading as the more compelling analysis and identifies him as the *tanna* who holds the prohibition of *matnat chinam*.

### Tosafot Qualifications

Tosafot significantly narrows the operative scope of *matnat chinam*. He cites a *Tosefta* on *neveila*: Rabbi Yehuda's prohibition applies to non-Jews who are strangers — but if one *knows* the non-Jew, *hamakiro mutar*, it is permitted, *mipnei she-hu ke-mochro lo* — because in the context of an ongoing relationship, what appears to be a gift functions more like a transaction with implicit reciprocity. You give now, they give later; there is no pure gratuitousness.

Tosafot further cites the *gemara* in *Perek Hadar*: even where one does not know the non-Jew, if one happens to be traveling together with him on the road, giving is permitted — *shehayah mislaveh imo ba-derech* — the context of shared journeying creates a momentary relational bond that removes the act from the category of *matnat chinam*.

And finally: *darchei shalom* — the rabbinic policy of supporting non-Jewish poor together with Jewish poor, of maintaining civil societal relations — is explicitly not *matnat chinam*. Tosafot states: *darchei shalom eino matnat chinam*, giving in the context of cultivating good relations is definitionally excluded from the prohibition.

### Chinam Meaning

The Koren translation renders *chinam* not as "free" but as "undeserved." The distinction is worth examining. Tosafot's framework suggests the operative concept is not deserving per se, but rather the presence or absence of any relational or purposive context. If there is a prior relationship, a shared journey, or a policy of *darchei shalom*, the giving has a context — it is not *chinam*. What Tosafot's qualifications effectively eliminate is the case of pure, contextless largesse directed at a random non-Jew with no relationship, no shared circumstances, and no communal rationale. In that narrow case, one's charitable impulses should be directed toward the Jewish community rather than to outsiders.

This reading, it should be noted, makes the prohibition far more about internal communal solidarity than about any hostility toward non-Jews. It does not forbid maintaining good relations — on the contrary, it explicitly permits and even encourages giving in any relational context. What it discourages is indiscriminate generosity extended to strangers who happen to be non-Jewish when that same generosity could be directed toward one's own community.

Tosafot raises a practical question about the *neveila* case specifically: the verse seems to say one must *give* to the *ger* rather than *sell* to him, even though one is normally permitted to sell one's property at fair market value. Tosafot resolves this by noting the particular economics of *neveila*: within a Jewish community where *neveila* is worthless to Jews, the commercial option would require exporting it to foreign buyers at considerable difficulty, whereas the *ger* living in your midst can receive it at the minimal local value. The verse is not insisting on pure charity at commercial cost; it is aligning practical reality with the *mitzvah* to sustain the *ger toshav*.

### Textual Censorship

A philological observation is worth making here. The original text of this *masechet*, like much of the *Talmud*, used the words *goy* or *nochri* when referring to non-Jews. Due to the attentions of church censors — and, more significantly, to internal Jewish self-censorship driven by fear that these passages would be reported as anti-Christian — the standard texts were systematically altered to read *ovdei kochavim*, "star-worshipers," or sometimes even *kena'ani*. The implication was that all such discussions referred only to ancient idolaters, not to contemporary Christians or Muslims.

The self-censorship becomes particularly visible at a telling moment in this *gemara*. Throughout the discussion of *matnat chinam*, the text consistently uses *ovdei kochavim*. But when the *gemara* reaches the statement that one is not obligated to sustain the non-Jew's life — *ve-kena'ani i ata metzuveh le-hachayoto* — the language shifts from *ovdei kochavim* to *kena'ani*. The rationale is transparent: a statement that one need not be concerned with a non-Jew's survival was apparently too sensitive to be left even with the already-censored *ovdei kochavim* designation, and required further distance through the term *kena'ani*.

The same phenomenon appears elsewhere in the Talmud. The famous *gemara* in *Bava Kamma* about whether *gezel* from a non-Jew is permitted reads, in censored manuscripts, *gezel kena'ani mutar* — as though it were speaking exclusively about Canaanites, not about any non-Jew. It was evidently not sufficient to replace *goy* with *akum*; the statement had to be attributed to an entirely different, historically extinct category of people.

What is remarkable is that over time, for many *poskim* who were more tolerantly minded, *halakha* eventually caught up to the censorship. What began as a face presented outward for self-protection gradually became internalized through genuine halakhic reasoning — whether by limiting the scope to actual idolaters, by arguing that contemporary non-Jews are not *ovdei avodah zarah*, or through other mechanisms. For many *poskim*, the internal halakhic position eventually converged with what the texts had been forced to say under external pressure.

---

## Lo Techonem: Favor (II)

### Complimenting Non-Jews

The *gemara* now turns to the second derivation from *lo techonem*: *lo titein lahem chein* — do not give them favor or express admiration. Rav states explicitly: *assur le-adam she-yomar kama na'eh avodat kochavim zu* — it is forbidden to say how beautiful this *avodah zarah* is. The original unedited text apparently reads *kama na'eh goy zeh*, *kama na'eh goyah zu* — how handsome is this non-Jewish man, how beautiful is this non-Jewish woman. The prohibition thus applies to statements *about* non-Jews, not only statements made *to* them.

The *gemara* immediately raises a challenge from a story about Rabban Shimon Gamliel. He was standing on the Temple Mount — itself a setting saturated with Jewish religious meaning — when he saw a strikingly beautiful non-Jewish woman, and he declared: *mah rabu ma'asecha Hashem* — how abundant are Your works, O God. Is this not a violation of Rav's ruling?

### R. Akiva's Reaction

The *gemara* adds a parallel story: Rabbi Akiva saw the wife of the wicked Turnusrufus — presumably also a woman of exceptional beauty — and his reaction was threefold. He spat (*rak*), he laughed (*shachak*), and he cried (*vacha*). The *gemara* explains each response. He spat because she came from *tipah sruchah* — a putrid drop, that is, from semen; all human beauty ultimately originates from something base and transient. He laughed because he foresaw that she would eventually convert to Judaism and he would marry her — a rather striking biographical note, given his celebrated marriage to Rachel. He cried because *hai shufra bali afra* — this beauty will ultimately dissolve in the earth; it is all passing.

There is a certain irony in Rabbi Akiva's laughing, consistent with his characteristic disposition. Just as he once laughed at the ruins of the Temple because he saw in its destruction the guarantee of ultimate restoration, here he laughs at what might seem like loss — the beauty that will perish, the woman who belongs to an enemy — because he perceives the irony of the situation, the hidden trajectory toward something different. The spitting and crying form the frame of transience; the laughing is the recognition that even within transience, things can turn.

### Rav's Resolution

The *gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction between Rabban Shimon Gamliel's statement and Rav's prohibition by explaining that Rabban Shimon Gamliel was engaged in *aduye hu de-kamode* — an act of thanksgiving to God, not an expression of admiration for the non-Jewish woman herself. The supporting principle: *ha-ro'eh beriyot tovot omer baruch she-kacha bara be-olamo* — one who sees beautiful creatures may recite the blessing acknowledging that God created such things in His world.

The distinction Rav draws is therefore not simply about whether one says something beautiful to a non-Jew versus about a non-Jew. It is about the direction of the admiration. If one says, "How magnificent these non-Jews are," or "How beautiful that church is" — that makes the non-Jewish world itself the object of esteem, and implicitly elevates its attractions. But if one redirects the aesthetic experience toward God — "How abundant are Your works, O God" — then the beauty of the created world, wherever it appears, becomes a vehicle for recognizing the Creator. The non-Jewish world is not thereby elevated; it is subsumed. It is not that those people or those institutions are remarkable; it is that God has created a world of remarkable beauty, some of which is visible here. This reframing deflects the concern that one is feeding the seductive pull of the non-Jewish world by celebrating it.

---

## Sexual Thoughts Ban

### Davar Ra Source

The *gemara* now raises a challenge to the story about Rabban Shimon Gamliel and Rabbi Akiva: *ve-le-istakulei mi sharei* — but were they even permitted to be *looking* at this woman? The *gemara* cites the verse *ve-nishmarta mi-kol davar ra* — you shall protect yourself from every evil thing — and understands it as a prohibition on the very act of gazing. The later part of the verse, which addresses *davar mikreh layla* — seminal emission at night — indicates that the *davar ra* is understood here as sexual thought that leads to involuntary emission. Rashi reads the verse's internal logic as: the way to protect oneself against seminal emission at night is not to indulge in sexual thoughts during the day.

### Looking Rules

The *gemara* elaborates a series of prohibitions on *histaklut* — intentional looking: one may not gaze at a beautiful woman, even if she is unmarried (*penuya*); nor at a married woman, even if she is unattractive; nor at women's colored garments; nor at donkeys, donkey-mares, pigs, sows, or birds when they are copulating. The concern in all cases is that such visual experiences will evoke sexual thoughts.

The question of how Rabban Shimon Gamliel and Rabbi Akiva could have found themselves in this situation is resolved by the *gemara* elsewhere: *keren zavit havai* — they came upon it at a corner, unexpectedly. The encounter was not a deliberate gaze but an inadvertent sighting.

The *gemara* goes on to discuss women's colored garments. Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel states that the prohibition applies even to garments laid out on a wall — i.e., not being worn by anyone. Rav Pappa qualifies this: it applies only when *makir ba'aleihen* — when one recognizes their owner, because in that case seeing the garment evokes the mental image of the woman who wears it. Rava confirms that the *gemara*'s precise wording — *bigdei tzeva shel isha*, "colored garments of a woman," rather than simply "colored garments" — supports Rav Pappa's reading: the prohibition is not about colored clothing as such, but about colored clothing associated with a specific woman in one's mind. Rav Chisda adds that even this applies only to garments that have been worn (*atikin*); new garments not yet worn (*chadatei*) are not subject to the prohibition.

The *gemara* proves this last point from a practical *reductio*: if new garments were also forbidden, how could we ever bring clothing to the *shapurya* (tailor or dry cleaner) for adjustments? The *gemara* responds that professional engagement constitutes a distinct category: *be-avideiteih tarid* — he is absorbed in his work — and this applies to the farmer who must handle copulating animals as well. However, this raises nuanced questions for *Shulchan Aruch* and later *poskim* about which professional roles may be assumed by men given the potential for *hirhur*; not every professional context suppresses arousal equally.

### Critique of Obsession

It is worth pausing here to note something that the *gemara*'s own framework suggests, even if it does not say it directly: *adam nitzal mehem be-chol yom* — a person cannot be saved from *hirhur aveira* every single day. Sexual thoughts are, as the *gemara* essentially concedes, an inescapable feature of human experience. The appropriate response would seem to be acknowledgment and equanimity, not obsessive suppression.

The intense religious focus in certain communities on the elimination of sexual thoughts — the elaborate *viduyim*, the *tefila zaka*, the architectural and sartorial measures designed to prevent male arousal — is, by any reasonable assessment, counterproductive even on its own terms. The effort to eliminate what cannot be eliminated tends to intensify the focus on precisely what one wishes to move past. If *lashon hara*, which violates multiple biblical prohibitions and causes tangible communal harm, received a fraction of the religious energy devoted to the policing of sexual thought, the community would be better served.

A related point: the *gemara*'s framing consistently locates the responsibility with the male observer, not with the woman observed. Rava's careful reading of *bigdei tzeva shel isha* emphasizes that the problem is what happens in the man's mind, not what the woman is wearing. Women are entitled to wear their colored garments; the obligation to manage one's response belongs to the one who sees. The widespread practice of imposing *tzniut* obligations on women as a mechanism for controlling men's sexual responses inverts this responsibility in a way the *gemara* itself does not support.

### Angel of Death

The *gemara* briefly digresses to discuss the *malach ha-mavet* (Angel of Death), prompted by the phrase *ve-afilu malei einayim ke-malach ha-mavet* — even if one is filled with eyes like the Angel of Death, one must not look. The *gemara* elaborates: the *malach ha-mavet* is described as entirely filled with eyes (*she-kulo malei einayim*). At the moment of a sick person's death, he stands above the person's head, his sword drawn, with a drop of poison (*tipah shel marah*) hanging from it. When the dying person sees him, he shudders, opens his mouth, and the drop falls in. That drop causes death, causes the body to rot afterward, and causes the face to change color.

The father of Shmuel is quoted as having been told by the Angel of Death himself: were it not for *kavod ha-beriyot* — respect for human dignity — he would slit the throat as an animal is slaughtered at the *beit ha-shchitah*. Instead, he cuts internally. The *gemara* reconciles this with the poison account by suggesting that the poison acts as an acid, effectively cutting through the *simanim* from the inside — it is both a drop and a type of cutting.

The thematic connection between the Angel of Death and the preceding discussion of sexual thoughts is not incidental. The *gemara* has been moving between the beauty of the created world — which evokes desire — and the fragility of that same world, which is subject to decay and death. Rabbi Akiva's three reactions to Turnusrufus's wife traverse exactly this terrain: the beauty, its transience, and the ironic consolation available to one who sees through the surface. The Angel of Death interweaving reinforces the point: the same physical beauty that evokes *hirhur* is also the body that will rot. The corrective to excessive investment in the world's physical attractions is not mere willpower, but a sustained awareness of their ultimate nature.

### Colored Garments & Excep…

The *gemara* returns to the looking prohibitions with a discussion of the farmer engaged in animal husbandry who must physically assist in animal copulation. Rav Yehuda states that *min be-mino mutar le-hachnis ke-michol ba-shoferet* — one may insert like an applicator into a tube — performing the act of insemination professionally. This would seem to contradict the prohibition on looking at copulating animals. The *gemara* resolves this, as noted above, through *be-avideiteih tarid* — professional preoccupation overrides the concern. The same principle explains why a tailor handling a woman's garments is not in violation: the professional context is determinative. But the *gemara*'s caveat is implicit and noted by later authorities: *be-avideiteih tarid* applies only where the professional engagement genuinely absorbs attention in a way incompatible with arousal. Professions that are themselves sexually charged, or that create extended intimate contact, require separate analysis.

---

## Rabbi Pinchas' Ladder

### Ten Steps

The *gemara* transitions to the famous statement of Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair, introduced as *mikan amar Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair* — from here Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair taught. The passage is the foundation upon which the *Mesillat Yesharim* is structured:

*Torah* leads to *zehirut* (carefulness against sin); *zehirut* leads to *zerizut* (alacrity in performing *mitzvot*); *zerizut* leads to *nekiut* (cleanliness from sin); *nekiut* leads to *perishut* (separation, ascetic withdrawal even from the permitted); *perishut* leads to *taharah* (purity); *taharah* leads to *kedushah* (holiness); *kedushah* leads to *anavah* (humility); *anavah* leads to *yir'at chet* (fear of sin); *yir'at chet* leads to *chasidut* (piety); *chasidut* leads to *ruach ha-kodesh* (divine spirit); and *ruach ha-kodesh* leads to *techiyat ha-meitim* (resurrection of the dead).

It is notable that *yir'at chet* — which one might expect to appear near the beginning as a foundational motivation — appears near the top of the ladder. At this level, it is clearly not rudimentary fear of punishment, but a refined, internalized aversion to sin that emerges from a life already deeply shaped by Torah, purity, and holiness. Similarly, *chasidut* here may not refer primarily to acts of *chesed*, but to a higher form of *prishut* — a quality of separation and dedication that transcends ordinary observance.

### Maharsha's Daily Schedule

The Maharsha offers a reading that is at once creative and practically grounding: these levels correspond not to a lifetime progression alone but to the stages of a single day's spiritual schedule. *Zehirut* — general carefulness — is the background disposition one carries always. *Zerizut* is awakening early in the morning, getting out of bed with alacrity to serve God. That early rising allows time for *nekiut* — washing and physical cleanliness before prayer. *Perishut* is the act of *davening* itself, in which one's hands are spread out (*perushos la-shamayim*) and one withdraws momentarily from the physical world. *Taharah* — a higher purity — represents one's *Torah* study undertaken after *davening* and the morning meal. *Kedushah* is the state achieved through immersion in *Torah* study, an entry into a kind of sanctified space analogous to the *Beit ha-Mikdash*. *Anavah* is the humility one carries into the workday that follows, tempered by the morning's spiritual activity. And so on through the ladder, until *ruach ha-kodesh* attends one's final waking hours and *techiyat ha-meitim* is, in a gentle metaphor, the re-ensoulment of the body each morning upon waking.

It is a charming and instructive reading, locating these elevated spiritual categories not only in the lives of great mystics and scholars but in the structured rhythm of daily Jewish life.

### Chasidus vs. Humility

The *gemara* records a dispute about which quality is the highest rung before *ruach ha-kodesh*. The text as cited by Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair places *chasidut* at the top, supported by the verse *az dibarta be-chazon la-chasidecha* — then You spoke in a vision to Your *chasidim* — implying that *chasidut* immediately precedes *ruach ha-kodesh*. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi disagrees: *anavah gedolah mi-kulam* — humility is the greatest of all. His proof is from the verse *ruach Hashem Elokim alai ya'an mashach Hashem oti levasser anavim* — the spirit of God is upon me, for God has anointed me to bring good tidings to the *anavim*, the humble. Since *anavim* rather than *chasidim* is the quality invoked in association with *ruach ha-kodesh*, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi concludes that *anavah* is the higher rung. The word *ya'an* — "because" — signals that *anavah* is the *reason* for the bestowing of *ruach ha-kodesh*, making it causally, and therefore hierarchically, more fundamental.

---

---

# Avodah Zarah 21

## Sale/Rental Restrictions

### Trees & Produce

The present daf picks up at the bottom of 20b, completing a *tana rabbanan* that addresses the core prohibition discussed in the preceding *mishna*: the restriction on selling items that are *mechubar lekarka* — attached to the ground — to non-Jews in the Land of Israel. This prohibition has obvious implications for contemporary debates about Jews selling land to non-Jews in Israel, though those debates must be understood in their proper context: the original prohibition was framed within the reality of a minority community struggling to maintain its foothold in the land, a context that differs substantially from present circumstances. The tradition, moreover, limits the scope of *matnat chinam* considerably — there is almost never a genuine case of *matnat chinam* — and allows for transactions rooted in *darchei shalom* and similar considerations. The preceding *gemara* had also addressed the question of *lo techonem* and when it does or does not apply. With those threads gathered, the *gemara* now returns to the *mishna*'s debate about selling something attached to the ground on the condition that the non-Jew immediately severs it.

### Yehuda vs. Meir

The *braita* records the dispute as follows. Rabbi Yehuda permits selling a tree (*ilan*) to a non-Jew on the condition that the purchaser chop it down — and the purchaser must then follow through and actually chop it down. Rabbi Meir is stricter: one may sell only what is already severed (*katzutz*). The same dispute repeats itself with *shachat* — the pre-grain stalks used for animal fodder — where Rabbi Yehuda permits selling it on the condition that the non-Jew cuts it himself (*vegozez*), while Rabbi Meir requires that it already be cut. And the same applies to *kama*, standing grain: Rabbi Yehuda permits the sale on condition of immediate harvest (*vekotzer*), while Rabbi Meir permits only what is already harvested.

### Three Cases Needed

The *gemara* asks: why does the *braita* need all three cases? Surely one would suffice, and the others could be inferred. The *gemara* answers: *utzricha* — each case is independently necessary.

Had the *braita* taught only the case of the tree, one might have said that Rabbi Meir's stringency applies specifically there because leaving a tree standing involves no loss to the owner — it just stands there indefinitely — and therefore the non-Jew has every incentive to delay severing it, prolonging his attachment to the land. But in the case of *shachat*, where delay actually causes a loss — the stalks spoil and become unfit for fodder — perhaps Rabbi Meir would concede to Rabbi Yehuda that the non-Jew's own self-interest guarantees prompt severance.

Had the *braita* taught only the tree and the *kama* (standing grain), one might have concluded that Rabbi Yehuda permits in both those cases precisely because in neither is there a clear, obvious gain to the non-Jew from delay. The tree simply sits; the grain will rot. But *shachat*, where leaving it a while longer actually improves the yield, might be different — perhaps even Rabbi Yehuda would agree with Rabbi Meir that such a sale is impermissible, since the non-Jew has a positive incentive to drag out the arrangement. And conversely, had only the *shachat* been taught, one would not know whether Rabbi Meir's ruling there (where there is a tangible gain from delay) also extends to cases where there is no such gain. All three cases are therefore needed.

### Animals Question

The *gemara* then raises a question: does Rabbi Yehuda's leniency — permitting a conditional sale before severance — extend analogously to the sale of an animal (*behema*) on condition of immediate slaughter? This question relates back to an earlier *mishna* (14b) about the prohibition on selling large or small livestock to non-Jews. The crux of the question is whether the rationale underlying Rabbi Yehuda's leniency in the land-connected cases applies equally here.

One might argue that Rabbi Yehuda's leniency by the tree and grain rests on the fact that the land itself remains in Jewish possession — the seller retains practical control and can enforce the condition. But once an animal is sold and passes into the non-Jew's domain (*reshus*), the seller loses any ability to ensure that the stipulation is honored. Perhaps Rabbi Yehuda would therefore agree with Rabbi Meir that a conditional sale of an animal is impermissible.

The *gemara* resolves the question with a citation: a *braita* teaches explicitly that Rabbi Yehuda permits selling an animal on condition of immediate slaughter, and the non-Jew may perform the *shechita* himself. Rabbi Meir, consistently, permits sale only of an already-slaughtered animal. The *gemara*'s concern was well-founded — one certainly cannot control what happens once the animal enters the non-Jew's possession — yet Rabbi Yehuda's more permissive general approach to these prohibitions holds even here.

## Geographic Scope

### Israel Restrictions

The *mishna* now makes explicit what was implicit in the earlier material: not only may one not sell land-connected items to non-Jews in the Land of Israel, one may not even rent homes to them. The *mishna* states: *ein maskirin lahem batim b'eretz yisrael* — one does not rent homes to them in the Land of Israel — and this is *ve-ein tzarich lomar sadot* — it goes without saying that fields are even more restricted.

The underlying prohibition is *lo techonem* in the sense of *chaniya bekarka* — granting them a foothold in the land. However, the *gemara* understands that rental alone does not rise to the level of this biblical violation; true *chaniya bekarka* requires an outright sale. Rental is prohibited by rabbinic enactment as a safeguard. One can trace the logic to the episode of Avraham purchasing the *me'arat ha-machpela* from the *Bnei Chet* — the entire elaborate transaction was necessary precisely because acquiring a burial plot signals genuine permanence and rootedness in the land. Rental carries no such permanence, and therefore the biblical prohibition does not apply to it directly.

### Fields vs. Homes

Why are fields more restricted than homes? The *gemara* identifies two distinct issues that attach to a field. The first is *chaniyat karka* — the presence and dwelling concern discussed above. The second is that renting a field to a non-Jew exempts the produce grown there from *terumos u-ma'asros*: once a non-Jew owns or effectively controls the land in the Land of Israel, the grain that grows there loses its obligatory status in tithes.

The *Yerushalmi* frames the distinction somewhat differently, in terms of *yispared* — the field is the source of livelihood and prosperity in an agricultural society, whereas the home is merely where one lives. A field therefore represents a more substantial and weighty presence in the land than a home, and restrictions around fields are correspondingly more severe. Whichever framing one adopts, the asymmetry is clear: a field carries a double weight of concern that a home does not.

### Syria Status

*Surya* — Syria, or the territory conquered by King David beyond the borders of *Eretz Yisrael* proper — occupies an intermediate halakhic status. The *mishna* reflects this: in *Surya*, one may rent homes to non-Jews but may not rent fields.

The *gemara* asks: why can one not sell homes in *Surya*? If the concern is merely rabbinic — a safeguard against conducting such transactions in *Eretz Yisrael* proper — then even renting homes in *Surya* should be prohibited as a further safeguard. The *gemara* responds: *hi gufa gezeira* — renting in *Eretz Yisrael* is itself already a rabbinic safeguard (the real prohibition being sale). To then prohibit renting in *Surya* as a safeguard to that safeguard would be *gezeira ligezeira* — which the rabbis generally do not impose.

But this answer raises a further difficulty: renting a field in *Surya* is also prohibited by Rabbi Meir. If renting a field even in *Eretz Yisrael* is only a rabbinic safeguard against selling, then prohibiting the rental of a field in *Surya* would seem to be *gezeira ligezeira* as well. The *gemara* resolves this by explaining that *Surya* is not treated as one degree removed from *Eretz Yisrael* in the first place — it is treated as functionally equivalent to *Eretz Yisrael*. The *tanna* who authored this position — Rabbi Meir — holds *kibbush yachid shmei kibbush*, that David's individual conquest of *Surya* constitutes a genuine annexation. Therefore *Surya* is halakhically part of the Land of Israel. Prohibiting the rental of a field in *Surya* is thus not a *gezeira ligezeira* at all — it is a straightforward prohibition applying within what is, in effect, *Eretz Yisrael*.

Yet since *Surya* is not *Eretz Yisrael* proper, the rabbis are more lenient with some of the ancillary safeguards. Fields in *Surya* carry the double weight (*tartei*) — the *chaniyat karka* concern and the exemption from *terumos u-ma'asros* — so the rabbis maintain a safeguard there. But homes, which carry only a single concern, are not subject to the same rabbinic stringency in *Surya*, and renting homes is therefore permitted.

### Outside Israel

In *chutz la'aretz* — fully outside the Land of Israel — the *mishna* permits even selling homes and renting fields. The logic follows the same graduated structure: homes, which carry only one concern, receive no rabbinic restriction at all outside Israel, and one may sell them outright. Fields, which always carry the heavier double concern, remain subject to a rabbinic safeguard even in *chutz la'aretz* — one may rent but not sell them. The *gemara* explains this restriction as a *gezeira*: if we permit selling fields outside of Israel, we might come to permit selling fields in the Land of Israel itself. This may strike one as somewhat far-fetched — the fields of Babylonia seem quite remote from the fields of *Eretz Yisrael* — but the safeguard is maintained nonetheless, perhaps limited in its rationale to cases where one owns fields in both places simultaneously, though the *halacha* is not formally restricted to such cases.

### Neighborhood Rule

Even in *chutz la'aretz*, where transactions are broadly permitted, Rav Yosef adds an important qualification: *u-vilvad shelo ya'asenu shechunah* — provided one does not turn the area into a non-Jewish neighborhood. A *shechunah* begins when there are at least three households. One therefore may not sell to enough non-Jews that a distinct non-Jewish enclave forms within the Jewish neighborhood. The concern here is not merely formal halakhic — it reflects the broader communal interest in maintaining the Jewish character of residential areas.

The *gemara* raises a practical concern: what if a Jew sells to one non-Jew, and that non-Jew subdivides his home and sells portions to two more families, creating three non-Jewish households without the original Jewish seller having directly sold to three? Abaye responds that the prohibition extends only to one's direct act — *a-lifnei mifakdinan, a-lifnei dilifnei lo mifakdinan* — we are enjoined against the direct enabling but not against the indirect consequences two steps removed.

## Exceptions

### Domicile Ban

Even in places where renting is permitted — whether to Rabbi Yossi's leniency allowing rental in *Eretz Yisrael* itself, or Rabbi Meir's allowance in *Surya*, or the broader permissions in *chutz la'aretz* — the *mishna* qualifies: *lo l'veit dirah amru*. The permission to rent does not extend to renting as a domicile. One may rent for a storehouse or other non-residential purpose, but not as a place of actual dwelling. The reason: *mipnei shemachnis l'tocho avodah zarah* — because the non-Jew will bring his idols into the home. The verse invoked is *lo tavi to'evah el beitecha* — do not bring an abomination into your house. Since a rented property is still halakhically considered the owner's house — as the *gemara* demonstrated earlier in the tractate when discussing the rental of animals on *Shabbat* — the non-Jew's worship within it constitutes a violation of this verse.

### Bathhouse Ban

The *mishna* adds a further restriction: in every location — even *chutz la'aretz* — one may not rent a bathhouse to a non-Jew. The reason is that the bathhouse continues to be associated with its Jewish owner by name, and when the non-Jew operates it on *Shabbat* and *Yom Tov*, the public perceives it as the Jewish owner's establishment running on *Shabbat*. Unlike the *beit dira* concern, which is rooted in the prohibition of *lo tavi to'evah el beitecha*, the bathhouse concern is distinctly a *Shabbat* violation concern — elaborated upon in the *Tosefta* and in the *gemara*'s subsequent analysis. These two exceptions thus rest on categorically different foundations, a distinction that will be important in the *gemara*'s discussion.

## Field/Home Analysis

### Two-Issue Framework

The *gemara* now examines the *mishna*'s statement that fields are more restricted than homes. The question is: *mai itztarich lemeimar sadot* — why is it obvious that fields are more restricted? The answer lies in the two-issue framework already introduced: *chada haniyat karka* — the presence-in-the-land concern — and *chada dekamfaka lah mi-ma'aser* — the field's exemption from *terumos u-ma'asros* once it passes to non-Jewish control. Fields carry both concerns; homes carry only one.

### Mezuzah Status

The *gemara* presses the point: homes too should have a second concern alongside *chaniyat karka*. Just as renting a field to a non-Jew removes it from the obligation of *terumos u-ma'asros*, renting a home to a non-Jew removes it from the obligation of *mezuzah*. Why then is a home treated as having only one issue? The *gemara* answers through Rav Mesharshia: *mezuzah chovas hadar hi* — the *mezuzah* is the obligation of the one who dwells in the home, not a status intrinsic to the land or structure.

### Tosafot Mezuzah

Tosafot elaborates this distinction with care. By the field, we speak of *kedushat eretz yisrael* — the land itself carries a halakhic status that renders its produce obligated in *terumos u-ma'asros*. When a non-Jew acquires that land, the land's status changes, and even a Jew who subsequently rents it and plants crops on it will find those crops exempt. This is the subject of the debate about *yesh kinyan l'akum l'hafki'ah mi-terumah u-ma'aser*, and this *gemara* proceeds on the assumption that non-Jewish ownership does indeed exempt the produce.

By the house, the situation is structurally different. We do not say that the house is obligated in *mezuzah* — we say that the person who lives in his own home is obligated. If one owns a house and is not living in it, there is no obligation to affix a *mezuzah*. More precisely, according to Tosafot, if one owns a house but rents it to another Jew, the owner is technically not obligated *mid'oraita* in *mezuzah* — because the obligation derives from *beitecha*, your house, and it is not the renter's house. The renter has a rabbinic obligation as the one dwelling there, but not a full biblical one. The non-Jew's entry into the home therefore does not change a status that inhered in the structure itself — there was no independent *mezuzah* status attached to the building to be lost. This is the fundamental asymmetry: fields have an intrinsic land-based sanctity that changes upon non-Jewish ownership; homes do not.

This distinction also bears on the practical question of *mezuzah* obligations in contemporary contexts. A rented apartment, according to Tosafot's framework, carries a rabbinic but not a biblical obligation. And the placement of *mezuzot* on commercial premises — retail stores, office buildings — where no one actually dwells, is without halakhic compulsion, whatever other reasons may motivate the practice.

## Kibbutz Yachid

### Syria Safeguard

Returning to the structure of Rabbi Meir's position, the *gemara* works through why *Surya* follows the rules it does. As established above, Rabbi Meir holds that *Surya* has the same halakhic status as *Eretz Yisrael* proper by virtue of *kibbush yachid shmei kibbush* — David's individual conquest counts as a genuine annexation. This means that selling a home in *Surya* is, in principle, a biblical violation of *lo techonem*, just as in *Eretz Yisrael* proper. Yet the rabbis chose not to impose a safeguard against renting homes in *Surya*, even though renting homes in *Eretz Yisrael* itself is prohibited as a safeguard against selling.

The *gemara*'s reasoning is that one cannot impose a *gezeira ligezeira* — a safeguard to a safeguard. Renting in *Eretz Yisrael* is itself already a rabbinic fence around the biblical prohibition of selling. To then prohibit renting in *Surya* as a further fence would be building a fence upon a fence, which the rabbis decline to do. Fields, however, are treated differently: since they carry the double concern, the rabbinic safeguard is maintained for them even in *Surya*.

There is an interesting subtlety here. If *Surya* were truly halakhically identical to *Eretz Yisrael* in every respect — if it were simply *lo techonem* applied equally — then any distinction between the two would be inexplicable. The *gemara*'s graduated treatment suggests that something beyond the pure *lo techonem* calculus is operating: the practical, communal, and quasi-political concern about where Jewish settlement most needs to be protected. *Eretz Yisrael* proper is treated with maximum stringency; *Surya*, even granting its biblical equivalence, receives somewhat more lenient rabbinic safeguards; and *chutz la'aretz* is treated most leniently of all.

### David's Conquest

The concept of *kibbush yachid* — individual conquest — requires explanation. Rashi understands it as follows: David waged his wars without the authority of the *Sanhedrin* and without the participation of *shishim ribo*, the six hundred thousand who represent *Bnei Yisrael* collectively. The question is whether a king's conquest is his private military achievement or whether it constitutes a conquest in the name of the entire Jewish people. If the land was not conquered as a national enterprise — if David was acting on his own initiative rather than as the representative of the collective — then that land does not become the patrimony of the Jewish people. It is land conquered by a king of Israel, not land conquered by the people of Israel.

Tosafot cites the *Sifrei* and offers a different framework. According to Tosafot, the problem with David's conquest of *Surya* was that he undertook it before *Eretz Yisrael* proper had been fully conquered. The conceptual structure of extending *kedushah* beyond the original borders requires that the base first be complete. If the territorial foundation of *Eretz Yisrael* has not yet been fully secured and settled, one cannot legitimately extend beyond it. There is something inherently problematic — from a priorities standpoint — in expanding outward while the core is not yet consolidated. David's preoccupation with these further territories, before *Eretz Yisrael* proper was fully in hand, renders the conquest structurally defective, and the *kedushah* of *Eretz Yisrael* cannot be extended upon it. Both Rashi and Tosafot agree on the bottom line — *kibbush yachid* does not establish full *kedushah* — but their conceptual accounts of *why* differ substantially and illuminate different dimensions of what makes a conquest nationally valid.

## Rabbi Yossi Lenient

### Yossi in Israel

The *gemara* now considers the opposing position, that of Rabbi Yossi, who rules more leniently at every level. The relevant ruling is recorded: *Amar Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel halacha ke-Rabbi Yose* — the *halacha* follows Rabbi Yossi.

In *Eretz Yisrael* itself, Rabbi Yossi permits renting homes. His reasoning follows the same internal logic as Rabbi Meir applied by *Surya*: homes carry only one concern (*chaniyat karka*), while fields carry two. Where there is only one concern, the rabbis did not impose a safeguard. Fields, carrying two concerns, remain restricted — one may not rent a field even in *Eretz Yisrael*. There may also be a pragmatic dimension to Rabbi Yossi's leniency: the economic realities of a community mean that restricting the rental of homes is simply not sustainable, and perhaps one cannot require people to bear that burden.

### Yossi in Syria

Rabbi Yossi's position on *Surya* diverges sharply from Rabbi Meir's, and this divergence reveals the deeper doctrinal disagreement between them. Rabbi Yossi permits selling homes in *Surya* outright. This is possible only if *Surya* is not treated as *Eretz Yisrael* — because if it were, selling a home there would be a biblical violation. Rabbi Yossi therefore holds *kibbush yachid lo shmei kibbush*: David's individual conquest does not constitute a valid annexation, and *Surya* does not carry the halakhic status of *Eretz Yisrael*.

Since *Surya* is not *Eretz Yisrael*, the biblical prohibition of *lo techonem* does not apply there. The rabbis impose safeguards nonetheless. Fields — carrying the double concern — may be rented but not sold, as a rabbinic safeguard against selling fields in *Eretz Yisrael* itself. Homes — carrying only one concern — are fully permitted, both for sale and rental. The rabbis do not feel that permitting the sale of homes in *Surya* will create a realistic risk of selling homes in *Eretz Yisrael*, and so no safeguard is imposed. In *chutz la'aretz*, Rabbi Yossi permits everything: *keivan demirchak lo gazrinan* — since the distance is great, we do not fear any slippage toward prohibited conduct in the Land of Israel itself.

## Exceptions (II)

### Tosafot Idols

The *mishna*'s exception prohibiting rental as a domicile — on the grounds that the non-Jew will bring his idols into the home — raised a pressing practical question for Tosafot: on what basis did Jews of their era rent and sell homes to non-Jews, including as places of actual residence? The *Tosefta* states that in both *Eretz Yisrael* and *Surya*, one should not rent a home to a non-Jew because it is known that they bring their idol into it — yet then qualifies that one may rent them barns, storehouses, and inns even so. Tosafot grapples with how to reconcile this with actual practice.

One reading of the *Tosefta* is that the distinguishing principle is permanence: when an idol is kept in the home on a fixed, permanent basis (*bikvi'ut*), the prohibition of *lo tavi to'evah el beitecha* applies. But when an idol is brought in only temporarily — as when a traveler stays at an inn — this does not constitute the forbidden "bringing an abomination into your house." On this reading, Tosafot suggests that the non-Jews of their time did not actually maintain idols in their homes on a permanent basis. They might bring in an icon when someone was dying or already dead, but even then they did not perform an act of actual worship; the statue was present for protective or ritualistic reasons, not as an object of formal veneration. Under these circumstances, the domicile restriction would not apply.

Tosafot then considers whether the *Tosefta*'s distinction might instead hinge on the word *beitecha* — "your house" — understood as a place where you yourself dwell. Inns, barns, and storehouses are not *beitecha* in that sense, and the prohibition therefore does not extend to them. But this interpretation offers no relief for the actual practice of renting residential homes, which would still seem to be prohibited.

Tosafot then cites Rabbeinu Chaim Kohen, who brings a proof from the *Yerushalmi*: the implication of the ruling itself — that even where renting is permitted, it is not permitted for a domicile — suggests that in places where selling is permitted, one may sell even for a domicile. One reading of this is that *beitecha* refers only to your genuine home, which is located in *Eretz Yisrael* — a house in *chutz la'aretz* is never truly *beitecha*.
