Tosafot finds this position difficult: does it mean there is no *mezuzah* obligation in *chutz la'aretz* because it is never truly *beitecha*? Ultimately, Tosafot's final resolution leans on the point that *beitecha* with its full biblical force applies only when one is actually living in the house. When the owner rents out the home and vacates, the biblical prohibition may not apply — it becomes only a rabbinic extension — and in that space the rabbis permitted more latitude, particularly in *chutz la'aretz*. As throughout this tractate, the tension between treating Christianity as *avodah zarah* and the practical realities of daily commerce in Christian Europe persisted well into the era of the *Shulchan Aruch* and the *Rama*, with various authorities proposing that perhaps Christians' idolatrous practice carries different weight for non-Jews than for Jews, or that their attachment to their icons is not sufficiently sincere to trigger these restrictions — all ultimately attempts to accommodate lived reality within the halakhic framework.

## Kibbutz Yachid (II)

### Rashi/Tosafot

The debate between Rashi and Tosafot on *kibbush yachid* repays further attention. For Rashi, the issue is one of representational legitimacy: did the king act in his own name or in the name of the nation? A conquest carried out without the *Sanhedrin*'s authorization and without the participation of *shishim ribo* — the full complement that embodies the national will — is a king's private military venture, not a national act. Since the Jewish people did not collectively conquer *Surya*, they have no collective claim to it, and it cannot carry the sanctity of *Eretz Yisrael* which was conquered and settled as a national inheritance.

For Tosafot, the issue is sequential rather than representational: *Eretz Yisrael* proper had not yet been fully conquered and settled when David turned his attention to *Surya*. The conceptual model is one of concentric completion — you must finish the core before the extension can take hold. The *kedushah* of *Eretz Yisrael* cannot spread outward until it has fully saturated the territory God designated as the Jewish homeland. David's premature expansion therefore lacks the foundation upon which *kedushah* can be built, and *Surya* consequently cannot participate in the sanctity of the Land. There is almost a rebuke embedded in Tosafot's reading: the question arises why David was concerning himself with these external territories at all when *Eretz Yisrael* itself had not yet been fully consolidated. That misordering of priorities itself disqualifies the conquest from generating genuine territorial *kedushah*.

## Bathhouse/Field

### Shimon ben Gamliel

A *braita* records the position of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: one may not rent one's bathhouse (*merchatz*) to a non-Jew, because the bathhouse continues to be identified by the owner's name, and the non-Jew will perform labor there on *Shabbat* and *Yom Tov*. The *gemara* notes that the *braita* is formulated as a prohibition specifically with respect to a non-Jew (*oved kochavim*), implying that renting to a *Kuti* (Samaritan) would be permissible, since a *Kuti* would observe *Shabbat*. The *gemara* then asks whether one need be concerned that the *Kuti* will operate the bathhouse on *chol ha-mo'ed*, since *Kutim* do not recognize the *issur melacha* of *chol ha-mo'ed*. The *gemara* dismisses this concern: we ourselves (*anan nami avdinan*) are permitted to heat water for bathing on *chol ha-mo'ed*, so there is nothing problematic about the *Kuti* doing so.

### Sharecropping Logic

A more substantial question follows: if renting a bathhouse is prohibited because the non-Jew's labor on *Shabbat* is associated with the Jewish owner's name, why is renting a field permitted? When a non-Jew is seen working a Jewish-owned field on *Shabbat*, surely the same concern applies — people will assume the Jewish owner directed him to work on *Shabbat*. The *gemara* answers: *arisuta arisuteih ka-avid* — people understand that work in a field is typically done under a sharecropping (*arisus*) arrangement. Sharecropping is sufficiently common in agricultural settings that observers naturally assume the non-Jew working the field on *Shabbat* is a *arisa* — a sharecropper — who works his own schedule, makes his own decisions, and keeps a portion of the harvest. The Jewish landowner's role is that of a passive beneficiary, not an employer directing the worker's Shabbat activity. The critical interpretive lens through which people see the situation is therefore the correct one.

### No Sharecropping

If the field's permissibility rests on the *arisus* presumption, the *gemara* asks, why not apply the same logic to the bathhouse? One could argue that the non-Jew has rented the bathhouse or entered a profit-sharing arrangement, and observers should assume accordingly. The *gemara* responds: *arisuta de-merchatz lo avdi inshi* — profit-sharing arrangements are simply not common for bathhouses. A bathhouse is a highly profitable enterprise, and owners do not typically give up those profits to a *arisa*-style partner. Consequently, there is no established cultural expectation through which observers will naturally read the non-Jew's operation of the bathhouse as anything other than employment by the Jewish owner. When the bathhouse runs on *Shabbat*, people will simply assume that Dov is running his business on *Shabbat*, collecting the fees, and having his workers heat the water — which presents the public appearance of a Jewish enterprise openly operating on *Shabbat*. This is more than a concern about suspecting the owner of a technical *issur de-rabbanan*; it violates the communal experience of *Shabbat* as a whole, analogous to *mechalel Shabbat be-farhesya*.

## Tosafot Framework

### Property Ownership

This *gemara* opens into one of the most practically significant discussions in the tractate for post-Talmudic communities. Tosafot here constructs a comprehensive framework for distinguishing permitted from prohibited arrangements involving non-Jewish labor on *Shabbat*. The *gemara*'s ruling about the bathhouse versus the field raises an obvious question: what about all the other contexts in which non-Jews perform labor on *Shabbat* in association with Jewish-owned enterprises or property — most prominently, the building of a Jewish-owned house?

The foundational distinction Tosafot draws is between work performed on the non-Jew's own property or in his own place of business versus work performed on the Jewish owner's property. When the non-Jew takes the job back to his own workshop — as in the paradigmatic case of *Beit Hillel* permitting one to drop off laundry before *Shabbat*, with the laundryman then working it on his own schedule at his own establishment — there is no visible association with the Jewish owner's name or property, and no *maris ayin* concern arises. When, however, the non-Jew is working visibly on land or property identified with the Jewish owner, the public association becomes the key variable.

### Contractor Logic

Within the category of work performed on Jewish property, Tosafot distinguishes between a day-laborer arrangement and a contractor (*kablan*) arrangement. A day-laborer is paid for each day of work and is presumptively under the Jewish employer's direction — people will naturally assume the owner told him to come on *Shabbat*. A contractor, by contrast, is hired to complete a project for a fixed sum and operates on his own timetable; the Jewish owner has no say in which days the contractor works. The public, sufficiently familiar with how contracting works, will understand that the non-Jew working on a Jewish-owned building on *Shabbat* is doing so on his own decision, not at the direction of the Jewish owner.

This is the basis on which Tosafot rules that a Jew may give a contract to a non-Jew to build his house, even though the work will be performed on *Shabbat*: *maskirim lahem urvot v'otzarot u'fundakaot* — the public interpretation will run through the correct lens of a contractor arrangement, not through the lens of directed Shabbat employment. The bathhouse is disanalogous precisely because no such *arisus* or contractor expectation exists in that context.

### Rabbeinu Tam

Tosafot records that Rabbeinu Tam ruled leniently on the contractor arrangement as a matter of practical *halacha* — *paskening* like Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel that the *arisus* logic applies, and that a contracted arrangement avoids the *Shabbat* concern even on Jewish-owned property. Nevertheless, Tosafot notes that when it came to his own affairs, Rabbeinu Tam maintained a personal stringency: when he was having his own house built, he did not permit the non-Jewish workers to build on *Shabbat*, even though the arrangement was structured as a contract. He ruled permissively for others, but for himself he would not rely on the leniency. The *sugya* thus closes with the image of Rabbeinu Tam navigating precisely the tension this entire passage has explored — between what is formally permissible under the *arisus* and contractor framework, and what the halakhic intuition of a leading *posek* demands of himself in practice.

# Avodah Zarah 22

## Field Rental & Shabbat

### Renting to Samaritans

The Gemara picks up three lines from the bottom of 21b with a *tanya*. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar rules that a person should not rent his field to a *kuti* — a Samaritan — because the field still carries the owner's name, and the *kuti* will perform *melachah* in it during *Chol HaMo'ed*, twice a year, on Sukkot and Pesach.

### Non-Jew vs. Samaritan

This ruling immediately raises a question: but we allow renting to an *oved kochavim*, an idolater — why? The Gemara's answer is that people could tell the *oved kochavim* is an *aris*, a sharecropper, and understand that he works the field in that capacity. The Gemara then pushes back: if so, we can say the same thing about the *kuti* — why not understand him as an *aris* as well? The answer lies in a distinction of visibility and social recognition: the *oved kochavim* is obviously a hired laborer, while the *kuti*, who resembles the Jewish owner more closely, generates greater ambiguity. Therefore it is specifically the *kuti* about whom we are stricter.

### Two Sources

The Gemara then asks: if the prohibition against renting to a *kuti* is due to the field carrying the Jew's name, why not simply derive the prohibition from *lifnei iver lo titein michshol* — the prohibition in Vayikra 19:14 against placing a stumbling block before another? The Gemara answers: *chada ve-od ka-amar* — both reasons are stated, one alongside the other. There are thus two independent sources for the *halachah*: the concern of *lifnei iver*, and the separate concern that the field is *nikret al shemo* — called by the Jew's name — while another performs *melachah* in it.

### Rambam Marit Ayin

The Rambam's ruling on this issue illuminates the practical *halachah*. He writes that if a Jew makes a deal with a non-Jew to build a yard, repair a wall, harvest a field, or plant a vineyard — or hires him for a year or two for such work — and this *melachah* is being performed within the *techum*, in a place where people can observe it, it is forbidden to allow the non-Jew to perform this work on Shabbat. The reason is *mipnei haroim* — because observers do not know the nature of the arrangement and will assume the Jew directed his worker to labor on Shabbat. This is a concern of *marit ayin*.

However, if the work is being done *chutz latchum*, outside the area where people would see it, it is permitted, since there is no one present who might draw the wrong inference.

Rambam further rules that one may lease a vineyard or field to a non-Jew even if the non-Jew will seed and plant on Shabbat, because observers understand that such fields are typically rented out or given over as *arisut*, sharecropping. But if the field carries the Jew's name and it is not the local custom to rent or give such property over in *arisut*, then it is forbidden to rent it to a non-Jew — because the non-Jew will work there on Shabbat while the field is publicly identified as belonging to the Jew.

## Shared Fields Cases

### Saffron Field

The Gemara presents a case: two parties — an *oved kochavim* and a Jew — shared a field of saffron (*karkom*), with the non-Jew working it on Shabbat and the Jew on Sunday. When they came before Rava, he permitted this arrangement.

### Ravina's Challenge

Ravina then challenged Rava from a *baraita*: a Jew and a non-Jew who jointly took on a field may not arrange that the non-Jew takes his share on Shabbat and the Jew takes his share during the weekdays. However, if this was stipulated from the outset (*hitnu mitechila*), it is permitted. If they calculated the arrangement after the fact (*ba'u lecheshbon*), it is forbidden — because this reveals that the Jew is effectively collecting the wages of Shabbat, making it appear that the non-Jew was his agent working on Shabbat.

When Ravina cited this *baraita* to Rava, *ichsif* — Rava was embarrassed. However, it was subsequently revealed (*iglay milta*) that in the original saffron field case the parties had indeed stipulated the arrangement from the beginning, so Rava's ruling was correct after all.

### Orlah Plants

Rav Geviha from Bei Katil recalled this same incident — or a parallel one — differently. In his version, it was not a saffron field but *orlah* plants: a Jew and a non-Jew had jointly taken a field, planted it, and agreed to divide the yield equally. The non-Jew worked the field and consumed the fruit of the first three years of *orlah*, while the Jew received the following three years of permitted produce. When they came before Rava, he also permitted this arrangement.

Rashi explains the case in detail: the *oved kochavim* worked the field and ate whatever he ate during the *orlah* years, and the Jew received the next three years of *heter* in return.

### Cases Distinguished

The Gemara asks whether the *orlah* case is comparable to the Shabbat case, such that one could draw a *ra'ayah* from it. The conclusion is that it is not, because the *orlah* situation involves no prohibition on the Jew's part regarding working the field in this manner — the only restriction is that the Jew may not eat the fruit. There is no prohibition on dividing the field's labor and produce in this way; the non-Jew may eat *orlah*. Therefore, the two cases cannot be compared, and no proof can be drawn from one to the other.

The Gemara then clarifies the role of Ravina's citation of the *orlah* case: rather than objecting to Rava, Ravina came to *support* Rava's ruling. The Gemara notes that the version in which Rava was embarrassed was not accurate — *lo hayu devarim me'olam*. That was not how the story unfolded.

### Tnai vs. Cheshbon

A dilemma is then raised: what is the *halachah* in an unspecified case — *stama* — where the Jew and non-Jew made no explicit condition from the outset and also did not calculate the profit after the fact? The Gemara suggests: come and hear — since *if they stipulated from the beginning it is permitted*, this implies that without any stipulation it is *asur*. But this conflicts with the other clause: *if they came to calculate it is forbidden* — implying that without any calculation it is *mutar*.

The two clauses thus contradict each other on the status of the unspecified case. The Gemara concludes: *ela meha leka l'mishma minah* — no definitive ruling can be derived from this source. The matter remains unresolved, functioning as a practical *teiku*, though the Gemara does not use that term explicitly.

## Second Chapter Intro

### Three Prohibitions

With *Hadran Alach Lifnei Ideihen*, we conclude the first chapter and open the second with its *Mishnah*, which contains three distinct prohibitions. First: we do not leave an animal (*behemah*) in the inn (*pundak*) of idolaters (*ovdei kochavim*), because they are suspected of *reviah* — bestiality. Second: a woman may not be in *yichud* — seclusion — with them, because they are suspected of *arayot*, immoral relations. Third: a man may not be alone with them, because they are suspected of murder.

### Rashi on Payment

Rashi explains *fundekaot* as establishments that take in travelers and charge them for lodging — that is, inns where payment is made. This specification of payment raises a question: what is the relevance of the payment? One suggested answer is that in a setting where a stranger is lodged without payment, there may be a greater sense of entitlement or casual familiarity that would make violations less likely. But even where payment is involved — certainly, *kal va'chomer* — one should not leave the animal there. The Rashi appears to be drawing a contrast: even in the more formal, paid-lodging context, the prohibition stands.

### Bestiality Preview

Tosafot, in the course of the discussion, raises a striking contradiction: the *Mishnah* prohibits leaving one's animal with non-Jewish shepherds, yet practice in Tosafot's own time — and as we will see also within the Gemara itself — was to purchase animals from non-Jews and to entrust animals to non-Jewish shepherds. Tosafot frames this as a genuine difficulty: on what basis do we rely? The resolution of this contradiction will occupy much of the remainder of the *daf*, and it will turn out that the Gemara addresses both challenges simultaneously. The answer, as will be seen, involves the distinction between *lechatchila* and *bedieved* — between ideal practice and the evaluation of a situation after the fact.

## Animal Contradiction

### Purchase Animals

The Gemara immediately raises a formal objection (*u'remihu*) to the *Mishnah*'s prohibition: we have a teaching that one may purchase an animal from a non-Jew for use as a *korban* — a sacrifice — without concern that it may have been used for *reviah*, that it may have been *nirba* (the object of bestiality), that it may be *muktzeh* (set aside for idol worship), or that it may be *ne'evad* (already worshipped as an idol).

This is a direct contradiction. The *Mishnah* says do not leave your animal with non-Jews because of concerns about *reviah*, and yet we have an established teaching that we do in fact purchase animals from non-Jews for the most sacred purpose — *korban* — without these concerns.

### Four Concerns

A *baraita* articulates the four concerns about animals that might disqualify them for use as a *korban*: *reviah*, *nirba*, *muktzeh*, and *ne'evad*. The Gemara works through each one. Regarding *muktzeh* and *ne'evad*, the answer is relatively straightforward: an animal that has been set aside for or actually worshipped as part of idol worship would not be sold by the non-Jew in the first place — it would be kept for that purpose. Therefore those concerns are practically eliminated when an animal is offered for sale.

### Non-Jew Cares

The concern about *reviah* and *nirba* remains. Here, Rav Tachlifa citing Rav Shila bar Avina in the name of Rav provides the key principle: an *oved kochavim* is *chas* — feels concern — for his animal, specifically that she should not become barren (*shelo te'aker*). The premise is that bestiality causes damage to a female animal's reproductive capacity, and the non-Jew, motivated by the desire to preserve the value of his livestock, will not engage in this behavior toward his own animals. This care for his property thus functions as a practical deterrent.

## Female Animals & Shepher…

### Female Barrenness

The concern for *akarot* — barrenness — explains why a non-Jew would refrain from sexually abusing his female animals: the act would cause irreparable damage to her reproductive organs, diminishing the value of his flock. Since the non-Jew's livelihood depends on his animals' fertility, he is motivated not to harm them in this way. This resolves the concern about purchasing female animals from non-Jews.

### Male Deterioration

But what about male animals? Here, Rav Kahana provides a different explanation: *ho'il u'machkhishin babasar* — the animal physically deteriorates from such treatment, becoming lean and weakened. Since a diminished male animal is worth less — both for work and for sale — the non-Jew refrains out of economic self-interest, providing the same practical deterrent as *akarot* does for females.

### Shepherd's Fear

A further *baraita* complicates matters: one may purchase an animal from their shepherds (*mero'eh shelahem*), and we do not worry that perhaps *reviah* occurred. The Gemara asks: should we not be concerned? The answer is that the shepherd fears financial loss (*hefsed secharo*). The shepherd has two related concerns: first, if the animal deteriorates, the flock loses value; second, and more directly, if the owner observes what happened to his animals, the shepherd will not be paid. These dual financial pressures deter the shepherd from harming the animals under his care.

This, however, generates a new tension. If the shepherd's fear of financial loss protects the flock, why does another teaching prohibit entrusting one's own animals to a non-Jewish shepherd? The answer begins to emerge: the shepherd fears loss of *his employer's* animals, but he has no such stake in a Jewish owner's animals placed temporarily in his care. Regarding the Jewish owner's animal, a different dynamic applies — one the Gemara will develop further.

### Non-Jews Know Each Other

Here the Gemara introduces a crucial principle: *inhu di'yad'ei bahadadei mirteti, anan d'la yad'inan behu lo mirteti* — non-Jews, being aware of each other's practices, would recognize the signs of abuse in an animal and hold each other accountable; we, not knowing what to look for, would not identify the problem and therefore cannot deter it. When the non-Jew's employer or peers would notice the harm, his fear of exposure acts as a restraint. When the owner is a Jew who would not recognize the signs, that restraint is absent.

Rava crystallizes this with an idiomatic expression: *machtava glei lei b'za, ragla b'chavreiah yada* — the chisel is apparent to the marble; those who move in the same circles know each other's behavior. The English parallel would be: it takes one to know one. This principle explains why, *vis-à-vis* a Jewish owner, the non-Jewish shepherd is less deterred — we would not recognize what had occurred and therefore cannot serve as a check on his behavior.

## Widow & Dog Case

### No Male Dog

Rav Yosef teaches: a widow should not raise a male dog (*kalba*, not *kalbata*), and she should not allow a single *bar bei rav* — a yeshiva student — to lodge in her home. The first prohibition appears puzzling given the preceding discussion: since a male animal's arousal would disclose the woman's transgression, should this not serve as a sufficient deterrent?

### Dog Arousal & Meat

The Gemara works through the logic. The prohibition against a *bar bei rav* lodging with her is straightforward: since the yeshiva student values his reputation for *tzniut*, if something occurred between them, he would not disclose it. He is, as a person, capable of concealing the relationship. The dog, by contrast, *keivan d'migri bah mirtata* — once aroused, it will follow her in a manner that publicly signals the relationship, thus generating fear that will deter her. On this reasoning, one might think she *should* be permitted to keep a male dog, since his very revealing behavior serves as a deterrent.

Yet the teaching prohibits the dog as well, and an alternative explanation is offered: *keivan d'ki shadya lei umtza u'mashrich batra* — when she throws the dog a piece of meat (*umtza*), it follows her, and people will simply attribute the dog's attachment to the meat rather than to any inappropriate relationship. Since the behavior can be innocently explained, the deterrent effect is neutralized, and therefore the prohibition stands.

### Female-Female Worst

One might then ask: why are we concerned about female animals in the care of female owners? In the cases of male animals with female owners, we noted that the animal would develop an attachment that would expose the woman. So what is the remaining concern?

Mar Ukva bar Chama explains: *ovdei kochavim* are known to frequent their companions' wives' homes. Sometimes when they arrive, they do not find the wife but do find the animal — and they will commit *reviah* with it. And if one wishes to push further: even when they do find the wife, *afilu motzah nami rova* — they will *also* abuse the animal. For, as the teaching states, the animals of Israel are more beloved to them than their own wives.

## Snake & Chava

### Zohama Doctrine

This remarkable statement — that the animals of Israel are more attractive to idolaters than their own wives — leads the Gemara to Rabbi Yochanan's foundational teaching: *besha'ah she-ba nachash al Chava hitil bah zohama* — at the time the snake came upon Chava, he instilled in her a *zohama*, a contamination or impurity. This is a striking *Gemara*. The teaching implies that the snake had an actual physical relationship with Chava, introducing into humanity a form of animalistic contamination that explains, at least in part, the tendencies being discussed throughout this *daf*.

### Textual Proofs

Two textual anchors are brought for this teaching. First, from Bereishit — Chava's declaration *ha-nachash hissi-ani*: Rashi, in Shabbat 146a, notes that *hissi-ani* can be read through the root of *nisu'in*, marriage. If so, the *nachash* had some form of engagement with Chava that resembles a marital relationship. Second, from God's words to the *nachash* following the sin: *ya'an ki asita zot* — because you did *this*. The demonstrative "this" has no other clear referent in the text, suggesting that what the *nachash* did was something beyond mere speech or temptation.

From this, the Gemara derives that humanity as a whole inherited a strain of *zohama* — a contaminating impurity that creates an orientation toward the animalistic. This is offered as the underlying explanation for why idolaters are drawn toward the animals of Israel.

### Sinai as Cure

The obvious question follows: if all of humanity descends from Chava, why are we not equally subject to this *zohama*? The Gemara's answer: *Yisrael she-amdu al Har Sinai paskah zohamatam* — Israel, who stood at Mount Sinai, had their *zohama* removed. *Ovdei kochavim she-lo amdu al Har Sinai lo paskah zohamatam* — idolaters, who did not stand at Sinai, retain it. Sinai functions here as a transformative counter-medicine to the contamination introduced at the beginning of human history. The Gemara elsewhere supports this with the verse from Shir HaShirim: *hinach yafah ra'ayati u-mum ein bach* — you are beautiful, my beloved, and there is no flaw in you.

One might ask what this implies about the generations before Sinai — the patriarchs, matriarchs, and all those who lived before *matan Torah*. The Gemara does not resolve this question here, and it remains an open point.

## Poultry Question

### Poultry Concern

Having worked through the various cases involving *behemot* — large and small animals — the Gemara raises a new question: *iba'it lehu ofot* — what about poultry? Are we concerned about *reviah* with fowl? The question is significant because we also take certain *ofot* as *korbanot*, and the same logic that applied to animals would seem to apply here.

### Goose Incident

Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel in the name of Rabbi Chanina offers testimony: *ani ra'iti* — I personally saw an *oved kochavim* who took a goose from the market, committed *reviah* with it, then choked it, roasted it, and ate it. This eyewitness account is brought as evidence that the concern about poultry is real and not hypothetical.

### Meat Incident

Rabbi Yirmiya from Difti then offers his own testimony, which is even more striking: *ani ra'iti* — I saw an *Arvi* (a member of the mixed tribes of the region, not to be identified with any modern people) who took a thigh — a piece of meat — from the market, fashioned it for the purpose of *reviah*, performed the act with it, then roasted and ate it. This account moves beyond a living bird to an already-dead piece of flesh, escalating the severity of what was witnessed.

### Lechatchila-Bedieved

Ravina then provides the resolution that draws together the contradictions of the entire *daf*: *Ravina amar la kashya — ha lechatchila, ha bedieved*. There is no difficulty. One ruling speaks to *lechatchila* — the ideal, prospective standard — while the other speaks to *bedieved* — the evaluation of a specific case after the fact, or when the transaction is already before us.

This is the key to reconciling the *Mishnah*'s prohibition with the established teaching that we purchase animals from non-Jews for *korbanot*. *Lechatchila*, we are concerned and therefore should not entrust our animals to non-Jewish shepherds or leave them in non-Jewish inns. *Bedieved* — when we are evaluating a particular animal that is now before us for purchase, the various considerations established throughout the *daf* (the non-Jew's concern for *akarot*, the male animal's *hekchesh*, the shepherd's fear of financial loss) give us sufficient grounds to conclude that in all likelihood this specific animal was not harmed. Therefore the animal may be purchased and brought as a *korban*.

The Gemara notes that this resolution is not complete, and the discussion continues into the next *daf*. But the essential framework is in place: the two bodies of teaching are not in contradiction — they operate on different planes of the same *halachic* question.

---

---

# Avodah Zarah 23

## Ethical Context

### Intro & Perek 2

Daf 23 marks our entry into the second *perek* of Avodah Zarah, which continues to elaborate on prohibitions governing interaction with the surrounding non-Jewish world, now moving explicitly into areas of a sexual and physical nature. We had already encountered a preliminary form of this concern on the previous daf, where the *mishnah* prohibited the sale of *behema daka* to non-Jews and the *gemara* explained that this was rooted in a concern over *riva'ah* — acts of bestiality. The current *perek* addresses these concerns more directly: an animal should not be left in a non-Jew's stable, a woman should not be in *yichud* with a non-Jew because of the concern of rape, and a man should not be in *yichud* because of the concern of murder.

### Prejudice & Fear

At this point in the learning, it is worth pausing to acknowledge the genuine discomfort these passages provoke. Concerns about commerce, about selling weapons, about building structures — even about land ownership — were all, however one interprets their ongoing applicability, at least rooted in a recognizable historical reality of persecution. But here, in the assumption that every non-Jew is searching for an opportunity to commit murder, rape, or bestiality, something qualitatively different is happening. The *yichud* concerns around rape and murder are, at least, somewhat understandable as a defensive posture born of real fear. People who see the outside world as hostile and their own community as safe will naturally be more guarded when venturing out. Rape and murder do occur, and a community that has experienced violence at the hands of outsiders may seek to minimize exposure.

### History vs. Today

The *riva'ah* concern, however — the assumption that non-Jews are constantly seeking opportunities to engage in acts of bestiality with animals, and specifically with Jewish-owned animals — is something else entirely. *Tosafot* himself will later note that he is not sure where the *gemara* draws this idea from. What makes this particularly troubling is not the historical emergence of the concern. One can understand, with a degree of sympathy, how a beleaguered community projects aberrant sexuality onto a threatening "other" — this is a well-documented human tendency. What is more troubling is the downstream effect: when such assumptions are absorbed into the *yeshiva* curriculum, learned year after year, they can quietly shape a generalized attitude toward non-Jews that outlasts whatever historical circumstances gave rise to the original fear. That is, the issue is less the historical genesis of the concern than its continuing internalization as received *halacha* and *hashkafa*. With that framing in mind, let us proceed to the *gemara* itself — where, as we shall see, the conclusion may turn out to be more measured than the premise.

---

## Ravina: Lechatchila/Bedi…

### Future vs. Past

The *gemara* on 23a opens with Ravina's answer to the apparent contradiction between the *mishnah*, which prohibits leaving an animal in a non-Jew's stable (out of concern for *riva'ah*), and the *baraita*, which permits purchasing animals from non-Jews for use as *korbanot*. *Lo kashya*, says Ravina — there is no difficulty. *Ha lechatchila, ha bedieved*: the distinction is between prospective concern and retrospective assessment. We are concerned about what might happen in the future, and therefore we do not leave the animal in the stable; but we do not assume that something already happened, and therefore we do not disqualify an animal purchased from a non-Jew for use as a sacrifice.

### Chezkat Chayim

The question immediately arises: in what sense is this a genuine *lechatchila*/*bedieved* distinction? Ordinarily, *bedieved* leniency is justified by the concrete loss that would result from invalidating a *fait accompli*. But here, there is no significant loss — if one cannot buy a sacrificial animal from a non-Jew, one simply buys it from a Jew instead. So why should the *bedieved* framework apply?

The answer lies in a different dimension of the *lechatchila*/*bedieved* distinction, one that the *gemara* in Gittin makes explicit. There, the rule is *shema yamut chayyishinan, shema meis lo chayyishinan* — we are concerned that someone might die, but we do not assert that he is already dead. The classic application: if a husband instructs that a *get* be delivered to his wife, we deliver it without worrying that the husband has died in the interim; but if the *get* is conditional on taking effect a moment before his death, we cannot deliver it, since at any moment could be that fatal moment. The asymmetry is not about loss — it is about the nature of assertion. To worry about a future possibility is legitimate and prudent. To affirmatively assert that a person's status has changed, overturning his *chezkat chayim*, is a different legal act entirely. The same principle applies here: to say "we are concerned something might happen to this animal" is reasonable caution; to say "we will assume something already happened" is to make a positive claim that overturns the animal's presumptive status. That, Ravina holds, we do not do.

---

## Woman Seized Debate

### Yichud Prohibition

The *gemara* now attempts to derive a proof for Ravina's distinction from the *mishnah*'s prohibition on *yichud*. Our *mishnah* states: *lo tisyacheid isha imahem mipnei shechashudim al ha'arayot* — a woman may not be alone with non-Jews because they are suspected of sexual violations. Against this, the *gemara* cites a *baraita* presenting two distinct scenarios. In the first, a woman is seized by non-Jews as leverage to recover a debt owed by her husband (*al yedei mamon*): she is permitted to return to her husband, and — as *Tosafot* notes — this applies even if her husband is a *kohen*, meaning we do not assume she was raped. In the second scenario, she is seized because she herself has been condemned to death (*al yedei nefashos*, as Rashi glosses: *shenischayeva hariga*): in that case she is forbidden even to a husband who is a plain *Yisrael*. The reasoning in this second case is that, facing execution, she may have chosen to trade sexual compliance for her life — a situation the *gemara* regards as *ratzon* rather than *ones*, notwithstanding the profound coercive context of such a "choice."

### Challenge to Ravina

The *gemara* challenges Ravina: if the *mishnah* prohibits *yichud* out of concern for rape, why — in the first scenario, where the woman was indisputably held in the captors' custody — do we not assume she was raped and forbid her to her *kohen* husband? This seems to support Ravina's principle: *lechatchila* we are concerned, but *bedieved* we are not. *Ela lav shema mina* — can we not infer from here that there is indeed a distinction between *lechatchila* and *bedieved*?

### Economics Protects

The *gemara* deflects this proof. *Dilma l'olam eima lach afilu bedieved nami* — perhaps even after the fact we would normally be concerned. The reason we are not concerned in the *mamon* case is not a general *lechatchila*/*bedieved* principle but rather a specific economic consideration: *d'mistapai mishum hefsed mamona*. The captor who is holding the woman to extract a debt from her husband has a financial incentive not to harm her. If he rapes her, the husband may reason that his wife has been "damaged" and refuse to pay the ransom. The captor's self-interest thus functions as a structural protection. By contrast, *Tosafot* notes that the *baraita* presents only two of three logically possible scenarios. A third case — a woman seized for no particular reason, neither *mamon* nor *nefashos* — is omitted, and in that case we would indeed be concerned after the fact, both for rape and for willing compliance. The *gemara* confirms this reading from the *seifa* of the *baraita* itself: the fact that she is forbidden when seized *al yedei nefashos* demonstrates that absent the protecting factor of economic self-interest, we do assume that sexual contact occurred. *V'su lo midi* — the *gemara* regards this as dispositive.

---

## Tosafot & Ashkenaz

### Ashkenazi Women

Having resolved the challenge to Ravina, the *gemara* proceeds. But *Tosafot*, commenting on the phrase *v'su lo midi*, raises a concern of immediate practical urgency for the Ashkenazi world. If even a brief period of *yichud* with a non-Jew suffices, in principle, to raise a concern of rape after the fact — such that a woman would be forbidden to her *kohen* husband — then *Tosafot* poses a startling challenge: *im kein lo hinachta bas l'Avraham Avinu, eishes Kohen yosheves tachas ba'alah*. If we take this rule seriously, there is not a single wife of a *kohen* who could remain with her husband. Why? Because, writes *Tosafot*, *d'ee efshar shelo tisyached im shum oved kochavim sha'a achas* — it is simply impossible in their society that a woman will never find herself alone with a non-Jewish man, even for an hour.

This is a remarkable window into medieval Ashkenazi reality. The assumption underlying *Tosafot*'s objection is that women in Ashkenaz were actively engaged in the public sphere — not confined to the domestic world as was more characteristic of Sefardic society at the time. Women in Ashkenaz participated in commerce and business, which inevitably meant private meetings with non-Jewish men.

### Isha Hashuvah

This reality had already left its mark elsewhere in *Tosafot*'s rulings. The *gemara* states that a woman need not recline (*haseiba*) at the Pesach Seder because her posture of submission to her husband means that reclining would not express genuine freedom — unless she is an *isha hashuvah*, a woman of recognized social standing, in which case she does recline. *Tosafot* there applies this exception universally in Ashkenaz, stating that all Ashkenazi women are *nashim hashuvot*. The elevated social and economic status of women in Ashkenazi society was sufficiently acknowledged that *Tosafot* could make this claim categorically. The same reality surfaces here: women who conduct business with non-Jews will, on occasion, find themselves alone with them.

### Business vs. Captivity

*Tosafot*'s resolution is to distinguish between *yichud* in a business context and captivity. *D'davka nishbis shani* — it is specifically the case of being taken captive that is different, *lefi shehi mesurah b'yado*, because then the woman is entirely at the captor's mercy, removed from the normal social and commercial context, with no exit and no recourse. A private business meeting, by contrast, does not carry the same presumption. *Tosafot* holds that after the fact, in a business setting, we do not assume rape occurred. He does not, it should be noted, attempt to justify the *lechatchila* violation of the *mishnah*'s prohibition on *yichud*. He acknowledges that the *mishnah* prohibits it and does not argue otherwise — his concern is only with the *bedieved* consequence. The practical resolution, of course, is that *lechatchila* one takes whatever measures are available — an open door, a glass partition, a third party present — to avoid *yichud* in the first place.

---

## Rabbi Eliezer Dispute

### Bestiality Dispute

With the *lechatchila*/*bedieved* approach of Ravina having been effectively challenged, the *gemara* turns to a second answer, proposed by Rabbi Padat. *Lo kashya*, says Rabbi Padat — the apparent contradiction between the *mishnah* and the *baraita* is not a logical tension at all. *Ha Rabbi Eliezer v'ha Rabbanan* — the two sources simply reflect a *machloket* between Rabbi Eliezer and the *rabbanan* as to whether we are concerned about acts of *riva'ah* at all.

This is itself a striking move. Up to this point in the sugya, the concern over bestiality has been treated as an unquestioned premise of the *mishnah* — a given, to be resolved and worked around, but not itself contested. Now Rabbi Padat proposes that this concern is not universal rabbinic consensus but rather a *da'at yachid*, the position of Rabbi Eliezer alone, with the *chachamim* holding that we are not concerned.

At this juncture it is worth pausing on a terminological question. The text as it stands uses the term *ovdei kochavim*, which is a censored formulation introduced in the Middle Ages. The original *girsa* of the *gemara* was simply *goy*. The substitution might suggest that the concern was specifically with idolaters, which could open a conceptual door: perhaps the rabbis were not characterizing all non-Jews this way, but only the specific pagan populations of their era, whose immorality they believed they had observed. However, there is nothing in the *gemara* itself that links the *riva'ah* concern to the fact of idolatry as such — no suggestion that these acts were performed as pagan ritual or that the concern would dissolve for non-idolaters.

The more systematic resolution along these lines is offered by the *Meiri*, who employs the formulation *gedurim b'darkei hadatot vehanimusim* — nations that are restrained by the disciplines of religion and civil morality. The *Meiri*'s argument is that the ancient pagans about whom the *gemara* legislated were characterized by a generalized moral dissolution, and that the *gemara*'s concerns were grounded in that reality. When dealing with non-Jews who live by moral codes — Christians, Muslims, and others who accept civilized norms — the *Meiri* holds that these concerns simply do not apply. *Tosafot*'s answers, by contrast, tend to be more localized: specific reasons in specific cases for why a particular practice is not followed in his time. The *Meiri* offers the global framework.

### Parah Adumah

The evidence for Rabbi Padat's claim is drawn from a *baraita* concerning the *parah adumah*. Rabbi Eliezer says one may not purchase an animal for the *parah adumah* ritual from non-Jews, while the *chachamim* permit it. The *gemara* proposes: *mani lav beha kamiflegi* — is this not precisely the debate between them? *Rabbi Eliezer savar chayyishinan l'revia* — Rabbi Eliezer holds we are concerned about acts of bestiality; *rabbanan savri lo chayyishinan l'revia* — the *rabbanan* hold we are not.

---

## Final Resolution

### Tosafot's Use

Before the *gemara* tests this proposed resolution, it is worth noting how *Tosafot* deploys it practically. On the previous *daf*, *Tosafot* confronted the question of why, in his time, Jews left their animals in the stables of non-Jews without concern — seemingly in violation of the *mishnah*. *Tosafot*'s ultimate answer was precisely this final resolution of the *gemara*: since the debate is between Rabbi Eliezer and the *chachamim* over whether to be concerned about *riva'ah* at all, and since the *halacha* follows the *chachamim*, we rule that there is no concern for such acts. For *Tosafot*, this is not an evasion but a clean *pesak*: the *mishnah*'s prohibition reflects Rabbi Eliezer's minority position, and the majority view of the *chachamim* — that we are not concerned — is the operative ruling.

---

## Burden Question

### Burden Hypothesis

The *gemara* now interrogates whether the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the *rabbanan* is actually about *riva'ah* at all. *Mimai* — how do we know that is the point of contention? The *gemara* floats an alternative: *dilma d'kulei alma lo chayyishinan* — perhaps everyone agrees we have no concern about acts of bestiality, and the dispute is about something entirely different, namely, whether a non-Jew may have put a burden on the animal. As Rav Yehudah said in the name of Rav, even placing a bundle of sacks on the animal — without it pulling any load — invalidates it, since the verse states *asher lo ala aleha ol*, that no yoke has gone upon it. For the *egla arufa*, the verse says *asher lo mashcha be'ol*, which requires actually pulling a burden. Perhaps the debate between Rabbi Eliezer and the *rabbanan* is simply whether we are concerned that a non-Jew may have momentarily placed something on the animal, thereby disqualifying it.

### Burden Rejected

The *gemara* rejects this hypothesis with a straightforward argument: *mishum hana'a purta lo mafsid tuva* — no rational person would risk losing something worth tens or hundreds of thousands of *dinarim* for one moment's trivial use. If a non-Jew happens to possess a *parah adumah*, which could be sold for an extraordinary sum, he would never jeopardize that value by carelessly placing a burden on it. This concern, therefore, need not be entertained.

### Bestiality Only

The *gemara* then asks: why does the same logic not dismiss the *riva'ah* concern? Should we not equally say that a non-Jew would not risk such a valuable animal for a moment's gratification? The *gemara* answers: *hatam yitzro tokfo* — there, his *yetzer hara* overcomes him. Unlike placing a burden, which offers no compelling psychological pull, the sexual drive can override rational calculation. Thus the only coherent explanation for the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the *rabbanan* remains whether we are concerned about *riva'ah*. The burden hypothesis is untenable; the *riva'ah* hypothesis stands.

---

## Everyone Not Concerned

### Verse Reason

The *gemara* makes a second attempt to argue that everyone agrees there is no concern for *riva'ah*, proposing instead that Rabbi Eliezer's reason for prohibiting purchase of the *parah adumah* from a non-Jew is textual. *Ki-detani Shila* — as Shila taught: the verse states *daber el benei Yisrael veyikchu elecha parah adumah temimah* — speak to the children of Israel and have them take for you an unblemished red heifer. The derivation: *benei Yisrael yikchu ve'ein ovdei kochavim yikchu* — it is the children of Israel who are to take it, not non-Jews. On this reading, Rabbi Eliezer's prohibition is a straightforward *derashah* on the verse, with no implication of any concern for bestiality.

### All Sacrifices

The *gemara* immediately challenges this: *de-katani seifa, ve-chen haya Rabbi Eliezer posel be-chol ha-korbanot kulan* — a *seifa* of the *baraita* states that Rabbi Eliezer would disqualify all sacrificial animals purchased from non-Jews, not only the *parah adumah*. This is precisely the position that conflicts with the *baraita* cited earlier, which permits buying animals for *korbanot*.

### Bestiality General

If Rabbi Eliezer's reason were purely textual — anchored in the verse *daber el benei Yisrael* unique to the *parah adumah* — there would be no basis for extending his prohibition to other sacrifices, where no such verse exists. *Bishlama parah, ktiv bah kicha* — for the *parah adumah*, the verse does say "take" from *benei Yisrael*. *Ela kuleihu korbanot, kicha ktiv behu?* — but does any such verse exist for other sacrifices? It does not. Therefore, the extension of the prohibition to all *korbanot* cannot be grounded in a specific verse. It must reflect a general concern — and the only coherent general concern is *riva'ah*. The attempt to frame the dispute as purely exegetical collapses.

---

## Final Resolution (II)

### Only R. Eliezer

The *gemara* now arrives at its conclusion. The dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the *rabbanan* is indeed over whether to be concerned about acts of *riva'ah*. Rabbi Eliezer holds that we are so concerned, and therefore prohibits both leaving animals in non-Jewish stables and purchasing animals from non-Jews for sacrificial use. The *rabbanan* hold that we are not so concerned, and therefore permit purchasing animals for *korbanot* — and by extension, the prohibition in the *mishnah* against leaving animals in non-Jewish stables represents Rabbi Eliezer's view. The practical *halacha*, as *Tosafot* concludes, follows the *chachamim*.

---

## Bestiality Invalidates

### Red Heifer Status

With the primary dispute resolved, the *gemara* turns to a structural question: how can an act of *riva'ah* invalidate a *parah adumah* in the first place? We know from a classic *midrash halakha* that *riva'ah* and *avoda zarah* disqualify animals from use as *korbanot*, derived from the phrase *min hatzon korbano* — from the flock and not all the flock. But the *parah adumah* is not a *korban* in the conventional sense. It is slaughtered outside the Temple precincts; it is burned, not offered on the altar. What is its precise sanctity?

### Sacrifice Sanctity

The *gemara* considers the possibility that the *parah adumah* possesses *kedushat mizbeach* — sacrificial sanctity, the same category of holiness as an animal brought to the altar. If so, whatever invalidates a *korban* would naturally invalidate the *parah adumah* as well, including *riva'ah*.

### Temple Only

The *gemara* raises the counter-possibility: perhaps the *parah adumah* has only *kedushat bedek habayit* — the more general sanctity of objects consecrated for Temple use but not for the altar. An animal consecrated for non-sacrificial Temple purposes — say, for the *kohanim* to use for transportation — would not be invalidated by an act of *riva'ah*, since that disqualification pertains specifically to sacrificial holiness. If the *parah adumah* has only this lesser sanctity, *riva'ah* should not affect it.

### Called Chatat

The *gemara* resolves the question by pointing to the Torah's own language: *shani parah d'chatas karya rachmana* — the *parah adumah* is different, because the Torah itself calls it a *chatat*. The verse reads *l'mei niddah chatat hi* — it is a sin offering. The *gemara*'s position is nuanced: the *parah adumah* does not possess full *kedushat mizbeach* for all purposes, but because the Torah designates it a *chatat*, the invalidating conditions that apply to a *chatat* apply here as well. This is a functional rather than ontological equivalence — for the specific purpose of determining what disqualifies it, the Torah's terminology controls.

---

## C-Section Question

### C-Section Test

The *gemara* now tests whether this reasoning is fully consistent. If the *parah adumah* shares the invalidating conditions of a *chatat*, it should also be invalidated by *yotzei dofen* — birth by Caesarean section. Ordinary sacrifices require natural vaginal birth, derived from the verse *ki shor o chesev o ez ki yivaled*, where *yivaled* is understood to mean birth from the place of conception, excluding C-section birth. Accordingly, if the *chatat* framework governs invalidation of the *parah adumah*, a *parah adumah* born by C-section should similarly be disqualified.

### C-Section Debate

The *gemara* cites a *baraita* that addresses precisely this question. According to the *chachamim*, a *parah adumah* born by C-section is indeed invalid (*pesulah*). According to Rabbi Shimon, it is valid (*machshir*). The *chachamim*'s position coheres smoothly with the *chatat* framework: just as C-section birth invalidates a *korban*, it invalidates the *parah adumah*. Rabbi Shimon's validation requires explanation.

### R. Shimon General

The *gemara* initially proposes that Rabbi Shimon is simply consistent with his general position: *d'amar yotzei dofen velad maalya hu* — Rabbi Shimon holds that a C-section birth is a fully valid birth in all respects, and does not distinguish it from vaginal birth in any area of *halacha*. The classic illustration is the law of *yoledet*: the Torah says *isha ki tazria v'yalda zachar v'tam'a shivas yamim*, and the rabbis derive that the *tumah* of a *yoledet* applies only to vaginal birth — *ad sheyalda mimakom shemazraas*. Rabbi Shimon disagrees, holding that the *parsha* applies even to a C-section birth. Perhaps, then, Rabbi Shimon simply never treats C-section birth as categorically different.

### R. Yochanan

This solution is undermined, however, by a ruling of Rabbi Yochanan. *Modeh hayah Rabbi Shimon l'inyan kodashim she'eino kadosh* — Rabbi Yochanan states that Rabbi Shimon himself concedes that for the purposes of *kodashim*, a C-section animal is not sanctified as a sacrifice. Rabbi Shimon's general position does not extend to *korbanot*; even he agrees that for ordinary sacrificial animals, C-section birth is a disqualification. This creates a problem: if Rabbi Shimon agrees that C-section birth disqualifies normal sacrifices, and if the *parah adumah* is governed by the same invalidating conditions as a *chatat*, why does Rabbi Shimon validate a C-section *parah adumah*?

---

## Blemish Answer

### Physical & Ritual

The *gemara* resolves this through a reconceptualization of what invalidates the *parah adumah*. According to the *chachamim*, one might explain the *parah adumah* as possessing *kedushat mizbeach*, which would mean all sacrificial invalidities — including C-section — apply to it straightforwardly. Rabbi Shimon, however, does not treat the *parah adumah* as having sacrificial sanctity. For him, the operating invalidating principle is *mum* — physical blemish. The Torah requires the *parah adumah* to be *temimah*, unblemished. Since *mum* invalidates, and since Rabbi Shimon extends the concept of *mum* beyond physical defect to include what might be called ritual blemish, a broader but still bounded category of invalidities applies.

### Corruption Blemish

The textual basis for treating acts of *riva'ah* and *avoda zarah* as constituting a *mum* is the verse *ki moshchasam bahem mum bam* — their corruption is in them, their blemish is in them. The verse identifies *hashchasah* (corruption) with *mum* (blemish). The *gemara* then invokes a *midrash* from the school of Rabbi Yishmael to define what *hashchasah* means.

### R. Yishmael

*Vetana devei Rabbi Yishmael: kol makom shene'emar hashchasa, eino ela davar ervah ve'avoda zarah* — wherever the Torah uses the root *hashchasah*, it refers either to sexual perversion or to idolatry. Two prooftexts anchor this: for sexual perversion, *ki hishchis kol basar es darko al ha'aretz* — all flesh had corrupted its way upon the earth (the classic rabbinic reading of the generation of the Flood as having engaged in, among other perversions, acts of bestiality). For idolatry, *pen tashchisun va'asisem lachem pesel* — lest you act corruptly and make for yourselves an idol. The conclusion: acts of forbidden sexuality and acts of idolatrous worship both constitute a *hashchasah*, and by the equation of *hashchasah* with *mum*, they constitute a ritual blemish on the animal. It is this *mum* that, for Rabbi Shimon, disqualifies the *parah adumah* — not its sacrificial sanctity, but the specific requirement of *temimah* interpreted to include the absence of ritual corruption.

---

## Shila Verse

### Verse Reason

The *gemara* now returns, in a section labeled *gufa*, to examine Shila's teaching in its own right. *Mai ta'ama de-Rabbi Eliezer?* — what is Rabbi Eliezer's actual reasoning for prohibiting purchase of the *parah adumah* from non-Jews? Shila teaches: *dechsiv daber el benei Yisrael veyikchu* — the Torah says speak to the children of Israel and have them take — *benei Yisrael yikchu ve'ein ovdei kochavim yikchu*, the children of Israel are to take it, and not non-Jews. On Shila's reading, Rabbi Eliezer's prohibition is a direct derivation from this verse, entirely independent of any concern over *riva'ah*.

### Terumah Challenge

The *gemara* immediately challenges this: *daber el benei Yisrael veyikchu li terumah* — the Torah also says speak to the children of Israel and have them take for Me a donation (*terumah*). Does this mean, by the same logic, that donations for the *Mishkan* may only be accepted from Jews, not from non-Jews? *Hachi nami de-benei Yisrael yikchu ve'ein ovdei kochavim yikchu?* Would Rabbi Eliezer hold that one cannot accept a non-Jew's contribution to the Temple building fund? The *gemara* considers the possibility — *v'chi teima hachi nami*, maybe so — but then raises a decisive counter-example.

---

## Dama ben Netina

### Filial Piety

The *gemara* introduces the story of Dama ben Netina in the context of Rabbi Eliezer's own teaching. Asked how far the obligation of *kibud av va'em* extends, Rabbi Eliezer responds: *tze'u ur'u mah asah oved kochavim echad la'aviv be'Ashkelon* — go and see what a certain non-Jew in Ashkelon did for his father. The choice to cite a non-Jewish exemplar is itself notable. Rabbi Eliezer appears to be pointing to something universal in the moral architecture of filial piety — something so deeply embedded in the fabric of human ethics that even one not commanded in *kibud av va'em* will enact it at great personal cost.

### Dama's Choice

The non-Jew is identified as Dama ben Netina. The *chachamim* came to purchase precious stones for the *eifod* from him. They were prepared to pay 600,000 *dinarim* — and according to Rav Kahana's version of the story, 800,000. The keys to the warehouse, however, were under the head of Dama's sleeping father. Dama refused to disturb his father's sleep, and the transaction fell through at the cost of an enormous sum. The *poskim* note, with some wryness, that presumably Dama's father would have wished to be woken for such a deal — which is why these extreme stories of *kibud av va'em* are sometimes understood as illustrating an exceptional standard beyond strict obligation rather than a normative ruling. But for purposes of the *gemara*'s argument, what matters is the outcome: the *chachamim* intended to purchase the *avnei eifod* from this non-Jew.

### Ephod Problem

This creates a difficulty for Shila's reading of Rabbi Eliezer. The *avnei milu'im* — the *avnei eifod* — appear in the same passage as the *terumah*: *vezos haterumah asher tikchu me'itam*, this is the donation you are to take from them — followed by a long list of materials including, at the end, *avnei shoham ve'avnei milu'im*. If the verse *daber el benei Yisrael veyikchu* limits contributions to Jews alone, how could the *chachamim* have purchased the *avnei eifod* from Dama ben Netina? And since Rabbi Eliezer himself is the one who cites this story approvingly, he cannot simultaneously hold that such a purchase was impermissible.

---

## Unresolved

### Contradiction

The *gemara* attempts to resolve the difficulty by noting that *avnei shoham* appears in the list without a preceding *vav* — *avnei shoham* rather than *ve'avnei shoham* — suggesting a syntactic break that might exclude this item from the limiting scope of *benei Yisrael yikchu*. However, the *gemara* immediately rejects this: *ve-ha ve'avnei milu'im kesiv dahadar arbeih* — the very next item, *ve'avnei milu'im*, does have a *vav*, which reconnects it to the earlier list and brings it back within the limiting phrase. The *vav* of *ve'avnei milu'im* reassimilates the entire unit into the *benei Yisrael* clause.

The *gemara* thus leaves us with an unresolved tension: Rabbi Eliezer, on Shila's reading, derives a prohibition against purchasing the *parah adumah* from a non-Jew from the verse *daber el benei Yisrael veyikchu*. Yet the same linguistic logic, applied to the *terumah* passage, would prohibit accepting the *avnei eifod* from a non-Jew — and Rabbi Eliezer himself approvingly recounts the story of their purchase from Dama ben Netina. The *gemara* ends here, without resolution, leaving this as the cliffhanger that will open the next session.

---

---

# Avodah Zarah 24

## Rabbi Eliezer's Prohibit…

### Intro & Dama Story

Daf 24 continues to grapple with the fundamental question of purchasing animals from non-Jews for use as sacrifices, and with the concerns about acts of bestiality that animate so much of this discussion. The previous daf concluded with the remarkable story of Dama ben Netinah — the ethically exemplary non-Jew who declined to disturb his sleeping father even to retrieve the precious stone needed for the *efod*, and who thereby forfeited a substantial profit. That narrative served as a striking counterbalance to the rather unflattering portrait of non-Jewish morality that had dominated the preceding discussion.

### Rabbi Eliezer & Verse

The story of Dama was introduced into the Gemara for a specific halachic reason. Rabbi Eliezer holds that the *parah adumah* may not be purchased from a non-Jew, deriving this from the verse *daber el bnei Yisrael veyikchu elecha parah adumah* — "Speak to the children of Israel and let them take for you a red heifer." The Gemara had pressed this position by noting a parallel verse concerning *terumah* — *daber el bnei Yisrael veyikchu li terumah* — and yet we know that *terumah* can come from non-Jews. This led into the Dama story, since the very end of that narrative involves the sages purchasing a *parah adumah* from him.

### Gemara's Challenge

The Gemara now presses further. Reading the continuation of the Dama story in the *baraita* on daf 24a, we find that the following year a *parah adumah* was born in Dama's flock, and the sages came to him. He said to them: "I know that if I were to name any price in the world you would pay it — but all I ask is that you reimburse me for the loss I suffered on account of my father." In the end, they purchased the *parah adumah* from him. This constitutes a direct challenge to Rabbi Eliezer: if the verse *veyikchu* requires that the purchase be made specifically from a member of *bnei Yisrael*, how could the sages have acquired it directly from a non-Jew?

### Middleman Solution

The Gemara resolves this: *hatam al yedei tagrei Yisrael zavnu* — they did not purchase it directly from Dama; rather, a Jewish merchant served as an intermediary. Dama sold to the Jewish middleman, and the Jewish middleman in turn sold to the Temple. The verse *daber el bnei Yisrael veyikchu* thus governs only the direct acquisition by the Temple itself, which must be from a Jew. The non-Jewish original owner remains permissible so long as the formal purchase is transacted through a Jewish party. In this respect the *tagrei Yisrael* functions as a kind of "sale Jew" — a Jewish cutout who *kasher*s the transaction, analogous in structure (if not in subject matter) to the familiar concept of a *shabbos goy*.

---

## Rabbi Eliezer's Concerns

### Bestiality Question

At this point the Gemara raises what is really the more fundamental question. A student might well ask: even granting that the verse is satisfied by using a Jewish middleman, what about the concern regarding acts of bestiality? If Rabbi Eliezer's objection to purchasing animals from non-Jews extends — as the *baraita* establishes — to all sacrifices and not merely to the *parah adumah*, then the concern cannot be rooted in the verse alone, since that verse is specific to the *parah adumah*. Evidently the broader prohibition on purchasing any sacrificial animal from a non-Jew must rest on a distinct concern: that non-Jews perform acts of bestiality with their animals, which would invalidate those animals for sacred use. If that is the case, then routing the purchase through a Jewish middleman solves nothing — the animal was still owned and presumably abused by the non-Jew.

The Gemara makes this explicit by quoting the *baraita* more fully. When the sages challenged Rabbi Eliezer — "But there was a case in which they purchased a *parah adumah* from a non-Jew named Dama!" — Rabbi Eliezer responded: *Yisrael hayu u'mishamrim otah mishe'noldah* — Jews were watching over it from the moment it was born, ensuring that no such act was ever performed upon it. This line is not addressing the verse issue at all; it is addressing the bestiality concern. And as Tosafot notes, Rabbi Eliezer's response here presupposes both issues simultaneously.

### Tartei — Twin Concerns

The Gemara draws the explicit conclusion: *Rabbi Eliezer tartei it leh* — Rabbi Eliezer has two distinct concerns operating in parallel. The first is the textual restriction of *kichah* — the requirement derived from *veyikchu* that the formal acquisition be by *bnei Yisrael*. This concern is specific to the *parah adumah*. The second is *vi'yah* — the concern about acts of bestiality — and because of this concern, Rabbi Eliezer extends his prohibition to all sacrificial animals.

### Both Issues Applied

The practical consequence of Rabbi Eliezer holding both concerns simultaneously is that the *parah adumah* presents a double requirement. For ordinary sacrifices, the bestiality concern can be resolved by having a *mashgiach* — a Jewish supervisor who monitors the animal from birth to ensure no prohibited act is performed. If that has been done, the animal may be purchased directly from the non-Jew (subject to the Rabbis' permissive position, of course). But for the *parah adumah*, resolving the bestiality concern through *mashgiach*-supervision is insufficient on its own — one must *also* transact the purchase through a Jewish middleman, on account of the independent textual requirement. Both problems must be solved; neither alone is sufficient.

---

## Bestiality & Pregnancy

### Fetus Contamination

The Gemara now takes the analysis considerably further. Even granting that the sages had stationed a Jewish supervisor to watch the animal from birth, there is a residual concern: what if the mother had been subjected to an act of bestiality while she was pregnant? The fetus, after all, was present in the womb at that moment. On the principle of *ubar yerech imo* — that the fetus is considered a limb of the mother, a single halachic unit — one might argue that an act done to the mother while she was pregnant was, in a meaningful sense, done to the fetus as well.

### Rava's Principle

Rava articulates this principle explicitly. He states: *vlad nogachat asurah* — if a cow that gores has a fetus in her womb, both she and her fetus are treated as having performed the goring (*hi v'valdah nagchu*). Similarly, *vlad hanirbaat asurah* — if an act of bestiality is performed upon a pregnant animal, the fetus is treated as having been subjected to that act as well (*hi v'valdah nirbu*). This is a striking application of *ubar yerech imo* that carries the taint of the act directly into the next generation, so long as the act occurred during the pregnancy.

Assuming Rabbi Eliezer accepts Rava's principle, it follows that simply watching the animal from the moment of its birth would be inadequate. One would have had to watch the *mother* during the period of her pregnancy, to ensure that nothing was done to her in that critical window. This complicates the scenario enormously: how did the supervisors know which animal to watch during pregnancy, before they knew the animal would give birth to a *parah adumah*?

### Invalidity Transfer

The Gemara anticipates a possible rejoinder. The *Mishnah* teaches that *kol hapesulim legabei mizbe'ach* — all animals that are themselves disqualified for the altar — have offspring that are *mutar*, permitted. In other words, if the mother's invalidity does not transmit to her offspring, then even if the mother was subjected to bestiality before she became pregnant, her offspring would be unaffected. If so, the concern reduces only to acts during the actual pregnancy, which is a much narrower window.

But the Gemara immediately notes that Rabbi Eliezer himself disputes this ruling and holds that the invalidity *does* transmit to the offspring. This reopens the problem: according to Rabbi Eliezer, even if the act occurred prior to the pregnancy, the resulting offspring would still be tainted.

### Transmission Debate

Rava, citing Rav Nachman, offers a crucial qualification. The debate over whether invalidity transmits to offspring, he says, applies specifically when the mother incurred her invalidity while she was already *mukdash* — sanctified as a Temple animal. But if the mother was *chullin* — unsanctified, as would certainly be the case here — then *divrei hakol mutar*: everyone agrees the invalidity does not transmit. This would neatly resolve the problem; since the mother of the *parah adumah* was never sanctified, acts done to her before pregnancy would not affect her offspring.

However, Rav Huna bar Chinena reads Rav Nachman's report differently. According to his version, the debate between the Rabbis and Rabbi Eliezer applies specifically when the mother was *chullin*, and Rabbi Eliezer holds that even in the unsanctified state, the invalidity transmits. If the mother was *mukdash* when she incurred the invalidity, everyone agrees it transmits. This is a considerably more stringent reading of Rabbi Eliezer's position, and it reopens the problem fully.

### When Watching Begins

According to Rav Huna bar Chinena's version of the dispute, simply watching the mother during the pregnancy is not sufficient — Rabbi Eliezer's position would require that one have monitored the mother from the moment of *her* own conception, to ensure that no act of bestiality was ever performed on her. And indeed the Gemara arrives at precisely this formulation: *Yisrael hayu mishamrim otah le'imah mishe'notzrah* — Jews watched over the mother from the moment the mother herself was conceived. At which point the Gemara asks the inevitable follow-up: what about the mother of the mother? To this the Gemara responds, *kulei hai lo chaishinan* — we do not extend the inquiry that far back. There is, in other words, a point at which the chain of suspicion must terminate — the grandmother's generation is beyond the scope of the concern.

---

## Red Heifer Breeding

### Mother's History

Even having established that the inquiry terminates at the grandmother's generation, a new question presses: if the sages were monitoring the mother from the moment of the mother's own conception, how did they know in advance which animal to monitor? A *parah adumah* is an extraordinarily rare phenomenon. What gave them reason to station a supervisor next to a particular cow during pregnancy, before they had any indication that the offspring would be a *parah adumah*?

### Red Cup Method

Rav Kahana offers an answer: *kos adom ma'avirin lefaneyha besha'ah she'oleh aleha hazachar* — they would pass a red cup before the animal at the moment of conception, while the male was mounting the female. The ancient belief — familiar from the story of Yaakov in Bereishit — was that whatever the female animal perceived visually at the moment of conception would influence the coloration of the offspring. By ensuring the animal was looking at something red, one could engineer a red offspring with some reliability. This is why the breeders would know to watch a particular animal: they had deliberately induced a red calf.

This belief enjoyed wide currency in the ancient world and extended to human beings as well. The Gemara elsewhere records that Rabbi Yochanan would position himself near the *mikveh* so that women leaving to rejoin their husbands would see his famously beautiful face, and their children would inherit his looks. The Yaakov story itself is more nuanced: Yaakov may have been attempting to use this technique, but the angel's subsequent revelation suggests that the actual result was brought about by divine intervention, not by the sticks and visual stimuli Yaakov had deployed.

### Expense Problem

The Gemara immediately raises an objection to Rav Kahana's explanation: if the red cup technique reliably produces red offspring, why were *parah adumah* animals so extraordinarily expensive? If any farmer could simply hold a red cup before his cow at conception and produce a red heifer, the market should be flooded with candidates and the price should be negligible.

### Genetic Selection

The resolution is that it is one thing to produce a red cow, and quite another to produce a cow that is *perfectly* red — one that lacks even two black hairs, since two black hairs suffice to disqualify the animal. The red cup technique might yield a generally reddish animal with some frequency, but a cow that is *completely* free of black hairs is a matter of genetics, not visual stimulus alone.

Rav Kahana therefore adds the concept of *muchzeket* — a known genetic line. The sages would identify a family of cattle with a proven track record of producing deeply, uniformly red offspring, and it was this genetic pedigree that gave them reason to station supervisors next to a particular animal. The red cup technique could improve the odds of redness, but only a *muchzeket* line could give confidence that the offspring would be flawless enough to qualify. In practical terms, this means the red cup explanation can largely be set aside as the primary rationale: the sages knew which animals to watch because they had identified the right genetic lineage, and the history of that line justified the investment of supervision going back, in some versions of the concern, to the mother's own conception.

---

## Challenges to R. Eliezer

### Ami & Nappacha

The Gemara now shifts to a broader challenge to Rabbi Eliezer's position. Rav Ami and Rav Yitzchak Nappacha were sitting together on Rav Yitzchak Nappacha's *kila* — Rashi explains this as a kind of antechamber or porch before the main room. One of them opened the discussion in an expansive, *midrashic* mode (*patach chad minayhu v'amar*), stating that Rabbi Eliezer's disqualification applied to all sacrificial animals without exception.

### Kedar Flocks Verse

The other then asked: but what did Rabbi Eliezer's colleagues say in response to his position? The obvious challenge comes from the verse in Yeshayahu: *kol tzon Keidar yikavtzu lach* — all the flocks of Kedar shall be gathered to you. These are the animals of the Ishmaelite tribes, and the verse clearly anticipates their being brought as sacrifices. If Rabbi Eliezer prohibits purchasing animals from non-Jews for sacrifice, how does he read this verse?

### Messianic Conversion

Rabbi Eliezer's answer is sweeping: *kulam geirim gerurim heim le'atid lavo* — in the messianic future, all the nations will have converted. The animals of Kedar will be brought as sacrifices, but by that time those who bring them will be full Jews, and the animals will have been raised and supervised in accordance with Jewish law. The verse is not describing the present legal order but the transformed reality of the End of Days.

This response opens onto one of the great theological questions of Jewish eschatology: what is our vision of the messianic era? Is it a world in which everyone becomes Jewish? A world in which Jews remain Jews and non-Jews remain non-Jews but all acknowledge God? Or — most radical of all — a world in which even the distinction of Jews and their particular *mitzvot* is dissolved, in line with the opinion that the *mitzvot* will be *batelot le'atid lavo*, abrogated in the future perfect world?

### Worship Question

Rav Yosef cites the verse: *ki az ehpoch el amim safah berurah likro kulam besheim Hashem* — "For then I will transform the nations to speak a pure language, that they may all call upon the Name of God." Abaye challenges this: perhaps the verse means only that the nations will abandon idolatry (*mei'avodas kochavim*), without adopting the full obligations of Jewish observance — in which case the bestiality concern would remain relevant. Rav Yosef responds: *le'ovdo shechem echad* — "to serve Him with one shoulder." The nations will serve God in complete unity with Israel, implying that they will observe all the *mitzvot* and will be, in every meaningful sense, indistinguishable from Jews in their religious obligations. The Gemara then notes that Rav Pappa and Rav Zevid each taught variant versions of which of these figures raised the question and which provided the answer, but the substantive content is consistent between the versions.

### Historical Cases

The Gemara turns from eschatological verses to historical cases, and presses Rabbi Eliezer with a series of biblical episodes where it appears that animals owned by non-Jews were used as sacrifices. The first is Moshe's demand of Pharaoh: *gam ata titein b'yadeinu zvachim v'olos* — you too shall provide us with animals for sacrifices. Rabbi Eliezer's answer is *kodem matan Torah shani* — that was before *matan Torah*, when the relevant restrictions had not yet come into force.

The second case is Yisro: *vayikach Yisro chosein Moshe olah u'zvachim l'Elohim* — Yisro took a burnt offering and sacrifices to God. Rabbi Eliezer can deploy the same answer if Yisro came before *matan Torah*. But the Gemara notes that this depends on a well-known dispute. The narrative of Yisro's arrival is positioned before *matan Torah*, yet the events described — Moshe sitting in judgment over the people, administering *chukei Elohim v'torosav* — only make sense after *matan Torah*. Tosafot (and Ramban on the Torah) resolve this by suggesting that Yisro arrived before *matan Torah* but the narrative encompasses events that occurred after: the Torah reports his arrival in full rather than splitting the story across the account of Sinai. If Yisro came before *matan Torah*, the pre-Sinaitic exemption applies; if he came after, the answer is that Yisro purchased the animals from Jews — *Yisro miYisrael zavin* — just as in the case of Dama.

The third case is Shaul and the Amalekites. Shmuel confronts Shaul: what is the sound of the sheep and cattle I hear? The people had spared the best of the Amalekite flocks, ostensibly *lema'an zvo'ach l'Hashem Elokecha* — in order to sacrifice them to God. Rabbi Eliezer reads *meitav* creatively: rather than bringing the animals themselves as sacrifices, the plan was to sell them and use the proceeds to purchase sacrificial animals (*ki heichi delikftzu alaihu zvini*). This is candidly a strained reading, but it allows Rabbi Eliezer to avoid a direct contradiction.

The fourth case is Aravna the Jebusite, who offered David his cattle directly for an *olah*. Here Rav Nachman supplies the answer: *Aravna ger toshav hayah* — Aravna was a *ger toshav*, a resident alien who had formally accepted the seven Noahide commandments.
