The sexual prohibitions are among those laws, and therefore there was no concern that his animals had been subjected to acts of bestiality. This is a relevant distinction: the concern about non-Jewish animals is not about idolaters per se — the Gemara had established on the preceding daf that mere recognition of God does not resolve the concern — but about those who have formally undertaken the *sheva mitzvot bnei Noach*, which include the relevant sexual prohibitions.

The Gemara also pauses to explain the *morigim* — the threshing implements — that Aravna offered alongside his cattle. Ulla explains: a *mita shel Turbil*, a bed of toothed pegs. Rav Yosef locates the term in the verse in Yeshayahu: *hinei samtich lemorag charutz chadash ba'al pipiyot* — behold I have made you like a new sharp threshing sledge full of teeth — and the subsequent verses confirm its use for crushing grain out of husks.

---

## Age Threshold

### Gevul Principle

Rabbi Yochanan now introduces a more measured position that occupies a middle ground between Rabbi Eliezer's blanket prohibition and the Rabbis' apparent blanket permission. *Gevul yesh lah* — there is a boundary to the Rabbis' permissive ruling. The Rabbis permit purchasing animals from non-Jews on the reasoning that non-Jews will not subject their own animals to acts of bestiality, since doing so renders the animals infertile and economically worthless. If that is the logic, then it has natural limits defined by age.

### Infertility Logic

The principle Rabbi Yochanan articulates is: *pachot mibat gimmel shanim ne'ekeret* — a female animal under three years old becomes infertile if subjected to such an act. Because non-Jews are motivated by economic self-interest to protect the fertility of their animals, they will not perform such acts on animals younger than three years. It is therefore safe to purchase animals under three years old from non-Jews, since the concern is operationally neutralized.

### Three-Year Cutoff

*Bat gimmel shanim einah ne'ekeret* — once an animal reaches three years, such an act will no longer render it infertile. At that point, the economic deterrent no longer operates, and one must therefore worry that non-Jews will perform such acts with animals of that age. Accordingly, animals three years old and older may not be purchased from non-Jews for sacrificial use.

### Verse Challenges

This position is then challenged by all the same verses that challenged Rabbi Eliezer — Moshe's demand of Pharaoh, Yisro's sacrifice, the Amalekite spoils, Aravna's cattle, the Philistine cows. The straightforward answer to the first set of these challenges is simple: *shani lehu pachot mibat gimmel shanim* — in all those cases, the animals involved were under three years old. That resolves the cases. But one case resists this answer.

---

## Philistine Cows Prob (II)

### Offspring Evidence

The Philistine cows present a specific difficulty that the three-year answer cannot address. The biblical narrative specifies that when the Philistines sent the *aron* back on the cart pulled by the cows, their calves were kept penned up at home. The cows, remarkably, did not turn back toward their young but proceeded straight to the Israelite camp. However, if these cows already had calves, they had already given birth — and if they had already given birth, they were necessarily older than three years, since, as the Gemara is about to establish, cows cannot give birth before three years of age. This directly contradicts Rabbi Yochanan's three-year solution.

---

## Age Threshold (II)

### Case Resolution

The Gemara's initial response to the Philistine cow problem is the same answer it gave to the other cases: those cows were under three years old. But this answer immediately generates a contradiction, as the subsequent discussion will show.

---

## Philistine Cows Prob (II)

### Bechor Status

The Gemara cites a *Mishnah*: if a cow or donkey gives birth within its third year (*mibat gimmel*), the offspring is definitively a *bechor* — a firstborn — and goes to a *kohen*. The logic is that, prior to three years of age, a cow cannot have given birth; therefore if she gives birth in her third year, this must be her first birth, and the calf is certainly a *bechor*.

### Age Contradiction

The problem is now fully articulated. If cows cannot give birth before three years — as the *Mishnah* assumes — then any cow that has already had a calf must be at least three years old. The Philistine cows had calves. Therefore they were at least three years old. Therefore Rabbi Yochanan's three-year cutoff cannot be used to rescue this case: these cows were already beyond the age limit.

### Special Ruling

The Gemara concludes: *ela michvarta kedishinu me'ikara* — the better answer, and the answer we should have stayed with from the beginning, is the one given for Rabbi Eliezer: *hora'at sha'ah hayah* — it was a special divine ruling for that moment, not governed by the ordinary rules. The Gemara confirms this reasoning: *hachi nami mistavra* — this indeed makes sense — because the cows were female and an *olah* ordinarily requires a male animal. The violation of two distinct rules simultaneously — a female *olah*, and an animal from non-Jews over three years old — makes it evident that the entire episode constituted a *hora'at sha'ah*, a temporary divine dispensation.

The Gemara considers whether the female issue alone might be resolved without recourse to *hora'at sha'ah*, by invoking the latitude of *bamot yachid* — private altars, which existed before the *Beit HaMikdash* and permitted females as *olot*, as demonstrated by Rav Adda bar Ahava from the verse about Shmuel's sacrifice. But this avenue is ultimately set aside, and the *hora'at sha'ah* answer stands as the *michvarta* — the clearest and most satisfying resolution.

### Nature Changed

Before moving on, the Gemara's assumption that cows cannot give birth before three years old invites a comment from Tosafot that touches on a methodological issue of broad importance. Tosafot observes that in their own time (*me'aseh bechol yom*) it was entirely routine for a cow of two years to give birth. If so, how can the Gemara's assumption — that birth before three years is impossible — be accepted?

Tosafot's answer invokes the principle of *nishtanah ha'et* — the times have changed. The biological reality of cows in the era of the Gemara was different from what Tosafot observed in their own world. This principle, sometimes formulated as *nishtanah hateva*, is not itself a Talmudic concept but emerged in the Geonic period as a tool for reconciling the empirical claims of the Gemara with observable reality. When the Gemara's descriptions of the natural world diverge from what later authorities saw, two responses are possible: either the rabbis were mistaken about the science, or the natural world has genuinely changed. Rambam held without hesitation that the rabbis were not granted supernatural knowledge in matters of science and could err in empirical claims — *mada'* was not transmitted from Sinai. Many *rishonim*, however, were reluctant to attribute error to the rabbis in areas that bore on *halacha*, and therefore preferred the *nishtanah hateva* answer.

Tosafot here adopts the *nishtanah hateva* approach and cites parallels elsewhere in the Talmud where similar divergences appear. It should be noted that in some cases this answer has genuine plausibility: when the Gemara addresses agricultural or zoological phenomena specific to the climate and fauna of Mesopotamia, *rishonim* living in France or Germany were sometimes dealing with genuinely different sub-species or growing conditions. In other cases — the classic example being the Gemara's permission to kill lice on *Shabbat* on the grounds that they reproduce by spontaneous generation — the *nishtanah hateva* answer strains credulity, since spontaneous generation was never a biological reality. For those cases, the more candid response is that the rabbis accepted the prevailing scientific understanding of their era, which happened to be incorrect.

---

## Cows' Song

### Vayisharnah

Having discussed the Philistine cows at length, the Gemara concludes the daf with a *midrashic* excursus on a single word in that biblical narrative. The verse states: *vayisharnah haparot baderech al derech Beit Shemesh* — the cows went straight (*yashar*) on the road toward Beit Shemesh, bringing the *aron*. The Gemara reads *vayisharnah* not merely as "going straight" but through a wordplay on *shirah* — song. The cows, on this reading, opened their mouths and sang as they pulled the *aron*.

### Song Dispute

A dispute breaks out among the Tannaim over what song the cows sang. Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Meir says they sang *Az yashir Moshe u'vnei Yisrael* — the Song of the Sea, the great song of triumph over Egypt's army. This reading emphasizes the defeat of an enemy: just as the Egyptians suffered for oppressing Israel, so the Philistines suffered for seizing the *aron*.

Rabbi Yochanan himself (in his own name, as opposed to in the name of Rabbi Meir) says they sang *Va'amartem bayom hahu hodu l'Hashem kiru bishmo* — "And you shall say on that day: give thanks to God, call upon His Name." This is a song of thanksgiving for salvation rather than a song of victory over enemies.

Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish says they sang what he calls a *mizmor yasom* — an orphan psalm. This is a psalm in *Tehillim* that lacks the standard introductory attribution: it begins neither with *Mizmor l'David* nor *livnei Korach* nor any statement of authorship or purpose. It launches directly into its content. The *mizmor* in question — *Mizmor shiru l'Hashem shir chadash ki niflaot asa* — celebrates God's wondrous deeds and salvation, again emphasizing divine praise.

Rabbi Eliezer says the song was *Hashem malach yirgezu amim* — God reigns, let the nations tremble. Rav Shmuel bar Nachmani says it was *Hashem malach ge'ut lavesh* — God reigns, He has clothed Himself in majesty.

### Nappacha's Version

Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha's version stands apart from all the others, as he does not cite an existing verse from *Tanach* but rather a distinct poetic composition. The song he attributes to the cows — or, as we will shortly see, to the Israelites — reads as follows: *Roni roni hashitah* — sing, sing, O acacia tree, from which the *aron* was fashioned. *Yitnofi berov hadrech* — be exalted in your magnificent glory. *Hamuchsheket berikmei zahav* — adorned with golden filigree. *Hamehulala bidvir armon* — praised in the *dvir armon*, the inner sanctuary. *Umefuara ba'adi adiyim* — and glorified with precious jewels.

The phrase *dvir armon* typically refers to the inner sanctuary of the *Beit HaMikdash*, but since the *Beit HaMikdash* had not yet been built at this point in the narrative, the Gemara will resolve this by reading *dvir* in a different sense — which leads directly into the etymological excursus at the daf's conclusion.

### Rav Ashi's Reading

Rav Ashi clarifies that the song attributed to Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha was not, in fact, the song the cows sang. It was the song the Israelites sang. The verse *vayehi binsoa ha'aron vayomer Moshe* — "And when the *aron* set out, Moshe would say, *Kuma Hashem*" — describes Moshe's words as the *aron* began to move. The Gemara then asks: what did the Israelites say in response? Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha's poetic composition, on this reading, was the Israel people's song of greeting to the *aron*, not the cows' song. The cows' song is the subject of the Tannaitic dispute above; Rabbi Yitzchak's song belongs to a different occasion entirely.

### Persian Etymology

Having read *dvir armon* in Rabbi Yitzchak's song as referring not to the Temple chamber but to something written — the *luchos* or the Torah scroll housed in the *aron* — the Gemara pauses for a brief etymological note. Rav asks: on what basis did the Persians adopt the word *dvir* to mean a book? The Gemara answers: *meihacha* — from the verse *veshem haDvir lifnim Kiryat Sefer* — "and the former name of Dvir was Kiryat Sefer." Since *sefer* means a book and the place was also called *Dvir*, the word *dvir* acquired the connotation of a written text. This explains how Persian came to use *dvir* for a book.

Rav Ashi appends a parallel question: why did the Persians call a *niddah* — a menstruant woman — *dashtana*? The answer is traced to the verse in which Rachel says to Lavan, *ki derech nashim li* — "for the way of women is upon me." The word *dashtana* is linked to *derech nashim* through shared consonants. The Gemara notes that this Persian term for a menstruant woman was indeed used in some of the Geonic literature as an alternative term for *niddah*, preserving the Aramaic-Persian linguistic bridge that the Talmud here traces to a biblical source.

---

---

# Avodah Zarah 25

## Sun Standing Still

### Sefer HaYashar Intro

The daf opens mid-discussion of miraculous episodes connected to earlier topics — specifically the debate between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani — and continues with a series of *drashot* on scriptural passages. The first of these concerns the miracle of the sun standing still for Yehoshua during his war against the kings of Canaan. The relevant verse reads: *vayidom hashemesh vayarei'ach amad ad yikom goy oyvav* — the sun was still and the moon stood in place until the nation took vengeance from its enemies — and the text adds: *halo hi k'tuvah al Sefer HaYashar* — behold it is written in the Book of the Upright.

The Gemara immediately asks: *mai Sefer HaYashar* — what is this Book of the Upright?

### Sefer HaYashar Identity

Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *zeh sefer Avraham Yitzchak v'Yaakov* — this is the book of Avraham, Yitzchak, and Yaakov, meaning Sefer Bereishit, *shenikru yesharim* — for the Patriarchs were called *yesharim*, upright. The proof text is Bilam's declaration: *tamut nafshi mot yesharim* — let my soul die the death of the upright. Since that verse praises Bnei Yisrael and refers to individuals of distinguished righteousness, it presumably refers to the Patriarchs themselves.

### Ephraim Blessing Hint

The Gemara then asks: *v'heicha r'miza* — if the miracle of the sun standing still for Yehoshua was indeed recorded in *Sefer HaYashar*, where exactly is it hinted in Bereishit? The answer is found in the blessing of Ephraim: *v'zaro yihye mlo hagoyim* — his descendants shall be the fullness of the nations. Yehoshua descended from Ephraim. *Eimatai yihye mlo hagoyim* — when would Ephraim's descendant fill the world? *B'sha'ah she'amdah lo chamma l'Yehoshua* — at the hour the sun stood still for Yehoshua, for then all the nations came to know of this miracle.

### Two Standing Moments

Returning to the miracle itself, the Gemara draws attention to two distinct moments described in the passage: *vaya'amod hashemesh b'chatzi hashamayim* — the sun stood at the center of the sky, meaning at midday — and *v'lo atz lavo k'yom tamim* — and it did not descend like a full day. The Gemara understands that the sun paused both at the height of noon and again at the point of setting, and asks: *v'kamma* — how long, in total, did it stand still?

### 24-Hour Standing

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says: twenty-four hours in total. The sun traveled six hours to reach midday, stood for six hours, traveled another six, and then stood again for six before setting. The entire passage of the sun across the sky — what would normally have been twelve hours — took twenty-four. This is the meaning of *k'yom tamim*: the whole event lasted a full day.

### 36-Hour Standing

Rabbi Eliezer disagrees and says the entire day was thirty-six hours. In his reading, the sun traveled six hours, stood for twelve, traveled another six, and then stood again for twelve at the point of setting. *Amidato k'yom tamim* — the standing itself was like a full day, meaning twenty-four hours of standing in total, on top of the normal twelve hours of travel, giving thirty-six.

### 48-Hour Standing

Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani says the entire day was forty-eight hours. The sun traveled six, stood twelve, traveled six, and then stood twenty-four before setting — *v'lo atz lavo k'yom tamim* — it did not move to set for a full day, meaning twenty-four hours. Since the verse implies the standing before setting was the full *yom tamim* of twenty-four hours, and the earlier standing was a separate and distinct episode, we infer it was half that — twelve hours. The two *pesukim* are in parallel: *vaya'amod b'chatzi* and *v'lo atz lavo k'yom tamim* — and Rashi attempts to explain how the derivation of twelve hours for the midday standing follows from that parallel, though the inference is admittedly not entirely explicit.

### Tosefta Reinterpretation

A second version of this debate is introduced: *ika d'amrei b'Tosefta* — some say, according to a *Tosefta*, that the figures of twenty-four, thirty-six, and forty-eight were not the total length of the day but the *additional* hours beyond the normal twelve. Under this reading, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's twenty-four means the sun stood an extra twelve at midday and an extra twelve before setting — *amidaso k'yom tamim*, the total standing amounted to a full day — giving thirty-six hours altogether for the day. Rabbi Eliezer's thirty-six means an additional twelve at midday and twenty-four before setting, for a total of forty-eight hours in the day. Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani's forty-eight means an additional twenty-four at each point — *makish amida l'vi'ah*, the standing at midday is equated with the standing at setting, both being twenty-four hours — giving a total of sixty hours for the entire day. Every opinion accordingly yields a number twelve hours larger than its counterpart in the first version of the debate.

---

## Moshe & Yehoshua Miracles

### Three Recipients

A *tanna* teaches: just as the sun stood still for Yehoshua, so too it stood still for Moshe and for Nakdimon ben Guryon. That the sun stood for Yehoshua is clear from the verses already cited. The miracle performed for Nakdimon ben Guryon is a tradition — a *gemara* — whose details are elaborated elsewhere, in Masechet Taanit. Nakdimon ben Guryon is, notably, a commoner in this context, not one of the great biblical figures, which makes his inclusion in this list striking. What requires derivation is the claim that a comparable miracle was performed for Moshe.

### Gezera Shava Links

The Gemara asks: *l'Moshe minalan* — what is the source that the sun stood still for Moshe? The answer is a *gezera shava* linking Moshe to Yehoshua. The word *acheil* — I will begin — appears in the context of Moshe's war against Sichon king of Emori and Og king of Bashan: *acheil teis pachdicha* — I will begin to give your fear before the nations. The same word appears in the promise made to Yehoshua: *acheil gadlicha* — I will begin to make your name great. Since the same miraculous context applies to Yehoshua's *acheil*, the same applies to Moshe's.

Rabbi Yochanan offers a different *gezera shava*, based on the word *teis* — to give. By Moshe: *acheil teis pachdicha* — I will give your fear. By Yehoshua: *b'yom teis Hashem es haEmori* — on the day God gave the Emori before you. Since both verses use the same root in connection with miraculous divine intervention, the parallel miracle is derived from that shared language.

### Shmuel bar Nachmani

Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani says there is no need for a *gezera shava* at all — the derivation can be made from the *pasuk* itself. The verse by Moshe concludes: *asher yishm'un shim'acha v'ragzu v'chalu mipanecha* — all who hear your report shall tremble and fear before you. The question is: *eimatai ragzu v'chalu mipanecha* — what event would cause that trembling and fear? It must be *b'sha'ah she'amdah lo chamma l'Moshe* — at the moment the sun stood still for Moshe. That fearsome celestial event is what made Moshe's reputation spread among the nations in the way the verse describes, paralleling precisely the miraculous effect the sun's standing had in the case of Yehoshua.

### Uniqueness Challenge

The Gemara raises a challenge: *v'lo haya k'yom hahu lifanav v'acharav* — there was no day like that one before it or after it. The verse by Yehoshua explicitly states that this miracle was unprecedented. Yet here we are saying that Moshe preceded Yehoshua with a similar miracle, and Nakdimon ben Guryon followed him with another. How can it be called unprecedented?

Two answers are offered. First: *sha'os hu d'lo havo nefishei kulei hai* — the uniqueness was in the number of hours. Yes, the sun stood for others, but for no one as long as it stood for Yehoshua. Second, and perhaps more telling: *avnei barad lo havo* — the hailstones were not present for Moshe. By Yehoshua, the miracle was not merely the sun standing still; it was accompanied by a miraculous barrage of great stones from the heavens: *v'Hashem hishlich aleihem avanim gedolos min hashamayim* — God hurled great stones upon them at the descent of Beit Choron until Azeka, and they died. That combined miracle — sun and hailstones together — was never replicated, neither before nor after. The Gemara thus preserves the uniqueness of Yehoshua's miracle while allowing the tradition that the sun had also stood still, in some form, for others. One senses the Gemara is navigating a delicate point: it does not wish to entirely overshadow Moshe, yet it allows Yehoshua his moment of singular greatness, as the verses indeed present it.

---

## Yehudah Archery

### Archery Teaching Intro

The Gemara now turns to another passage that mentions *Sefer HaYashar*, this one from Shmuel Bet: *vayomer l'lamed b'nei Yehudah kashet hinei k'tuvah al Sefer HaYashar* — and he said to teach the children of Yehudah archery; behold it is written in the Book of the Upright. Again the Gemara asks: *mai Sefer HaYashar* — what is this book? The same question that arose in the context of Yehoshua's miracle now recurs, and the three Amoraim offer three different answers.

### Yochanan: Bereishit

Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *zeh sefer Avraham Yitzchak v'Yaakov* — this is Sefer Bereishit, as before, since the Patriarchs were called *yesharim*. The supporting verse is the same: *tamut nafshi mot yesharim*. The question then follows: *v'heicha r'miza* — where is it hinted in Bereishit that the children of Yehudah would be archers? The answer is found in the blessing Yaakov gave Yehudah: *Yehudah atah yoducha achecha* — Yehudah, your brothers will praise you — and: *yadcha b'oref oyvecha* — your hand is against the neck of your enemy. The Gemara asks: *v'eizu hi milchamah she'tzrichah yad k'neged oref* — what type of warfare requires the hand to be against the back of the neck? The answer: archery. When drawing a bow, the hand that pulls the string back reaches behind, toward the nape of one's own neck. Thus *yadcha b'oref* alludes to the archer's draw, and this is the hint in Bereishit that archery is Yehudah's domain.

### Eliezer: Devarim

Rabbi Eliezer says: *zeh Sefer Mishneh Torah* — here, *Sefer HaYashar* refers to Devarim. Why is Devarim called the book of the *yashar*? Because Devarim opens the moral mandate with the words *v'asita hayashar v'hatov* — you shall do what is right and good in the eyes of God. The *yashar* is thus the defining theme of that book. The hint to archery in Devarim is found in the blessing of Yehudah there: *yadav rav lo v'ezer mitzarav tihyeh* — his hands shall be great for him and help shall come against his enemies. The word *yadav* is in the plural — his hands. The Gemara asks: *v'eizu hi milchamah she'tzrichah shtei yadayim* — what warfare requires both hands? *Hevei omer zeh kashet* — that is archery, since one hand holds the bow and the other draws the string.

### Shimon: Shoftim

Rabbi Shimon bar Nachmani says: *zeh Sefer Shoftim* — *Sefer HaYashar* refers to the Book of Judges. The identification is, notably, ironic: Shoftim is called the book of the *yashar* because its recurring refrain is *ish hayashar b'einav ya'aseh* — every man would do what was right in his own eyes — precisely because there was no king and no central authority. The hint to archery in Shoftim comes from the verse: *l'maan da'at dorot b'nei Yisrael l'lamdam milchamah* — so that the generations of Yisrael would know, to teach them warfare. The Gemara asks: *v'eizu hi milchamah she'tzrichah limud* — what warfare requires actual training and instruction? *Hevei omer zeh kashet* — archery, since it demands a level of skill and practice that other forms of ancient combat apparently did not.

One might then ask: the verse speaks of the children of Yisrael generally — how do we know it refers specifically to Yehudah? The answer is that Shoftim itself records the following: *mi ya'aleh lanu el haK'naani l'hilachem bo bat'chilah* — who shall go up first against the Canaanites to make war? *Vayomer Hashem Yehudah ya'aleh* — God said: Yehudah shall go first. Since Yehudah was designated as the vanguard of Israel's military campaigns, any general teaching about warfare in Shoftim is understood to refer primarily to Yehudah.

---

## Sacrificial Portions

### Portions Before Shaul

The Gemara now turns to a third dispute among the same Amoraim, this one concerning the interpretation of a verse in Shmuel Aleph describing the portions of meat set before Shaul: *vayarem hatabach et hashok v'ha'alyah vayasem lifnei Shaul* — the butcher raised the *shok* and the *alyah* and set them before Shaul. The question is: *mai v'ha'alyah* — what exactly is this *alyah*?

### Yochanan: Shok-Alyah

Rabbi Yochanan says: *shok v'alyah* — it is literally the calf and the fat tail of the animal. The *alyah* in the verse is the *alyah*, the fatty appendage near the tail that is characteristic of certain breeds of sheep. Why does the verse use the form *ha'alyah* rather than simply listing both items? Because *aleha* — it sits upon the *shok*, adjacent to it. The reading thus yields: the *shok* along with the *alyah* that rests beside it.

### Eliezer: Shok-Chest

Rabbi Eliezer says: it is *shok v'chazeh* — the calf and the breast. What then is the *alyah* of the verse? It is the breast, *d'manach lechazeh iluyei d'shok* — because when performing *tenufah*, the waving of the *shelamim* offering, the breast was placed on top of the calf. *Alyah* thus means "what is elevated upon it" — the breast elevated atop the *shok* for the waving ceremony.

### Shimon: Shok-Shufi

Rav Shimon bar Nachmani says: *shok v'shufi* — the calf and the thigh, which Rashi identifies as a portion of the upper leg. Why *alyah*? Because *shufi iluyei d'shokai* — the thigh is anatomically above the calf. *Alyah*, on this reading, simply means what is higher up on the limb.

---

## Yichud Laws

### Woman Seclusion

With the completion of these *drashot*, the Gemara returns to the *Mishna*. The *Mishna* rules: *lo tityached isha imahem* — a woman may not be secluded with non-Jews, out of concern for licentiousness — whether that means rape or seduction.

### Licentiousness vs Murder

The Gemara asks: *bemai askinan* — what is the scenario? If we are speaking of a single non-Jewish man being alone with a Jewish woman, that would be prohibited even if the man were Jewish, since *yichud* with even a single Jewish man is forbidden. And if we are speaking of multiple men, where the presence of multiple people might otherwise suffice to permit *yichud* in the case of Jewish men — that too is not straightforwardly resolved by their being Jewish, because even regarding Jews the law distinguishes between those who are *kesherim* and those who are *prutzim*, sexually loose. As the Gemara cites: *lo shanu ela bik'sherim* — this leniency applies only to upright men; *aval beprutzim afilu asara nami lo* — but with those who are dissolute, even ten men together with a woman would not suffice. And indeed, the Gemara records a troubling incident: *maaseh haya v'hotziu'ha asara bemitta* — it once happened that ten men smuggled a woman out in a manner suggesting the worst. The precise interpretation is debated — Rashi suggests the woman may have been a willing participant, though the image also evokes something far darker, and the incident itself reflects the broader question of whether the prohibition of *yichud* is primarily directed at seduction or at rape.

In any case, the Gemara's challenge stands: if the concern in the *Mishna* is simply about being *prutzim*, that concern applies to Jewish men as well and is not distinctive to non-Jews. What distinguishes non-Jews?

The Gemara resolves this: *lo tzricha* — the ruling is needed for the case of *b'ishto imo* — where even a man who is *parutz* has his wife present with him. In that circumstance, we trust that the wife will serve as a check on her husband's behavior; the concern is mitigated. This would apply even to a *parutz* — if his wife is with him, another woman may be in *yichud* with them. But that assumption does not hold for a non-Jew: *oveid kochavim ein ishto m'shamarato* — we do not trust a non-Jewish man's wife to keep him in check. *Aval Yisrael ishto m'shamarato* — but for a Jewish man, his wife keeps him in line. It is therefore specifically in that borderline case — where the wife's presence would ordinarily resolve the concern — that the *Mishna* needed to specify that a non-Jewish man's wife does not provide the same protection.

This resolves the licentiousness concern. But the Gemara then raises a further question: *v'tipok lei mishum shfichus damim* — why specify the concern about sexual misconduct at all? The next part of the *Mishna* will prohibit a man from being in *yichud* with a non-Jew out of concern for murder. Should that concern not extend equally to a woman? Why is the ruling about a woman framed around licentiousness rather than the fear of being killed?

### Important Woman Status

Rabbi Yirmiyah answers: *b'isha chashuva askinan* — we are speaking of a woman of status and importance. Such a woman would not face a realistic concern of being murdered, because the non-Jew would fear the repercussions of harming someone whose death would draw the attention of the authorities. Therefore, the murder concern that applies to an ordinary person simply does not apply here. Yet even an important woman still faces a concern of sexual misconduct — perhaps seduction rather than outright rape (which, as Rashi notes, might itself be deterred by fear of consequences), but seduction remains a real risk regardless of her social standing. Hence the *Mishna* frames the prohibition around that concern rather than murder.

### Rav Idi Position

Rav Idi offers a different framing: *isha klei zayna aleha* — a woman's weapons are upon her. Rashi and Tosafot offer somewhat different readings of this phrase. Rashi understands it to mean that non-Jews will not be interested in killing a woman — they see her not as a threat to be eliminated but as a potential object of sexual desire. Tosafot cites a *Yerushalmi* with an additional explanation: a woman can claim to be a non-Jew herself, whereas a Jewish man's circumcision would expose him. Since non-Jews would have no reason to kill someone they take to be one of their own, murder is not a realistic concern for a woman in the way it is for a man. This is not a contextual ruling dependent on the woman's status — it is a categorical statement that murder is simply never the operative concern when a woman is in *yichud* with non-Jews. The only concern is always *arayot*.

### Status Implications

This difference between Rabbi Yirmiyah and Rav Idi has practical implications, and the Gemara spells them out: *ika beinaihu isha chashuva bein hanashim v'she'eina chashuva bein hanashim*.

Following Tosafot's reading: the first case is an important woman who is among men. For Rabbi Yirmiyah, this was precisely the case of the *Mishna* — since she is important, there is no murder concern, but there is a sexual misconduct concern, hence *yichud* is forbidden. For Rav Idi, who says murder is categorically not a concern for any woman, the question would then turn on whether an important woman's status might also dispel the concern about sexual misconduct — since both rape and seduction may be deterred when the woman commands sufficient standing. If so, Rav Idi might permit *yichud* for an important woman with men, a leniency Rabbi Yirmiyah would not grant.

The second case is a woman of no particular status who would be in *yichud* among women. For Rabbi Yirmiyah, since she is not *chashuva*, the concern of murder is still present, and women may kill her as much as men might. He would therefore prohibit even *yichud* among women. For Rav Idi, murder is never a concern for a woman regardless of her status, and women among women present no concern of *arayot* either — so he would permit it.

The Gemara then cites a *baraita* that supports Rav Idi's position: *ha'isha af al pi she-shalom ima lo tityached imahen mipnei she-chashudin al ha-arayot* — a woman, even though there is peace with them, may not have *yichud* with non-Jews because they are suspect regarding *arayot*. The phrase *af al pi she-shalom ima* — even though there is peace with her — implies categorically that a woman is not in danger of being killed; and yet *yichud* remains forbidden because of *arayot*. This confirms Rav Idi's principle: for women, it is always and only the concern of sexual misconduct that drives the prohibition, never murder.

---

## Encounter Precautions

### Positioning Rules

The Gemara now moves to the next part of the *Mishna*, which deals with a man encountering a non-Jew while traveling. The concern here is *shfichus damim* — the possibility that the non-Jew will attempt to kill him. The *baraita* provides practical guidance: if a Jew encounters a non-Jew on the road, *toflo limino* — he should position him to his right.

### Weapon Placement

Rav Shimon, son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Broka, elaborates on why and how. If the non-Jew is carrying a sword, *toflo limino* — keep him to your right. The reason: a right-handed person wears his sword on his left side and draws it with his right hand crossing to the left. If the non-Jew walks on your right, his sword-bearing left side is adjacent to you, and any motion of his right arm to draw will be visible and interceptable. But if he carries a stick — *b'makkel toflo lismolo* — keep him to your left. A stick is held in the dominant hand, the right. If he walks to your left, his stick arm is oriented toward you, and you can more readily block or deflect it. The logic in both cases is the same: position the non-Jew so that the weapon he is most likely to use is on the side where you can most easily monitor and counter it.

### Elevation Advantage

When traversing an incline or a descent, *lo yehei Yisrael lemata v'oved kochavim lemala* — the Jew should not be in the lower position while the non-Jew is above, whether ascending or descending. Rather, the Jew should maintain the higher position. Rashi notes that one should still try to keep the non-Jew to the right or left as described, but that maintaining the higher ground is independently important — the elevated position is always the more defensible one.

### Avoidance Tactics

The *baraita* continues: *v'al yishach lefanav* — do not bow down in front of him. If one were to stoop — to pick up a coin, to tie a sandal — *shema yerotzetz gulgelto* — perhaps he will crush one's head. The vulnerability of bending over in the presence of a potentially hostile individual is obvious.

If the non-Jew asks where one is traveling, *yarchiv lo et haderech* — one should extend the destination. That is, one should name a location further away than one's actual destination. The non-Jew, believing he has a longer journey alongside his companion, will not feel urgency to act — and when the Jew departs at his actual stop, he will have avoided any window of opportunity the non-Jew might have sought.

### Yaakov Example

The Gemara grounds this tactic in the precedent of Yaakov Avinu: *kederech she'asah Yaakov Avinu l'Esav haRasha* — as Yaakov our Patriarch did before Esav the wicked. Yaakov told Esav: *ad asher avo el adoni Se'irah* — I will come to my lord in Seir. Yet the verse then records: *v'Yaakov nasa Succotah* — and Yaakov traveled to Succoth, not to Seir at all. By declaring a further destination, Yaakov created space between himself and Esav, allowing him to safely divert without confrontation.

---

## Evasion Narratives

### Akiva Students Story

The Gemara now offers two illustrative narratives. The first: *maaseh b'talmidei Rabbi Akiva shehayu holchim l'Chziv* — students of Rabbi Akiva were traveling to Chziv, a city north of Eretz Yisrael, somewhat short of Akko. Bandits approached them and, without immediately revealing their intentions, asked: *le'an atem holchim* — where are you going? The students replied: *le'Akko* — to Akko, a city even further than their actual destination. When they arrived at Chziv, they announced their departure: *parshu* — they took their leave. The bandits, realizing they had been misled, nonetheless expressed admiration: *ashrei Rabbi Akiva v'talmidav shelo paga bahen adam ra me'olam* — praised is Rabbi Akiva and his students, who have never been harmed by an evildoer. The technique had worked, the students were safe, and even those who sought to harm them acknowledged the wisdom of the teaching.

### Menasha & Cherem

The second story: Rabbi Menasha was traveling to Bei Torsa when he was similarly approached by robbers. Asked where he was going, he named Pumbedita — significantly further away. When they reached Bei Torsa and he departed, the robbers confronted him: *talmido d'Yehuda rama'a at* — you must be a student of Yehuda the deceiver. Notice the contrast with the previous story: in Eretz Yisrael, the robbers praised Rabbi Akiva; in Bavel, they insulted Rabbi Yehuda.

Rabbi Menasha was indignant. He turned to them and said: *yedaitu leih* — you know who he is? You dare call him a *rama'a*? He then declared: *yehei ra'ava d'leihavu hanu inshi b'shamta* — may it be that these people be under Rabbi Yehuda's *cherem*. The robbers went off and continued their criminal trade for twenty-two years — *v'lo atzlach* — with no success. The *shamta* had taken hold and affected everything they did.

### Weaver Curse

Eventually, when they realized that their persistent failure was connected to the *cherem* under which they had been placed, *atu kulhu tavu shamtayeihu* — they all came and sought to have their *cherem* removed, presumably asking forgiveness for the disrespect they had shown Rabbi Yehuda. The question of whether to remove a *cherem* from people who are seeking it primarily in order to resume their criminal activities is, of course, a pointed one, though the Gemara does not resolve it.

Among the robbers, however, there was one who stood apart: *chad giridna d'lo ata lishruyei shamtiah* — a weaver among them who did not come to have his *cherem* removed. *Achleih aryeh* — a lion ate him. The Gemara then invokes a folk saying: *giridna d'lo tivzan shata batzar mishnei* — a weaver who has no shame has a year deducted from his years. Rashi explains that weavers were associated with poverty and shamelessness, and the proverb reflects the idea that such a person — poor and without self-awareness — continues to suffer. The weaver's failure to seek *mechila*, his stubborn indifference, cost him his life.

### Bavel vs EY Respect

The Gemara draws a broader lesson from comparing the two stories: *ta chazi ma bein ganvei Bavel u'listim d'Eretz Yisrael* — come and see the difference between the thieves of Bavel and the bandits of Eretz Yisrael. In Bavel, the robbers mocked and insulted Rabbi Yehuda, calling him a *ramai*. In Eretz Yisrael, even the bandits recognized the greatness of Rabbi Akiva and blessed him and his students. The point is pointed and perhaps a little wry: even in the realm of those who live outside the law, the culture of Eretz Yisrael maintained a respect for Torah scholars that Bavel could not match.

---

---

# Avodah Zarah 26

## Midwives & Nurses

### Jewish Midwife/Non-Jew

The *mishnah* on 26a opens by transitioning from the theme of fear of non-Jews in private settings to the question of rendering assistance to them. The *mishnah* states: *bat Yisrael lo tialeid et ovadet kochavim* — a Jewish woman may not serve as a midwife for a non-Jewish woman, *mipnei shemeyaledet ben la'avodat kochavim* — because she is helping bring a child into idolatry. The framing is noteworthy: the concern is not a generalized prohibition against helping non-Jews but is specifically tied to the idolatrous character of the society. The worry is that one is actively facilitating the perpetuation of *avodah zarah* by bringing more practitioners into the world.

### Non-Jew Midwife/Jew

The *mishnah* then permits the reverse: *ovadet kochavim meyaledet bat Yisrael* — a non-Jewish woman may serve as a midwife for a Jewish woman. This immediately raises a question: given the concern about non-Jews and bloodshed that dominated the previous *mishnah*, why are we not worried here that the non-Jewish midwife might harm the Jewish mother or child? The *mishnah* itself does not explain this directly, but the *gemara* will clarify the conditions under which this is permitted.

### Jewish Nurse/Non-Jew

In parallel, the *mishnah* rules that *bat Yisrael lo teinik b'nah shel ovadet kochavim* — a Jewish woman may not nurse the child of a non-Jewish woman. Here again, the reasoning appears to track the same concern: one is helping raise a child destined for a life of idolatry, so the prohibition is similarly grounded in the idolatrous context rather than being a blanket prohibition against any assistance to non-Jews.

### Non-Jew Nurse/Jew

The *mishnah* allows the inverse: *ovadet kochavim meinket b'nah shel Yisrael b'reshutah* — a non-Jewish woman may nurse the child of a Jewish woman, but specifically *b'reshutah*, in the Jewish woman's domain. This word is a hint at the condition of supervision that the *gemara* will spell out more explicitly: it must not be conducted in total privacy, but in circumstances where the non-Jewish nurse is in someone else's space and therefore subject to oversight.

### Ramban/Rabbeinu Yonah

One might ask how this *mishnah* applies in practice when a Jewish professional is called upon to help non-Jewish patients. While the *Rambam* is well known as a physician, the *Ramban* — Nachmanides — was also a doctor and specifically practiced in the area of gynecology, assisting Jewish and non-Jewish women alike in matters of childbirth and pregnancy. His cousin *Rabbeinu Yonah* famously wrote him a letter of critique, saying with mordant irony: *tavo alecha berachah she-ata mechayeh zaro shel Amalek* — may blessings come upon you, for you are giving life to the seed of Amalek. The choice of the word *Amalek* is significant. The critique was not framed primarily around whether Christians count as *ovdei avodah zarah*, but rather around the fact that these were the oppressors of Israel — the people actively threatening Jewish survival. How could one help bring more of them into the world?

We have no record of the *Ramban*'s formal reply, but the *Beit Yosef* and later *posekim* offer the principle of *mipnei eivah* — for the sake of preventing enmity — as the operative justification. This concept, which the *gemara* will develop at length, holds that fostering positive relations with the surrounding non-Jewish society is itself a halachic value that can, under certain conditions, override the reluctance to render assistance. Refusing to help when one is capable of doing so, especially in a professional capacity, breeds hostility that can be more dangerous than the assistance itself.

---

## Meir vs. Sages

### Baraita Stricter

The *gemara* now introduces a *baraita* that takes a more stringent position than the *mishnah*. The *baraita* opens similarly: *bat Yisrael lo tialeid et ovadet kochavim mipnei shemeyaledet ben la'avodat kochavim* — a Jewish woman may not serve as midwife for a non-Jewish woman because she helps bring a child into idolatry. So far, parallel to the *mishnah*. But then the *baraita* adds: *v'ovadet kochavim lo tialeid et bat Yisrael* — and a non-Jewish woman also may not serve as midwife for a Jewish woman, *mipnei shechashudah al shefichut damim* — because she is suspected of bloodshed. This is the position of *Rabbi Meir*, and it is fully consistent with the stringencies he expressed in the previous *mishnah* regarding private contact. The question then becomes: whose opinion does our *mishnah* represent, if it permits a non-Jewish midwife for a Jewish woman? The next line of the *baraita* answers: *v'Chachamim omrim*, the Sages say, *ovadet kochavim meyaledet et bat Yisrael* — a non-Jewish woman may serve as midwife — *b'zman she-acherot omdot agabah* — as long as other women are present and supervising, so that she cannot use the opportunity to harm the mother or child. But *lo beina l'veina* — not when it is entirely in private. This represents the majority view and explains the *mishnah*'s ruling.

*Tosafot* notes regarding the *mishnah*'s language of *b'reshutah* — in her domain — that perhaps this does not require literally standing over her in the manner the *baraita* describes, but rather a situation of *yotzei v'nichnas*, people coming and going, which provides a sufficient ambient level of supervision.

### Crushing Skull

One might then ask: if other people are present and supervising, why does *Rabbi Meir* still object? The *gemara* explains: *de-zimnin de-mancha leh yadah a-pusa ve-katlah* — because sometimes during the delivery, she can place her hand on the soft spot of the infant's skull and kill him. *Ve-lo mitchazi* — and it would not appear to onlookers that she had done so. The act could be accomplished in the very moment of delivery, indistinguishable from a stillbirth, even with people watching. Thus, according to *Rabbi Meir*, supervision is simply insufficient to address this particular form of potential harm.

### Infanticide Story

The *gemara* then illustrates this concern with a striking narrative. *Ke-hai itteta de-amra le-chavertah* — it is told of a woman who was being mocked by another non-Jewish woman for being a midwife to Jews. The mocker called her a "friend of the Jews," using it as a slur. The midwife shot back: *nefishin be-sha'ata de-hai itteta* — may you receive evil in proportion to what I have done to them — *de-ka-mashpilna mineihu dama ke-ofya de-nahara* — for I have spilled their blood like the flow of a river. She was boasting that she had killed many Jewish infants in the course of her midwifery work. This anecdote is brought as a proof for *Rabbi Meir*'s concern.

### Sages Dismiss

The Sages, however, are not persuaded. *Lo hi* — that is not to be believed. *Be-milta de-amrah ve-kenisa* — she was responding in anger to someone who was mocking her, and the boast was an exaggeration born of that moment. In practice, where people are supervising, one can rely on the midwife's fear of being discovered, and the Sages maintain that supervision suffices.

### Poison Nipple

The same tannaitic debate applies to nursing. The *baraita* states that *bat Yisrael lo tanik beno shel ovedet kochavim mipnei she-megadelet ben le-avodat kochavim* — a Jewish woman should not nurse a non-Jewish infant because she is helping raise a child to idolatry. And *Rabbi Meir* says that a non-Jewish woman also should not nurse a Jewish infant, *mipnei she-chashudah al shefichut damim* — because she is suspected of bloodshed. The Sages again permit it with supervision. *Rabbi Meir*'s concern in this case is: *de-zimnin de-shaifa leh samma le-dad mi-berai ve-katlah* — sometimes she will apply poison to her nipple before entering the Jewish home, outside where no one can see her do it, and the poison will already be in place by the time she arrives. Unlike the crushing-of-the-skull case, where the act occurs in full view, here the preparation happens in advance and in private, making even the most diligent supervision ineffective.

### Both Cases Needed

The *gemara* then asks: *u-tzricha* — why is it necessary for the *baraita* to state both debates, the one about midwifery and the one about nursing? Could we not have inferred one from the other?

The answer is that each case is necessary to prevent a mistaken inference. Had we only been told the debate about midwifery, one might have thought: the Sages permit it with supervision because the act of crushing the skull occurs right in front of witnesses, and even *Rabbi Meir*'s concern is marginal — she would be too afraid to act. But in the nursing case, where she can apply poison *mi-berai* — beforehand, outside — one might have thought the Sages would agree with *Rabbi Meir* that supervision is useless. Therefore the *baraita* must tell us that even in the nursing case, the Sages are not concerned, relying on the deterrent effect of supervision in some form.

Conversely, had we only been told the debate about nursing, one might have reasoned: *Rabbi Meir* is only concerned in the nursing case because of the possibility of preparation outside, which renders supervision ineffective. But in the case of childbirth, where she could not have prepared beforehand — the act would have to occur on the spot — one might think *Rabbi Meir* would concede to the Sages when others are supervising. Therefore the *baraita* must tell us explicitly that even in midwifery, *Rabbi Meir* does not permit it. Both cases are indispensable.

---

## Eivah Concept

### Paid vs. Free

The *gemara* now raises a challenge against the *mishnah*'s apparent prohibition on serving as a midwife for non-Jewish women. A *baraita* states: *Yehudit meyeledes ovedet kochavim bischar aval lo bechinam* — a Jewish woman may serve as midwife for a non-Jewish woman for a fee, but not for free. This seems to contradict the rationale given in the *mishnah*: if the concern is that one is helping bring a child into idolatry, why does payment change anything? *Amar Rav Yosef*: *bischar shari mishum eivah* — when payment is involved, it is permitted on account of *eivah*, enmity. When someone offers to pay you for a professional service and you nonetheless refuse, that refusal will breed hatred and hostility. To decline an unpaid favor, however, is entirely natural — one's time has value and one is not obligated to provide free services — and so a refusal in that context does not generate *eivah*. Thus the distinction is not about the nature of the act but about the social dynamics of refusal.

### Eivah & Shabbat

*Rav Yosef* then sought to extend this principle further: *savar Rav Yosef lemeimar alodei ovedet kochavim be-Shabbat bischar shari mishum eivah* — he thought to say that one might even be permitted to assist a non-Jewish woman in childbirth on *Shabbat*, if paid, because of *eivah* concerns. The logic is that *eivah* can override rabbinic restrictions and resolve the concern expressed in the *mishnah* about aiding *avodah zarah*. Importantly, this reasoning only works if what is being overridden is a *d'Rabbanan* concern. *Eivah* is not a basis to permit a *d'Oraita* violation; for that, *pikuach nefesh* would be required. *Rav Yosef*'s position therefore implicitly assumes that the *Shabbat* activities involved in assisting childbirth in the case under discussion are, at most, rabbinic in character.

### Abaye Shabbat Reply

*Abaye* rejected this extension. He said the midwife can simply explain to the non-Jewish woman: *deedan demantrei Shabsah mechallelinan alei-hu* — for those of us who observe *Shabbat*, we are permitted to violate it on their behalf. *Deedchu d'lo mantrei Shabsah lo mechallelinan* — for those of you who do not observe *Shabbat*, I do not have the halachic authority to assist you on this day. In other words, she has a ready and honest explanation for her refusal that is rooted in religious observance rather than personal hostility, and therefore *eivah* should not result. The explanation is somewhat darkly amusing — it is not hard to imagine that a non-Jewish woman in labor receiving this particular theological explanation might not find it entirely satisfying, and one could argue it would exacerbate rather than defuse resentment. Nevertheless, that is *Abaye*'s answer.

### Chatam Sofer/Feinstein

Historically, Jews did assist non-Jewish women in childbirth on *Shabbat*, and there is a substantial responsa literature addressing how to ensure that any *Shabbat* activity involved would constitute only rabbinic rather than biblical violations, keeping the halachic concern at the level where leniency is possible. The *Chatam Sofer* engaged extensively with this question.

*Rav Moshe Feinstein* took the analysis a step further in addressing whether *Hatzalah* paramedics and Jewish doctors must respond to emergency calls from non-Jews on *Shabbat*. His position was that failing to answer such calls would generate such profound hatred and enmity that it would ultimately endanger Jewish lives — thus transforming the *eivah* itself into a *pikuach nefesh* concern for Jews. On this reasoning, even what would otherwise be a *d'Oraita* violation becomes permissible, not because *eivah* directly overrides *Shabbat* at the biblical level, but because the chain of consequences makes Jewish lives concretely at risk. This represents a significant extension of the *eivah* principle into territory the *gemara* itself does not explicitly reach.

### Paid Nursing

*Rav Yosef* then sought to apply the same logic to the nursing case: *anuka bischar shari mishum eivah* — a Jewish woman who is being paid to nurse a non-Jewish infant might be required to accept the arrangement because refusing payment without a good reason would create hostility.

### Abaye Nursing Excuses

*Abaye* again pushed back, arguing that here too a woman has ready-made excuses available to her. *Ei pnuya hi* — if she is unmarried, she can say: *ba'ina l'hinsuva* — I want to get married, and being seen nursing infants will make me appear either already a mother or less desirable as a wife, and men will not want to pursue me. *Ei eshet ish hi* — and if she is married, she can say: *lo migannina b'appei gavra* — I do not wish to become repulsive in the eyes of my husband, coming home smelling of milk and consumed with nursing another's child. Because plausible personal excuses are available, the refusal will not be interpreted as hostility, and therefore *eivah* does not compel her to accept even a paid nursing arrangement.

---

## Not Rescuing

### Idolaters & Shepherds

A *baraita* is then cited that marks a sharp shift in tone and subject matter. *Ovdei kochavim v'ro'ei behemah dakkah* — idolaters and shepherds of small animals, such as sheep and goats that graze close to the ground and damage agricultural land — *lo ma'alin v'lo moridin* — one does not raise them from a pit and one does not lower them into one. That is: one takes no active steps to save their lives, but neither does one actively cause their death. The *Rambam* reads this passage as referring specifically to idolaters, not to non-Jews in general, which is a significant limiting interpretive move.

This is a deeply difficult passage. It sits in considerable tension with other *sugyot* throughout the *gemara* — such as the principle of *mefarnesin aniyei ovdei kochavim im aniyei Yisrael mipnei darchei shalom*, that we support the poor of non-Jews alongside the poor of Israel for the sake of peaceful relations. *Tosafot* engages at length with how these sources are to be reconciled. One consistent approach is the limiting one: these harsh rulings apply specifically to idolaters, not to all non-Jews, and that distinction does meaningful work in narrowing the scope.

These texts also have a history of censorship. Later manuscripts often read *lo hayu ma'alin* — they did not used to raise them — using the past tense to soften the force of the ruling for non-Jewish readers. The historical reality of the communities in which these texts were generated, living under oppressive conditions, shapes the rhetoric of the rabbinic voice here.

*Rav Yosef* thought to say that even in this case, *eivah* applies: *asukei b'sachar shari mishum eivah* — if they are offering you payment to rescue them, it is permitted because of *eivah*. The reasoning is that if someone in desperate circumstances offers you money for help and you refuse, that refusal — and any knowledge of it that spreads through the community — will breed hostility. Even if the person drowns, others who learn of the refusal may become enemies. Or perhaps the person manages to escape on their own and then bears a grievance against you. Either way, refusing a paid offer of rescue in a visible way creates *eivah*.

### Apostates Harsher

The *baraita* then introduces a more severe category. *Rabbi Abbahu* taught before *Rabbi Yochanan*: for idolaters and shepherds of small animals, the rule is *lo ma'alin v'lo moridin* — no active rescue, no active killing. But *hamosrot vehamumrim* — the informers and the habitual violators — *hayu moridin velo ma'alin* — those one would actively throw into a well and not retrieve. These are figures who pose a direct existential threat to the Jewish community. Informers endanger Jewish lives by turning community members over to hostile authorities. The *mumer*, the habitual violator, is treated more severely than the ordinary non-Jew.

### Torah Obligation

*Rabbi Yochanan* challenged *Rabbi Abbahu* on the inclusion of the *mumer* in this harsh category. He cited the verse *lekhol aveidat achikha* — for all the lost property of your brother — reading the word *lekhol* expansively, as extending the obligation of concern for another's well-being even to the *mumer*. You still have a relationship with this person; he is still *achikha*, your brother in some sense. So how can it be said that one would actively throw him into a well? *Rabbi Yochanan* accepts the ruling for the *min* and the *masor*, but insists the *mumer* is different. The *gemara* responds accordingly: *semi mikan mumer* — remove *mumer* from this list. The harsh ruling of active harm applies only to *minim* and *masorot*, and the *Rambam* adds *apikoros* to that list as well.

### Appetite vs. Spite

The *gemara* then asks: why did *Rabbi Abbahu* not himself resolve the difficulty by distinguishing between two categories of *mumer*? There is the *mumer okhel neveilot lete'avon* — the person who eats forbidden food out of appetite, out of desire, or because it is cheaper or more convenient. He is not making a theological statement; his mundane desires simply override his religious commitments in a given moment. Such a person remains, in some meaningful sense, part of the community. He is a sinner, but sinners are still *achikha*. Then there is the *mumer okhel neveilot lehakh'is* — the person who eats forbidden food specifically to spite God. Even if you offer him perfectly good kosher food, he will *davka* choose the forbidden, as an act of defiance. This person has placed himself outside the community through intentional, principled rejection of its fundamental commitments.

Why couldn't *Rabbi Abbahu* have said: yes, a *mumer lete'avon* we have an obligation to, but a *mumer lehakh'is* is the one I said we throw into the well?

### Spite God Debate

The *gemara* explains that *Rabbi Yochanan* holds *okhel neveilot lehakh'is min hu* — someone who violates *lehakh'is* is already in the *min* category. *Rabbi Yochanan* agrees that such a person is to be treated like a *min*; he simply classifies him that way. What he objects to is the routine use of the term *mumer* for such a person, as though a violator acting from spite is in the same category as one acting from appetite. So the ruling stands — *min* and *masor* are treated harshly — but the ordinary *mumer lete'avon* retains the status of *achikha*.

The *gemara* then records an *amora'ic* dispute: *Rav Aha* and *Ravina* disagreed about precisely where the line falls. One holds that *lete'avon* is a *mumer* and *lehakh'is* is a *min* — exactly as articulated above. The other holds that even *lehakh'is* is merely a *mumer*, and the *min* category is reserved for one who genuinely worships idols, *ha-oved elilei kochavim*. On this second, more lenient view, *lehakh'is* does not amount to apostasy; the person is still engaged with God, however perversely, and therefore remains within the *mumer* classification rather than being cast entirely outside the community.

*Rashi* and *Tosafot* disagree about the practical implications of this second position. Even according to the view that *lehakh'is* is a *mumer*, it does not necessarily follow that all the obligations toward a *mumer lete'avon* apply equally here.

### Insect Proof

The *gemara* then challenges the first position — that *lehakh'is* already makes one a *min* — from a *baraita*: *akhal parosh ehad o yatush ehad harei zeh mumer* — if someone ate a gnat or a small insect, that person is a *mumer*. And presumably, who would eat a gnat except someone doing it *lehakh'is*, to be transgressive? Yet the *baraita* calls such a person a *mumer*, not a *min* — which seems to prove the more lenient position. The *gemara* rejects this inference: *hasam bitei'avon ta'ama de'issura* — in that case, the person may well be acting *lete'avon*, driven by the thrill of tasting something forbidden, curious about what the *issur* tastes like, rather than motivated by theological defiance of God. You therefore cannot prove from the insect case that *lehakh'is* falls within the *mumer* category.

---

## Prevention Methods

### Why State Lo Maalin

The *gemara* now revisits the formulation of the *baraita* regarding *minim* and *masorot*: *moridin velo ma'alin* — one casts them down and does not bring them up. An obvious question presents itself: if one is permitted to actively throw them into a pit, of course one is not required to pull them out afterward. Why does the *baraita* need to state *lo ma'alin* separately? The *gemara* seeks to identify a meaningful independent application for the phrase.

### Ladder Removal

*Rav Yosef bar Chama* said in the name of *Rav Sheshes*: *lo nitzrecha* — the phrase is necessary for a different scenario. *She-im hayta maalah babor megarerah* — if there was a ladder inside the pit, one removes it. *Lo ma'alin* thus teaches not merely that one refrains from active rescue, but that one may actively prevent the person from being able to climb out on their own.

### Lion Excuse

And when doing so, one offers an excuse: *de-lo tichos chayusa le-iloi* — I am removing the ladder so that lions and wild animals should not come down it and attack. The cover story provides plausible deniability and prevents the act of passive harm from generating liability or conflict.

### Tosafot Authority

This formulation raises two questions in rapid succession. First: if one can actively throw a *min* or *masor* into the well to begin with, why does it require any explanation to remove a ladder? And second: why is an excuse even needed? *Tosafot* addresses this by distinguishing between two political situations. The harsh ruling of *moridin* — actively causing death — applies when the Jewish community is in a position of control, where such an act can be carried out without consequence. The ruling of *lo ma'alin* — preventing rescue while offering an excuse — reflects a situation of living under non-Jewish authority, where one must be more circumspect. In that context, the ruling teaches not merely passive nonrescue but active prevention with a cover story, because overt action against such individuals would be dangerous or impossible.

### Stone Cover

*Rabbah* and *Rav Yosef* offer a parallel application: *she-im hayta even al pi habe'er mechaseh* — if there was a stone that could be placed over the mouth of the well, one covers it. The excuse offered is *le-vricha hu de-avdi lah* — I am covering the well so that my animals should not fall in. Perhaps one promises to remove the stone later and never does.

### Child Emergency

*Ravina* offers yet another variant: *she-im haya sulam mesalko ve-amar baina le-michas bri migra* — if there was a ladder, one removes it and explains that one needs it urgently to bring one's child down from the roof. The common thread across all these cases is the same: an act that prevents rescue is paired with a plausible innocent explanation to deflect suspicion and avoid generating hostile consequences.

---

## Non-Jew Mohel

### Purpose of Milah

The *gemara* then introduces a *baraita* that pivots the discussion toward the laws of *brit milah*. *Yisrael mal oveid kochavim leshum ger* — a Jew may circumcise a non-Jew for the purpose of conversion, which is straightforward. But not *leshum murna* — not for the sake of a worm, a medical condition, according to *Rashi*. This prohibition is continuous with the theme of not rendering active assistance to non-Jews in ways that primarily benefit them without a corresponding Jewish interest.

### Meir: Danger

The *baraita* then turns to the question of a non-Jewish *mohel* circumcising a Jew. *Ve'oveid kochavim lo yamol Yisrael mipnei shechashudim al shefichut damim, divrei Rabbi Meir* — a non-Jew may not perform circumcision on a Jew, because non-Jews are suspected of bloodshed. This is entirely consistent with *Rabbi Meir*'s characteristic stringency throughout this chapter. What is interesting, however, is the implication: the ruling is framed entirely in terms of danger, not in terms of halachic invalidity. The circumcision performed by a non-Jew would apparently be *kosher* in principle — the only objection is the physical risk of submitting oneself to a non-Jew with a blade.

### Sages: Supervised OK

*Chachamim* disagree, ruling: *oveid kochavim mal et Yisrael bizman she'acherim omdim al gabav* — a non-Jew may circumcise a Jew when other people are present and supervising, ensuring there is no opportunity for harm. *Aval beino leveino lo* — but not in private. This means the *Chachamim* accept a non-Jew as a halachically valid *mohel* for a Jew, which is a striking ruling that cuts against the intuition that entry into the covenant must be mediated by a covenantal member.

### Knife Slip

*Rabbi Meir*'s position is then explained: even with supervision, he says, there is a concern — *dezimnin dematzli bei sakina umashvei lei k'rut shofcha* — because sometimes the *mohel* may slip his knife and effectively render the person a *k'rut shofcha*, a eunuch. Even in front of witnesses, a subtle movement of the hand in the midst of the procedure could pass as an accident. Supervision, for *Rabbi Meir*, cannot eliminate this particular danger.

---

## Samaritan/Non-Jew

### No Jewish Doctor

The *gemara* now introduces another *baraita* that appears to contradict *Rabbi Meir*'s position. *Ir she'ein bah rofeh Yisrael* — in a city that has no Jewish doctor or *mohel* — *veyish bah rofeh Kuti verofeh oveid kochavim* — and there is both a Samaritan *mohel* and a non-Jewish *mohel* available — which of the two should perform the *brit milah*?

### Meir: Non-Jew Yes

*Yamol oveid kochavim ve'al yamol Kuti, divrei Rabbi Meir* — *Rabbi Meir* says: let the non-Jew do it rather than the Samaritan. This is initially puzzling on two counts. First, why not the Samaritan, who at least has some form of Jewish practice? *Rashi* explains that Samaritans performed *brit milah* with idolatrous intent, which disqualifies their *milah* on religious grounds. But the second and deeper problem: why does *Rabbi Meir* permit the non-Jew at all, given that he was just said to oppose it because of the danger of injury?

### Yehuda: Samaritan Yes

*Rabbi Yehuda* rules the opposite: *yamol Kuti ve'al yamol oveid kochavim* — let the Samaritan do it rather than the non-Jew. His reasoning is principled: Samaritans are halachically Jewish, and since a *brit milah* requires a member of the covenant to perform it, the Samaritan qualifies while the non-Jew does not.

### Gemara Reversal

The *gemara* considers reversing the attributions — assigning *Rabbi Yehuda*'s position to *Rabbi Meir* and vice versa — in order to achieve internal consistency: perhaps *Rabbi Meir* actually said Samaritan yes and non-Jew no, consistent with his danger concern about non-Jews. But this reversal fails. *Rabbi Yehuda* cannot be the one permitting non-Jews as *mohelim*, because we have an explicit *baraita* in which *Rabbi Yehuda* categorically excludes non-Jews from performing *brit milah* as a matter of halachic validity.

### Covenant Language

*Rabbi Yehuda*'s source is the verse *ve'ata et briti tishmor* — and you, Avraham, shall observe My covenant. The circumcision of Avraham and his descendants is a covenantal act, and the verse implies that only one who is himself within the covenant — a Jew — can perform it. A non-Jew stands outside the covenant entirely and therefore lacks the standing to perform the act that initiates others into it. This makes *Rabbi Yehuda*'s categorical exclusion of the non-Jew entirely coherent and textually grounded, and it means the reversal proposed by the *gemara* cannot work.

### Expert Removes Danger

The attributions therefore stand as originally stated. But this leaves the original question: how does *Rabbi Meir* permit the non-Jew, given his concern about danger? The *gemara* answers: *ve-hakha be-mai askinan be-rofe mumkhe* — here we are dealing with a professional expert. A *mohel* who has an established professional reputation would not risk that reputation by allowing something to go wrong, or by acting in any way that could be perceived as deliberate harm. The concern that a non-Jew with a knife might "accidentally" injure a patient does not apply to a recognized expert whose livelihood depends on his reliability and precision. Therefore, *Rabbi Meir*'s danger concern is not triggered in this case.

### Final Positions

To summarize the final positions: *Rabbi Meir* holds that a non-Jew is halachically valid as a *mohel* — he does not categorically exclude non-Jews from performing *brit milah* — but his concern about physical danger prevents him from permitting it in ordinary circumstances. When the non-Jew in question is a proven professional, that danger concern is resolved, and *Rabbi Meir* permits it. He objects to the Samaritan not on grounds of danger but on grounds of *avodah zarah* intent. *Rabbi Yehuda*, by contrast, does not share *Rabbi Meir*'s particular concern about physical danger from non-Jews, but holds that non-Jews are categorically excluded from performing *brit milah* as a matter of halachic principle, derived from the covenant language of the verse. He therefore permits the Samaritan, who is halachically Jewish, while categorically forbidding the non-Jew regardless of expertise.

---

---

# Avodah Zarah 27

## Context & Overview

### Mishnah Harshness

The *mishnayos* of this section of *Maseches Avodah Zarah* are, by any measure, striking in their severity. Having moved from earlier *mishnayos* that addressed concerns about bestiality, we now arrive at *mishnayos* that touch upon matters of life itself — who may care for you, who may heal you, and under what circumstances you may place yourself in the hands of a non-Jew. This reflects just how seriously *Chazal* regarded the dangers at stake. It is one thing to say: prefer a Jewish midwife over a non-Jewish one, or choose a Jewish nursemaid. *Tosafos* notes, interestingly, that the *Yerushalmi* is more permissive regarding non-Jews in such roles — a remarkable observation given that the *Mishnah* itself originates from *Eretz Yisrael*. But even granting that, we are about to encounter positions in the *Gemara* that go considerably further, extending these concerns even to the domain of medical treatment.

### Rabbi Meir v. Chachamim

The fundamental tension in these *mishnayos* runs between *Rebbi Meir* and the *Chachamim*. *Rebbi Meir* is concerned under all circumstances, a position consistent with his well-known tendency to be *chaish l'miuta* — to give weight even to unlikely possibilities. The *Chachamim*, by contrast, permit interaction with non-Jews when there is supervision or some form of public setting. *Tosafos* extends this leniency further, holding that even periodic, informal oversight — someone coming in and out of the house from time to time — is sufficient to remove the concern. Notably, a story is recounted of a non-Jewish nursemaid who boasted of having harmed Jewish infants, and the rabbis simply dismissed it as idle boasting. That dismissal itself illustrates how much the authority to interpret the law includes the authority to interpret the facts on the ground.

### Eivah Concept

A principle that threads through all of these discussions is *eivah* — the concern about inciting hatred. The *Gemara* permits certain forms of assistance to non-Jews, and certain forms of receiving assistance from them, when refusing would generate *eivah*. This functions as a kind of social pressure valve: where the refusal to help would breed dangerous resentment, *eivah* overrides the ordinary restriction. The *Gemara* even acknowledges that one can avoid *eivah* through artful excuses — "I'm sorry, my son is calling me" — as a legitimate strategy for extricating oneself without provoking hostility.

### Eivah & Shabbos

The concept of *eivah* takes on remarkable practical significance in the hands of later *poskim*. Rav Moshe Feinstein famously invokes this principle as the basis for permitting Jews — including *Hatzalah* volunteers and hospital workers — to treat non-Jewish patients on *Shabbos*. The reasoning is that if refusing to provide care would generate significant *eivah*, then that *eivah* is great enough to permit *chilul Shabbos*. *Tosafos* raises the objection: how can *eivah* alone justify desecrating *Shabbos*? Rav Moshe's response is that when the *eivah* rises to a sufficiently serious level, it does in fact carry that weight.

### Heretics vs Non-Jews

What emerged most starkly from the previous *daf* is that while the ordinary non-Jew is subject to restrictions that balance concern with pragmatism, the *moser* — one who hands Jews over to the authorities — and the heretic who has placed himself outside the community occupy an entirely different category. The *Gemara* treats these individuals with a severity that goes well beyond anything applied to an ordinary non-Jew. That harsh dimension of yesterday's learning sets the stage for what we will encounter at the end of today's *daf*.

### Brit Milah Intro

At the close of yesterday's *daf*, the *Gemara* pivoted to the topic of *bris milah* — specifically, who may perform a circumcision on a Jewish infant. The question arises in the context of healing and bodily intervention: if a non-Jew performs a *bris milah*, and that service is rendered for payment, is there an *eivah*-based permission? More fundamentally, is a non-Jew even a valid performer of *bris milah* at all? The discussion of *Rebbi Meir* established that his concern about placing an infant in the hands of a non-Jew stems from fear for the infant's safety. According to *Rebbi Yehuda*, however, such a concern does not apply in the same way. Yet conflicting *braitas* complicate the picture.

---

## Non-Jew vs Kuti

### Braita Conflict

The *Gemara* opens *Kaf Zayin Amud Aleph* by attempting to reconcile what appear to be conflicting *braitas* regarding who may perform *bris milah*. One *braita* seems to permit a non-Jew, another seems to permit a Samaritan (*Kuti*), and the positions of *Rebbi Meir* and *Rebbi Yehuda* seem to be inverted in different sources. The *Gemara* works through several reversals and un-reversals of these *braitas* before arriving at a coherent picture.

### Rofe Mumcheh

The resolution begins with the category of *rofeh mumcheh* — the expert physician. The principle, introduced by *Rav Dimi* in the name of *Rabbi Yochanan*, is that if a practitioner is an established expert recognized by the public, one may place oneself in his hands for treatment. The reasoning: a *mumcheh* will not risk his professional reputation by harming his patient. Applied to the question of *bris milah*, this means that *Rebbi Meir*'s safety concern can be satisfied by ensuring we are dealing with a recognized expert. In that case, the prohibition is not about safety but about *kavannah* — intention.

### Rabbi Meir's View

According to this resolution, *Rebbi Meir* holds that a non-Jew is permitted to perform *bris milah* — we are speaking of an expert, so safety is not the concern — but a *Kuti* (Samaritan) is not permitted, because *Rebbi Meir* is concerned about the *Kuti*'s *kavannah*. The *Kuti* may be performing the circumcision with the wrong religious intention entirely, directed not toward God but toward *Har Gerizim*.

### Rabbi Yehuda's View

*Rebbi Yehuda* takes the opposite position: a non-Jew may perform *bris milah*, but a *Kuti* may not. *Rebbi Yehuda* is not raising a safety concern but rather a *lishmah* concern — the requirement that *bris milah* be performed with proper intention. Strikingly, then, while *Rebbi Yehuda* does not exclude the non-Jew on grounds of obligation, he does exclude the *Kuti* on grounds of corrupted intention.

### Har Gerizim Issue

A *braita* is then cited that makes *Rebbi Yehuda*'s position explicit: *Yisrael* may circumcise a *Kuti*, but a *Kuti* may not circumcise a *Yisrael*, because the *Kuti* performs circumcision *leshem Har Gerizim* — in the name of their holy mountain. This was the theological focal point of the Samaritan cult, and the *Gemara* notes that over time the *Kutim* evolved from a people with a somewhat divergent practice to one that was essentially worshipping *avodah zarah* on *Har Gerizim*. Whether that is historically accurate is another question, but that is the *Gemara*'s understanding.

### Lishmah Debate

*Rebbi Yosi* challenges the entire framework of a *lishmah* requirement for *bris milah*: where in the *Torah* do we find any requirement for *milah* to be *lishmah*? His position is essentially that *milah* does not carry a *lishmah* requirement at all, and rather than worrying about bad *kavannah*, we might simply allow whoever performs the circumcision to do so as a technical procedure. The phrase he uses — *ela ma v'holech ad sheteitzei nishmato* — carries a note of sharp irony: let the Samaritan drop dead, but don't tell me we need *lishmah* for *milah*.

### Yehuda vs Rebbi

One remaining difficulty is that a *Rebbi Yehuda* cited earlier seemed to say that a non-Jew is also excluded — not just the *Kuti*. The *Gemara* resolves this by distinguishing between two figures: the *Rebbi Yehuda* who says a non-Jew may perform *bris milah* is the *Tanna Rebbi Yehuda* (son of *Ilai*), while the *Rebbi Yehuda* who excludes non-Jews entirely is *Rebbi Yehuda HaNasi* — *Rebbi* himself, a full generation later. A *braita* in the name of *Rebbi Yehuda HaNasi* derives this exclusion from the verse *v'atah et brisi tishmor* — "and you shall observe My covenant" — emphasizing that only one who is *commanded* in the *brit milah* may perform it.

---

## Lishmah Requirement

### Rav Chisda Proof
