Accordingly, when one obtains beer vinegar from a warehouse, one may assume with confidence that it contains no grape additive and is thus permissible.

These are the kinds of practical determinations that characterized *kashrus* practice across centuries and in many communities where certified supervision was unavailable. In the absence of a *hechsher* infrastructure, halakhic authorities made carefully reasoned assumptions about commercial practice, and those assumptions guided what people could and could not consume.

---

## Tosafot on Mead

### Mead Concern

Tosafot extends this discussion with practical application. Tosafot notes that just as the Gemara raises the concern of grape additives in beer vinegar, there is an analogous concern regarding mead — *shichra devash*, the drink of honey, referred to in the vernacular as *meet*. Tosafot writes: *tzrich lehizaher beshichra devash* — one must be careful with mead — *livdok im matilim bo shimrei yayin* — to check whether they add grape leaves or grape material to it, *le'hamid maher*, presumably to accelerate fermentation, much as a small amount of grape material can initiate or speed up fermentation in other contexts. *Ki yesh mekomos she'osim ken* — there are indeed places where this is done. *Ve'az vadai hu assur* — in such cases the mead is certainly forbidden.

The force of Tosafot's concern here is not derived directly from the Gemara's case; rather, Tosafot is drawing on independent knowledge of commercial practice to issue what amounts to a *kashrus* alert: in general you may purchase mead from a non-Jew, but in locales where it is known that grape material is added, one may not.

### Stored Beverages Rule

Tosafot then draws the broader conclusion from the principle established by Rav Ashi: *hilkach nira demutar liknos kol minei mashkeh min ovdei kochavim* — it appears permissible to purchase all varieties of drinks from a non-Jew, including apple juice (*yayin tapuchim*) and strawberry juice (*mei tutim*) and the like. The reasoning is the same as in the Gemara's discussion of stored beer vinegar: wine or grape additives, if introduced into a product held in storage, would cause the product to spoil. Tosafot generalizes this principle — assuming it holds true for all stored liquids — and concludes that one need not be concerned about possible wine admixture in any stored drink, unless one has specific reason to believe otherwise.

This permissibility, however, is conditioned on an important visibility requirement: *uvelvad sheyireh Yisrael moshech min hachavit* — specifically, the Jew must see the non-Jew drawing the liquid from the barrel. If the product is drawn from storage before one's eyes, one may rely on the principle that stored goods do not contain grape additives. Tosafot distinguishes between liquid held in storage — which is assumed safe — and freshly prepared liquid, where no such assumption applies.

### Back Room Caveat

A further caveat is added: *aval im lo ra'ahu moshech min hachavit* — if one does not see the non-Jew drawing from the barrel but instead the non-Jew goes to a back storage room and brings it out, the matter requires closer attention — *az hadavar mischalek* — the ruling then depends on further considerations.

### Price & Admixture Risk

Tosafot then refines the caveat based on economic logic. If the non-Jew retrieves the drink from the back room and the drink in question is more expensive than wine, then even though it is presumably stored goods, one must be concerned — *ye'aser shema eirev bo yayin* — that he may have mixed in some wine. Why? *Lehistaker o leharviach* — to make a greater profit, essentially watering down the product with something cheaper. If, on the other hand, wine is more expensive than the drink being sold, then *ein lachush shema eirev bo yayin lehachshilo* — there is no reason to fear that he deliberately mixed in wine merely to cause the Jew to transgress. No one adulterates a more expensive product into a cheaper one for profit; the concern only arises when wine is the cheaper of the two.

To summarize Tosafot's position: any stored drink may be purchased from a non-Jew without concern about grape admixture. The only additional concern arises when one does not witness the non-Jew drawing from the barrel, in which case the relative price of wine determines whether there is genuine grounds for suspicion.

---

## Hadrianic Pottery

### Definition

The Mishnah also lists *cheres hadiyani* — Hadrianic pottery — among the items that are *assur behana'ah*. The Gemara asks: *mai hadiyani?* What is Hadrianic pottery? *Amar Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel:* it is the pottery of Hadrian the Caesar.

### Rav Dimi's Explanation

When Rav Dimi came from Eretz Yisrael, he provided the following account of how this pottery was produced: *karka besula hayta shelo avda adam me'olam* — they began with virgin soil, land that had never been cultivated. Such land retains all of its nutrients and natural potency. They then plowed this land, planted it with grapevines, and produced wine from the resulting grapes. Because the soil had never been worked before, the wine produced from it was extraordinarily strong and concentrated. They then took this highly potent wine and placed it in *gufi chivri* — white pottery vessels — which were uniquely absorbent. The pottery absorbed the wine entirely into its walls.

### Wine Transport Method

The pottery was then broken into small shards. *Umitru lehu b'chafsabi* — the shards were collected, and *v'daru b'hadaihu* — the Roman army would carry these shards with them on campaign. Wherever they traveled, *taru lehu v'shatu* — they would immerse a shard in water, and the concentrated wine absorbed in the pottery would reconstitute, yielding wine. This was, in effect, a form of dehydrated wine — a portable concentrate for military use. The white pottery was the carrier medium, and the shards themselves were essentially solidified wine.

### Wine Quality

*Amar Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi:* our finest quality wine — *rishon she'bahen* — is equivalent only to their third-grade product — *kishlishi she'lahen* — meaning the wine reconstituted from these pottery shards at its third remove is still superior to the best Jewish wine. This gives a sense of just how intensely concentrated the wine absorbed into this pottery actually was.

---

## Pottery Status Debate

### Central Question

*Iba'ye lehu* — a question was posed: *mahu lismoch bahen karia d'mita* — what is the law if one wishes to use these pottery shards to support, for example, a wobbly bed leg? The shard is being used as pottery — as a structural prop — not as wine. Is that permissible, or do we treat the shard as though it were wine itself, making even such incidental use forbidden?

The stakes of this question are significant. Very few things are *assur behana'ah* entirely, and the question here is whether the Mishnah's prohibition on Hadrianic pottery extends to any benefit derived from it whatsoever, or whether it is limited to extracting the wine from it. Two considerations compound the question: first, the factual situation — these shards are so saturated with wine that the Romans used them to reconstitute actual wine, making them functionally indistinguishable from wine itself; second, the categorical consideration — this falls under *stam yeinam* and related wine prohibitions, which carry their own weight of stringency.

Additionally, the language of the Mishnah is itself suggestive: the Mishnah says the pottery is forbidden, without limiting the prohibition to situations where wine is extracted from it. This formulation invites the question of how broadly the prohibition extends.

*Rotzeh b'kiyumo yedei d'var acher sharya o assur* — if you want the pottery there and the benefit you derive is from the pottery itself, not from the wine in it, is that permitted or forbidden? The Gemara notes that Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yochanan disagree on this, one forbidding and one permitting — though this formulation, it should be noted, is the subject of textual debate, as many such rulings in the Bavli are suspected of being later Geonic glosses rather than original Talmudic text.

### Barrels & Flasks Baraita

The Gemara raises a challenge. A Baraita discusses *hardardurin* and *rokva'os* — various types of barrels and leather flasks belonging to non-Jews — and addresses what happens if a Jew stores his own wine in them. If a Jew places his wine in a non-Jewish vessel, there is concern that wine previously absorbed into the walls of that vessel will leach back out into the Jewish wine. Under normal *kashrus* principles, if everything is cold, such absorption is generally not a concern — *noten ta'am* under cold conditions does not typically create a prohibition. Yet here, the Gemara seems to indicate heightened concern, perhaps because wine vessels absorb so thoroughly, or perhaps due to the particular stringency applied in the domain of non-Jewish wine. The result: *assur b'shtiya u'mutar behana'ah* — the wine becomes forbidden for drinking but remains permissible for benefit.

This is another instance of the intermediate category that appeared earlier: not full *yayin nesech* status, not outright permission, but a middle level reflecting uncertainty or trace-level absorption. Notably, this is not the exotic case of Hadrianic pottery; this is ordinary barrels and leather flasks. The concern is entirely about wine leaching back out from the absorbed material — the vessels themselves have not been used in any idolatrous act.

### Rabban Gamliel Story

The Baraita continues: *heid Rabbi Shimon ben Guda lifnei bno shel Rabban Gamliel* — Rabbi Shimon ben Guda testified before Rabban Gamliel's son about his father, that Rabban Gamliel himself had drunk wine stored in such non-Jewish flasks in Akko, demonstrating that it is entirely permissible. *V'lo hodu lo* — and they did not agree with him. The sages around — whether or not Rabban Gamliel's son himself agreed is left unclear — rejected the testimony, effectively saying that Rabban Gamliel would never have done such a thing, or alternatively that even if he did, they do not accept that as the normative ruling.

---

## Leather Flask Ruling

### Saddle Cloth Prohibition

The Gemara then cites Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Kaphusai: *assur la'asos mehem davar acher* — specifically, one may not use a non-Jewish leather flask as a saddle cloth for one's donkey. Here the benefit derived is purely from the leather — there is no intent to extract wine from it — yet it is forbidden. This appears to support the position that even using the vessel itself for a purpose entirely unrelated to wine is prohibited.

### Challenge to Buy Jugs

The Gemara presses this logic: if we are genuinely concerned about the absorbed wine in non-Jewish vessels, why do we permit purchasing pottery jugs from non-Jews for use in storing our own wine? Clearly those jugs were previously used for non-Jewish wine. *Mai shna nod u'mai shna kankanim* — what is the difference between the leather flask and pottery jugs?

### Rava's Answer

*Amar Rava:* the distinction is not about the vessel per se but about a specific rabbinic concern — *gezeirah shema yibaka nodo* — there is a concern that if one uses a leather flask as a saddle cloth while traveling, the flask might split or crack, and *veyatilnu veyitferenu al gabei nodo* — one might then be tempted to use it as a patch for a leaking wine flask. In that case, the absorbed non-Jewish wine in the leather patch would leach into one's own wine. This is the specific danger the rabbis addressed with their decree. It does not reflect a general principle that one cannot derive any benefit from a vessel that absorbed non-Jewish wine. With pottery jugs, that particular concern does not apply — one does not patch a cracked pottery jug with a shard of pottery — and therefore purchasing and using them is permitted.

The implication is that in ordinary cases, deriving benefit from the vessel itself is not prohibited; only the absorption of the wine back into one's own wine is the concern. The saddle cloth prohibition is a *gezeirah* against a specific scenario, not a general rule.

### Concentration Logic

The Gemara then returns to the question of Hadrianic pottery and addresses it from the perspective of the opinion that holds using the pottery itself is forbidden: *hasam leseih le-issura be'einei hacha iseih le-issura be'einei* — in ordinary vessels the wine absorption is low-level and the wine does not exist as wine within the pottery in any meaningful sense. But in Hadrianic pottery, the wine is so fully absorbed and so intensely concentrated — the Romans reconstituted actual wine from it — that the pottery is treated as though it *is* the wine. It is not a vessel that once stored wine; it is effectively a solid form of wine itself. Accordingly, the prohibition extends not just to extracting the wine but to deriving any benefit from the shard.

This resolves the inner logic of the debate: for ordinary vessels, derived benefit is the prohibition only when wine leaches back out; for Hadrianic pottery, the pottery *is* the wine, and therefore even non-wine-related use is forbidden under the same principle as *stam yeinam* itself.

---

## Conflicting Testimonies

### First Version

The Gemara now returns to the testimony of Rabbi Shimon ben Guda, which ended with *v'lo hodu lo* — the sages did not concede. But a separate Baraita appears to relate the same incident with a different conclusion: *v'hodu lo* — they did concede. How are these two contradictory endings to be reconciled? The first reconciliation offered by the Gemara: *hatam chavraya lo hodu lo aval bno modeh lo* — when it says they did not agree, it means the other sages present did not accept the testimony, but Rabban Gamliel's own son did accept it. According to this resolution, the son accepted his father's conduct as authoritative, while the other rabbis rejected it. This version would leave the normative ruling on the side of stringency.

### Second Version

The Gemara offers a second resolution: *iba'it eima, Guda l'chud u'Guda l'chud* — the two accounts actually refer to two different people, both named Guda — one spelled with an *aleph* and one with an *ayin*. The first Guda testified and the sages did not accept his account. Subsequently a second Guda testified the same thing, and *l'zeh hodu acharei khen* — to him they eventually agreed.

### Storage Implications

According to this second resolution, the final normative conclusion may be that storing wine in non-Jewish vessels is actually permissible — *mutar b'shtiya* — which would in turn explain the practice of purchasing pottery jugs from non-Jews for wine storage without apparent concern. With the exception of the extraordinary case of Hadrianic pottery, where the shards are treated as the wine itself, the Gemara may be endorsing a position that ordinary cold absorption from non-Jewish vessels does not create a prohibition on the stored wine. This remains somewhat ambiguous, and the Gemara acknowledges that the question does not fully resolve; how long wine is kept in such a vessel, the nature of the materials, and other circumstances may all play a role. The extended treatment of these cases at the end of the tractate will revisit them in greater detail.

---

## Leather Heart Cutout

### Definition & Purpose

The Mishnah moves on to another category of items forbidden in benefit: *orot levuvin* — leather from which a piece has been cut out corresponding to the heart of the animal. The concern is that the leather was used in some idolatrous practice — apparently, cutting open the living animal over its heart in the course of a ritual act, reminiscent of the most extreme forms of pagan sacrifice. The leather with this characteristic excision is therefore suspect as having been used in idolatrous worship.

### Blood Indicator

The Rabbis taught: *eizehu or lavuv?* — what constitutes a *levuv* hide? *Kol she'karua k'neged halev* — any hide that is torn open opposite the heart area, in a rounded shape like a skylight. *Yesh alav koret dam assur* — if there is a trace of blood absorbed into the leather, it is forbidden, since the presence of blood indicates that the cut was made while the animal was still alive, i.e., as part of an act of worship. *Ein alav koret dam mutar* — if there is no blood, it is permitted, as the absence of blood suggests the cut was made post-mortem, during the flaying process, and thus had no idolatrous significance.

### Salted Leather Rule

*Amar Rav Huna:* this distinction applies only when the leather has not been salted. *Aval maluach assur* — if the leather has been treated with salt, it is forbidden even in the absence of visible blood. The reasoning: *eimar milcha avrateih* — one may say that the salt drew the blood out, eliminating any visible trace. Thus the absence of blood on salted leather cannot serve as exculpatory evidence.

### Shape Distinction

Rabban Gamliel adds a further criterion: the shape of the cut is determinative. If the cut is circular — *agol* — it is forbidden, as that shape corresponds to the characteristic form of the idolatrous practice. If it is elongated — *mashucha* — it is permitted, as that shape does not correspond to the ritual practice.

This might seem in tension with the earlier description of the cut as resembling a skylight — a shape one might associate with a square or rectangular opening with flaps — but Rabban Gamliel clarifies that the operative distinction is between circular and non-circular.

### Rav Yosef-Abaye Debate

*Amar Rav Yosef amar Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel: halacha k'Rabban Gamliel* — the ruling follows Rabban Gamliel. *Amar lei Abaye:* Abaye challenged Rav Yosef — when you say we rule like Rabban Gamliel, the implication is that he is *disagreeing* with the *Tanna Kamma*. But perhaps Rabban Gamliel is merely clarifying what the *Tanna Kamma* already meant, not introducing any novelty. If so, stating that we rule like him conveys nothing.

*Amar lei Rav Yosef:* what practical difference does it make whether he disagrees or clarifies, if the ruling is the same? *Amar lei Abaye: gemara gemorei zimurta tehei?* — are we to go around reciting our traditions like a meaningless little ditty? If Rabban Gamliel adds nothing beyond the *Tanna Kamma*, then declaring that we rule like him is a statement without content, and Abaye refuses to issue such a ruling. Halakhic precision requires that every ruling mean something; if Rabban Gamliel is only clarifying, then no ruling needs to be issued in his name. Even absent any practical *nafka mina*, the integrity of the tradition demands exactness in formulation.

---

## Meat & Worship

### Pre-Entry Permission

The Mishnah turns to yet another case: *basar hanichnas l'avodat kochavim mutar* — meat that is being brought into a house of idol worship is permissible. If one encounters a non-Jew carrying meat toward a temple of idolatry and purchases it before he enters, one may derive benefit from it — not for personal consumption since the non-Jew slaughtered it, but the meat may be resold or otherwise used. Despite knowing where the meat is headed, the act of bringing it to the temple has not yet occurred and no idolatrous act has yet taken place with it.

### Rabbinic Attribution

*Man tanna?* — who is the author of this ruling? *Amar Rabbi Chiya bar Abba amar Rabbi Yochanan:* this is not consistent with the position of Rabbi Elazar.

### Rabbi Elazar's View

For Rabbi Elazar holds: *stam machshevet avodat kochavim l'avodat kochavim* — we assume that the standard intention of a non-Jew who slaughters an animal is to offer it to his god. The act of slaughtering is a classic form of worship — one offers an animal to one's deity — and therefore, under Rabbi Elazar's view, any animal slaughtered by a non-Jew must be presumed to have been slaughtered with idolatrous intent, rendering the meat forbidden in benefit at the moment of slaughter. On that view, the meat was already problematic long before it arrived at the temple gates.

### Main Position

Our Mishnah, however, goes well beyond merely rejecting that position. It rules that even meat that is actively being carried into the temple at this moment is still permissible — we do not presume that the slaughter itself, performed this morning, was an act of idolatrous offering. The intent to use the meat in worship does not retroactively render the act of slaughter an act of worship. This is a striking ruling and represents a significant limitation on the scope of concern.

### Post-Exit Forbidden

*V'hayotzei assur mipnei shehu k'zivchei meitim* — but once the meat exits the temple, it is forbidden, because at that point it is considered like *zivchei meitim*, sacrifices to the dead. Whatever occurred inside the temple — and the Gemara notes *ei efshar l'likut shel avodat kochavim* — it is impossible that during his time inside the temple he did not in some way offer it up — the meat is now treated as having been presented to an idol and is therefore forbidden in benefit.

---

## Tumah & Dead Bodies

### Ba'al Pe'or Source

*Mani?* — whose position does this represent? *Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira hi* — it is Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira. The Gemara then cites the underlying derivation: *minayin l'tikroves avodat kochavim she'metamei b'ohel?* — from where do we know that an offering made to an idol conveys *tumah* under a tent, like a corpse? *She'ne'emar: Vayitzmadu le'Ba'al Pe'or vayochlu zivchei meitim* — as it says, "They attached themselves to Ba'al Pe'or and ate the sacrifices of the dead." The verse equates idolatrous offerings with the dead; just as a corpse conveys *tumah* to anything under the same roof, so too does an offering to idolatry.

### Tosafot's Question

Tosafot raises a sharp question: why does the Gemara need to attribute this to Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira at all? The prohibition against deriving benefit from *tikroves avodat kara* is universally agreed upon. No authority disputes that items offered to idolatry are *assur behana'ah*. So what is the novel contribution of Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira's derivation, and why does the Gemara feel it necessary to invoke his position?

### First Answer

Tosafot's first answer: the case in our Mishnah is not a classic *tikroves* in the recognized halakhic sense. A standard act of idolatrous offering involves an action one would recognize as a formal act of worship — slaughtering an animal on an altar, pouring a libation, burning incense, or the like. But what happened here? A non-Jew walked into a temple with some meat, did something unspecified, and walked out. Is that recognizable as a proper act of worship? One might have thought not — that without a formally recognized act of offering, the meat does not acquire the status of *tikroves*. It is to address this ambiguity that Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira's stringent derivation is invoked: by equating idolatrous offerings with dead bodies and insisting on the highest level of stringency in this domain, even an act that does not conform to a classic mode of offering is subsumed within the prohibition. The analogy to the *sheitel* controversy of recent memory is apt: when hair is brought into a temple and offered in the context of ritual practice, the question of whether that constitutes recognizable *tikroves* — and whether Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira's reasoning would apply — is precisely the kind of question this Gemara engages.

### Second Answer

Tosafot's second answer: the Mishnah itself signals that something beyond mere *issur hana'ah* is at stake. Throughout the Mishnah's list of prohibited items — wine, pottery, leather — the Mishnah gives reasons for the prohibition in each case. Here, uniquely, the Mishnah specifies that the meat is forbidden because it is *zivchei meitim*, sacrifices to the dead. This is not merely a restatement of the *issur hana'ah*; the phrase *zivchei meitim* is drawn from the verse about Ba'al Pe'or and carries the additional implication of *tumah*. The Mishnah's choice of this precise language signals that it intends not only to prohibit benefit but also to convey that the offering carries the *tumah* status of a corpse. And that additional ruling — *tumah be'ohel* from an idolatrous offering — is precisely the position of Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira. Hence the Gemara attributes the Mishnah to him: not because he alone prohibits benefit from *tikroves*, but because he alone extends the prohibition to include corpse-like *tumah*, and the Mishnah's phrasing indicates it is teaching that point as well.

Tosafot thus clarifies: no one disputes that *tikroves avodat kochavim* is *assur behana'ah*. The attribution to Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira addresses either the non-classic nature of the offering in this case, or the Mishnah's additional teaching about *tumah* — or both.

---

## Non-Jew Festival Travel

### To Festival Ban

The Mishnah introduces the case of *haholechin letarpot* — those going to the festival. *Tarpot* appears to be a contemptuous wordplay, perhaps on *tinofet* (filth) or *beit hartofet*, suggesting the pagan festival. A non-Jew traveling to such a festival: *assurin laset ulatet imahen* — one may not do business with him on his way there.

### Worship Benefit

The reason, as Shmuel explains: *bahalicha assur de'azlu modei kammai avodat kochavim* — because he is going to prostrate himself before and honor his idols. If you sell him goods or make a transaction with him, the money or merchandise will end up being used in, or contributing to, his act of idolatrous worship. This maps directly onto the concern from the first chapter of the tractate regarding business dealings in the days before a pagan festival: the worry is that the non-Jew's benefit or joy from the transaction will translate into enhanced participation in the idol worship.

### Return Permission

*Bachazara mutar* — on his way back, however, one may do business with him. The reasoning: *mai de'hava hava* — what was, was. He has already worshipped; no future transaction will contribute to or enhance the act that has already concluded. The business dealings on the return journey cannot be said to support idol worship that is already complete and past.

---

## Jew Festival Travel

### To Festival Permission

The rules are reversed for a Jew who is traveling toward a pagan festival. *Bahalicha mutar* — one may do business with him on his way there. The reason: *dilma hadar bei velo azal* — perhaps he will have second thoughts and turn back. We extend to the Jew the benefit of the doubt that he may yet have a change of heart, a *hirhur shel teshuvah*, and not participate in the idolatrous worship at all. Since there remains a real possibility that he will not actually engage in worship, his journey toward the festival does not yet render transactions with him problematic.

### Return Prohibition

*Bachazara assur* — on his return, however, one may not do business with him. *Keivan de'azik ba* — since he actually went, and presumably attended the festival, we now assume he worshipped. And unlike a non-Jew who practices idolatry as a matter of unremarkable routine, a Jew who has actively sought out pagan worship is now presumed to be genuinely devoted to it. One must fear that future transactions with him will in some way feed into continued idolatrous practice — *mehadur hadur azil* — he will return again to the festival.

### Habitual Worshiper

A Baraita challenges this, ruling that for a Jew, one may not do business either on the way there or on the return. *Amar Rav Ashi:* that Baraita refers to a *Yisrael mumar*, a Jew who is a confirmed and habitual idolater — *devai azil* — one who habitually goes to these festivals. For such a person, the going and the coming back are equally suspect: going will certainly culminate in worship, and returning signals that he will go again. The distinction between the going and the return applies only to a Jew who is not known to be habitual; for a confirmed idolater, all dealings are forbidden in both directions, just as with a non-Jew on the way to the festival.

---

## Market Day Fair Rules

### Non-Jew Fair Rules

The Gemara then teaches: *oved kochavim holech leyarid* — a non-Jew going to a market fair (*yarid*). *Bein behalicha bein bachazara mutar* — one may do business with him both going and returning. The market fair, unlike the festival, is not a site of idolatrous worship. There is no prayer, no prostration, no libation. Accordingly, transactions in connection with a market fair are free of the concerns that govern festival dealings.

### Jew Fair Rules

However, *Yisrael holech leyarid* — a Jew going to a market fair — the rules shift. *Behalicha mutar* — one may do business with him going, since the fair is not a place of worship and there is no reason yet to suspect any idolatrous activity. *Bechazara assur* — but on his return, one may not do business with him.

### Contaminated Money Logic

The reason: *de'amar avodas kochavim zavin* — we must suspect that he sold idols. In a pagan market fair, the trade in small idols and cult objects is a natural part of commerce. A Jew attending such a fair is suspected of having dealt in these items — perhaps buying from one non-Jew and reselling to another, perhaps acting as a middleman. Even if he did not manufacture them himself, any money in his possession after the fair may be *dmei avodat kochavim* — proceeds from the sale of idols — and one may not derive benefit from such money.

### Benefit of Doubt

But one may ask: a non-Jew returning from the same fair might equally have sold idols. Why do we not apply the same suspicion to him? *Oved kochavim amrinan glima zavin, chamra zavin* — for the non-Jew, we say he sold ordinary merchandise: a cloak, some wine. We extend him the presumption that he traded in legitimate goods.

Why is no such presumption extended to the Jew? *Ei is lei, dehacha hava mazvin lei* — if the Jew had ordinary merchandise to sell, he would have sold it within the Jewish community. The very fact that he made the effort to go to a non-Jewish market fair raises the suspicion that he was selling something he could not sell among Jews — and the most obvious candidate is cult objects, idols, and the like. Therefore, when a Jew returns from such a fair, we presume that some portion of his money may be proceeds from idol sales, and dealings with him are accordingly restricted.

---

---

# Avodah Zarah 33

## Returning Pilgrims

### Vhaba'im Mutarin

The daf opens twelve lines into 33a, at the break in the *mishnah* marked by the two dots. The *mishnah* had been discussing various scenarios involving foods, moneys, and other matters associated with *avodah zarah*. One such scenario concerned doing business with those traveling to an idolatrous pilgrimage site — which is forbidden, even if it is not within the three-day period before a holiday, since the pilgrim will experience some joy from the transaction and carry that into his worship. The *mishnah* continues, however: *vhaba'im mutarin* — those returning from such a pilgrimage are permitted. They are simply going home, and one may do business with them.

### Kshurim Zeh Bazeh

Reish Lakish qualifies this ruling: *lo shanu ela she'ein kshurin zeh bazeh* — this permission applies only when the returning pilgrims are coming back separately from one another. But if they are returning *kshurin zeh bazeh* — bonded together, traveling as a group — then it is forbidden. The reasoning is *eima daito lachzor*: when they return as an organized group, it suggests they are deeply committed and intend to go back. The implication is that they are still in some meaningful sense engaged with their worship. Admittedly, even if they plan to return next year, that does not directly affect a business transaction conducted now — the precise logic here is not fully clear, but Reish Lakish evidently regards the group dynamic as indicative of an ongoing relationship with the idolatrous practice.

## Leather Flasks

### Nodot Grudim Mutarin

The *gemara* turns to an entirely different issue: the absorption of wine by vessels, and particularly the question of whether vessels can absorb taste even in cold conditions. The normal principle is that the transfer of taste requires heat. Yet when pottery vessels or leather flasks are used with wine over a long period, and the wine remains cold, there is still a concern that the vessel has absorbed the wine's taste. This becomes halachically significant in the context of *yayin nesech* and *stam yeinam*.

The *mishnah* records a dispute about leather flasks (*nodot*) and pottery vessels (*kankanim*) that absorbed non-kosher wine: Rabbi Meir held the wine that absorbed and came back out renders one's own wine forbidden even in *hana'ah*, while the *chachamim* said it is only forbidden to drink but not forbidden in *hana'ah*. The *gemara*, however, does not pursue that dispute. Instead, it focuses on which types of vessels absorb in the first place.

*Tannu rabbanan*: leather flasks of non-Jews — if they are *grudim chadashim*, peeled and new, meaning the inside has never been lined with pitch and they have only been used briefly, they are permitted. They do not absorb the taste, especially given that all contact is cold. But if they are *yeshanim*, old — meaning used by the non-Jew for an extended period — or *mezufafim*, tarred on the inside (Rashi reads "or" rather than "and"), they are forbidden. Old flasks have had ample time to absorb, and tarred ones present additional concern because the tar lining is highly porous.

### Shikhur Bishvil Pariput

The *braisa* continues: if a non-Jew applies the pitch lining and also pours wine into the flask — which was apparently standard practice to season the pitch and neutralize its bad taste — and a Jew is observing, one need not be concerned. The *gemara* immediately asks: if the non-Jew is the one pouring in the wine, what difference does it make that a Jew is watching? It is still the non-Jew pouring wine, which ought to render it *yayin nesech*.

### Rav Papa's Reinterpretat…

Rav Papa resolves this by reinterpreting the *braisa*: the non-Jew applies the pitch, but it is the Jew who pours in the wine. And it is yet another Jew who stands and observes. Now the *gemara* asks again: if a Jew is the one pouring in the wine, why does he need a second Jew to observe? The answer is *dilma agav tirdei minaseich velav adaitei* — perhaps, because the Jew pouring is occupied and focused on his professional task of adding the wine at precisely the right moment during the pitch application, he is not paying close attention to the non-Jew's movements. The non-Jew might exploit that distraction to touch or sprinkle the wine in a manner constituting *nisuch*. A second Jew stands watch specifically to prevent that. This is a re-reading of the *braisa*, but it resolves the difficulty.

### Zorkeik Mayim Letit

Rav Zvid offers a different resolution. He maintains the original reading of the *braisa* — the non-Jew himself pours the wine — and explains why it is nevertheless permitted. *Be'idna dekeshadi lei*, at the moment he pours the wine in, *naasei kezoreik mayim letit* — it is as though one is throwing water into plaster. The wine is effectively going to waste, being swallowed up into the pitch. Rashi explains that since the wine becomes mixed with the pitch, the pitch absorbs and destroys the wine so thoroughly that no taste can later migrate back into wine stored in the flask. Others, citing the *Yerushalmi*, read the point as one about intent: pouring something into pitch is an act of destruction, not an act of *nisuch*. That rationale would be more relevant when it is the Jew's wine being poured — though admittedly, if it were the non-Jew's own wine, the concern would be different.

### Salt Processing

Rav Papa then draws an inference from Rav Zvid's teaching: *hai oved kochavim deshadi chamra lebei milchei* — if a non-Jew pours wine into a Jew's salt, perhaps the salt similarly burns away and destroys the taste, making it permitted. Rav Ashi challenges this: *mi dami?* The cases are not comparable. In the case of pitch, the wine actively goes to waste — *ka'azil le'ibud*. In the case of salt, no such active destruction occurs; the taste remains present in the salt.

Tosafot observes that the comparison would never have been drawn to ordinary salt — the contrast is obvious. Tosafot therefore explains that the comparison was to salt-processing facilities, where fires burn during production and the claim was that the intense heat destroys the wine poured in. Rav Ashi's response is that even in that context, the wine can still be absorbed more than in the case of pitch. Importantly, Tosafot cites Rabbeinu Tam, who notes that Rav Ashi's challenge is merely a *dechuyah* — it shows only that one cannot derive the ruling from Rav Zvid's case, but Rav Papa's underlying position remains correct. On the basis of this, Rabbeinu Tam rules that one may use salt commercially processed by non-Jews, even though it is common practice during the boiling phase to add a small amount of blood to whiten it. Since the processing occurs at such high temperatures, the blood is destroyed. This is, incidentally, consistent with the observation that even in certain modern food industries, small amounts of blood are used for particular processing effects.

## Kashering Method

### Bar Addi Taya

The *gemara* presents a case involving Bar Addi Taya, an Arab, who forcibly seized leather wine flasks from Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef, filled them with wine for his own use, and then returned them. The question was brought to the *beit midrash*: how does one restore these flasks to a permitted status?

### Memalim Mayim

Rabbi Yirmeya reported that Rav Ami had issued a practical ruling: *memal'im mayim shlosha yamim u-m'aran* — fill the flask with water for three days and pour it out. Rava adds the specification: *tzricha l'aran me'et l'et* — the water must be poured out every twenty-four hours. The procedure is thus three cycles of twenty-four hours, each time replacing the water. The logic is that the fresh water draws out the absorbed wine taste, but after twenty-four hours the water itself has absorbed what it can and must be replaced with clean water to continue the process.

### Aran Me'et L'et

Two assumptions underlie this ruling. First, that the flask absorbed the wine — which is not entirely obvious, since the earlier *gemara* indicated that new or briefly used vessels do not absorb. Here, though, the flask had been used by the Jew previously and was evidently considered capable of further absorption when seized by the non-Jew. Second, that a cold-water method can effect *kashering* — a notable departure from the standard heat-based methods. This is the source for the practice some observe of *kashering* glasses for *Pesach* through immersion in water changed over seventy-two hours, though whether that practice is warranted in other contexts is a separate discussion.

### Didan vs. Didehu

Following Rava's ruling, the *gemara* records that some thought this water method applied only to Jewish-owned flasks (*didan*) that had been temporarily used by a non-Jew — since such flasks had already been heavily conditioned by Jewish wine, the additional absorption during the non-Jew's use was minimal and could be extracted by water. But if the flask was one that had been used by a non-Jew for years (*didehu*), this method would not suffice. The *mishnah* never provides a method to *kasher* such vessels; it simply forbids them.

### Echad Shelanu

When Ravin arrived from Eretz Yisrael, he reported in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish: *echad shelanu ve'echad shelahem* — the water method works for both. Whether the flask is one that had been in Jewish use or one used entirely by non-Jews, the principle that cold absorption can be reversed by cold extraction applies equally.

### Kankanin Question

Rav Acha son of Rava then raised a question before Rav Ashi: perhaps this water method is effective for leather flasks (*nodot*), even if they have pitch lining — but what of pottery vessels (*kankanin*)? Pottery is highly porous. Would the three-day water method succeed there as well?

### Rav Ashi Response

Rav Ashi replied: *lo shena nodot velo shena kankanin* — there is no distinction. Just as taste was absorbed through cold, so too it can be extracted through cold. One might note the tension: absorption occurred over many years of use, while extraction is claimed to occur in seventy-two hours. But that is the ruling.

## Pottery Vessels

### Kankanin Chadashim

*Tanu rabbanan*: pottery vessels (*kankanin*) of non-Jews — if they are new and untarred (*chadashim grudim*), they are permitted, as brief use has not resulted in meaningful absorption. If they are old (*yeshanim*) or tarred (*mezufafim*) — Rashi reads these as alternative conditions rather than cumulative — they are forbidden. Old vessels have had time to absorb; tarred ones present additional absorption through the porous pitch lining.

### Non-Jew Wine, Jewish Wat…

If a non-Jew has used such a vessel for wine and a Jew then fills it with water, the vessel is *kashered*. Rashi reads this as a reference to the three-day water process described earlier — *noten letochan mayim* does not by itself specify the full procedure, but that is how Rashi understands the *braisa*. This passage also explicitly addresses earthenware pottery vessels, providing confirmation that the water method applies to them as well, which had been the subject of Rav Acha's question above.

### Tzir U'Moris

The *braisa* continues: if a non-Jew used the vessel for wine, a Jew may subsequently use it for *tzir umoris* — brine and fish sauce — without further concern. Rashi explains that these sharp, pungent liquids actively negate and counteract the taste of the absorbed wine. This is a stronger claim than simply the water method: rather than gradually drawing the absorbed taste out, the brine neutralizes it immediately. One might also consider the principle of *noten ta'am lifgam* — that a taste which imparts a detrimental flavor is halachically disregarded — as an alternative rationale, though Rashi focuses on the counteracting mechanism. This is presented as distinct from the water method, which requires the three-day process, whereas the brine works immediately.

### Lechatchila or Bedi'avad

A question is then raised: is using brine and fish sauce in such vessels permitted only *bedi'avad* — after the fact, if one already used them — or is it permitted *lechatchila*, from the outset?

### Rav Zevid Permits

The *gemara* resolves this by citing Rav Zevid bar Oshaya at the top of 33b: one who purchases pottery vessels from non-Jews — if new, he may simply use them for wine; if old, he may fill them with *tzir umoris lechatchila*. This explicitly permits the use of brine from the outset, not merely *bedi'avad*. It is a form of counteraction, not *kashering*, but it is fully permitted at the outset for old vessels.

## Fire Kashering

### Fire Method Question

Rav Yehuda Nesi'ah, grandson of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, posed a question to Rabbi Ami: *hechziran lechivshan ha'esh venitlabnu mahu* — if one places these pottery vessels back into the kiln and heats them until they become white-hot, does that constitute a valid method of destroying the absorbed taste?

### Fire Negates Taste

Rabbi Ami responded with a *kal vachomer*: if we have already permitted even simple brine — which merely counteracts the taste of the wine — then certainly real fire would be considered to destroy it. The underlying premise, which Rashi makes explicit, is that the brine does not merely permit use while the absorbed wine taste remains; rather, it goes in and destroys that taste, rendering the vessel fully permitted for any subsequent use. On that reading, the *kal vachomer* to fire is straightforward.

### Tar Melts Off

It was also taught: Rabbi Yochanan (and some say Rabbi Assi reported it in his name) ruled that once the inner tar of such vessels has melted off in the fire, the vessels become permissible. This makes sense: if the absorbed wine was primarily held within the tar lining, once the tar is gone, the vessel is restored to its untarred state.

### Softening Suffices

Rav Ashi takes this further: *lo teima ad denasran* — one need not wait for the tar to fully melt and slough off. *Afilu rifuy mirpu* — even if the tar only softens, that too is sufficient. The point is not literally about the tar being gone, but about the degree of heat applied. Softening of the tar is indicative of the vessel having been sufficiently heated to destroy the absorbed wine.

### Kinsa Debate

The *gemara* then raises the question of *kinsa* — placing small pieces of wood or twigs inside the vessel and burning them on the inside rather than firing the vessel from the outside in a kiln. Rav Acha and Ravina dispute this: one permits it and one forbids it. The *halacha* is ruled like the one who forbids.

### Outside vs. Inside Fire

Rashi explains the distinction carefully. When a vessel is placed in a kiln and fired from the outside: since the heat is applied externally, and the tar on the inside eventually melts, that means the pottery body itself became white-hot — *tanyas levana achris*. It is the pottery that was heated through. In the case of *kinsa*, however, putting fire on the inside causes the tar to soften immediately, but the pottery body itself is not meaningfully heated. The softening of the tar in the kiln case was merely a marker for the pottery reaching sufficient heat. Here, one has achieved softened tar without heating the pottery, and that does not *kasher* the absorbed wine in the pottery itself.

### Wine Barrels Kashering

Rashi draws a direct practical application: wine barrels and pottery jugs used for long-term storage are the classic case of *yeshanim* — they have genuinely absorbed wine over extended use. Such vessels require *kashering*. *Lo sagi behachsher bifnim* — firing from the inside is insufficient, as established. And since *kinsa* itself is forbidden, *kol shekein bemayim chamim* — certainly ordinary *kashering* with hot water will not work either. The options that remain are firing from the outside as in a kiln, or the three-day water method with the water changed every twenty-four hours. Rashi also mentions waiting twelve months as an additional possibility, though this does not appear explicitly in the *gemara* at this point.

It is worth pausing to note the underlying paradox: ordinarily, pottery cannot be *kashered* at all because the Torah indicates that absorbed matter cannot be extracted from it. On the other hand, the absorption here occurred through cold contact. The result is that standard heat-based *kashering* methods do not work — because it is pottery — but the cold water method does, precisely because the absorption was cold.

## Beer vs. Wine

### Beer in Wine Vessels

Having established that *tzir umoris* can counteract absorbed wine, the *gemara* raises the parallel question: *mahu lates lesochan shechar* — what about using beer in vessels previously used for wine? Can beer similarly neutralize the absorbed wine taste, or must one use only the specific substances mentioned?

### Rav Nachman vs. Rava

Rav Nachman and Rav Yehuda both forbid using beer for this purpose. Rava, however, permits it. Rashi gives an explanation similar to the brine case: the beer counteracts the taste of the wine. Whether the vessel is then fully permitted for any subsequent use is not entirely clear from the discussion.

### Ravina Permits

Ravina ruled leniently, permitting Rav Chiya son of Rav Yitzchak to use these vessels for beer. That person subsequently put wine in the vessels instead. Ravina, upon learning of this, was unconcerned.

### Teaching Correct Law

One might have expected Ravina to respond by tightening his ruling — if telling people beer is permitted leads them to use wine, perhaps one should simply rule beer forbidden to prevent the confusion. Ravina rejected this approach entirely: *lo chash lamiltei amikrei be'alma* — it was a pure coincidence that the mistaken substitution occurred. It does not justify altering the correct *halacha*. The correct ruling must be taught, and incidental errors do not change that.

## Temporary Use

### Dung Vessels Burst

Rav Yitzchak bar Bisna had vessels made from dried dung (*Pakusna*) that had absorbed wine. He attempted to *kasher* them using the water method but placed them out in the sun. The vessels burst.

### Issura D'Olam

Rav Abba rebuked him sharply: *assarta tinu alaich issura de'olam* — you have rendered them permanently forbidden, a prohibition for all time. By destroying the vessels through this improvised method, he made it impossible to ever *kasher* them properly. When did the Rabbis prescribe the water method? *Memal'im mayim* — simply filling with water and leaving them. *Achinu beshimsha mi amrei* — leaving them in the hot sun was never part of the prescription. The sun's heat caused the vessels to burst, and that was simply an error.

### Vessels of Nitron

Rav Hisda said in the name of Rav Ami: *klei netara ein lo tahara olamit* — vessels of nitron can never be fully *kashered*; they have no enduring remedy. When asked what *klei netara* are, Rav Yosef bar Avin explained that they are vessels made from the excavated earth around alum deposits — nitron being a mixture of sodium carbonate occurring naturally in desert terrain, often produced in antiquity from seaweed. The precise reason these cannot be *kashered* is not fully spelled out in the *gemara*, though the most natural understanding is that they absorb wine without being capable of releasing it.

### Temporary Use Rinsing

The house of Parzik — an official of some governmental authority — forcibly seized vessels from Pumbedita, filled them with wine, and then returned them. This closely parallels the earlier case of Bar Addi Taya. In this instance, the question was brought to Rav Yehuda.

### Lo Machnisan Lekiyomam

Rav Yehuda ruled: *keivan delo machnisan lekiyomam* — since they did not keep the wine in the vessels for long-term storage but only used them temporarily, *meshachshechan bemayim ve'in mutarin* — simply rinsing with water until no drips remain on the inside is sufficient. This contrasts with the earlier case, where the full three-day water method was required. The distinction may be that Bar Addi Taya's case involved longer use, constituting genuine *machnisan lekiyomam*, while here the use was plainly temporary. The *gemara* does not place these two cases in explicit dialogue with one another, but that resolution is available.

### Porous Assessment

Rav Avira taught: *hani chatzvei shachimei d'armaya* — these brown earthenware vessels of the Arameans, since *delo bal'u tuva* — they are not particularly porous — *meshachshechan bemayim ve'in mutarin* — rinsing with water suffices. Even though they are earthenware, the halachic concern is not a formal categorical one about the material but about the actual degree of absorption. Rav Pappi makes the same point regarding the *pasvasa* vessels of the region of Michsi, which were made from especially hard earth and were similarly not porous — rinsing suffices.

This reflects a *metzius*-oriented approach to the laws of absorption: the question is whether a given vessel actually absorbs, not merely what category of material it belongs to. This approach has implications for contemporary *kashering* questions as well. Some *poskim* take a formalist view — if a material resembles pottery it is treated like pottery, if it resembles glass it is treated like glass — while others assess actual porosity. The *gemara* here clearly endorses the latter framework, at least for cold absorption.

## Glazed Vessels Wine

### Glaze Types

Rav Zpidi taught: glazed vessels (*mani dekunya*) — if the glaze is white (*chivra*) or black (*uchma*), it is permissible. The glaze renders the vessel non-porous and prevents absorption, particularly since we are dealing with cold contact. However, green-glazed (*yeroka*) vessels are forbidden, *mishum demitzrif* — because green glaze contains alum, which is highly absorbent. This connects back to the earlier discussion of *klei netara*: alum absorbs and retains in a way that cannot be reversed. Therefore, even though the vessel appears glazed, the green glaze allows absorption.

### Cracked Glaze

Even for white and black glazed vessels, if the glaze has cracks (*kartufnei*), all are forbidden. Cracked glaze loses its protective function, allowing wine to penetrate and be retained by the earthenware beneath.

### Mareimar Permits All

Mareimar ruled more broadly: glazed vessels — *bein uchma bein chivra bein yeroka*, whether black, white, or green — are all permissible. This is a more lenient position than Rav Zpidi's, dispensing with the distinction based on glaze color. Rashi notes that these glazes were lead-based — a reminder of the ubiquity of lead in the ancient world's material culture.

## Pesach Glazed Vessels

### Pesach Question

The *gemara* then poses a striking challenge to Mareimar's leniency. The question was brought directly to him: *hani mani dekunya, mahu le'ishtamushi behu bePesach* — can these glazed vessels be used for *Pesach*? In this context, of course, the vessels would have been used with heat — *chametz* is cooked or baked, unlike wine which is consumed cold. So we are now in a different domain of absorption: hot rather than cold.

Mareimar's questioner lays out the parameters precisely. Green-glazed vessels need not even be asked about — *demitzrif uvala*, the alum-based glaze absorbs regardless, and it is certainly forbidden. Similarly, if the glaze has cracks (*kartufnei*), the answer is obvious — *devadai bal'u*, they certainly absorbed, and they are forbidden. The real question concerns white and black glazed vessels with smooth, intact glaze: what is the *halacha* for *Pesach*?

### Sweating Shows Absorption

Mareimar responded: *ana chazina lehu demadaytzi* — I see that they sweat. Even the smooth, white or black glazed vessels, after being used, exude moisture from their surface. *Vekivan demadaytzi, ve'azli bal'ei* — since they sweat, that demonstrates they absorb. *Va'asiri* — they are forbidden. The sweating is empirical evidence that liquid permeates through even smooth glaze when heat is involved. Mareimar, who had been entirely lenient regarding wine, is here fully stringent regarding *Pesach*.

### Torah's Testimony

Why is absorption through glaze concerning for *Pesach* but not for wine? The *gemara* invokes a broader principle: *datorah eidah al kli cheres she'eino yotzei miyedei dofno le'olam* — the Torah itself testifies that pottery vessels cannot release absorbed matter. The source is the *halacha* of cooking a *chatas* in a pottery vessel, which must be destroyed afterward — because once absorbed, the taste cannot be expelled. If the sweating demonstrates that the glazed vessel absorbed, then the Torah's rule applies: that absorbed matter stays in permanently.

### Heat vs. Cold

The *gemara* now resolves the apparent contradiction between Mareimar's leniency regarding wine and his stringency regarding *Pesach*. The response is: *zeh tashmisho bechamin vezehu tashmisho betzonen* — these are two different modes of use. *Chametz* is used with heat; *yayin nesech* is used cold. When contact is hot, the absorbed material penetrates through even intact glaze and embeds itself in the pottery beneath — whereupon the Torah's rule applies and it can never be fully expelled. When contact is cold, the glaze itself serves as an effective barrier and no meaningful absorption occurs at all.

This is one of the central distinctions running through the entire daf: cold absorption is a genuine phenomenon — vessels used with wine over extended periods do absorb even without heat — but it is categorically different from hot absorption. Cold absorption can, under certain conditions, be reversed; hot absorption into pottery cannot. Cold absorption may be blocked by an intact glaze; hot absorption will penetrate through it. And cold absorption permits more flexible methods of remedy — the three-day water process, brine, and other approaches — whereas hot absorption into pottery admits of no remedy at all, as the Torah itself attests.

---

# Avodah Zarah 34

## Rabbi Akiva's Three Ques…

### Fasting for Hours

The daf opens mid-discussion, picking up a few lines into 34a with the story of *Rabbi Akiva ikla l'Ginzak* — Rabbi Akiva's visit to Ginzak, where he was posed three questions. In each case, *lo hava b'yadei* — he did not hold the material and could not supply the *halacha* on the spot. The image is evocative: it would not have been sufficient for Rabbi Akiva simply to hazard an opinion; he would need to have the ruling firmly in hand, as a matter of received tradition.

The first question was *matnin l'shaot o ein mitanin l'shaot* — can one fast for hours, or must a fast be a full day? Rashi understands this as a question about whether one who incidentally did not eat in the morning may, upon reaching midday, formally accept a fast upon himself, thereby counting the entire day. There is, however, reason to read the question differently — in line with the *mishnayot* in Masechet Ta'anit concerning fast days that were called in the hope of rain. If rain fell during the afternoon, was one permitted to discontinue the fast at that point? The phrase *ve'im hishlim* — "and if he completed it" — appears to describe the scenario in which one might have terminated the fast early but chose not to, suggesting that the question concerns ending the fast before its conclusion rather than beginning it late. In any case, the *beit midrash* ruled *mitanin l'shaot*, and added that *ve'im hishlim yitpallel tefillat ta'anit* — if one did complete the fast, one recites the designated fast-day prayer, which in Tannaitic times meant the inclusion of additional *brachot* in the *Amidah*. Today this is reflected in the *Aneinu* paragraph. Conversely, one who does not complete the fast does not add those prayers.

This ruling opens an interesting side question regarding *Yom Kippur*: the *Shacharit* Torah reading on *Yom Kippur* is essentially a *Yom Tov* reading, reflecting the *kedushat hayom*, and there is general consensus that even one who is not fasting could receive an *aliyah* at *Shacharit*. The *Mincha* Torah reading, however, is more ambiguous — is it like a fast-day *Mincha* reading, which would require fasting, or like a Shabbat *Mincha* reading, which would not? This is a *machloket* between the *Shulchan Aruch* and the *Rema*, and Rabbi Akiva Eiger weighs in on the matter as well.

### Wine Jars (Kankanim)

The second question put to Rabbi Akiva was *kankanin shel ovdei kochavim asurim o mutarim* — are wine jars owned by idolaters prohibited or permitted? The question is understood to concern not their present status but whether they can be *kashered* and rendered permissible at all. Rabbi Akiva did not have the answer to this question either. The *beit midrash* ruled: *v'hilchta kankanin shel ovdei kochavim l'achar yud-bet chodesh mutarin* — the law is that such jars become permissible after twelve months of disuse, because whatever wine flavor was absorbed into the pottery becomes inconsequential over that span of time.

This ruling has broader implications. There is a lengthy discussion in *Yoreh Deah*, around simanim 121–122, and treated in the *Pitchei Teshuvah*, about whether porcelain and other ceramic vessels might similarly be *kashered* after twelve months, given that ordinarily we hold earthenware cannot be *kashered* by any means. The argument would be that after twelve months any absorbed flavor has fully degraded — through exposure to air, oxygen, or other environmental factors — such that there is simply nothing remaining. Of course, this remains a contested position and is not accepted *l'halacha* by many *poskim*. Moreover, for materials that can be *kashered* more readily — such as metal utensils, which require only immersion in boiling water — there would be little reason to resort to this more tenuous *kula*. The logic of the twelve-month leniency applies most naturally to cases where no other form of *kashering* is available, and even then, particularly given that the original prohibition of *stam yeinam* is itself *d'rabanan*, there are multiple layers of leniency operating simultaneously.

### Moshe's Clothing

The third question — *bameh shimmesh Moshe kol shivat yemei hamiluim*, what did Moshe wear throughout the seven days of the *miluim* — carries particular resonance given that Parashat Tetzaveh, which describes the inauguration of the *Kohanim*, was the week's *parashah*. During those seven days, Moshe Rabbeinu served as the *Kohen Gadol*, presiding over the induction of Aharon and his sons into the *Kehunah*. What he wore mattered, because it had to be clearly distinguishable from the *bigdei kehunah* worn by Aharon and his sons.

### Answers from Beit Midrash

The *beit midrash* answered: *b'chaluk lavan* — a plain white garment. And Rav Kahana later clarified, in the Amoraic period, that it was a white smock *she'ein bo imra* — one that lacked even an embroidered hem, so that no one would confuse it with the elaborate vestments of the *Kohen Gadol*. Thus the three questions encompassed an *Orach Chaim* matter, a *Yoreh Deah* matter, and a historical question about the *Beit Hamikdash* — none of which Rabbi Akiva could answer from his own knowledge, and all of which he resolved by consulting the *beit midrash*.

---

## Twelve-Month Drying Rule

### Grape Skins Classificati…

The *Gemara* now presents a *Baraita*: *tanu rabbanan hachartzanim vehazagim shel ovdei kochavim* — the grape seeds and grape peels belonging to idolaters. *Lachim assurim* — while moist, they are prohibited, because any residual grape liquid absorbed in them carries the status of *stam yeinam*. *Yeveshim mutarim* — once dry, they are permitted. The question the *Baraita* leaves unresolved is: *heichi dami lachim heichi dami yeveshim* — precisely what counts as moist and what counts as dry?

### Twelve Months Standard

The Amoraic clarification comes from *Amar Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel*: *lachim kol yud-bet chodesh, yeveshim le'achar yud-bet chodesh* — they are considered moist for the entirety of the first twelve months, and only after twelve months are they considered dry.

One might ask why twelve months is necessary — surely grape peels dry out more quickly than that. The answer lies in the realities of wine production: the skins and seeds are not laid out individually to air-dry but are discarded in large heaps together with all the waste from the winery. Clumped together in a mass, they retain their moisture for far longer than one might expect. One could also draw a suggestive parallel to the year-long mourning period, in which twelve months similarly marks the threshold at which something that was moist with connection begins to be regarded as fully separated.

A related procedural question arises: in a leap year, does "twelve months" mean twelve calendar months, or a full calendar year? Similar ambiguities arise with *kaddish*, *avelut*, and *yahrtzeit* observance — particularly in *Adar* years. The *halacha* regarding twelve months would seem to mean twelve months as such, though the question is not trivial.

It is also worth clarifying the distinction between *stam yeinam* and *yayin nesech*. *Yayin nesech* technically refers to wine actually used for libation to an idol, which is *assur behana'ah* by Torah law. *Stam yeinam* refers to wine touched or produced by non-Jews and is prohibited by rabbinic decree — a *gezeirah* that treats it as if it were *yayin nesech*. The difficulty is that throughout the *Gemara* and throughout the *Rishonim*, the terms are frequently conflated, and *yayin nesech* is often used loosely even where the prohibition is only *d'rabanan*. Keeping the distinction in view is essential for correctly parsing the level of prohibition being discussed.

### Wet/Dry Status Rules

*Amar Rabbah bar bar Channah amar Rabbi Yochanan*: the Gemara now records a *memra* that sharpens the rule considerably. *Keshen asurin asurin afilu behana'ah* — when the grape seeds and peels are in their moist state, they are prohibited even for benefit, not merely for consumption, because the liquid absorbed in them carries the full prohibition of wine that is *assur behana'ah*. *Keshen mutarin mutarin afilu be'achilah* — and once they become permitted after twelve months, they are permitted even to be eaten outright.

This formulation has potentially significant implications for the *kashrut* of raisins. If a non-Jew presses grapes or otherwise handles them in a manner that creates *stam yeinam* concerns, but the grapes are subsequently dried and allowed to remain dry for twelve months, they would become fully permissible. In practice, the production of raisins typically involves no pressing of juice at all, so the *stam yeinam* concern may not arise in the first place — though incidental dripping of juice during processing might still pose questions. The *halacha* regarding industrial grape and raisin production is complex and depends heavily on the specifics of each production process.

### Sediment & Vessel Types

The *Gemara* then records a series of Amoraic statements, each extending the twelve-month rule to a different substance or vessel type. *Amar Rav Zevid*: *hai dardaya dechamra de'armaye* — the wine sediment, the *shmarim*, the yeast-bearing dregs that settle at the bottom of a barrel of non-Jewish wine, also become permissible after twelve months, once whatever wine was in them has evaporated and only dry residue remains.

*Amar Rav Chaviva brei deRava*: *hani gulfi* — a different type of jug — are likewise permissible after twelve months. He adds a further ruling regarding *hani avata detayei* — the leather wine skins used by desert travelers, made of thick leather as Rashi describes. *Amar Rav Acha brei deRav Ika*: *hani purtzanei de'armai* — yet another category of vessels or pits and seeds — similarly follow the twelve-month rule. And *Amar Rav Acha brei deRava*: *hani gulfi dechimei ve'uchmei*, the black and brown pottery-type jars, also become permissible after twelve months. The cumulative effect of these statements is to establish a single overarching principle: wherever the concern is that a vessel or substance has been permeated with wine that carries a prohibition, twelve months of dryness renders it permissible. Each Amora addresses a slightly different case, but they all reinforce the same *psak*.

---

## Muryas & Fish Sauce

### Muryas Background

The *Gemara* turns to a discussion of *muryas*, a fermented fish sauce that was a staple of the Roman world, known in Latin as *garum*. The production process involved packing fish in salt and allowing them to ferment over an extended period. The liquid that resulted was the *garum* itself; the fish solids that sank to the bottom — corresponding to the Latin *hallex*, perhaps derived from *halos*, meaning salt — became what the *Gemara* calls *chilek*.

Archaeological evidence illuminates this world considerably. Jars found at Pompeii bear inscriptions identifying their contents as *garum castum* — pure *garum* — and at least one scholar has proposed that these were produced specifically from *kosher* fish for the Jewish inhabitants of Pompeii, though this theory is debated. The overwhelming majority of commercially produced *garum* appears to have been made from mackerel, which is a *kosher* fish, though cost pressures or availability could lead producers to substitute other species.

The *mishnah* — back on 29b — lists *muryas* as one of the items prohibited with an *issur hana'ah*, which points toward wine as the underlying concern, since a *kashrut* problem with non-*kosher* fish would ordinarily produce a prohibition on eating but not a prohibition on benefit. The role of wine in the production process will become clearer as the *Gemara* proceeds.

### Professional Production

*Tanu Rabbanan*: the *Baraita* states *muryas uman mutar* — *muryas* produced by a professional craftsman is permissible. The presumption is that a professional producer adheres to standard practice and does not adulterate his product with non-*kosher* fish or with wine — at least not in the initial stages of production.

The key distinction here concerns the stages of pressing. The first and second pressings of the fish are rich in natural oils and require no additives; the flavor is strong on its own. It is only from the third pressing onward — when the fish have been pressed multiple times and the resulting sauce is weak — that wine would be added to compensate for the diminished flavor. The price differential is decisive: where fish is inexpensive relative to wine, there is no economic incentive to adulterate the sauce with wine, and so the first-quality *muryas* from a professional can be assumed to be free of wine. This is analogous in structure to extra-virgin olive oil, where successive pressings yield progressively lower-quality product.

*Avimi brei deRabbi Abahu* taught: *muryas uman mutar*, and he himself both taught this ruling and applied it. He specified: *pa'am rishon vesheni denafish shumnayhu lo tzarich lemarmeihu chamra* — the first and second pressings, which are rich in fat and oil, require no wine addition. *Mikan ve'eilach remu behu chamra* — from the third pressing onward, wine would be mixed in, and therefore *shlishi assur* — the third pressing is prohibited.

### Chilek Permissibility

*Rabbi Yehuda ben Gamliel* stated in the name of *Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel*: *af chilek uman mutar* — even the *chilek*, the fish residue from the bottom of the production vessel, is permissible when it comes from a professional producer. The reasoning parallels that for *muryas* itself: there is a *chazakah* that a professional does not adulterate his high-quality product with non-*kosher* fish, and this presumption extends to the *chilek* as well.

One might raise the concern that after extracting the sauce, a producer could increase the volume of the *chilek* by mixing in other, cheaper fish — possibly non-*kosher* species — to bulk it up. Rashi raises a similar point, noting that *chilek* of non-Jews is prohibited when it is made from small fish mixed together in large quantities, since there is concern that non-*kosher* fish may have been included. The *Tannaim* nonetheless rule it permissible when coming from a professional, on the basis of the same presumption of honest practice. The parallel to contemporary *kashrut* supervision is worth noting: the presumption underlying these rulings — that a major commercial producer would not risk its reputation and business by adulterating its product — is structurally similar to arguments made about modern industrial food production.

### Akko Port Example

The *Gemara* relates a case: *hahu arba demuryasa de'atu lenamlya de'Akko* — there was a boat laden with *muryas* that docked at the port of Akko. Rabbi Abba of Akko went to inspect it. The question was whether this particular *muryas* could be presumed to be of the permissible variety.

Rava articulated the relevant concern: *ad ha'idna nichosh lah mishum demervei bah chamra* — the concern up to this point has been whether wine was mixed into it. The critical factor is the local price differential: *kista demuryas beluma* — if a measure of *muryas* costs one *luma*, and *kista dechamra bedaled luma'ei* — the same measure of wine costs four times as much, then there is no economic motivation to add wine to the *muryas*, and it can be presumed clean.

But Rabbi Yirmeya raised a complication to Rabbi Zeira: *dilma eidi deTzor atu deshavo chamra* — perhaps the boat came from Tyre, where the price ratio was inverted and wine was cheaper relative to *muryas*, making adulteration economically attractive. If it was produced in Tyre and then transported to Akko, the different price structure at the point of production would change the analysis entirely. The *Gemara* responds that sailing conditions near Tyre were poor, making such a route uncommon, so this scenario would be exceptional. The underlying principle, however, is clear: the permissibility of *muryas* is tied not only to whether it came from a professional producer but to the economic circumstances at the place of production, since those circumstances determine whether there was any incentive to adulterate the product with wine.

---

## Gevinat Beit Unaiki

### Reason for Prohibition

The *Gemara* now turns to the cheese of *Beit Unaiki*, which the *mishnah* (on 29b) listed as prohibited with an *issur hana'ah*. This is an *avodah zarah* question, distinct from the general *kashrut* questions about non-Jewish cheese that will be addressed later in the tractate.

*Amar Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish* — Reish Lakish — *mipnei mah asuru Gevinat Unaiki*: why did the Sages prohibit this cheese? *Mipnei she'rov agalim shel otah ir nishchatin l'avodah kochavim* — because the majority of the calves in that city are slaughtered for *avodah zarah*.

To understand why this matters, one must understand how cheese was made in Talmudic times. Cheese production required *or keva* — the stomach lining of a calf. The lining was fashioned into a bag, filled with milk, and the enzymes in the stomach lining caused the milk to curdle and become cheese. If the calf was slaughtered for idolatrous purposes, then the physical substance of the stomach lining carries the prohibition of *avodah zarah*, and any cheese made with it is prohibited even for benefit. That is why this is an *issur hana'ah* rather than merely a prohibition on consumption.

One might wonder: if a calf is slaughtered entirely for *avodah zarah*, would any part of it remain for sale in the market at all? The answer is that non-Jewish idolatrous sacrifice typically did not consume the whole animal. Just as in Greek mythology Prometheus teaches humans to offer the skin, bones, and fats to the gods while keeping the meat — a construction not entirely unlike the *korban shelamim* in its structure, though with the crucial difference that in our tradition the division is commanded by God rather than devised as a deception — it is reasonable that idolaters would dedicate specific portions of the animal to their worship while the remainder, including the stomach, entered commerce.

### Majority/Minority Logic

The *Gemara* presses further: *mai irya rov agalim* — why does it matter that it is the majority? *Afilu miyut nami* — even if it were a minority of calves being slaughtered for *avodah zarah*, shouldn't there still be a concern?

The answer invokes Rabbi Meir: *de'ha Rabbi Meir chayish l'miyuta* — Rabbi Meir, who is understood to be the author of our *mishnah*, is the opinion that is concerned even for a *miyut*, a minority. But a *miyut de'miyut* — a double minority — is another matter. If one says that the concern applies even to a minority, then one encounters the following analysis: consider all the animals in the city. Calves are a minority of all animals. Even if calves slaughtered for *avodah zarah* constituted the majority of calves, they would still be a minority of all animals — and their stomach linings, available in the market, would be a minority of all available stomach linings. That would make the problematic ones a *miyut de'miyut*, a minority of a minority.

### Rabbi Meir's Position

*Miuta de'miuta lo chayish Rabbi Meir* — even Rabbi Meir, who is concerned for a simple minority, is not concerned for a double minority. The *Gemara* therefore concludes that the *mishnah*'s ruling about *Beit Unaiki* specifically must rest on the premise that the calves slaughtered for *avodah zarah* constitute an actual majority of the calves in that city — not merely a majority of all animals. That way, the stomach linings from idolatrous slaughter are the majority among calf stomach linings available for cheese-making, while being a minority among all animal stomachs in general. This is a single *miyut* — a minority of all animals — which is exactly the kind of case Rabbi Meir does consider, and which the majority among calves makes sufficient to warrant prohibition. This also explains why the prohibition was specific to that one city: it was a local condition in which the majority of calves specifically, not animals in general, were dedicated to idolatrous slaughter.

### Intent Transfer Debate

The *Gemara* introduces a further question from Rabbi Shimon bar Elyakim directed at Reish Lakish: *ki nishchatin le'avodah kochavim mai havei* — even granting that most calves are slaughtered for *avodah zarah*, why should that render the stomach lining prohibited? Shouldn't Reish Lakish himself hold that there is no problem?

This question draws on a recorded *machloket* between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish. The case: *ha'shochet et ha-beheimah lizrok damah le'avodah kochavim ve'hiktir chalavah le'avodah kochavim* — one who slaughters an animal with the intention of subsequently sprinkling its blood for idolatrous worship, or burning its fats as an idolatrous offering. *Rabbi Yochanan amar asurah* — Rabbi Yochanan says the animal is prohibited. His reasoning: *kasavar machshivin me'avodah le'avodah* — the intent transfers from one act of worship to another. Even if what was ultimately performed differs from what was originally planned, the fact that the entire chain of actions was conceived as *avodah zarah* worship is sufficient to render the animal prohibited. Rabbi Yochanan derives this principle by analogy to the *Beit HaMikdash*: just as within the Temple the *machshava* — the mental intention during one *avodah* — can transfer to and affect another *avodah*, the same principle applies to *avodah zarah*. *Ve'alfinan chutz mi'pnim* — we extrapolate the definitions of *avodah zarah* from the definitions of Temple service.

The practical upshot for the *Beit HaMikdash* analogy is significant: *zerikat hadam* — sprinkling the blood — and *hekter chalavim* — burning the fats on the altar — are both recognized *avodot* in the Temple. The principle of *piggul* and related concepts in Masechet Zevachim turn precisely on how a disqualifying intent during one *avodah* can travel across the sequence of sacrificial acts. Here the same logic is applied to the realm of *avodah zarah*.

Reish Lakish says *muteret* — the animal remains permissible — because he does not accept this transfer of intent, at least not in all configurations. Rashi explains that Reish Lakish holds *lo yalfinan mipnim* — we do not extrapolate the laws of *avodah zarah* from the laws of the *Beit HaMikdash*.

When Rabbi Shimon bar Elyakim challenges Reish Lakish — if you say it is permitted, then how can our *mishnah* prohibit this cheese? — Reish Lakish responds: *tarmnach shatach*, a blessing upon you for raising it, and then clarifies: *uv'omer bigmar zevichah hu uvda* — the case of the *mishnah* is specifically where the person explicitly dedicated the *shechitah* itself as an act of *avodah zarah* worship. If the *shechitah* is itself the act of worship, then Reish Lakish agrees the animal is prohibited.
