What he disputes is only the case where the *shechitah* is neutral but the slaughterer plans to use the blood or fats for *avodah zarah* afterward — there, Reish Lakish holds that the subsequent *avodah zarah* does not retroactively taint the animal through the *shechitah*.

In other words, Reish Lakish does consider *shechitah* a significant *avodah* in the relevant sense — *dezevichah havei avoda chashuva kezrikah* — such that if the *shechitah* itself is performed with explicit *avodah zarah* intent, the animal is prohibited. He simply disagrees with Rabbi Yochanan about whether intent aimed at a *subsequent* act of worship can transfer back through the *shechitah* to prohibit the animal when the *shechitah* itself was not dedicated to *avodah zarah*.

This distinction allows Reish Lakish to uphold the *mishnah*'s prohibition on the cheese of *Beit Unaiki* — where the calves are slaughtered with explicit *avodah zarah* intent at the moment of *shechitah* — while maintaining his position in the broader debate with Rabbi Yochanan about the limits of transferred intent across distinct acts of worship.

---

---

# Avodah Zarah 35

## Cheese Mishnah Review

### Context & Framework

Daf 35 opens with an abundance of practically relevant material — non-Jewish cheese, milk, bread, and a range of other foods — but before engaging the *gemara* directly, it is necessary to review a *mishnah* from 29b, which the *gemara* on our daf references repeatedly. Without familiarity with that *mishnah*, the subsequent discussion would be difficult to follow.

### R. Yishmael vs R. Yehosh…

The *mishnah* records a conversation attributed to Rabbi Yehuda, in which Rabbi Yishmael questioned Rabbi Yehoshua while they were walking together: *mipnei mah asru gevinat ovdei kochavim* — why did the sages forbid non-Jewish cheese? Rabbi Yehoshua's initial answer was *mipnei shema'amidin otah bekeivat neveilah* — because non-Jews coagulate the cheese using stomach gunk from animals that were not slaughtered through proper *shechitah*, rendering the material *neveilah*.

### Olah vs Neveilah

Rabbi Yishmael immediately challenges this reasoning. He notes that the stomach gunk of an *olah* sacrifice is even more stringent than that of a *neveilah*, and yet we know that a *kohen sheda'ato yafah* — a priest who does not mind — may eat it directly, *sorfah chayyah*, without any further preparation. Moreover, the rabbis ruled *ein nehenin velo mo'alin* — one neither derives benefit from it nor violates the laws of *me'ilah* — indicating that the stomach gunk of the *olah* does not carry a full Torah-level prohibition. The upshot of this exchange is that eating stomach gunk of a *neveilah* would not itself be the real concern, thereby undermining Rabbi Yehoshua's first explanation.

### Idol Worship Reason

Forced to offer an alternative, Rabbi Yehoshua provides a second reason: non-Jews coagulate cheese using stomach gunk from animals that were dedicated to idol worship — *bekeivat eglei avodah kochavim*. Rabbi Yishmael responds sharply: if that is the case, then such cheese should be forbidden not merely to eat but also as an *issur hana'ah* — forbidden to derive any benefit from at all — since that is the standard rule for objects of idol worship. Rabbi Yehoshua has no answer.

### Closure & Diversion

At this point, *vehisio ledavar acher* — he changes the subject entirely. Rabbi Yehoshua pivots to a question about *Shir HaShirim*: how do you read the verse, *ki tovim dodecha miyayin* — "for your loves are better than wine" — in the masculine form, *dodecha*, or the feminine, *dodaich*? Rabbi Yishmael answers that it should be read in the masculine, since the parallel phrase *lere'ach shemanecha tovim* — "for the fragrance of your oils is good" — uses the masculine form. The apparent randomness of this digression will be explained shortly.

---

## Peresh Rulings

### Stoned Ox vs Idol

The *gemara* now opens with a statement from Rav Achdavoy: one who betroths a woman using the *peresh* — the excrement or stomach gunk — of a *shor haniskal*, an ox that was stoned to death for having gored a person, the betrothal is valid (*mekudeshet*). However, one who betroths using the *peresh* of an animal used for idol worship — *eglei avodat kochavim* — the betrothal is not valid (*einah mekudeshet*). The *gemara* proceeds to explain the distinction between these two rulings in two different ways.

### Logical Reasoning

The first approach is through *sevara*, logical reasoning. In the case of an animal dedicated to idol worship, it was in fact beneficial — *nichelei benafchei* — for the animal to have this gunk inside it, since a fatter, larger-looking animal was considered more impressive for purposes of idol worship. Because the gunk serves a purpose and benefits the animal's presentation, it is considered part and parcel of the prohibited animal, and is itself forbidden. By contrast, in the case of the *shor haniskal*, there is no benefit in having the gunk inside the ox — *lo nichelei benafchei* — and therefore it retains an independent status that is not subsumed under the prohibition of the animal.

### Textual Reasoning

The second approach is through *kra*, derivation from verses. Regarding idol worship, the verse states *lo tidbak beyadcha me'uma min hacherem* — nothing shall cling to your hand from that which is *cherem*, consecrated to idolatry. The word *me'uma*, "anything at all," implies by extension even the *peresh*. Regarding the *shor haniskal*, the verse states *sakol yisakel v'hashor lo ye'achel et besaro* — the ox shall be stoned and its flesh shall not be eaten. The verse specifies *besaro*, its flesh — which implies *ha pirsho mutar*, its excrement is permitted.

### Rava's Integration

Rava makes the striking observation that both of these conclusions — *tarveihu teni hi* — can in fact be derived from the very *mishnah* we reviewed at the beginning. The first derivation: the *mishnah* records that Rabbi Yehoshua initially said the prohibition on cheese was because the cheese was made with stomach gunk from a *neveilah*, and Rabbi Yishmael responded that stomach gunk from an *olah* offering — which is itself an *issur hana'ah* — is nevertheless permitted for a *kohen* to eat. This exchange implies by inference that objects which are themselves forbidden for benefit (*isurei hana'ah*) nevertheless have their *peresh* permitted. The second derivation: when Rabbi Yehoshua gave his alternative answer — that the cheese is made with stomach gunk from idol-worshipped animals — and Rabbi Yishmael countered that it should therefore be *asur behana'ah*, this implies that the *peresh* of an idol-worshipped animal is indeed forbidden.

The *gemara* then raises an interesting question. Given Rabbi Yishmael's challenge — that idol-worshipped animal gunk should be forbidden for benefit — why could Rabbi Yehoshua not have simply responded that there is no *issur* at all, since *leita l'issura be'einei*, the prohibition is no longer intact? After all, we find in other contexts (the case of *muryas*, a fish brine to which wine or vinegar is added in small amounts) that *rabbanan* did not forbid it for benefit precisely because the prohibited substance had lost its independent identity by being absorbed.

### Cheese Form Issue

The *gemara* answers that cheese is categorically different. Since the stomach gunk is the very substance that gives form and structure to the cheese — *keivan de'okmei ka mokim* — it has sufficient significance to be considered as though it remains fully present and intact. Therefore, Rabbi Yehoshua could not have deflected with that argument; the *issur* is treated as though it is still *be'einei*, still extant, by virtue of the coagulating function it performs.

---

## Shir HaShirim Diversion

### Oil Verse Chosen

We now return to the puzzle of why Rabbi Yehoshua specifically chose the verse *lere'ach shemanecha tovim* — "the fragrance of your oils is good" — as his subject-changing distraction. When Rav Dimi came from *Eretz Yisrael*, he reported that *Knesset Yisrael* said before the Holy One: *Ribbono Shel Olam*, the words of your beloved ones — meaning the sages — are more beloved to me than the wine of Torah itself: *arevim alai divrei dodecha yoter mi-yeinah shel Torah*.

### Sages Over Torah

This is a remarkable statement. The words of the sages — the Oral Torah, the elaborations and interpretations of the rabbis — are described as more pleasant than the wine of the written Torah itself. It is the oral tradition that is being celebrated, its capacity to extend and illuminate, and the verse from *Shir HaShirim* becomes a vehicle for that celebration.

### Kiss Verse Citation

One might ask: why was this particular verse chosen as the distraction, of all the verses in *Shir HaShirim*? Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi — and some say Rabbi Shimon bar Ami — answers that the choice was dictated not by this part of the verse but by its very opening: *yishakeni mi-neshikot pihu* — "let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth." Rabbi Yehoshua was using this verse to send a message to Rabbi Yishmael: *Yishmael achi, chashok siftotecha zo be-zo ve-al tivahel le-hashiv* — Yishmael, my brother, clamp your lips together and do not be so quick to respond. The citation of *Shir HaShirim* was a pointed, if poetic, request to stop asking so many questions.

---

## Decree & Secrecy

### New Decree Rule

This raises a further question: why did Rabbi Yehoshua not simply say he had no answer, rather than changing the subject entirely? Ulla — and some say Rav Shmuel bar Abba — explains: *gezeirah chadashah hi ve-ein mefakpekin bah* — this was a new decree, and one does not interrogate new decrees. When a new law is issued, one does not publicly challenge or undermine it, even if a compelling logical objection could be raised.

### Snake Venom Reason

What, then, was the actual substance of this decree? Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi says in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: *mishum nikur* — it was because of snake venom. The concern was that non-Jews were not careful about leaving their cheese exposed, and snakes could come and inject venom into it, rendering the cheese dangerous to eat. It is a striking reason, and the question naturally arises: if that was the reason, why was it not simply stated?

### Secrecy Period

The answer is provided by Ulla himself. When a new decree was issued in *Eretz Yisrael*, *lo megalu ta'ama ad treisar yarchei shata* — they did not reveal its reason for twelve months. The concern was that *dilma ika inish d'lo sevira leh*, perhaps there would be someone who disagreed with the reasoning, and he would come to treat the decree lightly — *atei l'zilzulei bah*. By keeping the reason secret for a full year, the practice would become established before anyone had the opportunity to argue against it. Only once people were already observing the law would the reason be disclosed. It is a telling insight into the politics of communal legislation.

---

## Yirmiya Challenge

### Aged Cheese Test

Rabbi Yirmiya is dismissive of the snake venom theory — the *gemara* says *megadef bah*, he mocks it. His challenge: if the concern is truly snake venom, then dried cheese should be permitted, and aged cheese should be permitted. Why? Because Rabbi Chanina rules in the context of *gilluy* — the broader laws of exposed liquids — that dried and aged substances are not subject to the snake venom concern: *yavesh mutar ein manichin l'yavesh, yashan mutar ein manicho l'yashan*. The venom does not allow substances to dry out or age; therefore, if a substance is dry or aged, one knows it could not contain active venom. Since non-Jewish cheese is not conditionally permitted when it is aged or dried, snake venom cannot be the actual reason for the prohibition.

### Milk Residue Theory

Rabbi Chanina therefore offers a different explanation: *lefi she'i efshar lah belo tzichtzuchei chalav* — because it is impossible to make cheese without leaving residual traces of milk in the final product. The concern is that the milk used by non-Jews may have included *treif* milk mixed in with otherwise permissible milk, and those residual traces of non-kosher milk remain present in the cheese.

### Stomach Lining

Shmuel offers yet another explanation: *mipnei shema'amidin otah b'or keivat neveilah* — because non-Jews coagulate the cheese not with the gunk itself but with an actual piece of the stomach lining of a *neveilah*, a piece of skin from the animal's stomach dropped into the milk to make it curdle. According to Shmuel, the gunk itself is not the problem — it is the stomach lining that is.

The implication of Shmuel's position is striking: *ha keiva gufa sharya* — the stomach gunk itself is permitted. But this creates a difficulty: a *mishnah* elsewhere states that *keivat oved kochavim v'shel neveilah harei zu asurah* — the stomach gunk of a non-Jew and of a *neveilah* is forbidden.

An additional difficulty with that *mishnah* is noted: the phrasing is itself strange. What does it mean to distinguish between the gunk of a non-Jew and of a *neveilah* as though they were separate categories? *Atu d'oved kochavim lav neveilah hi* — is the animal of a non-Jew not itself a *neveilah*? Shmuel resolves this: the *mishnah* is teaching that the slaughter of a non-Jew is to be treated as *neveilah* — they are in fact the same thing.

### Shmuel Resolution

There remains the contradiction between Shmuel's two apparent positions — one permitting the gunk, one forbidding it. The *gemara* resolves this: *kan kodem chazra, kan le'achar chazra* — one statement reflects Shmuel's view before he changed his mind, and the other reflects his view afterward. *Umishnah lo zazah mimkomah* — the *mishnah* was not rewritten to reflect the updated position, because that is simply not how we treat established texts. The earlier version remains in place as a historical artifact of what was once taught. The practical bottom line, according to Shmuel's final position, is that the stomach gunk is permitted, and it is the stomach lining itself that is the problem.

---

## Multiple Reasons

### Pig Fat Reason

The *gemara* now accumulates a striking series of additional reasons offered by various *amoraim* for the prohibition on non-Jewish cheese — a relatively unusual phenomenon. Rav Malachya in the name of Rav Ada bar Ahava states: *mipnei shemachlikim paneha beshoman chazir* — because non-Jews grease the surface or sides of their cheese with pig fat.

### Vinegar Reason

Rav Chisda offers a different reason: *mipnei shema'amidin otah bechomet* — because they use vinegar to coagulate the cheese. Since vinegar functions analogously to wine in halachic terms, this would render the cheese not merely forbidden to eat but also subject to the prohibition of benefit.

### Orla Sap Reason

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak offers yet another reason: *mipnei shema'amidin otah b'saraf ha'orla* — because non-Jews coagulate their cheese using sap derived from a tree whose fruit is *orla*, meaning a fruit tree within its first three years of growth, from which the fruit is forbidden.

### Orla Dispute

The *gemara* asks: whose opinion does this follow? It follows the position of Rabbi Eliezer in a *beraita*: *hamamid b'saraf ha'orla asur mipnei shehu peri* — one who coagulates cheese with sap from an *orla* tree is forbidden from the result, because that sap has the legal status of fruit. The *gemara* adds that one need not limit this to Rabbi Eliezer's view — even Rabbi Yehoshua could agree here. The only point of disagreement between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua in this area is regarding *kitpa d'goza*, the sap of a branch, which Rabbi Yehoshua holds is not considered fruit. But with regard to *kitpa d'peira* — sap that flows directly from the fruit itself — Rabbi Yehoshua agrees that it has the status of fruit and is forbidden. Rabbi Yehoshua himself says explicitly: sap of the leaves or sap of the roots used in cheese-making is *mutar*, perfectly permitted; but sap from the *paggim* — the young figs — *asur*, because *mipnei shehu peri*, it is like the fruit itself.

### Tension Unresolved

However, a sharp difficulty now surfaces with the vinegar reason and the *orla* sap reason. Both Rav Chisda and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak posit reasons that would logically render the cheese forbidden not merely to eat but also as an *issur hana'ah* — since vinegar has the status of wine, and *orla* is forbidden for benefit. Yet we know that non-Jewish cheese is in fact only forbidden to eat, not forbidden for benefit. The *gemara*'s response is simply *kashya* — it is a difficulty, and it is left unresolved. This unresolved tension suggests that none of these individual reasons is fully satisfactory as a standalone explanation, and that the prohibition may have originated as a broader decree that does not reduce cleanly to any single rationale.

---

## Torah Scholar Homily

### Balsam Oil Parable

Rav Nachman the son of Rav Chisda expounds: what is the meaning of the verse *lere'ach shemanecha tovim* — "the fragrance of your oils is good"? To what is a *talmid chacham* compared? To a covered plate of *paltin* — balsam oil. When the plate is uncovered, *reicha nodef* — its fragrance wafts and spreads, a beautiful and pleasant smell. When it is covered, *mekhusah ein reicha nodef* — the fragrance is contained and no one benefits from it. So too the Torah scholar: when he is out in public, teaching and sharing his wisdom, the fragrance of his knowledge spreads; when he is hidden away and not teaching, the world does not benefit.

### Revealed Secrets

But the homily goes further: *v'lo od ela devarim she'mechusim mimenu mitgalim lo* — not only does his fragrance spread when he teaches, but the things that were hidden even from himself become revealed to him. Rashi explains: *mitgalim lo me-aleihen belo torach k'shehu melamdan* — they become revealed on their own, without labor, in the very act of teaching. The teacher discovers, as he teaches, depths he had not previously accessed.

### Alamot Wordplay

There now follows a wordplay on the verse *alamot ahevucha* — "young women love you." The *gemara* says: do not read *alamot*, young women, but rather *alumot*, hidden things. The hidden things will love you — that is, they will come to you, they will be revealed to you, as you engage in Torah.

### Two Worlds Inherit

The homily continues: *v'lo od ela she'malach hamavet ohavo* — not only that, but the Angel of Death loves him. The *gemara* reads *alamot* as *al-mavet* — he who presides over death will love the Torah scholar, which is to say, the Angel of Death cannot touch him while he is engaged in Torah learning. And finally, *v'lo od ela she'nochel shnei olamot* — he inherits two worlds, *echad olam hazeh ve'echad olam haba*, this world and the world to come. The word *alamot* is now read as *olamot* — worlds. The Torah scholar inherits worlds.

---

## Food Mishnah

### Forbidden to Eat

The *mishnah* now shifts to a broader enumeration: *ve-eilu devarim shel ovdei kochavim asurin ve-ein isuran issur hana'ah* — these are things associated with non-Jews that are forbidden, but whose prohibition does not extend to *issur hana'ah*, forbidden benefit. One may not eat them but one may derive benefit from them.

### Non-Jewish Milk

The first item is *chalav she-chalavo oved kochavim ve-ein Yisrael ro'ehu* — milk milked by a non-Jew without Jewish supervision. This is the foundation of the well-known discussion around *chalav stam*. Rav Moshe Feinstein's *heter* — largely accepted in the Modern Orthodox community and in significant portions of the *Charedi* world in earlier generations — holds that government regulation of the dairy industry functions as a form of constructive supervision. Since the regulatory framework makes adulteration effectively impossible, it is *anan sahadei*, as if we are all present watching. Under this view, commercially produced milk is treated as *chalav Yisrael*. It is not that one abandons the requirement of *chalav Yisrael*; rather, one holds that the regulatory environment satisfies it.

### Bread & Oil

The *mishnah* continues: *ve'haphat ve'hashemen shelahem* — their bread and their oil. Regarding oil: *Rebbi u'veit dino hitiru ha-shemen* — Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and his court permitted non-Jewish oil, reversing an earlier prohibition. The *mishnah* thus records a historical leniency regarding oil.

### Brined Foods

The *mishnah* then lists a series of additional forbidden foods: *shlakot u-kvashim she-darkan latet letochan yayin ve-chometz* — cooked vegetables and brined foods into which wine or vinegar are customarily added; *tarit trufah* — a kosher fish that has been so thoroughly mashed that one cannot verify whether non-kosher fish has been mixed in; *sir she-ein ba daga kalbit shotetet bo* — fish brine in which a *kalbit* fish is not floating, since the *kalbit* fish, according to Rashi, floats only in kosher fish brine and therefore serves as a sign of kashrut; *ha-chilek* — a fish that is itself permissible but resembles a non-kosher species; *kurt shel chiltit* — a measure of asafoetida, a pungent spice used in ancient cooking and known in contemporary Indian cuisine; and *melach salkundit*. All of these are forbidden to eat but permitted for benefit.

It is worth noting that the appearance of *chiltit* here connects to a broader halachic principle discussed elsewhere in *Avodah Zarah*: *devarim charifim*, sharp and pungent substances, have the capacity to awaken dormant tastes. Even a taste that would ordinarily be considered *pagum* or neutralized by time can be reactivated when cooked or cut with something as potent as *chiltit* — a principle that is later applied to onions, garlic, and similar sharp foods.

---

## Milk Concerns

### Switching Worry

The *gemara* now probes the rationale behind the prohibition on non-Jewish milk. The challenge is direct: why worry? If the concern is *achlufi* — that a non-Jew switched out kosher milk for non-kosher milk — the answer seems obvious: *tahor chivver, tamei yarok* — kosher milk is white and non-kosher milk is a different color, greenish or yellowish. They look different. Switching would be immediately detectable.

### Cheese Test

If the concern is not outright switching but *eiruvei* — mixing a small amount of non-kosher milk into kosher milk — there is also an easy solution. One should simply attempt to make cheese from it, because *chalav tahor omed, chalav tamei eino omed* — kosher milk can be made into cheese, while non-kosher milk cannot. This is apparently a real physical phenomenon, having to do with the enzymatic composition of milk from non-kosher animals. If the milk coagulates properly, it is kosher; if not, there is a problem.

### Cheese Test Fails

However, the *gemara* notes that the cheese test only solves the problem if one is using the milk to make cheese. What if one intends to use it for *chamcha* — a dish that uses raw, uncongealed milk? One might still propose that a small amount be taken aside and tested. But the *gemara* responds: *keivan d'v'tahor nami ika nisyubei d'lo kaima*, even with fully kosher milk there will be *nisyuvei* — whey — that does not coagulate into cheese. Non-kosher milk mixed in with kosher could blend with the whey, and one would mistake the adulterated portion for ordinary kosher whey, rendering the test unreliable. Alternatively, even if one is making cheese, *ika d'ka bini atifei* — there will be milk remaining hidden within the holes of the cheese, much like the holes in Swiss cheese, meaning small pockets of non-kosher milk could be concealed within the finished product. The test therefore does not provide a reliable certification.

---

## Bread Story

### Admiration Question

The *mishnah* listed bread among the forbidden items. The *gemara* opens this discussion with an unusual statement. Rabbi Kahana says in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *pat lo hutra beveit dino* — bread was never permitted by his court, and some versions read *beveiti*, in his house. The very fact that Rabbi Yochanan felt compelled to say this implies that someone held otherwise. The *gemara* confirms: *in* — yes, there is indeed such a view.

When Rav Dimi came from *Eretz Yisrael*, he reported the following story. Once Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi went out into the countryside, and a non-Jew brought before him *pat purnei* — bread baked in a large oven, *ma'afeh se'ah*. Rabbi exclaimed: *kama na'eh pat zu* — how beautiful is this bread! And then: *mah ra'u chachamim le'osrah* — what did the sages see that led them to forbid it? This is a striking statement. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, the *redactor* of the *Mishnah* and the preeminent rabbinic authority of his generation, is expressing apparent bewilderment at the prohibition.

### Intermarriage Fear

The *gemara* responds with a *kasha*: what do you mean, what did they see? The reason is well established — *mishum chatnut*, because of the concern that eating together leads to social intimacy which leads to *chatnut*, intermarriage. But then the *gemara* reframes Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's question more precisely: *ela mah ra'u chachamim le'osrah basadeh* — what did the sages see to forbid it specifically in the countryside? In a rural setting, the social dynamics that lead to intermarriage are presumably absent. This was the real thrust of Rabbi's question — not challenging the prohibition in cities, but wondering about its application in the countryside.

### Jewish Baker Query

Rav Yosef — and some say Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda — disputes the story entirely. The incident did not happen this way. Rather, this is what actually occurred: Rabbi traveled to a certain place and observed that his students were *dachuk* — in real distress, without access to bread. He said: *ein kan palter* — is there no baker here? The people assumed he meant a non-Jewish baker, thus implying that even such bread would be acceptable under these circumstances. But Rabbi's intent was entirely otherwise.

### No Jewish Option

Rabbi Chelbo rules: even according to the interpretation that assumed Rabbi was asking about a non-Jewish baker, *lo amran ela delika palter Yisrael* — this leniency applies only where there is no Jewish bakery available. Where a Jewish baker exists, there is no dispensation to eat non-Jewish bread under any reading of the incident.

### City vs Country

Rabbi Yochanan adds a further qualification: even the lenient reading of Rabbi's statement — that non-Jewish bread might be permissible in some circumstances — *hani milei basadeh*, applies only in the countryside. *Aval ba'ir lo* — but in a city, one may not eat non-Jewish bread, *mishum chatnut*, because the concern of social proximity leading to intermarriage is fully operative in an urban setting.

### Avu Example

The *gemara* closes with a pointed anecdote. A certain Ibu would take and eat non-Jewish bread *abei metzrei* — along the borders of the fields, apparently reasoning that this qualified as the permitted countryside context. Rava — and some say Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak — declared to the people: *lo tishte'u minei* — do not associate with Ibu, because *dek'achil lachma arma'ei*, he eats non-Jewish bread. It is a striking conclusion: not merely a theoretical ruling, but a social distancing from one who treats the prohibition lightly.

---

---

# Avodah Zarah 36

## Oil Kashrut & Repealed D…

### Oil Prohibition Overview

The final line of 35b introduces the next topic of the *mishnah*: the *kashrut* of oil produced by idolaters. The *mishnah* records that *Rabbi u-veit dino* — Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and his *beit din* — permitted the oil, implying that at some earlier point a prohibition had been in force and was subsequently repealed. The discussion therefore proceeds on two tracks: when was the prohibition first instituted, and why, and how and why was it later repealed.

This case is notable as one of the relatively few examples in *Shas* of a rabbinic *gezeirah* that was formally abrogated, and it becomes an important test case for understanding the scope and parameters of rabbinic legislative authority.

### Cheese Prohibition Digre…

Before turning to the oil, it is worth noting the prior discussion of why non-Jewish cheese was prohibited. The *sugyah* canvassed numerous explanations, and *Tosafot*'s conclusion appears to follow Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's position that the concern is snake venom — a matter of *sakana*. Characterizing it as a *sakana* opens the question of whether, if the danger could be demonstrably eliminated, the prohibition might no longer apply, at least according to those authorities who reason that way. Indeed, some have argued that the *Rama*, the *Chazon Ish*, and even Rav Soloveitchik ruled in line with *Tosafot* in various circumstances.

By contrast, the *Rambam* and many other prominent *rishonim* hold that the prohibition stems from the *neveilah* concern: the rennet used in cheese production is derived from the stomach lining of an animal slaughtered without *shechita*, making it a piece of actual meat. Because this *ma'amid* — the coagulating agent — imparts the flavor of *neveilah* into the cheese and cannot be *batel*, the rabbis decreed against all cheese produced by non-Jewish manufacturers. On this view, even cheeses produced today with microbial or vegetable-derived curdling agents enter a debate already found among the *geonim* and *rishonim* about whether non-animal curdling agents fall under the *gezeirah* at all. The *Rambam* and many *geonim* were *machmir* on this point, though the Talmud itself leaves the matter open.

### Oil Repeal Question

Returning to the *shemen*: the discussion that follows asks both why the prohibition was originally instituted and what justification Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi had for repealing it.

---

## Rav's Daniel Theory

### Daniel Gazar Alav

*Rav amar*: *Daniel gazar alav* — it was Daniel and his *beit din*, during the period of the Babylonian exile, who decreed against the use of oil produced by idolaters. Daniel is not classified as a *navi* in the strict sense within the rabbinic tradition, but he occupies a role close to that of a prophet, and this attribution grants the *gezeirah* considerable antiquity and authority.

### Shmuel's Tamei Vessel Th…

*Shmuel*, however, offers a different rationale: *zelifatan shel keilim tmeiyim osartan* — the prohibition arose because of the seepage of *tamei* liquids from the vessels in which the oil was stored. The concern is that a jar already containing absorbed *tamei* substances would leach those substances into the olive oil placed within it, rendering the oil *tamei*.

### Tahara Not Universal

The *gemara* challenges Shmuel's formulation immediately: *atu kulei alma ochlei taharot ninhu?* — is everyone who eats food required to maintain *tahara*? Eating *chulin* in a state of *tahara* was a *midat chasidut*, a special stringency practiced by portions of the rabbinic class during the *mishnaic* period, but it was never obligatory for the general population. A *gezeirah* premised on that concern would rest on a very narrow foundation.

### Prohibited Vessels Seepa…

Shmuel accordingly revises his position: *zelifatan shel keilim assurim osartan* — the concern is not *tamei* vessels but prohibited (*assur*) vessels, that is, containers that had previously held non-kosher wine, lard, or other prohibited substances. The absorbed flavor of those prohibited materials would seep into the olive oil stored in the same vessels. One might initially object that such contamination would degrade the quality of the oil and therefore constitute *noten ta'am lifgam* — a detrimental flavor — which is ordinarily permissible. The *gemara* will address this directly.

---

## Shmuel vs. Rav Debate

### Shmuel's Logic for Repeal

Shmuel now presses his advantage. *Bishlama ledidi* — his own position explains coherently why the prohibition could later be repealed. As he notes, *Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta* reported that *Rabi Simlai* taught in *Ntzivin* that when Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and his *beit din* took a vote on the oil, *nimnu alav vehitiruhu* — they voted to permit it. Their rationale, according to Shmuel, was *kasavar noten ta'am lifgam mutar*: they ruled, or reassessed, that any flavor that would be transferred from the prohibited vessels into the oil would damage rather than improve the oil's taste, and a *noten ta'am lifgam* imparts no halachic prohibition.

One might ask whether *noten ta'am lifgam* was simply not a recognized principle before Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's time, or whether the earlier authorities had assessed the flavor transfer differently, or whether Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and his court were clarifying the proper application of an already-established rule. These are significant questions the *gemara* leaves open.

In any case, Shmuel's point is that if the original prohibition had a concrete and limited rationale — the seepage of non-kosher flavors into the oil — then a later *beit din* can reevaluate whether that concern still applies under current circumstances and repeal the *gezeirah* accordingly.

### Repeal Authority Challen…

Shmuel then turns the argument against Rav: *ela ledidach de'amarta Daniel gazar alav* — but on your account, Rav, that it was Daniel who decreed against the oil, how can you maintain that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi could subsequently come and repeal it? The concern here is one of institutional hierarchy and legal precedent. A *gezeirah* instituted by a figure of Daniel's stature, centuries earlier, represents a deeply embedded legal norm. And indeed, one must also consider how much of this was Daniel's personal stringency versus an actual promulgated decree — the *gemara* at this stage does not say *Daniel u-veit dino* but simply attributes the *gezeirah* to Daniel himself, which will become significant shortly.

### Ein Beit Din Yachol Leva…

The challenge is rooted in the well-known principle: *ein beit din yachol levatel divrei beit din chaveiro ela im ken gadol heimenu be-chokhma u-ve-minyan* — one court cannot abrogate the rulings of another court unless it is greater in wisdom and in number. This principle, discussed extensively in the first chapter of *Beitzah*, raises a fundamental question about the architecture of rabbinic law. There are at least two ways to read the principle. One reading addresses competing courts of equal standing within the same era, neither of which can override the other's local rulings — the remedy is to appeal to a higher authority, namely the *Sanhedrin*. The other reading, which appears to be the relevant one here, addresses the relationship between *batei din* across historical periods: can a later *Sanhedrin* repeal decrees issued by an earlier *Sanhedrin*?

The word *minyan* in the phrase *gadol heimenu be-chokhma u-ve-minyan* is itself subject to debate among the *rishonim*. It could refer literally to the number of members of the court — the *Sanhedrin* was normally seventy-one, though the *Anshei Knesset HaGedolah* had one hundred twenty members, which may be why certain enactments of Ezra's court are considered unrepeatable. Alternatively, *minyan* might refer not to the number of members but to the size of the court's constituency — the number of students and followers who adhere to that court's rulings, and thus a measure of its authority and reach. Both interpretations carry significant implications for how *dinim d'rabbanan* function over time.

### Ad Hominem vs. Lod

At this point in the debate, Rav attempts a different tactic. He questions whether the position that the oil prohibition was repealed really rests on a reliable source, asking: *amar lei Simlai Luda'ah ke-ha'amarta?* — is this really what Simlai from *Lod* said? And then: *shani Luda'ei de-mizalzelu* — people from *Lod* are known to be lax in their observance of rabbinic decrees, and therefore their opinions on the weight and bindingness of *dinim d'rabbanan* cannot be taken as authoritative. This is a remarkable move — an *ad hominem* attack on an entire community rather than engagement with the legal substance.

### Rav's Tradition Defense

The *gemara* indicates that this approach backfired: *ichsif* — Rav was embarrassed. The direction the argument had taken, attacking the community rather than the legal principle, was not the kind of reasoning Rav wanted to be associated with. He pivots to a substantive defense. *Amar Rav: im heim lo darshu ana lo darshinan* — if the tradition had not already interpreted the *pasuk* in this way, Rav himself would never have derived this law from the *drashah*. In other words, Rav concedes that the *pasuk* in Daniel is not independently compelling as a source for the prohibition; what makes the *drashah* meaningful is that it serves as a *mnemonic* for a law received through reliable tradition. The *drashah* is an *asmachta* that confirms what is already known from *mesorah*, not the source from which the law is derived.

---

## Daniel Proof & Binding N…

### Daniel 1:8 Citation

Rav proceeds to cite the verse: *vayasem Daniel al libo asher lo yisga'el bepas-bag hamelech uveyayin mishtav* — Daniel resolved not to defile himself with the king's bread or with his wine. The word *mishtav* is spelled *malei*, with a *yud*, which leads the *gemara* to read it as referring to two distinct types of drink: *bishtei mishta'ot hakasuv medaber*, the verse speaks of two kinds of drinking — one of wine and one of oil.

### Weak Drashah Admission

Rav openly acknowledges the weakness of this reading as an independent *drashah*. Left to its own devices, no interpreter would read the verse as referencing oil. The *drashah* is valid only because the tradition already establishes that Daniel avoided non-Jewish oil, and the verse provides a post-hoc textual anchor for that tradition.

### Personal vs. Binding Dec…

The real disagreement between Rav and Shmuel crystallizes around the question of whether Daniel's avoidance of oil constituted a personal practice or a binding legal decree. *Rav savar: al libo sam u-lechol Yisrael hora* — Rav holds that the phrase *al libo sam*, "he resolved in his heart," indicates that Daniel decided this for himself personally, but then *hora* — he issued a *hora'ah*, a legal ruling, making it binding upon all of Israel. The verb *hora* is significant: it implies a formal *psak*, not merely a personal stringency.

### Shmuel: Personal Decisio…

*Shmuel savar: al libo sam u-lechol Yisrael lo hora* — Shmuel holds that Daniel's resolution was purely personal. He decided this for himself but never promulgated it as a binding decree upon the community. On Shmuel's reading, there was therefore no *gezeirah* in the time of Daniel at all; the prohibition arose for entirely different reasons at a later period, as Shmuel explained, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's court had full authority to reassess and repeal it.

---

## Eighteen Decrees Question

### Oil Among Eighteen?

A new question is raised: was the oil prohibition counted among the eighteen decrees enacted by *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel* on the famous day when *Beit Shammai* outnumbered *Beit Hillel* and pushed through eighteen *gezeirot*? If oil was among those eighteen, the problem of repeal becomes even more acute.

### Daniel Rejected, Later A…

One possibility offered: Daniel did attempt to institute the decree, but the people did not accept it — *Daniel gazar velo kibeil*. Then, in a later generation, the students of *Hillel* and *Shammai* reinstated the same *gezeirah* and this time it was accepted: *va-atu talmidei d'Hillel ve-Shammai ve-gazur ve-kibeil*. If this is the case, one might ask: what was the point of Rav citing the Danielic origin of the decree if it was not accepted until the time of the students of *Hillel* and *Shammai*? The *gemara* regards this as a valid challenge.

### Urban vs. Rural Scope

An alternative resolution: *Daniel gazar alav ba'ir* — Daniel originally decreed against oil in urban settings, where the risk of adulteration or social intermingling was more acute. Later, the students of *Shammai* and *Hillel* extended the *gezeirah*: *va-atu inhu ve-gazur afilu basadeh* — they extended it to rural settings as well.

### Repeal Authority vs. Sha…

Either way, a serious difficulty remains: *ve-Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi heichi matzi l'mishrei takanta d'talmidei Shammai ve-Hillel* — how could Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi repeal a *takkanah* established by the students of *Shammai* and *Hillel*, who are of obviously far greater antiquity and seniority? The same principle reasserts itself: *ein beit din yachol levatel divrei beit din chaveiro ela im ken gadol heimenu be-chokhma u-ve-minyan*.

---

## Majority Acceptance Prin…

### All Decrees Repeatable E…

The *gemara* invokes an important principle from *Rabbah bar bar Chana* in the name of *Rabbi Yochanan*: *bechol yachol levatel beit din divrei beit din chaveiro chutz mi-shmonah asar davar* — in general, any *beit din* can repeal the rulings of an earlier *beit din*, except for those eighteen specific matters.

### Eliyahu Cannot Repeal Ei…

The principle is underscored dramatically: *she-afilu yavo Eliyahu u-veit dino ein shomein lo* — even if Eliyahu himself arrives in the Messianic era and convenes a *beit din* to repeal those eighteen *gezeirot*, the ruling is not to be heeded. This raises a fascinating question: why specifically those eighteen? They were enacted on a single day when *Beit Shammai* achieved a majority over *Beit Hillel* — what makes those eighteen uniquely immune to repeal while every other *gezeirah* from earlier or later periods remains in principle reversible? The *gemara* does not pause to address this directly, but notes that Eliyahu's *beit din* would be subject to the same rule — prophetic authority and legislative authority are categorically distinct, as the *Rambam* elaborates extensively: prophets legislate only in their capacity as heads of the *Beit Din HaGadol*, never by virtue of their prophetic powers alone.

### Rav Mesharshiya: Spread…

*Rav Mesharshiya* provides the underlying rationale: *ho-il u-fashat issuro berov Yisrael* — those eighteen *gezeirot* are irreversible because they spread throughout the majority of the Jewish people and became universally accepted. *Shemen lo pashat issuro berov Yisrael* — the oil prohibition, by contrast, never achieved that broad acceptance. This is why Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi was not only legally empowered to repeal it but had good reason to do so: the people were not observing it in any case.

### Investigation of Oil Acc…

This factual claim is supported by *Rabbi Shmuel bar Abba* in the name of *Rabbi Yochanan*: *yashivu raboteinu badku al shemen shelo pashat issuro berov Yisrael* — the teachers of that generation — Rabbi Yochanan's era, shortly after Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi — conducted an investigation and found that the prohibition against oil had not spread throughout the majority of Israel.

### Majority Uphold Principle

Upon this finding, *v'samchu raboteinu al divrei Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel ve-al divrei Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok* — they relied on the ruling of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok, two *Tannaim* who stated: *ein gozrim gezeirah al ha-tzibur ela im ken rov tzibur yecholim la'amod bah* — a *beit din* should not, or perhaps cannot, decree a law upon the community unless the majority of the community is capable of upholding it.

This formulation leaves a critical ambiguity: is this a formal limitation on the legal power of the *beit din* — such that a *gezeirah* which fails to achieve majority acceptance is retroactively invalid — or is it merely a counsel of prudence, warning against enacting decrees that will generate widespread violation? If the former, then the failure of a *gezeirah* to take hold might in principle render it void. If the latter, it remains a judgment call about good legislative practice, not a juridical nullity.

Further, even if the principle does function as a formal limitation, it does not appear to operate automatically. What is required is active judicial intervention: a *beit din* must investigate, find that the *gezeirah* failed to spread, and formally repeal it. That is precisely what Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi did. The law does not simply evaporate because people are not observing it; the authority of the *Beit Din HaGadol* is still necessary to give the repeal legal effect.

It is also worth noting that this position was in the minority: *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* and *Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok* represent a dissenting Tannaitic view, one the majority of *Tannaim* apparently did not share. The mainstream position seems to have been that *gezeirot* may be enacted even if the community will not fully observe them. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi found it necessary to invoke this minority view as the basis for the repeal.

---

## Malachi Source & Rov Tzi…

### Malachi 3:9 Proof

On the last line of 36a, *Rav Adda bar Ahava* provides a Scriptural peg for the principle that a *gezeirah* requires broad communal acceptance. The verse cited is from *Malachi* 3:9: *bame'era atem ne'arim ve-oti atem kovim ha-goy kulo* — "you are cursed with a curse, and you are robbing Me, the entire nation."

### Entire Nation Requirement

The operative phrase is *ha-goy kulo* — the entire nation. The verse associates the full force of a covenantal curse with the participation of the entire nation, not a partial constituency. Analogously, the argument runs, a rabbinic decree that binds with the force of law — and whose violation carries the weight of transgression — requires the acceptance of the entire community, or at minimum the majority. Only when *ha-goy kulo* is in play does the decree carry full operative force.

### Curse Acceptance Conditi…

*Rashi* notes that *bame'era atem ne'arim* refers to accepting a *gezeirah* in the manner of a binding oath or covenantal commitment, analogous to the acceptance at *Har Gerizim* and *Har Eival*. The implication: *ei ika goy kulo, in; ei lo, lo* — if the entire community is present as the accepting body, the decree takes effect; if not, it does not.

---

## Four Categories & Daught…

### Four Things Listed

The *gemara* now takes up a teaching attributed to *Bali* in the name of *Avimi*, quoting *Rav*: *pitan ve-shamnan ve-yenan u-venoteihem, kullan mi-shmonah asar davar hen* — bread, oil, wine, and their "daughters" are all counted among the eighteen decrees of *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel*.

### Benoteihem Definition

This prompts the question: *benoteihem mai hi* — what does "their daughters" mean in this context?

### Non-Jewish Women as Nidd…

*Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak* explains: *gazru benoteihem niddot me-arisotan* — the rabbis decreed that non-Jewish women are to be considered *niddot* from infancy, from the cradle. The background is that *mi-de'oraita*, the laws of *tumah ve-taharah* do not apply to non-Jews at all — with the possible exception of a non-Jewish corpse, itself subject to Tannaitic dispute. Non-Jews are not subject to *tumah* and cannot become *tamei* in the biblical sense. However, *mi-de-rabbanan* several forms of *tumah* were instituted with respect to non-Jews, presumably as an extension of the social boundaries constructed by the laws of *tumah ve-taharah* for the Jewish community itself. In this particular case, all non-Jewish women are treated rabbinically as if they were *niddot* from birth. The practical consequence is that any otherwise-prohibited sexual contact with a non-Jewish woman carries the added rabbinic violation of *niddah* as well.

### Gneiva: Avodah Zarah Rea…

*Gneiva*, however, quoting *Rav*, offers a different explanation: *kulan mishum avodah kochavim gazru bahem* — all four of these categories were decreed upon for the same underlying reason, namely *avodah zarah*, concern about idolatrous practice.

---

## Causal Chain of Decrees

### Bread-Oil-Wine Chain

*Rav Acha bar Adda* came from *Eretz Yisrael* and quoted *Rabbi Yitzchak* elaborating the causal chain: *gazru pitan mishum shamnan* — they prohibited the bread because of the oil. One might ask why the oil is considered a stronger basis for the decree than the bread itself, which prompts the clarification: *ela al pitan ve-shamnan mishum yenan* — in fact both bread and oil are prohibited because of wine. The connection is social: eating together leads to drinking together, and oil is part of the food that accompanies the shared meal, bringing one in proximity to the prohibited wine.

### Wine → Daughters

*Ve-al yenan mishum benoteihem* — and wine itself is prohibited because of "their daughters," meaning that sharing wine leads to social and ultimately sexual proximity with non-Jewish women.

### Daughters: Davar Acher

*Ve-al benoteihem mishum davar acher* — and the prohibition regarding their daughters is itself rooted in something referred to as *davar acher*, a rabbinic euphemism. According to *Rashi*, the first *davar acher* refers to *avodah zarah* — the concern is not so much the daughters themselves as the idolatrous practices to which proximity with them might lead.

### Davar Acher Reason Unkno…

*Ve-al davar acher mishum davar acher* — and the *avodah zarah* concern itself rests on some further reason, a second *davar acher* whose precise referent remains opaque. As *Rashi* notes, this second *davar acher* will be explained later in the *gemara*. The term *davar acher* is a well-known Talmudic euphemism that can refer variously to pork, sexual immorality, *avodah zarah*, *tzara'at*, or other sensitive matters depending on context.

---

## Intermarriage Prohibitio…

### Seven Nations Exception

The *gemara* probes the claim that the prohibition against non-Jewish daughters is rabbinic: *benoteihem de-oraita hi* — isn't it a biblical prohibition? The verse *lo titchaten bam* prohibits intermarriage with the Canaanite nations. The answer is that *de-oraita, zayin umot* — the Torah's explicit prohibition against intermarriage applies specifically to the seven Canaanite nations enumerated in the text. With respect to other idolaters, there is no explicit *de-oraita* prohibition against a Jewish man marrying an idolatrous woman. It was the rabbis who came and extended the prohibition to *shear ovdei kochavim*, all idolaters.

### Shimon ben Yochai: All I…

One might challenge this on the basis of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai's position: the verse *ki yasir et bincha me'achari* — "for she will turn your son away from Me" — teaches that the underlying concern is the risk of religious seduction, and Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai holds that *l'rabot kol ha-masirot*, this includes any idolatrous woman, since the same risk exists with all of them. On his reading, the *de-oraita* prohibition would apply universally, not only to the seven nations.

### Chatnut vs. Znut

The *gemara* resolves the difficulty: *de-oraita ishut derech chatnut* — the biblical prohibition, even on Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai's reading, applies to formal marriage, to the long-term relationship of *chatnut*, because it is in such a relationship that the risk of religious seduction is most acute. The later rabbis then came and extended the prohibition: *va-atu inhu ve-gazru afilu derech znut* — they prohibited even casual sexual relations between a Jewish man and a non-Jewish woman, not only marriage, on the ground that even such encounters fall under the concern of social and religious contamination.

### Asymmetric Prohibition

One might then ask: but was not *znut* with a non-Jewish woman already prohibited by *Beit Dino shel Shem* — the *beit din* of Shem, which Rav Elchanan Wasserman discusses in his *Kuntras Divrei Sofrim* as the source of universal rabbinic-style enactments in the wake of the Flood? The *gemara* distinguishes: *de-oraita oved kochavim ha-ba al bat Yisrael d'mashcha batrei* — the primary biblical concern is a non-Jewish man who takes a Jewish woman into his environment, drawing her after him into his culture and away from Torah. A Jewish man going to a non-Jewish woman presents a different profile of risk. That is the asymmetry that underlies the *de-oraita* formulation.

The rabbinic extension then fills in the gap: *va-atu inhu ve-gazru afilu Yisrael ha-ba al ovedet kochavim* — the *de-rabbanan* decree addresses the case of a Jewish man with a non-Jewish woman as well. However, the *gemara* then notes that the prohibition against a Jewish man having relations with a non-Jewish woman is in fact *halacha le-Moshe mi-Sinai*, derived from the episode of Pinchas — *ha-boel Aramit kana'in pog'in bo* — where anyone who witnesses the act may take the law into his own hands and kill the transgressor. This applies *de-oraita* only *be-farhesya*, in public, like the case of Zimri, who committed the act openly before *Ohel Moed*, in full view of Moshe and the *zekenim*. The *de-rabbanan* then extends the prohibition to *bitzina*, in private, as will be seen.

---

## Yichud Decree Progression

### Chashmonaim: Biah Decree

The *gemara* traces a layered historical progression of prohibitions. *Beit dino shel Chashmonai* decreed against the act of *biah* — sexual relations — between a Jewish man and a non-Jewish woman, formulating the violation as *nashga*: *niddah, shifcha, goya, ve-eshet ish* — the act constitutes a compound rabbinic transgression combining the prohibitions of *niddah*, *shifcha* (a slave woman), *goya* (a non-Jewish woman), and *eshet ish* (a married woman), even if she is not in fact married. *Ravin*, when he arrived from *Eretz Yisrael*, reported a slightly variant formulation of *nashga*: *niddah, shifcha, goya,* and *zonah* — a promiscuous woman — rather than *eshet ish*, on the reasoning that she may not be married but certainly falls into the category of *znut*.

### Biah vs. Yichud

The *gemara* emphasizes the precise scope of the Hasmonean decree: *ki gazru beit dino shel Chashmonai biah, aval yichud lo* — the Hasmonean court prohibited the act of *biah* itself, but did not extend the prohibition to *yichud* — seclusion — with a non-Jewish woman.

### David: Yichud with Jewis…

The prohibition of *yichud* with a Jewish woman, by contrast, was decreed by *beit dino shel David*. *Rav Yehuda* teaches that at the time of the rape of Tamar by Amnon, David's court enacted the decree against *yichud*. That decree, however, addressed seclusion between a Jewish man and a Jewish woman — *yichud de-bat Yisrael* — prompted by the specific violation that gave rise to the Tamar tragedy.

### Shammai/Hillel: Yichud E…

*Va-atu inhu ve-gazru afilu yichud de-oved kochavim* — the students of *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel* later extended the *yichud* prohibition to cover seclusion with a non-Jewish woman as well. David's court had not addressed this scenario, presumably because the concern at that stage was focused on violations within the Jewish community.

---

## Yichud Status & Drashah

### Yichud De'oraisa Source

With the prohibition of *yichud* with a Jewish woman now attributed to David's *beit din*, a question arises: is *yichud de-oraita*? The *gemara* suggests it is, or at minimum has a *de-oraita* basis — though the source is characterized only as a *remez*, a hint from the Torah rather than an explicit verse.

### Deuteronomy Remez

*Rabbi Yochanan* in the name of *Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak* asks: *remez le-yichud min ha-Torah minayin* — where in the Torah is there a hint to the prohibition of *yichud*? The verse cited is from the section dealing with *avodah zarah*: *ki yasitcha achicha ben imecha* — "if your brother, the son of your mother, entices you." The question is posed: does only a maternal brother entice, but not a paternal brother? The *gemara* explains: *ben misyached im imo* — a son may be secluded with his mother, because that relationship is not subject to the *yichud* concern.

### Son-Mother Exception

*Ve-ein acher misyached im kol arayot she-ba-Torah* — but no one else may be secluded with any of the *arayot* listed in the Torah. The verse specifies *ben imecha*, the son of your mother, because that is the one familial dyad for which *yichud* is permitted — a son and his mother. All other *arayot* are subject to the *yichud* prohibition. This *remez* from the Torah constitutes the basis for treating *yichud* with a Jewish woman as a *de-oraita* concern, or at least as something with a strong scriptural anchor, even though the formal enactment is attributed to David's court.

---

---

# Avodah Zarah 37

## Ad Hominem & Witness

### Ad Hominem Fallacy

There is a meaningful distinction between an *ad hominem* attack and the legitimate legal act of discrediting a witness. An *ad hominem* argument is a logical fallacy: rather than engaging with the substance of what someone has said, one attacks the character or conduct of the speaker as a way of dismissing the argument altogether. This is fallacious precisely because a person's character and the validity of their reasoning are, in principle, separable matters. Discrediting a witness, by contrast, is an entirely different operation — it removes the witness from the realm of credibility with respect to testimony, which is a legitimate and necessary halachic procedure. The two should not be conflated.

### Daily Opening

The shiur picks up on Avodah Zarah 36b, toward the bottom of the page, in the midst of the extended back-and-forth regarding what precisely the students of *Shammai* and *Hillel* enacted with respect to *binoteihem* — the relationships between Jewish men and non-Jewish women. Several aspects of the relevant laws had already been traced to earlier origins, including the *beit din* of *David*, the *beit din* of *Shem* the son of *Noach*, and the *Bnei Chashmonaim* during the Hasmonean period. The discussion now continues from where it left off.

## Yichud Laws

### Shammai & Hillel

The question before the *Gemara* is what specifically was established by the students of *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel*. Certain dimensions of the prohibition against intermarriage appear to have biblical origins, while others derive from *halacha l'Moshe miSinai*, and the precise scope of what the students of *Shammai* and *Hillel* added remained somewhat unclear.

### Brother's Seduction

The *Gemara* cites a teaching: *d'amar Rabbi Yochanan mishum Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotsadak — remez l'yichud min haTorah minayin?* — from where is there a hint or allusion in the *Torah* itself to the prohibition of *yichud*, the rule that a man and woman may not be together in private even absent any actual sexual contact? The verse cited is *ki yesitcha achicha ben imecha* — that your brother, the son of your mother, will seduce you to worship *avodah zarah*. The *Gemara* asks: does only a maternal brother seduce, but a paternal brother does not? Rather, says the *Gemara*: *ben mityached im imo* — the verse alludes to the fact that a son may be alone with his mother. This establishes that parent-child *yichud* is permitted, while *v'ein acher mityached im kol ha'arayot shebaTorah* — no one else may have *yichud* with any of those forbidden to him under *arayot* in the *Torah*.

### Yichud Levels

The *Gemara* then layers the prohibition: the *de'oraita* dimension of *yichud* applies specifically to *eshet ish*, a married woman. For the other *arayot* — the other categories of forbidden sexual relationships enumerated in the *Torah* — the prohibition of *yichud* is *d'rabbanan*, though it was established at an early period. Subsequently, *va-ata b'David v'gazar afilu al yichud d'penuyah* — the *beit din* of *David* extended the prohibition even to *yichud* between an unmarried man and an unmarried woman, or between a married man and an unmarried woman, even though no explicit prohibition is violated in such a case. One might ask why such *yichud* would be problematic at all, given that an unmarried woman could in principle marry the man in question, and indeed the marriage ceremony itself incorporates a moment of *yichud*. The *beit din* of *David*, however, was concerned with a broader fence against sexual encounters that were deemed socially problematic, even if not technically prohibited.

### Yichud Non-Jews

Finally, *v'atu talmidei Shammai v'Beit Hillel gazaru afilu al yichud d'avodat kochavim* — the students of *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel* extended the prohibition further still, to *yichud* between a Jewish man and a non-Jewish woman. The underlying assumption that originally might have rendered such *yichud* unproblematic — namely, that a Jewish man would have no business being involved with a non-Jewish woman — was set aside in favor of a more protective fence. The *Gemara*'s framing of *yichud* is generally from the perspective of the man's responsibility. The question of a Jewish woman secluded with a non-Jewish man is addressed differently, with concerns arising primarily in contexts involving coercion.

## Gezeirot Clarified

### Euphemism Usage

The list of *gezeirot* enumerated earlier had stated: *pitanu shemanan mishum yeinam* — they prohibited bread and oil because of wine — *v'yeinam mishum b'noteihem* — and wine because of their daughters, meaning non-Jewish women — and *v'davar acher mishum davar acher* — and something else because of something else. The *Gemara* has now reached the conclusion that the *gezeirah* attributed to *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel* regarding *b'noteihem* was the prohibition of *yichud* between a Jewish man and a non-Jewish woman, since the prohibition against intermarriage itself had already been established earlier. The question then becomes: what is the euphemism *davar acher mishum davar acher* pointing to?

### Non-Jewish Boys

*Amar Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: gazaru al tinok oved kochavim she'itamei b'zivah* — they decreed that a non-Jewish male child conveys impurity with the status of a *zav*, such that sitting on a chair or surface he has rested upon conveys *tumah* — *she'lo yeihei tinok Yisrael ragil etzlo b'mishkav zachor* — in order to prevent close association between Jewish and non-Jewish boys that could lead to homosexual relations or pederasty. From the *Beit Sheni* period there are many sources — both internal to the tradition and external — that reflect the rabbinic class's intense preoccupation with *tumah v'taharah*, sometimes to a troubling degree. The *Tosefta* in *Yoma* records the disturbing account of one *kohen* stabbing another in the *Beit HaMikdash*, whereupon the victim's father rushed to remove the knife before the young man died — not out of concern for his son's life, but lest the knife become *tamei*. That story is meant to sharply reorient our sense of priorities. The term *tinok* in the present context does not mean an infant but a child — and as will become clear, the relevant age is nine years old.

## Age & Tumah

### Age Tradition Chain

*D'amar Rav Zeira: tza'ar gadol haya etzel Rabbi Assi* — Rav Zeira reports that he experienced great difficulty with Rabbi Assi regarding this question, and Rabbi Assi had had the same difficulty with Rabbi Yochanan, who had it with Rabbi Yannai, who had it with Rabbi Natan ben Amram, who had it with *Rebbi* — that is, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi. This chain of student-to-teacher transmission traces the question back to its source. The question itself was: *tinok oveid kochavim me'ematai mitamei be'zivah?* — from what age does a non-Jewish child convey *tumah* with the status of a *zav*? *V'amar li ben yomo* — he was told it was from the very day of birth.

### Rabbi Chiya's Age

*U'keshebati etzel Rabbi Chiya, amar li ben tesha shanim v'yom echad* — but when Rav Zeira came to Rabbi Chiya, Rabbi Chiya said it was from nine years old and one day. *U'keshebati v'hirtzeiti devarai lifnei Rebbi, amar li hanach devarai v'echoz divrei Rabbi Chiya* — when Rav Zeira returned and reported Rabbi Chiya's position to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, *Rebbi* told him: set aside what I said, and follow Rabbi Chiya. This is characteristic of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's noted humility — he is the sage who consistently employs the phrase *omer ani*, placing his own opinion in a subordinate register, and here too he defers to Rabbi Chiya, his somewhat junior colleague and the compiler of the *Tosefta*, when he considers that Rabbi Chiya has the more reliable tradition or the more defensible position.

The *tza'ar gadol* that Rav Zeira experienced was the uncertainty of which opinion to follow — birth or nine years old. Nine years old represents a general halachic threshold for sexual significance with respect to certain questions, distinct from the age of legal majority which remains thirteen. It is worth noting that this threshold almost never corresponds to actual puberty, which is presumed at thirteen. The age of nine seems rather to reflect a recognition that from that age, a sexual act has certain legal consequences — which, in the context of widespread pederasty in the Greco-Roman world, represents a meaningful, if not fully developed, form of legal protection.

The *Gemara* clarifies Rabbi Chiya's reasoning: *ho'il v'ra'ui l'bi'ah mitamei nami be'zivah* — since from age nine and one day a boy's participation in a sexual act is legally significant, an analogous legal significance is created for the laws of *tumah v'taharah*, specifically the status of *zivah*. There may also be a connection to the medical phenomenon that *zivah* is sometimes associated with a condition resembling gonorrhea; in any case, the *Gemara* is creating a kind of constructed *zav* status for non-Jewish boys from age nine onward, linked to the threshold of sexual significance.

### Ravina Girls

*Amar Ravina hilkach, ha-tinoket ovedet kochavim bat shalosh shanim v'yom echad* — Ravina extends the same logic to non-Jewish girls, concluding that they convey *tumah* with the status of a *zavah* from age three years and one day, since that is the corresponding halachic threshold of sexual significance for girls. One might ask whether this ruling is not obvious — if we established the same analogy for boys, should it not follow automatically for girls? The *Gemara* addresses this: *mahu detema hai yada le-argulei* — one might have thought that a nine-year-old boy can actively entice or seduce, whereas a three-year-old girl has no such capacity or inclination. *Ka mashma lan* — Ravina's point is that the legal construction is applied across the board regardless of this asymmetry, even where it is considerably less intuitive. It should be noted that this decree regarding non-Jewish girls applies specifically to them; for a Jewish girl or woman, the laws of *niddah* and *zivah* apply from the time she has the relevant physical discharge, regardless of age. Medical literature attests to the fact that even newborn girls can exhibit vaginal discharge of a sort that *Chazal* engaged with halachically, and this will be developed more fully when *Masechet Niddah* is reached.

## Oil Court

### Rabbi Yehuda Nesi'ah

*Mistamich ve-azil Rabbi Yehuda Nesia a-katfei de-Rabbi Simlai* — Rabbi Yehuda Nesia was traveling, leaning on the shoulder of Rabbi Simlai, who was his attendant or servant. That Rabbi Simlai — one of the significant figures of the late *Tannaim* or early *Amoraim* — was serving in this role reflects the honor accorded to the *Nasi*, though it is notable that Rabbi Simlai was in many respects senior to him in scholarship.

The *Mishna* had stated that oil was prohibited by *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel*, and then permitted by *Rebbi*, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi the author of the *Mishna*. Rabbi Yehuda Nesia is the grandson of *Rebbi*, and the story as told here raises some difficulty: it seems to place the grandson in a first-person relationship to a court decision that one might have expected his grandfather to have made. It is possible that Rabbi Yehuda Nesia was a precocious young member of his grandfather's *beit din*, and thus present and involved when the oil was permitted — which would at least explain the personal terms of the narrative, even if some details remain puzzling.

*Amar lei Simlai: lav hayita emesh be-veit hamidrash keshe-hitarnu et ha-shemen* — so Rabbi Yehuda Nesia said to Rabbi Simlai: were you not in the *beit midrash* when we permitted the oil? *Amar lo beyameinu tatir af et ha-pat* — Rabbi Simlai replied: in your time you will probably permit even bread. He was alluding to the fact that *Rebbi* had already created some opening with respect to the conditions under which *pat akum* is prohibited, and now the grandson had permitted oil — it seemed a pattern was forming. *Amar lo im ken karu lan bei dina sharya* — Rabbi Yehuda Nesia replied: if so, they will call my court a permissive *beit din*, which is not a desirable reputation.

The basis of his concern is drawn from the precedent of *Masechet Eduyot*: *he'id Rabbi Yose ben Yoezer ish Tzeredah* — Yose ben Yoezer of Tzeredah testified three lenient rulings, and on account of them was given the epithet *Yosef Sharya* — the permissive Yosef.

### Yosef Sharya

Rabbi Yehuda Nesia explains the arithmetic of his reluctance. Yose ben Yoezer had permitted three things and earned the reputation of a permissive authority. Rabbi Yehuda Nesia had already permitted one thing — the oil — and had a second permissive ruling on another matter, which he reveals momentarily. Were he to permit bread as well, he would have three, and thus earn the same epithet. His interlocutor points out that even permitting bread would give him only two, to which he responds that he already has a second leniency that he had not yet mentioned.

This leads to the question: *mai hi?* What is this second permissive ruling?

## Get After Death

### Conditional Get

The answer is found in a *Mishna*: *ze gittech im lo bati mikan ve'ad shneim asar chodesh* — this is your *get*, if I do not return from here within twelve months. That is, a man departing on a long journey gives his wife a *get* now, contingent on his not returning within twelve months. *U'meit betoch shneim asar chodesh, eino get* — if he dies during the twelve months, it is not a valid *get*, because of the principle *ein get le'achar mita* — one cannot give a *get* retroactively after death. A deceased person has no legal standing to transfer a document, and moreover such a mechanism could be used to undermine the institution of *yibbum*, since the woman would not be subject to *yibbum* if she were already divorced.

### HaNasi Rejected

*Ve'amar Rabbi Abba breih de'Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba: de'Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi horah velo hodu lo* — Rabbi Abba, son of Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba, reported that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi — grandfather of Rabbi Yehuda Nesia — had attempted to institute a more permissive ruling on this question, but the other rabbis did not agree with him. *Kol sha'ato* — throughout his entire lifetime they never accepted his position. An alternative version reads *kol sayato* — not during his whole life, but during his tenure: none of his supporters accepted it.

### Nesi'ah Permits

*Ve'amrinan: man Rabboseinu? Amar Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel: be dina desharu mshacha* — when the text says *rabboseinu* permitted the woman to remarry, the *Gemara* asks whose court this was. Rav Yehuda, quoting Shmuel in *Bavel*, says it was the same *beit din* that permitted the oil. That is, it was the *beit din* of Rabbi Yehuda Nesia — which is again slightly puzzling, since the grandfather had tried to enact the same ruling and been overruled. The *Gemara* explains that this position rested on the view of Rabbi Yosi.

*Savri lah ke'Rabbi Yosei, de'amar zmano shel shtar mochiach alav* — the court followed Rabbi Yosi's principle that the date written in the *shtar* is indicative of when the document is intended to take effect. Applied to the *get*: if the man gives the *get* today with a condition about the future, the date on the *get* demonstrates his intent that it should take effect from the moment of delivery. Therefore, if he dies before the twelve months are up, the *get* is not a *get le'achar mita* — it retroactively took effect at the time it was given, the condition having subsequently been fulfilled. The woman is thus free to remarry.

The question was raised regarding Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's situation: does his opinion retain any validity if his court overruled him? The answer is clearly no — he is first among equals, a voting member of the *sanhedrin* with one vote. The *Nasi* holds great authority and seniority, and by convention speaks last, but he does not override a majority ruling. When his grandson later took the same position and convened his own court, that court ruled in accordance with Rabbi Yosi, and the ruling stood.

### M'nat vs Ki

*Amar Abaye: hakol modim l'chsheteitzei chamah minartikei* — Abaye introduces a related case. If a man gives his wife a *get* and says it should take effect *l'chi nafka* — when the sun comes out of its pouch — meaning at sunrise the next morning, and the man dies during the night before sunrise: *ki meit beleilaya get l'achar mita hu* — that is a *get le'achar mita*, because he used the language *l'chi nafka*, making the effectiveness of the *get* depend on the future moment of the condition's fulfillment, not on the present moment of its delivery.

But if he said *al m'nat sheteitzei chamah minartikei* — on the condition that the sun comes out of its pouch — then *me'achshav ka'amar lah*: using the formulation *al m'nat* is equivalent to saying the *get* should take effect now, contingent on the later condition. *Hu kidei Rav Huna, de'amar Rav Huna: kol ha-omer al m'nat ke-omer me'achshav dami* — this is consistent with Rav Huna's general rule that whoever says *al m'nat* is treated as though he said *me'achshav*, from right now. The *get* is thus a *get m'chayim* — a *get* given while the husband was alive — and the condition's subsequent fulfillment does not create the problem of *get le'achar mita*.

*Lo necheleku ela be-im* — the dispute between the authorities concerns the intermediate case where the man uses the word *im*, if: *im tetzei chamah minartikei*, if the sun comes out of its pouch. Is *im* more like *ki* — in which case the *get* only takes effect when the condition is fulfilled — or more like *al m'nat* — in which case the *get* takes effect now and the condition retroactively validates it? On this question the *poskim* divide.

It is worth noting in this context the distinction between *al m'nat* as a retroactive condition and *l'chi nafka* as a delayed effect. These two formulations have very different consequences precisely for the question of *get le'achar mita*. If the *get* only takes effect when the condition is fulfilled, and the husband has died before that point, then the *get* is *le'achar mita* and invalid. If the *get* takes effect now, with the later condition retroactively confirming its validity, then the husband's death in the interim is not an obstacle, provided the condition is ultimately satisfied.

### Shtar Date

*Rabbi Yehuda Hanasi savar la ke'Rabbi Yossi, de'amar zmano shel shtar mochiach alav, ve'hava lei k'me'hayom* — Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi held, following Rabbi Yosi, that the date written in the *shtar* demonstrates that the parties intended the document to take effect from that date, making it equivalent to saying *me'hayom*, from today, and thus *me'achshav im meti* — from now if I die. *Ve'rabbanan leit lehu de'Rabbi Yossi, ve'hava lei k'zeh giteich im meti gerada* — the other rabbis rejected Rabbi Yosi's principle and therefore read the *get* as saying: this is your *get* if I die, without any retroactive element, which then fails the *get le'achar mita* problem.

Why did Rabbi Yehuda Nesia not want to be called *beit din sharya*? A question along these lines was posed to Rabbi Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld, one of the leading *Charedi* authorities of early 20th-century Jerusalem. Someone pointed out: is it not a virtue to be lenient? Do we not say *koach de'hetera adifa lei* — that demonstrating the ability to permit reflects greater confidence and mastery of halacha than simply prohibiting? Rabbi Sonnenfeld replied: yes, *koach de'hetera adifa lei* applies, but there are limits that one does not cross. One should not develop a reputation of universal leniency, because that reputation erodes the credibility of one's rulings when stringency is genuinely required, and it can tempt people to treat uncertain cases as though they are clear. Rabbi Yehuda Nesia's hesitation reflects precisely this concern — not a rejection of the value of leniency, but an awareness of when that value has reached its threshold.

## Yoezer Leniencies

### Ayal Kamtza

*Gufa* — the *Gemara* now returns to the three rulings of Yose ben Yoezer themselves. *He'id Yossi ben Yoezer ish Tzreida: al ayal kamtza dachan* — he testified that the *ayal kamtza* locust is *tahor*, that is, kosher. *Ve'al mashke beit mitbachaya dachan* — that the liquids in the slaughterhouse of the Temple are *tahor*. *Ve'al di-krav le-meita mesta'av* — and that one who comes in contact with a corpse becomes *tamei*. *Vekaru lei Yosef Sharya* — and they called him the permissive Yosef.

*Mai ayal kamtza?* — What is the *ayal kamtza*? Rav Pappa said it is the *shushiva*, and Rav Chiyya bar Ami in the name of Ulla said it is the *susbil*. These are evidently two different species or descriptions of locusts, and we no longer have reliable knowledge of the precise taxonomy. Some communities still claim a *mesora* regarding which locusts are kosher; many have lost that *mesora*, which is a significant loss. *Rashi* gives the description in four words: *min chagav verosho aruch* — a type of locust with a long head.

*Rav Pappa amar Shushiva vekamipalgi berosho aruch* — the debate between Rav Pappa and Rav Chiyya bar Ami concerns the long head. One holds that a locust with a long head is prohibited; the other holds that one with a long head is in fact permitted. *Rav Chiyya bar Ami mishmei de'Ulla amar Susbil*, and *Rashi* explains regarding the *susbil* that it does not have a long head, *aval ein knafav chofin et rubo*, but its wings do not cover the majority of its body in a clearly visible way — only barely, *betzimtzum*. The question then is what kind of *rov* the halacha requires for the wings to "cover the majority of the body," one of the conditions for a kosher locust: does it suffice that the wings cover a bare majority of 50.0001%, or must the majority be visibly discernible? *Mar savar rova kol dehu* — one holds that any majority suffices; *umar savar rova deminchar ba'ina* — the other holds that a visible majority is required.

As for *kulei alma lo pligi de'assur* — all agree that a locust with a long head is prohibited. The debate concerns only the *susbil*, whose wings barely cover the majority of the body: *vehacha bichnafav chofin et rubo al yedei hadachak kamipalgi* — and this case is the subject of the dispute.

### Temple Liquids

*Al mashke bei mitbachaya dachyan* — regarding the liquids from the Temple slaughterhouse being *tahor*: this topic receives extensive treatment in the second chapter of *Pesachim*, and the *sugya* there should be consulted. It is worth noting the use of the Aramaic *dachya* for *tahor*, which is somewhat unusual in the *Talmud* in this form.
