This leads to the famous *chidush* of Rav Moshe Feinstein. Even according to the Ashkenazic position — which requires the formal presence of Jewish oversight and does not rely solely on the absence of non-kosher animals — Rav Moshe argued that under modern regulatory conditions, the situation is qualitatively different. Government oversight through agencies such as the USDA creates real legal and financial consequences for adulteration. There is no financial incentive, only a substantial financial disincentive, to mix in other milks. Under these conditions, the reality of oversight is so patent that it constitutes *anan sahdei* — we are all effectively witnesses — making it equivalent to *Yisrael ro'ehu*, a Jew observing. Rav Moshe's position thus holds that even for Ashkenazim who generally require formal Jewish supervision, modern commercial milk production meets that standard.

---

## Honey Analysis

### Honey Concerns

The Gemara examines why honey from non-Jews should be permitted. What concerns might apply, and why do none of them hold?

Three possible grounds for prohibition are considered and dismissed. First, concern for adulteration with wine: *sarvei misrei* — it would spoil the honey, so a non-Jew would never do it. Second, concern for *bishul akum* — that the honey was cooked by a non-Jew, which would normally prohibit it — is dismissed because honey *ne'echal kemo shehu chai*, it can be consumed raw, and the prohibition of *bishul akum* does not apply to foods that can be eaten without cooking. Third, concern for *gi'ulei akum* — that the honey was cooked in non-kosher pots, imparting a forbidden taste — is dismissed because even if such pots were used, *noten ta'am lifgam hu umutar*: whatever flavor was absorbed would only impart a bad taste to the honey, and *noten ta'am lifgam* is permitted.

### Non-Kosher Pots

This Gemara, along with other passages encountered in this tractate, assumes that cooking in non-kosher pots imparts a bad taste. This assumption is never stated explicitly in the Gemara itself, but is articulated by Tosafot here and by the *rishonim* generally in the form of the rule: *stam keilim shel akum einam bnei yoman* — we presume that the vessels of non-Jews are not *bnei yoman*, that is, they have not been used for non-kosher food within the past twenty-four hours, and therefore any absorbed taste they impart is considered *noten ta'am lifgam* and does not prohibit *bedi'avad*.

Tosafot goes further, explaining this assumption as a *sfek sfeika*: perhaps the pot was used today, perhaps yesterday; and even if today, perhaps it was used with something that gives a bad taste. This double doubt is what underlies the general assumption that non-Jewish pots are not a problem *bedi'avad*, though they may not be used *lechatchila*.

---

## Grape Clusters

### Shammai vs. Hillel

The *mishna*'s ruling that grape clusters are permitted even if dripping prompts a challenge from a well-known dispute. The *mishna* in *Tahorot* discusses *habotzer legat* — one who harvests grapes intending to press them for wine — where Shammai holds that the grapes become susceptible to *tumah* via *hechsher mashkeh* once liquid drips out, since the person desires that liquid. Hillel initially disagrees but ultimately concedes to Shammai. If so, dripping grape juice creates susceptibility — and that would raise a concern in our *mishna* as well. Why then are the grape clusters permitted?

### Intention Principle

The Gemara's answer is direct. *Hatam ka ba'ei lei lemashkeh* — in the case of the one harvesting to press wine, he desires the liquid; *hacha lo ka ba'ei lei lemashkeh* — here, the person wants to eat the grapes, not collect the juice. Since the dripping is not *leratsono*, not something the person wants, it does not activate susceptibility to *tumah*. The intention of the person handling the produce is determinative.

---

## Tarith Fish ID

### Definition

The Gemara cites a *baraita*: *eizehu tarith she'einah terufah?* — what constitutes a *tarith* that is "not chopped up" and therefore identifiable? *Kol she'rosh veshidra nikar* — anything whose head and spine can be identified. Rashi explains that this means you must be able to see the head and spine of each and every fish; if only some of them are visible, one would still have to be concerned about those whose identity cannot be verified.

### Huna vs. Nachman

A dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Nachman follows. Rav Huna holds that identification requires both the head and the spine to be recognizable. Rav Nachman holds that either one is sufficient — if the fish can be identified by the head alone or the spine alone, that is enough.

The practical analogy is instructive: may one purchase, say, a salmon fillet without fins and scales visible, relying instead on the color or texture of the flesh and the profile of the flesh itself? This is precisely the question — whether one identifying feature alone can vouch for the kosher status of the fish.

### Ukva Challenge

Rav Ukva bar Chama challenges both positions from the rules in Tractate Chullin: the identifying mark for fish is *snapir vekaskeset*, fins and scales. The *simanim* for fish are established by the Torah itself, and no mention is made of head or spine as alternative identifiers. This seems to undermine any permission based on those features.

### Abaye Resolution

Abaye resolves the difficulty. The ruling in Chullin that only fins and scales serve as *simanim* applies specifically to fish of the type *ara ufumda* — certain fish whose heads look similar to those of non-kosher fish and therefore cannot be relied upon for identification. For those fish, only fins and scales will do. But for fish whose heads and spines are distinctive enough to identify them, such features can indeed serve as valid indicators. The question in Chullin is therefore not addressing this situation.

### Body vs. Brine

Rav Yehuda in the name of Ulla introduces a further distinction. The debate between Rav Huna and Rav Nachman — whether one needs both head and spine or just one — pertains specifically to dipping in the *tzir*, the fish brine or oil that comes off the fish. When it comes to eating the body of the fish itself, however, everyone agrees that one must be able to see both the head and the spine; one alone does not suffice.

Tosafot raises the obvious question: why should there be any leniency for the *tzir*? Even the liquid that drains from non-kosher fish is itself non-kosher — *ta'am ke'ikar de'oraisa*. Tosafot answers that the leniency concerns a case where the *tzir* has been mixed with water, in which case the forbidden substance would be *batel berov* on a Torah level, even though rabbinic law would generally not permit that *bittul*. That explanation has an element of an *okimta* — it is somewhat forced — but Tosafot offers it as the basis for the distinction.

### Zeira Stringency

Rabbi Zeira reports his own evolution on this question. He had originally assumed that everyone agreed that for the *tzir*, even a single identifying mark was sufficient, and he would accordingly permit dipping in the *tzir* when only one of the two features was visible. Upon hearing the teaching of Rav Yehuda in the name of Ulla that the debate itself is about the *tzir*, and that eating the body is unanimously more stringent, Rabbi Zeira became *machmir* and resolved that he would not permit even dipping in the *tzir* unless both head and spine are visible.

### Rav Papa Ruling

Rav Papa rules definitively: *hilcheta ad sheyehei rosh veshidra nikar* — the *halacha* requires both head and spine to be recognizable, even when the question is merely about the *tzir*. This is the most stringent ruling and represents the final, authoritative position on the matter.

---

## Fish Pieces

### Baraita Teaching

The Gemara now addresses a challenge to Rav Papa's ruling that every individual fish must have its identifying marks visible. A *baraita* teaches that when pieces of fish are present — some bearing identifying marks, some not — whether the identifying mark is present on all of them, on some of them, or even on just one of them, they are all permitted. This is a striking ruling: a single piece with visible fins and scales, out of a hundred unidentifiable fillets, renders the entire batch permissible. The logic is that presumably the seller cut up a single fish and sold the pieces together, but it is nonetheless a significant leniency.

### Gamliel Story

The *baraita* recounts a supporting incident: a non-Jew brought a container of fish pieces, and an identifying mark was found on one of them. Rabban Gamliel permitted the entire container on that basis. This illustrates the principle in action at the highest level of *halachic* authority.

### Equal Pieces

Rav Papa resolves the apparent contradiction between this teaching and his own ruling requiring every piece to be identifiable: *keshechatichot shaveiot* — this applies only when the pieces are equal. Rashi explains that equal here means the pieces can be physically fitted together, demonstrating that they derive from the same fish — like a puzzle. They are not merely similar in appearance; one can verify their common origin by assembling them. The Gemara then asks: if so, is this not obvious? Why does the *baraita* need to state it?

The answer is that one might have thought to be concerned: even if the pieces seem to fit together, perhaps one of them is from a different fish and merely happens to fit. The *baraita* teaches that we do not entertain that suspicion.

### Huna Position

A separate incident: a boat carrying salted fish arrived at the city of Sichra. Rav Huna bar Chinana went out, saw scales mixed in among the fish, and permitted the entire load. This again suggests that a visible identifying mark found among a batch — here, loose scales — can render the whole permissible.

### Rava Objection

Rava objected: is there anyone who would permit on this basis in a place where scales are common? In a location where many fish with scales are processed and traded, loose scales in a boat could easily have arrived from a previous cargo, from different fish, or from other sources entirely. Their presence cannot reliably attest that these particular fish are kosher. Accordingly, Rava's announcement went out forbidding the fish. Rav Huna bar Chinana was undeterred and issued his own announcement permitting them.

### Ashi Report

Rav Yirmiyah miDiphti reported in the name of Rav Pappi that when Rav Huna bar Chinana permitted, he did so only for the *tzir*, not for the fish bodies themselves — consistent with the greater leniency already noted for *tzir* by Tosafot. Rav Ashi, however, reports a different version: Rav Pappi told him that Rav Huna bar Chinana actually permitted even the fish bodies. Rav Ashi adds that he himself would neither forbid — as Rava had announced — nor permit, because while Rav Pappi's report supports leniency, the ruling of Rav Yehuda in the name of Ulla establishes that for the fish body itself, everyone agrees one needs the head and spine visible for each individual fish. That ruling stands as a strong barrier against permitting the entire load on the basis of loose scales, and Rav Ashi therefore declined to rule definitively in either direction.

---

## Fish Brine Barrels

### Four Barrels

The Gemara proceeds to a new case. Rav Chinana bar Idi, seated before Rav Adda bar Ahava, posed the following scenario: a non-Jew brings a boat full of barrels, and *kilbis* fish are found in one of them. Can one extrapolate from that one barrel to permit the others?

### Open vs. Closed

The answer depends on whether the barrels are open or closed. If the barrels are open, all of them are permitted. Rashi's explanation here is that the presence of *kilbis* in one open barrel provides a basis for extrapolation: if the brine were from non-kosher fish, the *kilbis* would not be found there. And for the other open barrels, the absence of *kilbis* does not prove they are non-kosher — the *kilbis* may simply have swum out. One therefore extrapolates from the positive evidence in one barrel to permit the rest. If the barrels are sealed, by contrast, only the one containing *kilbis* is permitted, while the others are forbidden. Since they are closed, the *kilbis* could not have left, and their absence in the other barrels is genuine negative evidence that cannot be explained away.

### Three Authorities

When asked the source for this ruling, Rav Chinana bar Idi replied that he had heard it from three great authorities — Rav, Shmuel, and Rabbi Yochanan — and therefore relied on it with confidence.

---

## Fish Roe & Innards

### Expert Requirement

Rav Bruna in the name of Rav rules that *kirvei dagim v'ubaran* — the innards of fish and their *ubar*, meaning their roe or eggs — may only be purchased from an expert, a *mumche*. Since there are no fins and scales to observe, there are no standard external *simanim* to rely upon, and one must therefore trust someone with the knowledge and integrity to certify that these derive from a kosher fish.

### Ulla Challenge

Ulla challenged Rabbi Dostai with a contradiction. The requirement to buy roe only from an expert implies that non-kosher fish can also produce roe, which is therefore a concern. Yet a teaching in Tractate Bechorot states that *dag tamei mashritz* — non-kosher fish reproduce viviparously, gestating their offspring within their bodies — while *dag tahor matil beitzim* — kosher fish lay their eggs outside their bodies. If only kosher fish lay eggs, then all roe by definition comes from kosher fish, and no expert would be needed.

The Gemara's initial response is *sami mikan v'ubaran* — remove the word *ubaran* from Rav's ruling. The concern about experts applies only to innards, not to roe; roe need not be bought from an expert since it is always from kosher fish.

### Fish Reproduction

The resolution through deletion of *ubaran* is based on the premise that only kosher fish produce eggs. It should be noted that this is not biologically accurate — certain non-kosher aquatic animals, such as some species of shark, do lay eggs outside the body. The Talmudic sources work with the understanding available to them, and the ruling flows from that framework.

### Zeira Correction

Rabbi Zeira objects to the textual deletion: *lo tismi* — do not erase it. *Traivaihu matilei beitzim ninhu* — both kosher and non-kosher fish produce roe. The distinction of the *baraita* in Bechorot is not about the presence or absence of eggs, but about where the reproductive process takes place: *zeh mashritz mibachutz v'zeh mashritz mibifnim* — one deposits eggs outside its body, the other inside. Both have eggs, but in kosher fish the eggs develop and are deposited externally, while in non-kosher fish they remain internal. When one opens either a kosher or a non-kosher fish, one may find a cluster of eggs inside. The word *ubaran* therefore belongs in Rav's ruling, and roe must indeed be purchased from an expert.

Here too, the biological claim is not fully accurate by modern standards — certain non-kosher species do lay eggs externally. But the underlying *halachic* framework is clear: roe requires an expert because it can be found in both kosher and non-kosher fish.

### Roe Characteristics

The Gemara then asks: why rely on an expert at all? Why not simply examine the roe itself for identifying marks? A *baraita* teaches *k'simanei beitzim kach simanei dagim* — just as there are identifying characteristics for eggs from birds, there are similarly identifying characteristics for fish. If bird eggs have *simanim*, then presumably fish products do as well.

The Gemara initially takes *simanei dagim* to refer to fish themselves, and objects: of course fish can be identified — the Torah explicitly requires fins and scales, and no novel *baraita* is needed to tell us that. The *baraita* must therefore be read as: just as there are identifying characteristics for eggs from kosher versus non-kosher birds, similarly there are identifying characteristics for *uvrei dagim* — the roe of fish.

The *baraita* then details the *simanim* for kosher bird eggs: an egg that is rounded at one end and tapered at the other, with one wide end and one narrow end, is *tehorah* — kosher. An egg with both ends pointed, or both ends wide, is *temeiah* — not kosher. If the yolk is on the outside and the white on the inside, it is not kosher; if the white is on the outside and the yolk inside, it is kosher. If the yolk and white are mixed together with no distinction, that is the egg of a *sheretz* and is not kosher.

The question that follows is what the corresponding *simanim* for fish roe look like. Does the *baraita* mean the same *simanim* apply — one end wide, one end narrow — or something different? The Gemara understands the parallel to be exact: just as the kosher bird egg is wide on one end and narrow on the other, so too are the identifying marks for kosher fish roe based on shape, specifically the presence of one broader and one narrower pole.

### Expert Still Needed

If, then, one can identify kosher fish roe by its shape, why is a *mumche* still required? The answer is given by Rava at the top of 41b: *keshenimochu* — when the eggs have melted and congealed together into an undifferentiated mass, the identifying marks are no longer visible, and there is no way to inspect them. Under those conditions, which are standard for processed roe, one cannot rely on *simanim* and must therefore depend on an expert's testimony.

As for the position of Rabbi Dimi from Biri, who had argued for deleting *ubaran* from Rav's ruling on the grounds that all roe is kosher, the Gemara now addresses his view: once the *baraita* is properly edited to read *k'simanei beitzim kach simanei uvrei dagim* — just as there are identifying marks for eggs, so too for fish roe — this itself implies that roe can be non-kosher and therefore requires examination. Rabbi Dimi's counter-reading is that the *baraita* was never about roe at all, but about fish innards (*kirvei dagim*), and that the comparison is: just as eggs have identifying marks, so too do fish innards, specifically the *shalpucha*, the swim bladder of the fish, which can also present with one side wider and one side narrower. According to this reading, the *baraita* supports the need for examination of innards, not of roe — though we do not rule in accordance with Rabbi Dimi's position that roe requires no expert.

### Processor Claim

The Gemara now turns to what can be done when no *mumche* is available. Rav Yehuda rules: *keivan d'amar ani melachtim mutarin* — once the seller states "I salted these myself," they are permitted. The reasoning is that a person will stand behind his own work; if he claims personal responsibility for the processing, that testimony is credible even from someone who has not been previously established as a reliable expert. A middleman, by contrast, may not know the origins of what he is selling, but a processor who handled the fish himself can be trusted to know what they are.

### Show Fish

Rav Nachman is more stringent: *ad sheyomar elu dagim v'elu kirvehen* — it is not enough for the seller to claim he salted them. He must be able to show you the fish and their innards or roe together. Once you can see the gutted fish alongside the extracted material, you can verify for yourself that these are the innards or roe of the kosher fish before you, even if you cannot see them being extracted in real time. Rav Yehuda communicated his more lenient ruling to Ada, his attendant, instructing him that a seller's claim of personal salting is sufficient without requiring him to produce the fish alongside.

---

## Leaf & Cakes

### Chiltis Leaf

The Gemara now addresses the *aleh chiltit* — the leaf of the *chiltit* plant. The *chiltit* itself is an extremely sharp spice that can absorb flavor from non-kosher knives and render them *l'shevach*, imparting a beneficial absorbed taste. But the leaf is innocuous, and its permissibility seems self-evident — *pshita*.

The Gemara clarifies that the ruling is needed for a specific situation: *l'kortim shebah* — for the small pieces of *chiltit* that happen to be found attached to the leaf. One might have thought to be concerned that the non-Jew deliberately mixed cut pieces of *chiltit* into the leaves, which would be a problem since those pieces could carry absorbed flavors. The ruling teaches otherwise: *ishtaruki hu d'ishtaruq v'ati bahadah* — it is natural for small fragments of *chiltit* to find their way onto the leaves during harvesting and handling. No deliberate mixing need be suspected, and no motivation to do so exists.

### Olive Cakes

The Gemara turns to the case of *zeitei gluskaot hamigulgalim* — olive cakes that have been pressed together and are noticeably soft. This too seems self-evident: what concern should there be? The Gemara explains that the ruling addresses a case where the olives are *rafi tuva* — exceptionally soft. One might have thought that their softness indicates that wine was added to them. The Gemara rules otherwise: *hanei mechamat mishcha hu d'rafi* — they are soft because they are sitting in their own oil, not because of any added wine.

---

## Locusts & Produce

### Marketplace Wine

The Gemara discusses the case of locusts found in the marketplace. When the merchant displays his locusts for sale, he sprinkles wine over them to improve their smell or taste. This is the reason locusts in the basket at the front of the store — *habaim min hasalula* — are forbidden.

### Produce Rules

A *baraita* elaborates the general rule governing these concerns. Locusts, caper buds, and leeks — *hachagavim vehakafrisin vehakaplutot* — are all permissible if they come from the storehouse, the storeroom, or the boat: any stage before they are put out for retail sale. Wine would not be applied during storage or transport, only when the goods are displayed in front of the merchant for sale. Anything sold in the marketplace and placed before a storekeeper is forbidden on account of the wine he sprinkles over it.

A separate clause of the same *baraita* addresses apple cider made by non-Jews. Apple cider coming from the storehouse, storeroom, or even the basket is permitted. Unlike the other goods, where wine was applied specifically at the point of display, here even in the basket it is not yet a concern. However, once it is sold in the open marketplace — *hanimkar bekatloza* — it is forbidden because at that stage wine is mixed into it. The precise reason why wine is added to the apple cider only in the marketplace and not in the basket is not entirely clear from the *baraita*.

---

## Apple Cider Story

### Rabbi Illness

The *baraita* continues with a narrative: once, Rabbi suffered from a stomach ailment. He asked whether anyone knew if the apple cider of non-Jews — *yayin tapuchim shel ovdei kochavim* — was forbidden or permitted, implying that he thought it might help him.

### Yishmael Account

Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yossi responded: once my father, Rabbi Yossi, suffered from a stomach ailment, and they brought him apple cider of non-Jews that had fermented for seventy years — *yayin tapuchim shel ayin shana* — and it healed him.

### Cider Search

Rabbi thereupon exclaimed: if you had this knowledge, why did you allow me to suffer in pain? A search was conducted and a non-Jew was found who possessed three hundred flasks of apple cider that was seventy years old. Rabbi drank it and was healed.

### Praise

Upon his recovery, Rabbi declared: *baruch hamakom shemasar olamo leshomrim* — praised be God who has handed over His world to those who watch over it. The comment is striking in context: after an entire tractate focused on the dangers and prohibitions associated with the non-Jewish world, here Rabbi acknowledges that non-Jews can be instruments of healing and benefit, and expresses genuine gratitude. The entirety of this Gemara's concerns with the non-Jewish world does not preclude recognizing that there is much to gain from what that world has produced.

---

## Teruma Rules

### Suspect Kohen

The *mishna*'s closing phrase — *vechen litruma* — is now explained. Rav Sheshet interprets it as referring to a *kohen* who is suspected of selling his *teruma* while claiming it is *chullin*. *Teruma* is undesirable to many buyers: only *kohanim* may eat it, and if it becomes *tamei* it cannot be eaten at all. A suspect *kohen* might attempt to offload his *teruma* by misrepresenting it as ordinary produce. Items sold directly by such a *kohen* in his store or in front of him are forbidden, because there is genuine concern about this substitution.

### Storage Leniency

However, goods coming from his storehouse, storeroom, or basket — further removed from the immediate point of sale — are permitted. The reasoning is *irtzuyei mirtzei*: he is afraid. If he were to have his entire stock of *teruma* discovered and condemned, the Rabbis would cause him to lose everything. Selling a handful of *teruma* directly in the store to an unsuspecting customer may not expose him to much risk. But if the goods are coming from the storehouse or from a larger quantity in transit, the exposure is far greater, and he would not risk his entire supply. Therefore, one need not be concerned about *teruma* mixed into such goods.

This concludes the second *perek* of Avodah Zarah, which has addressed the full range of concerns governing interactions with the non-Jewish world: food, commerce, social proximity, and the dangers of idolatry by association. The third *perek* now begins, turning from those broader interactions to the laws of idols directly.

---

## Idols Introduction

### Rabbi Meir

*Kol hatzlamim* — all images, meaning statues or figures — are forbidden, according to Rabbi Meir, *mipnei shenevadin pa'am achas b'shana* — because they are worshipped at least once a year. Rabbi Meir acknowledges that such statues, including those of Roman emperors, are primarily decorative or civic in character, but holds that because they are worshipped at least annually — perhaps on the emperor's birthday or some other occasion within the Roman imperial cult — they are treated as objects of *avodah zarah* across the board.

### Rabbis

The Rabbis disagree and hold that not all statues are presumptively forbidden. Only a statue that holds a staff, a bird, or a globe is forbidden. These attributes indicate that the statue is regarded as divine — a staff may represent authority over the world, a bird some symbolic power, and a sphere the globe, representing universal dominion. An ordinary statue lacking these attributes does not warrant the presumption of worship.

### Rabban Shimon

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel goes further still: *af kol sheyeish beyado kol davar* — any statue holding any object in its hand is treated as the representation of a deity. Any object held by a figure suffices to identify it as an idol.

---

## Idols Debate

### Meir Minority

The Gemara now examines how Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis actually relate to each other. If the Rabbis concede that some statues are worshipped once a year, how can they permit them at all? Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef in the name of Rabbi Yochanan resolves this: in the locale of Rabbi Meir, statues were in fact worshipped once a year. The debate is therefore not about *metzius* — about whether such worship occurs — but about legal policy: does a minority practice in some places generate a universal prohibition?

Rabbi Meir, who is *chaish l'miuta* — who is concerned even with minority cases — extends the prohibition from places where such worship occurs to all other places as well. Since some locales worship these statues annually, he forbids all statues everywhere by extension.

### Rabbis Indifference

The Rabbis, who are *lo chaishi l'miuta* — not concerned with minority cases — do not apply this extension. A practice that exists in some locales does not generate a prohibition for all other locales where the practice does not occur. Accordingly, they require an affirmative indicator — a staff, bird, or globe — to presume that a given statue is an object of worship. Both positions agree on the underlying facts; their disagreement is entirely a matter of legal methodology in the face of geographic variation.

---

---

# Avodah Zarah 41

## Statues & Iconography

### Statues of Kings

The Gemara picks up from the bottom of 41b, continuing the exploration of the *mishnah*'s three-way *machloket* regarding which statues carry the presumption of being objects of *avodah zarah* — that is, actually worshipped rather than merely erected for decoration. The central question is how one determines, from the statue's appearance alone, whether it is an idol or simply a commemorative or ornamental figure.

Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel opens by clarifying the *mishnah*'s subject matter: *be'andarti shel melakhim shaninu* — the *mishnah* is speaking about statues fashioned in the image of kings. Rashi explains the practice: when a king died, his likeness was placed at the entrance of the city as a memorial. The question of whether such a statue is prohibited as *avodah zarah* thus turns on specific visual indicators — what the statue is holding, and the interpretive weight those objects carry.

### Villages vs. Cities

Rabba bar Bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan then offers a geographic clarification: *be'omdim al petach medinah shaninu* — the *mishnah* is specifically addressing statues placed at the entrance of a city. Rava then reframes the dispute entirely. He proposes that the *machloket tanna'im* concerns statues in small towns (*kefarim*) specifically, not cities. The reasoning is as follows: in large cities (*kerakhim*), statues are understood by everyone to have been erected *lenoi* — for beautification, as part of a kind of municipal aesthetic project. In small villages, however, there are fewer resources and less incentive for purely decorative sculpture, so the presumption shifts toward worship.

Rava's formulation is then revised: the *machloket* in fact concerns cities, while in villages everyone agrees that statues are prohibited. The reasoning is symmetrical but inverse — in villages, the assumption is *vadai demefalchin hu avdei lehu*, that they are built definitively for the purpose of worship. It is in cities that the tanna'im disagree, because urban contexts introduce genuine ambiguity.

### Staff, Bird, Globe

Having clarified the geographic parameters of the dispute, the Gemara turns to the position of the Rabbis — the middle position in the *mishnah* — which holds that a statue is presumed to be *avodah zarah* only when it is depicted holding one of three objects: a *makkel* (staff or scepter), a *tzippor* (bird), or a *kaddur* (globe or ball). The task is now to explain the symbolic significance of each.

### Symbolic Meanings

The staff (*makkel*): *she'rodeh et atzmo tachat kol ha'olam kulo kemakkel* — it presents the figure as ruling over the entire world with a scepter. A note of caution on the language: the Gemara employs inverted euphemistic phrasing throughout this passage, using *tachat* (under/beneath) where one would expect *al* (over), as a way of mocking the idol — implying it is being suppressed beneath the world rather than ruling over it. Readers must bear this in mind throughout.

The bird (*tzippor*): *shetofes et atzmo tachat kol ha'olam kulo ketzippor* — it presents the figure as controlling the entire world as one controls a trained bird of prey. Many pagan depictions showed the deity holding a falcon, eagle, or hawk, signifying mastery over the earth. The Roman statue of Jupiter, for example, holds precisely a staff, an eagle, and a globe — a first-century object now located in Russia that perfectly illustrates all three indicators simultaneously.

The globe (*kaddur*): *shetofes et atzmo tachat ha'olam kulo kekaddur* — it presents the figure as capable of holding and supporting the entire world like a ball. This implies awareness that the world is a sphere, a concept that goes back to Greek mathematical astronomy and was certainly current in the rabbinic era.

### Sword, Crown, Ring

A *baraita* then adds three further indicators beyond those in the *mishnah*: a *sayif* (sword), an *atara* (crown), and a *taba'at* (ring). These too are iconic objects of military power and royal authority, and their presence on a statue shifts the presumption toward worship rather than mere commemoration. The *baraita* frames each of these as undergoing an interpretive evolution — an original reading and a revised, more theologically charged reading.

### Symbols & Divinity

The evolution in interpretation is striking. For the sword (*sayif*): *me'ikara savur listim be'alma* — originally, they thought a statue holding a sword was simply depicting a bandit or military commander. *U'levasof savar she'horeg et atzmo tachat kol ha'olam kulo* — but the later interpretation is that the idol presents itself as capable of killing the entire world, asserting a kind of cosmic violent dominion. Again, the *tachat* formulation inverts the meaning.

For the crown (*atara*): initially they interpreted it as a craftsman's ornamental addition — *uman sam lo atara*, a craftsman placed a crown upon it. Later, it was understood as *k'atara lamelech*, the crown of a king, symbolizing supreme rule and mastery.

For the ring (*taba'at*): the initial reading was *ishtima be'alma* — it is simply a sign of delegated authority, like when Achashverosh gives Haman or Mordechai his signet ring, empowering the recipient to sign documents in the king's name. The idol was thus originally seen as merely serving as an agent of some higher power. But the later interpretation — *she'chotem et atzmo tachat kol ha'olam kulo l'mita* — reads the ring as a seal of death over the entire world, asserting life-and-death dominion over all creation. This imagery will be immediately recognizable: it is precisely the language of Yom Kippur, where God presses the royal stamp sealing human fate. The rabbinic tradition likewise teaches that *chotamo shel hakadosh baruch hu emet* — the seal of the Holy One is truth.

What these three additions share with the original three is the same conceptual arc: a shift from symbols of local or regional royal authority to symbols of cosmic, divine power. The iconography moves from "this depicts a king" to "this depicts a deity claiming dominion over all existence." That shift is the operative halachic distinction. Whether the object held by the statue merely demonstrates royal rule or asserts divine, universal power determines the presumption that attaches to the statue.

It is worth noting that these *chazakot* are presumptions calibrated to their historical and cultural context. The symbolic grammar of staff, eagle, and globe carried specific theological freight in the ancient world. Whether those same presumptions apply unchanged to modern sculpture — where the overwhelming majority of representational statues are created purely as civic or artistic objects — is a genuine question. The principle underlying the *mishnah* is not mechanical but contextual: one must assess what the iconography of a given time and place actually communicates to its audience.

## Rav Ashi Challenge

### Rabban Shimon View

The Gemara now turns to the stringent position of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel. According to this view, the indicator of *avodah zarah* is not limited to any specific object of symbolic weight. A *tanna* teaches: *afilu tzror afilu keysam* — even if the statue is holding a pebble, or even a splinter of wood, that suffices to establish the presumption that it is an idol. Even the most trivial or seemingly degrading object in the statue's hand renders it prohibited according to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.

### Waste Inquiry

Rav Ashi then pushes this position to its logical extreme: *tafas beyado tzoa mahu* — what is the law if the statue is holding human waste in its hand? This is not simply a provocative hypothetical. The question gains traction from the rabbinic treatment of *Baal Peor*, the constructed *avodah zarah* whose mode of worship involved defecating before the idol. The Rabbis used that case to establish that even the most degrading act, if it constitutes the recognized form of worship for a particular idol, remains halachically significant. Similarly, *Markulis* — which corresponds to the Roman god Mercury — was worshipped, according to rabbinic depiction, by throwing stones at it, a destructive and seemingly contemptuous act that nonetheless counted as its proper worship.

Rav Ashi's question thus has real analytical bite: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel said *any* object in the hand triggers the prohibition. Does that extend even to waste?

### Waste Symbolism

The Gemara entertains two possible readings of what waste in the hand of a statue might signify. The first: *kuli alma zil be'apei katzoa* — that this god treats all of creation as waste before him, that the entire world is contemptible and lowly in comparison to his magnitude. Under this reading, waste in the hand actually reinforces the divine pretension of the idol, and the presumption of *avodah zarah* would stand. The second reading inverts it: *de'azil be'apei kuli alma katzoa* — the statue degrades itself before the world, presenting itself as waste. Under this reading, no rational worshipper would erect such a statue as an object of veneration, and the presumption would not apply.

The Gemara leaves this unresolved: *teiku*. The question was posed to probe the outer limits of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's position and was left unanswered. It is worth noting that since the *halacha* does not in any case follow Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, the practical stakes of the *teiku* are limited. Yet the fact that Rav Ashi asked the question at all may itself be telling — it is possible that Rav Ashi was inclined to rule in accordance with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's view, and was therefore working out its precise parameters.

## Broken Statues

### Hands & Feet

The Gemara now transitions to a new *mishnah*: *hamotzi shivrei tzelamim* — one who finds broken statues. The ruling is *harei elu mutarim* — they are permitted. The fact of breakage is sufficient to remove the presumption of *avodah zarah* status. However, the *mishnah* adds an important qualification: *matza tavnit yad o tavnit regel, harei elu asurim* — if one finds a fragment in the shape of a hand or the shape of a foot, those remain prohibited. The Steinsaltz edition helpfully reproduces a Roman coin depicting the foot of the god Serapis — a genuine artifact confirming that the Rabbis were not speaking theoretically. Certain cults did in fact worship isolated depictions of a deity's hand or foot, and the *mishnah* reflects awareness of this practice. The reason given: *mipnei shekayotzei bahen ne'evad* — because objects of this kind are worshipped.

### Shmuel's Reading

Shmuel then makes a bold inferential move. He reads the *mishnah* as applying not only to *shivrei tzelamim* — broken pieces of ambiguous statues of unknown origin — but *afilu shivrei avodat kochavim*, even to broken pieces of objects that were known with certainty to have been worshipped as idols.

This reading is initially surprising. The *mishnah* says *shivrei tzelamim*, which is broader than confirmed idols — a *tzelem* is just a statue, not necessarily an object of worship. Why, then, does Shmuel extend the ruling to confirmed idols?

Shmuel's answer: *mishum de-ka-ba'ei le-matni seifa* — the reason the *mishnah* uses the broader term *tzelamim* rather than *avodat kochavim* is to set up the second clause of the *mishnah*, the ruling about hands and feet. The *mishnah* opens with the more general case in order to juxtapose it with the more specific prohibition that follows. Very often *mishnayot* are structured this way, with the first clause functioning as a foil or setup for the more pointed ruling in the *seifa*.

The practical implication of Shmuel's reading is significant: even pieces of confirmed idols, once broken, lose their prohibited status — with the exception of hands and feet, which retain their *avodah zarah* status regardless. Shmuel further qualifies his ruling on feet specifically: *be'omdim al besisan* — the prohibition applies specifically when the fragment is still attached to its base. A foot still mounted on a pedestal retains the character of an intact cultic object, while a detached fragment does not.

### Natural Breakage

The Gemara now raises a distinct but related question: *avodat kochavim she-nishbera me-eileha* — what is the law regarding an idol that breaks on its own, not through any human intervention? A dispute is recorded between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish.

Rabbi Yochanan says: *asura* — it remains prohibited. Reish Lakish says: *muteret* — it is permitted.

The stakes of this dispute concern the mechanism by which breakage affects the idol's status. Is it the mere fact of breakage that matters, or must there be an act of human *bitul* — an intentional nullification by a non-Jew — to remove the prohibition? Rabbi Yochanan holds that *deha lo batla* — because no person has come along to nullify it, the object retains its *avodah zarah* status. The breakage alone, without accompanying human intention, accomplishes nothing. Reish Lakish holds that *mistama bituli mevatla* — one may presume that the worshippers have nullified it in their minds, because *meimar amar i nafshei lo atzlah le-hahu gavra atzlah* — they will reason: if the idol could not even save itself from being broken, how will it save anyone else?

This reasoning consciously echoes the argument attributed to Avraham Avinu in the *midrash*. When Terach returned to find all the idols smashed and the large idol holding a staff, Avraham explained that the large idol had destroyed the others. Terach protested that this was absurd — idols cannot act on their own. And Avraham replied: *v'lo yishm'u oznecha mah she'motzi mipicha* — let your ears hear what your own mouth is saying. The same logic drives Reish Lakish's presumption: rational worshippers will draw the obvious conclusion.

That said, one should be careful not to take this rhetoric too far. The problem of *avodah zarah* is not that its adherents naively believe a stone statue possesses independent powers. The prophets — Hoshea, Yeshayahu, and others — employ this sharp polemic, but it does not fully capture the actual theology of ancient idol worship, in which the statue served as a vehicle or representation for a divine being. Reish Lakish borrows the prophetic rhetoric, but the psychological reality of the worshippers was more sophisticated than the argument implies.

### Dagon Proof

Rabbi Yochanan challenges Reish Lakish's position with a proof from the story of Dagon in Sefer Shemuel. The Plishtim captured the *aron* and brought it into the temple of their god. Each day, the statue of Dagon fell — and ultimately its head and the palms of both hands were severed. Yet despite this catastrophic destruction of the idol: *al kein lo yidrechu kohanei Dagon* — the priests of Dagon continued to be called the priests of Dagon, their devotion entirely unshaken. This is a remarkable proof: even in the face of the total physical destruction of their idol — manifestly broken by a superior power — the worshippers maintained their faith and their cult. Reish Lakish's presumption that worshippers will rationally conclude "the idol cannot even save itself" is flatly contradicted by the historical record.

### Threshold Transfer

Reish Lakish responds: *mishum re'aya?* — you bring a proof from there? *Hatam she-manichin et ha-Dagon v'ovdim et ha-miftan* — in that case, the worshippers did not simply continue with Dagon; rather, they stopped worshipping Dagon and transferred their devotion to the threshold of the temple, the *miftan*, against which the idol had broken. The reasoning attributed to them: *shavkei isurei l'Dagon* — they abandoned their devotion to Dagon and redirected it to what had apparently broken the statue. They assumed, in other words, that the threshold possessed a power greater than Dagon's.

This is precisely the mindset Reish Lakish is describing, just redirected: the worshippers did indeed conclude that Dagon had failed them. They drew the inference — just as Avraham in the *midrash* successively considered whether to worship fire, then water, then the sun — that something stronger had overcome their idol, and they transferred their worship accordingly. They did not abandon *avodah zarah*; they recalibrated it. But Reish Lakish's point stands: the breaking of the idol did effect a *bitul* of its status, even if new idolatry took its place.

## Safeik Vadai

### Principle Stated

The Gemara now introduces a new general principle emerging from the previous discussion. In the exchange about broken idols, the Gemara had posed the following challenge: a confirmed idol (*avodah kochavim vadai avaduha*) was definitely worshipped — it has unambiguous *avodah zarah* status. Even if you argue it is now broken, how do you know it was ever nullified? That remains a *safeik*. And *havei safeik vadai* — you have a *safeik* set against a *vadai*. The operative rule is stated: *ein safeik motzi midei vadai* — a doubtful status cannot extract an object from a status of certainty. The *safeik* of possible *bitul* cannot override the *vadai* of confirmed idol status.

Having articulated this principle, the Gemara immediately subjects it to scrutiny.

### Chaver Case

The first challenge comes from a *baraita*: *chaver shemet* — a *chaver*, a rabbinic scholar reliably known to be scrupulous in *terumah* and *ma'aser* obligations, died and left behind a storage basket full of produce (*megurah mlei'ah peirot*). Even if the fruit was freshly harvested that same day (*afilu hen bnei yoman*), the ruling is *harei hen b'chezkat metukanim* — we presume the *terumah* and *ma'aser* have already been separated.

This seems to violate the principle. The produce was *vadai tevel* — it was definitively untithed when it came off the tree. Whether this *chaver* actually separated *terumah* and *ma'aser* before he died is at best a *safeik*. Yet the ruling treats that *safeik* as sufficient to remove the produce from its *vadai tevel* status — precisely what *ein safeik motzi midei vadai* would seem to prohibit.

### Chazaka as Vadai

The Gemara's first resolution is conceptually important: *hatam vadai vadai hu d'vadai asrinhu* — in the case of the *chaver*, it is not truly a *safeik* against a *vadai*. It is *vadai* against *vadai*. The *chazakah* of a *chaver* is so robust that we treat it as *vadai* — we are as certain that he separated *terumah* and *ma'aser* as we are that the fruit was *tevel* when it came from the tree.

This is underscored by the ruling of Rabbi Chanina Choza'ah: *chazakah al chaver she'eino motzi davar she'eino metukan mitachat yado* — the presumption about a *chaver* is not merely that he probably separated *terumah* and *ma'aser*, but that he absolutely never allows anything to leave his possession without it being fully *metukan*. The *chazakah* carries the legal weight of a certainty. This broader principle is worth noting: *chazakot* in Jewish law are treated with extraordinary legal force — sufficient, in other contexts, even to support capital punishment. The rabbis were willing to execute based on *chazakot*, and the principle *ein onshin min hadin* — that one may not execute based on *kal v'chomer* — marks the outer limit, not the inner limit, of *chazakah*'s reach.

### Safeik vs. Safeik

The Gemara offers a second resolution: *v'iba'it eima, safeik v'safeik hu* — alternatively, the case of the *chaver* is actually a *safeik* against a *safeik*, not a *safeik* against a *vadai*. While the produce was on the tree, it was *vadai tevel* if it had reached the stage of *nigmar melachto* — completion of processing that triggers the obligation to tithe. But the Gemara introduces the possibility, based on a ruling of Rabbi Oshaya, that the produce might never have reached that obligatory stage at all.

Rabbi Oshaya rules: *maarim adam al tevu'ato u'machnisah b'motz shelah* — a person may employ a legal subterfuge (*ha'arama*) by harvesting grain together with its chaff and husks (*motz*), bringing it in that unprocessed state, *k'dei she'tehei behemtu ochelet u'ptura min hama'aser* — so that his animals can eat it without the obligation of *ma'aser* attaching. Since the produce was never fully processed, it never became obligated. Under this approach, the produce may never have been *vadai tevel* at all — it may have been *safek tevel* from the start, because the possibility of Rabbi Oshaya's *ha'arama* always existed.

This *ha'arama* is technically permissible according to Rabbi Oshaya, though it is a matter of some debate whether rabbinic law restricts it, and it carries obvious religious-ethical weight: one who exploits such subterfuges to avoid tithing is circumventing the spirit, if not the letter, of the *mitzvot hateluyot ba'aretz*. Nonetheless, the Gemara employs it to resolve the challenge: since the produce could theoretically have been brought in unprocessed, the *vadai tevel* status was never fully established, and the case is therefore *safeik* against *safeik*. The principle *ein safeik motzi midei vadai* thus remains intact.

## Corpse Impurity

### Miscarriage Case

A second and more complex challenge to *ein safeik motzi midei vadai* is now introduced. A *baraita* teaches: *ma'ase b'shifchatah shel metzik echad b'Rimon she'hetila nefel l'bor* — there was an incident involving a slave woman belonging to a certain wealthy person in Rimon, in the north of Israel, who had a miscarriage and threw the fetus into a water cistern. A *kohen* came to examine it — *leida im zachar im nekeivah* — to determine whether it was male or female.

### Animal Scavengers

The case came before the Sages, and they declared the *kohen tahor* — despite his having peered into the airspace of the cistern where the corpse lay, he did not contract *tum'at met*. The reason: *mipnei she'chuldah u'var metzuyim sham* — because weasels and other scavenging animals (the precise identification of the second creature remains uncertain, with some suggesting a polecat or similar animal) were commonly found in that area and could have removed the body before the *kohen* examined the cistern.

The challenge to *ein safeik motzi midei vadai* is sharp: she *vadai* threw a fetus into the cistern — that is a *vadai*. Whether the animals actually removed it is a *safeik*. Yet the Sages ruled leniently based on that *safeik*, apparently allowing it to override the *vadai* of corpse presence.

### Fetal Status

The Gemara's first resolution: *lo teima hitila nefel la-bor ela eima hitila ke-min nefel la-bor* — do not read the *baraita* as saying she threw a *nefel* (fetus), but rather that she threw something resembling a *nefel*. The laws of fetal development, discussed extensively in Masechtot Ohalot and Niddah, establish that at various stages, what emerges from a miscarriage may not yet have the status of a human body for purposes of *tum'at met*. If the object was not yet a fully formed *nefel*, then there was no *vadai* of corpse impurity in the cistern to begin with — the entire case was a *safeik* from the outset.

The Gemara then addresses the apparent difficulty with this reading: the *baraita* says the *kohen* came *leida im zachar im nekeivah* — to determine male or female — implying the form was human enough to carry that distinction. The Gemara reinterprets: *hachi ka'amar leida im ruach hepila im nefel hitila* — the examination was not to determine sex but to determine whether what she had expelled was a *ruach* (a wind or formless emission, implying nothing of human status) or an actual *nefel* (a recognizable fetus with *tum'ah*-bearing status). The use of *hepila* versus *hitila* as distinct verbal forms supports this reading. And even granting that it was an actual *nefel*, the examination to determine male or female may have been for the woman's own *tum'ah* calculations — a female fetus generates a longer period of *tum'ah* for the mother than a male.

### Animal Removal

The Gemara's second resolution circumvents the problem altogether: *v'iba'it eima, keivan she-chuldah u'vardelas metzuyim sham vadai giraruhu* — since scavenging animals of this kind were prevalent in that location, we may in fact treat their removal of the body not as a *safeik* but as a *vadai*. Animals of this type, given any opportunity to access meat, will invariably take it. Therefore the ruling of the Sages was not an instance of *safeik* overcoming *vadai* — it was *vadai* against *vadai*: the *vadai* of the fetus in the cistern is countered by the *vadai* that such animals would have removed it.

The principle *ein safeik motzi midei vadai* therefore remains intact. The discussion will continue on the following *daf*.

---

---

# Avodah Zarah 42

## Breaking Idol Debate

### Self-Broken Idols

The daf opens by returning to a *machlokes* between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish that was introduced the previous day: what is the status of an idol that breaks on its own, without any human intervention? Rabbi Yochanan holds that such an idol remains *assur*. His reasoning is that *bittul* of an idol requires an affirmative act — a non-Jew must deliberately break it, thereby expressing that the idol no longer holds significance for him. Spontaneous breakage, in his view, accomplishes nothing of the sort. Reish Lakish disagrees and holds the idol is *mutar*. His reasoning is that a non-Jew who sees his idol collapse and break of its own accord will reason: if the idol cannot even protect itself, it can hardly protect me. In his mind, therefore, he *mevatel*s it — he dismisses it as no longer possessing any power.

The Gemara proceeds to present a series of challenges — each introduced by the formula *eitivei* — in which Rabbi Yochanan attempts to demonstrate that Reish Lakish's position leads to untenable conclusions. In each case, Reish Lakish (or the Gemara in his name) offers a response, and the responses themselves follow a consistent pattern. That pattern is worth tracking carefully, as it recurs throughout the *amud*.

### Pieces on Pedestals

The first challenge draws on a ruling we have already encountered: if one finds a *tavnit yad* or *tavnit regel* — a form of just a hand or just a foot — these are *assur*, because they are *keyotzei bahen na'avad*, similar to something that has been worshipped. Rabbi Yochanan presses Reish Lakish: why should these be *assur*? They are, after all, *shevarim* — broken pieces. If a self-broken idol is *mutar* according to Reish Lakish, then broken-off pieces of a statue should similarly be *mutar*.

The Gemara answers by invoking Shmuel's interpretation: *b'omdin al basisam* — these are pieces that are standing on their own pedestals. In other words, the hand or foot is not a fragment broken off from a larger statue; it is, from the outset, a complete and independent idol in the form of a hand or foot. Such objects were evidently worshipped in their own right. The *shevarim* premise of the challenge simply does not apply here, because nothing has broken — the object is whole as it was always meant to be.

### Bending the Idol

Rabbi Yochanan tries again. The Gemara rules that a non-Jew can perform *bittul* on his own idol or on another non-Jew's idol, but a Jew cannot perform *bittul* on a non-Jew's idol. Rabbi Yochanan presses: according to Reish Lakish, why should a Jew's act of *bittul* fail? If a self-broken idol is *mutar*, then surely an idol that a Jew actively breaks should be at least as *mutar* — it should be *tehavi k'avodat kochavim shenishbeira me'aleha*.

Abaye clarifies that the case under discussion is not one of breaking the idol but of *pichasa* — a Jew who bends the idol out of shape, or in Rashi's formulation, takes a hammer to it and flattens it. This is a distinct act. The Gemara then asks: but what difference should that make? We even have an explicit *Mishnah* that says *pichasa af al pi shelo chasra batla* — bending the idol, even if nothing is actually removed, constitutes successful *bittul*. So why doesn't it work when a Jew does it?

Reish Lakish's first answer is that the *Mishnah* speaks of when a non-Jew performs the bending: *hani mili depichasa oved kochavim*, but *aval pichasa Yisrael lo batla*. Rashi explains that a non-Jew observing the bending would reason that the idol could not save itself — the same logic Reish Lakish employs for spontaneous breakage. But when a Jew comes and bends it, the non-Jew's reaction is simply: someone came and smashed my idol. There is no theological inference drawn. The distinction is psychologically coherent: spontaneous damage suggests divine disfavor or weakness; deliberate human damage does not.

### Rabba's Gezeirah

Reish Lakish offers a second, more structurally significant answer through the opinion of Rabba — and this answer will serve as Reish Lakish's primary defense for the remainder of the *amud*. Rabba says: *le'olam ki pichasa Yisrael nami batla* — in truth, when a Jew bends the idol, it theoretically *does* work as *bittul*. However, the Rabbis enacted a *gezeirah*: they were concerned that in order to bend or break the idol, the Jew would first pick it up — *magbah lah vehadar mivattelah* — and by picking it up, he would take ownership of it. And we know that *vechol avodat kochavim b'yad Yisrael einah betelah le'olam* — an idol that comes into Jewish ownership can never be subject to *bittul*. To prevent a Jew from inadvertently acquiring an idol and thereby locking it permanently into *assur* status, the Rabbis decreed that a Jew's act of *bittul* is simply ineffective. The practical consequence is that the Jew should not pick it up in the first place.

It is worth noting that this *gezeirah* is specific to Jewish involvement. There is no concern about a non-Jew picking up an idol and thereby acquiring it in a way that would block *bittul*, because the rule that an idol in Jewish ownership can never be *mevutal* applies only to Jews. This asymmetry is what allows Reish Lakish to maintain that self-broken idols — which involve no Jewish action at all — remain *mutar*.

---

## Successive Challenges

### Markolis Stones

Rabbi Yochanan continues with another *eitivei*. The ruling is: a non-Jew who takes stones from a *markolis* — a pile of stones dedicated to the worship of Mercury, into which worshippers would throw additional stones as their act of service — and uses those stones to pave roads or theaters (*v'chippa bahen drachim v'tarti'ot*), those roads are *mutarot*. One may walk on them and derive benefit from them. But if a Jew takes stones from the *markolis* and paves roads with them, those roads are *asurot*.

Rabbi Yochanan asks: according to Reish Lakish, why should a Jew's paving make these roads *assur*? The Jew has repurposed stones from idol worship into something mundane — should this not be at least as effective as an idol breaking on its own? Reish Lakish answers: *hacha nami k'deRabba* — this too is governed by Rabba's principle. Theoretically, the Jew's act should constitute *bittul*, but the Rabbis enacted the same *gezeirah*: we are concerned the Jew would pick up the stones and thereby take ownership of them, after which *bittul* becomes permanently impossible.

### Shaving the Idol

Rabbi Yochanan presses again. The ruling is: a non-Jew who shaves down an idol *l'tzarcho* — for his own personal benefit, to obtain the shavings — the idol itself and the shavings are both *mutarin*. The non-Jew's willingness to scrape material off his idol for personal use signals his contempt for it; he is effectively treating it as scrap. By contrast, if he shaves it *l'tzorkha* — for the sake of the idol itself, as a form of upkeep — then the idol remains *assur*, but the shavings themselves are *mutar*, since the shavings have been separated from the main object. However, if a Jew does either of these — whether shaving for his own benefit or for the idol's sake — both the idol and the shavings are *asurin*.

Rabbi Yochanan asks: according to Reish Lakish, should not the Jew's action be equivalent to spontaneous breakage, and thus *mutar*? And Reish Lakish again invokes Rabba: *hacha nami k'deRabba*. It is Rabba's *gezeirah* that renders it *assur* — the concern that the Jew will pick up the idol before shaving it, acquire it, and thereby block any future *bittul*.

One might ask: why does Rabbi Yochanan keep launching challenges when Reish Lakish has the same answer each time? Tosafot raises exactly this question. The implicit answer is that each challenge is slightly different in its structure, and the question is whether Rabba's *gezeirah* can plausibly be extended to cover each new scenario. Each application of *hacha nami k'deRabba* is its own halakhic move.

### Idol Dust

Rabbi Yochanan tries yet again, now citing the opinion of Rabbi Yossi. Rabbi Yossi holds that when one encounters an idol, one should grind it down to dust and scatter it to the wind or cast it into the sea. The Rabbis respond to Rabbi Yossi: but even that dust can serve as fertilizer — *af hi ne'eset zevel* — and thus one would be deriving benefit from it. And we have the verse *lo yidbak b'yadcha me'uma min hacharem* — nothing of what is forbidden should remain in your possession. The implication is that even the ground-up dust of an idol retains the status of *avodah zarah*, because it can yield benefit.

Rabbi Yochanan asks Reish Lakish: if this is so, and even idol dust remains *assur*, how does that cohere with your view that an idol breaking on its own becomes *mutar*? The Gemara answers: *hacha nami k'deRabba*. Rabba's *gezeirah* applies here as well — a Jew cannot pick up the idol to grind it, for doing so would acquire it and permanently foreclose *bittul*. This answer raises an interesting practical question: what, then, is a Jew supposed to do when he finds an idol? He cannot grind it, he cannot pick it up, he cannot break it. One is left wondering whether burying it — without picking it up — might be a workable solution, perhaps by digging a hole nearby and toppling it in.

### Dragon Head Cut

The final challenge in this series involves an image of a *drakon* — a dragon or serpent-like creature — whose head has been cut off. The ruling is: *safek oved kochavim chatacho, safek Yisrael chatacho* — if there is doubt whether a non-Jew or a Jew cut off the head, the image is *mutar*, since we may be lenient and assume a non-Jew cut it. But if it is known definitively that a Jew cut it, it is *assur*.

Rabbi Yochanan asks: according to Reish Lakish, this should be equivalent to an idol that broke on its own — *tehavi k'avodat kochavim shenishbeira me'aleha* — and thus *mutar* even when a Jew did the cutting. And once again, Reish Lakish responds: *hacha nami k'deRabba*. The same *gezeirah* applies.

---

## Asherah Trees

### Winter Planting

Having withstood all of Rabbi Yochanan's challenges, Reish Lakish now turns the tables and launches his own *eitivei* against Rabbi Yochanan. The topic shifts to the *asheira* — a tree dedicated to *avodah zarah*.

Rabbi Yossi rules that one may not plant vegetables beneath an *asheira* even in the winter months: *af lo yerakot biyemot hageshamim*. The background assumption is that in the summer, it is obvious one may not do so, because the shade of the *asheira* benefits the plants, and one thereby derives benefit from the *avodah zarah*. In the winter, one might have thought the shade is actually harmful to plants and thus no benefit is being derived. Rabbi Yossi nonetheless prohibits it, because *mipnei shehaniviana nosheret aleiha* — the foliage and leaves fall off the tree onto the vegetables below and act as fertilizer, which constitutes benefit.

Reish Lakish now poses this as a challenge to Rabbi Yochanan: those leaves fell on their own — *me'aleha*, of their own accord. According to Rabbi Yochanan, who holds that an idol that breaks on its own is *assur*, this is consistent. But since Reish Lakish holds that what breaks or falls of its own accord is *mutar*, he wants to know why Rabbi Yochanan finds this case troubling.

### Falling Leaves

Rabbi Yochanan's answer is: *shani hatam de'avodat kochavim kayamet* — this case is different, because the main body of the *avodah zarah* is still intact. The tree still stands. The leaves falling off do not diminish the idol in any meaningful way; the *ikar* of the *avodah zarah* is exactly as it was before. This distinguishes it from an idol that breaks on its own, where the idol itself has been damaged or destroyed.

### Natural Growth Rule

But the Gemara pushes back on Rabbi Yochanan's answer: what about the case of the shavings (*shipuyin*)? There, we said that if the non-Jew shaved the idol for the idol's own sake, the idol remains *assur* but the shavings are *mutar* — and in that case, too, the main body of the idol is still intact. So why are leaves that fall from an *asheira* any different from shavings that fall from an idol?

Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua answers: *lefi she'ein avodat kochavim betelah derech gedilata* — *avodah zarah* cannot be *mevutal* through the natural course of its own growth. It is built into the nature of a tree that its leaves fall. Since this is merely the tree's natural developmental process, it cannot constitute *bittul* in any form. This is a distinct principle from Rabba's *gezeirah*: it is not about the concern of Jewish ownership but about the inherent incapacity of natural growth processes to effect *bittul*.

### Nests on Trees

Reish Lakish continues his challenge to Rabbi Yochanan with a case involving nests. The *mishnah* or *baraita* distinguishes between two trees, each with a bird's nest at its top. The first is a tree that has been made *hekdesh* — dedicated to the Temple. Regarding the nest on this tree, the ruling is *lo nehenin velo mo'alin*: one may not benefit from the nest (*derabbanan*), but if one does benefit, there is no violation of *me'ilah* (*de'oraita*). The absence of *me'ilah* means that *de'oraita*, the nest does not carry the full sanctity of the *hekdesh* tree.

The second case is a nest at the top of an *asheira* tree, where the ruling is *yitiz bekaneh* — one may knock the nest off with a reed and take it. The natural assumption, Reish Lakish argues, is that a bird builds its nest by breaking off twigs from the very tree it sits upon. If that is the case, then the twigs of the nest are part of the *asheira* tree material — yet the ruling permits benefiting from them. This, Reish Lakish argues, supports his position: material that breaks off from the *avodah zarah* on its own becomes *mutar*, just as he holds for self-broken idols.

### Chicks Not Twigs

Rabbi Yochanan defends himself by rejecting Reish Lakish's factual assumption. The source of the *yitiz bekaneh* ruling is *Rabbi Yochanan* himself, who explains: *amai yatiz, yatiz be'afruchin* — what you are knocking out is the baby chicks, not the nest itself. The ruling permits knocking the chicks out of the nest, but it says nothing about benefiting from the nest's twigs. And the chicks themselves were not part of the *asheira* tree material — they belong to the bird, not to the tree. Rabbi Yochanan therefore argues that his permissive ruling does not support Reish Lakish's position at all.

Furthermore, the language of the *hekdesh* case — *lo nehenin velo mo'alin* — is itself evidence that the twigs come from elsewhere. If the bird built the nest from twigs of the *hekdesh* tree itself, those twigs would have the full sanctity of *hekdesh*, and benefiting from them would constitute *me'ilah* (*de'oraita*). The fact that the ruling says *velo mo'alin* — implying there is no *de'oraita* violation — demonstrates that the twigs are from some other tree brought in from outside: *de'aytei etzim me'alma vekinita bahen*. By external twigs, the nest carries only a *derabbanan* prohibition, which is why *lo nehenin* applies but *velo mo'alin* (no *de'oraita* violation) follows.

### Eggs & Young Birds

Reish Lakish attempts to sustain his challenge by pointing to the principle of *ain me'ilah begidulin*: even if the bird took twigs from the *hekdesh* tree itself, those twigs grew *after* the tree was made *hekdesh*, and there is a rule that growth occurring after *hekdesh* is declared does not carry the full force of *me'ilah*. This would explain *velo mo'alin* without requiring Rabbi Yochanan's interpretation that the twigs came from elsewhere.

Rabbi Yaakov clarifies the practical distinctions in this series of cases. Regarding baby birds (*afruchin*): in both the *hekdesh* case and the *asheira* case, the chicks are *mutar*. Regarding eggs (*beitzim*): in both cases, they are *asurin*. The eggs are considered an integral part of the nest in a way that the mobile chicks are not, and therefore the prohibition of the nest extends to them.

Rav Ashi adds a further refinement: *ba'afruchin shetzerichin le'iman k'veitzim damu* — chicks that are still dependent on their mother are treated like eggs and are likewise *assur*. Only chicks capable of independent existence are fully permitted.

---

## Vessels & Images

### Destroying Vessels

The Gemara now begins a new *mishnah*. One who finds vessels (*keilim*) bearing an image of the sun (*tzurat chama*), an image of the moon (*tzurat levana*), or an image of a *drakon*, must carry them to the Dead Sea and cast them in: *yolichim l'yam hamelach*. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds a qualification: it is only vessels that are *mechubadin* — important or distinguished — that are *assur*. Vessels that are *mevuzin* — humble or contemptible in appearance — are *mutar*. The precise meaning of this distinction will receive further treatment in the Gemara.

### Create vs. Find

The Gemara asks: is the *mishnah* implying that only these three images — sun, moon, and dragon — are worshipped by non-Jews, and that all other images are not? But that cannot be right. A *baraita* from Chullin enumerates a long list of things for which one may slaughter as worship: the sea, rivers, the desert, the sun, the moon, the stars and constellations (*kochavim umazalot*), Michael the great ministering angel, and even the smallest worm (*shilshul katan*) — all of these are classified as *zivchei meitim*, as idol worship.

Abaye resolves this: *miflach l'chol d'meshkach palchi* — non-Jews worship anything they happen to find. Whatever is in front of them, they will potentially worship. But when it comes to objects that they actually craft and create for worship, it is specifically those three things — sun, moon, and dragon — that they manufacture and venerate. Other images, when made, are crafted *l'noi b'alma* — purely for decoration — not as objects of worship. This distinction between what one creates and what one finds will prove to be structurally important going forward.

### Rav Sheshet's Rules

Rav Sheshet compiled the relevant *chumrot* from various sources and taught them together in a single *baraita*. He establishes three rules. First: all celestial bodies (*mazalot*) are *mutar*, except for the sun and the moon (*chama u'levana*). Second: all faces (*partzufin*) are *mutar*, except for the face of a human being (*partzuf adam*). Third: all shapes and images are *mutar*, except for the shape of a *drakon*.

The scriptural basis for singling out the sun and moon appears to come from *Shoftim*, where *hashemesh ve'hayareach* — the sun and the moon — are specifically mentioned. The *drakon* and the human face carry their own reasons, which the *sugya* will develop.

### Making Idols Problem

The Gemara immediately raises a difficulty with Rav Sheshet's first rule. If all celestial bodies other than the sun and the moon are *mutar*, in what context is this being said? If we are speaking of *making* such images, surely even making a representation of, say, a star or a constellation would be prohibited. The verse in *Shemot* states: *lo ta'asun iti elohei chesef ve'elohei zahav lo ta'asu lachem* — do not make alongside Me gods of silver or gold. And the Rabbinic interpretation of this verse is: *lo ta'asuni k'demut shimshai hamishmishin lefanai bamarom* — do not make images resembling My attendants who serve before Me on high. Those heavenly attendants include all the celestial bodies, not just the sun and the moon. Therefore Rav Sheshet cannot be speaking of a case where one is manufacturing these images.

### Finding vs. Making

The resolution is that Rav Sheshet's rules apply specifically to the case of *finding* such objects: *ella pshita bimotzei* — it is obvious that he is discussing one who finds an already-made vessel bearing one of these images. And the ruling aligns precisely with the *mishnah* we just read: *hamotzei keilim ve'aleihem tzurat chama tzurat levana tzurat drakon yolichim l'yam hamelach* — one who finds vessels bearing the images of the sun, the moon, or the *drakon* must cast them into the Dead Sea. Implicitly, other images found on vessels do not require this treatment. Rav Sheshet's three rules thus map onto the *finding* scenario: only the sun, the moon, the human face, and the *drakon* raise concern when found, while other celestial bodies, other faces, and other images, when merely found rather than crafted for worship, are *mutar*.

The Gemara is poised to analyze each of Rav Sheshet's three categories in turn — the celestial bodies, the faces, and the *drakon* — examining how each resolves into either the *finding* or the *making* framework. That analysis will continue in the next *amud*.

---

---

# Avodah Zarah 43

## Mishnah & Overview

### Mishnah Review

We pick up at the bottom of 42b, in the middle of a broader discussion that benefits from being surveyed as a whole before diving into the details. The *mishnah* states: *hamotze kelim ve'aleihem tzurat chama, tzurat levana, tzurat drakon — yolichem le'yam hamelach* — if one finds vessels upon which are depicted the form of the sun, the form of the moon, or the form of a dragon, one must take them to the Dead Sea. The *mishnah* then proceeds to distinguish between idolatrous objects that are *mechubad* — honorable or respectable — and those that are *mevuzeh* — disgraceful — a distinction that will occupy us later in the discussion.

It is worth pausing at the outset to appreciate the scope of the problem. The *mishnah*'s prohibition on the *tzurat levana* immediately raises a difficulty: we know from Tractate Rosh Hashanah that Rabban Gamliel kept images of the moon in his attic in order to show simple witnesses what shape they had observed in the sky, so they could properly testify to the new month. Similarly, the prayer books contain references to *Rav hitkin tzurat halevana* — Rav established the form of the moon in the liturgy. Where exactly are the lines between objects we encounter, symbolic depictions, and tools used for legitimate purposes? This is the overarching project of our *daf*.

### Rav Sheshet's Chart

A few lines below the *mishnah*, Rav Sheshet attempts to organize the various stringencies into a coherent framework. The result is essentially a chart of what is permitted and what is forbidden across three domains. Regarding the *mazalot* — the constellations — everything is permitted except for the sun and the moon, *chama u'levana*. Regarding *partzufim* — faces — everything is permitted except for a human face, *partzuf adam*. And regarding *tzurot* — figures or shapes generally — everything is permitted except for the dragon, *drakon*.

### Three Categories

This chart, however, immediately raises a question: with respect to which legal situation does each clause of Rav Sheshet's statement apply? The *gemara* identifies three distinct categories that must be kept in mind throughout: *oseh* — one who makes such an image; *oved* — one who worships it; and *motze* — one who finds it. Each of these categories carries different legal implications, and the permissibility or prohibition of any given figure depends heavily on which category we are discussing.

If Rav Sheshet's statement that "all constellations are permitted except the sun and the moon" refers to one who *makes* them, the question is immediate: how can any constellation be permitted to make at all? We have an explicit *pasuk* at the end of *Parshat Yitro* in *Shemot* chapter 20: *lo taasun iti elohei chesef v'elohei zahav lo taasu lachem* — "You shall not make with Me gods of silver, and gods of gold you shall not make for yourselves." The word *iti* — "with Me" — is notably unusual; it seems to say "do not make something 'with Me'" or "alongside Me." The *gemara* understands this as a prohibition against making images of God's heavenly *shamashim*, His celestial attendants. If so, making *any* constellation image would be forbidden, making Rav Sheshet's statement difficult to understand as referring to *making*.

The *gemara* therefore concludes that the first clause of Rav Sheshet's statement — about *mazalot* — must refer to *motze*, one who finds. This connects directly to the *mishnah*: *hamotze kelim va'aleihem tzurat chama...* — when one finds vessels bearing these images. But this creates a new tension with the middle clause. The *gemara* probes whether the statement can be internally consistent, or whether we must understand the beginning and end (*reisha* and *seifa*) as referring to *motze* and the middle (*metziaita*) as referring to *oseh*.

Abaye accepts this division: *reisha v'seifa b'motze, u'metziaita b'oseh* — the beginning and end address one who finds, while the middle clause about human faces addresses one who makes. Rava offers an alternative: the entire statement of Rav Sheshet refers to *motze*, and the middle clause — permitting all faces except a human face — represents the opinion of Rabbi Yehuda. For Rabbi Yehuda, as a *baraita* records, adds two further figures to the list of prohibited images: *dmut meinika* — a nursing mother — and *Sar Apis*.

The *meinika* is described as a mother nursing the entire world, *al shem Chava she'meinika kol ha'olam kulo* — in the name of Eve, who nurses all of creation. This figure is prohibited specifically when she is depicted holding a child and nursing it. The *Sar Apis* figure — identifiable with the Egyptian deity Serapis — is described as a minister who feeds and appeases the whole world, *al shem Yosef she'sar umefayes et kol ha'olam kulo*, associated with Joseph who governed Egypt's food supply during the famine. This figure is forbidden specifically when depicted holding a *geriva* — a dry-measure vessel — in the manner of one engaged in his work. The commentators note that Steinsaltz suggests the nursing figure may alternatively represent Isis from Egyptian mythology or Dionysus being nursed by nymphs, though the association with a universal mother goddess is the central concern.

## Dragon Definition

### Spikes Between Joints

A *baraita* opens the question: *ezehu tzurat drakon?* — what constitutes the form of a dragon? Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar defines it: *kol she'yesh lo tzitzin bein parakav* — any creature that has spikes between its joints. Rashi explains that *tzitzin* is the Aramaic translation of *snapir* — fin — and alternatively understood as hair-like projections.
