The *gemara* turns to a case of wine being transported: *hai oved kochavim de-dari zika ve-kazil Yisrael achorei* — a non-Jewish person is carrying wine in a skin (*zika*), a bag-type container, while a Jewish person follows behind to supervise and ensure the wine is not tampered with.

### Rav Papa: Full vs. Parti…

Rav Papa draws a distinction based on how full the skin is. If it is full — *malya* — it is permissible, *de-lo mekarkesh*: there is no air space, so the wine cannot be shaken around. If it is only partially full — *chasira* — it is prohibited, *dilma mekarkesh*: the non-Jew could shake the bag, agitating the wine in a way that could constitute prohibited handling.

### Open Jar: Opposite Rule

For an open jar (*kuba*), the rule is precisely the opposite. If the jar is full, it is prohibited — *dilma naga* — because the wine reaches near the top and the non-Jew might touch it. If it is only partially full, it is permissible — *de-lo naga* — because the wine level is too low for him to have made contact. So for the skin, full is better; for the open jar, less full is better. The different physical properties of each container drive the opposite conclusions.

### Rav Ashi: Skins Always OK

Rav Ashi disagrees with Rav Papa's distinction regarding wine skins. He holds that *zika*, a wine skin, is permissible whether full or partially full — *bein malya u-vein chasira shari*.

### Not Customary Manner

Rav Ashi's rationale is: *ein derech nisuch b'kach* — this is not the customary manner in which idolatrous libations are performed. The wine skin is a lesser, more disposable container, and it is not the kind of vessel through which one would conduct a proper act of *nisuch*. The *derech nisuch* — the standard mode of libation — requires a level of formality and presentation that a wine skin does not afford. Using a wine carried in a skin for idolatrous purposes would be, as it were, beneath the conventions of the practice.

---

## Wine Press Debate

### Mechanical Press Setup

The *gemara* now turns to the wine press. The setting is *me-atzra zeira* — a wine press of a specific kind. Rashi explains: *gat she-ein dorechin ela kofshin ba-kora* — a press where the grapes are not trodden by foot but instead crushed by a mechanical beam. The mechanism involves placing grapes in the press, using a lever or piston to apply downward force, and allowing the juice to flow out. The non-Jewish person operates this press without any direct physical contact with the grapes or the wine itself. The question is whether this kind of indirect involvement renders the wine prohibited.

### Direct vs. Secondary For…

Rav Pappi rules it permissible; Rav Ashi — or according to another version, Rav Shimi bar Ashi — rules it prohibited. The *gemara* then clarifies the scope of their debate. *Bekocho* — if the non-Jew applied his own physical strength directly to the press mechanism, pressing the lever down himself — *kulei alma lo peligi de-assur*: everyone agrees it is prohibited. That is equivalent to tilting the barrel: the wine is produced by his direct force.

*Ki peligi* — where they disagree — is *bekoach kocho*: a secondary degree of force. For instance, if the non-Jew loaded rocks into a basket that weighs down the press beam, so that it is the rocks, not the non-Jew's arm, that crushes the grapes — is that level of mediated control sufficient to prohibit the wine?

### Rashi: Two Degrees

Rashi spells out the distinction clearly. *Bekocho* is when the non-Jew presses the lever directly with his own strength — his body is the instrument of force. *Koach kocho* is when he does something that sets a secondary mechanism in motion — for example, *she-megalgel ve-hagalgal korei vaitz* — he turns a wheel, and the wheel operates the beam, and the beam crushes the grapes. His action is one step removed from the wine itself.

### All Agree on Direct

A second version of the dispute reframes its scope entirely. According to this version, *bekoach kocho kulei alma lo peligi de-shari* — everyone agrees that a secondary degree of force is permissible. The debate between Rav Pappi and Rav Ashi concerns *bekocho* — direct force — and even there, perhaps, there is room to permit it since the non-Jew never actually touched the grapes or wine. *Koach kocho*, two degrees removed, would be universally permitted.

### Rav Yaakov Case

A practical case was brought: *hava uvda bekoach kocho* — a real incident occurred involving secondary force, *ve-asar Rav Yaakov mi-nahar pekod* — and Rav Yaakov from Nahar Pekod ruled it prohibited. This ruling serves as a *ma'aseh rav*, a practical precedent supporting Rav Ashi's more stringent position as understood in the first version of the dispute.

### Modern Automation

This debate carries direct relevance to contemporary wine production. If a mechanical press is powered by hydraulics or an electric motor that operates entirely without human contact with the grapes, it is difficult to characterize the process even as *bekocho* in the classical sense — and certainly not as direct contact. If there is a step where a person presses a button or engages a lever, the question of *koach kocho* becomes live. The discussion cuts in more than one direction, however. The very same logic about automation and human intent that would tend toward leniency in the context of *yayin nesech* raises a stringency when applied to the requirement of *lishmah* — human intention — for items like machine-made *matzos* or *tzitzis*. Whether activating a machine that produces thousands of units constitutes sufficient intentional human agency for *mitzvah* purposes is the flip side of the same conceptual coin.

---

## Barrel Split Lengthwise

### Non-Jew Hugs Barrel

The *gemara* presents a case at the bottom of 60a: *hahu chavita de-itka'a le-orka* — a wine barrel that split lengthwise, meaning a crack running from top to bottom. The wine is about to spill. A non-Jewish passerby, wishing to prevent the loss, hugs the barrel — *chavkah* — pressing the two sides together to hold the crack closed.

### Two Versions

Two versions of the ruling are recorded. According to one, Rafram bar Papa permitted the wine even for drinking. According to the other, it was Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua who gave the ruling, and he permitted only *l-zavuney* — selling the wine to non-Jews — but not drinking it. This intermediate category, permissible to sell but not to drink, will shortly become the subject of broader discussion in the context of Rabbi Shimon's position.

### Lengthwise vs. Horizontal

The leniency in the case of a horizontally split barrel — cracked around its equator — is greater than in the longitudinal case. *Ve-hanei milei de-faka le-orcha* — this discussion applies specifically to a lengthwise split. *Aval le-futyeh* — but if the barrel was cracked horizontally — *afilu bi-shtiyah sharei* — even Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua would permit drinking the wine.

### Brick Analogy

The reason is: *ma'aseh leveinah ka avid* — the non-Jew is doing the work of a brick. To hold a longitudinal crack closed, the non-Jew must apply lateral force from both sides simultaneously, hugging the barrel and actively maintaining pressure. That constitutes a meaningful human intervention. But if the crack is horizontal and the barrel simply needs downward pressure to stay together, pressing down from above is no different from placing a brick on top of it — it is purely passive, mechanical pressure that any inanimate object could supply equally well. Such pressure does not rise to the level of halachically significant contact with the wine.

### Non-Jew in Press

Separately, Rav Ashi addresses a case where a non-Jew was found standing inside the wine press: *hahu oved kochavim de-ishtakach de-hava ka-ei be-ma'atzarta*. Rav Ashi rules based on the degree of moisture present. If the floor of the press was wet to the level of *tfo'ach le-hatpi'ach* — wet enough that contact with it would wet something else, a standard measure of moisture in *halacha* — then *ba-ei hadachah u-va-ei niggub*: the press must both be washed out and then dried thoroughly. The concern is that *yayin nesech* residue remains even in the wash water and must be eliminated entirely. If the moisture level was below that threshold, *be-hadachah be-alma sagi leh* — washing alone is sufficient, without requiring subsequent drying.

---

## Storage Pit Mishnah

### Debt as Motive

The *gemara* moves to the *mishnah* on 60b. *Oved kochavim she-nimtza omed be-tzad ha-bor shel yayin* — a non-Jewish person was found standing next to a storage pit of wine. The *mishnah* rules: *im yesh lo milveh alav assur* — if the non-Jew has a debt that the Jewish owner owes him, the wine is prohibited. The reasoning is that the non-Jew, believing the wine to be his practical collateral, may feel entitled to handle or take it. *Ein lo milveh alav mutar* — if there is no such debt, the wine remains permissible, as there is no motivation for him to have interfered with it.

### Touching Scenarios

The *mishnah* then lists several additional cases: *nafal la-bor ve-alah* — a non-Jew fell into the wine pit and came back out; *medado be-kaneh* — he measured the wine with a rod; *hetiz et ha-tzirah be-kaneh* — he removed a wasp from the wine with a rod; or he wiped the foam off the top of an open barrel. In all of these cases — *ve-chol elu hayah ma'aseh* — each was an actual incident that came before the authorities — *ve-amru yimacher* — and they ruled the wine should be sold (but not consumed by a Jew).

### Angry Throwing

The *mishnah* also records: *natal et ha-chavit ve-zarkah be-chamato la-bor* — a non-Jewish person, in a fit of anger, picked up a barrel of wine and threw it into the storage pit. *Zeh hayah ma'aseh ve-hikhshiru* — that too was a real case, and the wine was ruled permissible.

### Shmuel: Specific Wine

Shmuel qualifies the opening ruling of the *mishnah*: *ve-hu she-yesh lo milveh al oto yayin* — it is not sufficient that the non-Jew has any debt owed to him by the Jewish owner. The wine is only at risk if the debt is specifically secured by or against *that* wine. Only then does the non-Jew have reason to think of the wine as something he can lay claim to and therefore handle freely. A general debt without any connection to this particular wine does not create sufficient motivation for him to mishandle it.

### Rav Ashi: Contract Proof

Rav Ashi brings a proof for Shmuel's reading from the following *mishnah* in the same *perek*. That *mishnah* addresses a case of *ha-metaher yeino shel ovdei kochavim* — a Jew who undertakes to produce kosher wine using a non-Jew's grapes and facilities. The arrangement is that the non-Jew writes a *shtar* — a document — saying *hitkabalti mimcha ma'ot*, that he has already received payment, even before he actually has. Once such a document is written, the wine is permissible, because the non-Jew no longer thinks of the wine as having any claim on it.

However, if after writing the *hitkabalti*, the non-Jew refuses to let the Jew retrieve the wine until actual payment is made — *ve-ein menicho ad she-yiten lo ma'ot* — the *mishnah* rules that such a case occurred in Beit She'an and the wine was prohibited. The *ta'am* is: *ta'ama de-ein menicho* — the reason the wine was prohibited in that case is precisely because he would not release the wine. This shows he still regarded the wine as his collateral. Conversely, *ha menicho — shari*: had he permitted the Jew to take the wine freely, it would have been permissible. Rav Ashi concludes: *shema mina milveh al oto yayin ba'inan* — this proves that Shmuel's specification is correct: the concern applies only when the debt is specifically tied to that wine.

---

## Four Cases & Rabi Shimon

### Fell & Drowned Case

Returning to the case of the non-Jew who fell into the wine pit, Rav Papa rules: *lo shanu ella she-ala met* — the *mishnah*'s leniency applies only if the non-Jew drowned in the wine and was removed dead. *Aval ala chai* — if he emerged alive, the wine is prohibited.

### Yom Eidam Analogy

Rav Papa explains: *de-dami alei ke-yom eidam* — when a person's life was in danger and he survived, the experience is to him like a *yom eidam*, a celebratory occasion. Just as we are concerned about increased idolatrous fervor on the days that are holidays for non-Jews, so too a person who narrowly escaped death will feel intense gratitude and will likely want to offer a libation to his idol. That spontaneous religious impulse is sufficient reason to prohibit the wine.

### Rabbanan: Prohibit, Sell

The remaining cases in the *mishnah* — measuring with a rod, removing a wasp, wiping foam from the barrel — all represent situations where the non-Jew interacted with the wine in some way but did not directly handle it. The anonymous *tanna'im*, the *rabbanan*, rule that in such cases the wine is prohibited for Jewish consumption but may be sold.

### Rabbi Shimon Permits All

Rabbi Shimon takes a different position altogether: *matir* — he permits the wine in all of these cases, apparently even to drink. His view is that these incidental and indirect contacts do not rise to the level of prohibited handling.

### Rav Adda Praises

Rav Adda bar Ahava praises Rabbi Shimon's consistency: *yanuchu lo le-Rabbi Shimon brachot al rosho* — may blessings rest upon Rabbi Shimon's head. The reason for the praise: *ke-shehu matir matir afilu bi-shtiyah* — when he permits, he permits entirely, even for drinking; *u-che-shehu osser osser afilu be-hana'ah* — and when he prohibits, he prohibits entirely, even for any benefit. Rabbi Shimon has only two categories, with no ambiguous intermediate zone. Either the wine is fully permitted or it is fully prohibited, and he does not create the uncertain middle ground of permissible for sale but not for drinking.

There is a note by the *Rashash* that suggests the formula of blessing would only be appropriate if Rabbi Shimon were still alive, and therefore proposes that there were two scholars named Rav Adda bar Ahava. This is an interesting suggestion, though it may be questioned — not least because belief in *Olam Haba* means that *brachot al rosho* need not be limited to the living. The *Rashash*, it should be said, is frequently cited for his original and incisive observations, and the story is told that Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach, upon hearing someone suggest that the *Rashash*'s commentary was printed in the Vilna *Shas* only because his father-in-law was wealthy enough to pay for it, responded that he too would have happily paid to have the *Rashash* included.

### Halakha Not Like

Despite the enthusiasm of Rav Adda bar Ahava and the traditions transmitted in the names of Rav Chisda, Zeiri, and others that *halacha ke-Rabbi Shimon* — the *gemara* concludes: *ve-ein halacha ke-Rabbi Shimon*. The final ruling does not follow Rabbi Shimon. The *rabbanan*'s intermediate position, prohibiting the wine for drinking while permitting its sale, stands. In general, Rabbi Shimon's rulings are followed only in specific cases; when he disagrees with Rabbi Yehuda, for instance, the *halacha* typically follows Rabbi Yehuda rather than Rabbi Shimon.

---

## Angry Throwing Case

### Zav Contact Standard

Rav Ashi articulates a general principle: *kol she-be-zav tamei be-oved kochavim oseh yayin nesech* — whatever form of contact would render something *tamei* when performed by a *zav* will, when performed by a non-Jew, render wine *yayin nesech*. Conversely, *kol she-be-zav tahor be-oved kochavim eino oseh yayin nesech* — whatever form of contact would not create *tumah* when done by a *zav* does not create *yayin nesech* when done by a non-Jew.

This comparison is not arbitrary. The Rabbis decreed that non-Jewish people carry the status of *tumah* equivalent to a *zav* or *zavah*, even though they do not carry *tumah* under Torah law. Given that the Rabbinic level of impurity assigned to a non-Jew parallels that of a *zav*, it is a coherent move for Rav Ashi to use the *zav*'s contact standards as the benchmark for determining what level of non-Jewish interaction with wine creates *yayin nesech*. The association between idolatry and *tumah* is itself ancient: the *mishnah* in Shabbat already teaches that idols themselves are *metamei ke-sheretz*, and *kitvei kodesh* are *metamei et ha-yadayim*, though for different reasons and at different levels.

### Rav Huna Challenge

Rav Huna challenges Rav Ashi's principle by pointing to the very case in the *mishnah*: *natal ha-chavit ve-zarkah be-chamato la-bor ze hayah ma'aseh be-Veit She'an ve-hikhshiru* — the non-Jew picked up the barrel and threw it in anger, and the wine was ruled permissible. Rav Huna reads the word *be-chamato* — in his anger — as legally significant, not merely descriptive. The *mishnah* must be teaching: *be-chamato* — yes, when he threw it in anger, the wine is permissible; *she-lo be-chamato* — but had he thrown it calmly and deliberately, the wine would have been prohibited. If so, it is the absence of *kavanah* that makes the case permissible — and Rav Ashi's blanket principle, which ties the analysis purely to the *zav* contact standard without any consideration of intent, cannot stand.

### Rav Ashi Reinterprets

Rav Ashi responds by reinterpreting the *mishnah*. The word *zaraka* — threw — does not, he argues, describe a throw in the ordinary sense. Rather, Rashi explains: *she-holikh u-mitgalgel ha-kli kol sha'ah al yedei she-hu megalgelo u-morido la-bor* — the non-Jew was rolling the barrel to the edge and letting it tumble in. The wine only risked contact at the very moment when he lowered it into the pit, at the end of the roll, and the concern is that at that final point he may have touched the wine in the pit. *Hilkhakh she-lo be-chamato lo — de-haishinan dilma naga*: if he was not angry, we would be concerned that as he rolled it in he made actual contact with the wine. When he was angry, the act was more impulsive and less deliberate, reducing the likelihood of that final moment of contact.

### Amoraic Method

This exchange is itself a striking illustration of a broader Amoraic method. Rav Huna engages in what might be called *omni-significance*: the premise that every word in a *mishnah* carries independent legal weight. The word *be-chamato* is not merely coloring a story — it must be bearing a *halachic* distinction. From that premise, Rav Huna derives a rule that seemingly contradicts Rav Ashi's general principle, forcing Rav Ashi to stretch the language of *zaraka* to mean something other than what it plainly says — rolling rather than throwing.

What is notable is that the *mishnah* is recording an actual case that occurred: *zeh hayah ma'aseh ve-hikhshiru*. Yet the *amora'im*, working generations later, invest every detail of that narrative — including the emotional state of the actor — with binding legal significance, and then, having derived a rule on that basis, require the counter-position to reinterpret the very words of the *mishnah* in order to preserve a more general principle. It is a vivid example of how the *amora'im* engaged with *mishnayot* as texts of unambiguous legal density, where nothing is merely descriptive and every word bears legal consequence.

---

---

# Avodah Zarah 61

## Wine of Non-Jews

### Overview & Transition

Daf 61 concludes the *perek*. Most of the preceding discussion has concerned different types of touch — how a non-Jew's contact with Jewish-owned wine renders it prohibited — presented through a series of individual cases without a fully systematic treatment. This final *mishna*, however, introduces a distinct situation: wine that is owned by, or under the auspices of, a non-Jew. Whereas earlier cases addressed Jewish-owned wine and the circumstances under which non-Jewish contact creates a problem, here the starting point is the non-Jew's ownership itself. Whether this constitutes a conceptually distinct legal category, or merely a heightened version of the same concern, will be one of the central questions of the *daf*.

### Metaher & Tumah

The *mishna* opens with the phrase *hametaher yeino shel ovdei kochavim* — one who comes to *metaher*, to purify, the wine of non-Jews. The choice of the word *metaher* is striking and worth dwelling on. *Metaher* implies the existence of *tumah*, impurity, and it is no accident that the conceptual vocabulary of *tumah v'taharah* has become the dominant framework for thinking about this entire subject. The analogy is structurally apt: in the laws of *tumah*, an impure object communicates its impurity through touch, contaminating and invalidating whatever it contacts. With wine, the parallel is precise — Jewish wine is touched by a non-Jew and thereby rendered invalid. This was made explicit at the end of the preceding *daf*, where the *Gemara* drew a direct analogy between a *zav* and a non-Jew: just as a *zav* transmits *tumah* through various forms of direct and indirect contact, so too a non-Jew renders wine *tamei* through analogous modes of contact. The conceptual borrowings run even deeper — questions about whether a poured liquid constitutes one unit or two, whether touching the side of a barrel through an opening counts as contact, all of these are drawn from the world of *tumah v'taharah*.

### Non-Jews as Tamei

But this goes beyond legal analogy. The Rabbis explicitly treated non-Jews as *tamei*, categorizing them as *zavim* and *niddos* in certain respects. In a world where *tumah* and *tahara* no longer carry the practical weight they once did — when *kodshim* and *taharos* are no longer the daily preoccupation they were in the Tannaitic period — the one domain where the *tumah* of non-Jews continues to find expression is precisely in their contact with wine. The psychological and religious experience of wine contamination, then, is framed not primarily through the lens of *avoda zara*, but through the older and more visceral categories of *tumah v'taharah*. The non-Jew's touch is experienced as contamination in a quasi-ritual sense, and the discourse of *metaher* — purification — reflects how deeply that framework has been internalized.

---

## Case 1: Locked House

### Setup & Storage

The *mishna* then describes the first case: *v'nosno birshuso* — after processing the wine entirely on behalf of the non-Jew (who was kept away from contact throughout), the Jew places the filled barrels into the non-Jew's house. The non-Jew owns the wine; the Jew has processed it and is now storing it in the non-Jew's domain. The concern is that the non-Jew, feeling comfortable in his own home with his own wine, might quietly perform a libation to *avoda zara*. The *mishna* asks: under what conditions need we fear this, and under what conditions may we rely on available safeguards?

### Tosafot's Reading

*Tosafot*'s reading — which is the more cogent interpretation, and which corresponds to what was ultimately *Rashi*'s own final version before he raised difficulties with it — is that the case presupposes the Jew holds *maftei'ach v'chosam*, a lock and seal: the Jew has the key to the house and has affixed a seal to the door or barrels such that any unauthorized entry would be detectable. Given this, the non-Jew cannot simply walk in unnoticed; he would have to visibly break the seal or pick the lock, actions that expose him to scrutiny.

### Public Domain Effect

The *mishna* then adds that the house must be *patuach lirshus harabbim* — open to the public domain — and located in a city containing both Jews and non-Jews. The presence of Jewish passersby in the public street means that a non-Jew seen furtively attempting to access a locked and sealed house would appear suspicious. He knows this, and the deterrent effect is sufficient.

### Permission Conditions

Accordingly, in such a city — one with a mixed Jewish and non-Jewish population — the wine is *mutar*. But *b'ir she'kulo ovdei kochavim*, in an entirely non-Jewish city, it is *assur*. Non-Jewish bystanders would not provide the same deterrent: they would understand the context, see no reason to intervene, and might simply ignore the owner entering what is, after all, technically his own property. In such a case, a Jewish presence is required.

### Supervision Methods

The *mishna* clarifies, however, that the required supervision need not be continuous. *Ad she'yeishev umeshamer* — until you have a Jew sitting and watching — does not mean a Jew must be stationed there at all times. *Af al pi she'hu yotzei v'nichnas*, even if the supervisor comes and goes periodically, it is *mutar*. This is the mode of oversight known as *yotzei v'nichnas*, a form of *hashgachah* discussed at the very opening of *Masechet Chullin*: if a responsible party makes surprise visits at unpredictable intervals, that is sufficient to keep behavior honest. The non-Jew never knows when someone might appear, and this uncertainty functions as an effective deterrent.

---

## Wine of Non-Jews (II)

### Misleading Language

One might pause at the *mishna*'s opening phrase and note that *metaher* is actually misleading. The case described involves wine that has not yet been rendered *tamei* — the Jew processed the grapes himself, keeping the non-Jew away throughout. There is nothing to purify; the goal is *preventing* contamination from occurring in the first place. Once a non-Jew has actually handled wine and rendered it *stam yeinam*, there is no mechanism for *tahara* after the fact. The *mishna*'s language implies that the Jew is restoring something that had been lost, when in fact he is preserving something that was never compromised. What is implicit, perhaps, is that the only viable approach is to keep the non-Jew away during production — and the *mishna* then turns to the separate question of how to maintain that status during storage. Still, the phrasing is exaggerated, and the point stands.

---

## Case 2: Receipt

### Receipt Transfer

The second case presented by the *mishna* is *hametaher yeino shel ovdei kochavim v'nosno birshuso* — again, the wine is in the non-Jew's domain — but this time the Jew holds a receipt. The non-Jew has written *hitkabalti mimcha maot*, "I have received money from you," which functions as an acknowledgment that the wine now effectively belongs to the Jew, even if the actual payment has not yet been made. The receipt may be written in advance of the Jew actually paying, with the understanding that the Jew will sell the wine, collect the proceeds, and pay the non-Jew. But because the non-Jew has formally acknowledged Jewish ownership, his psychological relationship to the wine changes — he recognizes it as the Jew's property and is less inclined to treat it as his own to dispose of as he wishes. In this case, *mimcha maot mutar* — it is permissible.

### Beis She'an Case

The contrast case makes the principle clear. *Aval im rotze Yisrael lehotzi v'eino manicho ad sheyiten lo et meotav* — if the non-Jew has not truly relinquished control, and demands payment before allowing the Jew to remove the wine, then the non-Jew retains effective dominion. The Jew cannot exercise independent control over what is nominally his wine. *Ze haya ma'ase b'Veis She'an ve'asru* — this situation arose in Beis She'an and the Rabbis forbade it. The non-Jew's insistence on prior payment signals that he considers the wine still within his sphere of control, and given that it remains in his house with no lock-and-seal arrangement, the concern that he will take license with it is very real.

---

## Case 1: Locked House (II)

### Rashi vs. Tosafot

*Rashi*'s reading of the *mishna* differs substantially from *Tosafot*'s, and the difference reveals a fundamental conceptual disagreement. *Rashi* conflates the two cases of the *mishna* — the locked house and the receipt — treating them as cumulative requirements. According to this reading, both are necessary: the house must be accessible to a *reshus harabbim* where Jews might observe suspicious activity, *and* the non-Jew must have issued a receipt acknowledging the Jew's ownership. The underlying logic, which *Tosafot* makes explicit in citing *Rashi*, is the principle *havei k'yeino shel Yisrael* — it must become, in effect, the Jew's wine. For *Rashi*, and apparently for the *Rambam* as well, there is a categorical distinction: wine that belongs to a non-Jew is *stam yeinam* and presumptively problematic; wine that belongs to a Jew requires an actual event of contact before we begin worrying about the specific circumstances. These are not merely different points on a continuum of likelihood — they are different legal categories. The way to make non-Jewish wine permissible, on this reading, is to render it *not* non-Jewish wine: to establish Jewish ownership firmly enough that it falls into the other category.

*Tosafot* explicitly rejects this framework. In the first case of the *mishna*, the Jew has not paid and the non-Jew is the complete owner — yet *Tosafot* reads this as permissible with adequate safeguards. For *Tosafot*, there is ultimately one category: the question is always what is the likelihood that the non-Jew has touched the wine? When the non-Jew owns the wine and the house, that likelihood is substantially higher, and accordingly more robust safeguards are required. But the difference is quantitative, not categorical. As one might put it in contemporary terms: *Rashi* and the *Rambam* see a distinction between a Jew who has taken title to wine versus one who merely holds it on consignment with ownership remaining in the non-Jew; *Tosafot* sees only a spectrum of risk. This debate — conceptual categories versus likelihood analysis — is what structures much of the subsequent *Gemara*.

---

## Gemara Analysis

### Traveling Merchants

The *Gemara* challenges the *mishna*'s ruling that an all-non-Jewish city renders the wine *assur*. Even there, the *Gemara* asks, *v'ha'ika rochlin hamachzirin ba'ayarot* — there are Jewish spice merchants and peddlers who travel from town to town and periodically pass through. On *Tosafot*'s reading, one might wonder: what does it matter that a complete stranger passes by? Such a person would not know the context, would not recognize that the non-Jew is doing something suspicious with the locked house. *Tosafot*'s answer is precisely the point: the house is locked and sealed, so any non-Jew seen fiddling with the lock would appear furtive and criminal regardless of who is watching. Any Jew passing through who notices this will recognize that something is amiss. Even the occasional passage of Jewish merchants through an otherwise non-Jewish city is therefore sufficient to deter the non-Jew from attempting unauthorized entry — because looking like a thief in front of even one knowledgeable observer is too great a risk.

### Walled Cities

*Shmuel* addresses the case where even this deterrent is absent. *B'ir she'yesh la dlasayim u'vriach* — a walled city with controlled entry points, sealed at night, where strangers are either excluded or immediately identifiable — in such a city, no outsider would pass unnoticed, and the non-Jew knows it. The protection of anonymity-in-a-crowd is unavailable, and this changes the calculus. Even the occasional passage of Jewish merchants becomes unreliable as a deterrent when the city controls access so tightly that the non-Jew can account for every person present.

### Substitute Surveillance

*Rav Yosef* introduces several alternative forms of constructive surveillance that function equivalently to a *reshus harabbim*. *V'chalon k'reshus harabbim dami* — a window with a sightline from a Jewish neighbor's house is treated like a public domain; a neighbor who can observe the entrance to the storage house provides equivalent deterrence. *V'ashpah k'reshus harabbim dami* — similarly, a junkyard adjacent to the house creates a form of surveillance: people periodically come to forage or deposit garbage, and their random presence introduces enough uncertainty to deter illicit access. *V'dikla k'reshus harabbim dami* — a palm tree near the house is equivalent, since one who climbs to harvest dates gains an elevated sightline over the surrounding area, and a non-Jew contemplating unauthorized entry knows this.

### Barren Palm Tree

This last case generates a dispute. What if the top of the palm tree has been cut off and it no longer bears dates — *psik reisha* of its productive function? Is the non-Jew still deterred by its presence? *Rav Acha* and *Ravina* disagree. The one who forbids the wine reasons that without dates, no one has any reason to climb the palm tree, so the non-Jew has no cause to fear observation from above. The one who permits it counters: *zimnin d'avda leh beheima v'salik l'iyunei basrah* — sometimes a person loses an animal and climbs a tall tree to survey the neighborhood and locate it. A palm tree, even a barren one, affords an excellent vantage point, and the possibility that someone might ascend for this reason is sufficient to introduce deterrence. The underlying principle, as *Tosafot* emphasizes throughout, is that even a slight possibility of being observed — any credible chance of being seen and recognized as behaving suspiciously — is enough to deter the non-Jew from attempting to access a locked and sealed house.

---

## Baraita Cases

### Jew Owns Both

A *baraita* lays out four cases systematically. The first: a Jew purchases or rents a house in a courtyard owned by non-Jews and fills it with wine — wine that belongs to the Jew, in a house belonging to the Jew, but situated within a non-Jewish courtyard. If a Jew also lives in that courtyard, it is *mutar*, even without a *mafteach v'chosam*. The contrast with the *mishna* is instructive: in the *mishna*, the non-Jew owns the house and the wine, and a locked seal is essential because the owner feels entitled to enter freely. Here, where the Jew owns both house and wine, the non-Jew has no sense of entitlement toward the property — but his ease of physical access through the shared courtyard remains a concern. The presence of a Jewish resident in that courtyard, who would notice any suspicious activity, is sufficient without additional locks.

### Different Courtyard

If no Jews live in that courtyard but Jews reside in a neighboring courtyard, it remains *mutar*, but only *im hu she'hamifteach v'chosam b'yado* — only if the house is locked and sealed and the key is held by the Jew. Physical distance reduces the deterrent value of neighboring Jewish presence, and the lock-and-seal arrangement compensates.

### Non-Jew Owns Both

The third case: the wine belongs to the non-Jew and is stored in the non-Jew's house, but a Jew lives in that same courtyard. This is *mutar*, but here the *baraita* reinstates the requirement of *mifteach v'chosam*. The non-Jew's ownership of both the wine and the house means he feels fully at liberty to enter — Jewish proximity alone is not sufficient to override this sense of entitlement. The lock and seal are necessary in conjunction with the Jewish presence.

### Yochanan Lenient

*Rabbi Yochanan* intervenes and instructs the *tanna* to amend this ruling: *tani af al pi she'ein mifteach v'chosam b'yado mutar* — even without a lock and seal, if a Jew is living in the courtyard, it is permissible. *Rabbi Yochanan*'s reasoning is that a Jew actually residing in the courtyard creates a constant, organic presence that is more intimidating than a merely physical barrier. The non-Jew knows that his neighbor is there day and night, can step outside at any moment, and would notice immediately if anything were amiss. This ongoing presence provides a more effective deterrent than a lock that a determined person might eventually overcome.

### Jew Elsewhere

The fourth case: the non-Jew owns the wine and the house, but no Jew lives in that courtyard — the Jew is in a different courtyard entirely. Here, according to the *baraita*, even a lock and seal is insufficient: *divrei Rabbi Meir*. *V'chachamim osrim* — the *Chachamim* also rule it is forbidden — *ad sheyeih shomer yoshev umishammer*, unless a guard is present and watching, *o ad sheyavo memuneh haval kitin*, or a designated overseer who comes at appointed times.

---

## Case 4 Debate

### Rabbi Meir Strict

In the fourth case — non-Jew's wine, non-Jew's house, Jew in a different courtyard — *Rabbi Meir* holds that even a lock and seal on the door does not suffice. The non-Jew is the complete owner of both wine and house, feels total entitlement, faces no nearby Jewish presence, and could act with relative impunity. The mere physical barrier of a lock is not enough to overcome the cumulative weight of these factors.

### Chachamim View

The *Chachamim* similarly forbid the wine in this configuration unless either a guard is permanently stationed there or an overseer makes periodic visits. At first glance, this appears puzzling: the *Chachamim* seem to be responding to a lenient position, but *Rabbi Meir* himself has already declared it forbidden. The *Gemara* therefore asks precisely which case the *Chachamim* are addressing.

The *Gemara* rules out the possibility that they are responding to the fourth case (non-Jewish wine, non-Jewish house, Jew in a different courtyard), because the *tanna kamma* — including *Rabbi Meir* — has already forbidden that outright. The *Gemara* also rules out the third case (same courtyard), because *Rabbi Yochanan* has ruled so leniently there — not even requiring a lock and seal — that it would be strange to place the *Chachamim*'s strict requirement of a permanent guard in response to it. The *Gemara* therefore locates the *Chachamim*'s statement as addressing the second half of the first case: the Jew owns the wine and the house, but is living in a neighboring courtyard rather than the same one. The *tanna kamma* had ruled this permissible with a lock and seal; the *Chachamim* insist that even this is insufficient if there is no *reshus harabbim* passing by, since the only person positioned to notice anything is in the other courtyard and cannot actually see what is happening.

### Inspection Types

The *Gemara* then addresses the *Chachamim*'s alternative of a *memuneh haval kitin* — an overseer who comes at appointed times. This is puzzling in a different direction: fixed inspection times are arguably worse than nothing, since the non-Jew simply behaves properly during those predictable intervals and acts freely at all other times. The *Gemara* therefore adjusts the reading: *ella ad sheyavo memuneh she'eino ba l'kitin* — the requirement is an overseer who comes *without* fixed appointments, making surprise inspections. It is the very unpredictability of the visits that maintains the deterrent effect. This directly parallels the *yotzei v'nichnas* principle established in the *mishna* and discussed at the opening of *Chullin*: it is not the quantity of oversight but its unpredictability that keeps behavior honest.

---

## Shimon ben Elazar

### Two Readings

*Rabban Shimon ben Elazar* concludes the *mishna* with the statement: *reshus ovdei kochavim achas hi* — the domain of non-Jews is one. The *Gemara* immediately notes that this is ambiguous: *le-hakel o le-hachmir* — is he ruling leniently or strictly? *Rav Yehuda* in the name of *Ze'iri* says he is being lenient; *Rav Nachman* in the name of *Ze'iri* says he is being strict.

### Lenient: Own Domain

On the lenient reading (*Rav Yehuda* in the name of *Ze'iri*), the *tanna kamma* is the strict one. The *tanna kamma* holds that when the non-Jew's wine is stored in *any* non-Jewish domain — even a different non-Jew's house — the same precautions apply as when it is in the owner's own domain, because *v'chaishinan legomlin*: we are concerned about reciprocity. The non-Jew who owns the wine might approach the non-Jew who is housing it and say, in effect: allow me access to this wine for my libation needs, and when the situation is reversed, I will do the same for you. This is not necessarily an explicit arrangement, but a general laissez-faire attitude among non-Jews toward one another's religious needs. *Rabban Shimon ben Elazar* disagrees and is lenient: *b'mah devarim amurim bireshuso* — the precautions apply only when the wine is in the owner's own domain. *Aval bireshus oved kochavim acher mutar* — if it is in a different non-Jew's domain, it is permissible, *v'lo chaishinan legomlin* — and we are not concerned about reciprocal favors. The phrase *reshus ovdei kochavim achas hi* is then read as a question the *tanna kamma* might pose to *Rabban Shimon ben Elazar*: "Do you really treat all non-Jewish domains as identical?" And *Rabban Shimon ben Elazar* responds: no, I do not.

### Strict: Reciprocity

On the strict reading (*Rav Nachman* in the name of *Ze'iri*), the roles are reversed. The *tanna kamma* is lenient: precautions are required only *bireshuto*, in the owner's own domain; if the wine is stored with a different non-Jew, it is *mutar*, since the non-Jew who is responsible for it has no personal stake in the wine and would not casually compromise his custodial role. *Rabban Shimon ben Elazar* is strict: *kol reshus oved kochavim achas hi* — all non-Jewish domains are treated as one because of mutual cover — *mipnei harama'in*, on account of those who are devious. Non-Jews, he holds, will accommodate one another's religious practices regardless of ownership boundaries, and we therefore cannot distinguish between the owner's domain and any other non-Jewish domain.

### Tanya Support

A *braita* provides explicit support for the strict reading of *Rabban Shimon ben Elazar*: *amar Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, kol reshus oved kochavim achas hi mipnei harama'in* — his statement is declarative, not interrogative, and he explicitly grounds it in concern about deceptive reciprocity. The *halacha*, however, follows the lenient position — the *tanna kamma* on the strict reading, which limits concern to the owner's own domain. This is the appropriate conclusion not only because it produces a more lenient outcome, but because it reflects a more measured assessment of non-Jews rather than a conspiratorial one. When one enters into a business relationship with a non-Jew and entrusts him with wine, the concern is realistic when all factors point toward the owner's comfort and entitlement in his own space; it does not extend to a general assumption that all non-Jews collude to subvert Jewish interests.

---

## Gomlin Analysis

### Parzik Rufla Case

The *Gemara* offers a practical case that tests the limits of the *gomlin* principle. In the house of *Parzik Rufla* — *rufla* denoting a figure of high status, a second-in-command to the king — a Jew had deposited wine with a non-Jewish sharecropper (*arisa*) who worked *Parzik Rufla*'s land. This is a case of wine stored in a different non-Jew's domain: not the domain of the owner (*Parzik Rufla*) himself, but of someone subservient to him.

### Equals Reciprocity

The Rabbis sitting before *Rava* initially proposed that the concern of *gomlin* — reciprocal favors — applies only when the two non-Jews are social equals: I do you a favor, you do me a favor. That arrangement presupposes a relationship of mutual capacity and mutual need. But a lowly *arisa* could never be in a position to ask *Parzik Rufla* to watch wine on his behalf; the social gulf is too vast. Therefore, there is no realistic prospect of reciprocal accommodation, and the wine should be permissible.

### Rava Reversal

*Rava* counters with the opposite argument. Even granting that we would not normally worry about *gomlin* in an unequal relationship, the very inequality here creates a different and arguably greater problem: *kivan d'mirsas minei, machpia leh zechuseihu* — precisely because the *arisa* is subservient to and intimidated by *Parzik Rufla*, he will cover up for him. The sharecropper will not resist if *Parzik Rufla* arrives and demands access to the wine; he will look the other way, perhaps even actively facilitate it, to avoid antagonizing his powerful superior. Where equals might weigh the risk of being seen compromising their custodial role, a subservient person simply defers to the superior. The situation is therefore more dangerous, not less.

---

## Practical Applicatio (II)

### Wine Barrels Case

The *Gemara* closes the *sugya* with a practical case: in a certain city, Jewish wine was stored in barrels in the street. A non-Jew was found standing among those barrels. The question is whether we suspect he touched the wine and must therefore forbid it.

### Caught Criterion

*Rava* formulates the decisive criterion: *nitpas alav ke-ganav* — would he be caught like a thief? If the city is one where a non-Jew found tampering with barrels not belonging to him would face legal consequences — would be seized and held accountable — then the wine is *mutar*. Under those conditions, we may presume he did not touch the wine, because the risk of detection and punishment is too great. *V'ei lo assur* — but if it is the kind of place where such behavior carries no consequence, the wine is forbidden, because he has little to fear from having been found there. This criterion is directly analogous to the cases discussed throughout the *perek*: the controlling question is always how much liberty the non-Jew believes he has and how much risk he perceives in acting on it. The locked house, the seal, the Jewish passersby, the window sightline, the surprise inspections — all of these are instruments that increase the perceived risk and thereby remove the inclination to act. Where no such deterrents exist, we cannot rely on his restraint. And this, once again, confirms *Tosafot*'s reading: there is no categorical difference between Jewish-owned and non-Jewish-owned wine as a matter of fundamental legal status. In every case, the analysis comes down to the likelihood of unauthorized contact, assessed through the realistic conditions of deterrence and exposure.

---

## Conclusion

### Rules Summary

Very uncharacteristically, *Rashi* — or more precisely, *Rashi*'s students, as the text makes explicit after the *hadran* — appended a section at the end of the *perek* attempting to systematize what the *Gemara* itself left scattered across numerous individual cases. The paragraph is introduced as *maskana de-milta* — the bottom line — and represents a rare attempt at codification by a commentator who was not himself a codifier. That this was felt necessary is itself testimony to how unsystematic the *perek* was: the Talmud presented a vast range of cases involving different modes of contact without clearly articulating the organizing principles.

### Intent & Touch

The summary works through the relevant variables. *Maga oved kochavim kivan d'nitkaven liga she-shichshach, af al pi she-lo nizak, assur b'hana'ah* — if a non-Jew intended to touch the wine and moved his hand around among it, even without making a poured libation, the wine is forbidden even in benefit. *She-lo b'chavana, kegon she-lo hikkir bo she-hu yayin* — if he touched it without intent, not even knowing it was wine, it is *mutar b'hana'ah*, permissible in benefit. The analysis then proceeds through the full range of cases: direct touch and indirect contact, *kocho* (force applied indirectly), *kavanah* versus its absence, and whether in each case the wine is *mutar b'hana'ah* or *mutar b'shtiyah* — permissible in benefit only or also for drinking.

### Rashi's Ruling

The paragraph concludes with the note that *kach higgia ha-Rav u-pasak halacha le-ma'aseh* — "this is what the master [*Rashi*] arrived at and ruled as practical *halacha*." *Rashi*'s conclusions on these matters are not identical to those of all the *Rishonim*, but the attempt itself is significant: it acknowledges that the *perek*, for all its richness, did not leave the reader with a clear practical guide, and that someone had to do the work of integration.

---

## Practical Applicatio (II)

### Transport Distinction

*Tosafot* addresses one final practical question that the foregoing analysis raises: if a non-Jew is transporting Jewish wine from one city to another for sale, why is that not analogous to the case of a non-Jew left alone with wine and no deterrent to contact? *Tosafot*'s answer draws on the fundamental principle of perceived risk. In the *mishna*'s cases, the non-Jew exerted no effort to access the wine; he is simply present near it, and the question is whether he will take the opportunity to touch it for religious purposes. In that situation, there is little countervailing deterrence from consequences — he has nothing material to lose. But a non-Jew transporting wine for profit has a strong economic stake in the cargo's integrity. If he were to tamper with the wine and be caught, he would lose his commission and his livelihood, and face potential legal liability. That fear of consequences is itself a sufficient deterrent, and *Tosafot* rules that we are not concerned about contact in such a case. The principle is the same as *Rava*'s criterion of *nitpas alav ke-ganav* — it is the fear of being caught and suffering consequences that determines whether we may trust the non-Jew's restraint. With this ruling, the *perek* draws to its close.

---

---

# Avodah Zarah 62

## HaSocher Et HaPoel

### Intro & Chapter 5

We begin today the fifth *perek* of Masechet Avodah Zarah, on 62a. The chapter is entitled *Ha-socher Et Ha-poel* — "one who hires a worker" — and while it continues the *masechet*'s broader engagement with wine produced or owned or touched by non-Jews, its focus here shifts somewhat toward the monetary dimension of that prohibition. Additional topics arise over the course of the *daf* as well, including *shemittah* fruits and the prohibition of *etnan zonah* — the prohibition of bringing as a *korban* an animal given as payment for prostitution — a topic that surfaces in only a few places in the Talmud and is worth exploring carefully.

### Mishna: Worker

The *Mishnah* opens: *ha-socher et ha-poel la-asot imo be-yayin nesech — secharo assur.* If a non-Jewish employer hires a Jewish laborer to perform work associated with the production of *yayin nesech*, the wages are prohibited. Rashi clarifies this framing at the outset. However, if the worker was hired for some other task and was asked only incidentally to move a barrel of *yayin nesech* from one place to another, the wages are permissible — *secharo mutar* — because the agreed-upon terms of the contract concerned a different type of work.

### Mishna: Donkey

A parallel case follows: *ha-socher et ha-chamor lehavi aleha yayin nesech — secharah assur.* One who rents a donkey — or hires a donkey driver — to transport *yayin nesech* finds the wages prohibited. But if the donkey was rented for the owner to ride, and the non-Jew merely happened to place a wine flask on it, the wages remain permissible. The principle underlying both halves of the *Mishnah* is the same: if transporting or working with *yayin nesech* was the incidental byproduct of an arrangement made for other purposes, the wages are unaffected; if it was the core purpose of the hire, the wages are prohibited.

---

## Tofes Damav

### Mai Ta'ama

The *Gemara* opens with the obvious question: *mai ta'ama secharo assur?* Why are the wages prohibited at all? One's initial reading of the *Mishnah* might assume it refers to *stam yeinam* — the rabbinic prohibition of ordinary non-Jewish wine — since throughout the *masechet* the term *yayin nesech* is often used to describe even the rabbinic-level prohibition of *stam yeinam*, so as to underscore its severity. But as will become clear, the *Gemara*'s first question points toward a distinction between the two: whether the stringency applied here extends only to *yayin nesech* proper or also to the rabbinic-level *stam yeinam*.

### Issur Hana'ah

The *Gemara* proposes a first possible rationale: *ho'il ve-yayin nesech assur ba-hana'ah, secharo nami assur* — since the wine is forbidden to derive benefit from, perhaps the wages should be forbidden as well, as fruit of the poisonous tree. But the *Gemara* immediately challenges this: *orlah* and *kil'ei hakerem* are likewise forbidden to derive benefit from, yet the *Mishnah* teaches that if one sold such fruits and used the proceeds for *kiddushin*, the betrothal is valid — *mekudeshet*. That is, the money received in exchange for *orlah* or *kil'ei hakerem* does not itself become prohibited; the prohibited status does not transfer to the monetary proceeds. If *issur hana'ah* alone were the operative principle, wages received for work with *yayin nesech* should similarly remain permissible, just as the *kiddushin* money derived from *orlah* is valid.

### Money Laundering

The *Gemara* therefore advances a different rationale: *ela ho'il ve-tofes damav ke-avodat kochavim* — because *yayin nesech* has the property of *tofes damav*, of latching its prohibited status onto the money exchanged for it, just as is the case with *avodah zarah* itself. If one sells an idol, the money received carries the prohibited status of *avodah zarah*. So too, the wages received for work involving *yayin nesech* carry the prohibited status of the wine. This is the principle at stake — not a generic *issur hana'ah*, but the specific capacity of certain prohibited items to transfer their status onto the money. Notably, not all prohibited items possess this quality; it is a feature of only certain categories of prohibition, and which categories are included becomes the central question the *Gemara* will pursue.

---

## Shemittah Fruits

### Le'ochla Lo Sechora

The *Gemara* raises a comparison: *harei shevi'it de-tofes dame'ha* — what about *shemittah* fruits, which similarly transfer their sanctity onto the proceeds of their sale? *Shemittah* fruits, those that grew naturally during the seventh year, are in principle *hefker* — ownerless — and available for anyone to take. The verse states *ve-hayeta shabbat ha-aretz lachem le-ochla*, and the Rabbis derive from this: *le'ochla ve-lo le-sechora* — the fruits are to be eaten, not sold. If one harvests and sells them in the marketplace, that constitutes forbidden commerce with *shemittah* produce.

### Shemittah Worker

The *Mishnah* presents the following case: if one says to a worker, *heilach dinar zeh ve-likot li yarak ha-yom* — "take this *dinar* and go pick vegetables for me today" (during the *shemittah* year) — the wages are prohibited, *secharo assur*, because the money is explicitly linked to the produce, and *tofes damav* applies. But if one simply says *likot li yarak ha-yom* — "go pick vegetables for me today" — without specifying any wage, the wages are permissible, *secharo mutar*. In this latter case there is room to construe the arrangement as a favor, compensated by a gift, rather than as hired labor in exchange for *shemittah* produce. The explicit monetary linkage is what triggers the *tofes damav* concern. This stands in contrast to *avodah zarah*, where the status latches onto the money whether the arrangement is explicit or implicit.

### Rambam vs Ramban

It is worth noting a related debate between *Rambam* and *Ramban* regarding the *mitzvah* to eat *shemittah* fruits. *Rambam* understands the verse *le'ochla* as primarily conveying the prohibition of commerce — it defines the permitted use (eating) in order to exclude the prohibited one (selling). *Ramban*, by contrast, counts in his addendum to *Rambam*'s *Sefer HaMitzvot* a separate positive *mitzvah* to eat the fruits of *shemittah*, implying a higher level of *kedushah* attached to those fruits. Some have accordingly suggested that one should wash one's hands before eating *shemittah* fruits, and there are discussions about whether a special *berachah* — *asher kidshanu be-mitzvotav ve-tzivanu al achilat peirot shevi'it* — would be appropriate, all flowing from this underlying debate.

### Exports & Terumah

A related concern is the question of taking *shemittah* fruits out of the Land of Israel. This is generally prohibited until after the time of *bi'ur*, the point at which those fruits are no longer available in the field. After *bi'ur*, export becomes possible, but the issue remains live in practice: *shemittah* produce that makes its way to markets abroad raises questions of *kedushat shevi'it*, as does Israeli produce in general, which may carry obligations of *terumah* and *ma'aser* that consumers abroad must be aware of.

---

## Three Opinions

### Yochanan: Kenas

With the comparison between *yayin nesech* and *shemittah* established, the *Gemara* presents three *amoraic* attempts to explain the differences between them. The first is from Rabbi Yochanan, as quoted by Rabbi Abahu: *kenas hu she-kans'u chachamim ba-chamarin u-ve-yayin nesech* — there is a special *kenas*, a rabbinic fine and deterrent, that the Rabbis imposed specifically with respect to *chamarin* (donkey drivers) and with respect to *yayin nesech*. As for *yayin nesech*, that is what was already stated in our *Mishnah*. As for *chamarin*, the *Gemara* cites a *Baraita*: donkey drivers who transported *shemittah* fruits have their wages take on the *kedushah* of *shemittah* — *secharan shevi'it*.

But what does it mean for wages to have *kedushat shevi'it*? The *Gemara* considers two possibilities. First, perhaps the wages would be paid with *shemittah* fruits themselves — but that would mean the employer is paying off a debt using *shemittah* produce, which is itself forbidden commerce, contrary to *le'ochla ve-lo le-sechora*. Second, perhaps the money acquires *kedushat shevi'it* — but then the *Gemara* cites a *Baraita* in which the case of the *dinar* being explicitly mentioned yields a permissible result, which seems to cut against this. The tension in Rabbi Yochanan's explanation at this point is left somewhat unresolved, which is precisely why the *Gemara* proceeds to Abaye and Rava.

Under Rabbi Yochanan's framework, the stringency applied to *yayin nesech* — and to the donkey drivers in the *shemittah* context — is not derived logically from a general principle but is simply a *kenas* that the Rabbis imposed as a deterrent. This explains why *orlah* and *kil'ei hakerem*, which are less common and generally more repugnant, do not require the same *kenas*, and why the *shemittah* case may follow a somewhat different logic.

### Abaye: B'tzad Heter

Abaye accepts Rabbi Yochanan's framework that the donkey drivers' wages carry a special *kenas*, but offers his own explanation of what it means for the wages to be *shemittah*. He says: *le'olam yahavinan lei sechar mi-peirot shevi'it* — the wages are in fact paid using *shemittah* fruits. And when challenged that this amounts to using *shemittah* produce to discharge a financial obligation — which is *sechorah* — Abaye answers: *de-yahavinan lei be-tzad heter*, one must give the payment in a permissible manner. He draws a parallel from the laws of *ma'aser sheni*: one cannot instruct a friend to take *ma'aser sheni* fruits to Jerusalem *le-chalek*, meaning to receive a portion as payment for the transport — because that constitutes using the fruits to pay off a debt. But one may say "bring them to eat and drink in Jerusalem," and then give each other gifts in return. A gift exchange is not the same as a commercial transaction, even if it functions similarly in practice.

### Rava: Skilled Labor

Rava disagrees with Abaye and instead maintains: *le'olam de-kadosh bi-kdushat shevi'it* — the money does in fact take on *kedushat shevi'it*. The distinction Rava draws is between a *poel* — an ordinary day laborer who picks vegetables — and a *chamar*, a donkey driver. *Poel de-lo nafish agrei lo kansu rabanan* — since the day laborer earns relatively little, the Rabbis did not apply the *kenas* against him, because they wanted to protect his modest livelihood. *Chamarei de-nafish agraihu kansu rabanan* — donkey drivers, as a somewhat more skilled and better-compensated profession, did have the *kenas* applied against them. This is why the *Baraita* distinguishes between the cases: when the *poel* is hired without explicit mention of wages, the wages are permissible — not because the *kedushat shevi'it* does not attach to money in principle, but because the Rabbis chose not to extend the *kenas* to ordinary laborers.

### Yayin Nesech Chamura

The *Mishnah*'s ruling regarding *yayin nesech*, which prohibits wages even for a simple *poel*, deviates from the paradigm established by *shemittah*. The *Gemara* explains: *chumra d'yayin nesech shani* — the stringency applied to *yayin nesech* is of a different order. Because *yayin nesech* is so closely identified with *avodah zarah* itself, the Rabbis expanded the scope of the *kenas* beyond donkey drivers to encompass even ordinary laborers. The *shemittah* framework created by the Rabbis — applying the *kenas* to *chamarin* but not to simple *po'alim* — served as a template, but when it came to *yayin nesech*, that template was applied more broadly. This is the resolution of the *machlokes* among the three *amoraim*: all agree there is a special *kenas*, but they differ on exactly what it means for wages to carry *kedushat shevi'it* in the *chamarin* case, and on precisely why ordinary laborers were exempted from the *kenas* in *shemittah* but not in *yayin nesech*.

---

## Stam Yeinam

### Ibaia Lehu

Having established that the *Mishnah*'s prohibition refers specifically to *yayin nesech* proper and not merely to *stam yeinam*, the *Gemara* now raises the open question: *secharo le-stam yeinam mahu?* Does the same stringency of prohibited wages apply when one is hired to work with *stam yeinam* — ordinary non-Jewish wine, subject only to the rabbinic prohibition — as it does with *yayin nesech*? On one hand, since the Rabbis treated *stam yeinam* as equivalent in its level of *issur* to *yayin nesech*, perhaps the wages should be equally prohibited. On the other hand, perhaps when the Rabbis modeled the *kenas* they took into account the ways in which *stam yeinam* is more lenient than *yayin nesech*.

### Tumah Comparison

One metric of difference between *yayin nesech* and *stam yeinam* is *tumah*. *Avodah zarah* itself conveys *tumah*, but wine merely handled or produced by a non-Jew does not carry the same *tumah*-transmitting status as wine actually consecrated for idolatrous libation. Thus *tuma'ato kil* — the *tumah* of *stam yeinam* is lighter than that of *yayin nesech* — and one might argue that *af secharo nami kil*, the wages too should be treated more leniently. The question, then, is whether the Rabbis, in constructing the *kenas* on wages, modeled it after the ways in which *stam yeinam* parallels *yayin nesech*, or after the ways in which it differs. The *Gemara* leaves the question unresolved, then pivots to a practical case that sheds light on the matter.

---

## Boat Rental

### Rav Chisda's Case

A certain man rented out his boat to transport *stam yeinam*. As payment, the non-Jews filled the boat with wheat — a seemingly generous arrangement. After the fact, the man came before Rav Chisda with his question about the status of the wheat.

### Burn & Bury

Rav Chisda ruled: *zil kalinehu ve-kavrinehu be-vei kivrei* — go burn the wheat, and then bury the ashes in a cemetery. This is a striking ruling, requiring two separate acts of disposal, and the *Gemara* proceeds to interrogate each step.

### Temurah Rules

To understand the ruling, the *Gemara* invokes the final *Mishnah* of Masechet Temurah, which establishes a general principle: *kol ha-nisrafin lo yikaveru* — everything required to be burned should not be buried; *ve-chol ha-nikbarin lo yisarefu* — everything required to be buried should not be burned. Each category of prohibited object has its proper method of disposal, and the two methods are not interchangeable. Rabbi Yehuda dissents, holding that one may choose to burn items that should technically be buried, but the other Rabbis reject this: *eino rashai le-shanot*, one may not deviate from the designated method. A further principle applies: when something is classified as *nisrafin*, once it has been burned the ashes — *afran mutar* — are permissible, because burning actually transforms the object. We say *panim chadashot ba'u le-chan* — a new form has come into being. By contrast, *nikbarin* objects, once buried, remain prohibited even in decomposed form — *afran assur* — because burial conceals but does not transform.

### Why Both Steps

Given this framework, Rav Chisda's dual requirement demands explanation. Why not simply scatter the wheat? Because *ata bi-hehu lidei takala* — people will find it and use it, not knowing it is prohibited, thereby violating the *issur*. Why not burn it and scatter the ashes? Because *dilma mizavlei behu* — people might use the ashes as fertilizer, since ash is rich in potassium. So the object needs to be buried — but burning it first creates a transformation (*panim chadashot*) that addresses one dimension of the problem, and burying the ashes in a cemetery ensures they will not be retrieved and used. Both steps together accomplish what neither alone can.

### Execution Tools

One might ask: the *Mishnah* in Sanhedrin teaches that the implements of capital punishment — the stone used for stoning, the beam for hanging, the sword for beheading, the cloth for strangulation — are all buried alongside the executed criminal, and we are not concerned that people will dig them up and use them. Why should our case be different? The *Gemara* answers: *hatam de-kakavrei be-vei dina mukeach milta de-harugei bei dina ninhu* — there, the implements are buried adjacent to the *beit din*, and it is therefore evident to everyone that those graves belong to court-executed criminals. People understand what those graves contain and do not disturb them. *Hacha lo mukeach milta* — in our case, if a sack of wheat is buried in the ground, a passerby who finds it will simply assume a thief hid it there and will help himself to it, entirely unaware of its prohibited status. This distinction — between a burial whose context makes the prohibition evident, and one that does not — is what justifies the additional step of burning the wheat before burying the ashes in a cemetery.

---

## Yannai's Loan

### Loan Structure

The students of Rabbi Yannai had the practice of lending money against *shemittah* fruits. More precisely, they would borrow *shemittah* fruits from poor people during the seventh year and repay them — in money — in the eighth year. On its face, this arrangement appears to constitute commerce with *shemittah* produce, which is forbidden under *le'ochla ve-lo le-sechora*.

### Yochanan Approves

When this practice was brought before Rabbi Yochanan, he ruled: *yaot hem avdin* — they are doing it correctly. From a charitable standpoint, the arrangement represents a sophisticated form of *tzedakah*: the poor had gathered *shemittah* fruits for free, since the fruits are *hefker*, and then received a loan against those fruits. Being able to participate in what appears to be a regular business transaction preserves their dignity, making it a high-level form of *tzedakah*. But the question remains: is this not doing business with *shemittah* fruits? Rabbi Yochanan endorses the practice, and the *Gemara* connects his approval to the principle of delayed payment.

### Delayed Payment

Rabbi Yochanan further states: *u-knegdan be-etnan mutar* — and the equivalent arrangement in the context of *etnan* is similarly permissible. The connecting principle is temporal disjunction: when payment is delayed rather than simultaneous — when the monetary exchange does not happen at the same moment as the transfer of the prohibited or sanctified item — the *kedushat shevi'it* does not latch onto the money in the way that it would in an immediate transaction. The loan structure of Rabbi Yannai's students, in which the fruits are received in the seventh year and repaid only in the eighth year, exploits this temporal gap. It is not merely the fact that repayment occurs outside the *shemittah* year, but rather that the very structure of a loan, with its inherent time delay between receipt and repayment, is categorically different from a direct commercial sale.

---

## Etnan Zonah

### Intro to Etnan

To understand the principle of *u-knegdan be-etnan mutar*, the *Gemara* turns to the laws of *etnan zonah* and *mechir kelev*, which are discussed at length in Masechet Temurah. The Torah prohibits bringing as a *korban* in the *Beit HaMikdash* two types of animals: *etnan zonah* — an animal given as payment to a prostitute — and *mechir kelev* — an animal received in exchange for a dog. The sixth *perek* of Masechet Temurah defines these terms. *Eizo hi etnan?* — What constitutes *etnan*? *Ha-omer le-zonah ha lach zeh be-sichrech* — one who says to a prostitute "take this sheep as your payment," even if a hundred sheep are given, all become prohibited as *korbanot*. Similarly, if someone says "take this sheep so that your slave woman will sleep with my slave," Rabbi Yehuda counts that as *etnan* while the other Rabbis agree.

*Mechir kelev* is defined as exchanging a sheep for a dog: *ha-omer le-chavero hach lach taleh zeh tachat kelev zeh*. If two partners divided nineteen sheep and one dog — one taking ten sheep and the other taking nine sheep and a dog — the ten sheep given in exchange for the dog are prohibited as *korbanot*, while the nine that accompany the dog are permissible since they were exchanged only for sheep. Importantly, *etnan kelev* — payment for a dog used for breeding — and *mechir zonah* — money paid as the price of a prostitute — are both *mutar*, permissible, since the verse specifies only *shnayim shnayim ve-lo arba*: only the two named prohibitions, not the reverse combinations.

### Braita Case

A *Baraita* is cited: *natan la ve-lo ba'ala* — if a man paid the prostitute but never had intercourse with her — or *ba'ala ve-lo natan la* — if they had intercourse but he never paid her — *etnana mutar*, the payment is permissible. The *Gemara* immediately challenges this: if he paid her but they were never together, *peshita* — obviously the payment is not *etnan*, *matanah be'alma hi*, it is simply a gift. And if they were together but he never paid her, obviously there is no prohibited payment because nothing was given. The *Baraita* as stated seems to address either an impossible scenario or a self-evident one.

### Braita Logic

The *Gemara* therefore reinterprets the *Baraita*: *ela hachi kamar* — this is what it actually means. *Natan la ve-achar kach ba'ala* — he paid her first, and intercourse followed later. *O ba'ala ve-achar kach natan la* — or they were together first, and he paid her later. *Etnana mutar* — in both cases the payment is permissible. This is the operative content of the *Baraita*: time disjunction between payment and the act of prostitution removes the prohibition of *etnan*.

### Elazar's Answer

But this reading immediately invites a question: if he paid her in advance, why does the prohibition not take effect retroactively when intercourse eventually occurs? *Le-chi ba'ala le-chulei issur etnan le-mafre'a* — should we not say that once the act occurs, it retroactively renders the prior payment *etnan*? Rabbi Elazar answers: *ke-she-kadmah ve-hikravto* — the case in the *Baraita* must be understood as one where the prostitute took the animal before intercourse occurred and brought it as a *korban* before the act. Since the animal was already offered when the intercourse took place, there was no moment at which it could have become *etnan*. This raises a further structural question: how exactly does this work?

### Conditional Acquisition

The *Gemara* probes: *heichi dami?* How precisely must the transaction be structured? If the man said *kani lach me'achshav* — "acquire it from me now" — then *peshita de-shari*, it is obviously permissible, because *de-ha leita be-sha'at biah*, the sheep no longer exists at the time of intercourse — it has already been offered as a *korban* — and the initial transfer was simply a gift, *matanah be'alma*. If, on the other hand, he did not say "acquire it now," then *heichi matzi makriva* — how could she have offered it at all? She would not yet own it, and one cannot dedicate another's property as a *korban*.

The *Gemara*'s resolution: *ela de-amar lah le-havei gavach ad sha'at biah* — the man must have told her to hold the animal as collateral, keeping it in her possession until the time of intercourse, at which point she would acquire it. But *im mitztarech lach kani me'hashta* — if she needs it in the meantime — for example, if she wishes to bring it as a *korban* right away — she may acquire it now. This conditional acquisition structure — hold as collateral, with the option to acquire immediately if needed — allows for a scenario in which she offers the animal before intercourse, the man follows through, and yet the prohibition of *etnan* never attaches, because at the moment of acquisition the act of prostitution lay either in the past or the future, never coinciding with the moment the animal was acquired.

---

---

# Avodah Zarah 63

## Perek 5 Intro

### Perek Structure

Today's daf is 63, and with it we enter the fifth and final *perek* of *Masechet Avodah Zarah*. This represents a significant shift from what came before. We remain in the domain of *yayin nesech* and *stam yeinam*, but the angle of analysis changes considerably.

### Last vs. This Perek

The fourth *perek* was concerned primarily with the mechanics of how wine becomes *stam yeinam*: what stage of production qualifies a liquid as wine, and what types of physical contact — direct or indirect, intentional or incidental, deliberate in one context but performed for an entirely different purpose — render it forbidden. The *sugyot* of that chapter were often structured around vivid stories: an apple fell into a barrel of wine, someone plunged a hand in to retrieve it, bystanders physically restrained the arm from moving, and from there the *gemara* extracted its principles. The cases themselves were not technically complicated, but the theoretical questions they generated — about intent, about the underlying principles — produced enormous *Tosafot* that addressed not only the conceptual issues but also the practical applications relevant in their own time.

### Mishtaker Principle

This fifth *perek* opens with a different focus: the principle of *mishtaker be'issurei hana'ah* — being paid a salary for work performed in connection with objects that are forbidden in benefit. The opening *mishnah* addresses the case of a Jewish worker hired by a non-Jew to work with *yayin nesech*: the wages received are themselves forbidden in benefit. This concern will anchor the early discussions of the chapter before the *masechet* returns, toward its conclusion, to the *kashrut*-oriented themes more characteristic of the earlier chapters — questions of *ta'arovet*, mixtures, and wine that becomes commingled with other liquids.

---

## Payment Issue

### Gemara's Question

The *gemara* opens by interrogating the theoretical basis for this prohibition on wages. The *mishnah* states that payment for work with *yayin nesech* is forbidden in benefit — but why? Is this simply a consequence of the general principle governing *issurei hana'ah*?

### Issurei Hana'ah

This question has direct practical relevance, and it is one that arises with some regularity. Consider the question of whether a Jew may work as a waiter in a non-kosher restaurant that serves *basar bechalav* — a category that, unlike ordinary non-kosher meat, is genuinely *assur be-hana'ah*, forbidden in benefit. Is serving such food at a table, or working at a soup kitchen where *basar bechalav* is distributed, considered deriving benefit from a forbidden object, since one is being paid to interact with it?

The *gemara*'s answer is that as a general rule, this is not a problem under the category of *issurei hana'ah*. One is not deriving benefit from the *basar bechalav* itself — one is being paid to serve it. The *gemara* goes further: even if someone actually sells an item that is *assur be-hana'ah* and receives money for it — thereby transgressing through the act of sale, since receiving payment constitutes deriving benefit — the money itself does not carry a forbidden status, and continuing to use that money is not considered ongoing benefit from the prohibited object. Whether one may *lechatchilah* retain and use that money is a question that *Tosafot* engages with, but *bedi'avad* it is not problematic. If that is true even where money was directly exchanged for a forbidden object, it is certainly true that a worker being paid a salary for serving *basar bechalav* is not deriving benefit from the object itself.

### Issurei vs. Tofes

So if the general principle of *issurei hana'ah* does not account for the prohibition on wages for *yayin nesech*, perhaps the explanation lies in the concept of *tofes et damav* — the idea that in certain categories of prohibition, the forbidden status transfers to money received in exchange. By *yayin nesech* and *avodah zarah*, if one sells the prohibited object and receives payment, that money is itself forbidden in benefit, and the forbidden status continues to extend to whatever is purchased with it. The same principle applies to *shevi'it* produce. So here we have *issur hana'ah* — which applies to categories like *yayin nesech* and *basar bechalav* — and separately, *tofes et damav* — which applies to categories like *yayin nesech*, *avodah zarah*, and *shevi'it*.

But *tofes et damav* also cannot explain the prohibition on wages for *yayin nesech*. The *gemara* demonstrates this from *shevi'it*: if one is paid a salary to work *with* *shevi'it* produce, those wages do not themselves acquire *kedushat shevi'it*. The rule of *tofes et damav* applies only to money paid *for* the object itself — the object is exchanged for money and the status transfers through that exchange. A worker's salary for labor involving *shevi'it* is not money paid for *shevi'it*; it is payment for services. Therefore the *shevi'it* status does not transfer to it.

### Avodah Zarah Chumra

Thus, from the perspective of *issurei hana'ah*, payment for service should be permitted; and from the perspective of *tofes et damav*, salary for work is not the same as money paid for the object itself. Neither principle independently forbids taking wages for work with *yayin nesech*. The *gemara*'s conclusion is that the prohibition is a *chumra de'avoda zara* — a special stringency unique to the domain of *avodah zarah* — not derived from either of the two general principles. It is important to understand this precisely, because knowing that neither principle applies independently is itself practically significant.

### Liquor Store Question

This clarification matters for real-world questions such as whether one may work in a liquor store that carries non-kosher wine. Owning such a store is obviously a separate and more severe issue — there one is directly profiting from *yayin nesech* in ways that implicate both principles. But whether an employee who merely stocks shelves falls under the prohibition of *mishtaker be'issurei hana'ah* is a genuinely interesting question, one that the *mishnah* may well speak to.
