The *gemara*'s analysis of the underlying principles, and the conclusion that the prohibition in this domain is driven by the special *chumra* of *avodah zarah* rather than by either general principle, is essential background for reasoning through such cases. The final ruling, in any event, is that this *chumra* extends to *stam yeinam* as well: wages for work with *stam yeinam* are equally forbidden.

---

## Shvi'is Case

### Oranges Story

With the theoretical framework established, the *gemara* now turns to an illustrative case. The household of Rav Yanai (*debei Rav Yanai*) would borrow *peiros shevi'it* — fruit carrying the sanctity of the Sabbatical year — from poor people (*aniyim*). The likely motivation was charitable: the poor had gathered this produce from ownerless fields during the *shemittah* year, and as the time of *bi'ur* approached — after which the produce could no longer be kept and consumed — it became practically useful for a wealthy household to take the produce, use it promptly, and replace it with ordinary produce after *shemittah* ended. The arrangement allowed the poor to preserve the practical value of their *shevi'it* fruits beyond the *bi'ur* deadline.

A number of incidental complications surround this arrangement — there are questions of *ribbis*, since borrowing consumable goods and repaying in kind carries the risk of forbidden interest if values fluctuate; and separately, one might wonder whether *shemittah* at year's end cancels the loan entirely, although perhaps a *pruzbul* was in place. These questions are real but peripheral to the main discussion, which is this: when the borrowed fruit was repaid in the eighth year with ordinary non-*shevi'it* produce, were the workers who received that produce obligated to treat it as *peiros shevi'it*?

### Rabbi Yochanan

The people in Rav Yanai's household thought there might be a problem: perhaps the repaid fruit should be considered *chalifei shevi'it* — produce received in exchange for *shevi'it* — onto which the *kedushah* of *shevi'it* transfers. They brought the question to Rabbi Yochanan, and he replied: *ya'ot hen ovdin* — they are acting entirely properly, and there is no *kedushah* on the repaid fruit.

### Etnan Analogy

Rabbi Yochanan supports this ruling by analogy to the laws of *etnan* — payment given to a prostitute for her services, which the Torah forbids from being brought as a sacrifice in the *Beit HaMikdash*. From the laws of *etnan*, Rabbi Yochanan demonstrates a principle: the status of a prohibited object transfers to an exchanged item only when both objects are present simultaneously and a genuine exchange occurs between them. The *kedushah* of *shevi'it* produce, or the *issur* of *etnan*, extends to something received in exchange — but only if the original object and the replacement object exist together at the moment of exchange, so that the status can be understood as passing from one to the other. When the original fruit has long since been consumed and the replacement is delivered in the eighth year simply to repay a debt, there is nothing from which the *kedushah* can extend. The repaid fruit is merely the satisfaction of an outstanding obligation; it is not an exchange.

---

## Etnan Sugya

### Braisa Setup

The *gemara* now examines the laws of *etnan* directly. A *braisa* states: if the man gave the animal to the woman but had not yet had intercourse with her (*natan lah v'lo ba aleha*), or if he had intercourse but had not yet given her the animal (*ba aleha v'lo natan lah*) — in both cases the animal is permitted as a sacrifice (*etnanah mutar*) and does not carry the prohibited status of *etnan*.

### Logical Challenge

The *gemara* immediately challenges both halves of this *braisa*. The first case — giving the animal before the act — is obvious: *keivan d'lo ba aleha, matana b'alma hu d'yahav lah* — since the act has not yet occurred, the giving is simply a gift, with no connection to the services. There is nothing to give it the status of *etnan*. The second case, however, is incoherent: if he had intercourse but gave her nothing, *ha lo yahav lah midi* — he gave her nothing at all! There is no object that could be an *etnan*, permitted or otherwise. The question *etnanah mutar* is meaningless if nothing was ever given.

### Resolution

The *gemara* therefore reinterprets the *braisa*. It does not mean that both events happened but not the other — it means they did not happen simultaneously. The *braisa* must be read as: first he gave the animal and then later they had intercourse; or first they had intercourse and then later he gave her the animal. In both cases — payment followed by act, or act followed by payment — the *etnan* is permitted.

### Strictness

This is Rabbi Yochanan's ruling, and it is, as the *gemara* acknowledges, a striking position. Only if the giving of the animal and the act of intercourse occurred simultaneously — if the animal was in her possession as payment at the precise moment the services were rendered — does it acquire the status of *etnan*. If the payment came first and was finalized before the act, it does not retroactively become *etnan*. If the act came first and the payment followed, it does not acquire the status even though it is clearly being given as payment for services already rendered. One would naturally assume that payment delivered after the fact is precisely what defines *etnan* — yet Rabbi Yochanan says otherwise. The *etnan* status requires that the object be present, possessed, and defined as payment at the very moment the act is occurring.

### Sanctification Q

This leads to a question posed by Rav Hoshaia. The *gemara* had been discussing a scenario in which the man says to the woman: you will own this animal once the act is complete, but if you need it beforehand, you may take possession of it now (*lehavei gabaich ad sha'at bi'a, v'i itzterich lach kni me'achshav*). Under those terms, Rabbi Elazar explains, if she went ahead and brought the animal as a sacrifice before the act took place, the animal would not be *etnan* — since she sacrificed it while still fully owning it as her own property, before the act had occurred, and so the act did not define the animal's status.

Rav Hoshaia asks: what if, in that same scenario, she did not bring it as a sacrifice — she only *sanctified* it (*hikdishaso*), consecrating it to *hekdesh*, without yet offering it on the altar? What is the *halacha*?

One might argue that *amiraso lagavoah kimesiraso lahedyot* — when one consecrates an object to God, it is as though one has physically handed it over to another person; the *Beit HaMikdash* takes possession. On this reasoning, the moment she sanctified the animal, it was as though she had brought it as a sacrifice — she had exercised her early-possession right, the animal now fully belonged to *hekdesh*, and when the act of intercourse later occurred, the animal was no longer in the category of her property or payment. The act, therefore, would not have defined its status as *etnan*.

Alternatively, one might say: *hashta miha kai v'isa be'einayah* — right now, at the moment they have intercourse, the animal is still physically present. Even though she sanctified it, she has not yet actually used it or removed it from the scene; it remains present when the act is taking place, and therefore the act still defines it as *etnan*.

The *gemara* suggests that one could resolve Rav Hoshaia's question from the language Rabbi Elazar used — he specified *hikrivasah*, that she *brought* it as a sacrifice, which *davka* implies the animal was entirely out of the picture. If *hikdashasah* — merely sanctifying it — were equally sufficient, Rabbi Elazar would have stated that case rather than the more extreme one. This implies that sanctification alone does not save it from *etnan* status, since the animal remains physically present.

The *gemara* deflects this inference: it says that Rav Hoshaia's question is actually about Rabbi Elazar's own intent. Perhaps Rabbi Elazar himself was uncertain about the sanctification case, and therefore leaped to the clearer case of sacrifice — not because sanctification is obviously insufficient, but because he himself did not know the answer. The *gemara* concludes: *teiku*.

---

## Defend Yochanan

### Contradiction

The *gemara* now raises a direct contradiction to Rabbi Yochanan's ruling. A *braisa* explicitly states: if the act of intercourse occurred first and the payment was given afterward — even up to three years later — the *etnan* is forbidden (*afilu mikan ad shalosh shanim, etnan assur*). This is precisely the case that Rabbi Yochanan declared permitted.

### Nachman's Resolution

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between two scenarios, based on a *braisa* that employs two formulations: *hivali bi-bitla zeh* — "have intercourse with me in exchange for this specific animal" — versus *hivali bitla stam* — a general promise of payment without identifying a particular animal.

When a specific animal is designated at the moment of the act, the animal, though not yet in her possession, is already *identified* as the payment for that act. It is present, it is earmarked, and the act defines its status at that moment. Therefore, even if the physical transfer of the animal occurs three years later, the *etnan* status attaches — because the connection between the act and this particular animal was established at the moment of the act itself.

When no specific animal was identified at the time of the act — when the promise was general and no particular object was pointed to — then no object was present or earmarked at the moment of the act. Whatever is subsequently given in payment is not defined by that act; it is simply an outstanding debt being discharged. This is the case Rabbi Yochanan permitted.

### Non-Jewish Prostitute

The *gemara* presses further: even in the case where a specific animal is designated, it has not actually been given to her — she has not taken possession. *Ha mechusar meshicha* — it still requires *meshichah*, the act of taking physical possession, to effect transfer. So how does the designation of a specific animal give it *etnan* status?

The *gemara* answers: the case involves a non-Jewish prostitute. A non-Jew acquires movable property not through *meshichah* but through payment of money. Here, the giving of the services functions as the payment — it is the act of intercourse that constitutes the consideration. Therefore, at the precise moment the services are rendered, she acquires ownership of the designated animal. Possession transfers at the very instant of the act, and so the animal is simultaneously in her possession and defined as payment — exactly satisfying Rabbi Yochanan's requirement.

### Apoteke Lien

The *gemara* offers a second resolution for those who would apply this to a Jewish prostitute, where *kinyan chatzer* might be invoked if the animal happened to be in her yard. But the *braisa* speaks of delivery occurring three years later, which seems to preclude the animal having been in her yard at the time of the act.

The *gemara* answers with the concept of *apotiki*: the man declared this specific animal to be the *apotiki* — the lien — for his obligation. He said to her: if I bring you the money between now and a certain date, keep it; but if I fail to pay, take the animal in satisfaction of the debt. Under such an arrangement, although the animal was not physically delivered until years later, she held a legal property interest — a lien — in that specific animal from the moment the obligation arose. At the time of the act, this lien already existed with respect to a specifically identified object. It is therefore as though she had rights in that animal during the act itself, and it acquires the status of *etnan*, even though the physical transfer did not occur for three years.

The concept is noted in passing to have a cognate in modern languages — the word *apoteken* in certain languages carries the sense of a mortgage or pledge, likely from Greek or Latin.

The conclusion of this section is that Rabbi Yochanan's position is coherent but requires careful reading of the *braisot*: the *etnan* prohibition applies only when a specific object is present and owned — or subject to an existing lien — at the moment the act takes place, not when the payment is simply an outstanding debt to be discharged later.

---

## Workers' Food

### Rav Sheshet Q

The *gemara* now shifts to a related question raised by Rav Sheshet, which directly tests the principle that the *etnan* and *shevi'it* cases have been establishing. If an employer gives money to his donkey-drivers and workers to buy their own lunch (*lekhu ve-ikhlu be-dinar zeh*), does he bear any halachic responsibility for what they choose to purchase?

### Prohibited Foods

Three categories of concern are enumerated. First, *shevi'it*: the workers might take the money, go to a seller who is doing commerce in *shemittah* produce unlawfully, and purchase it — drawing the employer into a transaction involving *kedushat shevi'it*. Second, *terumos u'ma'asros*: if the workers are *amei ha'aretz* who purchase fruit from which tithes have not been properly separated, and the employer's money is what funded that purchase. Third, *yayin nesech*: if the workers are non-Jews and they purchase *yayin nesech* with the employer's funds.

### Rashi's Read

The question, as Rashi frames it, is not primarily about *lifnei iver* — not merely whether the employer is enabling others to sin by providing funds that might be spent on prohibited goods. The concern is sharper: is it as though the employer himself has *fed* his workers those prohibited foods? The *gemara* in *Sukkot* is cited by Rashi: one may not give *d'mei peiros shevi'it* — money in the place of *shevi'it* produce — to an *am ha'aretz* beyond what is needed for three meals, because he will not observe the laws of *shevi'it*. And with respect to *terumos u'ma'asros*, Rashi notes explicitly: since these workers are *amei ha'aretz* who will buy *eino me'ushar*, the employer is, on this framing, effectively feeding them untithed produce. Similarly for *yayin nesech*: since the employer has a legal obligation to provide his workers with meals, if we view his money as having directly purchased the food they ate, he has satisfied that financial obligation with *yayin nesech* and thereby derived benefit from it.

### Separate Transaction

The *gemara* answers that in the straightforward case — the employer gives the workers money in advance, and they go and make their own purchases — the employer bears no responsibility. The workers' choices are their own. We do not re-frame the transaction as the employer having purchased and fed them that food. Since the employer did not designate which specific goods the money would buy, the employer's funds are simply fungible money, and any subsequent purchase is a separate transaction initiated by the workers themselves.

### I Will Pay

However, the second case is different. If the employer says to his workers: *tze'u ve-ichlu va-ani pore'ah* — go out and eat, and I will pay the bill — then the employer *is* the one directly paying for whatever food they consume. In that case he is concerned about *shevi'it*, *ma'aser*, and *yayin nesech*, because he is now directly funding a specific food transaction, and we do treat it as though he fed them that food.

---

## Running Tab

### Chisda's View

Rav Chisda introduces a refinement. The distinction between the permissible and problematic case is not simply whether the employer said "here is the money" versus "go eat and I will pay." Rather, it turns on whether the storekeeper has a regular credit relationship with the employer (*chanvani ha-makifo*). If the storekeeper habitually extends credit to this employer, then the moment the storekeeper gives the workers their food, the employer becomes immediately obligated in the money to the storekeeper — *dimishtabed lei*. The debt is created instantaneously, not after a bill is rendered. In that case, it is as though the employer paid at the moment the food was given, and we regard him as having purchased and fed them that food.

### No Tab

By contrast, if there is no such ongoing credit relationship between this employer and this storekeeper, the bill merely comes later as a separate act, and the transaction is not regarded as having been direct on the employer's part.

### Raba's Resolution

Raba, however, rejects Rav Chisda's distinction. Whether or not there is a running-tab relationship, the employer always owes the storekeeper money once the storekeeper has given food to his workers at his direction. As the *gemara* demonstrates from a ruling elsewhere: if one says to another, *tein maneh li-ploni veyiknu kol nechasai lach* — give a hundred *zuz* to so-and-so and my entire estate shall transfer to you — this works as a valid transaction, on the logic that payment made on one's behalf is as if one received it directly. So too here: when the storekeeper gives food to the workers on the employer's behalf, it is as if the employer himself received the food and gave it to them, and he simultaneously becomes obligated to pay the storekeeper. This obligation exists regardless of whether there is a running tab.

### Outstanding Debt

Raba therefore rules that the distinction has nothing to do with the nature of the credit relationship. What matters is something different entirely: whether a specific sum of money has been pre-identified or designated. If the employer has not pre-designated a particular *dinar* or specific funds as the payment for this food, then what exists is simply an *outstanding debt* — an unspecified obligation to pay whatever the bill comes to, with no particular money identified as the consideration. An outstanding debt, where no specific object or amount has been earmarked, does not function like a simultaneous exchange. It is merely a financial obligation to be discharged later, and it does not render the employer's position equivalent to that of someone who directly purchased and distributed the food.

---

## Running Tab (II)

### Pre-payment Problem

The only case in which the employer would truly be regarded as having directly fed his workers the prohibited food is if he had pre-paid the storekeeper — given him specific funds in advance — and the storekeeper then distributed food to the workers out of those pre-paid funds. In that scenario, the prohibited food was directly purchased with money the employer already handed over, and there is no gap or separation between the employer's payment and the workers' receipt of the food.

### Text Reconciliation

The *braisa* that presents the problematic case — *tze'u ve-ichlu va-ani pore'ah* — must therefore be understood as describing either this pre-payment scenario, or the case in which the employer physically took the food from the storekeeper and handed it directly to the workers. The phrase *va-ani pore'ah* on this reading is reconciled by Rav Ashi as *kegon she-natal ve-natan be-yad* — the employer received the food from the storekeeper and placed it in the workers' hands himself. The language is somewhat strained, and the *gemara* acknowledges the difficulty — other *amoraim* proposed emending the text of the *braisa* to read *va-ani mchashev* (I will settle the account) or *telu ve-ichlu* (take it and eat) — but the underlying principle is clear: the employer is liable only if the money or the prohibited food was directly in his hands at the moment of the transfer.

---

## Practical Result

### Oranges Applied

This ruling now feeds directly back into the case of Rav Yanai's workers and the *shevi'it* oranges. When the fruit borrowed during *shemittah* was repaid in the eighth year, the repayment was simply the discharge of an outstanding debt. There was no pre-designated sum or specific object identified at the time of the original loan as the consideration. The original *shevi'it* fruit had long since been consumed; nothing was present at the moment of repayment to which the *kedushah* could transfer. The repaid fruit is therefore ordinary produce, free of *kedushat shevi'it*.

### Direct Principle

The broader principle is now in sharp relief: a transaction implicates an employer — or gives a prohibited status to money or produce — only when the money or the specific object is identified and present at the moment of the prohibited transfer. Where the connection between payment and prohibited item is established only after the fact, through the discharge of an outstanding and unspecified obligation, the two acts are treated as separate, and no status transfers between them.

---

## Breaking Barrels

### Breaking Q

The *gemara* closes the daf with a brief but pointed question. Rav Nachman, Ulla, Avimi bar Pappa, and Rav Chiya bar Ami were sitting together when they raised the following: if someone is hired to break barrels that had contained *yayin nesech* — not to transport the wine or work with it in any way, but simply to smash the empty barrels afterward — what is the *halacha*? Is this considered *mishtaker be'issurei hana'ah*, being paid for work in connection with a forbidden item?

The question has a slightly paradoxical edge: one might say that the worker *wants* the barrels to persist until his task begins, since without them there is no work and no pay. In that sense, he has a vested interest in the continued existence of objects associated with *yayin nesech* — similar to the perverse logic of someone who would want their *chametz* to remain a bit longer so they can enjoy the *mitzvah* of burning it. Does this interest in the barrel's persistence constitute a forbidden connection to the prohibited item?

### Nachman Ruling

Rav Nachman answers with characteristic brevity and warmth: *yishbor ve-tavo alav berachah* — let him break them and be blessed. His work is part of the process of eliminating and destroying objects associated with *yayin nesech*. We do not apply the strictures of *mishtaker be'issurei hana'ah* to someone whose labor contributes to the removal of the prohibited item from the world. The *gemara* will continue from this point in the following session.

---

---

# Avodah Zarah 64

*This shiur is dedicated to the memory of Rabbi Ozer Glickman of Yeshiva University, who passed away suddenly and unexpectedly. He was a tremendous inspiration to many. יהי זכרו ברוך.*

---

## Framework & Setup

### Opening

We begin at the bottom of 63b in order to pick up the sugyot that carry us through 64a–b. The material continues the masechet's sustained examination of *yayin nesech* and the complex halachic landscape governing interactions among *Yisrael*, *ger toshav*, and *oved kochavim*.

### Three Discussions

The passage opens with a gathering of rabbis — Rav Nachman, Ulla, and Avimi bar Pappa, joined by Rabbi Chiya bar Ami — who convene to address a series of questions arising at the intersection of these three categories. We encounter three such gatherings in succession, each structured around a distinct halachic scenario. The Gemara will revisit this sitting repeatedly, and in each instance it is Rav Nachman who emerges as the decisor.

### Gemara Structure

The Gemara's repeated use of the word *yativ* — "they were sitting" — is notable as a structural feature. Normally, when a second *yativ* appears naming an additional figure, it signals the arrival of a decision-maker. Here, however, the decisions in all three discussions belong to Rav Nachman, who was already present at the outset. The repetition of *yativ* thus serves to mark the transition from one distinct question to the next, rather than to introduce a new authority.

---

## Breaking Barrels

### Problem Setup

The first case: a non-Jew hires a Jew to break barrels of *yayin nesech* — real *avodah zarah* wine. On its face, this seems like straightforward prohibited benefit: the Jew is being employed in work that involves *yayin nesech*, and he stands to receive wages from it. But the scenario introduces a complication. The Jew's very livelihood in this case depends on those barrels remaining intact long enough for him to break them. He has a financial interest, in other words, in the preservation — *kiyum* — of the *yayin nesech*.

### Two Approaches

The Gemara frames the question as follows: *mi amrinan kevan d'rotze b'kiyumo assur* — since the Jew desires the preservation of these barrels (so he can be paid to break them), is his wage thereby forbidden? Or, *o dilma kol lemayutei tifla shapir dami* — can we reason that since the ultimate act reduces the *tifla*, the impropriety, the existence of *yayin nesech* in the world, the arrangement is permitted?

### Rav Nachman's Ruling

Rav Nachman rules: *yishbor vetavo alav beracha* — let him break the barrels, and may he be blessed for it. The Gemara then seeks a *beraita* to support this ruling, and the support comes from an unexpected direction — the laws of *kilayim*.

The *beraita* states: *ein odrim im oved kochavim bekilayim* — one may not hoe or till a field together with a non-Jew when that field contains *kilayim*. However, continues the *beraita*, at the top of 64a: *aval okrim imo kedei lemi'utei hatiflah* — one may uproot together with him, since the purpose is to reduce the impropriety. The parallel to the barrel-breaking case is clear: just as uprooting *kilayim* reduces something forbidden even though the worker temporarily benefits from its existence, so too breaking barrels of *yayin nesech* is permitted as an act of diminishing *tifla*.

### Kilayim Analysis

The Gemara pauses to identify whose opinion the *beraita* reflects. *Sevaruha ha meni Rabbi Akiva hi* — they initially assumed this follows Rabbi Akiva, who rules that *hamekayem bekilayim lokeh* — one who merely maintains *kilayim*, without even sowing or tilling, is liable to lashes.

This ruling of Rabbi Akiva requires its own exegetical foundation. The Torah in Vayikra 19:19 reads: *et chukotai tishmoru behemat'cha lo tarbia kilayim sadecha lo tizra kilayim uveged kilayim shatnez lo yaaleh alecha*. The plain reading offers three distinct prohibitions: forbidden crossbreeding of animals, forbidden sowing of mixed seeds, and the prohibition of *shatnez*. But Rabbi Akiva reads the verse with a different division: *behemat'cha lo tarbia* — [pause] — *kilayim sadecha lo* — and then *tizra kilayim*. By detaching the word *kilayim* from the animal prohibition and attaching it to the field prohibition, Rabbi Akiva derives an additional restriction: not merely *zorea* (sowing) is forbidden, but *kilayim sadecha lo* — any act of benefiting the *kilayim* field at all.

This is an elegant piece of midrash. It is worth pausing on the word *kilayim* itself. The root *keleh* means prison. As Rav Hirsch notes, the concept captures the idea that certain things imprison one another — when placed together, they deny each other full expression or growth. Whether applied to animal crossbreeding, mixed seeds, or *shatnez* (wool and linen, representing the animal and plant kingdoms respectively), the prohibition captures a spiritual incompatibility, a confinement that results from forced combination.

The *beraita* further specifies: *hamenakesh vehamachape bekilayim lokeh* — one who weeds to promote growth or covers the seeds of *kilayim* is liable. From this Rabbi Akiva extends the prohibition to *hamekayem*, one who supports or maintains the *kilayim* without directly interacting with the soil — for instance, by building a fence around the field.

Now the Gemara raises a difficulty. If this *beraita* reflects Rabbi Akiva's view — that even *kiyum* of *kilayim* is forbidden and punishable — then permitting the worker to temporarily maintain the field for the purpose of getting paid to uproot it seems to contradict Rabbi Akiva rather than reflect him. The Gemara registers this tension.

### Free vs. Paid

The Gemara resolves the difficulty by reframing the case entirely: *hacha bemai askinan? kegon dik'avid chinam* — what are we actually discussing here? A case where the uprooting was performed without any payment at all. And this, the Gemara says, is the view of Rav Yehuda, who holds that *liten lahem matnat chinam assur* — it is forbidden to give a free gift to a non-Jew.

On this reading, the *beraita* is not about someone being paid to uproot *kilayim*. It is about someone who uproots *kilayim* from a non-Jew's field as a *matnat chinam*, for free. Despite the prohibition on giving free benefit to a non-Jew, this gratuitous uprooting is permitted — because it reduces something forbidden.

### Reducing Issur

From Rav Yehuda's ruling, the Gemara derives a broader principle applicable also to Rabbi Akiva: *lechalot issur muttar* — to diminish or eliminate a forbidden thing is permitted. The Gemara states this with elegant economy: does not Rav Yehuda say it is forbidden to give a free gift to a non-Jew? — *aval lemi'utei tifla shapir dami* — and yet, to reduce an impropriety is permitted. *Lerabbi Akiva nami* — the same logic applies to Rabbi Akiva: even though he rules that *hamekayem bekilayim lokeh*, the act of *lemi'utei tifla* remains permitted. *Vetu lo midei* — and there is nothing more to be said.

---

## Avodat Kochavim Money

### Question Posed

The same rabbis reconvene — *hador yatvei vekamibayei lehu* — and a second question is placed before them. *Dmei avodat kochavim beyad oved kochavim mahu* — what is the status of money that a non-Jew has received as proceeds from the sale of an object of idol worship? May a Jew accept such money, for instance, in a commercial transaction?

### Rav Nachman Permits

Rav Nachman rules, *mistabra dmei avodat kochavim beyad oved kochavim mutarin* — it seems that such money, in the hands of the non-Jew, is permitted.

### Conversion Case

The Gemara adduces a case as apparent support: a group of non-Jews came before Rabba bar Avuha seeking to convert. He told them: *zilu zevinu kol mah de'it lechu vetu itgayeru* — go, sell everything you have, and then come and convert. The implication is that they could sell their idolatrous objects, receive money for them, and then enter the Jewish people with those funds — suggesting that *dmei avodat kochavim beyad oved kochavim* is indeed permitted.

But the Gemara immediately questions whether this constitutes a genuine proof. *Vedilma shani hatam dekeivan deda'ateih le'igyurei vadai batla* — perhaps that case is different, because since their intention was to convert, the status of the *avodat kochavim* was clearly already annulled in their minds before the sale took place. The money they received would thus not be *dmei avodat kochavim* in the ordinary sense. The story of Rabba bar Avuha, therefore, cannot serve as a clean proof for Rav Nachman's general ruling.

### Creditor Proof

The Gemara therefore looks elsewhere: *ela me'ha* — rather, from this case. A Jew was a creditor to a non-Jew for one hundred *dinar*. The non-Jew, in order to repay the debt, sold his *avodat kochavim* and brought the proceeds to the Jew — or sold his *yayin nesech* and brought the proceeds. In such a case, the Gemara rules: *mutar* — permitted. However, if the non-Jew said to the Jew: *hamten li ad she'emkor avodat kochavim ve'avi lecha* — wait for me while I go sell my idolatrous object and then bring you the money — that is forbidden.

### Timing Analysis

### Rav Sheshet

The Gemara asks: *mai shna reisha u'mai shna seifa?* — what is the difference between the first scenario and the second? Rav Sheshet explains: *seifa mishum dehava leh kerotzeh bekiyumo* — in the second case, where the non-Jew has told the Jew to wait while he sells the *avodat kochavim*, the Jew now has an active interest in the preservation of the idolatrous object. He wants it to remain intact, unharmed, unsold to anyone else, because his repayment depends on it. This is precisely the concern — *rotzeh bekiyumo* — that renders the arrangement forbidden. In the first case, the Jew receives payment without any such awareness or investment in the source of funds, and the money is therefore permitted.

---

## Inheritance Division

### Inheritance Scenario

The rabbis convene a third time. The case before them: a convert and his brother, an idol worshiper, are inheriting from their father who was a non-Jew. The estate includes objects of *avodah zarah*, *yayin nesech*, and ordinary property. The Gemara presents this scenario without any apparent surprise — such mixed families evidently existed, and the Talmud addresses their legal reality directly.

### Division Proposal

The convert proposes a division: *tol ata avodah zarah va'ani maot, tol ata yayin nesech va'ani perot* — you take the idolatrous objects, I'll take the money; you take the *yayin nesech*, I'll take the produce. On its surface this seems workable: each brother receives his share of the estate, and the *ger* avoids taking possession of prohibited items.

### Possession Problem

The Gemara identifies the problem: *im misheba'u lerashut hager assur* — if the prohibited items have already come into the *ger*'s possession, the arrangement is forbidden. Once the *ger* technically acquires the estate jointly with his brother, he has a stake in the *avodah zarah* and *yayin nesech*, and he has an interest in their preservation as the mechanism by which his brother will receive his share and the *ger* will receive his own. The concern of *rotzeh bekiyumo* applies here as well.

### Shards Limitation

Rav Bar Ula limits the scope of the ruling: *matnitin baavodah zarah hamithaleket lefi shevareha* — this ruling applies specifically to idolatrous objects that can be divided according to their shards or component pieces. If the *avodah zarah* is made of gold, for example, then breaking it apart creates valuable pieces that can be distributed. In such a case, even a fragmented object retains its worth, and the division is meaningful.

### Wine & Shards

The Gemara then asks about *yayin nesech*: how does the concept of division by shards apply to wine? One might think liquid cannot be divided by breaking. But the Gemara recalls the case of *cheres Adriani* — the distinctive clay vessels discussed earlier in the masechet, which were not fully fired and were soaked in wine during manufacture. The broken shards of such a vessel, when soaked in water, would release a concentrated wine essence, rendering them of significant value. Thus even *yayin nesech*, in the form of *cheres Adriani*, can have value in shards — and the *ger*'s desire for his own portion might cause him to want those shards preserved.

### Rav Papa's Leniency

This raises the question anew: does not the *ger* have an interest in the preservation of the idolatrous estate, given that his own inheritance depends on his brother receiving it? Rav Papa addresses this: *shani yerushat hager deakilu bah rabanan gezeirah shema yakhzor lekilkulo* — the inheritance of the *ger* is a different matter, because the Rabbis were lenient in this domain out of concern that if the *ger* is denied his inheritance, he might return to his former ways. The potential for *kibbul kilkulo* — his spiritual backsliding — justifies a leniency that would not otherwise apply.

### Inheritance vs. Partners…

A *baraita* at the top of 64b confirms and sharpens the ruling: *bamedebarim amurim sheyerashu aval nishtatefu assur* — these leniencies apply only when the *ger* and the *oved kochavim* are heirs; if they are business partners, it is forbidden. The distinction is clear: a halachic inheritance relationship carries leniencies that a commercial partnership does not. A Jew may be a business partner with a non-Jew, but not in a venture that involves deriving benefit from *avodah zarah*.

---

## Ger Toshav Annulment

### Ger Toshav Question

The third question posed in this series: *Ger Toshav mahu sheyevatel avodat kochavim?* — can a *ger toshav* annul the status of an object of idol worship? The question sits against the background of an earlier discussion involving Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan about whether a Jew can ever annul *avodah zarah* — and the elaborate concern about a Jew finding such an object in the marketplace, acquiring it through *kinyan*, and thereafter being unable to remove its prohibited status. The *ger toshav* occupies an intermediate category, and his ability to perform *bitul* is genuinely uncertain.

### Worship Principle

Rav Nachman articulates the operative principle: *dephalach mevatel delo phalach lo mevatel* — one who worships an idol can annul it; one who does not worship cannot. The question is then where the *ger toshav* falls. One might argue that since he does not actually worship idols — that is his defining characteristic — he lacks the capacity to annul. Alternatively, one might argue: *kol deminei mevatel vehai bar minei hu* — anyone who belongs to the same general category of idol-worshiping nations can annul, and perhaps the *ger toshav* counts as *bar minei*, of the same kind, even if he personally abstains.

### Marketplace Challenge

A challenge is raised from a *baraita*: if a Jew finds an object of idolatry in the marketplace, as long as it has not yet come into his possession, he may ask a non-Jew to annul its status, and it becomes permissible for him to take it. Once it has come into his possession, however, he may no longer do so, because *oved kochavim mevatel avodat kochavim shelo veshel chaveiro* — a non-Jew can annul the idolatrous status of his own object or that of his fellow — and the phrase continues: *bein ovdah uvein she'eino ovdah* — whether he worships it or does not worship it.

### Friend's Idolatry

The phrase *shel chaveiro* — of his fellow — raises its own question: who is this *chaveiro* whose *avodah zarah* the non-Jew can annul? The *baraita*'s language suggests that a non-Jew can cancel the idolatrous status of an object that was not his own. This was discussed in earlier passages as well: a Jew who encounters *avodah zarah* in the street can, before taking possession, request a non-Jew — not necessarily the original worshiper — to annul it, after which the object may be handled freely. The spiritual danger, whatever its precise nature, is thereby neutralized.

### Debate on Terms

The more pressing interpretive question concerns the clause *bein ovdah uvein she'eino ovdah* — between one who worships it and one who does not. This could be understood as referring to the same non-Jewish individual: whether he personally worships this particular idol or does not, he can still annul. Or it might be read as distinguishing between a full *oved kochavim* (*ovdah*) and a *ger toshav* (*she'eino ovdah*), thereby implying that the *ger toshav* too has the capacity for *bitul*. If so, the *baraita* would constitute a challenge to Rav Nachman's principle.

### Non-Jew Interpretation

The Gemara rejects the reading that would include the *ger toshav*: *le'olam eima lach idi ve'idi oved kochavim* — in all cases, both terms refer to the *oved kochavim*, the non-Jew proper. As for the distinction between *ovdah* and *she'eino ovdah*, the Gemara explains it through two sub-cases. *Reisha* — the first case — refers to *zeh vezeh lePe'or, zeh vezeh leMarkulis*: both the owner and the fellow worship the same deity, whether Pe'or or Markulis. *Seifa* — the second case — refers to *zeh lePe'or vezeh leMarkulis*: the one who annuls worships a different deity than the one associated with the object. Even so, the annulment is valid. The point is entirely about non-Jews of varying cultic affiliations — the *ger toshav* does not enter the picture.

---

## Ger Toshav Definition

### Multiple Opinions

Having determined that the *ger toshav* cannot annul *avodah zarah*, the Gemara steps back to define who the *ger toshav* actually is. The *baraita* presents a *machloket* among *tanna'im*, and the range of opinions reflects genuine disagreement about the legal and theological status of this category.

### Rabbi Meir's View

Rabbi Meir defines a *ger toshav* as *kol shekibel alav bifnei shelosha chaverim shelo la'avod avodat kochavim* — anyone who accepted upon himself, in front of three *chaverim* (a quasi-judicial body of punctilious observers), that he will not engage in *avodah zarah*. This is a formal, public commitment, analogous in structure to other acts of legal acceptance before a *beis din*.

### Chachamim's View

The *chachamim* offer a different criterion: *kol shekibel alav sheva mitzvot shekiblu aleihem bnei Noach* — anyone who accepted upon himself the seven *mitzvot* of the *bnei Noach*. This immediately raises a question: if the *ger toshav* is defined simply by his acceptance of the seven Noahide laws, why is he called a *ger toshav* rather than a *ben Noach*? The distinction must lie elsewhere — the *ger toshav* presumably does more than the ordinary *ben Noach*, even on the view of *chachamim*.

### Third Opinion

A third view (*acheirim omrim*) holds that the first two opinions do not describe a *ger toshav* at all. The true *ger toshav* is: *zeh ger ochel nevelot shekibel alav lekayem kol mitzvot ha'amurot baTorah chutz mi'issur nevelot* — one who accepted upon himself to observe all the *mitzvot* stated in the Torah, with one exception: the prohibition of *nevelot*, the requirement that meat be slaughtered according to halachic law. He is, in other words, nearly fully observant, living among Jews (*toshav* — a resident, not a transient), and distinguished only by this single leniency for himself.

One might ask: does this not create other complications? If the *ger toshav* observes all Torah law, including *Shabbat*, that raises a well-known concern derived elsewhere in the Talmud that a non-Jew who observes *Shabbat* is liable for a capital offense. The Gemara does not resolve this tension here, but the question merits attention.

### Wine & Oil

The *baraita* continues to define the practical parameters of the *ger toshav*'s status: *miyachadim etzlo yayin ve'ein mafkidim etzlo yayin* — we may leave wine with him briefly and unsupervised, but we may not entrust wine to him for extended safekeeping. The distinction between *yichud* (a brief, supervised deposit) and *hafkada* (a longer-term entrusting) reflects a calibrated level of trust. We do not suspect the *ger toshav* of actively mixing the wine with *yayin nesech*, but we worry that over time, inattention might lead him to mix it with his own wine, about which he is less careful. Even in a city with a Jewish majority, the brief deposit is permitted; even in a city with a non-Jewish majority, it is permitted. But the long-term deposit is forbidden in either circumstance.

*Shamno keyeino* — his oil is treated like his wine for these purposes: benefit (*hana'ah*) is permitted, but drinking (*shtiyah*) is forbidden.

### Wine Dispute

The Gemara immediately challenges the formulation: *shemen mi ka havi yayin nesech?* — can oil even become *yayin nesech*? The categories are being conflated. The Gemara corrects the formulation: it is not that his oil is like his wine, but that *yeino keshamno* — his wine is treated like his oil. That is, the wine of the *ger toshav* is permitted for *hana'ah* but forbidden for drinking, just as his oil would be.

Rabban Shimon, however, goes further: *yeino yayin nesech* — the wine of the *ger toshav* is full *yayin nesech*. His reasoning reflects a conservative concern: the *ger toshav* is not scrupulous enough for us to trust his wine at any level. Like a vegan restaurant that theoretically keeps no meat on the premises but may not have checked every ingredient — one simply avoids the uncertainty altogether. And at the other end of the spectrum, there is an opinion that holds *mutar bishtiyah* — the wine of the *ger toshav* is even permitted for drinking. He has committed formally, before a *beis din*, to full observance; there is no more reason to doubt his wine than the wine of a Jew.

### Like Oved Kochavim

Having surveyed these views, the Gemara returns to the original question. The *baraita* concludes: *velish'ar kol davar harey hu ke'oved kochavim* — for all other matters, the *ger toshav* is treated like an *oved kochavim*. The Gemara asks: *lemai hilchata?* — with regard to what specific halacha? Perhaps the intent is that he is like an *oved kochavim* for the purpose of annulling *avodah zarah* — which would contradict the ruling of Rav Nachman that he cannot annul.

### Reshut Rules

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves this: *lo, litten reshut u'levatel reshut* — no, the comparison to *oved kochavim* is limited to the laws of *reshut*, the domain rules that govern the creation of an *eruv* on *Shabbat*. The relevant *baraita* is cited: a Jewish *mumar* (apostate) who still observes *Shabbat* publicly can relinquish his domain rights for the purpose of establishing a shared *eruv*; one who does not observe *Shabbat* publicly cannot. The principle is that only a Jew — *noten reshut umevatel reshut* — can formally cede domain rights to enable a common *eruv*. A non-Jew cannot do this; he can only lease his domain to a Jew. How then does the *ger toshav* function? *Uve'oved kochavim ad sheyiskor* — for a non-Jew, the *reshut* must be acquired through a lease. The *ger toshav* falls into this same category for *eruv* purposes: despite his elevated status in many respects, he cannot participate in the domain-cession that only Jews may perform.

### Final Status

The conclusion of the discussion: the *ger toshav* cannot annul *avodah zarah*. His resemblance to an *oved kochavim* is limited to the specific domain of *reshut* and *eruv*. With respect to idol worship, Rav Nachman's principle holds: *dephalach mevatel delo phalach lo mevatel* — the one who worships can annul; the one who does not worship cannot. The *ger toshav*, who has formally committed to abstaining from *avodah zarah*, does not worship it, and therefore cannot annul it.

---

---

# Avodah Zarah 65

## Ger Toshav Status

### Opening Context

Today's *daf* is 65, and we pick up at the last line of 64b. The *Gemara* has been in the middle of a larger discussion — something of a return to unfinished business from the previous *perek* — concerning whether a *nokhri* can be *mevatel* *avodah zarah* that he himself does not worship. The *Gemara* had established that a person can be *mevatel* the *avodah zarah* of a god he does not personally follow; a Zeus-worshipper, for instance, can be *mevatel* Aphrodite's idol. But what of someone who is not an *oved avodah zarah* altogether? That question led into a broader discussion about who qualifies as a *ger toshav* — and what the relevant threshold is.

The categories under consideration represent a spectrum of standards. At one end is the minimal standard of simply not being an *oved avodah zarah*; at another is accepting the *sheva mitzvot bnei noakh*; and at yet another, more demanding end, is a position requiring observance of virtually all *mitzvot* save *nevelah*. The practical stakes of this classification are not merely theoretical. One central question is the obligation of *mitzvah le-hayoto* — the positive communal obligation to sustain and care for such a person. Another, immediately relevant to this *masekhet*, is whether such a person renders wine forbidden as *stam yeinam* by touching it.

### Formal Status Question

The *Gemara* poses the question sharply: must a non-Jew formally belong to the category of *ger toshav* in order for certain *halakhot* of *avodah zarah* to apply — or not apply — to him, or is it sufficient that he simply does not, in practice, engage in *avodah zarah*? This is the question the *Gemara* proceeds to address through a pair of stories.

It is worth recalling how *Tosafot* enters this discussion. *Tosafot* notes that there are Christians who are not *ovdei avodah zarah* — whatever *Tosafot* understood about the nature of Christian practice, or at minimum that they do not use wine in their *avodah zarah* worship outside of the specific act of communion and transubstantiation. On this basis, *Tosafot* reasons that their wine would not be *assur be-hana'ah* in the manner of true *yayin nesekh*, since it lacks the idolatrous dimension. It would, however, remain *assur be-shtiah* due to concerns of *benotayhem* — the intermarriage-related prohibitions. As the *Gemara* concluded at the end of the previous *daf*, their wine is comparable to their oil: the prohibition on oil, bread, and similar foods was never about *avodah zarah* but about social barriers against intermarriage. Accordingly, once someone falls into the *ger toshav* category, the *avodah zarah* concerns about wine are removed, but the intermarriage-based concern remains, so one may derive *hana'ah* from the wine but may not drink it.

### Avidrana Gift Story

With this framework in mind, the *Gemara* now presents the last line of 64b. Rav Yehuda sent a gift — the word used is *korbana*, a term with strongly sacrificial, religious overtones, which makes its deployment here particularly striking — to Avidrana on his pagan holiday. This raises an immediate question from the very first *mishna* of *Avodah Zarah*: is one not forbidden to conduct business with an *oved avodah zarah* on his *yom eida*?

The answer implied by the story is telling. Rav Yehuda apparently knew that Avidrana personally did not participate in the religious dimension of the holiday — he was not a genuine *oved avodah zarah*. The word *korbana* for gift is therefore suggestive: everyone else may have been sending gifts in a religious context, as a kind of cultic offering associated with the holiday, yet it was still permitted here because this specific individual was not participating religiously. Two aspects of this are worth emphasizing. First, it is striking that Rav Yehuda permitted this even on the day itself, when the surrounding cultural activity had a religious character. Second, and crucially, it is not stated that Avidrana was a *ger toshav* in any formal sense — he had not formally accepted the *sheva mitzvot bnei noakh* before a *beit din*. It was enough, for this purpose, that *lema'aseh* he did not worship *avodah zarah*.

### Rav Yosef Challenge

Rav Yosef challenges this reasoning. *Ve-hatanya*: who is a *ger toshav*? *Kol she-kibel alav bifnei gimel chaverim shelo la'avod avodah zarah* — anyone who formally accepted, before three *chaverim*, not to worship *avodah zarah*. Even if someone does not *lema'aseh* worship *avodah zarah*, and even if he observes the *sheva mitzvot*, the *halakhic* status requires a formal act of acceptance. Personal practice, in Rav Yosef's view, is insufficient.

### Status vs. Practice

The *Gemara* resolves this tension with a crucial distinction: *ki tanya hi le-hayoto*. The requirement of formal *ger toshav* status — the acceptance before three *chaverim* — applies specifically to the obligation of *le-hayoto*, the positive communal duty to sustain and care for the person. But for the *de-rabbanan* concerns of *avodah zarah* — such as the question of *yom eidam* — there is no requirement of formal status change. For those purposes, it is sufficient to assess the person's actual practice on a case-by-case basis.

This is a genuinely important distinction that goes to the heart of how *halakha* categorizes people. Not every *halakhic* consequence requires a formal personal status transformation. It may be enough to know that this individual does not worship *avodah zarah* in order to do business with him on his holiday. But for the more substantial social-communal implications — the positive obligation of care — a formal change of status is required.

### Religious Communities

Where does wine fall along this spectrum? The previous *daf* situated the question of wine squarely in the *ger toshav* discussion, suggesting that wine requires formal status change rather than individual practice. But *Tosafot* was working with a different model: not an individual's personal practice, but the practice of an entire religious community. All Christians — in *Tosafot*'s understanding — do not use wine in *avodah zarah* worship. That communal-level fact may occupy a middle position between individual practice (relevant for *yom eidam* questions) and formal individual acceptance of *ger toshav* status (required for *le-hayoto*).

A similar analysis applies to Muslims. The *Rambam* states that Muslims are like *gerei toshav* — since Islam entirely rejects *avodah zarah*, including all images, Muslims fall into the *ger toshav* category with respect to wine: one may derive *hana'ah* from their wine, though one may not drink it due to intermarriage concerns. The *Rambam* does not go so far as to say Muslims are formal *gerei toshav* for purposes of *le-hayoto*, but for the specific issue of wine, the entire religious community's non-idolatrous character is sufficient.

### Three Categories

This analysis yields three distinct categories. First, there is the individual who personally refrains from *avodah zarah* even while surrounded by a pagan community — a case with limited *halakhic* applicability, perhaps sufficient only for the *yom eidam* question. Second, there is the person who formally accepts *ger toshav* status before a *beit din* — this is sufficient for everything, including *le-hayoto*. Third, there is an entire religious people or community that, as a collective, is not *oved avodah zarah* — this intermediate category may be sufficient for questions like wine even without formal individual acceptance. Different *halakhot* shift depending on where a person or group is situated along this continuum.

## Lehachayoto Obligation

### Circumcision Requirement

The *Gemara* now cites a statement of Rabbah bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: a *ger toshav* who did not undergo *bris milah* within twelve months is treated as if he were a non-Jewish apostate — a remarkably harsh formulation that does not appear elsewhere in the *halakhic* literature and is not quoted as authoritative in the *poskim*. The implication of this statement is striking: it seems to suggest that *ger toshav* status is inherently transitional, a way-station between leaving *avodah zarah* and becoming a full Jew. If he has not converted within a year, his *ger toshav* standing is effectively forfeit.

### Conversion Intent

The *Gemara* immediately limits this ruling. *Hasam kegon she-kibel alav lamul ve-lo mal* — this applies specifically to a case where the person had explicitly committed to undergoing *milah* and then failed to follow through. In that case, if after a year he still has not done it, one gives up on him. But someone who inhabits the *ger toshav* status as a permanent condition — without ever having expressed an intention to convert — is not subject to this harsh characterization. He can comfortably remain a *ger toshav* indefinitely without any implication of blame for not completing conversion to Judaism.

## Rava & Bar Sheishach

### Gift on Holiday

The *Gemara* now presents: *Rava amti lei korbana le-Bar Sheishach beyom eida*. Rava presented a gift — again, *korbana*, the same suggestive term — to Bar Sheishach on a pagan holiday. Rava's justification: *yadana beih d'la palach l'avodat kochavim* — I know personally that he does not worship *avodah zarah*. This story thus reinforces the previous discussion: one need not establish formal *ger toshav* status in order for certain *avodah zarah* concerns to be set aside. Personal knowledge of this individual's non-idolatrous practice is sufficient for the purpose of giving a gift on *yom eidam*.

One might observe that the *Gemara* may also intend this story to make a further point: the fact that a person is morally problematic in other respects does not affect the narrow *halakhic* question. The approval of a non-Jew for purposes of *yom eidam* is not a general moral endorsement. This distinction becomes vivid immediately.

### Bar Sheishach Challenge

When Rava subsequently came upon Bar Sheishach, he found him *dyatib atzvarei be-varda* — seated amid rose petals — *ve-kaiman zonot arumot kameyh* — with naked prostitutes arranged before him. Bar Sheishach turned to Rava and asked: *it l'chu ki hai gavna l'alma d'atei*? Do you have anything like this in your *Olam Ha-ba*?

### Rava's Response

Rava replied: *didan adifa tfei mehai* — ours is better than this. Bar Sheishach pressed: *tfei mehai mi hava*? What could possibly surpass this? Rava answered: *atun ika l'chu eimta d'malchuta* — you live under subjugation to your king. *Anan lo havya lan eimta d'malchuta* — in our *Olam Ha-ba* we will not be subject to any human sovereign; we will stand directly before God. Of course, one might note that this response does not directly challenge the premise that *Olam Ha-ba* consists of physical sensory pleasure — it sidesteps that premise rather than refuting it, perhaps because Bar Sheishach could not have appreciated a response framed in purely spiritual terms.

Bar Sheishach then retorted: *ana mi it li eimta d'malchuta*? — I am so wealthy and powerful that I have nothing to fear from the king.

### King's Messenger

*Ad yatib* — while they were still sitting together — *ata hu pristaka d'malka* — a messenger arrived from the king. *Kum k'ba'i lach malka* — arise, the king requires you. The timing was perfect: Rava's point was proven on the spot.

### Blessing & Blinded Eye

As Bar Sheishach was rushing out, he said to Rava: *eina d'ba'i l'michzei l'chu bishuta tipaka* — the eye of anyone who seeks to look evilly upon you Jews should pop out. You Jews — clearly whatever you say, God makes come true. Rava responded: *Amen*. And the eye of Bar Sheishach popped out — presumably because, beneath the apparent blessing, his words carried an edge of envy.

### Alternative Verses

Rav Pappa then suggests that rather than making the argument about subjugation to a human king, Rava should have quoted a verse from *Tehillim*: *bnot melachim be-yikoroteicha, nitzva shegal liminecha be-chetem Ofir* — daughters of kings are among your honored ones, the queen stands at your right hand adorned with the gold of Ofir. This verse, interestingly, seems to play directly into Bar Sheishach's vision of *Olam Ha-ba* as sensory and physical — here they would be women of status and royalty rather than *zonot*, but it is the same basic fantasy, just elevated. Rashi reads *yikoroteicha* as connoting honor, while *Tosafot* offers a different reading.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak then proposes yet another verse: *ayin lo ra'ata Elohim zulatecha ya'aseh le-mechakeh lo* — no eye has seen, O God, other than You, what You will do for those who long for You. This verse entirely reframes the conversation: the nature of *Olam Ha-ba* is beyond all human imagination and sensory comprehension. No analogy to physical pleasure can capture it.

### Ultimate Principle

This concludes the *aggadata*, though its thematic connection to the *masekhet* as a whole is direct: when does a non-Jew exit the category of *oved avodah zarah*, and for which *halakhot*? The high *halakha* of *le-hayoto* requires formal status. The *de-rabbanan* concerns of *yom eidam* require only knowledge of personal practice. The intermediate issue of *yayin nesekh* appears to be more status-based. And as this story vividly illustrates, the narrow *halakhic* determination that one may give a gift to this person on his holiday says nothing whatsoever about general moral approval of the person's behavior.

## Earning from Wine

### Hiring Workers Rule

The *Gemara* now returns to the *Mishnah*. The rule under discussion is: if one hires a worker for general labor and in the course of that broader engagement the worker also handles *stam yeinam* or *yayin nesekh*, this is permitted. The general hire was for general work; the incidental contact with wine is folded into that broader arrangement. This is what the *Mishnah* claims.

### Nightfall Request

A *Tosefta* appears to complicate this, however. *Ha-socher et ha-poel, l'tutei erev, amar lo, hevei chavis shel yayin nesekh mi-makom le-makom* — if one hired a worker and then, toward nightfall, asked him to bring a barrel of *yayin nesekh* from one place to another, *secharo mutar* — his wages are permitted. The implication of the *Tosefta* is that this leniency applies specifically when the request comes at nightfall — after the worker has already effectively earned his day's wages. But during the workday itself, such a request would not be permissible on the worker's wages. This creates tension with the *Mishnah*, which appears to permit it without any such temporal qualification.

### Lump Sum Problem

Abaye resolves the tension by saying that the *Mishnah* too is speaking of the nightfall case — though this is not a natural reading of the text. Rava offers a cleaner resolution. *Lo kashya*: it depends on the payment structure. *Ha d'amar lei ha'aver li me'ah chavis be-me'ah prutos* — if the employer said, "move a hundred barrels for a hundred dollars" as a lump sum — and among those hundred barrels one turned out to be *yayin nesekh* — then *secharo assur*: none of the pay is permissible. Since the worker could not earn any of the lump sum without completing all hundred barrels, the single barrel of *yayin nesekh* is inextricably bound up with the entire payment. Every dollar he earned is, in a sense, connected to the *yayin nesekh*.

*Ha d'amar lei ha'aver li chavis chavis be-pruta* — if, however, the pay was one dollar per barrel — then *secharo mutar*: he keeps ninety-nine dollars and simply declines payment for the one barrel of *yayin nesekh*, saying in effect, "I'll move that one for free." A *beraita* confirms this distinction.

Accordingly, the *Mishnah*'s case of permitting mid-workday involvement with wine is when the worker is being paid per piece — he simply forgoes the unit of pay for the wine barrel. The *Tosefta*'s nightfall case applies to the lump-sum scenario, where the only way to permit it is if it occurs after the day's wages have effectively been earned. Yet even this is not entirely clean: if the pay is a lump sum tied to completing all the barrels, how does moving the wine barrel after hours change matters? *Tosafot* struggles with this and does not fully resolve it, and the *Gemara*'s treatment leaves the *l'tutei erev* question with limited scope.

### Animal Rental

The *Mishnah* continues: *ha-socher et ha-chamor le-havi'o aleha yayin nesekh, secharo assur* — if one rents out his donkey specifically to transport *yayin nesekh*, the rental income is forbidden, even though it is not the owner's personal labor that is being performed. The *Gemara* initially asks whether this is not already obvious from the first clause of the *Mishnah* — why repeat it for the case of the donkey?

In fact, one might have thought the donkey case is a genuine *chiddush*. The first clause involves the owner's personal labor. Here, the owner stays home; he is simply collecting a rental fee while someone else uses his animal. The connection seems far more attenuated. One might have thought that since the owner is not personally involved, and the renter does whatever he wishes with the donkey, the fact that the renter chose to use it for wine should be irrelevant to the owner. Yet the *Mishnah* rules it forbidden. The *Gemara*, however, says this is not actually the surprising case — the end of the *Mishnah* is what requires statement.

It also emerges that the standard model of donkey rental in this period is not like renting a car and staying home. The donkey owner typically comes along as the donkey driver — it is more like a limousine with a driver. This changes the intuition considerably: the owner is personally schlepping the *stam yeinam*, which makes the prohibition far less surprising.

### Donkey Driver Rights

The *Gemara* then asks about the end of the *Mishnah*: *sechara le-yeshev aleha* — if one rents out the donkey for the renter to ride on, as personal transportation, *af al pi she-hinniach oved kochavim legino aleha, secharo mutar* — even if the renter incidentally places his wine flask on the donkey, the owner's fee is permitted. The reason the *Gemara* initially suggests is that putting a wine flask on the donkey was not part of the rental agreement — the renter only paid for the right to ride, not to transport wine. Therefore, the owner is not being paid for anything connected to the wine.

The *Gemara* challenges this by pointing to a rule in *halakha*: one who rents a donkey for the day has the right to place on it his clothes, his wine flask, and his provisions for the trip. This seems to contradict the premise that the flask is outside the rental agreement.

Abaye resolves this: *nehi de-login dinei hu le-ozfei* — yes, it is true that the renter has a right to place his wine flask there — *mi ka amar lei mosif li, mi amar lei, nekhit li agra de-laginato* — but if he does not bring his flask, he gets no reduction in his fare. He does not pay separately for the flask; it is simply an implicit entitlement bundled into the ride. The owner is therefore not being paid for the flask at all. Just as a taxi passenger is not entitled to a discount for not placing luggage in the trunk, even if it would have been permitted — the price is the price. Accordingly, even if the renter does use the flask, the owner's fee is unconnected to it.

The *Gemara* then examines the rule distinguishing between the renter's right to carry a week's worth of provisions and the donkey driver's right to carry only a day's worth. If provisions are available for purchase along the route, the donkey driver could also be expected to buy as he goes, so the restriction to a day's provisions is justified. If provisions are not available, why should the renter have more right than the driver? Rav Pappa resolves this: in practice one can make the effort to seek out provisions at stops along the way, but it is burdensome. The traveler, who is the paying customer, is entitled to avoid that burden and bring everything in advance. The donkey driver, whose job is to handle logistics, is expected to manage his own provisioning along the way.

### Personal vs. Incidental

Abaye's ruling establishes the principle: the wages are for the personal transportation, not for the incidental use of the flask. Even if the flask is *yayin nesekh*, the owner is not earning money from it in any meaningful sense, because his pay would be identical whether or not the flask was there.

### Wine Pouring Story

The *Gemara* now presents a story. The father of the sons of Rav Acha son of Rav Ika — *avuh d'vnei Rav Acha brei d'Rav Ika* — would pour wine into the flasks of non-Jews who came to purchase it, and would then help them cross the river, receiving an empty barrel as his payment for that service. The practice was: the non-Jews would arrive, he would pour the wine from his barrel into their various flasks. Once the wine entered their flasks, it became forbidden — either by contact with residual *yayin nesekh* in the flasks, or simply by virtue of passing into the non-Jew's possession, a question *Tosafot* notes without fully resolving. The barrel was now empty. He would then help them transport the flasks across the river and keep the barrel as his fee.

When people brought this to Abaye's attention, he said: *ki katrach be-heteira katrach* — when he exerted himself, he did so with something that was still *heter*. The act of pouring the wine occurred while the wine was still permitted.

### Heteira & Rotzeh

The *Gemara* then raises two additional concerns. First, *rotzeh be-kiyumo*: while helping the flasks cross the river, he does not want them to break, since he is responsible for them — and this desire for the *yayin nesekh* to remain intact is an independent problem, analogous to *mekayeim kil'ayim*. The *Gemara* offers two resolutions: either he explicitly stipulated at the outset that if the flasks break in the crossing he bears no responsibility — so he is not *rotzeh be-kiyumo* — or he had spare jugs along, so that if the flasks broke the wine could be transferred, meaning he had no stake in the flasks' integrity.

The *Gemara* then raises the concern that he is *mistaker be-issurei hana'ah* by crossing the wine over the river and receiving payment for doing so. To this the *Gemara* says: *d'amar lei le-mavrumi me'ikara* — he had arranged payment with the ferryman in advance, so he himself was not personally ferrying the wine across; or, alternatively, *d'nakit pukitri* — he gave the ferryman a pass or voucher, so his own personal labor was not directly applied to transporting the wine.

The impression left by this passage is significant, and notably unremarked upon by *Rashi*, *Tosafot*, the *Rif*, and the *Rosh*: it appears that the problems of *rotzeh be-kiyumo* and *mistaker be-issurei hana'ah* are substantially limited when one is not personally and directly involved in the handling of the wine. The case of renting out a vehicle one does not personally operate may well fall outside the scope of these prohibitions for precisely that reason, though the *Gemara* does not articulate this explicitly.

## Wine Mixtures

### Wine on Produce

The *Mishnah* now turns to cases of mixture. *Yayin nesekh she-nafal al gabei anavim* — *yayin nesekh* fell on grapes. Since this is cold, there is normally no absorption. *Yedicham ve-hen mutarot* — rinse them off and they are permitted. *Ve-im hayu mevuka'ot* — if the grapes were cracked — *asurot* — they are forbidden, since cracked produce is porous enough to absorb even without heat.

### Min Bemino Rule

One might ask why the cracked-grape case requires rinse-and-permit at all for the uncracked grapes, rather than simply ruling it forbidden in any amount. The answer touches on a fundamental distinction in *halakha*: *min be-mino* — the same type mixed with itself — is forbidden in any amount, *be-khol she-hu*, at least by rabbinic enactment in the case of wine. But *eino mino* — wine mixed with something not of its kind — follows the standard rule of *nosein ta'am*, perceptible taste. Wine falling on uncracked grapes may be *min be-mino* in some sense, yet since the grapes have not absorbed and the wine is rinsed off, the *Mishnah* permits it. The cracked-grape case becomes *assur* because absorption has occurred.

### Veitos Ben Zonam

*Nafal al gabei te'einim o al gabei temarim* — if it fell on figs or dates, which are more porous: *im yesh bahen be-nosein ta'am, assur* — if there is enough to impart taste, it is forbidden. The *Mishnah* then cites a story: *u-ma'aseh be-Veitos ben Zonam* — a case involving Veitos ben Zonam, who was transporting dried figs by sea when a barrel of *yayin nesekh* broke and spilled on them. He brought the question to the sages, who permitted it. This seems puzzling: wine on figs would ordinarily seem to be a good taste and therefore forbidden. The *Gemara* concludes that the *Mishnah* is missing something — *chisore mekhsara ve-hachi katani* — and the story was meant to be preceded by the concluding principle.

### Good vs. Bad Taste

*Nosein ta'am li-fgam mutar* — if the mixture imparts a bad taste, it is permitted. This is the rule that was implicitly presupposed by the Veitos ben Zonam story: wine that broke open in a ship's hold and fell onto dried figs is not wine improving those figs — it is spoiled, off-putting, a negative taste. Accordingly it is *mutar*. The rule is thus two-layered: there must be perceptible taste, and that taste must be *li-shevach*, a positive improvement, for the mixture to be forbidden.

### Wheat Sale Ruling

The *Gemara* presents a case: a pile of wheat onto which a barrel of *yayin nesekh* broke and spilled. Rava permitted selling the wheat to a non-Jew. Rabbah bar Liva'i challenged him: even if the sale price excludes any value attributable to the wine, there remains the concern that the non-Jew will turn around and sell the wheat to a Jew — just as one may not sell a *kil'ayim* garment to a non-Jew lest he sell it back to a Jew. Rava conceded the point.

### Bread Solution

Rava then revised his ruling: *hadar sharya le-midchino, le-mifyeinu ve-lizvineihu le-ovdei kochavim, shelo bifnei Yisrael* — he permitted grinding the wheat into flour and baking it into bread, then selling the bread to non-Jews, but not in the presence of Jews. Why not in their presence? Because if a Jew were to see the transaction, he might assume it was bread baked by a Jew and purchase it, not knowing it had been contaminated. Outside Jewish view, it will be recognizable as bread of a non-Jew, which Jews will not purchase due to the prohibition of *pat akum* — unless one follows the *heter* of *pat palter* — so the concern of the wheat ultimately reaching a Jewish consumer is effectively eliminated.

### Wheat Kernel Grooves

A final question arises from the *Mishnah*: the *Mishnah* required only rinsing for uncracked grapes, implying that without cracks there is no absorption in cold. Why then was the wheat a problem? The *Gemara* answers: *amar Rav Papa, shani chiti, agav tzirayu ke-mevuka'ot dami* — wheat is different, because its kernels have a groove or nick in them. That groove functions like a crack, making wheat kernels porous in a manner analogous to *mevuka'ot* grapes. Even without heat, the wine seeps into the wheat through that groove. And since the taste imparted was *li-shevach* rather than *li-fgam*, the wheat became forbidden, requiring the indirect remedy of grinding and baking before selling it in a way that would not reach Jewish consumers.

# Avodah Zarah 66

## Nosein Taam Principles

### Mashechta Overview

The present daf continues in that portion of Masekhes *Avodah Zarah* that has become the classic locus for the study of *kashrus* and *bittul*. As we have seen in preceding pages, the *masechta* takes up questions of mixtures and prohibited substances with a rigor that has made it indispensable to later *posekim*. The *Mishnah* introduced the foundational concept of *nosein taam*: a prohibited substance creates a problem only if it imparts a detectable flavor to the permitted mixture in which it falls.

### Nosein Taam Lifgam

Even within the framework of *nosein taam*, there is an important qualification. If the prohibited substance imparts a *nosein taam lifgam* — a deteriorating or off-putting taste — it is not considered to have made its presence felt in any meaningful sense, and there is no prohibition. The question that drives the *sugya* forward is precisely how to measure and characterize the taste that a prohibited substance imparts, and under what conditions its presence is or is not regarded as legally significant.

### Absorption in Porous Foods

The physical mechanism of taste transfer also requires attention. The *Mishnah* addressed cases involving porous foods such as figs or dates, whose skins allow liquid to be absorbed even without heat. Grapes present a different case: ordinarily, wine or other liquids do not penetrate their skin, and rinsing the surface suffices. *Tosafos*, however, notes that this assumes the grapes remain attached to the cluster. Once a grape is plucked from its stem, the point of detachment creates an opening through which liquid can enter. In such a case, even cold liquid can be absorbed. This is a crucial distinction, as the principle of *nosein taam* applies equally whether heat drove the absorption or the porous nature of the food allowed it naturally.

### Yayin Nesech Principle

With these foundations in place, the *Gemara* opens *daf* 66a by taking up the special stringency that governs *yayin nesech*. In most areas of *kashrus*, prohibited mixtures are assessed through the lens of *nosein taam*: a substance is considered present and problematic only if it can be tasted. There is, however, a well-known category of *issurim* — *yayin nesech* and *chametz b'Pesach* being the paradigmatic examples — where the standard stringency is *batel be-mashehu*: even a negligible quantity, far below the threshold of taste, renders the mixture forbidden. For *yayin nesech*, this heightened stringency applies specifically when wine is mixed *min be-mino* — wine into wine, like with like. When *yayin nesech* falls into something that is not wine — soup, for example — the ordinary rule of *nosein taam* applies.

### Min BeMinο Debate

This distinction invites an obvious question: why should wine mixed with wine be *more* problematic than wine mixed with something else? The answer lies in a foundational dispute in *halacha*. The baseline rule, which reflects the majority position, is that *min be-mino* — a prohibited substance mixed with an identical permitted substance — is *batel be-rov*: as long as a simple majority of the mixture is permitted, the prohibited minority is nullified, because it imparts no distinct taste and therefore makes no independent impression. *Min be-eino mino* — a prohibited substance mixed with something of a different kind — is a stricter case, because there the prohibited substance *can* make its presence felt through taste, and therefore a mere majority does not suffice; one requires sixty times the prohibited amount.

*Rabbi Yehuda* takes the opposite position regarding *min be-mino*: he holds that *min be-mino* is never *batel*, not even in a majority. His reasoning is the mirror image of the majority view. Precisely because the two substances are identical in taste, the prohibited substance never loses its identity — every spoonful of the mixture contains the taste of the forbidden food, even if one cannot distinguish it. It does not make its presence felt distinctively, but neither does it disappear.

In practice, the *halacha* does not follow *Rabbi Yehuda* as a general rule. We do not say that every case of *min be-mino* requires more than a majority. However, when the *Rabbanan* wish to impose a heightened stringency in a specific area — as with *yayin nesech* — they construct that stringency by adopting *Rabbi Yehuda*'s reasoning selectively. They rule, in effect: for *yayin nesech*, we will apply *Rabbi Yehuda*'s principle, and *min be-mino* will be *batel be-mashehu*. Wine falling into wine, even a single drop, is forever forbidden. When wine falls into a non-wine mixture, one returns to the ordinary rule of *nosein taam*.

---

## Abaye-Rava: Taste vs Name

### New Wine in Grapes

This framing raises a question that the *Gemara* now confronts directly: how does one define *mino* and *eino mino*? The answer is not self-evident. Two substances might share the same name but taste quite different; conversely, two things with different names might taste nearly identical. The *Gemara* introduces its discussion with a carefully chosen case: *chamra atika be-invi* — old, fermented wine absorbed into grapes. Here there is no dispute: the case is governed by *nosein taam*. Old wine and grapes differ both in taste and in name, and therefore their interaction is assessed in the ordinary way.

The genuinely interesting case is *chamra chadta be-invi* — new wine, which is essentially unfermented grape juice, absorbed into grapes. Does this constitute *min be-mino* or *min be-eino mino*? Unfermented grape juice and grapes share a remarkably similar taste, yet they bear different names. This is precisely the question that divides *Abaye* and *Rava*.

### Abaye: Taste Determines

*Abaye amar be-mashehu* — *Abaye* holds that this is *min be-mino* and the mixture is therefore forbidden even in a negligible quantity. His principle is *batar ta'ama azlinan*: we follow taste.
