Because grape juice and grapes taste the same — *hai ve-idach chad ta'ama hu* — they are to be treated as identical substances. The logic connects directly to the underlying theory of *min be-mino*. The question is whether the prohibited substance makes its presence felt. If it cannot be tasted independently, it does not make its presence felt in the ordinary sense; but by the same token, it does not lose its identity either, because it is all there, tasting of grape with every bite. *Abaye* thus says: since they taste the same, they are the same, and the *mashehu* rule applies.

### Rava: Name Determines

*Rava amar be-nosein taam* — *Rava* holds that the mixture is governed by *nosein taam* and is effectively permitted once the grape juice is less than one-sixtieth of the grapes. His principle is *batar shma azlinan*: we follow the name. *Ve-hai shma le-chud ve-hai shma le-chud* — grapes and wine bear different names, and different names signal different categories. Therefore this is *min be-eino mino*, and the ordinary *nosein taam* standard applies.

One might ask whether there is something philosophically unsatisfying about *Rava*'s criterion. Categories defined by names seem like a social convention rather than an intrinsic property of the objects themselves. Yet this objection arguably misses the point: *halacha* operates with real human categories, and the names by which society classifies things are a precise reflection of the categories it recognizes. If we use different names, we are saying, as a society, that we have placed these things in different classifications. *Rava* holds that those social classifications are legally operative.

### Mishna Wine-Grape Case

Having set out the dispute, the *Gemara* attempts to resolve it by appeal to the *Mishnah*. The *Mishnah* states that if *yayin nesech* fell onto grapes and the grapes had cracked skins, they are forbidden — and it states this without any explicit condition of *nosein taam*. The implication seems to be that this is a case of *min be-mino be-mashehu*, which would support *Abaye*. The *Mishnah*'s end section, however, formulates the general rule as *kol she-natan ta'am assur, kol she-lo natan ta'am mutar* — the principle is always *nosein taam*. Since the *Mishnah*'s own stated rule is *nosein taam*, the earlier case involving cracked grapes must also be understood in those terms, which seems to support *Rava*.

### Gemara Resolution

*Abaye* responds to this challenge cleanly: *matnitin be-chamra atika be-invi* — the *Mishnah* is discussing old wine absorbed into grapes, not new wine. Old wine is fermented; it has a fundamentally different taste than the grape itself. When the *Mishnah* says the grapes are forbidden subject to the *nosein taam* rule, it is speaking of a case where the wine and the grapes are distinct in taste, just as both *Abaye* and *Rava* agree. The case of new wine — grape juice — absorbed into grapes remains unresolved by the *Mishnah*, and *Abaye*'s position that such a mixture is *mashehu* because taste determines identity still stands.

It is worth noting that *Abaye* and *Rava*'s positions are not simply a *chumra* versus *kula* in all cases. The case of new wine into grapes makes *Abaye*'s position the stricter one: since they taste the same, it is *min be-mino* and therefore *mashehu*. But the same principle can operate in reverse. If one has wine vinegar and beer vinegar — or sourdough of wheat and sourdough of barley — both examples bear the same name but taste quite differently. There *Abaye* would say they are *min be-eino mino* (different tastes, different categories, governed by *nosein taam*), while *Rava* would say they are *min be-mino* (same name, same category, governed by *mashehu*). The positions thus trade stringency and leniency depending on the case.

---

## Spices & Combined Issur

### Rashi's Caveat

Before proceeding, *Rashi* interjects an important qualification. The *Gemara*'s language in the line *ve-chol min be-mino be-mashehu* — "all *min be-mino* is *mashehu*" — is broader than the case of *yayin nesech* alone. It appears to assert, following *Rabbi Yehuda*'s reasoning, that in every domain of *kashrus*, *min be-mino* is forever forbidden even in a negligible amount. This is how *Rashi* reads the *sugya*, and indeed *Rashi* in various places in *Shas*, particularly in *Chullin*, rules accordingly. However, *Rashi* himself here acknowledges that the *halacha* does not actually follow this broad reading: *le-kaman paskinan de-lav hilchata hachi* — later we will rule that this is not the law. The rule of *min be-mino be-mashehu* is effectively limited to *yayin nesech*, *tevel*, and *chametz be-Pesach*. In most other areas, even *min be-mino* is governed by *nosein taam*. *Tosafos* roundly rejects *Rashi*'s broader position, and it is worth pausing to appreciate why: if every case of *min be-mino* required *mashehu*, the practical difficulties for *kashrus* observance would be considerable. *Rashi*'s inconsistency on this point — ruling one way in *Chullin* and another here — is flagged explicitly in the marginal notes.

For practical purposes, then, the *mashehu* stringency tied to *min be-mino* is primarily a *yayin nesech* concern. The broader dispute between *Abaye* and *Rava* over how to *define* *min be-mino* — taste versus name — has its main practical application there.

### Spice Mishna

The *Gemara* now brings *Abaye*'s proof for his own position. *Abaye* cites a *Braitah*: if you have spices of different types — some that are *orlah*, some *tevel*, some from *avodah zarah* — and they all fall into the same dish, they combine to render the dish forbidden. Furthermore, the case can involve spices that are different types entirely: pepper, cinnamon, and nutmeg, for instance, each forbidden for a different reason. Despite being different substances carrying different *issurim*, they combine. The double language of the *Braitah* — *assurin u-mitztatfin*, they are forbidden and they combine — addresses both wet and dry mixtures, but the essential point is the combination itself. If each spice individually would not constitute a sufficient quantity to render the dish forbidden, their combination together creates the requisite amount. The question *Abaye* presses is: why should fundamentally different things combine at all?

### Miney Metika

Before *Abaye* can complete his proof, *Chizkiyah* offers a clarification that proves essential: *hacha be-meinei matika askinan, hovrin le-mateik et ha-kedeirah* — the case here involves spices that are all of the sweet-giving type, all contributing a sweetness to the pot. The combination is possible precisely because, despite their different botanical origins, they all function in the same way in the dish: they all impart sweetness. This narrows the scenario considerably. The relevant case is not just any mixture of forbidden spices, but specifically those that all contribute the same kind of flavor profile.

### Abaye: Taste Proof

With *Chizkiyah*'s clarification established, *Abaye* presses his proof. *Ei amrat bishlama batar ta'ama azlinan, kulei chad ta'ama hu* — if you agree with me that identity is determined by taste, then the combination makes perfect sense. All these different spices ultimately produce the same sweetness; they are therefore to be regarded as a single category of substance, and they can combine to create a forbidden quantity. The proof, *Abaye* argues, is that we would not even *think* of combining things from fundamentally different categories. The fact that the *Braitah* permits combination reveals that shared taste creates a shared legal identity. That, *Abaye* says, is *batar ta'ama azlinan*.

It is true that this example involves *min be-eino mino* rather than *min be-mino*, which is where *Abaye* and *Rava* primarily disagree. The *mashehu* question does not arise here, since if you had enough of any one substance to be *nosein taam* you would not need combination. But *Abaye*'s point is structural: the very *possibility* of combination demonstrates that shared taste generates shared identity, and that is his underlying principle.

### Rava: Issur Identity

*Rava* responds that the *Braitah* proves nothing of the kind. *Ha mani Rabbi Meir hi* — this source reflects the position of *Rabbi Meir*, who holds that all *issurim* in the Torah share a generic identity, as derived from the verse *lo tochal kol to'evah*: do not eat anything that is an abomination. *Kol she-ti'avti lecha harei hu be-val tochal* — anything the Torah has forbidden shares this generic designation of *toeva*, of that which is abominable. That shared generic identity — we might call it *treifus* in the broad sense — is what allows different forbidden substances to combine. They need not taste the same; they merely need to share the identity of being forbidden. The combination follows from their shared status as *toeva*, not from their shared flavor.

*Rava* thus offers a coherent account of why the combination works that makes no reference to taste whatsoever. One might then ask: if combination follows from shared *toeva* identity alone, why does the *Braitah* specify that these are *meinei matika*, sweet-giving spices? According to *Rava*, if they were being eaten outside of a mixture, combination would follow purely from their shared *toeva* identity. But when these substances are mixed into a dish, they must still make their presence felt in order not to be *batel*. And in order to make their presence felt in a mixture, they must contribute a detectable flavor. Therefore, for the purposes of the mixture context, they also need to share a taste — not to create their shared identity, but to ensure that they are not nullified. The shared *toeva* identity is what conceptually unifies them; the shared taste is what preserves their presence in the mixture. *Abaye*'s position, by contrast, makes taste do double duty: it both creates the shared identity *and* preserves their presence in the mixture.

---

## Wine & Vinegar Debate

### Vinegar into Wine

The *Gemara* now takes up a new case that carries the *Abaye-Rava* debate into a domain where taste and smell diverge. *Chala le-go chamra* — vinegar falling into wine. This is straightforward: vinegar and wine have different names and different tastes. By both *Abaye*'s criterion (taste) and *Rava*'s criterion (name), this is *min be-eino mino*, and therefore *divrei hakol be-nosein taam* — all agree it is governed by the taste standard.

### Wine into Vinegar

The reverse case is more complex. *Chamra le-go chala* — wine falling into vinegar. At first glance, this seems equally simple: different names, different tastes, and therefore *min be-eino mino* by both positions. But the physical reality of the situation introduces a complication. When a drop of *yayin nesech* hovers above a large barrel of vinegar before falling in, the powerful smell emanating from the barrel envelops the drop. By the time the drop of wine actually enters the vinegar, it already *smells* like vinegar — even though, stripped of that smell, it would taste like wine. The question therefore becomes: when something smells like vinegar and tastes like wine, which property determines its *halachic* identity?

### Abaye: Smell Rules

*Abaye amar be-mashehu* — *Abaye* holds this is *min be-mino* and governed by *mashehu*. *Reicha chala* — the smell is vinegar, and for *Abaye*, smell determines the relevant category. The drop, as it enters the barrel, is to be treated as vinegar, and therefore it is vinegar meeting vinegar: *min be-mino be-mashehu*.

This result may seem surprising, since *Abaye*'s stated general principle is *batar ta'ama azlinan* — identity follows taste. Yet here *Abaye* is applying a deeper understanding of what "taste" means. There is a well-established physiological reality that the vast majority of what we experience as flavor is in fact olfactory: smell travels through the nasal passages and constitutes the dominant component of the tasting experience. When *Abaye* says we follow taste, and then in this case follows smell, he is saying that smell is the dominant determinant of taste. The two positions are therefore consistent: *Abaye* goes by the tasting experience, and in a case where smell overwhelms, smell defines the tasting experience.

### Rava: Taste Rules

*Rava amar be-nosein taam* — *Rava* holds this is *min be-eino mino* and governed by *nosein taam*. *Reicha chala ve-tama chamra, chamra* — if it smells like vinegar but tastes like wine, it is wine. *Ve-havei lei min be-she-eino mino* — it is therefore wine in vinegar, like with unlike, and the taste standard applies.

*Rava*'s position here connects naturally to his general criterion of *batar shma azlinan*. How would people refer to wine that has begun to smell of vinegar? Likely as "wine gone bad" or "vinegary wine" — still wine, even if deteriorating. The name has not changed, and therefore the identity has not changed. The smell does not override the category.

What makes this case especially interesting is that both the question of names and the question of taste pull in the same direction for *Rava*, yet *Abaye*, despite his general emphasis on taste, ends up calling it vinegar. The *Gemara* does not explicitly map this case onto the earlier *Abaye-Rava* debate about taste versus name, but the connection is clear. *Rava*'s position here is consistent with his broader principle; *Abaye*'s position reflects his view that smell is the dominant component of taste, and that where smell overwhelms, the tasting experience must be described in terms of that smell.

---

## Smell Standalone

### Bistia & Smelling Wine

The *Gemara* now moves to a case that fully isolates smell from taste: the *bistia*, a kind of pipette used to draw wine from a barrel and assess its quality by smell. The *Gemara* presents a two-part case. If a non-Jew smells a Jew's wine through the *bistia*, there is no issue — he has not touched the wine, has not moved it, and has not done anything that would create a problem of *yayin nesech*. *Tosafos* adds that if a Jew smells a non-Jew's wine, the assumption must be that he is doing so without payment; otherwise, there would be a separate problem of receiving benefit from *yayin nesech*. The harder question concerns the Jew smelling the non-Jew's wine itself. Has he done anything forbidden?

### Abaye: Smell is Real

*Abaye amar assur* — it is forbidden. *Reicha milta hi* — smell is a real thing. *Abaye*'s position is consistent with his earlier stance on the vinegary wine: smell is not merely an incidental property but is itself a vehicle through which one engages with and in some sense ingests the substance. To smell *yayin nesech* is, for *Abaye*, a meaningful form of engagement with it that triggers the prohibition.

### Rava: Smell Irrelevant

*Rava amar mutar* — it is permitted. *Reicha lav milta hi* — smell is nothing. *Rava* holds that if the physical wine itself does not pass down one's throat, if one has not actually drunk or eaten it, no prohibition is triggered. What precisely is the underlying dispute? The context of *yayin nesech* might suggest this is a question about *issurei hana'ah* — the prohibition of benefit. Wine that has been poured for idolatrous purposes is forbidden not only to drink but to derive benefit from, and one might ask whether inhaling its aroma constitutes benefit. However, the *Gemara* immediately connects this debate to a parallel in the laws of *terumah*, and *terumah* is not *assur be-hana'ah*. The question, as *Tosafos* explains it, is therefore not about benefit but about whether smell constitutes a form of *achilah* — ingestion or eating. When one smells something directly, tiny particles of that substance actually enter the body through the nose and mouth. *Abaye* holds that this constitutes a form of ingesting the substance itself. *Rava* holds that if the physical substance, in the form one recognizes as the food itself, does not enter the body, the act of smelling is not *achilah* and creates no prohibition.

### Terumah Bread Case

*Rava* supports his position from a *Mishnah* in the laws of *terumah*. *Tanur she-hisiko be-chamon shel terumah* — if someone heated an oven using cumin that was *terumah*, and then baked bread in that oven, the bread is permitted. *Lefi she-ein ta'am chamon ela reiach chamon* — the bread absorbed only the smell of the cumin, not the taste of the cumin. There is no actual cumin flavor in the bread; only the aroma permeated the baking environment. Since only the smell transferred, and smell is *lav milta*, there is no prohibition.

### Rava's Proof

This, *Rava* says, is his proof: *mana amina lah de-reicha lav klum hu* — from this *Mishnah* we learn that smell alone does not constitute a halachically significant transfer. Even though the *terumah* cumin's aroma permeated the oven and the bread baked within it, the bread remains entirely permitted, because smell is nothing.

### Abaye: Direct vs. Detach…

*Abaye* responds with a distinction that saves his principle: *shani hatam de-miklei issurei* — there the cumin was burned. The cumin itself was consumed by the fire; what remained in the oven was not the cumin but only a detached aroma, the smell floating independently in the air. A detached aroma, separated from the original substance by the act of burning, is genuinely "nothing" — it is not the thing itself in any form. But in the case of smelling wine directly, the wine is physically present; the particles entering one's nose are real particles of wine. That, *Abaye* argues, is qualitatively different from an aroma left lingering in an oven after its source has been destroyed.

The distinction *Abaye* draws is between direct smell — where the original substance is present and one's nose is in immediate contact with particles emanating from it — and detached aroma, where the source is gone and only a residual smell hangs in the air. The former, for *Abaye*, is a real form of ingestion; the latter is not. This maps onto what one might describe as the physical reality of smell: to smell something is to have particles of that thing enter one's body. *Abaye* holds that this is halachically cognizable when the source is present; *Rava* holds that without the physical substance passing one's lips, no *achilah* has occurred.

---

## Tannaim: Bread & Barrel

### Tannaitic Dispute

The *Gemara* now introduces a *Tannaitic* dispute that mirrors the *Abaye-Rava* debate and allows for a more precise mapping. The case: someone removes hot bread from an oven and places it directly on top of a barrel of *terumah* wine. Three *Tanna'im* weigh in.

### Rabbi Meir Position

*Rabbi Meir* forbids the bread. His position presupposes that the smell of the wine is absorbed into the bread and that this absorption is halachically significant — *reicha milta hi*. Because the hot bread is in direct contact with the barrel, the wine's aroma penetrates the bread, and since *Reicha milta*, that aroma renders the bread *terumah* and therefore forbidden to non-*kohanim*.

### Rabbi Yehuda Position

*Rabbi Yehuda* permits the bread. For him, *reicha lav milta hi* — smell does not transfer in a legally significant way, and the bread is unaffected by its proximity to the wine barrel.

### Rabbi Yossi: Wheat vs. B…

*Rabbi Yossi* takes a middle position: *mattir be-shel chittin ve-osser be-shel se'orin* — wheat bread is permitted, but barley bread is forbidden. The difference is absorption: *mipnei she-hase'orin sho'avot* — barley bread absorbs more, and therefore the wine's smell actually enters it in a physically meaningful way. Wheat bread does not absorb to the same degree, so it remains unaffected.

### Rava & Abaye Linked

*Rav Mari* notes that this *Tannaitic* dispute maps directly onto the *Abaye-Rava* debate: *Rabbi Meir* corresponds to *Abaye* (*reicha milta*), and *Rabbi Yehuda* corresponds to *Rava* (*reicha lav milta*). For *Rava*, this is straightforward: he acknowledges that his position aligns with *Rabbi Yehuda*, and he concedes that other *Tanna'im* disagree. For *Abaye*, however, the situation is more nuanced.

### Reish Lakish Conditions

*Abaye* argues that he need not read this as a fundamental dispute about the principle of *reicha*. He invokes a ruling transmitted by *Rabbah bar bar Chanah* in the name of *Reish Lakish*: *be-pat chamah ve-chavit ptuchah, divrei hakol assur* — if the bread is hot and the barrel is open, all agree the bread is forbidden, because in that case the smell is certainly absorbed. *Be-pat tzonenet ve-chavit megufah, divrei hakol muteret* — if the bread is cold and the barrel is sealed, all agree the bread is permitted, because nothing is absorbed. The debate among the *Tanna'im*, *Abaye* argues, is not about the principle but about the intermediate cases: hot bread with a sealed barrel, or cold bread with an open barrel — one factor favoring absorption and one disfavoring it.

### Abaye's Nuance

*Abaye*'s nuance is therefore this: he does not read *Rabbi Yehuda* as denying that smell is ever significant. Rather, he reads the entire *Tannaitic* dispute as operating within a shared framework that accepts *reicha milta* in principle, and debating only the threshold conditions under which smell is actually absorbed. *Ve-ha didi ke-pat chamah ve-chavit ptuchah dami* — the case of smelling wine directly, where one's face is over the barrel, is the equivalent of hot bread on an open barrel: there is no question that direct smell contact involves real absorption, and all would agree it is a problem. *Rava*, meanwhile, reads *Rabbi Yehuda* as a straightforward denial that smell matters at all, and aligns himself accordingly.

---

## Ovens & Pesach

### Tosafos Q on Reicha

*Tosafos* raises a question that has significant practical implications. The *Gemara* here, following *Rava*, rules *reicha lav milta hi* — smell does not create a prohibition. Yet in the *sugya* in *Pesachim* dealing with *reicha*, the conclusion appears to go in the opposite direction. Which ruling governs practical *halacha*, and do these represent the same type of scenario?

### Tosafos: Year Cooking

*Tosafos* addresses the question that arises in *Perek Keitzad Tzolin* in *Pesachim*, where *Rav* and *Levi* debate whether fatty kosher meat roasted together with *treif* meat is forbidden due to the transfer of taste through the oven. *Rav* forbids it; *Levi* permits it. The *Gemara* there brings a *Braitah* in support of *Rav*'s position. Nevertheless, *Rashi* in that chapter rules like *Levi*, permitting the practice — because *Rava* here rules *reicha lav milta hi*, and the *halacha* follows *Rava* against *Abaye*. Accordingly, *Tosafos* takes it as a baseline that during the year, cooking kosher and *treif* foods in the same oven — even simultaneously — does not violate the prohibition, because the transfer is only through smell, and smell is not a legally significant conduit of taste.

### Pesach Matzah Case

The *Pesach* context, however, changes the analysis. *Tosafos* addresses a case where *matzos* were baked and subsequently a kernel of grain was discovered in one of them, raising the concern that it may have been *chametz*. If the *matzos* were baked together in the same oven, has the smell of that potentially *chametz* kernel transferred to the other *matzos* and rendered them forbidden?

### Chametz Timing

*Tosafos* introduces a crucial timing distinction. *Chametz* is *batel be-mashehu* — forbidden even in a negligible amount — only once *Pesach* itself has actually begun. Even after midday on *Erev Pesach*, when eating *chametz* is already forbidden, *chametz* that becomes mixed into something else is still *batel be-shishim*: the *mashehu* stringency does not yet apply. Only from the night of *Pesach* onward is *chametz batel be-mashehu*. Therefore, if the *matzos* were baked on *Erev Pesach*, even after midday, the smell transfer — even if it were halachically cognizable — would still be *batel be-shishim*, and the other *matzos* would be permitted.

### Tosafos: Mashehu Issue

*Tosafos*'s critical distinction is this: ruling *reicha lav milta hi* means that smell-transferred aroma does not constitute a tastable flavor — there is no *nosein taam*. But this does not mean there is *nothing* there. Even when smell transfers, some trace particles of the substance have genuinely moved. Those particles, while insufficient to constitute *nosein taam*, still amount to *mashehu* — a negligible but real presence of the forbidden substance. During the year, when *issurim* require *nosein taam* to be operative, smell transfer is irrelevant: *reicha lav milta*. But by *chametz be-Pesach*, where even *mashehu* is forbidden, those trace particles become significant. The smell of *chametz* baking in the oven alongside *matzah* during *Pesach* itself would therefore create a *mashehu* problem.

### Final Matzah Ruling

*Tosafos* concludes: *aval im afu ha-matzos be-shiva yemei ha-Pesach ve-nimtza chita ve-chametz be-achas mehen, kulan assuros* — but if the *matzos* were baked during the seven days of *Pesach* itself and a kernel of *chametz* was found in one of them, they are all forbidden. And not only the *matzah* in which the *chametz* was found: even the other *matzos* baked in the same oven at the same time are forbidden. Though *reicha lav milta hi* — the smell carries no taste — *nehi de-ta'am leka, mi-kol makom mashehu be-alma ika* — even if there is no taste, there is still at minimum a trace quantity present, and *ve-afilu be-massa tanur* — this applies even in the context of a baking oven. The conclusion for *Pesach* practice is stark: *matzah* baked in the same oven as *chametz* during *Pesach* itself is entirely forbidden, not because smell is taste, but because *mashehu* does not require taste — and where *chametz be-Pesach* is concerned, *mashehu* is enough.

---

---

# Avodah Zarah 67

## Reicha & Ta'am K'Ikar

### Reicha Recap

Today's daf is 67, and we pick up at the top of 67a. Yesterday we covered a major topic in *halakha*: the issue of *reicha* — taste transfer through smell, or more precisely, the halachic status of smell itself. The question was to what degree ingesting smell through the nose or the mouth (for one also smells through the mouth, which is why smell figures into the definition of *mino* or *eino mino*) constitutes actual ingestion of the object itself. We have the principle of *ta'am k'ikar* — the taste of something is like the thing itself — but the question is to what degree we say *reicha k'ikar*.

This was the substance of the debate between *Abaye* and *Rava*, with *Rava* concluding that *reicha lav miltha hi* — smell is not halachically significant. *Tosafot* works through this carefully, noting that a parallel debate appears in the *Gemara* in Pesachim between *Rav* and *Levi* regarding *reicha miltha*, and that based on the standard *klalei pesak*, the conclusion there would seem to favor *reicha miltha* — that smell is a problem. *Rashi* essentially rules according to our *Gemara* against that *Gemara* and holds *reicha lav miltha*. *Tosafot* attempts to reconcile all the *sugyot* by constructing a hierarchy: there may be cases where *reicha* is *miltha*, but those cases are limited.

### Ovens & Communal Use

The cases *Tosafot* identifies as potentially problematic involve very condensed, closed environments — specifically, cooking two items simultaneously in a sealed oven while uncovered, generating substantial steam and transfer. *Tosafot* therefore arrives at the conclusion that one may not cook uncovered *milchigs* and *fleishigs* in the same oven at the same time. However, the extent of *Tosafot*'s concern is precisely this and no more. Cooking one after another — even *treif* after *kosher* — was never in question. Cooking covered items simultaneously was never in question. Even cooking uncovered items simultaneously, *Tosafot* permits in large ovens, and certainly in the ventilated ovens of today, the concern effectively disappears. The one residual stringency *Tosafot* acknowledges is in the *Pesach* context, where *reicha* may not reach the threshold of *ta'am*, but might still constitute a *mashehu*, and by *Pesach* items baked on *Pesach* itself there would be an *issur mashehu*.

Today, to the extent there is any discussion about the status of ovens, it follows *Tosafot*'s framework. The *Rosh*, however, introduces an additional concern — not *reicha* but *zeia*, the actual evaporated liquid, the condensed steam. This is notable precisely because the *Gemara* itself focuses only on *reicha*, and if *zeia* were a problem, one would have expected the *Gemarot* to discuss it. Some *poskim* therefore reject the *zeia* concern entirely; others accept it in principle but rule that in large and ventilated modern ovens it is not practically operative, and certainly not when items are covered.

One additional consideration *Tosafot* raises is that in his time people used communal ovens — if you baked *cholent* you would take it to the baker — which made individual supervision of these conditions impossible. This connects to a broader point about how affluence shapes *halachic* concern. The contemporary *hechsher* industry has trained us to assume that nothing is permissible without full supervision and certification. *Tosafot*, writing in a context where communal ovens were the norm, operated on reasonable presumptions about what the default facts were. Today, where two or more ovens are affordable and common, the practical question re-emerges — but *Tosafot*'s underlying analysis remains the baseline.

### Ta'am K'Ikar Intro

With the *reicha* discussion complete, we continue to topics that are foundational to anyone learning *kashrut*. The *Mishnah* states the governing principle — *ze haklal*, this is the rule — which takes us from *reicha* into the domain of *ta'am* proper, and specifically the principle of *ta'am k'ikar*.

---

## Ta'am Lifgam

### Positive vs. Bad Taste

The *Mishnah* establishes: *kol shebehana'ato benoten ta'am* — anything whose taste transfer is a positive taste is forbidden; if it gives a *ta'am lifgam*, a negative or off-putting taste, it is permissible. There is an interesting discussion among the *Rishonim* about a neutral taste; the working assumption is that neutral and positive are treated equivalently, such that only a genuinely negative taste carries the leniency.

### Hot vs. Cold Grits

*Rav Yehuda* in the name of *Shmuel* affirms: *hachi hilchata* — this is the ruling. But he immediately adds a qualification. *Lo shanu ela shenafal letoch grisin rotchin* — the case in the *Mishnah* where the vinegar is deemed to give a bad taste applies only when the grain — the oatmeal or grits — was already hot. *Aval nafal letoch grisin tzonenin ve'hirtichan* — but if the vinegar fell into cold grits and the mixture was subsequently heated, *na'aseh kemi she'hivshiach ulevasof pagam ve'asur* — it is treated as a case where the taste initially improved the mixture and only later became off-putting, and remains forbidden.

The logic is as follows. When the non-kosher vinegar — *yayin nesech* vinegar — is mixed into cold grits, vinegar with cold grits apparently produces a pleasing taste. The grits thereby become forbidden, having absorbed a positive taste from a non-kosher substance. When the mixture is then heated and the taste turns slightly unpleasant, the grits remain forbidden: having once acquired forbidden status through a positive taste, that status does not depart. *Na'aseh kemi she'hivshiach ulevasof pagam ve'asur.*

### Tzippori Grits Case

This same ruling is transmitted twice more — once by *Ravin* in the name of *Rabba bar bar Chana* in the name of *Rabbi Yochanan*, and once by *Rav Dimi* (the *Gemara* does not repeat the formulation a third time in full). The *Gemara* then notes: *vechach hayu osim be'arvei shabbatos beTzippori* — this is what they used to do on *Erev Shabbat* in Tzippori. It was apparently a classic *Shabbat* dish, mixing vinegar with cold grits — referred to as *shachlayim*. One might ask why they would mix it cold if heating it would produce an off-putting taste. *Tosafot* explains that they would mix it cold, heat it up, and then let it cool again; once cold again, the off-taste was no longer present.

### Reish Lakish Dispute

*Reish Lakish* now introduces a further nuance about the scope of *noten ta'am lifgam*. His statement — *lo she'yomru kedira zo chasera melach yetira melach chasera tavlin yetira tavlin* — defines when *ta'am lifgam* does not apply. The passage is admittedly difficult to parse, and two readings are presented.

According to the first, more stringent reading: *noten ta'am lifgam* as a leniency is unavailable in any case where the bad taste can be attributed to a contributing factor other than the forbidden additive — for instance, if the spices in the pot are slightly off. If one can say, "the reason this tastes bad is that the seasoning was already unbalanced, and had the seasoning been correct this additive would have improved the dish," then one may not invoke *ta'am lifgam*. *Ta'am lifgam* applies only when the spices are perfectly balanced and the forbidden additive alone is the source of the off-taste. This is the narrow, stringent reading — *ela kol she'eina chasera klum ve'eina ne'echelet mipnei zeh*: only when there is nothing else deficient and the bad taste is attributable solely to this additive.

The second, more lenient reading: we do not theorize about hypothetical circumstances. The relevant question is not what the taste would have been under ideal conditions, but what the taste actually is right now. If at this moment the additive contributed to an off-putting taste, that is sufficient for *ta'am lifgam* — regardless of whether, had the spices been better, the same additive would have enhanced the dish. *Ela hashta mei'ha pagma* — right now there is a bad taste, and that is what matters.

*Rav Ami* in the name of *Rabbi Yochanan* and *Rabbi Abahu* in the name of *Rabbi Yochanan* both affirm the practical ruling. The *halakha* follows the second, lenient position. One need not speculate about hypotheticals; as long as in the actual present circumstance the additive contributed to an off-putting taste, it is permissible. This is further confirmed by the *Gemara*'s language: *ve'hilchata k'lishna batra de'Reish Lakish* — we rule like the latter formulation of *Reish Lakish*.

One additional textual point: the *Gemara* uses the phrasing *riba* ("increased") rather than simply *natan* ("gave") a bad taste. This is intentional — *haka mashma lan d'af agav d'ika milei achrinaysa d'pogma bahadei* — even if there are other contributing factors also making the dish unpleasant (like imbalanced spices), if this additive increased the off-putting quality, it is still *ta'am lifgam* and therefore permissible. The forbidden substance need not be the sole source of the bad taste.

A further note on the phrase *einah ne'echelet mipnei zeh* — "it is not eaten because of this." *Rashi* immediately clarifies: *lav davka*. This is not literal inedibility. Any practitioner of *kashrut* knows that food cooked in a *treif keli* after twenty-four hours is not actually inedible — it simply tastes slightly less good. *Noten ta'am lifgam* requires only that the taste be rendered somewhat less desirable, not that the food become impossible to eat. Nevertheless, as we will see when we arrive at the source from *neveilah*, some *Rishonim* were drawn to read the *Gemara*'s cases as requiring actual inedibility, and the language here and the paradigm case together provide them a foothold. The *Ra'ah* offers a creative resolution: if a food is rendered off-putting, that is evidence that the *issur* taste, were it extractable in isolation, would be inedible. The logical connection is admittedly strained, but it allows the *Ra'ah* to honor the *Gemara*'s language while preserving the practical *psak* that mere off-putting taste is sufficient.

---

## Taste vs. Essence

### Three Levels

We now step back from *ta'am lifgam* to examine the broader principle of *ta'am k'ikar* itself. *Rabbi Abba* in the name of *Rabbi Yochanan* articulates three levels. First: *kol sheta'amo umamasho assur v'lokin alav* — any case where one has both the taste and the essence of a forbidden substance is forbidden, and one receives lashes. *V'zehu k'zayit b'khdei akhilat pras* — this is when the quantity of forbidden substance in the mixture is sufficient that one consumes a *k'zayit* of the forbidden item within the time it takes to eat a *pras* (half a loaf of bread). The debate between *Rashi* and *Rambam* regarding the size of a *pras* — eight *k'zeisim* or nine — yields the practical implication that if the forbidden substance constitutes roughly one-eighth to one-ninth of the mixture, and one eats the mixture at a normal rate, one will have ingested a *k'zayit* of the forbidden substance within the *achilat pras* window and will be liable to lashes.

Second: *ta'amo v'lo mamasho assur v'ein lokin alav* — if one has the taste of the forbidden substance but not its essence, it is forbidden but does not incur lashes. Third: *v'im riba ta'am lifgam mutar* — and if the taste is off-putting, it is permissible.

### Rashi's Distinction

What is the distinction between *ta'amo umamasho* and *ta'amo v'lo mamasho*? *Rashi* identifies a physical difference. *Ta'amo umamasho* — taste and essence — describes a case where the forbidden and permitted substances are physically of the same type and intimately commingled: *chazir* soup dissolved into chicken soup, or a piece of *chazir* that fell into *cholent* and cannot be located. In such cases, the forbidden substance is present as substance, not merely as flavor. By contrast, if a drop of *chazir* soup — liquid — is absorbed into a solid, such as a steak, *Rashi* considers that *ta'amo v'lo mamasho*: only the taste has been transferred, not the thing itself. The boundary between these categories is admittedly imprecise, but the distinction is a physical one.

For *Rashi*, this determines the scope of *ta'am k'ikar* as a question. The principle — "the taste of something is like the thing itself" — is only in question when dealing with *ta'amo v'lo mamasho*, the absorbed-flavor scenario. *Ta'amo umamasho*, like ground *chazir* mixed into ground beef, is not a *ta'am k'ikar* question at all; it is simply the thing itself, and everyone agrees it is *d'oraisa*. The question of *ta'am k'ikar* — is the taste treated like the substance? — only arises in the liquid-into-solid scenario. And since the *Gemara* concludes *ein lokin alav* in that case, *Rashi* derives that *ta'am k'ikar* is *lav d'oraisa* — not a biblical prohibition. All the concerns of pots and absorbed flavors are, according to *Rashi*, rabbinic in origin.

### Biblical vs. Rabbinic

*Tosafot* presents the matter differently and offers several alternative readings. The first alternative is that even if *ta'am k'ikar* is *d'oraisa*, it does not follow that one receives lashes. The letter *kaf* in *ta'am k'ikar* — "taste is **like** the thing itself" — may mean not that it **is** the thing itself, but that it is forbidden in the same way. It is an *issur* derived from a different *pasuk*, a more general prohibition. Under this reading, the absence of lashes does not disprove that *ta'am k'ikar* is biblical; it simply means it is a different category of biblical *issur* for which lashes do not apply.

A second alternative: the distinction between *ta'amo umamasho* and *ta'amo v'lo mamasho* is not a physical distinction but a quantitative one. *Ta'amo umamasho* is when the mixture meets the threshold of *k'zayit bichdei achilat pras*, and one is therefore liable because one has actually consumed a *k'zayit* of the forbidden substance. *Ta'amo v'lo mamasho* — no lashes — simply describes a proportion below that threshold. Under this reading, *ta'am k'ikar* is fully *d'oraisa*, but the *Gemara*'s no-lashes ruling is a consequence of insufficient quantity, consistent with the principle that *chatzi shiur assur min ha-Torah* but does not incur lashes. This reading was noted to align well with *Rabbi Yochanan*'s own ruling on *chatzi shiur*.

*Rambam* charts a middle course: *ta'am k'ikar* is *d'oraisa* when the proportion reaches *k'zayit bichdei achilat pras*, and *derabbanan* below that threshold. Regarding *keilim* specifically — the prohibition on cooking in a *chazir* pot — *Rambam* holds that a *kli bas yoma* is forbidden *d'oraisa*, even as a separate question from how the *Torah* generally treats *ta'am*. There is a *Gemara* that suggests *keilim* may be a *chiddush*, a standalone prohibition independent of the general *ta'am* principle: even if *ta'am k'ikar* is not fully biblical, the *Torah* may separately prohibit cooking in a vessel that absorbed *chazir*, as a *lechatchila* concern. The *Gemara* nonetheless treats the two as intimately linked — *Rabbi Meir*'s argument from *giulei ovdei kochavim* assumes that the vessel laws reflect the general *ta'am* principle — and so the debate about the biblical status of *ta'am k'ikar* carries weight in this domain as well.

---

## Rabbi Meir vs. Shimon

### Baraita Dispute

Having established that *noten ta'am lifgam mutar* is the ruling, the *Gemara* asks whether anyone would actually forbid bad taste. The answer: yes. *Detanya* — we taught in a *baraita*: *echad noten ta'am lifgam ve'echad noten ta'am leshevach assur* — whether the taste is positive or negative, it is forbidden. These are the words of *Rabbi Meir*. *Rabbi Shimon* says: positive taste is forbidden, bad taste is permissible — and it is like *Rabbi Shimon* that we rule.

This is, as one might note, an unusual *psak*. We do not ordinarily rule like *Rabbi Shimon* against *Rabbi Meir*.

### Rabbi Meir's Source

*Mai ta'ama de'Rabbi Meir* — what is the source for *Rabbi Meir*'s position? *Gamar migiulei ovdei kochavim* — he derives it from the *giulei ovdei kochavim*, the purging of vessels taken from non-Jews. The word *giulei* relates to *hagalah* — expulsion, purging — and refers to the taste expelled from those vessels. When the *Torah* commanded the Israelites, after capturing vessels from Midian, to pass them through fire and through hot water, *Chazal* understand this not only as a *taharah* process but as *kashering* — removing the absorbed *issur* taste. Now, the taste absorbed in those vessels after use would by definition be off-putting — it is the residual, stale taste of old food. Yet the *Torah* required *kashering*. This proves, says *Rabbi Meir*, that even an off-putting taste is halachically significant. *Lav noten ta'am lifgam hu? Ve'asrah Rachmana* — was it not bad taste? Yet the *Torah* forbade using those vessels. *Hacha nami lo shena* — the same applies generally.

### Rabbi Shimon Reply

*Rabbi Shimon* responds through the ruling of *Rav Huna son of Rav Chiya*: *lo asrah Torah ella kedeira bas yoma delav lifgamo hu* — the *Torah* only forbade those vessels on the day itself when the food was absorbed, because on that very day the taste is not yet off-putting. The *Torah*'s prohibition thus applied only when the taste was still good. Implicitly, had the vessels been used a day later, the *Torah* would not have forbidden them — *ta'am lifgam* being permissible. *Rabbi Meir* rejoins: *kedeira bas yoma nami ee efshar delo pagma purta* — even on the same day, the absorbed taste is already slightly off; the *Torah* forbade it even then, proving that bad taste is a problem. The dispute thus turns on an empirical question: is day-of absorption truly a good taste, or already slightly deteriorated?

A word here about the relationship between *keilim* and *ta'am k'ikar*: while *Rambam* may treat a *kli bas yoma* as a separate *chiddush* independent of the general *ta'am* principle, the *Gemara* here clearly treats the two as linked. *Rabbi Meir*'s argument works only if the vessel laws reflect the same principle as *ta'am* in general.

### Starkist Analogy

*Rabbi Shimon*'s broader position derives from a *baraita* on *neveilah*. The *pasuk* states: *lo tokhlu kol neveilah, lager asher bishe'arekha* — you shall not eat any carcass; give it to the stranger in your gates. The *baraita* derives: *kol haraui lager kriya neveilah* — only if it is fit for human consumption is it called a *neveilah* and subject to the prohibition; *she'eino raui lager eino kriya neveilah* — if it is not fit for consumption, it is not a *neveilah* and is permissible. From this *Rabbi Shimon* derives that a *ta'am* that is undesirable is not the *ta'am* the *Torah* forbade.

*Rabbi Meir* counters: *hahu l'motei srukha me'ikara* — that *pasuk* comes to exclude only an animal that was already putrid and inedible from the moment of death, never having held the status of *neveilah*. But if the animal died while edible and then became inedible, it remains *assur* — because once it acquired the status of *neveilah assur*, that status adheres. This is a general *halachic* principle: once something acquires a *halachic* status, a higher threshold is required to remove it than was required to confer it in the first place. *Rabbi Shimon* responds: *srukha me'ikara lo tzerikha mi'uta* — an animal that was never edible did not even need a *pasuk* to permit it. *Afra b'alma hu* — it is mere dirt, not food, not a *neveilah* at all. The *chiddush* of the *pasuk* must therefore be that even an animal that began edible and became inedible is permissible — teaching us that *ta'am lifgam* is permissible.

All the *Rishonim* ask the obvious question: what does an inedible *neveilah* carcass have to do with *ta'am lifgam*, which is merely slightly off-putting? As noted earlier, the *Ra'avad* attempts to read all the *Gemara*'s *ta'am lifgam* cases as involving genuinely inedible food — an approach that cannot be sustained. The *Ra'ah*'s creative solution — that off-putting taste is evidence that the extracted *issur* taste would itself be inedible — has an acknowledged logical gap. The general consensus among *Rishonim* resolves the matter by analogy, and it is worth spelling out.

For an object of food to become *mutar*, it must become something no normal person wishes to eat. For a *taste* mixed into a permitted dish to become *mutar*, the analogous standard is: it must be a taste that no normal person wishes to taste. The *Torah*'s prohibition of *ta'am* — "taste is like the thing itself" — refers only to taste that people desire. Taste that no one wants is not the *ta'am* the *Torah* meant to prohibit. The analogy holds structurally even if not physically: as the only *neveilah* that is forbidden is one fit for consumption, so the only *ta'am* that is forbidden is one fit to be tasted — a taste that is welcome and desired. The principle, as one might express it, is that the *Torah* does not want tunas with good taste; it wants tunas that taste good.

---

## Good Then Bad

### Ulla's Position

The *neveilah* debate between *Rabbi Meir* and *Rabbi Shimon* raises a sharp question about *ta'am lifgam*. *Rabbi Meir* argues that a *neveilah* that began edible and became inedible remains *assur* — the initial status sticks. If we analogize *ta'am lifgam* to *neveilah*, it would seem that when we say *ta'am lifgam* is *mutar*, we can only mean a case where the taste was bad from the very outset. If the taste started good and then became bad — *hivshiach ulevasof pagam* — by the *neveilah* analogy it should remain *assur*. This is precisely the question.

*Ulla* says: *machlokes she'hivshiach ulevasof pagam* — the debate between *Rabbi Meir* and *Rabbi Shimon* concerns specifically the case where the taste started good and became bad, paralleling their debate about *neveilah*. *Aval pagam me'ikara divrei hakol mutar* — but if the taste was bad from the outset, everyone agrees it is permissible.

### Rav Chaga Challenge

*Rav Chaga* challenges *Ulla* from a *baraita*: *yayin she'nafal le'toch adashim ve'chometz she'nafal le'toch grisin assur, Rabbi Shimon matir* — wine falling into lentils and vinegar falling into grits is forbidden; *Rabbi Shimon* permits it. *Rav Chaga* reads this as a case of *pagam me'ikara* — the taste was bad from the start — and yet *Rabbi Meir* and *Rabbi Shimon* still debate it, implying the debate extends to *pagam me'ikara*.

*Ulla* is dismissive: *Chaga lo yada mai kamri rabbanan* — *Chaga* does not even understand the *baraita* he is citing. The case was in fact *nafal le'toch grisin tzonanin ve'hirticham* — the vinegar fell into cold grits and they were subsequently heated. As we established earlier, that is a case of *hivshiach ulevasof pagam* — the mixture first tasted good, then became bad — and it is that case which remains in dispute.

### Rabbi Yochanan Clarifies

*Rabbi Yochanan* disagrees with *Ulla* entirely. *Be'pogem me'ikara machlokes* — *Rabbi Meir* and *Rabbi Shimon* debate specifically the case where the taste was bad from the very beginning. This prompts the question: does *Rabbi Yochanan* mean that when the taste *hivshiach ulevasof pagam* — started good and became bad — everyone would agree it is *assur*? Or does he mean that all cases, including *hivshiach ulevasof pagam*, are in dispute? The *Gemara* leaves this as *teiku*.

### Sourdough Cases

*Rav Pappa* asks: is it possible that *Rabbi Yochanan* is correct that the dispute concerns *pagam me'ikara* and yet this is never reflected in a *Mishnah*? He investigates and finds the following *Mishnah* supporting *Rabbi Yochanan*. Sourdough (*se'or*) of *chulin* fell into dough, sufficient to cause fermentation and duly fermenting it. Subsequently, forbidden sourdough — *se'or* of *terumah* or of *kilayim* — fell in, also in sufficient quantity to ferment. Because the dough was already fully fermented, this second addition only over-ferments — which is *pagam me'ikara* — yet it is *assur*, and *Rabbi Shimon* permits.

*Rabbi Zeira* counters: this may not prove the general point. The reason *Rabbi Meir* might forbid in the sourdough case is not that he treats *pagam me'ikara* as forbidden in general, but that sourdough over-fermenting dough is not truly *pagam* at all — the excess sourdough makes the dough better as a starter or culture even if worse as bread. So *Rabbi Meir*'s stringency here might be case-specific.

The *Gemara* therefore tries a second case: *se'or* of *terumah* and *se'or* of *chulin* that fell in simultaneously, each in sufficient quantity to ferment. Together they over-ferment. This is *assur*; *Rabbi Shimon* permits. But this case is ambiguous — one cannot clearly assign the *pagam* to either component alone.

A third sub-case resolves matters. When *terumah* sourdough fell in *first* — *divrei hakol assur* — everyone agrees it is *assur*. This is a classic case of *hivshiach ulevasof pagam*: the *terumah* fell in and initially enhanced the fermentation, then the whole became over-fermented and unpleasant. Yet everyone agrees it is forbidden. This is a direct proof for *Rabbi Yochanan*: *hivshiach ulevasof pagam*, everyone agrees, is *assur*.

### Final Resolution

The case where *chulin* sourdough fell in first and *terumah* fell in second is then the *machlokes*. From the moment the *terumah* sourdough entered the already-fermented dough, it added a bad taste — *pagam me'ikara*. That is the dispute between *Rabbi Meir* and *Rabbi Shimon*.

Now one might still object: perhaps *Rabbi Meir*'s stringency in the sourdough cases is due to *Rabbi Zeira*'s reasoning, not a general view on *pagam me'ikara*. The *Gemara* answers by pointing to the wine-into-lentils and vinegar-into-grits cases, which are straightforwardly *pagam me'ikara* and present the same *machlokes*. And one cannot read those as *hivshiach ulevasof pagam* (the cold-grits reading *Ulla* proposed), because the sourdough *Mishnah* already established that *hivshiach ulevasof pagam* is *divrei hakol assur* — if those cases were *hivshiach ulevasof pagam*, they could not be a *machlokes*. Therefore they must be *pagam me'ikara*, and the *machlokes* is there. *Ela lav shema mina bepagam me'ikara machlokes — shema mina.*

The conclusion: *noten ta'am lifgam* is *mutar*, but only when the off-putting taste existed from the moment the forbidden substance entered the mixture — *pogem mitechila*. That is the debate between *Rabbi Meir* and *Rabbi Shimon*, and we rule like *Rabbi Shimon* that *pagam me'ikara* is *mutar*. If, however, the substance initially improved the taste and only subsequently the taste became bad — *hivshiach ulevasof pagam* — then the mixture became *assur* when it tasted good, and that *issur* status does not leave it. Everyone agrees that in such a case one cannot rely on *noten ta'am lifgam*.

---

---

# Avodah Zarah 68

## Nosein Ta'am Lifgam Deba…

### R. Shimon vs. R. Meir

The daf opens eight lines from the top of 68b, at the Gemara's question *hani telasa bavei dekattani lamma li* — why were all three sections of the *braisa* necessary? To understand this question, we must first recall the parameters of the debate between Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Meir concerning *nosein ta'am lifgam*, the principle that a forbidden substance which imparts a bad taste does not render the food into which it falls forbidden. Our *mishnah* records that Rabbi Shimon holds *nosein ta'am lifgam* to be *mutar*, which is the source of many practical leniencies — particularly in cases where something is more than a day old. Rabbi Meir, by contrast, holds *nosein ta'am lifgam* to be forbidden.

### Pagum Me'ikara Focus

The Gemara has just established, based on a *braisa* supporting the position of Ulla, that the debate between Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Meir turns on a case of *pagum me'ikara* — where the forbidden substance gives a bad taste from the very outset. This is the case where Rabbi Shimon holds it to be permissible and Rabbi Meir holds it to be forbidden even so. However, if the substance was *hishbiach u-levasof pagam* — initially its taste was good and only later turned bad — then everyone would agree it is forbidden, since the forbidden status of the food was established at the moment the substance initially improved it.

### Two Cases Compared

This understanding aligns with the earlier discussion in the *mishnah* about vinegar that falls on cold lentils and is subsequently heated: since initially the vinegar's contribution was beneficial and only afterward became detrimental, the food remains forbidden. The critical distinction, then, is between *pagum me'ikara*, where the bad taste is present from the start and Rabbi Shimon permits, and *hishbiach u-levasof pagam*, where the taste was initially good and later deteriorated, which all agree renders the food forbidden.

### Braisa Necessity

The *braisa* in question contains three sections. The final section deals with forbidden wine or vinegar that fell on lentils, demonstrating that the debate of Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Meir applies to *pagum me'ikara* — even when the taste is bad from the beginning, Rabbi Meir holds it forbidden. The middle section deals with *se'or* — yeast — of *terumah* falling into dough, followed by additional yeast: since the *terumah* yeast initially improved the dough, its status was established at that moment, and even Rabbi Shimon agrees it is forbidden. Together, these two sections provide the full picture: *pagum me'ikara* is the disputed case, and *hishbiach u-levasof pagam* is agreed by all to be forbidden.

### Yeast Two-Stage Case

Given that, the Gemara asks: *ella reisha lamma li* — why was the first section of the *braisa* needed at all? The first section addresses a case where *se'or* of *terumah* and *se'or* of *chullin* fell into the dough simultaneously, resulting in over-fermentation from the outset. That appears to be simply another case of *pagum me'ikara*. The Gemara, however, notes an important nuance: over-yeasted dough, while not ideal for bread, could be used as sourdough starter. So this is not a pure case of *pagum me'ikara* with nothing but bad taste — there is also an element of benefit. The Gemara then presses the point further: if in the final section, where there is no benefit at all, Rabbi Meir already holds it to be forbidden, then obviously Rabbi Meir would hold the over-yeast case — where there is at least some benefit — to be forbidden as well. And by the same token, since that case is bad from the beginning (*pagum me'ikara*), why would Rabbi Shimon's lenient ruling here not follow automatically from what we already know? What does the first section add?

### Reisha Necessity

The Gemara answers: *reisha amar Abaye reisha le-Rebbi Shimon itztreech* — the first section was needed for Rabbi Shimon's ruling. It might not have been obvious that Rabbi Shimon would permit this case, and one might have thought he would agree with Rabbi Meir here. It is to forestall that possibility that the first section was required.

## Abaye's Explanation

### Initial Benefit Frame

Abaye frames the matter as follows: the case of the over-yeasted dough is one where there is an argument that the forbidden *se'or* contributed something positive before ultimately becoming detrimental — a possible instance of *hishbiach u-levasof pagam*.

### Fermentation Speed

The argument that Rabbi Meir would press against Rabbi Shimon runs as follows: *issa zu reuyah lehachmitz b'shtei sha'os mi garam lah shetachmitz b'sha'ah achas issur* — this dough would have fermented in two hours on its own, but the forbidden yeast caused it to ferment in one. The effect of the *issur* was therefore initially an improvement — it sped up the fermentation — and only later, when the dough became over-fermented, did the harmful effect manifest. On this analysis, the forbidden yeast was initially *mashbiach*, and the case should be treated as *hishbiach u-levasof pagam*, making it forbidden according to everyone, including Rabbi Shimon.

### Shimon's Combo Reply

Rabbi Shimon's response, as framed by Abaye, is: *keshehishbichu sheneihem hishbichu, keshepigu sheneihem pagmu* — when it improved, both of them improved together; when it deteriorated, both of them deteriorated together. The *issur* did not make it better on its own; it made it better only in combination with the *hetter*. Since the forbidden yeast was not acting alone in producing the initial improvement, it cannot be characterized as the *issur* making it *hishbiach* — and therefore the case cannot be framed as *hishbiach u-levasof pagam*. The status remains one of *pagum me'ikara*, and Rabbi Shimon permits it.

It must be acknowledged that this answer is not entirely clear. If we are already conceding that there were two stages — an initial period of improvement followed by deterioration — it is difficult to see why the fact that the *issur* did not act alone suffices to strip away the character of *hishbiach u-levasof pagam*. Rashi explains *she'ne-hem hispichu ve-lo ha'issur levado hispicho* — both improved and not the *issur* alone — but this alone does not resolve the difficulty: even if the *issur* contributed to the improvement jointly, the food still tasted good at first and only bad later, which would seem to trigger the *hishbiach u-levasof pagam* rule. A more satisfying answer may be that from the very outset, the dough had too much yeast, and the mixture was never fully good — it always had the character of excess and was always going to be problematic. In any event, the conclusion stands: the debate between Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Meir applies to *pagum me'ikara*, and we rule accordingly that *nosein ta'am lifgam* is *mutar*.

## Tziruf & Combination

### Combination Challenge

Having explained Rabbi Shimon's position, the Gemara raises a further challenge. If we accept Abaye's framing — that there were two phases, an initial improvement and a subsequent deterioration — then why can we not say that even according to Rabbi Shimon, the permitted and forbidden yeast should combine to constitute a meaningful *hishbiach*? The Gemara asks: *Rebbi Shimon litzterof hetter ve'issur bahadei hadadi* — why should Rabbi Shimon not hold that the *hetter* and *issur* combine to produce a status of *hishbiach*?

### Shimon's Principle

The Gemara answers that Rabbi Shimon goes according to his well-known principle: *afilu issur ve'issur lo mitstarfe* — even two separate forbidden items do not combine with each other if each one individually is insufficient. If Rabbi Shimon holds that even two items of *issur* do not combine for this purpose, then certainly a forbidden item and a permitted item would not combine.

### Orlah & Kilai

The source for this principle is a *mishnah*: *ha-orlah ve-khilai ha-kerem mitstarfin, Rebbi Shimon omer ein mitstarfin*. The case is where one has half a *kezayit* of *orlah* — grapes from a vine in its first three years — and half a *kezayit* of *kilai ha-kerem* — grapes that had grown in a vineyard planted with mixed species. The *tanna kamma* holds that these two half-*kezaytim* combine to constitute a full *kezayit* of forbidden grapes, such that sixty *kezaytim* of permissible food would be needed to render them *batel*. With only fifty-nine, the mixture retains the taste of forbidden grapes and remains forbidden. Rabbi Shimon disagrees: each of the two forbidden items operates independently, and each is *batel* on its own. From this ruling it follows that Rabbi Shimon does not recognize combination between two separate *issurim*, let alone between an *issur* and a *hetter*. The first section of the *braisa* was therefore necessary to teach us that even Rabbi Shimon permits the over-yeasted dough, since it is his view that combination between the permitted and forbidden yeast does not suffice to create a status of *hishbiach*.

### Tosafot Alternative

Tosafot raises an important conceptual observation. Rather than framing the question in terms of *tziruf* — combination — one might have framed it as a question of *zeh ve-zeh gorem*, mutual causation: when two contributing factors each play a role, does each one's involvement count as halachically significant even though neither acts alone? Tosafot responds with a key distinction: the question of *zeh ve-zeh gorem* properly arises when each factor is individually insufficient — when each one is necessary but not independently sufficient, and together they bring about the result. In that circumstance one could argue either that no single cause is meaningful, or that they operate as genuine partners. That is the classic *zeh ve-zeh gorem* question. Here, however, since either piece of yeast — the *terumah* or the *chullin* — would on its own have been capable of leavening the dough, the case does not present a true *zeh ve-zeh gorem* situation. Tosafot concludes that when each factor is sufficient on its own, there is actually stronger reason to regard the *issur* as significant — you could remove the other and the *issur* alone would have accomplished the result. Nevertheless, the Gemara chooses to frame the question through the lens of *tziruf* rather than *zeh ve-zeh gorem*.

## Rat in Beer Case

### Rav Forbids

The Gemara now introduces a new case: *hahu akhbra de-nafal le-chavita de-shikhra* — a rat that fell into a barrel of beer (or mead). Rav ruled that the beer is forbidden. Tosafot raises the preliminary question of how the taste of the rat could have transferred to the cold beer, and suggests either that it sat in the liquid long enough for the taste to seep out — implicating the principle of *kavush ke-mevushal*, the debate among the *rishonim* about whether extended immersion in a cold liquid suffices to transfer taste — or perhaps the incident occurred while the beer was being processed and the liquid was still warm.

### Questioning Position

Upon hearing Rav's ruling, the Rabbis posed the question to Rav Sheshes: *neima kasavar nosein ta'am lifgam assur* — does this mean Rav holds that *nosein ta'am lifgam* is forbidden? A rat, after all, is naturally disgusting, and its taste in the beer would be a bad one. If Rav forbids even this, it would seem to indicate that he rules like Rabbi Meir against Rabbi Shimon on the fundamental question.

### Rat Disgust Chiddush

Rav Sheshes rejected this interpretation. He said: *be-alma savar Rav nosein ta'am lifgam mutar* — as a general rule, Rav holds that *nosein ta'am lifgam* is permitted. The rat case, however, is a *chiddush* — a novel and distinct situation. The reason: *damimas ma'is u-vdili inish minei* — rats are genuinely disgusting and people naturally recoil from them.

### Torah Ignores Taste

Rav Sheshes continues: *ve-afilu hachi asrei Rachmana* — and despite being disgusting, the Torah forbade the rat anyway. *Hilkhakh nosein ta'am lifgam nami assur* — therefore, when it comes to rats, *nosein ta'am lifgam* should also be forbidden. The argument, as understood by the *rishonim*, is as follows: ordinarily, the Torah forbids things that taste good, and therefore when something imparts only a bad taste, the principle of *nosein ta'am lifgam* exempts it. But the Torah's prohibition of rats teaches us that in this domain, we do not operate through the lens of taste at all — the rat is forbidden regardless of any consideration of palatability. This argument works especially well if one assumes a rat to be under normal circumstances entirely inedible: the Torah is essentially saying that even something which no person would want to eat is still forbidden to place in one's mouth. If that is the Torah's stance *be-ein* — regarding the rat itself — then the same logic applies to its taste: even *nosein ta'am lifgam* does not exempt it, because the Torah, when it comes to rats, is not operating through ordinary standards of taste.

### Yavesh Sheratzim

The Rabbis press a counterargument against Rav Sheshes: *ela mei'ata letamei lach ve-yavesh* — if your reasoning is correct, that we set aside ordinary standards of edibility and palatability when it comes to rats and *sheratzim*, then a rat should convey *tumah* even when dried out and desiccated. Yet the *mishnah* rules explicitly: *metamin lachin ve-ein metamin yeveshin* — *sheratzim* convey *tumah* when moist but not when dried out. The logic of the objection, as Tosafot explains, is that if we are prepared to say that ordinary measures of fitness for eating are irrelevant for rats and *sheratzim* — that they are forbidden even when inedible, disgusting, or not in any normal sense "food" — then by the same token we should not require that they be moist (i.e., in a food-like state) to convey *tumah*. The dried-out state should be no different.

### Lach Specification

Rav Sheshes responds with a counter-analogy. He turns the Rabbis' logic back on them: *shichvas zera tetamei lach ve-yavesh?* — by your reasoning, semen should also convey *tumah* whether moist or dried out, since semen is obviously not in the category of food and we do not apply ordinary standards of edibility to it. Yet we also learn *metamin lachin ve-ein metamin yeveshin* by semen. The Gemara resolves both cases through scriptural specification: for semen, the Torah writes *shichvas zera*, "the laying of seed," which the Gemara reads as requiring a state in which conception remains possible — *bera'uya lehazria* — thereby excluding dried semen. For *sheratzim*, the verse *be-motam* — "in their death" — is read as *ke-ein motam*, meaning in a state resembling how they were at death, i.e., moist, not desiccated. Both limitations are thus derived directly from the text of the Torah, and their application to *tumah* law does not undermine Rav Sheshes's argument about taste and prohibition.

## Rava's Conclusion

### Halacha Ruling

Rava states the normative conclusion: *hilkheta nosein ta'am lifgam mutar* — the *halacha* is that *nosein ta'am lifgam* is permitted. This is of considerable practical significance, as it undergirds a broad range of leniencies.

### Rav's Reasoning Unclear

As for the case of the rat in beer, Rava states: *lo yadana mai ta'ama de-Rav* — I do not know Rav's reason for forbidding it. There are two possibilities. Either Rav holds that *nosein ta'am lifgam* is *assur* as a general rule — in which case we do not rule like him — or Rav actually holds that *nosein ta'am lifgam* is *mutar*, but he believed that in this specific case *achbara be-shichra ashvuchi meshvach* — a rat in beer actually improves the taste of the beer, making it a case of *nosein ta'am le-shevach* rather than *lifgam*. Tosafot notes this latter possibility with some puzzlement, suggesting that perhaps the rat lent a certain pungency or strengthened the beer in some way. In any event, Rava's fundamental ruling is clear: the principle of *nosein ta'am lifgam* applies even to naturally disgusting substances, and even a rat's taste, if it is a bad taste, would in principle fall within the *hetter* of *nosein ta'am lifgam*.

### Be'ein vs. Ta'am

This leads to an important conceptual distinction made by the *rishonim*. One might ask: if the Torah forbids a rat even though it is disgusting and people recoil from it, should not *nosein ta'am lifgam* also be irrelevant in this case? The *rishonim* answer by drawing a sharp distinction between *be-ein* and *ta'am*. When one eats the actual rat itself — *be-ein* — the Torah prohibits it as long as it is edible, regardless of whether it tastes good or bad. One is eating the forbidden object itself. But when it comes to *ta'am*, the Torah prohibits something that qualifies as *ta'am* — taste — in the halachic sense. The principle derived from *neveilah* teaches that *ta'am lifgam* is not halachically considered *ta'am* at all. Something that is not normally desired as a taste does not constitute the kind of *ta'am* the Torah forbids. The object itself, consumed *be-ein*, is forbidden because one is eating the rat regardless of taste; but the imparted taste, if it is a bad taste, does not rise to the level of halachically significant *ta'am*, and the food into which it falls remains permitted. This distinction is what allows us to say that even the naturally repugnant rat, whose very existence in a food product one finds disgusting, does not render the food forbidden when it operates only through *nosein ta'am lifgam*. The practical ruling is that even a cockroach that falls into scrambled eggs would be *nosein ta'am lifgam* and the food would be *mutar*, notwithstanding the natural revulsion one feels toward the food — since that sense of disgust is itself what qualifies the taste as *lifgam*.

## Rat in Vinegar

### Vinegar Pungency

The Gemara poses a new question at the top of 69a: what is the law if the rat fell not into beer but into vinegar? As Rashi explains, the question is whether the extreme pungency of vinegar might prevent the rat from imparting any detectable taste at all — *hachometz ta'amo kasheh ve-ein ha-sheretz mafigo litet bo ta'am* — since the vinegar's sharp flavor might dominate and neutralize whatever the rat would otherwise contribute.

### Rav Kahana Case

Rav Hillel reports to Rav Ashi that a case of this nature arose in the academy of Rav Kahana, and Rav Kahana forbade the vinegar. The precise reasoning is not entirely clear — whether it is because the rat did not give a bad taste but rather enhanced or neutralized the taste in a way that made it *nosein ta'am le-shevach* or simply imparted no taste at all, with the assumption that a neutral imparting of taste is also problematic.

### Pieces Problem

Rav Ashi, however, clarifies that Rav Kahana's case was not a question of taste at all: *ha'u imrutay imratay* — there were actual small pieces of the rat that remained in the vinegar, making the issue one of *be-ein* rather than *ta'am*. Since it was the actual substance of the rat present in the vinegar, the question of *nosein ta'am lifgam* did not arise.

### Honey Bee Legs

This clarification about *be-ein* prompts Tosafot to raise a striking practical question: *heikhan anu okhlim devash dvorim* — how is it that we eat bee honey? Bee honey regularly contains fragments of bee legs, which are *be-ein* of a forbidden *sheretz*. The principle of *nosein ta'am lifgam* would not help, since the problem is the actual physical presence of the forbidden item. Tosafot answers in the name of Rabbeinu Tam: *hanach raglei dvorim kivan de-atzmot be-alma ninhu mutarin* — bee legs are essentially bones with no meat, and the bones of a forbidden creature without any attached meat are not forbidden. This is a fascinating exchange that reflects how careful the *rishonim* were to reconcile theoretical halachic principles with the everyday foods they actually consumed.

## Shiurei Bittul

### Ravina 101 Measure

The Gemara now turns to the question of *shiurei bittul* — the measures of nullification required for a rat that fell into beer. Ravina was inclined to require a ratio of a hundred and one, analogous to the nullification of *terumah*, which requires sixty plus one, i.e., a hundred and one parts of permitted food against one of *terumah* — *truma olah be-echad u-meah*. The thinking seems to be that even if the rat's taste in beer is arguably *lifgam*, one might want to treat it more strictly than ordinary *issurim*, requiring a more substantial majority for *bittul*.

### Spices Exception

Rav Tachlipa bar Gizla challenged Ravina: perhaps the rat in beer should be compared not to standard *terumah* but to spices of *terumah* — *tavlin shel trumah* — or similar substances that are *avida le-ta'ama*, made to impart taste, and which therefore cannot be *batel* at the standard ratio. Even a minute quantity of such spices renders its presence detectable, and accordingly a far greater ratio of permitted food may be needed before the taste is truly undetectable. Tosafot is careful to note that *avida le-ta'ama* items are not categorically incapable of *bittul* — it is not that they belong to a more severe class of *issur*. Rather, the practical reality is that they impart taste even in minute quantities, and so one must determine just how much permitted food is needed before the taste is genuinely neutralized — which could be a thousand parts or two thousand, but eventually *bittul* does occur.

### Acha: Fifty

Rav Acha offered a different measure: when the rat fell into vinegar, fifty parts of vinegar are sufficient to render it *batel*. The implication seems to be that vinegar's sharp pungency reduces the rat's flavor impact, requiring a smaller ratio for nullification.

### Shmuel: Sixty

Rav Shmuel the son of Rav Ika measured differently: for beer, sixty parts are sufficient for *bittul*.

### Final Halacha

The Gemara rules: *ve-hilkheta adidi va-adidi be-shishin, ve-khen kol issurim she-ba-Torah* — the *halacha* is that whether the forbidden item fell into vinegar or into beer, sixty is the required ratio, and the same standard of sixty applies to all *issurim* in the Torah. This is the foundational rule of *bittul be-shishim*, sixty-to-one nullification, here derived and codified from this discussion.

### Rashi Bittul Types

The ruling opens a discussion in Rashi about the distinction between *min be-mino* — a forbidden item that falls into the same type of food — and *min be-she'eino mino* — a forbidden item that falls into a different type. Rashi argues that *min be-mino* follows the standard of sixty, while *min be-she'eino mino* would require *be-mashu* — any detectable quantity would render the mixture forbidden. This is a position we do not rule in accordance with; the accepted *halacha* is that *min be-mino* also goes by sixty. The ruling of *shishim* here, it should be noted, applies to cases where the taste of the forbidden substance is genuine — *nosein ta'am le-shevach*. If the substance imparts only a bad taste — *nosein ta'am lifgam* — then as Rava has already ruled, the mixture is entirely *mutar*, and the question of the sixty-to-one ratio does not arise at all.

---

---

# Avodah Zarah 69

## Supervision & Trust

### Opening

Daf 69 continues the tractate's broader sweep through various areas of *kashrus* and halachic concern. Having dealt with questions of earning wages from non-Jews and the laws of forbidden mixtures, the Gemara now shifts to a distinct but related area: the question of whether one can trust that wine left in the presence or custody of a non-Jew has not been touched or tampered with. The animating concern is not merely theft or adulteration but the possibility that the non-Jew, finding himself unobserved, will either pour the wine as a libation — *yayin nesech* — or handle it in a way that renders it forbidden.

### Topic Shift

The governing principle that structures this entire discussion is *chezkas ha-mishtamer* — the presumption that the wine is being guarded — and the conditions under which that presumption holds or dissolves. The Mishna presents a series of cases that progressively test the edges of this principle, and the Gemara then probes each one for its logical underpinnings.

---

## Transport & Presumption

### Transport Case

The Mishna opens with the following scenario: a non-Jew was transporting barrels of wine belonging to a Jew from one location to another — *oved kokhavim she-hayah ma'avir im Yisrael kadei yayin mimakom lemakom*. The question is whether the Jew can trust that the wine has not been touched or replaced.

### Chezkas Mishtamer

The Mishna rules: *im hayah be-chezkas ha-mishtamer* — if the wine is in a state of *chezkas ha-mishtamer*, it is permitted. The simple reading of this phrase is that the Jew has not informed the non-Jew of any extended absence; the non-Jew therefore cannot be confident that the Jew will not appear at any moment. The contrast case is *im hodio she-hu maflig* — if the Jew explicitly told the non-Jew that he would be away for a period of time, giving the non-Jew a window in which he knows he will not be interrupted. In that case, the wine may become problematic depending on how long that window is.

The phrase *chezkas ha-mishtamer* thus captures something more than mere physical presence. It describes a state in which the possibility of surprise inspection is alive enough in the non-Jew's mind that he will not risk acting improperly. This will be clarified further by the Gemara's analysis of the *beraita* on workers.

### Time Thresholds

When the Jew has informed the non-Jew of his departure, what period of time triggers concern? The *Tanna Kamma* says: *kedei she-yistom ve-yistom* — enough time to pierce a hole in the sealed top of the barrel, siphon off some wine (or substitute inferior wine), and then replaster and reseal the hole, waiting for the plaster to dry. The concern is that a hole of this kind might not be detectable once properly filled. If the non-Jew has been given enough uninterrupted time to accomplish this, the wine is forbidden.

### Tanna/Rabban Debate

*Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* disagrees. He is not concerned about hole-piercing at all — as the Gemara will later explain, such tampering is always detectable. The only tampering he fears is something more drastic: *kedei she-yiftach es ha-chavis ve-yigov ve-yisnagov* — enough time to completely remove the barrel's cover, draw off wine, fashion a replacement cover, reseal it entirely, and allow the new seal to dry. This requires considerably more time than making a small hole, and it is only this lengthier process that *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* treats as grounds for concern.

---

## Wagon & Ship

### Wagon/Ship Case
