The Mishna then presents a second scenario: *ha-meniach yeino be-karon o be-sefinah* — a Jew who left his wine in a wagon or on a ship and then departed. Specifically, he took a shortcut — *ve-halach lo be-kapandarya* — and entered a town, perhaps to bathe. He was away from the wagon or ship for some period, having left the non-Jew alone with the wine.

### Absence Indication

The Mishna rules this *mutar* so long as the Jew did not declare how long he would be away. Even though he was visibly engaged in some activity at a distance, since he gave no explicit statement of duration, the non-Jew cannot rule out a sudden return. However, if he did say *im hodio she-hu maflig* — that he would be absent for a defined stretch — then the same time thresholds apply: according to the *Tanna Kamma*, enough time to pierce and reseal; according to *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel*, enough time to fully remove and replace the cover.

---

## Store Case

### Store Scenario

The third case: *ha-maniach oved kochavim be-chanuto* — a Jew who left a non-Jew unattended in his store. Whether this is a hired storekeeper or simply a customer left alone is not entirely clear from the text.

### Coming & Going

Here too, the Mishna rules *mutar* so long as the Jew did not specify the length of his absence, even if he was *yotzei ve-nichnas* — going in and out repeatedly. The phrase *yotzei ve-nichnas* is the classical formulation for a type of supervision that falls short of constant presence, yet is sufficient because the person being supervised never knows when the supervisor will next appear. It is worth noting that the Mishna's formulation is in fact *yotzei ve-nichnas* — one who is fundamentally present but occasionally steps out — rather than the inverse pattern, which might describe someone who merely drops in at intervals. The whole point of the leniency is that the non-Jew perceives the possibility of surprise arrival at any moment.

If, however, the Jew did announce his departure and its duration, the same thresholds apply: *kedei she-yistom ve-yistom ve-yigov* according to the *Tanna Kamma*, and *kedei she-yiftach es ha-chavis ve-yigafeiha ve-yachzor ve-tigof* according to *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel*.

---

## Table & Vessels

### Table Drinking

A fourth scenario: *haya ochel imo al ha-shulchan* — the Jew was eating and drinking at the same table as a non-Jew, serving non-*mevushal* wine. It is remarkable that the Mishna describes this situation at all. The Jew was presumably pouring and the non-Jew was not being given license to handle the wine during the shared meal.

### Open vs. Sealed

The complication arises when the Jew steps away: *ve-hiniach laginim al ha-shulchan ve-lagin al ha-dulbeki ve-hiniach ve-yatza* — he left pitchers (*laginim*) on the table and also a pitcher on the *dulbeki*, a kind of wine stand or counter (translated by some as "cupboard"), and then departed. The Mishna rules: *ma she-al ha-shulchan assur* — whatever is on the table is immediately forbidden.

This is striking because in all the earlier cases, the wine was permissible as long as no specific departure time was announced. Here, the wine on the table is forbidden even without such an announcement and even without giving the non-Jew any extended period of unsupervised time. Two factors converge to produce this stringency: first, the non-Jew has been drinking at the table and already feels a degree of freedom with respect to the wine; second, as Tosafot notes, the pitchers on the table are already open, so no special effort — no piercing a seal or removing a cover — is required to touch the wine. Even the fear of a surprise return is insufficient to protect open wine in that kind of setting.

### Table vs. Cupboard

By contrast, *ma she-al ha-dulbeki mutar* — what is on the cupboard or counter is permitted. The non-Jew does not feel the same degree of freedom with vessels that are not right in front of him at the table.

### Permissive Language

However, if the Jew said to the non-Jew at some point during the meal — *hevei mazeg ve-shoteh* — "help yourself, pour and drink" — then even the vessels on the *dulbeki* become forbidden. Once such an encouraging and permissive statement has been made, the non-Jew feels entirely at liberty to take from wherever the wine is stored, and *af shel dulbeki assur* — even what is on the counter is forbidden.

### Sealed Exception

The exception concerns sealed barrels. Even after a permissive statement like "make yourself at home," *chaviyot stumot mutarot* — sealed barrels remain permitted, because the non-Jew does not feel sufficiently at ease with respect to vessels that require significant effort to open. The sealed barrels revert to the general rule: they only become problematic once enough uninterrupted time has passed — namely, *kedei she-yiftach ve-yigof ve-tigov*, the time to remove and replace the entire cover, in accordance with *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel*'s position, whose ruling frames the end of the Mishna.

---

## Workers Beraita

### Beraita Setup

The Gemara now probes the precise meaning of *chezkas ha-mishtamer*. The Mishna contrasted it with *hodio she-hu maflig* — telling the non-Jew of a departure — but the phrase itself implies perhaps a more active form of oversight. To clarify, the Gemara cites a *beraita*: *harei she-hayu chamrav u-fo'alav te'unim taharot* — a case where one's donkey-drivers and workers were carrying produce in a state of *taharah* (purity), and the owner stepped away. The concern here is not *yayin nesech* but rather *tumah*: the workers are *amei ha-aretz* who may be careless about handling *tahor* items. If the owner left without announcing his absence, the produce remains *tahor*, even if he traveled more than a *mil* away — because the workers remain afraid he may reappear without warning.

### No Limit vs. Stated

The key distinction is between leaving without specifying an absence and saying *lechu va-ani ba achareichem* — "go on ahead, I'll catch up." Once he says that, the workers understand they have a guaranteed window of unsupervised time, and the moment they pass out of his sight — *keivan she-nitalma eino mehem* — the *taharot* are deemed *tamei*.

### Friend Concern

The Gemara raises an internal difficulty, however. If this *beraita* is dealing with open barrels of wine (or open containers of *tahor* produce), the concern about *tumah* arises not only from the workers themselves — who have been made *tahor* beforehand — but from any passing friend of theirs who might touch the items. An *am ha-aretz* does not mind if his friend touches his produce: *ein am ha-aretz makpid al maga chavero*. So even in the first case, once the owner is out of sight, even if no explicit announcement was made, surely one must worry that a *tamei* friend will come by?

### Shortcut Fear

Rava resolves this: *de-ba lehu derech al-achlasson* — the workers remain fearful even of an apparently absent owner because he might take a shortcut and reappear suddenly. The owner's ability to cut across an alternate path and arrive unexpectedly is what keeps the workers on guard even when he has gone some distance. This is exactly what *chezkas ha-mishtamer* means in our Mishna as well: it is not merely the absence of an explicit announcement, but the active possibility — appreciated by the non-Jew — that the owner could appear at any moment by an unexpected route. Once the owner says "I'll catch up," that element of surprise is removed — *samcha da'ataihu* — they relax, knowing he is definitively behind them, and the protection of *chezkas ha-mishtamer* dissolves.

---

## Three Cases Need

### Case Redundancy Q

The Gemara now asks the obvious question: given that all three cases in the Mishna — the porter, the wagon or ship, and the store — involve the same basic principle (non-Jew alone with wine, departure announced or not), why enumerate them separately? If the rule is identical, one case would suffice.

### Scenario Risks

The Gemara answers that each case presents a counterintuitive consideration that makes it seem as though the general rule should not apply there. The Mishna therefore teaches explicitly that the same principle governs in each situation, despite the unique features that might suggest otherwise.

### Boat Opportunity

In the wagon or boat case, one might have thought that a non-Jew who sees the Jew depart from the boat into a town — engaging in what will clearly be a time-consuming activity — will feel entirely confident that he has a free hand. Even if no explicit time was stated, leaving a boat and going into a town seems to communicate an extended absence more clearly than simply getting a bit ahead on a road. The *chiddush* is that even here, the non-Jew cannot be certain: perhaps the owner will stand at the dock and observe him; perhaps he will take an alternate route back. The Gemara phrases this as *dilma atei be-orcha achrisi ve-kai aguda ve-chazei lei* — perhaps he will come by a different road and stand at the shore and see him. The fear of discovery through such means is sufficient to maintain *chezkas ha-mishtamer*.

### Store Discovery

Similarly, in the store case, one might reason that the non-Jew left alone in a locked store will simply lock the door and proceed to do whatever he wishes without fear of interruption. The Mishna teaches that this reasoning does not apply.

### Discovery Deterrent

The *chiddush* of the store case is the sufficiency of the fear of being caught having locked the door. If the owner returns and finds the door bolted from the inside, he will demand an explanation. That fear alone — even without any specification of time — is enough to keep the non-Jew in check. The principle at work here is that it is the psychological pressure of potential surprise discovery, not the formal announcement of a timed absence, that determines whether *chezkas ha-mishtamer* applies.

---

## Plaster vs. Tar

### Seal Material

Having established when *chezkas ha-mishtamer* fails and what window of time then becomes legally significant, the Gemara turns to the debate between the *Tanna Kamma* and *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* — specifically, the question of whether one must fear that the non-Jew made a small hole and resealed it, or only that he removed the entire cover and replaced it. Rabbah bar bar Chana said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *machlokes be-shel sid* — their dispute applies only where the seal of the barrel is made of plaster. When the seal is white plaster, a repaired hole on the surface may look identical to the surrounding material. That is the context in which the *Tanna Kamma* worries about undetectable tampering.

By contrast, if the seal is made of *tit* — a dark tar-like substance — *divrei ha-kol kedei she-yiftach ve-yigof ve-yigov*: everyone agrees we only fear the removal and replacement of the entire cover, because a hole patched with lighter material in a dark tar seal would be immediately obvious. There is no debate in the tar case.

### Plaster Detection

The logic of the plaster debate requires some elaboration. If the cover is plaster and a small hole is made from above and then refilled, the question is whether the repair is detectable. *Milma'alah* — from the top surface — it may look seamless, especially since plaster can be smoothed over to match the surrounding color. *Milmatah* — from underneath the cover — the repair may be more evident: the fill will not have been smoothed from below, may leave a visible gap, and the newer material may be a different shade from the older plaster that has been in contact with wine.

### RSBG Challenge

*Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* presents a challenge to the *Chachamim*: *ve-halo situmo nikar bein milma'alah bein milmatah* — is not the patching visible both above and below? The Gemara explains that *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* was not certain which material the *Chachamim* were discussing. His challenge was structured as a dilemma: if you are speaking of a tar seal, the patch is obvious both above and below, so there is no reason to fear hole-piercing at all — both sides should agree. If you are speaking of plaster, I still challenge you: even if the top looks fine, the underside will reveal the tampering.

### Thief Assumption

The *Chachamim* respond: *keivan de-lemala lo yedia, lo massik adaateih de-appik ve-chazei lei* — since from the surface nothing appears amiss, the would-be thief simply does not think ahead to the possibility that someone will remove the cover and inspect the underside. He convinces himself that the top looks normal, that he will get away with it, and does not mentally project far enough to realize that the bottom will reveal him. Furthermore, *zimnin de-chalim* — sometimes the fill does eventually blend in below as well, and the thief may count on this. This explains why the *Tanna Kamma* takes the hole-piercing scenario seriously in the plaster case: the thief believes he can execute it without detection.

---

## Halachic Ruling

### Halacha Decision

Rava rules: *halacha ke-Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* — the law follows *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel*. We do not fear the small-hole scenario; the only concern is the wholesale removal and replacement of the cover.

### Stam Mishna

The evidentiary basis for this ruling is the structure of the Mishna itself. The Mishna's final case — the case of eating at the table with a non-Jew — concludes with the ruling about sealed barrels: *chaviyot stumot mutarot, kedei she-yiftach ve-yigof ve-tigov*. This formulation quotes only the position of *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* and does so without attribution — it appears as a *stam mishna*, an anonymous ruling. An anonymous ruling at the end of a Mishna indicates the normative halachic position.

The Gemara briefly asks whether this is even a novel point — surely it is obvious from the *stam mishna* that we rule accordingly. The response is that one might have read the final passage of the Mishna not as a *stam* ruling but as a continuation of *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel*'s quoted position earlier in that same case. The Gemara therefore establishes explicitly: the closing lines of the Mishna function as an independent, anonymous normative statement, not merely as the tail of *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel*'s attributed opinion.

---

## Sealed Wine Problem

### Logic Problem

With the halachic ruling in place, the Gemara raises a searching and practically significant question. We have now established two things: first, that we rule like *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* and are not concerned about hole-piercing — only the wholesale removal of the seal; second, that we rule like Rabbi Eliezer (from an earlier chapter) that a single seal suffices to protect wine in transit. These two rulings together seem to eliminate nearly every ground for concern when leaving sealed wine in the custody of a non-Jew.

### Single Seal

The relevance of the ruling like Rabbi Eliezer is this: the earlier dispute about *chotam* and *chotam betoch chotam* — single versus double seal — was resolved in favor of Rabbi Eliezer, who holds that one seal is sufficient. The practical meaning is that a sealed barrel with one intact seal can be trusted; we are not worried that the seal was broken and forged.

### Permission Challenge

The Gemara therefore asks: *ve-chi me-achar de-kaima lan ke-vatteih de-Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel de-lo chaishinan le-situmi, ve-hilchesa ke-vatteih de-Rabbi Eliezer de-lo chaishinan le-ziyufa* — now that we are not afraid of a small pierced hole, and we are not afraid of seal-forging, what exactly are we afraid of when we restrict leaving sealed wine with non-Jews at all? Why not simply leave a sealed barrel of wine with a non-Jew indefinitely?

---

## Shaika Air Hole

### Siphon Method

The Gemara answers: *mishum sheika* — because of the *sheika*. The *sheika* is a tiny air hole that was made in the stopper of the barrel to allow the wine's aroma to escape — a standard feature of how barrels were constructed. Through this tiny hole, a non-Jew could insert a thin straw or tube and siphon off wine without breaking the seal at all. This does not require piercing a new hole (which would be detectable), forging a seal (which is prevented by the single seal's integrity), or removing the cover (which is the threshold *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* requires). It exploits a pre-existing aperture.

### Hole Authorities

Rashi explains *sheika* as *nekev dak me'od she-be-migufas chavit le-hotzi rei'ach ha-yayin* — a very fine hole in the barrel's stopper to allow the wine's scent to exit — and notes that the concern is that the non-Jew will *yashuf sham, yekadei'ach sham be-miktzat ve-yitom min ha-yayin* — probe that hole with a straw and taste or draw off wine. Tosafot offers a similar reading, differing slightly in the precise terminology but arriving at the same functional concern.

### Wood Plank Risk

For barrels made of wood rather than pottery, the concern is structurally analogous, as Tosafot explains. Wooden barrels are constructed from planks (*nissarim*) fitted together, and a thin knife blade inserted between the planks can create a gap through which a straw could be inserted to siphon wine — *she-yitkevuhu ovdei kochavim be-chudo shel sakkin bein ha-nissarim* — and this would not constitute the detectable tampering that *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* requires. Thus, even for the wooden barrels of medieval Europe, the *sheika* concern applied in a functionally equivalent form, and the question of what protections were required for transporting wine remained practically urgent.

---

## Tosafot Sealing

### Owner Inspection

Tosafot undertakes an extended analysis of how the rulings on *chotam* and *ziyuf* translate into practical guidance for transporting wine. One approach, consistent with ruling like Rabbi Eliezer, is that a single seal is sufficient when the owner himself will later inspect the barrel. If the owner knows what his own seal looked like and will examine it upon return, a single intact seal gives him enough information to determine whether it has been tampered with.

### Seal vs. Delivery

This basis for the leniency breaks down, however, in a delivery scenario. If the owner sends the sealed barrel with a non-Jew to a recipient — Chanan, for example — the recipient has never seen the original seal and cannot tell whether it has been broken and reforged. In such a case, more protection may be required.

### Minhag Olam

Tosafot acknowledges that the prevalent practice — *minhag ha-olam* — had already been to send wine with a single sealed barrel even without the recipient recognizing the seal. Tosafot is prepared to validate this practice *be-di'avad* at minimum, noting that the *stam* Gemara's ruling like Rabbi Eliezer supports it. The text reads: *vegam minhag ha-olam haya she-kevar lishloach yayin be-chotam echad belo chozer u-makiro* — the practice was already to send wine with one seal without the sender going back to inspect it personally.

### Wood vs. Pottery

Rabbeinu Yitzchak ben Yehuda raised the issue with Rashi that the barrels of the Talmudic period, being pottery, are not equivalent to the wooden barrels of medieval France and Germany. For pottery barrels, a single seal on the mouth of the barrel was sufficient. But for wooden barrels made of fitted planks, even with a seal on the top, the planks themselves are a vulnerability — *be-chudo shel sakkin bein ha-nissarim* — and wine can be extracted without disturbing the seal at all. Rabbeinu Yitzchak therefore held that wooden barrels require additional protection beyond what sufficed for pottery.

### Vessel Recognition

Even setting aside the question of how the barrel itself might be breached, Tosafot identifies a further concern: complete substitution of the barrel. The non-Jew need not break the seal at all; he can simply replace the entire barrel with a different one bearing an intact seal of his own. Against this concern, Tosafot argues that *hakarat ha-kli* — recognition of the vessel — is necessary: the recipient must be familiar enough with the specific barrel to know that it is the same one that was sent. If he cannot recognize it, he has no assurance that what he received is what was dispatched, regardless of the seal's condition.

### Multi-Layer Seal

Tosafot proceeds to enumerate additional protective measures that address these vulnerabilities. Wrapping the barrel in leather (*or*) affixed with nails prevents access between the planks. This leather covering functions as an additional layer of protection over and above the sealed top, ensuring that a knife cannot be inserted into the joins.

### Signature Seal

The most sophisticated protection Tosafot describes is the *signature-across-seam* method, analogous to signing one's name across the flap of an envelope. One writes Hebrew letters (*osiyot*) with half the letter on the leather covering and half on the body of the barrel itself — *chatzyan al ha-or ve-chatzyan al dofnei karshei ha-chavis*. If the non-Jew were to lift the leather, he could not realign it to restore the appearance of the original inscription. Moreover, since the letters are in Hebrew, the non-Jew cannot replicate them. Metal bands (*chashuk*) are then placed around the barrel to secure the leather in position.

The practical conclusion that emerges from Tosafot's discussion spans a wide spectrum. At the most lenient end, *be-di'avad* any single-sealed barrel may be trusted. At the other extreme, full protection requires leather wrapping, Hebrew lettering across the seam, metal bands, and recipient recognition of the vessel. The *lechatchila* standard sits somewhere in the middle: at a minimum, the air hole must be sealed — the *sheika* must be blocked — and ideally Hebrew lettering should be present so that any tampering with the seal would destroy the letters in a way the non-Jew cannot repair.

---

## Prostitute Cases

### Goy Prostitute

The Gemara now presents what is, by any measure, a striking scenario. Rava states: *zona ovedes kochavim ve-Yisrael mesubin etzlah* — a non-Jewish prostitute, with a Jewish man as her patron, eating and drinking wine at her table.

### Control Determinant

The ruling is: *chamar shari* — the wine is permitted. We are not concerned that the wine was touched improperly or used for libation.

### Separate Sins

The reasoning is carefully drawn: *nehi de-takif lei yitzra de-aveira* — granted that he has a powerful *yeitzer hara* for this particular transgression, specifically the sexual sin he is clearly committing. *Yitzra de-yayin nesech lo takif lei* — his inclination toward *yayin nesech*, toward using wine as a libation or permitting it to be handled improperly, is not similarly activated. The fact that a person transgresses in one domain does not mean he is reckless across all domains. One who will violate the laws of sexual morality does not necessarily give his companion license to touch his wine, and his own care for *kashrus* does not dissolve merely because he is sinning in another regard. The wine, therefore, remains his to control, and we assume he has not permitted it to be touched.

### Jewish Prostitute

The reverse scenario is then presented: *zonah yisre'elit ve-ovdei kochavim mesubin* — a Jewish prostitute with a non-Jewish patron.

### Follower Status

Here the ruling is reversed: *chamra asir* — the wine is forbidden.

### Patron Control Logic

The Gemara explains: *ho'il ve-zila aleihu, batraihu grira* — since she has made herself lowly before him, she follows after him. The logic is that in the relationship between a prostitute and her patron, it is the patron who holds the position of control and the prostitute who defers. When the patron is Jewish, he determines what happens to the wine — he controls the situation, maintains his own standards, and does not give her license to handle it improperly. When the patron is non-Jewish, the dynamic is inverted: she defers to him, and either she will permit him to handle the wine freely or she herself will act in accordance with his will, which may include offering the wine as a libation. In either case, the wine comes under his effective control, and since he is a non-Jew whose handling renders wine forbidden, the wine is prohibited.

---

---

# Avodah Zarah 70

## Crack in Door

### Locked Door Case

The daf opens with a case that tests the limits of supervision over Jewish wine. A house contained wine belonging to a Jew. A non-Jew entered, locked the door — closing it in the Jew's face — and was subsequently found standing among the barrels when the Jew gained entry. The locking of the door is significant: one of the standard concerns about leaving a non-Jew unattended in a store is precisely that he might lock the door, thereby gaining unsupervised access to the wine. Here, he has done exactly that.

Rava rules: *kol delehadi biza shari* — any barrel situated directly opposite the crack in the door is permitted. The barrels on either side of that crack, where there was no line of sight from outside, are forbidden.

### Line of Sight

The operative principle is that the non-Jew's awareness that he might be observed is what restrains him from handling the wine. Barrels positioned opposite the crack could, in principle, be seen from outside. Whether or not anyone was actually looking through the crack at the moment is beside the point; the non-Jew's knowledge that the crack existed and that those barrels were visible is sufficient to establish that he would have refrained from touching them. Barrels beyond the line of sight enjoy no such protection.

One might ask what the ruling would be had the non-Jew not been found among the barrels at all — had he been found, say, elsewhere in the house upon entry. It is not entirely clear how much his presence *among* the barrels is the generating concern here, as opposed to the mere fact that he locked the door. What the ruling establishes, in any case, is that even given the locked door and the discovery among the barrels, proximity to the crack rehabilitates those particular barrels.

---

## Housemates

### Upper/Lower Story

The Gemara continues with a related scenario. A Jew and a non-Jew shared a house: the Jew resided in the upper story, the non-Jew in the lower, with the wine — belonging to the Jew — stored in the lower story. Rashi explains that the arrangement itself constituted effective supervision: the Jew could look down at any moment, perhaps from a balcony or an interior overlook, and the non-Jew knew this. The possibility of being observed at any time kept the wine safe.

### Fighting Interruption

The normal arrangement is then disrupted. Both the Jew and the non-Jew heard the sound of a fight outside (*shamu kol tigra*) and ran out to see what was happening. When things settled, the non-Jew returned first and locked the door — he is now alone with the wine, behind a locked door, and the Jew is outside.

### Fear of Return

Rava rules that the wine is still permitted. The reasoning: the non-Jew will say to himself, *ki heichi dekadim ata'i ana, kadim ve'ata Yisrael* — just as I rushed back first, the Jew may well have rushed back too and is already sitting upstairs watching me. The non-Jew cannot be certain that his quick return gave him any exclusive advantage. He must assume, plausibly enough, that the Jew may be back in the upper story and observing.

This parallels the logic of the crack in the door: it is not actual observation that matters, but the reasonable possibility of it. If the non-Jew had good reason to think the Jew might be present and watching, the wine is protected. One might wonder whether the result would differ if the circumstances made it obvious to the non-Jew that the Jew was nowhere near — for instance, had the Jew visibly gone to summon the authorities. Rava's ruling does not address that scenario; it addresses the case as given, where the non-Jew simply cannot be certain.

---

## Nitpas K'Ganav

### Inn Barrels

The Gemara presents a third scenario. At an inn containing Jewish wine, a non-Jew is discovered among the barrels. There is no locked door, no interrupted arrangement — simply a non-Jew found in the middle of the barrels. Rava issues a conditional ruling.

### Consequences Test

*Im nitpas alav k'ganav shari* — if, had he been discovered mishandling the wine, he would have faced consequences, the wine is permitted. The concern that he would be caught and punished is what would have restrained him. An earlier comment from Rashi suggests that a person in a position of power or social protection — someone who knows that people would look the other way even if he were caught — falls into a different category, as does someone who could offer a plausible excuse for what he was doing.

### No Consequences

If, however, being discovered handling the wine would carry no consequences — whether because he has sufficient social cover, a ready excuse, or some other reason — the wine is forbidden. In that case, the deterrent does not operate, and one must assume he did handle the wine.

This is, as the Gemara frames it, a clarification and elaboration of the principle underlying the *mishnah*: the cases in the *mishnah* where wine left unattended remains permitted are precisely cases where the non-Jew fears the Jew might return unexpectedly. *Nitpas alav k'ganav* is the articulation of that fear: what holds him back is the prospect of being caught and facing consequences.

---

## Excuse vs Consequences

### House Barrels

A new case: a house — not an inn — containing wine, and a non-Jew found among the barrels. Rava rules conditionally.

### Has Excuse

*Ei it lei l'ishtamutei, chamra assur* — if he has an excuse for why he is in this room at all, the wine is forbidden.

### No Excuse

*Ve'ei lo, chamra shari* — if he has no excuse for being there, the wine is permitted.

### Rashi Explains

This seems, at first, precisely backwards. Surely a non-Jew found among the barrels without any excuse should be the *more* suspicious case? Rashi's explanation clarifies the distinction. If the non-Jew has an excuse for being in the room — some legitimate or semi-legitimate reason he can offer for his presence — then he feels at ease. He does not feel rushed, he does not feel exposed, and he therefore has the leisure to linger and handle the wine. It is precisely his sense of security that makes the situation more dangerous. If he has no excuse at all for being in the room, he knows he is entirely out of place. He is anxious, he feels the pressure of potential discovery at any moment, and that anxiety prevents him from tarrying long enough to handle the wine.

The Gemara confirms this reading by testing it against a related teaching: if a store was locked or a non-Jew was told to stand guard, the wine inside is forbidden. The apparent challenge is that this is a case where the non-Jew has no excuse for being inside — and yet it is forbidden. The Gemara answers: *lo, bede'it lei l'ishtamutei* — no, it is precisely a case where he *does* have an excuse. He has been stationed there with a role; he has reason to believe he is permitted to be present. It is that legitimizing context that creates the concern.

### Right to Be

The deeper structural distinction between *nitpas alav k'ganav* and *aishtemutei* now comes into relief. *Nitpas alav k'ganav* applies in cases where the non-Jew has a right to be in the location — he is at an inn, he shares a building, he is in a store where he belongs. The question in those cases is entirely about whether he would face consequences for reaching into the wine itself. As long as he would face consequences for that act, everything is fine. *Aishtemutei* applies in cases where he has no right to be in the room at all. There, the question shifts to his overall willingness to be in a compromised position. If he is willing to be in a room where he has no business being — and he has no excuse to offer — that very brazenness is a sign of anxiety and exposure, and paradoxically the wine is safer. If, however, he has a cover story that explains his presence, he has already demonstrated a readiness to enter compromised territory with a plan, and the wine is at risk.

---

## Companions

### Mincha Return

The Gemara turns to a series of cases involving a Jew and a non-Jew who are companions, where the Jew leaves wine unattended — and the question is whether the non-Jew believes the Jew will return. In the first case, the non-Jew is presumed to reason that his Jewish companion will remember he left wine behind and come back to check on it.

### Mincha Service

A Jew and a non-Jew are sitting and drinking wine together. The Jew hears the congregation beginning to pray in the synagogue — it is *mincha* time — and he gets up and leaves, leaving his wine at the table with the non-Jew. Rava rules that the wine is permissible. The reasoning: *meimar amar, hashta midkar lehu lechamra ve-hadar atei* — the non-Jew says to himself, my companion is not so scrupulous that he will forget about his wine; he will remember it is sitting here and he will duck out of *shemoneh esreh* to come back and check on me. The Jew's departure to *mincha* is not analogous to a declared absence with a known duration. It is an interruption, and the non-Jew has reason to think it will be a short one.

### Shabbat Preparation

A Jew and a non-Jew are on a boat together. The Jew hears the shofar blast at evening time — Rashi notes elsewhere that the sounding of the shofar at nightfall signaled the onset of *Shabbat*, as is still the practice in Jerusalem — and he disembarks to prepare for *Shabbat*. Now the non-Jew might well feel safe: the Jew has to prepare his *Shabbat* meal, attend synagogue, observe the day — surely he will not return to the boat on *Shabbat*. Rava again rules the wine is permissible.

### Shabbat Money

Why? Rava cites a remarkable teaching in the name of Issur Giyora, a convert who shared with Rava what non-Jews used to say about Jews when he was still among them: *yudai lo mantri Shabta* — Jews do not really observe *Shabbat*. The basis for this perception: *kama kissay mishtakchay b'shuka* — if they really kept *Shabbat*, you would find wallets lying all over the marketplace, because Jews trade in the marketplace right up until the moment *Shabbat* begins, and if they were genuinely committed to the day, they would simply drop whatever they were carrying the instant darkness fell. Since they do not, non-Jews concluded that Jewish *Shabbat* observance dissolves when money is at stake.

### Wallet Precedent

The Gemara acknowledges the uncomfortable accuracy lurking in this perception. The rabbis were aware that Jews would be tempted to violate *Shabbat* to protect their money, and so they instituted a dispensation: one may carry a wallet home on *Shabbat* by taking steps of less than four *amos* at a time, never technically performing a full *carrying* act in the public domain, following the ruling of Rabbi Yitzchak. The very existence of this dispensation is a concession to the reality that anxiety about money creates pressure on *Shabbat* observance. The non-Jewish perception was not unfounded.

In the context of the boat case, this means the non-Jew on the boat reasons: my Jewish companion left to keep *Shabbat*, but he also left all his wine here with me. He knows that Jews, when it comes to protecting their assets, are not inclined to let *Shabbat* stand in the way. So he expects the Jew to come back and check on his wine even on *Shabbat*. That ongoing apprehension keeps the non-Jew from handling the wine, and therefore it remains permitted.

---

## Thieves & Troops

### Lion Case

The Gemara presents a sequence of cases in which non-Jews are found among wine barrels under unusual circumstances. In the first, a lion was roaring in the winepress. A non-Jew, hearing the lion, fled and hid among the barrels for protection. Should one be concerned that, while hiding there, he drank some wine or performed some act of *nisuch*?

### Mutual Fear

Rava rules the wine is permitted. *Meimar amar ki heichi d'tashina ana, itshu nami Yisraeli achorei v'chazu li* — the non-Jew reasons: the same way I came running to hide among the barrels, so did the Jews, and they are watching me right now. The same emergency that drove the non-Jew to the barrels would equally have driven the Jewish owners there, and the non-Jew cannot be confident he is alone.

### Thieves Pumbedita

A gang of thieves (*ganavim*) came to Pumbedita and broke open many barrels of wine. Rava rules the wine is permitted.

### Thieves Jewish

Why? *Ruba ganvay Yisrael ninhu* — the majority of thieves in this context are Jewish. A note clarifies what Rava means: he is speaking of Mechuza, his own city, where the population was predominantly Jewish. In Mechuza, the majority of residents — and therefore the majority of thieves — were Jews. One should not assume that thieves who broke into Jewish wine storage were non-Jews; more likely they were Jews, in which case there is no concern of *yayin nesech*. Rava, who was known to have a complicated relationship with the people of Mechuza, was evidently not above characterizing his city's majority Jewish population as the primary source of local theft.

### Nehardea Case

The Gemara then records a case in Nehardea, where the population was not majority Jewish. Thieves opened barrels of wine, and Shmuel ruled the wine permitted. This is more striking, since in Nehardea one cannot simply appeal to a majority of Jewish thieves.

### Double Doubt

The Gemara asks whether Shmuel is following Rabbi Eliezer, who holds *safek bi'ah tahor* — that a doubtful entry into a domain where *tumah* is present does not render one *tamei*. The parallel is drawn from the teaching about one who entered a field during the rainy season (*yemot ha-geshamim*), when fields are considered *reshut ha-yachid* because their owners do not want them trampled, and a body is buried in one of the fields. If the person does not even know which field he entered, Rabbi Eliezer holds he is *tahor*, since there is a doubt about the entry itself (*safek bi'ah*), as distinct from a doubt about contact (*safek maga*) — the latter being *tamei* in a private domain.

The Gemara declines to rest the ruling on Rabbi Eliezer alone. Instead, it invokes a *sefek sefeka* — a double doubt. Even granting that the thieves were non-Jewish, there are two independent reasons to think they did not handle the wine: first, perhaps they did not touch it even after opening the barrel; and second — which Rashi identifies as the operative structure — their motivation was not wine but money. Thieves who systematically break open barrel after barrel are looking for hidden cash, not wine. Seeing wine, they likely moved on. Because the non-Jew's purpose was to search for valuables rather than to consume or handle the wine, there is a second layer of doubt even once his presence is established. The Gemara notes that Tosafot connects this to the structure of *safek bi'ah* itself: Rabbi Eliezer's ruling is also, in effect, a double doubt — whether one entered the right field at all, and whether one then walked over the body.

---

## Froth Case

### Froth Discovery

A non-Jewish girl was found among the wine barrels with wine froth on her hand. The concern: did she insert her hand into a barrel, producing the froth as evidence of contact with the wine?

### Outside Froth

Rava rules the wine is permitted. *Eimor migaba de'chavita shaklata* — assume she took the froth from the outside of the barrel, not from inside. Even if no froth remains visible on the exterior of the barrel — which might seem to eliminate that explanation — Rava adds: *eimor isrumei isramila* — assume it simply dried or disappeared by chance, and what was on her hand is all that remained. This reasoning is, as the discussion acknowledges, somewhat generous. The assumption that the froth came from the exterior rather than the interior, especially when none is visible on the exterior, does require a measure of interpretive charity.

### Child Awareness

Rashi adds a further consideration: she is a young girl. There was a prior discussion in the *masechet* about children who are not yet aware of the context of *avodah zarah*. For such a child, even actual contact with wine does not create a concern of *yayin nesech*, since the prohibition is predicated on the act being meaningful within an idolatrous framework — which a young child has not yet internalized.

---

## Thieves & Troops (II)

### Troop Barrels

A *polmusa* — a troop, or as Rashi explains, perhaps referring to a military commander — came to Nehardea and opened many barrels. Rav Dimi reported that a similar case came before Rabbi Elazar, who permitted the wine.

The Gemara considers two possible grounds for the ruling: perhaps Rabbi Elazar holds like Rabbi Eliezer (*safek bi'ah tahor*), or perhaps he holds that the majority of those accompanying such troops were Jewish, making it more likely that the barrels were opened by Jews. The Gemara then tests this: if the majority were not Jewish and the barrels were nonetheless opened, is that not a *safek maga* — a straightforward single doubt about contact — rather than a *safek bi'ah*?

The answer lies in the number of barrels opened. If only one or two had been opened, one might assume the troops were simply thirsty and took what they needed, making the question one of contact. But because they opened many barrels (*miftachi tuva*), it becomes apparent they were searching for money. That purpose — looking for hidden cash rather than wanting the wine — reintroduces the second layer of doubt even when the soldiers are presumed non-Jewish. They saw wine, but wine was not what they came for. Therefore, even though non-Jews definitively opened the barrels, one cannot assume they handled the wine itself, and the double doubt structure applies: the wine is permitted.

This clarifies the earlier discussion about the Pumbedita case. The critical variable is the searchers' motivation. When motivation is ambiguous — wine or money — that ambiguity produces the second doubt necessary to permit the wine. When thieves or troops open many barrels systematically, that pattern of behavior is itself evidence that money, not wine, was the goal.

---

## Tumah Parallels

### Key Guardian

The Gemara presents a case with a different structure. A female wine seller (*musavisa*, as Rashi explains it) gave the key to her wine cabinet to a non-Jew. Having handed him the key, must one now be concerned that he accessed the wine? Rav Yitzchak citing Rav Elazar reported that this very case was discussed in the *beit midrash*, and the ruling was: *lo masrah ella shemirat hamafteach bilvad* — she handed him the job of watching the key, not the right to access the cabinet. His mandate was custodial, not accessory. Since he was not authorized to enter the cabinet and he would face consequences for doing so without authorization — a clear instance of *nitpas alav k'ganav* — the wine is permitted.

### Tahara Keys

Abaye notes that this ruling has a precise parallel in the laws of *taharah*. A *mishnah* teaches: if one handed over keys to a storehouse containing *tahor* fruit to an *am ha'aretz*, the fruit remains *tahor* — *taharotav tehorot* — because the *am ha'aretz* was given custodianship of the key, not access to the fruit (*shemirat hamafteach bilvad*). The parallel is exact.

### Weights Compare

Abaye then draws a *kal va-chomer*: if this leniency applies in the domain of *tumah ve-taharah*, where we are more readily inclined to identify a problem, then *yein nesech* concerns — which Abaye treats as the less weighty category — certainly should not be more stringent. If guarding the key without the right of access is sufficient to protect *tahor* fruit, it is certainly sufficient to protect wine.

This comparative claim — that *tumah ve-taharah* is the weightier concern — is taken up explicitly by the Gemara as a substantive question.

### Adjacent Yards

Rav addresses a case of two adjacent yards separated by a low hedge or demarcating row of stones (*maspis*). On one side is a *chaver*, careful in matters of *tumah ve-taharah*; on the other, either a non-Jew or an *am ha'aretz*. Rav rules: if the neighbor is an *am ha'aretz*, the *chaver*'s fruit is *tamei* — the low boundary line is insufficient to prevent concern that the *am ha'aretz* crossed over and touched the fruit. But if the neighbor is a non-Jew, the wine is not rendered *yayin nesech* — the same boundary line is adequate protection in that domain. This is Rav's concrete expression of the hierarchical claim: we treat the possibility of *tumah* more seriously and are more ready to find a problem there than we are in the domain of wine.

What accounts for the asymmetry is not entirely spelled out. It may relate to the respective weights the tradition assigns these bodies of law, or to differing assessments of likelihood — an *am ha'aretz* neighbor may be considered more likely to casually cross a boundary line than a non-Jew is to cross into a neighbor's yard specifically to handle wine.

### Boundary Sufficient

Rabbi Yochanan disagrees. He rules *af taharotav tehorot* — the boundary line is sufficient protection even for *taharah* purposes. For Rabbi Yochanan, there is no meaningful hierarchy between the two domains at this level of analysis; the same logic of *ein lo lishtatmutei* (he has no excuse for crossing) applies equally in both. He has no right to be in the other yard; the demarcation is clear; and therefore one does not assume he crossed over.

### Rooftop Reach

The Gemara brings further cases to test the limits of these positions. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel rules: if a *chaver*'s rooftop is higher than the adjacent *am ha'aretz*'s rooftop, the *chaver* may spread fruit and place vessels there — provided the *am ha'aretz*'s hand cannot reach up to that level. If the hand *can* reach, it is a problem even for *taharah* purposes.

### Excuse Debate

A subsequent teaching presents the case of adjacent side-by-side rooftops, where the *am ha'aretz*'s hand can reach the *chaver*'s fruit — and yet the *chaver* may place fruit and vessels there. This appears to contradict Rav's position, since it suggests a boundary line (or in this case, rooftop demarcation) is sufficient even for *tumah ve-taharah* when there is no excuse for crossing.

The Gemara works through the apparent contradictions between these sources, distributing them between Rav and Rabbi Yochanan. Rav responds to the side-by-side rooftop case by aligning himself with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who takes the stricter position: if the hand can physically reach, it is a concern regardless. Rabbi Yochanan responds to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling about the higher rooftop by invoking *aishtemutei*: even there, the person stretching his arm up to a higher rooftop has an excuse — *meimar amri im mitzrei ka memtzina*, I was measuring how tall your building is, or as Rashi alternatively reads it, I was simply stretching, exercising, yawning. The excuse is admittedly weak, but Rashi's point is that some minimally plausible excuse exists, and that is sufficient to create concern.

When one distills the underlying agreement, both authorities accept the same framework: if there is a legitimate excuse for the reaching or crossing, the concern is real; if there is no excuse, the boundary is protected. Their dispute concerns only specific cases — whether, in a given configuration, a minimally colorable excuse exists. This same principle of *nitpas k'ganav* and *aishtemutei* that drove the wine cases applies throughout the laws of *tumah ve-taharah* as well.

---

## Peace War Troops

### Peacetime

The *mishnah* with which the daf concludes presents the case of *boleshet* — a troop — entering a city. Rashi explains the term derives from a root meaning to search out; these are soldiers moving through a town, confiscating food and supplies. If they enter *bi-sh'at shalom* — in peacetime — then open barrels are forbidden and sealed barrels are permitted. If they were already open, one assumes the troops helped themselves; sealed barrels they would have had no reason to open.

### Wartime

But if the troops are engaged in active combat — *bi-sh'at milchamah* — then both open and closed barrels are permitted, *lefi she-ein penai lenasech* — because they have no leisure to perform *nisuch*. This is a striking ruling. Even if the troops are non-Jewish and they are in the middle of the wine, the wine remains permitted because the context of active warfare leaves no room for the deliberate act of idolatrous libation.

One might ask: even if they have no time for *nisuch*, surely they have time to drink, and surely a non-Jew who handles wine and drinks it creates a concern even without explicit *nisuch*? The *mishnah*'s ruling seems to imply that absent a *nisuch* context — absent the intent and leisure associated with idolatrous ritual — even non-Jewish handling of wine is not forbidden. This would be a significant statement about the nature of the prohibition.

### Distraction

The Gemara challenges from a separate ruling: if a city is besieged, all the wives of *kohanim* within it are rendered forbidden (*pesulot*), because one must assume that the besieging soldiers, when they breached the city, engaged in acts of rape — and a *kohen*'s wife who has had relations with a non-Jew, even under compulsion, is forbidden to her husband. So even in the midst of war, soldiers apparently find the opportunity for sexual violence. Why then would we say they have no time for *nisuch*?

Rav Mari resolves this directly: *lenasech ein penai, livol yesh penai* — for *nisuch* there is no leisure; for sexual violence there is. Rashi explicates: *d'yeitzer ha-nisuch lo takif lehu ve-trudei b'milchamah* — the impulse toward *nisuch* is not so powerful as to break through the distraction of combat. *Livol yesh penai d-takif lehu yitzraihu* — for the other, a more overpowering drive is at work. The act of sexual violence is driven by a *yetzer* that overwhelms even the pressure of battle; the ritual act of libation is not. Soldiers distracted by fighting will not stop to perform a deliberate religious rite, even if they would stop for other things.

This distinction carries an implicit but important principle: the concern of *yayin nesech* is not simply about a non-Jew physically contacting wine. It is about contact in the context of, or with the capacity for, deliberate idolatrous intention. Troops in the chaos of active warfare, whatever else they may be doing, are not in a frame of mind that produces *nisuch*. The wine therefore remains permitted even if they have unquestionably touched it.

---

---

# Avodah Zarah 71

## Wine & Non-Jews Intr (II)

### Daf Overview

Today's *daf* is 71a. The preceding *dappim* were occupied with the question of wine left unattended with a non-Jew: under what circumstances may one assume, with sufficient confidence, that the non-Jew did not touch the wine or otherwise handle it? Now, with the *mishna* at the top of 71a, the discussion returns to an earlier cluster of themes — when does wine become the property of the non-Jew, and when is it still considered the Jew's wine? Related to this is the question of at what stage one is deemed to have derived benefit (*hana'ah*) from *yayin nesech*. These are the central concerns of the current *daf*.

## Workers Refuse Wine

### Non-Jew Payment

The *mishna* presents the following case: Jewish workers are employed by a non-Jewish owner. When the time comes to pay their wages, the employer has no cash on hand and offers them a barrel of wine instead. The *mishna* terms this *yayin nesech*, though as a practical matter, the non-Jew would not typically be setting aside wine dedicated to *avodah zarah*. Even *stam yeinam* — the ordinary wine of a non-Jew — is forbidden for benefit, and so the workers cannot simply accept this wine as payment.

## Wine & Non-Jews Intr (II)

### Chametz Tie-In

A notable feature of the upcoming analysis is how it connects to *chametz*-related discussions that have already appeared in this tractate. The question of how to define *bittul* — in particular, whether *chametz* is nullified like other prohibited substances or treated more stringently — has come up before, and the current *daf* will offer another such point of contact. Given that *Pesach* is imminent, this *chametz* tie-in is both appropriate and timely.

## Workers Refuse Wine (II)

### Request Cash

What are the workers permitted to do? The *mishna* rules: *mutar lomar lo ten lanu et dameha* — they may say to the employer, "Do not give us the wine; give us the cash equivalent instead." This is permitted because at the moment they make this request, the wine has not yet entered their possession. They are not selling *yayin nesech* or deriving benefit from it; they are simply declining the wine as payment and requesting an alternative.

### Possession Final

However, *mishe-nichnas le-reshutan assur* — once the wine has entered their possession, they may no longer reverse the arrangement by handing the wine back and demanding money in its place. At that point the wine is theirs, and returning it to the owner in exchange for cash constitutes selling *yayin nesech* and thereby deriving benefit from it. The rule is therefore straightforward: the request for cash must come before possession is established.

## Tax Payment via Non-Jew

### King's Tax Scenario

The *Gemara* does not pause to comment on the *mishna* directly but instead addresses a parallel case. Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: it is permitted for a person to say to a non-Jew, *tzei va-hafes alai menat ha-melech* — "Please go and pay the king's tax on my behalf." If the non-Jew then chooses to discharge this obligation using his own wine, that is the non-Jew's autonomous decision. The Jew never instructed him to pay with wine. The effect is simply that the non-Jew has covered the Jew's tax liability, and the Jew now owes the non-Jew the equivalent sum. The relationship between them is purely one of repaying a debt — the Jew is not using the *yayin nesech* in any meaningful sense.

This reasoning echoes an earlier discussion: if one tells a storekeeper to feed his workers and the storekeeper gives them wine, and then the storekeeper bills the Jew for the transaction, the Jew's only obligation is to pay the monetary debt. He did not direct the use of wine and is not considered to have derived benefit from it.

### Language Matters

The *Gemara* then raises a challenge from a *braita*: *al yomar adam le-oved kochavim amod tachtai la-otzar* — one may not say to a non-Jew, "Stand in my stead" with respect to the tax official. Rashi explains *otzar* as a reference to a tax collector or similar officer. The question is obvious: why is this formulation forbidden? If, even in the permitted case, the non-Jew might pay with wine, why does the phrasing make a difference?

Rav responds: *amod tachtai la-otzar ka-amrat?* — note the language you used. "Stand in my stead" is not the same as "please pay my taxes." The language of standing in one's stead carries the connotation of being a *shaliach*, a representative acting in the Jew's place. When the Jew frames the instruction as "be my representative," and the non-Jew then pays with wine, it is as though the Jew himself chose to pay with wine. The wine belongs to the non-Jew, but the Jew has effectively deputized the non-Jew to act on his behalf, and thus the non-Jew's choice becomes, in a legal and conceptual sense, the Jew's choice. By contrast, the permitted formulation — *matzileni min ha-otzar*, "save me from the tax collector" — leaves the non-Jew full discretion, and his decision to use wine remains his own.

### Rashi Tosafot Debate

This is how Rashi reads the passage. Tosafot, however, is uncomfortable with that analysis. Tosafot argues that if the entire debt were a cash debt — if the Jew owed the king ten thousand dollars — then even the language of "stand in my stead" should not be problematic, because the non-Jew is ultimately paying off a monetary debt. Whether he uses cash or wine to discharge it, the Jew is left owing the non-Jew a monetary sum, not wine. Tosafot finds it difficult to say that a mere choice of phrasing transforms a straightforward debt-payment scenario into a case where the Jew is considered to have paid with wine.

### Tosafot Leniency

Tosafot therefore proposes a more substantive reading. The problematic case, says Tosafot, is one where the Jew actually owes *wine* to the king — perhaps because the tax is assessed as a percentage of his annual wine production. In such a case, if the Jew says "stand in my stead" to the non-Jew, and the non-Jew then pays the king with his own forbidden wine, it genuinely does look as though the Jew is discharging a wine debt using *yayin nesech*. The non-Jew is paying wine for wine, and the Jew is in effect using that forbidden wine for his own benefit.

And yet Tosafot goes further with a remarkable *chiddush*: even if the debt is a wine debt, and even if the non-Jew ultimately pays it with wine, it remains permitted — provided the Jew framed his request as *matzileni min ha-otzar*, "save me from my obligation." The Tosafot explains: that phrasing implies "do whatever you can to get me out of this — bribe the official, pay in cash, negotiate, or pay in wine if necessary." It leaves full discretion to the non-Jew and signals that the Jew is not specifically directing the payment of wine. That degree of distancing is sufficient to ensure that even if wine is ultimately paid, the Jew is not deemed to have paid with wine himself.

The contrast between Rashi and Tosafot here is significant. According to Rashi, the entire analysis involves a cash debt, and the only variable is the language used to delegate the task. According to Tosafot, the more striking case involves an actual wine debt, and even there, a subtle shift in framing — from "be my agent" to "save me from my obligation" — is enough to sever the legal and conceptual connection between the Jew and the forbidden wine used to discharge it.

## Selling Wine Details

### Fix Price First

A new *mishna* now addresses the case from the opposite direction: not the non-Jew's wine being offered to the Jew, but the Jew's wine being sold to the non-Jew. The concern here is that the non-Jew must not come into contact with the wine — or be in a position to do so — before the sale is finalized. Once the sale is complete and the wine belongs to the non-Jew, whatever he does with it is no longer the Jew's concern. The question is therefore: what finalizes the transaction?

The *mishna* states: *pasak ad she-lo madad damav mutarin* — if the price was fixed before the wine was measured out, the payment is permitted. The wine entered the non-Jew's possession after the transaction was already concluded. But the *mishna* does not mention any exchange of money. The simple reading is that *meshicha* — the physical act of drawing the item into one's possession — or, in this case, its entering the non-Jew's vessel, is what finalizes the sale; and the role of price-fixation is to ensure that there is genuine *gemar da'at*, a settled intention, at the moment possession transfers.

### Two Cases

The two cases of the *mishna* are as follows. First: *pasak ad she-lo madad damav mutarin* — if you fixed the price first and then measured the wine into his vessel, the money is permitted. The moment the wine enters the non-Jew's vessel, the sale is final; the non-Jew gains access only after ownership has transferred to him, so whatever he subsequently does to the wine is irrelevant — it is now his wine. Second: *madad ad she-lo pasak damav asurin* — if you first measured the wine into his vessel before fixing the price, the money is forbidden. At the moment the wine enters his vessel, the sale is not yet final; the wine is still yours, and it is now in a vessel that the non-Jew can access. Once it becomes *stam yeinam*, you cannot then finalize the sale, because you would be selling forbidden wine and receiving payment for it.

## Meshicha vs. Kesef

### Ameimar Position

Ameimar draws a direct conclusion from the *mishna*: *meshicha be-oved kochavim koneh* — the act of *meshicha*, of the non-Jew drawing the item into his physical domain or taking physical control of it, effects a valid *kinyan* for a non-Jew, just as it would in transactions involving two Jews. This is the natural reading of the *mishna*, which makes no mention of monetary payment as the operative act of acquisition.

As a supporting observation, Ameimar notes that among Persians, the convention when exchanging goods or sending samples is that once the recipient takes physical possession, the transaction is not reversed. Rashi understands this as referring to cases where a sample is sent ahead of a larger delivery: once the buyer receives and accepts the sample, the sale is considered binding. Whether this is a formal legal norm or a matter of commercial etiquette, it at minimum reflects the understanding that physical taking of possession is the operative moment of finalization. Tosafot qualifies this by noting that the practices of Persians among themselves do not constitute a formal proof of what *halacha* recognizes, but the observation carries some weight as a supporting consideration.

### Rav Ashi Position

Rav Ashi disagrees. He asserts: *le-olam eima lach meshicha be-oved kochavim eino koneh* — I maintain that *meshicha* does not effect a *kinyan* for a non-Jew. As for the Persian practice of not reversing a transaction after physical possession is taken, Rav Ashi dismisses this as a matter of social convention or politeness — a form of *derech eretz* — rather than a legally operative norm.

The underlying debate here connects to the famous dispute in *Bava Metzia* between Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish regarding which act of *kinyan* the Torah itself prescribes for Jews. One position holds that according to the Torah, it is *kesef* — monetary payment — that effects acquisition; the Rabbis subsequently instituted *meshicha* for Jews and negated *kesef* for certain practical reasons. The other position holds the reverse. The relevance for non-Jews is as follows: whatever the Torah prescribes for Jews, the opposite applies to non-Jews. Thus if *kesef* is the Torah's *kinyan* for Jews, then *meshicha* is what works for non-Jews; and if *meshicha* is what the Torah prescribes for Jews, then *kesef* is the operative *kinyan* for non-Jews.

This debate has immediate practical implications, most notably for *mechirat chametz*, the sale of *chametz* to a non-Jew before *Pesach*. Because the *maskana* of this *Gemara* is not entirely clear, the practice emerged of performing every conceivable form of *kinyan* — *kesef*, *meshicha*, *chalipin*, *chatzer*, *dina demalchuta dina*, and more — in order to cover all possibilities.

Tosafot in this *sugyah* takes up the question of what our *psak halacha* should be with respect to sales to non-Jews, focusing primarily on the case of selling an interest in an animal to a non-Jew in order to exempt its offspring from the laws of *bechor*. The mechanism is that if the non-Jew holds even partial ownership of the mother at the time of birth, the *halacha* of *bechor* does not apply to the offspring. To accomplish this, Tosafot rules that one should ideally have the non-Jew both pay money (*kesef*) and perform an act of *meshicha* — and *meshicha* must be done either in a *simta* (a semi-public side alley that does not constitute a full public domain) or within the non-Jew's own domain. If the non-Jew has no domain of his own, Tosafot suggests a creative solution: first sell the non-Jew a room in the Jew's house, complete with its own *kinyan*, and then have the non-Jew draw the animal into that room. That establishes both the domain and the *meshicha* in a single sequence.

As for how much of the animal the non-Jew must own, Tosafot cites a debate among *amoraim* in the first chapter of *Bechorot*: some hold the non-Jew must own a portion significant enough that its removal would render the animal a *tereifa*; others hold even the ear suffices. Tosafot leans toward the more stringent position, recommending that one sell the non-Jew something like the lungs or the head. And as for the price: the non-Jew need not pay the full market value of what he is acquiring. Paying a *perutah* is sufficient, even though the portion of the animal is worth many times that amount, because — as Tosafot explains — everyone understands that the Jew's true intention is to transfer ownership for the purpose of exempting the offspring from *bechor*, and that sincere intention (*gemar ve-aknei*) supports the validity of the sale despite the token price. This is, of course, directly parallel to the structure of *mechirat chametz*, where similarly symbolic payment is combined with multiple forms of *kinyan*.

### Rav's Teaching

Rav Ashi now seeks to ground his position — that *kesef*, not *meshicha*, is the operative *kinyan* for non-Jews — in a teaching of Rav. Rav addressed wine merchants and instructed them: when you measure out wine for non-Jews, *shaklu zuzei mineihu ve-hadar haylu lehu* — first collect payment, and only then measure out the wine. If they do not have cash on hand, lend them the money and then take it back from them as payment, so that the purchase is actually transacted with cash before the wine changes hands.

The rationale Rav provides is explicit: *ki ka havei yayin nesech bi-reshuteichu ka havei* — if you measure out the wine before receiving payment, then at the moment the non-Jew's vessel receives the wine, the sale is not yet final, the wine is still yours, and it becomes *yayin nesech* while in your possession. Then, *vechi sheklitu dmei yayin nesech ka sheklitu* — when you subsequently take the money, you are taking payment for *yayin nesech*, which is forbidden.

The emphasis on receiving money upfront appears to support Rav Ashi's position that *kesef* is the operative *kinyan* for non-Jews. If *meshicha* were sufficient, one might argue there should be no problem: from the moment the wine enters the non-Jew's vessel, it is his, and he does not gain physical access to it until a moment later, by which time the sale is already complete. So why does Rav insist on payment upfront?

### Forbidden Drops

The *Gemara* offers an answer that attempts to preserve the possibility that *meshicha* also works, while still explaining Rav's instruction. The answer focuses on the physical mechanics of pouring wine into a vessel. We are not dealing with the case of pouring into a Jewish flask; the problem arises specifically when the wine is being poured into the non-Jew's own vessel. And here there is a complication: at the bottom of the non-Jew's vessel, there are residual drops of wine — *stam yeinam* — left over from prior use. The concern is that as the Jew's kosher wine is poured in, it mixes with those drops before the sale is finalized.

*Yayin nesech* is *asur be-mashehu* — even the smallest trace renders the mixture forbidden. So at the very moment the wine enters the vessel and mingles with those drops, it becomes *yayin nesech*, and this happens a millisecond before — or simultaneously with — any act of *meshicha* that might vest ownership in the non-Jew. The result is that the wine becomes forbidden while it is still the Jew's, and the subsequent "sale" is a sale of *yayin nesech*.

This is why Rav insisted on payment upfront: cash paid in advance means the non-Jew already owns the wine before any pouring takes place, and thus whatever happens when it enters his vessel is happening to his wine, not the Jew's.

### Vessel on Ground

The *Gemara* presses further. Even granting the drops of wine at the bottom, why does the non-Jew not take possession the moment the wine enters the airspace of his vessel? The principle of *kinyan kli* — acquisition through one's vessel — should operate from the point at which the wine enters the vessel's airspace. At that moment the non-Jew would own it, and the wine would only reach the forbidden drops at the very bottom a fraction later.

The *Gemara* considers whether the answer lies in the concept of *nitzok chibbur* — the idea that liquid connected by a stream of pouring is considered a single unit. If *nitzok chibbur* applies, then even though the wine at the top of the stream has not yet reached the drops at the bottom, it is halachically connected to them and thus forbidden. But the *Gemara* is reluctant to conclude *nitzok chibbur* simply in order to resolve this case — that principle remains contested and should not be treated as an established ruling merely to explain this difficulty.

An alternative resolution is therefore offered: the *Gemara* distinguishes between a vessel that the non-Jew is holding and one that is resting on the ground. If the non-Jew were holding his vessel, then *hagbahah* — lifting — would apply, since by holding the vessel he suspends its contents above the ground and is effectively *magbi'ah* the wine. But if the vessel is sitting on the ground, as is typically the case in a shop, then *hagbahah* does not apply. And the *Gemara* further establishes that the wine is not acquired through *kinyan kli* until it reaches the bottom of the vessel — it does not suffice for it to enter the airspace alone if the vessel is on the ground. Thus, acquisition through *kinyan kli* occurs only at the moment the wine reaches the bottom and mingles with the forbidden drops, at which precise moment the wine has already become *yayin nesech*. This is why Rav's instruction to collect payment first is necessary regardless of whether *meshicha* also works as a *kinyan*.

### Kinyan Kli Debate

At this point the *Gemara* raises a further question: even without *meshicha* or *hagbahah*, why does *kinyan kli* not take effect while the vessel is in the seller's domain? This is a general question about *kinyan kli*: does a purchaser's vessel effect a *kinyan* while it is situated in the domain of the seller? The concern is that if *kinyan kli* does not work in the seller's domain, that would itself explain why the non-Jew does not acquire the wine before it becomes forbidden, without needing to invoke either the drops at the bottom or the specific mechanics of *hagbahah*.

The *Gemara* declines to establish that *kinyan kli* fails in the seller's domain as a general principle, and instead reverts to a more concrete physical explanation. The real problem, the *Gemara* concludes, is that there is wine adhering to the lip of the vessel — the rim — left from previous use. As the Jew pours his wine into the vessel, the stream of wine contacts those forbidden drops on the lip before it ever enters the airspace of the vessel at all. Thus, the wine becomes mixed with *yayin nesech* at the very moment of pouring, before any *kinyan kli* can take effect. This explains, without recourse to either *kinyan kli* failing in the seller's domain or the contested principle of *nitzok chibbur*, why Rav required that payment be received before any measuring takes place.

### Wine Mixture Issue

Once this scenario is established, a further question arises. The wine that becomes forbidden is predominantly the Jew's kosher wine; only a minute quantity of *yayin nesech* from the residual drops is present in the mixture. The bulk of what is in the vessel is permissible wine. Why then may not the Jew simply accept payment for his own kosher wine, arguing that he is not being paid for and is not deriving benefit from the forbidden drops, only from his own portion?

This question opens onto a dispute between Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the Sages. When *yayin nesech* becomes mixed with permitted wine, and the entire mixture is thereby forbidden (*asur be-mashehu*), may one nonetheless sell the mixture to a non-Jew — charging only for the permitted portion and not for the forbidden drops? One view permits this: the Jew is not receiving benefit from the *assur* wine, only from his own. The other view holds that once the mixture is uniformly forbidden, one cannot selectively claim payment only for the permitted portion; the entire mixture must be treated as *yayin nesech* and none of it may be sold.

### Barrels vs. Liquid

The *Gemara* notes that if this case is to be considered a genuine prohibition, it must not accord with the position of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who would appear to permit collecting payment for the permitted portion of a mixture. But Rav himself ruled: *halacha ke-Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel chavis be-chavis* — the rule follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel specifically when sealed barrels are mixed up with one another but not when the liquids themselves are blended.

The distinction is significant. If ten barrels of kosher wine become intermixed with one barrel of *yayin nesech* and no one can identify which is which, Rav permits selling them all to a non-Jew and charging for ten barrels — because in principle the forbidden barrel remains conceptually separate and one can say "I am not selling you that one, whichever it is." But when the liquids themselves are physically combined into a single undifferentiated mass, that conceptual separation is impossible. The forbidden drops are inseparable from the permitted wine in any physical or practical sense, and the entire mixture must be treated as uniformly forbidden. Accordingly, one may not sell any of it, and payment for the permitted portion cannot be extracted separately. This is why Rav's instruction holds even in Rav Ashi's reading: the mixture is all one forbidden unit, and the entire justification for selling it falls away.

## Scrap Metal w/ Idol

### Idol Discovery

The *Gemara* now examines a *braita* about a different category of forbidden object in order to derive further conclusions about the operative *kinyan* for non-Jews. The case: a Jew purchases scrap metal from a non-Jew, and upon inspecting his purchase he discovers that some of the metal pieces are small discarded idols — *avodah zarah* — which are *asur be-hana'ah*. The *braita* distinguishes between two scenarios. *Ad she-lo natan ma'os mashach* — if he performed *meshicha* and took physical possession before paying — he may return the idol. *Im mi-she-natan ma'os mashach* — if he first paid and then performed *meshicha* — he may not return it but must cast it into the sea (*yolic le-yam ha-melach*), because returning the idol to the non-Jew in exchange for a refund would constitute selling *avodah zarah* and thereby deriving benefit from a forbidden object.

The question is whether this *braita* teaches us something about what finalizes the sale: is it payment (*kesef*) or physical possession (*meshicha*)?

### Abaye's Answer

On the surface, the *braita* seems to suggest that payment is the operative act, since it is the payment of money that makes the return of the idol impermissible. Abaye, however, resists this conclusion. He explains that *meshicha* does work as a *kinyan* — the Jew took possession of all the scrap metal through *meshicha* — but the idol is an exception because the entire purchase was a *mekach ta'ut*, a mistaken transaction. The Jew never intended to acquire an idol, and therefore *meshicha* cannot be said to have effected a valid acquisition of the forbidden item specifically. That is why, as a matter of principle, he can return it.

### Rava's Refinement

But this creates a problem, as Rava immediately points out: if the entire justification for returning the idol is *mekach ta'ut* — that the purchase was a mistake — then that should apply equally whether or not money has been paid. *Mekach ta'ut* nullifies the transaction with respect to the idol regardless of the sequence of payment and *meshicha*. Why then does the *braita* distinguish between having paid money and not having paid money?

Rava therefore refines the analysis. He accepts that in both cases — whether money was paid before or after *meshicha* — the situation is a *mekach ta'ut* with respect to the idol specifically, and the Jew does not genuinely own it in either case. The distinguishing factor is not whether a *kinyan* was made on the idol, but whether returning the idol to the non-Jew *looks like* a sale.

### Money Paid Effect

When money has not yet been paid: the Jew agreed on a price of, say, one thousand dollars for the scrap metal. The idol is worth ten dollars' worth of metal. He returns the idol to the non-Jew and when payment is eventually made, he simply deducts ten dollars and pays nine hundred and ninety. No money changes hands in connection with the idol itself; it simply never becomes part of the sale. This does not look like selling *avodah zarah* — it looks like correcting a mistaken purchase.

But when money has already been paid in full: to return the idol now, the Jew would hand back the object and demand ten dollars in return. That looks exactly like a sale — an idol is being transferred to the non-Jew in exchange for money. That appearance itself is prohibited: *seifa de-yahiv zuzei mitchazei ke-oved kochavim be-yad Yisrael* — it has the appearance of a Jew selling an idol.

The *kinyan*, on this reading, takes place at the time of *meshicha* in both cases. The only variable is whether the mechanics of returning the idol will carry the appearance of a forbidden sale. Thus, the *braita* does not prove that payment is the operative act of *kinyan*; rather, it turns on the distinct question of how the return of an idol appears in each case.

## Prepayment Analysis

### Measuring Question

Mar Kashisha the son of Rav Chisda raises a challenge to Rav Ashi directly: come and prove your position from our *mishna* itself — *hamocher yeino le-oved kochavim*, you sell wine to a non-Jew. *Pasak ad she-lo madad damav mutarin* — the price was fixed before it was measured, the money is permitted. Now, if *meshicha* does not work as a *kinyan* for a non-Jew, why would fixing the price before measuring be sufficient? The non-Jew has not yet paid money, so how is the wine his before he can touch it?

### Price Fixation Intent

Rav Ashi responds: *hacha be-mai askinan de-akdim lei dinar* — the case of the *mishna* involves a situation where the non-Jew prepaid. He gave money before the measuring took place. This is, admittedly, a difficult reading of the *mishna*, which never mentions money being paid. But Rav Ashi maintains that in the background of the *mishna*, money was already given; and without the price having been fixed, even prepayment does not finalize the sale, because *gemar da'at* — a fully settled intention — requires that both parties know the exact terms. Until the price is set, no amount of prior payment can close the transaction.

The *Gemara* then examines the second case of the *mishna* — *madad ad she-lo pasak damav asurin*, measured before the price was fixed, the money is forbidden — and asks: if money was already prepaid, why should this case be a problem? Rav Ashi's answer is the same: without *psak*, the sale remains open regardless of prior payment, because the buyer's *da'at* — his firm intention to complete the acquisition — is not settled until he knows the price.

### Kinyan Reading

The *Gemara* then poses the question symmetrically to the other side. If, by contrast, we read the *mishna* according to the view that *meshicha* is the operative *kinyan* — meaning that *madad* itself is the act of *kinyan* — why does the presence or absence of *psak* make any difference?
