In both cases the *mishna* describes the same act of measuring wine, yet in one case the money is permitted and in the other forbidden. The answer, applicable on either reading, is that *psak samkha da'atei* — fixing the price settles the buyer's intention and renders the *kinyan* effective. *Lo pasak lo samkha da'atei* — without fixing the price, even a completed act of *meshicha* or payment does not achieve a final acquisition, because the requisite *gemar da'at* is absent.

The upshot is that the *mishna* cannot be read as a decisive proof for either position. Whether *madad* is the operative *kinyan* (on the *meshicha* reading) or whether it merely marks the moment of the non-Jew's physical access to the wine (on the *kesef* reading), the role of *psak* is structural in both cases: it is the precondition for any *kinyan*, whatever its form, to be finalized. The debate between Ameimar and Rav Ashi therefore remains unresolved by the text of the *mishna* itself.

## Ben Noach Theft

### Theft Law

Ravina now cites a teaching in an attempt to settle the debate. Rabbi Chiya bar Abba said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: a *ben Noach* — a non-Jew subject to the seven Noahide laws — is executed even for stealing less than a *perutah*, and there is no possibility of restoring the situation through return of the object, since an amount less than a *perutah* is below the threshold of monetary claims in Jewish law.

### Theft Completion

The relevance to our debate: if *meshicha* does not effect a *kinyan* for non-Jews, and if *geneiva* — theft — is only legally completed when the thief has performed a *ma'aseh kinyan*, then by what act is the theft completed here? Where there is no payment of money — since one does not pay money when stealing — how is the theft ever legally consummated, so as to make the *ben Noach* liable for execution?

### Anguish Suffices

Rashi explains: even without a formal *ma'aseh kinyan*, a *ben Noach* who physically deprives a Jew of access to his property has committed a sufficient act of *geneiva* by virtue of the anguish (*tza'ar*) and deprivation caused to the owner. The transgression of the Noahide prohibition against theft does not require the identical formal conditions of *kinyan* that apply in intra-Jewish property law. One can lock a person out of his own house and prevent him from accessing his property without technically completing a *kinyan*, yet that is sufficient to constitute a violation of the prohibition against theft for *bnei Noach*.

### Second Theft

The *Gemara* then addresses the second case in the same source: if a second non-Jew steals the object from the first, he too is executed. This implies that non-Jew number one has genuinely taken possession of the object, such that non-Jew number two can steal from him. But non-Jew number two did not harm the Jewish owner at all — only non-Jew number one. If the liability of non-Jew number one rested purely on the *tza'ar* caused to the Jew, then non-Jew number two, who caused the Jew no anguish whatsoever, should incur no liability.

### Meshicha Works

The conclusion is therefore that non-Jew number one must have genuinely acquired the stolen object — through an act of *meshicha*, of physical taking of possession — so that non-Jew number two is stealing from a genuine owner, and that is itself a Noahide violation. *Shema mina meshicha be-oved kochavim koneh* — conclude from this that *meshicha* effects a *kinyan* for a non-Jew.

### Tosafot Caveat

Tosafot, however, adds an important qualification. Even granting that *meshicha* works as a *kinyan* for non-Jews in the context of theft, this does not necessarily prove that *meshicha* is sufficient in a transactional sale. Tosafot's position is that there is no dispute about *meshicha* functioning for non-Jews in non-transactional contexts — gifts and theft both operate through physical possession regardless of payment. The contested question is specifically whether, in a sale between a Jew and a non-Jew, *meshicha* alone can finalize the transaction without any payment of *kesef*. The proof from *ben Noach* theft therefore does not resolve the central debate between Ameimar and Rav Ashi regarding the mechanics of commercial *kinyan* for non-Jews. The *Gemara*'s apparent conclusion — *shema mina* — applies in the narrow context of non-transactional acquisition, and the question of which *kinyan* governs a sale of *yayin nesech* to a non-Jew, with all its implications for *mechirat chametz* and related matters, remains a matter of ongoing dispute.

---

---

# Avodah Zarah 72

## Conditional Sale

### Sale Story

The daf opens, five lines from the top of 72a, with a series of cases involving the finalization of a sale — a digression triggered by the broader discussion of selling wine to a non-Jew and when such a transaction is considered complete. The first story: a man said to his friend, *hahu gavra d'amar lei l'chavrei*, "If I ever wind up selling this land, I will sell it to you" — and they performed some form of *kinyan*, presumably a *kinyan sudar*, on that agreement.

Two assumptions must be in place for this case to be legally meaningful. First, that a *kinyan* was indeed performed. Second — and more critically — that the parties did not merely make a promise, but rather effected an actual *kinyan* on the sale itself, structured as conditional: if and when I decide to sell, the transfer shall take effect retroactively from this moment. A bare promise to sell, even accompanied by a *kinyan*, would constitute *kinyan devarim* — a legally unenforceable commitment, as discussed at the beginning of *Bava Batra*. The case is only interesting if the *kinyan* was substantive.

### Rav Yosef Ruling

Against that backdrop, *azal zavnah l'inish achrina* — the seller subsequently went and sold the land to a third party, breaching his conditional commitment. Rav Yosef ruled: *kana kama* — the first buyer acquires the land. The sale to the second party is ineffective. On the assumption that the conditional *kinyan* was properly structured, once the seller decided to sell, the earlier *kinyan* snapped into place and the land was already transferred to the first buyer.

### Abaye Challenge

Abaye challenged Rav Yosef: *vehalo lo pasak* — they never fixed a price. Even if the *kinyan* was otherwise properly executed, a sale cannot be final without an agreed-upon price — *psak damim*. The *ma'aseh kinyan* alone, without *psak damim*, is insufficient to finalize the transaction. No *kinyan* can be complete where the price remains undetermined.

### Wine Price Proof

Where does this principle derive from? Abaye cites our very own Mishnah: *hamocher yeino l'oved kochavim — pasak ad shelo madad, damav mutarin; madad ad shelo pasak, damav asurin.* One who sells his wine to a non-Jew: if the price was fixed before the non-Jew took possession (*meshichah*), the money is permitted — the sale is final before the non-Jew could touch the wine, rendering it *yayin nesech*. But if the non-Jew took possession before the price was fixed, the proceeds are forbidden — because the wine was not yet his when he was in a position to touch it, and it therefore became *stam yeinam*, producing a forbidden benefit. The Mishnah thus demonstrates clearly that no sale is finalized without a prior fixing of the price, regardless of whether physical possession has been taken.

### Yayin Nesech Exception

The Gemara deflects: *dilma chumra d'yayin nesech shani* — perhaps the Mishnah's ruling is a stringency unique to *yayin nesech*. In the laws of *mekach u'memkar* generally, a *kinyan* performed without a fixed price might well be final; but in the context of *yayin nesech*, the Sages treated the transaction as not fully consummated in order to impose the prohibition. One cannot therefore derive a general principle in monetary law from a Mishnah that may be operating under the special stringencies of *yayin nesech*.

### Meshicha & Price

The Gemara then seeks a proof from a source untainted by *yayin nesech* concerns. Rav Idi bar Avin reports that a case of this type arose in the academy of Rav Chisda — who was the son of Rav Huna — and was resolved from the following Mishnah: *mashach chammar u'poalav* — if a buyer led the donkey driver or the delivery workers carrying someone's goods and brought them into his house, the analysis is as follows. While the goods remain on the backs of the carriers, *shneihem yecholim lachzor bo* — either party may retract, regardless of whether the price was fixed before or after the act of drawing: the buyer has not yet completed a proper *kinyan*, since the goods are still in the possession of another person.

However, *parkan v'hichnisam l'toch beito* — once the buyer unloaded the goods from the carriers and brought them into his house, the outcome depends on whether the price was fixed: if the price was fixed before the goods entered the house, *ein shneihem yecholim lachzor* — neither party may retract. The *kinyan chatzer* combined with the *psak damim* finalizes the sale. But *madad ad shelo pasak* — if he brought them into his house before fixing a price — *shneihem yecholim lachzor* — either party may still retract. Here is an explicit Mishnah in the domain of monetary law, entirely unrelated to *yayin nesech*, establishing that even the most complete physical acquisition is insufficient to finalize a sale without a fixed price. Abaye's challenge to Rav Yosef therefore stands.

---

## Second Sale Story

### Rav Kahana Ruling

The Gemara presents a second, more refined case. A man said to his friend: *ee mizbanina lah l'ha ara mizbanina lach b'mea zuzei* — "If I ever sell this land, I will sell it to you for one hundred *zuz*." Here, crucially, a price was fixed. A conditional *kinyan* was performed. Subsequently, the seller went and sold the land to a third party for one hundred and twenty *zuz* — twenty more than the agreed price. Rav Kahana ruled: *kana kama* — the first buyer acquires the land. The condition was met — the seller decided to sell — and the *kinyan*, which had a fixed price, is now effective.

### Ones Challenge

Rav Yaakov mi'Nehar Pekod challenged this ruling: *hai zuzei ansuh* — the additional money coerced him. The seller argues that he was effectively forced by the higher offer. This is a striking claim. The condition of the sale was met in the most literal sense — the seller did decide to sell. And yet Rav Yaakov maintains that this form of financial pressure constitutes *ones*, coercion, sufficient to negate the effect of the conditional *kinyan*.

### Ones Analysis

The argument can be understood in two registers. The narrower reading: the seller's implicit intention when he said "if I ever sell it, I will sell it to you" was always limited to a case where he independently chose to sell at the market rate. It never occurred to him that someone would offer a dramatically above-market price, and he never intended his conditional commitment to cover such a scenario. The broader reading — captured by the word *ones* — is more absolute: the seller was not truly choosing to sell; rather, an irresistible offer compelled him. When he said "if I decide to sell," he meant a genuine, unforced decision. A sale driven by the overwhelming pressure of a windfall offer is not truly a free decision but a kind of financial coercion, and falls outside the scope of his original stipulation.

### Halacha Ruling

*Vehilchata k'Rav Yaakov mi'Nehar Pekod* — the halacha follows Rav Yaakov's position, which is a remarkable ruling: the *ones* of a dramatically higher financial offer is sufficient to allow the seller to retract from his conditional commitment to the first buyer.

---

## Assessment Dispute

### Three Assessors

The Gemara turns to a related case. A seller says to a buyer: *k'deshaimi bitlata* — "I will sell to you at whatever price three people assess it." The word *shaimi*, from *shuma*, is the technical language of *beit din* valuation. By using this term and specifying three people, the seller is implicitly constructing a *beit din* — a panel of three functioning as a court. Consequently, *afilu trei migu tlata* — even a majority of two out of the three suffices to determine the price, since this is the standard rule of judicial decision-making.

If instead the seller says *k'de'amri bitlata* — "as three people will say" — the verb *amri* ("will say") carries no *beit din* connotation. He is not structuring them as a court. Therefore, *ad de'amri bitlata* — all three must agree to the same price; majority vote is insufficient. Similarly, if he says *k'deshaimi b'arba'ah* — "as four assess it" — the word *shaimi* is *beit din* language, but four is not a standard *beit din* (which consists of three, and in any case must have an odd number). In that case too, *ad de'amri b'arba'ah* — all four must reach consensus. And certainly if he says *k'de'amri b'arba'ah* — neither *beit din* language nor a *beit din*-compatible number — full consensus of all four is required.

### Rav Pappa Objection

Now, assuming the seller said *k'deshaimi bitlata* — structured as a *beit din* — and three assessors came and set a price. The buyer objects: *leitu tlata achrinei d'kimlehu tfei* — bring a different panel of three who are more expert, because these assessors do not know what they are doing. This seems, on the surface, like a reasonable objection. After all, no particular *beit din* was specified in the agreement, and the buyer might reasonably argue that a *beit din* implies a competent one. Rav Pappa rules: *dina hu dema'akeiv* — the objection is legally valid; the buyer has a legitimate right to demand more qualified assessors.

### Rav Huna Counter

Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua challenged this: *mimai dehani kimlu tefei* — on what basis do we presume the next panel would be any more expert than the first? The objection assumes that the replacement *beit din* will be superior, but that is far from established.

### Halacha Assessment

*Vehilchata k'Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua* — the halacha follows Rav Huna: a bare assertion that the assessors are unqualified, without concrete evidence, is legally insufficient. A mere claim, unsubstantiated, cannot override the assessment that was already performed. It appears, however, that this ruling is specifically addressed to objections made without backup support. If the buyer could demonstrate that the assessors lacked expertise and that a more qualified panel was available — for example, licensed professional appraisers — a more concrete basis for the objection might succeed. The ruling forecloses objections made out of thin air, not necessarily all objections whatsoever.

---

## Funnel Case

### Mishnah Setup

With the digression concluded, the Gemara returns to *yayin nesech*. The next Mishnah: *natal et hamashpach u'madad l'toch tzluchito shel oved kochavim* — a Jew took a funnel and poured wine through it into a vessel belonging to a non-Jew. To visualize the scenario: the funnel sits atop the non-Jew's wine bottle; wine from a larger pitcher flows through the funnel down into the non-Jew's vessel. When the wine reaches the bottom of the non-Jew's vessel, it becomes *yayin nesech* — either because it is now in the non-Jew's possession and susceptible to his touch, or because it mingles with drops already there. The wine in the upper portion of the funnel, however, has not yet entered the non-Jew's vessel. *V'chazar u'madad l'toch tzluchito shel Yisrael* — the Jew then reuses the same funnel to pour wine for a Jew.

### Funnel Remnants

*Im yesh bahen akavat yayin assur* — if there remain droplets of wine (*akavat yayin*, the "footsteps" of the wine) inside the funnel from the earlier pouring, it is forbidden. The problem is that those remnant drops were in contact with — or can be traced back to — the wine that became *yayin nesech* at the bottom of the non-Jew's bottle, and now those drops will mix with the wine being poured for the Jew.

### Vessel Pouring

The Mishnah then addresses a related case: *hame'areh mikli l'kli* — one who pours from one vessel into another. *Et she-me'areh mimenu mutar* — what remains in the pouring vessel is permitted. *V'et she-ira l'tocho assur* — what has been poured into the receiving vessel is forbidden. This ruling seems straightforward enough: once the wine lands in the non-Jew's vessel, it is forbidden; what remains in the Jewish pouring vessel is untainted. But the case of the funnel raises a deeper question. The wine in the funnel never entered the non-Jew's vessel directly — so why is it forbidden? This is the question that opens the central debate of the daf.

### Nitzok Intro

The answer lies in the concept of *nitzok* — a flowing stream of liquid connecting two bodies. Before examining how *nitzok* applies to *yayin nesech*, the Gemara grounds the discussion in its treatment in the laws of *tumah* and *taharah*, drawing from a Mishnah in *Taharot*. Three types of liquid connections are catalogued there: *nitzok* — a stream of liquid poured from one vessel into another; *katafres* — liquid flowing down at an angle over a surface; and *mashkeh tofe'ach* — a thin film of liquid connecting two pools.

A brief clarification on the last: *tofe'ach* means a thin layer of moisture sufficient to wet the hand on contact, but not thick enough that the wet hand could, in turn, wet a third object. *Tofe'ach al menat le'hatpi'ach*, by contrast, is a layer thick enough that touching it leaves enough moisture to wet yet another surface — liquid that is genuinely transferable. The Mishnah in *Taharot* rules that *nitzok*, *katafres*, and *mashkeh tofe'ach* are all *eino chibur lo le'tumah velo le'taharah* — they do not constitute a *chibur*, a legal connection, for purposes of *tumah* and *taharah*. Only *ashboren* — a collected, standing pool of water — constitutes a *chibur* for *tumah* and *taharah*.

What does *chibur le'tumah u'letaharah* mean in practice? Two examples: First, if a person who is *tamei* touches one pool of water connected to another only by *mashkeh tofe'ach*, does the *tumah* transfer to both? If it is not a *chibur*, it does not — they are legally distinct bodies. Second, for *mikvah*: if a full *mikvah* of forty *se'ah* and a smaller pool lacking forty *se'ah* are connected only by such a thin film, are they considered a single body of water? If not a *chibur*, one cannot be *tahor* by immersing in the smaller pool — they are two separate entities. The ruling that these are not a *chibur* means each body remains legally discrete.

There are precedents for connecting *tumah* and *taharah* concepts to *yayin nesech* — for example, earlier in the tractate, the question of whether the touch of a *zav* is the operative model for what makes wine *yayin nesech*. The question now is whether *nitzok* constitutes a *chibur* for purposes of *yayin nesech* even if it does not for *tumah* and *taharah*. If it does, then the wine remaining in the funnel is forbidden because the stream connects it to the *yayin nesech* at the bottom of the non-Jew's vessel, making them all one legal unit. If it does not, the funnel wine is entirely distinct from the *yayin nesech* below, and there is no reason to forbid it.

---

## Nitzok Chibur Debate

### Rav Huna Position

Rav Huna opens the formal debate: *nitzok ve'katafres u'mashkeh tofe'ach — chibur le'inyan yayin nesech*. Even if these forms of liquid connection are not a *chibur* for *tumah* and *taharah*, they may nonetheless constitute a *chibur* for *yayin nesech*, because *yayin nesech* is treated more stringently.

### Rav Nachman Challenge

Rav Nachman challenges: where does Rav Huna derive this? If the source is the Mishnah in *Taharot* — which says these are *eino chibur lo le'tumah velo le'taharah* — perhaps the inference is: *le'tumah u'letaharah* they are not a *chibur*, but *le'inyan yayin nesech* they are. Rav Nachman rejects this inference by pointing to the *sof* of that very Mishnah: it states that *ashboren* — collected water — *is* a *chibur le'tumah u'letaharah*. If we use the specification "for *tumah* and *taharah*" in the first clause to imply a *chibur* for *yayin nesech*, then symmetrically we would have to read the second clause to mean that *ashboren* is a *chibur* for *tumah* and *taharah* but *not* for *yayin nesech* — which is absurd. You cannot apply the same inferential logic to both clauses without reaching contradictory results.

### Inference Problem

*Ela me'ha leika le'mishma minah* — from that Mishnah there is simply nothing to prove. The Mishnah neither establishes nor refutes Rav Huna's position. What remains is to derive the answer from our own Mishnah in *Avodah Zarah*. The most natural explanation of why the wine in the funnel is forbidden — when the wine in the funnel never entered the non-Jew's vessel — is precisely that *nitzok* is a *chibur*: the stream connected them into one unit, and when the bottom became *yayin nesech*, the entire connected stream was contaminated.

### Rabbi Chiya Baraita

Against this reading, Rabbi Chiya teaches in a *baraita*: *she'pachastot tzluchito* — the wine vessel of the non-Jew "slapped" the wine in the funnel. That is, the reason the funnel wine is forbidden is not because *nitzok* created a connection retroactively from the moment the stream began. Rather, the non-Jew's vessel filled up to the point where wine sloshed or doubled back upward into the funnel itself. The funnel wine is forbidden because actual *yayin nesech* physically re-entered it — not because of any *chibur* created by the downward stream.

### Doubling Back Case

The Gemara now presses: if the wine doubled back, it is certainly forbidden — that is clear from Rabbi Chiya. *Aval lo pachsa tzluchito mai?* — but if the wine did not double back, what then? Can we infer that the funnel wine would be permitted, and thereby conclude that *nitzok* is not a *chibur*? The Gemara refuses this inference. Rabbi Chiya's *baraita* defines the case where the wine is *definitely* forbidden — when it doubled back. He does not rule on the case where it did not double back; that case remains undecided, *teiku*. One cannot infer permission from silence. Rabbi Chiya says: here it is definitely forbidden. He does not say: and only here.

### Second Mishnah

The Gemara turns to the second clause of the Mishnah — *hame'areh mikli l'kli, et she-me'areh mimenu mutar* — pouring from vessel to vessel; what remains in the pouring vessel is permitted. This raises two separate questions: (a) what is the status of the wine remaining in the source vessel, and (b) what is the status of the wine in midair — the stream itself? If *nitzok* is a *chibur*, the midair stream should be forbidden as part of the connected unit with the receiving vessel.

### Midair Stream Status

The Gemara attempts to read the Mishnah as proving *nitzok* is a *chibur*: the source vessel is permitted, which implies that the midair wine *is* forbidden — otherwise the Mishnah would have told us about the midair wine rather than only the source vessel. *Ha d'beini beini assur* — what is in midair is forbidden. *Shema mina nitzok chibur.* The Gemara objects: if *nitzok* is truly a *chibur*, then not only the midair wine but even the wine remaining in the source vessel should be forbidden — it is all one connected unit. Yet the Mishnah says the source vessel is permitted. This actually argues *against* *nitzok* being a *chibur*.

### Stream Breaking

The Gemara responds: *d'kamkatef kitufei* — the case of the Mishnah is one where the pourer broke the stream mid-pour. He began pouring; then, before the wine struck the receiving vessel, he righted the source vessel back up, breaking the stream. The wine already in midair then continued falling into the receiving vessel — but by then the connection to the source vessel had been severed. The source vessel is permitted because it was disconnected before the stream reached the *yayin nesech*. The midair wine, however, had already been released before the break and so remains part of the *nitzok*. *Ein hachi nami* — had the stream not been broken, even the source vessel would have been forbidden, because *nitzok* is a *chibur*.

### Ambiguity Conclusion

But the Gemara ultimately rejects the proof. The Mishnah states: *et she-ira l'tocho hu d'assur* — it is what was poured *into* the receiving vessel that is forbidden. This implies: *ha d'beini beini sharei* — the midair wine is permitted. If the midair wine were forbidden, the Mishnah would have said so. The Mishnah's silence about the midair wine, combined with this implied permission, undermines the earlier reading. The Mishnah does not tell us that the midair wine is forbidden; it tells us only that what ends up in the receiving vessel is forbidden. *Ela me'ha leika le'mishma minah* — from this Mishnah too, nothing can be proven. The question of whether *nitzok* is a *chibur* remains unresolved.

---

## Barrel to Vat

### Stream Forbidden

The Gemara attempts once more: *ta shema, hame'areh mi-chavit le-vor* — one who pours from a barrel into a large vat belonging to a non-Jew. *Kilu'ach ha-yored mi-sefas chavit le-mata assur* — the stream descending from the rim of the barrel downward is forbidden. This seems to be a direct and explicit statement: the midair stream itself is prohibited. Since the stream connects to the *yayin nesech* at the bottom of the vat, and since the stream is declared forbidden, this should prove that *nitzok* is a *chibur*. One might also note that this still leaves open the question of why the wine remaining in the barrel is not forbidden — but that question is set aside momentarily.

### Non-Jew Pouring

Rav Sheshes reinterprets the *baraita* entirely: *targema b'oved kochavim ha-me'areh* — the *baraita* is speaking of a case where it is the non-Jew who is doing the pouring, not the Jew. This changes everything. When a non-Jew pours *lo mevushal* wine, the concern is not *nitzok chibur* at all. The problem is *kocho* — the energy or physical causation of the non-Jew. Since his force is propelling the wine, it is treated as though he has directly handled it. This is precisely the halacha relevant to the question of whether a non-Jewish waiter may pour *lo mevushal* wine at the table: because he is causing the wine to move, it is as if he touched it.

### Kocho Concept

The Gemara then raises an objection to the *kocho* interpretation: if the non-Jew is pouring and his energy is moving all the wine, why is only the stream forbidden? The wine inside the barrel is also being moved by his actions — as the wine pours out, even the wine inside the barrel shifts toward the opening. Should the barrel wine not also be forbidden on account of *kocho*?

### Kocho Rabbinic

The Gemara answers: *koach d'oved kochavim mid'rabbanan hu d'assur* — the principle of *kocho* is entirely rabbinic in origin. Since it is a rabbinic enactment, the Sages defined its parameters. *Hu d'nafik l'varai gazru bei rabanan* — only the wine that actually exits the vessel, moving into the open, was subject to the rabbinic decree. *Hu d'ligavai lo gazru bei rabanan* — the wine that remains inside the barrel was not included in the decree. The Sages drew the line at the point of exit.

This has a striking practical implication. If a non-Jew pours your *lo mevushal* wine — say, at a table — the wine that has already been poured into the glass is forbidden on account of *kocho*. But the wine remaining in the bottle should, according to this analysis, be permitted: *kocho* does not extend to wine that has not yet left the vessel.

One might, however, argue the opposite on a different ground: once the poured wine in the glass is forbidden, and the glass is connected to the bottle by the stream of *nitzok*, perhaps the *nitzok* causes the bottle wine to be forbidden as well. But this is precisely the question at the heart of the entire sugya — whether *nitzok* is a *chibur*. If *nitzok* is not a *chibur*, then the *kocho* prohibition extends only to the poured wine, and the bottle wine is entirely permitted. The *baraita* about the barrel pouring into the vat therefore proves nothing about *nitzok chibur*, since Rav Sheshes has established that it speaks of a non-Jew pouring — a *kocho* case, not a *nitzok* case. The question of *nitzok chibur* remains unresolved.

---

## Practical Instructions

### Rav Chisda

Rav Chisda addressed the wine merchants with a practical ruling: *ki chailisu chamra l'ovdei kochavim — katfey kitufey* — when measuring out wine for non-Jews, break the stream as you pour. The concern is that the stream, once it contacts the non-Jew's vessel, will create a *nitzok* connection back to the barrel. If the barrel wine becomes connected to what has entered the non-Jew's vessel and turned *yayin nesech*, the entire barrel is at risk. By breaking the stream mid-pour, the connection is severed before it can trace back. Alternatively, Rav Chisda suggested throwing the wine into the vessel rather than pouring it in a continuous stream — eliminating *nitzok* entirely. From this instruction it is evident that Rav Chisda was concerned about *nitzok chibur* as a live halachic risk.

### Rava Warning

Rava issued a related warning to those who poured wine commercially into large vats: *lo l'karev oved kochavim l'sayaya b'hadaichu* — do not allow a non-Jew to assist you in the pouring. The concern is *dilma mishtalisu v'shadisu leh aleh* — you may become distracted and allow the non-Jew to take over the pouring entirely. Once he is doing all the pouring, *v'kasi m'kocho* — his energy is the operative cause, and the wine becomes forbidden. Even if his initial involvement was only as a helper, if he ends up performing the majority of the pour, it is treated as his action.

### Siphon Story

A practical case arose: a certain person was extracting wine from a barrel through a siphon — a *gishta* fitted with a *bas gishta*. A non-Jew came and placed his hand on the lower portion of the siphon tube, stopping the flow. Rava ruled: *asrei l'kulu chamra* — the entire barrel of wine is forbidden. 

### Siphon Challenge

Rav Pappa, Rav Adda bar Matna, and Ravina all challenged Rava: on what basis did he forbid everything? *Be-nitzok?* Is this based on *nitzok chibur* — treating the siphon as connecting the non-Jew's touch at the tip to all the wine in the barrel? If so, *shema mina nitzok chibur* — should we infer from Rava's ruling that *nitzok* is indeed a *chibur*? The very framing of the challenge suggests that the questioners did not accept *nitzok chibur* as settled, making Rava's ruling surprising.

Rava responded: *shani hatam d'kulei chamra agishta b'agishta garir* — this case is different. Here, all the wine in the barrel is being actively drawn through the siphon. A siphon functions by suction — a vacuum pulls the wine upward and through the tube. When the non-Jew places his hand on the siphon, it is not merely that wine is falling onto his hand, as in an ordinary *nitzok* case. Rather, because the entire barrel is being actively drawn through that tube, touching the tube is tantamount to inserting one's hand into the barrel itself. The mechanism of suction makes the wine throughout the tube and barrel a single, actively connected unit in a way that a gravitational stream is not.

Rashi elaborates: in a standard *nitzok* case, the wine falls downward onto the finger, but the finger is not reaching upward into the source. Here, the siphon is the agent pulling the wine out — by touching the siphon, the non-Jew is, in effect, intervening in the vessel itself. The implication of Rava's distinction is that without this special feature of the siphon, *nitzok* would not be a *chibur* — otherwise there would have been no need to distinguish the siphon case from the general rule.

### Kaniskanin Case

One final case: Mar Zutra son of Rav Nachman states that a *kaniskanin* — a communal drinking vessel from which multiple people drink simultaneously through separate straws — is permissible even when a Jew and a non-Jew drink from it at the same time. The non-Jew's mouth contacts only the tip of his own straw; the wine he draws travels toward him and does not return into the vessel. This is a kind of reverse *nitzok* — the non-Jew's contact does not travel back through the stream to contaminate the shared vessel.

*V'hanei milei d'kadim pasek Yisrael* — this is only permitted if the Jew stops drinking first. *Aval kadim pasek oved kochavim* — if the non-Jew stops drinking before the Jew, the small amount of wine at the tip of the non-Jew's straw — touched by his lips but not yet swallowed — will flow back into the vessel. That reversal renders the shared contents problematic. *Tosafot* notes the question of how those present knew who would stop first, and why they were not concerned about the possibility that the non-Jew might finish first.

---

## Tosafot Analysis

### Rashi vs. Rabbeinu Tam

*Tosafot* addresses the major dispute head-on. Rashi rules that *nitzok* is a *chibur* for *yayin nesech* — and indeed states explicitly in his commentary earlier in the *sugya* (*d'issur lehu b'nitzok, d'savira leh nitzok chibur, v'chein halacha*) that this is the normative halacha. Rabbeinu Tam disagrees, ruling that *nitzok* is not a *chibur* even for *yayin nesech*. This is not merely an academic debate; it has extensive practical consequences.

### Hefsed Merubeh Leniency

*Tosafot* rules that in a case of *hefsed gadol* — significant financial loss — one may rely on Rabbeinu Tam's lenient position and permit wine that would otherwise be questioned on account of *nitzok*. *Aval b'hefsed mu'at* — where the loss is small, it is better to be stringent in accordance with Rashi, treating *nitzok* as a *chibur*.

### Mixture Bittul

*Tosafot* then makes a critical structural observation. The Gemara's concern about *nitzok* is framed around *yayin nesech* — wine that is forbidden even in the smallest quantity (*b'mashehu*). But in the overwhelming majority of practical cases, the relevant prohibition is *stam yeinam* — ordinary wine that has been touched by a non-Jew. *Stam yeinam* follows the standard rules of *bittul*: it is *batel b'shishim*, nullified in a ratio of sixty to one.

*Tosafot* therefore rules: if wine is being poured from a barrel into a vessel containing *stam yeinam*, and the barrel contains sixty times the quantity of the problematic wine, then even if we were to accept that *nitzok* is a *chibur* — and the entire stream is treated as one unit — the mixture would be permitted. *Nitzok chibur* would mean only that the few drops of *stam yeinam* at the bottom are considered mixed throughout the entire barrel. But since the barrel contains sixty times that amount, the *stam yeinam* is nullified. *Tosafot* cites Rabbeinu Tam explicitly on this point: *stam yeinam* is *batel b'shishim*, and therefore the *chibur* of *nitzok* creates nothing more than a *ta'aroves* — a mixture — which is resolved by *bittul*.

### Touching Context

When, then, does *nitzok chibur* matter in practice? *Tosafot* answers: it matters when a non-Jew physically touches the flowing stream itself. In that scenario, the question is not one of *ta'aroves* — of drops mixing with a larger body — but of *maga*, touching. If *nitzok* is a *chibur*, the non-Jew's touch at one point in the stream is as if he touched the entire connected unit of wine, all the way back to the source vessel. The wine he touched is forbidden not because of mixture but because of contact. In that case, *bittul b'shishim* is irrelevant — *bittul* applies to mixtures, not to wine that has been directly touched.

### Stam Yeinam Leniency

*Tosafot* concludes with a layered practical ruling. First, in cases of *hefsed merubeh*, one may rely on Rabbeinu Tam that *nitzok* is not a *chibur* at all. Second, even where one is stringent and accepts Rashi's position, *stam yeinam* — the category most relevant today — is *batel b'shishim* in any mixture scenario, such that *nitzok chibur* only affects cases of direct touching, not ordinary ta'aroves. Third, the broader halachic context of *stam yeinam* — involving non-Jews who are not genuinely immersed in *avodah zarah*, questions of indirect contact, and the principle of *kocho* being rabbinic — provides additional grounds for leniency in many practical situations.

The upshot is that this *sugya* — which traverses *nitzok*, *kocho*, *chibur*, and the distinctions between *yayin nesech* and *stam yeinam* — carries enormous weight for practical halacha: for the question of a non-Jewish waiter pouring *lo mevushal* wine, for the status of wine remaining in a bottle after such pouring, and for the conditions under which a *nitzok* connection creates a prohibited *maga* rather than a permissible or neutralized mixture. Any practical case touching on these issues warrants careful consultation with a competent halachic authority.

---

---

# Avodah Zarah 73

## Wine Mixtures Intro

### Yayin Nesech Basic

The *mishna* that opens our daf concerns *ta'aroves* — mixtures — and states a foundational principle: *yayin nesech osur v'oser bechol shehu*. Wine that has been used in idolatrous contexts is prohibited, and even the tiniest drop of it renders a mixture forbidden. This is one of the classic cases of *assur bechol shehu*, a prohibition that is not subject to the ordinary mechanisms of *bittul*. The other paradigm case, which the *Gemara* will reach shortly, is *chametz b'pesach*. As for the identity of the "water" that appears later in the *mishna* as an analogue forbidden substance, Rashi understands it to refer to water that was literally poured before an *avodah zarah* and therefore has the status of *tikroves avodah zarah* — a libation offered to an idol.

### Min B'Mino vs. She'lo

The *mishna* draws a fundamental distinction. When *yayin nesech* is mixed with wine — *yayin b'yayin*, like with like — it is forbidden *bechol shehu*, regardless of the ratio. But when wine is mixed with water or water with wine — unlike with unlike, *min b'eino mino* — the prohibition follows the principle of *b'nosein ta'am*: the forbidden substance renders the mixture forbidden only if it is present in sufficient quantity to impart a perceptible taste, which halachic tradition estimates as one part in sixty.

### Why Min B'Mino Hard

This distinction is not self-evident, and it is worth pausing to understand why *min b'mino* might be treated more stringently than *min b'eino mino*. There are in fact two competing logical positions pulling in opposite directions.

The argument for leniency runs as follows: if forbidden meat is mixed into kosher meat of the same species, no bite of the resulting mixture will carry the distinctive taste of the forbidden item, because the forbidden item has no taste that distinguishes it from the permitted majority. Since the taste of the forbidden substance cannot be isolated, it has no independent identity, and as long as it is the minority it should be *batel b'rov*. This is essentially the ruling we follow: *min b'mino* is *batel b'rov* at the Torah level, with rabbinic stringency requiring one in sixty even there.

The argument for stringency is the exact inverse. Precisely because there is no difference in taste between the forbidden and the permitted substance, the forbidden substance has no way to lose its identity. By contrast, when a drop of wine falls into soup, one can say: if the taste of the wine cannot be detected, that is proof that the wine has lost its identity. But when meat is mixed with meat, every bite carries the full taste of both the kosher and the forbidden component simultaneously. The forbidden substance never loses its identity, because there is no sensory criterion by which to declare it absent. This is the position of *Rebbi Yehuda*, who holds that *min b'mino* is *bechol shehu* — never subject to *bittul* — and this view is shared by Rashi.

### Rav Yehuda Position

Rav Yehuda's position — and Rashi's, as noted — is that *min b'mino* is *never batel* across all areas of Torah law. The *Gemara* ahead will present this as the view of Rav and Shmuel as well. Yet the normative *halacha* does not follow this position in general.

### Stringency by Yayin

The application to *yayin nesech* reflects a deliberate borrowing of the stringent position for contexts in which we wish to treat the prohibition with exceptional weight. Because *yayin nesech* involves *avodah zarah* — a prohibition of the gravest character — the decisors chose to apply the stricter logic of *min b'mino*, even though that logic is not the one we ordinarily rely upon. The stringency is a borrowed construct: we take a pre-existing rigorous model and apply it selectively where the severity of the prohibition warrants it. This is also why *chametz b'pesach* goes even further — not only is *min b'mino* governed by *bechol shehu*, but even *min b'eino mino* is treated as *bechol shehu* by *chametz*, a double exception that exceeds even *yayin nesech*.

---

## Rishon Rishon Batel

### Rav Dimi Statement

The *Gemara* introduces a statement brought by Rav Dimi when he came from Eretz Yisrael, citing Rabbi Yochanan: *ha'me'areh yayin nesech m'chavit l'bor, afilu kol hayom kulo, rishon rishon batel* — one who pours *yayin nesech* from a barrel into a vat, even if he spends the entire day doing so, each successive drop is *batel* as it falls in.

### Accumulation Question

The principle of *rishon rishon batel* is a substantive halachic concept that makes considerable sense in the right context. Consider the following scenario: a vat of kosher chicken soup is receiving drip after drip of *yayin nesech*. The *mishna* has already taught that wine mixed with unlike substances — wine in chicken soup — is governed by *nosein ta'am*: the forbidden substance is *batel* unless it can impart a perceptible taste. The first drop of wine falls in, and it cannot be tasted; it is *batel*. The second drop falls in, and it too is *batel*. This continues for hundreds of drips, until eventually the cumulative wine has reached one-sixtieth of the soup, and now the wine taste is perceptible. What is the *halacha* at that moment?

One might say: at drop number 2,000, the wine is now *nosein ta'am* and the mixture is forbidden. But another view says: one moment before that 2,000th drop, there was no wine in the soup — everything that had fallen had already been rendered *batel*, and the soup was 100% kosher at that stage. So the 2,000th drop lands in a kosher soup, and one drop of wine is not enough to render kosher soup forbidden. This is *rishon rishon batel*.

The opposing principle is *chozer v'neior* — it returns and wakes up. On this view, the wine that had been rendered *batel* was only dormant. When the 2,000th drop arrives and the proportion has shifted to the point of *nosein ta'am*, all the previously dormant wine "wakes up," reasserts its presence, and the entire mixture is forbidden. One might also pose the *chozer v'neior* question at the threshold of *rov* rather than *nosein ta'am* — would dormant forbidden substance reassert itself once the forbidden component has become a majority?

All of this reasoning makes excellent sense in a context where wine is dripping into chicken soup and the early drips are indisputably *batel*. The problem is that Rabbi Yochanan's application of *rishon rishon batel* involves wine dripping into a vat of wine — and the *mishna* has just declared that *yayin b'yayin* is *assur bechol shehu*. The very first drop of wine should never be *batel*. Rabbi Yochanan's statement appears to make no sense in this context.

### Contradiction Emerges

The *Gemara* confronts this directly. The *mishna* teaches *yayin nesech assur v'oser bechol shehu* — seemingly, one drop of forbidden wine falling into kosher wine creates a prohibition immediately. *Mai lav dekanfil issura lego heteira*? Is this not the obvious case, where the forbidden substance falls into the permitted? If so, Rabbi Yochanan's claim that each drop is *batel* flatly contradicts the *mishna*.

### Yayin B'Yayin Lenient

The *Gemara* resolves this by rereading the *mishna* entirely. When the *mishna* declares *yayin nesech* to be *assur bechol shehu*, it is not speaking of the ordinary case in which a drop of forbidden wine falls into a large vat of kosher wine. Rather, it speaks of the reverse: *dekanpal heteira lego issura* — the permitted substance is falling, drop by drop, into a large quantity of forbidden wine. In that scenario, each drop of kosher wine arrives already surrounded by a majority of *yayin nesech* and is rendered forbidden immediately. Even as more and more kosher wine is added, each increment is captured by the *issur* before it can accumulate into a majority. That is the meaning of *bechol shehu*: not that a single drop of *yayin nesech* contaminates a sea of kosher wine, but that even a large quantity of kosher wine pouring slowly into forbidden wine never achieves dominance.

The *Gemara* sustains this reading through the subsequent cases of the *mishna* as well. When the *mishna* addresses *yayin b'mayim b'nosein ta'am*, it is again the kosher wine dripping into a great volume of forbidden water, not the reverse. The entire *mishna*, on this reading, concerns *heter* falling into *issur*, not *issur* falling into *heter*. And according to Rabbi Yochanan, in the normal case — where a small amount of *issur* falls into a large amount of *heter* — *yayin b'yayin* is *batel b'rov*. This is, as Rashi is at pains to emphasize, a radical leniency — and not the position we rule by.

---

## Multiple Versions

### Yitzchak Limitation

A second report from Eretz Yisrael arrives with Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef, also citing Rabbi Yochanan. His version reads: *ha'me'areh yayin nesech mitziltzul katan labor, afilu kol hayom kulo, rishon rishon batel* — one who pours *yayin nesech* from a small vessel, drop by drop, into a vat, each drop is *batel* even over the course of the entire day. The language *tziltzul katan* — a small bottle producing individual droplets — is significant. Rav Yitzchak adds: *vedavka tsiltzul katan, dela nafish amudeih* — this ruling applies only to a narrow trickle that does not flow in a heavy stream. But *aval chavit*, if it were a full barrel pouring a thick, continuous column of wine, *denafish amudeih*, that would not be subject to *rishon rishon batel*. This version of Rabbi Yochanan thus pulls back from the broadest reading and limits the *bittul* to genuinely isolated drops, not to a continuous flow.

### Ravin's Roin

A third version arrives with Ravin, also in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, and introduces an entirely different conceptual framework. *Yayin nesech shenafal labor, venafal sham kiton shel mayim, ro'in et hamino ke'ilu eino, vehashear mayim rabim alav umevattlin oto.* When *yayin nesech* has fallen into a vat of wine, and subsequently a jug of water is poured in, we apply the principle of *ro'in* — we treat the kosher wine as though it were not there — and the remaining water, which stands in an *eino mino* relationship to the *yayin nesech*, is sufficient to create *bittul*.

This version represents an even larger *chiddush* than the earlier ones, because it does not require the water to have been present at the time the forbidden wine fell in. The *yayin nesech* fell first into wine alone, the entire vat was therefore forbidden at that moment, and yet retroactively — once the water is added — we apply *ro'in*, pretend the kosher wine is absent, and treat the matter as though one drop of forbidden wine fell into water. Ravin's Rabbi Yochanan, on this reading, never actually contradicted the *mishna*'s teaching that *yayin b'yayin* is *bechol shehu*. Rather, his leniency is specifically about the presence of *eino mino* — water — which can create *bittul* even after the fact, by means of the *ro'in* principle.

### Water First Rule

Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda cites Rabbi Yochanan with a qualification: *lo shanu ela she-nafal kiton shel mayim techilla* — the ruling that the water creates *bittul* applies only if the water fell first, before the *yayin nesech*. That is, when the wine drops into a mixture that already contains water, the water is immediately operative and performs *bittul* on the spot. *Aval lo nafal sham kiton shel mayim techilla* — but if no water had fallen prior to the *yayin nesech* — *matza min et mino venei'or*: the *yayin nesech* encountered the kosher wine, found its own kind, and they "woke up together." In such a case the wine's identity is reinforced and intensified rather than neutralized, and the subsequent addition of water cannot undo what has already congealed as *issur*.

The intuition behind *matza min et mino venei'or* is striking. In an ordinary *chozer v'neior* scenario, the forbidden substance had been dormant and reawakens when cumulative proportions shift. Here, the forbidden wine never even became dormant — it merged immediately with kosher wine and the entire vat was *assur* from the moment of contact. The addition of water at that stage cannot focus on a single isolated drop; the entire mixture is already forbidden.

### Timing of Roin

The *Gemara* notes that Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda's statement can be read in two ways depending on which earlier source it was meant to clarify. If it was offered as a clarification of the *mishna* directly, then it merely says: when water is added, *bittul* occurs, without specifying that the water must come first. In that case, the statement is lenient, allowing *ro'in* even when the water arrives after the *yayin nesech*. But if Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda was clarifying the statement of Ravin — who had already asserted that water added after the fact creates *bittul* — then Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda's refinement is a restriction: *only* if the water was there first. *Uman dematni lah adrevin vadai baei techillah.* If Ravin had already granted the more lenient position, Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda must be coming to limit it.

---

## Chizkiyah Position

### Hidgilu Debate

The *Gemara* now records a direct dispute between Chizkiyah and Rabbi Yochanan. The scenario is *yayin nesech shenafal labor venafal sham kiton shel mayim* — *yayin nesech* fell into a vat and water was subsequently added. Chizkiyah states: *higdilu b'issur — assur; higdilu b'heter — mutar.* If the mixture grew in a state of *issur*, it remains forbidden; if it grew in a state of *heter*, it is permitted.

Rashi reads Chizkiyah's position carefully. Both of the two cases under discussion — wine falling into wine alone, and wine falling into an existing mixture of wine and water — are classified by Chizkiyah as *higdilu b'issur*, because in both cases the *yayin nesech* encountered wine upon entry and the volume of *issur* increased. The only case of *higdilu b'heter* is the straightforward one: a single drop of *yayin nesech* falls directly into water from the start, whereupon *bittul* occurs immediately. According to Chizkiyah, once wine has merged with wine and the vat is already in a state of *issur*, the subsequent arrival of water cannot produce *bittul*. He rejects *ro'in* entirely.

### Yochanan Rejects

Rabbi Yochanan disagrees: *afilu higdilu b'issur — mutar.* Even in the case where the volume grew under conditions of *issur*, it remains permitted — provided that water was present when the *yayin nesech* fell in. Water, by virtue of being *eino mino*, generates *bittul* regardless of the presence of kosher wine in the vat. Rabbi Yochanan affirms the principle of *ro'in*: we disregard the kosher wine, treat it as though absent, and allow the water to perform *bittul* on the single drop of *yayin nesech*.

### Sourdough Analogy

Rabbi Yirmiyah poses a question to Rabbi Zeira: perhaps Chizkiyah and Rabbi Yochanan are simply reprising the ancient dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages concerning sourdough. The *mishna* teaches: *se'or shel chulin v'shel terumah shenafalu l'toch issa, lo b'zeh k'dei l'chametz v'lo b'zeh k'dei l'chametz, v'nitztarfu l'chimtzu* — two pieces of sourdough, one of *chulin* and one of *terumah*, each insufficient on its own to cause fermentation, fell together into dough and jointly caused it to rise. The question concerns *terumah*: since the *terumah* sourdough contributed causally to the fermentation, is the dough now forbidden as *terumah*?

Rabbi Eliezer says: *achar acharon ani ba* — I follow the last: whichever piece of sourdough fell in last bears causal responsibility for the fermentation, and the status of the dough is determined accordingly. The Sages say: it does not matter whether the *issur* fell first or last — if it did not have sufficient quantity to cause fermentation by itself, it never creates a problem.

The structural parallel being proposed is: Chizkiyah, who holds that sequence matters and that *issur* falling second is worse, seems analogous to Rabbi Eliezer, who follows the last act. Rabbi Yochanan, who says the water creates *bittul* regardless of sequence, seems analogous to the Sages, who ignore the order of events.

### Abaye Critique

Abaye, however, dismantles the analogy. He points out that Rabbi Eliezer's position, on closer examination, cannot be mapped onto Chizkiyah's. According to Abaye, Rabbi Eliezer's leniency applies only in the following circumscribed case: *lo shanu ela she-kadam ve-silek et ha-issur* — when the *issur* sourdough fell first and was then *removed* before the combined fermentation occurred. In that case, the *issur* is no longer operative at the time of fermentation. But if the *issur* sourdough remains present and participates actively in fermentation, even Rabbi Eliezer — who is sensitive to causal contribution — would render the dough forbidden regardless of whether it fell first or second.

This demolishes the proposed analogy. Chizkiyah holds that the case where wine falls into a mixture of wine and water is *mutar* — but according to Abaye's reading of Rabbi Eliezer, that same case by sourdough would be *assur* if the *issur* sourdough remained. Chizkiyah therefore cannot correspond to Rabbi Eliezer. The Sages, for their part, would say it is always *mutar* — which aligns with no qualified version of Chizkiyah's view either. *Chizkiyah damar keman* — Chizkiyah fits neither position.

The *Gemara* therefore concludes: *ella hacha beroin kemiflagi* — what Chizkiyah and Rabbi Yochanan are actually disputing is the principle of *ro'in* itself. *Lechizkiyah leit lei roin* — Chizkiyah does not accept *ro'in*. *Ulerabi Yochanan is lei roin* — Rabbi Yochanan affirms it. The debate about *zeh v'zeh gorem* — whether two partial causes jointly produce a prohibited outcome — is an entirely different discussion that does not map onto this one, as Rashi confirms.

---

## Two Cups Case

### Assi Question

The *Gemara* now asks whether Rabbi Yochanan truly holds the principle of *ro'in*, given that Rav Assi himself apparently posed the question to Rabbi Yochanan and received no immediate answer. The case Rav Assi presented was: *shnei kosos, echad shel chulin v'echad shel terumah, umazgan ve'irvan ze baze* — two cups, one of *chulin* wine and one of *terumah* wine. Each cup has water added (*mezigah*), and then the two cups are poured together. The question concerns *terumah*: water added to the *terumah* cup might, if considered in isolation, be sufficient to create *bittul* of the *terumah*. But the mixture now also contains *chulin* wine, which is *min b'mino* with the *terumah* wine. Does the *chulin* wine interfere with *bittul* — joining with the *terumah* wine and preventing the water from performing *bittul* — or does *ro'in* apply: we treat the *chulin* wine as absent and allow the water to act on the *terumah* wine alone?

Rav Assi's question received no immediate resolution from Rabbi Yochanan, which might cast doubt on whether Rabbi Yochanan was committed to *ro'in* as a firm principle.

### Ignoring Kosher

The *Gemara* resolves this: *meikara lo pashat lei ulevassof pashat lei* — initially he had no answer, but ultimately Rabbi Yochanan arrived at his view. And it is stated in his name — whether transmitted by Rav Ami or Rav Assi: *shnei kosos, echad shel chulin v'echad shel terumah, umazgan ve'irvan ze baze, ro'in et ze ke'ilu eino, veshaar mayim rabim alav umevattlo oto* — we regard the *chulin* wine as though it were not there, and the water — standing in an *eino mino* relationship to the *terumah* — creates *bittul*. This is the operative *halacha*, and the case of whether *ro'in* applies even when the water arrives second remains less fully resolved.

---

## General Bittul Rules

### Rav Shmuel Rule

With the case law of *yayin nesech* and *ro'in* behind us, the *mishna*'s closing words — *zeh haklal: min b'mino b'mashehu, shelo b'mino b'nosein ta'am* — serve as a springboard for the *Gemara* to set out the general positions of the *Amoraim* on *bittul*. Rav and Shmuel both rule: *kol issurin shebaTorah min b'mino b'mashehu* — for every prohibition in the Torah, when a forbidden substance is mixed with its own kind, even a trace amount is never *batel*. When it is mixed with something unlike itself, it follows *nosein ta'am*. The *mishna*'s statement of the "general rule" is understood by them to extend to every case in the Torah, making *min b'mino b'mashehu* the universal default.

### Yochanan Resh Lakish

Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish disagree. They rule: *kol issurin shebaTorah bein b'mino bein shelo b'mino b'nosein ta'am* — whether the forbidden substance is mixed with its own kind or with something different, the operative principle is always *nosein ta'am*. There is no categorical difference in stringency between *min b'mino* and *min b'eino mino*. If anything, *min b'mino* is *more* susceptible to *bittul*, not less. This is the position we rule by.

### Exceptions Listed

Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish, however, acknowledge two exceptions: *chutz mi'tevel v'yayin nesech* — *tevel* and *yayin nesech* are treated more strictly, such that *b'mino* is *b'mashehu* and *shelo b'mino* follows *nosein ta'am*. These two cases follow the exact structure of the *mishna*, whose *zeh haklal*, on Rabbi Yochanan's reading, comes precisely to include them.

### Yayin Reason

The reason *yayin nesech* receives exceptional treatment is stated plainly: *mishum chomer d'avoda kochavim* — because of the gravity of idolatry. We deliberatley impose the stringent logic of *min b'mino b'mashehu* on *yayin nesech* in order to prevent its easy nullification.

### Tevel Reason

The reason *tevel* is exceptional is formulated as *k'heteiro kach issuro*: as its remedy, so its prohibition. The principle means that the same measure that can fix the *tevel* problem sets the threshold for the prohibition. And what fixes *tevel*? Shmuel taught: *chita achat poteret et hakari* — a single kernel of wheat suffices to separate *terumah* and thereby discharge the most significant dimension of the *tevel* obligation from an entire heap. Since one grain of wheat effects the *heter*, one grain of *tevel* wheat creates the *issur* — and since that single grain is consequential, it cannot be *batel*.

### Single Grain Fix

Rashi adds that this reasoning explains specifically why *min b'mino* is the operative axis for *tevel*. The mechanism by which a single grain fixes the heap works only *min b'mino*: one cannot separate a grain of barley as *terumah* on a heap of wheat. The *heteira* — the fix — is inherently *min b'mino*, and therefore the *issur* follows the same *min b'mino* logic.

An alternative way of framing the exception, however — and one that applies equally to *yayin nesech* — is simply that when the *halacha* demands heightened severity, we borrow the stringent model even though it is not our normative position. There exists in the halachic system a logic under which *min b'mino* is the hardest case for *bittul*, and when a given prohibition is severe enough to warrant exceptional treatment, we apply that logic selectively.

### Chametz Exception

*Chametz b'pesach* goes still further, though the *Gemara* does not fully elaborate its reasoning here. The standard *machmir* position for *min b'mino* would be *bechol shehu*. But *chametz* exceeds even that: even *min b'eino mino* is governed by *bechol shehu* on Pesach, making it the most stringent category of all. This applies to mixtures that occur on Pesach itself; a mixture formed before Pesach follows the ordinary rules.

One might ask why the *Gemara* gives the *k'heteiro kach issuro* explanation for *tevel* rather than invoking the principle of *davar sheyesh lo matirin* — the rule that a forbidden substance which has a permissible avenue of remedy cannot be rendered permitted through *bittul*. Tosafos poses exactly this question. The most economical answer is that *davar sheyesh lo matirin* as a categorical principle is in fact a matter of debate among the *Tannaim*; while we rule by it *l'maiseh*, it is not the consensus position of the *Gemara*, and therefore the *Gemara* prefers to ground the ruling in the more universally accepted reasoning of *k'heteiro kach issuro*.

---

---

# Avodah Zarah 74

## Assur B'Chol Shehu

### Mishna Overview

The mishna at the top of 74 continues the tractate's discussion of *bitul* and related concepts, presenting a list of things that are forbidden and that forbid even in the tiniest admixture: *eilu assurin ve'ossrin bechol shehu*. The items enumerated are *yayin nesech*, *avodat kochavim* (an idol — Rashi understands this as a worshipped image mixed up indistinguishably with other decorative images), *oros levuvim* (skins cut from the heart of an animal as an offering to *avoda zara*, a form of *tikroves avoda zara* recalling an earlier mishna), *shor haniskal* (an ox stoned for killing a person), *egla arufa* (the calf whose neck is broken in the unresolved murder procedure), *tzipporei metzora* (birds used in the purification of the *metzora*), *se'ar nazir* (the shaved hair of a *nazir* at the conclusion of his period), *peter chamor* (a firstborn donkey whose owner declined to redeem with a sheep and whose neck is therefore broken), *basar bechalav*, *se'ir hamishtaleach* (the scapegoat of Yom Kippur), and *chulin shenishchatu ba'azara* (non-sanctified animals slaughtered in the *azara*). All of these share the common denominator of being *issurei hana'ah* — forbidden in benefit.

The straightforward reading of the mishna would be that things forbidden in benefit carry the rule of *assur bechol shehu*, that even the smallest admixture is forbidden. One important clarification regarding *basar bechalav* is worth noting at the outset. The Gemara in Chullin is explicit that *basar bechalav* as a forbidden mixture only comes into being in the first place if there is enough of one ingredient to impart taste to the other. An infinitesimal drop of milk that cannot be tasted in the meat does not create *basar bechalav* at all. Indeed, the Gemara even entertains the idea that the principle of *ta'am ke'ikar* — that taste is halakhically equivalent to substance — may itself be derived from the requirement that a forbidden *basar bechalav* mixture must involve a tasteable quantity. The rule of *assur bechol shehu* therefore does not speak to what constitutes *basar bechalav*; it speaks rather to whether, once you have a piece of *basar bechalav*, it can become *batel* in a further mixture.

### Why Chametz Missing?

The difficulty with the mishna's apparent logic is immediate. The Gemara asks: *tana mai kachashiv* — what principle organizes this list? If it is listing things that are *assur bechol shehu* because they are *issurei hana'ah*, then *chametz bePesach* should also appear — it is likewise *assur behana'ah*. And if the list is instead organized around the principle of *davar shebeminyan* — things sold individually rather than by weight or volume, such that each item retains its independent identity in a mixture rather than dissolving into a homogeneous mass — then why not list a *chatichas neveilah*, a presentable cut of non-kosher meat, which also retains its identity? That concept is the parallel principle of *chatichah harauyah lehitchabed*, a portion fit to serve to an honored guest, which confers the same kind of independent significance as *davar shebeminyan*. If the list is organized around *chatichah harauyah lehitchabed*, then a fine steak of *neveilah* should appear. Neither criterion alone explains the list as it stands.

### Two Criteria Rule

Rabbi Chiya bar Abba, and some say Rabbi Yitzchak Nafcha, resolves the difficulty: *hai tana tartei it lei* — this tanna actually requires the intersection of both criteria simultaneously. Only things that are both *davar shebeminyan* and *issurei hana'ah* appear on the list. That explains why *neveilah* is absent — it may be a *davar shebeminyan* through the principle of *chatichah harauyah lehitchabed*, but it is not *assur behana'ah*. And it explains why *chametz bePesach* is absent — it is *assur behana'ah* but not inherently a *davar shebeminyan*.

### Orlah Already Taught

The Gemara immediately presses further. Why not list the special nuts of the region of Perech and the pomegranates of Badan? Those items, familiar from the mishna in *Orlah*, are classic examples of *davar shebeminyan*, sold individually because of their significance. They are also *issurei hana'ah*, since both *orlah* and *kilayim* carry that prohibition. They would thus satisfy both criteria perfectly. The answer is that the mishna in *Orlah* already teaches them — *hatam tani lah*. The closing lines of that mishna state: *harauy le'orlah orlah, harauy lekil'ei hakerem kil'ei hakerem* — wherever the relevant fruits originate, they retain their status as *davar shebeminyan*, and they are also *issurei hana'ah*. Since they are already taught in their proper place, our mishna need not repeat them.

### Chametz B'Pesach

The same logic applies to the case of home-baked loaves, *kikarot shel ba'al habayit*, which the same mishna in *Orlah* lists as a paradigmatic *davar shebeminyan*. In the context of *chametz bePesach*, those loaves are also *assur behana'ah* — and both criteria are thus met. The Gemara notes that the position that *chametz bePesach* is at all *assur behana'ah* is actually a matter of dispute: *man shamit d'amar leh Rabbi Akiva* — it is Rabbi Akiva who holds that view. We of course rule accordingly. And the Gemara answers that Rabbi Akiva himself adds the home-baked loaves to the list in the mishna in *Orlah* — *Rabbi Akiva mosif af kikarot shel ba'al habayit*. Since that case is already taught there, there is no need to repeat it in our mishna.

### What Gets Excluded

The mishna's phrase *harei elu* — "these are the ones" — comes to exclude things that possess only one of the two criteria. *L'me'utei davar shebeminyan velo issurei hana'ah*, it excludes things that are *davar shebeminyan* but not *issurei hana'ah* — such as a presentable cut of *neveilah*. And *l'me'utei issurei hana'ah velo davar shebeminyan*, it excludes things that are *assur behana'ah* but are not *davar shebeminyan* — such as *chametz bePesach* that is not a fine home-baked loaf.

There is, however, a sharp difficulty here: those very examples the Gemara offers as excluded are in fact also not *batel* in practice. A fine *neveilah* steak is not *batel* because it is *chatichah harauyah lehitchabed*, functionally equivalent to *davar shebeminyan*. And *chametz bePesach* — even the smallest crumbs — is not *batel*, which is precisely why the stringencies of *bedikat chametz* extend to the most minute traces. Rashi appears to suggest, in a strikingly unusual comment, that *chametz bePesach* that is not a *davar shebeminyan* actually would be *batel* — a conclusion that is clearly not the operative *halacha*.

### Actual Rules Differ

Tosafot takes a different approach to resolve this tension, one that cuts sharply against the surface thrust of the Gemara. Tosafot argues that the Gemara here is not at all pronouncing what determines whether something is *batel* or not. Its sole concern is what determines which items are included in the mishna's list. The mishna chose to enumerate only things satisfying both criteria — *davar shebeminyan* and *issurei hana'ah* — but this tells us nothing definitive about the actual laws of *bitul*.

The actual rules are more complex and cannot be read off the mishna's structure. *Davar shebeminyan*, or its parallel *chatichah harauyah lehitchabed*, is always sufficient by itself to prevent *bitul* — regardless of whether the item is *assur behana'ah*. A *neveilah* steak and a *basar bechalav* steak are both not *batel*, the one despite not being *assur behana'ah*, the other because it is. That criterion stands alone and is always decisive.

*Issurei hana'ah*, on the other hand, is not a uniform category with respect to *bitul*. Some *issurei hana'ah* are *batel*, and some are not, and the distinction does not follow mechanically from the category. *Orlah* and *kilayim* — both *issurei hana'ah* — are *batel*. *Chametz bePesach* is *assur behana'ah* and yet is not *batel*. *Yayin nesech* and other *avoda zara*-related prohibitions are not *batel*, though that is partly because the gravity of *avoda zara* adds additional weight beyond the bare category of *issur hana'ah*. The mishna's two-criteria requirement thus reflects an editorial principle — what belongs on this list — not a halakhic formula for what is or is not *batel*. The actual determination of *bitul* for *issurei hana'ah* depends on separate, category-specific discussions and cannot be inferred from the mishna's structure alone.

---

## Yayin Nesech Falling

### Mishna Case

The next mishna addresses the case of *yayin nesech she-nafal l'bor* — *yayin nesech* that falls into a vat of wine. Since *yayin nesech* is *assur bechol shehu*, even a drop falling into a full vat renders the entire contents forbidden in benefit.

### Rabban Gamliel

Rabban Gamliel offers a practical remedy: sell the entire vat to a non-Jew, but charge only for the amount of kosher wine, not for the added *yayin nesech*. The elegance of this solution is that the seller receives payment only for the hundred gallons — or whatever the legitimate quantity is — and thereby derives no benefit from the forbidden drop. The *yayin nesech* has been absorbed into the transaction without the seller extracting its value.

### Rav's Limitation

Rav rules that the *halacha* follows Rabban Gamliel, but with a restriction: *chavit bechaviyot* — this applies when it is a barrel among barrels, *aval lo yayin b'yayin* — but not when it is wine mixed into wine. The logic is clear. When a barrel of *yayin nesech* is lost among a thousand kosher barrels, the seller can plausibly say: I am selling you a thousand barrels; the extra one — whichever it is — I am simply not selling, I am merely handing it over. Each barrel retains its independent identity. But when the wine itself is mixed in a vat, there is no discrete unit that can be conceptually set aside. The forbidden wine has dispersed entirely and redefined the identity of the whole vat. It becomes impossible to say "I am selling only the kosher portion."

### Lenient Views

Despite Rav's restriction, several Amoraim rule that even wine mixed into wine follows Rabban Gamliel's leniency. Shmuel states this explicitly, and his view is echoed by Rabbah bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, Rabbi Shmuel bar Barana in the name of Rabbi Chanina, and Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha — all permitting wine in wine.

### Practical Halakha

Notwithstanding this array of lenient opinions, Rav Nachman draws the operative practical distinction: for actual *yayin nesech* — wine actively used for *avoda zara* — wine mixed into wine remains forbidden and Rabban Gamliel's ruling does not apply; only barrel among barrels is permitted. For *stam yeinam* — wine that a non-Jew has handled or had access to but that was not actively used for *avoda zara* — even wine mixed into wine is permitted under Rabban Gamliel's approach. In practical terms, the overwhelming majority of cases we encounter are *stam yeinam*, so the leniency is broadly applicable.

### Rashi's Method

When it comes to the barrel-in-barrels case, Rashi notes a technique that appears more prominently in discussions of *avoda zara* than elsewhere: one takes a random barrel and throws it away entirely. This allows one to say — at least constructively — that the disposed barrel was the forbidden one. This is not sufficient to permit drinking from the remaining barrels, but it does provide an additional basis for the sale — allowing the seller to charge only for the remaining barrels and to represent that the *yayin nesech* barrel was not included in the transaction.

---

## Koshering Wine Press

### Mishna Cases

The mishna now turns from *bitul* to *hachsharah* — the koshering of wine presses and related vessels. The context is vessels that non-Jews have used in the production of wine, raising concern that the wine has absorbed into the walls of the vessel or into the pitch lining it.

The background is relevant: pitch (*zifta*) was used to line wine presses and barrels, in part to prevent the wine from seeping into the walls of the vessel itself. To prevent the resulting wine from tasting of pitch, wine was often mixed into the pitch before application — a kind of seasoning. The result is that the pitch itself contains wine from a non-Jew, which may then leach back into the next batch of wine pressed there.

The mishna presents a graduated series of cases. A stone wine press that was pitched by a non-Jew: scour it and it is permitted. Wood: Rebbi says the same — scour it; the Chachamim say scouring is insufficient, and the pitch must be peeled away. Pottery: even peeling off the pitch does not help, because the wine penetrates through the pitch into the pottery walls themselves, where it cannot be removed. Whether this last ruling regarding pottery reflects the Chachamim alone or is also conceded by Rebbi is left open by the mishna and will require clarification in the Gemara.

### Rava's Clarification

Rava clarifies that the mishna's requirement of scouring applies *davka zifsa* — specifically where the press was lined with pitch. If a non-Jew merely stomped grapes directly on the stone, without pitch, the concern is only surface contamination and a rinse suffices. Stone does not absorb; whatever wine was there is on the surface.

The Gemara initially questions this: the mishna explicitly mentions pitch, so of course it is discussing a pitched press — Rava's clarification seems unnecessary. The Gemara responds: one might have thought the mishna mentions pitch only because that is the typical situation (*orcha demilta*), but the same rule would apply to an unpitched stone press in which grapes were stomped. Rava therefore informs us that the leniency of mere rinsing applies specifically to the unpitched case; the mishna's scouring requirement is genuinely restricted to pitched stone.

A second, more stringent version (*ika deamri*) of Rava's ruling addresses a three-way distinction. There are three scenarios: stomping on bare stone (rinse is sufficient — the stone does not absorb); pitch with no stomping (scour — the wine is in the pitch but can be removed by scouring); and pitch with stomping on top of it (scouring is not sufficient). In this third scenario, the stomping drives the wine deeply into the pitch and likely into hidden cracks beneath it, such that even Rebbi would agree that the pitch must be entirely removed.

### Rav's Story

This three-way distinction is dramatized by a narrative involving Rav. A man approached Rabbi Chiya requesting that a student be assigned to assist him in koshering his wine press. Rabbi Chiya dispatched Rav, his nephew, with the instruction: *chazi dela mitzavchat alai bevei midrasha* — be careful that this man does not later come to the *beis medrash* and complain that I caused his wine to be forbidden.

Rav arrived and inspected the wine press. He found that the pitch surface was extraordinarily smooth, and concluded that scouring would suffice — the smoothness of the pitch indicated that even if grapes had been stomped there, the wine had not penetrated into cracks, and the situation was equivalent to the middle scenario of pitch without deep absorption.

But as Rav walked back and forth examining the floor of the press, he noticed a crack concealed beneath the pitch surface, and within it, wine. This transformed the case: whatever the surface had looked like, cracks existed and wine had penetrated deeply. The situation was now unmistakably the third scenario — pitch plus stomping — and Rav ruled that the pitch had to be entirely peeled away. He reflected: *vahainu deamar lei chavivi chazi dela mitzavcha alai bevei midrasha* — this is exactly what my uncle had warned me about. The instruction was not to be cavalier, but to inspect carefully enough that the koshering would truly hold up to scrutiny. The concern was not to burden the man unnecessarily, but to ensure that what was declared kosher was indeed kosher.

### Baraita Details

A *baraita* adds detail regarding other wine-press equipment. The *gat* (wine press), the *machat* (according to Rashi, the bucket used to draw wine from the press), and the *mishpach* (funnel) — all made of pottery according to Rashi's reading — when belonging to non-Jews: Rebbi permits scouring, the Chachamim forbid it. Rebbi himself concedes, however, that pottery *kankanim* — actual storage jars — belonging to non-Jews are forbidden even with scouring.

### Storage vs. Temporary

What is the distinction? *Zeh machniso lekiyum vezeh ein machniso lekiyum* — one type is made for long-term storage, the other is not. Pottery storage jars are designed to hold wine for extended periods — sometimes years. Even though all of this involves cold liquid and cold absorption, the prolonged contact causes genuine absorption into the pottery walls, and simple scouring cannot draw it out. Wine-press equipment, by contrast, is used intensively only during the pressing season and sits empty for long stretches of time; the sustained contact that causes deep absorption does not occur in the same way. Therefore Rebbi holds that scouring is adequate for the press equipment. The Chachamim disagree and require more.

When long-term pottery storage is involved and scouring is inadequate, Rashi notes that a remedy discussed earlier in the tractate (on 33a) is available: filling the vessel with water and emptying it over three consecutive days, changing the water each time. That solution addresses even pottery in which wine has been absorbed over time. It is worth noting, as an aside, that this very technique underlies the practice — familiar from the laws of Pesach — of soaking glass vessels in water for three days.

### Reconciling Views

A difficulty emerges: the baraita says that Rebbi permits scouring for pottery wine-press equipment without pitch. But the mishna states that if the wine press is pottery (*shel cheres*), even peeling off the pitch does not help. If pottery is that problematic, how can Rebbi permit mere scouring when it is just pottery without pitch?

Rava resolves this: *seifa dematnitin atya keRabbanan* — the closing clause of the mishna, which rules so stringently about pottery, follows the Chachamim, not Rebbi. According to Rebbi, pottery wine-press equipment without pitch can indeed be koshered by scouring, since it is not made for long-term storage. The mishna's stringent pottery ruling reflects only the Chachamim's position.
