According to the second version, *Rava* holds the opposite: *shogeg al pihem hu de-patur* — it is only the *shogeg* whose error is a *direct* result of their ruling who is *patur*; if he would have eaten it accidentally regardless, he is *chayav*. The *Gemara* ultimately cannot resolve the question from the *Mishnah*'s wording, since the phrase can be read either way, and the matter is left as a *plugta* — a standing dispute.

### Rav vs. Rabbi Yochanan

The question surfaces as an explicit dispute between *Rav* and *Rabbi Yochanan*. In a case where *beis din* ruled that *chelev* was *mutar* and the pieces got mixed up — *Rav amar patur*: he is exempt, because he would have eaten the piece anyway given *beis din's* ruling. *Rabbi Yochanan amar chayav*: he is obligated, because his eating the *chelev* was not caused by their ruling; he would have eaten it accidentally regardless.

### Shav Mideiato

A *baraita* is then brought to challenge *Rabbi Yochanan*'s position. The verse says *asher lo sa'aseinah bishgagah* — an act done unintentionally that one would otherwise not have done. *Rabbi Shimon* derives from this: *prat l'shav mideiato* — this excludes someone who, even had he known better, would have done the act anyway. *Hash-av mideiato mevi korban al shigagaso* — someone who would have stopped had he been informed brings a *korban* for his error; *lo shav mideiato eino mevi korban al shigagaso* — someone who would have proceeded regardless does not bring a *korban*.

Applied to our case: this person is no *mumar*, no apostate. He listens to everything *beis din* says. Had he known that what he was eating was *chelev*, he would have eaten it anyway — because *beis din* ruled it was permitted. He is therefore *lo shav mideiato*, and on that basis he should be *patur*. That supports *Rav*'s position and appears to refute *Rabbi Yochanan*.

## Talmid & Ra'uy

### Shev Mideiato Braita

The *baraita* develops the principle of *shav mideiato* in a way that is crucial for understanding the *Mishnah*'s cases. There is a fundamental distinction between two types of people who would have acted differently had they known better. The first is the ordinary *shogeg*: he did not know what he was doing, but had someone told him, he would have stopped immediately. He is *shav mideiato* and brings a *korban*. The second is someone like a *mumar* — an apostate who has rejected this category of law entirely. Even if told that he is eating *chelev*, he would not have stopped. He is *lo shav mideiato* and does not bring a *korban*.

The *baraita*'s contribution is to sharpen what "would not have stopped" means. In the case at hand, the person is entirely righteous. He is *not* a *mumar*. He follows *beis din* scrupulously. But: had someone told him in the moment that he was eating *chelev*, he would not have stopped — because *beis din* ruled it *mutar*. His willingness to continue is not defiance of the law but compliance with it as he understands it. The question of *shav mideiato* in this context is therefore not about the person's character but about the specific act: in this act, given *beis din*'s ruling, he is categorized as *lo shav mideiato* — not because he is a *rasha* but because the ruling created a context in which he would have proceeded regardless of knowing the facts.

## Shogeg al Pihem (II)

### Rav Pappa Resolution

*Rav Pappa* resolves the apparent contradiction between *Rabbi Yochanan* and the principle of *shav mideiato*. *Rabbi Yochanan* holds the person *chayav* in the mixed-up-pieces case, even though it seems he would not have stopped. *Rav Pappa* explains: *keivan de-ki mishtoda lehu le-vei dina hadari behu ve-hu nami hadar beih* — since, had *beis din* become aware of their own error and retracted their ruling, they would have retracted, and he, too, would have retracted. Therefore, in a deeper and more theoretical sense, he *is shav mideiato* — he is someone who, when we trace back through all the counterfactuals, would ultimately have preferred not to have done this.

The distinction *Rav Pappa* is drawing is between two levels of willingness. On one level: had he known in the moment that he was eating *chelev*, he would have eaten it anyway, because *beis din* said it was fine. On a deeper level: had he known the full picture — that *beis din* had actually made an error, that they would themselves have wanted to retract — he would not have eaten it. The *korban* exists for a person who ideally wishes he had not committed the act. That person, once the error of *beis din* is exposed, *does* wish he had not eaten it. He is therefore *shav mideiato* in the fuller sense, and *Rabbi Yochanan* holds him obligated to bring a *korban*.

*Rav Pappa* adds a further point on behalf of *Rav*: even though *Rav* holds that this person is personally *patur*, *modeh Rav she-eino mashlim le-rov tzibbur* — *Rav* concedes that this person does not combine with the fifty percent who consciously followed *beis din* to constitute the majority that obligates *beis din* itself to bring a *korban*. The reason: *amar kra bishgagah — ad she-kulam bishgagah achas* — all of those counted toward the majority must be following *beis din* in the *same kind* of error. Those who consciously ate because of *beis din's* ruling are following the ruling directly; this person accidentally ate the wrong piece. Even if we hold him personally *patur*, he is not acting *al pihem* in the active sense, and therefore he does not count toward the communal threshold.

## Talmid & Ra'uy (II)

### Doubled Language

The *Mishnah* says *o talmid ve-hu ra'uy le-hora'ah* — "or a student who is fit to rule." *Rava* explains why both terms are necessary. If the *Mishnah* had only said *talmid*, one might have read that as referring to someone who has both of the qualities required for *hora'ah*: *gamir*, broad knowledge of the relevant law, and *savir*, analytical acuity and good legal judgment. On that reading, a person who has only one of the two — who knows the law well but lacks the analytical sharpness, or who has fine analytical skills but gaps in knowledge — might be thought to genuinely defer to *beis din* when they issue a ruling that conflicts with his understanding. After all, he can say to himself: they are smarter than I am; surely they understand something I do not; I am genuinely trusting their superior judgment, not acting on my own.

The *Mishnah* therefore adds the phrase *ra'uy le-hora'ah* — fit to rule. *Rava* reads this as an extension: even one who has only partial qualifications, either *gamir velo savir* or *savir velo gamir*, is still considered to "know better" when it appears to him that the court has made an error. His sense that they are more capable than he is does not transform his act into genuine reliance on them. If the law looks wrong to him, even if he lacks the full scholarly package, he is considered *tולה b'atzmo* and brings a *korban*.

### Abaye's Challenge

*Abaye* challenges *Rava* at a more basic level. The *Mishnah* describes someone who is *ra'uy le-hora'ah* — comparable to Shimon ben Azzai or Shimon ben Zoma, who sat before the *Sanhedrin* and were fully qualified to serve on the court. If such a person knows that the court is wrong, and he follows them anyway, why does he bring a *korban* at all? He should be *meizid* — a willful transgressor — since he knows the ruling is an error. Where is the *shogeg* in his act?

The *Gemara* resolves this with a *baraita*: *yachid ha'oseh al pi atzmo chayav, u'mipi beis din patur* — one who acts on his own authority is obligated, one who follows *beis din* is exempt. The case where such a person is *chayav* is where he knows the substance of the prohibition — he knows this is *chelev*, he knows this is *chametz* — but he makes a mistake about a different thing: he believes he has a *mitzvah* to follow *beis din* even when they err, *de'ka ta'ei be'mitzvah lishmoa divrei chachamim*. He thinks the rule *lo sasur yamin u'smol* obligates him to submit unconditionally, even against his own correct judgment. That belief is itself the *shogeg*. He is not *meizid* with respect to the prohibition of *chelev* because he genuinely believed he was permitted — not because *beis din* ruled correctly, but because he believed he was obligated to follow them regardless.

This is a significant clarification of the principle of *lo sasur*. The famous *Rashi* formulation — that one must follow the sages even if they tell you your right is your left — cannot mean, according to this *Gemara*, that even a qualified scholar must follow an objectively wrong ruling against his own certain knowledge. That reading is categorically rejected here. A scholar in that position who follows them is making an error about the scope of the obligation to heed rabbinic authority — a sincere error, and therefore a *shogeg*, but an error nonetheless. He brings a *korban* on his own account, not as someone whose act was subsumed under the court's authority.

## Scope of Reliance

### Retracted Rulings

The *Gemara* turns to the final case of the *Mishnah*'s general rule: *hatoleh b'veis din patur*. What is included within "relying on *beis din*"? The case is: *horu beis din v'yadu she-ta'u v'chazru bahen* — *beis din* issued a ruling, subsequently recognized their error, and retracted. An individual who had heard the original ruling but had not yet heard the retraction goes ahead and acts on the original ruling. Since in his own mind he is following *beis din*, he is *patur*, even though the ruling was no longer in force at the time he acted. He did not know of the retraction, and therefore his reliance was genuine. The *Gemara* notes this case will be stated explicitly in the following *Mishnah*, though it is already implicit here.

### Rabbi Yehuda vs. Sages

*Rav Yehuda* in the name of *Shmuel* identifies the position in the *Mishnah* — that an innocent individual who follows *beis din* is *patur* when the majority has not followed them — as the view of *Rabbi Yehuda* specifically. The *chachamim*, however, disagree: *yachid she-asah b'horat beis din chayav* — an individual who acts on *beis din's* ruling is *chayav* even when *beis din* itself does not bring a *korban*. According to the sages, the individual must bring a *korban* regardless of his innocence, precisely because *beis din* is not bringing one.

### Guilt vs. Causation

This dispute cuts to a foundational question about the nature of *korban*. The instinctive assumption is that a *korban* is brought because of personal culpability — the person did something wrong, even if unintentionally, and now atones for it. But the *Torah*'s conception may be less about guilt and more about causation and cosmic repair. When a sin is committed — when *chelev* is eaten, when *chametz* is consumed on *Pesach* — something in the world has been disrupted, a kind of metaphysical rupture has occurred, regardless of the personal culpability of the one who committed the act. The *korban* is not primarily a statement of guilt; it is a repair. You caused it — even without fault — and therefore you are the one who must address it.

The paradigm here is the *tinok shenishba* — a Jewish infant taken captive who grows up entirely outside of any awareness of Jewish identity and observance, and who, upon discovering the truth after forty years, must bring a *korban* for all the violations of *Shabbos* committed in complete ignorance. That person is entirely blameless. Yet the *korban* is required. Why? Because the act happened, the rupture exists, and whoever is causally responsible for it — however blameless — is the one who must effect the repair.

The *chachamim*'s position follows this logic directly. The individual who followed *beis din* may be personally blameless. But *beis din* is not bringing a *korban*, because the majority of *Klal Yisrael* did not follow their ruling. The *aveirah* was nonetheless committed. Someone must bring a *korban*. The individual who committed the act — even innocently, even while relying fully on legitimate authority — is the one who caused it to happen, and therefore he is the one who brings the *korban*. *Rabbi Yehuda* disagrees: the individual's blamelessness is complete enough that he is exempt together with *beis din*. But the *chachamim* hold that blamelessness does not extinguish the obligation when the causal responsibility remains undischarged.

# Horayot 3

## Individual vs. Beis Din

### Yehuda: Exempt

The sugya opens with a ruling transmitted by Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel: *zo divrei Rabbi Yehuda* — the position that if an individual follows *beis din* and acts in accordance with their erroneous ruling, he is exempt from bringing a *korban*, and *beis din* itself is likewise exempt from bringing its special *par* (bull) offering, because the majority of the *tzibbur* did not follow the ruling. This position has an intuitive logic to it: if *beis din* itself is not liable for their special *korban* because the majority of the community did not act on the ruling, why should the individual bear any responsibility? He did nothing wrong by deferring to the highest halachic authority.

### Chachamim: Liable

The *chachamim*, however, disagree. *Aval chachamim omrim: yachid she'asah al pi beis din chayav* — an individual who acted on the ruling of *beis din* in such a case is nevertheless obligated to bring a *korban*. This is a striking and counterintuitive position. The person is entirely blameless from any subjective moral standpoint: he is not a scholar, he relied on the greatest rabbinic authorities of his generation, and yet he must bring an atonement offering?

### Sin & Tumah

The answer lies in understanding what *korbanot* are actually about. The *korban* in the Torah, at least the *chatas*, is not fundamentally a mechanism for expressing personal guilt. It is a response to the objective reality that a sin was committed — that something was done which, had it been done willfully, would have incurred *karet*. That act creates a kind of *tuma*, an impurity in the world, and it requires rectification regardless of the subjective culpability of the person who committed it. The analogy is instructive: if someone walks into a store and breaks something, they must sweep up and pay for it regardless of whether it was their fault. The act creates the obligation. So too here — a sin was done, and since *beis din* is not bringing the *korban*, the person who committed the act must clean up the mess, so to speak. A comparable principle appears in the *Gemara* in Shabbat regarding a *tinok shenishba* — a child taken captive who has no awareness of being Jewish — who nevertheless brings certain *korbanot* for sins committed in complete innocence.

---

## Baraita Interpretati (II)

### Case Analysis

Having established the positions, the *Gemara* now asks: *mai Rabbi Yehuda?* Where exactly do we see this dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the *chachamim*? The *Gemara* cites a *baraita* which begins: *adayin ani omer miyut kahal she-chatu chayavin she-ein beis din mevi'in aleihen par* — I would say that when a minority of the congregation sins, they are obligated, because *beis din* does not bring the special *par* offering for a minority. *Rov ha-kahal she-chatu hayu pturin* — but I might have thought that if the majority of the community sins, they should be exempt, *she-harei beis din mevi'in aleihen par*, because *beis din* would bring the *par* in that case. The *baraita* then derives from the verse *me'am ha'aretz* — "from the people of the land" — that even a majority, even the entire community, is still obligated.

### Logical Difficulty

The *Gemara* immediately presses: what case are we actually discussing? If the case is one of simple *shiggas ma'aseh* — accidental sin without any ruling from *beis din* — then why is the *baraita* drawing a comparison to what *beis din* would or would not bring? *Beis din mai aviditaihu?* If there was no ruling of *beis din*, *beis din* is simply not a relevant factor. Of course individuals who sin on their own are obligated in a *korban*. And if, on the other hand, the *baraita* is discussing a case where the community followed a ruling of *beis din*, then the verse *me'am ha'aretz* — which speaks about ordinary individual sin — cannot serve as a source for a case involving a *horat beis din*. Either way, the *baraita* seems incoherent.

The difficulty deepens when we think it through more carefully. If we are speaking of a case where there was no ruling of *beis din*, then the entire comparison — "since *beis din* would bring a *korban* in the analogous case, maybe the *tzibbur* should be exempt" — makes no sense, because there is no analogous case involving *beis din* to compare to. And if we are speaking of the case of a ruling of *beis din*, then the verse *me'am ha'aretz*, which applies to plain unintentional sin, cannot tell us anything about liability when the community followed an erroneous judicial ruling.

### Resolution

The *Gemara* resolves this by proposing a different reading of the *baraita*. The *baraita* must be understood as follows: in a case of *shiggas ma'aseh* with no *horaat beis din*, when a minority of the congregation sins, they are clearly obligated — *she-ein beis din mevi'in aleihen par be-hora'ah*, meaning that in the comparable case of a ruling of *beis din* followed by a minority, *beis din* would not bring the *par*, and yet those individuals are obligated. So certainly when there is no ruling at all and a minority sins, they are obligated.

But one might have thought: if the majority of the congregation sins through *shiggas ma'aseh* with no ruling, perhaps they are exempt — because in the comparable case of *horaat beis din* followed by a majority, it is *beis din* that brings the *korban* and the individuals of the *tzibbur* are not obligated. Perhaps the same would apply here — when the majority sins on their own, they too should be exempt? The verse therefore teaches: *afilu rubah va-afilu kulah* — even the majority, even the entire community, is still obligated.

### Parallel Logic

What this structure reveals is that the *baraita* is built on a parallelism between cases of *shiggas ma'aseh* and cases of *horaat beis din*. The *baraita* uses the *horaat beis din* scenarios as the reference points for reasoning about the *shiggas ma'aseh* scenarios. And critically, the *baraita* takes for granted, without needing to prove it, that when an individual follows *beis din* and commits a sin, he brings a *korban*. It only needs to *prove* the case of the majority sinning by *shiggas ma'aseh*, because that is the non-obvious result. If the *baraita* held that even in the case of *horaat beis din* an individual brings nothing, there would be no reason to treat the individual case of *shiggas ma'aseh* as obviously obligated and leave it unproven. The very structure of the *baraita* — that it takes the individual's liability for granted and must argue only about the *tzibbur* — demonstrates that the *baraita* presupposes individual liability in the case of *horaat beis din*.

This is the proof that there exists a position — call it that of the *chachamim* — that when an individual follows *beis din* and *beis din* does not bring the special *korban*, the individual is nonetheless *chayav*. And it is contrasted with Rabbi Yehuda's position, derived from the three *miutim* in the verse (*nefesh*, *bishgaga*, *ba'asotah*), each of which serves as an exclusion, among them the exclusion of one who acts under the direction of *beis din* rather than on his own initiative. The hermeneutical method of applying each *miyut* as a separate exclusion is itself a distinctively Rabbi Yehuda approach, as noted by both Rashi and Tosafos — since the standard rule is *ein miyut achar miyut ella lerabbos*, that a second *miyut* following another comes to expand rather than restrict. That Rabbi Yehuda applies each one independently as an exclusion is characteristic of his *derasha* technique, which is also attested elsewhere regarding the verse *zos toras ha-olah* at 3a, where he similarly enumerates three independent *miutim*.

---

## Reading Options

### Rav Papa Challenge

Once the *Gemara* establishes that there are two *stam* baraitot — one that appears to exempt the individual following *beis din* and one whose structure presupposes his liability — it asks: *mimmai* — how do we know which is Rabbi Yehuda and which is the *chachamim*? Perhaps the attribution is reversed, or perhaps neither is Rabbi Yehuda's. The *Gemara* answers that the one employing the threefold *miyut* is demonstrably Rabbi Yehuda's, based on the known characteristic of his exegetical method.

Then a parallel tradition is introduced: Rav Nachman citing Shmuel frames the same controversy differently — *zo divrei Rabbi Meir, aval chachamim omrim yachid she'asah al pi horat beis din chayav*. So now the same structural debate is attributed to Rabbi Meir versus the *chachamim* rather than Rabbi Yehuda versus the *chachamim*.

The *Gemara* then asks: *mai Rabbi Meir mai rabanan* — where do we see this as a debate between Rabbi Meir and the *chachamim*? A *baraita* is cited: *horu ve'asu* — they ruled and they acted. Rabbi Meir exempts; the *chachamim* obligate. But who are the actors? If it is *beis din* itself that followed its own ruling, the question of *chiyuv* would concern *beis din*'s special *korban*, not a *korban* of individuals — and there is already a *baraita* establishing that *ma'aseh taluy ba-kahal*, the criterion of action belongs to the *tzibbur*, not *beis din*. *Beis din* only brings its special *korban* when the *tzibbur* acts on the ruling, not when *beis din* itself acts. So the case in the *baraita* must be that *beis din* ruled and a minority of the congregation followed. And the debate is whether *yachid she'asah be-horat beis din* is *patur* (Rabbi Meir) or *chayav* (the *chachamim*). That appears to be the most natural reading.

---

## Baraita Interpretati (II)

### Underlying Assumption

However, Rav Papa challenges even this reading. He argues that the debate in the *baraita* may not necessarily be about whether the individual following *beis din* is *chayav* or *patur*. The *baraita* is sufficiently ambiguous that one could read it as reflecting a range of entirely different disputes. And the key observation that drives this point is the following: *ela lav — mi-de-lo mahader al miyuta l'chiyuvah bishgegas ma'aseh* — the *baraita* does not bother to first prove the case of the individual sinning by *shiggas ma'aseh*. It takes it for granted. If the premise of the *baraita* were that the individual following *beis din* is exempt — that there can be a sin with nobody obligated in a *korban* — then the *baraita* would have needed to prove both cases separately: first, why does the individual bring a *korban* when sinning by *shiggas ma'aseh* (since in the analogous *hora'ah* case no one brings), and then, why does the majority bring a *korban* by *shiggas ma'aseh* (since in the analogous *hora'ah* case *beis din* brings and the *tzibbur* does not). The fact that the *baraita* simply takes the individual case for granted — never arguing for it, going straight to the majority case as the open question — proves that the *baraita* assumes individual liability even in the *hora'ah* case. *Shema mina: miyuta be-hora'ah chayavin hein kisva us'ira* — the minority who follow *beis din* are still obligated in their own *korbanot*, and that is so self-evident to the *baraita* that it needs no proof. Only the *tzibbur* case, where in the analogous *hora'ah* scenario the individuals are exempt, requires a derivation.

This analysis is extremely important because it is precisely what the *Gemara* uses to assert that the *chachamim* position — that the individual following *beis din* is *chayav* — is baked into the very structure of the *baraita*, regardless of what specific controversy the *baraita* is ostensibly addressing. Whether we read the debate as Rabbi Yehuda versus *chachamim* or Rabbi Meir versus *chachamim*, and whether the explicit debate concerns one issue or another, the *baraita*'s assumption of individual liability in the *hora'ah* case is constant.

---

## Reading Options (II)

### Beis Din in Tally

With this established, Rav Papa proceeds to offer a series of alternative readings of what the explicit debate in the *baraita* might actually be about — alternatives that do not require us to say the dispute is over whether an individual following *beis din* is *chayav* or *patur*. The first alternative: *ela be-veis din mashlimu le-rov tzibbur ka-mifligi* — perhaps the debate is about whether the actions of *beis din* members themselves are counted toward the tally of whether a majority of the community has sinned. Imagine a scenario where the number of community members who followed the erroneous ruling falls just short of a majority, but if you add in the seventy-one members of *beis din* who acted on their own ruling, you reach the majority threshold. Does *beis din* count toward the *tzibbur* for this purpose, or are they always treated as a distinct entity whose personal conduct is categorically separate from that of the general community? The *chachamim* would hold that *beis din mashlimu le-rov tzibbur* — their actions do contribute to the tally — and Rabbi Meir would hold that *ein beis din mashlimu le-rov tzibbur*.

### Who Brings

The second alternative: the debate may concern not whether the individual is *chayav* or *patur* at all, but rather *who* brings the *korban* in the classic case where *beis din* ruled and the majority of the community followed. Everyone agrees a *korban* must be brought; the question is whether it is *beis din* that brings it or the *tzibbur* as a collective. *Man chachamim? Rabbi Shimon hi — de-amar tzibbur maysei* — the *chachamim* position that the community is *chayav* would be Rabbi Shimon, who holds that it is the *tzibbur* as a corporate body that brings the *korban*, not *beis din*. This is admittedly a somewhat strained reading of the language of *chiyuv* and *ptur* in the *baraita*, but it is offered as one viable possibility.

### Tribal Rulings

The third alternative is particularly interesting. Perhaps the debate is about whether a single *shevet* that followed the ruling of its own *beis din* — its tribal court — can trigger the special *korban* obligation. The picture here is something like a federal versus state court framework: the Torah speaks of a central *beis din* and a central *tzibbur*, but the tribes were themselves corporate entities with their own courts. If the majority of the tribe of Dan followed an erroneous ruling of Dan's tribal court, does that suffice to create a *chiyuv* for the special *korban*, or does the entire mechanism require the central *Sanhedrin* and *Klal Yisrael* as a whole? *Man chachamim? Rabbi Yehuda hi — de-tanya: shevet she'asah be-horat beis dino, oso shevet chayav* — Rabbi Yehuda holds that a tribe following its own court creates a *chiyuv*, while Rabbi Meir would hold it does not.

### Majority Definition

The fourth alternative is the most striking of all, and the *Gemara* frames it with explicit appreciation for the complexity. The debate may concern what constitutes a *rov* in the first place. Two criteria are conceivable: majority of population and majority of tribes. The scenarios map almost perfectly onto the structure of majority vote versus the Electoral College. In one scenario: six tribes sinned, which was not a majority of tribes, but those six happened to contain a majority of the total population. In the other scenario: seven tribes sinned, which is a majority of tribes, but those seven together represent a minority of the total population. Is either definition of *rov* alone sufficient, or do you need both? The *baraita* being discussed is attributed here to Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar citing Rabbi Meir, who holds that either definition is sufficient — *chatu shisha ve-hein ruba shel kahal o shiv'ah af al pi she-einam ruba shel kahal, chayavin*. Rabbi Shimon holds the opposite — you need a stricter confluence of both criteria. And the *Gemara* notes that this may explain which position is the *chachamim* in the *baraita*. In any case, the *Gemara* has now offered four entirely different readings of what the ambiguous *baraita* debate is about, none of which require us to say that the explicit controversy concerns individual liability when following *beis din*.

---

## Majority in Israel

### Land Requirement

Having spent considerable discussion on how a *rov tzibbur* is defined and counted, the *Gemara* now introduces a ruling from Rav Assi that draws a sharp boundary around who counts toward the *tzibbur* in the first place. *U-ve-hora'ah, halech achar rov yoshvei Eretz Yisrael* — when determining whether you have the requisite majority of the community to trigger the special *korban* of *beis din*, you count only those who are living in the Land of Israel. Jews living outside the Land are not included in the calculation.

### Identity Concept

This ruling carries a significant conceptual implication. The entire structure of a central *beis din* issuing rulings for the community presupposes a particular model of Jewish existence — not Judaism as a portable religious identity uncoupled from any land, but rather as a national corporate identity rooted in sovereignty over a specific territory. The idea of a central court, a *Sanhedrin*, is fundamentally about the law of the land and the people who live within it. Those living outside, even if halachically Jewish in every respect, are viewed in this framework as something like expats — part of the *am*, the people, but not part of the *kahal*, the tightly constituted corporate community. And it is the concept of *kahal* — the bounded, territorially-defined community — that is the operative category for the special *korban* of *beis din*.

### Verse Support

The *Gemara* supports Rav Assi's ruling from a verse in Melachim: *va-ya'as Shlomo ba-et ha-hi et ha-chag ve-chol Yisrael imo kahal gadol mi-lavo Chamat ad Nachal Mitzrayim* — Shlomo made the festival and all of Israel was with him, a great *kahal*, from the approach of Chamat to the Egyptian wadi. The verse says *kol Yisrael*, all of Israel, but then specifies the geographic boundaries. Why specify the boundaries if it means *kol Yisrael*? *Shema mina*: only those within those borders are called *kahal* in the operative sense. *Aval hanach lo ikri kahal* — those outside are not designated *kahal*. The verse by the special *korban* of *beis din* uses the term *ha-kahal ve-asu* — and it is that tight, territorially-bounded *kahal* that is the referent. One may be part of the *am* without being part of the *kahal*, and only the *kahal* counts for the purpose of this *halacha*.

---

## Status Changes

### Numbers Change

The *Gemara* now turns to what happens when the numbers shift between the moment of sin and the moment that *beis din* becomes aware of its error. The case: at the time the erroneous ruling was followed, a majority — fifty-one percent — of the community sinned. But before *beis din* became aware of its mistake, some of those who had sinned died, such that at the moment of *yediat beis din*, only a minority of the living community had actually followed the ruling. Does *beis din* bring its special *korban*? *Harei eilu plugta de-Rabbi Shimon ve-rabanan* — this is precisely the dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the *chachamim*.

### Sin vs. Awareness

The underlying debate concerns the halakhic weight of the moment of sin versus the moment of awareness. Rabbi Shimon holds that the status conditions must align at both moments — the sin must occur under conditions of *chiyuv* and the awareness must arise under the same conditions of *chiyuv*. The *chachamim* hold that you go by the moment of sin alone.

### Status Example

The clearest illustration of this dispute involves the *Kohen Gadol*. If a person sinned as an ordinary *kohen* — eating *chelev* or *chametz* on Pesach — and subsequently became *Kohen Gadol*, and only then became aware of his earlier sin, there is a mismatch: the sin occurred when he was a *kohen hedyot*, but the awareness came when he was *Kohen Gadol*. The *chachamim* say he brings the *korban* appropriate to his status at the moment of sin — as an ordinary individual. Rabbi Shimon says that since the awareness arose when he was in a different status, he brings nothing. The logic of *im kein leisei ke-hashata* — if it were all about the moment of awareness, Rabbi Shimon would say bring a *korban* now as a *Kohen Gadol* — makes clear that Rabbi Shimon does not simply follow the moment of awareness. He requires *both* the moment of sin and the moment of awareness to be aligned in terms of the level of obligation. *Rabbi Shimon chatas ve-yediah ba'i* — he requires both criteria to be met simultaneously.

### Application

The same principle applies to our case. When the sin occurred, *beis din* would have been *chayav* — the majority had sinned. According to Rabbi Shimon, since at the moment of awareness the majority no longer exists (some having died), there is no *chiyuv*. The *chachamim*, going by the moment of sin, would still obligate *beis din* to bring the *korban*.

The reverse case — *mu'atin ve-nisrabu*, a minority who sinned and then, before awareness, the tally shifts such that they become a majority (because people from the non-sinning side died off) — would work in the opposite direction. According to Rabbi Shimon, who goes by the moment of awareness, once there is now a majority at the moment *beis din* becomes aware, perhaps that would suffice. But the *Gemara* rejects this: *ve-tisbra?* Would you really think Rabbi Shimon holds that the moment of awareness alone creates an obligation when the moment of sin did not meet the threshold? *Rabbi Shimon chatas ve-yediah ba'i* — he needs both. If the original sin did not occur under conditions of *chiyuv*, the subsequent awareness under different conditions cannot create a *chiyuv* from nothing. The *chiyuv* must be rooted in both moments.

---

## Combining Rulings

### Same Sin Scenario

The *Gemara* raises a series of nested questions about whether separate rulings of *beis din* can combine to produce the necessary *rov tzibbur*. The first scenario: *horu beis din she-cheilev mutar ve-asu miyut ha-kahal*, they ruled that a certain fat was permitted and forty percent of the community followed them. Then *beis din* retracted. Then they issued the same ruling again, and another twenty percent followed. Can the two groups — forty percent from the first ruling and twenty percent from the second — be combined to reach a majority? On one hand, *keivan de-shtei yediot ninhu*, there were two separate moments of awareness and two separate rulings, which might make them independent events that cannot be combined. On the other hand, *keivan de-haidi ve-haidi cheilev hu* — since it is the same sin both times, perhaps they do combine.

### Same Sin Type

If you say that the same sin combines even across two separate rulings, then a further question arises: what if the two rulings concerned two different types of *cheilev* — one ruling permitted the fat over the stomach, and another permitted the fat over the intestines? These are technically different *issurim* derived from different verses. Does the fact that it is still called *cheilev* cause them to combine, or does the distinct textual derivation make them categorically separate — *keivan de-bitrei krai ka-asi, lo mitztaref*?

### Different Sins

And if you say that all types of *cheilev* combine, the *Gemara* asks about two entirely distinct prohibitions. *Beis din* first ruled erroneously about *cheilev*, thirty percent followed; then they ruled erroneously about *dam*, another thirty percent followed. Can those sixty percent be combined to constitute a *rov*?

### Korban Principle

Here the analysis becomes particularly refined. *Trei issurei ninhu* — these are clearly two separate prohibitions. But *keivan de-korban shaveh* — since a person who accidentally ate *cheilev* and a person who accidentally consumed *dam* each brings the same type of *korban*, a *chatas*, perhaps any two *aveiros* that carry the same *korban* can be combined for the purpose of *rov tzibbur* following an erroneous ruling of *beis din*. Under this view, any two rulings of *beis din* — no matter how different the underlying prohibitions — would combine, as long as the individual violation of each carries the same *korban*.

### Unresolved Edge

And if that is so, then the only edge case that might not combine is a ruling about *cheilev* paired with a ruling about *avodah zarah*. Why single out *avodah zarah*? Because when an individual accidentally worships idolatry, he brings a different *korban* than the standard *chatas* brought for other violations. So the *korban* is not the same. Does that distinction prevent combination? Or does the fact that both *cheilev* and *avodah zarah* carry the penalty of *karet* create enough of a shared category to combine them for *rov tzibbur* purposes? *Teiku* — the *Gemara* leaves this unresolved.

---

## Court Continuity

### Court Succession

The *Gemara* now addresses the question of whether the *beis din* that issues the ruling must be the same *beis din* that becomes aware of the error. The case: *horu beis din she-cheilev mutar ve-asu miyut ha-kahal* — *beis din* ruled, a minority followed. *Ve-meis oso beis din* — that *beis din* died. *Ve-amad beis din acher* — a new *beis din* arose, repeated the ruling, and another minority followed. Now, if these two minorities together constitute a majority, does the new *beis din*'s awareness of the error create the *chiyuv* for the special *korban*?

### Awareness Question

The *Gemara* reasons as follows. *Aliba de-man de-amar beis din maysei* — according to the view that it is *beis din* that brings the *korban* (rather than the *tzibbur*): *lo tiba'ei lach* — this case needs no deliberation. *De-ha leisnhu* — because the original *beis din* no longer exists. A *beis din* that did not issue the ruling cannot be obligated to bring the special *korban* for that ruling, and the original *beis din* is gone. But this reasoning itself raises a deeper question: is *beis din* a collection of specific individuals, or is it an abstract institutional entity? If *beis din* is an institution, then the same court — even if entirely repopulated with new judges — should remain liable for the rulings of its institutional predecessors. The *Gemara* appears to treat the court more as a collection of individuals than as an abstract entity, at least when the ruling itself has been superseded by a fresh ruling from a new court.

### Identity vs. Entity

*Ki tiba'ei lach aliba de-man de-amar tzibbur maysei* — the genuine *teiku* is according to the view that it is the *tzibbur* that brings the *korban*. In that case, the *tzibbur* is still around — the community members who sinned on the basis of the original ruling are still alive. Does the awareness of the new *beis din* suffice to trigger their obligation? Or does the *chiyuv* require specifically *yediat beis din de-horu* — the awareness of the very *beis din* that issued the erroneous ruling? Underlying this is a profound conceptual point: what defines an erroneous ruling as objectively erroneous? Perhaps only the recognition of error by the court that issued it constitutes a genuine retraction, not a later court pronouncing that an earlier court was wrong. *Teiku* — the *Gemara* does not resolve this either.

---

## Unanimity & Dissent

### All Must Rule

The *Gemara* introduces a new topic regarding the internal workings of *beis din*. Rabbi Yonatan states: *meah she-yashevu le-horos, ein chayavin ad she-yoru kulan* — if a hundred people sat together to issue a ruling, they are not liable for the special *korban* unless all of them ruled. The plain reading would suggest two things: first, that you need a full attendance of all court members, and second, that the vote must be unanimous.

### Verse Language

The source is the verse *ve-im kol adat Yisrael yishgu* — "if the entire congregation of Israel errs." The *diyuk* is from *kol* — the word "entire" or "all." *Ad she-yishgu kulan* — they all have to be in error. *Ad she-tishveh hora'ah be-chol adat Yisrael* — the ruling has to be uniform across the entire *beis din*. This would seem to mean unanimous agreement, which would of course make it nearly impossible ever to trigger this *chiyuv*, since one dissenting member would always break unanimity. The *Gemara* also observes that if the rule of *rubo ke-kulo* — majority is treated as the whole — normally applies throughout the Torah, why does the verse need to say *kol ha-edah*? The inference would seem to be that here, unlike the norm, actual unanimity is required, and therefore even if the court had more than seventy-one members, you would need all of them.

### Silent Dissent

A *baraita* is then cited: *horu beis din ve-yada echad mehen she-tatu* — *beis din* issued a ruling and one member knew they had erred, but said nothing. If that member then acted on the ruling — whether he acted alongside them, after them, or even if the others did not act and he acted alone — *harei ze chayav*, he is *chayav*. The reason: *she-lo talah be-beis din* — he did not rely on *beis din*, because he knew they were wrong.

### Verbal Dissent

A second *baraita* adds a different scenario: *horu beis din ve-yada echad mehen she-tatu ve-amar lahen — toin atem!* — one member explicitly told his colleagues: "You are mistaken!" In that case, *harei elu pturim* — the others are exempt. They relied on what appeared to be a ruling of *beis din*, and the verbal dissent of one member does not deprive the ruling of its status as a ruling of *beis din*.

But the *Gemara* notes: *ta'ama de-amar lahen toin atem de-pturim* — the reason they are *patur* is that he explicitly said *toin atem* (and then the conclusion: *ha shatik mashtik chayavin* — but if he merely remained silent and abstained, they would be *chayavin*). The implication appears to be that silent abstention, when it looks like a nod of acquiescence, does not prevent the ruling from being considered unanimous. But open verbal opposition does. And yet the *Gemara* asks: *ve-amai halo lo horu kulan* — but in the case of verbal dissent, why are they *patur*? Surely it was not a unanimous ruling! This is an apparent challenge to the idea that the vote must be unanimous, because even without unanimity (with a dissenter) it would seem the ruling is still valid.

### Community Burden

The *Gemara* challenges the unanimity requirement from a different direction as well, citing a principle attributed to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok: one does not issue a *gezeira* upon the community unless the majority of the community can withstand it. Rav Ada bar Ahavah identifies the verse: *ba-me'erah atem ne'arim ve-osi atem kovim, ha-goy kulo* — you are cursed with a curse and you defraud Me, the entire nation. The *diyuk* from *ha-goy kulo* — just as the earlier verse used *kol* to suggest unanimity, this verse says *kol* and yet is interpreted to mean the majority. *Ve-ruva ke-kulo dami* — majority is treated as the whole. *Tiyuvta de-Rabbi Yochanan, tiyuvta* — this is a decisive refutation of the unanimity requirement.

### Resolution

The *Gemara* concludes: *ve-ella mai kol ata kamma rachmana?* — if *kol* does not mean unanimous vote, what does it teach? *Ikka kullam, havya hora'ah; ve-lo, lo havya hora'ah* — the word *kol* requires that all members of *beis din* be present when the ruling is issued. Full attendance is required. But you do not need a unanimous yes-vote. If a member is silent, abstaining, or even quietly dissenting in his own mind while outwardly nodding, the ruling is valid. Only explicit verbal opposition — *toin atem* — disrupts the ruling. The resolution thus distinguishes two entirely different requirements: full attendance (*kullam*) is mandated by the verse; unanimous affirmative vote is not.

---

## Shared Liability

### Yoke Principle

Rabbi Yehoshua derives from this discussion a broader principle about judicial responsibility. *Yod she-yoshvin ba-din* — if ten people are sitting in judgment, even those who are technically superfluous to the *beis din* formation, *ha-kolar talui be-tzavar kullam* — the yoke of judgment hangs around all of their necks. Every member of the court, regardless of whether their presence was halachically necessary, shares in the responsibility for the ruling. The *Gemara* asks: *peshita* — is that not obvious? The answer: the novel teaching is *da-afilu talmid bifnei rabbo* — even a student sitting in the presence of his teacher, who in practice would simply follow the teacher's lead rather than exercising independent judgment, is nonetheless a participant in the court and shares in its collective responsibility.

### Rav Huna

Rav Huna took this principle to heart in a practical and somewhat poignant way. *Ki havei nafik le-vei dina* — when he would go out to *beis din*, he would bring ten of the *tarna'im* from Rav's study hall — essentially young scholars who served as memorizers and assistants — and seat them before him at the court. *Ki heichi de-nimti shiva meikashura* — so that each would get a splinter from the beam. The metaphor is of a heavy beam that, if lifted alone, would crush one person, but distributed across many bearers, each only carries a manageable share. By assembling ten people at the court even when they were halachically unnecessary for the ruling, Rav Huna was distributing the moral and spiritual weight of judgment. If the ruling turned out to be wrong, no single person would bear the full burden of responsibility alone.

### Rav Ashi

Rav Ashi applied the same logic to a different domain. *Ki havei meisi treifa le-kamei* — when he had to rule on a *treifa* case — determining whether an animal was halachically valid for consumption — *meisi asara tivchei me-masa Machasya* — he would bring ten of the *shochtim* from the city of Masa Machasya and have them present at the decision. Their practical expertise in *shechita* and *treifot* was certainly relevant and may have informed the ruling. But beyond their expertise, the same principle applied: *ki heichi de-nimti shiva meikashura* — so that each would receive a splinter from the beam. The responsibility for a consequential halachic decision should never rest on one set of shoulders alone.

---

---

# Horayot 4

## Individual Following Ret…

### Court Retracts Ruling

The Mishnah at the bottom of 3b opens with a case of *hora'ah* gone wrong: *horu beit din veyadu sheta'u vechazru bahen* — the court issued a ruling, became aware of their error, and retracted. Whether or not they have yet brought the sacrifice to which they are now obligated, an individual who never received the news and continued acting on the original ruling presents a problem. With no newspapers and no radio, it was entirely possible to remain ignorant of the retraction. *Rabbi Shimon poter* — Rabbi Shimon exempts such an individual from a personal *korban*. Rabbi Eliezer says it is a matter of doubt: *safek*.

### Shimon vs. Eliezer Dispu…

The disagreement between Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Eliezer maps onto a deeper conceptual question about the very basis on which an individual who follows a *beit din* ruling is ever exempt in the first place. There is a position — the *chachamim* — holding that even a blameless individual is obligated in a *korban*, since at the end of the day he is the one who committed the act. Our Mishnah assumes he is not obligated. But why?

### Two Models Debate

Two distinct conceptual models can explain the individual's exemption. The first focuses on blamelessness: the person legitimately believed the act was permitted and is therefore not culpable. The second frames the act differently — it is not so much the individual's personal act as it is an extension of the court's ruling; the individual is, in effect, acting under the court's authority and on the court's account.

These two models yield different results when the court retracts its ruling. If the exemption is grounded in blamelessness alone, then an individual who genuinely never heard of the retraction remains blameless even after the retraction — and should remain exempt. This is Rabbi Shimon's view. If, however, the exemption is grounded in the objective reality of operating under the court's authority, then once the ruling is retracted, the individual is no longer objectively acting under that authority — even if his subjective state of mind remains unchanged — and the exemption may no longer apply.

### Home vs. Away Cases

Rabbi Eliezer says it is a *safek*. The Mishnah then articulates what constitutes that doubt: *yashav lo betoch beito chayav, halach limdinat hayam patur* — if the person remained at home, he is liable; if he was traveling abroad, he is exempt. This requires careful reading. Rashi explains that *chayav* here does not mean obligated in a *chatat*, but in an *asham talui* — the suspended guilt offering brought when one has possibly committed a sin but cannot be certain. The *asham talui* is the appropriate *korban* in a case of objective doubt, as when one ate a piece of fat and cannot determine whether it was permitted *shuman* or forbidden *chelev*.

What emerges from this is that Rabbi Eliezer is not actually arguing with Rabbi Shimon's principle. Both agree: if the individual is truly blameless, he is exempt. Their dispute is over the application. When a person was abroad and had no means of hearing of the retraction, he is entirely blameless and therefore entirely exempt. When a person remained at home, however, it is possible he could have heard — perhaps he simply did not inquire or get out enough — and therefore his blamelessness is not so clear-cut. In that case, Rabbi Eliezer says the situation is a *safek*: perhaps he is blameworthy for failing to stay informed, perhaps not. That unresolved doubt requires an *asham talui*.

### Rabbi Akiva's Reasoning

Ben Azzai questions why the traveler's case warrants more complete exemption than the person who stayed home — the answer seems obvious, but he presses Rabbi Akiva to articulate it. Rabbi Akiva's response: *shehayoshev beiveito efshar hayah lo sheyishma velo hayah lo efshar* — the person at home had a realistic possibility of hearing, whereas the person abroad had none. That difference in practical capacity to hear is what determines the degree of blamelessness. Even that is refined further: if one was at home but in the midst of preparing to depart — packing, waiting for one's ride — Rabbi Akiva says he too is already sufficiently on his way that he counts as departed, while Ben Azzai maintains that as long as one is still physically at home, some possibility of receiving information remains.

---

## Court Liability Conditio…

### Detail vs. Whole Category

The Mishnah and Gemara now shift to an entirely separate point: not who follows the ruling, but the substance of the ruling itself — what kind of ruling makes the court liable for a communal *korban*. The principle, derived from the verse *vene'elam davar*, is *horu levatel miktzat ulekayem miktzat* — the court must have ruled to nullify a part of a *mitzvah* while upholding the rest. Only a ruling about a detail, erroneously gotten wrong, generates court liability. A ruling that eliminates an entire category of law altogether does not.

### Three Examples

The Mishnah provides three examples of a court ruling on a detail. If they ruled that the concept of *niddah* exists in the *Torah* but that a man who has relations with a *shomeret yom keneged yom* — a woman who bled mid-cycle — is exempt, that is a detail. If they ruled that *Shabbos* exists but that *hotza'ah*, carrying between domains, is permissible, that too is a detail. And if they ruled that *avodas kochavim* is prohibited but that *hishtachavaya*, prostration, is not a forbidden act of worship, that similarly constitutes a detail. In all three cases, *harei eilu chayavin* — the court is liable.

### Textual Proof for Detail

The Gemara derives the requirement that it be a *detail* rather than the whole from the word *davar* in the verse *vene'elam davar* — a matter was hidden — rather than the whole body of law.

---

## Shimon's State of Mind D…

### Court License Approach

Rav Yehudah cites Rav explaining Rabbi Shimon's position: *ho'il ubireshus beis din hu oseh* — since the individual is acting with the license of the court. Even though, objectively speaking, the court has retracted and the license is technically no longer in effect, in his own mind he is still operating under that license.

### State of Mind Purpose

A second version of Rav Yehudah's explanation frames it more precisely: *kol hora'ah sheyatzah berov tzibur, yachid ha'oseh osah patur, lefi shelo nitenah hora'ah ela lehavchin bein shogeg lemeizid* — any ruling that has been disseminated through the majority of the community exempts the individual who follows it, because the entire purpose of the court's ruling is to determine state of mind. This phrase — normally applied to the formal warning (*hatra'ah*) given before a sin — is here applied to the *hora'ah* itself.

The implication is this: what the court's ruling actually does is not create an objective legal reality that shields the individual, but rather it establishes the individual's subjective state of mind as one of legitimate reliance. Once we recognize that the exemption is grounded in state of mind rather than objective legal reality, it follows that the exemption persists even after the retraction — because the individual's state of mind has not changed. He still believes he is acting on the court's authority. That belief is sufficient.

### Fund Collection Challenge

A challenge is raised from a related law. The *par helam davar shel tzibur* — the communal bull brought when the court's erroneous ruling leads the public to sin — requires funding. Who pays for it? Rabbi Shimon says a special collection is conducted: the community is taxed specifically for this *korban*. Rabbi Yehudah says it comes from the general communal funds, *terumas ha-lishka*, normally used for the daily sacrifices.

The challenge proceeds as follows: Rabbi Shimon, who holds that exemption is entirely a matter of state of mind, rules in the Mishnah that an individual remains exempt even after the *korban* has been brought — that is, even after the court has not merely retracted but has fully closed the matter by bringing their sacrifice. But if the money for that *korban* was raised through a special public collection, as Rabbi Shimon holds, then surely the entire community would have learned of the retraction through that very collection. How then can anyone claim not to have known?

### Collection Resolutions

Three resolutions are offered. First, perhaps the funds were collected *stam* — without explanation, as a general campaign — so the public would not have known the purpose and thus not have learned of the retraction. Second, perhaps the individual in question was absent from his locale precisely during the period of collection. Third, and most striking, perhaps Rav who offered this explanation actually held the reverse of the standard attribution: perhaps it was Rabbi Yehudah who required a special collection and Rabbi Shimon who held the funds came from *terumas ha-lishka* — so no public collection occurred at all. This last resolution underscores just how central the state of mind doctrine is to Rabbi Shimon's position: even after every formal step has been completed — retraction, acknowledgment, and *korban* — if the individual genuinely did not know, he is exempt.

---

## Four Positions Compared

### Rabbi Meir Position

A *braisa* introduces a fourth position not seen in the Mishnah. Rabbi Meir holds that the individual who acted on the retracted ruling is *chayav* — obligated in a *korban* — straightforwardly and without qualification. This corresponds to the first conceptual model described above: Rabbi Meir does not accept that blamelessness alone exempts a person. His view is anchored in objective reality. Once the court has retracted, the individual is objectively no longer operating under their license, regardless of his subjective state of mind. The sin occurred, the individual committed it, and he must bring a *korban*. The fact that he is blameless is simply irrelevant to the question of obligation.

### Rabbi Shimon Position

Rabbi Shimon exempts the individual in all cases. As established above, his view is entirely anchored in state of mind and blamelessness. Since the individual genuinely believed he was operating under the court's authority, his exemption is complete.

### Rabbi Eliezer Position

Rabbi Eliezer says *safek*: it is a doubt, and the appropriate response is an *asham talui*. His position is that we are genuinely uncertain whether the individual's subjective state qualifies as sufficient blamelessness to exempt him.

### Sumchus Position

A fourth view is attributed to Sumchus: *taluy* — suspended. Rabbi Yochanan clarifies that the debate between Rabbi Eliezer and Sumchus concerns precisely the *asham talui*: Rabbi Eliezer holds this is a standard case of doubt requiring an *asham talui*, while Sumchus holds there is insufficient basis to bring any *korban* at all. This distinction will be unpacked through two separate analogies.

---

## Rabbi Eliezer Framework

### Forbidden Meat Analogy

Rav Zeira offers the analogy that illuminates Rabbi Eliezer's position. It is like a person who ate a piece of fat and does not know whether it was *shuman* — permitted fat — or *chelev* — forbidden fat, for which *karet* would apply. The reason the analogy uses fat rather than, say, *neveilah*, is that the *asham talui* mechanism applies only to sins that carry *karet* when committed deliberately. When the person later realizes he may have transgressed, he brings an *asham talui*. In Rabbi Eliezer's reading of our case, the individual's situation is structurally identical: there is a genuine factual uncertainty about whether the conditions for obligation are met. Just as we do not know whether that piece of meat was *chelev*, we do not know whether this person's state of mind qualifies as the kind of blameless reliance on the court that would exempt him.

### Two Layers of Doubt

There are in fact two layers of uncertainty at play. The first is whether the person's conscious reliance on the court's ruling — the fact that he subjectively believed he was acting on their authority — is sufficient to define his legal state of mind as one of legitimate reliance. The second is whether, even granting that he thought he was relying on *beit din*, we can treat that as the operative legal reality when objectively the ruling had been withdrawn.

### Court Publicity Analysis

One might argue that the more public the court's *korban* is — particularly if the community was involved in funding it — the harder it becomes to maintain that the individual genuinely could not have known of the retraction. Nevertheless, Rabbi Eliezer holds that this publicity does not resolve the doubt in either direction. Even if the collection was less public, as when *beit din* alone brings the *korban*, one could argue: *dehavei sho'el hava amrinan leh* — had he asked, people would have told him. There is an objective reality in which the information was available. We simply do not know whether his failure to ask rises to the level of culpable negligence. That unresolved question is the *safek*, and it mandates the *asham talui*.

---

## Sumchus Framework Analys…

### Twilight Sacrifice Analo…

Rabbi Yose bar Avin — some say Rabbi Yose bar Zvida — offers the analogy for Sumchus's position. A person brought his sacrifice right at *bein hashmashos* — the twilight period at day's end. It is uncertain whether the sacrifice was offered while it was still halachically day or once night had already fallen. *Safek mibod yom nitkapeir lo, safek mishehachishah nitkapeir lo* — we simply do not know. In such a case, *she'ein meivi asham talui* — no *asham talui* is brought. The person is not obligated to bring any further *korban*.

This is a striking analogy because the *asham talui* would seem even more justified here than in the forbidden fat case: with the fat, you at least know you ate something that might have been *chelev*. With the twilight sacrifice, you know an action was performed — the question is purely one of timing. And yet no *asham talui* is required. The Gemara pushes the analogy further: this holds even according to the position that the communal *korban* was brought publicly — *demifarsma milsa* — and even according to the position that perhaps he *could* have inquired: *ishal lo askach inish dumeshailei* — had he asked, he might not have found anyone who could have told him definitively, because the uncertainty in *bein hashmashos* is itself objective and irreducible.

### Doubt in Law Not Facts

This is Sumchus's innovation. For Rabbi Eliezer, the doubt is factual: we don't know whether the individual's state of mind meets the threshold for exemption or liability. For Sumchus, the doubt is not in the facts at all — the individual's state of mind is clear, his ignorance is uncontested — the doubt is in the law itself. Two legal frameworks apply simultaneously and point in opposite directions.

### Contradictory Lenses

What Sumchus is really saying is that there are two irreconcilable legal lenses through which to view this individual's act. Through the lens of Rabbi Meir — the objective reality lens — the court has retracted, and the individual is no longer operating under their license; he is therefore *chayav*. Through the lens of Rabbi Shimon — the state of mind lens — the individual genuinely believed he was relying on the court's authority, and he is therefore *patur*. It is worth noting that Sumchus was a student of Rabbi Meir, and what he seems to be saying is: I cannot choose between these two frameworks. Both are valid. Both apply. The individual stands exactly at the intersection of the status of *chayav* and the status of *patur* — not because we don't know the facts, but because the law itself generates a middle state when both frameworks are simultaneously true.

This is analogous to *bein hashmashos*: the doubt there is not about what time the sun set — it is an objective, irreducible twilight whose legal status is genuinely indeterminate. The period is neither day nor night in a legally resolvable sense. Similarly here, the individual is neither clearly *chayav* nor clearly *patur* — the legal frameworks themselves generate an irresolvable middle state, and that middle state is insufficient to generate the certainty required for any *korban* at all.

In summary, the Gemara has laid out two fundamentally different models — objective reality versus subjective state of mind — and three positions within the subjective framework: Rabbi Shimon holds blamelessness is always sufficient to exempt; Rabbi Eliezer holds it is a factual doubt requiring an *asham talui*; and Sumchus holds the contradiction between the two legal frameworks produces a legal suspension in which no *korban* is brought.

---

## Detail Definition Analys…

### Detail Principle

The Gemara now returns to the second major topic of the daf: what exactly constitutes a *davar* — a detail — as opposed to *kol haguf* — the entire body of law — for the purpose of determining court liability. The *braisa* sets up the problem: the verse says *vene'elam davar*, a matter was hidden. Perhaps *davar* refers to the whole matter? The *tana* anticipates this objection and resolves it: *davar* means a detail of the matter, not the entire category.

Several *amoraim* offer derivations. Ulla reads the verse as *vene'elam mi-davar* — hidden from a matter, meaning from an aspect of it — treating the *mem* at the end of *vene'elam* as a separate prefix. Chizkiyah derives it from the continuation of the verse: *ve'asu achas mi-kol mitzvos* — they did one thing from among all the commandments. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak notes that the word can be read as *mitzvas* rather than *mitzvos* — singular in construct form — meaning they erred in one aspect of a *mitzvah*, not in all the *mitzvos*. Rav Ashi draws a parallel to the *zaken mamre*, the rebellious elder. The verse by the *zaken mamre* uses the same language: *ki yipale mimcha davar*, when a matter is hidden. Just as the *zaken mamre* must be ruling on a detail rather than an entire body of law to be liable for his rebellious ruling, so too the court must be ruling on a detail for their error to constitute a *hora'ah*.

This parallel is more than a textual device — it is conceptually significant. The reason a court that eliminates an entire category of law is exempt is that such a ruling does not meet the threshold of *hora'ah* at all. It is so far off-base that it has no legal traction. If someone goes around saying there is no such thing as *Shabbos* in the *Torah*, he may cause people to sin, but he has not issued a ruling. The same logic applies to the *zaken mamre*: to be considered a competing authority to the court, his ruling must be within the system — a detail, gotten wrong — not a wholesale rejection of a category.

Rav Yehudah citing Shmuel adds another criterion alongside the *detail* requirement: *ein beit din chayavin ad sheyoru bedavar she'ein hatzeddukim modim bo* — the court is not liable unless they ruled on something that even the Sadducees would concede is halachically binding. If the ruling goes against something so obvious that even the Sadducees would say it is clearly the law, then the court is so manifestly wrong that it cannot be considered a legitimate *hora'ah*. As the Gemara puts it: *zil krei bei rav hu* — just go ask in *cheder* and the children will tell you the court got it wrong. A ruling that obvious is not a ruling; it is an embarrassment. The court is therefore exempt — paradoxically — precisely because they were too wrong.

### Niddah Example

The Mishnah's first example is a ruling that a man is exempt after relations with a *shomeret yom keneged yom*. One might ask: isn't the concept of *shomeret yom keneged yom* itself explicit in the verse? The Gemara says *vesafra lah* — she shall count for herself — and derives that she counts one day for each day of mid-cycle bleeding. That seems textually grounded, and even the Sadducees would presumably agree. How then could a court be liable for ruling erroneously about it?

The Gemara proposes several ways to refine the case so that it involves something the Sadducees would *not* necessarily concede. Perhaps the ruling concerns *ha'arah* — partial penetration — versus *gmar biah* — full penetration: the court ruled that partial penetration of a *shomeret yom* is exempt. The verse *es mekora he'erah* uses the word *he'erah*, which is read to refer to partial penetration — yet this reading is arguably not so explicit that even the Sadducees would agree. Perhaps the ruling concerns *kedarka* versus *shelo kedarka* — vaginal versus anal intercourse — the court ruled that anal intercourse with a *shomeret yom* is exempt. The Gemara says *mishkvei isha* — the lyings of a woman — in the plural comes to include both, but the court ruled otherwise. And perhaps the ruling holds that a *zavah* is only that status if she bleeds during the day, not at night, based on *kol yemei zovah* — all the days of her *zivah* — which emphasizes daytime. That is a reading that could be made from the verse, and one that the Sadducees would not necessarily reject, so it constitutes a genuine *hora'ah* that can generate liability.

### Shabbat Example

The second case is a ruling that *hotza'ah* — carrying between domains — is exempt. The Gemara asks: isn't *hotza'ah* explicit? It cites *velo totziu masa mibateichem* from the prophets — Yirmiyahu — which says do not carry a burden out of your houses. Even the Sadducees accept the *Tanach*, so this should be something they would agree is forbidden. To keep the case within the framework, the Gemara offers refinements. Perhaps the ruling held that *hotza'ah* — taking out — is forbidden, but *hachnasah* — bringing in — is permissible. Or perhaps both are forbidden, but *moshit* — handing an object through a window — and *zorek* — throwing — are permissible, since in those cases the person is not personally transporting the object across domains. Those latter distinctions are not explicit in the verse, and the Sadducees would not necessarily disagree with them.

### Idolatry Example

The third case is a ruling that *hishtachavaya* — prostration — is an exempt form of idol worship. The verse *lo sishachaveh le'el acher* explicitly prohibits bowing to other gods. But the Gemara proposes that the ruling concerned *shelo kedarka*: if a god is not normally worshipped through prostration, perhaps prostration before it would be exempt. That is not explicit. Alternatively, the ruling may have concerned the precise physical requirements of *hishtachavaya* — perhaps the court held that only a full prostration involving the spreading of both arms and legs (*pishut yadayim veraglayim*) constitutes the forbidden act, and partial prostration does not. That too is not derived from an explicit verse, and the Sadducees would not necessarily disagree. In these ways, each of the Mishnah's examples can be refined into a genuine detail — one that required real legal reasoning, that was not obvious even to the Sadducees, and that therefore constitutes a true *hora'ah* capable of generating court liability.

---

## One Melachah Question

### Plowing Question

Rav Yosef raises a *ba'ei* — an unresolved question. The court rules that there is no prohibition of plowing on *Shabbos*. Of the thirty-nine *melachos*, they have eliminated precisely one. Is this considered a ruling on a *detail* — and the court is therefore liable — or is it considered eliminating an entire category, making it equivalent to saying *ein Shabbos baTorah* — in which case they would be exempt?

### Two Interpretations

The two sides of the question are drawn cleanly. On one hand: *keivan d'kamodei b'kulhu milsa* — since they affirm all the other thirty-eight *melachos*, eliminating one is merely a partial ruling, a detail, and they should be liable. On the other hand: *keivan d'akrin leh l'charisha k'akira d'gufa damei* — since they completely eliminate the category of plowing, it constitutes the uprooting of an entire thing, and they should be exempt.

### Failed Resolution Attemp…

The Gemara attempts to resolve the question from each of the Mishnah's three examples. From the *niddah* case: the court eliminates the entire category of *shomeret yom keneged yom*, and yet this is treated as a detail. Since *shomeret yom* is a distinct personal status within the laws of *niddah*, this would seem to show that even eliminating a full sub-category is still considered a detail — supporting the view that eliminating one of the thirty-nine *melachos* would similarly be a detail. Rav Yosef rejects this: we already explained the *shomeret yom* case in a nuanced way — not as eliminating the whole status, but as a detail within it, such as a particular type of intercourse or timing. So that case cannot serve as a proof.

From the *Shabbos* case: the court eliminates *hotza'ah* entirely — one of the thirty-nine *melachos* — and is treated as liable. This seems directly parallel to the question. The Gemara rejects this as well: we already explained that the ruling was not about all of *hotza'ah* but about a specific aspect of it — taking out but not bringing in, or transporting but not throwing. So the Mishnah's *Shabbos* example is actually a detail within *hotza'ah*, not the elimination of *hotza'ah* altogether.

### Nuancing Problem

From the *avodas kochavim* case: the court eliminates *hishtachavaya* entirely, yet is liable. Again, the Gemara rejects this: we explained that the ruling was about *hishtachavaya shelo kedarka* or about the physical requirements of *hishtachavaya* — again a detail within the category, not its complete elimination. The difficulty is that precisely because the Gemara was forced to nuance all three of the Mishnah's examples into details — in order to satisfy the Sadducees criterion — none of them can now serve as a case where an entire sub-category was eliminated. The question of whether eliminating one complete *melacha* out of thirty-nine constitutes a *detail* or a *whole* therefore remains unresolved.

---

## Shemitah Year Question

### Plowing Harvest Verses

Rav Zeira poses a parallel *ba'ei*. Let the court rule that *Shabbos* does not apply during a *shemitah* year. The erroneous reasoning might proceed from the verse *b'charish u-v'katzir tishbot* — rest from plowing and from harvesting. One might read this to mean: *Shabbos* applies during years when plowing and harvesting occur, but during *shemitah*, when those activities are forbidden, perhaps *Shabbos* does not apply. That is a reading that could be derived from the verse's phrasing.

### Partial vs. Whole Framew…

Is such a ruling a *detail* or a *whole*? On one reading: *keivan d'mikayim leh b'sha'ar shnei shavua* — since the court affirms that *Shabbos* applies during the six other years of the seven-year cycle, they are only ruling on a partial matter. On the other reading: *keivan d'akrei leh b'shevi'is k'akirat gufa damei* — since during the *shemitah* year itself they are completely eliminating *Shabbos*, it constitutes the total uprooting of a *mitzvah* for that year. The question is left unresolved as stated, but it will be addressed by an analogy from the *navi sheker*.

---

## False Prophet Analogy

### Prophet Whole Law Liabil…

Ravina offers a resolution from the laws of the false prophet. *Navi she-nitnaba la'akor davar midivrei Torah chayav* — a *navi* who prophesies to uproot a word of *Torah* is liable. Here, strikingly, the framework is the inverse of the court. For a court or a *zaken mamre*, liability requires ruling on a *detail* — a wholesale elimination of an entire category is too far off-base to constitute a *hora'ah*. But for a false prophet who comes with prophetic authority — as the spokesman of God — the more radical the claim, the more clearly liable he is. If he says an entire category of law is abolished, he is *chayav*.

### Authority Distinction

The conceptual contrast is sharp. A sage operates within the legal system. His ruling has traction only when it engages with the law as it is — analyzing, applying, or misapplying a detail. A wholesale denial of a category is simply not within the domain of legal reasoning; it is not a *hora'ah*. A prophet operates outside the system, with claimed divine authority. For him, the most extreme assertion — that an entire category of Torah law is abolished — is precisely the kind of false prophecy that generates liability, because he is positioning himself as a divine voice against the entire *Torah*.

### Idolatry Exception

However, in the case of *avodas kochavim*, even Rabbi Shimon agrees that the false prophet is *chayav* even if he says only: worship today and do not worship tomorrow. *Afilu amar hayom ovdah u'lemachar bitlah chayav* — even telling people to worship the idol today while saying tomorrow it will be abolished is sufficient for liability. A time-limited instruction to worship *avoda zara* is still a partial ruling against *avoda zara*, not a wholesale elimination of the prohibition. Yet the prophet is liable. This establishes that a time-limited ruling — applying to some circumstances and not others — is legally categorized as a ruling on a *detail*, not on the whole.

### Inference to Court Case

This provides the resolution to Rav Zeira's question. If a false prophet who tells people that *Shabbos* does not apply during *shemitah* — limiting *Shabbos* to a subset of years — is analogous to the prophet who says worship today but not tomorrow, then such a time-based limitation is classified as a ruling on a *detail* rather than a complete elimination. The same framework applies to the court: a ruling that *Shabbos* does not apply during *shemitah*, since *Shabbos* remains in force the other six years of the cycle, is a *detail* and not *kol haguf*. The court would therefore be liable.

---

## Valid Ruling Conditions

### Dissent Prevention

The Mishnah returns to a condition for court liability that was introduced earlier in the tractate. If one member of the court explicitly tells the others *to'in atem* — you are making a mistake — and verbally dissents, the ruling does not generate the communal *korban* obligation. Even though the court normally operates by majority rule and a dissenting vote does not invalidate the ruling for purposes of *dinei Torah*, a verbal dissent is sufficient to prevent the court from being liable in this specific context. The concern, apparently, is not the formal legal validity of the ruling but whether the ruling carries the weight of a unified court acting on full authority.

### Missing Head or Unfit Ju…

Two additional conditions disqualify the ruling from generating liability. First, if the *mufla shebe-beit din* — the head of the court — was absent. Rashi specifies that this refers to a case where the court still had a full quorum, but the head had vacated his seat and someone else filled the number — so the court was technically complete but the leading decisor was not present. Second, if any member of the court was in a disqualified category.

### Disqualified Judge Categ…

The Mishnah lists four categories of disqualified members: a *ger* — a convert; a *mamzer* — a person of illegitimate birth; a *netin* — someone from the Gibeonites who attached themselves to Israel under Joshua in a problematic manner and whose descendants are of questionable lineage; and a *zaken she-lo ra'uy l'vanim* — an elder who has never had children. The disqualification of the *ger* is based on the requirement of *mikerev* — a position of communal authority requires being *mikerev* your brethren, which excludes the convert in this context. The *mamzer* and *netin* disqualifications relate to the genealogical integrity required for the court. Rashi acknowledges uncertainty about the *zaken she-ein lo banim*; the Rambam in his *Perush Hamishnayot* explains it as a concern about insufficient compassion — a person who has never raised children may not have developed the requisite empathetic judgment for capital cases, though this same concern is applied here by extension.

### Edah Textual Basis

The source for requiring that all members be fit for *hora'ah* is derived from the word *edah* appearing in two separate contexts — a *gezeirah shavah*. The concept of *edah* — congregation or court — is linked through textual parallel to a context where all members must be qualified to rule. The Gemara adds the verse *vahisyatzvu sham immach* — when God gathers the seventy elders alongside Moses — and derives *immach bidumim lach*: they must be like you, sharing the same qualities of lineage and fitness for authority.

### Tzaddukim vs. Missing He…

The comparison between the *Sadducees* criterion and the missing *mufla* criterion illuminates an important conceptual distinction.
