The Gemara concludes: *masnisin mani Rabbi hi* — our *mishnah* follows the view of Rabbi. A *braita* is cited which presents the Tannaitic dispute explicitly. Rabbi holds: *mashiach ba'avoda zarah — beshiggas ma'aseh* — for a *kohen gadol* transgressing *avoda zara*, the *shgagah* of the action alone is sufficient to generate liability, without requiring a *hora'ah*.

### Chachamim View

The *chachamim* disagree: *b'he'elam davar* — even for *avoda zara*, the *kohen gadol* requires the full *hora'ah* framework, the same as for any other sin. The silence of the *mishnah* on *vechen hamashiach* in the *avoda zara* clause reflects Rabbi's position that the *kohen gadol* in that context is simply like any other individual, for whom only action is required.

### Agreement Point

Despite this disagreement, both Rabbi and the *chachamim* agree on a critical point: the *kohen gadol* brings a *seirah* — not a *par* — for *avoda zara*. He is firmly within the category of *ve-hanefesh ha-achas* in *Parshat Shelach Lecha*, which encompasses all individuals regardless of their special status. This they do not dispute.

### No Asham

Both also agree that a *kohen gadol* never brings an *asham talui*. The basis for this agreement (and the difference in reasoning between the two positions) will be analyzed in the sections that follow.

## Rabbi Reasoning

### Vekhiper Pesuk

Rabbi's reasoning begins with the *pasuk* in *Bamidbar* 15 dealing with the *avoda zara* context: *ve-chiper ha-kohen al ha-nefesh ha-shogeges* — "the *kohen* shall atone for the inadvertently sinning soul." The *nefesh* here encompasses the *kohen gadol* (as well as the *nasi*), as both are subsumed within the *yachid* framework of *avoda zara*.

### Chet Bishgaga

Rabbi derives from the phrase *be-cheto bishgaga* — "when he sins through inadvertence" — that the *chet* for which this atonement applies is defined entirely by the *shgagah* of the action. For those within this category — including the *kohen gadol* when it comes to *avoda zara* — the *hora'ah* is simply not the operative criterion. The sin and the inadvertence are identical, and only the inadvertent act is *mechayev*.

## Chachamim Reasoning

### Pesuk Emphasis

The *chachamim* read the same phrase differently. *Ve-chiper ha-kohen al ha-nefesh ha-shogeges* — "for the inadvertently sinning soul": this describes the ordinary condition of individuals for whom the sin is defined entirely by the inadvertence of the action. That is the paradigm case.

### Exclusion

But the *kohen gadol* does not fit this paradigm. *Yatza mashiach she-ein cheto bishgaga ella b'he'elam davar* — the *kohen gadol* is excluded, because his sin is not defined by the *shgagah* of the action alone but by *he'elam davar* — the faulty ruling. Therefore, even for *avoda zara*, where he brings a *seirah* like any *yachid*, the *chachamim* maintain that the requirement of a *hora'ah* combined with a *ma'aseh* still governs his liability.

## Asham Talui

### Asham Source

The *mishnah* on 8b states, and both Rabbi and the *chachamim* affirm, that a *kohen gadol* does not bring an *asham talui*. The source *pasuk* is *ve-chiper alav ha-kohen al shigagato asher shagag* — "the *kohen* shall atone for him for his inadvertent act that he inadvertently did," which is the verse governing *asham talui*.

### Rabbi Exclusion

Rabbi derives from the doubling — *shigagato asher shagag* — that *asham talui* applies only to *mi she-kol cheto bishgaga*: someone all of whose sins are determined purely by the inadvertence of the action. The *kohen gadol*, though he is treated like an ordinary individual for *avoda zara* (requiring only *shgagah* of action), is nevertheless excluded from *asham talui* because the vast majority of his sins — everything other than *avoda zara* — requires a *hora'ah* in addition to the action. Since not all of his sins are defined by *shgagah* alone — *she-ein kol cheto bishgaga* — he is not in the class of persons for whom *asham talui* was instituted.

### Asher Shagag Q

The Gemara presses a textual question on this derivation: it does not actually say *kol* — "all" — in the verse. It says *asher shagag* — "that he inadvertently did." How does Rabbi derive from this the requirement that *all* of one's sins must be *bishgaga*?

### Entire Sin

The Gemara responds: *d'im kein yichtov al shiggaso* — if the verse merely intended to identify this particular act as inadvertent, it would have sufficed to say *al shiggaso*, "for his inadvertence." The addition of *asher shagag* is superfluous unless it is conveying something further: namely, that only a person for whom the entire structure of liability is always through *shgagah* — and nothing else — comes within the ambit of *asham talui*.

### Chachamim: Never

For the *chachamim*, the point is straightforward and unambiguous: *mi she-chataso bishgaga* — *asham talui* applies to someone whose sin is always defined by the inadvertence of action alone. The *kohen gadol* is excluded categorically — *lo ba'avoda zara velo bishe'ar mitzvot* — neither for *avoda zara* nor for any other prohibition. In every case, whether *avoda zara* or ordinary sins, the *kohen gadol*'s *chiyuv* requires *he'elam davar* combined with *shiggas ma'aseh*. He therefore never falls into the class of one whose liability is constituted purely by action, and consequently can never bring an *asham talui*.

Thus the daf concludes with the framework fully articulated: the *kohen gadol* brings a *seirah* for *avoda zara*; the Tannaitic dispute between Rabbi and the *chachamim* concerns whether *avoda zara* requires *hora'ah* or *shgagah* alone; and both agree that *asham talui* is entirely inapplicable to the *kohen gadol*, though they differ in the precise reasoning.

---

---

# Horayot 8

## Intro & Framework

### Overview

Daf 8 continues into the second *perek*, which deals not only with the *korban* of the *Beit Din HaGadol* when the people follow its incorrect ruling, but also with the *korban* of the *Kohen Gadol*. The *Kohen Gadol*'s situation is a striking one: his special *korban* is only triggered when he himself *paskens* incorrectly and then follows his own *psak*. If he simply commits an ordinary sin *b'shogeg*, he does not bring his special *korban* — a conceptually unusual idea. The *daf* also takes up the parallel cases of the *nasi* (the political head) and the special *korban* brought in the context of *avodah zarah*, where the *Beit Din HaGadol* brings both a *par l'olah* and a *se'ir l'chatas* when most of the *tzibbur* follows their erroneous ruling. In that latter case, there is a *machloket* between *Rebbe* and the *Chachamim* regarding whether the *Kohen Gadol* requires the same mechanism of *psak* and following, or whether he functions more like an ordinary individual.

### Mishna: Par Criteria

The *mishna* on 8a states: *ein Beit Din chayav ad she-yiru b'davar she-zidono karet v'shgegato chatas* — the *Beit Din* brings its special *korban*, the *par*, only when the ruling concerns a sin for which willful violation incurs *karet* and unintentional violation incurs a standard *chatas*. If the sin is of a category for which an ordinary individual would bring, say, an *asham vadai* or an *oleh v'yored*, the *Beit Din*'s special collective *korban* does not apply.

### Kohen Gadol & Nasi

The *mishna* extends this principle: *v'chen hamashiach* — the *Kohen Gadol* likewise brings his special *korban* only for that category of sin which would ordinarily obligate an individual in a *chatas*. Similarly, *v'lo b'avodah zarah ad she-yiru b'davar she-zidono karet v'shgegato chatas* — even the special collective *korban* for *avodah zarah* (the *par l'olah* and *se'ir l'chatas* brought when the *Beit Din HaGadol*'s erroneous ruling is followed) applies only to a form of *avodah zarah* for which willful violation would incur *karet* and unintentional violation a *chatas*. By contrast, an act such as hugging or kissing an idol — which *Rashi* identifies as expressing fealty rather than constituting actual worship — carries only a simple *lav* and would not ordinarily require a sin offering. If the *Beit Din* ruled erroneously on such a matter and people followed, no special *korban* would be brought.

---

## Karet Limitation

### Avodah Zarah Karet

The *Gemara* now asks: *menalan* — what is the source for the requirement that the *Beit Din*'s special *korban* applies only to sins for which *karet* is the penalty for willful violation?

### Arayot Deriv.

A *baraita* is cited: *Rebbe omer* — *Rebbe* derives this from a *gezeirah shavah* on the word *aleha*. In the *parsha* of *Beit Din HaGadol*, the verse uses the word *aleha* (*v'nodah hachatas asher chatu aleha*). The same word *aleha* appears in the *parsha* of *arayot* (*l'galot ervatah aleha*). Just as there — by *arayot* — the relevant sin is one for which willful violation incurs *karet* and unintentional violation incurs a *chatas*, so too here: the *Beit Din*'s *korban* applies only to such a category of sin. The *Gemara* notes that the *karet* dimension is clear from the *arayot* context; the requirement that unintentional violation produce a *chatas* is what links the two cases together. *Ashken tzibbur* — fine, that establishes the rule for the *Beit Din HaGadol*.

### Nasi Mitzvot

The *Gemara* then proceeds through each of the parties mentioned in *Perek Daled* of *Vayikra*. That chapter opens (*Perek 4, Pasuk 1*) with *nefesh ki techeta bishgaga mikol mitzvot Hashem* — introducing the general category of *chatas* — and then separately treats the *Kohen Gadol* (Pasuk 2 through 12), *Beit Din HaGadol* (Pasuk 13 through 21), the *nasi* (Pasuk 22 through 26), and finally the ordinary *yachid* (Pasuk 27 to the end of the chapter).

For the *Kohen Gadol*: the Torah says the *Kohen Gadol* sins *l'ashmat ha'am* — his sin is like the sin of the congregation. Therefore *harei mashiach k'tzibbur* — his *korban* follows the same rule as that of the *Beit Din HaGadol*, namely only for sins of *karet*.

For the *nasi*: *nasi yalif mitzvot mitzvot* — a *gezeirah shavah* on the word *mitzvot*. By the *nasi* the verse says *v'asah achat mikol mitzvot Hashem*, and by the *tzibbur* it similarly says *v'asu achat mikol mitzvot*. Just as the *tzibbur*'s *korban* — already established through the *aleha* link — applies only to sins of *karet* and *chatas*, so too the *nasi*: *af nasi davar shezidono karet ushgegato chatas*.

### Yachid Chatas

For the ordinary *yachid*: the *Gemara* notes that the verse introducing the *yachid*'s sin offering begins with *v'im nefesh achat techeta*, and the *vav* — *v'im* — links it to everything above. Since all the preceding categories were established to apply only to sins of *karet*, the ordinary *chatas* of an individual is likewise limited to such sins. This then works reciprocally: the individual *chatas* confirms that the class of sins punishable by *karet* is also the class for which an ordinary individual brings a *chatas* — and this is precisely the standard that all these special *korbanot* require.

The *Gemara* then raises an objection to this chain of reasoning. It works, the *Gemara* notes, according to *Rebbe*, who uses the word *aleha* in a *gezeirah shavah* to import *karet* from *arayot*. But the *Rabbanan* who require the *aleha* there to teach a separate *halacha* relating to *arayot* and *tzarot* and *yibum* — those *Rabbanan* cannot use that *aleha* for this purpose.

### AZ Yachid Se'ir

The discussion turns to *avodah zarah*. There is a separate *parsha* — *Bamidbar Perek 15* — which deals with the *korbanot* for *avodah zarah*, and this *parsha* applies to different categories: the *ציbbur* (verses dealing with *me'einei ha'eida*), and the *yachid* (*v'im nefesh achat techeta bishgaga*, who brings a *se'irah*, a she-goat). The *Gemara* establishes that the *Kohen Gadol* and *nasi* are included in the individual's category of *nefesh achat*, so that all of them — the ordinary individual, the *Kohen Gadol*, and the *nasi* — bring a *se'ir* for *avodah zarah*.

How do we know that the *tzibbur*'s special *korban* for *avodah zarah* is limited to *karet*-level offenses? The *Gemara* uses a *me'einei–me'einei* link: the verse in the *avodah zarah* context of *Bamidbar* 15 says *v'ne'elam davar me'einei ha'eida*, using the word *me'einei*; the verse by the *Beit Din HaGadol*'s standard *korban* in *Vayikra* 4 likewise uses the word *me'einei*. The *me'einei–me'einei* link connects the *avodah zarah korban* of the *tzibbur* to the *Beit Din HaGadol*'s standard *korban*, which is already established as applying only to sins of *karet*. Thus: *mah lehalan davar shezidono karet v'shgegato chatas, af kan davar shezidono karet v'shgegato chatas*.

That resolves the *tzibbur*'s *avodah zarah* case. But how do we know the same for the *yachid*, the *nasi*, and the *Kohen Gadol* in the *avodah zarah* context? The *Gemara* answers: *amar kra v'im nefesh achas* — the verse *nefesh achas* groups all three together, and then *v'yelamed tachton min ha'elyon* — the lower section learns from the upper. Once *karet* is established for the *tzibbur*'s *avodah zarah korban* via the *me'einei–me'einei* link, the individual cases follow.

The *Gemara* then notes a difficulty: this entire chain only works for the *Rabbanan* who cannot use the *aleha* link, if there is an alternative way to introduce *karet* into the *avodah zarah parsha* itself — without depending on *arayot*. This alternative comes from *Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi*, who taught his son from the verse *torah achas yihiyeh lachem la'oseh bishgaga* (Bamidbar 15:29). Immediately following the *avodah zarah* passages, the Torah says this "one Torah" for the one who sins inadvertently. Just before, it says *v'hanefesh asher ta'aseh b'yad ramah… v'nichretah hanefesh* — the one who acts presumptuously incurs *karet*. Once *karet* appears in this *parsha*, it can be propagated: just as *avodah zarah* done willfully incurs *karet*, unintentional *avodah zarah* incurs a *chatas*, and the *torah achas* generalizes this principle across all categories. *Huksha kol hatorah kullaha l'avodas kochavim* — the entire Torah is compared to *avodah zarah*: just as willful *avodah zarah* incurs *karet* and unintentional *avodah zarah* incurs a *chatas*, so too for every sin in this framework.

### Torah Achas

The *torah achas* verse thus serves as a general principle unifying the entire structure: whatever sin is in this category — whether by an individual, the *nasi*, the *Kohen Gadol*, or the *Beit Din HaGadol* — it is only a sin for which *karet* applies to willful violation and a *chatas* applies to unintentional violation. And then, in the manner described above, the *ציbbur*'s rule can also be learned back upward from the individual cases once *karet* is anchored below: *tzibur menalan yalif elyon mitachton*.

### Rav Hilkiya

The *Gemara* then asks: if *torah achas* is used to establish the *karet* standard, what was *Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi* teaching it to address? The answer is that *torah achas* is needed for a different purpose, as derived in a *baraita*: since we find that the Torah differentiates between a multitude and individuals in the case of intentional *avodah zarah* — a city that worships *avodah zarah* is executed by the sword and its property is destroyed, while an individual worshipper is stoned and their property is preserved — one might have thought (*yachol*) that there would similarly be distinct *korbanot* for unintentional *avodah zarah* by a city, as opposed to by ordinary individuals. The *torah achas* teaches otherwise: whether it is one individual or an entire city short of the full *tzibbur*, all bring the same *korban*.

*Rav Hilkiya me-Hagronya* challenges this: what distinct *korban* could we possibly have expected a city to bring? Running through the possibilities — a *par* (already the *tzibbur*'s *korban* for ordinary sins), a *par l'olah* and *se'ir l'chatas* (already the *tzibbur*'s *korban* for *avodah zarah*), a *se'ir* (already the *nasi*'s *korban* for other sins), a *se'irah* (already the individual's *korban* for *avodah zarah*) — there is nothing distinctly left for a city's *korban*. So what exactly was the *hava amina* that needed to be ruled out?

### AZ Korbanot

The *Gemara* responds: the *hava amina* would have been that a city brings the same elements as the *tzibbur* — a *par l'olah* and a *se'ir l'chatas* — but in reversed order, bringing a *par l'chatas* and a *se'ir l'olah*. Or alternatively, we might simply not have known which *korban* they would bring, and the *torah achas* informs us that they bring exactly what an individual brings. Thus *ka mashma lan* — the *torah achas* teaches that even for a city committing *avodah zarah* inadvertently, the rule follows that of individuals.

In any case, the conclusion reached by all opinions is that all these *korbanot* — the *par v'se'ir* of the *tzibbur* for *avodah zarah*, the *se'ir* for the individual, *nasi*, and *Kohen Gadol* — are written in the context of *avodah zarah*, and the *karet* requirement is established and propagated throughout. The *Gemara* identifies the *avodah zarah* context of these verses through three independent derivations: (1) *kol hamitzvot ha'eileh* refers to the *mitzvah* that is equivalent to all *mitzvot*, which is *avodah zarah*; (2) the verse mentions both *asher diber Hashem el Moshe* and *asher tziva Hashem aleichem b'yad Moshe*, and the only *mitzvah* heard both directly from God and transmitted through *Moshe* is *lo yihiyeh lecha* — the prohibition of *avodah zarah*; (3) the verse mentions that God commanded *min hayom… l'doroteichem* — from the first day of commandment onward — implying the very first *mitzvah*. The *Gemara* does note, however, that this third derivation is weak: the first *mitzvot* were actually received at *Marah*, before *Har Sinai*. So the better explanations remain the first two. Ultimately, one way or another, *karet* is introduced into the *avodah zarah* context and propagated throughout all the linked cases.

---

## Chatas & Oleh V.

### Mikdash Rules

The *Gemara* now introduces a second limiting principle. In addition to the *karet* requirement, all these special *korbanot* apply only when the underlying sin would normally obligate a *chatas kevuah* — a fixed-value sin offering. Where the sin ordinarily obligates a *chatas* that is an *oleh v'yored* — a variable-cost offering whose value shifts with the sinner's financial means — the *Beit Din HaGadol* does not bring its special *korban*. The *mishna* states: *ein chayavin al asei v'lo sa'asei sheb'mikdash* — the *Beit Din* is not liable for ruling on a positive or negative commandment relating to the *mikdash*. An example of a positive commandment would be expelling *temei'im* from the camp; a negative commandment would be the prohibition against entering the *mikdash* in a state of *tumah*.

### No AT Mikdash

An individual who is uncertain whether they ate *kodashim* while *tamei* — a case of *tumas mikdash v'kodashav* — would not bring an *asham taluy*, since *asham taluy* applies only where the underlying sin, if established, would require a *chatas kevuah*. An *oleh v'yored* does not support an *asham taluy*.

### Niddah Example

The *mishna* then provides a positive contrast: *aval chayavin al asei v'lo sa'asei shebeniddah* — the *Beit Din HaGadol* does bring its *korban* for an erroneous ruling about positive and negative commandments relating to *niddah*. The positive commandment is *perosh min haniddah* — separating from a woman approaching the time of her period; the negative commandment is the prohibition against intercourse with a *niddah*. The case the *mishna* envisions is one where the *Beit Din* ruled incorrectly and people followed — and where, for instance, a couple was engaged in relations at the moment the woman became a *niddah*, so the positive commandment's violation led directly into the negative's violation. This is a case of *karet* with a *chatas kevuah*, and the *Beit Din*'s special *korban* applies. Similarly, an individual uncertain whether such a violation occurred would bring an *asham taluy*.

It is noteworthy that the *mishna* does not actually quote the *pesukim* for these *mitzvot*. One might have expected textual citations. There is also a broader conceptual question lurking here, about the relationship between *hilchot niddah* and the frameworks of *dinei arayot* versus *dinei tumah* — but that discussion is for another time.

### Ve'Ashem Link

The *Gemara* asks: *minani milei* — what is the source that the *Beit Din*'s special *korban* and an individual's *asham taluy* apply only when the underlying sin is a *chatas kevuah*?

*Rabbi Yitzbar Avdimi* says: a *gezerah shavah* on the word *v'ashem*. In the passage of the ordinary individual *chatas* (*Vayikra* 4), the verse reads *v'im nefesh techeta v'astah achat mikol mitzvot Hashem asher lo te'asenah v'ashem* — it says *v'ashem*. In the passage of *asham taluy*, the verse reads *v'nefesh ki techeta v'astah achat mikol mitzvot Hashem asher lo te'asenah v'lo yada v'ashem* — also *v'ashem*. And in the passage of the *tzibbur*'s *korban*, the verse reads *v'asu achat mikol mitzvot Hashem asher lo te'asenah v'ashemu* — similarly *v'ashemu*.

The link between these three *v'ashem* formulations establishes a common requirement: just as the individual's *chatas* (the base case in *Perek 4 of Vayikra*) is a *chatas kevuah*, so too the *korban* of the *tzibbur* requires a *chatas kevuah* — *mah v'ashem b'yachid b'chatas kevuah, af v'ashemu b'tzibbur b'chatas kevuah*. And by the same logic, the *asham taluy*, which also uses *v'ashem*, is brought only in cases of doubt regarding what would otherwise be a *chatas kevuah* — *af asham taluy nami ein ba ela al safek chatas kevuah*.

### OV Challenge

The *Gemara* raises a powerful objection: if *v'ashem* is what defines membership in this "club" of *chatas kevuah* cases, then note that the *oleh v'yored* passage — precisely the category you are trying to *exclude* — also uses the very same word *v'ashem*. The verse in the *oleh v'yored* passage (*Vayikra* 5) reads: *v'hayah ki ye'asham l'achat me'eileh* — here the word appears as *ye'asham* (with a *yud* prefix). More pointedly, the *Gemara* notes that the *tumas mikdash v'kodashav* case — the archetypal example of *oleh v'yored* that the *mishna* explicitly excludes — contains the exact word *v'ashem*: *v'hu tamei v'ashem*. The *Gemara* thus challenges: how can one use *v'ashem* to create a link that excludes *oleh v'yored* when *oleh v'yored* uses the identical term?

The *Gemara* attempts a first answer: *danin ashemu me'asham v'ein danin asham mi'ye'asham* — the forms *ashem* and *ashemu* are sufficiently similar to create a link between themselves, but the form *ye'asham* (with the *yud* prefix) is different enough to be excluded. The *Gemara* immediately rejects this: what practical difference does that distinction make? The very logic of *gezeirah shavah* permits linking words that are not identical — the *Gemara* cites the *baraita* from *d'vei Rabbi Yishmael* concerning *tzara'at*, where the *kohen* "returns" and "comes," and even though those are distinct words, *zu hi shiva zu hi vi'a* — the link is made because they refer to the same idea. And in any case, the *tumas mikdash v'kodashav* passage uses *v'ashem* — the exact word — so the form distinction cannot do the work needed.

### Double Link

*Rav Papa* offers the resolution: *danin v'ashem umitzvot Hashem min v'ashem umitzvot Hashem* — the link is not based on *v'ashem* alone, but on a double link combining *v'ashem* and *mitzvot Hashem*. In the *tzibbur*'s passage (*Vayikra* 4:13), the verse says *mikol mitzvot Hashem asher lo te'asenah v'ashemu*. In the individual *chatas* passage (*Vayikra* 4:27), the verse says *achat mimitzvot Hashem asher lo te'asenah v'ashem*. Both passages contain both *mitzvot Hashem* and *v'ashem*. The *oleh v'yored* passages do not contain this double combination, and therefore they are not part of this exclusive club.

*Rav Shimi bar Ashi* raises a challenge to *Rav Papa*: by *oleh v'yored*, the text uses both *v'ashem* and *v'nasa avono* — a double link of its own. If the principle is that a double link creates a special category, then why not link the *asham taluy* to the *oleh v'yored* (via *v'ashem* and *v'nasa avono*) rather than to the *chatas kevuah* cases?

*Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak* provides the final answer: the decisive link is a triple combination — *v'ashem*, *mitzvot Hashem*, and *asher lo te'asenah* — all appearing together. Comparing the *tzibbur* verse (*v'asu achat mikol mitzvot Hashem asher lo te'asenah v'ashemu*) and the individual *chatas* verse (*v'im nefesh techeta v'astah achat mikol mitzvot Hashem asher lo te'asenah v'ashem*): these phrases are essentially identical, drawn from the same *parsha*, and constitute an unmistakably tight verbal parallel. The *oleh v'yored* and *asham taluy* passages lack this precise combination. The *Gemara* acknowledges, however, that it remains somewhat unclear at the end of the day precisely how *asham taluy* is linked to the *chatas kevuah* camp rather than to *oleh v'yored*; the primary derivation here is for the *korban* of the *tzibbur*, which is clearly linked to the *chatas kevuah* category by this multiple verbal parallel.

The *mishna*'s final formulation confirms: *ein chayavin al shemiat kol v'al bitui sefatayim v'al tumat mikdash v'kodashav* — these three are the classic cases of *oleh v'yored*, explicitly excluded from the *Beit Din*'s special *korban*. The inclusion of *niddah* as a case that does obligate the *Beit Din* — being a *chatas kevuah* carrying *karet* — is thus the positive counterpart demonstrating the rule.

---

## Nasi & Oleh V.

### Nasi Excluded

The next *mishna* introduces the *nasi*: *v'hanasi kayotzei bahem* — the *nasi* is like the *Beit Din* in this respect, and does not bring a *korban* for any of the three *oleh v'yored* categories. *Divrei Rabbi Yose HaGlili* — this is the position of *Rabbi Yose HaGlili*.

### R. Akiva Pos.

*Rabbi Akiva* disagrees: *hanasi chayav bekulan chutz mishemiat hakol* — the *nasi* is liable for all the *oleh v'yored* categories, and does bring the variable *korban* for each of them, with one exception: *shemiat kol* — the case of being sworn to testify.

### Court Testimony

The reasoning for *Rabbi Akiva*'s exception is *shehamelech lo dan v'lo danin oto, lo me'id v'lo me'idin oto* — a king neither judges nor is judged, neither testifies nor is compelled to testify. The *oleh v'yored* case of *shemiat kol* involves being bound by an oath to provide testimony; since a king cannot be summoned to court to testify, that category simply does not apply to him, and he therefore brings no *korban* for it. But the other two categories — *bitui sefatayim* and *tumas mikdash v'kodashav* — do apply to him, and he brings the corresponding *oleh v'yored* like anyone else.

The *Gemara* asks: why does *Rabbi Yose HaGlili* exclude the *nasi* from all three? One might suggest it is because the verse *v'hayah ki ye'asham l'achat me'eileh* — listing all three *oleh v'yored* obligations together — implies that liability for one entails liability for all: *kol shemis'chayev b'achat mis'chayev bekulan v'she'eino mis'chayev b'achat eino mis'chayev bekulan*. Since a *nasi* cannot be obligated in *shemiat kol*, he is excluded from the entire framework. The *Gemara* challenges this reading: perhaps *le'achat me'eileh* means that being obligated in even one of the three is sufficient to bring a *korban*, such that the *nasi* would still bring for the other two. The *Gemara* concedes that the exegetical basis from this verse is uncertain.

### Wealth Criteria

The *Gemara* then establishes the *tanna*'s actual reasoning, citing a *baraita* from *Rabbi Meir*: the *oleh v'yored* passages use the language *im lo tasig yado* (if he cannot afford) — the entire framework of variable-cost offerings presupposes a person who could be either wealthy or poor. *Mi sheba lidei aniyut v'ashirut* — only someone who may experience both poverty and wealth is within the scope of *oleh v'yored*.

### Always Wealthy

*Yatza nasi umashiach* — the *nasi* and the *Kohen Gadol* are excluded because they never enter into poverty. *She'ein ba'in lidei aniyut* — they are structurally prevented from becoming poor.

### Nasi Elohav

The textual source for the *nasi*: the verse describing his sin reads *v'asah achat mikol mitzvot Hashem elohav* — "the commandments of Hashem his God." The unusual phrase "his God" — as if God is specifically *his* — is interpreted to mean: *mi she'ein al gabav ela Hashem elohav* — he is a person over whom no human being stands in authority. This implies absolute primacy, not merely in political terms but in all respects, including wealth. The *nasi* must be the wealthiest person in the realm, such that no one stands above him even in material standing.

### KG Gadol

For the *Kohen Gadol*, the source is *v'hakohen hagadol me'echav* — the *Kohen Gadol* must be *gadol me'achav*: greater than his brethren in appearance, in strength, in wisdom, and in wealth. If a *Kohen Gadol* is appointed who does not possess sufficient wealth, *acherim* rule that his fellow *kohanim* must contribute to make him wealthy: *gadlohu mishel achav* — they elevate him from their own means, fulfilling the verse *v'hakohen hagadol me'achav*, make him greater from his brothers.

Thus the debate between *Rabbi Yose HaGlili* and *Rabbi Akiva* turns on this principle. *Rabbi Yose HaGlili* holds that since *nasi* and *Kohen Gadol* are always wealthy and can never be poor, the *oleh v'yored* framework — which presupposes the possibility of poverty — simply does not apply to them at all. *Rabbi Akiva*, by contrast, holds that they do fall within the *oleh v'yored* framework; the only exclusion is the *nasi*'s inability to be compelled to testify, which removes the *shemiat kol* category for him specifically.

---

---

# Horayot 9

## Par ha-Elam Davar

### Review: Chatat Keduma

We begin today at the top of daf 9, *amud aleph*. The *sugyot* we have been traversing concern the conditions under which a *par ha-elam davar shel tzibbur* is brought, and in parallel the conditions under which the *kohen gadol* brings his *par*. Several principles emerge from the prior discussion. Both require a *psak halacha*; both are only liable through a *hora'ah* involving *kiyum miktzat u'bittul miktzat*. The *hora'ah* must concern a matter for which one would otherwise bring a *korban chatat* — not a matter governed by *oleh v'yored*. A *korban chatat* itself requires a potential *chiyuv kares*, and, flowing from this, an *asham talui* is likewise linked only to the category of *korban chatat* and not to *korban oleh v'yored*.

### Nasi & Kohen Gadol

Within the discussion of *oleh v'yored*, a question arises: does the *kohen gadol* bring a special *korban* based on *oleh v'yored*, or are his *korbanot* categorically limited to those linked to a *korban chatat*? The same question applies to the *nasi*. He possesses a special *korban*, yet that uniqueness is not conditioned on a *psak* — it reflects his personal status when he commits an ordinary transgression. Does he nevertheless participate in the *oleh v'yored* structure?

The *mishnah* that concluded yesterday did not address the *kohen gadol* directly, but it did take up the *nasi*. According to *Rabbi Akiva*, the *nasi* is generally subject to *korban oleh v'yored* — when an act falls in the category of *chatat* he brings his designated *se'ir*, but for the *oleh v'yored* transgressions he is included, with one exception: the *oleh v'yored* arising from the oath to give testimony, which has no application to a king. *Rabbi Yose HaGlili*, by contrast, excludes both the *nasi* and the *kohen gadol* from *oleh v'yored* entirely — and, notably, not because their *korbanot* are limited to a different category, but because *oleh v'yored* is structurally designed for those who could conceivably become poor. A *kohen gadol* and a king are guaranteed against poverty by virtue of their office: the community ensures the *kohen gadol*'s wealth, and the king may always levy taxes to replenish his treasury.

This is a significant point: *Rabbi Yose HaGlili* is not arguing that their special *korbanot* crowd out the *oleh v'yored*. He is arguing that the very architecture of *oleh v'yored* — a sliding scale calibrated to wealth — is simply inapplicable to individuals whose poverty is structurally impossible.

---

## Nasi with Tzara'at

### Midcha Dachi Query

The *Gemara* continues roughly ten lines from the top of 9a, beginning with the word *minei*: *ba'ei minei Ravina me'Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak* — Ravina posed a question to Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak. Given that the *nasi* is excluded from *oleh v'yored* because he can never become poor, what is the law if the *nasi* contracted *tzara'at*? Since a king afflicted with *tzara'at* cannot continue serving, the question becomes: *midcha dachi o miptar patir* — has his royal status been permanently displaced such that the exemption from *oleh v'yored* is categorically removed, or has he only been temporarily suspended, such that during this interlude his prior exemption no longer shields him and he reverts to the ordinary obligation?

### Rashi: Wealth Exempts

The response, *dilach o deganza* — "is it from yours or from the treasury?" — is cryptic on its face. Rashi reads the exchange as follows: the question is, where does the money for the *korban* come from? Were the king to sin in office, the *korban* would be funded from the royal treasury — which, per Rashi, represents his personal wealth. Since even a king afflicted with *tzara'at* retains his wealth, and since the entire rationale for excluding the *nasi* from *oleh v'yored* is that he cannot become poor, the king remains exempt even while incapacitated. His wealth is intact; the exemption therefore persists.

### Ha-Rosh Challenge

The *Rosh* raises a powerful challenge to Rashi's reading. Mere wealth, he argues, cannot by itself be the criterion for exemption. Wealthy individuals who face no structural guarantee against eventual poverty still bring an *oleh v'yored*. The rationale for excluding the *kohen gadol* and the king is not wealth per se, but the institutional mechanism that ensures they will never fall into poverty — for the *kohen gadol*, communal support; for the king, the power of taxation. But a deposed king no longer commands that power. He can no longer reach into another's pocket. So what justifies his continued exemption?

The *Rosh* therefore reads *dilach o deganza* in the opposite direction: *dilach* — will the money come from your pocket, i.e., are you still able to compel others to fund your *korban*? Since the answer is no, and the money must come *deganza*, from his own stores, the deposed king now stands in the position of a private individual. And if that is so, he is no longer exempt — he would in fact be obligated to bring the *korban*. The *Rosh* concedes in the end that he prefers Rashi's reading, but the underlying critique stands: bare wealth, without the institutional guarantee, should not suffice for exemption. The unresolved tension in the *Gemara* is whether this period of *tzara'at* represents a complete displacement of the king's status or merely a temporary suspension of it.

---

## Kohen Gadol & Mincha

### Rava on Akiva

The *Gemara* now turns, via a *braita*, to *Rabbi Akiva*: *mashiach patur mikulan* — the *kohen gadol* is exempt from all categories of *oleh v'yored*. Rava explains the reasoning: *amar kra, zeh korban Aharon u'vanav* — the verse describing the daily *mincha* offered by the *kohen gadol*, half in the morning and half in the evening, is presented as his sole *mincha* obligation. *Zu ba-achovah lo v'ein acheres ba-achovah lo* — this, and no other *mincha*, is his obligatory offering. Since the lowest tier of *oleh v'yored* is a *mincha*, and since the *Torah* has said that a *kohen gadol* never incurs a *mincha* obligation beyond his daily offering, the bottom of the *oleh v'yored* scale is structurally inaccessible to him.

This distinguishes *Rabbi Akiva*'s position from that of *Rabbi Yose HaGlili* in a subtle but important way. *Rabbi Yose* excludes the *kohen gadol* because he cannot become poor. *Rabbi Akiva* excludes him because the *Torah* has categorically foreclosed the possibility of his ever bringing a *mincha* as an obligation. The two rationales overlap in practical outcome but diverge in conceptual basis.

### Me'achot Placement

The *Gemara* raises a challenge: perhaps we should read the verse as excluding the *kohen gadol* only from the lowest tier — the *mincha* of *dallei dalus* — while leaving him subject to the middle tier (the bird) and the upper tier (the large animal) when his means permit. Why not say simply that the *Torah* excluded him from *asiris ha'eifa* but not from the others?

The *Gemara* responds: *v'chiper alav ha-kohen al chataso asher chata mei-achas mei-eleh* — the verse states that the *kohen* shall atone for whoever sinned on "one of these." The principle derived is *ha-miskaper b'achas miskaper b'chulan* — one who can atone with any one of the three options may use all of them; *she-ein miskaper b'achas ein miskaper b'chulan* — one who cannot atone with one of them cannot use any of them. Since the *kohen gadol* is excluded from the *mincha*, he is excluded from the entirety of *oleh v'yored*.

### Me'achot vs L'achot

The *Gemara* presses further. A similar formulation appears in the verse describing the three categories of sin that trigger *oleh v'yored* — the oath about testimony, *tum'at mikdash v'kodashav*, and swearing falsely. That verse uses the phrase *l'achas mei-eleh* — sinned regarding "one of these." By the same logic, why not say: only if a person could be liable for any one of these sins may he be liable for any of them? If the *nasi* cannot be sworn to testify, he should be excluded from the entire *oleh v'yored*, just as *Rabbi Yose HaGlili* maintains. Yet *Rabbi Akiva* holds that the *nasi* is exempt only from the oath about testimony but remains obligated for the others. How can *Rabbi Akiva* invoke the *miskaper b'achas* principle to exclude the *kohen gadol* from the *korban*, while not invoking the same logic to exclude the *nasi* from the sin categories?

Abaye and Rava resolve this jointly: *mei-achas* and *l'achas* do not by themselves carry the implication that all possibilities must be available — the *mem* versus *lamed* is not the operative distinction. What matters is the *placement* of the word in the *pasuk*. The phrase *mei-achas* in connection with the *korban* appears specifically at the end, positioned adjacent to the *mincha* clause — *gabei asiris ha'eifa*. Had it been written alongside the bird or the large animal, it would carry no special exclusionary implication. But because the *Torah* placed it specifically at the *mincha* — the tier that a *kohen gadol* can never bring — the only way to make sense of that placement is to understand it as a signal: one who cannot bring the *mincha* is excluded from all tiers. The positioning is itself the *derashah*.

By contrast, the *l'achas* formulation governing the sin categories does not appear at a strategically chosen point that signals the exclusion of a class who cannot commit one of the sins. Therefore, the *nasi*'s inability to be sworn to testify does not cascade into a total exclusion from *oleh v'yored* — and *Rabbi Akiva* is not being internally inconsistent.

In summary: both *Rabbi Yose HaGlili* and *Rabbi Akiva* agree that the *kohen gadol* is fundamentally in the *parasha* of *oleh v'yored*, and that arguments must be marshaled to extract him. *Rabbi Yose* excludes him because he cannot become poor. *Rabbi Akiva* excludes him because the *Torah* has removed the *mincha* from his repertoire, and the *Torah*'s placement of *mei-achas* at that juncture signals a total exclusion. For the *nasi*, *Rabbi Yose* likewise excludes him from everything, while *Rabbi Akiva* retains him in the category except for the oath of testimony.

---

## Mishnah Classification

### Standard Chatat

Any transgression in the *Torah* for which willful violation incurs *kares* and inadvertent violation incurs a *chatat*: the *yachid* brings a female sheep or goat, *ha-nasi meivi se'ir* — the *nasi* brings a male goat, and *u'mashiach u'Beit Din mevi'im par* — the *kohen gadol* and *Beit Din* bring a bull.

### Avoda Zara Rule

In the case of *avoda zara*, the *yachid*, the *nasi*, and the *kohen gadol* all bring a female goat. *Beit Din*, when ruling leads the community to sin regarding *avoda zara*, brings a *par l'olah v'se'ir l'chatas* — a bull as an *olah* and a male goat as a *chatat*.

### Asham Talui

An *asham talui* — the conditional guilt offering brought when one is uncertain whether a sin requiring a fixed *chatat* was committed — obligates the *yachid* and the *nasi*. The *kohen gadol* and *Beit Din* are exempt. The *kohen gadol*'s exemption derives from the verse *al shegogaso asher shagag*: an *asham talui* is brought only by one whose liability arises purely from *shiggas ma'aseh* — inadvertent action alone. Since the *kohen gadol*'s obligation arises additionally from *hora'ah*, he does not fall within this category.

### Asham Vadai

For the specified cases of *asham vadai* — a definite guilt offering — the *yachid*, the *nasi*, and the *kohen gadol* are all obligated. *Beit Din* remains exempt, as its liability arises only through the *chatat* mechanism.

### Oleh V'Yored Sins

For the three sins that trigger *oleh v'yored* — *shmiat ha-kol*, *bitui sefatayim*, and *tum'at mikdash v'kodashav* — *Beit Din* is exempt, as its obligation is confined to the fixed *chatat* structure. The *yachid*, the *nasi*, and the *kohen gadol* are, in principle, obligated — though as we have seen, there are grounds upon which each may be excluded from particular instances of this obligation.

---

## Tum'at Mikdash Issue

### Contradiction Setup

The *mishnah* states: *ella she'ein kohen gadol mashiach chayav al tum'at mikdash v'kodashav* — the *kohen gadol* is not liable for *tum'at mikdash v'kodashav*. This is structurally parallel to the *nasi*'s exemption from the oath about testimony: each is excluded from one of the three *oleh v'yored* sins while retaining obligation for the others — according to *Rabbi Shimon*.

Yet the *braita* also states: *kol she-hu be'oleh v'yored, nasi kayotze vo, mashiach u'Beit Din peturin* — when it comes to *oleh v'yored* generally, the *nasi* is included but the *kohen gadol* and *Beit Din* are categorically excluded. These two positions contradict one another. The first says the *kohen gadol* is in the *oleh v'yored* category except for *tum'at mikdash*; the second says he is entirely outside it. *Hagufa kashya* — the *braita* contradicts itself.

---

## Rabbi Eliezer Rule

### Nasi Brings She-Goat

*Rabbi Eliezer* rules that when the *nasi* is obligated under *oleh v'yored*, he does not bring the standard sliding-scale *korban*. Instead, *ha-nasi meivi se'ir* — the *nasi* brings a male goat, which is the *korban* he would bring for a standard *chatat*. He is included in the *oleh v'yored* category, yet the *korban* he brings when obligated is his fixed designation, not the sliding-scale animal.

### Yochanan Limits Rule

*Rabbi Yochanan* clarifies that *Rabbi Eliezer* made this ruling only regarding *tum'at mikdash v'kodashav* — *ho'il v'ne'emar kares bo k'be'kavua* — because among the three *oleh v'yored* sins, *tum'at mikdash v'kodashav* is the only one that shares the structure of a standard *korban chatat*: it carries a *chiyuv kares* for willful violation. Had it not been incorporated into *oleh v'yored*, it would have been a regular *chatat*. Because of this structural kinship with *chatat*, *Rabbi Eliezer* reasons that when the *nasi* is obligated for this sin, he brings his standard *se'ir* rather than the variable *oleh v'yored* offering.

---

## Tum'at Mikdash Issue (II)

### Rav Huna Resolves

Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua resolves the internal contradiction in the *braita*: *kan bidalus, kan bidlei dalus* — one statement speaks of the middle tier (*dalus*, the bird), and the other speaks of the lowest tier (*dallei dalus*, the *mincha*). The first clause, which says the *kohen gadol* is in the *oleh v'yored* category except for *tum'at mikdash*, refers to the bird and the large animal. The second clause, which categorically excludes the *kohen gadol*, means he is excluded from the *mincha* tier. The contradiction dissolves: the *kohen gadol* participates in *oleh v'yored* at all levels except the *mincha* — and, additionally, for the sin of *tum'at mikdash v'kodashav* he is not liable even at the levels he could in principle bring.

### Rav Shimon's View

Rav Shimon agrees with *Rabbi Akiva* in one dimension and disagrees in another. He agrees — *sevira lei k'Rabbi Akiva bidlei dalus depatur* — that the verse *zeh korban Aharon u'vanav* excludes the *kohen gadol* from ever being obligated in a *mincha* as part of *oleh v'yored*. Where he diverges is in scope: *Rabbi Akiva* held that exclusion from the *mincha* tier entails exclusion from all tiers; *Rav Shimon* holds that the *kohen gadol* is excluded from the *mincha* but remains obligated at the other levels — save for *tum'at mikdash v'kodashav*, from which he is separately excluded for independent reasons.

---

## Tum'at Mikdash Reaso (II)

### Mitoch HaKahal

Why is the *kohen gadol* specifically excluded from *tum'at mikdash v'kodashav*? Chizkiyah provides the derivation: *venichresa ha-nefesh ha-hi mitoch ha-kahal* — "that soul shall be cut off from within the congregation." The phrase *mitoch ha-kahal* teaches that the *oleh v'yored* obligation for *tum'at mikdash* applies only to *mi she-korbano shaveh la-kahal* — one whose *korban* is the same as the congregation's. *Yatza zeh she-ein korbano shaveh la-kahal* — the *kohen gadol* is excluded because his *korban* for *tum'ah* differs from the community's. On *Yom Kippur*, the *Torah* emphasizes *vekiper al ha-kodesh mi-tum'ot Bnei Yisrael* — the bull and the goat atone for the *tum'ah* of the community, while the *kohen gadol*'s atonement for *tum'ah* constitutes a separate *korban* with a distinct structure. Since on *Yom Kippur* — the paradigmatic day of atonement for *tum'at mikdash* — the *kohen gadol* and the *kohanim* stand in a categorically different relationship to *tum'ah* than the rest of the community, the verse's limiting phrase *mitoch ha-kahal* excludes them from the *oleh v'yored* obligation for this sin.

### Challenge to Logic

The *Gemara* challenges immediately: if the criterion is that the *nasi*'s *korban* differs from the community's, then the *nasi* also brings a different *korban* for a standard sin — a *se'ir* rather than a *kesba* or *se'irah*. So why isn't the *nasi* also excluded from *tum'at mikdash v'kodashav*?

---

## Rabbi Eliezer Rule (II)

### Rav Papa's Question

Rav Papa raises a parallel question regarding *Rabbi Eliezer*'s ruling that the *nasi* brings a *se'ir* when obligated under *oleh v'yored* for *tum'at mikdash v'kodashav*. If the logic is that a person brings their standard *chatat* offering when this *oleh v'yored* sin is involved, then by the same reasoning, the *kohen gadol* should bring a *par* when he is similarly obligated. The structural parallel is clean: just as the *nasi* substitutes his standard *se'ir* for the sliding-scale animal, the *kohen gadol* should substitute his standard *par*.

### Why No Kohen Gadol

The very fact that *Rabbi Eliezer* did not extend his ruling to the *kohen gadol* demonstrates, by *diyuk*, that he was indeed speaking only of *tum'at mikdash v'kodashav* — and even then, only in the case of the *nasi*, because the *kohen gadol* is entirely exempt from *tum'at mikdash v'kodashav*. *Shma mina tumat mikdash v'kodashav ka'i de'mashiach patur* — the silence regarding the *kohen gadol* proves both that *Rabbi Eliezer*'s rule is limited to this sin and that the *kohen gadol* does not bring for it at all.

### Asham Talui Braita

A *tana* taught a *braita* before Rav Sheshet: *asham talui ba al tum'at mikdash v'kodashav* — one brings an *asham talui* in a case of doubt regarding *tum'at mikdash v'kodashav*. Rav Sheshet responds that this makes sense according to *Rabbi Eliezer*, who treats *tum'at mikdash v'kodashav* as structurally equivalent to a standard *chatat* — since *kares* applies to its willful violation and the sin has the architecture of a fixed obligation. If one follows *Rabbi Eliezer*'s principle that this sin is *k'be'kavua*, it is logical that an *asham talui* would be brought in a case of doubt, just as it would for any *chatat kavua*. *Rabbi Yochanan*, however, had limited *Rabbi Eliezer*'s position: *modeh Rabbi Eliezer she-ein meivi asham talui* — *Rabbi Eliezer* would concede that an *asham talui* is not brought. In *Rabbi Yochanan*'s reading, *Rabbi Eliezer* is making a narrow ruling about which animal the *nasi* brings — not a wholesale reclassification of *tum'at mikdash* as a standard *chatat*. This *braita* presents a difficulty for *Rabbi Yochanan*'s position.

---

## Tum'at Mikdash Reaso (II)

### Rava's Reframe

Rava reframes the entire reasoning behind the *kohen gadol*'s exclusion from *tum'at mikdash v'kodashav*. Rather than grounding it in the *Yom Kippur* atonement structure and the distinction between the *kohen gadol*'s *korban* and the community's *korban*, Rava focuses on the nature of the *sinner*: *mi she-chataso shaveh li-yachidim u'mai nihu kahal* — the verse *mitoch ha-kahal* refers to one whose sin is equivalent to that of a private individual. A private individual's sin is triggered by *shiggas ma'aseh* — inadvertent action alone. The *kohen gadol*, by contrast, achieves liability through a combination of *hora'ah* and *shiggas ma'aseh*. He is never, even when sinning privately, treated as a pure *yachid*. His entire identity is constituted by his public role — he does not leave the *mikdash* even to mourn his own parents — and therefore he never occupies the position of an ordinary private individual. Since the *oleh v'yored* obligation for *tum'at mikdash* attaches specifically to one who qualifies as a *yachid* in the full sense, the *kohen gadol*, who never qualifies as a *yachid*, is excluded.

The *Gemara* notes that this reasoning, if taken to its logical conclusion, would exclude all *kohanim*, not only the *kohen gadol*, from *tum'at mikdash v'kodashav* obligations — since *kohanim* also bring a distinct *korban* on *Yom Kippur*. The response is that *kohanim* are otherwise participants in the communal framework: when *Beit Din* rules and the community follows, *kohanim* are part of that community. But the *kohen gadol* stands apart even there — he is separate both in his *tum'ah* atonement and in his status vis-à-vis ordinary sin. The *Gemara* presses again: but the *kohen gadol* also participates in communal sin when *Beit Din* rules and the community acts. The discussion remains unresolved on precisely why *tum'at mikdash v'kodashav* in particular is the locus of his exclusion rather than other categories.

---

## Deposed Leader Korban

### Sin While in Office

*Kohen mashiach she-chata ve-achar kach avar mi-meshichuso* — a *kohen gadol* who sinned while in office and was subsequently removed from his position: *kohen mashiach meivi par* — he brings a *par*, in accordance with his status at the time of the sin. Similarly, *ve-chen nasi she-chata ve-achar kach avar mi-gedulaso* — a *nasi* who sinned as *nasi* and then was deposed brings a *se'ir*. The governing principle is that the *korban* follows the offender's status at the moment of the transgression, not his status at the time of atonement.

### Sinned After Deposed

*Mashiach she-avar mi-meshichuso ve-achar kach chata* — a *kohen gadol* who was first removed from office and only then sinned: *kohen mashiach meivi par* — he still brings a *par*, as though he remains a *kohen gadol*. *Ve-ha-nasi ke-hedyot* — but a *nasi* who was first deposed and then sinned brings as a commoner. This asymmetry is striking. The *kohen gadol*, even after being removed from his position, retains his *korban* status indefinitely. The *nasi* does not. The *kohen gadol* never fully loses his elevated halachic category; the *nasi*'s category is entirely contingent on his holding office.

### Stylistic Defense

The *Gemara* observes that the first ruling — that one who sinned while in office and was then deposed brings the elevated *korban* — is technically superfluous once the second ruling is stated. If a *kohen gadol* retains his *par* obligation even when he sins after being deposed, it is self-evident that he retains it when he sinned before being deposed. The *Gemara* defends the inclusion on stylistic grounds: since by the *nasi* there is a meaningful contrast — sinning while in office triggers a *se'ir*, while sinning after deposition triggers the commoner's *korban* — the *mishnah* presents the *kohen gadol*'s case in the same two-part structure for parallel clarity, even though the first clause is logically subsumed by the second.

### Ve'Hikriv Source

*D'tano rabbanan, ve-hikriv al chataso* — the *Gemara* identifies a *Torah* source for the *kohen gadol*'s retained status: the verse states *ve-hikriv al chataso*, he shall bring *upon* his sin — language oriented toward the past transgression. This past-oriented language is interpreted as *melamed she-meivi chataso mi-she-avar* — it teaches that he brings for a sin committed even under his former status. How exactly the past-tense formulation generates this ruling is not entirely transparent, but the *Gemara* takes it to mean that whatever category of *korban* was his at the time of the sin — or at the time of his *kohen gadol* status — remains the category of his atonement.

### Kal V'Chomer Logic

*Sheyachol velo dino* — one might attempt a *kal v'chomer* in the opposite direction: if the *nasi*, whose threshold for bringing a *korban* is relatively low — mere *shiggas ma'aseh* alone suffices — nevertheless loses his elevated *korban* status once deposed, then the *kohen gadol*, whose threshold is far higher — requiring both *hora'ah* and *shiggas ma'aseh* — should certainly lose his status once deposed, since the conditions that gave rise to that special *korban* are no longer present. The *Torah* therefore states explicitly *ve-hikriv al chataso* to override this *kal v'chomer*: the *kohen gadol* brings for his sin, even after his role has ended. The *kal v'chomer* would have led us to the wrong conclusion — that the *kohen gadol*'s stricter threshold means his status is more contingent, not less. The verse corrects this by anchoring his *korban* to the sin itself, not to his current office. It presumably follows that the conditions for bringing — including the requirement of a *hora'ah* — likewise attach to his former status; his *korban* as a past *kohen gadol* still demands the framework that made him a *kohen gadol*, even if he no longer holds the title.

---

---

# Horayot 10

## Chatu Ad Shelo Nitmanu

### Mishnah Setup

The third chapter of *Horayot*, continuing on 10a, takes up a comparison between the *kohen mashiach* and the *nasi* with respect to transgressions committed before either figure assumed his appointed role. The *mishnah* poses the case of *chatu ad shelo nitmanu* — they sinned before they were appointed. We are discussing the *kohen mashiach* and the *nasi* (who, as we shall see, is the king), and the question is: what is the status of a transgression — one whose deliberate commission would carry *karet* and whose inadvertent commission requires a *chatat* — committed before these individuals rose to their respective positions? *Ve-achar kach nitmanu* — and afterward they were appointed — *harei elu ke-hedyotot*: they are treated as ordinary persons and bring the sacrifice of an ordinary person.

### Rabbi Shimon's View

Rabbi Shimon refines this ruling. *Im noda lahem ad shelo nitmanu chayavin, u-mishe-nitmanu peturin.* For a transgression to generate liability, two elements are required: the act itself and the awareness of it. If both the act and the awareness occur before appointment, Rabbi Shimon holds the individual liable. If the awareness comes only after appointment, he is entirely exempt. The entire deliberation thus turns on precisely when the relevant status takes effect and how long it endures.

### Status Duration

The two offices differ in a critical respect established in prior discussion. The *kohen mashiach*, from the moment he is anointed, retains that status continuously — even during periods when he is not actively performing his duties. The *nasi*, by contrast, holds the relevant status only while he is actively exercising his role. As soon became apparent in that earlier *gemara*, the intermediate period raised its own question: what of the person who is a *kohen* but has not yet formally undergone the inauguration that would make him *kohen mashiach*? Rabbi Shimon addresses exactly this case — if such a person somehow became aware of his transgression in that liminal period, the *tanna kamma* would not hold him liable, since the full status of *kohen mashiach* had not yet been conferred.

### Who is the Nasi

The *mishnah* then asks directly: *eizehu nasi? Zeh melech* — the *nasi* in question is the king. The source is Leviticus 4:22, which speaks of one who violates *mikol mitzvot Hashem elohav* — from all the commandments of the Lord his God — and the *mishnah* reads this as meaning that there is no human authority above him, only God. He is therefore the highest temporal figure, and this identification will be important in the analysis that follows.

---

## Kal VaComer Deriv

### Leviticus 4:3 Source

The *gemara* asks *mena hani mili* — from where do we derive the rule about sinning before appointment? A *baraita* cites Leviticus 4:3: *im ha-kohen ha-mashiach yecheta* — if the anointed priest will sin. The *baraita* understands this as a *prat*, an exclusion, limiting the *kohen mashiach*'s special liability to transgressions committed while he already holds that status. Any transgression predating his anointment is treated as that of an ordinary person.

### Kal VaComer Rejected

But the *gemara* immediately questions the need for an explicit verse: *ve-halo din hu* — could we not derive this through a *kal va-chomer*? The *nasi* brings an offering only for *shgagat ma'aseh* — the inadvertent performance of an act — and does not bring for his prior transgressions. The *kohen mashiach*, whose threshold for liability is even more demanding (requiring *he'elem davar* — unawareness of the law — together with *shgagat ma'aseh*), should certainly not be liable for prior transgressions. Yet the *gemara* rejects this immediately: the *kal va-chomer* could be reversed. One might equally argue the other direction — the *kohen mashiach* brings a *chatat* for transgressions he committed while in his current status, whereas the *nasi* does not; perhaps therefore the *nasi* is more lenient and the comparison breaks down. The two cases are sufficiently different that neither straightforwardly implies the other, and the *kal va-chomer* cannot be sustained in either direction without challenge.

### Im vs. Asher

The resolution is that Scripture provides explicit language for both cases. Regarding the *kohen mashiach*, the verse says *im* — "if" — *ha-kohen ha-mashiach yecheta*: the conditional "if" signals that the obligation arises only when he transgresses in his current capacity, not for past actions. The *gemara* then concludes: *keshe-hu mashiach mevi, keshe-hu hedyot eino mevi* — when he is *kohen mashiach* he brings the offering, when he was still a *hedyot* he does not bring it.

The parallel is drawn for the *nasi* as well. *Ve-tanya nami gabi nasi ke-hai gavna: asher nasi yecheta — prat le-kodmot.* The verse says *asher nasi yecheta* — that the *nasi* transgresses — and this too excludes prior transgressions, since he must be *nasi* at the time of the sin for the special liability to apply. The push in both directions, from the *kohen mashiach* to the *nasi* and back again, eventually settles by showing that each case requires its own textual grounding, and the back-and-forth confirms that neither figure can fully derive from the other through logical inference alone.

### Asher Nasi Yecheta

The *gemara* now pauses to examine the precise language of the verse *asher nasi yecheta* more carefully, and this is a striking passage. *Yakhol gezeirah* — perhaps the word *asher* ("that") implies an inevitability, a divine decree that the *nasi* must sin? After all, unlike the *kohen mashiach*, where the verse uses *im* ("if") — a pure conditional — the *nasi*'s verse uses *asher*, which in other contexts carries a declarative or resultative force. Is the Torah telling us that it is simply inevitable that the king will transgress?

The *gemara* resolves this by reference to the *kohen mashiach*: *mah le-halan li-kshe-yecheta, af kan li-kshe-yecheta* — just as "if" in the earlier verse means "when and if this occurs," so too *asher* in the *nasi*'s verse means "when this occurs," not that it is decreed to occur. We learn the meaning of *asher* from the parallel context of *im*, even though the words differ.

But the *gemara* presses further: where else might we find a *gezeirah* — a divine decree — that someone will inevitably sin? The answer offered is Leviticus 14:34, the verse about *tzaraat* afflicting homes in the land: *ve-natati nega tzaraat be-veit eretz achuzatchem* — "I will place a plague of *tzaraat* in the houses of the land of your possession." The *gemara* notes, in the name of Rabbi Yehuda, that this is a *bsorah* — a tidings — and we know the tradition that it was ultimately good news, since dismantling these homes would reveal hidden treasures. Nonetheless, on its face it appears as a divine declaration of something that will occur.

Rabbi Shimon, however, limits the scope of this verse: *prat le-nig'ei onsin* — it does not apply to *tzaraat* that comes about through circumstances beyond the person's control, such as through supernatural forces. The *gemara* then asks whether *nig'ei onsin* at all render one impure, since regarding the *zav* the principle is that he does not become impure through *ones*. The comparison is pressed through a *kal va-chomer* between the *zav* and *nega'im*: *mah zav min ha-dibur va-eilach, af nega'im min ha-dibur va-eilach* — both become operative only from the giving of the Torah onward. This argument is rejected, however, because the *zav* does not become impure through *ones* while *nega'im* do, making the comparison asymmetric. The verse *adam ki yihiyeh* in Leviticus 13:2 establishes the *nega'im* rules as applicable from the time of *matan Torah* and going forward.

Rav Papa then distinguishes within Rabbi Shimon's ruling: when Rabbi Shimon exempts *nig'ei onsin*, he means specifically *nig'ei ruchot* — afflictions caused by spirits — and *nig'ei keshafim* — afflictions caused by sorcery. These supernatural causes are categorically different from ordinary circumstances of coercion, and it is only regarding these that Rabbi Shimon holds no impurity is transmitted.

---

## Choleh & Tzaraat

### Prat L'Choleh

Returning to the *nasi*, a *baraita* derives another limitation from the words *asher nasi yecheta*: *prat le-choleh* — this excludes a *nasi* who is sick. The logic is that if he is ill, he is not functioning as *nasi* at that moment, and the special liability of the *nasi* therefore does not apply. One might ask, however, just how serious must the illness be to remove a person from *nasi* status? Surely a cold or a headache does not suspend the kingship.

### Tzaraat = Spiritual

The *gemara* addresses this directly. *Amar Rav Avdimi bar Chama: prat le-nasi she-nitztzara* — we are not speaking of ordinary illness at all, but of a *nasi* who has been stricken with *tzaraat*. The understanding is that *tzaraat* is a spiritual affliction, not merely a physical one. Something has gone profoundly wrong — not a passing indisposition, but a condition that speaks to the person's very capacity to function in his role.

### Uzziah Story

The *gemara* cites the proof from Kings 2, chapter 15, verse 5: *va-yenagga Hashem et ha-melech va-yehi metzora ad yom moto va-yeshev be-veit ha-chofshit ve-Yotam ben ha-melech al ha-bayit* — God struck the king and he was a *metzora* until the day of his death, and he sat in *beit ha-chofshit*, while his son Yotam was over the royal household. This is the case of King Uzziah of Judah. Once stricken with *tzaraat*, he was removed from active kingship, and it was his son who effectively governed.

### Beit HaChutzfiyot

The *gemara* now pauses on the name *beit ha-chofshit* — the house of freedom — and asks a pointed question: *miklal de-ad hashta eved havah* — if we are now told that he went to the house of freedom, does that imply that until now he was a slave? The answer, and the transition it opens, is precisely yes: Rabban Gamliel will later say to his students, *avdut ani noten lachem* — I am giving you a form of slavery — and the understanding is that *serara*, the position of authority, is not a privilege but a burden. The king sitting in the *beit ha-chofshit* is now free — free from the crushing weight of royal responsibility. The phrase *chofshi min ha-mitzvot*, free from obligations, also resonates here, though the primary meaning in context is freedom from the responsibilities of governance.

---

## Boat & Comet

### Ship Provisions

The *gemara* develops this theme through the famous story of Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua traveling together on a boat. *Be-hadei de-Rabban Gamliel havah pita, be-hadei de-Rabbi Yehoshua havah pita ve-solta* — Rabban Gamliel had only bread for provisions, while Rabbi Yehoshua had both bread and fine flour, *solet*, something like cream of wheat. When Rabban Gamliel's bread ran out — *shalim pita de-Rabban Gamliel* — he relied on the *solet* that Rabbi Yehoshua had brought. Astonished, he asked him: *mi havah yad'at de-havah lan akuva kulei hai de-aitit solta* — how did you know the journey would be delayed so long that you brought extra provisions?

### Comet Knowledge

Rabbi Yehoshua's answer is remarkable. *Kochav echad le-shiv'im shanah oleh u-mateh et ha-sapanim* — there is a star that rises once every seventy years and confuses the navigators of ships, and he had calculated that it might rise during their voyage and lead them off course, so he came prepared. This is widely recognized as an early reference to what we now call Halley's Comet. According to calculations, the comet passed in the year 66, and this story is attributed to that period. Rabbi Yehoshua knew of this phenomenon and planned accordingly — it was, some have noted, Rabbi Yehoshua's comet long before Halley gave it his name centuries later.

There is also a *mashal* embedded in the story, developed by the *Maharsha*, who connects this narrative with the *aggadot* of Rabbah bar bar Chana at the end of *Sanhedrin*. In that reading, the *sfina* — the boat — represents the turbulent ocean of ideological conflict, and the seventy years alludes to *shivim shnot adam*, the span of a human life. Rabban Gamliel's *pita* represents *Torah*, which is solid and sufficient, while Rabbi Yehoshua's *pita* and *solet* together represent *Torah* augmented by other forms of wisdom — the kind needed to navigate and prevail in arguments with outside movements. The fuller treatment of this *mashal* warrants its own study.

### Gamliel's Question

Rabban Gamliel, deeply impressed by Rabbi Yehoshua's knowledge, exclaims: *kol kach be-yadcha ve-ata oleh be-sfina* — you have such knowledge and yet you travel on a boat like a common person? The implication is that someone of Rabbi Yehoshua's stature deserves far better circumstances.

### Two Students

Rabbi Yehoshua deflects the praise and redirects it: *ad she-ata tameh alai, tameh al shnei talmidim she-yesh lecha ba-yabashah* — rather than marvel at me, marvel at two students you have on dry land. He names them: Rabbi Elazar Chisma and Rabbi Yochanan ben Gudgada. *She-yod'im li-sha'er kama tipot yesh ba-yam* — they can estimate how many drops of water are in the ocean — and yet *ein lahem pat le'echol ve-lo beged lilbosh* — they have not a piece of bread to eat nor a garment to wear. Here are men of extraordinary wisdom and learning, living in absolute poverty.

Rabban Gamliel resolved then and there — *natan da'ato le-hoshivam ba-rosh* — to place them at the head of an academy or a position of communal responsibility. Rashi explains the purpose: *k'dei she-yihyu mitparnesim* — so that they would have *parnassah*, livelihood. The *Tosafot ha-Rosh*, however, notes pointedly: *ve-hoshivam — mai parnassah ika?* — if he is seating them in the *yeshiva*, what *parnassah* is actually there? This tension between Torah leadership and material sustenance was already alive in the *gemara*'s own time.

### Serara as Slavery

When Rabban Gamliel returned from the sea, he sent for them. They did not come — they did not wish for *serara*, for authority or position. He sent again and they came. He then delivered the essential teaching, which connects directly back to King Uzziah and the *beit ha-chofshit*: *ki-mdumin atem she-serara ani noten lachem? Avdut ani noten lachem* — do you think I am giving you authority? I am giving you slavery. The proof text follows immediately.

---

## Kingdom Split

### Elders' Counsel

The verse cited is from Kings 1, chapter 12, the pivotal moment when the united kingdom stood at its breaking point. The elders spoke to Rehoboam, son of Solomon: *im ha-yom tihyeh eved la-am ha-zeh va-avadtam va-anitam ve-dibarta aleihem devarim tovim ve-hayu lecha avadim kol ha-yamim* — if today you will be a servant to this people, serve them, answer them, speak good things to them, they will be your servants forever. This is the counsel of the elders: genuine leadership is servitude. Authority is not taken but earned through self-abnegation before the people one leads.

### Rehoboam's Hubris

Rehoboam rejected this counsel and delivered his notorious response: *avi yisser etchem ba-shotim va-ani ayasser etchem ba-akrabim* — my father chastised you with whips, but I will chastise you with scorpions. He refused to accept the position of servant-king that his advisors described.

### Schism Result

The consequence was the division of the kingdom. By refusing to serve, Rehoboam lost the unified throne. Jeroboam ben Nevat took the ten northern tribes and established the separate kingdom of Israel, while Rehoboam retained only Judah. The trajectory that followed was devastating: the northern kingdom drifted into idolatry. The lesson is stark — the willingness to accept *serara* as *avdut*, as a burden of service rather than a privilege of power, is what holds a people together.

---

## Asher → Ashrei

### Ashrei Drasha

The *gemara* returns once more to the words *asher nasi yecheta* and extracts yet another layer of meaning. *Amar Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakai: ashrei ha-dor she-ha-nasi shelo mevi korban al shigagato* — happy is the generation whose *nasi* brings a sacrifice for his inadvertent transgression. Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakai reads *asher* not as the relative pronoun "that" but hears in it *ashrei* — the formula of happiness or blessing. If the king is the kind of person who brings a *korban* even for an accidental sin, what does that tell you about the generation? *Im nasi shelo mevi korban, tzarich ata lomar mah hedyot* — if even the king brings a sacrifice, of course the common person will do so as well. *Ve-im al shigagato mevi korban, tzarich ata lomar mah zedono* — and if he brings a sacrifice for an inadvertent transgression, how much more will he do *teshuvah* for an intentional one. What an extraordinary standard of moral accountability for a king to set.

### Rava's Pushback

Rava challenges this *drasha* sharply. If we are going to hear *ashrei* every time the Torah uses *asher*, what do we do with the negative appearances of the same word? Jeroboam ben Nevat himself is described with *asher chata va-asher hecheti* — who sinned and caused others to sin. Are we to read that as *ashrei*? The parallelism would be absurd. More pointedly, if the word *asher* alone triggers the *ashrei* reading in Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakai's *drasha*, it should do so consistently across all contexts.

### Context Rules

The resolution is that context determines meaning. Here, in the verse *asher nasi yecheta*, we have an additional textual signal: the verse is being read against the backdrop of *im ha-kohen ha-mashiach yecheta*, where the parallel construction is unmistakably conditional and not a *gezeirah*. It is precisely this deliberate parallelism between the two verses that licenses the *drasha*. The same word *asher* in a completely different context — such as the description of Jeroboam's sin — carries no such interpretive invitation. The *drasha* belongs to this verse, in this context, and cannot be generalized.

---

## Righteous vs. Wicked

### Eccl 8:14 Cited

Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda expounds a verse from Kohelet, Ecclesiastes, chapter 8, verse 14: *yesh hevel asher na'aseh al ha-aretz asher yesh tzaddikim asher magia aleihem ke-ma'asei ha-resha'im, ve-yesh resha'im she-magia aleihem ke-ma'asei ha-tzaddikim* — there is a futility that occurs on earth: there are righteous people who receive what would befit the conduct of the wicked, and there are wicked people who receive what would befit the conduct of the righteous. Solomon concludes: I say this too is futility. The translation of *hevel* as "frustration" is offered in some editions, though it is worth noting that *hevel* more typically evokes vanity or nothingness — the famous *hevel havalim* of Kohelet.

### First Interp

The initial *drasha* on this verse reads it as describing a providential arrangement across worlds. *Ashreihem la-tzaddikim she-magia aleihem ke-ma'aseh ha-resha'im shel olam ha-ba ba-olam ha-zeh* — happy are the righteous to whom happens in this world what the wicked will experience in the world to come — i.e., suffering. *Oy lahem la-resha'im she-magia aleihem ke-ma'aseh ha-tzaddikim shel olam ha-ba ba-olam ha-zeh* — and woe to the wicked to whom happens in this world what the righteous will experience in the world to come — i.e., prosperity. On this reading, the righteous suffer now so that their full reward waits intact in the *olam ha-ba*, while the wicked enjoy now and will suffer then.

### Rava's Fix

Rava objects: *atu tzaddiki, i achlei terei olamei misnei lahu?* — is it really harmful for the righteous to enjoy two worlds? Why must they suffer in this one? The framing of the first interpretation implies that enjoyment in *olam ha-zeh* somehow diminishes the reward in *olam ha-ba*, and Rava finds no basis for that assumption. He therefore reframes the *drasha* entirely. *Ella amar Rava: ashreihem la-tzaddikim she-magia aleihem ke-ma'aseh ha-resha'im shel olam ha-zeh ba-olam ha-zeh* — happy are the righteous to whom happens in this world what the wicked experience in this world — that is, prosperity, enjoyment, material success. *Oy lahem la-resha'im she-magia aleihem ke-ma'aseh ha-tzaddikim shel olam ha-zeh ba-olam ha-zeh* — and woe to the wicked to whom happens in this world what many righteous people experience in this world — that is, hardship and suffering. On Rava's reading, the *felicity* belongs entirely in *olam ha-zeh* and the comparison is strictly this-worldly.

### Small Wealth

The *gemara* then illustrates Rava's teaching through an encounter. Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua came before Rava. He asked them: had they mastered this tractate and that tractate? They said yes. Had they become a little wealthy — *iatartu purta*? They said yes — *de-zavnan ketina de-ara* — they had purchased a small plot of land. Rava then applied to them the verse: *ashreihem la-tzaddikim she-magia aleihem ke-ma'aseh ha-resha'im shel ha-olam ha-zeh ba-olam ha-zeh* — happy are the righteous to whom happens in this world what the wicked experience in this world.

One of the commentators notes that the key word in Rava's question is *purta* — a little. He did not ask whether they had become rich; he asked whether they had become a *little* rich. And their answer is equally measured — a small plot of land, nothing extravagant. The implication is that modest *parnassah* alongside Torah learning is a blessing, but excessive wealth poses its own danger. The *Meiri* captures this with a striking metaphor: pursuing both Torah and *parnassah* is like trying to hunt two deer simultaneously. Hunting even one deer is extraordinarily difficult — they fast, they are alert, they hide. Chasing two at once approaches the impossible. A measure of worldly success is *ashrei*; unbounded pursuit of it is another thing entirely.

---

## Hosea Path

### Hosea 14:10

Rabbah bar bar Chana cites Rabbi Yochanan on a verse from Hosea, chapter 14, verse 10: *ki yesharim darchei Hashem, tzaddikim yelchu vam u-fosh'im yikashlu vam* — for the paths of God are straight; the righteous walk in them, but the wicked stumble in them. The provocative feature of this verse is that it is one path. The same road that the righteous walk successfully is the road in which the wicked stumble. This is not two different paths producing two different outcomes. It is the identical path producing opposite results depending on who is walking it. The *gemara* now undertakes to find concrete examples that capture this dynamic — situations where the very same act is a *mitzvah* for the righteous person and a transgression for the wicked one.

### Pesach Example

The first example is the *Pesach* offering. Two people slaughter and eat the *Pesach* sacrifice. One eats it *lishum mitzvah* — for the sake of the commandment. One eats it *lishum achilah gassah* — for the sake of gluttony. For the one who eats it as a *mitzvah*, this is *tzaddikim yelchu vam*. For the one who eats it for gluttony, this is *u-fosh'im yikashlu vam*. But Reish Lakish challenges this illustration: *rasha karit leih?* — you are calling him wicked? *De-nehi de-lo avid mitzvah min ha-muvchar* — granted he did not perform the *mitzvah* in the most elevated manner — *Pesach miha ka-achil* — but he still ate the *Pesach* offering. He fulfilled the commandment, even if not ideally. Calling him a *rasha* for that seems disproportionate. The example is therefore abandoned.

### Wife/Sister

The *gemara* proposes a more dramatic illustration. Two men are each at home with their wife and their sister. In one case, *nizdamna lo ishto* — it so happened that his wife became available to him; in the other, *nizdamna lo achoto* — it so happened that his sister became available to him. For the first man: *tzaddikim yelchu vam*. For the second: *u-fosh'im yikashlu vam*. The same moment of opportunity, the same domestic setting — one path, two outcomes.

This too is rejected. *Mi dami? Anan ka-amrinan chada derech, ve-hacha shtei drachim* — the comparison fails because we are looking for one path, and here there are in fact two: a wife and a sister are two different people, two different circumstances, two different choices.
